stories.title: Information Panel of Jeongjeon (Main Hall of Jongmyo Shrine)
stories.audioTitle: Information Panel of Jeongjeon (Main Hall of Jongmyo Shrine)
stories.script: The Main Shrine Hall of the Joseon's royal ancestral shrine houses spirit tablets of Joseon kings and their queen consorts for holding memorial rites honoring their achievements. Unfortunately, the shrine hall is not open to the public. Therefore, Jeongjeon, the information panel, provides an introduction to the hall.  The royal ancestral memorial rite takes place before the spirit tablets of Joseon kings and their consorts. Each tablet, made of wood, represents a specific royal ancestor. A total of 49 spirit tablets of kings and queens are enshrined in 19 chambers of the Main Shrine Hall, and 34 tablets in 16 chambers of the Hall of Everlasting Peace. A sacrificial table is offered in each chamber, allowing each king to share a table with one or more consorts. Offered foods are categorized as seasoned or unseasoned, wet or dry, along with specially brewed beverages.  The chart on the information panel contains the list of Joseon kings and queens whose spirit tablets are enshrined in the Main Shrine Hall of the Jongmyo Shrine. The chart also displays their posthumous titles and the locations of their spirit tablets. The Joseon Dynasty had 25 kings, with 19 kings, including those posthumously given kingly titles, having their spirit tablets enshrined in the Main Shrine Hall alongside the spirit tablets of their queen consorts. The original main hall was a five-bay building, but over time, it expanded into a long 19-bay structure through several extensions to accommodate more memorial tablets.  King Sejong, the fourth monarch of Joseon, constructed an annex to this shrine, known today as Yeongnyeongjeon or Hall of Everlasting Peace. The new shrine hall was exclusively dedicated to the four latest generations of ancestral tablets. When a king passed away and his tablet arrived at the Main Shrine Hall, the tablets of the oldest remaining in the shrine were relocated from the Hall to the annex. However, the royal family of Joseon retained the tablets of kings who had made extraordinary achievements in the Main Shrine Hall.

stories.title: Jeongjeon(Main Hall of Jongmyo Shrine)
stories.script: The Main Shrine Hall of Jongmyo Shrine is where ancestral rites are conducted using the spirit tablets of Joseon kings and their consorts. The shrine building stands at 101 meters, making it the largest remaining wooden building in Korea. The main hall has undergone several renovations and extensions to reach its current form. Originally a seven-bay structure, it expanded to a nineteen-bay structure through three large extensions. The original shrine building was destroyed in a fire during the Japanese invasion of Korea in 1592. The reconstruction project that commenced after the war took many years.  The architectural excellence of Jongmyo's Main Shrine Hall has been widely acknowledged by world-renowned architectural connoisseurs. One of the building's outstanding architectural features is its perfect symmetry. Maintaining such flawless symmetry and elegance is remarkable, particularly considering its several major renovations and expansions spanning hundreds of years. Despite different columns supporting the building's body, the roof, over 100 meters long, maintains a perfect horizontal line. Even today's architecture experts admire its scientific design and meticulous finish.  The columns supporting the roof exhibit a unique shape favored by Korean builders in the past. These entasis columns have a slight convex curve in the middle part, correcting the illusion of concavity produced by a straight shaft and creating a sense of stability. A series of twenty columns standing at regular intervals along the front of the building symbolizes the eternal prosperity of the Joseon Dynasty. The front doors of the shrine hall do not fit neatly when closed, leaving a gap between them at the lower part. This design is ingenious for improving ventilation, controlling humidity, and, more importantly, ensuring a comfortable passage for the royal ancestral spirits to enter and exit the shrine hall.

stories.title: Front yard of Jeongjeon Hall
stories.script: Jongmyo Jerye, or the Royal Ancestral Memorial Rite of the Joseon Dynasty, denotes a seasonal memorial rite conducted to honor the royal ancestors at the Jongmyo Shrine where their spirit tablets are enshrined. The rite epitomized all ceremonies performed to embody the ideal Confucian virtues of Loyalty and Filial Piety. Jongmyo Jerye remains the sole surviving rite, a significant reason why UNESCO listed this ritual on the Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2001.  During the Joseon period, state rites occurred five times a year, in the first month of every season: the first, fourth, seventh, tenth, and twelfth months. Additionally, special rites were held to mark celebratory events or disasters. The rite predominantly comprises three stages: burning incense and offering wine while invoking ancestral spirits in the first stage, reciting prayers and sharing food and beverages from the offering tables in the second, and bidding farewell to the ancestral spirits by incinerating written prayers and special gifts in the final stage. Presently, the rite is held once a year, on the first Sunday of May.  Jongmyo Jeryeak, or the Royal Ancestral Ritual Music, is the musical performance conducted at the Jongmyo Shrine as part of the royal ancestral memorial. Originally created for a royal banquet by King Sejong, the fourth king of Joseon, this music replaced the earlier Goryeo dynasty's music used at the Joseon court. King Sejong also developed an original music notation system called Jeongganbo, or Grid Notation. It is recognized as Asia's first Mensural notation and is often likened to the development of staff notation in the West due to its significance in music history. Regarding the artistic merit of the Royal Ancestral Ritual Music, experts commend the harmony between diverse artistic elements such as ritual, hymn, dance, music, costume, poetry, and more. This unique Korean musical heritage has been preserved in its original form for approximately 600 years.

stories.title: Gongsindang
stories.script: Gongsindang, or the Hall of Meritorious Subjects, situated across from the Main Shrine Hall, enshrines the spirit tablets of government officials who achieved distinction serving their king and the dynasty.  The original size of the shrine building for the meritorious subjects is documented differently in various historical texts. Over time, the building continued to undergo expansion, culminating in its present form as a sixteen-bay structure housing spirit tablets of eighty-three meritorious subjects of the Joseon era.  The requirements for designation as a meritorious subject varied depending on the political circumstances of the period. However, they predominantly related to contributions in restoring royal authority, uncovering treason, or suppressing rebellion. The fate of the meritorious subjects, whose spirit tablets are housed in this shrine hall, remained closely linked to the ruler they served, even after their passing. While their spirit tablets remained in the Gongsindang akin to those of their kings in the Main Shrine Hall, upon the removal of their kings from the Main Shrine Hall, the tablets of these subjects had to depart the shrine and were sent to their descendants.

stories.title: Chilsadang Government Office
stories.script: Chilsadang, or the Hall of Seven Deities, stands as another minor shrine hall across from the Main Shrine Hall, symmetrically positioned to Gongsindang. As its name suggests, it is a shrine constructed to honor seven deities revered by people of all social statuses, from royalty and aristocracy to commoners, while Jongmyo is a shrine dedicated to honoring royal ancestors, and Gongsindang is dedicated to meritorious subjects.  These seven deities are associated with various aspects of human life and actively engage in different facets such as auspicious occasions, entrances and exits, food, housing, and travel. Rites venerating these deities were conducted concurrently with those honoring the spirits of the royal ancestors. Each deity corresponds to one of the four seasons, and therefore, the rites are performed in the seasons associated with each deity. For example, during winter, a rite was held to honor the deity responsible for overseeing people's travel, aiding in preventing slips on icy roads and injuries. The tradition of worshipping the seven deities illustrates that the ruling class of Joseon acknowledged the common belief that even the smallest aspects of life are overseen by divine beings, thereby necessitating specific rituals to express gratitude to them.

stories.title: Yeongnyeongjeon Hall
stories.script: Yeongnyeongjeon Hall, also known as the Hall of Everlasting Peace, serves as an auxiliary shrine to the Main Shrine Hall. A chart displayed on the information panel presents the list of kings and their queen consorts whose spirit tablets are enshrined in this hall.  King Sejong, the fourth ruler of Joseon, made the decision to construct an auxiliary shrine hall, which is today's Yeongnyeongjeon Hall. Upon the death of a king and the arrival of his tablet at the Main Shrine Hall, the tablets of the oldest ancestors within the shrine were relocated from the Main Shrine Hall to the auxiliary shrine hall. As per tradition, only five ancestors?the Joseon dynasty founder and the four latest generations of the current king's ancestors?were to be honored at the Main Shrine Hall of the Joseon state shrine.  Presently, the auxiliary shrine hall houses 34 spirit tablets of Joseon kings and their consorts, inclusive of the dynasty founder's four latest generations of ancestors who were posthumously given kingly titles, as well as seven rulers. The Joseon Dynasty had a total of 27 kings, with two kings not permitted to be honored by enshrinement in the royal ancestral shrine. These two were deposed from the throne due to their ruthless tyranny and immoral behaviors. Conversely, there was a king who was dethroned but later reinstated with the kingly title posthumously, leading to the relocation of his spirit tablet to the royal ancestral shrine.

stories.title: Hamabi, Jongmyo Shrine
stories.script: Jongmyo Shrine  Hamabi, Jongmyo Shrine  During the Joseon Period, this area was a city center that many people traveled to and from just like today. By the entrance of Jongmyo Shrine seated at the center of our country, there stands a symbolic tablet that shows what kind of significance Jongmyo has had. It is none other than “Hamabi”. During the Joseon Period, no matter how noble or low-class you were, every passer-by had to get off his horse and show courtesy.  Hamabi in Jongmyo Park is estimated to have been erected in the 4th year of King Hyeonjong's reign (1663) and, on the stone, Chinese letters that say “Daesoinwon Gaehama” are carved in. The phrase means that “everyone shall get off his horse and show his courtesy.”  There were times when the king passed by in front of Jongmyo when he was moving to another royal palace or during a procession. At this time, the king would not get out of the palanquin or off his horse but, instead, stop the march briefly to pay his respects. Meanwhile, all of the vassals would get off their horses and stand around the king, and, before they restart their procession, they would bow as a way to show respect.  The area surrounding Hamabi during the Joseon Period was where everyone had to pause his or her journey so a town with a temporary station in which people and horses may temporarily stay and rest was established naturally. Whoever that was riding a horse was a man of high nobility and, most of the times, he was accompanied by a horseman or a servant who would lead the horse. While their masters show courtesy in front of Hamabi, the horsemen are able to take short rests during which they greet one another and talk about different subjects. Later, the information and rumors that they exchanged in front of Hamabi began to be known as Hamapyeong, and these stories often spread quickly throughout the village and, even, the royal palace.  If you have all paid your respects to Hamabi, let's go see Angbuilgu Daeseok right next to it.

stories.title: Angbuilgu Daeseok at Jongmyo Shrine
stories.script: Next to Hamabi of Jongmyo stands a stone staircase known as “Daeseok,” which serves as a stone pedestal supporting other objects. Atop Daeseok rests “Angbuilgu,” a type of sundial from the Joseon Dynasty. “Angbu” refers to “an iron pot looking up to the heavens.”  Angbuilgu was installed in Jongmyo Shrine during the 16th year of King Sejong’s reign (1434). However, during the Imjin War, the Japanese invasion of 1592, the sundial component vanished, leaving only the stylobate behind. During that period, people referred to the stylobate as “Iryeongdae.” In 1898, construction commenced to lay streetcar tracks, resulting in the burial of the stylobate underground and its eventual erasure from people's memories.  Fortunately, during the excavation to reorganize the Jongmyo area, Angbuilgu Daeseok resurfaced and was relocated to Tapgol Park on Jongno 3-ga. Subsequently, during the restoration of Jongmyo Park (Jongmyo Square), it returned to its original location in front of Jongmyo. Despite the disappearance of the sundial, which once sat atop the sturdy granite stone, Angbuilgu Daeseok has reemerged, rekindling people's interest.

stories.title: Jongmyo Jeongyo Bridge (King’s Road)
stories.script: Jongmyo Jeongyo Bridge (King’s Road)  When Jongmyo Park (Jongmyo Square) was restored, a bridge appeared for the first time. It is “Jongmyo Jeongyo (King’s Bridge)” that you see in front of you.  In the Joseon Dynasty, a small stream flowed in front of Jongmyo. During King Sejong’s reign, an artificial embankment was built to turn the waterway and prevent the stream from flooding. And, to enable people to walk over the new water route, a brand-new bridge was installed, which was Jongmyo Jeongyo. Since the royal palanquin and procession had to pass over this bridge, it was much wider than other ordinary bridges.  When it was first installed, it was made of wood but it was rebuilt as a stone bridge in the 3rd year of Sejong’s reign (1421) and then improved in the 4th year of Hyeonjong's reign (1663). This bridge is clearly marked in <Juncheonsasil> produced in 1760 and <Daedongjiji> made by Gim Jeong-ho in the 1860s. But, in the 1920s during the Japanese occupation period, a construction project proceeded in the Jongmyo area to repair the sewerage, which ended up burying the bridge and stream underground, no trace of the bridge had been found until recently.  Through the excavation survey conducted in 2010, the stylobate of Jongmyo Jeongyo and stonework by the stream were discovered and eventually restored after records and on-site checks. Although it was difficult to figure out the exact shape of the bridge from maps and images that still remain, a scene of installing Eodo, or the road through which the king's palanquin passed, was reproduced by referring to Eodo and Sindo in Jongmyo. On four corners of the bridge, Hwapyoju (pillars set up where a tomb is) were erected with the face of Haetae engraved on each of them.  On the king's road to Jongmyo, there is a well that the kings supposedly drank from. Shall we walk over the bridge to get to our next destination?

stories.title: Jongmyo Eojeong
stories.script: There is a well called Eojeong, situated in the middle of the path from Jongmyo Jeongyo to Oedaemun Gate, holds historical significance. It is said that Joseon's kings used to drink from this well during their visits to Jongmyo. Gyeongseong Baekgyeong documented in the 1930s that Eojeong never dried out during droughts, maintaining a constant water level. It was noted that the water was ice-cold in summer and steaming hot in winter, and renowned for its great taste. This historical importance is reflected in the naming of the neighborhood around Jongmyo as Hunjeong-dong.  However, during the Japanese colonial era, a concrete pipe was placed inside the well due to nearby construction activities. After Liberation, significant changes occurred for Eojeong. As the subway and underground parking lot beneath Jongmyo Shrine were constructed, the well's water completely dried up. Consequently, the well no longer retains any water today.  Presently, only remnants of Eojeong can be found, marked by a lid shaped like that covers the well. Adjacent to Eojeong, a stone in the shape of a turtle remains, believed to be the stylobate of a headstone that identified Eojeong.

stories.title: Statue of Yi Sang-jae
stories.script: In Jongmyo Shrine stands a statue of a man dressed in a hanbok on a pillar, named Yi Sang-jae. He was an independence activist and civic leader who spearheaded national movements against Japanese colonial rule, championing the Korean spirit.  He was born in 1850 as Yi Gye-ho, and later?changed his name to Sang-jae.?Yi served as the second secretary of the U.S. Legacy in Washington for a year. In 1896, he formed an independent civil rights association, along with notable figures such as Rhee Syngman, who became the Republic of Korea's first president. Yi also held the presidency of the Manmin Community, a significant enlightenment group.  Furthermore, Yi advocated for universal suffrage and proposed limitations on the absolute monarchy's sovereignty to Emperor Gojong, leading to his imprisonment. Upon release, he engaged with anti-imperialist organizations and endeavored to strengthen political relations with Americans.  Yi also became part of the Young Men's Christian Association (YMCA) and dedicated himself to educating young individuals. He actively participated in the March 1, 1919, independence movement. In 1922, he founded a domestic education association that aimed to establish a local private university, which unfortunately fell victim to the Japanese colonial rule. His enduring legacy remains symbolized by the statue in Jongmyo.

stories.title: Akgongcheong Pavilion (Musicians' Pavilion)
stories.script: Akgongcheong Pavilion, or the Music Office, served as the practice and rehearsal space for court musicians responsible for performing the Royal Ancestral Ritual Music at Jongmyo Shrine. The Akgongcheong Pavilion in Jeongjeon is situated between Jeongjeon Hall and Yeongnyeongjeon Hall. Unfortunately, the current building has undergone several transformations and does not precisely retain its original shape. Similarly, the Akgongcheong in Yeongnyeongjeon Hall, used by musicians like the Jeongjeon Akgongcheong, shares the same architectural structure and style.  The incorporation of music at Jongmyo Shrine stemmed from the belief of Joseon rulers that music would significantly contribute to the good governance of the people and the country.  The sequence of the Royal Ancestral Ritual Music at Jongmyo Shrine is interlinked like a vast epic poem. Musicians and dancers focused on performing to praise the establishment of Joseon, the remarkable rule and accomplishments of the kings, and to convey wishes for the dynasty's prosperity from their ancestors.

stories.title: Road to Haeinsa Temple Temple
stories.script: Welcome to the Haeinsa Temple. There is a 1.5 kilometer-long walk from the parking lot to the One Pillar Gate, the temple’s outermost entrance. While walking, take in the stunning view of Gayasan National Park.  Can you hear the melodious sound of water? It flows along the exquisite rocky valley on the left. The valley captivates visitors with its colorful scenery each season. Its beauty and the surroundings has earned it two nicknames. One is Ongnyudongcheon Stream, or Jade Brook Valley, inspired by the famous valley in Geumgangsan Mountain, often regarded as the most beautiful mountain in the Korean Peninsula. The other is Hongnyudonggyegok Valley, or Vermillion Brook Valley, derived from the autumnal colors of the trees reflected in the running water.  Gayasan National Park boasts breathtakingly beautiful peaks and valleys, symbolizing human spiritual growth in perfect harmony with nature.  Deep inside the park lies Haeinsa Temple, established about twelve centuries ago. Since then, it has evolved into one of the three most significant Buddhist sanctuaries in Korea, alongside Tongdosa Temple and Songgwangsa Temple. Each of them represents one of the Three Jewels of Korean Buddhism.  The First Jewel of Korean Buddhism comprises the true relics of the historical Buddha, or Shakyamuni, housed in Tongdosa Temple in Yangsan. The Second Jewel is the community of Buddhist monks symbolized by Songgwangsa Temple, which has produced sixteen eminent monks representing the spiritual maturity of Korean Buddhism. The Third Jewel is the dharma, or the Buddhist law, represented by the immense scriptural collection known as the Tripitaka Koreana. The collection comprises over eighty thousand scriptural woodblocks currently housed in two special depositaries in Haeinsa Temple. Some argue that Haesina Temple encapsulates the history of Korean Buddhism itself due to this treasure.

stories.title: One Pillar Gate
stories.audioTitle: The Road to the Haeinsa Temple
stories.script: The Road to the Haeinsa Temple  [Narration] Welcome to the Haeinsa Temple. You will now start a 1.5km-long walk from this parking lot to the One Pillar Gate, the temple's outermost entrance gate. As you walk from here to the temple, don't forget to feast your eyes on the stunningly scenic views of the Gayasan National Park.   Listen, and you can hear the melodious sounds of water running along the exquisite rocky valley on your left. The valley has fascinated visitors with colorful views that continue to change with the seasons. The scenic beauty of the valley with its surroundings has given it two nicknames. Ongnyudong, or Jade Brook Valley, came from the famous valley of the same name in Geumgangsan which is often regarded as the most beautiful mountain in the entire Korean Peninsula. The other, Hongnyudong, or Vermillion Brook Valley, came from the views of autumn colored trees reflected on the water running through the valley.  The Buddhist temple of Haeinsa is situated in the depth of the Gayasan National Park which contains breathtakingly beautiful peaks and valleys. It has long been regarded as an epitome of human spiritual growth in perfect harmony with nature.   Haeinsa has been admired as one of Korea's most valuable Buddhist treasures since its foundation some twelve thousand years ago. But before we visit the temple, why don't we ask one of its monks to give us a brief introduction?   [Buddhist priest in Haeinsa] Haeinsa was established about twelve hundred years ago. It has since grown into one of the three most important Buddhist sanctuaries in Korea.  Korean Buddhism has the Three Jewels represented by three main temples, Tongdosa, Songgwangsa and Haeinsa. The First Jewel of Korean Buddhism is the true relics of the historical Buddha, or Shakyamuni, housed in Tongdosa in Yangsan.  The Second Jewel is the community of Buddhist monks symbolized by Songgwangsa which has produced sixteen eminent monks representing spiritual maturity of Korean Buddhism. Finally, the Third Jewel is the dharma, or the Buddhist law, represented by the immense scriptural collection known as the Tripitaka Koreana. This collection of over eighty thousand scriptural woodblocks is currently housed in two special depositaries in Haeinsa. It is largely this treasure that makes Haeinsa stand out from other great Buddhist sanctuaries across Korea. And that is why some even argue that Haeinsa is the history of Korean Buddhism itself.

stories.title: Dead Trees (A withered Elm Tree)
stories.script: The short section of the road between the two gate buildings, One Pillar Gate and Cheonwangmun Gate, is lined with tall, and aged trees. The particular tree on the right side of the road near Cheonwangmun Gate might catch your attention.  This old zelkova tree died decades ago. It is believed to have been planted to mark the foundation of Haeinsa Temple in 802. The tree’s demise in 1945 marked the end of its millennium-long duty as a guardian of the temple. The thick and bulky trunk suggests that in its heyday, it had a majestic appearance.  The tree’s connection to the establishment of the temple is intertwined with an amazing story of two monks. They are known to have cured the ailing queen of Silla with the power of their prayers. Legend says they built a temple at the site of their prayers for her health. The king also planted a tree as a sign of gratitude. This dead zelkova before you is believed to be that tree.  There is a rectangular stone topped with a mound of gravel. The stone block is called yeomjuseok, or stone salt storage. While resembling a prayer cairn due to the gravel, it’s actually more related to traditional Korean feng shui theory.  Do you see the peaks to the south of the temple? Fengshui experts believed that the peaks contained fire energy. The belief could explain why the temple suffered at least seven disastrous fires, as recorded in old history books. With wooden structures housing treasures like Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks, fire has always been a major concern among the Haeinsa Temple community.  Consequently, they decided to counteract the fire’s malevolent energy by utilizing the power of the ocean, storing salt in the stone blocks. The tradition of this symbolic ritual is still maintained by the temple community, with the ritual held once every year.

stories.title: Bonghwangmun Gate
stories.script: You have now arrived at the Cheonwangmun Gate, or the Gate of Four Heavenly Kings. It is the second of the gates. It is also called Geumgangmun Gate and has been repaired a number of times.  As the name suggests, the gate houses murals depicting iconic images of the Four Heavenly Kings. These Buddhist deities typically appear as sculptural images in most other Buddhist temples in Korea, but here, they are painted on the walls.  The Four Heavenly Kings are the guardians of the center of the Buddhist universe called Sumeru in Sanskrit, and Sumisan in Korean. These fierce-looking warriors protect the holy place from evil forces invading from all four directions. Each warrior king watches over one cardinal direction with his own weapon: a sword for the East, lute for the West, a dragon for the South and a pagoda for the North.  Observe the evil creatures groaning under their feet. These embody all evil forces captured by the warriors while covertly infringing on the sanctity of the holy mountain.

stories.title: Haetalmun
stories.script: The Entrance to Nirvana  You have just conquered thirty-three grueling steps to arrive at Haetalmun, the Gate of Nirvana. As mentioned earlier, the center of the Buddhist universe is called Sumeru, and its summit consisted of thirty-three heavens. The stairway leading to this gate symbolizes the heavens forming the holiest place of the Buddhist cosmos.   The Gate of Nirvana features fine elements of the traditional Korean architecture. The word nirvana, or haetal in Korean, refers to the extreme bliss attained through liberation from all the desires and sufferings. So in passing, you are now entering the realm of complete bliss and peace.  Before you continue on to Gugwangnu Pavilion, I would like to touch upon the meaning behind the name of the temple. Haein originated from a Buddhist scripture and literally translates into seal of the ocean. More specifically, it means that Buddha's wisdom helped obtain enlightenment of the world.

stories.title: Gugwangnu Pavilion
stories.script: Gugwangnu Pavilion, also known as the House of Nine Lights, is situated opposite the Gate of Nirvana within Haeinsa Temple's front courtyard. This two-story building is prominently labeled with its name plaque.  Originally, Gugwangnu was constructed to accommodate lay visitors who came to the temple for prayer, meditation, or sermons. As time passed, its functions expanded to include storing and showcasing precious Buddhist artifacts, along with serving as a tourist information center. Additionally, it offers an English video detailing the temple's history, catering to international visitors.  You may have noticed a large, maze-like symbol in one corner of the courtyard, centered around a three-meter-tall stone pagoda. This symbol draws inspiration from a Buddhist hymn comprising 210 Chinese characters and the Buddhist swastika. It was devised by Using, a renowned Silla monk. Using intended for Buddhist devotees to use it as a path to enlightenment, inscribing each word of the hymn into their minds as they traversed the passage. Notably, the design allows the meditative walk to start and end at the same point.

stories.title: Beomjonggak Pavilion
stories.script: Beomjonggak Pavilion is the bell house of Haeinsa Temple. Although the name plaque of the building, Beomjonggak, denotes it as a bell house, it actually accommodates three other instruments alongside the bell, together forming the Four Dharma Vehicles. These include a drum, a wooden fish gong, and a cloud chime.  The bell is considered one of the most vital and frequently utilized instruments in a Buddhist temple. It tolls at least twice daily, summoning the entire Haeinsa Temple community for morning and evening prayer services. In the spiritual sense, its sound is believed to symbolize saving all sentient beings from the sea of suffering. The temple's ancient bell, carved with a benevolent image of Buddha, was crafted around five hundred years ago. It has since been replaced by a new bell and relocated to the temple's museum.  In the bell house, you'll notice a cloud-shaped bronze chime called Unpan hung under the ceiling. Striking it with a wooden mallet produces a light, clear metallic sound believed to liberate flying creatures and wandering spirits from suffering. The fish-shaped wooden gong, named Mogeo, is adorned with vivid colors. This instrument is played to seek salvation for water animals. Its fish shape symbolizes a devoted spiritual life, as fish do not close their eyes, remaining awake through night and day. The size of the fish gong was later reduced to create a portable version, allowing monks to strike it while reciting sutras and mantras.  Lastly, the dharma drum, Beopgo, is played for the salvation of land animals. Traditional rules govern the manner in which these instruments are played. They dictate the sequence of instrument play and the number of beats each instrument must hold. During the evening prayer, the bell is struck thirty-three times, symbolizing the thirty-three heavens at the core of the Buddhist universe. This is followed by the drum, fish gong, and finally, the cloud chime.

stories.title: Stone Lantern and the Central Pagoda (Three-story Stone Pagoda)
stories.audioTitle: Stone Lantern and the Central Pagoda (Three-story Stone Pagoda)
stories.script: The inner courtyard of the Haeinsa Temple, where two main stone structures, a lantern and a pagoda, stand adjacent to each other.  The lantern is lit during important religious ceremonies held at the temple. It features a square base adorned with lotus designs inspired by the patterns of elephant eyes. Beneath that, an octagonal body comprises upturned and downturned bowls of lotus petals, connected by a short octagonal pillar.  The upper section of the lantern includes an octagonal light chamber with four windows, featuring carvings of the Four Heavenly Kings. It is capped by an octagonal roof stone.  The style of an octagonal body was favored by Buddhist artists in the Silla period. However, the octagonal pillar supporting the upturned bowl of lotus petals appears to be a creation from a later period.  Standing behind the lantern is a three-story stone pagoda named jeongjungtap, which translates to 'the pagoda standing at the center of the courtyard.' The pagoda still maintains an elegant structure across its three stories, reflecting the refined aesthetic sense of Korean Buddhist artists during the Unified Silla Period.  While the pagoda's body remains intact, its original two-tier base was replaced by a three-tier base during a renovation in 1926.

stories.title: Daejeokgwangjeon Hall (Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon)
stories.script: Daejeokgwangjeon Hall   One of the most historically significant buildings at Haeinsa Temple is the central prayer hall known as Daejeokgwangjeon Hall, or the Hall of Great Quiescent Light. The original central prayer hall was a two-story building, but the successive fires razed the original and its replacements. The current building was built in 1817 and underwent renovation in 1971.  Take a look at the front six columns. You'll notice six vertical plaques bearing a seven-character prayer under the eaves. These famous handwritten prayers were penned by two renowned members of the late Joseon dynasty. The prayers on the right two columns were authored by a seven-year-old prince who later ascended to become King Gojong, the twenty-sixth king of the Joseon Dynasty and the inaugural emperor of the Korean Empire. The prayers on the left four columns were written by his biological father, Prince Regent Heungseon.  As you step inside the hall, focus on the altar where Buddhist images are enshrined, along with ritual objects, paintings, and decorative elements adorning the interior. Within this hall, seven Buddhist statues are present.  Most Vairocana Buddha statues usually take the hand gesture of wrapped the left index finger with right hand. However, the Vairocana Buddha statue enshrined in Daejeokgwangjeon Hall is different because both his hands are clasped, making this statue unique.  Remarkably, this particular Vairocana statue was initially housed in Geumdangsa Temple in Seongju, Gyeongsangbuk-do, before being relocated to Yonggisa Temple in Gayasan Mountain and eventually finding its current home at Haeinsa Temple in 1897. Enduring a long and turbulent journey, this Vairocana statue remains remarkably preserved in its original condition.

stories.title: Daebirojeon
stories.script: Haeinsa Temple houses twin wooden statues of Vairocana, believed to be the oldest of their kind in Korea. Historically, these Buddhist images were housed in separate shrines.  Recently, the statues were removed from their shrine for re-gilding, revealing a wooden strip with a historical inscription discovered by the temple's monks. According to this inscription, the images were carved in the year 883, commissioned by a high-ranking official of the Silla court.  Despite their invaluable status in Korean Buddhist art, being wooden, the statues are susceptible to fire damage. To safeguard them, the temple constructed a secure underground storage area. In case of an emergency, such as a fire outbreak, the images can be swiftly moved from the shrine hall to the underground strongroom located six meters below the hall.

stories.title: Entrance to JanggyeongPanjeon
stories.audioTitle: Tripitaka Koreana, a Symbol of Korean Spiritual Passion and Patriotism
stories.script: Tripitaka Koreana, a Symbol of Korean Spiritual Passion and Patriotism  You must now be somewhere near the stairway leading to the two remarkable buildings called Janggyeong Panjeon, or the Depositories for the Tripitaka Koreana Woodblocks. As for the original visitors, it is these buildings and the vast collection of woodblocks housed in them that made them make a long journey to this remote temple.   Many think that the Tripitaka Koreana is a World Heritage. However, it is the depositories rather than the collection of woodblocks that was put to the list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1995. UNESCO experts were amazed at the scientific design that helped safely store the treasures for several hundred years. It was later in 2007 that the Tripitaka Koreana was inscribed to the UNESCO Memory of the World Register.  The Tripitaka Koreana is called Palman Daejanggyeong in Korean, which literally means Eighty Thousand Scriptures. As the name suggests, it is a collection of over eighty thousand printing woodblocks carved with the canon of Buddhist scriptures. As for the 13th century Korean Buddhists, the project of carving the Buddhist scriptures, which took 16 years to complete, was their only defense to protect their country against a formidable enemy via their spiritual and cultural superiority.  Now let's move into the inner courtyard of the depositories, and learn more about how the medieval Koreans carried out such an epic project.

stories.title: Janggyeong Panjeon Depositories (Haeinsa Temple, Hapcheon)
stories.script: Janggyeong Panjeon Depositories   This building, which houses the Tripitaka Koreana, is called the Janggyeong Panjeon depositories. While its exact construction date is unknown, it was significantly rebuilt in 1457 during the reign of King Sejo of Joseon. The Janggyeong Panjeon depositories are the oldest buildings in Haeinsa Temple.   The buildings exhibit remarkable simplicity with minimal decorative elements, yet their structures are impressively scientific. The Janggyeong Panjeon depositories are situated with mountains blocking the north and open to the south, allowing winds from below to naturally flow through the buildings.  If you take a look inside, the floor is made of earth, with salt, charcoal, calcium oxide, and sand spread underneath to prevent harmful insects and maintain a constant humidity level. The Janggyeong Panjeon depositories were especially designed with airflow in mind. There is a space between the bottom of the bookshelves and the floor, ensuring good air circulation.  Most fascinating is the scientific secret behind the building's windows. Take a look at the windows from a distance, both above and below. The front windows of the building are smaller at the top and larger at the bottom. Conversely, the rear windows are smaller at the bottom and larger at the top. Why were the windows made this way?  Dry air enters through the large lower windows at the front passes through the racks and exits partially through the small windows at the bottom back. Not all air escapes through these small windows, and the remaining air stays inside, rising along the walls to exit through the large upper windows at the back. This mechanism helps maintain a constant indoor temperature and humidity.  The delicate design of the Janggyeong Panjeon depositories is so sophisticated that even modern scientists are amazed. Without these buildings, the Tripitaka Koreana might not have been preserved in its entirety for us to see today.

stories.title: Haksadae Pavilion
stories.script: Haksadae Pavilion, or Scholar's Hill, an old fir stands as if guarding the historical site. The tree is associated with the final days of Choi Chi-won, one of the greatest scholars of Silla in the 9th century.  Historical records state that he was a child prodigy who began reading and understanding Chinese classics at the age of four. With high hopes and aspirations for the people of his time, the strict hierarchical society of Silla hindered his pursuit of the desired government position. Disheartened, he left his home country for China at the age of twelve. Passing the imperial examination there to recruit foreign talents at the age of eighteen, he secured a government post. For ten years, he served the Tang Dynasty, participating in various important state affairs.  At twenty eight, Choi Chi-won returned home with plans to reform the country. However, Silla’s traditional class system was deeply rooted, and his proposals faced rejection by the aristocracy. Disillusioned, he chose to live as a hermit until his death.  The mountain ridge marks the hermitage where he spent his last days. According to folklore, the old fir was once his staff, planted and given life to grow tall and dense. Some of its branches droop downwards, as the tale goes, as they sprouted from the staff.

stories.title: Monument Street
stories.script: There stands an exquisite, aged granite pagoda beside the pond known as Yeongji, or Pond of Reflection. The pagoda displays the typical style of the Silla's three-story stone pagodas, similar to the one you saw at the inner courtyard of the temple. This pagoda is called Gilsangtap, which literally means 'pagoda of auspiciousness.' It is associated with the early Haeinsa Temple community's desire to protect the temple from wars and ensure everlasting peace.  Inside the pagoda, archaeologists discovered a record written by Choe Chi-won. It stated that the pagoda was built to honor those who sacrificed themselves to safeguard the temple's treasures from continuous wars.  Adjacent to the pagoda is a terrace of monuments, including the temple's history monument and the stupas honoring its most revered patriarchs. Situated nearby is the stupa of a Buddhist monk named Seongcheol. Widely regarded as one of the greatest Seon masters of our time, his austere life and sincere preaching inspired many Korean people, both Buddhists and non-Buddhists, making him one of the most admired religious leaders in Korea today.  This concludes our tour of Haeinsa Temple. We hope you enjoyed the tour, and if you wish, please don’t hesitate to visit again in the near future.

stories.title: Murals of the Founders’ Tale (Daejeokgwangjeon Hall)
stories.audioTitle: Murals of the Founders’ Tale (Daejeokgwangjeon Hall)
stories.script: Move to the right side of Daejeokgwangjeon Hall. Visitors can find the mural paintings depicting the life of Buddha. On the back wall of the building, a series of murals narrates the founding story of Haeinsa Temple.  One painting portrays a lady lying in bed, haloed by two monks, one above and the other below her. The lady is the queen consort of King Aejang, who ruled Silla during the early 9th century. Crowned at the age of thirteen, the king greatly relied on his wife's care. Consequently, he was deeply distressed when she fell ill.  Despite the efforts of physicians and the best available medicines, her condition did not improve. King Aejang sought a sincere prayer for her recovery and dispatched messengers across the kingdom to find a noble monk who could fulfill his request.  One of the royal messengers encountered two monks engaged in deep prayer at the foot of a mountain now known as Gayasan. The messenger relayed the queen's illness and asked for guidance to aid her. One of the monks instructed him to return to the palace, tie a string around her wrist, and affix the other end to a pear tree located at the front of the palace.  Following the monk's instructions, the king saw a miraculous recovery in the queen as she rose from her bed. However, the pear tree, connected to her healing, withered and died. Deeply moved by this miracle, the king erected a temple in honor of the two monks at the site where they had prayed. Over time, the temple grew into the Haeinsa Temple we know today.

stories.title: Tripitaka Koreana I
stories.script: These two unassuming yet meticulously designed buildings house the invaluable Tripitaka Koreana. If granted the opportunity to peer inside, you would immediately notice that they are filled with ancient printing woodblocks.  According to the historical records, these printing blocks were made of 'wild cherry' or Korean pear trees, aged over 40 years without any irregularities. The felled trees were left to rest for about a year to prevent warping or cracking during the slicing into boards. These boards were subsequently boiled in salted water and dried in well-ventilated spaces for two to three years. Each board was then joined with two sheets of paper, inscribed with scripture on both surfaces, and finally carved.  It is documented that the carvers ceremoniously bowed to Buddha three times before carving each character. Such dedication aligns with the aesthetic beauty and consistent size of all the characters engraved on the boards.  Following the carving, rectangular metal caps were affixed to both ends of each woodblock. These caps served multiple purposes: preventing warping, acting as handles, and safeguarding inscribed surfaces when stored piled up. Additionally, all woodblocks were lacquered to enhance durability, repelling insects and preventing moisture from compromising their integrity.  The intricate and time-consuming production process required around 15 years to complete the Tripitaka Koreana project. The accomplished work, borne from skilled artisans' dedicated efforts over such an extended period, is now revered not only as the world's foremost cultural and religious heritage but also as an artistic masterpieces.  These woodblocks, undoubtedly treasures of heritage, might not have survived were it not for the efficient storage chambers like the Janggyeong Panjeon. Now, let's delve into discussing these remarkable buildings. It's this sophisticated design rooted in scientific knowledge that continues to astonish even the esteemed architects of the 21st century.

stories.title: Tripitaka Koreana II
stories.script: The Tripitaka is a Sanskrit term referring to the complete canon of Buddhist scriptures, mainly comprising texts in three categories: sutras, the code of ethics, and the commentaries. Among the Tripitaka collections published in East Asia until the 13th century, the Tripitaka Koreana is generally regarded as the most comprehensive and accurate version of the Buddhist texts produced until that time. The significance of the Korean Tripitaka was reaffirmed when Japanese Buddhists chose it as the foundation for the Revised Taisho Tripitaka, published in the early 20th century with the aim of establishing a definitive edition of the Chinese Buddhist canon and its Japanese commentaries.  Numerous figures have been used to emphasize the historical and cultural significance of the Tripitaka Koreana as a world cultural heritage. For instance, the creation of the Tripitaka woodblocks in medieval Korea required over 13,500 logs and 160,000 sheets of paper.  Experts estimate that the project involved over 50,000 man-days to handwrite the scriptures and over a million artisans to engrave them onto the printing blocks. The engravers meticulously carved about 52 million characters onto the woodblocks. Assuming one can read approximately 5,000 characters a day, it would take about 30 years to read the entire scripture of the Tripitaka Koreana.  If all these Tripitaka woodblocks were stacked, they would reach about 3,250 meters in height, surpassing even the summit of Baekdusan, the tallest mountain on the Korean Peninsula, and nearly matching Mount Fuji, the highest mountain in Japan.  The weight of the Tripitaka Koreana is also remarkable. During the early 20th century, the Japanese colonial authority ruling Korea sought to transport this invaluable treasure to Japan but eventually abandoned the endeavor. The total weight of the woodblocks amounted to 250 tons, equivalent to requiring a hundred 2.5-ton cargo trucks to execute the plan, a logistical feat deemed unfeasible at that time.

stories.title: Hahoe Village
stories.script: Hahoe Village proudly holds a place of UNESCO’s list of world heritage sites. Its origin is traced back to Joseon Dynasty, fostering traditions that have endured for six centuries.  Among its many distinctions, Hahoe Village stands out as the birthplace of Hahoetal, traditional Korean masks used in performance. Visitors can catch a glimpse of these intriguing mask faces at the souvenir shop.  Take a look at the map displayed on the information panel. It illustrates the village’s unique setting, nestled amidst mountains on one side and bordered by a flowing river on the other side, with the Nakdonggang River curving along its boundary. The name ‘Hahoe’ literally means ‘a river that circles around.’  In Korea, traditional villages were established by both close and distant relatives of a family. Hahoe Village was largely populated by the Ryu family, which includes significant historic figures in Korean history. Notably, Ryu Seong-ryong played a crucial role during the 16th century war with Japan, significantly bolstering Joseon’s military power and contributing immensely to the nation’s recovery from a critical juncture.  Renowned as a haven for nobles and scholars, Hahoe Village’s legacy and customs persist through the ages, upheld by descendants of the Ryu family who continue to call the village their home, safeguarding its integrity and cherished traditions to this day.

stories.title: Hadong House
stories.audioTitle: Hadong House, Home of Seonbi in Hahoe Village
stories.script: Hadong House, Home of Seonbi in Hahoe Village  What you see before you now is Hadong House, one of the best-preserved traditional houses in the village. Hadong means East of Hahoe Village but it is better known as the Home of Seonbi in Hahoe Village among the local people.  If you want to understand the ruling philosophy of the Joseon Dynasty, it is very important to understand the meaning of “seonbi” and all that it refers to. Seonbi were virtuous scholars of the Joseon Dynasty, who had extensive knowledge of Confucianism. It was their virtue to serve the country and remain faithful to their ancestors. Even if they lived in honest poverty, they didn’t think it disgraceful, but devoted themselves to practicing Confucianism in the hope of realizing the ideal society.   Now let's take a look inside the house. The interior may not look very different from any ordinary house built during the Joseon Dynasty but you will notice a storage facility for oriental medicine in the wooden-floored living room. As you may have guessed already, the master of this house made medicine for poor and sick people who came to him for help. In this way, he tried to practice one of the Confucian philosophies of “virtue” during his life.  Now let's move on to the gate quarters, which leads to the outside. You will notice that while the rest of the buildings’ roofs are plated with tiles, as were most houses of the nobility during the Joseon Dynasty, the entrance gate of this house is simply topped with dry straw. This indicates the owner's effort to remain humble before his neighbors. It is probably why many people remember this house as the Home of Seonbi in Hahoe Village to this very day.

stories.title: Bukchondaek House, Hwagyeongdang (Hahoe Village, Andong)
stories.script: Bukchondaek House, Hwagyeongdang   Welcome to Bukchondaek House, greeted by its Tall Gate. The dignity of a noble house starts from its gate, and this house, with its splendid Tall Gate, represents the traditional homes nestled in the Bukchon area, a gathering place of noble families from Hahoe Village. Bukchondaek stands out for its size; originally constructed with 99 rooms, even the remaining 72 rooms make it the largest in Hahoe Village. A room in a Hanok is measured by the space between two pillars, so 72 rooms signify quite a large residence. The Tall Gate was designed to allow nobles in horse-drawn carriages to enter without stooping, with the gate's central section raised for this purpose. By the late Joseon period, wealthy and influential person could construct a Tall Gate to display their wealth and honor. The Tall Gate of this house is another testament to the family's social status and the prestigious authority of a prosperous noble.  Then who built Bukchondaek? The house was built by a true scholar Ryu Doseong , a descendant of Hahoe's meritorious subject, Ryu Seongryong, and a civil official of the Joseon Dynasty. In today's terms, Ryu Doseong held a position similar to the Chief Presidential Secretary. After retiring from public service, he returned to his hometown and dedicated his efforts to restoring Seowon (Confucian Academies) and so on.   What else makes Bukchondaek special? It's notable for separating living spaces for the father, son, and grandson. The central Sarangchae facing the main gate, called Hwagyeongdang, signifies harmony with parents and respect for the king, written by the famous calligrapher Han Seokbong. This area served as the master's living quarters.  The smaller Sarangchae on the left, Sushinwa, was for the master's son. The name Sushinwa teaches humility, reminding the family to consider their less fortunate neighbors and not to take pride in living in a fancy house. This lesson was heeded by descendants, who kept the plaque as a reminder against arrogance.  On the right, the large Sarangchae, Bukchonyugeo, served as the dwelling for the elder family members, where they lived after entrusting the household to their son. The pavilion offers a picturesque view of Hahoe, encapsulating filial piety and care.  Another attraction of this house is a pine tree near the shrine at the back of the large Sarangchae. Its bent shape, resembling the winding river around Hahoe, forms a Taegeuk symbol, unifying the house, people, and nature under the name of Hahoe.  Bukchondaek has also been a great benefactor to the village folks. Even when many nobles fell into decline in the late Joseon period, this house remained respected, thanks to the righteous actions of Ryu Doseong. One example was during the massive flood hitting the village in 1859. Despite having timber reserved for three years for his house construction, Ryu Doseong ordered his servants to throw it into the river to save villagers from drowning. His and his descendants' actions earned them respect throughout Hahoe Village.  So even during the Donghak Peasant Revolution in 1894, when Donghak peasant armies attacked other wealthy noble house, they passed Bukchondaek with respect. The ancestral virtues have influenced descendants positively, making Bukchondaek a respected noble house in the village.

stories.title: Earthen Wall and Stone Wall
stories.script: Walking along the path leading to Samsindang Shrine, there are exquisite walls lining the streets of Hahoe Village, each crafted from diverse shapes and materials.  These walls serve as great examples of traditional Korean beliefs. People held the belief that natural geographical formations directly impacted human lives.  In Hahoe Village, the act of digging wells or constructing stone walls has long been considered taboo due to the village’s specific geography. Locals envisioned the village as resembling a boat floating on a calm lake and believed that preserving this geographical configuration was crucial to maintain the auspicious energy of the area.  To uphold this belief, they opted to construct earthen walls instead of weighty stone walls. The wall on the left, known as ‘Toseokdam,’ is made of sand and stone, with the belief that it would prevent the ‘boat-shaped’ village from sinking. Additionally, the inhabitants refrained from digging wells for fear of damaging the ‘hull’ of this symbolic ‘boat.’  Meanwhile, the wall on the right is mainly made of sand and covered with roof tiles. The tiles were placed to prevent the sand from being washed away by the rain. This wall is called ‘Pandam,’ as these walls bear the marks left by the boards, or ‘pans,’ used during their construction.  In the village, visitors will encounter numerous narrow alleys lined with these traditional walls. Take a leisurely stroll through the village and marvel at the beauty inherent in each of these elements.

stories.title: Samsindang
stories.script: Samsindang, the Village's Spiritual Pillar  You will see Samsindang as soon as you make a sharp turn at the end of the narrow alley. It is the place which village commoners visited to call upon a higher being.  Do you see that very old tree? It is a zelkova tree planted by Ryu Gong-hye, one of the village's pioneer residents. The tree is now over six hundred years old.  Just as the Greeks believed that nymphs lived within oak trees, the people of Hahoe Village thought that their guardian deity lived in this zelkova tree. Two times a year the villagers would get together under the tree and hold a ceremony representing their hopes for the village's wellbeing and a bountiful harvest.  According to old tales, in years when the ceremony was not performed as fervently as in other years, tigers would appear in the forests around town. The ceremony is still performed to this day after hundreds of years. Indeed, it is one of the oldest village traditions to have survived to the present day.  The Samsindang Tree was also a shelter for the villagers. They would often be seen assembled under its cool shade either talking amongst themselves or making a wish. It is said that the women came to the tree to pray for childbirth and prosperity.  Still, people write down their wish on small paper notes and hang them on this tree. If there is something your truly heart desires, why not take this moment to make a wish?   The Legend of Hahoe Masks  [Narration] Each year, Hahoe Village performs a communal shamanistic rite which originated from a ceremony performed to entertain the village deity. This traditional mask dance has been designated as an Important Intangible Cultural Heritage of Korea.  A hahoetal, or Hahoe Mask, was traditionally used for this mask dance. These masks were made in different types of shapes and sizes, including one that does not cover the chin. There is an interesting legend that explains how this mask acquired the form it has today.  According to the legend, there was a young man named Heo, who was living in Hahoe Village.  [Heo] “The village is in grave danger. What should I do?”  [Narration] That night he went to sleep after many hours of tossing and turning in his bed. Then, the village's guardian deity appeared in his dream.  [Village Guardian] “You love and care for your village. I will help you solve this problem. Make twelve masks and use them in a shamanistic rite. Then all the plagues will be gone. But remember, if anyone sees you making these masks, you will die.”  [Narration] From that day on he locked his doors and devoted all his energy to making the masks. But alas, a village girl who secretly admired him came sneaking into his home one day and caught a glimpse of him putting the finishing touches to his last mask. As the guardian deity had warned, both souls were taken at that very moment. That is why one mask is missing its chin.   Mask Dance as Social Commentary  In Korea, traditional mask dance performances were popular throughout the nation, and Hahoe Village’s mask dance is one of the oldest one that passes on to this day. It was usually performed from the lunar New Year's Day to the fifteenth day of lunar January. In particular, the dance was basically a ceremony dedicated to the gods but it also functioned as an outlet for criticism for the common people.  Traditional Korea was a strict hierarchical society, and the common people were oppressed by the ruling class. In all ages, any society that lacks healthy criticism and communication is bound to negative side effects. So, this mask dance was a faucet for commoners to make fun of nobles and society's shortcomings. Any oppressed desires could be released through the performances.  The performers would wear a mask, harassing and mocking the nobles. Laughter would ripple through the audience. The satire did not end there. Fallen monks and other social classes were on the platter just the same. Observe the masks and you will find that each character is filled with humor.   Currently, the Andong International Mask Dance Festival is held in Hahoe Village and downtown Andong every October, so visitors can watch all sorts of mask plays and dances from all around the world.

stories.title: Yangjindang House
stories.audioTitle: Yangjindang House, Head House of the Ryu family
stories.script: Yangjindang House, Head House of the Ryu family  This is Yangjindang House, the head house of the Ryu family.   According to Korean traditions, the eldest son of a family has the duty of leading the family and carries out ceremonial rites for their deceased ancestors to show their respect. So, this house has been an important place for preserving the traditions and heritage of the Ryu family.  Also, there is an important aspect you should not miss. Ryu Seong-ryong, one of the greatest historic figures to be born in Hahoe Village, was born in this house.   What remains today is only a portion of the entire house as it was burnt down during the Japanese invasion in the 16th century. Legend has it that when the house was being built, something special happened.  The new owner of the site was determined to build a new house that would serve as a foundation for his family. But whenever he tried to erect a pillar, it kept tumbling to the ground. He prayed to his ancestors for help. He was told he must save the lives of ten thousand people in the course of three years in order to build a proper house.  So the man began to perform good deeds. He would go to the village square to help those in need, and never refused a request whether big or small. Before he knew it three years had passed.  The mountain deity was touched by his deeds and allowed him to build a home. When he tried erecting a pillar, it stayed up sturdy and strong. He was finally able to finish building his house, whereupon he named it Yangjindang House.   Construction Characteristics of Yangjindang House  The structure is perched atop a set of elevated pillars. This was to keep the wooden-floored hall cool during the hot summer months by promoting airflow. The pillars are fixed on a foundation that is carefully placed upon an unworked boulder.   As anyone would expect from a head house of a family, the wooden-floored living room of the outer quarters is very spacious. The Ryu family would gather in these quarters to discuss family matters and arrange ancestral ceremonies, which often required summoning four or five hundred guests to each event. An ancestral ceremony was and still is considered the most important family event, because it is the key event to show a virtue of respect for one's parents and ancestors.  Traditionally, it has been an honor for any Korean to honor a great ancestor. It must have been a great honor for the Ryu family to honor such a great ancestor like Ryu Seong-ryong. Ancestral ceremonies were practicing filial piety, according to Confucius teachings, and it took on a religious meaning beyond simply commemorating the deceased. That is why there were rules and procedures for every single detail regarding the ceremony down to how to layout the table to how to bow.  Now let's take a look at the inner quarters, in which the female members of the family resided. The windows would open up from the bottom. Back in Joseon, there were strict rules about how men and women should act around each other. The structure of the window was designed to help the women close them shut whenever they heard a stranger approaching.

stories.title: Chunghyodang House
stories.audioTitle: Chunghyodang House, the House Built in Memory of Ryu Seong-ryong
stories.script: Chunghyodang House, the House Built in Memory of Ryu Seong-ryong  The first thing anyone visiting Chunghyodang House will notice is the enormous tree that stands before the house. It is a Korean fir planted by Great Britain's Queen Elizabeth II in 1999 to celebrate her visit to Hahoe Village. The Korean fir is a native Korean evergreen tree that is known throughout the world for its qualities.  After the Queen's visit, this house and even the road before it enjoyed a great amount of publicity. The road that the Queen walked on near the house is now affectionately called the Queen's Road.   Actually, this house was built in memory of Ryu Seong-ryong, the great figure of the Joseon Dynasty. When he resigned after thirty years of faithful service, he came back home to Hahoe Village. The house was originally a small and humble abode while he was around, and was only expanded at a later date by his grandsons and students to commemorate his lifetime achievements. The name of this house, Chunghyodang House, literally means “a house of loyalty and filial piety”, and was thus named so as to commemorate Ryu Seong-ryong's devoted life.   The Life of Ryu Seong-ryong  Ryu Seong-ryong passed the civil service examination at the age of twenty-five. He served in many different official posts until he became the Chief State Councilor, in charge of all the policies that concerned the Joseon Dynasty.   When Japan invaded Joseon in 1592, he was appointed to direct the army of three provinces under the king's command. He distinguished himself in the national crisis by appointing great commanders such as Admiral Yi Sun-sin who led victories against Japanese navy during the war. Also, he made a significant contribution in many battles. And moreover, he negotiated with the Chinese army to wipe out any remaining Japanese troops left behind during their retreat.  He had returned home by the time the war was almost over. Despite the king's repeated requests, he refused to go back to serve the king's court. He personally felt responsible when the king had to leave the palace to avoid the vortex of war and when the people of the Joseon Dynasty were suffering from the war.  Ryu Seong-ryong was a man who was truly devoted to his people and his country in challenging times. He is still remembered as a great person because of his loyalty to the king and benevolence for people, and was the embodiment of Confucian virtues.

stories.title: Yeongmogak Exhibition (Hahoe Village, Andong)
stories.script: Yeongmogak Exhibition  Yeongmogak Exhibition, built in Chunghyodang Hall in 1966, serves as an exhibition hall preserving the relics of Ryu Seongryong. The name ‘Yeongmo’ means ‘waiting and longing for a long time.’  It showcases a variety of items including the royal decree appointing him as the Prime Minister (Yeonguijeong), the garments and shoes he wore in office, his written works, and personal belongings, allowing visitors to trace the life Ryu Seongryong led.   His achievements related to the Imjinwaeran (the Japanese Invasion of Joseon) especially offer profound lessons. It was Ryu Seongryong who, even before the outbreak of the war, appointed Yi Sun-sin as the Naval Commander of the Left Jeolla Province and Kwon Yul as the Governor of Uiju, preparing for the Japanese invasion. Without his foresight, would we have had the chance to meet the great heroes of the Imjinwaeran, Generals Yi Sun-sin and Kwon Yul?  Another significant achievement of Ryu Seongryong is the authorship of Jingbirok, The Book of Correction, a memoir that meticulously records the causes and events of the Imjinwaeran. The Jingbirok reflects on the mistakes that led to the national crisis, emphasizing the need to prepare for the future. Jingbirok, along with the Nanjung ilgi (War Diary) of Yi Sun-sin, serves as a valuable resource for studying the circumstances before and after the Imjinwaeran, offering profound lessons to future generations.

stories.title: Jakcheon Historic House
stories.script: Jakcheon Historic House was named after the scholar Jakcheon Yu-dogwan, who used to live here. Unfortunately, a portion of the house was swept away during a flood, leaving only the remaining straight-lined inner quarters.  What adds intrigue to this house is the low wall situated on one side of the courtyard. It’s strategically positioned between the outer quarters and the main room across from it. These walls, known as ‘Nae-oe-dam’ or ‘Hut-dam,’ served the purpose of maintaining a distance between the men and women.  During the Joseon Dynasty, Confucianism was the main value of the country. According to the Confucian philosophy, there are distinct roles for men and women, and they were expected to maintain separate spheres. Women were not to encounter male guests entering the house.  Therefore, a partition was installed between the guest room in the outer quarters and the main room in the inner quarters. Female members of the household would typically stay in the inner quarters, and the wall acted as a barrier to prevent their interaction with male guests.  Although these partitions are more commonly associated with tile-roofed houses, which were the dwellings of Joseon’s aristocrats, in the Andong area, such walls are also found in ordinary rectangular houses. This indicates that the people of Andong devised their methods to adhere to Confucian philosophy within their specific living environment.  Visitors will encounter several more of these walls when they explore Hahoe Village, serving as poignant reflections of Joseon’s enduring traditions.

stories.title: Damyeonjae
stories.script: Damyeonjae, a traditional house, holds loose connections to the global appeal of K-culture. This residence is owned by Ryu Si-won, a Korean actor and a descendant of Ryu Seong-ryong. His recent active engagements in Japan have drawn attention from his Japanese fanbase, some of whom have visited this village.  Damyeonjae House is also well-known for being the place where Queen Elizabeth II received a birthday gift during her visit to Hahoe Village in 1999. It was in this very courtyard that she witnessed a traditional mask dance performance.  If you observe closely, there is a small hole in the wall encircling the yard. During Joseon era, attaining a government official position was considered the greatest honor and aspiration. To become a civil servant, individuals had to undergo exams, which were held in the capital city. For those who lived outside the capital, the journey to participate in these exams was lengthy and often on foot.  During these travels, many of them faced financial difficulties. Rich nobles would discreetly stash money in holes within the walls of their houses to assist these aspiring officials on their way to the capital. These holes symbolize the generosity and benevolence of the nobles in Joseon.

stories.title: Pinewoods of Mansongjeong Pavilion
stories.script: Mansongjeong pine forest is home to approximately ten thousand pine trees and holds the designation as a Natural Monument of Korea.  The deliberate creation of the forest traces back to the time of King Seonjo of Joseon, when Ryu Un-ryong, brother of Ryu Seong-ryong, spearheaded the planting of ten thousand pine trees. This initiative aimed to mitigate the harsh energy emanating from the stone cliff, Buyongdae Cliff, and counterbalance the void from the northwest. As a result, the village now enjoys protection against flooding in summer and bitter cold winds in winter, thanks to the forest. The community continues the tradition of regularly planting young pine trees, further enriching the forest.  An ancient tale recounts how this forest became the savior of Hahoe Village. During the Japanese invasion of Korea in 1592, approaching Japanese troops sought an opportunity to attack the village. Suddenly, they encountered a dense, verdant pine forest. However, upon seeing pine cones strewn around the trees, they mistook them for soldiers' helmets, causing them to flee in fear. At that time, the forest was much denser, and the sight of the cones alarmed the troops.  On the opposite side of the forest lies the Buyongdae cliff, a prominent landmark of Hahoe Village. At the cliff's base stands Ogyeonjeongsa House, a house that encapsulates the narrative of Ryu Seong-ryong and Ryu Un-ryong, the village's most renowned brothers.

stories.title: Ogyeonjeongsa House
stories.script: Ogyeonjeongsa House was not originally a living quarters. However, Ryu Seong-ryong used this house as a place to pursue studies and mentor his students. It was also where he composed the famous Jingbirok, a memoir recounting the Japanese invasion to Joseon, following his retirement. Jingbirok attained the status of a Korean National Treasure due to its historical significance and is currently displayed in Yeongmogak Pavilion.  The house stands as a testament to its master’s hardships, being one of the most influential officials during challenging times in the nation’s history. The first chapter of the Jingbirok is title ‘Records of War Written in Tears and Regret.’ During the war, Ryu Seong-ryong had escorted the king during evacuation, feeling guilt-ridden for leaving behind the people. Upon the war's conclusion, he returned home and documented everything to remember the past and alleviate its torment.  Observe the narrow passage leading toward the cliff, known as ‘Rabbit Road.’ The path is so narrow that only a rabbit could pass through it. Ryu Seong-ryong used this route to visit his elder brother, Ryu Un-ryong, residing in Gyeomamjeongsa House, located across from the village, and it is believed that they frequently visited each other.  A short hike up from Ogyeonjeongsa House leads to Buyongdae Cliff. Visitors can enjoy a stunning view of the peaceful village from there.

stories.title: Buyongdae Cliff (Hahoe Village, Andong)
stories.script: Hahoe Village Seen from Buyongdae Cliff  Buyongdae Cliff offers a panoramic view of Hahoe Village from its position on a shallow rock mountain opposite the village. From the front of the village, the cliff appears as a steep escarpment, standing like a folding screen.  ‘Buyongdae’ means the cliff of Hahoe Village that resembles a lotus flower floating on water. It was also known as “Bugae, meaning the hill north of Hahoe from ancient times, and has been a symbol of the village ever since.  Buyongdae plays a crucial role as a buffer zone, guiding the fierce currents of the river to bypass the village, thus protecting it. The villagers believe that if Buyongdae were positioned slightly differently, they would have faced annual flooding, regarding this cliff as a remarkable safeguard.  From here, the picturesque village unfolds at a glance. Recognized as one of the sixteen scenic spots of Hahoe, Buyongdae allows for an appreciation of the harmony between the mountains, river, village, pine forests, and the lives of the Pungsan Ryu clan who have resided here through the ages.  The village, cradled by the river's embrace and blended seamlessly with the surrounding landscape, embodies Korean tradition. Hahoe's designation as a UNESCO World Heritage Site is attributed to the ongoing preservation and succession of nature, history, tradition, and family legacy through generations.

stories.title: Entrance of Yangdong Village
stories.script: Yangdong Village is a UNESCO World Heritage site. It has traditionally been the village of “yang-bans” since the Joseon Dynasty. Yang-bans, or “virtuous scholars,” were members of the nobility class of Joseon. They had extensive knowledge of Confucianism and were tasked with ruling the country based on its virtues while maintaining respect for their ancestors. Here in Yangdong Village, you can experience the lives of these nobles and learn about their ways.  During the Joseon period, people formed clan villages where they lived with their families. Yangdong Village was the home of the “Son” family from Wolseong and the “Yi” family from Yeogang. Many esteemed officials and scholars were born and raised in Yangdong Village. Their traditions and customs have been passed down for generations, remaining preserved to this day. This legacy has endured for six hundred years through the efforts and dedication of the families who consider this village their home. The village was registered as part of the UNESCO World Heritage in 2010 for its historic value.  In Yangdong Village, you can see many houses that were built during the Joseon Dynasty, now protected as cultural heritage. The Korean traditional houses, like the ones you see here, are called “hanoks.” A hanok usually consisted of more than one building, with inner spaces designated for the husband and wife, and outer spaces intended for guests. Separate quarters were designated for servants, and some hanoks even had storage facilities. A courtyard, enclosed by a fence and a front gate, linked the buildings together.  Koreans traditionally sat and slept on the floor, and anyone entering the building had to remove their shoes. The floor was heated with the traditional “ondols” during cold seasons, embodying Korea’s traditional lifestyle of sitting on the floor.  The segregation of spaces for men and women was also based on Confucian philosophy. Women occupied the inner portion of the house, farthest from the gate, while the exterior was reserved for men. As you walk through the village, you’ll be able to observe examples of these houses.

stories.title: Hyangdan House
stories.script: Hyangdan House stands as the largest and most splendid house in Yangdong Village, epitomizing the opulence associated with the Yi family.  Connected to Yi Eon-jeok and his brother Yi Eon-gwal, both iconic and prominent members of the Yi family, Hyangdan House remains closely intertwined with their legacy. While Yi Eon-jeok, a neo-Confucian scholar, ventured into government service, his younger brother Yi Eon-gwal chose to remain in the house, dedicating his life to caring for their mother and the family.   Distinct in its architectural structure, Hyangdan House features two courtyards, which is not commonly found in traditional Korean houses.  The main room and elevated floor are deliberately separated from the rest of the building, a design intended to offer increased privacy to the women residing in the house.

stories.title: Mucheomdang House
stories.script: In accordance with Korean tradition, the firstborn in a family inherits the house along its associated duties. In Yangdong village, there exist two principal houses: one for the Son family and another for the Lee family.  Mucheomdang House serves as the head house for the Lee family, upholding a tradition that is gradually fading in Korea but remains profoundly significant for the Lee family and numerous other households in the village. Over generations, the firstborn males of the Lee family have inherited responsibility for conducting ancestral ceremonies and overseeing family affairs.  The house's design reflects a blend of simplicity and refined beauty, with distinctive features that distinguish it from others. Notably, it boasts a spacious wooden-floored living room where Lee family members gather for monthly ceremonies, paying homage to their ancestors. These ceremonies necessitate considerable effort and emphasize the importance of honoring elderly and deceased family members, a fundamental Confucian virtue.  Another distinctive aspect of Mucheomdang House is its use of round foundation stones supporting the columns, a rarity in traditional Korean architecture. While squared foundations and pillars are commonplace, round pillars were typically reserved for royal palaces. Although Mucheomdang was originally a private residence, it was constructed in a style reminiscent of a public assembly hall.  The house encompasses a shrine situated in the northernmost corner, followed by a structure designated for ceremonies and living quarters. The architectural design showcases the two different roof styles, reflecting the separate timelines and purposes of the inner quarters and the annex building. The living quarters feature a gabled roof, known for its simplicity and grandeur in traditional Korean construction. In contrast, the annex building boasts a sleek and splendid hipped-and-gabled roof akin to those found in royal palaces.  The outer quarters and the annex building of Mucheomdang House were constructed in 1508 and 1543 respectively, and remarkably, members of the Lee family continue to reside in this historic house. The name ‘Mucheomdang’ originates from an old book phrase, emphasizing the value of leading a life that brings honor to one's ancestors a cherished virtue for the village's residents.
