However, these wooden tablets were used for short memos before the use of paper became widespread in Silla. They were easy to obtain and reuse after washing and shaving away the previous writing. Ancient Egypt and European countries also used papyrus stems prior to paper becoming more widely available.   The wooden tablets were used for a multitude of purposes, from making personal notes to administrative documents of the government. Thus they are an important historical aid to understanding the administration of ancient Silla society.   These exhibits document tax payments in the Silla kingdom, recording the names and addresses of taxpayers and the quantity of grain they paid as tax.   In addition, the wooden tablets also record information about palace guards, lists of medicines and their dates of manufacture, and lists of food and their dates of production. They record much valuable information about the life and society of Silla.

stories.title: Prehistoric and Ancient History Gallery 2: Funeral Urn
stories.script: Cremation and Funeral Urn  This relic is a funeral urn, and was designed to hold the ashes of a dead person after cremation. Silla accepted Buddhism as its national religion, so Buddhist cremation rites were widely adopted. In most cases, the ashes were placed in urns after cremation and buried underground.   A single funeral urn with a lid was generally used, but some of them comprised both an inner and an outer urn. The outer urn was usually highly decorated with beautiful patterns and had a knob on the lid, whilst the inner urn was rather simple and did not have a handle. Stamped patterns on the outer urn were very fashionable in Silla.  Funeral customs can be significant indicators to understand the changing culture of a nation, as they are very conservative and change very slowly. Therefore, funeral urns excavated in Silla area demonstrate that Buddhism exerted a strong influence on Silla people's lifestyle.

stories.title: Prehistoric and Ancient History Gallery 2: The Planned City, Seorabol
stories.script: The Planned City, Seorabol  Now let’s look around the 1000-year-old city of Gyeongju, the capital of Silla.   If you look at the picture closely you will see the way the roads are laid out in rows, forming a grid pattern. Gyeongju was well-planned and divided into neat areas. There was a palace, a residential area with a temple, a royal tomb complex, and an industrial iron and earthenware manufacturing area. Eighth-century Gyeongju was a flourishing city comparable to Constantinople, Baghdad and Chang’an.   In the middle under the painting of Gyeongju, you will see a crescent-shaped tract of land. It is the Silla palace known as Wolseong, meaning ‘moon-shaped palace’. The palace was built on a low hill along the river, which served as a natural moat to impede intruders.   Silla engaged in active cultural exchange with neighboring and western countries. This affected the foundation of aristocratic culture in Silla as many Silla nobles built ponds in their gardens and decorated their houses with gold.   As you can see in the picture, Gyeongju played an essential role as a planned city in leading the ancient society, and the marvelous culture of Silla flourished with Gyeongju as the heart of it. Large amount of relics representing the past glory of Silla has been excavated in Gyeongju, and thus, Gyeongju is often referred to as the treasure house of Silla Dynasty.

stories.title: Prehistoric and Ancient History Gallery 2: Gold Belt
stories.audioTitle: Gold Belt of Silla - the King’s Authority
stories.script: Gold Belt of silla - the King's authority  This is the gold belt of a Silla king. It was found with the gold crown that we saw earlier. The belt was not designed for practical use but rather as an ornament to display the authority of the king. A similar tradition also existed in Medieval Europe. To show wealth, Europeans also decorated their belts with jewels during the Middle Ages.  As a symbol of power, the gold belt was highly decorative. The part of the ornament encircling the waist consists of two thin gold plates. Small, round, gold decorations are strung together with gold thread. Just like a belly dancer’s costume, the glamour of the belt is enhanced by many pendant decorations.  Interestingly, numerous ornamental decorations inspired by diverse everyday items are attached to the belt by short gold strings. This derived from the customs of nomadic tribal peoples, who often carried various daily tools on their bodies. Each ornament has a different meaning and purpose. For example, a medicine pouch in a net symbolizes the wishes for health while a gold fish charm stands for fertility and eternal life.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR1: Relics of the Prehistoric Age (Potteries in the Neolithic Age)
stories.audioTitle: History of Earthenware and Stone Tools of the Prehistoric Age
stories.script: History of Earthenware and Stone Tools of the Prehistoric Age  We are now in the first room of the museum. This room is filled with stone tools and earthenware used by the Prehistoric occupants of the Korean Peninsula, long before the establishment of the Silla kingdom. The beginning of Prehistoric Age of Korea dates way back to around 500,000 B.C., and many traces of early human habitation have been found from this period.  From the exhibits in this room, we can see the technological development of the various stone tools and earthenware items. And with this information we can understand the lifestyles of the peninsula’s ancient inhabitants. Ground stone tools of the Neolithic Period, for example, indicate the beginnings of agriculture in Korea. We can also see how people cooked and stored grains.   The earthenware vessel in the middle of the room has a pointed base that is typical of artifacts dating from the Neolithic Period in Korea. While this type of clay earthenware was manufactured all over the world during the Neolithic Period, Korean vessels are distinguished by patterns of lines incised into the clay. The patterns were made by drawing or pressing the surface with a comb-like implement.  In the Bronze Age, more sophisticated tools were invented, and this made people’s lives easier. Earthenware from this age is characterized by a flat base and plain surface and is simple and practical. But in the Late Bronze Age, a more decorative and sophisticated style was introduced from China. We can see these exhibits in the big glass cases which lead us into the next room.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR1: Bronze Ware Culture in Korea
stories.audioTitle: Gojoseon’s Huge Leap to the Production of bronze Ware
stories.script: Gojoseon’s Huge Leap to the Production of bronze Ware  [Narration] Let us look at Korean bronze ware now. This room exhibits artifacts from the Korean Bronze Age. Bronze swords are the most representative items of the Korean Bronze Age. First, I’d like to draw your attention to the violin-shaped sword on your left. This sword was made in the Early Bronze Age in a Chinese province bordering the northern part of the Korean Peninsula.   [Visitor] Um, I am confused. Doesn’t that mean it is Chinese?  [Narration] Not exactly. During the Bronze Age, Korea was so powerful that it occupied some parts of main land China where this sword was made.   [Visitor] But as China is geographically close to Korea, I guess Chinese techniques and styles must have influenced Korean bronze ware, just like they influenced Korean earthenware in the Neolithic Period.   [Narration] No, they didn’t. While Chinese bronze swords were made as a single piece, the blade and hilt of Korean bronze swords were constructed separately. You can see this feature on the bottom of the sword.  [Visitor] Ah, I see. This sword looks unique but I doubt that it was very useful, was it?  [Narration] Ah, that is because the sword was not meant to be practical or functional. In the Bronze Age, powerful men carried these swords at their sides as a symbol of power. That’s why the swords were designed far more for appearance than for functionality. In Korea, functional bronze sword-making began during the Late Bronze Age. You can see some examples of these on the right. Comparatively, they have sharper and straighter blades.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR1: Clay Figurines of Various Kinds
stories.audioTitle: Clay Figurines, the Simplicity of Silla
stories.script: Clay Figurines, the Simplicity of Silla  From now on, we will examine the relics of the Silla kingdom. These small figures are called tou, which means ‘clay figurines’. The clay figurines of Silla generally represent human figures, common animals or tools.   Although the expressions of the clay figurines are simple and abstract, their audacious, funny faces inspire amusement. This group of clay figurines in the center looks like people dancing the night away at some crazy dance party. The two male figurines look devious and cheeky. As you can see, each of the clay figurines is simple but full of charm.  The various features of these clay figurines tell us about the lifestyle of the people of Silla, giving us valuable clues about their farming tools, musical instruments, and even their livestock. There are many examples of horse and dog clay figurines which indicate the popularity of the animals as well as their proximity to human life.   Usually, these clay figurines were made for burial with the dead. Tombs were furnished with necessities used in daily life, so that the dead would be prepared for the afterlife. This custom was also found in ancient Egypt. Egyptians used to bury their dead with a figurine named ‘The Answer Man’ to accompany them into the afterworld.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR1: Long-necked Jar with Figurines
stories.audioTitle: The People of Silla, the Drama of Life and Death
stories.script: The People of Silla, the Drama of Life and Death  The jar at the entrance to this room was found in the tomb of a Silla king. People believed that dead kings would live eternally in the next world, and that’s why they buried so many accessories with the dead.  This long-necked jar with figurines has a unique appearance. The body looks solid, with clay figurines decorating the shoulders of the jar. In Silla clay figurines were made not only for solo display but also for attaching to earthenware like this.  Similar to the clay figurines we saw earlier, many of the clay figurines on the jar show how the people of Silla lived. Look at the man sitting in the middle. He is playing a Korean traditional instrument that has many long strings. To the right of the player, there is a couple making love.  You may be surprised by the nudity and sensuality expressed by the ancient cultural heritage of the East. Actually, figurines depicting couples having intercourse or showing sexual organs were made from the Prehistoric Age onward, and have been found all over the world. They represent a way of praying for fertility and abundance, just like other animal-shaped clay figurines.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR2: Gold Crown of from the Cheonma Tomb
stories.audioTitle: Gold Crown of Silla, a Symbol of Dynastic Splendor
stories.script: Gold Crown of Silla, a Symbol of Dynastic Splendor  Buddhism and gold represent the culture of the Silla kingdom. Just as many gold relics were recovered from the tomb of Tutankhamen of ancient Egypt, many gold treasures have been excavated from the tombs of Silla’s kings. This room shows gold relics from the flourishing Silla kingdom. The most eye-catching artifact in this room is this gold crown. Of many glamorous gold crowns from Silla, this is regarded as the greatest masterpiece.   The Gold Crowns of Silla were shaped like branches, just like the laurel wreaths of Roman emperors, but the decorative symbolism was different. While the laurel wreath is a symbol of victory and glory, the upward-reaching tree motif of this gold crown symbolizes divinity. The round, gold ornaments represent leaves, and the crescent-shaped jade ornaments signify fruit. As such, these ornaments represent Silla’s desire for prosperity and perpetuation.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR2: Gold Belt of from the Cheonma Tomb
stories.audioTitle: Gold Belt of Silla - the King’s Authority
stories.script: Gold Belt of Silla - the King’s Authority  This is the gold belt of a Silla king. It was found with the gold crown that we saw earlier. The belt was not designed for practical use but rather as an ornament to display the authority of the king. A similar tradition also existed in Medieval Europe. To show wealth, Europeans also decorated their belts with jewels during the Middle Ages.  As a symbol of power, the gold belt was highly decorative. The part of the ornament encircling the waist consists of two thin gold plates. Small, round, gold decorations are strung together with gold thread. Just like a belly dancer’s costume, the glamour of the belt is enhanced by many pendant decorations.  Interestingly, numerous ornamental decorations inspired by diverse everyday items are attached to the belt by short gold strings. This derived from the customs of nomadic tribal peoples, who often carried various daily tools on their bodies. Each ornament has a different meaning and purpose. For example, a medicine pouch in a net symbolizes the wishes for health while a gold fish charm stands for fertility and eternal life.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR2: Silla, a Kingdom of Gold
stories.script: Silla, a Kingdom of Gold  The gold relics in this room were all crafted during the 5th and 6th centuries when the gold culture of Silla was at its height. Silla was described in the Chronicles of Japan as the ‘splendid kingdom of gold and silver’.  The gold culture of Silla was complemented by distinguished metal craftsmanship. The golden hat on the other side of the gold crown was made of thin and intricately patterned gold plates. It is as delicate as if it had been made by weaving gold threads.  The gold plate ornament on the side was used to accentuate the splendor of crowns or hats. This ornament depicts a butterfly with its wings extended in flight. On the front of the golden hat, there is a hole into which the butterfly-shaped ornament could be attached. Imagine how perfect the crown would have looked adorned with the butterfly ornament!   Can you see the small glittering gold spangles? These were originally attached to the gold crown. When the king wore this crown in sunlight, these spangles created a dazzling display, shining with the King’s every step.  The earring-shaped gold ornaments in the back glass case were pendants attached under the crown. They consist of little gold beads with half-moon-shaped jade ornaments or blue glass ornaments suspended by gold threads. They are also believed to have decorated the belt.  As we can see, members of the royal family and the nobility of Silla loved to use gold items not only during rituals but in their daily lives as well. The amount of gold excavated from the tombs in Gyeongju is very impressive, even by international standards.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR2: Glass Vessels and Other Relics
stories.audioTitle: Where Did Silla’s Glass Come From
stories.script: Where Did Silla’s Glass Come From  [Narration] Along with gold items, glass vessels were another luxury item of the Silla period. Since glass vessels were more expensive than gold, they were only used by the upper classes.  [Visitor] Glass was more expensive than gold? That’s difficult to believe…  [Narration] Yes, it was. Glass was first introduced to Korea during the Three Kingdoms Period. Such beautiful glass became popular among the nobility, but the manufacturers of Silla weren’t highly skilled and couldn’t keep up with the demand.   [Narration] Wait, are you serious? The glass vessels here are beautiful. I can’t believe there was a lack of quality workmanship. The colors and patterns are as good as those I have seen in Western countries.  [Narration] No wonder, because this is Roman glassware.  [Visitor] Wow! How can that be?  [Narration] This glassware is believed to have been made in the Mediterranean region and imported into Silla. The shape of the vessels and the components of the glass are different from the glassware made in Silla or China and are much more similar to Roman glass.  [Visitor] Can it be true that glassware was transported all the way from Rome to the far east of Asia? Was that possible?  [Narration] Yes, it was. Historians believe that merchants of Central Asia imported glassware along the Silk Road, a route that crossed the northern grasslands of China. Trade between Silla and other countries was very active at that time.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR2: Ornament Sheath of Precious Dagger (Scabbard Ornament)
stories.audioTitle: Ornament Sheath of Precious Dagger, Trace of Interchange and Communication
stories.script: Ornament Sheath of Precious Dagger, Trace of Interchange and Communication  The treasure in the corner inevitably catches one’s eye with its dazzling brilliance. It is the 1,500-year-old ornamental sheath of a precious dagger. At first sight, it looks exotic and unlike any of the other treasures. The unique patterns on the sheath and the wave pattern and yin-yang symbols on the surface are dissimilar to Korean traditional motifs. Also, the jewels and glass decorating it were a very rare type of decoration in the Silla kingdom. This is because this dagger was imported by way of the Silk Road like the glass vessels we saw earlier.   The origin of the dagger remained a mystery for a long time. The artistic technique using gold and colorful jewels is found across a broad swath of Europe, from Germany to West Siberia, but the exact providence of the item is unknown.  However, after 37 years of research, new information was uncovered and historians reached a temporary conclusion. First, the iron sword hidden in the sheath is a double-bladed dagger, which was mainly made in Middle Asia. Second, the red jewels on the right protrusion are garnets, which are commonly found in Eastern Europe. Thus, this dagger almost certainly was imported into Silla along the Silk Road. The dagger is proof of the vigorous exchange and communication Silla maintained with other parts of the world.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR3: Monument to the Martyrdom of Lee Chadon
stories.audioTitle: Execution Site and a Rain of Flowers
stories.script: Execution Site and a Rain of Flowers  This is the Monument to the Martyrdom of Ichadon made in the 6th century. Ichadon contributed to the propagation of Buddhism throughout the Silla kingdom. Just as early Christians were persecuted for their beliefs, it was initially difficult for Buddhism to gain acceptance in Silla.  When Buddhism was first introduced to Silla, the provincial nobility persecuted Buddhists with the aim of preserving their own folk religion. Nevertheless, Ichadon built a Buddhist temple and was subsequently executed. At the moment of his death, he predicted that a miracle from Buddha would occur and became a martyr for Buddhism.  In front of the monument, there is a sculpture depicting the martyrdom of Ichadon. Let’s have a look. Can you see his resolute expression? Instead of red blood, the sculpture shows white blood rising up to the sky. The wave pattern under his feet symbolizes the earth itself shaking and mourning his death. The rain of flowers falling from heaven honors his noble sacrifice.   Deeply moved by the martyrdom of Ichadon, the people of Silla started to accept Buddhism as a valid religion. This is how Buddhism became the national religion of Silla, and even today Buddhism remains one of the most popular religions in Korea.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR3: Human Face Roof Tile
stories.script: The Smile of Silla  [Narration] The first exhibit in the Silla Art Gallery is ‘the Smile of Silla’. If you look around downtown Gyeongju, you will see this face everywhere. How do you think this small, broken figurine became a famous symbol of Silla?  [Visitor] Was it made by a famous artist from the Silla kingdom?  [Narration] Maybe. But there’s no information about who made it, because it is just a common earthen roof tile. It was meant to be a building material, not a piece of art.  [Visitor] Then it must have come from a very famous building, like the Hanging Gardens of Babylon for example.  [Narration] That is interesting reasoning. However, this roof tile is famous for its face design, rather than for where it came from. Korean traditional roof tiles were usually decorated with lotus patterns, so the face design is very rare.  [Visitor] I see. In ancient Europe, faces of saints or devils are popular in architectural decoration. But smiling faces are rarely found. How interesting!  [Narration] Look at the face on the roof tile and you will understand why it has received so much attention. The smile of this Silla woman has a pure, natural beauty. Elongated eyes, a round nose and a mysterious demure smile… it can be compared to the smile of Mona Lisa!

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR3: Chaljubongi
stories.script: Chaljubongi, the Treasure of Treasures  These four metal plates were found under the pole of the pagoda. Originally, they formed a metal box joined by hinges. Now they are separate pieces. Can you guess what the box was for?  It was to hold the Buddha’s sarira. Cremation is a Buddhist funeral rite. After the cremation of a Buddha, or a person who had attained enlightenment, small crystalline fragments remained in the ashes. These rare relics, known as sariras, are kept in important temples in a box inside the pagoda. Christians have similar rituals to preserve the bodies of saints in churches.  This box has additional historic value. Three of the four plates are inscribed with records detailing the history of the pagoda. The nine-story, 80-meter-high structure was the tallest wooden pagoda in Korean history. Unfortunately, the original structure was burnt down by Mongol invaders in 1238. However, thanks to the excavation of Chaljubongi, we can clearly identify detailed information about exactly when, how, and by whom the pagoda was constructed and repaired.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR4: Miniature of Gyeongju Downtown
stories.script: The Planned City of Seorabeol  [Narration] Now, shall we look around Gyeongju as it was 1,300 years ago? Gyeongju, the capital of Silla, was a flourishing city and may have been comparable to the ancient cities of Constantinople, Baghdad and Chang’an. Well, what do you notice first?  [Visitor] The houses look identical. They are all single-storied and have roofs of the same color.  [Narration] Yes, you are right. All the houses have tiled roofs. During the Three Kingdoms Period, tile-roofed houses were built all over the Korean Peninsula. Did you notice that the houses are arranged in rows and form a grid pattern? This is because Gyeongju was a well-planned city. According to legend, the people of Gyeongju didn’t need an umbrella when it rained, as they were sheltered by the eaves of the houses. It was like walking under the arcades of Bologna.  [Visitor] Where is the palace by the way? I can’t find it. The buildings all look so similar.  [Narration] Do you see the crescent-shaped piece of land near the river? It is called Wolseong, meaning moon-shaped palace. Now, try to find the main street that runs from north to south. In China and Korea, it was common to have a wide road leading to the entrance of the palace. The biggest palace in Seoul, Gyeongbok Palace, also has a broad street leading to its main gate. Also, you can see there is a river to the south which functions as a natural moat.  [Visitor] What is the towering building on the right? The palace consists only of single story buildings, but that one is as tall as the spire of a cathedral.  [Narration] That building was also built by order of the king. It is the biggest temple of Silla and the top of the building is the temple’s pagoda. Buddhism was the national religion of Silla and many temples were built by royal command.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR4: The Tombstone of King Munmu
stories.audioTitle: Live Forever to Protect My Country
stories.script: Live Forever to Protect My Country  What do you think this broken rock is? If you take a closer look, you will see that it is a monument with inscriptions on the surface. The monument was erected to pay tribute to a Silla king Munmu and his great achievements. In ancient Korea, there were three kingdoms, including Silla. The king ended the long-standing conflict between the three kingdoms and united the Peninsula.  In accordance with his will, no tomb was built for King Munmu in Gyeongju. King Munmu had always worried about Japanese invaders crossing the East Sea and terrorizing Silla, so in his will he ordered that his body be cremated and his ashes scattered over the East Sea so that he could become a dragon and defend Silla forever. His wishes were respected, and a large rocky island off the coast near Gyeongju is regarded as his tomb.  His tombstone was erected in a temple in Gyeongju. The temple was built to honor and gain favor with Buddha, in order that Silla might be victorious in the war immediately preceding unification. The temple held great meaning for the king, and thus his tombstone was appropriately placed there.  On the front side of this tombstone, King Munmu’s achievements and the process of the unification of three kingdoms are described. On the back are inscribed the king’s will and eulogies. The tombstone in front of you is the lower half of the original one. The original tombstone was broken into two and the upper half remained missing until recently. But the missing upper half was discovered in 2009 and is currently under preservation process which will hopefully be completed soon.

stories.title: Silla History GalleryR4: Four Guardian Kings of Nogyu Temple
stories.audioTitle: Heavenly Guardian Kings who Protected Silla
stories.script: Heavenly Guardian Kings who Protected Silla  [Narration] These pieces are bricks depicting the Buddhist Heavenly Guardians, which are similar to guardian angels in Christianity. Do you see the devils under the guardians? The Buddhist Guardians were traditionally carved at the entrance to temples and served as gatekeepers.  [Visitor] But why are they in fragments?  [Narration] The bricks were found smashed into 200 small pieces and they remained that way for many years. The lower half of the body was excavated in 1936, but the upper part was only discovered 70 years later. Because several different excavation teams had worked on the project over many years, the fragments had been kept in five different institutes separately. But in 2009, they were finally assembled and a special exhibition was held to showcase the artifact. There is a picture of it in the middle.  [Visitor] Wow, even though it’s broken, it’s still very beautiful. I hope the missing parts are found soon.  [Narration] I agree. You can imagine the strong heavenly guardians bringing comfort to the people of Silla. People suffered during the long drawn-out wars and Buddhism provided relief and spiritual sanctuary. Just as Europeans fought for their nations buoyed by their Christian beliefs, the people of Silla united and defended their kingdom supported by Buddhism.   [Visitor] I understand. These heavenly guardians symbolized the population’s hope and desire for peace.  [Narration] Yes, they did. Even today, there are still many Buddhist temple sites and remnants of Buddhist statues and pagodas in the Gyeongju area. Most of them were built for the purpose of praying for peace and comfort.

stories.title: Silla Art Gallery 1F: Buddha and Buddihst Saints
stories.audioTitle: The World of Buddha Statues- Buddha and Buddhist Saints
stories.script: The World of Buddha Statues- Buddha and Buddhist Saints  Before walking into the next big exhibition room, let’s visit the small room on the right. The small statues in this room will help you to understand and appreciate the variety and symbolism of Buddha statues from the Silla kingdom.   These Buddhist saints practice the teachings of Buddha and lead people, and can be understood as a similar concept to the twelve apostles of Jesus. They are usually wearing jeweled crowns and accessories such as bracelets and brooches. To encourage a sense of familiarity and intimacy, they look more like humans than Buddha.   You will see many different statues of Buddha in different poses. ‘Buddha’ means an ‘enlightened one’. Unlike the monotheistic God of the Christian religion, in Buddhism any enlightened person can be a Buddha. Therefore, there are many different Buddhas. For example, there is a Buddha whose role is to guide people to heaven and a Buddha who cures disease and ignorance.  The four Buddhas in the glass case on the right are known as the VairocanaBuddhas, who symbolize the truths of Buddhism. The identifying characteristic of the VairocanaBuddhas is their hand gesture. The Buddha holds an index finger with the other hand, which signifies that foolishness and enlightenment come from the same root.   The statues in the glass case by the entrance are of Buddha and the Buddhist saints together. Of these, the small broken statue is the most famous one. They are standing together surrounded by the Buddha’s halo.   On the right is a statue in a unique pose. The Buddha is sitting on a lotus-shaped throne, with the right leg resting on the left knee. The right hand is placed on the chin. Doesn’t it bear a resemblance to Auguste Rodin’s ‘The Thinker’? Both depict a man in sober meditation.

stories.title: Silla Art Gallery 1F: Medicine Buddha (Bhaisajyanguru Buddha)
stories.script: This room is filled with tall statues of Buddha. Buddhism was the national religion of the Silla kingdom, and Buddha statues of varying sizes were crafted throughout the years. Statues of Buddha and temple architecture were a major part of Silla’s artistic tradition.  This Buddha statue in particular is aesthetically outstanding and one of the most famous Buddhist relics from the Silla kingdom. It is designated as a National Treasure of Korea. Let’s look at it in detail. The well-shaped body under the thin robe gives an impression of weight and solidity and the solemn face expresses quiet dignity.  The copper statue was originally gold-plated, a symbolic technique designed to represent the golden light of Buddha. As time passed, the gold plating eroded away and now only rusty copper remains.   The statue is of the Medicine Buddha, the deity who cures the illnesses and ignorance of humans. The hands are now missing, but they were supposed to have held a small earthenware jar containing medicines.

stories.title: Silla Art Gallery 2F: Ridge-end Ornament Tile
stories.audioTitle: Hwangnyong Temple with Golden Guardian Dragon
stories.script: Hwangnyong Temple with Golden Guardian Dragon  [Narration] What do you think this huge vertical structure is? Any guesses?  [Visitor] Well, this is the Hall of Hwangnyong Temple, so it must be something related to the temple, right? Is that a statue in the temple yard? It looks like an abstract sculpture.  [Narration] This is called a chimi (mangsae), which means a ridge-end ornament tile. It was originally on the corner of the roof at the main hall of Hwangnyong Temple. The dovetail design is believed to keep evil spirits away, just like the gargoyles of gothic cathedrals in the Middle Ages.  [Visitor] Awesome! But isn’t it too big to put on the roof? It’s huge!  [Narration] Hwangnyong Temple was the biggest temple in Silla, so its main hall was huge. This tile is famous for being the biggest and most brilliant ridge-end ornament tile made during the Three Kingdoms Period. And it has another interesting feature. Take a look at the back of the tile and tell me what you see.  [Visitor] Oh, the faces! How wonderful!  [Narration] Yes, you are right. Small, smiling faces are hidden there as if playing hide-and-seek. You can see the passion and delicacy of Silla artisans in the intricate details of the tile.

stories.title: Silla Art Gallery 2F: Wooden Pagoda of Hwangnyongsa Temple
stories.audioTitle: Wooden Pagoda of Hwangnyongsa Temple, the Nine-storied Guardian against Invasion by the Nine Neighboring Nations
stories.script: Wooden Pagoda of Hwangnyongsa Temple, the Nine-storied Guardian against Invasion by the Nine Neighboring Nations  This miniature is a replica of Hwangnyongsa Temple, which was the largest Buddhist temple of Silla. The lofty tower looking down over the temple is quite impressive. Hwangnyongsa Temple was built to protect and defend the nation using the power of Buddha. There is a legend about the construction of the temple. Whilst builders were working on a palace extension project, a golden dragon appeared from heaven. The king considered the appearance a sign from Buddha and ordered the buildings to be reconstructed as a temple. The golden dragon became known as the protective guardian spirit of the kingdom, keeping it safe from invasion. ‘Hwangnyong’ means ‘golden dragon’, so the name of the temple is also derived from the story.  The most significant structure of the temple is definitely the central pagoda. The nine-story wooden pagoda had outstanding architectural and artistic value. This tall, splendid pagoda was constructed to protect Silla against invasion by any one of its nine neighboring countries. Standing 80 meters in height, the pagoda was visible from all over Gyeongju. Even with modern technology, it would not be easy to build an 80-meter-high wooden pagoda strong enough to sustain its own weight and withstand strong winds, so this tower was an advanced architectural triumph.  According to a legend, Silla asked its neighboring countries for carpenters to help build the pagoda. A particular carpenter decided to work on the project, but during the night following his decision, he dreamt about the collapse of his own country. When he awoke from his dream, he refused to continue working on the Silla pagoda. Suddenly, the heavens and the earth shook and trembled, and an old monk and a strong man suddenly appeared. They built the columns of the pagoda and, just as suddenly, disappeared. The carpenter realized that finishing the pagoda was his destiny, and so he completed the project.  Unfortunately, we can’t see the original wooden pagoda now because it was burnt down during the Mongol Invasion in 1238.

stories.title: Wolji Hall: Miniature of the Wolji Pond
stories.audioTitle: Wolji Pond, the Fancy Pond of the Crown Prince
stories.script: Wolji Pond, the Fancy Pond of the Crown Prince  Wolji Pond was an artificial pond in the palace of the Crown Prince. The pond was built in the golden days of Silla, right after the unification of the three kingdoms. It was constructed in the grounds where open-air banquets for foreign envoys and nobles were held.   Korean traditional architecture placed great emphasis on harmony with nature. Buildings were designed and arranged to complement the beauty of the natural environment. Although Wolji Pond was an artificial pond, it was designed to look natural. Interestingly, this pond was constructed to remind one of the ocean. The shape of the pond was meandering, and a small islet was made in the pond. Given its shape and the presence of the islet, the other end of the pond was invisible, which led observers of the scene to feel as if they were looking at the ocean.  Furthermore, the garden surrounding Wolji Pond followed the tenets of Taoism, an East Asian philosophy that espouses withdrawal from reality and values meditative, peaceful environments. The twelve peaks around the pond were symbols of Taoist theology.   The site of this pond is located near the museum. We recommend you pay it a visit and spend some time there. You can see the classical grace of Silla, and the view at night is especially beautiful.

stories.title: Wolji Hall: Wooden Boat
stories.audioTitle: Rebirth of Silla Boat - Wooden Boat Discovered in Anap Pond
stories.script: Rebirth of Silla Boat - Wooden Boat Discovered in Anap Pond  The wooden boat in the middle of the exhibition hall was recovered from Anap Pond. The pond was large enough to accommodate the boats of Silla nobles for whom boating was a popular leisure activity.   But how was the boat preserved in such good condition? When Anap Pond was excavated, the water was drained from the pond. Many treasures had been well preserved in the oxygen-free mud layer at the bottom. This wooden boat was one of them.   Before the boat could be displayed here, there were many complications to overcome. The boat was found in an upturned position in the mud. Because it had been underwater for such a long time, the boat’s frame had become as soft as sponge. The excavation team struggled to find a way to remove it safely without damaging the relic. It was important to protect the boat from drying out and disintegrating. After much planning, the team disassembled the boat into three parts, covered each with wet cloth, and successfully extracted them from the mud.  The restoration process did not become easier once the boat had been moved to the museum. In order to be exhibited, the softened wooden boat needed to be restored to its original state. A chemical treatment process was applied in an underground warehouse to harden the timber. It took almost nine years – as many years as it took for the dust and soot to be stripped away from Michelangelo’s painting in the Sistine Chapel.

stories.title: Wolji Hall: Wooden Document
stories.audioTitle: Wooden Document, an Alternative to Paper
stories.script: Wooden Document, an Alternative to Paper  The relic on the steps to the second floor is a type of note pad from the Silla kingdom. Thin, small pieces of wood were used to write on instead of paper.  Wood wasn’t used for writing simply because there was no paper. As we know, paper was first invented in China, and Silla, being geographically close to China, began to use paper hundreds of years earlier than Europe. However, paper was a luxury in those times and so people used wood to write memos. Wood was also practical to reuse after sanding to erase the text.  The content of the memos is simple but varied and supplies valuable information about the daily lives of the people of Silla. For example, the names of the palace gates are written on wooden fragments of key rings. There are also “time cards” of the palace guards. By combining these pieces of information, we can glean an understanding of how palace security was managed.  There are also wooden pieces inscribed with lists of medicinal plants and prescriptions. From this information, we know how knowledgeable the pharmacists of Silla were. There are other pieces which record the names of fermented foods and their dates of production. Recording the date was crucial to knowing exactly when a food would be ready to eat. These notes provide information about the diet and food preparation methods of the time.

stories.title: Wolji Hall: Gilt-bronze Dragon Head Statue, Bronze Spoon and Other Relics
stories.audioTitle: Metal Craft Found from Anap Pond, Bountiful Life of the Royal Family
stories.script: Metal Craft Found from Anap Pond, Bountiful Life of the Royal Family  These exhibits on the second floor of Anapji Hall are all metal-crafted objects that belonged to members of the Silla royal family. Most of the relics exhibited in museums were recovered from tombs but these from Anap Pond were designed for daily use.  Let’s look at the tableware first. The hollow bowl with a lid was used as a rice bowl. The same small characters engraved on the bottom of the bowl and inside the lid indicate a matching set. The objects used by the royal family were much more detailed than those used by commoners.   Look at the spoons in the glass case on the right. How did people eat their meals with such large utensils? In fact, these were used as ladles to serve food out of large dishes.  Spoons like these have been found in Japan. A boxed set of ten Silla spoons found in Japan indicates that Silla exported goods there.  Stepping to the right, you will see various relics that once decorated Silla’s palaces. The king’s chair is decorated with carvings of dragon heads with bulging eyeballs and curved fangs. The dragon and the phoenix were the traditional symbols of the king in Korea, therefore many dragon and phoenix motifs would have been seen in palace interiors.

stories.title: Wolji Hall: Gilt-bronze Snuffers
stories.audioTitle: What was the Gilt-bronze Snuffer of Anap Pond used for
stories.script: What was the Gilt-bronze Snuffer of Anap Pond used for  [Narration] This is a gilt bronze candle snuffer that was used by the Silla royal family. It is too big to hold in one hand, and looks quite different to a modern candle snuffer.  [Visitor] Yes, it looks more like scissors.  [Narration] Indeed. In a way, this functioned as a scissors. Silla peoples used it to trim the wick of a candle. They cut off the burned part of the wick with this snuffer and the cut wick fell onto the ice cream scoop-like part of it.   [Visitor] Interesting! They handled candles with much care.  [Narration] It is probably because the candles were rare. Not many candles were produced, and even in Europe candles were expensive and only found in palaces and famous churches in those days.

stories.title: Wolji Hall: Gilt-bronze Buddha Triad
stories.audioTitle: Buddha Triad Holding the Wishes of the Royal Family
stories.script: Buddha Triad Holding the Wishes of the Royal Family  These cast metal pieces are also statues of Buddha. The flat gilt-bronze pieces were made throughout East Asia. This one, from Anap Pond, has been praised for its artistic value.   The statues were delicately made. First, a wax mold was crafted and then covered with mud and dried. Then the mold was heated to melt and remove the wax, leaving a hard clay cast. Molten bronze was then poured into the cast. This complicated procedure produced sculptures of high quality, compared to the Japanese and Chinese method of hammering metal plates. You can see the details up close.   As you can see, many statues of Buddha were excavated from Anap Pond, but the one in the middle is the only complete piece among them. Its discovery implies that other Buddha triads would also have been made in a similarly delicate manner. The Buddha in the middle of the triad has a toned body and a solemn facial expression. The two disciples at Buddha’s sides are very attractive, twisting at the waist.   Why do you think these triads were found in the palace garden and not at a temple site? Just as Europeans had chapels inside palaces, the Silla palace had a Buddhist sanctum, and it is thought that the triads were decorative. Their function may have been to remind the royal family to pray for the peace of the nation.

stories.title: Wolji Hall: Animal Bones
stories.script: A Zoo in Silla  [Narration] The last exhibition consists of animal bones from Anap Pond. Four hundred and thirty-four pieces of bone from livestock and wild animals such as mountain goats and boars were found there.  [Visitor] Shouldn’t they be kept in the Natural History Museum?  [Narration] Normally, yes. But there is a reason for displaying the bones here. They are evidence of the lavish lifestyle enjoyed by the nobility of Silla.  [Visitor] Animal bones and a lavish lifestyle… I don’t get it.  [Narration] According to historical records, the nobles of Silla kept imported and wild birds and animals here. The European nobility of the Middle Ages also collected rare animals.   [Visitor] It sounds like they raised very expensive pets.  [Narration] It would be more accurate to say that they created a kind of zoo near Anap Pond because the animals were mainly there to be seen and admired. The king of Silla used the animals to show off his wealth at banquets when nobles and foreign envoys were in attendance.  [Visitor] It seems strange that even cows and pigs were displayed in this way.  [Narration] Some of them were for eating of course. One of the wooden memos records a menu of fermented stingray, pig and roe deer. Such a varied diet was only available to the wealthy nobility and royalty.

stories.title: Outdoor Exhibition: Divine Bell of King Seongdeok
stories.script: The Sound of Devotion  The huge Divine Bell of King Seongdeok hanging outside the museum was made in 771. The bell was commissioned by King Seongdeok to commemorate his father, and took almost 20 years to make.  The bell is famous for its beautiful design and intricate patterns. The flying angel design on the surface is particularly beautiful. Look at the praying angel under the winds of heaven. His robes are fluttering in the wind. Silla people believed that angels rode on clouds in the sky, and on the bell the angel is depicted wrapped in a flower-shaped cloud. The king’s devotion to his father is manifested in this masterpiece of the 8th century.  The deep, full sound of the bell is internationally recognized for its originality. The sound you hear through the museum speaker system comes from this divine bell. Scientists have studied the bell in an attempt to replicate the beautiful sound quality, but so far it has proved impossible to imitate, even with modern technological methods.  The bell was used differently from western bells. In the west, bells are normally found at the top of church spires or bell towers to direct the sound towards the heavens. This bell was hung low, almost touching the ground, to spread the sound low and wide. It is believed to reflect the horizontal world view of Buddhism, the national religion of Silla.

stories.title: Outdoor Exhibition: Buddha Statues without Heads
stories.script: Unfortunate Buddha Statues  [Narration] Leaving the stone pagodas behind, let’s move to the back of the museum. There are tens of stone Buddhas standing in a line. After the unification of the three kingdoms, many stone Buddhas were made.  [Visitor] None of these stone Buddhas have heads.   [Narration] That’s true, and they were found in ponds, not in Buddhist sanctuaries.   [Visitor] I don’t suppose they were made without heads.  [Narration] Of course not. They were originally complete, but at some point their heads were removed. Why do you think this happened? Any guesses?  [Boy Student] Well, an earthquake could have done the damage, or maybe they were damaged during a war.   [Narration] Possibly, but historians believe that they were most likely vandalized by those in power during the 14th century. The governing group of the Korean Peninsula at that time was strongly influenced by Chinese Confucianism. They persecuted Buddhists and suppressed the Buddhist religion, which had been established in Korea for over 1,000 years. They destroyed many Buddhist temples and statues.  [Boy Student] It seems impossible to have peacefully co-existing religions, no matter where you are in the world.  [Narration] I agree. The new ruling group seized power in a coup. So they might have thought that introduction of a new belief system would help strengthen their political legitimacy.

stories.title: Outdoor Exhibition: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Goseon Temple and Other Relics
stories.audioTitle: Stone Pagoda, Beautiful Mercy of Buddha
stories.script: Stone Pagoda, Beautiful Mercy of Buddha  A pair of pagodas stands outside the Archaeology Hall. These are a reproduction of the pagodas from Bulguk Temple, one of the most famous tourist destinations in Gyeongju. The stone pagodas in front of us represent the Buddhist pagodas of the Silla Kingdom.  The purpose of the pagodas differs from that of western bell towers. During the Middle Ages, Europeans built bell towers as lookouts or to be closer to heaven. Buddhist pagodas, however, were made to enshrine the sariras of Buddha, so India was the first country to establish these types of pagodas. The pagodas in India resemble big upside-down bowls, whilst the towers of East Asia look like stacked cubes. The material used to construct the pagodas differs by region: mud brick in China, wood in Japan and stone in Korea.  Wooden pagodas were initially popular in Silla, but because of construction difficulties and their susceptibility to fire damage, they were superseded by stone pagodas. From the late 7th century onwards, stone pagodas were built with the same design and construction methods as the original wooden pagodas.

stories.title: Gyeongju National Museum
stories.audioTitle: Time capsule holding secrets from thousands of years ago
stories.script: Gyeongju is often described as an “open-air museum.” But some of its most important artifacts are showcased at Gyeongju National Museum. It houses genuine artifacts of all kinds. When you arrive at the courtyard, you will be welcomed by the genuine “Bell of King Seongdeok.” The bell has an enormous presence, fitting its designation as National Treasure No. 29. The Bell of King Seongdeok is also known as the “Emile Bell.” Do you think they really put a baby in the molten iron when they created the bell? Just like the legend tells us? Scholars have differing opinions. However, one thing is clear. More than 1300 years ago, engineers created an iron bell weighing at least 20 tons without a single air bubble inside. Everyone agrees that the technological expertise of Shilla engineers was beyond whatever was thought possible at the time. The sound of the bell proves their astonishing technology when it is broadcasted every 20 minutes. Although the museum does not physically hit the Bell for preservation purposes, the recorded sound of the bell still sounds extremely striking.   When you step inside the Museum, you will see a historical timeline of the Shilla Kingdom. Next to the timeline is a copy of the Petrogplyphs of Bangudae Terrace. Petroglyphs drawn on the rock faces thousands of years ago create a mystical atmosphere. The everyday lives of locals during the three kingdoms period or during the prehistoric era might have been similar to what it is today. What do you think? They might have been doing what we do today.  Gyeongju National Museum gives you a chance to feel connected with the glorious history and legacy of our ancestors. It is well worth your time, even if you have to spend a full day to see everything the Museum has to offer. The giant time capsule containing artifacts and stories accrued over thousands of years in Gyeongju is waiting for you with open arms.

stories.title: Gallery R1: Paleolithic Artifacts
stories.audioTitle: Cutting Edge Hunting Methods of the Prehistoric Age
stories.script: Cutting Edge Hunting Methods of the Prehistoric Age  Welcome to Gimhae National Museum. The first relics you will see are hunting tools from the Prehistoric Age. Because human culture changed along with the pace of tool development, tools had a significant effect on civilization. Among them, the development of hunting tools was a decisive factor in the survival of mankind and the development of civilizations.   You can see here the progression of hunting technology throughout the Prehistoric Age. Let’s start from the exhibits on the right. These are primitive tools such as stones for chopping and pointed stones. On the left are arrowheads and they were advanced weapons of the Neolithic Age.  People of the Paleolithic Age initially hunted animals using simple wooden and stone tools. They then began to make spears, which made hunting safer. Tool development accelerated around about 10,000 B.C., following the end of the Ice Age.   Mammals such as mammoth and reindeer were well adapted to cold climates and moved to the north, while smaller animals such as foxes and rabbits thrived. The proliferation of these small, fast animals prompted the development of long range weapons such as bows and arrows.  Now let’s look at the piece of earthenware in the glass case behind you. The Neolithic artwork is inscribed with a boar motif and expresses a desire for successful boar hunting expeditions.  Since the agricultural practices of the time were primitive at best, food supply primarily depended on the success of a hunt. Neolithic drawings of animals in caves or motifs on pottery expressed a desire for successful hunting. Murals discovered in Lascaux in France and Altamira in Spain were motivated by the same desires.

stories.title: Gallery R1: Stone Grinding Pestle&Saddle Quern
stories.audioTitle: A Warm-hearted Table of the Neolithic Age
stories.script: A Warm-hearted Table of the Neolithic Age  The exhibits in this glass case offer an explanation of the eating habits of the Neolithic people. The quern, which is shaped like an ironing board, and the baguette-shaped pestle were particularly significant tools of the Neolithic Age. They were used to shell or grind nuts such as acorns. Acorn cookies and jelly were staple foods of the Neolithic people who inhabited the Korean Peninsula.   Following the invention of ground stone tools, the diet of Neolithic people diversified. Since ground tools were more effective than the chipped stone tools of the Paleolithic Age, Neolithic people could accomplish more complex tasks. Various kinds of earthenware were produced in order to cook and store food.   These sudden changes were the result of a transition from a nomadic to a sedentary lifestyle. The population increased dramatically around 6,000 years B.C and Neolithic people began to settle down in groups. During the early period of the Neolithic Age, agriculture was non-existent, and so people still lived by hunting and gathering. As the groups of people developed into villages and communities, they were collectively able to gather large quantities of fruits and grains.

stories.title: Gallery R1: Fishing Net Sinkers, Bone Fishhooks
stories.audioTitle: Waves of Change and a Drawn Net
stories.script: Waves of Change and a Drawn Net  [Narration]  Thousands of years ago, grains and meat were not the only sources of food for Neolithic people. As Gimhae was surrounded by rivers and the sea, the people who inhabited this region enjoyed a diet supplemented with virtually every type of fish and marine food.  [Tourist]  Every type of fish and marine food! During the Neolithic Age! That must be an exaggeration.  [Narration]  No, not at all! The remains of fish, dolphins and even seals were identified from food waste heaps dating from the Neolithic Age.   [Tourist]  It’s funny that we have learned about ancient people from their trash.  [Narration]  Such trash heaps have revealed information about the diet of the Neolithic people, and also the fishing methods they employed. These net sinkers and bone fishhooks were found in food waste heaps as well.  [Tourist]  Are those fishhooks that I can see on the right? Sometimes I go fishing myself, so although they look clumsy I can see that they would work!    [Narration]  Yes. By using the divided fishhooks shown at the top, even large fish such as tuna and shark could be caught. Net fishing has also been in use from as long as 3,000 years ago. Just as communities of people worked together to gather food, the scale of fishing increased by their working together cooperatively. The artifact on your left is a weight. As we saw earlier, it was attached to a net to help it sink so that fish could not escape.  [Tourist]  Neolithic people were more intelligent than I thought.   [Narration]  They were intelligent. Although these artifacts are from the Neolithic Age, they are not primitive at all. They are functionally comparable to the modern fishing equipment used today. Now you know that the assertion that Neolithic people enjoyed all kinds of marine foods is not an exaggeration!

stories.title: Gallery R1: Polished Stone Daggers
stories.script: The Birth of the Farmers  [Narration]  Now we will take a look at the crescent-shaped stone knives. These knives were used for farming. The Neolithic people ground and sharpened the stones to cut the ears of grain. In fact, they were designed to remove and separate every grain.  [Tourist]  They remind me of Millet’s painting, The Gleaners. The women in the painting were so focused on removing every precious grain. By the way, what are these holes in the middle?  [Narration]  The two holes were threaded with string to form a handle for holding the knife securely.    During the Bronze Age, many other farming tools were employed besides crescent-shaped stone knives. Wooden and stone tools were generally used until they were superseded by bronze and iron farming tools. As farming techniques developed, tools became more functional and elaborate.  Let’s look at some of the other tools.

stories.title: Gallery R1: Crescent-shaped Stone Knives
stories.audioTitle: The Best Example of Stone-Craft, Polished Stone Daggers
stories.script: The Best Example of Stone-Craft, Polished Stone Daggers  [Narration]  These shiny, white, stone daggers are from the Bronze Age. It is difficult to believe that Bronze Age people produced such delicate and elaborate artwork.  [Tourist]  Wow, they’re fabulous! They also exude a sense of mystery. I’d like to have one in my living room.  [Narration]  How did you know that they were decorative daggers?  [Tourist]  Do you mean that Bronze Age people were interested in interior decoration? That’s unbelievable!  [Narration]  Ah, I mean that the daggers were designed to decorate tombs, not houses. Just like the pottery we saw earlier, these daggers were funerary goods used to signify the power of the deceased.   [Tourist]  Aha, I see. They remind me of the medieval European nobility who used to decorate their houses with swords and armor. But you said that these were from the Bronze Age. Why didn’t they make them with bronze? Bronze daggers would surely have been more prestigious.  [Narration]  That’s a good question. This style of stone dagger was only produced in the southern part of the Korean Peninsula. Since bronze manufacturing technology first developed in the northern part of the peninsula, it took a long time for the technique to spread south. Daggers were made of stone until they were superseded by the more popular bronze. Thus this polished stone dagger is regarded as a unique artifact that is only found in the south of the Korean Peninsula.

stories.title: Gallery R2: Korean Bronze Daggers
stories.script: Korean Bronze Daggers  [Narration]  Let us look at some Korean bronze ware now. The room exhibits artifacts from the Korean Bronze Age and bronze swords are the most representative relics of the time. First, I’d like to draw your attention to the violin-shaped sword on your left. This sword was made in the northern part of the peninsula, in what is now China, during the Early Bronze Age.   [Visitor]  Um, I am confused. Do you mean it is from China?  [Narration]  Not exactly. During the Bronze Age, Korea was so powerful that it occupied some parts of mainland China where this sword was made.   [Visitor]  But geographically, didn’t Chinese techniques and styles influence Korean Bronze ware, just like they influenced the earthenware of the Neolithic Age?   [Narration]  No, they didn’t. Chinese Bronze swords were constructed as a single piece, whereas the blade and the hilt of Korean Bronze swords were constructed separately. You can see this feature on the bottom of the sword.  [Visitor]  Ah, I see. This sword looks unique but I doubt it’s very useful, is it?  [Narration]  Ah, that is because the sword was not designed to serve a practical purpose. In the Bronze Age, powerful men carried these swords at their sides as a symbol of power. That’s why these swords were so impressively crafted. By comparison, Korean bronze swords made in the Late Bronze Age were more practical. You can see some examples of these on the right. They have sharper and straighter blades.

stories.title: Gallery R2: Brightening the Dawn of Gaya
stories.script: Brightening the Dawn of Gaya  [Narration]  The rise of Gaya was not only the result of exploiting an abundance of iron ore and establishing a prominent trade port. Rather, the splendid history of Gaya was the work of its people.  [Tourist]  Was this Gimhae region invaded or conquered?  [Narration]  No. During the late 2nd century B.C., people from the north migrated here after the collapse of their kingdom. Because they brought with them their own flourishing bronze culture, technology and products, Gaya endured for 600 years and successfully maintained a diverse, vibrant culture. In a way, similarities exist between Gaya’s cultural development and the classical scholars that became the driving force of the Italian Renaissance after the fall of Constantinople.  [Tourist]  Who were the people from the north? Were they Chinese? Was Gaya founded by Chinese people?  [Narration]  No, they weren’t. The people were survivors from the first kingdom in Korea called Gojoseon. Gojoseon was a powerful nation with a large territory that extended beyond the Korean Peninsula and into some regions of what is now China.   [Tourist]  I see. So you mean that these artifacts from the north were still ‘made in Korea’, right?   [Narration]  Yes, that’s right. This crown ornament, iron sword and writing brush were much more advanced than those being produced in the south at that time. For example, the brush provides evidence that a written language was in use. In addition, the iron sword and scabbard displayed on the front wall were elegantly designed.

stories.title: Gallery R2: Rule the World with Light
stories.script: Rule the World with Light  [Narration]  The artifact we can see here is a bronze mirror.   The bronze mirrors of the time were rather more symbolic than practical although they could serve the same functional purpose as modern mirrors. The people of Gaya believed that these round, shiny mirrors were imbued with the mystical power of the sun. They were usually possessed by noblemen and signified their authority.  [Tourist]  How can this be a mirror? I can only see designs on the surface.  [Narration]  Obviously, what we are seeing here is the back of the mirror. The backs of the mirrors were adorned with various patterns, paintings and scripts.   [Tourist]  What about the front of the mirror? Is it made of glass like modern mirrors?  [Narration]  No, no. Just like in ancient western countries, the people of Gaya polished thick plates of copper or bronze until they became reflective. After a thousand years, the bronze mirror has rusted and is in far less than perfect condition. However, it was originally the color of gold.

stories.title: Gallery R2: International Trade Port
stories.script: International Trade Port, Neuk-do Island  We have finally reached the section containing artifacts from the Iron Age. Korea was influenced by Chinese iron culture during the 3rd and 4th centuries B.C. From the 2nd century B.C., iron manufacturing technology rapidly spread throughout Korea. As a consequence, during the 1st century A.D, ironware was popularly used even in the south of the Korean Peninsula.  On display here is a collection of artifacts representing the lifestyle of the people of Gaya – a bone dagger, an iron ax, and the backbone of a whale among others. These relics were excavated from a small island off the south coast of Korea called Neukdo Island.  Many relics have been found on Neukdo Island. Surprisingly, some of the excavations conducted there have unearthed Chinese pottery, Chinese coins and Japanese earthenware. The artifact in the middle is an example of Japanese earthenware.  Do you know how Chinese and Japanese relics came to be found on Neukdo Island? Neukdo Island was an international trade port connecting the Korean Peninsula with China and Japan. Gaya exported high quality ironware to other countries via sea routes and simultaneously exchanged both culture and goods with different countries.  However, as navigation developed and the scale of sea trade expanded, the small trade port on Neukdo Island was no longer adequate. Gaya required a bigger port to accommodate larger vessels. As the port in south-eastern Gimhae developed, the era of Geumgwan Gaya began. Gimhae enjoyed an advantageous geographic location, sitting on the banks of the second largest river in the Korean Peninsula. The large port in Gimhae accelerated the development of Geumgwan Gaya.

stories.title: Gallery R3: The Foundation of Geumgwan Gaya
stories.script: The Foundation of Geumgwan Gaya  [Narration]  During the 20th century, an unusual incident occurred in Gimhae, the region located in the south-east of the Korean Peninsula. Heavy rains caused a landslide and unearthed a bounty of relics. Over 550 ancient tombs and some 5,000 artifacts were discovered in an area four times the size of a soccer field.   [Tourist]  That’s incredible! Which kingdom did the relics come from?  [Narration]  Considering the characteristics of the relics, historians presume that they belonged to the kings and nobles of the Geumgwan Gaya, as they date from the 1st to the 4th century. The display here consists of artifacts unearthed by the landslide. Many iron swords and spears were found. During that time, iron weapons were a symbol of power; whoever possessed iron dominated their world. Therefore, they could only have belonged to members of the ruling elite.   [Tourist]  I understand. But why did they bury these items in tombs? Did the ruling elite want to flaunt their power even in the afterlife?  [Narration]  Um… In a manner of speaking, yes. It was mainly because people believed that the life they led in this world would continue in the next world. Thus artifacts were buried with the dead in the hopes that the deceased person would maintain his authority and wealth. Ancient Egyptians also believed in the existence of eternal life in the next world and considered a tomb to be the new home of the deceased. The various treasures, including the famous golden mask and crown, excavated from Tutankhamen’s tomb in Egypt are good examples of this practice.  The iron pot displayed at the end on the left comes from the northern part of the Korean Peninsula. It provides evidence that Gaya enhanced its economy and political power by exporting iron and trading with other countries.

stories.title: Gallery R3: Sword with Round Pommel
stories.audioTitle: The Symbol of Authority, a Sword with a Round Pommel
stories.script: The Symbol of Authority, a Sword with a Round Pommel  These swords were excavated from the region formerly occupied by Gaya. Sword manufacturing was considered the epitome of quality metalwork. This sword was manufactured using a special integrated metal technique of Gaya. Only a very few of the highest-ranking members of society possessed this type of sword, which symbolized the authority of Gaya’s ruling elite.  Can you see the leaf pattern on the sword’s hilt? Motifs featuring dragons and phoenixes were also popular decorations for swords with round pommels. These opulent, elegant ornaments emphasized the authority of those who carried them.  The iron has rusted over time, so the sword’s current appearance is not as attractive as it would have been originally. However, it still retains a sense of dignity simply because it was produced by Gaya artisans using the most sophisticated methods available at that time.  This type of sword was manufactured throughout the Korean Peninsula in approximately the 1st century. Thus the same style of sword is commonly found in ancient tombs of kings and queens all over the Korean Peninsula, indicating that they were powerful, symbolic objects.

stories.title: Gallery R3: The New Leader, Dae Gaya
stories.script: The New Leader, Dae Gaya  Let’s now take a look at the relics of Dae Gaya, the rulers of the Gaya Confederacy during its later period. Geumgwan Gaya began to decline after it was attacked by two allied kingdoms during the late 4th and early 5th centuries. The rapidly developing polity of Dae Gaya soon took over Geumgwan Gaya’s position, and became the leader of the confederacy.   Just as the word Dae means ‘great’, the tombs of Dae Gaya kings possessed a profusion of great and luxurious artifacts. The most popular relic is the gilt-bronze crown displayed in the middle. The predominant motif of the crown features blades of grass and lotus buds. This type of crown was mainly found in Dae Gaya, and suggests that there was a strong leader who was deserving of such a crown, just like the king of a kingdom.   Let’s turn around and look at some more artifacts. Can you see the long sword? Although it is rusty, the sword retains dignity. The focal point of the sword is the hilt. If you look closely, you will see a small, delicate, oriental phoenix ornament. The higher the social status of a sword’s owner, the more elaborate the ornamentation became. Thus, mystical animals such as dragons and phoenixes were only used by people of the highest social status. This sword provides further evidence that Dae Gaya was indeed a wealthy country under strong leadership.

stories.title: Gallery R3: Ornaments of Gaya
stories.audioTitle: Fashion to Express Oneself, Ornaments of Gaya
stories.script: Fashion to Express Oneself, Ornaments of Gaya  Now we will learn something about the ornaments of Gaya. In those days, ornaments were not only used for personal beautification, but also to signify authority and to prevent misfortune.   In ancient western societies, similarly, kings and nobles wore extravagant crowns and accessories to accentuate their dignity and signify their authority.   By the 4th century, Gaya ornaments were mostly made of glass beads, crystal or jade. Compared to western jewels such as diamonds and emeralds they may seem humble, but they were rare and precious materials in Korea at that time.  When Gaya was under the influence of its neighboring kingdoms after the 5th century, jewelry made of gold and silver became popular. Many gold ornaments were then produced including gold earrings, rings and crowns.   This gilt-bronze crown is assumed to have been influenced by the style of Silla, a powerful kingdom neighboring Gaya. However, its shape differs from that of a Silla crown. This Gaya gilt-bronze crown possesses a unique beauty all its own. As we have seen, the ornaments of Gaya evolved with the introduction of innovative materials and advances in jewelry-making techniques. Such ornaments accentuated both the body and the social position of the person wearing them.

stories.title: Gallery R3: Crown Ornament
stories.audioTitle: Gaya Disappears in a Golden Flash
stories.script: Gaya Disappears in a Golden Flash  [Narration]  The artifacts we can see here are evidence of Gaya’s exchange with foreign countries. The pendant silver ornaments of the belt and the gold earrings were all made under the influence of Silla, a powerful neighboring kingdom of Gaya. Unfortunately, these luxurious ornaments were made around the time Gaya collapsed due to pressure from its more powerful neighbors.  [Tourist]  How is that? I would have thought that these extravagant ornaments were indicative of a strong, economically wealthy Gaya Confederacy.   [Narration]  I agree, but politically, the confederacy was continually embroiled in conflicts with neighboring countries over territorial expansion.  [Tourist]  I don’t understand. How could they make such luxurious items in the midst of defeat?  [Narration]  Most of the small Gaya polities were absorbed into the Silla kingdom without conflict. They engaged in pragmatic diplomacy and had already been under the cultural and economic influence of Silla for a long time. The ornaments and earthenware produced by those particular Gaya polities were influenced by Silla’s style.  [Tourist]  I see. Were most of the Gaya polities dependent on Silla at that time?  [Narration]  No. While a strong Gaya polity led the confederacy, Gaya experienced political peace. The independent culture of Gaya, represented by its iron industry and unique earthenware, was established during that period. Gaya’s stringed instrument called gayageum is now one of the most popular traditional Korean musical instruments. From this example, you can appreciate the sophistication of Gaya’s culture.

stories.title: Gallery R4: Storage of Gaya
stories.audioTitle: Beyond the Storehouses and Pottery of Gaya
stories.script: Beyond the Storehouses and Pottery of Gaya  [Narration]  Can you see the large jars in the middle of the exhibition room?  [Tourist]  Wow! What’s inside them? They’re huge!  [Narration]  Ha-ha! Follow me and you will find out. Besides those jars, other artifacts pertaining to the lifestyle of Gaya people are displayed in this room. First, let’s see what there is.  [Tourist]  That sounds interesting.  [Narration]  Please walk inside along the path to the right of the jars.  Can you see the pottery vessel resembling a house on the right? This object was made to replicate the storage houses of Gaya. At that time, food was extremely valuable and directly guaranteed survival. The people of Gaya built storage houses above the ground both to keep the stores dry and to prevent intrusion by wild animals looking for food.   [Tourist]  Um, that was wise.  [Narration]  I agree. Now let’s turn around and look at the large jars. These seven jars were made for different purposes. The wide-mouthed jar in the middle was used for storing grains and food. In the corner, there’s a charcoal gray-colored jar with four lugs which was used for holding water or alcohol.  [Tourist]  Hmm… these are all very ordinary. I’ve seen similar objects in other museums.  [Narration]  Only those two are ordinary. The other five jars were used in a very different way. Can you guess how they were used?  [Tourist]  Hmm… Besides food… Were they used to store leather or farming tools?  [Narration]  No, they were used to bury the dead.  [Tourist]  The dead! Why did they bury the dead in food storage jars?   [Narration]  When bodies were simply buried under the ground, they were often dug up and ravaged by animals. The bodies were placed in these jars to protect them.  [Tourist]  I see. Anyway, the people of Gaya appear to have been very wise.  [Narration]  Do you think so? As we can see, the food storage facilities of Gaya are important factors in explaining the ways of life and death of the Gaya people.

stories.title: Gallery R4: Birds, Spirit Messengers
stories.script: Birds, The Spirit Messengers  The earthenware object on the left is unique. The vessel, which resembles a duck, was buried with the deceased in a Gaya tomb.   The people of Gaya believed that birds had a unique ability to travel to the next world. Thus, bird-shaped objects were buried in a tomb because they were believed to escort the dead safely to the next world.   In ancient Andean culture, birds were also recognized as symbols of heaven. The condor, eagle and owl, in particular, were believed to be close to god. Nocturnal birds were thought to be related to death and the afterlife, and were believed to serve as guides on the journey to the next world.  Now let’s look at the artifact on your right. Can you see the iron plate adorned with a decorative bird? A wooden pole was inserted into the plate and it was used for large parades or funeral rites. Just like the duck-shaped pottery, this was also used for the funeral.  Relics featuring birds have been found throughout the world, including Gaya. It is obvious that ancient people considered birds to be special.

stories.title: Gallery R4: Agriculture and Cooking Culture of Gaya
stories.audioTitle: Cultivated Land of Gaya, Iron Agricultural Implements, and Cooking Utensils of Gaya
stories.script: Cultivated Land of Gaya, Iron Agricultural Implements, and Cooking Utensils of Gaya  These are iron farming tools from Gaya dating from the 4th century. From the 1st century B.C., Gaya produced swords and axes using their abundant deposits of iron ore. Iron farming implements enhanced agricultural productivity and thereby facilitated the development of Gaya.  The shovel-shaped farming tool on the right was used to dig channels for water and push the roots of plants into the soil. The next implement is an iron sickle that was used to reap rice. As these iron farming implements developed, the people of Gaya could farm the land with greater ease and efficacy.  So how did the people of Gaya cook and store their harvests? Look at the piece of pottery on the left. This is an earthenware steamer. Koreans have used steamers to cook food for a long, long time and they are still used to cook rice cakes today.   The people of Gaya boiled or steamed their crops in steamers such as this one. Isn’t it surprising that the same cooking equipment we use today was used 1,700 years ago? As we can see, Gaya’s agriculture flourished as a result of both abundant natural resources and advanced technology.

stories.title: Gallery R5: Gaya Pottery
stories.audioTitle: From Soft, Red Pottery To Hard, Grayish-blue Pottery, Gaya Pottery
stories.script: From Soft, Red Pottery To Hard, Grayish-blue Pottery, Gaya Pottery  When people of the Neolithic Age settled down in one place and began farming, they needed vessels to store the grain they produced. Earthenware was invented and made with soil, an obviously common and widely available material. This primitive pottery was “high-tech” at the time.  Gaya pottery generally refers to the popular pottery manufactured in the Gimhae region from the 1st century B.C. to the 7th century A.D. These particular vessels were manufactured between the 4th and 6th centuries.  Take special notice of the color of the pottery. The pieces are mainly red and gray. The different colors were produced using different firing methods. The red pottery in the middle of the glass case was fired outside in an underground kiln. The material used was soft and brittle when moist, but able to withstand high temperatures, so these vessels made ideal cooking pots.  The gray pottery, however, was fired in a cave-shaped kiln at higher temperatures. The temperatures caused the clay particles to bind tightly together, which resulted in hard, durable products. Preventing the influx of oxygen elevated the iron content and increased the depth of color.  As demonstrated here, the earthenware of Gaya evolved due to the advancement of manufacturing techniques.

stories.title: Characters and Symbols of Gaya
stories.script: Characters and Symbols of Gaya  These are pieces of earthenware inscribed with characters and symbols. The pieces at the end on the left in particular are inscribed with various symbols, but nobody has been able to interpret their meaning yet.  Some people insist that these are letters. Due to its vibrant iron industry, Gaya frequently traded with China. Writing brushes and knives used to erase inscriptions from wood have been found at historic Gaya sites dating from the 1st century B.C. It is suggested that the people of Gaya used letters from around that time.  Other people assert that these symbols were inscribed to indicate ownership of the pottery. It is possible that they were used to distinguish people’s earthenware possessions.  The symbols of Gaya remain a mystery today. You might be the first person to solve the mystery and understand their meaning, so please take a close look!

stories.title: Gallery R5: Earthenware Figurines
stories.audioTitle: Lofty and Elegant Individuality – The Beauty of Gaya Pottery 2
stories.script: Lofty and Elegant Individuality: The Beauty of Gaya Pottery 2  Now let’s turn around and see what is displayed on the wall. There is an earthenware figurine shaped like a duck.
