At the end of the alley is “Wonseo-dong Washing Place”, where you can imagine the lives of ordinary people who did the laundry here. Clean water still flows from where it meets the wall of Changdeokgung Palace.

stories.title: Choong Ang High School
stories.audioTitle: School with old history and great tradition
stories.script: School with old history and great tradition  At the end of the hill on Gyedong-gil Road, you will see a western-style stone building which stands out among surrounding hanoks. This is Choong Ang High School that has a history of over 100 years. This historical place is especially popular among foreign tourists because it is famous as the filming site of the Korean TV drama “Winter Sonata”. You can easily see tourists buy pictures of Korean pop stars at nearby shops.    Then, what is it like inside the school? The school, built in the early 20th century, looks like a college campus in foreign countries. It looks quite different from most other Korean high schools that are more box shape. It is said that the building was influenced by western schools in Europe and the U.S.    Unlike the main building in the front, the east and west buildings are made of red bricks. Between the buildings, you can see a small garden with old streetlamps, benches and garden trees, which are hard to find in other high schools. The three buildings have been designated as Historic Sites because the well-preserved buildings are helpful for research on Korea’s architectural style in the early 20th century, which features influences of foreign architectures.   For your information, the school is not open to the public on weekdays so as not to disturb students. Even if it is open for certain hours on the weekends, you should check the opening hours in advance.

stories.title: Bukchon 3rd View
stories.audioTitle: Harmony of hanoks and traditional craft workshops
stories.script: Harmony of hanoks and traditional craft workshops  Bukchon 3rd View is a hanok alley with hanoks on each side of a narrow alley. You cannot see inside most hanoks, as there are people living there. But, there are many famous museums and craft workshops where you can go inside and join experience programs with a small admission fee.      Han Sang-soo Embroidery Museum exhibits colorful embroidery artworks, and Gahoe Museum displays folk paintings, talisman and other folk relics. You can see beautiful traditional ornamental knots at Donglim Knot Craft Workshop or join various traditional craft programs without reservation at Bukchon Traditional Craft Experience Center.   Why are there so many traditional craft workshops in Bukchon? As hanoks began to disappear from the village due to development projects since the late 1960s, the government implemented a policy to preserve hanoks in the 1980s. Also, there were movements to preserve traditional culture. So, the city of Seoul purchased hanoks in the village and leased most of them to traditional craftsmen.   While Bukchon Cultural Center shows the traditional form of hanok, hanoks here feature a modern-style hanok structure of the 1930s, when a lot of small hanoks were built simultaneously. Most craft workshops have preserved their original form, so you can guess what people’s lives were like in the past. You can also join experience programs at these workshops.        At the end of the hanok alley, cross the road to Donmi Pharmacy to go to Bukchon 4th View. With almost 70 years of history, the Pharmacy is also a famous spot in Bukchon.

stories.title: Bukchon 4th View
stories.script: Sea of Hanok roofs  Hanoks in Bukchon look slightly different from typical hanoks. Then what is the difference?    At the fourth spot which is on the hill at 31st Gahoe-dong, you can see the largest cluster of hanoks in the village. Can you see them over the wall? If you can’t, get on the rocks at the base of the left wall. You will discover a sea of hanok roofs covering the hill in soft curves. This is one of the greatest hanok views in the village.   Large hanoks for upper class families of the Joseon Dynasty began to disappear in the 1930s, and they were replaced with smaller hanoks for lower class people, creating the unique view of closely located hanoks.   Among multiple roofs, one house will stand out. It is the House of Yi Jun-gu, a luxury western-style house with a blue roof. Yi’s family used granite brought from Gaeseong, currently a southern city in North Korea, and tiles from France for the walls and roofs. The family apparently spared no expense on their expensive materials. You can guess what it was like to live as the rich in the Joseon era through the House of Yi Jun-gu.       On your way down to Bukchon 5th View, you will see a tall locust tree. In the East, locust trees have symbolized scholars, as its freely growing branches are like a scholar seeking a new field of study. The tree was loved by upper class families in the Joseon period, as it was believed that if you plant this tree, someone in your family would become a famous scholar or official. At the intersection, go up the right hill to see Bukchon 5th View.

stories.title: Bukchon 5th View
stories.script: Dense collection of Hanoks  The hanok alley at 31st Gahoe-dong includes the fifth, sixth and seventh view spots. You will find many pictures of this alley in shops. Here, you can see how hanoks in Bukchon are different from traditional hanoks.      At the fifth view spot, take a look at the hanoks along the alley. You will see that many of them have a wall of fixed sized stones with a red pattern on it. Some of them have windows made of glass instead of Korean paper and wood shutters on them. Don’t they look too small for upper class families in the past?   Most of them were actually built in the 1930s. Back then, the upper class began to collapse, as the power of the Joseon royal family weakened gradually. So, they found it difficult to maintain a large hanok. At the same time, people needed more houses due to the growth in population in Seoul during the industrialization period. So, private construction firms began to remove large hanoks and build smaller ones, and leased them to common people.     This is why hanoks in Bukchon are similar in size and shape. Although they have a modern vibe with its new materials like glass and ceramic tiles, they have a traditional structure with the building surrounding the yard.

stories.title: Bukchon 6th & 7th Views
stories.script: Representation of Seoul’s 600-year history  Having followed a row of hanoks on both sides, look back once you reach the top of the hill. You will see a view of downtown Seoul filled with skyscrapers beyond the hanok roofs. You can also see Namsan Mountain with N Seoul Tower. The observatory on the mountain attracts people who want to enjoy a view of the whole city. You may feel strange when you see the skyscrapers of downtown Seoul beyond the hanoks. This is Bukchon 6th View.     Bukchon 7th View is the hanok alley to the right of the 6th View. It looks as if the hanok roofs touch each other across the alley, as it is gently curved to the left. You will see many small flower beds at the base of the stone walls.    You can go to Bukchon 8th View by walking up the back alley of the 6th View. On your way, you can visit “the Site of Maeng Sa-seong’s House”. Did you find the stone sign of the site? Maeng Sa-seong served as a Jeongseung, or prime minister of today, in the early 1400s. He was known as a man of integrity. He also taught King Sejong who created the Korean alphabet.    He led a frugal life, riding a cow instead of a sedan chair and enjoyed playing the pipe with a deep understanding of music. Here, you can also visit the Asian Art Museum where you can see rare Korean and other Asian relics.

stories.title: Bukchon 8th View & Samcheong-dong Observatory
stories.audioTitle: View of Samcheong-dong beneath Inwangsan Mountain
stories.script: View of Samcheong-dong beneath Inwangsan Mountain  Bukchon 8th View is a flight of stone steps that lead to Samcheong-dong. Let’s go down the steps. These stairs are of a modern style to the middle point, and then the style changes. These low steps are carved out of a single piece of bedrock. Why not walk up and down the steps to feel the charm of the alley.  On the way down from the top of the steps to Jeongdok Library, you can see Samcheong-dong Observatory. Here, you can see magnificent Inwangsan Mountain. It was originally called “Seosan Mountain” or a western mountain. But King Sejong changed its name to Inwang, meaning Buddhist guardian deity, with the hope that the mountain would protect the Joseon Dynasty.   On the left, at the bottom of the Mountain, you can see Gyeongbokgung Palace, the first palace of Joseon. King Taejo, the founder of Joseon, built the palace on the most auspicious site in the capital. Cheongwadae, the current Korean presidential residence, is located to the north of the Palace. This view reminds people of the 600-year history of Seoul.

stories.title: Gamgodang-gil Road
stories.audioTitle: Short trail telling the story of two queens
stories.script: Short trail telling the story of two queens  Besides the “Eight Scenic Views of Bukchon”, you can enjoy the charm of Bukchon in many small alleys. One of them is Gamgodang-gil, which is great for a walk. From Anguk Station to Duksung Girls’ Middle and High School, you can walk along the stone wall, enjoying the shade of the trees in the summer. Then, from the end of the stone wall to Jeongdok Library, you can visit various shops filled with an energetic atmosphere.  This road might feel short, but it represents a long history. Gamgodang, meaning a place where you look back on the past, was the name of a house built for Queen Inhyeon’s family by King Sukjong of Joseon in 1687. Her father lived here, and she also stayed here for five years after her dethronement caused by Lady Jang Hui-bin, the royal concubine of the king.   The house was named Gamgodang much later by King Yeongjo, who rose to the throne after King Sukjong and King Gyeongjong. He wrote the signboard himself in memory of the queen. Gamgodang means a place where you look back on the past. It is said that Queen Inhyeon, who was childless, loved King Yeongjo like her own son. So, maybe he felt sorry for the queen, who went through a hard time at this place.    Hundreds of years later, Gamgodang became home to another queen, Empress Myeongseong who was the wife of King Gojong, the 26th king of Joseon. The Min clan of Queen Inhyeon had lived in Gamgodang for generations, and Empress Myeongseong also lived here as a family member for eight years. Although  Gamgodang has been relocated to Yeoju in Gyeonggi-do Province where Empress Myeongseong’s birthplace exists, its name is still remembered as Gamgodang-gil in memory of the two queens.

stories.title: Jeongdok Library
stories.audioTitle: Library for citizens and rest area for travelers
stories.script: Library for citizens and rest area for travelers  Jeongdok Library, which opened its door in 1977, is at the center of the village where Bukchon-gil, Samcheongdong-gil and Gamgodang-gil roads meet together. You will see people reading books and taking a walk here. Then, what attracts people to this library? You can enjoy full-blown cherry blossoms in the garden in the spring and take a rest on a bench under wisteria vines beside a fountain in the summer.   The Library gained popularity right after its opening, as there were few libraries in downtown Seoul in the 1970s. People used to wait in a long line at dawn to get a seat. You might wonder why this library was built here in Bukchon.   The library building was formerly the Kyunggi High School. With the development of the southern part of Seoul in the 1970s, the government planned to relocate high schools to the south. Kyunggi High School was the first to be moved. Such decision met with severe opposition from students and graduates. They were worried that the history and tradition of their school would disappear.     Then, the Seoul Government promised to use the school as a library for citizens. It kept its promise by using the school building, schoolyard and affiliated facilities to make a great library.    It would also be fun to visit Seoul Education Museum next to the library. You can learn about Korea’s education history from the fourth century to modern time. The museum displays textbooks, school uniforms and stationery in a chronological order and it also shows a replica of classrooms and stationery stores in the past. You can enter a classroom with old desks, chairs and an organ. An exhibition room with school badges is also very popular.

stories.title: Gyedong-gil Road
stories.script: Old alleys  Bukchon has a variety of attractions besides hanoks, including the unique alleys. Among them, Gyedong-gil road is particularly popular to tourists.  Gye-dong was formerly called “Jesaeng-dong,” after Jesaengwon, a public hospital for the poor, was built here in the Joseon Dynasty. In front of the Hyundai Building next to Anguk Station, you can find a stone sign with the words, “Site of Jesaengwon.” Beside it, you will see another stone sign with the words, Ministry of Health and Welfare. It is interesting that the current ministry in charge of public health is located on the site of Jesaengwon, which treated the poor back in the old days.   Gye-dong is a reminiscent of Seoul in the 1970s and 1980s. You will see small restaurants with tiled roofs and shops with old handwritten signs, which attract tourists to this town.   In maze-like alleys on the sides of the road, you can see how local residents lead their daily lives in hanoks.    You can also visit hanok experience centers or join experience programs at craft workshops. Hanok Homestay Information Center, located in front of Jaedong Elementary School and across the Constitutional Court, provides information about hanok homestay and traditional culture programs. Why not stay overnight at a hanok to have more fun in Bukchon?

stories.title: Samcheondong-gil Road
stories.audioTitle: Great place for sightseeing and for a stroll
stories.script: Great place for sightseeing and for a stroll  Samcheongdong-gil road is quite popular among tourists and couples. You can take a walk along the stone wall of Gyeongbokgung Palace and look around and see unique products in small shops. You can also see many famous restaurants here. This might make the road look different from other places in the village, but it also has a long history.      The name “Samcheong-dong” was derived from “Samcheongjeon Hall,” which enshrined Three Purities, meaning the three highest gods in Taoism. Some argue that this area was named Samcheong, literally meaning three pure things: pure water, pure mountain and pure-hearted people. It was once known as a tranquil town with no convenience stores, franchises and neon lights.   How was this possible in downtown Seoul? Samcheong-dong is located near Gyeongbokgung Palace, Changdeokgung Palace and Cheongwadae, the presidential office. So, development was limited in this area to protect cultural properties and maintain security. Even now, you can easily see police officers standing guard for the presidential office and the prime minister’s office nearby. Thanks to limited development, this area could maintain its unique view of small buildings and hanoks with no tall buildings.    Samcheongdong-gil is now filled with restaurants, cafes, galleries and shops, after the development restrictions were partly lifted in the 1990s. Galleries and shops in Gangnam and Insa-dong moved here. This has made this area what it is today. How about having fun on Samcheongdong-gil?

stories.title: Wonseo-dong Public Laundry Site
stories.script: Wonseo-dong Public Laundry Site  If you come inside along the Wonseo-dong Workshop Road, you will reach the Wonseo-dong Public Laundry Site. Water follows from Sohacheon Stream where the Oesammun Gate of Changdeokgung Palace and Bukchon end, and this is where the court ladies gathered, sat together and repetitively struck their laundry bats to wash clothes.  If you look from the inside of Changdeokgung, the laundry site is the area that corresponds to Sinseonwonjeon Hall. A small stone bridge was installed where water flows naturally beneath the palace walls, and Gungjang (walls encompassing the palace) were established on top of the bridge. The water from Sohacheon flows out from Changdeokgung's backyard, which had an abundance of water. So, there was an ample flow of water in the area all year long, and the water flowed up to Sohacheon.  Along with Cheonggyecheon stream, this is one of the oldest laundry sites in the Joseon Dynasty and was also the innermost neighborhood in Wonseo-dong where the palace and the private residence came into contact, which is why this laundry site was also used by commoners as well. Therefore, it was a place where court ladies inside the palace walls and commoners outside the palace were able to gather and exchange whispers over the walls while doing laundry. That is why it was a place of communication where the court ladies could hear the news of the outside through the common folks who, in turn, could listen to the stories from the inside of the royal palace walls through the court ladies.  Nowadays, there is not as much water flowing as before, and you may easily see the water frozen in the wintertime. As a part of the river was reclaimed during the construction of a new road, the waterway became narrower, and iron fences were installed underneath the walls for protection of Changdeokgung Palace so the space seen from the laundry site is the vacant lot of Sajumun and Sinseonwonjeon.  Now, shall we go back to the entrance of Wonseo-dong to meet the first Western-style painter of Korea?

stories.title: House of Go Hui-dong (Go Hui-dong Art Museum)
stories.audioTitle: House of Go Hui-dong (Go Hui-dong Art Museum)
stories.script: House of Go Hui-dong (Go Hui-dong Art Museum)  In 1918, a modernized hanok was built in the alleyway of Wonseo-dong where the sun shines brightly. It was the house designed by Painter Go Hui-dong himself upon his return from studying abroad in Japan. Go Hui-dong lived in this house for 41 years to train his students while working on the creation of his artworks.  While he was studying in Japan, Go frequently came across the Western and Japanese architecture styles, from each of which he took and harmonized the strengths to apply to hanok. That is why it became a unique hanok featuring glass windows, a rare element in traditional hanok at the time, as well as long hallways and modern bathrooms.  A native of Wonseo-dong, Go Hui-dong grew up to be a modern intellectual, learning French when he was a child under the influence of his father believing in idea of enlightenment. In 1904, he served a government post as Jusa of Gungnaebu.  But he soon resigned after the Eulsa Treaty was signed in 1905 and, instead, became a pupil of a pair of Eastern-style painters, Ahn Jung-sik and Jo Seok-jin, to study Oriental paintings. Then, in 1908, he became the first Korean to enroll in Tokyo University of the Arts where he learned Western paintings for 5 years before coming back to Korea to teach Western painting at various schools.  The most notable works he painted in this house are “Geumgangsan Jinjudamo and “Tapseung. His works are exhibited inside the house along with the works of his pupils so you can check out Go’s world of art that expresses a mix of the Eastern and Western painting styles.  Originally consisted of Sarangchae, Munganchae and Gokganchae, the house went through a number of deformations and was neglected after his passing, which left it seriously damaged. But, as it was designated as Registered Cultural Heritage No. 84 in September 2004, Anchae and Sarangchae were repaired and restored. Sarangchae was reproduced by utilizing the furniture from the era in which Mr. Go actually lived, and there is a studio in the room next to Sarangchae so you can get a glimpse of his work space where he freely produced Western and Oriental paintings.  When you stand in front of the bust sculpture of Go Hui-dong on your way out after touring the house, the house and a large tree protecting the front yard can be seen at a glance. Don’t forget to take a picture!

stories.title: House of Baek Inje
stories.script: House of Baek Inje  * You may tour the House of Baek Inje with a tourism commentator after making a reservation on the public service reservation website of Seoul (free admission).   You will reach the House of Baek Inje with a huge gate at the entrance after a walk along the alley between Gahoe-dong Community Center and Bukchon Museum. It was named the House of Baek Inje because Mr. Baek Inje, a medical doctor and a surgeon, and his family were the ones who last lived here.  Originally, this was a modernized hanok built in 1931 by Han Sang-ryong, an infamous pro-Japan businessman and the son of Ye Wanyong's cousin, to host parties for Japanese high officials. For construction of the house, even Korean black pines were brought all the way from Amrokgang River, showing the wealth and power of one of the uppermost families in the country at the time. In particular, the Sarangchae and Anchae are connected by a hallway so you do not need to go outside to move between the two rooms and, also, a portion of the Sarangchae is located on the 2nd floor, all of which are unique elements that were not typically seen in hanok architecture of the time.  The house is largely divided into the Munganchae, Sarangchae, Anchae and Byeoldang. The Sarangchae front yard that you see as soon as you enter through the main entrance is broad for parties and banquets. As you walk from the garden along the walls, you will get to Byeoldang from which you can come inside to Anchae so you can see that the house is connected even on the outside. There is a unique space in the front yard of Anchae, and that is an air-raid shelter established to prepare for surprise air strikes. But it is said that the shelter was used more as a wine cellar or storage.  In 1944, Dr. Baek Inje purchased this house and lived with his family and, after he was abducted to North Korea, his wife, late Choi Gyeong-jin, stayed here until she passed away, waiting for news of her husband. That is why it was decided that many traces of his family be left behind during the restoration of the house.  The House of Baek Inje became famous when it appeared in the film, Assassination, as the house of Kang In-Gook, an evil pro-Japanese businessman. Here, you can see and feel the scenes from the movie including the attic where Lee Jung-jae stayed and the hallway Jun Ji-hyun walked through. The city of Seoul purchased this house in 2009 and, after repair and reinforcement, began to open it to the public in 2015.

stories.title: Hwangudan (Wongudan) Altar
stories.audioTitle: An altar representing the dreams of the Great Korean Empire
stories.script: Hwangudan (Wongudan) Altar  The first character of the altar’s name means “circular” or “round” hence Hwangudan translates to “round altar.” The altar was built to protect the king’s authority at the end of the 19th century, when King Gojong’s power was being threatened. Here, Gojong declared Joseon as the “Daehan Empire,” offered a ritual to the heavens, and was proclaimed as emperor.   In 1910, Japan took over Joseon and began building Western-style buildings in Seoul to assert their power. In the process, Hwangudan was destroyed and a hotel was built in its place. Today, Hwanggungu, a three-storied octagonal shrine, remains along with a gate and three drums with dragon decorations. The drums were constructed in 1902 inside Hwangudan Altar to commemorate Emperor Gojong’s 40-year reign. The stairs of the arched gate in front of Hwanggungu, which enshrines ancestral tablets for the gods of heaven, had a central stone slab called the “Dapdo” for the Emperor to walk on. The stone fence is adorned with stone statues of Haechi, a mythological animal believed to offer protection against fire and disasters.   Hwanggungu enshrines the ancestral tablets for the gods of heaven and it is lit by natural sunlight coming in from the 24 windows on the third level. On the ceiling, there is a painting of a “Chil-jo-Ryong,” a dragon with seven claws. This dragon symbolizes the authority of the King of Joseon or the Emperor of the Daehan Empire, and Korea’s desire to become a great nation.

stories.title: Myeong-dong
stories.audioTitle: A major shopping and economic hub of Korea
stories.script: A major shopping and economic hub of Korea  The streets of Myeong-dong are always crowded with shoppers, couples, office workers, and tourists. Popular fashion brands, famous Korean cosmetics stores, and great tasting food can be found here.   The modernization of Myeong-dong began in the 1920s. With Cheonggye Stream dividing the city, the people of Joseon settled north of the stream while the Japanese settled south of the stream. Located south of Cheonggyecheon, Myeong-dong was developed into a commercial district by Japanese residents.   In 1945 (the year Korea gained independence from Japan), plenty of small theatres opened up, thereby attracting many actors, musicians and artists to the area. The coffee shops and bars were frequented by artists discussing and sharing their talents, eventually making Myeong-dong the center of Korean arts and culture.   In the 1960s, redevelopment took place and all the coffee shops and theaters were replaced by commercial stores, making Myeong-dong the main shopping district that it is today.    Today, shopping malls, cosmetics stores, currency exchange stalls, coffee shops and restaurants can be found all around UNESCO Street, Myeong-dong 8-gil Street, Quan Chen Ru Street and the other major streets of Myeong-dong. Between 5pm and 11 pm, the streets become even more livelier with street performances and street vendors.

stories.title: Myeongdong Theatre
stories.audioTitle: The beginning of arts and culture in Myeong-dong
stories.script: The beginning of arts and culture in Myeong-dong   Designed by Ishibashi Ryosuke, Myeongdong Theater opened its doors for the first time in 1934 as a movie theater called “Meiji jwa.” After the independence of Korea, the name was changed to Sigongkwan and it became a venue for live performances.Beginning 1957, the theater served as the National Theatre. After the National Theater moved to Jangchung-dong, the building was sold to a finance company.    With the commercialization of Myeong-dong, artists left the area and the buildings became office space. Myeongdong Theatre also lost its place as the center of the arts. The Theater was about to be torn down in the 1990s but locals and artists who still cared for the theater fought to save it. The Korean government purchased the building in 2003, and after undergoing renovations, it finally opened its doors once again as a theater in 2009.     The Baroque-style exterior was preserved and only the interior was renovated. On the roof of the theatre is a dome-shaped glass structure that symbolizes the “light of culture.” The sunlight passing through the glass brings light and warmth to the audience. The seats are situated close to the stage, allowing the audience to get a closer look at the actors and performers.

stories.title: Myeong-dong Cathedral
stories.audioTitle: The symbol of the Korean Catholic Church
stories.script: The symbol of the Korean Catholic Church  Located on the highest hill in Myeong-dong, Myeong-dong Cathedral is the seat of the Archbishop of Seoul. It became even more famous after the Pope’s visit in 2014.  The Cathedral was designed by the French priest Father Coste, and constructed by Korean Catholic volunteers with the help of skilled bricklayers from the Qing Dynasty of China. The building was completed in 1898. It consists of a 45-meter-high (148 feet) bell tower, the main sanctuary, and an underground sanctuary. The bell is rung three times a day as a reminder for prayer time. The stained glass window of the chapel illuminates the gray brick columns and creates a serene and tranquil atmosphere. By the choir platform on the second floor is the first pipe organ to be installed in a Catholic church in Korea. Remains of the five saints and four martyrs are enshrined in the underground sanctuary.  Behind the main chapel is a statue of the Virgin Mary, the Patroness of Korea and people’s guardian during the pro-democracy movement in the 1970s and 1980s.

stories.title: Korea Postage Stamp Museum
stories.audioTitle: History of Korean postal services and postage stamps
stories.script: History of Korean postal services and postage stamps  Located on the basement level of the Korea Post Tower, the Korea Postage Stamp Museum displays all the postage stamps that have been printed in Korea, as well as stamps from around the world. Here, you can see the world’s first postage stamp, “Penny Black,” and Korea’s first postage stamp, “Moonwe Stamp.”  In the exhibition room, you can see how Korean postmen and the postal services have changed over the years. Through the changes you can also see how the Korean society and culture have progressed.  Unique stamps from around the world like vinyl record stamps, 3-dimensional stamps, hologram stamps, coded stamps, and many more can be seen at the museum. The cartoon character stamps section is very popular among kids. You can also make your very own stamp here.

stories.title: Bank of Korea Money Museum
stories.script: Money and Humanity  Construction of this Renaissance-style building began in 1907. The building was originally intended to be used for The First National Bank of Japan. Halfway through the construction, the Bank of Joseon purchased the site. Construction was completed and the building was used as the head office of the Bank of Joseon from 1912 onwards.  In 1945, the bank changed its name to the Bank of Korea. In 2000, it was renovated and reopened as the Bank of Korea Money Museum. The museum consists of two exhibition halls: one on the first floor and one on the second floor. The first floor takes you through the history of Korean currency and other currencies from around the world. You’ll also find ancient Japanese coins and a currency plate from China. If you have any Korean bills, try scanning them through the counterfeit detector to check whether your money is real or not.  On the second floor, you will find a model of a vault. You can take pictures holding bags of money in front of the vault. There is also a digital money waterfall, in which you can put your hand to touch the money of the country you want to learn about. If you touch the money, the information corresponding to the country you chose will pop up on the screen. On the hallway of the second floor is a bench made of recycled money. If you sit on the bench, you’d be sitting on approximately 86 million won!

stories.title: Namdaemun Market
stories.script: 600-year-old Traditional Market   In 1414, Joseon Dynasty’s King Taejong established a market in the Namdaemun area of the Seoul City Wall where circulation of goods and commodities was greatest. The government built shops around Namdaemun and rented out the shops to traders. Word spread very fast and soon enough, the market thrived with merchants and goods from around the nation.  In the wake of the Korean War, items from American military bases including chocolates, army supplies, cameras, watches, and other imported goods began to circulate secretly in the market. Whenever officers would enter the market, traders would instantly pack up and disappear. Over a period of 40 years, the city of Seoul redeveloped and modernized the market little by little. New buildings were erected, and the Namdaemun Market you see today was completed in 2005.   The Namdaemun Market houses over 10,000 shops that carry mostly children’s clothing, accessories, eye glasses and cameras. But with the increasing number of foreign tourists, shops selling traditional Korean goods like dried seaweed and ginseng have also increased.  The back alleys lined with delicious eateries also attract plenty of visitors. Home-made noodle soup, braised cutlass fish, king-sized dumplings, and fried fish cakes are just a few of the mouthwatering dishes you’ll find here.

stories.title: Entrance to Seoul Namdaemun Market
stories.script: Seoul’s finest traditional market   Welcome to Seoul’s Namdaemun Market. It is a place where you can find a wide array of products from Korea. Situated at the South Gate, Namdaemun, built during the Joseon Dynasty, it boasts a 600-years history and stands as the largest traditional market where everyone can immerse themselves in Korean market culture.  At Namdaemun Market, you can purchase almost everything you need for daily life at an affordable price. Operating as a wholesaler and retailer, it offers products at reasonable prices to customers worldwide, including international traders.   Though the market offers a variety of goods, you will find similar product vendors in each alleys, making price comparison easy for visitors. The children’s clothing alley features year-round clothes printed with kid’s favorite characters and patterns. The eyewear alley presents different kinds of glasses, both functional and fashionable. In the jewelry alley, there are both retail and wholesale stores offering a wide range of choices, from earrings to necklaces at affordable prices. It is greatly recommended to stop by the tourist information center or customer service center for details on tax-free shops or kiosks before shopping.  Once you are done with your shopping, don’t forget to explore K-Food Street. You can find famous dishes like seolleongtang (ox bone soup), galchi-gui (grilled cutlass fish), kalguksu (fresh noodles in seafood soup), and mandu (Korean dumplings).

stories.title: Tour Attractions near Namdaemun Market
stories.script: A place where major tourist attractions in Seoul are gathered   There are many major tourist sites near Namdaemun Market, with the most renowned spots being the Sungnyemun Gate, Myeongdong and Namsan Seoul Tower.  Sungnyemun Gate is regarded as the oldest among the existing wooden buildings set up in the fortified city of Seoul, featuring an arched entrance in the middle. Positioned to the south of the capital, it is also known as Namdaemun or the South Gate. The gate held significant importance, being used for major national events and as the passage for the king’s parade during the Joseon Dynasty. Despite its long history, it now finds itself surrounded by roads and modern tall buildings, creating an enigmatic space where the past and the present coexist.  Myeongdong stands out as one of the most visited tourist attractions for foreigners, a bustling place and one of the primary shopping districts in Seoul. Visitors can find clothes, shoes, cosmetics, and accessories at reasonable prices. Different from Namdaemun Market, Myeongdong also features sales of designer brands and is teeming with various restaurants and street food vendors.  Furthermore, Namsan Mountain lies adjacent to Namdaemun Market. At the mountain’s peak stands the Seoul N Tower, a must-visit spot. Visitors adore the breathtaking view of Seoul from the observatory deck and engage in the tradition of locking the “padlock of love” onto the railings, expressing wishes for everlasting love. The stunning view has made the tower an attractive filming site for many dramas and variety shows, such as “My Love from the Star”, “Running Man” and “Infinite Challenge.”

stories.title: Sungnyemun Gate
stories.script: The main gate of the 600-year-old city of Hanyang  King Taejo of the Joseon Dynasty constructed a fortress wall to encircle the entire capital city for defense. The fortress wall had four gates on north, south, east, and west. While the south gate is commonly known as Namdaemun Gate, which translates to the Great Southern Gate, its official name is Sungnyemun Gate, signifying the “Gate of Exalted Ceremonies.” It was the gate used by the king during official processions, and it served as the main entrance for goods and products from various provinces that entered the capital city.  Different from other gates, Sungnyemun Gate has its name written vertically. King Taejo believed that the palace, Gyeongbokgung, and the capital city were vulnerable to fires as they faced Gwanaksan Mountain, which had a shape resembling flames. To safeguard against fire, he chose the characters Sung and Nye in the gate's name, which indicated the shape of fire and represented the element of fire within the five elements.  The bullet marks left on the faded walls reveals the traces of a fierce battle between Korean and Japanese forces when the armies were forced to disband in 1907. In 2008, a significant fire caused severe damage to the gate, resulting in the destruction of the roof and the second level. After extensive research and reconstruction efforts, Sungnyemun Gate has been meticulously restored to its original appearance.

stories.title: Culture Station Seoul 284
stories.audioTitle: The old Seoul Train Station becomes a cultural space
stories.script: The old Seoul Train Station becomes a cultural space  Seoul Station began operation in 1900 as a small train station and was originally called Namdaemun Station. Japan’s South Manchuria Railway Company wanted to use the station to gain a foothold on Manchuria, so in 1925, the station was renovated into a building with the same architectural style as Tokyo Station and renamed as Gyeongseong Station.  After Korea’s liberation from Japan in 1945, Gyeongseong Station was renamed Seoul Station and became a meeting place for locals. With the completion of a new Seoul Station in 2004, the old Seoul Station was vacated. The project to restore the former Seoul Station and convert it into a cultural complex began in, 2008. The restoration project was known as “Culture Station Seoul 284,” reflecting the building’s designation as Historic Site No. 284. When you enter “Cultural Station Seoul 284,” you will see the Main Hall and the dome. On the ceiling, there is a stained glass depicting a traditional Korean dance symbolizing unity called Ganggangsullae. The second floor was once used as a barber shop and restroom when it was first built. Now, the space displays photos of the station before and during renovations.

stories.title: Ahn Jung-Geun Memorial Hall—Introduction
stories.audioTitle: A Memorial Hall that commemorates the achievement of Ahn Jung-geun.
stories.script: A Memorial Hall that commemorates the achievement of Ahn Jung-geun.  With the goal of colonizing Asia, Japan invaded Korea in 1909 and established an era of imperialism. In March of the same year, Ahn Jung-geun, along with 11 comrades, got together in Primorsky Krai, Russia and formed a secret group called Dongui Danjihoe, a secret society whose name roughly translates into the Society of Patriots. The members severed the top part of their left-hand ring finger to convey their loyalty and determination to the underground liberation movement. With his blood, Ahn wrote “Daehan Dongnip” (Korean Independence) on the Korean flag. In October 1909, Ahn assassinated Ito Hirobumi, a four-time Prime Minister of Japan and former Resident-General of Korea, at Harbin Station in China, shouting “Hurrah, Independence of Korea!” He was arrested on the spot and taken to a Japanese jail in Lushun, China. He was executed in 1910.  The Memorial Hall was built to commemorate Ahn Jung-geun and his fellow Dongui Danjihoe members. The memorial hall is configured as a cluster of 12 columns that shoot up from the sunken base. The number 12 symbolizes the unsung heroes of Dongeui Danjihoe. The transparent column represents the patriotic sacrifice of Ahn Jung-geun.  The memorial stones at the Memorial Hall were inscribed with writings of Ahn. In front of the Hall, you can see the statue of Ahn Jung-geun holding the Korean flag. On the way to the Memorial Hall there’s a black piece of granite with the inscription of one of Ahn’s writing.

stories.title: Ahn Jung-Geun Memorial Hall—Exhibit Halls
stories.audioTitle: A look into the noble life of Ahn Jung-geun
stories.script: A look into the noble life of Ahn Jung-geun  In the Worship Hall, on the 1st basement level, there is a seated statue of Ahn wearing a white hanbok (traditional Korean clothes). Behind it hangs a large Korean flag with “Korean Independence” written in Ahn’s blood.  Exhibition Hall 1 takes you through the life of Ahn beginning from his childhood to the social circumstances that shaped Ahn into the Korean independence activist that he was.  Exhibition Hall 2 displays Ahn’s activities in and outside of Korea including the justice army and the Danjihoe.  Exhibition Hall 3 contains materials related to the Harbin incident, and the autobiography which Ahn recorded during his imprisonment called “Ahn Eung-chil’s Life History”. Ahn Eung-chil was his childhood name. “On Peace in East Asia,” a book that Ahn wrote to encourage peace in the three Eastern countries (Korea, China and Japan) can also be found here.   Although Ahn was only 31 years old when he died, his martyrdom inspired Korea’s strong will of independence against Japanese imperialism. His sacrifice must be remembered by today’s youth and by the future generations.

stories.title: Namsan Bongsudae Beacon Tower
stories.script: Bongsudae, Joseon’s System of Communication  Located next to Palgakjeong Pavilion on Namsan Mountain, Bongsudae was used to send signals during the Joseon Dynasty. This communication facility sent out smoke in the daytime and fire at night to let people in the area know what was going on. One beacon was lit at normal times, two when an enemy appeared, three when an enemy approached the border, four when an enemy invaded the border and five beacons were lit when a battle with an enemy had begun at the border.  In 1883, Percival Lowell, an American astronomer visiting Joseon, saw the torch of the Namsan Bongsudae and remarked that it looked like a light coming from another world. This news traveled around the nation and made it to the King at Gyeongbokgung Palace, from where the beacon can be clearly seen.  The Bongsudae’s system of communication disappeared in 1895 when telegraphs and telephones were introduced in Korea. The tower you see today is a restored version. It was rebuilt in 1993 after careful study and research of maps from the Joseon era. Guards patrol the area and reenact the Beacon Fire Lighting Ceremony for tourists. When the last smoke is let out, which represents peace, you can take pictures with the Bongsudae guards.

stories.title: Namsan Palgakjeong Pavilion
stories.script: Palgakjeong Pavilion on Namsan Mountain  Palgakjeong was built in 1968. Initially, Mokmyeoksinsa Shrine, which was built by King Taejo in 1395, used to sit here. So, the people of Joseon used to call Namsan Mokmyeoksan Mountain. King Taejo used to refer to the mountain god as Mokmyeok the Great and built Mokmyeoksinsa for rituals performed in the spring and fall. To protect this sacred mountain, he closed off the mountain to the public, and prohibited cutting trees or using the mountain as burial ground. But in the 1920s, Japan built botanical gardens and parks on the mountain and moved Mokmyeoksinsa to Inwangsan Mountain.  Since 1945, Namsan has become a place for rest leisure. A pavilion was built to provide a sitting area for visitors and it was designed following an ancient Eastern philosophy that compares the world of the gods to a circle and the human world to squares, thereby creating an octagon in the center. This octagonal pavilion signifies a place between the world of the gods and the world of humans.    At the square in front of the Palgakjeong is a water fountain. This place that offers peace and relaxation to tired hikers and locals amidst the hustle and bustle of the city life.

stories.title: Seoul City Wall - Namsan Mountain Trail
stories.script: A 600-year-old Fortress Wall  The Seoul City Wall has lived through the 500 years of Joseon and it has survived until today. The Namsan trail is part of Zone 3, which runs from Gwanghuimun Gate to Namsan Mountain and all the way to Sungnyemun Gate. It is 5.2 km (3.2 mi) long and takes about 3 to 4 hours to finish.   The wall was constructed in three phases, 1396, 1422 and 1704. You can tell when a section was built just by looking at the bricks. The bricks were inscribed with the village name from where the construction workers were from. So if a section of the wall collapsed, the village people who built that section would be responsible for rebuilding it. Between 1910 and 1950, many parts of the wall were destroyed due to the Japanese occupation and the Korean War. Major reconstruction took place from 1975 to 1981. As you walk along the Namsan area, you will find a hidden gate. This gate was built to secretly deliver army supplies and forces.   During the Joseon era, there was an activity called “Excursions Along the Wall,” where people would walk along the wall and enjoy the scenery of Hanyang.

stories.title: N Seoul Tower
stories.script: N Seoul Tower stands on the top of Namsan Mountain. It was the first general radio wave tower in Korea and was built to promote the future of broadcasting and the tourism industry. Since it opened to the public in 1980, it has become the most famous tourist attraction and a landmark in Korea.  The tower stands at 236.7 meters, which brings its overall height above sea level to 479.7 meters. It has seven floors, including the ground floor, which is the fifth floor at the top of Seoul Tower Plaza. The tower's observation decks provide a breathtaking panorama of the entire city, making it a popular destination for locals and visitors from all over the world. Visitors can reach the observatory decks on the ground floor, the fourth floor, and the fifth floor by using the OTIS traction high-speed elevator, which only takes 30 seconds.  The outdoor observatory on the ground floor is well known for its love locks. Visitors lock their “padlock of love” onto the railing and pray that their relationship can last forever. On the other hand, the observatory on the fourth and fifth floors offers a panoramic 360-degree view of downtown Seoul. On a sunny day, visitors can even see the view of Yongmunsan Mountain in Yangpyeong on the east, Hangang River and the Yellow Sea on the west, Namhansanseong Fortress on the south, and Songaksan Mountain in North Korea on the north. Also, the restaurant above the observatory deck is famous for its complete rotation every 90 minutes.  There is a hidden message in the light of the tower. The tower lights up the city with colorful illuminations, which indicate the level of air pollution to the public. The blue, green, yellow, and red lights represent the serious level of air pollution, from good to extremely bad. It also actively participated in the Earth Hour event by turning off the lights every last Saturday of March.

stories.title: Overview of Namsangol Hanok Village
stories.script: Discovering Joseon Lifestyle at a Traditional Korean Village  Namsangol Hanok Village was developed by relocating five traditional Korean houses from the Joseon Dynasty to the northern foot of Namsan Mountain over a period of four years starting in 1933. These houses were gathered from different parts of the city and brought to this location.  In addition to the houses, the village features traditional gardens and the Seoul Millennium Time Capsule Square. Five pavilions have been constructed in the traditional garden to recreate the appearance of a traditional garden where visitors can enjoy the surroundings. These pavilions include Cheongnyujeong Pavilion, Gwaneojeong Pavilion, Cheonuagk Pavilion, Mangbungnu Pavilion and Pigeumjeon Pavilion. The Seoul Millennium Time Capsule Square is built in the shape of a meteorite crater, symbolizing perpetuality. The Seoul Namsan Gukakdang, a traditional music hall, was also built to provide a venue for visitors to listen to traditional music.  Namsangol Hanok Village was previously known as “Cheonghakdong,” where “Cheonghak” literally means “a blue-green crane,” signifying the beautiful green nature that surrounds the village. During the Joseon era, scholars and aristocrats walked around the pavilions and houses while enjoying the beauty of nature. Although its appearance has changed over time, the harmony between Namsan Mountain and Hanok Village remains attractive.  At the hanok village, you can experience the lifestyle of Joseon era by exploring the houses, furniture, and everyday objects that reflected the resident’s social class at that time. Various traditional experience programs are available, such as entering traditional Korean houses or taking pictures in hanbok, the traditional Korean clothing. Behind Cheonuagk Pavilion, a stage hosts various performances, including traditional music, traditional dance, and traditional martial arts shows, allowing visitors to get up close to Korean traditional culture. The Traditional Crafts Center showcases a variety of products crafted using traditional Korean techniques.

stories.title: Traditional Korean Houses (Namsangol Hanok Village)
stories.script: Walking around a beautiful traditional Korean village  Namsangol Hanok Village is home to five traditional Korean houses. They are the Carpenter Yi Seung-eop’s House, General Kim Choon-yeong’s House, Min Family’s House, Yun Take-yeong’s Jaesil, and Yun Family’s House. These houses exhibit different building structures that vary based on their utility and the social status of their owners.  Towards the end of the 19th Century, Korean society underwent significant changes due to corruption, Western cultural influences, and the rise of modern philosophy. This upheaval led to the disappearance of traditional cultural boundaries and class distinctions. It became common to find items and features in commoners' houses that were originally associated with noble houses. For example, adobe bricks or railing on the maru, which is equivalent to today’s living room, are originally the features of noblemen’s houses could then be seen in commoners’ houses at that time. However, distinct features such as the raised gate, low chimney, or separate ritual room were still characteristic in a nobleman’s house.  These traditional Korean houses at Namsangol Hanok Village offer various seasonal programs that allow you to experience traditional Korean culture firsthand. You can enter the house, try on traditional Korean clothing known as hanbok, and take pictures. You can also try traditional teas and desserts. On specific days, you may have the opportunity to witness an authentic traditional Korean wedding ceremony.

stories.title: Jangchungdan Park
stories.audioTitle: A shrine built by Emperor Gojong
stories.script: A shrine built by Emperor Gojong  Jangchungdan Park has great significance in Korean history. During the Eulmi incident of 1895, when Japanese forces invaded Gyeongbokgung Palace and assassinated Joseon’s Empress Myeongseong, the guards and servants who stood by the empress and protected her until the very end were also brutally killed. Emperor Gojong built a shrine called Jangchungdan to remember and comfort the souls of the dead. But in 1932, Japan destroyed Jangchungdan and in its place built Bakmunsa, a temple that commemorates Ito Hirobumi, who led the Korean invasion. Bakmunsa was eventually torn down in 1945.       The inscription on Jangchungdan Monument, a symbol of Jangchungdan Park, was written by Emperor Sunjong, the last emperor of Korea, while he was the crown prince. There are also many relics related to Korean independence such as the Parijangseobi Monument. This monument was erected in memory of a petition for Korean independence sent to the 1919 Peace Conference in Paris during Korea’s March 1st Independence Movement. There is also a statue of Martyr Lee Jun, a Korean independence activist who was sent by Emperor Gojong as a secret envoy to the Hague in 1907.   Supyogyo Bridge and a supyo, an instrument used to measure the water level during the Joseon Dynasty, were both located on Cheonggyecheon Stream in Jongno. But when restoration of the Cheonggyecheon Stream began, they were both moved to this park. If you walk under the bridge, you can have a better look of the granite stones used to build the bridge.

stories.title: Baeksu Coastal Road
stories.audioTitle: An amazing drive along the coast, Baeksu Coastal Road
stories.script: An amazing drive along the coast, Baeksu Coastal Road  Welcome to the coastal road that winds its way to and fro along the West coast. One might even mistaken themselves to be on the east coast. The 16.8 km of coastal road here in Yeonggwang is the perfect location to gaze at the beautiful scenery of sunset as it illuminates the sea beneath, You may also go for soothing drives that make it a worthwhile journey.  Baeksu Coastal Road. Baek means “white” and su is the Chinese character for “tightly crowded mountain peaks.” Thus, the name denotes either “white mountain,” or “white peaks,” and the coastal road is located in Baeksu-eup, hence the name for the road. Here’s a quick quiz. Can you guess how many peaks there are in total?  The villagers in Baeksu-eup say there are 99 peaks in total. The character for “white” is also the same syllable for the character “100,” and it’s only a difference in one brush stroke too. So, erasing one stroke from “100” becomes “white,” and that’s the explanation villagers give as to why there are 99 peaks in total. It’s an old wives’ tale passed down through generations by the villagers at Baeksu-eup regarding Mt. Gusu, so don’t be counting the peaks literally!   Instead, try cruising down Baeksu Coastal Road. Awarded Korea’s Most Scenic Road, and ranked as one of the top ten amazing driving courses in Korea, the road is well renowned, especially during May and June, when the sweetbriers are in full bloom. The backdrop of the ocean connecting to the red hues of the sweetbriers is a sight to behold.   When in Yeonggwang, be sure to stop by one of the beautiful viewpoints of the Baeksu Coastal Road.   Chilsan Gazebo / Chilsan Sea  At the entrance to Baeksu Coastal Road is the 3-story Chilsan Gazebo. When looking out from the gazebo on a clear day, one can see Chilsan Island and its nearby islands scattered here and there throughout Chilsan Sea in one amazing view, in absolute clarity. It’s a refreshing treat for the eyes.   Korea’s one and only Sunset Exhibition Hall  Past Chilsan Gazebo, along Baeksu Coastal Road, there are several rest points for travellers to enjoy spectacular views. A word of advice to travellers coming to this area just before sunset is to park their vehicles at the Sunset Exhibition Hall. You won’t regret it, guaranteed.  Just being able to view the sunset across Chilsan Sea from the Sunset Exhibition Hall will be an “illuminating” experience. Yeonggwang’s slogan, “A Millennia of Illumination” will come to mind as you gaze upon the dazzling sunset melding the sea and sky into one brilliant display. If so, it would be a lucky millennial enlightenment, so to speak.  For travellers that come a bit early to the exhibition hall, be sure to check out the 4D Virtual Theater to look at sunsets from around the world, or go to the Rider Theater for a virtual reality experience while you await sunset. On the first floor is the Sunset Experience Hall, and on the second floor is the Sunset Science hall. The second floor is surrounded by glass windows, with binoculars available for visitors to scour even the farthest reaches of the Yellow Sea as the sun paints the scenic horizon. It will be an experience like no other.  Within the vicinity of the Sunset Exhibition Hall is a wooden path built for people to enjoy the glow of the setting sun. Starting from the “365 Steps to Health,” the wooden walkway winds its way around the coastline, and is often called “Sunset Coast Walkway.” This particular walkway had the honor of being awarded the Grand Prize in Korea’s first natural scenery designation awards.  Come autumn, there is a special sunset festival that takes place. There are a variety of programs prepared for this event, and will make any autumn trip even more charming.   Turtle Rock, Mother and Son Rock, and the sad tales they hold within  Along the Baeksu Coastal Road, there are various cliff sides and rock formations that stand out prominently. Among these formations, Turtle Rock and Mother and Son Rock in Baeksu-eup’s Daeshin-ri are points of interest visitors won’t want to miss.  Long ago, it is told, that an old woman and her son lived on Hanakweol Island, which could be seen from the Baeksu coast. On one very windy day, her son had failed to return from fishing no matter how much the old woman had waited. So the old woman began to pray to the sea god, “Please, if you will allow me to meet with my beloved son once again, I would dearly pay that price with my life.” The old woman prayed night after night, and the sea god, touched by her devotion and bond to her son, answered her prayers. “Your devotion has touched me, and so I will let you meet your son, but you must make a promise not to let anyone know, and must come alone.”   And so, the legend goes that the old woman was allowed to meet her dear son every night, in secrecy. Then, on one day, a neighboring couple who thought odd of this woman heading towards the sea night after night, decided to follow her footsteps in silence. When the couple saw the son whom everyone had thought was surely dead, they screamed in horror. The sea god, angered by the broken promise, turned the son into stone in the shape of a turtle far from Nakweol Island towards the Baeksu coastline. The Turtle Rock is shaped like thurtle stretching its neck trying to climb the coast. As for the old woman, she too was turned to stone on Hanakweol Island, yearning for her son.   Not far from the Turtle Rock is the Mother and Son Rock. This rock formation itself has a sad tale to tell, a young wife and her son waiting for her husband who has yet to return from the sea. The wife, with her child on her back, waited for her husband from the coastline, praying every day, staring out into the sea. And so they both turned to stone, forever facing the sea, awaiting her husband.

stories.title: First Sanctuary of Baekje Buddhism
stories.script: First Sanctuary of Baekje Buddhism  India’s Buddhist monk Marananta left China’s Eastern Jin kingdom and headed east by sea. After days and nights of rough sailing, he arrived on the central region of the Korean peninsula, at a harbor port in Inam. The year was 348CE, and Marananta, who traveled all the way from India through China to Baekje, brought with him religious texts and began to spread Buddhist ideologies. This was how Buddhism first entered Korea, through Baekje. It is recorded that Marananta first arrived at Baekje through Beopseongpo Harbor in Yeonggwang.  Centuries have passed, and now we’re at the location, which commemorates Korea’s milestone in history, the entrance to the First Sanctuary of Baekje Buddhism. The sight here may seem very foreign and different from other historical sites. The commemoration gate takes on the role of the Ilju gates found at the entrance of every Buddhist temple, but this one takes a very different form. The architecture here takes on the form of those in Marananta’s hometown of Gandhara, present day Pakistan. The pagoda garden and souvenir shop also takes on this architectural style, influenced heavily by the main pagodas found in Takht-i-Bahi, Gandhara. This was where the monks practiced meditation.  To learn more about Gandhara architecture in detail, be sure to visit the Gandhara Relic Hall. At the relic hall, the facial features of Buddhist statues have distinctive profiles, sharp nose lines, and curly hair. They look almost Greco-Roman. Though Sakyamuni Buddha was of Indian descent, Alexander the Great’s conquer of the Gandhara region ignited an exchange of east/west cultures, ergo influencing even Buddhist art to adopt Hellenistic Greek attributes. As such, the first images of Buddha created in the Gandhara region carry uncanny resemblances to Greco-Roman statues, more specifically, that of the sun god Apollo.   Four-face Grand Buddha and Buyongru Hall  What can easily be seen from the First Sanctuary of Baekje Buddhism is the tall standing four-face grand Buddha statue, uncommon throughout the peninsula. It stands 23.7m tall, or 78ft. The statue that can be seen from Mandhara Square straight ahead is that of the monk Marananta. For his troubles of travelling so far across the land and seas, solely to help spread the Buddhist religion, it is said even the king of Baekje came to formally and officially greet him, and allowed Marananta to stay at the royal palace, to encourage the teachings of Buddhism.  Little is known about Marananta’s life thereafter, but the Haedong Goseungjeon, or “Lives of Eminent Korean Monks,” a compilation of hagiographies of famous monks from the Three Kingdoms period up until the Goryeo, states as such: “[He] travelled throughout many regions to spread his doctrines, and never stayed in one place for long…[He] faced many perils and difficulties, but even through such adversities continued to spread the word, and there is no place his foot has untouched.”  1600 years later, until today, Marananta continues to stand in silence, staring out towards the Yellow Sea, reminding us of the influence his travels had left behind. Behind his statue, the statue facing Beopseongpo is that of Amitabha Buddha, with Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to his left, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva to the right.   Underneath the four-face Buddha statue is the Buryong Hall, characterized by traditional Korean-style roofing. Situated at the center of the 108 steps towards the statue, the walls surrounding the first floor depict the life of Sakyamuni, from his birth to asceticism and enlightenment. Maybe it’s the climbing of the 108 steps, each representing the 108 earthly desires, or the unrestricting view of the ocean as seen from the Mandhara Square, but one thing for sure is that while on the site grounds, the world and its problems melt away in peace, if only for a few moments.

stories.title: Won-Buddhism Yeongsan Shrine
stories.audioTitle: Won-Buddhism’s first shrine, Won Master’s childhood home
stories.script: Won-Buddhism’s first shrine, Won Master’s childhood home  This is the birthplace of Won-Buddhism, a religion that started in relatively modern Korean history. The founder of the religion, Jung-bin Park was born and raised in Yeonggwang, and this was where he achieved Bodhi status. He is referred as the “Grand Master” to his followers, and his formal title is “Founding Master Sotaesan.”  This is the birth home of Founding Master Sotaesan. Park spent his days here until he was ten years old, when a large village flood forced him to move to neighboring Guho-dong. The original home was burnt to the ground during the Korean War in 1950, and this thatched hut standing today is a restoration that was completed in 1981 to commemorate the 90th year of the Grand Master’s birth.   On March 27, 1891, a third child was born to a peasant farmer named Park, in Yeongchon Village located in Yeonggwang’s County Baeksu-eup, Gilryong-ri. The boy was named Jung-bin, and was said to be quite different from his peers, and exceptionally intelligent. He was always curious about nature and the universe, and when he turned 11, he followed his father to pay respects at an ancestral grave. Watching adults perform ritual rites for the mountain spirits, Park became puzzled.  “Father, why are they paying respects to the mountain spirits in front of our ancestors?” “That’s because there are spirits far greater than our grandfather that lives here.”  Jung-bin Park, upon hearing his father’s reply, began climbing the mountain 4km away day after day, praying for the mountain spirits to appear and answer his questions. This continued for 5 years, today, halfway up Gusu Mountain, at the Sambatjae ridge (now considered a sacred site) stands a marker that commemorates his prayers.   Norumok Bodhi Site  Jung-bin Park changed his meditation locations twice, when he was 20 and 24. As he continued his prayers, villagers ridiculed him. The place where the head stone stands is where an old hut stood where the founding master achieved Bodhi, or enlightenment. That is why this site is called Norumok Bodhi Site. Norumok refers to the hill people used to pass by, and is named as such because the hill looks like the neck, mok, of a crouched deer, noru.  This site, where Founding Master Sotaesan (Jung-bin Park) achieved Bodhi is one of, if not the most, important cultural relics for Won-Buddhism here in Yeongsan Shrine.  On April 28, 1916, when Park was 26 years old, he had achieved enlightenment early in the morning, while still pondering deeply about nature and the universe. It was early in the morning. Even though the thatched hut where he achieved Bodhi is now long gone, the Man-go-il-weol headstone was erected to mark the location.  So what does Man-go-il-weol mean? It means that even through tens of thousands of years, the truths about the universe do not change, like the sun and the moon, and that social morals of enlightenment are eternal.   It is said that on clear days or on drizzling rainy days, especially early in the morning, energy vibes of Won-Buddhism from Guho-dong and Norumok can be felt strongly. Even non-followers of the religion can come to this place deep within nature for a comforting rest, and experience the awe of spiritualism.   Oknyeobong, Jeongwanpyeong, and Gugandoshil   The mountains which can be seen from the Won-Buddhism Yeongsan Shrine are called the Gusu Mountains. The name suggests that the mountains are shaped like nine tigers protecting the shrine, and there is one peak that stands out called Oknyeobong. It has the symbol of Won-Buddhism engraved on it.  Though there are countless peaks named the same throughout Korea, this peak is located 140m above sea level and resembles a heavenly woman using the oceans as a mirror to comb her hair, hence the name of the peak.  The time Jung-bin Park established Won-Buddhism was during a tumultuous era when Japan had annexed Korea and the lives of the people were oppressive and difficult. With the spiritual energy he received from Gusu Mountain, Oknyeobong, and Norumok, he began disseminating his teaching with the mantra, “The material is at the dawn of a new era, and so we must awaken our minds towards a new dawn as well.” The religious sect began with the title “Thinkers of the Buddhist Way,” and though its main roots are identical to Buddhism, Won-Buddhism also outlined a very detailed set of lifestyle that must be followed. It stressed the importance of labor and shunned idling extensively.

stories.title: Christian Martyr Museum
stories.audioTitle: Yaweol Church, the site of Christian martyrs
stories.script: Yaweol Church, the site of Christian martyrs  Yaweol Church has over a hundred years of history. It was built by Eugene Bell, a missionary, and within its grounds, a rich tapestry of events took place as well as equally painful and horrifying moments.   On the evening of June 22, 1950, a platoon from the North Korean army clandestinely landed on the shores under the cover of darkness. The South’s punitive army forces clashed with the north in a brutal battle in the nearby mountains, and as the south crushed most of the forces, where the remaining few sought refuge towards the church’s grounds. A villager discovered a North Korean soldier in the back mountains, and a churchgoer reported it to the police. The soldier was shot and killed, and the remaining soldiers in hiding deemed the entire village as foul and plotted their revenge. On September 29, as the once-retreating South Korean army and UN forces recaptured Yeonggwang, Christians and right-wing nationalists alike rejoiced and welcomed these armies, as the communist forces retreated into the mountains in hiding, planning to murder the Christians.   The Christians were captured by the communist forces and were buried alive, stabbed with knives and bamboo spears, or drowned. The church was burned to the ground, and the entire congregation of 65 Christians were wiped out. It’s a part of history which is uncommon even in other parts of the world.   The Yaweol Church Christian Martyr Memorial Hall was completed in 2009 to commemorate the 65 martyrs and their devotion. Inside the memorial hall, there are pictures of the martyrs, and efforts to find these pictures involved the painstaking process of locating the distant relatives of the martyrs. As the martyrs’ homes were burned to the ground, portraits of these Christians were difficult to obtain. The large sculpture at the memorial hall titled “Hands Held Together” depicts a bruised and torn hand finding forgiveness and reconciliation through the hands of God.   Yeomsan Church and its 77 martyrs  The Korean War created many martyrs in the Yeonggwang area. Of the eight churches found in Yeonggwang, six have witnessed the martyrs of 194 Christians.   The western coast’s small fishing village of Yeomsan-myeon has another sacred martyr site aside from Yaweol Church, at Yeomsan Church. Yeomsan Church’s martyrs of 77 Christians is more than that of the entire congregation martyred at Yaweol Church, unfortunately, this church was burned to the ground as well, with two thirds of the congregation including priests and elders were killed.  Even before the Korean War broke out, this region was the hiding grounds of North Korean spies deemed extremely dangerous. They would hide in the mountains during the day, and come to the village during the night to pillage for food and cattle, harassing villagers. They would pick on the priests as well, and as the Korean War broke out, communist forces took over Yeomsan Church to use it as the People’s Committee Office. The newly designated priest and his family were forced out, and in September of 1950, as the war went unfavorable to the north, the communist forces burned the church and began murdering Christians in retaliation.  A total of 77 Christians, including the priest, his son, and young grandchildren were slaughtered, and in some cases, entire families were murdered. The 77 memorial stones at the entrance of Yeomsan Church pays respect to these brave martyrs who till their last moments supported each other and sang hymns of praise.

stories.title: Catholic Martyr Museum
stories.script: Catholic Martyrdom  Over two hundred years ago from today, in 1801, King Jeongjo died unexpectedly and King Sunjo ascended to the throne. This particular year was an important milestone in Korean history as it represents the period where Yak-yong Jeong, one of Choseon Dynasty’s brilliant intellects, was exiled. Korean history calls this the Catholic Persecution of 1801, or Shin-yu-bak-hae in Korean.  What led to the persecution of Catholics? At the end of the 18th century, there became an increase of progressive ideologists who realized the limits of Choseon Dynasty’s longstanding patriarchal authority and Confucian-based society. The newly introduced Catholic doctrine began to spread among these idealists, and to the general population as well, who had grown weary from the incompetence and corruption rampant within the authorities. With the sudden death of King Jeongjo who had relatively lenient views towards Catholicism, an 11-year-old king ascended to the throne. The political parties manipulated the king’s authority to persecute those who challenged their authoritative rule.  As there were many progressive ideologists practicing the Catholic faith, this persecution quickly became a religious persecution. As a result, countless Catholics were exiled or executed.  It was during this time when two Catholics lost their lives.  The Catholic doctrine spread relatively early in Yeonggwang. The martyr that took place here was a first for Korean Catholicism as well as the South Jeolla region. During the Catholic Persecution of 1801, Hwa-baek Lee of Yeonggwang and another man only known by his surname Oh had been executed at the main gates of Yeonggwang Cathedral, The cathedral was designated as the Martyr Memorial Cathedral in 2010.    The new two-story cathedral was completed in 2014 and houses the martyr memorial gates and statues of martyrs In August of 2014, Pope France’s visit to Korea raised awareness of the Catholic faith, and this place is a great place to ponder about the religion’s doctrine.

stories.title: Gamami Beach
stories.script: Gamami Beach  The three representative beaches in the southwestern region of Korea are Buan’s Byeonsan Beach, Yeosu Beach, and Gamami Beach. The waters are clear and shallow, at depths of around 1~2 meters. The beach is rather wide and in the shape of a half-moon surrounded by coniferous trees, Every summer a festival takes place with bands and dance teams.   The name Gamami has its origins in horses. Gama means “saddle,” and mi means “tail.” The backdrop of nearby Geumjeong Mountain is said to resemble a horse’s saddle and tail. In 1627, Choseon Dynasty’s Bomyeongdaesa visited here and said it looked like a horse galloping towards the beach, and named it, marae. The village town by the beach looked like the tail of a horse, and thus the name Gamami was given.   Gamami Beach opened in 1925, and its popularity extends pretty far back. Just simply watching families enjoying the beach with hammocks hitched between the pine trees, or friends pitching tents and basking in the sun brings a sense of relaxation in itself. The sunset off the Yellow Sea is a spectacular sight to behold, and will surely remind visitors again why Yeonggwang’s slogan is “A Millennia of Illumination.” It’s another great place for sunsets other than the Baeksu Coastal Road, and surely another illuminating experience.

stories.title: Cheonwangmun Gate(Bulgapsa Temple, Yeonggwang)
stories.script: Cheonwangmun Gate of Bulgapsa Temple, Yeonggwang  Bulgapsa Temple was built by the Indian Monk Marananta who traveled to Baekje to spread the Buddhist faith. “Bul” means “Buddha” and “Gap” means “first,” suggesting that the temple is the first Buddhist temple.  There are many legends associated with Bulgapsa Temple. One of them is about the four heavenly kings located within the Cheonwangmun Gate, near the entrance of the temple. The four heavenly kings are the protectors of the Buddhist doctrine and followers. They can typically be seen with their eyes wide open with gaping mouths, standing on sinners or evil spirits below them, presenting an ominous atmosphere. These gates are located at the temple entrance to allow the protectors of the north, west, south, and east to prevent evil spirits from entering.  During the Joseon Dynasty, in 1870, when Bulgapsa Temple was being restored, a residing monk by the name of Master Seoldu had a dream. In it the four heavenly kings spoke to him in the rain, “We are the four heavenly kings residing at Yeongisa Temple. Move us to Bulgapsa Temple and put a roof over our heads and we will protect your temple and your monks.”    Finding the dream odd, he searched for Yeondusa Temple, located on Soyosan Mountain in Mujang, Chungcheongbuk-do. However, despite his efforts, the temple could not be found, and no one knew its whereabouts. Lost in the woods, he stumbled upon a deserted temple, where he found the Four Heavenly Kings. Using four boats, he loaded each large statue onto a boat and headed back to Bulgapsa Temple, just as his dream had instructed.  Yeongisa Temple was a very large temple, but the authorities that governed that area burned the temple to the ground knowing that the place was a valuable site to use. The monks were murdered and the temple was destroyed. Ever since Master Seoldu moved the four heavenly kings to Bulgapsa Temple, it is said the temple has withstood several potential fires unscathed.

stories.title: Daewoongjeon Hall(Bulgapsa Temple, Yeonggwang)
stories.script: Daewoongjeon Hall of Bulgapsa Temple, Yeonggwang  Daewoongjeon Hall is the main hall that houses the Shakyamuni Buddha statue. Found in most temples, it is usually located at the center of the temple grounds. But the  Daewoongjeon Hall here at Bulgapsa Temple is slightly different from the outside.  Atop the center of the roof ridge of the main hall is a Botap, which means treasure tower. The Botap was an ornamental piece added to the ridge when roof tiles were laid during construction. Having its origins in Buddhist architecture found in Indian and southern China’s temples, it’s an important clue that shows where Buddhism originated.  Upon a closer look, the Botap is in a rare comical shape. With round bulging eyes and bulbous nose, there’s a face that looks rather like a demon. In fact, it’s not a demon, but a dragon, and serves a purpose to drive out bad spirits.  When at Bulgapsa Temple, visitors should look at the doors carefully. These doors are known to be exceptionally beautiful compared to those found at other temples. Lotus flower shapes and chrysanthemum shapes adorn the doors with comb patterns. Through the doors, one would expect the Buddha statues to be facing head-on, but in fact, the statues are turned away, facing south. Though Daewoongjeon Hall is facing west, the Shakyamuni Statue at the center, the Bhaiṣajyaguru Buddha to the left, and the Amitabha Buddha to the right are facing south.   In Korea, Magoksa Temple in Gongju and Buseoksa Temple in Yeongju are the only temples that have the main Buddha statues turned away from direct view. This layout is due to the architectural preferences of early Buddhist cultures in the southern region.

stories.title: Resurrection Lily Festival(Bulgapsa Temple , Yeonggwang)
stories.script: Resurrection Lily Festival of Bulgapsa Temple, Yeonggwang   The popularity of the Bulgapsa Temple and Bulgapsan Mountain is represented by the Resurrection Lily Festival,  held every year in September. During this time, this area is colored with resurrection lilies, also known as red spider lilies. The Chinese character for this flower means love that was never meant to be, and unlike other flowering plants, the leaves do not grow together with the flowers. When the plant loses all of its leaves during June and July, the flowers begin to bud and bloom starting in September. A month after the blooms fade, the leaves then take over again, all through winter.  Visitors may be curious and wonder why there are so many flowers with romantic connotations growing around the temple grounds. For Buddhist followers here at the temple, the Resurrection Lily symbolizes enlightenment within the world, reminding the faithful about freeing oneself from life’s greed and selfish desires. Given the meaning behind these flowers, it’s no wonder they’re found here in such abundance. Another reason these flowers are found here is practical rather than symbolic. The roots of this particular lily have preservative properties used for painting wooden buildings and portraits found on altars. Applying the root concentrate prevents mold growth on the paint and helps preserve its natural colors.  Visit Bulgapsa Temple in September, when fields of Resurrection Lilies bloom from the temple entrance to the reservoir deep within, creating a dazzling backdrop. Families and couples visiting this area may see a connection in the way leaves and flowers bud in alternation, symbolizing that there is no need for longing when two become one.

stories.title: Naesan Memorial Hall
