stories.script: Naesan Memorial Hall  There is a Korean movie released in 2014 titled The Admiral: Roaring Currents  that depicts the maritime battle that ensued on September 16, 1597, between the Japanese navy and Korea’s infamous Admiral Sun-shin Yi. The battle, which Korea had won, is called Myeongryangdaecheop, and the period when the Japanese invaded Korea was called Jeongyujaeran.  A week after the naval battle on September 23, 31-year-old Hang Kang served in the Korean army in Yeonggwang when he was captured as a prisoner-of-war. Kang was a famous Confucian scholar who had passed the national exam just 4 years prior, and during his 3-year captivity in Japan, he collected geographical, military and wind information of the Japanese and sent it to Korea. Through this, he preached that Choseon must empower itself to defend itself from invaders. In the meantime, Kang exchanged his wisdom with a Japanese intellect, spreading Choseon academics and upholding his status as a scholar  Naesan Memorial Hall was erected to commemorate the life of Hang Kang. Behind the memorial are the graves of Kang and his two wives, looking down on the memorial grounds. When he returned from captivity, he proclaimed that he was a willing prisoner-of-war, and began to foster and teach his wisdom to his students.   The memorial exhibition hall within Naesan Memorial Hall preserves the collection of books Kang had written. Among them, one is titled Ganyangrok. While in captivity, Kang wrote a book titled The Cart a Sinner Rides, which was retitled to Ganyangrok by one of his students. Ganyang means to “herd sheep,” and refers to a story in Han China where a loyalist returned upon herding sheep, after enduring much adversity far away from home. The revised title was in honor of Kang’s loyal allegiance to his nation during perilous captivity.   The story and teaching of Hang Kang are not that popular among the masses in Korea, but during the 80s, a hit Korean drama titled Ganyangrok aired in the nation, causing awareness of this great teacher, with the theme song sung by then popular Yong-pil Cho.

stories.title: Beopseongjin Castle Supjaengi / Supjaengi Park
stories.audioTitle: The old Beopseongjin Castle Supjaengi and the modern Supjaengi Park
stories.script: The old Beopseongjin Castle Supjaengi and the modern Supjaengi Park  The newly modern Supjaengi Park is an extension of the beautiful lush forest flourishing in the National Cultural Heritage Site No. 22 Beopseongjin Castle Supjaengi forest, near the First Sanctuary of Baekje Buddhism. It has a walking trail, rest areas, and an artificial waterfall, During spring, many different types of flowers in full bloom create a wonderful scenery. In the summer and fall, the park offers shade from the heat as well as a dazzling display of the changing leaves.  The Korean word for “forest” is sup, and jaengi refers to the castle and/or hill. So, the name supjaengi can be interpreted as “a castle built via the forest,” or “forest on a hill.” Visitors traveling from the coastline may ask locals where the Supjaengi is, to which locals interestingly most often reply, “Supjaengi, supjaengi.”  Designated as a national heritage site in 2007, the Beopseongjin Castle Supjaengi is lush with Zelkova trees planted over 450 years ago during the Choseon Dynasty, an artificial forest formed along the ridge of a mountain. There are a total of 150 Zelkova trees in this forest, and the it is known not only for it historical and cultural values, but also as one of the top ten most beautiful forests in South Korea.  Throughout Korea, at least one very old Zelkova tree can be found in almost every traditional village, but to find an entire forest of them is very rare indeed. This begs to ask the question, “Why so many here?” The main reason is actually to act as windbreakers. The trees block the strong breezes that flow in from Beopseongpo coast, and as such, the breezes felt within the forest and park are gentle and comfortable, and aided in the growth of the village nearby. However, there is another purpose for the trees being planted here, and to find the secrets to these 400-year-old trees, we need to understand another very important cultural heritage that occured here in Yeonggwang’s Beopseongpo. Sit underneath the shade within the lush forest, and listen for it, you’ll understand soon enough.   Beopseongpo Dano Festival and Zelkova tree habitat  Every May 5th in Korea’s east coast city of Kangneung, there is a festival held called the Kangneung Dano Festival, and, the Beopseongpo Dano Festival In the west coast  There is a reason as to why such a big festival is held here every year. The lunar months of February through April is the clam season, where lots of manual labor gather together. As the volume of clams captured is huge, so is the amount of money traded. It’s during this time that all the specialty foods of South Jeolla Province gather in this area, and long ago this was where tax was collected in the form of rice crops which were stored or sent to Seoul. It was around May 5th when all the labor for digging up clams was finished, and markets thrived and flourished  The Beopseongpo Dano Festival was held in the Zelkova tree habit at in Beopseongjin castle. It was the home ground of the celebration and the trees growing along the ridge were optimal natural theater seating. By today’s standards, it would be akin to amphitheaters with step seatings.   The breeze in this area are stable, calm, cool. The trees provided shade for people, allowing thousands to gather and take seat. Taking a look at the old pictures of previous Beopseongpo Dano Festivals, it’s easy to see the mass of crowds gathered here to enjoy the festivities.  The supjaengi still provides a place of rest for visitors, and the forest is divided into east and west by a paved road developed during the Japanese colonial Era. During the festival, both sides are used for the festivities, and visitors should take note of Buyong Bridge that connects the east and west sides. Unlike other bridges, this one has a tree growing at the center. The reason for this is because of the belief that the road had disconnected the energy of the area, and the villagers remedied the problem by planting a tree in the middle, to connect the two sides, so to speak. The bridge is seldom used except during the festival.

stories.title: Beopseongpo Yellow Corvina Street and Yeonggwang Dried Yellow Corvina Promotion Hall
stories.script: Beopseongpo Dried Yellow Corvina Street  Yeonggwang is synonymous with yellow Corvina as it’s a delicacy here. And when Koreans think of Beopseongpo, they think of the Dried Yellow Corvina Street. Yellow corvinas are famous in Yeonggwang, and the term gulbi refers to the female yellow Corvina species.   The question has to be asked, “Why does yellow Corvina taste exceptionally more delicious here than in other regions?” The first reason is that the corvinas caught off Chilsan Sea in front of Beopseongpo have unusually high amount of roe, and the fish have a high content of fat. The corvinas are dried in the wind, and hence wind is a very important factor in curing the corvinas. The northwesterly winds from the Yellow Sea are drier than other areas, making it perfect for curing the corvinas. It’s the geographical location, which controls the humidity of the winds and its speed, along with temperatures in this region that make the corvinas an exceptional delicacy.  When curing fish, the insides are usually removed beforehand, but in the case of yellow corvinas, sea salt aged at least one year to reduce its bitter taste is liberally applied to the insides, specifically in the gills. Then, with the stable temperature breeze flowing through the area, the curing process begins. During the night, moisture from inside the Corvina moves towards the outside, enhancing the curing process altogether. Another crucial factor in making these corvinas so delectable is the salt that is used, all natural of course. The salt is also produced within the Yeonggwang region, and that in itself has spurred its own cultural traditions when it comes to salting foods.  Along the Beopseongpo Dried Yellow Corvina Street, visitors can see these salt cured fish, tied with eco-friendly twine made also in Beopseongpo, cleansed of its salt and hung to dry. Almost every restaurant on this street serves yellow Corvina in a traditional Korean table d’hôte style, or multicourse fashion.   Tying dried yellow corvinas at the Yeonggwang Dried Yellow Corvina Promotional Hall  For those that are interested in learning more about the famous dried yellow Corvina, head over to Beopseongpo’s Yeonggwang Dried Yellow Corvina Promotional Hall. Here, visitors will get to learn how to distinguish regular yellow corvinas from those that are caught in Yeonggwang, as well as the history of yellow corvinas of the region. The corvinas that are just caught off of the sea are called jogi, in Korean, which means “full of energy”, and once it undergoes the curing process, it is called gulbi. There is a very specific reason as to why the name changes, and the answer can be found here at the promotional hall.  The term gulbi was given to the cured fish by Ja-gyeom Lee, a nobleman during the Goryeo Dynasty of prestigious lineage. Lee had hoped to become a king himself by marrying off three of his daughters to kings, but failed to do so due to a rising coup, and was banished to Yeonggwang. He came to Beopseongpo and tasted the jogi that was on his dinner table and found it to be so delicious he decided to send it to the king.   “The taste of this amazing fish reminded me of our king, and as such I wish to offer this fish, caught off of Chilsan Sea to the king.”  He further added, “Though I live banished and in exile, I regret not my past deeds, and refuse to submit (gul) or be servile (bi).” And as such, Ja-gyeom Lee named the dry fish gulbi before sending it to the king, as a symbolic message of “I will not be subdued.”  This is the reason as to why the name gulbi stuck to the dried yellow Corvina. So whatever happened to Ja-gyeom Lee? The man that had vowed never to be subdued or be servile, in that very year, fell ill and died in Yeonggwang, still in exile. Although the food has survived through over a millennia of popularity, this little known traitor to the throne and his story of attempting to steal the throne has been less popular, and forgotten to most through the ages.

stories.title: Songi Island
stories.audioTitle: The small island of Songi Island, and Mongdol Beach
stories.script: The small island of Songi Island, and Mongdol Beach  The shape of Songi Island looks like a person’s ear, and has a lot of pine trees , which the name of the island derives from. Past the docks and up the coast a little is Songi Island’s representative Mongdol Beach, which stretches for about 2km.  At Mongdol Beach, there is an interesting legend being passed on. Long ago, the villagers of the island were protected by a mountain spirit family from disasters. The mountain spirit family went into meditation after witnessing ten years of peace on the island, and during then, numbers of evil spirits began causing trouble on the island. The spirit family ceased their meditation and battled with these evil spirits for ten days. The island was once again returned to peace. During the battle, a large boulder on the beach broke and was so called Mongdol, or Mong Rock.   On Songi Island’s low-lying mountains is a habitat full of giant pine trees. With 106 trees, it’s the nation’s largest of its kind, and what’s odd is that these trees are usually found along the coasts of Korea, and to have them form a lush forest as they do on the island is exceptionally rare to see.  Every morning and evening, beyond Songi Island’s village, in a mud flat, a phenomena called Moses’ Miracle occurs daily. During low tide, the ocean splits apart to reveal a land bridge connecting Songi Island and Gaki Island. Low tide is the best time to go out onto the mud flats to collect different kinds of clams for consumption. Many people come here to pick clams and enjoy the spectacular sunset that occurs every day. A boat that connects Songi Island to Anma Island comes in two hours after the boat arrives from the mainland arrives, only once a day. If you miss this boat travelers would have to stay on the island for the night. But then again, being able to see a spectacular sunset on one of these remote islands is meaningful enough to stay a night.

stories.title: Bay Salt Flats
stories.audioTitle: Bay salt flats and the salt flower crystals
stories.script: Bay salt flats and the salt flower crystals  There is an old story about a salt merchant in Yeomsan. A salt merchant by the surname Yeom, fell asleep under a tree, and dreamed of two monkeys fighting over a crystal ball. When he awoke, he found the crystal ball beside him, and as he unconsciously put it in his mouth, it turned out that nobody in the village could see him. Being invisible, his form would reappear when he took the ball out of his mouth. Yeom told the people who had gathered at the market, “I’ll become invisible right in front of your eyes, and if what I say is true, I ask that each of you buy a bit of salt, and if I am wrong, the salt will be free.” The tale goes on to say that Yeom became incredibly rich this way quickly. Fearful that he’d lose the crystal ball, he buried it in his yard. When he tried to look for it, it couldn’t be found, as if a mole had stolen it from him underground. To this day, farmers around the area dig deep into the land in hopes to find the ball, so they say, and consequently, harvests here are said to be more bountiful than other areas.  Maybe it is just an old wives’ tale to console the hardships of salt merchants long ago, but it is true that there were and are a lot of salt merchants here. Salt produced here is high in mineral content, and low in sodium chloride content, making it somewhat healthier than salt from other regions. The floors of the salt flats found in the Duwoori Mud Flats are lined with clean porcelain, and hence the flats here are considered to be environmentally friendly.  The breeze coming off the shores of Chilsan Sea and the sunlight are gifts from nature here at the salt flats.  Experience the Duwoori Mud Flats as well as the process of making salt, and watch the beautiful sunset to end the day here in Yeonggwang.

stories.title: Chilsan Tower
stories.script: Chilsan Tower   Chilsan Tower is the tallest observatory in the Jeollanam-do area. The three-story tower comprises a waiting hall, snack store, and local specialty store on the first floor, restaurants and a raw fish center on the second floor, and an observatory deck on the third floor. The observatory commands a breathtaking panoramic view of the wide open waters and neighboring inland areas during daytime and a dramatic landscape of beautiful red colors on the waters of Chilsan during the sunset hours.

stories.title: Train Exhibition Hall
stories.audioTitle: Train Exhibition Hall: The last stop for your time travel.
stories.script: Train Exhibition Hall: The last stop for your time travel.  There is a train station inside the Hapcheon Movie Theme Park. You won't be able to find it in the KORAIL list of train stations, because it's not in service. It's called 'Gaho Station', and only actors and actresses have any business visiting the station. The word Gaho literally means beautiful lake in Korean, and it's the name of a town that exists in the Movie Theme Park. The official name of the town is Gaho-ri, Yongju-myeon, Hapcheon-myeon. After the construction of Hapcheon Dam in 1988,  asaddleorauxiliarydamwasbuilt in this town, and wet fog started rolling in over the town every dawn. The saddle dam is a popular place among Korean photographers.   The train station named after the town has an old electric locomotive. But the train never departs the station, although it actually can. However, it takes about 6 million won worth of coal to move the train just one meter. In movies or TV dramas, it appears to be traveling 100 kilometers when it moved only 1 meter.   Once you have finished your tour of the Movie Theme Park and pass by Gaho Station, you'll come to the last stop of your time travel. It's a wholesale market selling local food. It's where tourists can purchase local produce and little souvenirs. How about buying some healthy local food as a gift for your friends and family?

stories.title: The Bank of Korea
stories.audioTitle: The Bank of Korea: The first bank building built in Korea.
stories.script: The Bank of Korea: The first bank building built in Korea.  This building was intended for the Seoul branch of Japan's Cheil Bank. However, when it was completed in 1912, it became the main branch of the Bank of Joseon. It's because in 1909, when the building was still under construction, the Bank of Korea was founded as the central bank of Korea to serve as the Seoul branch of Japan's Cheil Bank. Shortly after the Bank of Korea was founded, Korea was occupied by Japan and the 'Bank of Korea Act' was enacted, changing the name of the bank from 'The Bank of Korea' to 'The Bank of Joseon'. It wasn't until Korea was liberated from Japanese rule in 1950 that the Bank of Joseon was renamed to its original name, the Bank of Korea.   This bank building resembling a Renaissance-style castle has a large vault in the basement floor, and it has a capacity of 1,600 people. A new building was built in 1987 right behind this historic building, which now serves only as the Bank of Korea Money Museum.  Here is one interesting fact about the replica of the original Bank of Korea in the Hapcheon Movie Theme Park: It serves as a motel despite how it looks from outside. That means you can sleep in the bank with your family or friends. Who knows? You might hit a jackpot in your dreams!

stories.title: 70-80 Jongno Streets
stories.audioTitle: The 70-80 Jongno Streets: When Mom and Dad were young.
stories.script: The 70-80 Jongno Streets: When Mom and Dad were young.  When you enter the 70-80 Streets of Memories on the right side of the Hapcheon Movie Theme Park, the first thing you'll see is the Railroad Underpass at Namyeong Subway Station. Namyeong Station is located between Seoul Station and Yongsan Station on Subway Line 1. The name 'Namyeong' simply means the military camp in the southern part of Seoul in Korean. The replica railroad of the Namyeong Station in the Movie Them Park is not made of iron, but wood. The railroad and houses of the 70's and 80's are about 40% the original size. The stair steps between the houses and restaurants nearby may appear to be leading to the neighbor, but it actually leads to a dead end alley. It's only in movies and TV dramas that the alley opens out onto a street.   The most memorable place for Koreans who still remember the 70's and 80's is Jongno with its narrow alleys. At the time, Jongno was the hottest place for young men and women to be in, as it was the center of the Korean pop culture. There were many music cafes where the disc jockey played acoustic guitar music among the array of theaters, bars, publishing companies and bookstores. These shabby buildings are nowhere to be found nowadays, because starting from the 80's, the old shabby buildings began to give way to the rise of tall buildings, particularly in and around the Gwanghwamun district.   However, you can still see the old signboards of the 70's and 80's at the Hapcheon Movie Theme Park.  If you're a Korean belonging to the older generation, you might find yourself diving into your memories just by walking in the street, and some of the restaurant signboards might make you hungry as well. If they do, go to 'Pimatgol' in Jongno. The word pimatgol literally means avoid the horses. The word came to use and eventually became the name of a small district in Jongno because it was where high officials of the Joseon Dynasty used to pass through on horseback, and people were forced to give way to them to avoid getting run over by a horse. The heavy traffic of pedestrians made the narrow streets a perfect place to open a restaurant, and many restaurants actually opened in the area. Even today, 'Pimatgol' is still a great place to dine. The 'Pimatgol' in the Movie Theme Park actually has an array of restaurants, serving hot rice soup, noodles in anchovy stock, makgeolli bars and street vendors selling roasted sweet potatoes. Take a pick and have your fill - the traditional way.

stories.title: Seoul Central Post Office
stories.audioTitle: The First Central Post Office of Korea: The Beautiful Building in Gyeongseong.
stories.script: The First Central Post Office of Korea: The Beautiful Building in Gyeongseong.  Built in 1915, Gyeongseong Post Office was the first central post office built in Korea. At that time, the capital of Korea was called 'Gyeongseong', not 'Seoul'. Just like the Bank of Korea and Japanese Government-General of Korea, the Gyeongseong Post Office building had a dome in the center and arched windows. Being one of the most modern buildings in the country, this three-story red brick building with a band of granite stone around was regarded as the 'Beautiful Building' of Gyeongseong. But only the framework of the building remained after the Korean War. So it was demolished and replaced by a new modern building in 1957 for the Seoul Central Post Office.   The Hapcheon Movie Theme Park has a replica of the original post office building with red bricks, just as it once looked like in the past. What's odd about the building is that while the facade of the building takes the form of a post office building, the side resembles the Embassy of the United States in Seoul. It was built by attaching a reinforced concrete structure to the post office building. The 80's style structure was added in order to shoot a scene of a protest. It's a film set after all.  The inside of the post office building will take you by surprise as well. It's a vampire mansion inside!  The inside of the building was designed to serve as an event hall for students to test their guts by lodging there. There are other buildings where you can enjoy various activities. At the Daehan Ilbo Building, you can get to use the real broadcasting equipment and pretend to be a news anchor or weatherman. You can also take photo stickers and make a reservation to participate in one of the traditional art programs such as pottery and beads craft. You can even hold wedding ceremony at Sogong-dong with a streetcar and all. How about it? Why don't you indulge in the fun activities that the Hapcheon Movie Theme Park has to offer?

stories.title: Gyeonggyojang
stories.audioTitle: Gyeonggyojang, where the Korean political leader  ’Baekbeom’ Kim Gu was killed.
stories.script: Gyeonggyojang, where the Korean political leader 'Baekbeom' Kim Gu was killed.   'Baekbeom' Kim Gu was a Korean independence activist and one of the most respected politicians in Korea during the Japanese Occupation of Korea. He served as the President of the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea, which was organized in Shanghai, China in 1919 during the Japanese Occupation of Korea. 'Gyeonggyojang' is a two-story building on the left side of the street that starts from the front gate of the Movie Theme Park. Kim Gu used 'Gyeonggyojang' as his official residence and headquarters of the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea upon his return from China after Korea's Liberation from Japan in 1945.   After his assassination, the building was used as the Embassy of Taiwan and then headquarters of the U.S. Special Forces before it was purchased by the Samsung Foundation in 1967 to be used as the main building of Gangbuk Samsung Hospital. In 2004, it was rented out to the Seoul Metropolitan Government and was restored. Now it serves as a memorial hall. The restoration took four years. The window glass with two bullet holes was also restored at the memorial hall. The two bullet holes were made when the bullets killed Kim Gu. The memorial hall also displays the bloody traditional Korean vest that he wore when he was killed.  In movies and TV dramas, the buildings may look as big as the actual building, but most of the buildings in the Hapcheon Movie Theme Park are only about 60% of the original size. It's the same with 'Gyeonggyojang'. While this building mostly appears as 'Gyeonggyojang' in most of the movies, it's also sometimes transformed into a school in some other movies. It can be fun to find out what other purposes this historic building serves in the movies and TV dramas.

stories.title: Ihwajang
stories.audioTitle: Donamjang and Ihwajang, where the First President of the Republic of Korea Rhee Syngman lived.
stories.script: Donamjang and Ihwajang, where the First President of the Republic of Korea Rhee Syngman lived.  After Korea's Liberation from Japan in 1945, Dr. Rhee Syngman returned from the U.S. with his Austrian-born wife Francesca Donner. At first, they unpacked at the Chosen Hotel. They checked out of the hotel and moved to 'Donamjang' in Dongsomun-dong, Seongbuk-gu, Seoul. They didn't buy or rent the house because the house owner was a man of wealth and let them stay there for free.  After two years of living there, Dr. Rhee and his wife moved to a house called 'Mapojang' and lived there for a short period, and then moved to another house called 'Ihwajang'. The money to buy this house was raised by more than 30 of his friends, and they gave this house to him as a gift. 'Ihwajang', located at the foot of Naksan Mountain, Seoul, is a historic place not only because Rhee Syngman lived there, but also because it was the residence of one of the princes of the Joseon Dynasty.  He and his wife lived there for two years until he moved to the Blue House after becoming the first President of the Republic of Korea. And after living at the Blue House for 12 years as the President, he moved back to Ihwajang upon his resignation on April 28, 1960. But this time, he stayed there for only one month because he left for Hawaii as a political refugee. He died in Hawaii five years later. Francesca Donner, the widowed first First Lady of the Republic of Korea, returned to Korea in 1970 and lived in Ihwajang until her death.   In the Hapcheon Movie Theme Park, 'Ihwajang' is located right next to 'Gyeonggyojang', the official residence of Kim Gu. It is ironic to have the two buildings next to each other, since they were political rivals when they were alive. The 'Ihwajang' in this theme park serves as a traditional Korean restaurant despite its exterior resemblance to the original one.

stories.title: Jeoksan Gaok
stories.audioTitle: The Houses of the Enemy where Japanese People Lived and Japanese-Style Houses
stories.script: The Houses of the Enemy where Japanese People Lived and Japanese-Style Houses  In South Korea, there still are many Japanese-style houses in many regions. These are the houses that were built during the Japanese Occupation of Korea. This type of houses are most common in Gunsan, Busan, Ulsan, Pohang, Yeosu and other port cities where a majority of the Japanese lived.   Such houses are called Jeoksan Gaok in Korean, which literally means the real estate properties of the enemy within my country or within the land occupied by the enemy. In a real sense, they refer to the houses and buildings abandoned by the Japanese when they returned home in 1945.   The Movie Theme Park has a small town designed to look like one of the actual Japanese towns with alleyways and such houses. When filmmakers shoot a scene of horse-mounted Japanese police officers patrolling the area, some of the Korean tourists nearby would still get mad and curse at them even though they know it's just a scene for the movie.   These Japanese-style houses come in handy for the filmmakers who need to go to Japan to shoot their movie but can't. When you step into the Japanese-style house named 'Punggyeong' with a garden and pond, or dine at the ryokan-style restaurant called 'Hyangwon', you will feel as though you're in Japan.  The movie 'My Way' starring the Hallyu star Jang Dong-geon, Japanese actor Joe Odagiri and Chinese actress Fan Bingbing was also filmed here. The movie was about the friendship between a Korean marathoner who dreams of winning the gold medal at the Olympics and the best Japanese marathoner during the World War II. This Japanese-style house is where some of hottest actors and actresses shot their film.

stories.title: Jongno Police Station
stories.audioTitle: The Japanese Government-General of Korea Building as a symbol of Japanese occupation
stories.script: The Japanese Government-General of Korea Building as a symbol of Japanese occupation  The Japanese Government-General of Korea was headquarters for Japan's colonial rule of Korea. In 1926, the Japanese Forces built their Government-General of Korea building in the Gyeongbokgung Palace grounds in order to demonstrate their power. This reinforced concrete structure covered with granite slabs, this domed building represented the most modern architecture at that time. The building was used by the Korean government after the Korean War and then as the National Museum of Korea after 1986. However, the building was demolished in 1995 to give way to the restoration of Gwanghwamun, the main gate of Gyeongbokgung Palace.  Japan ruled the Korean Peninsula for 35 years from 1910 to August 15, 1945, and such oppression was unprecedented in the history of Korea. The Japanese Government-General of Korea demanded Koreans to have a Japanese name and live as a Japanese citizen. Even Sohn Kee-chung, the 1936 Olympic Marathon gold medalist, had to wear the Japanese flag. After the Olympics, some of the Korean newspapers put him on their paper with the Japanese flag erased on his chest. However, they couldn't escape the watchful eyes of the Japanese Government-General of Korea. Those newspapers were forced to shut down or suspended, and their employees were arrested. Sohn Kee-chung is still one of the most loved athletes of all time in Korea.

stories.title: Daeheung Theater
stories.audioTitle: Daeheung Theater and The movies of the good old days.
stories.script: Daeheung Theater and The movies of the good old days.  The first movie theater in Korea was 'Danseongsa'. It opened in 1907. It was followed by Umigwan, Gyeongseong Theater, Hwanggeum Yeonyegwan, which was renamed to Gukdo Theater in the 1940's, and many others. Only those who are middle-aged and older still remember these theaters. And two of the most popular movie theaters were Gukdo Theater on Euljiro-4-ga and Daeheung Theater in Mapo, Seoul.  The 'Daeheung Theater' in the Movie Theme Park still plays 'Daehan News'. It was a three- minute news on Korean government affairs, and all the movie theaters in the past played it before the movie. Every old Korean would still remember watching the news at the theater. The 'Daeheung Theater' in the Movie Theme Park plays the news saying that a farewell ceremony was held for the Korean soldiers who are being sent to Vietnam and that Gyeongbu Expressway is now open. These events took place in the 60's and 70's. You'll also get to see some of the old commercials as well as one of the old movies still paying at the theater. Anyone who was a student during this period would remember watching a movie in one of the in the darkness of the theater. This kind of theater will be a new experience for younger generations who are used to going to multiplex theaters.   In the lobby, there are old movie posters and equipment that were used at the time. The theater also stages performances and events. You can even make a reservation to borrow the theater. The theater with 100 seats can be used also as a lecture hall, singing room, or recreational space just for you.

stories.title: Gyeongseong Station
stories.audioTitle: Gyeongseong Station: A Gateway to the Seoul of the Past.
stories.script: Gyeongseong Station: A Gateway to the Seoul of the Past.  I went to Gyeongseong Station, despite the fact that I got nearly hit by the streetcar several times. The seat in front of me was empty, and I wanted to get rid of the bitter taste in my mouth. Coffee? A good idea. But as I stepped into Gyeongseong Station Hall, I suddenly remembered that I didn't have a penny in my pocket.  This is a passage from the short Korean novel called 'Wings'. The book was written by Yi Sang, one of the most famous poets of the 1930's. This poverty-stricken poet frequented the tea cafe on the second floor of Gyeongseong Station, where he would sit there until the closing hour. Sometimes, he was penniless just like the hero in his novel, and had to turn on his heels at the door. Gyeongseong Station was one of the most popular backgrounds of the poems and novels of the time.  'Gyeongseong Station' opened in 1900, changed its name to 'Namdaemun Station' in 1905 and then renamed back to 'Gyeongseong Station' in 1923. The station building was completed in 1925. It was designed by Tsugamoto Yasushi, one of the students of Tatsuno Gingo, the architect of Tokyo Station in Japan. Although Yasushi insisted that the train station is modeled after Lucerne Station in Switzerland, anyone would agree that it somehow resembles Tokyo Station. For this reason, the Japanese people at that time boasted that Tokyo Station is the best and Gyeongseong Station is the second best in the Orient. Gyeongseong Station is regarded as the most beautiful structure among the ones built during the Japanese occupation of Korea.   It wasn't until 1946 - 1 year after Korea's Liberation from Japan - that the station was renamed to Seoul Station. This is how the station looked like in 1925. It was restored to its original shape and designated 'Culture Station Seoul 284' to serve as a cultural space. Here, the number '284' means that the Old Seoul Station is now a cultural heritage site designed 'Historic Site No. 284'. The tea cafe that Korean poet Lee Sang frequented is also on display in the exhibition room.

stories.title: Bando Hotel
stories.audioTitle: Bando Hotel, the first business hotel in Korea.
stories.script: Bando Hotel, the first business hotel in Korea.  'Daebul Hotel' in Incheon was the first hotel ever built in Korea. It was built in 1889 by a Japanese man, who saw business opportunities in the tourists who flocked to the city after the opening of Incheon Port.  Then which was the first hotel built in Seoul? It was 'Sontag Hotel', built in 1902 in Jeong-dong, Seoul. It was the first European style hotel established by Antoinette Sontag. The building was bestowed to this French-born German woman by Gojong of the Korean Empire and then renovated into a hotel. Neither Daebul Hotel nor Sontag Hotel remains today. The oldest hotel still in service is the 'Chosun Hotel', which is now called the 'Westin Chosun Hotel'. Built in 1914, it was the first hotel furnished with an elevator, European restaurant, buffet and ballroom. This hotel was one of the reasons why Sogong-dong became the center of the new western culture in Korea.  But the first business hotel built in Korea was Bando Hotel. It was built by a Japanese entrepreneur named Noguchi Shitagau. A story has it that he decided to build a bigger hotel right next to the Chosun Hotel after being rejected by the Chosun Hotel for having shabby clothes on. He ended up building an eight-story hotel next to the four-story Chosun Hotel.  After Korea's Liberation from Japan, Bando Hotel was used as the headquarters of the U.S. Forces and lodging for their officers. In the 1950's, Korean politicians used to meet there. Bando Hotel was sold to Lotte in 1974 and replaced by Lotte Hotel, which has been in service ever since. On the first floor of Lotte Hotel Seoul, there is the Hotel Museum displaying the items used at some of the first hotels built in Korea as well as photos of the hotels. It should be easy for you to recognize some of the items if you saw the replica of Bando Hotel in the Hapcheon Movie Theme Park.

stories.title: Gaho Station
stories.audioTitle: Hapcheon Movie Theme Park, The place where you can start a time travel to the past.
stories.script: Hapcheon Movie Theme Park, The place where you can start a time travel to the past.  The Hapcheon Movie Theme Park was first built to film the Korean blockbuster movie titled 'Brotherhood', which was directed by Kang Je-gyu and released in 2004. The movie is about a tragic story of two brothers who were drafted into the South Korean Army at the break of the Korean War in 1950. Hallyu stars Jang Dong-geon and Won Bin played the two brothers, and over 2,500 extras were hired for the movie. For this movie, large film sets were built to reproduce the city of Pyeongyang and streets of Jongno in South Korea. These are the film sets.  They became a popular tourist attraction after the movie became a blockbuster hit. It was only after the release of the movie that people decided to reproduce Seoul in the 1920s during the Japanese Occupation of Korea, Seoul in economic development after the Korean War and also Seoul in the 1970s and 1980s. As a result, these film sets became streets of history and memories as you see today. There is an array of buildings showing the everyday lifestyle of the city as well as the modern politics, economy, society and culture of Korea.   The buildings in these film sets of 'Brotherhood’ were originally built for temporary purposes, but were given street addresses later. Today, there are more than 150 buildings in the film sets, all with an actual street address. Having a street address means that they're registered as a real estate property. Still, the buildings are used for filming movies, and it's fun to watch how they can be changed to serve different purposes simply by switching the hanging board. Inside the buildings, you can enjoy various exhibitions, learn how movies are made and watch old movies.  The theme park also turns into a ghost park during the summer nights. Theculturalheritagecommentatorwilltellyousomeinterestingstoriesaboutthemoviestarswhocameheretoshootafilm.If you're lucky, you might be able to see a filming location in action - all because you're here in the Hapcheon Movie Theme Park.

stories.title: Hwangmae Plain on the Miracle Trail of Hwangmaesan Mountain
stories.audioTitle: Hwangmae Plain Covered with Royal Azalea in the Spring and Silver Grass in the Autumn.
stories.script: Hwangmae Plain Covered with Royal Azalea in the Spring and Silver Grass in the Autumn.  Along with Gayasan Mountain, Hwangmaesan Mountain is often regarded as one of the two most beautiful mountains in Hapcheon. There are quite a few stories behind the name of the mountain. One of them is that the mountain was named after its color. The name 'Hwangmaesan' literally means yellow mountain in Korean.   Halfway up the mountain about 800 to 900 meters above sea level, the area is an extensive plain. The hill area was occupied by a ranch in the past. Today, the whole place is covered with royal azalea in every May. There is a road leading to the entrance to the habitat of royal azalea, allowing cars to enter, and this is one of the reasons why the place is packed with people in early and mid-April. There are wooden decks in the natural garden of royal azalea, making it easier for both children and old people to hike the area.   The top of the mountain is a plain where a ranch used to be with grazing livestock. That's why most of horse riding scenes for many Korean movies and dramas were filmed here.  The place serves as a natural garden of royal azalea in the spring and auto camp with a cool breeze in the summer. It turns into a silver grass field in the autumn and then a land of snow covered trees in the winter. You can drive around the area, but if time allows, it would be a good idea to hike the trail to the top.

stories.title: Guksadang Shrine on the Miracle Trail of Hwangmaesan Mountain
stories.audioTitle: Guksadang Shrine, the place where Muhak prayed for the founding of Joseon
stories.script: Guksadang Shrine, the place where Muhak prayed for the founding of Joseon  'Guksadang Shrine' was where people used to pray to the heavens for the prosperity of the country. There are many shrines all over Korea bearing the same name of 'Guksadang', and most of them are located in a auspicious site. Hwangmaesan Mountain is one of the many mountains where a 'Guksadang Shrine' located.   The Guksadang Shrine in Hwangmaesan Mountain in particular is where a great Buddhist monk stayed to pray for the founding of a new kingdom in the 14th century. During the Joseon Dynasty, local governors held a ritual here every year. Even today, people living below Mosanjae still come here on March 3rd every year to hold a ritual.  Most Koreans know who Muhak was, but not many people know that he was born here in Hapcheon. In Hwangmaesan Mountain, there are many stories about this famous Buddhist monk. The local people call Hwangmaesan Mountain a mountain lacking three things because of him.   While Muhak meditated and prayed in Hwangmaesan Mountain, his mother was the one who took care of him by bringing him food and other necessities. A story has it that when his mother was climbing the mountain as usual, she tripped over a wichuraiana and arrowroot vine. When she fell, she panicked at the sight of a snake in front of her. After she told her son what happened, the Buddhist monk prayed for 100 days that he wanted all the three things removed from the mountain. That's why people still say that Hwangmaesan Mountain is a mountain lacking three things. Needless to say, the three things are wichuraiana, arrowroot vine and snake. But it's just a story, because all the three things can be found in the mountain.  If you stand on the top of Hwangmaesan Mountain, you will see three peaks in a row. They're called 'Sambong' or 'SeoSambong' in Korean. Legend has it that if anyone earnestly prays to the three peaks, three people from his family or descendants including himself can become a sage.  The local people say that so far, two sages were born in Hapcheon. They're Muhak and 'Nammyeong' Cho Sik. Who's the third one? Well, he wasn't born or hasn't shown himself yet. Maybe he will in future.

stories.title: Sungyeol Bawi on the Miracle Trail of Hwangmaesan Mountain
stories.audioTitle: Sungyeol Bawi, the Rock of Purity
stories.script: Sungyeol Bawi, the Rock of Purity  On the Miracle Trail of Hwangmaesan Mountain, you'll see many strangely shaped rocks on Mosanjae. Each of the rocks has an interesting story to tell, adding more fun to the hike.   If you come down the top of the mountain on the opposite side of Dotdae Bawi,  you'll come across a rock named 'Sungyeol Bawi‘. It's the rock at the end of the cliff. The rock is divided in the middle with enough room for a person to pass through, and legend has it that if a person unfaithful in the marriage won't be able to pass through it because the opening will close a little to trap the person.  The myth is somewhat similar to that of the Mouth of Truth in the portico of the church of Santa Maria in Cosmedin, Rome.  Whatever the legend, please don't try to pass through the opening between the split rocks. Even if you're faithful to your spouse, you might not be able to pass through and get stuck if you're too big for the opening. After all, most hikers come here to refresh their mind and body while enjoying the view of the strange bunch of rocks.

stories.title: Mosanjae on the Miracle Trail of Hwangmaesan Mountain
stories.audioTitle: Mosanjae with the Best Feng Shui Site
stories.script: Mosanjae with the Best Feng Shui Site  Mosanjae is a cliff 767m above sea level, located in Hwangmaesan Mountain, which is a little over 1,000m high.   There are many stories about how the cliff was named 'Mosanjae'. But the most interesting story is about the Rainbow Site right under the top of Mosanjae. The name 'Mosanjae' literally means the mountain with a pond in Korean. It was named as such because the Rainbow Site has a pond that never dries up. Since ancient times, the local farmers would come here to pray for rain during the time of a drought, because they believed this to be the best 'feng shui' site in the country. The funny thing is that it always rained after they held a ritual here. In Korea, using an auspicious place like this as a family grave site for your parents or grandparents can make you rich and famous for generations to come. However, there is the downside of causing a drought in the area if anyone uses such place as a burial site. So the townspeople never allowed anyone to use it as a burial site.  If you look at the opposite side from the top of Mosanjae, you'll see a giant rock in the shape of a triangle. The rock is named 'Dotdae Bawi' because it looks like a sail. The word 'dotdae' means sail in Korean. Located at the end of the cliff, it looks like it's going to fall at any moment. If you take a look at the rock from the bottom, you will see why it was named as such.   Once you have seen Dotdae Bawi and the Rainbow Site, why don't you go all the way to the top? Many hikers say that they feel refreshed and more energetic at the top of this mountain.

stories.title: Yeongamsa Temple Site on the Miracle Trail of Hwangmaesan Mountain
stories.audioTitle: Yeongamsa Temple Site, a Sacred Place under Mosanjae
stories.script: Yeongamsa Temple Site, a Sacred Place under Mosanjae  If you follow the signpost to Yeongamsa Temple Site, you will see a big zelkova tree. The 600-year old tree is still there, but Yeongamsa Temple is not. There are no records of when the temple was built or why it was destroyed.   Twin Lion Stone Lanterns are only in three places in South Korea. While both of the Twin Lion Stone Lanterns in two other places are designated as a National Treasure, the Twin Lion Stone Lantern here is designated only as a Treasure. If you take a closer look at the lions, you will see that the paws of both lions were cut off and had to be restored. Some Japanese cut the paws off to take them to Japan during the Japanese Occupation of Korea in 1933, but the local people found out about it and stopped them from taking the paws. It was not designated as a National Treasure because of the damage.   The secrets of the Yeongamsa Temple Site are yet to be revealed, but the temple site still shows some unique characteristics that can't be found in other temples. They include the stone retaining wall holding back the hillside of Hwangmaesan Mountain, which is held in place by driving in a number of square stones like nails, and the pieces of stones with relief carving on them. What makes this temple site more mysterious and beautiful must be that it's located right below Mosanjae, receiving all the auspicious energy from the best feng shui site in Korea.

stories.title: Changuisa Memorial Hall in Hwanggang River
stories.audioTitle: Chunguisa Temple Dedicated to the Souls of Volunteer Soldiers from Hapcheon
stories.script: Chunguisa Temple Dedicated to the Souls of Volunteer Soldiers from Hapcheon  In the early stage of the Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1592, Korea didn't have enough military power to protect the homeland. Men from many regions of the country formed an army of their own to protect their country, and Jeong In-hong was the general who represented the towns of Hapcheon. After being appointed a general, Jeong In-hong led an army of 3,000 to protect Hapcheon and other towns nearby. He and his volunteer soldiers stopped the Japanese forces from getting drinking water from Nakdonggang River, and also protected the farms along the river so that the Japanese can't use them as a source of food. He and his men didn't leave the army until the war was over. For his services to the country, he was appointed to various government positions and then Prime Minister at the age of 84. This memorial hall was built in 2001 in commemoration of General Jeong In-hong and his soldiers. To reach the shrine from the entrance, you must climb four steep flights of stone steps. On the first flight, you'll see a 17m-tall monument and statues of peasant soldiers. On the third flight, there are a lecture hall and an exhibition hall, where an audio guide tells a story of the volunteer soldiers at the time with an array of relics on display. Changuisa Memorial Hall is located at the top of the last flight, housing the mortuary tablets of 113 people, including General Jeong In-hong.   Hapcheon is the birthplace of more than 50 generals who rose fought against the Japanese forces. It was possible because of a great scholar and teacher named 'Nammyeong' Cho Sik. All the generals were students of this great scholar whose hometown was also Hapcheon. Thanks to his teachings, the generals were able to protect also the wooden printing blocks of the Tripitaka Koreana stored at Haeinsa Temple.

stories.title: Hapcheon Dam Water Museum in Hwanggang River
stories.audioTitle: Hapcheon Dam Water Museum and What Hapcheon Dam Created
stories.script: Hapcheon Dam Water Museum and What Hapcheon Dam Created  Hapcheon Dam in Hwanggwang River was completed on the last day of 1988. For the construction of the dam, more than 1,700 people had to move out of the area. Hapcheon Lake was created by blocking Hwanggang River. Today, it serves as a great place for recreational fishing, driving and water sports.   If you walk along Hapcheon Lake, you'l come across the Hapcheon Dam Water Museum. It was established to provide information on Hapcheon Dam, and inform people of the importance of water. The two-story building with a dome has the lake as the backdrop, so the observatory platform on the ceiling commands a picturesque view of the lake. The exhibition hall on the first floor shows the relationship between mankind and water resources throughout the history, while the exhibition hall on the second floor is dedicated to the natural surroundings of Hapcheon and Hapcheon Dam as well as which part of the area had to be submerged for the construction of the dam. The exhibition hall shows details of other rivers in the Korean Peninsula and the water shortage of the world. It also has a model of Hapcheon Dam as well as the process of electric generation on display. It makes the museum a great stop for families with young children.  One more thing has changed with the construction of Hapcheon Dam. The waterside ecology trail along the auxiliary dam below the main dam became a very popular place for taking pictures. When early morning sunlight seeps through the wet fog rolling over the river, you will hear the sound of camera shutter all over the place, since most the photographers come here to capture the very moment. It's their lucky day if migratory birds fly in at the right moment. In the spring, the 40km lake trail from downtown Hapcheon to Hapcheon Dam is filled with cherry blossoms in full bloom. Cherry blossom trees were planted along the trail soon after the completion of the dam, and they create a picturesque view in April every year. Although the trail of cherry blossoms was built less than 30 years ago, it's considered one of the Eight Scenic Views of Hapcheon along with Haeinsa Temple that's been there for over a thousand years.

stories.title: Monument of General Juk Juk in Hwanggang River
stories.audioTitle: A monument dedicated to General Juk Juk of Silla who died for his country.
stories.script: A monument dedicated to General Juk Juk of Silla who died for his country.  The 'Battle of Daeyaseong' was not only an important event in the Koran history, but it was also an interesting and dynamic one as well.   Kim Pum-seok seduced and took away the wife of one of his soldiers, and the soldier was justifiably held a grudge against the Lord of Daeyaseong. So when Baekje invaded the fortress, the soldier betrayed Silla and set the castle on fire. The internal enemy was the reason why Daeyaseong lost half the battle from the beginning. Kim Pum-seok lost the will to fight, and he almost opened the gate to the invading Baekje force, believing the promise of a Baekje general that he will spare his life if he surrenders. However, one of the Silla generals named Juk Juk tried to dissuade him, but Kim Pum-seok and his soldiers still surrendered. The Baekje general didn't keep his promise and killed all of them.   Despite all this, General Juk Juk didn't give up and continued on to fight with the help of the remaining soldiers. Sadly, he didn't stand a chance against the Baekje force.   The name 'Juk Juk' literally means bamboo in Korean.  The general said, My father named me 'Juk Juk', because he wanted me to be a man who is like a bamboo, which never withers even in cold and breaks in half rather than yielding to the wind. So I will never surrender in fear of death! General Juk Juk stood up to his name, and died fighting until his fortress fell to the hands of the enemy.  On the ground where General Juk Juk fought to his death now stands a monument dedicated to his bravery. Named 'The Monument of Loyal Subject Juk Juk' was built in 1644. Just like the Silla general who didn't wither in cold nor yield to a strong wind, this monument still stands to greet those who come to this place to pay tribute to his bravery and loyalty.

stories.title: Yeonhosa Temple in Hwanggang River
stories.audioTitle: Yeonhosa, a temple dedicated to the souls of the war victims 1,400 years ago.
stories.script: Yeonhosa, a temple dedicated to the souls of the war victims 1,400 years ago.  There are traces of an ancient fortress in a low mountain where Hambyeoknu is located. The entire mountain was a fortress called 'Daeyaseong'. It was built by Silla to protect their land against invading Baekje. Despite having this large fortress, Silla was no match for Baekje at the time. At the time when the battle took place in 642, the Lord of Daeyaseong was Kim Pum-seok, the son-in-law of Kim Chun-chu the 29th King of Silla. Both Kim Pum-seok and his wife were killed during the battle, and the fortress was taken over by the invading enemy. In the year following the battle, Silla built Yeonhosa Temple to pray for the souls of Kim Pum-seok and his wife as well as more than 2,000 soldiers who died in the battle.   Eighteen years after the battle, Silla conquered Baekje in 660 and then Goguryeo in 668, ultimately unifying the Korean Peninsula. The man who made this possible was Kim Chun-chu, the king of Silla who lost his daughter and son-in-law in the Battle of Daeyaseong. It is said that the king of Silla vowed to conquer Baekje after losing his loved ones. Driven by anger, he had his revenge by conquering Baekje, and then inevitably Goguryeo after the balance between the three kingdoms was broken.   The story of the battle was shown in a popular TV drama titled 'Queen Seon Deok', which was filmed here.

stories.title: Hambyeoknu Pavilion in Hwanggang River
stories.audioTitle: A picturesque scenery from Hambyeoknu Pavilion: The silver beach of Hwanggwang River
stories.script: A picturesque scenery from Hambyeoknu Pavilion: The silver beach of Hwanggwang River  People say that the history of Hapcheon began with Hwanggang River. Just like Hanggang River runs through Seoul, Hwanggang River cuts through Hapcheon, a city 1.6 times bigger than the capital city. The name 'Hwanggwang' simply means Yellow River in Korean, and it's named as such because the 111km-long river turns brown after a heavy rain.  If you walk down the river from downtown Hapcheon, you'll come across Chwijeoksan Mountain that stands 90 meters tall. And Hambyeoknu Pavilion is located at the foot of the mountain. Built in 1321,  the pavilion has a large rock behind it, engraved with the name 'Hambyeoknu'. It's a calligraphic work of 'Uam' Song Si-yeol, a writer and scholar of Joseon in the 17th century. Inside the pavilion, there are poems and writings by a number of renowned scholars of the time including those of Song Si-yeol, who is regarded as one of the best scholars in the history of Joseon. They mostly wrote about the blue river and beach of fine sand while visiting this place.  The pavilion still commands a breathtaking view of the river.   Hambyeoknu Pavilion is particularly a good place to visit on a rainy day because its ceiling and eaves are designed to channel the rainwater directly to the river.

stories.title: 'Nammyeong' Cho Sik and the Seonbi Road: Noeryongjeon Pavilion and Yongam School
stories.audioTitle: Noeryongjeong Pavilion and Yongam School: The teachings of ’Nammyeong’ Cho Sik, who dared to criticize the king at the risk of his life.
stories.script: Noeryongjeong Pavilion and Yongam School: The teachings of 'Nammyeong' Cho Sik, who dared to criticize the king at the risk of his life.  'Nammyeong' Cho Sik, a renowned scholar of the Joseon Dynasty in the 16th century, built a pavilion named 'Noeryongjeon' in his hometown to teach students there. The word 'Noeryong' is a word from a book written by Zhuang Zhou, an influential Chinese philosopher who lived around the 4th century BC.   In 1955, the King of Joseon appointed Cho Sik as a local administrator, but he refused by sending a written appeal to the king. His written appeal titled 'Danseongso' created quite a stir in the kingdom, and that's what made his famous.   In his written appeal to the king, he wrote: Your Majesty, the country lost ground, the will of the heavens is gone and the trust of the people has already been lost because of the bad decisions you're making in your court. Your mother is wise, but she's just a widow living in the palace hidden away from the world, and you're just a young son of the late king. Now that your people don't know where to turn to, how are you going to bear the burden, and how will you restore their trust in you? He explained that he turned down the king's offer for a government position because he doesn't have enough ability to serve the king, especially when they're in hard time. Needless to say the king was very upset and wanted to punish him, but the government officials dissuaded him. Even the king couldn't slight him.   Cho Sik's appeal to the king is engraved on a large monument at the entrance to Yongam School next to Noeryongjeon Pavilion.

stories.title: Nammyeong Cho Sik and the Seonbigil Trail (Birthplace of Nammyeong)
stories.audioTitle: Nammyeong Cho Sik and the Seonbigil Trail (Birthplace of Nammyeong)
stories.script: Nammyeong Cho Sik and the Seonbigil Trail  Nammyeong Cho Sik is a great scholar of the 16th century from Hapcheon. He was born in the house of his maternal grandparents in Hapcheon in 1501. The site where he was born is called 'Togol', named for its shape resembling a rabbit lying down. This place was prophesied to give birth to a great sage.   Cho Sik moved to Seoul when he was five and then to other cities after his father passed the state examination but returned to his hometown at the age of 26 after his father passed away. When he was 30 years old, he moved to Gimhae where his parents-in-law lived but returned to Hapcheon when he was 45 after his mother passed away. He stayed in Hapcheon, teaching his students throughout his stay until he was 61 years old. Although he was buried in Sancheong below Jirisan Mountain, he spent most of his life in his hometown, Hapcheon.  He always carried around two small bells tied to his coat belt, and a knife in his jacket. He named the bells 'Seong-Seong-Ja'. Here, the word seong is to realize in Korean. And he had a phrase engraved on his knife, which reads: To light up your inside is to have reverence, and to make hard decisions to act is to be righteous. It was his way of saying out loud: I will awaken my mind with the bells for the growth of my mind and spirit and strike down the evils of the world with this knife. This was his belief and philosophy in his life.  He lived out his philosophy, and his teachings have greatly influenced his students. When the Japanese forces invaded Korea 20 years from his death, men from Hapcheon and neighboring towns volunteered to raise an army to protect the country, and most of them were his students. Among his students, there are more than 50 army generals.   One of the most well-known generals was Jeong In-hong, who led an army of 3,000 volunteer soldiers to protect Hapcheon from the invading Japanese forces. Nammyeong Cho Sik was a great teacher to many, and he remained an influential figure even after his death. It may be worthwhile to visit the birthplace of Cho Sik, and to understand what it meant to be a true scholar in the 16th century.

stories.title: Hapcheon Museum: Golden Storytelling Course Trail of Daraguk 2
stories.audioTitle: Hapcheon Museum: The only museum in Korea dedicated to Daraguk
stories.script: Hapcheon Museum: The only museum in Korea dedicated to Daraguk  Hapcheon Museum has the only exhibition room dedicated to Daraguk in Korea. The main hall is designed after the jar tray of Daraguk. Across from this hall is Dara Culture Room, where you can take the stairs to the second floor where Dara History Room is located.  A number of 'swords with ring pommel' decorated with dragon and phoenix were excavated from the Ancient Tombs in Okjeon. One of them was 116cm long, the longest among the similar swords excavated from other sites of the Gaya confederacy. It shows how advanced Daraguk was in iron works. In addition to the swords, the museum also has displays various ironware such as hammers, tongs and whetstone. They tell us that Daraguk was able to build its economic power based on these ironware.  The tomb of a king who reigned during the most flourishing period was restored, and it's displayed in Dara History Room. The royal tomb was made by digging a big hole, covering the surfaces with stones, burying the king and the relics representing his power as a king on one side, and also burying a set of earthenware on the other side. The tomb named 'M3' also included antlers of two or three deers, hinting that the deers were buried as well. However, they are not the spotted Formosean deers that are common in Korea, but moose from Siberia. It's a proof that Daraguk traded with the northern part of the Asian continent.  Forty pairs of earrings were also unearthed from the tombs. None of the ancient tombs of Gaya had this many earrings. The jewelry craftsmanship and decorations are just as elaborate and beautiful as the ones made in other kingdoms and states of the same period. However, one of them is a half a pair, and it's the fanciest one of them all. It seems that only one of the earrings was excavated.

stories.title: Hapcheon Museum: Golden Storytelling Course Trail of Daraguk 1
stories.audioTitle: Hapcheon Museum: The stories told by 1,500-year old relics.
stories.script: Hapcheon Museum: The stories told by 1,500-year old relics.   In the ancient past, the Korean Peninsula was occupied by the three kingdoms of Goguryeo, Baekje, Silla, and also the Gaya confederacy. Gaya was a confederacy of several states. Unlike Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla, Gaya was not a centralized state. The states of Gaya generally considered equal to one another, although 'Geumgwan-Gaya' and 'Dae-Gaya' were the two more powerful states that prospered by trading outside the confederacy.   Around 400 AD, King Gwanggaeto of Goguryeo invaded Geumgwan Gaya. By the way, he was the most well-known king of Goguryeo, commonly known as 'Gwanggaeto the Great' for his conquests and victories among Koreans. Geumgwan Gaya lost the war against the great conqueror and his army. The ruling class of Geumgwan-Gaya fled to Japan and other regions in the Korean Peninsula along Nakdonggang River. One of the groups that fled settled here in Hapcheon and founded the state called 'Daraguk'. Daraguk existed for around 200 years, until it was merged into Silla.  There is not much historical material about Daraguk, save for the ones confirmed in the documents in China and Japan. The lack of historical documents make these relics much more valuable. According to the relics, the kingdoms and states in the Korean Peninsula independently traded with Japan and China.  The relics on display in Hapcheon Museum are a proof that Daraguk was indeed a proud member of the Gaya confederacy in the latter Gaya period.

stories.title: Ancient Tombs in Okjeon: Golden Storytelling Course Trail of Daraguk
stories.audioTitle: Ancient Tombs in Okjeon, the hidden history unveiled.
stories.script: Ancient Tombs in Okjeon, the hidden history unveiled.  There is a hill called 'Guseulbat' since ancient times in one of the low mountains along a tributary of Hwanggang River. It was named as such because the local farmers sometimes found jade beads while cultivating their land, and the name Guseul-bat literally means Bead-Field in Korean.  The historic site of the Ancient Tombs in Okjeon has been regarded as a part of the Gaya confederacy that occupied the eastern and western sides of Nakdonggang River in southern Korea in the period of between the 4th and 6th centuries. However, the tombs found had a different structure from those of other states of Gaya that were excavated in the past. Having different type of tombs means that even though the region was very close to other well-known states of Gaya, it was nevertheless under the reign of another monarch.  These are the most well preserved ancient tombs of the Gaya period. It's because they were relatively kept safe from tomb robbers. While the ancient tombs of Gaya that were excavated in the neighboring region called Goryeong were made by digging a hole, burying the coffin and then placing a slab of stone over it, a wooden board is placed over the coffin instead of a stone slab before covering it with a mound of dirt in the case of the Ancient Tombs in Okjeon. Most grave robbers distinguish ancient tombs by the slab of stone. But no such slabs are found in here, and that's what kept this place safe from tomb robbers whose main interest is usually in royal tombs.  More than 2,500 relics were discovered from the Ancient Tombs in Okjeon. With these relics, archaeologists discovered that the tombs belong to the rulers of 'Daraguk' during the Gaya period. This archaeological discovery was both sensational and controversial at the time of the excavation. Just who were the rulers who were buried here? And what kind of a state was Daraguk, which was never taught in the Korean history textbooks?

stories.title: Haeinsa Sorigil: Nakhwadam
stories.audioTitle: Nakhwadam, the scenic beauty in Hongnyudong that the French ambassador loved.
stories.script: Nakhwadam, the scenic beauty in Hongnyudong that the French ambassador loved.  If you ask anyone who has visited this valley which part of the valley is most beautiful, chances are, he would say 'Nakhwadam' without any hesitation. The roaring waterfall and the strangely shaped rocks all around are what make this place really beautiful. The name 'Nakhwadam' literally means the pond with fallen flowers.  The French ambassador to South Korea Roger Chambard wrote in his will that he wished to be cremated and have his ashes spread here.  He was the first French Ambassador to South Korea. He was sent to South Korea in 1959 and served as the French ambassador to South Korea for 10 years. An archaeologist and linguist who also had a Bachelor of Law and Doctor of Literature degrees, Roger Chambard traveled all over South Korea during his tenure. By doing so, he tried to understand Korea as much as possible.   He frequently visited Hongnyudong Valley because he was particularly impressed by Haeinsa Temple and the Tripitaka Koreana. He wrote in his will: After my death, have me cremated and my ashes spread in my second home, Hongnyudong Valley in South Korea. When he died at the age of 78 in 1982, his ashes were indeed spread in Hongnyudong Valley. For some reason, fallen flowers float in the pool of water and don't get swept away. It could be because so many people have fallen in love with the place.

stories.title: Gilsangam Hermitage and Nakhwadam Reservoir (Haeinsa Temple Temple Sorigil II)
stories.audioTitle: Gilsangam Hermitage and Nakhwadam Reservoir (Haeinsa Temple Temple Sorigil II)
stories.script: Starting from Haeinsa Temple Temple parking lot, the 600-meter stretch along Sorigil offers both beautiful scenery and an accessible walk. Along the path, there is a hermitage nestled beneath the mountain ridge, where stones ascend skyward resembling flames, the Gilsangam Hermitage.  Established in 1972 as one of Haeinsa Temple Temple’s 16 hermitages, Gilsangam Hermitage features the Jeokmyeolbogung, the Shine of Sakyamuni Buddha's Sarira, and Deungsinbul, which draws considerable attention. ‘Jeokmyeol’ denotes the stage of enlightenment, while ‘Bo-goong’ refers to a splendid palace, housing true relics of the Buddha.  When a monk attains Parinirvana in a seated posture and their body remains incorruptible for years, they may be adorned with gold and enshrined as Buddhas ?known as 'Deungsinbul.' Gilsangam Hermitage houses Deungsinbuls from Mongolia, Myanmar, and Sri Lanka. Though the stone steps along the mountain path are steep, it is highly recommended not to miss a visit to Jeokmyeolbogung.  Following Gilsangam Hermitage, visitor can reach the Nakhwadam Reservoir, undoubtedly the highlight of Haeinsa Temple Sorigil. A poet once wrote that fallen flower petals linger near Nakhwadam Reservoir, dancing and swirling rather than easily drifting away.  Ros? Chambard, the former French Ambassador to South Korea, served from 1959 for a decade. He extensively explored various regions of Korea, developing a deep affection for Haeinsa Temple and Nakhwadam Reservoir. He frequented the Hongnyudonggyegok Valley and expressed in his will the desire his ashes to be scattered there upon his death. His wish was eventually fulfilled in 1982.

stories.title: Nongsanjeong Pavilion (Haeinsa Temple Temple Sorigil I)
stories.audioTitle: Nongsanjeong Pavilion (Haeinsa Temple Temple Sorigil I)
stories.script: Haeinsa Temple Sorigil is a 6km-long road that runs alongside the Hongnyudonggyegok Valley, stretching from Theme Park of the Tripitaka Koreana to Yeongsangyo Bridge at the entrance of Haeinsa Temple.    Monk Hoegwang was appointed as the chief monk of Haeinsa Temple in 1918. He, along with Master Choi Dong-sik, identified 19 attractions compared to the folktales passed down from the past. They installed signposts and left their own poems at each location.  The name 'Hongnyu’ implies that the flow of the water in the valley appears red, likely referring to the vibrant and beautiful autumn foliage reflected in the water.  Hongnyudonggyegok Valley was where Choi Chi-won spent his final days. He was a distinguished scholar at the end of the Silla Dynasty. In his youth, he studied abroad in China and attempted to reform his home country but was unable to overcome the class barrier. Consequently, he abandoned government work and came to live in Gayasan Mountain.  Choi built a pavilion called ‘Nongsanjeong Pavilion’ in the Hongnyudonggyegok Valley. It served as his place for reading, practicing, and resting. The name ’Nongsan’ means ‘to cover up the mountain,’ originating from a poem he wrote expressing the idea of living outside the worldly concerns.  Along Haeinsa Temple Sorigil, a dense pine forest is present. Visitors may notice that the bark is peeled off from each pine tree. During the Japanese colonial era, resin was randomly collected from these trees for use in aviation oil and gunpowder. Subsequently, people attempted to gather the inner shells of the trees as a food source during challenging times in the 1960s. Scars from those times remain visible as well.

stories.title: Haeinsa Sorigil: Entrance
stories.audioTitle: Haeinsa Sorigil, a trail that covers 16 of the ’19 Scenic Views of Gayasan Mountain’
stories.script: Haeinsa Sorigil, a trail that covers 16 of the '19 Scenic Views of Gayasan Mountain'  'Hongnyudong' is the narrow valley that leads to Haeinsa Temple in Gayasan Mountain. The name literally means the valley with a red stream of water and it's named as such because the reflection of red autumn leaves on the water creates a picturesque landscape. 'Haeinsa Sorigil' is a six-kilometer stretch of a narrow valley from Daejanggyeong Theme Park to Yeongsangyo Bridge, which is right in front of the entrance to Haeinsa Temple called 'Yeongsangyo'. This is the a beautiful trail that covers 16 of the '19 Scenic Views of Gayasan Mountain'.   Hongnyudong is where Choi Chi-won, a genius scholar of the 9th century, spent the last years of his life. He went to study abroad in the Tang Dynasty at a young age, and he was regarded as one of the best writers even in China. Upon his return home, Silla, he tried to reform his home kingdom that was on a rapid decline. He tried to become a government official, but he couldn't overcome his status in the hierarchical society and lived a life of seclusion here in Gayasan Mountain. One day, he suddenly disappeared after fixing his fir wood staff on the ground of Haeinsa Temple. A folk legend has it that he became a mountain deity.   On Haeinsa Sorigil, you'll pass by a lush pine grove. If you look closely enough, you'll see that the bark every pine tree has been stripped on the waist. The damage was done in the early 20th century by the Japanese forces, who extracted resin from the pine trees to make aviation fuel and chemical materials. Further damage to the trees was done in the 1960's by famine-stricken Koreans, who were left with no choice but to eat the flesh of the tree. Now, why don't you leisurely hike up the trail in Hongnyudong, so you can listen to the nature and follow the tracks left by people some 1,000 years ago?

stories.title: Donggureung: East Nine Royal Tombs in Guri
stories.audioTitle: Donggureung, the Largest Royal Cemetery of the Joseon Dynasty
stories.script: Donggureung, the Largest Royal Cemetery of the Joseon Dynasty  Donggureung literally means the “Nine Tombs of the East”. This royal cemetery was named so because they are located in the east of Seoul, today’s City of Guri.  Joseon Dynasty was built on the basis of Confucian ideology and highly regarded virtues such as loyalty, filial piety and humility. Naturally, the ideology affected all aspects of the Joseon Dynasty including the establishment and management of the royal tombs. As humble Confucian followers, the Joseon kings wanted the tombs of their ancestors to be simple and modest. However, the royal ancestors were regarded as parents of all their people and symbols of the state itself. So, the royal tombs still should be solemn enough to pay maximum respect to them.   That is why the Royal Tombs of the Joseon Dynasty feature comfortably small sizes, giving little burden to the surrounding nature and creating a peaceful harmony with it. Of course, the nine royal tombs in this royal cemetery are no exceptions.   Especially, Donggureung tends to attract more attention than others, because it includes the Royal Tomb of King Taejo, the founder and the first king of the dynasty. This huge royal cemetery was established as his successors built royal tombs near this area for more than 400 years.   Now then, let’s move and meet at each tomb.

stories.title: Donggureung: Sureung
stories.audioTitle: Crown Prince Hyomyeong and His Consort, Queen Sinjeong
stories.script: Crown Prince Hyomyeong and His Consort, Queen Sinjeong  Sureung is the royal tomb of Crown Prince Hyomyeong and his consort. He was the eldest son of King Sunjo, the 23rd king of the dynasty, and his consort was posthumously titled Queen Sinjeong. Traditionally, husband and wife were buried under a single mound in the belief that such burial would help the couple continue the marital relationship even after death. And this tomb is a fine example for this tradition.   According to historical records, the prince was a devoted filial child and an ambitious young man full of reformative ideas. When he was eighteen, he started active participation in political affairs on behalf of his sick father and continued to make distinguished achievements in the political arena in the 19th century. For instance, he tried hard to restore royal sovereignty by counteracting the political influence of maternal relatives. He also maintained politically impartial stance in recruiting capable resources for the government.   Also, he was a talented man of letters and performing arts enthusiast. He wrote many poems and published essay collections. He even wrote lyrics for the musical works and choreographed dances performed in the court.    Unfortunately, the prince died at the age of twenty two before receiving the opportunity to be crowned. Accordingly, his tomb was built as that of a crown prince at first. His tomb was changed later to fit the status of a king, after his son was enthroned to be King Heonjong, the 24th king of the Joseon Dynasty.   Queen Sinjeong  Crown Prince Hyomyeong, the occupant of this royal tomb, died young before he was given an opportunity to be crowned. However, his consort relished a long, prosperous life, and she is generally referred to by her posthumous title Queen Sinjeong. History shows that she was a powerful charismatic figure and actively engaged herself in the state and royal household affairs until her death in 1890 at the age of eighty two.   After the prince died in 1830, an eight-year-old boy born between the prince and his consort was enthroned. The new king, Heonjong, honored his deceased father with a king’s title, and raised his mother’s royal status to a queen dowager. Sadly, King Heonjong died young, too, leaving no heir to succeed to the throne. It was eventually given to a minor royal who had been leading a poor farmer’s life. The farmer king died only fourteen years after he was crowned, again, leaving no heir. By then, Queen Sinjeong was in the status of the queen grandmother and the most senior member of the royal family. It meant that she had the right to appoint the heir to the crown.  After much consideration, she adopted the twelve-year-old son of a distant relative of the royal family, and crowned him into the 26th king of the dynasty. She expected the alliance with the boy king’s biological father to help her remove her political rivals and move ahead with various reform plans. In the following ten years, the two regents drove out corrupted officials and reformed the tax system. Also, they decided to abolish private Confucian academies because their political influence had been a lot of threats to royal sovereignty.   Crown Prince Hyomyeong’s untimely early death deprived him of the opportunity to be king and rule the country as he had planned. Ironically, however, the opportunity was given to his consort. While relishing a long life, she had a large influence in the history of Joseon during the late 19th century.

stories.title: Donggureung: Hyeolleung
stories.audioTitle: A Tragic Chapter in the History of the Joseon’s Royal Family
stories.script: A Tragic Chapter in the History of the Joseon’s Royal Family  Hyeolleung is the royal tomb of King Munjong, the 5th king of the Joseon Dynasty. He is buried with his consort, Queen Hyeondeok, under separate mounds. The mound in the west is the king’s and that in the east the queen’s.  He was the first child of King Sejong, the 4th king of the dynasty who is generally regarded as the greatest king in Korean history. Historic records say that King Munjong was a devoted filial son and a man of great knowledge. Even when he was a crown prince, he played a very important role in the political arena and actively helped his father ruling the country.
