Walk around behind the lions and take a closer look at their hips. The wider hips represent the fecundity of a lioness and the sharp hips next to the female are those of a male lion. This expression of yin and yang demonstrates the wit and wisdom of our ancestors. The writing engraved on the statue says, “Regardless of social rank, a person must dismount their horse here. Visitors and outsiders are strictly prohibited from entering the premises.” The writing expresses the gravity of the place where a portrait of the king was enshrined.  Gyeoggijeon is famous because the main building enshrines the portrait of Taejo Seongge Yi, the founder of Joseon. We have lots of places to see in Gyeonggijeon, including the main building, bamboo forest and Jeonju Sago (historical archives that once stored the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty). Now, let’s enter Gyeonggijeon through the red gate, outer gate and inner gate, one after another. The audio file will continue in front of the red gate.

stories.title: Gyeonggijeon: Hongsal Gate
stories.script: Gyeonggijeon: Hongsal Gate  [Narration] There are three gates to pass through before we reach the main building where the portrait of Taejo Seongge Yi was enshrined. At the entrance to Gyeonggijeon, you will first see the red gate, topped with arrow-shaped wooden spikes between two columns. A yin and yang pattern is painted in the middle of the gate. This red gate is called ‘Hongsal Gate’ in Korean, meaning ‘Red Arrow Gate’. Hongsal gates were generally built at the entrances to shrines, tombs, palaces and government offices to indicate that these places were sacred precincts. The gate is also intended to prevent evil spirits from entering. It is said that Korean ghosts fly and therefore the wooden spikes on the gate would catch them, while Chinese ghosts bounce around on the ground and therefore the door thresholds are high in China to trip them up.  Shall we now move to the next gate, the outer gate? The outer gate consists of three smaller gates, and the gate in the middle is only to be used by spirits. Colorful paintwork under the eaves represents the prosperity of the Joseon Dynasty, and the flower pattern on the inner gate symbolizes the offering of flowers. Please pass through the inner gate and play the next audio file at the main building of Gyeonggijeon.

stories.title: Gyeonggijeon: Jeongjeon
stories.script: Gyeonggijeon: Jeongjeon  [Narration] Here we are at the main building of Gyeonggijeon where the portrait of Taejo Seonggye Yi, the founder of Joseon, is enshrined. The portrait was newly copied in the 9th year of King Gojong in 1872, and it is the only remaining portrait of Taejo. As a formal and elegant shrine for Taejo’s portrait, this building is designated a National Treasure.   In the portrait, King Taejo is depicted wearing a blue royal robe embroidered with golden dragons on the chest and shoulders, sitting on a throne and looking straight ahead. This portrait of Taejo provides important historical data and contributes to the research of portraits from the early Joseon Period. For a moment, shall we listen to the story of how Seonggye Yi founded Joseon?  [Narration] One day, General Seonggye Yi of the late Goryeo Dynasty dreamed a mysterious dream, so he visited the Buddhist Great Master Muhak to ask for help to interpret it.  [Seonggye Yi] I had such a strange dream last night, and I’d like to ask you to interpret the dream. Would you please help?  [Master Muhak] How was the dream strange?  [Seonggye Yi] I dreamt I was passing through a country village and the chickens started clucking and all the householdswere milling rice.   [E]  Sound of chickens clucking and milling rice.  [Master Muhak]  That’s interesting.  [Seonggye Yi]  And then I went into a barn and carried out three rafters. Then I woke up.  [Master Muhak]  Hmm… that is a lucky dream. All the village chickens clucking means that you will soon rise to a high position, and the sound of milling rice means you will be congratulated on your advancement.  [Seonggye Yi]  Then what do you think the three rafters mean?  [Master Muhak]  You laid the three rafters on your back, and they formed a shape that looks just like the Chinese character, ‘Wang’, meaning ‘king’. Do you understand?  [Seonggye Yi]  If so…  [Master Muhak]  Your face has the full spirit of a king. But you should not speak about your dream.  [Narration]  At that time, Goryeo was going through a difficult period, invaded frequently by barbarians from the north and Japanese pirates from the south. Hence, King Gongmin ordered Seonggye Yi to conquer the Liaodong region of China. However, Seonggye Yi withdrew his troops at Wihwa Island on the way to Liaodong and founded a new country named Joseon. Thus the five-hundred-year history of the Joseon Dynasty began with Taejo Seonggye Yi from the Jeonju Yi family.   [Narration]  What do you think of the foundation story of Taejo Seonggye Yi? Telling fortunes by interpreting dreams was common throughout history.  Sharing the positive spirit of Taejo, you may have a good dream today.   We will move now to Jeonju Sago, one of the historical archives of the Joseon Dynasty. After looking around the area, please walk out the inner gate and we will meet again at the small gate on the left.

stories.title: Gyeonggijeon: Jeonju Sago
stories.script: Gyeonggijeon: Jeonju Sago  [Narration] This time, we will introduce you to Jeonju Sago, across the bamboo forest. If you move to the small gate on the left between the inner gate and outer gate, you will see the forest on the right side of the yard. This bamboo forest is famous as a film location, used in TV dramas such as ‘Tears of the Dragon’ and ‘King and Queen’, and so it attracts many tourists. If you keep walking along the road, there is a memorial stone commemorating the preservation of Jeonju Sago. You will find Jeonju Sago on the left. ‘Sago’ is the name of the historical archives that held important national publications. The term ‘sago’ had been used from the last period of the Goryeo Dynasty to the late Joseon Dynasty, and Jeonju Sago was where the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty were preserved. The 2,124 volumes of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty are a precious historical asset and are registered on the UNESCO World Heritage list. The annals contain all kinds of historical facts of the 472-year-period (1392-1863), from the first King Taejo to the 25thKing Cheoljong. Covering many different fields including politics, society, economy and culture, the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty were preserved in sagos in Chunchugwan of Seoul, Chungju, Seongju and Jeonju. However, when the Japanese invaded Korea in 1592, the annals in other sagos were burnt, with Jeonju Sago being the only exception. Thanks to a few government officials, Hongrok Sohn, An-eui and others, the annals of Jeonju Sago were safely removed to Yonggulam on Naejang Mountain. After a while, during the Japanese Invasion in 1597, the building that housed the annals was completely burnt down and the present building was only rebuilt in 1991.  Five hundred years of the Joseon Dynasty! We hope you have an interesting time here, learning about how the details of the long history of the dynasty were protected and preserved through Jeonju Sago.  Next, we will go to King Yejong’s Taesil. Please pass through the gate on your right and walk to the right for about 30 meters.

stories.title: Gyeonggijeon: King Yejong’s Taesil
stories.script: Gyeonggijeon: King Yejong’s Taesil  [Narration] This stop on the tour is King Yejong’s Taesil and the monument which is registered as Jeolla Provincial Folk Material Number 26. From ancient times, when a baby was born into the royal family, the newborn’s placenta was buried in a chamber. This holy place is called ‘taesil’ in Korean. The taesil in Gyeonggijeon is the chamber of King Yejong of the Joseon Dynasty. The place where the taesil was buried was destroyed and the chamber abandoned in 1928 by the Japanese, but the chamber was replaced in its original location in 1970. A foundation stone was surrounded by an octagonal stone railing, and a round stone was placed on the foundation and sheltered with a stone roof. The monument standing next to the taesil has a well-preserved turtle-shaped foundation stone and a cornerstone with a dragon design. The design of the monument is engraved on the front and on the back of the monument writings reveal that this taesil belonged to King Yejong.  There are benches near the walls next to the monument for visitors. It’s a good place to sit and take a rest for a moment, and listen to the breeze rustling through the bamboo forest over the walls. We hope you enjoy the great scenery here for a while.  We will next visit Jogyeong Shrine. Jogyeong Shrine is located just to the left of the restroom near the taesil monument. You can see a tall ginkgo tree standing in front of Jogyeong Shrine, and the view of the tree with the shrine is regarded as the most photogenic spot in Jeonju Hanok Village. In autumn especially, the changing leaves of the ginkgo tree are amazingly beautiful and you wouldn’t want to miss an opportunity to take a picture here! Let’s meet at the Jogyeong Shrine.

stories.title: Gyeonggijeon: Jogyeong Shrine
stories.script: Gyeonggijeon: Jogyeong Shrine  [Narration]  We have just arrived at Jogyeong Shrine, located to the north-east side of the Gyeonggijeon grounds. Jogyeong Shrine (North Jeolla Provincial Tangible Asset Number 16) served the Han Yi, the founder of the Jeonju Yi family, and his wife. The Jeonju Yi family first hadn’t had the shrine of the founder, hence Jogyeong Shrine was built in the 47th year of King Yeongjo’s reign. With the establishment of Jogyeong Shrine, Jeonju became the real homeland of the royal family, rather than an ideological one. The founder of the Jeonju Yi family, Han Yi, served the government during the Silla Period. The founder of Joseon, King Taejo, was the 21st generation of the family and the ancestral tablet here was also written by King Yeongjo himself.   Jogyeong Shrine was repaired in 1854 along with Gyeonggijeon, and when Jeonju Fortress was about to be captured during the Donghak Pleasant Revolution in 1894, the portraits were temporarily enshrined in Wibong Temple before being returned to Jeonju. Later, during the Japanese Occupation period, most of the buildings here were destroyed, with the exception of the main building of Gyeonggijeon and Jogyeong Shrine. The annexes were restored only recently and now, including the annexes Jogyeong Shrine has been completely restored.  Jogyeong Shrine, representing Jeonju, is the source of the Joseon Dynasty! After appreciating the shrine, we will now introduce the Royal Portrait Museum.

stories.title: Gyeonggijeon: The Royal Portrait Museum
stories.script: Gyeonggijeon: The Royal Portrait Museum  [Narration]  The Royal Portrait Museum is located to the right of Jogyeong Shrine. This is the only museum in Korea that specializes in royal portraits and preserves the portrait of King Taejo and relics regarding royal portrait enshrinement. Before we look around together, let us provide you with some information about the museum tour. The museum opens from 9am to 6pm in the summer and from 9am to 5pm in winter, and it is closed on Mondays. The museum has three permanent exhibition halls – Royal Portrait Exhibit, History Exhibit, and Palanquin Exhibit. In the Royal Portrait Exhibit, there are seven portraits of Joseon kings, including the only existing portraits of King Taejo, King Yeongjo and King Cheoljong. The exhibit creates a similar ambience to Jinjeon of Gyeonggijeon. Out of the seven royal portraits, those of King Sejong and King Jeongjo were artists’ impressions, and not drawn from the actual kings. The portraits of King Gojong and Sunjong were painted, copying earlier images of the kings.   In the History Exhibit, there are relics related to the portrait of King Taejo, such as the foundation of Gyeonggijeon, the enshrinement of King Taejo’s portrait, and the history and preservation of King Taejo’s portrait. In the Palanquin Exhibit in the basement, there isa palanquin used in 1771 to enshrine the tablets in Jogyeong Shrine and other palanquins used in 1872 to enshrine the portrait of King Taejo in Gyeonggijeon.   The Royal Portrait Museum offers a variety of exhibitions with detailed guides available, and so it must be an interesting and educational place for tourists to visit.  The Royal Portrait Museum, where the 600 year history of King Taejo’s portrait enshrinement continues! When you finish looking around, we will take you to the last stop in Gyeonggijeon, the annexes. The annexes are all located near the entrance to Gyeonggijeon. If you walk along the walls opposite the museum, you will soon come to the annexes.

stories.title: Gyeonggijeon: The annexes
stories.script: Gyeonggijeon: The annexes  [Narration]  We introduce you this time to the last tour stop in Gyeonggijeon, the annexes. The annexes were built to guard Gyeonggijeon and prepare for ancestral rites. From here, there is a clear view of Jeongdong Catholic Church over the roof tiles of the traditional buildings, so you can take a great photo showing the harmony of the Eastern and Western architecture.   Shall we then go into the annexes? On the left side of the entrance gate, there is an office building named Subokcheong. Starting from Subokcheong, we will take a tour of the buildings in a clockwise direction. Each audio guide will begin with a ringtone and, if you press the pause button after you hear the ringtone, you can play the guide again when you are ready. Let’s begin with Subokcheong. Subokcheong was an office building where low-ranking government officials stayed and took care of ceremonial matters in Gyeonggijeon. Although its interior is similar to a normal house, the building was only used for short periods, in the lead up to important events. According to Sejo Sillok (Annals of King Sejo), one slave and eighteen civilians guarded Gyeonggijeon in turn, and this means that there were always a few people staying at Subokcheong. Next, we’ll move to Macheong, to the left of Subokcheong.  As the name indicates, Macheong is a horse stable, used to house the horses of government officials. When ancestral rites or ceremonies were held at Gyeonggijeon, the attending officials kept their transport, horses, in Macheong. Next, let’s go to Seojae at the back of Macheong.  ‘Seojae’, or in other words ‘Jaegak’, was built besidetombs or shrines in order to hold ancestral rites. It is where the attending officials performed ablutions before holding ceremonies. The ablutions werea purifying ritual, a way to prepare to welcome spirits with a clean body and mind. We will now move to Jegigo.  Jegigo was used for the storage of the utensils used in ancestral rites. Unlike everyday dishes, utensils used in ancestral rites were regarded as holy and they had to be stored in a separate building. The floor of Jegigo was made of wood, built above the ground, to prevent the utensils from getting wet. After looking around Jegigo, please pass through the side gate at the back.  The building on your left is called Yongsil. Yongsil was the mill used to make the food for ancestral rituals. Food used for all kinds of ceremonies at Gyeonggijeon was prepared here with kitchen equipment such as a mortar and millstone. No unclean facilities were allowed to be around the holy cooking place, Yongsil. From here, let’s walk down until we come to the building at the end on the right, Jobyeongcheong.  Jobyeongcheong is where food for ancestral rites was made and stored. Yumil and Dasik were popular Korean traditional foods used for ancestral rites: Yumil is similar to Yakgwa, a honey-coated rice cake, and Dasik is a mixture of powdered grain and honey. We will now go down to Jeonsacheong.  Jeonsacheong is the office of Jeonsagwan who was in charge of food preparation for ancestral rites. Shall we pass through the side gate again and go to Eojeong on the left?  ‘Eojeong’ is referred to as the ‘well of the king’. The water in Eojeong was the drinking water of king and was often used to cook the king’s meals. The wells at Jongmyo Shrine and Sajikdan Altar are also called ’eojeong’because the king used to attend ceremonies there. As eojeong had to be kept clean and sacred, they were generally surrounded by a wall and had a separate entrance gate. Next, we’ll go to Dongjae.  Just like Seojae where we have already been, Dongjae (in other words, Jaegak) is the building beside the tombs or shrines. It is where ancestral rites were prepared and the attending officials performed their ablutions before starting the ceremonies. Let’s pass through the side gate again and move to the last stop, Gyeongdeokheon.  Gyeongdeokheon is the office of the chief gatekeeper of Gyeonggijeon. Gyeongdeokheon is the last stop and our tour Gyeonggijeon will finish here.   Gyeonggijeon, a symbol of Jeonju, as well as a renowned place imbued with Korean cultural heritage! We hope you have had a pleasant time here.  The following tour begins at Choi Myeong Hee Literary Museum. From the entrance of Gyeonggijeon, pass by the tourist information center on the left and turn left again at Jungang Elementary School. Let us introduce you to the writer, Choi Myeonghee, on your way to the museum.

stories.title: Jeondong Catholic Church
stories.script: Our walking tour begins at Jeondong Catholic Church, the largest and oldest modern western building in Jeolla Province. It is open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. and is situated to the right of the Taejo-ro signpost, amidst the traditional houses of the Hanok Village, which creates a mystical atmosphere.  Jeondong Catholic Church is a grand and beautiful piece of architecture that features unusual and rare curved lines. With the bell tower in the center and small belfries on each side, this solid building looks exceedingly splendid. While most visitors are busy taking photos of this picturesque building, the history behind it enhances its beauty beyond its appearance. The secrets begin to be revealed near the wall behind the reception area, to the right of the entrance.  The church was built in honor of the Roman Catholic martyrs of the Joseon Dynasty at the same spot where they lost their lives. A stone monument stands against the wall of the flower garden engraved with 'the first martyrdom place in Korea'. The inscription refers to two pioneering Catholic martyrs, Yun Jichung and Gwon Sangyeon, who were executed at Pungnammun Gate during a period when Catholicism was not accepted in Korea. The soil and stones from Pungnammun Gate, soaked with the blood of the two martyrs, were used as the cornerstones to build Jeondong Catholic Church. The founder of Jeondong Catholic Church is French Father Xavier Baudonet, and a bust sculpture of him stands in the garden on the left. The missionary Xavier Baudonet served as a provost at Jeondong Catholic Church for 26 years since 1889 and was truly believed to be the 'Father' of the church.

stories.title: Jeondong Catholic Church: Statues of Martyrs
stories.audioTitle: Jeondong Catholic Church: Statues of Martyrs
stories.script: After listening the story about Yun Jichung and Gwon Sangyeon from the previous chapter, let’s delve deeper into their history as they play a crucial role in the narrative of Jeondong Catholic Church.  A statue of Yun Jichung and Gwon Sangyeon was placed next to the statue of French Father Xavier Baudonet. Yun Jichung and his maternal cousin, Gwon Sangyeon, were martyred in Korea during the Joseon Dynasty, considering the social context of that time.  Confucianism was deeply rooted in the Joseon Dynasty. It emphasized the concept of ‘Sin-che-bu-mo, Su-ji-bal-bu’, translating to ‘your body, including hairs and skin, are inherited from your parents, cherish them as the beginning of your filial duty.’ During that time, devotedly serving your parents was of utmost importance. People believed that even in times of starvation, holding ceremonies to honor ancestors was necessary. This reflects how significant ancestor worship was in Joseon society.  Now, imagine the reaction when someone deviated from these practices. Especially, scholars who studied and practiced Confucianism not following ancestral rites would be deemed outrageous. However, when Catholic Yun Jichung’s mother passed away, he held a Catholic funeral to honor her instead of the traditional Confucian ancestral rites. This act, amidst the scholars of the Joseon Dynasty, was unprecedented. Consequently, Yun Jichung was arrested by the Jeolla Local Government Office, branded as a disruptor of Confucian society's order, and sent to Jeonju.  Eventually, Yun Jichung and Gwon Sangyeon were executed at Pungnammun Gate at the ages of 41 and 33, respectively. The incident occurred in the Sinhae Year, marking the Sinhae Persecution as the first two martyrs' deaths. Today, Jeondong Catholic Church stands as a significant pilgrimage site, contrasting the historical persecution faced by these martyrs.

stories.title: Jeondong Catholic Church: Inside of Jeondong Catholic Church
stories.audioTitle: Jeondong Catholic Church: Inside of Jeondong Catholic Church
stories.script: Jeondong Catholic Church: Inside of Jeondong Catholic Church  [Narration]  Have you come into the cathedral? The previous audio files talked about quite serious stories, but this time we will be a little more positive.  [Through microphone] Testing, testing~ Firstly, I’d like to announce a few things that you should keep in mind as you look around the cathedral. The walls of Jeondong Catholic Church have been perfectly preserved in their original condition, so please don’t touch or scribble on the walls. Please appreciate them only from a distance. Secondly, I’m sure you already know, but please keep quiet in the chapel. Thirdly, when taking photographs of the building, using a flash can distract people attending mass, so please be careful.    Let me now tell you about the architectural beauty of the cathedral. If you look up at the ceiling, you will notice the curved arch shape, which looks just like that of European churches. Natural lighting floods into the building through the windows on all sides and soft sunlight shines through the colorful stained glass, giving visitors a feeling of comfort, just like a mother’s embrace. The unpainted cathedral walls are the color of the original red and grey bricks, and the color coordination is impressive. For city people, familiar only with concrete buildings, this classical and natural design must warm their hearts. Please have a look at the chapel altar where Mass is held. It was used as the location for a scene in the Korean movie entitled ‘A Promise’, where Shinyang Park and Doyeon Jeon, the lead actor and actress, are secretly wed. One of the most famous quotes from the movie is “If I am asked to name my greatest sin, it must be to have met her, loved her, then left her alone.” If you visit with your loved one, it would be very romantic to confess your love with quotes from the movie!

stories.title: Jeondong Catholic Church: Exterior of Cathedral and Chief Priests Office
stories.audioTitle: Jeondong Catholic Church: Exterior of Cathedral and Chief Priests Office
stories.script: Jeondong Catholic Church: Exterior of Cathedral and Chief Priests Office  [Narration]  Have you come to the back of the cathedral? Visitors normally do not walk around the back of the buildings, thinking there would not be much to see. But Jeondong Catholic Church is different. We will see.   Please look at the dome-shaped exterior of the building from the back. If you have ever visited Myeongdong Cathedral in Seoul, you might be able to see the similarity. Myeongdong Cathedral in Seoul was built in 1882, the first Korean Catholic church, and French Father Poisnel oversaw the construction. This Jeondong Catholic Church was also designed by Father Poisnel, and that’s why the two buildings have a lot in common. The different buildings have the same features! Isn’t it very interesting!?   In the back yard of the cathedral, there is a statue of Virgin Mary holding the body of Jesus Christ. The sculpture expresses the peacefulness of Jesus and the calmness of the Virgin Mary. The statue is an imitation of the Pieta Statue, one of Michelangelo’s three masterpieces. What do you think? We hope that your walk to the back of the cathedral was worth it!    On the left side of the statue, there is an office that was built along with the cathedral. The office was used as the living quarters for chief priests and assistant priests. Founded in 1926, and western in style, it is a valuable historical modern construction along with the chapel.

stories.title: Jeondong Catholic Church: The statue of Jesus
stories.audioTitle: Jeondong Catholic Church: The statue of Jesus
stories.script: Jeondong Catholic Church: The statue of Jesus  [Narration]  A trip to Jeondong Catholic Church with a variety of points of interest! Was it fun? In front of the statue of Jesus next to the cathedral, we conclude our visit to Jeondong Catholic Church. Looking up at the statue, you can see Jesus Christ posed, extending open arms. On the marble sculpture in front of him is written the history of Jeondong Catholic Church. It would be helpful to read the inscriptions on the marble to learn more about the cathedral. Also, this is a photogenic spot where you can take a photo of yourself visiting Jeondong Catholic Church. If you crouch down and have a picture taken with both the statue of Jesus and the cathedral in the frame, you will get the most beautiful shot of Jeondong Catholic Church, so don’t miss the opportunity! If you stay late at the Hanok village, don’t forget to take another picture of the cathedral at night. This is the end of our tour of Jeondong Catholic Church.

stories.title: Gunsan Modern History Museum
stories.script: Gunsan Port, an Archive of Korean Modern History  Gunsan is a city in Jeollabuk-do, Korea, and due to its geographical and historical characteristics it has many cultural heritages of modern Korea. The city is also well-known for its port. Gunsan is located between the West Sea and Geumgang, which is one of the largest rivers in Korea. So for centuries, Gunsan Port has been serving as a hub for trade. In particular, it was where agricultural products from the fertile plains of the south-western regions were shipped to the capital city.   But the city’s optimal location and abundant supply of goods were also the very reason why it was often invaded by foreign countries. In 1899, the Japanese realized the value of the port’s strategic location, and forced their way in to turn it into an international trade port. After the Korea was occupied by Japan, a number of extension and reconstruction works were carried out at the port for efficient operation of Japanese colonial exploitation policy. The Japanese even built railroads and bridges near the port preparing required infrastructures for the system.  After the opening of the port, a huge number of Japanese people settled down in Gunsan. It is said Japanese people accounted for nearly 50% of the city’s population.  So Japanese-style buildings, railroads and bridges can still be seen all over the old downtown area near the port. The traces of the Japanese Colonial Period make up a majority of the modern cultural heritage of Korea. And they’re some of your destinations here in this city.  The first place we are going to visit is the Gunsan Modern History Museum. This museum sheds light on the city’s identity as the center of sea trade and the operation base of colonial exploitation. You'll also learn more about how ordinary people live in this city with arrays of exhibits including replicas of modern shops and mud huts and rickshaws.

stories.title: Former Bank of Joseon
stories.script: A Major Hub of Exploitation  This building was used as the Gunsan Branch of the Former Bank of Joseon.  During the Japanese Colonial Period, banks helped Japanese businessmen to enter the Korean market. They were also involved in the illegal transfers of Korean rice to Japan. They even forced Korean people to sell their land at cheaper prices, and made poor people suffer as loan sharks. In short, banks were a symbol of colonial rule and exploitation, and the Bank of Joseon was at the center of the entire operation.   Now, let’s look at the building. It was designed by a Japanese architect in 1922, featuring classical architecture styles. It’s a two-story building, but the total height of this building is as high as that of four-story building because of the lofty ceilings. As you can see, the building and its sloped roof have a command presence.   A rumor has it that there was a secret path to the sea at the basement of this building. However, there is no way to verify this story now. Because after the Liberation of Korea in 1945, this building was used as a branch office of banks, and it then it was transformed into a bar by a private owner. So, going through of this period of transition, the interior of this building has changed a lot after many renovations and reconstruction works, and it was also damaged by fire several times.

stories.title: Pontoon Bridge
stories.script: Floating Pontoon Bridge  The West Sea has a large tidal range. Sometimes, it reveals mud flats when the tide is extremely low, making it difficult to dock a boat at the pier. And this pontoon bridge is a solution for the problem.   A pontoon bridge is constructed by connecting a long series of decks that float on water. It’s a kind of temporary pier or wharf, but some are used for long periods of time. Only one side of the structure is fixed to the ground, so that the height of the bridge varies by the tidal change.  However, this pontoon bridge at Gunsan Port has witnessed a tragic part of Korean history. It was constructed in 1918, when Japan continued to wage wars after annexing Korea by force. A long period of wars caused severe food shortage in Japan, and to ease this problem, the Japanese government illegally transferred rice from Korea to Japan. The exploitation was carried out nationwide, and nearly 25% of the total harvest was taken out of Korea at this very port. So, this pontoon bridge was built to move as many boats as possible without a break, despite the ebb and flow of the tides.

stories.title: Former Gunsan Customs Office
stories.script: Harmony of Eastern and Western Architecture  This is the former Gunsan Customs Office, which is the most well-preserved building among the modern cultural heritages in this city.   This modern building was constructed in 1908, following the opening of Gunsan Port. As the international trade began in Korea, the government established a customs office in Gunsan, and this building was constructed by domestic funds. Since the Japanese Colonial Period, taxes for products traded at Gunsan Port were set and collected at this office.  Allegedly, this building was designed by a German architect, but it displays unique characteristics of modern Japanese buildings which combined various European architectural styles. For example, it has a Gothic roof and Romanesque windows, and the protruding eave at the entrance is in English style.   The inner part of the building consists of a hall at the center and several rooms on each side. In particular, this building has many windows, and it shows the Japanese architectural characteristics as well. The humidity is pretty high in Japan, so Japanese buildings usually have a lot of windows to improve natural ventilation.  This building continuously functioned as the customs office, until the current office building was built in 1993. Now, the former building is used as an exhibition hall.

stories.title: Haemanggul
stories.script: Finding Peace in Haemanggul  Haemanggul is a tunnel that links Jungang-ro in front of the formal Gunsan City Hall and Haesin-dong, which was the center of fishing industry. The hemisphere tunnel is 4.5 meters high and runs through for 131 meters.   When Korea was ruled by Japan, many construction works were carried out to build diverse infrastructures in Gunsan. For example, as a part of the Gunsan Port improvement work in1926, the cargo area was expanded, and more pontoon bridges and storehouses were built near the port. This tunnel was established at that time, and was opened in October of the same year.   During this period, Gunsan was frequently visited by many people and the trade and business were in high gear. The Japanese colonists wanted to build a tunnel linking the downtown and the port, so that they could deliver the goods and products to the port in a faster and easier way.  This tunnel still had to face more adversities even after the independence of Korea. During the Korean War, it was occupied by the North Korean forces stationed in Gunsan, and was used as their commanding post. It became a target of an intensive attack by the Allied Forces, and a number of bullet marks still remain at the entrance demonstrating the harsh battle of that day.  After all, Haemanggul is now in peace. Its vicinity is also very quiet, providing a good walking trail for visitors. If you pass the tunnel and follow the walking path again, you will find an observatory at Wolmyeong Park, where you can see Geumgang meeting the West Sea.

stories.title: House of Hirotsu
stories.script: Splendid Trace of the Dark Period  As Gunsan was populated by many Japanese people during the colonial period, many of their houses still remain in the city. This house is one of the examples. It was once owned by a Japanese merchant named Hirotsu, who ran a draper’s shop and made a fortune by exporting rice and speculative investments. He grew to a well-off merchant in the city and even became a member of city council.   Showing off his wealth, he constructed a two-story wooden house accompanied with a large courtyard in a rich village. His house displays the original characteristics of Japanese residence. It consists of two-story main building attached by a one-story guesthouse, and a courtyard located between these two buildings. The entire house is surrounded by tall outer walls, and the gate stands on one side of the walls. Interestingly, you can’t see the entrance to the main building from this gate.   The inner courtyard is a typical Japanese garden. It is full of flower trees, juniper trees and natural stones, and is decorated with a stone pagoda and lantern standing between the trees. Also, there is a pond, presumably filled with koi fish in its heyday.  After the Liberation of Korea, this house was used as an employee’s house of a private company, and later it was featured in some Korean movies as well.  There are many more Japanese houses left in the neighborhood. So, take a walk around the area and imagine how this village was like in the modern times.

stories.title: Dongguksa Temple
stories.script: Japanese-style Buddhist Temple  Originally, Dongguksa was a Buddhist temple named Geumgangsa, established by a Japanese monk in 1913. It is the only survived Japanese-style Buddhist temple and it consists of the main hall, monk’s living quarters, and a belfry. Its name was changed to Dongguksa after the Liberation of Korea in 1945  Followed the architectural style of the Edo Period of Japan, the main hall has a steep roof and many windows. Its eaves are simply painted in black and white, while the eaves of Korean traditional temples are decorated with multiple colors. You might notice this hall is attached by a corridor, and it leads to the living quarters for monks.   The temple has a Japanese garden as well, and there is a bamboo grove as a part of this garden. It is said that these bamboos used to grow bigger, but it gets smaller due to the changes in environment.   The bronze bell in the belfry was made in Kyoto, Japan, in 1919, and moved to this temple. Unlike Korean Buddhist bells, it sounds for a short time at a high note. Also, a writing that praises the forced annexation of Korea is engraved on its body, indicating the tragic history of Korea.   Last but not least, don’t miss the unique alley on the way to the temple. It will provide you a pleasant walk, accompanying with art studios and galleries. The walls in this alley are splendidly decorated with murals and artworks, and interesting store signs will catch your eyes.

stories.title: Seonyudo Ferry Terminal1
stories.script: Gogunsan Islands, the Shield of Gunsan  Welcome to Seonyudo! This is the starting point of your journey to Gogunsan Islands.   Gogunsan Islands refer to an archipelago located about 50 kilometers from the city of Gunsan in Jeollabuk-do. There are 16 inhabited islands and 47 uninhabited islands in the archipelago, including Munyeodo, Jangjado, Daejangdo, Sinsido, Yamido, and Gwallido.   Munyeodo used to be famous for large salt farms, and Gwallido is famous for its coasts with oddly shaped rocks. As for Jangjado, the island has an interesting and yet tragic story about a woman was turned into a rock after waiting for her husband for a long time.   In addition to the beautiful nature and interesting stories, Gogunsan Islands have been an important place for Korea as the center for international trade and national defense. It’s because the islands are right in the middle of a sea route taken by Japanese, Chinese, and even Arabian merchants. So while the islands served as a trade hub in times of peace, they were one of the first regions to be taken over by the enemies during a war.   It’s time to have a short trip to the islands, and your first destination is Seonyudo Island.

stories.title: The Gunsan Naval Base
stories.script: Seonyudo, the Shelter for Admiral Yi Sun-sin  This is called the Gunsan Naval Base, because it’s where navy forces were stationed centuries ago.  For the longest time, Seonyudo had served as outpost as well as a hub for maritime trade. It’s mostly because the island is located right in the middle of a sea trade route in Northeast Asia, and also the safest port in the West Sea of Korea in terms of storms. These features made it an important strategic location in Korea. That’s why most of the ancient Korean kingdoms that ruled over this region had their army and navy stationed on this island.  The Joseon Dynasty was no exception. The kingdom built a navy port here on this island to defend against invaders, namely the Japanese. Among Koreans, the island is most famous for being the island where Admiral Yi Sun-sin rested with his soldiers and sailors. He's one of the most revered historical figures in Korea, because he had defeated the Japanese fleet numerous times at the end of the 16th century. He's also known as one of the “Three World’s Greatest Admirals of All Time”. He’s also famous for keeping a diary widely known as the ‘War Diary’ in Korea. In the diary, he says that after winning a naval battle against the Japanese, he and his men would come to Seonyudo to recuperate and write a draft for an official report to the King.

stories.title: Seonyudo Ferry Terminal2
stories.script: Seonyudo, the Flower of Gogunsan Islands  Seonyudo is the most visited island in the archipelago. Its name literally means ‘the playground for the gods’. It was named as such because of the breathtaking scenery.   The most beautiful scenic places in and around the island are called the “Eight Scenic Views of Seonyu”. As their title suggests, they are definitely the must-see attractions.  The first scenic view is Mangju Falls. It has 7~8 streams falling from Mangjubon Peak, but they're visible only after a heavy rain. The second scenic view is Woryeongbong Peak on Sinsido Island nearby. It’s famous for its gorgeous autumn leaves. Other scenic views include the Chinese nettle tree standing alone on a beach, and the three inhabited islands located to the west of Seonyudo.  But the most beautiful sight of all is the sunset viewed from the island. The beautiful sunset over the nearby islets is truly a sight to behold.

stories.title: Sandbar and Wild Goose Island
stories.script: White Sandbar with the Vitality of Nature  This sandbar is formed naturally by the tides between the main island and nearby islets, which are all connected by the bar of sand. It’s one of the finest quartz sand beaches in Korea, and the glitter of the sand is why people call it the ‘White Sandbar’. It’s nothing short of a work of nature.  The beach stretches for about 3 kilometers and the width is about 200 meters. Thanks to the sandbar, the water is shallow, making it one of the best beaches for a family vacation.  The surrounding natural environment is awesome as well. Mangjubong Peak stands at the end of the beach, and small islets are dotted throughout the sea. You’ll also find a wide range of sand dune plants growing in the beach, making it an ecologically valuable place as well.  In between Mangjubong Peak and Seonyudo Port, there is a small islet formed by sedimentation of quartz sand. It is called a ‘Wild Goose Island’, because it looks like a sitting goose. You might not find this small islet very attractive, but it is to rare and endangered species.

stories.title: Mangjubong Peak
stories.script: Missing the King  This is Mangjubong Peak, located in the northernmost part of Seonyudo Island. It’s consisted of two rocky peaks, and it is said that those peaks look like a woman lying down with loose hair. The highest point of Mangjubong is 152 meters above sea level, and it commands a great view over the sea.   The peak is famous for Mangju Falls, which is one of the Eight Scenic Views of Seonyu. With seven to eight streams falling from the top of the peak, the waterfall offers a magnificent view particularly on rainy days.   Mangjubong has some interesting stories to tell, just like other beautiful sites in Korea. In Korea, scenic spots are named after a story.  One of the stories is about an official who was exiled to this remote island. During his long exile, he climbed the peak every day, longing to see the King again. Hence the name Mangjubong, which means “the peak for missing the king” in Korean.  There is another story for the origin of the name. A prophetic book written around the 15th century said that the founder of a new dynasty would come to this island and build his capital here. A young couple living in the island believed the prophecy, and they went up to the peak every day waiting for the new king. However, the king never came, and they were so disheartened that they were turned into rocks. The big rock is called the ‘Husband Rock’, and the small rock is called the ‘Wife Rock’.

stories.title: Oryongmyo
stories.script: Oryongmyo, the Traditional Shrine  Oryongmyo is a shrine hidden from the view in the southern part of Mangjubong Peak. There are actually two shrines in Mangjubong, and the one in the lower part is called “Oryongmyo”, which means the “dwelling place of five dragons”.  This shrine was once the biggest one on the west coast of the country, and it’s where people held rituals praying for good catch and safe return of seamen. There were music and dance at the rituals that were held regularly. The local people even invited famous entertainers to perform at their rituals. But the tradition is not observed any more.  As its name suggests, this shrine has a story about five dragons. Once upon a time, a ship delivering roof tiles stayed at this island to take shelter from a storm. The captain of the ship had a dream while he stayed here. In his dream, the dragon god told him that the violent storm will cease if he put five roof tiles on the roof of the shrine. He woke up and did what the dragon god told him. To his amazement, the storm really subsided.  The other shrine has a unique story as well. A couple living in the island had a daughter who never opened her left hand. When the girl grew up, her parents found a man for her to marry. But the girl went missing, and was soon found dead at the shrine. The grief-stricken parents collected her body, and saw the word ‘King’ written on her left palm which never opened in her lifetime. They realized that their daughter was destined to marry the king, but it was too late. All they could do was hold a ritual at the shrine to comfort her soul.

stories.title: Chobun Park
stories.script: Affection and Respect at the Grass Graves  This is Chobun Park, where you can learn about the unique funeral rituals of the southern regions of the Korean Peninsula.  Seonyudo has a tradition of holding funeral services, twice. When someone dies, the corpse is placed on a heap of stones or wood to be covered with straws, and then tied with straw ropes. The locals call this type of grave the ‘chobun’, meaning “grass grave”. After making the grass grave, several branches of pine tree is placed near the grave. It was to prevent animals from harming the body, as well as for the descendents to show respected to the deceased.  The actual funeral service is held two or three years later after the grave is made. They would separate the bones from the flesh at the grass grave, and then clean and bury only the bones.  This type of funeral service originated from the ancient practice of keeping the corpse in a place for a while before the actual burial. Also, it is related to the traditions that were observed in this island. They never buried the dead at the same place where their ancestors were buried, and they didn’t dig the ground during the first month of the year.   Moreover, the tradition was a way of expressing survivor's deepest love for the deceased. The reason being is that when they had a death in the family while they were fishing in the sea, they couldn’t be at the deathbed. So they wanted to hold the funeral service in the sincerest way, by taking care of the grass grave for a long period of time.

stories.title: Jangjado Island
stories.script: Jangjado Island  Jangjado is a quiet island on the east of Seonyudo. It’s a small island, but it offers a beautiful view since it’s covered with rocky hills.   You can either walk or ride a bicycle to cross the bridge leading to the island. There is a small, peaceful island village over the other side of the bridge. Despite its small size, this island used to be one of the major ports in the West Sea of Korea. It's because the island served as an excellent shelter for boats and seamen against unexpected typhoons and storms.  The sea around the island used to be rich with fish. So the area offered a beautiful night time view, with a countless number of fishing boats that light up the surface of the water with lamps. That’s why it used to be one of the Eight Scenic Views of Seonyu.   Sadly, the island is not as lively as it once had been today. So enjoy the serenity of this simple village, and the peace of mind instead.

stories.title: Munyeodo
stories.script: Munyeodo, the island of diversity  Your last destination is munyeodo island, where you’ll see various life styles of the island. To reach the island, however, you need to cross Seonyu-daegyo bridge. The name of this island means a female shaman and the origin of this name is quite interesting. The main mountain of this island faces small islet called Jangusam-seom and the shape of these islet resembles a Jangu or the hourglass drum of Korea. There is another islet in front of Munyeodo and it looks like a wine glass.  Traditionally Korean female shamans usually play musical instruments and dance during a ritual. And the shapes of the three islands reminded people of a female shaman performing a ritual.   By the way, this island used to be famous for salt farms until the mid 20th century. However, the salt farm industry dwindled and the last salt farm of the island closed in 2003. So only the old deserted salt farms are what we can see today.  Take a walk along the salt farms in the southern part of the island. And you’ll come across a small beach at the end. The beach is covered with pebbles instead of sand. And it’s regarded as one of the hidden beauties of this island.

stories.title: The Donghak Peasant Revolution Memorial 1
stories.script: Donghak, the Incomplete Revolution 1  [Narration] This is the Donghak Peasant Revolution Memorial.  The Donghak Peasant Revolution began at the end of the 19th century during the Joseon Dynasty. The nation was going through major changes at the time. In addition to the modernization, the country was being invaded China and Japan, and the dynasty could no longer ignore the encroachment of powerful European nations either. The corrupt government was incapable of coping with changes. So peasants joined the movement to reform their country, and restore sovereignty.  In many aspects, it was similar to the French Revolution. However, there was one major difference between the two. Unlike the French Revolution that was won by the bourgeoisie, peasants were at the core of the revolution. This is the main reason why the movement is still highly regarded.  What is ‘Donghak’? It literally means “Eastern Learning”, but it gradually evolved into a religion in Korea. The term was first introduced at the end of the 19th century, to teach people that they’re all sons and daughters of the Heavens”. The main purpose of the doctrine is to make people understand that everyone should be respected equally, since they all share the same root. It was a modern idea based on equality and humanism, but it also aimed at countering foreign influence and achieving complete independence of the nation.  And Jeongeup is where it all started. They even built a memorial to commemorate the historical importance of the revolution. In the lobby, you’ll see an old persimmon tree. It was brought to this place from Malmok Marketplace, where the first assembly of peasants was held. On the first and second floors, you’ll see a number of exhibition halls showing how the country looked like during the time and how the revolution took place, in a chronological order.

stories.title: The Donghak Peasant Revolution Memorial 2
stories.script: Donghak, the Incomplete Revolution 2  [Narration] Welcome to the historical site of Donghak Peasant Revolution. But before we go on, you might want to learn a little about the revolution.   The revolution began in 1894 here in Jeongeup. The local governor at the time was Cho Byeong-gap. He was a corrupt and vicious official who made the local people’s lives a living hell.  The peasants couldn’t take the abuse anymore because suffered the most, and they charged in to the government building to drive him out.   That’s how everything started. After their first victory against the government forces, they continued to conquer other cities. The central government eventually conceded their demand for reform. The peasants proposed twelve reform articles, including the abolition of the caste system, punishment of corrupt officials, and improvement of the taxation system.  It seemed as though the peasants have succeeded, but the government ended up bringing in a foreign army to drive the peasants away because high ranking officials were afraid that the revolution would spread beyond control.  The foreign army was from Japan, and they ended up killing nearly 350,000 peasants in the process of putting an end to the revolution.   So it was an incomplete revolution. The story begins from the Donghak Peasant Revolution Memorial.

stories.title: Hwangtohyeon Battlefield
stories.script: The Victory of People  [Narration]  This is the Hwangtohyeon Battlefield. This is a monumental site where the peasants defeated the government forces.  The future seemed bright for the peasants when they took over the government building, drove away the governor, and shared food with the poor, heavily taxed people. The newly appointed governor also gave meat and wine to the peasants, and promised that those involved in the incident won’t be held responsible. The peasants went home. But after the mob dispersed, the governor had many peasants arrested in order to catch the leader, and coerced the followers of Donghak.   After hearing about this, more peasants revolted and asked the government to reform the system. More than 4,000 peasants came to Hwangtohyeon under the leadership of General Jeon Bong-jun, and a battle between peasants and government soldiers took place.  The peasants won the battle, and they proceeded to conquer other nearby areas. Their victory at Hwangtohyeon fueled the revolution.  That’s why the Hwangtohyeon Battlefield was officially recognized as a historical site. Here, you’ll see a number of other historical monuments, such as Korea’s first peasant revolution tower, the statue and shrine of General Jeon Bong-jun, and an exhibition hall of artifacts.

stories.title: Jusan Village
stories.script: The Movement Conspiracy  [Narration]  This is Jusan Village! This is where people prepared for the Donghak Peasant Revolution. The village has three historical sites related to Donghak. Let’s go take a look.   The first one you’ll see is the Donghak Revolution Conspiracy Monument, built in 1969 at the village entrance. They built this monument after finding documents on how they came up with the plan to revolt.   Further inside the site is a memorial tower. It was built in 1994, to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the Donghak Peasant Revolution and for the memory of the peasants who died fighting.   And lastly, there is the house of Song Du-ho. The house is where the twenty leaders of the Donghak Peasant Revolution vowed to work together and signed their name on a document.  The list of conspirators was discovered in December 1968 at the house of a person named Song Hu-seop.  They even wrote down the month of their meeting: November 1893. The date is before the first uprising, meaning that the uprising was carefully planned. For this reason, it's a document of high academic value.

stories.title: Malmok Marketplace
stories.script: A Persimmon Tree and Jeon Bong-jun  [Narration]  This is Malmok Marketplace. It used to serve as a center of trade, where merchants from other regions came to buy and sell commodities. But something very extraordinary happened here on January 10, 1894. Thousands of angry peasants suffering under the tyranny of the local government came to this place. The records have it that it’s where General Jeon Bong-jun, the leader of the movement, gave a very moving speech, telling the peasants that they need to rise up. All the angry peasants yelled in agreement.  There is a legend about the assembly. After his speech, General Jeon Bong-jun sat down on the ground and leaned his back against an old persimmon tree in the marketplace. And as soon as he sat down, the branches stretched down as if to protect him.  The story shows the affection of the peasants for General Jeon Bong-jun, and their appreciation for their leader in fighting against the corrupt government. The persimmon tree has been a landmark of this place for many years. But it was moved to the Donghak Peasant Revolution Memorial after it was knocked over by a typhoon in 2003.

stories.title: The Old House of Jeon Bong-Jun
stories.audioTitle: The Old House of Jeon Bong-Jun
stories.script: We Are the Children of the Heavens  [Narration] This is the old house of General Jeon Bong-jun, the leader of the Donghak Peasant Revolution.  He was a short man born from a poor noble family in Gochang.  His family was so poor that they had to move quite often ever since he was a child. When he finally settled down in this town, he opened a small school to teach children and made a living by selling herbal medicine and working as a ghostwriter. He was leading an ordinary life until he learned about Donghak and the reformation. He joined the school of Donghak in 1890. And he soon became the leader of the Jeongeup branch school.   He tried to reform the society based on the ideals of equality, which are what Donghak was mostly about. That's why he volunteered to lead the Donghak Peasant Revolution.  But his dreams were shattered when the revolution came to a failure. He was arrested in Sunchang as the leader of the revolution, handed over to the Japanese army, and executed by hanging in Seoul.   He died fighting for a cause, but his small house is still here in this town.

stories.title: Irrigation Resorvoir
stories.script: Destroy the Embankment  [Narration]  This site used to be an irrigation reservoir used by the farmers in Jeongeup, Jeollabuk-do. Ironically, it’s also one of the main causes of the Donghak Peasant Revolution in 1892.   It all started when Cho Byung-gab, the local governor at the time, ordered people to build an embankment right below the reservoir for no good reason. He not only didn’t pay the peasants for the labor, but he also charged them for using the new reservoir they didn’t need. To make things even worse, the rice fields began to be flooded when it rained hard because of the second reservoir. The peasants suffered.   Cho Byung-gab collected too much tax, stole from people by accusing them of a crime they didn’t commit, and even killed those who protested. The angry peasants charged into the government building and drove the governor away. That was the beginning of the Donghak Peasant Revolution.

stories.title: About the Trail Course
stories.script: About the Trail Course  The Gwanghalluwon Garden is the background of “The Story of Chunhyang”, a Korean love story about a young couple named Chunhyang and Mongnyong. It’s also a traditional garden of Korea, with the place landscaped in a way to take the shape of an original garden of the Joseon Period.   Traditionally, gardens in Korea have been landscaped to blend in with the natural surroundings, and they usually included a wooden pavilion, trees, and lake. The trees and other parts in a garden were carefully arranged and located in a way to form a representation of people’s idea of a utopia, or in some cases, loyalty to the king.   As for the Gwanghalluwon Garden, it’s a representation of a utopia. So this can be your chance to see and stroll in the Korean version of utopia.

stories.title: Wanwoljeong Pavilion (Gwanghallu Pavilion, Namwon)
stories.script: Wanwoljeong Pavilion  Upon entering Gwanghalluwon Garden, the first structure you encounter is Wanwoljeong Pavilion. Constructed in the early 1970s as part of the renovation of Gwanghalluwon Garden, Wanwoljeong Pavilion means Pavilion for Enjoying the Moon. Positioned with its pillars extending over a pond, Wanwoljeong Pavilion is also referred to as a water pavilion, adding charm with its reflection in the water. Climbing up to Wanwoljeong Pavilion, one can view the moon rising over the pond and enjoy the beautiful scenery of Gwanghalluwon Garden from behind.  Visitors initially seeing Wanwoljeong Pavilion might mistake it for Gwanghallu Pavilion, but it could be aptly described as a space substituting for Gwanghallu. Since Gwanghallu Pavilion, designated as a treasure, has restricted access for visitors, it's challenging to appreciate Gwanghalluwon from the pavilion. However, the view of Gwanghalluwon from beneath and atop Wanwoljeong Pavilion is incomparable. Ascending Wanwoljeong Pavilion and looking towards the lake, you'll nod in understanding why Joseon's nobility, Yangbans enjoyed their time in pavilions, indulging in the arts. Wanwoljeong Pavilion is open to the public year-round, and it is especially welcoming during the annual spring Chunhyang Festival, making it a familiar spot for tourists.

stories.title: Ojakgyo Bridge
stories.script: Ojakgyo Bridge  The name of the girder bridge between Wanwoljeong and Gwanghallu is ‘Ojakgyo’. This name literally means “the bridge of crows and magpies”, and this bridge was mentioned in a Korean folk story that’s been told for many centuries.   The story goes something like this: Once upon a time, a married couple was punished by a god to live on the opposite sides of the Milky Way. They were allowed to meet only once a year, on July 7th, in the middle of the Milky Way. But they couldn’t be reunited even on the promised date, because they didn’t have a bridge between them. Their sad story was known to all, even the crows and magpies. So the birds flew up to the Milky Way to form a bridge with their bodies. And people started calling the bridge ‘Ojakgyo’.  Then what’s the bridge doing here? The ancient people regarded this garden as the palace on the moon, and called the nearby lake the Milky Way. So they started calling this bridge 'Ojakgyo’, because it’s built over this little Milky Way.  A legend has it that couples who cross this bridge will have healthy children and love each other forever.

stories.title: Gwanghallu Pavilion
stories.script: Gwanghallu Pavilion  Just across the Ojakgyo Bridge is the Gwanghallu Pavilion, which is located right at the center of the garden. Again, this garden means the “Moon Palace” of people’s imagination. The scenery of the place is as beautiful as its name implies. No wonder the author of Chunhyangjeon chose this place as the main scene.   The original pavilion was built in the 1400s, but it was burned down in a war. So this is actually a reconstructed version of the original built in the 1600s. It’s still the oldest building in the garden.

stories.title: Chunhyang Shrine (Gwanghallu Pavilion, Namwon)
stories.script: Chunhyangsadang Shrine  Given that Gwanghalluwon Garden is where Chunhyang and Mongnyong fell in love, there is a space dedicated to commemorating Chunhyang. This is Chunhyangsadang Shrine, established to honor Chunhyang's integrity. The gate leading into the shrine is named Dansim Gate, which means Wholehearted Devotion to One's Love. Inside the shrine, a portrait of Chunhyang is enshrined.  Built during the Japanese occupation, Chunhyangsadang Shrine subtly embodies the secret desire for national independence. Our ancestors aimed not only to emphasize external beauty when creating something but also to imbue it with meaning. For example, if you look closely beneath the hanging board, you can see a carved rabbit riding on a turtle, referring to the well-known Pansori (epic chant) Sugungga or The Tale of the Underwater Palace. In Sugungga, the rabbit symbolizes wisdom, while the turtle represents loyalty. Given the historical context of the Japanese occupation, it's reasonable to interpret the symbols of the rabbit and the turtle, along with Chunhyang's integrity, as a desire for national independence.

stories.title: House of Wolmae
stories.script: House of Wolmae  The last stop you’ll make is the House of Wolmae. Follow the path on the left side of the front gate to the garden, and you’ll see an adult-sized swing. Go past that, and you’ll reach a small straw thatched house where Wolmae lived. Wolmae is the name of Chunhyang’s mother, so this is also Chunhyang’s home.  Can you see the life-size dolls designed to look like Chunhyang and Mongnyong?   You’ll see them in the middle of the pond, with a stone jar in front of them. The jar is there for visitors to toss a coin into, and wish for long-lasting love. A song will be played if your coin goes into the jar. But it won’t be easy to score a goal.  This house is the last destination of your tour of the Gwanghalluwon Garden. We hope you have enjoyed your tour of a traditional Korean garden. Thank you.

stories.title: Chapter of First Encounter
stories.script: Chapter of First Encounter - Chunhyang and Mongnyong, Korea’s Romeo and Juliet  Welcome to Chunhyang Theme Park.   This theme park celebrates “The Story of Chunhyang”, a Korean love story about a young couple who come together despite overwhelming adversities. Along with Gwanghalluwon Garden, it is one of the main tourist attractions in Namwon. It has recently become more popular among foreign tourists after being featured in a number of popular TV series and movies.  Chunhyang was the name of a beautiful young girl who fell in love with a young man from a family of much higher social status. Their love story resembles that of Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet, although the stories have a different ending. Just as Romeo and Juliet fell in love despite their family feud, Chunhyang and Mongnyong fell in love and overcame the gap in their social status. Instead of taking a tragic turn of events, they lived happily ever after.  Chunhyang Theme Park consists of five areas, each representing a chapter of the story. This is the very beginning of the story where the couple meets for the first time. The story continues on to a pledge, love and separation, trials and tribulations, dramatic reunion, then culminates in a happy ending for the two love birds. Besides the story, the park also offers many activities and shows for you to enjoy.

stories.title: Chapter of Vows
stories.script: Chapter of Vows - Where an Everlasting Love was Born  Do you see the ring-shaped structure at the entrance? It's where the Chapter of Vows, the second chapter of Chunhyang Theme Park, begins. This area includes the Fence of Love, Fence of Vows, Altar of Vows, and a swing, each representing the couple's everlasting love.  What is the Altar of Vows? As its name suggests, it is a place for couples who want to pledge their undying love. The altar is surrounded by stone sculptures describing scenes from the story of Chunhyang and has a heart-shaped “vow plaque”. Couples can place their hands on this plaque to make a vow, and a tone will sound blessing their love. This is perhaps the most intriguing place for couples in love. Don't forget to leave a padlock of love at the bridge before you move on. In Ponte Vecchio, Italy, couples leave a padlock on the bridge rail to promise their devotion, a practice which has become popular around the world. So why not do something memorable here with the one you love as a celebration of your relationship?

stories.title: Chapter of Love and Forced Separation
stories.audioTitle: Chapter of Love and Forced Separation
stories.script: Chapter of Love and Forced Separation - Separation from the Loved One  This is the third chapter of Chunhyang Theme Park, and the most trying part of the story. It is also where you can see a variety of filming locations. There are traditional houses including Chunhyang's House and a village school, and Korean traditional furniture items are on display as well. In particular, Chunhyang's room, called Buyongdang, is where the couple spent their first night together.  But their happiness was short lived. After a short period of blissful rendezvous, the two were left with no choice but to part ways. His father was a local administrator and was dispatched to another province, so he had to leave town with his family. He promised her he would return a successful man and she watched him leave. She never doubted his return.  But she didn’t realize that she would have to overcome more than her longing for her beloved. Let's find out what happened.

stories.title: Chapter of Trials
stories.script: Chapter of Trials - Chunhyang Stays True to Her Love  These life-size replicas show what Chunhyang had to endure in her wait for Mongnyong.  She didn’t hear from him for months. She spent her days in awful longing and misfortune. The new magistrate urged beautiful Chunhyang to serve him in private.  But she refused to meet him because she wanted to keep her promise to Mongnyong. As a result, she was sent to jail and tortured for insubordination. The Chapter of Trials describes what she had to go through.  Then, one day, Mongnyong returned dressed as a beggar. They met at last, but their future seemed as dark as the prison she was in.

stories.title: Chapter of Celebration
stories.script: Chapter of Celebration - Namwon, the City of Chunhyang  Now to the last chapter, the Chapter of Celebration. What awaits Chunhyang and Mongnyong after their struggle to stay together?  On the magistrate’s birthday, she was dragged out to the courtyard and tortured for refusing him once again. Suddenly, Mongnyong appears dressed in the robes of a high official. He had returned to his hometown disguised as a beggar to divert the evil magistrate's attention so that he could capture him red handed!  See the long parade at the entrance of this chapter? Mongnyong is leading the march on a horseback while Chunhyang is sheepishly peeping out of her decorated carriage. It's a grand finale, with the villagers giving their blessings.  Chunhyang Theme Park has a number of places for you to partake in joyous activities and get a taste of Korean traditions. In one of the places, you can also try some of the traditional Korean musical instruments.  If Verona is the city of Romeo and Juliet, Namwon is the city of Mongnyong and Chunhyang. It will be interesting to note that Namwon and Verona actually became sister cities for cultural exchange.

stories.title: About the Course
stories.script: About the Course  These places were constructed with the purpose of carrying on the legacy of Korean traditional music.  Have you heard of Korean “pansori” before? Pansori is one of the types of folk music native to Korea. It comprises songs that provide a narration while weaving in the stories of a long script and sounds matching the drum-beat of a drummer, aided by their gestures.   Namwon is especially famous for being the home of pansori, and it is setting for the renowned works such as “Song of Chunhyang” and “Song of Heungbu”. Also, the region is the birthplace of dongpyeonje, which is a singing style of pansori popular in the eastern area of Jeolla-do. In addition to this, various genres of Korean traditional music from long ago have been studied and passed on here.   This is the place for Korean traditional music with all kinds of things to see and activities to try. Shall we go and have a look?

stories.title: The Resting Place of the Masters of Korean Traditional Music
stories.audioTitle: The Resting Place of the Masters of Korean Traditional Music
stories.script: The Resting Place of the Masters of Korean Traditional Music  Firstly, we are going to visit the graveyard where the ancestors of Korean traditional music lay sleeping. Do you see the circular stage? If you go past here, up the steps, and through the door, you will see the Akseongsa Shrine commemorating Korean traditional musicians. In the shape of a traditional Korean building, this place is home to the ancestral tablets of the resting traditional musicians. An ancestral ceremony is performed here to honor their souls.  The front side of the tomb is in the shape of a drum, which is a musical instrument that accompanies pansori performances. There are five tombs here, all of which inform you about the masters of Korean traditional music.

stories.title: Acquiring Sound through Personal Battle
stories.script: Acquiring Sound through Personal Battle  This area is especially devoted to deugeum, a pansori singer’s most important challenge. Deugeum literally means “to acquire the vocal sound”, and refers to the intensive training that singers have to go through to attain the perfect stage of the superior, advanced quality of vocalization techniques. Here is the special area devoted to this training. These rooms can be used by anyone, and was designed to reflect the image of musicians who perfected their sound alone in the mountains or alongside waterfalls or other natural spaces. Also, visitors can first-hand experience the training methods of the master singers. How about trying out the sound for yourself?

stories.title: Folk Songs and Instruments
stories.script: Folk Songs and Instruments  Inside this stylish building, right in the center of the precincts, you can experience exhibitions and activity programs about Korean traditional music. The first place that we come to is the Folk Music Pavilion. A wide variety of items related to Korean folk songs are exhibited in this hall, and you might notice that the folk songs have slight regional differences in tone and the atmosphere that they create. We hope that this is a chance for you to listen to whichever songs you like best and for you to discover what Korean traditional folk music really is. In addition to folk music instruments, primitive instruments such as dried sticks, bells, and water containers, along with Korea’s traditional stringed instruments are on display here.

stories.title: Everything about Pansori
stories.script: Everything about Pansori  You can find out here exactly what pansori is, and how its history unfolded. Pansori is an art form combining the harmony of the drumming and verbal sounds of a drummer, and the songs, descriptive speech, gestures, and foot movements of a singer. If you take a good look around, you will learn all kinds of information about the origins of this performance, its formative elements and the 12 pansori pieces. There is even an introduction to the master singers of each generation.  Have you ever heard of the terms dongpyeonje and seopyeonje? Chances are, anyone interested enough in Korean traditional music to visit this museum should have heard of them. Additionally, there is a famous Korean movie called ‘Seopyeonje’ which is quite well known to foreigners. Dongpyeonje and seopyeonje are types of pansori music from the southern regions of the Korean Peninsula. The former is a singing method commanding emotional restraint, while the latter could be described as a very decorative and technical singing style. There is a corner here where you can hear the songs of master singers, so we hope that you can spend a little time listening to the music.

stories.title: Korea’s Cultural Heritage, Registered by UNESCO
stories.audioTitle: Korea’s Cultural Heritage, Registered by UNESCO
stories.script: Korea’s Cultural Heritage, Registered by UNESCO  Shall we go and see the 2nd floor?  On the right, belongings and keepsakes of the Namwon master singer Kang Do-geun are proudly displayed. You can see items such as the props and instruments that he used, his performance costumes, and certificates of various awards.  On the left, examples of decorative, traditional dancing costumes are on display. These costumes are extravagant and very colorful.   The objects displayed here will inform you about the history of Korean court music. In particular, there are many items associated with the Royal Ancestral Ritual Music which was performed at Jongmyo, the royal shrine of the Joseon Dynasty. This extends to the singing and dancing which praise the good deeds of Korean ancestors, while performing with an instrument in a style in keeping with each part of the ceremony.   This ritual music is the first intangible cultural heritage of Korea which was selected as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2001. Pansori was also selected by UNESCO in 2003.

stories.title: Time to Try Singing a Part like a Master Singer
stories.audioTitle: Time to Try Singing a Part like a Master Singer
stories.script: Time to Try Singing a Part like a Master Singer  Here you can learn more about Korean traditional music firsthand. You can learn a part of pansori and learn to move in time to the rhythm of Korean traditional percussion music called samul nori. Also, you can try making a small janggu, an hourglass-shaped drum. Of these activities, dancing to the tune of the drum while wearing a traditional hat decorated with long ribbons can be especially appealing to people from other countries. You might have seen this kind of dancing from any videos promoting tourism in Korea.  Learning pansori is also very popular. You can learn the most popular part, and although it might be a little hard to keep up with the rhymes in Korean, feel free to have a go!  In making the mini hourglass-shaped drum, you’ll be given the same materials used to make a real drum. It will sound like a real drum too. It’ll just be smaller. Making a mini drum can be a fun activity particularly for families and children.  If the weather permits, you can also participate in various activities outside.

stories.title: Performance Hall
stories.script: Performance Hall  This is the Performance Hall. There is a regular concert held here every Wednesday, but you must make a reservation in advance. If you are visiting in a large group, then it is possible for you to see a performance on days other than Wednesday too.  The performers are from the Namwon Municipal Traditional Music Orchestra. Here on the stage, they show various elements of folk music including the playing of instruments and singing, dancing, and pansori. In order to develop a closer intimacy with the public, some of their traditional music is infused with modern elements as well. The performance is about one hour long, but time will fly.  Pansori performers try to communicate with the audience during their performances. Listen closely and follow the points in the middle of the performance when Koreans in the audience call out. You can call out too! Eolssu! This short word of encouragement spurs the performers on into giving a really exciting performance.

stories.title: The Sound Still Remains Where the Master Singers Lived
stories.audioTitle: The Sound Still Remains Where the Master Singers Lived
stories.script: The Sound Still Remains Where the Master Singers Lived  This is the birthplace of the master singer Song Heung-rok. The exterior of the building looks like a traditional Korean farmhouse. If you go inside, there is a sculpture to the left of the entrance. Made from stone, the 24 large and small orbs represent the teardrops of the audience listening to one of his performances.  In spite of already being famous, he had to put much time and effort into his practice in order to become a master singer. He is also known for being one of the founders of the dongpyeonje type of singing. His achievements were praised by the king and government.   Have you seen the statues in the center of the house? The statues show him performing pansori with his drummer.

stories.title: Park Cho-wol’s Thatched House
stories.script: Park Cho-wol’s Thatched House  In the birthplace of Song Heung-rok, there is also the restored, thatched house of the master singer Park Cho-wol, who lived here when she was young. She was the leading female master singer of pansori. Her singing ability was so great that she had already made a clean sweep of the prizes at many singing competitions before she had even turned 16.  She learned from several master singers, and her ability had been acknowledged in performances in both Seoul and Japan before she was twenty years old. In the early 1930s, she entered the ‘Joseon Society of Singing’, and became known as the lead female performer there. Additionally, she struck a chord with many as she travelled all around the country with her accomplished singing and acting. She was a pop star of those days.

stories.title: Koreans' Efforts to Control Water
stories.script: The Efforts to Control Water  [Narration] Byeokgolje in Gimje is the oldest and largest artificial reservoir in Korea.  Korea has been an agrarian nation for hundreds of years, so flood control and irrigation have always been an important issue for all. Reservoirs were built on a national scale: More than three hundred thousand people were commissioned to build reservoirs each year.   It was the same with Byeokgolje. According to historical records, it was built in 330 A.D. and its circumference reached to 41㎞ when it was first built. People used to say, “If Byeokgolje dries up, everyone will go hungry.” That’s how important this reservoir was in the old days when irrigation made a world of difference between good and poor harvest.  Today, only a small portion of the embankment and floodgates remain in the Byeokgolje Tourist Complex, but restoration works based on historical records continue to bring back its original splendor.
