stories.script: The School for the Ruling Class  This is the school that once educated the ruling class of the region. Here they prepared for the state examination. In addition, they also held the rituals for people of great learning and moral character.  Not only is this building preserved today just as it was 600 years ago, but it also stores a variety of documents which are an invaluable resource for researching the history and culture of the region.  When you enter the school, you can see that it is divided into two different areas. One of these is the place where students studied and the other was where the rituals were held. In addition to book learning, the building was also a place for character development.  Surrounding the building can be seen some ginkgo trees, and ginkgos used to be planted near all of Korea's schools. The reason for this is that the Chinese scholar Confucius, the founder of Confucianism, used to teach his disciples underneath a ginkgo tree.

stories.title: The Building Where Rituals Were Held for Saints of Old
stories.audioTitle: The Building Where Rituals Were Held for Saints of Old
stories.script: The Building Where Rituals Were Held for Saints of Old  The most famous place here is the building where the rituals were once held for holy men of the past. This building has been designated as an important cultural heritage. Among the 200 buildings remaining in Korea used for the same purpose, it is the oldest. It has been around for more than 600 years.  The pillars that support the roof are not inside the building but rather on the outside. Because of this architectural characteristic, the building is considered to have high historical and cultural value.  In addition, the name of the building on the front below the roof was written by the greatest calligrapher of that time, further increasing the structure’s value.  The big stone slab in the front yard was discovered buried in the ground. This kind of fine road paving stone was once used in palace architecture. It adds to the aura of the place.  At this building, the rituals are held for 27 wise men from China and Korea including Confucius, the founder of Confucianism. Twice a year, a large ritual is held, and at such times many people come from around the country to honor the memory of these scholars.

stories.title: The Person Who Risked His Life for the School
stories.audioTitle: The Person Who Risked His Life for the School
stories.script: The Person Who Risked His Life for the School  To the right of the school is an old stone memorial.  This monument was built in remembrance of Jeong Gyeong-son who did everything to protect this school from the invading Japanese army. During the late 16th century, the Japanese army was sweeping across the Korean Peninsula, pillaging and destroying as it moved. When the invaders reached this school, it is said that he stood his ground alone in front of the Japanese forces and stopped them from destroying the school.  Awed by the spirit of the man who was ready to lay down his life to protect his school, the Japanese soldiers could not enter the school. Instead, it’s told that the Japanese general had a notice written that said, “Do not trespass since this is holy ground,” and withdrew of his own accord.  Thanks to this man's courage, the school has been preserved in its original form as you see it today.

stories.title: The Beautiful Pine Tree
stories.script: The Beautiful Pine Tree  When you reach Jangsu-gun Office, you will notice an extremely unusual yet beautiful pine tree standing in front of the building.   Estimated to be around 400 years old, this huge pine tree is a grand sight, measuring 9 meters tall and 3.22 meters in circumference.   Twisting upwards in a spiral, the tree is said to resemble a dragon twirling its body as it soars into the sky. Then there are the abundant branches at the crown of the tree, which stretch out on both sides like the horizon.  No one knows who planted the tree, but it has been lovingly tended by locals for centuries, and it has been designated as a natural monument.

stories.title: Bangchon Park
stories.script: Bangchon Park  Now it’s time for you to walk through a park.  This park is connected to Hwang Hui, one of the most renowned civil officials in the early Joseon Period. He rose to the highest position, just below the king, and maintained this position for 18 years. He was highly regarded for his integrity and the strength of his convictions.  His family’s roots were in this region, and when at one point he disagreed with the king about an issue related to the royal succession, he was banished here. This park was made by those who appreciated him all the more during his exile.  The bronze statue standing in the middle of the park shows us what he looked like.

stories.title: Noha Forest
stories.script: Noha Forest  Do you remember the bronze statue of a man? You are coming to a forest where you will learn more about him.  This forest of old Zelkova and Chinese hackberry trees is said to have been planted by his father, because his mother had been here when she prayed that she might give birth to a great son. His father apparently started to plant the trees to protect the spot. I guess you could say that a great historical figure was born as a result of the mother's prayers and the father's work planting the trees.  While today the forest has been split into two areas by a road, the 600 years of history in the forest and the streams that flow through the area give it a lovely ambience.

stories.title: Private School
stories.script: Private School  You are now about to take a look at another school.  You could say that what you saw before was a public school authorized by the government. This school, however, was more like a private school where the local scholars continued their studies and revered the intellectual giants of the past.  Among the schools of this kind, this one was built to commemorate the great civil official, Hwang Hui. At one time, the school fell on hard times as government policy forced it to shut its doors. Later, though, it was restored, and today the areas for studying and for performing the ritual remain.  If you go up the narrow, steep stairs behind the educational building, you will find another shrine.  Even today, people who study Confucianism come here each year to offer the ancestral rites

stories.title: Taru Park and Taru Memorial
stories.script: Taru Park and Taru Memorial  The last stop on this course is a park whose name means “shedding tears”.  The Jangsu region has been famous for its virtuous people. You have already met two of them, such as the woman who jumped with the Japanese general into the river and the man who singlehandedly protected his school from the Japanese army. Along with them, a man named Baek has been highly respected for his loyalty, and this park was established to commemorate him.  He was the servant of a certain household long ago. He and his master were on a journey and, as they were following a path that led along a cliff on the hill behind this park, a pheasant suddenly flew out of the woods. Startled by the bird, the horse that the master was riding reared up, and the master fell from his horse, rolled off the cliff, and plunged to his death in the river below. Overcome with guilt for not being able to protect his master, the servant bit his finger and used the blood to write the story about the pheasant and horse and, next to it, he left a phrase shedding tears. After this, he leaped into the river after his master and ended his life.  A government official who heard this sad story had these memorial stones and the park built in their honor.  Of the two stones, the large one was built for the servant, while the smaller one was built for the master.

stories.title: About the Course
stories.script: About the Course  Today we will take a stroll along this historical and cultural trail through Muju, Jinan, and Jangsu regions. Jangsu, where we will begin our journey today, is known for both its remoteness and its water. As you walk along the trail, you’ll hear the story of the kingdom that existed for 500 years prior to Korea’s independence from Japan. The trail takes four hours on foot but these stories will entertain you every step of the way.

stories.title: Tteunbongsaem Spring
stories.script: Tteunbongsaem Spring  This spring that wells up at the top of the mountain is the source of the Geumgang River. Starting its journey here, the river flows hundreds of kilometers to the Yellow Sea to the west of the Korean Peninsula. The thirst you must have worked up while walking through the rough mountain terrain can be quenched by this spring.   There is also a legend about the spring that relates to the foundation of one of Korea’s great kingdoms, the Joseon Dynasty, which was established in 1392. When the general who founded the dynasty was having difficulty making decisions, he wandered from mountain to mountain offering sacrifices to the heavens. It wasn’t until he arrived here that he received a revelation. A rainbow appeared in the sky and legend has it that a bird rose up from the ground by the spring and took flight. This is how the general came to notice the spring. After receiving his revelation here, it is said that the general made his decision to establish a new nation. So it may be a small spring, but its role in the birth of the new dynasty was rather important.

stories.title: Tteunbongsaem Ecological Park
stories.script: Tteunbongsaem Ecological Park  If you pass the spring and face towards the bottom of the mountain, you will see a lovely, well-maintained park. There are many attractions relating to water here at the park, including a water experience hall you can visit.  The “Water Square” has a model demonstrating how the spring becomes a river and flows into the ocean, allowing you to appreciate the long journey the water makes.  A small building in the shape of an apple might attract your attention, but it is just a quirky restroom facility! The significant diurnal range, clear water and clean air of this region make it ideal for growing fruit. The region is particularly known for producing delicious apples so maybe that’s why the restroom is shaped like an apple!

stories.title: Geumgang Water Experience Hall
stories.script: Geumgang Water Experience Hall  At the Geumgang Water Experience Hall located inside the park, you can see how water first formed and learn about Korean river systems and the current status of water resources. In addition to the water-related educational exhibits, there are also displays featuring prehistoric culture and artifacts from this region and rare insects specimen on display.

stories.title: Subun Village
stories.script: Subun Village  The small village that you can see from the experience hall is located at the head of Geumgang River as it begins to flow in earnest. The current name of the village means, “where water divides,” and the old name meant “source of water”. One branch of the stream courses into Geumgang and the other flows into another large river called Seomjingang.   The village is designated an “exemplary village” due to its outstanding natural ecology, so you may enjoy taking a walk around and experiencing the clean, pure environment.

stories.title: Subun Chapel (Baekdudaegan Trail)
stories.script: Subun Chapel of Jangsu Catholic Church  As you stroll through Subun Village, you're likely to notice a building with a red slate roof. Approaching it, the contrast of the red roof with the vivid white cross immediately catches the eye. In the backyard, there's a statue of Jesus on the cross and the Virgin Mary looking on in sorrow. This is the Subun Chapel of Jangsu Catholic Church. Although no priest resides here permanently, it serves as a place for the faithful to pray.  Originally, the Subun Chapel was established in 1866 when Catholic believers fled here during the Byeongin persecutions, the largest-scale Catholic persecution in Korean history. At that time, the community grew to over a thousand members, since Father Choe Yang-eop, a significant figure in the history of the Catholic Church in Korea, used this place as a base for the missionary work. Then, in 1913, the believers built a new Chapel, marking the beginning of what is now Subun Chapel. Now, a priest from Jangsu visits once a month to hold Mass. Given its role in helping establish churches in Jangsu and Janggye, Subun Chapel is recognized as a significant site in the history of the Catholic Church in Korea and is listed as a modern cultural heritage of Korea.   Because it's a Korean modern cultural heritage site, the Subun Chapel is usually locked, but you can ask the village head for permission to enter. Inside, the space is slightly larger than a primary school classroom and has a quite exotic atmosphere, reminiscent of a small church in a European village. The harmony between Korean tradition and Western religious symbols offers visitors a fresh experience.

stories.title: Subullyeong Pass
stories.script: Subullyeong Pass  Having passed through the village, you will come to one of the well-known passes on this trail. It is where two mountain ranges come together and the stream that you saw flowing through the village divides into two branches at this junction. Although only a pass, it stands high like a mountain with an elevation of 539 meters.  In use since the olden days, this was a pass travelers had to go through to get to other regions or to the capital, so there were many taverns and inns nearby. Even now, there is a rest stop here.  After passing over the pass, you will have to climb another pass. Even though the road is paved with asphalt, the steep ascent is still quite difficult. When you get to the top, the road down the other side winds around the pass and descends to the valley. If you continue down the pass, you will come to the next section of our journey.

stories.title: Banghwadong Family Holiday Village
stories.script: Banghwadong Family Holiday Village  This is a family holiday village, ideal for a short break. It is surrounded by natural forests, mountains with elevations close to 1,000 meters, and you can catch a glimpse of scenic, flowing water.  With beautiful scenery that differs every season and convenient, well-equipped facilities, the holiday village is a great place for camping. It has a large nature education center, excellent campsite, a picnic area, a water park, a communal kitchen and restroom facilities. At night you can have a barbecue, relax with your family, and watch the stars in the night sky.

stories.title: Banghwadong Natural Recreation Forest
stories.script: Banghwadong Natural Recreation Forest  If you follow the valley from the family holiday village for about ten minutes, you will arrive at the natural recreation forest. This place has accommodation facilities so if camping isn’t your thing, you may prefer to spend the night here.  The therapeutic forest and a “house-in-the-forest” are ready for you to explore with your family. There is a path next to the house-in-the-forest that leads to the valley floor. It is the most therapeutic walking path that you could possibly take! If you walk along the path in the morning, when trees release therapeutic oils and other elements, on a clear, windless day between early summer and fall when the growth of trees is most vigorous, you might just feel your body and mind becoming stronger and healthier.

stories.title: Deoksan Valley
stories.script: Deoksan Valley  If you follow the road next to the house-in-the-forest for about one kilometer, you will come to a valley, and if you follow that valley for a while into the forest, you will come to another picturesque road. This road, through dense forest and alongside clear water, has been designated as one of the “most beautiful roads” of the region.   Compared to the rugged mountain terrain, this road is rather flat. Your walk is accompanied by the pleasant sound of flowing water year round, even in the winter as the snow melts. Since the water is icy cold even in the summer, you can take a break and cool down by dipping your hands and feet into the water.  Walk a bit farther on and you will see an artificial waterfall. The water falling from the tall rocks offers a pleasant sight.

stories.title: Pool under the Waterfall
stories.script: Pool under the Waterfall  If you follow the valley road for about 30 minutes, you will soon reach a wooden boardwalk. After traversing some rough terrain, from this point on you can relax, stroll at your leisure and enjoy the surrounding environment.   At the end, you will arrive at the deep pool under the waterfall, which is the final destination of our course. From here you can enjoy spending time in the lush forest, relaxing by the clear water, and marveling at the strange-looking rocks. The water cascading over the rocks is deep blue in color.  Legend has it that this pool was created when a dragon ascended to the heavens. The local residents are very proud of this place and in the olden days, writers gathered here to write poems and enjoy the natural environment.

stories.title: Stone Buddha in Osu-ri
stories.script: The Stone Buddha from the Mountain  [Narration]  Welcome to Osu-ri! Osu-ri is a small village in Imsil-gun, Jeollabuk-do, located in the south-western part of the Korean Peninsula. The village became famous for the “Osu Dog”, which died saving its owner. We'll get to the story a bit later.   Before going into the village, let’s go see a stone Buddha statue.  This is a stone relief of Buddha carved on a slab of rock. The Buddha carving is about 2.4 meters in height, and the rock stands about 3.5 meters tall. The feet of the Buddha can't be seen because it's buried under the ground.  There are no records to show when it was carved, but it's presumed to be from the 13th or 14th century because of its sculpture characteristics.   Look at the aura around the Buddha’s head. It's almond-shaped and carved with various patterns.   His face is impassive, and the carving is quite flat so the overall figure is distinguishable. The upper torso is wide, while the lower torso is thin. And there are many pleats on the robe. This stone Buddha is worshipped as a tutelary deity of this village by local residents.

stories.title: Monument for Loyal Dog
stories.script: Heroic Death of a Loyal Dog  [Narration] Now, back to the story about the Osu Dog. There are historical records about a loyal dog that saved its owner, and there is a monument commemorating the dog in Wondongsan Park.  Once upon a time, there was a dog lover named Kim Gae-in who lived in Imsil. He loved his dog so much that he took it with him everywhere he went. And one day, he went to the marketplace with his dog. He met his friends at the market, got drunk, and fell asleep on a grassland while on his way back home. A fire started near him while he was asleep. His dog realized that his owner was in danger and tried to wake him, but the man was too drunk to wake up. The dog didn't give up trying to save him. It ran to a nearby stream, soaked his hair with water, and rolled over the man's body to put out the fire. The dog did this several times and finally put out the fire, but died in the process.  After a few hours, the man woke up and found his dog lying dead next to him. He soon realized what happened, and grieved for the dog. He then buried the dog on the spot and placed his walking stick over the grave as a tombstone. Later, the stick grew to a zelkova tree. People called it Osu, which literally means Dog Tree in Korean. They even renamed their village after it in 1992.   They also built a monument dedicated to the loyal dog, as well as a statue of the dog near it.

stories.title: Osu Watchtower
stories.audioTitle: Osu Watchtower, the Guard of Imsil
stories.script: Osu Watchtower, the Guard of Imsil  [Narration] The Osu Watchtower in the middle of downtown was built around 1940 during the Japanese Colonial Period.   It's 12 meters high and 2.4m wide at the bottom. It's the tallest watchtower in Korea. Why did they build such a large watchtower in such a small village?  Osu has been the center of Imsil for a long time, and was famous for silk during the Japanese Colonial Period. The chimney of a silk factory still standing in front of the watchtower is a testament to the fact. Because of the booming economy of this region, many Japanese people flooded to Osu to take over the economy and people. And they had this watchtower built in the center of the village as a reminder of their existence.  But as time went by, the purpose of this watchtower changed. After the Liberation of Korea, it was used to watch for mountain fire, as well as a guard post during the Korean War. And in the 1960s, clocks were uncommon, it was used as a town clock. It was particularly useful for farmers, because it chimed at noon and people would know it's lunch time.  In 2005, this brick tower was designated as Cultural Heritage No. 188. The cylindrical tower and hexagonal turret make a great combination, and it is regarded as a rare example of architecture at the end of the Japanese Colonial Period. In short, it's a symbol of the changes that took place during the modernization of Korea.

stories.title: Osu Dog Park
stories.script: Park for Loyal dogs  [Narration] You are now in Osu Dog Park. This park is dedicated to the Osu Dog and promoting animal companions.  It's a great destination for families and couples since it has a number of excellent facilities, such a grass sports field, walking trails, octagonal pavilion and pond, and a playground for children.  Being a park dedicated to the famous Osu Dog, it also has a monument inscribed with the dog's story as well as a statue of the dog. Besides these, there are several more statues of other famous dogs from other parts of the world. Let's go see them.  The first one is Siberian Husky sled dog named Balto. In 1925, he led his team to deliver serum to more than one thousand children infected by deadly diphtheria. The roads were blocked due to heavy snow, and sled dogs were used to deliver the vaccine. Balto and his team ran over 1,100 kilometers in a temperature of minus 30 degrees Celsius.   And here is Bobby. He was a Skye Terrier in Edinburgh. After his owner died, he stood guard of his owner’s grave for 14 years, until he died next to the grave in 1872. Bobby was now buried near the grave of his beloved owner.  This park tells a number of stories of other heroic dogs. The Osu Dog Festival is held here every April in the memory of loyal dogs.

stories.title: Birthplace of Kim Gae-in
stories.script: Osu Dog's House  [Narration] This is the Birthplace of Kim Gae-in, the owner of the Osu Dog. Despite the name, it's not where he actually lived. The house was built based on the story and it's open to the public, so that more people can learn about the story of a heroic dog.   Look at the large monolith in front of the house. It's not directly related to the Osu Dog or this house either. It was originally used as a washboard or a stone bridge. Then why did they move the heavy rock to this place? It's because in Korea, people traditionally place a large monolith in front of a sacred place. So it's like a tribute to the dog.  In April every year, the Osu Dog Festival is held in the front yard of this house. To the local people, it's more like a ritual for the heroic dog, and a way of comforting the soul of the dog and saying thanks.

stories.title: Gangcheonsan and Natural Trails
stories.script: Gangcheonsan and Natural Trails  [Narration] Gangcheonsan Mountain is small, but has a number of valleys and peaks that make up a beautiful scenery. From its summit, the mountain looks like two dragons flying from the east to the west. Some even argue that the mountain resembles a woman lying down with her legs stretched out.  The name 'Gangcheon' literally means 'clear spring water pouring out of a rock'. The water flowing from the west flank to the east is so cold that no moss can grow around it. Try to listen to the sound of the clear water streaming down while walking on the trail. It will add to the pleasure of walking in the nature.  Most of the trails in this mountain are gently sloped, and it only takes about seven hours from one end of the main trail to the other. No wonder it's one of the most popular hiking trails in Korea.  In particular, a small section of the trail called the 'Barefoot Trail' is very popular among visitors. The trail section, covered with loess and pebbles, continues for 2.5 kilometers between rocky cliffs and streams in the ravine. These sand and pebbles stimulate the soles of your feet and blood circulation.   Well, are you ready to take a hike?  See if you like the sound of birds chirping and water flowing. Smell the wild flowers and plants too. Listen to the nature.

stories.title: Byeongpung Falls, the Guardian of Gangcheonsan Mountain
stories.audioTitle: Byeongpung Falls, the Guardian of Ganfcheonsan Mountain
stories.script: Byeongpung Falls, the Guardian of Gangcheonsan Mountain  [Narration] Pass through the mountain entrance, and you will see a waterfall named Byeongpung Falls. This man-made waterfall measures 40m in height and 15m in width, and 5 tons of water pours down every minute. As the waterfall perfectly mingles with the surroundings, it provides a magnificent view to visitors while also preserving the natural environment.  As you can see, there is a smaller fall next to the main one. You’ll also see a large rock right under it. A story has it that you will be cleansed of your sins if you successfully pass by the rock. The rock looks normal from a distance, but when you get closer, it looks as though it’s going to fall over you. In the old days, it was the only way to get to Gangcheonsa Temple. So people had no other choice but to cross this area. When they did, they placed flat stones on the ground so they can take careful steps on them. With every step they took, they repented of their sins. So the moral of the story is that, the more you repent, the more your soul will be cleansed.   When you stand in front of the waterfall, you’ll feel the wind blowing from the falling water. The air contains lots of anion, which is good for your health. So take your time to breathe in fresh air.  This waterfall is the starting point of every hiking and walking course in this mountain, including the Wooden Deck Trail, on which you can take a slow walk. The popular 2.5 kilometer-long Barefoot Trail to Gujanggun Falls also starts here. So when you see Byeongpung Falls, you’ll know that you’re at the starting point of the trail, which will take you to five other waterfalls.

stories.title: Gangcheonsa Temple, Under the Protection of the Nature
stories.audioTitle: Gangcheonsa Temple, Under the Protection of the Nature
stories.script: Gangcheonsa Temple, Under the Protection of the Nature  [Narration] Gangcheonsa is a Buddhist temple established in 887.  It's located between two waterfall ponds, because the founder of the temple thought the site between two ‘dragon ponds’ is an auspicious place to build a temple. Ancient Koreans called a waterfall pond the ‘dragon pond’, because they believed dragons live in a waterfall pond. So did the people in this region. According to a local legend, a blue dragon lived in the upper pond and a golden dragon in the lower pond. The temple did flourish for many years, since it once had between 500 and 600 resident monks. They also built 12 hermitages around the temple as well. But it was heavily damaged during the Korean War, and it began to be restored in 1959.  The founder also said, “We need those who can’t grow a beard if we want this temple to flourish and the place to be purified.” By saying this, he wanted Buddhists nuns to live and pray in the temple. So this temple always had more Buddhist nuns than priests.  There is another interesting fact about this temple. In Korea, most Buddhist temples have the Four Guardian Kings at the entrance. They are the Buddhist gods who keep watch of the four cardinal directions. This temple doesn’t have them. It’s because they didn’t have to, since there are rock figures that look like them just outside the entrance.  Did you see the mounds of stones in front of the temple? There are many stone mounds around the stream. It’s because many Koreans often place a stone on top of the mound when making a wish, particularly around a temple. Over the years, it became a landmark of the temple.

stories.title: Three Seals on a Pine Tree
stories.audioTitle: Three Seals on a Pine Tree
stories.script: Three Seals on a Pine Tree  [Narration] Alongside the stream in front of Gangcheonsa Temple is a special building. It houses a monument called ‘Samindae’ dedicated to a number of loyal officials of the Joseon Dynasty.   At the end of 15th century, the country was under the reign of one of the worst tyrants in Korean history. So in 1506, a group of officials ended up dethroning the tyrant king, and making his stepbrother the new king. They also exiled and executed those who opposed them, even the new king's father-in-law. In the process, the queen consort was also dethroned and exiled.   After this incident, three local officials in this province gathered at the valley in Gangcheonsan to have a discussion on restoring the unfairly dethroned queen's title.   At the time, the country was still in political turmoil, and those who went against the new regime were killed or at least exiled. Nonetheless, the three officials vowed to reinstate the queen, at the risk of losing their government positions and even lives. They submitted a petition to the king, but their petition was denied.  It took more than 200 years for their petition to be accepted. In 1739, the queen was finally restored, and five years later, a stone monument and a memorial building were built here to commemorate the courage of the three officials. The place was named ‘Samindae’, meaning ‘three seals’, because the officials hung their seals on a pine tree made the vow. Since 1995, Samin Cultural Festival is held in August of the lunar calendar to honor their loyalty to the country.

stories.title: Suspension Bridge
stories.script: Suspension Bridge  [Narration] After Gangcheonsa and Samindae, you will see a suspension bridge that will make you giddy. Built in 1980, the bridge is a 76-meter long structure 50 meters above the ground.  To cross the bridge, follow the trail on the right side of Sipjangsaenggyo Bridge. The bridge is only one meter wide, and it will sway under your feet. But there is no need to worry. As you can see, the deck is hung below suspension cables on vertical suspenders on each side. The bridge sways because the cables are installed to be too tight so they can support more weight without breaking the deck.  While on the bridge, you will have a panoramic view of the mountain with its rocky cliffs. In the autumn, these cliffs are covered with colorful leaves of trees growing from between the rocks. The mountain is particularly beautiful late in the autumn.   The bridge is a perfect place to appreciate the beauty of the mountain. On the bridge, you'll have a great view of Yongmeori Falls and a pond underneath. Far off to the west, you'll see a fortress named Geumseongsanseong Which starts from Sanseongsan Mountain and stretches out for about 7,345 meters.

stories.title: The Strong Resolution on Nine Generals
stories.audioTitle: The Strong Resolution on Nine Generals
stories.script: The Strong Resolution on Nine Generals  [Narration] A short 10-minute walk from the suspension bridge plaza will take you to Gujanggun Falls, at the end of the Barefoot Trail. You'll see two streams falling from about 120 meters above. The story has an interesting story about nine generals of ancient Korea.  During the 1st and 3rd centuries, the southern part of Korean Peninsula was ruled by a confederacy called Mahan. When the allied states had a war against neighboring states, nine generals of the confederacy lost a series of battles and retreated to this place. At first, they were going to kill themselves out of shame. But instead, they made a resolution to fight once again and die in the battlefield.   Just as they were ready to return to the battlefield, nine horses suddenly appeared out of nowhere. So they mounted the horses and headed back to the battlefield. This time, they won the battle despite all odds. The generals celebrated, and when they came to their senses, they were astonished to see that their horses were turned into a rock. So the rock was named ‘Gujanggun Rock’, which means the ‘Rock of Nine Generals’. They even named the waterfall after the rock, hence the name Gujanggun Falls.

stories.title: Gochang Eupseong Fortress 1
stories.script: The Purpose of the Fortress  [Narration] Let’s start the tour of Gochang Eupseong Fortress and nearby historical sites.   Your first stop will be Gochang Eupseong Fortress.  It was built in 1453 to protect the southwestern region of the Korean peninsula. That’s why the site includes a number of military facilities. The most outstanding facility is a rampart within the interior of the fort. Can you see a circular wall just in front of the gate? That’s the rampart of this fortress. A circular rampart is built behind all the gates in this fortress. Their primary role is to make it as difficult as possible for the enemies to come in. While the rampart had a very practical purpose in the past, it’s now a popular tourist spot because of its beautiful shape.   In fact, the entire fortress walls are a piece of art in itself. It’s mostly because they’re made of natural stones, which help the walls blend in with the natural surroundings. Unlike the outer walls, the inner walls are made of stones and clay. It even follows the curve of the mountain ridges.  Let's go into the fortress.

stories.title: Gochang Eupseong Fortress 2
stories.script: The Fortress as a Tourist Site  [Narration] To go into Gochang Eupseong Fortress, you must go through the north gate.   The fortress has a total of 14 administrative buildings restored inside. It originally had 22 buildings in the past, but most of them were destroyed over the years. They’re still trying to restore all of them. Normally, fortresses in Korea were built around a village. But that wasn’t the case of Gochang Eupseong Fortress, since the fortress only had administrative buildings.   Today, Gochang Eupseong Fortress is one of the most popular places to hike because of its beautiful interior. There is a beautiful flower trail which leads to a lush forest of pine trees. Right next to the pine forest is a bamboo grove.   The fortress has yet another trail just outside the walls. It’s another popular attraction in the region. Let’s go take a look.

stories.title: Gochang Eupseong Fortress 3
stories.script: The Own Customs of Fortress  [Narration] Inside Gochang Eupseong Fortress, you’ll see a trail adjoining the inner walls and a mountain ridge. That’s the famous “Fortress Road”. Since it’s on top of the wall, you can have a panoramic view of the town below.   They have a old, strange custom of circling around the fortress walls with a rock on their head. Mostly practiced by women, the tradition has been passed down for centuries. The locals believe that good things will happen if they do this. They say your legs will feel better if you circle the walls once, you'll have a long healthy life if you circle twice, and you’ll go to Heaven if you circle three times.   There was a practical reason why they adopted the custom. It was created in 1678 right after a war. The walls collapsed during the war, and the local governor had it repaired with stone and clay. But the walls were more like a loose mixture of clay and stones, and he had to make them hard and sturdy. So he encouraged people to walk on the walls. He even asked them to bring a rock to add more weight of their body, and more pressure to the wall. He needed as many volunteers as possible, so he spread the rumor that good things will happen if you circle around the walls.  It became established as a tradition, and you can witness it at the annual ‘Gochang Moyang Seongje Festival’.

stories.title: The Old House of Shin Jae-hyo
stories.audioTitle: The Old House of Shin Jae-hyo
stories.script: The Old House of Shin Jae-hyo  [Narration] This is the old house of Shin Jae-hyo. Born in 1812 in Gochang, Shin Jae-hyo was one of the greatest contributors to pansori, a form of traditional musical theater in Korea.   Pansori is like opera, in that the soloist sings an entire story. But unlike opera, it’s performed by only one singer on the stage.  Not only that, there aren't any musical accompaniments except for the drummer. So the soloist sings to the beat of the drum with occasional rhythmic gestures and storytelling. Are you ready to listen to a pansori?   This is 'Chunhyang', which is one of the most well-known classical pieces. But pansori wasn’t always like this in the past. The lyrics weren’t even composed, and ordinary people sang in whatever fashion they liked. Then a legendary singer named Shin Jae-hyo came along, and recreated the genre of music by composing lyrics, tunes, and choreographed the performance. He didn’t stop there, as he composed more than 30 pansori songs.  Some of his other achievements include the establishment of ‘Soricheong’, the first pansori school. He opened a music school right in his house. He was at center of controversy at the time, because he became the first person to teach pansori to women. Before him, pansori was a male-dominated genre of music.   He was the one who established principles and theories for pansori, and dedicated his whole life teaching and composing pansori. He never stopped changing and developing pansori until his death in 1884. That’s why Koreans call his the ‘great master’ of pansori.

stories.title: Pansori Museum
stories.script: The Sacred Ground of Pansori  [Narration]  This is the Gochang Pansori Museum. The museum is dedicated to honoring the lifetime achievements of Shin Jae-hyo, who taught and improved pansori throughout his life.  He’s the one who laid the theoretical basis for pansori and compiled a list of every pansori classics.   He also built the country’s first pansori school here in Gochang. It makes Gochang the birthplace of the pansori education system, and that’s why so many pansori masters came from this region. The first female pansori singer was educated here as well. In short, Shin Jae-hyo turned this region into the center and sacred place of pansori education.  The tradition of teaching pansori is still there in Gochang. Some of the top pansori singers have trained here, and many young people still come to study pansori.   The Gochang Pansori Museum is the only museum of pansori, established on the traditions of Gochang. The museum houses thousands of objects that highlight the history of pansori. It also has a section dedicated to Shin Jae-hyo and other pansori singers from Gochang. The section displays arrays of their articles and music records.   The museum also has special pansori classes and performances. So it would be a good idea to check the schedule before visiting the museum.

stories.title: The Five Shrines
stories.script: The Stone Pillar Guardian  [Narration] Welcome to the Five Shrines. Since ancient times, Koreans prayed at the shrine for their wishes. Here, the shrine refers to a mountain, tree, rock, or any other natural objects that are thought to be imbued with a divine spirit. Koreans regarded them as a their guardian.  The practice of nature worship is not uncommon in other parts of the world.  The people of Gochang were nature worshippers we well. After having a serious flood in the early 19th century, the villagers set up five pillars on the four directions and at the center of their town to pray for their safety. Those are known today as the Five Shrines.   The people of Gochang revered the Five Shrines as sacred, and held religious ceremonies at the shrines. But the religious ceremony is no longer practiced. They do, however, hold the ceremony at the Five Shrines to preserve their tradition.

stories.title: Seonunsa Temple: Dosolcheon, the Road Cleanses Your Soul
stories.audioTitle: Seonunsa Temple: Dosolcheon, the Road Cleanses Your Soul
stories.script: The Road That Cleanses Your Soul  [Narration] Welcome to Seonunsa Temple in Gochang.  The distance between Seonunsa Temple entrance and Dosoram Hermitage is 3.2 kilometers. Follow the trail along Dosolcheon Ravine, if you want to climb Seonunsan Mountain. The name 'Seonunsan' means “a mountain to meditate in the clouds”. It's also called Dosolsan Mountain. It’s a Buddhist name, meaning, “learn the teachings of Buddha”. As its name suggests, it’s a special mountain for those wishing to attain enlightenment and live by the Buddhist doctrines.   If you’re here in the summer, the stream in the ravine makes a great place to rest in the shades. After the heat of the summer, you’ll see red spider lilies all around you as you walk on the lower trail of the mountain, making your walk more pleasant. Some people think it's sad that the flowers bloom only after all the leaves have fallen.   More people come to this place in the early autumn to see the red tinged leaves. In your walk on the trail, listen to the clear sound of the water flowing. It may relax your mind.

stories.title: Seonunsa Temple: A Cup of Tea at Manseru Pavilion
stories.audioTitle: Seonunsa Temple: A Cup of Tea at Manseru Pavilion
stories.script: A Cup of Tea for You  [Narration] Take a short walk along the trail flanked by maple and zelkova trees, and you’ll reach Cheonwangmun Gate before you know it. Just inside the gate, you’ll see statues of Buddhist guardian deities whose primary role is to protect the world of Buddhism and defeat evil. It’s common to see statues or paintings of these deities at other Buddhist temples in Korea, since they’re believed to uphold the Buddhist doctrine and protect the temple.   The first thing you’ll see after passing through the gate is a pavilion called Manseru. Manseru Pavilion is the last building to be built on the temple ground, but it’s the first building to greet visitors.   Manseru Pavilion is primarily used as a lecture hall where Buddhist priests give lectures and Buddhists pray. The building also has a tea room open to all the visitors.  All the columns of Manseru Pavilion are shaped differently and bent in the middle. It’s because only natural tree trunks are used to make these columns. The corner columns in particular are made of a whole tree, with only its bark removed.    Some of them had to be repaired every once in a while, but there are still those that are over 700 years old.

stories.title: Seonunsa Temple: Daeungbojeon, and Foundation Stories
stories.script: Daeungbojeon and Foundation Stories  [Narration] Just in front of Manseru Pavilion and surrounded by camellia shrubs, is Daeungbojeon. It houses a seated Vairocana and a mural behind. The ceiling is painted with four dragons in different colors. Many visitors to this place find themselves overwhelmed by the imposing statue of Buddha and the dragons, which seem as though they’re soaring up to the sky.  There are two different stories about the foundation of this temple. According to a legend, this place used to be a pond with a dragon living there. A Buddhist priest came to this one day and drove the dragon away. But when he was filling up the pond by throwing stones into it, a very contagious eye disease spread in the village around the pond. The villagers soon learned that they can be cured of the disease if they pour a sack of hardwood charcoal into the pond. So every villager brought a sack full of hardwood charcoal and stones to fill up the pond. And when the large pond was soon filled with charcoal and stones, people built a temple on top of the reclaimed land.   There is another story about how the temple was built. According to the story, there was a poor village right under Seonunsan Mountain. A Buddhist priest came to the village one day, and taught the villagers how to take salt out of seawater as well as how to make hardwood charcoal and paper.  In other words, the Buddhist priest taught them the means to survive. The villagers were so grateful for him, that they built him a temple.  The village prospered, and the villagers donated salt to the temple every year in return for his service. During the time, salt was a very valuable commodity. The villagers still observe the tradition, even after 1,500 years.

stories.title: Seonunsa Temple: Camellia Forest
stories.script: Camellia Forest  [Narration] The Camellia Forest at the temple has always been a famous place in the country, and that’s why many poets wrote about it.  In Asia, camellia represents “the devotion of lovers”. It blooms in the spring, and when it falls, the whole bud falls and not just the leaves like most of other flowers.  Poets related the bud falling to pure love, and that’s why they wrote about the flower.   You’ll find about three thousand camellia trees right behind Seonunsa Temple. The monks at the temple have been growing camellia trees for hundreds of years to protect the temple against mountain fire, and use it as a lamp oil substitute. Camellia trees that are over five hundred years old are dark blue in color, and they have a sacred air about them. Camellia flowers at the temple bloom in March, which is much later than those in other regions. So March is the perfect month to visit the temple if you want to see the spring flowers.

stories.title: Seonunsa Temple: Ksitigarbha, the Protector of the Heavens,Land, and People
stories.audioTitle: Seonunsa Temple: Ksitigarbha, the Protector of the Heavens,Land, and People
stories.script: Ksitigarbha, the Protector of the Heavens, Land and People  [Narration] Seonunsa Temple also has three seated statues of Ksitigarbha, as the protectors and saviors of every living creature in the world, namely “All Heavenly Beings”, “All Earthly Beings”, and “All Aquatic Beings”.   In Buddhism, calling out his name can end all the suffering and help you attain Nirvana.   So most temples in Korea have a portrait of Ksitigarbha enshrined in the altar. But Seonunsa Temple is different from the rest, because it has a statue of Ksitigarbha enshrined instead of a portrait.  Since 1472, Seonunsa Temple has been receiving special support from the Joseon Dynasty, and many Buddhists came to this place to pray to Ksitigarbha.   There are many strange stories about the seated statue of Ksitigarbha. One of the most well-known stories goes something like this: The statue was stolen and smuggled into Japan in 1936, only to be returned in just two years.   The reason being is that the holder of the statue dreamed about Ksitigarbha one night, and the bodhisattva told him, “I was originally in Korea, so have me returned to the country right now. He didn’t like the dream, so he gave the statue to someone else. But the new holder also saw the bodhisattva in his dream, and gave it to another person. This went on and on, and the last person to have possession of the statue reported to the Gochang Police Station. After the report came in, a priest from Seonunsa Temple and a number of police officers went to Japan and brought back the seated bodhisattva.   After the incident, the seated statue was designated as a National Treasure and placed in the Seongbo Museum at Seonunsa Temple.

stories.title: Seonunsa Temple: Jangsasong and Jinheunggul Cave, the Places of Enlightenment and Caring
stories.audioTitle: The Places of Enlightenment and Caring
stories.script: The Places of Enlightenment and Caring  [Narration]  The stream in Dosolcheon changes color every year.   Can you see the pine tree with several branches pointing toward the sky? The branches start splitting about three to four meters from the bottom of the trunk, and they split even more at the top. When looking up from the bottom of the tree, the pine tree named “Jangsasong” looks like a blue umbrella.   The tree has been there for the past 600 years. Over the centuries, people came up with a number of myths about the tree. One of them is the transformation of a woman into a pine tree. She was the wife of a soldier who was sent to a battlefield, and she died waiting for her husband. And the tree grew from her body.  There is a cave right next to the pine tree. A story has it that in the 6th century, the King left his throne to meditate in this cave and attain enlightenment.  It’s a natural cave, about 4 meters high and 10 meters long. There is a small Buddha statue and burning candles in the cave, because some people still come to this place to pray. The candles are always lit for this reason. It’s been more than a millennium since the first person came to this quiet cave to be immersed in a deep meditation to attain enlightenment, and yet people still continue their spiritual journey.

stories.title: Seonunsa Temple: Maitreya Statue with Secrets
stories.audioTitle: Seonunsa Temple: Maitreya Statue with Secrets
stories.script: Maitreya Statue with Secrets  [Narration] There is a rock-carved Maitreya on the rocky cliff to the west side of Dosoram Hermitage. The carving is 13 meters high and 3 meters wide. It has a square face, upward slanted eyes, sharp nose, and thick lips. The huge figure seems to be looking down from the sky. Although the skills of those who carved Maitreya into the cliff are far from being refined, it seems like they did their best. As a proof, the rock carving is still visible today, even after one thousand years.    There is a famous story behind this Maitreya carving. There is a square hole near the naval of the bodhisattva. It was a common practice to make a hole on the rock when carving a Buddha figure into a rocky cliff so the workers can store jewels and books. In the case of this Maitreya carving, people believed that a book written with great secrets to change the world was stored in the hole next to the bodhisattva's navel up until about 120 years ago. A rumor has it that the book was stolen in 1892 by the leaders of the Donghak Peasant Revolution. Upon hearing this, tens of thousands of peasants joined the movement, believing that the book contains the secrets to change the world. In a way, the peasants rebellion became a national movement because of the Buddhists who believed in the secret messages in the book. No one can tell if the peasant soldiers actually took the book or not, but one thing is for sure. They were desperate to change the world they live in.   Now let’s move on to Naewongung, a pavilion on top of the bodhisattva’s head, and where a statue of Maitreya is housed. It’s also the last place you’ll visit in your journey to Seonunsa Temple.

stories.title: Seonunsa Temple: A Hermitage with Maitreya in Meditation
stories.audioTitle: Seonunsa Temple: A Hermitage with Maitreya in Meditation
stories.script: A Hermitage with Maitreya in Meditation  [Narration] To get to Naewongung, you need to walk up a stone stairway, and the top of the staircase won’t be visible from the ground level because it’s circular. The stairway to Naewongung has a total of 161 steps.  Buddhists say that you should repent for your sins on the first 108 steps, and think about how to attain wisdom and enlightenment on the last 53. What they’re trying to tell you is to clear your mind while climbing the stairway.   According to a story, Naewongung is where Maitreya meditates, while enlightening the world. Although you won’t find any Maitreya statues here, you will see a golden seated statue of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva. With a round, elegance face and well-balanced body, the statue is very elaborately carved.   While you’re up here, why don’t you take in the scenery of Seonunsan Mountain?  Just look at the Seonunsan Peaks from Naewongung, and you'll see clouds over them.   Okay, you have seen every corner of Seonunsa Temple while walking along the stream. Seonunsan Mountain is where you can feel enlightened in a thick silence. Your tour of the temple ends here, where you can have a panoramic view of the mountain.

stories.title: Chaeseokgang, the Landform Created by the waves Over a period of 70 Million Years
stories.audioTitle: Chaeseokgang, the Landform Created by the waves Over a period of 70 Million Years
stories.script: The Landform Created by the Waves over the Period of 70 Million Years  [Narration]  What you see in front of you is called Chaeseokgang.  Formed by coastal erosion, the cliff has been hit by the waves over a period of 70 million years. Today, it looks like a tall stack of books. There are many caves of different shapes on the cliff as well. The sunset seen from one of the caves is quite extraordinary. The ocean turns red as the sun goes down.   Chaeseokgang is a more beautiful place at night. The ocean turns white when the moon is full, and the cliff and caves become more visible under the moonlight.   The beautiful scenery of Chaeseokgang is a gift of the nature.

stories.title: The Place to Bid Farewell to the Century, or the Year
stories.audioTitle: The Place to Bid Farewell to the Century, or the Year
stories.script: The Place to Bid Farewell to the Century, or the Year  [Narration] This scenic viewpoint is very popular among Koreans because it’s where the sun sets the latest in the country. That's why the New Millennium Festival was held on December 31, 1999.  On the last day of the 1999, thousands of people came to this place to start fire with a lens to celebrate the last sunset of the millennium. And the first sunrise of the new millennium was celebrated in Homigot, Pohang, because it’s where the sun rises first in the peninsula.   The celebration didn’t end there, since they put the fire from two different places together at a torch-shaped sculpture specially made for the occasion. They even gave a name to the fire: “The Eternal Fire of the New Millennium. The torch is still lit in Homigot, Pohang.   There is a great viewpoint at Gyeokpo Beach, offering a panoramic view of the beautiful place. This promenade stretches about seven kilometers from Chaeseokgang to Jeokbyeokgang, on which you can take a walk while taking in the beautiful scenery of the coast.   The walk on the promenade along the beach and the beautiful sunset will make your visit a memorable stay.

stories.title: The Tree Growing in the Sea Breeze
stories.audioTitle: The Tree Growing in the Sea Breeze
stories.script: The Tree Growing in the Sea Breeze  [Narration] Under the hill behind Suseongdang is a grove of silver magnolia trees, which usually grow in the southern islands of the Korean Peninsula. So this is as north as it gets in Korea for silver magnolia to grow. A silver magnolia tree can grow as tall as twenty meters with a girth of six meters. It’s a beautiful tree characterized by glossy red leaves.    There are a little over twenty silver magnolia trees that are about four meters tall in this grove, which are just enough to block the strong wind blowing from the sea. Since the trees serve as a windbreak, the local people can cultivate their land and grow crops without having to worry about the wind.   People living in a coastal village like this cherish silver magnolia trees for another reason as well, which is that they look neat and clean until the end of their life cycle.

stories.title: Jeokbyeokgang, with the Glow of the Sunset Over the Sea and Cliff
stories.audioTitle: The Glow of the Sunset over the Sea and Cliff
stories.script: The Glow of the Sunset over the Sea and Cliff  [Narration] Welcome to Jeokbyeokgang, where the sea and cliff are tinged by the red glow of the sunset in the evening.   The place was formed by the volcanic activity. You can still see the traces of lava on some of the rocks in the beach. They’re the igneous rocks, and the cliff around the area is also dark red.   Jeokbyeokgang is a pebble beach, with the pebbles worn down to the size of a bean by the waves. The whole beach is red all over, thanks to the volcanic rocks and cliffs.    That’s why the sunset is particularly beautiful in this place. In the evening, the rocks along the coast are tinged by the crimson glow of the setting sun. Another advantage of this place as a tourist site is that not many people come to this place, making it a perfect place to enjoy the view of the west coast in leisure.

stories.title: Suseongdang, the Shrine of a Guardian Deity
stories.audioTitle: The Shrine of a Guardian Deity
stories.script: The Shrine of a Guardian Deity  [Narration] This is Suseongdang, the cliff house on the rocky site of Yongdusan Mountain overlooking Jeokbyeokgang. It’s the only shrine and the last remnant of the folk religion of this coastal village. The archaeological excavation in 1992 revealed that people first started having rituals in this place about 1,700 years ago.   This shrine was dedicated to the guardian goddess of the West Sea. The local legend has it that the old goddess is so tall that the sea is only ankle-deep for her even when she’s standing in the deepest part of the West Sea.  The sea route in front of the shrine is known for having high waves.    The local people believed that the goddess protected their fishermen and boats by filling the deeper areas and calming the waves. So the people in this region performed rituals for the goddess, and prayed for the safety of their boats and prosperity of their town.  And the villagers still observe the tradition. It’s of a grand scale too, since a number of well-known shamans from other regions are invited on January 3rd of each year. Individual rituals are also held by different shamans throughout the year. Suseongdang has a strange, mysterious air. It must be because the ancient tradition of having rituals is still carried on.

stories.title: Naesosa Temple: The Fir Grove Trail for Walking Meditation
stories.audioTitle: Naesosa Temple: The Fir Grove Trail for Walking Meditation
stories.script: The Fir Grove Trail for Walking Meditation  [Narration] Welcome to Naesosa Temple! You’re in an ancient temple built in 633, but it's most well-known for its Fir Grove Trail. The trail has been there for over 150 years. It was created by the resident Buddhist monks, who had to plant over 500 fir trees to form a trail as you see today. The trail is only about 600 meters long, but while you’re on it, you’ll find that it’s a perfect place for a ‘walking meditation’.  Except for the scent of the trees, the scenery changes by season. You’ll see cherry blossoms in the spring, lush fir trees in the summer, tunnel of autumn leaves in the autumn, and snow covered trees in the winter. It’s no wonder this place is listed as one of the ‘Most Beautiful Groves’ as well as the 'Most Beautiful Trails in Korea’.

stories.title: Naesosa Temple: Shrine Tree, the Guardian of the Village
stories.audioTitle: Naesosa Temple: Shrine Tree, the Guardian of the Village
stories.script: The Guardian Tree of the Village  [Narration] Just inside the Cheonwangmun Gate is an old zelkova tree wrapped around with a golden rope. It’s called the ‘shrine tree’ because it’s regarded as a place of worship and the guardian deity of the village. It's a good example showing how Korean Buddhism goes hand in hand with folk beliefs.    The shrine tree is one thousand years old, and there is another shrine tree at the first gate to the temple. That one is about seven hundred years old.   These shrine trees are also the guardians of the village where the temple is located. The monks hold a Buddhist ritual in front of the shrine tree inside the temple on January 15th of the lunar calendar, and then hold a folk-style ritual with the villagers in front of the shrine tree at the entrance. In the second ritual, people mostly pray for a good harvest and prosperous life.

stories.title: Naesosa Temple: The Bronze Bell for Your Spiritual Ears
stories.audioTitle: Naesosa Temple: The Bronze Bell for Your Spirtual Ears
stories.script: A Bell for Your Spiritual Ears  [Narration] The Bronze Bell at Naesosa Temple was made in 1222. A story has it that a farmer found the bell while working on the farm, but the strange thing was that it didn’t make any sound no matter how hard he hit it.  So he took the bell to a number of temples to see if the Buddhist monks can make it work, but none of them could. But when a monk at Naesosa Temple struck the bell, it rang. So the bell was donated to Naesosa Temple.   The Bronze Bell of Naesosa Temple is not only known for its serene and clear sound, but for its beautiful shape. The elaborate patterns engraved on the bell are also what make this bell so unique.  The Bronze Bell is not in use anymore, but you can still hear the temple bell in the morning and evening. Right behind the temple is a hermitage, where you can enjoy the clear sound of the bell while looking down at the West Sea. It’s one of the best places to enjoy the scenery and the serene sound of the temple bell at the same time.

stories.title: Naesosa Temple: The Beauty of the Main Hall of Naesosa Temple
stories.audioTitle: Naesosa Temple: The Beauty of the Mail Hall of Naesosa Temple
stories.script: The Beauty of the Main Hall of Naesosa Temple  [Narration] The 'Daeungbojeon', or the main hall of Naesosa Temple is a well-preserved cultural heritage made by using traditional joint construction methods, in which no nails are used.   It's not as big or colorful as most other Buddhist temples in Korea, but it blends in with the nature of Neunggasan Mountain behind. It’s also an important cultural heritage both in the aspects of architecture and art.   Go take a look at the murals of Maitreya on the back wall of the wall. You’ll see a painting of bodhisattva Avalokitesvara. It’s the biggest painting of bodhisattva Avalokitesvara in Korea. There is a legend about this painting. The legend has it that your wishes will come true you if the eyes of the painting follow you when you walk to the side while looking directly into the eyes.

stories.title: Naesosa Temple: The Flowers in Daeungbojeon Make the World More Beautiful
stories.audioTitle: Naesosa Temple: The Flowers in Daeungbojeon MAke the World More Beautiful
stories.script: The Flowers in Daeungbojeon Make the World More Beautiful  [Narration] This is Daeungbojeon, or the main hall of the temple is famous for the flower carved doors. They're the oldest flower carved door in Korea.   There are a total of eight doors elaborately carved with sunflowers, lotus flowers, and chrysanthemum flowers. Since they’re paper sliding doors, the flowers are carved on the frames. They were originally painted, but the colors are completely washed out with time, wind, and rain. But the carved flowers are still there, still beautiful even after hundreds of years.   The flowers on the door frames represent the beauty of the world of Buddhism. The woodworker who carved the flowers into the wood somehow managed to make it look like the flowers are blooming on the door. Everything had to be caved down to the finest detail, since even the slightest slip with the chisel meant redoing the whole thing again.  Thanks to the woodworker’s devotion to his work, we can still appreciate the beauty of these doors. Looking as though they were carved into the wood today, the carved flowers will make your visit to the main hall of Naesosa Temple a memorable experience.

stories.title: Naesosa Temple: Seolsandang and Dormitory, the Places of Meditation for Monks
stories.audioTitle: Naesosa Temple: Seolsandang and Dormitory, the Places of Meditation for Monks
stories.script: The Places of Meditation for Monks  [Narration] The buildings in front of you is where the monks of Naesosa live. Surrounded by Neunggasan Mountain, the buildings are connected to each other to form a perfect square. Connected on all four sides, the buildings share a front yard with a well in the middle.   Built in 1640, the buildings are particularly unique in that the ground under them is not leveled even though there is a slope. Instead, wood columns of different lengths are placed on top of the foundation stones to level the floor. This traditional building technique was employed because traditionally, Koreans tried not to destroy the nature around them.  This is where your journey from the Fir Grove Trail ends. Breathe in the fresh air of Neunggasan Mountain in front of the living quarters of the Buddhist priests.    We hope you have taken some of the burden off your shoulders during the journey, and feel a little more light-hearted on your way back down.

stories.title: Namhansanseong
stories.script: Along with Bukhansanseong, Namhansanseong is a fortress built in Joseon Dynasty to defend the capital Hanyang. It began construction during King Injo’s reign.  What event comes up to your mind when you hear King Injo of Joseon Dynasty? Most likely the Second Manchu Invasion, or Byeongjahoran. King Injo took refuge in Namhansanseong during the Invasion. Namhansanseong is extraordinarily advantageous in terms of defense thanks to its height and rough terrain. Additionally, with a circumference of 12 kilometers, Namhansanseong encompasses a vast basin large enough to house an entire city. As such, it served as a perfect refuge for the Joseon court, providing a safe haven for both the king and his people in times of crisis.   Currently, defense facilities, secret passage, well, military training grounds, and government offices remain in Namhansanseong. Many artifacts from the early Baekje period are discovered in the area, making some believe that Namhansanseong must have had been a palace for King Onjo, the founding father of Baekje. This theory is supported by the presence of Sunhnyeoljeon, a shrine built to store King Onjo’s spirit tablet.   However, excavations at the site of the Namhan Temporary Palace have uncovered roof tiles and stone structures from the Unified Silla period. Inside the fortress walls, granite stones presumed to be part of Jujangseong Fortress, constructed during the reign of King Munmu of Silla, have also been found. These findings have led to speculation that Namhansanseong may have originated as Jujangseong Fortress during the Unified Silla era.  Regardless of its origins, what remains unchanged is Namhansanseong’s critical role as a bastion of defense for Joseon. Its facilities are meticulously maintained, making it one of the most well-preserved fortresses in Korea. Namhansanseong also showcases the evolution of fortification techniques across different historical periods. Namhansanseong was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, for its historical and cultural significance.

stories.title: Namhansanseong Haenggung
stories.script: [Narrator] December 1636, King Injo was taking refuge here, in Namhansanseong Haenggung, to evade the attack of the Qing Dynasty. [Juhwapa (Pro-Qing) Member 1] Fight Qing? Are you out of your mind? We can’t afford a battle against Qing soldiers! [Cheokhwapa (Anti-Qing) Member 1] That’s why we must be smart about it! Are you suggesting we betray the Ming? Have you forgotten that the Ming is our closest ally?  [Juhwapa (Pro-Qing) Member 2] Even if they were once our brother nation, they’re now nothing more than a toothless tiger! [Cheokhwapa (Anti-Qing) Member 2] No matter how strong Qing may be, I absolutely cannot agree with the idea of making peace with them! [Narrator] King Injo felt a heavy heart. Leaving behind his ministers, who argued every time they met, he quietly stepped outside. Sensing the king’s concerns, his chamberlain followed silently. Outside, snowflakes swirled in the icy wind. It didn’t take long for King Injo to realize that things were much worse outside the Haenggung. No matter where he turned his gaze, the sight was unbearable. Beyond the fortress walls, the mighty Qing army, 100,000 strong, loomed in their camps, high in morale. Within the fortress, soldiers and civilians suffered from hunger and cold. The king’s heart felt as if it were being torn apart. To soothe his heavy heart, he began wandering aimlessly through the Haenggung. The palace was unusually quiet and dark. Then, he saw a group of generals and soldiers patrolling the palace grounds. But their clothing was completely soaked. [King Injo] Why are you in wet clothes? [General] Your majesty, it’s because it is impossible to dry our clothes in this weather.  [Narrator] King Injo’s eyes started to water. [King Injo] Go straight to my chamber! Tear apart my blankets and clothes and give them to the soldiers to wear. [Narrator] The soldiers knelt, bowing their heads, tears streaming down their faces. King Injo looked up, glaring at the heavens with eyes full of despair. Soon, his own tears began to fall. [King Injo] Oh, Heaven! Why do you abandon us? Please, do not let my people suffer for my sins. Let me bear the punishment alone. Oh, Heaven! Please! [Narrator] Tears continued to roll down the faces of King Injo and his soldiers. Snowstorm gradually subsided, and through the clouds, a few starts began to glimmer faintly.  Haenggung is a temporary palace for kings when they left the royal palace in Seoul for travels outside the capital. Namhansanseong Haenggung was constructed in the fourth year of King Injo’s reign as a refuge in case of war or rebellion. As a matter of fact, when the Second Manchu Invasion (Byeonjahoran) broke out, King Injo took refuge and fought against the Qing army for 47 days.

stories.title: Sueojangdae
stories.script: [Narrator] King Jeongjo led the final years of Joseon’s golden age. The following even occurred when he visited Namhansanseong to inspect the military. [King Jeongjo] Ugh… Ah! Another nightmare… [Narrator] King Jeongjo suffered from chronic insomnia and frequently experienced nightmares. [Chamberlain] Your Majesty, are you feeling unwell? [Narrator] The elderly chamberlain, Jang Han-yong, quietly approached and sat by his side. A loyal servant, he had faithfully served Jeongjo for many years. [King Jeongjo] Ah, Chamberlain Jang… It’s nothing to worry about. [Narrator] King Jeongjo was a wise and virtuous ruler. To avoid burdening his people, he ate only two meals a day and insisted on wearing coarse hemp clothing. Even in his quarters, he preferred a straw mat over luxurious bedding. However, King Jeongjo bore deep pain. After his father, Crown Prince Sado, was executed in a rice chest, King Jeongjo, then a young prince, was often the target of assassination attempts orchestrated by his political enemies. To protect himself, King Jeongjo mastered martial arts while dedicating himself to rigorous study to become a ruler so capable that no one could challenge him. His efforts earned him the reputation of a king who was both academically and physically excellent. Yet, the repeated threats to his life left him deeply anxious, ultimately contributing to his battle with insomnia. [Chamberlain] Your Majesty, since you’re already awake, why not take a walk around Namhansanseong? [King Jeongjo] Yes, that sounds good. [Narrator] When King Jeongjo and the chamberlain strolled through the night and arrived near Sueojangdae, they encountered a well glistened in the moonlight. [King Jeongjo] Ah, just what I needed. Let’s have a drink of water—it looks refreshing. Ah, so crisp and cool. [Chamberlain] Yes, Your Majesty. This is the water our soldiers drink while guarding the fortress. [King Jeongjo] It’s nice to know that they have clean and clear water to drink. [Narrator] King Jeongjo stepped into the courtyard of Sueojangdae and gazed at the signboard on the second floor. [Narrator] The name on the signboard, Mulmang meaning ‘do not forget,’ was personally written by his grandfather, King Yeongjo. But what should not be forgotten? It was the humiliation of the Second Manchu Invasion (Byeongjahoran). [King Jeongjo] The Second Manchu Invasion (Byeongjahoran) was one of the most shameful events in Joseon’s history. We must remember it and ensure it never happens again. I will strengthen Joseon to prevent such humiliation from ever recurring. [Narrator] King Jeongjo lived his life with this conviction. Although his sudden death prevented him from fully realizing his vision, his enduring spirit continues to inspire us. A Jangdae is a commander’s post, typically built in a secure location with a clear view of the surrounding area. Unfortunately, the Jangdae built at Namhansanseong during wartime were all destroyed. In the mid-to-late 18th century, Sueojangdae (West Command Post) and Namjangdae (South Command Post) were rebuilt as pavilions. Today, only Sueojangdae remains.

stories.title: Sungryeoljeon Shrine
stories.script: [Narrator] Several days after fleeing to Namhansanseong Fortress to escape the Qing attack, King Injo was physically and mentally exhausted. One evening, while pondering state affairs, he drifted off to sleep. [King Onjo] The enemy is at your doorstep, and yet you are sleeping? [Narrator] Startled by the sudden scolding, King Injo woke with a jolt. Standing before him was an elderly man with a stern expression. Dressed in an embellished golden robe, the man radiated an air of authority. [King Onjo] You fool! Time is running out. Go to the northern wall immediately! [King Injo] W-who are you? [King Onjo] I am Onjo, the master of this fortress. [Narrator] The old man was none other than King Onjo, the founding monarch of Baekje. Onjo pressed King Injo further. [King Onjo] Hurry! There is no time to waste. Send your generals to the northern wall at once! [Narrator] At that moment, King Injo awoke from his dream. Wasting no time, he summoned General Yi Seo. [Kig Injo] Go to the northern wall immediately and check for any enemy activity! [Yi Seo] Yes, Your Majesty! [Narrator] General Yi Seo, one of King Injo’s most trusted commanders, headed toward the northern wall. Before long, Yi Seo and his soldiers discovered hundreds of Qing soldiers attempting to climb up the fortress walls. Yi Seo and his men repelled the invaders, securing a decisive victory. Deeply grateful for the warning in his dream, King Injo constructed a shrine to honor King Onjo’s spirit and held a ceremony with his court. Several days later, King Injo had another dream. Once again, King Onjo appeared. [King Onjo] I am grateful that you have offered a ceremony in my honor. [King Injo] Great King, thank you for protecting the fortress. [King Onjo] I have one more request. The shrine feels too empty. Could you send me one of your loyal subjects to keep me company? [Narrator] For a second, King Injo hesitated. Fulfilling King Onjo’s request would mean the death of one of his subjects. Yet, he could not refuse. [King Injo] I understand. Who shall it be? [King Onjo] I will take care of it. [Narrator] The next morning, King Injo woke up with a heavy heart. As he contemplated his dream, his chief secretary burst into the room with a panicked expression. [Chief Secretary] Your Majesty! Tragic news! Last night... General Yi Seo passed away! [Narrator] King Injo collapsed, overwhelmed with grief. General Yi Seo had been one of his most beloved commanders. He was a loyal patriot and a fearless warrior who had played a pivotal role in building Namhansanseong Fortress. For days, King Injo mourned the loss of his faithful servant. After the war ended, in 1638, King Injo enshrined King Onjo’s spirit tablet in a hall originally known as Onwangmyo (Shrine to King Onjo) and had General Yi Seo honored alongside him. Later, in 1795, King Jeongjo renamed the shrine Sungnyeoljeon Shrine(Hall of Revered Loyalty). To this day, an annual memorial ceremony is held at the site on the 5th day of the 9th lunar month.

stories.title: Cheongnyangdang
stories.script: [Narrator] During the construction of Namhansanseong Fortress, a loud scolding voice echoed from the tent of General Yi Seo, who was overseeing the massive project.  [Yi Seo] What? The work in this area is still at such an early stage?  [General 1] Yes, sir. We’ve sent out numerous pressing orders, but General Yi Hoe is incredibly stubborn.  [Yi Seo] Arrest Yi Hoe at once! [Narrator] Soon, Yi Hoe was tied with ropes and dragged in front of the Sueojangdae, a military pavilion.  [Yi Seo] Yi Hoe, you scoundrel! I trusted you with this critical task. Why have you neglected your duty? [Narrator] Despite the fierce scolding from General Yi Seo, known as “the Tiger,” Yi Hoe remained calm and composed. [Yi Hoe] General! The southeast section I’m responsible for has extremely steep and rough terrain. That’s why the construction is taking longer. We had to proceed with extra care. [Yi Seo] How dare a government official who makes a living on valuable tax make excuses for his laziness? Execute Yi Hoe immediately! [Yi Hoe] General... [Narrator] The executioner started dancing and swinging his sword to the beating of a drum. Yi Hoe closed his eyes, awaiting his fate. [Yi Seo] Yi Hoe! Do you have any last words? [Yi Hoe] Everything is the will of heaven! I do not fear death. However, I cannot accept the false charge of negligence. Something extraordinary will happen at the moment of my death. Please take that as evidence of my innocence. [Narrator] At that very moment, the executioner’s blade sliced through the air, severing Yi Hoe’s neck. But then— [Soldier 1] What is that? [Soldier 2] It’s a bird! A bird just flew out from Yi Hoe’s neck! [Narrator] Indeed, no blood spilled from Yi Hoe’s severed neck. Instead, a large hawk emerged, flying into the sky. The hawk perched on a rock, bowed its head toward the south, where the king resided, and then soared into the sky, disappearing from view. [Soldier 1] Look, General! There’s a footprint on the rock! [Narrator] Sure enough, the hawk’s footprint was clearly imprinted on the rock. General Yi Seo recalled Yi Hoe’s final words. [Yi Hoe] Something extraordinary will happen at the moment of my death. Please take that as evidence of my innocence. [Yi Seo] Ah, Yi Hoe... You were telling the truth... I have wrongfully killed a loyal subject. [Narrator] People mourned Yi Hoe’s death and built a shrine near Sueojangdae to honor him. The rock where the hawk perched became known as Hawk Rock (Mae Bawi). Unfortunately, the hawk’s footprint is no longer visible. Does this mean the legend is false? No. During the Japanese colonial period, a Japanese official carved out the section of the rock with the hawk’s footprint and took it. Only a rectangular mark remains today. Afterward, Yi Hoe was referred to as Hoengsu Daegam (The Lord of Tragic Fate) due to his unjust death. Among the many spirits worshiped at Namhansanseong, he is regarded as one of the most powerful and divine.

stories.title: Hyeonjeolsa Shrine
stories.script: During the Second Manchu Invasion (Byeongjahoran), the Joseon court took refuge in the temporary palace or Haenggung at Namhansanseong. The invading Qing Dynasty demanded that Joseon cut ties with the Ming Dynasty and form an alliance with them. The Joseon court was divided into two factions. Juhwapa and Cheokhwapa. Juhwapa argued that Joseon should accept the Qing’s demand and strike new alliance.   Juhwapa: Although it is true that the Ming Dynasty has been a close ally for a long time, it has weakened. The world will soon be dominated by the Qing Dynasty. It would be wise for the future of Joseon to align with the Qing.   Cheokhwapa: You should be ashamed of yourselves! The Ming helped us during the Imjin War. How dare you suggest we abandon our loyal friend and befriend the Qing?  As the war progressed, it became increasingly unfavorable for Joseon. Having backed Joseon into a corner, the Qing issued a harsh demand.   General Yong Gol-dae: I, General Yong Gol-dae of the Qing, deliver the order of our emperor.
