Send the most resolute Cheokhwapa members of the Joseon court to our camp as hostages.   Three loyal officials volunteered. They were O Dal-je, Yun Jip, and Hong Ik-han.   Yun Jip: Your majesty, I Yun Jip, offer my life for Joseon.  At the time, Yun Jip’s position in the court was Gyori, responsible for drafting government documents. This role is equivalent to a mid-level officer, fifth-grade civil servant, in today’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs or Ministry of Culture, Sports, and Tourism.   O Dal-je: Your majesty! I, O Dal-je, as Vice-Gyori, will join Yun Gyori and sacrifice my life for the nation.  O Dal-je served as Vice-Gyori, a close assistant to Yun Jip.  Hong Ik-han: Your majesty, I, Hong Ik-han, as a government inspector, dedicate my life to Joseon.   Hong Ik-han’s position was Jangnyeong, responsible for state inspections, similar to modern-day senior auditor in Board of Audit and Inspection, a third-grade civil servant.  These three men were one of the younger members of the court, in their late 20s and early 30s. Filled with passion, courage, and unwavering patriotism, they stood firm even when brought in front of General Yong Gol-dae.  Yong Gol-dae: Look at you! You are just young pups. Aren’t you afraid to die? Why don’t you give in and work for the Qing court instead?  Yun Jip: Ha! I am Yun Jip, a Gyori of Joseon. My duty is to draft loyal documents. I doubt your barbaric country even have documents for me to work with.  O Dal-je: I am Vice-Gyori. Why do you even need Gyori and Vice-Gyori when you don’t even have documents? All you would have us do is scoop horse feces. I have no interest. Just go ahead and kill me.  Hong Ik-han: I am Hong Ik-han, a Jangnyeong of Joseon. I oversee audit. I root out corruption and uphold justice. In your lawless country, there would be so much filth for me to clean up, I’d end up dying of overworking. You might as well kill me here.   Finally, Yong Gol-dae lost his patience.  General Yong Gol-dae: Enough of your insolence! Just thinking about working with you gives me a headache. Fine, I’ll grant your wish and kill you!  The three men were eventually executed, but their unwavering loyalty moved even the Qing soldiers, who treated their remains with respect and provided them with honorable burials. The three became known as the Three Loyal Subjects (Samhaksa).  Hyunjeolsa Shrine was built to honor these three patriots. Today, it is designated as a Gyeonggi Province Tangible Cultural Heritage. Later, the spirit tablets of other notable Cheokhwapa figures, such as Prime Minister Kim Sang-heon and Second Minister of Personnel Jeong On, were also enshrined here. Collectively, these five figures are referred to as the Five Loyal Subjects (Ohhaksa).

stories.title: Chimgwaejeong
stories.script: [Narrator] Our nation has endured countless wars throughout its history. Among them, the Second Manchu Invasion (Byeongjahoran), was particularly harsh. Even the king and his officials had to abandon the capital, Hanyang (modern-day Seoul), and take refuge here at Namhansanseong Fortress.  At the time, King Injo suffered the humiliation of kneeling before the Qing emperor and bowing his head to the ground in surrender. Moreover, Crown Prince Sohyeon, Prince Bongnim, and other members of the royal family and high-ranking officials were taken as hostages to the Qing court.  Later, King Hyojong, who ascended the throne after King Injo, could not forget the disgrace of Byeongjahoran.  [King Hyojong] We must ensure that we never bow to the barbarians again. To achieve this, I pledge to pursue Bukbeol!  [Narrator] Bukbeol! It means Northern Expedition, or the determination to conquer the Qing Dynasty. Following this declaration, Bukbeol became a guiding principle for the Joseon court.  Chimgwaejeong symbolizes this vow for Bukbeol. It served as a military office, with nearby facilities for manufacturing and storing weapons. As such, it became the central hub for the soldiers stationed at Namhansanseong Fortress.  However, a rumor circulated among the soldiers working at Chimgwaejeong during the Joseon Dynasty.  [Soldier 1] Hey, did you hear? It showed up again! Kim saw it last night.  [Soldier 2] What? That ghost of old man appeared again?  [Soldier 1] Exactly! A man in a blue robe with a gold crown—it must be him!  [Narrator] The ghost reportedly appeared during the soldiers' night patrols, wearing a blue robe and a gold crown.  [Old Soldier] That’s the spirit of King Onjo.  [Soldier 1] King Onjo? Is he the current king?  [Soldier 2] Ugh, you fool! King Onjo was the founding king of Baekje.  [Soldier 1] Why would a king from Baekje appear in Joseon?  [Old Soldier] Well, they say that Namhansanseong was originally Baekje's capital. Perhaps he appears to support us. We are his descendants.  [Soldier 2] Then that ghost—no, the great king—is on our side, so we don’t have to fear him.  [Old Soldier] Of course not. If you see him, pay him respect with a bow. Haha!  [Narrator] The origins of Chimgwaejeong are unclear. In 1624, King Injo ordered the construction of Namhansanseong Fortress to strengthen national defense. During the construction, General Yi Seo, the overseer, discovered the remnants of a building in the dense forest. While the walls and roof were gone, the pillars, foundation stones, and even the ondol (Korean underfloor heating system) were intact. Based on these remnants, the Chimgwaejeong was rebuilt.  The current structure, however, was restored in 1751 during the reign of King Yeongjo. The signboard originally read ChimGWAjeong, not ChimKWAEejeong. The name ChimGWA translates to ‘resting one’s head on a spear,’ symbolizing readiness and vigilance. Over time, the name evolved into Chimgwaejeong.  Chimgwaejeong serves as a reminder of the painful defeat during the Second Manchu Invasion, emphasizing the importance of guarding against external threats while strengthening the nation from within.

stories.title: Yeonmugwan
stories.script: [Soldiers] Hup! Hup! Hup! [Yi Mu-hyeong] Your arms are still too low! Again! [Soldiers] Hup! Hup! Hup! [Yi Mu-hyeong] Raise the tip of your swords! One more time! [Narrator] Yeonmugwan was the most energetic and intense place within Namhansanseong Fortress. It was where soldiers were trained. Those who performed exceptionally here were sent to Hanyang (modern-day Seoul), where the king resided. The men would continue their training until the sun was high in the sky.  [Yi Mu-hyeong] Take two hours of rest. This afternoon, we will practice archery. Eat your meals and gather at the archery range! [Narrator] Yi Mu-hyeong, the drill instructor at Yeonmugwan Pavilion, shouted at the men without showing any signs of fatigue. The soldiers adjusted their uniforms. [Yi Mu-hyeong] It looks like it’ll rain soon. Be careful not to get wet. Dismissed! [Soldiers] Yay! [Yi Mu-hyeong] Haha, during training, you're all strong men, but at times like this, you turn into little boys. [Narrator] Just then, someone entered the training ground. [Gu Goeng] Drill Instructor Yi Mu-hyeong! [Yi Mu-hyeong] Ah, Minister Gu Goeng! What brings you here? [Narrator] Gu Goeng, the Minister of Public Works, was also a deeply committed military official like Yi Mu-hyeong. Having passed the military service examination early in life, Gu Goeng became a trusted minister of King Injo. [Gu Goeng] Why do you think I’m here? I came to see if there are any competent soldiers worth sending to Hanyang. [Narrator] Gu Goeng often visited Yeonmugwan Pavilion to select outstanding warriors and send them to Hanyang. [Yi Mu-hyeong] If the soldiers knew the minister was here, they would train even harder. By the way, how are things in the royal court? [Gu Goeng] A Qing envoy visited recently. What do you think they demanded? [Yi Mu-hyeong] It’s obvious. They want us to abandon the Ming Dynasty and strike alliance with the Qing, don’t they? [Gu Goeng] Exactly. At first, everyone dismissed the idea as ridiculous, but now, some are saying aligning with the Qing might not be such a bad idea. [Yi Mu-hyeong] Opinions are divided even among the soldiers here. Some argue we should ally with the Qing, while others insist we must resist to the end. What are your thoughts, Minister? [Gu Goeng] I’m still unsure. But I can’t shake the ominous feeling that war is inevitable. [Yi Mu-hyeong] A war… If that happens, I can’t imagine the suffering the people must endure. [Gu Goeng] If we consider the people’s suffering, allying with the Qing seems like the right choice. [Yi Mu-hyeong] But if we do that, the government will be abandoning its principles. [Gu Goeng] And if we consider that, we mustn’t sever our ties with the Ming. [Yi Mu-hyeong] It is truly a dilemma. [Gu Goeng] We are soldiers. Whatever decision is made, whatever happens, our duty is to fight for Joseon and its people. [Yi Mu-hyeong] Indeed. That is our duty, General. [Narrator] As the two feared, the Second Manchu Invasion (Byeongjahoran) broke out soon after, plunging Joseon into the chaos of war. However, thanks to the courageous soldiers trained by dedicated military men like Gu Goeng and Yi Mu-hyeong, the nation was ultimately defended. The name Yeonmu means to showcase martial skills. Yeonmugwan was built specifically to train soldiers in martial arts. Military training and competitions were held here to select outstanding soldiers, who were then sent to serve in the royal court. During the reign of King Jeongjo, the civil and military service exams were also held at Yeonmugwan.

stories.title: Jisudang
stories.script: [Narrator] Jisudang was a leisurely fishing spot for high-ranking officials in the past. It served as a space for reflection, communication, and discussion. What if Kim Sang-heon and Choi Myung-gil, two key figures from the story of the Second Manchu Invasion (Byeongjahoran), had fished here together? Perhaps their conversation might have gone like this. [Kim Sang-heon] Sighs deeply… [Narrator] Minister of Rites, Kim Sang-heon, had been sitting in the same spot for hours, staring at his fishing float, but hadn’t caught a single fish. [Choi Myung-gil] Minister Kim, it seems you haven’t had any bites yet. [Kim Sang-heon] Ah, Minister Choi… [Narrator] The man approaching was Minister of Personnel, Choi Myung-gil. The two were the respective leaders of the opposing political factions. At that time, the Joseon politics was divided between the isolationist Cheokhwapa faction and the accommodationist Juhwapa faction. The Juhwapa, led by Choi Myung-gil, advocated for breaking ties with the weakening Ming Dynasty and forming an alliance with the Qing. In contrast, the Cheokhwapa, led by Kim Sang-heon, argued against betraying their long-time ally, Ming. Naturally, the two often found themselves at odds. [Choi Myung-gil] I came to fish as well. May I sit beside you, Minister Kim? [Kim Sang-heon] Go ahead. It’s the king’s reservoir, after all. Who am I to object? [Choi Myung-gil] Thank you. [Narrator] Choi’s fishing float soon disappeared underwater with a lively splash. The two men sat silently, focusing on their floats. [Choi Myung-gil] Minister Kim, fishing is about using bait to catch fish, isn’t it? Politics and diplomacy are similar in that we use strategies to achieve our goals. Don’t you think fishing and our work have much in common? [Kim Sang-heon] I suppose they do. [Choi Myung-gil] If the goal is to catch fish for dinner, wouldn’t it be best to use the most efficient method? Perhaps casting a net and catching them all at once? [Kim Sang-heon] I disagree. If a fisherman only thinks about tonight’s meal and catches all the fish he can, there will come a day when he’ll find no fish at all. Even in fishing, there is an order and a principle to follow. [Choi Myung-gil] Ha! But if we keep hesitating, worrying about the future, we might miss the chance to catch the fish we truly want. [Kim Sang-heon] Then I will wait until I catch the fish I want. [Choi Myung-gil] So, are you willing to let go of the fish already in your hand just because it’s not the one you desire? [Kim Sang-heon] The purpose of fishing isn’t merely to catch fish but to embrace the waiting. I find it hard to concentrate to be sitting here with someone so impatient. I’ll be leaving now. [Choi Myung-gil] Ha! Believe it or not, Minister Kim, I admire your unwavering principles. [Kim Sang-heon] Unfortunately, I dislike your reed-like flexibility, Minister Choi. [Choi Myung-gil] Ah, so you’d like to uproot the reeds, then? [Kim Sang-heon] Though I dislike them, I wouldn’t remove them. [Choi Myung-gil] And why is that? [Kim Sang-heon] A forest needs bamboo, but a riverside must have reeds. [Narrator] Indeed, sometimes the steadfastness of bamboo is necessary, while at other times, the flexibility of reeds is essential. Despite their differences, both Kim Sang-heon and Choi Myung-gil shared the same love for their country, though their methods were different. Today, Jisudang is designated as Gyeonggi-do Cultural Heritage Material No. 14. It was built in the 13th year of King Hyeonjong's reign by Governor Lee Se-hwa. Originally, there were three ponds surrounding Jisudang, but only two remain today. This spot wasn’t just for fishing. It was a place where scholars and officials composed poetry, practiced calligraphy, and sought personal growth.

stories.title: ﻿Janggyeongsa Temple
stories.script: ﻿[Narrator] A long, long time ago, there lived a monk named Geomdan Seonsa at this site. He was a virtuous and kind-hearted monk, renowned across the country. One day, a cute little boy visited him.   [Boy] Monk, do you like wild vegetables?  [Narrator] The boy’s basket was filled with fresh wild vegetables.   [Boy] I live down the street. I brought some wild vegetables. I heard monks like them.  [Geomdan Seonsa] Thank you. I’ll enjoy them.  [Narrator] From then on, the monk and the boy became friends. They played pranks together, foraged for wild vegetables, played Go, and enjoyed each other’s company. But one winter, when the cold was at its worst…  [Boy] Monk, monk! My mom has collapsed!  [Narrator] The boy’s mother, who had been raising him alone after her husband’s early death, suddenly fell ill. A doctor examined her and shook his head.  [Doctor] This is serious. There is a cure, but…  [Boy] A cure? What is it? Where can I find it?  [Doctor] If you brew dried persimmons and jujubes, she might recover. But in this freezing winter, where would you find such things?   [Narrator] Geomdan Seonsa couldn’t just stand by.  [Geomdan Seonsa] Child, I will find those persimmons and jujubes. You stay and look after your mother.  [Boy] Really? But I feel so bad to trouble you.  [Geomdan Seonsa] Don’t say that. We’re friends, aren’t we?  [Narrator] Geomdan Seonsa traveled to Mount Myohyang, said to be the dwelling of divine beings. There, he managed to obtain the ingredients and hurried back, only to find out…  [Woman] Oh, monk, it only you had come a little earlier. The boy’s mother passed away just two days ago.  [Geomdan Seonsa] What? Then where is the boy?  [Woman] He cried endlessly at his mother’s grave and then disappeared. We searched everywhere but couldn’t find him.  [Narrator] Geomdan Seonsa was heartbroken to see the mother’s humble grave. He placed a stone as a headstone to mark it. One day. During a violent storm, lightening struck the stone and broke off a piece.  [Geomdan Seonsa] Ah, I should erect a new headstone. Wait, is this… is this the Buddha?  [Narrator] To his astonishment, Geomdan Seonsa discovered that the broken fragment bore the image of the Buddha.   [Geomsan Seonsa] This must be a sign to build a temple here.   [Narrator] Geomdan Seonsa built a temple at that very place and named it Janggyeongsa. The name means long-lasting prosperity, symbolizing the hope that the boy and his mother, who had suffered in life, would find eternal happiness in the afterlife.  Geomdan Seonsa enshrined the Buddha-engraved stone inside the temple. It is said that when he passed away, the stone disappeared with him. People believe that the boy’s spirit had followed Geomdan Seonsa.  However, this is merely a legend. In fact, Janggyeongsa was built during the Joseon Dynasty by order of King Injo. It served as a temple for monk soldiers, monks who fought to protect the nation during times of foreign invasion. Janggyeongsa was a training and living site for these monk soldiers, embodying the temple’s patriotic role. Today, Janggyeongsa is designated as Gyeonggi-do Cultural Heritage Material No. 15.

stories.title: ﻿Gaewonsa Temple Site
stories.script: ﻿[Narrator] A bell rings in a quiet mountain temple. A Buddhist monk sits in the great hall, quietly playing a wooden fish. He is Master Myeongjo, better known as the commander of the monk soldiers among the public.   In 1627, the Qing Dynasty invaded Joseon, an invasion referred to the Later Jin Invasion (Jeongmyohoran). At this time, Master Myeongjo makes an important decision.   [Master Myeongjo] I shouldn’t kill as I am a monk. But how can I stand idly by while my country, which I have bonded with, is trampled on like this! I will gather the monks and defeat the Qing army!  [Narrator] Led by Master Myeongjo, the monk soldiers defeated the Qing army in various places and managed to find peace, or so it seemed.  [Monk 1] Master, Master, we’re in trouble.   [Narrator] In winter of 1636, the surprising news arrived.   [Monk 1] Master! The Qing army has invaded again. The Joseon army fought bravely but they were overwhelmed and the king and his servants took refuge in Namhansanseong Fortress.  [Master Myeongjo] It happened again.  [Narrator] Master Myeongjo did not hesitate to send out news to temples across the country that he is recruiting new soldiers.   [Master Myeongjo] Monks of Joseon, today, we go out to fight. Buddha taught us to refrain from killing but today, we have chosen to put aside Buddha’s words and fight for this country and people who need us.  [Narrator] The monk soldiers clenched their fists.   [Master Myeongjo] Today, we must go out to fight. We must leave this castle to walk a path more important and greater than our own enlightenment. We may die. However, our spirits will be etched into the history of this land. We will be remembered for not turning our backs on the suffering of this country and the people.   [Monk Soldier 1] For my country!  [Monk Soldier 2] For the people!  [Monk Solders] Waaaaaah~  [Narrator] From then on, until the end of the Second Manchu Invasion (Byeongjahoran), Gaewonsa Temple served as the headquarters for monk soldiers. Monks were regarded to be of lowly status during the Joseon Dynasty. But in times of national distress, they would rise up and give their lives without a second thought.   Gaewonsa Temple in Namhansanseong is a patriotic temple that reflects the fervent patriotism of those monks.   Unfortunately, nothing remains of the original temple. It was rebuilt in 1971, and then again in late 1986 to take on its current form. Currently designated as Gyeonggi-do Monument No. 119, Gaewonsa Temple Site was a patriotic temple that protected the capital Hanyang (today’s Seoul) for over 270 years until it was abolished during the Gabo Reforms.

stories.title: Gangchon Rail Park
stories.audioTitle: Walk through memory lane of the old Gyeongchun railway
stories.script: Walk through memory lane of the old Gyeongchun railway   In Gangchon Rail Park, there are rail bike courses that remind visitors of the memory and nostalgia of the Gyeongchun railway which ceased its operations. The rail bikes run on some sections of the railway, which start from Gangchon Station, Gyeonggang Station, and Gimyujeong Station. If you take a Chuncheon City Tour bus, you can ride the rail bike from Gimyujeong Station. Gimyujeong Station was named after Kim Yu-jeong, a famous writer known for many works, such as Spring, Spring and The Camellias. The village, where the station is located, is the birthplace of the writer, which is the main backdrop in most of his novels. The exterior of Gimyujeong Station is surrounded by rows of gigantic books that are lined up as if they were on a bookshelf. You may feel like you have just arrived in a land of giants. Now, shall we go ride the rail bike? The bike course that starts at Gimyujeong Station is mostly downhill, so it is easy and exciting to pedal. You can enjoy picturesque scenery along the railroad surrounded by small flowers and old signposts. The tunnels you will pass have different themes, such as a club tunnel with flashy lights and exciting music and a galaxy tunnel with the milky way in the night sky. At the service area, transfer onto a train, called the romantic train, and enjoy the rest of the course that will leave lasting memories.

stories.title: Gongjicheon Recreation Area
stories.audioTitle: A long beloved tourist attraction in Chuncheon
stories.script: A long beloved tourist attraction in Chuncheon  Gongjicheon Recreation Area is a resting area for its residents as well as a famous tourist attraction of the city. People of all ages love to visit this place. Some just take a rest on mats, and others enjoy inline skating. Now, let's look around the Gongjicheon Recreation Area. First, there are bicycle rental shops at both ends of Gongjicheongyo Bridge. The bike course will make you enjoy the best bike experience. And, duck boat riding on Gongjicheon Stream is another experience that you must not miss. You can take the boat at the quay located next to the Memorial Hall for Ethiopian Veterans in the Korean War. Then, cross Gongjicheongyo Bridge to visit Gold Scales Theme Street. The street was the backdrop of the novel <Hwanggeum Bineul (Gold Scales)> written by Korean author Lee Oe-su who was born in the city. Walk along the calm river, while indulging in the literary world of the writer. Then, you will reach Chuncheon MBC. Climb up to the observation deck in the building to overlook the entire city. The magnificent panoramic view will capture your eyes. If you have some time left, visit the Chuncheon site of KT&G Sangsang Madang, a multi-culture complex. Facing Uiamho Lake, the elegant red-brick architecture is the work of late Kim Su-geun, a master architect in Korea. As described, Gongjicheon Recreation Area is a favorite tourist attraction in Chuncheon, where you can get some healing while enjoying culture and art amidst nature.

stories.title: Cafe Street near Gubongsan Observatory
stories.audioTitle: The harmony of a clear view and a cup of coffee
stories.script: The harmony of a clear view and a cup of coffee   Cafe Street near Gubongsan Observatory is the best place to enjoy a cup of coffee with an uninterrupted view of Chuncheon city. From here, you can see the geographical characteristics of the city, which is located in a basin formed by erosion. Cafe Street, created along the well paved hillside road, offers an exotic atmosphere with distinctive features. There is a cafe with a wide observation deck and a skywalk. At night, another cafe that has a large outdoor garden is crowded with visitors who come to see the summer night view of the city. Besides the cafes that provide a wonderful view of the city, there are also various types of restaurants, such as snack bars, a high-end Italian restaurant, and a bakery that sells naturally fermented bread. While Cafe Street near Gubongsan Observatory provides a spectacular view throughout the year, it is recommended to visit the place on a warm day so that you can sit outdoors to enjoy a clear view. And, the best view you can have is from when the sky starts to glow with the setting sun to when the night glitters with lights in the dark.

stories.title: Kim Yu-jeong Literature Village
stories.audioTitle: Where the novels of Kim Yu-jeong live on
stories.script: Where the novels of Kim Yu-jeong live on  Kim Yu-jeong Literature Village was built to honor Kim Yu-jeong, a Chuncheon-native author who wrote a number of novels with the city as its setting. In the village, there is a Kim Yu-jeong Memorial Exhibition Hall as well as the Birthplace of Kim Yu-jeong. The exhibition hall displays materials about the life and works of the author who died young at the age of 29. In the exhibition hall, the first thing you will notice is a large sculpture of an open book titled <Spring, Spring>, one of his major works. There is a pot of yellow flower that symbolizes his other major novel titled <The Camellias>. Most camellias are red color, and the yellow flower placed in the hall is actually ginger flower. The reason for this is because residents in the province mistook ginger flowers as camellias. Ginger flowers that are in full bloom in early spring are also found at the Birthplace of Kim Yu-jeong, which is located beside the exhibition hall. The house was restored almost to its original form based on the testimonies of the villagers and historical research. The thatched house exudes rustic elegance, along with the old barn, treadmill and traditional crocks. And, in the yard, there is a pond and a pavilion, as well as interesting sculptures that depict a scene in one of his novels.

stories.title: Namu Walkway on Namiseom Island
stories.audioTitle: The island of trees with year-round beauty
stories.script: The island of trees with year-round beauty  When you walk along the trails on Namiseom Island, you will understand why the island is also known as 'Namu Island' or the island of trees. The island is known for its trails such as the Metasequoia Walkway, Pine Nut Tree Walkway, Ginkgo Tree Walkway, and Cherry Blossom Walkway. The Metasequoia Walkway, in particular, is the most famous trail and the best spot for photos on the island. It was also a filming site of the Korean drama, 'Winter Sonata', which still attracts many foreign visitors. The Pine Nut Tree Walkway is just as popular as the Metasequoia Walkway as the best spot for photos. When you arrive on the island, you can walk the center trail which leads to the Pine Nut Tree Walkway. This is the center of the island, so it bustles with visitors. To take photos of tranquil scenery, it is recommended to visit the island in the early morning or late in the evening. As its nickname, the island of trees, suggests, Namiseom Island offers a different landscape for each season. In the spring, cherry blooms are in full bloom. In the summer, metasequoia and many other trees bestow deep shades over the trails. In the fall, ginkgo trees spread yellow carpets along the river. And, in the winter, the bare branches are covered with pure white snowflakes. As the island changes its landscape like this, you may want to visit the place each time the seasons change.

stories.title: Nami Library on Namiseom Island
stories.script: Play with picture books   One of the symbolic icons of Namiseom Island is books. On the island, there are picture books placed on benches and even in washrooms. As such, the island has a children's library called Nami Library. The library has over 20,000 children's books and about 5,000 picture books from 86 countries around the world. Inside the museum, there is a wall filled with picture books and a tower of thousands of books that make it look like a tall wooden post. Both are impressive sights. The slide installed between bookshelves allows children to read books and play. The outdoor playground also has books placed all around. It is a large 'book playground' where children can encounter books amidst nature. During the Nami Island International Children's Book Festival period, various events take place, adding a more special experience to your trip. The biennial book festival was first held on Namiseom Island to celebrate the 200th anniversary of the birth of Hans Christian Andersen. Thanks to this effort, the island was designated a UNICEF Child Friendly Park in 2010. If you visit the island with your children, be sure to visit Nami Library for a wonderful time together.

stories.title: Overview of Namiseom Island
stories.script: Namiseom Island, located in Gangwon Province, is a breathtaking place renowned for its stunning landscape. It was initially called ‘Namseom’, which means the island in the front. It acquired its current name from General Nami, whose body is believed to be buried in a pile of stones on the northern hill of Nami Island.  Namiseom Island was artificially created in 1944 following the construction of Cheongpyeong Dam north of the Han River. For about two decades, it remained a barren wasteland until 1965 when Sujae Minn Byeong Do purchased the island and began reforestation efforts. The Kyeongchun Tourism Development was established to build the tourist facilities next year. From solely serving as a commercial vacation resort before 2000, Namiseom Island has evolved into an international hub for art, culture, and eco-friendly tourism.  Nowadays, Namiseom Island hosts various cultural events, concerts, exhibitions under the themes of “Fairy Tale Village and Song Village”. Visitors can partake in activities such as the Song Museum, exploring the Picture Book Lounge, attending events at the MICE Centre, and engaging in activities like the Charity Train and Story Tour Bus. Additionally, the island provides restaurants and accommodations, offering visitors a place to rest and ensure they can create countless special memories on Namiseom Island.  In addition, there are two ways to access the Namiseom Island. Visitors can take the ferry or the zipline to the island. For those seeking a more adventurous experience, trying the zipline is recommended as it offers a unique perspective to explore the island's charming views.

stories.title: Chuncheon Nangman Market
stories.audioTitle: Add romance to your time at the traditional market
stories.script: Add romance to your time at the traditional market   In Chuncheon, known as the city of romance, you can find Nangman Market, otherwise known as the Romantic Market. Chuncheon Jungang Market, which opened in 1960, changed its name to Nangman Market in 2010, after it was designated a culture and tourism market as part of an effort to promote traditional markets as tourist attractions. Since then, the old and narrow alleys of the market have been transformed into galleries with beautiful wall paintings and sculptures. Each store has a sign hanging outside with distinctive figures and letters. The glittering mirror balls on the ceiling of the market arcade add to the excitement. The traditional market also offers a variety of things to eat, such as buckwheat crepes, rice soup, and noodle soup with dough. What’s more, there are culture and art spaces that were created in once empty stores in the market. When you walk the central arcade, a sign that reads Gunggeumhan Icheungjip, meaning a curious second-storey house, will arouse your curiosity. This place was designed to help people communicate about travel and culture, so you can take a break here over a cup of coffee. As said, Nangman Market is full of things to please your eyes and mouth. It is also an attractive tourist spot, as it is connected to Myeong-dong Street, where the famous Korean drama, <Winter Sonata> was filmed. It is also very close to Dakgalbi Alley with restaurants that serve spicy stir-fried chicken food.

stories.title: Chuncheon Makguksu Museum
stories.audioTitle: Make makguksu, or buckwheat noodles, yourself
stories.script: Make makguksu, or buckwheat noodles, yourself  Chuncheon-style makguksu, or buckwheat noodles, is one of the two iconic foods of the city, along with dakgalbi, or spicy stir-fried chicken. So, there are many famous makguksu restaurants in the city. To learn about the essence of makguksu, Chuncheon Makguksu Museum is just the right place to visit. The exterior of the museum embodies the shape of the traditional noodle machine and the traditional cauldron, which capture the eyes of the visitors. First, in the exhibition hall on the first floor, you can learn about the origin and tradition of makguksu and the effects of buckwheat, among other things. A large millstone sculpture, installed at the center of the hall, depicts an interesting sight of ground buckwheat slipping out of the stones. Moving up to the experience hall on the second floor, we see a makguksu experience room and a restaurant. In the makguksu experience room, you can participate in the whole process of kneading and pressing buckwheat dough to the process of boiling the noodles. As the name, makguksu, means instant noodles, you can enjoy the taste as soon as you've made the noodles. However, it is hard for unskilled individuals to knead 100% pure buckwheat dough. And, the buckwheat noodles that you just made and the one served in the restaurant next door have different buckwheat content. So, it will be an interesting culinary experience to try both and compare the subtle differences in taste and texture.

stories.title: Mulle-gil
stories.script: Uiamho Lake meets wooden canoes  In general, 'Mulle-gil' refers to 'a path traveling along a waterway,' which differs from specific paths such Olle-gil in Jeju and Dulle-gil in Jirisan Mountain. It is a special experience to ride a classic wooden canoe and float on Uiamho Lake, which is known for its spectacular landscape. Moving without an engine, canoes do not cause noise or acrid fumes. So, you can slide through the surface of the water quietly while fully enjoying the sound of nature and the refreshing air. The classic wooden canoes were introduced in Uiamho Lake by Moksoon Boaz Jang, the president of the Mulle-gil Corporation. He was fascinated by canoes in Canada and learned canoe making from a craftsman, which eventually led to the creation of the Mulle-gil water trail. Then, shall we go and enjoy a canoe ride on the lake? Even beginners can easily complete the Uiamho Dam course, which starts from the Mulle-gil Management Office located in the Songam Sports Town. When you paddle down on a canoe, you can see a bike lane stretching along Uiamho Lake and the Skywalk observatory. It is very interesting to look up the observation deck that is made with reinforced glass installed 12m high above the water surface. Why don't you enjoy a canoe ride along the Mulle-gil water trail, which follows the flow of the lake to where nature leads you.

stories.title: Soyanggang Dam
stories.audioTitle: A walkway on the rock-filled dam
stories.script: A walkway on the rock-filled dam  When you face Soyanggang Dam where shadows of the magnificent mountains are reflected on the serene surface of the river, you will first notice the white sign that reads Soyanggang Multi-purpose Dam of the Korea Water Resources Corporation (a.k.a. K-Water) located on the mountain across the river. Built in 1973, Soyanggang Dam is the largest multi-purpose dam in the country. Take a closer look at the dam to find that it is made with rocks and soil, instead of concrete. As a typical rock-filled dam, its center was built with clay, which was enclosed by stones and sand. The dam blends more harmoniously with nature than concrete dams. On the embankment of the dam, which was formed with stones and sand, you can see a trail known as the 'zigzag path'. It is also called Yongneomi-gil, which literally means the path of a rising dragon, as the track resembles the shape of a dragon ascending to the sky. This path is connected right to the top of the dam, which, however, is normally closed and is only open once a year when the Yongneomi-gil walking event is held. If you cannot visit the dam at that time of year, you can walk another trail called Jeongsang-gil, which is open throughout the year. The trail is accessible from 10 a.m. to 4 or 5 p.m. depending on the season, except when the weather is extremely severe. Why don't you walk from the top of the dam to Octagonal Pavilion Observatory on the opposite side while enjoying the beautiful landscape of the dam?

stories.title: Animation Museum
stories.audioTitle: An exciting imaginary world for both adults and children
stories.script: An exciting imaginary world for both adults and children  Animation Museum displays various animated works and characters from the 1960s to today, which makes it attractive to people of all ages. At the entrance of the museum, you can see the house of Hongbi and Hongsi, the main characters of Cloud Bread. Here, you will feel as if you were drawn into the scene of the cartoon. Then, inside the Animation Museum, on the first floor, there is an exhibition hall that illustrates the history and development of animation, as well as a 3D theater that screens animated films. In the center hall, major animated works and their characters, such as Robot Taekwon V and Dooly, greet visitors. On the second floor, there is another exhibition hall that shows animated works of countries around the world, including the United States, Japan and Europe, as well as a sound studio where you can experience sound effects used in animated movies. In a dubbing experience room, you can be a dubbing artist yourself and try doing some voice-over. Next to the Animation Museum, there is Robot Experience Center. Here, you can watch a robot performance with robots dancing in formation to the exciting beats of music, and you can also control robots yourself in a boxing or soccer match. Outside the museum, one can find a large lawn area beside Uiamho Lake where one can take a stroll and rest.

stories.title: Jade Garden
stories.audioTitle: A European-style garden famous as a filming site of dramas
stories.script: A European-style garden famous as a filming site of dramas  Jade Garden is an arboretum designed with the concept of 'a small European town in the forest.' It was created by keeping the geographical features of the valley. Flowers, trees, and architectural styles and layouts were arranged in a European style. When you enter the arboretum, the first thing you will notice is an exotic red-brick building. It is the visitor center which was built in the architectural style of the Tuscany region of Italy. It is the iconic structure at Jade Garden, which frequently appears as the backdrop of dramas and films. It is a popular photo spot for visitors. Besides the visitor center, the Cottage Garden located at the center of the trails and the Wedding Garden, which stands in the innermost part of the arboretum, were all built in a European style. There are also European theme gardens, such as the British Border Garden and the Italian Garden. You can choose one of the three walking courses: Namunaeum-gil, which has larch woodchips spread on the path, Danpungnamu-gil, which is lined with various kinds of maple trees, and Supsokbaram-gil, which is filled with enormous trees. Each course takes about 40 minutes to one hour one-way, so you can drop by cafes located at the start, middle and end of the trails to have something to drink. Take the guide map placed at the entrance of Jade Garden and start your journey into the European-style arboretum.

stories.title: Cheongpyeongsa Temple
stories.audioTitle: A beautiful temple surrounded by exquisite nature and ancient tales
stories.script: A beautiful temple surrounded by exquisite nature and ancient tales  Cheongpyeongsa Temple is a small Buddhist temple, but it has a long history and many ancient tales. Due to the spectacular surrounding landscape, it was designated a national scenic point in 2010. Built during the reign of King Gwangjong of the Goryeo Dynasty, Cheongpyeongsa Temple has the legend of 'The Princess of the Tang Dynasty and the Lovesick Snake'. According to the story, a young man, who falls in love with a princess of the Tang Dynasty, dies and becomes a snake. The snake sticks to the body of the princess, but is eventually forced away from her here at the temple. The tale lives on to date as a sculpture that is found in the temple. One can also find 'the cave of the princess', where the princess stayed, and a three-story stone pagoda called 'the tower of the princess' which was built by the Chinese emperor in return for having the snake removed from his daughter. There are other picturesque views and historical sites, such as the Gusong Falls, which can be encountered on the way to the temple. And, two of them are particularly worth noticing: Yeongji Pond and Hoejeonmun Gate. Yeongji Pond was created by Lee Ja-hyeon, a nobleman from the Goryeo Dynasty period, when he stayed in the temple for 37 years. The pond was named 'yeongji', meaning the pond of the shadow, because the shadow of Obongsan Mountain was reflected on the surface of the water. And, while Hoejeonmun literally means a revolving door, here, the name implies the Buddhist concept of reincarnation. The gate replaces the Sacheonwangmun Gate, or the gate of four heavenly kings, which is typically found in temples. Look around the rustic temple and other beautiful sights, and your mind will soon become clear and peaceful, as the name 'cheongpyeong' suggests.

stories.title: Ganjeolgot Cape
stories.audioTitle: The place where the sun first rises on the Korean peninsula
stories.script: The place where the sun first rises on the Korean peninsula  The name 'ganjeolgot' originated from 'ganjitdae' meaning a long bamboo pole. It was named so because the land appears to be stretched towards the sea when it is seen from a distance. Ganjeolgot Cape became famous as a place where one could see the first sunrise on the Korean peninsula on the first day of the year 2000.  The sun rises here at the Cape about five minutes earlier than Jeongdongjin in Gangneung and about one minute earlier than Homigot Cape in Pohang, which are both popular sunrise spots in Korea. Sculpture Park at the Cape provides a picturesque view towards the sea. Visitors can sit in chairs and listen to the sound of waves or watch boats sailing far away in the sea. Meanwhile other visitors can write heartfelt letters on postcards that can be easily sent in a mailbox here at this park where the sun first rises. You can walk past the white lighthouse at the top of the hill in the park and stroll along the coastal walk. There, you can see the Drama House, a large mansion built in a European style, where a number of dramas had been filmed. At the end of the embankment of Daesong Port, located in front of the Drama House, one can see the Propose Lighthouse where a fanfare is sounded when lovers stand in front of the lighthouse together.

stories.title: Cape Ganjeolgot
stories.audioTitle: New hope rises in the East Sea
stories.script: Ganjeolgot Cape is a popular natural tourist attraction thanks to the fact that it is the very first place on mainland Korea where you can see the sunrise.     The name “Ganjeolgot” comes from the Cape’s distinct shape - it resembles a long pole if you look at it from the sea.      The Cape Ganjeolgot lighthouse has guided seafarers for close to a century now. Built under the Japanese colonial rule of Korea, the lighthouse has witnessed all the joys and sorrows of the Korean people as they endured war and earned their peace. You can climb up the lighthouse, look out into the vast East Sea, and imagine a pack of whales swimming by the Cape.      The Wishing Postbox is another popular feature at Cape Ganjeolgot. Don’t you want to sit down next to the 5m-tall, giant postbox and write a little postcard as a keepsake?    Meanwhile, Pohang is home to Cape Homigot, one of the best places to enjoy the sunrise in Korea along with Cape Ganjeolgot. Pohang is also known for its “Sunrise Alliance” with Ulsan and Gyeongju.     Every year, Cape Ganjeolgot hosts a Sunrise Festival on the 1st of January, and it invites everyone to witness the hope of a new year rise above the horizon.

stories.title: Whale Culture Village
stories.audioTitle: Traces of Jangsaengpo Port when it was vibrant with whaling
stories.script: Traces of Jangsaengpo Port when it was vibrant with whaling    Jangsaengpo Port in Ulsan was well known for whaling in the 1970s and 1980s. It was the center of the whaling industry until 1986 when whaling was prohibited. At its peak, about 20 whaling boats captured over 1,000 whales a year. People would laughingly utter, even dogs walk around holding money in their mouths or no one would trade being a whale catcher in the port with the city governor, suggesting that the town was awash with money. The old days of the port was revived at the Whale Culture Village. The alleys of the village is full of things that evoke a sense of nostalgia, such as a bookstore with old magazine photos, a bicycle shop, an old tea house, and a mom-and-pop grocery store. Behind the alleys are model houses of fishermen who went out to the sea for whaling. In the catcher's house, you can see harpoon cannons and knives that were used to cut up whales. Outside the houses, there is a whale cutting facility, whale oil extraction facility and a whale meat store, among other things. The scene will vividly conjure up sights that could not be seen since the prohibition of whaling. Now, as one walks up the hill from the Village, one will find the Whale Sculpture Park that overlooks the sea. The park is decorated with life-size sculptures of gray whales, humpback whales, minke whales, sperm whales, blue whales and killer whales. The blue whale sculpture is particularly famous, as visitors can enter and explore the body of the whale.

stories.title: Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village
stories.audioTitle: Jangsaengpo, the home of whales ‘Where did all those whales go?’
stories.script: Have you seen the Petroglyphs of Bangudae Terrace depicting whaling techniques used by our ancestors? If so, it’s clear that, Jangsaengpo served as a whaling village since ancient times. At one point, Jangsaengpo was a whaling base with more than 20 whaling ships and 10,000 people involved in whaling in some capacity.    It was truly an affluent fishing village. But in 1986, when the international community banned whaling, people in Jangsaengpo lost their way of life.   Whales used to be a symbol of hope for the villagers in Jangsaengpo. With the whaling ban, hope was gone. Recently, however, people have begun to restore hope in Jangsaengpo. As one of the 12 must-see tourist attractions in Ulsan, Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village offers plenty of features to see and enjoy, including Whale Park (shows the local history with whales since prehistoric times) and Whale Sculpture Park.   In particular, “Jangsaengpo Old Town” is a popular attraction for all tourists with its diorama-type reproduction of the village and its people in Jangsaengpo’s heyday when whaling was still legal.    You can walk along around the village, visit the old butchery where people used to carve up freshly caught whales, or see the whale meat restaurants that served steamed whale dishes, and travel back in time.   Jangsaengpo was the home of whales for a very long time. Immerse yourself in some wonderful memories from the East Sea right off the coast of Jangsaengpo, all the way to Guryongpo in Pohang.

stories.title: Whale Museum in Jangsaengpo Port
stories.script: Exploring the mystery of whales   The Whale Museum in Jangsaengpo Port collects and exhibits various relics and items about whales and whaling, which began to disappear in 1986 when whaling became prohibited. When you visit the museum, which stands with an open sea view, the first thing you will notice is a whaling boat installed outdoors. The boat, equipped with a harpoon on the prow, had actually been in operation, and after whaling was prohibited, it was long abandoned and later moved to this site. The Whale Museum consists of three floors. You can start on the second floor, which is the entrance of the museum and move to the third floor and finish on the first floor. In the first exhibition room, located on the second floor, there is a gigantic skeleton of the bryde's whale that measures 12.4meters-long. Also on display are various whale bones, whaling tools, and the history of whaling of Jangsaengpo Port and the world. The theme on the second exhibition room is gray whales. You can see life-size models of the whale and the processes of whale cutting and whale oil processing. You can also listen to the sound of a whale. Lastly, the third exhibition room on the first floor offers children a chance to experience whales. It provides an interesting learning experience, such as touching whale skeletons, listening to the sound of whales and making whales with clay.

stories.title: Introduction(Daewangam Park)
stories.script: Introduction of Daewangam Park  Daewangam Park is steeped in the legend of King Munmu, who unified Korea’s Three Kingdoms. After the King’s death, he was buried in an underwater tomb off the coast of Gyeongju. According to legend, when the Queen died, she joined him in the afterlife and became a dragon guarding the East Sea. Daewangam Park is also one of the Twelve Scenic Places of Ulsan City. Beyond the tale of the Queen and the dragon, the park is rich with other mythical stories.   Today, let’s dive into Daewangam Park and uncover its secrets, some of which are over a thousand years old.   Let’s get started!

stories.title: Yonggul Cave(Daewangam Park)
stories.script: Yonggul Cave(Daewangam Park)  If you walk past the Daewangam Stairs that lead up to the Jeonseolbawi-gil Trail, you’ll reach a place called “Haekkaebi,” located between the outer and inner “Makgujigi” borders. In the past, mysterious will-o’-the-wisp lights were often observed here. The term “Makgujigi” is a compound of “Mak,” meaning dead end, and “Gujigi,” meaning corner in the local dialect. At the inner Makgujigi, a drum-like sound can be heard when a large wave crashes against the cliff. Interested in knowing the source of this sound?  Beneath the cliff lies a mysterious cave associated with the legend of the blue dragon. One day, a blue dragon appeared in the area and began to harass the fishermen. Furious at the dragon’s behavior, the Dragon King blocked the cave entrance with a massive boulder, trapping the dragon inside. According to legend, whenever a large wave hits the cliff, the dragon inside the cave thrashes against the boulder. That’s the source of the mysterious sound.

stories.title: Minseom(Daewangam Park)
stories.script: Minseom(Daewangam Park)  If you look across the inner Makgujigi, you’ll see a rocky island that acts as a natural breakwater for Ilsan Bay. From certain angles, the island resembles a beautiful lady lying down. Interestingly, nothing grows on the island, and there is a story behind this.  A long, long time ago, the seven angels of the Great Jade Emperor would cross a rainbow bridge once a year to visit Earth. Each time, the Emperor warned them sternly that if they did not return before sunset, the gates of heaven would close.  One year, the seven angels arrived near Daewangam, where they met Geobukbawi, head of the royal guard protecting the Dragon King. Geobukbawi, brave and handsome, transformed into a turtle-shaped rock by day and became a man by night. Min, the youngest of the angels, fell in love with Geobukbawi and disobeyed the Emperor’s decree. She chose not to return to heaven, deciding instead to stay on Earth.  Once the Great Jade Emperor found out about Min and Geobukbawi, the infuriated Great Jade Emperor turned Min into a rocky island. Barren and as smooth as a bald head, the island became known as “Minseom.”  Heartbroken over losing his beloved Min, Geobukbawi’s heart grew cold and hard, and he eventually lost the ability to transform into a person. Minseom stands as the center of this tragic love story between Geobukbawi and Min. How about taking a walk along the beach and sharing this story with your loved one?

stories.title: Ulgi Lighthouse(Daewangam Park)
stories.script: Ulgi Lighthouse(Daewangam Park)  At the end of Jeonseolbawi-gil Trail, you’ll find the final destination of this magnificent path, the Ulgi Lighthouse. For over 100 years, this lighthouse has stood in the same spot, guiding travelers across the sea. After the Russo-Japanese War in 1906, the Japanese began calling this location “Ulgi,” meaning the “end of Ulsan.” However, when the municipal government celebrated the lighthouse's centennial anniversary, they changed the Chinese character for “gi” from meaning “rough” (崎) to “energy” (氣) to remove traces of the colonial era. As a result, Ulgi gained a new meaning, “the energy of Ulsan.”  The lighthouse emits a sound known as “Musansori,” symbolizing how fog scatters and disappears into thin air. Today, Ulgi Lighthouse continues to serve as a guiding beacon for passing vessels.  In 1987, the government built a new lighthouse next to Ulgi Lighthouse. According to legend, two brothers separated in childhood were reborn as these two lighthouses. It is said that on foggy days, they call each other's names, and this sound is known as “Musansori”.  This seaside trail starts from Jeonseolbawi-gil and is part of the Haeparang Trail Course 8 in Ulsan. Following the coastline past Daewangam Park, it takes roughly forty minutes to reach Seuldo Island. It’s a wonderful trail for a leisurely walk along the coast.  The Four Seasons Trail Course is popular among tourists, especially families and couples.

stories.title: Seuldo Island(Daewangam Park)
stories.script: Seuldo Island(Daewangam Park)  Seuldo Island is scattered with porous rocks across its entire landscape. When the wind and waves pass through these holes, carved over millions of years, they create a sound reminiscent of a sorrowful Geomungo (a traditional Korean instrument). Try closing your eyes and listening to these natural tunes.

stories.title: Jujeon Mongdol Beach(Daewangam Park)
stories.script: Jujeon Mongdol Beach(Daewangam Park)  If you drive about thirty minutes from Seuldo Island, you’ll reach Jujeon Mongdol Beach. As one of Ulsan’s “12 Must-See Tourist Attractions,” Jujeon Mongdol Beach is known for its smooth, round black pebbles. When waves hit the pebbles, they produce a soft “clinking” sound, and the frothy air bubbles created by the waves resemble buckwheat flowers from afar, making for a beautiful sight.  Continuing along the Haeparang Trail from Jujeon Mongdol Beach, you’ll eventually arrive at the Jusangjeolli Padosori-gil Trail in Gyeongju. Along the way, listen to the legend of King Talhae, who gathered his forces in Dalcheoncheoljang in Ulsan before journeying to Gyeongju to become the King of Silla.   This journey across Ulsan uncovered the history of Korea’s eastern seaboard.  If you can still hear the sound of waves echoing in your ears, it’s time to visit Ulsan!

stories.title: Myeongseongyo Bridge
stories.audioTitle: A beautiful bridge shining with colorful lights over the sea at night
stories.script: A beautiful bridge shining with colorful lights over the sea at night   To enjoy the best night view in Ulsan, visit Jinha Beach where you can see Myeongseongyo Bridge from the beach. The bridge sits on two beaches and connects Jinha Village and Gangyang Village. It was originally built for pedestrians only, so the local residents can now come and go within just 5 minutes without having to make a detour that would otherwise have taken over 30 minutes. Myeongseongyo Bridge resembles a pair of cranes soaring up to the sky with their wings wide open. The pier looks like the head and body of the cranes, and the stairs at both ends appear to be the tip of the wings. The smooth curves look like a masterpiece, coupled with a view of the sea. When it gets dark, in particular, the beauty of the bridge shines brighter when it is seen from the beach. The LED lights are lit along the pier and change colors, providing a fantastic night view. Besides the wonderful night scenery, the bridge is an observation platform itself. Climb up the spiral stairs to stand on the bridge and enjoy a clear view of the wide sandy Jinha beach and the East Sea, as well as the port landscape.

stories.title: Seosaengpo Japanese Fortress
stories.audioTitle: The largest Japanese fortress that remains in Korea
stories.script: The largest Japanese fortress that remains in Korea  Under the control of Japanese commander Kato Kiyomasa, Seosaengpo Japanese Fortress was built in the year after the Japanese invasion of Korea in 1592 in the style of Japanese fortresses. During the invasion, about 30 Japanese fortresses were constructed in the eastern and southern coasts. Among them, Seosaengpo Japanese Fortress was the largest in size. It is different from Korean fortresses in that the ramparts were erupted in several layers. Japanese fortresses served as footholds for the Japanese to move inland of the Joseon Dynasty. Seosaengpo Japanese Fortress was an important bridgehead for Japan's invasion of Korea, where 7,000 soldiers once resided. It is known that during the Japanese invasion, signals that were set off from the beacon mound of the fortress were relayed to Gijang Jukseongniseong Fortress and Busan Jinseong Fortress, so it is also called 'bonghwaseong' or a beacon fortress. The pain and suffering of Koreans who were forced to cut and carry heavy stones to build the fortress can be felt here. While some traces of Seosaengpo Japanese Fortress can be found near the entrance of the village, the tour to the fortress begins in earnest from the information center of the cultural heritage guide. Walk up the trail along the outer fortress to reach the citadel, which offers a quiet and meditative ambience, surrounded by tall and branchy pine trees. When you reach the fortress, you can enjoy a panoramic view towards Myeongseondo Island and the arched Jinha Beach.

stories.title: Sinhwa Village
stories.audioTitle: From a hillside village to a roofless art museum
stories.script: From a hillside village to a roofless art museum   Sinhwa Village is a village of murals with its fences and walls painted with lovely pictures. The wall-painted alleys of different themes spread out like a spider web. Sinhwa Village was formed by people who began to settle in the 1960s when a petrochemical complex was established in the neighborhood. It is known that the settlers started to call the village 'Sinhwa,' which reflected their wish to live happily in this place together. This place became a mural village thanks to a film titled 'Bicycle Looking For a Whale'. To shoot the film, the alley near the house of the brother and sister, the lead characters in the movie, was painted, and this inspired the whole village to turn into a world of painted walls. Later, the village was selected as part of the '2010 Village Art Project' organized by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, which engaged local painters, sculptors and poets in Ulsan to transform the place into a beautiful mural village. In the village, houses built in the 1960s and 1970s have remained almost intact, so the paintings drawn on the walls of narrow old alleys look more attractive. The alleys were painted with different themes, such as a flower alley with blooms of beautiful flowers, an illusive alley with impressive three-dimensional drawings, and an alley of innocence that illustrates old retro plays. This is why the village is called 'a roofless art museum'.

stories.title: Oegosan Onggi Village
stories.audioTitle: The largest traditional onggi (earthenware) cluster in Korea
stories.script: The largest traditional onggi (earthenware) cluster in Korea  Oegosan Onggi Village is the largest traditional onggi, or earthenware, cluster in the country. It has handicraft workshops, an onggi academy and an onggi museum, among other things. The whole village features onggi and offers exotic sights. The origin of the onggi village dates back to when the potter, Heo Deok-man, tried to seek refuge in Busan after the outbreak of the Korean War and eventually settled down in this place. Since then, the village rapidly developed, as potters and people, who wanted to learn pottery making, flocked to the village from across the country. But, in the 1980s, plastic products began to replace earthenware, and today, about 40 potters are here to carry on the tradition. When you walk a path in front of the information center of the village, you can easily spot onggi workshops. It is fascinating to visit and look around workshops that display and sell various traditional pottery items. In particular, the workshop of craftsman Heo Jin-gyu is open to anyone, so visitors can watch the process of onggi making. If you want to make one by yourself, visit the onggi academy located past the workshop, which provides anyone with a chance to make onggi. In order to learn more about pottery, visit the onggi museum which displays exhibitions about the history of Korean and world pottery, as well as the world's largest pottery that is over 2meters long.

stories.title: Oegosan Onggi Village
stories.script: Oegosan Onggi Village  [Woman] In Ulsan, there’s something that has lasted longer than Shilla. A tradition that has survived thousands of years. Of course, I’m talking about “Onggi,” a type of distinctly Korean crockery used since the prehistoric period. Ulsan is home to the only village in Korea that specializes in Onggi crockery. It protects its traditions no matter how much the world around it changes. Let’s head over to Oegosan Onggi Village in Ulju-gun, Ulsan-si.    [Man] Onggi Village produces more than 50% of all Onggi products made in Korea. 	With seven dedicated artisans producing various Onggi crockery, Oegosan Onggi Village is the largest folk village specializing in Onggi culture in Korea. Here, there is a special reason why the Onggi artisans use traditional techniques to make their products  [Interview with Shin Il-seong, Master Onggi Artisan] If you use oil to bake an Onggi product, it cannot “breathe.” That’s a fake Onggi.Traditionally, Koreans have made Onggi products that can “breathe.”  [Women] Onggi artisan Shin Il-seong says he wants to give people genuine traditional Korean Onggi products. His passion for Onggi burns brighter and hotter than the kiln that fires above 1000oC. Then, how long does it take to bake a hand-made Onggi product?  [Man] Preparing a traditional kiln takes ten days. Baking the Onggi product takes another ten days. That means, Onggi artisans have to stay by their kiln for close to 20 days. It’s tough work. For 10 days, when the fire has to be tended to constantly, artisans work around the clock in three shifts to make sure the temperature inside the kiln stays at optimum levels, and to check if the Onggi are being baked properly.  Over the course of those 10 days, the kiln consumes approximately 15 tons of firewood. It is the equivalent of burning all the trees on a small mountain. Preserving this tradition requires enduring pain and being patient.  [Interview with Shin Il-seong, Master Onggi Artisan] who produces Onggi products using traditional Onggi techniques. As an Onggi artisan, I’ve led a principled life. I live with a sense of mission and purpose. I live as an Onggi artisan because I love Korean Onggi that breathes. Even at this very moment, I am trying to teach my apprentices and make sure they can carry on this tradition after me.  [Woman] The Ulsan Onggi Museum has more than 1,000 pieces of pottery-related artifacts. Have you ever seen an Onggi that is more than 2m-tall? This Onggi, the largest of its kind in the world, was built on the 6th attempt. Of course, it has been registered in the Guinness Book of World Records! It was a project led by Onggi Village. By producing the largest Onggi in the world and achieving that proud record, the artisans showed how outstanding our traditional Onggi production techniques can be.    Onggi Academy   [Man] The Onggi Academy is available only at the Onggi Village. Here, you can learn how to make and use Onggi products with fun and easy interactive programs. Onggi products are born with clay, water, fire, and wind. Behind each Oegosan Onggi product inspired by the wisdom and know-how of our ancestors is the care and dedication of artisans working extremely hard to preserve our traditional culture.    Jujeon Fishing Experience Village   [Woman] Now, shall we move on from Onggi to Haenyeo divers? Jujeon Village boasts some rich history and tradition that dates back more than 200 years. It is home to plenty of veteran Haenyeo divers who have been diving these waters for at least 30 years. Astonishingly, most of them are in their 60s, 70s, or even their 80s!.  All Haenyeo divers are members of a group called “Najamhoe” and they work as instructors in Haenyeo activity programs. In particular, the “Haenyeo Meal Table” program led by veteran Haenyeo divers is a popular choice among visitors. The “Haenyeo Meal Table” features fresh seafood, including sea mustard, abalone, and fresh sashimi, all of which have been famous local delicacies since the Shilla period!   [Man] Fresh sashimi with some sweet red pepper paste is just... perfect. You’ll fall in love with the savory, yet spicy flavor. Apart from the “Haenyeo Meal Table,” you can also enjoy other unique programs such as the “Sea Mustard Rice Cake Cooking” and “Natural Soap Making” programs.   [Woman] Jujeon Village is perhaps best known for Mongdol Beach. Waves breaking apart on the black Mongdol pebbles create a beautiful harmony that tickles your ears. Walking on the pebbles without shoes can leave you with a memorable sensation as well. The Jujeon Fishing Experience Village features some great natural marine resources. Recently, access to Jujeon Village has vastly improved with the opening of Maseong Tunnel. More and more people are choosing the village as a quick getaway from the city.    Story of the Gangdong Jejeon Village   [Man] “Gangdong Jejeon Village” is a hidden gem in the Buk-gu area.As its nickname “Eel Village” - suggests, Jejeon Village has been a popular destination for people looking for eel. During Ulsan Folk Culture Year in 2017, Jejeon Village was designated as a Folk Research Village. The village worked with the National Folk Museum of Korea and opened the first Village Corporation in Buk-gu called “Saranggil Jejeon Eel.” The company tells people about the traditional lifestyle of Haenyeo divers, who have tended to eels and sea mustard throughout their entire lives, and the tragic legend of the eel who fell in love with the Princess.     [Woman] We took a trip through the past and modern features of Ulsan. What is your verdict? I believe it would have given you an opportunity to understand our traditions better. In particular, Oegosan Onggi Village in Ulsan is even better with children. So, if you’re looking for a place for your next family trip, don’t forget to check out Onggi Village

stories.title: Ulsan Petroglyph Museum
stories.script: Meet life-size petroglyphs of Bangudae Ulsan,city tour,Ulsan Petroglyph Museum   When you visit the Ulsan Petroglyph Museum, you can see life-size models of the Bangudae Petroglyphs of Ulju and the Cheonjeon-ri Petroglyphs of Ulju, both designated as a national treasure. Petroglyphs refer to images carved on rocks by prehistoric people, and these are important materials in understanding the lifestyles of these people. In the exhibition room on the first floor, you can see full-size replicas of the Bangudae Petroglyphs and the Cheonjeon-ri Petroglyphs, which show the engraved images in detail. The models of the Bangudae Petroglyphs, which were presumably created in the Neolithic Age, mainly depict the figures of animals and people. And, the replicas of the Cheonjeon-ri Petroglyphs illustrate abstract patterns that were assumed to have been made through generations of people in the Bronze Age. In another exhibition room on the second floor, there are models of animals that appear in the Bangudae Petroglyphs. Land animals, such as tigers, deer and wolves, are displayed in stuffed forms, and sea animals, such as whales, are depicted in painting. What is noticeable in the Bangudae Petroglyphs is the highly realistic portrayal of whale fishing, which has significant implications that whaling was not a figment of one's imagination but something that was actually performed off the coast of Ulsan.

stories.title: Bangudae Petroglyphs of Ulju
stories.audioTitle: Petroglyphs with the world's first portrayal of whale hunting
stories.script: Petroglyphs with the world's first portrayal of whale hunting  Bangudae Petroglyphs of Ulju is an important relic that suggests Ulsan's age-old relationship with whales. Petroglyphs refer to images carved on rocks by prehistoric peoples. The Bangudae Petroglyphs is found on a cliff of Daegokcheon Stream in upper Taehwagang River. The carvings were presumably created through many generations from the Neolithic Age, and most of them have been found on a rock surface that is about 8-meters wide and 3-meters high. The Bangudae Petroglyphs feature interesting illustrations of land and sea animals, hunting of prehistoric people, and whaling. The land animals depicted include deer, boars, tigers, leopards and foxes, and the notable sea animals include whales, tortoises, fish and cormorants. It is said that no other petroglyphs in the world provides such detailed expressions of various animals than the Bangudae Petroglyphs. Whales take the largest part in the petroglyphs with 58 carvings, and two of the petroglyphs illustrate cutting whales. It is assumed that prehistoric peoples guided whales that entered the bay near the villages of Ibam-ri and Gulhwa-ri in Ulju, where the waters were shallow, and hunted them with spears or harpoons. With the discovery of the Bangudae Petroglyphs, which is the first whaling relic of mankind, it is considered that men began to hunt whales in around the 10th and 11th century.

stories.title: Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace
stories.audioTitle: A whale’s dream, embarking on a journey back in time
stories.script: [Man]	  Whales seem to spend an eternity swimming across the deep blue ocean. Where could they be right now?  [Woman] Whales swim across the ocean, but so do fishermen.They sail across the open sea, hoping to catch a glimpse of whales breaking the surface.   [Man] Whalers were the envy of all fishermen! Today, our destination is Jangsaengpo in Ulsan, a port that used to be a forward base for whalers. It’s a place with fascinating tales from the waters off the coast of Ulsan!  [Together] A whale’s dream. Let’s embark on a journey back in time.     Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace    [Man] Daegokcheon is a tributary of the Taehwagang River in Ulsan. The sound of water rushing through the tranquil valley is the only thing that breaks the silence here. There is a special boulder here.A special boulder in Ulsan.. Hey Suji, can you guess which boulder I’m talking about?  [Woman] Of course, I can. You’re talking about the “Petroglyph Rock,” right? Petroglyphs are found almost all over the world across different points in time, and they are known as the oldest form of art created by humans.  [Man] You’re absolutely right. features more than 300 pieces of illustrations scattered  across an 8m x 5m patch of rock face on a cliff. Most of the illustrations depict marine animals such as sharks and seals, or land animals such as deer and tigers. But, if you take a closer look, you might find something strange.  [Woman] Let me see... you said most of the drawings are about animals...But here, the Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace seem to have a lot of whales!   [Man] You’re right. In total, there are 58 whales. Whales live in the deep ocean. Why do you think people drew whales on a rock in the middle of the mountain?  [Interview with Park Ki-nam, a Cultural and Tourism Commentator working in the Ulsan area.] Given the high concentration illustrations created using a side relief technique, we can estimate that the drawings were created 7,000 years ago during the prehistoric era. The Neolithic Era to be precise. The reason why there are so many whales is because our ancestors who settled in Ulsan 7,000 years ago hunted whales. Nearby, we have found artifacts such as a harpoon embedded in whale bone. That is why we think there are so many illustrations related to whaling in Bangudae.  [Woman] Now I get it. The illustrations are so detailed, I can’t believe they’re from the Neolithic Era. Some pictures even show the detailed features of whales and depict how they like seaweed. They are so intricate, I almost think people may have actually gone into the water to observe the whales with their own eyes.  [Man] We can enjoy these amazing pieces of art thanks to the artists astonishing powers of observation. You can spend several hours looking at different illustrations, but there is one particular picture that attracts my attention. It’s the picture of people dragging a whale that appears bigger than their boat.  [Woman] How on earth did they manage to catch a whale that appears to be as large as a house?  [Male] The key to answering that question lies in the Petroglyphs. Do you see that long, sharp thing jutting out of the whale’s back?  [Woman] Is that a ‘harpoon’? You mean, those prehistoric people fought whales with harpoon?  [Man] That’s correct. They caught giant whales with tiny harpoons that appear ridiculous compared to the size of the whales. This is a remarkable series of events that happened 7,000 years ago in the sea.  [Woman] But, there are several other parts at the Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace, apart from whale hunting, that do not make much sense. How did people manage to preserve these Petroglyphs for thousands of years?  [Man] That involves some sophisticated calculations. Did you know that archaeologists discovered the foundations of old houses from the prehistoric period near the banks of Taehwagang River?  [Woman] They found it on the banks of Taehwagang River... isn’t that almost 30km away from Bangudae?  [Man] That’s right. But there is a reason why prehistoric humans traveled all the way from their houses to Bangudae. The answer lies on the top area of the rock. Bangudae has a rock that juts out between 2m to 4m out at the top like a roof. In other words, the Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace was the only place in the area where people could find protection against wind, rain, or snow.  [Woman] Wow!.. I guess all the leg work looking for clues linked to the Petroglyphs paid off.  [Interview with Park Ki-nam, a Cultural and Tourism Commentator working in the Ulsan area. ] The Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace are widely acknowledged as the first record of humans hunting whales. It contains information about the distinct maritime culture in the North Pacific during the prehistoric period, which is why it has been included in the tentative list of World Heritage Sites. Also, the illustrations of whales seems to indicate that whales were an important food source for Neolithic humans. They caught whales together as a group, and shared the meat as well  [Man] Whalers who fought the rough seas with high hopes of a good catch tried to pass on the wisdom of whaling to their children with petroglyphs because they did not yet have a written language system. That’s why prehistoric humans drew the illustrations on the Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace    Ulsan Petroglyph Museum    [Man] If you travel a little further from Bangudae, you’ll arrive at the Ulsan Petroglyph Museum.Also nearby is the Cheonjeon-ri valley. Cheonjeon-ri valley used to be a popular road for Hwarang cadets during the Shilla Dynasty. They even created a visitor’s log on the rocks. That’s just another thing that makes the Ulsan Petroglyph Museum so special. First of all, it’s the only petroglyph museum in Korea.  If you want to visit a petroglyph museum, Ulsan is the only place you can go to. Also, from the sky, the museum looks like a whale. The museum was built thanks to the sheer fact that Bangudae Terrace had such historically important petroglyphs.  [Woman] If you want to learn more about petroglyphs, it might be a great idea to visit the museum and take your time touring its exhibits.  [Man] Bangudae Terrace has beautiful petroglyphs, but it is also famous for its gorgeous scenery. “Gyeomjae” Jeong Seon, a famous painter who lived during the late Joseon Dynasty used to come to paint the landscape near Bangudae...enough said, right? Meanwhile, “Poeun” Jeong Mong-ju, a noble official who lived during the late Goryeo Dynasty, was so enamored with the strange rock formations of Bangudae when he was exiled, called it “Poeundae.”  [Woman] Historical figures loved this place, too. All those whales in Ulsan and the Petroglyphs...I feel like really want to go on a trip now.  [Man] If you’re heading to Ulsan, there’s another place I want to recommend.    Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village    [Man] I’m talking about Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village.  [Woman] I’ve heard of Jangsaengpo in Ulsan. Apparently, you can see whales in the area from time to time.  [Man] In fact, there is an interesting story about Jangsaengpo Village. In the not-so-distant past, whaling made the entire village so rich that, people used to say, “even the village dogs carry rolls of cash.”   [Woman] Haha! Imagine dogs around the village carrying rolls of 	cash... I know there’s a 		statue of a dog holding money in its mouth. How did people catch so many whales near Jangsaengpo?  [Man] Well, that requires a little history lesson. In 1899, a whaling company in Russia decided to butcher whales in Jangsaengpo because they needed a whaling base to process large whales caught in the East Sea. After that, when Japan defeated Russia in the Russo-Japanese War, Japan monopolized the whaling base in Jangsaengpo. During the Japanese colonial rule of Korea, the waters near Jangsaengpo remained extremely profitable. Each year, whalers caught more than 100 whales, including gray whales and white whales. Here, Korean people mostly served as petty crewmen. But after our country won independence, Korean fishermen opened a company named the Joseon Whaling Corporation.  [Woman] Wow. That just seems so much fairer.  [Man] During the 1970s, whalers began using 100-ton iron ships, the whaling industry became much more substantial in size. But soon, the success story of Jangsaengpo came to an abrupt halt.    [Interview with Park Chang Hye-gyeong, a Cultural and Tourism Commentator working in the Ulsan area. ] Jangsaengpo in Ulsan is a port city that has a rather unfortunate history. It suffered from numerous raids and attacs from Japanese pirates, and it had to endure wars such as the naval battle of Ulsan and the Korean War. Today, it has become a place where countless people visit to get a taste of how things were during the days when whaling was a prominent industry.  [Man] Despite countless raids and attacks from Japanese pirates, Jangsaengpo survived. But, after some reckless whaling practices around the world drove a few whale species into extinction, the International Whaling Commission decided to ban all commercial whaling as of 1986.  [Woman] That means the fishermen at Jangsaengpo lost their livelihood literally overnight.  [Man] That’s right.. Whaling ships were moored in port, never to sail again. Soon, they disappeared into the history books.  [Woman] Whaling used to represent a glowing dream for the fishermen in Jangsaengpo. It took up their entire lives. Does Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village tell the same story you just told me?  [Man] Yes it does. Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village was created to show people how things looked and felt during the heyday of whaling.   [Woman] If you take the monorail from Whale Cultural Square, you will pass by the blue skies and arrive at Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village! Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village offers plenty of features to see and enjoy, including the “Goraemadang (Whale Plaza)” that shows you the history of whales since prehistoric times, and the Whale Sculpture Park with a life-size representation of a whale.
