Although this fortress is only 683 meters long and 7 meters tall, it was enough to fend off the enemy army. It’s particularly because the steep mountain made it harder for the enemy to approach. You can say that it has all the important factors of victory. The hill is now covered with wild flowers and pine trees but in the past, there was a well inside the fortress, providing ample drinking water to the soldiers. A number of bowls were also discovered around the well. Most likely, it was where they used to cook. Records indicate that while soldiers went about their daily life inside the fortress, invading soldiers got too tired and gave up invading.   The hardness of the walls is a factor we must not overlook. The wall is made of layers of granite slabs. No clay was used, but it’s still very solid and there was no worry of collapsing because all the crevices were filled with small stones. The slabs on the outside and those on the inside were stacked over each other to make the wall more solid. That’s why most of the wall except the portion near to the river is still intact even after 1,500 years.

stories.title: Ondal Tourist Sites: Ondal Cave
stories.script: Ondal Cave  [Traveler] Oh! Didn’t you feel the cool breeze brushing over the nape of your neck? Where is the wind coming from? Oh! So this is the Ondal Cave. I was told that this cave is about 450 million years old. The cave is nearly 800 meters long, and the rocks are still growing. The pale white stalactites and stalagmites are growing ever so slowly because there is plenty of water inside. That’s why this place looks so mysterious and grand.  But what does this ancient cave have to do with Ondal? There are many myths about him. One of them is that this was where Ondal and the Princess lived after eloping. And the holes were made when Ondal had the rocks carried away to build the fortress.   They say the cold breeze is from the crystal clear waters that are cold during summer but don’t freeze in winter. A myth has it that there is a snake, that failed to become a dragon, still lives here. Shall we go see where about that snake could be? It’s relatively safe at the entrance, but at one point, the ceiling gets very low. So don’t forget to wear your safety helmet!

stories.title: Uirim Reservoir: Entrance
stories.script: Uirim Reservoir Entrance  [Traveler] Since ancient times, agriculture was the main industry and basis of all economic activities in Korea. In order to produce greater yields, farmers cultivated rough land and created reservoirs by digging pools everywhere to facilitate water usage. As it was difficult to access water for farming purposes around here, local people established a reservoir here a very long time ago. The reservoir’s name is ‘Uirim.’ Uirim Reservoir is thought to be the oldest irrigation facility in Korea. Its original appearance has been preserved to the present day, making it a valuable heritage. A long time has passed since its birth, but its basic purpose hasn’t changed. Even today, farmers use water from Uirim Reservoir to irrigate their fields. So Uirim Reservoir can be said to give birth to their crops.  There are many theories about the date of construction of Uirim Reservoir. From careful analysis of the reservoir’s sediments, it seems most likely that Uirim Reservoir was built some 2,000 years ago.   Uirim Reservoir is more than a superb reservoir: it also attracts many tourists due to its wonderful scenery. Pine trees provide cool shade during spring, summer and fall. During the winter, people can break the frozen surface of the reservoir and catch the fish swimming below the layer of ice. You can also enjoy a 2km walking path around the reservoir, or simply enjoy the cool breeze and the great scenery. Uirim Reservoir is number one among the ten famous attractions of Jecheon, a town renowned for its beauty.

stories.title: Uirim Reservoir: Yongchu Falls
stories.script: Yongchu Falls  [Traveler] Looking down from the bridge above the waterfall, is a dazzling cliff about 30 meters in height, and a cool waterfall. Interestingly, on one side of this bridge there is a gentle flow of water and on the other there’s a dynamic waterfall.  A long time ago, people thought this waterfall resembled a dragon penetrating the valley before flying up into the sky. That’s why the word ‘Yong,’ which means ‘dragon’ in English, forms part of its name - Yongchu Falls. The high copper content in the water makes the waterfall look red, so the area is also called, the Red Dragon Valley. Look where the dragon left his mark, and listen to a folk tale. The story of <Five strong men and a python> has been passed down for generations here at Uirim Reservoir.  Once upon a time, there were five very strong brothers. Not only were they strong, but they also had scales on their bodies like dragons. One day, while the five brothers were playing around in Uirim Reservoir, a gigantic python came up behind the eldest brother. A python is an imaginary beast that frequently appears in Korean legends. It’s basically a baby dragon that has yet to acquire its mysterious powers. While the eldest brother fought with the creature under the water, his four brothers watched in shock, hoping for their brother to come back safe.   The brothers picked up wooden sticks from the waterside and started attacking the python. With help from his younger brothers, the eldest finally struggled back on land, while the angry beast whipped its tail at the five brothers.  The five brothers quickly dodged the attack, and the creature’s tail got stuck in a giant pine tree. The brothers beat down the evil beast with their bare hands and feet.   The beast’s scales broke off and were scattered all around, and its blood turned the waterfall red. The python was so big that when they hung it from the top of a giant tree, its tail reached all the way down to the ground. Thanks to the five brothers who defeated the python, the townspeople were able to go to Uirim Reservoir without fear.

stories.title: Uirim Reservoir: Jerim
stories.script: Jerim  [Traveler] The pine trees surrounding Uirim Reservoir are all more than 2,300 years old. There are 183 trees in total. Did you know that phytoncide is good for the human body? A pine tree is an excellent source of phytoncide. Phyton means “plant” and cide means “anti-bacterial,” and as the name indicates, it is an anti-bacterial substance that the plant secretes to protect itself. You’ve probably noticed the thick scent from a broken stick or a bunch of grass.   Phytoncide is very good for people, too. Just smelling it improves our immune system and stabilizes our entire body. It is known to have incredible effect in lowering stress hormones. It also kills various harmful bacteria in our body. What’s fascinating is that phytoncide has the same or a better effect than the antibiotics we take. It is a natural medicine without any side effects. Since that you are here in this forest of old pine trees, breathe in as much phytoncide as you can. It’s a valuable gift from our old pine tree friends.

stories.title: Uirim Reservoir: Ureuk Pavilion
stories.script: Ureuk Pavilion  [Traveler] ‘Ureuk’ is one of the three most famous musicians in Korean history, and was a master of the traditional string instrument called the gayageum. The gayageum consists of twelve strings connected to a long strip of royal foxglove wood. People play the gayageum by flicking the strings with their fingers. Ureuk was an exceptionally skilled player of the instrument, and this pavilion was his favorite place to visit. It still feels like his music lingers on in the area.  There are many stories about the Ureuk Pavilion in Jecheon. In a place called Janggeumdae, Ureuk is said to have brought three students and taught them how to play the instrument and how to perform various songs and dances. The story says that they looked like music gods enjoying themselves like no humans ever could. Ureuk got his water from the Ureuk well, whose water stays cool even during the hottest days of summer. Legend has it that drinking water from this well can cure many diseases. While you take a look around, I’ll tell you one more story about Uirim Reservoir.  Once upon a time, there was a huge wealthy house in Uirim Reservoir. The owner of the house was a very stingy man, like Scrooge. One day, a monk visited his house and asked for some food. The miser didn’t even want to donate a bowl of rice. When he saw that the monk hadn’t left his garden, the man got nasty. He dug up a bowl of soil and gave it to the monk. But the monk didn’t look surprised at all. He received the soil in his pouch, bowed to the man, and moved on. Having witnessed this, the daughter-in-law followed the monk. She asked him for forgiveness and gave him a bucket of rice. In a quiet and solemn voice, the monk told her to run far away, for there would be rain, wind, thunder, and lightning here. And he told her not to look back.  When the daughter-in-law returned, her stingy father-in-law was accusing the servants of stealing the missing portion of rice. When the daughter-in-law confessed that she had given the rice to the monk, he became infuriated and locked her up in the store room.  After some time, thunder and lightning came, and rain started to fall just like the monk had said. While the daughter-in-law was trying to figure out what to do, a violent noise and a spark of light passed around her. The storage door miraculously opened up, and the daughter-in-law quickly went outside and started running towards the mountain.  As she was running senselessly, the daughter-in-law suddenly remember the children she had left behind in the house. In a sudden reflex, she looked back.  For having disobeyed the monk, the daughter-in-law was turned to stone. The house was filled with water and became Uirim Reservoir. According to the legend, the stone form of the daughter-in-law is still somewhere around here, forever looking backwards.

stories.title: Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex: Entrance
stories.audioTitle: Entrance to the Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex
stories.script: Entrance to the Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex  [Traveler] Welcome to Cheongpung. Blessed by beautiful scenery and waterways extending in all directions, Cheongpung was the center of regional commerce. As indicated in its name, it is a complex of cultural relics of the area. When the relics were at risk of being immersed underwater due to plans to build a dam, local residents and civil workers joined hands to transfer the precious relics here, to the Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex, and ultimately formed a small folk village.   At the entrance of the complex, Paryeong Pavilion welcomes visitors. It was originally the entrance to the village. Let’s walk through the gate and go up to where we can see the entire place.   Please look up as you pass through the gate. Can you see the big tiger? It was drawn there so that it will protect the village from negative energies and floods.  Have you come up? Can you see the writing on the ceiling? It says paryeongsi, which means “paryeong poem.” This pavilion was named after this poem, which was written an official of the Joseon Dynasty about the 8 scenic views of this town. The original name of the gate was Namdeok Gate, and there is an inscription with the name on the inside. Okay, now let’s go and take a closer look at a traditional house of the Joseon era house.

stories.title: Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex: Dohwari House
stories.script: Dohwari House  [Traveler] This is a typical house from the Joseon era where the traditional beauty and styles of Korea can be seen. As you walk through the low gate of the straw-topped fence is a small cozy house across the courtyard. By the looks of the remaining construction, it can be estimated that there was an annex building before the main house.  Directly in front is an elevated wooden hall measuring 3 kan. A Kan refers to the distance between two columns and is used to describe the size of wooden buildings. Inside each section of the main hall is a door which can be opened wide to let the breeze in. Back in the days when there were no fans or air conditioners, such halls provided a perfect sanctuary from the scorching summer sun. Most traditional homes have doors between the rooms, but this one is blocked off completely, which indicates that this home was built earlier than most homes here.  Now take a look up at the roof. This is an example of a typical Korean building. The font and back of the roof are trapezoidal while the sides are triangular. It may not be as elaborate as a Chinese structure or as elegant as certain Japanese buildings, but these roofs have a unique charm, they feel cozier and more stable.    Moving on to the ground, you can see that the house is slightly elevated. The raised base is made of stones and dirt, and it was made to prevent flooding and humidity.   The houses here provide a visual testimony of life in the olden days. Take a close look at the gadgets and tools hanging on the walls or laying on the ground. Rusty old things always have a story to tell.

stories.title: Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex: Multaeri Standing Stone Buddha
stories.script: Multaeri Standing Stone Buddha Statue  [Traveler] This Buddha statue was moved here due to the construction of a dam. It was found waist deep underground, but has since then been preserved in good condition.  Korea was a Buddhist nation long before Christianity was introduced. People would erect Buddhist statues and pray for peace and prosperity, and seek tranquility from Buddhist teachings.   Let’s take a closer look at the Buddha statue. There is a small bump on the crown of his head, which represents the hair. It has a square head and a large and chubby face that makes the Buddha look kind and gentle. His small eyes look as if they were closed, and his nose is wide and bulky. The creases in the cloth around his shoulders are thick, and there is a belt around his waist. His arms hang to the sides of the belt, with the palm of his left hand facing up and his right arm is raised with a finger slightly bent. The facial expressions and hand gestures of Buddha statues are different according to the country they were made in. It is said that Buddha’s profound learning can be seen in his face and the shape of his hands.   The expression on his face and the wrinkles in this Buddha’s neck are distinct features of the time. Judging by the overall style, this statue is estimated to have been made in the 10th century.

stories.title: Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex: Geumbyeong House and Eungcheong Pavilion
stories.script: Geumbyeong House and Eungcheong Pavilion  [Traveler] This is Geumbyeong House. It was built in 1721, and was moved here during the construction of the dam. Officials dispatched from the capital would stay here while managing the region, and some high-ranking officials even used the building as their official residence.  Inside the building is a panel engraved with a number of characters. The original panel of this building was lost, so a panel was brought from another building. The overall layout of the building is rectangular with part of the floor being ondol, traditional underground heating system. The house is quite small compared to most official buildings, and has been built and restored so many times over the years that its original form is barely recognizable.   The building on the right is Eungcheong Pavilion. We don’t know when it was exactly built or what it was used for, but it was most likely a resting place for officials or an annex building for government work. It is said that Yi Hwang, the great scholar of Joseon, personally named this building. Now, let’s move on to the next stop, which is a pavilion where royalty and dignitaries of the Joseon Dynasty hosted banquets and parties.

stories.title: Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex: Hanbyeok Pavilion
stories.script: Hanbyeok Pavilion   [Traveler] Hanbyeok Pavilion was built in 1317 to celebrate the appointment of a great monk as the king’s teacher. It was built and managed by the government and was usually used for entertaining guests or holding banquets.  This building has undergone a number of renovations over the years, but its elegance was not lost. It has a hipped-and-gabled roof, and as you can see, the ends of the roof’s surfaces meet at one end. It is the most common type of roof in Korean traditional houses. You can tell the interior structure of a house just by looking at the roof.   Now, let’s take the stairs to the left.  The flooring was made of natural stone. You may think it was made of a few large boulders, but the gaps in between were filled with dirt and rimmed with stones to elevate the building.  If you stand here, you can see the beautiful surrounding landscape. Just before us is Cheongpung’s most representative lake and bridge. What a refreshing view!  Not far from here is Mangwol Fortress. The fortress walls are about 500 meters long, and it takes about 15 minutes to look around, so be sure to walk up and enjoy the spectacular view of the lush mountains and clear waters.

stories.title: Tangeum Terrace: Tangeum Pavilion
stories.script: Tangeum Pavilion  [Traveler] The road to Tangeum Terrace starts here. If you follow the signposts and walk through the forest along the soft mossy rail, you will be greeted by a sudden brightness, the Tangeum Terrace. Some 1,500 years ago, the court musician named Ureuk would immerse in the natural surroundings and perform along amidst the beautiful landscape of the lake. He is considered to be among the top 3 musicians of Korean history.  The gayageum, the 12-stringed instrument he played, was a gift from the king of the Gaya Kingdom, his home nation, personally invented by the king himself. He showed his gratitude to the king by writing twelve musical pieces about the people of Gaya. But unfortunately, due to invasion and attacks from neighboring countries, Gaya collapsed and Ureuk was forced to surrender.   An embittered Ureuk aimlessly roamed around the streets with his instrument slung over his shoulder. One day, the royal court of the country that had taken over Gaya recognized Ureuk’s talent and invited offered him a house, land and pupils if he entered the palace as a court musician.  However, he refused the fame and dignity of a court musician and chose to live a simple and free life instead. The graceful and delicate music he created from the twelve silk strings of the gayageum drew people close to him, gradually constructing a village.   No Western musical instrument can imitate the sound of a gayageum, what do you think about the unique sound of the gayageum? Doesn’t it blend exquisitely well with the scenic view of the Namhan River seen from Tangeum Pavilion? Look afar and concentrate on the music for a moment. The scent of the pine trees, the lush mountains and rivers that Ureuk loved so much will be communicated on to you through his music.

stories.title: Tangeum Terrace: Yeoldu Cliff
stories.script: Yeoldu Cliff  [Traveler] To the north of Tangeum Terrace is a cliff called Yeoldu Cliff, which literally means ‘twelve cliffs.’ It was named so because it was said that the great General Sin Lip of the Joseon Dynasty had climbed the cliff twelve times. Why do you think he climbed up this cliff so many times?  In 1592, when the Japanese army attacked Joseon and reached Chungju within ten days, General Sin Lip came up with a plan to drive back the enemy troops, with the cliff at his back. Such strategy is called “Baesujin,” the battle formation was initially developed by Chinese General Han Xin. General Han pitched his camp with a river behind his army’s back so that none of his soldiers could retreat, leaving them no choice but to fight like devils. This word is still used to express one’s strong determination.   Because he was greatly outnumber, General Sin believed that the best way to fight the large Japanese army, who were armed with guns, was the Baesujin strategy. He and his soldiers fought to the end and gave everything they had, however, they were pushed against the cliff and died heroically fighting for their country.  The name of this cliff shows how fierce the battle was. General Sin and his soldiers had to climb up and down to the river twelve times cool their bows, because they had become too hot to pull. The intensity of this battle show how fiercely people fought to close all roads to Seoul.

stories.title: Tangeum Terrace: Seven-story Stone Pagoda of Tappyeong-ri
stories.script: Seven-story Stone Pagoda of Tappyeong-ri  [Traveler] According to a local legend, two men, both with the same walking pace, started to walk. One departing from the northern tip of the peninsula, and the other from the southern tip, and this was where they came to meet. This place was then designated as the middle of the peninsula and this tower was erected. (Laugh) Whether this story is true or not can’t be proved, but seeing that this tower is better known as “Central Tower” rather than by its actual name, the story may have some truth to it.   The more practical history as to why the tower was erected, was to alleviate the anxious and unstable souls of the nation by encouraging faith in Buddhism.  The king wanted to announce such purpose to the nation by establishing this pagoda at the center of Silla territory.  Before the 10th century, Chungju was known as “Jungju,” literally meaning “center village” or “village at the center.” At that time, the Korean Peninsula was divided into three kingdoms, namely, Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla, which were constantly engaged in territorial wars. Chungju was regarded as a highly strategic point and hence was dominated by each of the three kingdoms in turn. Interestingly, all three kingdoms gave this place a name with the meaning “origin of the country” or “the central area of the territory.”  This pagoda measures 14.5 meters in height, which is quite rare for structures built in those days. The seven-story stone pagoda with a wide double-layered pedestal looks as if it is about to fly up to the sky. I think perhaps it may have represented the people’s pride of living at the very center of the country.

stories.title: Chungju Ancient Tombs of Nuam-ri
stories.script: Ancient Tombs of Nuam-ri  [Traveler] After passing the fruitful apple orchards, smoothly rounded tombs will come into view. This cluster of about 1,000 tombs is known as the Ancient Tombs of Nuam-ri, but is more frequently referred to as the “Hill of Tombs.”  These ancient tombs date back to Silla, an ancient kingdom that dominated the Korean Peninsula about 1,400 years ago. Its capital, Gyeongju, located about 240 km southeast of here, is home to many tombs of Silla’s kings and royal family members. Regardless of the country, tombs of the nobility are generally found close to the capital. That being the case, why were so many Silla royal tombs established here, so far away from Gyeongju?  The Korean Peninsula was divided into three kingdoms, namely Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla, which were constantly engaged in territorial wars. Around 1,400 years ago, a Silla king managed to capture this place from his northern opponent and set up a small capital to preserve the kingdom's victorious spirit. He even had some nobles and their families move from Gyeongju to the new city. In other words, you can feel the “frontier spirit” of our Korean ancestors who wanted to take over the peninsula’s central area after the unification of the three kingdoms.

stories.title: Chungju Goguryeo Stele Exhibition
stories.script: Goguryeo Stele  [Traveler] This monument is called the Goguryeo Stele. Before Silla took control of the central region of the Korean Peninsula, the biggest kingdom among the three was Goguryeo, which occupied the northern part of the peninsula. This stele is assumed to have been erected by the Goguryeo people around 432 B.C. The majority of Goguryeo territory is currently North Korean territory, so this is the only Goguryeo stele in South Korea.  But how did we know that this stele was actually from Goguryeo? Gratefully, its identity is explained by the 400 or so characters tightly inscribed on all four sides of the stele. Because the inscription was so severely worn by the passing time, it was quite hard to make out the meaning. Various advanced technologies including an infrared imaging system had to be used to figure out the inscription, and, as a result, a lot of historical information including the territorial boundaries of Goguryeo were successfully discovered.   Interestingly, this historically significant stele was found by an amateur cultural research organization. Before its discovery, its surface was entirely covered with moss and the inscriptions were unreadable, so the stele was believed to be nothing more than a common stone built to represent wishes for the prosperity of a nearby village. But one day, a member of the research organization had to leave the town and happened to pass by the stone after a farewell party with some villagers. Thinking that this might be the last time he would pass that way, he took a closer look at the stone, and realized that some characters were inscribed on its surface! Such simple and honest passion on the part of an amateur researcher is what ultimately saved a national treasure.

stories.title: Temple Site of Mireuk-ri: Entrance
stories.audioTitle: Entrance to the Temple Site of Mireuk-ri
stories.script: Entrance to the Temple Site of Mireuk-ri  [Traveler] Welcome! This is the entrance to Haneul Pass and the Temple Site of Mireuk-ri where traces of a stone Buddha statue and a pagoda are located. In order to get to the top of Haneul Pass, you have to pass by this temple site. Known as the oldest uphill path in Korea, many historical relics and old tales and stories are hidden here.  Approximately 1,800 years ago, a king of Silla, an ancient kingdom located in the southeastern area of the Korean Peninsula, made this uphill path to expand the territory northward. The nearby area was also the border area of three ancient Korean kingdoms, namely Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla. It was a very important area since it served as a route for Silla to enter the Han River basin and to prevent Baekje and Goguryeo’s enemies from invading from the south. It is also famous because Buddhist civilization began here. Fierce battles often took place around this site because it connected the peninsula from south to north. According to historical records, the last king and princess of the Unified Silla Dynasty passed through here, when the nation collapsed, to escape the fallen city and get to Geumgang Mountain. Now, this area has put such stories behind it and serves the residents as a recreation area and an eco-tour course. So, I hope you will enjoy the course and the beautiful scenery as well.  Although this is a temple site where only a pagoda and a stone Buddha statue remain, originally a huge Buddhist temple called Daewon Temple stood in this area. The people who visited this temple to make their wishes used to spend the night here. For a long period of its history, the temple remained severely damaged as wars occurred frequently. However, it is regarded as a mystical place where the story of Silla’s last prince and princess is often told.   Now, shall we look over the Temple Site of Mireuk-ri? First, let’s take a look at the Five-story Stone Pagoda of Mireuk-ri.

stories.title: Temple Site of Mireuk-ri: Five-story Stone Pagoda
stories.script: Five-story Stone Pagoda   [Traveler] Let’s look at this big stone pagoda. Stone pagodas, which enshrine the sarira, or the relics of the Buddhas that remained after the cremation of their bodies, have long been objects of worship. In China, pagodas were made by cutting rocks into a brick-like shape, while they were made with wood in Japan. In Korea, pagodas were primarily made with granite. So, pagodas tend to vary according to the country in which they are made. And the large pagoda standing before you is a traditional Korean five-story stone pagoda.  The roof-shaped stones are the basis for counting the number of stories of a pagoda. When counting the stories of a pagoda, the pedestal that supports the pagoda and the capstone on top are excluded from the count. You can see that this pagoda has five roof-shaped stones, so it is a five-story stone pagoda. Its impressive stability is due to the structure, in which smaller parts are placed on the higher story. This pagoda displays the typical structure of Korean and Chinese pagodas.  Now, shall we look at the stone lantern standing between the stone pagoda and the stone Buddha statue?  Can you see the octagonal stone lantern? Usually, a stone lantern is placed in front of the main hall of a Buddhist temple, and is said to be lit by the Shakyamuni’s enlightenment of the truth to deliver it to mankind. The windows on the four sides of the stone lantern are intended to spread this light wider and further. Also, this stone lantern features lotus patterns, the lotus flower being one of the major symbols of Buddhism. Lotus patterns have been widely used to stand for Buddhist doctrine and applied to most Buddhist relics, as lotus flowers bloom clean and pure even in dirty, muddy places.

stories.title: Temple Site of Mireuk-ri: Stone Buddha
stories.script: Stone Buddha   [Traveler] There are two stone Buddha statues in this area, which are located at the end of the southern part of the Mireuk Temple Site. You are looking at the first one, which wears a gentle smile. The other one is carved on the rock cliff to the north of Worak Mountain. Regarding these Buddha statues, there is a story about Silla’s last prince and princess who lived in about the 10th century. Would you like to hear their story?  Over one thousand years ago, as Silla, the dynasty which had unified the three ancient kingdoms of the Korean Peninsula, collapsed, the prince and princess left to build a new kingdom. When they stayed at this mountain, Buddha appeared in the prince’s dream, and told him they would find a wide area across a hill to the west, and that they should establish a Buddhist temple and a stone Buddha statue there. The Buddha also told him to carve a stone Buddha on the peak on the opposite side of the area.  As the prince told his dream to the princess, she was surprised to find they’d had the same dream. Hoping to restore his kingdom, he built a temple and the stone Buddha you saw earlier. The princess also carved a Buddha statue on the peak of Worak Mountain, and it is now called the Rock-carved Buddha of Deokju Temple.  However, their wish did not come true. The prince left, but the princess stayed in the temple and prayed for the prosperity of their kingdom.  As you can see, this stone Buddha statue is 10.6m high and consists of five granite stones. At the top, there is a wide stone that looks like a Korean traditional hat, and under that, there are four stones which form the Buddha’s face and body. His long eyebrows are like crescent moons, while his slightly closed eyes make him seem lost in meditation. The long and wide nose also brings comfort to watch. Compared to the face, which is expressed in detail, the wrinkles on his robes and the Buddha’s gestures look very simple.  Unlike other Buddhist temples of Korea, the Temple Site of Mireuk-ri uniquely faces north. Presumably, this is because the founder of the temple wanted to display his wish to expand the kingdom’s territory in a northerly direction.   Now, shall we go back to the entrance to look for the tortoise-shaped pedestal?

stories.title: Temple Site of Mireuk-ri: Tortoise-shaped Pedestal
stories.audioTitle: Tortoise-shaped Pedestal in the Temple Site of Mireuk-ri
stories.script: Tortoise-shaped Pedestal in the Temple Site of Mireuk-ri  [Traveler] The large tortoise-shaped stone is a pedestal for a stele. Actually, this is the biggest pedestal found so far in Korea. The dented part on the tortoise’s back was used to erect a stele. This pedestal is thought to have been derived from Chinese counterparts, and took the shape of a tortoise, which was regarded as a symbol of longevity, to express the eternal existence of the stele. The stele of this pedestal has not been found, and it is presumed that it was never completed.  It appears that this pedestal was made of a large stone that was located on this site. There is no hexagonal pattern on the tortoise’s back. Instead, there are two baby tortoises carved on its back. Shall we find the baby tortoises? Take a look around the tortoise’s shoulders. Can you see two baby tortoises climbing up its back? Such a feature clearly reveals the wit of the person who made this pedestal.  If you walk 200m up from the entrance of the Temple Site of Mireuk-ri to Haneul Pass, you can see the Three-story Stone Pagoda in the Temple Site of Mireuk-ri. Shall we move on to see the pagoda?

stories.title: Haneuljae Three-story Stone Pagoda
stories.audioTitle: Three-story Stone Pagoda in the Temple Site of Mireuk-ri
stories.script: Three-story Stone Pagoda in the Temple Site of Mireuk-ri  [Traveler] There is a three-story stone pagoda located about 500m away from the Temple Site of Mireuk-ri. It is assumed to have been placed there either to notify people coming over the uphill path about the temple or to serve as a map that enshrines the remains of a Buddhist monk.  Normally, when people think of a western tower, they think of a high and imposing structure that shows its greatness. But Korea, Japan and China which accepted Buddhism refer to towers as pagodas. In other words, they expressed the fact that they were living in a Buddhist kingdom by erecting such pagodas.  Now, shall we take a look at the stone pagoda. This pagoda looks like it has four stories, but actually it’s a three-story pagoda. There are two pedestals to support the pagoda, and on top of them there is a three-story body. The simple and elegant structure of this pagoda has greater aesthetic value than the five-story stone pagoda.   On the way up here, did you see the stele engraved with characters indicating Haneul Pass? That is the entrance to Haneul Pass. If you have time, I recommend you take a walk up the pass. It should take about 2 hours, and is a fairly comfortable walk. It is not like climbing a mountain, so don’t worry.

stories.title: Entrance to Haneul Pass
stories.script: Entrance to Haneul Pass  [Traveler] Known as the oldest pass in Korea, Haneul Pass connects North Chungcheong Province and North Gyeongsang Province. The word haneul means “sky” in Korean, so its name indicates that it is located very close to the sky. When you climb up to the top of this pass, it will lead you into North Gyeongsang Province.   The pass in the area of Chungcheong Province is located in Woraksan National Park and therefore maintained its original appearance. However, the pass in Gyeongsang Province has unfortunately been covered with asphalt. As it has gentle slopes, you can easily enjoy the trails of Haneul Pass without any climbing gear.  This pass was an important transportation route from the Three Kingdoms Period on, and also served as a key point in military and economic strategies for a long time. Now, it is an excellent place of relaxation for many visitors.  Haneul Pass has two trails. One is the original trail, and the other is a newly developed eco-tour course. The eco-tour course is equipped with many environmentally-friendly facilities that help visitors fully enjoy the fauna and flora of Worak Mountain. Also, visitors can learn about Korea’s native species of trees and other abandoned passes in Korea on this course.  When you arrive at the top of this pass, you will see an asphalt-covered trail. And just before the summit, there is a memorial stele standing on the right-hand side of the pass. If you climb further up the slope of the pass, you will find the height of scenic beauty. Then you will realize why this pass is called Haneul Pass even though it is not very high. A fair view of Worak Mountain and the beautiful scenery of grasses will welcome you.   Take off your earphones for a moment and listen to the sounds of the mountain birds, the wind and the flowing water of the valleys. And also enjoy a chat with friends and family.

stories.title: Haneuljae Pass Trail Route
stories.script: Haneuljae Pass Trail Route   Shall we go up Haneuljae Pass, Korea’s first pass? This is a trail where both history and nature can be enjoyed because it encompasses the clean nature of Woraksan Mountain and Mireukdaewon Stone Temple Site.  Mireukdaewon Stone Temple Site can be seen after walking for about 1km on the paved road stretching from the Mireuk-ri parking lot. It is the only stone temple facing north in South Korea. Legend has it that Prince Maui, the son of King Gyeongsun(r. 927-935), the last king of the Silla Dynasty(57-935 B.C.), established the temple while grieving for the loss of the country to the Goryeo Dynasty(918-1392). After observing the cultural heritages at Mireukdaewon Stone Temple Site, go on to see Haneuljae Pass in earnest.  Anybody can walk to Haneuljae Pass with ease because the slope of the road is gentle and the mountain is not rough. If you set out for the road on the left side of the stone monument at the entrance to Haneuljae Pass, a forest dense with fir and oriental oak trees with a long history unfolds. While strolling on the forest path with phytoncide filling the air, you will encounter the “friend tree,” which is a conjoined tree where the trunks of two trees with different roots are combined and grow as one tree. You can also see “Yuna-like Pine Tree,” a pine tree that resembles the figure skating pose of the world-famous figure skater Yuna Kim. Why not pose like Kim here at this popular photo zone to keep in your memories?

stories.title: Summit of Haneuljae Pass
stories.script: Summit of Haneuljae Pass    After walking for about an hour along the forest path, the summit of Haneuljae Pass, where it feels like you could reach out and touch the sky, will be in sight. Haneuljae means “a place that merges with the sky,” though its low altitude of only 525m makes it easy to hike. But because it is open in all directions and the sky and mountains are merged in harmony, a scenic view like a painting spreads out before your eyes.   It is written on a stone monument at the summit of Haneuljae Pass that in 156 during the Silla Dynasty(57-935 B.C.), it was discovered to go to the Hangang River basin and was called Gyerimnyeong Pass in the past. Thus, it is a pass with over 2,000 years of history. Also, there is a story that Prince Maui and Princess Deokju of the Silla Dynasty, which surrendered to the Goryeo Dynasty(918-1392), crossed Haneuljae Pass dreaming of the revival of Silla.  At the summit of Haneuljae Pass, take a look at the bondstone of the stone monument. Two addresses are engraved there: Mireuk-ri, Suanbo-myeon, Chungju-si, Chungcheongbuk-do and Gwaneum-ri, Mungyeong-eup, Mungyeong-si, Gyeongsangbuk-do. With Haneuljae Pass at the center, one side is Chungju-si, Chungcheongbuk-do and the other side is Mungyeong-si, Gyeongsangbuk-do. The village in Chungju is called Mireuk-ri and the village in Mungyeong is called Gwaneum-ri. Gwaneum means “this life,” while Mireuk means “the afterlife.” That is, Haneuljae Pass is a special road that connects Chungju and Mungyeong and at the same time connects this life with the afterlife.

stories.title: Nine-story Stone Pagoda of Sajabinsin Temple Site
stories.audioTitle: Nine-story Stone Pagoda of Sajabinsin Temple Site
stories.script: Nine-story Stone Pagoda of Sajabinsin Temple Site  [Traveler] Let me introduce another stone pagoda on Worak Mountain. It is the nine-story stone pagoda located at the Sajabinsin Temple Site. The date and purpose of the construction are inscribed on the lower part of the pagoda. The 8th King of the Goryeo Dynasty built this pagoda and dedicated it to the nation’s safety, his personal longevity, and the spread of Buddhism.   This stone pagoda has many unique characteristics. Instead of pillars, four lions can be seen supporting the pagoda on their heads. A lion was not a usual animal on the Korean Peninsula in those days, but it was used to decorate the pagoda as it represents the Buddha in Buddhist symbolism. If you look closer at the lions, they all have different facial expressions.   There is a small statue of Buddha inside the pagoda. If you look at the seated statue, you will see it has a funny facial expression and is wearing a fabric headgear. The lotus flower that is inscribed on the ceiling of the niche inside the pagoda is beautifully preserved as it has not been damaged by wind or rain. The pagoda was originally nine stories high, but it was caught in a fire during the Korean War and only four stories survived the blaze.

stories.title: South Gate of Deokju Fortress
stories.script: South Gate of Deokju Fortress   [Traveler] If you follow the valley for 5km, you will find a towering rock cliff along the way, and an old fortress on the opposite side. That is Deokju Fortress, which was built during the Silla Kingdom. In ancient Korean kingdoms, fortresses were built in mountainous areas by exploiting nearby geographical features, while fortresses in western countries were usually constructed high by digging a well on a plain.  The east gate of this fortress is located at the temple’s entrance while the north gate is located on the road leading to the nearby village. The south gate is the most beautifully constructed of the three gates. This fortress was named after Deokju Princess, who suffered a tragic fate.   The construction of another fortress outside its walls gave Deokju Fortress a double-layered defensive structure. Overall, it is a very large, defensive fortress comprised of four layers.  Thanks to its defensive power, this fortress, which linked Chungcheong Province to Gyeongsang Province, played a very important role in Korean history. As it was located at the center of the Korean Peninsula, it was a border area of the three ancient Kingdoms, so a great variety of political and military events took place near here. And, because of its advantageous location, people from the surrounding area used it as a refuge whenever there was a war.  This fortress was as a candidate to be listed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in January 2010. I hope we can all see Deokju Fortress on the World Heritage List along with Bulguk Temple, Seokguram Grotto and Hwaseong Fortress.  If you drive for about 5 minutes from here, you will meet a path leading to the temple. About a one-hour walk up the path is a Buddha statue carved on a large rock cliff, which is presumed to have been made at the command of the princess. This statue typifies not only the traditional style of Buddhist culture in Korea, but also that of China, Japan and India. Now, let’s follow the path along the valley to see the statue.

stories.title: Gwana Park
stories.script: Gwana Park   Chungju is a city that represents Chungcheong-do as well as a historically meaningful region. It was a ferocious battlefield for fighting over territories during the Three Kingdoms period(57-668 B.C.) and was an important traffic hub during the Goryeo Dynasty(918-1392) and the Joseon Dynasty(1392-1910). The first character in Chungcheong-do, “chung,” is derived from Chungju.   Such historical meanings of Chungju can be discovered in Gwana Park. The park was formed on the site of a government office(Gwana) that had jurisdiction over the administration of Chungju. After passing by the quaint two-story gate tower, Cheongnyeongheon Magistrate's Office, the main building, can be seen. This was where business was carried out, and the name means “clear and comfortable.” A hip-and-gable roof, which is one roof structure types used in traditional Korean houses, is impressive. Jegeumdang Hall, at opposite Cheongnyeongheon Magistrate's Office, is where central government officials who came down to Chungju stayed. Sangosucheonggak Hall at the back of Jegeumdang Hall was used as a secretary’s office or a kitchen.   Other things to see include the Martyrs’ Monument that pays tribute to Roman Catholics who were taken to Gwana during the oppression of Roman Catholics and died as martyrs, and a zelkova tree that is over 540 years old. There is also an information board on Chungjueupseong Walled Town, estimated to have been built over 1,000 years ago. Why not take a walk through Gwana Park and imagine the old Chungjueupseong Walled Town?

stories.title: Jayu and Muhak Markets
stories.script: Jayu and Muhak Markets   A visit to markets where the liveliness of local people can be directly felt cannot be left out of the schedule. In particular, the fun of eating and people watching as well as touring traditional attractions can all be enjoyed in Chungju’s traditional markets. Five markets gathered along Chungjucheon Stream are located where the north gate of the old Chungjueupseong Walled Town was. Each market has its own characteristics, making it fun to visit each one. Among the markets, Jayu Market is easily accessible due to its location near a big road and has many stores that handle dry goods, clothes and jewelry. Muhak Market, where various kinds of food such as vegetables, fish and side dishes are sold, is also worth visiting.  In particular, Sundae-Mandu Alley stretching from Jayu Market to Muhak Market is a course you should take: Blood sausage and rice soup with dried radish leaves and chewy-textured potato dumplings are popular. After filling your stomach, why not check out Jayu Café run by the Jayu Market Merchants’ Society. A variety of beverages can be enjoyed at a low price, and the joy of requesting the music you want to listen to from a DJ can be experienced.     Also at Nuri Market near Jayu and Muhak Markets there is the Samhwa Blacksmith’s Shop run by Kim Myeong-il, a blacksmith designated as Chungcheongbuk-do’s intangible cultural heritage. Watching the master craftsman, who has handled iron for about 60 years, work the bellows and hammer and temper the iron to make a variety of tools is phenomenal. Nearby there is Banseonjae House, the house where UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon lived in during his school days.

stories.title: Chungju Jayu  Muhak Market
stories.audioTitle: The market where you can meet culture
stories.script: Along the Chungju Stream, Jayu, or the Free Market was formed on one side, and Muhak Market on the other. Through their origins might differ, they emerged as one entity, developing along with the people of Chungju City. Jayu Market was formed naturally on the outskirts of Chungju Eupseong, or Fortress, during the Joseon Dynasty. Muhak Market was created by street vendors along the Chungju Stream.  It takes about 15 minutes to get to the market from Chungju Station or Chungju Bus Terminal. There is also a public parking lot for visitors coming by car. Jayu Market is most famous for its alley full of handmade potato dumplings, as well as an alley for dried-radish-greens soup. The dumplings made a particularly strong impression on the renowned celebrity chef, Baek, Jong-won. Along with a generous serving of dried radish greens and blood sausages, these dumplings, with their chewy potato-flour skins and spicy kimchi or meat fillings full of vegetables, await passersby at affordable prices at many venues on this street.  Jayu Muhak Market has also been branded by locals for its quality cultural programs. This makes it the best-known marketplace in downtown Chungju City. Just like the cultural centers run by many department stores, the market has adopted this concept. So, several cultural programs are open to local patrons, giving them the chance to enrich their cultural intelligence.  On Fridays and Saturdays in the summer and fall, “Nuri Night Market” opens in the evening. Along the alley leading into the market, the streets full of food and activity vendors provide great entertainment for all visitors. Families dining out with their children can enjoy these exciting activities, and also choose from a variety of delicious dishes, spending the whole night here.

stories.title: Chungju World Martial Arts Park
stories.script: Chungju World Martial Arts Park   Chungju is the home of Taekkyeon, a traditional Korean martial art that makes use of fluid, rhythmic dance-like movements to strike or trip up an opponent, which is listed as a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Also, it’s the place where the Chungju World Martial Arts Festival is held. Chungju World Martial Arts Park is the main stage of the festival, which is officially sponsored by UNESCO.  The outdoor stage of the park located along the Namhangang River is loved by citizens as a rest place where people usually ride bicycles or go inline skating. It gained popularity because next to the stage is the Chungju World Martial Arts Museum and Chungju Lava Land, a theme park for “Lava,” popular animation characters loved by children.   There are amusement facilities that can be enjoyed for free. A forest playground and a rock maze are places for children. The forest playground was made with five big plane trees in the park. Children can run around in nature with its suspension bridges, tunnels, moving stairs, single log bridges, slides, etc. placed between the trees. There is a rock maze, made with boulders from the Namhangang River, which looks like an apple, Chungju’s regional product, and a taegeuk symbol, when seen from above. Other facilities include a large soccer field, a water fountain, and the Neungam Bog Ecological Park, making it an enjoyable rest area for both children and adults.

stories.title: Chungjuho Lake and Jongdaengigil Path
stories.script: Chungjuho Lake and Jongdaengigil Path   Chungjuho Lake, Korea’s largest artificial lake, is also called the “sea of the land.” Many people visit this popular place because the landscape is beautiful. Although tourists usually tour Chungjuho Lake on a cruise, if you walk along Jongdaengigil Path, which was created in 2013, you can also enjoy the whole of Simhangsan Mountain.  It takes about 3 hours to walk Jongdaengigil Path, a 7.5-km course. But for the core course of touring Simhangsan Mountain and appreciating Chungjuho Lake, you can walk it in just one and a half hours. The name Jongdaengi is derived from an old place name in a neighboring village.   Dullegil Trail, which is connected to Chungjuho Lake, starts at the end of Jongdaengigil Path, where the natural forest is emphasized. The core course along Jongdaengigil Path looks like a heart. Therefore, people say if one walks on this road with a lover, their love comes true. There is also an interesting story that whenever one crosses over Jongdaengi Pass in the middle of the path, that person gets a month younger. When the trail around the lake comes to an end, there is a suspension bridge.   If you cross the bridge you can go to Sanjong Village, and if you do not cross the bridge you return to Jongdaengigil Path going through the forest interpretation information center.

stories.title: Suanbo Hot Springs
stories.script: Suanbo Hot Springs   Suanbo Hot Springs was the first naturally erupted hot spring among the many hot springs in South Korea. This means it’s a hot spring where thermal water naturally gushes out from the earth without an artificial drilling process. The quality of the thermal water is first grade. This is because it erupts naturally at a high temperature of 53℃ from 250m below ground, and is colorless, odorless and flavorless clean natural thermal water with weak alkaline of 8.3 acidity. Suanbo Hot Springs is traditionally known as having remedial effects for skin diseases, etc. because it includes various minerals that are beneficial to human bodies.   In Joseon wangjo sillok(Annals of the Joseon Dynasty) designated as a UNESCO Memory of the World, there is a record that says King Taejo(Yi Seong-gye, r. 1392-1398) went to Suanbo to treat his malignant skin disease. There is a record in the Cheongpung hyanggyoji(Cheongpung Local Confucian School Newspaper), a historical record, which says King Sukjong(r. 1674-1720) enjoyed the hot springs at Suanbo and recuperated there. Thus, Suanbo Hot Springs is also known as the “King’s Hot Springs.”  The thermal water of Suanbo Hot Springs is managed directly by Chungju-si to control and preserve its quality. The best quality thermal water can be used at any facility that has a thermal water usage permit within the Suanbo Hot Springs area. If circumstances don’t allow you to bathe in the hot springs, then visit Multang Park. There is a foot bath area called Naganjeong where travelers can rest for a while and recover from fatigue.

stories.title: Jungangtap Park(Seven-story Stone Pagoda)
stories.script: Jungangtap Park(Seven-story Stone Pagoda)   The Seven-story Stone Pagoda in Tappyeong-ri, Chungju(National Treasure No. 6) is located in Jungangtap Park with the beautiful scenery of the Namhangang River. The stone pagoda was built during the Unified Silla period(676-935) to mark the middle of Korea’s territory and was called Jungangtap Pagoda(“Jungang” means middle in Korean). According to a legend, during the Silla period, King Wonseong(r. 785-798) had two men start travelling from the southern and northernmost tips of the country several times to identify the center point, and they repeatedly ended up meeting at the same location. Accordingly, a big granite pagoda was erected to indicate the center of the territory, and it is said to be the largest among others built back then.   Jungangtap Park was created to protect this national treasure from being damaged. A trail around the pagoda offers a place for visitors to relax. Along the trail, sculptures made by national artists are displayed. The seven-story stone pagoda, in harmony with the contemporary art pieces, allows visitors to experience a mysterious feeling of time transcending a thousand years.    Other popular places to visit include Liquorium, the world’s first liquor museum where you can enjoy a glass of wine or a cocktail while appreciating the beautiful views of the Namhangang River, and the Pungnyu Culture Center, where you can spend some relaxing moments with tea. Also, there is Chungju Museum where you can look into the diverse history of Chungju, Tangeum Lake International Rowing Regatta and a camping site, all of which make the area a great one-day trip course.

stories.title: Chungju Museum
stories.script: Chungju Museum   Due to its geographical location, Chungju was a fierce battlefield for fights over territory among the three ancient states of Goguryeo, Silla and Baekje(A.D. 57-668) as well as a major traffic hub. Therefore, lots of cultural properties and historic sites are scattered throughout the area. Among others, Chungju Museum in Jungangtap Park houses representative relics from the Three Kingdoms period.      The museum comprises two exhibition halls and an outdoor exhibition area. Hall 1 consists of the History Hall with Buddhist art pieces including Buddha statues, Buddhist paintings and shaman paintings on display, and the Folk Hall, where visitors can take a look at the lives of our ancestors in the Chungju area. Hall 2 is composed of four connected exhibition halls: The Prehistoric-Three Kingdoms Hall, Goryeo-Joseon Hall, Noted Men of Chungju Hall, and Chungju’s Struggle Hall. The Prehistoric-Three Kingdoms Hall exhibits replicas of the Goguryeo Monument, Chungju and the Jeokseongbi Monument of Silla, Danyang, representative relics of the Three Kingdoms period. The Goryeo-Joseon Hall displays celadon and white porcelain from the Goryeo and Joseon periods, while Chungju’s Struggle Hall houses reproductions of battles in Chungju including the Chungjuseong Fortress Battle, Tangeumdae Battle during Imjinwaeran(Japanese Invasion of Joseon in 1592), etc. The outdoor exhibition area exhibits stone relics.   For more about the exhibits, a commentary service on the exhibits is available upon request. You can apply for the service at the Information Center from 10 am to 4 pm on all days except Mondays when the museum is closed. Currently, commentary in English is available. You can contact the Tourism Promotion Team in the Tourism Division of Chungju City Hall.

stories.title: Liquorium
stories.script: Liquorium   There is a unique museum in Chungju, a place of glorious beauty, full of flavor. It is Liquorium, a museum with exhibits on global liquor cultures next to the Pungnyu Culture Center. Liquorium is a compound of “Liquor” and “-rium,” which is a Latin word for space. It introduces various kinds of liquor and culture from around the world.    At the entrance to the museum are two stills that were actually used to distill whiskey for over 100 years, acting as a main gate. Also, the oak casks from around the world stacked at the entrance of the exhibition hall will delight your eyes even more. The first exhibition hall is the History of Wine, Wine Culture Hall. It is full of exciting exhibits, from the history of wine to the variety of grapes, how to read the labels on bottles of world-famous wines and trademarks, and how to choose wine. The next exhibition hall, the Cooperage Hall, displays oak casks that were used for storing, aging and transporting wine, brandy and whiskey. The exhibition corner called “The Angel’s Share” is eye-catching. It explains that “Alcohol and fragrances evaporate when alcohol is matured in oak barrels, and the amount that evaporates is called ‘the angel’s share.’”  In addition, you can learn about the history and culture of liquor while touring around the Beer Hall, Aqua Vitiate Hall, Tradition Hall, Korea Liquor Hall, and Fermentation Education and Science Hall. If looking around the exhibition halls is not enough for you, you might want to try some wine or make a cocktail yourself.

stories.title: Pungnyu Culture Center
stories.script: Pungnyu Culture Center   The Pungnyu Culture Center, inside a stylish hanok(traditional Korean house), is located in front of the quiet scenery of the Namhangang River. It is a place of relaxation and learning to recall the beauty and wisdom of the arts left by our ancestors in beautiful nature. Pungnyu refers to the enjoyment of tasteful activities that combine the elements of nature, life, and art.   Anyone visiting here can get a taste of pungnyu while looking at the gentle flow of the river and the low hills. It is also great to have some relaxing moments over a cup of healthy tea made with apple blossoms, the symbol of Chungju, or chrysanthemum, the flower of the city. You can also experience a tea ceremony where you can learn about the origins of tea, and the etiquette of making and drinking tea with an application in advance.  Various experience programs are also available. In the Writing a Family Motto corner, you can write a phrase that you want to let your descendants know or a lesson passed down from ancestors(called gahun, or family motto) or you can ask a calligrapher to write it for you. You can also try making traditional Korean cookies, tea confectionery, or playing traditional folk games such as tuho(throwing arrows), biseokchigi(hitting stone slabs), etc. However, since the programs available may vary depending on the season, it is recommended to check before visiting the Pungnyu Culture Center. Sitting with a brush and writing on traditional Korean paper will make you feel calm and relaxed both physically and mentally.

stories.title: Tangeum Lake International Rowing Regatta
stories.script: Tangeum Lake International Rowing Regatta   The Tangeum Lake International Rowing Regatta is next to the Namhangang River near Jungangtap Park, Chungju. Now is the time to enjoy the river and appreciate its magnificent views. Why not experience a one-day boat rowing session, moving through the waters of the Namhangang River?  The sport of rowing, propelling a boat with long oars, started in the UK in the 17th century. It’s a sport that is unfamiliar to Korean people. However, an easy and systematic program, which ordinary people can enjoy, is prepared in the Tangeum Lake International Rowing Regatta. In the one-day rowing program, theory education is conducted first and this is followed by rowing machine education and a water experience, and ends with physical exercise. After the theory education, you sit on a rowing machine and practice rowing for 20-30 minutes. The instrument panel shows the distance and the time required, so racing is possible with the rowing machine. After that, you set a boat afloat on the water and make a 500-meter round trip. Four people board a five-person racing board with an instructor.    It is not easy for several people work together and row in one direction, but it becomes an exciting memory. The one-day experience program, which will familiarize you with the sport of rowing, is conducted for free, and you can participate after making a reservation online.

stories.title: Changdong-ri Rock-carved Buddha
stories.script: Changdong-ri Rock-carved Buddha    There is a historic site on the road between Jungangtap Park and Tangeumdae Overlook & Park, the representative tourist attractions of Chungju that cannot be missed. It is the Rock-carved Buddha in Changdong-ri, Chungju. This standing Buddha carved into the rock cliff next to the Namhangang River is Chungcheongbuk-do Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 76.  From the location of the Buddha overlooking the Namhangang River, it is assumed that the sculpture was made to pray for the well-being of water transportation. It is thought to be a heritage of Goryeo(918-1392) in light of its sculpture type with a huge size, facial expression, and drapery of clothes. Although it has been partially damaged over the years, the round face exudes softness and gentleness. Also, the thin and long slanting eyes, broad nose, slightly retracted lips, and lengthy ears touching the shoulders are very impressive. To properly appreciate the Rock-carved Buddha, it is recommended to view it from a boat on the river.   After appreciating the sculpture, if you walk for 5 minutes from there, you will find the Changdong-ri Five-story Stone Pagoda and Standing Stone Medicine Buddha. They are also recommendable to view. Both of them are Chungcheongbuk-do tangible cultural heritages, thought to be works from the Goryeo period.

stories.title: Chungju Goguryeo Astronomical Science Museum
stories.script: Chungju Goguryeo Astronomical Science Museum   In Chungju, there is Chungju Goguryeo Astronomical Science Museum, where you can experience a longing for night sky and the secrets of the universe. From traditional astronomy, such as the visions of the universe of ancient people and world of astronomy during the Goguryeo period, to cutting-edge astronomical observation using digital devices, you can view various things. The museum has two stories. There is an exhibition room, audiovisual room and planetarium on the first floor and the main observatory and sub-observatory on the second floor.  There is a permanent exhibition of thousands of photos of the night sky in Chungju and neighboring areas in a room on the first floor. You cannot take your eyes off from them, as they are mysterious and beautiful. Also, the planetarium has a 360-degree screen, so you can view a virtual night sky along with explanations from the staff.  After the tour of the planetarium, shall we go upstairs now? There are the main observatory and a sub-observatory, and they are formed as a round dome and sliding dome, respectively. When the weather is nice, you can observe nebulas, clusters and the planets of our solar system through the large reflecting telescope and small auxiliary telescopes in the second-floor observatory. If you visit in the daytime, you can only see the sun, so it is recommended to visit there after sunset. Also, as the observation schedule differs a little every month, please check it on the web page before visiting.

stories.title: Chungju Happy Forest
stories.script: Chungju Happy Forest   The Chungju Happy Forest, located along the foot of Jajubongsan Mountain, is composed of recreational forests such as Moonsung Recreational Forest, Bonghwang Recreational Forest, and Gyemyeongsan Recreational Forest, an eco forest, and the Wood Cultural Experience Center. If you walk along the hiking trail on the lush forest path, you will feel that even your heart is green and clean. There are three hiking trails along the forest path in Moonsung Recreational Forest. You can choose from one-hour to two-hour courses according to your taste. If those courses are a little too much for you, why not take the monorail? You can also spend a night in a log cabin or an auto camping resort.  In addition, there are lots of things to enjoy. The Wood Cultural Experience Center consists of an exhibition building, which has exhibition room and 3D image room, and an experience building. There, you will find various wooden crafts and can have an experience making small items such as hairpins or brooches and furniture such as chairs or beds. The forest library, forest kindergarten and eco pond are built in the eco forest for children to get familiar with nature. In Small Mountain Spring, a meditation healing center, a unique forest culture experience with meditation is available. If you want more dynamic memories, how about flying through the forest like Tarzan on a zip-line?

stories.title: Binaegil Path and Binaeseom Island
stories.script: Binaegil Path and Binaeseom Island   Binaegil Path has a simple rural landscape and was listed among the “Top 10 Green Ways of Our Village” in 2012 by the Ministry of Public Administration and Security. Binaegil Path is composed of two zones, and the starting and ending points of both zones is Angseong Hot Springs Plaza.   Zone 1 of Binaegil Path is a friendly path, which takes 2 to 3 hours to walk, consisting of an unpaved path and bicycle road. Walking on the path in a leisurely manner, you will come across Byeoseulbawi Rock. It is known as a magical rock and scholars who wanted to enter government service used to come and pray in front of it. The highlight of Zone 1 is the path from Migratory Bird View Park to old Jodae Quay. You can walk on the path while viewing a beautiful landscape.  It takes 4 to 5 hours and 30 minutes to walk along Zone 2 of Binaegil Path. If you turn at the end of this zone, you will find Binaeseom Island. Thanks to its natural views, a lot of dramas were filmed on the island, such as “Jeong Do-jeon,” “Six Flying Dragons,” and “King Geunchogo.” If you enter Binaeseom Island following the words of guidance in “the seventh sight out of 36 sights of the Hangang River,” an abundance of silver grass comes into view. You should check the restriction period in advance before you visit. When you return to Angseong Hot Springs Plaza, the ending point, how about relieving the fatigue of your feet at Korea’s representative carbonate hot springs complex?

stories.title: Cheongnyongsa Temple Site
stories.script: Cheongnyongsa Temple Site   Cheongnyongsa Temple Site is the site of a temple that no longer exists, and is Chungju’s representative temple ruin site along with the Mireukdaewon Stone Temple Site. Cheongnyongsa Temple is thought to have been established in the late Goryeo period(918-1392). A folk tale is told that the temple was established in the place where a dragon came down from the sky to look for a magic pearl it had dropped.    Cheongnyongsa Temple Site is said to have been a small hermitage. After State Preceptor Bogak, who is known as the teacher of King Taejo(Yi Seong-gye), the first king of the Joseon Dynasty(1392-1910), retreated there, King Taejo built a large temple. Of course, since no traces of temple are left, it is difficult to tell what the temple looked like. However, only national treasures and gems you come across while walking on the silent forest path are valuable enough.  The Stupa of State Preceptor Bogak at Cheongnyongsa Temple Site in Chungju(National Treasure No. 197) is a pagoda that King Taejo built with the name “Jeonghyewonyung” when State Preceptor Bogak passed away. As it has an unusual form that is unlike the bell-shaped pagodas, which were prevalent in the Joseon Dynasty, its value is higher. There are also the Lion Stone Lantern in Front of the Stupa of State Preceptor Bogak at Cheongnyongsa Temple Site, Chungju(National Treasure No. 656) established for the repose of State Preceptor Bogak's soul in front of the pagoda, and the Stele for State Preceptor Bogak at Cheongnyongsa Temple Site, Chungju(National Treasure No. 658) behind the pagoda.

stories.title: Mokgye Quay
stories.script: Mokgye Quay   Mokgye Quay was the hub of water transportation trading at the Namhangang River long ago. As one of the top 5 river ports in the late Joseon Dynasty, it was major waterway connecting central inland area of Chungcheong-do, Gangwon-do and Gyeongsang-do with Seoul. It was a large inland port capable of holding about 100 merchant ships. Byeolsinje Ritual, at which people prayed for the success of the village, was held on a large scale here, and a lot of people gathered for it. Thus, a big market was held here.  However, the quay declined after Korail Chungbuk Line was opened and a road was developed in the 1920s, and it finally disappeared when Mokgyedaegyo Bridge was built in 1973. Now, a big standing stone with the words “Mokgye Quay” written on it and a poem carved in stone titled “Mokgye Market” by poet Sin Gyeong-rim commemorate the prosperous old days.   This place recently began to draw attention again as a tourist attraction in Chungju. It is because of the beautiful landscape created by rape flowers in spring and buckwheat flowers in fall. Also, the Mokgye Quay Culture Complex was built, and Mokgye market is revitalized, so a lot of tourists visit this place. You can look into history and meaning of Mokgye Quay and experience making a wish paper boat in the River Boat Experience Center. There are abundant exciting things to enjoy such as Mokgye Byeolsinje Ritual, which is held every year, where Byeolsingut(shamanistic ritual) and a tug of war are staged.

stories.title: Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral: Entrance
stories.audioTitle: Front of Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral
stories.script: Front of Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral   [Traveler] Hello!  The word ‘Maegoe’ from the name of Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral is composed of the Chinese characters for ‘rosario,’ which means rosary in English. It’s used in Catholicism and symbolizes the rose bouquet dedicated to the Virgin Mary. As its name indicates, this church, which has more than one hundred years of history, is dedicated to the Virgin Mary. The church was founded by Father Camille Bouillion from Lourdes, France, a town famous for an apparition of the Virgin. You can see a statue of the bearded priest holding his hat in front of the priest’s office built with red bricks. Inscribed below the statue are the words he always used to say.   [Bouillion] “I loved you long before I ever met you.”  [Traveler] After entering the clergy in 1893, Father Bouillion entered Korea to carry out missionary work. While searching for a location to build a church, he found just the spot he was looking for, but there was already an extravagant house there. The Father asked the townspeople who the owner of the house was. People told him that the house belonged to a family of the empress. So the Father had no choice but to give up on the location.   Soon after October 1895, there was a national tragedy in Korea. Japan assassinated the empress in order to gain control of Korea, and the big house that belonged to the family of the empress was also burned down. After hearing the news a little later, Father Bouillion acquired the land from the owner and built a small church there for temporary use.   As the small church attracted more and more believers, it was expanded through a number of reconstructions until it gained the appearance it has today.   Father Bouillion was French, but he loved Korea as much as any Korean. Maybe because of the Father’s endless love, an astounding miracle occurred in this church. I’ll tell you a couple of stories from the Korean War in the next file.

stories.title: Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral: Interior
stories.audioTitle: Interior of Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral
stories.script: Interior of Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral  [Traveler] : Inside the church, there’s a beautiful statue of the Virgin Mary from Lourdes, France. With her hands put together, the Virgin Mary looks as gracious as ever. On the clothes of the Virgin Mary, there are a number of black pits here and there. These are the seven bullet marks from the Korean War in 1950. The story takes place when a group of North Koreans invaded Eumseong, back in the days when South and North Koreans fought with each other.   A group of North Koreans decided to use the church as their command post. When they entered the church armed with guns, the glowing statue of the Virgin Mary greeted them. Although they didn’t understand the significance of the statue, they were overwhelmed by its solemn aura. But they looked away, and started to plan their attack on the town. They discussed how to steal food and hurt people. However, although they pretended everything was fine, the North Korean soldiers were becoming edgy. They couldn’t shake off the feeling that someone was watching them. So the North Korean major aimed his gun at the statue of the Blessed Virgin and pulled the trigger like a mad man.  Among the bullets shot by the North Korean soldiers, seven hit the statue of the Virgin Mary. But the statue, which is made of plaster, was only left with seven bullet marks, remaining intact. In the eyes of the scared North Korean soldiers, the statue of the Virgin Mary shed tears and turned her head. The soldiers screamed ‘Save us!’ and ran out of the church. Until they left this town, they couldn’t come close to the church. The bullet marks left by the scared North Korean soldiers remain in the statue of the Virgin Mary to this day.

stories.title: Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral: Virgin Mary Square
stories.script: Virgin Mary Square  [Traveler] The Japanese colonial era lasted from 1910 to 1945. On a summer’s day in1943, Father Bouillion witnessed Japanese troops walking up the mountain behind the church with some workers. Stricken with an ominous feeling, he followed them. There was a pile of wood and construction equipment in the middle of the mountain. When Father Bouillion asked what they were for, the Japanese answered that they were going to build a Japanese temple there. In order to sap the energy of the Korean land they’d invaded, the Japanese were building their temples everywhere. Father Bouillion fiercely opposed them, but they drove him away with guns and knives.   But the Father wouldn’t let them be. He left his priest’s office late at night and went up the mountain by himself. And he buried the Medal of the Miracle he’d received from his mother there. Shedding tears, he prayed to the Virgin Mary for protection.   The next day, the weather suddenly became violent.   There was heavy thunder and lightning every day, and an enormous amount of rain fell from the sky. The land prepared for construction of the temple was ruined. All the construction equipment was covered with mud, broken, or lost in the water. The Japanese army feared that it was a punishment from above, but they didn’t halt the construction work. More similar events followed. There was more flooding, hail storms assailed the workers, and the icy winter weather froze the ground. Finally, World War II ended. The construction of the temple had not progressed, and Korea was liberated.   The Japanese army left Korea. People believed that the priest’s prayers and the power of his medal had protected the location in the mountain behind the church. So they named the area Virgin Mary Square. Even today, the statue of the priest and a giant cross look upon the church from the top of the mountain.

stories.title: Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral: Maegoe Museum
stories.script: Maegoe Museum  [Traveler] During the Japanese colonial era, not only did Japan ruin Korea but it also stole everything that could help them with the war effort. In particular, they stole metal for use in the production of weapons. They also stole dishes, spoons, and chopsticks from civilian houses, and raided schools, temples, and churches. And this place wasn’t an exception.   After threatening the priest and the believers with their guns, the Japanese army went up to the bell tower of the church. Japanese soldiers forcefully removed the bells of the church, which were the St. Bernadette Bell, St. Maria Bell and the St. Therese of Lisieux Bell. The bells were treasures of the church that father Bouillion had brought with him from France. They were called the ‘three sister bells,’ and the locals loved and respected them. But the Japanese army loaded them onto a truck and dumped them into a smelting furnace.   The three sister bells were dumped into a burning furnace. But something incredible happened. Unlike other metals, the three sister bells didn’t melt. The Japanese troops were confused. When the rising temperature still didn’t melt the bell, the head of the Japanese unit took out the bells to break them with a hammer.   But no matter how hard they hammered them, the bells didn’t break. Infuriated, the Japanese buried the three sister bells in the ground.  The congregation of the church never gave up looking for the bells. At the very time of Korea’s liberation, they miraculously found the spot where the bells were buried. The believers went there themselves with shovels and dug up the ground, and the three sister bells were brought back to their home in the church.  Everyone shed tears of happiness. Unfortunately, the bells were damaged, showing cracks here and there. People did everything they could to repair the bells, but only the Bernadette bell regained its original sound.   The three sister bells didn’t lose their shape even in the burning furnace or under the hammer. Today, Bernadette, Maria, and Therese of Lisieux greet visitors to the church from the bell tower, on the 1st and 2nd floors of the museum.

stories.title: The Birthplace of General Kim Yu-sin
stories.audioTitle: The Birthplace of General Kim Yu-sin
stories.script: The Birthplace of General Kim Yu-sin 1  [Traveler] Born in this place, General Kim Yu-sin is one of the most famous military leaders in Korean history. He played a key role in the unification of three ancient Korean kingdoms.   He was born in 595 and thereafter devoted his life to winning the battles which led to the unification of the three ancient Korean kingdoms, namely, Silla, Baekje and Goguryeo. The three kingdoms fought against each other for over 700 years until their unification.  Few expected that Silla, the weakest of the three for much of that long period, would be the ultimate winner in the conflict for unification. General Kim Yu-sin was one of the few leaders who nurtured Silla’s strength to enable it to overpower its two rivals. History says that he was a brave fighter and outstanding strategist who left no record of defeat during his forty years as a battlefield commander.  His decisive role in Silla’s success in the unification of the early Korean kingdoms has been widely admired among the Korean people, and both his birthplace and his grave have been transformed into a major place of pilgrimage.
