The village you are currently visiting is where he was born and grew up. Before you stands a stone monument erected in his honor, and on your left is his birthplace, which was restored in 1983. The mountain behind his home contains a well used by his family during the period when his father served as a government official. And, on the peak of the mountain is a mound in which his placenta is buried.  Another interesting point is that his home was in Jincheon, a town situated about 200 km from Silla’s capital, although he was one of Silla’s most powerful political figures in the unification period. This is particularly interesting, given that Silla’s aristocrats at that time clung to the capital as it was the source of their power and wealth. The situation surrounding Kim Yu-sin at the time is closely related with the history of the three preceding generations of his family.  While Kim Yu-sin was a great warrior who obtained fame and power through his successive victories on the battlefield, he was always careful about his family background. The fact that he overcame his inferior social status using his own outstanding personal capabilities makes his life comparable to that of Julius Caesar.  History tells that he was born in a country which was later defeated and incorporated into Silla. His grandfather, the last king of the fallen country, surrendered to Silla and became a Silla aristocrat. However, he was ostracized by the Silla aristocracy because he had not been born in Silla. The fallen king felt that he needed to achieve distinguished exploits in battle to prove his loyalty to Silla and open up a new future for himself. He succeeded, and was eventually promoted to the highest position in government.  His remarkable success, however, did not prevent further discrimination. His son, that is, Kim Yu-sin’s father, came up with a new plan, and seduced a Silla princess. His behavior infuriated the Silla royals, who sent him into exile here, which was at the time a remote border area. Meanwhile, the Silla princess had fallen in love with the seducer and fled the palace to the border town, where she married him and gave birth to a boy who would later become General Kim Yu-sin.    Grown into a man of noble character and looks, Kim Yu-sin was admitted to his maternal grandmother as a royal offspring, but he could never remove the tag that he was a descendant of a foreign, ruined country. He had to repeat what his grandfather had done to be accepted by the Silla aristocracy; that is, fighting and winning victories for Silla. He continued to rush to the battlefield and brought numerous victories to Silla until he was 70. His spirit of self-sacrifice and devotion to the dynasty moved the Silla ruler to honor the general with a title and a position of the highest rank. These remarkable achievements made through three generations finally brought Kim Yu-sin what he and his ancestors had longed for.

stories.title: Jincheon Gilsang Shrine
stories.script: Gilsang Shrine  [Traveler] Surrounded by scenic landscapes with raining cherry blossoms in spring and golden ginkgo leaves in fall, Gilsang Shrine and the surrounding area has grown into one of the most popular tourist attractions in Korea. The shrine is also famous as a shrine honoring the life and achievements of the great Silla General Kim Yu-sin. The shrine is a venue for the ceremonies of honoring the general, which take place twice a year, in spring and fall.  Worshippers offer four deep bows to his funerary tablet at each ceremony because 160 years after his death, the king at the time praised his feats and loyalty and granted him the status of king. Kim Yu-sin is the only subject in Korean history to have been given a kingly title for his distinguished achievements. That this large building was built to honor only one man also attests to how great his achievements truly were.  The unification of the Korean kingdoms by Silla in the 7th century is widely regarded as one of the most significant events in Korean history. Silla enjoyed a golden age for about 300 years after the unification, which some historians compare with France under the rule of the Sun King Louis XIV. Historians say that as the capital of Silla, Gyeongju in the 8th century was one of the four largest cities in the world, along with Constantinople, Bagdad and Chang’an.  We are now at the top of the stairs of Gilsang Shrine, which is located at the highest point in the shrine’s precincts. Kept in the shrine is a portrait of General Kim Yu-sin in armor, with a long sword at his side. An interesting fact concerning the portrait is that it was made from the photos of 50 men selected from among the general’s descendants.

stories.title: Entrance (Botapsa Temple, Jincheon)
stories.script: "Entrance to Botapsa Temple  If you take a walk along the passages that wind about the gentle hills, you will see numerous treasures that are protected by the government. One of the nearest attractions is the birthplace of General Kim Yu-sin, who is widely regarded as one of the greatest figures in Korean history. There is a reservoir containing a piece of land whose shape is very similar to that of the Korean Peninsula and a bridge in the shape of a centipede. The key attraction in this area is, of course, Botapsa Temple.  The main entrance to the temple enshrines the statues of the Four Guardian Kings, although some regard the 300-year-old zelkova tree standing below the gate as a more reliable guardian. While the temple itself is much younger as it was only built in 1996, it is widely regarded as one of the finest architectural pieces of our time, as it was designed by some of Korea’s greatest architects. The temple’s pagoda was built to symbolize hopes for the Korean reunification and is regarded as a rare architectural jewel.   As we enter the temple, this site is surrounded by scenic mountain peaks and ridges and is thus said to resemble a lotus blossom. In spring, the area is filled with plants and flowers that bloom in diverse colors, and it looks like a flower bloomed within a larger flower. Visitors can enjoy such beautiful scenes because the temple and the surrounding area are taken care of by the temple’s Buddhist nuns. As with the Catholic tradition, Korean Buddhism does not allow monks and nuns to live in the same temple or monastery.  Before we visit the pagoda, which is the temple’s landmark monument, let’s go to a house containing a large temple bell 'beomjong' and a gong 'beopgo'. The house does not only have a bell and a drum, but it also has a wooden fish 'mogeo' and a bronze gong named 'unpan' in the shape of a cloud. They are Buddhist musical instruments that played for the salvation of all suffering beings. They are played not just for human beings but for other creatures as well. The bell is sounded for mankind, the drum is beaten for field animals, the wooden gong for fish, and the cloud chime for birds. The instruments represent the Buddhist tradition of respecting all living things on earth.  These instruments are played daily before and during the morning and evening prayer session. They create sounds that help all the creatures of this world to alleviate their suffering and spend each day in peace and harmony. This explains why the Buddhist bell is hung so low. It helps spread the sound deep and wide. You may compare it with Christian church bells, which are hung high up in lofty bell towers so that their sound reaches heaven easily.   Why not participate in a temple stay program at Botapsa Temple and enjoy a rare opportunity to hear the superb sound of the temple bell spreading deep and wide like thick fog in the depths of the night. "

stories.title: Botap Temple: Wooden Pagoda
stories.script: Wooden Pagoda of Botap Temple   [Traveler] You have now arrived at the tall wooden pagoda that has held your attention all the way here. Let’s walk upstairs, and before you take off your shoes, why don’t you walk in a slow circle around the pagoda?  Although it’s only a three-story building, it looks quite tall. The Botap Temple is in fact 42.7 meters tall, the height of an ordinary 14-story building. It can’t have been easy to build such a tall building using timber alone. More remarkably, all that woodwork was erected without using any nails. Instead, the builders used various traditional joinery techniques developed for the construction of traditional Korean homes. The use of such techniques helped prevent the timber from corroding and twisting.  The construction of this pagoda was carried out by master builders who were the leaders in their fields. Accordingly, all the features of the building display the characteristic style of Korean architectural masterpieces. If you look at the areas under the eaves, for instance, you will notice they are lavishly decorated with complex colored patterns. These patterns, known as dancheong, have long been an important element of Korean architecture, and are generally used for the decoration of ceilings and columns of temple and palace buildings. The decoration of the ceiling of this pagoda was completed after a 100-day project carried out by a 72-year-old master artist. It was his last work and, quite naturally, one of the greatest works of its kind. 	 Well, we’ve now gone full circle around the pagoda. Didn’t you notice something extraordinary around the building? That’s right. The pagoda has many name plaques each hung on each side of each floor. Why did they need so many different names for a single building? You may find the reason inside the pagoda. So, aren’t you curious about what the inside will be like? Let’s go in.  As you walk up, look closely at the top of the stone steps, where you will see elaborately carved lotus blossoms on each of them. The lotus blossom is a symbol of the Buddha’s enlightenment. The lotus carvings on the stairs suggest that you need to prepare yourselves as you step on them to gain enlightenment in the world of Buddha.

stories.title: Botap Temple: First Floor
stories.audioTitle: First Floor of the Botap Pagoda
stories.script: First Floor of the Botap Pagoda  [Traveler] The first thing you should notice inside the pagoda is the column standing at the center of the hall. There are 999 white porcelain pagodas arranged around it. What makes the column a major attraction is that it enshrines the relics of the Shakyamuni Buddha, who was sent to Korea from Sri Lanka. A pagoda, as you may already know, was originally a structure built to enshrine sariras - the pearl-like relics left over after the cremation of a Buddha or Buddhist saint.     You can also see four golden Buddha statues arranged around the column, looking out in all four directions. The Buddhas face the four cardinal directions, and represent the Buddhist vision of the creation of a Buddhist country run according to Buddhist teachings. Some see the arrangement of the Buddhas as a symbol of the wishes of the Korean people for the reunification of the divided Koreas.   Let’s now take a look at the Buddhas one by one. Unlike Christianity, which is a monotheistic religion, Buddhism venerates many saints who became Buddhas by attaining enlightenment. The statue facing the courtyard is the temple’s principal Buddha, Shakyamuni, while the one on his left, in the west, is Amitabha, who created the Land of Bliss, the Buddhist utopia. The statue in the north is Vairocana, who represents wisdom, and the fourth one, in the east, is the Medicine Buddha. His worshippers still practice the age-old tradition of offering him 100 watermelons in the 4th lunar month of every year. What is amazing is that the watermelons offered to the Medicine Buddha are shared by the worshippers in December. The sharing of the watermelon during wintertime has now become the most famous celebratory event held at the temple. Isn’t it amazing that the fruit can retain its freshness for almost half a year? I’d like to cut one open and see if it really is still fresh.   Do you remember the name plaques hung on all four sides of the pagoda? The names are related with these Buddha statues. Likewise, the names reflect the characteristic features of each storey  Let’s go upstairs. This is the only wooden pagoda in Korea with stairs built inside it. The stairs also display the technical excellence of a master builder. By the way, be careful not to slip, for the steps are very steep.

stories.title: Botap Temple: Second Floor
stories.script: Second Floor of Botap Pagoda  [Traveler] While the pagoda’s first floor is devoted to Buddhas in general, the second floor is made for the Buddha’s teachings. The hall is packed with the Buddhist scriptures. Just as the Bible is the basis for the teachings of Christianity, so are the Buddhist scriptures for the teachings of Buddhism. The Buddhist teachings have traditionally been regarded as one of the Three Treasures of Buddhism.  The green book cabinet at the center of the room contains a Korean translation of the Tripitaka Koreana, whose original edition, printed in 1236, is now a UNESCO World Heritage. The scriptures were carved on over 80,000 woodblocks, taking 16 years to complete. The carving techniques as well as the calligraphic scripts of the woodblocks have been widely praised for their artistic excellence. The original woodblocks are currently stored in Haein Temple in South Gyeongsang Province.  Was this vast collection of Buddhist scriptures put here to be read by visitors? Probably not! You can see that the circular book cabinet is designed to be turned. According to tradition, you will be regarded as having read all the scriptures in it if you spin it repeatedly, and the scripture reading will grant you a magical power that will protect you against evil and see your prayers fulfilled. They say that the object was invented in the past when ordinary people were not educated to read and write. 	 Let’s now go to the third floor. I’ll tell you a secret about this pagoda before we get there. The pagoda looks like a three-story building but, in fact, it is a five-story structure because there are two hidden floors between the stories. The hidden floors are designed to give a more stable structure to the pagoda by fitting the inner structure to its outer appearance. The secret floor between the 2nd and 3rd stories is open to the public as a museum specializing in pagodas of the world.

stories.title: Botap Temple: Third Floor
stories.script: Third Floor of Botap Pagoda  [Traveler] Now you are on the third floor of the pagoda. What is its purpose, you may wonder? Oh, there are some Buddhist images, of course, all facing in a single direction. You may think that the ones in here are the same as those you saw on the first floor. But the Buddha enshrined in here is the Maitreya. All the hanging plaques on the third story also show that this hall is devoted to him.   The statue flanked by two assistants is Maitreya, the Buddhist messiah who will rule the future. The Buddha was worshipped widely among the common people in Korea and therefore almost all the villages and towns across Korea once had one or more stone statues in them. The promise of a better future was a great comfort to the common people, who led hard lives. Interestingly, some experts argue that the name Maitreya has the same origin as that of Messiah, the Christian savior.    Hold on! It’s too early to leave yet, because the landscapes you can see from here are too good to miss. Go out through the open doors in all four directions, and then walk around the pagoda while admiring the stunning landscapes surrounding it. Waves of mountain peaks will gently cover your spirit like a serene lotus blossom. If you find the doors closed, why don’t you leave the pagoda and go to the stairs behind the stone lantern, as it will also offer you a good vantage point from which to view the fine landscapes.

stories.title: Botap Temple: Yeongsan Hall
stories.script: Yeongsan Hall  [Traveler] Let’s move on to the dainty octagonal building on the right. (E – sound of footsteps) First you should see an ordinary gilt Buddha statue, but then you will notice that the room is so tightly packed with tiny figurines, it looks like a can of sardines. Has the Buddha been besieged by evil forces?   Of course not! It represents a historic event in which Buddha Shakyamuni gave a sermon to 500 of his followers gathered on a holy mountain. The name, Yeongsan Hall, literally means “Hall of the Holy Mountain,” and it was derived from that event. The famous historic event has been honored in numerous paintings and drawings in the Korean Buddhist community, but here the event is represented by the art of sculpture.   The people seated closest to Shakyamuni Buddha are his Ten Disciples, who are in turn surrounded by 526 saints who attained enlightenment through ascetic practices. Interestingly, all these figurines are arranged to look in different directions. By the way, did your eyes meet the eyes of any of the figurines? If you did, the first one whose eyes met yours is your guardian.

stories.title: Botap Temple: Stone Monument of Yeongok-ri
stories.script: Stone Monument of Yeongok-ri  [Traveler] Didn’t you think that this particular stone monument stands out from all the others? If you did, it was probably because it is much older than the others. It has been worn away by hundreds of years, but the decorations on the monument clearly display the excellent skills of the stone carver. The nine dragons with magic pearls in their mouths carved on the capstone are vividly rendered to exhibit a dynamic movement, as if they might fly into the air at any moment. The turtle pedestal is also elaborately carved down to the minutest details.  What makes this monument so special is, more than anything else, its body. The monument has been given the nickname of “White Stele” because, remarkably, no inscriptions were ever engraved on its surfaces. No one knows whether it bore no inscription from the start or whether inscriptions were somehow removed.  The blank surfaces of the monument tend to incite viewers to think about its background. What made the builders of the monument decorate it so elaborately and then decide to inscribe nothing upon it? Was it some unrequited love, or the remorse of a child who had failed to fulfill its filial duty to its parents? Try to create your own story about this extraordinary memorial stone.

stories.title: Botap Temple: Sansin Shrine
stories.script: Sansin Shrine  [Treveler] Being here now, you are among those who are fortunate enough to be able to enjoy all the hidden beauties of the temple, because this Sansin Shrine is located at its remotest part. Let’s go in and see what’s inside.  Ah, there is no Buddhist image in this room. There is instead a portrait of an old man suspended above the altar. What does it mean, you may wonder? Well, it means that Sansin Shrine was devoted not to a Buddha or a Buddhist saint but to a mountain deity. The old man in the portrait represents the kind of mountain spirit worshipped by the Korean people since even before the arrival of Buddhism in Korea.  How, then, did they come to honor this native deity at a Buddhist sanctuary? Early Buddhists in Korea realized that they, as the worshippers of a foreign religion, would need to establish a harmonious relationship with the Korean native religion in their efforts to spread Buddhist teachings more effectively. They accepted shrines for Korean native gods and goddesses as part of the Buddhist institution. It helped Buddhism to become firmly rooted in the hearts of the Korean people.  Now you may start to understand the identity of the old man in the portrait. What about the tiger, then, which seems to be snuggled up in the old man’s arms like a pet? It has a funny face that makes it look more like a household cat. There were many tigers in the Korean mountains in the past, and the Korean people regarded the animal as an incarnation of the mountain god. That explains why it always appears with the old man in portraits of the mountain god. The tiger in Korea has never been portrayed or regarded as a ferocious killer beast but as a friendly guardian who protects us from evil.

stories.title: Botap Temple: Jeokjo Hall
stories.script: Jeokjo Hall  [Traveler] What! A Hollywood star was here? We can see a footprint on the floor in front of this building.That’s right, it is the Buddha’s footprint. Carving the Buddha’s footprint is an expression of honor towards Shakyamuni Buddha, who never stopped walking to guide humankind to enlightenment. There are fish in the sunken part of the sole which symbolize fertility and prosperity. The print of a wheel beside it symbolizes the Buddha’s teachings, as it continues turning to break down the bonds of ignorance.  Let’s take a look at the inside of Jeokjo Hall above the stairs. Oh, there is a recumbent Buddha. Is he tired because he has had to work for humanity 24 hours a day, 7 days a week?  The truth is that it represents the Buddha after his attainment of nirvana, that is, after his physical death in this world. The word ‘nirvana’ originally meant ‘blowing out’. Blowing out what, you may well ask? Blowing out the lights of greed, obsession, and agony! That is why he looks so comfortable, so calm. The landscape unfolding behind him is Kushinagar, the Indian village where Shakyamuni entered nirvana.  Now, why don’t you look up at the ceiling of the hall, where a scene of the Buddhist land of bliss will unfold before your eyes? Can you see the five dragons intertwined amongst each other, the blue birds, and the heavenly maids playing pipes while they fly through the air? They represent the utopian world of Buddhism. For Buddhists, who believe in the cycle of life and death, rebirth in this blissful land is the happiest result of their life and death.

stories.title: Jeungpyeong Folk Museum
stories.script: In front of the Museum  [Traveler] Welcome to our museum! This museum features exhibits and experience corners where you can learn about and experience Korea’s traditional rural cultures. In Hall No. 1, located in front of the parking lot, you can learn about agricultural folksongs and try playing some traditional Korean instruments. Every second week of June, the villagers hold a festival in the vicinity of the museum and invite visitors to attend. The festival features planting rice in the local paddies, and ploughing fields with oxen. Of course, tourists are welcome to join in these events. You can also catch mud snails and dig up potatoes. Since experienced farmers are ready to help, this is your chance to try your hands at farming.    Hall No. 2 features a collection of folk dolls from all around the world. Some 700 dolls from about 100 countries are displayed here. Each doll is pretty and unique. Korean blacksmith’s tools and a variety of ancient weapons are also exhibited in Hall No. 2.   Hall No. 3 exhibits native materials. Over 90 percent of them were donated by local residents. Another corner showcases the four-season farming, and ancient market places and other agriculture-related items.  After taking a tour of the museum, you can take a look at the Buddha images that are believed to guard Jeungpyeong Village. This tangible cultural heritage was discovered at a temple site. The Buddha images were thought to serve as guardians of the village. First, you will see the Namha-ri Stone Maitreya Bodhisattva next to the museum. The other Buddha images are a 10-minutes drive away from here. These Buddhas are not elaborate or fancy, rather they are a bit old but give off a friendly aura. Shall we go to meet the Namha-ri Stone Maitreya Bodhisattva?

stories.title: Buddha Sculptures of the Town: Maitreya
stories.script: Maitreya Bodhisattva  [Traveller] These three stone Buddhas standing in the field are wearing a smile. They are like three close brothers, and appear to be gazing towards a far view. The tallest Buddha is the Maitreya Bodhisattva, who could be compared to the Christian Messiah. He is said to come to this world 5.7 billion years later to save the people. Bodhisattva means “an enlightened man who leads people to the right way in order to save them.”   Bodhisattva can be distinguished from the Buddha by his ornate crown, bracelets and necklaces. You see that this Bodhisattva is wearing a jewel crown and bracelets. The long crown has grooves carved on both sides, and ornaments appear to have been studded into them. The neck shows three lines of wrinkles, which symbolize the process of people repeating their lives. The carved hair between the eyebrows is believed to have the power to see the past, present and future. The left hand, which is holding a lotus flower, is cautiously placed on the heart.    These images are believed to have been sculpted between the 10th and 14th centuries. Over time, they have been damaged in various parts, but they still exude a gentle ambiance and have a kind smile of a guardian deity.   In the next course, you will see Buddhas from the temple site. It takes seven minutes by car to get there.

stories.title: Buddha Sculptures of the Town: Rock-carved
stories.script: Rock-carved Buddhas  [Traveler] Just as many unique relics have been found at ancient temple sites, rock-carved Buddhas can be seen at this temple site. These Buddhas were carved on the broad surface of rocks. They are believed to have been crafted sometime between the 9th and early 10th centuries, and have consequently been worn down by wind and rain over the centuries.   The carved Buddha in the middle stands 3 meters tall. On both its sides you can see the Bodhisattvas, who were Buddha's assistants.   On the right face of the large rock there is a carved Buddha, although it is not very clear. On the triangle-shaped rock, to the left of the big rock, a Buddha sits on a lotus flower with its legs crossed, and as if in deep thought. This carving is also not too easy to see.  A square well was carved around the central Buddha. Lit candles and small bowls are placed near it, showing that people still come here pray to Buddha. Although the carved Buddha is not clearly visible, it has long remained a place of worship.   Korean people have followed the Buddhist faith for many centuries. In the past, they sought comfort from the religion when they experienced such difficulties as poverty and disease. Buddhist temples were places where people sought comfort, much like Christian churches. The presence of so many Buddha images in the vicinity of this small village tends to confirm that.   Next, we will go to see the Miam-ri Temple Site, which is about 15 minutes away by car.

stories.title: Buddha Sculptures of the Town: Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva
stories.script: Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva  [Traveler] Standing near to the Bodhisattva image is a gigantic zelkova tree which is over 300 years old. In the vicinity stands a stone Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva image which is even older than the tree. Avalokiteśvara and Maitreya are the most beloved figures of Buddhism. Maitreya symbolizes future salvation, while Avalokiteśvara is believed to save people from the pain and suffering of the real world.   Let’s study the stone Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva image. It is wearing a jewel crown, its body is a little fat, and its neck is carved with three lines. Although not clearly visible, a single hair, which is said to have mysterious power, can be seen between the eyebrows. The right hand is raised with the palm facing outwards, while the left hand is placed on the upper part of the abdomen. Judging by the sculpting technique, the image is believed to have been crafted somewhere between the 10th and 14th century.    Every New Year’s Day, the villagers hold a rite before the stone Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to pray for its mercy. This gigantic old zelkova tree and the stone Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva must be very precious to the villagers.    Now we will move on to Gwangdeok Temple. It takes about 15 minutes by car.

stories.title: Standing Stone Buddha of Gwangdeok Temple
stories.audioTitle: Standing Stone Buddha of Gwangdeok Temple
stories.script: Standing Stone Buddha of Gwangdeok Temple  [Traveler] Gwangdeok Temple, standing next to the stone Buddha, was built in 1949. The temple was named after the village after a monk dreamed an auspicious dream about the stone Buddha.   This majestic-looking stone Buddha stands on a pedestal festooned with lotus flowers. The pedestal is 83 cm tall, and the Buddha is an imposing 4 m tall. Judging by the sculpture technique, it appears to have been crafted around the 10th century. The Buddha has a high nose and big ears, and its eyes appear to be gazing towards a far away place. The Buddha appears to be conversing deeply with the opposite mountain.   This Buddha was made from granite, and shows signs of wear. To prevent further cracking in the neck and head, strong ropes have been wrapped around.

stories.title: Sanmagi Trail: Entrance
stories.audioTitle: In Front of the Guide Panel
stories.script: In Front of the Guide Panel  [Traveler] Welcome. What you see here is a map of the trail from Saorang Village to Sanmagi Village. There are plenty of things to see on all corner of this trail, and there are also many seasonal delights to savor.   Sanmagi Village was an ordinary mountain village until 1957, when Goesan Dam was constructed and a part of the village was submerged beneath Goesan Lake. Because not enough people lived Sanmagi to run a boat across the lake, a narrow trail was naturally formed along the lake. Villagers would go through this narrow trail to go to the market or go visit friends across the lake.   What you are about to experience is the narrow road that was created fifty years ago. With an increasing number of visitors, villagers reinforced the path with wooden boards, making the trail safe. To your left, the glittering lake is just at your finger tips, and to your right are green tree branches of the mountain forest. The more you walk, the stronger and healthier you will feel.   If you take your time to enjoy Nature, it'll take about 2 hours to walk the trail and come back. There are various rest areas on the way, so there's no need to worry. There are a total of 26 attractions, and all are very close to the trail. The elevated bridge that passes through the pine forest is popular among young hikers. You can look down to Goesan Lake from the 40-meter high observatory, and you can also quench your thirst at the Nanjaengi Mineral Spring. The next bathroom is at the village, so if you have to go to the bathroom, make sure you go we leave.

stories.title: Sanmagi Trail: Pine Tree Hill
stories.script: Pine Tree Hill  [Traveler] A dense pine forest covers a 33,000 square meter area. Put your hands around the trunk and breathe with the tree. You will feel cleansed from head to toe.   Pine trees release a great amount of phytoncide. I'm sure you've heard of the benefits of phytoncide, right? “Phython” means plant, and “cide” means ‘to sterilize’ therefore phytoncide is a sterilizing agent the tree emits to protect itself from harm. You know the smell of freshly mown lawn, or of a broken tree branch? Well, that is the scent plants release as a defense mechanism. It is the result of millions of years of evolution that cannot be replicated with our technology. Research has shown that this substance is very good for the human immune system too. All you have to do is breathe in and breath out, breathe in and breath out. It not only enhances your immune system but it also decreases stress hormones in your body. And what is more surprising is that it is as beneficial if not better than antibiotics we may find at the pharmacy. This is a natural antibiotic without any side effects.   Aside from all the phytoncide we get to breath in, isn’t it so nice to walk under the shade of these trees? Look far away into the distance and let your eyes rest. Release all the stress and polluted air you took in from the city and breathe in as much freshness from these trees as possible. You will notice your body feel much lighter as we continue our hike.

stories.title: Sanmagi Trail: Lake Observatory
stories.script: Lake Observatory  [Traveler] This is the lake observatory, and it floats on the tranquil waters of Goesan Lake. From here it looks as if the mountain is embracing the lake. You can also see Goesan Dam from here, and as I also told you before, this path was built because the dam submerged parts of the village.   Goesan Dam was the first dam to have been built using Korean technology, complete with the smallest hydroelectric generator. It was built after the Korean War to strengthen the devastated power infrastructure. Back then, only big cities and towns had electricity, and even that was until midnight only. Building a dam was a major project, and due to its size and scale, construction was often put on hold. Korea’s first president visited attended the opening event, and it became a popular field trip destination for students for many years to come. However, with the construction of a much bigger dam nearby, Goesan Dam became less and less popular, but it still remains Korea’s first dam.   Sanmagi Village has become isolated from the local network of villages since the construction of the dam. When parts of the town were submerged under the lake, most residents moved away, but a few chose to remain in their hometown. With a mountain behind and a lake in the front, the winding path along lake was their only way out of the village. The path was often very lonely and dangerous, but with an increasing number of tourists and facilities, it has gradually transformed to a rejuvenating hiking trail.  Now that you know the history of Goesan Dam, do you feel any differently about it? A dam built to supply power, locals leaving because of its inconvenience, and then gradually making a tourist attraction out of the once dangerous winding path. The joy and pain of the locals can be felt through the story of the dam.   Now, we are heading to our last stop, which is the Exile House of Roh Su-sin. You will feel quite hungry by the time we get there, but don’t worry. The kind residents of Sanmagi Village will have prepared delicious dishes for us. Don’t forget to look for unique rock formations and trees on the way there!

stories.title: Sanmagi Trail: Roh Su-sin’s House of Exile
stories.script: Roh Su-sin’s House of Exile  [Traveler] Roh Su-sin was a scholar who lived in the 16th century. He made his debut in politics at the age of twenty-nine, and was praised for his competence during his period of service, but was ousted by the powers that controlled the Joseon Dynasty. He was exiled to an isolated town where he lived for twenty-three long years.   The Joseon Dynasty lasted for six centuries, until the beginning of the 20th century. In those times a common form of punishment was exile. The sentence was usually passed to eliminate officials who failed to adjust to the harsh power struggles between the various factions. The king, being reluctant to kill nobles, sent them far away from the capital. They had to live in isolated villages where they would wait, sometimes for many years, for the king to summon them once more. But unlike what most people might think, life in isolation was not always bad. For many scholars who had lived busy and hectic lives, it was a chance to read in peace and silence. Poems and writings by exiled nobles constitute a major genre in Joseon literature. Roh Su-sin was sent from village to village where he continued his studies. After twenty years of roaming, he was finally reinstated. Later, he made his way to the highest government post in Joseon. All this was possible because he continued to study despite the seemingly hopeless conditions.   This house is the last place he stayed in during his time of exile. Shall we go in?.  The house is a bit rugged , but can you see the wooden board inscribed with Chinese characters hanging under the roof? From right to left, each character represents water, moon, and pavilion. It means that the only things you can see from here are the moon and water. There is a wood-floored space separating two rooms: one was for Roh Su-sin, while the other was for his servant.

stories.title: Hwayang Valley: Entrance
stories.script: Towards the Valley  [Visitor] This valley, where an abundance of cold, clear water flows, is called Hwayang Valley. It is also a popular summer resort. Besides the clear water of the valley, there are other nine tourist attractions that are worth seeing. This place was selected by Song Si-yeol, who has had a huge impact on Confucianism and politics in Korea since the 17th century.  Song Si-yeol, the top politician of his day, wrote a large number of books and achieved excellent academic results. Also, a lot of his disciples entered government services, so he was very influential in the political sphere. In particular, his name appears over three thousand times in The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, which has recorded the 500-year history of the Joseon Dynasty, and historically speaking it’s hard to find a comparison. Therefore, he is sometimes likened to the Confucius of Korea. He was a teacher of King Hyojong, the 17th King of the Joseon Dynasty, as well as a supporter and a faithful servant of the King. In a history book, it was recorded that a close relationship between the King and the servant was recognized.    However, he was famous for his stubborn character, and when he thought he was right, he never compromised. Thus, when he was in government service, there was often friction between him and the King, which resulted in him being exiled several times. Eventually, he died insisting on the principle regarding the succession to the 18th throne of Joseon.  He studied and taught his disciples while staying here, and visited this place 23 times. Then, in his late 60s, he settled down here while filled with anguish about a crisis following the death of the King.   It takes about one and a half hours to look around the nine attractions and their beautiful landscapes. The first attraction, Gyeongcheon Cliff, is located slightly to the rear of the parking lot. After getting off the bus, walk back a bit to the road you came along. You will see the fantastic site of the cliffs supporting the sky.

stories.title: Hwayang Valley: The 3rd Valley, Eupgung Rock
stories.script: The 3rd Valley, Eupgung Rock  [Visitor] In this valley there is a memorial monument representing Song Si-yeol’s thoughts. It is presumed that our ancestors erected the stone to tell us of the event. This monument was found here in 2010.  There are white flat rocks just below the memorial monument, and in these rock  is a story about Song Si-yeol. Song served the 17th King of Joseon, and after the King passed away, he would come to this rock every morning and cry in grief, bent on the ground with his back hunched like the bow of an arrow. And this is why the rock is called “Eupgung,” meaning “crying bow.”  Song experienced as many ups and downs in his life as he received great honors. Upon seeing the prince, who had also been a disciple of his, being taken hostage by China after losing a war, he resigned from government service and concentrated on his studies. After the prince came back and ascended the throne, he prepared for war to avenge the indignity he had suffered in the past, but his plan was annulled when the King passed away.  He wrote poems here while in great grief. Can you feel the depth of his despair? Now, shall we continue learning about his story on the next course?

stories.title: Hwayang Valley: Hwayang Confucian School
stories.script: Hwayang Confucian School  [Visitor] Song Si-yeol underwent several crises due to friction with the 18th King of the dynasty, and was eventually executed by the King. Six years later, he was proven innocent and his honor was restored. Later, temples and Confucian facilities were built around the country in memory of Song, of which the most representative is Hwayang Confucian School. Here, many students of Confucianism continued to respect Song Si-yeol’s studies and pursued their learning.  Specially important of this school is the shrine located on the highest point of the school, which was built according to Song’s wishes. The stairway leading to the shrine are very steep and can barely fit one foot. Even these stairs contain Song’s philosophy of concentrating while going up the stairs.   The memorial service for the Chinese Ming Dynasty’s last emperor and his servants, who supported Joseon during the Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1592, used to be held at this shrine by national support. When the memorial service was held, scholars from around the country would gather and join the services. Additionally, disciples of Song kept his memorial tablet in this shrine and conducted memorial services for him every year.  Thus, the Hwayang Confucian School had a powerful influence on the local society, but with the passing of time it became corrupt and persecuted the people. So it was forced to close by a later king. During the Japanese Colonial period, it suffered the indignity of its memorial monument being buried. However, after remaining buried for quite some time, the monument dug up again, and we can now see traces of Korean traditional Confucianism before our eyes.

stories.title: The 4th Valley, Amseojae House (Hwayanggugok Valley)
stories.script: The 4th Valley, Amseojae House  The building standing on the shimmering rock in harmony with the golden sand under the water is called Amseojae House, it was used as Song Si-yeol’s study and his villa. This building has the best location among the nine sites selected by him. If you sit on the ground and look down, you will see a splendid view of clean waters crashing against the rocks, and, if you look upwards, there is a great view of the mountains.  As mentioned, this is where Song stayed, so there are many writings engraved on rocks. At that time, the Chinese Ming Dynasty, which had a close relationship with Joseon, was helpless against attacks from a newly emerging power on mainland China, the Ching Dynasty. Joseon supported Ming Dynasty, which was a Confucian country like Joseon, and regarded Ching as an uncivilized country. As if to prove the friendly relationship between Ming and Joseon, the King of the Ming Dynasty sent a signboard to Joseon that he had personally written. That signboard hangs here in this building, and there is also a poem here written by Song Si-yeol, that contains lines about worshipping Ming but boycotting Ching.  After Hyojong, the 17th King of Joseon passed away, Song could not get close to the 18th King Hyeonjong, so he left government service for a while and stayed here. He probably let go of all his troubles and worries and enjoyed his time here as a commoner. There are still five more wonderful sights left to see, so let’s take a break here as Song Si-yeol did.

stories.title: Hwayang Valley: Chaeun Temple
stories.script: Chaeun Temple  [Visitor] The temple you are looking around now is called Chaeun Temple. It was built by the Seon Priest Doil during the Goryeo era in 1277, and was later combined with Hwanjang Temple, which was built by Song Si-yeol in 1655.  The temple built by Song Si-yeol was designed to keep the writings sent from the Ming Dynasty. Some time thereafter, an auxiliary building was built beside the temple owing to the increasing amount of books written by Song Si-yeol, the growing body of documents of the King, and so on. In addition, another building for storing relics was built between Hwanjang Temple and Song’s villa. However, no traces of those buildings remain. When soldiers who fought against the Japanese invasion stayed here, the Japanese army attacked and set fire to eight of the buildings. Only the main building of the temple, where a statue of the Buddha was enshrined, survived the conflagration.  Meanwhile, Chaeun Temple, which was located around Domyeong Mountain, was badly damaged by a flood. Locals felt bad for the loss and decided to build a new temple by combining two temples. The people built a residence for the monks right next to Hwanjang Temple, and they also named the new temple ‘Chaeun Temple’. With this, the two historical temples were joined together as if to support each other, and their peaceful spirits were restored.

stories.title: The 5th Valley, Cheomseongdae Observatory (Hwayanggugok Valley)
stories.script: The 5th Valley, Cheomseongdae Observatory  At the entrance of Domyeongsan Mountain, there is “Cheomseongdae,” a tower of huge rocks cut into pieces and it boasts a magnificent view. The name was given to mean “Observatory where people could see the stars from atop a rock piled up.” It is somewhat different from how Western people observed stars through a telescope. However, it is a place where you can feel our ancestors' desire to research and study the stars.  There are as many writings engraved on Cheomseongdae as anywhere else. For example, a writing by Song Si-yeol illustrated the political relation between Joseon and Ming Dynasty at that time.   Besides, there is another writing that took reference from the work of a Ming Dynasty’s servant. The interpretation of such writing is “A King should be as clean as a jar for ice cubes; Joseon should be loyal to the Ming Dynasty.”   Also, King Seonjo engraved the words in gratitude to Ming Dynasty for sending reinforcements during the Imjinwaeran (the Japanese Invasion of Korea), stating, 'Even though the Yellow River in China bends and turns over ten thousand times, it always flows eastward.'  While you are enjoying the refreshing atmosphere here in Hwayanggugok Valley, don’t forget to check out the Cheomseongdae!

stories.title: Hwayang Valley: The 9th Valley, Pacheon
stories.script: The 9th Valley, Pacheon  [Visitor] Pacheon is located in the highest region among the other nine attractions. This place is called “Pacheon” because of the waters of the valley flow vigorous between white rocks.  One reason why Song Si-yeol stayed here was because he was so greatly charmed by the surroundings. This valley has many good qualities including clear water, strong waterflow, and a peaceful atmosphere. The surfaces of the stones are soft enough to walk on. The bubbles foaming on the stones look as if they were washing away the fatigue and color of the people. This valley is the perfect place for the grand finale of the nine attractions.  You’ve now seen all nine of the attractions. Unlike the beautiful scenery, the attractions contain the sadness of history, but I hope you feel refreshed after seeing the mountain, rocks and valley water.

stories.title: Sangdang Fortress: On the Way to the Gate
stories.audioTitle: On the Way to the Gate
stories.script: On the Way to the Gate   [Traveler] Welcome to Sangdang Fortress, a symbolic site of North Chungcheong Province. This mountain fortress serves as a place of relaxation for many Chungju citizens and is a hotspot where various historical dramas have been filmed. Today, the 4.2-km-long fortress trail is open to citizens who want to take a walk, but the original purpose of this fortress was to prevent enemies during war.  European countries or Japan usually built their fortresses on plains with moats and waterways around them as a defensive measure. However, Korea has a lot of mountains that served as refuges for the king and his citizens. They fought off enemies from the mountaintop. This kind of history led to the country being described as “a nation of fortresses.”  Sangdang Fortress, which you are about to enter, has gates on the east, west and south. The northern gate was omitted because the steep slope of the mountain acted as a natural defense mechanism. This fortress was situated at an important crossroads in the central plain, and was successively ruled by Baekje, Goguryo and Silla. The large number of relics discovered in the area indicates the importance and value of this location.  Then, let’s go to the first gate, Gongnam Gate, and find out what treasures are hidden there.

stories.title: Sangdang Fortress: Gongnam Gate on the South
stories.script: Gongnam Gate on the South  [Traveler] More than 70 % of the Korean peninsula is mountainous, so fortresses were built at all strategic points. Whenever a war broke out, the people from the surrounding towns and villages were evacuated to the fortresses, where they lived on food stored there in advance until the enemies abandoned their siege. Each fortress had its own town and reservoir, so the people had no worries about food. Throughout Korea’s war-torn history, such fortresses were very valuable to kings and their people.   Sangdang Fortress was built in the Baekje Period, which lasted from 18 B.C. to 660 A.D. The original wall was made of dirt, but after recognizing its importance during the Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1592, the walls were re-built with stones. When you look at the fortress from high ground, it displays soft curves in line with the topography, which was optimal for shooting arrows or stones at the enemy troops as they climbed up the hill.  Let’s take a look at Gongnam Gate, the main gate of Sangdang Fortress. Doesn’t it look like a rainbow? The name of this gate is inscribed on the gate and it means “knocking on the south.”  Take a look at the walls spreading out on both sides. Can you see the small stone fence over the fortress walls? Soldiers used to hide behind those walls and fire at enemies with guns and bows and arrows. I’ll explain further as we go up.  When you enter through the rainbow-shaped gate, you will see two phoenixes depicted on the ceiling. The red phoenix stands as the protector of the south, and like a dragon, it is said to be a mythical creature.  Do you see the stone wall right passed the gate? It was used for keeping the enemies that came through the gate at bay, and for launching final attacks against them. They must have shot arrows from above. Let’s go see what's up there.   You can see the green grass field and mountain trails on both sides. With such a wide open view soldiers must have been able to spot enemies from afar. Now let’s go outside.   The small walls can be seen from here too. The holes here were used for firing through with guns and bows and arrows. Some of the holes are slanted, while the others are horizontal. The slanted ones were used to fire down on enemies positioned right below, while the horizontal holes were used to shoot at enemies a bit further down the mountain. There are only a few holes left around the gate now, but they used to be located in regular intervals all along the wall.  If you look a bit further you’ll be able to see a small section sticking out. That’s where guards were posted, and it was also used for attacking the enemy from the sides. We’ll be passing by one of these on the our way to the next course, so take a close look.

stories.title: Sangdang Fortress: Namam Gate
stories.script: Namam Gate  [Traveler] If you walk from the south gate to the west gate you will find a second battlement of small walls, below which is a small gate called Namam. It was constructed as a secret door.  Sangdang Fortress has two secret doors: one on the south and one on the east, and they are called Namam Gate and Dongam Gate, respectively. They were used as secret passages for bringing in food and weapons. Right behind the gates were piles of dirt and stones, which were used to block the doors in case they were found by enemies. Imagine how the soldiers would have felt as they secretly walked through the gates hiding from enemies, and then hurriedly blocking the doors after being found!   Next up is the west gate, which will take us about 20 minutes to reach.

stories.title: Sangdang Fortress: Miho Gate on the West
stories.script: Miho Gate on the West   [Traveler] This western gate was the hardest for enemy soldiers to get through. It is called Miho Gate, and the name translates to tiger conquering the steep, bow-shaped mountains of the west.   The protruding part of the fortress is the interior of the gate, while the sunken part is the exterior. Let’s walk to the exterior of the fortress.  Miho Gate is not as elaborate as the south gate, but it seems the sturdiest. There’s a reason for covering the already tight entrance with stones, namely, to drive the enemies inside and attack them from above.   Of the three gates, Miho Gate is the closest to the downtown area, and has the highest and strongest walls. If the people in the fortress found it too hard to keep the enemy troops away, they all ran to this gate to hide. More than 5,000 soldiers were needed to keep this long wall safe from enemies, so the king built a Buddhist temple inside the fortress and brought monks to live here, who also served as reserve forces during wartime. Although none of the temple have survived to this day, at one time there were three temples.  Next, we'll be going to the east gate, but before we go there, we’ll be stopping by Dongam Gate, which is quite similar to Namam Gate. It'll take about 50 minutes to get there.

stories.title: Sangdang Fortress: Jindong Gate on the East
stories.script: Jindong Gate on the East  [Traveler] Jindong Gate seems lower and simpler than its western counterpart, but it was the site of one of the biggest incidents in Korean history, which was the Rebellion of Yi In-Jwa during the Joseon Dynasty. Yi In-Jwa was a government official who formed one of the major factions that came into conflict over who would be the ultimate successor of the king. When Yi’s opposing candidate finally became the successor, Yi immediately came under threat.  So he decided to strike first with conspiracy and rebellion. He started from the fortresses in the downtown area, and ultimately conquered Sangdang Fortress. But his revolt came to an end by the king’s army after 12 days, when Yi was arrested.  After this incident, the king rebuilt most of the facilities in the fortress in the hopes of preventing such a tragedy from ever happening again. He added a high post to the east so that soldiers could guard the point and provide greater protection for the fortress.  There’s a memorial stone inscribed with the names of the righteous army soldiers who kept fighting the rebels after Yi’s arrest. You’ll see that on the way down.   Shall we check out the road where we can see the shining reservoir? There you can see the rooftop where the general shouted out orders to his soldiers, with some very beautiful scenery in the background. We’re almost done now. Let’s take a break and move on to the next course.

stories.title: Sangdang Fortress: Bohwa Pavilion of the East Commanding Post
stories.audioTitle: Bohwa Pavilion of the East Commanding Post
stories.script: Bohwa Pavilion of the East Commanding Post  [Traveler] What a clear view we have from here! As I mentioned before, the king recognized the importance of this place and built the East Commanding Post.  Generals used to assemble their troops and give orders here. There were originally two commanding posts, one on the east, and another on the west, but only the East Commanding Post was recovered. This East Commanding Post marks the end of this course.   Did it take too long? Thank you for times, and please be sure to go down to the hanok village and have a drink and taste the great food before you go. Also, don't forget to take a break at the reservoir surrounded by beautiful mountains and trees.

stories.title: Heungdeok Temple Site
stories.script: Heungdeok Temple Site  [Traveler] We have now arrived at the Cheongju Early Printing Museum. However, you probably saw more of the characters JIKJI than the name of the museum as you were coming here. That is because the museum was built to commemorate Jikji. Although you may be unfamiliar with it, Jikji is the world's first metal type-printed book, and it was produced in Korea in 1377. These metal types were produced 78 years earlier than those made by Gutenberg of Germany in 1455.  	 Why did we come to this desolate yard instead of entering the museum to see Jikji? What is this traditional building in the yard? This is the workshop where Jikji was made. 600 years ago, at Heungdeok Temple, on this expansive plot of land, typography was invented. That is why Korea's printing museum was built here.   This location was discovered by chance. The last chapter of Jikji says that it was produced at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju, but its accurate location was still unknown. The temple was destroyed in the 15th century, and thereafter this location remained just an expansive plot of land. In 1984, when this site began to be developed into housing land, a small bronze drum was discovered, and the characters reading “Heungdeok” inscribed on the bell's surface led to the discovery of the accurate location of the temple.   This place is more than just the place where metal types were invented. According to the US magazine Life’s 1997 choice of 100 events that impacted humanity over the last 1,000 years, the no. 1 event was the invention of typography. So, you are now standing on that dramatic and historic site.   Typography is able to print books faster than humans can read them. In ancient times, the manual copying of books took up a lot of time and effort, making books expensive and rare, so they were owned only by rich people. Metal types enabled the widespread distribution of books, knowledge and information, so the invention of typography was more revolutionary than the birth of the Internet.   Koreans knew the value of recording the details of even trifling things, having pursued a fierce and passionate recording culture since ancient times. That is why Korea came to possess as many as seven items on the UNESCO Memory of the World, including Jikji. Notably, Jikji is the world's first metal type-printed book, making it even more special.   Now, shall we enter the museum to see the most special book in human history?

stories.title: Cheongju Early Printing Museum: Jikji and Heungdeok Room
stories.script: Jikji and Heungdeok Room  [Traveler] Finally, we have come to see Jikji. Jikji is a Buddhist book, which is why it was made at a temple. Just like monks in medieval Europe, ancient Korean monks produced religious books profusely to preach their religion widely.   Two books are contained in the glass chest. The one on the left is a photographic copy of the original Jikji, while the middle one was printed using the recently restored metal types placed on the right. Jikji originally comprised two books, but only one book has been discovered so far. At the end of the 19th century, the French diplomat Plancy took the original copy of Jikji from Korea, and it is currently being kept at the National Library of France.   It's a pity not to be able to see the book at its very birthplace. However, what is fortunate is that although it has left its home country, UNESCO was able to recognized and designated Jikji as a UNESCO Memory of the World. It was given special treatment probably because the invention of metal types had a remarkable influence on the development of humanity's culture.   By the way, take a look at the metal type plate behind the two books. What could that be used for? It features closely knitted patterns of lozenges. The same pattern can be found on the reinstated cover of the book. That is the metal plate used to print decorative patterns on the book. Jikji is a masterpiece that involved a lot of technical and aesthetic efforts. Shall we now move on to see the relics discovered at the Heungdeok Temple Site?  This broad cylinder is the drum that helped find the birthplace of Jikji. Indeed, characters are inscribed on the edge of the drum. This bronze drum was used to gather people together or to inform them of urgent news, therefore must have made a very particular sounds. What do you think are those sculptures on the far left shaped like turban shells? That's Buddha’s curly hair. These sculptures suggest that Heungdeok Temple also had iron Buddha statues.  The peculiar-shaped item on the right was used by female monks when going through religious training. It was made after a weapon used by a god of India. Monks believed that this item could dispel their worries and distracting thoughts while they disciplined themselves.

stories.title: Cheongju Early Printing Museum: Metal Type Workshop
stories.script: Metal Type Workshop   [Traveler] Wow! The monks of Heungdeok Temple are making metal types here. Some 600 years later, you can finally inherit the world-class technology here. Let's observe closely and learn about the technology.   What would be the first thing to do when making a metal type? It is selecting the font. Just as we choose a font when writing a document on a computer, monks copied fonts from books or created new fonts. After deciding the font, the characters are individually written down on paper. What should we do next? Let's go to the left.   The second process consists in purifying the beeswax. The people squatting on the left are squeezing honey out of beehives to melt and collect beeswax. The melted beeswax is filtered through sieves and cleansed. But! Why is beeswax needed to make metal types? Let's walk further down and see the next process.   Let's look at the process of producing beeswax type matrices first. It looks like the three people dressed in white are making something out of melted beeswax. They are pouring it into a plate frame and making bars. Then, the characters from the first process are attached to the bars row by row, and the outer parts are trimmed with a knife. By cutting out each character from the bars, metal types are created, and then each individual metal type is fixed onto the end of the thick beeswax bars. Now, turn around and see the completed beeswax bars.   People dressed in purple are working hard next to a big container of dirt. Those small things on the right of the container are beeswax bars. They are like fruits hanging from a thick branch. These beeswax bars will be completely wrapped in well kneaded dirt. They will then be shaped into round lumps of dirt, like the ones on the left of the container. Then, they'll be left to harden. The next process is shown on the left.   In this process, beeswax is heated and melted. This job is being carried out by those who are holding tongs in both hands. When melted beeswax is let out, the area where the characters were will be vacant. Then, boiling molten bronze is poured into mold. , As you can see, this job is being performed very cautiously by the man standing on the left of the furnace. Beeswax types are attached to the end of radial-shaped leaves to allow the molten bronze to flow completely fill the mold. And now the final process. Let’s move over a little bit?   The three men dressed in purple are hammering and sawing before a log. The person on the right is breaking soil lumps with a hammer, which suggests that the molten bronze has now completely cooled down. Now, the individual types have to be detached from the bronze character tree. This job is being done by the man in the middle who's holding a saw. The types are handed to the man on the left, who trims their shapes. Next, the metal types are carried to the printing room in containers with compartments to prevent them from being mixed with each other. This is the end of the process of making the types. Only the printing process is left. The workers in the printing room on the left are busy typesetting.   You can probably see the men in white and the men in grey. They are typesetting the types on a broad panel. First, the metal types should be arranged in order. And, if we melt some beeswax a little and spread it on the panel to fix the types, this secret process will prevent blotting. After the typesetting, finally, we start printing. Let's move on to see the next part of the work.   Now let's look at the process of printing and correcting the press. The process consists of applying ink to the types with a brush. A special ink, which adheres well to the metal, is used. After applying the ink, put Korean paper on the types and closely rub it. It may be an embarrassing story, but the best rubber was a large lock of human hair. After finishing the printing, they fill in any unpainted areas with a brush.   Now, the last process is to bind the printed books. In ancient times, no glue existed, so books were closely sewn with sturdy threads. Then, the cover of the book was dyed yellow with gardenia to protect against harmful insects; beeswax was applied to the cover to prevent it from being torn; and the previously introduced metal plate was pressed on the cover to create beautiful designs. Finally, a book has been completed! The ancient printing process requires unimaginably hard work and masses of time compared with these days when we can make electronic books with a smartphone alone. We are happy to be able to easily make, buy and read books today, aren't we?

stories.title: Cheongju Early Printing Museum: Spotless Pure Light Dharani Sutra
stories.script: Spotless Pure Light Dharani Sutra  [Traveler] Next, we will see some ancient Korean printed materials that are even older than Jikji. This scroll is a reproduction of a woodblock-printed book made in the eighth century on the Korean Peninsula. The original copy is kept at the Seoul Central Buddhist Museum. Why is a reproduction exhibited here, although the original copy is just two hours’ drive away? This printed material is as important as Jikji. While Jikji is the world's first metal type-printed book, this material is the world's oldest woodblock-printed book.   This scroll concerns Dharani, a special spiritual Buddhist power. Its name means “tremendously clear, clean, and shining Dharani.” It was believed that if a transcription of a phrase from the scroll was enshrined in a pagoda, health and peace will be bestowed upon the believer. This object, discovered inside a pagoda, has a unique shape. This small scroll measures 6.6cm in width and 6cm in length, so it could fit in a small containers.   Interestingly, this discovery was made thanks to an unsuccessful robbery. In 1966, a robber tried to dismantle the pagoda and steal treasures from it, but since he had no time, he roughly reassembled the pagoda and ran away, pledging to come back again later. Monks found the disrupted pagoda, and tried to repair it, when they found a treasure inside it. Even 1200 years later, the paper was not seriously damaged. This proved the superiority of ancient Korea's typography, paper and ink to the world.

stories.title: Cheongju Early Printing Museum: Tripitaka Koreana
stories.script: Tripitaka Koreana  [Traveler] One of Korea's representative items in the UNESCO Memory of the World is the Tripitaka Koreana, a Buddhist scripture printed on as many as 81,258 woodblocks. The Tripitaka Koreana shows the excellence of ancient Korea's woodblock printing technology, some 140 years before metal types were invented, when the ancient country's woodblock printing technology was in its heyday. Notably, the character carving skills and contents of the printed materials have been highly evaluated for their excellence.  This masterpiece was made possible because Buddhism was widely spread across the country and because woodblock printing was actively carried out at temples. Specifically, whenever the country was in a crisis, Koreans resorted to Buddhism to save the country from the crisis. They thus endeavored to produce these scriptures, build temples, and pray for peace with the Buddha. The Tripitaka Koreana was produced in the desire to repel Mongol invaders. A dedicated office was established to exclusively undertake this printing work, which took as much as 16 years to complete, from 1236.   The interesting thing is that the depository of the Tripitaka Koreana boasts outstanding technology, enabling it to be designated as a UNESCO World Heritage. Thanks to its scientific architecture, the 750-year-old wooden building has been able to preserve its original appearance despite a long period of exposure to rot and insects. Under the building, charcoal was laid deep in soil to automatically control moisture according to the changing seasons, and the sizes and locations of the windows in the building were made to vary so as to allow the incoming air to circulate around evenly inside the building before being channeled out again. Furthermore, specially devised shelves allowed air to flow between the woodblocks.   As such, the Tripitaka Koreana is the best example of ultimate memory culture and preservation culture.

stories.title: Cheongju Early Printing Museum: Dr. Park Byeong-seon
stories.script: Dr. Park Byeong-seon   [Traveler] What are these medals and prizes? They are dedicated to the Korean (laughter) Dr. Park who promoted Jikji to the world. When Jikji was kept at the French National Library, and its existence virtually unknown to most Koreans, she was working there. Knowing about the existence of Jikji, a metal-type printed book, she proved that it was Korea's great treasure after three years of research. Thanks to her efforts, Jikji came to be known at home and abroad, finally leading it to be listed as a World Heritage.   Her efforts did not stop there. She persistently tried to persuade the French to return to Korea the books that the French took in 1866 during its invasion of Korea. Of 340 books, many are precious materials about important royal ceremonies and protocols. Thanks to 36 years of effort on her part, 296 precious ancient books were returned to Korea in 2011.   Those royal books were finally returned to their home in Korea 145 years later. Though not a Hollywood super star celebrity, they were met with a great welcome at the airport by 100 journalists and many citizens of Korea. At the one-month exhibition of the books after their return to Korea, as many as 100,000 people came to see them.   Moreover, another 100,000 precious pieces of Korea's cultural heritage are said to be kept overseas. They were smuggled to foreign countries in the course of the Imperialist era, like the Elgin Marbles of the Greek Parthenon and the Egyptian Pharaoh's relics. Cultural heritages connect a country's past and present spirit and culture. It is to be hoped that our cultural heritages scattered around the world will one day be returned to Korea.

stories.title: Cheongju Early Printing Museum: Joseon Period
stories.script: Joseon Period  [Traveler] After the dynasty that produced Jikji and the Tripitaka Koreana faded at the end of the 14th century, the last dynasty on the Korean Peninsula, the Joseon Dynasty came into being, and, printing technology was further developed.   In Joseon, printing work was shifted from temples to government offices. Joseon adopted Confucianism as the state religion over Buddhism, allowing it to publish books with diverse themes in addition to works on Buddhism. In the early Joseon period, however, metal types made by government officials were said to be of poor quality. Later, perfect typesetting technology was developed. Those books before you exhibit different typefaces.   From the mid-15th century, diverse typefaces were developed. They were unique Korean brands, shedding foreign brands. This means that the country developed its own typefaces instead of imitating the then famous Chinese typefaces.   In the 17th century and subsequent periods, not only government offices but also the private sector made metal types, allowing typography to reach its peak. Notably, books produced by government offices were nearly immaculate, and featured very refined printing, because of the strict rules imposed on printing workers. One character error would result in punishment by 30 strokes of the cane, as would the application of too thick or too soft a coat of ink. Even an error of five characters or more would lead to deprivation of one's position. They knew the importance of accurate recording, thus compelling them to efficiently manage their printing work.   In Joseon's history of printing technology, one particular event occurred that is truly remarkable. I'm talking about the invention of hangeul, the Korean Alphabet, in 1443. Worin cheongang jigok, exhibited here, is the first book to have been printed in hangeul. It contains the words of a song, authored by King Sejong, one of the inventors of hangeul, praising the virtues of Buddha. Other diverse books written in hangeul were widely distributed to the common people. Hangeul boosted the people's literacy. These days, Koreans boast the world's lowest level of illiteracy, at 0.3%, thanks to its easy-to-learn writing system and the early development of printing technology.

stories.title: Cheongju Early Printing Museum: Gutenberg's Metal Type Printing
stories.script: Gutenberg's Metal Type Printing  [Traveler] As you know, Gutenberg was the first person in the West to print books using metal types. The diverse objects before you were used by him in type printing. Some of them are similar to the printing facilities of Korea, as explained above. His type-printing involved pouring a molten alloy into molds and making types, and then arranging them in a wooden frame. This is similar to the method used in ancient Korea. However, the difference is that he developed a compressor capable of printing on both sides of paper and an ink mixed with oil varnish to ensure quick drying.   In 1452, 78 years after Jikji was printed in Korea, Gutenberg opened a printing house. He wanted the Bible - which at that time was available only to priests and aristocrats - to be read by a greater number of people. He thus developed metal types and printed 180 bibles in three years. One of them is the thick book you see before you. A few months of writing by hand would have been required to produce a book like this, but metal type printing shortened the period tremendously.   His typography revolutionized Europe. Printing houses were established across Europe, and 20 million copies of the Bible were printed in 50 years up to 1500. This number was far greater than the amount of books produced in the preceding 1,000 years. Typography also liberated knowledge that had been buried for one thousand years. Notably, commoners were able to read the Bible, which eventually developed into the driving force behind the religious reformation.   His typography did not stop here, but triggered a flood of information, influencing humanity's culture, religion, science and all other areas of knowledge. Which is why to this day, Gutenberg is even cited as the founder of the media industry.

stories.title: Suam Valley: Samchung Market
stories.script: Samchung Market  [Traveler] Hello! This place, which is called Suam Valley, is located between Su-dong and Uam-dong in Cheongju. Many refugees who escaped to the south of the peninsula during the Korean War in 1950 eventually moved back here. These houses, in which two or three households lived together under one roof, have retained their original appearance, despite having undergone little restoration work. Villagers, who have been through difficult times together, always support each other and share their warmth. Well, their walls are adjoining together like this, so it's not a surprise they are so close. In 2008, when the public art project was started, this place, which used to be a hillside town occupied by the poor, changed considerably. Painters and neighboring university students started painting the walls under the theme of “Memorable Journey into the Side Streets.” Once the grey walls were colorfully painted, the side streets gradually came to look like a rainbow, and because of that, Suam Valley has appeared in several TV dramas and movies.  In spite of all the urban development, this old town has survived along with the pretty wall paintings. Isn’t it a bit ironic how a place that was once the home of refugees is now a popular tourist attraction that is often featured on television dramas? Maybe that's why warmth and longing can be felt here. And the hills and side streets, bring back memories of childhood.   Before taking a look around the side streets, please take a tour information pamphlet from the small store at the entrance. Go wherever your feet make you, and because all the streets and alleys here are connected, you won’t get lost. When you finish the tour, and have seen all the colorful houses introduced in the pamphlet, go to the highest point and look down. Because of the high altitude, it provides a great view. After looking around the side streets, you can head towards the Cheongju Cultural Industry Promotion Foundation via the Uam Mountain detour. At the Cheongju Cultural Industry Promotion Foundation you will find the King of Baking, Kim Tak-goo exhibition hall, which was a TV drama about love and success as a baker. You can see the sets used in the drama, bake bread, and watch a performance as well. You can even taste famous Cheongju noodles and sample various tasty breads too. I’ll see you back at the exhibition hall.

stories.title: Suam Valley: Kim Tak-goo Exhibition Hall
stories.script: Kim Tak-goo Exhibition Hall  [Traveler] Can you see the oven-shaped exhibition building? That is the exhibition hall for King of Baking, Kim Tak-goo, which was a famous Korean drama watched by one out of every three Korean people. Aired in 2010 against a background of the rapid growth of the Korean economy in the 1980s, this drama told the story of a man who overcame many hardships to succeed as a baker.  This place used to be a cigarette factory. Although old and a bit torn, this historic building was ideal as a set for a drama based in the 1980s.  The exhibition hall was built by remodeling the interior of the factory. The grey warehouse was colorfully painted, and the actual sets and props used in the drama were brought in. Usually, drama sets are disassembled as soon as a drama ends, but because of the fame of Kim Tak-goo, this set has still been kept. The structure and even the circulation system of the exhibition hall were all designed to recall the touching scenes of the drama. So, if you have seen the drama, imagine yourself as being in the kitchen with Kim Tak-goo and Gu Ma-jun.

stories.title: Suam Valley: House of Chairman Gu Il-jung
stories.script: House of Chairman Gu Il-jung  [Traveler] As you enter the room, there is a staircase, and to each side is the dressing room and the make-up room. In this room, everyone can become the main character of the drama. You can also try on a bakers' uniform and take picture.  At the center are the stairs of the house of Gu Il-jung, the main character’s father. I can still see Gu’s wife, Seo In-suk, dressed up in an elegant dress and walking on the red carpet. Most of her breathtaking scenes took place here. The first thing you see as you enter Gu's house are the grandiose European stair. The carpet, the chandelier, and even marble floor seem to reflect the characters’ desires and feelings. To the left of the staircase, Gu’s reception room, the CEO’s office at Geoseong Foods, and the baking room have been re-created. In the CEO’s office the best scenes of the drama are shown through a projector, so take your time to enjoy the scenes.  The baking room was where Tak-goo would peak through a crack in the door to see Gu Il-jung making bread. And it is also where Gu Il-jung’s passion and devotion to bread could be seen.

stories.title: Suam Valley: House of Palbong’s Family
stories.script: House of Palbong’s Family   [Traveler] To the right of the staircase is Seo In-suk’s mini bar, and the 1st and 2nd stories of bakery where Kim Tak-goo lived were re-created.
