Passed the antique mini bar, you can see vivid scenes of the drama set. Places where the camera doesn’t reach are quite messy, like you see here. This is the front door of the house where the bakery family lived. Shall we knock and go in?  The atmosphere of this house is the very different than that of Gu’s house. Unlike the western-style home of Gu, this is a typical Korean family home. Although it looks a bit small, the entire bakery family would gather around for to eat or talk, and thus their love and warmth can still be felt in these walls. Passed the living room, you can see Tak-goo’s small room. Here, Tak-goo fell asleep holding his mother's hand after having found her again. The two were very happy to have met after so many years of being separated. That particular scene was very special and touching to Korean people, who value family affection above everything else.  When you’ve finished looking around the bakery family’s rooms, you can enjoy a meal of bread and noodles. On one side of the restaurant, the bakery where Tak-goo used to look at the mouth-watering breads and buns beyond the glass window, has been recreated.  After you've finished eating, you can try baking your own bread at the baking room in the drama exhibition hall. Baking is available everyday at 10:30, 2:30, and 6:30, except Mondays. While fermenting the dough mixed with red beans and crumb topping, an exciting show will be performed. It is a way of waiting while the dough rises by pounding on the dough. After the show, you can go home with your own bread and remember the day as a very satisfying day.

stories.title: Cheongnamdae: Presidential Museum of History and Culture
stories.audioTitle: Presidential Museum of History and Culture
stories.script: Presidential Museum of History and Culture  [Traveler] Hello everyone! Welcome to Cheongnamdae, the Presidential villa. Before we start our tour, let’s stop by the Museum of History and Culture and take a quick look at the presidents of Korea. Knowing what happened in the past will make our next course more interesting.   This museum was originally a barrack for soldiers and a dormitory for the guards of Cheongnamdae.On June 20th, 2011, it was redecorated, and it now houses a number of interesting exhibits.   The interior of the museum is divided into the Presidential Hall and the Cheongnamdae Hall.Spanning from the first to the current president of Korea, the Presidential Hall summarizes major events and issues that occurred throughout modern Korean history. Videos and photos of the most important and most memorable moments of former presidents of Korea can be seen here.  The Cheongnamdae Hall features a collection of items left behind by successive presidents, including tableware and furniture. Not only that, there are also items used by the guards, presenting a vivid picture of the past. Take your time to look around and I’ll meet you in front of the main hall!

stories.title: Cheongnamdae: Heading to the Main Hall
stories.script: Heading to the Main Hall  [Traveler] In December 1983, the Cheongnamdae, Korea’s presidential villa, was constructed on an expansive site covering 1.8㎢ at the president’s instructions. The name of Cheongnamdae means “a warm southern Cheongwadae”. The Cheongwadae or Blue House is the Korean presidential office. In addition to this villa, there used to be four more presidential villa compounds. However, all of them disappeared with the end of Korea’s military government, and now, only the Cheongnamdae remains.   The villa compound is surrounded by mountain peaks, as if skirted by defensive walls. When Cheongnamdae was initially built, it was kept secret from the public. That’s why people thought it was just a rumor as nobody could find it. It was not even indicated on maps for reasons of security, and photos of the house were only disclosed for the first time in 1999, 16 years after its construction.  So for 16 years, no one was allowed to enter the Cheongnamdae except presidents and their family. Now, let's take a tour of the Cheongnamdae. I’ll also tell you about how the villa came to be opened to the general public.

stories.title: Cheongnamdae: Main Building (Reception Room, Living Room and Restaurant)
stories.audioTitle: 1F, Main Building (Reception Room, Living Room and Restaurant)
stories.script: 1F, Main Building (Reception Room, Living Room and Restaurant)  [Traveler] Did you change your shoes to the slippers at the door? The first things you will see are the table and chairs inside the clean lobby. There’s a huge window behind it, and a golden elevator to the left. The elevator was an addition built for the Nobel Peace Prize winner President Kim Dae-jung, who had difficulty walking. Now the elevator is used by tourists who have difficulty walking up and down the stairs.  The first place you’ll look around is the Reception Room. Please enter through the door on the right.  Presidents used this reception room when receiving guests. At the front of the room, there are a national flag called Taegeukgi and a blue flag with a golden bird. The blue flag symbolizes the president. We can also see several chairs here. The chair with a golden bird carved on the back was made for the president, while the chair with a rose of Sharon on the back was made for the first lady.   Please look around the room, and you will find an old-looking calendar. It’s on the page for April and May. Why are they hanging there?   This is a calendar for 2003. It has been left here to commemorate April 18, 2003, when the ownership of the Cheongnamdae was transferred to North Chungcheong Province by the president. The Cheongnamdae appears to be caught in the past. The furniture and pictures, presumably bearing the fingerprints of former presidents, also look like leftover relics from past times.  President Roh Moo-hyun, who was a presidential candidate in 2002, pledged to return the Cheongnamdae to the province. It was a decision made to relieve the complaints of townspeople, who suffered considerable inconvenience due to the omnipresent security. Also, it represented a break from authoritarianism. After his election, President Roh stayed at the Cheongnamdae for just one day, and handed over the villa to the provincial government of North Chungcheong Province. After 20 years of secrecy, the historical presidential villa was finally opened to the general public, and a lot of people visited it out of sheer curiosity. Many people visited this place out of curiosity. It has also been used as a filming location of various Korean dramas and movies.  Shall we move on to the living room? Let’s leave the reception room and enter by the door on the right. The area with the pearl-colored sofa and the big window is the living room.  The view out the window is just magnificent. Don't you think you could sit around this table with friends for dinner and a chat about anything, and everything? There’s a fireplace next to the window, and there is a dining table and an extra table outside that big door on the right. Presidents may have had chats with their guests here before dinner. Let's now move to the kitchen.   Here is the place where presidents enjoyed their meal together with family or guests. Opposite the window, the door to the left leads to the kitchen. Whenever a president visited the villa, chefs specializing in Korean, Western, Chinese, and Japanese cuisine would come over from Cheongwadae. All the ingredients were brought from Seoul. However, presidents also ate fresh vegetables from the small garden in the villa compound.

stories.title: Cheongnamdae: Bedroom and Office on Main Hall, 2nd Floor
stories.audioTitle: Bedroom and Office on Main Hall, 2nd Floor
stories.script: Bedroom and Office on Main Hall, 2nd Floor  [Traveler] Did you come up to the second floor through the stairs? The 2nd floor of the Main Hall was the VIP floor where the president and his family stayed. Inside the living room are the president’s bedroom, a bathroom, and an office. We can’t go inside the room, so look inside while listening carefully.  Whenever a new president took office, new beds and tableware were brought in, but the furniture and electronic appliances were not replaced with new ones. You can see the bathroom door to the left of the bedroom closet. When the Cheongnamdae was closed to public access in the past, rumors abounded that even the tap faucets and door handles were made of gold. People often ask me if it’s true. Of course not! It’s only painted gold. Inside the tub, handles and safety bars, a telephone, and a pager were installed for President Kim Dae Jung’s convenience and safety.   Now, let’s move to the office next door. This office is where the president conducted his daily business.  Do you see the green table? Cheongnamdae was built as a vacation villa, but seeing this work office makes me feel bad for the presidents.   At Camp David in the USA, important meetings take place between the US president and leaders of other countries. The peace treaty signed by President Jimmy Carter, the President of Israel, and the President of Egypt is also called the ‘Camp David Treaty.’ Cheongnamdae has a similar word, and it is so called the “Cheongnamdae Plan.” When a president left for the villa to take a holiday, news media reported that the president had now begun to devise the “Cheongnamdae Plan.” This means that president formulated new political ideas while relaxing at the Cheongnamdae, and then returned to the Cheongwadae. In reality, the presidential decisions made here changed the country's political movements several times. So to speak, you are now standing in that special place. Because of the great interest people had in Cheongnamdae, articles on what types of books presidents read, and even th titles of books and magazines they read were published. Those books mainly concerned how to overcome the major difficulties of the times.

stories.title: Cheongnamdae: 2F, Main Building (Office, Living Room, Restaurant, and Family Living Room)
stories.audioTitle: 2F, Main Building (Living Room, Restaurant, and Family Living Room)
stories.script: 2F, Main Building (Living Room, Restaurant, and Family Living Room)   [Traveler] There's a secret inside this living room with the round table and white sofa. Are you curious? The window here is bullet-proof ! But, as you can see, they don't look much different from regular glass. And, even if they're bullet-proof, it can still break if you hit it too hard, so be careful.   Opposite the living room is the restaurant used by the president's family. The dining hall window was originally quite small, but it was enlarged because one president wanted it to be brighter inside. On April 18th, 2003, when Cheongnamdae was opened to the public, President Ro and his family had their last dinner here. Let's move on.   The wide space to the right is the family living room. When many family members gathered  here, the presidents pushed the sofa to one side and enjoyed little games. President Ro’s daughter played the piano in the living room, and the president also played his favorite songs  there. Although we only saw them from an authoritarian perspective, behind closed doors, while with their families, they must have been just like the rest of us.   If you walk past the living room through the hallway, you will see a hansil, or Korean-style room, which is quite different from the rest of the house. This room uses the ondol heating system, which means the floors are heated through underground pipes. Like most Korean people, the president also enjoyed sitting on warmly heated floors in the cold winter days. This is where the president and first lady received their New Year’s bows from their children. It’s the most Korean-style area in the villa.

stories.title: Cheongnamdae: Pentagonal Pavilion
stories.script: Pentagonal Pavilion  [Traveler] Did you enjoy the pine scent and fresh air? Former presidents really enjoyed walking along the road leading to this Pentagonal Pavilion. They were able to breathe in the fresh scent of the pine trees crowding both sides of the road, look at flowers, and forget their worries. There is also a lake, called Daecheong Lake, with a beautiful reflection of mountain ridges, making it look like a tree forest.   In the past, straw mats were laid on the floor of the Pentagonal Pavilion, so presidents took off their shoes to enter the pavilion. In the cold winter weather, knee covers, outer socks and stoves were provided to presidents. Just imagine a president wearing outer socks and looking at this splendid scene.

stories.title: Cheongnamdae: Shade House
stories.script: Shade House  [Traveler] The Shade House was the best place to have tea and relax. Through the front window, you can enjoy the view of the lake.  At the fishing pond in front of the Shade House, President Kim Young-sam and his second son are said to have enjoyed angling. Oh, I have an interesting story to tell you about the Shade House. Back then, there were ‘duck soldiers’. Huh? duck soldiers? you may ask. Literally, ‘duck soldiers’ were responsible for raising and training ducks. The Military Unit 338 was charged with guarding the Cheongnamdae area, and they also needed to raise ducks and mallards. The mallard ducks were so well trained that they all gathered at the sound of a trumpet, creating a beautiful scene. President Kim Dae-jung was caught on camera wearing a straw hat and feeding ducks from a basket.   Just outside the Shade House is Daecheong Lake. Can you see those buoys floating on the lake? They are holding nets installed at the bottom of the lake to protect possible underwater invasions. They also prevent the influx of other floating objects.

stories.title: Cheongnamdae: Jogging Track
stories.script: Jogging Track   [Traveler] This is a jogging track which was built with a mixture of coarse clay and loess. This coarse clay comes from weathered granite sand, and is good for acupressure of the feet and blood circulation. It also makes you feel very refreshing when you tread on it. In summer, tourists take off their shoes and walk along this road. Try it and you will feel the fresh touch of earth on your feet.  This road was built for President Kim Young-sam, who enjoyed a daily early morning run. Other diverse functions were added to the Cheongnamdae depending on presidents' favorite pastimes. A playground was built in the garden for the presidents' grandchildren, and an elevator was installed in the main building to support the President Kim Dae-jung, who was physically disabled. There’s also a small pavilion at the end of the trail.   On the way to the next point, statues of some of our former president will welcome you. The presidents are depicted jogging, reading, biking, and walking. So strike a pose with them.

stories.title: Cheongnamdae: Presidential Plaza
stories.script: Presidential Plaza  [Traveler] The bronze statues of Korea’s presidents on the Presidential Plaza are all life-sized. On the advice of their family members and secretaries, their clothing and postures were elaborately designed to be close to reality. They are standing in the same place, but each exudes a different aura. It's like looking at a summarized history of Korea.   From the left, we can see the first, second and third president and so on. Each president's name and mandate are inscribed at the bottom of the statues. The first statue is Korea's first president Rhee Syng-man. The second president Yun Po-sun was unfortunately unable to serve out his term due to a military coup. The third president Park Chung-hee brought about the great economic development of South Korea, Which helped lift the country out of poverty. The second statue from the right is President Kim Dae-jung, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of his efforts toward reconciliation with North Korea. We can also see President Roh Moo-hyun.   At the far left, an empty space has been prepared for a future president. If you take a picture there, you’ll look like you’re standing side by side with all the presidents.

stories.title: Cheongnamdae: Choga Pavilion
stories.script: Choga Pavilion  [Traveler] This place was established during Kim Dae Jung’s presidency. Inside the Choga Pavilion, there are traditional Korean appliances collected from around here, and agricultural tools that President Kim brought from his hometown. President Kim loved this place so much that he often took a walk around here - with the first lady next to him, of course. The president often sat here and pondered quietly, much like the surface of the Daecheong Lake.  Sitting on the pavilion, we can get a glimpse of the surrounding scenery. In particular, look at the long stick with a wooden bird at the top. It’s called a sotdae, which is a type of decoration used to wish for the security of a town and a great harvest. Also, it’s meant to connect people with the sky. The wooden geese and ducks symbolize hope. They’re cute, right! Rest for a while with the sotdae as you look over the lake. The way to the next course, which is the observatory, has many, many steps.

stories.title: Cheongnamdae: Observatory
stories.script: Observatory  [Traveler] Wow, you made it to the observatory!  Welcome. You’ve just walked up a total of 645 steps. These steps bring good fortune to those who step on them!!  From the observatory, you can see the entire Cheongnamdae. And it’s really is surrounded by the a forest and a lake. The view of the Daecheong Lake from the observatory is so beautiful that people refer to it as an in-land archipelago. It almost feels like we’re floating right in the middle of the ocean.   Before being opened to the public, this observatory was the site of 338 vulcuns. It was built to prepare for air raids. After opening Cheongnamdae to the public, the weapons were transported back by helicopter. Now, this place is only meant for tourists. It’s relatively low at 265 meters above sea level, but the open view provides a great view of the natural surroundings. This is the last course of Cheongnamdae, so please enjoy the scenery!

stories.title: Munui Cultural Heritage Complex: Yangseong Gate
stories.script: Yangseong Gate  [Traveler] Welcome to Munui Cultural Heritage Complex. This is a small folk village where various cultural heritage - which were rescued from the construction of Daecheong Dam in Cheongwon-gun and which would otherwise have been submerged - have been preserved.   In 1980, Daecheong Dam was connected to this area in order to develop the local water resources and this area was entirely submerged. 6,000 residents had to leave their long-time residences. Deprived of their hometown, they were unspeakably sorrowful. They moved to nearby areas and began to settle down. Munui-myeon is one of those new settlements. Outwardly, Daecheong Dam is beautiful, but such a sad story lies behind it.   As you walk along the path through the village, you will discover a seemingly close Yangseong Mountain and the shining surface of the water. You will also see different scenes as you walk up this high land. Now, let’s take a look at the precious cultural heritage, beginning with the traditional house in Gwanjeong-ri.

stories.title: Munui Cultural Heritage Complex: Traditional House in Gwanjeong-ri
stories.script: Traditional House in Gwanjeong-ri   [Traveler] This is a house with a straw-thatched roof. Most Korean commoners lived in such houses in the past. From the outside, it looks simple, but many inventive ideas are hidden in various parts of the house. Koreans designed the structure of the house to secure cooling and heating effects and hygienic facilities, allowing them to live in a pleasant environment throughout the four seasons.   [Docent] Welcome to this house. This house was built in the second half of the Joseon Dynasty, which lasted from the 14th to the 20th century. Can you see the thick-straw thatched roof? In the cold winter, when the floor is heated, the hot air permeates even inside the roof, while in the hot summer, the roof screens out the sunshine like a straw hat. And in spring, swallows nestle in the roof. The earthen brick walls remove poisonous substances, foul smells and mold. The walls absorb moisture and discharge it when it is dry, so they function as a kind of humidifier. There is a kitchen on the far left, and there are three rooms with a big floor at the center.   [Traveler] Do you dine and sleep in this room?  [Docent] Yes. In a Korean house the bedroom and kitchen are not strictly divided. When you get out the sleeping mats, it becomes a bedroom, and when you set the table, it becomes a dining room. This makes the furniture simple. The rooms are few and small in size.  [Traveler] I see.   [Docent] The floor, located at the center, is where family members sit and look at the garden. In the heat of summer, if you lie on that floor, it is so cool, that there is no greater paradise. The floor of this house has another unique characteristic. There is a box containing mortuary tablets. Korean people believed that the souls of the dead were contained in that box, so they regarded this boxes as precious items. On the wall, you can see a horizontal panel. When you unfold the panel, it becomes a wide table. Various foods are set on that table, and an ancestral rites is held for the box. And so the room is now a living room, and then a room for ritual services.   Shall we look around the room on the far right over there? That room has an elevated floor, under which a fire hole has been made to heat the stone floor. This structure is called ondol. The ondol floor structure is perfectly designed to suit the Korean climate with its four distinctive seasons. When it is hot, the doors are left over for cool air to flow in. A cool wind blows in from the open gate to the floor, cooling the people in the house. When it is cold, the floors are heated. Inside the room there is a heated stone floor, and outside the room there's a cool wooden floor. Isn't it an inventive structure?   [Traveler] Modern-day high-rise apartments also have an ondol system. Ondol is comfortable and familiar to Koreans.   [Docent] There's more to show and tell in the back, so let's go to the back .  [Traveler] The back garden is pretty spacious.   [Docent] Look at that low chimney over there. Actually, I invited you to this house to boast about that chimney. The chimney is below the roof, not above it. There are several reasons for this. First, it keeps the roof clean. Smoke from this low chimney permeates into the straw, and automatically disinfects it. This rids the roof of moisture and harmful insects in winter, allowing it to usher in the spring as a new roof. Second, it adjusts the temperature. When the ondol floor is heated, the air is not so hot. So, the hot air from the low chimney helps heat the room. Isn’t it a good idea? Noblemen in the Joseon period made meticulous efforts to build houses. Let’s look around the nobleman's house over there.

stories.title: Munui Cultural Heritage Complex: Nobleman's House
stories.script: Nobleman's House  [Docent] Welcome. A tall gate like this was built only for the houses of high-ranking aristocrats. So, rich commoners made their gates wider rather than higher. Please come on in.   You can see that the gate opens inwards, believing that opening in that direction could usher in blisses  This house consists of the servants’ quarters, the men’s quarters, and the women’s quarters. It also has a bathroom, a shed, and a space for rites. The small servants’ quarters are located to the left of the gate. Whenever a guest visited the house, a servant would quickly welcome him and open the gate. A fire hole has been installed in the floor. However, bad house owners did not put a fire hole in the servants’ quarters to save fuel. Fortunately, this servants’ quarters has a fire hole.   Can you see that large building over there. That's the men’s quarters. The man of the house and his guests stayed there. In this building, guests were served, and children were taught literature. Aristocrats in the Joseon period enjoyed their comfort in this snug house. They mainly sat on the floor and read books. They also painted pictures and enjoyed walking. Noblemen studied literature throughout their life if they failed to pass the state examination to become officials.   [Traveler] In Joseon agricultural society, who took care of the fields?  [Docent] Agricultural work was performed mainly by servants and tenant farmers. The noblemen would lease his land to them. Work varied according to people’s status. Buildings also varied according to the status of the residents. Look at the roof of the men’s quarters.   [Traveler] A small gable is placed on top of the roof, and the ends of the eaves are slightly raised, making the roof appear more attractive.   [Docent] This type of roof was used mainly in luxury, decorative or luxury buildings. On the other hand, the roof of the servants’ quarters is far smaller and simpler.   Iron rods are hanging down from the ceiling to the floor. They are part of a system for latching or unlatching the door. This house door can be latched or unlatched. In summer, they unlatch the door to let in air and make the rooms cool.  Now, let’s move to the women’s quarters. A door from behind the men’s quarters is linked to the women’s quarters, where the wife stays.  [Traveler] Both quarters face each other, which makes them look friendly.   [Docent] Is that so? Actually, the women’s quarters are located higher than the men’s quarters, so that the wife can check if there are guests in men's quarters. The women’s quarters were built not to directly face the men’s quarters, so that the wife could keep her privacy. The low-lying wall between the two buildings appropriately hide the women’s quarters. In the Confucian society of the past, women and men were not allowed to sit close to each other.     Behind the women’s quarters is a ritual space. In this nobleman’s house, an ancestral ritual space was located in a higher space as a means of showing respect. Our ancestors bowed down to the ritual space when they left the house in the morning, and offered the first crop of their harvest to the souls of the deceased.

stories.title: Munui Cultural Heritage Complex: Shrine
stories.script: Shrine   [Docent] Welcome! This house was built here so the children could take care of their parents’ tombs. They serve food to them every day and keep the tombs clean. They had to lead this life for three years. Three years is probably a long time, but the children are so grateful to their parents for having raised them, expecially for the first three years after they were born. The children want to return that love to their parents.    If the man was too busy with a job, he would have his servant take care of the tombs. If a servant faithfully performed the job for three years, he would be released from service. If a son did that job, the state erected a monument to commemorate such filial piety. This practice was very important to Koreans in the past. It was a rigid Confucian practice.   This bamboo cane he is holding signifies that his father has died. If it were his mother who had died, he’d be holding a paulownia or willow cane. The bamboo symbolizes the rigid, strong character of the father, whereas the soft, flexible paulownia and willow trees symbolize the mother.   [Traveler] In the past, such symbols were probably necessary since cameras did not exist to photograph the portraits of dead persons.

stories.title: Munui Cultural Heritage Complex: Munsan Guesthouse
stories.script: Munsan Guesthouse  [Traveler] In front of Munsan Guesthouse are three staircases. Seen from the guesthouse, the staircase to the left is for ascending, while the staircase to the right is for descending, and the middle staircase symbolizes sacredness, and thus is not often used.   [Docent] Here, this Munsan Guesthouse used to be a lodging facility for local officials as well as those from Seoul.   [Traveler] The building seems to be divided into three parts.   [Docent] That’s right. In the middle building, officials held meetings twice a month. They bowed to the north where the king resided as a gesture of respect. The building on the left was a banqueting hall. Officials ate and drank together and enjoyed performances by female entertainers there. The building on the right was a lodging facility.   [Traveler] The roof of the building blends well with the mountain ridge.  [Docent] I agree. The curved lines and upward lines harmonize with mother nature. They are part of Korean beauty.  Munsan Guesthouse has a fine view. From the garden, you can look down at the clean, mirror-like lake which reflects the sky. The guesthouse appears to be floating between the mountain, the lake, and the sky. Isn't it just the best place? Why not take a stroll here in the garden as you admire the straw-thatched roof and the earthen-tile roof.   [Traveler] When you've finished your tour of the Munui Cultural Heritage Complex, please visit the presidential villa, the Cheongnamdae, which was built in the 1980s. It is not far from here. The villa is now open to the general public. It boasts an amazing vista with a beautiful dam. Have a good trip!

stories.title: Beopju Temple: One Pillar Gate
stories.audioTitle: From Ori Forest to the One Pillar Gate
stories.script: From Ori Forest to the One Pillar Gate   [Traveler] Welcome everyone. Do you hear the merry singing of birds? Yes you do, because you are now in Ori Forest. You must walk along this famous path to get to Beopju Temple. I wonder if you know the meaning of the forest's name. In Korean, Ori' means a distance of 10 kilometers. Walking through this forest, which is packed with oak and pine trees as old as one hundred years, you can easily fall into meditation.  You will gradually feel that the only sound you hear is the sound of your footsteps. Also, you will lose in deep thought until you finally arrive at the entrance to Beopju Temple. The name of this temple means that it is a temple of the Buddha's Law. It was founded some 14 centuries ago by a monk of the ancient Korean kingdom of Silla, who was charmed by the stunning beauty of the area. He believed that a temple built here would make a perfect academy to teach the Buddhist scriptures he had brought with him from India.  The temple has long been a sanctum for Buddhist followers waiting for the arrival of the Buddhist Savior. Just like Christianity has been divided into many different denominations according to differences in doctrines or interpretations of the Bible, each Buddhist temple in Korea performs different functions. For instance, Beopju Temple had grown into a home of the worshippers of the Future Buddha who will save all sentient beings from suffering. You could compare the Future Buddha with the Messiah of Christian belief.  Beopju Temple is now revered as one of the Korea's most important temples, largely because of its history and religious authority. The temple’s reputation is also due to the stunning natural beauty of Songni Mountain that embraces it. As a resident of Chungcheong Province, I visit the temple as the seasons change and indulge myself in the fantastic transformation of the landscapes. Such visits to the temple lead me, or indeed any visitor, to find peace of mind, and to ponder over what changes in the world and what does not.   We will shortly be arriving at the Ilju Gate, which translates to One Pillar Gate. The important element in the name of the gate is one. It signifies that visitors passing through the gate need to focus their mental energy before entering the Realm of the Truth. The gate represents the main entrance to a Buddhist sanctuary ruled by Buddha. It typically has its name plaque hung at the center under the eaves. The entrance gate of Beopju Temple also has a hanging plaque inscribed with an epithet. It The Primary Temple of Chungcheong Province.   If you have passed through the One Pillar Gate, then you are now in the precincts of Beopju Temple. Korean Buddhist temples and monasteries have maintained unique architectural layouts. As for Beopju Temple, the layout is marked by buildings arranged along a single line. Are you already beginning to wonder which building will come next? Let's go and find out.

stories.title: Geumgangmun Gate (Beopjusa Temple, Boeun)
stories.script: Geumgangmun Gate, the Guardian’s Gate of Beopjusa Temple  There is another entrance gate here called Geumgangmun Gate which means the Guardian's Gate. It is generally regarded as the main entrance to Beopjusa Temple as the wall enclosing the temple starts here. Why did they had to put up two or more gates? Was there any specific reason for Korean temples to adopt such security measures? Maybe. But what they really wanted to protect the temple from with these gates was not any tangible threat such as a thief or an intruder but rather intangible evil forces.  Then, what's the difference between the Iljumun Gate, One Pillar Gate you saw earlier and this Guardian’s Gate? Like most other buildings, this gate has four pillars supporting the four corners of the roof. In this gate, four Buddhist figures are enshrined. The first two are Diamond Warriors whose main role is to protect the Buddhist Law from evil. The other two are Buddhist saints, one riding a lion and the other an elephant. They symbolize wisdom and physical power, respectively.  Now, moving to the next building, there is another gate building waiting for you to pass through. As you may have noticed by now, you can access to the main hall only after passing through several gateways. The symbolism behind such a layout is that you need to empty your mind more and more as you pass through the gates one by one and get ever closer to Buddha.

stories.title: Beopju Temple: Iron Cauldron
stories.script: Iron Cauldron   [Traveler] Now, why don't we turn aside from this straight path for a moment and make a short visit to a tiny building on our right? There is a huge iron bowl shaped like a tin helmet worn by British soldiers during the First World War. What was it used for? Was it a whirlpool tub used by the monks some hundreds of years ago?  No, it was not. Remarkably, it was a cauldron used for cooking rice or soup.  Is there anyone who can guess how many monks were fed with rice cooked in this pot in one go? Don't be surprised. They say that the pot can hold as much as 3,200kg of rice. Considering that an ordinary Korean consumes 200 grams of rice in one meal, it’s enough for 16,000 people. Isn't that amazing? It is said that there were more than 3,000 monks in this temple when this cauldron was used. So the cauldron provides clear evidence of the prosperity the temple once enjoyed.  The temple is currently made up of about 30 buildings. However, according to historical records, it was a large monastery with about 60 main buildings and 70 subsidiary buildings until the end of the 16th century. When the seven-year war waged between Korea and Japan following the Japanese invasion of Korea in 1592, the greater part of the temple was destroyed. But thankfully the cauldron was never harmed. Today this majestic vessel is regarded as a “living witness” of the glorious past of Beopju Temple.

stories.title: Beopju Temple: Gate of the Four Heavenly Kings
stories.audioTitle: Gate of the Four Heavenly Kings
stories.script: Gate of the Four Heavenly Kings  [Traveler] Now, let's pass through the Gate of the Four Heavenly Kings. This is the last gateway to the World of Buddha. The Four Heavenly Kings enshrined in the gate are fierce protectors of the Buddhist world. Are the two tall trees soaring in the air before us the guardians?  Well, the trees boast a majestic appearance, indeed, but no, they are not. The Buddhist guardians are in fact inside the gate building.  The Four Heavenly Kings were originally Hindu deities who protected the four cardinal directions, East, West, South and North. They were later adopted by Buddhism and turned into four of the most widely admired guardian deities among Buddhist followers around the world. Their appearance changed, too. As you can see here, they became fully armored warriors with a robust physique. In the early period, they had a much more benign and gentle appearance.  The main role of these guardians is to protect Buddhist followers from evil influences. Interestingly, each of the four protectors is in charge of a different emotional state of human beings. The guardian with the ancient Korean lute called a bipa governs pleasure, while the guardian with a sword governs love. The third carrying a dragon with magic pearl controls anger, and the fourth carrying a pagoda controls joy. Korean Buddhists also believe that these divine protectors are keenly interested in good and evil in the human mind to punish or reward people according to what they find in their minds. It's somewhat scary, isn't it? Do you think you can get safely past their sharp eyes without betraying your darkest thoughts?

stories.title: Palsangjeon Wooden Pagoda (Beopjusa Temple, Boeun)
stories.script: Palsangjeon, the Wooden Pagoda of Beopjusa Temple  This beautiful building is widely regarded as the most valuable treasure preserved in Beopjusa Temple today as it is the only five-story wooden pagoda to have survived to the present day in Korea. Until the 7th century, Korean Buddhists built many wooden pagodas, but these valuable assets were destroyed by fire during the wars throughout its history.  Besides, Palsangjeon is also the tallest ancient pagoda that remains in Korea today. There are numerous towers across the world. While majority of them were used for observation or for housing bells, most of the old towers in Korea are pagodas that are used to enshrine the holy relics of Buddha or eminent monks. Most Korean pagodas are in similar size and height, but this pagoda is exceptionally tall, measuring 23 meters. It is comparable to the height of an eight-story building.  It seems to be a five-story building from the outside, but it is in fact a single-story structure. If you look closer, there are eight paintings, The Eight Great Events, and two are attached to each of the four-square pillars standing inside the hall. The name of this pagoda originated from these paintings.  Some people believe these paintings are invaluable because these paintings show the eight most important scenes from the Shakyamuni Buddha’s life. Korean Buddhism has left a vast collection of art works on the Buddha's life and teachings, just as the Christian Church has given us great works on important events in the life of Jesus Christ, such as the Annunciation and the Last Supper.   Now, why don’t we take a closer look to each of the paintings. The first painting is on the right of the entrance gate, it illustrated a young child riding an elephant inside a circle located on the upper right. This painting describes how the Buddha came down from the sky to be born as a prince of India. In Buddhism, the white elephant is an auspicious creature symbolizing wisdom and mercy.   The second painting depicting the birth of the Shakyamuni Buddha. At the bottom, you will find a queen who is the Buddha’s mother, standing and holding on to a stick while giving birth through her right side. Upon his birth, the Baby Buddha took seven steps in each of the four directions, and announced his arrival in a loud voice, pointing the heaven and the earth.  The next painting is on the left of the pillar. It shows the Indian prince returning to his palace after witnessing people in pain. The fourth painting on your right depicts the prince leaving the palace to lead an ascetic life and seek the Truth. By then he was a 29-year-old heir apparent to the throne, living happily with his loving wife and children. As the horse riding the Buddha crosses the wall, the four kings suddenly appeared and hold up the hooves of the horse. That is depicted in the upper part of the picture near the cloudy area. You can see the Buddha on a horse, along with many people.  The fifth painting on the right-hand side of the next pillar shown the scene of the prince who spent six years leading an ascetic life on a snow-covered mountain. One day, he realized that all these self-tormenting ascetic practices were of no use, and he finally took a bath in the river after six years. When his five followers found out his decision, they left the prince with disappointment. One time, while the Buddha is in agony under a tree, a young girl named Sujata brought the Buddha some porridge made of milk. The food helped the prince return to life and continue with his meditation. Eventually, he reached to enlightenment and ultimately became Buddha.  The sixth paintings on the left illustrated the background of how the Satan witnessed all this and felt a sense of crisis. There is the Buddha under the barley tree and the Satan in his extravagant outfit. To test the Satan, the Buddha asked him to knock down a small water bottle placed in front of him. Innumerable demon soldiers tied strings to the bottle and start pulling, but the bottle did not move a bit. This very scene of the demon soldiers hanging from the bottle is painted in the picture. Later, the Satan finally acknowledged his defeat and fled.  The seventh painting shows the Buddha spreading his teachings after he defeated the Satan. If you look at the bottom of the picture, the five followers that had left the Buddha are kneeling facing backwards. To the right, there is the final picture showing the Buddha’s death. People generally refer death as “Nirvana”, which means a state of complete freedom from suffering. In the upper part of the picture, where it’s painted blue, reliquaries from the Buddha’s body after his cremation, are pouring down like rainfall.  Looking through the Buddha’s life in paintings is fascinating. Spend some time and appreciate these masterpieces in detail as if you are in an ancient gallery!

stories.title: Beopju Temple: Double-Lion Stone Lantern
stories.script: Double-Lion Stone Lantern   [Traveler] Now we are going to meet a pair of lions that have lighted the precincts of Beopju Temple for 1,300 years. The lions supporting the heavy stone lantern are characterized by sturdy shoulders and buttocks. Some people feel rather sorry about their posture because it looks like as if they are getting punished. Others say that they look very cute and cuddly. The reputation of this particular stone lantern is largely because of the pair of lions. Regarding typical Korean stone lanterns, an octagonal pillar supports the middle part of a stone lantern. But for this one, two lions replaced the pillar.   Remarkably, these two animals are not of the same sex. That’s to say, one is surely a lion and the other a lioness. Can you tell us which is which? Experts say that the one with the wide open mouth saying Ah! is a female, while the other with the closed mouth saying Hum! as if to gather more strength is a male. Ah and Hum are two Sanskrit syllables of a Buddhist mantra, and each represents the beginning and the end of all things in nature. They form an Indian version of Alpha and Omega' in the Greek alphabet, which stands for the first and the last.  Actually, lions were not in Korea at that time. So, some people have wondered how Korean people in the 10th century knew about and carved these foreign animals. The truth is that the lion, along with the elephant, is a symbolic animal of Buddhism. And Buddhism introduced the animals to Korea when it arrived from India via China.   Now I will tell you about an interesting secret hidden somewhere in the lantern. Please take a look at the ceiling of the lantern's light chamber. You might find a white pictograph similar to the sharp symbol. This symbol resembles the Chinese character, which means “a well”. Also, there is even a lotus flower in the well. The image represents the people’s wish to protect the temple from fire.

stories.title: Beopju Temple: Stone Lantern of the Four Heavenly Kings
stories.audioTitle: Stone Lantern of the Four Heavenly Kings
stories.script: Stone Lantern of the Four Heavenly Kings  [Traveler] Let's go and look at the stone lantern standing in the yard in front of the main hall of Beopju Temple. This Stone Lantern of the Four Heavenly Kings is characterized by a roof with corners that curve gently upwards. As I said earlier, these four Buddhist deities are guardians of the Buddhist Law, and you can see them carved between the faces between the light windows.  Please take one step closer to the lantern and look at each of the four guardians closely. The lions of the earlier lantern create a rather cheerful atmosphere, but this lantern is a fine piece of art work exhibiting a unique elegance and dignity. Time has worn the carved images quite significantly, but you can’t miss the artistic value of the elaborate carvings.   A stone lantern is an essential architectural element of a Korean Buddhist temple. It stands in front of the major prayer halls of a temple, shedding light on the world with the Buddhist truths. As in many other religions across the world including Christianity, giving light is a very important symbolic religious act in Korean Buddhism. In particular, lighting a temple with a large lantern is regarded as a great offering to Buddha.

stories.title: Daeungbojeon Hall (Beopjusa Temple, Boeun)
stories.script: Daeungbojeon Hall of Beopjusa Temple  This is the Daeungbojeon Hall, the main hall of Beopjusa Temple. In most Buddhist temples in Korea, the Daeungbojeon Hall is devoted to the Shakyamuni Buddha and forms the central point in the temples. Likewise, this hall can be referred as the heart of the entire Beopjusa Temple precinct. Before you enter the hall, have a look at the pairs of trees standing on both sides of the hall's front section. These are the Bodhi trees, and it is said that the Shakyamuni attained complete enlightenment under these trees. The trees bloom glorious golden flowers in spring and summer as if to celebrate his enlightenment.  The Daeungbojeon Hall of Beopjusa Temple displays a stunningly beautiful appearance and is regarded as one of the three greatest masterpieces of Korean Buddhist architecture. The beauty of the roof is particularly highly praised, as it displays the core characteristic of Korean architectural beauty. For instance, try to follow with your eyes the elegantly curved lines running along the ridges from the top of the roof to the corner eaves. You will find that the delightfully simple and attractive roof lines create a dramatic contrast to the straight lines of most Western architecture.  The beauty of the roof of Korean classical buildings is further enhanced by the ornamental bracket sets under the eaves. These structures of ornately carved wooden brackets have the practical function of dispersing the roof’s weight. Also, they form an important element of the building adornment with their complex geometrical forms. The bracket sets are typically further embellished with even more complex color patterns, although they continue to exhibit their artistic excellence even without it. Some classical buildings are lavishly ornamented with complex bracket clusters, while others exhibit simpler, more controlled ones. For instance, the architecture of Palsangjeon Hall is a fine example of the latter.  Let's now enter the hall where the Shakyamuni Buddha is enshrined.  Can you feel the serene and solemn atmosphere created by the three Buddhas standing at the altar? Unlike Christianity and other religions that worship a unipersonal God, there are many Buddhas in Buddhism. The name Buddha means a person who attained enlightenment, and you can also attain Buddhahood if you can enlighten yourself.  As I explained earlier, all three Buddhas display hand gestures of their own, revealing the content of the Truth they wish to deliver. The Buddha at the center symbolizes the Universe and the Truth. His one hand is covering the index finger of the other hand, and it means that folly and enlightenment are originally one. The one on the left is a Buddha devoted to rescuing sentient beings suffering in the mundane world. His hand gesture reveals that he is summoning the land deity to defeat the Devil King. The Buddha on the right has been devoted to good deeds since time immemorial, and his one palm is raised upwards, and the other is pointing forwards. His hand gesture shows that he is delivering Buddhist teachings to the world.

stories.title: Wontongbojeon Hall (Beopjusa Temple, Boeun)
stories.script: Wontongbojeon Hall of Beopjusa Temple  Let’s make a brief visit to an attractive temple building now. This building was erected to honor a Bodhisattva. As I said earlier, Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva assist Buddha in saving all sentient beings who are suffering in agony. The Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva enshrined in this hall is called Gwanseumbosal in Korean. Gwanseumbosal is widely admired as a deity of compassion and mercy.  Let's enter the hall and have a look at the Wooden Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva.  Although the statue stands an imposing 2.8 meters tall, many feel a sense of intimacy or affinity with the image. It’s probably due to the benign look on the face. She has not yet attained Buddhahood, but her image here is lavishly adorned with a bejeweled headdress and a veiled robe decorated with floral bands. Such Bodhisattva statues are often luxuriously decorated with the same types of ornaments worn by ordinary people in the mundane, everyday world.  When you look at Buddhist images at a temple, you will surely be attracted to the variety of gestures they make with their hands and fingers. These symbolic hand gestures represent what a Buddha or Bodhisattva intends to do to help ease the suffering of sentient beings in this world. The hand gestures of Gwanseumbosal enshrined here reveal that her goal is to save sinners and send them to the most comfortable world.

stories.title: Beopju Temple: Standing Stone Buddhist Saint
stories.script: Standing Stone Buddhist Saint  [Traveler] Now, it's time to see the most mysterious Buddhist saint enshrined in Beopju Temple. The statue is carrying a large bowl with a tray on the head. The identity of the statue is yet to be known.   This figure is not wearing any shoes but displays a half-naked, well-built body standing in a determined manner. Doesn't he look like someone engaged in a very important task? Even the bowl he carries on his head does not look like an ordinary, simple object. Some experts regard him as an apostle of the Shakyamuni Buddha, and his main function is passing on the vessels used by the Buddha to future Buddhas. Still, others believe that he is the carrier of an incense burner who immolates himself to pay respect to the Shakyamuni Buddha. In Buddhism, self-immolation is often regarded as one of the noblest religious acts.  What's your idea about the vessel? Is it a bowl used to hold food or an incense burner?

stories.title: Beopju Temple: Gilt-bronze Future Buddha
stories.script: Gilt-bronze Future Buddha  [Traveler] We are now standing at a huge gilt-bronze Buddha, the main landmark of Beopju Temple. It measures 33 meters in height, and is known as the tallest statue of its kind in the world. Its construction required a large amount of time and energy, all the more so because it is the Future Buddha. The hand gesture shows that he will help people dispel their fears and realize their wishes.   This statue of the Future Buddha had a long history filled with many twists and turns before it acquired its current golden appearance. The Buddha was first erected as a bronze figure 1,200 years ago, when Buddhism was enjoying its prosperous heyday in Korea. This Buddha continued to display its imposing figure for more than 1,000 years. However, 150 years ago, a powerful politician decided to pull it down and use the bronze to mint coins, because he believed it would help the country overcome the financial crisis of that time. The statue was then restored as a cement work in 1939 by a local sculptor who hoped the Future Buddha would help liberate his country from the oppression of the Japanese colonial rulers. Unfortunately, the statue began to sustain damage before long and had to be transformed into a new bronze work. The bronze had to be gilded later on to prevent it from rusting. The thickness of the gold foil used for the gilding is only 0.003 millimeters, but the whole statue required as much as 80 kilograms of gold in total.   Why did the Korean people of more than one thousand years ago want to build such a big Buddha statue? According to a local legend, the Shakyamuni statue was 4 meters tall. It’s because his followers in later periods wanted to express their admiration for him by making his statue larger than life size. Some also wanted a taller Buddha because it would help him look farther and guide more creatures to the right path. Their decision may have been proved right because quite a few travelers visit the temple to have a look at this tall, imposing Buddha.

stories.title: Beopju Temple: Stone Lotus Basin
stories.script: Stone Lotus Basin  [Traveler] This stone basin was made about 1,200 years ago. Why do you think the old Korean Buddhists made this strange stone work? For use as a kitchen pot like the huge iron cauldron we saw earlier? I am afraid not. This stone basin is called a Seoknyeonji, and it means a stone pond in the shape of a lotus flower. Usually, lotuses are grown in a pond, but the maker of this stone work seems to have wanted to contain a pond in a lotus flower. Quite amazing, isn't it?  The outer part of the basin is heavily embellished with carved lotus petals. In Buddhism, the lotus symbolizes pure nobility because it blooms beautifully clean flowers even in dirty muddy water. The little pillar supporting the lower part of the flower features clouds which represent the lotus in heaven. Hence, this lotus pond is not of earth but of heaven. What is amazing is the artistic courage and creativity of the stone carver, who clearly wanted to turn the heavy stone into a light cloud.   The basin was used as a pond for floating lotus blossoms, but today it remains dried due to a crack. Just imagine the fully open lotus flowers floating in a small manmade pool in the shape of a lotus blossom.

stories.title: Beopju Temple: Iron Flagpole
stories.script: Iron Flagpole  [Travel] What do you think this iron pole was used for? Iron poles like this one are easily found in Korean Buddhist temples because they were widely used in the past. What kind of flags did they hoist on poles like this, then? Mostly, they hoisted temple flags to indicate the denomination each temple belonged to or flags bearing an ode to the greatness of Buddha.  This particular flagpole was also used to signal that the nearby area was a sacred place. The custom is closely related with the folk tradition. In Korea, people erected a long piece of bamboo or a wooden pole at the village entrance as its guardian.  These iron poles generally measured 22 meter in height and 30 centimeters in diameter. So, a special device was required to fix such huge poles to the ground. Please look down at the pair of stone blocks that are as tall as a man. They are tightly fastened to each other by iron bands. The original relics were heavily damaged by time and were later replaced by these newly restored supports. I hope that these stone supports and the flagpoles will be safely preserved for future generations.

stories.title: Beopju Temple: Seated Rock-carved Buddha
stories.script: Seated Rock-carved Buddha  [Traveler] Let's move to a rock cliff carved with a Buddha image, which attracts Buddhist followers from all over the country. The Buddha is carved in low relief on a rock cliff, but it has been preserved for about a millennium. While other images carved on the front of the large rock have been worn away, this particular image has survived to reveal the original condition.  This Buddhist image is regarded as a rare piece of art largely because of the position it takes. The Buddhist figure is seated on a fully-bloomed lotus flower.  Please look at the figure's characteristic curly hair style. The conch-shaped hair is one of many characteristic physical features of the Buddha. But what is truly remarkable is the skill that the carver used to create such a fine piece of art work. Just imagine how hard and intricate was the working process required to carve these clear-cut images in such a high place.

stories.title: Seon Byeong-guk’s House: From the Rear Gate to the Front Gate
stories.audioTitle: From the Rear Gate to the Front Gate
stories.script: From the Rear Gate to the Front Gate  [Traveler] The gate you can see from the parking lot is the rear gate of Seon Byeong-guk’s house. Let’s walk along the stone fence to find the front gate.  Let me tell you a bit about the history of this house while we’re walking to the front gate.  This Korean traditional house was built by Seon Jeong-hun and took ten years to complete. Today, Seon Byeong-guk, the son of Seon Jeong-hun is the owner of this house, and hence called Seon Byeong-guk’s House. Seon Jeong-hun chose this place as the best and most auspicious site to build a house because it is suffused with the clean and pure spirit of Songni Mountain. He believed that if he built a house on this site, his descendants would prosper.  However, he ran into an unexpected problem while building the house. The villagers were jealous that strangers who had appeared from nowhere could build such a huge house here, so they set fire on the building materials and burnt all the timber. This meant the Seon family had to spend more time preparing new materials and wood, which is why it took a total of 10 years to build, although the actual construction period was only three years. Also, Seon Jeong-hun hired carpenters who had worked on the king’s palace. The work required highly sophisticated and exquisite management, and Seon Jeong-hun treated the workers to feasts of meat every three days. That’s how much he valued the house.  Back in the days of the Joseon Dynasty, only royal palaces were allowed to be built with dimensions of more than 100 kan. Kan is a unit of measurement which refers to the space between two columns. But such regulations were relaxed later on, and new construction methods became available, allowing Seon Jeong-hun to work on this house, which displayed a traditional Korean beauty. Originally, Seon Byeong-guk’s house measured 138 kan, but parts of the building have been lost over the years and it now measures about 110 kan in total.   This traditional house exhibits some of the common characteristics shared by houses built in the modern period in Korea. The walkway with its stone fence is a fine example of this. If you go around the corner to the front gate, you will find a towering gate. Opposite the gate, there is a memorial stone and a pine tree forest. Shall we move to the front of the memorial stone?

stories.title: Seon Byeong-guk’s House: Memorial Stones
stories.script: Memorial Stones  [Traveler] Newspapers and TV sometimes feature news about rich people contributing their wealth to less fortunate people, and you’ll be hearing about one more similar story here from the Joseon Period. The person in question was from the Seon family, who made a fortune by trading goods. His generosity to the poor is commemorated by these memorial stones. Let’s take a closer look at the four stones one by one.  The memorial stone standing furthest to the right was set up by one of the most intelligent scholars of Chinese literature to celebrate Mr. Seon’s love for students. He supported poor students with free tuition, board and lodging so that they could continue learning from good teachers. This memorial stone represents his heart-warming generosity towards the poor.  The memorial stone to the left of the first stone was granted by the government in recognition of his huge contribution to the construction of royal tombs when the national economy was in a bad situation. He was also given a position in government but declined the offer.  Can you see another small memorial stone to the left? It was erected by the villagers to express their gratitude to the Seon family. In lean years, he imported crops from China and shared them with the village, and also provided acres of land for free.  The last memorial stone on the far left is not actually a stone, but is made of metal, which is quite rare in Korea. It looks old and rusty, but it still shows the message of appreciation dedicated to Mr. Seon for sharing land and paying taxes for them.  There is a small door to the left. Inside there is another memorial stone which was erected in memory of the devoted sons and virtuous ladies of the Seon family. Let’s go inside.

stories.title: Seon Byeong-guk’s House: Hyoyeol Monument Pavilion
stories.script: Hyoyeol Monument Pavilion  [Traveler] You have to lower your head to enter this pavilion. The entrance was built with such a low ceiling in order to compel visitors to show their respect.  Korea has been deeply influenced by Chinese Confucianism, of which one of the most important virtues was filial piety. In order to promote this virtue, memorial stones for the most devoted sons and daughters around the country were established, so that people could follow their example. The memorial stone you are looking at now was made for a devoted son named Seon Cheo-heum and his wife. I have some stories to tell you about those respectable people.  One day, Seon Cheo-heum’s father had a serious problem with his eye. Seon was nursing his father and tried to find the right medicine, but it was not an easy task. A doctor told Seon that the meat of a hawk would cure the disease in no time, so Seon set about looking for a store that sold hawk meat, but all his efforts were in vain. Eventually Seon decided to go to the mountains to catch a hawk himself, but didn't know how to do what first. So he prayed, and a hawk descended to the nearby ground for him. He caught the hawk and cooked it for his father. It really worked and his father quickly felt better, meaning that more hawk meat was needed. Wishing for his father’s full recovery, Seon climbed up the mountain again in a heavy snowstorm.  In the end, Seon’s sincere prayer worked again. Another hawk came to him and he was able to serve his father with hawk meat to completely cure the disease after much suffering.  Also, it is said that Seon’s wife also nursed her husband with the utmost care when he was suffering from a terrible disease. Her virtuous deed is also commemorated by the memorial stone standing here.

stories.title: Seon Byeong-guk’s House: The Tall Gate and Outer Quarters
stories.audioTitle: The Tall Gate and Outer Quarters
stories.script: The Tall Gate and Outer Quarters  [Traveler] When you enter the gate, you will find a building standing amidst refreshing scenery. Called the sarangchae, or outer quarters, this structure was designed for male guests of the house. They would spend their time there reading books and taking rests. In other words, this room had similar purposes to those of today's reception room. Each side of the room is hidden by a fence, which is a unique feature of this traditional house.  That orange, tin-roofed building is a bathroom. The hole in the floor indicates that it is very old. Korean traditional houses were usually constructed with beautiful tiles, and tin was a rare and expensive material back then.   We are in front of the outer quarters. The building looks like an “H” from above, and half of the “H” is attached in the back. What you’re looking at is an example of the general structure of a traditional house.  Let’s take a closer look. From the three granite stones, other stones under the pillars, and to railings around the two wings, all these components exude richness and prosperity. Notably, the pillars are not square-shaped like those of ordinary houses, but are rounded like the pillars of royal palaces. Their great width also make a magnificent impression.  Now let’s look at the roof – have you noticed its triangular shape? That’s typical of Korean traditional houses. The colors of the bricks and tiles seem mysterious. Down there is a long pole on the eaves for some atmospheric appearance. I wouldn’t mind spending some free time relaxing on the spacious floor under the eaves.  Speaking of free time, these outer quarters have a café, which opens from 11 am to 9 pm, except at weekends and during holidays. Teas brewed with the sincerity of the owner are available. Looking out to the garden from the room made of thick logs and soil would feel different from what you see from the outside.

stories.title: Seon Byeong-guk’s House: Servants’ Quarters and Inner Quarters
stories.script: Servants’ Quarters and Inner Quarters  [Traveler]  Now, we will look at the anchae, which are the inner quarters. These were mainly frequented by ladies. I’ll give you more details later about that. Let’s take a look at this door to the inner quarters. It has a lock inside to maintain the privacy of the women living here.  Opposite the door is a house with walls of red clay. This is the haengnangchae, which means an annex next to the main gate. It used to be occupied by servants, but nowadays it is occupied by candidates for national examinations. Let’s take a quiet stroll around the building and move into the inner quarters.   Recently, soybean paste, Korean chili paste and soy sauce have been available for purchase at the inner quarters under the brand name of “Adanggol.” This is another popular name associated with the Seon family, whose long history guarantees a rich flavor. You can also make those pastes or pickled vegetables yourself while staying at this Korean traditional house.   Now let’s enter the inner quarters. Both the outer quarters and the inner quarters form part of the H-shaped structure, which connects seamlessly to the interior, creating a comfortable space. The inner quarters were cozy spaces for the ladies who lived here. The floor was made of a soft soil and emitted warmth. Did you notice several layers of fence on the way inside? They too were designed to maintain the privacy of the ladies.  Though it’s not noticeable from outside, here we can see a long supporting beam with its natural curves maintained across the ceiling. It is highly representative of the Koreans’ aesthetic sensibility, who hope to preserve natural features as much as possible.    Can you see the characters engraved beneath the roof? They say that “the biggest pleasure in life is to practice goodness, which fits quite well with the Seon family’s history of sharing wealth with their neighbors. Behind the inner quarters is a big kitchen, an exclusive space for women. The food containers and dishes will give you an idea of how Korean women managed their households. Take your time to look around here and then meet me at the shrine at the rear of the building.

stories.title: Seon Byeong-guk’s House: Shrine
stories.script: Shrine  [Traveler] Here, we are in a Korean ancestral shrine. China and Japan also have similar shrines where people pay their respects to their ancestors, but the Korean shrine falls somewhere between Chinese shrines in terms of their large scale and splendid appearance, and Japanese shrines in terms of their simplicity and aura of calmness. A more controlled and moderated beauty can be found in Korean shrines.  The shrine in Seon Byeong-guk’s house is located on higher ground than the inner and outer quarters that we've just visited. This feature was intended to provide more dignity to the building, while the long distance between the gate and the shrine was made in consideration of the topography and the other buildings here.   The shrine has three entrances, of which the central one is for the ancestral gods. It is kept open during memorial ceremonies so that the gods can go in and out freely. You are supposed to enter through the door on the right and leave through the one on the left.  The shrine of Seon Byeong-guk’s house is a little different from other shrines. Each space has a door like the one between the main hall and a room, so it is often mistaken for a small outer quarter. The shrine consists of three layers of stones piled up on flat ground with stone steps built at the center.   The most unique feature of this shrine is its small annex, which was used for storing containers and cooking foods for memorial ceremonies. It is connected with a roofed corridor to enable the convenient delivery of food. It also shows how much respect the family accorded to their ancestors.

stories.title: Near the Birthplace of Jeong Ji-yong
stories.audioTitle: Near the Birthplace of Jeong Ji-yong
stories.script: Near the Birthplace of Jeong Ji-yong   [Traveler] Streams and low mountaintops surrounding the town – this is a typical farming town scenery in Korea. In 1902, Jeong Ji-yong, a representative poet of Korea, was born here. In the year he turned 22, he wrote a love poem, <Nostalgia>, for his hometown. This poem was later made into a song, and became very popular with the public. You can listen to the original song in the memorial hall right near here.  The poem <Nostalgia> describes the typical farming town scenery of Korea in a delicate, lyrical fashion. A typical scene from the poet’s hometown includes streams, spotty yellow cows, humble thatched houses, families gathering around dim lights, a tired father lying down on a straw pillow, a gleaning young sister and barefoot wife, mind grown from soil. All these create a pastoral scene much like those depicted in the French artist Millet’s [Angelus] and [Gleaners].    Leaving his beloved hometown behind, he crossed the sea and went to Japan. While studying abroad and experiencing a different culture and another world in Kyoto, Japan, he wrote the modernist poem <Café Frans>. This poem describes young people heading to Café Frans on a rainy day. He compares young men wearing Bohemian neckties to ‘swallows soaked in rain,’ and a gloomy mind to a ‘worm-eaten rose.’ In this poem, he describes the sorrow and lamentation of intellectuals who had to leave their colonial homes in Korea to study. The poem also reveals a sense of deep loneliness. Around this time, he published works in both the Korean and Japanese literary worlds and built up his reputation as a poet. You can see the translated version of <Café Frans> in the Memorial hall.   Now, shall we go to the birthplace of Jeong, which was restored in 1996. Let’s wind up the story in the place he was born. While we’re making our way to his birthplace, listen to <Nostalgia>.    < NOSTALGIA >  The place where a rill, babbling old tales,  Meanders on eastward toward the end  of a broad plain  And a mottled bull ox lows  In dusk's plaintive tones  of golden indolence-   Could it ever be forgotten, even in one's dreams?   The place where ashes grow cold in a clay brazier  While over empty fields the sound of the night wind  drives the horses  And our aged father, overcome with drowsiness,  Props his straw pillow-   Could it ever be forgotten, even in one's dreams?   The place where I got drenched  in the rank weeds'dew,  Searching for an arrow recklessly shot  In the yearning of my earth-bred heart  For the sky's lustrous blue-   Could it ever be forgotten, even in one's dreams?   The place where little sister, dark earlocks  Flying like night waves dancing in a fairy-tale sea,  And my wife, not pretty but passable  and all the year barefoot,  Bent their backs to the sun's tingling rays and  gleaned ears of grain-   Could it ever be forgotten, even in one's dreams?  The place where sprinkled stars  wend their way in the sky  Toward sand castles just beyond our ken,  While beneath drab roofs,  hoary crows cawing past,  People sit, softly murmuring,  round the faint firelight-   Could it ever be forgotten, even in one's dreams?

stories.title: Birthplace of Jeong Ji-yong
stories.script: Birthplace of Jeong Ji-yong  [Traveler] We can see Cheongseok Bridge and a stream here. This is where the poet Jeong Ji-yong was born and raised. He showed outstanding talent in literature, even when he was in high school, where he produced a literature magazine with his friends.  He wrote sensuous poems that generated clear images of the emotions, by comparing emotions to objects rather than directly expressing them. A few examples include ‘a soaked star’ and ‘clear glass’ to symbolize sadness and a ‘crowd of blue lizards’ is used to picture a wave.  Upon completing his studies in Japan, he returned in Korea in 1929 and worked as an English teacher in the high school he graduated from. He was passionate about educating the future generations.  When socialism swept the world in 1930, it had a profound influence on his literary world. The School of ‘Poetry Literature,’ which included Jeong Ji-yong, took Korean poetry to the next level with its superb techniques. In the autumn of 1935, his first book of poetry was published and he became the best poet of the 1930s. He also introduced the major talents of Korean literature to the world.   Jeong Ji-yong was loved and respected by many. But his departure from us was too sudden. When the country was plunged into chaos by the Korean War, he went out one day and never came back. The government concluded that he had entered North Korea and consequently banned his poems. His great poems, which brought great delight to many of us, were banned for a while. Jeong never came back, but the ban was fortunately lifted in 1988. Anywhere you go in Okcheon, his poems are there. Any Korean citizen who became nostalgic for their home would turn to his poems. The poets and scholars who loved him created an organization for him, and the Okcheon Literature Festival is held every May to celebrate his poetry.   As a poet who majored in English literature, Jeong elevated the beauty of Korean language into a unique and mature form. If you wish to learn more about him, we recommend participating in the festival in May. In the next course in the exhibition hall, you can enjoy his poems and poetry. You’ll find yourself immersed in his poetry in no time.

stories.title: Okcheon Confucian School
stories.script: Okcheon Confucian School  [Traveler] On the way up to this Confucian school, the first thing you will see are the red doors. Red doors were built in dignified buildings such as palaces, lecture halls, and Confucian schools. To the right, there is a headstone inscribed with the words: “Get down from your horse and walk from here.” As the saying suggests, this place is very solemn and important.   Confucian schools were built by government offices to educate local residents and hold commemorative rites for great scholars during the Joseon Dynasty. In 1398, the king who founded the Joseon Dynasty built Okcheon Confucian school. It consists of an educational facility for students at its front and a shrine for commemorative rites at the back.   Now, are you at the entrance to the Confucian school? The big building you saw on the way up here was the lecture hall, where students used to learn. The building to the right, which stands opposite the lecture hall on the left of the entrance, is a shrine to Confucius of China and Korean scholars.   As a place of education and ritual, even the building’s location and position follow strict rules. Let’s look at the lecture hall first. The splendid roof with the ears pointing upwards is a traditional style of Joseon architecture designed to avoid rain with wide eaves. The wide floor was used to hold lectures, and the teachers dwelled in the two rooms. For heating, the traditional under floor heating system called ondol was used.  Now let’s look at the shrine across the lecture room. There’s a reason why the entrance consists of three doors. The middle door was built for deities, so ordinary people didn’t use it. It was customary to enter through the door on the right and exit through the one on the left.  The roof looks different from the one we saw before. It looks like a half-closed book hanging on the top. This type of Korean roof architecture has its own meaning. For buildings that emphasized tradition, such as shrines, a simple and humble roof was used, while for residential buildings such as schools and temples, more extravagant roofs were used.   During the Joseon Dynasty, Confucius’ teachings were selected by the elite as the national ideology, and the general way of life including customs, manners and traditions were formed within a Confucian framework. That’s why the ancestral tablets of Confucius, the founder of Confucianism, and those of four additional scholars are housed inside this shrine. It also houses the tablets of 18 people who contributed to the development of Korean Confucianism.   Finally, the humble building between the hall and the shrine is a dormitory for students. Originally, there were an east building and a west building, but only the latter remains now. The next course will take us to where Korea’s first lady used to live. We will see a traditional Korean house there. Shall we move on?

stories.title: Birthplace of Yook Young-soo 1
stories.script: Birthplace of Yook Young-soo  [Traveler] When we evaluate a person, we look at where the person was born and raised. Lady Yook Young-soo resembles the cozy geography and rivers of Okcheon. She was the first lady of President Park Chung-hee, who left a significant mark on Korean history. Many people who still remember her, visit this place, as she grew up here.    President Park Chung-hee is one of the most important people in the modern history of Korea. While he was in office during the 1960 and ‘70s, Korea accomplished record economic growth, which is known as ‘The Miracle of the Han River.’ But his opponents criticized him as an enemy of democracy.   Yook Young-soo was born here in 1925, graduated from high school, and worked as a teacher in a middle school. When the Korean War broke out, she escaped to Busan, met Park, and married him. She was 26 years old then, and became the first lady of Korea 12 years later.  Although she was at the center of an important change in Korean history, she is remembered as a humble and upright person. She frequently visited leper colonies and slums and helped the poor and sick, and she always lived a thrifty life. Koreans remember her as a person who suited Korean traditional dress the best, and as a person with a gracious quality.   Also, she critically and objectively delivered certain truths to the President. People called her the opposition party of the Cheongwadae. In 1974, when she was 50 years old, she was killed by an assassin who was after the President. Many Koreans mourned her death and shed tears. Now, let’s take a look at the house she lived in.   In addition to being her birthplace, this house is an important heritage that shows the style of housing enjoyed by modern rich people. It is constructed in the upper class style of the 17th century Joseon Dynasty.   The entrance alone tells us that this house is pretty big. After entering by the traditional Joseon-style gate, you will see a detached house for guests. The building that looks to be hidden right behind the detached house is the main building where the women lived. There’s the room that she used to live in until she left this house. If you go around the front of the main building and head to the back, you will see her small, humble room.  Let’s take a look around. There are photos and writings about her all around the house. Among the many exhibited writings, one concerns her folksy and open-minded thoughts.
