She cooked noodles for soldiers on Christmas Eve, and crossed the Han River in a boat during a flood to encourage isolated people. She also gave 20 female pigs to a leper village as a gift, and those pigs gave birth to piglets and financially helped the poor lepers of the village. After her death, the president wrote many poems expressing his longing for her. The poems are so mournful that you can feel his heartache and sorrow when reading them.

stories.title: Birthplace of Yook Young-soo 2
stories.script: Coming Out  [Traveler] Okcheon gave birth to the poet Jung Ji-yong and First Lady Yook Young-soo. There’s a road here that commemorates them. It’s known as the ‘30-ri of Nostalgia’ course, which runs from the Jung Ji-yong Literature Museum to the Great New World. There’s an elementary school about 10 minutes by foot from here that both Jung Ji-yong and Yook Young-soo attended. Also, about a 15-minute drive away, is a small park called the Great New World, next to Daecheong Lake. The walkway consists of statues depicting images from Jung’s poems. In spring, the road to ‘Great New World’ is covered in white cherry blossom trees, creating an artistic masterpiece.   There’s also an outdoor café with 19 poems and traces of writers still living today. ‘Great New World’ is an art belt of the utopia that poets dreamed of. It’s a place of utopia project – presenting a harmony among poetry, literature, art, and education. In Okcheon, literature and nature come together in a harmonious marriage. Pay a visit to this place and indulge in nostalgia created by virtuous people.

stories.title: Nangye Gugak Village: From the Entrance to the Achievements of Nangye
stories.audioTitle: From the Entrance to the Achievements of Nangye
stories.script: From the Entrance to the Achievements of Nangye   [Traveler] Master Park Yeon is better known by his pen name, Nangye, which literally means “orchid and stream”, reflecting his enthusiasm for orchids. He was born here in Yeongdong in 1378, and grew to become one of the three greatest musicians in Korean history. Park Yeon also represents the musical achievement of the Joseon Dynasty, Korea's last kingdom, which existed from the late 14th to the early 20th century. He won the favor of King Sejong, the creator of the Korean alphabet known as hangeul, and under his auspices invented Korea’s unique twelve-note scale and the musical instruments required to play it, as well as studying Chinese court music for systematic arrangements of Korean folk music. Now, let’s enter the museum to learn more about the life and achievements of this master musician.   You can see his bust in this room, and the entrance to the exhibition hall is on your left.   Do you see the chronological chart hung on the wall? It contains information on the development of Korean music. On the opposite side are exhibits related with the life of Park Yeon. And as for those golden sticks placed side by side in the display case, Master Park Yeon has this to tell us.  [Park Yeon] Hello, everyone! The metal tubes in the display case are called Twelve-pitch Pipes. They can correctly make the twelve sounds of Korean music mentioned in the historic records when they are blown. The sounds became standards for the sounds of other instruments. Tuning other instruments was difficult, if not impossible, without this instrument.   [Traveler] It’s amazing to know that Korean traditional music has twelve scales.   [Park Yeon] The pentatonic scale is the norm, but they are hard to create musical harmony. So I had to make the more balance twelve scales. I will tell you how.   [Traveler] Please do!  [Park Yeon] His majesty King Sejong generously granted me a position in the government, expecting me to help liberate Korean musical theories and instruments from the Chinese heritage. It was a period when Joseon had just emerged and hence needed new systems to represent it, and music was one of them. I was encouraged to focus on the court music, first of all, and to study the existing music books, correct the scales, collect and recreate court music scores, and create new instruments. His commitment to Korean music resulted in the creation of an instrument known as the pyeongyeong, or stone chimes, and then, finally, the pipes displayed before you.  [Traveler] Your explanation makes me look at the instrument from a different point of view. Now I can see that the instrument was a valuable object regarding the Korean traditional 12-pitch pipes. And, by the way, what kind of musical instrument are the stone chimes you invented?   [Park Yeon] The manufacturing process of the instrument is displayed at the next exhibit, let's go see.   The instrument over there, which is similar to the pyeongyeong but is hung with bells rather than chimes, was imported from China. The bells are made of iron so their sounds are subject to change according to changes in the weather. The pyeongyeong, however, is not influenced by the weather and makes a constant sound because the chimes are made of stone. If you look at the chimes more closely you will find that all the chimes have different thicknesses which means they resonate at a different pitch.   Now, let’s move on to the next exhibits. There you will see a scene composed of miniature figurines and other objects that represent musicians performing Jongmyo Jeryeak (Ceremonial Music of the Royal Ancestral Shrine of Joseon) to honor the royal ancestors of the Joseon Dynasty.

stories.title: Nangye Gugak Village: A Scene of Jongmyo Jeryeak with Miniature Model Figures
stories.audioTitle: A Scene of Jongmyo Jeryeak with Miniature Model Figures
stories.script: A Scene of Jongmyo Jeryeak with Miniature Model Figures   [Park Yeon] The model figures shown here represent a ceremonial musical performance regularly held at the Jongmyo Shrine to honor the royal ancestors of the Joseon Dynasty. The building enshrining the memorial tablets of Joseon’s royal ancestors displays a majestic feature. Jongmyo was one of the most revered and sacred state institutions in the Neo-confucian dynasty and a venue for seasonal rites held to honor royal ancestors of the dynasty. The rites, called Jongmyo Jerye, consist of the actual rituals accompanied by songs and dances performed by 64 players in red robes to an accompaniment of grand orchestral music.   You are now listening to the music of Jongmyo Jeryeak. The original music played during the ritual was derived from the Chinese court, but King Sejong of the Joseon Dynasty thought it was inappropriate.   [King Sejong] My ancestors enjoyed folk music when they were alive, so it will be very sad if they have to hear Chinese music in heaven.   [Park Yeon] That is how today’s music for the royal ancestral memorial rites became based on Korean folk music. His Majesty’s interest in music also resulted in the publication of music books we never had before, and the invention of new musical instruments. The effort to replace Chinese court music with Korean folk music contributed to the formation of a rich and concrete musical foundation for both ordinary people and the ruling class, including the royal family. Now we Koreans have finally equipped ourselves with the power to enjoy Korean music.    [Traveler] How wonderful! So, it is you and King Sejong who played a crucial role in establishing Korean music’s rightful position in Korean history.   [Park Yeon] It took as long as ten years to invent the Twelve-pitch Pipes and get them to produce the twelve correct sounds. I kept failing continually, but His Majesty King Sejong never wavered in his support for me and for the project.   [Traveler] So he had full confidence in you.  [Park Yeon] My study of music would have been impossible without his support and encouragement. The development of Korean music would have been badly affected, too.   [Traveler] The Jongmyo Jeryeak is now included on UNESCO’s World Heritage list. It is quite amazing to think that this ritual music has survived the turbulence of Joseon’s five-hundred-year history and is still performed today.   [Park Yeon] The annual performance of the ritual music takes place on the first Sunday of May at Jongmyo Shrine as part of the royal ancestral memorial rite of the Joseon Dynasty. I hope you will enjoy this unique and wonderful event.

stories.title: Nangye Gugak Village: String Instruments
stories.script: String Instruments  [Traveler] In this exhibition room you will be introduced to Korean traditional musical instruments and the sounds they make. Let’s start with stringed instruments, whose sound is produced by plucking, striking, or drawing a bow over the taut strings.   If Western stringed instruments are represented by the violin and cello, Korean stringed instruments are represented by the geomungo and gayageum, both of which are zithers with a long, rectangular body, with six and twelve strings, respectively. The two instruments displayed before you may look similar, but the six-stringed instrument produces low-pitched male sounds while the twelve-stringed instrument emits high-pitched female sounds. Let's now listen to a short piece of music played on the geomungo.   And this is the sound of the gayageum.   The gayageum and geomungo are divided into several different types according to the techniques used to play them and the sounds they produce. The geomungo, for instance, is largely divided into two types: the geum, which is larger than the other and has a colorful body, and the seul, which has a smaller, back body. In Korea, a happily married couple is often compared with the two instruments, which create a wonderful harmony when played together. Listen!   Beside them is another stringed instrument, called a bipa, which has a shape similar to that of ordinary guitars, and next to it are three gonghus whose shape is comparable to that of the harp. In fact, they say that the prototype of the gonghu was born in ancient Egypt and transmitted to Europe to become the harp as it is known today. Sadly, no one really knows how to play the instrument. The flat instrument displayed beneath the gonghu is ayanggeum, or Western dulcimer, whose characteristic features include iron strings. The player strikes the strings with a bamboo hammer to produce sounds. I wonder what kind of tunes it can make.

stories.title: Nangye Gugak Village: Wind Instruments
stories.script: Wind Instruments  [Traveler] This room contains a large number of interesting instruments. I can see, for instance, a shell trumpet called a nagak, and a saenghwang, which is similar to the bagpipes of Scotland, and then a hun, which looks like an ocarina. I wonder what attractive sounds they can make. I am dying to hear them. First, let's hear the sounds of the nagak, whose pitch height is dependent upon its size.   The next instrument, the saenghwang, consists of several pipes gathered together just like bagpipes, and is the only Korean instrument that can produce chordal sounds. It makes sound when air is blown into it and also when it is blown out, just like a harmonica does. Let’s hear it.   Next is the hun. Most of the remaining instruments are painted black because they were used at state memorial rites. This particular hun exhibited here, however, has a beautiful jade blue color. Let's see what sound it makes.

stories.title: Nangye Gugak Village: Percussion Instruments
stories.script: Percussion Instruments  [Traveler] Can you see the green wooden box among the exhibited instruments? It is called a chuk, an instrument played to signal the start of a performance. You play it by striking the wooden stick put into the hole of the box. The sound symbolizes the act of waking up the darkness.  The tiger-shaped instrument beside the chuk is an eo. The instrument is played by scraping the protrusions on its back with a bamboo stick. This instrument is played to end a performance of court music. It is placed to the west of the orchestra whereas the chuk, the instrument played to start a performance, is placed to the east. The location of the two instruments is related with the movement of the sun, which rises from the east and sets in the west.  You have been introduced to some musical instruments and their sounds, that best represent the musical heritage of the Joseon Dynasty. Now we will guide you to the hall where you can experience these Korean traditional instruments via a touch screen.

stories.title: Nangye Gugak Village: Gugak Instrument Experience Hall
stories.script: Gugak Instrument Experience Hall (Floor 1)  [Traveler] We are now on the first floor of the Gugak Instrument Experience Hall. Press a button to hear the sounds of the traditional instruments, including the melody of Arirang, one of the most widely known Korean folk songs. You can even try playing the gayageum.  After this exciting cultural experience, why don’t you visit the birthplace of Master Park Yeon, which is very close by, and his shrine, where memorial rites are performed regularly to honor his life and achievements. Don’t forget that the Okgye Falls, a renowned tourist attraction widely known as the place where Master Park Yeon liked to play the bamboo flute to praise the surrounding beautiful landscape, are also situated nearby. stories.title: Paldalmun
stories.script: Paldalmun  This is the southern gate of the Suwon Hwaseong Fortress, ‘Paldalmun’. The name ‘Paldal’ has the interesting meaning of “being open to all directions”. The Paldalmun was built in order to protect the Hwaseong Fortress. It had a semicircle shaped Ongseong standing on the outside, and had a device that allowed soldiers to dump hot water on enemies climbing the wall.  When the Hwaseong Fortress was being constructed, there was a policy which required people involved in the construction to engrave their names on the building. It was to give pride to those working for the construction of the fortress. Their names were engraved on the buildings, and the outer stone wall of the Paldalmun. You can check the engraved names and numbers of the people who built the gate.  As a representative palace gate of the second half of the Joseon Dynasty, the Paldalmun has been designated a National Treasure No.402.

stories.title: Namchi
stories.script: A bastion known as 'chi' was constructed to jut outward from a fortress wall, serving as a defensive position against approaching enemies. The name 'chi' originates from Chinese characters denoting 'pheasant' because of the pheasant's adeptness at hiding and peering. Hwaseong Fortress features ten bastions strategically positioned at regular intervals, approximately every 150 meters. Each bastion's configuration varies, adapting to the surrounding terrain.  Namchi, literally translated as the Southern Bastion, stands among these fortified structures. Positioned between Paldalmun (South Gate) and Namporu (Southern Sentry Post), Namchi was erected on a steep western slope, resulting in a shorter and narrower structure compared to other bastions situated on flat terrains. What sets Namchi apart is its inclusion of a small staircase leading inside. Remarkably, Namchi has maintained its original shape over time.

stories.title: Namporu
stories.script: Poru, also known as artillery pavilions, protrude outward and were utilized for attacking enemies by housing artillery called ‘Hwapo’ within them. These pavilions are structured across three floors. The lower level was designated for artillery storage, while the upper levels served as vantage points for soldiers to surveil the surrounding area and engage the enemy using firearms and arrows. Soldiers fired upon approaching enemies through holes in the fortress walls. Hwaseong Fortress features a total of five artillery pavilions, with Namporu situated to the south of the fortress.  These artillery pavilions were distinctive facilities introduced during the latter half of the Joseon Dynasty, scarcely found in traditional settlements and mountain fortresses prior to the construction of Suwon Hwaseong. Among the five artillery pavilions within Hwaseong Fortress, Namporu remains in the best original condition.

stories.title: Seonam Ammun and Seonamposa
stories.script: Seonam Ammun, Seonamposa  The Fortress had several secret gates here and there, which permitted people to move around unnoticed by the enemies. The Seonamammun was one of them. Ammun is a military facility set up in a deep and secluded spot, through which war supplies would be secretly carried into or taken out from a castle. In a case of emergency, the gate should be closed and covered up with stones and earth so that enemies could not find it.  As the Seonamammun was located close the Seonam Gangnu, the command post, and the Yongdogil, which was a road used to move military provisions, the gate was considered to be among the especially important among secret gates. This is why the Seonam Gangnu has a building attached to it unlike other such gates Yongdo Road is seen in a movie entitled Man of the King.  Normally, the secret gates did not have buildings above them, as they were meant to be hidden from the enemies. But the Seonamammun had a structure called the Posa, which was used to observe the enemy and relay signals. It was more of a guard post, and did not have offensive facilities.

stories.title: Seonam Gangnu
stories.script: Seonam Gangnu  The Gakru was used as the military command post during emergencies, and there were a total of 4 Gakrus in the Fortress, the Seonam Gangnu being one of them. It was situated in an elevated area, and was therefore suitable for observing the situation both inside and outside of the Fortress. Its proximity to the Yongdogil also made it a strategically important point during wars.  On the other hand, there was a great chance of having our troops’ situation being exposed if the enemies occupy the Seonam Gangnu. This was why there is a long wall built along the side up to the mountain, so that enemies unaccustomed to the local geography would not be able to see everything. The Seonam Gangnu was also called the “Hwayangru”, which meant a structure built to the south of the Hwaseong Fortress.

stories.title: Seosamchi
stories.script: Seosamchi, literally meaning the Western Bastion, is a structure projecting outward from the wall, designed to repel approaching enemies. Hwaseong Fortress comprises 10 bastions, and one of them is Seosamchi, measuring only about four meters wide.  Seosamchi is a Chiseong located between Seoporu or the Western Guard Pavilion and Seonamammun or the Southwestern Secret Entrance. Chiseong structures were typically built solely with Seonggakwi. However, due to the uneven ground, various facilities were installed to protect the fortress, resulting in curves and sharp edges within the fortress walls. Seosamchi is characterized by its Seonggakwi, which slightly bends inwards towards Hwaseong Fortress. Seonggakwi served as a low wall within the fortress, enabling Joseon soldiers to defend themselves while repelling enemy attacks.

stories.title: Seongshinsa
stories.script: Seongshinsa  The Seongshinsa was a shrine which venerated the gods of the Hwaseong Fortress. King Jungjo himself would write the scripts for the veneration rites and oversee the ceremony, showing his affection for the place. The Seongshinsa is also the only shrine the Japanese Empire altered. The Japanese originally planned to build a Shinto shrine at its place, but as furious citizens blocked it, the Seongshinsa structure was moved to the side. The original site was left empty for a long time, until it was restored to its original form in October 2011.

stories.title: Seoporu 1
stories.script: Seoporu(1)  The Seoporu is a Poru that stands on the Seobuk Gangnu to the direction of the Seojangdae. Because it is located closest to the most important military command post of the Fortress, the Seojangdae, Seoporu is the most fully armed poru among the other five Porus of Hwaseong.

stories.title: Seoammun Gate (Hwaseong Fortress, Suwon)
stories.script: Seoammun Gate    Due to Seoammun Gate‘s unique construction to the side, it was less likely to be discovered by enemies. It was also difficult to break in, as it was covered in steel. Even if the steel gate was destroyed, the stairs leading to the Fortress had a sharp curve, so that allies on the other side could attack the enemy. It was truly the most secretive gate among the other secret gates.

stories.title: Seojangdae Command Post and Seonodae
stories.script: Seojangdae served as a location for generals to oversee their soldiers, providing a vantage point both inside and outside of Hwaseong Fortress. The term Seo in Seojangdae signifies west, as it was positioned on the western side of the fortress. In 1795, King Jungjo personally trained his soldiers at this site. The painting capturing this moment is referred to as the 'Seojangdaesungjodo,' constituting one part of the Palpokbyungpungs.  This two-story building, Seojangdae, contains an interior staircase. The lower floor consists of three rooms arranged vertically and horizontally, with the central room designated for the use of generals. Standing at Seojangdae evokes the spirit and legacy of the esteemed generals of old.  Suwon Hwaseong features two balconies, Seonodae and Dongbuknodae, elevated positions from which catapults were employed against enemy attacks. Additionally, Hwaseong Balcony served for monitoring enemy movements and transmitting signals, using five-color flags and other means, to a command post and throughout the entire castle.  From Seonodae, when observing the surroundings, a vast water pool becomes apparent in the front. Originally a reservoir, this water source was utilized for agricultural purposes. During the construction of the fortress, King Jungjo excavated four reservoirs to support farming, as it was essential for attracting settlers to the fortress. King Jungjo's concern for both the construction of the fortress and the livelihoods of the people is evident. Presently, only two of the reservoirs, constructed by the king in the west and north, remain.

stories.title: Seoyichi
stories.script: Seoyichi, also known as the Western Bastion, is a Chiseong constructed between the Seojangdae or the Western Artillery and the Seoporu or the Western Command Post. Chi refers to a pheasant, symbolizing soldiers who could conceal themselves like pheasants within the Chiseong before launching attacks against enemies approaching the fortress walls. Hwaseong Fortress, encompassing 10 bastions, features Seoyichi, which is relatively small compared to the other bastions due to its location on a steep slope leading to the summit of Paldal Mountain.  Originally, Seoichi was built in 1796 in the 20th year of King Jungjo of the Joseon Dynasty, and it was restored in 1975 by retaining its original appearance. Various sized stones with a reddish hue are still well preserved, and a rectangular stone, larger than the flat wall, was positioned in the lower part to provide additional support.

stories.title: Seoporu 2
stories.script: Poru, an artillery pavilion, protrudes outward and serves to attack the enemy by housing artillery inside. Among the five artillery pavilions in Hwaseong Fortress, Seoporu is one of them. Seoporu was originally built in 1796 during the Joseon Dynasty and was restored in 1975. Although they all appear similar, each pavilion possesses its unique characteristics.  Seoporu was built near the top of Paldal Mountain and was designed to help soldiers attack the enemy effectively by taking advantage of the geographical characteristics of the steep slope. Particularly, Seoporu is slightly smaller and features a staircase. Its construction on a slope resulted in a smaller size compared to the northwestern and northeastern artillery, which were installed on flat land. Consequently, the number of artillery pieces and shooting holes was also reduced.

stories.title: Seoilchi
stories.script: Seoilchi  The Seoilchi is a Chiseong standing between the Seobuk Gangnu and the Seoporu. It has the unique characteristic of having a brick cover over the low tower.

stories.title: Seobuk Gangnu
stories.script: Seobuk Gangnu  The Seobuk Gangnu was a Nugak constructed on the fortress wall to command the army around the Hwaseomun area. A Nugak signifies a house built on a high level without doors or walls in order to provide a wider view of a large area.  The Seobuk Gangnu had four rooms, among which one held a staircase going above. Some of the rooms downstairs had a stone heating system for soldiers to take a rest. The Seobuk Gangnu was situated in a protrusion along the fortress wall and had holes above and under it, making it convenient to observe the movement of the enemy’s.

stories.title: Hwaseomun Gate (Hwaseong Fortress, Suwon)
stories.script: Hwaseomun Gate   This gate with its elegant octagonal roof is the Hwaseomun. Unlike the Paldalmun Gate or the Janganmun Gate, it does not have a separate gate for the semicircular Ongseong, a defensive wall structure, but is open to its side. The Hwaseomun Gate is also famous for being built with the most advanced machinery of the time, such as the Geojunggi and the Hwalcha.  The Geojunggi was a machine used to pick up heavy objects, and was invented by the scholar Jeong Yakyong, who had produced the inventions by studying Chinese and Western books. It implemented a pulley system, and enabled a person who can lift an object of 24kg to lift 25 objects weighing 60kg each.  When the Fortress was built, other machines such as the Gupan, Seolma, Dongcha, and Nokro, and so on were used to facilitate carrying and lifting stone blocks.

stories.title: Seobuk Gongsimdon
stories.script: Seobuk Gongsimdon  The Seobuk Gongsimdon was constructed in order to defend the Hwaseomun area. It had holes called Pohyeols on each floor, and the upper floor wall had arrow slits. Soldiers entered through a small gate called the Hongyemun on the lower floor.  The Gongshimdon is a unique facility which was built only at the Hwaseon among the other fortresses of Joseon Dynasty. This is why King Jungjo was satisfied with the structure, and told his vassals to freely observe it, as it was the first of its kind to be built in our country.

stories.title: Bukporu
stories.script: Bukporu  Hwaseong has many defensive facilities, among which is the Bukporu. It had a hole in a low wall through which it could directly fire cannon at enemies approaching from below.

stories.title: Bukseoporu
stories.script: Bukseoporu  The Bukseoporu, built with black bricks, partially protrudes from the fortress walls like a Chiseong. Its interior is divided into three floors, and the wall has holes for cannon firing.

stories.title: Bukseo Jeokdae
stories.script: Bukseo Jeokdae  The Bukseo Jeokdae, situated to the northwest of the Janganmun, was a Jeokdae built in 1795. A Jeokdae signifies a fortress installation that had a rather high elevation, situated inside the fortress, and spaced every 82.6 meters from the center of the fortress. This was where soldiers would observe movements of the enemies and store weapons.  As guns were already in use by the time the Fortress was built, the Bukseo Jeokdae also had crenels for guns as well as bows and arrows.

stories.title: Janganmun
stories.script: Janganmun  The Janganmun is the main gate of the Fortress, situated to the north. It is adorned with curved rainbows both inside and outside, and is surrounded by an auxiliary fortress wall called the Bukonseong.  The name ‘Jangan’ came from the name of an old capital city of China, ‘Jangan’. This name carried King Jungjo’s wish that Hwaseong would prosper long as a new capital city.  The Janganmun originally had a similar shape and size to the southern gate, the Paldalmun. But as the gate and the fortress walls were connected to each other during its restoration, we can now go above the gates unlike its counterpart.

stories.title: Bukdong Jeokdae and Bukdongchi
stories.script: Bukdong Jeokdae, Bukdongchi  The Bukdong Jeokdae was a defensive structure built to the sides of the fortress gates in order to block the enemies. The inner wall was equipped with ports to attack enemies in case of emergency. Crenels are holes in a rampart or fortress through which bullets would be shot secretly at enemies.  While Porus and Chiseong completely protruded from fortress walls, this Jeokdae has half of it inside the walls.  The Bukdongchi was a Chiseong connected to the Bukdong Jeokdae. It had a Seonggakwi, a low wall that permitted soldiers to hide themselves from the enemy. The Seonggakwi had three openings which one could view outside through them.

stories.title: Bukdong Poru
stories.script: Bukdong Poru, or Northeastern Artillery Pavilion is one of five artillery pavilions built in Suwon Hwaseong Fortress. Similar to the other artillery pavilions, Bukdong Poru was built to protrude outward and used to attack enemies by housing artillery within. It was built by King Jungjo in 1794 during the Joseon Dynasty and was restored in 1977. Bukdong Poru is located in the northeast between Janganmun Gate and Hwahongmun Gate, which was built relatively high on the ground allowing for easy surveillance of the surrounding area.  The roof structure of Bukdong Poru differs between its exterior and interior. While the exterior features a Wujingak-type roof, the interior boasts a Matbae-type roof resembling an open book. Both designs represent traditional Korean roof structures and preserve the original beauty of curved roofs. The Wujingak roof consists of four Chunyeohmarus converging on Dongmaru, while the Matbae roof style, the oldest of the two, omits Chunyeomaru from the front and back.

stories.title: Hwahongmun Gate
stories.script: In the past, there was a large water stream around Buksumun Gate, but during the rainy season, it would often flood. That's why when Hwaseong Fortress was built, both a waterway and Buksumun Gate were constructed. Buksumun refers to the northern gate of Hwaseong Fortress among the two main gates, which was constructed to control the flow of Suwoncheon Stream that cuts through the fortress. Buksumun Gate is also known as Hwahongmun Gate, meaning a shining rainbow.  Hwahongmun Gate has seven Hongyemuns, arched water gates in varying sizes. These arched floodgates were designed to slow down fast streams and were constructed wider and larger as they approached the center. Additionally, Hwahongmun Gate had iron gates to prevent enemies from entering. Furthermore, the stone installed at the bottom of Hwahongmun has been sturdy enough to last until today.

stories.title: Banghwasuryujeong
stories.script: Banghwasuryujeong  The Dongbuk Gangnu situated on the hill next to the Hwahongmun, the Banghwasuryujeong, was used as an emergency military command post. However, it is also quite decorated with various trees and a Yongyeon, a King’s pond. Its manifold Paljak roof also displays an architectural beauty rarely seen in other structures in Hwaseong.  The building costs for the Banghwasuryujeong was ten times that of the Dongnamgakru and the Seobuk Gangnu. This is why King Jungjo, who sought modesty as a virtue, chastised the construction manager.

stories.title: Bukammun
stories.script: Bukammun  This rainbow shaped gate is the Bukammun, another one of the secret gates. Isn’t it surprising that such a beautiful gate, so conspicuous, was a secret gate? But this is also a type of camouflage, as no one would have thought such a beautiful gate would be a secret gate.  The Bukammun is situated in the southern corner of the Banghwasuryujeong, and not easily seen from outside the Fortress. The door is inlaid with timber, and is hard to open. Thus, the Bukammun has the various characteristics that made such a perfect secret gate.

stories.title: Dongbuk Poru
stories.script: Dongbuk Poru  The Dongbuk Poru was a Poru to the Northeast, built in September 23rd, 1794. Built in a 3-story structure, it has holes on stone in various spots to allow cannons to fire.

stories.title: Dongammun Gate (Hwaseong Fortress, Suwon)
stories.script: Dongammun Gate  The Dongammun Gate was a secret passageway situated between the Gakgeondae and the Dongjangdae, utilized for inconspicuously moving soldiers and equipment.  The Dongammun Gate is situated deep within the Fortress in a secluded area, as most secret gates are. The Hongye, rainbow arch, inside the gate has been narrowed by bricks, so that only one horse could barely pass. There are bricks above the gate, and it does not have a roof.

stories.title: Yeonmudae(Dongjangdae)
stories.script: Yeonmudae  The Jangdae was where the general would stand and order his troops. They were normally built on fortresses or beams by piling stones. Hwaseong has the Seojangdae and the Dongjangdae – the latter was where soldiers were trained during normal times, and the Seojangdae was used during actual wartime. The Dongjangdae was also called the Yeonmudae, which meant a place where people practiced martial arts.  Should we walk around the Yeonmudae? Although it is now a quiet lawn, this place once bustled with armed men and horses 210 years ago. The large yard to the back is still used as an archery range.

stories.title: Dongbuk Gongsimdon
stories.script: Gongshimdon is a watchtower built in the northeast of Hwaseong Fortress to surveil and defend against surrounding threats. Gongshimdon was originally built by King Jungjo in 1796 during the Joseon Dynasty. However, it was heavily destroyed during the Korean War (1950-1953) and was rebuilt in 1976.  The name of Gongshimdon means hollow outpost. The three-story cylindrical tower is built with circularly laid bricks and has no other facilities except a spiral staircase inside. In Korea, Namhansanseong Fortress and Ganghwa Island's coastal areas are similar in shape, but only Hwaseong Gongsimdon is constructed with hollow inside. In addition, the winding path up the stairway is shaped like a conch, called Sora in Korean, so the place was also called Soragak, literally meaning conch tower.

stories.title: Dongbuk Nodae
stories.script: Dongbuk Nodae  The Dongbuk Nodae was where soldiers could observe approaching enemies and signal nearby allies. The Nodae was originally used as an archery post, but in Hwaseong it had the role of alerting the castle of the enemy’s status.  When the Fortress’ main command post, the Seojangdae, gave its orders, the Seonodae would wave flags with five different colors to relay the message to the Seonodae. The Dongbuk Nodae would then receive and carry out the message.

stories.title: Changnyongmun Gate (Hwaseong Fortress, Suwon)
stories.script: Changnyongmun Gate  There are black, white, red, and blue flags on the Fortress walls. These colors represent the guardian animals of the four cardinal directions. The east is the blue dragon’s blue, the west  is the white of the white tiger, the north is the Hyunmu (Black Tortoise and Serpent)'s black, the north is the Jujak (Vermilion Bird)’s red, and the center is yellow, representing the king.  Now you can guess why the flags around the Changnyongmun Gate are blue – this is because the gate is situated to the east.  The eastern Changnyongmun Gate is a sibling gate of the Hwaseomun Gate to the west, and is decorated with a Paljak roof, a Mullu and an Ongseong, rivaling it in its splendor.

stories.title: Dongil Poru
stories.script: Dongil Poru  The Dongil Poru is one of the Fortress’ five Porus, situated in the east.  Unlike the Northeastern Porus , it is on slightly elevated and flat ground, and the fortress walls are greatly protruded.

stories.title: Dongilchi
stories.script: Dongilchi  The Dongilchi is a Chiseong situated between the Dongil Poru and the Bongdon. The Chiseong is a defensive structure built in specific intervals, and Hwaseong has ten.  Why were there so many Chiseongs? Joseon had undergone the Imjin invasion attacked by Japan in 1592. Then the government realized that Joseon fortresses had weak defenses. This was why various defensive structures were built in Hwaseong.

stories.title: Dongporu
stories.script: Dongporu  The Dongporu is a Poru located in the east. A Poru is a wooden structure that makes the soldiers in a Chiseong unobservable by the enemies. It functioned as a type of military fallout base.

stories.title: Dongyichi
stories.script: Dongyichi  The Dongyichi was a Chiseong between the Dongporu and the Bongdon. Our soldiers would stand here and shoot bows or guns to enemies trying to climb or destroy the wall.

stories.title: Bongdon
stories.script: Bongdon  The Bongdon was where signal fires were lit. Fire and smoke were used to relay urgent messages. Rabbit droppings were burned during the day to make the smoke visible, and fires were lit during the night. The five pyres were used in different combinations to signal different situations.  In normal times, one pyre was lit to show that everything was well. However, when enemies were sighted far away from the border, two pyres were lit. Three would be lit when the enemy approached the borders, and four were lighted when they had entered Joseon borders. Five pyres meant a battle was going on with the enemy.  A stone heated room was provided under the Bongdon so that the signal fire soldiers could stay in.

stories.title: Dongyiporu
stories.script: Dongyiporu  The eastern walls of the Fortress have two Porus. One of them is the Dongil Poru, and the other is the Dongyiporu. The latter was made to the south of the Bongdon to fend off attacking enemies.  The interior of the structure is composed of two rooms. One has laid boards on the floor, and the other has a ladder installed.

stories.title: Dongsamchi
stories.script: A Chi is a bastion or turret-shaped projection strategically positioned at regular intervals along Hwaseong Fortress, enabling soldiers to defend the fort and repel approaching enemies. Hwaseong Fortress comprises 10 bastions, with slight variations in shape depending on the topography. Along the Eastern Wall, there exist three Chiseong known as Dongilchi, Dongyichi, and Dongsamchi. Ordinarily, numbering started from the north, making the southernmost bastion Dongsamchi, literally meaning the eastern third bastion.  Dongsamchi is located between Dongiporu or Eastern Guard Post II and Dongnamgangnu or Southeastern Corner Pavilion. Due to the steep slope in the area, Dongsamchi possesses the widest width and the shortest length among the bastions. Initially erected by King Jungjo in 1796 during the Joseon Dynasty, it underwent restoration in 1979, preserving the bastion and its surrounding fortress in their original appearance.

stories.title: Dongnamgakru
stories.script: Dongnamgakru  The Dongnamgakru was situated in a corner of the wall on a hill next to the eastern Suwon stream, and therefore best suited for observing the enemy and defending the Namsumun. It could be used to direct the army as it faced the Dongbuk Gongsimdon .  The Dongnamgakru has a similar structure to the Seobuk Gangnu. However, all four rooms have wooden flooring, and the lower room has a staircase. To the southwest of the building is a stone heated room.

stories.title: Hongsalmun and Sinpunggyo
stories.script: Hongsalmun, Sinpunggyo  The Hongsalmun was a symbolic gate raised in front of lecture halls, Confucian temples, and graves. It was made by raising two pillars to each side and linking the top with two long wooden beams, and sticking in Hongsals in regular intervals. There are no records of when the Hongsalmuns started to be built, but as they were invariably raised in sacred areas, it is thought that they carried the meaning of sanctity and respect.  Immediately behind is there a small bridge called Sinpunggyo. In the old days, the Myeongdangsu, sacred water coming from the Paldalsan, would flow from the right of the Hwaseong Haenggung’s rear area to the front gate of the Sinpungnu. The Myungdangsu had the meaning of making the palace officials, who passed it every day upon entering the palace, see it and make their minds pure. The Shinpunggyo was lost during the Japanese occupation, but was excavated and restored.

stories.title: Sinpungnu
stories.script: Sinpungnu  The gatehouse before you is the front gate of the Haenggung, the Sinpungnu. It was originally named the Jinnamru, which changed under the orders by King Jungjo. On the day following his mother Haegyeonggug Hong’s 60the birthday, he gathered widows, widowers, unmarried people and orphans who had nowhere to rely upon, and distributed rice and salt. The also held a Jinhyul celebration for the hungry, and himself tasted the porridge that they were given. We can see how much he loved his people.

stories.title: Jipsacheong
stories.script: Jipsacheong  The Jipsacheong was one of Joseon’s offices, where various office works were carried out. The work included managing miscellaneous jobs such as equipment maintenance and gardening.

stories.title: Buk Gunyeong
stories.script: In 1785 during the Joseon Dynasty, King Jungjo reorganized the military system and created the royal guard to symbolize his powerful royal authority. During the expansion of the palace in 1794, new guard buildings called ‘Gunyeong’ were placed on the left and right sides of the main gate. Among these, the guard building located on northern side is referred to as the ‘Buk Gunyeong.’ The initial construction of Gunyeong occurred in 1789, with subsequent extensions in 1794, resulting in a size of 62 units. Buk Gunyeong is one of the two military units within Hwaseong Temporary Palace, where King Jeongjo's Guard was stationed. The primary force in Jangyeongwaeyoung, composed of cavalry known as Chingunwui, entered Buk Gunyeong in two rows, each consisting of 100 people.   However, two years after King Jungjo’s death, the Royal Guard was disbanded in 1802. Furthermore, Hwaseong Seongyeokwuigweh is classified as a government office due to its documentation of the construction of Hwaseong Fortress.

stories.title: Jwaingmun
stories.script: Jwaingmun  The name “Jwaing” of the Jwaingmun comes from “helping from nearby”. The writing on paper on the gate, the Pyeonaek, was written by literary official Jung Dongjun under King Jungjo’s orders. You can observe that the floor of the Jwaingmun consists of uneven stones. These are called Bakseok. It normally protects our eyes by diffusing bright light, and prevents water from forming puddles during rain.

stories.title: Jungyangmun Gate
stories.script: Jungyangmun Gate was built in 1790 by King Jungjo. It is also known as Naesammun Gate, which literally means three gates on the inside, it serves to protect the immediate vicinity of Bongsudang, the central court of Hanggung Palace. The name ‘Jungyang’ is derived from the village where Gojo Yubang resided during the Han Dynasty, a name chosen by King Jungjo. Initially named ‘Jungyakmun,’ the gate underwent a name change when it was relocated to the front of the Wuhwagwan. Jungyangmun Gate comprises the central gate, Wuhyup Gate, and Jwahyup Gate on its sides. Moreover, a lengthy Haenggaek was constructed on both the left and right sides of the gate to regulate access.  In 1795, Queen Heonyeong's (Hyegyeonggung Hong) 60th birthday celebration, known as Jinchanrye, was hosted at Jungyangmun Gate in front of Bongsudang. King Jungjo, along with other royal relatives and ministers, graced the occasion.

stories.title: Gyeongnyonggwan
stories.script: Gyeongnyonggwan  The Gyeongnyonggwan was an attic building built over the door to the Jangrakdang. The Kyungryong means a dragon, which represents the king. This was built for the king to rest and plot Joseon’s prosperity and peace.

stories.title: Bongsudang Hall
stories.script: Bongsudang Hall serves as the primary hall within Hwaseong Temporary Palace. King Jungjo conducted various national affairs and received morning greetings from his officials at Bonsudang Hall. Additionally, during normal times, Hwaseong's administrative officials, called Yusu, stayed and worked at Bongsudang. However, Bongsudang Hall was never overly large or extravagantly decorated due to King Jungjo's philosophy of maintaining modesty.  It was originally built in 1789 and named Jangnamheon Hall. However, in 1795, the name was changed to Bongsudang after Hyegyeonggung Hong’s 60th birthday, who was King Jungjo’s mother. The name Bongsudang translates to “praying for ten thousand years of life,” symbolizing King Jungjo’s wishes for his mother's longevity. Bongsudang was destroyed during the Japanese occupation and restored in 1997.

stories.title: Noraedang and Nangnamheon
stories.script: Noraedang was constructed for King Jungjo to reside in after his abdication from the throne. It also served as a resting place during the numerous events hosted at the Nangnamheon and Deukjungjeon.  The name 'Norae' conveys the sentiment that 'Aging is left to fate, and home is where one lives comfortably,' reflecting King Jungjo’s desire to dwell at Hwaseong Haenggung.  In addition to Noraedang, another historically significant building to explore is Nangnamheon. Nangnamheon served as the venue for national exams, banquets for the elderly, and army feasts during the 60th birthday celebrations of King Jungjo’s mother, Haegyeong Hong. During major events, Nangnamheon’s folding doors on three sides were widely opened to accommodate a large number of attendees. Notably, Nangnamheon is one of the Suwon Hwaseong structures that remained intact during the Japanese occupation.

stories.title: Deukjungjeong Pavilion
stories.script: Deukjungjeong Pavilion is a hall designed for archery enjoyment. It was originally constructed in the 14th year of King Jungjo's reign during the Joseon Dynasty in 1790. When Hwaseong Temporary Palace expanded in 1794, the hall was relocated to its current position behind Nangnamheon Hall. Additionally, a shooting platform for the king was installed in front of the hall. King Jungjo named the hall using a phrase from the Book of Rites, which reads, 'He who hits the mark is permitted to become a prince, but he who doesn’t hit the mark cannot be a prince.'  Whenever King Jungjo visited Hwaseong Temporary Palace, he enjoyed archery from the shooting platform in front of the palace. An enduring scene of King Jungjo engaging in archery and watching fireworks with his attendants during his mother Hyegyeonggung Hong's 60th birthday celebration in 1795 is captured in a painting called ‘Painting of King Shooting Arrows at Deukjungjeong Pavilion.'

stories.title: Mirohanjeong
stories.script: Mirohanjeong  The Mirohanjeong was a pavilion with the meaning of a place where one could rest leisurely after reaching an old age. It was also called the “Yukmyeonjeong” when it was built, signifying its hexagonal roof.

stories.title: Naeposa
stories.script: Naeposa  The Naeposa was made to signal danger from outside the Hwaseong Haenggung. Shouts and flags were used to alert the Haenggung of danger. One can imagine that those with small voices would have had a hard time working here.

stories.title: Bongnaedang
stories.script: Bongnaedang is a building within Hwaseong Temporary Palace, constructed in 1789. During his visits, King Jungjo used Bongnaedang as his sleeping chamber. However, after the establishment of Jangrakdang in 1794, it was utilized by local officials. The name “Boknae” signifies that ‘if everything goes right on the outside, blessings will come from within.’ King Jungjo personally named the building and inscribed the hanging board called Pyeonaek. Unfortunately, the hanging board has been lost.  In the early 20th century, with the construction of Gyeonggi Provincial Hospital, Boknaedang was demolished. However, it was rebuilt in 1997 during the restoration of Hwaseong Haenggung Palace. Additionally, Bongnaedang has gained popularity among tourists as several major scenes of the Korean drama Dae Jang Geum and numerous Korean movies and dramas were filmed there.

stories.title: Jangrakdang Hall
stories.script: Jangrakdang Hall was built in 1794, during the 18th year of King Jungjo's reign in the Joseon Dynasty. It served as a residence for King Jungjo's mother, Haegyeong Hong, during her 60th birthday banquet at Hwaseong Temporary Palace. The devoted son, King Jungjo, built this place with the wish for his mother's good health and personally inscribed the Pyeonaek, a hanging board. Additionally, King Jungjo installed two gates on the fence between Jangrakdang Hall and Boknaedang, named Dabokmun and Jangbokmun. These gates symbolize a door for abundant blessings and a door for enduring blessings, reflecting King Jungjo's filial piety and his prayers for his mother's well-being.  Jangrakdang also served as a sleeping chamber for Joseon kings during their visits to Hwaseong Temporary Palace for rituals near the tomb of King Jeongjo and his father, Crown Prince Sado.  It was constructed using a method where different parts were made separately and then assembled during the construction process, reducing both construction time and costs. Furthermore, it is connected to Bonsudang, the main hall. Notably, the famous Korean movie 'The King’s Man,' directed by Yi Jun-ik, was filmed at Jangrakdang.

stories.title: Yuyeotaek
stories.script: Yuyeotaek  The Yuyeotaek was where the King would stay for a while during his visits and meet his vassals. Normally it was used as the Hwaseongyusu’s office. It was also used as King Jungjo’s quarters after Haegyeong Hong’s 60th birthday in 1795.

stories.title: Oejeongriso and Bijangcheong and Seoricheong
stories.script: In Hwaseong Temporary Palace, there are several historically significant buildings such as Oejeongriso, Bijangcheong, and Seoricheong.  Firstly, Oejeongriso served as a provisional bureau responsible for preparing and overseeing all expenses related to the Joseon king's visits to Hwaseong Temporary Palace. Originally established in 1795 during the 19th year of King Jeongjo's reign in the Joseon Dynasty, it was organized for the preparation of his mother, Hyegyeonggung Hong's 60th birthday royal banquet when it was held at Hwaseong Temporary Palace. It was named Oejeongriso to distinguish it from Jeongriseo in the capital. Typically, the role of the Jeongrisa, similar to the minister of finance, was carried out by Hojo Panseo, but in Hwaseong, the role was usually fulfilled by Hwaseong Yusu, a counterpart to the local administrative minister.  Bijangcheong is another noteworthy site. It served as the workplace for Bijang of Hwaseong Yusubu, who were staff officers serving various officials. Despite being secretaries, they wielded significant power as they worked for influential authorities. Bijang would conduct audits and discreetly examine the lives of people.  Additionally, Seoricheong functioned as a place where clerks carried out their duties within a town. Seoris were officials responsible for recording village events and related tasks. A small village typically had about 20 officials, while larger ones like Hwaseong Yusubu had around 80 officials. Moreover, during King Jungjo’s mother, Haegyeong Hong’s 60th birthday banquet, Seoricheong was utilized as Suragan, the royal kitchen.

stories.title: Namgunyeong
stories.script: King Jungjo, during the Joseon Dynasty, established his own royal guard named Jangyongyeong in 1785 to fortify and symbolize his royal authority. Naeyeong was entrusted with protecting the capital, Hanseong, while Wehyeong was assigned the task of safeguarding Hwaseong Fortress. Bukgunyeong and Namgunyeong were the locations where Wehyeong troops were stationed, symmetrically arranged on the left and right sides of Sinpungnu, the main gate of Hwaseong Temporary Palace. These two structures served as quarters for the cavalry of Jangyongwehyeong, accommodating 100 people each for eating and sleeping.  Furthermore, the royal guards stationed at both Bukgunyeong and Namgunyeong received special privileges. Those who held the top positions twice a year in spring and fall were granted high government posts. However, two years after King Jungjo’s death, the royal guard was demobilized in 1802. Namgunyeong was built in 1794 by King Jungjo and was restored relatively recently in 2002.

stories.title: Gicheungheon
stories.script: Gicheungheon  The Gicheungheon was where various musical instruments such as Pyungyung and Pyungjong played during the formal court music were stored.

stories.title: Hwaryeonjeon
stories.script: Hwaryeonjeon  The Hwaryeonjeon was where King Jungjo’s portrait was kept and ancestral rites were held every year. It was built by King Sunjo, who wished to learn from his father’s own filial devotion. King Sunjo personally wrote the signboard on the Jeongjeon. When the structure was built, it had the Yiancheong, Jaeshil, Hyangdaecheong, Jaegigo, Wehsammun, Naesammun, and Jung Hyeopmun, besides the Unhanjeong where King Jeongjo’s portrait was kept. The southern Hyangdaecheong and the Jaegigo no longer remain. King Sunjo would hold banquets for the elderly here, and personally hold ancestral rites on the days his father was born and died.

stories.title: Jaejung
stories.script: Jaejung  The Jaejung is a well whose water was used for religious services, and was also called an Eojeong. Its water supply was bountiful, and nearby villagers and refugees during the Korean War would use the well, and it never dried. It was 5.5m in height, and the water stands about 4m high within the well.

stories.title: Punghwadang
stories.script: Punghwadang  The Punghwadang was a building where officials would stay a while ancestral rites were held at the Hwaryeonjeon. Small and large banquets were held here as well.

stories.title: Yeomingak
stories.script: Yeomingak is a Jonggak, a house of bells, situated across the street from Hwaseong Haenggung Square. Similar in appearance to the Bosingak Bell in Jongno, Seoul, Yeomingak was built in 1796 during the establishment of Hwaseong Temporary Palace under King Jungjo's reign. Its creation aimed to bestow well-being upon the Suwon people and convey King Jungjo's intentions throughout the city.  Unfortunately, Yeomingak mysteriously vanished at some point. Though exact details remain unclear, it is believed to have been removed following orders from the Japanese Government General in 1911. However, there's a fortunate turn of events?visitors can now admire Yeomingak. It was meticulously restored on October 8, 2008, based on records from ‘WonHeng Ulmyo Jeongri Euigwae’ and Lee Hwee-pyeong's 'Hwaseongyilgi.' These historical records comprehensively documented all constructions and events related to Suwon Hwaseong.  Yeomingak serves as the location for the annual New Year's Eve bell tolling ceremony. This ceremony, held on the night of December 31, marks the beginning of the New Year.

stories.title: Value of Suwon Hwaseong
stories.script: Value of Suwon Hwaseong  The value of Suwon Hwaseong as a ‘UNESCO world cultural heritage’ is recognized worldwide. A cultural asset is not just valued as a relic. It also represents the artistic level of its age, the social maturity and the hopes its age had and was pursuing.  In this sense, Suwon Hwaseong is considered a world cultural asset because it is recognized as a cultural heritage and the cultures in which it was constructed are also recognized worldwide. Gyeonggi Province takes pride in Suwon Hwaseong, which is worthwhile and deserves to be well favored. It is a great cultural heritage and it is a crystal of construction made during the rule of King Jeongjo in the latter period of the Joseon Dynasty, during which cultures flourished the most. Its construction is scientific, artistic and beautiful. Moreover, it comprises vivid dreams of the figures who led the age in which it was constructed.  Travelers will be greatly touched and impressed when they understand the proper value of a cultural heritage. Travelers will be even more attracted to Suwon Hwaseong when they overall understand the city of Suwon, Hwaseong which was a product of the age, the festival celebrating the 60th birthday in 1795 which was artistically conducted, King Jeongjo the contemporary conductor of all the events, and scholars of the Realist School of Confucianism.

stories.title: Suwon Hwaseong a planned city for a new age
stories.audioTitle: Suwon Hwaseong a planned city for a new age
stories.script: Suwon Hwaseong a planned city for a new age  Suwon Hwaseong stands magnificent and grand while it is looking over the downtown. The city is naturally and smoothly stretched outside the castle.  Suwon Hwaseong does not stand as a defensive castle only. It is also referred to the whole area of the city, which is more advanced than any other planned modern city around the world. 300 years ago, just a vast expanse of waste land stood east of Mt. Paldal. That time, King Jeongjo the 22nd ruler of the Joseon Dynasty believed that the area was quite fit for a new planned city, which should be constructed as he dreamed. King Jeongjo decided to construct a new city on the site where the people should live together in peace and harmony and assured safety from enemies.   King Jeongjo set up the tomb (called Yung-neung) for his biological father or Crown Prince Sado at the foot of Mt. Hwasan, from where he moved a village called Suwon to this current site below Mt. Paldal. And the village grew to be a commercial city which had roads running in all directions in the south and was connected with Hanyang which was the largest city in the Joseon Dynasty. Unlike any other cities surrounded by mountains and defended from enemies, commercial city Suwon was situated at the center of crossroads running vertically through Paldal Gate and Jangan Gate and horizontally through Haseo Gate and Changryong Gate and being connected with surrounding villages and towns. It was constructed according to the determination of King Jeongjo, who called a southern gate Paldal Gate and a northern gate Jangan Gate with a view to making Suwon an active large city stretching in all directions. Furthermore, he changed the name of the city into Hwaseong and had an impregnable castle safe from any enemies constructed under the management of Yak-yong Jeong who was the most favored vassal of King Jeongjo.  Yak-yong Jeong designed a very defensive and beautiful castle after having considered all the strengths of Eastern and Western castles. Based on the design, gradual adjustments were made according to the local conditions so that a new 5.7km-long castle called Hwaseong might be established. In addition, King Jeongjo established Manseokgeo which was a reservoir for agriculture and turned a wilderness into farms, for the purpose of making Hwaseong a self-sufficient and affluent city.

stories.title: The 60th birthday festival at the temporary palace of Hwaseong for Lady Hong of Hyegyeong Palace, the greatest event during the rule of King Jeongjo
stories.audioTitle: The 60th birthday festival at the temporary palace of Hwaseong for Lady Hong of Hyegyeong Palace, the greatest event during the rule of King Jeongjo
stories.script: The 60th birthday festival at the temporary palace of Hwaseong for Lady Hong of Hyegyeong Palace, the greatest event during the rule of King Jeongjo   The temporary palace of Hwaseong was a special place for King Jeongjo. It was a residence set up so that the king might stay there after visiting the tomb of Crown Prince Sado in Suwon. It was also a place where King Jeongjo would spend the rest of his life after retiring from the throne. This building initially had 30 rooms and up to 576 rooms in 1796, which was the largest temporary palace in the Joseon Dynasty. King Jeongjo desired to stay after retire at Hwaseong since he wanted to live near to his father and develop new politics in there apart from his vassals who opposed his reformed policies.  1795 when Hwaseong was almost completely constructed, King Jeongjo lavished a startling amount of money on the 60th birthday festival held at the temporary palace of Hwaseong for Lady Hong of Hyegyeong Palace who is his biological mother. For the splendid party, the king stayed for 8 days along with his mother at Hwaseong.  Such a long stay of his at Hwaseong was because he wanted to console the spirit of his father who was killed in a pitiful manner and especially comfort his mother who had never visited for 23 years the tomb of her husband. Not only that. The king also desired to show off the magnificent appearance of Hwaseong and his pride in the city before the presence of his opponents who drove his father to death in the Joseon Dynasty. It was why he personally commanded his royal guards to be drilled in a very stately manner for two times on the evening and at night of the 4th day of his visit, to which training all the residents within the castle were invited and positively responded. Besides, on his way to the castle, the king closely looked at the living of the people and paid attention to their difficulties and troubles or solved their problems.  King Jeongjo was a reformed monarch, who paid a visit to outside the palace 66 times and dispatched his secret commissioners about 60 times in order to catch up with the changing trends of the age and take care of the life of the people. Now, the temporary palace of Hwaseong holds a performance of 24 skills of martial arts at 11 and 15 hours everyday except Mondays. King Jeongjo ordered warriors Dong-su Baek and Je-ga Park and others to complete the compilation of a military science textbook, which his father longed to publish. 24 war techniques reported in the book are still handed down to us and demonstrated before us.

stories.title: The Principles of Behavior and Manner, Another World Heritage
stories.audioTitle: The Principles of Behavior and Manner, Another World Heritage
stories.script: After the Korean War, Suwon residents would remark, “The East Gate went away, the West Gate ran away, the North Gate broke away, but the South Gate stands alone.” However, Suwon Hwaseong has now been nearly completely restored. Following the death of King Jungjo, who devoted much attention and support to Hwaseong, memories of the fortress gradually faded. Suwon Hwaseong suffered extensive damage during the Korean War, and after the war ended, most of the palace collapsed, except for several facilities.  The restoration work commenced in 1975 and was almost finished within three years. The rapid and comprehensive restoration of Hwaseong was made possible by the book entitled “The Principles of Behavior and Manner for Sacred Precincts of Hwaseong.” This book meticulously details the construction of Hwaseong, encompassing records of construction costs, schedules, personnel in charge, major structures, tools, and even includes pictures. It also elucidates on the proposals made to the king by his servants, workers' earnings during their labor, and other specifics.  For recognition as a World Heritage site, the historical and artistic nature of the heritage is crucial, alongside its maintenance and preservation in its original form. In this regard, many of Hwaseong’s facilities were lost, posing difficulties for UNESCO recognition. However, thanks to the detailed documentation in “The Principles of Behavior and Manner for Sacred Precincts of Hwaseong,” the original appearance of the palace was nearly completely restored.  Furthermore, the record, “The Arranged Principles of Behavior and Manner for the Royal Visit to His Father,” written in 1795, is also an important document. This record comprehensively details the royal visit of 1795, the 60th birthday banquet held that year, preparations, mobilization of personnel and goods, scenes from the banquet, catering, aspects of the royal event, the royal procession, and military training, accompanied by corresponding pictures and explanations. It's reported that UNESCO investigators found no faults in Suwon Hwaseong due to the detailed and thorough records. Consequently, it was listed as a World Heritage site.

stories.title: Nearby historic sites
stories.script: When discussing the historical sites near Suwon Hwaseong Fortress, one of the foremost mentions is the tomb of Crown Prince Sado, the father of King Jungjo. These tombs, where Crown Prince Sado and King Jungjo rest, are situated in a serene and auspicious location accessible through a tranquil forest path near Yongju Temple.  King Jungjo's dedication to relocating Crown Prince Sado's tomb to the most auspicious site in the country eventually led to the selection of the current burial place. It's noteworthy that both King Jungjo and his mother are also interred here, making it one of the most renowned burial sites during the Joseon Dynasty.  Additionally, the sculptures within the royal mausoleum are a testament to the cultural richness and beauty of the era. Created by esteemed artists of the time, such as Hong-do Kim, Yun-bok Shin, and Deuk-sin Kim, these sculptures are a visual feast. Behind the Buddha image at Yongju Temple, commissioned by the king for the restoration of Crown Prince Sado, there is an altar portrait of Buddha that King Jungjo himself drew using Western painting techniques.  The roads leading to the royal mausoleum and Yongju Temple offer more than just a glimpse into King Jungjo's profound reverence for his father, Crown Prince Sado. They reflect the cultural flourishing during the reigns of King Yeongjo and King Jungjo, marked by the rise of the realist school of Confucianism and genre paintings.  After enshrining Crown Prince Sado in this auspicious location, King Jungjo experienced a series of positive events, including the birth of his son, King Sunjo, fulfilling his wish. In a dream, King Jungjo saw his father transform into a dragon carrying cintamani in his mouth as he soared high into the sky. This vision inspired him to name the temple 'Yongju,' which means 'dragon cintamani.'  The construction of Yongju Temple faced resistance, primarily from vassals who believed that a Buddhist temple should not be erected in a Confucian nation to commemorate someone. However, with the support of people from across the country, King Jungjo overcame these obstacles. The deep filial affection King Jungjo held for his father is evident at Yung-neung and Yongju Temple.  Touched by a sermon delivered by a Buddhist priest, King Jungjo inscribed the ten major graces of parents, excerpted from 'The Graceful Favors of Parents,' on a plate. This precious relic still exists and is preserved within Yongju Temple.

stories.title: Overview of Suwon Hwaseong Fortress
stories.script: Suwon was one of the four main regional government centers during the Joseon Dynasty. The Hwaseong Fortress was built to protect the city, which was designated as a cultural asset for its historical value.   Suwon Hwaseong Fortress was built in 1796 by King Jeongjo under the general supervision of the former prime minister, the head of central government affairs, and the vice envoy. During the two years of construction, many new machines were specifically designed to move and pile up big stones. Following the completion of the fortress, other minor facilities were smoothly built. However, most of them were destroyed in wars and riots, and part of the fortress was destroyed or lost during the Japanese Occupation Era and the Korean War. Fortunately, the fortress was repaired afterwards.  The fortress is a piled-stone and brick fortress that surrounds the center of Suwon. Its massive walls are 5.74 km in length and remain almost as they were in their original form, constructed 200 years ago. The Suwoncheon Stream, the mainstream of Suwon, flows through the center. The walls include a number of defensive features, most of which are intact, such as floodgates, observation towers, command posts, multiple arrow launcher towers, firearm bastions, angle towers, secret gates, beacon towers, bastions, and bunkers.   There are four main gates at the cardinal points. The Paldalmun Gate in the south and the Janganmun Gate in the north are impressive with their two-story wooden structures on stone bases. Both sides are built with gated platforms and half-moon-shaped ravelins. In addition, the Hwaseomun Gate in the west and Changnyongmun Gate in the east are one-story structures that are protected by ravelins.  King Jeongjo built the fortress to show filial piety towards his father and create a new pioneer city with its own economic power. The fortress had a great influence on the development of Korean architecture, urban planning, and the arts. Not only is it a defensive weapon, but it also shows its uniqueness in combining military, political, and commercial functions.

stories.title: Entrance to Gukje Market in Busan
stories.audioTitle: Entrance to Gukje Market in Busan
stories.script: A market with the modern and contemporary history of Korea   After the National Liberation on August 15, 1945, the Japanese commenced a flea market to sell off their belongings before their return home following their defeat in World War II. The market expanded, and by 1948, it evolved into what's known as Jayu Market.  During the Korean War, many refugees sought livelihoods in this market. While vending American military and relief supplies, they also traded goods from Korea, Japan, and the United States. Thus, since the 1950s, the market has been called Gukje Market, literally translating to 'international market' in Korean.  Today, Gukje Market stands as one of the largest markets in Busan. It retails imported products like second-hand clothes, tools, and industrial items. Along Tool’s Alley in the market, numerous hardware retail and wholesale stores offer various kinds of tools, with one of these stores serving as the backdrop for the film Ode to My Father. When shopping in the market, seek out stores displaying the 'Global Tax Free' sticker, providing tax breaks for tourists.  Additionally, the market features numerous famous and delectable snacks such as yubujumeoni, tofu pouches filled with vegetables; mul-ddeok, water rice cake; and bibim-dangmyeon, spicy glass noodles. After a meal, consider exploring Korean desserts by visiting shops that offer traditional red bean sherbet during summer and hot red bean paste porridge in winter.

stories.title: Gukje Market in the Films and Other Broadcasting Programs
stories.audioTitle: Gukje Market in the Films and Other Broadcasting Programs
stories.script: Gukje Market showed up in various media contents  Korean films and dramas set in Busan often include at least one scene filmed at Guje Market. For those interested in the market's development progress and the lives of Koreans in the past, watching the 2014 movie Ode to My Father would be worthwhile.  When discussing Korean films, another famous attraction near Gukje Market is the Busan International Film Festival Square (BIFF Square), which hosts celebrations on the eve of BIFF. This presents an excellent opportunity for fans to closely encounter their favorite stars, as many celebrities attend post-festival events. The streets surrounding the square feature handprints of famous actors and directors.  Not only are films and dramas shot at Guje Market, but many popular variety shows also film there. In an episode of Running Man, the members played games in the market and savored some food, such as sweet red bean shaved ice and hoddeok, a flat, round cake with sugary fillings. Tourists can even find the Running Man members’ name tags at souvenir shops around the market. Other well-known shows like 'Infinite Challenge' and 'One Night Two Days' have also filmed segments in and around the market. Visitors can follow the routes taken in these shows and enjoy a comprehensive market tour!

stories.title: Entrance to Daegu’s Seomun Market
stories.audioTitle: The largest wholesale market in Youngnam area
stories.script: The largest wholesale market in Youngnam area   Youngnam region is used to designate the southern area between ‘Jukryeong” and “Joryeong” at Korean Sobaek Mountain Range. Daegu Seomun Market is the largest in this area by far.  Daegu Seomun Market was deemed as one of three largest markets during the Joseon Dynasty, and became Seomun Market in the 17th century, moving from the outskirts of Northern Gate of Daegu city walls to the outside of the Western Gate after “Gyeongsang-gamyeong” was installed which the provincial governor administered. It was moved to the current location in 1922.  The major product sold at Seomun Market is the fabric used to make clothes.  The fabric wholesales have greatly contributed to the development of the area’s textile industry. In addition, with fabric suppliers and garment cutters available right inside the market, it is possible to have custom-made clothes as soon as possible. There is an underground shopping center in the District #2, and it has become a new attraction of Seomun Market, with many cafes opening up   Tourists can find many of Daegu’s famous foods, including Gyeongsangbuk-do Province style foods such as napjak-mandu (flat Korean dumpling), ggoma-kimbob (miniature cooked rice with stuffs inside wrapped in laver), maewun-odeng (spicy fishcake), and kalguksu, (fresh noodles inside seafood soup).  The flat mandu always perks up visitors’ curiosity with its unique shape, and bite-size miniature kimbob is everyone’s favorite.  With the opening of the night market since 2016, Seomun Market has led new trends and offered a variety of entertainment and fun to all visitors. It is easily accessible by Daegu Subway Line #3.

stories.title: Daegu’s Seomun Night Market
stories.audioTitle: Night market with a variety of cultures and tastes
stories.script: Night market with a variety of cultures and tastes   The night market at Seomun Market is the largest in the country, and can be easily reached by getting off at the Seomun Market Station on Daegu Subway Line #3. The market is open up to midnight and the visitors can enjoy Daegu’s one of kind dishes such as napjak-mandu (flat Korean dumplings), makchang (grilled beef entrails), and matefaim (tasty bread).  There are other international menus such as Vietnamese noodles, spring rolls, and lumpia, which are also available for the visitors to enjoy as they tour around the market.  On top of that, there are numerous places where the visitors can enjoy Korean traditional games and watch entertaining shows on the stage while eating their snacks. With many regular stores open until late, the tourists can enjoy late shopping at night.    There are many shops that sell handmade accessories and idea items, and with small-scale credit card transactions available, visitors can conveniently pick up their ‘it’ items.

stories.title: Entrance to Cheongju’s Yuk-geori Market
stories.audioTitle: The hub for products from three nearby provinces
stories.script: The hub for products from three nearby provinces   Cheongju was a place where products from Gyeongsang-do Province, Jeolla-do Province, and Chungcheong-do Province got together during Joseon Dynasty.  Most of all, Yukgeori General Market is the largest in that area, having inherited the traditions of “Cheongju Market” among nine markets that thrived in Cheongju area. It was initially named Yuk-geori Market because there were six-way crossroad, but now it turned into a four-way intersection.  Because Cheongju is far from the seaside, food made by ingredients from forests or farms have been developed.  The most famous among these are various kinds of ‘jeon’ or pancakes, and meat dishes. All day long, the smell of different kinds of pancakes sizzling on hot grill entices the visitors, and there are many varieties from Korea represented here. Jokbal, seasoned pig’s feet, are also a favorite item at Yuk-geori Market.  Made of pig’s feet, there are also a variety of different sizes and tastes available at the market. Fishcakes, which are great as desserts, are made fresh and warm at the site.  The early-morning market at Yukgeori Market bustles lively and operates from 4 AM in the morning to 8 PM at night.  So it is possible to shop for breakfast ingredients or to take care of breakfast at the market

stories.title: Cheongju’s Seongan-gil Road
stories.audioTitle: The center of Cheongju’s trend and tourism
stories.script: The center of Cheongju’s trend and tourism   There is a place called ‘Seongan-gil’, located just north of Yukgeori Market, and it has got its name in that it was called ‘the inside the wall’ (seongan) of the old Cheongju town wall. This is one of the busiest parts of the town, and with Sangdang-gu office as the center that is in the middle of the street, there are many restaurants, shops, and movie theaters for people to get around and enjoy.  The area called Rodeo Street in Seongan-gil filmed a drama called, “Doctors,” with a famous Korean actress Park Shin-hae. In one of its scenes, the actress was on the run with her friends in this area. In a movie called “The Veterans,” which was seen by more than ten million moviegoers in Korea, actors Hwang Jeong-min and Yu A-in filmed a fight scene at Seongan-gil, making this place even more famous.  A five-minute drive from Seongan-gil, there is a famous tourist site called Suamgol. It is a place that served as setting for many Korean dramas including: ‘Cain and Abel,’ starring So Ji-seop and Han Ji-min and ‘Healer,’ starring Ji Chang-wook and Park Min-young.  How about taking pictures as the Korean drama or movie stars at Seongan-gil and Suamgol and leaving some memories of the trip behind?

stories.title: Entrance to Jeonju’s Namboo Market
stories.audioTitle: Market with all of Jeonju’s flavors
stories.script: Market with all of Jeonju’s flavors   Along with ‘Hanok Village’ in Jeonju, Jeonju Nambu Market is the most famous tourist attraction in the area. It has originated from a local market called “Nammun-jang” which was located outside the Pungnam-gate of Jeonju Castle during Joseon Dynasty. Known for local specialty food, the market offers a variety of Jeonju’s flavors.  Some of the most famous menus include: kongnamul guk-bob (bean sprout soup with rice), pisundae (blood sausages), muljjajang (noodles with watery bean-paste sauce), and bibimbob (rice mixed with vegetables).  These were all created and developed to satisfy the hunger and nutritional needs of the busy market workers.  Although these menus are available in different regions throughout Korea, they are prepared with Jeonju’s own special recipes, a reason why they are so very popular among many tourists from Korea.  There are programs such as “Indi-food Class” and “Nambu Market Mission Tour” in which the tourists can cook their own food with their own ingredients purchased from the market.  The tourists can also visit “Hanok Village” and “Gyeongijeon” next to the market and experience Korea’s traditional architecture and history.  At “Hanok Village,” the visitors can spend the night at Hanok guest houses or rent ‘Hanbok,’ the traditional Korean garments to try on.  There are many opportunities to experience Korean culture at Literary Gallery, Hanji Experience Center and Traditional Craft Experience Center.

stories.title: Jeonju Namboo’s Night Market and The Youth Mall
stories.script: Night market with youthful energy    In 2011, the rooftop of an abandoned two-story building in the market was renovated into a place called “Real New Town” (Young Adult Mall) and has become a hub for the youngsters, attracting younger crowd to the market. The place holds different kinds of exhibitions, concerts, and flea market events and has contributed to create a more vibrant market and a new paradigm for the market culture.   At the Young Adult Mall, you can come across many unique handmade items. “My postcard” area sells postcards with the pictures around Jeonju, and postcard is a great way to write down and keep memories of the time spent in Jeonju.
