Among them, the humanities program that is related to “fostering the next generation” of Seowons, is Salon de Wolbong.  Salon refers to the meetings of social leaders in the upper class of France in the 17th and 18th centuries, which were cradles of culture and intelligence. During the Joseon Dynasty, there was also a culture of writers enjoying the arts in the setting of nature’s beauty called “Gyesanpungnyu.” In that sense, Salon de Wolbong is a place for cultural exchanges where Gyesanpungnyu is revived in modern times with the participation of citizens.  The Salon de Wolbong program is held in “Gangsudang,” the education experience hall of Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy. It consists of cultural performances such as gugak, classical, jazz and fusion music performed on stage, “Theme Story Madang,” where various experts are invited to give lectures, and “Dadam,” in which participants and lecturers talk over tea. The annual program of Salon de Wolbong can be found on the homepage of Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy.

stories.title: Day of a Scholar in Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy
stories.audioTitle: Day of a Scholar in Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy - Live like a Scholar for a Day
stories.script: Day of a Scholar in Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy - Live like a Scholar for a Day    Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy operates the program “Day of a Scholar” where tourists can experience the life of scholars during the Joseon Dynasty. Scholars were talented and highly learned, being well-read, and good at poetry, painting and calligraphy, and represented an ideal human character in the Joseon Dynasty.  The day of a scholar starts by putting on a Confucian school uniform. Scholars wear a jade-green robe and a black jute cap shaped like the Chinese character for “scholar.”  After putting on this attire, the participants live out five keywords: etiquette, thinking, play, arts and socializing. First, they experience etiquette by bowing to ancestors at Sungdeoksa Shrine and spend time thinking while walking along Philosopher's Trail behind Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy. They can play by throwing arrows, and experience the arts by making a mirror scroll to reflect on themselves with. Finally, they talk over tea and the program comes to an end.

stories.title: Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy,Kids Philosophers’ Imagination School
stories.audioTitle: Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy, Kids Philosophers’ Imagination School, a Philosophy Class that Develops the Power of Thinking
stories.script: Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy, Kids Philosophers’ Imagination School, a Philosophy Class that Develops the Power of Thinking    The “Kids Philosophers’ Imagination School” program is held in Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy. In this program, children can raise the power of their thinking with fun. Gi Dae-seung (penname: Gobong) showed the importance of thinking differently via the debate over “Sadanchiljeong” (four impulses and seven emotions of humans) with Yi Hwang (penname: Toegye), a great scholar of the time.   The Kids Philosophers’ Imagination School combines “Sadanchiljeong” with amusing activities. Sadan refers to the four moral instincts a human inherently has and consists of: compassion, justice, modest behavior, and deciphering right from wrong. Chiljeong means seven human emotions: joy, anger, sorrow, pleasure, love, hatred and greed.    The Kids Philosophers’ Imagination School is composed of three series. “Square of Philosopher” teaches how to practice Sadan correctly with the theatrical play “Mugunghwa Gochi Pieosseumnida.” “Treasure of Philosopher” helps to control “Chiljeong” with the game Yunnori. Lastly, in the “Bingwol in My Mind” series, children learn the value of togetherness with the activity Ganggangsullae. You can find out how to participate in the Kids Philosophers’ Imagination School on the homepage of Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy.

stories.title: Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy, Iandang Dasi Dasi Café
stories.audioTitle: Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy, Iandang Dasi Dasi Café, a Traditional Culture Café You Can Visit in the Region of Scholars
stories.script: Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy, Iandang Dasi Dasi Café, a Traditional Culture Café You Can Visit in the Region of Scholars     In Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy, down a stonewall walkway near the entrance of the village, is a nicely kept hanok, or Korean traditional house, “Iandang,” which means “happy and comfortable house.” It has a guesthouse and a traditional café.   The café, “Dasi Dasi,” allows visitors to Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy to take a break from their busy daily lives. The first “Dasi” means “again” and the second “Dasi” means “tea and time.” In other words, “Dasi” represents the time when scholars of the Joseon Dynasty organized their thoughts before making an important decision.   The café sells coffee and various kinds of fruit tea and traditional tea. In particular, the Bamboo Dew Green Tea is collected from wild tea trees in a bamboo grove and can be tasted in April when the tea leaves are collected. Unlike other cafés, there are abundant things to do here. You can experience the life of a scholar by wearing a Confucian school uniform, making a Korean painting frame, writing letters on traditional Korean paper, hanji (Korean paper), and playing traditional games such as throwing arrows and jegichagi.

stories.title: Neobeusil Village
stories.audioTitle: Neobeusil Village, a Scholar’s Village in a Broad Valley
stories.script: Neobeusil Village, a Scholar’s Village in a Broad Valley    Located on the border between Gwangju and Jangseong-gun, Jeollanam-do, Neobeusil Village is where descendants of Gi Dae-seung (penname: Gobong), a Confucian scholar from the Joseon Dynasty, live. The name of this village, in an impressive landscape encompassing the east of the Hwangnyongang River to Baegusan Mountain, originates from the Chinese characters for “Gwanggok,” which means “broad valley.”   It is said that the Haengju Gi Clan took root in Neobeusil Village after the father of Gi Dae-seung moved to Gwangju. After Gi Jun, Gi Dae-seung’s uncle, who led reform politics with Jo Gwang-jo, was assassinated while in political persecution, the father of Gi Dae-seung went to the rural village and turned his back on the world. Gi was then born in 1527.  There are traces of Gi Dae-seung throughout Neobeusil Village. The representative places include Wolbongseowon Confucian Academy where his tablet is enshrined, his tomb in the middle of Baegusan Mountain, and Chilsongjeong Pavilion, which was built in the place where his first son mourned. Also, there is the site of Gwijeonam Rock, where Gi cultivated his mind and studied until his death, as well as Gwihujae Shrine, which had been used as a Seodang for the Gi family and is now being used for observing the family’s ancestors.

stories.title: Chilsongjeong Pavilion
stories.audioTitle: Chilsongjeong Pavilion, Filial Piety Contained in Seven Pine Trees
stories.script: Chilsongjeong Pavilion, Filial Piety Contained in Seven Pine Trees    If you enter a plain path at the entrance of Neobeusil Village, there is Chilsongjeong Pavilion on a low hill. It is a pavilion that was built on the place where Gi Hyo-jeung, the first son of Gi Dae-seung (penname: Gobong), mourned.  In the Joseon Dynasty, when parents passed away their children built a mud house around the tombs of their parents and lived there for three years to mourn. After mourning, with a regretful mind that he didn’t serve his parents with devotion, Gi Hyo-jeung built a pavilion named Chilsongjeong and planted seven pine trees there.  There is an interesting story that has been passed down about the grave site of Gi about 300 m away from Chilsongjeong Pavilion. Gi conceded a good grave site based on feng shui to his older brother and decided on a site for his grave that was predicted to prevent continued offspring, before he died. When his son and pupils were discouraged, he said, “Aren’t the offspring of siblings my offspring?” This  example shows the great personality and brotherly love of Gi.

stories.title: 1913 Songjeong Station Market
stories.audioTitle: 1913 Songjeong Station Market, the Transformation of a 100-year-old Traditional Market
stories.script: 1913 Songjeong Station Market, the Transformation of a 100-year-old Traditional Market    The revitalized 1913 Songjeong Station Market is a traditional market that boasts a history of over 100 years. It was originally “Maeil Songjeong Station Market,” but the name was changed to commemorate its long history.  The new chapter of 1913 Songjeong Station Market, which had once been on its way out, started with the remodeling of 10 empty stores as a revitalization project for the traditional market. Young vendors brought in energy with fresh ideas, and existing store owners refreshed their old signboards. Also, they added a written history and photos showing the origin and history of the establishments on the storefronts. Looking around the market and reading up on the history of the stores is one good way to enjoy 1913 Songjeong Station Market.   When it comes to a traditional market, food should be included. There are countless things in the market that will stimulate your appetite such as homemade fishcakes, fresh fruit jelly with red beans, croquettes, boiled barley rice, and homemade Choco Pies. On top of that, the charming array of shops, such as blanket stores, shoe stores and fish stores provides fun things to look at in 1913 Songjeong Station Market.

stories.title: House of Kim Bong-ho
stories.audioTitle: House of Kim Bong-ho, a Traditional Farmhouse in the Center of the Town
stories.script: House of Kim Bong-ho, a Traditional Farmhouse in the Center of the Town     The House of Kim Bong-ho in Hanam-dong, Gwangsan-gu is conspicuous in the urban landscape where there is a concentration of tall buildings and sophisticated cafés. But it is Gwangju-si Cultural Heritage No. 25 because of its invaluable data of architectural history and folklore, as it is still in its original state. Various agricultural tools and household items are still preserved here.  The House of Kim Bong-ho, a typical upper-class farmhouse built in the 1940s, is a quite large wooden Korean-style tile-roofed house. The main building’s layout starts with a scullery, followed by the kitchen, main room, center floored hall and opposite room. In the main building, pay attention to the attic, called “Gongnu.” An attic is usually a room with one kan (the space from one column to the next), but this one is wide with three kans, encompassing the main room, center floored hall and opposite room. In particular, since the attic of a hanok, a Korean traditional house, with a tile roof has an insulation effect, it’s cool in summer and warm in winter.  Besides the main building, the stable, warehouse, well and outdoor bathroom have been preserved. There is a wood-burning stove in the outdoor bathroom that was used to heat water in a pot. If you look around the House of Kim Bong-ho slowly, you will fall in love with a hanok that has weathered the years and feel as if you were in a scene in a historical drama.

stories.title: Asia Culture Center in Gwangju
stories.audioTitle: Asia Culture Center, Korea’s Largest Cultural Complex
stories.script: Asia Culture Center, Korea’s Largest Cultural Complex     The Asia Culture Center behind the old Jeollanam-do Provincial Office, a symbol of Korea’s democratization movement, holds exhibitions, performances and research on themes of Asia and culture. With a total area of 156,000 ㎡, this is the largest cultural space in Korea. Despite its huge size, all the spaces are constructed in the basement with the design concept, “forest of light.” It harmonizes well with the surrounding landscape.   The center is composed of various spaces. The Democracy and Peace Exchange Center, remodeled from the old Jeollanam-do Provincial Office, was made into the 5.18 Democracy and Peace Memorial Hall and Cultural Exchange Center. Meanwhile, the ACC Children’s Center, where children can experience culture by watching plays, is composed of an experience hall, library, theater and creation laboratory.   The Cultural Information Center is a new cultural space which includes a library, museum, gallery and theater. One wall of the theater can be opened to become seats or a stage. The Culture Creation Center next to the art theater holds video screenings, performances and seminars on the history and culture of the world.

stories.title: Sancheong-gun, Gyeongsangnam-do
stories.audioTitle: Sancheong-gun, Gyeongsangnam-do - Healing with Oriental Medicine and Nature
stories.script: Sancheong-gun, Gyeongsangnam-do - Healing with Oriental Medicine and Nature    Sancheong has a magnificent landscape that includes the popular Jirisan Mountain, and is full of various tourist destinations and interesting stories. In the valley at the foot of Jirisan Mountain is the picturesque Daewonsa Temple. You can also find Namsa Yedamchon Village, in Sancheong which was designated as “the most beautiful village in Korea.”  Sancheong is called the “region of medicinal herbs” as countless medicinal herbs are found in its untainted natural environment. Sancheong successfully hosted the 2013 World Traditional Medicine Expo and the Sancheong Medicinal Herb Festival is held every year. You can see exhibitions related to oriental medicine in Donguibogam Village, where the Korean Medicine Museum and Experiential Themed Park are located.  Sancheong also has many significant sites of historical figures. There is the stone tomb of King Guhyeong, the last king of Gaya, and the remains of Jo Sik (penname: Nammyeong), who, along with Yi Hwang (penname: Toegye), are representative Confucian scholars from the mid-Joseon Dynasty. You should not miss the birthplace of the great Buddhist monk Seong Cheol who is famous for the saying, “mountains are mountains, and rivers are rivers.” Sancheong, in which nature, history and traditional culture harmonize, is an interesting tourist destination for everyone.

stories.title: Donguibogam Village
stories.audioTitle: Donguibogam Village, the Nation’s First Healing Travel Site for Korean Medicine
stories.script: Donguibogam Village, the Nation’s First Healing Travel Site for Korean Medicine    Donguibogam Village is a large theme park which has various experiences, exhibitions and resort facilities. The village’s name originates from “Donguibogam,” a book on traditional Korean medicine, which is listed in the UNESCO Memory of the World Register.  The exhibition facilities include the EXPO Themed Hall, Korean Medicine Museum, which help in the understanding of traditional medicine, and Sancheong Medicinal Herb Hall, which exhibits rare medicinal herbs and plants that grow on Jirisan Mountain.  At the popular “Ki” (qi - vital force) Experience Hall there are three rocks of “Ki” where you can receive good energy. Also, the Donguibogam Village Experiential Themed Park, Heo Jun Trail, and Hanbang Maze Park are good areas to enjoy a walk.   There are various recreational and accommodation facilities here such as a recreational forest, hotels, a hanok stay – a stay at a Korean traditional house, and condominiums. There are also restaurants that sell bibimbap with medicinal herbs and dishes with oriental medicine, as well as a store that sells Sancheong specialties.  Although Donguibogam Village is quite large, walking is recommended, as the trails and roads are well organized. If you take a leisurely tour of the village while taking breaks in pavilions and on benches between courses, it’s a good chance to energize your body and mind.

stories.title: Donguibogam Village, Expo Themed Hall
stories.audioTitle: Donguibogam Village_Expo Themed Hall, a Place which has Various Exhibitions from Insects and Ötzi the Iceman to Korean Medicine
stories.script: Donguibogam Village_Expo Themed Hall, a Place which has Various Exhibitions from Insects and Ötzi the Iceman to Korean Medicine    Upon entering Donguibogam Village’s main gate, you will first see the EXPO Themed Hall. It looks like two buildings from the outside since it was built with two different shapes, but it is one structure, with traditional Korean architecture symbolizing Gyeonghoeru Pavilion on one side and Western architecture symbolizing the Parthenon on the other.  The EXPO Themed Hall was used during the 2013 World Traditional Medicine Expo in Sancheong. In the Insect Exhibition Hall there are specimens of insects and butterflies collected from Jirisan Mountain in Sancheong. In the Iceman Ötzi Exhibition Hall, you learn about the secrets of medicine with “Ötzi,” the 5,300-year-old mummified man discovered in the ice of the Otzal Alps in 1991. Birch mushrooms, which are used as a natural antibiotic, were found along with parasites in the intestines of Ötzi. Also, 59 tattoos were found on the meridian points of his body, suggesting that Ötzi used medicinal herbs to treat diseases and used acupuncture to control pain.  The Korean Medicine Healing Park is an exhibition hall that introduces the excellence of Korean medicine. The basic principles of Korea medicine based on the principles of the universe and royal traditional Korean medicinal health management methods are exhibited. Also, you can watch related videos and 4D animations for children in the 4D Image Hall and Theme Image Hall.

stories.title: Donguibogam Village,Korean Medicine Museum
stories.audioTitle: Donguibogam Village_Korean Medicine Museum, where Korean Medicine is Taught and Experienced with Fun
stories.script: Donguibogam Village_Korean Medicine Museum, where Korean Medicine is Taught and Experienced with Fun    If you climb a low hill at the back gate of the EXPO Themed Hall, you will find the Korean Medicine Museum, which has Donguibogam Hall and the Korean Medicine Experience Center.  The first floor of Donguibogam Hall introduces the value, status and excellence of “Donguibogam,” a book on traditional Korean medicine listed in the UNESCO Memory of the World Register. In particular, the exhibit “Donguibogam in daily living,” which shows practical aspects of “Donguibogam,” is very interesting as it recreates scenes from Korea’s old way of life. An old Korean medicine clinic, herbal medicine shop, Korean medicine doctor and patients are very realistically portrayed.  In the Korean Medicine Experience Center on the second floor there is the Korean Medicinal Herbs Forest and Korean Medicine Dulle Road. The Herbs Forest has exhibits of medicinal herbs that grow naturally in Sancheong, the region of medicinal herbs, and you can experience them. The Korean Medicine Dulle Road introduces Korean medicine health management methods according to gender and age. You can learn how to grow your brain and height, how to slim your body and face, how to be healthy, and how to live a long life of 100 years. You can apply the information you obtain from the Korean Medicine Experience Center to your daily life.

stories.title: Donguibogam Village,Experiential Themed Park
stories.audioTitle: Donguibogam Village_ Experiential Themed Park, a Korean Medicine Story Enjoyed in Nature
stories.script: Donguibogam Village_ Experiential Themed Park, a Korean Medicine Story Enjoyed in Nature    Between the EXPO Themed Hall and Korean Medicine Museum is a huge sculpture of a bear, and there is a sculpture of a tiger in the lower area of the Experiential Themed Park. These sculptures at the start and end points of the park refers to the myth of Dangun, the myth of the founding of the Korean people.  There is a mural depicting the myth of Dangun on the bear sculpture, and the park is seen in the bear’s mouth. The golden leatherback sea turtle sculpture, which is located in front of the sculpture, is the largest of its kind in the world. Gold symbolizes luck and wealth, and the turtle symbolizes longevity. It is said that if you touch the Chinese characters for “luck” and “longevity” carved on the neck of the leatherback sea turtle, you will be blessed and live to a great age.  Other sculptures in the center of the park depict the mysterious human body’s organs based on Sinhyeongjangbudo (illustration of the human body) in “Naegyeongpyeon,” the first section of Donguibogam. After passing the sculpture of a heart, liver and small intestines, you will arrive at the end of the park.  Above the Experiential Themed Park there is the Korean Medicinal Herbs Experience Theme Park where various medicinal herbs that grow on Jirisan Mountain are displayed. Take a walk and enjoy the seasonal medicinal herbs and their scent.

stories.title: Donguibogam Village -Sancheong Medicinal Herb Hall
stories.audioTitle: Donguibogam Village_Sancheong Medicinal Herb Hall, a Beautiful Hanok-Style Greenhouse
stories.script: Donguibogam Village_Sancheong Medicinal Herb Hall, a Beautiful Hanok-Style Greenhouse    Between the Korean Medicine Museum and Observatory, Sancheong Medicinal Herb Hall is a hanok-style, a traditional Korean house-style, glass greenhouse where you can see rare medicinal herbs that grow naturally on Jirisan Mountain. It is a beautiful building that goes well with Donguibogam Village.  In Sancheong Medicinal Herb Hall, 60 woody plants and 100 herbs are exhibited. Woody plants have large, hard stems and roots, while herbs have soft, moist stems.  It takes about 5 minutes to tour the entire hall quickly, but if you look at the plants in detail, it can take over 30 minutes. The name and efficacy of each plant is written on a name plate in front of the medicinal herb, with the age written for old trees. For example, you can learn that sand pear is effective for treating a cough, phlegm, a fever, tuberculosis, and constipation, and it is 100 years old.   The exhibition theme in the Sancheong Medicinal Herb Hall is “Recipe for Good Health - Donguibogam Garden.” If you look around while taking notes on the efficacy of medicinal herbs, you can make your own “health recipe.”

stories.title: Donguibogam Village -”Ki” Experience Hall
stories.audioTitle: Donguibogam Village_”Ki” Experience Hall, Good Energy Spreading in the Mind
stories.script: Donguibogam Village_”Ki” Experience Hall, Good Energy Spreading in the Mind    The “Ki” (qi – vital energy) Experience Hall is a place where you can heal your body and mind with Korean medicinal energy training and meditation, and it is located in the upper area of the circulation path. It has hanoks (traditional Korean houses) placed in a circle, and a mountain unfolds behind it. It’s beautiful like an oriental painting.   The three rocks of “Ki,”, Seokgyeong, Gwigamseok, and Bokseokjeong around the “Ki” Experience Hall are said to provide good energy. Seokgyeong is a mirror made of stone. Gwigamseok looks like a turtle and is so named because all good things under the sky are written on it. Bokseokjeong means “a bowl containing luck.” It is said that energy from Jirisan Mountain runs through Seokgyeong and Gwigamseok and ends in Bokseokjeong next to Gicheonmun Gate. It’s also said that if you pray while circulating Bokseokjeong, your prayers will come to fruition.  Donguijeon, in the center of “Ki” Experience Hall, has an exhibit related to Korean medicine, including a sasang constitution diagnosis. Jeongakjeon next to Donguijeon is a seal engraving that was used for manufacturing Korea’s top four Great Seals, and the kiln that was used for it still remains. The chimney seen behind Jeongakjeon was created by accumulating ceramics one by one, and it looks like a work of art.

stories.title: Donguibogam Village, Heo Jun Trail
stories.audioTitle: Donguibogam Village_Heo Jun Trail, a Meditation Trail Through a Forest
stories.script: Donguibogam Village_Heo Jun Trail, a Meditation Trail Through a Forest    Heo Jun Trail is named after a medicinal scientist in the mid-Joseon era. The trail, which has three courses, goes through a forest with evergreen trees, an area with a magnificent landscape of Korean chrysanthemums, and a pavilion next to flowing water, a nice place to  take a break.  Course 1 includes the observatory where there is a panoramic view of Donguibogam Village, and a farm where deer run freely. On Course 2, you will find Autopsy Cave, which represents Heo Jun Trail. In the novel and drama about Heo Jun, his teacher Ryu Ui-tae passes away, leaving a note that his body should be dissected to save many lives, and the scene that Heo Jun dissects his teacher’s body in the cave is recreated. Course 3 goes from Autopsy Cave to the Ryu Ui-tae Mineral Spring.  Since Heo Jun Trail is connected to various popular places in Donguibogam Village, it’s easy to access, anytime during the tour of the village. It is interesting to walk on the wooden stairs, wooden deck road, dirt path and stone road. Also, it is good to meditate while walking on the forest path.

stories.title: Donguibogam Village, Korean Medicine Recreational Forest
stories.audioTitle: Donguibogam Village_Korean Medicine Recreational Forest - Enjoy the Essence of Rest
stories.script: Donguibogam Village_Korean Medicine Recreational Forest - Enjoy the Essence of Rest    If you want to have a healing trip in Donguibogam Village, stay for a night. The village has various accommodations such as a recreational forest, hotels, hanoks – traditional Korean houses, and condominiums. Among them, Korean Medicine Recreational Forest is particularly attractive because you can relax in nature.  Korean Medicine Recreational Forest, in the uppermost area of Donguibogam Village, has a beautiful landscape and clean air because it has Wangsan Mountain and Pilbongsan Mountain behind it. The forest has accommodations called Forest Rest Hall and Forest House, which are like condominiums and single-family houses, respectively. They are decorated with hinoki cypress, so you enjoy a healthy stay.  On the outdoor deck for campers, there is a restroom, shower room and kitchen. Also, you can use the outdoor swimming pool, seminar room, volleyball court, and trail. Korean Medicine Recreational Forest is attractive as it is good for a light walk and hiking and has paths to Wangsan Mountain and Pilbongsan Mountain. Enjoy a real Korean medicinal healing trip while looking at the green trees, wild grass and flowers.

stories.title: Donguibonga Healing Town
stories.audioTitle: Donguibonga Healing Town, a Healthy Experience with Medicinal Herbs, from a Herbal Spa to Wrapping Medicine
stories.script: Donguibonga Healing Town, a Healthy Experience with Medicinal Herbs, from a Herbal Spa to Wrapping Medicine    Donguibogam Village has the Korean medicine clinics Donguibonga and Bondiol. Donguibonga offers an experience program and hanok stay (accommodations at a traditional Korean house) as well as Korean medicinal treatments.  The Korean medicinal experience program is mainly composed of making Korean medicine and Korean medicine treatments. The former includes making medicinal toothpaste, wrapping for medicine, and a pretty scent bag to hold medicine prescribed by a Korean medicine doctor.  The latter includes experiencing a longevity pillow, called “Sinchim,” made with medicinal herbs that help get sound sleep. If you lay on a Sinchim and have a moxa on your belly button in a hanok ondol (heated floor) room, you will feel very comfortable because it warms your belly and clears your head.  The medicinal herb spa is a lower-body bathing experience with a medicinal herb bath. Experience a well-known longevity secret from “Donguibogam,” “Keep your head cold and your feet warm.” We recommend that you try moxa and a medicinal herb spa and stay one night in a Donguibonga hanok.

stories.title: Korean Medicine Permanent Program Experience
stories.audioTitle: Korean Medicine Permanent Program Experience, a Way to Enjoy Donguibogam Village with More Fun
stories.script: Korean Medicine Permanent Program Experience, a Way to Enjoy Donguibogam Village with More Fun    If you participate in the permanent experience programs of Donguibogam Village, your trip will be more enjoyable. The most popular program is trying on an “Eouibok” and “Uinyeobok.” Eoui refers to a court physician who treated the king and royal family, and Uinyeo refers to a female doctor who only treated female patients during the Joseon Dynasty when men and women strictly kept their distance from each other.  You try on these clothes on the first floor of the EXPO Themed Hall. The Eouibok includes a cap called “Samo,” and the Uinyeobok comes with a “Heukdan Garima”. There is a fee to try on the traditional clothes. If you tour Donguibogam Village in these costumes, you will feel as if you were a person in the Joseon Dynasty.  A Korean medicine thermal experience is conducted on the second floor of Donguijeon in the “Ki” (qi – vital energy) Experience Hall. When the weather is good, you can relax on a thermal bed for 30 minutes while looking out at the landscape through an open window. There are also various permanent experience programs. These experiences will make exploring Donguibogam Village more fun.

stories.title: Namsa Yedamchon Village
stories.audioTitle: Namsa Yedamchon Village, a Picturesque Combination of Old Houses and Walls
stories.script: Namsa Yedamchon Village, a Picturesque Combination of Old Houses and Walls    Namsa Yedamchon Village was designated as “the most beautiful village in Korea” in 2011. The name means “village of lovely walls,” and the lengthy walls around the village are famous and are Registered Cultural Heritage No. 281. Nigusan Mountain behind the village and the watercourse surrounding the village, Sasu, were named after Qufu, China, where Confucius was born.  The village boasts a long history and has a lot of old trees. In particular, there are two 300-year-old sophora trees that cross trunks to make the letter “X,” and are called “the couple tree.” It is said that if a couple passes under this tree, they will live in conjugal harmony.  Another source of pride of Namsa Yedamchon Village is the group of hanoks (traditional Korean houses) that have been beautifully preserved for a long time. The House of the Yi Clan, built in the 1700s, is the oldest one in the village, and you can stay overnight in Sayangjeongsa Shrine, which has dignity and restraint. Leisurely enjoy the grounds, wandering along the stone walls laid out like a labyrinth, to  experience the charm of this cozy village.

stories.title: Jo Sik Historic Site in Sancheong
stories.audioTitle: Jo Sik Historic Site - Learn from the Life of a Lofty Scholar
stories.script: Jo Sik Historic Site - Learn from the Life of a Lofty Scholar    There are reminders of Jo Sik (penname: Nammyeong), a representative Confucian scholar of the mid-Joseon era, around Sancheong-gun with Jirisan Mountain stretching to the southeast. Although Jo Sik was respected as a “great teacher of the Yeongnam region” along with Yi Hwang (penname: Toegye), who was the same age, the two lived different lives. While Yi entered the government service, Jo refused a government post and concentrated on studying and training junior scholars.  Sancheonjae House, the place where Jo trained junior scholars until he died, has a humbleness to it, similar to his pure and lofty personality. Splendid Jirisan Mountain unfolds behind it, and the Deokcheongang River flows in front of it. In the yard, there is a Japanese apricot tree that is said to have been planted by Jo, and a monument of “Ueum” that means “a poem extempore.”    On the opposite side of Sancheonjae there is Nammyeong Memorial Hall, which was established to pay tribute to his learning and virtue, as well as to preserve and exhibit relics. One and a half kilometers away from Sancheonjae House toward Jirisan Mountain is Deokcheonseowon Confucian Academy.  It was established by Jo’s disciples four years after his death, to preserve his spirit and studies. The central building, “Gyeonguidang,” originates from the representative teaching of Jo. He taught that “Gyeong” means being upright by brightening the mind internally, and “Ui” means deciding and practicing it externally. This is still enlightening modern people today.

stories.title: Royal Tomb of King Guhyeong
stories.audioTitle: Royal Tomb of King Guhyeong, a Stone Grave Containing a Chapter of History
stories.script: Royal Tomb of King Guhyeong, a Stone Grave Containing a Chapter of History    About 5 minutes by car from Donguibogam Village toward Hamyang  is Deogyangjeon Shrine, where the tablets of Gaya’s 10th king and queen are enshrined. One kilometer up the left road from Deogyangjeon Shrine is a unique stone grave at the foot of Wangsan Mountain. It is said to be the tomb of King Guhyeong, who was the 10th and last king of Gaya and the great-grandfather of Kim Yu-sin. In front of the tomb, at the center, is a stone tablet with the words “Royal Tomb of King Yang of Garakguk” written on it, as well as recently made stone sculptures. King Yang was the posthumous epithet of the king Guhyeong. It is said that he left a will that said, “make a stone grave,” because he was pained that his kingdom had surrendered to Silla.  The Royal Tomb of King Guhyeong is made up of stones piled in a pyramid shape. From the front, it looks like it has seven layers and there is a small space in the stylobate in front, the use of which is not known. Take a moment to think about the Gaya Kingdom, which has faded into the mists of history, while looking around the tomb.

stories.title: Daewonsagyegok Valley
stories.script: Daewonsagyegok Valley - Walk along a Clean Waterway on Jirisan Mountain  Daewonsagyegok Valley is regarded as the most beautiful valley in Jirisan Mountain. A stream originating from the mountain’s largest ridge flows refreshingly down to Daewonsa Temple. The valley is named after the temple, which is famous for being one of Korea’s Top 3 bhikkhuni (female Buddhist monastic) temples.  Daewonsagyegok Valley has a magnificent landscape in which water, strange rocks, bizarre stones, and trees come into harmony. The water flowing in the valley between small rocks is clean and clear. Scholars used to enjoy “Takjok,” a traditional way to find reprieve from the heat in the summer by dunking one’s feet in the cold, pure water of nature, in the valley.  The picturesque Daewonsa Temple, which harmonizes with the clean, beautiful valley, was built during the Silla Dynasty. The temple was rebuilt a few times due to fire and is elegant and nicely presented. While you are at the temple, do not miss the multi-story stone pagoda located on the hill. It is one of the few stone pagodas from the mid-Joseon period and has a fine, tall shape.   If you go up a little from Daewonsa Temple, there is Yongsopokpo Falls, legend has it that a dragon went up into the sky after living in it for one hundred years. The rocks here are mysterious because they have holes and look like small caves.   Since there are a few parking lots in the middle of Daewonsagyegok Valley, you can take a nice break while enjoying the beautiful valley landscape.

stories.title: Birthplace of Great Monk Seongcheol
stories.audioTitle: Birthplace of Great Monk Seongcheol - Mountains are mountains, and rivers are rivers
stories.script: Birthplace of Great Monk Seongcheol - Mountains are mountains, and rivers are rivers    “Mountains are mountains, and rivers are rivers.” This is a representative Buddhist saying of monk Seongcheol, the Great Star of Korean Buddhism. Seongcheol, who was born in Sancheong, strengthened his ties with Buddhism while going back and forth to Daewonsa Temple. The Birthplace of Great Monk Seongcheol, his home before becoming a Buddhist, was restored.  Geoboesa Temple was built to pay tribute to the monk, who received the designation of Great Master (Daejongsa).  The name Geoboesa means “a temple that transcends time and space.” There is a bronze statue of monk Seongcheol, a Buddhist rosary, and a sculpture of a moktak (a wooden percussion instrument used for chanting by Buddhist clergy) in the large yard of the temple.  His life story, from becoming a Buddhist to his cremation rite, is depicted in a painting on the outer wall of Daeungjeon Hall.  The Birthplace of Great Monk Seongcheol is behind the bronze statue. His birthplace is composed of a main building, detached house, and the Relics Exhibition Hall. The main building is a reproduction of Yeomhwasil in Baengnyeonam Hermitage of Haeinsa Temple. In this reproduction of Yeomhwasil, which is a room where a monk lives, there is an old desk and a chair that he used and satgat (a conical hat  made of bamboo) that he wore to avoid the sun. In the Relics Exhibition Hall, the Buddhist robe and rubber shoes he wore are on display. These are the representative relics that show the non-materialistic spirit of monk Seongcheol.

stories.title: Introduction
stories.script: Introduction   “Surrounded by refreshing mountains and beautiful water, Yeoju of Gyeonggi-do Province used to be known as the heavenly soil. In the midst of Yeoju lies Silleuksa!”  “These are the words of Suon Kim, a writer from the early Joseon Dynasty period. As this ancient writer indicated, Silleksa Temple, nestled along the curvy southern part of Han River, has been a famous attraction representing Yeoju for a thousand years .”  “Unlike most temples located amongst mountains, Silleuksa rests on a riverside, overlooking the clear blue water beside an open sandy beach and spacious fields.”  “A glance at the historical record reveals that the outstanding beauty of Silleuksa in Yeoju has been known for over a thousand years, proving that the millennial temple is true to its name.”   “Of the eight must-see attractions of Yeoju, Silleuk Mojong—the sound of the evening dharma bell at Sillueksa Temple—is at the top. This experience itself is a cultural asset representative of Yeoju City.”  “Alongside the calmly flowing water of the southern Han River, Silleuksa has silently kept the history of the land for a thousand years. Inside this beautiful millennial temple, where air, soil, water and wind create such harmony, why not meet your true self by setting aside the confusion in your mind?”

stories.title: The Legend of Silleuksa
stories.script: The Legend of Silleuksa   “Silleuksa, the millennial temple, is said to to have been founded by Venerable Wonhyo during the reign of King Jinpyeong, the 26th ruler of the Silla Kingdom. It is said that one day, an old man in white clothes appeared to Venerable Wonhyo in a dream…”  “Wonhyo, do you see that pond over there? In the future, there will be a sacred temple overlooking that pond!”  “Venerable Wonhyo then prayed sincerely for seven days, until nine dragons emerged from the pond to which the old man had pointed and flew into the sky. Venerable Wonhyo went on to found a temple overlooking the pond, which came to be known as Silleuksa Temple.”  “Since ancient times, dragons were known as loyal vassals. Rough waves were called ‘Yongma,’ or swift dragons. As the southern part of Han River has long been known for frequent flooding, the desperate wish of the local people to quiet this rough weather has been included in another foundation legend.”    “During the reign of King U, the 34th ruler of the Goryeo Dynasty, a bizarre uncontrollable horse appeared and caused damage to the people at a place called Maam near Silleuksa. According to legend, Seon Master Naong tamed the horse with a magical bridle, so the temple came to be known as Silleuksa.”  “In another legend set during the the time of King Gojong, the 23rd ruler of the Goryeo Dynasty, a wild horse appeared in a village across from the temple. An old master named Venerable Indang approached the horse and pulled on its reins. The horse was immediately tamed, indicating a god’s power had magically controlled the savage. As a result, the temple came to be called Silleuksa.”  “Sil, leuk…, the temple overpowers misfortune with the power of god, Silleuksa! With just the name alone, its mystical power can be felt.”

stories.title: Iljumun of Silleuksa Temple
stories.script: Iljumun of Silleuksa Temple   “Ah, finally, it’s Silleuksa! Honey, this is Iljumun of Silleuksa!”  Iljumun? Is this the main gate of the temple?”  “That’s right! The first gate into a temple is called Iljumun. This symbolizes ‘oneness’ or ‘one mind!’ Originally, Iljumun meant that the pillars were lined up as one. Rather than having four pillars like a common house, a roof was placed on just two pillars!”  “Oh, you’re right, there are only two pillars. Are these beams made of rock rather than wood?”  “Are they? In Iljumun of Silleuksa, the distinctive technique of entasis for stone pillars was used; with this technique, the middle part of the pillars was slightly thicker in diameter! Look, there is some writing carved here! Can you read it? Now, from the right…”  “Samilsusim Cheonjaebo, even a short period of cultivating the mind can be treasured for a thousand years!”  “Baenyeontamyog Iljojin, a hundred years of greed becomes dust overnight!”  “These sound wise. It would be nice if people could live like that!”  “Why not live like that? It is said to contain the teaching that one should clear worldly afflictions with the Buddha’s words, and go in with one mind toward the world of wisdom before entering the sacred temple!”  “Oh, really? That’s why I feel that my mind is being cleared…”  “Now, shall we go into Silleuksa Temple, the world of wisdom, with our clear minds?”

stories.title: Josadang of Silleuksa
stories.script: Josadang of Silleuksa   “Standing in the northwest part of Silleuksa Temple, Josadang, the Shrine of Patriarchs, which is the oldest among all the buildings, houses the portraits of the three famed masters Jigon, Naong and Muhak, and serves as a place to pay tribute to their deeds.”  “Josadang is a hall that houses the tablets and portraits of preeminent priests, or great masters who have formed Buddhist sects, allowing visitors to pay tribute.”  “In the midst of the downfall of Buddhism in the late Goryeo Dynasty period, as a close knit group of teachers and disciples, the three venerables Jigon, Naong and Muhak were a strand of hope. Josadang is a uniquely structured hall that consists of one column in the front and two at the sides, standing on low stone steps.”   “Registered as Treasure No. 180 in 1963, the current Josadang structure is believed to have been built using the early Joseon style, though a number of repairs have been conducted up to the present day. The presence of Josadang in Silleuksa can be verified by historical record to at least as far back as 1379, in the fifth year of King U, the 34th ruler of the Goryeo Dynasty. ”  “Thick trees tell me to to live without words, and the sky orders me to stay without any defilement; without any greed and letting go of anger, dwell and leave like water and wind! The teaching of Seon Master Naong, who entered nirvana in Silleuksa, continues to encourage practitioners at the temple to endeavor to abandon greed and seek righteous paths.”

stories.title: Bell-shaped Stupa and Stele of Buddhist Monk Boje (Silleuksa Temple, Yeoju)
stories.audioTitle: Bell-shaped Stupa and Stele of Buddhist Monk Boje (Silleuksa Temple, Yeoju)
stories.script: Bell-shaped Stupa and Stele of Buddhist Monk Boje of Silleuksa Temple  The vital energy of the main range of Odaesan Mountain is rising here in Bongmisan Mountain from Yeogang River through Yeonbangsan, Gongjaksan, Oeumsan, and Godalsan Mountains! This place is considered the best among the surrounding area.  The current location of the Bell-shaped Stupa and the Stele of Buddhist Monk Boje of Silleuksa Temple is where Master Muhak, an expert in feng shui, believed it was suitable to enshrine his teacher, Zen Master Naong. The name “Bojejonja” was the posthumous title given to Zen Master Naong by King Gongmin, the 33rd ruler of the Goryeo Dynasty.  Bell-shaped Stupa of Buddhist Monk Boje was built in 1379, three years after Zen Master Naong reached Nirvana. It was called “Seokjong” or stone stupa because it was shaped like a bell made of stone, and a stupa containing the relics of Zen Master Naong was enshrined in the middle.  Facing the Namhangang River, Silleuksa Temple and its stone stupa stands tall. When the moon rises, it will tilt and submerge in its river of shadows, with the reflections of azure water, lanterns, and incense smoke blending and fading into it. The solidity of the stone bell not only shares the beginning and end of Silleuksa Temple, but also the river and the water. The epitaph ‘We will be together forever!’ on the Bojejonjaseokjong stele is written by Goryeo scholar Mogeun Lee Saek.   Zen Master Naong was a great revolutionary who compiled Korean Zen Buddhism and advocated practical rebirth relief for the persecuted people. Standing in front of the Bell-shaped Stupa and Stele of Buddhist Monk Boje at Silleuksa Temple, you can feel the presence of Zen Master Naong, whose teachings of truth and wisdom continue to inspire many to this day.

stories.title: Dacheung Seoktap and Jeontap of Silleuksa
stories.audioTitle: Dacheung Seoktap and Jeontap of Silleuksa
stories.script: Dacheung Seoktap and Jeontap of Silleuksa   “….As you can see, this Dacheung Seoktap, or multi-layered stone pagoda, was, interestingly enough, made of white marble. The sense of formation that it exhibits  is outstanding, making the stone pagoda exceedingly elegant! Though the original structure has suffered much damage, making it difficult to determine how many stories it once had, superbly carved dragons and clouds illustrate the application of excellent techniques at the base of the pagoda!”  “Professor, the structure of this pagoda seems to adhere to techniques of the Silla or Goryeo periods, does it not?”  “Yes, you have made an excellent observation! However, the details of this pagoda are quite different from others of the Silla or Goryeo periods. This one displays a unique sense of formation!”  “I see! As I look at it more closely, I see that lotus designs have been carved on four sides between the pagoda and the ground, and the exquisite techniques applied to create the realistic dragons and clouds at the bottom of the body were extremely skillful!”   “This is the Dacheung Jeontap of Silleuksa! Do you know what a Jeontap is?”  “Of course, this is a pagoda made of bricks. I also know that this multi-layered brick pagoda is the one and only jeontop from the Goryeo period!”  “Haha, of course! As Silleuksa has a pagoda made of stacked bricks, it has also been known as ‘Byeokjeol since ancient times. As the water flowing down the stream often flooded Silleuksa, this jeontap functioned as a lighthouse.”  “Wow, a pagoda functioning as a lighthouse! This structure now seems much more interesting!”

stories.title: Gangweolheon Pavilion (Silleuksa Temple, Yeoju)
stories.script: Gangweolheon Pavilion of Silleuksa Temple  From Gangweolheon Pavilion, you can see Namhangang River at a glance. This beautiful pavilion, Gangweolheon, rests on a steep cliff along the riverside of the Namhangang River.  As a riverside temple, there are many places like this within the temple grounds.  Gangweolheon Pavilion is named after the Zen Master Naong’s posthumous dharma name. It was built to pay tribute to his achievements after he reached Nirvana.  When Zen Master Naong was alive, he advocated realistic ideas for saving all human beings, and many people followed him because of his high virtue. However, he had to come all the way to Silleuksa Temple as he was being chased by some Confucian scholars.  Silleuksa Temple was Zen Master Naong’s last residence and he vowed to dedicate his entire life to attain enlightenment. This very site of Gangweolheon Pavilion is where his cremation service was done.   This pavilion with such stunning scenery is loved by Zen Master Naong when he was still alive. It is said that he used to talk to his disciples at a spot that overlooking the river with the moon beaming in the sky. And now, Gangweolheon Pavilion still remains here overlooking the river long after the death of Zen Master Naong.

stories.title: Geuknakbojeon of Silleuksa
stories.script: Geuknakbojeon of Silleuksa   “Geuknakbojeon, the Hall of Utmost Bliss, enshrines Amitabha Buddha and serves as the main dharma hall of Silleuksa. Amitabha Buddha, overseeing the Utmost Bliss of the Pure Land of the West, assists the blissful rebirth in the Pure Land of the dead, and the longevity and comfort of sentient beings.”  “Silleuksa was appointed as Wonchal, a royal shrine, to pay tribute to King Sejong the Great, the fourth ruler of the Joseon Dynasty, and his tomb, Yeongneung. Geuknakbojeon can therefore be seen as a hall dedicated to prayer for the repose of the deceased king, as well as for the well-being of the royal family.”  “Registered as Tangible Cultural Property of Gyeonggi-do Province No. 128, Geuknakbojeon has three columns, with two on the sides. Palgak-jibung, a half-hipped roof over triangular walls on the sides, sits on top, giving an extravagant, yet majestic appearance.”   “Enshrined with the Amitabh Triad inside the hall are various Buddhist paintings depicting guardian Devas, Buddha giving a sermon, and the Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva, which are hung behind the Buddha statues. There is also is a hanging sign board upon which, “Cheonchumanse,” was supposedly written by Seon Master Naong himself.”  “Geuknakbojeon is a miniature of the Utmost Bliss of the Pure Land, depicted in an elaborate and majestic manner. For those sentient beings dreaming of blissful rebirth in the Pure Land, it is a precious portal allowing a short escape from this world.”

stories.title: Introduction_Yongjoosa
stories.script: Introduction   “Located in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi-do Province, Yongjoosa is a famous temple based on filial piety, or the virtue of respect to parents, elders and ancestors. King Jeongjo, the 22nd ruler of the Joseon Dynasty, sublimed his heartbreaking love towards his deceased father, Prince Sado, into his Buddhist faith. This millennial temple continues to remind us of the true meaning of filial piety.”  “After Prince Sado was wretchedly killed by his father, his heartbroken son, King Jeonjo, came across a sutra called, ‘Bumo Eunjungyeong’ which espoused the profound relationship between parents and children, and the love of a mother and father. Inspired by this, he decided to found a temple to ease the suffering of his father's spirit.”  “Yongjoosa was originally founded under the name of Galyangsa in 854, the 16th year of King Munseong, the 46th ruler of the Silla Kingdom, but it was burned during the Manchu War of 1636. The temple was moved by King Jeongjo when he moved his father’s tomb to what is now Hwaseong, and the temple was renamed  Yongjoosa.”  “Yongjoosa took on the role of watching over and protecting Hyeonreungwon, Prince Sado’s tomb, while also being developed as a committed ground for strict cultivation.”  “Yongjoosa was one of the five Gyujeongso, which oversaw the lives of monks and together formed a center called ‘Pallodoseungwon,’ which systematically managed temples around the country.”  “Even today, Yongjoosa operates Hyohang Education Center, which honors King Jeongjo by offering various programs for practicing filial piety and strengthening character.”

stories.title: King Jeongjo (Yongjusa Temple, Hwaseong)
stories.script: King Jeongjo and Yongjusa Temple  Yongjusa Temple in Hwaseong was founded by King Jeongjo, who reigned over the country during that time. Under the atmosphere of suppressing Buddhism and promoting Confucianism as the ruling idea, this temple was founded because the Buddhist ideology was deeply rooted within the royal family.  There are a few symbolizations of Yongjusa Temple.  King Jeongjo built Yongjusa Temple as a way to fulfill his filial piety and to pray for the soul of his father, Prince Sado. It is said that when the devoted son, King Jeongjo, missed his father from time to time; he will always visit his father’s tomb in person and always stopped by Yongjusa Temple and asked the people to take good care of his father’s tomb.  Other than King Jeongjo’s filial piety, Yongjusa Temple was built to consolidate his regime and the change of view in Buddhism. King Jeongjo was prone to the suppression of Buddhism in the early days of his reign. However, the fact that he founded Yongjusa Temple indicated his change of attitude toward Buddhism. Besides, King Jeongjo built Youngjusa Temple to regain his father’s honor, and in doing so, he also solidified his own orthodoxy.  After learning the background of Yongjusa Temple and King Jeongjo, maybe you can spend some time here and feel the calm combining the filial piety and faith in Buddhism.

stories.title: The Origin of Yongjoosa
stories.script: The Origin  “It is said that a temple called Galyangsa once stood in this location, but it was renamed Yongjoosa in 854, the 16th year of the reign of King Munseong of the Silla Kingdom.”   “Then who founded Galyangsa and when was it established?  “Galyangsa was founded by an old sage called Preceptor Yeomgeo in the late Silla Kingdom! The dharma bell in Yongjoosa was designated as National Treasure No. 120. According to the record on the bell, it was cast in May during the 16th year of King Munseong of the Silla Kingdom at the time of the foundation of the temple! Seonghwangsan is modern-day Hwaseong, and Galyangsa is Yongjoosa, isn’t it all clear!?”   “Dad, why did Galyangsa become Yongjoosa?”  “When King Jeongjo moved his father’s tomb to Hwaseong, he reconstructed the temple. As for why it came to be called Yongjoosa, it is said that one day King Jeongjo had a dream...”   “I had a dream last night! A dragon held a legendary precious mani-gem and ascended into heaven! I therefore command that the name of the temple be changed to Yongjoosa!”  “Oh, so it is called Yongjoosa using the Chinese letters of ‘Yong’, a dragon, and “Joo’, the legendary precious mani-gem!”  “Oh, my! My little girl is so smart!! Hahaha…”

stories.title: Sammun of Yongjoosa
stories.script: Sammun of Yongjoosa   “Upon entering Yongjoosa, one may notice that its entrance is a bit different from other temples. Like palaces or loyal tombs, one must pass the Sammun. The Sammun, or Three Gates, of Yongjoosa clearly illustrate the background of the temple’s establishment.”  “Sammun are most often used at palaces or ancestral shrines, and are characterized by the servants’ quarters which are laid out along the sides of the door. Since Yongjoosa enshrines the tablet of Prince Sado, it is considered to be part of a royal tomb or palace.”  “The entrance to the Sammun of Yongjoosa has three doors; two side doors on the east and west and a main door at the center. A sign board written by Sunhwan Ahn, a famous calligrapher who wrote under the pen name Jungnong, stands at the main door and displays his impressively delicate yet strong writing style.”  “The top section of the four pillars of the Sammun is made of wood, while the bottom is made of stone, and each pillar is exceptionally tall and large. Upon each of these pillars is written a poem beginning with the four letters of Yong Joo Sa Bul. The poem goes like this…”   “While a dragon was hiding in the midst of shining clouds, it acquired a legendary precious mani-gem and began to play tricks. However, when it arrived at the temple gate, it learned about Seon, or goodness and virtue, and came to save sentient beings under the teachings of the Buddha.”  “In front of the Sammun of Yongjoosa are two mystical unicorn lions, which were thought to stop the spread of fire. These animals were humorously carved with simple, thick lines, so that they seem to reflect the tranquility of our people.”

stories.title: Cheonboru of Yongjoosa
stories.script: Cheonboru of Yongjoosa   “Wow, that’s fabulous! What do you think, honey? Doesn’t this temple look a bit different?”  “You’re right! The name of the building is Cheonboru…”   “Passing the Sammun and entering the main facility of Yongjoosa, the first thing that comes into view is Cheonboru Pavilion! Though it is a temple, it is said that this structure is also often used in palaces.”  “Here is some information regarding its history: Venerable Kwaeseong of Eunhyesa Temple in Yongcheon supervised the construction of Cheonboru Pavilion, while Venerable Paljeong of Yeongensa Temple in Samcheok, Gangwon-do Province was in charge of the multi-colored painting. Wow, these monks were so talented!”   “Honey, look! The lower floor of Cheonboru Pavilion connects to Daeungbojeon! Are these the high foundation stones supporting the six wooden pillars?”   “As King Jeongjo placed his father’s tablet, I bet he wanted Yongjoosa to stand tall for a long time! Come to think of it, doesn’t that stone pagoda seem to be one of a kind?”  “Yes, indeed! That stone pagoda is called Sejon Saritap in Cheonboru Pavilion because it is said that it has enshrined the relics of the Buddha since 1702!”  “Everywhere I look, I can see justification for Yongjoosa’s reputation as a traditional temple!”

stories.title: Daeungbojeon of Yongjoosa
stories.script: Daeungbojeon of Yongjoosa   “Daeungbojeon, the main Buddha hall of Yongjoosa Temple, is reached after Passing underneath Cheonboru Pavilion. The landscape of Daeungbojeon, framed by the pillars of Cheonboru, resembles a painting on a canvas.”   “This historical Dharma hall of Daeungbojeon was founded in 1790 at the time of the establishment of Yongjoosa. Since that time, it has gone through a number of repairs and reconstructions, though maintaining its original appearance.”  “At the corner of both sides of the staircases of Daeungbojeon, daewooseok have been installed as end stones. Daewooseok are generally decorated with lotus flowers or plants called dangcho, and are carved with clouds and peonies. It is said that this style is the same as that of Hyunreungwon, Prince Sado’s tomb.”  “Daeungbojeon in Yongjoosa serves as an enormous art gallery. Kim Hongdo, one of the most famous painters at that time, was known to contribute to the paintings hung behind the Buddha statues, which were a massive four meters long. It was said that he utilized rare techniques of perspective and shading at that time.”  “King Jeongjo’s love for his parents, combined with 1,700 years of Korean Buddhist art, have created such beauty that Daeungbojeon of Yongjoosa has become a delightfully precious piece of cultural heritage incomparable to anything else in the world.”

stories.title: The Dharma Bell of Yongjoosa
stories.script: The Dharma Bell of Yongjoosa   “The dharma bell is used to signal the time or the beginning of a ceremony. Its clear resonating sound signifies the rescue of all sentient beings in heaven and on earth.”  “Oh, I see! Venerable, that’s why I feel peaceful when I hear the sound of the dharma bell. Hoho…”   “Haha, do you? This rare dharma bell was designated as National Treasure No. 120. Now, shall we take a closer look?”    “First of all, the front of the bell has lotus flowers carved at the bottom, and there is a heavenly being on each side at the spot where it is struck! As it is a dharma bell cast from the early Goryeo period, it is quite large.”   “The top of the bell also looks rather unique. Isn’t it a dragon?”  “You’re correct! The dragon’s head on top is biting the upper part of bell, its two legs seem to support the overall structure, lifting it into the air. The main body is carved with lotus flowers which are unique in Korean Buddhism, and it can resonate majestic sounds.”  “Look over here. The main body of the bell also looks fabulous! Oh my! Are these the Triad Buddha, Venerable?”  “Yes, they are! As you can see, there are heavenly beings on the sides of the main body and the seated Triad Buddha are carved on top of lotus flowers!”   “Oh, your thin clothes seem to be ascending into the sky as if you were in heaven! Haha…”

stories.title: Hoseongjeon of Yongjoosa
stories.script: Hoseongjeon of Yongjoosa   “As Yongjoosa was founded as a result of King Jeongjo’s filial piety, it features a unique hall, called Hoseongjeon, that can’t be found in other temples.”  “Listen! Build a structure for holding memorial ceremonies for my father, Prince Sado, within Yongjoosa Temple!”  “Hoseongjeon was built with the sole purpose of holding Prince Sado’s tablet. Consequently, elaborate palace architecture was adapted in Hoseongjeon, which now also holds the tablets of King Jeongjo and his mother, Princess Consort Hyegyeong, as well as his wife, Queen Hyoul.”  “In Buddhism, parents’ love is described in ten ways: as conceivers; enduring the pain of labor; their endless worries after giving birth; swallowing bitterness and giving sweetness; and lying us down in a dry, rather than wet, place.”  “Feeding us with breast milk; washing us clean; worrying before long journeys; willingness to do difficult deeds in place of children; and feeling pity until the end. Likewise, parents’ love should be repaid, which is the teaching of the sutra called “Bumo Eunjingyeong.”  “King Jeongjo was enormously moved by Bumo Eunjingyeong. As he wanted to tell his people about parents’ love, he ordered Kim Hongdo, one of the most famous painters at that time, to create wooden blocks featuring Bumo Eunjingyeong. Now Bumo Eunjingyeong is carved in the Stone Pagoda in front of Hoseongjeon, so that everyone can see its contents.”  “Standing at Hongseongjeon, the ardent prayer of King Jeongjo for his father’s blissful rebirth in the Pure Land, and his sincere consolation for his father’s pain, is unmistakable.”

stories.title: Introduction (Bomunsa Temple, Incheon)
stories.script: Introduction of Bomunsa Temple  A 10-minute boat ride across the water from Oepori Dock in Ganghwado Island takes you to Seongmodo Island Dock. There, you will meet the cool sea breeze and rural scenery on the 20-ri road that goes to Bomunsa Temple in Nakgasan Mountain.  Boriam Hermitage in Guemsan Mountain of Namhae, along with Hongnyeonam Hermitage in Yangyang County of Donghae and Bomunsa Temple is one of the three sacred Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva sites (Gwaneum sites). The Avalokiteshvara sites are traditional temples where Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva is said to reside.  The name Bomunsa Temple, where Bomun stands for “virtuous door”, meaning a door that spreads virtue equally to all without discrimination. It also carries meaning of saving the common people by sharing the relationship with the Buddha in various forms.  With beautiful landscapes, mysterious tales and earnest prayers, Bomunsa Temple served as a “Avalokitesvara Sanctuary” where everyone are welcomed to pray at any time, hence, it continuously attracts both Buddhist practitioners and visitors.

stories.title: The Origin of Bomunsa
stories.script: The Origin of Bomunsa   “Bomunsa was founded in 635, the fourth year of Queen Seondeok, the 27th ruler of the Silla Kingdom, by Great Master Hoejeong after he had a vision of Gwamseumbosal, the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, while practicing on Mt. Geumgangsan. He called it Bomunsa Temple, meaning that Gwanseumbosal resides in the sacred ground from a broad and deep perspective!”  “On a spring day like any other fourteen years after the foundation, a number of fishermen from a village down the mountain from Bomunsa Temple went out to fish…”    Now, pull the net! (working hard) Wow! (surprised) What are these?”  “They netted more than twenty stones, which appeared quite strange in their net. The fishermen threw the stones back into the sea and cast their net again a further distance away. That night, each of the fishermen had the same dream.”   “We are holy men from India, and have come to give dharma to achieve all the wishes of sentient beings. Please lead us to Nakgasan Mountain so that we may rest in comfort!”  “When morning broke, the fishermen cast their net at the spot where they had thrown the stones the previous day, and up came twenty-two stone statues. The fishermen placed the statues of Maitreya, the Future Bodhisattva, Dipankara, the Past Bodhisattva, and the Arhats in a cave at Bomunsa Temple. At the time, it was said that the sound of sutra chanting and delicate scents came out of the cave. That night the fishermen had another dream….”  “I have come with Shakyamuni Buddha and two bodhisattvas, as well as eight others, all the Buddha’s disciples. We are very thankful that you have taken good care of us. Hahaha….”

stories.title: Five Hundred Arhat Statues (Bomunsa Temple, Incheon)
stories.audioTitle: Five Hundred Arhat Statues (Bomunsa Temple, Incheon)
stories.script: Five Hundred Arhat Statues in Bomunsa Temple  These are the five hundred arhats of Bomunsa Temple. Each of the five hundred arhats here has different facial expression and its individual features are well-articulated.  There is a 40-meter-long and 5-meter-wide large rock named Cheonindae, which was used in Buddhist ceremony. The name ‘Cheonindae’ is a Korean compound word formed by 'cheon' and 'in', which mean ‘one thousand’ and ‘people’ respectively. This signifies that it is large enough for a thousand people to sit.  “Nahan” is a saint who is respected by the world for breaking all anguish and gaining endless wisdom, and is also called “Arhat.”  Whoever studies according to Buddha’s teaching can eventually become an arhat and most of these were actual people from history. In other words, all five hundred arhats are real people from the past.  Bomunsa Temple was originally a temple that valued the Arhats’ faith. There are nineteen arhats who came from the sea have now been enshrined in the stone hall, and five hundred of them have been place here as well.   While visiting Bomunsa Temple, do not forget to take a look at the five hundred arhat statues!

stories.title: Wabuljeon, Reclining Buddha Hall (Bomunsa Temple, Incheon)
stories.audioTitle: Wabuljeon, Reclining Buddha Hall (Bomunsa Temple, Incheon)
stories.script: Wabuljeon, the Reclining Buddha Hall of Bomunsa Temple  Wabuljeon, the Reclining Buddha Hall of Bomunsa Temple is a pavilion built on “Cheonindae,” a rock wide enough to seat a thousand people. Reclining Buddha Hall refers to a shrine that houses a Buddha image when he was in Nirvana.  Reclining Buddha Hall in Bomunsa Temple enshrines the image of the Buddha who is lying comfortably on his side in the form of Nirvana. It is 10 meters in height, and is incredibly detailed and realistic considering that it is carved with stone.  The “Nirvana Altar” where the Buddha in repose, is carved in the shape of cloud, presenting a beautiful and elegant appearance. Next to the Reclining Buddha Hall, the statues of 500 Arhats and the stupa containing the relics of 33 Avalokitesvara Bodhisattvas are harmoniously arranged.  When you enter the Reclining Buddha Hall of Bomunsa Temple, the Buddha's head and feet seem to touch the ends of the hall, conveying a strong sense of dignity due to its immense size. The fact that it was carved from a single massive rock without piecing together is also astonishing.  Lying comfortably with a pillow and armrest, the Buddha in the Reclining Buddha Hall of Bomunsa Temple brings a calmness that sets everyone at ease.

stories.title: Seoksil of Bomunsa Temple
stories.script: Seoksil of Bomunsa Temple   “Seoksil, or Stone Dharma Hall, enshrines the Triad Buddhas which emerged from the sea 1,300 years ago, one statue of Gwanseumbosal, the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, and nineteen arhats.”  “I heard that Bomunsa Temple is one of the sacred Gwaneum sites. Is it because of these arhats in Seoksil that it came to be known as one of the renowned temples for this faith?”  “That’s correct! Seoksil, or Stone Dharma Hall, is a rare cave hall in South Korea which corresponds closely with the foundation of Bomunsa Temple. The significance of Seoksil was recognized by Incheon Metropolitan City and it was registered as Tangible Property No. 27!”  “Oh, I see! Then, how is Seoksil structured?”  “Seoksil, or Stone Dharma Hall, was created out of a natural cave; that is, a natural rock wall was used in its construction. On the rock wall, semi-circle pedestals and support beams were installed at intervals between these pillars, and tabernacles were created for each statue to be enshrined!”  “On the upper altar rest the Triad Buddhas, followed by Gwanseumbosal, the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion and Arhats?”  “Yes, that is correct! Furthermore, Sinjung Taenghwa, a Buddhist painting depicting the guardian Devas of Buddha-dharma sits in the middle of the altar, behind which is enshrined the Buddha’s picture.” “After seeing all of the arhats in Seoksil, I can see why Bomunsa is called an arhat site!”

stories.title: The Millstone of Bomunsa Temple
stories.script: The Millstone of Bomunsa Temple    “In a flower garden to the right of the entrance of Seoksil, the Stone Dharma Hall, sits an ancient millstone. How did this millstone end up here at Bomunsa?”  “Bomunsa was once a huge temple home to over 300 monks and practitioners. That’s why this millstone is two times bigger than an ordinary one!”  “It is! It looks like it is made of strong granite, which must have been difficult to carve, yet its lines are smooth and beautiful! The bottom part looks round and the drainpipe has been carved with great precision.”  “You are correct. As you know, even a single grain of rice is considered precious in a temple, and this seems to have been designed to minimize any waste. The top stone has two holes for the sticks which turn it. It seems that it may have required two people to turn it!”  “That’s true! The millstone is so large that several people had to work together to turn it! Currently, most remaining millstones found in temples consist of only the top part, but the one at Bomunsa has been well-preserved, with the bottom part still intact. It is therefore considered highly valuable!   “By just looking at the size of the millstone, it’s hard to imagine how many people have come to Bomunsa Temple to practice!”  “I know what you mean. Though this millstone is no longer used, many visitors have still come today to pray. Its reputation as one of the three sacred Gwaneum or Avalokiteshvara sites is well-deserved!”

stories.title: Geuknakbojeon of Bomunsa Temple
stories.script: Geuknakbojeon of Bomunsa Temple   “With five columns in front and three on the sides, Geuknakbojeon is the central structure of Bomunsa Temple. With an area estimated at approximately 200 square meters, this spacious structure welcomes all the visitors of Bomunsa!”  “Oh, I see. It is magnificent! Can you tell me a little bit more about this Geuknakbojeon?”  “Geuknakbojeon generally refers to the dharma hall that enshrines Amitabha Buddha, who governs the Utmost Bliss of the Pure Land in the West! After Daeungjeon, or the Great Hero Hall, Geuknakbojeon ranks second in importance among Korean temple architecture hierarchy!”   “Is that Buddha statue on the top altar towards the back made of jade? The hall feels more majestic with three thousand of them!”  “That’s right! Please look at the top. Do you see the small house there? It is called Datjip, a canopy over the Buddha statue. It is used to represent the palace of the Utmost Bliss of the Pure Land.”  “Ah, it looks very exquisite! Is that a carved dragon toward the ceiling?”  “Yes, it is. Actually, there are two carved dragons, one on each side of the ceiling, and another pair push their heads outward from inside the dharma hall!”  “Even the doors look quite unique! These colorful floral designs on the doors seem to add to its grandeur!”  “Do they? You are very observant! Haha…”

stories.title: Rock-carved Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva (Bomunsa Temple, Incheon)
stories.audioTitle: Rock-carved Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva (Bomunsa Temple, Incheon)
stories.script: Rock-carved Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva of Bomunsa Temple  The Rock-carved Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva of Bomunsa Temple is always packed with practitioners and visitors. This statue is enshrined on a huge rock on the middle of Nakgasan Mountain. When you quietly memorize the word Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva while climbing the 419 stairs next to Daeungjeon Hall, you will find yourself standing in front of the Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva sooner than you think!  The rock-carved seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva statue of Bomunsa Temple has a special crown named ‘Bokwan’ on its head and it is a symbol of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva. Another symbol is the bottle that the statue holding, named “Jeongbyeong.” This simple yet elegantly carved smooth lines will definitely put the viewer’s mind at ease.  The bottle that the statue holding is the holy nectar which is used as a medicine for the sick, and symbolizes the benevolence of the Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva.   The Rock-carved Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva of Bomunsa Temple stands at an impressive height of 9.2 meters and width of 3.3 meters. It also symbolizes the thirty-two forms in which Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva appears if it is converted into Korean units.  It is loved by everyone as it helps countless people to find their inner peace. If you need a moment away from your busy lifestyle, why not spend this opportunity to visit Bomunsa Temple?

stories.title: Ganghwado Gwangseongbo
stories.script: Gwangseongbo Battlefields of the U.S. Expedition to Korea  You are now at Gwangseongbo, where you can view the Ganghwa Strait. This historic site was one of the Battlefields during the Shinmi Yangyo of 1871, a significant conflict between the United States and Joseon. The war began when the U.S. fleet entered Sondolmok (Ganghwa Strait) without permission from the Joseon government.  When the American forces, who had already taken Choji Jin and Deokjin Jin, arrived at Gwangseongbo, they faced 600 soldiers led by General Eo Jae-yeon. However, the Joseon army's weapons were outdated, they only had old matchlocks and cannons. Despite efforts to defend with ‘Myeonje Baegap’, a bulletproof vest designed to counter Western firearms, these protections were no match for modern weaponry, leading to a devastating defeat.  One remarkable aspect of this battle is that photographs from the event exist. For the first time in U.S. naval history, a photographer accompanied the fleet and captured images of the battle. These photographs not only show moments of negotiation but also the aftermath of the battle, documenting the brave and unwavering spirit of the Joseon soldiers who fought to defend their country, undeterred by fear.

stories.title: Yongyang Bongjeojeong Pavilion
stories.script: Yongyang Bongjeojeong Pavilion  Yongyang Bongjeojeong Pavilion: The king’s procession road that boasts the outstanding technology of Joseon   Hello everyone! I’m Yeo Reum of Hello Venus. The place you’re standing right now is Yongyang Bongjeojeong Pavilion where King Jeongjo stopped by for lunch on his way to Hwaseong Fortress in Suwon for the 60th birthday party of his mother, Lady Hyegyeong. The name Yongyang Bongjeojeong means “a pavilion where dragons run around and phoenixes fly high.” It is said that it was named by King Jeongjo who was looking at the mountains and the Hangang River in the north of Hanyang.  King Jeongjo took a pontoon bridge from the palace to cross the Hangang River and arrive at the pavilion. This pontoon bridge was designed by Jeong Yakyong, who was one of the greatest thinkers at the time. The pontoon bridge made at this time weaved boats into double and triple layers with solid wood and covered the bridge with a board to make it flat. Parapets were also installed on both sides of the bridge so that people could cross safely. Grass was laid on the board to decorate it splendidly. According to the records, the bridge was made in just 11 days, so you can guess how amazing the technology was back then. You can see the scene of King Jeongjo’s procession crossing the pontoon bridge through a drawing, Hangang Jugyohwaneodo.  Don’t forget to leave your name on the guest book on your way home after seeing the Yongyang Bongjeojeong Pavilion!

stories.title: Site of Mangwonjeong Pavilion
stories.script: Site of Mangwonjeong Pavilion  Site of Mangwonjeong Pavilion: A place where you can get a clear view of the Hangang River far away   Hello, this is Shownu from “History Repletion: Oh! Cool Guys”. The place where you are now is the Mangwonjeong Pavilion, which means “a pavilion with a good view of the distant scenery.” This pavilion was built along the Hangang River and was a place frequented by many kings because of its magnificent scenery.  It is said that the kings climbed up to this pavilion and watched the people farming and the naval training of his army in spring and autumn. However, there was a man who watched the naval training here even though he was not a king. His name was Heungseon Daewongun, the father of King Gojong.  Heungseon Daewongun is said to have built a battleship called Hagujobiseon, meaning a flying ship made of crane feathers, to counter Western ships.  He thought that the light crane’s feathers wrapped around the ship will prevent the ship from sinking even when attacked.  Heungseon Daewongun showed his passion on making this ship by ordering catchers from all over the country to catch cranes. Despite his wish, however, the ship was not used eventually. Because as soon as the boat was on the waters, the glue that attached the feathers melted, and water began to fill the ship, resulting to sinking.  Although it ended in a failure, we can feel Heungseon Daewongun’s desire to develop a new weapon for the country.

stories.title: Unhyeongung Palace - The entrance to the Unhyeongung Palace
stories.audioTitle: Unhyeongung Palace - The entrance to the Unhyeongung Palace
stories.script: Unhyeongung Palace - The entrance to the Unhyeongung Palace  Unhyeongung Palace: A palace over the hill of clouds   Hey guys, I’m Hyoseong of Secret. Today, I am going to guide you to the Unhyeongung Palace. The Unhyeongung Palace was the home of Heungseon Daewongun, who was famous for being the father of King Gojong, the 26th king of Joseon.  It was upgraded to the Unhyeongung Palace because it was the royal residence of King Gojong until he was twelve. There is only one door left now, but records say that the palace was so large that it had four gates like other palaces. It is also said that the site of the high buildings surrounding the Unhyeongung Palace was also a part of the palace.  Just as the size of this royal residence, the power of Heungseon Daewongun became influential. Although he had many enemies, royal guards were dispatched from the palace to protect him.  The place where Heungseon Daewongun engaged in politics instead of King Gojong. The place where King Gojong and Empress Myeongseong had an auspicious ceremony. Although its scale is not as enormous as it was in the past, let's go inside the Unhyeongung Palace while imagining its dignity of the past!

stories.title: Unhyeongung Palace - Noandang Hall of Unhyeongung Palace
stories.audioTitle: Unhyeongung Palace - Noandang Hall of Unhyeongung Palace
stories.script: Unhyeongung Palace - Noandang Hall of Unhyeongung Palace  Noandang Hall of Unhyeongung Palace: The sarangbang of Heungseon Daewongun   Hello everyone! I’m Hana from Secret. We are now in the inside of the Unhyeongung Palace. The building in front of you is called the “Noandang Hall.” which was Heungseon Daewongun’s sarangbang, or detached house.  This building was named by Heungseon Daewongun himself. It means that he was satisfied to spend his old age in a good house due to his son becoming a king.  The handwriting on the signboard was written by Chusa Gim Jeong-hui, the best calligrapher of the time.
