It is said that Heungseon Daewongun, who was a student of the calligrapher, made the signboard by attaching the letters written by his teacher to give him respect.  Heungseon Daewongun decided on all policies right here on behalf of young King Gojong. Here at the Noandang Hall, Heungseon Daewongun removed all corrupt Confucian academies, which were the stronghold of the aristocrats who harassed the people, and commenced hopoje, a policy of reducing the taxes of the people and imposing taxes on the aristocrats instead.   As you see, Heungseon Daewongun had the power equal to a king. Now, look to your side and let's go to the most splendid building in the Unhyeongung Palace.

stories.title: Unhyeongung Palace - Norakdang Hall of Unhyeongung Palace
stories.audioTitle: Unhyeongung Palace - Norakdang Hall of Unhyeongung Palace
stories.script: Unhyeongung Palace - Norakdang Hall of Unhyeongung Palace  Norakdang Hall of Unhyeonggung Palace: A place where an auspicious ceremony of King Gojong and Empress Myeongseong took place   Hello everyone! I’m Ji Eun from Secret. This is Norakdang Hall, the largest building in the Unhyeongung Palace and located in the center. This hall, which means a place to entertain the elderly, was where various feasts were held.  Among the numerous feasts was the birthday party of Sunmok Budaebuin who was the wife of Heungseon Daewongun and also the mother of King Gojong. The biggest feast was an auspicious ceremony of King Gojong and Empress Myeongseong.  When King Gojong grew old enough to get married, Heungseon Daewongun considered carefully a spouse for his son and chose Empress Myeongseong, who was polite and intelligent even she was from a poor family. All preparations for the auspicious ceremony were carried out here at the Unhyeongung Palace, and the ceremony was so grand and luxurious that it mobilized 1,600 attendants and 700 horses.  It was Heungseon Daewongun who blessed the marriage of his son and Empress Myeongseong and wished for their happiness, but later, Heungseon Daewongun and Empress Myeongseong saw the worst relationship due to political conflicts.  Now what remains in front of us is a historical place of the three people who had different dreams.

stories.title: The War Memorial of Korea - The Story of the Korean War 1
stories.audioTitle: The War Memorial of Korea - The Story of the Korean War 1
stories.script: The War Memorial of Korea - The Story of the Korean War 1  The Story of the Korean War 1: Saving General Dean   Hello, I’m Jo Se-ho from “History Repletion: Oh! Cool Guys”. This is the War Memorial of Korea where records of numerous wars in our country are preserved. We, Oh! Cool Guys, heard about the sad history of the Korean War here that began on June 25, 1950.  The Korean War left numerous victims along with the tragedy of division of the two Koreas. Today, I’m going to tell you the story of the late train driver Kim Jae-hyun, who was a victim and a hero of the Korean War.  After the outbreak of the Korean War, Task Force Smith, the U.S. ground forces, were dispatched to stop the North Korean troops from advancing southward. However, they were pushed back by the power of the North Korean troops, which used a powerful tank called the T-34 tank. Meanwhile, General William F. Dean, the commander of the Task Force Smith, was taken as a prisoner.  And to rescue this key military figure at the time, special U.S. troops were urgently sent, but no one came forward to drive a locomotive to the enemy's camp since it involved risk. However, there was a Korean man who showed his braveness; it was the late Kim Jae-hyun. Unfortunately, the military operation came to a failure, leading to the death of the driver and numerous soldiers of the special U.S. troops.  Driver Kim was the first Korean to receive the Secretary of Defense Exceptional Civilian Service Award from the U.S. Department of Defense in 2012. There is a monument and a statue to commemorate him at Daejeon Station. But what I want to tell you today is that we should keep in mind that many more people were sacrificed during the Korean War while helping the refugees evacuate or after being dispatched to military operations. They are the hidden true heroes of our nation.

stories.title: The War Memorial of Korea - The Story of the Korean War 2
stories.audioTitle: The War Memorial of Korea - The Story of the Korean War 2
stories.script: The Story of the Korean War 2: Last bastion, the Nakdonggang Riverfront  Hello, I’m Han Sang-jin from “History Repletion: Oh! Cool Guys”. The story I’m going to tell you today is about the Hakdo student soldiers who took part in the Korean War and were sacrificed.  Less than two months after the outbreak of the Korean War in 1950, Korea was in a crisis of being pushed back to the Nakdonggang River after a series of battles. And there were people who rushed to the war to protect the last defense line of the Nakdonggang River.  They fought just like the soldiers to make up for our lacking forces. They were the Hakdo student soldiers who were as young as 15 and 16.  The young boys came out from their schools and entered the battlefield with guns instead of pens. They weren't even trained soldiers. They were someone’s precious sons and brothers, and they were miserably sacrificed in the crossfire without leaving any military service number behind.  The death of these young students brought the war of an unfamiliar country called Korea to the world, and thanks to them and the help of many countries, we could reverse the flow of the war.  A letter written by a young boy who were one of the student soldiers remains in this memorial: “Mother, why do we have to be in a war?” This sad line broke the hearts of many.  Let us remember the countless sacrifices buried in this county where we live today and take the tour to the War Memorial of Korea.

stories.title: Chinese Matrimony Vine (Solanaceae family)
stories.script: Chinese Matrimony Vine (Solanaceae family)   There is an old Korean folktale about the effectiveness of the Chinese matrimony vine. One day, a Confucian scholar was passing by a village when he saw a young girl lashing the legs of a gray-haired old man with a cane. Startled, the scholar said to the girl, “How come you, such a young girl, are lashing this old man?” Then she replied, “I am 400 years old and he is my son. His hair has turned gray because he has not taken the very effective elixir of youth like I have.” When he asked her what the elixir was, she answered: The fruit of the Chinese matrimony vine.  In fact, every part of the Chinese matrimony vine can be used to make medicine, including the fruits, leaves, and even the roots. Indeed, many generations of Koreans have made wine with the fruit and tea with its young leaves.

stories.title: Common Jujube Tree (Rhamnaceae family)
stories.script: Common Jujube Tree (Rhamnaceae family)   There is an interesting Korean folktale about the effectiveness of the jujube. Once upon a time, a woodcutter entered a deep forest where he came across two mountain gods playing the game of go with each other. He took off his carrier and watched the game for a while. Then the mountain gods gave him a jujube which tasted delicious. He then returned to his village, but it had changed so much that he couldn’t even find his house. In fact, a very long time―as much as two hundred years―has passed while he was watching the mountain gods playing go! The lesson of this tale is that he did not even feel hungry for two hundred years although all he ate during those years was a jujube - which just goes to show how nutritious the jujube is.

stories.title: Oriental Persimmon Tree (Ebenaceae family)
stories.script: Oriental Persimmon Tree (Ebenaceae family)   In ancient Chinese literature, the persimmon tree is widely praised for its seven merits. First, it lives for a long time; second, it provides a large shaded area; third, birds do not build nests in it; fourth, worms do not infest it; fifth, it has beautiful autumnal leaves; sixth, its fruits taste good; and seventh, it has leaves so wide that one can write on them. Along with the chestnut tree and the jujube tree, the persimmon tree is one of common fruit trees and bears many fruits. The persimmon is both a good healthy snack and an important ingredient of herbal medicine. The stalk end of the persimmon is effective in stopping hiccups, while a ripe persimmon has a sobering effect. The persimmon tree leaf is also consumed as tea as it is rich in Vitamin C and lowers blood pressure.

stories.title: Box-leaf Holly (Aquifoliaceae family)
stories.script: Box-leaf Holly (Aquifoliaceae family)   In Korea, the box-leaf holly is known as kkwangkkwangnamu. That sounds rather funny, doesn’t it? Koreans of old times named this tree as it makes a sound something like a kkwangkkwang when burnt in a furnace. The secret is in the leaf itself: air is contained in the leaf, which is as small as a grown-up person’s fingernail yet quite thick; and the heat of fire causes a sudden expansion of the air inside the leaf that makes it explode with a kkwangkkwang sound.  This Aquifoliaceae Family Section contains the Curiosity Plant Pot where you can see the nine most representative sights of Seoul in a time-lapse video.

stories.title: Katsura Tree (Cercidiphyllaceae family)
stories.script: Katsura Tree (Cercidiphyllaceae family)   The old Korean children’s song Bandal (Half Moon), which starts with the lyrics “Pureun haneul eunhasu” (The Milky Way in the Blue Sky), describes how a gyesunamu and rabbits live on the moon. In modern Korean, a “gyesunamu” is a “katsura tree.” But the “gyesunamu” of this song is actually not the katsura tree. The tree that we see today was brought to Korea from Japan during the Japanese occupation of Korea. So the katsura tree and the gyesunamu in the song, which is considered an imaginary tree, are not the same tree. Meanwhile, ancient Chinese literature includes many records on the gyesunamu. However, again, this tree is not the same as either of the two trees mentioned so far: it is actually the fragrant olive tree. These three countries in the Chinese character cultural sphere have long used the same Chinese character “桂 (pronounced “gye” in Korean)” to signify different trees, which naturally causes some confusion.

stories.title: Siberian Chrysanthemum (Compositae family)
stories.script: Siberian Chrysanthemum (Compositae family)   Do you like chrysanthemums? The Compositae family is one of the most difficult plant families for botanists to study, as there are over 20,000 species worldwide, with more than 200 species in Korea alone. Furthermore, it is not easy to distinguish among them because of their resemblance. Hence, they are the most evolved dicotyledonous plant. The flower of the chrysanthemum is unique. Although it looks like a single blossom, it is in fact a group of numerous blossoms that are gathered together. Every long petal is actually a blossom. In botany, this form of flower is called an “inflorescence.” The inflorescence of the chrysanthemum is referred to as a capitulum.

stories.title: Lilac Self-heal (Labiatae family)
stories.script: Lilac Self-heal (Labiatae family)    Labiatae plants have hairs that exude a unique scent on almost every part of the leaf or stem. Each hair is called a pilus. Plants such as rosemary or lavender, often called herbs, belong to the Labiatae family. They are used as the raw materials of perfume for their pleasant fragrance, and are grown as ornamental plants for their beautiful flowers.  Koreans eat lilac self-heal sprouts in spring by seasoning them with other ingredients. They also make an herbal medicine ingredient, called hagocho, with the plant’s cut and dried inflorescence.

stories.title: Metasequoia (Taxodiaceae family)
stories.script: Metasequoia (Taxodiaceae family)   The metasequoia tree has existed since the age of the dinosaurs. Isn’t it amazing that this tree of the Cenozoic era some 65 million years ago is still living beside us today? Once thought to be completely extinct, the metasequoia tree attracted the world's attention when it was rediscovered in China in 1946. The metasequoia was brought to Korea around 1950. In Damyang, Jeollanam-do, you can still see the metasequoia trees that were planted to line the streets at that time. The avenue of metasequoia trees in Damyang is one of the most beautiful tree-lined streets in Korea.

stories.title: Burning Bush Spindletree (Celastraceae family)
stories.script: Burning Bush Spindletree (Celastraceae family)   The burning bush spindletree is called hwasalnamu in Korean, the word “hwasal” referring to “arrow.” The tree was given this name because its branches have arrow-shaped, flaky wings. Koreans eat the young leaves of the tree by seasoning them with various ingredients, and use the bark of the branch to make herbal medicine. In many cases, plants that humans eat are also edible by herbivorous animals. The burning bush spindletree evolved to avoid being eaten by herbivores before it could grow fully by enlarging the wings so that the branches would look twice as large as they actually were. Herbivores only eat young and thin branches, not old and thick ones. Moreover, the wings are corky and taste bad. In brief, the burning bush spindletree has developed its wings as a unique survival strategy.  This Celastraceae Family Section has the Seoullo Information Center where you can obtain a guide to the Seoullo.

stories.title: Blunt-lobe Spicebush (Lauraceae family)
stories.script: Blunt-lobe Spicebush (Lauraceae family)   The hometown of Kim Yu-jeong, one of the greatest Korean writers of the twentieth century, is Chuncheon in Gangwon-do Province. So the “yellow dongbaek kkot” (camellia flower) that appears in his novels is, in fact, the flower of the blunt-lobe spicebush. As the names of trees and plants differ slightly depending on the region, in Gangwon-do Province the flower of the blunt-lobe spicebush is called dongbaek kkot. The Korean name of the blunt-lobe spicebush is saenggangnamu, the word “saenggang” meaning ginger; however, the tree has nothing to do with the ginger used in cooking. The plant was given this name because it smells like ginger when branches are cut. Koreans have long made tea with the flowers and wine with the blooming branches.

stories.title: Sawleaf Zelkova (Ulmaceae family)
stories.script: Sawleaf Zelkova (Ulmaceae family)   While the pine is regarded as a tree that symbolizes the spirit of the Korean people, the tree that best represents ordinary Koreans’ way of life is the sawleaf zelkova. Its branches extend outwards in four directions from the trunk, which grow thick and straight, and cast a wide, cool shade. In rural areas where the shade of the tree was used as a natural pavilion, it is also called jeongjanamu (pavilion tree). The wood of the sawleaf zelkova has a soft and beautiful pattern and a nice color, so it is a preferred material for construction. In olden times, noble families in Korea lived in houses built with zelkova and used furniture made with zelkova; while the deceased were laid in coffins made with it. Most of the coffins excavated from the Cheonmachong Ancient Tomb of the Silla Dynasty in Gyeongju were also made with zelkova.  The Seoullo Shop where you can buy souvenirs is located in this Ulmaceae Family section.

stories.title: Palmate Maple (Aceraceae family)
stories.script: Palmate Maple (Aceraceae family)   The palmate maple boasts a beautiful color in autumn, so it is preferred as a garden or landscape tree. This tree’s palm-shaped leaf is its most distinctive feature. The Korean indigenous maple has a leaf that splits into 5 to 7 parts, while the Manchurian full moon maple from China has a leaf that splits into 9 to 11 parts. The mono maple is distinguished from other species by its wide leaf that shortly splits into 5 to 7 parts, while the trident maple has a long leaf whose tip splits widely into 3 parts in the shape of a flipper.  Most trees of the Aceraceae family contain water in the trunk, and some of them even contain sugar. For example, the sap of the sugar maple is used as the raw material for maple syrup. Koreans also drink sap from the mono maple as a restorative since it contains vitamins that strengthen bones.

stories.title: Orange Stonecrop (Crassulaceae family)
stories.script: Orange Stonecrop (Crassulaceae family)   The orange stonecrop is called a girincho in Korean. The word girin is likely to remind most Koreans of the giraffe, which has a long neck and lives in the African savannah, so one of the common misconceptions about the girincho is that it is the preferred food of the giraffe. In this case, however, girin does not refer to the giraffe but rather to an imaginary animal of the same name: In the old days Koreans thought that the fruit of the orange stonecrop resembled the horn of this legendary animal. Its elongated leaves grow three centimeters long and have serrated edges. In spring, Koreans season and eat the orange stonecrop's young leaves, or blanch and enjoy them with red chili-pepper paste with vinegar.

stories.title: Prickly Castor Oil Tree (Araliaceae family)
stories.script: Prickly Castor Oil Tree (Araliaceae family)   In the olden days, Koreans used to hang branches from a prickly castor oil tree on the gates of their houses as they believed that these thorny branches would prevent evil spirits from entering their homes because their fluttering robes would get caught on the thorns. For the same reason, people would often plant a prickly castor oil tree in their front yard.  There was also a custom of making hexagonal accessories with its branches and hanging them around the waist of children's clothes in the belief that this would prevent common childhood diseases as well as repel evil spirits. These accessories were called eum, which is the reason why the Korean name for the prickly castor oil tree is eumnamu.  Among Korean dishes, a chicken boiled with the branches of this tree is called eomnamu baeksuk. However, the correct name for it is eumnamu.

stories.title: Snowbell Tree (Styracaceae family)
stories.script: Snowbell Tree (Styracaceae family)   It is said that you can catch fish using the fruit of the snowbell tree. In fact, if you place some pounded snowbell tree fruits in a stream and wait a little while, fish will float up to the surface of the water. This is because the fruit of the snowbell tree is rich in a component called ego saponin, which instantly paralyzes a fish's gills. So the fish that float on the water are not dead, but have simply fainted. It’s a great way to catch fresh fish easily.  The snowbell tree grows up to about 8 meters tall. Although it is not taller or thicker than other trees in the forest, and its leaves are plain, its flowers and fruits are very beautiful. In May, the tree blooms white flowers shaped like little bells hanging from long flower stalks. The outer diameter of the blossom is about two centimeters, and is directed toward the ground. During the blossoming season, the snowbell tree is the most beautiful tree in the forest.

stories.title: Nandina (Berberidaceae family)
stories.script: Nandina (Berberidaceae family)   The nandina is a unique and highly unusual evergreen tree. While other evergreen trees are green all year round, the leaf of the nandina turns red in autumn, and seems to be a sign of the imminent season of falling leaves. However, this tree passes the winter without shedding a single red leaf. The nandina fruit, which is as small as a bean, also has a reddish color that nicely matches the red leaf. The color and shape of the nandina are beautiful in winter, so it is usually grown for ornamental purposes. Still, the nandina likes a warm environment, thus great care is required to grow it in the central region of Korea.

stories.title: Magnolia (Magnoliaceae family)
stories.script: Magnolia (Magnoliaceae family)   The magnolia, which is indigenous to Korea, grows naturally only on Jeju Island in relatively small numbers. At first glance, it resembles the yulan tree of China, but the blossom of Korea’s native magnolia has six petals while that of the yulan has nine. Moreover, unlike the yulan, the blossom of the Korean native magnolia blooms by spreading out the petals. The trees of the Magnoliaceae family are called living fossil plants. Even in fossils dated to 130 million years ago, traces of these trees can be found. The magnolia is the oldest of all phanerogamous, or angiosperms, (flowering) plants which bloom flowers and bear fruits.  In the Magnoliaceae Family Section, you can enjoy a variety of Korean traditional teas and beverages at the Magnolia Cafe and various performances on the Magnolia Stage.

stories.title: Golden Rain Tree (Sapindaceae family)
stories.script: Golden Rain Tree (Sapindaceae family)   This tree is named Golden Rain Tree as it blooms bright golden yellow flowers in summer. Although the diameter of a single blossom is less than one centimeter, the blossoms are gathered together in a conical shape and look voluminous and splendid overall. The fruit of the golden rain tree resembles the Chinese lantern plant: the inside of a shell is empty, and only three black seeds are attached to it. When the seeds are ripe, the shell opens spontaneously and the seeds are blown away in the wind. In Korea, it is also called yeomjunamu as solid black seeds are often used to make yeomju, or Buddhist prayer beads.

stories.title: Water Hyacinth (Pontederiaceae family)
stories.script: Water Hyacinth (Pontederiaceae family)   The water hyacinth grows and floats on the surface of the water instead of putting down roots in the soil beneath the water. As the middle part of the leafstalk contains air, it floats well on the water. In fact, this part of the leafstalk functions like a fish’s air bladder, which is referred to as a bure in Korean, so the Korean name of the plant is bureokjam.  The water hyacinth is used as feed for livestock, and is also grown for the purification of water. It is known to be very effective in removing heavy metals from water, and is a helpful plant that cleans up the environment.

stories.title: Retusa Fringetree (Oleaceae family)
stories.script: Retusa Fringetree (Oleaceae family)   The retusa fringetree is a particularly friendly plant for Korean farmers, who have long believed that if the flower of the retusa fringetree blooms abundantly, they will have a bumper crop and, conversely, if the flower blooms poorly, they will have a bad harvest. Interestingly, this belief is in fact scientifically grounded. During the blooming season of the retusa fringetree, farmers plant rice in the fields. For a good harvest, the initial rice planting must be successfully carried out, and this requires good weather conditions including moderate rainfall and a warm temperature, which also happen to be the conditions in which the flowers of the tree bloom. It is remarkable that the farmers of ancient times had such great wisdom.  The Oleaceae Family Section also contains the ‘Seoullo Travelers’ Café’ where visitors can relax and refresh themselves.

stories.title: Big Blue Lilyturf (Liliaceae family)
stories.script: Big Blue Lilyturf (Liliaceae family)   The big blue lilyturf is better known as an ingredient of herbal medicine rather than a plant in Korea. Some dictionaries include it in the category of medicine, and not as a plant. In Korean traditional medicine, the tuberous roots clustered at the end of its main root, almost like peanuts, are used to make herbal medicine. These tuberous roots relieve coughing and asthma, and also have an antipyretic effect. Many generations of Koreans have boiled the root and drunk the water as tea or made wine with it.  The big blue lilyturf is native to Korea, and is known as maengmundong. Before Koreans named this plant, the Chinese gave it the same name, and it is presumed that Koreans started to use it as well.

stories.title: Chinese Sweetleaf (Saxifragaceae family)
stories.script: Hydrangea (Saxifragaceae family)   The Hydrangea is appreciated for its abundant flowers in summer. The flowers blossom into diverse and splendid colors including clean white, fresh blue and warm light purple. The plant also looks voluminous as small blossoms gather and form into bunches as big as a ball used in a handball. The language of the Hydrangea's flower is a change of heart. Interestingly, its flowers change color depending on the season or the nature of the soil in which they are planted. If it is strongly alkaline, their pink color becomes darker, but if its acidity is stronger, the blue color turns darker.  Although the flower changes color, it blooms for a long period from June to autumn, without withering or falling to the ground. In the Saxifragaceae Family Section, you can visit a small cafe named Hydrangea Bread that sells Korean-style grilled toast and coffee.

stories.title: Purple Maiden Silvergrass (Gramineae family)
stories.script: Purple Maiden Silvergrass (Gramineae family)   When autumn comes, purple maiden silvergrass blooms flowers that dance gracefully in the wind. They are gathered in the shape of fan ribs at the end of the stalks and waving in the wind.  These flowers make the silvergrass look much more gracious in autumn. When you climb mountains in autumn, you are sure to come across silvergrass fields in full bloom. The rays of sunlight passing through silvergrass flowers create a magnificent spectacle. This Gramineae Family Section features the Curiosity Plant Pot which includes an augmented reality space set against the background of Sungnyemun Gate; the Bang Bang Playground, where children can run around and play freely; and the Citizens' Natural Rest Space, where you can relax and enjoy nature.

stories.title: Autumn Oleaster (Elaeagnaceae family)
stories.script: Autumn Oleaster (Elaeagnaceae family)   The autumn oleaster is called borisunamu in Korea. Many Koreans regard this tree as the one that provided shade for the Buddha when he was seeking enlightenment. But the borisunamu in Korea is actually a different tree.  Botanically speaking, the Buddhist borisunamu is the bo tree. It is a fig tree of the Moraceae family and, being a subtropical plant, cannot grow in Korea. Perhaps Korean monks would have liked to plant the bo tree in their temples, but the fact is they could not. However, there was a similar tree that grew in Korean forests, so the monks planted and grew it in order to recall the Buddha's pursuit of asceticism. This tree was the amur linden, which has nothing to do with the (borisunamu) tree.  In short, the autumn oleaster that grows in Korea is different from both the bo tree and the amur linden.

stories.title: Crape Myrtle (Lythraceae family)
stories.script: Crape Myrtle (Lythraceae family)   The crape myrtle blooms flowers for over 100 days. In Korea, this tree was originally called baegilhongnamu, but due to gradual changes in its pronunciation, it is now referred to as baerongnamu, although some elderly people still call it baegilhongnamu. Koreans often confuse the crape myrtle with the zinnia, which is usually planted in small pots, because the latter also has the name baegilhong. However, although each of the plants remains in bloom for over 100 days, the crape myrtle and the zinnia are, from a botanical perspective, entirely different plants. The former blooms flowers, bear fruits, sheds leaves and then survives the subsequent years, while the latter is an annual plant that perishes at the end of the blooming season. Also, the crape myrtle belongs to the Lythraceae family, while the zinnia belongs to the Asteraceae, so the two are not related to each other.

stories.title: Iris (Iridaceae family)
stories.script: Iris (Iridaceae family)   The great German writer Hermann Hesse was so fond of the iris that he described the period when the iris is in bloom as a moment of grace. He also likened the iris to the key to the secret of creation, and the door to heaven. The scientific name of the iris is also iris, which is derived from the name of the rainbow goddess in Greek mythology. In Korea, the iris is called butkkot” (brush flower) because it resembles a brush soaked in ink.

stories.title: Rainbow Pink (Caryophyllaceae family)
stories.script: Rainbow Pink (Caryophyllaceae family)   The rainbow pink starts to bloom light purple flowers at the beginning of summer and continues to embroider the lowlands of the forest with its colorful flowers until autumn. The vivid deep purple pattern inside the blossom with five petals helps the rainbow pink to stand out among all other flowers. The horizontally divided petals resemble the hat called a paeraengi that Koreans used to wear, so its Korean name is paeraengikkot. The rainbow pink is commonly perceived as a small weak flower, but it is actually a (hardy) plant whose stalk grows to over 50 cm in length. It is considered small because it grows flat on the ground, and has many stalks that tilt downward and are unable to straighten up due to their thinness.

stories.title: Korean Red Pine (Pinaceae family)
stories.script: Korean Red Pine (Pinaceae family)   In the olden days Confucian intellectuals in Korea regarded pine trees as a symbol of their culture. The evergreen pine tree inspired them to maintain their pride as scholars. When they had children, they would plant pine trees, representing their hope that their offspring would grow into great scholars. During the Joseon Dynasty, the Geumsongnyeong ordinance was enacted to protect the Korean red pine, with the result that it has become the most widely distributed tree in Korea's mountains. Koreans have long used pine wood to build houses as well as to make furniture such as wardrobes and rice chests, and farming implements such as spades and spinning wheels. As such, it would not be an exaggeration to call Korean culture a pine culture. In fact, Koreans love pine trees very much. According to a recent survey of the Korea Forestry Service, nearly half of Koreans selected the pine tree as their favorite tree.

stories.title: Water Lily (Nymphaeaceae family)
stories.script: Water Lily (Nymphaeaceae family)   In Korea, the water lily is called a suryeon. Many Koreans believe that this name is composed of the Chinese characters su” (水), which means water, and ryeon” (蓮), which means lotus. But in fact, this word uses a different Chinese character pronounced su” (睡), which roughly means sleeping, so the name suryeon means sleeping lotus.  The water lily blooms in the morning and sleeps with its petals closed in the evening. Using this characteristic of the water lily, Koreans have made a special way to drink tea. In the evening, before the water lily closes its petals, tea leaves wrapped in hemp cloth are placed inside the blossom; and in the morning when it opens its petals, the tea leaves are taken out of the blossom ready to be brewed in warm water. This tea, which exudes the fragrance of the water lily, is called suryeoncha. The water lily, which blooms in summer, is a popular gardening plant that can be found in most Korean ponds.

stories.title: Mugunghwa (Malvaceae family)
stories.script: Mugunghwa (Malvaceae family)   The flowers of the mugunghwa bloom in the morning and fall in the evening, only for new flowers to bloom the next morning. A mugunghwa tree has about thirty blossoms at any one time, and remains in bloom for about 100 days throughout the summer, which means a single tree blooms around 3,000 flowers during the season.  During the Japanese colonial period, Korean independence activists regarded the mugunghwa as a symbol of Korea for its great vitality. In response, the Japanese imperialists began to slander the flower, claiming that just looking at or touching the flower would be enough to make one’s eyes bleed or cause boils to erupt on one’s skin. So they called it the “bloody eye flower” or the “boil flower.” The Japanese even went to schools that were trying to instill the spirit of independence in their students and burned all the mugunghwa flowers in their gardens. This may be the only case of oppression of a plant for political reasons in the entire history of the world. The mugunghwa survived these trials and became the national tree and flower and a source of pride for the Korean people.  This Malvaceae Family Section contains the Seoullo Gallery where you can enjoy various art works.

stories.title: Maidenhair Tree (Gingkoaceae family)
stories.script: Maidenhair Tree (Gingkoaceae family)   The maidenhair tree is the only tree belonging to the Gingkoaceae family. This tree first appeared on Earth some 300 million years ago and has survived until the present day. It is a living fossil plant that survived both the glacial age and successive global extinctions. The tree is also well known for its long lifespan of 1000 years or longer. There are twelve maidenhair trees that are known to be more than 1,000 years old in Korea. The one at Yongmunsa Temple in Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi-do is a 1,100-year-old giant with a height of 42 meters. Almost every Korean village has at least one maidenhair tree, which, along with the pine and the zelkova, is the tree most preferred by Koreans.

stories.title: Golden-and-silver Honeysuckle (Caprifoliaceae family)
stories.script: Golden-and-silver Honeysuckle (Caprifoliaceae family)   The golden-and-silver honeysuckle is a wall-climbing plant that blooms splendid flowers. Its Korean name indong consists of the Chinese characters in” (忍) meaning patience and dong” (冬) meaning “winter.” It was given this name because it does not shed leaves in winter and can endure extreme coldness. Koreans also call it indongcho, but this name is botanically inaccurate. The Chinese character cho” (草) means a plant that loses the upper part of its stalks, which are exposed on the ground, at the end of the year; but the golden-and-silver honeysuckle maintains its stalks. When its new white blossoms bloom as the older ones have turned yellow after pollination, you can see golden and silver flowers at the same time. That's why it is called the golden-and-silver honeysuckle.

stories.title: East Asian White Birch (Betulaceae family)
stories.script: East Asian White Birch (Betulaceae family)   The East Asian white birch is distinguishable from other trees by its white trunk. Many people like the wonderful white color of its bark which is also the key to explaining the birch's ability to survive a cold climate. It is thin but multi-layered, and rich in oil, which helps the tree endure cold winters without freezing. The Korean name for this tree is jajak namu, which derives from the fact that Koreans thought it made a sound like jajak jajak when it is burned. The sound is created when the oily components of the bark catch fire and burn.  In the olden days when there were no candles, Koreans would light its bark and use it as a candle. In Korean, the expression to light a hwachok (colored candle) means to hold a wedding ceremony. Here, the Chinese character hwa” (華) originates from hwa” (樺), which represents the East Asian white birch.

stories.title: Peony (Paeoniaceae family)
stories.script: Peony (Paeoniaceae family)   The peony is the most loved plant of all Asian garden plants and is likened to the king of flowers. Koreans first called the peony mokdan under the influence of its Chinese name, but its pronunciation gradually changed to moran, the name by which it is now known in Korea. The peony was introduced to Korea from China during the reign of King Jinpyeong of the Silla dynasty, after which it was frequently described in the poems and paintings of the nobility and came to be regarded as a symbol of wealth. In May, the peony blooms eight-petal flowers with a diameter of 15 centimeters. The vivid contrast between the red petals and yellow stamens creates a splendid scene. Certain varieties that have been developed in recent times for ornamental purposes have multiple folded petals or bloom white flowers.

stories.title: Japanese Apricot Tree (Rosaceae family)
stories.script: Japanese Apricot Tree (Rosaceae family)   The Japanese apricot tree is the most fascinating messenger of spring. Some people, no doubt with its splendid flower in mind, call it the “apricot flower tree,” but it should really be called the “apricot tree” to be more precise. This is because - as with the pine, persimmon, and chestnut tree - trees are generally named after their fruit in principle. So the correct name for this tree is apricot tree and not apricot flower tree, although it is true that it blooms apricot flowers.  In the Rosaceae Family Section you will find the Rose Gimbap restaurant, which serves delicious mini-gimbap (dried seaweed rolls), and the Rose Stage where various performances are held.

stories.title: Manchurian Violet (Violaceae family)
stories.script: Manchurian Violet (Violaceae family)   The Manchurian violet is a flower that blooms in the middle of spring. Its blossom has five petals that resemble a swallow flying above with its wings spread, so it is called jebikkot (swallow flower) in Korean. There are many other Korean names for this flower, one of which is orangkaekkot” (barbarian flower). It is said that this name was given to the flower at a time when foreign forces invaded Korea in spring, its blooming season. However, some people say that it was named this way after its corolla, which is elongated to the back of the blossom and reminiscent of the hairstyle of the barbarians who invaded Korea. This flower is also called anjeunbaengikkot” (cripple flower) for its shortness, and byeongarikkot” (chick flower) for its cute appearance. The various names given to this one single flower prove that it has always been a familiar presence in the daily life of the Korean people.

stories.title: Witch Hazel (Hamamelidaceae family)
stories.script: Witch Hazel (Hamamelidaceae family)   The English name of this plant, witch hazel, originated its use in water dowsing. Japanese people call this plant mansaku (まんさく, 万作), which means good harvest, out of the belief that its abundant flowers will bring a good harvest. In Korea, it is called pungnyeonhwa, which also carries the meaning of a bumper year. Koreans started to use this name when the plant was first brought to the country in the early 1930s during the Japanese occupation, doubtless influenced by its Japanese name. Witch hazel plays the role of a messenger in spring by blooming in early spring. It grows quite tall, usually up to 5 meters, which is the reason why it is a popular garden plant.

stories.title: Rigid-branch Yew (Taxaceae family)
stories.script: Rigid-branch Yew (Taxaceae family)   Koreans often describe the rigid-branch yew as a tree that lives for 1,000 years before death and for another 1,000 years after death. This tree, known for its very long lifespan, is used for many purposes even after (its) death. For example, its leaves and fruits are used as medicine in Korean traditional medicine. Recently, research have been conducted on the components of its leaves and fruits, which are thought to have a tumor suppressant effect.  Its trunk is used to make furniture or for building materials as it is easy to manage, solid, and resistant to decay. Its trunk is red, so the Korean name for this tree is composed of the Chinese characters ju” (朱) meaning red and mok” (木) meaning tree. In some areas of Gangwon-do Province, where there are large colonies of the tree, the Chinese character jeok” (赤), which also means red, is used instead of ju” (朱) to form another name for the tree, jeok mok. Its scientific name also includes the meaning red tree with pointed leaves, thus emphasizing the most distinctive feature, the red trunk.

stories.title: Korean Rhododendron (Ericaceae family)
stories.script: Korean Rhododendron (Ericaceae family)   When the forsythia blooms along the low fences of villages and heralds the advent of spring, the rhododendron blooms in the distant mountain behind the villages. The rhododendron and the azalea are very difficult to distinguish, because the flowers of the two trees closely resemble each other. However, the two must be accurately distinguished for the following reason: The rhododendron flower is edible, while that of the azalea contains a poisonous substance. So, in the olden days, Koreans called the rhododendron flower chamkkot” (true flower) and the azalea gaekkot” (false flower). The easiest way to distinguish between the two trees is to see if they have leaves or not. The rhododendron blooms flowers before its leaves come out, while the azalea’s leaves appear before its flowers. So the rhododendron tree can be distinguished by the fact that its flowers are in bloom when there are no leaves, and the azalea tree can be recognized by the presence of both luxuriant leaves and flowers.

stories.title: Korean Stewartia (Theaceae family)
stories.script: Korean Stewartia (Theaceae family)   The Korean stewartia has a trunk that is mottled but as smooth as silk. So in some regions of Korea, it is called bidannamu (silk tree). At first, this tree was called nokgaknamu (deer horn tree) due the surface of its bark resembles that of a deer's horn. However, it later came to be called nogaknamu. The wood of the Korean stewartia is a useful material for making traditional wooden bowls as it is solid and moisture-proof. The trunk of this tree grows straight upward and is very big. The bark has a gray and brown pattern which can be seen much clearly when the tree sheds its leaves in autumn.

stories.title: Sawtooth Oak (Fagaceae family)
stories.script: Sawtooth Oak (Fagaceae family)   The sawtooth oak was given its Korean name sangsurinamu during the Japanese Invasion of Joseon in 1592. When the war broke out, King Seonjo left the palace and fled to another region, but there was not enough food to eat. His servants made jelly with the fruits collected from the trees in the area and served it to the king. He liked this jelly so much that, upon his return to the palace after the war, he ordered that it continue to be served on his surasang (king's dining table). The jelly that King Seonjo ate was similar to today's dotorimuk (acorn jelly). Sangsurinamu means the tree that bears fruits that are served on surasang, and its original name was sangsuranamu.  In the Fagaceae Family Section there is a shop called Acorn Sweets that sells pulppang bread and traditional Korean snacks.

stories.title: Balloon-flower (Campanulaceae family)
stories.script: Balloon-flower (Campanulaceae family)   The balloon-flower root is a Korean native health food that is well known to the world as the deodeok root. The root of the balloon-flower is rich in saponin, which is effective in treating bronchial-related diseases, and thus is used to make herbal medicine. Its boiled root is a particularly effective medicine for people suffering from coughs or asthma. Traditionally, Koreans have dug the root every spring and autumn and eaten it with various spices and other ingredients, so the balloon-flower is a friendly plant for Koreans, as reflected in the traditional folk song Doraji Taryeong (Balloon-Flower Root Song).

stories.title: Oriental Arborvitae (Cupressaceae family)
stories.script: Oriental Arborvitae (Cupressaceae family)   The Chinese have long regarded the oriental arborvitae, which grows throughout the vast expanse of mainland China, as a symbol of longevity and prosperity, and still plant it to pray for their families' happiness. The oriental arborvitae was originally brought to Korea from China, but as that was a very long time ago, it is now fair to say that the tree is a Korean tree. The Forest of Oriental Arborvitae in Dodong, Daegu is Korea’s Natural Monument No. 1.  This tree has a characteristic feature in that its leaves grow sideways; and its Korean name cheukbaengnamu includes the Chinese character cheuk” (側), which means side. All the trees of the Cupressaceae family, including the juniper, are notable for horizontally extending leaves.  In the Cupressaceae Family Section, you can find the restaurant, 7017 Seoul Bibimbap, where you can taste bibimbap (rice mixed with vegetables).

stories.title: Japanese Cornelian Cherry Tree (Cornaceae family)
stories.script: Japanese Cornelian Cherry Tree (Cornaceae family)   The Japanese cornelian cherry tree announces the arrival of spring by blooming yellow flowers at the beginning of the season. Its flowers bloom on every branch before the leaves come out, creating a dazzling spectacle. In areas such as Jirisan Mountain, Uiseong in Gyeongsangbuk-do, and Icheon in Gyeonggi-do, well-known habitats of the Japanese Cornelian Cherry Tree, various festivals are held in spring to celebrate its blossoms.  The tree bears fruits after shedding all its flowers, creating an impressive spectacle. The fruits are greenish at first but turn red as they ripen throughout autumn. The red fruits hanging on empty branches against a blue winter sky show a beautiful contrast between primary colors. The Japanese cornelian cherry is used as a medicinal ingredient in Korean traditional medicine.

stories.title: Horse Chestnut Tree (Hippocastanaceae family)
stories.script: Horse Chestnut Tree (Hippocastanaceae family)   Did you know that the horse chestnut tree is known as the “marronnier” in France? The use of the French name spread among Koreans as it was known that the trees planted on the slopes of Montmartre in Paris were called by this name among the French. The horse chestnut belongs to the Hippocastanaceae family, and its exact English name is horse chestnut tree.  The horse chestnut tree became widely known to Korean people after it was brought into the country from Japan in the 1920s, so it is often referred to by Korean names meaning Japanese horse chestnut tree. However, the official name used in Korea simply means horse chestnut tree. Actually, a very similar kind of tree was brought to Korea a few years earlier to celebrate King Gojong's 60th birthday in 1912, when the Dutch ambassador presented the king with a horse chestnut tree from Montmartre which can still be seen in the grounds of Deoksugung Palace to this day.

stories.title: Chinese Scholar Tree (Leguminosae family)
stories.script: Chinese Scholar Tree (Leguminosae family)   The Chinese scholar tree extends its branches in various directions and shapes, and the bark of its trunk is smooth. It is a graceful tree that is reminiscent of the dignity of a prestigious scholar. In ancient Korea, Confucians would take the state examinations around the time when the tree blossomed, so Koreans used to call this tree seonbinamu (Confucian student tree) or hakjasu (scholar tree). The Leguminosae Family Section has the Gardening Learning Center where you can learn about various plants or read books.

stories.title: Lilac Daphne (Thymeleaceae family)
stories.script: Lilac Daphne (Thymeleaceae family)   In Korea, the lilac Daphne is often called by its nickname joginamu (croaker tree). The people of the West Sea coastal villages believed that shoals of croaker would come when the lilac Daphne growing on the shore bloomed flowers and therefore, gave it this nickname. It is a sad fact that nowadays, even if the flowers bloom on the tree, few croakers are caught in the West Sea.   Patkkonnamu (red bean tree), the Korean name for this tree, originated from the color of its flowers, as it is similar to that of the red beans used to brew patjuk (red bean porridge). Strictly speaking, the color is a bit lighter than that of the red bean, but it seemed that Koreans thought of the red bean whenever they looked at the flower. The blossoms hanging from the branches are also small and pretty like red beans.

stories.title: Boston Ivy (Vitaceae family)
stories.script: Boston Ivy (Vitaceae family)   Boston ivy is a climbing plant that cannot stand on its own and grows by leaning on other objects. It can climb walls, rocks and many other objects, as well as nearby trees, thanks to the tendrils that sprout from the stems. At the end of each tendril is a kind of sucker that enables it to stick to any object.  In Korea, this plant was originally called damjangdeonggul as it grows well on walls (damjang). However, it is now known by the name damjaengideonggul. This Vitaceae Family Section has the Ivy Theater where puppet shows, storytelling shows, and mime performances are held for children.

stories.title: Korean Boxwood (Buxaceae family)
stories.script: Korean Boxwood (Buxaceae family)   The Korean boxwood grows slowly but provides a dense and solid wood, so it has long been used to make objects requiring solid wood. Koreans also used Korean boxwood to make wooden printing types, as well as combs and Korean chess pieces. Today, the wood of the Korean boxwood is usually used to make seals (dojang). As such, this tree is often called dojangmok or dojangnamu in Korea. This Buxaceae Family Section has the Peeping Pot which shows the eighteen representative sights of Seoul in video.

stories.title: Greetings, Gwangmyeong Cave
stories.script: Greetings   Welcome to Gwangmyeong Cave, a former gold mine with over 100 years of brilliant history turned into a cave theme park in the heart of the city. In the 1910s, Gwangmyeong Cave was the largest metal mine in the metropolitan city. It produced not just silver, bronze, and zinc but also a lot of gold, earning it the name of “Gold Mine.” In the 1970s, the mine closed its doors and served as a ground for curing salted shrimp. Now, it is a theme park with where visitors can experience caves, as well as Gwangmyeong’s beautiful heritage. Gwangmyeong Cave is 7.8km long, and made up of 8 layers total. Waiting for you inside these maze-like tunnels is a thrilling adventure where you can savor the history of Korea’s modern mining industry and the mystery of caves at once. These include a massive Cave Art Center as well as the Cave Aqua World, which can only be found in Gwangmyeong Cave. Explore the Golden Road, the Golden Waterfall, and the Golden Palace, or retrace the steps of miners from 100 years ago in the Cave Underground World and gaze upon the Miner’s Spring Water, the Modern History Museum, and the Wine Cave. Now, are you ready to begin? Let’s start our adventure into Gwangmyeong Cave, where 100 years of history and mystery a wait.

stories.title: Wind Road (Horizontal Mine Photograph Panel)
stories.script: Wind Road (Horizontal Mine Photograph Panel)   From this point, we will be following the tunnels that miners once traversed over 100 years ago to head into the cave. Tunnels refer to roads that were formed by penetrating the veins of ore spread out inside a cave. Whenever miners found a vein, they would create a hole and blow it up to collect ores or find cracks and break down the bedrock to head deeper and deeper within to create a path. As we walk along the tunnels, please enjoy the tale of how this forgotten mine came to be reborn as a cave theme park, Gwangmyeong Cave and open up the future of Gwangmyeong City. 100 years ago, during the period of Japanese occupation, a mine appeared in this cave, which was devoid of human activity. Our ancestors fled into the mine in order to avoid being drafted. In the depths of darkness, they mined the rich veins of the cave while shedding blood, sweat, and tears tinged with sorrow over the loss of their country and a longing to see their homes. The mining continued even after liberation from Japanese rule until 1972, when the mine was submerged under water by a flood. After being abandoned, the cave was once used to store the pickled shrimp Sorae Port, filling it with the smell of brine instead of ores. The people who once toiled as the sweat rolled off their backs vanished along with the sound of machinery, and the cave looked to fade away into the annals of history, leaving its golden days behind. However, in 2011, a new light was shone on the empty cave. Efforts were made to spread word of the cave’s history and roots, as well as to transform it into a space that would once more be frequented by people. The cave, once an industrial heritage of the past, opened its door to a new golden era as a theme park where many people could come and have fun. This is Gwangmyeong Cave where we are standing now.

stories.title: Wormhole Square, the Light Space
stories.script: Wormhole Square, the Light Space   We are now at Wormhole Square. What is the most beautiful thing in a cave shadowed by darkness? A light that shines brilliantly inside the dark may be the answer. Let’s head right to the “Light Space” that brightens up the tunnel. The bright light blasts away the darkness. Yet, it is precisely because darkness exists that we can further appreciate the beauty of light. Follow the tunnel and you’ll see a small space to the right. Here, within the darkness of Gwangmyeong Cave, is an exhibition of works that go beyond the confines of space and time. These works of art are based on the theme of a light that shines hope in the past, present, and future. Please take your time and appreciate these works, which are filled with a hope bright enough to light up the entire cave.

stories.title: Cave Art Center
stories.script: Cave Art Center   This is the “Cave Art Center”, the first cave performance stage in Korea. There are over 50 empty rooms in Gwangmyeong Cave, and the “Cave Art Center” is the largest of them all. The empty rooms had passages connected the upper and lower levels of a mine, meaning that they served as hubs of sorts. Back when this cave was a mine, the empty rooms used by miners are rest areas or shelters to hide in when blowing holes in vein with dynamite. Not only is this Cave Art Center massive, but it also has a unique trait that can’t be seen in other performance stages. Try shouting “Yahoo” as loud as you can. Wasn’t the echo amazing? Because the cave itself acts as a wonderful microphone, there is no need for any additional sound equipment. Thus, the “Cave Art Center” makes the most out of the cave’s characteristics to become a very special stage you can’t find anywhere else. The powerful echoes also make the art center popular among vocalists and musicians as a stage they absolutely wish to perform in. Every week during the opening hours, fantastic performances take place to greet the visitors, so you may look forward to it.

stories.title: Cave Aqua World
stories.script: Cave Aqua World   Welcome to Gwangmyeong Cave’s Aqua World, an underwater world inside a cave! First up are golden fish that symbolize the essence of the Gold Cave and reflect prayers’ wealth and fortune. Please to look for the bright Yellow Prince Cichlids, the red-eyed Gold Severum, and the popular and adorable Blood Parrot Cichlid! Gwangmyeong Cave’s Aqua World uses natural bedrock water from the Underground Level 1 of the cave to provide an environment capable of housing various types of fish from around the world. Enjoy a unique experience and meet an underwater ecosystem with native fish such as Korean Splendid Dace or Korean Rose Bitterling, which can only exist in clean areas with Grade 1 water quality. Gwangmyeong Cave is made up of 8 floors total, and from the below of the Underground Floor 2  are all full of bedrock water. These waters are clean and free from heavy metal pollution, making them ideal habitats for the fish. They also supply the coolants that go into the incinerator of the resource recovery facility located in front of the cave, saving 100 million won in expenses every year. Now then, feel free to see for yourselves the types of fish that coexist in this clear and pure underwater world made using clean underground bedrock water.

stories.title: Golden Road
stories.script: Golden Road   Now, we’ll be walking along the Golden Road. Gwangmyeong Cave was originally developed as a gold mine, and it is assumed that hundreds of kilograms of gold were mined here before it was abandoned due to the flood. According to experts, there should still be a great amount of gold buried here to this day. In fact, there may be gold under the road that you are walking on this very moment! The Golden Road is made up of higher levels of anions than forests, meaning that you can enjoy both affluence and good health. By walking along the Golden Road, which prays for both health and wealth with the energy of gold, you will find a beautiful statue of a goddess. The goddess is none other than Fortuna, the Roman goddess of wealth and production. The cornucopia held by Fortuna was called the horn of plenty, and legend holds that Fortuna handed the riches and good luck that flowed out of the horn to other people. Now that we’ve received the essence of health and wealth, it’s time to make a wish. Do you have the golden plaque that was prepared at the entrance? The plaque comes in four shapes of Su, Bok, Gang, and Nyeong that symbolize a desire for long life, fortune, good health, and comfort. Write a wish on the plaque and hang it. The plaque will be preserved on the Golden Road and pray along with you.

stories.title: Golden Waterfall
stories.script: Golden Waterfall   The sound of the waterfall’s current ringing around the cave is quite refreshing, isn’t it? This waterfall is the Golden Waterfall, and it is the pride of Gwangmyeong Cave that can’t be seen in any other caves. Originally, this area was full of underground water. However, when water was drawn up and pumped out in an attempt to let the water out, this amazing 9m tall waterfall was born in the process. The waterfall’s hole served as a hole to drop ores down back when the cave was a mine. Now, with the Golden Waterfall we have concluded our tour of the horizontal level. What you have seen until now is Level 0, the horizontal level and one of the 8 levels of Gwangmyeong Cave. We will proceed to explore the Underground World of Gwangmyeong Cave, which is also known as Underground Level 1. The road from the horizontal level to the underground level was once used by miners to load and transport mined ores. It has a 32 degree slope and a particularly large number of stairs, so pregnant women, the elderly, the infirm, and those with disabilities should receive guidance from operating personnel before continuing.

stories.title: Golden Palace , Golden House
stories.script: Golden Palace, Golden House   The fairy Aixia, who lives in Gwangmyeong Cave, protects the 6 Golden Pillars here. According to legends, Aixia is known to be in caves full of gold. This is because of the golden hammer that Aixia carries around. Whenever the golden hammer is used to strike rocks, they become gold. The gold bars scattered around the Golden Palace are Aixia’s work as well. Let’s try memorizing the chant Aixia yells out when making gold with the hammer. “Hiss hisshoihoiAixia~” You can yell it out loud or just follow along in your mind. “Hiss hisshoihoiAixia~” Once you have memorized this chant, you’ll be able to receive a mystical energy if you ever manage to touch Aixia’s hammer. If you look inside, you’ll find the Room of Gold where all the golds turned by Aixia have been gathered. As entry is not permitted, please take a glimpse of the room while standing outside. Now, let’s head to Underground Level 1. Currently, it is the lowest floor in Gwangmyeong Cave that you are allowed to travel to. The stairs on the path down are incredibly steep, so please watch your step as you make your way down.

stories.title: Cave Underground World
stories.script: Cave Underground World   We are now at Underground Level 1, the lowest floor that visitors in Gwangmyeong Cave are allowed into. Gwangmeyong Cave is made up of 8 floors total, and visitors are only allowed on Level 0, which is the entrance to the cave, and Underground Level 1. Underground Levels 2 to 7 are flooded with water, and operations to remove the water are still underway. We will do our best to ensure that you will one day be able to see Gwangmyeong Cave as it was 100 years ago. Furthermore, the deepest part of the underground cave is located a horror attraction. Thrilling horror felt in darkness, in Gwangmyeong Cave, you can feel not only in summer, but throughout all 4 seasons.

stories.title: New Zealand’s Weta Workshop Fantasy Exhibition
stories.audioTitle: New Zealand’s Weta Workshop Fantasy Exhibition
stories.script: New Zealand’s Weta Workshop Fantasy Exhibition   Gwangmyeong Cave and its 100 years of history, fantasy, and mystery have joined up with New Zealand’s Weta Workshop, a world-renowned special effects company known for their work on The Lord of the Rings, King Kong, and Avatar, to hold a fantasy design contest exhibition. Now, you can find the prize-winning works from the contest at this very spot. Furthermore, Gwangmyeong Cave and Weta Workshop are set to collaborate on several projects in the future including another International Fantasy Conceptual Design Contest Exhibition. We are constantly giving it our all so that we can spread the beauty and cultural value of Gwangmyeong Cave around the whole world, develop contents using the cave, and turn the city of Gwangmyeong into a global city of culture and art.

stories.title: Miner’s Spring Water
stories.script: Miner’s Spring Water   Back in the mining days, when clean water inside the underground tunnels was a valuable commodity, miners would drink water and rest at this mineral spring whenever they were thirsty and tired from mining ores. For those miners, water was as precious as life itself. The water here comes from Underground Level 1, and according to water quality inspections, it is natural bedrock water that is suitable for drinking. Now then, why not try having a taste of the Miner’s Spring Water that miners themselves used to quench their thirst in the old days?

stories.title: Salted Shrimps Storage
stories.script: Salted Shrimps Storage   After the mine was abandoned in 1972, people started filling the cave with containers of salted shrimps. This was because the salted shrimp merchants of Sorae Port had begun to cure their pickled shrimp inside Gwangmyeong Cave by paying 10,000 won per container. Pickled shrimp requires an environment surrounded by bedrock, with enough moisture to keep a constant flow of water dripping from above and most importantly, a set temperature that does not waver. Gwangmyeong Cave had all these conditions, making it the ideal place for storing pickled shrimps. During certain periods, you can relive the tradition and taste from the past and purchase pickled shrimp cured right here in Gwangmyeong Cave. Gwangmyeong Cave Salted Shrimps! It’s highly recommended that you try a taste.

stories.title: Bullomun Gate
stories.script: Bullomun Gate   By piercing through a boulder in the cave, a sturdy gate capable of withstanding the tides of time was created, and came to be called “Bullomun Gate.” Originally, Bullomun Gate was a stone gate created to pray that the king would live a long and healthy life. The Bullomun Gate of Gwangmyeong Cave was prepared to pray for the good health of visitors for a long, long time of over 100 years, so please enter with a merry heart. After passing through Bullomun Gate, you’ll see a mine cart that was used to transport ores on display. The cart and the rails underneath it were actually used back when the cave was a mine. They were found and restored to their current state today, lending to the authenticity of the cave experience. Once we move to the next area, we’ll be able to meet even more realistic aspects of Gwangmyeong Cave’s past, as well as the history of a once-thriving era of mining.

stories.title: Tunnels Around the Modern History Museum
stories.audioTitle: Tunnels Around the Modern History Museum
stories.script: Tunnels Around the Modern History Museum   This is a Modern History Museum where you can take a look at 100 years of history of the cave from 1912 to 2016 at one glance. Inside the main exhibition hall is composed of life-sized figures and videos so that visitors can understand each era and affairs related to the Gwangmyeong Cave. The tunnels and past entrance of the cave, and the site of the Mine Processing Plant were reproduced and displayed as diorama. Behind it is displayed a video that expresses the appearances of the tunnel in sections. It expresses Japanese colonial period, which is fraught with painful history of invasion and resource-stripping by the Japanese,  industrialization period where over 500 people worked in one day, closure of the cave due to the great flood, and the birth of the cave theme park after that. The tunnels of the cave is made up of total of 9 layers. Where you are standing right now is the level 0, and there are 1 layer above and 7 layers below. Total depth is 275m and total length is 7.8km. Of these, the sections that are open to public for display is level 0 and underground level 1, and below that level is full of underground bedrock water, so you may not take a look at it, but through continuous development, it is expected that it would be gradually open to public for display some day.

stories.title: Jogutong
stories.script: Jogutong   The small hole you see above you was called the “Jogutong” during the mining period. The hole was a way to conveniently transport mined ores in a tunnel that was 7.8km long. When making the Jogutong, the miners bore through in a zig-zag pattern instead of a straight one so that ores would bump into the walls as they fell. This would naturally break the ores down, saving the miners the trouble of having to smash and break the ores into small pieces. Currently, only three areas with Jogutong remain, including the one you see before you. During the mining period, a Jogutong could be made anywhere when needed to make transporting ores easier. The ores would be broken into small pieces after going through the Jogutong and fall into the cart right in front of the hole, and then transported outside of the mine using the rails.

stories.title: Relics Exhibition
stories.script: Relics Exhibition    On top of the model mine cart, which is manufactured a little smaller than life-size, tools that were used in the cave and mined minerals are on display. According to the records, 52kg of gold, 6,070kg of silver, 1,247 tons of bronze, and other various minerals were produced, which is the number between 1955 and 1972. Thus, if you go back to 1912, when the history of the mine began, it is estimated that much more amount of gold and other minerals were mined.

stories.title: Japanese Colonial Period
stories.script: Japanese Colonial Period   Perhaps you have heard about resource-stripping and enforced enlistment during the Japanese occupation. In 1910s, Japanese Governor-General of Koreaset up ’Mineral Deposit Investigation Agency’ and began to investigate vein of ore throughout the whole country. Further, only Japanese were allowed to own mines, and they monopolized the mining rights of Korean peninsula. The establishment of Siheung Mine by the Japanese in 1912 is probably in that context. When Sino-Japanese War and Pacific War broke out in the 1930s, the stripping and labor mobilization were at their peak. Most minerals mined here at the Gwangmyeong Cave were sent to Japan in the form of rough gemstone. They went through smelting and metallurgy process and then imported back again. In those days, the Japanese Imperialism only allowed part of smelting, chemistry and iron industry, and would not train Koreans to become engineers. Under these backgrounds, it led to lack of mining technology and engineers after the independence, so the mining industry in Korean peninsula had to go through a period of recession for some time.

stories.title: A Shelter During the Korean War
stories.audioTitle: A Shelter During the Korean War
stories.script: "A Shelter During the Korean War   During the Korean War in 1950’s, this place was used as a shelter, and even babies were born inside the cave. The babies had beautiful names that their parents gave to them, but the refugees called them Guldaenggi (meaning cave companion). These are the graffiti of the miners. The miners applied soot produced from carbide lamps, which were called ‘Gandeure’, and left graffiti all over the cave. You can read the minds of the miners who missed their home and wished for their safety. There were even graffiti of pictures and writings in Chinese characters and English. These graffiti are currently left in the underground or in the upper space of the cave in their original form. "

stories.title: Industrialization Period
stories.script: Industrialization Period   According to the stories from nearby villagers, “The mine was closed with the independence of the country, and we worked right after the war was over.” In the 1956 issue of <Almanac of Major Enterprises in Korea>, the name “Siheung Mine” appears, so it seems as though it was around that time that the mine had become bustling again. In the mid-1960s, it had placed itself as the biggest metal mine in the metropolis area. In 1964, mining amount was 35,530 tons, and in 1968, 250 tons of ores were mined per day. During its glory days, more than 500 workers worked in the mine, and it was given the nickname of ‘Dogonae Mine’. It is recorded as the place of first labor movement in the Gwangmyeong region. Here is a man who had worked as machinery repairman for over 20 years from 1950s to the closure of the cave. He mostly was in charge of cutting iron for the shelf. His first salary was KRW 6,000 and later went up to about KRW 13,000. Other general workers received KRW 3,000 to KRW 4,000. In those times, there was no smelting factory near the mine, so the mined minerals were transported to the smelting factories in Janghang, Pohang, Busan, or other cities.

stories.title: Closure of the Mine and Salted Shrimp Storage
stories.audioTitle: Closure of the Mine and Salted Shrimp Storage
stories.script: Closure of the Mine and Salted Shrimp Storage   In August 1972, there was a great flood in Seoul, which led to the eventual closure of the Gwangmyeong Cave. After that, there were efforts to resume mining business, but the surrounding area was designated as a green belt zone to limit the development. Plus, making the most of the cave, which is optimized for maturing, the local merchants used it as pickled shrimp storage.

stories.title: Exploration and Development of the Cave from 2011
stories.audioTitle: Exploration and Development of the Cave from 2011
stories.script: Exploration and Development of the Cave from 2011   The explorers (government officials) who recognized the value of the cave searched numerous materials, and finally found out with difficulty that there was a ‘tunnel map’ in the Korea Resources Corporation (KORES), and started exploring the cave using that map. It was told that the exploration team were very afraid because they had no knowledge about the cave. They found out that inside of the cave was made up of solid rock, so there was no concern of collapsing. They pumped out the water that filled the tunnel, organized the channel of movement within the cave, and installed basic lightings. The place where you are standing right now used to be filled with water when they were exploring the cave. Wine Cave was made by using the horizontal tunnel. At first the height and width of the horizontal tunnel was only about 1.5m, which was widened to 4–5m to make a Wine Cave. The construction of Cave Art Center was also very difficult. To prepare for safety accidents, which might occur, they tried to make sure that safety reinforcement work, such as installing lock bolts and rockfall protection nets, was done. They set up numerous scaffolds, and had to do all the work manually by going up and down the ladders and stairs hundreds of times. Just as the miners had to work hard by digging the tunnels, they had to work in the same conditions. The construction site of Cave Art Center in 2013 has been moved to this place.

stories.title: Mine Hoist
stories.script: Mine Hoist   Almost no data about Gwangmyeong Cave remains today.  In particular, most of the materials from 1912 to 1945 during the Japanese Colonial Period was taken back to Japan by the Japanese miner owner,  and the others from 1955 to the closure of the cave had been swept away by the great flood in 1972. Some information that was fortunate to survive those incidents was disappeared by the fire in the mine office and storage. In 2011, when Gwangmyeong-si announced that they were going to purchase and develop the abandoned mine, there were many raised eyebrows. Many concerned that how  this abandoned mine that we know almost nothing about would be developed, and who would be willing to come down and inspect inside of the mine. Despite of the opposing voices and concerns, having the courage and writing the history of challenge were the foundation in making the miracle of today’s Gwangmyeong Cave. The mine hoist placed in the middle seems to be symbolizing the 100 years of record, wounds and pains during the Japanese Colonial Period, blood and sweat from the miners who had worked here, and all the courageous and challenging moments so far experienced by the Gwangmyeong Cave. Even though some people might say that it is just a mass of steel that does not work, please place your hands on top of the mine hoist, and say, “You have worked hard”, “Thank you for your service”, and “Please rest peacefully.” It is probably waiting for someone to embrace its 100 years of trace, becoming rusty and had been put on top of another. The history of Gwangmyeong Cave lies here. Close your eyes for a moment and feel the 100 years of breath.

stories.title: Wine Cave
stories.script: Wine Cave   With its sturdy bedrock, Gwangmyeong Cave is like a natural fortress cut off perfectly from the rest of the world. For miners, it was a secure workplace. After its abandonment, it became a place to cure delicious salted shrimp. Once we arrive at our destination, please see for yourselves what role the cave plays today. Many famous wineries in foreign countries use underground caves to store their wine. This is because caves where maintains best temperature of 12 degree and consistent temperature and humidity are optimal conditions for aging wine. Most importantly, wine must be stored in an area without vibrations to ensure the highest quality. As such, caves are ideal for storing not just wine but other types of fermented food as well. They are all-natural refrigerators that cannot be matched by man-made-products. At Gwangmyeong Wine Cave, you can receive an explanation on wines produced in Korea, from the types of fruits used to brewing methods and characteristic flavors. Wine sampling is also available. Furthermore, the cave displays over 1,000 bottles of wine from around the world, and you can purchase various types of wine as well as cheese to go with the wine.  With this, we have concluded our exploration of Gwangmyeong Cave. The more the cave is being developed to this day, the newer experience you will enjoy on your next visit. We hope that the rest of your journey will prove to be a meaningful one. Thank you for your visit.

stories.title: History of the Cheonggyecheon Stream
stories.script: History of the Cheonggyecheon Stream ‘Gaecheon Stream’ to ‘Cheonggyecheon Stream’, covering construction to restoration project.    In 1392, Joseon Dynasty was established, and in 1394, it moved its capital to Hanyang, which is now called Seoul. There was a natural stream in Hanyang, and it often flooded. When a series of flood damage followed after the movement of the capital, King Taejong embarked on a construction to enlarge and deepen the natural stream. From that moment, the stream was called ‘Gaecheon’. During the 17th Century, Joseon’s weather was frigid. Thus, people of Joseon engaged in illegal lumbering in order to secure fuels. This resulted in deforestation and soil erosion. Soil leaked into the stream’s floor, and even a slight rain would lead to submergence of Hanyang. After a long consideration, King Yeongjo undertook a dredging construction in 1760 to dig up the soil at the stream’s floor, and the stream was recovered. During the latter period of Joseon Dynasty and the earlier period of Japanese Colonial Era, the stream’s name changed from ‘Gaecheon’ to ‘Cheonggyecheon’. From 1923, drain pipes were reclaimed in Hanyang, and as domestic sewages were discharged at the Cheonggyecheon Stream, it became severly contaminated. In 1937, Japan started the Sino-Japanese War. Therefore, in order to smoothen the transportation of military supplies, Japan began the covering construction from the Cheonggyecheon’s upstream to Kwangtonggyo Bridge.  When the Korean War ended in 1953, refugees crowded in Seoul and formed a shantytown around the Cheonggyecheon Stream. As population grew, tremendous amount of sewage were discharged, and this polluted the stream. After the war, Korea placed postwar reconstruction ahead of everything. Thus, they covered the entire Cheonggyecheon Stream with concretes, and built roads and overpasses above it.  The Cheonggyecheon Stream, which was buried under the covered roads for 40 years, was unearthed in 2005 through 2 years of restoration work. However, running water is being discharged at the stream, and the bridges are only partially restored. Despite of several defects, refreshing air and clear sky has returned to the Cheonggyecheon Stream, since the concretes and overpasses were removed. The stream now became a resting place.

stories.title: Mojeongyo Bridge
stories.script: Mojeongyo Bridge Mojeongyo Bridge that leads to fruit markets becomes Palseokdam, a place for making wishes.  In 1412, King Taejong mobilized 50,000 soldiers to repair Cheonggyecheon Stream and reduce flood damage. The stream was widened and deepened, and several stone bridges were built. Mojeongyo Bridge was one of them. At the street corner of the north Mojeongyo Bridge, there were fruit stores called ‘Mojeon’. ‘Mojeongyo Bridge’ was named after them since it was in their vicinity.  Under the Mojeongyo Bridge, there is Palseokdam. The word ‘Palseokdam’ means a pond built with stones brought from all eight Provinces of Korea. However, actually there are nine stones at Palseokdam including one extra basalt stone brought from Jeju island . In the middle of Palseokdam, there is ‘Somangseok’, which is a wish stone. It is said that the strength and spirit of the entire country is centered at Somangseok, so wishes made by throwing coins there will come true. Coins collected in Somangseok are donated to ‘Korean Committee of UNICEF’ and ‘Dream Scholarship Foundation’. Enjoy the romance of Cheonggyecheon Stream by making wishes under the cool waterfall of Palseokdam!

stories.title: Gwanggyo Bridge
stories.script: The Main Bridge of Cheonggyecheon Stream   Originally, Gwangtonggyo Bridge occupied the current location of Gwanggyo Bridge. Gwanggyo Bridge was newly constructed during the 2005 restoration of Cheonggyecheon Stream. It was built on the site where Gwangtonggyo Bridge, a remnant of the original structure, had been moved 155 meters upstream.  Gwanggyo Bridge is a bridge connecting a huge road heading towards Jongno on the North and Namdaemun Gate on the South. Considering the convenience and mobility of vehicles and people, a new bridge was constructed and named after Gwangtonggyo Bridge.  During the era of Joseon Dynasty, Gwangtonggyo Bridge served as the main passage to ‘Yookcho Street,’ the location of the executive branch of Joseon, ‘Jongru’, the bell tower, and ‘Sungnyemun Gate’, the south gate of Hanyang. Therefore, it was mainly used by the king during a royal march or by the Chinese ambassadors when they entered Gyeongbokgung Palace from their official residence.
