Also, it was always bustling because Sijeon, the greatest marketplace of Joseon, was located at its north side. As a result, the width of the bridge exceeded its length. Today, Gwanggyo Bridge, like its ancient counterpart Gwangtonggyo Bridge, stands out as the most widely used bridge among all 22 bridges along Cheonggyecheon Stream.

stories.title: Jangtonggyo Bridge
stories.script: Bridge in Jungchon Village, a town translators and doctors lived   Jangtonggyo Bridge was named after ‘Jangtongbang’, one of Hanyang’s administrative district. During the period of the Joseon Dynasty, the bridge was the confluence of Cheonggyecheon Stream and Namsandongcheon Stream, which originated from Namsan Mountain. It was also a spot where the width of the stream suddenly broadened to 20 meters from its original 10 meters. Thus, it had to be longer than other bridges upstream. This is why it was also called ‘Janggyo Bridge,’ which literally means ‘long bridge.’ The bridge was demolished during the covering construction of Cheonggyecheon Stream, and the current Jangtonggyo Bridge was newly built during the restoration work of Cheonggyecheon Stream in 2005.  Jungchon Village is a town that starts from Jangtonggyo Bridge and ends at Supyogyo Bridge. Jungin, the middle-class people of Joseon, were the main residents of the village who primarily worked as translators or doctors. Since the official translators often went in and out of China and Japan and were authorized to trade ginseng and silk, most of them were affluent; some said the wealth of ten translators equaled to that of the country. On the other hand, since many doctors lived in Jungchon Village, many people crossed Jangtonggyo Bridge to receive treatments.

stories.title: Samilgyo Bridge
stories.script: Samilgyo Bridge Samilgyo Bridge, alongside with Samil building and Samillo Street, commemorates the March 1st Independence Movement  Samilgyo is a bridge built during the restoration project of Cheonggyecheon Stream in 2005, and it is called ‘Samilgyo’ due to its northwards connection with Samilro Street. Joseon became a colony in 1910 due to Japan’s annexation of Korea. On March 1st, 1919, people of Korea held a major demonstration to resist against Japan and demand independence. People gathered at the Tapgol Park at the north of Samilgyo Bridge and began to read the Declaration of Independence as they marched on the road in front of the park. In 1966, this road was named ‘Samilro’, signifying the numbers one and three, to commemorate the March 1st Independence Movement. Above the Samilgyo Bridge, there is a black rectangular building, which is the Samil Building. This building with 31 floors was completed in 1971 to commemorate the March 1st Independence Movement. It was the tallest building and the most famous tourist attraction in Seoul, Korea until 1985, when the 63 Building was built. Along with the Cheonggye Expressway that is now demolished, Samil Building was a symbol of economic growth in the 1970s.

stories.title: Gwansugyo Bridge
stories.script: Gwansugyo Bridge Gwansugyo Bridge, meaning ‘looking at the Cheonggyecheon Stream from the Juncheonsa Government Office’    Gwansugyo is a bridge made by Japan in 1918 during the Japanese Colonization Era that connects the Changdeokgung Palace and the Joseon Governor-General Building that existed in Namsan Mountain. Because there was a government office called Juncheonsa near the bridge, Japan named it ‘Gwansugyo’, meaning, ‘looking at the Cheonggyecheon Stream from the Juncheonsa Govt. office’. This bridge was lost during the covering construction, but it was newly built in 2005. During the 17th Century, the Cheonggyecheon Stream flooded due to blocked waterways caused by soil erosion of mountains. Therefore, King Yeongjo mobilized over 200,000 people and undertook 57 days of major dredging construction. The amount of dredged sands were as immense as two low hills. After the dredging construction, King Yeongjo established a government office called Juncheonsa at where the Gwansugyo Bridge is located today. Juncheonsa dredged the stream’s bottom once in every two to three years, and undertook the same construction on a larger scale every ten years until 1882.

stories.title: Seungyo Bridge
stories.script: Seungyo Bridge Hyogyeonggyo Bridge next to a village of Joseon’s blind people becomes the Seungyo Bridge beneath the Seun Marketplace  During the Joseon Dynasty, Hyogyeonggyo Bridge was located where the Seungyo Bridge is built today. Next to Hyogyeonggyo, there was a town where the blind people gathered and lived. Those disabled people were called ‘Sogyeong’, so this bridge was also known as the Sogyeong Bridge. During the Joseon Dynasty, these people exclusively dominated the field of fortune-telling.  Hong Gye-gwan was the most renowned blind fortune teller of Joseon. In fact, he was so famous that the village where he lived was even named after him. One day, the king showed Hong Gye-gwan a box, and asked him what was in the box. Hong immediately answered that there were rats. When asked, “How many?” Hong said that there were five. However, there was only one rat in the box. The king put him to death, accusing him for misleading people through divination. However, there were four cubs inside the rat’s belly. Unfortunately, Hong Gye-gwan was already decapitated.  Hyogyeonggyo Bridge was demolished during the covering construction of Cheonggyecheon Stream. In 2005, the bridge was newly constructed and named ‘Seungyo Bridge’, after the Seun Shopping Center next to the bridge. ‘Seun’ means 'gather the energy of the world'

stories.title: Baeogae Bridge
stories.script: Baeogae Bridge Baeogae Bridge and Baeogae Market    Baeogae Bridge was newly constructed during the restoration work of the Cheonggyecheon Stream. There was a hill called ‘Baeogae’ at the north side of the bridge. Baeogae means a hill with many pear trees. When the Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1592 ended after six years,  refugees crowded in the capital and formed a vegetable market at Baeogae Hill. As the market grew, many ruffians formed a gang and used violence to extort the peddlers’ properties. However, those peddlers had nowhere to plead their grievous situation because the market itself was illegal. In 1791, King Jeongjo, the 22nd king of Joseon, officially authorized the Baeogae Market, and it became the largest vegetable market in the capital during the latter period of Joseon Dynasty.  Today’s Gwangjang Market under the Saebyeok Bridge has its roots in the Baeogae Market.

stories.title: Saebyeokdari Bridge
stories.script: The Vibrant Feeling of Market at Early Dawn   Saebyeokdari Bridge was newly constructed during the restoration project of the Cheonggyecheon Stream in 2005. Near the bridge, two traditional markets, Gwangjang Market and Bangsan Market, thrive. The merchants in the markets begin their day early in the morning, preparing for store openings by pitching tents and arranging items. Thus, the bridge earned the name ‘Saebyeok,’ meaning dawn in Korean, encapsulating the vibrant atmosphere of Gwangjang and Bangsan Market at early dawn.  In November of 1905, merchants in Jongno organized a large marketplace named Gwangjang Market on Saebyeokdari Bridge. At first, the market mainly focused on trading agricultural products and seafood. It shifted to selling rescue kits and goods leaked from the US military base after the Korean War. In the 1960s, it gained fame for its textile and apparel markets, and now it is renowned for its food alleys.  Bangsan Market is located on the south of Saebyeokdari Bridge. Originating as a small market for grocery and food additives, it later evolved into a specialized market for printing and packaging.

stories.title: Majeongyo Bridge
stories.script: Majeon, a marketplace for horse and cow trade, where snake hunters lived   Majeongyo Bridge, an ancient bridge in Cheonggyecheon Stream, held different names throughout history. It was initially called ‘Changseongbang Bridge’ during the reign of King Taejong and was later changed to ‘Taepyeong Bridge’ in the era of King Sungjong. However, it acquired its current name during the reign of King Yeongjo, the 21st king of Joseon, when the Majeon, a market for trading cattle and horse, relocated near this bridge.  To the south of Majeongyo Bridge lies Hullyeonwon Park, historically used for military training and martial arts examinations during the Joseon Dynasty. Admiral Yi Sun-sin, a renowned figure in naval history, underwent a martial arts test. A famous incident involving him occurred in this park when he was injured while riding a horse during the test. Despite the injury, he wrapped his wounded leg with willow bark and persevered to complete the examination.  In Bangsan-dong near Majeonggyo Bridge, two artificial hills were created using soil from construction during the reign of King Yeongjo. Flowers and trees were planted in the garden to prevent the soil from being washed away by the flood. The fragrant environment led to the area being named “Bangsan-dong,” signifying a 'mountain with flower scents' in Korean. Furthermore, the garden attracted many impoverished individuals who dug a tunnel to reside there. These individuals, labeled 'snake hunters,' were granted exclusive rights by King Yeongjo to catch and sell snakes.

stories.title: Narae Bridge
stories.script: Narae Bridge The soaring clothing business of Dongdaemun Gate    Narae Bridge was newly built in front of the Pyeonghwa Market during the restoration work of the Cheonggyecheon Stream in 2005. Pyeonghwa Market was created by the refugees who formed a shantytown around the Cheonggyecheon Stream and sold clothes in street stalls during the Korean War. Most of the refugees were from North Korea, who left their hometowns, and they named this market ‘Pyeonghwa', which means 'peace' in Korean language, with the hopes of peaceful reunification. Shantytown and street stalls that were concentrated at the Cheonggyecheon Stream burned down by a massive fire in 1958 and 1960, but the Pyeonghwa Market was rebuilt during the covering construction of the stream. Dongdaemun Market, which includes the Pyeonghwa Market, is the center of clothing commerce. The bridge near the market was designed to embody the flutter of butterfly wings with the meaning of rising clothing business in Dongdaemun.

stories.title: Buddle Bridge-Jeon Tae-il Bridge
stories.script: Buddle Bridge-Jeon Tae-il Bridge The 1970s, when Jeon Tae-il awakened the reality of working condition    Buddle bridge was newly built in 2005. The name ‘Buddle’ means willow in Korean. Its name changed to Jeon Tae-il Bridge on the 40th anniversary of Jeon Tae-il(1948-1970)’s suicide by fire.    Jeon Tae-il, who was 17 years old in 1965, was a worker in a clothing factory of the Pyeonghwa Market. He worked for more than 14 hours a day in a factory that was crammed with dusts, but received a wage that was below the minimum cost of living. Tailors like Jeon Tae-il had a fixed monthly salary of 3,000 won to 3,500 won, but young girls who were elementary assistants received 70 won per day. At that time, the price of a cup of coffee was 30 won. Jeon Tae-il, who was unable to ignore the reality of laborers, started a labor movement. However, there was no one who listened to the voice of a laborer. On November 13th, 1970, when a labor organization was forcefully dispersed by the police, Jeon Tae-il shouted, Obey the Labor Standards Act, we are not machines. And burned himself to death.  His death was the trigger that brought social problems about the workers who were victimized during the government's process of industrialization into focus.

stories.title: Malgeunnae Bridge
stories.script: Malgeunnae Bridge Malgeunnae, a pure Korean word for Cheonggyecheon Stream    Malgeunnae Bridge was newly constructed during the restoration project of the Cheonggyecheon Stream in 2005. The bridge was named ‘Malgeunnae’, which is a pure Korean word for Cheonggyecheon Stream. When Joseon moved its capital to Hanyang, Cheonggyecheon was a natural stream, so it often flooded during summer. Therefore, King Taejong, the third king of Joseon, embarked on a construction to enlarge and deepen the stream. After that, this natural stream was called ‘Gaecheon’. The name ‘Gaecheon’ became ‘Cheonggyecheon’ during the Late Joseon Dynasty. In 1914, the Japanese Government General of Korea investigated the current condition of the stream and arranged every names of rivers. Since then, the term 'Cheonggyecheon' was featured in newspapers. The origin of the name 'Cheonggyecheon' is unknown. It is said that this term is from the Chinese characters that means 'clear and flowing stream', and it is also said that the name came after ‘Cheongpung Gyecheon’, which is a river located at the upper region of the Cheonggyecheon Stream.

stories.title: Dasangyo Bridge
stories.script: A bridge built to honor the life of Dasan   Dasan is the pen name of Jeong Yak-yong, a great scholar during the latter period of Joseon Dynasty. Rising to a key position at the remarkably young age of 28, he later became a trusted advisor to King Jeongjo.  Following the passing of King Jeongjo, the 22nd ruler of Joseon, in 1800, the conservative Noron Party, opposed to reform, gained power. Jeong Yak-yong, an advocate of change, found himself at risk and named his birthplace 'Yeoyudang' at the time, signifying 'live carefully as if crossing a stream during winter.' Jeong barely survived eventually, but he was banished for 18 years to Gangjin, Jeollanam-do.  During his banishment, Jeong Yak-yong built a thatched house under the mountain, surrounded by natural tea plants, and created the pen name ‘Dasan’, referring to ‘tea mountain.’ He persevered, authoring numerous books, including Mokmin shimseo. He became a great scholar who compiled the idea of practical study in the late Joseon Dynasty.  The Dasangyo Bridge leads to Dasan Street, an homage to Jeong Yak-yong's pen name, further immortalizing his legacy.

stories.title: Yeongdogyo Bridge
stories.script: A bridge tells the tragedy of King Danjong and Queen Jungsun   Originally known as the ‘Wangsimpyeong Bridge’, Yeongdogyo Bridge underwent several transformations throughout history. In 1452, King Danjong, the 6th king of Joseon, ascended the throne at the tender age of 11, and married Queen Jungsun two years later, who was a year older than him. Their affectionate union was marred by the interference of Grand Prince Suyang, King Danjong's uncle. In 1455, King Danjong was dethroned by his uncle, and exiled to Yeongwol, Gangwon-do Province where he bid a poignant farewell to Queen Jungsun at what came to be known as Yeongdogyo Bridge. Since then, people called this bridge ‘Yeongyibyeol’ or ‘Yeongyeong Gunnun’, signifying a lifelong parting. Subsequently, King Sejo’s grandson, King Seongjong, renamed it ‘Yeongdogyo’, symbolizing a bridge perpetually crossed with no return.  During the reign of King Gojong, the 26th Joseon king, Yeongdogyo Bridge was dismantled and repurposed as construction material for Gyeongbokgung Palace. Japan reconstructed it with concrete in 1933, only for it to be destroyed once more during the covering of Cheonggyecheon Stream. The current Yeongdogyo Bridge was erected during the Cheonggyecheon Stream restoration project.

stories.title: Hwanghakgyo Bridge
stories.script: Hwanghakgyo Bridge Doggaebi Market, an antique market where poor women sold their hair   Hwanghakgyo is a bridge connecting Cheonggyecheon Stream and Hwanghak-dong, a town with a legend that ascetics came in and out riding Hwanghak, a stork.  After the Korean War, the refugees settled around Hwanghak-dong, running street stalls for their livelihood. Hwanghak-dong Market was famous for a market where poor women sold their hair. Their hair was later made into wigs, which was a major export in the 1960s.  In 1969, after the construction that covered the Cheonggyecheon Stream around Hwanghak-dong, legally permitted antique stores entered the Hwanghak Market. Hwanghak Market was also called ‘Flea Market’ because of the merchants who ran across the country like fleas to collect antiques. In 1983, a shopping district that traded antiques was created in Janganpyeong, so the antique stores of Hwanghak Market moved to there.  As the antique shops moved out, the street stalls began to enter this market. From this time on, Hwanghak-dong Market was called ‘Doggaebi Market’, which means goblin. This name was given because those street vendors quickly disappeared during the crackdown, and then appeared again. It was also because the secondhand goods sold in the Hwanghak-dong Market were reformed like new products through repairs. It was also called ‘Gaemi Market’, which means an ant. This name was created because the street vendors diligently collected old items like ants. Today’s Hwanghakgyo Bridge was newly constructed in 2005.

stories.title: Biudanggyo Bridge
stories.script: Biudang, the symbol of righteous life   Biudanggyo was named after the renowned scholar Yi-Su-gwang's house, Biwoo-dang. Lee Su-gwang honored the spirit of his honorable grandfather, Yu Gwan, by renovating his house and naming it 'Biudang' to commemorate his integrity and noble character. The bridge, constructed during the restoration of Cheonggyecheon Stream, was named Biudanggyo Bridge, inspired by the splendid name meaning 'shielding rain'.  Adjacent to Biudanggyo Bridge, along the North Cheonggyecheon Stream, lies a street named Jibongno. It was named after the pen name of Yi Su-gwang, who wrote the first encyclopedia of Korea, Jibong Yuseol.   After a 40-minute stroll along Jibongno Street, you will encounter a quaint thatched house named “Biudang.” It was the residence of Yu Gwan, the prime minister during the reign of King Sejong, the fourth king of the Joseon Dynasty. As Yu Gwan spent his wages on the needy, he had no money to repair his thatched house. During heavy rain, when water leaked into the house, he had to use the umbrella to avoid getting wet. Yet, he remained concerned for those without umbrellas in such circumstances. After that, people praised the integrity of Yu Gwan and called his house ‘Usangak’, meaning ‘an umbrella house.’  Although Yi Hui-geom, the Yu Gwan’s descendant, was from a royal family and was a minister of King Seonjo, the 14th king of Joseon, Yi Hui-geom continued to reside in Usangak. One day, a guest visited and asked, Isn’t this house too shabby for a government official to live in? Yi Hui-geom answered, “this house is too luxurious compared to an umbrella.” Coming to the generation of Yi Su-gwang, Yi Hui-geom’s son, he called this house ‘Biudang,’ meaning ‘a house that would barely shelter the rain.’

stories.title: Muhakgyo Bridge
stories.script: A folk tale of Great Master Muhak and Hanyang, the capital of Joseon   Muhakgyo Bridge was newly built and designed with the inspiration of sunrays during the restoration work of Cheonggyecheon Stream. The name of the bridge was originated from a highest priest, Master Muhak, in the early Joseon Dynasty. He assisted King Taejo to examine the configurations of the ground with the purpose of establishing a capital.  On the south side of Muhakgyo Bridge, there was Muhak Street with a wide field during Joseon Dynasty. The Great Master Muhak surveyed this area, contemplating its suitability for the future capital. During his evaluation, an intriguing encounter occurred when an old man herding cattle passed by. Astonished by the old man’s manner of reprimanding the cattle for his own hesitation, Master Muhak sought the man’s advice on the area’s suitability for a new capital site.  The old man suggested him to move forward 10 ‘ri,’ an ancient distance unit equivalent to about 4 kilometers. Muhak followed his words and discovered an ideal site for the new capital. He recommended this location to King Taejo, and it later became the site of Hanyang.  The place where Muhak encountered the old man is now known as ‘Wangsimni,’ reflecting the old man's advice to move forward ten 'ri,' with 'wang' signifying 'to' and 'simni' denoting 'ten ri' in Korean.

stories.title: Dumuldari Bridge
stories.script: Dumuldari Bridge where two streams met during the Joseon Dynasty   Dumuldari Bridge was newly constructed as part of the restoration project of the Cheonggyecheon Stream in 2005. The name of the bridge means ‘two streams merge.' Positioned at the confluence of two streams, it marks the junction where tributaries, such as the Jeongneungcheon Stream and the Samgaksan Valley’s flowing water, merge with the Cheonggyecheon Stream.  The bridge not only bears a name signifying the merging of two streams but also embodies this symbolism in its design. Today, if you walk from Dumuldari Bridge toward Gosanjagyo Bridge, you can see the confluence of two streams. Furthermore, a short downstream stroll from Dumuldari Bridge reveals the Jeongneungcheon Stream flowing leftward, presenting an enchanting sight in front of Gosanjagyo Bridge.

stories.title: Gosanjagyo Bridge
stories.script: Gosanja, the pen name of Kim Jungho, made Map of the Great East   Gosanjagyo Bridge, among the bridges constructed during the restoration of Cheonggyecheon Stream, is situated at the very end. “Gosanja” is the pen name of Kim Jungho, a Korean geographer and cartographer during the latter period of the Joseon Dynasty.  Kim Jungho is renowned for compiling the most extensive collection of maps and geographies of the Joseon Dynasty. His most significant accomplishment is the woodblock, known as “Daedongyeojido,” the Map of the Great East. It took him 30 years to complete which contains the entire Korean Peninsula engraved onto 22 wooden plates. When folded, it is a map; and when opened, it unfolds into a comprehensive map. Notably, it featured distinct symbols and scaled roads every four kilometers, providing accuracy comparable to modern map.  Despite Kim Jungho’s low social status and limited economic resources, he had a sponsor to support his cartographic endeavors. Moreover, the flourishing commerce during the later years of the Joseon Dynasty resulted in increased demand for his maps, particularly from merchants who required detailed maps for their travels. However, the strong tenacity of Kim Jung-ho was the main reason led to the completion of the Daedong-yeojido, a map that integrated all previous Joseon maps. Today, Gosanjagyo Bridge stands as a tribute to the life of Kim Jung-ho and achievements.

stories.title: Yongdusan Park
stories.script: Yongdusan Park houses Busan Tower, the city's iconic landmark. The term Yongdu in its name literally means the head of a dragon, depicting the mountain's shape resembling a dragon rising above the sea. Initially, the area held Konpira Shrine and Benzaiten Shrine, signifying a sacred site for the Japanese. However, post-liberation, the shrines were demolished, and Yongdusan transformed into a refugee shanty town.  Unfortunately, everything turned to ashes during the Great Fire of Yongdusan Mountain in 1954. Subsequently, Yongdusan Mountain underwent reconstruction, becoming the park we know today. Presently, the park boasts the dragon-shaped Busan Tower, along with various facilities. Ascending Busan Tower offers a panoramic view of the entire city, with a chance to glimpse Tsusima Island on clear days. Despite being just a three-minute walk from Nampo-dong, the heart of the city, the park emanates a serene ambiance.  Once teeming with pigeons, most were eventually dispersed due to eradication efforts. For first-time visitors to Busan, a visit to Busan Tower in Yongdusan Park promises to create lasting memories by offering a singular view of the entire city.

stories.title: Busan Modern History Museum
stories.script: Built in 1929 during the Japanese colonial period, it is the history museum where you can see the modern history of Busan. In the beginning, it was used as the Busan Branch of Oriental Colonization Company, an agency responsible for exploiting colonies, but after the Liberation, it started to serve as Busan Cultural Center for the United States Information Service in 1949. However, due to ceaseless demands from Busan citizens for its return, the American cultural center left the building in the end. It was returned to the Korean government in 1999 before the city of Busan took it over in June of the same year. As it was a symbol of invasion and exploitation, the building became the Busan Modern History Museum to be able to utilize it for education to teach the citizens on our painful history. The museum opened on July 3, 2003. The exhibition hall has a map that shows the opening and reclamation of Busan Port with modern stories of the city through various videos. Busan Modern History Museum tells us a lot of interesting stories about the city's modern history.

stories.title: Daegagsa Temple
stories.script: Located in Sinchang-dong, Jung-gu, Busan, Daegagsa Temple became famous when it appeared in the movie, Hi! Dharma 2: Showdown in Seoul. In the 9th year of Meiji restoration of Japan, the country's first-ever Japanese temple called Busan Branch Temple of Dongbonwonsa Temple was established. At first, it only had Inbeopdang Hall but later built a school and a hospital as well. It is a historical site where Yu Tae-chi (a Korean medical doctor), a key member of the Enlightenment Party, consulted Lee Dong-in (a monk at Bongeunsa Temple) on enlightenment policies and, together with over 40 members of the party such as Kim Ok-gyun, Park Yeong-hyo, Seo Gwang-beom and Yun Chi-ho, left a huge mark in the enlightenment of modern Joseon as they frequently traveled Japan. After the Liberation, it became a property of the Korean government, which transformed it into a Korean temple that we see today. As it is located at the heart of the city, it boasts a unique charm that feels much different from typical temples seated at the top of mountains.

stories.title: Ibagu-gil - Old Baekje Hospital
stories.script: The old Baekje Hospital is an old yet elegant and antique building made of red bricks. It is one of the modern structures still remaining in Busan that have been preserved over a long period of time for a variety of uses and purposes. It is the first modern private general hospital built by a man named Choi Yong-hae from Myeongji in 1922. In the days when most buildings had only one or two floors, the hospital made of red bricks featured five floors and hired foreign medical staff to carry a profitable business. However, as he became mired in malicious rumors and, eventually, a financial crisis, Choi handed the hospital's managing rights over to a Chinese man and fled to Japan. Afterwards, the building went from a Chinese restaurant called Bongnaegak to a wedding hall, and today, it is being utilized for a rental business. It is a registered cultural property of Busan, and you will instantly fall in love with its history along with its antique look.

stories.title: Ibagu-gil - Choryang Presbyterian Church
stories.script: Ibagu-gil - Choryang Presbyterian Church  It is the first church built in Busan in 1892 by a missionary named William. Being “first” carries great significance as it was the first church built by a missionary in the south of Hangang River in Seoul. Choryang Presbyterian Church founded during the port opening era opened with the goal of proclaiming the gospel through history and establishing a church that gives joy to the Lord. It is a historically meaningful place that is not only closely related to the Anti-Japanese Independence Movement but also served as the cradle of the Anti-Shrine Worship Movement. During the Korean War when the existence of the nation was in danger, ministers and Christians from all over the nation came together to host a prayer movement for salvation of the country. As you can see, Choryang Presbyterian Church continues to grow into a church that knows the depth of its long history and where the workplaces of the believers are.

stories.title: Ibagu-gil - 168 Stairs
stories.script: It is a steep, six-story-high vertical staircase, which is a unique characteristic of old mountainside roads. As the name suggests, the number of the stairs is 168 and it is said that there used to be three wells at the bottom of the stairs. Currently, only one of the wells that was used for drinking water remains, so you can imagine how people waited in long lines to draw water in the time when clean water was a rarity. Though the times were tough, it is a pleasant, convivial scene if we think about it now. 168 Stairs are so steep that even the residents who live in the area still have to take two to three rest stops in the middle to climb the entire stairs. It also gained more fame when it appeared in the MBC TV series, Shopaholic Louis.

stories.title: Ibagu-gil - Kim Minbu Viewing Point
stories.script: Kim Minbu Viewing Point  When you stand at Kim Minbu Viewing Point, which is named after a person, you will see Bukhang Port unfolds right in front of your eyes. People think about a person who will never return, whom they will never see again. Commemorating Poet Kim Min-bu who is famous for Heart of Waiting, it is an observatory built next to 168 Stairs from which the Busan Port is seen very clearly, offering an awesome view of Busan. Kim Min-bu was a genius poet who first came into the poetry scene when he was only a freshman in high school. Kim is widely known as the producer of a radio show called “Jagalchi Ajimae.” When you stand on the observatory and look down the sea, you will be able to feel the heart of longing for the loved ones to return. It is a sentimental place where you can feel a little bit of such longing and earnestness.

stories.title: Ibagu-gil - Ebagu Archive Center
stories.script: Ebagu Archive Center  The name Ibagu means a “story” in Gyeongsang-do dialect. Ebagu Archive Center is located at the end of Choryang Ibagu-gil, a themed street that holds the history and culture of Busan. It was constructed in the shape of a ship and as a local hub of the “Mountainside Road Renaissance Project,” which is an urban regeneration project of Busan. It is an archive center that collects the stories of residents on Ibagu-gil. When it first opened, it hosted an exhibition titled Yogangjeon, which collected Yogang or chamber pots from the elderly living in the area and exhibited them along with their stories. It stores the history of individuals who live on the mountainside road in their own unique ways. It will evolve into a warehouse that gathers a variety of cultural content and processes them for novel outputs. Visitors can enjoy a clear, panoramic view of the beautiful Busan at the observatory set up on the roof of Ebagu Archive Center.

stories.title: BIFF Square [Peeping Around Gukje Market]
stories.script: BIFF Square  It is a symbolic place established when the Busan International Film Festival, or BIFF, was first held in 1996. Here, you can find countless hand prints of renowned actors and directors. Located between Jagalchi Market and Gukje Market, a great number of people always pass this area. It is full of delicious snacks such as ssiat hotteok (griddlecake with sugar and seeds filling). In the early years of BIFF, films were often played in theaters of Nampo-dong, but ever since the Busan Cinema Center opened in Haeundae, most of the events related to the film festival relocated to the Haeundae area. Today, performances held on the stage in the Square continue its tradition. In recent years, it has become more than just a movie-playing attraction; instead, it has transformed into a cultural complex where you can enjoy shopping and entertainment at the same time, which has attracted young people around the area, thereby contributing to revitalization of the commercial district.

stories.title: Bosu Book Street [Tour Around Gukje Market]
stories.audioTitle: Bosu Book Street [Tour Around Gukje Market]
stories.script: Bosu Book Street  After the Korean War, many tent classes were set up in Seo-gu, Busan that taught refugees who had fled to the city. Some children in this neighborhood who had difficulties in getting books they needed were able to read used books here and continue their studies. This street is Bosu Book Street. Bookstores started as street stalls, which gradually evolved into temporary buildings to form a street. At that time, impoverished refugees and numerous students and intellectuals from economically disadvantaged households sold and loaned valuable books they owned. They were also able to purchase pre-owned books they needed at affordable prices to continue their studies. In the middle of the street, there is Bosu Book Street Cultural Center where you can get a glimpse of the circumstances back then. Why don’t you take a moment and get lost in old memories at Bosu Book Street full of secondhand books?

stories.title: Bupyeong Kkangtong Market [Tour Around Gukje Market]
stories.audioTitle: Bupyeong Kkangtong Market [Tour Around Gukje Market]
stories.script: It is a combination of Bupyeong Market and Kkangtong Market. This place became famous after the Korean War when supplies and canned goods from U.S. military bases began to be sold. It is one of the famous markets representing Busan along with Gukje Market and Jagalchi Market. As the nation's first-ever night market which opened in 2013, it is extremely popular among tourists, offering a variety of traditional foods and snacks from around the world. Along with porridge restaurants, there are many stores specializing in side dishes such as kimchi, salted seafood, seasoned vegetables and eomuk (fish cakes). In particular, restaurants and entertainment districts are thriving from Jokbal Alley to Bupyeong Market, and ever since Bupyeong Kkangtong Night Market opened in 2013 and started to offer exotic foreign foods, the place became a popular attraction for many tourists.

stories.title: Jeoryeong Coastal Trail (Huinnyeoul-gil)
stories.script: The Jeoryoung Coastal Trail, established along the coast and commencing at the Huinnyeoul Culture Village Information Center, is a 3-kilometer-long path created through a public labor project in 2001.  The trail showcases a picturesque landscape adorned with beautiful pebbles and offers expansive views of the sea. In the past, Yeongdo used to be known as Jeoryoungdo Island, and the name ‘Jeoryoung’ persists along the trail.  As soon as you step onto the trail, you are greeted by the endless expanse of the blue sea. The pathway unfurls like a red carpet, extending from the apartment area all the way to the Piano Stairs, which mark the endpoint of the Huinnyeoul-gil trail.  For a panoramic view of the entire trail, head to the Namhangdaegyo Bridge, which connects Seo-gu and Yeongdo-gu. From there, you can observe the trail in its entirety, with ships and boats moored close to the coast providing a striking backdrop, akin to a masterpiece painted by a legendary artist.

stories.title: Huinnyeoul-gil
stories.script: Huinnyeoul-gil was named after how 'the water stream starting from Bongnaesan Mountain and rapidly winding down into the sea looks like white snow falling.' When looking at the path from an alley, you'll find houses nestled under a steep hillside, bringing to mind thoughts of Santorini, Greece.  Recently, it has become a popular filming location for movies and TV series such as 'The Attorney,' 'Nameless Gangster,' and 'Crossing Yeongdo Bridge.' The Yeongdo-gu Office remodeled empty houses in the village near Dongshin Apartment into art workshops, allowing local artists to use the spaces. At the village entrance, on the way to Jeoryeong-ro where buses pass, there is a storytelling map and information sign about the Huinnyeoul Culture Village. You can enjoy the peaceful scenery where relaxed street cats and homeless dogs patrol the alleyway.  You might also hear some people calling the mountain 'Gogalsan,' meaning 'a mountain whose water has completely dried up.' This misleading name was given during the Japanese colonial era with the purpose of degrading Korean people’s pride.  Despite this misleading naming, Bongnaesan boasts a rich body of water running through it. It is famous for offering many mineral springs that produce easily accessible natural water. Hikers can quench their thirst even if they haven’t brought their own bottles.  By calling this area 'a village where water falls and crashes in white,' perhaps the people of the village had a hidden desire to strike back in their own way for the country's stolen history.

stories.title: The Filming Location of “The Attorney” (Huinnyeoul-gil)
stories.script: ‘The Attorney’ is a film based on a true story and holds the distinction of being the 9th movie in Korean cinema history to attract over 10 million moviegoers. As you walk along Huinnyeoul-gil, you’ll see the Jeonin Gajok Research Institute, known as a vacation villa. A bit further down the road, you'll reach the very location where The Attorney was filmed.  Your first encounter will likely be with a wall bearing the famous line from the movie: This makes no sense! This is wrong. I'll do it! I'll be the attorney! This impassioned declaration was made by Attorney Song as he resolved to defend Jinwoo during the trials under the military dictatorship. Continuing along the road past this wall will lead you to the actual filming location of the movie.

stories.title: Isongdo Observatory (Huinnyeoul-gil)
stories.script: If you continue along the road, following the laundry pieces hung on the walls facing the cliff, you'll eventually reach Isongdo Observatory. Here, you can bask in the stunning views of Songdo from the opposite side. On clear days, you may even catch a glimpse of Tsushima Island. This spot is also perfect for taking in the breathtaking vistas of nearby islands, such as Jujeonja, Mokdo, and Hyeongjedo Islands, making it an ideal location for capturing memorable photographs.  Among the many islands in this area, Jujeonja Island holds a special significance as it is considered sacred. When you visit, keep in mind the three taboos: refrain from making fires and falling in love. Additionally, don't forget to plan a visit to Isongdo Observatory yourself; it's an experience you won't want to miss.

stories.title: Suyeong Paldo Traditional Market
stories.script: Suyeong Paldo Traditional Market   Suyeong Paldo Traditional Market has been selling products brought by fishermen and farmers from Gwangalli, Cheongsapo, Gijang and many other places. It is known that the name, Paldo Market, was derived from the fact that it was a marketplace where products from all across the country came to be sold, but most locals believe that it was originated from a Korean-Japanese man named Kim Paldo who had returned to Korea in the 60s or 70s and renovated the marketplace to its present form. Established as a general market in 1969, on August 10, 1981, it was officially registered as a traditional market. At the time, there had been no big market in the area and since its foundation, Suyeong Paldo Traditional Market quickly became a huge marketplace with over 150 stores that cover a broad region from Suyeong-dong and Millak-dong to Mangmi-dong, Yeonsan-dong and Namcheon-dong.

stories.title: Black Pine and Muku Tree at Jwasuyeong Fortress Site
stories.audioTitle: Black Pine and Muku Tree at Jwasuyeong Fortress Site
stories.script: Black Pine and Muku Tree at Jwasuyeong Fortress Site   The Korean name of black pine, “Gomsol,” is said to have stemmed from “Geomeunsol,” which means pines with black-colored bark. As it is highly resistant to sea breeze and salt, it is popularly used as a windbreak forest, which is also being referred to as “Haesong,” meaning sea pine. The “Black Pine at Jwasuyeong Fortress Site” is designated as Natural Monument No. 270. There is a shrine next to it called Godang where ancestral rites used to be held. At Jwasuyeong (Left Naval Headquarters) during the Joseon Dynasty, soldiers believed that this tree ruled over military ships so they treated it as a divine tree and performed ancestral rites. You can find more black pines that are over 200 years old within the South Gate of Suyeongseong Fortress, along with many old, armful trees. In particular, the Muku Tree, which is designated as Natural Monument No. 311, is said to be over 500 years old. Its size and branches spread out dynamically and vigorously, seemingly showing off its old age and freshness at the same time. It has been providing the villagers a generous and cool shade like an umbrella, which is why it has been revered as a sacred tree of the village for a long time.

stories.title: Shrine to General An Yongbok
stories.script: General An Yong-bok from Suyeong, Dongnae during the reign of King Sukjong of the Joseon Dynasty was a sailer of Jwasuyeong naval forces. He achieved a great feat of driving out Japanese invaders who raided Korea’s Ulleungdo and Dokdo Islands on the East Sea twice in the 19th and 22nd years of Sukjong’s reign and eventually went over to Japan to get their confirmation that Dokdo is indeed Joseon’s land. On October 30, 1967, General An Yong-bok Commemoration Society built the Memorial Tower in Suyeong Historical Park to commemorate his accomplishments. But since people felt sorry that the size of the Memorial Tower was too small compared to the magnitude of what he achieved, construction of a shrine and a statue as well as relocation of the existing tower took place to raise his achievements and status. A memorial service is held by General An Yong-bok Commemoration Society every year, around 12 PM on every April 18th of the solar calendar.

stories.title: Altar to Twenty-Five Heroes
stories.script: Jwasuyeong was a superior administrative office that commanded and oversaw Busanjin, which was the first battlefield of the Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1592. Moreover, it was the center of the local naval forces that had to mobilize military forces to fight in the outbreak of war. However, as soon as Busanjinseong and Dongnaeseong Fortresses were in danger of falling by the attack of the invaders, Bak Hong, the head of Jwasuyeong who had to lead his naval forces and fight against the enemies, ran away, only thinking about his own safety. This left only the commander-less soldiers and the residents in the face of the Japanese raiders who were stampeding into the fortress. The Japanese used Dongnae as their base and carried out brutal and habitual plunders and slaughters. Under such circumstances, 25 soldiers and residents of Jwasuyeong — Jeong In-gang, Choi Song-eup, Choi Soo-man, Park Ji-soo, Kim Paeng-ryang, Park Eung-bok, Shim Nam, Lee Eun-chun, Jeong Soo-won, Park Lim, Lee Su, Shin Bok, Kim Ok-gye, Lee Hee-bok, Choi Han-yeon, Choi Han-son, Choi Mak-nae, Choi Keut-ryang, Kim Dal-mang, Kim Deok-bong, Lee Sil-jeong, Kim Heo-nong, Ju Nam-geum, Kim Jong-soo and Kim Jin-ok — decided to die fighting and started a guerrilla battle to protect themselves, their families and neighbors.

stories.title: F1963
stories.script: F1963 is a cultural and art complex in Mangmi-dong, Suyeong-gu where Suyeong Factory, the first factory of Kiswire, was located. F stands for Factory, and 1963 is the year when Kiswire completed the construction of Suyeong Factory. The Kiswire Suyeong Factory produced wire ropes for 45 years from 1963 to 2008 and was later used as a warehouse after the factory moved. Ever since it was utilized as a special exhibition hall for Busan Biennale in 2014, it went through remodeling in 2016 and was eventually reborn as a Busan Biennale Exhibition Hall. Spaces inside F1963 are set up under the concept of “three squares.” It consists of a section where academic conferences, performances and concerts are held, a commercial space featuring cafes and beer pubs, and a cultural space once used as an exhibition hall for 2016 Busan Biennale that is planned to be used as a library, bookstores, etc.

stories.title: Provisional Capital Trail — Hidden Biseok Cultural Village in Ami-dong
stories.audioTitle: Provisional Capital Trail — Hidden Biseok Cultural Village in Ami-dong
stories.script: The Hidden Biseok Cultural Village in Ami-dong by a mountainside road is a village built on top of a cemetery. This neighborhood speaks volumes about the history of Busan. Refugees who had fled to the city during the Korean War built a town here but before that, there had been a cemetery for Japanese people built in the colonial period. Walking through the alleys of Hidden Biseok Cultural Village, you will be able to see angled upper stones and tombstones used as stepping stones for steep stairs or foundation stones for retaining walls and houses. When you walk out of Toseong Station, you will find a trail information board, and there is a village map at the peak of the hill. Friendly murals are painted in the alley, and there is also a sign in front of a structure made of a tombstone. To feel the essence of Hidden Biseok Cultural Village in Ami-dong, look for traces of tombstones as if finding hidden pictures.

stories.title: Provisional Capital Trail — Choi Min-Shik Gallery
stories.audioTitle: Provisional Capital Trail — Choi Min-Shik Gallery
stories.script: Choi Min-Shik Gallery   Choi Min-shik is one of the most notable documentary photographers of Korea who was known for capturing the hard, strenuous lives of ordinary people in the aftermath of the Korean War. His article through which he posed the question, “Aren’t the unnamed people called ‘grass roots’ the source of life and vitality?” represents the philosophy of a great photographer who has now been gone from this world. Choi Min-Shik Gallery exhibits more than 30 of his relics including photos he took from the 1960s and 1970s, his cameras, handwritten lecture materials, and pictures taken of him over the course of his life. It is a place where you can picture Busan in the past with the help of his pictures. Many who love photography visit the gallery, but since it is not extremely well-known yet, visitors are able to enjoy a true taste of photos in a quiet, tranquil environment.

stories.title: Provisional Capital Trail — Gyeongmudae (Currently Provisional Capital Memorial Hall)
stories.audioTitle: Provisional Capital Trail — Gyeongmudae (Currently Provisional Capital Memorial Hall)
stories.script: This building was built in 1926 by the Japanese General Government of Korea as the official residence for the governor of Gyeongsangnam-do Province. Whereas the exterior is in the form of a Japanese tile-roofed house, the interior architecture is a mixture of the Western and Japanese traditional styles. When Busan was the temporary capital during the Korean War, it was also used as the official residence of the president. At the time, President Rhee Syng-man lived here together with the first lady and his secretaries to not only command and be reported on the state affairs and Korean politics but also welcome important state guests. As you can imagine, many of the historical moments of the time took place in this very building.  After the war ended, the presidential residence relocated back to Seoul, and this building became the official residence for the governor of Gyeongsangnam-do Province. The residence, however, moved to Changwon soon after. The Busan Metropolitan Government purchased the building and opened it on June 25, 1984 as the Provisional Capital Memorial Hall. The first floor has replicated an old appearance from the days when the building was used as the presidential residence while the second floor exhibits many artifacts, which include relics from the war and of President Rhee. It is a place where records of the hope of recovery even in the history of hardships still remain. Moreover, it is a valuable asset that we must pass down to future generations so that no national tragedy of war will ever repeat.

stories.title: Provisional Central Government Complex (Currently Seokdang Museum of Dong-A University)
stories.audioTitle: Provisional Central Government Complex (Currently Seokdang Museum of Dong-A University)
stories.script: In the days of Busan as the wartime capital, this building, which had been the Gyeongsangnam-do Provincial Government Office, was utilized as the Government Complex for the Temporary Capital. It featured the Office of the Prime Minister and the six government departments that oversaw the core administrative and legislative functions of a wartime capital. Here, the members not only responded to pressing wartime circumstances but also established and executed various policies. The building indeed was the center of politics of Busan as the wartime capital as well as the heart of the country that dealt with major national agendas. This was also the place where historical events took place during the war from the Busan Political Crisis to the Bodo League Massacre. Many of the important policies for reconstruction of the nation, which include actions to take for refugees and financial assistance, were decided here as well.  After the war was over, it was used as the Busan District Court and Busan District Prosecutors' Office before Dong-A University began to utilize it as a museum in 2002. The inside is a museum, and the exterior still well maintains how the building looked in the beginning. Recognized for its great historical and architectural value, it is currently designated as Busan's Registered Cultural Heritage No. 41.

stories.title: Provisional Capital Trail — Central Meteorological Office (Currently Busan Meteorological Station)
stories.audioTitle: Provisional Capital Trail — Central Meteorological Office (Currently Busan Meteorological Station)
stories.script: When and where do you think weather observations began in Busan? In 1904, it started as a temporary rain gauge station for the Japanese Meteorological Observatory and Busan Meteorological Observation Station in Bosu-dong, Jung-gu. In 1934, it moved to the new building in Bokbyeongsan Mountain. It is currently the Busan Meteorological Station. During the wartime capital days, it was used as the Central Meteorological Office. Here, the weather was observed at every hour, thus 24 times every day, to provide important weather data needed for military operations. In addition, Ilgan Cheongido that recorded daily weather was published to inform refugees with useful weather-related information. The weather forecast at the time was an important task that determined victory or defeat of military operations as well as critical information that helped decide departure or anchorage of ships.  The exterior is made in the shape of a ship, which is fitting for the port city Busan. Forming an exquisite harmony with the natural landscape, the building was built on a hill of Bokbyeongsan Mountain where it is easy to observe the weather. Both the interior and exterior of the building have been well preserved over a long period of time, which makes it a perfect place for history and culture learning.

stories.title: Provisional Capital Trail — U.S. Embassy and U.S. Information Service (Currently Busan Modern History Museum)
stories.audioTitle: Provisional Capital Trail — U.S. Embassy and U.S. Information Service (Currently Busan Modern History Museum)
stories.script: This building was constructed as the Busan Branch of the Oriental Development Company. After the Liberation, the U.S. military was stationed here and used the facility, and during the Korean War, it served as not only the U.S. Embassy, which was a diplomatic window for the country, but also the U.S. Information Service, a cultural window for communication and exchange. During the war, it was a popular venue to hold lectures, rallies and teenagers’ oratorical contests about defeating the Chinese People's Volunteer Army. After May 18 Democratization Movement in 1980, Busan citizens demanded the building's return, which is why the American Cultural Center moved out. In the same year, the city of Busan took the building over and turned it into Busan Modern History Museum after expansion and remodeling. Once a symbol of invasion and exploitation, the place now serves as a space for education to learn about the painful history of our ancestors.

stories.title: Provisional Capital Trail — Busanhang Port Pier 1
stories.audioTitle: Provisional Capital Trail — Busanhang Port Pier 1
stories.script: As one of the city's notable landmarks, Busanhang Port is Korea’s first-ever trading port opened in 1876. Pier 1, in particular, is a modern port facility constructed in connection to the Gyeongbu Line railway. During the Japanese colonial period, it was connected to Shimonoseki Port and utilized as an important hub for Japan's invasion of the mainland continent. In the days of Busan as the wartime capital, ships carrying refugees as well as war supplies and relief goods of the UN forces came into Busanhang Port, which played a critical role in transport during the war. This also subsequently created many logistics-related jobs in the area, contributing greatly to the livelihood of the refugees. As you can see, Busanhang Port contains not only the joys and sorrows of refugees but also the spirit of pioneers of our maritime industry. As it is a place that has historical significance as well as the value of our maritime culture, make sure to check the port as thoroughly as you can.

stories.title: Provisional Capital Trail — Camp Hialeah (Currently Busan Citizens Park)
stories.audioTitle: Provisional Capital Trail — Camp Hialeah (Currently Busan Citizens Park)
stories.script: This is Camp Hialeah, a place for which Busan citizens carried out a “campaign that demanded the return of the land” for 17 years and that has now become a park for the citizens. It was first established as a horse racetrack in 1930 and used as a warehouse for Japanese military supplies until the Liberation. When the Korean War broke out, the United States Forces Korea (USFK)’s Busan Command was set up here, serving as the command center to supply military goods and support the UN forces.  It is said that the unit name of “Hialeah,” which means a “beautiful meadow,” was also coined in this period. Even after the war was over, it played an essential military role as a military command base. Though it was an independent space for the execution of the U.S. military functions, it lived on within the city for a long time, conveying and communicating each other’s cultures. With the closure of Camp Hialeah in 2006 and its transformation to Busan Citizens Park, you can now visit the symbolic places such as the commissioned officers’ club where meals and banquets were held for the U.S. soldiers as well as the dormitories for noncommissioned officers. As you take a slow walk in this large park, I hope you will also be able to feel the history infused in this place.

stories.title: Provisional Capital Trail — United Nations Ground Forces Command (Currently Walker House)
stories.audioTitle: Provisional Capital Trail — United Nations Ground Forces Command (Currently Walker House)
stories.script: Students are able to enjoy relaxing lunch in this cafeteria thanks to the tense, 18-day history that happened here in the past. The war started by the invasion from the north and over 90% of the entire Korean Peninsula was taken over by the North Korean troops, but here at the Walker House, the Allied Forces were able to score a victory. In the time when the front line at Nakdonggang River was in danger of being destroyed, this building was used as the temporary headquarters of the Nakdonggang front line command center. It is a hastily built stone house made of a mixture of natural stones and concrete. A U.S. general named Walker commanded the troops here to defend the Nakdonggang front line, which served as a turning point for the eventual Incheon Landing Operation. Walker House holds countless sacrifices and efforts put forth to protect Busan, the last bastion. Today, it is used as a cafeteria of Pukyong National University.

stories.title: Provisional Capital Trail — United Nations Cemetery (Currently United Nations Memorial Cemetery in Korea)
stories.audioTitle: Provisional Capital Trail — United Nations Cemetery (Currently United Nations Memorial Cemetery in Korea)
stories.script: The UN troops who fought in the Korean War for the freedom and peace in Korea are buried in the United Nations Cemetery. During the war, a total of 16 countries sent troops and five sent medical assistance groups. Approximately 11,000 fallen soldiers were originally buried in this place, but due to the requests from the bereaved or their governments, many of the remains continued to be returned, which leaves only about 2,300 from 11 countries still remaining at the cemetery. On the 12-meter-high Monumental Stone for the UN Soldiers, built by the Korean government in 1978, the status of combat equipment, number of the dispatched and the fallen during the Korean War are engraved. The Memorial Cenotaph for the British Commonwealth, which was built by the British government, honors the noble sacrifices that unfortunately have not been found among the dead of the Commonwealth. It is a historical space where you can feel the breaths of young and noble lives that were sacrificed for the world peace.

stories.title: Taebaek Gumunso
stories.script: Gumunso: The Harmony of Softness and Strength  Gumunso is a beautiful spot where the water flowing from Hwangji Lake gently passes through Dongjeom-dong, carving its way through a large mountain to form a stunning stone gate and a deep pool. Known for its grace, it is sometimes called “Dduru-nae ” (穿川), meaning the river flowing through the mountain, and is also referred to as Gumunso (求門沼) in Chinese characters.  The Nakdong River, starting from Hwangji Lake, reaches Gumunso, where the water flows beneath a massive rock arch, about 20–30 meters high and 30 meters wide. This formation has created a deep pool beneath the arch. The term Gumun(求門) refers to an old word for a hole or cave, which translates to a swamp or lake with a cave,   Gumunso is designated as Natural Monument No. 417, and it is a truly remarkable site where the river flows beneath a massive cave. This natural wonder vividly brings to life the saying water can carve through rock. The cave's unique geographical features are rare and hard to find elsewhere in the world. It is particularly fascinating because the waterway of Hwangji Stream flows through this stone gate, merging with Cheoramcheon Stream and then adjusting its course toward the Nakdong River. This makes Gumunso not only a stunning sight but also a place of great natural significance.  The story of Gumunso goes back even further in time. A long time ago, the Baekdu Mountains were submerged under the sea. One day, a massive tectonic plate collision occurred beneath the ocean, and the force from this impact pushed the Baekdu Mountains upwards, emerging above the surface. As a result, the Baekdu Mountains, including the area around Gumunso, bear traces of the ocean that existed about 470 to 450 million years ago. These remnants can still be observed today in the region's rocks.  As you walk near Gumunso, you can spot wave-like patterns in the rocks, salt traces, and fossils of ancient sea creatures like trilobites. These discoveries add a unique charm to the experience. Walking through Gumunso feels like stepping into an ancient ocean, with the lush surrounding forests resembling seaweed and the sound of water flowing through the cave echoing the distant crash of waves.

stories.title: Three Tales of Gumunso
stories.script: Three Tales of Gumunso  The first tale is about a large willow tree. The river that flowed from the Huangji Pond to Gumunso originally turned toward the Sagun Bridge and flowed toward Marigeorang. One day, a great flood caused the river to swell massively. The water from Huangji Pond couldn’t drain completely into Marigeorang, and the entire Huangji area became a vast sea. At that moment, a massive willow tree, carried from the willow grove in Hwajeondong, crashed into the wall of Gumunso. With a thunderous sound, a large hole appeared, changing the course of the water. The river that had been flowing toward Marigeorang suddenly flowed through this hole, becoming Cheoramcheon Stream.  The second tale is deeply related to the sacredness of Gumunso. Long ago, before the hole was formed in Gumunso, there was Cheoramcheon Stream a large pond on the eastern side, which was home to the Blue Dragon, and the western side, Huangji Stream, was inhabited by the White Dragon. The two dragons always fought for control of the Nakdong River. The clash between them created thunderous roars and thick fog, obscuring the boundary between heaven and earth. One day, the White Dragon came up with a plan and, while fighting on top of the stone wall, swooped down and breached the wall beneath to ambush the Blue Dragon. The Blue Dragon, unable to recover in time, was caught off guard, the White Dragon emerged victorious and ascended to the heavens. The mountain that the White Dragon passed on his way to the sky is called Yonguwisan (Dragon's Peak), and it rises right in front of Gumunso.  The third tale emphasizes the global significance of Gumunso. In ancient times, when the entire world was flooded, the villages below Taebaeksan Mountain, including Huangji and Jangseong, were submerged. During this time, an emperor from China, known for leading the prosperous era, appeared. This emperor, Hao Xi, was a divine-like figure who understood the laws of mountains and rivers. Hao Xi took a large sword and, with one strike, pierced the stone wall beneath Gumunso, causing the water to flow into Cheoramcheon Stream and revealing the land once again.  These three tales, full of vivid and contrasting elements, reveal just how mysterious and enchanting Gumunso is. From the cave walls that seem to have been scratched by the branches of willow trees, to the twisting water that echoes the movements of dragons, to the deep pond that might have fascinated even the emperor of China, the three stories seem to come alive as you gaze at the swirling waters of Gumunso, where Huangji Stream meets Cheoramcheon Stream.

stories.title: Tales of the Gumunso People
stories.script: The Unfortunate Eom Jong-han and the Fortunate Son-in-law, Mr. Cho  Once upon a time, near Gumunso, there lived a kind-hearted man named Eom Jong-han(嚴宗漢). He devoted his life to caring for his elderly parents, catching fish at Gumunso each day to provide for them.  One evening, as Eom went to prepare dinner, he discovered that his precious fishing net was missing. It was all he owned, and losing it was devastating. Determined, he searched tirelessly around Gumunso, but as he stepped on a mossy rock, he slipped and fell into the swirling waters.  When he woke up, he found himself in the magnificent palace of the Dragon King. The Dragon King, furious, accused Eom of stealing his “chickens.” Only then did Eom realize that the fish he had been catching were sacred creatures from the Dragon King's domain. He humbly apologized, explaining he had no choice but to fish to feed his aging parents. For three days, Eom sincerely begged for forgiveness.  The Dragon King, moved by Eom’s earnestness, forgave him and even held a grand feast in his honor. During the meal, Eom thought of his family and discreetly tucked a piece of rice cake into his pocket to share with them. When the feast ended, the Dragon King guided Eom out of the palace. To his surprise, he found himself back at Gumunso, but a strange scene awaited him.   Villagers were gathered for a ritual, and when they saw Eom, they were shocked—everyone thought he had been dead for three years. What felt like only days in the Dragon King's palace had been years in the human world.  Eom returned home and remembered the rice cake in his pocket, but it had hardened into a small stone. Still, he placed it in the family’s rice jar. The next day, his wife discovered something miraculous: the rice jar was full, and no matter how much rice they took, it never ran out. Naming it Baekbyeongseok(白餠石) which means White Rice Cake Stone, Eom treasured it and kept it safe.  News of this miracle reached their daughter, married into the Cho family in Hanyang. She begged her parents for the stone and eventually sneaked it away. Without the stone, Eom's family fell into poverty again. His wife repeatedly visited her daughter to retrieve the stone but was only given imitations. Meanwhile, the Cho family prospered, moving to a fertile silk farm in Andong, where they enjoyed great success. Sadly, Eom’s family remained impoverished.  Despite their wealth, the Cho family felt a lingering guilt over taking the Baekbyeongseok. To make amends, they always treated Eom’s descendants with warmth and generosity whenever they visited Andong. After each visit, they would send them home with sacks of rice, a gesture said to be rooted in their remorse over the stone.

stories.title: Gumunso Stone Gate Tunnel (Seokmun)
stories.script: The Subtle Colonial Logic Behind the Stone Gate Tunnel  Now, let's take a look at the tunnel entrance along the road next to Gumunso. It's so narrow that only one car can barely fit, and the ceiling is too low. Though vehicles coming from Gyeongsang-do pass through this tunnel on their way into Taebaek, it feels too crude to be a product of human craftsmanship and too artificial to have formed naturally.  The term Seokmun (stone gates) refers to an entrance made of stone, commonly used for describing tunnel or cave openings. In the case of Gumunso and the nearby tunnel, both can be considered stone gates. However, the stone gate at Gumunso is specifically referred to as the  Jagae Gate. This name comes from historical records, such as in the Jeonggamrok, which describes how, ... the stone gate opens at Ja-si and closes at Chuk-si. When it opens at Ja-si, if you quickly enter, you will find a place called Obokdong, an ideal land where flowers bloom year-round, there is no famine, no illness, and no misfortune. This passage inspired the naming of the stone gate as Jagae Gate, symbolizing a place believed to be blessed and free from misfortune.  The Obokdong refers to what is now the Taebaek area, while the Stone Gate is the entrance to the cave at Gumunso, where the Nakdong River makes its way through the mountains. In the book Samcheok Gukgi Nojeonggi (三陟局基路程記), it is said: There is a remarkable stone called Jibusuk, which resembles a bow, with two pillars standing on either side. This is the Stone Gate, which opens at Ja-si and closes at Chuk-si. When it opens, anyone who steps inside will find a paradise called Gunghaeyeomji (弓海鹽之地) a place of eternal spring where flowers bloom all year round, there is no famine, no illness, and no misfortune.  The phrase opens at the hour of Ja-Si comes from the term Ja-si-gae (子時開), which refers to the opening that happens at Ja-si. This is why the entrance to Gumunso is lovingly called Jagae Gate (子開門), which translates to The Opening Gate of Ja-si. For the people of Taebaek, as well as those who believe in the teachings of Jeonggamrok, this gate holds a deep spiritual significance. It's considered so sacred that the idea of desecrating it was simply unthinkable. Gumunso has also long been a place for important rituals. People would offer prayers to the heavens, and during times of drought, they would perform rain dances. This sacred belief remained alive even into the late 1980s. Those from Gyeongsang Province would enter Taebaek through Gumunso, hoping to find prosperity, but when leaving, they took a much longer route around the sacred site, passing through Tongri and Cheolam instead. Even today, some people still follow these traditions, giving us a glimpse into just how deeply Gumunso is cherished by the people of Taebaek.  The man-made tunnel next to Gumunso was constructed in 1937, during the Japanese occupation, when a coal mine was developed in Jangseong. The tunnel was built with the sole purpose of transporting coal quickly, with little regard for the beliefs of the local people. The Japanese dug the tunnel right next to Gumunso, and it’s said that this act drained the energy of Taebaek from below according to feng shui. If we consider the locals' beliefs, this act may have been even more brutal than the iron stakes driven into the Baekdu mountains range. While the iron stakes are hidden, the artificial tunnel is visible every day, constantly serving as a reminder. Moreover, inscribed above the tunnel is the phrase Woo Hyul Mo Gi (禹穴牟奇), meaning as strangely same as the hole made by Yu the Great (referring to Yu the Great, a legendary figure in Chinese history). The implication of this inscription was that it placed Japan on the same level as the legendary benefactor Yu the Great, subtly crafting the colonial logic that Japan is Korea's benefactor.  Several years ago, a new tunnel, the Dongjeom Tunnel, was constructed next to the artificial tunnel built by the Japanese. Now, there are three main pathways around Gumunso: The Gumunso Jagae Gate, the stone gate of the tunnel, and the modern Dongjeom Tunnel where the distinction between gates is no longer necessary. If you visit Gumunso, be sure to explore all three tunnels—they symbolize the spirit, the pain, and the progress of Taebaek.

stories.title: Gumunso Samhyeongje Waterfalls
stories.script: The Gift from the Three Brothers  A long time ago, the three brothers were joyfully playing in the water near the waterfall. They were so caught up in the fun that they didn't notice the cliff and fell right into the water below. But don’t worry—they were so happy they didn’t realize they had crossed into another world.  As they played even more joyfully in the water, and as they followed the rain falling from the sky, they all turned into dragons and soared into the heavens. Their splashes were so powerful that the traces they left on the waterfall rocks became the waterfall itself. That’s how the Samhyeongje (Three Brothers) Waterfall was formed. The villagers like to joke that if one of the waterfalls has less water during a drought, it’s because the youngest brother is upset, feeling left out by his older brothers who won’t play with him.  Near the waterfall, there used to be a spring and laundry area, though now only the remnants of the spring remain. The waterfall has always been a favorite spot for photos, so if you're raising brothers who tend to bicker, you might want to capture a playful moment with the waterfall as a backdrop while sharing the heartwarming story of the three brothers.

stories.title: Gyeongsang Gamyeong Park
stories.script: Gyeongsang Gamyeong Park in Daegu is where the Gyeongsang Gamyeong used to be during the Joseon Dynasty. Gyeongsang Gamyeong was the government office that oversaw Gyeongsang-do, which was one of the eight provinces of Joseon. Originally located in Gyeongju and then Sangju, it moved to Andong later before relocating to Daegu in the 34th year of King Seonjo’s reign. Since 1910 when the local administration system was restructured to 13 provinces, its role changed to be the center of Gyeongsangbuk-do, not Gyeongsang-do. Gyeongsangbuk-do Provincial Office was here from 1910 to 1966, and after the office moved to Sangyeok-dong, it turned into a park in 1970 to commemorate the site.  Inside the park, Seonhwadang Hall (Daegu Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 1), which was the office of the governor of Gyeongsang Gamyeong, and Jingcheonggak Hall (Daegu Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 2), the residence of the governor, still remain. There are a total of 29 distinguished service monuments erected by commoners to pay respects to the good service by governor and executive assistant to the magistrate of Daegu. These days, the elderly of the village gather together to play janggi (Korean chess) or chat with one another for a relaxing time. A small pond and a pavilion, which were also installed when building the park, are popular spots to take pictures.  <This guide was recorded by Kang Gyeong-hwa of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Daegu Modern History Museum
stories.script: Daegu Modern History Museum  Originally built as the Daegu branch of Joseon Siksan Bank in 1932 during the Japanese colonial period, the building was remodeled and eventually reopened as the Daegu Modern History Museum in 2011. During the colonial era, it was an infamous symbol of financial domination over Joseon and colonial exploitation. Boasting a Renaissance style, the building still preserves its original form well and possesses great value as cultural heritage. It was later designated as Daegu's Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 49.  There is a permanent exhibition hall on the first floor of the museum that exhibits the scenes of modern Daegu and the lives of our ancestors. You can also step inside a huge safe that existed since the days when the building was used as a bank. A ticket-taking lady who speaks a nostalgic dialect kindheartedly guides you through a video that introduces the central area of the modern Daegu. Make sure to visit the second floor as well by taking an elevator as it is a planned exhibition that displays the newest exhibits related to the city of Daegu.   <This guide was recorded by Kang Gyeong-hwa of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Hyangchon Cultural Center, Daegu Literature Museum
stories.audioTitle: Hyangchon Cultural Center, Daegu Literature Museum
stories.script: Hyangchondong-gil refers to a 30-meter-long street that runs from the eastern path of Mugunghwa Department Store to Bukseong-ro. There once were Jungyeong and Daegubu of Gyeongsang Gamyeong on this street but most of them were torn down during the Japanese colonial era. After that, major government offices, bars, pubs and inns began to be established here, making it the most popular city center of Daegu. After the Liberation, music teahouses such as Nokhyang and many other types of cafes and teahouses were created in this area, thus attracting many artists. Some of the most famous artists who stayed in Hyangchon-dong include Artist Lee Jung-seob and Poets Ku Sang and Yu Chi-hwan. Their traces that have been long gone can now be seen at Hyangchon Cultural Center located by the entrance of the street.  Having replicated the street of Hyangchon-dong once filled with romance and artists’ spirits in the 1950s, Hyangchon Cultural Center sits on the location where Daegu's first-ever general bank, Seonnam Commercial Bank, had existed in 1912. The bank carried its business as the Daegu Branch of the Commercial Bank of Korea before being transformed into a cultural exhibition hall in 2014 for the preservation of the original downtown area of Daegu. The first and second floors feature a permanent exhibit that shows the yesterday, today and tomorrow of Hyangchon-dong in addition to a planned exhibit and a multi-theme video room.  On the third and fourth floors of the building, you will find an exhibition hall and an experience hall that commemorate the history of Daegu literature. The black tower you see as soon as you enter the entrance signifies the birth of Juksun, a literary coterie magazine published after the Liberation, in Daegu. Writings and faces of some of the famous writers who carried out their literary activities in the city are engraved on the tower. Once you pass the Hyangchon-dong alley where literature and arts were discussed, you will reach the Hall of Fame for several writers from Daegu such as Hyun Jin-geon, Yi Sang-hwa and Yi Jang-hui. On the fourth floor, there is an experience space where you can record a children’s story or a children’s poem on your own and listen to it as well as a space for reading books.  On the basement floor, there is Nokhyang music listening hall. Opened in 1946, Nokhyang was the country's first-ever traditional music listening space. It is said that Nokhyang first started when Yi Chang-su, a member of Yeyukoe, who was looking for a place to gather the group, set up a meeting place underground in Hyangchon-dong and played classical music gramophone that he owned. After the Korean War broke out in 1950 and as artists fled south from all over the nation, the greatest artists of the time from Poet Kim Yo-seop and Composer Kim Dong-jin of Gagopa (“I wish to go”) to Yu Chi-hwan and Shin Dong-jip frequently visited Nokhyang, which naturally served as a meeting place for the artists. Take a seat and enjoy the music playing to feel Nokhyang from the tumultuous but romantic days.   <This guide was recorded by Kang Gyeong-hwa of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Daegu Bukseong-ro Tool Museum
stories.script: Daegu Bukseong-ro Tool Museum  In 1906, Japan tore down the northern fortress of the Daegueupseong Walled Town to establish “Bukseong-ro.” At the time, at Namseong-ro and Seoseong-ro lived many of the Joseon community leaders whereas Dongseong-ro and Bukseong-ro were home to, primarily, Japanese. The presence of Minakai Department Store built by Japanese on Bukseong-ro helped raise the street’s splendor to its zenith. After the Liberation, tool shops and manufacturers relocated from Ingyo-dong to establish the Industrial Tools Street of today. This area also used to have many high-class restaurants and cafes, and, especially after the Korean War, artists who had fled in such a chaotic period gathered together in these cafes to carry out their artistic activities.  Today, there is Bukseong-ro Tool Museum on the street filled with tool shops. The building was used as a rice warehouse in the 1930s, but a tool store was set up here after the Liberation. Once you enter the shop located at a corner, you will see the “Technician's Room” that has reproduced a tool work space. The eye-catching desk and large parts attached to the floor enable you to feel the vibe of the tools district.  If you go up the small stairs in the front, “Tool Box Room” and “Tool Salesman's Room” welcome you. A countless number of parts are neatly organized in shelves that are taller than an average man. Next to the shelves display office supplies that were once actually used by tool merchants like ledgers, desks, chairs and phones as if they have just been utilized.  It will be a unique experience to sit at a tool salesman's chair and look towards the entrance while expecting customers.

stories.title: Police History Experience Hall
stories.script: Police History Experience Hall  Daegu Police has bravely faced any danger and crisis for the wellbeing of Daegu citizens. Here at Daegu Jungbu Police Station, an experience hall is set up where the citizens can learn the history and roles of police in a more familiar manner. The experience hall on the 1st floor of the main building used to be a jail back then. Also on the 1st floor are a costume exhibit hall and a memorial, and the 2nd floor has a history hall, a theater, and a weaponry exhibit hall.  The most popular area in the experience hall is the police costume experience hall and police motorcycle photo zone. Here, you can wear the actual police outfits and hats and take selfies either with Podori and Posooni, the Korean police mascots, or by getting on the motorcycle in the front. Here, we hope that you spend valuable time as you experience and understand various activities of the police and feel more familiar with them to comprehend their efforts and endeavor.

stories.title: Heeum - The Museum of Military Sexual Slavery by Japan
stories.audioTitle: 3. Heeum - The Museum of Military Sexual Slavery by Japan
