stories.script: Heeum - The Museum of Military Sexual Slavery by Japan  Heeum - The Museum of Military Sexual Slavery by Japan is a place that remembers the painful history suffered by “comfort women” who were forced into sexual slavery by the Japanese army. The museum takes a wide variety of actions to resolve the issue in a proper, reasonable way.  Having reconstructed a two-story, Japanese-style wooden building from the mid-1920s, the museum presents the lives of comfort women in greater echoes and tremor through its 90-year-old building and a lilac tree in the courtyard that endured the same cruel period.  A variety of programs are in place at the museum to give more opportunities for the citizens to learn and experience the value of peace and human rights. When you take photos while a program is in progress or during a tour at the museum, remember to focus on the exhibited items and works instead of photographing the victims’ faces.  For your small attention today to blossom as a piece of hope in the future, take as much time as you want in this meaningful place where you can encounter the history that you should never forget.

stories.title: Tree of Choe Je-u in Jongno Elementary School
stories.audioTitle: Tree of Choe Je-u in Jongno Elementary School
stories.script: Past the main gate and between the schoolyard and a playground, there stands a 400-year-old pagoda tree since the days when there was a prison around it.  Choe Je-u (1824–1864) is a national philosopher from Gyeongju. Based on the idea of Innaecheon (Human beings are Heaven), Choe created a national religion of “Donghak,” which was a belief that all men were equal, and spread to many people. As the Joseon government back then believed that such an idea would disturb the public sentiments, it immediately arrested Choe and imprisoned him in the Gyeongsang Gamyeong prison in Daegu.  His execution was decided soon after, and he eventually passed away in nearby Amisan Mountain. This pagoda tree must have witnessed everything that had happened. The tree had probably been very small when Choe Je-u was still alive but, today, it has grown to be taller than the elementary school building and become a nurse-tree.  If you do go see the Tree of Choe Je-u, please check the schoolyard opening hours posted by the main gate before you enter since you will not be able to get inside when the students are still at school.   <This guide was recorded by Kang Gyeong-hwa of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Site of Dalseomun Gate
stories.script: Site of Dalseomun Gate  Dalseomun Gate, which was the west gate among the four gates of the old Daegueupseong Walled Town, was destroyed when Bak Jungyang, a pro-Japan official, tore down the town for Japanese merchants between 1906 and 1907 without the permission of the Korean Empire. At Dalseomun Gate, there had been a gate tower made of a gambrel roof, which has three cells in the front and two cells on the sides, on top of the fortress.  During the Joseon Dynasty, the area used to host one of the three largest markets in Joseon and attract goods from all over the nation. This market by the west gate of the Daegueupseong Walled Town has been relocated to the “Seomun Market” today to continue on its history. Today, only a small sign stone remains on the site.

stories.title: Samsung Trading Company
stories.script: The Samsung Trading Company is the forerunner and the birthplace of the Samsung Group, which has become a global corporation. In 1938, Hoam Lee Byung-chul opened the Samsung Trading Company near Seomun Market. Having made money by exporting Daegu apples and dried seafood of Pohang to Manchuria and China, Lee also made a fortune by founding “Byeolpyo Guksu” in addition to the trading business.  This noodle company was here until the 1960s. At the time, all it had were about a 16.5 m2 office, a small factory, a phone and a noodle machine. Now, there is a bronze replica created in 2001 by reducing the original building to a 1/25 size in commemoration of the Site of Samsung Trading Company as well as a pine tree and bamboo, which represent the spirit of Lee Byung-chul.  It would be a good idea to stop by the house where Hoam lived, which is located nearby.   <This guide was recorded by Kang Gyeong-hwa of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Dalseong Park
stories.script: It was the site of a fortress of a tribal state called Dalgubeol during the Three Hans period. It was also the place where the Dalseong Seo clan lived for generations after the mid-Goryeo Dynasty. The Dalseong Seo clan donated the land to the country during the reign of King Sejong and from then on, it became a state-managed land.  In 1905, a park was first created here by Japan, and in May 1967, the city of Daegu set up a new comprehensive park construction plan and eventually established a grand park that we see today. Dalseong Park currently has a 1,300 m rampart trail, a lawn square, a zoo, and Gwanpungnu Pavilion. It also features the Local History Museum, thus serving as a resting place for Daegu citizens.  On a sunny day, you can take beautiful pictures in a square full of green grass, or go on a date at the zoo and on the trail, which makes the park a popular spot for lovers. Dalseong Park is free of charge, but as the admission hours are limited, please check the hours of operation at the entrance first.   <This guide was recorded by Kang Gyeong-hwa of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Dongsan Cheongna Hill
stories.script: Cheongna Hill has been the center of Christianity since the religion first settled in Daegu and it has grown as today's Keimyung University Dongsan Medical Center which carried out a great deal of community service. The houses of missionaries who had come from overseas to spread Christianity still remain today, which exude an exotic atmosphere.  The House of Switzer, which is being used as Dongsan Medical Missionary Museum and designated as Daegu's Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 24, was built around 1910 and named after Martha Switzer, the American missionary who had lived in the building. The red bricks and a roof made of tiles create a unique vibe. It is also special in that stones from Daegueupseong Fortress were used as cornerstones for the foundation.  The House of Chamness (O.V. Chamness) regained its original form in 2002 through repair and reinforcement work on cultural properties. It is currently used as the Museum of Medicine. Here, you can find medical tools and equipment from the 1890s to the 1900s. Even after Missionary Chamness, many other missionaries continued to live here including Howard F. Moffett who revived Dongsan Hospital.  The House of Chamness appeared in the TV series Bridal Mask as the house of Kimura Shunji (Park Ki-woong) and is also where Yoon-ah was hospitalized in a series called Love Rain. Featured in numerous TV series and films, it shows how beautiful the exterior of the house is while antique furniture and decorations within the house enable us to vividly feel the scenes of life from those days.  Cheongna Hill is also known as the musical setting of a song, Dongmu Saenggak (“Thinking About My Friend”). It is a song composed by Park Tae-jun, the pioneer of Korean modern music, based on his own story of a secret crush he had when he was a student at Keisung Academy in Daegu. Upon listening to Park's story, Poet Yi Eun-sang wrote a poem about it. After adding a melody to the words, a timeless song was born. As the lyrics suggest, Cheongna Hill was covered with green ivy, and it is said that the lily is the girl from Sinmyeong School whom he had a crush on.   <This guide was recorded by Choi Hyun-min of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: March First Independence Movement Road
stories.script: In 1919, the March First Independence Movement, which started in Seoul, spread to Daegu by the afternoon on March 8. Starting from the March First Independence Movement Staircase located to the left of the new building of the First Presbyterian Church of Daegu to the Cheongna Hill, the Independence Movement Road is the path that Daegu students took during the March First Movement to evade the Japanese police. Students and teachers from Keisung Academy, Sinmyeong School and Daegu High School as well as many other citizens marched on this road to gather for the March First Independence Movement.  On one side of the wall, pictures of Daegu taken around that time are exhibited. On the other side, there are fences decorated with Taegeukgi, the Korean national flag, from which you can imagine the Korean flags that the students secretly carried during the movement.  The steps are also known as “90 Stairs” named after the number of the steps. The stairs are not steep, and there is a gentle slope so it wouldn’t be too difficult to climb up if you walk slowly. In summertime, cooling fog is installed at the upper part of the wall to cool down the summer heat. This mist in combination with sunlight often creates small rainbows, which attract many enthusiastic photo-takers.   <This guide was recorded by Choi Hyun-min of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Kyesan Catholic Church
stories.script: Kyesan Catholic Church was built in 1899 as a hanok by Father Achille Paul Robert. However, it was burned down in 1901 and rebuilt in 1902 as a Western-style structure, which is what we see today. The church has been designated as Historic Site No. 290 in recognition of its historical value including beautiful design and a 100-year tradition.  Kyesan Catholic Church, known for its tall twin towers, is also a popular wedding venue due to its antique interior and classic buildings. Inside the building, people wearing hanbok are engraved on stained glass, representing the saints who were martyred during the persecution of Catholics in Joseon period.  The persimmon tree standing next to a wisteria bench between Kyesan Catholic Church and the Cultural Center is called “Lee In-sung Tree.” It got its name from Lee In-sung, a genius painter from Daegu who was active during the Japanese colonial era and even after the Liberation, who depicted the church and a tree together in his paintings.  Kyesan Catholic Church is the oldest of its kind in Gyeongsang-do Province and has existed for over a century as the center of the history of Catholicism not just in Daegu but also in Gyeongsang-do Province.   <This guide was recorded by Choi Hyun-min of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: House of Yi Sanghwa and House of Seo Sangdon, Gyesan Yega
stories.audioTitle: House of Yi Sanghwa and House of Seo Sangdon, Gyesan Yega
stories.script: On the path leading to the House of Poet Yi Sang-hwa from Kyesan Catholic Church, a phrase from his famous poem, Will Spring Come to the Lost Land, is engraved. As you read the poem and enter into the alley, you will reach the house where Yi Sang-hwa, an anti-Japanese artist and poet, lived from 1939 to 1943 just prior to his passing.  Yi kept his artistic spirit alive and carried out remarkable literary work right up to the moment he passed away due to deterioration of his health. Worried that his poetry would influence Joseon people, however, Japanese colonial police confiscated all of his original manuscripts. That’s why Yi is unfortunately remembered as a poet who could not publish a single book of poetry during his lifetime. It was in danger of being demolished recently for development, but thanks to the citizens’ help, the building transformed into a memorial hall that pays respects to Yi's literature. His life and world of creativity are summarized well in the house.  Next to the house, you will find “Gyesan Yega,” a Modern Culture Experience Center. The video room, which plays videos and displays materials related to modern culture, shows the lives and stories of artists who lived in Gyesan-dong. The exhibition hall features videos and chronological tables that show our history divided into the Korean Empire period, Japanese colonial era, the Liberation and the Korean War, and the industrialization era.  On the opposite side of the House of Yi Sanghwa, there stands the House of Seo Sangdon, a national activist who sought to restore the sovereignty of the state through the so-called National Debt Repayment Movement. Born in 1850 in Gimcheon, Seo began to work as a peddler at the age of 17 to eventually earn a great fortune and become a huge landowner. During the Japanese colonial period, he proposed and started the National Debt Repayment Movement, striving to save his country. Just like the House of Yi Sanghwa, the House of Seo was also nearly demolished when high-rise buildings were planning to be built in the area, but thanks to signature-seeking campaigns and sponsorships from the citizens, the house still stands in its location.   <This guide was recorded by Choi Hyun-min of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Mulberry Alley (Du Sachung)
stories.script: Mulberry Alley (Du Sachung)  Du Sachung, a general from Ming dispatched to Joseon during the Japanese invasion of 1592, did not return to his home country even after the war was over. After becoming a naturalized Joseon citizen, the King of Joseon bestowed upon him a land in Daegu, but he gave it away when Gyeongsanggamyeong Provincial Office was established there. He then built a home in the Gyesan-dong area where he and his family made a living by planting mulberry trees. So, even today, this area is known as the Mulberry Alley.  There is a neighborhood in Daegu named Daemyeong-dong”, which originates from “Daemyeong Cheosa”, the name that people called Du Sachung who had longed for Ming.  Among the tales of Du Sachung that are painted on the street walls, his love story is where the expression, “Meet one's loved one as well as pick mulberries”, comes from. One day when Du Sachung and his two naturalized sons were planting mulberry trees, he saw a beautiful woman over the wall of his house and fell lovesick. One of his sons who caught his father’s romantic feelings for the woman spoke to her. It turns out that the woman had lost her husband at a young age and was interested in Du Sachung as well. This tale ultimately ends in a happily-ever-after.  The story of Daemyeong Cheosa Du Sachung who settled down in Joseon is still told on this mulberry alley to show his traces.

stories.title: Oriental Medicine and Ecological Wellbeing Experience Center
stories.audioTitle: 6. Oriental Medicine and Ecological Wellbeing Experience Center
stories.script: Oriental Medicine and Ecological Wellbeing Experience Center  For about two years from October 2012 to June 2014, a project was commenced to remodel the former Lee Hae Young Orthopedic Surgery Hospital building. The building was refurbished into Oriental Medicine and Ecological Wellbeing Experience Center, a resting place during every visitor’s modern street tour.  Built in 1966, the old hospital building featured a white appearance, large windows, and a unique shape of the roof railings, and many at the time regarded the building as the most modern hospital building in Daegu. Traces of the inner and outer walls, balcony, chimney, and stairs have been preserved to display the spatial characteristics of the time.  After the remodeling, the first floor features the Eco Exhibition Hall that talks about the climate, environment, and future of mankind. Visitors can play games related to the environment, learn about the changing environment, and take part in country-wide efforts to reduce CO2 emissions. The 2nd floor has “Healing Time” and Herb Gallery. At Herb Gallery, you can check out various herbs used in oriental medicine while at Healing Time, you can take a rest for your weary body during the tour.  There is also a traditional teahouse on the 1st floor outside, and the kiosk tells you various herbal tea that suits you. It would be great to stop by here to regain your energy and get ready to move to the next location!

stories.title: Former First Presbyterian Church of Daegu
stories.audioTitle: Former First Presbyterian Church of Daegu
stories.script: This is the old chapel building of the First Presbyterian Church of Daegu, which is designated as Daegu's Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 30. Since the construction of a new chapel in 1994, this building has been used as a mission house and an exhibition hall.  The Church evolved from Namseong Church, the first Christian church established in Daegu and Gyeongsangbuk-do region in 1893. At first, it purchased a tile-roofed house to hold services, but as the number of believers and the scale of the church increased, it eventually built a new, two-story church in 1908. In 1933, it newly constructed a red-brick chapel and in 1936, a bell tower was installed to complete the look we see today. In particular, it is said that some of the stones used for the stylobate of the building came from Daegueupseong Fortress, which had been torn down in 1907.  The first floor of the building, currently used as an exhibition hall, displays many relics and artifacts that tell the history of the church. You will be able to check out items that the churchgoers and missionaries at the time actually used and walls that show the history of suffering.   <This guide was recorded by Choi Hyun-min of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Daegu Yangnyeongsi Oriental Medicine Museum
stories.script: First established during the Joseon Dynasty (1658, the 9th year of King Hyojong’s reign), Daegu Yangnyeongsi is one of the nation’s three largest marketplaces specializing in oriental medicinal herbs and ingredients. To preserve, inherit and advance the culture of Korean traditional medicine of the nation's oldest Yangnyeongsi Market, the “Permanent Exhibition Hall of Oriental Medicine” was opened on the second floor of the National Federation of Fisheries Cooperatives Namdaegu branch, located at Yakjeon Alley, on September 25, 1985.  The exhibition hall on the third floor starts from the Bullomun Gate, which is the gate with the meaning that “if you walk past this gate, you will live forever.” The exhibition offers scenes from the Yangnyeongsi Market in the Joseon Dynasty through animations and oriental medicine pharmacies replicated in actual sizes. In addition, the chronology of the Yangnyeongsi Market continues from the floor of the entrance to the walls, giving you a feeling that you are going back in time.  On the second floor, there is an Oriental Medicine Hands-On Experience Zone where you can learn about the difficult concepts of oriental medicine in an easy-to-understand manner through various experiences. You can get diagnosis by the great Heo Jun, and in the Oriental Wellbeing Experience Hall, you can learn about ways to stay healthy that can be applied in your everyday life.   <This guide was recorded by Choi Hyun-min of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Yeongnam-daero
stories.script: There was a road called Yeongnam-daero behind Yeommae Market and Hyundai Department Store in the Joseon Dynasty. Yeongnam-daero was one of the nine principal roads in the Joseon Dynasty that ran from Dongnaepo, Busan to Hanyang (Seoul). It was also a famous route that scholars living in the Yeongnam region took on their way to Hanyang for state examinations.  During the Joseon period, Yeongnam-daero in Daegu was an important road since it was possible to get to Yangnyeongsi Market and Seomun Market, which were formed around the fortress. This enabled people to visit pharmacies where they could get treatment, taverns for food and drinks, and clothing or shoe stores where they could purchase items they needed on the way to Hanyang. It is said that peddlers also bought and sold goods on Yeongnam-daero, and all the successful merchants in Daegu went through this route.  Today, murals and trick art about Yeongnam-daero are drawn throughout the street for people to remember and reminisce the old Yeongnam-daero. Take a picture with kings, vassals and scholars whom you may have seen somewhere before, and set out on a journey to the past.   <This guide was recorded by Choi Hyun-min of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Daegu Jongno
stories.script: Daegu Jongno  The name, Jongno, means the street with Jonggak (or belfry), and places of the same name exist in Seoul and Suwon as well. Once the center of Daegu downtown during the Joseon Dynasty, Jongno was home of Gyeongsanggamyeong Provincial Office and Yeongnamjeilgwan, the south gate of Daegueupseong Walled Town. Also, as Jongno was close to Jin Alley, a wealthy neighborhood, and Yakjeon Alley on Namseong-ro, it served as the city center that saw many people come and go every day.  In particular, an immense amount of cash dealt in Yakjeon Alley (Yangnyeongsi Market) flowed into the area, which led to many entertainment establishments such as high-class restaurants and gisaeng call offices. Overseas Chinese have moved since 1905 and reside in this neighborhood until present.  From 1950s to 1970s, carpentry and furniture workshops were established here and thrived, and then hardware stores and safe shops came into the area to add to the vigor. However, as large furniture manufacturers emerged, furniture stores on Jongno faced a decline.  Jongno in Daegu is the setting of “House with a Sunken Courtyard”, a famous novel by Kim Won-il, and, in fact, there are paintings and statues in places where the main character of the novel, Gil-nam, could have been. In particular, Gil-nam's mother carrying a baby and Gil-nam sitting on a bench and looking onto the street are great spots to take photos.

stories.title: Jingolmok Alley
stories.script: Jingolmok is a name derived from the term, “jilda,” of Gyeongsang-do provincial dialect, which means gilda, meaning “long” in standard language. The alley existed since the Joseon period and at the time, many of the local leaders of Daegu lived in the area. It was also known as place where Seo Byeong-guk, a wealthy local of Dalseong, Daegu, and his brothers and sisters lived together. However, as they left the area one after another, the houses on this alley were then used by the Chinese Residents Association, Jeong Pediatrics and a restaurant.  Mido Dabang, which was nicknamed as “Yangban Dabang” because of frequent visits by scholars, still maintains the original form of a traditional teahouse, a thing of rarity today. That’s why it is a popular meeting place for the elderly and artists. Nowadays, young tourists often stop by to experience traditional teahouse. A wall of Mido Dabang has a poem titled Mido Dahyang, which was written by Poet Jeon Sang-yeol in admiration of this place.  The building of “Jeong Pediatrics” was the city’s first-ever Western-style structure built by private capital in 1937. It was the house of Seo Byeong-jik, a wealthy man from Daegu. Dr. Jeong Pil-su purchased it in 1947 to use as his own clinic. Many Daegu locals used this clinic insomuch that it makes an appearance in the novel, The House with a Sunken Courtyard, which depicts the lives and scenes of Daegu before and after the Korean War. The building itself has gone through nearly zero changes or deformations, which makes it an essential modern structure for us to understand the residential culture of the upper class families during the Japanese colonial era. The house features curved walls, sunlight room on the first floor, Western-style bathtub and many other elements from which we can learn about how the wealthy lived in those days and what kind of modern architectural technology was used.  Today, the actual length of the alley is only about 100 m but it has still kept the name, Jingolmok, because the time that has been embraced by this street is not short at all. Try to feel the life that people carried in those days on this path, and immerse yourselves in the charm of Jingolmok Alley.   <This guide was recorded by Choi Hyun-min of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Daegu Korean Chinese Association (Overseas Chinese Primary School)
stories.audioTitle: Daegu Korean Chinese Association (Overseas Chinese Primary School)
stories.script: The history of overseas Chinese is captured in Jong-ro, Daegu. Overseas Chinese refer to people from China who settled in a foreign country. In modern times, overseas Chinese found economic stability through draper, construction, and food businesses, created schools and established a residents’ association, forming a society for the overseas Chinese community.  In front of the entrance of the Chinese Association building is Gilnam, the main character in the novel House with a Sunken Courtyard. Pass the entrance are the yellow-colored primary school building and bright red bricks that form the Chinese Association building. Originally built in 1929, the Chinese Association building was both the home and office of a wealthy Korean named Seo Byeong-guk. After his death, the Chinese Association bought the building and built the Overseas Chinese Primary School on the opposite side. Although more than 80 years has passed since the establishment of the Chinese Association building, it is very well preserved and thus registered as Korea’s National Registered Cultural Heritage No. 252.  The Chinese Association and Overseas Chinese Primary School is still in operation today and visitors may enter the area on weekdays after 3:30 PM. Visiting before 3:30 PM is allowed outside the buildings as long as visitors do not interrupt the classes.   <This guide was recorded by Choi Hyun-min of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Daejeongseong Fortress Site, Seogwipo-si, Jeju-do
stories.script: During the Joseon Dynasty, Jeju's administrative districts were divided into Jejumok, Jeonguihyeon and Daejeonghyeon, the last of which used to be right here in today's Daejeong-eup. Daejeongeupseong Fortress, which encompassed Daejeonghyeon, was constructed in the 18th year of King Taejong’s reign with a 1,481 m circumference and a 3.3 m height. It installed pavilions on the east, west and south gates as well as a total of 10 beacons for communication. Inside the fortress, there once were Confucian schools, guesthouses, shrines, magistrate's offices, jail cells and other government-related facilities, all of which only remain as a site now. Today's Boseong Elementary School sits on the site of the magistrate's office while the historical site of Chusa is where the east gate and a jail cell used to be.  You can also find Dol Hareubang on the side of the streets. Four Dol Hareubangs each were installed in front of the east, west and south gates of the fortress. The term “Dol Hareubang” began to be used as a name of the cultural asset in 1971 and up to that point, it had been called as Useongmok, Museongmok or Beoksumeori. Currently, 12 Dol Hareubangs exist in Daejeong-eup; the one in front of the Memorial House of Chusa wears a scarf while the one at Boseong Elementary wears a simple-looking hat.  Daejeongeupseong Fortress is being continuously being restored. The fortress walls that have been restored are 1,260 m in length, and the large stone wall that you see next to the Memorial House of Chusa is actually a part of the fortress. As you walk along the Chusa Exile Trail, check out the fortress walls as well.  Daejeongseong Fortress Site is designated as Jeju Special Self Governing Province's Monument No. 12.

stories.title: Chusa Exile Trail
stories.script: There are a total of three courses on Chusa Exile Trail.  Course 1, also known as the “Road to Tenacity,” is a 6.7-km-long village road that starts from the Memorial House of Chusa and passes the House of Kang Do-sun where Chusa lived in exile, the Songjuksa Site, the Site of Song Gye-sun's House, Deuremul, the site of a modern school named Hannamuisuk, the Tomb of Mary Jeong Nan-ju, Nammunjimot Pond, Dansan Mountain and Stone Pagoda, and Semimul before ending the journey at Daejeonghyanggyo Local Confucian School. As it goes from where Chusa lived in exile to the Confucian school, it is indeed a local road on which Chusa probably traveled frequently every day.  Course 2, also known as the “Road to Human Relationships,” is an 8-km-long road that also starts from the Memorial House of Chusa and passes the Suworimot Pond, a park where you can enjoy the poems composed by Chusa, Jeju Onggi Museum, Pyeonji Stone Pagoda, Gotjawal, and finally the Osulloc Tea Plantation.  Course 3, the “Road to Contemplation,” is a 10.1-km-long road that starts from the Daejeonghyanggyo Local Confucian School and ends at Sanbangsan Mountain. It goes around the mountain and offers great views of the trees, the sea and different flowers that blossom every season. It is said that Chusa actually walked this road with his pupils and took a stroll to Andeok Valley in Seogwipo.

stories.title: Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School
stories.script: There is Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School underneath the Dansan Mountain that resembles a bat with its wings spread out wide. It was initially constructed within Daejeongheon in the 16th year of King Taejong's reign. After having been relocated a few times, it finally settled in this location in the 4th year of King Hyojong's reign.  When you look at this Confucian school, a black basalt wall will catch your eye. It is the typical image of Jeju. Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall where students studied and Dongjae and Seojae Dormitories are located in the front while Daeseongjeon Shrine, which enshrines sages, is at the back. In addition, the lecture hall and the shrine are built in a way that they are at different heights.  Next to the Sammun Gate, there are huge Japanese hackberry and pine trees, which follow the tradition of planting the Samgangoryunmok trees at a place that enshrines Confucius. Among them, the pine tree is known to be the model for Sehando, which is why it is also referred to as the “Sehansong.” Whether or not it really is the model for the painting, if you look at it after seeing Sehando in the Memorial House of Chusa, you may feel as though the two trees look alike.  Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall has a plaque that says “Uimundang” written by Chusa himself, meaning “Never cease to doubt and ask questions in your studies.” The plaque here at the Confucian school is a replica while the original is on display at the Memorial House of Chusa.  Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School is designated as Local Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 4.

stories.title: Sanbang Beacon
stories.script: At the roadside in front of Sanbangsan Mountain in Sagye-ri, there stands Sanbang Beacon. It was used as a means of national defense and communication during the Joseon Dynasty, delivering urgent political or military news with torchlight or smoke. Unlike the typical beacons that are often installed at the top of a mountain, this one is installed on a hill. In Jeju, you will find these types of beacons in pretty much every beach you go. In the early Joseon Dynasty, there were 39 of them in Jeju and then 30 by the 19th century.  Commonly referred to as “Yeondi Dongsan,” Sanbang Beacon was built in the 19th year of King Sejong’s reign (1437) in preparation for Japanese invasions. It is said that six byeoljangs and 12 bongguns of Daejeonghyeon were stationed here and divided into six groups, each of which guarded the coastline five days a month. It communicated with Dangpo Beacon about 5.7 km away to the east and Musu Beacon about 6 km to the west. Much of it was destroyed during the Korean War in 1950 and only left some stones on the ground. It was restored in 2000 to what we see today. It is surrounded by protective walls. In its middle, a large, rectangular brazier is installed and stairs are set up to the south.  Sanbang Beacon is Jeju Special Self-Governing Province's Monument No. 23-21.

stories.title: Andeok Valley, Seogwipo
stories.script: This is Andeok Valley of Seogwipo where stories say that Chusa came sightseeing with his pupils.  Andeok means “cozy and comfortable” in Korean. Rocks and cliffs of unique shapes stand like a folding screen and a thickly wooded warm-temperate forest holds the valley in its arms while the ground is a bedrock, which adds to the mystical vibe of the valley. On the way to the valley, there is a cave in which primitive men once lived, meaning that the area was a great place to live even in the prehistoric ages.  We must be especially careful here in regard to protection of nature. The valley, which is designated as Natural Monument No. 377, has rare plants such as whisk ferns, Korean hornbeams and horned hollies as well as a thickly wooded evergreen forest with over 300 different species including Itajii chinkapins, evergreen oaks, silver  magnolias, muku trees and camellias, not to mention many pteridophytes.   How about staying here quietly while becoming a student of Chusa who let go of all greed, talked poetry and meditated?

stories.title: Osulloc Tea Museum
stories.script: Explore the Osulloc Tea Museum and its captivating garden, with the entire building resembling the shape of a teacup. This is where you can immerse yourself in everything related to Sulloc Tea, delving into the world of green tea and traditional Korean tea culture.  Osulloc Tea Museum was first established on September 1st, 2001, serving as a cultural space and nature-friendly rest area. The ‘O’ in ‘Osulloc’ signifies an exclamation and stands for ‘origin of sulloc,’ ‘only sulloc,’ and ‘of sulloc tea.’ The museum is renowned for its harmonious blend of Eastern and Western cultures, seamlessly combining tradition with modernity.  The first exhibition room houses about 130 artifacts dating between the 4th and the 19th centuries. It displays approximately 30 ceramic artists and 70 teacups from China, Japan, and Europe.  Upon entering the Tea Cup Gallery, you can immerse yourself in the rich history of Korean tea culture, the global propagation routes and the art of tea making. The gallery leads to a coffee shop where you can enjoy warm cups of tea, ice cream, and roll cakes.  Don’t miss the ‘O Observatory.’ Here, you can take in the scenic views of sprawling Seogwang Dawon Tea Plantation just outside, providing a smoothing experience for your mind and legs.

stories.title: Tea Stone
stories.script: Tea Stone was designed by Architect Cho Min-suk who was inspired by Chusa Kim Jeong-hui. Do you notice that the color of the building is charcoal black? It was designed in this way to remind its visitors of the inkstone of Chusa who had had a great influence on Jeju tea culture. The building contains the story of Chusa creating his unique calligraphic style of Chusache after making holes on 10 inkstones and wearing out thousands of brushes. It was named Tea Stone and “stone” here refers to an inkstone.  Concrete and glass windows hold a contrast of opacity and transparency and warmth and coldness. Such a clear contrast is gently covered by the wooden roof. The interior also has charcoal black walls, and the outside seen through the window is green with flowers, trees and water in harmony. Hong Dong-hee, a Western-style painter who was in charge of the interior design, is said to have been fascinated by the tea culture himself. Indeed, Hong has created a great atmosphere to drink tea.  Tea culture experience classes are held in here. It’s a 50-minute program hosted by tea masters. It will be a special experience of encountering our tea in a place that features premium teaware and diligently roasted organic tea amid the beautiful scenery.

stories.title: Innisfree Jeju House
stories.script: Innisfree Jeju House is the one that will make you feel the greatest openness among the three buildings that stand side by side. It is the work of Cho Min-suk who also designed the Tea Stone. Whereas the Tea Stone is finished in a dark tone, Innisfree Jeju House seems to exude a more natural and bright vibe. A wood shingle roof is laid, but at the same time, it allows the beautiful sunlight of Jeju to be reflected. The stone wall at the entrance reminds of the wall of a typical Jeju stone house. In addition, the natural connection between the inside and the outside through a large window also shows the nature-friendliness by the architect.  The architect was already fascinated by the beautiful Seogwang Dawon Tea Plantation and Gotjawal, and wanted to create a comfortable and harmonious building that did not go against these sites. Therefore, the structure was completed so that nature, not the building, takes the center stage.  What is also meaningful is that it uses solar energy sources with photovoltaic equipment based on fundamental principles of eco-friendly construction and recycling in architecture and design. Here, you can taste beverages and food made of Jeju ingredients,   experience Innisfree indirectly through fragrance-tasting of natural ingredients, or sit at a desk and make soap on your own. Even if you don't do anything in particular, it will be a delightful trip just walking on the lawn.

stories.title: Sulloccha Green Tea R&D Center
stories.script: There is Sulloccha Green Tea R&D Center on one side of Seogwang Dawon Tea Plantation. This is a factory and an R&D center of AmorePacific. It was designed by Sun Eun-soo, one of the leading architects of Jeju. The building area is 2,832 ㎡ and the total floor space is 3,423 ㎡. It is a three-story structure made of iron frames and ferroconcrete, and its exterior uses Merbau, which is a premium type of wood.  Sulloccha Green Tea R&D Center went through two extensions. A powder tea factory was built during the first extension and an R&D center was added through the second extension. The assignment through the two extensions was to naturally connect the factory and the research building. In the office building, the office space is set up on the front for lighting and viewing of Seogwang Dawon Tea Plantation, and in the section that connects to the existing factory, service facilities and main stairs are installed.  Sulloccha Green Tea R&D Center offers field trip tours on a non-regular basis. On this tour, visitors can check out products of AmorePacific on display and understand the products and production processes.  Sulloccha Green Tea R&D Center won an award at the 2008 Korean Architecture Awards.

stories.title: Seogwang Dawon Tea Plantation
stories.script: The name of the tea field you see now is Seogwang Dawon, which is the largest tea production field in Korea. Your heart will feel open and calm just looking at the field that spreads out under the Namsongi Parasitic Cone. It is the broadest and the largest tea plantation in the country. In fact, this area used to part of Gotjawal until the 1970s.  The tea plantation that has become Jeju’s best attraction for landscape agriculture is the result of an entrepreneur’s will. Late Seo Seong-hwan, the founder of AmorePacific, once thought that Jeju climate is great for tea production, so he decided to cultivate a tea plantation here by bringing soil, making compost with pig manure to improve the earth, planting windbreak forests to block winds and drawing water to achieve a miracle over 793,388 m2.  It is now one of the nation’s leading tea-producing areas along with Hadong-gun, Gyeongsangnam-do Province and Boseong-gun, Jeollanam-do Province. It is also a popular filming location for many TV series, movies and commercials.  Since you’re here, try taking the best photo of your life. When sprinklers are running, you would be able to take a unique photo with fresh spray of water.

stories.title: Jeju Green Tea Land
stories.script: Jeju Green Tea Land is a traditional tea garden that produces, processes and sells green tea. It is the first private green tea plantation designated by the Jeju Special Self-Governing Province. In the late 1990s, a land of about 231,404 m2 of a tangerine plantation began to be developed as tea fields, becoming a tea plantation of what we see today. It was also a notable case in which green tea was grown as an alternative crop in tangerine plantations.  Jeju Green Tea Land is currently operated as a green tea theme park. There is a green tea maze built by green tea trees that are as tall as a person. Finding your way out from here won't be as easy as you think. In addition, there are trails such as Olle Course, Saitgil Course and Dullegil Course on which you can enjoy a 30 to 90-minute walk. The green tea plantation observatory can't be missed out on. If you look down upon the green tea field, which is located at about 500 m above sea level, from a slightly higher ground, you will be able to get a wide open view of Munseom, Beomseom and Marado Islands as well as Dansan and Sanbangsan Mountains together with the tea plantation.  As this is a tea plantation, don’t forget to have a cup of tea here, a handmade leaf tea roasted in an iron pot with deep flavor.

stories.title: Seogwi Dawon Tea Plantation
stories.script: If you are a traveler in Jeju, you would probably have one or two hidden places that only you know about. From today on, Seogwi Dawon Tea Plantation will be on the list of your secret travel spots. It has no special attractions and the size is not that big, but it is known as a tea field that you can’t help but visit again.  In the 66,000 ㎡ green tea plantation, cedar and camellia trees form a windbreak forest, and a scenery of basalt fragments and rows of green tea will captivate your heart. The stone walls and stone towers stacked around the plantation are unique. These stones had originally been underground when the tea fields were being cultivated. Overall, the tea plantation looks much more three-dimensional because they have slopes and curves like low hills. The picturesque tea field and a small tea room with Hallasan Mountain seen in the distance is a scenery that is nowhere to be found.  This actually used to be a tangerine farm for more than 30 years before being cultivated into a tea garden in 2005. If you are lucky, you may meet the owner and share a good time over a cup of good tea.

stories.title: Seogwipo Performance Art Theater
stories.script: This is Seogwipo Performance Art Theater, which you can enter after passing through a small ticket office. It opened in 1963 as an exclusive film theater with 667 seats over a 240 ㎡ area. But it hasn’t played movies only; it has also hosted various cultural events of Seogwipo from presentations and speaking contests for nearby elementary schools to performances by pop singers and musical group and even an invitational event of Ahn Eak-tai who composed the Korean national anthem. It is indeed a place filled with nostalgia of the local elderly.  In 1973, a short circuit caused injuries for over 100 people, which led to an indefinite closure of business ordered by the provincial authorities. Later, the ban was lifted and it kept its role as a neighborhood theater before it went out of business for good in 1999. It was even on the verge of becoming demolished as the building collapsed once, but after remodeling in 2012, it was transformed into an arts performance hall that maintained the collapsed ceiling as it was, reopening as an outdoor theater. The front where the screen was installed is a wonderful stage with black Jeju rocks exposed, and through the ivy-filled windows, you can see Lee Jung Seop Art Museum nearby and Seopseom Island in the distance. Seopseom is famous for its appearance in Scenery With Seopseom Island in the Distance, a work of Lee Jung-seop.  The theater hosts various performances and the lobby of the theater holds exhibits from time to time as well as experience programs on weekends.

stories.title: Lee Jung-seop Residence and Lee Jung-seop Park
stories.audioTitle: Lee Jung-seop Residence and Lee Jung-seop Park
stories.script: Happy Road of Lee Jung-seop — Lee Jung-seop Residence and Lee Jung-seob Park   This small room, which was restored in September 1997, is where Lee Jung-seop and his family used to live. He fled from Busan to Seogwipo during the Korean War, and the family of four had to live in a 4.6 m2 room in a warehouse. They stayed in Jeju for 11 months and later became forever separated in Busan.  He gave his wife, Masako, a Korean name of Lee Nam-deok. It is said that the couple called each other by nicknames of “Agori” and “Mr. Toe.” The way his family is portrayed in his countless works tells us how much he loved his family and how much he valued the time he spent with them. Many critics also say that this period was the spiritually richest and the happiest time in his life. In addition, it is said that the works in which he expressed his dreams for utopia were influenced by his days in Jeju.  His wife, Lee Nam-deok, visited the site for the restoration of his birthplace in 1997, for the establishment of the museum in 2002, and for the palette donation ceremony in 2012. The residence leads to Lee Jung Seop Art Museum and a small park along the alley. On Lee Jung Seop Street, you can find younger artists’ works that commemorate Lee, including Dream of Lee Jung-seop by Kim Bum-soo and A Family Setting Off by Song Jae-kyung.

stories.title: Gidang Art Museum
stories.script: Seogwipo Art Travel — Gidang Art Museum   Gidang Art Museum opened on July 1, 1987 and became Jeju’s first municipal museum in 1988, which made it the first-ever municipal museum in the country. It was established by Gidang Kang Gu-beom, a Korean-Japanese businessman who was originally from Jeju. He later donated the museum to the city of Seogwipo.  It has a permanent exhibition of the works of late Byun Shi-ji (the first honorary director of the museum) dubbed the “artist of the storm.” It also owns around 660 paintings, sculptures, crafts, prints and calligraphic works from Korea and overseas.

stories.title: Seogwipo Chilsimni Poetry Park
stories.script: Seogwipo Art Travel — Seogwipo Chilsimni Poetry Park  This is a “poetry” park of Seogwipo. There are 16 monuments on which poems or songs about Seogwipo are engraved, all of which were written by Kim Chun-su, Lee Dong-ju, Park Nam-su and other senior authors or writers who have passed away. There are many things that would make you pause on the way to the poetry monument.  First is Saeseom Observatory. Along with Seogwipo Port, Seyeongyo Bridge is seen to the right and to the left, Saeseom, Munseom, Beomseom and Seopseom Islands are seen in a row. The blue sea and sky are beautiful during the day and reflection of lights is gorgeous around sunset while the night view of Seyeongyo Bridge greets us with a splendid look in the evening. This is one of the few nightscape spots in Jeju.  Many people take pictures at the pergola pond where a mirror is installed. Jeju's sky is reflected on the water while the travelers are reflected on the mirror located on the other side over a stepping-stone. The entire scene creates a marvelous atmosphere.  The highlight is the Cheonjiyeon Falls Observatory. Typically, a waterfall is viewed upward from below but here, you can look down upon the Cheonjiyeon Falls. How the water falls over a cliff filled with trees and plants is a spectacle like that of a jungle in Africa. As you look up, you will be able to see a beautiful scenery created by Hallasan Mountain and Cheonjiyeon Falls.

stories.title: Soam Memorial Hall
stories.script: Seogwipo Art Travel — Soam Memorial Hall   This is a place that commemorates Soam Hyeon Jung-hwa, a renowned calligrapher from Seogwipo. It was built in Jobeom Sanbang where Soam resided and worked. It officially opened on October 4, 2008, designed by Kim Sang-eon and Hyeon Gun-chul  in a way that it does not go against a steep slope, and thus form a natural harmony with the environment. It has one underground and two ground floors with a total floor space of 1,523 ㎡. The overall exterior looks quite modern but the interior space and design exude the vibe of old architecture.  Soam is originally from Beophwan-dong, Seogwipo. He went to study in Japan at the age of 18 and learned a variety of calligraphic styles. Later, he mixed Yukjohae and Haengchoseo and added an aesthetic sense to develop his own unique style of calligraphy. The memorial hall features two permanent exhibitions that well explain his world of works as well as one planned exhibition and Jobeom Sanbang. In particular, the first floor of Jobeom Sanbang has a variety of relics on display, and on the second floor, artifacts from the days when Soam carried his private and artistic lives here have been preserved and exhibited in their original appearances. The art museum also hosts memorial exhibitions in commemoration of Soam as well as art lectures for citizens and students.  It is the country's first-ever private art museum of a calligrapher. It even won the grand award in the Completed Building category at the 2008 Jeju Architecture Awards.

stories.title: Jaguri Cultural Park
stories.script: Seogwipo Art Travel — Jaguri Cultural Park The first thing you will notice at the Jaguri Cultural Park is a large hand that is drawing on paper. This is an installation artwork titled Drawing Crab and Children by Artist Jeong Mi-jin. What's drawn on this work is Crab and Children by Lee Jung-seop, so these hands must be his. Jaguri Beach is known as the place where Lee Jung-seop went out with his family to catch crabs and appease their hunger. This scene is expressed vividly in several works of Lee including Beloved Jeju Scenes and Crab and Children.  In addition, there are sculptures by other artists such as Silk Road: Wind Path by Song Pil and Art Pergola by Ko Jung-soon. This is because the park not only is a trail that Lee Jung-seop loved but also part of the Utopia Trail. In particular, Art Pergola is a work and a rest area that embody Teu, a traditional Jeju boat, and Mangsari, a device used by haenyeo, or female diver. On the ground, there is the work called Culture Story Walked on Foot, which was created by over 150 calligraphers.  As you walk down along a trail, a fresh water beach with spring water adjoins the sea. In summertime, many locals come to dip their feet in the clean and cold spring water.

stories.title: Wal Chong Art Museum
stories.script: Seogwipo Art Travel — Wal Chong Art Museum  This is a house that holds the dream of a painter. The designer and architect of the building is Lee Wal-chong himself who had come to Jeju for the artistic works. Lee later made the workshop of his dream into pottery. Architects Han Man-won and David Macculo refined the design for two years, and Lee tore down his workshop to build a house in its place. Finally, just like the pottery, Wal Chong Art Museum, which resembles a Joseon porcelain, was completed.  A lot of windows are installed in the building to enable visitors to enjoy artworks without artificial lighting, and the light coming through the ceiling windows makes paintings look more three-dimensional. The first floor features a storage, pottery room and children's art classroom, and the second floor has an exhibition hall while the third floor consists of the artist's workspace. There is also a small rest area on the rooftop garden alongside pottery works.  The view from here includes the Castle of Shell. Lee was a close friend to the late Kim Cheol-ho, the owner of the Castle of Shell. When Kim suddenly passed away in 1998 from cerebral hemorrhage, it is said that Lee hung a picture of his friend in his room for a year and burned incense. Prior to that, he actually couldn't find an incense burner that he wanted so he set up a pottery kiln in his workshop to make it on his own. This is why the art museum has as many incense burners as paintings.

stories.title: Gidang Art Museum
stories.script: Gidang Art Museum opened on July 1, 1987 and became Jeju’s first municipal museum in 1988, which made it the first-ever municipal museum in the country. It was established by Gidang Kang Gu-beom, a Korean-Japanese businessman who was originally from Jeju. He later donated the museum to the city of Seogwipo.  It has a permanent exhibition of the works of late Byun Shi-ji (the first honorary director of the museum) dubbed the “artist of the storm.” It also owns around 660 paintings, sculptures, crafts, prints and calligraphic works from Korea and overseas.

stories.title: Seogwi Jungang Girls' Middle School (Former College of Agriculture of Jeju National University)
stories.audioTitle: Seogwi Jungang Girls' Middle School (Former College of Agriculture of Jeju National University)
stories.script: Built in 1971, this building is a work of Kim Jung-eop, a master of Korean architecture. Today, it is Seogwi Jungang Girls' Middle School but it once housed the Department of Fisheries, College of Agriculture of Jeju National University.  Shall we take a look at the building? What grabs our attention before anything else is the western surface, especially the shade, which is attached to the windows to prevent sunlight or rain from coming directly into the inside. On days with strong sunshine, shadows created by the shade look like an abstract work of art. This also serves to alleviate the strong sunlight in the afternoon. The windows on the front are very unique as well. They all have different sizes like a typical Mondrian’s work. There is nothing ordinary about this place, from stairs to entrances. As you calmly look at one surface after another, you will realize that it is impossible to predict other sides from the current angle.  Kim Jung-eop was born in Pyongyang and studied architecture at Yokohama Industrial School, which is today's Yokohama National University. After the Liberation, he became a lecturer at Seoul National University and in 1952, he attended the 1st International Conference of Artists, which was held in Venice, Italy, as a representative of Korea. This turned out to be a fateful event because at the conference, Kim met Le Corbusier, a globally renowned master in architecture, and ended up studying and working at his architecture institute for four years until 1955. After his return to Korea, he produced a few artworks while living and working in Jeju. One of the works that still remains today is Former College of Agriculture of Jeju National University, which is what you're looking at right now.  As we encounter his aesthetic sense that does not fade or regress over time, we realize how Kim Jung-eop is an architectural virtuoso who transcends generations.

stories.title: Seogwipo Miracle Library
stories.script: This children library has pine trees at its heart, which is a work of Architect Jung Gi-yong.  Its construction was completed in 2004. It is actually related to an MBC TV show called Exclamation Mark! that aired from 2003. The show started a nationwide movement to read books and even led to formation of a civic organization named Movement to Create Reading Society. It also selected a city where a small children's library was going to be built. Seogwipo was chosen in the end and Architect Jung Gi-yong took the job.  Having various nicknames such as the architect of sympathy, the poet of spaces and a public service worker in architecture, Jung successfully carried out an epitome of collaboration. He led a process of integrating opinions of an architect and civic organizations while stubbornly holding onto his principle of keeping the trees in the surroundings intact and undamaged. As a result, the structure was completed while maintaining the pine tree colony, which had been at risk of destruction. This is how the inner courtyard of the library hugs a pine forest. Pine trees are great for children's emotions and sentiments, and natural lighting that falls through the tree branches also provides a nice reading environment.  The Miracle Library won the 2004 Seogwipo Chilsimni Architecture Award. It is considered as a wonderful example of a civic movement, democracy production process and a model for children.

stories.title: Former Castle of Shell
stories.script: The building you see is a work of art that is most certainly believed to have been designed by Kim Jung-eop. Evidence lies in the method of how the curves are finished and usage of architectural materials, both of which has elements that are unique to Kim Jung-eop. Though it is still a strong assumption, not many architects were capable of completing a work like this in the 1960s. If it is indeed a work of Kim Jung-eop, it has great significance since it is perhaps the only work of his that has kept its original shape and look to this day.  Built in 1969, it is most widely believed to have been built as a dormitory for the president's guards since there is a vacation home of former President Park Chung-hee nearby. Considering how the designer and the purpose of the building are still unclear due to security reasons, the anonymity behind the creator of this artwork seems quite convincing.  The building has no specific name so it is still called by the name of the restaurant that was once in business here. The most distinct element of the design is the aesthetic beauty of curves that wind and turn. The visibly protruded section on the second floor reminds you of Gaudí's architecture, and the falling columns and interior curves, which seem to break in between but still run without pause, gently wrap the space and softly continue. It is open without any doors but the inside and the outside are divided, which shows a unique and interesting twist. Round pebbles on the exterior walls show a sense of wit and meticulousness.  If you've come up to the roof after looking around the building, don't forget to enjoy the beautiful scenery of the Seogwipo sea.

stories.title: Shinyoung Cinema Museum
stories.script: This is the country's first-ever cinema museum that opened its doors in 1999. It is a place filled with the passion of Shin Young-kyun, a veteran actor, for films. It was designed by Architect Kim Seok-cheol who is known as the designer of the Seoul Arts Center and a pupil of masters Kim Jung-eop and Kim Su-geun.  When viewed from the outside, the museum looks very familiar; the entire building looks like a huge camera. But the motif behind the design, as explained by the architect, is DNA that symbolizes life. When you step inside, opening and closing continue naturally, and artificial lighting, natural lighting, closed spaces and open spaces intersect as well. As Kim once said, “It’s my first time in a long time to make a drawing without a ruler,” the building shows a very organic form only consisted of free curves. It won the Gold Award in the Outstanding Architectural Works category at the Asian Congress of Architects.  The museum narrates the 100-year history of Korean film. Here, you can check out great actors in history, beloved movie characters to this day, films that attracted over 10 million viewers, old cameras, films and projection materials. You may also watch a movie in the underground theater. Collaborated works of sculptors and media artists, circle riders, 5D riders and other experience elements enable you to communicate with and enjoy the films. The indoor exhibition leads to the outdoor exhibition, and it would be good to take a walk through palm trees and shrubs while looking at major scenes, sculptures of characters, and posters of famous movies.

stories.title: Jeju Teddy Bear Museum
stories.script: This is Teddy Bear Museum where a glass cone greets travelers. It was built in 2001, and at the time of its construction, it was quite revolutionary to establish a museum with just the theme of “Teddy Bear” alone. Teddy Bear Museum was introduced in numerous Korean dramas such as All In and Princess Hours and became well-known both nationwide and overseas. Subsequently, it was able to establish branches in other foreign cities including Hainan and Chengdu.  When you look at the building from the road, you can only see the garden and the cone-shaped entrance. The structures on the ground are minimized, and the cone-shaped entrance to the atrium allows people on the inside to view as much of the outside as possible. Typical museums want you to focus on exhibited items by using pin spotting while trying to diminish other elements, but this museum enables visitors to watch the sea through glass windows and enjoy the exhibits at the same time.  It consists of a history museum, an art museum, a planned exhibition hall, an Elvis performance, and an outdoor sculpture park of over 9,917 m2 area. The spaces are set up for you to comfortably view the exhibits, starting with the indoor exhibition and then naturally walking out to the Teddy Garden.  The exhibited works are antique teddy bears, which have been collected from all over the world with great effort, as well as those created by famous artists both in Korea and overseas. Since each of them has its own story, you won’t be simply looking at stuffed animals but instead, you will be able to travel the world and encounter history and many different characters.

stories.title: International Peace Center Jeju
stories.script: International Peace Center Jeju adds another meaning to Jeju. On January 27, 2005, Jeju was designated as an “Island of Peace” by the Korean government, which then decided to establish a facility that would symbolize this designation. What you're looking at is that facility.  Built over a total floor area of about 7,120 ㎡, it has one underground and two ground floors, and all of the elements in the building have their meanings. First of all, the building embodies columnar joints while the roof has a large structure made of special glass that reflects regionality as well as a pigeon sculpture spreading its wings of peace.  The inside features the central hall, exhibition halls 1, 2 and 3, planned exhibition hall and a seminar room. Exhibition halls 1 and 2 have items that symbolize peaceful lives of Jeju and those that have been donated by world leaders who visited the island in the past. Exhibition hall 3 displays wax figures of global celebrities, people who have striven for world peace, and famous Korean actors, making it a perfect place to take commemorative photos.  It won the Excellence Award in the Completed Building category at the 2006 Jeju Architecture Awards.

stories.title: Jeju Booyoung Hotel & Resort
stories.script: Booyoung Hotel is a work from the latter phase of the career of Ricardo Legorreta, a world-renowned Mexican architect. Legorreta is well-known for architecture with warmth that sufficiently applies natural elements such as water, wind, air and sunlight. He always put human and environment at the core of his architecture. For Booyoung Hotel, he brought the Caribbean passion and sensitivity and slightly modified them to suit the geographical characteristics of Jeju. The building with unique colors and palm trees go well together, and the windows and walls built to receive as much sunshine as they can seem to exude the architect's philosophy. It is built in a terraced style without going against the topography, which makes it nature-friendly, and as a result, this enabled every room to have a view of the sea. It would depend on whom you ask, but some believe that, among all hotels in Jeju, the most outstanding view of the sea can be enjoyed here.  Booyoung Hotel is also famous for the “Gallery Casa del Agua” that had existed nearby. It used to be the model house of the Jeju International Convention Center Anchor Hotel. It is especially significant because it was a posthumous work of Ricardo Legorreta. Moreover, it was the only work of his in Asia whose interior was made public, which is why it had much value in terms of history of architecture. However, since it was built as a temporary structure, it ended up being torn down after its retention period expired. Because it does not exist any longer, it has become a house in our imagination filled with curiosity and sadness for the lost legend.

stories.title: International Convention Center Jeju
stories.script: This is the International Convention Center Jeju where the Korea-Asean Special Summit was held. Designed by Nihon Sekkei and Cheonil Architecture, it began its construction in 1997 and opened in 2003. The construction period was delayed due to the IMF financial crisis of 1998, which resulted in a few design changes from the original plan. Having an oval shape with transparent glass that well receives light from the sky and the sea, the building is the country's only resort-style convention center that embodies Jeju as well as the island within an island. In addition, small hills that express oreum, or parasitic cone, a waterfall that embodies columnar joints, and a green space established by Jeju's native trees and plants are seen outside the building, all of which constitute a smaller version of Jeju.  With the goal of being a green convention, the building installed the province's largest solar power generation facilities throughout the venue. Moreover, through continuous efforts including application of insulation films, introduction of eco-friendly energy management system and replacement with highly efficient, eco-friendly LED lighting, it acquired the EarthCheck certification by an Australian global eco-friendly certification agency called EC3 Global.  It has seven ground floors over the building area of 15,218 ㎡ and a total floor space of 63,477 ㎡. There are meeting rooms, exhibition halls, outdoor banquet hall, food and beverage corners and many other convenience facilities within the building. The large conference room has the total capacity of 4,300 people. Seogwipo's large events, exhibitions and performances are held here every day.

stories.title: Jeju World Cup Stadium
stories.script: Jeju World Cup Stadium was designed by Hwang Il-in for 2002 Korea-Japan World Cup. Its construction began in 1999 and completed in 2001. The Guinness World Record selected this stadium as the most beautiful stadium in the world thanks to its design in harmony with the environment. The first characteristic that grabs our attention is how it is an underground stadium. Instead of going against the natural topography that descends from Hallasan Mountain, most seats were installed along the slope below the ground level, which led to the establishment of the soccer pitch at 14 m underground. This helped block the wind and thus, reduce construction costs, and only one side of the roof is covered to minimize the section that protrudes above the ground level. It added the elements that symbolize parasitic cones and craters to the shape of the stadium, and also expressed Teu and nets, which are Jeju's traditional tools used by haenyeo, on the roof. In addition, the number of the pillars and the spaces in between them represent five oceans and six continents while 11 Dol Hareubangs symbolize the soccer players. Connecting the Olle Trails with the entry plaza is another unique Jeju's characteristic. Above all, the fact that Hallasan Mountain and the sea can be viewed even from the seats is a special feature of this island stadium.  After the World Cup was over, it modified its structure in a practical way; it originally had over 40,000 seats, but the seats initially installed as temporary seats were removed and installed in a nearby soccer field (Citizens’ Jungmun). Thus, the world cup stadium reduced the number of seats down to a little fewer than 30,000 now.  It boasts a remarkable award-winning history as well; it was selected as a Beautiful Architecture of the city of Jeju, won an award at the 2002 Korean Institute of Architects Award and won another award at the 2002 Kim SwooGeun Cultural Award. Currently, it is used as the home field of Jeju United, a team that relocated its home from Bucheon, Gyeonggi-do Province in 2006.

stories.title: Soesokkak Estuary
stories.script: Strange-shaped rocks and cliffs continue like a Chinese landscape painting here in Soesokkak Estuary. This unique name that you can’t forget once you hear it is derived from “Soedunudun,” which is the old name of this area, Hyodon-ri. “Soe” and “So” mean a pond and “Kkak” means an estuary in Jeju dialect, so it means something like an “estuary of a pond in an ox village.” It is mostly a dry stream with no water flow, making the detailed features of the rocks and cliffs to be seen clearly. Thanks to its oriental and primitive vibe, it has become the background of several Chinese movies as well as numerous Korean dramas and films including Fate, The Great Merchant, The Slave Hunters, Swallow the Sun, Dae Jang Geum and Life is Beautiful.  At the end of the dry stream, an estuary appears, and all of a sudden, deep, green-colored water is seen underneath pine tree shades. Many travelers consider this as the must-see point in Soesokkak Estuary. However, if it was a stream that had completely dried up once, where do you think all this water has come from? It is so thickly wooded and abundant with water that it feels like a valley deep in a mountain, not an estuary of a stream. Soon after, the vast sea comes into sight. It has become a beloved filming spot for many, perhaps because of a series of pleasant surprises hidden behind its ordinary exterior.

stories.title: Cafe de Seoyeon
stories.script: Have you watched the movie, Architecture 101? This is the house of Seo-yeon, the main character. It is quite rare for the background to take the center stage of a film, but in the movie, the story flows around Seo-yeon’s house. Seo-yeon asks Seung-min to remodel her old house in Jeju, and this brings back memories of innocent love from their youth. That is why some people say that this house is the third main character of the movie.  The house was built to film the movie but it was later replicated into a gallery cafe in 2013. It was designed by Architect Koo Seung-hoe who served as an adviser of the film and the interior was done by Art Director Woo Seung-mi. With the addition of ideas from Director Lee Yong-joo, traces of memories from the film were able to come alive. The essence of the house lies in the grass rooftop and whole glass folding windows through which the vast sea is seen in a single view. These were accurately replicated as they were in the movie although there were design changes in other areas to meet the requirements of the Building Act. Inside, there are movie-related props such as scenes and lines, autographs of actors and directors, and hand prints of actors. It also sells beverages and side menus with movie lines written, such as “What should I do with you?” and “Seo-yeon,” as well as Nabddeuckyi muffins.  There is also Seung-min’s studio next to the Cafe de Seoyeon. As it is a little less crowded compared to the cafe, it is a perfect place for those who want a quiet rest.

stories.title: Jeju Folk Village
stories.script: Jeju Folk Village, which was a filming location for a Korean TV series Dae Jang Geum, has a mini Dae Jang Geum theme park. Many other dramas like The Slave Hunters, The Great Merchant, Queen & I and King's Doctor were also filmed here, and Tamra the Island filmed over 80% of its scenes here. In particular, Tamra the Island is a fusion historical drama centered on Hamel, a Dutch man who drifted to Jeju in the mid-17th century, that depicts a variety of people in exile to Jeju haenyeo, portraying how Jeju looked like in the old days.  This is why Jeju Folk Village is a popular filming spot in Jeju for historical dramas and TV shows.

stories.title: Pyoseon Beach
stories.script: One may think that beaches are everywhere on Jeju Island, but actually, that is not the case. Pyoseon Beach, which I am introducing now, is the only beach in the southeastern part of Jeju. It is a shallow and peaceful beach with a length of 200 m, a width of 800 m, and a depth of about 1 m.  Several scenes of the TV series Phoenix aired in 2004 were filmed here, and the ending scene of the drama Iris was shot at the white lighthouse located at the end of the sandy beach, which is why it has the nickname, the “Iris Lighthouse.” Swallow the Sun was also filmed at this lighthouse.  This place is known as a great spot to watch sunrise because you can see the sun ascend into the sky from the front. The beach's another name, “Haebichi,” means the place where the sun comes up first. At low tide, the white sandy beach looks round-shaped, and when the water comes in, it looks like a lake. The sand of the beach after water recedes is hard and firm, which is good for children to play with. Sand is made of crushed and pulverized clamshells. It is said that a sand bath helps with neuralgia, so it is a great beach for adults and children alike.

stories.title: Sinyang Seopji Beach and Cape Seopjikoji
stories.audioTitle: Sinyang Seopji Beach and Cape Seopjikoji
stories.script: The movie Love Wind, Love Song was filmed here in 1998. Jang Dong-gun and Ko So-young, handsome and beautiful celebrities of the time, were the main characters of the film and this itself was the talk of the town, but the movie became a hot topic once again years later when they married each other in real life in 2009.  Love Wind, Love Song is a tranquil love story in which Ko, a tour guide in Jeju, and Jang, a traveler, come to have romantic feelings for each other. It is considered one of the most notable movies that use Jeju in the background, thanks to the much-loved soundtrack, Still Our Love Continues and the beautiful scenery of the island.  In the film, Seopjikoji Beach appears as a place where the two main characters sit in a cabin and talk about their memories. The beach has nearly no rocks or pebbles, and shows a crescent moon-shaped outline with fine, light brown-colored sand. Having an average depth of about 1 m, it is also a beach where waves are calm and gentle. Pine trees form a colony on the small beach, which is about 300 m long and 80 m wide, and Jeju Special Self-Governing Province's windsurfing and board sailing training centers are located close by.  Cape Seopjikoji is located near the beach where several dramas and movies including All In, My Girl, Eyes of Dawn, The Legend of Gingko, The Uprising and Ae-ran were filmed. It is a great place to see Seongsan Ilchulbong Tuff Cone. In addition, there are works of Tadao Ando as well as Agora and Bella Terrace here, attracting many travelers for various reasons like sightseeing, exploration and accommodation.

stories.title: Jeju Horse Park
stories.script: This is a museum that hold the 600-year horse farming culture of Jeju. Since the old days, there have been vast grasslands in Gasi-ri, which is why the largest horse farm of Jeju called Noksanjang was located here. The best horses that were offered to the king were raised at Noksanjang and such horses were known as “Gamma.” Numerous communal horse farms are still in business throughout Jeju, and among them, Gasi-ri is said to be the leader of them all.  Jeju Horse Park is the country's first museum established by the people of an administrative town “ri,” not by the national or provincial government. Opened on September 8, 2012, it is a cultural complex built as a part of the new cultural space establishment project aided by the Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs.  It was designed by Yoon Eung-won and Kim Jung-joo, and the round exterior made of exposed concrete symbolizes Jeju oreum, or parasitic cone. In the exhibition hall, you will be able to examine the history and culture of the village, especially various aspects and details of horses and livestock farming. Here, you can see how the horse culture of Jeju has been developed and also check out how horses were raised in the old days through Tamna Sullyeokdo of Yi Hyeong-sang, a magistrate of Jeju, during the Joseon period, and many other horse-related relics from Korea and overseas. After checking out the exhibition, don’t forget to stop by the rooftop garden where you can get a 360-degree, panoramic view of Hallasan Mountain and nearby oreum.  In addition, there is a horse riding facility and a horse campground, and you can also participate in several experience programs.

stories.title: Photo Gallery Jayeonsarang Art Museum
stories.script: Seo Jae-cheol has worked as a photographer-reporter of the Jeju Press and the head of photography department at the Jemin Ilbo since 1972 to take hundreds of thousands of pictures of Jeju's nature. Then, in 2003, he randomly discovered Gasi Elementary School, which was a discontinued school at the time. He remodeled it and reopened it as Jayeonsarang Gallery on March 1, 2004.  The gallery consists of four exhibition halls with different themes in each of the classrooms. In “Baramjari” hall, you can check out the four seasons of Jeju while in “Ddarabi,” you will be able to see remarkable landscapes unique to Jeju. “Heukbaek Sarang” has black-and-white photos of haenyeo and old docks that have disappeared now, which arouses nostalgia for Jeju locals and offers travelers a chance to examine the old stories of Jeju.  The “Hwasantan Gallery” outdoors is the nation's only exhibition hall of Hwasantan, or volcanic bombs. These volcanic bombs are related to the formation of Jeju, a volcanic island, and will help you understand the land of Jeju.  In addition, there are photos of the old Gasi Elementary School, a camera exhibition hall, an education room and a rest area.  As the gallery has an enormous volume of materials, the exhibited items are replaced once in three to six months. Once a year, it also hosts planned exhibitions of various privately owned artifacts, sculptures and artworks.

stories.title: Kim Younggap Gallery Dumoak
stories.script: We introduce to you Kim Young-gap, an artist who passionately loved Jeju ever since he moved to the island. From the day he settled on the island in 1985 to his passing from Lou Gehrig's disease in 2005, he captured different aspects and scenes of Jeju with his camera for 20 years. Kim Younggap Gallery Dumoak you’re seeing right now was once Samdal Elementary School, which was a discontinued school, and Kim turned it into a gallery after he repaired and decorated it on his own. Though it was extremely difficult for him to move around after getting the disease, he still placed his heart and soul into the work.  He is especially famous for panorama pictures that captured Jeju’s nature. Among the gallery's total area of 13,223 m2, about 991 m2 is utilized to store and exhibit over 200,000 photos. You will find his workshop on the left side as soon as you enter the indoor exhibition hall. He actually used this room while he was alive, and his books, cameras and workstation are all still there.  The exhibit spaces are divided into two zones just as how the school buildings are separated. “Dumoakgwan” mainly has photos of the sky and clouds while “Hanaloreumgwan” shows Jeju’s oreum, Jungsangan, Marado Island and haenyeo. Pictures that were taken several times in the same place after a long wait are contained in a single work. From these photos, it is possible to feel the time rather than the moments.  In the front yard of the gallery, there are human-shaped sculptures in harmony with flowers and trees, and an unmanned cafe is also available in the back. Moreover, cultural performances for the locals are sometimes held in the outdoor performance stage.

stories.title: Dongbaek Village
stories.script: Since the old days, camellias have been used as windbreak trees in Jeju. Camellias that block strong winds of Jeju bloom beautiful flowers in the early spring. Once the flowers fall, they produce camellia oil, which is utilized in food, cosmetics and folk remedy.  Here in Sinheung-ri, there is a camellia colony, which is designated as Jeju-do Local Monument No. 27.
