Cheoninjeong, the name of the pavilion, was quoted from the phrase, “A phoenix does not eat a jujube even if she is hungry.” A pheonix is known as a mystical creature that only builds its nests on royal foxglove trees as well only eating bamboo tree seeds. The name itself, which holds the spirit of scholars in pursuit of fidelity and integrity, tells us the nature of Cheoninjeong.  Cheoninjeong was a pavilion built by the Gwangju Yi Clan to teach and train students but a Japanese shrine was almost established here during the occupation period. Japanese coveted the site after learning that the land gave off the most positive energy and vitality. But, by the strong resistance from the Dangchon Village residents, the Japanese failed to build a shrine here. During a repair that took place later, the scholars of Cheoninjeong took down the “Meiji”, which was a Japanese year name, from the Sangnyangmun and instead wrote an estimation year, in the Joseon way, thus displaying an unwavering national consciousness. You can see how much pride and affection the people have for this village from such nicknames like “Hanggeojeong” or “Hangiljeong”.  A wooden building boasting a stable and elegant beauty, Cheoninjeong has sufficient value of cultural heritage both architecturally and historically, which is why it is a shame that it’s not even registered as a local cultural heritage.  At the entrance of the village, you will see a large pine tree that stretches its branches extensively. The zelkova tree that is often used as a tree for shade is known as the guardian tree. People believe that, if you break a branch or leaf of a zelkova tree standing at the entrance of a village, a disaster will come to the village. To villagers, a zelkova is not an ordinary tree. A zelkova creates shade blocking the scorching sunlight on a summer day thus, providing a place for people to rest comfortably. Not only that, it is also a tree to which people pray for their health and illness-free lives for their families, as well as a year of good harvest. Byeolsindang is a place that enshrines the gods responsible for grains and land. Commonsensically, it is quite a strange combination for Cheoninjeong, where scholars used to discuss studies, to stand next to Byeolsindang. However, if you do look at them in person, they give off an amiable feel of old neighbors.  Together with Bongcheon-ri Five-story Stone Pagoda located nearby, Bongnae-myeon offers the coexistence of Buddhism, Confucianism, and even folk religions. On the back of Byeolsindang and Cheoninjeong, aged pine trees stand around like a folding screen to block off the cold winter wind. Originally, this shrine was seated at the mid-slope of Bibongsan but it was too far from the village especially for January, where too many of the days have harsh weather conditions, making it difficult for people to climb up to the shrine for rituals. So, in 1897, it was relocated to the current site and has gone through several repairs. The former name of Bongnae-myeon was Bokseong-hyeon. The name, Dangchon Village, was brought about as it was a village with a dang, or a shrine, where Sajiksin, or gods of land and grain, were enshrined during the days when it was called Bokseong-hyeon.

stories.title: Boseong Byeolsindang - Byeolsindangje of Bongnae-myeon
stories.script: Order and cooperation of the village  Byeolsindangje, which is held between 11:30 PM and 12:30 AM on the 15th day of the New Year, is also called “Gyomokje” or “Dangsanje”. In the beginning of every January, the head of a village and other community leaders meet to elect the Jegwan, or the person to oversee rituals, for the year's Dangsanje. One could not become a Jegwan if he has suffered a sickness or has a death in the family, or has visited a funeral, has a pregnant woman in the family, or has tried dog meat.  Hwaju who serves as the Choheongwan during Dangsanje has important responsibilities along with the Jegwan. Starting on the day on which one is given the duties of Hwaju, he keeps his body and soul clean and pure and hangs golden strings on the front gate of his house where he also spreads out red clay. This is to prevent himself from being entangled in disgraceful events with ahead of the ritual. From this point on, the villagers also refrain from entering the house of the Hwaju until the ritual is over even if they have any business there.  The Hwaju and the head of the village purchase the offerings together, and it is customary not to bargain the prices of the items under all circumstances. The food for the ritual is made by the Hwaju couple, and the water for cooking must be carried from a well. When cooking, they are prohibited to taste the food to check for seasoning, and if they go to the restroom, they must change into new clothes and take a bath. Because it was a hassle to take a bath every time they went in and out of the restroom on a cold day, it was typical for the Hwaju couple to be unable to eat anything during the ritual period.  The village does not celebrate Jeongwol Daeboreum separately, which is substituted instead with Dangsanje. So, starting from the evening before the day of Dangsanje, the entire village goes into a festival featuring nongak, which is the type of folk music played in the countryside to accompany agricultural labor. Women would tie up rope onto the guardian tree to make a swing, and men would twist straw to make thick ropes, which they would then place on their backs, then going around the village while singing songs, before performing a moon house burning with them. Most of the rituals were conducted in the Confucian style. One difference was that the pork meat that would be used as an offering would be buried underground after the ritual was over. Once Dangsanje was finished, it was customary to bring the offerings out into the village for Isaje, which is a ritual specifically held for those who pass away without any children.  The ritual continues until the break of dawn. In the morning, the villagers would gather at a village school to partake in the sacrificial food and drinks as well as to hold village meetings. In old times, the wages to be paid to farming laborers that year were decided in a village meeting as well, and it is said that no one could go against a resolution that was made in the meeting. It seems like we are now able to understand more about the reason that Cheoninjeong and Byeolsindang coexisted in such close locations in a traditional Confucian society.  Cheoninjeong scholars were no naive academics. They were patriots imbued with devotion for the country and mental leaders respected by the residents. That is why the villagers placed their lives on the line to stop the Japanese' dirty ambition of building a shrine here, thus Cheoninjeong has become a place that elevates the pride of our people. Perhaps, the virtue of the coexistence of these two structures for such a long period stem from the fact that Byeolsinje, which is based on folk belief, follows the Confucian format and demonstrates an emphasis on the order and cooperation of a village by, for instance, holding funerals for those without family or friends.

stories.title: Seokjangseung in Haepyeong-ri, Boseong - Seokjangseung in Haepyeong-ri, Deungnyang-myeon
stories.audioTitle: Seokjangseung in Haepyeong-ri, Boseong - Seokjangseung in Haepyeong-ri, Deungnyang-myeon
stories.script: Strong patron god protecting a village  Our ancestors believed that Jangseung would protect a village against all misfortune, and because its powers were so incredible, one who harms it would be punished severely. This shows how they believed in and relied upon the power of Jangseung.  Jangseung is a long, wooden signpost. Some say that it is the origin of Korean traditional masks and the face of Dangun and that Jangseung is the expression of the grand achievements of Chiu Cheonwang, the 26th king of Dangun Joseon, in the form of a mask. Though it looks expressionless at a glance, Jangseung actually has many different faces. If you look at it with a sad heart, it seems full of deep sorrow, but if you look at it with a bright mind, its facial expression seems joyful as well. The reason for such a variety of expressions hidden in the face of Jangseungs is so that it can be closer to the people. Very considerate, as a guardian god of a village should be.  The roles of Jangseung are as diverse as the appearances. The most common of them all are the landmark Jangseung, which distinguishes boundries between regions, and the road sign Jangseung that helps guide your journey. There is also a Jangseung that drives ghosts away. Jangseung normally stands in a pair consisting of a male and a female. Typically, one that wears a crown or a hat is a male Jangseung and, the one not wearing anything is a female Jangseung.  Some say that the Seokjangseung, or stone Jangseung, standing in the entrance of Haepyeong-ri Village in Deungnyang-myeon was erected by righteous army soldiers but the exact story is unknown. The two Jangseung standing face to face are both square-shaped. On their bodies, letters of “Sangwonju Janggun” and “Hawondang Janggun” are engraved in intaglio.  Sangwonju Janggun has an appearance of a woman with a shaved head and a nearly flat face. She also has round eyes, a wrinkled forehead, seagull eyebrows, a bat-shaped nose and distinctly expressed nostrils. The teeth are seen to be vaguely engraved between the slightly opened lips, and a vine pattern is sculpted on her chin. On the other hand, Hawondang has the appearance of a male. It also has a shaved head and its entire body resembles a square pillar. Thick wrinkles are found on the forehead, and his eyes, which are slightly raised upward, protrude out. His bulbous nose also shows clearly expressed nostrils, and the mouth is closed gently. Moreover, the elaborately engraved ears and its thick mustache make the Hawondang very memorable.  These Jangseung are known to have originally been placed at the entrance of the Gaeheungsa Temple. Then, since the guardian saint of the temple was moved to the village, it served as a sort of civil working Jangseung. Haechang Village in Haepyeong-ri used to be where a tax storage warehouse existed during the Joseon Period. The role of the stone Jangseung was to protect the tax filled ships that had set out to sea and to help them carry out their missions safely. As generations passed, cargo ships began to disappear, thus, the functions of Haechang died out, but since the existence of the reclaimed land here, the Jangseung has been serving as a charm against evil influences and a protector of peace for the villagers.

stories.title: Jangjwa-ri, Boseong - Gibaji Byeolsinje of Jangjwa-ri, Beolgyo-eup
stories.audioTitle: Jangjwa-ri, Boseong - Gibaji Byeolsinje of Jangjwa-ri, Beolgyo-eup
stories.script: Story-filled Seongeun Bridge  Seongeun Bridge in Jangjwa-ri, Beolgyo-eup used to be the only bridge to go from downtown Beolgyo to Yeongdeung-ri Village in Jangjwa-ri or Goheung before the Beolgyo Bypass was built. Up till the Goryeo Dynasty, Jangjwa-ri was not part of the main land and instead it was an island called Jangjwado. Thanks to small stepping-stones, an island village with a thousand-year history turned into a mainland village with beautifully golden reed fields.  There are several myths being passed down regarding the origin of this bridge. The most widely known among them is the one about a fifteen-year-old Seongeun, a son with great love and respect for his parents. His mother passed away when he was young, which left his father alone with him. One day, curious of his father leaving the house every night and returning in the early morning, Seongeun followed his father.  He crossed a stream, barefoot, in cold weather to save his shoes and socks from getting wet and went into a house in Jangjwa-ri. Seongeun found out his father fell in love with a woman who had lived there alone. To help his father cross the stream without getting his feet wet in the winter, Seongeun collected large stones and made stepping-stones within the water. Having learned of this later, the people from the village were touched by Seongeun’s love for his father and installed a wooden bridge, which they named Seongeun Bridge.  Another myth speaks of a Bodhisattva named Yeonan, with the secular name Kim Seon-gun before turning herself to Buddhism, who built this bridge. The Yeonan Bodhisattva myth begins with a young 19-year-old bride getting deserted by her husband on the first day of their marriage. The husband was attacked by a tiger on that night and, though he survived the life-or-death situation, he decided to wed another woman instead of the one he had already married because he thought she had been the bringer of bad luck. Unable to muster up the courage to return to her own family, she went into Myohyangsan Mountain and became a Bodhisattva by the name of Yeonan. 30 years after, she received the calling from Buddha and went down to stay in a remote island, which is where Jangjwa-ri is today. Setting a bridge that leads to the mainland was the ultimate wish for the people of Jangjwado. So Yeonan Bodhisattva built a bridge for the village and donated all of her assets and properties just before her death. The village named the bridge after her secular name, Seongun, and every January, held a funeral service, which is said to be the origin of the Byeolsinje of Jangjwa-ri.  In Yeonggubong Peak at the top of Jangjwa-ri, there are two shrines, Sangdang and Jungdang. Jungdang is a shrine to commemorate Yeonan Bodhisattva Kim Seon-geun, and Sangdang is known to have been donated by a merchant with the last name, Kim. According to a story, a man with the last name, Kim, once went on a journey to sell goods but ran into strong winds. Luckily, he was saved by mountain spirits of Jangjwa Village and out of gratitude for his survival which led to his life of wealth later on, he built a shrine for them.  Whether it be the love for parents or devotion to Buddha, the reason that Jangjwa-ri myths have a touching story is because, at the core of them all, the story involves neighbors. Stepping-stones made by a good son who diligently carried one stone after another eventually led to a construction of a safe wooden bridge thanks to help from the village neighbors. Also, the custom of a village that holds rituals every year in remembrance of the Bodhisattva's virtuous deeds is in line with our tradition of mutual dependence and cooperation. Boasting an 800-year old history, Jangjwa Gibaji Byeolsinje is a communal ritual through which people pray for the well-being and abundance of the village and also strengthen order and harmony, and it received the Grand Prize at the 18th Namdo Culture Festival and the Minister of Culture award at the 31st National Folk Art Contest.

stories.title: Daepo-ri, Boseong - Beolgyo Daepo-ri Gaetgwisinje
stories.script: A place of communication that supports a community   Gaetgwisinje is a traditional custom that has been passed down for over 400 years, and is the biggest event in Daepo-ri. This event, which is held by the entire village community, possesses a sacred meaning for the people for whom gaetbeol, or mud flat, has been the source of life. Originally, it is said that there used to be three shrines in Daepo-ri -  Sangdang, the grandfather shrine; Hadang, the grandmother shrine; and Jecheong underneath Hadang - so rituals had to be carried out in all three locations. Today, people only perform Gaetgwisinje in the grandmother shrine and Jecheong. Gaegwisinje, which prays for an abundance of fish and harvest as well as prosperity of the village to Gaetgwisin, or mud flat ghost, and Dangsan Grandmother, takes place around the 15th day of the lunar calender new year. Prior to the event, villagers must follow several taboos such as hanging golden strings and spreading golden clay at the entrance of the village and in the shrine, and keeping their bodies clean and pure. All of the residents participate in the event voluntarily. Conflicts, big or small, that have occurred throughout the year are settled during this event to form a harmony. Gaetgwisinje is not just an offering of a ritual but, rather, a place of communication through which the spirit of community is raised.  Gaetgwisinje starts with nongak music in front of the village hall. Nongak proceeds like a festival in which all villagers participate. The head of an ox and a sacrificial table sincerely prepared by the people are set up in front of Jecheong, and it takes two full days just to carry out the rituals, which include Saemgut, Naldangsangut, Deuldangsangut, Dangsan Grandmother Munangut, Yongwanggut, Mungut, Dangjujipgut and Dangsan Sangdanje. The final event is Yongwanggut that takes place at 11 PM on the second day. Once Doposu and Changbu go out to a dock right in front and sacrifice the head of an ox as the offering to Gaetgwisin, all the villagers prostrate on the ground to pray for the offering to go off in peace. After the sacrificial offering, Jecheong is burned down, which marks the end of Gaetgwisinje. In the morning after, if the offering was found to still remain without being carried away by the sea, the people would believe that they inadequately performed the ritual, and would carry out another one.  Gaetgwisinje of Daepo-ri is a valuable traditional cultural heritage that was awarded first-place at the 14th Namdo Culture Festival in 1985 and second-place at the 1997 National Folk Art Contest. These are the fruits borne by our ancestors, who have protected this precious custom that could have very well disappeared thanks to the era of advanced civilization, which further adds to its value. Recently, a conservation society for Daepo-ri Gaetgwisin was organized, adding life to it, which has also been a welcoming sight.

stories.title: Taebaek Paleozoic Museum
stories.script: Taebaek takes you on a fascinating journey back to the ancient seas that once covered this land. The museum's exhibits guide you through the geological changes from the Cambrian to the Ordovician periods, making it easy to understand why this area was once a sea and how life evolved here, from its birth to extinction.  On the first floor, you'll find a series of videos that vividly illustrate the environment from the Precambrian era to the Middle Paleozoic. These visuals bring to life the shallow seas that once spread endlessly across the Taebaek region. In those seas, salt crystals shimmered, dried under the harsh sun, and within the waters, the presence of trilobites could still be felt, moving through the ancient world.  At the museum and in the surrounding area, you can enjoy your own little treasure hunt, just like when you were a child. As you explore, you might find traces of ancient life—cracked rock surfaces, wave patterns, fossils of animals that once roamed these lands, and gentle folds of the earth’s layers. One of the fascinating highlights is the display of trilobite fossils, which feature clearly segmented bodies and delicate, ridged joints. These fossils, once commonly found around the museum, especially near the Hwangji Stream, give a glimpse into the past. You’ll also see brachiopods, shaped like pencils, and cephalopods, which are the ancestors of squids. Trilobites have bodies divided into three parts: the head, thorax, and tail. Since their bodies often broke apart when they died, it's rare to find them fully intact. However, after observing them carefully in the exhibition, you might find it easier to spot fragments in the rocks near the stream. The more you learn, the more you'll discover!  The older villagers fondly recall how, as children, they would wander near the Taebaek Jangseong Double-tier Bridge, not knowing what trilobites were. They were simply intrigued by the bug-like patterns on the rocks, and as they found one, they couldn’t help but search for bigger, better-preserved specimens. It became a friendly competition, who could find the biggest and best? Fossil hunting was not only a way to spend time but also a way to connect with friends, and even to gain their admiration.  In the 1960s, Japanese fossil collectors began coming to the area, buying fossils from locals. They even paid children to collect them, which wasn’t difficult, as fossils were abundant along the Hwangji Stream. This area continues to be a wonderful geological classroom, with traces of various ancient creatures still visible on the rocks. Even today, local universities conduct field studies and research here, continuing the tradition of learning from this rich natural history.

stories.title: Cheoram and My Father
stories.script: Cheoram Station Cheoram and My Father  During the heyday of the coal industry, children who moved to Cheoram with their parents felt as though they had entered a world painted in black. The water was black, the houses were black, and sometimes even the sky appeared to be tinted with shades of dark. Even their fathers, returning home from the mines, wore clothes that were covered in black dust. In no time, the children became so accustomed to their surroundings that when they began to draw, they often painted the river black as well.  Black, as it turns out, is the color that holds all others within it. The people of Cheoram, with their different dreams and stories, lived in a town bathed in this deep, rich black. But this wasn’t just any darkness—it was a black full of hopes and dreams, like a rainbow waiting to emerge from the shadows.  For the sake of their families, the miners didn’t only unearth black stones from the depths of the earth; they unearthed their lives, their sacrifices, and their hopes for a brighter future. Working in those harsh, shadowy mines, they prayed that their children would be spared the same struggles. While some might say that the coal mine marks the end of the road, for these fathers, it was a place of hope.  As time passed, coal, once an essential industrial fuel, was replaced by oil and gas. The mines closed, and the familiar sight of coal ash scattered across alleyways faded into memory. Even the cold winter nights, when people would delay fetching coal to warm their homes, are now cherished memories. The white dog that once wandered through the neighborhood as if it owned the place, sniffing around every corner, no longer has black soot on its nose.  The hard work in those black mines secured a brighter future for their children, who grew up surrounded by hope. The fathers, who had been miners in their youth, sometimes longed for the days when they were industrial warriors. Like coal burning to ash, they grew old, and so did Cheoram. Maybe that’s why Cheoram feels like a quiet, steadfast father—someone who gave everything for his children and his country.

stories.title: Taebaek Cheoram Station
stories.script: The small houses gently line the streets, though the area remains quiet, with hardly any passersby. Behind Cheoram Station, you'll find a coal yard, its piles of black coal standing tall—this is the kind of view you can only find in a coal mining region. While some places grab your attention with their vivid, natural beauty, Cheoram quietly captivates with a landscape reminiscent of charcoal drawings. The simplicity and warmth of a charcoal sketch mirrors the soft, comforting atmosphere of Cheoram.  The station building itself stands larger than its surroundings. Originally built in the 1930s, it was moved about 100 meters in 1985 to its current location, replacing a single-story structure. During the coal industry's golden era, Cheoram was at the heart of it all, serving as a key hub for coal transport across the nation. During the 1970s and 80s, the station handled as much as 12,000 tons of coal a day, with around 300 employees making it a bustling center. I wonder if Cheoram Station recalls the golden days of old?  Cheoram Station is also home to murals—beautiful works created by artists, sculptors, photographers, and others. Between 2001 and 2011, these talented individuals adorned the walls of the station and surrounding buildings with large-scale murals about Cheoram and its coal history. These murals are known as the Wall of Memories, a heartfelt tribute that offers the people of Cheoram a way to reminisce about their beloved hometown.

stories.title: Taebaek Coal Preparation Plant at Cheoram Station
stories.audioTitle: Taebaek Coal Preparation Plant at Cheoram Station
stories.script: Get Ready for Modern Culture No. 21!  As you pass through the waiting hall of Cheoram Station, a fascinating sight awaits dozens of railway tracks stretching out in every direction. Cheoram Station offers a unique experience that surprises visitors in two distinct ways: first, the quiet emptiness, with hardly anyone around, and second, the striking view of the station tracks, with the Coal Preparation Plant just beyond.  Once, Cheoram Station was the largest coal distribution point in Korea. During the prosperous 1970s and 1980s, when the mining industry was thriving, Cheoram was known as the heart of Korea’s coal industry, a “land of black jewels” where economic power was unmatched. Despite the hardships, it became a place where people with big dreams came, hoping to turn despair into hope. The unyielding will and dreams for a new life were the forces behind Cheoram’s growth, contributing significantly to Korea's economic development.  The coal loading facility grew alongside Korea’s industrial progress. Raw coal was extracted from the Baekdu Mountains, processed at the facility to remove impurities, and then loaded onto trains to be transported across the country and even to Japan. During the Japanese occupation, the facility's conveyor belts started running, and they continue to function to this day.  The Coal Preparation Plant at Cheoram Station was designated as a Registered Heritage Site in May 2002, due to its well-preserved original structures that have remained largely unchanged for nearly 80 years, since 1935. Not only the buildings, but also the equipment inside the facility reflect the difficult lives of the miners and their families. It’s a source of pride that this place is perhaps the best-preserved testament to the history of Korea’s coal industry.  The Coal Preparation Plant is where raw coal brought from nearby mines is sorted, processed, and prepared for transport by train. Even today, you can still see key operational elements, like the hopper beside the building, where coal is poured into wagons. While the facility is no longer in full operation, it still plays an important role in the supply of coal.  If you contact Cheoram Station in advance, the staff will guide you to the Coal Preparation Plant, and you’ll be able to take photos of the tracks. However, it’s essential to remember that crossing the tracks is very dangerous, so please ensure your safety while enjoying the visit.

stories.title: Taebaek Sambang-dong
stories.script: People from all over the country once came to Cheoram, dreaming of a happy life with their families. Traveling in six-wheeled, five-ton GMC trucks, they settled wherever coal mines could be found, no matter how harsh and long the winters were in the valleys of Gangwon-do. With their own hands, they built homes and worked tirelessly. Seeing the coal neatly piled at the preparation facilities near Cheoram Station brought them a sense of pride and contentment. Their neighborhood, Sambang-dong, felt so close to the sky that it seemed you could reach it with just one leap.  As the mining industry declined, many of those who had come left the same way they arrived, and now only a few families remain. Walking through Sambang-dong today, it’s hard to imagine that this quiet little village was once home to over 900 households.   If the countless miners who once lived here hadn’t worked in three shifts, what would mornings and evenings in this place have been like? There’s an old saying in Sambang-dong: “Even brushing shoulders here means it was meant to be.” The alleys are so narrow that you’d often need to step aside to let someone pass, and as you stroll through them, the meaning of those words starts to make sense.  The houses in Sambang-dong, made from simple planks, have walls that are truly unique. They’re covered with layers of paper—newspapers, calendars, and even children’s test sheets. Surprisingly, while cement walls have crumbled over time, these paper-covered walls have stood firm. In a place known for strong winds and heavy snow, it’s amazing that these walls have lasted. It almost feels like Sambang-dong has its own secret method for wallpapering.  The answer lies in the many layers of paper. In some houses, the wallpaper is said to be thicker than the walls themselves. Residents didn’t bother removing old wallpaper; instead, they just pasted new layers on top. Sometimes, they only patched up the areas that needed it. Over the years, as neighbors added layer after layer to their shared walls, these layers became a kind of support system. Even as the cement walls behind them started to crumble, the layers of wallpaper held everything together. Today, those thick walls of paper quietly tell the stories of Sambang-dong and the lives of the people who lived there.

stories.title: Taebaek Cheoram Market
stories.script: Cheoram Market is a traditional market that opens on the 10th, 20th, and 30th of every month. One of its unique features is the direct coal sales store (yeontan jikmaeso), which catches the eye of visitors. In the Taebaek region, many homes still rely on coal for heating, and with the direct sales method, there are fewer intermediaries, allowing coal to be sold at much lower prices than in Seoul.  On days when the market isn’t open, it’s quite rare to find a restaurant in Cheoram Market that is open. In Taebaek, you can find delicious pork dishes almost everywhere. After a long, hard day of work, miners would unwind by enjoying stir-fried pork with a glass of soju, known as doeruchigi. Pork belly, often grilled to wash off the coal dust from a miner’s neck, became a beloved food, second only to kimchi.  Pork in Taebaek is quite magical in its versatility—whether stir-fried as doeruchigi, boiled as suyuk, grilled as samgyeopsal, or seasoned into tender pork ribs. On cooler days, locals enjoy grilling meat on large stones by the stream with family or friends, a delightful tradition known as stone grilling (dolgui). Over time, this has become a symbol of friendship, and when people catch up with old friends, they often say, “Let’s go for some dolgui.”  There’s also another touching memory related to pork in Cheoram. In the 1950s, the wives of miners would trade their monthly rice rations for cheaper grains or flour to save money and secretly buy pork, setting it aside just for their husbands and keeping it hidden from the children. It’s a bittersweet yet heartwarming memory that came from the struggles of poverty.

stories.title: Taebaek Cheoramcheon Maple Grove
stories.script: The red glow along the Cheoramcheon Stream recalls the vibrant past of Cheoram. It’s none other than the autumn foliage. On the right side of the widened road, you'll see Cheoram Elementary School, and on the left, the graceful arch of the iron bridge. Beneath the bridge, the colorful autumn leaves float on the water, painting the rocky peaks of Cheoram in late fall. While the autumn colors here may be modest compared to more famous spots, the sight of these red leaves in Cheoram is truly a rare and magical experience.  Taebaek, nestled in the highlands of the Taebaek Mountain Range that divides Yeongdong and Yeongseo, enjoys cool summers and very cold winters due to its mountainous climate. That’s why coniferous trees like yew, pine, and fir thrive here. It’s amazing to see vibrant autumn leaves growing in clusters alongside these evergreen trees!  Perhaps it’s the warmth that the red leaves seem to exude, but the Cheoramcheon Stream maple grove has long been a popular spot for couples. Today, there’s a lovely walking path that winds through the grove. As you cross the bridge and ascend towards the rocky peaks, you’ll even find a foot massage path along the way.  If you walk a little further along the Cheoramcheon Stream, you’ll reach a viewpoint where you can take in a stunning panoramic view of the town. From here, you can spot Cheoram Station, coal loading docks, coal mines, the old streets of Cheoram, Cheoram Elementary School, and the residential areas. In the distance, you’ll see the rocky mountain ridgeline. On the left, there’s Pinaegol, a peaceful place that has long been a refuge. On the right, the Cheoramcheon Stream winds through the autumn grove you’ve just passed.

stories.title: Taebaek Tongri 5-Day Market
stories.script: Which rural market is beloved by itinerant vendors? It is said that the best markets are those where many people gather, and business thrives. In this regard, Tongri 5-day market can certainly be considered the best, as it is bustling with people and goods sell well.   A typical 5-day market refers to a market that opens every 5 days, but Tongri 5-day market is held on the 5th, 15th, and 25th of each month, which is why it is called a 5-day market. This schedule was decided with consideration for the local merchants, as a result of mutual understanding and cooperation among the vendors.  One of the special things about Tongri market is that it still preserves the charm of old rural markets. Stretching at least 500 meters along the roadside, it leads all the way to the Tongri traditional market. Taking a walk through the entire market can feel like a bit of a workout! On market days, the area around Tongri Kyungdong Apartments gets busy with people selling their goods, shoppers browsing, and many just enjoying the lively atmosphere. During holidays, it can get so bustling that it’s hard to tell where the entrance and exit are!  What makes Tongri 5-Day Market unique is that it’s only about an hour away from the East Sea, so the seafood here is as fresh and plentiful as you would find in big city markets—but at much more affordable prices! You can even enjoy fresh sashimi right at the fish stalls. You’ll also find a wonderful variety of wild herbs, vegetables, and locally grown products like mushrooms from the deep mountains of Gangwon-do, as well as homemade tofu and mung bean jelly. One of the most fascinating parts of the market is the section selling farming tools, offering a rare sight you won't often see in city markets.

stories.title: Taebaek Tongri
stories.script: Tongri Hill, located at an altitude of 720 meters, was once known as Neureupnyeong (Yuyoung) and, even earlier, as Usan-hyeon. In the Silla Dynasty, it was the pass that the kings used to cross on their way to perform celestial rituals at Mount Taebaek. During the Goryeo and Joseon Dynasties, it served as a path through which the people of Samcheok would bring cattle for the celestial rites, earning it names like Usan-hyeon or Ubo-hyeon.  In the mid-to-late 1700s, the heart of Neureupnyeong Tongri was near what is now Tongri, roughly in the middle of National Route 38, connecting Tongri to Hwangji. At that time, the village was known as Yojeonggol, named after a pond, Yongjeong, where water springing up was quite special. The water from Yojeonggol still flows into Cheoramcheon and eventually merges with the Nakdong River.  By 1842, Yojeonggol became Yomulgol, and later, it was called Yongjeong. In 1916, the name changed to Tongri, which means a village surrounded by towering mountain peaks, like a well, symbolized by the characters for barrel (桶) and village (里).  Today, Tongri’s center is near the Kyungdong Apartment area and the vicinity of Tongri Station, where you can find a traditional market. The area once used to be a vast swamp, and the spring water flowed into Cheoramcheon, eventually joining the Gu-mun stream, and then merging with the Sodo and Hwangji streams. During the mining boom, as the development in Simpo-ri occurred, the water flow shifted toward the Oship stream, gradually reclaiming the land and transforming the swamp into the land we see today.

stories.title: Taebaek Cable Railway
stories.script: After the village of Yeojeongol became known as Tongri, a railway was laid from Cheoram to Tongri in the 1930s, with a strong railway line extending about 1km from Tongri to Simpo-ri. Although Tongri and Simpo-ri stations are quite close to each other, the elevation difference of about 250 meters made it necessary to create a unique type of railway, called Gangsakcheoldo (cable railway).  A gangsakcheoldo is like a cable car that runs on rails laid along steep slopes. It uses a steel cable wound around the rails to pull vehicles, either carrying passengers or cargo. Unlike regular cable cars, which hang from the cables in the air, the gangsakcheoldo pulls the train along the ground using ropes. Freight trains could manage, but passenger trains, being heavier, couldn’t make the climb.  Because of this, passengers arriving from the East Sea would disembark at Simpo-ri, carry their luggage up the hill to the elevated Tongri Station, and then catch another train waiting for them. This led to the need for about 200 porters who would carry the luggage up the mountain paths. The steep hills made the work tough, so porters were a necessity.  In winter, when snow would cover the paths, passengers could borrow special shoes called ssaka at the station. These shoes, with nails in the soles, were like modern crampons. If a passenger couldn’t borrow ssaka, they would buy a piece of rope to tie around their shoes and climb the slopes. What was especially thoughtful about the ssaka system was how the shoes were returned. The person lending the ssaka would go up the hill with the passenger who borrowed them, get the ssaka back, then lend the ssaka to a passenger coming down from the opposite train. Afterward, they would descend together and retrieve the ssaka again.  When the Yeongdong Line, connecting Yeongju and Gangneung, was completed in 1963, the need for the gangsakcheoldo disappeared. People no longer had to walk up the steep hill, and as a result, the number of visitors around Tongri Station significantly dropped. The porters who used to call out ssaka, ssaka or I’ll save you a seat during the winter gradually disappeared, as did the scenes of people buying and selling goods while utilizing the about 2 hours of free time while waiting at Simpo-ri and Tongri stations.  It’s a relief that the hardships of life have eased and that things have become more convenient. One should feel at peace, yet why does the longing for those old landscapes still remain?

stories.title: Gangsan Village, Daeya-ri, Boseong - Gangsan Village, Daeya-ri
stories.audioTitle: Gangsan Village, Daeya-ri, Boseong - Gangsan Village, Daeya-ri
stories.script: Gangsan Village, Daeya-ri, Boseong - Gangsan Village, Daeya-ri  Cradle of Seopyeonje  Mr. Park Yu-jeon, originally from Sunchang, Jeollanam-do, began his life in Boseong at the age of 18. Born as the second (or third, according to some) son to a vocalist father, he built a mud hut in the mountains behind Daeya-ri, Boseong-eup, where he trained in the art of pansori.  Danjae Shin Chae-ho, an independence fighter and a pansori specialist from the Joseon Period, once said, “The most important elements of a singer are Inmoolchirae, Sasulchirae and Dukeum.” Having lost an eye due to an unfortunate accident when he was young, Mr. Park was far from having Inmoolchirae, or good looks, which is, according to Danjae, the primary necessity for a singer.  Back in the old days, people used to call singers entertainers. It is the nature of this vocation to put a greater emphasis on looks rather than skills if one wishes to succeed within the field. But Mr. Park was riddled with smallpox scars on his face in addition to his one blind eye. Even though he had several handicaps to be a successful singer, he used his talents alone to establish a unique stage that no one else was able to reach.  Gangsan Village in Daeya-ri is the cradle of Seopyeonje, both in name and reality. Here, he invented Seopyeonje, which is also commonly referred to as Park Yu-jeon Ryu. He also created Gangsanje that merged the singing styles of Dongpyeonje and Seopyeonje, eventually reaching the rank of a pansori master and one of the eight great singers of the late Joseon Period.  According to a famous story, Heungseon Daewongun who loved pansori was moved by Mr. Park's voice, saying “You are Gangsan, the greatest in the world!” before bestowing upon him the position of Seondal. Daewongun also presented to him a bracelet and colored glasses made of gold, and gave Park the pen name Gangsan. The name, Gangsan Village, came to be because Mr. Park taught a great number of pupils here. Some of the bigger names of Korean pansori, such as Leenalchi and Jeong Jae-geun, were also fostered in Gangsan Village.  Behind the pavilion, after his passing, according to stories, an echo that cried, “Take my voice”, lasted for three days in the mountains out back. Whenever it rains amidst the pine forest, a passage from his Jeokbyeokga, to which even Emperor Gojong weeped, grabs the people's attention.  The end of the Korean Empire is full of misfortune, bringing forth boils The Yellow Turban Army is suppressed but Dong Zhuo rises And Dong Zhuo's rebellion is suppressed but the rebellion of Li Jue and Guo Si rises

stories.title: Boseong Sori Village
stories.script: Boseong Sori Village  Hill of sounds, hill of tears  Botjae appears in the first scene of the film, 〈Seopyeonje〉, as a place where the male protagonist is lost within his memories at a tavern. Soritjae that is mentioned in the movie is another name for Botjae. Dogang Village below Botjae in Hoecheon-myeon, Boseong-gun is the birthplace of Songgye Jeong Eung-min, a student of Gangsan Park Yu-jeon and the creator of Boseong Sori.  Boseong Sori is known as a vocal technique that combines Gangsanje created by Mr. Park Yu-jeon, the Bijo (the one who has founded or started something for the first time) of Seopyeonje; Junggoje of the central region; and Gyeongje of Seoul (the sijo vocal style in the Seoul and Gyeonggi regions) to which Mr. Jeong Eung-min added his own dose of musicality.  Songgye Jeong Eung-min was born with musical talent but had to go through a much more difficult path compared to others because of his vocal cords that were not suited for singing. He revised the lyrics of pansori, which had been quite coarse and wild previously, to dignified words through discussions with his pupils. He also forbids his students from producing the same sounds as their teachers and to always conduct themselves to the likes of a crescent moon.  During the period of the late Korean Empire, his family was widely regarded as a reputable pansori family. His uncle, Jeong Jae-geun, was a singer so renowned that he was even invited to the Emperor Gojong's coronation ceremony. Mr. Jeong Jae-geun was a student of Mr. Park Yu-jeon. Thus, Boseong Sori was born through the lineage that started from Park Yu-jeon, passed through Jeong Jae-geun, then finally went on to Jeong Eung-min.  Mr. Jeong Eung-min was known to be infinitely benevolent and tender but also known to not hesitate in denouncing his pupils in the strictest way when he felt a need to do so. This is why, in Dogang Village, Botjae was not only a hill of sounds from singers on their way to meet their teachers but also a hill of tears from when they traveled back and forth, weeping from harsh beatings from a pipe or a drumstick. Singers such as Park Chun-seong, Jeong Gwon-jin, Jo Sang-hyeon, Seong Chang-sun and Park Gye-hyang learned how to sing from him.  While training alone in Seoul, after the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1910, Mr. Jeong Eung-min, one winter, heard the shocking news of the death of his teacher Mr. Park Yu-jeon. Rumors had it that Mr. Park even decided to starve himself in order to leave this world, while others speculated that he had frozen to death. Heungseon Daewongun loved Mr. Park Yu-jeon's talents insomuch that he even bestowed a house upon him. We can only guess how Jeong Eung-min felt when he had learned of his teacher severing ties to this world immediately after Daewongun's passing.  After the death of Daewongun, who had loved pansori more than anyone else, the world of pansori went through a slump in the 1920s. Around this period, Mr. Jeong who traveled over Botjae for one last time, taught his students in Dogang Village before his life eventually came to its end. The title of Yi Chong-jun's novel, 『Seopyeonje』, writes, “To live is to accumulate sorrows, and to accumulate sorrows is to live.” The Yejeokbi Monument of Songgye Jeong Eung-min stands proudly in Dogang Village of Yeongcheon-ri, Hoecheon-myeon where Boseong Sori Village is.

stories.title: Buyongsan Mountain, Boseong - Buyongsan the Song
stories.audioTitle: Buyongsan Mountain, Boseong - Buyongsan the Song
stories.script: Buyongsan Mountain, Boseong - Buyongsan the Song  Elegy for a sister  In 1947, a young and beautiful woman, 24 in age, from Beolgyo passed away due to tuberculosis. After burying his sister, who had died at a young age, at the foot of Buyongsan Mountain, the poet coughed out his sorrow through bloody poetry. The name of this poet is Park Ki-dong, originally from Dolsan in Yeosu, Jeollanam-do. He moved to Beolgyo with his family when he was 11 years old following his father who was a doctor of Korean medicine. When he turned 14 years old, he went to study abroad in Japan at a young age where he finished middle school and eventually enrolled in the Department of English Literature at Kansai University. He was a brilliant student. Learning literature in Japanese was probably too much for him to bear. In 1943, he decided to discontinue his studies and returned to Korea where he wrote poems whenever he had a chance while also serving at first as a teacher  at Beolgyo Boys' Elementary School and then at Beolgyo Commercial Middle School and the Suncheon School of Education. He cared for his sister throughout his whole life so the news of her sudden death brought him heartbreaking sorrow. 〈Buyongsan〉was not only a funeral ode to his sister but also a poem of warm, sad tears shed by a brother who had to live the rest of his life with endless longing.  Buyongsan Ori-gil, only the grass is green In between the pine groves On a whirlwind You went Without any word A sick rose does not bloom and only withers Buyongsan peak, only the sky is blue  In 1948, the death of a student from Hangdo Girls’ Middle School in Mokpo buried the entire school in grief. The name of the 16-year-old girl full of dreams was Kim Jung-hee. A girl with literary sensibility so full she even won the grand prize at a national writing contest. The girl who passed away was also one of Poet Park Ki-dong's, who had been serving as a Korean teacher at this school for about a year, favorite students.  He was invited specially by the principal to teach the girl, who had been studying at the Gyeongseong School of Education, where many of the brilliant students were enrolled in, but transferred to Mokpo after Liberation. As everyone at the school, from the principal to all the students, faced deep sorrow at the news of the girl's sudden passing, the song, 〈Buyongsan〉, began to be heard throughout the school's campus. It was a tribute song that combined a poem written by Park Ki-dong, in remembrance of his sister's death, and a melody composed by Ahn Seong-hyeon, a music teacher at the school.  Coincidentally, Ahn also had lost his one and only 15-year-old sister around the same time that Park lost his. Ahn Seong-hyeon is the composer of a children's song known as 〈Mother, Sister〉, a famous poem of Kim So-wol. Ahn acted as the head of his household after his father, a master of the gayageum, defected to North Korea. It was no coincidence that he, who had been more devastated than anyone else after losing his obedient sister, became the composer of 〈Buyongsan〉.

stories.title: Buyongsan Mountain, Boseong - Buyongsan, Beolgyo
stories.script: Buyongsan Mountain, Boseong - Buyongsan, Beolgyo  Only the sky is blue in the distance  It did not take long for 〈Buyongsan〉, the song that was sung amongst the students of Hangdo Girls' Middle School, to overcome the school's walls. As people were deeply moved by the mournful melody and lyrics, the song spread quickly to the neighboring regions. During the tumultuous period, post Liberation, when the conflict between the Left and the Right was at its worst, North Korean partisans who were hiding in mountains sang this song as they thought of their hometowns.  As time passed, the song, Buyongsan, spread throughout the Honam region. This song was never officially released in an album but it perfectly empathized with the sorrowful sentiments of the Namdo people. Though the lyrics were slightly modified here and there, the song still spread quickly by mouth.  However, the situation unfolded in an unexpected way. The Rhee Syngman regime prohibited this song after the Yeosu–Suncheon rebellion on the grounds that the North Korean partisans enjoyed the song. In the midst of all this〈Buyongsan〉still survived as it was passed by mouth from one person to another. During the era of the democratization movement, it gained popularity as a protest song among university students.  So, as you can imagine, it was unavoidable for Po et Park Ki-dong to face imminent hardships. Ahn Seong-hyeon who married the daughter of Choi Seung-hee, a dancer who had defected to North Korea, went over to the north as well with his wife during the Korean War. Moreover, the fact that Park once signed a statement issued under the name of Namjoseon Educators' Association during his tenure at the Suncheon School of Education also followed him like a scarlet letter. As news that the composer of 〈Buyongsan〉had defected to North Korea, as well the song's lyricist being Park Ki-dong spread, searches of houses and close surveillance ensued endlessly. Eventually, Park left his home country and immigrated to the faraway foreign land of Australia where he lived a life of a poor immigrant until he became 80.  〈Buyongsan〉, tightly wrapped in its veil until the early 80s, finally had its prohibition lifted in 1987, when the song faced its turning point. Professor Kim Hyo-ja of Kyonggi University, one of Park's students at Hangdo Girls' Middle School, discovered the original copy of the song. Then, the story behind the birth of the song was explained in a newspaper, which helped it spread throughout the country.  Having wandered around only as a blacklisted song of protest by word of mouth, it has since touched the hearts of the people through the voices and albums of various singers including Han Young-ae, An Chi-hwan and Lee Dong-won. In Buyongsan, Beolgyo where the poet's sister lies, a poetry monument and the Buyongjeong Pavilion were established. And, in 2002, the song's 50th anniversary, Park returned home and published a book of his own essays titled 『Buyongsan』before his tumultuous, life of 87 years ended in Seoul in 2004.  Having had to depart the strenuous life of this world after leaving an elegy for a sister who withered like a flower without a goodbye, the poet finished the lyrics for the second verse of 〈Buyongsan〉 only in his later years.  Longing becomes a river flowing around my heart The sunset over the hill is already far away If it is a lily, your sweet dream is nowhere to be seen now Unable to turn around, I stand here all alone Only the sky is blue in Buyongsan in the distance

stories.title: Chae Dong-seon Music Hall, Boseong - Chae Dong-seon Music Hall
stories.audioTitle: Chae Dong-seon Music Hall, Boseong - Chae Dong-seon Music Hall
stories.script: Chae Dong-seon Music Hall, Boseong - Chae Dong-seon Music Hall  Songs of people's sorrows  Boseong is famous for its many singers since old times, and this history naturally led to Korean contemporary music. Mr. Chae Dong-seon was born in Beolgyo in 1901 and graduated from Gyeonggi Gobo. He started in the field of music by learning violin from Hong Nan-pa in 1918.  But he was expelled due to participating in the March 1st Movement in 1919, and went onto study at Waseda University in Japan and the Stern School of Music in Berlin, Germany before returning to Korea in 1929. He even refused to adopt a Japanese name and continued to build a foundation for Korean music. After Liberation, he also stressed unity among Korean musicians and formed the “Goryeo Music Association.” He composed symphonies like 〈Motherland〉, 〈Hangang River〉 and 〈Independence Celebration Song〉 as well as songs like 〈My Hometown〉 and 〈Until Peonies Bloom.〉  Chae Dong-seon's songs are much more meaningful as they were composed without the use of the styles that were popular at the time.  Not too long after Liberation, the Korean War broke out, and the war was a brutal reality even for the son of a wealthy family. Stories say that he barely survived in Busan where he had found refuge by selling American cigarettes and canned goods. He passed away in February 1953 due to malnutrition and pleurisy. Before he left to Busan, he had tightly sealed and buried his sheet music in his front yard so that no one could discover them.  10 years after his death, his wife Mrs. Lee So-ran, found these valuable materials, which could have very well gone missing over the course of the war, in the Seongbuk-dong house. Starting from 1999, Beolgyo residents have held small concerts every fall in memory of Mr. Chae Dong-seon.  The Chae Dong-seon Music Hall was built in 2007 by Boseong-gun to highlight and pay tribute to his world of music. The music hall has 344 seats for its audience and, in the exhibit room, the original copies of the sheet music, which were personally written by Mr. Chae and later found by his wife, Mrs. Lee So-ran, are on display.

stories.title: Chae Dong-seon Music Hall, Boseong - Chae Dong-seon’s Songs
stories.audioTitle: Chae Dong-seon Music Hall, Boseong - Chae Dong-seon’s Songs
stories.script: Chae Dong-seon Music Hall, Boseong - Chae Dong-seon’s Songs  Music that has persevered through the ages  〈My Hometown〉and 〈Missing You〉, two songs that we all know, are works of the Poets Jeong Ji-yong and Lee Eun-sang, respectively, yet they both use the same sheet music. When you also listen to 〈Nostaliga〉, with the different lyrics created by Poet Park Hwa-mok, the sorrowful melody still touches your hearts. What do you think is the reason behind using three different poems written by three different poets as the lyrics of a song composed by just a single person? This is because there was a poem that Mr. Chae Dong-seon particularly had in mind when composing this song.  If you visit Chae Dong-seon Music Hall, established in Beolgyo-eup in 2007, and go up to the second floor lobby, you will see 〈My Hometown〉, a poem by Jeong Ji-yong, on display. Written in calligraphy and hung inside a large frame, it exudes a sense of pride. 〈My Hometown〉was the poem that Mr. Chae had chosen when releasing this song in 1933. But, after the Korean War, the song was banned along with the poem of Jeong Ji-yong whose defection to North Korea had given him a scarlet letter, which is why it changed its lyrics to the poems of Lee Eun-sang and then Park Hwa-mok before finally returning to its original lyrics in 1988.  The time at which this song was released to the world was 1933, the height of Japanese exploitation. A collection of songs, filled with desperate nostalgia, that seemed to represent the sadness of our people, sold very well. Meanwhile, Mr. Chae refused to adopt a Japanese name and lived a life in seclusion to spend all his efforts in making gugak music. 〈Chunhyang and Yi Doryeong〉, 〈Hangeul Norae〉, 〈Hangeonnim〉, 〈Gaecheonjeol〉, 〈Song of Mugunghwa〉, 〈Seungpyeong Manse Jigok〉, 〈Ilche Tonggok〉…. They are all songs whose titles alone portray a certain message.  Because he sacrificed everything he had to preserve our valuable traditional music, even when the country had been handed over to Japan, forcing us to use their language and names, it is not undue to call him our proud national musician.

stories.title: Fossil Site of Dinosaur Eggs, Boseong - Fossil Site of Dinosaur Eggs, Deungnyang-myeon
stories.audioTitle: Fossil Site of Dinosaur Eggs, Boseong - Fossil Site of Dinosaur Eggs, Deungnyang-myeon
stories.script: Fossil Site of Dinosaur Eggs, Boseong - Fossil Site of Dinosaur Eggs, Deungnyang-myeon  Remnants of dinosaurs stimulating our imagination  Wherever you are in the world, dinosaurs are children’s favorite characters. In any business that targets children, whether it be cartoons, movies, games, stationery and characters, Dooly the Little Dinosaur is considered a guarantee for success. How interesting would it be to tell our children, fascinated by dinosaur cartoon characters and computer graphics, that there is a place where dinosaurs actually existed?  The Bibong-ri Fossil Site of Dinosaur Eggs, which spans 3㎞along the coast of Seonso in Deungnyang-myeon, is a living educational site where you can experience the reality of dinosaurs that had only existed in your imaginations before. It was September of 1988 when the fossil of a dinosaur egg, estimated to have existed in the late Cretaceous period of the Mesozoic Era, was discovered for the first time on the coast of Seonso. ​​Scholars who had been observing coastal rocks discovered here a nest of herbivorous dinosaurs and fossils of eggs that existed here at least 100 million years ago.  Some of the nests that contained at least six to thirty large and small fossilized dinosaur eggs were up to 1.5m in diameter, and some eggs with 8 to 12 overlapped layers of shells were discovered as well. This is an extremely rare case even throughout the world, and meets enough requirements to be listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.  At the entrance to the fossil site, the dinosaur's eggs and nests, which are in a near-perfect state of preservation, are widely distributed into 5 different regions. This place where about 20 dinosaur eggs have been found so far proves that the Korean Peninsula was one of the main habitats of East Asian dinosaurs during the Cretaceous period.　More than 10 locations for dinosaur egg's nests and 100 dinosaur egg　fossils are observed on the bedrock along the coast. The largest of the dinosaur egg nests are 1.5m in diameter, and the size of　the dinosaur egg fossil is 9to 15㎝ while the thickness of the　dinosaur eggshell is 1.5㎜ to 2.5㎜ . The shapes of the eggs are disciform, oval or globular, and the surfaces have uneven bumps or, in some cases, exhibit severe curvatures. Inside the dinosaur eggs, the dinosaur embryos or their skeletal structures were not found, which makes us estimate that they were fossilized after the eggs hatched.  The Fossil Site of Dinosaur Eggs in Bibong-ri, Boseong is not only evidence proving that the location was a habitat for dinosaur, but also an important and valuable source in revealing how and which dinosaurs lived here. The site was designated and is protected as a Natural Monument No. 418 as there is a possibility that fossils of other dinosaur eggs and additional data of ancient organisms may still be buried. Along with the Hwaseong Dinoistenesaur Site in Gojeong-ri, this site is one of the more well-known dinosaur egg fossil sites that have been discovered in relatively recent years. Therefore, this place has an interesting correlation with other major dinosaur remains on the South Coast, which are the Dinosaur Footprint Fossil Site of Uhang-ri, Haenam and Dinosaur Footprint Fossil Site of Deokmyeong-ri, Goseong, and is expected to contribute significantly to the restoration of the dinosaur ecological environment in Korea.  The small park set up around the dinosaur egg fossil site is popular among children because of its cutely shaped dinosaur mascot. The rock face where the fossilized dinosaur eggs were found is a crust layer with an unusual structure and features unique ad bumpy rocks that have many holes, big and small, and are purple in color. Another thing to do is to enjoy the purple shaped rocks that nature has created. Nearby is the Boseong Green Tea Field and Haesu Nokchatang so it is perfect for families to visit and tour around.

stories.title: Ganggol Village, Boseong - Ganggol Village, Deungnyang-myeon
stories.audioTitle: Ganggol Village, Boseong - Ganggol Village, Deungnyang-myeon
stories.script: Ganggol Village, Boseong - Ganggol Village, Deungnyang-myeon  The preciousness of things that do not change  In 2012, Ganggol Village was designated as the “Record Love Village No. 5”by the National Archives of Korea, the first of its kind in the Honam region. “Record Love Village” is a project that has been implemented by the National Archives of Korea since 2008 and aims to strengthen the foundation for preservation of archival materials that contain the villages' unique history and cultures, thus spreading the archival culture and the importance of managing archives.  Before a breakwater was installed in 1937 during the Japanese occupation period, sea water used to come up right to the village, which was subsequently called Ganggol or Gangdong. Ganggol Village is a typical country town. The Deungnyang Field spreads wide in front, and over the field, Deungnyang Bay, a repository blessed with a variety of marine products, stretches out. Because such a vast field and sea exist nearby, the village has enjoyed abundance from both land and sea, making it the wealthiest town in the region since old times.  Ganggol Village has preserved its original traditions and cultures including over 500 village archival materials like Wonam Gongyumuk, Sojakjeung and Sojakdaejang from which we can catch a glimpse of the village's history and the lives of residents from the early 1990s to the modern era. Also, the three houses of Yi Geum-jae, Yi Yong-uk and Yi Sik-rae as well as the Yeolhwajeong Pavilion were designated as important folk cultural properties. Also, “Record Love Village No. 5 Exhibit Hall,” located within Ganggol Village, stores and exhibits old documents from the early to late 1900s, that were collected by the Record Love Village Operating Committee, such as inspection records of the great-grandfather, the accounting book of Sojakjeung and Sojakryo, various receipts and farming diaries from Yi Sik-rae's Residence and the Achisil House, as well as election archival materials from the birthplace of the late Yi Jung-jae, and over 500 other tools related to daily life and farming.  In Ganggol Village, a family village of the Gwangju Yi Clan, about 30 traditional hanok buildings are neatly gathered together as they all face Obongsan Mountain. It is not a traditional town with just a facade; there are residents actually living here. As you step into the village, you will instantly feel as if you have traveled back in time.  Old roads, narrow alleys, deep wells, a bamboo forest, chimneys, and toenmaru still remain intact, to the point that when standing in the frontyard of one of these old houses, it feels strange to see tourists dressed in suits and dress shoes. There is an abundance of things to enjoy nearby ranging from Kalbawi Rock and Obongsan Mountain to Yongchu Waterfall, the mud flat and Boseong Tea Field, as well as the traditional culture experience, which features countryside meals, not to mention the mud flat experience run by the village, being a popular educational site for children. It is also one of the best location for foreigners to witness the traditional look of Korea.

stories.title: Yeolhwajeong Pavilion, Boseong - Yeolhwajeong Pavilion in Ganggol Village
stories.audioTitle: Yeolhwajeong Pavilion, Boseong - Yeolhwajeong Pavilion in Ganggol Village
stories.script: Yeolhwajeong Pavilion, Boseong - Yeolhwajeong Pavilion in Ganggol Village  A pavilion with its traditional landscaping preserved  A place you just cannot skip over in Ganggol Village is Yeolhwajeong Pavilion, which was built by Ijae Yi Jin-man to train students during the reign of King Heonjong of the Joseon Dynasty. At Yeolhwajeong, Yi Bang-hoe, a grandson of Yi Jin-man, talked about learning with Yi Geon-chang, praised as a great scholar of the time, and many others. Famous righteous army generals of the late Korean Empire days such as Yi Gwan-hoe, Yi Yang-rae and Yi Ung-rae were produced here.  Seated in the middle of a forest, up in the highest ground in the village, Yeolhwajeong faithfully follows the Korean traditional landscaping technique that maintains a forest surrounding the building to produce an aesthetic space. At the pavilion located in the east, there is a front gate with two pillars and a roof. Once you step into the gate, you will find a house with an L-shaped loft. Once you come into the front yard, there is a small pond and a well which forms natural harmony with the cherry blossom trees, magnolias, and bamboo trees in the garden to add to the grace and dignity. Leaning against the handrail of Yeolhwajeong Pavilion, it feels as though all my worries and concerns have disappeared from my head as I listen to the brisk sound of the wind coming in and out of the bamboo forest.  This place makes frequent appearances in movies and dramas because many directors love the fact that a filming set does not need to be newly built here. In 〈The Sword with No Name〉, a film by Director Kim Yong-gyun, elegant architectural beauty and an organized vibe unique to hanok is on full display through Yeolhwajeong, which is set as the house where Empress Myeongseong had lived before moving into the palace. In addition, the pavilion appeared in several other films including 〈Seopyeonje〉and 〈The Taebaek Mountains〉 by Director Im Kwon-taek, and 〈Blood Rain〉  by Director Kim Dae-seung.  While people these days yell, “Hurry, hurry”, and try their best to keep up with the speed of the world that seems to change every day, Ganggol Village quietly remains where it has been all along and makes us realize the value of being steady and not changing so easily.

stories.title: Boseong Hyanggyo
stories.script: Boseong Hyanggyo  Striking terror into the hearts of the Japanese Government-General  Since the old times, Hyanggyo has been an important educational institutions of the country similar to today's public schools in different regions. The true purpose of Hyanggyo was to develop local talents with government expenditure. Though they all had different building sizes, all Hyanggyo around the country were built in the same structure as Seonggyungwan in Seoul. A typical Hyanggyo consists of Munmyo where scholars held funeral rituals for Confucius, Myeongnyundang where they studied, Daeseongjeon that enshrines ancestral tablets of saints, and even a dormitory.  Boseong Hyanggyo, which was originally constructed in the 6th year of King Taejo's reign during the Joseon Dynasty (1397), was burnt down during the Jeongyu Wars but, after relocation to its current whereabouts, it underwent numerous repairs. In front of Myeongnyundang at Boseong Hyanggyo, which has many stories to tell over the course of its long history, you will see a memorial stone that you cannot find at any other Hyanggyo. I am of course talking about“Yurim Hangil Sajeokbi.” The establishment of an anti-Japan memorial stone in a Hyanggyo, an institution made purely for education, stemmed from the “Boseong Hyanggyo Ritual Wine Distress Incident.” The incident began when Japan ruled ritual wine for Confucian shrines in Hyanggyo as bootleg liquor on the grounds of the Liquor Tax Law,  a law promulgated in 1907 by the Japanese. Its primary objective was to prohibit all liquor making at homes, leading to more taxes collected and extermination of our traditional customs. They even banned our people from brewing wine that was offered to our ancestors during funeral rituals. It was such an evil law for people who had faithfully obeyed the tradition of presenting diligently brewed wine up to the meals of our ancestors on every national holiday and memorial service. Another hidden goal of the Liquor Tax Law was to  track down anti-Japanese activists. Under the pretext of cracking down on bootleg liquor, Japanese officials frequently encroached upon private homes whenever they wanted to look for any suspicious activities or individuals. Hyanggyo was no exception.  In August 1921, Boseong Hyanggyo was preparing a ritual ceremony to get ready for Seokjeonje, one of the most important events in Confucianism. During Seokjeonje, people held rituals for Confucius as well as 4 Seong, 10 Cheol and 18 Hyeon at Munmyo on Sangjeongil in February and August every year. The Confucian scholars of Boseong Hyanggyo had secretly brewed ritual wine to be used for Munmyodaeje. However, a Japanese official suddenly rushed into the Hyanggyo, knowing of the fact that wine was a must-have element during ancestral rites. The official insisted that the Hyanggyo violated the Liquor Tax Law and committed an atrocious act of sealing the ritual wine on the day of a great ceremony. This naturally resulted in an uprising of infuriated scholars.

stories.title: Boseong Hyanggyo - Ritual Wine Distress Incident
stories.audioTitle: Boseong Hyanggyo - Ritual Wine Distress Incident
stories.script: Boseong Hyanggyo - Ritual Wine Distress Incident  Confucian scholars who defended the tradition  The Confucian scholars tied up the Japanese official whose disrespect had crossed the line, placed him up on a pile of firewood, and proclaimed that a burning ceremony would be carried out if the Japanese do not remedy the situation. Surprised at the news, the Japanese police station chief came running with his men. They lay down flat on the grounds of the Hyanggyo garden and bowed many times as an apology.  The naive scholars accepted this apology from the police station chief and released the official who had caused the issues, however, as soon as he stepped out of the Hyanggyo, the police station chief requested the provincial police headquarters for more men. Soon, a few dozen policemen broke into the Hyanggyo and arrested the scholars. A few days later, all 70 scholars who were present at the scene received brutal torture for interfering with an officer in his line of duty as well as for the violation of the Liquor Tax Law. The torture was done to make the scholars admit their guilt. Despite severe intimidation and appeasement by the Japanese police, the scholars did not yield,  and the incident magnified significantly. All Confucian scholars in Boseong gathered at the Hyanggyo and held a protest to accuse the Japanese police of brutality and to demand for the abolition of the Liquor Tax Law. Moreover, they sent out Gyeonggo Paldo Hyanggyo Tongmun, a writing that appeals to all Confucian scholars in the country for a general rally. An incident that took place in a small Hyanggyo in the Honam region evolved into a catalyst that incited the anti-Japanese spirits in all scholars of Joseon and, subsequently, terrified the Japanese Government-General. Having already been smacked across the face by the March 1st Movement, the Government-General eventually released all prisoners in just one year and ten months after the incident.  But this did not cool down the powerful anti-Japan sentiments that had spread like a wildfire amongst the scholars. In the end, the Japanese government held an emergency cabinet meeting during which they decided to replace the governor-general and at the same time declared a partial amendment of the Liquor Tax Law which allowed Hyanggyos and scholars to brew the liquor used specifically for rituals and ceremonies. The “Boseong Hyanggyo Ritual Wine Distress Incident”, which forced Japan to take a step back and even amend its laws, was a feat achieved by the unity among all local Hyanggyos and scholars around the country.  Today, Boseong Hyanggyo has installed a Confucianism college in Chunghyo Hoegwan to be able to utilize it for a variety of social education. Notable projects include Giroyeon, which invites local senior citizens every spring and fall and prays for their long, illness-free lives, and General Choi Dae-seong Memorial Ceremony. Loyalty and filial piety are the foundations of Confucianism. Even as generations pass, Boseong Hyanggyo still practices the unchanging duties of mankind and services as the protector of beautiful traditions.

stories.title: Boseong Honggyo - Beolgyo Honggyo, Sohwa Bridge
stories.audioTitle: Boseong Honggyo - Beolgyo Honggyo, Sohwa Bridge
stories.script: Boseong Honggyo - Beolgyo Honggyo, Sohwa Bridge  Walking over the shackles of history  Designated as Treasure No. 304, Honggyo is the scene of pain that still maintains the scars of our history marred by confrontation between the Left and Right after Liberation. Here, countless gunshots were fired and many people died in vain.  Honggyo, which still has a defined arch-type structure along with the Seungseongyo at Seonamsa Temple, has a shape in which a semicircular arch supports the bridge. A stone carved in the shape of a dragon’s head protrudes downward at the midpoint of the ceiling underneath the bridge. During the old days, a wind chime used to be hung at the tip of the dragon’s nose, which generated a soft tinkling of the bell. Considering both its scale and aesthetic beauty, it is considered the best among the existing arch bridges. Installed where the river water of Beolgyocheon meets the seawater, Honggyo exposes most of its bottom at a low tide and, once water flows in, most of the bridge is submerged.  In Buddhism, building a bridge for people to travel conveniently is considered as the so-called “Wolcheon Gongdeok,” the greatest offering one can make. Until the days of King Sukjong's reign during the Joseon Dynasty, a floating bridge made of hardwood existed here, and Beolgyo's name is also derived from this floating bridge. Then, in 1728 during King Yeongjo's reign, the floating bridge collapsed due to a great flood in the Jeollanam-do region, and there is a record saying that, in the following year, monks named Choanseonsa and Seupseong of Seonamsa made an offering to build a stone bridge. The bridge went through repairs since then, and that is what we see today.  On the five headstones standing next to Honggyo, the records of the origin and repairs of the bridge are engraved. Unfortunately, it is difficult to decipher the headstones because the letters are severely worn. Only three headstones constructed in 1737, 1844 and 1899 are somewhat readable.  If you walk down for about 100m from Honggyo, you will see Buyonggyo Bridge (also known as Sohwa Bridge), which was built during the Japanese colonial era. The novel, 『The TaeBaek Mountains』, narrates the tragedy of a fratricidal war that took place on this bridge during the Yeosu-Suncheon Rebellion.  The indifferent river water speaks of nothing and the bridge carrying painful scars of our people continues to silently connect the daily lives of the Beolgyo people from here to there even today.

stories.title: Nodong-myeon, Boseong - Nodong-myeon Village Story
stories.script: Nodong-myeon, Boseong - Nodong-myeon Village Story  A story of a village name  Feng Shui geography-wise, Nodong-myeon is Bianhamno, or a shape of a wild goose flying with a reed leaf, and is formed centered around Garisil Village known to have Myeonghyeolji of Oknyeobongban, which is how it acquired the name, Nodong-myeon. It borders Jangpyeong-myeon of Jangheung-gun to the west and neighbors Boseong-eup and Miryeok-myeon to the south.  Byeokoksan Mountain in Yongho-ri, Nodong-myeon are known for magnificent clouds and mist that spreads below the mountain in October and November every year. It is also where many photographers visit to capture the beautiful landscape in images. In the old times, it is said that Sanjeok, or bandits, often made appearances in the valleys of Byeokoksan. Stories say that one day a monk who was passing by the valley built a temple to edify the bandits. This temple is Wollimsa, or also known as Byeokoksa. Wollimsa was originally constructed during the early Goryeo Period and lasted for about 400 years but was destroyed during the Japanese invasion of 1592.  The five-story stone pagoda located in the Wollimsa Site in Okma-ri is called Byeokoktap, which is known to have been built during the late Goryeo Dynasty, and the village where the Okma-ri Five-story Stone Pagoda stands used to be called as Tap-dong. It was designated as Provincial Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 141 in 1986.  There are many interesting stories behind the name of Nodong-myeon. For instance, the original name of Musaengi Village of Daeryeon-ri was “Moreumji.” Named by one great monk who was passing by the area and realized that the mountain in front of the village resembled a horse's shade. Then, later during the reign of King Jungjong of Joseon, a member of the royal family was exiled to this area. While in exile, he realized how deep in the mountains the village was located and how only a small number of people came and went, so he called the village Musa, which means, in Chinese characters, “a place that no one knows.”  Jeogyeongol of Daeryeon-ri was initially named due to the presence of Myeonghyeol of Yeonhwadosu but, every year, red lotus flowers are in full bloom in the Gochisil Reservoir here, which is why it is also written as “Jeokryeon.” Moreover, Hagamjeong Village in Geumho-ri used to be called Gamjeong-dong, meaning“the water of the well is sweet.” Since the old times, the well located in the middle of the village was known for its sweet and tasty water. For people of the village, this water still serves as a source of drinking water.  Meanwhile, Daeyeo Village of Geumho-ri has a name that highlights a page of its sad history. It was during the reign of King Sejong when the village came to have its name. In the early stages of the Joseon Dynasty, politically tumultuous events took place frequently. Mrs. Wonju Yi, the wife of Sujumoksa Son Chaek who settled in the area away from all the turmoil, later told her children not to get involved with any government positions or get entangled with the turbulent age. Out of hope that her children would live with the same mindset and heart for generations later, she named the village Daeyeo.

stories.title: Donda Village, Boseong - Donda Village, Geumho-ri
stories.audioTitle: Donda Village, Boseong - Donda Village, Geumho-ri
stories.script: Donda Village, Boseong - Donda Village, Geumho-ri  Story of Son In-guk  Donda Village of Geumho-ri was named after the five brothers of the Park family who were the first ones to live in the village and showed immense love and respect for their parents and each other. Although the village in which he is born is not specified, there is a story in Nodong-myeon about another son with great love for his parents - Son In-guk, the 8th-generation son of Gaseondaebu Hong Yun.  In 1813, Son was born in Nodong-myeon during the reign of King Sunjo. His father passed away when he was young, leaving him to devotedly serve his single mother. Years passed and it was the winter of 1853, the 4th year of King Cheoljong’s reign. When he reached 40 years of age, his mother suffered from a severe case of malaria. A great son with much love for his mother, Son visited every well-known clinic and pharmacy to try everything but her condition only became more and more critical.  One day, Son heard of a doctor far over the mountain whose medical skills were said to be phenomenal, so he rushed to pay him a visit. The doctor told Son that he had to feed her tiger meat.
