How could he possibly catch a tiger by himself? As Son headed home while lamenting with a deep sigh, his eyes suddenly opened wide in surprise. A tiger that had recently passed was lying down on the mountain road. He took home a leg of the tiger at once and saved his mother who was in critical condition.  Son's mother eventually passed away during the following year. He wanted to serve his mother in good health and with devotion but her death greatly disappointed the son. Son missed his mother so much to the point where the sadness took a physical toll on his body. To make things worse, Son's older brother also became bedridden for many years. He nursed his brother with all his heart and never left his side. When his brother’s condition still became critical, Son even stopped eating and shed tears all day long.  People of the village who were touched by Son's filial piety and brotherly love informed the government about him and recommended that he be awarded a prize. Then in 1875, the 12th year of King Gojong's reign, the rank of Tongjeongdaebu Dangsanggwan was presented to Son according to the records from 『Boseong History of People』. The story involving the tiger's leg might be a bit of an exaggeration but, given that there is a record of him being given a government position, the love and respect Son In-guk had for his mother was probably true.

stories.title: Boseong Myeongbong Station - Myeongbong Station in Nodong-myeon
stories.audioTitle: Boseong Myeongbong Station - Myeongbong Station in Nodong-myeon
stories.script: Boseong Myeongbong Station - Myeongbong Station in Nodong-myeon  Train station within our memories where a phoenix cried  As a village with warm legends, Nodong-myeon generally has a cozy and stable vibe. The poem, 〈Station where Birds Cry〉, written by Poet Moon Chung-hee originally from Homi Village in Hakdong-ri, Nodong-myeon, Boseong-gun, is Sweden's Cikada Prize winner of 2007. The station where birds cry where my father and I parted last, and the station where a phoenix cries after seeing the icy road ahead is Myeongbong Station located in Myeongbong-ri, Nodong-myeon, Boseong-gun.  Myeong means to cry and Bong means a phoenix. Phoenixes cry because the male and female are  separated from each other. The birds had their wings bound with the Myeongbongcheon Stream between them. Thus, the male phoenix and the female phoenixes became rocks facing each other from the mountain village behind Bonghwachon and Bongdong Village, respectively. And, to this day, the birds cry every day as they miss each other dearly.  Myeongbong Station whose name means a station of crying birds according to a story of feng shui geography is now a temporary station forgotten in people’s memories. People began to visit this small rural station, that did not even have a ticketing office, as it became a popular spot for filming movies and dramas such as the 〈Summer Scent. 〉 A temporary station in itself makes one sentimental. What coexists in the temporary station is the loneliness or longing for the times cannot travel back to and the sadness for a space that will eventually disappear without a trace.  The original title of 〈Station where Birds Cry〉, which contains Poet Moon Chung-hee’s affectionate love towards her father as she left him to go to Seoul to study at the age of 14, is 〈Myeongbong Station. 〉 An unmanned station without any station staff today, Myeongbong Station first opened in December 1930. A building with over 80 years of history blends with the typical rural landscape to create an atmosphere that looks like a scene from a movie.  As you walk past a huge mural painted by someone, probably to fill the emptiness of the unmanned station before stepping into the building, a long wooden bench, quite rare to see these days, offers you a seat. By pressing your camera shutter at any direction within the station building, the picture instantly becomes a magnificent painting.  By the time white ume flowers are in full bloom and armful cherry trees stretch out their branches on the way to Myeongbong Station, the quiet village approaches your heart as a beautiful fairy tale. Anyone who takes a look around would understand why directors of dramas and films covet this area. Myeongbong Station is definitely one of Boseong’s valuable cultural contents.

stories.title: Boseong Yulpo Beach - Seawater Green Tea Spa at Yulpo Solbat Beach
stories.audioTitle: Boseong Yulpo Beach - Seawater Green Tea Spa at Yulpo Solbat Beach
stories.script: Boseong Yulpo Beach - Seawater Green Tea Spa at Yulpo Solbat Beach  Romance and health at the same time   Selected as one of the “Top 3 Excellent Beaches in the country”by the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs in 2012, Yulpo Solbat Beach boasts things people can enjoy that is not found anywhere else in Korea - the one and only seawater green tea spa. Seawater green tea is a completely novel concept of bath culture that has combined seawater brought up from the rock formation 120m underground with good quality Boseong tea leaves. It is more reliable since it is a business directly run by Boseong-gun.  The seawater green tea spa well utilizes the characteristics and natural environment of the region where green team is very common and is also well-suited to the needs of modern people who value health. How fascinating it is to enjoy a seawater spa while admiring the beautiful white sand of Yulpo Solbat Beach and the sunset glow in the evening. Another point that attracts people to the seawater spa is its small size, which means that only a handful of people are able to use it at the same time. This means that it can be enjoyed in a cleaner and more elegant manner.  It has been revealed by an official verification agency that the Yulpo Seawater Green Tea Spa contains over 10 times more potassium and magnesium than the seawater in other regions. This proves its great affinity with the human skin. The seawater from the underground rock in Yulpo, which is used for the spa, does not contain any harmful substances that it can even be developed as drinking water as long as the salinity is removed. It is a beautiful gift from the sea.

stories.title: Beolgyo Boseong Inn
stories.script: Beolgyo Boseong Inn  A lodging in time   Boseong Inn became a famous attraction of Beolgyo since the establishment of the Taebaek Mountain Range Literary Museum at the foot of Jeseoksan Mountain in Beolgyo-eup in November 2008. Its outward appearance is still the same when compared to the days when it was the setting of a novel. Most people who visit here are tourists from other areas.  For tourists who did not live through the harsh, rigorous era, perhaps it may be remembered simply as a space that brings forth cinematic imagination. Elderly tourists are often seen here. Some of them may have lived here in the past or have connections through parents or relatives. There are things that are not erased even as time passes by and worlds change. Some may fall into deep, sudden contrition as they stand in front of a building that still holds the same appearance from old times. The street corner of Boseong Inn, which has kept its place since the Japanese occupation period, is a space that gives you much to reflect on.  Boseong Inn was first built in 1935. It is a wooden, two-story structure with a design that mixes the Korean and Japanese styles. There were ten rooms on the first floor and four large rooms with the tatami floor, which could also be opened up to be used as one huge space. From the second floor, you can have a clear view of the schoolyard of Beolgyo Elementary School. During every National Assembly member election, candidates stood inside the room on the second floor, treating it like a makeshift podium, and made speeches to the crowd gathered in the schoolyard. Regarded as a five-star hotel at the time, it used to be the largest accommodation in Boseong-gun until the early 1980s.  Today, the first floor is utilized as a cafe and an exhibit space, and the second floor decorated as a four-cell Japanese-style tatami room is used as a multi-purpose cultural experience space. A building used as accommodations is also decorated in the Japanese tatami style and located in the back. It is a good place to travel back in time as you look around the different scenes that are backdrops do novels such as Honggyo Bridge, ​​Sohwa Bridge, Boseong Financial Association, Hyunbuja's House, Sohwa's House and Kim Bum-woo's House.

stories.title: Beolgyo, Boseong - Premium Boseong Sambe
stories.script: Beolgyo, Boseong - Premium Boseong Sambe  Masterpiece created by the hands of masters   Cut the hemp, cut the hemp Cut the hemp with fingernails over a thousand time a day As soft hemp cloth is cut again and again, even the spade has been cut My once-lovely hands have become that of a man’s  It is a part of 〈Samjjaegi Norae〉 that talks about the hardships and sorrow of the women making cloth. An old saying has it that Boseong girls never get married to Boknae because it was evident that they would grow old and die after working all their lives to make cloths.  Boseong Sambe, or hemp cloth, is a specialty product of the region that is also registered as Geographical Indication No. 45. If you look closely at the manufacturing process, you will understand why Boseong women did not want to marry men whose families were rooted inn the hemp cloth making business. Regarded as a masterpiece among all traditional Sambe products, Boseong Sambe has reproduced the traditional manufacturing techniques to make Sambe, which means it goes through an extremely difficult and arduous process. It is not something people in today's world would love to learn and it is even tougher to find those who will perform the work.  From the beginning to the end, there is not a single stage within the entire process of making Boseong Sambe that does not require a human intervention. Workers put their hearts into every stitch and embroidery. Also, the process completely rejects chemical dyes and, instead, only uses natural dyes of 100% purity that are collected in the wild. This means obtaining the raw materials is not an easy task. Possessing traditional colors that are elegant and simple, Boseong Sambe is shared with the world thanks to the sweat- and blood-filled hands of the masters who strive to protect our traditions.  Boseong Sambe is regarded as a premium masterpiece anywhere in the country. It is sold at a higher price than typical Sambe but the supply cannot keep up with the demand. It is more critical to find workers than to sell the products. Fortunately, the elderly of the village still carry out the tradition and life of Boseong Sambe. Their craftsmanship and devotion to protecting our valuable tradition amidst all the difficulties and hardships is something that we cannot help but admire.

stories.title: Beolgyo, Boseong - Boseong Deombeongi
stories.script: Beolgyo, Boseong - Boseong Deombeongi  Premium pottery made with unique techniques  Boseong, famous for being the largest green tea plantation in Korea, also has the finest tea cups, which are known as “Deombeongi”, a kind of Buncheong ware. Deombeongi is a combination of “Deombeong”, an orginal Korean word, and “i.” It got its name because of the way the ceramic object is made with clay and then dunked, or “Deombeong,” into white clay water for decoration.  Ever since a Deombeongi kiln site was discovered in Deungnyang during the Japanese occupation era, it was called “hozokobiki” in Japan. However, a local potter who reproduced the Boseong Buncheong ware in 2007 affixed a new original Korean name to it. The reason that it is more famous in Japan even though it is our own indigenous ceramic products stems from historical facts.  Deombeongi requires an extremely difficult manufacturing technique that has a high failure rate as it must be cooked in a kiln at least three times. What do you think led to the emergence of such an inefficient pottery technique in a period when white porcelain was already widely manufactured and used? Towards the end of the 15th century, there was a time when the use of white porcelain in private homes was banned temporarily. As Joseon’s Sagijang, or ceramic making masters, were no longer able to produce white porcelain, they used a new technique to create Buncheong ware that gave a similar feel as white porcelain. A few pieces of bowls made in this method found their way to Japan before and after the Japanese invasion of 1592, and they became popular among the Japanese ruling class as they began to be used as tea bowls for drinking matcha.  As you can see, Boseong Deombeongi is a very rare kind of teacup that emerged suddenly at a specific point in time and was produced for about a generation before ceasing to exist. Boseong Deombeongi is special because not only is it high in scarcity but it also contains unique manufacturing techniques that you cannot find anywhere else. Most of the celadon, Buncheong ware, white porcelain and blackware produced in the Korean Peninsula were from ceramic-making techniques that had been introduced from China. However, Deombeongi, which was produced primarily in Boseong as well as in Goheung and Jangheung in the late 15th century, was made from our own ceramic-making method that existed nowhere else in the world, even in China. It is a proud cultural heritage of not just the Boseong area but also our nation.  Boseong Deombeongi is excellent in function as well as aesthetic beauty. Deombeongi, which is made of weathered clay of elvan containing plenty of metallic oxides, has the function of neutralizing tannin that produces the bitterness in green tea to purify the tea's taste. Also, even if water is kept in the bowl for a long time, the water doesn't go bad because the bowl itself breathes. In particular, once you pour tea water into a cup, a water flower blooms inside the cup, and Deombeongi is the best premium tea ceremony tool in which which you can enjoy an elegant scene of the water flower blooming. So Manbojeonseo, which is the oldest book of tea in Japan, even praised it as “on the greatest level created by humans.”  As you can see from the background of its creation, Boseong Deombeongi was not a work of art that sought the highest level of perfection from the beginning. It was a byproduct created by the Joseon’s Sagijang in place of white porcelain in their attempt to survive in the changing environment and, from the perspective of the product, it is an unfinished piece of work. However, countless changes stemming from the imperfections have given birth to unique beauty and functionality that no one could have ever expected. Boseong Deombeongi is considered as ceramic pieces of the highest elegance in the famously picky tea circles and the antique art business of Japan as well as China, Europe, and America. This is because of the beauty that is presented by such unexpected possibilities.  Deombeongi contains the sorrow of Joseon's grassroots and the affectionate energy and life of the people of Boseong. The fact that world-class ceramics were born in Boseong is a great cultural heritage of the region. If Deombeongi continues to be developed as a great partner to Boseong green tea, it will be able to contribute greatly to promoting Boseong’s unique tea culture.

stories.title: Miryeok-myeon, Boseong -  Miryeok Onggi and Cheonggwang Doye
stories.audioTitle: Miryeok-myeon, Boseong -  Miryeok Onggi and Cheonggwang Doye
stories.script: Miryeok-myeon, Boseong -  Miryeok Onggi and Cheonggwang Doye  Dishes and bowls that hold art and practicality   If you visit Dogae-ri, Miryeok-myeon, you will realize our traditional living onggi, or earthenware, is more diverse than you think. Boasting a 300-year old history over nine generations, Miryeok Onggi does not use any glaze but only natural lyes. Mr. Lee Hak-su, the Onggijang or artisan of earthenware (Important Intangible Cultural Property No. 96) currently runs the Miryeok Onggi experience site following in his father's footsteps, the late Lee Ok-dong. An exhibit hall and a workshop are also available there.  Meanwhile, Cheonggwang Doye is a ceramics workshop where Potter Kim Ki-chan makes and cooks bowls, teacups, dishes and Moon Jars. In addition to the ceramics workshop where the potter performs his work, there is also a hanok pension. Inside you can also find a ceramics exhibit hall and a traditional tea house that also serves as a restaurant specializing in delicious Namdo cuisine.  Between Mongjungsan Mountain and Cheonggwang Doye, the green tea field owned by the Juksan Ahn Clan, a renowned family in Boseong, lies on a slope. This is why it is a perfect place where you can experience ceramics as well as enjoy the traditional hanok’s peace and comfort as well as tasty teas and indigenous foods that Namdo has to offer. As you settle in the open space inside the teahouse, you feel as if you are sitting on top of the tiled roofs of the hanok below your feet, and the mountains fill up the windows in a broad and open view in the distance, giving you true sight to see.

stories.title: Juwolsan Mountain, Boseong - Juwolsan Paragliding Experience Site
stories.audioTitle: Juwolsan Mountain, Boseong - Juwolsan Paragliding Experience Site
stories.script: Juwolsan Mountain, Boseong - Juwolsan Paragliding Experience Site  Running on the sky   In 『Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam』, a mountain was named Juwolsan after the phrase “a boat climbed over it.” ​Now, it has become a mountain in which a man is able to float around in the sky. On weekends, the shouts of youth, flying up in the air and decorating the Boseong sky in a splendid way, echoes throughout the mountain of Juwolsan. If you look at the colorful paragliders in the sky above the blue mountain and sea of Boseong before your eyes, it looks like a choreographed dance of large birds with extensive wings.  There is a saying that the term, world, is Sesang in Korean because it consists of three images or Sang. It means that the world seen from the ground, the world seen from the sky, and the world seen from under the sea are all different. As people’s desires for leisure and sports have diversified, paragliding is becoming increasingly popular among the younger generation. Currently we are in the era of self-satisfaction. Even those who had fear a flying, thought the equipment was too expensive, or simply assumed that paragliding was a luxurious hobby are ready to make bold investments for new experiences.  Every human being has a desire to soar high. It could be a simple dream of physical flight or even just a psychological desire. Paragliding is a healthy flying activity that can satisfy these two elements at once. Looking at the ecstatic faces of those leaving the Juwolsan Paragliding Experience Site are enough to make anyone feel great as well. They are the ones who have already experienced two of the three worlds that a human can experience.

stories.title: Na Cheol of Boseong - Hongam Na Cheol
stories.audioTitle: Na Cheol of Boseong - Hongam Na Cheol
stories.script: Na Cheol of Boseong - Hongam Na Cheol  Living two lives with a single belief  Originally from Geumgok Village in Childong-ri, Beolgyo-eup, Boseong-gun, Jeollanam-do, Mr. Hongam Na Cheol is a pioneer who founded Daejonggyo upon being a great teacher to our people. When a country is in crisis, the lives of individuals cannot help but be powerless much like a candle in the wind. But he wholeheartedly resisted the oppression and let the entire world know his will for restoring national rights, striving to revive the dying Joseon.  Having lived 53 years of fiery life, he chose two different paths as a politician and a religious leader to live one life as Na In-yeong and the other as Na Cheol. Na In-yeong is his original name and Na Cheol is the name he changed to when founding Daejonggyo. They say, Cometh the hour cometh the man. 1863, the year in which he was born, was when King Gojong was enthroned and, at the same time, Heungseon Daewongun's regency began. During this period, Joseon was a center stage of heated competition among imperialistic world powers, and 1891, the year in which Mr. Na passed the Daegwa examination, was when the impure ambitions of Japan that eagerly sought to take over Joseon was at its peak.  It is an improvised poem narrated at a poetry meeting in Namsan where officials of high levels were in attendance because of Hongam, in his 20s, who had come to Seoul with the dream of rising in ranks. This poem, which represented the agony of young intellectuals who are lost within the raging waves of the era, instantly captivated Kim Yun-sik, a great scholar of the time. Mr. Na then came under Kim Yun-sik's wings, passed the Daegwa examination at the age of 28, and served as an official of Seungjeongwon and Seungmunwon. Then, in April 1895, he became the head of a tax office but soon quit. As his teacher, Kim Yun-sik, was involved in the murder of Empress Myeongseong and exiled to Jeju, Mr. Na followed and served his teacher.  In February 1904, Japan forced Joseon to sign the Japan–Korea Treaty and had its policy of colonizing Joseon approved or overlooked by the U.S., the U.K., and Russia. Emperor Gojong refused to sign the treaty and attempted to protect the country's sovereignty but the fate of the nation was already on an irrevocable decline. Determined to come face-to-face with the reality in which the fate of his country was placed in the last extremity, Mr. Na formed an underground organization known as Yusinhoe together with patriots from the Honam region to start a national salvation movement.

stories.title: Na Cheol of Boseong - Na In-yeong, National Salvation Activist
stories.audioTitle: Na Cheol of Boseong - Na In-yeong, National Salvation Activist
stories.script: Na Cheol of Boseong - Na In-yeong, National Salvation Activist  The path of a country in decline  One of the first activities was to go to Japan and convince the Japanese emperor and the senior foreign affairs statesmen. In June 1905, just before the Eulsa Treaty was signed, he sent letters to the Japanese government as well as Ito Hirobumi, demanding that Joseon, Japan, and Qing form a mutual alliance for peace in the East. Furthermore, he also wished for the sovereignty of Joseon to be assured and respected. However, already bold and impertinent enough to pressure the emperor of a nation in forcing him to sign a treaty, Japan looked down upon Joseon and its exploitation was not going to be stopped by anything. Mr. Na held a three-day fasting demonstration in front of the Japanese royal palace to urge the emperor and government officials to do something about the situation but he did not receive any responses.  Meanwhile, a humiliating event had been taking place in Joseon. Ito Hirobumi led a few dozens of his Japanese military policemen into Deoksugung Palace and pressured the Joseon ministers to sign the so-called Eulsa Treaty. Mr. Na's fury had now then targeted the traitors of Joseon. Unable to suppress the bitter grief and sorrow, Mr. Na returned home with two swords to be used to punish the traitors, although he did not execute his plan right away. Instead, he decided to go to Japan one more time in 1906. During this visit, he met with groups that were the in opposition of Ito Hirobumi and urged them to interfere with the Japanese government's policy to colonize Joseon.  But, at the end of the day, they were Japanese as well and were not willing to stand up for Joseon. Unfortunately, he came home with not much accomplished. But, on the way back from his second visit to Japan, he came back with a bomb that he had kept hidden. Soon after his return, he rallied his comrades including Oh Ki-ho and Park Dae-ha to form Jasinhoe and, as their first project, they resolved to take care of the traitors who painted the future of their country and their people dark with their own hands. Formed in February 1907, Jasinhoe was a group that had over 200 members that sought to enlighten the people while fighting against the Japanese. Mostly consisting of enlightened officials from the Honam region, Jasinhoe included followers of the late Chungjeonggong Min Young-hwan who showed resistance to the Eulsa Treaty with his own death. Many of Chungjeonggong's followers were former government officials from Seoul or generals of the anti-Japan righteous armies, and they sought to restore national sovereignty by raising an army. Mr. Na persuaded them to organize the Five Eulsa Traitors assassination team.  But, after many twists and turns, the assassination attempts ultimately failed. Armed with pistols, the assassination squad members given different roles and responsibilities were commanded to stake out near the traitors’ residences, at Seodaemun and Gwanghwamun, but the faithful day was postponed twice and eventually led to a leak of intelligence. Not only that, but members who had failed to kill Gwon Jung-hyeon were captured, which unfortunately led to most members of the group being arrested.

stories.title: Na Cheol of Boseong - Na Cheol, Religious Leader
stories.audioTitle: Na Cheol of Boseong - Na Cheol, Religious Leader
stories.script: Na Cheol of Boseong - Na Cheol, Religious Leader  Founding Daejonggyo  The July 2, 1909 edition of Daehan Maeil Sinbo printed an article that said, “Mr. Na In-yeong and Oh Ki-ho have recently given up all political activities and, now, only devote to and serve in the religious world with the goal to promote a national religion.” After facing limits of his roles as a politician, Mr. Na decided to start a new kind of independence movement. The path he chose was to resurrect Dangungyo and uniting all national spirits. He also changed his name from Na In-yeong to Na Cheol.  Together with those who shared the same view, he held a harvest ritual in Jae-dong, Seoul, and officially proclaimed the beginning of Dangungyo. Dangungyo claimed to be a national religion that sought the equality of humans and world peace based on humanitarian ideals and saw its number of believers rise to 20,000 in just a year.  In 1910, Joseon became completely deprived of its national sovereignty in the aftermath of Gyeongsul Gukchi and was incorporated into Japan as a colony by force. As it became difficult to evangelize in Korea due to the Japanese’ oppression, Daejonggyo relocated its headquarters to Manchuria. Based on his immense interest surrounding education, Mr. Na established the Bakdal Institute,  ongchang School, Baeksan School and Daejong Institute to instill the love for our people and the spirit of independence. He also formed numerous anti-Japan movement groups, most notably, Jeonguidan, Bukro Gunjeongseo, Sinminbu and Seoro Gunjeongseo. Most soldiers of Bukro Gunjeongseo who were the heroes of the Battle of Qingshanli were Daejonggyo believers.  As Daejonggyo became the head temple for the independence movement, the number of its believers grew to 300,000. Threatened by the explosive expansion of the religion, Japan announced its plans to control religions in 1915. It was a scheme to illegalize Daejonggyo, a religion of the Joseon people, and neutralize its will and vigor to fight against Japan. Japan classified Daejonggyo not as a religion but as an anti-Japan organization, thus prohibiting all of its propagation activities. This was the biggest crisis Daejonggyo had faced, and Mr. Na became determined to execute one last resistance with his life on the line.  One day in August 1916, he went to worship at Samseongdan in Guwolsan Mountain, Hwanghae-do Province. After a harvest ceremony finished up, he grieved about the brutality of Japan and chose the path of martyrdom. Soon after, his two sons, Na Jeong-ryeon and Na Jeong-mun, also passed away at Mokdangang Prison with the sorrow of their lost country still in their hearts.  Born in a poor Confucian scholar family, Hongam Na Cheol was the most nationalistic and practical intellectual as well as a pure independence fighter. It seemed a bit overdue, but in 1962, the Korean government conferred the Order of Merit for National Foundation in memory of his unswerving loyalty, and Presidential citations were also given to Mr. Na’s two sons. Though he lived two lives in a single body, what both Na In-yeong the politician and Na Cheol the religious leader solely aimed for was the independence of his people.

stories.title: Park Gwang-jeon of Boseong - Jukcheon Park Gwang-jeon
stories.audioTitle: Park Gwang-jeon of Boseong - Jukcheon Park Gwang-jeon
stories.script: Park Gwang-jeon of Boseong - Jukcheon Park Gwang-jeon  The maverick teacher of a prince  Born in Yongjeon-ri, Joseong-myeon, Boseong-gun in the 21st year of King Jungjong's reign (1526), Jukcheon studied under Yang Eung-jeong and Toegye Yi Hwang who were close friends with Jeongam Jo Gwang-jo. Miam Yu Hui-cheon recommended Jukcheon, regarded as one of the top literary men of the Honam region, as the Jeollado Governor. The reason behind this recommendation was that, “Park Gwang-jeon served his parents with great devotion, fulfilled his manners, has a custom in cherishing himself, and shows no idleness in teaching others so his excellent behaviors shall be thought highly of.”  The Seonggyungwan incident that happened in the first year of King Seonjo's reign sheds light on his maverick like character. One day, Chinese envoys visited Seonggyungwan to pay tribute to Munmyo and greet the Confucian scholars. Suddenly, heavy rain came and all of the scholars rushed over to under the eaves except Jukcheon who stayed still. While standing in the middle of the compound with heavy rain pouring all over him, Jukcheon reprimanded the scholars by saying, “Do not scatter away. How can students of Confucius’ teachings be afraid of getting rained on!” At his rebuke, scholars who had quickly run away and, even, the Chinese envoys immediately returned to their original places.  All his life, Jukcheon strictly followed his principles and lived a life of thorough self-censorship. His upright character served a pivotal role in his appointment as the teacher of the prince. During the time, it is said that the royal court “selected Jukcheon to be responsible for leading the prince to righteousness as his teacher because of his good behaviors devoid of corruption. His character was not a matter of debate even for those who did not approve of Gwanghaegun.  King Seonjo who was also well aware of Jukcheon's upright personality had immense confidence in him insomuch to tell Gwanghaegun, “Whatever you do not know or understand, ask Teacher Park.” To Gwanghaegun, Jukcheon was a strict teacher. For instance, he learned that Gwanghaegun's family on his mother's side set up a sign in front of a temple to prohibit access. To this, he insisted that a temple is not private property and advised to remove the sign immediately. When Jukcheon had to leave the royal palace to serve his post as the prefect of Hamyeol, Gwanghaegun who had followed and relied on Jukcheon dearly wanted to see him off even outside the fortress walls. But Jukcheon dissuaded Gwanghaegun, stressing that a prince stepping outside the fortress for such a petty event would go against customs.

stories.title: Park Gwang-jeon of Boseong - Park Gwang-jeon the Righteous Army Captain
stories.audioTitle: Park Gwang-jeon of Boseong - Park Gwang-jeon the Righteous Army Captain
stories.script: Park Gwang-jeon of Boseong - Park Gwang-jeon the Righteous Army Captain  White-haired captain of the righteous army  The Japanese invasion of 1592 broke out when Jukcheon was 67 years old. By then, he had already retired from his government post and was living in Boseong, his hometown. Despite a national crisis, many of the high-ranked officials of the government ran away to spare their own lives but Jukcheon, just a man in the countryside at the time, gathered himself about 700 men to raise a righteous army.  “The reason that the country did not worry was because of the three provinces, Gyeongsang, Chungcheong and Jeolla. But Gyeongsang-do and Chungcheong-do had already fallen at the hands of the enemies and now only the Honam region preserves its corner. All rations have already been collected and sent, and all soldiers have also been commandeered so everyone putting his hopes in Honam and the fate of the entire nation hinged virtually on this region. Moreover, now, the royal palace is in imminent danger and Sunchalsa plans to lead the troops past the sea to the king, and a thousands soldiers are crossing Geumgang River. Both righteous armies already left the province to protect the king. Many men from various towns are also getting ready to go to war so there is not much left. (...) How lamentful it is. This is really the time for righteous commoners to rise up.”  This is a declaration written by Jukcheon while he was recruiting his righteous army. By then, he was already aware of the fact that the core of the nation would collapse if all three provinces of Gyeongsang, Chungcheong and Jeolla were to fall. Jukcheon was already well advanced in age and ill so he was not in a situation to fight in the war. Instead, he appointed Im Gye-yeong as the captain, An Bang-jun as the head of military affairs, and his eldest son as an adviser. Meanwhile, he himself visited Gwanghaegun and proposed ten ways to overcome the crisis. Unfortunately, there are no records remaining that detail the proposal.  There is a record, however, that Gwanghaegun treated Jukcheon well for three days. We can get a glimpse of the close relationship shared between Jukcheon and Gwanghaegun even during the times of war from a letter Jukcheon sent to Gwanghaegun 20 months later from this point. In the letter, Jukcheon advised that a country can truly be empowered only when it prevents tyranny from officials to stabilize the public sentiments and allows people to carry on with their lives in peace.  In 1597, Japanese raiders who had been quiet attacked Joseon again and started the Jeongyu Wars. Jukcheon was a white-haired 70-year-old at this time but his love and loyalty for the country was no less than that of a young, hot-blooded man. “The crisis is urgent and the illness of the body is critical but, as long as I still breathe, I cannot live on the same land as these Japanese raiders.” The spirit of the white-haired Jukcheon helped raise the morale of the righteous army to its highest levels. He actually led the troops in a battle and even defeated the Japanese raiders at the red cliffs but eventually passed away from old age inside the military camp at the age of 72.

stories.title: Seo Jae-pil of Boseong - Songjae Seo Jae-pil
stories.audioTitle: Seo Jae-pil of Boseong - Songjae Seo Jae-pil
stories.script: Seo Jae-pil of Boseong - Songjae Seo Jae-pil  An ill-fortuned independence fighter  Dr. Seo Jae-pil was born on January 7, 1864 in Ganae Village of Yongam-ri, Mundeok-myeon,  Boseong-gun. After spending his childhood in his hometown, he was sent to his uncle in Hanseong when he was seven. Serving as a Champan, or a vice minister-level official at the time, Seo's uncle, Kim Seong-geun, was close with Kim Ok-gyun, Park Yung-hyo, Hong Yeong-sik and many of the Gaehwapa members. During his stay at his uncle’s house while preparing for a national examination, Seo naturally came into contact with them and became fascinated with the new culture. He took the national examination at the age of 18 and won first place. Then, based on advice from Kim Ok-gyun, he enrolled at an army school in Japan as a government scholarship student.  In December 1884, 21-year-old Seo took part in the Gapsin Coup led by Kim Ok-gyun and became a member of the new regime. But the coup ended with Kim’s Three-Day Reign. The failure of the Gapsin Coup was the beginning of a long period of adversity. Dishonored as traitors, he defected to Japan together with Kim, Park Yung-hyo, Seo Gwang-bum, and others but the Japanese government greeted them with cold shoulders as they wanted to evade the responsibility of the coup. Eventually, they ended up leaving to the United States a few months later.  While he wandered in foreign countries from Japan to U.S., his parents and siblings had to live their lives as the family of a traitor and his wife and children were also dragged into a terrible calamity. His parents, older brother, and wife committed suicide by taking poison and his younger brother was executed while his young, two-year-old son ultimately died from starvation. Meanwhile, Seo became naturalized in U.S. and, after much difficulty, settled down in the city of San Francisco. He worked during the day and learned English at night, spending desperate efforts to adapt to the life there.  In 1889, Seo entered Columbia Medical College, now known as George Washington University. Because he had to earn money for tuition during the day, he went to night classes. Having lost his entire family, studying was his only hope. He went through many struggles but successfully graduated from college and made a living by working as a part-time lecturer. He then married a woman and opened up a hospital in Washington. Around this time, the Gabo Reform took place in Joseon and false charges on the leaders of the Gapsin Coup were also cleared.  In 1895, Park Yung-hyo who had become the Interior Minister as an important figure of the reformation government came to visit Seo in the U.S. By the advice of Park, Seo decided to return home and was appointed as the adviser of Jungchuwon in January of the following year. Philip Jaisohn or Pi Jai-sohn or Seo Jae-pil. As you can see from the different names he used in various circumstances, the life of Dr. Seo Jae-pil was full of twists and turns. Perhaps, he thought that it would be safer for him to work as an American citizen and a defected politician. Upon his return to Joseon, he primarily used his American name, “Philip Jaisohn” or “Pi Jai-sohn,” a Korean version of the American name, rather than his original name.

stories.title: Seo Jae-pil of Boseong - Story of Dr. Pi Jai-sohn
stories.audioTitle: Seo Jae-pil of Boseong - Story of Dr. Pi Jai-sohn
stories.script: Seo Jae-pil of Boseong - Story of Dr. Pi Jai-sohn  Publishing the Dongnip Sinmun  〈Dongnip Sinmun〉, published in April 1896 for the first time, was born by government funds thanks to an arrangement made by Yu Kil-chun. He was simply overloaded with work at that time. In July of that year, he formed the Independence Association together with Yi Sang-jae, Yun Chi-ho, Rhee Syngman, and others, as well as establishing the People's Joint Association. In addition, he taught Thursday lectures at the Paichai School with the goal of enlightening the people. It was also around this time when Mohwagwan, which had been taken over to abolish the flunkeyism towards China, was remodeled into Dongnipgwan, or Independence Hall. In 1897, Yeongeunmun Gate was torn down to build Dongnipmun in the same location . Dongnip Sinmun, an integration of Seo's thoughts and beliefs, was published 100% in Korean thanks to the efforts of Ju Si-gyeong, a Korean linguist, and the final page was produced in English, which aimed at informing the foreign media on the reality that was faced by the Korean Empire. Starting in the second year of foundation, it published two versions, English and Korean, as the scale of the newspaper grew significantly. In 1898, the total number of newspaper issues published in Seoul at the time was about 2,500, and it is estimated that nearly 2,000 of them were issued by Dongnip Sinmun. It is said that a single copy of Dongnip Sinmun was circulated and read by 85 people so you can understand how great its influence was.  Through Dongnip Sinmun that could be easily accessed by not only government officials and intellectuals of the society but also the general public, Seo wrote articles that criticize Russia's policies for East Asia and also demanded the withdrawal of the Russian advisory committee, thus utilizing the newspaper pages to its fullest. Such articles led to a confrontation against the pro-Russian regime and increased wariness by the Japanese government.  When Dr. Seo returned, the Korean Empire's government at the time appointed him as the advisor of Jungchuwon and stipulated the term of contract to be 10 years. There was also a condition that they would pay him a certain amount of money for living expenses. But, threatened by the growing power of the Dongnip Sinmun, the extremely conservative regime together with Russia and Japan fired Seo from his position as a Jungchuwon advisor and suspended all assistance of funds. Seo eventually left to U.S. on May 14, 1898, and delegated all operations of the newspaper to his colleagues. The ownership of the newspaper was still vested in him but it was virtually a deportation.  A few months later, the Independence Association was disbanded and the government demanded a return of the newspaper company building by insisting that it was a state-owned property, which led to the government's takeover of the publication rights and printing facilities of the newspaper at an extremely cheap price. This pretty much resulted in the discontinuance of the publication. How devastated must he have felt, being driven out of his motherland twice.

stories.title: Seo Jae-pil of Boseong - The Last of Seo Jae-pil
stories.audioTitle: Seo Jae-pil of Boseong - The Last of Seo Jae-pil
stories.script: Seo Jae-pil of Boseong - The Last of Seo Jae-pil  Will for independence in the U.S.  Even after returning to the U.S., Dr. Seo Jae-pil did not let go of his ties to the independence movement. When the March 1st Movement happened, he appealed for our independence to global media and, also, secured funds with his own properties. Furthermore, he formed “The League of Friends of Korea”with Americans who showed pro-Korea tendencies and also established the Bureau of Information for The Republic of Korea to publish 〈Korea Review, 〉 performing a variety of sponsorship activities. But, mostly he was using his own money which meant that his everyday was unavoidably in need of assistance. Under such difficult circumstances, however, he did not stop serving as the sponsor for independence fighters in the U.S.  When he returned to his liberated home country in 1947, he was already 83 years old. Some people talked about recommending Dr. Seo as a candidate for presidency. As he received heavy spotlight from the media irrelevant to his own intentions, Seo went back to the U.S. despite his old age. Then, in 1951, sad news came during the middle of the Korean War that Dr. Seo Jae-pil who had been bedridden passed away at the age of 85. Many who heard of the news shed tears of mourning. In 1977, the Korean government conferred the Order of Merit for National Foundation, Republic of Korea Medal in commemoration of his meritorious deeds.

stories.title: An Bangjun of Boseong - Eunbong An Bangjun
stories.audioTitle: An Bangjun of Boseong - Eunbong An Bangjun
stories.script: An Bangjun of Boseong - Eunbong An Bangjun  A life lived with integrity  Eunbong An Bangjun (1573-1654) sought practical studies primarily as a commoner rather than as an official. His high level of learning and virtue were widely recognized by Maesan Hong Jik-pil, a Neo-Confucian scholar of the late Joseon Period, once said, “Yi Eonjeok, Jo Sik and Jeong Gu are the most renowned Yeongnam scholars while Kim Inhu, Gi Daeseung and An Bangjun are the most prominent Honam scholars.” His lifelong teachers at heart were Poeun Jeong Mong-ju and Jungbong Jo Heon. Eunbong is a combination of two letters, which are from each of these two great scholars' pen names.  Jeong Mong-ju and Kwon Geun were leaders of all Confucian scholars at the time but they were placed at the crossroads of destiny when Joseon was established. One chose the path of staying loyal to Goryeo which ended in his murder, whereas the other survived by cooperating with Joseon and extensively promulgated his teachings. The fact that Eunbong An Bangjun's heart and thoughts leaned more towards Jeong Mong-ju among the two allows us to predict what the remainder of his life would have been like.  Until he passed away at the age of 82, Joseon had four kings - Seonjo, Injo, Gwanghaegun and Hyojong - and a series of national calamities occurred during the Japanese invasion of 1592, the Jeongyu Wars, and invasion by Later Jin and Qing while the famous factions of Joseon repeatedly gathered and separated in a chaotic fashion. Considering that most living things surrender themselves to powerful stimulation from the outside, it is extremely interesting to reflect on the life of a man who lived at the core of rapid changes.  If we were to choose one work that described his life, it would be “integrity.” Integrity means to act by putting one's life on one's strong belief in loyalty and justice. In other words, it is reverence to fidelity and righteousness. High-ranked officials of the government fought among themselves first as Dongin and Seoin and, after Dongin seized power, they were again divided into Bukin and Namin. Then, once Namin became powerful, they were further separated into Noron and Soron to scratch and gnaw at each other. Such factional politics made Joseon unable to prepare for Japan's impure ambition of invading our land even though we had already been aware of it. As conflicts between factions overlapped with the wars, the public sentiment became increasingly anti-government to the point that even a plot of treason occurred to the point where the country had to worry about the collapse of Confucianism, the national foundation. Eunbong then chose integrity as the means to solve the issues presented by factional politics. This is the famous Jinyuron.

stories.title: An Bangjun of Boseong - Writings of An Bangjun
stories.audioTitle: An Bangjun of Boseong - Writings of An Bangjun
stories.script: An Bangjun of Boseong - Writings of An Bangjun  Getting through the crisis  When the Japanese invaded Joseon in 1592, Mr. An raised a righteous army together with his teacher, Jukcheon Park Gwang-jeon. In the outbreak of the two consecutive foreign invasions, he himself became the captain of a righteous army and marched to the battlefront. His age was already past 60 at this point. After the Japanese invasion ended, he wrote about the deeds of the fallen righteous army soldiers and actively worked to highlight their loyalty. Setting justice right is another aspect of a life of integrity. If we read the appeal he submitted to the government prior to the outbreak of the Japanese invasion of 1592, we would shudder with fright.  “An extremely disgraceful rumor is spreading around even in the remotest of regions. Though the words passed between the mouths on the streets are not always true, it all stems from the king's own faults so you shall heed the situation.”  It is a direct appeal talking about how the king shall take responsibility for the chaos that the country is facing because of his improper behavior, so his definition of integrity did not just emphasize loyalty but entailed uprightness that maintains righteousness. Henceforth, he continued to submit appeals to the king to insist in earnest that factions shall be suppressed and talents shall be carefully selected while the public sentiment shall be soothed. Such a spirit of practice was manifestation of a consistent conviction that “integrity is the vitality of a country.”  He was recommended for a government post during Gwanghaegun's reign but he declined it. Instead, he went to live in Usan-ri, Boseong-eup to train the younger generation and to also write 『Samwongisa』. After the Injo Restoration, he sent letters to Kim Yu who had become a prominent figure in the royal court to advise him on appointing talent from all around and making sure to differentiate between public and private matters. He had had academic fellowship with some of the key members of the restoration including Kim Yu. After King Injo was enthroned, the royal court bestowed the Jeong-6-pum position upon him. He declined the invitation once again and instead returned to his hometown to teach students.

stories.title: An Bangjun of Boseong - The Last of An Bangjun
stories.audioTitle: An Bangjun of Boseong - The Last of An Bangjun
stories.script: An Bangjun of Boseong - The Last of An Bangjun  Tasanjiseok, learning from something to benefit oneself  In 1627, the Later Jin invaded Joseon. Mr. An himself became Hososa of the Honam and Hoseo regions to lead the righteous army and, when the Qing invasion broke out in 1636, he sent declarations to every corner of the province to recruit righteous army soldiers. On his march to Cheongju, he heard the urgent news that Namhansanseong Fortress was under siege. The Qing invasion ultimately ended with the “Humiliation at Samjeondo” in which the king kowtowed three times and bowed nine times towards the Qing emperor.  Upon learning this news in Cheongju, An kneeled and weeped bitterly towards the north where the king had lived and returned home. From then on, he trained his pupils at Daegye Seowon at the foot of Jangwonbong Peak in Wonbong-ri, Boseong-eup. An eventually passed away at the age of 82 while staying at Eunbongjeongsa in Maejeong-ri, Iyang-myeon, Hwasun-gun.  In commemoration of An, King Hyojong posthumously appointed him as Ijopanseo, or the Minister of Interior, and assigned him the pen name Mungang. He left a countless number of books whlie spending most of his life in Usan-ri, Boseong-eup. 『Eunbongjeonseo』, which was published at Daegye Seowon in the first year of King Gojong’s reign, is a compilation of his books collected by his descendants over six to eight generations.  In particular, 『Eunbong Yasa Byeolrok』, which recorded what An had seen and heard while he was leading the righteous army, is regarded as a masterpiece that describes the scenes and conditions of the Japanese invasion of 1592 in even greater detail than the Annals of King Seonjo. The stories of important historical figures such as Jo Cheon, Yi Sun-sin and Gim Si-min were compiled in three books, which were also translated and published in Japan. In 1850, a Japanese man named Watanabe in Edo published these books,even adding a preface and an epilogue through which he stated that he would learn from the books to benefit himself.  At the Eunbong Head House located in Usan-ri, Boseong-eup, many materials related to Daegye Seowon are stored. From letters exchanged with scholars he associated with to old documents passed down within the house for generations, these materials preserve an extremely important value in understanding the political situation of the Joseon Dynasty, relationships among scholars of the time, their values, and companionship among family members and relatives. The materials related to the Eunbong Head House and Daegye Seowon are currently designated as Jeollanam-do Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 303.

stories.title: Jeon Bangsak of Boseong - Gyuam Jeon Bangsak
stories.audioTitle: Jeon Bangsak of Boseong - Gyuam Jeon Bangsak
stories.script: Jeon Bangsak of Boseong - Gyuam Jeon Bangsak  Hero of Jukjeonbeol  General Jeon Bangsak was someone whom the Japanese during the colonial period were eager to erase all traces of by ruining the lives of his descendants and even by setting his house on fire in an effort to destroy all of his relics. This speaks to how great his performances were during the Japanese invasion of 1592.  Gyuam Jeon Bangsak was born in Taekchon Village in Usan-ri, Boseong-eup as a son of Yun Bu, Jangheung Dohobusa at the time, during the first year of King Injong’s reign in 1545. He loved to ride horses and shoot arrows since he was young, and, when he was 20 years old, he passed the military service examination in the 8th year of King Seonjo’s reign before entering a training institute. Around when the Japanese invasion broke out in 1592, Gyuam’s position was General Geongong, Jong 3-Pum Hullyeonwon Bujeong. The war quickly swept through the entire nation and people were shocked at the news that the Japanese raiders that had landed in Busanpo swiftly took over Hanyang. Before the shock subsided, people found out that Pyongyang also fell to the hands of the raiders. All of these events took place in less than two months.  While waiting for the order to go to war, Gyuam joined the camp of Admiral Yi Sun-sin of Jeolla Jwasuyeong together with Generals Choi Dae-seong and Song Hee-rip. Here, he helped General Yi in defeating a countless number of enemies in numerous battles out at sea. Although commanders and soldiers united and fought with their lives on the line, Joseon's forces were at a severe disadvantage in all aspects as the Japanese troops were armed with advanced weaponry whereas our soldiers were inferior in terms of firearms as well as provisions. However, thanks to the naval forces led by General Yi who prepared for the Japanese raiders’ assaults in advance as well as the righteous armies from all the different regions, the enemies’ spirits began to slowly subside.  Gyuam used this opportunity to make a quick return to his hometown. Once he arrived at his house in Taekchon, Boseong-up, he scraped every last asset and property his family had owned and offered 50 seok of rice for military provisions. Touched by his love and loyalty for the country, other villagers also donated rice and other grains. Everyone was in need during these times of war but gladly and generously offered whatever they had, whether it be a doe of beans or a handful of barley.  Some time later, Gyuam was given the role of guarding Gwanghaegun who had set out to lead the war as the crown prince. Around this period, Gwanghaegun was  going around the Jeonju region to encourage people to offer provisions as well as to join the righteous armies. Gyuam personally visited Jeolla Byeongsa Yi Gwangak and Jeon Baekok, his relative and the governor of Boseong, to ask for cooperation. Also, when Gwanghaegun returned to Hanyang, Gyuam proposed to the crown prince that he should remain in his hometown and recruit a righteous army to prepare for the future. Well aware of Gyuam's sincerity, Gwanghaegun accepted this idea. Soon, a righteous army of about 300 men from the Boseong region who were familiar with the geography and terrain of their hometown came to possess excellent fighting skills comparable to those of well-trained soldiers, thanks to the leadership of Gyuam.

stories.title: Jeon Bangsak of Boseong - Eomojanggun Jeon Bangsak
stories.audioTitle: Jeon Bangsak of Boseong - Eomojanggun Jeon Bangsak
stories.script: Jeon Bangsak of Boseong - Eomojanggun Jeon Bangsak  Destroying the Japanese army  In 1597, the Jeongyu Wars broke out finally. Over 13,000 Japanese invaders led by Ukita Hideie toppled Namwonseong Fortress in Jeollabuk-do. As the fate of the nation was in a dire extremity after the Noryang Battle that ensued, the righteous army led by Gyuam played a remarkable role. At the time, battles, big or small, took place every day in Boseong, Suncheon, Gwangyang, Goheung, and other places. In the end, Gyuam led over 20 battles to victory. The Japanese raiders who invaded Yejinpo in Boseong and Mangjepo in Goheung fell helplessly at the hands of Gyuam’s army. The battles continued for months  and, starting from March to July 1598, not a single day went by quietly and calmly in the Yeosu and Goheung Peninsula region. Gyuam as well as Choi Dae-sung, Song Dae-rip, Hwang Won-bok and Jeong Hee all led their own armies to fight fiercely against the Japanese. Having defeated the invaders in the consecutive battles at Yejin, Nakan, and Anchi, Gyuam’s army overpowered the enemy once again at the Battle of Cheomsan in Goheung and marched to the fateful Jukjeonbeol in July of the same year.  Jukjeonbeol is today's Seongjeokgol of Seongjae Village in Samjeong 3-ri, Deungnyang-myeon. As our soldiers roared and fought with their lives on the line against the Japanese raiders armed with matchlocks, Jukjeonbeol looked a lot like hell on earth. Jeon Baekok, the governor of Boseong-gun, took part in this battle as well. In the first do-or-die battle of our royal forces and righteous armies versus Ukita Hideie's unit, our troops scored a huge victory.  Also, in the second battle, Gyuam took the helm to command the soldiers and halted the enemy's attack with everything he had. As the troops witnessed their general not sparing himself and courageously leading the army, their spirits were soared. In the battles that followed, the only target of the Japanese enemy was General Jeon. No matter how brave the general was, he still could not stop bullets from coming at him. Mourning for the death of a general who died in battle at the age of 54, King Seonjo bestowed the ranks of Seonmu Wonjong Gongsin Ideung Hullyeonwonjeong Eomojanggun upon him in July 1598.  Yeongdeungpogu Dock in Beolgyo was the base for the righteous armies and a place where numerous commanders including General Gyuam Jeon Bangsak annihilated the Japanese raiders. Jeon Hongrye, a son of Gyuam who once served as Pangwan of Hullyeonwon, established Yeongdeung Village here in memory of his father. At Chunghyosa Temple in Yeongdeung Village, Beolgyo-eup, his portrait and ancestral tablet are enshrined, and his descendants hold annual memorial ceremonies to reflect on his loyalty.

stories.title: Im Chang-mo of Boseong - Woldam Im Chang-mo
stories.audioTitle: Im Chang-mo of Boseong - Woldam Im Chang-mo
stories.script: Im Chang-mo of Boseong - Woldam Im Chang-mo  A venerable patriot  There used to be a time when a child would stop crying at once if he or she heard Japanese policemen approaching. Mr. Im Chang-mo, a righteous army general from Boseong, is the type of person who boldly shouted and reprimanded Japan in a court room under the Government-General. Woldam Im Chang-mo was born in Usan-ri, Boseong in 1868. His family was the noble Joyang Im Clan that had also been wealthy for generations. In years of bad harvest or whenever the neighbors were in need, the family offered their private properties to relieve them. In today's terms, they can be said to be a family that practiced noblesse oblige.  By the influence of his grandfather who once served as Tongjeongdaebu Owijang Buchonggwan, he grew up into a well-rounded young man with hero-like dignity, courage, and resourcefulness. At the age of 28, he passed the military service examination and began to serve the country as Uigwan of Jungchuwon. In the same year, the murder of Empress Myeongseong took place in Joseon. As any Joseon person would, he too, became infuriated at the unpardonable atrocities carried out by the Japanese. To Mr. Im who was living the days in frustration, the Eulsa Treaty and the Jeongmi Treaty finally blew his fuse.  The Korean Empire lost its sovereignty and its army was disbanded. Im returned to his hometown at once and began to take part in the independence movement. Yang Hoe-il, An Chan-jae, Yi Gwang-seon, No Eung-hyeon, Yun Hyang-won, Im Bong-su, Yu Tae-gyeong, Shin Tae-hwan and many others from Neungju decided to stand alongside Mr. Im. Im Yeon-mo, his brother and a former Uigwan of Jungchuwon, also joined the group. Im Yeon-mo recruited an army of about 50 dismissed soldiers and outstanding shooters.  Hearing the news that Woldam was recruiting to organize a righteous army, men from every corner of Boseong region gathered. The military provisions prepared by Im’s family were over 400 seok. The first date they decided upon was March 10, 1907. Im held a small ceremony with his comrades at Honam Changuiso. Meanwhile, the scale of the army grew to about 200 men. After electing Yang Hoe-il as the captain and Woldam as the commander of the central unit, the righteous army set Hwasun-gun Office on fire and attacked a Japanese military police outstation and tax office. As night approached, they retreated towards Dongbok-myeon, Hwasun to spend the night.

stories.title: Im Chang-mo of Boseong - Im Chang-mo the Righteous Army General
stories.audioTitle: Im Chang-mo of Boseong - Im Chang-mo the Righteous Army General
stories.script: Im Chang-mo of Boseong - Im Chang-mo the Righteous Army General  Raising an army for his country  At noon on the following day, the army carried out a surprise attack on the Dongbok military police dispatch station and continued to march to Gwangju without stopping. In the afternoon, Japanese military policemen flocked to the area from Gwangju and Suncheon. Overwhelmed by the number of policemen, the righteous army battled with desperate resistance in Domachi but, eventually became besieged by the Japanese forces. At this time, six key leaders of the righteous army, including Woldam, Yang Hoe-il, An Chan-jae, Yu Tae-gyeong, Shin Tae-hwan and Yi Baek-rae, were transferred to Gwangju Regional Court. The final verdict ruled 15 years of imprisonment for Woldam and Yang Hoe-il, the captain of the army, and the other members received 10 years of exile all in different regions. Doing his just part retake his stolen country was considered a crime, and he was exiled to a small island in Sinan, Jeollanam-do.  Then, in January 1908, a decree of amnesty was announced in celebration of Emperor Sunjon's enthronement. Released on a special pardon at this time, Im began to recruit an army again with his own funds as soon as he returned home from the exile. He was doing something, which would not be done even once by most people, for the second time. From Im Yang-on and Im San-won who were widely regarded as men of wealth in Boseong-eup to Park Nam-hyeon of Miryeok-myeon, Im Jong-won of Boknae-myeon and Yi Won-suk of Hoecheon-myeon, many influential people in the area supported his righteous army activities. Over 500 men gathered at the ceremony held at Honamuiso in Seokhosan Mountain, Miryeok-myeon, and Im was appointed as the captain of the army.  Having learned from his experience of failure in the past, he and his comrades were extremely careful in keeping the righteous army activities strictly confidential. All commanding officers were to use nicknames or aliases, and a valley deep into Gyedang-ri, Boknae-myeon was established as the base. To secure fighting power comparable to that of the Japanese soldiers, they made sure to purchase new weapons and procured a sufficient amount of war supplies. Starting with a surprise assault on Japanese military police, which was marching to Boseong, in Beodeulgogae, Yedang-ri, Deungnyang-meyon in April 1908, the righteous army led by Woldam terrified the Japanese military police forces stationed in Boseong and Goheung. Im Hak-sun, his other son, also joined the second righteous army. It is rare for brothers to serve in a righteous army together but they did not hesitate to follow his father into the battlefield.  This is believed to be a byproduct of the family tradition that did not focus on seeking individual distinctions. As the army moved constantly and attacked Japanese forces in various places over ten days, they became infuriated and anxiously tried to locate the whereabouts of the army leaders. Then, in October 1909, the Japanese attacked to subjugate the righteous army in Boseong and Goheung area. Im obtained intelligence in advance that the Japanese would attack Boknae-myeon on October 13 and summoned the commanders the night before. This strategy meeting to come up with plans to defeat the Japanese forces was held in a remote house of Park Chae-ik, a righteous army commander, in Mukseok-dong, Boknae-myeon.

stories.title: Im Chang-mo of Boseong - The Last of Im Chang-mo
stories.audioTitle: Im Chang-mo of Boseong - The Last of Im Chang-mo
stories.script: Im Chang-mo of Boseong - The Last of Im Chang-mo  Do not harm my country  Jeong Taehwa, the spearhead of the army; An Chan-jae, the commander of the central army; and Woldam as well as his son, Im Hak-sun, all arrived at the meeting place around midnight. By then, no one could have expected that there had been a compromise of information. About thirty minutes later, suspicious movement was detected outside. The Japanese punitive forces and hundreds of military police had already set up a camp. After learning that they were under siege, the righteous army resisted desperately but it was not enough. Not too long after, devilish gunshots were fired off in Mukseok-dong valley. The so-called 『Jeonnam Pokdosa』 is a book that described the resistance of the Joseon righteous army from the viewpoint of the Japanese.  Your eyes cannot help but tear up when reading the about the depictions of the brutal scenes that took place on this day. “You bastards, do not harm my country!” As his father let out his final breath with this cry, his son, Hak-sun, embraced his father's body and wailed. “Shameless thieves, do not harm my father!” Before his cry ended, another gunshot carried out. Woldam was 42 years of age and Hak-sun was just 22 years old at the time.  Sadly, his brother, Captain Im Yeon-mo, also passed away on the same day. Captain Im led another righteous army and performed victoriously in various battles at Ssangam, Ungchi, and Bakgok. The Battle of Cheongpo, which took place in Gaeksan-ri, Hoecheon-myeon in August 1909, was the final battle for Captain Im Yeon-mo. With a gunshot wound from battle he had to run away into hiding for nearly two months without any proper medical care. Eventually, he passed away at the age of 38 on the same day as his older brother and nephew. The cause of death was excessive bleeding.  When the sad news of the family's divine death was heard, many people came to pay their condolences even though the times were rough. Among the mourners, there was a Japanese man named Buseok. He came with his subordinates and tried to pay money as a show of condolence but Woldam's wife refused it to the very end. The Japanese government conferred medals of merit to the two pro-Japan Joseon policemen who led the Japanese forces that night. While these traitors were treated as patriots in Japan, how do you think Woldam's family stood by?  An entire family fought for their country and faced courageous deaths in the end but not many people remember their names. After Liberation, the Im Clan and the villagers combined small amounts of subsidies given by the government with their own offerings to build a monument in front of the grave of the father and the son, located at the foot of the mountain next to Jueum Village, Yongmun-ri, Boseong-eup.

stories.title: Baek Hong-in of Boseong - Sesimdang Baek Hong-in
stories.audioTitle: Baek Hong-in of Boseong - Sesimdang Baek Hong-in
stories.script: Baek Hong-in of Boseong - Sesimdang Baek Hong-in  Student of Myeonam  Mr. Sesimdang Baek Hong-in is someone who lived his entire life until the day he died with devotion to national salvation. He famously wrote Gyeonggo Seomun, which makes us solemn in this present age even 60 years after his death. Sesimdang was born in Buchun Village, Yusan-ri, Ungchi-myeon, Boseong-gun in 1874, and learned the Chinese classics and Zhouyi at an early age. Once he reached 20 years of age, he studied Seongnihak, or Neo-Confucianism, under teachers like Gi Woo-man, Song Byeong-seon, Song Byeong-sun and Choi Ik-hyeon,  all of who had significant influences on Sesimdang to come to possess the spirit of upright resistance. Songsa Gi Woo-man carried out righteous army activities against the Japanese after the Eulmi Incident, and Yeonje Song Byeong-seon and Simseok Song Byeong-sun committed suicide once the Eulsa Treaty was signed while Myeonam Choi Ik-hyeon tenaciously performed anti-Japanese righteous army activities with his pupils before eventually passing away at the end of a hunger strike in protest against the ordinance prohibiting topknots. Baek Hong-in's relationship with Myeonam, in particular, had great psychological and ideological influence on him throughout his entire life. Myeonam was the last glimmering hope for Confucian scholars during the days of the late Korean Empire. It is said that Baek's pen name, Sesimdang, was given by Myeonam himself.  Every April, a joint memorial ceremony is held for five independence patriots including Myeonam Choi Ik-hyeon at Mochungsa Temple in Buchon Village, Yusin-ri, Ungchi-myeon. Buchon Village in Yusin-ri is the home of Jangchunjae where Baek trained a countless number of students after he had returned from studying under Myeonam at the age of 29. Jangchunjae is also where he launched a righteous army together with his pupils such as Kim Gwan-jung and Kim Jun-su.  Jangchunjae was the cradle of dreams, disappointment, agony and the fury of the patriots of the late Korean Empire. In the winter of 1905, he and his 40 or so students who had gathered from Boseong, Jangheung, Hampyeong, Hwasun, and Gangjin took an oath to save and protect their country at all costs. They were dispersed throughout the Honam region again to distribute Gyeonggoseosa. When Sesimdang brought a copy of Gyeonggoseosa to Choi Ik-hyeon, the great teacher of all Confucian scholars,  yeonam gave him three instructions.  The first was to go to Isan Ganghoe and determine the great cause. The second was to draft a declaration to all people. And the third, keep the base of the righteous army in Neungju, Jeollanam-do and store military provisions there.  Isan is today's Nonsan. In January 1906, Myeonam hosted a lecture meeting on present situations to urge the Confucian scholars from all over the nation to join the sovereignty restoration movement. It is not exactly known whether or not Baek Hong-in was present at this meeting. But the 『Boseong History of People』 does state that, on New Year’s Day of the same year, Sesimdang delivered the words of Myeonam by revealing 〈Geungo Paldo Saminseo〉 in front of about 100 patriots which included Baek Hyeong-chil, Yang Hoe-il, Yi Nam-jae, Yi Won-suk, Yi Baek-rae, Yi Gyo-mun, Sim Nam-il and Im Chang-mo.

stories.title: Baek Hong-in of Boseong - Sesimdang Ganghak Yujibi
stories.audioTitle: Baek Hong-in of Boseong - Sesimdang Ganghak Yujibi
stories.script: Baek Hong-in of Boseong - Sesimdang Ganghak Yujibi  No memorial stone for a scholar of a fallen country  〈Geungo Paldo Saminseo〉 written by Baek Hong-in by the order of Myeonam was a manifesto that urged people throughout the country to rise up. Gyeonggoseosa and Geungo Paldo Saminseo were distributed throughout the nation. Deeply moved by the manifesto, people from various regions donated military provisions and activity funds, and all of the accumulated supplies were then sent to the house of Yang Hoe-il in Neungju. In the meantime, numerous patriots were arrested by the Japanese and served time in prison. Sesimdang was no exception. He was taken into custody by the Japanese military police and spent about five months in prison. So the day they had planned for in May of that year on which an army had been scheduled to be raised had to be pushed to the following year.  In 1907, Ssangsan Uiso in Gyedangsan Mountain area became the base for righteous army activities. In March of the same year, Sesimdang led an army of about 700 men and held a dispatch ceremony at Ssangsan Uiso. 50 soldiers under Yi Gwang-seon who spearheaded the army and 20 shooters under Im Chang-mo as well as many other righteous army commanders joined the ceremony. At first, the army successfully took over government offices, military police detachments and tax offices in Neungju, Hwasun and Dongbok. Their next target was Gwangju Gwanchalbu, or the provincial office. But the crafty Japanese policemen and military forces knew in advance that the righteous army would march to Gwangju so many of them waited in ambush in Domachi to carry out a surprise attack. In this battle at Domachi, six leaders of the righteous army including Changui Dodaejang Yi Baek-rae were captured. Most of them were exiled to Jido Island in Sinan-gun before being released on a special pardon in the following year for the enthronement of Emperor Sunjong.  From January 1908, a righteous army based in Ssangsan Uiso decided to divide the entire Jeolla-do region in eight zones to carry out guerrilla warfare. The unit from the 5th Zone, which had joined the headquarters in June of the same year, raided the Japanese military police in Jangheung and scored a victory but its leaders ended up being arrested. This is when the army led by Mr. Baek Hong-in began to face hardships and trials. The arrested army leaders refused to take any food and eventually passed away in prison. Then, in May 1909, Dodaejang Yi Baek-rae was arrested in his own house by the Japanese military police who had received a tip on Yi’s location. Not only that, but, Yi Ok-rae who tried to rescue Yi Baek-rae was also tragically shot to death. In the end, Ssangsan Uiso disbanded but this did not stop Sesimdang’s resistance towards Japan.  He himself took part in the March 1st Independence Movement of 1919 and returned to his hometown to lead a local independence movement as well before being arrested and serving time in prison. Even after he was released from prison after undergoing brutal torture, his conviction was still vigorous even though his health was not. After years of suffering from the after effects of the torture, he attempted to burn all of the books he had written and planned to commit suicide in the fall of 1923. Fortunately, his family found out in advance and stopped him but the incident ended up blinding his eyes. When his students erected a Ganghak Yujibi out of respect for him, he felt as if he was responsible for failing to protect his country and decided to bury the memorial stone underground. He also refused to cut his topknots or change his name to one that was Japanese, which was persistently coerced by the Japanese. When he passed away at the age of 79 in 1953, his funeral was conducted together by local scholars and people of the county.  After his death, his students unearthed the Ganghak Yujibi that had been buried at Jangchunjae in order to set it up again. The Gyeonggoseosa, which had been kept in secret by his descendants, is now stored at Gyujanggak. In 1980, the Korean government conferred the Presidential Citation of Merit for National Foundation and, in 1990, the National Medal of the Order of Merit for National Foundation was bestowed upon him.

stories.title: Yeolseonru, Boseong - Yeolseonru
stories.script: Yeolseonru, Boseong - Yeolseonru  Seeing the tears of Chungmugong   Boseong, which neighbors the sea, is a historic place where young Chungmugong bravely demonstrated the spirit of our people. During the Japanese invasion of 1592, he secured a great volume of provisions from Boseong's Joyangchang (Gonae Village, Yucheon-ri, Joseong-ri, Joseong-myeon, Boseong-gun) and scored a huge victory against the Japanese raiders on the waters in front of Uldolmok. Not only that, but he also went to battle in 1597 during the Jeongyu Wars after preparing rations, weapons, a navy, and ships from Boseong and achieved the feat of overpowering the Japanese raiders once again.  As you can see, no one can deny the fact that Boseong provided great aid for Admiral Yi Sun-sin's victories. Boseong is also where his in-laws lived. He married at a young age to the only daughter of Bang Jin, the governor of Boseong at the time, which solidified his ties to Boseong. Bang Jin was actually the one who recommended Yi Sun-sin to take the military service examination.  Chungmugong's wife was also an incredible heroine. There is a story about her in 『Yi Chungmugong Jeonseo』. When she was 12 years old, a group of robbers raided her house. Bang Jin who was a sharp shooter fought against them with his bow and arrow. Soon after, when he ran out of arrows he yelled at his servants to bring him more. But the servants had already colluded in secret with the robbers and hidden all of the arrows. This is when Bang Jin's daughter utilized her wits. She grabbed a bundle of bamboo sticks that were used to weave hemp cloths and threw them up to the attic as if they were arrows. Then she shouted, “Father, here are the arrows!” The robbers ran away immediately after hearing this exclamation as they knew that they would not able to survive the presence of Bang Jin and his arrows.  Boseong is the place that helped the admiral in being victorious in his battles as well as the place that gave birth to and raised his loving wife, however, it is also smeared with agony, passion, and contrition of Yi Sun-sin as a person. The historic site that connects Admiral Yi Sun-sin and Boseong is a place called “Yeolseonru.” Unfortunately, there are no traces of Yeolseonru that still remain today. The Boseong Gwana government office where the admiral probably stopped by every time he visited his in-laws and the hackberry that used to guard Yeolseonru are also nowhere to be seen. A few years ago, a bibliographer named Lee Jong-hak revealed the original copy of 〈Hansandoga〉 of Admiral Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin, and this copy was confirmed to be the handwriting of Chungmugong himself. This shed light on the presence of an agony- and suffering-filled human under the thick armor and helmet of the admiral. And Yeolseonru was a place that kept him company during his inner struggles.  Then, where exactly was Yeolseonru? Today's Boseong-gun Office site is where Boseong Gwana used to be, and Boseong Elementary School was the location of the official residence of the Boseong-gun governor and a dormitory for visitors. If you walk into the elementary school and hike up the path in the back, the Seventh-day Adventist Boseong Church stands, and Yeolseonru existed near this church.

stories.title: Yeolseonru, Boseong - Yeolseonru and Chungmugong
stories.script: Yeolseonru, Boseong - Yeolseonru and Chungmugong  Loyalty spoken through Hansandoga   In August of the year of Jeongyu, Admiral Yi Sun-sin received a letter carried by Seonjeongwan Park Cheon-bong at Yeolseonru. The letter, which contained the royal command from King Seonjo, had the admiral quite puzzled. The letter said, “Our naval forces are too weak so join forces with Gwon Yul's army at once and fight the war together.” It quite literally meant the abolition of the navy, and for Admiral Yi, it was an extremely shocking command from the king because of an order that was issued to him less than two weeks ago to strengthen the navy once again in order to rescue the country. Now, the king wanted to abolish the navy and commanded them to join the army. The admiral felt devastated as he had been working tirelessly to rebuild the naval forces even under unfavorable circumstances.  Around that time, Japanese raiders kept about 600 ships at their Busan headquarters alone. In contrast, Joseon's navy only carried 12 ships but even these ships were all once damaged and discarded Panokseons that the admiral encouraged his subordinates to fix and repair. From what was happening, you can guess that the royal court believed that this is a war was unwinnable. “If you wish to die, you will live. If you wish to live, you will die.” This is something that the admiral habitually emphasized in front of his men. So you can imagine how it was an unacceptable order for someone like Admiral Yi who truly believed that there would be no defeat if one is determined to die in battle.  Unable to fall asleep that night, he wrote a letter in response to Seonjo's command.  “This is exactly what I am afraid of. We still have twelve battleships left. If we fight with our lives on the line, we will be able to thwart the enemy's push. The mere number of the ships we have is small but as long as the lowly body of mine still breathes, the enemy will not look down upon us.”  As we read this famous writing, it is possible to estimate the depth of agony he was feeling at the time.
