If he were to obey the royal order, he had to give up his navy, which in turn would undoubtedly hand over the country to the Japanese raiders. He spent many sleepless nights and his grief continued to deepen as time passed. 〈, Hansandoga〉, which he recited ardently on one of those nights, is still remembered as a song that touches the hearts of all people even several hundred years later.

stories.title: Yeolseonru, Boseong - Hansandoga
stories.script: Yeolseonru, Boseong - Hansandoga  Agony harbored in Yeolseonru  Walk up the tower alone on a moonlit night of Hansando While in deep grief with a big sword tightly held in my hand A sound of a pipe from somewhere adds more anxiety - Recited by Yi Sun-sin on Jungchu, Jeongyu  Jungchu of the year of Jeongyu refers to August 15, 1597. The Nanjung Ilgi, or War Diary of Yi Sun-sin, says that the admiral stayed at Boseong Gwana for eight days during this period and also walked up to Yeolseonru on August 15, the same day as when he wrote this poem. This is a definite proof that, unlike what is understood among the general public, the stage of Hansandoga was indeed Yeolseonru of Boseong.  Admiral Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin is a histroic hero that is respected by naval forces, not just in Korea, but worldwide. And the fact that a site of such huge historic importance, which could have been one of the greatest cultural heritages of our people, has disappeared is an immense loss for locals and the nation alike. What we have lost is not a mere pavilion.  In Boseong, Admiral Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin became the husband to a woman and vowed to serve his king and country based on his own principles until the day he dies, and Yeolseonru smiled and cried with him. The pavilion in itself provided immense support for a man who was known as a never-retreating commander and, at the same time, a human being under agony. Recently, Boseong-gun decided to carry out a project to restore the site and develop it into a tourist attraction where people can reflect on its historic significance. We hope to reminisce about the spirit and soul of Chungmugong here in Boseong some day.

stories.title: Soesil Village of Boseong - Soesil Village, Deungnyang-myeon
stories.audioTitle: Soesil Village of Boseong - Soesil Village, Deungnyang-myeon
stories.script: Soesil Village of Boseong - Soesil Village, Deungnyang-myeon  Special village of Baekbeom Kim Gu  For Baekbeom Kim Gu, the father of Korean independence, Soesil was an extremely special village. From this small town, Baekbeom who had devoted most of his life to independence movements and even seen death up close took away a warm heart that he could never forget.  On the way to Suncheon from Boseong-eup, there is a place called the Gireogijae Service Station. Beneath the station, if you go about 1km to the left, you will reach a little village surrounded by high mountains and deep valleys. This is Soesil Village of Samjeong-ri, Deungnyang-myeon. Roads and the town have been expanded these days but, in the old days, Soesil was located deep in the valley that is difficult to be seen from the outside. Here, young Kim Gu lied low for nearly two months under the alias of Kim Du-ho. It was when the entirety of Joseon had become infuriated by the murder of Empress Myeongseong.  In May 1896, Kim Gu ran into a suspicious Japanese man named Tsuchida near Chiha Port in Hwanghae-do. Tsuchida was disguised in Joseon attire but Kim Gu saw through an opening of his clothes that he was keeping a sword close to his chest and was convinced that the Japanese man was the murdurer of Empress Myeongseong. At that moment, the only thing that went though his mind was to take revenge on behalf of all Joseon people. After following Tsuchida into a restaurant, Kim Gu was engaged in a bloody fight and, ultimately, avenged the empress’ death. People sitting and standing nearby were shocked but Kim proudly declared that he just brought down judgment upon the scum that had killed the empress and then revealed his identity.  The Japanese judiciary sentenced the 21-year-old Kim Gu to death. He was subject to various types of torture at Haeju Gamyeong Provincial Office and, after he was transferred to Incheon, he attempted to break out of prison. After going through many hardships after the escape, he finally came to Soesil Village,  which was home of the Andong Kim Clan. Kim Gu probably knew about this from the genealogy or words of the elder members of the family. When young Kim Gu arrived there, his appearance was unspeakably shabby and miserable. He visited the house of Kim Kwang-eon, one of his distant relatives, and introduced himself as “Kim Du-ho” who lives in Songdo. Kim Kwang-eon readily offered him a place to rest for the time being.  For about a month and a half, Soesil Village became a warm hideout for an independence fighter who was about to set out on a lifelong journey filled with hardships and obstacles. While in jail, Kim Gu taught his fellow prisoners how to read and write because he thought that people who do not know the language or do not engage in learning cannot be self-conscious. As he stayed in a guest room at Kim Kwang-eon's house, Kim Gu taught the language and Dongguksagi to the workers. During that time, he became very attached to the villagers. Finally, his time for goodbyes arrived. As all villagers were sad to see him leave, the mother of a young man gave him a bag for writing brushes that she had sewed herself. Kim Gu's way of saying thanks was presenting a book titled 『Dongguk Yeokdae』 and leaving a poem of farewell on its cover.

stories.title: Soesil Village of Boseong - Difficulty of a Farewell
stories.audioTitle: Soesil Village of Boseong - Difficulty of a Farewell
stories.script: Soesil Village of Boseong - Difficulty of a Farewell  Baekbeom’s words of gratitude  It is difficult to abandon and leave this land. I have lived leisurely for about a month but I must leave even though I am sad to say goodbye. If you read this later on, it may allow you to reminisce about me of today, so I leave this letter as a token and go far far away.  No one had known that such a polite and sentimental man would become Baekbeom, the head of the Korean provisional government in Shanghai later on. 48 years passed since his final day in Soesil. Upon his return to Korea after Liberation, he visited the village once again in September 1946 not as a man named Kim Du-ho but, rather, as Kim Gu, the leader of the Korean people.  Later, he wrote 『Baekbeom Ilji』 about the touching encounters he had during this visit. He looked around every corner of the village that he revisited and delivered words of gratitude to the villagers who had shown compassion to him in the past. He also brought out the writing brush bag sewn by Mrs. An that he had treasured all his life, and promised that he would return again some day.  But, in the end, this promise could not be kept. On June 26, 1949, the death of Baekbeom Kim Gu brought the entire village to tears. Next to the main entrance of Kim Kwang-eon’s house, which was Kim Gu’s hiding place at the time, there stands a memorial stone that says, “Baekbeom Kim Gu’s Hideout.” In commemoration of Baekbeom's actions and signficance, Boseong-gun set up the “Kim Gu Retreat Monument” and also established the “Kim Gu Retreat Memorial Hall.” Fragrant pine trees and upright bamboo trees of Soesil Village resemble Baekbeom's character quite a lot. Although Baekbeom has long been gone, his thoughts about the country still live on in Boseong.

stories.title: Chungjeolsa Temple, Boseong - Story 1 of Chungjeolsa Temple in Deungnyang-myeon
stories.audioTitle: Chungjeolsa Temple, Boseong - Story 1 of Chungjeolsa Temple in Deungnyang-myeon
stories.script: Chungjeolsa Temple, Boseong - Story 1 of Chungjeolsa Temple in Deungnyang-myeon  Moui Janggun Choi Dae-seong  Sagok-ri, Gyeombaek-myeon, Boseong-gun is where General Choi Dae-seong was born. During the Japanese invasion of 1592, he served as an adviser and the commander in charge of defenses in the rear unit under Admiral Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin and took part in a countless number of battles. From the famous Battle of Hansando Island and the Battle of Busanpo to battles in Okpo, Dangpo, Ungpo, Happo and Angolpo, wherever Admiral Yi scored a victory, General Choi was there as well.  General Choi is also the one who proposed to Chungmugong a scheme to lure the Japanese army in the well-known Battle of Hansando Island. King Seonjo praised his meritorious deeds and bestowed upon him the post of Hullyeonwonjeong as well as a sword and something that was called a “hol.” The Jeongyu Wars in 1597 disintegrated the government army and decimated the coast of the South Sea. As the government forces became nearly devoid of the ability to defend themselves or the country, General Choi put on his armor once again and began to recruit a righteous army. Upon hearing the news that General Choi was recruiting men to fight against the Japanese, a great number of people gathered, even reaching a few thousand later on. Patriots from the Boseong region also joined General Choi, which included figures like Song Dae-rip, Kim Deok-bang, Jeon Bang-sak and Hwang Won-bok.  His nickname of “Moui Janggun” was also created around this time because he had been recruiting an army. His two sons, Eon-rip and Hu-rip; his younger brother, Dae-min; his younger cousin, Dae-yeong; and, even, his servants, Duridong and Gapsul, all followed General Choi. His righteous army engaged in over 20 battles against the Japanese troops led by Gato Kiyomasa and won every single time, which is why the Japanese raiders shuddered even when they merely looked at the flag that had Moui Janggun written on it. Up to this point, almost all of the Japanese raiders invading Boseong, Suncheon, Goheung and Gwangyangman regions were routed by Moui Janggun's righteous army.  Anchi, located on the border of Boseong-gun and Deungnyang-myeon, was the most ferocious battlefield, and, in June 1598, a fierce bout between the two sides took place here. Moui Janggun commanded the army at the front. With their fighting spirits lifted more than ever, the righteous army soldiers fought bravely against the Japanese raiders who began slowly be pushed back as they were overwhelmed by the righteous army's energy and force. But, sadly, Moui Janggun who chased after an enemy captain on the run was shot by a Japanese soldier lying in ambush and passed away at the age of 45. At the Battle of Anchi, Duridong and Gapsul also died along with the general while his eldest son, Yeon-rip, suffered a serious injury. Also, the general's brother, Dae-min, returned from Suncheon with serious wounds but eventually passed away, and the general's younger cousin died in battle in the Goheung.

stories.title: Chungjeolsa Temple, Boseong - Story 2 of Chungjeolsa Temple in Deungnyang-myeon
stories.audioTitle: Chungjeolsa Temple, Boseong - Story 2 of Chungjeolsa Temple in Deungnyang-myeon
stories.script: Chungjeolsa Temple, Boseong - Story 2 of Chungjeolsa Temple in Deungnyang-myeon  Protecting the country over three generations   When the Qing invaded Joseon later on, three grandsons of Moui Janggun raised righteous armies. Moui Janggun had been left out of the list of meritorious vassals until this point. In any era, there were those who like to indulge in armchair arguments and empty talks. Three generations dedicated their lives for the country but the royal court, blinded by factional politics, tried to ignore the general's noble sacrifices. Even the Annals of King Seonjo assessed the general in a slightly negative and passive manner. It was the patriots from Boseong who restored the honor of General Choi Dae-seong. Local Confucian scholars including Munganggong An Bangjun persistently submitted appeals to the king to have the general's meritorious deeds recognized. Then, finally in 1752 (28th year of King Yeongjo's reign), he was posthumously conferred with the rank of Tongjeongdaebu Hyeongjocham Moui Janggun. This was over a century after his death.  The old name of Choamsan Mountain in the back of Sagok-ri, Gyeombaek-myeon is Geumhwasan. A 300-pyeong plain in the mid-slope of the mountain is said to be the Geumhwasa Temple site during the Baekje Period. Geumhwasa once was an enormous temple but, because of its severe bedbug problems, it was eventually burned to ashes. Who knew the old saying “To burn one's house to get rid of the bedbugs” was actually a true story. But, still, it is hard to imagine how many bedbugs there were insomuch to burn down such a huge temple in Choamsan, which is one of the three renowned royal azalea mountains of Boseong along with Jeamsan and Illimsan.  When you walk up for about 300m from the Geumhwasa site and its strange legend, you will reach a natural cave called Beteulgul between the cliffs. It is said that the younger sister of Moui Janggun carried looms into this cave with female servants of the house and weaved cloths for military uniforms of over a thousand righteous army soldiers, which is where the name, Beteulgul came from.  Even just the men of the family not being enough, the younger sister volunteered to support the righteous army activities. In April and May every year when the royal azalea are in full bloom, Choamsan becomes a sea of red. Deep inside the cave, a group of women sewed a great quantity of clothes without even realizing that flowers bloomed, birds chirped, and spring came in the burning red Choamsan. It feels as if we can visualize the beads of sweat forming on the foreheads of these women.

stories.title: Ochungsa Temple, Boseong - Ochungsa Temple, Boseong-eup
stories.audioTitle: Ochungsa Temple, Boseong - Ochungsa Temple, Boseong-eup
stories.script: Ochungsa Temple, Boseong - Ochungsa Temple, Boseong-eup  An outsider who kept their fidelity to Goryeo   Toehyudang Seon Yun-ji is a Chinese man who used to be a scholar of Munyeongak during the Ming Dynasty but became naturalized in Goryeo after visiting the late Goryeo Dynasty as an envoy. According to the 『Boseong History of People』, Zhu Yuanzhang, the empreror of Ming at the time, said, “Goryeo has seen invasions by Japanese raiders and flourishings of Buddism so the duties that a man must fulfill continue to disappear and upright academics are gradually declining,” and dispatched Seon to Goryeo.  Upon arriving in Goryeo, he was appointed as Jeollado Gwanchalsa, or governor, and Honam Allyeomsa to sweep the Japanese raiders from the Honam region and to spread Confucianism. He also stabilized the livelihoods of the people and ruled justly and wisely, and the people of Boseong who were touched by his learning and virtue built a Saengsadang in Hansik-dong in his honor.  Saengsadang is where a ritual is held for someone who is still alive out of respect and praise for a just and wise rule of Gamsa or Suryeong of a village. This tells us how much affection Mr. Seon had for the country of Goryeo. From the day he first arrived in Goryeo in 1382 (8th year of King U's reign) until the day he died, Mr. Seon lived strictly as a Goryeo person. One of the closest academic colleagues of his was Yaeun Gil Jae who was known as one of the three great scholars of the late Goryeo Period along with Mogeun Yi Saek and Peun Jeong Mong-ju. After Goryeo collapsed, Seon resigned from government posts together with Gil Jae and went back to the country life. The pen name he made for himself around then was Toe, which means to avoid; Hyu, which means to rest; and Dang, which means a house. For the remainder of his life, Toehyudang dwelled in Boseong, formed a family and became the progenitor of the Boseong Seon Clan.  His years of birth and death are not clearly known. Ochungsa located in Boseong-eup is a family shrine where five loyal subjects of the Boseong Seon family are enshrined. Mr. Seon Yun-ji together with Seon Hyeong, Seon Geo-i, Seon Se-gang and Seon Yak-hae are known as the Five Loyal Subjects of the Seon Clan. In 183, King Sunjo bestowed a plaque of a funeral oration upon Ochungsa and lauded Seon's achievements as follows.  “The scholar came to the country in the east to show the virtue of the emperor. Also, he did not consider a life in this nation an undesirable one but, instead, entered the Goryeo family. He valued the beauty of our custom through three-years of mourning and excluded Buddism to walk on the path of righteousness. Teachings of loyalty and filial piety are bestowed and only joy will come for his descendants in return for the good deeds he performed for others throughout his life.”  Ochungsa was torn down during the reign of Daewongun and restored in 1961 to the shrine we see today. It features a shrine with three rooms in the front and a gambrel roof, the L-shaped Chunguidang,  Naesammun, Oesammun and Munganchae. Chunguidang was originally built as a sarangchae of a private residence but later changed to an auditorium, the same as you can see today. Having been recognized for its architectural significance and rarity as a structure with a specific purpose, Ochungsa was designated as a Jeollanam-do Folk Cultural Heritage.

stories.title: Bideulgogae, Boseong - Bideulgogae in Yedang-ri, Deungnyang-myeon
stories.audioTitle: Bideulgogae, Boseong - Bideulgogae in Yedang-ri, Deungnyang-myeon
stories.script: Bideulgogae, Boseong - Bideulgogae in Yedang-ri, Deungnyang-myeon  The legend that became the root of the anti-Japan movement   The character in the drama, 〈Bridal Mask〉, who appears as Damsari the righteous army commander is said to be inspired by Mr. An Gyuhong, a righteous army general from Boseong who once famously said, “Do not boast about your fist in Beolgyo.” In fact, as we trace back to the origin of the term, Beolgyo Fist, we will learn that it ties to the anti-Japan righteous army activities that took place in Boseong. According to 『100 Years of Beolgyo: Korean Modern History of a Colony Port』, a book published by Beolgyo residents in 2007, that famous saying began to spread after the incident in which An Gyuhong, the general of a righteous army and a former house servant, beat up a Japanese military policeman to death at a Beolgyo marketplace.  The Honam region where the anti-Japan independence movement was carried out in the fiercest manner was a serious headache for Japan. Righteous army activities, which had taken root in the region through the Donghak Peasant Revolution, gained more energy as most of the Korean Empire government soldiers joined after they were disbanded by the Jeongmi Treaty. People called the righteous army led by General An Gyuhong the “Damsari Unit.” In Jeolla-do dialect, Damsari means a house servant. The Damsari Unit was the primary subject for monitoring by the Japanese military and police. The Damsari soldiers disguised themselves as farmers during the day to engage in an intelligence war while, at night, they carried out guerrila attacks. Their primary targets were Japanese police, military, and members of Iljihoe as well as the evil men of wealth who lived like parasites sucking at Japan.  The life story of General An Gyuhong is described in detail in 『Damsansilgi』 written primarily by the Confucian scholars in the Boseong region and 『Boseong History of People』 published by Boseong Cultural Center. Damsan is a pen name that was assigned to him after his death. Born in Taekchon Village, Usan-ri, Boseong-eup, An Gyuhong is a tenth generation of Munganggong An Bangjun. His father passed away when he was young and with the responsibility to take care of his mother and younger siblings, he worked as a servant for 20 years in the house of one of his cousins in Beophwa-ri, Mundeok-myeon.  Since the early stage of his life, he was very strong and great at martial arts. He also possessed upright, chivalrous spirits, which made him unable to restrain himself upon witnessing acts that were unjust. A story has it that, when he saw an official from a tax office beating up a poor neighbor, he tied the official to a pillar and scolded them harshly. It's safe to assume that he must have had a fiery temper as well. The Jeongmi Treaty of 1907 set the heart of young An Gyuhong on fire. He had harbored animosity towards the Japanese imperialism and, after this treaty took place, he formed “Ilsimgye”with Yeom Je-bo, Lee Jeong-pyo and Park Cheol-hyeon and agreed to raise a righteous army.

stories.title: Bideulgogae, Boseong - Damsari Unit
stories.script: Bideulgogae, Boseong - Damsari Unit  Achievements of the Damsari Unit  An Gyuhong organized Ilsimgye and recruited servants like him, woodcutters, farmers and even a few disbanded soldiers. Just before an uprising, he asked local influential figures for assistance but only cold shoulders were received in return. Then, Damsan led Ilsimgye and joined forces with Kang Seong-in's righteous army in Suncheon but, soon, decided to form his own unit because, as he found out later, Kang Seong-in was leading a group that was disguised itself as a righteous army when in fact they were actually thieves plundering the properties of the common people. Damsan punished Kang for his deeds with a gunshot and was elected by Ilsimgye as the general of the righteous army.  Since then, the Damsari Unit scored incredible victories everywhere it went from Boseong to Hwasun and Gwangyang. They carried out a surprise attack on an elite unit of the Japanese army to secure a great volume of weapons and military secrets, and, in Gwangyang, they also raided the Japanese who had taken the fishing rights of our fishermen by force and destroyed their surveying units while killing pro-Japanese traitors of Iljinhoe. As you can see, behind every incident of significance, lies the Damsari Unit was there. Their fearless anti-Japan resistance received active support and sponsorship from the locals.  In March 1909, Damsan led local righteous army troops as Honam Haenggun Sojang to completely annihilate about 70 men of the Japanese military police in Geoseong-dong, Naju. Feeling the pressure, the Japanese army executed the Honam righteous army extermination plan in September of the same year and assigned a separate infantry regiment exclusively responsible for the Damsari Unit. No matter how brave and courageous An Gyuhong's army was, they would never be able to withstand this full might. Damsan's resistance, which had last for a year and seven months since February 1908, ended on the night when a temporary disbandment of the righteous army was decided.  After parting with his comrades with hopes to reunite in the future, he returned to his hometown but was arrested by the Japanese police near his home in Mundeok-myeon. Japan sentenced him to death.  After Liberation, a monument that commemorates Damsari Unit's Pacheong Seungcheop was erected on Bideulgogae in Yedang-ri, Deungnyang-myeon. Pacheong Seungcheop is the incident where An Gyuhong's army, which had obtained intelligence that a company of the Japanese army was scheduled to move from Suncheon to Boseong, lied in ambush at Bideulgogae, killed every last Japanese soldier and acquired many of the enemy weaponry including matchlocks and ammunition.

stories.title: Mun Ikjeom of Boseong - Bujomyo Shrine of Mun Ikjeom in Miryeok-myeon
stories.audioTitle: Mun Ikjeom of Boseong - Bujomyo Shrine of Mun Ikjeom in Miryeok-myeon
stories.script: Mun Ikjeom of Boseong - Bujomyo Shrine of Mun Ikjeom in Miryeok-myeon  Village that breathes the warmth of cotton   Cotton flowers blossom and fall several times from spring to late autumn excluding winter so they are the type of flowers that really cater to their fans. He went to a foreign country far away as an envoy but was soon put in an exile. When he was released, he hid three cottonseeds inside the lid of a brush and smuggled them home. Two of the seeds died on Goryeo's land but the last and only surviving cottonseed brought about a remarkable revolution in our history of clothing.  It reminds you of a scene from an intelligence war movie. Some suspect that the circumstances are a bit exaggerated but it is an undeniable fact that cotton was introduced to our land by Mr. Mun Ikjeom's efforts. Thanks to him, poor commoners who could not afford anything other than hemp cloth and animal skin for clothing were now able to make clothing out of cotton.  Cotton had an impact on not only the regular people but also the royal family. Queen Jeongsun, the second queen married by King Yeongjo when he was 66 years of age, was 15 years old at the time, setting the record for a marriage with the largest age gap in the history of the Joseon Dynasty. The reason that Queen Jeongsun was chosen as the queen over many other competitors was because of cotton flowers.  Before the final selection, Yeongjo asked the candidates, “What do you think is the most beautiful flower in the world?” While everyone else replied ume, peony or other flowers that are fancy and colorful, Jeongsun chose cotton flowers. The king asked why. She responded, A cotton flower does not have exceptional beauty but it keep the people warm during the cold winters so it is the most beautiful flower in the world.” Considering a tender and benevolent heart as the greatest virtue of a queen, Yeongjo chose her over a number of ladies from prominent houses.  Mun Ikjeom first brought cottonseeds into the Korean Peninsula during the reign of King Gongmin in the late Goryeo Period. Nammyeong Jo Sik, a scholar of the mid-Joseon Dynasty, later said, “Putting clothes on people is as great as Hou Ji who first started to farm,“ highly praising his contribution. Bujomyo refers to construction of a shrine by royal command for someone who has made significant contributions to the country as well as the order to hold rituals for the person forever. Bujomyo of Mr. Mun Ikjeom used to be in Sancheon, Gyeongsangnam-do but it was burned to ashes during the Japanese invasion of 1592 and, years later, it was relocated to Dogae-ri, Miryeok-myeon, Boseong-gun by the descendants of the Nampyeong Mun Clan and local Confucian scholars.  Bujomyo is a special privilege to enshrine the ancestral tablet of a person who has performed great merits for the nation while rituals in the shrine are also conducted eternally. When you enter Chungsinmun, which is the Oesammun, you will find Dongjae and Seojae and, in Yumulgak, documents related to Ikseon of Bujomyo are stored. Consisted of 15 documents total, these materials are designated as Jeollanam-do Tangible Cultural Property No. 165, and are valuable data for understanding the customs and truth of the relocation of Bujomyo during the Joseon Period.

stories.title: Jeamsan Mountain, Boseong
stories.script: Jeamsan Mountain, Boseong  A place that holds the myth of Gomjae  In Boseong, there are three famous mountains whose names include the letter Je, meaning king - Jeamsan, Jonjesan and Jeseoksan. Standing at the end of Honam Jeongmaek in Ungchi-myeon, Boseong-gun, Jeamsan is the tallest among the numerous mountains representing Boseong.  A unique 30m-high rock at the peak that resembles the Chinese letter Je is formed with 3 levels, exuding a magnificent and masculine vibe. Standing tall on the border of Jangheung and Boseong, Jeollanam-do, the mountain stretches its branches out even to the Goheung Peninsula. The rocks and peaks seen in the surroundings look as if they are politely bowing to the rocks at the top, which is why the mountain is also known as “Imgeumbawisan”, or the mountain of the rock king. The rock at the top of the mountain is broad and flat enough for about 100 people to sit on at the same time. The myth of Jeamsan originates from Gomjae where this rock is seated.  Once upon a time, a kind and beautiful queen lived in Gomjae. Rumors of her beauty and virtue spread even to the prince living up in heaven Infuriated by the fact that the prince of heaven had fell in love with a woman from earth, the Great Jade Emperor struck the prince with a long stick. The prince immediately fell down onto Gomjae, where he turned into a huge rock at the top of a mountain. The prince of heaven then became the guardian saint of the village. The villagers originally called Gomjaesan Mountain, Imgeumbawisan or Hwangjebawisan, however it eventually evolved into what we refer to as Jeamsan in the present. The name of “Ungchi” also came from this myth.  A great thing about myths is that, no matter how sad a story is, it mostly ends with a happy ending. But there are indeed stories that do not end in a pleasant way. For such stories and myths, people hold rituals or memorial ceremonies to comfort the victimized souls.  Gomjae, the main peak of Jeamsan, is connected to Sajasan (666m) and Illimsan (664m) to the south by its ridge. Once you stand at the Gomjae observation deck, you can enjoy the great scenes of Boseong, such as Deungnyangman Bay, Boseongman Bay, Juamho Lake, Boseonggang River and the tea plantation. You are also able to see the Ungchi field which is famous for Ungchi olbyeo rice, which acquired the Geographical Indication Registration No. 74 following Boseong green tea, Beolgyo cockles, and Boseong Sambe. On a sunny day, Mudeungsan Mountain in Gwangju and even Jeju Island are within sight. As you stand at the top and look out in all directions, you will realize why Jeamsan is considered the eldest brother of all mountains.  Royal azalea are in full bloom during the spring, clouds and mist swarm all around during the summer, maple leaves and silver grass welcome you to fall, and the snowy landscape is magnificent to watch come winter. The four seasons of Jeamsan, with mother nature boasting its banquet, are always beautiful.

stories.title: Jeamsan Mountain Recreational Forest, Boseong - Jeamsan Mountain Recreational Forest
stories.audioTitle: Jeamsan Mountain Recreational Forest, Boseong - Jeamsan Mountain Recreational Forest
stories.script: Jeamsan Mountain Recreational Forest, Boseong - Jeamsan Mountain Recreational Forest  A quiet place for meditation  Located in Daesan-ri, Ungchi-myeon, Boseong-gun, Jeamsan Mountain Recreational Forest is a beautiful recreational forest facility that was opened in 1996 by Boseong-gun. Once you step into the forest, that features large trees such as Cypress, Acer mono, oriental oaks, and pine trees, a refreshing energy will instantly flow through your body, wiping out all your stress away.  Equipped with a variety of facilities such as trails, streams to play in, camping grounds, and mountain pensions built with natural wood, Jeamsan Recreational Forest is a famous attraction of Boseong that welcomes more than 200,000 visitors yearly. It was originally operated as a free-admission facility but now it charges an admission fee thanks to the increase in burden of facility management.  The clear water of the valley originating from Seomjingang River forms a three-level waterfall, and it has been recognized as first-grade, zero-pollution water that is okay for people to drink as is, which makes it a popular summer vacation spot for families who want to enjoy the cool water with their children.  The construction of a recreational forest here should be credited to the efforts of the Ungchi-myeon residents. At the time immediately after Liberation, Jeamsan was a mountain with no large trees or old pine trees. It was in fact just covered in thickly wooded scrubs. The indiscriminatory logging of the Japanese had been performed in the area, moreover, after the Yeosu-Suncheon rebellion, the mountain, which was a hiding place for the leftists, became a target for deforestation. A countless number of innocent trees were cut down as scapegoats of history. Since then, the residents of Ungchi-myeon have diligently planted trees for about half a century, which made today's Jeamsan Recreational Forest possible.  If you go in a little further while breathing in the scent of phytoncide that spreads throughout the forest, you will find a trail covered with sawdust. When walking along the trail that seems to emit the fragrance of nature, amidst the of sounds of water, birds and the wind, the vast forest becomes a space just for yourself. Anger filled hearts are carried away by the gentle wind, and all you hear is the sound of birds, water, and the wind.  The 5.2km course, which starts from the recreational forest to Imgeumbawi Rock at the peak before returning to the forest, is a course that takes about two and a half hours. Sometimes, the course feels a bit short as you lose track of time all the whilst your soul is being purified through the journey. Jeamsan Recreational Forest is still progressing. There are planned facilities still under construction. Because there is still much to show, it is a place that leaves you full of anticipation while imagining its developments for the future.  Currently, the forest operates various subsidiary facilities such as an eco-friendly leisure sports and eco-adventure facility, Deoneum-gil (mountainous trekking road), and the Environmental Disease Prevention Management Center. There is no better cure for the ever-stressed people of the modern society than the Jeamsan Mountain Recreational Forest.

stories.title: Obongsan Mountain, Boseong
stories.script: Obongsan Mountain, Boseong  Little Seorak of Namdo   People of Deungnyang-myeon call the two Obongsan Mountains in the area“Obongsan” and “Kalbongsan.” The taller of the two is Kalbongsan. If you think about it, there is nothing more common than the names of mountains, valleys, or rocks. Another Kalbongsan exists in Gapyeong, Gyeonggi-do and there is a valley called Yongchu there as well, which has the exact same name as the one in Obongsan, Boseong. It is probably because there are many geographies that look similar throughout the country, which features a countless number of low mountains and small ranges.  Obongsan in Deungnyang-myeon, Boseong is also not a tall mountain. It is only 324m in altitude, but there are a variety of things to see everywhere you climb and the view of Dadohae from the ridge is excellent. The petite rocks that stand starting from the entrance give off a cute and adorable aura.  You can climb Obongsan in two different ways. One is to take the trail set up towards Kalbawi and the other is to walk on the path that leads to Yongchu Waterfall.  At Yongchu Waterfall, which has a myth that a dragon once ascended to heaven at this location, its basin is mostly filled up now. It is not an enormous or high waterfall but, according to the elderly in the area nearby, the basin used to be big enough for a complete pack of silk threads to go in.  As you walk up the trail that heads towards the waterfall, you will find a stone slope made up of flat stones, which are also known as Bangdol. In old times, flat stones from Obongsan were popularly used as stones for the floors of the traditional heating system. Thanks to its uniform sizes, small thickness, large, and neat shapes, these stones were perfect for the floor heating system and quickly sold in great volumes in Gwangju, Daejeon, Seoul as well as many other places.  During the era when people used floor heating systems at home, they climbed the mountain to obtain Bangdol for every year of the poor harvest. Though it is only used by few people today, the Boseong Cultural Center works to inherit and maintain the technique of setting the traditional floor heating systems before it is forgotten.

stories.title: Kalbawi at Obongsan Mountain, Boseong
stories.script: Kalbawi at Obongsan Mountain, Boseong  Greatest peak of Obongsan  The landscape you see at the peak of Obongsan Mountain is magnificent. Some of the landscapes you can see apart from the indigo blue sea of Dadohae are the Deungnyang-myeon breakwater that stretches out in a straight line, the broad plains of the reclaimed land of Deungnyang-myeon, the Joseong-myeon area including the Bibong-ri Dinosaur Eggs Fossil Site, the Deungnyangdo where the protector of the South Sea Admiral Yi Sun-sin collected military provisions, and finally the Goheung Peninsula in the distance.  Steep cliffs spread out like screen doors underneath, giving off the imagery of sharp swords standing side by side. Kalbawi, which is over 30m tall, is the highest peak of Obongsan that seems as if the tip of a sharp-edged sword is pointing to the ever-stretching cliffs with 340 peaks on the other side. It also reminds you of the toe of a sock, or Beoseon. This is why people in the area also call Kalbawi as “Beoseonbawi.”  It is the same rock as Ingeomam, explained in the book 『Sceneries of Korea』, which is described to be located in Deungnyang-myeon, Boseong-gun, Jeollanam-do. In the surroundings, large, strange-shaped rocks such as Horangibawi, Beoseonbawi, Gaksibawi and Josaebawi are erected here and there, and there are also a number of caves of different sizes. Moreover, there is a broad space underneath that is encompassed by tall, rocky walls. Though it is small, it would be hard to find another mountain in Korea that features a greater variety of things to see, which is why, since old times, Obongsan has been known as the “Little Seoraksan.”  On Kalbawi, which can be said to be the symbol of this mountain, a vague silhouette of Hwasang (traces of a drawing) are engraved. Normally you can't see it, but it often makes its appearance on the morning of a sunny day. There are many theories behind this Hwasang,  one of which says that Wonhyodaesa engraved a statue of Buddha here as he left. One day, Wonhyodaesa was passing by the area and was captivated by the profound beauty of Obongsan and Kalbawi. So, he stayed in a cave below and practice asceticism before engraving the shape of Buddha as he left the area.  According to another theory, it is the Hwasang of Taejo Yi Seong-gye who, prior to his enthronement, is said to have engraved his own image on this rock after defeating the Japanese raiders and staying at the fortress he had built here.  Even the local residents have different opinions regarding the true identity of the image carved on this rock. According to 『Cultural and Academic Survey of Boseong-gun』 published by Chonnam National University Museum, a large Yukgye (the protruding part on top of Buddha’s head) is carved on the head of the Hwasang and Baekho (the jewel located at the center of Buddha’s forehead) is engraved on the forehead while Suin (the hand motion of Buddha, its meaning varies depending on the shape) of the right hand is also found close to the chest. Considering all of these elements, it is estimated to be a Maitreya or Tathagata statue carved during the early Goryeo Period.  Underneath the rock, there are caves on the left and right. The one on the left is Jangjegul where Wonhyodaesa is said to have practiced asceticism, and the cave on the right is Beteulgul. In 1949, a guerrilla unit of North Korean partisans attempted an attack on Boseong Police Station. A few dozens of the partisan members ended up running away from the police into Obongsan but they were eventually killed in this Jangjegul. As you go into a crack in the rock and look up, Kalbawi that stands tall into the sky blocks your vision, leaving you shuddering in awe of the empty space. We are curious to know what kind of enlightenment Wonhyodaesa reached inside such a quiet and still cave.

stories.title: Hackberry Forest of Jeonil-ri, Boseong - Hackberry Forest, Jeonil-ri
stories.audioTitle: Hackberry Forest of Jeonil-ri, Boseong - Hackberry Forest, Jeonil-ri
stories.script: Hackberry Forest of Jeonil-ri, Boseong - Hackberry Forest, Jeonil-ri  Trees that have endured the ages   In front of the head house of the Yeonggwang Jeong Clan by the entrance of the village, 18 armful hackberry trees and a zelkova are lined up towards the coastline right in front of the sea. Every fall, the hackberry trees bear bean-sized fruits, a handful of which were popular snacks for children in the countryside.  A hackberry tree is also known as a Paeng Tree in Korean because, when you make a Paeng gun out of a bamboo tube and insert hackberries into the gun before blowing it with your mouth, the berries would fly like bullets making a noise that goes “paeng.” If the hackberry trees are full of leaves, the village believes that a year of good harvest was upon them, and in turn they would hold a Dangsanje Ritual.  The Hackberry Forest of Jeonil-ri actually doesn't have enough trees to be called a forest but it still forms good harmony with the surrounding topography and mountainous terrain, giving off a vintage atmosphere. The hackberry trees found in Jeonil-ri are old trees that are at least 200 to 400 years of age. They are about 9 to 15m-tall and line up along the 155m-long embankment. It is rare to find a place in Korea where this many trees of the same species inhabit and grow in a region. Old hackberry trees are designated as one of the three nurse-trees of Korea, therefore receive extremely delicate care. If trees have names like people do then some even have completed their ownership registration procedures and pay taxes to the government.  As more and more of these hackberry trees continue to grow here over a long period of time, the forest will become even more antique.

stories.title: Rock-carved Triad Buddha Statue in Yureo-myeon, Boseong - Rock-carved Triad Buddha Statue in Yureo-myeon
stories.audioTitle: Rock-carved Triad Buddha Statue in Yureo-myeon, Boseong - Rock-carved Triad Buddha Statue in Yureo-myeon
stories.script: Rock-carved Triad Buddha Statue in Yureo-myeon, Boseong - Rock-carved Triad Buddha Statue in Yureo-myeon  A smile revealed in moonlight  The Rock-carved Seated Buddha Statue in Yusin-ri is considered the treasure of treasures that is responsible for making Yureo-myeon and Ilwolsa Temple, established at the northern foot of Jonjesan Mountain, famous. Originally, the Ilwolsa site is known as the location where Jonjesa Temple was built during the Goryeo Dynasty however it was destroyed in the 19th century. The existence of a Buddhist temple was discontinued for a long time until in 1978 when Ilwolsa was newly constructed here.  Large rocks of various shapes including elephants, dragons, swords, fish, pigs, and Sapsal dogs stand throughout the temple exuding a divine atmosphere. Among them, the so-called “Toad Rock”, which is also known as 12 Jisin Rock, showcases different animal shapes, all depending on the direction you look at it from. An area that is indented beneath Toad Rock is where monks of high ranks went about their Zen meditations since ancient times.  Dolneodeul, where flat rocks spread like a valley, produces a magnificent scene in which the stones seem to flow like water. On the rock face next to this stone valley, the Rock-carved Seated Buddha Statue of Yusin-ri is engraved and overlooks the world below the mountain.  Being complete in form, which is rare for rock-carved statues, this Rock-carved Seated Buddha Statue is estimated to be from the pre-Goryeo period and is designated as the country's Treasure No. 944. Over the centuries, the statue's nose and mouth have been weathered and damaged, which brings about an air of sadness for the visitors. Still, the rock-carved statue is displaying a smile that's as radiant as a smile could possibly be.  The smile doesn't show when one observes simply with the naked eye. Why do you think that is? There was a photographer who visited a few times to take pictures, and he found out that the bright smile of the statue was able to be captured only when a subdued moonlight would shine upon it. During the day, it boasts an enigmatic smile, like any other Buddha statues, but, under the soft moonlight, it exhibits a smile that beams much like a baby's would.  What do you think this Rock-carved Seated Buddha Statue, which has survived for thousands of years in this exact location, is trying to tell the world with its bright smile revealed in the moonlight? Ilsim, which means to become one even though the world may be stormy. Perhaps, the statue's smile is tied to these two letters of Seolju.

stories.title: Daewonsa Temple, Boseong
stories.script: Daewonsa Temple, Boseong  A temple with a gorgeous cherry blossom tunnel  Daewonsa, which still holds the mystique of a millennial temple, is famous for its cherry blossom tunnel that runs over 5km, with Juamho Lake in its background, all the way to the entrance. Established in the 1980s, this cherry blossom road boasts such beauty that it was selected as one of the “100 Most Beautiful Roads of Korea.” As you walk along this path, you will see Daewonsa Temple in the distance at the foot of Cheonbongsan Mountain. According to feng shui topography, Cheonbongsan is shaped like the nest of a phoenix.  Daewonsa and the phoenix are deeply related to Monk Ado Hwasang who spread Buddhism in Silla. About 1,500 years ago during the reign of King Jijeung of Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje at the time had already authorized Buddhism, which was widely promulgated both in the royal palace and among the general public, but Silla still had a deeply rooted indigenous belief so they did not want to accept another religion. It was common for monks from foreign countries who had traveled to Silla to spread the teachings of Buddha to lose their lives at the hands of indigenous religion worshipers.  Even in such circumstances, Ado Hwasang took the risk and headed to Silla. Upon arriving in the country, he hid in the house of More in Seonsan-gun, Gyeongsangbuk-do and preached Buddhism to the people. One night, he heard a cry of a phoenix in his dream. The phoenix cried out loud to tell Ado Hwasang to run because the Silla people were on their way with swords. He immediately woke up to see a phoenix flapping her wings out the window. Ado was guided by the phoenix and safely escaped to Bonghwangdae in Mudeungsan, Gwangju. Here, the phoenix disappeared.  Having survived thanks to the phoenix, Ado Hwasang roamed around the mountains and fields in the Honam region for three months. One day, when he finally saw a mountain shaped like a phoenix holding an egg under its wings, he became so ecstatic that he danced with joy. The mountain he discovered was Cheonbongsan and the temple built by Ado later on is Daewonsa, according to the popular myth.  Once you enter the precincts, a scene of young monks wearing red hats and sitting side by side stops you where you stand. Daewonsa is a temple that enshrines Taean Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva and is specialized as Gido Doryang for Taearyeong, which refers to an aborted child. Taean Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva says that Buddha's heart and sorrow expresses the hearts of parents that have burned to ashes. There are especially many events held at Daewonsa that hold special meanings. Among them, the lotus flower festival, which takes place in July and August of every year, enables you to enjoy several dozens of different kinds of lotus flowers as well as over a hundred aquatic plant species. The festival's theme is to wash away a turbulent mind like a lotus flower that purifies muddy water.  Another unique element of Daewonsa is the Tibet Museum located on the outside. Once you enter this museum, that exudes an exotic vibe, you find a congratulatory letter sent by the Dalai Lama for the opening ceremony. In the underground floor of the museum, there is what is called the “Death Experience Room.” It's a room where you may actually pretend that you are dying and experience the entire process from writing a will to stepping into a coffin and closing the cover to lie in there for some time. This place gives you a perfect chance to experience the time and place of your own death. Death is a reality that no one can avoid. Perhaps, the true goal of the Death Experience Room is to teach you to remember this day and leave room for no regrets in every moment of your life.

stories.title: Five-story Stone Pagoda in Bongcheon-ri, Boseong - Five-story Stone Pagoda in Bongcheon-ri
stories.audioTitle: Five-story Stone Pagoda in Bongcheon-ri, Boseong - Five-story Stone Pagoda in Bongcheon-ri
stories.script: Five-story Stone Pagoda in Bongcheon-ri, Boseong - Five-story Stone Pagoda in Bongcheon-ri  Answering your wish   The Five-story Stone Pagoda in Bongcheon-ri inherits the stone pagoda style of the Silla Dynasty. It is said to have been built when Odongsa Temple was established in the 7th year of King Hyeonjong’s reign during the Goryeo Dynasty (1016). The temple now, however, is nowhere to be seen and only a stone pagoda remains for us to interpret what went down in history. The five-story stone pagoda, which is now only two-stories tall and overlooks the quietly flowing Boseonggang River, ultimately lost its balance at the third level due to grave robbers. But the Bodhisattva statue engraved on the southern face of the upper platform and its delicate relaxed smile attracts people's attention in a mysterious way. erhaps, people of the old days also felt the same. There is a myth about the Five-story Stone Pagoda in Bongcheon-ri that has been passed down for a long time.  During the late Goryeo Dynasty, a poor farmer lived in this village. He was so impoverished that he could not even get married at an age of over 40 years and lived alone without any parents or siblings.  In the afternoon of a spring day, as he lamented his misfortune while leaning on the stone pagoda, he fell asleep. All of a sudden, he sensed something very bright right in front of his eyes. As he looked closely, he found two huge eggs beaming in a golden light by the river ahead. t was too vivid to be a dream so he ran towards the river at once. There, a young woman was about to dive into the water.  The surprised farmer hurriedly followed her into the river. She had become a widow due to her husband's death the day before their wedding.  She continued to refuse the farmer’s help and tried to dive back into the water, saying that, since she was not accepted by neither the in-laws nor her own family, her only option was to commit suicide. The farmer persuaded her earnestly and eventually brought her to his house. Some time later, the two became husband and wife. Feeling a sense of responsibility for the newest member of the family, he worked diligently and their livelihood gradually improved. His wife served her husband well and the husband treasured his wife.  Now the only thing left that the farmer could wish for was to have a son who would carry on his family's name. No one knew why but this happily married couple was not lucky when it came to fostering a child. Feeling as if they had to try anything they could possibly try, the couple prayed to the stone pagoda every night.  Then, finally, the wife gave birth to twin boys at the age of 50, and the couple continued to pray to the pagoda with more diligence and sincerity than ever before. It is said that these boys grew up to be great military generals. This was the beginning of the myth that your wish will come true if you come and pray in front of the Five-story Stone Pagoda in Bongcheon-ri.

stories.title: Three-story Stone Pagoda in Joseong-myeon, Boseong - Three-story Stone Pagoda in Joseong-myeon
stories.audioTitle: Three-story Stone Pagoda in Joseong-myeon, Boseong - Three-story Stone Pagoda in Joseong-myeon
stories.script: Three-story Stone Pagoda in Joseong-myeon, Boseong - Three-story Stone Pagoda in Joseong-myeon  Keeping watch faithfully, the lost temple site  The Three-story Stone Pagoda of Ucheon-ri, which was designated as Treasure No. 933 in 1988, stands in the middle of a barley field. Slightly different from the typical stone pagoda style of the Silla Dynasty, this pagoda was dismantled and restored in 1970. The exact timing and method of its construction are unknown. Some claim that it was a pagoda built in the branch temple of Jinggwangsa located in Beolgyo nearby but this theory is not a confirmed one.  Known as the birthplace of traditional green tea, Jinggwangsa was a temple that published Buddhist books and was so large that it had Ssanggyesa and Songgwangsa as its branches. Jinggwangsa, too, only has mere traces that remain today. The Three-story Stone Pagoda of Ucheon-ri has quietly guarded a temple site filled with weeds for several hundred years, possibly, even longer.  Because the lower structure of the pagoda's platform is buried underground, we are not able to verify its exact style but the manufacturing technique of the pagoda as a whole is very refined, sophisticated and tidy. It was designated as Local Tangible Cultural Property No. 6 on January 29, 1972 and was promoted to state-designated Treasure No. 943 on April 1, 1988.  Could the pagoda possibly remember a time when this land was in fact the sea? Standing alone on the side of an expressway where the Gyeongjeon Line railroad tracks tell us about the flow of ever-changing time, the stone pagoda continues in its quiet stillness.

stories.title: Buan Celadon Museum Enterance
stories.audioTitle: Explanation of the Museum History and Facilities, and Building External Design
stories.script: Welcome to the Buan Celadon Museum! The Buan region is known for the inlaid celadon that was made here about 1,000 years ago, during the Goryeo Dynasty, and which is reputed to be one of the best ceramics in the world. Opened in 2011, the Buan Celadon Museum was established as a three-storied building, with a land area of 69,452㎡ and a total floor area of 5,610㎡, by restoring and maintaining various national historical sites including Goryeo celadon kiln sites and relics.  The museum consists of two buildings – the exhibition building, which is used mainly to hold exhibitions, and the building on its left, which houses a special experience space where visitors to the museum can actually try their hand at producing celadon.   So if you have the time, why not try making your own celadon with the help of an artisan’s one-to-one explanation. It will be a truly worthwhile experience.   Now, in the park on the right of the museum, can you see the building with a semicircular wooden roof? Inside that building is a kiln site where Goryeo celadon was baked about 800 years ago. When it was discovered during an excavation conducted by the Museum of Wonkwang University in 1998, it was found that the arch-shaped ceiling of the kiln had been damaged, so only the furnace which was used to bake celadon and a part of the firing chamber remain at present. If you have enough time, we recommend you take a walk around the site.  Now, shall we discover the Goryeo celadon with its mysterious autumnal sky blue color at the Buan Celadon Museum? As you were entering the museum, did you notice the shape of the building? It features a unique design that takes the shape of a cup. In fact, our museum building was designed after the shape of the Bowl, celadon with inlaid chrysanthemun and scroll design (National Treasure No.115), that was excavated from the tomb of an eminent Goryeo official named Moon Gong-yu. The building was designed this way to represent the high-quality celadon that used to be made in Yucheon-ri in Buan, and the external wall was coated with oxide copper to represent celadon’s green color.    Explanation About the Glass Entrance Door  This entrance door is made with a special glass that was fabricated by gluing pieces of broken glass together to express the fine cracks on the surface of Goryeo celadon. Speaking in technical terms, it is ‘glazing cracking’ which indicates that the surface of the glaze is cracked like broken ice. These fine cracks occur mainly for two reasons. First, it often happened when, after baking the pottery in a kiln at a high temperature of about 1,250℃, the kiln door was opened and cold air flowed into the kiln before the temperature of the kiln had completely cooled down. This caused thick and irregular cracks to appear on the surface of the glaze. The other reason is due to a problem resulting from the combination of kaolin and glaze. In other words, when baking pottery at a high temperature, if the percentage of contraction between the glaze and the clay is not exactly the same - and even a tiny difference of 0.1% can cause a breach between them – this difference in contraction inside the cooled kiln will cause the glaze to crack. In this case, fine and regular cracks would appear on the entire surface of the pottery.  Technically speaking, when baking Korean kaolin over a fire, it shrinks by 15 to 20%, so it is not a great material for making celadon. The fact that Goryeo’s potters made such excellent celadon despite this disadvantage only serves to highlight their outstanding techniques and artistry.   Museum Exhibition Guide  Our museum’s exhibition rooms are situated on the first and second floors. We recommend you take a lift to visit the Celadon History Room, where you can appreciate a wide range of genuine celadon in the Celadon Masterpiece Room on the second floor first, and then go down to the first floor to visit the Celadon Production Room, Celadon Experience Room, and 4D Theater.

stories.title: Celadon History Room
stories.audioTitle: Celadon History Room: Chronology of Korean Pottery
stories.script: Now, let’s take a look around the exhibition room which displays genuine Goryeo celadon.  This is the Celadon History Room, where we can learn about the history of celadon. People first began to make and use pottery in Korea about 10,000 years ago in the Neolithic Age. Generally speaking, the pottery used in the Neolithic Age is characterized by a sharp body with a comb pattern or a V-shaped bottom. As people settled near rivers or beaches where there was a lot of sand, they made pottery with a V-shaped bottom so it could be inserted into sand easily for stability.   From the Neolithic Age until the North South States Period, people used viscous clay to make pottery or earthenware. Because clay is the main raw material of pottery, if the baking temperature rises above 1,000~1,100℃, the pottery collapses. So, they baked their pottery at a temperature below 1,000℃, resulting in lower strength.   On the other hand, from the Goryeo Dynasty onwards, Goryeo’s celadon and Joseon’s Buncheong (grayish-blue-powered celadon) and white porcelain were mainly made of a stone powder called kaolin (China clay) and glazed. These types of pottery are called porcelain. In Korea, we generally use the term dojagi, a Korean composite of dogi, which means ‘pottery’ in English, and jagi, which means ‘porcelain’ in English.   China was the first country in the world to produce glazed ‘porcelain’ made with stone powder, some 2,000 years ago, while Korea’s Goryeo Dynasty began to make porcelain about 1,000 years ago. China and Korea are the two only countries to have a tradition of making porcelain for more than 1,000 years.

stories.title: Relationship Between Chinese and Korean Porcelain
stories.audioTitle: Relationship Between Chinese and Korean Porcelain
stories.script: When did people start making and using porcelain in Korea? The first porcelain was made in Korea sometime in the late tenth century during the early days of the Goryeo Dynasty. At that time, it is said that Wuyue - an independent coastal kingdom of the tenth century located in present-day Zhejiang Province, China - was well-known for making excellent celadon, and amassed great wealth by selling celadons throughout China. However, when Wuyue was destroyed by China’s Song Dynasty around 978, its celadon craftsmen dispersed around East Asia. Some of them became naturalized citizens of Goryeo and passed down their celadon and white porcelain techniques to Goryeo’s potters. From then on, the Goryeo Dynasty produced and used solid and beautifully-colored celadon and white porcelain made of stone powder.   The circumstances in which porcelain making techniques were transmitted from China to Korea were revealed by archeological investigations and artifacts discovered at the Celadon and White Porcelain Kiln Site in Bangsan-dong of Siheung in Gyeonggi Province, and the Kiln Site in Wonsan-ri of Baecheon in South Hwanghae Province. As you can see in the photo, the Yuezhou celadon kiln site in Silongkou, Zhejiang, China on the left and the kiln site in Bangsan-dong, Siheung on the right share similar features including a 40m-long tunnel and kiln walls made of bricks. The brick kiln has a unique structure unlike those of Korea, and clearly shows the influence of Yuezhou celadon of China.

stories.title: Celadon Flower-shaped Bowl and Dish
stories.script: This celadon flower-shaped bowl and the accompanying dish were made about 950 to 1,000 years ago. They feature a cloudy green glaze with a simple floral pattern, and no inlaid design. As the early celadon and white porcelain of the Goryeo Dynasty were made with imported Chinese techniques, it is difficult to distinguish between Korean and Chinese artifacts because of similarities in their color and shape.

stories.title: 『Xuanhe Fengshi Gaoli Tujing』and Goryeo Celadon
stories.audioTitle: 『Xuanhe Fengshi Gaoli Tujing (宣和奉使高麗圖經, Travelogue of a Song China envoy named Xu Jing who visited Goryeo in 1123)』
stories.script: Xuanhe Fengshi Gaoli Tujing is a travel report written by Xu Jing, a Chinese envoy who was sent to Goryeo during the first year of the reign of King Injong of Goryeo for one month by Emperor Huizong of Song in 1123. This valuable record covers virtually every aspect of Goryeo society including its politics, society, culture, economy, military, arts, technology, clothes, customs, and so on. In particular, it contains detailed information about Goryeo celadon, including names, shapes, sizes, and usages, and describes the sophisticated shapes and beautiful jade color of celadon bottles and incense burners. It is considered an invaluable record as it contains a wealth of unique details about the features of Goryeo celadon at that time.

stories.title: Goryeo Celadon Kiln Site
stories.audioTitle: Goryeo Celadon Kiln Site Uncovered During an Archaeological Dig in Buan
stories.script: The archaeological features of a number of Goryeo celadon kiln sites were discovered during an investigation of Kilns 18 and 20 in Jinseo-ri, and Zone 7 in Yucheon-ri in the Buan area. The discovered kiln, which exhibits a 20m-long tunnel-style shape, consisted of mud walls, a furnace, a firing chamber, and a chimney - all of which are connected together by a long hole; and an arch-shaped ceiling.  The relics recovered from these ancient kiln sites were made in the heyday of Goryeo celadon, sometime between the late twelfth century and thirteenth century. They include dishes, bowls, saucers, bottles, pots, chairs, and other objects decorated with a wide variety of designs and motifs, including lotus, parrot, cloud and crane, lightning, chrysanthemum, vine, peony, fish swimming through waves, waterfront views, and so on. Goryeo celadon is generally known to have been used only by members of the upper class, such as kings and aristocrats. However, judging from the celadon found through actual research, plain rice bowls and dishes without patterns were baked in significant quantities by piling up ten or twenty of them together at a time; and were then supplied to the public at a low price. As for the high-quality celadons inlaid with designs of clouds, cranes, or pomegranates, they were fabricated only in small quantities and supplied to the upper class at a high price.

stories.title: Celadon-tiled Wall
stories.script: Here at the museum we have a total of 56 celadon-tiled walls that feature inlaid designs handmade by Buan potters who drew their inspiration from authentic Goryeo celadon tiles made in Buan about 800 years ago. Try to imagine a scene in which a Goryeo nobleman, wearing elegant silk clothes, spends his time leisurely drinking tea in a celadon cup, sitting in a celadon chair, writing a poem, and playing music on a traditional musical instrument in his house, whose walls, floors and even the roof are beautifully decorated with celadon materials. What a beautiful life!  One of the most impressive patterns on the celadon tiles can be found in the celadon maebyeong (prunus) vase possessed by the National Museum of Korea.   It depicts a scene in which a Confucian scholar is playing the geomungo, a Korean traditional instrument with six strings, under a pine tree while a crane descends to the ground and begins dancing to its beautiful melody. Filled with joy by this playful scene, the pine tree also joins the dance with the crane, twisting its body to the music. The potter who inscribed this uniquely creative pattern on a celadon vase 800 years ago must have been full of imagination and rather humorous.

stories.title: Explanation of the General History of Goryeo Celadon
stories.audioTitle: Explanation of the General History of Goryeo Celadon
stories.script: Goryeo Celadon is a representative handicraft of the Goryeo Dynasty that holds both practical and decorative value, and was used throughout the entire Goryeo period, from the initial introduction of the production technique toward the end of the tenth century to the fall of the dynasty in 1392.    Goryeo celadon is particularly well known for jade-colored celadon and inlaid celadon; however, jade-colored celadon was not produced from the early period of Goryeo. Just as a person is born, grows up to become an adult, gets old, and finally dies, so Goryeo celadon also assumed distinctive patterns and shapes at each stage of its existence, from its emergence and development to its prime and ultimate decline.

stories.title: The Emergence of Goryeo Celadon
stories.script: Shortly after the invention of celadon in the tenth century, the Korean people of the Unified Silla Dynasty learned about porcelain, an advanced commodity from China, through exchanges with the Tang Dynasty of China. In Korea drinking tea became fashionable among the nobility, students who had studied in the Tang Dynasty and Buddhist monks.   Furthermore, with the importation into Korea of celadon teacups and white porcelain teacups produced at the Yuezhou celadon kiln and the Jingzhou kiln in China, respectively, many people wanted to acquire a set of porcelain teacups. Around the same time, the Goryeo Dynasty was established and its ruling class began to import Chinese commodities via the west coast of the Korean peninsula; and as the demand for Chinese porcelain increased, it became necessary to produce porcelain directly in Goryeo.   Around this time, the small independent coastal kingdom of Wuyue in China, which was famous for making celadon and exported its products to Korea, was destroyed by the Song Dynasty in 978. It is thought that around that time a few celadon master craftsmen from the Yuezhou celadon kiln fled to Goryeo and transmitted their celadon production techniques to Goryeo craftsmen. This theory is supported by the discovery of a pottery kiln built with bricks of the same shape as Chinese kilns of the period. Among the diverse celadon wares made in Goryeo at that time were saucers with a halo-shaped foot, flower-shaped teacups, ewers, cups and saucers - all of which exhibited similar colors and shapes to the Chinese ones.

stories.title: The Development of Goryeo Celadon
stories.script: After an initial period of receiving and imitating Chinese celadon production techniques, Goryeo celadon followed its own course of development from the eleventh to the early twelfth century, resulting in changes in the shapes and patterns of celadon, and various changes related to the construction of celadon kilns.   A new type of clay kiln emerged, replacing the Chinese-style brick kiln, and the number of firings was increased to two. Thus, celadon wares were baked lightly at a low temperature first, then coated with a thin glaze and baked again, thereby conferring a unique transparent effect on Goryeo celadon. This method led to the development of the famous jade-colored celadon. The most representative celadon wares from this intense period of development are green celadon (low-grade celadon) and jade-colored celadon. Various decorative techniques were developed for celadon, such as the plain (pattern-less) style, intaglio carving (depressed engraving), relief carving (raised carving), impressed engraving in relief (i.e. the stamping of patterns on the surface of an object in relief), pictogram (patterns resembling the features of animals and plants), openwork (with a lotus, peony, or ring pattern of openings or holes on the sides of a bowl, usually used for chairs, pillows, etc.), and underglaze iron brown (i.e. the painting of patterns on the surface of an object with a brush dipped in iron pigment).

stories.title: The Heyday of Goryeo Celadon
stories.script: During the heyday of Goryeo celadon between the late twelfth and thirteenth century, various decorative styles of jade-colored celadons - such as plain, intaglio carving, relief carving, impressed engraving in relief, pictogram, openwork, and underglaze iron brown - were developed, culminating in sanggam inlaying, Goryeo’s renowned and unique pattern carving technique. Sanggam inlaying is an advanced decorative technique in which craftsmen would engrave an item of pottery with lines or designs, and then insert materials such as white clay or porcelain clay into them, in order to create an attractive colored effect. It was widely used not only on pottery but also on metal craftworks (metalwork inlaid with gold and silver) and wooden craftworks (lacquerware inlaid with mother-of-pearl). Common decorative themes included cranes flying freely through clouds, floral patterns consisting of chrysanthemums or peonies, water birds swimming in a body of water surrounded by reeds and a willow tree, and so on. The main production areas of Sanggam celadon were Buan in Jeollabuk-do and Gangjin in Jeollanam-do, and their products were distributed to Gaegyeong, and from there to all over the country by sea.

stories.title: The Decline of Goryeo Celadon
stories.script: Goryeo celadon entered an abrupt decline between the late thirteenth and fourteenth century. Sanggam celadon remained in fashion until the end of the Goryeo Dynasty, and some high-quality celadons continued to feature patterns and shapes reminiscent of the classic blue and white porcelain made in China during the Yuan Dynasty. During this period, celadons were decorated with diverse patterns, with repeatedly stamped patterns of chrysanthemum, cloud, and circle becoming particularly popular. The repetition of such patterns on the surface of pottery wares may look superficially glamorous, but they lack the clear jade color of celadon’s heyday, and look thick and crude. The main patterns include birds sitting on branches, flowers, butterflies, simple pictures of a bird in water with willows and reeds, a phoenix with a long tail flying through clouds, cranes depicted as simple dots between clouds, star-shaped peony vines, a dragon with a magic pearl, and so on. The Sanggam celadon produced at the end of the Goryeo Dynasty had a strong influence on the patterns and shapes of the Buncheong wares made in the newly founded Joseon Dynasty during the fourteenth century.

stories.title: Celadon Maebyeong Vase with Inlaid Chrysanthemum, Peony, Willow and Reed Design
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Maebyeong Vase with Inlaid Chrysanthemum, Peony, Willow and Reed Design
stories.script: This celadon maebyeong (prunus) vase with inlaid design was made around the thirteenth century. Maebyeong vases were generally used to contain alcohol, drinks, or other foods and ingredients such as honey or sesame oil. Nowadays, honey and sesame oil are commonly used ingredients in Korea, but 800 years ago only high-ranking officials could afford them. For its celadon name, the Korean word ‘maebyeong’ originated from the Chinese words 梅 (mae meaning ‘prunus’) and 甁 (byeong meaning ‘vase’ or ‘bottle’) during the Song Dynasty, signifying ‘a bottle with a small mouth containing two to three sprays of plum flowers’, so it is presumed that this celadon maebyeong vase was used to hold flowers.   The vase is inlaid with a beautiful scene of animals and plants, and features various motifs including a water fowl swimming gracefully in water surrounded by plants and willows, another water bird swimming amid reeds, a large hibiscus flower, and a chrysanthemum in full bloom, all of which are set within a ‘water chestnut window.’

stories.title: Celadon Pitcher with Inlaid Reed Design
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Pitcher with Inlaid Reed Design
stories.script: This celadon pitcher with inlaid reed design was made around the twelfth to thirteenth century. Its body is of a similar shape to that of a metal pitcher, while its spout takes the shape of dragon’s head and neck; and both sides of the body are inlaid with three reeds. While the top of the celadon exhibits elaborate features including an angular shoulder and a dragon-headed spout, the body is simply decorated, revealing the aesthetic sensibility of Goryeo people of that time.

stories.title: Celadon Jar with incised flower design
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Jar with incised flower design
stories.script: This patternless celadon jar, made around the twelfth to thirteenth century, features a round and thick outward edge and a flat but rounded body shape. It is presumed to have been used to hold water or tea as part of a tea set. This beautiful celadon is evenly coated with a thin, clear bluish glaze.

stories.title: Celadon Maebyeong Vase with Incised Lotus Design
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Maebyeong Vase with Incised Lotus Design
stories.script: This celadon maebyeong vase with incised lotus design was made around the twelfth to thirteenth century. It features a curved, S-shaped body viewed from the side, and exhibits a vivid incised design consisting of a lotus flower and a lotus leaf stem in three places on its body, and three large floral patterns on its shoulder. Below the body is a single lightning design, which was engraved was engraved obliquely with a knife to create the impression of relief work. It attests to the excellent carving skills of Goryeo celadon potters.

stories.title: Celadon Bottle with Incised Cloud Design
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Bottle with Incised Cloud Design
stories.script: This celadon bottle with incised cloud design was made around the twelfth to thirteenth century. It exhibits a sack-like body with a bulging lower body and a long neck that spreads like a trumpet. It forms a set with a lid.   The rings attached to the top of the lid and the neck of the bottle were designed to thread a string through them with which to attach the lid. Unusually, this celadon bottle retains its original lid, as the lids of most celadon bottles and ewers have been lost. The bottom part of the lid has a 2.0cm-long point designed to insert into the mouth of the bottle, while a leaf pattern is engraved on its upper part. The body bears a design of three large and four small incised clouds of different sizes. In particular, the clouds feature a straight head with a zigzag tail, resembling a pine tree. Normally one would draw a cloud horizontally, but in this case the clouds appear to represent the courageous and elevated spirit of the Goryeo people.

stories.title: Celadon Pipe with Inlaid Chrysanthemum Design
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Pipe with Inlaid Chrysanthemum Design
stories.script: This celadon pipe with an inlaid chrysanthemum design was made sometime between the late twelfth and thirteenth century. A similar artifact was discovered in Yucheon-ri, Buan, and is now housed in Ewha Womans University Museum. While each end of the pipe bears a single line of lightning design, the surface of the pipe is fully decorated with a black and white inlaid chrysanthemum design. The pipe has nine finger holes for controlling the sound – two at the back and seven at the front.  Some people ask whether it makes a sound or not. As it is an authentic celadon ware, I have never played it, but I am sure that this pipe will produce a clear flute-like sound.

stories.title: Celadon Gourd-shaped Pitcher with Inlaid Chrysanthemum Design
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Gourd-shaped Pitcher with Inlaid Chrysanthemum Design
stories.script: This celadon pitcher with an inlaid chrysanthemum design was made around the thirteenth century. The pitcher, which is made in the shape of a gourd, forms a set with a small lid that has a ring with a 1.5cm-long point. The mouth of the pitcher is hexagonal, and its gourd-shaped body consists of a spout and a band-like handle, and features six lobes decorated with a black and white inlaid chrysanthemum design. Judging from its transparent, clear bluish glaze, its well-balanced shape, and its surface full of chrysanthemum patterns, this object was most likely made during the golden age of Goryeo celadon. The pitcher was used to keep alcoholic drinks, including wine. The alcohol in the pitcher can be served as a warm or cold drink simply by pouring hot or cold water into the seungban, which is the bowl-like saucer that forms a set with the pitcher. Unfortunately, the original seungban that came with this pitcher has been lost.

stories.title: Celadon Melon-shaped Pitcher with Incised Lotus Design
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Melon-shaped Pitcher with Incised Lotus Design
stories.script: This celadon melon-shaped pitcher with an incised lotus design forms a set with a lid, and was made around the twelfth to thirteenth century. The body of the pitcher and the lid feature ten lobes, in each of which the design of a lotus flower and lotus leaf stem is vividly incised; while the lower sides of the lid, mouth and body are decorated with a single line of a lotus flower pattern. The pitcher is evenly coated with a transparent, clear bluish glaze and has fine cracks in places. As middle and upper class people of the Goryeo Dynasty prized melons as refreshments at that time, the body of many celadon pitchers and vases are shaped like a round melon.

stories.title: Celadon Oriental Melon-shaped Vase with Inlaid Chrysanthemum Design
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Oriental Melon-shaped Vase with Inlaid Chrysanthemum Design
stories.script: This celadon oriental melon-shaped vase with an inlaid chrysanthemum design features a widely flaring mouth and a high foot, and was made around the thirteenth century. The body of the vase features six lobes, in each of which the design of a chrysanthemum stem is inlaid in black and white; while a single line of a lotus leaf pattern is inlaid in white on the lower part of its neck. The mouth of the vase flares delicately outwards in the shape of a morning glory, while the tip of the foot is round and thick, giving it a sense of balance and stability. This celadon vase was found in the corner of the room of a beautiful maiden about 800 years ago.

stories.title: Celadon Bottle with Inlaid Chrysanthemum Design
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Bottle with Inlaid Chrysanthemum Design
stories.script: This celadon bottle with an inlaid chrysanthemum design was made around the thirteenth century. It was used to contain alcohol, and exhibits a sack-like body with a bulging lower body and a long neck that spreads like a trumpet.  The body features six lobes, in each of which two sprays of chrysanthemum vine are inlaid in black and white. As the body widens from the neck toward the lower part, the size of the chrysanthemums increases accordingly to form a delicate design.

stories.title: Celadon Bowl with Inlaid Willow, Reed and Waterfowl Design
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Bowl with Inlaid Willow, Reed and Waterfowl Design
stories.script: This celadon bowl with an inlaid willow, reed and waterfowl design dating back to the thirteenth or fourteenth century was used to contain rice, soup, or tea.
