The inside of the bowl features splendid inlaid work of a peaceful waterfront scene depicting a waterfowl swimming on water and a bird sitting on a willow branch; while the bottom is decorated with a pair of fish. Many celadon vessels made in Buan tend to feature such surrounding scenery or a seasonal view, showing the sentiments of Goryeo people who loved a simple and peaceful daily life.

stories.title: Celadon Jar with Inlaid Lotus, Reed and Waterfowl Design
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Jar with Inlaid Lotus, Reed and Waterfowl Design
stories.script: This celadon jar with an inlaid lotus, reed and waterfowl design was made around the late thirteenth century. The jar is characterized by a unique, flat shape on two of the four sides of the body, which is closer to the style of the Yuan Dynasty of China rather than the typical style of Goryeo. Around this time, the political influence of the Yuan Dynasty increased dramatically, which in turn influenced Goryeo’s culture and customs. That’s why the shapes or patterns of Goryeo celadon made at that time partially exhibit the styles of the Yuan Dynasty.   The flat sides of the body are decorated with an inlaid doubled-water chestnut window pattern containing a waterside scene composed of a lotus flower, lotus leaf stem pattern, bird, willow, and reeds. Both the narrow and round sides of the body feature a design depicting two birds tidying their feathers or playing peacefully under a tree with fruits.

stories.title: Celadon Oil Bottle
stories.script: This small celadon oil bottle dating to the thirteenth century was used to contain oil, especially expensive imported perfumed oils such as musk, oriental orchid, red or white sandalwood oil, during the Goryeo Dynasty. Perfumed oils were mainly consumed by the aristocracy, so oil bottles were generally decorated with attractive patterns including crane, peony, and chrysanthemum in the sanggam technique or the underglaze iron brown technique. You can perhaps imagine what the Goryeo people’s tastes and styles were like at that time!

stories.title: Lacquerware Cabinet Inlaid with Mother-of-pearl at the Hanok Corner of the Celadon Masterpiece Room
stories.audioTitle: Lacquerware Cabinet Inlaid with Mother-of-pearl at the Hanok Corner of the Celadon Masterpiece Room
stories.script: This corner of the museum is designed to display the lifestyle of Goryeo people. Among the representative craftworks of the Goryeo Dynasty, lacquerware inlaid with mother-of-pearl is comparable to celadon in terms of its beauty and reputation. The combination of celadon with a lacquerware cabinet inlaid with mother-of-pearl creates a delicate harmony. If a white porcelain ware of the Joseon Dynasty was placed here instead of the celadon, the white color of the porcelain would not go well with the cabinet.   I believe this is how a culture is formed; arts associating with spirit and ideology of the time.

stories.title: Table Used by a Confucian Scholar of the Goryeo Dynasty
stories.audioTitle: Table Used by a Confucian Scholar of the Goryeo Dynasty
stories.script: This table was used by a Confucian scholar. Along with the chair, there are various accessories that were considered essential when writing calligraphy, including an ink-stone, a water dropper, and a writing brush holder, all of which are celadon wares. A Confucian scholar of Goryeo would have passed his time reading and writing at this table. In particular, the water dropper is decorated with an interesting depiction of a young boy and girl, and a monkey.

stories.title: Celadon Go Board
stories.script: Next to the table, there is a celadon go board. The palm-sized top board on the left is an authentic celadon go board, while the one on the right is a reproduction of a complete celadon go board. Playing ‘go’ was one of the favorite hobbies of Confucian scholars. It is interesting to know that go boards could be made of celadon.

stories.title: Celadon Tea Service and Tea Table
stories.audioTitle: Celadon Tea Service and Tea Table
stories.script: On the lacquerware table inlaid with mother-of-pearl placed at the very end of the room, there are a number of craftworks associated with the tea culture of Goryeo. The people of Goryeo loved drinking tea very much. Small teacups were used when drinking green or red tea made by infusing tea leaves, while teacups with a wide mouth were used for drinking thick tea made by grinding clumps of tea leaves, such as Chinese puer tea, and mixing it with water in a teacup. It is interesting to learn about the tea culture of Goryeo people through the celadon teacup.

stories.title: Pottery Kiln Site of the Goryeo Dynasty in the Honam Region, Together with Pottery Fragments
stories.audioTitle: Pottery Kiln Site of the Goryeo Dynasty in the Honam Region, Together with Pottery Fragments
stories.script: In Korea, we use the names ‘Honam’ or ‘Jeolla-do’ to refer to the combined area of the two provinces known as Jeollabuk-do and Jeollanam-do.   Compared to other areas, the Honam area - which includes Buan in Jeollabuk-do and Gangjin in Jeollanam-do - is famous for producing beautiful pottery of outstanding quality. Because the people of Goryeo mainly used sea routes to transport goods, the southwest coastline of the province was the ideal location to produce celadon wares and other potteries and then transport them to Gaegyeong, the capital of Goryeo. Another reason why Goryeo celadon was manufactured in large quantities in Buan was that the area had an abundant supply of firewood (pine trees), which was needed for baking the pottery. Therefore, convenient transportation by sea and the abundance of trees were the most important conditions for the mass production of Goryeo celadons.

stories.title: Replica of a Celadon Kiln Site
stories.audioTitle: Replica of a Celadon Kiln Site
stories.script: This is a 1/10 scale replica of a Goryeo celadon kiln that was built about 800 years ago, and was excavated in 1998. The kiln consists of a firing chamber in which celadon wares were baked at high temperature by making a fire in the furnace.  Many celadon fragments were discovered in the area to the right of the kiln. These fragments are the remains of defective wares that were discarded next to the kiln. Generally speaking, the large quantities of celadon fragments of defective wares discovered at kiln sites are important materials for academic research. We can also see several cylindrical shaped objects made of clay on the left of the kiln. These are what are known as ‘dojimi’, which were placed under the celadons to prevent them from getting stained by dirt from the kiln floor during baking. We can see the wisdom of potters of the Goryeo Dynasty.

stories.title: The Quest for Celadon Buried Deep in the Sea
stories.audioTitle: The Quest for Celadon Buried Deep in the Sea
stories.script: This room recreates the discovery of Goryeo celadon wares lying buried deep in the mud of the seabed in front of Biando Island, and screens a video of the relics as they were brought up to the surface of the sea. During the construction of the Saemangeum seawall in 2002 and 2003, about 3,000 relics were discovered and brought to land by the National Maritime Museum, which is now known as the National Research Institute of Maritime Cultural Heritage. These relics are thought to have been produced in Jinseo-ri and Yucheon-ri in Buan, and to have played an important role in identifying the existence of Buan celadon and also its production, consumption and transportation by sea. Let’s try to imagine a scene in which a ship loaded with celadon wares was wrecked during a storm while sailing to Gaegyeong about 800 years ago, sending the celadons to the bottom of the sea, where they remained buried deep in the muddy seabed for many centuries.   Interestingly, although they remained buried in salty mud for over 800 years, they did not decay, and were found with their color and condition perfectly preserved.

stories.title: Production Process of Inlaid Celadon
stories.script: Now, let’s take a look at the production process of Goryeo inlaid celadon made in Buan! Before looking at the production process, let’s think again about the reasons why celadon wares were made in Buan. It was mainly because Buan had good quality clay, which is viscous or sticky and fictile (in other words, it’s a fatty clay that tends to keep its shape), abundant firewood, and a convenient sea route for transporting goods to the rest of the peninsula.  The first step in the production of celadon consists in selecting good clay that is viscous and fictile, and then molding the clay on a molding frame or spinning wheel. As you can see, the molded bowl will be decorated with the sanggam inlay technique by cutting lines or shapes into which white clay and kaolin (or china clay) are inlaid together. Kaolin turns black when heated. The inlaid wares are dried in the shade and baked at 600 to 800 degrees, and then glazed and baked again at around 1,250 degrees, resulting in jade-colored celadons.   Now let’s take a look at the model of the kiln. Inside the kiln are dojimi and gapbal. A dojimi is a type of support that was placed under the celadons to protect them from dirt on the floor of the kiln, while a gapbal is a lid that was used to cover and protect them from alien substances falling from the ceiling of the kiln. The completed products are then placed one by one in a long wooden frame whose four corners are tied tightly; while straw ropes are put between the vessels to prevent them from breaking. These bundles are then put in a wooden box for transportation by ship. Nowadays, air caps or styrofoam are used to pack glass or pottery wares safely, but 800 years ago the conditions would have been very different. The package you see here is a reproduction of the packaging condition it was found in when it was unearthed from the seabed.

stories.title: Information About the Special Exhibition Room, Celadon Experience Room, and 4D Theater
stories.audioTitle: Information About the Special Exhibition Room, Celadon Experience Room, and 4D Theater
stories.script: The first floor of the museum also contains the Special Exhibition Room, Celadon Experience Room, and 4D Theater. The Special Exhibition Room holds diverse exhibitions in each season.  The Celadon Experience Room is designed to allow visitors to learn all about Goryeo celadon through a variety of interesting games and experience programs, including Puzzle Making, Celadon Quiz Game, and Photo Taking Activity. The 4D Theater offers visitors an opportunity to enjoy a three-dimensional animated film that features various special effects related to water, fire and wind produced by a large simulator.   The film consists of two stories: The first story is about the exciting adventure of ‘Yucheonyi’, a boy from Buan during the Goryeo Dynasty, who makes inlaid celadons and transports them by ship to Goryeo’s capital, Gaegyeong. The second story tells the tale of Yucheonyi, his friend, and a celadon elf who try to protect celadon from a nasty grave robber. If you have enough time, we recommend you watch them.

stories.title: Closing Comments
stories.script: During your visit, you have received detailed explanations of the authentic Goryeo celadons housed in our Buan Celadon Museum and the celadon production process. We sincerely hope that it has been very helpful and interesting.  Finally, before finishing this guide, we would like to make a brief digression. Recently, someone asked us how to describe the color of Goryeo celadon in a simple word or phrase that anyone can understand easily.  So, we would like to emphasize that the color of Goryeo celadon, which resembles the clear blue autumnal sky of Korea, is perhaps the most natural color ever made by humans in imitation of the color of nature. So when you leave the museum, please raise your head and look at the clear sky. And don’t forget that that is the color of Korea’s Goryeo celadon! Thank you!

stories.title: The Origin of the Korean People
stories.audioTitle: Exhibit Hall No. 1, The Origin of the Korean People.
stories.script: You have just entered Exhibit Hall No. 1, The Origin of the Korean People. This hall shows how Koreans endeavored to keep their history, culture and the grounds of their history and culture. Now, you will see a film introducing the country’s long history. We hope that this will be a nice opportunity for you to see how the country’s history and culture have developed.

stories.title: Koreans' Proud Culture
stories.script: This ceiling-high glass showcase displays relics that represent the country’s culture throughout the long period from prehistoric times to the days of the Joseon Dynasty. Let’s start with those which originate from prehistoric times and the Northern and Southern Dynasties.

stories.title: Joseon (The Independence Hall of Korea)
stories.script: Joseon  Joseon was not only a cultural powerful nation with advanced knowledge and technology but also a strong military nation that took a tough stance against foreign invasions. Based on the agricultural policies, it developed scientific technologies capable of reading time, weather, and seasons, and it flourished in various fields of study.   Joseon devoted considerable efforts to protect its well-developed technology, unique culture, and its own national foundation from ceaseless foreign invasions. From the saddles used by General Gwak Jae-woo, who played a major role as a righteous army commander during the Imjinwaeran (Japanese Invasion of Korea), to the merit certificate named “Chamwae Gongshincheop” awarded to those who beheaded Japanese soldiers during the Imjinwaeran.  Also, a memoir of the Imjinwaeran named Jingbirok, written by the scholar Yu Seong-ryong has as well illustrated the dedication and devotion people had to Joseon during that era.

stories.title: Joseon’s Struggle Against Foreign Invasions and the Turtle Ship
stories.audioTitle: Joseon’s Struggle Against Foreign Invasions and the Turtle Ship
stories.script: The dragon head-shaped structure erected at the bow of the geobukseon, the iron-clad turtle ship, looks impressive. Inside the two-tiered ship, gunners and oarsmen are busy at work. Weapons are stored on the lower deck of the ship. The gunners are in position on the upper deck. The geobukseon was the world’s first iron-clad ship. A fleet of them was employed by Admiral Yi Sun-shin during the Japanese Invasion of 1592-1598. The turtle ship played a leading role in the many victories won by the country’s navy against the Japanese invaders.

stories.title: Undaunted Determination
stories.script: Joseon defended itself against ceaseless invasions. The country developed various excellent weapons besides bows and arrows. The armor worn by Joseon troops was made of layers of cotton sewn together. It was durable enough to protect the body from Japanese rifle bullets. The Bimongpo was a cannon that shot pot-shaped poison balls. There were also cannons that could fire five to ten balls in succession. They must have been a marvel at that time. It is said that the Japanese invaders were frightened at their thunderous sound and destructive power.

stories.title: National Crisis by Japanese Imperialism
stories.audioTitle: Hall No. 2 “National Crisis by Japanese Imperialism.”
stories.script: You have just entered Hall No. 2 “National Crisis by Japanese Imperialism.” The materials in this exhibition hall range from the 1860s to the 1940s, a period in which the country opened its doors and underwent successive waves of change until its long history ground to a halt with the Japanese colonial rule. In this hall, you will have the opportunity to look at various scenes of Korean life during the colonial period and how Korea’s neighboring countries are still engaged in attempts to distort Korea’s history.

stories.title: Weapons Used by the Donghak
stories.script: In the mid-19th century, the country ushered in an era of change. Now, you will see how the country struggled to achieve national self-reliance through the Donghak Peasant Movement (1894), the Gabo Reform (1894-1895), and the launch of the Dongnip Hyeophoe (Independence Society) (1896) and the Great Han Empire (1897-1910). The flags and spears displayed here are of the kind used by the Donghak Army during the Donghak Peasant War of 1894. They protested against exploitation of farmers by the government and the landlords, and the economic invasion of the country by the Western powers. They were also engaged in an anti-feudalistic, anti-imperialistic movement, calling for the abolition of the social class system.

stories.title: Preamble of the Eulsa Illegal treaty
stories.audioTitle: Preamble of the Eulsa Illegal treaty
stories.script: Japan forced the Great Han Empire to sign the treaty in order to deprive the country of its diplomatic rights. Generally speaking, treaty should be submitted to the process of entrusting, signing, and ratification. However, this one failed to go through any such procedures. This document even lacks the term “treaty.”

stories.title: Korean Independence Activists
stories.script: Please get closer to the wall and have a look inside. Many people were forced to stand here, their bodies still bleeding. There was no space for sitting down. This was one of the 70-plus methods of torture used by Japanese colonists on Korean independence fighters. The torture methods used by the Japanese colonists were notorious for their cruelty.

stories.title: A Report Document Drawn up by a U.S. Intelligence Unit
stories.audioTitle: A Report Document Drawn up by a U.S. Intelligence Unit
stories.script: The document stamped “confidential” at the top and the bottom is a record drawn up by the Office of Strategic Services (OSS) of the U.S. to report the result of their interrogation of Korean women found by the U.S. troops in Kunming, China after being abandoned by the Japanese military in 1945 after the Japanese defeat in the war. The document tells that the 23 Korean women were taken away from Korea either forcefully or by deceit and had to serve as sex slaves. It is an important material attesting to the fact that the Japanese military was involved in recruitment of those women.

stories.title: Struggles for National Rights
stories.audioTitle: Hall No.3, Struggles for National Rights.
stories.script: You have just entered Hall No.3, “Struggles for National Rights.” This hall is dedicated to the movements carried out for the recovery of the country’s sovereignty towards the end of the brief era of the Great Han Empire, particularly the anti-Japanese struggles of the righteous army and the patriotic enlightenment movements.   The long line of footprints signifies the struggle waged by the Korean people to defend their country’s sovereignty. Let’s look at the ways in which Koreans struggled to defend their homeland.

stories.title: The Sword that Sparked a Righteous Army of Kim Do-hyeon (The Independence Hall of Korea)
stories.audioTitle: The Sword that Sparked a Righteous Army of Kim Do-hyeon (The Independence Hall of Korea)
stories.script: The Sword that Sparked a Righteous Army of Kim Do-hyeon  The sword displayed here belongs to Kim Do-hyeon, a righteous army commander who was active in the Yeongyang and Andong regions of Gyeongsangbuk-do Province at that time. The characters Chang-ui geom (Sword that Sparked a Righteous Army) engraved on the scabbard seem to display the firm resolve sworn at the start of the righteous army's struggle. Commander Kim Do-hyeon, mourning the loss of his country, walked into the sea and died for his nation in 1914.

stories.title: The Fifteen Crimes of Ito Hirobumi
stories.audioTitle: The Fifteen Crimes of Ito Hirobumi
stories.script: This material refers to the fifteen crimes that An Jung-geun singled out as having been perpetrated by Ito Hirobumi, including the assassination of Empress Myeongseong; the forcing of the Korean Empress to sign the Eulsa Illegal Treaty; the forcing of Emperor Gwangmu to abdicate; and the plunder and expropriation of Korea’s resources.

stories.title: Daehan Maeil Sinbo
stories.script: Co-founded by Yang Gi-tak and a British subject named Ernest Thomas Bethell in 1904, the newspaper spearheaded the anti-Japanese struggle.

stories.title: Report on Funds Collected document
stories.script: This confidential document, dated August 22, 1906, is a report submitted to the Japanese Residency-General by Maruyama, the Japanese advisor in charge of police affairs.

stories.title: Pyeonghwanuri,Entering
stories.script: You have now entered Pyeonghwanuri, the 4th exhibition hall. Unlike other exhibitions that display specific contents or data related to the independence movement, it is a place where we think about how we should remember the true meaning and value of independence movement and how we should continue such legacy.  The theme of this exhibition is “path”; there are paths of Resolve, Activism, Unification, and Echoes. From now on, as you walk on the path, you will get to explore the true meaning of the independence movement opening up the future and transcending the space-time barrier.  For each path, you will be asked questions about the independence movement. There are a total of four questions: what the independence movement was, why people did it and how it proceeded, which tasks it has, and finally, how we should remember the meaning and value of independence and maintain the legacy. Please take a moment in this exhibition as you think about your answers to the questions above. So, shall we start touring? First, enter the entrance on the left.

stories.title: Quotes
stories.script: In a dark forest, there are small lights gathering together, lighting up the dark path. In the forest that turned bright, you can see the words and quotes of three independence activists; Ahn Jung-geun, Han Yong-un, and Ahn Chang-ho. On October 26, 1909, Ahn Jung-geun assassinated Ito Hirobumi at the Harbin Station in China. Later, he was arrested and questioned by the Japanese police multiple times. During questioning, Ahn confessed that his act of assassinating the source of evil who not only invaded Korea but also destroyed peace in Asia was a justifiable act, stating that the way to seek peace in Asia was through Korea, China, and Japan’s concord to strive for peace.   Han Yong-un completed the Three Pledges contained in the March 1st Declaration of Independence. Han had to endure imprisonment after attending the independence declaration ceremony as one of the 33 Korean leaders on March 1, 1919. During his imprisonment, he also wrote an article titled “Introduction of impression for the Independence of the Joseon Dynasty.” In the article, which clarified the legitimacy of the independence of Korea, he expressed his belief that the independence movement was an act of freedom and peace that the entire humanity required.  Ahn Chang-ho, again had to endure imprisonment as Imperialist Japan fabricated the so-called “Donguhoe Incident” in order to suppress intellectuals. Despite being imprisoned repetitively, he never compromised or gave up his beliefs; in fact, during his questioning, he strongly stated that the independence of Korea was what the justice of the world wanted. Can you feel their beliefs on independence, freedom, peace, and justice through the words and quotes above by the three independence activists during their hardships in prison? The resolution and willingness of the independence activists, which never wavered despite Japan’s suppression and imprisonment of the independence movement, are the true meaning of the independence movement as well as the light that brightened the dark world.

stories.title: Path of Unification : The nation of which the independence activists dreamed
stories.audioTitle: The nation of which the independence activists dreamed
stories.script: At this point, you have entered the path of Unification. Here, we should inherit the spirit of independence after liberation as we remember the achievement of Korea and the tasks that we should deal with in the future. If you approach the bright light that you see, you will hear someone telling a story. The story is about a nation that independence activists dreamed of. Independence activists believed that the challenges were not only to take back the country and its sovereignty but also to establish a single independent nation. Then, what kind of nation did activists hope to establish? Through the March First Movement, a country where the people became the owner was established, followed by the establishment of the Republic of Korea after liberation. Is this country the one that independence activists had dreamed of? Stop for a moment and listen to the voices of independence activists.

stories.title: Path of Echoes : Path of Remembrance and Legacy
stories.script: You have now entered the path of Echoes. This is a place where we remember and succeed the meaning and value of independence as we expand such values and meanings to the globe. First of all, walk up the path of Remembrance and Legacy. We should never forget patriotic martyrs who made every sacrifice required in order to take the country back and to pass to their descendants a world where freedom and justice are fully realized. Without their noble sacrifices, we may not be standing where we are now. Please slowly take one step at a time and walk along the path of Remembrance and Legacy, which has total length of 75.4m. Think about the patriotic martyrs as you take your steps. If you take a look at the left side of the path, you can see the words that our patriotic martyrs had left for us.   There is a screen on the center if you keep walking until you reach the 3-meter top. The bubbles on the screen symbolize the approximately 14,000 independence activists who made sacrifices to take the country back. If you touch a bubble with your finger, each bubble will turn into the name of one of the activists. At this point, please write down your name and let it flow along with the water stream. This means that you will remember and succeed patriotic martyrs. Just as small bubbles shape the river and the wide sea, bubbles that you let go will spread to our hearts as the echo of peace following the path of Remembrance and Legacy and will also get delivered to descendants in the future, never to be forgotten.

stories.title: Patriotic Struggle for National Independence
stories.audioTitle: Hall No. 5. Patriotic Struggle for National Independence.
stories.script: You have just entered Exhibition Hall No. 5: Patriotic Struggle for National Independence. This hall displays materials illustrating Korean independence fighters and activists’ unyielding commitment to the armed struggle against the Japanese. Among them, you can see a group of people carrying rifles and swords. Let’s take a look at how unknown independence fighters sacrificed their lives in combat against Japanese troops in the mountainous regions of Manchuria or the in Maritime Province of Siberia, shall we?

stories.title: Uniforms and Weapons of Korean independence fighters
stories.audioTitle: Uniforms and Weapons of Korean independence fighters
stories.script: Here, you can see some of the uniforms that were worn by Korean independence fighters and the types of weapons they used. These quilted uniforms give us a good idea of how cold the winter can be in Manchuria. Korean civilians in Manchuria provided both uniforms and money to purchase weapons to the independence fighters.

stories.title: A Public Notice Put up by Uiyeoldan
stories.audioTitle: A Public Notice Put up by Uiyeoldan
stories.script: Some letters are written on the mirror on your right side. They were part of a public notice put up by the Uiyeoldan, an organization formed in Jilin Province, Manchuria in November 1919. The Uiyeoldan carried out such activities as sabotaging the Japanese institutions which played a leading role in the invasion of foreign countries, and assassinating Japanese leaders. The public notice and the Declaration of the Korean Revolution stress that violent revolution is the only way to gain freedom and independence.

stories.title: Yun Bong-gil’s Heroic Deed in Hongkou Park
stories.audioTitle: Yun Bong-gil’s Heroic Deed in Hongkou Park
stories.script: This is a reconstruction of Yun Bong-gil’s heroic deed in Hongkou Park, Shanghai. On April 29, 1932, a crowd of people are gathered in the park. The Japanese flag is fluttering in wind. A man stealthily enters the park amid the exalted atmosphere during the commemoration of the Japanese Emperor’s birthday and Japan’s victory in the Shanghai Incident. Seconds later, he threw a bomb at the Japanese military leaders seated on the platform.

stories.title: A Taegeukgi Containing the Signatures…
stories.script: On this flag, soldiers of the Korean Independence Army based in Fuyang, Anhui Province wrote a few words on how they felt about the country’s liberation and what they hoped to do upon their returns to Korea. The flag was designated as Registered Cultural Property No. 389.

stories.title: Establishing the Great Korea
stories.audioTitle: Hall No. 6. Establishing the Great Korea.
stories.script: You have just entered Hall No. 6 “Establishing the Great Korea.” This hall displays materials relating to anti-Japanese movement of the Korean people and movements for the preservation of national culture during the Japanese colonial period, and the establishment of the Korean Provisional Government that played a pivotal role in the independence movement. Here in this hall, you can see how Korean from various walks of life took part in the independence movement, tried to protect the spirit inherited from their ancestors, and finally established a new republic.

stories.title: Manuscript for Joseoneo Keunsajeon
stories.script: This is the manuscript for the Joseoneo Keunsajeon (Comprehensive Korean Dictionary). The Korean Language Society made corrections and additions to the manuscript for 13 years, i.e. between 1929 and 1942 in which it was ordered to be closed. The 17-volume manuscript was confiscated by the Japanese police. In September 1945, one month after the country’s liberation, it was found in a storage space near Seoul Station. It was designated as a State-designated document in November 2008 for its historic value as the first unabridged Korean language dictionary.

stories.title: Development of the Gwangju Student Independence Movement
stories.audioTitle: Development of the Gwangju Student Independence Movement
stories.script: Here, you can see how the Gwangju Student Independence Movement was developed through miniature models and films. On the right, members of Seongjinhoe, a clandestine anti-Japanese student organization in Gwangju, are making a decision to boycott classes at school. In the middle, students are staging demonstration in front of Gwangju Prison, asking for the release of their friends unlawfully imprisoned during the public rallies held after November 3, 1929. Finally, on the left, students are engaged in demonstration after boycotting classes amidst the independence movement spread nationwide.

stories.title: The Korean Provisional
stories.script: These are leaders of the Korean Provisional Government. Please click on the figure you would like to know more about.

stories.title: Declaration of Independence
stories.script: This declaration of independence issued by the Korean Provisional Government contains the text of the March First Independence Declaration, the provisional charter of the Shanghai Provisional Government of Korea and the list of the cabinet members, as well as national symbols of Taegeukgi and mugunghwa (rose of sharon).

stories.title: A Sheet of Cloth Containing
stories.script: The leaders of the Korean Provisional Government put their autographs and expressed how they felt about the liberation of their homeland on a sheet of cloth on the eve of their returning home to Korea in November 1945.

stories.title: Deoksugung Doldamgil
stories.script: Deoksugung Doldamgil Deoksugung (Gyeongungung) Doldamgil was naturally formed along the outside of the stone wall that encompasses Deoksugung Palace. Since Joseon opened its port during modern times, this place has served a central role in history. Shall we listen to those stories one by one as we walk along the Doldamgil?  In November 1902, Carlo Rossetti, the Italian consul who had come to Joseon for the first time, wrote in his book, “Pass the royal palace named Jeongdonggung (today's Deoksugung), which is the current residence of the emperor of Korea, you run into another major arterial road of Seoul that leads to Namdaemun. On this path, there are shops selling Korean drawers or traditional Ham on both sides of the road, which is why the area is known to foreigners in Seoul as an English name of Cabinet Street.” It literally meant that it was a street where furniture such as desks and drawers were sold. It is said that foreigners loved this street and the shops because they could buy in person the oriental furniture with gorgeous decorations.  However, the beautiful Deoksugung Doldamgil was reduced in size as the country went through the Japanese colonial era. In 1920, a new road was built in the back of the present-day Deoksugung Palace, and it was called “Yeongseongmun Gogaegil” because it used to be where the old Yeongseongmun Gate existed in the past. Jeong Bi-seok’s 〈Madame Freedom〉, which was released in 1954, described this palace as the “hill of love.” It talks about how big trees stretched over the walls to create a tunnel of nature and young lovers who wanted to avoid the eyes of others liked to come here for dates. This gives us a sense of romance of Deoksugung Doldamgil.  However, the suffering of Deoksugung Doldamgil did not end here. After Liberation, the walls were replaced with iron fences in 1961 under the pretense of allowing the interior of the palace to be more visible, and, in 1968, the fences were moved back 16m for road expansion before being replaced with stone walls.  Also, around Deoksugung Palace, which was reduced in size during the Japanese occupation period, colonization organizations such as the high court, Jungchuwon and Korean History Compilation Committee were established. Because of this, the High Court and Family Court continued to be settled here even after the unification. Moreover, there were many stories in which couples who sue each other at the Family Court walk along Deoksugung Doldamgil and into the court together but are separated when they come out, which gave birth to a myth that “lovers who walk along the Doldamgil together will eventually break up”.  From the joy of foreigners’ encounter with Joseon's culture and civilization and trials of the Japanese occupation era to the love and farewell of lovers, Deoksugung Doldamgil holds all these emotions and sentiments and accompanies the lives of citizens.

stories.title: Seoul Museum of Art
stories.script: Seoul Museum of Art  If you follow along Deoksugung Doldamgil, you will soon find Seoul Museum of Art at the end of the path covered with a garden. This is where Pyeongniwon (Hanseong Jaepanso), the first court of Joseon used to be in 1895. Next to Pyeongniwon was Yugyeong Park, the first-ever modern public educational institution in Korea.  In 1891, Yugyeong Park moved to another location and, instead, the German consulate was established here. Emperor Gojong who had declared the Korean Empire as the name of the country tried to expand Deoksugung to suit the authority of the emperor, and it came under the jurisdiction of Gungnaebu of the Korean Empire in 1902.  After Gyeongsul Gukchi, the Temporary Bureau of Cadastral Survey became the tenant and, after 1928, the so-called 3 Gyeongseong Courts, which are the High Court, Gyeongseong Reexamination Court and Gyeongseong District Court, settled here. The building we see today was newly constructed around this time, and a countless number of independence activists were tried in the building before being sent to Seodaemun Prison.  After Liberation, the place was used by the Supreme Court and, before the court moved to Seocho-dong in 1995, it served to protect the Korean constitution. Seoul Museum of Art became the resident after the Supreme Court had moved. In order to use it as an art museum, the existing central entrance building was preserved while a three-story modern structure was built in the back to host exhibits of a greater number of contemporary artists.  The central entrance building was designated as Registered Cultural Property No. 237 in 2006, showing its historical significance. From the three main gates, the length of the building, size and number of windows are identical. This was one of the popular styles of architecture in Japan at the time, and it is precious heritage with not only architectural meaning that shows the phases of the times but also historical significance as a place where independence fighters were tried.

stories.title: Appenzeller Noble Memorial Museum
stories.script: Appenzeller Noble Memorial Museum  Paichai School was the first modern, privately-established educational institution and was granted the name, “Paichai Hakdang” by King Gojong in June 1886. “Paichai”, which means “a school that educates talented people”, also used the name “American School” in English. Paichai School's history began when Pastor Appenzeller purchased a two-room hanok in Jeong-dong and tore down the walls to build a classroom.  American missionaries taught students at Paichai School, which was like a symbol of America to Joseon people along with the U.S. legation. It also served as a place for discussions and gatherings of foreigners who stayed in Joseon at that time. Not only that, it sometimes provided a meeting place or refuge for the leaders of the Independent Club and People's Assembly.  Paichai produced a countless number of independence activists and scholars, including Ju Si-gyeong, a Korean linguist; Novelist Kim Sowol; Na Do-hyang; Rhee Syngman, the first president. It was an institution where many Joseon people who were striving to overcome a gloomy age with modern education were able to be educated. The present-day Appenzeller Noble Memorial Museum building was originally the east wing of the Paichai School, which was established in 1916. The building constructed at the time still remains today.

stories.title: Jeongdong Jeil Church
stories.script: Jeongdong Jeil Church  Chungdong Jeil Church is Korea's first Protestant church. Jeongdong Jeil Church started on October 11, 1885 when Appenzeller, a pastor from the North Methodist Mission of the U.S., held a worship service for Koreans at his home called “Bethel Chapel”. Four believers conducted their worships and were baptized that day.  For the cornerstone laying ceremony for the completion of construction of the “Bethel Chapel” in its present-day location in 1895, many officials including Soh Kwang-pom, Minister of Justice, and Yun Tchi-Ho, the Vice Foreign Minister, attended the event. The chapel, which was completed in 1897, held its first public service and opened Pokunyokwan, the first hospital for women and children in Korea, during the same year. In addition, many of the students who attended Paichai School where he worked as a teacher were able to learn about the Christian culture at this church.  Jeongdong Jeil Church was a symbolic building on Jeongdong Street during the Korean Empire days and served as the center of the anti-Japanese movement in the Japanese occupation era. Independence fighters once hid inside the pipe organ, which was installed for the first time in a Korean Protestant church, away from Japanese police, and Pastor Lee Pil-ju and Missionary Park Dong-wan among the 33 national representatives participated on behalf of the Protestant church.  The pipe organ and chapel, which were destroyed after the Korean War, have been restored to the shape we see today, and, because this is the only church building built in the 19th century that still has the original appearance intact, it was recognized of its value and designated as Historic Site No. 256.

stories.title: Jeongdong Rotary
stories.script: Jeongdong Rotary  Jeongdong Rotary is a place that connects the roads that were created from the forced demolition of a part of Deoksugung Palace during the Japanese occupation period. The term, “Rotary,” comes from the English prefix of “Rot”, which means “going round and round”, and it refers to a “circular intersection” without any traffic lights.  The four roads that meet at Jeongdong Rotary are “Deoksugung-gil” from the main gate of Deoksugung Palace, “Seosomun-ro 11-gil” from the Seoul Museum of Art, “Deoksugung-gil” also known as Yeongseongmun Gogaegil, and “Jeongdong-gil” towards the Jeongdong Theater. A fountain stands where the four roads meet to relieve the summer heat for citizens; allowing cars driving on narrow streets to be able to yield to one another.  The circular Jeongdong Rotary was actually one of the demonstration areas of Seoul’s “Historic Cultural Walk Establishment Plan,” which began in 1994. Before that, a circular rotary did not exist here. Professor Kim Sung-gyun, the person in charge at the time, and his research team proposed to install a rotary to preserve the cultural assets nearby while creating roads for anyone to walk comfortably on, and, after an agreement among various agencies, the present-day Jeongdong Rotary was born.  At the time, Yeongseongmun Gogaegil was owned by the U.S. Embassy and the British Embassy since 1959, which prohibited civilian access, but certain sections became open to public in 2015 before more parts were opened in 2017, thus completing Jeongdong Rotary in the true sense that is accessible by all.

stories.title: Jeongdong Theater
stories.script: Jeongdong Theater  Jeongdong Theater was founded in 1995 with the idea of restoring “Wongagsa”, the first-ever modern private theater of Korea. Although this is not the original location of Wongagsa, it has become a new cultural space in the city that distributes traditional art and seeks culture in the midst of life together with other cultural venues nearby.  Although it was the last of many cultural facilities settled in Jeongdong, it became a symbol of Jeongdong arts and culture as it put on stage various genres from traditional art and music to dance and theater every year. In particular, “Jeongdong Theater Regular Gugak Performances”, which was the first case of traditional arts commercialized as a tourism product carried out by a Korean theater, of 1997 has established itself as a program through which the audience can enjoy the traditional Korean art performances in a more friendly and diverse fashion.  The reason that Jeongdong Theater was able to survive as an independent theater was because it inherited the spirit of modern art and continues to develop new performances to communicate with today's audiences. As a result, high-quality performances are produced insomuch to attract enthusiasts and foreign tourists who come just to watch the Jeongdong Theater performances.  On the exterior wall of the Jeongdong Theater’s outdoor yard, there is an artwork called “Myths, Plays and Vision of Planets” that shows the image of an ideal cultural space that Jeongdong Theater aims at. Also, the statue of Lee Dong-baek, a famous Pansori master singer from the 19th century, tells us that Jeongdong Theater succeeds the spirits of modern artists.

stories.title: Jungmyeongjeon Hall, Deoksugung Palace
stories.script: Jungmyeongjeon Hall, Deoksugung Palace  Jungmyeongjeon Hall was called Suokheon when it was initially used as a royal library. The name, Suokheon, has the meaning of “wiping the jade.” In 1904, Emperor Gojong stayed here to avoid a great fire that broke out in Deoksugung and, later, its name changed to Jungmyeongjeon.  Why did its name change from Suokheon to Jungmyeongjeon? Buildings in a royal palace are named differently depending on the people who use them and their purpose, and these are classified by the last letter of the building names including Jeon, Dang, Hap or Gak, Jae or Heon, Ru or Nu and Jeong. When naming Suokheon, “Heon” was used since the building executes official functions for the royal family but, later when King Gojong stayed here, “Jeon”, which is attached in case a building is used by the elders of the palace such as the king, queen, queen of the abdicated king or queen dowager, was affixed at the end of the name to become Jungmyeongjeon.  Jungmyeongjeon Hall was where Emperor Gojong ordered the Hague Secret Emissary to go to the Second Peace Conference. Moreover, it was the the stage for the compulsory signing of the Eulsa Treaty of 1905 and the Korea-Japan Agreement of August 1904, which served as a stepping stone for Japanese colonization. On the 1st floor of Jungmyeongjeon, the events that took place at the time are reproduced in miniature models so you can witness the miserable scenes of our history. During the Japanese occupation era, Jungmyeongjeon was utilized as a gathering place for foreigners.  Behind Jungmyeongjeon is where Manheedang once existed. Manheedang was the building used as Emperor Gojong's bedroom after he had relocated to this place due to the great fire of Deoksugung Palace, but it was eventually torn down once the emperor returned to Hamnyeongjeon Hall in 1907. Then, during the Japanese colonial period, Jungmyeongjeon was used as a meeting place and, in the location where Manheedang once was, a swimming pool was built for foreigners. The pool, however, disappeared after the Korean War. An excavation survey in 2009 identified the traces of the swimming pool and columns of Manheedang in the area.

stories.title: Ewha Hakdang
stories.script: Ewha Hakdang  Founded in Seoul in 1886, Ewha Hakdang was a private educational institution providing elementary, middle and high school curricula, and is also the first-ever educational institution for women. The number of students slowly grew after Mary Fletcher Benton Scranton, a missionary for the Methodist Episcopal Church, recruited a female student through much difficulty and started to teach her in 1886, which was how Ewha Hakdang began.  It was quite a tough task to recruit female students and operate a school in the late Joseon Dynasty, a period during which no one regarded education of women as important. When the number of students increased to 7 in 1887, Emperor Gojong praised the hard work and bestowed the name, “Ewha Hakdang” upon the school.  The student body of Ewha Hakdang consisted of a handful of of high-class folks such as children and wives of the enlightenment activists and children from working class families. The school pioneered a new path for women’s education and gender equality in the late Joseon Dynasty dominated by the Confucian ideology. Some of its renowned alumnae include Ryu Gwansun, a female independence activist, and Esther Park, the first female doctor.  Ewha Hakdang was a hanok building at the time of its establishment but, as the number of students increased, a new Western-style building was built. One of the remaining buildings from the time of establishment is the Simpson Memorial Hall whose construction was funded by an American woman named Sarah Simpson in 1915. The building was damaged during the Korean War but it was restored, and is currently designated as Registered Cultural Heritage No. 3.  Today, only the section used as the Ewha Museum within the Simpson Memorial Hall is open to the public whereas the areas other than the museum prohibits access for students’ classes.

stories.title: Former Russian Legation Site (Jeongdong Park)
stories.script: Former Russian Legation Site (Jeongdong Park)  Former Russian Legation Site (Jeongdong Park)  During the days of the Korean Empire, the Russian Legation was seated where today’s Jeongdong Park is. After signing the Korea-Russia Treaty of 1884, the Korean Empire established the Russian Legation at the site of Sangnimwon, an agency in charge of supplying fruit to the royal family, in the following year.  In the beginning, the Russian Legation used a hanok but a new building was constructed at the Paichai School Site in 1900. The newly built legation boasted the largest size among all legations located in Jeong-dong at the time of the Korean Empire, and it was also seated on a high ground, which entailed numerous geographical advantages for Russia.  At dawn of February 11, 1896, King Gojong and the crown prince (Sunjong) evacuated to the Russian Legation due to the heightened level of threats by the pro-Japan forces and, here, Gojong elected a new cabinet to govern the country. He also ordered preparations that were neededin founding the Korean Empire as well as to repair the Gyeongungung Palace. Russia was called “Arasa” at the time so this event is known as “Agwanpacheon,” which means that “the king leaves the palace he has stayed and flees to the Arasa Legation.”  The once-enormous Russian Legation now only has the tower part of the original building remaining, and the new Russian Consulate and Embassy has replaced the site and functions.

stories.title: Habib House
stories.script: Habib House  Habib House  * Habib House prohibits photography except when it is open during the Jeongdong Culture Night.   After signing the Korea-United States Treaty of 1882, the U.S. established its legation in Jeong-dong before anyone else in 1883. Other legations that had purchased lands in Jeong-dong built structures in their own styles but the U.S. used a Korean traditional hanok. The old U.S. Legation is not only the most aged building that still remains in the Jeong-dong area but also the oldest among all overseas diplomatic establishments that the U.S. have operated.  When the U.S. Legation was established in Jeong-dong in 1883, legations of other countries such as the U.K., Russia and France were also constructed soon after, and all of these foreign legations served as the center of diplomacy and missions. Ever since its legation was installed, the U.S. led friendly diplomacy with Joseon through missionaries and diplomats and kept the foreign affairs relations with Joseon in various ways including arrangement of outstanding Joseon students to be able to study abroad in America.  This building, which was used as the legation until 1905, was then used as the consulate until 1941 and as a reception hall after the Korean War. Philip Habib who served as the U.S. ambassador to Korea in the 1970s built the new embassy in hanok, which is still being used today. The former U.S. Legation was designated as cultural heritage in 2001 since it is a space that shows well the historic diplomatic relations between the U.S. and South Korea.  It currently prohibits any civilian access but it is temporarily open to the public during the Jeongdong Culture Night period so don’t miss out.

stories.title: Central Hall of the Salvation Army
stories.audioTitle: Central Hall of the Salvation Army
stories.script: Central Hall of the Salvation Army  Have you seen the people that ring a bell with a red donation box every December? They are the Salvation Army who live a life of service to help the needy and alienated. The Salvation Army is a denomination founded by William Booth, a British Methodist pastor. He came to Joseon in 1908 and started his missionary work.  The construction of the Central Hall of the Salvation Army, which is currently used as the main building of the Korean Salvation Army, began in 1926 and was completed in 1928. A triangular roof is placed on huge pillars on the porch to make the porch look quite large. The walls used red bricks that were popularly used at the time for Western-style buildings. The hallway and stairs inside are made of wood, and they are a part of a building from which you can feel the passing of time.  Although there were some renovations over time and the back of the building was also extended, it has still maintained the original appearance overall, which led to its designation as Seoul Metropolitan Monument No. 20 in 2002.  Since the inside of the building is currently used as an office and a worship space, visits by non-members are allowed only after asking the office for permission.

stories.title: Yeongnangho Lake
stories.script: Located in a 15-minute walking distance from Sokcho Intercity Bus Terminal, Yeongnangho is a large lake that holds countless stories. This lake is a lagoon. As seawater comes in, sand begins to accumulate and ends up separating a body of water from the sea. This is how a lagoon is created. There are two of such lagoons in Sokcho.  A long time ago, there lived a dragon that was destined to ascend to heaven soon. For the dragon to do so, it needed to shine a magic pearl on a moonlit night. But one day, an imugi, or a monster serpent, that had been secretly coveting the pearl, snatched it away and rose up to the sky. Having lost its pearl, the dragon sorrowfully wept and the legend has it that its tears turned into Yeongnangho Lake.  Yeongnang, who belonged to the elite youth corps called Hwarang, had gone to Geumgangsan Mountain for training during the Silla period and found this beautiful lagoon on his way back to Gyeongju. He instantly became enamored with the view of the lagoon and decided to settle down near Beombawi Rock where he both trained and enjoyed the arts without any knowledge of the time. This is how it became known as Yeongnangho Lake.  Beombawi Rock of Yeongnangho Lake is famous for being one of the Eight Sights of Sokcho. It is nice to simply look at the rock but, in the old days, many literary scholars climbed up the rock and looked down the waters as they wrote poetry. Lee Jung-hwan, a Silhak scholar from the Joseon period, described the lake as “a place that seems to have hidden a magic pearl” in his work Taengniji. Traces of names and poetry engraved on rocks still remain today.  There is a pavilion named Yeongnangjeong next to Beombawi Rock. This was originally built in the name of Geumjangdae during the Korean War to commemorate the feat of a military commander at the time but was later damaged. When it was restored in 2005, it was reborn with a new name. When you look down the lake from the pavilion, you can see the migratory birds flying over as well as the sun and the moon reflecting on the water.  Yeongnangho is a large lake with a circumference of approximately 8km. That is why an annual marathon is held here. You can also ride a bike to take a look around the lake with a tour guide. The lake features resorts and pensions around it so visitors can stay and relax while looking onto Yeongnangho Lake.

stories.title: Sokcho Lighthouse Beach
stories.script: As there are many beaches in Sokcho along the East Sea, you need to check the name of the beach before you pay a visit. Sokcho Lighthouse Beach stretches for about 400m along the coast to the north of Sokcho Lighthouse. The beach first opened to the public in July 2004.  Named after a lighthouse nearby, the Lighthouse Beach has a calm and tranquil vibe unlike other beaches in Sokcho, which makes it a popular spot for anglers. The beach, which is formed on both sides of an embankment, consists of sand and rocks. On the other side of the Lighthouse Observatory, you will also notice a small lighthouse colored in white and red.  If you stop by the beach in an off-season, you will see flat, large rocks being used to dry seaweeds or plaice, which is to make a popular dish in the East Coast called gajami sikhae (salted and fermented plaice). When people hear the word sikhae, many of them misunderstand it as sikhye, or sweet rice punch; sikhae is a type of salted seafood whose name is a combination of sik, which means food, and hae, which means salted seafood. Gajami sikhae, which is typically enjoyed in Hamgyeong-do Province, spread in Sokcho by people from Hamgyeong-do Province who settled in Sokcho in the aftermath of the Korean War.  Along the National Road No. 7 on the way up to the Lighthouse Observatory, there is a sculpture that symbolizes the legend of Yeonggeumjeong Pavilion. If you look down the Lighthouse Beach from here, you will get a clear view of the entire seaside. Lighthouse Beach only opens in July and August. As water is freezing cold other than those two months, please remember that, without proper gear, swimming may be prohibited.

stories.title: Sokcho Lighthouse Observatory
stories.script: Sokcho Lighthouse Observatory is also known as Yeonggeumjeong Lighthouse Observatory since it is located right next to Yeonggeumjeong Pavilion. From both side of Lighthouse Beach and Yeonggeumjeong Pavilion, you can go up to the observatory by climbing up the stairs. If you wish to take a more gradual path, I recommend you take the one from the Lighthouse Beach.  While climbing up from Lighthouse Beach, you will see a small stage where events for Sokcho citizens are held. It is said that the Lighthouse Observatory was built over a large space to accommodate a great number of people since it also serves as a shelter in case of a disaster.  No. 1 of the Eight Sights of Sokcho, the Lighthouse Observatory began its operation in June 1957 and the building that serves as the observatory today was constructed in 2006. You can check out the history and views of the Lighthouse Observatory on the second floor, and enjoy the cool sea breeze outdoors on the third floor.   East Sea, Lighthouse Beach, Yeonggeumjeong Pavilion and Dongmyeonghang Port unfolds right in front of you. From here, it is possible to see the entire Sokcho from Cheongchoho and Yeongnangho Lakes to Cheongdaesan and Seoraksan Mountains as well as Daepohang Port, so be ready to take out your phone and capture the wonderful scenery.   Once you take pictures and go down to Yeonggeumjeong Pavilion, you will get to Yeonggeumjeong Certification Center that looks like a red phone booth. It was established for many tourists who travel the eastern coast on bicycles. If you visit here on a bike, don't forget to check in here before you go!

stories.title: Yeonggeumjeong Pavilion, Sokcho
stories.script: On the coast where Sokcho Lighthouse Observatory and Dongmyeonghang Port meet, there is a pavilion that faces a small stone mountain and the sea called Yeonggeumjeong. Most people think that it is the name of the pavilion but, in fact, the stone mountain and the rocks that had existed in the area were collectively referred to as Yeonggeumjeong in the past.  East Sea has carried powerful waves into Sokcho every day. Every time the waves crashed into the stone mountain and enormous rocks, it is said that it sounded like geomungo, a traditional Korean musical instrument. That is why the area got the name Yeonggeumjeong, which means a place with numinous geomungo sounds. Another legend has it that fairies from the heavens came down, took a bath in the sea, and played geomungo before returning.  Some stories also say that Yeonggeumjeong holds large and flat rock where the hoofs of a general's horse are said to still remain and Jingbawi Rock from which the sounds of a gong are heard. It is unclear exactly when such stories began to be told, but what is certain is that the rocks and stone mountains at Yeonggeumjeong have lived countless years with the villagers.  During the Japanese colonial period, rocks of Yeonggeumjeong were gathered and used for constructing breakwaters and extending facilities in Dongmyeonghang and Sokchohang Ports. The size of Yeonggeumjeong continued to be reduced to become what you see today.  There are two pavilions at Yeonggeumjeong. The one at the top of the stone mountain offers a view of the sea at a higher ground while the one on the sea, which extends long towards the waters, enables you to examine the stone mountain and the sea more up close. Many people come to see the first sunrise of the year at these pavilions because it is the perfect place to watch the sun slowly come up from the waters while listening to the waves that sound like a geomungo playing.  However, it is not open when the waves are too high or if the area is under a high seas watch, so make sure to check the weather forecast before you go.

stories.title: Sokchohang Port (Dongmyeonghang Port)
stories.script: Sokchohang Port is one of the eastern coast ports in Gangwon-do Province where you can see the greatest variety of ships. It is a huge port where you can find a variety of ships from small fishing boats that catch squids or plaice to coast guard vessels that patrol the waters, as well as battleships, cruise ships and ferries.  Known by the name of Sokchohang or Dongmyeonghang today, this port was built during the Japanese colonial period through a large-scale harbor and bank revetment construction. At the time, the port was built by forcibly mobilizing fishermen and other Joseon people living nearby and, because the rocks of Yeonggeumjeong and sand from the shore were thoughtlessly taken, it caused great damage to nature.  Known for a variety of things to eat and see, there are many foreign international who visit Sokcho on cruise ships. Dongmyeonghang Port features many restaurants that sell snow crabs, red snow crabs and mulgomtang (spicy moray eel stew). A long breakwater extends towards Yeonggeumjeong and you will find many people fishing or standing around to get a closer view of the sea.  Towards Sokchohang Port, there are coast guard pier and a ferry ticket office. Food stalls are set up night and day where you can enjoy fresh, just-caught seafood. Because each stall has its own fishing boat, it is interesting that these stalls have the exact same names as the fishing boats. In summertime, people gather to hold small parties where they can enjoy great food and company, so it'd be a good idea to pay a visit during the summer season.

stories.title: Cheongchoho Lake, Sokcho
stories.script: There are two lagoons in Sokcho: Yeongnangho Lake and Cheongchoho Lake. Among them, Cheongchoho Lake is located in the downtown of Sokcho, making it an easily accessible lake. Unlike Yeongnangho Lake whose name had existed since the Silla period, Cheongchoho Lake had remained a nameless lagoon for quite a long period of time. In those days, it was often called Ssangseongho Lake to refer to it as a twin lake of Yeongnangho Lake. A legend has it that Cheongchoho Lake got its name because Cheongnyong, a blue dragon, used to live here whereas Hwangnyong, a yellow dragon, once lived in Yeongnangho Lake. This is why there is a sculpture related to the two dragons installed by Cheongchoho Lake.  During the Joseon period, Manhoyeong Garrison was located by Cheongchoho Lake to anchor warships mainly because, though it was located right next to a sea, it was subject to a lesser severity of wind and waves. In the late Japanese colonial era, Japan widened a narrow entrance and built embankments on its sides for large ships to be able to pass through in order to turn Cheongchoho Lake into a large port.  Cheongchoho Lake is also a famous habitat for migratory birds. Although it is located at the center of the city, the lake is so large that migratory birds spend as much time and eat as much food as they want here before it is time for them to leave. These migratory birds attract many visitors who wish to take their pictures. In particular, as Cheongchojeong Pavilion and the migratory bird habitat observatory built on the lake provide a more up-close view of the migratory birds, you will see a lot of people getting settled in the area even from early in the morning.  There is Cheongchoho Lake Park near the lake, and because it was built in time for the International Tourism Expo in 1999, it is also known as the Expo Park. You can enter the Expo Tower, which was constructed before the expo opened, with an admission fee. Here, you can get a night view of downtown Sokcho as well as Cheongchoho Lake. If you go from the lake to Sokcho City Hall, you will reach Central Market (Sokcho Tourist Fish Market) where you can easily lose track of time visiting different stores in the marketplace and enjoying delicious food.  Where the East Sea and Cheongchoho Lake meet, there are Seorakdaegyo and Geumgangdaegyo Bridges, both of which can be walked over. In particular, when you go up to Seorakdaegyo Bridge, you will be able to see ships that enter Cheongchoho Lake. It is a wonderful place where you can feel the scale of the lake whose circumference is nearly 6km.

stories.title: Abai Village and Gaetbae
stories.script: During the Korean War, people from Hamgyeong-do Province who fled to the south either got on a ship heading to Busan in Sokcho or settled in the area. Near the end of the war and when peace talks continued, they were optimistic that they would be able to get back to their hometowns. But five long decades have passed and they have yet to return home, longing to meet their families they had left behind in the north.  In Hamgyeong-do dialect, Abai means father and Eomai means mother. This village used to be a small sandbank by a coast. People from Hamgyeong-do Province who were unable to return home began to set up a shantytown here, which eventually became Cheongho-dong of today, also known as “Abai Village.”  Today, many of those who first settled in Abai Village back in the day and remembered their homes in Hamgyeong-do Province are long gone. Instead, their descendants live here to continue the culture and cuisine of Hamgyeong-do Province. In Abai Village, the famous Abai sundae and gajami sikhae (salted and fermented plaice) are foods that you will be able to eat in any restaurant you walk into. In addition, you can try a variety of Hamgyeong-do dishes including pollack sundae, squid sundae and Hamheung naengmyeon (cold buckwheat noodles).  There are two ways to go in and out of Abai Village from downtown Sokcho: one is to walk over Geumgangdaegyo or Seorakdaegyo Bridges, and the other is to use a Gaetbae. “Gaetbae” is a non-powered boat that you can only find in this area. It is a unique type of boat that moves only when the boat's passengers themselves hook and pull a rope. Sokcho citizens who present their IDs can use it for free whereas those from other regions must pay a fee every time they ride it. If you take a boat from the Gaetbae boarding platform beneath Seorakdaegyo Bridge, you can get to Central Market (Sokcho Tourist Fish Market) on the other side in just two minutes.

stories.title: Sokcho Beach
stories.script: One of the most famous summer vacation spots run by the city of Sokcho, Sokcho Beach is where people all over the world visit every summer to swim. As it is open year-round, it is a great place to feel the different charms of the East Sea from one season to the next.  Over the 1.2km-long sandy beach, you will see the blue sea and Jodo, the island of birds. Black pines stand tall like a folding screen behind the beach. Black pines prevent loss of sand and serve as a windbreak forest that blocks strong sea wind. There are small trails and rest areas like benches among the black pines where you can have a unique experience of walking through the forest while listening to the waves. When snow falls on the black pine grove in wintertime, it looks as if white foam is settled over the green trees, which creates a unique scenery.  As you walk down to Oeongchi Beach along the black pine grove of Sokcho Beach, you will find a sea garden filled with golden-waves and orange cosmos. These flowers that blossom from spring to fall boast their own colors and make our eyes delighted.  If you come to Sokcho Beach for summer swimming, make sure to check the hours during which swimming is available, which are posted on the notice board. And don't forget to take all the trash with you!

stories.title: Jodo Island, Sokcho
stories.script: Jodo, which has stood the test of time with the sea of Sokcho, is literally the “island of birds.” The owners of this huge island featuring black pines growing from rocks and a small lighthouse are sea birds and migratory birds.  The landscape of Jodo Island was famous since Joseon Dynasty. It is known as Sokcho Gwibeom or Jodo Gwibeom among the “Eight Sights of Soya” described by Samyeon Kim Chang-heub, a Joseon scholar. The terms, which means the “scenery in which a sailboat traveling far away makes a return to Sokcho Port,” praise the beauty of Jodo Island in harmony with the East Sea.  Since Jodo Island is an uninhabited island, you can get the closest look only when you go on a ferry from Sokchohang Port and pass by the island. From time to time, there are people who rent fishing boats and go to the island for fishing. Using a telescope located on Sokcho Lighthouse Observatory, Geumgangdaegyo Bridge or Expo Observatory, you can get a better view of which birds are on the island right now.  However, the peaceful Jodo Island began to witness chlorosis, the phenomenon in which the black pines slowly turned white and withered. Environmental organizations and the city of Sokcho investigated for its cause, which was eventually revealed to be the excretion of migratory birds and environmental destruction by tourists. Due to thoughtless development in other areas, many habitats for migratory birds were gradually destroyed one by one, which led to too many birds flying over to Jodo Island. And as food wastes and trash thrown away by swimmers or fishermen nearby were carried over to the shores on waves, more and more migratory birds started to flock to Jodo Island, ultimately resulting in deterioration of the island's ecosystem.  Together with the environmental organizations, the city of Sokcho chose to clean Jodo Island on a regular basis in order to prevent chlorosis of the black pines of the island. The authorities conduct education sessions and campaigns every year for tourists so that they do not discard trash and food wastes into the sea. We must all do our best to keep the beautiful landscape of Jodo Island for a long time.

stories.title: Oeongchi Beach
stories.script: The original name of Oeongchi is “Dok Quay,” which stems from how the shape of the village looks like a dok (pot) placed upside down. As this name started to be written in Chinese characters in the Joseon Dynasty, it became “Ongjin.” In Choesin Joseonjiri published in 1918 during the Japanese colonial period, it is recorded as Naeongjin and Oeongjin. In 1966, Naeongjin became Daepo-dong (Daepohang Port area) and the name Oeongjin survived in a stone mountain called Oeongchi as well as the port.  The Armistice Agreement in 1953 halted the Korean War but a line at the 38th parallel was drawn, which turned Sokcho and its coast the front lines. To protect the safety of the citizens, soldiers began to guard and patrol the eastern coastline, and most of the sections became a military zone restricting civilian access.  In the 2000s, the confrontation between the South and North Koreas was alleviated and the city of Sokcho carried out a special tourist zone vitalization project, which made certain areas open to the local residents. In 2014, a trail was established along the large-sized resorts and cliffs. The name of the road opened in 2018 is Badahyanggiro. As the name suggests, it is a trail where you can enjoy the scents of the sea as much as you want.  The 1.74km-long Badahyanggiro that continues from Oeongchi Beach to Oeongchi Port along the coast has become a famous attraction of Sokcho. Because it is still a military security zone, civilians can only access it from 9AM to 6PM (5PM in wintertime), but the picturesque scenery of Oeongchi ceaselessly attracts people.  As you walk along the road, you will encounter the superb view of Oeongchi created by waves, Madangbau Rock that is as vast as a front yard, and rocks where seals played around, as well as other rocks of diverse sizes. There is an enormous rock called Deokdaebau by the shore on the way to Daepohang Port. Its name came from how deok, or blessings, will come to you if you pray to the rock. Make a prayer to Deokdaebau for the safety of your travel and joy for your family and take home the rock's blessings.

stories.title: Daepohang Port
stories.script: Daepohang Port of Sokcho was once an area that was referred to as Naeongjin and Oeongjin; in 1966, Oeongchi-ri and Naemulchi-ri were merged to become “Daepo-dong,” which is how the name of the port also became “Daepohang.” It is said that people used the name Daepohang, which means a large port, from a long time ago.  Located at the southernmost part of Sokcho, it became an enormous tourist fishing port complex today. A variety of high-end fish such as halibut, flatfish and amberjack come to the fish market, which subsequently attracts many tourists who want to enjoy fresh fish.  Daepohang Port has a fish market that sells marine products as well as Daepojang Market, which is held on days that end in 1 and 6. The main items are, of course, fresh seafood. From large fish to squids and red snow crabs, such a variety of marine products makes you think about what to eat today.  The embankment of Daepohang Port is tall and long, which makes it a great place to watch the East Sea. You can also take beautiful pictures with the sea and the red lighthouse in the background. There are many people who fish or are on standby to watch the sunrise, but when the waves are high and the weather conditions are bad, you need to evacuate to a safer place.  While walking from the breakwater towards the port, you will find people working on the freshly caught seafood, and their fast and nimble hands instantly capture your eyes. When you take a picture, be sure to ask for their understanding first so that you do not interrupt their daily tasks.

stories.title: Seorak Sunrise Park
stories.script: Where Seorak Sunrise Park is located is the southern tip of Sokcho seaside and an entrance to Seoraksan Mountain. Past this park is the Naksan area of Yangyang. This is an area that used to be known as Naemulchi, and the name is related to Uam Song Si-yeol, a famous Confucian scholar from the Joseon Dynasty.  During Joseon period, Uam was on his way to exile from Hamgyeong-do to Geojedo Island along the eastern coast. One day when he was passing the Sokcho region, the sun set and the day turned dark so he had to stay here overnight. Then, all of a sudden, a heavy rain fell and the water rose fast, which made Uam remain in the neighborhood for a few more days. Since then, the area became known as Mulchi, which means “a village submerged in water.” And, as the population grew in Mulchi Village, it was naturally divided into Naemulchi and Oemulchi.  Seorak Sunrise Park was established in 1999 in time for the International Tourism Expo. It consists of paths and sculptures in various topics such as the Sunrise Square, Path of Lovers, Path of Happiness and Path of Love. The coast consists of pebbles and rocks, which is peculiar since most other beaches in Sokcho are sandy beaches. As it is an entrance to Seoraksan Mountain, there is a sculpture that symbolizes the mountain.  In the park's plaza, there is the “time capsule commemorating the 50th anniversary of the elevation of the region's status to a city,” which was erected in 2013. Scheduled to be opened on October 12, 2063, the time capsule contains materials that record the past and the present of Sokcho. It's curious to see what the future citizens of Sokcho will think of when they open up this capsule.  In the shore by Seorakhang Port, you will be able to find mermaid statues that hold a dolphin. This is the most popular statue among many sculpted works here. They say that photos taken with the mermaid statue and the rising sun in the background are views that many photographers can't wait to capture. The area is crowded on every January 1 with people who come to see the first sunrise of the year, but on a normal weekday, visitors can enjoy the sea and the mountain in a relaxing way.

stories.title: Cheongdaesan Mountain, Sokcho
stories.script: Cheongdaesan Mountain is more familiar to Sokcho citizens than Seoraksan Mountain. It is close to Cheongchoho Lake and has hiking trails that start from anywhere in the city center. It has a relatively low altitude of 230m, so even children can climb this mountain. The name Cheongdaesan came from the pine trees that are thick and green.  Cheongdaesan appears in Cheongdae Hwabyeong among the “Eight Sights of Soya” described by Samyeon Kim Chang-heub, a scholar from the Joseon Dynasty, and it means, “a mountain rising tall looks like a folding screen drawn in a painting.” It has recently become more famous as one of the Eight Sights of Sokcho.  Cheongdaesan Mountain is home to various kinds of trees including chestnut trees, maple trees and pine trees. There are benches and pavilions at every peak where you can take rests along the way. As you near the top, you will begin to get a view of the East Sea, Cheongchoho Lake, Yeongnangho Lake and Seoraksan Mountain one after another before seeing all of them at once at the peak. It basically serves as a natural observatory.  Though Kim Chang-heub called Cheongdaesan Mountain a folding screen, once you reach the top of the mountain, you will realize how the entire city of Sokcho is actually the folding screen that wraps the mountain. It feels as if one is standing in the heart of Sokcho and watching a panoramic image. This scenery, which refreshes your mind, is probably the greatest treasure you can take from Cheongdaesan Mountain.

stories.title: Hangmujeong Pavilion, Sokcho
stories.script: Ssangcheon Stream in Sokcho that originates in Daecheongbong Peak of Seoraksan Mountain passes Domun-dong and flows to the sea. Munil-ri Hanok Village is located near the middle of Ssangcheon and a good number of hanok houses still remain in this old village. Today, many tourists on the way to Seoraksan Mountain stop by this village for overnight stays.  During the reign of King Gojong, a scholar named Oh Yun-hwan who was also known as Maegok Cheosa lived in this village. Oh was born in 1872 and only concentrated on his studies without ever serving a government position all his life. He opposed Japan's orders to shave his head and change his last name to a Japanese name, and steadfastly held onto white clothing all his life to keep the pride of a Joseon scholar. In opposition to the Japanese-style education, he opened up a village school to train younger students. His birthplace, which still remains in the village today, is designated as Cultural Property Material No. 137.  In 1934, Oh built Hangmujeong Pavilion in the southern part of the village. He had deep respect for Yulgok Yi I and thought that, just like Gosan Valley in Haeju, Hwanghae-do where Yulgok had lived, there was a valley also in Ssangcheon. He depicted that rocks are piled up by the stream where it corresponds to the second bend and water flows on both sides, making them look as if a boat is afloat. He named the pavilion Hangmujeong to depict how hak, or cranes, visit this pine forest for mu, which means to dance and play around. Many of the literary visitors who came to see Oh composed and exchanged poetry here. As the pavilion was shaped like a hexagon, it was also referred to as Yukmojeong.  Plaques with different names are hung on four of the six sides of the pavilion, but it is unclear exactly when these were installed. Hangmujeong is written on the plaque on the south, Yeongmoje in the north, Injidang in the northeast and Gyeonguije on the southwest. Next to the pavilion, there are Monument to the Chunghyo Gangneung Bakgong Hwijiui erected in 1955 and Hangmujeong Monument installed in 1971.

stories.title: Cheoksan Footbath Park
