stories.script: Known as the area that has hot springs, Cheoksan is loved by tourists who visit Seoraksan Mountain and resorts in the region. There is a small space here where visitors can enjoy quick footbaths it is Cheoksan Footbath Park.  The park was established by utilizing the spring water of Cheoksan. It is open from 9AM to 6PM and is closed in wintertime. It is a great place from spring to fall for those who have just completed their hikes in Seoraksan Mountain to relax and recover momentarily.  Once you enter through the main gate decorated with stone towers, you will find a well-prepared outdoor footbath facility. You need to take off your shoes and socks here and wash your feet first before entering the footbath. The facility is divided into a hot bath and a cold bath so you can choose the type you want and enjoy a relaxing footbath.  The floor of the footbath has acupressure stones installed. They may hurt a little bit at first, but as you take slow steps forward, you will no longer feel any pain but start feeling pleasantly light-footed. Most of the stones are round-shaped but you may get injured if you run around or walk carelessly, so you must watch your steps.  Next to the park store, you can rent towels and small cushions at reasonable prices. You just have to return used towels and cushions after fully enjoying the footbath. Take a soothing stroll in the footbath park where you can surely get rid of all the fatigue of the day.

stories.title: Suncheonman Bay National Garden
stories.script: Suncheonman Bay National Garden  Suncheonman Bay National Garden, which was created for the Suncheonman Bay Garden Expo in 2013, has become the most famous tourist attraction in Suncheon since its opening. Built around Dongcheon, that heads towards the sea from downtown Suncheon, the garden exhibits beautiful styles from different countries and, by utilizing the inherent characteristics of this place that once was a wetland, creates breathtaking scenery in which people, animals, and plants coexist.  Suncheonman Bay National Garden is divided into four main sections. If you go through the east gate, you can reach the World Garden Zone first, and, if you enter through the west gate, you can get to the arboretum section (Suncheonman Bay WWT Wetland Zone). No matter which gate you decide to go to, the same beautiful scenery awaits you.  If you come to the World Garden Zone, you can see what gardens from various countries look like, as well as gardens that are decorated with specific concepts. The gardens, spread around the Lake Garden in the center, show off their beauty and exhibit different appearances that change by the season and time. The most famous garden is Bonghwa Hill in the middle of the Dutch Garden and Lake Garden. Since the World Garden Zone is so vast, you can easily tire yourself if you decide to walk. Fret not for there is a platform in front of the Kkumteul Garden and Chinese Garden where you can get on a shuttle to go around and enjoy the gardens in a relaxing manner at a small riding cost.  To go over to the arboretum section from the World Garden Zone, you have to cross the “Dream Bridge.” Built with the concept of a “Floating art museum” as well as a “Long-roofed footbridge,” the Dream Bridge is decorated with over 10,000 tiles on which the works of Artist Kang Ik-joong, along with the dreams of children from around the world, are drawn. Created by volunteers and Artist Kang Ik-joong at the 2013 Expo, this bridge became a bridge of dreams that connects nature, the people, and everyone around the globe.  If you come over to the Arboretum Zone, there are various gardens and facilities surrounding the Suncheon Bay WWT Wetland, including the Wild Zoo, Suncheon International Wetlands Center, Korean Garden, Sky Cube and many more. Here, you can check out various animals and plants living in the garden, and also view the entire Suncheonman Bay International Garden from the Korean Garden Observatory and Arboretum Observatory. The Azalea Garden, which bursts into bloom in spring, and the pink flamingos of the Water Birds’ Playground are popular stars in the Arboretum Zone.  Once you have finished enjoying the Arboretum Zone, you can swiftly move on to the Suncheon Literary Museum and Suncheon Bay Wetland by using the Sky Cube (with a fee). The Sky Cube is an eco-friendly means of transportation that runs off electricity. It is an unmanned automated driving system so a user has to press the button to open or close the door. Shall we move on over to the Suncheon Literary Museum now?

stories.title: Suncheon Literary Museum
stories.script: Suncheon Literary Museum  If you take the Sky Cube and get off at the Suncheon Literary Museum station, you will be able to find the museum right away. It is also possible to get there via public transportation. The thatched houses, neatly gathered together, give off the sense that they are a small village of their own.  The authors who had settled down here were Kim Seung-ok and Jeong Chae-bong. Well-known for his work, “Mujingihaeng”, Kim Seung-ok was born in Osaka, Japan but spent most of his school life after the Liberation in Suncheon. He once said that his experience during his school years as well as the nature surrounding Suncheon had a great influence on his literary works. Though he became famous for his novel, he was also deeply interested in movies and plays, even winning the Best Screenplay at the Daejong Film Awards in 1969  In front of Kim Seung-ok Hall, you will see Jeong Chae-bong Hall. Born in Suncheon and raised in Gwangyang, Jeong Chae-bong was known for writing “fairy tales for adults.” His notable works include “Oseam“ and “Crescent Moon and Night Boat.” In particular, “Oseam” was a children's story written based on a Buddhist tale, and it became more famous when it became produced as an animated film. The author continued to write as he fought against liver cancer but eventually passed away in 2001. He and his works still live in many of his fans’ memories.  Once you come out to the front yard of the museum, you will find a number of Korean traditional toys like the hoop, Jegi, and Tuho. On the broad earth, you can draw with rocks and play “Sabangchigi” or the game of “The Rose of Sharon Blooms.”  As you walk down towards the Suncheon Bay Wetland Reserve, the Nantes Garden awaits you. It is a garden established in collaboration with the city of Nantes, France, a famous destination hotspot. You can see the cultivation of various flowers and grapes in this garden as well as a laundry boat, which well expresses the vibe of Nantes. Similar to village laundry sites in Korea, in Nantes of the 1900s, there used to be laundry boats that moved along rivers in order to do the laundry for the people. The laundry boat in the Nantes Garden is currently used as a cafe whose hours of operation varies by season so make sure to check out the hours in advance.  On the bank path heading to the Suncheon Bay Wetland Reserve, you will find the stories of “Duri”, a hooded crane that is one of the most notable migratory birds found here, and the wetland reserve itself. As you walk along the path and read these stories, before you know it, you will reach the Suncheon Bay Wetland Reserve.

stories.title: Suncheon Bay Wetland Reserve
stories.script: Suncheon Bay Wetland Reserve  The Suncheon Bay Wetland Reserve is a unique habitat where the Dongcheon River meets the sea. The wetlands are filled with reeds that produce beautiful sounds when the wind blows through them. Here, you can discover various marine creatures such as Japanese ghost crabs, mudskippers, and cockles. The area is also renowned as a habitat for a diverse range of migratory birds that arrive during different seasons.  Suncheon Bay Wetland Reserve was designated as a Wetland Protected Area in 2003 and registered under the Ramsar Convention (The Convention on Wetlands of International Importance) in 2006. Then, in 2008, it was designated as Scenic Spot No. 41, a state-designated cultural heritage, ultimately becoming a well-known wetland area all over the world. In order to stop the destruction of the ecosystem and preserve the wetlands and their resources, the Suncheon citizens as well as the people around the world cooperate to protect the area.  Numerous bird species visit the Suncheon Bay Wetland Reserve each year, including internationally protected species, such as hooded cranes and Saunder's gulls, as well as white-naped cranes, shelducks, and dunlins, which are seldom found in urban areas. The well-preserved ecosystem here benefits from the absence of nearby industrial complexes and the constant, natural ebb and flow of tides. Additionally, the presence of tall reeds, towering over adults, creates an ideal environment for birds to hide and forage for food.  Visitors to the reserve can observe the wetlands by walking along paths made from wooden decks. The observatory located on Yongsan Mountain, directly facing the wetland, is a popular spot for taking photographs, especially capturing stunning views during sunrise and sunset. The journey from the wetland to the Yongsan Observatory takes about 40 minutes, so it's advisable to plan your schedule accordingly. If you stay until after sunset, you might be fortunate enough to enjoy a starry night.

stories.title: Suncheonwaeseong Fortress
stories.script: Suncheonwaeseong Fortress  In Sinseong-ri where Suncheon, Yeosu and Gwangyang meet, Suncheonwaeseong still remains to show the traces of the Japanese invasion of 1592. Originally, the sea used to come right up to the fortress but, since the establishment of the Yulchon Industrial Complex, the area has all become land. During the invasion, Japanese raiders are said to have dug moats and set up bridges to get to the fortress during the day before cutting off the bridges at night. Thus, it was also called Waegyoseong or Yegyo.  Suncheonwaeseong only has a stylobate of the inner fortress walls remaining today but it was one of the 28 fortresses that the Japanese raiders built along the southern coast during the invasion in 1592 and the Jeongyu Wars. By constructing fortresses at key locations on the shores, the Japanese raiders not only secured sea routes but also defended themselves against the Joseon navy. It was built with rocks and soil for about three months by the hands of Japanese soldiers as well as the Joseon people who had been prisoners of war.  As you walk along the trail from the parking lot, you will reach the fortress walls in Munji, the first gate. The easiest difference you can find between Korean and Japanese fortress construction styles is the shape of the walls. Japanese typically built walls with a steep and sharp curvature to make it difficult for enemy soldiers to climb up, and then set up structures on top so that, even if each of these buildings gets captured, battles could continue from other structures.  If you continue to follow the trail between the fortress walls, you will reach the second gate. Within a Japanese fortress system, the place where a general dwell is known as the Cheonsugak (or Tenshukaku), and this Gate No. 2 is the final barrier that protects the Cheonsugak. Once you go past the gate, you will find the stylobate of Cheonsugak that remains in its highest position. If you stand on this stylobate, all of the surroundings can be viewed like a panorama.  The most famous battle that took place at Suncheonwaeseong is the Battle of Waegyoseong during the Battle of Noryang. It was the battle in which Admiral Yi Sun-sin and General Chen Lin of the Joseon-Ming joint forces fought against Konishi Yukinaga and his Japanese troops. History says that it was a difficult and desperate battle as some of the Ming soldiers who had been bribed by the Japanese did nothing to contribute. It ultimately ended in the Joseong-Ming forces victorious, but in the naval battle that followed, Admiral Yi Sun-sin perished.  The fortress was designated as a national treasure during the occupation era but the designation was canceled after Liberation. Then, in 1999, it was re-designated as Jeollanam-do Provincial Monument No. 171 to serve as a site where we can reflect on our sad history. There is the Chungmusa not far from the fortress and the temple enshrines three of our greatest military figures (Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin, Chungjanggong Jeong Un and General Song Hee-rip) who protected Suncheon during the Japanese invasion of 1592 so make sure to check it out as well.

stories.title: Suncheon Drama Set
stories.script: Suncheon Drama Set  Once upon a time, there was a village in Suncheon where good-hearted lepers gathered and lived together. In the old times, leprosy, or the Hansen's disease, used to be known as Nabyeong or Mundungbyeong but, regardless of the name, it was a horrible disease that would make victims' eyebrows fall out while deforming their hands and feet. It was called Mundungbyeong because, as a side effect, one’s hands and feet would decay, and those who have this disease were known as “Mundungi”, or lepers.  These Mundungi lived together in a specific region in order to stop the spread, and the foot of the mountain in Jorye-dong where the Suncheon Drama Set is located today was one of those regions. The lepers who had dwelled here had kind hearts and had no trouble with other villagers in living in peace. However, once a hospital specializing in leprosy was established in Sorokdo Island, most of them relocated to Sorokdo, leaving small shelters and shacks behind.  The city of Suncheon utilized these facilities to create a drama set that reproduced poor hillside villages that may be seen in Seoul, downtown Suncheon, and other places. Exhibiting our country's appearances from the 1960s to 1980s, the drama set has become an attraction known for its nostalgia. Once you pay an admission fee and enter through the main gate, you can see a lot of tourists walking around in school uniforms that were around during the 60s and 70s. You are able to experience things that cannot be experienced today such as movie theaters from that time, Gogojangs, (indoor roller skating rink) and old classrooms.  You can also find a set that has reproduced a hillside neighborhood, and pictures taken with this set in the backdrop have become so famous that the set is designated as a photo zone now. It is possible to walk through and between the hillside neighborhoods. In the yard in front of Chilbok Market, a community well and a rice store bicycle remind us of tough times. If you walk up a bit more, you can also check out the house of the main character from the drama, “Love and Ambition.”

stories.title: Jogok-dong Railroad Cultural Village
stories.script: Jogok-dong Railroad Cultural Village  Suncheon and Yeosu are cities located near the end of the Honam Line. That is why these locations are where the trains are stored as well as the locations from which they depart. The village created as a result behind Suncheon Station is the Jogok-dong Railroad Cultural Village.  Jogok-dong is originally the home of the villages named Yuljeon, Duksil and Jaegyeonggol. Yuljeon got its name because of a large number of chestnut trees in the south of Jukdobong, Duksil got its name since there used to be an embankment here, and Jaegyeonggol was named after a valley where Jaegung was located. As Suncheon Station and the railroad tracks were built during the Japanese occupation period, large-scale construction was carried out to build a residential village for station employees. This village was called Jogok-dong.  Established in 1936, this official residence village was available for station employees and their families only and was a well-planned city with the latest welfare facilities at the time such as a playing field, hospital, bathhouse and swimming pool for their convenience. After Liberation, the Honam Regional Office of the Korea Railroad Corporation began to manage the village, and the houses were sold to the general public during this time. Now it has become a village where everyone lives together.  Jogok-dong Railroad Cultural Village starts from the Railroad Culture Museum. Made up of a museum on the first floor and a guesthouse on the second, it is already a famous place for college students who go on train trips during school breaks. Across from the museum, there is a village playground, which was built during the Japanese occupation period and has been maintained well ever since, and Gijeoksori Cafe. It is a cafe that has an information board for traveling around the Railroad Cultural Village and where the latest, up-to-date news of the village are noticed, which is why many people begin their trips here after taking a village map.  From the cafe to the inner part of the village, there are murals, which are, of course, related to trains, and this is a great spot to take pictures. If you have a map of the village, you can find the residences for station employees along the road but the houses are privately owned houses now so please refrain from entering the residences without the owners' permission or, even, looking over the walls. If you follow the road to the highest point of the village, you can see a panoramic view of it. It is recommended to take a picture of a train passing by in front of the sunset village.

stories.title: Suncheon Hyanggyo
stories.script: Suncheon Hyanggyo  Located close to Suncheoneupseong Fortress from the Joseon Dynasty, Suncheon Hyanggyo was first established in 1407. It moved several times as time went on and finally settled in its present location in 1801 (the first year of King Sunjo’s reign). Suncheon Hyanggyo moved frequently because of the war and the flooding of the Okcheon Stream. Suncheon was not properly equipped with a bank at that time so the damages in the surrounding areas were very serious whenever the river flooded.  Nevertheless, the reason Suncheon Hyanggyo has been able to continue its name and legacy to this day was that it formed the largest group of Confucian scholars in the Jeollanam-do region along with Namwon Hyanggyo. Hanhwondang Kim Goeng-pil, a renowned scholar of the mid-Joseon Dynasty, built a Seowon and trained pupils as he settled in Suncheon. To enter a Joseon Seowon, it came without question for one to take a basic education at a Hyanggyo, an educational institution established by the country. Therefore, Hyanggyo had excellent teachers who eagerly nurtured bright young minds.  If you follow Hongsalmun Gate of Suncheon Hyanggyo, you will find the main building. Most of the buildings, including those that form the core of the Hyanggyo like Myeongnyundang, the Temple of Confucius, Dongjae, and Seojae; the auxiliary buildings such as Yangsajae and Punghwaru still maintain their original appearances. On both sides of Myeongnyundang, there are trees that are more than 100 years old. It is said that they have witnessed all the famous people that came and went from the Hyanggyo, making them quite significant.  Hyanggyo still runs programs that teach traditional culture. In the spacious yard between Myeongnyundang and Daeseongjeon, you can partake in various traditional games such as neolttwigi, tuho, and meongseoknori. Except for the period of Seokjeon, which is held in spring and fall, the Hyanggyo is open for the general public, free of charge, and you can tour around in a convenient way.  If you come out from the Hyanggyo to a small door near Punghwaru and follow an alley, you will reach “Okridangil.” There are famous restaurants and cafes along the streets around Okcheon so it would be good to look around the Hyanggyo of the past and then wrap up your trip on Okridangil of the present.

stories.title: Naganeupseong Fortress
stories.script: Naganeupseong Fortress  During the Joseon Period, Naganeupseong Fortress was the greatest downtown of Nagan-eup. It used to be earthen ramparts, but after General Im Gyeong-eop was appointed as the governor during the mid-Joseon Dynasty, it was reconstructed into a stone fortress. Inside the fortress, whose circumference is about 1.4km, there is a village with impressive thatched roofs  and residents still live here even today. Some of them had moved outside the walls over the course of the repairs that went on in the fortress, but many residents who chose to stay within the walls currently make a living through pensions, folk handicraft, and restaurants. This is why the fortress is able to live on even to this date instead of having become a manmade folk village.  No matter which of the four gates in the north, south, east and west you come in from, we recommend you to walk up the fortress wall to enjoy the view of the village first. There are no fences on the walls so, as you carefully walk around, you will be able to see a fortress filled with thatched roofs and its surroundings featuring green fields and mountains. The location that offers the best view is the hill between the west gate and south gate.  Most of the residents’ houses are located on the south and east gates of the fortress while the area encompassing the west and north gates have the governors’ residence, Dongheon, and the drama set of Daejanggeum. In particular, the monument house of General Im Gyeong-eop standing in front of the governors’ residence is still regarded as a guardian saint of the village, and many old trees that can be found throughout help us estimate the age of the fortress.  It is said that Admiral Yi Sun-sin once visited Naganeupseong during the Japanese invasion of 1592 and, behind the governors’ residence, there is a Muku tree known to have been planted by the admiral himself. Also, “Paljinmi,” a meal cooked by using 8 ingredients cultivated in Nagan at the time, was served to the admiral, according to records. “Paljinmi” is served at a restaurant inside the fortress so enjoy the food while imaging yourself as a citizen living in a Joseon village.  If you walk for just 5 minutes from the south gate, you will get to the “Ppurigipeunnamu Museum,” which houses the collection of relics of the late Han Chang-gi, the publisher of 〈Ppurigipeunnamu,〉 a magazine that promulgates Korean elements and traditions. It is a museum where you can see the efforts of Mr. Han who aimed at protecting our roots, which had been regarded as old and crude and mostly neglected due to urbanization, while creating a new culture within.  After taking a look around a modern museum, you can also check out the hanok of the late Baekgyeong Kim Mu-gyu located at the entrance. It was built in 1922 and relocated here in 2006. Baekgyeong was the holder of Gurye Hyangje Jungpungryu, the Important Intangible Cultural Property No. 83. It possesses the form of a typical Yangban house, which features a sarangchae and anchae divided by a wall. You can check out the appearance of a southern-style hanok yourself, while taking your shoes off to enter the building of course, so make sure to stop by.

stories.title: Juamho Lake, Suncheon
stories.script: Juamho Lake, Suncheon  In 1992, an enormous 57m-high and 330m-long dam was built in a quiet mountain valley. It was Juam Dam, which was to be responsible for the drinking and farming water in the Jeollanam-do region. As the construction of Juam Dam was completed, a lake to store water appeared naturally and it was named Juamho.  Juamho is a huge lake that spans across Boseong-gun, Suncheon and Hwasun-gun in Jeollanam-do, and the water from this lake is provided for daily use in Gwangju, Naju, Mokpo, Hwasun-gun, etc.  Juam-myeon, Suncheon is the place where you can get an expansive view of Juamho. As you follow along a small road from the Juam-myeon Post Office, you will find Juamho Observatory. You can see up close the water being discharged from Juam Dam and, when the water is not discharged, you can really get a feel for the massive size of the dam. Juam Dam you see here, in harmony with the surrounding environment, will leave you in awe.  If you come down from Juamho Observatory towards Gwangwongyo Bridge, you can see Juam Dam from the front. You may cross Gwangwongyo by car or on foot and this is where Boseonggang River and Juamho meet so you can also see the river far away.  If you cross the bridge and head to the opposite side of the observatory, you will find the Juam Auto Camping Ground. Here, you can glamp as well as auto camp with a lake and the mountains in the surroundings. It is popular among family travelers as it is well equipped with facilities like a shower room, sink and children’s playground. The view of the dam is available also from the campground and there is a small water facility for you to play in as well so it is a perfect place for summer vacations.  There are many famous tourist attractions around Juamho, including the Dolmen Site in Hwasun, Seo Jaepil Memorial Park and a sculpture park in Boseong and Songgwangsa Temple and Jogyesan Provincial Park in Suncheon. Hope you enjoy trip filled with activities in Juamho, full of its various tourist attractions and sceneries.

stories.title: Songgwangsa Temple, Suncheon
stories.script: Songgwangsa Temple, Suncheon  The three sacred jewels of Buddhism comprise of “Bul”, which means the Buddha; “Beop”, the dharma or the doctrine and teachings of Buddha; and “Seung”, which means the sangha or the monk who practices and preaches Buddha’s teachings. These three elements are called “Sambo”, or the three jewels, and are valued with the utmost importance. Songgwangsa Temple in Suncheon is one of the Monasteries of the Three Jewels that inherits the element of “Seung.” That is why it serves as Seungbo Jongchal for the monks of the Jogye Order.  The Songgwangsa site is said to be where Gilsangsa used to be, which is a temple built during the late Silla Period. It nearly became a ruined temple during the Goryeo Dynasty but Bojoguksa Jinul developed it again and King Heejong of Goryeo later bestowed the name of “Suseonsa of Jogyesan”upon the temple, which then became Suseonsa. The name was changed again during the Joseon Dynasty to Songgwangsa and that name continues to this day. There is a theory behind the name, Songgwang, that Jogyesan was originally known as Songgwangsan because it had many pine trees.  As you walk for about 20 minutes from the parking lot along the valley, you will reach Iljumun Gate of the temple. Sewolgak and Cheokjugak that are seen right after you pass through the gate are spaces reserved for the souls of the dead. It is interesting that separate houses were built for men and women; Cheokjugak is for male souls whereas Sewolgak is for female souls. In Buddhism, the place where dead souls purify all the resentment and memories they had in the secular world is known as “Gwanyokso” or “Gwanyokcheo”, which is what Cheokjugak and Sewolgak are. Imgyeongdang and Uhwaru located right next to them are well-known through numerous picture works. You can also take a photo while passing through the stone bridge in front of Iljumun.  Walking past Sacheonwangmun and Jonggoru, you will reach the center of the temple that features Daeungbojeon, Seungbojeon and Jijangjeon. Among them, “Seungbojeon”is a hall unique to Songgwangsa because of its identification as a Seungbo Jongchal. Also, you can check out “Bisarigusi,” one of the three specialties of Songgwangsa that refers to gusi (place where rice is stored) made of bush clover. It is said that this bisarigusi can hold enough rice to feed 4,000 people so we can tell how many people used to eat meals (or “gongyang”) at Songgwangsa in the old days.  The temple has a number of hermitages, and Burilam that you see along a Jogyesan trail is where the Venerable Beopjeong, the author of “Musoyu,” once stayed. It is known that, while writing “Musoyu, he lived a life devoted to practicing the ways of the monk. Sanggwangsa is a temple where monks practice asceticism so we recommend you to walk around the site quietly and politely.

stories.title: Seonamsa Temple
stories.script: Seonamsa Temple  Seonamsa is the headquarters temple of the Taego Order of Korean Buddhism located at the eastern skirt of Jogyesan Mountain. It is a well known fact that Baekje's Ado Hwasang stayed here before anyone else and, in late Unified Silla Period, Doseonguksa named the temple “Seonamsa”, which means “a rock bestowed by a god.” The temple's heyday was in the Goryeo Dynasty when Daegakguksa Uicheon stayed here.  The Korean Buddhism has several orders and, among them, Taego Order is the one branched out from the Jogye Order after the Japanese occupation period, and one of its notable differences from the Jogye Order is that it allows monks to marry. It is an order whose monks are able to get married but are required to practice asceticism at the same time.  As you walk for about 25 minutes from the parking lot along the Seonamsa Valley, you will reach Seungseongyo Bridge of the temple. The image of an arch bridge reflecting on the valley water is really famous. Because the volume of water in the Seonamsa Valley is not uniform every year, people say that the best time to take a picture of Seungseongyo's reflection on the valley water is spring after all the snow melts or when the water rises due to a monsoon.  Upon entering the Seonamsa precincts past Iljumun Gate, you will find Manseru and Daeungjeon. In front of Daeungjeon, you will see Dongtap and Seotap Pagodas as well as Dangganjiju, which is a pillar erected in front of a temple gate or a large hall. It lets people know that it is an entrance but it's also there to hang the enormous Gwaebul Taenghwa (a painting of Buddha of 2m or greater in height) whenever a Buddhist ceremony is held to preach the teachings of Buddha.  Seonamsa's Haeuso (restroom) is famous for a sign written in pure Korean. Its interior is designed in the same way as a typical countryside bathroom that many felt inconvenience when using it so a new Haeuso was built to the right of the existing one.  In 2018, its value was recognized when it was designated as UNESCO World Cultural Heritage. The opportunity for diverse experiences ranging from temple stays to traditional tea ceremonies while being surrounded by nature is another appealing aspect of Seonamsa.

stories.title: Sangsaho Lake, Suncheon
stories.script: Sangsaho Lake, Suncheon  Sangsaho is an artificial lake created by the completion of the 106m-high, 575m-long Sangsa Regulation Dam.The water from Sangsaho Lake is used for hydroelectric power generation, agriculture and everyday living, and supplied to Suncheon, Yeosu and Gwangyang. It is named “Sangsaho” because it is located in Sangsa-myeon, Suncheon.  Sangsaho is a famous driving route, for dates, in Suncheon. In spring, the mountains are covered with cherry blossoms and azaleas in full bloom and during the summer, the mere sight of the blue sky and lake cool you off. In fall, the area is colored with maple leaves, giving you the chance to really feel the vibe of the lake. In winter, the snow-covered scene is magnificent but you should be careful when you drive on icy roads since it is in the mountains.  The place where you can relax and enjoy the scenery of Sangsaho is in front of the Juam Dam Water Culture Center, which opens at 10 AM. Here, you can learn about the history of water in Korea and in-depth stories on the construction of Juam Dam. You can also find out here that, even though Juamho and Sangsaho are located far apart from each other with a mountain in between, they are actually connected by a headrace tunnel.  On the way from Sangsaho to Seonamsa Temple, there are several temporary rest areas here and there at which you are able to park your car and enjoy the view of the lake. The scenery of Sangsaho varies depending on the location and angle so, if you take your car, we recommend you to park in a safe place and appreciate mother nature in a relaxing manner.

stories.title: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Baby Bottle Lighthouse
stories.audioTitle: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Baby Bottle Lighthouse
stories.script: The Seoamhang Port Southern Breakwater Lighthouse, which was first lit in September 2009, is the world’s first baby bottle-shaped lighthouse. Baby Bottle Lighthouse contains the meaning to congratulate births of precious lives and to encourage childbirth in an era of low birth rates. It features a roof in the shape of a ceramic-baked nipple at the very top of the 5.6-meter-high lighthouse.  The handprints and footprints of 144 babies under the age of 2 in Busan were imprinted on plaster and made into tiles, which are attached on the outer wall of the lighthouse. They express promotion of childbirth and productive future of Busan. Korea was the country with the lowest fertility rate among all OECD nations, and Busan, in particular, was scoring the lowest fertility rate. In the midst of this, Busan actively utilized this Baby Bottle Lighthouse to host the 2013 World Population Conference.

stories.title: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Cockscomb Lighthouse
stories.audioTitle: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Cockscomb Lighthouse
stories.script: The Cockscomb Lighthouse was established in 2009 to create a tourism infrastructure and an attraction in Gijang-gun. Its official name is Seoamhang Port Northern Breakwater Lighthouse. The lighthouse was initially installed in the form of a terrace-style observatory where people can view the sea, but many tourists who saw the lighthouse said that it resembles a cockscomb, which is why the nickname, Cockscomb Lighthouse, is popularly used.  To public officials, cockscomb means practicing integrity while to the general public, it means to pay respects to the spirit of Mongmingwan of Dasan Jeong Yak-yong. Therefore, the Busan Regional Office of Oceans and Fisheries added the meaning of cockscomb to the lighthouse for storytelling and utilized it as a part of the “road for determination to practice integrity,” making the lighthouse to serve as a commemorative lighthouse.  You can climb the Cockscomb Lighthouse through stairs and enjoy the view of the sea. As you can see, the Cockscomb Lighthouse today delivers messages to all ships and people traveling to and from the area that they will all “succeed as they wish.”

stories.title: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Jangseung Lighthouse (Mazinger Z and Robot Taekwon V)
stories.audioTitle: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Jangseung Lighthouse (Mazinger Z and Robot Taekwon V)
stories.script: The official name of Jangseung Lighthouse is “Daebyeonoehang Port Southern Breakwater Lighthouse.” It was installed to pray for the well-being and abundance of fish for the fishermen traveling around Daebyeonoehang Port in Gijang-gun, which was an advanced base for anchovy production.  Jangseung Lighthouse is located on the breakwater seen behind the Baby Bottle Lighthouse. White and yellow lighthouses stand side by side in harmony. These lighthouses are also known as Mazinger Z and Taekwon V by the locals.  The white lighthouse overlooking the sea is “Cheonha-daejanggun,” and is nicknamed Taekwon V Lighthouse. The yellow lighthouse is “Jiha-yeojanggun,” and because the way it emanates light resembles the face of Mazinger Z, it is also called the Mazinger Z Lighthouse.

stories.title: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — World Cup Lighthouse
stories.audioTitle: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — World Cup Lighthouse
stories.script: Located in the Daebyeonoehang Port Southern Breakwater in Gijang-gun, World Cup Lighthouse features a red lighthouse building with a soccer ball in the middle. Depicting a red-colored jersey and a soccer ball, it was established in 2003 in commemoration of the successful hosting of Korea-Japan World Cup during which Korea accomplished the unforgettable feat of reaching the semifinals.  The soccer ball in the middle is Fevernova, which was the official ball for the World Cup. On one side of the lighthouse, the list of participating countries, players and scores from all matches are recorded. In addition, at the bottom of the breakwater in front of the lighthouse, the slogan of “Let’s Run Korea” is engraved over an image of Taegeuk.  World Cup Lighthouse continues to pray even today for the growth of Korean soccer and for the nation to move forward vigorously towards a new and hopeful tomorrow.

stories.title: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Woljeonhang Port Breakwater Lighthouse
stories.audioTitle: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Woljeonhang Port Breakwater Lighthouse
stories.script: The square-shaped, concrete Woljeonhang Port Breakwater Lighthouse was first lit in 2009. It is dubbed as the Eel Lighthouse because it was built in a fishing village known as Jangeo Maeul, or Eel Village. In fact, the road to the lighthouse is full of smell of grilling and roasting eels, so its reputation still continues to this day. Woljeonhang Port is small but famous for its live fish market. There is a silver grass field on a hill on the opposite side of the lighthouse. It is said that, in the past, the island villagers cultivated high hills to create fields and produce foods. These kinds of fields were referred to as “Dalbat,” which can be written as Woljeon in Chinese characters, and the lighthouse was also created in the shape of a Chinese character “jeon,” or a field.  The Woljeonhang Port Breakwater Lighthouse flashes red lights once every four seconds like a red square-shaped lighthouse. The lighthouse has an observatory, which is on the first floor as well as the second floor to which you can walk up by steel stairs. It is an excellent course for meditation with a quiet view of the sea outside the lighthouse window.

stories.title: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Baseball Lighthouse
stories.audioTitle: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Baseball Lighthouse
stories.script: The official name of the white Baseball Lighthouse built in 2010 in Chiramhang Port, Gijang-gun is Chiramhang Port Southern Breakwater Lighthouse. It was constructed to commemorate the gold medal won in baseball at 2008 Beijing Olympics as well as to promote to the world the image of Busan as a baseball city.  The Baseball Lighthouse flashes green lights once every four seconds to illuminate the night sea. The lighthouse is an 11-meter-high steel sculpture structure, consisting of a baseball bat, a glove and a baseball, which go well together and form a great harmony. The empty space in the center of the baseball serves as a window to view the open sea and also depicts the championship won at the Olympics through graphics in a classy manner.  The sculpture on the inside of the baseball displays the players of the national baseball team who won the first-ever Olympic gold medals as well as their handwritten autographs and their thoughts on winning the championship. This lighthouse is said to stand out for its formative beauty, which expresses the image of Busan as a baseball city in a very unique way.

stories.title: Busan Tour of Unique Lighthouse — Seagull Lighthouse
stories.audioTitle: Busan Tour of Unique Lighthouse — Seagull Lighthouse
stories.script: The Seagull Lighthouse, built in 2012 in Chiramhang Port in Ilgwang-myeon, Gijang-gun, expresses the image of three seagulls, which are the symbolic birds of Busan, flying together with the rising sun. The reason why the sun is there is because the name of the village is Ilgwang-myeon, meaning daylight. The Seagull Lighthouse faces the Baseball Lighthouse, which was already constructed earlier on the opposite side, and creates an atmosphere of singing “Busan Seagull.”  Thus, the motif of the Seagull Lighthouse is Busan Seagull, the cheering song of a professional baseball team, Lotte Giants, where it got its nickname from. The official name of the lighthouse is Chiramhang Port Northern Breakwater Lighthouse. The red light flashes once every four seconds. The Seagull Lighthouse is a 12-meter-high steel structure and a notable example of lighthouse storytelling and revitalization of Galmaetgil Trails with a lighthouse theme. It is also one of few sports-related lighthouses in the country along with World Cup Lighthouse and Baseball Lighthouse on the coast of Gijang-gun.

stories.title: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Conger Eel Lighthouse
stories.audioTitle: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Conger Eel Lighthouse
stories.script: The yellow Conger Eel Lighthouse, built in Chiramhang Port, Gijang-gun in 2012 along with the Seagull Lighthouse, expresses the shape of a wriggling conger eel, which is famous in this region. The official name of the Conger Eel Lighthouse is Chiramhang Port Northern Breakwater Lighthouse, and the lighthouse flashes yellow lights once every four seconds. A conger is a sea eel which is commonly referred to as anago, which is the Japanese word for sea eel. The sea in front of Chiram made of sand and rocks is a perfect environment for sea eels to inhabit. It is also a great course on which you can take a stroll around the lighthouse and Chiramhang Port and enjoy the delicious tastes of raw and grilled conger eels while watching the sea.

stories.title: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Fish Lighthouse
stories.audioTitle: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Fish Lighthouse
stories.script: Imnanghang Port in Gijang-gun is a port of a beautiful pine forest and sparkling silver waves as its name suggests. This port is the starting point of the 12.2-km-long walking course, the Lighthouse Galmaetgil Trails. The Fish Lighthouse was installed at Imnanghang Port in 2014. The reason that the lighthouse was installed here was to not only serve as a guide for ships’ safe navigation together with Baseball Lighthouse in Chiramhang Port, Baby Bottle Lighthouse in Seoamhang Port and World Cup Lighthouse in Daebyeonhang Port scattered throughout Gijang-gun, but also utilize the lighthouse as a tourism resource in fishing villages.  The image of the Fish Lighthouse was designed by Park Jong-man, a famous sculptor from Busan, and it dramatically expresses the joy of catching big fish with a golden fishing rod. Ultimately, it was intended to symbolize the hearts of fishermen wishing for the abundance in fishing villages. Imnanghang Port is a small port where about 40 households engage in fishing, but it is also a fishing village with a long history with a fortress and a palisade to show off its neat coastline and set up a defense against enemies. It is a good marine tourist destination for a quiet walk along with nearby Wollae Beach.

stories.title: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Gadeokdo Lighthouse
stories.audioTitle: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Gadeokdo Lighthouse
stories.script: Established in 1909, Gadeokdo Lighthouse in Gangseo-gu is designated as Busan's Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 50. While most of the lighthouses built during the Korean Empire have been damaged, Gadeokdo Lighthouse still preserves its original form from a century ago.  The lighthouse you see today was newly built before the opening of the new port in 2002 and was designed in the form of a sailing ship. Inside the lighthouse, you can go up round and round to climb up the 198 spiral stairs. Lights flicker once every 12 seconds and reach as far as 44 km.  As Korea’s second-tallest lighthouse with the height of 40.5 m, you can get a view of numerous domestic and foreign ships sailing through the blue sea from on top of the lighthouse. The whole scene reminds you of a ship museum.  Due to the topographical location in front of Geojedo Island and 7.4-km-long Gadeok Channel, Gadeokdo Lighthouse had been at the center of fierce battles since the Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1592. Japan had always invaded Joseon through this waterway. In addition, there are countless islands and reefs scattered in the sea, which makes the presence of lighthouses essential.  As Gadeokdo Lighthouse is an area controlled by military, you must make a reservation 4 to 5 days in advance before your visit. If you want the lighthouse experience accommodation, you can apply on the Busan Regional Office of Oceans and Fisheries website.

stories.title: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Yeongdo Lighthouse
stories.audioTitle: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Yeongdo Lighthouse
stories.script: Yeongdo Lighthouse is Busan’s first manned lighthouse built in 1906. It is installed at the southeast end of Taejongdae Park and has served as a guide for the safe operation of ships sailing between Busanhang Port and nearby seas. Yeongdo Lighthouse was reborn in 2004 with a new lighthouse tower as well as an outdoor performance stage and exhibition hall, proclaiming to be a marine cultural space with stories.  The exhibition hall is used as a place to introduce artworks to Busan citizens and visitors alike, and various concerts in which people can also take part are held on the outdoor performance stage.  Yeongdo Lighthouse is 35 m high with a white circular reinforced concrete structure. The lighthouse's lights flicker three times every 18 seconds and are able to reach as far as 44 km into the sea.

stories.title: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Oryukdo Lighthouse
stories.audioTitle: Unique Lighthouse Tour in Busan — Oryukdo Lighthouse
stories.script: The original lighthouse was built as a guide for ships’ safe navigation as countless ships began to travel to and from the coast of Oryukdo Islets, a gateway to Busan, after the opening of Busanhang Port in 1876. Constructed in 1937, Oryukdo Lighthouse became a symbol of Busanhang Port along with Oryukdo Islets since it was a must-pass structure for every ship entering and leaving the largest international port in Korea.  The existing lighthouse facility was extremely inadequate so the new Oryukdo Lighthouse was built in 1988. The height of the lighthouse increased from 6.2 m to 27.5 m, and the lights also became much brighter. The light from the lighthouse serves as a safe guide for ships’ passage to the entrance of Busanhang Port and as a sign that warns countless reefs, which include Oryukdo Islets, near Igidae Cliff. The light from the lighthouse flickers once every 10 seconds and reaches out 35 km into the sea.  The first lighthouse in Korea designed by a citizens’ design contest, Oryukdo Lighthouse is open to the public and also has an observatory where you can get a clear view of the entire Busanhang Port.

stories.title: Yangnim-dong Penguin Village
stories.script: Yangnim-dong Penguin Village  Yangnim-dong in Gwangju started to become famous because of the “Penguin Village” located by the entrance to the village. The name of the neighborhood, Yangnim-dong, is a combination of yang, which means willow trees, and nim, meaning a forest. It was named after a great volume of willows on Gwangjucheon Stream that flows in front of the village. So how did the name, Penguin Village, come about all of a sudden?  In the post-Korean War period, most of the people who settled in Yangnim-dong were poor. Those who had no land formed a dosshouse near Gwangjucheon Stream. Most of the people who lived here had physical disabilities, illnesses, or advanced ages at which they could not perform any arduous labor; they scrubbed along by collecting and selling junks and scrap metal they found on streets.  Fire often broke out in empty houses to turn residences into ashes, and garbage began to pile up in houses and streets, gradually changing the place into a dangerous neighborhood. In order to transform the vibe of the town, the leader of the village and the residents cleaned out empty houses and set up a vegetable garden. The residents decided to name the garden as “Penguin Garden” after an elderly gentleman nicknamed “Penguin Ajae” (ajae is a dialect expression of ajeossi, or an older gentleman) who walked in a different way because of a leg that he had injured from an accident in the past. Also, the villagers thought the word, penguin, was cute. The name, Penguin Garden, spread through its people, and the name of the village also became “Penguin Village.”  A unique vibe of Penguin Village was created from walls and the vegetable garden built with garbage and junk metal that were produced from the village. Various sculptures are standing by the village’s entrance as well; as you enter the village along the Statue of Peace and a robot made of scrap metal, you will reach the cultural rest area of Penguin Village. Here you can check out photos and artworks of the village. If you wish to enjoy the view of the neighborhood, take a picture in front of walls decorated on each street and small vegetable gardens set up in between.

stories.title: Yangnim Church
stories.script: Yangnim Church  In 1904, an American missionary named Eugene Bell arrived in Gwangju. Together with Clement C. Owen who accompanied him on the journey to Korea, they chose where they were going to live. The first worship on Christmas in their home marks the beginning of Yangnim Church.  As the church saw the number of its members grow, it relocated to within Bukmunan Gate of Gwangjuseong Fortress in 1906 and changed its name to Bukmunan Church in 1912 and then Geumjeong Church in 1919. In 1924, Yangnim Church branched out from Geumjeong Church (today's Gwangju Jeil Church) and has continued its existence to this day. After the separation, members of Yangnim Church held their worship services at Owen Memorial Hall. The church constructed its own chapel in 1926.  The missionaries and doctors of Yangnim Church concentrated on education and medicine, which have ultimately led to the establishment of the Christian Hospital, Christian College of Nursing, and Speer Girls' Middle School and High School. Christians of Yangnim Church took part in the March 1st Movement and a movement in opposition of the shrine worship forced by Japan in order to defend their faith and pride as Joseon people in the colonial period.  The chapel built in 1926 features impressive red bricks and long windows. The year of foundation is written on the left-side wall, so you can estimate how old this building really is. Owen Memorial Hall sits right next to the church, and the memorial briefly served as the chapel for Yangnim Church.

stories.title: Owen Memorial Hall
stories.script: Owen Memorial Hall  Upon his arrival to Gwangju, Clement C. Owen, an American missionary and medical doctor, began to perform medical activities with his wife, who was a nurse. At the time, Yangnim-dong was a neighborhood inhabited by impoverished Joseon people so his Western medical practice helped greatly. To get closer to Joseon people, the missionary even changed his name to a Korean one, “Oh Won” or “Oh Gi-won.”  Even before he moved to Korea, Owen wanted to set up a space for memorial of his grandfather, William Owen, so his plan was to construct a building in Yangnim-dong to serve as a memorial and his clinic. His plans seemed to be vanishing, however, when Owen passed away in 1909 due to pneumonia from overwork.  But the people of Yangnim-dong remembered Owen who had dedicated his life for them. In 1914, the villagers delivered the missionary's will to his relatives in America. Not too long after, Owen’s grandfather and his relatives sent 4,200 dollars in remembrance of him. M. L. Swinehart, known as an architect missionary at the time, and other Westerners designed a building whose exterior was made of gray-colored bricks and interior was made of wooden frames. The marble signboard at the memorial says, “IN MEMORY OF WILLAM L. AND CLEMENT C. OWEN,” in both English and Chinese so you can tell that this space pays tribute to the two men of the Owen family.  There are two main gates to the building, which is an evidence of the social atmosphere of the era when it was built. Considering the distinctions that existed between men and women, men used the west gate while women passed through the north gate. Today, the inside of the building is used as the chapel for the Christian College of Nursing, so it is not open to the public. As the Gwangju Metropolitan City Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 26, Owen Memorial Hall shows the will of the missionaries who settled in Yangnim-dong.

stories.title: Jo Ahra Memorial Hall
stories.script: Jo Ahra Memorial Hall  Jo Ahra was a female activist who is known as the mother of Gwangju. Her pen name, “Sosimdang,” means “pure and innocent.” She was born in Naju in 1912 but graduated from Gwangju Speer Girls' High School and settled in Gwangju when she became a teacher at the Neel Bible School.  The era in which Jo lived is the modern period widely regarded as the turbulent history of Korea with some of the most important events in the country's modern and contemporary history; she went through the Japanese colonization when she was in school, the Korean War when she was a young adult, and the Gwangju Uprising later in her life.  When shrine worship and forced name change to Japanese names were implemented in 1936, Jo firmly refused to accept such ideas, which led to her imprisonment. The country was liberated soon after, and, in 1947, she oversaw the Gwangju YMCA to protect women's rights. Also, she operated Seongbinyeosa and Gyemyeong Women's Welfare Center aiming to educate women and protect the socially disadvantage.  Even after the end of the Korean War, she carried out relief project and women's education project after another, and when the Gwangju Uprising commenced in 1980, Jo served as a member of the situation control committee and led the discharge of the imprisoned people and treatment for the wounded. Her work actually got her jailed on the charge of conspiracy of a rebellion.  Jo spent her life for the citizens of Gwangju and the marginalized classes in our society. When she passed away in 2003, she was conferred with the Grand Order of Mugunghwa, and people who were supported and aided by her came together to establish the Jo Ahra Memorial Hall in 2015 in the present-day location.

stories.title: House of Missionary Wilson
stories.script: House of Missionary Wilson  Missionaries who came to Jeollanam-do Province arrived in Gwangju and settled down on a hill in Yangnim-dong where not many people had come and gone. One of the missionaries, Robert Manton Wilson, changed his name to “Woo Il-seon” to get closer to Joseon people.  Wilson, a missionary and a surgeon, initially rented a hanok building for his missionary work before building a Western-style house later here. At first, the structure was used as a church and a house, but once the Yangnim Church building was established, it became solely the house of his family.  The house is currently the oldest Western-style building in Gwangju and is designated as Gwangju Metropolitan City Monument No. 15. As a doctor at Jejung Hospital (Jejungwon), today's Kwangju Christian Hospital, Wilson led the efforts to treat and educate patients with leprosy and helped the completely cured to live new lives through vocational training.  Consisted of a basement and two ground floors, the house is currently used as the church's mission work building, so it is not open to public. The gray bricks on the exterior are construction materials that were widely used in Netherlands at the time, and granite, a material that is easy to acquire in Korea, was also used in the building. With the materials used, the building boasts a unique structure combining Korean and Western components.

stories.title: Chinese Holly Tree of Yangnim-dong
stories.script: Chinese Holly Tree of Yangnim-dong  A Chinese holly tree is a species often found on the southern coast of Jeollanam-do Province and Jeju-do Island. As the first missionaries of Yangnim-dong decided to settle down on this hill forested by Chinese holly trees, the Chinese Holly Tree Hill turned into the so-called missionaries’ hill.  The reason this particular tree is special is that it has kept its place for over 400 years. The expected lifespan of a typical Chinese holly tree is short. It mostly grows on coastal areas, which is why it does not grow tall in order to withstand the sea winds. So Chinese holly trees were popularly raised at home for admiration and enjoyment, and because of this, many people pulled them out from the original habitats.  A Chinese holly tree has sharp, strong thorns at the tips of its leaves; people back in the day called them a tiger’s claws. White flowers blossom in spring and red-colored fruits are borne in fall. The leaves are widely used as herbs in Oriental medicine. If you decoct the leaves and drink the extract, it is known to be effective for treating osteoporosis and high blood pressure—the extract is loved by many elderly people.  In Christianity, the green leaves and red fruits of Chinese holly trees are used as decorations for Christmas because the leaves are dark green even in winter. They believed that the tree symbolizes eternal life and defends against all evil spirits. It is not a coincidence that Chinese holly trees were planted in many of the areas where foreign missionaries settled in the Jeollanam-do region.  This particular 40-year-old Chinese holly tree also stood in front of the missionaries’ houses and served to connect them with the residents of Yangnim-dong. Perhaps, the missionaries who had moved to a foreign land felt nostalgic when they found this tree.

stories.title: Yangnim-dong Missions Museum
stories.script: Yangnim-dong Missions Museum  One day on a hill in Yangnim-dong where sky burials used to be performed for those who are ill, Westerners with white skin and blonde hair appeared. Villagers were scared of them, calling them the ghosts from the West, but these Westerners treated people who did not have any access to medicine with Western medical techniques and educated those who are illiterate, gradually becoming a part of the village.  Among them, a missionary named Eugene Bell was the first one to settle here, and the building constructed in commemoration of him is Eugene Bell Memorial Hall. In 1895, Bell founded Jejungwon (today's Kwangju Christian Hospital) and a church to evangelize and bring significant changes to Yangnim-dong.  The memorial hall exhibits photos and materials, showing how Eugene Bell and other foreign missionaries who arrived in Yangnim-dong gradually became a part of the town. In particular, their efforts and dedication for the marginalized can be seen through Yangnim Church, Jennie Speer Memorial School for Girls, and Christian Hospital that still hold traces of the missionaries. Here, you can also meet the people of Yangnim-dong who have been a part of the neighborhood's history.  Next to the Memorial Hall is Yangnim Art Center, which is a cultural space where new exhibits of different artists are held year-round. Make sure to stop by these places if you have a chance to visit Yangnim-dong.

stories.title: Gwangju Sajik Park
stories.script: Gwangju Sajik Park  During the reign of King Taejong during the Joseon Dynasty, a Sajikdan Altar was installed in Gwangju. “Sajikdan” is a place where people held rituals to the gods of grain and land in the Joseon Dynasty when farming was extremely important. The name, Sajikdan, comes from sa, the god of land, and jik, the god of grains.  In 1908 during the occupation period, Japan abolished all rituals at Sajikdan and, instead, built zoos and parks in its locations to do away with the tradition of Joseon people. After the Liberation, the zoo was relocated to Uchi Park to revive the significance of Sajik Park, and eventually in 1993, Sajikdan was restored.  After Sajikdan turned into a park, an octagonal pavilion was established at the top of the hill. However, it was decided to be torn down in 2014; now, only its columns remain to tell the trace of the pavilion. Next to the columns is the “Sajik Park Observatory Tower” from which you can see the entire city of Gwangju.  The tower accepts no admission fees from its visitors. You can either take the elevator from the 1st floor or walk up the stairs to reach the observation deck at the top. Here, you can have a panoramic view of Yangnim-dong as well as Gwangju as a whole. Of course, you can also view Mudeungsan Mountain, which is the symbol of Gwangju. The 3rd floor exhibits the city’s historic moments, so be sure to stop by and check them out!

stories.title: Hyangiram Hermitage
stories.script: Hyangiram Hermitage  Hyangiram Hermitage, located at the end of Yeosu Dolsando, is one of the first places mentioned when talking about the landscapes of Yeosu. This is because you can see not only the sunrise and sunset but also various islands in the southern sea called Dadohae in the distance, which is why it is also considered as one of the four major Haesu Gwaneum Gido Doryang in Korea.  Since Hyangiram is located at the tip of Dolsando, you can only access it by car or bus. The way up from the ticket office where you have to pay the admission fee is extremely steep so you need to be prepared as if you would climb a mountain. But, the closer you get to the hermitage, the broader the scenery unfolds before your eyes, so you will be missing out if you only look ahead and hike up the hill.  Wonhyodaesa, a high-rank Buddhist monk of the Silla Period, was said to have fallen in love with the scenery here and practiced asceticism every day while sitting on a rock here. The original name that Wonhyodaesa gave was Wontongam, which changed several times since then and has now become Hyangiram. There is still the Jwaseondae Rock remaining where Wonhyodaesa once sat down.  One of the old names of Hyangiram is Yeongguam for its resemblance to the back of a turtle. In fact, if you climb Hyangiram and look towards the sea, you can actually see a turtle trying to set out to the sea with its front fins pushing forward. According to the feng shui topography, Hyangiram's location corresponds to the turtle’s back, which is why many turtle-shaped sculptures are seen throughout the hermitage. Also, if you actually look closely at the rock in Hyangiram, fine cracks are found on them, which resemble what a real turtle's back looks like.  Since Hyangiram is a hermitage made by utilizing the natural terrain as much as possible, it possesses a unique passageway through a crack on a rock that you need to pass to get to the hermitage and a place of asceticism. If you go up the stairs set up in between the rocks, you will see the statue of Haesu Gwaneum Bosal, which is said to take care of Hyangiram and the sea. Why don’t you make a wish to the benevolent Bodhisattva at Hyangiram during sunrise?

stories.title: Yeosu Maritime Cable Car
stories.script: Yeosu Maritime Cable Car  Yeosu Maritime Cable Car is the first of its kind installed in Korea and the fourth throughout Asia. It is a 1.5km-long cable car that connects Dolsan Park and Jasan Park and offers you an amazing experience of passing over the sea of Yeosu in a cable car.  You can get on the cable car from either Dolsan Park or Jasan Park. You can go for a round trip or simply take a one-way trip. There are two types of cable cars; one is the regular cable car with glass on all four sides and the other is the crystal cable car whose floor is also made of glass.  As you float above the sea in a maritime cable car, you can see all of the major tourist attractions of downtown Yeosu, including Geobukseondaegyo Bridge, Dolsandaegyo Bridge, Janggundo Island and Yi Sun-Sin Square. You may also watch the fishing boats setting out to sail, and cars driving over the bridge pass below your feet, which makes it feel as if you are looking at a miniature village.  The three landscapes that you should not miss here are the seascape of sunlight reflecting in the water on a clear day, the golden sea of Yeosu at sunset, and the night view of Yeosu embroidered with night lights.  Food is not allowed when riding the cable car so you have to finish your snacks and food before getting on. Also, standing up inside the cable car to shake it or jump around can be dangerous so please be careful!

stories.title: Odongdo Island
stories.script: Odongdo Island  Odongdo Island, located between Yeosu Expo Park and Jasan Park, where you can get on the cable car, was originally an island as the name suggests. The name, Odongdo, came from the shape of the island that resembles a paulownia leaf when viewed at a distance as well as the fact that a lot of paulownia trees grow here.  But the species that has the biggest population on the island is actually camellia, which blooms red flowers. Covered with camellia flowers every spring, Odongdo is famous as the largest camellia habitat in the country, and a countless number of tourists from all over visit every year to see Odongdo filled with camellia flowers.  During the Joseon Dynasty, the island was used as a training ground for naval forces, and arrow shafts made of paulownia trees grown in Odongdo were one of the main weapons of the Joseon Navy during the Japanese invasion of Korea in 1592. In 1935, the 758m-long breakwater was completed to connect the island to the mainland, and this breakwater now serves as an entrance to Odongdo Island.  You cannot enter Odongdo by car but you may take the Dongbaek Train at the entrance or walk inside. The Dongbaek Train is available at an one-way fare but you can get on or off the train only at designated stops. As you follow the breakwater, you will find a large square and a music fountain. The fountain that shoots water according to the music at every hour seems to dance along to the song.  If you continue onwards, you can meet the camellia forest, Odongdo Lighthouse, coastal cliffs and observatory. You will be able to see all of the places on the island in less than half a day even if you walk slowly so please take your time for a stroll around the island.

stories.title: Yeosu Expo Ocean Park
stories.script: Yeosu Expo Ocean Park  In 2012, a world expo was held in Yeosu. The theme of the world exhibition was “The Living Ocean and Coast,” which symbolizes a dream of the most desirable future of the sea. The place where the expo venue was built used to be a small hillside slum on the coast with a coal briquette factory but the area completely changed into a new look through the expo.  After the expo, it became a new tourist attraction in Yeosu. The building, which was used as the main expo venue, is now used in various ways including as an exhibition hall, aquarium, convention hall, guest house and restaurants, which still attract many tourists for diverse experiences.  The two most famous things you can experience here are the Sky Fly and Big-O Show (with a fee). The Sky Fly, which goes back and forth between the aquarium and the theme exhibition hall, is an experience in which you fly through the sky and cross the sea by hanging on a rope. Many people take on this challenge as it gives them a thrill of flying in the sky.  The Big-O Show begins on a huge circular stage in the park, and it uses water to put up a screen in the circle and portrays the story of the sea. It is a performance that takes place out at sea, which allows you to watch the show outdoors in a cool weather.  Both experiences require pre-purchasing of tickets online, and the Big-O Show doesn't open during wintertime. However, if you want to experience the sea in a different way in Yeosu, make sure to stop by the Expo Park.

stories.title: Manseongri Black Sand Beach
stories.script: Manseongri Black Sand Beach  After passing Marae Tunnel from Yeosu Expo, you can see a beach with quality black sand. It is the Black Sand Beach called Manseongri Beach. The reason this beach is the only one with black sand among many beaches in Yeosu-si is because of its unique topography, where the sand and pebbles contain a high amount of iron.  The Black Sand Beach is famous for its hot sand bath, rather than sea bath. It is said that, if you take a sand bath by covering yourself with black sand and pebbles, pleasant warmth heats your body, and far-infrared rays coming out from the black sand containing iron produce a positive effect on the body.  On April 20th of the lunar calendar every year, an event called “The Day When Black Sand Open Eyes” is held, which originated from a folk tradition that has been passed onto villages around here since ancient times. As the hot geothermal heat accumulates deep in the sand and rises above the sand, it is good for the body to take a sand bath around this time. People from all over the country come to experience this heat, so the venue becomes incredibly crowded on the day of the event.  Another reason why the sand on the Black Sand Beach is particularly great to take a sand bath in is that the sand grains here are about four to six times thicker than regular sand grains so they have a high degree of conduction of sunlight. That’s how it can deliver well the geothermal heat coming from below and the sunlight coming from above. The sand grains are too thick to play with or build a sand castle out of but they are perfect for you to bathe in.

stories.title: Jinnamgwan Hall, Yeosu
stories.script: Jinnamgwan Hall, Yeosu  Yeosu was the base of the Joseon naval forces during the Joseon Dynasty. In today's world, it is where a naval base is established. As it was a strategic point for coastal defense of the Jeolla-do region, it became the military headquarters of Jeolla Jwasuyeong that utilizes the topography along the shores.  Jinnamwan was originally used as the main military headquarters of Jeolla Jwasuyeong by Admiral Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin but it used to be where a pavilion named “Jihaeru” used to stand. Jinhaeru was burned down by the Japanese raiders during the Jeongyu Wars, and Yi Si-eon, the Jeolla Jwasusa who succeeded Yi Sun-sin, built Jinnamgwan.  Jinnamgwan was also burned to ashes in 1716 but was rebuilt in 1718 and has remained in its place to this day. After Gyeongsul Gukchi of 1910, it was also used as a classroom for the Yeosu Public School and Yeosu Middle School.  Jinnamgwan has both historical and architectural significance; being an enormous single building with 68 pillars and 75 rooms as well as having used to being the main building of Jeolla Jwasuyeong. Rightfully so, it was promoted to National Treasure No. 304 in 2001 and has continued to be well preserved to this day.  On the left side of Jinnamgwan, there are Yi Ryang Janggun Bangwae Chukjebi and Jeolla Jwasuyeongbigun, and the Japanese Invasion of 1592 relic museum is located on the right. After touring these two venues and then climbing up Jinnamgwan, the sea of Yeosu awaits you where you can see Janggundo and Dolsando Islands. It is where you can view the old town of Yeosu and the sea at the same time so don’t miss it!

stories.title: Yi Sun Sin Square
stories.script: Yi Sun Sin Square  Yi Sun Sin Square, which takes only about 5 minutes on foot from Jinnamgwan, is the main square of the old town Yeosu. It is not hard to find thanks to the statue of Admiral Yi Sun-sin standing at the rotary and the Geobukseon Exhibition Center near the square by the beach.  This square is presumed to have been where military ships of Jeolla Jwasuyeong were anchored and repaired during the Joseon Dynasty. According to the records, there was a Geobukseon, or Turtle Ship, known as “Yeonggwiseon” at the headquarters of Jeolla Jwasuyeong. This is why a Turtle Ship model was built and set up here, to let people know that this used to be the base of Jeolla Jwasuyeong.  The Turtle Ship exhibition can be accessed at free admission. Inside, you can check out the miniatures of the Joseon navy and wear the outfits and wield the weapons used at the time. You are welcome to take pictures as well. The Turtle Ship was a remodeled version of Panokseon so the model in the exhibition was reproduced by conjecturing Panokseon and the Turtle Ship described in the records.  At the tail side of the Turtle Ship exhibition, there is the the Peace Monument and the head section leads to Yeosu-gu Port Marine Park, which turns into the “Nangman Pocha” street at night. At Nangman Pocha that runs from Yi Sun Sin Square to Hamel Museum, you can eat and drink everything from seafood dishes made of Yeosu’s specialties to convenient snacks. Busking performances take place here and there, providing fun and enjoyable nights for tourists and Yeosu citizens alike. How about spending a great evening at a pocha with the quiet night sea in the backdrop?

stories.title: Hamel Lighthouse
stories.script: Hamel Lighthouse  In 1653, Hamel, a Dutchman who drifted to Jeju Island, was sent to Seoul and then exiled with his colleagues to Jeolla Byeongyeongseong in Gangjin. Hamel and his colleagues, who had experienced difficulties in the place of exile due to forced labor and a great famine, were dispersed to Suncheon, Namwon and Yeosu to continue their exiles in Jeolla Jwasuyeong.  At that time, Jeolla Jwasuyeong was located in today's Jinnamgwan and they performed forced labor here as well. Then, Yi Do-bin, the newly appointed Susa, felt pity for Hamel and his colleagues to exempt some of the labor and also distribute some food. Yi Do-bin knew that Hamel and his colleagues missed their country dearly, so one day he told them subtly that there were many boats by the beach.  In September 1666, they managed to find a ship, which they loaded with food while pretending to be having a feast, and left Yeosu in time for the low tide before arriving in Nagasaki, Japan, after 10 days. After being investigated in Nagasaki, they eventually returned to the Netherlands in 1669 via Batavia (today's Jakarta), Indonesia.  Hamel had originally been adrift in a voyage as a member of the East India Company and, when he found out that no wages were paid for the period in which he was adrift, he claimed the wages by submitting written records about everything that had happened during the drift period. These records are the book, “Story of the wreck of the Sperwer yacht” that we all know of.  The city of Yeosu built Hamel Museum and Hamel Lighthouse where the Dutch sailor is believed to have left by boat in order to remember his final footsteps. An alien who suddenly appeared in an exclusive Joseon society in the 17th century went through all kinds of hardships and the records he left are valuable materials from which we can get a glimpse of Joseon through the eyes of an outsider.  Hamel Lighthouse is one of the places where you can see the Yeosu Marine Cable Car up close. It is a photo zone where you can take pictures of all the famous attractions of the old town of Yeosu, including the red Hamel Lighthouse, the blue sea, the Marine Cable Car and Geobukseondaegyo Bridge so make sure to stop by for a picture!

stories.title: Soho Dongdong Bridge
stories.script: Soho Dongdong Bridge  With the integration of Yeocheon with Yeosu, many “dongs” that used to belong to Yeocheon became a part of Yeosu. One of them is Soho-dong, which was originally “Soho-ri, Ssangbong-myeon,” and it is an area that is widely known to those who have lived in the region for a long time as “Ssangbong.”  Soho-dong, which once was a quiet fishing village, became developed when a national industrial complex was established in Yeosu, which led to construction of numerous company houses and apartments. After the decision to host the Yeosu Expo 2012 was finalized, large hotels, a marina and resorts were built and Yeosu City Hall was moved here. This helped Soho-dong in becoming one of the central neighborhoods of the city.  There is a 700m bridge over the sea from Soho Yacht Marina to the raw fish center, and this is Soho Dongdong Bridge. It was already quite famous thanks to its appearance in a romantic scene from the drama, “Temperature of Love.” Soho Dongdong Bridge has merit as a place where you can enjoy a view of the sea up close during the day. At night, it is decorated with subdued lights and enables people to take a walk by the night sea.  Soho Dongdong Bridge in the nighttime hosts busking performances and also has various sculptures and benches throughout the bridge so you may stop by and rest on your stroll. A middle section of the bridge is made of a glass floor where you can see the water sloshing down below. At night, people gather to view the water of the sea, which changes depending on the color of the lights, through the glass floor.

stories.title: Yeosu Seonso
stories.script: Yeosu Seonso  The Joseon navy of Jeolla Jwasuyeong that had scored victories during the Japanese invasion of 1592 and the Jeongyu Wars had powerful partners of Geobukseon, or the Turtle Ship, and Panokseon. And, of course, a place to serve as a shipyard was needed to build and repair the Geobukseon and Panokseon. That place is “Seonso,” which is located in today's Sijeon-dong.  It is said that, originally, there had been a shipyard in the Sijeon-dong area where Seonso is located since the Goryeo Dynasty. Seonso was seated in the back of Mangmasan Mountain and, as you can guess from its name, it was the mountain where they trained cavalrymen. We assume that the cavalrymen who were trained in the mountain also played a role in patrolling the seaside.  The first thing you see when you enter Seonso is an artificial lake called “Gulgang.” It is a place where ships were kept to be built or repaired, and, since the area cannot be seen from the sea due to Mangmansan in the middle, it is also the best location to hide a ship.  A small blacksmith’s workshop appears on the way to Segeomjeong Pavilion from Gulgang. In fact, traces of a blacksmith’s workshop were found here at the time of the excavation, and it was presumed that some of the weapons or iron used on ships were produced here. We can imagine that technicians like blacksmiths stayed at Seonso and performed work on ships.  In the inner most part of Seonso lie the Segeomjeong Pavilion and Seonsochang building. The buildings were restored based on document records and foundations unearthed during the excavation in 1985, and they are assumed to have been used as an office for Seonso and a storage of the equipment.

stories.title: Soswaewon Garden
stories.script: Soswaewon Garden  Soswaewon Garden was built by Yang San-bo, a scholarly politician of the mid-Joseon Dynasty, after he left the royal court and returned home. Yang San-bo’s pen name was “Soswae”, which means “clean and cool” so the name of the garden became Soswaewon. Soswaewon was originally a larger garden but most of it was burned down during the Japanese invasion in 1592, leaving only a pair of pavilions, Jewoldang and Gwangpunggak.  If you enter after paying the admission fee, a forest of bamboo trees, which are the symbol of Damyang, welcomes you. If you continue to follow the bamboo forest, you will see Aeyangdan Terrace and Jeungamcheon Stream. Aeyangdan is the best place to view Soswaewon in harmony with nature. The name, Aeyangdan, is believed to be named by Song Si-yeol, a Confucian scholar in the later era.  As you follow the fences of Aeyangdan, you can see the Ogokmun where the valley water comes in. Large stones were placed in the valley and these made the water bend around five times, which is why it became Ogokmun.  If you continue to follow the valley water, you will reach Jewoldang and Gwangpunggak.Jewoldang was a space that the owner personally used, and Gwangpunggak was the reception room meant for greeting guests. While you sit on the floor of Gwangpunggak and gaze at Ogokmun, you will feel your mind cleaned and refreshed as everything around you comes together in perfect harmony.

stories.title: Sigyeongjeong Pavilion
stories.script: Sigyeongjeong Pavilion  Sigyeongjeong Pavilion from which one can see Gwangjuho Lake was built by Seohadang Kim Seong-won, a scholarly politician of the Joseon Dynasty, for his father-in-law, Seokcheon Im Eok-ryeong.
