The name of this pavilion, which was named by Im Eok-ryeong, means, “The surrounding scenery shown at this place is so beautiful that even shadows take their rest here.”  After the construction of Sigyeongjeong was completed, four scholars known as the “Sigyeongjeong Saseon” came here to make poems for fun. They are none other than Kim Seong-won, Im Eok-ryeong, Jebong Ko Kyŏng-myŏng well-known as the general of a righteous army, and Songgang Jeong Cheol, the great master of Joseon poetry.  Songgang Jeong Cheol, in particular, composed “Seongsan Byeolgok” based on traditional poems and stories shared here with them. Originally, it was based on the story of “Sigyeongjeong 20 Yeong”, which was composed by the four of them to discuss the good places of Seongsan (former name of the surroundings of Sigyeongjeong Pavilion). It is told that the format of Seongsan Byeolgok was influenced by “Myeonang Jeongga” written by Song Sun, his teacher.  On the way up to the pavilion, “Seohadang,” which is known to be built together with Kim Seong-won, as well as Buyongjeong Pavilion are restored. Although it has changed significantly since the construction of Gwangjuho Lake, there used to be large rocks, trees and other pavilions around the river in Sigyeongjeong, which offered beautiful sceneries to be enjoyed. Why don’t you sit on the floor for a while and enjoy the scenery with your shadow?

stories.title: Myeongokheon Wonrim Garden
stories.script: Myeongokheon Wonrim Garden  There is a beautiful garden deep in Husan Village in Goseo-myeon, Damyang-gun. It was built by Janggye Oh Hee-jeong, the fourth son of Myeonggok Oh Hee-do from the mid-Joseon Dynasty. If you translate the Chinese meaning of Myeongok in a literal manner, it means “cry of beads” but, if you interpret the term, it means “beautiful sound like beads touching one another”, which is an expression of the sound of water in Myeongokheon Wonrim Garden.  Myeongokheon is located in the innermost part of Husan Village. It appears as you leave the parking lot and walk up a narrow alley, on which only one car seems to be able to pass, for about 15 minutes, and there is a sign on the alley wall that says, “To Myeongokheon” so you can get there easily if you just follow the sign on the wall.  Since Myeongokheon is a garden, a pond was created and the surrounding area was decorated with a beautiful forest of trees, and it is famous for camellia in spring and crape myrtle and lotus flowers in summer. In accordance with the idea of “Cheonwonjibang”, which means that “the sky is a circle and the land is square”, the pond is square while the artificial island inside the pond is circular.  Behind the pond, there is a pavilion built by Oh Hee-do to educate his son and pupils, and you are allowed to go up and enjoy the view after taking off your shoes. The pond and the garden viewed from the pavilion show off different colors from season to season.  Oh Hee-do was well-known as scholar with integrity and high erudition, which is why Neungyanggun (King Injo in the future) who had wanted to dethrone Gwanghaegun and become the king himself visited Oh Hee-do personally at Myeongokheon to ask him to serve as his vassal. The Ginkgo Tree of Husan-ri (or Gyemahaeng of King Injo), which is said to be where King Injo tied up his horse, is nearby so make sure to stop by before you leave.

stories.title: Myeonangjeong Pavilion
stories.script: Myeonangjeong Pavilion  “Song Sun”, a prime minister from the mid-Joseon Period who was a renowned gayageum player and a poet, returned to Damyang after his retirement and spent the rest of his life here. Just like Song Sun who loved arts and culture, he built a pavilion under Jewolbong Peak and composed “Myeonangjeong Sameonga” from which you can find the origin of Myeonangjeon Pavilion in the first part that reads, “If you look down, it is a land and, if you look up, it is the sky”.  As Song Sun was a prime minister, many people paid a visit to him even after his retirement. Friends of Song Sun include include Toegye Yi Hwang, Gijae Sin Gwang-han and Soswae Yang San-bo, and some of his pupils are Songgang Jeong Cheol, Gobong Ki Dae-seung and Jebong Go Gyeong-myeong. This tells you how great his knowledge and virtue were.  If you walk up the stairs from the parking lot, you will see Myeonangjeong across from an oak, which is a nurse tree. Sung Sun left a poem called “Myeonangjeongga” while enjoying the surrounding landscape for four seasons. Known to be influenced by “Sangchungok” written by Jeong Geuk-in, this poem, in turn, influenced “Seongsan Byeolgok” of Songgang Jeong Cheol, a pupil of Song Sun's.  The original Myeonangjeong was completely burned down during the Japanese invasion in 1592 and a new pavilion was rebuilt in the same place in 1654. Through several repairs and renovations over the years, it finally came to exhibit the current appearance in 1972. Although the appearance has changed, the surrounding landscapes are magnificent throughout the year so please come and visit any time.

stories.title: Juknokwon
stories.script: Juknokwon  The most notable bamboo forest of Damyang, Juknokwon was built by Damyang-gun in March 2005. It is a large bamboo forest garden in downtown Damyang created by making paths and shelters in between a preexisting bamboo forest in that location. It is across from the Noodle Street and Gwanbangjerim Forest so it is easy for you to find it.  Once you go through the main gate after paying the admission fee, you get to “Unsudaetong-gil”. If you go to the right from the crossroads, you will find an observatory called Bonghwangnu. Here, you can enjoy the view of Gwanbangjerim Forest and the downtown of Damyang.  If you chose to go left from the crossroads, you can walk along “Jukmagou-gil” on which there is “Leenam Lee Art Center”, which was created under the theme of “Museum in Juknokwon, Juknokwon in Museum”. It is a great place to calmly enjoy the works of Leenam Lee, a media art artist known as the next Nam June Paik.  Inside Juknokwon, you pass by the filming site of the movie, R-Point, and the TV show, 2 Day& 1 Night, to get to where “Pango” are, the mascot pandas gathered in front of a waterfall. Pango, which are seen playing together in a group in different places throughout the venue, is a good friend to take pictures with. As you follow along the road, you will reach Shiga Culture Village near the back gate. Shiga Culture Village was established by reproducing one pavilion after another where scholars who stayed in Damyang made poetry. You may check it out together with Chuseong Memorial Hall. If you apply online or by phone, you can also enjoy a Hanok stay in the Hanok Experience Center so please make a reservation in advance before you visit.

stories.title: Gwanbangjerim Forest
stories.script: Gwanbangjerim Forest  Damyangcheon Stream, which cuts across downtown Damyang, is one of the branches that form the Yeongsangang River. The stream starts from Yongso. It is said that, during the Joseon Dynasty, there was a flood whenever it rained, causing severe damages to private houses and farmlands nearby.  There are many stories revolving around the creator as well as its time of erection. The most well-known story is that Seongiseong Busa performed a bank revetment in 1648. The artificial bank and forest, which were established during the Joseon Dynasty, have maintained their original appearances until now and were designated as the Natural Monument No. 366.  If you start from Juknokwon or Damyang Noodle Street, you will see huge trees running along Damyangcheon. Each of these old nurse trees has a tag with a number and a name on it so you can see what kind of trees they are. About 200 nurse trees are in this area, including the Aphananthe, cherry trees and zelkova trees. The biggest population of them all is the Aphananthe, which is one of the more common trees seen in Jeollanam-do.  You may bike or roller skate on the riverside trail, and the trail on the riverbank has benches and tables where you can sit and enjoy the Gwanbangjerim. From spring to fall, it is hard to find seats here as many people visit to enjoy starlight-filled nights. When you take a night stroll with the stars and the moon reflecting across the stream, the road leads to the Metasequoia Trail.

stories.title: Moonlight Art Warehouse
stories.script: Moonlight Art Warehouse  When Chuseong Stadium starts coming into vision while following Gwanbangjerim Forest, look down the opposite side. On the lawn, you can see statues inspired by traditional fairy tales. And, as you follow the sculpture garden where the statues are, you will see an impressive building built by red bricks.  This building at which you are welcomed by pandas at the main entrance is the Moonlight Art Warehouse. It originally served as a granary and bamboo product processing factory but it has been remodeled since 2015 and is currently used as a cafe and exhibition space. There is a reason why it emerged as a famous Damyang attraction from the opening. Shall we take a look around?  The Moonlight Art Warehouse is divided into an exhibition hall and cafe. At the entrance of the cafe, it says “Namsong Warehouse” in Chinese characters, which is an old name of the Moonlight Art Warehouse. Click the camera shutter at a location where Namsong Warehouse and the cafe entrance are seen together to take the first souvenir photo before entering the cafe.  Look to the right side of the cafe to find a huge pipe organ, which is the first bamboo pipe organ created in Korea. The organ was made here to commemorate the Damyang Bamboo Festival in 2015, and it was manufactured by a pipe organ manufacturer in the Philippines. Regular organ performances are usually held for about 30 minutes in the afternoon but the playing time varies on the day of the week so you should check it out in advance before you visit.  While the organ is being played, beverage orders are not received so it is better for you to order one beforehand and then find seats. As cell phones or noisy photo-taking during a performance can be disturbing, it is essential to read the etiquette guide in advance. After the performance is over, take another souvenir picture in front of the pipe organ.  As you leave the cafe and go to the exhibition hall right next to it, you can check out the various exhibits. Taking advantage of its strengths of having a high ceiling and a broad space, the exhibition hall offers diverse forms of art ranging from photography, sculptures, and even painting. When entering an exhibit, you are not allowed to bring any beverages that you may have bought at the cafe so make sure to finish your drinks before you go inside.

stories.title: Metasequoia-lined Road
stories.script: Metasequoia-lined Road  Route No. 24 is the road that connects Damyang and Sunchang. The name of the big street trees standing along this road is Metasequoia. These trees, which were planted when the Street Tree Planting Project began countrywide in the 1970s, grew large over the decades.  The name, Metasequoia, is comes from “sequoia”, which is a type of tree in North America, with the English prefix, “Meta” in front, for its resemblance to the tree. It was originally known as a tree only discovered in fossils but an actual tree was found in the northern part of Yangtze, China, and has been imported into Korea since the 1950s to be planted mainly in the southern provinces of the country. In Chinese characters, it is “Susam,” which refers to “a cedar that grows well even by the water.”  The reason that Metasequoia has been used as a street tree was because it is too weak for its grand size to be used for anything except for pulp. Therefore, it is highly valued as an ornamental tree, but because it deteriorates rapidly as it ages, it is known to be difficult to raise in places other than those with the right climate.  Lined up along a nearly 8.5km-long section, the Metasequoia is over 10m-tall and grows up to 35m. If you drive through a wooden tunnel, you can see in between the sceneries of Damyang and, if you choose to walk, you can proceed slowly while calmly enjoying the trees.  There is an admission fee for the Metasequoia Trail. You may buy tickets at a ticket office located in each section. Motorcycles and bicycles are not allowed on the trail so you may relax and walk freely. Now, shall we walk together along the Metasequoia that people say have lived since ancient times to the present?

stories.title: Damyang Bamboo Theme Park
stories.script: Damyang Bamboo Theme Park  There is a large bamboo forest in a quiet village a little away from downtown Damyang. It is the Bamboo Theme Park filled with bamboo trees from the entrance. Once you pay an admission fee and enter, the best place for a bamboo forest bath awaits you. It'd be a shame if we moved on without learning about the bamboo trees here, right?  A bamboo forest is also called a “Daebat,” or a bamboo field. Why do you think people used the expression, “field”, when it is full of trees? Botanically, bamboo is not actually a tree. It is written as “Bamboo” in English and “Juk” in Chinese so the expression of tree,” is not actually added. Even according to the encyclopedia, it is also defined as “a generic term for indeciduate perennial plants, which belong to monocotyledonous plants in the order of Poales of the Poaceae and Bambusoideae family.” In other words, it is a type of grass, not a tree.  When many scholars had to define the designation of bamboo, there were said to be many controversies. Usually, to become a tree, the volume and growth rings have to increase as it grows. However, a bamboo grows thick for about a year in the state of a bamboo shoot and only grows upward to form joints while it is empty inside. And, whereas most trees grow by planting seeds inside their fruits, a bamboo is unique in that a bamboo shoot grows when the roots are cut and buried in the ground similar to how a seed potato planted eventually becomes a potato.  Moreover, it blooms only once in a lifetime and, after that, it naturally breaks or rots and dies. This phenomenon is called “broom disease” and there is an old story saying that, when bamboo flowers bloom, one should avoid the land as its vigor has run out. However, bamboo has been raised in Korea for a long time and widely recognized as a tree by people as it has been utilized for making various objects so the name “bamboo tree” stuck around.  In spring, bamboo shoots sprout from the ground in a bamboo field. Bamboo shoots that get rained on grow rapidly and become bamboo trees in no time at all. These bamboo trees gathered to form a huge bamboo forest. You can enjoy various sizes of bamboo trees at Damyang Bamboo Theme Park so please come and take a bamboo forest bath anytime.

stories.title: Damyang Geumseongsanseong Fortress
stories.script: Damyang Geumseongsanseong Fortress  On the top of Geumseongsan Mountain located on the border between Damyang and Sunchang, there is Geumseongsanseong Fortress, one of the three mountain fortresses of the Honam region. Geumseongsanseong is estimated to have existed since the Baekje Period, and it has become the greatest fortress by utilizing the inherent geographical features of the mountain.  According to records, it was built in 1409 during the reign of King Taejong of Joseon Dynasty and, in the Japanese invasion of 1592, it became a base for righteous armies in the Honam region along with the Namwonseong Fortress. Later, a donjon was constructed to enhance its utilization and, in 1653, a lower wall was built on top of the fortress wall to make it a more solid military fortress. Inside the fortress, it features a large military rice storage that could hold up to 16,000 grains as well as government offices and guesthouses to be able to carry out military administration.  In the cold winter of 1894, the Donghak Peasant Army fought against the Japanese based in Geumseongsanseong but was eventually defeated, which led to the fall of the fortress and the complete destruction of both guesthouses and the storage area by fire. Later, the fortress restoration project began in the 1990s and the fortress has come to have the appearance it does today. It also became a cultural heritage when it was designated as Historic Site No. 353.  The fastest way to climb Geumseongsanseong is to take the hiking trail up from the south. Once you come up about halfway on the hiking trail, you will see “Donghak Peasant Revolution Army Monument” next to the snack bar so you would think that you will see the South Gate soon but it is just the start of a steep section so it is better to check your equipment before you proceed.  Since large rocks are protruded outward right in front of Eonammun Gate so you need to be careful not to miss a step. Knowing that the soldiers of the Joseon Dynasty and the Donghak Peasant Army carried weapons and military gear through this rough terrain leaves you marveling at them. When you enter through “Bogukmun Gate,” which is Eonammun, and climb up the gate tower, you will then get a view of Damyang. If you go towards the direction of the donjon, you will find “Chunghyomun Gate,” which is Naenammun, and a crossroad to Boguksa Temple and Dongheonteo.  Since the entire length of the fortress is about 7,345m it may be a little difficult to check it all out in one day. Since all fortress wall sections except the four gates in the east, west, south and north are cliffs, it is extremely dangerous to go on a path that is not a designated hiking trail or to climb up at the end of the wall. Take a safe tour by following the information signs and the hiking trail and make the scenery of Damyang yours.

stories.title: Damyang Memory Street
stories.script: Damyang Memory Street  On the way to Damyangho Lake, there is a street of memories that has recreated an alley from the old days. An old motel building was remodeled into the Modern History Exhibition Hall by maintaining its old vibe and it continued to grow in size, which eventually became the Memory Street. Now, it is used as both a movie studio and the Modern History Exhibition Hall.  Once you stand in front of the street after paying the admission fee, you will encounter an alley boasting a non-contemporary atmosphere from the 1950s to the 1980s. Signboards that are not easy to see these days and unfamiliar store names such as “Geumseong Electronics Store,” “Godeung Barber Shop,” and “Kkeutsuni Jeomppang” greet us with a very friendly and welcoming feeling.  If you pass through the alley and go to the left, there lies the Cheonmak Movie Theater and Obong Primary School. In the countryside where there were no fancy movie theaters, there used to be those who carried projectors and films all over the country to set up tents in a broad, vacant lot and show movies to people. This has been reproduced here. At Obong Primary School right next to it, a mother who came to walk her children to school in a beautiful hanbok and the children who are listening to a teacher in class are reenacted via mannequins.  If you come out of the school, another street awaits you, and you will find ordinary houses and shops. You will also see terms that are unfamiliar in today's world such as “dress mishin” and “type.” “Mishin” refers to a sewing machine or an alteration shop we see today, and “type” is a typewriter, a machine used to prepare documents in the days when we did not have computers and copying machines. This type of shop not only sold typewriters but also prepared urgent news or documents for money by using a type.  Once you have arrived at “Chamsae Mill,” it is time to enter the movie theater. In the movie theater with a large movie sign, there are spaces that reproduced a“Gogojang (roller-skating rink)” and a “discotheque.” It is exciting to have fun under the splendid lights and music here. If you pass “Myeongbo Sajang (photo studio)” towards the exit, an old animation film is being played. You can come back out to the yard and play games on old machines as well as some traditional games.  If you wish to enjoy more of the atmosphere, we recommend you to rent old school uniforms and walk around. As you take pictures as if you are back on the streets in the old days, you will come to have precious memories to talk to your friends and parents about.

stories.title: Damyangho Lake Yongmaru-gil
stories.script: Damyangho Lake Yongmaru-gil  Damyangho, created by Damyang Dam completed in 1976, is an artificial lake surrounded by Geumseongsan Mountain and Chuwolsan Mountain. The water gathered here is streamed from “Yongso” in Gamagol and is responsible for daily use and agricultural use in Damyang and nearby cities. As the lake in harmony with the mountains became famous for its surrounding landscape, an amusement park was created and the area shortly became an attraction of Damyang.  There is an entrance to Yongmaru-gil across the parking lot of Chuwolsan. It is a wooden bridge and a 3.9km-long trail that were created along the border of Geumseongsan and the lake. There is a slow post box in front of the wooden bridge on the way over to Yongmaru-gil so it is not difficult to find the entrance.  The wooden bridge that cuts across Damyangho Lake is the best place to take pictures of the surrounding scenery. It is good to taking photos of Geumseongsan and Chuwolsan from the front and back or of Damyangho that holds the reflection of the sky under the bridge. If you look towards Geumseongsan from the observatory in the middle of the bridge, you can also see an artificial waterfall.  As you walk over the bridge and come towards Geumseongsan, Yongmaru-gil officially begins. Bicycles and kickboards are prohibited so you need to either walk or run to proceed on this road. Some sections are well made of wood but there are also sections that have kept the surrounding topography and maintained the rocks and dirt roads as they used to be so it is recommended to walk in comfortable shoes. The scenery when spring flowers bloom and autumn leaves fall is so beautiful and attracts many tourists, which is why, during these seasons, we suggest that you come early in the morning for a view.

stories.title: Gamagol Ecological Park
stories.script: Gamagol Ecological Park  Gamagol, which has Yongso widely known as the origin of Yeongsangang River, got its name for many kilns used to burn dishes that existed from the old times. The name was proven to be true when the remains of the kiln sites were actually discovered during an excavation survey conducted in 1998.  Gamagol Ecological Park is a natural park centered on Yongchusan Mountain. It is a well-known summer resort thanks to several valleys and waterfalls. As soon as you enter by paying an admission fee, you will be able to enjoy clear valley water, huge cliffs and rocks.  The road from the entrance to Yongso is a gentle path along with the valley water flows, which does not keep you bored while walking. There is a myth behind how the area was named as Yongso. During the Joseon Dynasty, a new Busa, or governor, is appointed in Damyang. The new Damyang Busa who had a taste for the arts is enamored with the scenery here and tells his subordinates that he will see more of the place on the next day. That night, a white-haired virtuous man appears in his dream and kindly asks him not to visit the next day as the day is on which he will ascend to heaven. After this request, the man disappears.  Waking up from the dream, Busa ignores the words from the white-haired man and goes to Gamagol anyway. He arrives at a pond enraptured with the scenery and all of a sudden a yellow dragon rises from the pond. However, the yellow dragon is not able to reach the sky and, instead, falls into the valley before coughing up blood and passing away. The Damyang Busa sees this and passes out as he is too surprised. Unfortunately, he forever does not wake up from this. After that, the village people name it “Yongso” because it is a pond where a dragon has risen; they also call the valley where the dragon coughed up blood and died as “Pijaetgol.”  If you look up from Yongso, you will see the suspension bridge. If you follow the road up the bridge, you can see Yongso, which is where we were until a few minutes ago, under our feet. There is a small observatory at the end of the suspension bridge from which you can look at Gamagol Ecological Park as a whole. As you go further up, you can see Yongchusa and the kiln site so look around diligently and come back down to put your feet in the cool valley water.

stories.title: Entrance to Gamcheon Culture Village (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.audioTitle: Entrance to Gamcheon Culture Village (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.script: The Beginning of Gamcheon Culture Village  The stream flowing at the foot of Cheonmasan Mountain used to be called “Gamnae,” which literally means sweetness in Korean, referring to its sweet taste. During the period of Japanese occupation and the Korean War, approximately 4,000 Taegeukdo religion believers gathered in this area. Subsequently, more people, including merchants and refugees, moved to the area, forming a village. Initially named Cheondeok-dong, the area eventually split due to increased population, forming a new area named “Gamcheon-dong,” which further separated into “Gamcheon 1-dong” and “Gamcheon 2-dong.”  Gamcheon-dong was initially constructed with around 1,000 shacks on slopes when the Taegeukdo followers relocated to this site. In the aftermath of the war, severe shortages of supplies and living spaces afflicted the residents. Originally, the village was built as a communal residence village, all inhabitants shared wells and bathrooms, leading to increased inconvenience as the population grew. Moreover, shacks were susceptible to fire hazards. Therefore, three 6-meter-wide vertical stairs were installed as a safety measure, which still exist in the village today.  From its initial planning stages, Gamcheon Village was designed to ensure houses at the back would not obstruct the view and to maintain a pedestrian lane in front of the houses. These planning considerations contribute to the colorful and well-organized village seen today. Unfortunately, the village started to decline as its facilities deteriorated, prompting residents to seek better living conditions elsewhere. To revitalize the village's atmosphere, the government initiated the “Gamcheon Village Art Project.” This project involves installing artwork in the village annually, aiming to enhance residents' quality of life. The renovated village eventually became a popular tourist spot for visits and photography.  An information center is situated at the village entrance, where visitors can purchase a map of the village. Additionally, visitors can converse with village guides who provide course guidance and explanations. It's essential to note that touring the village is permitted only between 9 AM and 6 PM, and visitors should refrain from peeping into residents' houses or taking photos without their consent.

stories.title: Little Museum (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.script: Fitting into the Old Gamcheon Culture Village  Walking along the Gamcheon Culture Village Tourist Information Center, you will see a small museum painted over a sky blue background. The mural on the museum's outer wall is Gamcheon Arirang, created by Artist Jeon Mi-gyeong in 2012. It vividly depicts the representative scene of Gamcheon Culture Village, offering visitors a fresh visual experience with its detailed expression.  The museum is open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on weekdays and does not charge an admission fee, allowing all visitors to freely enter and enjoy their time there. It narrates the village's history by showcasing old photographs and household items collected from residents, including rotary dial phones, a fulling block, and hand warmers. Towards the end of the exhibition, there's a display of an old house from Gamcheon Village in its actual size. Visitors find it fascinating for taking pictures and immersing themselves in the ambiance of the old Gamcheon Village.

stories.title: Fish in the Alley (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.audioTitle: Fish in the Alley (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.script: Fish Swimming Through the Alleys  After finishing tour at the Little Museum, visitors may encounter a large, colorful fish swimming through the village's alleys. This artwork, named Fish in the Alley, was created by Artist Jin Yeong-seop in 2012. The narrow alleys of Gamcheon Village serve as communication paths for residents, laundry areas for mothers, and family front yards. Consequently, this artwork conveys a message of creating a vibrant living space by depicting a fish freely swimming around the living area.  The large fish in the artwork is constructed by assembling a group of small fish, each adorned with different colors, which are scattered throughout the village's alleys. As there is a sizable open space in front of the artwork, you can capture photographs from various angles. However, for a complete view of the entire fish in the photo, it is recommended to take the picture from the tail side.  If you look above the fish's body, you'll notice grapevines growing on the side of the building. This is another art piece called A Landscape with Grapes, crafted by Artist Ha Yong-ju in 2012. This artwork portrays a vine with an abundance of grapes stretching out in a way that evokes images of an affluent village. To capture a picture with both artworks, position yourself at the center of the fish and shoot vertically.

stories.title: Gamcheon Village Haneulmaru Overlook (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.audioTitle: Gamcheon Village Haneulmaru Overlook (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.script: Looking at the heartbreaking scenery from Haneulmaru Overlook  To reach Gamcheon Village Haneulmaru Overlook, you will need to pass by a caf? operated by the village community. It is called “Gamcheon Cafe” which is painted a beautiful flower on the wall by Artist Na In-ju in 2012. It allows you to feel like you are walking along a flowery path on the way to the Haneulmaru Overlook.  Haneulmaru Overlook is the observatory that offers the best view of Gamcheon Culture Village. Standing from the rooftop of Haneulmaru Overlook building, you can see the vividly colorful scenery of the village unfolding at the end of the green floor. Not only the stunning view of the village, but you can also see the scenery of Cheonmasan Mountain, the coast of Busan and Yongdusan Observatory. As Gamcheon Culture Village is built on a mountain slope, you can definitely enjoy all of the magnificent view from Haneulmaru Overlook which is located at the peak. Looking down from Haneulmaru Overlook, you will first find out the maze-like streets of the village. If you look at them in details, you will soon find out that they are all connected to one another. It would be as if you have discovered a secret passageway of the village.  Haneulmaru Overlook has a seasonal timetable for its operation. It is from 9 AM to 5 PM between November and February and from 9 AM to 6 PM between March and October. Eating or drinking is prohibited in the building so make sure to finish eating them before you enter the village.

stories.title: The Little Prince and the Desert Fox (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.audioTitle: The Little Prince and the Desert Fox (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.script: Story about the Little Prince and the Desert Fox  As you walk along the widest road in Gamcheon Culture Village, you will see a familiar sight: a figure seated on the railing. It is the Little Prince and the Desert Fox, the most famous artwork in Gamcheon Village.  The artwork was created by Artist Na In-ju in 2012, depicting the story of the prince and the fox. The Little Prince departed from his planet and met the Desert Fox on Earth. They embarked on a long journey, transcending space and eventually arriving at Gamcheon Culture Village. Seated on the railing, they enjoyed the view of the village, gazing at the rooftops and the coast of Busan. The story originates from The Little Prince, a novel written by the French author Saint-Exup?ry, depicting the tales of a little prince living on an asteroid in space. The Little Prince and the Fox in Gamcheon Village are incredibly famous, even among foreigners, and there's always a line of people waiting to take a picture with them.  When taking pictures with the Little Prince and the Fox, please be mindful of a few things. Sitting on the rail next to the statue exposes only the roof of a house below, so extra caution is necessary to prevent accidents. Also, please pay attention to passing cars and motorbikes while queuing up for pictures.

stories.title: Cheondeoksu Well's Story (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.script: A story about the wishing well  After passing the statue of the Little Prince and walking towards the House of Peace, you'll come across the Book Staircase. As the name implies, it resembles a stack of books painted with various book covers. Once you climb the Book Staircase, you'll encounter the story and the Cheondeoksu Well.  ‘Cheondeoksu’ translates to 'the great water comes from heaven.' Near the well, several illusion paintings create an immersive experience within the story about a kind young man.  This young man was renowned throughout the village for his kindness. He cared for his mother and younger brother diligently. During a severe drought, the village's land began to dry up, and the existing wells ran dry. Determined to provide water for the village, the young man resolved to dig a new well. Without sleep or food for days, he tirelessly dug. Eventually, he was too weak to continue and could only pray to God before he collapsed. Sadly, he never woke up again after completing his prayer. Touched by his integrity, God decided to send rain to the village. Since then, the well dug by the young man has always been filled with clean water.  The villagers named it Cheondeoksu Well, believing that earnest prayers made at the well could reach God and make wishes come true. Why not take a few seconds to make a wish here?

stories.title: House of Peace (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.script: A house fulfilled by peace wishing messages  Making a wish in front of Cheondeoksu Well and walking down a wide road, you'll encounter a huge fish on the wall. This artwork, named 'Fish in the Alley,' was created by Artist Jin Yeong-seop and is similar as the village entrance. It's placed at the end of the village to notice visitors that they're still within the area of Gamcheon Culture Village. On the floor, you may notice the words 'House of Peace' written in white, guiding you toward its location.  The House of Peace is painted in white, an artwork created by Artist Jeong Hui-uk, formally known as 'House of Peace ? Bowl Room/ Moon Room.' The artist aims to commemorate the history of Gamcheon-dong, originally established due to the Korean War. Additionally, the artist hopes to encapsulate the meaning of wishing for peace by recording and attaching messages and signatures of visitors to the wall, embodying hopes for national peace and human prosperity. That's why there's a bowl for collecting wishes and a representation of the moon in the house, symbols of prayer and peace. The color white is regarded as a symbol of peace. The house is adorned with many writings and notes containing messages of peace. Although it is not immediately visible from afar, numerous traces left by many people can be found upon close inspection.  Adjacent to the House of Peace, a small park offers a quick resting spot. While seated on the rocking chair and observing Gamcheon Village, you can take in the deeply peaceful scenery. To explore other artworks within the alleys, you'll need to pass through a narrow path from the House of Peace. The path is so narrow that if someone approaches from the opposite direction, you may have to step back, demonstrating the virtue of compromise. Such simple acts contribute to maintaining peace... don't you think this is precisely what the House of Peace aims to promote?

stories.title: Stairs to See Stars (148 Stairs) (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.audioTitle: Stairs to See Stars (148 Stairs) (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.script: See the stars on the 148 Stairs  As you stroll through the alleys of Gamcheon Culture Village, you'll encounter a staircase known as the '148 Stairs.' It's also referred to as the 'Stairs to See Stars.' Following the staircase to the bottom, you'll arrive at the Gamnae Eoulteo Center building; ascending the stairs leads to the road where the Little Prince and the Desert Fox statues are situated.  The staircase is named the '148 Stairs' due to the number of steps it comprises. However, there's another reason behind its moniker, the 'Stairs to See Stars.' In difficult times of the past, residents who lived atop these stairs had to climb with carrying large bags or yokes laden with water. Climbing such a long and steep staircase while burdened was incredibly exhausting. Midway, they often stopped and adjusted their posture, causing dizziness and resulting in the sensation of seeing stars. This led people to start calling the staircase the 'Stairs to See Stars.'  It's difficult to imagine the hardships faced by people at that time. Presently, the view of the stars on the '148 Stairs' is rare, as buses navigate around the village, and delivery services alleviate the situation. If you're up for the challenge, you could attempt to climb it from the very bottom.

stories.title: Daejeon Jungang Market
stories.script: Daejeon Jungang Market  Boasting the greatest scale in Daejeon and a rich history of 100 years, Daejeon Jungang Market is close to Daejeon Station and connected to Subway Line 1, ensuring convenient access to the people. Here, you will not only see the energetic merchants and bargaining customers but also feel the unique vibe of a traditional market. The market is divided into different areas of specialties and named as stations—Jewelry Station, Living Station, Bedding Station, Clothing Station, Fabric Station, International Station, Yori Station, and Food Station!  In particular, near the entrances of Yori and Jori Stations, which are food alleys, delicious smells and sounds of fried foods and Korean pancakes attract your nose and eyes. Spicy tteokbokki, fried fish cake, deep-fried and braised chicken, and sundae are must-have dishes as well. You must try dipping a crispy fried dish into tteokbokki sauce—it's like a matchmade in heaven. An old owner of a bakery suggests every passerby to try their food, and you might wonder, 'how he could make money with all the food he's giving out for free.' Here at the market, you can enjoy a sufficient amount of snack despite a light wallet. Would you believe that there is a restaurant where you can have a bowl of seonji soup with just KRW 1,000? If you head south from Daejeon Station, you will find “Seonjiguk Sikdang”, the oldest restaurant in the city. Not only the price makes your heart warm but will a hot and delicious soup. The price has remained the same for a long time. At Jungang Market, there is a place where you can make your own seal—unique and one-and-only seal! Under the motto that reads, “Individuality is what a seal is all about,” this store interprets your name and time and date of birth to make you a special seal, and this is another place you must definitely visit.  As you walk to different corners of the market to find more hidden treasures, you may also encounter the Pig of Luck, which supposedly brings good health and wealth. A legend has it that, if you see both the boar and the sow, your wish will come true, so make sure to find them and make a wish!

stories.title: Former Chungcheongnam-do Governor's Residence
stories.script: Former Chungcheongnam-do Governor's Residence  The former Chungcheongnam-do Governor's Residence, located at about a 10-minute walking distance from the Daejeon Modern History Exhibition Hall, is registered as Daejeon Cultural Heritage No. 49. Built in September 1932, this building was the official residence used by Chungcheongnam-do governors until the Chungcheongnam-do Provincial Office relocated in 2013. During the Korean War, it was used as a temporary residence of President Rhee Syngman who made a formal announcement here to urge the UN troops to join the war. Also, it is a historical site where the “unequal treaty on the Korea-U.S. status forces agreement” was signed.  Near the residence is a cluster of other residences built in the 1930s to 40s that were provided to high-ranked director-level officials, which makes it one of a kind in the country. The whole area was designated as a national registered cultural heritage. They are important modern cultural heritage that tells us the history of the modern city of Daejeon.  Overall, the exterior of the residence exudes an Art Deco architecture while the interior is a combination of Japanese and Western styles. Its main rooms are set up in a way that they face southward, and the reception area and the family residence are separated with a hallway. Reopened under the new name of “Temiorae” selected by the citizens, the building is being utilized as a modern architecture museum, a small library, a workshop of the citizens and artists, a support center, and a residence.

stories.title: Daejeon Gallery
stories.script: Daejeon Gallery  The auditorium building of the old Daejeon Girls’ Middle School was well preserved and reproduced into Daejeon Gallery (Daejeon Cultural Heritage Material No. 46). The gable-roofed building constructed in 1937 is regarded as an exquisite structure of a unique shape that is rarely seen within the region. The Art Nouveau structure forming smooth curves remind people of the traditional thatched roof of Korea, and it was in fact a popular style in the United States and Europe from the late 19th to the early 20th century. Below the eaves are bricks that are stacked up in a classical tooth form piling to support the eaves line—emphasizing the smoothness.  The front and back of the red brick walls are installed with three wide windows each to bring in natural light indoors and reduce the stuffy feel of a brick building. The lintels near the windows are in more indented design than the walls and finished with concrete. Such styles make the building look sturdy and well-organized.  Reopened as a cultural exhibit hall for local artists, Daejeon Gallery is a space that has preserved a modern structure and holds historical significance.

stories.title: Daeheungdong Cathedral
stories.script: Daeheungdong Cathedral  Celebrating its 100th anniversary in 2019, Daeheungdong Cathedral (Registered Cultural Heritage No. 643) represents the history of the Catholic church in Daejeon. The exactly symmetric features of the exterior imitates praying hands faced toward the heaven. At the time of its completion in 1962, this cathedral was the tallest building in Daejeon, big enough to be seen from anywhere in the city. According to the history, Daeheungdong Cathedral was planned to be built larger than Myeongdong Cathedral in Seoul, but the architects realized that they had made an absurd mistake of incorrectly measuring the size of Myeongdong Cathedral.  Daeheungdong Cathedral is an epitome of Korean modern cathedral architecture of the 1960s, featuring a bell tower—which has interpreted the Gothic style in a contemporary fashion—and the enormous interior of the cathedral made of a reinforced concrete structure with no columns. What makes this place special is that Jo Jung-hyung has served as the cathedral's bell ringer for 50 years. So famous that everyone in Daeheung-dong knows who he is, this bell ringer has been climbing up and down the 20 m-high bell tower every day at the same time to ring the bell. If you ever visit the cathedral, it would be great to meet him as well.

stories.title: Daejeon Museum of Art Creation Center
stories.audioTitle: Daejeon Museum of Art Creation Center
stories.script: Daejeon Museum of Art Creation Center  Daejeon Museum of Art Creation Center is a government office building where Chungcheong Branch of the National Agricultural Products Quality Management Service used to be located in 1958. It is currently designated as Registered Cultural Heritage No. 100, a valuable modern cultural heritage of the Daejeon region. It is a two-story brick building designed by Bae Han-gu, a Daejeon-based architect. With the main entrance forming an arch, each floor features two to three column-less, “L”-shaped spaces centered on the staircase. This shows well the trend of the Korean contemporary architecture style, which was largely influenced by the functionalism of the Western world in the mid-20th century.  Being the nation’s first case of remodeling a modern structure, the center officially opened in 2008 after restoring the old appearances of interior, exterior, ceiling, stairs, and box-shaped window frames that are protruded from the outer walls of the building—this has resurrected the building's lost time and history. The building is now used as a complex cultural center and a downtown museum showing the vivid coexistence of the past, present, and future, and it is actively utilized as a space where the audience communicates with various art projects and encounter different cultures.

stories.title: Fried Korean Streusel Bun and Bomunsan Meari
stories.audioTitle: Fried Korean Streusel Bun and Bomunsan Meari
stories.script: Fried Korean Streusel Bun and Bomunsan Meari  There is a place in Daejeon that boasts a 60-year tradition. “Fried Korean streusel bun (or soboro bread)”, the most famous menu here, is widely loved by many thanks to its excellent and harmonious taste combining the chewy texture of a donut and sweetness of red-bean bread. More known as a bread that delights the taste when it has cooled down, fried soboro bread was came out to the world in 1980 and has since grown immensely popular, selling over 15,000 breads in a single day. This single bread even became the first in the Korean confectionery industry to be listed on the “Michelin Green Star”, which highlights great restaurants worldwide. There is a truth behind this—the bread was never made to be baked this way. After frying the bread, it was supposed to add another layer of bread crumbs, but, since it was too hot, this baker, or the first who invested this bread, put the bread down for a brief moment. This was when some customers tried the bread and loved the taste of it. This is how an incomplete fried soboro bread turned into a completion.  Along with the fried soboro bread, “Bomunsan Meari” is a rising star that bread lovers crave for. Also recommended by Lee Young-ja, a famous comedian in Korea, the name comes from its resemblance of the shape of Bomunsan Mountain, one of the more well-known mountains in Daejeon. Its design of like a spinning whirlpool reminds us of an echo from Bomunsan Mountain. People chase after its moist texture and sweet taste.  What began as a shabby steamed bun store in 1955 has transformed into a local enterprise that has over 400 employees, establishing itself as one of the three best bakeries in the country. Its dedication and efforts for the local community made a mere local bakery grow as a huge company. The company always cares for neighbors in need insomuch that a famous saying goes, “Not even a single person in Daejeon starves to death thanks to Sung Sim Dang.” During Pope Francis' visit to Korea, the bread of Sung Sim Dang was served on his meal table. When you get a chance to visit Daejeon, make sure to try the fried soboro bread and Bomunsan Meari.

stories.title: Jangtaesan Recreational Forest
stories.script: As you along the forest paths of Jangtaesan Recreational Forest, it feels as if you are growing taller, just like metasequoia trees stretched straight up toward the sky.  Opened in 1991, Jangtaesan Recreational Forest is the first forest in Korea to be developed by private efforts. It was acquired by Daejeon Metropolitan City in 2002 and reopened in 2006 as a forest for the public. The forest features accommodations such as the Forest Culture and Recreation Center, forest lodges, a forest retreat center, and camping sites, as well as educational facilities like insect experience center. Visitors can also join a forest guide to walk the trails and participate in activities that bring the vibrant life of the forest to light.  You can enjoy a leisurely walk around the ecological pond while children have fun in the shaded forest playground, safe from the strong sunlight. Notable attractions include the spiral staircase leading to the forest adventure course and the Skywalk, where you can stroll at treetop level, looking eye to eye with the upper reaches of towering trees.  At an elevation of 374 meters, the summit of Jangtaesan offers a scenic viewpoint that is easy to reach, providing a rewarding experience. Many cycling enthusiasts, including international riders, are also drawn to the challenge of biking to the top.  Plan ahead and book your accommodations early to fully immerse yourself in the peace of the forest and breathe in the crisp, fresh air.

stories.title: Maninsan Recreational Forest
stories.script: Maninsan stands 538 meters above sea level. Beyond its peaks lies Geumsan, South Chungcheong Province. Due to its height and strategic location, a beacon fire station was built at its summit during the Gojoseon period. According to a legend, following advice from the great monk Muhak, the tomb of King Taejo Yi Seong-gye, originally located in Hamgyeong Province, was relocated to Maninsan.  The peaks of Maninsan are said to resemble a lotus flower. The well-maintained hiking trails and forest paths make it a perfect destination for trekking. The mountain is the source to Daejeoncheon Stream, one of the three major rivers in Daejeon, which originates in the Bongsuremi Valley of Maninsan.  The rest area at the mountain's entrance is popular among those who enjoy scenic drives. Behind the rest area lies a pond where swans and ducks swim, and visitors can enjoy a peaceful stroll along the circular trail. Another option is to take a walk along the elevated exploration path through the forest.  Opened in 1997 and newly renovated in 2017, the Maninsan Green Learning Center features an exhibition hall, an observatory, educational spaces, a mini zoo, and group lodging facilities that can accommodate up to 150 people.  The Maninsan Natural Recreation Forest is especially beautiful in autumn, with its vibrant foliage from dense broadleaf forests. Slowly walking along the well-groomed forest trails, you’ll eventually reach the Taejo Daewang Tomb, where sections 2 and 3 of the Daejeon Dulle-gil trail meet. For the adventurous, there’s a swaying rope bridge along the trail.

stories.title: Leeungno Museum
stories.script: If you were to name the most internationally renowned cultural and artistic venue in Daejeon, it would undoubtedly be the Leeungno Museum. When the museum hosts exhibitions featuring works by French artists associated with Goam Lee Ungno, even the members of the French Embassy in Korea come to celebrate the exhibition.  The Lee Ungno Museum, designed by French architect Laurent Beaudouin, opened in 2007. The city of Daejeon built the museum in recognition of a notable, though modest, connection: Lee Ungno spent time at Daejeon Prison in the late 1960s. Professor Beaudouin deeply understood and reinterpreted Lee Ungno's abstract calligraphy, particularly his work Su (壽), symbolizing it through architectural design. The museum features pine trees at the front, a central courtyard, and bamboo planted along the outer corridors, creating a harmonious blend of Eastern and Western aesthetics with elegance.  The museum’s built on the same level as the ground which creates a welcoming appearance to visitors. Large windows let in natural light, and the views of the wide lawn and a quaint fountain in the adjacent Dunsan Grand Park transform the scenery into a piece of art.   In 2016, a new Storage Annex was built behind the museum, which enables the transfer of numerous works by Lee Ungno from France to Daejeon. On the first floor of this annex is the Project Room, which hosts the Lee Ungno Art Lab, a relay exhibition program supporting emerging artists.  In Paris, the École d’Art Oriental de Paris was co-founded in 1964 by Lee Ungno and his wife Park Inkyung, who now serves as the honorary director of the Lee Ungno Museum. Additionally, Goam House, a traditional Korean-style residence with tiled roofs, is placed in the suburbs of Paris. The museum also operates the Paris Lee Ungno Residency Program for selected Korean artists.

stories.title: Daejeon Sky Road
stories.script: Daejeon Sky Road  Marvelous screens decorate the ceiling of the street. People take out their phones to take pictures. When the sun is about to set, a splendid, the ceiling screens a three-dimensional video along with stereo music at every hour. Is there actually a place like this? Yes! It is Euneungjeongi Skyroad in Eunhaeng-dong, Jung-gu, the original downtown of Daejeon. Euneungjeongi Skyroad is formed of a large-sized, arcade-style LED screen, measuring 20 m in height, 13.3 m in width, and 214 m in length. It is the largest of its kind in Korea to date. Typically, it features letters or love proposals of individuals, but it hosts different themes depending on the season. In summer, Euneungjeongi Skyroad hosts a dance party along with a video show while in winter, it celebrates a countdown festival where people gather for an end-of-year celebration. But you may wonder, what does Euneungjeongi mean? Euneungjeongi is a term that originated from “a village with a ginkgo tree pavilion, and is a pure Korean name of Eunhaeng-dong. On both sides of Euneungjeongi Street, stores of various brands loved by the young people are standing in lines. Euneungjeongi Street of Daejeon is like Myeongdong of Seoul. On weekends, the street is filled with so much events and things to see, where free busking performances and other city-hosted cultural performances are held. Euneungjeongi Street is an exciting cultural space especially loved by the young people as it is packed with tasty foods, pretty cafes, and inexpensive beauty salons.

stories.title: Ilgwang Beach
stories.script: Ilgwang Beach  Ilgwang Beach in Gijang-gun where Busan and Ulsan meet is a beach located at the east end of Busan. You can head to the beach by taking the Donghae Nambu Line subway and getting off at Ilgwang Station.  The name was naturally given due to the area being called Ilgwang-myeon which in turn came from “Ilgwangsan Mountain” located nearby. It used to be just a village where fishermen gathered and lived in a small community, but after it was incorporated into the city of Busan, development began in the area and now it has become a beach where locals usually come for the clear southern sea.  There is a big wooden boat in the middle of Ilgwang Beach. This boat, which also looks like a wreck, is actually a musical fountain as well as an observatory. Waterspouts from the bottom of the wood, and the height of the water varies according to the music so it looks as if it is listening and dancing to the music. You can usually see children who cannot go into deep water enthusiastically playing here.  On one side of the sandy beach, there are various facilities where you can enjoy leisure sports every summer with your friends ranging from motor boats and banana boats to all other exciting water sports. If leisure sports are not your thing, it is also nice to sunbath under a parasol.

stories.title: Jukseong Catholic Church
stories.script: Jukseong Catholic Church  In a tranquil fishing village, a small catholic church can be seen where the village and the sea meet. Located in Jukseong-ri, Gijang-gun, this catholic church is called the“Jukseong Dream Catholic Church”. The building that was collapsed by Typhoon “Chaba” in 2016 was restored in 2017 and has been used as a tourist attraction and event venue ever since.  Jukseong Catholic Church is a famous filming location for a drama named “Dream”. At first, there were mostly drama fans who came to see the filming take place but it has become more famous as a wedding and social media photo spot thanks to hype through word-of-mouth describing its opportunities for beautiful pictures and its exotic scenery.  Normally, the inside is not open to the public but, since its restoration, you may look around on days the location is rented out for an exhibition or event. Since it is irregular, you have to look up the schedule in advance if you want to see the inside; otherwise, you must hope you're accidentally lucky.  The photo zone where everyone comes to take pictures is under the gray arch in front of the church gate, next to each of the doors. You can even take a picture with the sea in the background as long as you get the right angle from the arch so naturally people will be standing in long lines. The sea gets closer as you come around next to the church so many people take pictures of the sea here as well. Also, what is most famous about Jukseong Catholic Church is its view at night. Colorful lights flash towards the church so you can enjoy a wonderful view of the church in harmony with the night sea.  If you feel unsatisfied with just the Jukseong Catholic Church, take a slow walk towards the Jukseong Breakwater and the Jukseong Lighthouse. The street murals of “Duho Happiness Village” await you, hiding ever so slightly.

stories.title: Yonggungsa Temple
stories.script: Yonggungsa Temple The temple that has protected Yeongjongdo Island since the Unified Silla Dynasty City Tangible Cultural Property No. 15  According to records, Yonggungsa Temple was established by Won Hyo in the 10th year of King Munmu's reign (670) in Silla. It was then rebuilt by Heungseon Daewongun in the 5th year of King Cheoljong's reign (1854) during the Joseon Dynasty, until it got its current name. In front of the Yosachae House located at the entrance of Yonggungsa Temple, there is a plaque that reads “Yonggungsa,” which as written by Heungseon Daewon himself.  The Gwaneumjeon Hall of Yonggungsa Temple was built as a house with a gambrel roof whose side looks like a walking man, and on the pillars, there remain four verse couplets written by Haegang Kim Gyu-jin. It is said that there used to be a Gwanyin Statue carved with jade in the hall, but it was stolen during the Japanese occupation period. Now, the hall enshrines a bronze Gwanyin Statue.  In front of Yonggungsa Guesthouse, a zelkova tree estimated to be about 1,300 years old still stands. The Yonggungsa zelkova tree, which is Incheon City Monument No. 9, is an enormous, 20m-tall tree with a circumference of 5.63 m, and it is also known as the grandfather or grandmother tree.

stories.title: Cheongsapo Daritdol Observatory
stories.script: Cheongsapo Daritdol Observatory  A new attraction has emerged in Cheongsapo, famous for its mural filled street and grilled clams. It is called the “Daritdol Observatory”. It is also a work of art that embodies the blue dragon (or a big blue snake) that was regarded by the residents of Cheongsapo Village as a guardian since the early times.  If you travel to Cheongsapo by public transport or car, walk along the Daritdol Observatory information board to reach the “Daritdol Observatory Tourist Information Center”. From here, you may go up to the 3rd floor using the stairs or the elevator and walk directly to the entrance of the Daritdol Observatory along the railroad track.  If you want to choose a slightly different path, follow the small coastal cliff path on the right side of the information center. Nature here has remained undamaged with the cliffs and rocks intact, and here, you can take pictures with the Daritdol Observatory and the Busan Sea in the background. It is a narrow and steep path so be safe here.  The observatory’s operation hours are fixed. The hours are different in the summer and the winter so it is recommended that you check the hours in advance before your visit. Before entering the observatory, you need to wear a pair of special shoes over your shoes as to not damage the floor. Leave your food at the entrance for a while and focus on the scenery.  Walking toward the sea on a floor made of tempered glass, you can witness the waves crashing into the large rocks under the bridge, the ever-deepening color of the sea and sky, and the horizon far away. Then before you know it, you will be standing in the middle of a wide, blue ocean and finally, you will fully realize why it is called Cheongsapo, meaning blue sand and blue snake.

stories.title: Haeundae Beach
stories.script: Haeundae Beach  Haeundae Beach is the first name that probably pops up in your head when talking about the beaches of Busan. The beach became even more popular thanks to the film “Haeundae” and is one of the beaches in Busan that attracts the most visitors.  The name, “Haeundae”, comes from Choe Chiwon, one of the geniuses from the Silla Dynasty, who built a stone platform here and engraved “海雲臺 (Haeundae)” in Chinese characters. One of the pen names used by Choe Chiwon was “Haeun (海運)” but the character “Un” is different when it comes to the name and place. But, because they are both pronounced as “Haeun”, people theorize that one of those two names was created here. The letters known to have been engraved by Choe Chiwon are located on the southern rock face.  Haeundae Beach spans broadly between Dongbaekseom Island and the Dalmaji-gil cliffs, and thanks to the cool sea breeze that continues to blow, no matter how hot the day is, it has the advantage to letting you enjoy yourself in the water. Parks and trails are nicely set up around the beach making it great to go for a walk to warm up.  Haeundae is most known for its view at night; fancy hotels and high-rise apartments near the beach allows for an urban night view, which can be enjoyed from a variety of chic cafes nearby. It is visited by a grand number of people during the summer but there are many tourists wanting to take photos of their trip to Busan who come to Haeundae even during the winter, so it is a beach that is always filled with people all year long.

stories.title: Dongbaekseom
stories.script: Dongbaekseom  Named Dongbaekseom due to its abundance of Dongbaek Trees, it was transformed into a place for the 2005 APEC Summit Meeting in Busan and has since become a famous attraction where many world leaders have visited.  Dongbaekseom used to be a small island just off the coast of Haeundae however due to sedimentation, over a long period of time, became connected to the mainland. The island was also called “Darimiseom” for its resemblance to an iron. In “Come Back to Busan Port”, a song by Cho Yong-pil, there is a line that goes, “Spring came to Dongbaekseom, where flowers are”, and the Dongbaekseom in the lyrics is in fact this island itself. Every spring, it becomes a red island on top a blue sea due to its complete covereage in red flowers.  Dongbaekseom is where the “Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit Meeting” was held in November 2005. APEC is an international organization and summit of countries on the Pacific Rim that discuss a variety of topics such as economics and politics while solidifying their partnerships. When the summit was held in Busan, the status and details of the meeting were reported in real time around the world showcasing the amount of attention that the event had gotten globally.  No cars are allowed on Dongbaekseom. Instead, one can only walk throughout the island because while the yacht club side has flat paths, the Haeundae side is made of cliffs. Where the flat road meets the cliffs sits the “Nurimaru House,” the place where the APEC Summit Meeting was held. The inside of the meeting house still remains as it was so visitors can see with their own eyes the desks and chairs that were used by the leaders of the countries in attendance.  On the side where the Dongbaekseom lighthouse is, there is a stone on which the story of Choe Chiwon, who is known to have created the name “Haeundae,” and the name in Chinese characters are engraved. As you walk along the cliff path from the lighthouse you will see a short suspension bridge and a mermaid statue depicting the legend of Princess Hwangok who came for marriage from the kingdom of mermaids. The cliff section is narrow and has steep steps so make sure to pass safely and let other people pass by first, if needed.

stories.title: Gwangalli Beach
stories.script: Gwangalli Beach  A place to visit at least once, every time you're in Busan, to see the view of the night sea, Gwangalli Beach is where Gwangandaegyo is located. It is where the Busan International Fireworks Festival is held, which splendidly decorates the black sky and sea every fall.  Gwangalli Beach is named after its location in Gwangan-dong, which was created during division of administrative districts during the Japanese occupation period. Gwangan-dong means, in Chinese characters, “wide coast.” It is the region that was guarded by the naval forces of Gyeongsangjwa-do Province during the Joseon Dynasty. A long time ago, the sand at Gwangalli Beach used to break and disappear easily, so it was deemed unfit to swim in. So, instead, it was used as a shore where small fishing boats were tied up or a place people could go for a walk at.  When Gwangandaegyo was constructed by the sea in front of Gwangan-ri in 2003, the landscape of Gwangan-ri began to change. At the time of the construction, it was the longest bridge in Korea and people from all over the country gathered to see the beautiful sight of Gwangandaegyo reflecting the night sea with various colored lights that changed hourly. Fully living up to its wonderful nickname the “Diamond Bridge”, Gwangandaegyo and its bright lights that shined on soon became a landmark of Gwangan-ri.  Subsequently, a beach was formed there and the Fireworks Festival came around, making the area a tourist attraction with various facilities. Especially during the Fireworks Festival in the fall, the beach is full of people from the shore all the way to the roads so some people even camp out starting midday in order to secure the best spots.  If you are interested in seeing Gwangalli Beach from a different angle, you could try driving over Gwangandaegyo by car. Gwangandaegyo is a bridge made of two levels, each of which is one-way only. If you take your car, there is a toll fee so make sure to prepare it in advance.

stories.title: Oryukdo Skywalk
stories.script: Oryukdo Skywalk, a transparent glass bridge built on the cliff  Oryukdo Skywalk is situated at Seungdumal Hill, named for its saddle-like shape. At one point, Seungdumal Hill served as an area where patients of Hansen's disease resided. Nevertheless, in 2003 and 2007, the island was designated as a Marine Protected Area and National Scenic Spot No. 24, respectively. This recognition highlights the area's diverse marine animals and volcanic landforms, providing a window into Earth’s history.  The construction of the Oryukdo Skywalk began in September 2012, and was officially opened in October 2013 under the theme of “Walking over the Sky.” This 15-meter glass bridge comprises 24 glass plates built on the edge of 35-meter-high coastal cliffs, featuring unique rock formations. Additionally, the glass bottom is specially produced and coated with a bulletproof film to ensure safety.  It's important to note that to enjoy the skywalk, visitors must wear overshoes while walking on the tempered glass bridge. While admission is free, items such as walking sticks, umbrellas, parasols, and selfie sticks are prohibited inside to prevent any actions that could cause damage to the ecosystems of Oryukdo Island and its surrounding marine sanctuaries. Looking from the skywalk bridge, visitors may notice the islands appearing overlapped, offering glimpses of the lighthouses on Usakdo Island, Suriseom Island, and Deungdaeseom Island. On the opposite side, visitors can observe Igidae Coastal Trail and even Haeundae in the distance.

stories.title: Overview of Oryukdo Island
stories.script: Oryukdo Island, a changeable island from different time  There is a skywalk located at the end of Igidae Natural Park in Nam-gu, Busan, offering a view of Oryukdo Island. It serves as the starting point of Haeparang-gil, a path leading to the Unification Observatory Tower in Goseong-gun, Gangwon-do. visitors can reach there by bus or car, and transfer to a small cruise ship docked at the pier for a closer exploration of the island.  The rocky Oryudo was formed nearly 80 million years ago, towards the end of the Cretaceous period in the Mesozoic Era. Approximately 120,000 years ago, rising sea levels transformed it into an island. Over time, through the effects of the Ice Age, erosion, and weathering, it evolved into the current Oryukdo.  Oryudo Island refers to a cluster of rocky islands off the southern coast of Busan. Depending on the viewpoint and time of observation, the number of islands visible may vary. This variability in sight led to the name Oryukdo, which literally translates to five or six islands. According to the Sancheonjo of Dongnaebuji, a historical record mentions seeing six islands from the east and five islands from the west. Hence, the island was named Oryukdo, composed of Bangpaeseom Island, Solseom Island, Suriseom Island, Songgotseom Island, Gulseom Island, and Deungdaeseom Island in order of their proximity to the mainland. During low tide, the lower portions of Bangpaeseom Island and Solseom Island nearly connect, creating an appearance of a single island known as Usakdo, which reverts to two distinct islands during high tide.

stories.title: Taejongdae
stories.script: Taejongdae  King Taejong Muyeol of Silla who unified the three states of the Korean Peninsula stopped here to rest and gazed into the sea during his tour of the country. From that point on the place became known as “Taejongdae”. After many years later, Taejong, the 3rd king of the Joseon Dynasty, also visited Taejongdae on his tour around the country.  What views did Taejongdae present to grab the attention of the kings? The Taejongdae we see today is a sedimentary rock topography originally formed between about 80 to 100 million years ago. This is known as the Cretaceous period of the Mesozoic Era, and most of the uniquely shaped rocks and cliffs near the Taejongdae Lighthouse were created during this period and have survived to this day.  As land, crashed onto and cut away by waves, experienced numerous volcanic activities and earthquakes, it is uplifted (rise of the land in a specific region over the surrounding area due to natural causes), and since the degree and period of the cuts vary, a flat, stair-shaped topography appears. We call this type of land a “coastal terrace.”  Near the coastal terrace, we find smooth-surfaced bedrocks that were carved by waves, and thus, have a gradual incline. We call this “wave-cut platform” and, since it is carved with a slope towards the sea, we may deduce that it has been affected by the waves. Such topography, which exists in Busan from Taejongdae to Dongsam-dong, was probably quite a marvelous sight to behold even to the eyes of King Taejong Muyeol of Silla and King Taejong of Joseon.  To see the unique topography of Taejongdae, you need to go from the entrance to either the observatory or the lighthouse. You can get to the destination more comfortably by riding the Danubi Train. If you wish to see Taejongdae from a different angle, you may go down and board a cruise ship to enjoy the wonderful sight. In the evening, you may enter by car, with a fee, or walk inside for free.

stories.title: Songdo Beach
stories.script: Songdo Beach  Songdo Beach of Busan has everything you want from things to see, things to eat and things to play with. It especially attracts many visitors since the beach offers views of Busan from the land, sea, and sky.  The Marine Cable Car offers the sky view of Busan at Songdo Beach. It goes back and forth between the building in front of Songnim Park and Amnam Park, travels over the sea and presents a view of Geobukseom Island, Namhangdaegyo Bridge, Haeparang-gil and Sinseondae Cliff. From large fishing boats to motor boats for leisure sports, you can see a variety of ships that depart from the Port of Busan and float along the sea in front of Songdo.  The view from the sea can be enjoyed from the Skywalk on Geobukseom Island. Geobukseom  Island is named for its resemblance to a turtle but it is also called Songdo because of the pine trees that populate the island. It is connected to the mainland through the cloud trail. If you walk along the trail and enter Geobukseom Island, you reach the entrance to the Skywalk. Here, you may look around with your shoes on, and if you look up at the sky from the Skywalk, you will see the cable car pass right above you.  The most popular attraction on land is, of course, the sandy beach. Looking at Geobukseom Island, the Cable Cars and the blue sea of Busan from the beach, you are due for a great and exciting time of fun. At night, it is possible to enjoy the beautiful sea in harmony with the bright lights emitted by the Cable Cars and large ships.

stories.title: Dadaepo Beach
stories.script: Dadaepo Beach  “Dadaepo,” one of the oldest names in Busan, is located where Nakdonggang and the South Sea meet. In 『Samguk Sagi (historical record of the Three Kingdoms of Korea: Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla)』, there appears a place named “Dapdal”, and this is presumed to refer to “Dadae” of Dadaepo. During a similar period, a book named 『Nihongi』 revealed the names of places such as “Dadara” or “Dadarajin” and it is assumed that these words eventually evolved into “Dadae”.  Japanese invaders frequently appeared in this area so, during the Joseon Period, a military camp was installed here to make it one of the 7 military zones that protected the Gyeongsangjwa-do Province. This is also the ground for the historic “Battle of Dadaepo”, which was one of the earliest battles that took place during the Japanese invasion of 1592 along with the Battle of Busanjin. Today, it has become a peaceful and relaxing coast thanks to its beach and Sunset Fountain of Dreams.  You can get to the beach and park by getting off at Dadaepo Beach Station (Morundae Station), the final stop of Busan Subway Line 1. Known as the “Fantastic Music Foundation”, the Dadaepo Sunset Fountain of Dreams is located inside the beach park.  Operating from April to October of every year, the Sunset Fountain of Dreams first opened in 2010. The first music fountain installed in Busan, it is a beautiful fountain that shoots streams of water upward in sync to the music and lighting. Thanks to its enormous size and height, it was listed as the “world's largest ground fountain” by the Guinness World Records in 2010.  As the name suggests, the Sunset Fountain holds music performances in the evening for about 20 minutes, and, since the hours of operation and frequencies vary depending on the season and date, we recommend you to check the times in advance. Music performances are popular even on weekdays and the seats are on a first-come, first-served basis in an open space so you need to be there early in order to get good seats.  If you post a story and song request in advance onto the Saha-gu District Office website, you may be able to see the music fountain dancing to the song you want. It's a great opportunity to do something special for your loved one or for families to make long-lasting memories.

stories.title: Jangnimpogu
stories.script: Jangnimpogu  Located near the end of Nakdonggang, Jangnimpogu used to be a small port from which the village residents would go out to sea on small boats or fishing vessels to farm laver or to catch marine products such as freshwater eels, gizzards, flounders and anything else that could be seen in the sea and river which then they sold at the marketplaces. “Jangnim Laver” was famously known as the best laver in Busan.  However, since the construction of the Nakdonggang Estuary Bank in 1987, a large-scale reclamation took place to establish an industrial complex, which eventually led to the disappearance of the fish, fisheries and, subsequently, the fishermen as well. Yongsinje, a ritual to Yongsin, the guardian of the fishing villages, was discontinued as well. In particular, as the surrounding region was designated as 5 different types of cultural heritage protection areas including the ecosystem preservation protection area and national resource cultural heritage protection area, development was restricted so even the factories that had been residing in the industrial complex also relocated to other areas, leading to a rapid decline of Jangnimpogu.  Fading even from the minds of the citizens of Busan, Jangnimpogu began a gradual transformation through the “Jangnimpogu Enhancement Project” by the Saha-gu District Office, which started in 2012. The port that once featured rusty containers and old fishing boats has become neatly organized with colorfully decorated containers and repaired boats.  People who had once come here by chance in the past, visit again to re-encounter the unique scenes from the pictures they had taken, and these exotic images attract others, turning today's Jangnimpogu into a famous photo zone. It also has the nickname “Bunetia” as some say that pictures taken here look like they are from Venetia, Italy. If you are looking for an exotic attraction in Busan, how about Jangnimpogu and its diverse array of colors?

stories.title: Imdang-dong Catholic Church
stories.script: Imdang-dong Catholic Church  Imdang-dong Catholic Church is a historic Gothic architecture featuring the pointed peak of the bell tower, roof ornaments, and arch-shaped windows. Its history began in 1921 when Father Cheol-yeon Francisco Lee built a church in Geumgwang-ri in Gangneung. The church had to move around several times, going through the Japanese colonial rule and the Korean War, until it finally settled in its current location thanks to the missionaries of the Missionary Society of Saint Columban. Many churches have been established in the Yeongdong region, centering on Gangneung's oldest church.  Stepping into the church, the first thing you will notice is the domed ceiling and beautiful stained glass window. From the birth to the death and resurrection of Christ, stories in the Bible are depicted in colors that luminously glow when the sun shines through.   Take a closer look at the walls, ceiling, and shape and ornaments of the altar. It’s not something you commonly see in an ordinary Catholic church. The unique interior decorations and exterior retain their original appearance, and it has been designated as Registered Cultural Property No. 457 of the Modern Cultural Heritage of Korea.

stories.title: Cheoneunsa Temple, Gurye
stories.script: Cheoneunsa Temple, Gurye  Cheoneunsa, which is regarded as a temple with one of the most beautiful sceneries in the Jirisan Mountain area, has become a famous filming site after it appeared in various scenes of 〈Mr. Sunshine〉. Now, let's pay the admission fee and enter to take a look around the temple.  To get into the temple, the first place you have to pass is “Suhongru.” In the drama, it is where Ae-shin and Hee-sung bid the last farewell. The tower erected on the stone bridge looks, in a way, like a watchtower on a fortress gate or a pavilion.
