Regardless, it is a small tower known for its beautiful reflection on the water during sunrises and sunsets. If you wish to shoot a video like a scene from a drama, try it on the stone bridge located behind Suhongru.  Upon entering through Cheonwangmun past Suhongru, you get to the place where Dong-mae tried to find the traces of Ae-shin in the same drama. If you wish to reenact the scene in which Sacheonwang inside Cheonwangmun Gate seemed as if they are watching Dong-mae, sit by the entrance and look towards the inside. It looks just like the scene in the drama, doesn't it?  Once you enter through Sacheonwangmun, you will see Bojeru where a righteous army once fought against Japanese soldiers on the day of the 49 Jae ritual of the late Go Sa-hong. Here, you may be reminded of the scene in which Ae-shin's shadow appeared on the roof of Bojeru. Unfortunately, it is strictly prohibited to climb up onto the roof so please enjoy the simple beauty of Bojeru from the ground.  On the opposite side of Bojeru, there is Geukrakbojeon Hall where the ancestral tablets of Ae-shin's parents are enshrined in the drama. Here, Dong-mae famously uttered,”I won't be able to be with you, will I?” , which created one of the most memorable scenes from the drama. The painting Dong-mae was looking at is known as the “painting of Tripitaka Bodhisattva of Cheoneunsa Temple, Gurye,” which is designated as Treasure No. 1888. I know you would also like to reenact the famous scene here as well but, right now, the place is being used for religious ceremonies so make sure to keep quiet while you are here.  What did you think of Cheoneunsa where a number of memorable scenes from Mr. Sunshine were filmed? If you wish you check out Cheoneunsa for a little while longer, you may RSVP and participate in a temple stay, which we recommend for those of you who would like to feel the lingering impression of the drama.

stories.title: Kyungdong Catholic Church, Mokpo
stories.script: 8. Kyungdong Catholic Church, Mokpo  Kyungdong Catholic Church was designated as Mokpo’s Local Heritage No. 22 in 2012 and is very close to the Oriental Development Company Mokpo Branch. Constructed in 1953, Kyungdong Catholic Church carried out a remodeling project in 1966 due to a ground subsidence of the front of the building and was newly renovated to the appearance we see today. However, all of the other sections have remained the same since the time of the original construction.  The first priest of this church was Father Kim Seong-hwan Victorio. He was the first one to introduce Legio Mariae to the Korean church in 1953, and organized “Praesidium, Refuge of Sinners.” Legio Mariae, or the Legion of Mary, is a church-authorized organization of believers that was formed to actively participate in the church's ceaseless fight against evil forces. Members of the organization are said to have actively engaged in visiting the believers’ homes as well as in carrying out missionary work since the beginning.

stories.title: Mokpo Modern History Museum I and II
stories.audioTitle: Mokpo Modern History Museum I and II
stories.script: Mokpo Modern History Museum I and II  Mokpo Modern History Museum, located in Yudal-dong, Mokpo-si, Jeollanam-do, is the oldest building in Mokpo and was built as a consulate after Mokpo Port opened in 1897 and the Mokpo Japanese Consulate was established in 1898. Before 2014, the building of the Oriental Development Company Mokpo Branch was the main building but, now, the old Mokpo Japanese Consulate, which is located not too far from the Oriental Development Company Mokpo Branch building, is used as the main building. The style of the building is neoclassicism and it still preserves much of the appearance of the time it was constructed so it has a high historical and architectural value related to the opening of Mokpo port. Because of this, it was designated and is managed as National Historic Site No. 289.  The site on which Modern History Museum II is located was where the Oriental Development Company existed during the Japanese occupation period and, also, where the Military Police of the Mokpo 3rd Naval Sector Command was stationed during the May 18 Democratization Movement in 1980. Chun Doo-hwan’s New Military Regime, who had suppressed the resistance by military force, later made arrests of many involved in the democratization movement. Important figures of the movement in the Mokpo area who were arrested were detained here in the guardhouse of the Military Police after being forced to confess through beatings and tortures at the Mokpo branch of the security forces.  The museum exhibits symbolic materials related to the opening of Mokpo Port, the history of modern Joseon and the Japanese’ false ambition and exploitation during the occupation period as well as a vault used by the Oriental Development Company. The second floor is also used as an exhibition hall. Mostly, photo exhibits of materials from the modern era are planned and displayed.

stories.title: Seongok Memorial Hall and Lee Hun-dong Garden
stories.audioTitle: 6. Seongok Memorial Hall and Lee Hun-dong Garden
stories.script: 6. Seongok Memorial Hall and Lee Hun-dong Garden  Situated at the foot of Yudalsan Mountain in Mokpo, Seongok Memorial Hall is a cultural space established in 2004 by the children of Mr. Seongok Lee Hun-dong, the founder of Joseon Naehwa and the publisher of Chonnam Ilbo, in commemoration of Mr. Lee.  The memorial exhibits not only potteries but also the works and Korean paintings of contemporary calligraphy masters that Seongok had diligently collected all his life. In the exhibition room, visitors may enjoy over 80 pieces of artworks including the landscape painting plaque of Gongjae Yun Duseo, Yeseo Igokbyeong of Chusa Gim Jeong-hui, Mukrando Sipgokbyeong of Seokpa Yi Ha-eung, Palgok Baeknapbyeong of Uijae Heo Baek-ryeon, and a landscape scroll of Liu Songnian, a painter from the Southern Song Dynasty in China. In addition, Buncheong ware kettles, long-necked jars, white porcelain lamp support and many other earthenwares are on display. Today, the memorial serves as an artistic and cultural shelter for both Mokpo locals and tourists who visit the city.  Lee Hun-dong Garden is a Japanese-style garden established by a Japanese person (Uchidani Manppei) in the 1930s. After the Liberation, a congressman from Haenam named Park Gi-bae owned the facility and, later, it was purchased by Lee Hun-dong in the 1950s who still owns it today. Though there have been slight changes over the 60 years, the characteristics of a Japanese garden are still well preserved. Inside the building that boasts a smooth appearance, contemporary artworks collected by Mr. Lee and his children are on display. The largest private garden in the Honam region, it consists of the entrance garden, an inner garden, a forest and stream garden and a back garden, and is famous as a filming site of the drama, Rustic Period.  There are a five-story and a seven-story Japanese-style stone pagodas inside, and there are also a greater number of Japanese plant species. However, the garden itself was built in the Korean Seowon style, and a narrow stream is made to flow through the woods.

stories.title: National Route 1 and 2 Starting Point Monument
stories.audioTitle: 5. National Route 1 and 2 Starting Point Monument
stories.script: 5. National Route 1 and 2 Starting Point Monument  The National Route 1 and 2 Starting Point Monument is located on the right side of the path leading up to Mokpo Modern History Museum I. Mokpo is the starting point of Route 1, which is the first-ever modern road network of Korea. Route 1, which began its construction in 1906 and opened in 1911, is a 939.1km section that runs from Mokpo to Sinuiju in P'yonganbuk-do Province, North Korea. In commemoration of the route, there is a monument standing next to Yudalsan Post Office.  When Mokpodaegyo Bridge was opened in 2012, the starting point of Route 1 was changed to Gohado Island in Chungmu-dong, the last stop on Mokpodaegyo, in 2013 and the length also increased to 943.37km. As a result, the city of Mokpo revised the existing monument that said, “National Route 1 and 2 Starting Point”, to “National Route 1 and 2 Starting Point Monument”.  Behind the monument, you see a red building that had long been used as the Japanese consulate. It was first constructed in 1897 when the Mokpo Port opened. As international relations between Korea and Japan changed over time, the purpose of the building also changed to Mokpo City Hall and Mokpo City Library. For its architectural value and historical significance when considered together with the opening of Mokpo Port, it was designated as a National Historic Site in 1981. If you wish to check out the starting point of the national route and port of Mokpo, you can stop by the National Route 1 and 2 Starting Point Monument.   Guide on the change of the National Route 1 and 2 Starting Point The starting point of National Route 1 and 2 was changed as follows, and it has been decided that the word 'Monument' is to be engraved in the sign stone installed here; marking the starting point to commemorate the beginning of National Route 1 and 2 forever.  Change of Route 1 starting point (February 28, 2013) 11-beonji, Daeui-dong 2-ga, Mokpo→Dal-dong, Mokpo (Gohado)  Change of Route 2 starting point (August 25, 2001) 11-beonji, Daeui-dong 2-ga, Mokpo→Jangsan-myeon, Sinan-gun, Jeollanam-do  May 1, 2013 Mayor of Mokpo

stories.title: Dongbonwonsa Temple, Mokpo (Ogeori Culture Center)
stories.script: 12. Dongbonwonsa Temple, Mokpo (Ogeori Culture Center)  Ogeori Culture Center used to be known as Dongbonwonsa. The building was first established as the Mokpo Branch of Dongbonwonsa, which was the first-ever Japanese Buddhist temple built in Mokpo after the opening of the port in 1897. Its official name is “Jinjong Daegokpa Dongbonwonsa.” The Dongbonwonsa Mokpo Branch was constructed in 1898, and was authorized to establish Mokpo Simsang High School. For some time, it was also operated officially as a primary school for Japanese students, the first of its kind in Mokpo.  Initially, a mission was installed close to the Japanese consulate site near the open port, and was relocated to the current location in 1904.. Though this was somewhat away from the open port area where the Japanese people lived at the time, it was located on the border between the Joseon and Japanese districts, which made it a great location for a temple to be built in. It was controlled by Jeong Gwang-san after the Liberation and, starting in 1957, it was used as the Mokpo Jungang Church, which makes it unique in the sense that it is a church that turned into a temple.  Mokpo Jungang Church was a place where conscientious religious leaders who were concerned about the country's situation frequently met since the days of the Yusin Dictatorship. During the period of the May 18 Democratization Movement, the church constantly hosted leadership meetings for the Democratization Protest Committee of the Mokpo citizens. Protestant leaders gathered here to denounce the new military regime of Chun Doo-hwan that had committed the Gwangju massacre and adopt the resolution asserting, “The cost of blood cannot be bought on credit. Chun Doo-hwan shall resign immediately.” This was a turning point for many of the Protestant clergymen in Mokpo to join the democratization movement after the 25th.  It became Registered Cultural Heritage No. 340 in 2007 and, since 2010, it changed its name to Ogeori Culture Center to be utilized as a place for various cultural events and exhibits. In the front yard of the building, you can find a monument letting the visitors know that it is a historical site related to the May 18 Democratization Movement.

stories.title: Yudalsan Mountain
stories.script: Yudalsan Mountain  The 228m-tall Yudalsan Mountain spans across Yudal-dong, Mogwon-dong and Jukgyo-dong of Mokpo, Jeollanam-do. Listed as a spot that offers one of the eight places to offer the best views of Mokpo, it is the pride and symbol of Mokpo. It is also known as the spiritual mountain of the city. From the peak, you can take in a view of Dadohae and the city of Mokpo, and, since the old times, it has had the nickname of “Gaegolsan” of Honam for its resemblance to a vigorous folding screen despite being a small mountain. There are Ildeungbawi, Ideungbawi, Samdeungbawi Rocks and Dalseongsa Temple, and it is also the habitat of Kalkora mimosa.  Mokpo Sculpture Garden, the first of its kind in Korea, was established at the entrance of Yudalsan Mountain and currently exhibits 100 sculptural works. At night, lights are turned on at each peak from the top of Yudalsan to show off a wonderful nightscape. On clear nights, you can check out the magnificent view yourself. Also, there is a monument of 〈Tears of Mokpo〉, a song by singer Lee Nang-young, and the statue of Admiral Yi Sun-sin.  In April, the Yudalsan Flower Festival attracts a lot of visitors. The view of Dadohae from the top of Yudalsan is magnificent. Dadohae seen from the center of Mokpo is beautiful, and many people visit Yudalsan Nakjodae. In addition, there are the Omokdae, exhibition hall, the orchid park, and the specific wild plant garden to provide shelters and attractions for those who visit.

stories.title: Yudalsan Mountain: Sculpture Park
stories.script: Yudalsan Mountain: Sculpture Park  The first-ever outdoor sculpture park in Korea  Korea in 1980 suffered and sacrificed too much for democratization. And, in 1982, the government established the first-ever outdoor sculpture park in Korea at Yudalsan, Mokpo located at the end of Honam region. At that time, people who were living tough lives lived like slash-and-burn farmers but the government relocated them to permanent rental houses and built a sculpture park regardless of the city's intentions. This outdoor Yudalsan Sculpture Park in Mokpo is a beautiful resting place with a great view of the city but its beginning was as shabby as it gets. Trees were planted sparsely in an empty plain and about 40 works of famous Korean sculptors were exhibited few and far between so people wondered if this could be a legitimate sculpture park. However, as nearly four decades of time passed by, it became arguably one of the most outstanding sculpture parks in the country. It not only serves to purify the emotions of the Mokpo citizens much like an oxygen tank but also plays a big role in attracting tourists from other regions. Even if you just climb up to the midpoint of the park, you will be able to see downtown Mokpo, the flowing Yeongsangang River, as well as the Jeollanam-do Provincial Office at the same time so don’t you think this is one of the best tourist attractions? In particular, there are 41 excellent works of art, various native wildflowers as well as crape myrtles on the central aisle of the park, which are also known as tickling trees. Also, the street trees are not red crape myrtles that we typically see on streets. Instead, they are what's called Cheollihyang, which got its name because it has the scent that travels a thousand miles, attracting the footsteps of the tourists. Most common flowers bloom in spring and their fruits are harvested in fall but Cheollihyang blossoms around Chuseok. Every late September, the scent of Cheollihyang pauses the people passing by at Yudalsan Sculpture Park. As you can see, Yudalsan Sculpture Park forms harmony between sculptures and trees, and features wonderful artworks with the themes of nature, culture and sculpture, all of which symbolizes the marine-centered city of Mokpo. Inside the park, there is also an outdoor music hall, a fountain, rest areas, and Gwaneumsa Temple as well as strange, bizarre-looking rocks of the mountain’s sacred peaks, which wear different colors every season. All of these form a great harmony and create beautiful memories for those who visit the park. Now, take your time and enjoy this wonderful space!

stories.title: Yudalsan Mountain: Yudalsan Dulle-gil
stories.script: Yudalsan Mountain: Yudalsan Dulle-gil  Heal along the Yudalsan Dulle-gil  What comes to your mind when you think of Mokpo? For Mokpo citizens, it is Yudalsan. It is not an exaggeration to say that Yudalsan is the symbol of Mokpo and the soul of the locals from Mokpo whether it be from the lyrics of a school song or popular music. From the old days, Yudalsan was also known as “Yeongdalsan”as people believed it was where souls passed through. It is a rocky mountain of 228m in altitude but is not so rugged. The themed Yudalsan Dulle-gil has become a healing route in the center of a city for both Mokpo locals and tourists. Then, let us introduce to you a few of the 7 courses in which you can find harmony between the city and nature.  The first course starts at the Yudalsan parking lot near Nojeokbong Peak and continues through – Daehangnu – Dalseonggak – Song Monument of Lee Nan-yeong – Yuseongak – Madangbawi – Ildeungbawi – Soyojeong – Ideungbawi – and finally to the Sculpture Park. This is an appealing route on which you can purify yourself and be healed while enjoying the strange-shaped rocks of Yudalsan, beautiful sceneries of Dadohae, and downtown Mokpo all at a single glance from the top of Ildeungbawi Rock.  The second route is the one-and-a-half-hour course that is the most accessible and least burdensome. You begin from the Yudalsan parking lot near Nojeokbong, make a brief stop in front of the statue of Admiral Yi Sun-sin to be reminded of his bravery during the Japanese invasion of 1592 and then stand on top of Daehangnu to look at the sea in front of Mokpo and Samhakdo Island. According to a sad legend, Samhakdo became an island when three young women who loved a Yudalsan general turned into cranes and eventually fell into the sea. Today, the island is becoming a popular tourist attraction of Mokpo thanks to Samhakdo Cruise and Harbor Pocha. Then, move to the Song Monument of Lee Nan-yeong who was a great singer from Mokpo, and recite the 〈Tears of Mokpo〉, which sings about the sorrow of the city during the Japanese occupation period as well as Admiral Yi Sun-sin. “A boatman's song is faintly heard...” As you wipe the sweat off your forehead and walk past Dalseonggak, you will pass through a fragrant forest where you will be able to slowly recover your breath. Then, you will find Dalseongsa, a temple that is known to have been built by Seonsa No Dae-Ryeon in 1913. The Kṣitigarbha Triad Statue, which is Treasure No. 2011, provides hope for the footsteps of passers-by. By the time when the refreshing sea breeze brushes past the tip of your nose, you will find a wild plant garden where you can encounter many of the wild flower species of Korea. A wild flower complex is operated throughout the year to stimulate the eyes and hearts of those who visit the Dulle-gil. In addition to wild flowers, there are over 500 different species of plants inhabiting Yudalsan. Oak trees and chrysanthemum trees form colonies, and Hyun poplars, glossy-leaf paper plants, loquats and horned hollies will also welcome you.  At the end of the path of narrowleaf firethorns, which is a foreign species, you will find the Sculpture Park. Established in the 1980s as the first-ever outdoor sculpture park in the country, it exhibits works of prominent Korean and international artists. While looking at the sculpted artworks with the themes of taste, chicness, and the sea, the view of downtown Mokpo also unfolds before your eyes. On Yudalsan Dulle-gil, even the gasps and short breaths of those who climb up and down the mountain sound pleasant. As you walk along the path immersed in the scents of trees, earth and sea, you will realize that there is a marine cable car flying above your head, another unique scenery you cannot easily see in other areas. Now, move your steps quickly to head to the Fisherman's Hill, which was established in 1995 to soothe the souls of fishermen who lived their entire lives out at sea, to pay tribute to the spirits of fishermen who pioneered the waters to provide for the rest of the citizens.  Yudalsan Dulle-gil has a variety of courses thanks to many paths that branch out. It is 8.37km long in total and takes about 3 hours 40 minutes on foot but the time and course can be chosen and adjusted according to individuals' preferences. Dulle-gil is accessible from anywhere through Ilju Road and enables anyone to enjoy a safe hike. It is a trekking course so people of all ages and genders may walk in comfortable clothes and shoes, another reason that Yudalsan Dulle-gil is appealing. Throughout the Dulle-gil, there are signposts, rest areas and sports facilities where you may engage in simple stretching and exercises so you may heal and promote health at the same time. Now, enjoy the sea breeze and the scent of the forest to be healed on the Yudalsan Dulle-gil!

stories.title: 210. Yudalsan Mountain: Nakjodae
stories.script: Yudalsan Mountain: Nakjodae  Where the sunset is the most beautiful  Yudalsan is the final peak of Noryeong Mountains located at the southwestern tip leading to Dadohae. It is the symbol of Mokpo and Yudalsan Nujeong is a precious rest area for the citizens. Nujeong is a term that combines Nu, which means a tower, and Jeong, which means a pavilion built in a place with a great landscape. It is one of the structures utilized as a place for spiritual training, enjoying of art in nature, and quiet appreciation of the surroundings.  Nakjodae is one of the 6 Nujeong installed on the Yudalsan ridge way and, because it is seated at a great location for you to view the scenery of Dadohae, you may easily enjoy the nightscape of Gohado Island lined up lengthily over the sea as well as the sunset. It is popularly used as a rest area for Mokpo locals thanks to its convenient accessibility but it is also a famous attraction of Yudalsan that greets a countless number of tourists every year.  Everyone standing on Nakjodae, could you please look at the signboard? Don't you feel a force from the writing? The signboard of Nakjodae is Yeoseoche, also known as a clerical script, and is the work of Yucheon Seo Jong-gyeon, an influential figure in Mokpo calligraphy. It is interesting to note that the term, Yeoseoche, means a simple calligraphic style for even slaves to be able to understand. As long as one knows Chinese characters, he or she will be able to comprehend this style of writing.  Now, enjoy your much-needed rest before a beautiful scenery of the coast offered by Nakjodae of Yudalsan.

stories.title: Yudalsan Mountain: Fisherman's Hill
stories.script: Yudalsan Mountain: Fisherman's Hill  A beloved trail for Mokpo citizens  Fisherman's Hill is the place where people pray for abundance and full load of fish for fishermen who are central figures of Mokpo's local economy. It is also a place to pay tribute to their spirits. It is equipped with various facilities and a great view of Dadohae, which makes it a popular date spot and walking trail for Mokpo citizens.  The beautiful gardening of the Fisherman's Hill was established as an eco-friendly hill with themes. Water is made to flow year-round in the pond through, for instance, a nightscape program fountain, and the hiking course is also well-organized for people to walk comfortably. Did you happen to see a mineral spring by the entrance that looks like a ship? Have a cup of cool water here and take your time to enjoy the Fisherman's Hill! Throughout the hill, there are also several statues and poetry monuments in the shape of boats including the Fisherman statue, which expresses the joys and sorrows of fishermen, and a monument on which 〈Sea〉, a poem by Kim Ji-ha, is carved. It would be fun to look for these monuments. On the trail, a fountain stands at a location from which Ideungbawi Rock of Yudalsan is seen. At night, the fountain wears colorful lights to present a fantastic nightscape featuring Mokpodaegyo Bridge and Gohado. As you walk up the stone path past the fountain, you will reach a rest area in the midst of a green forest so make sure to stop by if you get a bit tired from walking. Lastly, you can also check out the Fisherman's statue, which is installed at the top of the Fisherman's Hill, and a waterfall. Though the volume of water is not great, the waterfall still cools the hot and humid weather. Enjoy the Fisherman's Hill whenever you want!

stories.title: Gatbawi Culture Town
stories.script: Gatbawi Culture Town  Gatbawi Culture Town is one of the most notable cultural spaces of Mokpo and is located near Gatbawi Rock, which is designated as Natural Monument No. 500. It is also a popular driving route with an outstanding view at night. You may immerse yourself into the fragrance of culture and arts all day long here through a tour of the National Maritime Museum, Culture & Arts Center, Natural History Museum, Literary History Hall, Ceramic Livingware Museum, Mokpo Literature Museum, Namnong Memorial Hall, etc., all of which are located at the foot of Ibamsan Mountain that clearly exposes its rocks. Also, you may walk along the Ibamsan dulle-gil and enjoy the scenery of the sea in front of Mokpo.  Gatbawi is made of tuff, which is created by deposited volcanic ashes in the past, and the particles of tuff are visibly large even to human eyes. Gatbawi has been formed over a long period of time through erosion by waves and chemical weathering by salt. A combination of the shape of gat, or a Korean traditional hat for men, on top of the rock and a weathering pit shown below results in a beautiful topography that resembles a man wearing a gat. The original shape of Gatbawi continues to change little by little due to humidity and sunlight. Gatbawi's surroundings display a typical eroded topography and also feature developed sea cliffs, sea notches, wave-cut terraces and tafonis, which are highly likely to turn into a similar form as Gatbawi some day. A sea pedestrian walk is installed in front of Gatbawi so you can conveniently enjoy the work of art created by mother nature. About a ten-minute walk also gets you to the Peace Square  where you can find a seat in the seaside park and enjoy the “Dancing Sea Fountain,” a combination of a fountain, lights and music. A cultural space where families and lovers may spend great time together with the cool sea breeze and fantastic music. This is the “Gatbawi Culture Town”of Mokpo.

stories.title: Chungmugong Yi Historic Site in Gohado Island
stories.audioTitle: Chungmugong Yi Historic Site in Gohado Island
stories.script: Chungmugong Yi Historic Site in Gohado Island  It is the place where Admiral Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin stayed from October till March of the following year during the Jeongyu Wars in the 30th year of King Seonjo's reign in the Joseon Dynasty; storing military provisions and supplies to get ready for the war. Here, we may find the traces of Admiral Yi. It was designated as Historic Site No. 113 in 1963 and continues to be maintained under the name we know today. The fortress here was built by stones to divide the interior and the exterior and, to collect war funds, 1 to 3 seok of grains were taxed from ships passing through, which led to 10,000 seok of military provisions collected in just 10 days. Weapons and ships for the war are also said to have been manufactured here.  Gohado is a small island located about 2km to the southwest of Mokpo, and its name first appeared in 《Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam》. 《Nanjung Ilgi》calls it Bohwado, and, on the Chungmugong Yi Monument in Gohado (Jeollanam-do Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 39), it is engraved as Gohwado.  There was a shrine called Mochunggak in Gohwado and, here, the Chungmugong Yi Monument is enshrined. It was installed by Yi Bong-sang, the 5th descendant of Chungmugong, in 1722 and Nam Gu-man came up with the words of the inscription while Jo Tae-gu actually inscribed them. Although gunshot marks created by Japanese soldiers during the occupation era exist on the body of the monument, it is almost in perfect condition. It was once thrown away and left neglected on a hill nearby during the occupation period but was installed at the current location again post Liberation.

stories.title: Gohado Island: Yongmeori and Coastal Deck
stories.audioTitle: Gohado Island: Yongmeori and Coastal Deck
stories.script: Gohado Island: Yongmeori and Coastal Deck  The rocky mountain lined up like a wide folding screen in front of Mokpo is known as Yongoreum-gil or Byeongpungsan Mountain. As you walk along Yongoreum-gil, you will run into several photo spots and, at the end of the road, you will be able to find Yongmeori. Here, take a photo for a special memory of your Mokpo trip. By the time your legs ache from the walk along Yongoreum-gil, you will reach Gohado Observatory, which is made of piling 13 Panokseon in the form of a grid. Why do you think it was built this way? This is because the structure, which is utilized for education and tourism, pays tribute to the spirit of Admiral Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin who led the Battle of Myeongnyang to victory with just 13 Panokseon and stayed in Gohado for 106 days to brace up for battle. The observatory is a perfect place to enjoy the view of Mokpo. Ongeum-dong seen on the other side is shown as a beautiful, heartwarming neighborhood insomuch that there is no explanation needed on why it is named Ongeum. If you walk out of the observatory and towards a path leading to the sea, it connects to the coastal deck, which was first opened to Mokpo citizens in November 2019. The path from Gohado Observatory to Yongmeori is an easy, 1km course. Sea water splashes beneath the coastal deck, and there are sections made of transparent glass floor here and there, which gives you a fun experience. Also, you may enjoy a landscape that you will never be able to see when hiking up a mountain. That my friends is none other than sea cliffs. A sea cliff, or Haesigae in Korean, refers to a precipice formed on a coast by the waves' erosion and weathering effects. In areas that are protruded from a coast where waves are strong, erosion proceeds actively and you can see rocks that are cut away. It is not a high cliff but still a magnificent scenery. The way each cliff is cut is different so it would be fun and meaningful to observe the cliffs one by one as you walk. You can also see that seaweed grows at the point where the water and rocks meet. In particular, Australian laurels, which are often gifted as congratulatory plants, are found in between the rocks and they are huge unlike their flowerpot counterparts.  If you have reached the end of the deck, you may now walk up the ridge of Yongoreum-gil towards Yongmeori. This is a secret but there is a seriously steep slope on the way down from the observatory to the coastal deck. It would be pretty tiring to climb up this path again, right? Many people look at this slope and complain, “Do we really have to walk up this path again?” but, actually, you don't need to. If you go up from the end of the coastal deck to Yongmeori and then walk on the ridge, you will be able to return to the starting point. Now, shall we walk together to enjoy the scenery while indulging in a little bit of exercise at the same time?

stories.title: Gohado Island: Observatory
stories.script: Gohado Island: Observatory  Gohado, which is also known as Yongseom for its resemblance to the shape of a dragon, is a patriotic island. There is also an observatory here that is made of Panokseon, the warship that brought victory to the Battle of Myeongnyang, piled up in the shape of a grid. From this Panokseon Observatory, you can see the cruise ship carrying passengers going around Yongmeori of Gohado, yachts powerfully cutting through the blue sea and white waves, Mokpo Port, Yudalsan and colorful houses. Especially at night, lights on the Panokseon are turned on to showcase the ultimate nightscape, completing the painting-like scenery. The lights of Gohado also become a dragon that roams around the night sea. Whenever we witness this, it feels as if Admiral Yi Sun-sin has become a dragon with dignity and is protecting Mokpo. During the Jeongyu Wars of 1597, Japanese raiders invaded Jindo with 333 ships. Admiral Yi lured the enemies into the narrow Uldolmok and scored a huge victory with just 13 Panokseon against 133 Japanese ships. Also, to get ready for a possible pursuit by the Japanese raiders, he himself patrolled the southern coast to make the people feel safe and to secure a suitable place for a navy camp. It is said that Admiral Yi was very pleased when he first saw Gohado.He recorded in Nanjung Ilgi, “It is extremely suitable to block the northwestern wind and hide warships. As I looked around the island, the topography seems well-suited so I decided for us to stay here.” Gohado is the best location to secure military provisions and the granary in the Yeongsangang region. Admiral Yi reorganized the Joseon navy here in Gohado before leaving to Wando and Gogeumdo to annihilate the enemies trying to retreat to Japan. He also set up Byeoljangjin where military rations are stored and garrison farms are managed to save up foods for military purposes and for tribute to the king. You can see his loyalty and willingness to prepare, right? Oh! There is also a myth behind Nojeokbong Peak in Yudalsan in relation to Byeoljangjin of Gohado. Rice straws were placed around Nojeokbong to be disguised as military provisions and, upon seeing this, Japanese raiders were shocked and ran away immediately as they thought the Joseon naval forces were great in number. The peak has been called Nojeokbong since then. Tongjesa Yi Bong-sang, the 5th descendant of Admiral Yi, erected his memorial stone in 1722 to tell the future generations about the importance of Gohado. During the occupation period, Japanese left it neglected on purpose or, even, damaged it with gunshots but, after the Liberation, Mochunggak was installed here in admiration of the achievements of Admiral Yi. Gohado is a historical island that made significant contributions to ending the 7-year Japanese invasion of 1592.

stories.title: Noeul Park, Mokpo
stories.script: Noeul Park, Mokpo  In addition to Mokpo Port, there is Bukhang Port to the north of Yudalsan Mountain in Mokpo. Bukhang, which had a relatively small floating population compared to Mokpo Port, established Noeul Park in June 2014.  Since then, Noeul Park has been used as a place to feel and experience the sea with a waterfront deck, Noeul Plaza, event plaza, green area and a trail. A variety of rest facilities such as sea fountains, pergolas and benches are set up to transform the venue into an environment-friendly space with characteristics of the sea.  During fall, the “Sunset Party,” which perfectly suits the name of Noeul Park, takes place. Diverse street foods and performances help create a vibe of a fall festival. Sushi restaurants and convenience facilities are gathered around the area, which is a beloved attraction for both Mokpo locals and tourists. Moreover, there is a large parking lot and a vacant lot nearby so parking is easy for not only passenger cars but also large buses.  The park has a long, rectangular shape and is a great dating course for lovers as well as a place where families and children can have a great time while enjoying the sun setting over the waters.

stories.title: Bukhang Noeul Park
stories.script: Bukhang Noeul Park  Bukhang, the final destination of the Seohaean Expressway, is close to a residential area crowded with apartments while also being located on the beach, which is why it has become a popular attraction for not only the locals but also tourists from outside Mokpo. With the creation of a cultural space that is Noeul Park in Bukhang, which had been just a small pier of Mokpo, a new vitality was generated within the city.  Noeul Park was established in 1984 when the Bukhang began developing according to the “National Trade Port Development Plan. Mokpo has four ports which include the Bukhang, Sinhang, Naehang and Namhang but, among them, Bukhang was only a small wharf also known as “Dwitgae.” Then, when the Seohaean Expressway was constructed in 2001, the wharf was renamed “Bukhang” and emerged as a central axis for the revitalization of the original city center along with the opening of Mokpodaegyo Bridge in 2012.  Noeul Park is equipped with various convenience facilities such as a waterfront deck where you can feel and experience the sea as well as an event plaza, green area, trail, floor fountain and rest facilities; small sculptures also decorate the park beautifully. Even at night, you can take a walk relatively safely thanks to the luminated floors.  It would be nice to take a stroll in the peaceful Bukhang Noeul Park during day or night, whenever you need the rest.  If you become hungry during a stroll, try any one of the seafood restaurants in the live fish distribution sector of Bukhang for the delicious taste of Mokpo. When you enter the Bukhang Seafood Town, king crabs and snow crabs welcome you from the entrance. You may buy fresh live fish in the complex space on the 1st floor and enjoy the taste of Mokpo with various dishes in the seafood town on the 2nd floor. Now, enjoy the great combination of beauty and flavor of the Bukhang Noeul Park!

stories.title: Yeonhee's Supermarket
stories.script: 7. Yeonhee's Supermarket  Yeonhee’s Supermarket is the filming site of the movie, “1987” starring Gang Dong-won as Lee Han-yeol and Kim Tae-ri as Yeon-hee. Inside the supermarket, briquettes, daily supplies, snacks, freezer, radio and many other antique props from the movie are on display to reproduce a scene that is exactly how it was in the film. The most impressive prop out of them all is an old, yellow taxi.  As you follow a small alley behind the supermarket, you will find a small silver door on your left, and there is a large air-raid shelter there. Inside the shelter, lights and information boards are installed for visitors to reflect on the painful history of the Japanese occupation era. It is said that this air-raid shelter was built by Korean people who had been mobilized compulsorily by the Japanese in preparation for aerial bombings by the Allied Forces towards the end of the Pacific War.  The Sihwa Alley near Yeonhee’s Supermarket is an area that still has scenes of the 1980s remaining from which you can feel the old vibes yourselves. It would be no exaggeration to say that the entire village is a modern museum as old structures still remain in Seosan-dong, a section of the city where a red-light district had existed for the Japanese.

stories.title: Nojeokbong Art Park Museum
stories.script: 2. Nojeokbong Art Park Museum  Nojeokbong Art Park Museum is a rural art gallery where you can appreciate not only the natural landscape but also the artworks. When Nojeokbong Art Park opened on July 29, 2009, the museum also opened on the 1st floor of the main building, and it was registered as a public art museum on January 27, 2014.  The main building and the annex building each have three floors, and the 1st floor of the main building is run as the art museum. The art museum consists of Exhibition Rooms 1 and 2 and, since the reorganization of the exhibition rooms in July 2015, various planned exhibitions have replaced permanent exhibitions.  On the 2nd floor of the main building, there is a Mokpo public relations center. The public relations center enables visitors to understand overall contents related to Mokpo, including its vision, history, economy, culture, art, figures, and tourism resources. On the 3rd floor of the main building, regular performances by the city art organization take place. There is also an outdoor stage where local art organizations and individuals can perform. The annex building is being used as a management office as well as a culture and arts organization.  The panoramic view of downtown Mokpo, which you can see from the art museum garden, is so beautiful that it reminds you of a magnificent painting.

stories.title: Namnong Memorial Hall
stories.script: Namnong Memorial Hall  Namnong Memorial Hall is an art museum established by Namnong Heo Geon who is the grandson of Sochi Heo Ryeon, the master of Korean Namjonghwa paintings, and the third owner of Ullimsanbang for the purpose of preserving the relics of his ancestors and continuing the development of Korean Namjonghwa (Namhwa) paintings. So what are Ullimsanbang and Namjonghwa? Ullimsanbang was where Heo Ryeon used to live and paint, and it is also a beautiful place that was chosen as one of the Top 100 tourist attractions that a Korean must visit. Namjonghwa is the opposite of Bukjonghwa, which was the style of paintings produced by professional painters from Hwawon and is the type of paintings mostly produced by noble literati who were not professional painters with a focus on expressing the inner world by light ink and colors. One of the most notable works of Namjonghwa is Chusa's Sehando, the National Treasure No. 180 which boasts the beauty of blank space.  The museum primarily exhibits the works of three generations from Heo Ryeon whom Chusa Gim Jeong-hui praised as the best in Joseon to Misan Heo Hyeong and Namnong Heo Geon. In other words, it is where the works of the family who continued the tradition of Korean Namjonghwa and those of Namnong's pupils are on display, including Namnong's 〈Nosongdo〉, which depicts three old pine trees, as well as 〈Peonies〉 by Sochi. There are also the works of Painter Illang Lee Jong-sang who drew the portraits of Yulgok Yi I and Sinsaimdang that are printed on the current 5,000-won and 50,000-won bills. In addition, earthenware and potteries from Gaya, Silla and Joseon as well as China and Japan are on display so take your time to enjoy all the works!

stories.title: Mokpo Peace Square
stories.script: Mokpo Peace Square  The Peace Square is a plaza located on the beach of Hadang New Town in Mokpo, Jeollanam-do. In a narrow sense, it refers to the square in front of the Dancing Sea Fountain and, in a broad sense, it encompasses everything from Gatbawi Rock in the south to the Bridge of Peace in the north. Its original name was Migwan Plaza but it was renamed to the Peace Square to celebrate the Nobel Peace Prize awarded to the late Kim Dae-jung, a former president. Every summer, the biggest festival of Mokpo, the Mokpo Maritime Culture Festival, is held here as well.  The world’s first-ever ultra-large floating sea music fountain also makes the night sea beautiful by the Peace Square. The “Love Gate” located in the middle of the square is a heart-shaped sculpture installed recently with the concept of a door of love towards the sea of Mokpo. It is a place where lights are lit one by one for many lovers and families to visit and take beautiful pictures with the sea fountain in the backdrop.

stories.title: Mokpo Natural History Museum
stories.script: Mokpo Natural History Museum  Mokpo Natural History Museum collects and exhibits global rare data such as dinosaur fossils and minerals that show the Earth’s 4.6 billion years of natural history, as well as materials introducing the history and culture of the southwest region.  It exhibits not only the original “carnivorous dinosaur egg nest fossils”, which are Korea’s first-ever carnivorous dinosaur fossils registered as a National Monument in 2012, but also about 20,000 original fossils and well-preserved specimens from which we can speculate the Earth's past, such as one of the two “Prenoceratops” fossils discovered in the world, “Conchoraptor fossils” as well as rare marine reptiles. Also, the wide grass area in front of the Natural History Museum is a great place for you to rest under the shades of trees while checking out the various animal-shaped structures on display outside.  The museum also has a venue where you can assess the cultural and artistic world of Yehyang Mokpo including art history, dance, music and art, and an experience section at which visitors may participate themselves. The 4D stereoscopic theater inside the museum gives you a chance to experience more vivid and realistic videos. The Natural History Museum is both a lifelong learning center and a tourist attraction where you can learn natural ecology and, at the same time, experience human culture and art.  In the Literary History Hall, you can examine the history of various local cultures in the 4 art galleries of Ullimsanbang, a living museum, and the viewing stone gallery. The Literary History Hall also operates the Ceramic Livingware Museum and Children’s Sea Science Museum. At the Ceramic Livingware Museum, you can feel and experience the pottery industry of the Jeollanam-do region and, at the Children’s Sea Science Museum, the first of its kind opened in Korea in 2013, you can check out the development history of the high-tech ceramics industry at a glance.

stories.title: Samhakdo Island, Mokpo
stories.script: Samhakdo Island, Mokpo  On the sea in front of Mokpo, Jeollanam-do Province, there exists Samhakdo Island, which was reclaimed in the 1960s into land, and it still contains the intact modern history of Mokpo. In the past, it was a park-like island where people used to go over by boat to pledge their love but it has become what it is now after reclamation and renovation. Sitting where the three little peaks meet the sea and the river, the island is considered a representative scenic spot of Mokpo along with Yudalsan.  Samhakdo railway, which connects Mokpo Station and Samhakdo, actually branches out to various lines such as the Hangukjebun Line, Seoktanbudu Line and Samhak Line. However, the main line started at Mokpo Station and ran toward Samhakdo, which is why people often called it “Samhakdo Coal Railroad.” Samhakdo Island, which had been flattened due to reclamation and reckless development, began belated restoration work in 2004, and much of it has now been returned to the Mokpo citizens. This interesting railroad is now undergoing a construction to become a park.  Recently, the “Forest of Gyeongbuk Province Residents” is being established, thus becoming a symbol of harmony and coexistence of Youngnam and Honam Regions. In fact, the Forest of Jeonnam Province Residents was created in Gumi, Gyeongsangbuk-do while the Forest of Gyeongbuk Province Residents was established in Samhakdo for harmony, exchanges and cooperation between the east and the west.Each forest is a symbolic place of harmony established over a 15,000m² area where provincial trees and flowers were planted, under the theme of Gudongjoni, which means to respect differences and to seek for things to be together. There is also the Kim Dae-jung Nobel Peace Prize Memorial nearby, which you can stop by for a tour as well.

stories.title: Samhakdo Island, Mokpo - Samhakdo Cruise
stories.script: Samhakdo Island, Mokpo - Samhakdo Cruise  Samhakdo Cruise that will fill the Mokpo sea with romance  Welcome everyone to Samhakdo Cruise! Samhakdo Cruise held a sailing ceremony on June 12, 2020 and started its operation by departing from the old Mokpo Coast Guard Wharf and crossing Naehang. This is a 969-ton cruise ship that is the most advanced and largest of its kind in Korea, and its capacity is 578 passengers. Now, let me introduce to you the convenience facilities that can be used during the voyage. Restrooms to answer an urgent call of nature are located in the back on the floor of the main ship, and snack bars selling sweets for people and Saewookkang for seagulls are located by the stairs on the 2nd and 3rd floors. If you want to sing a song while floating on the Mokpo night sea, a karaoke room is available on the 3rd floor. Also, if you want to dance by any chance, there is a banquet hall on the 1st floor where you can dance with Gakseori, or a Korean gypsy. When the ship departs, the excitement towards the sea is felt and everyone's heart would beat like the sound of an exhaust pipe. Is your heart pounding as well? The ship travels for about an hour and a half through 9 piers and 5 tour zones, which are Samhakdo Zone, Yudalsan Zone, Gohado Zone, Peace Square Zone and Gatbawi Zone, before returning to the port. From April to November, you can watch 〈Dancing Sea Fountain〉, located in front of Peace Square, from the ship. It is the world’s first-ever sea fountain and is also listed in the Guinness Book of Records. The Dancing Sea Fountain offers an even more fantastic enjoyment since, from the ship, you can watch the front and sides of the fountain three-dimensionally.  Carrying not just passengers but also the culture, Samhakdo Cruise is equipped with friendly and comfortable convenience facilities for both Koreans and foreigners to visit and enjoy the global port of Mokpo, and also presents the locals with relaxation and delightful memories as a soul-recharging station in the city. Moreover, Samhakdo Cruise hosts various cultural and artistic performances to rewrite the history of Mokpo tourism on the sea. Now, please enjoy the Samhakdo Cruise trip that will fill the waters of Mokpo with romance.

stories.title: Ganghwasanseong Anglican
stories.script: Upon the invasion of the Mongolians during the Goryeo Dynasty, the Goryeo royal family started the “Cheondo (relocation of the capital)” to Ganghwado Island, which can be reached from the current capital, Kaesong, by following along a river. The Ganghwado Goryeo Dynasty, the only time in Korean history when the capital was on an island, began in an attempt to avoid the Mongolian invasion.  When they built Igung (a palace built for temporary stay when a royal family was on the move), known as the Goryeogung Palace Site, they also built ramparts in three layers on the coast of Ganghwado and around the palace to prepare for the invasion of the Mongolian army. This fortress is known today as Ganghwasanseong Fortress. Gates were constructed on the east, west, south, and north sides, and walls were connected along the ridge of the mountain to block off the Mongolian invaders into Goryeo.  Mongolia imposed various conditions to form a friendly relation with Goryeo, and among them, there was a condition requiring both the inner and outer fortress walls of Ganghwasanseong be torn down. But, choosing peace over resistance, the Goryeo royal family demolished all of the walls as they left Ganghwado.  Later in the Joseon Dynasty, the fortress walls were built once again on the island because the structures that used to be the Goreyo fortress were now utilized as a government office, annex buildings, and as a Oegyujanggak. These fortress walls also served as strong blockades in protecting Ganghwado Island during the battles of the Japanese invasion in 1592, the French invasion in 1866, and the U.S. Invasion in 1871. Today, Ganghwasanseong has done its restorations centering the inner walls closest to the palace, and the gates of the east, west, south, and north have also been recovered, now serving as a center of the island. stories.title: Goryeogung Palace Site
stories.script: Goryeogung Palace Site where Goryeo resisted the Mongol invasion  Goryeogung Palace Site marks the location of the royal palace of Goryeo, which unified Korean Peninsula for 450 years from 936 to 1392 after its founding by Wang Geon in 918. Goryeo faced the relentless challenge of the Mongol Empire’s expansion while confronting invasions at that time.  During this period, Goryeo functioned as a military regime where actual power lay in the hands of military officials rather than the nominal kings. King Gojong, reigning for 45 years, endured the most among the successive kings.  Mongolia launched six invasions against Goryeo. After the first invasion, Goryeo encountered internal meddling and substantial tribute demands. To avoid those issues, Goryeo, under the leadership of its subjects, decided to relocate the capital to Ganghwa-do. The original capital, Gaegyeong, situated in Gaeseong city, North Korea, was about 20 km from Ganghwa-do, easily reachable by boat. Ganghwa-do was chosen for its strategic advantages. The several tides on the west coast thwarted the less adept Mongolian navy from accessing Ganghwa-do. Furthermore, the self-sufficiency of agriculture and fishing industries facilitated easy travel to and from other provinces by boat. As a result, the Goryeo royal family moved the capital to Ganghwa-do in July 1232.  With the sudden capital relocation, soldiers and residents mobilized to build palaces and government offices. Two years later, Goryeo Palace was completed in Ganghwa-do, serving as the Goryeo capital for 39 years until its relocation back to Gaegyeong in 1270.  After the fall of Goryeo Dyansty, THE GORYEO PALACE was torn down almost immediately in 1392. The Goryeo Palace site CONTINUES to serve various purposes.

stories.title: Goryeogung Palace Site in Joseon Dynasty
stories.audioTitle: Goryeogung Palace Site in Joseon Dynasty
stories.script: History of Goryeogung Palace Site in Joseon Dynasty   The Goryeogung Palace Site, the royal palace of the Goryeo Dynasty, continued to hold significance even after the fall of Goryeo in 1392 and the rise of the Joseon Dynasty.  Following the establishment of the Joseon Dynasty by Yi Seong-gye in 1392, the Goryeogung Palace Site served as the military zone, the Yusubu. It also served as a royal library known as Oegyujanggak during the reign of King Jeongjo, the 22nd king of the Joseon Dynasty.  During the French expedition to Korea in 1866, also known as Byeongin-yangyo, French troops invaded Joseon and took 359 royal books from Oegyujanggak to France. Approximately 100 years later, in 1975, Dr. Park Byung-seon, an employee of the French National Library, rediscovered these books housed there. Upon this discovery, the Korean government persistently requested the return of the books from French government. After extensive efforts and negotiations, an agreement was reached during the G20 Summit in November 2010 for a contract stipulating a five-year renewable lease scheme for the 297 books taken from Ogyujanggak. Eventually, in June 2011, the books were returned to Korea.  While the Goryeogung Palace has already been torn down, most of the buildings at the Goryeogung Palace Site, including Yusubu, the library, and the pavilion, were destroyed during the French expedition to Korea. Regrettably, only a few buildings remain today. It is crucial for people to value these invaluable resources and spend time contemplating the ancient times at the Goryeogung Palace Site, where a turbulent history resides.

stories.title: Ganghwa Anglican Church of Korea
stories.script: When you look up the hill from Yongheunggung Park, you will see a unique hanok building. This is Ganghwa Anglian Church (Catholic church), a hanok building with a unique two-story structure. The Anglian Church came to existence in this area in 1900 during the Korean Empire period, and it was constructed by British Bishop Charles John Corfe.  Bishop Corfe wanted to build a church in a more friendly form for the Joseon people in Ganghwado Island and brought the master builder and the carpenters who were responsible for building Gyeongbokgung Palace. Since Joseon architects did not know any Western-style church architecture, they simply thought of temples and shrines when they heard that it would be a place to worship God, whereas the inside was designed in the style of a church through Bishop Corfe’s advice, which resulted in a very unique building.  A signboard that says “Catholic Church” hangs on the second floor of the main gate, which is awfully similar to hanging a name sign on the buildings of a Buddhist temple. Even Juryeon, or the long vertical plaques, are hung on the five pillars in front of the gate, giving the place a more temple like feel rather than a church but from the Western-style hinged doors, and the cross atop the roof, it is easy to guess that this is in fact a Western Catholic church.  Usually, hanok buildings use the width as the front and the lengths as its sides but this church utilizes the length as its front, adding more depth to the inside while not making the overall building look awkward despite all the chairs and a Western-style altar. People must take off their shoes to go inside, and since men and women stayed in separate spaces during the Joseon Dynasty, doors from both sides were used in order to have men and women sit apart from each other. Because the space on the second floor is open, there are no stairs, and sunlight comes through the windows to fill the interior with warmth.  The place is still operated as the Anglian Church and is a place where Catholic believers actually come to attend Mass. That is why taking pictures without permission or interrupting a Mass is strictly prohibited. Let’s all be respectful and quietly look around.

stories.title: Yongheunggung Royal Residence
stories.script: Cheoljong, the 25th king of Joseon, is a king with somewhat of an unusual past. A typical king is born inside the palace and receives the education necessary in being a crown prince; however, King Cheoljong upon birth had the unusual status of both a member of the royal family and a commoner. According to the genealogy of Cheoljong, he is a great-grandson of the Crown Prince Sado but Prince Euneon, the grandfather of Cheoljong and brother of King Jeongjong, was executed for being a Catholic, and his descendants had been exiled to Ganghwado Island.  Cheoljong’s family was exiled as well and lived a commoner's life in a thatched house. Cheoljong also had lived an ordinary life as a farmer named “Yi Won-beom”. However, in 1849 when King Heonjong died without leaving behind a son, Queen Sunwon gave an order to find a descendant of the royal bloodline. And the person eventually chosen was Cheoljong, also known as the “Woodcutter Prince of Ganghwa Island”. In fact, when people came to find Cheoljong, he hid because he thought he would be taken captive. This goes to show that he really had no idea that he would become king of the country.  Yongheunggung Royal Residence is the tile-roofed house that renovated the thatched house where Cheoljong used to live after his ascension to the throne. Because it was a Jamjeo (a house in which a king had lived before ascending to the throne), it had to be equipped with proper class and dignity. After becoming the king, Cheoljong tried to participate in politics and attempted a political reform but he was often thwarted by the power politics of the Andong Kim clan and experienced many setbacks. In his later years, his health deteriorated and he eventually passed away in 1863.  Cheoljong left this place when he was 19 and could never return to this place that hard turned into a tile-roofed house. The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty have records talking about how Cheoljong missed his life in Ganghwado, his life as Won-beom. The thatched house has long been gone but it would be fun to imagine the time when Won-beom lived here and walk through the yards and alleys where the Woodcutter Prince of Ganghwa Island had once roamed.

stories.title: Ganghwa History Museum
stories.script: One of the phrases that describe Ganghwado Island is “a museum without a roof.” It expresses the characteristics of Ganghwado, which seems to have miniaturized the history of the Korean Peninsula, and this is the “museum with a roof” that shows the history of Ganghwado Island. It is right next to the Bugeun-ri Dolmen Site and Ganghwa Natural History Museum so it is a place you absolutely must visit when coming to the island.  The life on Ganghwado, whose history began in prehistoric times, can be pictured through the dolmens, flint arrowheads, and ornaments that have been found in the surroundings, and it exhibits the dolmen-making process as well as models to resolve any curiosity you may have.  You can also learn about the culture of Ganghwado, which served as a trading warehouse from the period of the Three States all the way to the Goryeo Dynasty thanks to its close proximity to Byeongnando Island, a famous trading port, so it briefly flourished when it became the capital of Goryeo.  In addition, it shows the stories of the experiences of Ganghwado during foreign invasions in the Joseon Dynasty. In particular, the French invasion and the U.S. Invasion have been reproduced in life-size models, giving you the feeling of viewing a scene directly from history in person.  In the garden outside the museum, there are various stone relics that were found throughout Ganghwado including Munsinseok and Musinseok at tombs, stone lanterns, and components of dolmens, so it is fun to look for them one by one.

stories.title: Ganghwado Dolmen Site
stories.script: In the Korean Peninsula also known as the dolmen kingdom, there are three areas where clusters of dolmens are located. These areas are Ganghwado in Incheon, Hwasun-gun in Jeollanam-do, and Gochang-gun in Jeollabuk-do. Dolmens in these three regions were registered as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 2000, meaning that they were recognized as important historic sites that tell us the prehistoric culture in East Asia.  Dolmens in Ganghwado are dispersed throughout the island but, before they were revealed to be dolmens, people had thought of them simply as rocks with unique shapes. There were dolmens gathered up in the mountains, but there were also those that existed in the middle of a village field or on a street, and the meaning of the latter type of dolmens was more difficult to grasp.  Dolmens found in the Korean Peninsula are commonly divided into the Northern style (table style) and Southern style (go-board style), and you are able to see both types in Ganghwado. If you want to check out enormous Northern-style dolmens, we recommend you visit the dolmens in Bugeun-ri, which are located across from the Ganghwa History Museum. These are famous dolmens that are explained even in Korean History textbooks. If you go see them in person, their size, much greater than that of an average adult, will surprise you.  If you want to see a group of dolmens gathered together, we recommend Osang-ri Dolmens. The site has a parking lot as well so you may visit anytime on your trip to and from Ganghwado. Here, dolmens of various sizes are all in one place so people think of the site as some kind of cemetery. Dolmens dispersed throughout the island all have different shapes and sizes so it is interesting to compare them to find their discrepancies.

stories.title: Ganghwado Peace Observatory
stories.script: Ganghwado Island is renowned for its weekend resort and historical sites, being an area that borders North Korea. With the atmosphere of reconciliation between North and South Korea since 2000s, a peace-wishing observatory was established on the island in 2008.  The Ganghwa Peace Observatory is a four-story building, one story below the ground. Constructed on forest land in the northern area of the Civilian Passage Restriction Line, entry was strictly restricted from the public since late 2006. Following by its public opening in September 2008, it offers visitors with access to observe the unique cultural ecosystem of North Korea. The most frequent visitors are foreigners and individuals with family ties or hometowns in the North. Visitors may see grandmothers and grandfathers are shedding their tears while foreigners are often filled with curiosity as they gaze towards the North.   Entering the Ganghwado Peace Observatory, the basement and forth floor are exclusively used for military purposes. The first floor houses restaurants, administrative offices, guest rooms and specialty shops selling goods originated from Ganghwa-do and North Korea. The second floor features a high-performance telescope and an exhibition room allowing visitors to witness the traces of war and various images, including the background of the Korean War, the occurrence of wars in Korean and overseas, and the war-related damages. Lastly, the third floor houses an observatory facility offering visitors a panoramic view of North Korea’s mountain and rivers. An audio-visual room displays comprehensive view of North Korea through videos.  Visitors can observe the life and scenery of the North using the telescope when the weather is nice. The areas include Byeokrando Island, which flourished as a trading port in the Goryeo Dynasty, and Songaksan Mountain in Gaeseong, where the Gaeseong Industrial Complex is located.   As the Ganghwado Peace Observatory is situated in the area of the Civilian Access Control Line, please be reminded that inspection may occur upon entry. Furthermore, filming and uploading images of military facilities or North Korean sites may be against the law.

stories.title: Yeonmijeong Pavilion
stories.script: Yeonmijeong, whose name comes from the shape of the waterway, where Imjingang River and Hangang River meet, resembling the tail of a swallow, was a pavilion famous for moon gazing in Ganghwado Island. The current was strong and the tide fluctuated severely at the point where the two rivers met, so the boats entering Hangang from the West Sea took short breaks under the pavilion.  It is not clearly known since when Yeonmijeong Pavilion has existed but there is a record of students studying here during the Goryeo Dynasty. The pavilion we see today is the restored version of what was damaged during the Japanese invasion in 1592, the Qing invasion in 1636, and even the Korean War.  After passing through Johaeru and the rampart, you will see Yeonmijeong Pavilion under giant zelkova trees. In fact, what will grab your attention more than the pavilion itself are the two huge zelkova trees. These trees have stood here even as the pavilion and fortress walls fell during the wars, and it seems like they hold all those years of history in every one of its growth rings.  If you look towards the river from the fortress wall where the zelkova trees are, you can see Udo Island and Kaepung-gun of Hwanghae-do Province in North Korea. There is a special story in Udo. When there was a big flood in North Korea in 1996, a bull floated down to Udo and remained there. Since Udo is a demilitarized zone, one can only go into the island after an agreement between South and North Korea so they conducted a negotiation, which helped save the bull as a result. The bull eventually came to live in the south where he got the nickname, “Bull of Peace.” The island has since been known as Udo, as it was an island to which a bull floated down.  Yeonmijeong Pavilion is located within the Civilian Access Control Line so you may be subject to an inspection upon entry, and it may be against the law to film any military facilities or North Korean land and to upload them online so be sure to take extra caution.

stories.title: Gapgot Dondae Fort
stories.script: Gapbigocha is the name of the Gapgot used during the period of the Three States. Some believe that the name, Gapgot, comes from an event in history. During their invasion of Goryeo, the Mongolian army and its weak naval forces were disappointed in not being able to cross this body of water and said, “We could march over the waters if all of our soldiers just take off their Gabot, or armor, and fill up the sea,” which is another possible origin story.  During the Joseon Dynasty, Gapgot was the French army base at the time of their invasion. The French Far Eastern Squadron came to Ganghwado in 1866 because of the execution of French priests that happened in Joseon which had been persecuting Catholics. Father Félix Clair Ridel who was able to escape the persecution fled to Qing and told the French army stationed in Tianjin about the situation in Joseon. Then, the French troops began to march towards the Korean Peninsula after notifying Qing not to interfere with their war against Joseon. Furious at hearing this news from Qing, Heungseon Daewongun intensified the persecution of Catholic believers and strengthened defense in the Ganghwado area.  In September later that year, 3 French battleships sailed past the sea in front of Incheon and up to an area near Seoul. As the Joseon army reinforced their defenses, the French eventually returned to Qing after only surveying the river currents and coastal regions. Then, during the second intrusion that began in October, they brought 7 battleships and about 600 marines. Four of these warships landed in Gapgotjin (Dondae) and prepared to march towards Ganghwaseong Fortress.  Once landed on Joseon territory, the French army carried out indiscriminate assaults on both military facilities and private residences, setting everything in the fortress on fire and stealing weapons and books. But, after they began to spread throughout Ganghwado, the French troops suffered a huge loss in Jeongjoksanseong Fortress at the hands of the Joseon army led by General Yang Heon-su, which ultimately resulted in their retreat to Qing in November.  Once you enter Gapgot Dondae, with an admission fee, you will find cannons used during the Joseon period and restored fortress walls. Although these are not the cannons that were used during the French invasion, the fort still presents to us historical significance as a place where the technically inferior army of Joseon took advantage of the geography to defeat the French.

stories.title: Deogjinjin Fort
stories.script: Our first encounter with the United States of America, an unknown country to us then, was the “General Sherman” incident that took place in Pyongyang. At the time, hostility to foreigners was at an all-time high due to the French invasion in 1866, but this is when the U.S. and the General Sherman showed up in Taedonggang River and demanded trades. Based on the culture of treating strangers well, Joseon treated the Americans warmly but did not accept their request to trade. Time passed by but there was no progress in trading. Moreover, the once-rising river water began to dwindle making sailing of ships difficult. Then, one day, the General Sherman decided to attack the Joseon people. As the number of Joseon soldiers and commoners killed by the American cannons increased, Pyongyang Gamsa Bak Gyusu carried out a counterattack with fire, and burned down the General Sherman and wiped out its crew.  In fact, Robert Jermain Thomas who led the General Sherman had introduced himself as an Englishman so Joseon only found out that it was an American ship after receiving a memorandum of protest from the U.S. Then, the U.S. brought five warships to Ganghwado Island in 1871, demanding responsibility for what happened to the General Sherman as well as openings of trade.  The place where the U.S. Navy first landed was Chojijin Fort and, after capturing the fort, they continued to move northward and arrived at Deogjinjin Fort to carry out fierce battles. The Joseon Navy with only aged weapons could not help but suffer from the U.S. cannons, which eventually led to the fall of Deogjinjin Fort. As a result, most of the ramparts, gates and gate towers of Deogjinjin were destroyed and only their sites remained.  Having passed Deogjinjin and headed to Gwangseongjin Fort (Gwangseongbo), the U.S. army engaged in hard-fought battles against Joseon’s General Eo Jae-yeon who was ultimately killed during the battle. As a response, the Joseon Navy planned a night attack on Chojijin which was successful, and ultimately lead to the U.S. troops' retreat. Having realized that any more attacks would simply pile up the loss of lives, the U.S. Navy returned to Qing after about 40 days. One of the trophies that they took at the time was “Sujagi” (a flag with the Chinese character of Su, which means general), which was later returned to Korea in 2007.  Today's Deogjinjin Fort refers to the rampart and fortress that were completely renovated in the 1970s. A turret, which was also renovated during the same period, is located here as well. It is said that President Park Chung-hee inspected the traces of the fortress near the Ganghwa Strait himself and ordered the restoration.

stories.title: Chojijin Fort
stories.script: Chojijin Fort, which serves as the gateway to the Ganghwa Strait, is related to two major events in history - the United States invasion in 1871 and the Ganghwa Island incident in 1875. Chojijin Fort has a relatively short history among many of the fortifications and turrets in Ganghwado Island but its importance grew significantly as it became the main stage for these two incidents.  Today's Chojijin has only the dondae, or fortification, section where gunpoints and cannons are located, restored. It is presumed to be much bigger originally than it is now. You will see a black hole on the huge pine tree next to the fortification, showing how the tree survived even a hit from a cannonball. The decisive event that wounded Chojijin this way was the Ganghwa Island incident.  On August 21, 1975, a Japanese warship called the Un'yō anchored in Nanjido Island located southeast of Ganghwado. They started to approach Chojijin on the grounds of a plan to survey the coast and look for water. The Joseon Navy, which was guarding the fort, warned the Un'yō not to approach any further but the Japanese ship ignored the warning. Eventually, when the Joseon troops at Chojijin began firing at the Un'yō, the Japanese fired back as if they had been waiting for it and destroyed the fort.  While the Japanese invaders used high quality cannons imported from the West, the only cannon that Chojijin Fort had was its Large Mortar, which could only fire up to about 700m. Dominated by the weaponry, Chojijin was destroyed and only its traces remained. Japan used this incident to force the Joseon government to sign a treaty, which is none other than the Japan-Korea Treaty of 1876.  After the construction of Chojidaegyo, more and more visitors have come to Chojijin Fort. Once you enter the fort with an admission fee, you can see Chojidaegyo and Gimpo at the same time, which makes it a great place to take pictures along with the sunset. Stop by Chojijin Fort, a must-visit attraction for anyone who comes to Ganghwado and take a few photos.

stories.title: Jeondeungsa Temple
stories.script: Jeondeungsa Temple is most famous temple in Ganghwa-do and is known to be one of the oldest temples in Korea. It was first constructed within the Samnangseong Fortress and was named Jinjongsa Temple during the early Goryeo Dynasty. Later, when the queen of King Chungyeol donated a precious jade lantern to the temple, it was renamed the current Jeondeungsa Temple. ‘Jeondeung’ in Korean signifies the ‘donation of a lantern’.  Initially established during the reign of King Sosurim in Goguryeo Dynasty, there was limited historical information about the temple until the Joseon Dynasty. However, the temple faced two major fires in 1605 and 1614, which destroyed it. Reconstruction began the following year, and by 1621, during the 13th year of King Gwanghaegun’s reign, the temple was restored to its original appearance.  The Daeungbojeon Hall serves as the main building of the temple. Positioned in front of the temple precinct, it is accessed by passing underneath the entrance gate of Daejoru Tower. The hall stands as significant architectural feature, enshrining the Sakyamuni Buddha Traid. Its architectural design showcases a hip-and-gable roof with simple bracketing styles, notable for its mid-Joseon Dynasty architecture. Visitors can find the names of soldiers written on the walls and columns. These soldiers had fought against the French troops and wrote their name in the temple to pray for good fortune in war.   Observing the gabled roof closely, you can notice four little crouching figures placed in the corners to support the eaves. They are known as Nabusang, which depict naked women. There is an interesting story behind these figures. Would you like to learn about it as we walk around the temple?

stories.title: The Story of the Carpenter and Nabusang
stories.audioTitle: The Story of the Carpenter and Nabusang
stories.script: Daeungbojeon Hall is the main building of Jeondeungsa Temple. It showcases significant architectural work with a heartbreaking story behind. Now, let’s listen to the story and delve into the architectural design of the hall.  After Jeondeungsa Temple was burnt down in the fire, King Gwanghaegun sent Dopyeonsu, the chief carpenter in Korean, to rebuild the temple. Dopyeongsu resided in a nearby inn during the reconstruction. Over time, he fell in love with the innkeeper. As bank facilities were absent then, he entrusted all his asset to her for safekeeping. Dopyeonsu worked diligently, as they had promised to marry each other once the reconstruction work was completed.  However, one day, when he finished the work and returned to the inn, he found out that she had vanished a few nights prior and never returned. Outraged at her betrayal, Dopyeonsu decided to take a revenge. Consequently, he sculpted four crouching figures of naked women, known as Nabusang, under the eaves of Daeungbojeon Hall. These figures were destined to forever support the hall’s roof.  The Nabusang figures are positioned at the hall’s four corners. Upon closer inspection, an interesting detail emerges. While three figures support the roof with both hands, one supports it with only a single hand. If observed closely, their facial expressions differ, suggesting a sense of cunning even while enduring punishment. The hall, owing to its exquisite carving skills, is regarded as a significant research asset for mid-Joseon architectural history and is currently designated as Treasure No. 178.

stories.title: National Archive of Jeongjoksan Mountain
stories.script: In 653, a national archive located in Manisan Mountain was burned down, and the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty that had been stored in Ganghwado went missing. Hyojong, who was the king of Joseon at the time, ordered the build of a new archive in Jeongjoksan Mountain to keep the Annals there. It was during the reign of King Hyeonjong when all of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty and other books were finally moved to the archive in Jeongjoksan, which marks the beginning of the National Archive of Jeongjoksan Mountain.  The history of crises of this national archive dates back to the French invasion in 1866 when French troops stole books that had been stored here. So, Joseon relocated some of the other books back to Seoul, and Chunchugwan itself started to manage the archive. During the days of the Korean Empire, according to the records, a government official was dispatched from Uijeongbu to manage the archive in cooperation with the Governor of Ganghwa-gun.  During the Japanese occupation period, the books in the Jeongjoksan National Archive were moved to the school affairs section of the Japanese Government General along with the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty that had been stored in Taebaeksan National Archive. Then, in 1930, they were moved to Keijō Imperial University (Seoul National University today) for research and, after Liberation, the Gyujanggak Library of Seoul National University took over the books for preservation and management.  The vacant Jeongjoksan National Archive disappeared after 1931. There are no records on exactly when it ceased to exist but, since a picture of it was seen in a book called 〈〈Joseon Gojeok Dobo〉〉in 1931, we presume that the archive disappeared after this point. The building we see right now is what was newly restored in the 1970s  based on the records and photos that still remain. Consisted of two buildings called “Seonwonbogak” and “Jangsagak”, the Jeongjoksan National Archive is currently used as an auxiliary building of Jeondeungsa Temple. Exhibits are held during festival periods, but usually the place shows itself as an ancient library that once stored the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty.
