stories.title: Maehwamarum Habitat
stories.script: Class 2 Endangered Wild Plant. 9th Ramsar wetland on the Korean Peninsula. Do you get the feeling of how valuable the Maehwamarum Habitat is by looking at these two descriptions alone? Maehwamarum Habitat in Ganghwado used to be a common wetland in a small village near Chojijin Fort.  People of this village were farmers so they had been planning for a construction project that would reorganize and expand farming lands. But, because of the disappearance of this wetland, there was a chance that the flower species known as Maehwamarum was going to be never seen again not just in Korea but in the whole world. So, in 2000, the National Trust of Korea made a commitment to preserve and manage the wetland through an agreement with its residents, which has led to the habitat we see today.  Maehwamarum used to be one of the more common plants people were able to see in Yeouido or Yeongdeungpo in Seoul, but due to the disappearance of many wetlands from excessive development and reclamation, it can only be found in Ganghwado these days. In April and May every year, white flowers bloom and nearly fill up the wetland. The flower is also called “Minarimarum” or “Minarimal” depending on the region. In fact, it was originally known as “Marum” but became “Maehwamarum” since the way it blooms makes it look like a Maehwa, or ume, flower.  The existence of Maehwamarum itself means that the wetland ecosystem in the surrounding environment is ideal. The habitat is a clean area where you can meet a pair of endangered species of Seoul, the pond frogs and boreal digging frogs as well as natural monuments such as black-faced spoonbills and Swinhoe's egrets. In 2003, a Maehwamarum habitat was also discovered in the Dangsan-ri area of Ganghwa-gun, which is under preservation as well.  The Maehwamarum Habitat can be enjoyed through a trail made of wooden decks. Attempts to catch or collect any of the animals or plants inhabiting this area are strictly prohibited so we recommend that you only observe or take photos and videos of them.

stories.title: Jeokseoksa Temple, Ganghwado
stories.script: Located in Goryeosan Mountain famous for azalea, Jeokseoksa is one of the oldest temples in Ganghwado. It is known to have been established during the reign of King Jangsu of Goguryeo by a monk from India who had traveled through Qin of China before arriving in Ganghwado. Upon arriving at Goryeosan, the monk discovered a pond, where five-colored lotus flowers bloomed, he then let the flowers fly in the air, and built a temple in the location on which each of the five flowers landed.  Because a red lotus flower fell in this area, the temple was named Jeongnyeonsa, which was later on renamed to Jeokseoksa, the name we use today. There is no definite story behind the change of its name but considering that the temple is built on an enormous stone stylobate, we can estimate that it means a temple built by stones.  Jeokseoksa became famous for its Nagjodae, or sunset viewpoint. Widely regarded as one of the three best sunsets in the Korean Peninsula, it presents incredible scenery together with Goryeosan and the West Sea. The final burning light just before sunset is more beautiful in the fall when accompanied by the maple leaves of Goryeosan and in the spring when it forms perfect harmony with the brilliantly blossomed azalea, which makes you wonder if this sunset was what the Indian monk referred to as the red lotus flower.  The road up to Jeokseoksa is an extremely narrow and steep trail so tour buses cannot go through. The hike may seem a bit long, but as you slowly take one step after another while enjoying nature, you will be rewarded with the sunset on the West Sea that resembles the red lotus flower leaves flying away into the sky.

stories.title: Seodaemun Prison History Hall Main Entrance
stories.audioTitle: Seodaemun Prison History Hall Main Entrance
stories.script: Seodaemun Prison History Hall Main Entrance  There is a prison built of red bricks in the middle of downtown Seoul. It is Seodaemun Prison, which is a sacred site of the Korean Independence Movement and where democracy fighters were imprisoned.  If you come out from Exit 5 of Dongnimmun Station on Seoul Subway Line 3, you can see the main gate of Seodaemun Prison. It is a place that frequently appears in dramas and movies whenever they film a scene of someone being released from prison. During the Korean Empire days, it was where many righteous army soldiers were killed and, in the Japanese colonial era, it was a noble site where independence fighters did not break their will for independence. Then, in our modern history, it was a place that imprisoned a countless number of activists who fought for the democratization of our country.  In 1907, Emperor Gojong of the Korean Empire was forced to abdicate and the army of the Korean Empire was disbanded as a result of the Korea-Japan Treaty. In response, righteous armies from all over the country were raised and fought against the Japanese army. In the process, captured righteous army soldiers were imprisoned and, as the number of the captured increased, Japan built Gyeongseong Gamok in 1908 with a plan to build a new confinement.  The name, Gyeongseong Gamok, had been used from Gyeongsul Gukchi in 1910 to 1912, and then, it changed to Seodaemun Gamok before it became Seodaemun Prison. It came to have an appearance that is similar to what we see today since the 1920s, and it is said to have been built by compulsorily mobilizing the prisoners. The watchtower you can see from the entrance was constructed to watch the prisoners and prevent them from breaking out.  Now, when you enter through the main entrance and purchase a ticket, your tour of Seodaemun Prison History Hall will officially begin. Since it is a noble place of great significance, please look around as quietly as possible.

stories.title: Seodaemun Prison History Hall Administration Building
stories.audioTitle: Seodaemun Prison History Hall Administration Building
stories.script: Seodaemun Prison History Hall Administration Building  The first exhibition hall you see is the building that was used as the main wing of Seodaemun Prison. This particular building was primarily used by the warden of the prison and other Japanese prison officers as well as detectives. On the outside, it looks to be a two-story structure but, in the basement, there was a torture room where independence activists were beaten and tormented.  Most independent activists were dragged here after trials as mere formality at the Gyeongseong Court (former Supreme Court building) or even without any trial, and this was the building they were headed to first once they entered through the prison gate.  The 1st and 2nd floors of the exhibition hall exhibit the history of Seodaemun Prison and contents of righteous army activities and independence fighters up to the post-Liberation Seodaemun Prison. Among the relics on display are objects used to restrain and suppress prisoners, such as Yongsu used to cover prisoners’ faces, shackles to prevent prisoners from escaping, and self-protection canes utilized by prison officers. These show contrasting images to articles actually used by prisoners like rubber shoes and wooden laundry bats.  Past the exhibition hall, you will see prison records attached all over the room that tell what it was like at the time of imprisonment of the independence fighters. You can see that people of all ages from 13-year-old children to 60-year-old seniors were put in jail because of their actions for national independence. There are both well-known independence activists and unknown independence fighters here so you can witness the will of a countless number of our patriots and martyrs.  On the basement floor, there is a place where independence activists were actually tortured and interrogated. The images of not only independence activists who were forced to confess and make false accusations but also the Japanese torturing them are exhibited as mannequins, showing a vivid picture of the brutality of the time. Tools that were actually used to torture people are on display as well, and you can go inside and get a first-hand look and feel of the narrow wall coffin in which only one standing person can fit. It is known that many independence fighters were locked up in this space for more than a day.  When you get out of the basement, it will lead to the central office connected to the prison building. It is a building where you can see the actual appearance of the prison so let’s walk along while thinking about the pain of our patriots.

stories.title: Seodaemun Prison History Hall Prison Cell
stories.audioTitle: Seodaemun Prison History Hall Prison Cell
stories.script: Seodaemun Prison History Hall Prison Cell  When you enter the central office building, you will find the space that the prison officers used to use as an office as well as the door that leads to the prison building. The office space has become a place that exhibits the prisoners’ meals, clothes and shelter. Here, you can see the tools used to differentiate the distribution of meals and the clothes that the prisoners actual wore at the time.  As you enter the central prison officers’ room and the letter room, you will realize that they directly lead to the prison building. In fact, the imprisoned independence fighters were allowed to exchange letters with their families but, because the contents of what they exchanged were censored, they could not talk directly about the poor situations in the prison or the fact that they were being tortured.  Now, when you enter the prison building, you will find a Japanese prison officer mannequin watching you from the hallway of the two-story prison building. Each prison building has reproduced images of independence activists imprisoned during the Japanese colonial era in mannequins and exhibition materials, and you may enter the room that is open.  Meokbang, which is the name of the one-person jail, got its name because the room had no light coming in and, thus, it was pitch dark like the color of Meok, or the Korean traditional ink. Designed to inflict pain upon any prisoner who causes trouble, it is the type of confinement that does not let even a single ray of sunlight in to make you feel physically and mentally exhausted.  The prison buildings were built in the way that it was good for surveillance. Heavy iron doors were used to make it difficult to open, and, if you look inside from the outside, the inside could be viewed clearly but, when looking outside from inside of the room, only a limited portion was able to be seen. Also, a restroom existed in the room, it was filled with odor and insects in the summer so it was not clean at all, and, during the period when many independence fighters were arrested and imprisoned, more than 15 people were put in a single cell, creating an environment where they could not eat and sleep properly.  Once you exit the prison building and look at the outside wall, there is a small window where you can see the ventilation structure of the building. It was installed for ventilation within the prison but, in most occasions, things were unable to be solved by that small window alone. It is also said that the prisoners in solitary confinement were controlled by making them use separate restrooms outside to prevent contact with others. The traces of these also remain on the exterior walls.

stories.title: Seodaemun Prison History Hall Execution Building
stories.audioTitle: Seodaemun Prison History Hall Execution Building
stories.script: Seodaemun Prison History Hall Execution Building  Those who were imprisoned in Seodaemun Prison were forced to perform arduous labor or tortured, and, if one was sentenced to death from a trial, he or she was martyred in the execution ground inside the prison.  For independence activists, the trials were too unfavorable. Most of the independence activists of the Japanese colonial era were sentenced to death, and they either died on the execution grounds or became ill as they could not overcome the harsh tortures. There were many cases of deaths caused by a failure to overcome the aftereffects of torture.  It is said that, after being sentenced to death, most of the independence fighters let out their deep resentment while holding a poplar tree in front of the execution ground. Therefore, this poplar got the name, “the Wailing Poplar.”  There is another poplar tree built during a similar period on the inside of the execution grounds but stories say that this particular tree could not grow well because of the sorrow and resentment of the independence fighters. The execution grounds building looks like a house made of wood but about 5m-tall walls were set up so that no one from the outside could see what is happening inside. It is said that executions took place at dawn or night rather than daytime.  In case families or relatives existed, the dead bodies of independence fighters were handed over to their families but, if not, most of them were thrown away in a nearby hill or cremated. There was a separate gate in the back of the execution ground through which dead bodies were transferred to outside. This was because the Japanese were worried about the Joseon people becoming infuriated if the corpses were moved in and out through the main gate.  Seodaemun Prison History Hall is now a place in the city center surrounded by apartments. It is a place that we can easily miss and pass by but we must never forget that it is a precious space holding the spirit of many independence fighters and righteous army soldiers who sacrificed their lives for our country as well as those who strove for democratization.

stories.title: Dongnimmun Gate
stories.script: Dongnimmun Gate  The western gate of Hanyangdoseong Fortress is “Yeongeunmun” where envoys from Qing were greeted and instructed to stay temporarily before entering the royal palace. Upon his return from the U.S. In 1896, Dr. Seo Jae-pil formed the Independence Club and proposed to construct Dongnimmun Gate. His intention was to demolish Yeongeunmun and erect Dongnimmun in the same location as an expression of will for independence. With the support of Emperor Gojong and other activists who agreed to Mr. Seo's idea, the construction of the Dongnimmun began in 1896 and was completed in November 1897.  Dongnimmun is a Western-style building completely different from the existing Joseon-style architecture, and it was modeled after the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, France. In fact, the architect was a Westerner but it was built by Joseon people so it is said that the gate was constructed as if they were building Joseon fortress walls. But, regarding the architect and the builders, the records from Seo Jae-pil’s autobiography are different from that of “Gyeongseongbusa” so the accurate details are not known.  Dongnimmun is about 14.28m tall and 11.48m wide, and a stone staircase leading to the top is located on the inside of the gate. The most famous element of Dongnimmun is its signboard, which has “Dongnimmun” engraved in Korean and Chinese letters on the front and back, respectively. And, on both sides of the signboard, Taegeukgi flags are carved in. By the way, a story says that the one who wrote the letters on this signboard is Ye Wanyong, the most famous pro-Japan traitor in our history. It is said that Ye Wanyong was well-known for his writing skills at the time. Before he became one of the Five Eulsa Traitors, he was a young nobleman who actually sponsored the Independence Club, and it is speculated that he actively participated and supported the construction of Dongnimmun because the gate meant independence from Qing. But there are also some people who claim that Kim Ga-jin, another renowned calligrapher of the same period, wrote the letters so the mystery about the gate’s signboard has yet to be solved.  The place where Dongnimmun Gate is currently located is known as “Seodaemun Independence Park” and, here, there once was a building called “Mohwagwan where the Qing envoys used to stay. In front of Mohwagwan, there was a gate called “Ilgakmun, and one of its pillars still stands in front of the gate. It was standing there in front when the gate was being built, according to sources. The pillar was moved to the south in 1934 and then, in 1979 when Seongsandaero Bridge was completed, it was removed from its original place along with Dongnimmun to settle in the present-day location.

stories.title: Taeryeongjeon Hall of Gyeonghuigung Palace
stories.audioTitle: Taeryeongjeon Hall of Gyeonghuigung Palace 경희궁지 태령전
stories.script: Taeryeongjeon Hall of Gyeonghuigung Palace   In 1760, King Yeongjo of the Joseon Dynasty renamed Gyeongdeokgung Palace, which was also called the “West Palace”, as Gyeonghuigung Palace, and Prince Jeongwongun, the father of King Injo, received an official warrant from the Qing Dynasty, along with the posthumous title of “King Wonjong (Great King Wonjong Gyeongdeok Inheon Jeongmok Janghyo).” Because Gyeongdeokgung Palace and Wonjong’s posthumous title contained the same letters, King Yeongjo, who could not use his ancestors' posthumous title as it was, named the palace as Gyeonghuigung Palace to include “hui”, meaning to shine.   Taeryeongjeon Hall was built by restoration work that began in 1988. In order to restore Gyeonghuigung Palace at that time, materials such as “Seogwoldoan”, “Seogwol Yeonggeon Dogam Uigwe”, and “Gungwolji” were referred to, and the location of the stylobate was confirmed and restored through actual excavation work.  The meaning of the Chinese characters of Taeryeongjeon Hall is “a large and comfortable pavilion”, denoting a great place for the king’s portrait to stay. It is known to have been repaired during King Yeongjo's reign, but it is not known what the place was used for prior to the restoration. Since King Yeongjo served as king for a long period of time, his portraits were regularly drawn, and a royal portrait painted in 1744 during the 20th year of King Yeongjo’s reign was enshrined here, and after King Yeongjo's death it was used as “Honjeon”, a place where the spirit of King Yeongjo stayed.  Thereafter, it is not known exactly what it was used for, but now it is used as a building for storing the royal portrait (copy) of King Yeongjo. Since King Yeongjo lived in Gyeonghuigung Palace for about half of the period of his reign, his affinity towards Gyeonghuigung Palace was unusual.  If you go behind Taeryeongjeon Hall, you will see the rock of the king upon which Gyeonghuigung Palace was built. Shall we go to take a look?

stories.title: Overview of Gyeonghuigung Palace
stories.script: Gyeonghuigung Palace is located in Jongno-gu, Seoul. It is the site of Gyeonghuigung Palace, which was a secondary palace in the late Joseon Dynasty. Changdeokgung Palace and Changgyeonggung Palace are called Donggung Palace, while Gyeonghuigung Palace is called Seogung Palace. The kings have used it as a place to take charge of political affairs since the reign of King Injo.  Gyeonghuigung Palace is known as the palace built by King Gwanghae in the late Joseon Dynasty. Its original name was Gyeongdeokgung Palace, which was renamed by King Yeongjo as it was pronounced similar to the posthumous name of King Wonjong. Initially, it was a large palace that was built with a lot of halls. However, its halls were mostly burned down in 1829. The remaining buildings were torn down during the Japanese Occupation. The palace was severely damaged and reduced to its current size.   Gyeonghuigung Palace has five gates: Heunghwamun Gate, the main gate; Heungwonmun Gate, the east gate; Mudeokmun Gate, the north gate; Sunguimun Gate; and Gaeyangmun Gate, the south gate. In addition, there are more than 100 large and small buildings, including Sungjeongjeon Hall, Jeonghyeonjeon Hall, Jeongjeon Hall, Jungbokjeon Hall, and Songnyeonjeon Hall. Also, Gyeonghuigung Palace has a different building arrangement from Gyeongbokgung Palace. Instead of building the inner and outer courts in a vertical line, they were built side by side in Gyeonghuigung Palace. Furthermore, it’s usual to see the main gate of a palace in the right corner. Perhaps it’s because it is a detached palace, which allows it to be built differently from the formal palace architecture style.  Gyeonghuigung Palace completely lost its status when it was turned over to the Japanese Government-General of Korea in 1910. The temples in Gyeonghuigung Palace were later used for completely different purposes than the palaces, including the Gyeongseong Middle School Teacher Training Center (currently the Seoul High School), the main hall of Jogyesa Temple, lecture rooms, and the main gate of the hotel. Currently, Gyeonghuigung Palace has been partially restored to its original form through the restoration project of the Seoul Metropolitan Government.

stories.title: Heunghwamun Gate (Gyeonghuigung Palace)
stories.script: Heunghwamun Gate was the main gate of Gyeonghuigung Palace. Its name literally means “to educate the people”. It did not only act as the entrance of the palace, but the king also listened to the difficulties of his people, gave out food to the poor, interrogated the criminals, and released the prisoners at the gate.  After Gyeonghuigung Palace was demolished in the Japanese colonial era, Heunghwamun Gate was removed and used as the main gate of Bakmunsa Temple in 1915. After liberation, it was used as the main gate of the hotel and lost its original role. Eventually, although its original site was already occupied by the Salvation Army Building, it was relocated to its current location and restored to its former state in 1988 through the restoration project.   Heunghwamun Gate, as the main gate of a secondary palace, has revealed the palace's specialty through its appearance. Heunghwamun Gate was built on a single floor, as opposed to the two-story main gates of other palaces. It has four columns in front that support the entire intricately carved wooden structure and tiled roof. There are also three entrances, each between two columns. The central entrance was built with an arrow fence up on top.   Gyeonghuigung Palace initially had more than 100 buildings. All the buildings were either burned down or torn down by several hardships in the past. Although the restoration of Gyeonghuigung Palace began in 1988, only some buildings could have been restored, and currently only three main halls are left. Heunghwamun Gate is one of them. Now let’s find more stories hidden in this secondary palace!

stories.title: Sungjeongjeon Gate (Gyeonghuigung Palace)
stories.script: Sungjeongjeon Hall, the central building of Gyeonghuigung Palace, was the royal audience hall that served as the king's office since the reign of King Injo in the Joseon Dynasty. Sungjeong means honoring state affairs. It was a place where the king managed and discussed politics or the affairs of the nation. The king had a morning assembly with his courtiers or held official events such as feasts and envoy receptions. Jeonggung, the main palaces during the Joseon Dynasty, were primarily comprised of Gyeongbokgung Palace and Changdeokgung Palace. However, regardless of being a secondary palace where the king only stayed temporarily, Gyeonghuigung Palace served as the main palace. The most prominent kings of the mid- and late-Joseon Period have stayed here, including King Injo, King Sukjong, King Gyeongjong, King Yeongjo, and King Jeongjo. There are various reasons why the kings stayed in the Gyeonghuigung Palace. King Injo had to live here because Changdeokgung Palace was burned down during the “Injo restoration”. King Sukjong was born in Changdeokgung Palace, but he often visited Gyeonghuigung Palace, where there is a record of the demise of King Yeongjo. As King Gyeongjong, King Jeongjo, and King Heonjong held their coronation ceremonies at Sungjeongmun Gate, it actually pointed out that all events were held at Sungjeongjeon Hall. Sungjeongjeon Hall in the current Gyeonghuigung Palace was restored in 1988 during the restoration project of Gyeonghuigung Palace. The actual building of Sungjeongjeon Hall was sold during the Japanese invasion of Korea and is currently located at Dongguk University's Seoul Campus. It is said that the restoration was carried out by using the original building as a reference. However, since the interior of the former building had changed significantly, the interior restoration could only be conducted by referring to Geunjeongjeon Hall of Gyeongbokgung Palace and Injeongjeon Hall of Changdeokgung Palace. The building that connects the back of Sungjeongjeon Hall is Jajeongjeon Hall. Aren't you curious what other stories are hidden here?

stories.title: Jajeongjeon Hall (Gyeonghuigung Palace)
stories.script: Whereas official events of the nation were held at the royal audience hall of Sungjeongjeon Hall, the Jajeongjeon Hall right behind it served as the king's office, where he actually worked. Halls like this were called Pyeonjeon, such as the Sajeongjeon Hall of Gyeongbokgung Palace and the Seonjeongjeon Hall of Changdeokgung Palace. The king reviewed the documents written by the people and his courtiers and discussed important state affairs with the courtiers. King Injo, King Sukjong, King Yeongjo, and King Cheoljong were the kings who handled state affairs here.  However, Jajeongjeon Hall of Gyeonghuigung Palace also served as Binjeon for storing coffins after the king's death. When King Sukjong died, it became the Binjeon for King Sukjong, and when Emperor Gojong died, his portrait and ancestral tablet were enshrined here. Following the damage to the buildings of Gyeonghuigung Palace during the Japanese invasion of Korea, Jajeongjeon Hall was also torn down. Until 1988, it was restored to its present state through the restoration project.  If you look at the corridor leading from Jajeongjeon Hall to Taeryeongjeon Hall, you will see the actual floor bricks used in the old times that were discovered in an excavation. The newly restored floor bricks next to them allow you to compare their size and color. In fact, when the king moved around in the palace, he was supposed to avoid stepping on the ground as much as possible, instead sitting in a sedan chair or walking through roofed corridors. The stepping bricks for the king were not rough arch stones but flat bricks. This is no doubt an impressive design.  Now, let's walk on the floor bricks where the king stepped and head to the Taeryeongjeon Hall.

stories.title: Taeryeongjeon Hall (Gyeonghuigung Palace)
stories.script: In 1760, King Yeongjo renamed Gyeongdeokgung Palace as Gyeonghuigung Palace. It was also called the Western Palace. He changed the name of the palace because it contained the same letters as the posthumous title of King Wonjong. Therefore, he renamed the palace by adding the letter “hui” to replace “deok” with the meaning “to be happy and shine”. Taeryeongjeon Hall was rebuilt through restoration work that began in 1988. In order to restore the original state of Gyeonghuigung Palace, the construction has taken reference to some reading materials from the Joseon Dynasty, such as Plan of the Western Palace, Construction Process Record of the Western Palace, and History Record of the Palaces. Also, it was restored at the location of the stylobate, which was confirmed through actual excavation work. The meaning of the Chinese characters in Taeryeongjeon Hall is a large and comfortable pavilion, denoting a great place to enshrine portraits of the kings. It is known that the hall was repaired during King Yeongjo's reign, but no one knows what its utility has been since then. Since King Yeongjo had a long reign as monarch, his portraits were regularly drawn. A royal portrait of him painted in 1744 during the 20th year of his reign is enshrined here. After King Yeongjo had passed away, it was used as Honjeon, where the spirit of King Yeongjo stayed. Thereafter, no one could figure out what it was used for exactly, but now it is used as a building to store the original copy of King Yeongjo’s royal portrait. As it is said that King Yeongjo lived in Gyeonghuigung Palace for about half of his reign, his affinity for Gyeonghuigung Palace was unusually special. If you go behind Taeryeongjeon Hall, you will see the rock of the king, which was the reason why Gyeonghuigung Palace was built here. Shall we go and take a look at it?

stories.title: Seoam Rock (Gyeonghuigung Palace)
stories.script: As King Gwanghaegun of Joseon was crowned after the Japanese invasion of Korea in 1592, rebuilding Hanyang after the war became his first top mission. At first, he planned to stay in the Eastern Palaces, which are Changdeokgung Palace and Changgyeonggung Palace, instead of Gyeongbokgung Palace, which had been burned down. However, as he believed they were inauspicious sites, he built Ingyeonggung Palace at the foot of Inwangsan Mountain. King Gwanghaegun only received a little affection from his father, King Seonjo. In contrast, while he was still a crown prince, King Seonjo only cared about his sibling, the fifth son of the king, Prince Jeongwongun, and played favorites. Even after ascending to the throne, he recognized Prince Jeongwongun as a threat to his throne and never stopped keeping the prince in check. One day, a rumor began to circulate that the Saemoondong site where Prince Jeongwongun lived was filled with the energy of a king. The rumors quickly spread to King Gwanghaegun, and a written memorial said Prince Neungchanggun, the third son of Prince Jeongwongun, was vying for the throne. As a result, King Gwanghaegun exiled Prince Neungchanggun to Ganghwa-do. Two years later, the king tore down the house of Prince Jeongwongun and built the Western Palace on the site. The Western Palace was the present Gyeonghuigung Palace. However, the first son of Prince Jeongwongun, Prince Neungyanggun, had actually seized power. After he had staged a coup, he expelled King Gwanghaegun and ascended the throne. He was then titled King Injo. The Chinese characters of Seoam originally meant a rock in the west, but when King Sukjong heard about the story of King Gwanghaegun, he changed its Chinese character to carry the meaning of “an auspicious rock”. Thereafter, he wrote the name in his own handwriting on the stone laid around a square mound to announce its new name. Looking at the Seoam behind Taeryeongjeon Hall from a distance, it looks merely massive in size, but its inside resembles a cave. This looked like something was kept inside. If you get closer to it, you will see it is not a cave but a fountain in a rock. Furthermore, looking at the buildings of Gyeonghuigung Palace from Seoam, it may appear as a huge rock behind the palace, but in fact, the palace was built by taking advantage of this topography.  Why not take in the uplifting energy of Seoam before moving on to the next trip?

stories.title: Yeouido Park - Yeouido Park (Yeouido Airfield)
stories.script: Yeouido Park - Yeouido Park (Yeouido Airfield)  Yeouido is one of the islands created by Hangang River as earth and sand having flowed by the river water were accumulated and piled up. During the Joseon Dynasty, a ferry was built here where boats to go into the city were set afloat. We can tell its traces by the name, “Yeoinaru”, that we still use today. Can you believe that Yeouido Park, a popular location for strolls and exercises, used to be a runway where airplanes departed and landed?  In 1916 during the Japanese colonial era, Yeouido was a piece of land that belonged to Goyang-gun, Gyeonggi-do, not Seoul. In their search of a place to land airplanes close to Gyeongseong (Seoul), Japan built a runway and a hangar to store the planes in Yeouido and operated it under the name of “Gyeongseong Airfield.” So the runway was built where today's Yeouido Park is located.  On August 18, 1945, a C-47 transport plane arrived at Gyeongseong Airfield, which was celebrating the Liberation after Japan’s surrender. The people on the flight were Kim Jun-yeop, No Neung-seo, Lee Beom-seok and Chang Chun-ha who were commissioned officers of the Korean Liberation Army. They arrived on a U.S. military plane as a part of the U.S. military mission, not as members of the Liberation Army.  Chang Chun-ha’s autobiography “Tolbegae records, “When we arrived at Gyeongseong Airfield and were waiting in a Japanese army barrack, Colonel Shibusawa who was in charge of Gyeongseong Airfield and Major Ueda Hideo knelt and offered us a drink so we accepted drinks from the Japanese people for the first time in our lives.” Later, Japanese troops that had been stationed in South Korea returned to Japan by the U.S. and UN forces.  Gyeongseong Airfield was used until 1971 while serving as Yeouido International Airport and Air Force Base, and, ever since Yeouido began to be developed, it has been used as a plaza and a park. Once a plaza was established here, it started to hold national events and also offer citizens a place to relax.  If you go to the basketball court in Yeouido Park, there is an aircraft on display that is exactly the same as the C-47 transport plane that the commissioned officers of the Korean Liberation Army had flown to Korea with. The plane with which the provisional government officers arrived at Gimpo Airfield was the same model, and you can actually walk in and sit inside the machine, and also watch a video to see the photos taken the day when the provisional government officers returned home. Now that we are celebrating the 100th anniversary of the establishment of the Provisional Government, shall we go and greet the provisional government officers who have returned to us?

stories.title: Former Capitol Hall and Gwanghwamun Gate
stories.audioTitle: Former Capitol Hall and Gwanghwamun Gate
stories.script: Former Capitol Hall and Gwanghwamun Gate  During the Japanese occupation period, the Japanese Government-General building was seated where today’s Gwanghwamun Gate is. After Gyeongsul Gukchi in 1910, Japan established an administrative system to colonize and govern Joseon, and a governor-general was appointed to oversee the system to begin colonization.  In 1916, Japan relocated Gwanghwamun, the main gate of Gyeongbokgung Palace, to destroy the spirit and culture of Joseon people, and demolished its walls and structures to construct the government-general building. Completed in 1926, the government-general became the symbol of imperialistic colonization that completely concealed Gyeongbokgung from people's sight.  After Liberation in 1945, the U.S. military came into Seoul and used this place as the military government office. Upon their return to Korea, President Kim Gu and Dr. Rhee Syngman continued to discuss with the U.S. Military on the establishment of a government, and, as a result, an independent government of South Korea was founded. The South Korean government used this place as the Capitol administrative office that housed the presidential office and other administrative departments.  Then, starting in 1986, the administrative departments were moved out as the building was considered to be a symbol of Japanese imperialistic invasion so, instead, the National Museum of Korea became the tenant. In 1993, discussions began to take place regarding demolition of the building, which eventually started to be torn down in 1995, the 50th anniversary of the Liberation. Then, in November 1996, it was completely demolished to disappear into history. The demolition of the Capitol was broadcast live on TV nationwide.  Once the Capitol was gone, the original owners, Gwanghwamun and Gyeongbokgung, returned to this place. Since its return to the Korean people, Gwanghwamun continues to be with us as important cultural heritage that symbolizes our history and culture.

stories.title: Gwanghwamun Gate
stories.script: Gwanghwamun Gate  [Eunuch Officer Kim] Welcome to Gwanghwamun Gate, where the king's great virtue shines across the country. Gwanghwamun Gate, the main gate to the south of Gyeongbokgung Palace, serves as a symbolic gate for the royal family of the Joseon Dynasty. During the Joseon Dynasty, there was Gyeongbokgung Palace on the inside of the gate, while the area of Hanseong City Administration (the department that now serves as Seoul City Hall), commonly referred to the 'Street of Six Ministries' as well as Jongno Street where the people lead their lives, were on the outside. Gwanghwamun Gate, which is in the center of everyone's passage, also served as a reminder of the time and the news by hanging a bell and a drum in the upper section.  [Lady Officer Kim] It's like the pair of Haechi (Haetae or mythical lion) at the gate are saying 'I defend justice!' with their stern stare.   [Eunuch Officer Kim] It is, isn't it? You may feel that because they were erected to denote that these Haechi are watching over the officials in the Street of Six Ministries and the king to conduct administrative affairs in a righteous manner.  [Lady Officer Kim] It's reassuring to have Haechi at both sides! Wow, Lord Kim! It's my first time to pass through this gate! There's a phoenix drawn on the ceiling!  [Eunuch Officer Kim] How wonderful! Originally, Gwanghwamun Gate was used by envoys from China and the royal families for their official visits. I have passed through the side gates many times before, but this is also my first time to enter through the central gate. It feels amazing! For your reference, the left gate has Nakguibuseo, or the painting of a tortoise, and the right door has Hamabuseo, or the painting of a horse.   [Lady Officer Kim] We had to go to a lot of trouble to move Gwanghwamun Gate back here in 2010, so of course we have to dress it up nicely! Gwanghwamun Gate was pushed back on the priority list by the Japanese Government-General of Korea during the Japanese occupation, and having moved near the Geonchunmun Gate, it was bombed out during the Korean War. It was restored in 1968, but it wasn't until the Joseon Governor-General's building, called the Capitol building, was removed in the 1990s that it was returned to its original location.  [Eunuch Officer Kim] So during the restoration, 7 roof tiles with symbols (ten objects symbolizing immortality) were correctly placed on the hip! And the aesthetic elements that blend with the ridges of Bugaksan Mountain in the back were revived just right! Whether long ago or today, everyone probably knows how overwhelming it feels to have Gwanghwamun Gate here!  [Lady Officer Kim] Wow, we finally agree on something! Well then, let's buy a ticket and begin our journey towards the Royal Court!

stories.title: Gimpo Airport - Gimpo Airport (Gimpo Airfield)
stories.script: Gimpo Airport - Gimpo Airport (Gimpo Airfield)  Gimpo International Airport, which is the place that has seen many scenes of greetings and good-byes, was the airport that had served as a gateway to Korea until the construction of Incheon International Airport. It was 1937 when airplanes began to fly to this area that had previously been filled with rice paddies and fields. Having started the Sino-Japanese War, Japan started to strengthen its military power with a focus on Joseon, one of their colonies. Japan constructed factories across Korea to produce war supplies, as well as training centers and bases to train their troops. It was here that bases and runways for the training of the air force were built, which belonged to Gimpo-si, Gyeonggi-do at the time. That is the origin of the  history of Gimpo Airfield .  For the construction of the runways, Joseon workers living nearby were mobilized against their will. Between the time of its completion and Japan's final surrender to the Allied Forces at the end of World War II, the runways served as a training ground for “Kamikaze”, suicide attack units of Japanese Air Force.  In November 1945 after the Liberation, a C-47 transport plane, which left Jiangwan Airfield of Shanghai, arrived at Gimpo with 15 key figures of the Provisional Government of Korea including Kim Gu, the president, and Kim Kyu-sik, the vice president. But, at the airfield, they could not find a single Taegukgi let alone any crowd welcoming them home. It was because the U.S. considered the provisional government members as a threat to the U.S. military regime and, thus, arranged their return to home quietly as ordinary civilians.   Chang Chun-ha, a Korean Liberation Army officer who came to Korea at the same time, recorded the moment when they arrived at Gimpo Airport in his autobiography, “Tolbegae as follows - “When we descended down the steps one by one, we were greeted by a handful of American soldiers. Our expectations were completely shattered into thin air.” The U.S. military made sure to block any contact between the provisional government members and civilians, and, immediately upon their arrival, the provisional government officers were transported to Seoul by U.S. military vehicles.  The officers stayed at Gyeonggyojang and Myeongdong Hotel in Seoul and put in great efforts to establish a unified government on the Korean Peninsula. However, the nation was divided into North Korea and South Korea, with respective governments founded on both sides of the DMZ.  Gimpo Airfield, which held the dreams and sorrows of the provisional government officers, received a new name of “Gimpo International Airport” after the renovation work during the post-Korean War period. It still operates as an international airport to this day.

stories.title: Daemyeongheon House, Ganghwa-do
stories.script: Within the south gate of Ganghwasanseong Fortress, there is a hanok that has since turned into a guesthouse. Known as Daemyeongheon House, it is a historic hanok that was once visited by Mr. Baekbeom Kim Gu.  In 1896, a young man named Kim Chang-su killed a Japanese person, who had been on the run after murdering Empress Myeongseong, in Chihapo, Hwanghae-do. He was imprisoned in Incheon Gamniseo, awaiting his final verdict. Of course, the Japanese people insisted on a death sentence but Emperor Gojong had no intention of it so Kim continued his prison life as a prisoner on trial without a finalization of his sentence. At this point, there was a man named Kim Ju-gyeong who was moved by the justness of Kim Chang-su so he consistently communicated with the prisoner via letters and advised him to break out of the jail. Finally in 1898, Kim Chang-su successfully escaped.  He wandered throughout the country before coming to Ganghwado in search of his supporter but unfortunately, Kim Ju-gyeong had already disappeared to Vladivostok to aid the independence movement. Instead, Kim Chang-su stayed at the house of Kim Jin-gyeong, the younger brother of Kim Ju-gyeong, and opened an academy for three months to teach the children in Ganghwado. Around this time, Kim became acquaintances with Yu Wan-mu, a friend of Kim Ju-gyeong’s, and, based on a suggestion from Yu, Kim Chang-su changed his name to Kim Gu.  Upon his return to Korea after the Liberation, Kim Gu visited Kim Ju-gyeong’s house again but he could not meet Kim Ju-gyeong who had been missing in Vladivostok. Together with Kim Jin-gyeong and others who had supported the independence movement, Kim Gu took a commemorative photo at Daemyeongheon and also left a note saying, “Taking a picture in front of an old building”, in Baekbeomilji.  The Daemyeongheon building we see today was built by Hwang Guk-hyeon, a wealthy farmer in Ganghwado, in 1928. Hwang was an active supporter of the independence movement and known to offer a place to hide to the independence fighters who had been on the run from the Japanese army. It is a hanok constructed in the modern era so you can see a unique combination of the Western and Korean architectural elements in one space.  Daemyeongheon is currently a privately owned guesthouse so those of you who wish to visit need to RSVP to view the place with an admission fee.

stories.title: Hyochang Park
stories.script: Hyochang Park  Hyochang Park (Hyochangwon)  If you come out of Exit 1 of Hyochang Park Station on Seoul Subway Line 6 and walk up the hill for about 10 minutes, you will get to Hyochang Park. There is the statue of Lee Bong-chang near the main gate so you can easily find the park. Today, locals like to rest and relax here but it is also a place with noble significance that is home of the graves of three patriotic martyrs and members of the provisional government who dedicated their lives to independence.  Its original name was Hyochangwon where the tomb of Prince Munhyo, the first son of King Jeongjo of Joseon, was located. There was also the tombs of the Royal Consort Uibin Seong, Prince Munhyo’s mother, and of Park Suk-ui who was a concubine of King Sunjo of Joseon. When the tombs were relocated to Seosamneung in Goyang, Gyeonggi-do during the Japanese occupation period, this area turned into a park.  In 1946 after Liberation, the remains of Patriots Lee Bong-chang, Yun Bong-gil and Baek Jeong-gi returned to Korea and were buried here as a national funeral, and then, in 1948, the remains of Yi Dong-nyeong and Cha Ri-seok who had served as members of the provisional government were returned and buried in this park as well. Cho Seong-hwan, the head of the provisional government’s military department who had passed away in the same year, was also buried here, and, when Mr. Kim Gu’s remains were laid to rest in 1949, Hyochang Park became a haven for those who devoted their lives to the nation and the people. There is a fake grave for An Jung-geun next to the graves of the three patriotic martyrs, and it is still empty because Mr. An's remains have not been found yet. In 1979, Uiyeolsa was established to enshrine the portraits of the patriots laid to rest here and hold annual joint memorial ceremonies.  100 years have passed since the foundation of the provisional government. If you visit Hyochang Park, why don’t you courteously give silent prayers in front of the graves of the independence patriots and Uiyeolsa?

stories.title: Kim Gu Museum & Library
stories.script: Kim Gu Museum & Library  Not far from the main gate of Hyochang Park is a memorial hall commemorating Baekbeom Kim Gu. The reason why a memorial hall was established here is that there is a cemetery in Hyochang Park where Baekbeom and his wife, Mrs. Choi Jun-rye, are buried together.  Baekbeom dedicated his entire life to the independence of Korea and strove to overcome the Japanese colonial era by the power of the Joseon people and to found one, unified government after the Liberation. He is also well-known to us as the President of the Provisional Government of Korea.  At Kim Gu Museum & Library, you can see his life story from his childhood as Kim Changahm and the days of his youth as Kim Changsoo and to the period before becoming the president of the Provisional Government. Kim Gu’s story begins with a large statue in the center of the exhibition room's 1st floor.  In 1876, he was born as Kim Changahm in Haeju, Hwanghae-do Province and grew up in a fallen Yangban family. When he was a young boy, he learned letters and texts through Chinese classics (Confucianism) was awakened to the reality of the country under the tutelage of his lifelong teacher and a Confucian scholar, Ko Neung-seon. As he grew up to be a young man, he joined the Donghak Movement and changed his name to “Kim Changsoo”. His will to defend the country against foreign powers even after the struggles of the Donghak Movement were thwarted by the Japanese army can be seen through the Chihapo incident and activities as a member of Sinminhoe. While he was wandering around the country, he changed his name again to “Kim Gu” and defected to Shanghai after the March 1st Independence Movement of 1919, participating in the provisional government of Korea. Starting his career there as the Police Minister, he served as a key figure of the provisional government.   From the 2nd floor of the exhibit, you can learn about the life including the final days of Kim Gu as a member of the provisional government. From inside the memorial, you can quietly pay your respects to Kim Gu’s grave outside through the window. Photo-taking is prohibited in all exhibition rooms so please watch quietly.

stories.title: Changnyeong Uponeup Marsh (1988)
stories.script: In Changnyeong, which has been long referred to as the “Fire Village” from the Gaya Era, there is a large marsh. Uponeup Marsh, located about 10 minutes by bus from downtown Changnyeong, is the second marsh designated as the Ramsar Wetland in Korea. It is the largest of the wetlands in the country.  Uponeup Marsh is so large that, depending on where you depart from, you can see and experience whole different things. In general, visitors start at the Ecological Center. This route is suitable for a walking trip or bicycle trip, which is recommended to those who want to take a slow stroll. If you want to see migratory birds, start at the parking lot of Somok Village.  Uponeup Marsh includes Upo, Sajipo and Mokpo sections, as well as Jjokjibeol and sanbakbeol wetlands.These are the names made during the Japanese colonial period, and their original Korean names are Sobeol, Namubeol, and Moraeboel. People who lived here for a long time prefer to call them by their old Korean name. The marsh was created by Topyeongcheon Stream and Nakdonggang River nearby. It is assumed that the bank was piled up following the flow of the river and stagnated water, thereby creating the Uponeup Marsh today. It used to play the role of the reservoir in the past. It was also a fishing spot to catch freshwater fish by riding a boat or throwing a net. Now is the home to migratory birds, freshwater fish, and wild plants. Ecological Wetland School and Ecological Experience Center provide both educational and scientific opportunities to see and learn about the ecosystem of the wetland and experience dugout canoe riding, loach fishing, and aquatic insect hunting. Come and see the famous Uponeup Marsh.   <This guide was recorded by Kwon So-hyun of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Birthplace of Park Sang-jin
stories.audioTitle: A flower blooming on arid and desolate land.
stories.script: Birthplace of Park Sang-jin  [Woman] In 1910, a smart young man became the first candidate to successfully pass the examination to become a judge in Korean Empire history. But when he was ordered to take up a judgeship in Pyongyang Court, he immediately refused.    [Park Sang-jin the Patriot] “I cannot punish an independence fighter!”  [Man] The young man, who was 26 at the time, had a strong conviction in his voice. Who was this man?   “Goheon” Park Sang-jin was born in 1884 in Songjeong-dong, Buk-gu, Ulsan-si. He was the eldest son of Park Si-gyu. Although he married the daughter of the famous Choi family in Gyeongju, and later on became a judge, Park Sang-jin chose to be an independence fighter instead of having the decadent life of an aristocrat.    [Park Sang-jin the Patriot] “Hit that wagon and rob the Japanese of their taxes!”  [Subordinates] “Yes, sir!”   [Man] July 1915. The Korea Liberation Corps was created in Dalseong Park in Daegu-si, and Park Sang-jin served as its inaugural commander. Under his command, the Korea Liberation Corps robbed a mail wagon carrying taxes from Gwangmyeong-ri in Gyeongju, and instigated the Daegu handgun incident. The Korea Liberation Corps continued to escalate its attacks against Japan. When Lee Seok-dae, the lieutenant commander of the Korea Liberation Corps, died, Park Sang-jin appointed Kim Jwa-jin as his replacement.   [Woman] Park Sang-jin swore a blood oath of brotherhood with Kim Jwa-jin and Shin Dol-seok. He invested his entire fortune into the independence movement and fought  against the Japanese. But when the Japanese apprehended Jang Doo-hwan, the person who assassinated pro-Japanese figure Park Yong-ha, they discovered the Korea Liberation Corps as well. Park attempted to flee overseas. But he was captured on his way home upon learning that his mother was gravely ill.   [Park Sang-jin the Patriot] “I was fortunate enough to be born as a man in this difficult life. Nevertheless, I leave this earth without achieving anything. I see the mountains and rivers laughing at me.”  [Man] August 1921. Park Sang-jin was executed at a penitentiary in Daegu. His last poem shows how grief-stricken he was. Park Sang-jin spent all of his money funding the independence movement. Thus, Park’s house was sold to another family. Fortunately, the municipal government of Ulsan restored the house in 2007. The birthplace of Park Sang-jin and Park Sang-jin History Park  will give you a chance to feel his passion to win independence for his country. Even when his country was lost, Park Sang-jin made the ultimate sacrifice. His memory will live on forever for generations to come.    “Oesol” Choi Hyeon-bae       [Woman] It was the 1940s, the final years of Japanese colonial rule of Korea.   [Man] “We will perfect our language!”   [Man] If you watch the character Ryu Jeong-hwan in the movie “MAL-MO-E,” you will learn about the life of “Oesol” Choi Hyeon-bae.   [Man] Born in Ulsan, Choi Hyeon-bae created the Korean Language Society, and led the “Malmoe (dictionary in pure Korean)” movement. As an independence fighter and Korean language scholar, Choi was arrested by the Japanese just before he was able to publish the Joseon Language Dictionary in 1942.  “Oesol” Choi Hyeon-bae insisted that the “Korean language is his life.” To commemorate his dedication to the Korean language, the government built Oesol Memorial Hall where Choi Hyeon-bae was born. Here, you can learn about his work researching and promoting Korean language.   [Woman] Thanks to his passion and willingness to risk his own life protecting our language in the face of strong oppression from the Japanese Empire, we were able to perfect our language to what it is today.    Ugasan Mountain Yupo Beacon    [Man] Let’s move on to another place in Ulsan that will awaken the true patriot inside you. We are going to head to Ugasan Mountain to see the Yupo Beacon, which people used during the reign of King Sejong to defend against Japanese pirate attacks.   [Woman] This is part of the Beacon Fire Network along our eastern seaboard. Records of the Yupo Beacon can be found in the “Sejong Chronicles” and the 	“Donggukyeojiseunglam.” Back then, if the guards lit the fire at the Military Beacon, guards at the old Nammokcheon would receive the signal, relay it to Haseoji in Gyeongju, then all the way up to Hanyang. In total, Ulsan has eight beacons. Given its strategic importance,  Ulsan did suffer numerous attacks from Japanese pirates. However, the beacons always did their job to keep Korea safe.   [Man] In 1894, the 32nd year of King Gojong’s reign, Joseon introduced the telephone system. As a result, the Beacon System was abolished. Currently, Yupo Beacon only has a round fireplace made with naturally sourced rocks, a protective wall, and the foundations of a barracks that housed the guards stationed at the beacon. Our Coastal Beacon system is an important historical resource, and a proud part of Ulsan’s history.

stories.title: Ulsan Daegyo Bridge Observatory
stories.audioTitle: “Yooha” Hong Se-tae with poems describing the beautiful views of Ulsan
stories.script: If you cross the Ulsan Daegyo Bridge that connects the Whale Cultural Village in Jangsaengpo, Nam-gu, with the Dong-gu region in Ulsan, you’ll arrive at the Ulsan Daegyo Bridge Observatory, which is quickly becoming the signature landmark of Ulsan.   Atop the Ulsan Daegyo Bridge Observatory, you can enjoy panoramic views of the three major industrial complexes in Ulsan - the petrochemical, automobile, and shipbuilding complexes - in addition to Ulsan’s 7 largest mountains.   In particular, the crimson sunset and the glittering lights scattered across the industrial complexes make the entire area look like a magical palace at night.     300 years ago, a new official was sent to the Nammok area of Magolsan Mountain in Dong-gu, Ulsan, to manage the military horse ranch.   His name was “Yooha” Hong Se-tae. Also known as one of the most prominent poets during the late-Joseon Dynasty era, the history books say that Hong Se-tae often communicated with Buddhists monks at Wolbongsa Temple (a temple built to pray for the spirits of horses) and wrote poems where the Ulsan Daegyo Bridge Observatory stands today.         ‘Living a trapped existence deep in Nammok,       I find myself in a wider world at last.       The spring breeze wafts across my face       and my sleeves flutter in the wind.        The vast blue ocean spreads before me       where the shadows of horses can travel afar.       Magnificent clouds rush overhead       carrying a boat traveling ten thousand miles.       Oh, the poor fishermen.’  The above is an excerpt of a poem titled, “Poem for Yeompo on the way to Gyeongju.” It is a Chinese-style poem written by Hong Se-tae as he took in the views of Yeompo from where the Ulsan Daegyo Bridge Observatory is today.    Born as the bastard son of an aristocrat during the Joseon Dynasty, Hong Se-tae led a tragic life. Most notably, he had to endure the premature death of his own son and seven daughters.  Despite these tragedies, Hong channeled his emotions into poetry that blossomed like beautiful lotus flowers blooming in muddy waters. In all, he composed more than 200 poems depicting the everyday lives of commoners in Ulsan.     Wolbongsa Temple, located near the Ulsan Daegyo Bridge Observatory, was built during the fourth year of King Gyeongsun’s reign (Shilla Dynasty), and the temple has been revered as an auspicious site ever since.   Gleaning some of that auspicious energy from Wolbongsa Temple, Ulsan Daegyo Bridge Observatory has also become apromising site for visitors.   You can enjoy some truly beautiful views of the East Sea during both day and night from the Observatory. In terms of great views of the East Sea, the glittering lights of the steel mills in Pohang serve as a must-see attraction, and the Gyeongju Yangnam Jusangjeolli Cliff Observatory offers a unique experience as well.

stories.title: Gangdong Jejeon Village
stories.audioTitle: A tale of blind love, “The eel that loved the princess”
stories.script: Gangdong in Buk-gu has a magnificent trail (Sarang-gil) along its beautiful coast. If you follow the trail past the mural street, you will arrive at a peaceful little village.     This village, which features layers of terraced rice paddies, is called Gangdong Jejeon Village. In the past, the village was also known as Jejeon Village due to the abundance of Paper Mulberry trees in the area.     Jejeon Village is a hidden gem in the Buk-gu area. It is best known for its delicacies - eel and sea mustard.   Meanwhile, Jejeonhang Port - a destination along the Sarang-gil trail - is famous for a love story that features an eel.    One day, an eel fell in love with the daughter of the Dragon King (king of the sea). He begged the Dragon King to let him marry the princess but he only managed to anger him. Eventually, the Dragon King ordered his soldiers to remove the eel’s eyes.  Even without his eyes, however, the eel remained persistent. So, the Dragon King came up with a cunning plan.         (Dragon King speaks)    “If you swim across the Pacific Ocean and return without eating anything, I will let you marry the princess.”    The eel danced with joy at the King’s proposition. He immediately went on his adventure to traverse the Pacific. However, because he didn’t have any eyes, legend says that the eel is still fumbling his way through the ocean somewhere.    Once news of the blind eel spread through the sea, countless other eels gathered around Jejeonhang Port to support him.     Jejeon Village is home to “Sarang-gil Jejeon Eel” (first-ever registered Buk-gu village corporation) and a museum that gives visitors a chance to learn about the history of Jejeon Village.     Come and enjoy the sea breeze and some healthy eel dishes on the beach, and experience the unique ambiance of an authentic fishing village.

stories.title: Yeongnam Alps
stories.audioTitle: Lady Jeong, the virtuous widow, and the tiger’s grave
stories.script: The Yeongnam Alps - or the “Korean Alps” - gets its name thanks to some truly beautiful mountains and landscapes.   More specifically, the Yeongnam Alps features nine mountains, including Gajisan Mountain that sits on the border of Gyeongsangnam-do and Gyeongsangbuk-do, each of which are at least 1,000m above sea level.   In winter, the fantastic silver grass plains stretching across 33,058m2 along with the snowcapped peaks turn the Yeongnam Alps into something you might read in an ancient myth.  Gajisan Mountain is one of the top-100 mountains in Korea.   It features the historic site of Seoknamsa Temple (the premier temple of the Yeongnam region), Seonbawi (home to a white dragon), Ssalbawi (a rock that use to spout rice from its hole), and other mysterious legends.   Among all of the tales in Sangbuk-myeon (in Ulju-gun), where Seoknamsa Temple is located, the strangest story involves a monument built to house a tablet commemorating a virtuous lady from the region and a tiger.    During the early years of King Taejong’s reign (Joseon Dynasty), a lady named Jeong spent three years at her late husband’s grave in mourning as was custom at the time.   Tending to a grave alone as a woman was an immensely difficult task.   One night, someone with glowing eyes carefully approached the grieving widow.   Surprised by the approaching stranger, Jeong tried to take a step back. But the visitor with glowing eyes did not attack her. It rubbed its back against the ground and sat down.        The glowing eyes belonged to none other than a tiger.   The tiger helped the lady tend to her husband’s grave for a while. But soon, it stopped visiting. One night, the tiger appeared in Jeong’s dream and begged her to save him.     What happened to the lady and the tiger? Why did they have this connection? Did the widow finish her three years mourning by the side of her husband’s grave?    Nature and people become one, and people can enjoy a relaxing break while healing themselves at the Yeongnam Alps. The annual paragliding competition and International Climbing Center have turned the region into a popular trekking destination for mountaineers and trekking enthusiasts.

stories.title: Jujeon Mongdol Beach
stories.script: Romantic Pebble Beach, Jujeon Mongdol Beach   At 19.1km-long, Haeparang Trail Course 9 will take you from Ilsan Beach all the way to Jeongjahang Port in Ulsan. The course features a great ocean trail and the famous Jujeon Mongdol Beach.  The word “Mongdol” is what locals call round pebbles with no discernible sharp edges. Jujeon Mongdol Beach, which stretches from Jujeon-dong to Gangdong-dong, is filled with these pebbles instead of sand. That is why you will often see people walking on the pebble beach to massage their feet using the Mongdol pebbles.  Jujeon Mongdol Beach also produces a distinct acoustic effect that sounds like pebbles rolling in the water instead of the typical sounds you would expect from a sandy beach when waves wash up against the sand. The sound of Mongdol pebbles rolling in the waves has even been selected by the Ministry of Environment as one of the Top 100 beautiful sounds of Korea.  If you walk along the ocean trail listening to the beautiful sounds of the beach, you will reach Jujeon Fishing Experience Village which is home to seven small villages with just over 300 households. Residents of Jujeon Fishing Experience Village catch fish and farm the nearby fields and rice paddies. Here, you can try your hand at a number of different activities, including the Haenyeo experience program, fishing boat program, bare hand fishing program, and agriculture program.

stories.title: Ugasan Beacon Fire Station
stories.audioTitle: Beacon at the top of Ugasan Mountain
stories.script: The Ugasan Beacon Fire Station is atop the peak of Ugasan Mountain, where our ancestors used to send urgent messages with fire and smoke.  Historians believe this beacon fire station was used since approximately half-way through the Goryeo Dynasty, primarily for military purposes.  During the final years of Goryeo, the government began reinforcing its beacon fire system to defend against the plundering of Japanese pirates, and later on, the system was fully refurbished during the reign of King Sejong (Joseon Dynasty).  The Yupo Beacon Fire Station at Ugasan Mountain was part of a coastal system. It received signals from the beacon fire station in Nammokcheon (known as Jujeon today), then relayed them to a place called Haseoji in Gyeongju.  Also known as the Yudeungpo Bonghwa, the Yupo Beacon Fire Station still features the remains of a stone platform (1m~2m tall), and a circular fireplace made with unprocessed (natural) rocks, a protective wall, and a barracks site for guards on duty at the station. Today, it remains an extremely valuable historical resource for the research of coastal beacon fire systems.

stories.title: Ulsan Grand Park
stories.audioTitle: Enjoy a comfortable spot of healing in the bosom of nature
stories.script: With 3.71km2 of parkland, Ulsan Grand Park is a landmark urban eco-park fin Ulsan. Developed with cleanness and the comfort of nature in mind, the park gives people a place where they can enjoy nature without leaving the city. Ulsan Grand Park offers a variety of facilities, including landscaping features, recreational equipment, sporting equipment, and other amenities.  In particular, if you walk past the entrance of Ulsan Grand Park, you will see the reservoir and windmill, both of which are the park’s signature features. Why not take a walk along the shores of the reservoir, and enjoy the scenery with the picturesque windmill in the background?  Moreover, as you would expect from a landmark urban eco-park fin a great city like Ulsan, the Grand Park hosts various festivals and has plenty of facilities for cultural activities.  From spring to early summer when it is time for beautiful flowers to bloom, the park hosts the Rose Festival. With a sweet and fragrant aroma of roses filling the air, the Rose Festival is the perfect event for couples. When the cold winds start to blow in winter, Ulsan Grand Park hosts the Light Festival that features light fixtures installed with different themes and live busking performances.  If you feel exhausted - both physically and mentally - and you need a pick-me-up, take a walk through Ulsan Grand Park. Unique events will be waiting for you each season.

stories.title: Cheoyongam
stories.audioTitle: Origins of the Tales of Cheoyong
stories.script: Sometimes, we call certain people “bigger” than others. We call them bigger when they act calm and rational even in the face of events that would make most of us overly emotional. What if there was a person who was so much “bigger” than everyone else, he even impressed ghosts?   According to one episode in the “Tales of Cheoyong,” an evil spirit that was spreading sickness and disease met someone who made it repent for its past transgressions. That someone was Cheoyong, the son of the Dragon King.   One day, King Heongang, the 49th monarch of Shilla, traveled to Gaeunpo (today’s Ulsan) on a retreat. But suddenly, the weather turned and the entire realm became overcast with dark clouds and fog. Frightened at the thought that he may have angered the Dragon King, King Heongang built a Buddhist temple. Pleased with King Heongang’s offering, the Dragon King introduced King Heongang to his seventh son, Cheoyong. Cheoyong was soon appointed to the position of Geupgan, upon which he helped King Heongang rule his kingdom. He even married the most beautiful woman in all of Shilla.   However, one day, Cheoyong witnessed something devastating when he returned home. He saw his wife was in bed with someone other than himself. Despite catching his wife committing adultery, Cheoyong kept his temper, came back outside, and began to sing and dance. The song and dance Cheoyong performed was called “Cheoyongmu” And was designated as a UNESCO intangible heritage in 2009.   Surprised by Cheoyong’s reaction, the evil spirit begged for forgiveness. It promised never to do anything bad in a location with Cheoyong’s picture. Thereafter, people posted pictures of Cheoyong’s face on their front doors.   Today, you can still visit the place where, according to legend, the Dragon King and Cheoyong first appeared It is at a rock (the “Cheoyongam”) sitting 150m off the coast of Sejuk Village in Hwangseong-dong, Nam-gu (Ulsan-si).

stories.title: Eunwolsa Temple
stories.script: There is a saying, “revenge is best served cold.” It means to remind yourself of the humiliation you suffered and never forget until you have exacted your revenge.   Sinjeong-dong in Nam-gu, Ulsan-si, is home to Eunwolsa Temple which tells the heart-wrenching story of those who wanted to seethe resurgence of the Geumgwan Gaya Kingdom. Eunwolsa Temple is a modest establishment in the heart of the city. Most notably, it houses the ancestral tablets of Muryeok Gong and Seohyeon Gong, the grandfather and father of General Kim Yu-sin.   But that begs the question. General Kim Yu-sin and his family were from Jincheon in Chungcheongbuk-do. Why did he enshrine his father and grandfather in Ulsan? When the Geumgwan Gaya Kingdom dissolved, their noble families were accepted into the noble class of the Shilla Dynasty. Despite their seemingly equal status, however, descendants of the former Gaya Kingdom were forced to endure discrimination and bigotry. So, the noble families of Gaya met in secret to develop plans to resurrect the Geumgwan Gaya Kingdom, and Ulsan was the covert base for the insurrection.   But soon, Queen Jindeok discovered these plans for rebellion. To bring the disgruntled former Geumgwan Gaya aristocrats into the fold once again, Queen Jindeok built the Taehwasa Temple. Here, “Taehwa” means “grand harmony.” It was a far more acceptable name than “Shilla,” which means “a new land.”   Historians believe that Taehwasa Temple was a fairly substantial temple. Unfortunately, theyre do not know the exact location where it stood. Luckily, you can see a restored version of Taehwaru Pavilion - which was built together with Taehwasa Temple - near Eunwolsa Temple today.

stories.title: Jinha Beach
stories.script: Beautiful Blue Sea, Jinha Beach   Approximately 20km south of Ulsan-si is Jinha Beach which continues to be a popular destination for tourists. Opened to the public as a beach in 1974, Jinha Beach stretches across 96,000㎡. It has a 1km-long white sand beach and pristine waters, making it the perfect place to go on a summer holiday. It constantly attracts people looking to enjoy some marine sports or a spot of fishing.   Moreover, thanks to the Hoeyagang River, which flows from Munsusan Mountain to Hoeya Dam, you can bathe yourself in some freshwater streams as well. Nearby, Jinha Beach has Ideokdo Island which features two reefs jutting out from the sea and Myeongseondo Island, which is an island you can walk over to. Myeongseondo Island is an uninhabited island facing the Palgakjeong Pavilion but it is a great fishing spot for sea bream, halibut, and rockfish.  The island is also known as a great place to take photos of the sunrise among photographers. The name “Myeongseondo” means an “island where heavenly beings used to play.” Originally, the island was accessible on foot during a specific period of the year when the tidal difference was severe. More recently, however, you can now walk over to Myeongseondo Island anytime you want thanks to an artificial structure installed in order to prevent the sedimentation of sand.   Just a 20-minute drive from Ulsan and a 40-minute drive from Busan, Jinha Beach attracts more than 300,000 visitors during the summer peak season. If you travel 10km more, you can visit the lighthouse at Cape Ganjeolgot, which is open to visitors 24- hours a day. Watching the sun rise above the ocean with someone special can be a truly unforgettable experience.

stories.title: Jangsaengpohang Port
stories.audioTitle: Thin and long like a Jangseung totem pole
stories.script: Jangsaengpohang Port is a port located in Nam-gu, Ulsan-si. In the past, this beautiful port was known as “Jangseungpo,” as the configuration of the port resembled a thin and long Jangseung totem pole. Despite its beauty, Jangsaengpohang Port has a sad history.   The year was 1899. Back then, the waters near the port were home to large packs of whales. But pressure from the Russian Empire forced the Korean Empire to permit Russian whalers to hunt whales in its sovereign waters. In 1905, when the Japanese defeated the Russians in the Russo-Japanese War, Japan won the exclusive whaling rights in Korean waters. Prolonged whaling drove whales in Korea to the brink of extinction. By the 1960s, it became almost impossible to see large whales off the coast of the Korean Peninsula.   Later on, the global community collectively banned whaling in 1986. This pushed Jangsaengpohang Port and the nearby village into further decline, and most residents chose to abandon the area. It was an unfortunate turn of events. A few decades later, the government and local residents started some initiatives to revive Jangsaengpohang Port.  In 2008, it was even designated as a Special Whale Culture Zone. Thereafter, people created the Whale Cultural Village, a Whale Museum, Whale Life Experience Museum, and other facilities under the overarching theme of whales. Today, Jangsaengpohang Port continues to build upon its unique and distinct character.

stories.title: Gyeongju Gyochon Village
stories.script: [Woman] I’m planning a trip to Gyeongju. Do you have any places that I absolutely should not miss?  [Man] Right...you’re looking for some recommendations. Let me think for a bit. Hey, what comes to your mind when you think of a trip to Gyeongju?   [Woman] When it comes to Gyeongju, I know that it has Seokguram, Bulguksa Temple, and a lot of other heritage sites.  [Man] You’re right. Gyeongju does have plenty of heritage sites with significant historical value. If you plan your trip to Gyeongju as a historical tour, it might be a little more fulfilling. What kind of city do you think Gyeongju is?   [Woman] More than anything else, Gyeongju is a city of aristocrats.  [Man] That is correct. But did you know that Gyeongju is a city of romance? (Pause) Did you know?  [Woman] Don’t be ridiculous. Gyeongju and romance don’t seem to match.  [Man] No, they actually do match! Gyeongju is home to a surprising number of historical and romantic sites.If you're dreaming of a sweet and romantic experience like the flowers fluttering in the spring breeze, follow me to the Gyochon Village in Gyeongju.    Introduce Gyochon Village and its ties to Shilla   [Man] Gyochon Village in Gyeongju was home to “Gukhak,” the first national university of Shilla built during the reign of King Sinmun. Gukhak of Shilla, later on, became Hyanghak in Goryeo, and Hyanggyo during the Joseon Dynasty. The reason why the village is called “Gyo-dong,” “Gyochon” or “Gyo-ri” is because it has a Hyanggyo inside the village.  [Woman] In other words, Gyochon Village in Gyeongju was like the eight competitive school districts in Seoul. But their roots go back to Shilla, not Joseon. That’s amazing.  [Man] That’s right. A few years ago, Gyeongju, Ulsan, and Pohang joined forces under the “Sunrise Alliance” to carry on the legacy of Shilla which was built across a thousand years. Historically, Ulsan and Pohang used to protect Seorabeol and the kingdom against Japanese pirates looking to raid the country through the sea. Thanks to their dedication, Shilla was able to unify the three kingdoms and survive for a thousand years despite being the smallest country in the region.   [Woman] Wait a minute. Now I’ve come to think about it, I have never heard of a royal palace or palatial ruins belonging to Shilla, despite the fact that the kingdom went on for a thousand years.   [Man] Oh.. I suppose that’s true. Where did you go on your school excursions?  [Woman] My school excursions...they were such a long time ago...I think I went to Gyeongju when I was in high school.  [Man] Well then, you would have seen the palatial ruins that belonged to Shilla..    Gyeongju Travel Spot 1: Wolseong District   [Man] Do you see that hill with all the trees next to Cheomseongdae Observatory? That’s Wolseong District. It’s the place where all the royal palaces were during the Shilla Dynasty. In other words, it was the center of Gyeongju back then. Thanks to its historical value, the district has been designated as Historic Site No. 16.  The name “Wolseong” comes from the fact that the palace site is shaped like a half-moon. That is why the district is also known as “Banwolseong (half-moon palace).”  [Woman] I thought the palatial ruins of Shilla would feature some grand palaces. But I don’t seem to see any.  [Man] You’re right. Unfortunately, we only have the foundations today. At first, the palaces were built near Changnimsa Temple Site, right underneath Namsan Mountain. During the reign of King Pasa (the 5th monarch of Shilla), the palaces were relocated here.  [Woman] What a pity. It would've been so great to see the palaces today.  [Man] Don’t worry. I’ll take you to an even better place.Now, you might be able to see a long forest stretching north from Wolseong.That forest is called “Gyelim.”     [Woman] Wow. It’s such a dense forest. I feel like all the fine dust would be filtered away there.  [Man] Although it might look like an ordinary forest, it is an extremely important place. Gyelim is where Kim Al-ji was born. Kim Al-ji was the man who created the Kim clan, a powerful family that was famous for producing the largest number of monarchs during the Shilla Dynasty.  [Woman] Kim Al-ji? Even his name seems special. I bet there’s a story about his name.  [Man] You’re quick, aren’t you? The story behind Kim Al-ji’s name can be found in the History of the Three Kingdoms. One day, a bright light began pulsating in Gyelim.So, a man went to check the light source. There, he discovered a handsome baby boy  inside a golden chest. Since then, people started calling the forest “Gyelim.” With regards to the boy, he came from a golden (“geum”) chest, so people gave him a surname that sounded similar: “Gim (later on Kim).”  [Woman] You know, people who appear in these legends become king. Did he become a king?  [Man] It seems a lot of them do. But Kim Al-ji himself did not become king.It was his great-great-great-great-grandson that became a member of the Kim clan that became the monarch of Shilla (King Michu).Starting with King Michu, the Kim family produced a staggering 38 monarchs for the Shilla Dynasty.   [Woman] 38 monarchs? My god! They must have been an extremely powerful royal family.   [Man] They guarded Gyelim as a sacred place and banned anyone from cutting down any trees from the forest.  [Woman] Now that I’ve learned the history behind Gyelim, it feels a little scary.  [Man] Okay. I’ll show you a place that is a little more romantic. Shall we go?    Gyeongju Travel Spot 2: The love nest for Wonhyo and Princess Yoseok - Yoseokgung Palace    [Woman] Wow. A romantic spot in Gyeongju. I’m so curious.   [Man] The place I’m talking about is the Yoseokgung Palace, which is home to the beautiful love story between Wonhyo and Princess Yoseok. The story goes like this.
