King Muyeol of Shilla had a daughter, Princess Yoseok. But during a battle against Baekje, Princess Yoseok lost her husband.  King Muyeol was sad to see his daughter heartbroken. After all, he was as much of a father as he was the king of his country. According to court rules, he could not move his widowed daughter back into the royal palace, so he had her live in a palace near Wolseong Yoseokgung Palace.    [Woman] Doesn’t Yoseokgung Palace have something to do with Wonhyo, the Buddhist monk?  [Man] You’re absolutely right. This is where the love affair between Wonhyo and Princess Yoseok began.  [Woman] A romantic love affair between a monk and a princess. That’s exciting.    [Man] There’s a song that Wonhyo supposedly sang for the princess. Shall we take a listen?  [Wonhyo] “Someone give me an ax without a handle. I’ll make a column that props up the heavens. Using that ax without a handle, I plan to make a column that props up the heavens.”  [Woman] Those lyrics aren’t romantic at all!  [Man] You’ll feel different if you dig a little deeper into the meaning of those lyrics. Here, an ‘ax without a handle’ means the widowed Princess Yoseok, and the ‘column that props up the heavens’ means a great person that will help the kingdom thrive.  [Woman] I see..… now it seems that way.  I want to know more about Wonhyo!  [Man] Wonhyo established some of the key philosophies of Buddhism in Korea such as “Ilcheyushimjo (everything depends on the mind)” and “Hwajaengsasang (principle of harmony).” At the time, Buddhism was the official religion of the kingdom. Nevertheless, common people did not understand the religion all that well. Wonhyo popularized Buddhism among the masses.  [Woman] I can’t believe such a prominent monk would fall in love with a woman and serenade her like that.  [Man] ‘Someone give me an ax without a handle.I’ll make a column that props up the heavens.’  You too? You don’t have to. It’s no wonder Princess Yoseok fell for a man who serenaded her with a special love song. How did they meet?  According to history, Wonhyo always looked like a beggar.Despite his appearances, the royal family and Buddhist worshipers recognized him and invited him to lead a Buddhist ceremony.   [Woman] Then, did Princess Yoseok fall in love at first sight with Wonhyo at the royal Buddhist ceremony?  [Man] That’s right. It was rare for a monk to appear at a royal Buddhist ceremony. Princess Yoseok saw how honest Wonhyo was, and fell immediately in love. Soon, she became lovesick. When King Muyeol saw his daughter suffering, he summoned Wonhyo into the palace.   [Woman] I assume Wonhyo, the beggar that he is, didn’t comply with the King’s request so easily?  [Man] You’re right. When he saw the court officials approach with the king’s decree, Wonhyo fell into Muncheongyo. He used his wet clothes as an excuse to step into Yoseokgung Palace where Princess Yoseok was staying, instead of the royal palace where King Muyeol was waiting for him.  [Woman] They were so deeply in love, the entire area around Yoseokgung Palace supposedly smelled like flowers for a while. But unfortunately, their love didn’t last.  [Woman] Why not?  [Man] After a while, Wonhyo had to leave.He broke the rules as a Buddhist monk, so he put his Buddhist robe away and became a commoner. 10 months after Wonhyo left, Princess Yoseok gave birth to a boy. That boy grew up to be Seolchong, the genius scholar who invented Idu script.As his lyrics said, Wonhyo helped bring a ‘column to prop up the heavens’ into this world.  [Woman] Wow. Love stories are always so interesting I think I should call Gyeongju the city of love.    Gyeongju Travel Spot 3: The love nest for Wonhyo and Princess Yoseok - Woljeonggyo Bridge   [Man] Hey Suji, did you know that Woljeonggyo Bridge has become a popular place for couples when they go on a date?  [Woman] I’ve heard that the view from Woljeonggyo Bridge is magnificent!  [Man] In the evening, the soft lights come on,	and create a romantic ambiance. If you get a chance, visit Woljeonggyo Bridge at night!    Gyeongju Travel Spot 4: Gyeongju Hyanggyo and Old Family House of the Choi Clan    [Man] We’ve seen Woljeonggyo Bridge. So now, it’s time to head over to the Gyochon Village in Gyeongju. Can you guess why Gyochon Village is also known as “Gyo-dong” or “Gyochon”?  [Woman] That’s because it has a Hyanggyo inside the village!  [Man] You remembered.As I mentioned earlier, Gyochon Village in Gyeongju was home to Gukhak, the first national university in Korea built during the reign of King Sinmun.Gukhak evolved into Hyanghak during the Goryeo Dynasty, and eventually into Hyanggyo during the Joseon Dynasty. Naturally, people created an aristocratic village nearby.  [Woman] That’s why the village was created. Their legacy carries on to this day. I thought the village was simply a collection of traditional Hanok homes that belonged to aristocratic families. Now that I know the reason why it was created, the village seems more dignified.  [Man] At the time, Gyochon Village had houses with blue tiled roofs and refined scholars. So, most people wanted to move into the village.       [Woman] I think I can hear some aristocrat calling out at the door, “Is there anyone at home?”  [Man] Haha... Gyochon Village has several old houses that belonged to the Choi clan. It has a great environment to see what Gyeongju looked like culture-wise during the Joseon Dynasty.One of the reasons why Gyochon Village become so famous is because it had the Choi family mansion. Supposedly the Choi family was the richest family in all of Joseon.  [Woman] I’ve heard of the mansion before! The Choi family mansion! It’s the family that was extremely charitable to other poor neighbors. Right?  [Man] You’re so smart! Throughout the family’s 400-year history, the Choi clan produced court officials for eight generations and remained one of the richest families for 12 generations. They were the wealthiest family during the Joseon Dynasty.There’s another story I want to add to the list of good deeds they did for the community. Whenever the country suffered from a poor harvest, the Choi family did not eat rice. either. People say, that the Choi family would cook porridge 	and share it with the entire village.  [Woman] They seem to be the embodiment of noblesse oblige. I’m really impressed.   [Man] I have another story about the Choi family. The last prominent descendant of the Choi clan was Choi Joon. During the Japanese colonial rule of Korea, Choi Joon funded the Provisional  Government of Korea. Despite ruling Korea with an iron grip, the Japanese could not ignore the wealth and reputation of the Choi family that had stood the test of time for hundreds of years.After our country won its independence, Choi Joon donated his money to help educate talented individuals.Although they do not enjoy the immense wealth held before, the reputation of the family still lives on.     [Woman] They truly are the quintessential example of noblesse oblige during the Joseon Dynasty.  [Man] A few years ago, they restored their guest house which was lost to a fire in the 1970s.If you walk past the guest house, you’ll arrive at a storage building  that is larger than a typical house.The Choi family used to be so rich, they could fill the entire storage unit with food. People say, the Choi clan donated all of it to the community.   [Woman] I think the leadership the Choi clan showed us  gave us an opportunity to appreciate the value of sharing and wisdom our ancestors believed in. I think it will be a good lesson for our children as well.    Gyeongju Travel Spot 5: Traditional Liquor of Gyeongju   [Man] Do you like to drink?   [Woman] I do.   [Man] We came all the way to the mansion of the Choi clan. It would be a shame to leave without having some traditional local liquor, right? This is called Gayangju. Made with water sourced from the old mansion of the Choi family, they used to send Gayangju to the king as tribute.This traditional Gyeongju liquor is made with the roots of Chinese matrimony vine that are more than 100 years old. It has a subtle aroma and an amazingly smooth taste!  [Woman] It seems smooth but honest! Just like the values the Choi family used to believe in.  [Man] So, we took a tour around Gyochon Village in Gyeongju. What did you think?  [Woman] I feel like I took a time machine back into the past. It was so fun. I learned about stories hidden behind your history. It was a truly meaningful trip.  The more you know, the more meaningful your trip can be. We’ll come back with more stories to make your trip across Gyeongju more exciting.  [Together] History Tour of Korea! Thank you for joining us.

stories.title: Jusangjeolli Padosori-gil Trail
stories.audioTitle: Beautiful rock formation on the eastern seaboard
stories.script: [Woman] There is a place in Gyeongju that can show you the city goes further back in time than ancient Shilla. In fact, it shows you that Gyeongju is tens of millions of years old.   [Man] To check it out, we must go to a peaceful little beach in Yangnam-myeon, Gyeongju. Here, I’m going to tell a new story to those of you who aren’t so familiar with the coastal area of Gyeongju. This place is called the “Jusangjeolli Padosori-gil Trail” and it is one of Gyeongju’s hidden gems.  [Woman] Can you hear the refreshing sound of waves washing over the beach? As you can see, this place has everything cool sea breeze and the sound of cresting waves. This place is called the “Jusangjeolli Padosori-gil Trail” in Gyeongju. You might know Jusangjeolli Padosori-gil Trail as the longest trekking course in Korea that starts from Busan and ends in Goseong. To tell you the origin story for the Jusangjeolli Padosori-gil Trail, we have to go back approximately 26 million years into the past.   [Man] A long, long time ago, the Korean peninsula and Japan were connected by land. But gradual crustal movements pushed Japan to the east and water filled in the gap, creating the East Sea.During this process, magma from deep inside the crust vaulted up to the surface and created volcanic features. The Jusangjeolli (columnar joint formations) in Gyeongju were created by magma rising to the surface.  [Woman] Jusangjeolli refers to a naturally-formed, long column-like features made by magma. As magma rises, it takes shape, then hardens when it cools down. These formations are made with no human interference, and simply by the forces of nature. If you look at them, you might divine power of the planet.  [Man] If you walk inside the trail near Jusangjeolli formation, the first thing you’ll see is the “fan-shaped Jusangjeolli.” At more than 10m-long, Jusangjeolli is shaped like a fan, which is why it gets its name.  [Woman] Jusangjeolli formations typically have distinct features. Some lean in a particular direction, while others lie horizontal to the ground. But a fan-shaped Jusangjeolli is a rarity. Apparently, there aren’t many formations like this anywhere in the world. If you climb on top of Jusangjeolli Observatory, you can truly appreciate the grand scale of the fan-shaped Jusangjeolli formation.  [Man] Meanwhile, the Padosori-gil Trail is ideal if you want to enjoy a walk. Here, you’ll see a heart-shaped coastline adjacent to the observatory. This geographical feature was created naturally as large boulders blocked waves and gradually turned the coastline into the shape of a heart. If you walk along the trail, listening to the waves, you’ll soon arrive at Eupcheonhang Port which is famous for its murals. Murals are on most of the walls across the village. It almost makes the entire village feel like an art gallery.  [Woman] Naari Beach near Eupcheonhang has an interesting story that involves Shilla. It is the origin myth of Seok Talhae, who was one of the founding fathers of 			Shilla along with Bak Hyeokgeose and Kim Al-ji. According to the Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms, Seok Talhae (4th monarch of Shilla) first arrived in Shilla through Naari Beach. The story goes as follows  [Man] The Queen of Dapana gave birth to a giant egg after seven years of marriage. This was considered a bad omen. Soon after, a boy hatched from the egg, but the King put the boy on a boat then set it off ointo the sea. Thereafter, the boat was discovered by an old lady as it arrived at a port called Ajinpo. There, as if to welcome his arrival, a flock of magpies were standing guard around the boat. Ultimately, the boy was given the surname “Seok” (if you remove the Chinese character for bird from the Chinese character for magpie, you get “Seok”). In terms of his given name, he was named “Talhae” which meant “escaping from a box.”    [Woman] The boy grew up to be an extraordinary man. He even ushered in powerful iron-age technology and culture into Shilla. Today, Naari Park has a stone tablet known as the “Seoktalhaewang Tangangyuheobi” that commemorates the mysterious arrival of King Talhae.  [Man] 26 million years ago, a beautiful rock formation appeared along our eastern 			seaboard! We call it Jusangjeolli. If you’d like to learn more about the history of those mysterious geographical features, come and visit the “Jusangjeolli Padosori-gil Trail” in Gyeongju.

stories.title: Hwangnidan Street
stories.script: There is a place in Gyeongju that is creating new history for the city. That place is Hwanglidan-gil Road, built by the hands of young entrepreneurs in Gyeongju. A few years ago, distinct and unique-looking shops started popping up one after another at a neighborhood in Hwangnam-dong, Gyeongju-si, set aside for redevelopment.  From cafes roasting aromatic coffee beans, characterful fusion restaurants, and retro pubs lighting up the streets at night, customers began pouring in Each shop had its own unique ambiance and ideas, which were perfect for satisfying younger generations in the Gyeongju area.  The narrow street soon became known as Hwanglidan-gil, and today, it continues to bustle with a never-ending stream of people. It was even listed on the “100 Must-Visit Tourist Spots of Korea” by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism recently. In other words, it has become an extremely popular destination among Korean people.   In less than five years, Hwanglidan-gil has transformed itself into a landmark representing the city of Gyeongju. It is so great to see young local entrepreneurs channel their love for the community and successfully create new hope. Don’t you agree? If you are interested, there are similar places brimming with passion such as Gonglidan-gil in Ulsan and Yeongildae in Pohang. Hwanglidan-gil blends a retro atmosphere that reminds people of the 1960s and 70s, and cultural elements that are distinctly from Shilla. So, come and interact with fun-loving young people at Hwanglidan-gil.  What makes this place even better is that it is full of people looking to live in harmony with one another. If you still think Gyeongju is like that old city you saw in your textbooks, you might be in for a surprise.

stories.title: Bomun Tourist Complex
stories.audioTitle: Walk, rest, and enjoy the seasons
stories.script: If Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond are places that represent historical Shilla, Bomun Tourist Complex and Bomunho Pond are places that represent the modern Gyeongju. As its name suggests, Wolji Pond can offer a beautiful view of the moon reflected on its surface at night. On the other hand, Bomunho Pond can show you different elements of each season in Gyeongju. Although it is a joy to visit all year round, Bomunho looks particularly striking in spring and autumn. Bomun Tourist Complex features a hotel, resort, and other amenities in addition to Donggungwon (a modern recreation of Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond) and Gyeongju World (a popular theme park for children). The complex offers a variety of attractions for all visitors. Meanwhile, Bomunho Pond has a nice trail along its circumference called “Bomunhoban-gil (Bomunho Trail).” If you walk at a leisurely pace, it takes 90 minutes to complete the course. But the trail offers some spectacular views, so it may take a little longer than that. This could be the reason why so many people like to return to Bomunho.   In fact, every city has that type of place. Ulsan has Ulsan Grand Park, and Pohang has its Greenway Railroad Forest.   Meanwhile, Myeonghwalsan Mountain, which lies to the west of Bomunho Lake, has a mountain fortress that protected Seorabeol (the capital city of Shilla). During emergencies, the fortress served as a temporary palace for the King. During the reign of Queen Seondeok (the 27th monarch of Shilla), Crown forces quelled the rebellion led by Bidam at Myeonghwalsan Mountain. Unlike today, it was a battlefield that determined life or death. The mountain no longer has that legacy. Today, Myeonghwalsan Mountain and Bomun Tourist Complex have turned into great places for rest and recuperation. Over time, Gyeongju became a peaceful city, and peacefulness created the foundation upon which Bomun Tourist Complex can offer different shades of colors during each season.

stories.title: Gampohang Port
stories.audioTitle: A major fishing port in the southern regions of the eastern seaboard
stories.script: In 2020, Gampohang Port in Gyeongju-si, Gyeongsangbuk-do, will celebrate 100 years as an open port. Gampohang earned its name from the fact that the geographical layout of the area resembled the Chinese character for “sweet (gam), ”, and that it was a port close to Gameunsa Temple. The waters near Gampohang Port have schools of mackerel pike, cod, anchovy, squid, etc., which attracts plenty of fishing vessels. Thanks to the sheer volume of traffic in the area, Gampohang Port has become a major fishing port in the southern regions of the eastern seaboard.   In particular, the port offers great access, meaning that it is always brimming with freshly caught seafood. This also makes Gampohang a popular destination for anglers and epicures. The coastal road between the underwater royal tomb of King Munmu and Gampohang Port is lined with fresh sashimi restaurants that serve seafood from the Port.   But Gampohang is not all about food. There are plenty of things to see as well. Songdaemal, which features plenty of old pine trees (300~400 years old), has a lighthouse inspired by the three-storied stone pagoda at Gameunsa Temple The lighthouse was designed to celebrate the achievements of King Munmu who unified the three kingdoms. Also, Najeong Sandy Beach, with its seawall, is a popular place to watch the sunrise.   Meanwhile, Haeguk-gil (a road near Gampohang Port) has several features from our modern history, including old Japanese-style houses and a shrine built by Japanese fishermen who lived in the area during the Japanese colonial rule of Korea.   There are plenty of other attractions such as the Gampoyeongseong Fortress, underwater royal tomb of King Munmu, and Bonggil Beach, which means you don’t have to worry about running out of places to visit. The Gyeongju municipal government is in the process of developing a variety of marine tourism items and related content to celebrate the centennial anniversary of Gampohang Port. So, check them all out next year.

stories.title: Tohamsan Mountain
stories.script: Each person has his or her own distinct character and personality. This is the same with mountains and other natural objects. Each has its own unique character Although the entire city of Gyeongju is like a giant historical heritage site, there is one particular place that has the strongest ties to Buddhism. That place is Tohamsan Mountain.   As one of the four major mountains of Shilla, legend says that Tohamsan Mountain is home to the spirit of Shilla. Atop its peak, you can see the beaches of Gampo where the underwater royal tomb of King Munmu is located. The Mountain itself has several stone pagodas and other artifacts that link it with Shilla, including a shrine dedicated to Seok Talhae of Shilla near a headstone at its peak (745m above sea level).   Other notable historical sites are very close in proximity with Tohamsan Mountain. The mountain’s peak is close to Seokguram, and Bulguksa Temple lies at its foothills. Of course, Bulguksa Temple is home to beautiful historical artifacts such as Seokgatap Pagoda, Dabotap Pagoda, Cheongungyo Bridge, and Yeonhwagyo Bridge. Thanks to all of these heritage sites, the entire mountain has been designated as Gyeongju National Park.   Meanwhile, the name “Tohamsan” means a “mountain brimming with fog.” Due to its proximity to the East Sea, the Mountain always seems like it is brimming with fog blown in from the sea. Isn’t that just amazing?   In particular, the sun rising above the sea off the coast of Gampo is nothing short of spectacular. That is why tens of thousands of people from all over the country flock to Tohamsan Mountain on New Year’s day. At midnight on New Year’s Day, the National Gyeongju Museum strikes the Bell of King Seongdeok to usher in the new year, then tourists walk up to Seokguram, and make new resolutions for the first sunrise of the year.

stories.title: Bomunjeong Pavilion
stories.audioTitle: One of the best places for cherry blossoms in Korea
stories.script: Have you ever tried to catch cherry blossoms fluttering in the spring breeze? If you have, where was the best place you saw cherry blossoms? Or, are you still looking for a great place to see and enjoy them?  If so, we have the perfect place for you. This place was introduced on CNN, a famous news network in the US, as one of the best places to see cherry blossoms in Korea.  Next to a modest pond called Bomunho inside Gyeongju Bomun Tourist Complex, there is a small pavilion known as Bomunjeong. In January 2012, world-famous news channel CNN ranked Bomunjeong Pavilion at No. 11 on the list of ‘50 beautiful places to visit in South Korea’ through its tourism and travel website, CNN Go.   In spring, Bomunjeong and its pond become shrouded in cherry blossoms. In summer, lotus flowers fill Bomunho Pond, while beautiful leaves surround the pavilion to create some truly stunning views. Unlike typical cherry trees found in other areas where the branches grow upwards, the cherry trees near Bomunjeong Pavilion have willowy branches that hang over the surface of Bomunho Pond. In spring, when flowers bloom along those willowy branches, Bomunjeong Pavilion looks magical.   Surprisingly, when the municipal government in Gyeongju originally built Bomun Tourist Complex, Bomunjeong Pavilion was not a particularly popular feature. However, as the cherry trees grew enough to produce spectacular cherry blossoms, the newly built pavilion went viral. Photos of Bomunjeong spread through various SNS platforms, and soon the pavilion became a popular attraction.   Every year, during the cherry blossom season, photographers flock to Bomunjeong Pavilion. How about creating a few unforgettable memories on a special day out in Bomunjeong this spring?

stories.title: Yeonorang and Seonyeo Theme Park
stories.audioTitle: A land of history and myths
stories.script: [Man] Tell me Suji, what is the first thing that comes to your mind when you think of Pohang?   [Woman] When I think of Pohang, I always think of the steel mills and Cape Homigot. I visited both places on a field trip when I was in school.   [Man] I see. The steel mills and Cape Homigot are the most famous landmarks in Pohang. But today, I want to introduce you to somewhere a little more special. I’m talking about the ‘Homi Peninsula Seaside Trial’ which sits on the easternmost point in the Korean peninsula.    [Woman] Wow, I love it. I think I can smell the sea already.  [Man] A land of history and myths! Let’s head over to Pohang.    Yeonorang and Seonyeo Theme Park   [Woman] That park is so gorgeous. But, where are we exactly?   [Man] We are at ‘Yeonorang and Seonyeo Theme Park.’This park was inspired by the Tale of the Sun and Moon in the Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms that involved Yeonorang and Seonyeo. Yeonorang and Seonyeo Theme Park is based on the only myth featuring the Sun and Moon in Korea. The tale of Yeonorang and Seonyeo is also the most famous folk story from the entire Pohang region. It has a trail called the Homi Peninsula Seaside Trail that lets you walk along the sea while listening to the waves. At dusk, you can enjoy the bright lights illuminating the steel mills in Pohang as well.  [Woman] Fresh air, panoramic view of the sea. This place is heaven on earth. I see a house with a thatched roof. What is that?    Shilla Village   [Man] This is called the “Shilla Village.” It is a historical reproduction of the village where Yeonorang and Seonyeo used to live. The jar-shaped art piece at the Village’s entrance is made out of iron. This is meant to represent the fact that Shilla introduced its iron-age culture to Japan.      Twin Turtle Rocks   [Woman] Right! I get it. What about those two rocks that look like they’re on top of each other? I think they might have a special meaning.  [Man] They are called the Twin Turtle Rocks. According to legend, Yeonorang and Seonyeo were forced to part ways because of a rock. But, they were able to reunite because of a rock as well. After they were reunited, they never wanted to part again, so they fused two rocks together. Those rocks became the Twin Turtle Rocks.  [Woman] I think I can feel their desperate love from these rocks.    Gwibigo Exhibition Hall   [Man] Now then, shall we move onto the Gwibigo Exhibition Hall? “Gwibigo” was the name of a warehouse that used to store the silk sent by Seonyeo. The exhibition hall is full of various interactive features and exhibits, so it might be a great idea to take your time and tour the hall with your children.   [Woman] Didn’t you also tell me that the ‘Yeonorang and Seonyeo Theme Park’ had a special legend?   [Man] Indeed, I did. Now! I’ll tell you a passionate love story between a couple that will certainly bring tears to your eyes.  [Woman] Once upon a time, a young married couple, Yeonorang and Seonyeo, lived in a small fishing village near Yeongilman Bay. Seonyeo wove textiles, while Yeonorang caught fish to sell in the market  [Man] They were poor, but they were thankful for their work. Every day, the couple prayed to the Dragon King of the sea as well as the Sun and Moon.  [Seonyeo] “Dear Gods of the Sun,,. please protect my husband who ventures out into the rough sea today. Keep the waters calm and protect him from any dangerous winds or waves.”  [Yeonorang] “Dear Gods of the Moon,. my wife has to work through the night to 				weave her silk. Please protect her from illness, and protect her hands 			from injury.”  [Woman] Day after day, the couple prayed for the safety and well-being of each other to the gods of the Sun and Moon. Then, one day, Yeonorang headed out to sea as usual  [Yeonorang] “My dear! I’m going now. Don’t worry about me.”  [Woman] However, Yeonorang did not return home, even as dusk approached. Worried about her husband, Seonyeo went out to look for Yeonorang  [Seonyeo] “Excuse me, have you seen my husband?”  [Villager] “I’m not sure. We divvied up our catch today and said good-bye a while ago. Didn’t he come home yet?”  [Seonyeo] “What?”  [Woman] Despite her racing heart, Seonyeo ran as fast as she could towards the sea.  [Seonyeo] “Oh, my dear husband!! Yeonorang!! Where are you?”  [Woman] Despite her plea, she could not hear Yeonorang’s voice. But then, she discovered a pair of shoes on a rock by the shore.   [Seonyeo] “Thes are my husband’s shoes. I am certain. That means....,”   [Woman] The shoes did indeed belong to Seonyeo’s husband. Yeonorang.   [Woman] Maybe he was accidentally swept up by a wave, maybe he slipped while he was collecting seaweed. Seonyeo sat on the rock where she found Yeonorang’s shoes and spent day after day crying.   [Man] Then, something amazing happened. The rock Seonyeo was sitting on began to move slowly. Then it started gliding towards the sea.   [Seonyeo] “What on earth is happening? The rock is moving! Did the same thing happen to my husband? Then, maybe this rock can take me to him.”   [Woman] Seonyeo held on to the rock as hard as she could. She was worried she might fall into the sea, but she didn’t let go throughout the long journey.   [Villager 1] “I don’t know what happened. Seonyeo just disappeared.”   [Villager 2] “Did you look carefully across the entire village? Did you look for her on the beach?”  [Woman] The small fishing village where the couple used to live became rife with rumors. Then, the Sun and Moon, which rose and fell beautifully every day, suddenly disappeared. The entire village fell into darkness. The Sun and Moon didn’t rise the next day either. In fact, the entire kingdom descended into total darkness.   [Court official] “Your majesty, I think this could be because of Yeonorang and Seonyeo. They used to pray to the Sun and Moon so devotedly every day. Now that they are gone, the entire kingdomhas gone dark.“  [Woman] So, King Adala sent an emissary to Japan and asked Yeonorang and Seonyeo to return home to Shilla.   [Court official] After the both of you, Yeonorang and Seonyeo, left Shilla, the Sun and Moon disappeared from our kingdom. The people are terrified in the darkness. Please come back with us to Shilla.”  [Woman] The emissary begged the couple. But, instead of agreeing to come home, Yeonorang and Seonyeo gave the emissary a surprising answer.  [Yeonorang] “We do not dream of declining His Majesty’s request. However, if we leave this place now,  it will descend into darkness as well. Also, we have lived here for a while now. Please understand we are in an impossible situation.”  [Seonyeo] “Instead, please take this silk. I wove it myself.Although it might not be the best silk in the world, I wove it for days, thinking about my homeland.”  [Man] So, Seonyeo’s silk came back to Shilla instead of Yeonorang and Seonyeo themselves. Immediately, the villagers used the silk to perform a ritual.Then, something amazing began to happen   [Villager 1] “Look over there. That must be the sun, right?”  [Villager 2] “Yes, yes. The sun is rising. The sun is rising again!”  [Man] From that day forward, Yeonorang and Seonyeo became symbols of the Sun and Moon, and their love story became legend.   [Woman] Oh, then the exhibition hall we visited a few moments ago was Gwibigo, the warehouse built to store the silk Seonyeo sent to Shilla.  [Man] That is correct. Now that we have seen Gwibigo, shall we move outside and head up to Ilwoldae?    Ilwoldae Pavilion    [Woman] Wow!~ The view from Ilwoldae is astonishing.~ I feel like I can let go of all the stress pent up inside of me.It almost seems as if I’m standing in the middle of the sea! It’s so refreshing.  [Man] Ilwoldae is a pavilion inspired by the Sun and Moon. The view from Ilwoldae is just as lovely as the beautiful love story between Yeonorang and Seonyeo.     Homi Peninsula Seaside Trail   [Man] Now, let’s go to the highlight of our trip to Pohang - the Homi Peninsula Seaside Trail~ Homi Peninsula Seaside Trail sits on the easternmost point of the Korean peninsula. It is the only seaside trekking road in Korea that features Yeongilman Bay.Here, the trail starts with the Yeonorang-Seonyeo Trail, then continues on to Homigot Square, and snakes around the entire coastline of Homigot Peninsula. In all, the trail is 58km -long.   [Woman] That’s great! Why don’t we take a leisurely walk along the trail? Wait! I have a question. Aren’t most trekking trails found on mountains? I think this is my first seaside trail.   [Man] You’re right. Opened in 2017, Homi Peninsula Seaside Trail is the only seaside trekking trail in Korea.  [Woman] Is the trail divided into different courses?   [Man] It is divided into four courses. Course number- 1 is the Yeonorang-Seonyeo Trail. Now, Yeonorang-Seonyeo Trail is 6.1km -long. It starts from the landing drill site used by the Marine Corps, then leads onto Dogu Beach, and Yeonorang and Seonyeo Theme Park. The Marine Corps landing drill site near the beginning of the course trains our Navy and Marines. At times, Korean and American troops hold joint tactical training exercises. If you’re lucky, you might get to see them train. If you walk past the training site, you’ll come to a colony of pine trees. The sea, the pine trees... (Pause) Wow. The view is simply amazing.   [Woman] There are plenty of rest stops and benches along the way, too. If you get tired from walking, you can sit for a break  and take in the magnificent view. You did the heavy lifting so far. So, I’ll take over for course number-2. Take a break here.  Course number -2 is the Seonbau Trail. Seonbau Trail starts in Ibam-ri, Donghae-myeon, then leads to Honghwan Beach, and Honghwaneohang Port. In total, the entire section is 6.5km. If you arrive at the halfway point of the trail, you’ll see a giant rock called “Hindigi.”The rock was originally named “Heungdeok” which meant “live in prosperity.” The Roh clan that settled the area gave the rock its name, but as time went by, the local dialect slowly changed the pronunciation of Heungdeok into Hindigi. That’s how the rock came to be the Hindigi rock. Oh! According to legend, if you make a wish in front of this white rock, you become rich. Believe it or not, it’s up to you.   [Man] Wow, Suji! You did a lot of research. That was great. Applause  [Woman] This is what I do.. Hahaha Well, then take us to course number -3 please.  [Man] Okay. Course number -3 is the Guryongso Trail. Guryongso Trail starts from the fishing port in Honghwan-ri, Donghae-myeon, then goes onto Daedongbae in Homigot-myeon. In total, the trail is 6 .km -long. Guryongso Trail gets its name from a legend about night dragons ascending into the 	heavens. On the west side of the Daedongbae Beach, there are nine holes on the sheer cliff face looking out into the sea. According to a legend that can be traced by to the reign of King Jinheung of Shilla, nine dragons came out of these holes and rose up to the heavens.   [Woman] The thought of dragons ascending into heaven makes the place look more 		auspicious. The sea looks deeper and darker, too. Haha    [Man] Hold on a moment! Can I give you a quiz? What shape best describes our country?  [Woman] Come on, I know that. Our country looks like a tiger.  [Man] Okay then. Which part of the tiger would Pohang be?  [Woman] Well..…you have the chest, the head...Oh, no! (In the dialect of ethnic Koreans in China) I don’t know...  [Man] Here, the Homi Peninsula is where the tiger’s tail would be. A tiger’s tail is the symbol of a nation’s fortune. That means Homi Peninsula sits in the most auspicious area in all of Korea.   Kim Jeong-ho, a Joseon Dynasty cartographer, visited the Homi Peninsula seven times just to make sure it was at the easternmost point of Korea when he was drawing the Daedongyeojido Map.  Also, according to legend, “Gyeokam” Nam Sa-go (a famous Fengshui geomancy expert who lived during the reign of King Myeongjong of Joseon) named Homi Peninsula as the most auspicious location in Korea.Meanwhile, “Yukdang” Choi Nam-seon listed the sunrise at Cape Homigot as one of the ten best views of Joseon in his book, the Joseon Sangsikjiri.  [Women] It seems like our ancestors were all correct! Everywhere I go, I see something beautiful. In terms of gorgeous views, Pohang and its coastline are the best!  [Man] Course number -4, the last leg of the Seaside Trail, is called the Homi Trail. At 5.3km -long, Homi Trail features “Ggaggurigae” rock (also known as Eagle Rock) and Cape Homigot Sunrise Square. The name Ggaggurigae comes from a Gyeongsang-do dialect “Ggagguri” which refers to a rake. People living along the Homi Trail used rakes to gather all the herring whenever they washed ashore.That is why the rock was named Ggaggurigae.     If you walk along the trail, you will come across a commemorative tablet for Yi Yuk-sa’s Green Grapes poem, a commemorative tablet called “Kwaeeunghwanhonan Ginyeombi,” The National Lighthouse Museum, the Hand of Mutual Sake, and the New Millennium Memorial Hall.  [Woman] Wow. I think we’re doing an amazing job. We started out with Yeonorang and Seonyeo but now, we’ve arrived at Homigot Square. That means we have walked 25km. Shall we give ourselves a round of applause before we move on? Despite the fact that we walked a lot, I don’t feel that tired. It must be because of the vast East Sea, right? I don’t think I can come up with a better trekking trail if I’m looking for a place to enjoy the indigo-colored sea and the music of waves.  [Man] You’re right. In particular, the trekking trail here does not have any steep hills. That makes it perfect for everyone, from children to the elderly, to walk together. I heartily recommend the trail if you want to go on a family trip.  [Woman] So far, we’ve picked out some of the most beautiful places in Pohang. What did you think? If you want to enjoy beautiful landscapes all year long, don’t hesitate. Why not head over to the blue waters of Pohang?

stories.title: Homigot Village
stories.script: People say that the Korean peninsula has the shape of a tiger preparing for a leap into the Maritime Province of Russia. From that perspective, Pohang is located at the tiger’s tail.  Homigot Village in Pohang is known as the home of the best sunrises in the country. The word Got in Homigot refers to a piece of land that protrudes into a lake or sea but is smaller than a peninsula.  There’s a secret story behind Homigot Cape dating back to the 16th century Joseon era during the reign of King Myeongjong. Nam Sa-go, a renowned Fengshui geomancy scholar, wrote about visiting the Homigot Cape and its coastline: “Geographically, this place sits where the tiger’s tail would be. It’s the most auspicious place in the land.” Tigers use their tails when they sprint forward or command others, which are the most essential ways a tiger’s energy is expressed. Therefore, Pohang’s location has been considered the symbol of the nation’s fortunes and security.  During Japan's colonization of Korea, they recognized the geographical significance of Pohang. They attempted to drive an iron stake through Homigot Cape to sever the flow of auspicious energy through Joseon. The oppression didn't end there. When a Japanese military vessel ran aground while attempting to infiltrate Joseon through the East Sea, they blamed Joseon for not having a lighthouse in the area. They argued that Joseon must pay for the damages and build a lighthouse immediately.  However, Joseon lacked technicians capable of constructing a lighthouse. Japan forced the country to invite foreign engineers at a high cost.  This is why the lighthouse in Homigot Cape was designed by French engineers and built by Chinese construction workers. The lighthouse takes the shape of an octagonal pagoda. Bricks without rebars were used in its construction. The interior comprises six floors, each bearing the pattern of a plum blossom, symbolizing the royal Korean family. Despite its creation under tragic circumstances, it has safeguarded numerous vessels passing through the East Sea for more than a hundred years.

stories.title: Deokdong Cultural Village
stories.audioTitle: A land of history and myths, Pohang
stories.script: Deokdong Cultural Village  [Woman] Pohang-si, Gyeongsangbuk-do, is home to a remote village that is more than 300 years old. The entire village is like a museum. Of course, I’m talking about Deokdong Cultural Village.   [Man] Let’s travel to Deokdong Cultural Village where nature, history, people, and culture all coexist in harmony.  Deokdong Cultural Village features a dense forest and plenty of old houses that feel like they would belong to aristocratic families. There is a special reason why Deokdong Cultural Village was first created. Shall we rewind the clock 360 years?  [Woman] When the Japanese invaded the Joseon Dynasty in 1592, the entire country was engulfed in turmoil. “Nongpo” Jeong Mun-bu, a court official who served during the middle years of the Joseon Dynasty, had organized a militia to fight against Japanese invaders. But during battle, he was shot and injured.   [Jeong Mun-bu] “Surely, we’ve out-run the Japanese soldiers. But, where are we exactly? Hold on. I didn’t know such a place existed in Joseon. This is an auspicious piece of land I have never seen before.  [Man] Jeong Mun-bu organized a militia during the Japanese invasion of Joseon in 1592.The place he discovered during the war becam Deokdong Cultural Village.   [Woman] When Jeong Mun-bu returned home after the war, he gave his house to his grandson-in-law, Lee Gang. Lee Gang was one of the five wise men in the Yeongnam region during the Joseon Dynasty. He was the great-great-grandson of Lee Eon-gwal, the younger brother of “Heejae” Lee Eon-jeok. Lee Gang, who was living in Yangdong Village in Gyeongju, soon moved to Deokdong Cultural Village. As a result, his children stayed in Deokdong Cultural Village to carry on the legacy of orthodox Confucianism developed during the Joseon Dynasty. Now, this aristocratic village is more than 360 years old. Deokdong Cultural Village was also registered as “Archive-friendly Village No.4 by the National Archives of Korea. But there is a special story behind that as well.   [Man] One day, villagers gathered around to fix the old pavilion. They used a ladder to get to the roof and started to peel off the old material. But inside, there were several volumes of old dusty books. The villagers were all taken aback. They carefully removed all the books and the name plate, gathered them on the floor of the pavilion, and paid their respects.  [Woman] Oh my god. What are all these old books? Let’s open them up, quick!   [Man] Aren’t these books more than 230 years old?  [Woman] That day, the villagers discovered old books from the Joseon Dynasty that were more than 200 years old inside Yonggyejeong Pavilion.   [Woman] Look here. There are records of when people planted gingko trees, bamboo trees, zinnia trees, and juniper trees.”  [Man] There are records on the Yonggyejeong Pavilion, Saeuidang Hall, and Sedeoksa Temple.  We have four name plates as well. It seems to be the writing of Kang Se-hwang, who served as the Minister of Culture and Education. These definitely seem to have significant value as historical records. Let’s report it to the authorities!  [Woman] The villagers took all the books and records to the National Archives of Korea.  [Government official] “I’ve never seen these kinds of documents before. I think your ancestors were worried they might lose the documents for some reason, and hid them inside the roof of the pavilion to make sure their children got them.”  [Woman] That is how Deokdong Cultural Village became an archive-friendly village via the National Archives of Korea. Their ancestors had left records across more than 140 years from 1780 to 1922.  Deokdong Cultural Village has Saudang (home of “Nongpo” Jeong Mun-bu and 		Lee Gang), Aeeundang and Yeoyeondang (home to Lee Gang’s family), Deokgyeoseodang (study hall for villagers), and other modern Hanok buildings. If you take your time and walk the streets of the village, you’ll feel like you’ve gone on a time machine back to the Joseon Dynasty.  [Man] People of Deokdong Cultural Village can look back on their history because they were careful enough to preserve and carry on the legacy of their ancestors from 400 years ago. Perhaps it is a reward for their dedication. So, come visit Deokdong Cultural Village, a village that looks like it came out of an oriental artwork

stories.title: Bogyeongsa Temple
stories.audioTitle: History in the bosom of beautiful nature Pohang
stories.script: Bogyeongsa Temple  [Man] Korea is a country with pristine waters and magnificent mountains! There is a special place in Pohang that was so beautiful, it made a fan out of “Gyeomjae” Jeong Seon, a master landscape painter who lived during the Joseon Dynasty!  [Woman] He’s referring to Bogyeongsa Temple and Naeyeonsan Waterfall in Pohang. Let’s head over to Bogyeongsa Temple at Naeyeonsan Mountain, which makes an appearance in one of Jeong Seon’s paintings.    [Man] Built during the reign of Kin Jinpyeong of Shilla, Bogyeongsa Temple is a branch 		temple of Bulguksa Temple. King Gojong of the Goryeo Dynasty rebuilt it as a bigger temple. Eventually, it became a major temple during the Joseon Dynasty.  [Woman] During the Joseon Dynasty, monks at Bogyeongsa Temple mainly produced paper using paper mulberry and supplied it to the government. From time to time, they also took high-ranking officials into the beautiful valleys of Naeyeonsan Mountain on retreats.  [Man] The valleys near Bogyeongsa Temple are so beautiful, they have been listed as one of the top-8 beautiful destinations in Gyeongsangbuk-do.  [Woman] According to history, “Gyeomjae” Jeong Seon, a painter during the Joseon Dynasty, frequented Naeyeonsan Mountain and Bogyeongsa Temple when he was stationed as an official at the Cheongha-hyeon office.  [Jeong Seon] “It is amazing. The Buddhist painting in Jeokgwangjeon Hall at Bogyeongsa 			Temple is so elegant, as the artist used white lines without a hint of any hesitation. The facial expression of Gwangmokcheonwang giving the side-eye is extremely interesting as well.”  [Man] Here, Jeong Seon was commenting about the “Birojanabuldo” painting which has been designated as a national treasure. It is a Seonmyo-style Buddhist painting that uses a coat of red painted on help canvass and white paint to draw the characters and their clothes.   [Woman] This Seonmyo-style Buddhist painting was created by monks called Noehyeon, Milgi, and Seokjam who lived during the 18th century. In particular, when looking at the painting, it becomes apparent that Noehyeon was an exceptionally talented painter.    [Man] Seonmyo-style Buddhist paintings during the Goryeo Dynasty used silk as canvass and golden paint to draw the lines. They were only painted for the royal family or noble families. Common folk could not even dream of seeing them. But, when the Joseon Dynasty rolled around, Buddhism became much more of a people’s religion. Naturally, artists started replacing silk as the canvass for Buddhist paintings with help.   [Woman] Apart from its Seonmyo-style paintings, Bogyeongsa Temple has another example of how Buddhism spread across the common people. These paintings are called hanging paintings. The Hanging Painting at Bogyeongsa Temple is widely regarded as one of 	Eugyun’s best  works. On a 10m canvas, the artist drew a lone Buddha in the Bodhisattva form holding a lotus stem.   [Man] During the Joseon Dynasty, if the temple had to host a large service that could   		not fit everyone inside its halls, the monks used to hang a large painting of Buddha outdoors and let people pray outside. For particularly large ceremonies, monks performed dance routines, such as the Nabichum and Barachum, and played music. In short, they were distinctly comprehensive Buddhist, art performances.   [Woman] When the temple hung a large painting of the Buddha, and held a service outdoors, the common people would flock to the temple to learn from the words of Buddha. That is where the oft-used term “Yadanbeopseok” comes from - preparing a stage outdoors (“Yadan”) for a Buddhist ceremony (“Beopseok”).  [Man] Indeed, the term we use to describe a loud and bustling event or place comes from these outdoor events at Buddhist temples.   [Woman] Now, Bogyeongsa Temple came to own six treasures because it enjoyed a renaissance during the Joseon Dynasty.     [Man] Another thing we shouldn’t forget about is the gorgeous view of Naeyeonsan Mountain. When “Gyeomjae” Jeong Seon was serving as the governor of Cheongha-hyeon, he drew the landscape of a valley at Naeyeonsan Mountain.  [Woman] Naeyeonsan Mountain had a special place not only in the heart of Jeong Seon, but also the hearts of other high-ranking officials at the time. Boulders near the beautiful Jamryong Waterfall, Mupung Waterfall, Gwaneum Waterfall, and Yeonsan Waterfall bear the names of more than 200 people who visited the mountain. They were the modern equivalent of ‘selfies,’ to show that they had actually been there.   [Man] So, we took a look at Bogyeongsa Temple at Naeyeonsan Mountain... Did you enjoy tranquil trip to the temple? The more you know about the history of a place, your trip becomes more meaningful.I hope this serves as a valuable resource when you plan for your next trip

stories.title: Jukdo Market
stories.script: Jukdo Market started out as a temporary market right after the Korean War. Today, with more than 2,000 shops, 200 of which are fresh sashimi restaurants, Jukdo Market has become a massive establishment.    Labeled as the largest traditional market for tourists along the eastern sea border, it takes two hours to cover the entire marketplace on foot. What makes Jukdo Market special is the fact that fishing boats can come right up to the market entrance and supply freshly caught seafood. Shopkeepers try to win over customers, saying, “(In the local dialect) Let me know what you’re interested in. I’ll guarantee dirt-cheap prices.” These little interactions withof customers haggling with shopkeepers for a better price will entertain your ears and add character to the market experience.    Another peculiar sight you can expect to see at Jukdo mMarket is the long lines of people waiting to eat a bowl of “Kaljebi.” Kaljebi is a hybrid dish between Kalguksu (chopped noodles) and Sujebi (hand-pulled dough soup). It has an amazing spicy flavor you will not find anywhere else. The portions are extremely generous as well. Aside from Kaljebi, there is one other thing you simply cannot miss at Jukdo Market.   It is called shark “Dombaegi.” In Pohang-si, to see if you’re a ”somebody” all you have to do is look at what they serve on the table during their ancestral rites and family banquets. According to tradition, affluent families in the area used to serve shark Dombaegi (matured shark meat) for ancestral rituals and sunfish during family banquets or festivals. As you walk past the shark Dombaegi shops, you might catch a glimpse of something else that attracts your attention. Now might be time for you to try matured whale meat.  Pohang is home to Guryongpo Port, which appears in a children’s story titled “Ghost Whale,” and Damupo Port, a well-known whaling village. In all, Pohang used to be a major producer of whale meat.   Now, you might be thinking of another great tourist attraction when you think of whaling - the Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village in Ulsan. So, how about starting your trip in the Jukdo Market in Pohang, visit Guryongpo and Damupo to learn more about our whaling history, then travel all the way out to Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village in Ulsan?

stories.title: Pohang Canal / Pohang Cruise
stories.script: Pohang Canal is often called the Venice of Pohang. Pohang Canal was built when the city government of Pohang decided to reopen the waterways of the Dongbin Inner Harbor.   As a forward base for the fishing industry during the Japanese colonial rule of Korea, Dongbin Inner Harbor played an integral role in developing the local economy. After Korea won its independence, Pohang became an international port city and a gateway into the Gyeongsangbuk-do region.   Pohang Canal flows through Dongbin Inner Harbor and into the heart of the city. It offers some spectacular views with canola flowers in spring and cosmos flowers in autumn. Moreover, there are plenty of steel art pieces showcased along the canal, which gives visitors a chance to enjoy art as they walk along the embankment.   Another place you should absolutely visit is the Pohang Canal Observatory. Here, you can take in the almost mystical view of Yeongilman Bay, where the Hyeongsangang River flows into the East Sea, and the magnificent view of lights illuminating the steel yards in Pohang at night.     You can also board a Pohang cruise, which is another way to immerse yourself into the beautiful landscape of Pohang Canal.  Meanwhile, Songdo Beach is a great place if you want some time to think. It has a dense forest with hundreds of pine trees and flocks of seagulls gliding overhead in the sky. The Daewangam Park in Ulsan has a staggering 10,000 Haesong (a type of pine tree) trees. So, it might be a great idea to visit the Songdo Beach near the Pohang Canal, then head over to Daewangam Park to see how the trees and the surrounding landscape are unique.

stories.title: Japanese-style Housing Street in Guryongpo
stories.script: According to legend, nine dragons (“guryong”) ascended to heaven near Guryongpo Port. Despite its auspicious name, Guryongpo Port was used as a forward base for fishing throughout the Japanese colonial rule of Korea.    At the time, the waters near Guryongpo were so bountiful, fishermen apparently had to dump some of the fish they had caught and their fishing tools in the sea to make sure their boats returned to port safely without sinking. Naturally, it became the most popular target for the Japanese Empire.    Some Japanese people eventually settled down in Guryongpo and amassed substantial amounts of wealth by exploiting the fishermen and other resources at Guryongpo Port. They even built a department store, pharmacy, and a park which, eventually, led to the modernization of the Guryongpo area.    When the Japanese Empire surrendered to the Allies, the Japanese in Guryongpo were forced to flee as well. Their houses were left abandoned. Instead of demolishing those houses, the Pohang-si city government decided to restore those houses and the Japanese-style street to educate the public and raise awareness about how the Japanese exploited our country.  Today, Guryongpo residents actually live inside the Japanese-style houses. Guryongpo Port also has a Modern History Museum that gives visitors a glimpse into the interior of the former Japanese-style houses, what fishing tools people used, and how they went about their daily lives.   However, the most striking feature of the Japanese-style housing street in Guyrongpo is, the 120 stone columns lining each side of the stairway leading up to the park, and the “Togawa Yasuburo Commemorative Monument” made with cement, the Chunghontap Tower, Chunghongak Pavilion, and the sculpture of an ascending dragon . Recently, the Guryongpo Gwamegi Museum has also become an extremely popular destination. You can experience the distinct fishing culture that developed throughout history along our eastern seaboard.  If you are looking for a similar place to Guryongpo (a forward base for fishing under the Japanese Empire), you can check out the Japanese-style Street in Bangeojin, Ulsan, and Jangsaengpo Port also in Ulsan. How about visiting these historical locations and learning about the sacrifices locals had to make under the colonial rule of Japan?

stories.title: Sabang Memorial Park
stories.audioTitle: Bird’s eye view of the natural eco-road
stories.script: The Korean government launched its first “Sabang” project in 1907 near Bukhansan Mountain. “Sabang” refers to the act of preventing the erosion of sand into the sea and stopping landslides to protect forests.   Sabang Memorial Park in Pohang was built in 2007 to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the first Sabang project in Korea.  It was developed as part of a green industry initiative alongside the steel manufacturing business. According to the locals, people did not use any special tools for this extraordinary They used their hands to carve out cascading mountains and waterways to help preserve the forest. That could be the reason why?  Sabang Memorial Park boasts unrivaled scenery. The forest, the sky, and the cobalt-blue ocean create the perfect sense of harmony. The small harbor with a red lighthouse and soot-black rocks create a tranquil ambiance. People call the view at Sabang Memorial Park the “Odori.”  Pohang realized the public value of forests from early on. The city’s catchphrase is “Greenway.”    The “Healing Road” at Ulsan Grand Park and Bomun Tourist Complex in Gyeongju also have some great eco-tourism attractions. Put Sabang Memorial Park in Pohang on your list of places to visit when you are making plans for your next trip. Enjoy a “green” and refreshing walk in the Park.

stories.title: Pohang city that looks beautiful at night
stories.audioTitle: A steel-making mecca in Korea, a city that looks beautiful at night
stories.script: Yeongildae Beach and Yeongildae seaside pavilion, both of which are in the Buk-gu area of Pohang, are two great places the enjoy the beautiful nightscape of Pohang. Stretching 2km-wide, Yeongildae Beach offers romantic busking performances on weekends, and it hosts the International Fire and Light Festival organized by the Pohang-si municipal government.    Most notably, the brilliant view of the steel mills in Pohang at night is so beautiful; it will make you feel like you have somehow traveled all the way to New York City.  The brightly lit fresh sashimi restaurants and cafes along the coastline will also add to the romantic ambiance of your trip. On a different note, a few years ago archaeologists discovered fossils of marine animals from the Mesozoic era at the Sunrise Park near Yeongildae. Naturally, it comes up in conversations when people visit Yeongildae to enjoy the view at night.    So, what do you think? Enjoying the nightscape along the Yeongildae coast will prove to be a great idea. Would you like to go on another “night tour” after that? If you do, head over to the “Street of Youth” and “Hwanglidan-gil” in Gyeongju. Alternatively, we recommend a trip to the Ulsan Daegyo Bridge Observatory in the evening.

stories.title: Greenway Railroad Forest
stories.audioTitle: A walking trail that will entertain your eyes and ears
stories.script: The Greenway Railroad Forest used to be a patch of land with old, abandoned railway tracks. Today, it is a public park that symbolizes the Greenway philosophy of Pohang as a city.    When the city government was removing the old tracks, workers accidentally discovered natural gas buried under the site. A flame that was lit to get rid of unnecessary gas still burns to this day, which is why the park is also known as the “Garden of Fire.”   Greenway Railroad Forest also features steel art. In particular, there is an interesting piece that reveals different faces as you move closer.    You can spend time thinking or walking along the tracks. As you walk along, you might find the ceremonial tree planted for the Korea-Russia Regional Cooperation Forum 2018. The tree is a symbol that shows that the Greenway Railroad Forest has become a place for international cooperation and exchange.   The beautiful Greenway Railroad Forest has blooming flowers in spring and yellow Gingko leaves in autumn.    This year, welcome the new spring season at the Railroad Forest, and then head over to Ulsan Grand Park for a nice, leisurely walk along the Healing Road.

stories.title: Oeosa Temple in Pohang
stories.audioTitle: “Temple of my fish,” a clever play on words by the famous monk
stories.script: According to history, it seems the Buddhist monk Wonhyo knew how to enjoy himself in the company of friends  when he was not busy writing or pursuing spiritual enlightenment.    The literal translation of the name “Oeosa” amounts to the “temple of my fish.” The Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms tells the story in detail. One day, after a long day of studying, Hyegong and Wonhyo (both Buddhist monks) decided to catch some fish from the river. After they ate their fish, they went to the toilet.  But soon, two fish appeared from the toilet. One went upstream, while the other swam downstream. As they watched the fish swimming upstream, Hyegong and Wonhyo jokingly argued that the fish belonged to them. Thereafter, inspired by this story, the nearby temple was named the “temple of my fish,” in other words “Oeosa.”   Frankly, it might sound a little strange to hear a story about the “stool” of such a great monk However, the well-known story of how he slept with Princess Yoseok who then gave birth to Seolchong, and other anecdotes of Wonhyo interacting with the common people in the market seem to suggest Wonhyo was an extremely free-spirited monk. The Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms even gave Wonhyo the moniker “Wonhyo Bulgi” which means “a monk who is not bound by anything.”  Meanwhile, Oeosa Temple is home to the 8km-long Oeoji Reservoir trail nearby. If you walk along the trail, you can visit Oeoho Lake, Metasequoia Forest, and Naehangsa Village.

stories.title: Long-term Exile Culture Experience Zone
stories.script: Along with Jeju-do Island, Gangjin in Jeollanam-do, and Namhae in Gyeongsangnam-do, Janggi-myeon in Pohang-si (Gyeongsangbuk-do) was a well-known place of exile during the Joseon Dynasty. Known as “Janggi-hyeon” at the time, famous scholars such as “Dasan” (Jeong Yak-yong) and “Uam” (Song Si-yeol) as well as prime ministers were once exiled to Janggi-myeon. Over time, the presence of high-profile exiles gave birth to a distinct exile culture.  According to the “Shinjeungdongguk Yeojiseungram,” Janggi-myeon was approximately 864 ri (distance unit used during the Joseon Dynasty) away from Seoul. Its remoteness was one of the primary reasons why it became such a popular place of exile.  The region once stood at the heart of the Shilla Kingdom. Once Shilla collapsed, however, it was relegated to an unremarkable frontier area. As the number of prominent scholars, (who previously enjoyed great power and authority in the central government), exiled to Janggi-myeon grew, the local culture became much more sophisticated.  Despite the fact that they were forced to endure incredible hardship, exiles made time to read books, write papers, and educate scholars within the region. This created a culture where people valued academics, and a community that prioritized loyalty and courtesy.   If you visit Janggi-myeon today, you can still see the site where the famous “Dasan” (Jeong Yak-yong) spent his time in exile. Charged for his involvement in the Catholic persecution of 1801, he composed  hundreds of poems and wrote several books on practical subjects while in exile.   In addition to Jeong Yak-yong’s house, Janggi-myeon has a variety of other attractions, including the house of exile where “Uam” (Song Si-yeol) used to live, the private residence of Oh Do-jeon, carts used to transport prisoners to their place of exile, the site where officials used to flog prisoners, a natural healing forest, Manghyangjeong Pavilion, natural embankments and facilities along the river, and a stage for traditional folk plays or games.   This is the only place in the country where you can experience cultural features created by exiles. It sounds interesting, right?

stories.title: Malmokjangseong Trail
stories.script: Located in Guryongpo-eup (Nam-gu, Pohang-si, Gyeongsangbuk-do), Malmokjangseong Trail follows along the stone fence of the largest government-owned horse ranch during the Joseon Dynasty. Originally, the 8km-long trail connected Guryongpo Port and Heunghwan-ri in Nam-gu. Today, only 5.6km of the trail remains.  According to the Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms, the horse ranch first opened approximately 1400 years ago.  An official of the “Jong-6 pum” rank supervised the ranch, and a dedicated military force was stationed at the ranch to perform janitorial duties (including the removal and cleaning of horse droppings).   The ranch now features a two-story observation deck more than 200m above sea level, which gives visitors a bird’s-eye view of Guryongpo Port and the ridges along Homi Peninsula. There are plenty of other things to see near the site, including the ruins of a beacon fire station, and a colony of Korean Dendranthema.   The Malmokjangseong Trail is the perfect place to learn about the history of war horses used during the Joseon Dynasty, and enjoy some breathtaking views. Walk along the old trail, and take a relaxing break.

stories.title: Dokseok Village
stories.audioTitle: Backdrop of the Pohang Evacuation Operation in movie “The Front Line”
stories.script: Dokseok Village is best known as a registered historic site for patriotic deeds. From August 15 to August 17 of 1950, the 3rd Infantry Division fought the invading forces of North Korea. Once its rear flank was cut off from its allies, the 3rd Infantry Division decided to evacuate people through an extraction point near the coast of Dokseok-dong. The village made an appearance in movie “The Front Line” which reenacted the Pohang Evacuation Operation that took place on the beaches of Dokseok-dong at Pohang-si (Gyeongsangbuk-do).  The beautiful eastern seaboard of Dokseok-dong Is home to several skin diving and scuba diving companies, making it the ideal place to try some marine activities.   You can explore the pristine waters of the East Sea, catch some seafood like conchs or sea squirts, and enjoy them on the spot. All of it is so exciting.   Today, Dokseok-dong has become an important strategic location in the defense of our country. It even serves as a location for joint maritime training exercises between Korean and American forces. Continued military activity clearly shows how Dokseok-dong still serves as a military position even though half a century has passed since the Pohang Evacuation Operation.   If you get a chance to visit Dokseok-dong in Buk-gu, Pohang-si, re-watch a few scenes from “The Front Line” beforehand. You will realize that Pohang, a beautiful city on the eastern seaboard of our country, survived because of all the soldiers who gave their lives for one last mission.

stories.title: Yeongildae Beach
stories.script: Maximizing Blue Water, Yeongildae Beach   Pohang has two fantastic beaches to offer, the Songdo Beach and Yeongildae Beach. With a vast white sandy beach stretching across 380,000㎡, Yeongildae Beach is popular among tourists who want to walk along the soft sandy shores of the East Sea.   The beach also has a bicycle road along the coastal road, making it the perfect place for cycling enthusiasts. Adjacent to Yeongildae Beach is “Gomsol (Japanese Black Pine)” Forest with more than seventy pine trees. Gomsol Forest features more than twenty geometrically shaped steel art pieces with striking names, “Life,” “Birth of Venus,” “Mrs. Kim’s Excursion,” etc., along the footpath as well. Thanks to the mix of pine trees and steel artwork, Gomsol Forest is a popular photo zone for visitors. These are photos exhibited at the ‘Pohang Steel Art Festival,’ which has been held annually since 2012. Additionally, Yeongildae Beach has various benches, a parasol-shaped resting area, and five busking stages for musicians.   Here, you can enjoy a special view that features the steel mills in Pohang and Yeongilman Bay. Together, the bright lights illuminating the steel mills at night and view of Yeongildae Pavilion (a seaside pavilion) are known as one of the Top 12 Must-See attractions of Pohang. Every year, Yeongildae Beach hosts a New Year’s Festival, then the First Full Moon Event, the National Marine Leisure Sports Games, the Lunchbox Festival, Pohang International Fireworks Festival, the Sand Sculpture Festival, Yeongildae Fire and Light Parade, and the Christmas Festival for Pohang Citizens, etc.   With so many events, Yeongildae Beach has so much entertainment to offer.

stories.title: Aeeundang Gotae k
stories.script: In Pohang-si, Gyeongsangbuk-do, you can find a village that is full of so many interesting artifacts, the entire village almost seems like a museum. That village is the Deokdong Cultural Village. Here, the name “Deokdong” means, “home of the virtuous.”   Deokdong Village also serves as the home village of the Lee clan, a family that originated from the Yeogang region. The village, which boasts 400 years of tradition, has a forest that features some beautiful old trees, and some old houses. Among all the antique houses, the most famous are Aeeundang Gotaek, Saujeong Gotaek, and Eoyeondang Gotaek. In particular, Aeeundang Gotaek used to belong to “Nongpo” Jeong Mun-bu, a high-ranking official during the Joseon Dynasty who served his country admirably during the Japanese Invasion of 1592. The house offers a prime example of how aristocratic families used to live during the medieval times.   Jeong Mun-bu evacuated his family to Aeeundang Gotaek during the invasion, then gave it to his son-in-law when the war ended. From a “fengshui” geomancy  perspective, Aeeundang Gotaek stands on a parcel of a tortoise-shaped land. The annex and mill is located where the tortoise’s front legs should be, while the silkworm-raising room is located where the head is, and the toilet is found where the tale should be. Overall, the house has a rectangular shape and features a main building, storage room, and guest house. It allows you to imagine how aristocratic families used to live during the Joseon Dynasty.   The Gyeongsangbuk-do government acknowledged the value of Aeeundang Gotaek as a cultural heritage and designated it as Folk Cultural Heritage No.80 in 1988. Please note that someone actually lives at Aeeundang Gotaek today. So, if you do visit the village, be courteous to the elders and refrain from being too loud or inconveniencing the villagers.

stories.title: Mural Street at Imgok Village
stories.audioTitle: A place to enjoy charming little murals
stories.script: Do you remember the tale of “Yeonorang and Seonyeo,” the story about a fisherman from Shilla named Yeonorang who migrated to Japan with his wife, then became the king?   Unfortunately for the Shilla Kingdom, Yeonorang and Seonyeo were the symbols of the sun and moon. After they left the kingdom, the sun and moon became dim and other strange things started to happen. The King of Shilla begged the couple to return home. But they told the emissary that they could not disobey the gods in heaven. Instead, they instructed the emissary to take the silk woven by Seonyeo herself back to Shilla and use it to perform a ritual.  When the King followed the instruction of Yeonorang, the sun and moon started to shine again like a miracle. Of course, the story is not a factual description of what actually happened. It is best understood as an anecdote laden with symbolic meaning.   The place where Yeonorang and Seonyeo used to live according to this legend is Imgok Village in Pohang-si, Gyeongsangbuk-do. Here, you will find a black boulder known as “Meokbau.” Locals say that Yeonorang and Seonyeo rode Meokbau when they traveled to Japan.   Apart from Meokbau, Imgok Village features Yeonorang and Seonyeo Theme Park. It also has a seaside trail that runs along the Homi Peninsula, which is part of course number 16 of the Haeparang-gil trail. If you walk along this trail, you will come across murals illustrating the tale of Yeonorang and Seonyeo. These murals are hidden across the entire village, particularly along the walls of the Imgok Community Youth Center and on the street leading up to Yeonorang Seonyeo Theme Park. These murals have turned the village from a quiet little fishing village to a charming tourist attraction. So, why don’t you head over to Imgok Village, enjoy the colorful murals, and take a long walk along the seaside trail?

stories.title: Guryongpo Port
stories.audioTitle: A port where nine dragons appeared
stories.script: Guryongpo. The name literally means a port where nine dragons appeared.   The story begins during the reign of King Jinheung of Shilla.  One day, the administrator of Janggi-hyeon was patrolling his county. But suddenly, a violent storm broke out, bringing gale winds and thunder. As the storm kept raging, ten dragons began ascending into the heavens. One, however, did not make it all the way to the sky. In the end, only nine dragons ascended to heaven, and that is how Guryongpo Port got its name.  In fact, Guryongpo has a sad and painful past. During the late-19th century, Japanese fishermen began fishing in the waters near Guryongpo. In 1883, the Regulations for the Conduct of Trade between Joseon and Japan gave Japanese fishermen complete freedom to fish in the sovereign waters of the Joseon Dynasty.   This, inevitably, led to the severe exploitation of our marine resources. Despite the damage, the Korean Empire and Japan signed the Treaty on Fisheries in 1908, which brought more Japanese fishermen into Korea. In 1923, under the Japanese colonial rule of Korea, port facilities and a seawall was built, transforming Guryongpo into a more modern port. Because of this heritage, the Modern History Street in Guryongpo, which sits adjacent to the port, still bears several traces of Japanese-inspired buildings and structures including Japanese-style traditional houses.  Meanwhile, Guryongpo Port is the largest producer of Gwamegi (semi-dried herring) and snow crabs in the country. Early in the morning every day, fishermen auction off their haul at the market. Especially, when snow crab fishing boats make port, Guyrongpo really comes alive and gives visitors a taste of a vibrant seafood market. The port is also close to Guryongpo Market, so you can enjoy the warm and friendly hospitality of a local market as well as its delicious food.

stories.title: Haemieupseong Walled Town Jinnammun Gate (South Gate)
stories.script: Haemieupseong Walled Town was built around the bottom of Jinesan Hill, connected to the west side of Seongmunbong Peak of Gayasan Mountain. Construction of the fortress began during the Joseon period in 1417, under the reign of King Taejong, and was initially completed in 1421, under the reign of King Sejong, to defend against attack from Japanese invaders. The entire complex was completed in 1491, under the reign of King Seongjong. The fortress is 4.9 meters in height, 1,800 meters in length, and the area of the walled town of the old barracks is 190,000 square meters. Of the original gates, the East and West Gates were destroyed, to be reconstructed in 1974; only the South Gate Jinnammun has been kept in its original form; the North Gate is an auxiliary gate. Jinnammun Gate is a rainbow-shaped arched gate, on which is a three-kan-wide, two-story pavilion with a hip-and-gable roof. The signboard of Jinnammun Gate was written by Yi Jin-baek, who was a county magistrate of Taean from  Yeomi-ri, Unsan, well-known for his righteousness and calligraphy. Lots of people from Chungcheong-do were mobilized for the construction of the fortress, and under Jinnammun Gate is an engraved phrase that reads it was built by the people from Gongju. Haemieupseong Walled Town is Historic Site no.116 and Must-visit Destination of Seosan no.1 out of nine. Also, it is one of the three well-preserved walled towns in South Korea.

stories.title: Haemieupseong Walled Town Jamyangnu Gate (East Gate)
stories.script: Jamyangnu Gate, the East Gate of Haemieupseong Walled Town, is built toward the eastern mountainous area and Hamicheon Stream. Its wall is not equipped with a defense system and was constructed to overwatch the invasion of the enemy. The gate had once been destroyed, but was restored in 1974. During the persecution of Catholics in the Naepo region (the southwestern part of Chungcheongnam-do), the Catholics from Deoksan moved through this gate, were inspected, and then went out through the West Gate to be executed. At the bottom of the wall around the gate, it is written that the wall was built by the people from Chungju up to a certain point, and by those from Imcheon from a certain point. The reason for leaving this engraved phrase seems to clarify their respective responsibility by section.

stories.title: Haemieupseong Walled Town Jiseongnu Gate (West Gate)
stories.script: Jiseongnu Gate is the West Gate of Haemieupseong Walled Town. Outside the wall, trifoliate oranges were planted in order to defend the enemy’s attack, so the walled town itself was once called Jiseong-myeon (‘Ji (枳)’ means trifoliate orange). The Great Admiral Yi Sun-sin of the Joseon Dynasty also worked here as a commissioned officer. Inside the wall were three springs, and with a 8-meter gap outward of the trifoliate oranges, there was a moat—10-11 meters wide on the top, 5 meters wide at the bottom, and 1.4-2.4 meters deep. The northern part of the moat has been partly restored. Outside Jiseongnu Gate, there is a broad rock where Catholics were executed. It is one of the three Catholic execution grounds in Chungcheongnam-do, and it is known that 405 Catholics, the least in Haemi, were executed here.

stories.title: Haemieupseong Walled Town Emplacement (Fortification)
stories.script: The Haemieupseong Walled Town has two emplacements. An emplacement is the structure around which the wall protrudes so that a cannon can be installed and fired from a higher position. During the Japanese invasion of Korea in 1592 and the Manchu War of 1636, the Joseon government realized the power of modern weapons and wisely started to build the fortification for effective defense.

stories.title: Haemieupseong Walled Town Gaeksa (Guesthouse)
stories.script: In Haemieupseong Walled Town, there were various buildings including Dongheon (Magistrate's Office), Naea (Living Quarters), Gaeksa (Guesthouse), Janggwancheong (Office of Military Affairs), Gyoryeoncheong (Drilling Center), Jakcheong, Saryeongcheong, Chaeksil (Book Publishing Building), Naesammun Gate, Oisammun Gate, Naechang, Gungigo, Hwayakgo, and Oksa (Jail). Among these structures, the largest was the guesthouse. It provided accommodations for officials or envoys from the central government or a superior office. A wood plate symbolizing the king was enshrined at the guesthouse, and every first day of the month and middle of the month, the local magistrate led a ceremony to pay respect with the officials on their business trip. The guesthouse in Haemieupseong Walled Town was excavated and surveyed in 1981 and restored in July 1999.

stories.title: Haemieupseong Walled Town Dongheon (Magistrate's Office)
stories.script: The Magistrate’s Office was a hall where the provincial governor, provincial military commander, naval commander, and local magistrate administered public affairs. From inside the 102-square-meter office, the county magistrate and garrison commander managed the affairs of the district. This was the person in charge of military affairs, administration, and arresting thieves of the neighboring 12 gun (counties) and hyeon (small prefectures). The Magistrate’s Office included a book publishing building, and is entered by a gate connected to the living quarters.

stories.title: Haemieupseong Walled Town Naea (Living Quarters)
stories.script: The living quarters in Haemieupseong Walled Town was inhabited by officials and their families, like today’s official residence. It was excavated and surveyed in 1981 and restored in November 2000. It is located to the west of the Magistrate's Office, surrounded by a square-shaped wall, composed of two buildings facing each other, with an area of 40 square meters. There is a wicket door that leads to the living quarters from the Magistrate's Office.

stories.title: Haemieupseong Walled Town Cheongheojeong Pavilion
stories.script: Cheongheojeong Pavilion was constructed on the Eastern hill in Haemieupseong Walled Town. Jo Suk-gi, the provincial army commander of Chungcheong-do, built it in 1491, but the building was so dilapidated that it was reconstructed into an octagonal pavilion in 2011. From the pavilion, one can take in the view of Cheonsu Bay; once, the poetry club gathered and the literati improvised poetry at Cheongheojeong Pavilion. In 1894, the Donghak Peasant Army camped and was defeated on the right side of the pavilion; under the Japanese Occupation, there was once a shrine, but it was burned down by anti-Japan residents.
