stories.title: Haemieupseong Walled Town Oksa (Jail) / Pagoda Tree
stories.script: In front of the jail in Haemieupseong Walled Town, there is a pagoda tree that is around 300 years old. The tree was once called Hoya Tree, and its East branch was where Catholics were checked and hung. The great-grandfather of Kim Taegon, the first Korean-born Catholic priest, died a martyr in the jail. The jail was restored based on historical records of Haemi martyrs that were published in 1935. In 2014, Pope Francis visited Haemieupseong Walled Town and prayed to give comfort.

stories.title: Haemieupseong Walled Town Traditional Houses
stories.script: In Haemieupseong Walled Town, there were public facilities like the township office, schools, and 94 private houses, but they were demolished in 1974. Then, three traditional houses were restored—a farmer’s house, a merchant’s house, and an official’s house. The farmer’s house is L-shaped and has an attached building where farming tools were kept. The merchant’s house is an I-shaped, straw-roofed, three-room structure, with two bedrooms and a kitchen, where the process of weaving by hand is represented. The official’s house is as large as the merchant’s and shows the simple living arrangements, along with stationary. There is a vegetable garden in front of the house, and a chicken run and toilet behind the house.

stories.title: Haemieupseong Walled Town Traditional Weapons
stories.script: Come in through Jinnammun Gate and you will see, in the green lawn leading to the Government Office, several weapons of the Joseon period in a row: the Frankish gun, geomcha, cannon, general’s cannon, and unje. The Frankish gun is a kind of cannon that was originally invented in Europe, and then China and Joseon made and used it. Geomcha is a weapon to defend the charge of the enemy’s troops. It looks like a wagon with a shield and swords attached. Every October, Haemieupseong Festival offers diverse, hands-on programs to citizens and tourists that allow them to learn about the history of the Joseon Dynasty: Experience of Army Life, Making Swords and Bows, Soldier Contest, Struggle Experience, and Exchanging and Using Coins of the Joseon period.

stories.title: Haemi Martyrium Cathedral (Entrance of the Cathedral)
stories.script: Haemieupseong Walled Town had been where the provincial army commander of Chungcheong-do stayed for 233 years, but on November 13, 1652, the place was moved to Cheongju. Afterward, a county magistrate and garrison commander became responsible for military affairs, administration, and police of the neighboring 12 gun (counties) and hyeon (small prefectures). The person became in charge of punishing the prisoners of the 12 gun and hyeon. This is the reason Catholics who were arrested in other places were moved to Haemi and executed there. In 1814, the great-grandfather of Kim Taegon died in the jail of Haemieupseong Walled Town, and in 1866 (during the Byeongin Persecution), more than a thousand Catholics were martyred. The Catholics came into the East Gate, were hung on the pagoda tree in front of the Jail and tortured, and then were executed after going out through the West Gate. Some of them were buried alive in the hold near the small stream of Josan-ri. Facing death, they prayed calling out “Jesus” and “Maria,” and the villagers who heard them misunderstood it as Yeosu, so they named the place “Yeosugol.” In 1935, the priest Beom Baro of Seosan Catholic Church made the martyrium widely known, and a Cathedral was completed there in 2003. The overall round shape symbolizes the hole in which the martyrs were buried alive, and the outer appearance is built to represent the walled town.

stories.title: Haemi Martyrium Memorial Hall (to pay respects to the remains of the martyrs)
stories.audioTitle: Memorial Hall (to pay respects to the remains of the martyrs)
stories.script: Behind Haemi Martyrium Cathedral, there is a memorial hall shaped like a tomb of a martyr. In the hall, you can find paintings and sculptures that commemorate the martyrdom, and the remains of the martyrs that have been excavated are lying in state for visitors to view and pay their respects. In 2014, Pope Francis held a Mass for the closing of Asian Youth Day at Haemieupseong Walled Town and led the unveiling ceremony of the monument for the Haemi martyrs in front of the memorial hall and beatified it.

stories.title: Haemi Martyrium Martyrdom Tower
stories.script: In 1935, the priest Beom Baro of Seosan Catholic Church listened to the testimony of the witnesses who had seen the Catholics killed at Jindumbeong (puddle), and he excavated the remains and articles like rosaries. The remains of the martyrs that had been buried at the Chapel in the mountain at Sangheung-ri, Eumam-myeon were moved here, the original place the martyrs were executed, in 1995, and the 16-meter Martyrdom Tower was constructed.

stories.title: Haemihyanggyo Local Confucian School Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall
stories.script: Haemihyanggyo Local Confucian School is known to have been constructed in 1407, under the reign of King Taejong of the Joseon Dynasty. At the entrance stand a dozen of giant saw-leaf zelkovas over 200 years old. The Haemihyanggyo Local Confucian School was designated as Chungcheongnam-do Cultural Property No.117 in 1997, and Daeseongjeon Hall, Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall, Dongjae East Dormitory, and Seojae West Dormitory are located on the sunny hill. At Daeseongjeon Hall, the ancestral rituals take place, and Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall was where lectures were given. ‘Myeongnyun’ means ‘enlightening the ethics of human society.’ Dongjae East Dormitory and Seojae West Dormitory are where the students used to stay.

stories.title: Haemihyanggyo Local Confucian School Daeseongjeon Hall
stories.script: In Daeseongjeon Hall, the sacrificial tablets of five Chinese saints (Confucius, Yan Ying, Zengzi, Zisi, and Mencius), four sages of the Song Dynasty (Cheng Hao, Zhu Xi, Zhou Dunyi, and Cheng Yi), and eighteen sages of the Joseon Dynasty (Choi Chi-won, Jeong Mong-ju, Jeong Yeo-chang, Yi Eon-jeok, Gim In-hu, Seong Hon, Jo Heon, Song Si-yeol, Bak Se-chae, Seol Chong, An Yu, Gim Gwang-pil, Jo Gwang-jo, Yi Hwang, Yi yi, Gim Jang-saeng, Gim Jib, and Song Jun-gil) are enshrined. The Confucian circles of Haemi-myeon, Gobuk-myeon, and Unsan-myeon gather every Spring and Autumn to hold the ancestral ritual, and burn incense every first day and middle of the month. Also, the Haemihyanggyo Local Confucian School keeps various copies of Confucian texts, including Cheonggeumnok and Seonan.

stories.title: House of Kim Gihyeon
stories.script: House of Kim Gihyeon, located in the north of the birthplace of Queen Consort Jeongsun, is a traditional tile-roofed house at the foot of the low hill facing the East, presumably built in the middle of the 19th century. Its C-shaped inner quarters and L-shaped gentlemen’s quarters form the overall square-shaped layout. The C-shaped women’s quarters is six kan wide and there is a two-kan wood-floored hall at its center. On the left and right side of the hall are the women’s quarters and an opposing room, and the kitchen and shed respectively connected to them. The house has a hip-and-gable roof with single-layer eaves, and the there remains a thatched cottage in the backyard. The place offers hanok stay since 2010, and the rooms are equipped with air conditioners. Designated as Important Folklore Cultural Heritage no. 199, the House of Kim Gihyeon also holds events for tourists, like poetry recitals and wildflower exhibitions.

stories.title: Birthplace of Queen Consort Jeongsun
stories.script: The birthplace of Queen Consort Jeongsun, which is presumed to have been constructed in the middle of the 17th century, is at Yugye-ri, Eumam-myeon, Seosan-si. The overall layout of the house is square-shaped and its size is five kan wide and two kan deep. On the left and right side, three-kan structures are attached, making the layout of the inner quarters C-shaped. It has a wide wood-floored hall, linked to the shed, the women’s quarters, and the kitchen on the right and to the shrine, the room opposite to the women’s quarters, and the shed. Beside the shed is the inner gate that leads to the gentlemen’s quarters and the women’s quarters. The wall around the backyard, the women’s quarters, and the gentlemen’s quarters is made of natural stones, the height of the main gate equals that of the house, and the roof has single-layer eaves. There is a tale about how Jeongsun was chosen as the queen consort. For the contest, the queen consort candidates came into the room, where they found sitting cushions, on each of which their own father’s name was written. Jeongsun, unlike other candidates, put her cushion aside. When she was asked why, she answered she couldn’t dare sit on her father’s name. When, in turn, she was asked what her favorite flower was, she answered “cotton,” because it makes the clothes that warm people. From these behaviors, she was considered worthy to be married to the king of a country.

stories.title: Tourist Information for Samgilpo Port
stories.script: Samgilpo Port is at the northeast shore of Samgilsan Mountain in Hwagok-ri, Daesan-eup, Seosan-si. In the early 1980s, before the Daeho Embankment was built, over 50 boats for fishing young white grunnels opened the pasi market on the sea from spring to autumn. At Samgilpo Port, you can participate in events all year round including the Rockfish Festival, Doksal (traditional fishing with bare hands) Experience, Cruise Tour, and Ships for Filleting Raw Fish. As the must-visit destination of Seosan no.9, Samgilpo Port is home to Haewolsa Temple, Hwanggeumsan Mountain, and Beolcheonpo Beach in the vicinity for you to enjoy the seascape.

stories.title: Samgilpo Port Hoe Tteuneun Seonsang (Ships for Filleting Raw Fish)
stories.audioTitle: Hoe Tteuneun Seonsang (Ships for Filleting Raw Fish)
stories.script: Past the signboard that reads “Hoe Tteuneun Seonsang (Ships for Filleting Raw Fish)” and across the bridge over the sea, you will see the ships where raw fish are filleted. You can choose any fish to be made into hoe (sliced raw fish): fresh rockfish, spotty-bellied greenling, flounder, flatfish, etc. You can also have the heads and bones of the fish cooked into the broth of a spicy stew for your meal. Make your own memories with the pleasant smell of the sea on the boat.

stories.title: Samgilpo Port Rockfish Lighthouse
stories.script: Built in January 2009 at the end of the embankment, the Rockfish Lighthouse lights up the path on the sea where the ships come and go. 11.5 meters high, it is painted red, marking a stark contrast against the blue ocean. Beside the lighthouse is the sculpture of a rockfish, the lighthouse's namesake. With the yearly Rockfish Festival, the Rockfish Lighthouse provides the tourists with unforgettable memories.

stories.title: Samgilpo Port Observatory
stories.script: Although it is a relatively low mountain, Samgilsan Mountain gives a grand and imposing impression since it is located on the seashore. It is said that Samgilsan Mountain has brought about three advantages: first, the stronghold called Pyeongsinjin was built at the South foot of the mountain in the Joseon period so that the army officers could work there; second, the mountain has embraced the historic and scenic Haewolsa Temple at its east foot; third, there are abundant populations of fish offshore. If you climb up the mountain to its summit and reach the beacon, you can enjoy an extraordinary landscape.

stories.title: Samgilpo Port Beacon
stories.script: Established in the Joseon period, the beacon at Samgilsan Mountain was where our ancestors communicated with the beacons of other places using smoke during the day and firelight during the night. When invaded by a foreign enemy, they made immediate communication for coast defense. The landscape that is viewed from the beacon contains the islands of the Yellow Sea, which looks like natural embankments and includes Nanjido Island, Sonanjido Island, Sojodo Island, and Daejodo Island. They look so beautiful that you may forget what time it is. The beacon is also a good place to enjoy the sunrise and sunset.

stories.title: Entrance of Hwanggeumsan Mountain
stories.script: Hwanggeumsan Mountain is located at the end of the Northwest shore of Daesan peninsula in Dokgot-ri, Daesan-eup, Seosan-si. It is said that the mountain was once called Hanggeumsan because it had gold (geum), and it was later renamed Hwanggeumsan. It is only 156 meters above sea level, but it looks higher since it is bordered to the seashore. Its west edge is a rocky cliff that adjoins the Yellow Sea, and it is famous for Elephant Rock which was created by coastal erosion. Also, there are two caves—one that is 10 meters deep and 10 meters high, and another that is 20 meters deep and 2 meters high—both of which were once gold mines. On the top of the Hwanggeumsan Mountain are dozens of oak trees that are considered to be auspicious by the local residents. On the mountain ridge is a shrine with the portrait of the general Yim Gyeong-eop--it is a sacred place where the ritual for bountiful fishing and the ritual for rain took place.

stories.title: Hwanggeumsan Mountain Mountaintop (Shrine to Yim Gyeong-eop)
stories.script: Pass the forest trail through pine trees and wild flowers to reach the top of Hwanggeumsan Mountain, and you will see the site of the ritual for rain and the shrine with the portrait of Yim Gyeong-eop. There is a tale about him: the General Yim Gyeong-eop was sailing toward Ming across the Yellow Sea in order to attack Qing, which was expanding its territory. On the way, he drifted off course and had to stay on a deserted island for a few days. For meals, he caught fish with his sword and made the soldiers cut thorny trees and lay them in the mud flat so that fish would get caught in the thorns during high tide. There is another legend as well, saying that he beheaded the evil dragon that tried to remove the fish from the Yellow Sea, allowing the fish population to thrive. The villagers were grateful for this deed, which is why they built the shrine and held the rituals. The shrine was restored in 1999, and the tutelary rituals take place every April 1. The seascape and the setting sun are stunning when seen from the top of Hwanggeumsan Mountain, and Deokjeokdo Island and Uldo Island are also visible far in the distance.

stories.title: Hwanggeumsan Mountain Sageori Rest Area
stories.script: If you go toward the sea from here, you will see the road split into the path to Pebble Beach and to Kkeutgul, and the descending path that leads to the pine forest. Take a rest and go down to take the path to reach the Elephant Rock and Gulgeum. You will certainly enjoy Pebble Beach with its outstanding landscape.

stories.title: Hwanggeumsan Mountain Elephant Rock
stories.script: The pebbles have been created by the waves, and they are characterized by their round rather than angular shape. As you walk down the beach, listening to the rustling of the pebbles, you will reach the 5-meter-high Elephant Rock. The rock looks like an elephant drinking the seawater with its long nose, and is so impressive that everyone wants to take out their camera. Via the wooden stairs behind the Elephant Rock, you can reach the beach beyond, where you can encounter the columnar joints that have been carved out over a long period of time.

stories.title: Hwanggeumsan Mountain Gulgeum Cave
stories.script: Walking down along the sea road as you breathe in the odor of pines and wildflowers, you will reach the sea caves Gulgeum and Kkeutgul. Around 50 meters deep, Gulgeum Cave can be visited only at low tide. Formed over a long period of time, the cave is said to have once been a gold mine. The giant Elephant Rock, Gulgeum Cave, the columnar joints, and Pebble Beach, all along with the myths about the blue and yellow dragons, will offer visitors a long-lasting memory of Hwanggeumsan Mountain.

stories.title: Seosan Buseoksa Temple Iljumun Gate
stories.script: Located at Dobisan Mountain in Chwipyeong-ri, Buseok-myeon, Seosan-si, Buseoksa Temple was established in 677 by the Buddhist monk Uisang of Silla and later rebuilt by the Buddhist monk Muhak. The record of its construction was found in the crossbeam of Geungnakjeon Hall during the reconstruction of the hall in 1995. The bronze-gilded Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, which was enshrined in Buseoksa Temple in 1330, the late Goryeo period, had been brought from Tsushima Island of Japan into South Korea without proper process, resulting in a pending legal issue. The Geungnakjeon Hall, Yosachae Dormitory, Anyangnu Pavilion, Simgeomdang Hall and Muryangsugak Hall are found in Buseoksa Temple, and therein are enshrined the statues of the Amitayus Buddha, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva, and Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva. Drawing the attention of tourists with its beautiful natural environment, Buseoksa Temple also offers temple-stay programs. Dobisan Mountain, where Buseoksa Temple is located, used to be the gangmu site where King Taejong and his third son Prince Chungnyeong held military training events (gangmu refers to the hunting contest for military training that was attended by the king).

stories.title: Seosan Buseoksa Temple Geungnakjeon Hall
stories.script: Three kan wide (kan refers to the space between two pillars) across the front and two kan on the side, Geungnakjeon Hall is a wooden, gable-roofed structure with column-top complex brackets, and is a significant object of study in the architectural style of the Goryeo period. In the hall is enshrined a hanging scroll behind the Amitayus Buddha, along with the guardian spirit of a mountain and the guardians of the Buddhist philosophy. On picking out the site for building the temple, the Buddhist monk Uisang regarded buseok (the floating rock) in Jeokdolman Bay as the location where the energy of Dobisan Mountain was gathered, and moved the rock near the temple to construct a pond beside the Yosachae Dormitory. Buseok, in turn, became the name of a nearby myeon (township). There you can find the Seonmyogak Shrine in front of a natural cave to the Northeast of Geungnakjeon Hall. A beautiful tale has been handed down about Lady Seonmyo who turned into a dragon to follow the monk Uisang and help him build the temple using miracles.

stories.title: Outside of the Ryubangtaek Science Museum
stories.script: The Seosan Ryubangtaek Science Museum was established in memory of Ryu Bang-taek, an astronomer from Seosan of the Goryeo Dynasty who made the Celestial Chart. The Celestial Chart is the second oldest celestial chart in the world, made in 1395 based on a rubbing of the celestial chart of Goguryeo. Twelve scientists including Ryu Bang-taek completed the chart, and it was designated as National Treasure no.228. If you look at the Korean 10,000-won bill, you can see the Celestial Chart drawn in the background of the Celestial Globe. The museum consists of the Main Observation Station, Auxiliary Observation Station, Celestial Hall, Exhibition Hall, and Audiovisual Room. At the Main Observation Station, you can observe the dark star clusters, nebulae, and galaxies through the 600 mm Ritchey-Chretien reflector telescope. At the Auxiliary Observation Station, you can observe sunspots, solar prominences, and various stars with a number of astronomical telescopes. For adolescents with hopes and dreams, the museum is the education center that offers experiences in space science.

stories.title: Ryubangtaek Science Museum At the Center of the Celestial Hall on the 1st Floor
stories.audioTitle: At the Center of the Celestial Hall on the 1st Floor
stories.script: On the first floor of Seosan Ryubangtaek Science Museum are the Celestial Hall, Exhibition Hall, and Planetarium. At the Celestial Hall, you can find the Celestial Chart Stone and the records about Ryu Bang-taek. In the Exhibition Hall are replicas of old-time scientific tools such as the celestial globe and the rain gauge. The planet-scale and astronomical telescope help visitors to feel and learn about astronomical principles. At the Planetarium in front of the Celestial Hall, you can watch the videos related to space and see various astronomical phenomena including constellations on the 8.8-meter dome screen.

stories.title: Songgokseowon Confucian Academy
stories.script: Songgokseowon Confucian Academy is also called ‘Songgok Hyanghyeonsa’ (hyanghyeon means ‘sages in the village’), as there are enshrined nine ancestral tablets of the sages who lived in Seosan: Wonoerang Jeong Sin-bo, Yangryeolgong Jeong In-gyeong, Geumheon Ryu Bang-taek, Husong Yun Hwang, Jeojeong Ryu Baek-yu, Wichon Ryu Baek-sun, Mudongcheosa Ryu Yun, Danguja Gim Jeok, and Miam Gim Wi-jae. The rituals take place every appointed day in February and August of the lunar calendar. It was later that the building was used as a Confucian academy. The structure is three kan wide (kan is the distance between two pillars) across the front and two kan on the side, with a hip-and-gable roof and single-layer eaves. At its entrance is a pair of Chinese Junipers that are over 500 years old and were designated as Natural Monument no.553 on May 13, 2018. Beside the Songgokseowon Confucian Academy is the Seosan Ryubangtaek Science Museum.

stories.title: Seosan Birdland Ticket Office at the Entrance
stories.script: Located at Chang-ri, Buseok-myeon, Seosan-si, Seosan Birdland is an eco-park on the hill along the seashore. Over 300 thousand winter migratory birds visit the nearby Cheonsuman Bay due to the grains left behind on the ground after the harvest from the mechanized, modern farming around the area that produces 1% of South Korean rice. Aquatic plants and fish are also abundant in the nearby lake, which is ample reason for the birds want to stay in the area. Since it opened in 2011, Seosan Birdland has run various education and hands-on programs with the theme of migratory birds. Its main facilities include a museum, 4D theater, and a Nest Observatory. Seosan Birdland is definitely the place to visit during a trip to Seosan, as it is located near other tourist destinations including the Ganworam Hermitage and Buseoksa Temple.

stories.title: Seosan Birdland Exhibition Hall, 2nd Floor of the Migratory Birds Museum
stories.audioTitle: Exhibition Hall, 2nd Floor of the Migratory Birds Museum
stories.script: The shape of the Migratory Birds Museum symbolizes the forest of Cheonsuman Bay where the migratory birds live. The specimens and educational materials are on display in the exhibition hall on its second floor, with more than 200 kinds of migratory birds that inhabit the Cheonsuman Bay including the bean goose, spectacled teal, spoonbill, and whooper swan. You can also obtain information on natural ecology of Cheongsuman Bay through videos and enjoy the sounds of birds.

stories.title: Seosan Birdland 1st Floor of the 4D Theater
stories.script: The 4D theater is a pyramid-shaped structure, decorated with colorful glass on the outer wall, drawing the attention of visitors. The 4D theater is equipped with facilities that allow you to enjoy the fantastic, realistic flight of the 300 thousand migratory birds of Cheonsuman Bay. While watching the video, your chair moves, wind blows, and water drops spatter--you will feel as if the birds are flying right in front of your eyes.

stories.title: Seosan Birdland Nest Observatory
stories.script: Built in 2013, the Nest Observatory stands atop a four-story, 30-meter-high building. The lower part of the building looks like a large ship. Its outer wall is decorated with oval patterns that differ in sizes, symbolizing the eggs of migratory birds, which makes it easier to recognize as an observatory for watching birds. With its stylish design, the Nest Observatory was awarded the Junior Grand Prix at 2011 Good Public Design Awards. Going up to the 4th floor, you can look down on the landscape of Cheonsuman Bay, and through the viewing binoculars you can observe the various migratory birds living there such as the spectacled teal, bean goose, Korean buzzard, stork, and hooded crane.

stories.title: Ganworam Hermitage A Stairway Leading to the Sea Path
stories.audioTitle: A Stairway Leading to the Sea Path
stories.script: There is a small hermitage with a mysterious ambiance in Ganwoldo Island, Buseok-myeon, Seosan-si. Ganworam Hermitage has deep connections with the Buddhist monk Muhak, the mentor of Yi Seong-gye, the founder of Joseon. Born in 1327 in Seoju (now Seosan) in Chungcheong-do, the monk Muhak was suddenly enlightened about the Buddhist law by looking at the moon during training of the mind, and therefore his successors called the island and the hermitage ‘Ganwol’ (ganwol means ‘looking at the moon’). He made great efforts in reviving Buddhism between the late Goryeo period and the early Joseon period. It is said that he was named Muhak (‘舞鶴’ meaning ‘dancing crane’) when he was a child, and later given the precept name Muhak (‘無學’ meaning ‘needing no more learning’). The old tale regarding his birth is written on his birth monuments at Hakdorijae of Mowol-ri in Inji-myeon, and in Aejeong-ri of Inji-myeon. He was a royal teacher, a state ambassador, and a great master under the reign of King Taejo of the Joseon Dynasty, and the person who played a decisive role in making Seoul the present capital of the nation. With Ganwolho Lake and Cheonsuman Bay in the vicinity, Ganworam Hermitage has a wonderful view, particularly extraordinary during the sunset. At high tide, the island appears lonely in the middle of the sea, but in low tide is connected to the mainland. If you visit, you’ll have to check the times that the tide comes and goes beforehand.

stories.title: Ganworam Hermitage Daeungjeon Hall (Gwaneumjeon Hall)
stories.script: Ganworam Hermitage in Ganwoldo Island was once famous as the place where the Buddhist monk Muhak cultivated ‘the Way’. In the Joseon Dynasty, however, the hermitage became dilapidated under the government’s oppression of Buddhism. In 1914, it was restored by the Buddhist monk Mangong, and he also re-enshrined the Avalokiteshvara that had been enshrined by the monk Muhak. Monk Mangong is one of the great masters of Korean Buddhism, a monk and independence activist in the late Joseon period and under the Japanese Occupation. It is said that he prayed for 1,000 days for the country’s liberation, and Korea was liberated the day after he finished his prayer. The Wooden Seated Bodhisattva in Ganworam Hermitage is a seated Avalokiteshvara of which the frame was first made with wood and paper then gilded. The statue is small in scale compared to ordinary statues, but it has a long history--it is said it was constructed by the Buddhist monk Muhak himself, who built the Ganworam Hermitage. There are also portraits of Buddhist monks Muhak and Mangong in Daeungjeon Hall, and ‘Ganworam’ was written on the signboard by Song Man-gong.

stories.title: Rock-carved Buddha Triad in Yonghyeon-ri, Seosan Entrance to the Path
stories.script: Under Inbawi Rock flows the clear water following the Yonghyeon Valley. Cross the Sambulgyo Bridge, and you will face the uphill slope that leads you to the ‘Smile of Baekje.’ Nearby is the school of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism where Goeun Choi Chi-won pursued studies in the late Silla period. If you continue straight, you will reach Bowonsa Temple Site, where one of the ten representative temples of Silla once existed. At the site, you can find five Treasures forming an outdoor museum in one spot—the Stone Basin, Flagpole Supports, Five-story Stone Pagoda, as well as Stupa of State Preceptor Beobin and Monument to State Preceptor Beobin, all of which have stood the test of time for over one thousand years.

stories.title: Rock-carved Buddha Triad in Yonghyeon-ri, Seosan Rock-carved Buddha Triad
stories.script: The Rock-carved Buddha Triad in Yonghyeon-ri, Seosan was presumably carved in the late 6th century. Known as the “Smile of Baekje,” the sculpture is 2.8 meters high, carved in relief on the wall facing the Southeast, giving different smiles in the morning, noon, and at sunset, depending on the angle of the light. The standing Sakyamuni Buddha (a Buddha of the present) in the middle, standing Dipankara Buddha (a Buddha of the past) on the left, and pensive Maitreya Buddha (a Buddha of the future) on the right are smiling the eternal smiles. Some say the sculpture represents the peace of mind belonging to the people of Baekje, and others say it represents the benevolent appearance of King Muryeong and Seong of Baekje. The Rock-carved Buddha Triad in Yonghyeon-ri, Seosan was designated as National Treasure no.84 in 1962 and has been visited by many visitors from Korea and abroad.

stories.title: Tourist Information at Bowonsa Temple Site
stories.audioTitle: Tourist Information at Bowonsa Temple Site
stories.script: Today, there only remains the site, but it is said that, when it flourished, the temple was counted as one of the 10 greatest temples of Unified Silla and there were more than 100 hermitages nearby and over 1,000 monks. You could also imagine how it thrived by the saying that people could avoid getting rained on under the eaves of the temple buildings, and the stream in front of Bowonsa Temple used to be milky white as it was used to wash rice, day and night. As Historic Site no.316, Bowonsa Temple Site has Stone Basin (Treasure no. 102), Flagpole Supports (Treasure no. 103), Five-story Stone Pagoda (Treasure no. 104), Stupa of State Preceptor Beobin (Treasure no. 105), and Monument to State Preceptor Beobin (Treasure no. 106). Among them, Five-story Stone Pagoda and Monument to State Preceptor Beobin are being considered to be re-designated as National Treasures. Behind Bowonsa Temple Site, there are Naepo Cultural Forest Trail, Aramegil Hiking Trail, and diverse trails to climb Gayasan Mountain, which is Must-visit Destination of Seosan no.6. for those who want to enjoy an undemanding hike.

stories.title: Bowonsa Temple Site Flagpole Supports
stories.script: Flagpole supports refer to the pair of columns used to support the flagpole during rituals like prayers or Buddhist services at the temple. The Flagpole Supports at Bowonsa Temple Site in Seosan are presumed to have been made in the Unified Silla period as they follow the basic style of the period of the Three States; with an overall refined look and outstanding carving, it has a high value as a cultural asset. Today, there is no longer a flagpole and there only remains the two supports that are 4.2 meters high and 37 centimeters wide.

stories.title: Bowonsa Temple Site Stone Basin
stories.script: The Stone Basin at Bowonsa Temple Site is the largest among those that exist in South Korea today. It was designated as Treasure no. 102 in 1963. There is no decoration or carving on the basin, only an eight-centimeter hole at the bottom for drainage—which may seem too simple but also can be considered as rightfully focusing on its use. As a kind of stone water container used by monks, the imposing basin is rectangular-shaped, made by digging out the inside of the granitic rock, able to contain about four tons of water.

stories.title: Bowonsa Temple Site Five-story Stone Pagoda
stories.script: The Five-story Stone Pagoda at Bowonsa Temple Site is approximately 9 meters high, and its five-story main body has been placed on a two-story platform. On the lower platform are carved lions, and on the upper platform are sculpted palbujungsang, the eight guardians of the teachings of the Buddha. The first two stories of the main body (two-story roofs) is composed of four stone plates, and the rest of the body (three-story roofs) single stone plate. The wide and thin stones for the roof part are made following the style of Baekje and the platform the style of Silla. The pagoda was designated as Treasure no.104 in 1963 and is being considered to be re-designated as a National Treasure.

stories.title: Stupa of State Preceptor Beobin and Monument to State Preceptor Beobin at Bowonsa Temple Site
stories.audioTitle: Stupa of State Preceptor Beobin and Monument to State Preceptor Beobin at Bowonsa Temple Site
stories.script: Tanmun was a renowned monk who lived between the late Silla and the early Goryeo period. He became the royal tutor in 968 and the state preceptor in 974. In 975, he passed into Nirvana and, in 978, his sarira was enshrined in the stupa. His posthumous title is Beobin and his courtesy name is Daeo. The Monument to State Preceptor Beobin is where you can read about his life of 76 years in 5,500 engraved characters of the epitaph. The monument is 2.3 meters high and 1.15 meters wide. Reportedly, over 1,000 monks of Zen and non-Zen Buddhism welcomed him when he came back to Bowonsa Temple, and even animals and tiny insects respected his power of merit and virtue. In 1963, the Stupa of State Preceptor Beobin was designated as Treasure no.105 and the Monument to State Preceptor Beobin as Treasure no.106; however, scholars maintain that the latter is cultural property with such a high value that it should be re-designated as a National Treasure.

stories.title: Iljumun Gate (Gaesimsa Temple, Seosan)
stories.script: Iljumun Gate of Gaesimsa Temple, Seosan  Gaesimsa Temple located on the hillside of Sangwangsan Mountain, Unsan-myeon, Seosan, is one of the four major temples in Chungcheongnam-do Province. There is a record indicating that the temple was founded by State Preceptor Hyegam during the reign of King Uija of Baekje.  At Gaesimsa Temple, you can see various buildings such as the Daeungjeon Hall, Muryangsugak House, Simgeomdang Hall, Anyangnu Pavilion, Myeongbujeon Hall, Palsangjeon Hall, Beomjonggak Hall, and the Five-story Stone Pagoda.   The temple holds numerous cultural heritage, including the Daeungjeon Hall, the Treasure Hanging Painting (The Vulture Peak Assembly), Wooden Seated Amitabha Buddha, Buddhist Paintings (Five Emperors of the Five Cardinal Directions), and Printing Woodblocks of Dalmadaesa hyeolmaengnon (Treatise on the Bloodstream Sermon by Buddhist Monk Bodhidharma).   Gaesimsa Temple, as the Traditional Temple and the fourth scenic spot of “Seosan’s 9 Scenic Views” is renowned for its donarium cherry blossoms in Spring, particularly the jade-colored donarium cherry blossoms that enhance the surrounding landscape. The path leading from Iljumun Gate to the temple is gorgeous and hikers can enjoy the Naepo Cultural Forest Trail and the Arame-gil Hiking Trail after passing through Gaesimsa Temple.   Looking for some leisure activity around Seosan? Gaesimsa Temple would be the perfect place for you!

stories.title: Gaesimsa Temple Daeungjeon Hall
stories.script: Treasure no. 143, Daeungjeon Hall was burned down in 1475 and rebuilt and renovated in 1484 and 1740. The Daeungjeon Hall is a single-story gable-roofed building that is 3 kan wide and 3 kan deep. The building displays a mixture of dapo (multiple column heads) and jusimpo (single column head) styles, having outstanding artistic and historical value. In the hall is enshrined the triad statue of Buddha—Amitabha, the main statue, the Avalokitesvara, and the Ksitigarbha. The Wooden Seated Amitabha Buddha of Gaesimsa Temple is Treasure no. 1619, and it is presumed to be the oldest wooden Buddha statue in South Korea. In the front yard of the Daeungjeon Hall is the Five-story Stone Pagoda and on its sides are Simgeomdang Hall and Muryangsugak House, facing each other.

stories.title: Gaesimsa Temple Beomjonggak Hall
stories.script: The downstairs of Beomjonggak Hall of Gaesimsa Temple is made of concrete and the upstairs is made of wood. The upstairs is one kan wide across the front and one kan deep on the side. For the columns that support the double-layer eaves and the pyramid hip roofs, the curved trunks of trees are used without being straightened out, making its overall appearance unique. On the left side of Beomjonggak Hall is Anyangnu Pavilion. In the pavilion, the Dharma drum, the wooden fish-shaped drum, and the cloud-shaped gong are preserved. The pavilion is five kan wide across the front and three kan deep on the side, with double-layer eaves and a hip-and-gable roof. On its front hangs a signboard, on which ‘Sangwangsan Gaesimsa’ has been written by Haegang Gim Gyu-jin in regular script style. The calligraphy is said to be impressed on the viewer’s memory for a long time. Gaesimsa Temple holds the ritual every year for Buddha's birthday, with Hanging Painting (The Vulture Peak Assembly) open to the public.

stories.title: Gaesimsa Temple Myeongbujeon Hall
stories.script: Cultural Property Material no. 194 of Chungcheongnam-do, Myeongbujeon Hall of Gaesimsa Temple was built in 1646. Myeongbujeon Hall is gable-roofed, three kan wide across the front and three kan deep on the side, and its gongpo (the column head that supports the roof) shows the ikgong style, which means it looks like the wing of a bird. On its side, there is pungpan to block the rainstorm, and its inner space, with no column, is spacious. Myeongbujeon Hall is the place to pray for the deceased’s rebirth in the Pure Land, and Ksitigarbha (Jijang Bosal in Korean) is mainly enshrined in it, so it is also called Jijangjeon. A path that passes Myeongbujeon Hall and goes behind Gaesimsa Temple leads to the trail that goes through Bowonsaji Temple Site, Illaksan Mountain, and Gayasan Mountain.

stories.title: Illaksa Temple Daejeokgwangjeon Hall
stories.script: Illaksa Temple is known to have been built by the Buddhist Monk Uihyeon in 663, under the reign of King Munmu of Silla, and was renovated several times in the Joseon period. Originally, there were only Daeungjeon Hall and Three-story Stone Pagoda; and in 1933, Daejeokgwangjeon Hall was newly constructed in place of the small Daeungjeon Hall. In front of Daejeokgwangjeon Hall, which is three kan wide across the front and two kan deep on the side, there is the Three-story Stone Pagoda of Illaksa Temple, built in the Goryeo period. The structure is made of a two-story foundation on which the three-story main body is placed. It is now not in the best condition. The scenery beyond the wall around the wide front yard of Daejeokgwangjeon Hall, where the Three-story Stone Pagoda is located, is magnificent. You can also enjoy following the trail from Illaksa Temple to the top of the Illaksan Mountain and Seongmunbong Peak of Gayasan Mountain.

stories.title: Illaksa Temple Daeungjeon Hall (Myeongbujeon Hall)
stories.script: Daeungjeon Hall, the central hall of Illaksa Temple, was renovated in 1919. It was disassembled and moved to the current location in 1933, when the signboard was attached. In its original location, Daejeokgwangjeon Hall was newly built. Three kan wide and two kan deep, Daeungjeon Hall has a gable roof and its gongpo (the column head that supports the roof) shows the ikgong style, which means it looks like the wing of a bird. The Buddha triad in the hall is plated with gold now, but originally the Vairochana Buddha in the middle was made of soil, the Shakyamuni Buddha on the left wood, and the Sambhogakaya Buddha on the right iron. The Sambhogakaya Buddha is named Iron Buddha of Illaksa Temple and was designated as Cultural Property Material of Chungcheongnam-do no.208.

stories.title: Gayasan Mountain Entrance of Gaesimsa Temple (Rest Area)
stories.script: This is the Rest Area at the entrance of the Gaesimsa Temple, where you can fully enjoy pure nature of the Naepo Cultural Forest Trail and the Aramegil Hiking Trail. From the entrance, descend 400 meters toward Haemi-myeon and you will reach Gaesimsa Temple; or go toward Illaksan Mountain and you will come to the three-way road where you can find the belvedere; you can enjoy trekking and hiking to Gayasan Mountain. When you go down 1.7 kilometers toward Yonghyeon Valley, you will see Bowonsa Temple Site.

stories.title: Gayasan Mountain Belvedere
stories.script: Enjoying the Naepo Cultural Forest Trail and the Aramegil Hiking Trail, you can take a rest at the belvedere—go up to Palgakjeong Pavilion and enjoy the view of the serene landscape of the Yonghyeon Valley. The belvedere is about 300 meters from the Rest Area at the entrance of the Gaesimsa Temple, and it leads either to the path to climb the Illaksan Mountain or the path to descend to the Yonghyeon Valley.

stories.title: The Summit of Illaksan Mountain
stories.script: On the summit of Illaksan Mountain, there is a small pavilion where you can take a short rest. From the pavilion, the ridge of Gayasan Mountain that is part of the Geumbukjeongmaek Mountain Range and Ogyangbong Peak will come into sight. Descend 500 meters from the summit, and you will come to Saitgogae Rest Area, the entrance to Seongmunbong Peak of Gayasan Mountain. Going down toward Haemi-myeon, you can reach the historic Illaksa Temple and Haemieupseong Walled Town, Must-visit Destination of Seosan no.1. Taking the path leading to Sangwangsan Mountain, you can enjoy the landscape of Gaesimsa Temple, famous for the donarium cherry blossoms in Spring, and the cultural properties like Bowonsa Temple Site, and Rock-carved Buddha Triad.

stories.title: Saitgogae Rest Area
stories.script: Saitgogae Rest Area is a well-known rest area before ascending the paths to the summit of Illaksan Mountain and Seongmunbong Peak of Gayasan Mountain. At the hillside, you can have the unusual joy of reading the poem written on the stele standing at one corner, and the deserted mountain pass gives the feeling of separation from secular affairs. Following the path in the direction of Illaksa Temple, you will arrive the parking lot for temple visitors. If you take the opposite path and go down toward Northeast, you will come to the road across the expansive champaign that leads to Bowonsa Temple Site.

stories.title: Seongmunbong Peak
stories.script: Seongmunbong Peak is a rocky peak 1.7 kilometers Westward from Gayabong Peak. Look up at the peak from a far distance and you will find two stone pillars appearing like a large gate—this is why it is also called ‘Mundarami’ or ‘Tongcheonmun’ (‘mun’ means ‘door’ or ‘gate’). When you climb up to the peak and look around, the fair view of Ogyangbong Peak, Gamtubong Peak, Illaksan Mountain, Sangwangsan Mountain, and the West coast will come into sight. Seongmunbong Peak is famous for its beauty all year around—royal azaleas in Spring, leafy green trees in Summer, yellow and red foliage in Autumn, and snow in Winter. Must-visit Destination of Seosan no.6, Gayasan Mountain is mainly located in Unsan-myeon, Seosan-si, Chungcheongnam-do, and its whole body lies in three si (cities) and gun (counties)—Seosan-si, Yesan-gun, and Dangjin-si. From Gayabong Peak, the main peak, the peaks of Wonhyobong Peak, Ogyangbong Peak, Illaksan Mountain, Sujeongbong Peak, Sangwangsan Mountain are connected and the mountain pass is varied but not very hard to follow, so everybody can enjoy mountain climbing without difficulty.

stories.title: Baegamsa Temple Site
stories.script: At Baegamsa Temple Site, you will find the temple site to be around 6,600 square meters and partly remaining masonry works that seem to have been done when the temple once existed. The style of the stone lantern, with its platform and roof, tells us that it would have been made in the early Goryeo period. According to an old tale, there once were a total of 99 hermitages and temples on this mountain. It is said that, after the construction of Baegamsa Temple, the 100th, every hermitage and temple was burned. A modern theory is that it was in the process of arresting Yi In-jwa (a rebellious subject of the Joseon Dynasty), who hid in the Baegamsa Temple, that 100 hermitages and temples including the Baegamsa Temple were all set on fire and destroyed.

stories.title: Sabangdaem Forked Road
stories.script: At Sabangdaem Forked Road, you can see Suri Cliff and Suribawi Temple Site. It is said that the cliff was named so because a pair of eagle-owls nested and lived there (‘suri’ refers to the eagle-owl), and on the cliff is Suribawi Temple Site. If you take the right road at the fork, you will reach a pond which is the starting point of Yonghyeon Valley; around the pond spreads a plain with a primeval forest. Follow the valley for about 3 kilometers, and you will arrive at a road across the expansive champaign that leads to Bowonsa Temple Site. When you follow the hilly ridge toward Ogyangbong Peak for 1 kilometer, you will find Baegamsa Temple Site; go up following the mountain pass alongside the valley and reach Saitgogae Rest Area. In the direction of Sangwangsan Mountain, there is a zigzag path, and by climbing it you will enjoy the view from the belvedere and the scenery of Gaesimsa Temple, renowned for its donarium cherry blossoms.

stories.title: Tungtunggogae Rest Area
stories.script: From Tungtunggogae Rest Area, located in the middle of Naepo Cultural Forest Trail and on the path leading to the ‘Smile of Baekje’ (Rock-carved Buddha Triad), you can enjoy, from the pavilion that is beautifully built at the three-way road, the landscape of the Yonghyeon Valley, surrounded by the mountains. If you take the road in the direction of Yonghyeon Valley from the rest area, you will pass Yonghyeon Recreational Forest and reach Bowonsa Temple Site. There is also a hiking path that leads to Ogyangbong Peak and Seongmunbong Peak of Gayasan Mountain. Before climbing toward Ogyangbong Peak, you will find Baegamsa Temple Site right at the starting point of the slope. Going behind the pavilion at Tungtunggogae Rest Area, you can enjoy climbing the trail that leads to Sujeongbong Peak and Gopung Reservoir.

stories.title: The Entrance of the House of Yu Gibang
stories.audioTitle: The Entrance of the House of Yu Gibang
stories.script: Built in 1919 under the Japanese Occupation, House of Yu Gibang is a traditional house located at the innermost part of the village, facing South, with a low hill in back. The I-shaped inner quarters are on the North, and the servants’ quarters are on the West. In 1988, part of the building was demolished and the current gatehouse was constructed on the East. On the Eastern hill, there stands a Japanese Torreya which is over 330 years old. Behind the house is a daffodil habitat, which is visited by many tourists in Spring and is the starting point of Aramegil Hiking Trail Route 1. Also being a filming location of various TV drama series, the House of Yu Gibang has a high architectural and historical value to be preserved. In 2015, the house was designated as Folklore Heritage of Chungcheongnam-do no.23.

stories.title: Placenta Chamber and Stele of Great King Myeongjong / on top of the stairs
stories.audioTitle: Placenta Chamber and Stele of Great King Myeongjong
stories.script: The Placenta Chamber of King Myeongjong and the Stele on its right were built in 1536, the Stele on its left in 1546, and the Stele in the middle in 1711. The monuments were not well managed during the Japanese Occupation, but the stoneworks were restored in 1975 as they are today. A replica, as large as 3/4 of the original, is on display at the National Palace Museum of Korea, and it was designated as Treasure no.1976 in March 2018. At the time of constructing the placenta chamber, the site was selected among the most auspicious locations in terms of feng shui. Also, the places with the names of ‘taebong’ or ‘taesan’ throughout the country are where the placenta chambers were located as ‘tae’ means ‘placenta’ in Korean.

stories.title: Hanwoo Ranch Path to Cherry Trees Road
stories.script: Seosan Hanwoo Ranch (‘Hanwoo’ means ‘Korean beef’), which is called a cradle of mountainside stockbreeding, was created in 1969 by developing the gigantic mountain slopes of Wonbeol-ri and Yonghyeon-ri, Unsan-myeon, Seosan-si. On the ranch’s 21.06 square kilometers, the cows graze in peace, presenting a pastoral type of scenery. Entering the ranch is prohibited because of the risk of spreading diseases to the cattle, such as foot-and-mouth disease. However, the cherry tree road that stretches approximately one kilometer along the slope of the ranch is well-known. Visit the place in Spring, when the cherry blossoms are in full bloom, to enjoy the neighboring landscapes of Sinchang Reservoir and Gaesimsa Temple.

stories.title: Entrance (Palbongsan Mountain, Seosan)
stories.script: The Entrance of Palbongsan Mountain, Seosan   Palbongsan Mountain, the fifth scenic spot of “Seosan’s 9 Scenic Views” is a 362-meter mountain located in Yanggil-ri, Palbong-myeon, Seosan. The mountain was named so because of its eight peaks extend from the North to the South. In Korean, 'pal' means ‘eight’ and 'bong' means ‘peak’, and the name of the myeon (township) is derived from the name of the mountain.   In the year of Imjin, when the Japanese invasions broke out and invaded Joseon, the government planned to build a fortress refuge on the mountain. During a severe drought in 1582, the county magistrate Go Gyeong-myeong held the ritual for rain in the Cheonjedan Altars, and on the same day, it began to rain. Afterward, other county magistrates came to this mountain to hold the ritual when there was a drought in their county. In recent times, the villagers gather together and hold a religious ritual for the mountain spirit. On the East ridge of the mountain’s third peak, you can find the natural altar stone there.   The time needed to complete a hike across all eight peaks of Palbongsan Mountain is around three hours, allowing hikers to enjoy the scenic beauty within a short duration.  Come and spend a morning hiking at Palbongsan Mountain now!

stories.title: Palbongsan Mountain The First Peak
stories.script: Follow the eastward path through the forest from the parking lot, and you will reach the forked road that leads to either the first or the second peak. 210 meters above sea level, the first peak is also called Nojeokbong Peak or Gamtubong Peak. When viewed from the middle of the iron stairs built on the narrow rocky slope that leads to the second peak, the first peak looks wonderful and invites applause with its wide open landscape of Garorimman Bay to the north.

stories.title: Palbongsan Mountain The Second Peak
stories.script: The path leading to the second peak is set in the form of a metal stairway between the rocks to facilitate the climb. When you look around from the metal stairway, various rocks including a turtle rock, elephant rock, and rockfish rock will capture your eyes. The landscape of the first peak to the north and Garorimman Bay will also offer a fresh sensation. The first peak is also called Nojeokbong Peak or Gamtubong Peak because it looks like piled up nojeok or gamtu (a kind of cap formerly worn by the gentry). If you look at the third peak from the top of the second peak, you will notice that the third peak looks like the shoulders of a strong man, which is why it is also called Eokkaebong (eokkae means ‘shoulder(s)’).

stories.title: Palbongsan Mountain The Third Peak (Cheonjedan Altar)
stories.script: You can climb up the 362 meter third peak, the highest peak of Palbongsan Mountain, by a metal stairway. The peak is also called Eokkaebong (eokkae means ‘shoulder(s)’) since it resembles the shoulders of a strong man. There is also Yonggul Cave, where the guardian dragon of the eight peaks is said to have lived. To the north of the Mountain you can look down on Garorimman Bay with the sprinkling of sea fog, and to the South is the embankment at Cheonsuman Bay and Hwanggeumsan Mountain just coming into sight. When you have almost reached the top by the metal stairway, you will see the Cheonjedan Altar, where the county magistrate Go Gyeong-myeong held the ritual for rain, after which it is said to have rained a lot. Other county magistrates also held the ritual for rain afterward. Recently, the rituals for the abundant harvest and peaceful days are also held here.

stories.title: Unamsa Temple Site (Palbongsan Mountain, Seosan)
stories.script: Unamsa Temple Site of Palbongsan Mountain, Seosan  The Unamsa Temple Site is a rest area on the path along the ridge going down from the second peak. Unamsa Temple is an ancient temple known for its name, which means 'always surrounded by clouds.' During the rainy season or after a heavy rain, the temple and the rocks nearby are wrapped with white clouds, looking like a fairyland. The exact dates of its establishment and abandonment are unknown, and only a well remains at the site of the temple. You may try to go through the state of ‘freedom from distraction’ like the old Buddhist monks of the Unamsa Temple. It may also be one of the delights of hiking.

stories.title: Palbongsan Mountain The Fourth Peak
stories.script: The climbing route to the fourth peak is steep and jaged, so you will have to go up the long and steep metal stairway. The 330-meter peak is formed of rocks with soft curves. Sitting on the rock on the summit, you can catch your breath for a moment while slowly appreciating the wide open view and the appearance of the nearby rugged precipice of the third peak. The fourth peak is located at a five-minute walk from the third peak with a steep path between the two, so you should proceed with caution so as to prevent any accidents. The hike up to the eighth peak would be a relatively light course up and down following the 600-meter ridge, but the trail leading to and from the fourth peak is precipitous and rugged, so you will have to move carefully while following the metal stairway.

stories.title: The Eighth Peak (Palbongsan Mountain, Seosan)
stories.script: The Eighth Peak of Palbongsan Mountain, Seosan  To enjoy hiking on Palbongsan Mountain, you can start from either the parking lot in Yanggil-ri and head towards the first peak or from Eosong-ri to the eighth peak. If you leave from Eosong-ri, you will pass through Seotaesa Temple and the eighth peak will be the first peak you reach.   At the foot of Palbongsan Mountain and in its west valley are a number of home-sized hermitages. The eighth peak which is 319 meters above sea level, provides a landscape as wonderful as the other peaks. You can enjoy climbing the peak in around 3 hours, and even a hike of such short duration will be rewarded with a magnificent landscape.

stories.title: An Gyeon Memorial Hall
stories.script: Located in Hwacheon-ri, Jigok-myeon, Seosan-si, An Gyeon Memorial Hall was established in October 1991 in memory of An Gyeon, the master of landscape painting of the Joseon Dynasty. An Gyeon is one of the three greatest painters of Korea, along with Solgeo of the Silla Dynasty and Yi Nyeong of the Goryeo Dynasty. The original ‘Dream of Strolling in a Peach Garden’, his major work, is a National Treasure of Japan and is housed at the central library of Tenri University. At the Memorial Hall, 18 works are on display including the replica of Mongyudowondo (Dream of Strolling in a Peach Garden), Jeokbyeokdo (Red Cliffs), Sosangpalgyeongdo (Eight Views of the Xiao and Xiang Rivers), and Sasipalgyeongdo (Eight Scenes of the Four Seasons). You can enjoy all of these refined landscape paintings in one place.

stories.title: Hong Geonik's House
stories.script: Hong Geonik's House  This guide is recorded by the voice of Mr. Kim Young-ha.  In Seocheon where the middle-class people of the Joseon Dynasty lived, hanok buildings that represent various eras are gathered in clusters. Among them, this house, which is called “Hong Geonik's House”, is a modern hanok built in the 1930s. There is little data left on Hong Geonik but his name was given to this house because he was the one who tore down the previous house and built the current one.  Before Hong Geonik lived in the house, it is said that a Yeokgwan named Ko Yeong-ju and his family had lived here. Three generations of Ko Yeong-ju's family, from the father and brothers to nephews, served the post of Yeokgwan. “Yeokgwan” served the same role as today's interpreter and diplomat, and they were able to meet foreigners in person to interact with them and, also, learn about various cultures and obtain new information faster than anyone else. So, despite their status as middle-class people, they were able to gain wealth and honor.  Ko Yeong-ju was Yeokgwan who had learned the Chinese language (and literature). His brothers were actually more famous as Yeokgwan; his second younger brother, Ko Yeong-hee, was a Japanese interpreter who was a member of Susinsa dispatched to Japan after the Treaty of Kanghwa of 1876. The youngest, Ko Yeong-cheol, had studied English in China and went to America as a part of Bobingsa (delegation). Ko Yeong-ju sold the land to another person in the 1910s and, years later, Hong Geonik purchased it. The house was much larger when Hong Geonik built it but there is only half of it left now.  As soon as you enter through Ilgakmun of Hong Geonik’s House, you will see the taste and sense of its owner. While Munganchae and Sarangchae give off a neatly organized vibe, Anchae feels more cozy and comfortable. Underneath Daecheongmaru of Anchae, you will find holes in the shape of the eight trigrams, which are also used in Taegukgi. These holes have the function of letting wind through. As it was a modernized hanok, its doors and windows are made of glass, and this was a way to boast the family's wealth at the time.  If you go to the left of the Anchae, there is a small door leading to a Byeolchae and the garden. What you see first after going through the door is a large well, and it is said that having a well inside a private home meant that the family was extremely rich. The Byeolchae is being used as a small library that anyone can use at free of charge. Once you pick out a book you want to read and sit on a cushion, you will be able to read the book while enjoying the scenery of the garden.  If you want to get a full view of this house, climb up to the top of the garden. It is beautiful to see the scenery of the roofs of Byeolchae, Anchae, Sarangchae and Munganchae in harmony with the present-day buildings of Seochon. Take a seat on a bench in the garden and relax and enjoy this nice scenery.

stories.title: The House of Yi Sang
stories.script: The House of Yi Sang  This guide is recorded by the voice of Mr. Kim Young-ha.  Yi Sang, a famous literary man in the Japanese colonial era for his unique literary world, was adopted by his uncle when he was a child and raised as a native of Tongin-dong. His uncle’s house used to be an enormous hanok, which was inherited by Yi Sang later. But, when his business failed, he was forced to sell it. The house sold was divided into five pieces of land whose owners have continued to change to this day. Where Yi Sang’s house is located today is one of those five lands.  His real name was Kim Hae-gyeong and he was adopted into this family when he was 3 years old. His uncle adopted Yi Sang because he had no son but his aunt who had remarried did not have much affection for him. Yi Sang showed special talents in painting since he was young but his uncle forced him to become an architect, a job that could make a lot of money. Eventually, Yi Sang enrolled in the department of architecture at Gyeongseong Engineering High School and later became an architect.  Hired as an architect working for the government-general, Yi used his pen name to write, mainly expressing confusion of his identity and chaos of the times through literary works. His pen name, “Yi Sang”, also has many different meanings when read in Korean so we can tell that the name contains both the frustration and wishes of a person with genius talents.  Although Yi Sang is imprinted on us with an abstruse literary world and an agonizing image, he was said to be a good son and a reliable older brother to his real family. According to his sister’s testimony, “My eldest brother was always polite to our mother and used to fret about not being able to do more for her.” In turn, Yi Sang treasured his sister, calling her “the only one who could understand him.”  This house is a place that keeps both the darkness and hope of Yi Sang’s childhood. You can encounter a small story about his life in the darkest and innermost space of the exhibition room. Once you open the heavy sliding door at the end of the stairs, you will see the front yard and roof of Yi Sang’s house. Try to look for Yi Sang in the house of a literary man who ceaselessly agonized to find an exit to freedom.

stories.title: Tongin Traditional Market
stories.script: Tongin Traditional Market, nestled within the alleys of Tongin-dong, supports the livelihood of the neighborhood.  The history of Tongin Traditional Market dates back to the 1950s. Seoul was in disarray due to the Korean War, and some private houses in the Jongno area, where Gyeongbokgung Palace and the Capital were located, survived. After the war, people returned and gathered in the area, initiating the buying and selling of various items along the Tongin-dong alley, eventually forming the Tongin Traditional Market.  The market offered delicious food and durable goods. Additionally, many people exchanged news, from the life and death of family members separated during the war to those left behind in the North. Conversations flourished among individuals over dishes, shaping the market into a place where everyone's news was shared.  As this area adjacent to Gyeongbokgung Palace became a neighborhood close to Cheongwadae (The Blue House), it was designated as a development-restricted area. Consequently, residents began to move away, leading to an increase in vacant stores. However, the remaining merchants were determined to sustain the market. They devised a plan to use Yeopjeon as currency, reminiscent of the marketplace in the Joseon Dynasty. By leveraging their proximity to Gyeongbokgung, one could use Yeopjeon to purchase various foods from different stalls in the market, creating an exhilarating experience while choosing their desired meal.  At the 'Yeopjeon Dosirak Cafe,' situated in the market's center, visitors can exchange cash for Yeopjeon and a lunch box tray. As they explore the market with the tray, they can fill it with diverse flavors such as oil tteokbokki, deep-fried and braised chicken, kimchi, and salad, reliving the Joseon Dynasty era through the use of Yeopjeon.

stories.title: Park No-soo Museum
stories.script: Park No-soo Museum  This guide is recorded by the voice of Mr. Kim Young-ha.  Namjeong Park No-soo, considered as a master of Korean Oriental paintings, moved to a house in Ogin-dong in 1973. This house, which boasted a French-style exterior, captivated the artist's heart with its beautiful garden and unique interior.  The house has extraordinary style featuring various architectural techniques including a French exterior and interior element that were Korean, Japanese, and Chinese. The original owner was the daughter of Yoon Deok-young, a pro-Japan traitor. Yoon Deok-young cherished his daughter very much and wanted to give her the best house. So he requested Park Gil-yong, one of the greatest architects at the time, to design and build a house.  A two-story Western-style house stood out amongst tile-roofed and thatched houses in the surroundings. It is said that it stood out even more after Yoon’s Western-style mansion called Byeoksu Mountain Cabin caught fire and was burned to ashes. As assets and properties of all traitors and their families were confiscated after Liberation, the owner of the house continued to change before, eventually, the family of Painter Park No-soo came to live here. Park No-soo ended his life in this very house and, later, Jongno-gu bought the property and has opened it to the public since 2013.  Park No-soo Museum exhibits his paintings, collections amassed in his lifetime, and different tools he actually used. The contents of the exhibit change every year but some of the relics used by Mr. Park as well as viewing stones are permanently on display in the hallways and garden. Artist Park No-soo had a hobby of collecting viewing stones, and he once stated that a stone contains all the images of nature and is an inspiration for his paintings.  The inside of Park No-soo Museum is not available for taking photos or videos. Instead, the exterior and the garden can be shot or filmed. Since it is an old house that is more than 80 years old, the floors may creak when you look around inside, and you also need to walk up the stairs carefully. However, the sound and atmosphere that only time can provide you with add a dose of mystique of this house.  The garden, which is highly praised by anyone who has ever visited here, is small in size and encompasses the house but it gives you an opportunity to check out the viewing stones and well-managed trees. Artist Park No-soo’s paintings and their ability to embody well the lines, spaces and composition as well as the nature that inspired him so much are manifested in the garden. Slowly and carefully look around and appreciate a house that resembles its owner.

stories.title: Yun Dong-ju's boarding house site
stories.script: Yun Dong-ju's boarding house site  This guide is recorded by the voice of Mr. Kim Young-ha.  On the street leading from Park No-soo Museum up to Suseong-dong Valley, there is a place that is known as where Poet Yun Dong-ju once lodged. Today, the house has become a private home and only a sign attached to a pillar still holds the traces of the old times.  Poet Yun Dong-ju was from North Gando and, for about four years from 1938 to 1942, he lived in Seoul (Gyeongseong at the time) for high school. He originally stayed in the school dormitory but, during his junior year, he boarded at the house of novelist Kim Song together with a younger student named Jeong Byeong-wook.  The memoirs by Jeong Byeong-wook talk about stories of his boarding days with Yun Dong-ju. After deciding to get out of the dorms, Yun and Jeong were looking for a boarding house. One day, they saw an ad by someone who was recruiting boarders so they went right away to find out that it was the house of Kim Song, an author they both had loved and respected. They started to board at Kim's house and, while he lived here, Yun Dong-ju climbed up Inwangsan every morning to meditate or wash his face anywhere there is flowing valley water. Over dinner, he liked to exchange literary stories and thoughts with Kim Song.  Kim was an anti-Japanese author from Hamgyeong-do Province and a person who was on the blacklist of Japanese police. So, almost every evening, detectives came by to search the entire house and write down the titles of all the books Yun Dong-ju was reading. On some days, they inspected all the luggage in the house and even took the letters and postcards. Kim Song repeatedly apologized for this and, by the time when the fall semester began, Yun and Jeong moved to a new boarding house for their safety.  Yun's new boarding house was in Bukahyeon-dong and another famous poet named Chong Ji-yong was already living here. Also, Song Mong-gyu, Yun's cousin on his father's side, also lived in the same neighborhood so Yun resided in Bukahyeon-dong until he went abroad to study.  While he was saying in Kim Song's house, Yun Dong-ju wrote a poem titled <Another Hometown>, which is known as a poem that talks about his own experiences and the tough reality of the time. While reciting <Another Hometown>, take a stroll on the streets that Yun Dong-ju probably walked to and from.

stories.title: Suseong-dong Valley
stories.script: Suseong-dong Valley  This guide is recorded by the voice of Mr. Kim Young-ha.  A stream of water flowing from Inwangsan Mountain turned into a valley and, as the area is relaxing and peaceful with loud sounds of the water, it became Suseong-dong. The water flowing from Suseong-dong Valley runs past Gyeongbokgung Palace to Hyejeonggyo Bridge to the east before meeting with Cheonggyecheon Stream. So it is a place that is always mentioned when explaining the geomancy of Gyeongbokgung.  Inwangsan is a rocky mountain with rugged terrains. It does not have many trees, which is also why valleys were developed between large rocks and the few trees standing here and there. In the early Joseon Period, the third son of King Sejong, Grand Prince Anpyeong, especially loved this landscape.  Anpyeong was a prince who was adept in poetry, calligraphy and painting, all of which were skills that a typical scholar of the Joseon Dynasty needed to have. When Grand Prince Anpyeong built a house in Suseong-dong and went into Gyeongbokgung, King Sejong bestowed the name, Bihaedang, upon the house that means to serve only one king without idleness. A novel from the Joseon Dynasty called <<Unyeongjeon>> talks about Suseonggung located at the foot of Inwangsan and the owner of this palace is Anpyeong. In the novel, Anpyeong is depicted as someone who has great appreciation for the arts and proficiency in poetry, calligraphy and painting. It is this love for the arts that is believed to be at the core of his character. Grand Prince Anpyeong had utmost affection for Bihaedang; he, even, wrote a poem called Bihaedang 48-yeong and enjoyed the scenery.  During the mid-Joseon Period by the time when Anpyeong's Suseonggung had disappeared, another genius painter visits this place - it was Gyeomjae Jeong Seon, the master of Jingyeong Sansu. Jingyeong Sansuhwa is a type of paintings produced by observing and examining the actual landscapes of our country, and Gyeomjae Jeong Seon was the one who took Jingyeong Sansu to whole new heights.  Jeong Seon is believed to have been born in Cheongun-dong situated between Bugaksan and Inwangsan Mountains, and, at the age of 41, he took his first government post as a professor in astronomy at Gwansanggam (department that observed weather and sky during the Joseon Period). Because he started his government career at such a late stage in his life, he was already 58 years old when he became Hyeongam of Cheongha, Gyeongsang-do Province and, at the age of 81, he rose to Dongji Jungchubusa of Jong 2-pum (a post for extension of favor to an old, aged official).  History books states that he started to live in Inwanggok Valley at the eastern foot of Inwangsan when he was 52 years old and, that it was here that he painted some remarkable works that depict the landscape of the mountain, including those of Inwangjesaekdo and Suseongdong. In particular, the work titled Suseongdong displays a scenery that is similar to today's Suseong-dong Valley, and you can find the stone-made “Giringyo Bridge” on the painting, which allows you to figure out the composition and location of the painting.

stories.title: Inwangsan Mountain
stories.script: The Mountain guarding Gyeongbokgung Palace, the royal palace of Joseon Dynasty  Inwangsan Mountain, situated to the west of Gyeongbokgung Palace, was originally named Seosan Mountain until the 4th King Sejong of the Joseon Dynasty. The name ‘Inwang’ was derived from one of the Buddhist guardian gods, Geumgangshin, and the mountain was subsequently renamed with the hope of protecting the Joseon Dynasty, just as the god protects Buddhism.   Comprised entirely of granite, Inwangsan is a rocky mountain with a rugged shape, adorned with numerous strange-looking rocks. These rocks are associated with various special stories, leading to names inspired by animals, objects, and gods such as pigs, toads, elephants, snails, tigers, headgear, skulls, skirts, and Buddha statues.  In accordance with Chinese geomancy, royal palaces and tombs were traditionally built with a huge and tall mountain at the back and a smaller one in the front. This principle was applied to Hanyang, the capital of Joseon, and the current Seoul. Gyeongbokgung Palace, the center of Seoul, features Bukaksan Mountain at the rear and Namsan Mountain in the front.  In the traditional layout, the left and right sides are designated as the Blue Dragon and the White Tiger, respectively. Inwangsan Mountain takes on the role of the White Tiger. It is said that Inwangsan Mountain was once inhabited by many tigers, and the ancient stories of the mountain and its tigers have been passed down through the ages.

stories.title: The Story of Inwangsan and the Tiger
stories.audioTitle: The Story of Inwangsan and the Tiger
stories.script: A story of many tigers living in Inwangsan Mountain  Legend has it that Inwangsan Mountain has been home to many tigers since ancient times, with numerous anecdotes passed down through generations. Let’s delve into an anecdote from the Goryeo Dynasty.  One day, the General Gang Gam-chan, a military commander in the early Goryeo Dynasty, encountered an old monk in the mountain while patrolling in the Inwangsan Mountain. The general yelled at the monk in a grim voice, asking him to leave the area immediately. In an instant, the general realized it was the leader of the tigers disguised as an old monk. In response to the general’s rebuke, the tiger ended up leaving Inwangsan Mountain with its group.  Anecdotes about Inwang Mountain and tigers often appeared in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, which records the history of the Joseon Dynasty for 472 years. Most records about Inwangsan Mountain found in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty are about tigers that came down from the mountain, and tigers at Inwangsan Mountain frequently damaged palaces and private houses at the time.  There is a proverb about Inwangsan Mountain and tigers: “Is there even a tiger that doesn’t know Inwangsan Mountain?” This proverb emphasizes that no one could possibly not know themselves. If a tiger did not know what Inwangsan Mountain is, it would be isolated from the group of tigers. From the proverb, we can also infer that many tigers lived in Inwangsan Mountain.   Inwangsan Mountain banned all access to civilians for the security of Cheong Wa Dae from 1968 to 1993. However, starting from February 1993, it has been fully opened to the public. Today, it has become a popular spot where anyone can climb up and see Seoul at a glance. If you want to trek lightly, it is highly recommended to walk along the trail from Suseong-dong to Cheongun-dong.

stories.title: UNCURK Street
stories.script: UNCURK Street  This guide is recorded by the voice of Mr. Kim Young-ha.  The hill going over from Tongin-dong to Cheongun-dong is called “UNCURK Street” by the natives of this neighborhood. Since when was this hill referred to as such a foreign name?  The origin of UNCURK Street dates back to 1945. This area was the land owned by Yoon Deok-young, a pro-Japan traitor, during the Japanese occupation period, and Yoon established here a huge Western-style mansion called “Byeoksu Mountain Cabin. After the Liberation, however, Byeoksu Mountain Cabin was recovered by the U.S. military government. After the Korean War broke out in 1950 and as Seoul was lost and then recovered, the U.S. and UN forces came into the city, and they used this building, which had been called Byeoksu Mountain Cabin, as the U.S. 8th Army officers’ quarters.  In June 1954, an organization named UNCURK (United Nations Commission for the Unification and Rehabilitation of Korea) started to use this building. UNCURK is a special agency founded in 1950 by the resolution of the UN General Assembly for the purpose of unification, independence and establishment of a democratic government in the Republic of Korea as well as its economic reconstruction and restoration of peace. However, the agency was disbanded later in December 1973 as it was deemed that South Korea and North Korea are now capable of achieving the goals on their own independent and autonomous efforts.  People who returned to the neighborhood after the war found it strange and interesting that foreigners went in and out of the large building. When people asked these foreigners where they had come from, they simply replied, “UNCURK”, which was then pronounced the way Koreans heard and understood. So the name of the street became the “UNCURK Street”.  The building that was used as the UNCURK headquarters was completely burned down by a fire in April 1966. Today, the area is filled with residential structures so the splendor of the good old days is long gone but the name left on the hill and the pillars of the main gate Byeoksu Mountain Cabin on the roadside still maintain the old memories.

stories.title: Udang Memorial Hall
stories.script: Udang Memorial Hall  This guide is recorded by the voice of Mr. Kim Young-ha.  During the Japanese occupation period when it was hard to produce even a single independence fighter in a family, there was a house whose six brothers all sacrificed their lives for independence movement. It is none other than the house of Udang Lee Hoe-yeong. His father was Lee Yu-seung, a scholar who once served as Ijo Panseo under King Gojong. In today's world, Ijo Panseo is a minister who oversees Ijo, which works to hire officials.  Mr. Lee Hoe-yeong was the fourth son out of the six and one of the people who had devised a plan to send the Hague secret emissaries to the Second Peace Conference in 1907. When the Hague emissary plan failed and the Korea-Japan Treaty of 1910 was forced to be signed by the Japanese, Lee gathered his brothers for a meeting.  The brothers thought that they needed a powerful army to take their country back and, to fulfill their plan, they decided to move to Manchuria and establish schools. At once, they disposed of all of their properties to secure cash and foods and traveled to Manchuria along with all of their family members and servants who wished to follow. The lands they sold at the time were mostly in Myeong-dong and Jongno in Seoul, and their total monetary value was about 600 billion won in today’s currency.  Settled in Samwonbo, Manchuria, the brothers founded the “Sinheung School” to educate and train Joseon people into independence activists. And this was expanded later into “Sinheung Military Academy” based on their wish for more people to receive education. As they were teaching a great number of students, the funds ran out and the wife of Mr. Lee Hoe-yeong even sewed for money to contribute to the independence funds. Such dismal times continued until not too long after. As the level of oppression by the Japanese army intensified, Sinheung Military Academy had to eventually be shut down in 1920.  Mr. Lee Hoe-yeong still carried out anti-Japanese fights after that but, in 1932, he was arrested by Japanese forces in China and ultimately passed away in November of the same year after suffering from torture. His brothers also died while participating in independence movement or ended their lives after dealing with poverty and hunger for a long time. Only Lee Si-yeong, the fifth son of the family and the lone survivor, was able to tread the soil of the liberated homeland.  The stories of Udang Lee Hoe-yeong and his family were passed down to his descendants and the independence army soldiers from Sinheung Military Academy fought bravely to continue the legacy of the six Lee brothers. Even after the Liberation, people did not forget about them and built “Udang Memorial Hall” in commemoration of their spirit.

stories.title: Mugunghwa Hill
stories.script: Mugunghwa Hill  This guide is recorded by the voice of Mr. Kim Young-ha.  In the southern half of the Korean Peninsula that was celebrating the Liberation, the democratic government of the Republic of Korea was established, and key government positions, most notably the president, were elected. Now, the president, one who represents our country, needed a place to stay so Gyeongmudae” located behind Gyeongbokgung Palace was chosen.
