But, as industries and the population grew in Yeongdo, people could no longer bear the inconvenience so a big decision was made to install water pipes along Yeongdodaegyo. Having lost its character since then, the bridge was treated as the less preferred brother to the juxtaposed “Busandaegyo ” before eventually facing the risk of being demolished. However, the people of Busan would not let a bridge that had been with them through the ages of turbulence be torn down so easily. For nearly 3 years, they put a great amount of efforts into building a sturdy, durable bridge while trying to reproduce the old appearance as much as possible. Looking at the stone steps and walls at the entrance of the bridge, you will see old, stained stones meshed with new, smooth stones. This seems to show the age of Yeongdo Bridge that embraces the turbulence of yesterday while protecting the daily lives of today with great vigor.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 2. Monument of Songs for Hyeon In
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 2. Monument of Songs for Hyeon In
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 2. Monument of Songs for Hyeon In  〈Be Strong, Geumsun〉is a famous song whose melody has probably been heard at least once even for those who have no idea where the windy, blizzard-raging Heungnam Pier is in the Korean Peninsula. What could possibly be the story behind this song, released during the Korean War that managed to linger at the tip of tongues of the Korean people for over half a century, protecting one end of Yeongdo Bridge along with the statue of Mr. Hyeon In?  The reason Yeongdodaegyo is special to the Busan people is not because it is the only bascule bridge in Korea. Instead, it is probably an unforgettable place where the sorrowful lives were lived in the midst of a tragic war. A countless number of refugees,who were stranded at Heungnam Pier at the time of the January–Fourth Retreat in 1950, fought for their lives to board the southbound ship as they failed to hold onto the hands of their mothers, wives and sisters, ultimately reaching Busan, just as the words of the song by Mr. Hyeon In. As they had to do whatever it took to survive, many of the refugees became merchants and settled on the edges of the Busan Port. This was not only because the port was bustling with opportunities for jobs. It was based on the slimmest hope that they may run into their separated families or, at least, hear the news of their beloved ones somewhere within the crowd of people. Whenever their longing for families filled them to the brink, they would go on Yeongdo Bridge to blame the innocent night sea and swallow their bloody tears. 〈Be Strong, Geumsun〉, released in 1953 around when the Korean War finally came to a truce, is a testament to their devastated hearts.  For urgent refugees who did not know where to designate their place of reunion in a strange land, Yeongdo Bridge, which they had barely known by its name, was a place of gathering. “Get to Busan first. I will follow. Meet me on Yeongdo Birdge.” People who had to head south away from the hometowns promised to their families while letting go of their hands. That is why, for a long time even after the war was over, flyers with names, ages and hometowns of separated family members filled up every handrail of Yeongdo Bridge. Jeombachi Street was created around this time along the shore below the bridge on the Nampo-dong side. “Is my mom alive?”, “Did you hear when we'll be able to return home?” Because of the refugees who frequently visited the fortune-tellers below the bridge out of desperation, over 70 of such shops were crowded in the area during the immediate post-war period.  As you can see, Yeongdo Bridge has stood in its place as a witness to the history of modern Korean, stained with the tears of sorrow from a life away from home and the hand prints of those who endlessly waited. The reason that 〈Be Strong, Geumsun〉sung by Mr. Hyeon In is special is probably because of the weight of the memories this bridge has shouldered for decades.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 3. Kangkangee Guide Center (formerly Doseonjang)
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 3. Kangkangee Guide Center (formerly Doseonjang)
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 3. Kangkangee Guide Center (formerly Doseonjang)  If you start smelling a hint of pungent iron powder from within the salty smell of the sea, you have arrived at Kangkangee Village. “Kangkangee” Where do you think such a rhythmical name came from? For nearly a century of time, this area was known as the best ship-repairing site in Korea. Even today, from different corners of the streets, we can see before our very eyes the large vessels waiting to be checked by technicians. When a ship comes in for repair, the first thing they have to do is to take off the rust, seaweeds, barnacles, amongst other things that are attached to the sides of the ship. Before the invention of the grinder, and electronic tool, they had to use hammers to strike each of these things individually in order to remove them. The sound, “Kangkang”, was produced every time an iron hammer hit a ship and was even heard by people living around the mid-level of the mountains across the sea. So it's easy to imagine how the name, “Kangkangee Village” came about naturally.  Here, people were able to get whatever they needed to make or repair a ship. Ships built all around the world have different shapes of for the parts they use, that are as various as their nationalities are, so it is extremely difficult to secure the correct parts whenever they are in need. However, here, the parts and even the machines that create the said parts are manufactured in-house so any malfunction that occurs on any vessel from anywhere in the world can be repaired. It is not an overstatement that “even a submarine can be built if you go through about ten factories in Kangkangee Village”.  But the world-class ship building and repairing industry is not the only business that boasts a long history within this village. The history of a ferry service that connects the mainland to this island also dates back over 100 years. Even though four bridges stretch out to the mainland, small boats have been an essential means of transportation in Yeongdo. At the location where Kangkangee Guide Center is now, there used to be a dock at which people got on boats that would travel to Jagalchi across the sea. The ferry service began in the early 1900s, when a large Japanese population immigrated to Yeongdo, and served as feet to the residents of Kangkangee Village until it stopped its operation in 2008. The creation of Yeongdo Bridge in the 1930s made it much more convenient to travel between the mainland and Yeongdo but here in Kangkangee Village, which resembles the toes of a sock that protrudes towards Jagalchi, it was still faster to cross the sea. A 15-minute drive on land could be shortened to just 5 minutes by boat. The elderly of Yeongdo still remember the days of their childhood when they would jump off the boats in the middle to avoid paying the fare or when they dress out to go to the music cafes in Nampo-dong.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 4. Kangkangee Street Museum
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 4. Kangkangee Street Museum
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 4. Kangkangee Street Museum  Over these walls you see above, the shipbuilding industry of Yeongdo began. Today, this place continues its existence under the name of 〈Woori Shipbuilding〉but, about 100 years ago, it was called 〈Tanaka Shipyard〉. Tanaka Shipyard is regarded as the birthplace of the Korean modern shipbuilding industry as it was the place where the first powerboat driven by an engine instead of wind or steam was developed in the country. The reason that a street museum, presenting the history and sceneries of Kangkangee Village like a panorama, was set up here is because this is the heart of the Yeongdo shipbuilding industry that still lives on vibrantly for over a century.  But even before the Japanese built a shipyard, there had already been many workshops in the village where Korean technicians built and repaired ships using their own technology. Up until the 1920s, a narrow but long bay existed from the sea on the Jagalchi side to the center of the village. Thanks to the sea stretched deep into the land as well as a broad mud flat, the area lacked wind and waves, which made it a perfect place to build small ships. Moreover, the Busan Port opened in 1876 and it was a great location for Japanese fishing boats, which had operated up to Joseon's coasts, to make a pit stop for rests and repairs. After the Korea-Japan Annexation, it was natural for the Japanese to construct numerous shipyards and ship repair facilities in this area.  In the 1930s, Yeongdo's shipbuilding industry welcomes its first heyday as the Japanese exploitation intensified, which necessitated large-sized cargo vessels and eventually led to a broad-scale expansion of the infrastructure by the Japanese. Small boats can be brought up to the ground for repair but large vessels had to be anchored first near land and drained of all water before starting repairs. This was also the time when enormous advanced facilities, which served to fill and drain water to set ships afloat or to sink them, were produced. As the tension of the war arose in the 1940s, military vessels such as battleships and transport ships were of dire need so Japan made another broad-scale investment. As a result, Yeongdo became equipped with the technology and infrastructure to build and repair 1,000-ton vessels and beyond. That such a remarkable growth entailed exploitation of resources and, more importantly, people of the Korean Peninsula is a sad chapter in our history.  But, fortunately, the second peak of the Korean shipbuilding industry was achieved by the hands of our own people after Liberation. Tanaka Shipyard and other Japanese shipbuilding facilities were sold to Korean technicians in the village and, through internal development of techniques and methodologies, Kangkangee Village evolved into a global mecca of the shipbuilding and repair industry in the 70s and 80s. Even to this day, based on the pride that, “If it can't be found in Daepyeong-dong, it can't be found anywhere in the world”, Kangkangee Village powers on in its passionate voyage.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 5. Daepyeong Village Museum
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 5. Daepyeong Village Museum
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 5. Daepyeong Village Museum  In addition to the “Village Guide Center”, there is another building here in Kangkangee Village that is difficult to find anywhere else - the “Living Culture Center” . Boasting a nice facade; a village cafe; and even a village museum, the building is unique from any other typical village hall or welfare center. The building itself and the land it stands on are both properties of the village. After Liberation, the Daepyeong-dong Village Council purchased land where there used to be a Japanese temple and has been using it for various purposes ranging from a kindergarten to even a temporary shelter for the homeless refugees of the Korean War. It is rare for a city village to own public property but it seems like the Daepyeong-dong people had understood the importance of life together since a long way back.  Though the name is not used anymore, “Daepyeong-dong” was the official name of Kangkangee Village for the past 60 years. Before that, it was called “Daepungpo”, which means a port that waits or prepares for the wind. This piece of land, which resembles a fish hook protruding out from the main island of Yeongdo, got its name by serving as a natural embankment for the island. A large-scale reclamation project in the 1920s changed the shape of the land significantly and administrative districts were restructured after Liberation, eventually giving a new name to Daepungpo - “Daepyeong-dong” , which means, “wish for great peace” . . Thanks to its name, the area thrived until the 80s to the point where people joked about how “even puppies would carry around 10,000 won bills in Daepyeong-dong” . Unfortunately, the name “Daepyeong-dong” no longer exists as ships that continued to increase in size after the 80s moved to larger shipyards nearby, leading to many losing their jobs and ultimately leaving the town. Then, in 1998 when a fierce tsunami known as the IMF struck the nation, Daepyeong-dong lost its name by becoming incorporated into the nearby Namhang-dong. However, many of the residents in the area are proud of the name insomuch to still introduce themselves as Daepyeong-dong people, and you can guess how proud they are by seeing the lettters of “Daepyeong” written boldly on the signboard of this building.  Because it is an island village close to Japan, there have been many people going in and out of Yeongdo since old times. From compatriots freed from forced labor after Liberation, refugees who had been pushed southward due to the war, to even the female divers of Jeju who came all the way to Busan waters to make a living, outsiders who had left their homes were welcomed in Daepyeong-dong, whose people readily shared what they had. Traces of dividing a small, 5- to 6-pyeong residence for many people to reside in are still found in the area under the names of Ibukdongne, Jeju 18-tong, etc. The heart of Daepungpo, which opened its arms to more ships as the wind grew more vicious, is once could say, the true valuable heritage of Kangkangee Village.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 6. Ultra-large apartment mural
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 6. Ultra-large apartment mural
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 6. Ultra-large apartment mural  The face that seems older than the very apartment wall on which it is painted is the Kangkangee Ajimae. The sounds of the hammers struck by workers hanging on the ships for over 40 years have become their name. When a ship, which was as large as two tile-roofed houses combined, came in, about 15 to 30 Ajimae, or middle-aged women, worked to remove the rust while holding hammers as heavy as 3kg and leaning their bodies only on long and narrow wooden plates hanging onto the ship. As three to four workers sat on the same wooden plate to get to work, even the slightest movement of one person would shake up the entire plate so everyone had to exert forces that would cause numbness to their bodies just to not to fall off. If one person wanted to come down, all of them had to go so they would not take any breaks aside from the 20 minutes they were given daily. Of course, going to the bathroom was not easy as well, which is why, even in the midst of all this hard labor, most of them merely wet their lips with water just to bear with the thirst. But they still lived with the mere grateful thought of avoiding a fall from the weak platform, 5m off from the ground.  The daily wages for the Kangkangee Ajimae were a measly 1,000 won even during the 70s when the village was thriving. A bag of flour was about 800 won at the time, so even if they worked hard all day long, their living standards did not improve much. However, they could not stop hammering these ships because most of them were the heads of their households who had to take care of the livelihood of their families. Many of them were widows of the war, daughters who inherited poverty from their refugee parents, or those who had left their impoverished hometowns to make a living in the city. In a village that did not have many jobs other than the rough fishing work, the women had to become Kangkangee Ajimae who had to put up with heavy labor for just a little bit of money.  Tears filled the hearts of mothers who would go to work at dawn, shrouded in darkness, after placing a large bowl of rice, a bowl of water, and a chamber pot next to their young child and locking the door from the outside. Many of the women who had to use hammers with their bare hands without any protective gear on shabby platforms eventually acquired sicknesses of the shoulders, waists, legs, and even lost their hearing. But Kangkangee Ajimae ached more for their children, whom they could not care for, than their own bodies that were slowly deteriorating. Perhaps, the bold earring worn by the Kangkangee Ajimae painted on the outer wall of Daedongdaegyo Mansion in Daepyeong-dong is a medal of honor presented to these women for the loss of their hearing and lifelong sacrifices.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 1. Choryang Modern History Gallery
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 1. Choryang Modern History Gallery
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 1. Choryang Modern History Gallery  A long line of Chinese-style red lanterns lights up a brilliant street and portray the portraits of old Busan people, strolling through thatched houses in their simple hanbok, quite exotic. This place is the Choryang Modern History Gallery. As you can see from the pictures, Choryang used to be a small coastal village with a wide spanning beach of white sand under green pine trees, at least it was, until Cheonggwan Street, which later became today's Chinatown, was established in 1884. After the Busan Port opened, Chinese merchants attempted to open up shops in the Japanese residential district located in Nampo-dong but conflicts ensued between the two groups. Thus, the Joseon government provided the Choryang area as concession for the Qing. The Qing consulate was then set up in the location of an overseas Chinese school nearby. Concessions may sound a bit unfamiliar to you but it was a place where foreigners resided and traded freely similar to today's special economic zones. Behind the installation of such establishments, however, lay the imperialistic greed of the two nations in trying to hastily occupy the Korean Peninsula before the other. From this point on, Choryang, once a peaceful village that used to be called “Saetti”, which meant a village of reed fields, suddenly is dragged into the whirlwind of East Asian modern history.  Would you believe me if I said that the ground you stand on right now was a part of the sea just a century ago? Continuously increasing its forces at the beginning of the 1900s, Japan carried out a large-scale reclamation project to fill up the sea in front of Choryang. Their goal was to expand the residential district and simultaneously secure a base in Busan from which they could advance into China more conveniently. In the same sense, the Japanese who had built the Gyeongbu Line railroad established Busan Station at a close distance to the Busan Port in order to allow those traveling from Tokyo to Seoul to be able to quickly transfer on to the train once they got off their ships. As you can imagine, Choryang had to bear the sad fate of being exploited as the base for the Japanese' Korean Peninsula colonization policy for four decades. The rough times Choryang had endured did not end with the Liberation. As the Korean War that immediately followed produced a countless number of refugees who threw themselves into trains and ships and were pushed southward, their destination being Busan Station and Busan Port. Although the city managed to avoid the sorrows of war, Choryang soon becomes overcrowded due to the increasing number of refugees. In the photo on the wall, you will see lines of houses constructed on a mountain like a terraced paddy field, this was the last resort to accommodate the ever-increasing refugees by any means necessary.  Not too far from the shade of this hillside slum rooted in poverty, the U.S. troops stationed in Korea during the war began to flock to Texas Street next to Chinatown, which ultimately turned Choryang into an entertainment district where foreign currency flowed. Then in the early 90s when diplomatic ties were established with Russia, a great number of Russian peddlers came to Busan, and also indulged in Texas Street. Recently, it is said that there are many Chinese and Southeast Asians in the area. As you can see, Choryang reflects, like a mirror, the state of international affairs surrounding the Korean Peninsula as an interchange of the country, as well as a gate to the city of Busan.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 2. Busan Chinatown
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 2. Busan Chinatown
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 2. Busan Chinatown  Perhaps, to tourists, Chinatown is simply where you go for real Chinese cuisine cooked by chefs from mainland China. But in fact, it is more than that; it is the home of the fierce and tenacious lives of overseas Chinese who have laughed and cried along with the Korean people for over a century. The history of overseas Chinese in Busan dates back to the 19th century when Cheonggwan Street was first established. Considering the long history of back and forth exchanges between Korea and China, the history of overseas Chinese in Korea is rather short. But, unlike those who received tough treatment as immigrants in other countries, the overseas Chinese in Korea were able to settle down relatively easily during the early days thanks to much support from the Qing. There is a familiar term among the overseas Chinese - “Sampado”, which means “three knives”. When Chinese people went overseas, they carried one of the three following knives - a cooking knife, a haircutting knife and a linen/cotton cutting knife, which tells you why most of the overseas Chinese made their living from restaurants, barbershops and/or linen shops.  But a lot of the Chinese we meet in Chinatown today are not the descendants of the Qing merchants who settled during the aforementioned period. Most of the Chinese at the time returned home in the aftermath of the Sino-Japanese War, the purpose of which was an invasion of China, started by Japan in the 1930s. Thus, the Chinese who live in Busan today are mostly the descendants of those who fled from the oppression of a post liberated communist China or refugees of the Korean War who had been living in other parts of the country. Many of the first-generation and second-generation overseas Chinese who settled in Busan are not very proficient in Korean, and one of the reasons is that much like most refugees in general, they had never imagined to call the city their home forever.  Not a single moment in the lives of the Chinese settlers was easy. The Cold War era that lasted nearly half a century pressured the overseas Chinese in becoming people of Taiwanese nationality, a country that they had never been to. Most of the Chinese living in Korea at the time were from the Shandong Province in the Chinese mainland. In the days of the Third Republic, economic activities of the overseas Chinese were strictly regulated so they could not own real estate or open up stores larger than a designated area. Such discrimination drove a significant number of Chinese out of Korea. Even after a century-long coexistence, the overseas Chinese continued receiving the cold shoulder as strangers.  It is sometimes easy for us to ask, why don't you change your nationality when you live in Korea? To this, they reply. They were treated as Chinese in Korea, as Koreans in China and as mainland Chinese in Taiwan and lived as outsiders their whole lives but Korea never provided a home for them. In the “era of diversity”, shouldn't our genuine respect for diversity begin from the way we view our neighbors?

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 3. Old Baekje Hospital
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 3. Old Baekje Hospital
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 3. Old Baekje Hospital  Old Baekje Hospital is a building with a unique appearance that would grab the attention of passersby even without any historical knowledge. Not the broadest or tallest of buildings but what kind of history and stories are held inside this dignified and vintage structure?  The history of the building dates back nearly 100 years. A man named Choi Yong-hae from Gimhae, Gyeongsangnam-do returned from Japan, where he was studying medicine, in 1927 and built a building 5 story building, with 1 underground floor, which he named “Baekje Hospital”. There were large medical institutions such as the Busan-bu Hospital and the Railway Hospital in the city at the time but Baekje was the first general hospital of that scale that was founded by an individual. A total of 60,000 won was used for its construction and given that a bag of rice was worth 10 won back then, it was an incredible amount of money equivalent to over 1 billion won today. The hospital also hired about 30 foreign medical staff including, German and Japanese doctors, and installed over 40 beds, thus boasting an unprecedented level of expertise for a private hospital. Thanks to this, the hospital began to see people in droves immediately after it first opened. However, its boom ended in just 5 years because of the rumors surrounding the use of corpses of homeless people and charity patients in making human cadavers and storing them inside the hospital. As people criticized the hospital, the number of those who came for checkups and exams dwindled. Then, one day in 1932, 39-year-old Choi Yong-hae handed the hospital building over to the Oriental Development Company and fled to Japan.  Ironically, the fate of Baekje Hospital became inextricable from the political situation of East Asia. In the following year, the Oriental Development Company sold the building to a Chinese salesman named Yang Momin and, after the remodeling of its interior, Baekje Hospital was reborn as “Bongnaegak” , a Chinese restaurant. From that point on, it was used as a place of business reception by the Chinese who ruled the Cheonggwan Street. But, as the war intensified in 1942, Yang Momin rapidly shut down its business and returned to China. Afterwards, Japan's Akazuki unit stationed in Busan used this building as a dormitory for its officers. Then, after Liberation, the building, which had been abandoned by the fleeing Japanese army, was used for the Busan Public Safety Headquarters. The iron bars seen at the building's main entrance are proof of the buildings use as a detention center. In 1950, it was used as a temporary embassy for Taiwan and then, in 1953 after the end of the war, it was sold to an individual to become the commercial building we see today. Fortunately, there have not been any major change to the inside or outside of the building since the internal repairs that were conducted in 1933. In an era where similar modern structures disappeared due to reasons of safety and politics, the old Baekje Hospital is a valuable cultural heritage that sheds light on how buildings looked at the time.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 4. Namseon Warehouse Site
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 4. Namseon Warehouse Site
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 4. Namseon Warehouse Site  After busily snapping shots while being captivated by the picturesqueness exuding from the old Baekje Hospital building, if you turn your attention this way you can't help but feel a sense of loneliness. This place, which only has a wall on one side and seems to be in direct contrast to the soundly preserved old Baekje Hospital, is where Namseon Warehouse, once considered as one of the 5 biggest logistics warehouses worldwide in the early 20th century, used to be.  Originally, this used to be a rice paddy located by the sea. Before the Japanese reclaimed the sea in front of Choryang, the seawater would come all the way up to this wall. This field used to be nicknamed“Tteongnon” , which stems from a story of the owner of the field who was starving because of a severe drought in 1877 selling a few acres of the field to buy himself some tteok, or rice cake.  Finally in 1900, 5 warehouse buildings whose total area was 1,000 pyeong were constructed on this land. As you can see from the images on the wall, wooden pillars were erected, rafters were placed in a triangular formation, and the walls were built with red bricks. It was the first warehouse built in Busan. There were also installations of temporary waterways to lower the humidity and maintain a constant temperature regardless of the weather outside, from which we may glimpse the level of excellent warehouse construction technology that our ancestors had.  It actually started with the name “Bukseon Warehouse” and primarily unloaded and stored pollack that had been caught in Hamgyeong-do Province before distributing them to Gyeongsang-do, Chungcheong-do and even Seoul. The volume of pollack it once handled was enormous, which is why it was also known as “Myeongtae Gobing”. There's even a saying that goes “no Busan local has ever not had the eyes of a pollack from Bukseon Warehouse”. A special economic zone in which the Chinese and Japanese traded freely was nearby and the Gyeongbu Line railroad constructed in 1905 reached its front yard so Bukseon Warehouse enjoyed great prosperity. But, after a railroad connecting Seoul and Wonsan, Hamgyeong-do was established in 1914, all Seoul-bound cargo no longer had to go through Busan. Furthermore, a few fast-thinking businessmen even built a warehouse in Wonsan of the same name. To prevent any confusion caused by the identical name, Bukseon Warehouse in Busan changed its name to “Namseon Warehouse”.  Even after Liberation, the warehouse continued to handle all sorts of goods from seafood to chemicals, plywood, shoes and even items of Russian peddlers, serving as the foundation of the Busan economy until November 2009 when Namseon Warehouse was finally torn down. “By the walls and buildings standing as they always have, under rain, wind, and the scorching sun, I was able to turn the moments of the past into an eternity. … Who wouldn’t have a time they would desire to pause and places they wish to never forget?” Mr. Cho Gap-sang, an author and a Busan native, expressed the sadness he felt at the disappearance of the Namseon Warehouse by this statement. The feeling of loss as if a fragment of time has evaporated along with the disappearance of a space is perhaps something we all experience.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 5. Choryang Presbyterian Church
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 5. Choryang Presbyterian Church
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 5. Choryang Presbyterian Church  Choryang Presbyterian Church has great historical meaning in that it not only was the first church established in the south of the Hangang but also firmly stood by the Busan people through the anti-Japanese movement and the Korean War, two of the most important moments in Korean modern history.  Choryang Presbyterian Church was founded in 1892 by William Baird, an American missionary. You may not be familiar with the name, Baird, but you have probably heard of the Soongsil School, which was one of the national institutions that instilled the spirit of independence and democracy in the students during the Japanese occupation period. Missionary Baird was the founder of the Soongsil School.  Originally founded under the name of “Yeongseonhyeon Church”, Choryang Church changed its name several times since then. In 1922 when the church building was newly constructed, it was named “Choryang Samil Church”, adding the spirit of the March 1st Movement, one of the more famous anti-Japanese movements, into its name. When Japanese policemen, who had sensed the rebellious nuance, asked what “Samil” meant, the church told them that it referred to “Samwi Ilche”, or the Holy Trinity. Fully living up to its name, “Samil Church” had many clerics and believers who actively devoted themselves to the anti-Japanese movement. The March 1st Movement in Busan first began with the independence demonstration by the Ilshin Girls' School in Busanjin on March 11, 1919, and the one who led this movement was Joo Kyung-ae, a teacher and a member of Choryang Church. Also, Choryang Presbyterian Church is famous for having been deeply involved in collecting war funds to support the Provisional Government of Shanghai and the Korean Liberation Army. Yoon Hyun-jin, a deacon of the church and the head of the Masan Branch of the Gyeongnam Bank, defected to Shanghai, China immediately after the independence demonstration and took 300,000 won with him, an amount that could buy 4 fighter jets at the time. Also, Pastor Chu Ki-chol who was appointed to the position in 1925 is widely known as the one who led the movement against shrine worship. Asserting that we should never bow our heads to where the Emperor of Japan is enshrined as a god and where Japanese warlords were revered as guardian gods of the state. Pastor Chu was martyred in a Pyeongyang prison in 1944, just a year prior to Liberation, after 7 long years of hardship inside the cells. As he had gained such great respect and trust from the Busan people because of his unbending anti-Japanese spirit, both the believers and non-believers alike did not hesitate to reach into their pockets when the church collected tithes for the construction of a new chapel.  The days of which the Choryang Presbyterian Church shared their fate along with the people did not stop here. When refugees from all over the country fled to the city due to the war in 1950, the church gladly opened its gates to be used as a refugee shelter. The front yard and inner garden of the church were covered in tents and the church members distributed things to eat and wear to the refugees. Not only that, but they also encouraged refugee ministers and believers to host a national salvation prayer service for the country to overcome its present sufferings.  Providing psychological support for the commoners who had been shocked and worn down due to the repeated national hardships, Choryang Church was the epitome of fulfilling the true value of a religion.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 6. 168 Stairs
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 6. 168 Stairs
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 6. 168 Stairs  As you hike up a road between Choryang Elementary School and Choryang Presbyterian Church, you cannot help but yell, “Wow!” in front of some terrifyingly steep stairs. They are the 168 Stairs made of a whopping 168 steps on a steep sloped hillside. The area surrounding the 168 Stairs is known as the Yeongju-dong Mountain Village, and the fastest route to travel back and forth between the upper and lower sides of the village is these stairs.  When people think of 168 Stairs, their memories naturally go back to the lives of the refugees during the Korean War but the history of this mountain village dates back to much earlier than that. Because of the geological nature of Busan, which has more mountainous regions than flat lands, the life on hillsides began at an earlier time than we think. Especially in the early 1900s when the Japanese carried out a project to cut away Yeongseonsan Mountain, which had been blocking Choryang from the Busan Port, to reclaim the sea, a great number of people came to the city for jobs and, subsequently, shack houses began to populate the hillsides. At the time, people called those who performed physical labor as “Dogada” from which the term “Nogada” came, a slang that refers to daily manual laborers.  More and more shacks continued to be built up the mountain like a pyramid due to the Koreans who had returned from Japan after Liberation and the refugees who had come from every corner of the country immediately after the start of the war. There was a story that many foreigners who were about to arrive in Busan on a flight in the middle of a night were surprised at the scene as they mistakenly thought Busan was a huge city densely populated with high-rise buildings. It was impossible to supply Water to these shacks that had been built in a hurry so the most arduous task for women of the hillside village was to carry water all the way from a well in the lower side of the village. The well, which was used at the time, still remains near the bottom of the stairs. It was tough to stand in line for many hours just to access the well but it was an even more daunting task to climb up the seemingly endless stairs with buckets full of water. With babies on their backs and buckets filled to the brim with water, walking up the stairs with extra care as to not spill any of the precious water, surely this situation would leave many breathless. Moreover, the stairs at the time were not properly built as the ones we see today and were made with only a few stones in the middle for people to step on, so you can assume the hardships the hillside women had to endure while straining to not slip on the steps.  Meanwhile, men had to find odd jobs in order to make a living, so they often would take a seat at the top of the stairs, where an observatory is located today, and wait around all day long. Upon seeing the trains and ships entering Busan Station and Busan Port, people would pretty much roll down the 168 Stairs. This was possible because of the Busan weather at that time, which was void of snow.  If you decide to take the stairs, you feel the weight of life of the old days, every step you take.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 7. Kim Min-bu Observatory
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 7. Kim Min-bu Observatory
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 7. Kim Min-bu Observatory  At the middle of the 168 stairs, a place to take a breather and enjoy the beautiful scenery, this place is the Kim Min-bu Observatory. Located at a lower level compared to other observatories, it is especially attractive as the sea afar in the background is overlapped with the scenes of life right before your eyes. It seems fitting to name this observatory after Kim Min-bu, a poet who grew up witnessing the pain and agony that plagued the area.  It is widely known that the composer of a famous song, 〈The Waiting Heart〉, is Mr. Jang Il-nam but not many people know that Kim Min-bu wrote the lyrics for the song. This is understandable because 〈The Waiting Heart〉 is not included in the two books of poetry left by the poet who passed away at a young age of 31 years old from a sudden accident. Fortunately, the story of his versification was revealed thanks to composer Jang Il-nam.  At the time of the January–Fourth Retreat, Mr. Jang left his mother in his hometown of Haeju, Hwanghae-do and moved south alone to stay in Yeonpyeongdo Island for a year. Here, he stumbled upon a poem written in the old Korean language. The poem, which was in the Jeju dialect, wrote, “Dreaming of a life on land, a man from Jeju comes to Mokpo with much difficulty. The greatest pain of a weary life away from home is when you can't see the person you love. Every time he missed her badly, he would go up to Wolchulbong at the back of Yudalsan Mountain in Mokpo and gaze at the sea towards Jeju. The woman, missing the man as well, also climbs up Seongsan Ilchulbong but the seemingly eternal wait turns her into stone.” Mr. Jang chokes up as he interprets the meaning of every letter because he likened himself, who is not able to visit his hometown even though it is only a few miles away, to the man from the poem. So, Mr. Jang went up to the tallest hill in Yeonpyeongdo and finished the song in just 10 minutes. One day after over a decade since the completion of the song, Mr. Jang who had been requested by a TV show that introduced new songs brought this song with him to the TV station. Working as a scripter at the TV station at the time, Poet Kim Min-bu was so touched by this story that he instantly started to write the lyrics.  The poet probably knew very well what kind of reverberation the story of the Wolchulbong man and the Ilchulbong woman gave Mr. Jang, who was a displaced person, because he grew up right where you stand now, walking up and down this hill from which we can see the ocean. He breathes in the sighs of the refugees missing the homes they left, waiting for their separated families. Perhaps, it is an incredible inevitability planned by history that Kim Min-bu became the lyricist for 〈The Waiting Heart〉.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 8. Chang Kee-ryo Memorial Hall
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 8. Chang Kee-ryo Memorial Hall
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 8. Chang Kee-ryo Memorial Hall  “I woke up thinking the raindrops beating onto the window were you. I knew it couldn't be but I ran over to the window with a sense of hope but only darkness awaited me there. With a dispirited heart, I light up a lamp to write this letter. … I know no religion is accepted in the North for anyone but I believe you will always pray. I can finish this letter with a delightful heart because I truly believe the 38th parallel will vanish in our lifetime and the separated families will finally meet to share their love once again. —In Busan after 40 years of separation, from yours truly Kee-ryo”  This letter, composed to make readers’ hearts ache, is a nostalgic letter written by Dr. Chang Kee-ryo to his wife whom he had left in the North after being separated during the escape to the South. We can never imagine the shade and magnitude of the feeling of longing for a man who was separated from his family and lived alone for 40 years. While he was treating patients at an army field hospital after the recapturing of Pyongyang, Dr. Chang's family started on the journey with other refugees during the January–Fourth Retreat. He let his wife and five children leave first and then he himself followed with his second son, escaping Pyongyang on an army ambulance. As he was on his way out of the Jongno Street in Pyongyang, he saw out the ambulance window, his wife moving briskly while holding the hands of his young son. But the doctor could not ask the driver to stop the car because it wasn't possible to pick up only his family in the midst of the countless refugees running away from the city, their faces deadly pale. Once arriving in the South, the doctor heard the news that his family had been caught by the Chinese army and forced to return to Pyongyang. This event left a scar in his life that would never heal.  As you can see at this memorial, Doctor Chang produced great achievements as not only a doctor but also a medical policy maker and educator, and also practiced medicine for the impoverished at no cost, being revered as the Schweitzer of Korea. During a reunion of separated families from the two Koreas, the government proposed Dr. Chang a special reunion, which would allow him to see his family from the North over other families who could only get a chance for a reunion through a lottery. Although everyone believed that he more than deserved the chance, Dr. Chang did not accept this opportunity of a lifetime since he believe it to be unfair when considering all the other separated families. This did not mean that the love he had for his family was any less than others. Having lived all his life without any extravagance, the doctor told the people around him that one day he wishes to travel to another country. When people asked him where he wishes to visit, his answer was East Germany, which was a socialist state at the time. He had heard that one of his sons who grew up in the North and became a doctor was planning to attend a conference to be held in East Berlin. Even though he had no chance to see him face-to-face, he strongly wished to be on the same earth that his son would be on. He then silently wiped away his tears while saying so. Until the moment he passed away, Dr. Chang is known to have hummed a song that his wife had taught him during their days together. Some call him a cold man of principle who even refused a chance to reunite with his loving family. But, looking back on his life, we can't help but wonder if this principal stems from his deep empathy for feeling a greater pain from a thorn under another’s finger than the pain from his own broken leg.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 9. Yu Chi-hwan Postbox
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 9. Yu Chi-hwan Postbox
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Choryang-dong Ibagu-gil: 9. Yu Chi-hwan Postbox  This tranquil road leading up to the observatory here is Sanbok Road, a lifeline of Busan. Sanbok Road literally means a road that cuts across the abdomen” area of a mountain, and Busan can be said to be a mecca of the Sanbok Roads. As a result of topography featuring narrow flat lands and many mountains combined with the history of the frequent influx of people from other parts of the country, one hillside village after another began to be established in Busan starting from a long time ago. It was extremely inconvenient to walk down to a flat part of the village and then climb up a mountainous hill again just to get to a town nearby, which eventually gave birth to roads connecting one hillside village to the next. This particular road, which was built in 1964, is the first Sanbok Road in Busan.  Now, shall we turn our attention to the postbox and poetry monument standing below this tranquil road with the sea as its backdrop? This cozy-looking observatory is a space that commemorates the Poet Cheongma Yu Chi-hwan. Cheongma also served as the principal of Gyeongnam Girls' High School, one of the traditionally prestigious schools in Busan that is located just about 5 minutes away from here by car. He was said to be a romantic Korean teacher who would lead a group of students up a mountain on a clear, sunny day and recite poems for them. The boundless view of this place seems to match well with his character.  “I was happy for I loved/​ Loving someone/ gives a greater happiness than being loved./ Today, I come to a window at the post office again/ where the emerald sky is clearly seen, to write you a letter.” 〈Happiness〉, which is engraved on the monument, is a song that anyone who had spent their teenage years before the 90s recited at least once in their lives for someone they loved. People can easily empathize with this poem perhaps because it is a song that stemmed from the poet's own love story. After Liberation, Mr. Yu Chi-hwan returned to his hometown and became a Korean teacher at Tongyeong Girls' Middle School where he encountered the Poet Lee Young-do. Known for her good looks and writing ability, she was a housework teacher at the same school. Cheongma instantly fell in love with her but, unfortunately, he was a married man who was nine years older than the Poet Lee. But, unable to hold his overflowing feelings for her, Cheongma went to a post office from which a handicraft shop where Poet Lee spent most of her time after work can be seen and started to write love letters. Though her heart had been locked away tightly at first, Poet Lee began to stagger at the rock-like persistence that Cheongma displayed. Thereafter, they exchanged over 5,000 love letters for 2 decades to share their platonic love, which ended abruptly in 1947 when Mr. Yu became 60 years old and passed away as a result of an accident.  The two individuals' love, years of repetition of writing precious, hard-thought words on paper, folding neatly in an envelope, firmly pressing down a stamp on the outside, sending it out and then waiting days in earnest. If you feel nostalgic for slow and hefty love during an age of quick and light encounters and breakups, how about sending out a postcard to someone today?

stories.title: 1. Jagalchi Market (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.audioTitle: 1. Jagalchi Market (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.script: What do you think Jagalchi means in Jagalchi Market? One might assume it's the name of a famous fish in Busan, like hairtail or sauries, but Jagalchi actually refers to the beach here, named for the large number of pebbles (jagal in Korean). The name is a blend of Jagal and Chi, the Chinese character for hill. Originally, this fishing village, where pebbles chattered along with the waves, was known as Nambin, meaning southern waterside. Interestingly, the land you're standing on was once the rippling sea, not the top of a pebble hill. Traces of the embankment, built to prevent seawater from flooding, can be found from BIFF Square, indicating extensive land reclamation.  In 1928, Japanese invaders reclaimed Nambin and established Namhang Port, named after Nampo-dong. The port facilitated frequent incoming and outgoing fishing boats, leading to the establishment of a fish market called Nambin Market. It primarily traded seafood, agricultural produce, and vegetables. Later, some merchants began selling small amounts of fish caught by small boats, marking the inception of the Jagalchi Ajimae. Following the Liberation and subsequent war, Busan's population nearly doubled. Facing financial constraints, many opted to start small seafood stands. The Busan Metropolitan City cracked down on these stands post-war. Despite this, the resilient Jagalchi Ajimae fiercely resisted. In one incident, an elderly woman, desperate about the situation, hugged a police officer, dragging both into the sea. Subsequently, Busan City abandoned restrictions on the Ajimaes, instead constructing a three-story building to house all the stands.  Officially, Jagalchi Market refers only to the glass building adorned with a structure resembling a flying seagull. However, locals consider all the old markets and stores, between the stock fish market near Yeongdodaegyo Bridge and the fish market in Chungmu-dong, as part of Jagalchi Market. This is because Jagalchi Market was a community-created space. It boasts over 300 fish types, including hairtail, mackerel, minke whales, great white sharks, and sunfish. You can glimpse into the lives of Busan's people here. Undoubtedly, Jagalchi Market reflects the map of Busan citizens’ lives.

stories.title: 2. History of BIFF Square (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.audioTitle: 2. History of BIFF Square (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.script: The Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has been a massive event since its establishment in 1996. It injected new energy not only into the struggling Korean film industry but also into the aging original city center of Busan. In fact, the current global festival's location in BIFF Square is not a coincidence. The history of Korean cinema surrounding Nampo-dong Street dates back nearly 100 years.  In 1903, the first Korean theater, “Haengjwa,” was built in the alley opposite the current hand printing street. Other theaters such as Ukgwan, Boraegwan, and Sangsaenggwan were established successively, following the triumph of Haengjwa. Since then, Nampo-dong Street became a hub for films. The reason theaters were concentrated in this area was the significant Japanese population that settled here since the establishment of Choryang-Waegwan in the 1600s. During the Japanese occupation period, these residents enjoyed extravagant lives using assets they had exploited from the Joseon people. This influx led Busan to build numerous early leisure facilities such as hot springs, theaters, golf courses, and race courses. Notably, film theaters were a necessity for the Japanese who founded a large film production company and collaborated with Western companies in the early 1900s.  The establishment of theaters was a significant catalyst for the Joseon people. Children raised in these theaters began producing their own films in the 1920s, leading to the founding of the Chosun Kinema Corporation in Busan. Na Un-kyu, a founder of Chosun Kinema and a pioneer of Joseon film, expressed a strong desire to produce films that conveyed Korean national thoughts and emotions. Chosun Kinema's inaugural film, “Sorrowful Song of the Sea,” found commercial success in Japan, leading to the production of three more films in its first year. However, discrimination by Japanese film distributors against Korean films forced Chosun Kinema to halt operations within a year. The spirit of these artists, however, became the cornerstone of Busan's present film industry.  The Nampo-dong Film Street existed until the 1990s but disappeared due to multiplex film theaters. With the establishment of the Cinema Center at Centum City in 2011, the public's enthusiasm for BIFF shifted. Nonetheless, the century-long presence of Korean films in this area will always be vividly remembered by the citizens of Busan.

stories.title: 3. Gukje Market (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.audioTitle: 3. Gukje Market (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.script: Would you believe that the vast Gukje Market emerged as a result of chance, stemming from a series of overlapping historic events? Since the mid-Joseon Dynasty, numerous Japanese immigrants resided in the Choryang-Waegwan area. Consequently, the region was densely populated with buildings during the Japanese occupation. As all these structures were made of wood, any fire outbreak quickly escalated into a large inferno. Before liberation, while the Allied Forces’ continuous attacks that inflicted significant damage, the Japanese imperialists left Lighting Street, currently named as such, vacant as a refuge area. This strategic measure aimed to contain any fire outbreak within this street and prevent it from spreading.  Following liberation, many Japanese gathered at the port to depart from Korea. Due to restrictions on the number of carry-on luggage, numerous sold their bags at scrap value, containing items collected over decades. Some bags contained not just expensive household goods but also valuable artworks and rare antique books. Setting up goods for sale in the vacant refuge area marked the inception of Guje Market. Locals often refer to Gukje Market as Doddegi Market, derived from the Japanese term “Dori,” meaning grab and take, illustrating the fierce competition among Joseon merchants striving to acquire Japanese items.  With the outbreak of the Korean War in 1950, a multitude of refugees fled to Busan, and the U.S. Army brought in an overflow of war supplies and munitions, significantly expanding Gukje Market. However, its success was short-lived as a massive fire in January 1953 reduced the entire market to ashes. A small bar fire engulfed over 4,000 stalls within 7 hours, resulting in a catastrophic event that caused 1.4 billion won in damages and nearly 10,000 victims. Amid Busan's mourning, General Whitcomb, commander of the U.S. Logistics Supply Base, brought hope and support. He erected tent villages for those who lost homes overnight, rebuilt schools and churches, and remained committed to safeguarding Busan's citizens throughout his life. Recovering from this tragedy, Gukje Market once again thrived until the 1990s, trading aid goods and contraband from America. It served as an all-in-one marketplace that met various life needs. Though the market's peak has passed, it retains its status as Busan's foremost traditional market.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 4. Bupyeong Kkangtong Market
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 4. Bupyeong Kkangtong Market
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 4. Bupyeong Kkangtong Market  Just across the street from Gukje Market, there exists another enormous market. It is rare to see two such large-sized markets right next to each other even when looking throughout the whole country. While Gukje Market was a market that came about by chance during a period of historic upheaval through Liberation and war, the Bupyeong Market had been a major marketplace in the area since the Joseon Dynasty.  After the port was opened to foreign trades, the Japanese came into this market that had been here since the days of Joseon and began to call it “Ilhan Market”. “Ilhan Market” opened everyday except for the first day of every month, and since during the time, a market that would open five-days a week was the norm, many Joseon people stood in lines to check out the first permanent market they had ever seen in their lives. Thanks to this Bupyeong Market was able to stably and also endured the troubled times of Liberation and the war in a relatively peaceful manner. It was definitely a different vibe from Gukje Market, which was also known as Doddegi Market with its many shabby stands. As the Joseon people took over the stores that had been abandoned by the Japanese, Bupyeong Market was reborn as a market of Joseon. This was also around about the time when “Busan Fish Cakes”, one of the most famous foods of Busan, was created. In 1910s, many stores that cook and sell fish cakes were set up here to respond to the needs of the increasing Japanese population. In one of the official records of the Japanese Government-General of Korea, it even describes how “rice, fish cakes, vegetables and fruits were primarily sold at Ilhan Market”. The fish cake alley in Bupyeong Market was also a natural outcome of merchants who had taken over stores from the Japanese after Liberation, while competitively developing their own recipes.  Bupyeong Market began to enjoy great prosperity when American soldiers replaced the fleeing Japanese. The name, Kkangtong Market, was coined around this time because the main goods sold and purchased then were canned foods that trickled out from the U.S. Army bases in the aftermath of the Korean War. Then, as those who had taken part in the Vietnam War brought and sold C-ration, a type of combat food of the U.S. Army, the name stuck for good. Another name for Bupyeong Market is Dokkaebi Market. Even after the Vietnam War, peddlers obtained foreign goods and sold them to the Bupyeong Kkangtong Market, however, the trading of items that had not gone through customs was not legal at all. So merchants would briefly unpack their bags of goods, and once the police showed up, quickly pack up everything and disappear. The nickname, Dokkaebi, stems from how they repeatedly appeared and disappeared.  During the days when supplies were nowhere near abundant, Bupyeong Kkangtong Market was a new world for the Busan people. There were no “foreign imports” that one could not buy at the market, from the latest electronic devices to liquor and cigarettes, and even cosmetics. The reputation of Bupyeong Kkangtong Market has slightly faded in an era where it is not so difficult to find foreign products or travel overseas, but for tourists, the market still offers a variety of things to see.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 5. Bosu-dong Book Street
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 5. Bosu-dong Book Street
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 5. Bosu-dong Book Street  “The very first to start here was Mr. Son Jeong-rin who fled from the North and built a shack over there on the hillside slums. He had to feed himself so he put everything he had brought from his hometown up for sale. The first things to sell were books. Why? It was because there were many schools in Daesin-dong on this street and a lot of students at the time did not have enough money so they walked instead of taking the tram. And this was on their way to school and many of them would be around the area in the mornings and evenings so books were the first to sell. That's when he realized that he should become a bookseller. I asked him about 2 or 3 years later. I was studying under adversity and I wanted to make a living out of something so I asked, Can I do this, too? and he said yes. So, I put a box out here and bought books from him to sell them myself.”  This is the story of Mr. Kim Yeo-man, a first generation Bosu-dong resident who still runs his bookstore to this day since it first opened in 1953. During the days when everyone was facing tough times, there were not a lot of books being published so students had a hard time finding books even though they wanted to study. Students were grateful if they could even get a hold of used books. A few refugees who had realized the circumstances opened up street stalls for used books, and Bosu-dong thrived as the number of stalls grew from 6 to 7 in the beginning to over a few dozen in just a couple years. One of the more popular items here were English magazines and other foreign books, which had mostly been left behind by U.S. troops who frequently traveled to and from the Busan Port. They were collected by the booksellers and resold to refugee intellectuals. There were also those who made great profit by selling antique books that they had purchased inexpensively without much thought from the Japanese after Liberation. Merchants who secured seed money from their stall operations opened stores and officially launched the used books business, which has become the Book Street that we see today. When a frequent customer orders a book he or she needs, the bookseller finds and secures it from another used book street in Cheonggyecheon, Seoul or near Daegu City Hall, and makes a trip around the country once a month to transport the books before delivering it to the customer. At the time, books in specialized fields such as law or engineering had a waiting period of about 1 to 2 months. Refugees or students facing hard times would sell relatively high-priced books among the ones they owned and then buy the other used books that they needed. In the 60s and 70s when there were over 70 bookstores, Bosu-dong street was always crowded especially before the start of new semesters with people carrying around bags of books, looking to buy and sell textbooks and reference materials.  “A bookstore is innocent. 90% of those who come to buy a book are good people. When you talk to them, there is a lot of things you can learn. There are no better teachers. Everyone who comes to buy a book is a teacher. I have lived my whole life in gratitude.” In an era where online bookstores dominate the publishing world, these words of an old bookstore owner who still protects a corner of the alley seem to symbolize the unchanging value of the Bosu-dong Book Street.

stories.title: Busan Modern History Museum
stories.script: Built in 1929 during the Japanese colonial period, it is the history museum where you can see the modern history of Busan. In the beginning, it was used as the Busan Branch of Oriental Colonization Company, an agency responsible for exploiting colonies, but after the Liberation, it started to serve as Busan Cultural Center for the United States Information Service in 1949. However, due to ceaseless demands from Busan citizens for its return, the American cultural center left the building in the end. It was returned to the Korean government in 1999 before the city of Busan took it over in June of the same year. As it was a symbol of invasion and exploitation, the building became the Busan Modern History Museum to be able to utilize it for education to teach the citizens on our painful history. The museum opened on July 3, 2003. The exhibition hall has a map that shows the opening and reclamation of Busan Port with modern stories of the city through various videos. Busan Modern History Museum tells us a lot of interesting stories about the city's modern history.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 7. Daegagsa Temple
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 7. Daegagsa Temple
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 7. Daegagsa Temple  The sign that says, 〈Daegagsa〉, seems out of the ordinary as it is seated unawkwardly amidst the signs of stores lined up in disarray. Upon pokin your head just a little bit into the main gate, you cannot help but make eye contact with the Buddha who is lying down in front of Daeungjeon Hall, gazing at the bustling city with a subdued smile. Then, you will grow curious about the story behind this temple that stands in the middle of the original city center as if it owns the area. On the land, where Daegagsa sits today, was an official residence where Japanese delegations, that frequently visited Busan to conduct trades with Joseon, had stayed for over 200 years since the 17th century, the period when Choryang-Waegwan was established. As the number of Japanese immigrants to Busan grew after the port opened, one facility after another began to be built for the newer members of the community, and temples were one of them. Originally called Dongbonwonsa Busanbyeolwon, which was established in 1877 by renting out a dormitory within the Waegwan, the temple then became the first Japanese-style Buddhist temple of the Korean Peninsula.  Although it initially started as a temple house for the Japanese, it soon became an outpost of modernization for Joseon. In the late Joseon Dynasty, Heungseon Daewongun implemented the policy of refusing to form diplomatic ties with foreign countries, however, within the Joseon society, many were already beginning to think that they must open up the gates and accept Western culture. People who aimed to implement this thinking into action were called the GaeHwa-Pa and, among them, radical members such as Kim Ok-gyun, Park Yung-hyo, Yun Chi-ho and Seo Jae-pil promoted active exchanges with Japan. And Daegagsa served a pivotal role during this period. In particular, Yi Dong-in, a Buddhist monk, known as a pioneer of the GaeHwa-Pa, smuggled himself through this place into Japan and stayed in Kyoto for about 10 months to survey the Japanese society. When he came back to Korea, he helped the young men of the GaeHwa-Pa to travel to and from Japan to set up a foundation for autonomous enlightenment, and, after Liberation, Dongbonwonsa Busanbyeolwon was reconstructed as a Korean Buddhist temple and renamed to “Daegagsa”. Just as the Choryang Presbyterian Church was support on which Christian refugees could lean on during the war, Daegagsa faithfully served as the bastion for Buddhism in the provisional capital. This is why, towards the end of the war, important Buddhist organizations such as the Headquarters of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism and Dongguk University came to establish their bases in this area.  Once you step into Daeungjeon of Daegagsa, you encounter an unfamiliar scene in which exotic-looking statues of Buddha completely fill one side of the wall before a broad and open Buddhist sanctuary with no pillars, which is why it is often misunderstood that this place is exactly how it used to be when it was the old Japanese temple house. Actually, the sanctuary and the house for monks at the time all burned to ashes during the war, and the buildings we see today are those that were newly constructed in 1969. From a temple house built by advanced architectural techniques to unique Buddha statues delicately enshrined, different and novel things come together to form perfect harmony at Daegagsa, and we may cautiously presume that the present of Daegagsa is deeply rooted in the spirit of enlightenment, fearless for the unknown, from the Joseon Period.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 8. Gwangbok-ro Fashion Street
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 8. Gwangbok-ro Fashion Street
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 8. Gwangbok-ro Fashion Street  What attracts people to this street, which would thrive even when put up against the likes of Myeongdong in Seoul, is perhaps the stores that tightly populate the street. This particular area on Gwangbok-ro was known as the Fashion Street because these stores led the trends of not just Busan but the entire country during the 80s.  But it was actually long before that when this area first began to be crowd with people looking to buy and sell goods. The history of commerce on Gwangbok-ro started along with the installation of Waegwan in the late Joseon Dynasty. Joseon people were not allowed to enter Waegwan, which was a Japanese-only residence, and even the Japanese could not travel beyond certain limits. That is why the markets, near the three gates into Waegwan, that sold fresh vegetables, fruits and fish to the Japanese prospered. As the Japanese population grew even more after opening the port, development of the commercial district of Gwangbok-ro took off. By the Japanese occupation era, many restaurants, movie theaters and department stores were established so the area began to be known as “Jangsutong”, which means “Prospering”. Two-story store buildings began to populate either side of the street and an increasing amount of energy came about every day to the point where it was nicknamed Byeoncheonjeong, which stood for “the look of the sky has changed”. In 1902, street lamps were lit on this street for the first time in Busan to be able to set up a night market, enabling the street to gain extreme popularity as one of the leading commercial districts within the city.  The Gwangbok-ro shopping district continued to maintain its fervor even after Liberation, and Mihwadang Department Store, established in 1949, was at the center of it all. It was the first-ever department store in Busan and the second in the country, behind Seoul's Hwasin Department Store, built by our own national capital. The concrete annex building constructed in 1956 was not only the tallest building in Busan at the time but also an advanced structure with elevators and escalators. In particular, the pedestrian overpass leading from the roof of the annex to Yongdusan Park made a name for itself as a romantic date hot spot for young lovers. Thanks to its reputation, Mihwadang was considered as a place of gathering amongst Busan people. Everyone from Busan probably has fond memories of briskly walking along Gwangbok-ro towards the main entrance of the department store, filled with excited anticipation of seeing a friendly face.  Where the people gathered, so gathered tea houses on the streets. Gwangbok-ro especially featured many music cafes. It was a natural outcome of cultural artists, who had fled to Busan due to the war, gathering in cafes at Gwangbok-ro. Here, the artists transcended the pain of our history into literary, artistic, and musical works to motivate themselves to carry on. A novel by Kim Dong-ri written in the setting of “Mildawon”, a cafe on Gwangbok-ro, depicts a writer who refuses a comfortable bed and instead takes naps in a corner spot of the cafe. Through a confession stating, “I can't stand not being in the midst of our crowd of refugees,” we are given a glimpse of an artist's conscience in desiring to be with history and destiny. As a result, the Nampo-dong area became the mecca of Busan culture teemed with musical halls and movie theaters until the 70s. Today, many of the traces from those times have disappeared but the dignity of the original city center, built by a long history, can be felt anywhere.

stories.title: 9. Yongdusan Park (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.audioTitle: 9. Yongdusan Park (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.script: Yongdusan Park, a mountain situated at the center of Busan since the late Joseon Dynasty's Waegwan period, was historically envisioned as a traditional park rather than an antique landmark. However, the lack of historical traces today can be attributed to a story that sheds light on this absence.  Legend has it that Yongdusan was once known as Songhyeonsan due to its densely wooded pine trees. It was later renamed by the Japanese during the Waegwan period, who perceived the mountain's shape resembling the head of a dragon rising above the sea. Additionally, Yongmisan, symbolizing the dragon's tail, once stood at the present location of the Lotte Department Store. Three shrines were erected after Japanese housing settlements were established. Two shrines were situated in Yongdusan, while one was located in Yongmisan. The shrines in Yongdusan closely resembled traditional temple houses and served as places of prayer for fishermen's safety and prosperity. Conversely, the Yongmisan shrine historically enshrined military officials who invaded the Korean Peninsula.  In 1934, Yongmisan was razed, making way for the construction of the Busan government office. The shrine from Yongmisan merged with the shrine on Yongdusan, eventually becoming a symbol of Japanese imperial spirit, adorned with 102 Japanese national flags. Since 1935, Koreans were coerced by the Japanese to visit the shrine, facing humiliation as they had to bow to Yongdusan even when riding the tram.  Post-liberation, Koreans burnt most of the shrines, which had been constant reminders of their suppression. The peninsula was engulfed in the chaos of war, deflecting attention from discussions about rebuilding the site previously tainted by Japanese imperialism. During this period, Yongdusan provided refuge to displaced people. However, a massive fire in 1954 destroyed the village huts. To honor the souls lost in the fire, Buddhist monks constructed Jeongsusa, a small temple within the park. A stone tablet called 'Suhwayebangbi' along the east entry path bears fire and water Chinese characters, symbolizing Yongdusan's enduring position as a spiritual center for the citizens of Busan.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 10. Gwangbok-ro (Gwangbok Rest Area)
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 10. Gwangbok-ro (Gwangbok Rest Area)
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 10. Gwangbok-ro (Gwangbok Rest Area)  Until about a century ago, Gwangbok-ro was a small stream of water, not a land on which people and cars would come and go. Spring water from Yongdusan would pass through today's Busan Modern History Museum and Daegagsa Temple then flow along Gwangbok-ro before entering the sea by the entrance of Yeongdodaegyo. This used to be called “Soljaenae”, which means a stream that flows down from a pine tree hill, and when Choryang-Waegwan was established here in 1678, Japanese immigrants planted cherry trees along the water so its name changed to “Aengcheon”. “Waegwan” refers to an official residence built by Japanese who frequented Joseon for diplomatic and trading related activities, and Choryang-Waegwan occupied up to 100,000 pyeong of land left and right of Yongdusan Park. The Japanese were zealous about installing Waegwans due to Korean teacups. The Japanese monks who had studied abroad in Tang brought the tea culture of China with them, which led to increased demands in teacups. The monks valued meditation and naturally became captivated by Joseon's teacups that were calm and appeared to be empty. At the time, Japan did not have the adequate skills to produce such products. The Japanese who moved to Joseon started to build kilns and brought potters from all over the country to make teacups. Busanyo located below Yongdusan Park was installed around this period as well. The Japanese’ exploitation of pottery finally ended when the entire Gyeongnam region ran out of earth.  A rapid increase of the Japanese population within the area was the reason that Aengcheon began to lose its clear appearance. After the ports opened, the Waegwan turns into a Japanese Concession or a special economic zone in which Japanese people were free to trade in. Harboring unethical intentions of invading China through Joseon, Japan continued to expand the concession thus the Japanese population grew to 10,000. In a letter written by a Westerner who visited Busan in the late 19th century, he writes, “In every aspect, Busan's residences are of a Japanese style. In addition to 5,508 Japanese living here, over 8,000 Japanese fishermen would come and go. The consulate general of Japan resides in a fancy European house. Services of Tokyo's Dai-Ichi Bank would be provided and even postal as well as telegraph services were also dominated by the Japanese...” As you can see, the Gwangbok-dong area was already exhibiting the appearance of an exotic and contemporary city where it was not difficult to see foreigners. Eventually, the odor filled stream of Aengcheon was covered as is today.  After the Liberation, Aengcheon looks after the Busan citizens in their daily lives with a new name, “Gwangbok-ro” in commemoration of that overwhelming moment.

stories.title: 2.1 Today’s BIFF Square (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.audioTitle: 2.1 Today’s BIFF Square (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.script: BIFF Plaza, a cultural complex area  The Busan International Film Festival Square (BIFF Square) was established when the festival was held in 1996. It is located between the Jagalchi Market and Gukje Market, attracting a great number of tourists to pass through. It has been transformed into a cultural tourist attraction to promote the advancement of Korea’s film industry.  Back to the early years of BIFF, films were screened in the theaters of Nampo-dong. However, since the opening of the Busan Cinema Center, most of the film festival events have relocated to the Haeundae area. The Busan Cinema Center has evolved beyond just a venue to watch films, it has become into a cultural complex where visitors can enjoy shopping and entertainment at the same time. In addition, numerous street snack stalls can be found in the BIFF Square, offering popular street food such as Ssiat Hotteok, the griddle cake with sugar and seeds filling; and Dakkochi, the Korean Chicken Skewer. These offerings attract more young people to gather in this place, helping revitalize the area.

stories.title: Overview of Changdeokgung Palace
stories.script: Changdeokgung Palace was the second palace built in the Joseon Dynasty after Gyeongbokgung Palace. It is located at the foot of Eungbongsan Mountain, which is on the left of Bugaksan Mountain. It was also built on the east side of Gyeongbokgung Palace.
