By the way, this tomb looks somewhat unique.”  [Villager 1] They say it is a combination of northern and southern styles to suggest the permission for their marriage after her death.”  [Villager 2] “I knew there was something about the dolmen. That's why the dolmen is built like that.”

stories.title: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 2
stories.audioTitle: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 2 고창 고인돌 유적 제 2코스
stories.script: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 2   [Teacher] “Everyone! Attention! We are now near the entrance of the Gochang Dolmen Site Course 2.”  [Student] Is course 2 long?  [Teacher] The second course is about 276 meters long. There are 41 dolmens located in course 2.”  [Student] 41? That's less than course 1.  [Teacher] It is indeed less than course one, but there is still a lot to see here. There are go-board dolmens, pad-stone dolmens, a semi-exposed dolmen, nine dolmens of unknown styles, and five traces of dolmens.   [Student] What's the go-board dolmen? Sir?”  [Teacher] Go-board dolmens are also known as based dolmens. Go-board dolmens have a burial chamber built underground made of flagstones or broken and natural stones, and 4-8 supporting stones are erected around them with a large capstone placed on top.”  [Student] What about the pad-stone dolmens?“  [Teacher] “The pad-stone dolmens have a capstone placed right above the burial chamber built underground. The pad-stone dolmens that cover their burial chambers without any supporting stones are alternatively referred to as no-support, lid, or footstone dolmens. In this style, a burial chamber made of stone is almost always found. Those dolmens were originally built to serve as tombs.   [Student] What is the semi-exposed dolmen?  [Teacher] The semi-exposed dolmen is a type of table dolmen, and it used several pieces of flagstones to build a burial chamber. As its burial chamber is half underground, this dolmen has both the characteristics of table dolmens and go-board dolmens.”  [Student] Oh, I see.  [Teacher] You have half an hour to take a look around course 2. Let’s meet up at course 3 afterwards!”  [Student] “Alright.”  [Man] Located on the second course of the Gochang Dolmen Site, dolmen No. 2019 is a representative dolmen that displays the semi-exposed style. The propping stones, also known as supporting stones of rectangular shape, and flagstones or small broken stones are used to build a stone coffin above the ground. The capstone is not a heavy rectangular shape, but rather a disk shape, and its overall shape is completely different from that of go-board dolmens.  [Woman] Among the go-board dolmens, dolmen No. 2406, estimated to weigh between 120 and 150 tons, is built as an altar on its own or as a monument symbolizing the graveyard, maintaining a certain distance from the dolmen graveyard. A society building dolmens needed symbolic monuments to strengthen the cooperation and solidarity of different groups. A dolmen with a huge capstone was a very symbolic monument.  [Man] Dolmens No. 2419 and No. 2433, which were damaged by Typhoon Rusa in 2003, were excavated prior to their restoration according to plan, and the excavation found 55 pieces of undecorated pottery and a piece of burnished red pottery. During this process, a burial chamber was found about 8 m away from No. 2433, where one complete clay striped pottery item was excavated.   [Woman] The large dolmens were landmarks of the graveyard, indicating the sacred space of the community that built them, as they were visible from a distance due to their large size, as well as the symbol displaying the collective power of the community.

stories.title: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 3
stories.audioTitle: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 3 고창 고인돌 유적 제 3코스
stories.script: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 3   [Tourist] Is this the third course of the Gochang Dolmen Site?  [Guide] Gochang Dolmen Site Course 3 is located at the center of the dolmen site in Gochang, in the valley running down from the mountain range between Seongteulbong Peak and Jungbong Peak. The dolmens are located along the gently sloped ridge of Juklim-ri.  [Tourist] How many dolmens are here?  [Guide] There are a total of 128 dolmens located on the third course, including 36 go-board dolmens, 2 semi-exposed dolmens, 49 pad-stone dolmens, and 41 dolmens of unknown styles. As the capstones, propping stones, and piles of stones with destroyed and moved propping stones are also found here, it is believed that there were once even more dolmens here.  [Tourist] What is the difference between a go-board dolmen, semi-exposed dolmen, and pad-stone dolmen?  [Guide] “Go-board dolmens have a burial chamber built underground made of flagstones or broken and natural stones, and 4 to 8 supporting stones are erected around them with a large capstone placed on top. They are called go-board dolmens because they resemble a go-board.  The semi-exposed dolmens are only found in Juklim-ri, Gochang, so they are also called Gochang-style dolmens. Like a table dolmen, a burial chamber was built using several flagstones. The burial chamber is slightly of semi-underground form and has a thick capstone. This dolmen has the characteristics of a table dolmen, while at the same time it displays the characteristics of propping stones that are found in go-board dolmens.   The pad-stone dolmens have a capstone placed right above the burial chamber built underground. The pad-stone dolmens that cover their burial chambers without any supporting stones are alternatively referred to as no-support, lid, or footstone dolmens. In this type, a stone burial chamber is almost always found, indicating that they were originally intended to serve as tombs. As they are widely distributed in the Liaoning Peninsula, the Korean Peninsula, and Kyushu, Japan, they are the most common type of tombs among the dolmen types.”  [Tourist] What are the characteristics of course 3?  [Guide] The course features dolmens with column-shaped propping stones, and above all, unique-shaped dolmens tilted at an angle are clustered in open spaces along the ridge.    [Woman] In course 3, there are dolmens that remain well-preserved and elegant, while some dolmens with heavy roof shapes and naturally cut stone surfaces are located to display the formativeness of their kind. The site gives you the chance to enjoy dolmens of various shapes in a large space.

stories.title: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 4
stories.audioTitle: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 4 고창 고인돌 유적 제 4코스
stories.script: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 4   [Guide] This is the Gochang Dolmen Site Course 4, where a quarry is located.  [Tourist] A quarry? Do you need a quarry to build dolmens? Aren't you suppose to build one out of rocks that exist naturally?  [Guide] The most important part of a dolmen is the capstone. There is also an example of a capstone being obtained from naturally existing rock. However, it was very difficult to find stones to be used for capstones from among natural rocks. That is why people mined stones from a quarry to build dolmens.   [Tourist] It's very interesting to know that people had stone-cutting techniques at that time. How did the people at that time remove the stone?  [Guide] There were three or so ways to remove the stone. First, find a suitable stone and drill a small hole in it at intervals of 10 to 15 cm. The first method was to drive a wedge into the hole and continue to hammer it down, while the second method was to drive wood into the wedge hole then pour water into it to remove it using the tension of the wood. Third, pour water into the wedge hole and wait for the water to freeze. Once the water freezes and its volume increases, cracks are created in the stone.  [Tourist] The technology sounds amazing.  [Guide] That's right. Our ancestors were quite wise. It has been found that the main ingredients of the capstones for dolmens in Gochang match those in the quarry on course 4. What we can see from this is that most of the stones at the dolmen site in Gochang were quarried here.  [Man] Traces of stones quarried were found in 23 places around Seongteulbong Peak and Jungbong Peak, the mountains behind where the dolmens are located. Fifteen sites were found around the summit of Seongteulbong Peak and eight around Jungbong Peak, and it has been shown that they are clustered mainly on the ridges, covering a wide range. You can find the quarry at the K point by following the sign to the north, which shows “To the quarry for dolmens” behind course 3. It is located between 80 and 85 meters above sea level.  [Woman] The traces of stones falling from the rough stone are usually clearly displayed on the front, the V-shaped groove was made lengthwise on the joint plane of the rough stone, and a wedge was inserted into the point plane and its top was struck to remove it. There remain traces of wedge holes in the rough stone, and rocks that fell from the rough stone and rolled down remain in the surrounding area.  [Man] The dolmen distribution on course 4 consists of the section covering the area from the western end of the triangular valley field on course 3 to Sanggap-ri. A total of 41 dolmens have been discovered, including 10 go-board dolmens, 26 pad-stone dolmens, and 5 dolmens of unknown styles at the foot of the mountain running from Seongteulbong Peak and on the flat ground.  [Woman] Go-board dolmens, also known as foundation dolmens, have a burial chamber underground, and four to eight supporting stones are placed around it, with a large capstone placed on top of them. Their characteristic is their grand appearance as they are raised above the ground's surface.   [Man] The pad-stone dolmens have a capstone placed right above the burial chamber built underground. The pad-stone dolmens that cover their burial chambers without any supporting stones are alternatively referred to as no-support, lid, or footstone dolmens. In this type, a stone burial chamber is almost always found, indicating that they were originally intended to serve as tombs. The capstone is thin in the north, but in the south it tends to be thicker.

stories.title: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 5
stories.audioTitle: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 5 고창 고인돌 유적 제 5코스
stories.script: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 5   [Guide] The 5th course of the Gochang Dolmen Site is located on the southern slope of Seongteulbong Peak, adjacent to Gochangcheon Stream. There are 220 dolmens at the foot of a mountain that runs about 900 meters along Gochang Stream.  [Student] There are 220 dolmens here? That's a lot. By the way, what kind of dolmens are there?”  [Guide] The dolmens on Gochang Dolmen Site Course 5 are divided into four clusters, consisting of 135 go-board dolmens, 25 semi-exposed dolmens, and 60 dolmens of unknown styles.   [Student] Can you tell us the type and characteristics of each dolmen?”  [Guide] Yes, certainly. First of all, go-board dolmens are also known as foundation dolmens. Go-board dolmens have a burial chamber built underground made of flag stones or broken and natural stones, and 4 to 8 supporting stones are erected around them with a large capstone placed on top. These dolmens, which look grand as they are raised above the surface, have large capstones, and some of them are large with oddly-shaped stones, many of which do not have distinct burial chambers.  The semi-exposed dolmen is a type of table dolmen, and it used several pieces of flagstones to build a burial chamber. The burial chamber is of a slightly semi-underground form and has a thick capstone. The unique feature of these dolmens is that they belong to the table dolmens, while they have propping stones that are found on go-board dolmens.  [Student] What are the characteristics of the dolmen site course 5?  [Guide] The most distinctive characteristic of course 5 is that there are four clusters covering the area of about 800 meters, and each cluster has a series of dolmens in a line. It also features over 2 to 3 large dolmens of various shapes by cluster, and a significant number of modified table dolmens like semi-exposed dolmens are located here.   [Man] Large dolmens are built in the best locations of each cluster, such as No. 1117 in the first cluster, No. 1239 in the second cluster, and No. 1321 in the third cluster. Among them, No. 1321 is estimated to weigh about 100 tons, and it is believed to have served as an altar to mark the graveyard, as it is located independently on relatively high land.   [Woman] Given that the dolmens on course 5 are formed in groups, and most of them appear in rows, it is sometimes regarded as a cemetery for a group based on blood ties or as a graveyard for a ruling group.

stories.title: Gochang Jungnim Prehistoric Village
stories.audioTitle: Gochang Jungnim Prehistoric Village 고창 죽림 선사마을
stories.script: Gochang Jungnim Prehistoric Village   [Student] Hello.  [Staff] “Hello. What can I do for you?  [Student] What kind of place is Gochang Jungnim Prehistoric Village?  [Staff] Gochang Jungnim Prehistoric Village is an outdoor experience center built between the Gochang Dolmen Museum and the dolmen site course 3, allowing visitors to closely examine the lifestyles of the Bronze Age.”  [Student] How big is the Prehistoric Village?  [Staff] The Gochang Jungnim Prehistoric Village was built on 28,000 square meters of land.     It has an experience hall, an experience center, seven pit dwellings, and eight experience spaces.”  [Student] What can we experience in the Prehistoric Village?  [Staff] The experience programs of the Jungnim Prehistoric Village are largely divided into free and paid programs. You can experience the goblin needle experience, hunting experience, watchtower experience, cattle pen experience, fire-making experience, pit-dwelling experience, pitch-pot games, metal inscription experience, and chilgyo gonu games for free.  [Student] What kind of paid programs do you have?  [Staff] Paid programs include making semicircular stone knives, making stone arrowheads, making pottery, making 3D paper pit-dwellings, and making moromoro mobile phone rings.”  [Student] What is a semicircular stone knife?”  [Staff] A semicircular stone knife is a harvesting tool used for cutting off grain ears, and it is characterized by its half-circle shape. At first it was used as a harvesting tool for various grains, but during the mid-Bronze Age, triangular stone knives appeared for rice farming.  [Student] So the semicircular stone knife was a farming tool?”  [Staff] Yes, you could say that. However, it wasn't just used as a farming tool. There is a view that the semicircular stone knife was used not only for livelihood but also for ceremonial purposes. For example, it has been found in a broken state around tombs. This is regarded as evidence demonstrating its burial after intentionally breaking it, rather than it simply being broken during use.   [Student] Could you tell us the operating hours of the experience center?”  [Staff] The outdoor experience center of Jungnim Prehistoric Village is open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and it is closed every Monday and on January 1st each year.

stories.title: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 6
stories.audioTitle: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 6 고창 고인돌 유적 제 6코스
stories.script: Gochang Dolmen Site Course 6   [Man] Dosan-ri dolmens are known as dolmens in Dosan Village, 1 km away from the Gochang Dolmen Museum. A total of five dolmens, including one table dolmen, two go-board dolmens, and two pad-stone dolmens, are located on the hill 43 meters above sea level, and they have been designated as Historic Site No. 391 along with the dolmen cluster in Juklim-ri.  [Woman] The table dolmens have a burial chamber made of 4 or 6 wide flagstones that are exposed above the ground with a flat capstone placed on top of the burial chamber, and they are called table dolmens as they resemble a table. They are mainly distributed north of the Han River and in the Liaoning region of China.  [Man] Go-board dolmens have a burial chamber underground, with four to eight supporting stones placed around the chamber and a large capstone on top. They are called go-board dolmens because they are similar in shape to a go-board.  [Woman] The pad-stone dolmens have a burial chamber underground and a large capstone placed on top to cover the chamber. The pad-stone dolmens are alternatively referred to as no-support, lid, or footstone dolmens. In this style, a burial chamber made of stone is almost always found. The dolmens were built to serve as tombs.  [Man] Dosan-ri dolmen are also known as Jangdokdae dolmen because they have been preserved in the Jangdokdae of a private house. The capstone, which is 350 cm long, 310 cm wide, and 38 cm thick, and two propping stones, or so-called supporting stones, are used. On the side of the capstone, there is a groove mark for securing the rope for moving the stone, and between the supporting stones and the capstone, a wedge stone measuring about 20 cm in length is used, while the gaps are filled with earth.  [Woman] The table dolmens on course 6 are called Mangbukdan or Mangbukdae, which dates back to the time of the Qing invasion of Joseon.   [Song Gisang] We will fight against the Qing Dynasty. How can we stand idly by while our country is in danger? Let's fight for our country! Let's show the spirit of Koreans to the Qing Dynasty!!”  [Woman] When the Qing invasion of Joseon broke out, Song Gisang raised an army in the cause of justice. They then marched toward the north.  [Soldier] “My Lord!! Sir!!!”  [Song Gisang] What is the matter? Why are you in such a hurry?”  [Soldier] My... Lord! Joseon and the Qing Dynasty have signed a peace treaty. But... it was a very humiliating arrangement for us...  [Song Gisang] “Wh... what...?”  [Woman] Upon hearing the news, Song Gisang returned to his village and spent his entire life wailing towards the north where the king was, in front of the dolmen.   [Villager 1] My goodness. Song Gisang is wailing in the direction of the king’s palace again.   [Song Gisang] Your Highness!!! This cannot be!!!”  [Villager 1] “With him wailing like that every day, I'm worried about his health.

stories.title: What is dolmen?
stories.script: What is dolmen?  [Teacher] There are stone statues and tombs made of large, heavy, sturdy rocks in the world. Examples include the pyramids, which are large tombs in Egypt, Stonehenge, the mysterious megalithic monument in England, and the Moai statues, the huge face sculptures on Easter Island. It is called megalithic culture.  [Student] Is there also megalithic culture in Korea?  [Teacher] “Of course there is.”  [Student] What is it?  [Teacher] The representative megalithic culture of Korea would be the dolmens. “  [Student] The dolmen was part of the megalithic culture?  [Teacher] Most of the dolmens are prehistoric tombs with a large stone placed above a burial chamber made on the ground or underground. The dolmens are also called Jiseokmyo, which are made of a flat stone or an oddly shaped stone with supporting stones placed underneath.  [Student] Sir, dolmens aren't only found in Korea, are they?”  [Teacher] Starting from northern Europe, the dolmens are concentrated in the United Kingdom in Western Europe, throughout France, Switzerland, and the Iberian Peninsula, then in the northern part of the Mediterranean sea, the Middle East, India and Southeast Asia, and in China's Fujian, Zhejiang Province, Shandong Province, Liaodong Peninsula, the southern part of Jilin Province, the entire Korean Peninsula, and in Kyushu, Japan.   [Man] Dolmens were generally built on plateaus around a river basin and on low hills. Dolmens are more frequently distributed in slightly higher plains near mountains and hills and coastal areas than in large plains. In the river basin, they are largely placed to match the direction that the stream flows, mainly because the human dwellings primarily developed in those areas. The reason that there are no dolmens in the vast plains is that most of them were there before the areas were developed, and those areas were not used for human living. It is highly likely that the residential areas, farmland, and tombs were built here, as the plateau or a slightly higher hill was located at the foot of a sunny mountain, thus making it easy to get water and firewood for living while the hunting ground also remained close. It was because it was highly accessible.  [Woman] The dolmens are alternatively referred to as Dokbaegi, Baubaegi, or Dokbau, as they have natural stones buried underground, while go-board dolmens are alternatively called Gwanbau or Amdakbau. They may also be called Baebau, Geobukbau, Duggeobibau, or Gaeguribau depending on the shape of their capstones. A dolmen was also called Chilseongbau due to its shape of arrangement in connection with folk beliefs, or Janggunbau in a belief that a Janggun, meaning army general in Korean, moved the stones but then stopped. The names of the villages are sometimes related to dolmens, such as Juam, which resembles Baebawi Rock, Guam, meaning turtle rock, and Chilam, which means chilseong rock.

stories.title: Types of dolmens
stories.script: Types of dolmens  [Man] Dolmens are different from ordinary tombs because they are made with huge rocks erected above the ground. Their simple structure allows detailed insight. The dolmens are classified into table dolmens, go-board dolmens, pad-stone dolmens, semi-exposed dolmens, and exposed dolmens.  [Woman] The table dolmens have a burial chamber made with 4 or 6 wide flagstones that are exposed above the ground, with a flat capstone placed on top of the burial chamber. They are called table dolmens because they resemble a table. They are mainly located in the northern part of the Korean Peninsula and the Liaoning area of China, and thus they used to be called the northern style. Among the table dolmens, the large ones are estimated to have been built mainly as altars or monuments. Among these dolmens, the super-large dolmens, which are more than 8 meters long, 5 meters wide, and 2 meters high, are usually found in the Liaodong Peninsula and the Daedonggang River basin in Korea, and only one is built on each hillside or mountainside.   [Man] Go-board dolmens have a burial chamber built underground made of flagstones or broken and natural stones, and 4 to 8 supporting stones are erected around them with a large capstone placed on top. This is called a go-board dolmen because it resembles a go board. The go-board dolmens, which look magnificent as they are raised above the surface, are often devoid of distinct burial chambers. A large dolmen usually exists at the foot of a mountain, hill, or flat area at the end of a valley, but in a cluster of dolmens, it is located at the center or in an independent location.  [Woman] The pad-stone dolmens have a burial chamber with a lid right above the top. Since there are no propping stones, the pad-stone dolmens are alternatively referred to as no-support, lid, or footstone dolmens. For this type, a stone burial chamber is almost always found, indicating that they were originally intended to serve as tombs. Being widely distributed in the Liaoning Peninsula, the Korean Peninsula, and Kyushu, Japan, they are the most common type of tombs among the dolmen types. The capstone is thin in the north, but in the south it tends to be thicker. Most of the artifacts excavated from dolmens were also found in this type.  [Man] Semi-exposed dolmens have a structure like a stone coffin on the ground with a flagstone that is lower than the typical table-style flagstone or that has multiple overlapping flagstones. On the outer covering, the remaining styles are those with propping stones erected to match the height of the flagstone; with only the flagstone part without any propping stones; and with all propping stones missing. The burial chamber is also located either on the ground and in the semi-basement, and it is difficult to spot the location of the burial chamber without checking each and every part.  [Woman] The exposed dolmens are also called Jeju-style dolmens. The burial chamber is exposed to the ground, and multiple flagstones are erected along the edge of the capstone. The number of flagstones exposed to the ground amounts to six or more, forming a burial chamber similar to the flat shape of the capstone, while the burial chamber is usually shaped like an oval or square. The exposed dolmen is a unique type of dolmen only found on Jeju Island in Korea. Similar burial chamber structures have also been found in Zhejiang Province, China.

stories.title: Functions of dolmens
stories.script: Functions of dolmens   [Man] The dolmen, part of megalithic culture, has three key functions. First, the dolmen, a prehistoric tomb with a huge capstone placed above the ground or an underground burial chamber, serves as a tomb.   [Woman] In 1962, the National Museum of Korea conducted two excavations of dolmens in Hwangseok-ri of Chungcheongbuk-do.  [Archaeologist 1] “Huh? What are these?”  [Archaeologist 2] “What? What's going on?”  [Archaeologist 1] “Sir, I think you should see this. Please take a look.” What...? Is this what I think it is? It looks like a human bone, doesn't it?  [Archaeologist 2] “Yes! That's right. This is indeed a human bone.”  [Archaeologist 1] “Then it must have been a tomb.”  [Woman] Among them, a human bone of a [male] adult was found in its complete form, and its function as a tomb was reported to the academic world. Although no human bones have been discovered in Jeollanam-do, it is assumed to have served as a tomb given the size of the burial chamber inside the dolmen. The evidence demonstrating its use as a tomb is that dolmens are distributed in groups at each location, that human bones have been found, and that grave items buried during the construction of the tomb have been discovered.   [Man] Second, the dolmen served as an altar. The dolmens that have the characteristics of an altar have three different conditions from dolmens that served as tombs because they were the venue for religious events or ceremonies. First, each of these dolmens stands independently, maintaining a certain distance from the cluster. Second, it is supported by a large oddly-shaped stone capstone and large propping stones which show distinct size and appearance from other dolmens. Third, it is located on high ground overlooking the surrounding area. Based on the combination of these factors, it is assumed that such dolmens served as altars rather than tombs. A society building dolmens needed symbolic monuments to strengthen the cooperation and solidarity of different groups. It is thus estimated that dolmens were built and used as altars.  [Tribe member 1] “Move the stones, quickly!”  [Tribe member 2] “Why are we building this, anyway?”  [Tribe member 1] To show off the strength of our tribe. A few days ago, our neighboring tribe bragged about building a dolmen! The chief saw it, and said we should build one too! We can't let them beat us at it!”  [Tribe member 2] Of course! “We can do better! We should build it bigger and grander!  [Woman] The third function of dolmens is to serve as a headstone. They were used to demonstrate the authority and power of the group that built the monument, symbolizing the graveyard or being the graveyard itself. In some cases, dolmens form a cluster, and a dolmen that is unusually large compared to other dolmens or is located differently from other dolmens served as a headstone.

stories.title: How to build dolmens
stories.audioTitle: How to build dolmens 고인돌의 제작 방법
stories.script: How to build dolmens   [Man] The biggest feature of dolmens is that they used huge capstones. Dolmens were constructed based on the method of placing capstones on top of supporting stones above the ground. So how did they build dolmens?  [Woman] The most important thing in building dolmens was to obtain capstones. Capstones were difficult to obtain because they ranged from just a few tons to as heavy as hundreds of tons. It was necessary to trim the naturally separated stones from nearby mountains or to remove capstones directly from rock walls.  남1 [Chieftain] How much work have you done so far?”  남2 [Laborer] “Sir! We are now ready to remove the capstone. We have drilled several holes into the stone and we are now nailing wooden wedges into these holes. We are almost done with that as well.”  남1 [Chieftain] “Good. Then you'll have to pour water into the wooden wedges to soak them in it. Have you collected the water yet?  남2 [Laborer] Other tribesmen have already gone to get the water. You don’t need to worry too much, sir!”  남1 [Chieftain] This dolmen will demonstrate the power of our tribe. So make sure you build it with special care.  남2 [Laborer] “Sir! I will!”  [Man] When removing the capstone from the quarry, several holes are artificially drilled into the stone. And then wooden wedges are nailed into the holes. After that, the wooden wedges are soaked in water and the wet wooden wedges thereafter expand, causing the stone to be cut out.  [Woman] Various methods were used to transport such capstones. It is generally believed that a transportation route was opened to move the obtained capstones. It is assumed that the capstone was moved by paving a log rail underneath it, placing several logs across the rail, and then raising the capstone to make it easier to move. It is also assumed that they used Y-shaped wooden sleds or even ice in cold climate areas.  [Man] The burial chamber was built next once the capstone was moved. First, the tomb was dug up and plates or broken stones were used to shape the burial chamber. When the burial chamber was built, stone swords or burnished red pottery as well as weapons, accessories and earthenware were sometimes buried together.  [Woman] Once the burial chamber was complete, supporting stones were erected around it, and a hill was built with soil to make it easier to pull up the capstone.  남2 [Laborer] Build a hill out of soil! To raise the capstone!  남3 [Villager] Do we really have to work this much?  남2 [Laborer] Of course, you have to! Raising the capstone is the most difficult task. You have to do your best!”  남3 [Villager] Why is it difficult?  남2 [Laborer] It's because the capstone must strike a balance above the supporting stones. Otherwise, they'll just collapse! We can’t let our efforts be in vain! Hey there! Firm the soil!”  [Woman] Raising the capstone required a high level of civil engineering technology. Once the capstone is raised, they need to dig out the soil from the hill.  [Man] When the construction of the dolmen was completed, as the final event, people held a rite for the dead or a feast for the mobilized. This is an estimation based on the discovery of broken earthenware or stone tools around the grave. Dolmen construction was part of community ritual that required the mobilization of the same kin group as well as the labor force of the neighboring kin. The dolmen construction required a large number of people, including those who built a burial chamber, those who built a transportation route, and those who pulled up the capstone. Dolmens serve as an important historical source that informs the existence of communities that could mobilize this collective labor force.

stories.title: Whose dolmens were they?!
stories.audioTitle: Whose dolmens were they?! 고인돌의 주인은?
stories.script: Whose dolmens were they?!  [Man] There are many stories about the status of those who were buried underneath a dolmen. It is very difficult to determine the identity of the buried person. Many arguments were raised because the dolmens in Korea come in different shapes and densities depending on the region, and because they display various aspects in the cluster and shape of burial chambers.  [Woman] The person buried underneath a dolmen underwent a transformation in their status, as it took a long period of time to build each dolmen. The structure and layout of the burial chamber differs depending on the cluster of dolmens, making it difficult to assume that each tomb belonged to a particular class or stratum. That is why some argue that the dolmen served as a tomb for a ruler like a chieftain and their family members, as a joint tomb for a community of blood ties, or as a tomb for the fallen in battle.  [Man] Building a dolmen requires a large workforce. This is because a capstone weighing as little as a few tons to as much as several hundred tons had to be collected and transported. Thus, there must have been a lot of people to be mobilized as the workforce. Some view the dolmen as the tomb of a leader based on the bronze ware, ornaments, and other grave items excavated.   [Woman] While excavating a series of dolmens, one was found to have no burial chamber. What this suggests is that dolmens were not built solely to serve as tombs. Dolmens were also used as headstones and altars.  [Man] Why were dolmens built? They were built because powerful rulers began to emerge. In the Bronze Age, inter-tribal wars created classes, and rulers needed a reason to flaunt their power. In this process, they came up with building the dolmens. The most ideal way to show off and strengthen one’s authority and demonstrate the power of their tribe was to build a dolmen. The rulers of the time used the dolmen to strengthen their control and further unite the tribes. Dolmen served as a symbol of power and authority.

stories.title: Daesan-ri Dolmen in Ganghwa
stories.audioTitle: Daesan-ri Dolmen in Ganghwa 강화 대산리 고인돌
stories.script: Daesan-ri Dolmen in Ganghwa    [Man] The dolmens located in Korea include table dolmens, also known as northern-style dolmens, go-board dolmens, also referred to as southern-style dolmens, pad-stone dolmens with no supporting stones, and the exposed dolmens found in Jeju Island.   [Woman] The table dolmens have a burial chamber made with 4 or 6 wide flagstones that are exposed above the ground, with a flat capstone placed on top of the burial chamber. They are called table dolmens because they resemble a table.  [Man] Go-board dolmens are built with a burial chamber underground, and four to eight propping stones or so-called supporting stones are placed on top of it. They are called go-board dolmens because they look like a go board due to the shape where a large capstone is placed on top of these supporting stones. The go-board dolmens, which look magnificent as they are raised above the surface, are often devoid of distinct burial chambers.  [Woman] The pad-stone dolmens have a burial chamber with a lid right above the top. The pad-stone dolmens that cover their burial chambers without any supporting stones are alternatively referred to as no-support, lid, or footstone dolmens. It is estimated that the pad-stone dolmens were originally built as tombs, as their stone burial chambers are almost always found. Being widely distributed in the Liaoning Peninsula, the Korean Peninsula, and Kyushu, Japan, they are the most common type of tombs among the dolmen types.  [Man] As for the exposed dolmens, which are also known as Jeju-style dolmens, their burial chambers are exposed to the ground, and multiple flagstones are erected along the edge of the capstone. The number of flagstones exposed to the ground amounts to six or more, forming a burial chamber similar to the flat shape of the capstone, while the burial chamber is usually shaped like an oval or square. Among the dolmens in Korea, the exposed dolmens are only found on Jeju Island.  [Woman] The Daesan-ri dolmen in Ganghwa is located at the last foot of the northern ridge of Buksan Mountain, the eastern peak of Goryeosan Mountain. It is on a ridge 20 meters above sea level.  [Friend 1] “Hey, look over here.”   [Friend 2] Why? “Huh? Is this a dolmen?”  [Friend 1] Yes, the dolmen collapsed and the capstone fell down.”  [Friend 2] So dolmens collapse, too!”  [Friend 1] A table dolmen could topple down. By the way, it would be unfortunate for the tomb's owner. It would mean the collapse of your own tomb.”   [Friend 2] A tomb?  [Friend 1] The dolmens are known to represent the tombs of the Bronze Age. Of course there are also others dolmens used as headstones or altars.”   [Friend 2] “The Bronze Age? Are they that old? I didn’t know dolmens were so old.”  [Friend 1] “Yes, they sure are. What a pity. It would have been great if it had kept its original form.   [Friend 2] “At least some part of it has been preserved.”  [Woman] The Daesan-ri dolmen in Ganghwa has collapsed with its capstone fallen to the ground. The dolmen is 2.4 m long, 1.5 m wide, and 0.45 m high on its right, and 1.6 m long, 1.3 m wide, and 0.3 m high on its left side. The capstone is 3.68 m long, 2.6 m wide, and 0.5 m thick. The table-shaped stone of the Daesan-ri dolmen in Ganghwa collapsed, giving it its current shape.

stories.title: Dolmen Cluster in Araenmal, Hado-ri, Ganghwa
stories.audioTitle: Dolmen Cluster in Araenmal, Hado-ri, Ganghwa 강화 하도리 아랫말 고인돌 군
stories.script: Dolmen Cluster in Araenmal, Hado-ri, Ganghwa   [Man] The dolmen cluster in Araenmal, Hado-ri, Ganghwa is about 400 meters away from the dolmen cluster in Bugeun-ri to the northwest, with a plain in between. Unlike most dolmens of Ganghwado Island, it is located on a flat surface. In 1916, a Japanese person named Imanishi Ryu conducted an investigation on these five dolmens during the Japanese occupation.   [Woman] When Imanishi Ryu studied the dolmens, the records show that two horizontal propping stones or so-called supporting stones and the finishing stone in the northwest remained well-preserved, but now only the supporting stone on the north side is propping the capstone while the other stones are missing, thus losing their original form.  [Man] According to the composition of the dolmens in Araenmal of Hado-ri, Ganghwa, there are 1 table and 4 pad-stone dolmens. The table dolmens have a burial chamber made of 4 or 6 wide flagstones that are exposed above the ground, with a flat capstone placed on top of the burial chamber. They are called table dolmens because they resemble a table.   [Woman] The pad-stone dolmens have a capstone placed right above the burial chamber built underground. The pad-stone dolmens that cover their burial chambers without any supporting stones are alternatively referred to as no-support, lid, or footstone dolmens. In this style, a burial chamber made of stone is almost always found, and thus they are known to have been built as tombs. The capstone is thin in the north, but in the south it tends to be thicker.  [Man] Among the dolmens in Hado-ri, Ganghwa, the table dolmen has a propping stone or a supporting stone on its north side with a length of 2.15 m, thickness of 0.28 m, and height of 0.7 m. As the supporting stone on its south side is buried underneath the capstone, its exact length is unknown. The size of the capstone is 2.62 m long and 1.95 m wide, and its maximum thickness is 0.65 m.  [Woman] The dolmens in Hado-ri, Ganghwa were once located in the middle of privately owned farmland. Ganghwa-gun then purchased the land where dolmens are located, and has managed them since.

stories.title: Dolmens in Bugeun-ri, Ganghwa
stories.audioTitle: Dolmens in Bugeun-ri, Ganghwa 강화 부근리 고인돌
stories.script: Dolmens in Bugeun-ri, Ganghwa   [Woman] “Here they are! The dolmen site in Bugeun-ri, Ganghwa.”  [Man] What is the dolmen site?  [Woman] A dolmen site refers to a tomb built by people of the Bronze Age. This tomb is also called a dolmen.”  [Man] Aha! Dolmen!  [Woman] There are around 40 dolmens near Hajeom-myeon in Ganghwa-gun, and this table dolmen, called a dolmen site in Bugeun-ri, was designated as Historic Site No. 137 in 1964.  [Man] Table dolmen?”  [Woman] Yes. In the past, they were often found in the northern part of the Korean Peninsula and China, so they used to be called northern-style dolmens. However, as this type of dolmen was also found later in the southern part of the Korean Peninsula, they are not referred to as northern-style dolmens anymore. They are called table dolmens because of their resemblance to a table.   [Man] “But the dolmens are tombs. This dolmen doesn't look like a tomb.”  [Woman] It may or may not be a tomb, because dolmens don't always serve as tombs.  [Man] “What do you mean by that?”  [Woman] The dolmens are known as tombs, but they were also used as altars or headstones for graveyards.”  [Man] Really?   [Woman] The dolmen burial site in Bugeun-ri, Ganghwa is not regarded as a dolmen to serve as a tomb, but rather as an alter, because it has no flagstone constituting a burial chamber.   [Man] I see. So dolmens had other functions, too.”  [Woman] The table dolmens have a burial chamber made of 4 or 6 wide flagstones that are exposed above the ground, with a flat capstone placed on top of the burial chamber. Among these dolmens, the super-large dolmens, which are more than 8 meters long, 5 meters wide, and 2 meters high, are only found in the Liaodong Peninsula and the Daedonggang River basin in Korea, and only one is built on each hillside or mountainside. In North Korea, they are called Odeok-style dolmens according to the name of the area where they were found, and in China, they are called Seokbung.    [Man] The dolmen in Bugeun-ri has not yet been excavated, and thus it is not known what kind of artifacts it may hold. However, considering the grave items excavated from the nearby Samgeo-ri site, it is estimated that the dolmen in Bugeun-ri will also contain artifacts similar to those found in the Samgeo-ri area. The dolmen in Bugeun-ri, Ganghwa has a height of 2.6 m, and its capstone is made of a granite slab 7.1 m long and 5.5 m wide. The supporting stone is tilted about 70 degrees from the surface. It is unknown whether this was the original form or if it was tilted later, but many scholars assume that the weight of the cover stone may have caused the supporting stone to lean. Next to this dolmen is another destroyed dolmen with its propping stone missing and the cover of its flagstone tipped upside down.

stories.title: Dolmen in Jeomgol, Ganghwa
stories.audioTitle: Dolmen in Jeomgol, Ganghwa 강화 점골 고인돌
stories.script: Dolmen in Jeomgol, Ganghwa   [Man] The dolmen in Jeomgol, Ganghwa located in Hajeom-myeon of Ganghwa-gun, Incheon is positioned in a bean field in the middle of the road connecting Bugeun-ri and Mangwon.  [Cultural Commentator] The Dolmen in Jeomgol, Ganghwa first became known through a study of dolmen burial sites in Korea. As you can see, the relatively well-preserved dolmen was first surveyed in 1991, revealing its size and style.”  [Tourist] The dolmen here is shaped like a table.  [Cultural Commentator] Yes. The dolmen in Jeomgol, Ganghwa is a table dolmen. It gets its name because it looks like a table. In the past, it was called a northern-style dolmen.   [Tourist] Oh! I have learned that before. Northern-style dolmens and southern-style dolmens!  [Cultural Commentator] Table dolmens are those with burial chambers made of flagstones exposed to the ground. They usually used 4 to 6 flagstones. Each of these dolmens was made by placing a capstone on top of the burial chamber built above the ground. They used to be called the northern-style dolmens because they were mainly located north of the Han River and in the Liaoning province of China.  [Tourist] Why do we call them table dolmens now?”  [Cultural Commentator] The discovery of table-style dolmens in the south of the Korean Peninsula has led us to call them table dolmens instead of northern-style dolmens. The supporting stone you see here had previously collapsed from the dolmen in Jeomgol, but it has been restored to its original form.   [Tourist] I have a question. When was this dolmen made? Can we find out the specific year it was built or anything like that?”  [Cultural Commentator] There is no record showing when the dolmen was built. That is why we determine the time period by making assumptions using the chronology of the artifacts found and the time order between styles, or by resorting to the natural scientific age-dating technique. The data on absolute age commonly displays the measurement showing that the dolmen was built between the 12th and 9th centuries B.C. We thus assume that the dolmen was built around the 12th century B.C.  [Tourist] So until when was the dolmen still being built?”  [Cultural Commentator] “According to the discovery of artifacts dating back to the late Bronze Age, its construction ceased between the 3rd and 2nd centuries B.C. It is believed that dolmens in Korea were built over about 1,000 years from the 12th century B.C. to the 2nd century B.C.  [Tourist] Dolmens indeed go back far in time.”  [Man] The dolmen in Jeomgol, Ganghwa is located in a farming field at a low altitude of about 15 m above sea level. To its north, the finishing stone is not missing and remains preserved, making it a valuable source of information to identify the structure and shape of dolmens built in the Ganghwa area.

stories.title: Dolmen Cluster in Samgeo-ri, Ganghwa
stories.audioTitle: Dolmen Cluster in Samgeo-ri, Ganghwa 강화 삼거리 고인돌 군
stories.script: Dolmen Cluster in Samgeo-ri, Ganghwa   [Friend 1] “Wow, I love the fresh air.”  [Friend 2] “It's nice, isn't it?”  [Friend 1] “Yes. By the way, why is there a rock here?”  [Friend 2] “Oh, that is a dolmen!”  [Friend 1] “A dolmen?”  [Friend 2] You know that dolmens represent the tombs of the Bronze Age, right? The tombs are located here on the western ridge of Goryeosan Mountain in Ganghwa.”  [Friend 1] The tombs? There is more than one tomb?  [Friend 2] Sometimes dolmens form groups of 10 to 20. The Dolmen Cluster in Samgeo-ri, Ganghwa is also built in groups. There are five dolmen clusters on Ganghwa Island that are built in groups as they are here.  [Friend 1] I see.  [Friend 2] There are nine table dolmens located here in total. However, the ones here are not that large, and they do not maintain their original shape, either.   [Man] The table dolmens have a burial chamber made with 4 or 6 wide flagstones that are exposed above the ground, with a flat capstone placed on top of the burial chamber. They are called table dolmens because the their exterior appearance resembles a table, but they were once called northern-style dolmens as they were mainly found in the region north of the Han River and the Liaoning area of China. Among the table dolmens, large ones were primarily built as altars or monuments.   [Woman] Among these dolmens, the super-large dolmens, which are more than 8 meters long, 5 meters wide, and 2 meters high, are only found in the Liaodong Peninsula and the Daedonggang River basin in Korea, and only one is built on each hillside or mountainside. On the other hand, the table dolmens in the south usually have a capstone that is 3-4 m tall, and the height of their burial chambers is less than 1 m, making the dolmen smaller and the burial chamber narrow.  [Man] Among the dolmens in Samgeo-ri, Ganghwa, there is one with a small hole on its capstone called Seonghyeol, which is sometimes associated with constellations. Although dolmens are known to be the tombs of the ruling class with political power, they also served as altars or headstones symbolizing graveyards. The dolmens in Samgeo-ri, Ganghwa were registered as a UNESCO World Heritage Site along with the dolmen sites in Gochang and Hwasun on December 2, 2000.

stories.title: Dolmen cluster in Gyosan-ri, Ganghwa
stories.audioTitle: Dolmen cluster in Gyosan-ri, Ganghwa 강화 교산리 고인돌 군
stories.script: Dolmen cluster in Gyosan-ri, Ganghwa  [Man] Ganghwa dolmens are located in Bugeun-ri, Samgeo-ri, Gocheon-ri, Osang-ri, and Gyosan-ri of Hajeom-myeon in Ganghwa-gun, Incheon. The dolmens are mainly located at the northern foot of Goryeosan mountain, with 127 dolmens dispersed. Since Ganghwa, an island at the mouth of the Han River, has been an important area historically, the dolmens there have also been widely known from early on.   [Teacher] In Europe, megalithic monuments began to be built during the Neolithic Age, and in other regions such as Asia, dolmens were built during the Bronze Age and the Iron Age. The shape of dolmens varies from region to region, but the table shape is commonly found around the world.  [Student] Sir, are all dolmens table-shaped,then?  [Teacher] No, they are not. In addition to the table dolmens, there are also go-board dolmens with supporting stones placed under a huge capstone. There are also pad-stone dolmens that used a huge capstone like a lid covering the burial chamber underground, and exposed dolmens built with supporting stones surrounding them. Among those, go-board dolmens are the ones mostly found in Korea.  [Man] The dolmen cluster in Gyosan-ri, Ganghwa-gun, which is located in Gyosan-ri of Yangsa-myeon in Ganghwa-gun, Incheon, was designated as Natural Monument No. 48 of Incheon Metropolitan City. There are 11 dolmens on the northern hill of Byeollipsan Mountain. The dolmens here are generally well-preserved, with only parts of the supporting stones and capstones showing damage.  [Woman] In the dolmen cluster in Gyosan-ri, Ganghwa-do, there are table dolmens with supporting stones, finishing stones, and capstones, while some of the dolmens are go-board dolmens with a capstone measuring 3-4 m. Their original shapes are well-preserved because they are located on a desolate hill, resulting in little damage caused by humans.  [Man] The table dolmens have a burial chamber made of 4 or 6 wide flagstones that are exposed above the ground, with a flat capstone placed on top of the burial chamber. They are called table dolmens due to their resemblance to a table. They were once called northern-style dolmens because they were mainly found north of the Han River and in the Liaoning province of China.  [Woman] Go-board dolmens have a burial chamber built underground made of flag stones or broken and natural stones and 4 to 8 supporting stones erected around them with a large capstone placed on top, and they are called go-board dolmens because of their resemblance to a go board. A large dolmen is usually found at the foot of a mountain, hill, or flat area at the end of a valley, but in a cluster of dolmens it is located at the center or in an independent location. These dolmens usually have round, egg-shaped capstones that are 3-6 m in length to 2-4 m in thickness, or rectangular-shaped capstones with each side leveled.

stories.title: Dolmen Cluster in Osang-ri, Ganghwa
stories.audioTitle: Dolmen Cluster in Osang-ri, Ganghwa 강화 오상리 고인돌 군
stories.script: Dolmen Cluster in Osang-ri, Ganghwa   [Man] The Dolmen Cluster in Osang-ri, Ganghwa is located at the southern foot of Goryeosan Mountain in Ganghwado Island. Twelve dolmens are gathered on a gently rolling hill at 75 m above sea level. All 12 dolmens are table dolmens, and large, medium, and small sizes are evenly distributed.   [Woman] The table dolmens have a burial chamber made of 4 or 6 wide flagstones that are exposed above the ground, with a flat capstone placed on top of the burial chamber. They are called table dolmens because they resemble a table. They were once called northern-style dolmens because they were mainly found north of the Han River and in the Liaoning province of China. However, as these were also found in the southern part of the Korean Peninsula, they were later renamed as table dolmens.   [Man] The dolmens in Osang-ri, Ganghwa were excavated in 2000.  [Archaeologist 1] How's it going? Would you like some coffee?  [Archaeologist 2] “Thank you. The excavation is almost finished here, too. Have you made any progress?  [Archaeologist 1] Yesterday, we excavated the old stoneware of the Paleolithic Age, and today we found the pieces of comb-pattern pottery and patternless pottery of the Bronze Age.   [Archaeologist 2] That means Ganghwado Island has been inhabited since the Paleolithic Age.  [Archaeologist 1] That's right. How about you?”  [Archaeologist 2] We found a half moon-shaped stone knife and a stone arrowhead. What we are excavating now is likely to be...”  [Archaeologist 1] “Likely to be what?”  [Archaeologist 2] We still have to dig up a bit more, but it is probably going to be Daerongok (tube-shaped jade beads).”  [Archaeologist 1] “Hmm, I see. I’ll be getting back to work. Keep up the good work.”  [Archaeologist 2] Thanks for the coffee.”  [Woman] Daerongok is also called Gwanok or Jo-ok, and there are pieces that are less than 1 cm long and some that are more than 10 cm long. Among the beads, it was the first of its kind that emerged, and it was primarily used to make necklaces. It is estimated that Daerongok was first made by cutting hollow bones like bird bones, and in fact, Daerongok made of bird bones have been excavated from Neolithic sites. During the Neolithic Age, Daerongok was also made of either earth or stone.  [Man] The semicircular stone knife was a stone used for cutting grain ears. Although they are mainly semicircular, square knives were made in the Hamgyeong-do area, while triangular knives were made in the coastal areas of Chungcheong-do and Jeolla-do. At first it was used as a harvesting tool for various grains, but during the mid-Bronze Age, triangular stone knives appeared for rice farming. The semicircular stone knife was used as a ritual object as well as in real life, and it is presumed that the ones found broken around the tomb were not broken during their use, but were rather intentionally broken and buried underground.   [Woman] Among the dolmens in Osang-ri, Ganghwa, the largest dolmen located at the top was designated as Gyeonggi-do Monument No. 9 on July 3, 1972, and was re-designated as Monument No. 16 by the Incheon Metropolitan Government on March 1, 1995.

stories.title: Dolmen cluster in Gocheon-ri, Ganghwa
stories.audioTitle: Dolmen cluster in Gocheon-ri, Ganghwa 강화 고천리 고인돌 군
stories.script: Dolmen cluster in Gocheon-ri, Ganghwa   [Teacher] We've arrived. This is where the dolmen cluster in Gocheon-ri, Ganghwa is located.  [Student] These dolmens are located on higher ground.”   [Teacher] Yes, this is the western ridge of Goryeosan Mountain. There are 18 dolmens distributed over the surfaces, 250-350 m above sea level. It is located on much higher ground than the average dolmen tombs of Korea. That would be the unique characteristic of these dolmens here.”  [Student] That's why it was a bit hard to climb up. But the dolmens here are generally...”  [Teacher] “Damaged a lot?”  [Student] Yes, on our way up, I saw a lot of stones in the forest that were the right sized for dolmens.”  [Teacher] That's right, that would be what they were.”  [Student] And yet, the table-type dolmen seems relatively well-preserved.  [Teacher] Yes, that's right. The capstone of the dolmen is 3.35 m wide, 2.47 m long, and 0.65 m thick, making it one of the most well-preserved dolmens here.”  [Student] Sir. The dolmens here must have been made of stones quarried from around here. There are traces of stones that have been removed.  [Teacher] Yes, that is most likely. Since this is a mountain, we can infer that they were made of stones found here.   [Student] Yes, they would have required a lot of manpower, and it must not have been easy to carry them, either. Right?  [Teacher] “That's right. It took a lot of manpower to build dolmens. At that time, they had to be hand-built.”   [Student] That’s amazing. They were able to build dolmens in those days. We can do all the hard work with machines these days, but they didn’t have them at the time. It's kind of awe-inspiring to think that dolmens were built by hand.”  [Teacher] “That's right. You can't make a dolmen like this on your own. The fact that dolmens were built demonstrates that a society was already able to mobilize such manpower. Dolmens indeed provide interesting historical records.  [Woman] Among the cultural heritages of humankind, dolmens are widely located throughout the world. These remains effectively reflect the social aspects of the times when they were built. Dolmens in Korea are more densely distributed than anywhere else in the world. The dolmens in Ganghwa show a wide variety of locations, including at the foot of mountains, hills, flatlands, and ridges. Among them, the dolmens in Gocheon-ri of Ganghwa are located on the ridge of the mountain, with around 18 dolmens that are shaped as table dolmens.   [Man] The table dolmens have a burial chamber made of 4 or 6 wide flagstones that are exposed above the ground, with a flat capstone placed on top of the burial chamber. They are called table dolmens because they resemble a table. They were once called northern-style dolmens because they were found mainly in the northern part of the Korean Peninsula or China. However, the discovery of this type of dolmens in the southern part of the Korean Peninsula has given them the new name of table dolmens.  [Woman] Among the table dolmens, the largest dolmens are found only in the Liaoning Peninsula and the Daedonggang River basin in Korea, and only one of them is located on a hillside or mountainside. The table dolmens in the south usually have a capstone that is 3-4 m long and a burial chamber that is about 1 m high. These dolmens are small, with narrow burial chambers.

stories.title: What is dolmen?
stories.script: What is dolmen?  [Teacher] There are stone statues and tombs made of large, heavy, sturdy rocks in the world. Examples include the pyramids, which are large tombs in Egypt, Stonehenge, the mysterious megalithic monument in England, and the Moai statues, the huge face sculptures on Easter Island. It is called megalithic culture.  [Student] Is there also megalithic culture in Korea?  [Teacher] “Of course there is.”  [Student] What is it?  [Teacher] The representative megalithic culture of Korea would be the dolmens. “  [Student] The dolmen was part of the megalithic culture?  [Teacher] Most of the dolmens are prehistoric tombs with a large stone placed above a burial chamber made on the ground or underground. The dolmens are also called Jiseokmyo, which are made of a flat stone or an oddly shaped stone with supporting stones placed underneath.  [Student] Sir, dolmens aren't only found in Korea, are they?”  [Teacher] Starting from northern Europe, the dolmens are concentrated in the United Kingdom in Western Europe, throughout France, Switzerland, and the Iberian Peninsula, then in the northern part of the Mediterranean sea, the Middle East, India and Southeast Asia, and in China's Fujian, Zhejiang Province, Shandong Province, Liaodong Peninsula, the southern part of Jilin Province, the entire Korean Peninsula, and in Kyushu, Japan.   [Man] Dolmens were generally built on plateaus around a river basin and on low hills. Dolmens are more frequently distributed in slightly higher plains near mountains and hills and coastal areas than in large plains. In the river basin, they are largely placed to match the direction that the stream flows, mainly because the human dwellings primarily developed in those areas. The reason that there are no dolmens in the vast plains is that most of them were there before the areas were developed, and those areas were not used for human living. It is highly likely that the residential areas, farmland, and tombs were built here, as the plateau or a slightly higher hill was located at the foot of a sunny mountain, thus making it easy to get water and firewood for living while the hunting ground also remained close. It was because it was highly accessible.  [Woman] The dolmens are alternatively referred to as Dokbaegi, Baubaegi, or Dokbau, as they have natural stones buried underground, while go-board dolmens are alternatively called Gwanbau or Amdakbau. They may also be called Baebau, Geobukbau, Duggeobibau, or Gaeguribau depending on the shape of their capstones. A dolmen was also called Chilseongbau due to its shape of arrangement in connection with folk beliefs, or Janggunbau in a belief that a Janggun, meaning army general in Korean, moved the stones but then stopped. The names of the villages are sometimes related to dolmens, such as Juam, which resembles Baebawi Rock, Guam, meaning turtle rock, and Chilam, which means chilseong rock.

stories.title: Types of dolmens
stories.script: Types of dolmens  [Man] Dolmens are different from ordinary tombs because they are made with huge rocks erected above the ground. Their simple structure allows detailed insight. The dolmens are classified into table dolmens, go-board dolmens, pad-stone dolmens, semi-exposed dolmens, and exposed dolmens.  [Woman] The table dolmens have a burial chamber made with 4 or 6 wide flagstones that are exposed above the ground, with a flat capstone placed on top of the burial chamber. They are called table dolmens because they resemble a table. They are mainly located in the northern part of the Korean Peninsula and the Liaoning area of China, and thus they used to be called the northern style. Among the table dolmens, the large ones are estimated to have been built mainly as altars or monuments. Among these dolmens, the super-large dolmens, which are more than 8 meters long, 5 meters wide, and 2 meters high, are usually found in the Liaodong Peninsula and the Daedonggang River basin in Korea, and only one is built on each hillside or mountainside.   [Man] Go-board dolmens have a burial chamber built underground made of flagstones or broken and natural stones, and 4 to 8 supporting stones are erected around them with a large capstone placed on top. This is called a go-board dolmen because it resembles a go board. The go-board dolmens, which look magnificent as they are raised above the surface, are often devoid of distinct burial chambers. A large dolmen usually exists at the foot of a mountain, hill, or flat area at the end of a valley, but in a cluster of dolmens, it is located at the center or in an independent location.  [Woman] The pad-stone dolmens have a burial chamber with a lid right above the top. Since there are no propping stones, the pad-stone dolmens are alternatively referred to as no-support, lid, or footstone dolmens. For this type, a stone burial chamber is almost always found, indicating that they were originally intended to serve as tombs. Being widely distributed in the Liaoning Peninsula, the Korean Peninsula, and Kyushu, Japan, they are the most common type of tombs among the dolmen types. The capstone is thin in the north, but in the south it tends to be thicker. Most of the artifacts excavated from dolmens were also found in this type.  [Man] Semi-exposed dolmens have a structure like a stone coffin on the ground with a flagstone that is lower than the typical table-style flagstone or that has multiple overlapping flagstones. On the outer covering, the remaining styles are those with propping stones erected to match the height of the flagstone; with only the flagstone part without any propping stones; and with all propping stones missing. The burial chamber is also located either on the ground and in the semi-basement, and it is difficult to spot the location of the burial chamber without checking each and every part.  [Woman] The exposed dolmens are also called Jeju-style dolmens. The burial chamber is exposed to the ground, and multiple flagstones are erected along the edge of the capstone. The number of flagstones exposed to the ground amounts to six or more, forming a burial chamber similar to the flat shape of the capstone, while the burial chamber is usually shaped like an oval or square. The exposed dolmen is a unique type of dolmen only found on Jeju Island in Korea. Similar burial chamber structures have also been found in Zhejiang Province, China.

stories.title: Functions of dolmens
stories.script: Functions of dolmens   [Man] The dolmen, part of megalithic culture, has three key functions. First, the dolmen, a prehistoric tomb with a huge capstone placed above the ground or an underground burial chamber, serves as a tomb.   [Woman] In 1962, the National Museum of Korea conducted two excavations of dolmens in Hwangseok-ri of Chungcheongbuk-do.  [Archaeologist 1] “Huh? What are these?”  [Archaeologist 2] “What? What's going on?”  [Archaeologist 1] “Sir, I think you should see this. Please take a look.” What...? Is this what I think it is? It looks like a human bone, doesn't it?  [Archaeologist 2] “Yes! That's right. This is indeed a human bone.”  [Archaeologist 1] “Then it must have been a tomb.”  [Woman] Among them, a human bone of a [male] adult was found in its complete form, and its function as a tomb was reported to the academic world. Although no human bones have been discovered in Jeollanam-do, it is assumed to have served as a tomb given the size of the burial chamber inside the dolmen. The evidence demonstrating its use as a tomb is that dolmens are distributed in groups at each location, that human bones have been found, and that grave items buried during the construction of the tomb have been discovered.   [Man] Second, the dolmen served as an altar. The dolmens that have the characteristics of an altar have three different conditions from dolmens that served as tombs because they were the venue for religious events or ceremonies. First, each of these dolmens stands independently, maintaining a certain distance from the cluster. Second, it is supported by a large oddly-shaped stone capstone and large propping stones which show distinct size and appearance from other dolmens. Third, it is located on high ground overlooking the surrounding area. Based on the combination of these factors, it is assumed that such dolmens served as altars rather than tombs. A society building dolmens needed symbolic monuments to strengthen the cooperation and solidarity of different groups. It is thus estimated that dolmens were built and used as altars.  [Tribe member 1] “Move the stones, quickly!”  [Tribe member 2] “Why are we building this, anyway?”  [Tribe member 1] To show off the strength of our tribe. A few days ago, our neighboring tribe bragged about building a dolmen! The chief saw it, and said we should build one too! We can't let them beat us at it!”  [Tribe member 2] Of course! “We can do better! We should build it bigger and grander!  [Woman] The third function of dolmens is to serve as a headstone. They were used to demonstrate the authority and power of the group that built the monument, symbolizing the graveyard or being the graveyard itself. In some cases, dolmens form a cluster, and a dolmen that is unusually large compared to other dolmens or is located differently from other dolmens served as a headstone.

stories.title: How to build dolmens
stories.audioTitle: How to build dolmens 고인돌의 제작 방법
stories.script: How to build dolmens   [Man] The biggest feature of dolmens is that they used huge capstones. Dolmens were constructed based on the method of placing capstones on top of supporting stones above the ground. So how did they build dolmens?  [Woman] The most important thing in building dolmens was to obtain capstones. Capstones were difficult to obtain because they ranged from just a few tons to as heavy as hundreds of tons. It was necessary to trim the naturally separated stones from nearby mountains or to remove capstones directly from rock walls.  남1 [Chieftain] How much work have you done so far?”  남2 [Laborer] “Sir! We are now ready to remove the capstone. We have drilled several holes into the stone and we are now nailing wooden wedges into these holes. We are almost done with that as well.”  남1 [Chieftain] “Good. Then you'll have to pour water into the wooden wedges to soak them in it. Have you collected the water yet?  남2 [Laborer] Other tribesmen have already gone to get the water. You don’t need to worry too much, sir!”  남1 [Chieftain] This dolmen will demonstrate the power of our tribe. So make sure you build it with special care.  남2 [Laborer] “Sir! I will!”  [Man] When removing the capstone from the quarry, several holes are artificially drilled into the stone. And then wooden wedges are nailed into the holes. After that, the wooden wedges are soaked in water and the wet wooden wedges thereafter expand, causing the stone to be cut out.  [Woman] Various methods were used to transport such capstones. It is generally believed that a transportation route was opened to move the obtained capstones. It is assumed that the capstone was moved by paving a log rail underneath it, placing several logs across the rail, and then raising the capstone to make it easier to move. It is also assumed that they used Y-shaped wooden sleds or even ice in cold climate areas.  [Man] The burial chamber was built next once the capstone was moved. First, the tomb was dug up and plates or broken stones were used to shape the burial chamber. When the burial chamber was built, stone swords or burnished red pottery as well as weapons, accessories and earthenware were sometimes buried together.  [Woman] Once the burial chamber was complete, supporting stones were erected around it, and a hill was built with soil to make it easier to pull up the capstone.  남2 [Laborer] Build a hill out of soil! To raise the capstone!  남3 [Villager] Do we really have to work this much?  남2 [Laborer] Of course, you have to! Raising the capstone is the most difficult task. You have to do your best!”  남3 [Villager] Why is it difficult?  남2 [Laborer] It's because the capstone must strike a balance above the supporting stones. Otherwise, they'll just collapse! We can’t let our efforts be in vain! Hey there! Firm the soil!”  [Woman] Raising the capstone required a high level of civil engineering technology. Once the capstone is raised, they need to dig out the soil from the hill.  [Man] When the construction of the dolmen was completed, as the final event, people held a rite for the dead or a feast for the mobilized. This is an estimation based on the discovery of broken earthenware or stone tools around the grave. Dolmen construction was part of community ritual that required the mobilization of the same kin group as well as the labor force of the neighboring kin. The dolmen construction required a large number of people, including those who built a burial chamber, those who built a transportation route, and those who pulled up the capstone. Dolmens serve as an important historical source that informs the existence of communities that could mobilize this collective labor force.

stories.title: Whose dolmens were they?!
stories.audioTitle: Whose dolmens were they?! 고인돌의 주인은?
stories.script: Whose dolmens were they?!  [Man] There are many stories about the status of those who were buried underneath a dolmen. It is very difficult to determine the identity of the buried person. Many arguments were raised because the dolmens in Korea come in different shapes and densities depending on the region, and because they display various aspects in the cluster and shape of burial chambers.  [Woman] The person buried underneath a dolmen underwent a transformation in their status, as it took a long period of time to build each dolmen. The structure and layout of the burial chamber differs depending on the cluster of dolmens, making it difficult to assume that each tomb belonged to a particular class or stratum. That is why some argue that the dolmen served as a tomb for a ruler like a chieftain and their family members, as a joint tomb for a community of blood ties, or as a tomb for the fallen in battle.  [Man] Building a dolmen requires a large workforce. This is because a capstone weighing as little as a few tons to as much as several hundred tons had to be collected and transported. Thus, there must have been a lot of people to be mobilized as the workforce. Some view the dolmen as the tomb of a leader based on the bronze ware, ornaments, and other grave items excavated.   [Woman] While excavating a series of dolmens, one was found to have no burial chamber. What this suggests is that dolmens were not built solely to serve as tombs. Dolmens were also used as headstones and altars.  [Man] Why were dolmens built? They were built because powerful rulers began to emerge. In the Bronze Age, inter-tribal wars created classes, and rulers needed a reason to flaunt their power. In this process, they came up with building the dolmens. The most ideal way to show off and strengthen one’s authority and demonstrate the power of their tribe was to build a dolmen. The rulers of the time used the dolmen to strengthen their control and further unite the tribes. Dolmen served as a symbol of power and authority.

stories.title: Mupunghansolgil Trail of Tongdosa Temple
stories.audioTitle: 1. Mupunghansolgil Trail of Tongdosa Temple_통도사 무풍한솔길
stories.script: 1. Mupunghansolgil Trail of Tongdosa Temple  [Friend 1] “Wow! This is great!”  [Friend 2] “I told you.”  [Friend 1] “I love this cool breeze!”  [Friend 2] “This place is the Mupunghansolgil Trail!”  [Friend 1] “Mupunghansolgil Trail? Mupung means windless, so does that mean a windless pine tree trail?”  [Friend 2] “Nope! That’s not it! It means a cool pine tree trail with dancing wind!”  [Friend 1] Oh, I thought it would be weird to call this place windless, since this place is full of cool breezes. So, mu means dancing, right?  [Friend 2] That's right!  [Friend 1] “The trail is so beautiful!”  [Friend 2] It was selected as the most beautiful trail in the National Forest Competition in 2018.  [Friend 1] I see. It does seem that beautiful.  [Woman] Tongdosa Temple was founded in Yeongchuksan Mountain by Jajang Yulsa, a Buddhist monk during the Three Kingdoms Period. It was 646, the 15th year of Queen Seondeok. The name of the mountain was Yeongchuk because its shape was very similar to that of Yeongchuk Mountain in India.  [Man] The temple was founded enshrining the sarira and kasaya of the Buddha that were brought by Jajang Yulsa when he returned home from Tang China, along with 400 chests containing the Complete Collection of Buddhist Sutras, making it a very important temple since the early days.  It was the first temple in the history of Korea to enshrine the Complete Collection of Buddhist Sutras as well as the sarira and kasaya of the Buddha. Tongdosa Temple became the fundamental Bodhimandala of the Buddhist rules of Silla.   [Woman] At the time of its foundation, it is assumed that there were just several Dharma halls around the stairs called the Ordination Platform, and it was not a large temple like today.  In the early Goryeo Dynasty, the temple was expanded to cover a large area, to even have symbol signs for boundaries.   As the major stone structures that currently exist were constructed during the reign of King Seonjong in early Goryeo, it is estimated that the maintenance of its garden was also conducted primarily during this period.   [Man] There are two ways to get to Tongdosa Temple, one being by crossing the bridge from the entrance and taking a car, and the other is by walking along the Mupunghansolgil Trail. Mupunghansolgil Trail, which starts from the Tongdosa Temple ticket office, extends about 1 km through the valley to the Buddha-stupa field in front of Iljumun Gate. Mupunghansolgil Trail is a forest path where 100- to 200-year-old pine trees stay green all year round, allowing visitors to enjoy the quaint beauty of Tongdosa Temple.

stories.title: Three-story Stone Pagoda of Tongdosa Temple
stories.audioTitle: 2. Three-story Stone Pagoda of Tongdosa Temple_통도사 삼층석탑
stories.script: 2. Three-story Stone Pagoda of Tongdosa Temple  [Woman] Standing in front of the Yeongsanjeon Hall of Tongdosa Temple, this pagoda has a three-tier pagoda body on top of the two-tier stylobate. The stylobate is decorated with a column shape, and the lower tier has a shallow carving of the eye shape. The pagoda body was constructed by alternating body and roof stones, and the curved eaves of the roof stone and the lifted corners are visible at a glance.   The stone pagoda is about 3.5 meters high and has four long footstones carved into the foundation stone. It displays a double stylobate, a typical style of stone pagodas from the Unified Silla Period. The upper stylobate is carved with a pillar in the corner, and the lower stylobate is carved with three ornaments on each side. This style is characteristic of those found in the late Unified Silla Period or after the 9th century, during which the decorative function of stone pagodas was emphasized.  Each pagoda body has only a corner pillar with no particular carving, and the roof stone reduces the roof support to the four layers, reflecting the trend of the times.  The upper part is installed with an ornament made of a two-layered pedestal on top of the roof stone on the third tier, and there is a semi-spherical finial ornament and jewel canopy on top of it, but it remains inconclusive as to whether the part above the ornament was originally a part of this pagoda.   [Teacher] We estimate that stone pagodas began to be built in Korea around the year 600 at the end of the Three Kingdoms Period.  [Pupil] Are you saying there was technology for building stone pagodas around 600?”  [Teacher] Buddhism is believed to have been introduced to Korea between the late 4th and the late 6th century.”  [Pupil] Yes, that's right.”   [Teacher] During those 200 years, we had been building wooden pagodas. The technology required to build stone pagodas was gained through building wooden pagodas.”  [Pupil] “Wow! That sounds about right. The know-how gained from the building of the wooden pagodas led us to build the stone pagodas?”  [Teacher] That's right. Stone pagodas cannot be built overnight.  [Pupil] By the way, Has the Stone Pagoda of Tongdosa Temple always been here?”  [Teacher] “No, it hasn’t.  The pagoda was dismantled and restored in 1987. It was then moved to the northeast, about 1.5 meters from its original location. To the location where it stands now.  [Pupil] I heard that relics are usually found when a tower is dismantled and restored. Were there any such relics in this pagoda?”  [Teacher] Of course there were. At that time, a white porcelain vessel dating back to the Joseon Dynasty was found among the rubble in the upper stylobate. Two gilt-bronze Buddha statues and bronze spoons were found in the lower stylobate.”  [Pupil] Bronze spoons and white porcelain from the Joseon Dynasty... That’s an odd combination.  [Teacher] We regard the relics as showing that it has been rebuilt once before.”  [Pupil] “Ah! I see!”  [Woman] The stone pagodas of Silla tend to undergo partial changes and become smaller over time following the 8th century. In general, with the beginning of the 9th century, the transformation gradually took off, and in the late 9th century, a significant change was made. After the 9th century, the society experienced unrest due to family discord and the rise of many local rival leaders in Silla, withering artistic values. In particular, the formative arts were affected, undergoing a transformation from the vibrant spirit into wanness and frailty.  As a result, the size of each sculpture naturally decreased, and the style of each part became weakened or omitted.  The Three-story Stone Pagoda of Tongdosa Temple is a valuable resource for understanding the stone cultural assets of Tongdosa Temple along with the kneeling stone in front of the pagoda. The worship stone is decorated with a rectangular pattern of lotus flowers, and according to the engraved calligraphy writing, it was built in 1085, the second year of King Seonjong.

stories.title: Yeongsanjeon Hall of Tongdosa Temple
stories.audioTitle: 3. Yeongsanjeon Hall of Tongdosa Temple_통도사 영산전
stories.script: 3. Yeongsanjeon Hall of Tongdosa Temple  [Man] It is unknown when Yeongsanjeon Hall of Tongdosa Temple was built.
