It was one of the main institutions that led the economic growth of Joseon along with the Oriental Development Company during the Japanese colonial rule. While the Oriental Development Company plundered the land and resources of Joseon, Joseon Siksan Bank funded the Japanese industry by issuing bonds and fooling the Joseon people to make savings in the bank. The Daegu branch of Joseon Siksan Bank, in particular, was built firmly to withstand the frequent bombings by activists of the resistance movement. A century has passed since its establishment, yet it still maintains its original shape.   After liberation from Japanese colonial rule, the building was used as the Daegu branch of Korea Development Bank until it was renovated into the Daegu Modern History Museum in 2011. A building that was once built by the greed of the Japanese colonization and Imperialism has now become a place to reflect on the brutality of the colonial rule.   In 1905, after the opening of the Gyeongbu Line, a road that connects Seoul with Busan, which was built by the Japanese to facilitate the exploitation of Joseon and the invasion of China, made Daegu an even more attractive destination to the Japanese. After around 800 Japanese who resided in Daegu ruled over the city with a population of not more than 20,000, they ordered a pro-Japanese collaborator named Park Jung-yang to lead the destruction of Daegueupseong Walled Town that outlined the city of Daegu.   Tour to the Daegu Modern History Museum starts by covering the peaceful landscape of the Gyeongsanggamyeong Provincial Office where the Gwanpungnu Pavilion used to be situated in the early 1900s, followed by the painful traces of the contemporary history of Korea — the Japanese colonial rule and the Korean War. The museum also features Helen Keller who visited the city to spread hope to the colonized Joseon and Marilyn Monroe who arrived at the Dongchon Airfield (currently the Daegu International Airport) for her performance in front of war veterans. Should you be interested in tracing the footsteps of Daegu, visit the Daegu Modern History Museum.   "

stories.title: Choe Je-u Tree (Daegu Chongno Elementary School)
stories.audioTitle: (6) Modern Streets of Daegu: Choe Je-u Tree (Daegu Chongno Elementary School)
stories.script: "There is a special tree that grows on the campus of the Daegu Chongno Elementary School. Taller than the school building, the tree casts a shadow onto the schoolyard where children run and play. This 400-year-old Japanese pagoda tree is also known as the “Choe Je-u Tree” by the residents of Daegu. So, what is the relationship between Choe Je-u (1824-1864), the founder of Donghak movement, and this old tree?   Choe Je-u was convicted of sedition and heresy, meaning that he disoriented the world through distorted belief. He, who criticized the corrupt society and spread the belief that all people are equal, was incarcerated behind the bars of Gyeongsanggamyeong Provincial Office before he was eventually beheaded one fine day in spring in April 1864.   Choe never lost his dignity and kept his belief despite all the interrogations and torture he went through. Every night, he would look at the Japanese pagoda tree standing outside the bars to find peace of mind. Had Choe's embittered soul reached the spiritual tree? Legend says that the bountiful leaves of the tree fell on the ground and the sap seeped out like tears the day Choe was sentenced to death.   Exactly 30 years later, the Donghak Peasant Revolution took place. The first modernization movement that was started by peasants and believers of the Donghak religion who fought against feudalism and foreign powers led to anti-Japanese protests and the March 1st Movement. This is the reason why the death of Choe was not for nothing. The democracy of Korea bloomed from the seed of Donghak spirit Choe sowed in this country.   Chongno Elementary School was established in 1900 and is the oldest elementary school in Daegu. It was once known as the educational institution for children of Japanese residents during the Japanese colonial rule, a period when there was segregation between the oppressors and the oppressed, and between men and women. This was also a time when people were exploited and persecuted, their human rights trampled on. Countless deaths of the innocent also took place. Choe Je-u tree witnessed it all throughout the years. "

stories.title: Birth Home of Poet Yi Sanghwa in Geundaero, Daegu
stories.audioTitle: (7) Birth Home of Poet Yi Sanghwa in Geundaero, Daegu
stories.script: Are you aware of Yi Sanghwa (1901-1943), often known as “the modern boy,” who was a trendsetter in the 1920s? Many recall him as an anti-Japanese poet for his famous piece “Will Spring come on the lost land,” but he was also a true romanticist as can be seen from his other work titled “To my private chamber.” Yi lived a life of romanticism and resistance with an intellect ahead of the time. What must have been Yi’s childhood like, inspiring him with such poetic spirits and leading him to become a poet?   The site of the Birthplace of Poet Yi Sanghwa located in 11, Seomun-ro 2-ga, currently has a coffee shop in a small hanok with Korean lilacs that fill its front yard. In the past, when Yi was living here, it was a large house covering over 1,300 m2. Yi was born in 1901 to a wealthy and noble family. He was raised by his uncle after his father died when he was a child. His uncle Yi Il-woo ran the Uhyeonseoru School to promote Korean nationalism during the Japanese colonial rule. It was here that several anti-Japanese patriots were fostered.   At the age of fifteen, Yi persuaded his uncle to allow him to study in Seoul. He was more into pondering philosophical questions on life, however, and began to spend his life on the streets. During that time, when the March 1st Movement took place in Daegu, he created publications including the Korean Declaration of Independence right here at sarangchae, or the master's quarters, at the tender age of eighteen. The good looking and popular modern boy with good manners gave up his dream of studying in France and stayed in his sarangchae that he named Damgyojang. It was here that he dreamt of Korean independence with nationalists and intellectuals from the region.   A 200-year-old Korean early lilac stands on the site of sarangchae to this day. We can only imagine what the old scenery could have been like. This boy, while spending a lazy day, may have experienced the joy of spring on a fine day, gazing at the tree in the front yard blooming with flowers. The poet may have been longing for that spring, the peaceful spring that no one has ever stolen from him.   The Korean early lilac, commonly known as lilac, is a native tree to Korea. The fragrance of its light purple flowers is known to make lovers fall in love deeper with each other. This tree, meaning “a portrait of younger days” and “a beautiful promise,” fully blooms in April. Coincidentally, Yi was born in the month of April and also passed away in April.

stories.title: The Site of Samsung Trading Company
stories.audioTitle: (8) Modern Streets of Daegu: The Site of Samsung Trading Company
stories.script: "A 29-year-old young man who had not been successful in his studies or business all his life settled in Daegu, known to be the center of commerce at the time, after leaving his hometown. In 1938, he built a small Japanese-style wooden structure at the end of Seomun Market in Jung-gu and put up a signboard that read “Samsung Trading Company."" This man strove for success, making noodles while his hair got white from scattered flour. This is the story of Chairman Lee Byung-chul (1910-1987), the founder of the global company Samsung.   Chairman Lee was already married, a father to four children at the time. He quickly adjusted to the keen competition of the marketplace, as he had already experienced the bitterness of failure. He focused on his work and slept in one corner of the office. He engaged in the export of agricultural and fishery goods to Manchuria and Beijing, until he later established a factory to manufacture noodles. The brand “Byeolpyo Guksu” (Star Noodles) made by Samsung Trading Company at the time had three big stars in its logo, and this was the beginning of Samsung.   The building of Samsung Trading Company was torn down in 1997 and only the site remains today. However, it still functions as a “refueling station” for those praying for success and achievement, as it holds the spirit of Chairman Lee as a young man that he kept reminding himself of until Samsung Trading Company became the Samsung of today. If you are interested in seeing what Samsung Trading Company actually looked like instead of this mockup, it is recommended to visit the Samsung Creative Campus in Buk-gu, Daegu. It features a replica of the company of the 1940s that was built with the exact same old materials.   Chairman Lee stated in his critical biography as follows: “There is nothing such as a waste in life... (omitted) Even if you feel that time was spent for nothing, there must be something meaningful in it. The problem is not spending time for nothing, but how to accept reality and take it as a meaningful experience for the future.” The lesson Chairman Lee has emphasized seems to be that if you are standing at a critical turning point of life, not to hesitate, but to make the most of each valuable moment.."

stories.title: Dalseong Park (Dalseongtoseong Earthen Fortification)
stories.audioTitle: (9) Modern Streets of Daegu: Dalseong Park (Dalseongtoseong Earthen Fortification)
stories.script: "A golden statue of King Sunjong, the last king of Joseon, stands in front of the main gate of Dalseong Park. It was erected in January 1909 at a point of the Royal Tour of Emperor Sunjong to commemorate his visitation to Daegu. The expressions on the Emperor’s face and the people looking at it, however, seem somewhat gloomy. What could have made the Emperor take the painful journey all the way to Dalseong Park in the late period of Joseon, one of the bleakest moments of Korean history?  Dalseong Park is a place where many people of Daegu have spent joyful moments during their childhood. V of BTS, who was born in Daegu, also said that he still has pictures of himself playing in Dalseong Park as a child. During the Three Kingdoms Period, there used to be a fortress wall built of clay on the site of the park. People living inside the wall were some of the most powerful in the region. The hill in the middle of the basin-shaped Daegu was the optimal spot to observe the area, especially when fighting against the invasion of enemies. Dalseongtoseong Earthen Fortification, still holding countless ancient relics from the Bronze Age, was the fertile ground of Daegu with a 1,800-year old history.   Under the Japanese colonial rule, however, this historic site later became the first park of Daegu in 1905. The park was designed in Japanese style and even had a Japanese shrine for worshiping Japanese gods, where bowing took place in the direction of the seat of the Japanese king. And this was the “Shinto shrine” that Emperor Sunjong personally visited to pay respects. It was truly a heartbreaking moment when the last emperor was made to worship the ancestors of the enemy who not only took his nation’s sovereignty, but also killed his mother. He spent his last years in sorrow until he died in Changdeokgung Palace.   The ordeals of Dalseongtoseong Earthen Fortification continued even after liberation, with the opening of a zoo. The zoo that was built in 1970 became one of the largest zoos of Daegu, holding more than 1,500 species of animals. It was deemed not appropriate to be on a site, however, that held invaluable cultural heritage. This realization came after awareness grew of another zoo that had been built on the sites of Changgyeonggung Palace by the Japanese.   From a fortification to a park, Dalseongtoseong Earthen Fortification underwent many transformations. Its existence of more than 2,000 years in a single spot, however, is of great value in itself. Currently, the Dalseongtoseong Earthen Fortification, built by our ancestors over a hill, is having its century-old disgrace removed and having its original form restored. It is a shared hope of a majority of citizens that this site of great historic significance will be handed down to future generations as a historical site, rather than simply being known as one of the largest parks of Daegu. "

stories.title: Cheongna Hill
stories.audioTitle: (10) Modern Streets of Daegu: Cheongna Hill
stories.script: There is a small hill also known as the “East Hill” as it is situated in the eastern part of Dalseongtoseong Earthen Fortification. It was in the early 20th century that this hill slowly began to be covered in ivy. American missionaries came to the mysterious land of Joseon to settle in this area, but the scorching heat of summer in Daegu may have been a challenge for them. The missionaries began to plant ivies on the facades of their houses to cool down the heat, which later became the origin of the name of the hill, Cheongna Hill.   There are three western-style houses that remain to this day in this beautiful garden that offer a picturesque scene in this hectic city. They are the houses of American Christian Missionaries Switzer, Chamness, and Blair, built around 1910 and named after the missionaries. The houses that create a harmony with nature and the architectural design indeed put the visitors in awe. In 1907, the Japanese teared down the Daegueupseong Walled Town, claiming that it was unnecessary. The stones of the fortress were then sold at extremely low costs. That was when the missionaries took notice that the stones had more value, and brought them to Cheongna Hill to use them as base stones of the houses. The bungalow-style buildings that were trending in California at the time were built over the fortress stones of the time of King Yeongjo. They were two stories tall made of red bricks with Korean roof tiles covering the top. The intelligent and harmonious qualities of the missionaries can be seen from these observations. Although the missionaries have passed away long ago, their houses are well-preserved and currently listed as Tangible Cultural Heritages of Daegu, each functioning as the Museum of Mission, Museum of Medicine, and Museum of Education and History.   Apples are Daegu's specialty. Urban legend has it that the people of Daegu people have fair skin because of the large amount of apples they consume. The first apple tree that made Daegu the home of apples was planted right here on Cheongna Hill and has been passed down to three generations. It was American missionary Dr. Woodbridge O. Johnson (1869-1951) who brought in a young apple tree from his country and planted it here in 1899. Not only did he plant an apple tree, but he also established Jejungwon, the first western medical institution of the Yeongnam region. Jejungwon treated the diseases of Joseon people and taught western medicine to the youth of Joseon. It is the root of the current Keimyung University Daegu Dongsan Hospital.  There is a small graveyard called Garden of Mercy where the souls of the missionaries and their family members lay. Even the chittering birds take a break as if paying respect in here. There is an old gravestone of a missionary with a short but powerful quote. He who died at an early age from a typhoid infection during his mission left this quote: I'm Going To Love Them. He had great love for the people of Joseon, even in the moment he was facing death away from home.  Composer Park Tae-jun (1900-1986) from Daegu was once passing by this hill when he was a student of Keisung Academy. He fell in love at first sight with a girl who went to Sinmyeong Girls’ School, but never had the chance to tell her his feelings. The love story was then composed as a song titled “Thinking of My Friend, which the lyrics were written by poet Lee Eun-sang. This song was released in 1922 and became popular among youngsters despite the dull political scene during the Japanese colonial rule. “When white lilies bloom on a green ivy hill, a symphony of spring reverberates...” The song of springtime that is heard on Cheongna Hill delivers countless love stories to this day.

stories.title: Samirundong -gil Road (Manse-gil)
stories.audioTitle: (11) Modern Streets of Daegu: Samirundong -gil Road (Manse-gil)
stories.script: The March 1st Movement occurred on March 1, 1919 starting from Tapgol Park in Seoul until the movement spread nationwide and reached Daegu on March 8. Thousands of people across all genders, ages, and statuses gathered in Seomun Market to claim back their nation, shouting “Daehan dongnip manse!” (Long live the independence of Korea!) The streets were flooded with Korean flags, showing the desperate feeling of the people at that time. This was the first Manse Movement of the Daegu-Gyeongbuk region. Young students of Keisung Academy, Kyeongbuk High School, and Sinmyeong Girls ‘School were at the center of this movement.  Four days prior to this big event, teachers and students who gathered at the basement of Keisung Academy printed the Korean Declaration of Independence they secretly brought from Seoul and made Korean flags. But these items had to be brought to Seomun Market where the demonstrations were to take place, without being caught by the strict surveillance of the Japanese police. Then, the students took the lead. They hid the flags and leaflets inside their shirts. The boys wore their father's overcoat and disguised themselves as merchants. The girls carried laundry baskets and pretended as if they were headed to the stream to wash their clothes. They did not take the shortcut, but chose to go through the woods of Dongsan Hospital. The 90-step stairway in Cheongna Hill that leads to the direction of Kyesan Catholic Church was the steep slope the students passed with pounding hearts to get to the demonstration venue. It was also the secret path that led the demonstration to succeed.   The demonstrators gathered in the marketplace on a Saturday afternoon at 2 p.m. and recited the Korean Declaration of Independence. They marched, yelling manse as hard as they can. The copies of the Korean Declaration of Independence and Korean flags that were brought by the students scattered in the air. Nationalist leaders, religious people, gisaeng (female Korean entertainers), students, servants... Everyone, regardless of status, cried for independence. The armed Japanese police, however, violently put down the demonstration. The demonstrators dispersed, covered in blood and dirt.   Numerous leaders and students of the movement were arrested and put in jail, but the impact of the event was significant. The movement spread across the Daegu-Gyeongbuk region, prompting more than 90 demonstrations to occur from over 80 spots for two months. The Japanese way of suppression continued to become more brutal, but no one saw the Manse Movement in Seomun Market as a failure, nor regretted having taken part in it on March 8.   Looking up towards the steep 90-step stairway, let us remember the young boys and girls who sacrificed their precious lives to fight for the independence of Korea. While it may easily be passed as a spot for a photo op to us, it is in fact a staircase that represents the spirit of patriotism. Thanks to their brave struggles and sacrifices, the flags on the Samirundong-gil Road (or the Manse-gil) fly proudly to this day.

stories.title: Kyesan Catholic Church
stories.audioTitle: (12) Modern Streets of Daegu: Kyesan Catholic Church
stories.script: In the early 19th century, a large religious group was formed in Daegu after groups of Roman Catholics arrived from Hanyang, escaping the religious persecutions that had been taking place. Kyesan Catholic Church was the chapel and refuge of the pitiful souls. The first outline of the church was designed by Father A.P. Robert (1853-1922) of the Paris Foreign Missions Society. The priest arrived in Korea in January 1877, eight months after his departure from Paris. He withstood persecution, threats, and deportation orders, and engaged in missionary work for 45 years. He was the first priest of the Catholic Archdiocese of Daegu.   On December 25, 1899, Kyesan Catholic Church was revealed in a cross-shaped hanok with beautifully painted roof tiles. Unfortunately, it is no longer available to see this unique hanok, as it had been burnt down after two years since its construction due to an earthquake. Father Robert did not fall in despair, but began to build the foundation all over again. The second blueprint was handed over by Father V.L. Poisnel who had designed both Myeongdong Cathedral in Seoul and Jeondong Cathedral in Jeonju. Kyesan Catholic Church is the first western-style architecture of Daegu that was built in 1902 under Cheongna Hill according to the strong will of Father Robert and the devotion of the followers.   The layers of 120 years of history is visible on the facade built with red and gray bricks. Above the glass window with a rose figure and the arched windows stretched vertically are two spires. The bell on the left is the Augustine Bell, while the one on the right is the Germana Bell, each named after the baptismal names of nationalist activist Seo Sangdon who led the National Debt Redemption Movement and Kim Germana, the wife of nationalist activist Jeong Gyuok, who donated the bell. The Augustine Bell is still rung three times a day from the attic on the second floor by three bell-ringers employed by the church to let know the time for Angelus.  The history of the church is more visibly evident from inside of the church. The stained glass windows through which light passes were brought from France, via Vladivostok, finally reaching Daegu of Joseon through the Trans-Siberian Railway. The colorful windows that surround the altar and the statue of St. Mary of Lourdes, the guardian of Kyesan Catholic Church, are designed with St. Francis Xavier, who greatly contributed to spreading Catholicism in Asia, the Sacred Heart of Jesus, St. Mary, and St. Joseph. The stained glass with the martyrs of Korea in hanbok were newly installed during the building repair and restoration in the 1990s.   The “interesting and pointy house” as it was known by the people of Joseon 120 years ago still maintains its original shape welcoming pilgrims even today. How about taking a peaceful moment here, taking in the view of old columns and chairs that witnessed the prayers of those throughout the past century? Take time to also appreciate the healing light that come in through the stained glass windows.

stories.title: House of Yi Sanghwa and House of Seo Sangdon
stories.audioTitle: (13) Modern Streets of Daegu: House of Yi Sanghwa and House of Seo Sangdon
stories.script: In Gyesan-dong, Jung-gu, next to tall apartment buildings, stand two small old houses facing each other. They are the old houses of anti-Japanese poet Yi Sanghwa (1901-1943) and nationalist activist Seo Sangdon (1851-1913). The two hanoks still stand as if time has frozen in the middle of this hectic city. Let's take a deeper look into the story behind this street where the new and old are oddly intertwined.  Some people may want to demolish old and abandoned structures to make way for newer buildings that would carry greater value in the real estate market. These two houses also came to the brink of being brought down as part of the city's urban development project. Luckily, citizens of Daegu who opposed to the idea made a petition. They collected signatures of one million citizens and raised funds to preserve the old houses. Thanks to their efforts, the houses were restored to their original shape and returned to the citizens in 2008.   The House of Yi Sanghwa has a small front yard with persimmon and pomegranate trees and it is where the poet had spent the last four years of his life focusing on writing more of his works. In 1937, he was in great despair when he was let free after serving three months in prison for meeting Gen. Yi Sangjeong, who was his older brother and an independence activist. He spent his darkest days until he was diagnosed with stomach cancer. In the spring of 1943, he passed away just before Korea’s independence took place, the day he had been longing for such a long time. His death came at the rather young age of 42.   Seo Sangdon is another figure of Daegu who fought to get our nation back in the late period of Joseon. While poet Yi Sanghwa fought for independence through literature, Seo Sangdon led the National Debt Redemption Movement by proposing to quit smoking to save money and restore sovereignty. Although it ended up a failure due to Japanese intervention, it was a meaningful attempt that proved the unity of the people. Only a part of Seo Sangdon's house has been restored as it has had greater damage. Nevertheless, his noble spirit still remains the way it used to be.   Yi and Seo may not be from the same generation, but they both fought in their own ways to get away from the restraints imposed by the Japanese. History clearly says that they were models of patriotism to many people. Now, they have become close neighbors, warmly welcoming their descendants. Take time to walk along the houses and send your gratitude for the passion and struggles of the nationalist activists who passed away before witnessing the joy of independence.

stories.title: Kim Won-il's Madang Gipeun Jip
stories.audioTitle: (14) Modern Streets of Daegu: Kim Won-il's Madang Gipeun Jip
stories.script: Kim Won-il's Madang Gipeun Jip located in the Modern Street of Daegu is a space that focuses on literature and encourages visitors to experience the spirit of literature. Visually speaking, it was designed to take after the house as depicted in the novel House with a Sunken Courtyard by Kim Won-il. There are several literary spaces nationwide that are named after writers, but this is the first of its kind that recreated the setting of a novel as a stage. Let's find out more about the story that realistically reproduced the landscape of Jung-gu in the 1950s.   Gil-nam in the novel is a 13-year-old boy who lived in the fourth room attached to a house with a sunken courtyard. His single mother took care of four children and frequently scold Gil-nam, the first son. Gil-nam would often be made to deliver newspapers and chop woods. It was his mother’s way to teach him how to become the head of a household. Gil-nam was hungry all the time and was upset with his mother treating him harshly as if he were a servant. He would  run away from home, but soon get caught by his mother the very same day.   Gil-nam's family shared the house with other families from Gyeonggi, Pyeongyang, and Gimcheon, who were all war refugees who left their hometowns. Author Kim Won-il was in the same shoes. This vivid story reflected the actual childhood days of the author. The main character Gil-nam was an autobiographical figure of the author Kim whom he projected his own soul in.   Kim’s House with a Sunken Courtyard (1988) is recognized as a masterpiece depicting the division of the two Koreas, and is still a steady seller with more than 20,000 copies sold every year. It was recreated as a TV series in the 1990s, gaining nationwide popularity. The novel was then sold internationally after it was translated into French, German, Spanish, and Japanese. This proves that the story of a boy who was forced to live a sorrowful life after the Korean War had touched the people of the world beyond race, nationality, and mind.   The story ends with the demolition of the house, but the doors to this literary piece where you can experience the spirit of the novel still remain open to everyone. When in this space, it doesn't matter whether you have read the novel or not. Take a look around the exhibition halls that are a mixture of fiction and non-fiction, and you can come to meet the spirit of the character Gil-nam in the sunken courtyard.The visit is sure to offer you a sense of calm and consolation.

stories.title: Christian History Museum of the First Presbyterian Church of Daegu
stories.audioTitle: (15) Modern Streets of Daegu: Christian History Museum of the First Presbyterian Church of Daegu
stories.script: The sign set in stone reads “Jeil Chapel” and allows us to imagine how old this church must be. The grandeur gothic-style structure stacked with red bricks is the third church of the First Presbyterian Church of Daegu that holds a history of over 120 years. Built in 1933, a five-story bell tower was built three years later, completing its shape of today. This church became the Christian History Museum of the First Presbyterian Church of Daegu in 1994 after a new building of the church was built on Cheongna Hill.   The church underwent changes to its name, appearances, and location over time, but the fact that Christianity of the Daegu-Gyeongbuk region was born here remains. The American Presbyterian missionary William Martyn Baird (1862-1931) was the one who sowed the seed of Christianity in the region in 1893. He was the first missionary from overseas who came past Busan to Daegu.   Baird found Daegu to be a very attractive city. It was the core city of politics and commerce as both Gyeongsanggamyeong Provincial Office and Yangnyeongsi Market were located there, and it had a great transportation system and a large population. The late 19th century was when Christian mission had spread across Joseon and the people's interest toward foreigners and Christianity was higher than ever. However, it was different in Daegu. People of Daegu were extremely hostile to “foreign strangers.   This was when the missionaries started using Korean names to show intimacy. Baird called himself “Bae Wi-ryang”, Adams as “Ahn Eui-wa”, and Johnson as “Jang In-cha” to get closer to the people of Daegu. Ahn Eui-wa and Jang In-cha, or James E. Adams (1867-1929) and Woodbridge O. Johnson (1869-1951), respectively, were the ones who established Daenam Primary School (current Chongro Elementary School), Keisung Academy, and Sinmyeong School in this foreign land despite religious persecutions as well as “Miguk Yakbang” (American Drugstore) that later became Jejungwon (current Keimyung University Daegu Dongsan Hospital), the first western-style hospital in Daegu.   The First Presbyterian Church of Daegu that started with one member has now accumulated a history of 120 years. It is also known as the “Mother Church” of the many churches that branched out to all regions of Daegu-Gyeongbuk. The leaders of this church did not simply focus on spreading the gospel and increasing the number of its followers, but they also created a new vision for the future on a barren land by establishing educational and medical institutions. They also actively participated in the March 1st Movement in Daegu in March 1919, consoling the souls of the poor who had lost their nation. This must be the guidance of Jesus Christ that Christianity had always wanted to spread in this world.

stories.title: Yakjeon Alley – Daegu Yangnyeongsi Museum of Oriental Medicine
stories.audioTitle: (16) Modern Streets of Daegu: Yakjeon Alley – Daegu Yangnyeongsi Museum of Oriental Medicine
stories.script: The history of Yakjeon Alley traces back to the 17th century during the Joseon Dynasty (1658, 9th year of King Hyojong's reign). The Yangnyeongsi Market that sold seasonal medicinal herbs would stay open for about a month every spring and fall near an inn inside the Gyeongsanggamyeong Provincial Office. The place was crowded with medicine vendors and dealers from across the country, and the market also benefited greatly from the foot traffic to and from nearby restaurants, pubs, and inns. The market, initially formed to collect medicinal herbs of good quality for the royal family, became a cultural institution in itself, also serving as a festival promoting good health of ordinary citizens.   The Yangnyeongsi Market later opened in Jeonju and Wonju as well, making the three Yangnyeongsi Markets the “Big 3” markets of the country. It is only the one in Daegu, however, that remained as one of the longest standing markets for Korean medicine. This was possible because Taebaek and Sobaek Mountain Ranges surrounding the Gyeongsang-do Province, as well as the regions of the Nakdonggang River, were rich in medicinal herbs and minerals. Daegu also had the advantage of having an excellent transportation system. There was even a saying that medicinal herbs that cannot be found in Hanyang would often be found in Daegu Yangnyeongsi Market.   The humble but festive market, however, was shut down in 1908 after the Japanese demolished the Daegueupseong Walled Town as well as the inn where the market was held. What used to be a hub for the trading of medicinal herbs that would then be distributed to all parts of the nation and overseas, including Japan, China, and Europe, was forced into near extinction during the Japanese colonial rule. But it was saved by the persistent efforts of merchants who gave their all to protect the traditional medicine of Korea. This is how the Daegu Yangnyeongsi Market was relocated to “Yakjeon Alley” in Namseong-ro.  With a 350-year old history, the market of medicinal herbs is the pride of Koreans, standing out even in the global historical context not only for the abundant supply of various medicinal herbs, but also for the practices of Koreans that made the most of such ingredients. If you wish to learn more of and experience the history and culture of Daegu Yangnyeongsi Market, it is highly recommended to visit the Daegu Yangnyeongsi Museum of Oriental Medicine.  The market is not as big as it used to be, but the unique smell of the herbs will definitely “heal your body and soul as you walk along the street. The sceneries of old-fashioned Korean medicine shops will also offer you a glimpse of the past. You can enter any of the shops to have your pulse taken. Take a stroll and enjoy healing energy that the Yakjeon Alley brings you.

stories.title: Yeongnam-daero
stories.script: Have you ever imagined an ultrafast train that goes from Seoul to Busan in just 16 minutes? Well, the idea actually already exists. It is called Hyperloop and is hailed as the mode of transportation of the future. While still in its planning stage, the train nonetheless appears set to become a reality in the near future, given the rapid pace of railway development. But perhaps what is more unimaginable than a train that moves at the speed of light is the fact that not so long ago, people used to travel from Seoul to Busan on foot.   In the past, when there were neither cars nor railways, Daedong Yeojido (Map of the Great East) showed that Yeongnam-daero was the fastest route that connected Seoul and Busan. The route that started from Busan went past Daegu, Mungyeongsaejae Pass, Chungju, Yongin, and finally reached Seoul. It was along this route that people and goods moved. Scholars who went to Hanyang (Seoul) to take government exams especially made use of this road. They would start their journey from Dongnae, Busan after having an early breakfast at dawn, and it took them 14 days on foot to get to Gwanghwamun Gate in Seoul.   The scholars used the term “gwangwang,” or to go see light, when they left their homes to take the government exam. The light, representing the king, was a sign of strong determination that they would bring honor to the family by passing the exam. The word “gwangwang” now means to travel in Korean, but this is the background of the origin of the word.   Mungyeongsaejae Pass, which is now a popular tourist attraction, was known to be extremely difficult to pass, even for birds. But scholars chose to go through this tough course instead of easier routes such as Chupungnyeong Pass or Jungnyeong Pass to show their strong will for passing the exam. They believed that if they went through Chupungnyeong Pass, they would fail the exam like falling leaves, and if they went through Jungnyeong Pass, they would fail the exam like slipping from bamboo trees. If they went through Mungyeongsaejae Pass, however, they would hear joyous news.   Try walking along the old path of Yeongnam-daero where the scholars took their way to the light of gwangwang. “A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step” is a quotation in the Tao Te Ching ascribed to Laozi. Although it is not recommended these days to take a walk from Busan to Daegu the way scholars of old times did, we can learn the value of taking time in this world where all emphasis is placed on speed.

stories.title: Jingolmok Alley
stories.audioTitle: (18) Modern Streets of Daegu: Jingolmok Alley
stories.script: “Jin,” a dialect of the Gyeongsang-do Province meaning “long, “Jingolmok Alley” literally means “a long alley. Although it may look like a rather quiet, curved and narrow street today, it used to be a busy alley where most of the wealth of the city was known to pass through a century ago.   This alley that connects from Jongro to the Chinese Elementary School has a century-old history. The map of Daegueupseong Walled Town (1905) shows that when commoners came in and out of Gyeongsanggamyeong Provincial Office, a government office of Gyeongsang-do, they went through Jingolmok Alley to avoid the street that the noble class called yangban would take. It is also said that the female nationalist activists' group originated from this street. The group was called Namildong Paemul Pyeji Buinhoi and participated in the National Debt Redemption Movement during the Japanese colonial rule.   Jingolmok Alley saw its traffic at its peak when Seo Byeong-guk of the Dalseong Seo clan and his brothers arrived to live in the area. Later, the late Founder and Chairman Lee Won-man of Korea Nylon Inc. (current KOLON Industries), the late Founder and Chairman Kim Hong-sik of Kumbokju, and other influential figures of the region gathered around the alley forming a wealthy neighborhood. Today, only the few houses that remain are witness to the glorious days of the past.   Those who wish to trace back historical moments in modern times usually start with a tour of Jeong Pediatrics first, located at a mid-point of the alley to the western side. It is the former house of Seo Byeong-jik and Seo Byeong-guk, designed by architect Mo Mun Geum who came from China in 1937. It was later purchased by Dr. Jeong Pil-su in 1947 and passed down for generations until present. The two-story house was built on a site that covered about 660 m2 and has a garden with old and beautiful trees, an open-air area, a western-style tub and other features that show the luxurious lifestyle during the Japanese colonial rule.   If those at Jeong Pediatrics  only allow you to take a peep inside the yard, you can head to Mido Teahouse instead to experience something similar to what would have been experienced by the “modern boy” of the romantic period. The teahouse  was where artists, politicians, and high-profile figures of Daegu usually gathered. Poets Kim Chun-su, Shin Dong-jib, and Jeon Sang-yeol also wrote pieces about this teahouse, proving how much this space was loved by the people of Daegu. Inside, you will be greeted with a typical traditional teahouse of Korea, such as the five-colored sitting cushions, beautiful western-style paintings that fill the walls, and an enormous fish tank. Senior citizens still come to Mido Teahouse to drink ssanghwacha (medicinal herbal tea) with an egg yolk on top of it. It is only the young visitors that are something new in this space.

stories.title: Chinese Elementary School
stories.audioTitle: (19) Modern Streets of Daegu: Chinese Elementary School
stories.script: This place where the Flag of the Republic of China flies in the wind is the Chinese Elementary School located in Daegu. The entrance to the school has wall paintings depicting influential figures of China, including Emperor Taizong of Tang, Qin Shi Huang, and Confucius. At one corner of this yellow building, you will find an adorable painting of a panda, a significant symbol of China. What is the significance of this small school with a bust of the President of the Republic of China Chiang Kai-shek for the city of Daegu?  It appears that Daegu was considered attractive to the Chinese who frequented the Yangnyeongsi Market to purchase medicinal herbs. In 1905, when the Gyeongbu Line, a railroad that connects the north and the south, opened, many Chinese migrated to Daegu and formed a community. This is the beginning of the history of the Chinese diaspora in Daegu. Those who we call “the Chinese diaspora” in Korea are the Chinese and their descendants who arrived and settled in Korea before the establishment of official diplomatic ties between Korea and China in 1992.  Architect Mo Mun Geum who greatly influenced the modern history of architecture in Daegu was also Chinese. The architect, who was nicknamed “the master of brick architecture,” built numerous structures that remain as significant architectural heritages of Daegu. As he was especially renowned for designing religious architectures, such as the Kyesan Catholic Church, Holy Mother's Shrine, and Community Building of Sisters of St. Paul, Daegu's greatest man of wealth Seo Byeong-guk came to him and asked to design his private house.  The location of this school of over 3,300 m2 used to be the private land of Seo Byeong-guk before the national liberation. He used to live in a mansion on the site. But his wealth was worthless when it came to treating cholera that swept across Daegu. After Seo died in 1946 due to the epidemic, Mo raised funds from overseas Chinese that were scattered around the country, and purchased Seo’s lot. Later, a signboard that read “Overseas Chinese Association” was put up on the building that Mo personally built himself. The building of the Association decorated with white granite over red bricks still boast a beautiful appearance despite its more than 100-year history.  Many overseas Chinese later left Korea with the upheaval of world history. Mo, who lived a prosperous life mingling with people of Daegu, also sold Gunbanggak, the first Chinese restaurant in Daegu that he operated, and returned to Taiwan. Is it appropriate to call members of the Chinese diaspora who gave us marvelous architectures, restaurants known for their good food, the tea culture, antique shops, and other aspects of Chinese culture strangers? Are these people who lived with us for over a century indeed strangers? In October, take a walk along the street of Jongno dressed in red. The members of the Chinese community in Daegu, amounting to approximately a thousand will be hosting an exciting festival that is worth seeing.

stories.title: Gukchaebosang Memorial Park - The National Debt Redemption Movement Memorial Hall
stories.audioTitle: (20) Modern Streets of Daegu: Gukchaebosang Memorial Park - The National Debt Redemption Movement Memorial Hall
stories.script: In the early 20th century, the Empire of Japan established roads, railroads, ports, banks, hospitals, and schools on the Korean Peninsula, justifying its policy of modernization of the Korean Empire. As such projects required tremendous amount of money, the Japanese government manipulated pro-Japanese Ye Wanyong to force the Korean government to take out a loan to execute the projects. The loan at that time was KRW 13 million, which is around KRW 860 billion in current value. Despite the situation where the Korean government suddenly found itself burdened with a huge debt, they had no power to complain against the absurd deal, nor the capacity to repay the amount. This pushed the Korean Empire into bankruptcy.  Then came along Seo Sangdon (1850-1913), the greatest merchant of Daegu during the time, who argued that Korea would be able to claim back its sovereignty once the debt is paid back. Other nationalist activists including President Kim Kwang-je (1866-1920) of Gwangmunsa helped Seo promote this idea. They formed a National Debt Redemption Group and published a letter through the media, including Korean Daily News. That was the beginning of the National Debt Redemption Movement, the first movement aimed at restoring the economic sovereignty of Korea.  The Korean population of 20 million joined in on the movement. Men quit smoking for three months and women donated their jewelry to help fund the movement. Women especially played a critical role, so much so that some call this movement the first women's movement of Korea. Patriotic gisaeng (female Korean entertainers) in particular showed great devotion. Gender, age, wealth, or social class did not matter in saving the country.  Unfortunately, this movement had a low chance of success from the very beginning. Even if it would lead to collecting a great amount of money, the Japanese Empire made other sabotages and had the pay greater amounts. As expected, the movement resulted not only in failure in regaining the economic sovereignty, but also loss in the valuable assets of the people. Nevertheless, thousands of records of the movement were later registered as UNESCO World Heritage in 2017. The light of hope that was shown by the people of a small nation in 1907 was an unprecedented movement in the world.   Gukchaebosang Memorial Park, where National Debt Redemption Movement Memorial Hall is situated, is a well-maintained site featuring the Dalgubeol Grand Bell, a bell that is rung in the New Year. There are also paths through the green forest with quotes by ancient sages marked along the way. Take a moment to walk through the park, imagining the passion of people participating in the National Debt Redemption Movement over a century ago here in Daegu. Feel the never-ending passion for the movement that was participated by King Gojong, independence activist An Jung-geun, overseas Koreans, and even thieves and panhandlers. The March 1st Movement during the Japanese colonial rule, the gold-collecting campaign to repay the debt to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in the 1990s, and the citizenship that the Koreans have shown during the COVID-19 crisis that hit the global community in 2020 are some of the movements that prove Korean passion never dies.

stories.title: Kim Kwang Suk Memorial Mural Road
stories.audioTitle: (21) Modern Streets of Daegu: Kim Kwang Suk Memorial Mural Road
stories.script: There was once a Korean singer who would often pose the question , Are you happy? to the public. There was no way to find out if he was happy with his own life, but he always prayed for everyone's happiness with a smile on his face when singing his songs. The name of this singer is Kim Kwang Suk (1964-1996). Though several years have passed since his sudden death, his name still evokes powerful emotions in many fans, as he is known as a singer who captured moments in the lives of ordinary people and expressed those moments through beautiful songs and poems. People from all parts of the country now visit the Kim Kwang Suk Memorial Mural Road to feel the soul of the singer.  This 350-meter-long road was established to commemorate the singer who was born and raised in Daebong-dong, Daegu. You can see his portraits and songs everywhere that never get old. Kim who put the audience in awe with his lyrics “My music is my strength, my music is my life” sang along with a classic guitar and harmonica shows his attitude toward music and life. “Hey, do you know what goes best with soju? Kim Kwang Suk's songs. His songs are a perfect match with soju...” This short dialogue written on the wall is rather making the people crave for a glass of soju.   Until 2009, this road used to be surrounded with a filthy retaining wall. The Bangcheon Market located on the right side of the road was going old and saw a drop in the number of visitors with each passing day. Then, merchants and artists gathered to prompt change. The empty shops in the market turned into workshops of artists, and their passion brought liveliness to the market. The market regeneration project led to establishment of the Kim Kwang Suk Road, which vitalized the market and converted the region into a national tourist attraction.  Kim made over 1,000 performances in small stages for six years from 1989 to 1995 and always wished to perform near the audience. He may have left us years ago, but his songs sound more vivid as times go by. He still remains as a brother, a friend, a son, and a lover in our hearts. And just like his walk of life, works of many artists that are exhibited in the Kim Kwang Suk Road continue to change, striving to bond with the public.  During his performance on August 15, 1995, Kim said: “There is something I wish to do when I turn 40. I want to buy a motorbike. A Harley-Davidson. A very nice one. I even made savings. But my acquaintances are concerned that my feet won't reach the ground. Haha. I want to navigate the world riding it.” However, in less than six months since he made that comment, he passed away at the age of 33. He never got to travel the world nor buy a motorbike. Once you exit the Kim Kwang Suk Road, you will reach the Bangcheon Market. The large structure on the market entrance attracts the attention of visitors. It was built under the theme of “Door of Happiness,” which is one of Kim's songs. If you still miss the singer after humming some of his songs, then nothing would be more amazing than visiting one of the old shops in the market and taking a drink paired with the traces of Kim Kwang Suk.

stories.title: Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School
stories.audioTitle: (22) Modern Streets of Daegu: Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School
stories.script: There is a stone sign that reads “Hamabi” by the stairway to the Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School. “Hama” means to get off the horse and walk. This sign was put in front of palaces, royal tombs, temples of Confucius, and royal ancestral shrines during the Joseon Dynasty, where it was necessary to pay respect to a subject. Those who ignored the sign were severely punished. The reason why this sign was placed here was because this place was a school where the scholars of the Joseon Dynasty studied Confucianism and admired ancient sages, including Confucius.  Hyanggyo was a national secondary education institution of the Joseon Dynasty. Scholars of over 16 years of age who completed seodang, or a private village school, were eligible to enroll. The students practiced proprieties and studied and learned Confucianism. The history of hyanggyo begins from the Goryeo Dynasty, but it was most appreciated after the establishment of the Joseon Dynasty in 1392. As hyanggyo were established in large and small villages throughout the country, Joseon was able to strengthen its position as a Confucian nation. 600 years since then, there are about 200 hyanggyo left on the Korean Peninsula today.  Past an outer three-door gate with a message that wishes you good luck and health, you will be greeted with a marvelous and peaceful landscape as if you have entered a different world. Inside the school you can find: Daeseongjeon Shrine where the tablets of Confucius and other ancient sages are enshrined; Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall that was used as the classroom of scholars; Dongjae East Dormitory and Seojae West Dormitory; and a white statue of Confucius who founded Confucianism. Imagine the young scholars of the period passing through Daeseongjeon Shrine, studying hard without break, and going in and out of the dormitories.  Built in 1398, the Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School saw a lot of events take place throughout history. It suffered a series of fires and repairs, reconstruction and relocation, until it finally settled down in 1932 at the current location. Despite the fact that all villages that had or have a hyanggyo are called “Gyo-dong”or “Myeongnyun-dong,” the Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School is currently located in Namsan-dong. It was the Japanese colonialists that forced the relocation of the school to the outskirts of Daegu, so that it could not be used as the base of independence movement by scholars.  Confucianism is often misinterpreted as an old-fashioned idea that does not fit in with the contemporary world. The belief in the relationship of people and the true meaning of being human as promoted by Confucianism, nevertheless, still has a place in contemporary life. Especially so in this hyper-competitive world where courtesy, respect, social order, and stability often take a back seat. Take a moment to get a deeper insight into Confucianism values from the Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School.

stories.title: Banwoldang
stories.script: Gangnam Station is to Seoul as Banwoldang Station is to Daegu. Banwoldang Station, Daegu Metro’s first-ever interchange station, is the busiest subway station in Daegu as bustling as Gangnam Station, which is always jam-packed with a floating population of the Seoul metropolitan area. The station boasts 23 exits — making it the subway station with the most exits in Korea. These exits provide convenient access to Dongseong-ro, a street of youth often comparable to Seoul’s Myeong-dong, and several large department stores. As such, Banwoldang has long been widely regarded as the main gate of downtown Daegu and as the meeting place for not just citizens, but also a place where different cultures and trends mingle. It is more than likely that every citizen of Daegu probably has a fragment of his or her youth planted somewhere in Banwoldang Negeori (four-way intersection).  Surprisingly, however, there is a saying that “Many people know of Banwoldang, but not many people actually know Banwoldang.” That is, apart from senior citizens who have stood the test of time, not many people are aware that Banwoldang used to be a “place” before it became a “name of a place.” Banwoldang is one of the leading examples where the significance of the place has been lost with the passage of time and urban development. Still, Banwoldang survived as the name of a place, ready to bring us the memories of the past if we are willing to look into it.   During the Japanese colonial rule, Daegu became a large city locked in by land, where four department stores opened. As it can be assumed from their names, the Ibishya Department Store, the first department store of Daegu that was built in Dongseong-ro in 1932, and the Minakai Department Store, opened in Bukseong-ro in 1934, were both established with Japanese capital. Meanwhile, Banwoldang and Muyeongdang were the first department stores that were built with Korean capital around the same time.   Banwoldang opened a year ahead of Muyeongdang in 1936 in a building with a wooden structure of two stories. It was built by Cha Byeong-gon, a merchant of the Yakjeon Alley. Most of the products here were for women, such as luxury cosmetic brands, parasols, and handicrafts, but its glorious days did not last long. It had two big fires in just a year since its opening, and the building eventually burned down. The sad fate of Banwoldang eventually came to an end when it was completely torn down in 1981 to make way for a road expansion project.  Have a moment in Banwoldang and imagine the fashion lovers of the 1930s who would have frequented the Banwoldang Department Store for the latest trends. The area surrounding Banwoldang was nothing more than a land near Amisan Mountain until the opening of department stores started a golden era for the commerce of Daegu, building up to what we see today. There may not be many people who recall Banwoldang Department Store as the first department store that was built in Daegu with Korean capital, but its name still carries significance in the cultural history of Daegu.

stories.title: Gwandeokjeong Martyrs' Memorial
stories.audioTitle: (24) Modern Streets of Daegu: Gwandeokjeong Martyrs' Memorial
stories.script: In front of Gwandeokjeong Martyrs' Memorial lies an odd-looking structure made of stone. It is not a tablet, a sign, or a sculpture, but a brutal torture device called the “stone hyeonggu” that was used for hanging people in the Joseon Dynasty. A person's head with a rope around the neck was put inside the hole on the stone, which then an animal from the other side of the stone pulled the rope to execute the person. The device was also called a “stork stone, saying that the executed person with the head pulled out of the body looked like a stork. This inhumane device is an original piece that was actually used in 1866 (6th year of King Gojong's reign) by Heungseon Daewongun to execute nine French missionaries and over 8,000 Roman Catholics during the Byeongin Persecution.  Gwandeokjeong Pavilion, also referred to as Gwandeokdang Pavilion, was a government building built to train the military with archery and martial arts. The front yard was also a military training ground where the government exam for military officials took place. Since Gyeongsanggamyeong Provincial Office was established in Daegu after the Japanese invasion of Korea, this yard was then used as an execution site to behead criminals who were transferred from the Gyeongsang-do Province. Gwandeokjeong Pavilion became more notorious in the 19th century when Joseon was frantically repressing and persecuting Cheondoists and Roman Catholics. The persecution stole the lives of many religious people including Founder Choe Je-u (1824-1864) of Cheondoism and Catholic saint John Yi Yun-il (1815-1867).  In 1991, in commemoration of the 200th anniversary of Catholicism making it to Korea, Gwandeokjeong Martyrs' Memorial was built on the very site where many martyrs lost their lives at the foot of Amisan Mountain. The white and strong granite surrounding the building represents the pure and firm faith of the Catholics, while the facade, a reproduction of the old Gwandeokjeong Pavilion, is colored with dancheong (Korean traditional decorative colouring), representing the shapes of Catholic symbols and figures. This memorial hall that houses a small chapel, an exhibition hall of the martyrs' relics, and the remains of John Yi Yun-il should be the most significant and holiest place of the Roman Catholic Church in Yeongnam area with a sorrowful history.  Catholicism was introduced as a field of study from the West in the late Joseon Dynasty before it became known as a religion. The Catholics, however, went through brutal repression and persecution as a result of political unrest. This was because the belief of Catholicism that stated all people, including women and the lowest class, are equal and this was perceived to harm the social class system of Joseon. Accordingly, Heungseon Daewongun installed steles condemning reconciliation in every parts of the country, showing extreme hostility against foreign influence. Later, with the establishment of the Korea-France Treaty of 1886, Catholicism was finally accepted as a religion. It was after 20 years since the Byeongin Persecution in 1866 and 100 years since the religion was first introduced to the Korean Peninsula.  Take your time to go up to the pavilion of Gwandeokjeong Martyrs' Memorial and take in the sweeping view of Namsan-dong. The current view may make it quite unbelievable that this site was once used as an execution site for Catholics who sacrificed their lives for their belief. One must wonder where their courage came from. No matter what your own religion is, take a moment to ponder about what belief is in our lives as you walk along the Namsan-dong Catholic Trail with a history of 100 years.

stories.title: St. Justin Seminary - Catholic Priests Cemetery
stories.audioTitle: (25) Modern Streets of Daegu: St. Justin Seminary - Catholic Priests Cemetery
stories.script: Catholicism in Korea saw an end to persecution it had faced with the turn of the 20th century. In October 1898, among a group of French missionaries of Paris Foreign Missions Society who arrived to Korea, there was a young priest at the age of 23 who just graduated from a theological seminary. It was Bishop Florian Demange (1875-1938) who came to this small and poor country of the East to serve for the people, strove for the development of Korean Catholicism, and transformed the barren land of Namsan-dong into a holy Catholic town.  In 1911, as the Joseon diocese was the core of Korean Catholicism, it was classified as the Daegu diocese with the expansion of the religion. Bishop Demange who was appointed as the first head of the diocese proclaimed Our Lady of Lourdes as the patron saint and made three wishes to her: “If you allow me to construct a house for priests and a seminary and to expand the cathedral (Kyesan Catholic Church), I vow to build a shrine just like the Grotto of Lourdes in France at the best spot reserved for the house for priests.” It did not take very long until his prayer was heard.  Seo Sangdon, one of the wealthiest merchants of Daegu and a devout Catholic, volunteered to take on this project. He donated a lot of more than 33,000 m2 in Namsan-dong and it was soon filled with large trees as well as Romanesque and Gothic architectures. In 1913, the two-story house for priests, followed by the St. Justin Seminary were completed. Finally expanded in 1918, Kyesan Catholic Church was the fruit of the contributions from Catholics around the world. This all happened with the prayer of Bishop Demange. The architectures were designed by the master of Korean Catholic church constructions Father V.L. Poisnel and completed by the delicate work of Chinese technicians, and they still remain as priceless heritages that hold 100 years of the contemporary history of Daegu.  The St. Justin Seminary opened in 1914 and cultivated seven bishops and 67 priests until it was forced to close down by the Japanese Empire in March 1945. The seminary was where Cardinal Stephen Kim Sou-hwan (1922-2009), born in Namsan-dong in Daegu, started his theology studies, enduring the tough boarding school programs at the age of ten. He, who was ordained a priest at Kyesan Catholic Church, was assigned the first cardinal of Korea by Pope Paul VI in 1969. His age of 47, he was the youngest cardinal at the time among the 134 cardinals across the world. All of these happened in half a century since Bishop Demange established the seminary in Daegu. The seminary where Cardinal Kim spent his young days is currently operated as the St. Justin Seminary Centennial Memorial Hall.  Walking along a small path in the seminary, you will see a place that looks like a secret garden. It is the Catholic Priests Cemetery, where life and death, the past and future co-exist. At the entrance is a Latin inscription that reads “Hodie Mihi, Cras Tibi, which is translated as today me, tomorrow you.” It means that the death that these priests have faced will come to us tomorrow. This beautiful cemetery was also built by Bishop Demange in 1915 to comfort the souls of the priests of Daegu diocese. Bishop Demange  was also buried in this place in 1938.

stories.title: Holy Mother's Shrine
stories.audioTitle: (26) Modern Streets of Daegu: Holy Mother's Shrine
stories.script: Past the tranquil path in the forest comes a peaceful and magnificent view that will put you in awe. A shrine dedicated to Our Lady of Lourdes, the patron saint of the Daegu diocese, Holy Mother's Shrine is where people make earnest wishes through lighted candles and where the desperation of the pilgrims are conveyed through prayers. The shrine is also the symbol of the Daegu archdiocese.  The story takes place in 1858, when a 14-year-old girl named Bernadette who lived in Lourdes, a small town located in southwestern France, experienced Marian apparitions on a total of 18 occasions. The first of those 18 visions took place at a cave now known as the Grotto of Massabielle. The little girl immediately knelt down in front of the beautiful lady and prayed with her Rosary. The story spread quickly, forming a Lourdes investigation committee consisted of theologians, scientists, and physicians. In two years, the “Marian Apparitions at Lourdes” was determined to be true. Later, a large cathedral was built over the cave, attracting millions of pilgrims from all over the world every year. The cathedral has become the world's most recognized Marian apparition site.  In 1918, as he had made a pact if his three wishes were to come true, Bishop Demange decided to build the Holy Mother's Shrine at the highest and most beautiful location of the diocese. He enshrined the statue of dedicated to Our Lady of Lourdes in an arched brick structure and it was an exact copy of the Grotto in France. An inscription at the upper side reads “EX VOTO IMMACULATAE CONCEPTIONI (the promise of the immaculate conception),” expressing the gratefulness of the bishop. The numbers on each sides represent the year the bishop made his promise (1911) and the year that he kept the promise (1918). “He had made the promise before God asking for his wishes to come true.”  As a place that proved to be one where “dreams come true”, Holy Mother’s Shrine is also where the mother of Cardinal Kim Su-kyeong was known to have also desperately prayed to the Holy Mother. It is said that her prayers led to a miracle that allowed the cardinal to come back home after he had been forcedly enlisted by the military while he was studying in Japan during the Japanese colonial rule. This anecdote is part of what brings the pilgrims to the site to this day.   The Holy Mother's Shrine of the Daegu archdiocese is a shrine visited by pilgrims throughout the year. It has been a century since the Holy Mother's Shrine has been listening to the countless prayers of petition, appreciation, confession, and blessing. All prayers may be different, but the energy of noble minds are enough to create a miracle. It does not matter whether you are at a church or a chapel. People who constantly pray regardless of the place and time are indeed dignified and beautiful. Pray. Pray not for yourself, but someone around you.

stories.title: Community Building of Sisters of St. Paul of Chartres
stories.audioTitle: (27) Modern Streets of Daegu: Community Building of Sisters of St. Paul of Chartres
stories.script: In 1888, with the arrival of the four French missionary sisters to Joseon for the first time, the Sisters of St. Paul of Chartres formed a small community in a poor country of the East. After the three sisters were sent to Daegu in 1915 as the first sisters of the region, the Community Building of Sisters of St. Paul of Chartres was built in Seoul followed by Daegu. This was also one of the wishes of Bishop Demange that eventually came true.   During the Japanese colonial rule, Daegu became a busy city that was pleasant enough for the Japanese to live in, but there were countless orphans, seniors, and the sick in the streets who had been neglected. There were too many of them for the Catholics to take care of. The people desperately needed nuns. After hearing the news, the French sisters agreed with Bishop Demange and commenced their apostolate by taking care of 30 orphans as soon as they made themselves at home in Namsan-dong, Daegu. This was the nation's first orphanage, the Baekbaekhap Orphanage.  There was a time when the orphanage took care of 400 children immediately following the Korean War. The sisters educated the orphans and visited homes of the sick to provide them with medical care. Their devotion and dedication had a purpose to raise the humane and spiritual dignity of the people. The orphanage closed down in the 1990s, but it has since been converted to “Baekhap Daycare Center,” taking care of the children in the region.  There is a small garden where a St. Mary's statue is enshrined in front of the community building and a history hall that was originally built as a chapel in 1927. At one side of this beautiful setting with large trees and flowers are “meju” blocks, or blocks of fermented soybeans. This practice of placing these blocks originated from the beautiful tradition of the nuns who made and sold meju blocks themselves to make a living and take care of those in need. Preserving the tradition, the “Meju Baekhap Foods” is currently recognized as a well-known food brand produced by the convent.  The history of the Community of the Sisters of St. Paul of Chartres dates back to France in the 17th century. A community was formed when a priest, after discovering hopeless people suffering from poverty and diseases after war, began to gather ladies who could devote themselves to recovering the dignity of these people. The devoted hearts of the priest and the sisters have endured for over 130 years, including through the oppression of the Japanese Empire and horrors of the Korean War. They surely deserve respect. Their home is situated near the residential area rather than in a deep forest. It would have been quite small to fit more than 150 sisters who lived together, but the smiles on their faces shine brighter than diamonds.

stories.title: 2.28 Democracy Movement Hall
stories.audioTitle: (28) Modern Streets of Daegu: 2.28 Democracy Movement Hall
stories.script: Sunday, February 28, 1960. An election campaign of vice presidential candidate Chang Myon of the opposing party was expected to take place near the Suseongcheon Stream in Daegu. At the time when the fourth presidential and vice presidential election was just around the corner, the Liberty Party that wished for the permanent ruling of Syngman Rhee plotted a scheme. The party ordered, rather unexpectedly, high school students of Daegu to go to school on that very Sunday, so that they could not take part at Chang's campaign. Kyeongbuk High School held the final exams; Daegu High School organized a rabbit hunt; Daegu Commercial High School had a farewell party for the senior year students; and Kyungpook National University High School held a special class on that day to follow the orders that had no legitimate grounds.  That Sunday morning, students of Kyeongbuk High School went to school as ordered by the school authorities. The students in uniforms gathered at the school yard, when Lee Dae-woo, the president of the student council, stood behind the podium and read out a resolution. “Fellow students! We are the future of this country, pure and innocent souls that are not influenced by the social evil! Fellow students! There has never been a time throughout history when life has been so oppressive and threatening like today! There has never been a time when such inhumane and violent incidents happened every day! Fellow students! If there is blood flowing inside of you, do not hesitate and stand up!”  As soon as his speech ended, over 800 students took to the streets. They denounced the injustice, corruption, and dictatorship of the Liberty Party and marched to the Gyeongsangbuk-do Provincial Office. Students of Kyeongbuk High School and Daegu High School participated in the demonstration the first day, followed by students of Gyungbuk Girl's High School, Daegu Girls’ High School, and Daegu Commercial High School the next day. Although some schools severely opposed to such movement — Kyungpook National University High School confining students inside the auditorium and Gyungbuk Girl's High School locking down the school gate — there was nothing they could do to discourage the students. The students chanted, citing a poem that was written by Indian poet Rabindranath Tagore which he dedicated to Korea after he was moved by the March 1st Movement. “Light up your lamps! Lamps of the East!” The lamps for anti-dictatorship and democracy had been lighted for the first time since the establishment of the government of the Republic of Korea.  The student protest that ignited in Daegu soon spread to other regions, building up to a nationwide protest. Despite the strong opposition and demonstrations of students, the Liberty Party engaged all sorts of disgraceful activities to manipulate the election. Syngman Rhee had won the election, after all. But the truth was meant to be revealed sooner or later. The March 15th Movement that protested against the electoral fraud began in Masan until it led to the April 19 Revolution with enraged citizens taking to the streets. Syngman Rhee’s dictatorship violently cracked down on these protests and even declared martial law. Shortly after, however, he proclaimed his resignation in front of the furious crowd and quietly stepped down from presidency.  The 2.28 Movement for Democracy that took place in Daegu was not just a rebellion of students who refused to go to school on a Sunday. It was the students’ call for justice against corruption, incompetence, and dictatorship. Hundreds of students were investigated by the police and school teachers were held responsible for the commotion. But they will still be forever remembered as the light of the East that brought democracy into reality.

stories.title: Suncheon Aretjang Market
stories.script: The Biggest 5-day Market in Honam Region  There are several markets in Suncheon but the biggest one is Aretjang. Originally, it was referred as Nambu Market in 1977, but among the local people of Suncheon, it was called “Aretjang.” Naturally, it was officially renamed as “Aretjang,” after revising the ordinance in 2009.  Aretjang of Suncheon is open at all times but a 5-day market is on the 2nd and 7th (2, 7,12,17,22, and 27). On those days, the marketplace is packed from the entrance, Pungcheongyo Bridge, leading to the mouth of the alley of Suncheon Pharmacist. Fresh goods from daily caught seafood from the coastal waters of Suncheon to rare herbs and products from nearby Mt. Jiri are on display. Specifically, local farmers bring out their produces for sales so that you can get same quality products at various prices and quantities.  On Friday and Saturday evenings, there is a night market. In summer, they open from 6 to 11 P.M., and in winter, from 5 to 10 P.M. Unlike the daytime, various food stalls come in and fill the space with lively energy. Since they offer various fusion dishes, it’s a lot of fun to choose from. On a stage, they also hold a singing contest or a music concert so that people from various regions can come together and enjoy the night market.  The following are must-not-miss dishes at Aretjang Market of Suncheon – patjuk, or red bean porridge; sundae gukbap, or blood sausage and rice stew; and jajangmyeon, or black bean sauce noodles. These dishes are popular for their affordable prices and generous portions. The dishes from the daily market, the 5-day market, and the night market are different so you can always stroll around the markets on a full stomach.

stories.title: Seocheon Special Market
stories.script: A Thousand Delights in the Western Sea  Seocheon Special Market is only 5 minutes away from Seocheon Intercity Bus Terminal on foot. It was rebuilt as the modernized special market by integrating street stalls and the old market place scattered around Seocheon in September 2004. The special market is sectioned by fishery, general goods, agricultural produces, eateries, and fish drying so that you can enjoy shopping indoors in any season.  In the special market, all of the unique goods of Seocheon are assembled. The freshest catches and dried seafood of the western sea are waiting to be tasted, and the special goods of Seocheon, such as dried seaweed, Hansan Sogokju, a traditional Korean liquor from Hansan, Seocheon’s old name, and rice cake made with ramie leaves can be purchased here. In the eatery section, you can enjoy menus from simple banquet noodle soups to Korean-style fast food dishes filled with the warmth and generosity of local people.  Seocheon Special Market is also famous for their efforts to renew their traditional marketplace in various ways. They run diverse clubs and provide special courses for local merchants so that they can cope with the fast-changing environment. In fact, they started “Noljang Broadcasting Station” in June 2020 and have been running a community broadcast where the merchants host shows engaging visitors.   The special market is held every 5 days on the 2nd and 7th (2, 7,12,17,22, and 27). It takes place in the parking lot behind the general goods section. On those days, there are many eye-catching diversified goods by street vendors that will surely entertain while strolling around.

stories.title: Sokcho Central Market (Sokcho Tour & Fisheries Market)
stories.audioTitle: Sokcho Central Market (Sokcho Tour & Fisheries Market)
stories.script: Meet All the Specialties of Sokcho!   Welcome to the biggest market in Sokcho! This is Sokcho Central, or Jungang Market. It sprang out amid the Korean War in 1953 when the refugees, soldiers, and local people simply came to live together. It ended up with two names when the new title “Sokcho Tour & Fisheries Market” came to be selected after a naming contest held back in 2005.  The market is a popular place that won the Presidential Award for the “Best Traditional Market” in 2017. The market consists of alleys of seafood vendors, restaurants, and a raw fish center at the underground level. On the second floor, there are clothing shops and other facilities for everyday services for local residents of Sokcho.  The hot spots for tourists are the raw fish center and the food alley. The merchants in the raw fish center underground keep their seafood fresh in facilities that bring in pure seawater. Unquestionably, raw fish is the freshest, and you can enjoy spicy and sour cold raw fish soups. The food alley is filled with famous local delicacies: like stuffed squid, fermented righteye flounder, and millet pancake. Also, whether it is a king crab or red crab, or other seafood, you can have them fried, steamed, or fermented. There are also popular restaurants on social media that serve sweet and sour chicken, or Dak gangjeong, sweet rice punch, and mega gimbap.  Inevitably, eating and sightseeing can make you tired, so go up to the second floor toward the clothing shops, and you will see a resting place. Eating is not allowed in that section, but the market officials hold various events for visitors so you may just get lucky.

stories.title: Hyangho Beach (BTS Bus Stop)
stories.script: Hyangho Beach (BTS Bus Stop)  You all love BTS, don’t you? The K-pop sensation BTS is now the world’s biggest boy band, having recently taken the top spot on the Billboard singles chart. There is a bus stop named after BTS in Hyangho Beach in the Jumunjin district of Gangneung. No bus will ever stop there, but it’s a famous attraction that millions of BTS fans from all around the world come to visit. Hyangho Beach became world-famous when BTS shot their second album cover there in 2017, and fans started to swarm into the area as the fan tour, dubbed the “BTS Tour,” in which fans travel around the sites of BTS’ hottest shooting locations, became popular.   The bus stop at Hyangho Beach has been voted the favorite travel destination among BTS fans around the world! You can see fans sitting on the same exact seat where their favorite stars used to sit and taking photos. BTS also shot the music video for the song “Spring Day” from their second album at Hyangho Beach, which quickly made it on to the fans’ list of hot destinations along with the BTS bus stop. The beautiful horizon where sky meets sea, endless sands, and a remote bus stop near the beach will conjure up your sweetest memories of BTS. Hyangho Beach will be missed as the intro of “Spring Day” goes, “Bogo Shipda”.

stories.title: Chungnyeolsa Temple: Main Hall
