stories.script: 〈 Chungnyeolsa Temple Main Hall 〉  Chungnyeolsa Temple is a hall that enshrines martyrs who sacrificed their lives while fighting against the Japanese invaders in Busan during the invasion in 1592, and the Main Hall is the center of Chungnyeolsa. It was newly constructed in 1978 as a part of the cultural heritage purification project, which has led to its current appearance. The Main Hall enshrines 89 patriotic martyrs including Busa Song Sang-hyeon, Captain Jeong Bal, Commander Yun Heung-sin as well as 23 killed in battle, 4 unknown soldiers and 62 righteous army troops. Although Joseon was a feudal society, people believed that there should be no discrimination in enshrining souls that lost their lives while serving to protect the country, so all of the precious sacrifices are now enshrined in “one place.” In addition, there are the ancestral tablets of Cheol-su and Mae-dong, a pair of loyal servants who collected the body of Busa Song Sang-hyeon.  At the Main Hall, a sacrificial rite is held every year on May 25, of the solar calendar, that corresponds to April 15, 1592 of the lunar calendar, which is the date of the Battle of Dongnaeseong. Chungnyeolsa Jehyang is a rite that has materialized the traditional ideology of Confucianism, and the temple is the only place in the country that enshrines Busa, Gunsu, Cheomsa and servants all together regardless of the class the martyrs had belonged. Also, meritorious deeds of even the faithful servants and concubines are praised through a ritual, and a woman participates as the head of the sacrificial rite at Uiyeolgak to serve in the ritual, which is another unique characteristic of Chungnyeolsa.  During a Simin Jehyang in which citizens may take part, court musicians from the National Gugak Center come and play Jongmyo Jeryeak, or the Royal Ancestral Ritual in the Jongmyo Shrine and its Music, presenting a more realistic vibe. Try to attend a Simin Jehyang if you ever get a chance.

stories.title: Uiyeolgak Shrine (Chungnyeolsa Temple, Busan)
stories.script: Uiyeolgak Shrine of Chungnyeolsa Temple, Busan  Uiyeolgak is a shrine that dedicated to two righteous women and two virtuous women who sacrificed themselves during the Japanese invasion in 1592. Although these individuals were honored together in the main shrine regardless of their status at the time, due to the prevailing norms separating men and women, the four women were specially enshrined in Uiyeolgak Shrine.  The virtuous women are “Aehyang” and “Han Geum-seom”. “Aehyang” was a concubine of Captain Jeong Bal and “Han Geum-seom” was a concubine of Busa Song Sang-hyeon, both of whom died in the Battle of Dongnaeseong while fighting against the Japanese invaders until the end. “Yi Yang-nyeo”, another concubine of Busa Song Sang-hyeon was taken to Japan as a captive, but a Japanese general was moved by her righteous, upright character and integrity, honored her as the teacher of the wives of Japanese warriors. She eventually returned to Joseon at her strong insistence and was posthumously buried next to Busa Song and Han Geum-seom. After knowing their stories, we cannot help but show great respect for these two Joseon women who had sacrificed their lives to protect their precious beliefs and values.  During the Battle of Dongnaeseong, while numerous Japanese soldiers fought with swords and muskets, the people of Joseon fought back using farming tools such as hoes, pitchforks, and sickles, and resisted by throwing stones with their bare hands. The two righteous women climbed onto rooftops, throwing roof tiles at the Japanese invaders and fought back until they were killed by Japanese invaders’ swords. These women, known only as “Ichonnyeo,” lived in Dongnaesang Fortress, and their names remain unknown. You can see what they looked like from “Dongnaebu Sunjeoldo,” the Patriotic Martyrs at the Battle of Dongnaebu Fortress displayed in the memorial hall.

stories.title: Chungnyeolsa Temple: Memorial Hall
stories.script: 〈 Chungnyeolsa Temple Memorial Hall〉  The Memorial Hall, which opened in 1978, features painting records such as the〈Busanjin Sunjeoldo〉 and the 〈Dongnaebu Sunjeoldo〉 from which we can see the situation during the Japanese invasion of 1592 as well as signboards from the old Chungnyeola Temple, Allak Seowon and Sojuldang Hall. Items left behind by the martyrs are also on display here. The most notable exhibit items of them all, 〈Busanjin Sunjeoldo〉 and 〈Dongnaebu Sunjeoldo〉, were created by Byeon Bak, a painter in Dongnaebu, in 1760, and the Chungnyeolsa Temple Memorial Hall currently owns their photoprints. The originals are stored in the “Korea Army Museum.” 〈Busanjin Sunjeoldo〉 depicts in detail the Battle of Busanjinseong, which was the first battle that took place during the Japanese invasion in 1592, in a single painting. 〈Dongnaebu Sunjeoldo〉 also shows contrasting images between Busa Song Sang-hyeon and his troops, throwing a sign that says “Jeonsaigadonan” out the fortress walls for one last deadly showdown at the Battle of Dongnaeseong, as well as the depiction of Yi Gak running away cowardly. You're probably not very familiar with the term, “Jeonsaigadonan,” right? It means that “it is easy to die in battle but it is difficult to give way”. Dongdoisibeop, which is the method of painting events at different points in time within a single drawing, is applied even though the two events did not occur simultaneously. Do you feel the loyalty of our ancestors in these paintings?  The 6 pieces of record paintings hung on the inner wall of the memorial hall include 〈Busanbunjeon Sungukdo〉, which shows the Battle of Busanjinseong and Captain Jeong Bal; 〈Dadaejinseong Gyeoljeondo〉, which depicts the Battle of Dadaejinseong and Commander Yun Heung-sin; and 〈Suyeongyugyeok Jeontudo〉 showing the people of Suyeongseong Fortress forming a righteous army to engage in guerilla warfare against the Japanese. The 3 remaining record paintings are those that describe different battles at Dongnaeseong and the final moments of Busa Song Sang-hyeon based on the 〈Dongnaebu Sunjeoldo〉. They are individually named 〈Naeseongsusa Gyeoluido〉, 〈Dongnaeminjung Bunjeondo〉 and 〈Dongnaeboguk Chungjeongdo>〉, respectively. Looking at the paintings in detail, there is a scene in which the people of Dongnaeseong throw tiles and hold farming tools in their hands to fight against the Japanese invaders immediately prior to the fall of the fortress. There is also Busa Song Sang-hyeon wearing an official dress over his armor, deeply bowing towards the north where the king is, knowing that his time has come. One of the paintings has a scene in which he writes his will onto a fan before being martyred by the Japanese invaders. In addition, the Memorial Hall exhibits 《Cheongok Supil》 , a book written by Busa Song Sang-hyeon himself, as well as other valuable books from Allak Seowon and pieces of armor and helmets worn by the masters of religious rites for the Busa. Now, take as much time as you want to enjoy the memorial hall.

stories.title: Sojuldang (Lecture Hall) (Chungnyeolsa Temple, Busan)
stories.script: Sojuldang of Chungnyeolsa Temple, Busan  Before talking about Sojuldang, let’s explore the history of Allak Seowon Confucian Academy. In 1605, seven years after the Japanese invasion was over, Dongnae Busa Yun Hwon built a shrine called “Songgongsa” on the Nongjusan Observatory near the South Gate of the fortress to honor Busa Song Sang-hyeon. This shrine hence marked the beginning of Chungnyeolsa Temple. Later in 1624, the name “Chungnyeolsa” was bestowed upon the temple and the ancestral tablet of Captain Jeong Bal was also enshrined there.  In 1652, Busa Yun Mun-geo believed that the location of Chungnyeolsa Temple was not appropriate for conducting memorial services as it was humid and noisy. Thus, he moved it to Allak-ri and expanded its size. During this relocation, he also established a Seowon, also known as Confucian Academy, to teach loyalty and scholarly virtues of the patriotic martyrs to future generations and to foster academic diligence.  Sojuldang, which served as the lecture hall for Allak Seowon Confucian Academy, derives its name from the Chinese characters ‘昭’ meaning bright and ‘崒’ meaning high, signifying that the loyalty and scholarly virtues of the martyrs were as bright as the sun and moon and as high as a mountain. This name originates from a poem titled Yi Qing Song by the Tang dynasty writer Han Yu. The couplets on the pillars of Sojuldang is written by Dongnae Busa Gwon Yi-jin, expressing his profound sorrow over the severe suffering endured by ancestors in the aftermath of the Japanese invasion.  In the late Joseon society, Seowon became the center of factional politics and hotbeds of corruption, leading to various societal issues. Consequently, under Heungseon Daewongun reign, he ordered the closure of all seowons except for 47 across the country. However, Chungnyeolsa Allak Seowon Confucian Academy was exempt from this order because it was a shrine honoring the patriotic martyrs of the Imjinwaeran. As a result, it survived the abolition decree, endured the Japanese colonial period, and continues to exist today. In 1976, during a nationwide cultural heritage restoration and purification project, the existing seowon was demolished and reborn in its current form.  A replica of the old Chungnyeolsa Allak Seowon Confucian Academy is displayed inside the memorial hall. By observing the structure of the former Sojuldang replica, you can imagine how the Confucian scholars read and study in Sojuldang at that time!

stories.title: Chungnyeolsa Temple: Song Sang-hyeon's Wisdom Monument
stories.audioTitle: Chungnyeolsa Temple: Song Sang-hyeon's Wisdom Monument
stories.script: 〈Song Sang-hyeon's Wisdom Monument〉  When you look through the precincts of Chungnyeolsa Temple from the main entrance, you will see the Main Hall as well as several tile-roofed buildings and stairs. On the left side of the entrance, there is a pond called Uijungji and an administration office of the temple, and near the staircase up to the Main Hall, 6 crepe myrtle trees can be found. There is a special space in the yard on the right side where these trees are. It is a stele in the name of 〈Song Sang-hyeon Wisdom Monument〉  on which a phrase that reads “Jeonsaigadonan” is engraved. It means that “it is easy to die in battle but it is difficult to give way.”  On April 13, 1592, 18,700 Japanese invaders arrived at the sea in front of Busanpo. The day after, Busanjin Cheomsa Captain Jeong Bal led his troops to fight against the Japanese, however, eventually the captain perished in battle and Busanjinseong Fortress also fell to the hands of the invaders. Records state that the number of people inside Busanjinseong at the time was fewer than 1,000, even when counting government officials and commoners in addition to all the soldiers, all of whom passed away after desperate resistance. After capturing Busanjinseong, one unit of the Japanese invaders headed to Dongnaeeupseong while the other marched to Dadaejinseong. Upon arriving at the south gate of Dongnaeeupseong, it is said that the Japanese troops set up a wooden board that read,  “Jeonjeukjeonui Bujeonjeukgaado”, which means, “Fight if you wish to fight but give way if you do not.”  In response, Song Sang-hyeon wrote a phrase on a wooden tablet and threw it straight to where the enemies stood and this is the famous “Jeonsaigadonan”, which means “it is easy to die in battle, but it is difficult to give way.”  Determined for one last battle, Song Sang-hyeon arrived at his lodge, made a deep bow towards the north to his King and bid his final farewell to his father through a “will poem”.  Goseong Wolun - The ring around the moon has set on a lonely fortress. Yeoljin Gochim - Several camps have fallen into a long sleep. Gunsin Uijung - Though loyalty of vassals towards their king is heavy, Buja Eungyeong - the affection between father and son is light.  In a situation where the Japanese invaders surrounded Dongnaeeupseong like the ring around the moon, yet no commanders from the regions nearby came to rescue, he comforted his sorrowful heart by reciting this poem and said goodbye to his father.

stories.title: Chungnyeolsa Temple: Military Office
stories.script: 〈Military Office〉  As you hike up Mangwolsan Mountain behind Chungnyeolsa for about 15 minutes, you will see the Military Office building. Since ancient times, a piece of land that is ideal to live on refers to one where there can exist a village, and during the Joseon Period, Dongnae was exactly that kind of land. Dongnaebu at the time was the center of the Busan area and Gwana, or government buildings, was also located here. Similar to today's government offices, Gwana was a place for performance of public works and, according to the 《Dongnaebuji》(1740), there were up to 50 structures related to government offices in Dongnaebu. A number of such government offices were built inside the eupseong for administrative and military purposes, and it is typical for these offices to be set up around Dongheon. Dongheon is the office building for the local chief and gaeksa whose job was to enshrine the royal tablet, known as a jeonpae, and to hold rituals.  Cheongsajo from 《Dongnaebuji》has records on the existence of many military offices including Jungguncheong, Janggwancheong, Gyoryeoncheong, Oegungwancheong and Byeolmusacheong. But most of these military offices disappeared when they went through the Japanese occupation period. Only Janggwancheong inside Dongnae Market and Gungwancheong, which had been relocated on the path to Mangwolsan Mountainm, behind Chungnyeolsa Temple we are looking at right now, remain today.  The military office was for military officials of Dongnaebu and though the year of its establishment is not accurately known, some records say that Dongnaebusa Eo Ik-jin rebuilt it in 1675. Its original location was near Dongnae Market but due to the urbanization of the surrounding area, it was moved to near Chungnyeolsa in 1983. When it was dismantled and reconstructed in 1982, the Sangnyangmun discovered underneath a ridge beam of the building has a written record that says, “Dongnaebusa Jo Jeong-cheol extended in 1812”, from which we are offered a glimpse of its history. Although it stands alone up in a mountain, the appearance of a building with 6 cells on the front and 2 cells on the sides standing proudly reminds us of the military officials working at the military office during the time.

stories.title: Chungnyeolsa Temple: Dongjangdae Command Post and Remains of Dongnaeeupseong Fortress
stories.audioTitle: Chungnyeolsa Temple: Dongjangdae Command Post and Remains of Dongnaeeupseong Fortress
stories.script: 〈Dongjangdae Command Post and Remains of Dongnaeeupseong Fortress〉  After looking around the military office and hiking up the mountain for a little bit, you will find Dongjangdae Command Post situated on top of Mangwolsan Mountain and the Remains of the Dongnaeeupseong Fortress. During the Joseon Period, Dongnae was the center of Busan, and Dongnaeeupseong was the fortress built to protect Dongnae. An eupseong was a fortress encompassing the administrative hub, including local government buildings and major infrastructure, and since Dongnae was a coastal area close to Japan, Dongnaeeupseong also served as defense against foreign enemies. Considering that there are records in Dongnae-gun about fortress repairs that took place in 1021 during the Goryeo Dynasty (12th year of King Hyeonjong's reign), the fortress is believed to have existed for a very long time in the Dongae region. The size of the fortress around this time is estimated to be that of today's Mangmi-dong, Suyeong-gu. Then, in the late Goryeo Period, in 1387 (13th year of King U's reign), “Bak Wi”contructed the eupseong in today's Dongnae Market area to block off the Japanese. The eupseong maintained its appearance until the early Joseon Dynasty, and its circumference was about 1.4km (3,090 cheok) while its height was about 4 to 5m (13 cheok).  When the Japanese invaded Joseon in 1592, heroic battles in which Dongnaebusa Song Sang-hyeon and most of the soldiers, government officials, and commoners died took place, and after that, the fortress was left neglected for a while. In 1731 (7th year of King Yeongjo's reign), Dongnaebusa Jeong Eon-seob recognized the importance of Dongnae as a gate into the country, thus constructing a fortress at a much grander scale than before. The details of this event were engraved on a stone known as the “Naejuchukseongbi”by Dongnaebusa Choe Myeong-sang in 1735. The Dongnaeeupseong constructed by Busa Jeong Eon-seob was a typical “pyeongsanseong fortress”, which compromises mountains with flat lands by using the natural topography. There were 6 gates into Dongnaeeupseong and the area connecting Ammun, the west gate, the south gate, and the east gate was a flat land, while the area connecting the east gate, Inseongmun, the north gate, and Ammun featured walls along the ridge of Maansan Mountain. And, among the four command posts of Dongnaeeupseong, the east, west, and north posts, all but the south post, were restored along with the surrounding fortress walls from which we can get a glimpse of the Dongnaeeupseong of the past. On the inside of Dongjangdae, or the east command post, hangs a name sign that says, “Mangwoldae”, which is the writing of Mr. Han Hyeong-seok, an independence fighter from Dongnae, Busan. Mr. Han received a Patriotic Medal of the Order of Merit for National Foundation for his service in the independence movement through artistic activities for national salvation as a part of the Liberation Army during the Japanese occupation period.

stories.title: Baeksan Memorial Hall — 01. Birth of Baeksan – 05. Foundation of Baeksan Sanghoe
stories.audioTitle: Baeksan Memorial Hall — 01. Birth of Baeksan – 05. Foundation of Baeksan Sanghoe
stories.script: Baeksan Ahn Hui-je was born on August 4, 1885 as the eldest son in the house of a local elite and a small landowner in Uiryeong-gun, Gyeongsangnam-do Province. He was so brilliant even at a young age; at the age of 10, he became highly proficient in Saseo Ogyeong (Four Books and Five Classics), the essence of Confucianism, and at the age of 17, he even won a village essay contest. He studied Chinese classics until he turned 20 years old, but as the Japan–Korea Treaty, also known as the Eulsa Treaty, was signed by force in 1905, and Japan deprived of Joseon’s diplomatic rights and interfered with the internal affairs, he resolved to study the new learning for restoration of the national sovereignty. In that same year, he enrolled as a member of the first-ever class of the Department of Economics at Boseong College, which later becomes Korea University.  Lee Yong-ik, the founder of Boseong College, had defected to Russia in opposition of the Eulsa Treaty but met an untimely death in 1907. His grandson, Lee Jong-ho, ran the school in place of him but could not avoid financial difficulties, so it was not an atmosphere in which Baeksan was able to concentrate on studies. For that reason, together with 23 of his fellow students, he transferred to the “Department of Economics at Yangjeong Eui-suk,” which is today's Yangjeong High School, in 1906 and graduated four years later.  As Joseon collapsed due to Korea-Japan merger, he went to Vladivostok, Russia in 1911 where he met independence activists such as Ahn Chang-ho, Lee Gap and Sin Chae-ho. Baeksan figured that it is crucial to procure funds and establish a secret communication base to support the independence movement. Thus, he returned to Korea and founded Baeksan Sanghoe.  In 1914, he sold fields and rice paddies in his hometown and persuaded wealthy men in Yeongnam region to establish Baeksan Sanghoe in Donggwang-dong, Busan. Baeksan Memorial Hall you are standing right now used to be Baeksan Sanghoe. It initially began as a small-scale private shop that sells grains, cotton, seafood, etc. but in 1919, Choi Jun, the wealthiest man in Gyeongju, and many other large landholders of Yeongnam were gathered to expand the business to Baeksan Trading Co., Ltd.  Headquartered in Busan, the trading company began its business in July 1919 and operated three branches in China in addition to 18 in Korea. Baeksan Trading was an ordinary trading company on the outside, but in reality, it provided a secret communication base for independence activists and procured funds needed for the independence movement, serving a variety of roles as a clandestine headquarters for the anti-Japan movement. Moreover, he brought Tongnip Sinmun, the newspaper of the Shanghai Provisional Government at the time, into Korea and secretly distributed it.  This led to intensified surveillance and investigation of Japan. Coupled with serious financial hardships, the business ultimately closed its doors in January 1928, the 14th year since its foundation.

stories.title: Baeksan Memorial Hall — 06. Baeksan’s National Salvation Movement Through Education – 09. Published Works
stories.audioTitle: Baeksan Memorial Hall — 06. Baeksan’s National Salvation Movement Through Education – 09. Published Works
stories.script: Now, let’s examine Baeksan's national salvation movement through education. While he was studying in Seoul, Baeksan Ahn Hui-je converted to the ideology of enlightenment and began to lead foundation of schools and scholarship projects. He built Uisin School and Changnam School in his hometown of Uiryeong, and together with Yun Sang-eun, he founded Gumyeong School in Busan where he served as the principal for two years. Gumyeong School is today's Gupo Elementary School.  He recognized the urgency of fostering the next generation of leaders to resurrect the waning country and launched a scholarship foundation known as “Gimi Yukyeonghoe” in 1919. 10 young and competent talents were chosen every year and sent to foreign countries like the United Kingdom, Germany and Japan to study abroad.  Ahn Hui-je did not just work as an educator. In October 1909, he formed a secret society known as “Daedong Cheongnyeondan” with about 80 young and patriotic people who are passionate about taking part in the independence movement, and carried out an Anti-Japanese Movement. Members of the organization include Nam Hyeong-woo, Seo Sang-il, Yun Se-bok, Kim Dong-sam, Shin Chae-ho and Yun Byeong-ho. Daedong Cheongnyeondan was a secret Anti-Japanese society that practically led the independence movement in Korea during the colonial era, and the organization was so thoroughly covert that some of the accurate details and inside stories of the group are still unknown today.  Then, how was Daedong Cheongnyeondan, a secret organization, revealed to the world? It was because of a memoir of Changnam Yun Byeong-ho that he had written himself before he passed away. Changnam was a long-time comrade of Baeksan who also served as a member of the Third National Assembly after the Liberation. To become a member of Daedong Cheongnyeondan, one had to be recommended by at least two of the existing members, and upon being accepted into the group, the newcomer had to make a vow with his blood. In addition, a member shall never write on paper about the name or details of the organization. In case he is arrested, he shall take the sole burden for all the relevant matters and never expose involvement of any other members. These extremely strict rules enabled Daedong Cheongnyeondan to work as a secret, Anti-Japanese organization.  Baeksan took part in the foundation and management of the newspapers Dong-A Ilbo and Jungoe Ilbo and strongly criticized and attacked the Japanese General Government of Korea's politics, carrying out an independence movement through media activities as well. In 1920, he took part as one of the 78 initiators for the foundation of Dong-A Ilbo and served as the head of the Busan Branch. Then, in 1926, he took over Sidae Ilbo and renamed it as “Jungoe Ilbo,” which he managed and served as the publisher for four years. Moreover, he launched the “Gyonam Education Society” together with local leaders of Yeongnam region in 1908 and published a magazine named Gyonam Education Society, contributing to the enlightenment of the public. Currently, the memorial hall exhibits copied volumes of the Gyonam Education Society from Issue No. 1 to No. 12.  Now, take your time looking around the memorial hall to feel Baeksan's spirits and passion for salvation of his country.

stories.title: Korean War and Background for the Creation of the Forty Stairs
stories.audioTitle: Korean War and Background for the Creation of the Forty Stairs
stories.script: " On August 15, 1945, the Korean Peninsula was liberated at the news of Japan's collapse and was full of hope to establish a new country. However, the joy did not last long; the 38th parallel north was drawn and the Soviets and the Americans began to rule in the north and the south, respectively, to begin the US-Soviet military government era. Moreover, the U.S. and the Soviet Union, though they had worked together during the World War II, started to confront each other in different matters, and subsequently, divergence in ideologies and philosophies was becoming more apparent in Korean politicians as well. Eventually in 1948, two different regimes were established in the Korean Peninsula, and the Republic of Korea of liberal democracy was founded in the south whereas the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, a communist state, was founded in the north.  Since the establishment of its regime, Kim Il-sung of the north constantly sought an armed southward invasion and ultimately carried it out at 4 AM on June 25, 1950 after obtaining an approval from Stalin on the date of commencement of the southward attack. This was the start of the Korean War, the tragedy of a fratricidal war.  Unlike the south that was not prepared for the sudden invasion by the north, the invaders had been in a state of war long before that and was able to bring in a massive amount of weapons thanks to full-scale support from the Soviets and China. There was simply no way for the south to thwart the north’s invasion with dominating firepower. This abrupt start of a war led to the fall of Seoul in just three days and many South Koreans had to hastily pack things up and begin their journey of evacuation. The final destination for these refugees was “Busan.”  The city was already jam-packed to its full capacity due to countless people who had come from all over the nation to avoid war. In order to accommodate this explosive increase in refugees, the city of Busan and the government quickly set up refugee camps and shelters in 40 locations throughout Busan. Those who were able to live in one of these camps were fortunate. There was still a great number of refugees who had nowhere to go, and as they could not secure any legal residential spaces, they started to build shacks one by one in the vacant lot next to the Forty Stairs with hopes to simply avoid rainstorm.  During the colonial era, Japan carried out the construction project to flatten Yeongseonsan Mountain (1909–1912) to expand the urban district and build port facilities, thereby turning Busan into a bridgehead for advancement into the main continent. As most of Yeongseonsan (Ssangsan) Mountain disappeared as a result, a staircase was built for convenient travel from Yeongju-dong to the old Busan Station and International Yeonan Pier, and because the number of steps is 40, it began to be called the Forty Stairs. Also known as Dottegi Market where people sold and traded the Korean War relief supplies, Forty Stairs became famous along with Gukje Market, serving as a place for reunion of separated families of refugees.  Forty Stairs gained national popularity after Park Jae-hong's song, Gyeongsang-do Lady, became a mega hit in 1951. In those days, one could see Yeongdo Bridge from the Forty Stairs, and refugees often sat and leaned on these stairs to comfort the weary and exhausted souls.  However, the Forty Stairs and the surrounding neighborhood, which had consoled the hearts of the refugees, were completely annihilated by the “Great Fire of Busan Station” in November 1953. When the area was cleaned and remodeled later on, the Forty Stairs were also moved to where they are found today, about 25 meter south of the original location. In 1993, the Stone Monument for the Forty Stairs was installed, and the lyrics of Gyeongsang-do Lady, which sings the sorrows in the lives of refugees, as well as the origin story of the stairs are engraved on the monument’s back side."

stories.title: Forty Stairs Cultural Center — Forty Stairs, the Second Home
stories.audioTitle: Forty Stairs Cultural Center — Forty Stairs, the Second Home
stories.script: 2. But we must live on. Forty Stairs, the Second Home  Lives still carried on even during a war. For those who had fled their homes and taken shelter in the Busan, surviving each and every day was more important than the feeling of shame and social status.  The area surrounding the Forty Stairs to which refugees flocked from all over the country was where relief supplies came from the port right in front. Some men sold these relief goods for a living while others engaged in physical labor as port handling workers or A-frame carriers. Women mostly maintained a livelihood by odd jobs or selling things on display stalls. It was difficult to obtain proper clothes so they often picked up garments thrown away or offered by soldiers to sew their own clothing. Being shameful or disgraced was petty compared to earning money and raising children because it was a time when you could not survive if you are not persistent and tenacious.  The fervor for education was also ablaze even in the midst of a war. An academic background was a valuable asset that would never be destroyed by a war. Together with schools that had fled to the city, Busan schools set up street classes on the hill behind Bosu-dong at the foot of Gudeoksan Mountain among many other locations. Because of a sudden increase in population, all schools in Busan faced a shortage of classrooms, which led to some holding classes on a mountain while others held theirs in valleys or on streets under tents. National, public and private universities united under the Wartime Nations University; Seoul National and Yonsei Universities established schools in Busan whereas Korea University settled down in Daegu. Though people had to fight to survive each day of the war, Koreans' great passion in education was a huge driving force that eventually led to the remarkable economic growth the country has achieved today.  Meanwhile, a countless number of artists were also included in the hundreds of thousands of refugees who came to Busan. No different from other refugees, they had to perform manual labor at the port or in the U.S. military bases to carry on difficult and exhausted lives. The tough circumstances did not quench their thirst for arts, and out of desperation, they gathered in coffee and tea houses, or dabang in Korean, in Gwangbok-dong and Nampo-dong areas. Dabang served as a place of creative thoughts and activities for writers, painters and musicians. Yoon Yong-ha composed a song known as Boribat, which means a barley field, and Painter Lee Jung-seob frequently hung out at Dabang. As you can see, dabang in those days was not just a place to drink coffee or tea; it was where you could come in contact with foreign cultures imported through the port and where a new world of culture and arts was formed through exchanges with local artists.  The war made people desperate but they still had to carry on. Therefore, even in the hardscrabble lives as refugees, they did not give up on their children's education while artists expressed the anxiety of a war in their respective forms of art to quietly perform their duties.  As such, a foreign land can still become one's hometown. As they sat on the Forty Stairs, they looked onto Yeongdo Bridge to forget about the grief of the war and hardships of their refugee lives. At night, they watched the flickering lights of ships anchored at Busanhang Port to soothe their nostalgia. As you can imagine, Forty Stairs were a shelter for these people almost like a second home.  In the gloomy days of war that they wanted to undo if they had a chance, Forty Stairs were there for those who could not give up hopes and dreams.

stories.title: Forty Stairs Cultural Center — Hope Left on the Forty Stairs
stories.audioTitle: Forty Stairs Cultural Center — Hope Left on the Forty Stairs
stories.script: 3. Hope left on the Forty Stairs  Until the ceasefire agreement was made on July 27, 1953, the Korean War left indelible wounds and colossal sacrifices on our people. Nearly all the infrastructures including houses, schools, public facilities, roads, railways and bridges as well as various industrial facilities such as factories were destroyed, and the number of casualties, soldiers and civilians together, was greater than 60 million people for the south and the north combined. The war has caused hundreds of thousands of war orphans and widows as well as over 10 million separated families.  But people simply refused to give up. No matter how difficult it was to climb these stairs, they did so numerous times each day to perform various daily labor and chores during the war. As they returned to their shacks after a long day of work, they took a moment to lean on the Forty Stairs and consoled themselves for the yearning of their homes and wretchedness of the refugee life. As you can see, the Forty Stairs are the traces and history of refugees, still holding countless stories that we must remember today.  On different corners throughout the area surrounding the Forty Stairs, you will find sculptures that depict the moments of rest and pause in the midst of a war.  The “Heart of the Mother” expressing a mother who raised her children with all she had even in the tough lives as refugees; “Rest of the Father” who takes a short rest from difficult labor he performs for his family; “Children Carrying Water Jars” depicting two girls who helped house chores even at a young age; and “Rice Puff Man” who nervously awaits the moment at which the rice puff machine makes the exploding sound are all sculpted works that remind people of those good, old days.  Now, the Forty Stairs are transforming into a “cultural theme street.” The Forty Stairs, which have added the class of arts as a mural street, utilize the painful history as cultural assets to evolve into an attraction for local growth and coexistence for energetic future. The refugees’ will and hope to carry on with their lives even with the pain and wounds of the modern times are permeated on every step of the Forty Stairs along with the value of peace and unification.

stories.title: Foundation Origin and Tale (Beomeosa Temple)
stories.script: 1. Foundation Origin and Tale of Beomeosa Temple  Welcome to Beomeosa Temple located on the eastern side of Geumjeonsan Mountain. It is a thousand-year-old temple where sacred water and air circulate through the mountain, and the clear sound of the Moktak wakes up the quiet dawn. Now, let’s go back to the time of 1,300 years ago and learn how Beomeosa Temple was originally established.  King Munmu of Silla spent day after day in worry due to the continuous threat of Japanese raiders, who were actively seeking opportunities to invade Silla. One day, he dreamt that a man told him about a great monk named Uisang in Taebaeksan. Uisang preached Hwayeombeommun with a holy assembly of 3,000 at all times, indicating that many gods and kings stayed by his side. Also, there was an over 160-meter-high rock standing at the top of Geumjeongsan Mountain on the east coast. On the top of the rock, there was an ever-flowing well that glistened with a golden hue color throughout the year. Inside the well, a golden fish, descended from the heavenly realm on iridescent clouds, swam and played. The man in the dream told the king that if he went to the rock with Uisang and read the Hwaeomsinjung for seven days and nights, he would be capable of conquering the Japanese raiders in the East Sea.  The next morning, the king summoned his vassals to discuss his dream and read the scriptures with Uisang for seven days and nights at Geumjeonsan Mountain. All of a sudden, the ground shook greatly, and many Buddhas, heavenly kings, Buddhist guardians, and Child Manjusri appeared, all with weapons in hand to fight the Japanese raiders in the East Sea, leaving no enemy alive. Returning after a remarkable victory, the king was ecstatic and built a large temple at the foot of Geumjeongsan Mountain together with Uisang. This is the Beomeosa Temple built in 678 with the spirit of protecting the country.

stories.title: Jogyemun Gate (Beomeosa Temple)
stories.script: 2. Jogyemun Gate  Jogyemun Gate is located at the entrance of the temple and serves as the Iljumun Gate of Beomeosa Temple. The name 'Iljumun' signifies not only that it has a single pillar but also that 'the pillars stand in a line.' It is a gateless gate that allows entry into the world of Buddha?a space free from agony and delusion.  There are two large plaques hanging on the front of the gate, written ‘Seochal Daebonsan’ on the right and “Geumjeongsan Beomeosa” on the left. ‘Seonchal Daebonsan’ means ‘the center of the Zen Buddhism-practicing Temples.’ It indicates that Beomeosa Temple is the preeminent temple of Zen training, where Buddha's followers cultivate their minds, set aside various distracting thoughts and illusions, and engage in ascetic practices through Zen meditation. The plaque in the middle, displaying ‘Jogyemun,’ indicates that this is a temple affiliated with the Jogye Order, preserving the teachings of Buddha, Gaseobjonja, Dalmadaesa, and Hyeneungdaesa.  Jogyemun Gate, a nationally designated cultural heritage treasure, represents the temple with a history dating back 400 years. In 1614, Myojeon Hwasang built the initial Iljumun Gate, and in 1718, under Monk Myeongheup's supervision, four stone pillars were added to the original two. In 1781, the 5th year of King Jeongjo’s reign, short wooden pillars were placed atop the stone ones. The thick, rough texture of the original stone pillar, still supported by wooden pillars, reflects the enduring and warm-hearted character of Busan's people.  Jogyemun Gate is regarded as one of the country's greatest architectural masterpieces, blending aesthetic beauty with structural ingenuity. Its unique design features wooden pillars erected on four natural rocks, supporting a substantial roof weighing approximately 60 tons. This distinctive architectural technique, known as 'Graengijil,' involves affixing stones or wood to natural rocks, showcasing an exquisite Korean craftsmanship that harmonizes with nature and minimizes artificial elements. Over its 300-year existence, Jogyemun has demonstrated remarkable resilience against typhoons, rain, and wind, standing as a testament to its robust construction. Above the pillars, a finely crafted Dapo-style roof adorned with lotus flower patterns symbolizes the pure heart of Buddha, untainted by the distractions of the secular world. This signifies the aspiration for a pristine and pure heart, akin to the lotus flower, even amidst the complexities of our worldly existence.

stories.title: Beomeosa Temple: Cheonwangmun Gate
stories.script: 3. Cheonwangmun Gate  Cheonwangmun is the second gate of the temple and serves as the main entrance. This is also where the statues of the four warrior spirits protecting the four directions are enshrined. When Jasu Jangno founded the temple in 1694, the 20th year of King Sukjong’s reign, a Buddhist painting of the four warrior spirits was hung up, however it was taken down when remodeling in 1989. Wooden statues of the four warrior spirits were enshrined later on only to be completely burned to ashes in a fire that happened in 2010. They were restored in March 2012 to the appearance we see today. According to Buddhism, Mount Meru is seen as the center of the universe below which there is hell. At the foot of the mountain, humans and animals live, and then past the 28 levels of heaven, above the top of the mountain, exists Pure Land Buddhism where Buddha resides. The four warrior spirits were originally folk gods of ancient India however, after listening to the teachings of Buddha, they became kings that turned to Buddhism. They are seated on the mid-slope of Mount Meru, the closest heaven to earth, and protect the east, west, south and north. They also help those who seek truth and enlightenment in climbing up to the top of Mount Meru. Now, please turn your eyes to below the warrior spirits’ feet. As you can see from the spirits trampling over the demons and suppressing all the evils of the world that are trying to come into the temple, Cheonwangmun was built with the purpose to make the good citizens feel safe and to make them believe that the temple is a sacred place. On “Juryeon”, which is a vertically written piece on a pillar or wall, it reads,“The wisdom of Jeseokcheonwang is bright so he knows everything of this world in a single thought and loves mankind like they were his own children. Thus, I devote myself in veneration.”. The four warrior spirits who protect the heaven nearest from our world and look down upon us! Whenever you pass by them, try to spend time repenting for the sins committed in this world with a humble and modest attitude.

stories.title: Beomeosa Temple: Burimun Gate and Bojeru Pavilion
stories.audioTitle: Beomeosa Temple: Burimun Gate and Bojeru Pavilion
stories.script: 4. Burimun Gate and Bojeru Pavilion  Burimun is the third and final gate leading into Beomeosa. It is also known as “Haetalmun”, which means “teaching one, not two, truths”. In 1699, the 25th year of King Sukjong’s reign, Jasu Jangno built this simultaneously with Cheonwangmun, which later burned in a fire in 2010 and was restored to what you see now in March 2012. “Buri”means that, though Samnamansang, or all things and phenomena that exist in the universe, seem to be two separates things from one another, they are “one, not two”when looking at their essences. It's worded a little difficultly, right? In other words, it expresses that life and death, Buddha and mankind, good and evil, and all things relative are ultimately not different from each other. On “Juryeon”, which is a vertically written piece on a pillar or wall, a poem composed by Monk Dongsan, once the highest serving monk of Beomeosa, is engraved. On the right, it says, “Singwangbulmae Mangohwiyu - Hope that a mystic heart is not dark and fills the universe throughout the ages”, and on the left it says, “Ipchamullae Makjonjihae - Upon stepping through this door, all knowledge created by the thoughts of this world shall be thrown away and one shall enter with an empty heart.” They say all truths that exist in the universe come from our hearts. In other words, good, evil, and narrow-minded thoughts, all created from our own thoughts, produce pain and suffering. So, according to these teachings of Buddha, when you enter through Burimun, try to empty your mind and seek the path to true “nirvana,”away from greed, hatred, and foolishness of the secular world. Now, shall we head to Bojeru Pavilion? The name, Bojeru, means to “save all creatures of this world”, and it is a hall where various Buddhist services and rituals such as the Beobyosik are held. You see the plaque that says “Geumganggyedan”in the front at the center? Geumganggyedan is used as stairs on which “Sugye Haengsa”, or a pledge to precepts, that a student of Buddha must obey, takes place. On the pillar, there is a“Juryeon”written by Monk Dongsan as a commemorative piece for Geumganggyedan Bosalgye prior to his entrance into nirvana in 1965. “Bulseol Ilchebeop - All laws spoken by Buddha, Wido Ilchesim - are to make the hearts of all creatures right, Yangmu Ilchesim - If a person does not have any thoughts, Hayong Ilchebeop - where would every one of these laws be used?”

stories.title: Beomeosa Temple: Jongru Pavilion, Stone Pagoda and Stone Lantern
stories.audioTitle: Beomeosa Temple: Jongru Pavilion, Stone Pagoda and Stone Lantern
stories.script: 5. Jongru Pavilion, Stone Pagoda and Stone Lantern (Seven-story Stone Pagoda)  “Jongnu”is a pavilion built in order to preserve the Buddhist objects at a temple. These objects, called Buljeon Samul, refer to Beomjong, a Buddhist temple bell; Beopgo, a Dharma drum; Mogeo, a wooden clapper; and Unpan, a cloud-shaped bronze plate, all of which are related to sounds to propagate and reform the truth of Buddha to the people. The terms are quite esoteric, right? Let's examine each of them in detail. Having a noble and elegant appearance with a majestic and brilliant sound, Beomjong is struck 33 times at 4 AM and 28 times at 6 PM to save all living things in hell. Beopgo, a large drum struck, full of the Chinese character of “heart” during a Buddhist service, aims to touch the hearts of all animals born with skin and to enlighten them with the mercy of Buddha. Mogeo, a piece of wood carved in the shape of a fish that is made hollow inside, is hit by a small wooden stick to produce sounds and its purpose is to edify all creatures under water. Additionally, it means for ascetics to be awake like fish that always keep their eyes open when practicing asceticism and devotion. Unpan is a cloud-shaped bronze plate struck to save the birds flying in the sky or the souls roaming around in the air. It is shaped like a cloud and since clouds hold rain, it was often hung in a kitchen and struck to pray for prevention of fires. Every day at Beomeosa begins by waking up all the creatures asleep through striking the aforementioned items in the order of Unpan, Mogeo, Beopgo and Beomjong. The sounds of these objects ringing their entire bodies, emptying themselves in order to salvage the living creatures. Listen to the significance and meaning held inside them and feel the genuine value of all things in the universe.  Now, let's look at the three-story stone pagoda. Known as Treasure No. 250 with the properties of a stone pagoda from the late Silla Dynasty, around the time when Beomeosa was established. The period of its foundation can be estimated by the fact that Ansang, though small, is engraved on both the top and bottom stylobates and that the Okgaeseok Stone and its support, Myeonseok and Uju, are in their simplified forms. When the pagoda was repaired in 1937 during the Japanese occupation, the stone at the very bottom of the stylobate was added and Japanese-style stone handrails were also installed in the surroundings. On the back of a stone post, “Japanese Government-General of Korea” was engraved, however during the dismantling and restoration project of 2010, the handrails around the pagoda were torn down and the pagoda was restored to its original form. At this time, only broken glass bottles and newspaper pieces were discovered inside the core stone on the 1st floor so they were newly enshrined in a sarira case along with the 6 sariras of Buddha, historical records of the three-story stone pagoda, scriptures such as Banyasimgyeong, Geumganggyeong and Beophwagyeong in addition to five-colored fabrics, five-colored strings, five treasures, and five fragrances. A pagoda is a unique Buddhist sculpture created based on the Sarira faith. The first sariras were obtained in India after cremating the body of Shakyamuni Buddha upon his reaching of nirvana, and what was built to enshrine these brilliant sariras was a pagoda. Since ancient times, Buddhist believers have hosted “Tapdori events”during which they circle around a pagoda all night long to wash away the agony in their hearts and wish for their prayers to be answered. Three-story stone pagodas that have shared the longings of countless people. How about laying down any burden harbored within your heart right now next to a stone pagoda?  Now, shall we move to the stone lantern? A stone lantern is an offering tool that lights up the front yard of a temple, as well as a lamp of Dharma that sheds light on Buddha's nature by reflecting the truth of Buddha onto the hearts of all creatures. Looking at the engravings and ornaments, it is estimated to have been set up together with the Beomeosa Three-story Stone Pagoda in the late Unified Silla Period. “Stone lantern”literally refers to a lamp made of stone used to shed light, and in Buddhism, light symbolizes the wisdom to govern foolishness of people and lighting a lantern was regarded as the highest form of offering. To be able to shed light onto Sangdaeseok, a Hwasaseok with four windows is supported, and a roof stone covers the top. Also, on the top of the Hadaeseok, a lotus flower with 8 leaves is engraved. Enjoy the subdued beauty of the stone lantern that has lit up the wisdom necessary to drive away the agony.

stories.title: Beomeosa Temple: Daeungjeon Hall
stories.script: 6. Daeungjeon Hall  Daeungjeon is Treasure No. 434 and the greatest hall at Beomeosa that enshrines Sakyamunī. Daeung is a kind of a pen name in praise of Buddha's virtue and a term that alludes his virtue to that of a great hero. It is said that the term originated from a Chinese emperor who dedicated the title to Buddha. As the Jubuljeon situated in the center of the Garam, a garden where monks live and practice to be better students of Buddha, Daeungjeon is located upon the highest ground in the Garam to look over everything in the temple below. Beomeosa's Daeungjeon is regarded as one of the leading architectural works of Joseon Buddhist culture that employed elaborate construction techniques that cannot be seen at other temples. From the dynamic composition of Chang-Bang and Pyung-Bang that connect hand-carved cornerstones with pillars, we can catch a glimpse of the structural beauty of the Korean traditional wooden architecture. 4 Juryeon, excerpted from 《Geumganggyeong Ogahae》and written by Monk Dongsan, are hung on the pillars of Daeungjeon. Let's look at it together starting from the right. “Maha Daebeobwang - Great and holy Buddha, Mudan Yeongmujang - Neither short nor long, Bollae Bijobaek - Neither black nor white in its inherent appearance, Sucheo Hyeoncheonghwang - Shown in blue or red depending on the relation.” Now, let's look inside Daeungjeon. Three statues of Buddha are seen on top of the altar in the center - Sakyamuni Buddha, the Buddha of the Present, situated in the middle; Dipankara Bodhisattva, the Buddha of the Past, on the left; and Maitreya Bodhisattva, the Buddha of the Future, on the right. The Buddha Triad means that, even if Sakyamuni dies, Buddha exists in all moments of history, past or future, allowing for Buddha's teachings to continue. Exquisite and fancy canopy ornaments of dragons, fairies, and cranes shown above Sakyamuni Buddha create additional dignity. There are 14 murals painted on the walls. The Buddha Triad represents time while Yaksasamjondo on the east and Amitasamjondo on the west represent space, and together they signify transcendence over time and space to save all living creatures symbolized by the fish. Now, try to feel the mercy and virtuous spirit of Buddha, the ruler of all things in the universe, here in Daeungjeon, the sanctuary of enlightenment at Beomeosa.

stories.title: Beomeosa Temple: Mireukjeon Hall and Birojeon Hall
stories.audioTitle: Beomeosa Temple: Mireukjeon Hall and Birojeon Hall
stories.script: 8. Mireukjeon Hall and Birojeon Hall  Mireukjeon is the hall that enshrines the future Buddha. If the main Buddha happens to be Maitreya, they are also referred to as Yonghwajeon. Known to come down to our world 5.67 billion years after Buddha’s nirvana, Maitreya is the Buddha who descends to the human world after “Sakyamuni Buddha” of the present and exists to wash away the fears and worries of the future that people have. But its hard to see Mireukjeon's Buddha statue when outside, right? It is because Maitreya Buddha in Beomeosa is not facing the front but, instead, seated towards Daeungjeon with his back against the right wall. There is a story behind why Maitreya Buddha is seated towards the west. When people dug the ground below Mireukjeon that had been destroyed during the Japanese invasion of 1592, the Buddha, which had probably been facing the front, was found to be sitting with his back against Japan. And, despite the efforts to correct it, the statue did not move at all so they kept it in its position. If you look at the pedestal below the statue, you can see traces left by the fire. There are several theories as to why the statue was discovered with his body turned, and the most popular one is that the statue itself turned its body away from Japan, not wanting to face a country responsible for invading Joseon.  Now, let’s move to Birojeon. Birojeon of Beomeosa is a hall that enshrines Vairocana Buddha who holds the true appearance of all life that exists within the universe. It was destroyed during the Japanese invasion of 1592 before being rebuilt in 1721. Vairocana Buddha, the Dharmakāya that symbolizes truth itself, is enshrined in the center with Manjushiri Bodhisattva, the symbol of wisdom, and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, the symbol of compassion, on the left and right, respectively. The name, “Vairocana” means that “hope shines the entire universe”; in other words, it means that the light and wisdom of Buddha will spread evenly to all living creatures in this world. If you look at the Wooden Seated Vairocana Buddha Triad enshrined in Birojeon, you will see that their hands look different from other statues, right? Wrapping of the right index finger with the left palm is known as “Jigwonin”, which represents the merciful heart of Buddha sheltering all living creatures in order to bring them into the clear and pure world of Buddha. They say, in the human world, love follows hatred and hatred follows love. Buddhism teaches not to view love and hatred as two separate elements. An eternal heart hinges on how I handle my own mind and soul, don’t you think so?

stories.title: Beomeosa Temple: Palsang, Dokseong, Nahanjeon Hall and Sallyeonggak Shrine
stories.audioTitle: Beomeosa Temple: Palsang, Dokseong, Nahanjeon Hall and Sallyeonggak Shrine
stories.script: 9. Palsangjeon, Dokseongjeon, Nahanjeon Halls and Sallyeonggak Shrine  Firstly, Palsangjeon is a hall that enshrines Palsangdo, a painting of the eight main events of Buddha’s life and shares the same building as the two other halls - Nahanjeon and Dokseongjeon. It was first constructed in 1704 and rebuilt in the 9th year of Gwangmu, 1905. The 80-year life of Sakyamuni Buddha from when he comes to the human world from Tusita to his nirvana is depicted in eight paintings. Then, let’s all enjoy Palsangseongdo, four of which can be found on each side, before moving to Dokseongjeon on the right. Also known as “Dokseong”, Dokseongjeon is the hall that enshrines “Nabanjonja” who became a saint by reaching enlightenment on his own without any help from others. It was originally detached from Nahanjeon and Palsangjeon but it was eventually connected as one building in 1905. A round, arch-shaped entrance that exudes the exotic aura of India is a unique trait of Dokseongjeon, and you can catch a glimpse of the excellent handicraft techniques as well as the elaborately engraved scene of two pious man and woman holding up heaven on the side of the door. The sight of these two, heads completely shaved, standing in longing for the next life, leaves quite an impression, doesn't it? Among the three halls, Nahanjeon is the one located on the very right and it enshrines the sixteen outstanding disciples of Buddha. In Buddhism, “a saint who could not become a Buddha but gained insight into the true nature of existence and achieved nirvana” is called a arhat or arahant. You can see that the 16 arhats divided equally on the left and right all have distinct appearances. Nahanjeon is a hall that enshrines saints, not Buddha, so it is known for a non-majestic decoration of the altar and the shrine hall itself. Enjoy the beauty of Nahanjeon along with Soseulmaehwa Kkotsalmun of Palsangjeon and Soseulbit Kkotsalmun of Dokseongjeon, a pair of the most beautiful Kkotsalmun, or even the floral design lattice doors, found in Korean temples.  Finally, let’s move over to Sallyeonggak Shrine. Sallyeonggak is where the mountain spirit of Geumjeongsan is enshrined. Since old times, our ancestors have cherished the energy of the mountains which lead to them enshrining mountain spirits. Installing Sallyeonggak behind the highest shrine hall of a temple and enshrining a mountain spirit here is a unique characteristic of the Korean Buddhist culture that values harmony instead of exclusion and is also an element that expresses its natural embrace of the traditional shamanism or folk beliefs. In Sallyeonggak, a painting of a mountain spirit and a tiger that protects the mountains and the temple is enshrined. Here in the shrine of the mountain spirit, enjoy the beauty of the Buddhist culture completed through balance and harmony.

stories.title: Beomeosa Temple: Other Halls
stories.script: 10. Other Halls  Now, let’s learn about the remaining 6 spaces of Beomeosa Temple. The first is “Simgeomdang Hall,” which means “a house where one finds the sword of wisdom to eliminate the agony of ignorance.” It was originally a meditation hall for beginning ascetics but as the size of the temple grew, the meditation hall was relocated to today's Geumeoseonwon and currently this hall is used as the office of the proctor who handles the housekeeping of the temple. After it was first constructed by Myojeon Hwasang in 1614, it was rebuilt in 1648 and during the dismantling and repairs conducted in 2016, it was confirmed by Sangnyangmun as the oldest structure at the Beomeosa Temple. The second building we want to look at is “Geumeoseonwon,” which has a sign that says, “Yeongju Seonjae.” Since ancient times, Geumjeongsan Mountain has been called Yeongju, a place where mountain spirits dwell thanks to its great mountain range and has boasted beautiful sceneries. It is a place of practice where believers devote themselves to reach the world of enlightenment under the sole determination for Hwadu. It is also where the traditional Zen Buddhism, which had slowly been disappearing, was promoted once again along with Monk Gyeongheo in 1899. This is said to represent a meeting between new Zen thoughts and Buddhism. The third is the “Josajeon.” It is a place that enshrines 10 monks who have served as patriarchs of Beomeosa - Gaesanjo Uisang and Wonhyo in the center; Jungheungjo Myojeon, Gyeongheo, Seongwoldang, Simhaedang and Seongundang Seonsa on the left; and Samyeongdang, Hwanseongdang, Geumbongdang, Yongseongdang and Dongsan Hyeil Daejongsa on the right. Juryeon is the Beopseonggye of Uisangdaesa and makes you rethink the story of realization told by the “Wonhyo and the human skull” mural. The fourth building is the “Seolbeopjeon”that enshrines Amitabha Buddha, Avalokitesvara and Ksitigarbha. It is the place that performs various Buddhist ceremonies and features a kitchen on the floor below. The fifth is the “Chimgyeryo”. It was originally one of the most notable meditation halls of Beomeosa that was built together with Daeungjeon in 1614. During the late Joseon Period under the Japanese occupation, it was also known as the Myeongjeong School, a modern educational institution that served a pivotal role in the national movement and local social movement. Today, it is used as the Vinaya Graduate School of Buddhism. The last is the “Hyuhyujeongsa”. It was built based on the principle of resting comfortably without even the smallest thoughts within our hearts, and before the opening of the Zen Cultural Education Center in 2019, it had been used for “temple stays” for Buddhist temple culture experiences. Originally, “Geukrakam Chilseongdo” and “Geukrakam Sinjungdo”existed here but they were both taken overseas after the Korean War. Fortunately, both “Geukrakam Chilseongdo” and “Geukrakam Sinjungdo”returned to Korea through auctions held in Switzerland and Los Angeles, U.S., respectively, in 2015. Chilseongdo, gained particular attention as the first-ever case of returning to its original nation via an auction.

stories.title: Seongbo Museum
stories.script: The repository of Buddhist culture where the essence of the religious culture lies, it was opened in 2003 in order to preserve, manage, comprehensively research, and exhibit the Seongbo cultural properties scattered throughout Beomeosa Temple in a more efficient and systematic manner. The exhibition hall and storage possess Buddhist paintings from the late Joseon Period, 40 portrait paintings, 1,000 books and documents, 15 kinds of woodblocks, 23 kinds of signboards, and a variety of other Buddhist relics and artifacts. The most notable cultural properties stored here include Buddha's sariras, Samguk Yusa, portrait of Uisangdaesa, Baeguigwaneumdo, the largest Sacheonwangdo in the nation, and 3 kinds of scriptures of Buljo Samgyeong, which is designated as a Treasure, as well as Geumjang Yojipgyeong and Jubeom Manggyeong. As you can see, the Seongbo Museum offers a chance for you to meet in person the various relics such as records of the temple's history, printing blocks, and construction that hold the tradition of Beomeosa's 1,340-year-old history. Here at the Seongbo Museum that presents the beauty and elaborateness of the Buddhist culture to those who visit Beomeosa, check out the meaningful traces left by the temple's old stories through its history, culture, and planned exhibits.

stories.title: History Hall for the Korean People and Women
stories.audioTitle: History Hall for the Korean People and Women
stories.script: History Hall for the Korean People and Women  We first came across the existence of Japanese military “comfort women” on August 14, 1991 when late Mrs. Kim Hak-sun publicly testified, the first Japanese military comfort women survivors to do so, what she had suffered at a press conference.  Towards the end of the Asia–Pacific War that Japan had started, Japan lured countless women, as young as little girls to those in their 30s, with lies that they would provide them with jobs, and took them to where Japanese troops were stationed. What awaited these innocent women whose sole goal was to get a job and contribute to the livelihood of their families back home were sexual abuse and exploitation. They lived each and every day in despair under the inescapable watch and monitoring.  Japan probably knew and realized how inhumane the existence of “comfort women” is, because after they lost the war, they did all they could to erase the evidence of forced mobilization of Joseon women as Japanese military “comfort women.” They burned all the related documents and left the victims in the battlefields to die or, even worse, killed those women. Some women did survive the hardship but it was nearly impossible for them to carry normal lives again because of the horrendous trauma of the sexual abuse and exploitation they had had to endure. But they eventually overcame the long-endured pain and wounds and testified about them, which allowed everyone to learn about what they had suffered. Many private organizations both in Korea and overseas were founded to help resolve the Japanese military “comfort women” issue.  Among them, Kim Mun-suk, the president of the “Citizen's Coalition for Volunteer Korea,” met over 250 women who had been taken as “comfort women” and sexual slaves of Japanese military to record and collect a great volume of materials and evidence, based on which she and her group began a legal battle against the Japanese government in 1993 and demanded the nation’s official apology and reparation.  They ceaselessly traveled between Korea and Shimonoseki, Japan for a total of 26 trials. After six years of the fight, they won the first trial. However, in 2001, they lost the following trial held at the Hiroshima High Court after the appeal of the Japanese government. Kim filed an appeal in 2003 but unfortunately, lost at the Supreme Court. Though it was a lost legal battle, what Kim and her organization did is extremely significant in that it was the first time for a Japanese court at any level to acknowledge exploitation and abuse inflicted upon the “comfort women.”  After this, Kim invested her own assets to build and open the History Hall for the Korean People and Women in Suyeong-gu, Busan. In three exhibition halls, it exhibits photos, newspaper articles, videos, books, etc. on the women who were taken and brutally suffered as Japanese military “comfort women.” Even a film called Herstory was produced based on the materials on display here.  Thanks to countless testimonies and evidential materials, everyone now knows about the “comfort women” and also knows that this is something that must never happen again. However, Japan continues to downscale, conceal and deny the evident facts, which wearies and tires the victims all of whom are now well advanced in age.  When will Japan sincerely apologize and make reparation? What we do know is that, until then, we need to make sure to never forget the Japanese military “comfort women.”

stories.title: Chodang Dubu Village
stories.script: Chodang Dubu Village  Did you know that Chodang Tofu” is the most popular local specialty in Gangneung? We are at Chodang dubu Village in Chodang-dong, Gangneung. Tofu, which is an essential staple food in Korea, is made by grinding soybeans and then boiling them. The soymilk thus obtained is then stirred with salty water, or Gansu, to coagulate the protein and oil. Unlike regular tofu, Chodang tofu is made with seawater from the deep East Sea. When used as a coagulant, seawater increases the moisture in tofu, resulting in silky soft texture.  Chodang tofu is the only food in Korea to have the name of a local city placed before its name, making it a proper noun. Chodang is also the pen-name of Heo Yeop, the father of Heo Gyun, who wrote the first Korean novel, titled Hong Gildong Jeon. Since Heo Yeop, a governor of the Joseon Dynasty, was the first person to use seawater to make tofu, any tofu that uses seawater as a coagulant is called Chodang tofu.   The savory aroma of tofu will welcome you the moment you step into Chodang’s alleys packed with restaurants. Their signature menus include freshly-made tofu squares, soft sun dubu, and hotpot tofu in broth. Visit Chodang dubu Village and try its delicious, earthy Chodang tofu.

stories.title: Old Daegwallyeong Road
stories.script: Old Daegwallyeong Road  The Old Daegwallyeong Road, a mountain path rising 823 meters above sea level, used to be the gateway connecting the east and west sides of Daegwallyeong. During the olden days, when there was no other road, people had to climb this hill to get to Gangneung. ‘Daegwallyeong’ is infamous for its rugged terrain. One of its many nicknames is the road with 99 bends.” There is a local story about a scholar who started out with 100 dried persimmons when he embarked his journey over Daegwallyeong Hill, but ended up with only one as he took one out and ate it every time he came to a bend on this serpentine road.  Today, the Old Daegwallyeong Road is an 8-km-long trail that passes through a dense forest. It starts from the Daegwallyeong Museum, crosses over Wonuri Hill and then passes by the ruins of an old public restaurant to reach its midpoint, Banjeong, before finally reaching the summit of a hill called Guksa Seonghwangdang. Guksa Seonghwangdang is the starting point of Gangneung's famous Dano Festival (designated by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity), which commemorates both General Kim Yu-shin of the Silla Dynasty, who is considered the indigenous god of Daegwallyeong, and the main deity of the Dano Festival. Here you can enjoy a leisurely walk along a footpath surrounded by beautiful forest, wild flowers, and stories from the past.

stories.title: Jumunjin Adeul Rocky Park
stories.script: Jumunjin Adeul Rocky Park  Sodol village is a small port village in the Jumunjin district. On the beach behind the dock of Sodol is a row of oddly formed rocks and strangely shaped stones created by crustal movements that occurred about 150 million years ago. This place is called Adeul Rocky Park. Of all these strange rocks, Adeul Rock is the most popular one because of the legend that has sprung up around its particular shape. According to the legend, a long, long time ago a husband and wife were waiting for their son to return home from a war. One night, the Dragon King appeared in the couple's dream and told them that they would hear good news if they prayed diligently until a hole appeared in a rock on Sodol beach. As soon as the couple awoke from the dream, they went to the beach and prayed in front of a rock. They prayed and prayed every day and finally a hole appeared in the rock. And shortly thereafter, they heard their son’s voice through the hole in the rock, and the wife bore a son, ‘adeul’ in Korean, who looked just like their first son. Rumor has it that if you pray on Adeul Rock, your deepest wish will be granted. As such, many people visit the site to this day.

stories.title: Jumunjin Port
stories.script: Jumunjin Port  Located in the northernmost part of Gangneung, Jumunjin Port is the city’s largest port. Both passenger and cargo ships started to dock at Jumunjin port in 1917 when it became a major port of call. Korea’s East Coast is a ‘golden’ fishing ground where warm and cold ocean currents meet, yielding up huge catches of fish. Some 400 fishing boats travel in and out of Jumunjin Port every day, bringing in a wide variety of freshly caught fish including squid, mackerel, sand lance, and herring. Next to the port is Jumunjin Fish Market, the biggest fish market in the whole Yeongdong area, which opens every day. The market is always packed with visitors looking for fresh fish at low prices and dried goods. If you head further north along the costal road from Jumunjin Port, you will come to the very first lighthouse built in Gangwon Province back in 1918. The Jumunjin Lighthouse is well known for its high architectural value and modern Korean lighthouse architecture, and commands panoramic 2700views of the ocean. If you follow the route from the lighthouse to Seonangdang, you will find a panoramic view of Jumunjin Port. Seonangdang enshrines Seonang, the village and land guardian, and three Seonang guardians are cherished here in Jumunjin Seonangdang. Meanwhile, at the observatory next to Seonangdang, you can take in the white lighthouse against the blue ocean and the lively Jumunjin Port in a single glance.

stories.title: Youngjin Beach (shooting location of the TV series Goblin <Guardian>)
stories.audioTitle: 4. Youngjin Beach (shooting location of the TV series Goblin <Guardian>)
stories.script: Youngjin Beach (shooting location of the TV series Goblin <Guardian>)  Six sand groins stand in a line on Youngjin Beach, but only one of them has become a famous tourist spot. This is the place where the Korean TV series Guardian: The Lonely and Great God, a story of a goblin who is destined to find a human bride to end his immortal life, was filmed. The so-called “Goblin Groin” is an important place in the drama where the main character Eun-tak (played by Kim Go-eun) meets Kim Shin, the goblin (played by Gong-yoo) for the first time, as well as the place where she comes back whenever she faces adversity or changes her mind. The scene where Kim Shin presents buckwheat flowers to Eun-tak at the end of the wave-lashed sand groin became the most beloved scene in the entire series. The groin is now a special stage where visitors create their own dramatic moments. The formerly quiet Youngjing Beach is now writing a new story after forming the backdrop to a beautiful love story. Why don’t you come and play a dramatic role by yourself against a backdrop of blue sea and pristine white sand?

stories.title: Sacheon Mulhoe Village
stories.script: Sacheon Mulhoe Village  You must try ‘mulhoe’ if you visit the village of Sacheon Jin-ri. Mulhoe is a famous summer delicacy of Gangwon-do that is served with sliced seafood like raw fish or squid and vegetables mixed together in a spicy cold broth. Jin-ri has earned the name of Mulhoe Village because it has an abundance of fresh seafood due to its close proximity to Sacheon Port, a small port famous for lance fishing, and because it has more mulhoe restaurants than fish markets and raw fish restaurants.  Originally, mulhoe was eaten by fishermen who liked to put slices of freshly-caught fish and rice in gochujang soup to quickly relieve their hunger while out at sea in their fishing boats. So what was once a fast food for fishermen is now a popular low-calorie summer dish! There are about twenty restaurants specializing in mulhoe in the village. The recipe for mulhoe may seem simple, but the flavor varies depending on the types of seafood and the broth, so you can enjoy a unique mulhoe in any restaurant.

stories.title: Sogeumgang
stories.script: 6. Sogeumgang  Sogeumgang refers to a large area that occupies one-third of ​​Odaesan National Park and which has been designated as the No. 1 Scenic Site in Korea. Sogeumgang, meaning “the small Mount Geumgang”, boasts a view that is as outstanding as the Mount Geumgang, which has long been known for its spectacular beauty. Yulgok Yi Yi, one of the most prominent Korean scholars of the Joseon Dynasty, made a pilgrimage to the area and left behind a poem praising its beauty, feeling that more people should know about it. If you climb the 1338-meter-high mountain, you will come across some of the famous scenic spots of Sogeumgang along the way. Follow the mountain path and you will arrive at a rock called ‘Sikdangam’, whose upper surface is spacious enough to accommodate dozens of people. This huge rock is believed to have been used as a dining table by the last prince of Silla, an ancient kingdom of Korea, when he trained with his army to win back the lost kingdom. The ruins of Amisanseong Fortress, which was built in preparation for the war, still remain. If you pass by Guryong Falls, a series of nine waterfalls, and the strangely-shaped Manmulsang rocks which change shape depending on your viewing angle, you will finally arrive at the summit, Noinbong peak. Please note that Korea’s No.1 Scenic Site is even more beautiful when it changes color in the fall.

stories.title: Chamsori Gramophone Museum
stories.script: 7. Chamsori Gramophone Museum,  At Gyeongpo Lake are three museums. The Chamsori Gramophone Museum is a sound museum that exhibits early acoustic devices such as phonograph and music box. There is a music room where you can listen to music through professional theater speakers.   The Edison Science Museum has a collection of over 2,000 inventions made by America's greatest inventor Thomas Edison. From incandescent light bulbs invented in 1879 to household items like telephone, typewriter, and iron, early tinfoil phonography, and class M, including the first-ever phonograph introduced in Korea and an electric vehicle he made in 1913, there is so much to see here.    At the Son Seong-mok Film Museum, you can learn about the history of film technology through various filmmaking gears including a kinetoscope, an early motion picture exhibition device invented by Edison. Just like a scene from the movie Cinema Paradiso, you can watch an old movie in a theater equipped with the theater speakers of the 1940s, sitting on a chair used in American theaters 100 years ago. There are over 10,000 items including radio, TV, and speakers from around the world on display.

stories.title: Gyeongpodae Pavilion
stories.script: Gyeongpodae Pavilion   On a small hill north of Gyeongpo Lake, overlooking the lake and the East Sea, is a pavilion built in the Goryeo Dynasty. Gyeongpodae is the name of the pavilion, but the surrounding areas including the lake and the beach are also called Gyeongpodae. In other words, the beach and the pavilion are both called Gyeongpodae. The pavilion was originally built in 1326 at the Inwolsa Temple site on a mountain behind Banghaejeong Pavilion before moving to its current location under the reign of King Jungjong of Joseon. Today, the eight scenic spots over the Gwandong region, the northeastern boundary of Korea, are called Gwandong Palgyeong,” and the view of Gyeongpo Lake from Gyeongpodae Pavilion is one of them. It was the dream of every Joseon Dynasty scholar to take a tour of the Gwandong region to enjoy the views of the mountains and the sea and write a poem about them. Gyeongpodae, too, was constantly visited by tourists and featured as a subject in literature and paintings. The inside of Gyeongpodae Pavilion is decorated with calligraphy and poems written by many famous Joseon dynasty scholars, including both King Sukjong and Yulgok Yi Yi.

stories.title: Gyeongpo Lake
stories.script: 9. Gyeongpo Lake  Gyeongpoho literally means a lake as clear as a mirror. Gyeongpo Lake is the most well-known lagoon on the east coast. A lagoon is a lake formed when the mouth of a bay was closed by sand and pebbles brought in by the sea currents. Gyeongpo Lake is a clear and serene lake surrounded by the East Sea and Daegwallyeong. For a long time, the 8 scenic views around Gyeongpo Lake have been called “Gyeongpo Palgyeong.” The first view is the sunrise from Nokdujeong Pavilion south of the lake. The second view is the moonlight observed from the Jukdo area, and the third and fourth views are the lights of a fishing boat floating on the sea of Gangmun and the smoke from chimneys in Chodang Village in the evening. The fifth and sixth are the night scene in the rain as viewed from Hongjangam Temple on the northern hill and the sunset from Sirubong Peak in the northwest. The seventh and eighth are the sound of a flute heard from Hwanseonjeong Pavilion east of Gyeongpo Lake and the evening bells at Hansongsa Temple. There are about 10 pavilions in Gyeongpo Lake thanks to the phenomenal views. Tourists are said to have visited here since the olden times to enjoy the landscape and write poetry. Today's Gyeongpo Lake is a natural playground where citizens can relax and enjoy the atmosphere. There are scenic trails and bicycle paths circling the lake. The Prickly Water Lily Wetlands and the annual Gyeongpoho Cherry Blossom Festival are also fantastic.

stories.title: Prickly Water Lily Wetlands
stories.script: Prickly Water Lily Wetlands  Have you ever seen a prickly water lily? The stems, leaves, and flowers of prickly water lilies are covered with sharp thorns. Classified as a second-class endangered species, it topped the list of Rare and Endangered Plant Species by the Korea Forest Service.  Prickly water lilies used to bloom in Gyeongpo Lake, but they completely disappeared in the 1960s. Gyeongpo Lake was originally three times larger than it is now. In the 1960s, the waterway entering the lake was channeled into the sea to turn the wetlands into farmlands. As a result, the living organisms there died, and the water was contaminated, causing the ecosystem of the lake to collapse. From that time on, the prickly water lilies no longer bloomed. Then, in the 2000s, efforts to save the wetlands began, and prickly water lilies made a surprising return after a while. The buried seeds in the soil spontaneously germinated as the wetlands were revived. Now, you can the bright purple flowers in full bloom from July to August.
