If you take a boat from Mokpo that operates 5 to 6 times a day and go for about 50 minutes, you will arrive at the dock of Oedaldo, and, in front of the dock, there is a flower garden on a low hill. Once you climb the wooden stairs, you will reach an octagonal pavilion, which is covered in flowers during the spring and summer, presenting a spectacular scene. To the left of the pavilion, there is a small, approximately 400m-long beach. A seawater pool, sunbathing area and sand playground are found near the beach. In the seawater pool, there is an artificial pool created by bringing in seawater for people to enjoy swimming even during low tide. In front of the pool, a pine forest and the blue sea of Dadohae stretch out, and a variety of convenience facilities are also available. When the tide goes down, the beach transforms itself into a fishing village learning site where you can experience collecting various kinds of shellfish, oysters and so on. If you go right from the dock, you will find Oedaldo's second beach, which is a deserted island called “Byeolseom.” It is an impressive island with two pine trees sticking out and is seen on the right as you come from Yuldo to Oedaldo. You may walk into the island once the water is pushed out but you will not be able to walk out when the tide is high so the island offers you an experience of a natural phenomenon of the sea. If you go past “Oedaldo Pension Village”and head towards “Hanok Pension Town,” you will reach the southeast end of Oedaldo, which is called “Solmeorikkeut.” In front, you can see Siha Bada, a sea with strong currents, Sinan Amtaedo Island and Palgeumdo while, on the left, you can catch a fantastic view of the picturesque Mokpogu Lighthouse on the Haenam Hwawon Peninsula located across the sea. As you follow the trail around the pensions, you will reach the top of Maebongsan, the tallest mountain in Oedaldo. The island is not that big, enough for an average person to go around in about an hour, but its beautiful sceneries and awesome views of the small but rich shores attract many people to visit consistently. Moreover, Oeadaldo is also called as the “Island of Love” or Island of Lovers” so check out why it has such a nickname with your own eyes!

stories.title: Oedaldo and Dalido Islands – Dalido
stories.script: Oedaldo and Dalido Islands – Dalido  An island with 8 beautiful natural sceneries   Dalido Island is located about 3km from the western end of Mokpo and seems like the entrance to the Dadohae. Dalido is the largest of the four inhabited islands of Mokpo and, as of 2020, has the largest population at 400. Because the island resembles a half-moon, it used to be called Dal-dong or Daldo and, now, the name is fixed as Dalido. Most of the residents are engaged in agriculture to produce rice and barley as well as sweet potatoes, beans, garlic, cabbage, red pepper, radishes, etc. Marine products from the island include bass, clam and ocean quahog, and laver farming also takes place in the surrounding waters. It has an educational institution that is the Dali branch of the Yudal Elementary School, and ferries between Mokpo and Dalido are operated six times a day.  Near Dalido, there is an island called Oedaldo. And, in the near future, Dalido and Oedaldo will be connected so that people can walk between the two islands.  Oedaldo, the Island of Love, was selected as “the island people want to visit for the holiday season” in 2017 thanks to its well-established tourism infrastructure including seawater pools and hanok pensions while Dalido owns beautiful natural sceneries such as the “8 Scenic Views of Dali.” Once the “pedestrian bridge on the sea,” which connects the two islands, is installed, don’t you think they will show great synergy in becoming a fantastic marine tourist destination?   And, by 2030, it will be possible to go to Dalido by car. This is because the National Route 77 project to connect Aphaedo, Yuldo, Dalido and Hwawon Peninsula began in 2020. The National Route 77 is an 897km large-scale coastal road that runs from Incheon to Busan along the west and south coast, and a fantastic driving course connecting bays and islands. It is expected that Mokpo and Dalido will serve as the hub for rest and maintenance for those who depart and arrive. Dalido has many things to see and experience and will increase in importance as time goes. Surely you will visit again, right?

stories.title: Mokpo Literature Museum - Cha Beom-seok Hall
stories.audioTitle: Mokpo Literature Museum - Cha Beom-seok Hall
stories.script: Mokpo Literature Museum - Cha Beom-seok Hall  Cha Beom-seok who has completed the Korean realistic plays  Mokpo Literature Museum located within Gatbawi Culture Town is a literature complex opened in October 2007 that exhibits the works of four people - Kim Woo-jin, the pioneer of Korean theatrical art; Park Hwa-seong, an author who wrote the first full-length novel as a woman; Cha Beom-seok, the consummator of the Korean realistic plays; and Kim Hyeon, an unrivaled figure in Korean criticism literature. Now, let's first take a look through Cha Beom-seok Hall on the first floor. Are any of you a fan of plays? Cha Beom-seok, one of the most notable playwrights and directors of our country, was born in Mokpo in 1924. His play titled 〈Moonshine〉was selected as a runner-up in the Chosun Ilbo's annual spring literary contest in 1955, and he made his debut in the literary world when his work, 〈Returning Home〉, won the contest in the following year. He was an author and a man of theater who wrote many works that possess social consciousness and popular appeal at the same time. Do you see the writing in the exhibit that says, “Sanha is our home and motherland?” Mr. Cha founded a theater company named “Sanha”in 1963 and served as the president for 20 years. To him, the people he met and the things he experienced in Mokpo where he was born and raised were the yarn and needles with which he weaved his works. One day during his young and sensitive years, he was deeply moved by the performance of Choi Seung-hee, a modern dancer, on stage at the Pyeonghwa Theater in Mokpo. He once wrapped himself with his mother's skirt and mimicked the dance moves of Choi Seung-hee only to be caught by her and reprimanded. Two of his earlier works, 〈Moonshine〉 and 〈Returning Home〉, are staged on the shores of Mokpo, his hometown. He once said that the sounds of waves and seagulls and the salty and fishy smells carried by the sea breeze are the memories of his youth when the sea was conceived within his body and soul. He was also employed by Munhwa Broadcasting Corporation and wrote scripts for dramas. Do you know the farming village drama known as 〈Country Diaries〉that everyone loved at the time? Starting with the very first script on October 21, 1980, Mr. Cha wrote 48 scripts for about a year. Country Diaries went on to air 1,088 episodes over 22 years and become the “longest drama beloved by the entire country.” Raised as the son of a wealthy landlord when he was young, Mr. Cha witnessed a countless number of dead bodies and starving people during the 18 days of evacuation from Seoul to Mokpo immediately after the outbreak of the Korean War in 1950. “Ah, what can't even the son of a wealthy family do to survive?” “Rich or poor, every human being is powerless before a war.” These thoughts engulfed his mind even in the distant future and had a significant influence on his writing. Mr. Cha's play titled 〈Burning Mountain〉, which is praised as the masterpiece of realistic plays, is famous as a modern artist's work that hosts the greatest number of performances. Starting with the premiere by the National Drama Company in December 1962, over 30 different theater companies have put the play on stage. At the premiere, it is said that the doors and windows of Myeong-dong National Theater were broken because of the audience flooding in. 〈Burning Mountain〉is a realistic play that talks about a tragedy stemming from a conflict between North and South ideologies and love, lust, jealousy of man and woman. It is regarded as a masterpiece that well expresses the essence and dignity of mankind in the midst of the cruelty of a war. Once you leave today, why don't you go grab one of Mr. Cha's plays to feel the power of his words?

stories.title: Mokpo Literature Museum - Park Hwa-seong Hall
stories.audioTitle: Mokpo Literature Museum - Park Hwa-seong Hall
stories.script: Mokpo Literature Museum - Park Hwa-seong Hall  Park Hwa-seong, the first Korean female author to write a full-length novel  The godmother of all Korean women's novels, Mrs. Park Hwa-seong was born in Mokpo in 1903. Her original name was Park Gyeong-sun and her pen name was Soyeong. Hwa-seong was her nickname as well as literary name. She came up with the name, Hwa-seong, herself and began to use it when she was 11 years old. It means that “white gourd flowers cover a castle,”according to her. She was so smart that people considered her a child prodigy; she learned Hangul at the age of 4, wrote her first novel at 11, and even skipped a few grades in a year. She also began to teach students when she was just 15 years old, hence the nickname, the “Baby Teacher.” Mrs. Park made her official debut in the literary world in 1925 when she released ≪The Eve of Chuseok≫ to 〈Chosunmundan〉 by the recommendation of Yi Kwangsu. The work received positive literary reviews for the fact that it depicted female laborers encountering the reality of colonization for the first time by a female author, that it accurately understands the distorted distribution of economy in the colonized Joseon, and that a perception on money is exposed in a detailed and realistic way. Her most memorable work is 〈Baekhwa〉, the first full-length novel written by a female author in Korea. Thanks to the recommendation of Yi Kwangsu once again, Baekhwa was serialized for 180 days on Dong-a Ilbo with illustrations of an artist named Cheongjeon Lee Sang-beom. The first full-length novel written by a female author, 〈Baekhwa〉 boasted an epic novel-like flow and excellent reality, and was highly praised by Lee Tae-jun to be a work of art that could be regarded as an exceptional achievement in our history of literature. Because she was a woman, however, many people suspected whether or not she actually wrote 〈Baekhwa〉, and she had to go through a number of other ordeals as well. In 〈Stories of Pain on the Road to Become a Female Writer〉, she wrote about the hardships she faced as follows. “In order to write novels, I am doing things that are totally unsuitable for my livelihood and income. In the morning, my two beautiful devils are sent off to the kindergarten and, before I get to spend any time thinking about a story, they return for lunch and come running back in a few hours when kindergarten finishes. At home, they nag me and pester me to give them the squared manuscript paper I spread out on my desk. I would then lock the door, bring out a beating stick and shout at them. I may scribble a few words but, when things go over the tipping point, I would even hit them. What divine punishment it is to be trying to push the children away, being a furious tiger mom, not being a good daughter to my own mother, and secretly thinking all the time about how I can possibly have my alone time like a thief devising ways to rob a house but failing miserably to let go of this pen even as I hear a good amount of gossip and criticism.” She was also interested in young literati so she trained future writers and artists at “Sehannu,” her own writing area. Her lifestyle was simple but very chic. She wore gloves even in the summertime, and always appeared presentable every time she met with people. This is why she got the nickname of “Summer Gloves.” Stories have it that she once changed her profile picture several times until she found the one she liked.In doing so, she met with the president of a publishing company somewhere in the middle between Seoul and Mokpo to replace the photo. In addition to exchanges with Korean authors, she also actively communicated, as the first president of the Society of Women's Literature, with Pearl Buck, a winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature; as well as Luise Rinser, a German female novelist; Arthur Miller, an American playwright; and a number of Taiwanese female writers. From the year of 1903 when she was born to 1988 when she passed away, Mrs. Park Hwa-seong wrote about 20 full-length novels, 100 short stories and over 500 essays and poems. I hope all of you get a chance to read her exquisite works.

stories.title: Mokpo Literature Museum - Kim Woo-jin Hall
stories.audioTitle: Mokpo Literature Museum - Kim Woo-jin Hall
stories.script: Mokpo Literature Museum - Kim Woo-jin Hall  Kim Woo-jin, the first-ever modern playwright of Korea  Playwright Kim Woo-jin was born in Jangseong, Jeollanam-do in 1897 as the eldest son of Kim Seong-gyu, an enlightenment thinker and a former Muan Supervisor, and began to live in Mokpo when he was 11 years old. After graduating from Mokpo Public Ordinary School, he went on to Kumamoto Agricultural School in Japan and graduated from Waseda University with a degree in English literature, as advised by his father who wanted his son to manage the lands and properties of the family. His pen name is Choseong or Susan. He performed in plays since he was in college and, in 1920, he formed the Theatrical Arts Association, a theater research group, with other study abroad students. Then, in 1921, he organized the Dongwoo Association Touring Theater Group to go on a performing tour around the country. Until he passed away in 1926, he lived a life of a pioneer who researched and materialized the modern play. During his short but passionate, flame-like life of 29 years, he produced 50 poems, 5 plays, 3 novels and 20 critiques. A true pity, because he would have left behind a much greater number of works if he had lived longer. He is also the first-ever modern artist produced by the city of Mokpo, considering the period in which he was active. If we call the plays before his time melodramas, we can say that a foundation of the new play was established with Kim Woo-jin. Kim was a pioneering playwright who had gone beyond the existing literary world and was even called a genius. When he was 16 years old, he wrote a novel titled 〈Fancy Literature〉 (not published) and, at the age of 18, he produced a modern free verse called 〈Ah, What Must I Gain〉, which is a Japanese poem. Upon graduating from Waseda, he returned to his hometown of Mokpo and began to work under his father, following his wish. During the day, he worked at his father's company and, at night, he set up a study he named “Baeksujae” where he engaged in ceaseless writing. Here, he wrote 〈Lee Young-nyeo〉 among many other works. Lee Young-nyeo is one of the best depictions of how Mokpo looked during the Japanese occupation period. The dialect of Jeolla-do region used at the time is shown accurately and realistically in the conversations within the work, which also vividly shows the horrific lives of the impoverished who lived below Yudalsan Mountain.  As a person who produced the first modern play written in Korean, the title of the first-ever modern playwright was perennially attached to him, and he also became the first theater activist who led the new play movement in the country. Moreover, Mr. Kim was active in the field of critiques as well. Through his paper titled 〈Bury the Yi Kwangsu-style Literature〉, he sharply criticized the fabrication of enlightening nationalism and humanitarianism. He then insisted on the revival of the pure Joseon language, organization of the dictionary, and collection of children's songs. Despite such literary achievements, however, his world of arts is not widely known perhaps because he has always been labeled as the “tragic protagonist of the Hyeonhaetan suicide” ever since he intentionally fell into the sea together with Yun Sim-deok. On his voyage back to Korea during which he was accompanied by Yun Sim-deok, the first soprano in the country's history, in August 1926, he and Yun jumped off from the ship into the Straits of Korea (Hyeonhaetan) but many view this as a death already foretold many times in his works and diaries rather than a surprising accident.

stories.title: Mokpo Literature Museum - Kim Hyeon Hall
stories.audioTitle: Mokpo Literature Museum - Kim Hyeon Hall
stories.script: Mokpo Literature Museum - Kim Hyeon Hall  Kim Hyeon, an unrivaled figure in Korean criticism literature  Kim Hyeon's original name is Gwang-nam. He was born in Jindo Island in 1942 and began to live in Mokpo when he was 8. In 1962 when he was in college, he began his literary career by releasing 〈Narcissus Poetics〉 on the 《Free Literature》 critique under the pen name of “Kim Hyeon”. He led the foundation of 《Sanmun Sidae》, the first literary coterie magazine for novels in Korea, together with Author Kim Sung-ok and Poet Choi Ha-rim. Mr. Kim is the first generation that was educated and performed literary activities purely in Korean, not Japanese. And this may be the reason that he was deeply interested in restoring the beauty and purity of the sentiments of our language. We call this generation the 4.19 Pure Korean Literature generation. Mr. Kim passed away on June 27, 1990 at the age of 49. He read a remarkable volume of books during his short life, and was a comprehensive intellectual equipped with a delicate but sharp analysis of works and an ability to encompass the humanities as a whole. With a lucid and beautiful style of writing, he was regarded as the first critic in history to raise the level of critique to an independent literary genre instead of something that is parasitic to creative works. The final diary entry he wrote on December 12, 1989 starts with, “I look at a mirror under a fluorescent light in the early morning... I am shocked at how wasted I look” and ends with, “I shout desperately and barely wake up... Ah, I am alive,” encouraging us to be thankful for the fact that we are alive. Some call him “a person who had read the whole world and passed away.” His appealing sentences and writing style are still setting an example today under the name of “Kimhyeonche.” He also discovered a number of new authors, which included Poet Gi Hyeong-do, Kim Seung-ok and Poet Lee Seong-bok.  Later, his pupils and friends described Kim Hyeon the literary critic as follows. Poet Hwang Ji-woo called him “an once-in-a-century type of critic”, and Poet Kim Hyung-young said, “He is still alive with us even after his death.” Poet Kim Ji-ha stated, “Kim Hyeon is the only person who will read my poetry” while Critic Lee Gwang-ho even claimed, “The passionate symbol that is Kim Hyeon comes to life under the name of literature and by the beauty of absent things.” Kim Hyeon once said, “I lack the skills to work with the language to write poetry and lack the power to fight against the reality to write novels,” showing truly how humble he was when it came to literature, and he served as a critic who always lowered himself. But his critiques resounded just as powerfully as poetry and unearthed the hidden structure of reality just as transparently as novels. It is said that he loved to meet up with other literary people at a chicken restaurant in Banpo to enjoy some delicious chicken and beer. They visited the place so many times that he was widely known as the “saint of Banpo chicken.” Because of the presence of a master of criticism literature, many other literary people naturally visited the restaurant as well. Chicken and literature are a bit strange combination but, in fact, Lee Cheong‐jun, Hwang Ji-woo and other renowned writers and intellectuals in the literary circles visited here as regulars, and, according to stories, many literary aspirants also visited on a whim for a chance to meet with Mr. Kim Hyeon.

stories.title: Kim Dae Jung Nobel Peace Prize Memorial
stories.audioTitle: Kim Dae Jung Nobel Peace Prize Memorial
stories.script: Kim Dae Jung Nobel Peace Prize Memorial  Welcome to the Kim Dae Jung Nobel Peace Prize Memorial. The memorial is designed as a building that symbolizes the five oceans and the six continents. The six protruded parts when you look from the outside symbolize the six continents, and the area filled with water is called Ullim Pond, which was constructed to represent the five oceans. The entire architecture holds the hope that President Kim Dae-jung’s spirit of peace spreads to the five oceans and the six continents of the world. Kim Dae Jung Nobel Peace Prize Memorial was opened on June 15, 2013, on the day of June 15th North-South Joint Declaration.  On the first floor, you will see the state car that the late President Kim Dae-jung used after his retirement. if you look at the license plate of the car, it says 1987. Let’s think about the meaning of this number. 1987 is the year in which not only his long-term house arrest was lifted after six years in prison and two exiles in Japan and the U.S. but also the democratic uprising took place.  Now, let’s move to Exhibition Hall 1. The video that is playing right now is the one that captured scenes from the actual Nobel Peace Prize ceremony, and this exhibition hall is a miniaturized reproduction of Oslo City Hall, Norway where the Nobel Peace Prize ceremony was held. Do you see the picture on the certificate of the award? The contents of this picture change every year depending on the award winner and show a summary of reasons why the person has been chosen for the prize. There are two main reasons that President Kim Dae-jung was selected for the Nobel Peace Prize. The first was his efforts in improving human rights in Korea and East Asia, and the second was his work in promoting reconciliation and cooperation between the two Koreas. If you take a closer look at the picture of the certificate, the shape of the road on which the two people are standing embodies a map of the Korean Peninsula. The difference in color between the bottom and the top symbolizes the division of Korea, and the use of red symbolizes the Sunshine Policy. The one dressed in white and the other dressed in black represent the leaders of two the Koreas. Since black and white respectively symbolize good and evil in the view of Westerners and North Korea was widely viewed as evil that used nuclear weapons to threaten world peace, perhaps that is why the North Korean leader is displayed in black. Finally, the branch on the side embodies a dove and symbolizes peace.  The Exhibition Hall 2 exhibits about Nobel and the Nobel Prize, and Exhibition Hall 3 displays President Kim’s biography and activities as a politician so please take your time to look around.  The Exhibition Hall 4 explains about the reconciliation of the North and the South as well as the Sunshine Policy, which helped the president receive the Nobel Peace Prize. There is an episode from his first trip by a South Korean president to Pyongyang since the Korean War. The movements of heads or guests of state are tightly planned in minutes, and accurate understanding of such movements is directly related to national security. On the way to Pyongyang Baekhwawon banquet hall, President Kim Dae-jung and Chairman of the National Defense Commission Kim Jong-il were supposed to move separately in their owns vehicles. However, as Chairman Kim decided to ride in President Kim's car, the predetermined plan faced serious issues.As a result, South Korea issued the highest emergency alert equivalent to that of an imminent war, and it was said that a situation on the verge of a war was actually generated. As he revealed through an interview later on, this was the most nervous moment in his life, according to President Kim, even more than numerous near-deaths he had experienced up to that point. Unlike President Kim who was quite strained, however, it is said that Chairman Kim actually tried to be humorous to ease the tension that President Kim was feeling. Now, hope you have a great time at the memorial hall.

stories.title: Lee Nanyeong Park
stories.script: Lee Nanyeong Park  Nanyeong Park is a park established in memory of Singer Lee Nan-yeong who sang Mokpo is a Port, and there is also the place of her natural burial, the first of its kind in Korea. What is a natural burial? It is a nature-friendly funeral method in which the ashes of a cremated body are buried under the roots of a tree, and her remains are laid to rest under a crape myrtle.  Before you enjoy the park, let me explain to you who Lee Nan-yeong was and why she is such an inconic figure for Mokpo citizens. She was born in extreme poverty in 1916. Her family was so poor that she could not even finish elementary school. Later on, she sang as an understudy for a traveling theater but, her big break came at the age of 19. It was then that she got to sing the song of her life, Tears of Mokpo, which became so popular to sell over 50,000 albums. Tears of Mokpo was released when Mokpo Port was filled with exploited goods such as rice and cotton. Perhaps, that is why the song was received as an expression of resentment towards Japan and the spirit of resistance and comforted the joys and sorrows of Joseon people like our sad Arirang.  All her life, she expressed the resentment and agony she and our people felt through songs before ending a short-lived life at the age of 49. Her grave was originally in a cemetery park in Paju, Gyeonggi-do but, by Dr. Choi Tae-ok, a local influential figure in Mokpo, and others, she was relocated to Nanyeong Park here in Samhakdo in 2006 and a natural burial ceremony was held.  She had three daughters to whom she herself became a strict teacher of music to raise them as singers as well. In 1953, her daughters debuted as “The Kim Sisters,”the first Korean girl group that went overseas. The Kim Sisters made an appearance at a Las Vegas show in 1959 and also released an album in America, achieving great success. They also appeared several times on 〈The Ed Sullivan Show〉, a show that made the Beatles famous and was a gateway to success for all future stars. Mrs. Lee was a great singer, too, but her children also scored remarkable success as singers. Aren't they amazing?  Near the song monument in Nanyeong Park, there is the “Lee Nan-yeong Song Button.” If you press the button, it will play her songs such as Tears of Mokpo and Mokpo is a Port. Make sure to press it and feel her voice and melody.

stories.title: Harbor Pocha
stories.script: Harbor Pocha  There is an old saying that the bird who has eaten is the best. Now, shall we look around the Mokpo Harbor Pocha and enjoy a variety of dishes together?  When Mokpo was selected as one of the four tourist hub cities nationwide, the city declared itself as 〈Mokpo, the City of Taste〉 in 2019 and opened the Harbor Pocha in Samhakdo in 2020. So why was Mokpo proclaimed as the City of Taste? First off, you all probably know that Jeollado is the most famous region in Korea in terms of food. This was the case during the Joseon Dynasty as well. In ≪Domun Daejak≫ written by Heo Gyun that evaluates foods from all over Joseon, the ingredients and tastes of Jeollado food are considered as the best. But Mokpo, especially, is located close to both the West and South Seas and, also, can conveniently be supplied with agricultural produce from other parts of Jeollado, which made the city famous since the old times as where a generous amount of inexpensive foods and all kinds of delicacies would nearly break the legs of the dinner tables. Notable dishes of Mokpo include Hongeo Samhap, or fermented skate and steamed pork slices served with kimchi; Nakji Tangtangi, or sliced raw octopus; Kkkotge Muchim, or seasoned crabs; and Junchi Muchim, or seasoned slender shad. You may be a bit unfamiliar with “Junchi Muchim,” though, right? You probably all know of an old saying, “Junchi is still better even if it is rotten.” Junchi is called Jineo or Sieo in Chinese letters, which mean that all the fish other than Junchi is fake. Taste-wise, you would agree that Junchi is the only real fish; if you enjoy the lustrous Junchi with a kick of sourness, there is nothing better to stimulate your appetite. But it does have a lot of tough bones so you must be careful when you eat it. There is more to enjoy at Harbor Pocha than just food. The sunset at the harbor is a well-known spectacle and, near the Harbor Pocha entrance, there is a deck from which you can get on the Samhakdo Cruise to enjoy the sea breeze and nightscape after dinner. Now, take full advantage of the great food and beautiful night scenery at Harbor Pocha!

stories.title: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 1. Start as
stories.audioTitle: 4. Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 1. Start as Mokpojin
stories.script: 4. Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 1. Start as Mokpojin  Hello, welcome everyone to Mokpo Modern History Museum I. This building used to be the Japanese consulate established to protect Japanese people and perform consular tasks since the opening of Mokpo Port in 1897. But, after the port opened, it served to seek the interests of Japanese merchants and transport rice and other specialty products of Jeollanam-do to Japan through the port of Mokpo. To the front of the building, a Japanese concession and the port were seen and, in the back, Yudalsan stood like a folding screen so it was a prime location. After the Eulsa Treaty, it was changed to Isacheon, an organization aimed at controlling local administration, and then, after Liberation, it was used as Mokpo City Hall, Mokpo City Library and Mokpo Cultural Center.  It is the oldest modern structure in Mokpo but still maintains most of the original appearance, thus receiving the highest praise for its historical and architectural significance and eventually accepting the designation as National Historic Site No. 289. Then, since 2014, it has been used as the History Museum.  Before you entered, did you get a good look at the exterior walls and surroundings of the building by any chance? The exterior walls still have bullet holes from the Korean War, and there is also an air-raid shelter remaining in the back of the building. Make sure to check them out after looking through the inside of the museum.  Okay, then we will begin with 〈Mokpojin Fort〉, the first of the seven themes of Mokpo Modern History Museum! First of all, the name, Mokpo is recorded in ≪Goryeosa≫ and ≪Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam≫ but its actual origin is not clearly known. Some speculate that it means a port filled with trees or cotton but this is said to be a baseless story that the Japanese made up during the occupation period. The most likely theory is that, because this area was a Mok, or an entrance, through which the Yeongsangang River water flows into the sea, it was initially called “Mokgae,”which then changed to its Chinese name of Mokpo.  Mokpojin Fort is an area of defense of the southwestern sea of the Korean Peninsula, located at a geographically key position that leads to the waters so it was home of the Joseon naval base and where Manho of Jong 4-pum was stationed for defense against the Japanese raiders. Based on the principle of “Seonsangsueo,” which means to pile up military provisions and weapons in a camp while waiting on ships to fight against the enemies rushing in from the outside, Manho diligently executed its duties of leading the ships to travel the waters back and forth for defense and search. As you can see, Mokpojin served as not only a military camp but also a passageway for propagation of culture and a maritime route on which tax grains were transported to the center.  However, Mokpojin that had been guarding a strategic point on Yeongsangang was abolished on July 15, 1895 by Gojong's Royal Edict No. 141. Unfortunately, no traces of the walls and government office of Mokpojin remained after going through the Japanese occupation period but, in 2014, some of the structures were restored including Hongsalmun, which symbolizes the entrance at the Mokpojin site, as well as an inn and parts of the surrounding walls. FYI, Mokpojin is the 6th of Mokpo 9 Views so make sure to stop by.

stories.title: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 2.
stories.audioTitle: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 2.
stories.script: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 2.  Restart as Gaehangjang, the Open Port  What comes to your mind when you think of “Mokpo”? A harbor? As it is popularly known, Mokpo still diligently fulfills its role as a harbor so let's examine together its past history.  On October 1, 1897, Mokpo opened the fourth port of the country following Busan, Wonsan, and Incheon. But it was the first independently opened port by Gojong's royal edict for invigoration of commerce to increase the wealth of the nation, which is why the beginning of Mokpo Port was dynamic and lively. In fact, the concessions in Mokpo at the time of the port-opening were either rice paddies or mud flats, which were difficult for people to dwell on, so projects were implemented to expand the concessions and stabilize the lands through reclamation. But almost all of these lands were occupied by the Japanese, leaving little space for Joseon people to live in. So the Joseon people who had to move to Mokpo for labor at the docks began to settle near Ssanggyo-ri after relocating the tombs that had existed in the area.   In order to increase government finance and income through tariffs, the Korean Empire installed Haegwan, which is today's customs, and Gamniseo to handle the business. Gamniseo strove to not only perform the tasks of foreign consulates and general affairs but also to protect the lives and properties of both Koreans and foreigners as well as safeguard the rights and interests of the Joseon people against foreign powers but it was eventually abolished in 1906 after the nation's diplomatic rights were stripped by the Eulsa Treaty of 1905. The functions of the port were maximized during the Japanese occupation period. Since it was in a great location to plunder rice and grains that were being produced abundantly in the Honam region, the port was exploited as a hub for fabric and grains.   Now, let's look at the distribution of concessions in the Open Port. On October 16, 1897, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Korean Empire met with the representatives of Japan, U.S., France, Germany, U.K. and Russia in Hanseong for Mokpo concessions regulations. As a result, it was decided that concessions for each of the countries within Mokpo were to be installed near Dongmyeon-dong fish market in the east, Seosan-dong in the west, Mokpojin in the south, and an area near Nojeokbong Peak in the north. After that, the concessions of different countries, which had extended their lands by construction of breakwaters and reclamation, entrusted the urban district plan to Staden of the Netherlands and, excluding the land for roads, consulates, tax office and parks, divided housing sites into three zones of A, B and C, which they put up for a public auction.  Then, the Japanese advanced to the inland based on Mokpo Port, purchased farmlands throughout Jeollanam-do and encouraged farmers to cultivate raw cotton. Have you heard of the word, upland cotton? It is the plant that corresponds to most of the cotton production worldwide. Since it was impossible to cultivate upland cotton in the humid climate of Japan, it had to be imported entirely from the U.S. and China. Then, Wakamatsu Tosaburo, a newly appointed Mokpo consul at the time, succeeded in a trial cultivation of upland cotton in Gohado Island of Mokpo and, subsequently in 1906, the Residency-General entrusted all rights to cotton cultivation to Japan’s Cotton Cultivation Association. Since then, Japan began to plunder Joseon for its cotton and volumes of cotton transported skyrocketed, which ironically resulted in Mokpo becoming a Top 3 trading port and the 6th largest city in the country.

stories.title: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 3. Becoming the frontline resistance
stories.audioTitle: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 3. Becoming the frontline resistance
stories.script: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 3. Becoming the frontline resistance  Becoming the frontline resistance  Mokpo experienced a great deal of suppression during the Japanese occupation period as numerous agencies were installed for Japan's rule over Joseon. However, Joseon people carried out numerous movements to resist the Japanese’ reign.  After the “Korea-Japan Treaty of 1910” was signed compulsorily by Japan, the jurisdiction of Mokpo Police spanned a broad region including Mokpo-bu, Muan-gun and Chuja-myeon of Wando-gun. In Mokpo-bu, precinct stations were established in Yeongjeong and Hangjeong where Japanese people lived while a police substation was installed in Juk-dong where Joseon people lived. After the military police system was changed to the general police system in 1919, another precinct station was additionally installed in front of the station within Mokpo-bu. Around 1930, there were 5 precinct stations, 19 police substations, 1 quarantine office, and 2 patrol crafts under the Mokpo Police Station. The chief was the police director under whom there were 2 police officers, 3 assistant police officers and 136 common policemen. You can tell just by these numbers that Japan's iron rule and pressure on the people of Joseon were heavy and harsh. But, as the suppression intensified, resistance and struggle by Joseon people continued.  Then, what kind of resistance and struggle were there? Mokpo is not a rootless city that happened to rise from wasteland as Japanese claimed but, rather, it is a city that was developed based on Mokpojin Fort, which was the naval base of Joseon. After Mokpo Port opened in 1897 by Gojong’s royal edict, trading began to increase significantly and laborers from all over the country flocked to the city for jobs. How many? According to ≪Mokpobusa≫, the Korean population that was 2,600 in 1897 increased to 23,488 by 1930. So, the men of the wharf formed an organization called Dojung to improve the inadequate labor conditions. As Japanese merchants lowered wages under the pretext of setting the wage standards for wharf men, the laborers caused general strikes against the wage cut in February and September 1898 and then in January 1901. It was the first labor movement and resistance movement in our country's history. After the abdication of Emperor Gojong and the disbandment of the army in 1907, rebellions of righteous armies grew more fierce and competitive especially in the Honam region. Notable generals of righteous armies that were active in the Jeollanam-do region are Jeon Hae-san, Sim Nam-il and An Gyuhong. They not only fought against Japanese forces but also took money and properties from corrupt Japanese officials and evil men of wealth and distributed them to Joseon farmers while interfering with inland trades of the Japanese. As you can see, Mokpo was an exploitation port and, at the same time, a city of resistance.

stories.title: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 4.
stories.audioTitle: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 4.
stories.script: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 4.  Foreign cultures are spread  Since the opening of the port, Mokpo was introduced with different forms of Christianity such as Catholicism and Protestantism and other foreign religions like an order of Japanese Buddhism and shrines. Also, within Joseon, Cheondogyo and Sicheongyo were created. After a failed mission in Naju, missionaries from the Presbyterian Church in the United States sought to establish Mokpo as the base for mission work in Jeollanam-do Province especially once the port was opened in 1897. Thus, they came to Mokpo in the spring of 1898 to begin their mission. A missionary named Eugene Bell first began the missionary work but, at the time, there were not that many believers and the environment was extremely inadequate so he had to set up tents to conduct mission work. But the number of believers continuously grew and, in 1910, Pastor Yun Sik-myeong constructed a stone chapel, which is today’s Yangdong Church building. Missionary Eugene Bell gathered and taught a handful of students in his sarangchae, and this was the beginning of Yeongheung School. A female missionary named Straeffer also educated a group of women, which evolved into Jeongmyeong School. Evangelism of the Catholic Church began when Father Albert Deshayes first settled in Mokpo in July 1898 and, in 1923, Sanjeong-dong Church opened Seongsim Primary School to contribute to education of children. The Catholic holy site of Mokpo established in the area surrounding Sanjeong-dong Church was where Legio Mariae, which is an international group of members of the Roman Catholic Church, was introduced for the first time in Korea. Also, the Korean Legio Mariae Memorial was established within the site to provide a place for pilgrimage and education of Legio organizations nationwide.  For Buddhism, ever since Dongbonwonsa of Jinjongdaegokpa of Japanese Buddhism was introduced in 1898, Shingon Buddhism also came into the country, and, by 1910, there were a total of 8 temples built by Japanese Buddhism. The Japanese government also built a shrine in Songdo Park, Mokpo and actually appointed an official there to manage it.  When foreign cultures come into our country, religions and schools are not the only ones that are introduced. Mokpo's very first hospital was a public hospital established by a Japanese in 1898. Then, in 1906, the Japanese settlement corporation built a commissioned hospital whose ownership was transferred to Mokpo-bu in 1914 to become Mokpo Prefecture Hospital. But, because all of the doctors here were Japanese, the Joseon people who could not speak Japanese were not able to use the hospital. How ironic, right? So most of the Joseon people used a French hospital, instead. This French hospital was built and managed by the Mission of the Presbyterian Church in the United States starting in 1909, and it is said that about 7,000 to 8,000 Joseon people used it every year.

stories.title: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 5.
stories.audioTitle: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 5.
stories.script: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 5.  Age of pop culture  Mokpo Ogeori was the Myeongdong of Mokpo, always crowded with Mokpo locals meeting one another. It was because seven movie theaters were concentrated in the area surrounding the Ogeori. Among them, Mokpo Theater was the second theater built by the Joseon people during the Japanese colonial period. Newly released movies were always the center of people’s interests. The one-handed man at Wonjin Theater capable of picking out those who were sneaking into the movies like a demon was one of the four most famous people of Mokpo. In 1904, the Japanese established a permanent entertainment theater called “Sangbanjwa”, which also gave birth to Sangnak-dong, which means an always fun place. Cha Bum-seok, a playwright from Mokpo, watched a performance by Dancer Choi Seung-hee at Pyeonghwa Theater when he was young and, after that point, he liked to wear his mother’s skirt and stand in front of a mirror to vaguely dream of a job for which he would stand on stage. Meanwhile, there were many children who were caught sneaking into and then dragged out of the Nylon Theater where people set up tents and engaged in entertainment. What do you think? Can you picture the scenes from that time in your head?  There are as many as 120 songs composed and written with Mokpo as the background. It is probably because of the beauty of Yudalsan Mountain, Yeongsangang River and Mokpo Port, right? People of Mokpo had a lot of artistic talents and flairs and many popular singers have been produced from the city. When we think of singers from Mokpo, the first one who comes to our mind is Lee Nan-yeong who sang 〈Tears of Mokpo〉. 〈Tears of Mokpo〉 was created by Mun Il-seok’s poem, which won the nationwide Top 10 city local song contest in 1935. Lee Nan-yeong sang this song when she was 18 to gain immense popularity, and the song instantly became a national favorite. The saying, “Let’s go to Mokpo to see Lee Nan-yeong,” even became famous among people. It was a turning point for Mokpo to be be known nationwide. 〈Tears of Mokpo〉 is an immortal masterpiece that is great to sing whether you are happy or sad. Also, it is a mysterious song that sounds sorrowful if you sing it alone and exciting if you sing with others. During the Japanese colonial era, it was a song of mourning that talked about the loss of the country, and, under the military dictatorship that alienated the Honam region, it was a song of Honam. People in Mokpo call it the anthem of the city so someone is probably singing it now at the top of his or her voice, right? The song titled 〈Mokpo is a Port〉, which was created by Lee Nan-yeong’s older brother, Lee Bong-ryong, was also sung by her so the siblings imprinted their hometown of Mokpo on the entire nation. The PR of Mokpo by the siblings is amazing, right?  You have probably heard of 〈Southbound Train〉 by Singer Kim Soo-hee. But there is also 〈Southbound Train〉 sung by Lee Nan-yeong in 1939! The sentiment about the warm southern country where Mokpo Port is located at the end of the Korean Peninsula has led to the nickname, Southbound Train. Mokpo Station on the Honam Line is the final stop but it has a greater significance as the departure station since there are more people getting off than getting on. Meanwhile, 〈The Hymn of Death〉 has a special connection to Mokpo as well. 〈The Hymn of Death〉, which is also the title of a famous drama, was originally sung by Yun Sim-deok, the first-ever soprano singer of Korea. Yun Sim-deok had fallen in love with Kim Woo-jin, a married playwright since her days of studying abroad in Japan. Kim Woo-jin was the son of a Mokpo millionaire and the nation’s first modern playwright who generated the new play movement and experimented with expressionist works on his own. It is also said that Kim wrote the lyrics for 〈The Hymn of Death〉. Mokpo, which was quicker to accept advanced cultures thanks to the open port, was at the forefront of the modern pop culture era.

stories.title: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 6.
stories.audioTitle: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 6.
stories.script: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 6.  Independence demonstration together  On March 1, 1919, the Declaration of Independence was announced in Tapgol Park, Seoul, which was filled with Taegukgi, or the Korean national flag, and cries for independence. The March 1st Movement was a colossal resistance to Japan's oppressive colonial rule. This can be said to be one of the greatest and most significant events in Korean history and a national resistance in which nearly the entire population took part. It was also a movement that acted as a historical driving force for the Korean national movement and united all of our people under the hope for independence. The shouts for liberation echoed and spread throughout the country even to Mokpo. Until the day on which the cries of Mokpo citizens were heard in resistance against Japan, they made the Taegukgi and planned to publish the Declaration of Independence, the independence song and resolution and an underground newspaper, all in the dark away from the strict surveillance of the Japanese. Then, the day finally came. At 10 AM on April 8, 1919, waves of Taegukgi flooded out sporadically from various locations along with the cries and shouts of the students of Jeongmyeong Girls’ School, Yeongheung School and Commercial School as well as members of Yangdong Church, merchants and other citizens. They were all heading to Mokpo Station. The independence demonstration proceeded fiercely throughout downtown Mokpo. Japanese police were greatly surprised by this and even mobilized mounted troops and military to swing their swords at the leaders of the movement. Protesters fell to the ground with severe wounds, which resulted in a great number of people injured. About 80 people were arrested in the end and suffered harsh beatings and tortures in prison. Many of them eventually passed away because of the aftereffects of merciless tortures. What do you was going on in their minds on that day?  Around the time of the March 1st Movement, Mokpo was a battleground of colonial exploitation versus resistance. Japan had set its eyes on Mokpo and its abundant local products as well as its port, and built the Japanese consulate, the Oriental Development Company, etc. While plundering rice, cotton, salt and many other products, Japan also thoroughly suppressed the resistance and fights displayed by Mokpo citizens. However, the people of Mokpo did not succumb to the oppression but, rather, marched towards independence more powerfully than any other region. Even under the strict monitoring of Japanese authorities, a variety of social groups from students and young people to church members, merchants and other citizens carried out systematic and organized protests. The April 8 Independence Protest, a famous independence movement of Mokpo, was a turning point for national awakening and was a driving force that led to national movements in various fields after the 1920s. Youth movements, in particular, were very active. In 1926, Mokpo Youth Hall was built and, in the following year, the Mokpo branch of Singanhoe, the largest national cooperation association during the Japanese occupation period, was launched at the Youth Hall in 1927. To commemorate the cries of that day and pay tribute to the noble cause of our patriots, Jeongmyeong Girls' High School reenacts the independence protest on every April 8. High school girls wearing white jeogori, or a Korean traditional jacket, and black skirts wave Taegukgi and depart the school to march past Mokpo Station towards Nojeokbong Peak in Yudalsan Mountain. In front of Nojeokbong, the event ends with a bodily expression of the day's brutality and the three cheers for independence. As you walk along Ilju Road of Yudalsan, there is a sign for the Mokposisa Pavilion, and, at the end of the path on which you follow this sign, you will reach the March 1st Independence Movement Monument. This monument was built in 1983 to commemorate and develop the noble patriotism of those who participated in the independence protest in Mokpo on April 8, 1919. On the back of the monument, which is designated as a facility related to independence movement by the Ministry of Patriots and Veterans Affairs, a list of independence patriots from Mokpo is engraved. Every March 1, the city of Mokpo invites the families of independence patriots and heads of veterans agencies and citizens' organizations to the Citizen's Bell and the March 1st Independence Movement Monument in Yudalsan to hold the Citizen's Bell Blast ceremony and events to pay respects. As we remember once again the noble spirit of independence of those who protected their country, people, hometowns and fellow citizens from the brutal colonization of Japanese imperialism and sacrificed their lives for independence on that day 100 years ago, let's shout, “Long Live Korean Independence!”

stories.title: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 7.
stories.audioTitle: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 7.
stories.script: Mokpo Modern History Museum I - Theme 7.  Modern city special exhibit  The beginning of a modern city can be said to have taken place when the port was opened. Mokpo Port opened on October 1, 1897 as the fourth of its kind in the country following Busan, Wonsan and Incheon. Unlike other ports that had been opened unfairly by the coercion of foreign powers, Mokpo Port was opened solely based on the determination of the Korean Empire government that such a port is in need. We can tell from the ≪Records of Japanese Embassy in Korea≫ that the government actually decided the date of the port opening on its own. Mokpo began to move forward as a modern city based around Mokpojin, the naval base during the Joseon Dynasty. However, the opening of the port also led to unfortunate events. Mokpo Port primarily exported rice and cotton, which were primary products while mainly importing secondary products for factories for a low-development trading structure so-called rice-cotton exchange system, which was the turning point at which the port was subordinated to the global capitalism market. Thus, the opening of Mokpo Port not only affected the limited area of Mokpo but also brought huge changes to the entire Honam region. Also, the port-opening led to a new world in which people were able to do away with the existing Yangban governance system. Various groups of people sought new possibilities, and the contemporary Western culture and Japanese culture introduced through the open port had a significant influence on everyone from merchants and farmers to, even, Yangban landowners. In particular, the first region in Korea to which Christianity was evangelized by missionaries was Jeollanam-do, which led to the establishment of modern schools and medical institutions in the region. Convenience facilities such as financial institutions, barber shops, billiards halls, pawn shops, public bathhouses and fire stations were established where the Japanese people lived and, in the process, a variety of modern structures were built. In particular Dongbonwonsa, Honam Bank, Yangdong Church and Japanese houses near the Ogeori, which was the center of the city at the time, produced scenes of a modern city. During the Japanese occupation period, it seemed as if Mokpo was divided in two in discrimination around Bukchon, which was the primary residential district for the Joseon people, and Namchon, which was where the Japanese people lived together.  As the function of a trading port became increasingly important after the port-opening, a greater population began to flow in from other regions which has led up to this day. Mokpo is a city that still has many traces of the Japanese colonial period. I hope that this is an opportunity for all of you who are looking for the scenes of life in Mokpo as a modern city to rethink about what colonization and modern mean to you.

stories.title: Modern History Museum II
stories.script: 9. Modern History Museum II  From a symbol of colonization to the modern history museum  Mokpo Modern History Museum II is the building that was used as the Mokpo branch of the Oriental Development Company during the Japanese occupation era, and is the symbol of colonial rule and exploitation. The Oriental Development Company was founded in December 1908 specifically to exploit the Joseon economy. Its headquarters was in Tokyo, Japan and had 9 branches in Joseon and 8 in China. The branch was initially installed as a local office in Yeongsanpo, Naju in 1909 but, as Mokpo grew rapidly as an open port, it was relocated to Mokpo in June 1920. The date on which the Mokpo branch building is believed to be November 7, 1921.  The company started with dual nationalities of Korean and Japanese but it became solely Japanese-owned after 1910 and, since then, served as a window for colonial exploitation. The tasks that had focused on land management in the early phase began to diversify into colonial landowner development, farm management, finances, etc. The primary role of the Mokpo branch, which was located within Jeollanam-do where agriculture was quite developed, was to purchase land at cheap prices; then to distribute it again to the Joseon tenant farmers. The Mokpo branch was controlling 17 farms located throughout Jeollanam-do and collected the largest amount of farm rent among any other branches of the Oriental Development Company nationwide. It also served as a financial institution that exploited the Joseon farmers through real estate mortgage loans.  In 1946 after Liberation, the Department of Naval Security was founded and stationed in this building until 1974. Then, from 1974 to 1989, it was used as the Military Police of the Mokpo 3rd Naval Sector Command. The participants of the May 18 Democratization Movement who had been suppressed by Chun Doo-hwan's new military regime were detained in the guardhouse here. Afterwards, command was relocated to Yeongam and the building was left vacated and neglected for about a decade before beginning to be dismantled on August 7, 1999. However, citizens who believed that the building held great value as a cultural heritage carried out a preservation movement, which eventually suspended the demolition. Then, on November 20, 1999, it was designated as Jeollanam-do Monument No. 174 and is currently used as the Mokpo Modern History Museum II.

stories.title: Archive Building of Former Mokpo-bu Office
stories.audioTitle: 3. Archive Building of Former Mokpo-bu Office
stories.script: 3. Archive Building of Former Mokpo-bu Office  Behind the Mokpo Modern History Museum I, which had been used as the Japanese consulate, Mokpo-bu Office and Mokpo City Hall since it was built in 1900 below Nojeokbong Peak in Yudalsan, there lie the Archives building and air-raid shelter of the former Mokpo-bu Office. It is estimated that the gable-roof, two-story stone structure, which looks like an opened book placed upside down, was used as the archive in the annex building of Mokpo-bu Office during the Japanese colonial period. The total floor area is 82㎡, which is not that large, but it is built with maximum effort overall, some people question whether or not its true purpose was an 〈archive〉. Normally, a structure isn't built with this much effort and elaboration just to store typical administrative documents. That is why some people think that “it is a place where valuable items were stored,” rather than just ordinary documents. But most experts in architecture agree that it was indeed an archive from the Japanese occupation period.  It was built in 1932 but the stone staircase leading from the 1st to the 2nd floor is still preserved as it was. The surfaces of the stones are finished in the “Hokdugi” technique, which makes each brick look as if it has a Hok, or a bump. If you count them well, the bricks are piled up in 21 levels but only both corners of the front of the building are processed with a round, dabbed finish. The Japanese mobilized prisoners who were captured at Mokpo Prison for this construction project. There is a quarry behind the prison located in Sanjeong-dong, Mokpo at the time, and the prisoners were forced to work on stone-cutting and construction.  The air-raid shelter, which is designated as Registered Cultural Property No. 588 along with the archive, was also built by the labor of our own people, which is quite sad. Now, let's move to the air-raid shelter.

stories.title: Archive Building and Air-raid Shelter of the Former Mokpo-bu Office - Air-raid Shelter behind the Mokpo Modern History Museum I
stories.audioTitle: Archive Building and Air-raid Shelter of the Former Mokpo-bu Office - Air-raid Shelter behind the Mokpo Modern History Museum I
stories.script: Archive Building and Air-raid Shelter of the Former Mokpo-bu Office - Air-raid Shelter behind the Mokpo Modern History Museum I  Behind the Mokpo Modern History Museum I, there is a huge air-raid shelter presumed to have been built between 1944 and 1945. The air-raid shelter is 82m long and there are three doors leading to the outside. It is estimated to have been created by the 150th Division of the Japanese army stationed in Yudalsan at the time for possible use in case of emergency. The cave is equipped with a cooking facility and even an air purification facility. After the start of the Pacific War in 1941, the Government-General of Joseon strengthened the war footing. They conducted air defense training through government offices and schools to prepare for air bombardment, and established air-raid shelters, which are manmade caves to be utilized as evacuation spaces, in many places. And they mobilized the Joseon people to war by force and exploited their labor.  Inside the shelter, you can find sculptures of Joseon men who were mobilized compulsorily for the construction of the cave. It is indeed a historical site that proves compulsory mobilization of the Joseon people during the Japanese colonial period. Can you feel the sweat, tears, and sighs of our ancestors who labored arduously under the watch of the Japanese?  As you walk up the stone steps between the central entrance of the air-raid shelter and the stone-built annex building, you will find the Bonganjeon site still remaining. Bonganjeon was where the Japanese king's photo and imperial edict on education were placed for coercion of worship. As it had no value to be preserved in terms of the architectural history and it was also believed to be a symbol of humiliation and disgrace, it was completely demolished in 1996, the 51th anniversary of the Liberation.

stories.title: Morundae Peninsula — Morundae Peninsula and Sunset
stories.audioTitle: Morundae Peninsula — Morundae Peninsula and Sunset
stories.script: Do you know the story of Morundae Peninsula, a place full of fog and clouds? It was named as Morundae because the island is often concealed in fog and clouds that are caused by sea currents. Up to the 16th century, Morundae was actually an island called “Morundo.” As time passed, soil and sand were gradually deposited here to connect the island to Dadaepo, which completed Morundae Peninsula that we see today.  Boasting a wonderful scenery, Morundae Peninsula is one of the three most picturesque places in Busan along with Taejongdae and Haeundae. It is especially known for the best sunset in the city. The glowing sun setting into the night creates unforgettable scenery.  If you view Morundae Peninsula from the sky, it looks like a crane stretching her wings and flying in the air. It is said that Yi Chun-won, magistrate of Dongnae Magistracy during the reign of King Seonjo, narrated a poem after looking around Morundae Peninsula. On the way to Dadaejin Magistrate's Office, there is a poetry monument on which this poem is engraved. It reads as follows: “Intrepid winds and waves continue thousands and thousands of miles, and the sky and Morundae are buried in white clouds. The sun that rises over the early morning sea is a red wheel, and Taoist hermits always come riding on cranes.” What do you think? You can tell from the poem that this has always been a beautiful place, right?  Moreover, the 15-km-long “Saha Sunset Road” from Morundae Peninsula to Eulsukdo Island is considered the most beautiful road in Busan. Now, shall we take a walk together?

stories.title: Morundae Peninsula — Dadaejin Magistrate's Office
stories.script: There is a place called “Dadaejin Magistrate's Office” within the famous Morundae Peninsula with the beautiful sunset. Dongheon, or magistrate's office, used to be a building where officials during the Joseon Dynasty performed duties related to politics or national administration at local government offices. Here, magistrate of town also bowed to pay respects to the royal palace. But did you know that the name of this structure had been “Dadaepo Guesthouse” until July 2020?  Busan Metropolitan Government called it “Dadaepo Guesthouse” when the structure was designated as the city's Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 3 in 1972. However, because the restored structure was not even close to a typical gaeksa, or guesthouse, it led to heated debates among local historians and scholars.  Gaeksa is a structure that served as the official residence in each village whereas dongheon was a magistrate's office to work on the matters of the state; the two are completely different structures. Through analysis and investigation of various historical sources and materials later, it was confirmed that this building was not a guesthouse but instead a magistrate's office. After deliberation by the Busan Cultural Heritage Committee, it was renamed from “Dadaepo Guesthouse” to “Dadaejin Magistrate's Office” as of July 2020. For your information, Dadaepo Guesthouse building actually existed but was lost in the 1900s after the Japanese colonial period.   Not too far from here, there is the Monument to the Loyalty of Jeong Un, also known as Nokdo Manho, who died in the Battle of Busan during the Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1592. Let me tell you a story about General Jeong Un for those of you who don’t know him that well. During the Japanese invasion, commander of Gyeongsang Right Navy Camp Won Gyun requested General Yi Sun-sin who was the commander of Jeolla Left Navy Camp at the time for military aid. As General Yi was unable to make a decision, General Jeong Un said, “There is no such thing as our province and theirs when it comes to defeating the enemy. We have to break the brunt of the enemy to preserve Jeolla-do Province,” insisting to fight the battles together as a nation. He helped protect the waters of Joseon alongside General Yi Sun-sin in countless naval battles including the Battle of Okpo and the Battle of Hansando Island. Thanks to the efforts and sacrifices of our ancestors who fought the Japanese invaders and defended our country, we are able to enjoy the beautiful Morundae Peninsula today.

stories.title: Eulsukdo Island — Nakdong River Culture Pavilion
stories.audioTitle: Eulsukdo Island — Nakdong River Culture Pavilion
stories.script: Nakdong River Culture Pavilion was first opened to tell the diverse stories of Nakdonggang River, which flows up to 317 miles and holds beauty and lives in its arms. Nakdonggang Estuary is a brackish water zone where river water and sea water meet. It features reed fields and an abundance of foods, which makes it a perfect seasonal home for over 170 kinds of migratory birds.  Inside the culture center, you may not only check out the culture surrounding the river but also enjoy world-renowned artworks with the theme of river. It is also a great experiential learning space that teaches why living organisms in water cannot live in a polluted river or what we have to do to protect our environment in a very detailed and transparent manner even for children to easily understand.  When you look at Nakdonggang Estuary from the rooftop garden of the building, you may witness once in a while fish that jumps out and back into the river as if it were dancing. You can also find birds who are waiting for those fish. The culture center offers a live view of the river, which you have only learned through pictures and texts.  Now, shall we move onto Nakdonggang Estuary Eco Center?

stories.title: Eulsukdo Island — Nakdonggang Estuary Eco Center
stories.audioTitle: Eulsukdo Island — Nakdonggang Estuary Eco Center
stories.script: Nakdonggang Estuary Eco Center exhibits materials on the ecology of the estuary in an easy-to-understand manner and also runs various nature learning programs for visitors including students. In addition, it serves as a research center that studies and investigates the ecology of birds and wetlands.  Established in an area where men, nature and birds coexist in harmony, Nakdonggang Estuary Eco Center was designed by an architect named Yasuhiro Yamashita who had won an international architecture contest. Korean pinewood was used on all three surfaces — floors, walls and ceilings — to set up an atmosphere in which you feel like strolling in a forest. What do you think?  If you look above from the section that connects the first and second floors, you will find indoor sculptures depicting flying birds, which add a dose of vividness to the environment. Moreover, if you look out the windows, you will be able to observe in person different kinds of migratory birds in the wetlands right in front. As there is a telescope near a window, especially in cold wintertime, it is the perfect place to observe birds from the warm indoors.  The second floor features a permanent exhibition hall and a mini library where you can learn more in detail about the birds you have just observed with your own eyes. The library, in particular, has a wide variety of books from those for children to professional literature on ecology, so children and adults alike will be able to enjoy it. Now, I hope you have a great time at the Nakdonggang Estuary Eco Center.

stories.title: Eulsukdo Island — Nakjojeong
stories.script: Nakjojeong is the name of the observatory located inside the Nakdonggaram Park near Nakdonggang Estuary Embankment. If you look at Nakjojeong from the outside, it is a two-story, triangular building. As you walk up the stairs inside or get on a sloped elevator, you will be able to reach a place where you can observe migratory birds.  The name, Nakjojeong, contains the meaning that, here in a migratory bird reserve, we do not interrupt the activities of these birds but rather, enjoy their company in the appearance of a migratory bird. There are footholds for children and telescopes for observation installed, which allows anyone to easily check out the birds.  But why do you think that Nakdonggang Estuary is a popular habitat for migratory birds? It is because the area has an excellent natural environment and an abundance of foods on a vast sandbank and mudflat, and also because it is located in the middle of the East Asia-Oceania flyway, which is one of the world’s three routes of migratory birds’ movement.  Since we are at Nakjojeong, shall we learn about birds as well? Depending on their movements, birds are divided into resident birds, migratory birds, passage migrants and vagrant birds. A resident bird is a species of birds that spend the whole year in a specific region to breed. Kestrels, hawks and sparrows are famous resident birds. A migrant bird is a type that moves its habitats from one season to the next, primarily to areas that have the adequate temperature, abundant foods and good places to build a nest. A passage migrant is the species that passes Korea and either flies north to breed in the tundra of Siberia and Alaska in springtime or flies south in fall to spend the winter in warm Australia or New Zealand. Finally, a vagrant bird refers to the one that got lost.  What kind of birds are you looking at right now? Enjoy an exciting time of observing different species of birds!

stories.title: Eulsukdo Island — Nakdonggang Estuary Embankment Fish Gallery
stories.audioTitle: Eulsukdo Island — Nakdonggang Estuary Embankment Fish Gallery
stories.script: Here, you can watch with your own eyes the fish swimming.  The walls are made of transparent glass windows, which enables you to make eye contact with the fish that are using fishway at this very moment. It almost feels like a natural aquarium. Then, what does fishway means? It literally means a “path that fish passes” and refers to a facility that has removed all the obstacles for fish to move and swim through more easily. This helps preserve the fish ecosystem.  Nakdonggang River, which begins from Hwangji Pond all the way up in Taebaek, Gangwon-do, winds and flows to the estuary where it enters the sea. The type of fish swimming from the sea to the river is called anadromous fish whereas those that swim from the river to the sea is known as catadromous fish. The species of anadromous fish you can find in Nakdonggang River are flathead mullets, sweet fish and three-spined sticklebacks. Flathead mullets are found from March to December while sweet fish and sticklebacks are seen between March and May. On the other hand, one of the most famous species of catadromous fish is eels and, in the Nakdonggang Estuary Embankment Fish Gallery, you can see eels going down to the sea and laying eggs in the period from August to October. Now, enjoy a great time with the swimming fish!

stories.title: Eulsukdo Island — Nakdonggang Estuary Experience Center
stories.audioTitle: Eulsukdo Island — Nakdonggang Estuary Experience Center
stories.script: Nakdonggang Estuary Experience Center is established for the purpose of preserving the excellent natural and ecological resources of the estuary and promoting the value they have. But originally, it was a marine processing station to handle human wastes generated in the city of Busan. However, the facility was remodeled and reborn as Nakdonggang Estuary Experience Center, which even won the grand prize at 2013 Busan's Most Beautiful Landscaping Awards.  In the Education Hall on the underground floor, you can listen to lectures on ecological experiences and safety related to ship explorations while the Eco Small Library on the first floor is offering books on ecology and various other fields. Though it is small, it still has over 6,000 books so visit the library whenever you can to read many different books.  Now, let’s use the elevator to go up to the rooftop observation deck. The surroundings are so beautiful that it is hard to believe that it once was a human waste marine dumping site emitting a bad odor in the past. If you look to the right from the observatory, you will see a longshore bar, which is a sandbank. If you look to the left, you can find a vast sea as well as Morundae Peninsula in the direction of Dadaepo. If you can’t see it well, try using one of the free telescopes installed on the observation deck. If you want to look for birds from the rooftop, be careful not to make too much noise! We shouldn’t make the resting birds stressful and disturb them who are taking a good rest here.

stories.title: Hwangnyeongsan Mountain — Hwangnyeongsan Mountain
stories.script: If you ask Busan locals what they think about Hwangnyeongsan Mountain, they will say that it is “a place with a beautiful nightscape,” “a great place to stroll or exercise at night,” “a place where you go to see a sunrise” and “a perfect place to watch the Busan International Fireworks Festival.” During the Japanese colonial era, it used to be a mine where copper and gold were dug up. Today's Hwangnyeongsan Mountain is not that vast so it is possible to take a hike in about three hours. It has become a very attractive trail on which you can have a great time even at night. Hwangnyeongsan Mountain’s nightscape is especially famous among Busan locals. There is a cafe near the Hwangnyeongsan Beacon where you can enjoy a cup of coffee while enjoying the scenery.  By the way, when do you think Hwangnyeongsan Beacon was first established? The beacon, which is an important means of military communication, was installed at the peak of the mountain in 1422 (the 7th year of King Sejong's reign). Although they are no longer in use nowadays, beacons were a system that used smoke in daytime and lights at night to deliver information quickly to even remote places. This particular beacon was the one restored in 1976 to teach the future generations the spirit to protect local and national lands. Every year, religious rituals for the mountain spirit are held at the restored beacon in addition to the reenactment of a signal fire. For those who are interested, make sure to visit again at the right time.

stories.title: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation and Tunnel of Memories
stories.audioTitle: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation and Tunnel of Memories
stories.script: “A museum to remember and learn about history together” This is the goal and value pursued by the National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation. It is because painful and disgraceful history has no meaning if we don’t remember it.  Why do you think National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation was established in Busan? Having won the Russo-Japanese War in 1904, Japan decided to use Busan as a base for its advancement into the mainland continent and began full-scale development of Busanhang Port. Subsequently, starting in 1905, it installed ferries that regularly traveled between Busanhang Port and Shimonoseki Port to begin a full-scale exploitation. In addition, for procurement of military goods and supply of manpower, Japan implemented the manpower exploitation policies that forcibly mobilized Joseon people. Most of those who left Joseon as a part of the forced mobilization at the time got on ships from Busanhang Port and a majority of the victims were from Gyeongsang-do region. Based on these facts, a plan to construct a museum in Busan began in September 2008,  and National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation finally opened its doors in December 2015. The walls of the building, which is in the form of terra-cotta produced by firing clay, were made to have rugged, uneven surfaces to express the pain and wounds from those days. Relatively dark colors were used to depict a gloomy atmosphere of the times while the overall appearance of the building not only symbolizes the ferries that traveled between Busan and Shimonoseki but also expresses the dynamics of overcoming pain and moving forward. Next to the building, a path called “Memorial Stairs” is established to enable visitors to walk up to the memorial tower on the rooftop.  In the exhibition hall of the museum, over 400 pieces of relics that aim to tell the truth are on display, from the materials collected by the government to essays and photos donated by the victims of forced mobilization and their families. As such, visitors can witness the reality of forced mobilization committed by Japan.  Now, let’s take a tour of the inside together. When we take the elevator and get off on the fourth floor, we can get to the permanent exhibition hall. As we enter the hall along a gradual slope, what awaits us before anything else is the “Tunnel of Memories.” On dark walls, shapes of those setting off on a journey are shown in white shadows. You can hear a sorrowful music and voices that flow through the dark road.  Every time I was beat with a stick, I cried and looked up at the ceiling. Many have died but no burial has been made...  The stories of a boy laborer who was dragged to Japan at a young age of 15 and of those mobilized as suicide commando are narrated at a low-tone voice.

stories.title: Concept of Forced Mobilization (Permanent Exhibition Hall 1) (FOMO Museum)
stories.audioTitle: Concept of Forced Mobilization (Permanent Exhibition Hall 1) (FOMO Museum)
stories.script: Forced mobilization is an inclusive term that encompasses conscription, enlistment carried out by force, and “Sexual slavery victims for the Japanese imperial army“, the so-called “comfort women.  Japanese Imperialism, which invaded mainland China in 1937, enacted the National Mobilization Law in 1938 and mobilized all of the people, resources and funds necessary for war in colonial Joseon until its defeat in 1945. They even controlled and mobilized ideas. The Korean government calls all of those who were forcibly mobilized to become soldiers or laborers as “victims of forced mobilization.”  Forced mobilization happened in nearly all regions that were ruled by Japan at the time.According to the official data from the Japanese government, the scale of forced mobilization in both local and overseas has reached a total of 7.8 million Joseon people. Considering that the population of Joseon was 26 million in the 1940s, this means that one person from each household was mobilized. Japan also enacted various laws to secure the labor power needed to carry out an invasion war and forcibly mobilized countless Joseon people to munitions factories, road construction sites and coal mines, thus exploiting their manpower.
