The period from 1910 when Joseon was deprived of its national sovereignty to the liberation in 1945 is called the Japanese Colonial Period. Starting with extortion of Joseon’s sovereignty, Japan carried out a full-scale invasion of neighboring countries and even attacked Manchuria in 1931. Having won in Manchuria, Japan founded Manchukuo and then started a Sino-Japanese War in 1937 to subsequently conquer neighboring countries one by one. Ultimately in 1941, it executed a sudden attack on Pearl Harbor in the U.S. to start the Asia-Pacific War. Japan called it the “Great East Asia War.” They exaggerated it as a holy war which protected Asian people from the land of white people, such as the U.S. and Europe to glamorize and justify their invasion. This is still what conservatives in Japan believe to this day.  As the invasion of mainland China has become a long-term war, Japan enacted the “National Mobilization Law,” in 1938 which aimed to transform not only Japan but also the colonies including Joseon and Taiwan into a system for war execution. In other words, they tried to mobilize everything they needed for the war. Forced mobilization of Joseon labor force continued to be evolved and strengthened from “recruitment” in 1939 and “public labor mobilization” in 1941 to “forced draft” in 1944.

stories.title: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 1: True Nature of Forced Mobilization
stories.audioTitle: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 1: True Nature of Forced Mobilization
stories.script: During the Joseon Dynasty, many Japanese companies in Joseon and Japan grew rapidly. A lot of these companies are now global corporations thanks to the growths they had experienced in this period. And, the blood and sweat of forcibly mobilized Joseon people lie at the foundation of their development. Types of forced mobilization include mobilization of soldiers, army civilians, laborers and sexual slaves.  “Mobilization of soldiers” literally refers to an act of mobilizing soldiers to fight in battlefields. In 1938, Japan started to mobilize Joseon people as soldiers based on a system they called an Army Special Volunteer System. The name suggested that people “volunteered,” but since a quota was assigned to each region, it was virtually forced mobilization.  “Mobilization of army civilians” refers to an act of mobilizing workers to perform all necessary tasks during a war in military administration. Such workers included nurses, prisoner guards and translators but most of them were those mobilized for simple labor at airfields or road construction sites in life-or-death battlefields.  “Mobilization of laborers” refers to forced mobilization of Joseon people to supplement labor forces that became insufficient since most Japanese men had been enlisted in military as the war was prolonged. Forcibly mobilized Joseon laborers suffered from racial discrimination and low-wage, long-hour labor at mines, coal mines, munitions factories, civil construction sites and unloading stations at ports in not only mainland Japan but also Sakhalin, Hokkaido, Taiwan and East Asia.  “Mobilization of sexual slaves” is a crime against humanity in which Joseon women were forcibly mobilized by employment frauds and human trafficking as sex slaves to be taken to battlefields where Japanese soldiers were stationed. The women who had had no idea of where they were being taken to experienced indescribable sexual abuse and exploitation.  The reason we now know about the history of forced mobilization is the testimonies from those who had survived the atrocities. Despite their countless testimonies, however, Japan denies, reduces and conceals evident facts, which is one of the reasons why the magnitude and scope of such inhumane damages from war crimes such as those who suffered as comfort women are still not clearly known.  Over half a century has passed since our country was liberated from Japan, but there are still a lot of issues that have not been solved, including remains that have not returned, failure to pay psychological compensations for forced mobilization, violence by the Japanese government that unlawfully placed war criminals in Yasukuni shrine without the consent of the bereaved, discrimination against Siberian detainees and B- or C-grade war criminals, and proper apologies for their inhumane actions performed on Japanese military “comfort women.”  Solving these issues is a way to overcome colonialism that the 20th-century Japanese imperialists have left us with as well as the assignment of mankind in pursuit of universal values for restoration of men's dignity and rights that had been infringed upon by national violence.

stories.title: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 1: Liberation and Return
stories.audioTitle: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 1: Liberation and Return
stories.script: What do you think these steel bars represent? Yes, they represent prison.  After Japan lost the war, international war crime trials were held in Tokyo and many other places in East Asia. In these trials, a number of Joseon people were also prosecuted and punished as Class B or C war criminals. Why do you think people from a colonized territory who didn't even start the war were prosecuted as war criminals? It is because many of them were forced by the Japanese military to serve the role as prisoners’ guards who oversaw forced labor by Allied Forces’ captives. Since they were the ones who directly dealt with the prisoners, all the responsibility for starvation and brutality was placed upon Japanese soldiers and Joseon-born prisoner guards at the prison camps. As a result, many of these Joseon men ended up being executed or locked up in jail cells as war criminals.  The long-awaited liberation finally came, but there was almost no possible way for them to return to their homes. Even after executing governmental authority for forced mobilization of Joseon people, Japan treated them as “foreigners” as soon as they lost the war and chose not to help with their return to Joseon, which is why Joseon people had to find their own difficult routes back home. Depending on the policies or circumstances of the countries they had been living in, some of them had to see their returns postponed indefinitely while others actually settled down for good in the foreign land.  There was an unfortunate sinking of a vessel named “Ukishima” by explosion. The ship, which was traveling from Japan's Maizuru Bay to Busan with thousands of Joseon people onboard, supposedly sunk by intentional attacks and explosions carried out by Japan. To this day, we still do not clearly know how many Joseon people died or went missing and exactly what caused the explosions.  The Japanese government also showed its duplicity in the matter of return of Joseon people from Sakhalin. When the Soviet Union returned Japanese people, they were able to go back to their home country safely but Joseon people were unable to return because they were no longer Japanese citizens. Japan abandoned Joseon people they had been using, and even after being demanded by the Korean government later on, has not shown any actions to take responsibility for the return of Joseon people from Sakhalin.

stories.title: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 1: Never-Ending Forced Mobilization by Japan
stories.audioTitle: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 1: Never-Ending Forced Mobilization by Japan
stories.script: The Korean-Japanese Conference and the Agreement on the Settlement of Claims took place in 1965 but issues of inhumanity such as Japanese military “comfort women” and forced labor victims were never brought up for discussion. The Japanese government also interprets in a different way the nature of the money that Joseon received through a claim. Moreover, Japan claims that everything was “completely and finally” resolved by the Korean-Japanese Agreement of 1965.  The Supreme Court of Korea, however, ruled that Japan's rule over Korea was unlawful and therefore, all National Mobilization Laws enacted as a result were also illegal, thereby requiring Japanese companies to pay compensations for psychological damages inflicted upon victims of forced labor. The court clearly stated that Japan's colonial rule was illegitimate and the money received through a claim was a mere settlement of the claim-obligation relationship between Korea and Japan, so the Japanese companies are liable for damages. However, the Japanese government and companies completely refuse to accept this ruling. They are denying the claim rights of individuals that even the Japanese judiciary had acknowledged.  Even if a certain agreement was signed between the two nations, international laws state that, in principle, the rights of the victims cannot be overlooked for inhumane crimes such as Japanese military “comfort women” and the forced labor issue. In 1997, the International Labour Organization (ILO) stressed the fact that wartime sexual violence and forced labor issues by Japan had not been resolved and advised the Japanese government to take immediate actions for resolution of these issues. Such recommendations are valid even today but the Japanese government is still irresponsibly repeating their lame claim saying that they are no longer liable as all issues have been resolved.  Now, please take a look at the commemoration space for victims and donors. There are photos of young men who are at a physical examination for military draft, child laborers at Shin-Shimokawa mine, young soldiers of a suicide squad, military officers, laborers in front of a minehead, Joseon soldiers in front of a Japanese shrine, prisoner guards, soldiers wearing traditional Japanese underwear called fundoshi, drafted soldiers and their wives, mothers covering their mouths and holding back tears at the end of a line in a schoolyard, and a child holding a portrait of his father in his arms...  We should never forget about what happened so that this painful history does not repeat itself.

stories.title: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 2: Process of Forced Mobilization
stories.audioTitle: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 2: Process of Forced Mobilization
stories.script: In 1938, Japan enacted the National Mobilization Law to forcibly mobilize from Joseon everything they needed to carry out a war. Every sector of the public and governmental authorities including Japanese General Government of Korea, local administrative agencies and police were utilized, and means of fraud, threats, conciliation and even abduction were used to fill the quota that had been assigned to each region. They called this “offering of men.”  “They promised to give us good jobs, but it was all lie.” “I wasn’t sure if I would come back alive or dead. It made me difficult to leave in the first place...” This is a line that I can’t forget. Most people who were recruited in this manner left Busanhang Port on ferries and arrived at Shimonoseki Port in Japan. Here, they were either made to stay in Japan or dragged to China, Russia or Southeast Asia to be stationed where Japanese troops were.  You might wonder, was there anyone in Joseon who refused the forced mobilization? Of course there was. Chang Chun-ha, Kim Jun-yeop and their fellow comrades who had been taken as student soldiers made a successful escape and joined the Korean Liberation Army to fight for the independence of Korea. Some young men who had avoided forced draft hid in Jirisan Mountain and confronted Japanese policemen that came to arrest them. There were many instances where Joseon people escaped in the process and sites of forced mobilization. To prevent such escapes, Japan utilized Concordia Association and local police agencies to strengthen surveillance and crackdown.  Now, let’s enter a room called “Mirror of an Era.” The road of invasion, the road where they were taken by force, that railroad... The mirror contains those that look like our family and friends. As we read each and every name engraved in battlefronts, coal mines, munitions factories, sugar cane farms, refineries and military brothels, we are reminded of the lingering wounds. There is a saying, “A nation that forgets its past has no future.” This can't be emphasized enough.

stories.title: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 2: Joseon Laborers’ Dormitory
stories.audioTitle: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 2: Joseon Laborers’ Dormitory
stories.script: What do you think “takobeya” is? It is a Japanese word for dormitory of Joseon laborers. Takobeya is another term for the hanba system, which was an old-fashioned labor management system in civil engineering and construction industries where managers of labor organizations not only supervised labor of the manpower and wholly controlled contracts, wages, etc. but also dominated workers’ bodies and souls through violence. Also known as “Prison beya,” it was a type of labor organization from the days when workers’ human rights were not respected. The Naya system at coal mines is a similar kind of labor management organization. “Takobeya” is translated into Korean as an “octopus room.” There are several theories behind the origin of this term but what they all say in common is that it refers to both a labor management system and a dormitory in which even the slightest human rights are easily infringed upon by violence.  Look at the young Joseon men who lie down shoulder to shoulder in a cramped space like in a military barracks. They are so weary and fatigued that they expect to fall asleep within seconds but couldn't do so due to the aching body, hunger, and longing for home and family. Tears fall from their eyes, which they once believed to have run dry, slowly running down their cheeks.  Their typical lunch was two rice balls made by mixing bean cakes, which were suitable for animal feeds or fertilizers. In addition, they did not have any place to comfortably lay down their bodies that had been fatigued from hard labor all day long. We can’t imagine how many young men of Joseon were starved and cried themselves to sleep, longing for their parents.  In To Hokkaido Over Nine Hills, a collection of oral statements of victims forcibly mobilized to Hokkaido in those days, there is a passage that reads as follows: “You can’t get out or do anything because takobeya is where they beat you up like there’s no tomorrow. The bathroom’s inside and they lock the only door that leads to the outside so you can’t go out at all. There's someone who watches lights at night, a Japanese who doesn’t sleep to watch lights all night long. There’s nothing you can do.”

stories.title: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 2: Coal Mines
stories.audioTitle: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 2: Coal Mines
stories.script: Coal and iron ores are extremely essential commodities in a war. So where can these be obtained? That's right, in a mine or a coal mine. Coal mines were very dangerous places where burying or gas explosions often occurred so no Japanese men wanted to work in such places, which is why Japan mobilized Joseon people by force. Joseon men were dragged to anywhere that has a lot of coal, from the northern region of Joseon and the entire Japan including Hokkaido to South Sakhalin and Manchuria in China.  There is a Korean term, “Insaeng Makjang.” “Makjang” refers to the innermost end of a mine, and it is also a metaphor for a state of despair with absence of possibility. Japan even pushed little Joseon children into these hellholes, and forced grown men to dig coal from these narrow mines where they were unable to even stand up. Because it was difficult to get out of a mine once you are deep inside, workers alleviate hunger with bean cake rice balls and took care of their urine and feces in the mines as well all the while suffering from hard labor for over 12 hours a day. They continuously inhaled coal dust without masks on because of the heat of the environment. They were allowed to get out of a mine only if they finished their quota. You can imagine how laborious and taxing the working environment was.  Have you all seen the movie, The Battleship Island? The name of the island is actually Hashima, but it’s called the Battleship Island because it looks like a battleship. Coal mines on this island were over 1,000 meters deep down into the ground and the working environment was also infamously poor, which is why it was also known as a “hell island” or “prison island.” On this hell-like island, Joseon people who had been forcibly mobilized like this saw the end of their lives from hard labor, starvation, suffering from accidents or diseases, or deaths during escape attempts.  In 2015, the Japanese government designated the Battleship Island, still freshly holding the blood and sweat of Joseon people, as “Modern Industrial Heritages in Kyushu and Yamaguchi” to register them as the UNESCO World Heritage site. However, in doing so, they showed cowardice in intentionally omitting all the facts about Joseon and Chinese victims of forced mobilization while only stressing the aspect of the place as a modern industrial heritage site. When it inscribed the Battleship Island as a world industrial heritage, the UNESCO General Conference made a formal recommendation to reveal its “complete history” including that of forced mobilization, and the Japanese delegate to UNESCO publicly promised at the conference that the country would fulfill such recommendation. However, Japan changed their mind on the following day, before the ink on the inscription hadn't even dried up yet, denying forced mobilization of Joseon people and even went as far as to blatantly lie to the world that there was no such thing as racial discrimination and forced mobilization.

stories.title: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 2: Midwest Pacific Front
stories.audioTitle: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 2: Midwest Pacific Front
stories.script: During the Asia-Pacific War, Japan expanded their front lines even to the Midwest Pacific regions and called them “Nambang” or “Namyang.” This area used to be a German colony prior to World War I, but as Germany collapsed after the war, Japan took it by force afterwards. To these distant places, over 55,000 Joseon people were forcibly mobilized as soldiers, army civilians, laborers and Japanese military “comfort women.”  There is a bridge called “Aigo Bridge” in Palau, Southeast Asia, and people say that the name originated from how Joseon workers at the time cried, “Aigo, aigo,” as they were starved and exhausted from hard labor. In addition to difficult labor and hunger they had to endure, they also faced deaths as human shields on battlefields, or even worse, by a slaughter.  Have you ever heard about a film called The Bridge on the River Kwai? A part of the “Thailand-Burma Railway” that connects the two countries, the Bridge on the River Kwai was initially constructed to aid Japan in its war. In the movie, there is a prisoner guard who is a Joseon man. They become prisoner guards by an order of Japanese army and make the prisoners of war from the Allied Forces perform hard labor, but once the war is over, they faced trial as a war criminal and eventually receive prison terms. When you watch this movie, you will be able to better understand how ignorant Japan was when it came to obeying international laws and how brutally they treated the Allied prisoners of war.

stories.title: Sexual Slavery Victims for the Japanese Imperial Army (Permanent Exhibition Hall 2) (FOMO Museum)
stories.audioTitle: Sexual Slavery Victims for the Japanese Imperial Army (Permanent Exhibition Hall 2) (FOMO Museum)
stories.script: ‘Sexual slavery victims for the Japanese imperial army’, the so-called ‘comfort women’, refer to female victims who suffered sexual violence from Japanese soldiers and whose human rights were abused. Japan unlawfully and forcibly mobilized Joseon women, from little girls to those in their 30s, in a variety of ways including employment frauds and human trafficking then took them to the battlefields where Japanese soldiers were stationed. These women who had basically been abducted not knowing where they were going became deprived of freedom and suffered brutal sexual violence and abuse in an unfamiliar place. This horrific experience left trauma so enormous that they could never live a normal life again.  As we pass through a barbed-wire gate, we see a brothel. Barbed-wire fences represent military camp. In this tiny boarded up room, we can only see a wooden bed and a washbasin. It is no different from a prison cell. There is also a nametag attached on every door. Sachiko,” “Michiko,” “Miyoko”... These are the names of the sexual slavery victims for the Japanese imperial army who were called by their Japanese names.  Besides, an animation about the cruel journey from being taken from Joseon to Japan as a ‘Sexual slavery victims for the Japanese imperial army’ begins with a sad tune of a piano. The song you can hear is called ‘To Me, Girls and Grandmas.’  Despite these historical facts, Japan ceaselessly tries to ignore and evade their responsibilities without making any sincere apologies. Why is it so difficult to apologize for what they have done wrong?  Now, the victims who were once known as Sachiko,” “Michiko” and “Miyoko” have broken a long silence, bravely stepped forward to tell the truth and are currently working for women’s human rights.“  Being Sexual slavery victims for the Japanese imperial army was forced down our throats. We are going to let everyone know the accurate details of what really happened and record them in history so that such tragedy never ever happens again to mankind.”

stories.title: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 2: Return
stories.audioTitle: National Memorial Museum of Forced Mobilization under Japanese Occupation — Permanent Exhibition Hall 2: Return
stories.script: In 1938, Japan enacted the “National Mobilization Law,” taking and arresting countless Joseon men for military and labor force under the name of the emperor and nation of Japan. However, after they lost the war, they immediately took a stance to ignore and evade their responsibilities for the return of Joseon people whom they had mobilized by force.  Once the country was liberated, Joseon people wished to go back to their homes as soon as they could. The road back home, however, was not easy. The Japanese government was virtually in a state of anarchy so they could not receive any help from Japan while the U.S. government, too, did not make policies with a focus on the return of Joseon people. Therefore, Joseon men and women were forced to make the journey home by their own efforts and hard-earned money, which was used to buy boats. But many died or suffered injuries from storms and various accidents. The road to home as they held onto the corpses of their friends and colleagues was filled with mixed feelings of joy, sorrows and pain.  Though most of these Joseon people were able to return to their homes, there were those who could not make it. In the midst of the cruel international state of affairs and chaotic circumstances on the Korean Peninsula, many had to continuously remain or be detained in areas to which they had been mobilized, and some have not been able to return even after their passing.  What do you think happened to Joseon people who failed to return to Joseon and stayed in Japan? At first, they were viewed as people of an enemy country, prisoners of war, stateless people, minorities or foreigners. Even under unfair treatment and discrimination, they gradually settled down and took deep root in local communities. As diplomatic relations between Korea and Japan later returned to normalcy, many of these Joseon people have been able to visit their home countries or permanently move to Korea, thus generating active exchanges between the two nations. Today, the Korean government continuously strives to raise the legal status of overseas Koreans, protect their rights and interests, ensure their political right and revitalize exchanges.

stories.title: Meeting Point (Frontyard_01)
stories.script: Pleasure to meet you, my name is Song Puga and I am your culture and tourism guide today. The “Historical Tour of Samjeondo-gil” that we are going to take today is to look back at the 47-day period during which Joseon fought against the Qing Dynasty at Namhansanseong Fortress. As you all may already know, Joseon eventually surrendered to the Qing Dynasty in a humiliating manner. It was one of the most disgraceful moments in the history of Joseon. Nonetheless, the stories of various events and people we are about to learn today give a lot of messages. Let's follow the trail and take on a journey through the history of Namhansanseong Fortress. There are a total of five courses at Namhansanseong Fortress, each of which takes from one hour to three-and-a-half hours. Today, we are going to tour the entire fortress by combining all of these five courses. The course will begin at the North Gate and pass West, South and East Gates to look around the fortress. And lastly, we are going to look at Haenggung, the temporary fortress. Namhansanseong course is well-prepared like any other trail you find around your neighborhood, which is a great place to enjoy history and nature at the same time. However, please be mindful of safety as there are steep uphills and downhills from the East to North Gates. Also, if you feel excessive fatigue or any other abnormality with your body while we move on, please let me know immediately. If anyone wants to use the restroom before we leave, you may use the ones behind you. There are also restrooms throughout the fortress so you can use any of them during our tour.

stories.title: Meeting Point (Frontyard_02)
stories.script: Okay, everyone. Please gather around here. Before we start, let me introduce to you a little bit about Namhansanseong Fortress.  Namhansanseong is a fortress built by King Injo in 1624 over the foundation established during the period of the Three Kingdoms. During the Joseon Dynasty, Namhansanseong Fortress was the last bastion that defends Hanyang, the capital, and at the same time, a key military point. However, the fortress was not properly managed after the Japanese colonial period. Dangerous telephone poles were installed on the fortress walls and the temporary palace where the king stayed became a hotel. It was only after 1998 that Namhansanseong Fortress started to regain its original looks. A number of scholars, locals and organizations joined together for resurrection of the fortress and, at last, the work to excavate and restore the fortress began. What were discovered from the excavations were full of surprises, and it was a series of Namhansanseong Fortress to regain its old, forgotten appearance. And the last step of this process was to restore Haenggung, the temporary palace. Temporary palace at Namhansanseong Fortress was open to the public in 2012 after a decade of restoration work. Finally, Namhansanseong Fortress, which served as a temporary capital in times of wars and disasters, came to life once again. The history of Namhansanseong Fortress, its characteristics as a military base, and its role as a temporary capital in case of emergency, all of which helped protect the country's independence, were highly regarded, and this is the reason why it was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site to be protected by mankind.  Now, let's take a look around the fortress. The first place we will be visiting is the North Gate of Namhansanseong Fortress.

stories.title: North Gate Entrance
stories.script: Before we move on, let me explain briefly about the surrounding topography of Namhansanseong Fortress.  Everyone, could you please take a look around you? From Namhansanseong Fortress, there is Namhansan Mountain to the east and Cheongnyangsan Mountain to the west. Among them, the main mountain of Namhansanseong Fortress and its temporary palace according to geomancy is Cheongnyangsan in the west. In the old days, people also called Cheongnyangsan Mountain as Iljangsan Mountain. Our ancestors even made a song to praise the beautiful nature. There is a song that praises Cheongnyangsan Mountain in a book of poetry titled Donggyejip from the late Joseon period. Let me recite it for you. “Green Iljangsan Mountain stands tall, gathering and holding the righteous spirits of the world. It looks the same from every direction, south or north, reminiscent of a solid rock that has never weakened.” It is a poem that makes you feel and understand how spiritually great the Cheongnyangsan Mountain is.  Let's go up the Namhansanseong Fortress that stands in the presence of good energy and spirits of Cheongnyangsan and Namhansan Mountains. We need to walk about 10 more minutes from here to the North Gate.   (4) Temporary Palace at Namhansanseong Fortress (Samjeondo-gil)

stories.title: North Gate (North Gate)
stories.script: ㅇ Everyone, the gate you see in front of you is the North Gate of Namhansanseong Fortress. Namhansanseong Fortress has four gates in the east, west, south and north. The North Gate is close to Hangang River so it was the gate through which war supplies that had come through the river were transported. Then why do you think our ancestors built Namhansanseong Fortress during the Joseon Dynasty?  The capital during the period was Hanyang, which is today's Seoul. Joseon built several defense facilities to defend Hanyang. First, they used mountains and natural topography in the east, west, south and north and constructed fortress walls to set up a defense line. They are Bugaksan, Naksan (Taraksan), Namsan (Mongmyeoksan) and Inwangsan Montains. And they considered Bukhansan, Deogyangsan, Gwanaksan and Yongmasan Mountains on the outside as a natural defense line. Then, last bastions to protect Hanyang were set up in all four directions in case enemies approach the capital. These last bastions were Gaeseong in the north, Suwon in the south, Ganghwa in the west and Gwangju in the east. The fortress built to keep off enemies attacking from the south and north is Namhansanseong Fortress. Injo, the 16th king of Joseon, commanded the construction of the fortress in 1624 as a measure to check and counter the Jurchens in the north whose became more powerful. Jungjeong Namhanji described Namhansanseong Fortress as a “tall fortress built by the heavens as its inside is vast and the outside is blocked.” It is indeed a fortress equipped with the greatest natural conditions. Namhansanseong is a fortress constructed at the top of a 500-meter-tall mountain, and its surroundings are so steep that the mountain itself serves as a fortress. On the contrary, the area inside the fortress has a gradual slope, which allowed a great number of people to live in it. It also had an abundance of water.  Korea has many fortresses. Whenever there was a war, our ancestors immediately destroyed all the weapons and foods around them and locked themselves up in such fortresses for resistance. Such a tactic is known as “Cheongyajeon” and, for Cheongyajeon to succeed, it is paramount to arrange a good, continuous supply of water within the fortress. Having over 80 wells inside, Namhansanseong was a fortress that had a great supply of water. Hangang River that encompassed the fortress as a natural boundary created perfect conditions for Cheongyajeon as well. In addition to these natural topography, 7.5-meter-tall walls stood tall to cover a 11.76km distance including naeseong (inner fortress) and oeseong (outer fortress). Therefore, Namhansanseong was a fortress that has never been conquered. Although King Injo surrendered during the Qing invasion, the Qing forces were not able to take the fortress down. As such, it was a strong and well-built fortress that utilized the natural terrains. Another name for the North Gate is “Jeonseungmun.” There is a plaque that says Jeonseungmun on the exterior of the gate. This name was given when the gate was repaired during the reign of King Jeongjo. If you hear the name, you may think that it commemorates a victory at the fortress. It actually meant to win the war, delivering the memories from the Qing invasion to future generations. During the Qing invasion, the North Gate was the only place where Joseon army battled Qing troops. Joseon soldiers went out through this gate to engage in numerous battles, big and small. King Injo himself climbed up the gate to command and encourage the troops. As a result, Joseon army was victorious in small-scale battles in the early stage of the invasion. Though the results could be seen as trivial as killing 6, 10 or 30 Qing soldiers, the victories gave Joseon army enough confidence to believe that they can fight against Qing. Soon after, however, Joseon faced its greatest defeat at the North Gate. About 300 Joseon soldiers rushed out through the North Gate to raid the enemies but the Qing army pretended to be fleeing before staging a counterattack. In the end, most of the 300 soldiers were killed and the troops faced a crushing defeat, which completely demoralized the Joseon forces.  The memory of disgrace and humiliation suffered during the Qing invasion had a huge influence on the kings who followed. They made sure to never forget the defeat and left their will in many different places. North Gate is one of them. You will be able to witness this in a number of different places we are going to visit today. Now, let's go to the West Gate.

stories.title: North Gate → West Gate (Namhansanseong Fortress)
stories.script: Namhansanseong Fortress was built in 1624 by the royal command of King Injo during the Joseon Dynasty. In fact, the fortress was constructed upon a foundation that had been established during the period of the Three Kingdoms. The people of Joseon believed it was originally built by Onjo, the progenitor of the Kingdom of Baekje, based on the traces they found, hence they referred to it as “Onjoseong”.  However, recent excavations revealed that the Baekje relics discovered in this area were minimal, simple, and modest for the ruling class. Although the Baekje people inhabited this region in clusters, it appears implausible that they constructed the fortress. The records in Samguk Sagi (“History of the Three Kingdoms”) mention, “Jujangseong Fortress was built in Sanju in the 12th year of King Munmu's reign, with a length reaching 4,360 bo.” King Munmu ruled Silla, unifying the Three Kingdoms of the Korean Peninsula. When Silla allied with the Tang Dynasty to conquer Baekje and Goguryeo, the Tang attempted to annex Baekje and Goguryeo territories. This prompted King Munmu to erect a fortress to halt the southward advance of the Tang Dynasty and safeguard the Hangang River basin, a vital military hub for Silla, known as Jujangseong Fortress. However, it exists only in records, and discussions regarding it have been ongoing.  As excavation and restoration work commenced at Namhansanseong Fortress, archaeological evidence started supporting the theory that this location was Jangjuseong Fortress. Then, in 2004, a substantial site of an ancient Silla building was excavated within the fortress. Moreover, the remnants of a house with Goryeo Ondol, a floor-based heating system, were discovered within the fortress. Records of the Mongolian army attacking Gwangjuseong Fortress further indicate that the fortress served as a military defense facility during the Goryeo period. Therefore, Namhansanseong Fortress has safeguarded the heart of the Korean Peninsula for over 1,500 years, boasting an incredibly extensive history. We hope you enjoy the well-established trail in harmony with the beautiful natural scenery, offering an authentic experience of Namhansanseong Fortress.

stories.title: North Gate → West Gate (trail)
stories.script: As I have told you earlier, Namhansanseong Fortress is a place that stood the test of time. The first thing that will come to your mind when you think of Namhansanseong Fortress would be the Qing invasion. Let me take this opportunity to explain to you about the Qing invasion.  To truly understand the Qing invasion, it is essential to first look at the relationship between Joseon and China at the time. As you may already know well, the Japanese Invasion, which began in 1592 and lasted seven years, changed the fate of Joseon, Ming and Japan forever. When the invasion was over, Joseon had to be in a subservient relationship with the Ming Dynasty. Though some of us today criticize such subservience displayed by Joseon at the time, it was a means of diplomacy for Joseon to not only accept the advanced Chinese culture but also avoid unnecessary conflicts to keep the country safe. On the contrary, Joseon practiced both hard-line and conciliatory policies towards Japan and Jurchen in Manchuria. But such external relations began to change dramatically in the aftermath of the Japanese Invasion. Starting in late 16th century, Ming's influence and power were dwindling due to corruption of the ruling class and rebellions by the commoners. Sending troops to Joseon to fight against the Japanese during their invasion also consumed a great portion of Ming's national power. Towards Ming that provided military and other aids in a tough time, Joseon started to feel much more than subservience; they felt a need to repay the debt they had owed, and tried to further solidify their relationship with the Ming Dynasty. As Ming was losing its grip and authority in this part of the world, Jurchens conquered Manchuria and grew powerful enough to wait for a chance to challenge the Ming Dynasty. And, eventually, when the powerful Nurhaci founded the Later Jin and took over Shenyang, the central hub of the Ming Dynasty, Joseon found itself at a crossroads to make a critical diplomatic decision.  Gwanghaegun who ascended to the throne after the Japanese invasion was over employed what is called neutral diplomacy. The gist of it was to maintain suitable relationships with both Ming and Later Jin without siding with any one party. It can be viewed as an extremely appropriate policy between the two countries that both needed Joseon's support and backing. However, many of the government officials were taken prisoner of the idea that Ming is the country Joseon has to repay debts to and, for them, Gwanghaegun's policy would make Joseon an ungrateful country that is ignorant of everything Ming had done for them. Eventually, Gwanghaegun was dethroned as a result of the Coup of 1623, also known as the Injo Restoration or Injo Banjeong. Banjeong in Korean means to restore justice. The “restoration” army executed the coup under the cause of setting justice right by dethroning Gwanghaegun who had murdered his half brother, Grand Prince Yeongchang; imprisoned his step-mother, Queen Inmok; and, above all, failed to keep his fidelity to Ming. King Injo who became the king as a result of this naturally carried out Ming-friendly policies. Joseon discarded the neutral diplomacy policy and ignored the Later Jin that had been growing with such powerful forces. However, Ming's authority and power were gradually becoming weakened by the Later Jin. Around this period, a huge incident took place in Joseon. In 1624, Yi Gwal who participated in the Injo Banjeong raised up in rebellion because he believed that he was discriminated in the process of giving out rewards for his role and merit during the coup. Yi Gwal was eventually murdered by the betrayal of Gi Ik-heon, and Gi defected to Qing. To solidify his position within the Qing Dynasty, Gi exaggerated Joseon's present situation and Qing, which needed a reasonable cause to attack Joseon, quickly invaded Joseon with 30,000 troops. As the Qing Dynasty continued to march southward from Uiju, King Injo fled to Ganghwa region and sent O Yun-gyeom and Choe Myeong-gil to Qing to conclude a peace treaty. As a result, Joseon and Qing formed an amicable relationship. This whole incident is known as the Later Jin Invasion of Joseon, or Jeongmyo Horan, as it took placed in the Year of Jeongmyo. The subsequent decade was a peaceful one. Then, in 1636, Joseon dispatched a delegation to the Qing Dynasty. While the Joseon delegation was in Qing, Hong Taiji of Qing named himself the emperor and held an emperor's coronation ceremony. Though it had signed a peace treaty with Qing, Joseon was serving the Ming Dynasty at the time, so they could not accept the king of Qing as the emperor.  When the Joseon delegation returned home, Qing gave them a letter in which Hong Taiji is referred to as the emperor, but the delegation intentionally left the letter on its way back. However, this event turned Joseon upside down as many of the high-ranked officials criticized the delegation for accepting the Qing's letter in the first place. Qing was deeply offended by this series of events. Then, the second incident occurred. When the queen of Joseon passed away, Qing sent Ingguldai as the leader of a delegation to offer condolences. Upon arrival in Joseon, they became upset as they thought Joseon's reception was poor. When Ingguldai came into the royal palace to offer his condolences, the tent where he was standing at collapsed over him. At that instant, Ingguldai saw a group of Joseon soldiers training in the back garden, misunderstood the situation, and escaped from the palace. The Confucian scholars of Joseon became upset at the Qing delegation that did not properly and faithfully offer their condolences for the queen's passing, and submitted appeals to the king, requesting immediate execution of the Qing envoys. Upon hearing this news, the delegation hurriedly returned to Qing. This led to King Injo immediately issuing a royal statement that denies the peace treaty signed in the year of Jeongmyo. Unfortunately, a copy of this statement fell into Qing's hands. As Joseon was at the brink of war, the court was divided into two groups: one insisting to resolve any misunderstanding and make peace while the other willing to break ties with Qing even if it meant a life-or-death confrontation. One of the leading officials who stressed the importance of making peace again with Qing was Choe Myeong-gil. Choe played a pivotal role in signing the original peace treaty in the year of Jeongmyo. In the end, King Injo accepted Choe's opinions and sent envoys to Qing. As a response, Qing told Joseon that the prince and vassals need to be sent to Qing by November 25 to request for peace and, otherwise, it would mean war. But this led to another round of heated debates on whether or not the prince should be sent to make peace and which vassals are to be dispatched. With nothing decided, the deadline expired. Though war was imminent, Joseon was not properly prepared for it. They had a relaxed mindset because it was a cold winter at the time and it is unlikely for anyone to make an assault in such a season. But on December 6, a fire was seen at the beacon on Yonggolsan Mountain, indicating the invasion of enemies. However, Kim Ja-jeom who was overseeing the Pyongan-do Province ignored this signal fire and informed Hanyang of the invasion only after the Qing army crossed the Amnokgang River.  Due to the fast advance of the Qing troops, King Injo and his officials decided to take shelter in Ganghwado Island on December 13 as they did in the year of Jeongmyo. The Qing army that had crossed the borders swiftly moved south and approached the capital, Hanyang, in just three days. King and his vassals set out for Ganghwa but it was going to take two full days to get to Ganghwado Island and the route had already been cut off by the Qing army. Choe Myeong-gil proposed the king to stay at Namhansanseong Fortress while he meets with the Qing general to buy some time. So King Injo and his company changed their destination to Namhansanseong Fortress. Even at Namhansanseong Fortress, however, the officials argued against one another about whether they should escape to Ganghwado Island again or not. While they were wasting time in debating and arguing, the Qing troops were already heading towards Namhansanseong Fortress. In the end, the plan to go to Ganghwa failed and the Qing army set up a camp in Samjeondo in front of the fortress. This is how the Qing Invasion of Joseon broke out and a 47-day resistance at Namhansanseong Fortress began.  Now, let's talk more about the Qing invasion as we move on. We are quite close to the West Gate now. Let's walk a little more.

stories.title: West Gate
stories.script: This is the West Gate of Namhansanseong Fortress. West Gate was the closest gate to Hanyang, so it was utilized for military purposes. It is also the gate through which King Injo set out to surrender to Qing after a 47-day resistance.  On January 30, 1637, the once welded shut West Gate of Namhansanseong Fortress finally opened as King Injo and his vassals who had fought from inside the fortress for 47 days ultimately chose to surrender. They walked out through this gate and headed to the Qing camp. Namhanilgi records the scene at the time as follows: “The king walked out the West Gate and the crown prince followed. All civil and military officials stood at the gate and lamented.” Injo left the fortress on a white horse followed by about 50 of his vassals. They headed towards Samjeondo with Ingguldai, the Qing commander. Samjeondo was a dock that connected Hanyang and Namhansanseong Fortress during the Joseon period, and it was located in today's Samjeon-dong, Songpa-gu. The method of surrender demanded by Qing was “Samgwegugodu,” which required three kowtows and nine prostrations to pay respects to Hong Taiji. In Samjeondo, Injo kowtowed three times and bowed nine times at the bottom of a platform towards the north where Hong Taiji is. This was a sign of surrender and an expression of his service to Qing. For Joseon that had regarded Jurchens as a group of savages who do not know any manners, this was a huge disgrace. Having accepted the surrender, Hong Taiji left a road open for Injo and his vassals to return to Hanyang. However, those who remained behind at Namhansanseong Fortress had to suffer immensely from plundering and pillaging of Qing and Mongolia. This is how the Qing invasion ultimately came to an end. But Joseon's humiliation continued thereafter. Qing demanded Joseon to erect a stele that commemorates the surrender. This is Samjeondobi Monument whose official name is “Daecheonghwangje Gongdeokbi.” The most humiliating moment for Joseon was the merits, virtue and achievement of the Qing emperor. The writing on the stele was engraved in Mongolian, Manchurian and Chinese characters. The contents of the stele were written by Yi Gyeong-seok. Yi only wrote the contents of the stele by King Injo's command but, still, he was greatly criticized in years to come. In addition, the letters were engraved by O Jun, a great calligrapher of the time. It is said that O Jun was so humiliated by this that he pounded his hands on a stone and did not write ever again. This stele that was in the center of controversy when it was first erected has consistently suffered from various disgraceful events thereafter as well. In the late Joseon period, it was buried underground by the Japanese force. Competing with Qing at the time over the Korean Peninsula, Japan aimed to erase any traces of Qing on Joseon land. The stele was later recovered but was buried again in 1956 as it was considered a part of the nation's humiliating history. In the end, it was re-excavated and designated as a historic site. Samjeondobi Monument was relocated several times before being installed in Seokchon Lake in Songpa-gu today. Samjeondobi Monument contains painful history of our country, which is why there has been no shortage of demands to tear it down. In 2007, there was an incident in which someone wrote “tear it down” in red paint on the stone. Although it represents painful history for us, we all need to have the mindset of trying to learn the bigger lesson through it. You can find a number of different traces throughout Namhansanseong Fortress that Joseon kings have left in the aftermath of the Qing invasion to keep the memories from those days. Our ancestors tried to remember their history rather than to forget it, no matter how painful and humiliating it was. We in the present day need to learn such wisdom from our ancestors.  Whenever you have a chance, stop by Seokchon Lake to check out not only its beautiful scenery but also Samjeondobi Monument. I am sure you will have novel feelings that you have never felt before. Now, let's head towards Sueojangdae Post. There is a restroom you can use on the way there.

stories.title: Sueojangdae Post (Sueojangdae Post)
stories.script: Sueojangdae Post you see in front of you is the most colorful and splendid building in Namhansanseong Fortress. It is one of the four posts set up when the fortress was constructed during the King Injo's reign, and it is the only one that still remains today. Let's get a little bit closer to Sueojangdae Post.  Jangdae refers to the platform established on a high ground for a commander to stand and lead a battle. As Sueojangdae Post is located at the highest ground at Namhansanseong Fortress, from here, you can view the interior of the fortress as well as its surroundings. When Joseon was fighting against Qing at the fortress, King Injo himself rose up to this post to encourage his troops. Sueojangdae Post was originally a single-story pavilion but during the King Yeongjo's reign, a two-story pavilion was constructed and a signboard that says “Sueojangdae” was hung on the front exterior. Sueojangdae refers to the Jangdae commanded by Sueosa of Sueocheong installed at the fortress. The kings who ruled after the Qing invasion watched and commanded military training at Sueojangdae Post whenever they visit Namhansanseong Fortress. Here, they remembered the humiliating history in the past and pledged not to endanger the country ever again. In this context, King Yeongjo installed a plaque that says Mumangnu on the inside of the pavilion on the second floor. “Mumang” means to never forget. What do you think it refers to? That's right. They were determined not to forget about the humiliation of Qing invasion from the days of Injo and King Hyojong who died without seeing the conquest of the north come to fruition.  Sueojangdae Post is one of the places in Namhansanseong Fortress where visitors take the most pictures. You may also capture the beautiful moments in photos.

stories.title: Sueojangdae Post (Maebawi Rock)
stories.script: If you look here, you will see a huge rock on which it says “Sueojangdae.” This rock is called Maebawi. People in Namhansanseong Fortress believed that this rock had magical powers. There is a famous story here.  The person who oversaw the entire construction of Namhansanseong Fortress during the reign of King Injo was Yi Seo, the Sueosa of Sueocheong. Yi Seo then entrusted General Yi Hoe with the task of constructing Dongnamseong Fortress. General Yi immersed himself in constructing the fortress night and day. But the expenses for fortification were severely deficient, and General Yi invested even his own personal assets into the construction project. As he deliberated long and hard to procure funds and to build a strong fortress, the construction continued to be delayed, and this led to a few of the high-ranked officials defaming Yi, claiming that Yi is blinded by his selfish interests and desires and has fallen into booze and women while neglecting the construction. In the end, General Yi was imprisoned and executed here at Sueojangdae Post. Just before he was executed, General Yi said, “If nothing happens at the moment I die, that means I am guilty. If a hawk flies over, however, this means that I have not sinned.” General Yi is executed and, at that very moment, a hawk flies over and sits on this rock. Later, people checked if the fortress was built properly and it was revealed that Dongnamseong, the fortress that General Yi was responsible for, was constructed in the strongest, sturdiest manner. Only then they realized that General Yi had died for no reason.  But this is not the end of his story. Let's walk over to Cheongnyangdang Shrine and we'll continue with General Yi. Please follow me.

stories.title: Cheongnyangdang Shrine (Entrance to Cheongnyangdang Shrine)
stories.script: This place enshrines General Yi Hoe who died on a false charge. But this place exudes a more shamanistic vibe than any other typical shrine. In fact, among the generals that shamans serve and worship, General Yi Hoe is regarded as one of the most powerful gods.  As I have explained earlier, General Yi died because of a false accusation. Once people realized that he died for no reason, they built a shrine to pay respects to his spirits, and that shrine is Cheongnyangdang. On the inside of Cheongnyangdang Shrine, you will find a portrait of General Yi. On both sides of his portrait, portraits of Great Monk Gakseong and two women can be seen. Great Monk Gakseong was the one who led the Buddhist monks mobilized for the construction of Namhansanseong Fortress, and the two women are his wife, Lady Song, and his concubine, Lady Yu. When General Yi faced difficulties of securing funds to construct the fortress, the two women traveled through the southern regions themselves to collect funds. On their way back with hard-earned money, however, they learned that their husband was killed by execution and, together, committed suicide by throwing themselves into a river. It is one of the sad stories in relation to Namhansanseong Fortress. To appease the souls of those who died on false charges, the shrine hosts Dodanggut, a shamanistic ritual of Gyeonggi-do to this day.  One of the reasons Namhansanseong Fortress still possesses vigor and vitality is the fact that old traditions continue even today. Dodanggut at Cheongnyangdang Shrine is a proof of that. Now, let's head to the South Gate.

stories.title: South Gate (South Gate)
stories.script: This is the South Gate of Namhansanseong Fortress. South Gate is the largest and grandest gate in Namhansanseong Fortress, serving the role of the central gate. During the Qing invasion, King Injo and his vassals came into the Namhansanseong Fortress through this South Gate.  As Qing forces crossed Amnokgang River and advanced down to Hanyang, King Injo and his vassals hurriedly fled to Namhansanseong Fortress. And the gate through which Injo entered the fortress was the South Gate. The Qing invasion took place in December, during an extremely cold winter, and one soldier after another started to abandon their duties of protecting the king on their way to Namhansanseong Fortress. When they had to cross the river at Songpa Quay, there was not a single boatman to carry them across. By the time King Injo arrived at the fortress, his body and soul were already exhausted. It even snowed over Injo and his vassals who had fled from their home in Hanyang. Under such circumstances, it was extremely difficult for the king to climb up the tall Namhansanseong Fortress. That is when one man suddenly came forward and carried the king on his back to head to the fortress. He was a low-class commoner named Seo Heun-nam. Having no proper shoes on his feet, Seo carried King Injo on his back and hiked up a winter mountain barefoot. Deeply touched by this act, King Injo bestowed a royal robe upon him. Later on, when all communication between Namhansanseong Fortress and the outside world was interrupted due to the siege by the Qing forces, Seo Heun-nam carried the letters written by the king himself and traveled around the country to deliver the royal command. Eventually, Seo was acknowledged for such deeds and merits and received the position of second-Jeong class Gauidaebu.  Though it is a beautiful and magnificent gate, the South Gate holds such a sad story within it. There is a restroom nearby so let's take a quick break before we move on.

stories.title: South Outwork (2nd South Outwork)
stories.script: We have just passed the halfway point of the Namhansanseong course. What do you think? As you know more and more about Namhansanseong Fortress, doesn't the fortress look differently now compared to when you saw it at the very beginning? Let's look at an important facility called the South Outwork on the southern wall of Namhansanseong Fortress.  An outwork is a structure that defends a gate of a fortress. The most vulnerable part of a fortress is the gate since the enemy is likely to attack the gates rather than the tall, rock-solid fortress walls. If a gate is opened, enemies are going to flood into the fortress like waves, so it is important to defend the gate. At Namhansanseong Fortress, outworks were installed by protruding a portion of the fortress walls outward to not only defend the gates but also to attack more easily. These south outworks were all created by the royal command of King Injo in the aftermath of the Qing invasion. They fixed a vulnerability of Namhansanseong Fortress after an upheaval. There are a total of five outworks at Namhansanseong Fortress: Janggyeongsa-sinji Outwork is in the east, Yeonjubong Outwork in the north, and as you can see, three South Outworks in the south. There are many outworks in the south because people of Joseon believed that the southern part is the biggest vulnerability of the fortress because, unlike the east, north and west whose slopes are steep, the area in the south had gradual slopes and grounds. Outworks were connected to ammun, or hidden gates, to set up a passageway to the outside and to maximize the effect of attacks from the back. We are going to look at the ammun more in detail later. Now, let's examine what kind of attacking facilities there were. What you see right now is Yeojang. Yeojang is where soldiers hide when enemies attack. If you see a Yeojang up close, you will find these holes that are known as Chongan.  Soldiers fired through these Chongan. Ever since the Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1592, guns became extremely important weapons in Joseon. Do you see these cracks between one Yeojang and another? These cracks are called Tagu, which is where soldiers were able to shoot arrows. Bows and arrows are traditional weapons of our ancestors. Yeojang and Tagu are the most notable attacking structures installed on the walls of Namhansanseong Fortress, which is why you can locate them everywhere on these walls. There are 87 Yeojangs on the 2nd Outwork here. And the structures that were newly installed when constructing outworks were Poru. As they went through the Qing invasion, people of Joseon realized the power of the Qing cannons. So when they installed outworks, they also set up Poru, which enabled the troops to carry out cannon attacks. There are a total of seven Porus at the 1st Outwork. I am going to explain to you about Poru more in detail later at Janggyeongsa-sinji Outwork.  We can say that Namhansanseong Fortress has continuously evolved along with the changes of the eras, and the South Outwork is a proof of such transformations. Now, let's move to the East Gate.

stories.title: Site of South Command Post
stories.script: We are now at the Site of South Command Post established in the southern part of the fortress. This is where military training took place. Let me take a moment to explain to you about internal conflicts that happened within the fortress during the Qing invasion.  As I explained earlier, responses to Qing were divided into two different factions: those who insisted on fighting until the end and those who sought for peaceful relationships through reconciliation. The confrontation between the two factions continued within the walls of Namhansanseong Fortress. The symbolic figure that argued against making peace with the Qing was Kim Sang-heon, and the one that insisted on maintaining friendly relations with the Qing was Choe Myeong-gil. Choe was the one who wrote the surrender document himself based on the past experiences, but Kim ripped the surrender document into pieces. Even if Kim teared the document apart, Choe picked up the ripped parts and put them together, thus strongly asserting the need for peace. It is said that Kim fasted for six days in opposition to the surrender. Kim Sang-heon was 67 years of age at the time. Choe Myeong-gil was 50 years old at the time as well. After the Qing invasion came to an end, the two met in Shenyang, China. Kim was taken to Shenyang for having acted in opposition to Qing while Choe was also dragged to Shenyang on the charge of collusion with the Ming Dynasty. The two dramatically met each other again in a jail cell in Shenyang, and they eventually reached reconciliation as they were both moved by how each other faithfully kept their loyalty and integrity for the country even in the presence of impending death. In the end, the two loyal vassals understood each other that their actions in the past were all for the country.  Later, Kim Sang-heon was released from prison and escorted Crown Prince Sohyeon back to Joseon. Kim peacefully passed away at the age of 87. Choe Myeong-gil was also released and returned to Hanyang in 1645, but passed away two years later at the age of 62. There are others whom we need to remember in addition to Kim Sang-heon and Choe Myeong-gil. They are Hong Ik-han, Yun Jip and O Dal-je. Before accepting Joseon's surrender, Qing demanded to capture all those who had insisted on fighting until the end. Qing sought to shift responsibility of their invasion on them. At the time, Hong Ik-han, Yun Jip and O Dal-je opposed friendly relations and urged to fight until the end. Hong was initially pointed out as the leader, which he acknowledged it, and Yun and O also voluntarily came forward to call themselves the leaders of the opposing faction. Eventually, the three were taken to the Qing Dynasty where they faced cruel torture and threats. As they did not surrender, Qing started to conciliate them. However, the three men rejected Qing's attempts for conciliation and kept asserting the great cause of rejecting peace. In the end, all of them were executed by Qing. Prior to the execution, Hong Taiji himself came to interrogate them. Even at the gate of death, the three did not change their mind for anything. They stayed loyal to the country until the end. That is why they are referred to as the Samhaksa. At Namhansanseong Fortress, a shrine called Hyeonjeolsa was established to pay tributes to the spirits and loyalty of Samhaksa. Hyeonjeolsa Temple was originally built for Samhaksa but, later on, it came to enshrine Kim Sang-heon and Jeong On as well, who were on the opposing faction.  Between the assertions of the two factions, it is difficult to judge who were right and who were wrong. However, the story of Kim Sang-heon and Choe Myeong-gil who met each other in a foreign country and came to understand and reconcile as well as that of Samhaksa who sacrificed their lives for the country deeply touches our heart.

stories.title: East Gate
stories.script: We are at the East Gate of Namhansanseong Fortress. Unlike other areas, the East Gate has a gradual slope, making the enemies to easily carry large-sized weapons. So they installed stairs to prevent this.  Here, you can see a path where water flows. As Namhansanseong Fortress was a place abundant with water, if there remained food to eat, a great number of people were able to survive here. But such abundance of water means that there must be a good drainage system. If water does not drain well, it would become stagnant and deform the fortress walls, which may even lead to the collapse of fortress. As you go down along the East Gate, you will reach a valley. In this valley, there is a rock where King Jeongjo briefly rested on his way to pay respects at Yeongneung, the royal tomb of King Hyojong. King Yeongjo spent half of the procession to Yeongneung Royal Tomb here at Namhansanseong Fortress where he looked around facilities and inspected training of the soldiers. The importance of Namhansanseong Fortress increased since the Qing invasion, so the kings themselves came to the fortress to inspect the conditions. To King Jeongjo, Namhansanseong Fortress has a special significance. Namhansanseong Fortress was a good reference for Hwaseong Fortress, which was being designed by King Jeongjo at the time. When Hwaseong Fortress was constructed, King Jeongjo commanded that military training must be carried out according to the rules and regulations established at Namhansanseong Fortress. The military operations of Namhansanseong Fortress had a huge influence on Jeongjo's Hwaseong.  Let's take this trail towards the North Gate.

stories.title: Songamjeong Pavilion Site
stories.script: Because of its geographical location, Namhansanseong Fortress was a place where countless people traveled back and forth even before the fortress was built. The place you see in front of you is where a pavilion called Songamjeong used to be located prior to the construction of a fortress. This place is related to Hwang Jin-yi  who was a gisaeng, a female entertainer, from Gaeseong. Her name was famous all over the Korean Peninsula for her beauty and talents. She tried to seduce Seo Gyeong-deok, a Confucian scholar, but actually ended up respecting him for his erudition and personality. After she met Seo, Hwang went into Geumgangsan Mountain to take up Buddhism. Years later, Hwang came down from the mountain and was passing by this place when a group of scholars who were drinking with gisaengs at Songamjeong Pavilion begin to harass her. Without being embarrassed or disconcerted, Hwang taught the scholars about Buddhism. One of the gisaengs who was with the scholars saw Hwang, felt ashamed and started to weep. Then, she jumped off from the Songamjeong cliff. Since then, people say that, on a bright moonlit night, they can hear the sorrowful cry of a woman nearby. Do you see a pine tree at the Songamjeong Pavilion Site? That pine tree has a special name called Daebusong. Daebu was a high government position that corresponds to third-Jong class and the king who granted this official position was Jeongjo. During a royal procession, King Jeongjo once stayed at Namhansanseong Fortress where he found a beautiful pine tree rooted in a rock. Amazed by this tree, he bestowed a government post upon it. Isn't it interesting that the natural scenery was so beautiful that the king granted a government position? Let's walk along the fortress walls.

stories.title: Janggyeongsa Temple
stories.script: There is a Buddhist temple over there. There used to a total of nine temples inside Namhansanseong Fortress but Janggyeongsa you are seeing right now is the only temple that still remains today.  When the fortress was constructed in 1624, the largest group of people that were mobilized for the construction was Buddhist monks. They were outstanding during the Japanese Invasion of 1592. Once the invasion broke out, monks formed an army to fight the Japanese raiders in a number of regions and scored different scales of victory. Namhansanseong Fortress was built primarily by the monks who also served an important role in managing and protecting the fortress. And the person who led the construction of Namhansanseong Fortress was Great Monk Gakseong. King Injo appointed Gakseong as Dochongseop to gather the monks and build the fortress. Dochongseop was the highest position given to a monk during the Joseon Dynasty. King Hyojong who ascended to the throne in the aftermath of the Qing invasion commanded to train monks here at Janggyeongsa Temple for the goal of forming a strong army of monks. King Hyojong witnessed his father, King Injo, surrendering to the Qing troops as well as his older brother, the crown prince, being taken hostage to the foreign country. So, upon rising to the throne, King Hyojong began to prepare a war against Qing. To strengthen his military forces, Janggyeongsa Temple served a pivotal role as a national defense temple and the center for raising the monk army.  When Namhansanseong Fortress became inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site, the element that received the most attention was the fact that Buddhist monks, a group of religious leaders, took part in the construction of a fortress and even fought against the enemies to protect it. And Janggyeongsa Temple is where their traces still remain today.

stories.title: Janggyeongsa-sinji Outwork
stories.script: This is Janggyeongsa-sinji Outwork, which is the outwork on the eastern side of Namhansanseong Fortress. As I have mentioned earlier, an outwork was a structure that enhanced the soldiers' attacking power.  Prior to the Qing invasion when Namhansanseong Fortress was being built, the fortress had no Poru, or emplacements, installed. When the war began, Joseon was helpless against the Qing's cannon attacks. After the invasion was over, Joseon made sure that cannon attacks can be made from the fortress, which naturally necessitated emplacements from which cannons are fired. To fire a cannon, a sufficient amount of space is required since when the cannon is discharged, it moves backward due to a recoil. Moreover, several people were needed to fire a cannon: the one who inserts a cannonball for an attack; the one who grabs the cannon; and the other who lights it up, which means that securing an adequate amount of space was a must. That is why an outwork was a great place to install an emplacement. If you look here, you will find Yeojang and Tagu on top of the fortress wall and an emplacement at the bottom. It is a summary of how methods and weapons of attack have evolved from bows and arrows to guns and cannons. This was an important element considered when UNESCO designated Namhansanseong Fortress as a World Heritage site. The criteria for the registration as UNESCO World Heritage site included architecture, structure and technology that show important stages of mankind's history, and this served as an important evidence of the development of weapons and how our ancestors responded to it.  Please remember how Yeojang, Tagu and these cannons look like. They tell us how our ancestors were able to respond to a new breed of weapons.

stories.title: Bongamseong Fortress
stories.script: This is the Site of East Command Post, which was built on the east side of the fortress. Here, generals and commanders trained soldiers. You will see a hidden gate in front of you, and we are going to pass this gate and walk head to the Bongamseong Fortress. We are about to move out of the fortress but be careful as we move since the path is narrow and steep.  Okay, everyone. Come over to this side, please. Here, you will see fortress walls stretching out long and wide. This is the outer fortress of Namhansanseong Fortress known as Bongamseong Fortress. Prior to the Qing invasion, Bongamseong Fortress had not existed. During the invasion, Qing took over this area, which threatened Joseon in a great way especially because it had a high ground so the inside of the fortress was clearly seen from here. Besieging Namhansanseong Fortress, Qing stationed its troops in Beolbong located at the apex of Bongamseong Fortress. The top surface of Beolbong was flat and level so it was possible to install cannons. The Qing army surveyed the fortress from Beolbong and fired Honguipo to attack. Honguipo was an extremely powerful and lethal cannon which was one of the Qing's representative weapons. It also boasted a long shooting range, which enabled it to attack even the inside of Namhansanseong Fortress directly. When Honguipo fired by the Qing struck a pillar of the temporary palace at Namhansanseong Fortress where King Injo was staying, he and the vassals were greatly surprised and shocked. Records from December 23 that year reveal that the Qing did not stop firing cannons from the peak. Joseon troops countered with Cheonjapo, but it could not overcome Honguipo. People inside the fortress were terrified at the time as cannonballs were flying from such a far away. The thundering sounds of these flying cannons were extremely intimidating for King Injo. Moreover, because they were being monitored from a higher ground, they worried about the fortress being destroyed at any given moment, further raising the sense of anxiety among them. The Qing invasion made Joseon to realize once again how important Namhansanseong Fortress is, and through the war against Qing, they figured out the vulnerabilities of the fortress as well. To fix this issue, King Sukjong commanded to construct an outer fortress called Bongamseong Fortress, which includes Beolbong. The name Beolbong stems from the shape of the rock located at the peak; when you look at this rock from outside the fortress, it resembles a bee. According to another story, bees built nests on this rock since the old times, which is why people called it Beoram, Beolbawi or Beolbong.  As you can see, excavation work at Bongamseong Fortress is still on-going today. This also means that the old fortress walls still remain in good conditions. It would be great for us to go up to Beolbong together but, since the road is not properly set up yet, it may be a bit dangerous. We will have to look at Bongamseong Fortress from here and move on. Please be careful on your way back as well.

stories.title: Northern Fortress Walls (Fortress Walls_01)
stories.script: Namhansanseong Fortress can be said to be the textbook and history of Korean fortresses. It shows very well how Korean fortresses and their walls have developed and evolved.  Take a moment to look at the outer fortress walls from here. Do you see that they are slanted? They were built this way so that they can withstand the pressure both from the inside and outside, while preventing the walls from collapsing. Such fortress construction techniques were typically utilized by the people of Goguryeo when they had built fortresses. Silla introduced the technology of Goguryeo, a state with developed fortress construction skills, to build its own Jujangseong Fortress, and also utilized it during the construction of Namhansanseong Fortress later on. As I have mentioned earlier, Namhansanseong Fortress was built upon a foundation of a Silla fortress, using the fortress walls that were still standing at the time. People of Silla commonly utilized granite for stones that made up their fortresses. They carefully trimmed the hard granite and piled them up densely. But granite was not able to be obtained in this region, which forced Silla craftsmen and artisans to bring granite from a far away. Then, by the Joseon Dynasty, fortress wall stones became much bigger than those from the Silla period. The shape also changed as well as they became more rectangular and lengthy in the left and right direction. They were made to be wider to enable the stones to make greater contact with one another, thus strengthening the durability. The stones are gneiss, which can easily be collected in the neighboring area. The major reason for a change in the shape of these stones is the change in the weaponry used to attack fortresses. In the ancient societies, the primary weapons used to attack fortresses were bows, arrows and swords, which means that battles mostly featured hand-to-hand fights after soldiers climb up fortress walls. So the sizes of stones that make up fortress walls weren't that big. In the 16th century, however, the type of weapons used to attack fortresses changed with the introduction of cannons. If the walls were constructed in the same way as before, they were extremely vulnerable to cannons being fired by enemies. So they started to make the stones thicker and longer. Changes in fortress walls were inevitable as a response to changes in weapons, and the fact that traces and materials about these changes still remain is what makes Namhansanseong Fortress incredible.  Let's move along the fortress walls.

stories.title: Northern Fortress Walls (Fortress Walls_02)
stories.script: Let me give you a pop quiz. Who is the first Westerner to visit Namhansanseong Fortress? Right. It is Hamel who wrote the Story of the Wreck of the Sperwer Yacht, which is a book that introduced Joseon to the Western world.  Hamel was an employee of the Dutch East India Company and, on his voyage to Nagasaki, Japan, he was adrift and later arrived in Jeju Island. It was 1653, the fourth year of King Hyojong's reign. Magistrate of Jeju arrested 35 crew members including Hamel and Bak Yeon traveled from Hanyang to translate for them. Bak Yeon was a Dutch who had been naturalized in Joseon. Hamel and others were imprisoned in Jeju for about 10 months before being transferred to Hanyang. Surprisingly, King Hyojong gave them a special duty instead of punishment. He commanded them to develop new weapons at Hullyeon Dogam (Military Training Command). Having witnessed his father, King Injo, disgracefully succumbing to Qing at Namhansanseong Fortress, King Hyojong only had revenge on his mind. He was planning a conquest of the Qing after strengthening the country and its military. So he reinforced Hullyeon Dogam and renovated and repaired all of the weapons while commanding Hamel and others who were good with cannons to develop weapons. While Hamel and others were staying in Hanyang, a news of a visit of Qing envoys was heard in 1654. Seeing a group of Westerners developing weapons in a period where Joseon was planning a northern conquest, the Qing envoys became suspicious. So the government officials isolated Hamel and others at Namhansanseong Fortress to conceal them. They stayed at the fortress for about a month. After staying in Hanyang for a while, negotiations for his release with the East India Company were completed in 1667, so he finally returned to Netherlands through Japan in 1668. This finally marked the end of a 14-year detainment. Once he returned home, Hamel wrote what he had seen and experienced in a report format, which is the famous Story of the Wreck of the Sperwer Yacht. It was actually a report Hamel wrote to be paid with the wages that had been overdue for 14 years but, as soon as it was published as a book, it became an instant hit throughout Europe. An interesting fact is that his book has records of Namhansanseong Fortress. Hamel writes about Namhansanseong Fortress as follows: “Because Namhansanseong Fortress was used as the king's shelter in case of a war, it was built in an extremely strong and sturdy way, and others with fame or of nobility also stayed in the fortress. It had enough food for a great number of people to endure three years within its walls.” Even to an outlander's eye, the solid walls and abundant resources of Namhansanseong Fortress were impressive.

stories.title: Northern Fortress Walls (Fortress Walls_03)
