stories.script: Did you know that the first food delivery in our country's history happened here in Namhansanseong Fortress? It was the food called Hyojonggaeng.  When you hear the name, you may think that it is somehow related to King Hyojong, perhaps something that the Joseon king enjoyed eating. But the name itself actually has nothing to do with the king. If we dissect the name, Hyo means dawn and Jong means a bell, so the word literally means a “bell ringing at dawn.” And Gaeng means soup. A combination of a bell ringing at dawn and a soup-style food. It's a bit difficult to imagine what kind of dish it is judging by its name. Records on Hyojonggaeng can be found in a book titled Haedongjukji which was published in 1925. Haedongjukji describes Hyojonggaeng as follows: “People at Namhansanseong Fortress know how to cook Hyojonggaeng well. Cabbage heart, bean sprouts, pine mushrooms, shiitake mushrooms, beef ribs, sea cucumbers and abalones are mixed with doenjang and boiled sufficiently for an entire day. The jar boiled overnight is wrapped in a cotton and sent to Seoul. By the daybreak bell rings, it arrives at the prime minister's house.” According to these records, the name Hyojonggaeng came from the fact that it was often delivered to homes until the bell rang at dawn. When it was delivered, the container was wrapped tightly and thoroughly with a cotton blanket to prevent the soup from going cold. Looking at the ingredients that go into Hyojonggaeng, you will understand why it was so delicious. From various vegetables and seafood to beef ribs, it contains an ample amount of delicious and healthy ingredients, which made it a popular haejangguk, or hangover soup, for the nobility of Seoul.  We are getting closer to the North Gate where we first met.

stories.title: 4th Hidden Gate (Entrance to Hidden Gate)
stories.script: Please come over here for a second. Here at Namhansanseong Fortress, there are several gates that lead to the outside. However, in addition to the four gates I've talked about earlier, there are also hidden gates, which are called Ammun.  This is an Ammun. Ammun is a fortress gate built at a location that cannot be viewed and surveyed by enemies and, strategically, it was a very essential piece of structure. People inside the fortress were secretly supplied with foods, weapons and, even, reinforcement troops through these hidden gates. If enemies approached the fortress, soldiers inside the fortress were able to counterattack from behind through this Ammun. There are a total of 16 Ammun at Namhansanseong Fortress. Today, many of these gates are no longer present but you will find traces of their installation. It is an interesting activity to look for these hidden gates in different locations within the fortress.  Okay, let's move to the North Gate along these walls. The path is a bit rugged so let's walk slowly and carefully.

stories.title: Sungnyeoljeon Shrine (Entrance)
stories.script: This is a shrine built by King Injo to enshrine the ancestral tablets of Onjo, the founder of Baekje. Why do you think a shrine for Onjo is located here at Namhansanseong Fortress?  While staying at the temporary palace after fleeing to Namhansanseong Fortress, King Injo had a dream one night. A man appeared in the dream and yelled at Injo on why he does not fight against the enemies that just showed up at Bukseong Fortress. And the man called himself King Onjo. Shocked by his dream, King Injo immediately woke up and sent troops to Bukseong. Surprisingly, Qing soldiers were actually there and about to attack the fortress but Injo's forces defeated them. Out of gratitude and respect, King Injo built Sungnyeoljeon Shrine to enshrine King Onjo. If you look at the shrine, you will find one more person other than King Onjo. It is none other than General Yi Seo who oversaw the construction of Namhansanseong Fortress. After building Sungnyeoljeon Shrine and enshrining King Onjo there, Onjo appeared again in Injo's dream. Onjo said that, since he is alone at the shrine, he commands Injo to enshrine him along with a loyal vassal. King Injo woke up from this dream and, on the next day, he learned that General Yi had passed away. Believing that King Onjo from the dream wanted Yi Seo as the loyal vassal, Injo enshrined the general at Sungnyeoljeon Shrine as well. In fact, Yi Seo was the one who proposed Injo to reinforce Namhansanseong Fortress. When General Yi was serving as Sueosa at the fortress, he made sure to store as much provisions, salt, paper and firearms as possible. Thanks to his foresight, King Injo, his vassals and a countless number of commoners were able to fight for 47 days at Namhansanseong Fortress. The fact that General Yi is enshrined next to King Onjo is the proof that his efforts were recognized in the end. Sungnyeoljeon Shrine holds a ritual on every September 5 on lunar calendar.

stories.title: Zelkova Tree (Namhansanseong Fortress)
stories.script: As we approach the temporary palace, a solitary old zelkova tree bears silent witness to a poignant tale from the time of the Qing invasion. This venerable tree has a somber story to tell. On a cold mid-December day during King Injo's 11th day at Namhansanseong Fortress, it seemed as if the heavens had opened up, releasing relentless rain. The king emerged, tears blending with the raindrops, and beseeched the skies, 'I bear responsibility for our nation's tragedy, so I implore you to punish me and spare my soldiers and people.' His heartfelt plea moved all those who watched, and together they wept. It's a testament to the desperate circumstances when superstition and prayers to the heavens were the only solace they could find.  According to the Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty, King Injo and his vassals, while staying at the temporary palace, awaited positive news signaled by the cries of magpies perched upon this tree. In the beliefs of our ancestors, the presence of a magpie building its nest on the south side of the house was seen as a highly auspicious sign. One day, a magpie alighted on this very tree to establish a nest, offering a glimmer of hope. Yet, it underscores the dire and trying circumstances of the time, where magpies, traditionally regarded as heralds of good news, became the sole source of hope for the people of Namhansanseong Fortress, encircled and suffering at the hands of their adversaries just beyond the fortress gates.

stories.title: Hannamnu Gate_01 (Namhansanseong Fortress)
stories.script: Haenggung, or a temporary palace, holds paramount importance within Namhansanseong Fortress as it serves as a functioning capital during times of war. Upon the designation of Namhansanseong Fortress as a UNESCO World Heritage site, the committee emphasized, “Namhansanseong Fortress stands as the sole fortress city constructed as a temporary capital during emergencies to safeguard Joseon's autonomy and independence.” This highlights the crucial role of the temporary palace in UNESCO’s recognition of the historical significance of Namhansanseong Fortress.  Throughout history, numerous kings sought refuge in Haenggung, particularly during the Qing invasion. King Injo notably resided in this palace for an extended period of 47 days, marking it as the location where Joseon kings endured the longest stays during such crises. Furthermore, this temporary palace stands out as it included areas for Jongmyo Shrine and Sajikdan Altar, setting it apart from the ten temporary palaces found elsewhere in Joseon. These two areas symbolized the traditions and the essence of the nation itself.  However, after the Japanese colonial era, the temporary palace suffered extensive destruction due to inadequate management. In 1895, the Joseon empress faced brutal violence at the hands of Japan. This led to the formation of numerous righteous armies across the country, known as Eulmi Uibyeong. The armies from the Gyeonggi region utilized Namhansanseong Fortress as their base, prompting Japan to destroy eight Buddhist temples and parts of the temporary palace, suspecting the temples of aiding these righteous armies. In efforts to fully restore Namhansanseong Fortress, the restoration works primarily focused on reinstating the temporary palace to its original state. After a decade of restoration efforts, the temporary palace was finally opened to the public in 2012.  The temporary palace within Namhansanseong Fortress comprises Sanggwol and Hagwol, constituting the palace itself, alongside Huwon, the secret garden, and Jwajeon, corresponding to Jongmyo Shrine and Sajikdan Altar. It accurately replicated the center of Hanyang (currently Seoul). Passing through Hannamru, the main gate, visitors encounter Hagwol, Sanggwol, and Huwon, before reaching Jwajeon. Additionally, in the Hagwol area, one can observe the extensive housing sites of the Silla Dynasty that were excavated.

stories.title: Temporary Palace at Namhansanseong Fortress (Hannamnu Gate_02)
stories.audioTitle: Temporary Palace at Namhansanseong Fortress (Hannamnu Gate_02)
stories.script: Please come over this way. This is the main gate of the temporary palace at Namhansanseong, Fortress, which is called Hannamnu. When the temporary palace was initially constructed, it only had Naehaengjeon and Oehaengjeon Halls, which are the central buildings of Sanggwol and Hagwol. Then, in the days of King Sukjong, Jwajeon, which corresponds to Jongmyo Shrine, and Usil, a stone wall that corresponds to Sajikdan Altar, were established. And this gate was made during King Jeongjo's reign. Let's take a closer look at Hannamnu Gate.  When restoring the temporary palace at Namhansanseong Fortress, the greatest focus was on resurrecting its old looks as much as possible. So the people who were in charge of the restoration referred to the records from various literature and the building site exposed through the excavation, and tried to use the old materials as much as possible to find their right places. But it was not an easy task to find the materials of temporary palace that had already been in ruins. In order to construct Hannamnu Gate, a total of 12 cornerstones were needed. People who were responsible for the restoration ransacked the entire village to find two cornerstones. Soon after, they also located two additional cornerstones that were being used as pillars of the main gate of Namhansan Elementary School. With four old cornerstones and eight new ones, the restoration work began. What greatly helped the restoration was a single photo of Hannamnu Gate taken by a French man in the 19th century. Where do you think the original four cornerstones are right now? That's right. You can find them easily, right? That's because these stones did not go through any artificial processing in order to clearly identify the old stones from the new ones. Some say that there should be no traces of restoration but there was also a need to tell people which materials are the original ones. This is why the old materials were not chemically processed.  Okay, let's go inside.

stories.title: Temporary Palace at Namhansanseong Fortress (Stylobate)
stories.script: This is the Hagwol section of the temporary palace. Haenggung is divided into Sanggwol, the upper palace, and Hagwol, the lower palace. Sanggwol was the king's living space whereas Hagwol was his office. Before we walk up to Oehaengjeon Hall, please take a closer look at this stylobate.  As I have told you earlier, when they built the temporary palace, they put the greatest emphasis on well-utilizing old materials. This stylobate was also made with this objective as the utmost priority. A stylobate is a stone structure built to raise the status of a building. Looking at this stylobate, you see that stones that formed the old stylobate and new stones were brought to be piled up together, but since cracks were created between the old stones and the new ones, small stones were used to fill in the cracks. However, if one of these stones is inserted incorrectly, the entire stone structure may collapse. In order to prevent this, it is said that they tore it down three times to rebuild it.  You can tell how much care they put into restoring temporary palace at Namhansanseong Fortress. Let's go up to Oehaengjeon Hall now.

stories.title: Temporary Palace at Namhansanseong Fortress (Oehaengjeon Hall)
stories.audioTitle: Temporary Palace at Namhansanseong Fortress (Oehaengjeon Hall)
stories.script: Oehaengjeon Hall was the central building of Hagwol which served as the king's office. It is where King Injo discussed with his vassals night and day on how they were going to respond to Qing. Now, let's examine the building more up close.  Considering the order of ranks, Oehaengjeon Hall is lower than Naehaengjeon of Sanggwol, and this is shown in the structure's ornaments. Please take a look at the roof of this building. These self-assembly wooden materials added to the tip of pillars are called Gongpo. They are made to withstand the weight of the roof. On certain Gongpo, a long wooden decoration is extended outward and, because this resembles a bird's wings, it is referred to as Ikgong. The style of Ikgong in Oehaengjeon Hall is called Murikgong, which has a rounded tip rather than a sharp end. Remember how this looks like and compare it with the Ikgong style in Naehaengjeon Hall.  Okay, before we move up to Sanggwol, let's briefly stop by the front yard of Oehaengjeon Hall where a large Silla building site was excavated.

stories.title: Temporary Palace at Namhansanseong Fortress (Site of Structure from Silla Period)
stories.audioTitle: Temporary Palace at Namhansanseong Fortress (Site of Structure from Silla Period)
stories.script: Namhansanseong boasts a history of over 1,000 years, and many pieces of evidence that prove it are revealed through excavations. The site of the Silla Period structure that we are going to look at now is an important proof that this used to be Jujangseong Fortress from the Unified Silla Period. Let's move together.  As I have said earlier, excavation began in the 1990s for restoration of Namhansanseong Fortress and, by 2004, the work was nearly coming to an end. However, as temporary palace was excavated, a building site was discovered 4m underground in Hagwol's front yard. The excavation, which continued until 2007, unearthed a large-scale building site that is 53m long and 18m wide. This was the site of a structure from the Unified Silla Period. It is considered one of the largest Unified Silla building sites excavated and is assumed to be a storage of weapons at Jujangseong Fortress. A discovery as marvelous as that of this building site was a great volume of tiles from the Unified Silla Period. The sizes of the tiles were extraordinary. Each of these gigantic tiles was 64cm long and weighed about 20kg. These tiles were more than five times larger than those from the Joseon Dynasty. They were tiles from the Unified Silla Period about 1,300 years ago. For such heavy tiles to be installed on a roof, the structure needed many pillars for support, which also tells us that these structures were probably quite large as well.  If weapons were stored in a structure of this magnitude, we can assume how strategically important Jujangseong Fortress was at the time. Now, let's move to Sanggwol.

stories.title: Temporary Palace at Namhansanseong Fortress (Naehaengjeon Hall)
stories.audioTitle: Temporary Palace at Namhansanseong Fortress (Naehaengjeon Hall)
stories.script: This place is Sanggwol where the king lived and slept. The building in front is Naehaengjeon Hall, which is the central structure of Sanggwol. You remember seeing the Gongpo at Oehaengjeon Hall, right? Then, let's check out the Gongpo of Naehaengjeon Hall as well.  If Gongpo of Oehaengjeon Hall is Murikgong, which is a bit lower in status, Gongpo of Naehaengjeon Hall is Iikgong which is much more lavish. When King Injo was staying in the fortress, the amount of his concerns was great. One day, King Injo lamented as he saw a royal meal table serving baeksuk, a chicken soup, with only half a chicken. “When we first arrived at Namhansanseong Fortress, we could not sleep because of the cries of roosters and hens, but seeing only half of a chicken on my table, it tells me all the roosters and hens of the fortress have disappeared,” lamented King Injo. When he first came into Namhansanseong Fortress, he was in a hurry and had no idea that he would be staying here for 47 days. King Injo was not able to bring any food and supplies with him on the way to Namhansanseong Fortress, and was forced to use the limited resources available in the fortress. Cries of roosters and hens were too loud at first to prevent people from falling asleep; all of them are long gone now as can be seen from the half chicken on the king's royal table. You can tell how bad the circumstances were inside the fortress. Though they wanted to fight, they lacked in weapons and soldiers. They wanted to fight and protect Namhansanseong Fortress until the enemies gave up, but the amount of supplies and resources was too little to do so. Naehaengjeon is the place that still holds their sadness and agony.  Let's now move to the secret garden.

stories.title: Secret Garden (Namhansanseong Fortress)
stories.script: At the northern end of the temporary palace in Namhansanseong Fortress lies a secret garden called Huwon. As Haenggung mimics the layout of the royal palace, it incorporates Oehaengjeon and Naehaengjeon Halls, respectively corresponding to Oejeon and Naejeon, alongside the secret garden. Kings often sought respite or engaged in archery practice within Huwon.  Within Huwon stands the Iwijeong Pavilion, where kings would stay during their archery practice sessions. Constructed in 1817, the 17th year of King Sunjo's reign, it was built by Sim Sang-gyun, who served as Sueodaejang. Sim enlisted Chusa Gim Jeong-hui to create calligraphy for a plaque, which, though only 31 years old, has unfortunately disappeared and is no longer extant. However, traces of Chusa's calligraphy can still be found in a rubbed copy of Iwijeonggi, a document written by Sim and calligraphed by Chusa, describing the origins and history of the establishment of Iwijeong Pavilion. The rubbing reveals Chusa's strong and powerful calligraphic style from his younger days.  The name Iwijeong translates to a dignified pavilion, and Iwijeonggi elaborates on its profound meaning. It suggests that while one can rule the world with bows and arrows, true dominion over the world requires the practice of righteousness and loyalty. The irony behind the name Iwijeong becomes apparent as it denotes the governance of the world by righteousness and loyalty in a war and military establishment at Namhansanseong Fortress. However, upon closer reflection, the name holds a deeply meaningful significance.

stories.title: Jwajeon (Namhansanseong Fortress)
stories.script: Jwajeon, within the context of Korean historical dramas depicting the Joseon Dynasty, serves as a symbol of profound significance. Viewers often witness loyal vassals beseeching the king with impassioned pleas, Your Majesty, safeguard the Jongmyo and Sajik. Jongmyo is the sacred place where the ancestral tablets of past kings rest, while Sajik is the hallowed ground for rituals honoring the deities overseeing the land and harvests. Consequently, Jongmyo and Sajik stand as the very embodiment of Joseon's royal court traditions and, by extension, the essence of the nation itself. When King Taejo, the dynasty's founder, relocated the capital to Hanyang (modern-day Seoul), he prioritized the establishment of Jongmyo Shrine and Sajikdan Altar before constructing the royal palace. In essence, Jongmyo and Sajik are foundational structures in the capital, where the king's authority resides.  The temporary palace at Namhansanseong Fortress holds exceptional significance as it houses Jwajeon, a site where the ancestral tablets of past Joseon kings, enshrined in Jongmyo Shrine, find their place. Jwajeon underscores the fortress's enduring commitment to defending and preserving the nation under any circumstance. Beyond this, the fortress city's acclaim extends far beyond the role of a royal sanctuary, incorporating remarkable architectural mastery and formidable defense, culminating in a reputation well beyond that of a mere temporary residence for the kings.

stories.title: Front Yard (Namhansanseong Fortress)
stories.script: The front yard of Namhansanseong Fortress, known as Samjeondo-gil, offers a captivating blend of natural beauty and historical significance. As you explore this area, you'll be immersed in the picturesque landscape of lush vegetation and serene pathways, providing a tranquil setting for visitors to reflect on the fortress's storied past. The vibrant colors of the changing seasons only add to the charm, making it a delightful spot for leisurely walks and outdoor activities. While taking in the scenery, you'll also encounter informative signposts and engaging narratives that unveil the layers of history preserved within the fortress walls. Overall, Samjeondo-gil serves as a remarkable gateway to the rich heritage and enduring spirit of Namhansanseong Fortress.

stories.title: Overview of Namhansanseong Fortress
stories.script: Namhansanseong Fortress served as a temporary capital of the Joseon Dynasty in a mountainous site 25 km southeast of Seoul. It was significant during the Japanese invasions of Korea in the late 16th century and the Byeongjahoran war with the Qing Dynasty in the mid-17th century. The length of the trail is approximately 12.4 km, with the main fortress 8.9km, the external fortress extending 3.2km, and Sinnamsanseong Fortress covering 0.2km. Its height stands at 7.3m. Visitors can find themselves awestruck by the large scale and remarkable sophistication. Although the earliest remnants date back to the early 7th century, the fortress has undergone several reconstructions in anticipation of potential attacks, notably by the Qing-Manzhou Qing Dynasty.  Today, only a few buildings remain within the fortress, notably its four gates, Sueojangdae, and some sections within the middle of the West Gate that retain their original appearance.  This fortress embodies a military defense concept that synthesizes changes in fortress construction technology due to the introduction of Western-style weapons while incorporating influences from China and Japan. It stands as a connected heritage, encompassing Bonseong, including Hanbongseong and Bonghamseong, and Sinnamseong, East and West Dondae, demonstrating the mutual exchange, accumulation, and urban planning among East Asian countries from the 16th to the 18th centuries. Additionally, it showcases the developmental stages and alterations in the weapon system from the 7th century to the 19th century, serving as a valuable living heritage where residents have dwelled for generations.  Moreover, it symbolizes Korea's independence and embodies the diverse religions and philosophies present in Korean history. Recognizing these values, Namhansanseong is listed as a World Heritage site and designated as Korean Historical Site No. 57

stories.title: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 1: Tombs From the Prehistoric, Three Hans and Three States Eras
stories.audioTitle: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 1: Tombs From the Prehistoric, Three Hans and Three States Eras
stories.script: How do you think the tombs of our country have changed since the Neolithic Era to the Period of the Three States? We’re going to examine these changes together.  Now, shall we first look at the tombs from the prehistoric times? It was the Neolithic Era when our ancestors first began to make tombs. One of the most notable tombs from this era is “stone axe tombs” in Hupo-ri, Uljin where bones were collected and buried in natural pits. Most of the Neolithic Era tombs dug shallow pits, buried bodies and covered them with earth or clamshells. Beombang Shell Mounds in Busan are a great example.  The most notable characteristic of tombs from the Bronze Age is the wide use of stones. In particular, Korea has a volume of dolmens that is unparalleled compared to other nations. There are also stone-coffin tombs and stone-mound tombs. Why do you think people back then liked to use stones as materials for tombs? There are several theories. First, a lot of people is needed to move large stones. In other words, using stones to build tombs literally meant power and authority. Because people of lower classes had no ability or status to use stones for their tombs, their traces disappeared completely in the course of time. That's why we believe that tombs from this era are mostly made of stones since they are the type of tombs capable of surviving for a long time. In later periods, jar coffin and wooden coffin tombs also appeared. A jar coffin tomb puts two jars together to make a coffin whereas a wooden coffin tomb refers to the one that features a wooden coffin.  After the Bronze Age, ironware culture officially began and this led to the advent of “states” in different regions of the Korean Peninsula. Three Hans of Mahan, Jinhan and Byeonhan to the south of the middle region later evolved into Baekje, Silla and Gaya, respectively, and tombs of various styles started to be constructed depending on the state and region. In the early phase of the Three Hans, small-sized tombs made of wooden coffin were popularly built. Towards the end of the era, however, tombs began to grow in size and wooden chamber tombs, which buried a lot of relics along with the body, became widely applied. A wooden chamber tomb has a structure of a room surrounded by boards with a wooden coffin in the center. This enabled them to place a greater amount of relics into tombs than before.  Now, in the period of the Three States, many different burial structures were seen, from wooden chamber tombs and stone-lined tombs to stone chamber tombs and corridor-style stone chamber tombs. How diverse and difficult to differentiate, don't you think? Although their life spans vary, most of them were made from the early 4th century to the 7th century. “Wooden coffin tombs,” which had appeared during the Three Hans, were still popularly used in the Gaya period. A variety and abundance of relics were also buried with bodies, and in particular, there are traces of Sunjang, which buries the living with the dead, so you can tell how powerful and dominant the leaders of those days were. In the 5th century, pit dwelling-style stone-lined tombs, which bury the dead vertically from the top, became popular, and the burial of relics and the living still continued. Then, after the late 5th century, Gaya’s tombs began to be made in entrance and corridor-styles that set up an entrance to enable several additional burials after the initial one.

stories.title: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 1: Ancient Tomb Culture of Busan and Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong
stories.audioTitle: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 1: Ancient Tomb Culture of Busan and Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong
stories.script: The Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong was first known to the world when they were accidentally discovered during the development and construction of a housing site in September 1969. Before that, shacks that had been built after the Korean War were densely crowded in the area. Starting with Dong-A University Museum's investigation of Tomb No. 1, a full-scale excavation took place in the 1980s. The excavation that ensued helped reveal not only the ancient history and cultural identity of Busan, which had been somewhat unclear, but also served as a turning point for Gaya’s outstanding ironware culture to become widely known.   Bokcheon Museum, which opened in October 1996 based on the discovery at the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong, vividly displays the history from the Three Hans to the Three States. In particular, it offers an in-depth look at the Gaya culture that was not easy to find in other museums.  Looking at how tombs are scattered here, there is a large tomb equipped with a subordinate outer coffin at the top of the hill while small- to medium-sized tombs without any subordinate outer coffin are seen on the hill's slopes and surroundings. The large-sized ancient tombs at the center were created as they gradually moved from the south to the north of the hill, and it seems like they were constructed in a neat, sequential order.  191 tombs and over 12,000 pieces of earthenware and ironware have been excavated from the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong. In particular, Tomb No. 57 revealed not only Haman-style earthenware but also Japanese earthenware, which sheds light on us the external exchanges our ancestors had with Japan at the time.  At Bokcheon Museum, try to solve the mystery of Gaya, which still remains as an unknown kingdom.

stories.title: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 2: Earthenware in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong
stories.audioTitle: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 2: Earthenware in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong
stories.script: At the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong, a variety of unglazed earthenware including pedestal dishes, doilies and necked jars were discovered. Unglazed earthenware is the type of earthenware made by blocking outside air and burning all oxygen on the inside when firing it to enable metallic components in earth to emanate their true colors. Gaya’s earthenware culture was centered on this unglazed earthenware.  During the Three Hans period in the past, gray-colored and ductile gray earthenware was more popularly used. Then, starting in the period the Three States in the 4th century, unglazed earthenware and gray earthenware coexisted and this officially begins the earthenware culture of the Three States period. The earthenware in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong clearly tells us the change.  By the late 4th century, many pedestal dishes were made. In particular, the earthenware of Aragaya and Hajiki of Japan were excavated, and this sheds light on the exchanges between the two states at the time. Then, by the 5th century, it is unified as unglazed earthenware, making the legs of pedestal dishes longer and the holes punched downward. There are dishes whose holes are in a vertically straight line or staggered. Considering that the latter type is Silla's earthenware, people assume that this was the period around which Busan region began to be under the influence of Silla. The amount of Silla earthenware began to gradually increase after the mid-5th century, and by the end of the century, nearly all of the earthenware made was Silla earthenware. This tells us that this region was now completely under the influence of Silla. It’s interesting how you can learn about history just by looking at pottery, right?  In addition, a wide variety of earthenware that display excellent forms and shapes have been excavated from those that are shaped as a shoe, duck and a horse head horn chalice. Among them, the earthenware in the shapes of birds such as ducks is the majority. Ancient people believed that birds guide the dead to heaven and bring seeds of grains in spring so they often placed birds’ feathers and duck-shaped earthenware into tombs.

stories.title: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 2: Ironware in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong
stories.audioTitle: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 2: Ironware in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong
stories.script: Around the 3rd century B.C., ironware from China began to slowly spread to the southern regions and the Korean Peninsula entered the era of ironware culture. As the technology of smelting iron was developed, people began to make and use a variety of ironware, which significantly increased their agricultural production capacity. Subsequent population growth and generation of states led to rapid development of societies. During the period of the Three States, iron was an indispensable material used to make farming tools, weapons and armors so it was not only a symbol of wealth and power but also a means of external exchanges.  At the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong, iron ingots, which is a material used in ironware, was the single most excavated relic. Iron ingots were found in large tombs primarily in Busan and Gimhae regions from the late 4th to 6th centuries. In the beginning, iron ingots were made in a variety of shapes and sizes, but in the 5th century, the sizes became uniform including the ones larger than 40 cm or those smaller than 20 cm. However, the size shrinks significantly by the 6th century. The size and shape of iron ingots were mainly related to the size of ironware to be produced with it but it had also a close relationship with the producers of iron ingots and the overall volume of iron production.  At the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong, iron ingots started to be installed at the bottom of the tombs in mid-4th century but they disappeared by the early 6th century. When burying iron ingots in a tomb, several pieces were tied together and spread on top of the wooden boards. In those days, iron was like money in today's world, so placing iron ingots in a tomb was an act of boasting wealth and authority of the dead. Iron ingots were used the most in the 5th century, which tells us that iron production began to increase around this period. Items like whetstones, hammers and tongs, which were used in iron production, were also excavated from some of the tombs but most of the ironware discovered here were weapons and farming tools. There was also unique ironware such as iron ritual implement and bent iron hand knives, and such relics either represent one's social status or were used in burial rites so they are often called as spiritual relics. Spiritual relics were popular in those days not because of their practicality but their shamanistic and symbolic functions. In addition, depending on the region, they served as a means to boast one's wealth just like iron ingots.

stories.title: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 2: Armor in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong
stories.audioTitle: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 2: Armor in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong
stories.script: Weapons were the second most unearthed burial accessories in tombs from the Three States period. Normally, when you think of weaponry,” you mainly think of swords and other tools of attack, but armor is actually a type of defense weapon as well. Notable defense weapons include helmets, gorgets and shields. Excavation of Tomb No. 11 revealed that this particular tomb is fully equipped with not only lamellar armors but also various accessories such as helmets, gorgets, shoulder pieces, greaves and brassards.  Armor was often used not only to protect the chest, the part of a body that a warrior is most vulnerable to fatal injuries, but also as a symbol of power. The iron armors excavated in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong were considered the quintessence of ancient iron-making technology and an unprecedented type of armors only discovered in the Gaya region. These armors are divided into laminar and lamellar armors. Laminar armors are made by connecting large triangular or rectangular iron plates whereas lamellar armors are made by connecting small, scale-like pieces of iron. A lamellar armor looks like fish scales, which is why it is also referred to as a scale armor. It weighs about 10 kg and is typically made with 1 mm thickness. Now, do you think these different types of armors and accessories actually served as defense weapons in actual battlefields? The answer is “Yes.” It is said that iron armor of Gaya showed excellent defense as even arrows shot from 30 to 40 m away would simply bounce off the armor. It also added practicality and convenience in wearing or taking off the armor by attaching hinges. As soldiers were engaging in battles wearing actual armors, there shouldn’t be any inconvenience in their movements, right?  Now, take your time to examine Gaya’s scientific and high-class weapon relics.

stories.title: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 2: Horse Equipment in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong
stories.audioTitle: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 2: Horse Equipment in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong
stories.script: In the ancient society, domestication of horses was important for the broadening of the scope of human activities. Since it was possible to move speedily between areas on a horse, exchanges among different local groups and populations were actively carried out, which proved to be quite useful. That’s why the ability to control horses was vital.  Horse equipment refers to various tools and items hung on a horse to able to ride and control it in a stable manner as well as to decorate it and report on it. It includes control tools such as bits that help handle a horse, devices like footrests and saddles for convenient riding of the horse, decorations such as belt-end ornaments and horse bells, and protective equipment like horse armor and horse helmets. Though they are not familiar items, they are explained on the walls of the museum's Exhibition Hall 2 with images.  Such horse equipment was widely spread from the northern region of the Korean Peninsula during the period of the Three States to be accepted as military and cultural tools. At the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong, a variety of horse equipment was excavated around the large tombs, which tells us how advanced the horse-riding culture in the Busan region was.  Horse equipment is divided into practical ones for battles and ornamental kinds. Looking at the unearthed relics, the 4th century was a period during which practical ironware was primarily manufactured, and starting in the mid-5th century, production of decorative gilt bronze products increased due to Silla's influence. Check out these relics with your own eyes to examine their characteristics.

stories.title: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 2: Jewelry in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong
stories.audioTitle: Bokcheon Museum — Exhibition Hall 2: Jewelry in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong
stories.script: Mankind started to wear jewelry on their bodies probably from the middle of the Old Stone Age. Jewelry at the time had more of a shamanistic meaning for self-defense or repelling of ghosts than bodily decorations. The custom of wearing jewels began to be emphasized as not only physical protection and aesthetic ornament but also a symbol of power and status. The jewelry of Gaya includes coffins, belt decorations, earrings, necklaces, and bracelets, and there are more gilt bronze, silver and glass products than gold. Most of the necklaces were made of glass but gem minerals such as crystal, agate, amber and jade were also used. From the Three Hans period to the 4th century, people preferred beads made of crystal, agate and glass but from the 5th century, jewels such as gold, silver and gilt bronze made by metal crafts were produced under the influence of Silla whose national power had become strengthened in the Three States period. However, it is rare to find products that are more colorful or refined than Silla's. Look for gold or gilt bronze earrings in the exhibition room. Unlike Silla’s colorful earrings, you can see that most of them are simple with only small rings.  A coffin is a symbolic item of the ruling class. In the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong, a total of three gilt bronze coffins were excavated — two of them decorated in the shape of a Chinese character 出 (chul) from Tomb No. 1 and one branch-shaped diadem ornament from Tomb No. 11. In particular, the gilt bronze coffin from Tomb No. 11 is estimated to be the oldest among all items excavated to the south of Hangang River.  The most excavated kind of jewelry from the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong is glass jade necklaces. Glass jade was produced from the Three Hans by the influence of China and became widely used as a jewelry material by the people of the Three Hans. Since the Three States period, manufacturing techniques were further developed, which led to creation of beads of various shapes and forms. If you mix a proper amount of iron, copper, lead, manganese, etc. when making glass, different shades of colors are created. Isn’t it amazing that the colors have been maintained to this day? The most widely used colors were blue and navy. Take a close look at the beautiful old necklaces to see if the color is blue or navy.

stories.title: Bokcheon Museum — Bokcheon Museum Outdoor Exhibition Hall
stories.audioTitle: Bokcheon Museum — Bokcheon Museum Outdoor Exhibition Hall
stories.script: The Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong are the only tombs in Busan that are for the ruling classes from before the 6th century. It is also a cultural site that vividly shows the prosperity of Gaya culture and the process of its incorporation into Silla.  The interesting characteristic of the outdoor exhibition hall is that it was established in the place where the actual tomb was excavated. In addition, it exhibits the exact scene from when the inside of the tomb was excavated and thus, allows us to take a peek at the burial custom from those days.  Tomb Nos. 53 and 54 are displayed inside the outdoor exhibition hall. Tomb No. 53 is a “pit dwelling-style stone-lined tomb” equipped with a secondary outer coffin built in a large size with stones in the mid-5th century. As the name suggests, it has a structure of a wooden chamber tomb with a secondary outer coffin. When it was discovered, it was found in a perfect condition so we were able to clearly see the structure of the tomb and the state of the tomb relics. Over 310 grave goods were excavated from inside the tomb, including earthenware, ironware, jewelry, whetstones and iron products. In particular, the excavated pedestal dishes are divided into several types — Silla's, local natives’ and Haman's — and here, a lot of earthenware of the Haman region are also found, which shows that the one buried in this tomb was once a person from western Gyeongnam region. Most of the ironware was excavated from the main outer coffin, and since the total amount excavated is smaller and the percentage of weapons is less compared to other tombs in the Ancient Tombs in Bokcheon-dong, it is presumed that the person buried was a woman. In an empty spot of the secondary outer coffin, there are traces of bones of a person who seems to have been sacrificially buried.   Tomb No. 54 is a large-sized wooden chamber tomb equipped with a main outer coffin and a secondary outer coffin that was constructed in the late 4th century. A portion of it was damaged due to disturbances in later generations but the tomb was so deep that the grave relics were in good condition. About 200 artifacts, including earthenware, ironware and necklaces, have been excavated, and most of them were earthenware. The area inside the tomb that is dug in a round shape like a puddle was where a pillar was standing at the time. Thanks to this, the tomb could not be destroyed. In Tomb No. 54, artifacts from the western Gyeongnam region centered on Haman and those of the Japanese style were excavated, indicating that the Gaya group in Busan region had personal and physical exchanges with the surrounding area as well as Japan far away.  Besides, you can get a beautiful panoramic view of Busan outside the outdoor exhibition hall so take your time and enjoy the scenery.

stories.title: What is the UN Memorial Cemetery? (UN Memorial Cemetery)
stories.audioTitle: What is the UN Memorial Cemetery? (UN Memorial Cemetery)
stories.script: The United Nations Memorial Cemetery is the only UN-certified cemetery. It is a place where fallen UN soldiers, who sacrificed their lives for world peace and freedom, rest in peace. There are several main sites and memorials including the Memorial Service Hall, Memorabilia Hall, two Turkish Monuments, Greek Monument, Australian Monument, British Commonwealth Monument, and two ponds.  As soon as the Korean War broke out on June 25, 1950, the UN immediately dispatched Allied Forces to fight. This was the only incident in history where UN forces were sent to a troubled region worldwide. A total of 22 nations participated in the war, with 16 providing combat forces and weapons, and 5 contributing hospital ships, medical staff, and supplies. Throughout the war, which lasted about 3 years (from June 25, 1950, to July 27, 1953), 40,896 UN soldiers from the 17 participating nations lost their lives, including those who provided medical assistance like Norway.  From 1951 to 1954, around 11,000 fallen UN heroes were buried at the UN Memorial Cemetery. However, the remains of soldiers from 7 countries including Belgium, Colombia, Ethiopia, Greece, Luxembourg, the Philippines, and Thailand, along with some from other nations, have since been repatriated to their home countries. Currently, 2,309 fallen soldiers from 11 countries, including 36 Korean soldiers who died in battle alongside the UN troops, are buried in this cemetery.  Every year on November 11, the Turn Toward Busan International Memorial Ceremony in honor of the Fallen of the Korean War is held at the cemetery. Under the slogan of “Moment to Be One, Turn Toward Busan,” the entire world observes a minute of silence towards Busan at 11 AM on November 11. Let us all remember this day and pay a silent one-minute tribute to the deceased heroes.

stories.title: The Symbolic Area and the Main Cemetery Area (UN Memorial Cemetery)
stories.audioTitle: The Symbolic Area and the Main Cemetery Area (UN Memorial Cemetery)
stories.script: The UN Memorial Cemetery consists of three main areas: the symbolic, main grave, and grass areas. First, let's take a look at the symbolic and grave areas.  In the symbolic area, the national flags of the 22 UN nations that participated in the Korean War are raised year-round, symbolizing the interred soldiers from 11 nations. The main grave area houses the majority of the fallen soldiers from Australia, Canada, France, Netherlands, Turkey, the United Kingdom, and the United States.  Entering the main grave area, you'll encounter several notable monuments and statues. The Australian Memorial situated in the Australian cemetery area, sculpted by Australian artist Ross J. Bastiaan in 2010, commemorates the actions of the Australian Air Force during the Korean War. It was initially installed in 1988 but underwent reconstruction due to weathering.  Another significant feature is the Canadian Memorial Statue located in the Canadian cemetery area. Erected by Canadian Veterans of the Korean War on November 11, 2001, the statue portrays a soldier without a hat, weapon, or unit patch, symbolizing Canadian individualism and informality. The two flower bouquets held by the boy and girl represent the maple leaves and roses of Sharon, Canada's national flowers. Each bouquet contains 21 flowers, symbolically representing the 21 Canadian soldiers listed as Missing in Action (MIA). Notably, the statue was designed by Mr. Vincent R. Courtenay, a Canadian Korean War veteran, and sculpted by Mr. You Young-moon, a Korean artist.  Lastly, the Commonwealth Memorial was erected in 1965 to honor the 386 MIAs of the Commonwealth Nations whose remains were not recovered. Engraved on the walls are the names, ranks, and units of these soldiers from the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, and South Africa. Please take a moment to honor and appreciate their noble sacrifices.

stories.title: Green Area (UN Memorial Cemetery)
stories.script: The Green Area, which spans over 70,000 square meters, is preserved as a buffer zone to maintain the grave areas of the UN Memorial Cemetery in a quiet and reverent manner. It encompasses the Veterans' Graves Area, the UN Forces Monument, the Wall of Remembrance, and more.  The Veterans' Grave Area is where surviving UN Forces who participated in the Korean War have been approved for interment since 2015. The graves here are arranged chronologically by date rather than by nation. The UN Forces Monument, constructed by the Korean government in 1978, bears a pair of doves on the front symbolizing peace. It features an engraving that reads “UN Forces Monument” in Korean, inscribed by Park Chung-hee, a former president. The monument's side walls display brass plaques detailing combat assistance provided by various nations and their casualty counts. Initially used to house a list of UN troops killed during the war, it was renovated into an exhibition hall in September 2007, now exhibiting photos and other information related to those buried there.  Additionally, the Wall of Remembrance was established in October 2006 with support from the Korean government. It aims to honor the fallen soldiers of the UN Forces who sacrificed their lives to protect the Republic of Korea during the Korean War, contributing to the cause of world peace and freedom.  Lastly, the round pond, symbolizing the universe, holds the sky where the souls of the fallen died in the war rest, alongside the monuments. Inside the pond, the helmet symbolizing war transitions to the peaceful lotus flower on the opposite side. Engraved on the black stone monument are the names of 40,896 fallen soldiers provided by war-participating countries, including those who are Missing in Action (MIA). The names are arranged alphabetically by countries and individuals. Let us all look at the eternal flame in the middle of the pond and pray for everlasting world peace.

stories.title: Memorial Service Hall (UN Memorial Cemetery)
stories.script: The Memorial Service Hall was built by the UN on August 21, 1964, to commemorate the fallen soldiers of the UN Forces during the Korean War. It was designed with six support beams and a triangular shape by Mr. Kim Jung-up, a pioneer of Korean modern architecture. This design was carefully considered to accommodate the diverse religious backgrounds of the fallen. Isn't the geometric triangular shape very unique?  The windows adorning both sides of the hall are made of stained glass instead of ordinary glass, containing intricate artistic designs. Each symbolizes different images and meanings such as peace, sublimation, the tragedies of war, love, and peace. You can see there are 16 lines radiating from the center of the floor through the UN logo and up to the ceiling, signifying the 16 nations that participated in the war. These lines also symbolize the wish and will for the prevention of war tragedies.  Moreover, visitors can watch a 10-minute-long documentary on the Korean War and the history of the UN Memorial Cemetery in five languages. This enables visitors from different countries to understand the content without language barriers.

stories.title: UN Memorial Cemetery: Memorabilia Hall and Memorabilia Hall II
stories.audioTitle: UN Memorial Cemetery: Memorabilia Hall and Memorabilia Hall II
stories.script: The Memorabilia Hall was built by the UN in 1968 along with the cemetery office and other auxiliary buildings. Photos and memorial artifacts of the UN troops during the Korean War are on display, and the first-ever UN flag used in history is exhibited at the front.  Shall we take a closer look? The photos showing the actions of the UN soldiers during the war are arranged in alphabetical order and by nation. And, below the photos, various memorial artifacts like items left by the fallen and visitor memorial tablets are on display as well. You can also see the pictures of the UN Memorial Cemetery that has changed over the years as well as various Korean War monuments throughout the nation. It is also interesting to see the images of the VIPs who visited from different countries including Margaret Thatcher, former prime minister of the United Kingdom, and those from Australia, Canada and New Zealand who attended the APEC Summit in 2005. Take your time to look at the photos and once you are finished, let's move to Memorabilia Hall II.  Memorabilia Hall II was a place that originally stored a list of all the UN troops who died during the war but it became Memorabilia Hall II after the Wall of Remembrance was installed in 2006. The hall exhibits a panel consisting of photos of the buried, which were provided by the bereaved from different countries, arranged in a table, and also features a permanent exhibit of various relics and paintings related to the fallen soldiers. Please remember that there are also a continuing number of special exhibits with new themes planned.

stories.title: History Museum of Joseon Tongsinsa — Exhibition Hall 1
stories.audioTitle: History Museum of Joseon Tongsinsa — Exhibition Hall 1
stories.script: Exhibition hall on the 1st floor  What greets us at the entrance of the History Museum of Joseon Tongsinsa is a sculpture of Masangjae, a person who rides a horse and performs acrobatic movements, from a procession of Tongsinsa. Masangjae was one of the most popular elements of cultural exchange amongst Tongsinsa to the point that Japanese considered watching Masangjae as a lifetime honor.  By the way, what does Tongsinsa mean? Tongsinsa means envoys that communicate with trust and refers to diplomatic delegations sent by the king of Joseon to the shogunate who was the power-holder in Japan. They were dispatched to Japan a total of 12 times between 1607 and 1811 after the Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1592. Up to 400 to 500 people were sent, and it consisted of Jeongsa, Busa and Jongsagwan who are the highest responsible persons in addition to people from a variety of fields, including interpreters, Jesulgwan in charge of writing diplomatic documents, doctors, Sajagwan who are good writers, scribes, painters, soldiers, Masangjae, captains, performers, riders, junior interpreters, cooks, trumpeters and naval officers.  Tongsinsa took Seogye, the official diplomatic document delivered by the king of Joseon, and Byeolpok, gifts to be delivered to Japan. They departed from Hanyang and took a ship from Busan through Tsushima to Osaka. From there, they traveled to Edo, which is todays’ Tokyo, on foot, and completed an average of eight-month round trip journey. Lords of the regions in Japan through which the Tongsinsa delegations were passing spent much of their budget to entertain Tongsinsa by preparing food and gifts and repairing roads, and many Japanese people filled the streets to see the parade of the Joseon Tongsinsa.  The History Museum of Joseon Tongsinsa opened in 2010 as an exhibition hall for historical education on cultural exchanges between Korea and Japan, promoting the historical value and meaning of Joseon Tongsinsa.  The ground of the exhibition hall on the first floor has a map with which you can figure out different locations. The exhibition hall on the first floor is a place where you can learn through various content the historical background and role of Joseon Tongsinsa as well as their efforts for Korea-Japan exchanges. It also displays the definition and role of Tongsinsa, the appointment ceremony of Samsa, etc. on numerous panels to help you better understand them. In the History Museum’s video room, you can think about the historical and present meaning of Joseon Tongsinsa through various videos related to them, such as introduction videos and festival videos of Joseon Tongsinsa as well as 3D images for children. Besides, you can also check out the costumes of Jeongsa, Jongsagwan and military officers dispatched as Joseon Tongsinsa, and there is also a small library, so take your time to look around!

stories.title: History Museum of Joseon Tongsinsa — Exhibition Hall 2
stories.audioTitle: History Museum of Joseon Tongsinsa — Exhibition Hall 2   Exhibition hall on the 2nd floor
stories.script: On the passageway to the exhibition hall on the second floor through the first floor stairs, you will find traces of various writings and paintings by our ancestors that were created based on their travels and experiences as members of Tongsinsa.  Joseon Tongsinsa conversed and shared drinks with many writers in Japan they met on their journey. They also received an enthusiastic welcome from Japanese commoners and had a huge influence on people of various classes in Japan. In the exhibition hall on the second floor, you can take a closer look at the “Documents on Joseon Tongsinsa,” which are registered as a Memory of the World, containing various traces of Tongsinsa. During the registration process, “Documents on Joseon Tongsinsa” were applied as a UNESCO Memory of the World by emphasizing the fact that they were a symbol of “peace” and “good-neighborly diplomacy,” and on October 31, 2017, 111 cases and 333 pieces were registered.  The exhibition hall on the second floor displays maps and models that show the route the Joseon Tongsinsa took from Hanyang to Edo, which is today's Tokyo, as well as Panokseon that Joseon Tongsinsa traveled on during their journey. In addition, it plays a video of a replicated procession of Tongsinsa entering Edo Fortress in Japan so you can visually see the activities of Tongsinsa at the time.  After looking around the exhibition halls on the first and second floors, head to Yeonggadae Pavilion, which is connected to the History Museum of Joseon Tongsinsa. Yeonggadae is the place where Joseon Tongsinsa held rituals for sea gods to pray for their safe voyage to Japan, and it is also where the governor of Gyeongsang Gwon Ban built a pavilion on the hill in front of Jaseongdae in 1614 (the 6th year of King Gwanghaegun’s reign). The name, Yeongga, was derived from the old name of Andong, Gwon Ban’s hometown. Today, it is replicated on one side of Jaseongdae Park.

stories.title: Cheonmasan Sculpture Garden
stories.script: Cheonmasan Sculpture Garden is a sculpture park established at the top of Cheonmasan Mountain. Cheonmasan Mountain possesses excellent natural conditions that since the old days, dense grasslands here were a popular habitat of horses. A legend has it that once a dragon horse descended from heaven. At Cheonmasan Sculpture Garden, the mythical Cheonmabawi Rock and 44 sculpted works are on display. In fact, when it first opened, the garden had 45 works but unfortunately, a bronze statue was stolen in 2010, which only leaves 44 works today.  At Cheonmasan Sculpture Garden, there is a general guide to all the works that explains in detail every single work so even those who have considered art to be difficult to understand will be able to appreciate and enjoy them. In addition, a forest of cypress trees surrounds the works, which makes a perfect place for the visitors to enjoy a therapeutic walk. After checking out the works, take deep breaths in the cypress forest. You will feel refreshed like your soul is being cleansed. Moreover, the area surrounding the park features various sports facilities, trails, observatory, rest areas and many convenience facilities, which is why it is a popular spot for field trips and cultural experiences.  Now, take your time looking at the sculpted works and enjoy a relaxing stroll through Cheonmasan Sculpture Garden.

stories.title: Cheonmasan Sculpture Garden
stories.script: Cheonmasan Observatory  There are two observatories in Cheonmasan Mountain — “Nuribaragi Observatory” also known as the observatory at the bottom of the mountain, and “Cheonmasan Observatory,” which is located a bit higher. Whichever observatory you go up to, you can enjoy a magnificent view of the city, but we recommend you to check out “Cheonmasan Observatory” though it may be a little tougher to get to.  The city of Busan viewed from the observatory features diverse looks, from Yeongdo Bridge and Yeongdo close by to Oryukdo Islets, the Scenic Site No. 24 in the distance. Since the old times, Yeongdo was known for horse breeding farms and it is said that horses trained here ran so fast and people could not even see their shadows, which is why the island was also called Jeoryeongdo. Today's Yeongdo is famous for “Taejongdae Park” with gorgeous coastal scenery, so make sure to stop by. Oryukdo’s name stems from how it shows six peaks when viewed from the east and five peaks when viewed from the west. Among the six peaks, Bangpaeseom and Solseom Islands are connected at the bottom, which is why the number of peaks shown varies depending on the height of the seawater.  From the South Port, Jagalchi Market is seen. The name Jagalchi means outskirts with many Jagal, or pebbles. The building with a shape of a flying seagull is that of Jagalchi Market, a seafood cooperative. There is a Jagalchi Cruise ship seen nearby that departs Jagalchi and sails to Jujeonja Island on the sea in front of Taejongdae Park.  Isn’t it exciting to see the diverse Busan at a glance? When you go down, follow the “To the End Point” sign to enjoy a beautiful forest path. Make sure to be careful as you head down.

stories.title: Jeongnamjin Hinoki Woodland
stories.script: A healing trip to the Hinoki Forest filled with the scent of phytoncide  Jeongnamjin Hinoki Woodland is known to be a “therapeutic forest,” and a site of great healing. It is the best out of the nine fascinating destinations that represent Jangheung-gun. Since it cures the mind and body of modern people tired of city life, it was designated as a “Wellness Tourist Attraction” by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Korea Tourism Organization in 2017. Hinoki Forest contains 470,000 hinoki trees carefully tended for over 60 years. Considering phytoncide secreted from hinoki trees helps antibacterial action, strengthens intestinal functions and cardio pulmonary functions and mitigates atopic dermatitis, Jeongnamjin Hinoki Woodland is a remarkably healthy place to visit.  You can inhale phytoncide to your heart’s content by simply walking along the scenic trails meandering through Hinoki Forest. The walking courses vary from a 1-hour course, which starts from the ticket booth and leads to Hinoki Owl Fountain, Forest of Meditation, Anion Fall, foot bath and Aromatherapy Garden and back, to a 3-hour course. If you are looking for a more comfortable way to enjoy the forest, simply go straight to the Forest of Meditation where you can relax in rattan chairs and low wooden benches or recline on hammocks skillfully hung between trees.  After walking through Hinoki Forest trails, taking a Hinoki Salt Sauna is the ideal next stop. Here you can experience salt detoxification using natural salt, luxuriate in the many inviting sauna facilities, including a salt cave, visit the salt massage shop and salt detoxification room. Staying one night at Eco Experience Pension in the woods is a great way to add to your visit’s unforgettable memories.

stories.title: Jeongnamjin Jangheung Saturday Market
stories.script: Fun festival held every Saturday  Jeongnamjin Jangheung Saturday Market is a traditional market that represents Jangheung-gun. It is full of exotic things to see, eat and enjoy. There is a regular market open every day and a five-day market held on days that end with a 2 or 7. Visit the weekend market on Saturday to see exciting performances in the circular plaza like the Beoggu Nongak Show that is the traditional farm music of Jangheung-gun and native folk plays such as Pumba.  You can find shiitake mushrooms, pen shells and beef that are representative specialties of Jangheung-gun in the Jangheung-gun Local Specialties Market. Jangheung shiitake mushrooms are fragrant and chewy and pen shells grown clean in the Deungnyangman Bay tideland have especially large scallops and are rich with healthful nutrients. Jangheung-gun beef, from native Korean cattle fed good feed and raised in a clean environment with mild weather year-round, is famous for its tender texture and satisfying taste.  There are many restaurants selling “Jangheung Samhap,” a combination of grilled shiitake mushrooms, pen shells and beef, in the Jeongnamjin Jangheung Saturday Market. Especially during the busy weekends, there are people inside and outside of the market enjoying Jangheung Samhap. Visit Jeongnamjin Jangheung Saturday Market—one of nine representative tourist attractions selected by Jangheung-gun where you’re sure to find happiness.

stories.title: 7080 Mural Street
stories.script: Murals depicting old days that all generations can relate to  In the Yeyang-ri and Giyang-ri areas, which used to be the center of Jangheung-eup in Jeollanam-do, there is the 1.8-km-long mural street. Like the name “7080 Mural Street” implies, the scenes of 70s and 80s are drawn in murals. Visitors who spent their school days in those areas will be lost in their memories.  The murals show the scenes of classrooms that cannot be seen these days and scenes of kids following a fumigation truck as well as snacks, such as cinder toffees, sold in front of school. When you walk along the winding street, it seems you are travelling back in time. There is a street that shows games including leapfrog and jump rope in the good old days and there is another street that reminds visitors of the time when people wearing jeans sang songs accompanied by a folk guitar.  There is a street showing popular animations highlighted by Korean and foreign animations from Dooly, the Baby Dinosaur, Galaxy Express 999 to Inspector Gadget, which are sure to catch eyes of visitors. Even Slam Dunk that was a big hit in the 90s is shown at the end of the animation street. A 5-minute walk from the Jeongnamjin Jangheung Saturday Market, 7080 Mural Street is the perfect spot for a casual stroll down after looking around the market.

stories.title: Cheongwansan Mountain
stories.script: Cheongwansan Mountain Famous mountain in the Honam region filled with waves of silver grass  You will join other visitors to Cheongwansan Mountain in Jangheung-gun in searching for just the right words to describe this special place, one of the five famous mountains in the Honam region. It is called a mountain with unique and stunningly beautiful rock formations or a mountain with gently waving silver grass on a sunny autumn day. It probably means that Cheongwansan Mountain has made a lasting impression on you after just one visit.  The reason why this mountain is one of five famous mountains in the Honam region, together with Jirisan Mountain, Wolchulsan Mountain, Naejangsan Mountain and Naebyeonsan Mountain, can be also found in its name, “Cheongwan” that is given because dozens of unique rock formations rising sky-high look like an emperor’s crown. In addition to this beautiful unique rock formation, Cheongwansan Mountain also hosts the Cheongwansan Silver Grass Festival in Hwanhuidae Hermitage and Yeondaebong Peak in mid-October when silver grass is at its peak. Waves of these heavily topped silver grass stems dancing in the wind create a picturesque landscape with a backdrop of Dadohae.  There are up to 10 courses to the top of Cheongwansan Mountain, but three courses starting from Jangcheonjae Shrine, Tabsansa Temple, and Cheongwansan Recreational Forest are most commonly used. In the most popular Jangcheonjae course, don’t forget Jangcheonjae Shrine, where Confucian scholar of the Joseon Period studied. It is also where Wi Baek-gyu, a neo-Confucian scholar, who was the representative scholar of the Honam region, studied when he was young and trained younger students later in his life.   There is Cheongwan Literary Museum and Cheongwansan Literature Park in the Tapsansa Temple course, so you can experience the true nature of Jangheung-gun, the home of literature. If you want to see the largest camellia grove in Korea, take the Cheongwansan Recreational Forest course. Since the level of difficulty and the time required for each course is different, please make sure to check course details before starting your hike to ensure a pleasant trip.

stories.title: Cheongwan Literary Museum
stories.script: Base camp of Jangheung-gun literature tour  Cheongwan Literary Museum, the only literature tourist zone in Korea, offers visitors an overview of the real value of Jangheung-gun. From Gwanseo Byeolgok (Song of the Sceneries of Gwanseo) by Baek Gwang-hong that was 25 years ahead of Gwandong Byeolgok (Song of the Sceneries of Gwandong) by Jeong Cheol to modern literature, you can discover Jangheung-gun’s literary strength. It is a bonus that you can enjoy the amazing scenery, as the literary museum is located at the foot of Cheongwansan Mountain, one of the Nine Sights of Jangheung-gun.  In Exhibition Room No. 1 of the literary museum, the works of renowned local writers are displayed. In Exhibition Room No. 2, the works of writers from Jangheung-gun are introduced and even their press interviews are carefully categorized. Famous writers such as Song Gi-suk, the author of Nokdu General, children’s book writer Kim Nok-chon, and Yi Seung-u, a candidate for the Nobel Prize in Literature, are from Jangheung-gun. In addition, the works of writer Han Gang who is the first Korean writer to win the Man Booker International Prize and also the daughter of writer Han Seung-won are also proudly displayed.  In particular, the exhibition of comparing the lives and works of writer Yi Chong-jun and writer Han Seung-won is very interesting. They are of the same age and were born in Jinmok Village and Singsang Village, respectively. Don’t miss the corner introducing movies and TV shows based on their novels, such as Seopyeonje and Come Come Come Upward.  After viewing, write your feelings on a postcard prepared by the literary museum and send it to someone. If you put it in the Wish Mailbox and Slow Mailbox at the entrance, it will be delivered to the address after 1 year. It’s fun to write your precious memories of the visit and send it to yourself, so when you get the postcard 1 year later, it will help you relive your visit to the museum.

stories.title: Cheongwansan Literature Park
stories.script: Examine the works of writers from Jangheung-gun  Take the winding 1 km path along the road with stone towers from Cheongwan Literary Museum to Cheongwansan Literature Park. All the stone towers were built by residents of Daedeok-eup. The villagers’ devotion to the village is quite impressive.  The 15-m high Literature Tower that greets you upon arriving at Cheongwansan Literature Park is also the work of residents of Daedeok-eup. It contains a buried time capsule of the handwritings and messages of famous writers in Korea, which is very fitting for Jangheung-gun, the area of literature.  When you pass the Literature Tower and enter the park, you will see the literature monuments engraved with the excerpts of works from 54 famous writers in Korea including Song Gi-suk, Kim Nok-chon, Yi Chong-jun, Han Seung-won and Yi Seung-u, who are from Jangheung-gun, and other writers including Park Beom-sin and Yang Gwi-ja. All the stones used for the literature monuments were brought from Cheongwansan Mountain. Reading these inscriptions on the uniquely shaped stones will make you feel like enjoying a sculpture and literature at the same time. More literature monuments are scheduled to be added in the future, so let’s look forward to the future of Cheongwansan Literature   Cheongwansan Literature Park greets visitors with different appearances in each season. In spring, fresh tender shoots of green are beautiful under the warm sunlight, and in summer, lush green trees create cool shade under which visitors can recite a poem. In autumn, brilliant burning red autumn leaves create a picturesque landscape, and in winter, white snow blankets the grounds so a tranquil phrase of an essay can warm a cold heart.

stories.title: Cheongwansan Recreational Forest
stories.script: A natural recreational forest in Cheongwansan Mountain  Cheongwansan Recreational Forest is located at the foot of Cheongwansan Mountain, one of the famous mountains in the Honam region. When you arrive at the entrance to the recreational forest, you will see a forked road centering on the management office. The left fork leads to the hiking and forest trails and the right fork takes you to the House in the Forest and a campground.  How about taking up the challenge and hiking to Cheongwansan Mountain, starting from Cheongwansan Recreational Forest? Since Cheongwansan Recreational Forest is already located at a high altitude, the course to the top is somewhat easy. It takes about 3 hours from Cheongwansan Recreational Forest to the top and back. If hiking is burdensome, how about taking on the trails in Cheongwansan Recreational Forest? There are no uphill or downhill areas, so people of all ages can enjoy meandering along these easy to navigate trails.  To spend a night in the forest, simply make a reservation for the House in the Forest or the campground at the Cheongwansan Recreational Forest homepage. We recommend participating in various experience programs provided by the recreational forest. Reservations for nature-friendly programs including Camellia Broach Making and Natural Dyeing can be made on the spot. Each program takes about 30 minutes.

stories.title: Cheongwansan Camellia Eco Forest
stories.script: The largest natural camellia habitat in Korea  The Camellia Eco Forest located in the mid-slope of Cheongwansan Mountain is famous for silver grass, and more than 20,000 camellia trees fill the valley. It is recognized as the largest habitat for a single variety and was listed in the Guinness Book of Records of Korea in 2007. The “Best in the World Cheongwansan Mountain Camellia Forest” monument was put up at the observatory in the upper Camellia Eco Forest to celebrate the designation.  When you drive on Local Road No. 827 and turn towards the sign of Cheongwansan Recreational Forest and continue for about 2 km, you will see Camellia Eco Forest. You will be amazed at how the camellia forest densely fills the valley. Camellia flowers in Cheongwansan Mountain are at their peak in late March to early April, which is slightly later than those in coastal areas, and thick green leaves and red blooms sparkling in the sunshine are spectacular.  After looking at the camellia forest in the upper section of the observatory to your heart’s content, come down to the lower section of the observatory along the trail. When you enter the forest tunnel dense with camellias, you will feel as if you are in a beautiful fairy tale forest. The trail is mostly a dirt road, except for some sections, so it is convenient to walk. While walking, it is easy to see white-eyes that carry pollen instead of bees.

stories.title: Jeamsan Mountain
stories.script: Feast of royal azaleas unfolds along the spring path  Jeamsan Mountain is a celebrated mountain famous for its unique rock formations and royal azalea fields. It is also a mountain representing Jangheung-gun, along with Cheongwansan Mountain. It is called Jeamsan because there is a lofty rock in the shape of Chinese character “帝 (Je),” which means a king, at the 800 m top of mountain, and what makes it even more fascinating is that other surrounding rocks look like they are reverently lying prone towards the top of mountain.  At the top of the mountain, you can see the southern sea far away as well as Cheongwansan Mountain, “one of five famous mountains in Honam,” Wolchulsan Mountain that is called “Geumgangsan Mountain of Honam” and Mudeungsan Mountain that represents Gwangju Metropolitan City. In May when mountain hiking is at its peak, the royal azalea community spreads from Jeamsan Mountain to neighboring Sajasan Mountain along the ridge, so these vistas look covered with a pink carpet. Hence, Jeam Royal Azalea Festival is held around early or mid-May every year.  There are many courses to take when scaling Jeamsan Mountain. Among them, the typical courses either start at the Jeamsan Mountain royal azalea field parking lot, passing through Gomjae Pass before reaching the top, or take the course from Ganjae Pass, hiking through the royal azalea field and Gomjae Pass and making your way to the top. If you have enough time and stamina, take on the long-distance course starting from Gamnamujae Pass in Jangdong-myeon, passing through the top, and leading to Gomjae Pass and Sajasan Mountain.

stories.title: Tamjingang River
stories.script: Lifeline that wets the land of Jangheung-gun  Tamjingang River, one of the Nine Sights of Jangheung-gun, is considered as three great rivers of the Honam region along with Seomjingang River and Yeongsangang River. Tamjingang River penetrates Jangheung-gun and flows 55 km through Gangjin-gun to meet the southern sea. It was named Tamjingang River as the envoy of Tamna, the old name of Jeju-do during the Silla period, anchored a ship to pay a tribute, by combining “Tam” from Tamna and “Jin” from Gangjin.  Tamjingang River Marsh Eco Park, embraced by the long river course of Tamjingang River, is a popular site for family outings and relaxing walks by locals for its many trails and ecological observation trails, Picturesque stepping stones connect to Jeongnamjin Jangheung Saturday Market from the riverside parking lot. Don’t miss the fun as fish swim under your feet as you cautiously use the stepping stones to cross the river.  From the end of July to early August each year, the huge “Jeongnamjin Jangheung Water Festival” is held around the Tamjingang River area. The festival offers a host of fun programs including the “Biggest Water Fight in the World” where you can relieve the stress of daily life by dousing your “enemies” and “Catch the Gold Fish” where you can win a prize by catching a certain fish. “Jangheung Water Rock Pool Party” with a famous EDM DJ is certainly in vogue these days. The Jeongnamjin Jangheung Water Festival is considered one of the major summer festivals of Korea and offers visitors a wide range of popular water-related leisure sports to make their stay especially memorable.

stories.title: Yonghojeong Pavilion and Garden
stories.script: A pavilion built in filial piety for generations  Built in 1828, the 28th year of King Sunjo’s reign during the Joseon Dynasty, Yonghojeong Pavilion is not very old among pavilions in Jangheung-gun. There is another difference in Yonghojeong Pavilion from other pavilions around Tamjingang River. While Sainjeong Pavilion, Buchunjeong Pavilion and Dongbaekjeong Pavilion were built in loyalty, Yonghojeong Pavilion was built in filial piety.  Choe Yeong-taek, a scholar who lived in Jangheung-gun, visited his father’s grave on the mountain across the river every day for three years after his father’s death. For the days he could not cross the river because of heavy rain, he built an alter and made a deep bow. His son Choe Gyu-mun felt sorry for his father and built a pavilion at the site so that he could take shelter from rainstorms, and that’s how Yonghojeong Pavilion and Garden started. A thick forest formed around Yonghojeong Pavilion built on a stiff cliff in the upper Tamjingang River and became Yonghojeong Pavilion and Garden. Maybe trees know about the filial piety passed down from the father to the son. There are 23 interesting tablets telling this fascinating story, including “Yonghojeonggi”, hanging in the pavilion.  Yonghojeong Pavilion was built with chestnut and zelkova trees and has one room surrounded by wooden floors. When you sit on the small wooden floor of the pavilion, the lazy Tamjingang River spreads out before you like a landscape painting and the forest embraces the surroundings to release cool air even on the hottest summer days.

stories.title: Buchunjeong Pavilion and Garden
stories.script: Loyalty of Righteous Army Commander dwelling in a pavilion  In the course of Tamjingang River in Jangheung-gun, Jeollanam-do, there is Buchunjeong Pavilion where loyalty resides. Buchunjeong Pavilion stands on a little hill lush with many types of tress including pine trees, offering a clear view of Tamjingang River.
