The gallery has portraits of five saints that spread the gospel near Sinri Catholic village and 13 paintings that tell the story of martyrs.  Sinri Shrine is famous for its beautiful and exotic views and known as “Jeju Island of the Mainland.” Take a moment to feel the sacred atmosphere and listen to our hearts.

stories.title: Beogeunae Pilgrimage Route
stories.script: Camino de Santiago of Korea - Beogeunae Pilgrimage Route was used by Korea’s martyrs since the early days of the history of Catholics in the country. Stretching from an inland port of Sapkyocheon Stream, the route is where the family of Saint Andreas Kim Daegon developed their faith. It also served as a secret path and passageways for the religious activities of foreign missionaries.  A one-way trip on foot along the 13.3 km-long route from Solmoe Shrine to Sinri Shrine takes about four hours. The route was awarded the Asia Townscape Award in 2016 and selected as Trail of the Month in 2019. It has become more popular after a stamp tour began in 2018. In October 2010, Beogeunae Pilgrimage Route and Camino Corea, the official Camino de Santiago certification organization in Korea, signed a memorandum of understanding, making the course an undisputed major pilgrimage route in Korea.  Hapdeokje Jungsubi Monument, the birthplace of martyrs Won Sijang and Won Sibo, the tomb of an unknown martyr and other cultural heritage sites can be found along the way, making Beogeunae Pilgrimage Route ideal for looking back on your religious journey through nature.

stories.title: Arirang Literature Village
stories.script: Arirang Literature Village  Arirang of the Korean people  Welcome to Gimje Arirang Literature Village. Arirang Literature Village was established based on the story of Arirang, an epic novel written by Jo Jung-rae. The novel is set in the Japanese occupation period and talks about the lives of Joseon people whose lands and roots were taken away by the Japanese. Located in Hongsan-ri, Juksan-myeon of Gimje-si, the Literature Village is the very location mentioned in the novel and where both the traces of the colonial period and valuable modern cultural heritage still remain. The city of Gimje reproduced the buildings and streets from the novel, including police substation, which was a modern agency of exploitation; a myeon office; a post office; and a rice mill. Your presence in the place will make you feel like you are in the middle of the novel. It is also a site that teaches you about the patriotism and sacrifices of anti-Japanese fighters such as An Jung-geun.  The village consists of the promotion hall (Japanese exploitation hall), modern exploitation agency, Naechon and Oeri Villages, the house of immigrants, and Harbin Station building. The promotion hall is divided into Exhibition Halls 1 and 2. Exhibition Hall 1 on the 1st floor explains the policies implemented by the Japanese to colonize and exploit Joseon while Exhibition Hall 2 on the 2nd floor displays the lyrics of Arirang on the walls. As you read them, the story of the novel, Arirang, unfolds before your eyes.  Among the four modern exploitation agency buildings, the myeon office exhibits a telescope, compass, camera, abacus, mimeograph and other tools that were used at the time, and you can even try using them your own. Once you step into the police substation, you feel a bit frightened by the sounds of interrogation, and various tools of torture such as a whip are displayed on the walls. Naechon and Oeri Villages are the replica of the houses of Son Pan-seok, Ji Sam-chul, Gamgoldaek and Song Su-ik, the major characters of the novel. They are a countryside community seated by a small hill and consisted of simple, thatched houses standing next to one another in a friendly, pastoral fashion. The lives of the home owners as depicted in the novel, however, were not as peaceful as the exterior.  The house of immigrants is also a replica of the one where the main characters lived before they moved to Gando and Yeonhaeju Provinces. The place offers a peek into the lives of the people back then who had left their hometowns empty-handed and carried difficult lives in strange, unfamiliar regions. Harbin Station is a reproduction of the scene in which An Jung-geun, a Korean-independence activist, shot Ito Hirobumi, an event that is also talked about in the novel. It is a miniature version of the actual Harbin Station building back in 1910. On the back of the building stands a life-size statue that replicates the shooting scene.  Shall we now embark on our journey to the novel, Arirang?

stories.title: The historical background of the novel
stories.audioTitle: The historical background of the novel
stories.script: The historical background of the novel  The Arirang Literature Village Promotion Hall was built in the shape of a straw rice bag and a rice field. In the lobby, there are clothes and shoes from the era of the novel, Arirang, so anyone can try them on (currently not available due to COVID-19).  Exhibition Hall 1 explains the policies implemented by Japan in order to colonize and exploit Joseon. In Juksan-myeon of Gimje, which is the setting of the novel, the work to exploit Joseon’s rice had started from an early stage, and Japan executed a land survey project from 1910 to 1918 to extort lands from Joseon farmers, most of who were forced to become tenant farmers around this time. Many farmers who were robbed of their lands became laborers, and some had no choice but to move to Gando or Maritime Provinces for survival. In addition, Gimje, which had shown the greatest rice production amount in Joseon, turned into one of the poorest regions after being incorporated into Japan's colonial economy.  In resistance against Japan's colonial policies, the people of Joseon began the Independence Movement on March 1, 1919. Gimje farmers also took part in the movement and, later, formed Gimje Youth Association to carry out youth and enlightenment movements. They installed night schools to invigorate education and led farm tenancy disputes, the funding for the Independence Army, the promotion of rights of laborers and farmers, and these efforts contributed to increasing the national consciousness and thoughts on independence.  Exhibition Hall 2 gives you a tour to the lives of Gimje people in the 1900s through the novel. As you enter the hall by following the lyrics of Arirang engraved on the walls, the story of the novel unfolds before you. The story about Gimje and Mangyeong Plains is depicted in detail in Part 1 whereas the lives and actions of the protagonists who have left their hometowns are described vividly in Parts 2 and 3.  When your tour ends, come out to the yard, and you will get to experience various traditional plays. Try a rickshaw, which was an important means of transportation in the 1900s, and be sure to take your best photos!

stories.title: A front line colonization agency
stories.script: A front line colonization agency  At the entrance of the myeon office built with red bricks shows a sign that says “Juksan-myeon Office.” The office is where chief Baek Jong-du, a pro-Japan chief in the novel, Arirang, worked. Most of the chiefs of myeon offices with huge political and financial influence and power during the Japanese occupation period were pro-Japan. The novel describes people who try their best not to displease the chiefs so that they would not end up being sent away for labor or military service by the chiefs. The employees at myeon offices, most of whom were elementary school graduates, also belonged to the pro-Japan group. Financially, they were from a class higher than or equal to middle-class farmers, and many of them were chosen from influential families of the region. Thus, the chiefs and employees of myeon offices served as the lowest authority on the totem pole and were guaranteed of their security.  The “Juksan-myeon Office” is the reproduction of the myeon office that appears in Arirang. Pieces of furniture from the era are set up in the office where chief Baek Jong-du in the novel worked in, and a mannequin of the office secretary engaging in administrative tasks stands in the center of the myeon office. The wall next to the mannequin displays various photos and materials related to patriotic group activities, which were executed by Japan as a part of the colonial rule, as well as brassware that was compulsorily offered to Japan and the patriotic aircraft donation movement. It was one of the office secretary’s tasks to manage patriotic groups.  The tools and utensils that were popularly used at the time are also exhibited in the civil affairs room and the mimeograph room on the left. The mimeograph room, in particular, is something we rarely see these days. At the time, the technology of printing, publication, and preservation of materials was not as developed as today, so a separate mimeograph room was installed to write and manage materials. And because acts of printing and publishing were strictly controlled during the colonial rule, myeon offices also served to censor rumors or handbills.

stories.title: Rice Mill
stories.script: Rice Mill  A rice exploiting agency for Japanese people  The wooden building with a red roof situated next to the myeon office is a rice mill, which has a sign that says “Juksan Rice Mill”. A rice mill is a place where rice is produced by threshing, pounding, and polishing harvested rice. But the rice produced at “Juksan Rice Mill” in Arirang was polished to be offered to Japanese landowners or export to Japan. In the novel, chief Baek Jong-du operated the rice mill. During the colonial period, machines were widely distributed to exploit more rice, but for the tasks that needed manpower, Joseon labor forces were exploited at extremely small wages or no wage at all.  The room on the left side of an enormous thresher located in the middle of the rice mill is the supervision room. You can see rice seeds dispersed on the floor and the tools that were used during that time including a winnow, A-frame, and straw bags.  If you walk a bit further inside, you will find a reenactment of “Miseonso” with working women and a chief monitoring them. Here, women were ordered to pick out unbroken, sound rice seeds in order to offer the highest-quality rice to the powerful and rich Japanese people. On the other hand, the impoverished Joseon people slaved away in the face of harsh, unfair treatment, even being called not by their names but by their numbers, to make money and simply not to starve. If a hungry worker who picks up and eats rice seeds on the floor is caught by the chief, the worker gets beaten in public and kicked out.  Rice mills during the Japanese occupation period were agencies that exploited both the labor and rice of Joseon. In 1939, Japanese enacted the rice distribution cooperative control law to prohibit the distribution of rice in the market, and they even took the minimum consumption amount of Joseon people and exported to Japan. What was typically distributed to Joseon people in place of rice were foods for animals, such as beans or barnyard millets brought from Manchuria and other regions.

stories.title: Post Office
stories.script: An intelligence agency for colonization  You will easily find the gray-colored Juksan Post Office with a mailbox standing in front of it. In 1905, Japan took over Joseon’s communications network and attempted to repair and expand it nationwide to solidify its colonial rule over politics, military, and economy.  Hayagawa, the chief of Mokpo Post Office’s Gunsan branch from the novel Arirang, was a post office worker on the outside, but he actually was a Japanese spy. He was fluent in Korean and amicable to the people of Joseon, and he used these strengths to collect information and also deliver messages utilizing the communications network. Also, he developed Yang Chi-seong, an errand boy at the post office, into an excellent informant for Japan and a member of the pro-Japan group.  Post offices at the time handled telegrams, communications, and mails, but in reality, they monitored the movements of Joseon people and collected intelligence for Japan's colonial rule. In 1929, post offices sold “temporary life insurances” and forced Joseon people to subscribe for the sake of war funding. Most of the insurances were used as a part of Japan's war funds, but due to the fall of Japan, Joseon people ended up receiving no compensations, not even the principals.  In the night-duty room, mail sorting room, and operating room, office supplies and furniture are on display. Communications were not as developed then as they are now, so there used to be telephone switchboards that receive, operate, and then deliver a communication. Also, letters or documents were created by using a typewriter. But because the cost of ink and maintenance was quite considerable, a typewriter at the time was a premium office supply that can only be used by a few.

stories.title: Oeri Village
stories.script: Oeri Village  A village of common Joseon people  Beyond the exploitation agencies, you will see a village where thatched houses are standing in a huddle. This is the replica of “Oeri Village”, which is the setting of the novel, Arirang. Oeri Village is an actual name that exists in Hongsan-ri, Juksan-myeon, Gimje-si, and it is called Oeri because of its location on the outside of Naechon Village. In the novel, the characters of the greatest importance among the Oeri Village residents are Gamgoldaek and her family. After her husband who served in the Donghak Army during the Donghak Peasant Movement fell sick, Gamgoldaek owes Mr. Kim 18 won for her husband's treatment. But as soon as he passes away, Kim pressures Gamgoldaek to either pay the money back or give up her daughter. In the end, the debt is paid when her son, Yeong-geun, is sold to Hawaii as a laborer. The remaining family of Gamgoldaek moves to Manchuria, and after years of hardships and ordeal, she is eventually murdered by Japanese soldiers. Gamgoldaek is a character who embodies a great mother urging to keep her family together in the midst of poverty and steadfastly holds on to the hope of Joseon's independence. The one behind the house of Gamgoldaek is the house of Song Su-ik who was from a noble, yangban family widely respected by the villagers and owns progressive and enlightened thinking. Song Su-ik openly rebuked Joseon informants for Japan who tried to lure the villagers to sell their rice fields, but this incident got him locked up in a jail by the military police. Released some time later thanks to a campaign by his family, Song raised a righteous army and scored some success but when the army was soon disbanded by the Japanese forces, he moved to Manchuria There he participated in the independence movement; however, he was later captured on the charge of conspiring to assassinate the commander-in-chief of Kwantung Army for which he got 15 years of imprisonment. He passed away in a prison cell. Song Su-ik, the commander of a righteous army and the army for national independence, displays the lives of countless independence activists who resisted to Japanese invasion and fought hard towards independence. Once you pass by the house of Song Su-ik, you will reach the house of Cha Deuk-bo. Cha’s father was publicly executed by a firing squad for opposing the government-general's land survey project, and his mother passed away soon after, which leads Cha and his younger sister to live a wanderer's life. But when he ultimately got separated with his younger sister, he met Shin Se-ho who took him in. Cha began to help with Shin's household matters. His sister who grew up to be a great singer bought Cha a rice field with which he became a farm owner and got married as well. But he was drafted by force and performed hard labor before making an escape and taking refuge thanks to the help of the Ainu people. What an unfortunate life he lived. Oeri Village has an appearance of a small and simple farm village. Perhaps, all the residents of Oeri Village, from Gamgoldaek to Song Su-ik and Cha Deuk-bo, wanted to live a simple and honest lives just like their village.

stories.title: Naechon Village
stories.script: Naechon Village  They ordinary lives of a Joseon farmer's household  Once you walk past the bamboo forest and the guardian tree, “Naechon Village” welcomes you. One of the main settings of the novel, Arirang, Naechon Village is also an actual village that exists in Hongsan-ri, Juksan-myeon, Gimje-si. In the novel, Naechon Village was established earlier than Oeri Village, and it is depicted as an ordinary village inhabited by people who make a living from cultivating rice fields. Here, the houses of Son Pan-seok and Ji Sam-chul from the novel are replicated.  A former righteous army soldier, Son Pan-seok was arrested by the Japanese army and performed hard labor at the construction site of a new highway before fleeing to Gunsan-si. He then began to work at the wharf but, after a fight with Chinese laborers, he injured his leg and lived the rest of his life as a handicapped person. Unable to follow Gamgoldaek, Ji Sam-chul and Song Su-ik when they moved to Manchuria, he remained in Gunsan-si and served as a contact for the Independence Army, carrying out his life while refusing to give in to misfortune.  Ji Sam-chul was a former servant who later became a righteous army soldier. He was close with Gamgoldaek’s husband and Son Pan-seok, and, in particular, took care of Gamgoldaek’s family as his own. After being released from forced labor at the Gyeongbu Line railroad construction site, Ji returned to Naechon Village and followed Song Su-ik to resume his service in a righteous army. Once the army was disbanded, he began to work at the Gunsan Wharf with Son Pan-seok and, later, moved to Manchuria He served in the Independence Army with Song Su-ik to live his entire life as a fighter for his country's independence.  Inside Ji Sam-chul’s house, there is a space where you can experience a life in a thatched house. Here you can get your hands on living and farming tools that were used around that time, including maettong, millstone, water-carrying yoke, A-frame, mortar, fulling block, and other necessities of a farming household. Get a first-hand experience of an old farmer’s life and make lasting memories with commemorative photos in Naechon Village.

stories.title: 1st Floor of Harbin Station
stories.script: 1st Floor of Harbin Station  Those who left for Manchuria  Harbin Station was a railway station located in Harbin in the northeastern part of China. The Harbin Station in Arirang Literature Village was built in a 60% miniaturized size of the real Harbin Station in the 1910s. The station’s 1st floor consists of a waiting area (lobby), Exhibit 1, and a complex theater. The waiting area features mannequins that replicate people who are waiting for a train's arrival, from which you can feel the vibe of Harbin Station at the time.  Exhibit 1 displays materials and situations related to An Jung-geun's heroic assassination in 1909 detailed in the novel, Arirang. If you go further inside, you will see a space that has reproduced the cafe that existed inside Harbin Station at the time, and, here you will meet the mannequin of An Jung-geun sitting on a chair and looking outside the window. On October 23, 1909, An arrived in Harbin and met up with his colleagues to discuss the assassination. Then, he wrote a letter to Yi Gang, the editor-in-chief of Daedonggongbo, regarding the decision and funds for the assassination.  The next day, he received a message from a station clerk that Ito Hirobumi would arrive at Harbin Station two days later, and this was when An decided to carry out the plan. Around 7 AM on October 26, he waited at the cafe inside Harbin Station for the train that carries Ito Hirobumi to arrive.  The road that the novel takes from the lives of the commoners to the story of An Jung-geun is full of ups and downs. People were deprived of their hometowns, fertile lands, precious families, and mother country. Some of them were forced to move to Manchuria while others had no choice but to stay even in the midst of suppression by the Japanese. It would give you memorable moments to think about An Jung-geun as a person who was sitting at the cafe while brooding over the pain and suffering of his people in Joseon.  Now, shall we go outside through the door from the Harbin Station cafe?

stories.title: Police Substation
stories.script: Police Substation  The symbol of suppression  “A Japanese police officer will come and get you.” This was an expression that many of our grandparents used to calm a rowdy or crying child. As you can imagine, a “Japanese police officer” was an object of terror. Police officers were the lowest-ranked position of the police system during the Japanese occupation period, and police substation was where the officers worked. You can recognize Juksan Police Substation by its entrance and windows featuring iron bars. Police substation was a facility that the government-general installed throughout Joseon based on its policy of one substation in every myeon,” and the highest-ranked official-in-charge was the substation chief appointed by the chief of police in the particular region. In the early 1920s, a police officer was an “occupation that one could attain relatively easily without any high-level education but with considerable benefits.” If someone passed the police exam, he received a “warm, hospitable sendoff by 50 to 60 villagers and relatives standing in line,” and once he was placed to a substation, “about 80 residents of the myeon gathered to throw him a welcoming party.” You can see that it was a profession that received kind, cordial treatment from people.  But police officers at police substations wielded serious suppression and surveillance and, thus, were objects of hatred and fear to Joseon commoners. In particular, many of Joseon police officers were especially infamous as they were voluntary members of the pro-Japan group. As you walk into the Juksan Police Substation, you can feel the atmosphere of the time through the photos and Japanese flags hung on the walls. The materials from which you can witness the government-general's evil deeds are also exhibited on the walls of the substation chief's office. In the novel, Arirang, Ji Sam-chul and Song Su-ik find themselves in the middle of an incident, which makes them locked up in the police substation jail. Shin Se-ho gets arrested for teaching the national ideology to Joseon children and is severely tortured here. In fact, a countless number of independence fighters and innocent Joseon people were dragged to and tortured at police substations.  An interrogation room is where the police tried to threaten or conciliate those who had been arrested. Inside this room, the instruments of torture that were used to induce confessions are on display. In particular, a wall coffin that looks like a wardrobe places a person inside it, which is barely large enough for one adult to stand straight, and locks the door from the outside to make the person immobile and spend the whole time in pain and darkness.  Although they are only replicas of the scenes from a novel, you will be able to feel the horror of the times as you slowly look through the experience facilities and materials that show the atrocity of the colonial rule.

stories.title: The House of Immigrants
stories.script: The House of Immigrants  The hardscrabble reality of those who left their hometowns  As you depart Naechon Village and walk past a pond and along a narrow path, you will see Harbin Station, and at the end of the road, you will reach the house of immigrants. The house of immigrants is a replica of a typical house that Joseon people who had lost their country in the Japanese occupation era built for a new life and fought for independence in Manchuria and Jiandao. In the novel, Arirang, Gamgoldaek and her family, Ji Sam-chul, Song Su-ik, and many other villagers relocated to Manchuria. Their only option for housing in Manchuria where they have no friends or lands was a reed house barely capable of blocking rain and wind.  A reed house was built by reeds that were easy to find by rivers or in the fields. Joseon people who had left their hometowns constructed their dwellings with basic materials that they were able to obtain easily in the plains of Manchuria, and one of such materials was reeds. A reed house was built by using only earth, trees, and reeds. Since reeds weren't enough to block the wind, reed houses had poor insulation and could not even maintain the warmth of a furnace; it was a type of housing that was close to a mud hut.  Neowajip, or a shingle-roofed house, was another kind of residence for immigrants in the Japanese occupation period. Popularly seen in the mountainous regions of Manchuria, it places barks of trees on the roof like tiles. With the extreme cold in the mountainous areas of Manchuria, people would only install the minimum number and size of doors and windows. And because most of the trees growing in these areas were needleleaf trees, instead of broadleaf trees, people used long and segmented wooden tiles to replace broad wooden tiles. You can see that the wooden roof is tied and fixed with earth and strings so that it is not blown away.  The house of immigrants is also a place where you can see the traces of Joseon people who moved to the foreign land of Manchuria and tenaciously lived and fought so that their children would not inherit the sorrow of statelessness. Although the novel only depicts reed houses, but you must not miss the shingle-roofed house as well, which is replicated in the Arirang Literature Village in the form of an immigrants’ house during the Japanese colonial period.

stories.title: Statue of An Jung-geun Assassinating Ito Hirobumi
stories.audioTitle: Statue of An Jung-geun Assassinating Ito Hirobumi
stories.script: Statue of An Jung-geun Assassinating Ito Hirobumi  October 26, 1909  Behind Harbin Station, there is a life-size statute that shows the scene of assassination carried out by An Jung-geun. Around 9:30 AM on October 26, 1909, Ito Hirobumi got off a train, inspected the honor guard, and greeted the delegations from different nations. All of a sudden, he fell to the ground by three bullets that were fired from nowhere. Immediately after, a shout of “Corea Ura” echoed throughout Harbin Station. “Corea Ura” means “Korea Hurrah!” in Russian. Having suffered a deadly wound, Ito died about 20 minutes later while An was arrested on-site by Russian military police and ended up being locked in an underground jail inside the Japanese consulate.  The heroic feat of An made headlines in Joseon and other related countries such as China, Japan and Russia, and the news of Ito's death also spread worldwide. After being imprisoned in the Japanese consulate for a few days, An and his colleagues who had planned the assassination together—Woo Deok-soon, Jo Do-seon, and Yoo Dong-ha—were transferred to Lushun Prison on November 1. During the trial process, he proudly stated that killing Ito Hirobumi is a war for independence and an extension of righteous army executed as the lieutenant general of the Korean Army.”  An was eventually sentenced to death through six hearings held at Lushun Court, and Woo Deok-soon was given three years of imprisonment. His other comrades, Jo Do-seon and Yoo Dong-ha, both received one year and six months of imprisonment. After giving up his right to appeal, An wrote The History of Ahn Eung-chil, his autobiography, and The Theory of Oriental Peace in his prison cell. On March 25, 1910, he had his last visit by his brothers, Jeong-geun and Gong-geun, and left six farewell letters, and he delivered his will to his people” through a lawyer. On March 26, 1910, he passed away by hanging at Lushun Prison.  Even after the heroic deed of An Jung-geun, Japan's invasion to turn Joseon into its colony continued, and tales of the commoners who suffered oppression and hardships in the colonized Joseon are well-depicted in the middle and final parts of the novel, Arirang.

stories.title: 2nd Floor of Harbin Station
stories.script: 2nd Floor of Harbin Station  The birth story of Arirang  On the 2nd floor of Harbin Station are Exhibit 2 and an experience hall for children. Exhibit 2 displays the story of the novel, Arirang, after the noble undertaking of An Jung-geun in 1909 as well as Author Jo Jung-rae's investigation diaries.  In 1910 after An Jung-geun’s assassination of Ito Hirobumi, Joseon became a colony of Japan, and those who have sorrowfully left Joseon to join the independence movement continued their fight to recover their country. Those who remained in Joseon lived painful lives as they were being persecuted under Japan's colonial rule. Especially after starting the Sino-Japanese War, Japan began to utilize the Korean Peninsula as its logistics base for war supplies, and, subsequently, Joseon people were harshly and brutally exploited of their human, physical, and financial resources. Author Jo’s diaries contain details of his investigation into Joseon people during his travel in order to write the novel, Arirang. The materials collected by the author on his journey through China, Mongolia, United States, and Korea were compiled into a novel that we read today. Bang Yeong-geun, Gamgoldaek’s eldest son who went to Hawaii for work; Song Su-ik and Ji Sam-chul, soldiers of both a righteous army and the Independence Army; the families of Baek Jong-du and Jang Deok-pung who harassed other villages for their own success; Yang Chi-seong, a pro-Japan informant raised by the Japanese, and; and Suguk, a woman who was forced to be sacrificed simply because of her gender: these are all characters from the novel, but the book is also the history that our ancestors had to go through themselves.  From the Arirang Literature Village’s promotion hall to the Harbin Station exhibit, certain sculptures catch our eyes in all places. They are the works of Artist Kim Rae-hwan that display Joseon people who were sacrificed not just in the novel but also throughout the history, especially during the Japanese occupation era. As we see innocent commoners falling victims to invasions and wars, we are faced with our painful history once again.  How was your time at the Arirang Literature Village as you reflected on the modern history of the Korean Peninsula through the novel, Arirang? A history of ordeal and adversity is also a part of our history. May your time at the Arirang Literature Village allowed you to understand and value the history of our nation and people.

stories.title: Supullo
stories.script: An ecological restoration site that returns clean water to the Hangang River  Have you ever heard of a supullo? A supullo is an ecological space created by the Ministry of Environment and the Han River Basin Environmental Office. Its purpose is to keep clean the Hangang River water that citizens in the Seoul metropolitan area drink.  Take a moment to imagine the following: Apartments and buildings are built along the Hangang River. Wouldn’t this make it easy for contaminants to flow into the river? That’s why the Ministry of Environment and the Han River Basin Environmental Office purchased the land around the Bukhangang River, the Namhangang River, and the Gyeongancheon Stream. They have transformed the purchased land into green land and maintained it as a supullo. Through such waterside green space development projects, it is said that a supullo, back in the arms of nature, blocks contaminants from directly flowing into the Hangang River and plays a role in purification.   Anyone can visit a supullo, which has been established in three places, Unsim-ri, Yangsu-ri (in Yangpyeong-gun, Gyeonggi-do), and Samhoe-ri (in Gapyeong-gun, Gyeonggi-do). When visiting a supullo, which is abundant with clean water and green grass, you’ll be able to see the restoration process of the Hangang River and its surrounding ecosystems. Experience ecology firsthand by taking a walk or just relaxing in nature. These supullo locations are quite popular especially since the admission fee is free.  Then what’s the atmosphere like in the three supullo locations? At Supullo Unsim-ri, you can see purified water flowing out towards the Namhangang River. Supullo Yangsu-ri is an ecological space beautifully decorated with flowers, trees, and ponds, and Supullo Samhoe-ri is where you can walk along the Bukhangang River and observe waterside ecology. Make a reservation for any of three locations through the Han River Basin Environmental Office ecological experience website to receive guidance and experience education from an expert guide. Moreover, visitors can enjoy exploring on their own, non-face to face content tailored to each age group is provided.  A supullo, revived by the Han River Basin Environmental Office for the Hangang River’s water quality restoration and ecosystem restoration! Shall we walk a supullo, a path with clean water and green grass?

stories.title: Supullo - Unsim-ri  (Previously known as Hangang Eco Learning Center)
stories.script: Voice actor/ 	Exploring a supullo, where the water is clean and the grass is green! 		The first story!  Mother/	Starting today, you and I are going to have a very special ecological exploration! The very first location we’ve arrived at is Supullo Unsim-ri.  They say it’s the size of 10 soccer fields.  Son/	Wow, that’s enormous! I see a marsh over there.  There are Dragonfly Pond and frogs. And, what’s so special about this place?  Mother /	You can’t tell with your eyes, right? Supullo Unsim-ri has a lot to do with the water of the Hangang River we consume daily.   Son /	What do you mean by that?  Mother /	 Every day, the water we use becomes wastewater. You know that it then goes through a sewage treatment plant for purification, right? The purified water comes here to Supullo Unsim-ri.  As it goes through the six ponds and waterways, it becomes even more purified  thanks to the aquatic plants, and flows into the Hangang River.  Son /	Wow, then it’s not just an eco-experience center but an eco- experience center  that manages water quality. But, has it always been a beautiful place where water is purified and where various animals and plants live?  Mother /	They say that Supullo Unsim-ri was previously an aggregate collection site.  The sand or gravel used in constructing buildings was taken from here.  As a result, areas around the river were hollowed out and devastated.  The ecosystem, of course, became a mess. Not wanting the environment to be ruined any further,  the Ministry of Environment and the Han River Basin Environment Office  wanted this place to be able to support animals and plants again.  So, they planted a lot of trees and revived the wetland.   Son /	Oh! With a revived wetland, countless insects and animals returned.  Mother /	That’s right. It’s said that the leopard cat and the Eurasian otter, both endangered, live here.  Son /	Whoa! Really? I can’t wait to see them!  Mother /	That’s going to be difficult. Plants and animals that need protection  are being taken care of in conservation and buffer zones. The place we’re allowed to see is the excursion area. But, I’ve heard that they’ve discovered evidence  that the leopard cat had come to this area to mark its territory in the dead of night.  Should we go look for one?  Son /	Yes, that sounds great! Mom, by going in a counterclockwise direction from the entrance,  I can see at a glance the process in which the water becomes clean as it flows.  And the place with a thick layer of gravel and sand at the bottom  seems to act like a water purifier filter by filtering out contaminants.  Mother /	That’s right. You’re very observant. It’s hard to believe that this beautiful place  was once an aggregate collection site where flowers and trees couldn’t live.  The forest and ponds are quite beautiful, aren’t they?  This is all thanks to planting trees and grass on devastated land, which gave birth to the wetland. It’s said that it has become a more valuable park since native Korean aquatic plants, from Purple maiden silvergrass to lesser cattail, and water lilies,  and animals, such as spot-billed ducks, Wang-eun-jeom-pyo-beom-na-bi, and Geom-eun-mul-jam-ja-li, can be found here.  Son /	It’s quite fortunate. But, Mom! Close your eyes for just a second. 	(효과음 ins.) You can hear the water flowing and also the birds chirping.   Mother /	Oh! I feel my mind more at ease. I applied for guidance and experience education  from an expert guide on the website beforehand.  There is also non-face to face content for all age groups, starting from kindergarten. Shall we go to hear more about Supullo Unsim-ri?  Son /	All right! I can’t wait!

stories.title: Supullo - Yangsu-ri (Previously known as Yangsu-ri Environmental Eco-Park)
stories.script: Voice actor/ 	Exploring a supullo, where the water is clean and the grass is green! 		The second story!   Mother/	Today, we’re going on another very special ecological exploration.  The second location is Supullo Yangsu-ri. The atmosphere is very different from  that of Supullo Unsim-ri, the first location we went to, right?  Son /	Yes, there is a wildflower square and a pretty waterway, and  the Bukhangang River can even be seen from here. It’s quite beautiful.  Mother /	That’s right! Supullo Yangsu-ri is also a special ecological space that was created to save the Hangang River and preserve the ecosystem!  Originally, apartment buildings were planned to be built at this location,  but the Ministry of Environment and the Han River Basin Environment Office purchased this land and created Supullo Yangsu-ri instead of constructing buildings.  Son /	Wow! That’s so cool! If apartments were built here, wastewater,  which includes the water from washing up, laundry, and food preparation  from the apartments, would flow directly into the river, right?  Mother /	No doubt! If apartments were built here, numerous trees and plants  would have had to be cut down, and the animals, such as birds and insects,  would have lost their homes. Just thinking about it is very sad, isn’t it?  What’s even more terrifying is that the water from the Hangang River is what people in metropolitan areas consume.  It’s their drinking water. Something serious would have surely happened.  Son /	Phew~ That’s quite fortunate! Since Supullo Yangsu-ri lies between cities and the river,  the wastewater from cities doesn’t directly enter the Hangang River.  This space is very precious since it purifies the water.  Mother /	Right! This natural shelter contains abundant grasses and trees,  not densely packed concrete buildings. The air has become cleaner,  and the beautiful walkways benefit many people, not just the residents.  Now, shall we look around Supullo Yangsu-ri?  Son /	Mom! On the left, there’s a square where children can run and play, and on the right,  there’s a watercourse that looks like a snail. I want to play at the Snail Watercourse.  Mother /	All right, it looks fun. You can find watercourses in two locations in Supullo Yangsu-ri. One of them is the Snail Watercourse, where purified water from the Bukhangang River flows from April to October. The water is very clean, right?  But don’t put your hands in the water.  The other is free-flowing water in the center of the park.  Okay, shall we go to the forest now?  Son /	Yes, I’d love to! The forest air is refreshing, and I feel more at ease.  Mom, I hear a bird nearby.  Mother /	Oh, it sounds like a song. This preserved Eucommia forest was here  before the park was made. And I heard that they hung bird houses on many trees, such as retusa fringe and sawleaf zelkova, so that birds can rest.  That probably explains the continuous bird song.  Son /	Mom! Let’s take a break at the lookout that looks like a shelter!  Mother /	That’s a good idea. You can probably see the water that flows into the Bukhangang River  if you stand on the wooden bridge in front of the viewing platform. After resting a bit, how about crossing that wooden bridge and walking all the way to the bench near the river?  Son /	That sounds like a great plan. Oh! Mom, didn’t you say that you applied for experience education?  Mother /	Oh, how time flies! If you apply for an expert guide on the Han River Basin Environment Office’s ecological experience website, you can learn about Supullo Yangsu-ri from an expert guide.  And they also have tailored content for all age groups  for those who want non-face to face guidance.  Now, shall we go meet our guide?  Son/	Yes, let’s go!

stories.title: Supullo - Samhoe-ri (Previously known as Gapyeong Samhoe Ecological Restoration District)
stories.script: Voice actor/ 	Exploring a supullo, where the water is clean and the grass is green! 		The third and last story!   Mother/	This is Supullo Samhoe-ri, the last location of our very special ecological exploration. Its atmosphere differs from Supullo Unsim-ri, our first stop,  and Supullo Yangsu-ri, our second stop, right?  Son /	It does! It’s amazing that there’s such a place between the river and the road  where cars speed along. There must be a reason… right?  Mother /	Correct~ Originally, there was a retaining wall made by piling soil along the river.  They set up a retaining wall to prevent dirt that has been dug to make way for houses from being washed away down the river. As a result, animals lost their homes and couldn’t help wandering since their travel routes were blocked. It also created habitat loss for plants.  That’s why the Ministry of Environment and the Han River Basin Environmental Office  purchased the land and then tore down the retaining wall.  They created Supullo Samhoe-ri. Of course, it would’ve been impossible  without the participation of residents of the surrounding area!  Son /	Oh, I see! Then what happened to the plants and animals after the removal of the retaining wall  and the creation of a wide trail and eco-experience space?   Mother /	Many wonderful things happened. They were like miracles! Eurasian otters, mandarin ducks,  and grey herons returned, and many animals now call this place their home. Moreover, pollutants from cities undergo another stage of purification  before flowing into the river. And oak trees planted in Supullo Samhoe-ri play a role  in controlling flooding by absorbing water. Isn’t it amazing?  Son /	Wow! What an incredible change!  	Mom, I want to see Supullo Samhoe-ri in more detail!  Mother /	Then, shall we walk along the waterside walkway? The waterside walkway is the pride of Supullo Samhoe-ri.  You can walk along the river where the retaining wall used to be.  And since it’s connected to the oak tree forest, you can easily walk into it.  Son /	I love it! Mom, Supullo Samhoe-ri’s scenery is really fantastic.  Mother /	You’re right. It’s like a painting in which more than a thousand trees  continue along the Bukhangang River.  Planting trees where the retaining wall used to be works with nature  and provides people with a place to rest. Isn’t it wonderful!  Son /	Mom! Now, the Supullo Samhoe-ri walk is almost over.  We’re going to meet an expert this time as well, right? I’m really looking forward to it.  Mother /	Of course we are! If you apply on the Han River Basin Environment Office’s ecological experience website,  you can receive guidance and experience education from an expert guide!  Or, if you want to explore on your own, you can also apply for non-face to face content  that is tailored to various age groups!  Hmm... Since this is our last excursion, I’m curious what your thoughts were  of the three supullo locations as you explored them.  Son/	If we care for nature, it will provide generously.  I should pay more attention to the protection of our environment from now on.  Mother /	 Great! You learned a valuable lesson. Don’t forget that saving nature  ultimately saves us. Now, shall we go meet our guide?

stories.title: Geumseonggwan Hall
stories.script: No. 1 location for exploring Naju Geumseonggwan Hall  Naju is a region often referred to as “Cheonnyeon Moksa Goeul as it has been maintained for nearly a thousand years since it became Naju-mok during King Seongjong’s reign in Joseon dynasty. It has been the center of Jeolla Province’s administration, economy, military and culture from the Goryeo dynasty. Not only that, Gyeon Hwon founded Later Baekje based in the Naju area, and King Taejo of Goryeo won the Battle of Geumseongsan Mountain to establish the foundation for Goryeo. Later, King Taejo changed the original name of Geumseong to Naju but this is why there are still many places whose names have “Geumseong'' in them such as Geumseongsan and Geumseonggwan.  There must be a lot of historical sites since it is a town that boasts a thousand-year history, right? One of the most notable attractions is Geumseonggwan Hall, which is a guest house where domestic and foreign VIPs who visited Naju stayed and had banquets. It was also a countryside palace where tablets of Jeonpae and Gwolpae that symbolize the king were enshrined and people observed courtesy to the king on the 1st and 15th of every month. It was the largest in the country during the Joseon dynasty and also served as a regional palace that the king himself stayed and used so you can guess how much power the area of Naju had at that time.  The guest house is believed to have existed since the Goryeo dynasty considering the records that remain in the magistrate's office of Byeokoheon from the 3rd year of King Taejong’s reign in early Joseon dynasty. Later from the 18th to 20th year of King Seongjong’s reign (Apr. 12, 1487–Jul. 20, 1489), Magistrate Yi Yu-in rebuilt Geumseonggwan Hall in the appearance we see today. It is a single-story, gambrel-roofed type with five bays on the front and four on the side, and the ceiling is high while each of the bays is broad so you can feel a sense of grandeur. Geumseonggwan Hall was designated as Jeollanam-do Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 2 on Jan. 29, 1972, and was upgraded to Korea’s Treasure No. 2037 on Oct. 25, 2019.  To enter Geumseonggwan Hall, you have to go through Manghwaru, which is the main gate. The present-day Manghwaru is a two-story Oesammun that restored what had disappeared during the Japanese occupation period to the original form in 1977. You have to pass through three gates to get into Geumseonggwan Hall, and the one located at the outermost part is called Oesammun. If you enter inside through Manghwaru, you will find Geumseong Topyeongbi on the left and wall-less Jungsammun ahead of you. Although what remains of Naesammun here today is only the ground, the gate itself is currently located by the entrance of Naju Namsan Citizens' Park. The series of these three gates is of the same structure as a typical royal palace.  After passing through Jungsammun, majestic Dongikheon and Seoikheon stand on both sides of Geumseonggwan Hall where Jeonpae and Gwolpae are enshrined. These used to serve as lodgings; the larger Dongikheon was where high-ranking officials above jeong 3-pum stayed whereas Seoikheon was where low-ranking officials below jong 3-pum stayed.  As generations passed, Geumseonggwan Hall also became a place that showed the spirit of Naju. The anti-Japan movement was active during the Japanese invasion of 1592 and towards the end of Joseon dynasty, and the shouts of May 18 Democratization Movement spread like wildfire in this region as well. Geumseonggwan Hall was the center of Naju’s power and the gathering place of the city's spirits. After the Liberation, it was used as Naju-gun Office and Naju City Hall for a long time and, thanks to the efforts to keep the original shape overall, it was restored very close to its original appearance in 1976 and continues to exist to this day.  Geumseonggwan Hall is a symbolic site of history proving that Naju once served a central role for Honam and remains the “No. 1 location for exploring Naju.” Geumseonggwan Hall, which has been welcoming guests with its magnificent appearance even after many years, is filled with rich breaths of our ancestors and righteous spirits.

stories.title: Romantic Gosat-gil
stories.script: A path of love as warm as much as it is narrow Romantic Gosat-gil  David Le Breton, author of Praise of Walking, once said that “every road in the world is a memory carved on the ground and is like a vein of leaves left on the earth by countless walkers who have been in and out of the places for many years.” Just as water and nutrients flow along the vein of leaves, history, life and stories also run along the road.  Such a road is called gosat in Korean, which means a narrow village alley. Walled towns of old Korean society comprised a multitude of gosat insomuch that residents' lives were almost definable by their town's gosat. This place we call Romantic Gosat-gil got its name from the belief that a man and a woman are destined to fall in love as soon as they walk into a gosat because the narrow path forces their shoulders to touch when they walk side by side each other. It is said that the path was even narrower in the past.  The images of cute, romantic looks of lovers who just began their relationships are painted on the walls of houses in the front, in the back and on the side, all of which stand tightly but affectionately shoulder to shoulder, and the ivy adds to the beauty of the low walls. It makes you feel as if your heart would palpitate instantly when you run into someone here. It is said that many men and women actually have become couples thanks to Romantic Gosat-gil.  Come to think of it, Naju must be a city of romance because King Taejo of Goryeo also enjoyed sweet love in Naju. It was when Wang Geon went to war in Naju and engaged in battles against Gyeon Hwon of Later Baekje. One day, he went to where five-colored clouds rose at the bottom of the mountain to find a beautiful lady doing the laundry by a spring. Thirsty at the moment, Wang Geon asked her for a bowl of water and the lady politely offered water with a willow leaf floating on it. It was to make him drink the water slowly because she was worried that he may get a stomachache if he drinks it too quickly. Wang Geon was enamored with her sagacity and beauty and got married with the lady who later became Queen Jangwha of the Naju Oh clan. The spring where the willow leaf romance was born is today's Wansacheon Stream.  Romantic Gosat-gil teaches us “how to live as a decent human being.” You run into others on such a narrow path that you have to be considerate of them and have to share a bow at least. Even if you run into an enemy of your life, someone has to yield to the other so a mood of reconciliation can sprout. Romantic Gosat-gil, a narrow but heartwarming path, is filled with footprints of love, consideration and reconciliation.

stories.title: Jeongsuru Pavilion
stories.script: Govern right and love the people Jeongsuru Pavilion  Central Square is the quintessential starting point of a trip to Naju because not only is it located in the very heart of Naju, but it is also home to Geumseonggwan Hall, Magistrate's Living Quarters, and Naju-mok Cultural Center. When you step foot into Central Square, Jeongsuru is the first structure to welcome you. This two-story pavilion with its magnificent stance used to be the gate of Naju’s Government Office. Passing through Jeongsuru will take you to Jegeumheon, the government office of Naju-mok. Jegeumheon had been torn down in the Japanese colonial era, and is currently being excavated for restoration.  Jeongsuru is believed to have been built during the term of Moksa U Bok-ryong (Oct. 1602–Jan. 1605); the first book of Yonggye Yugo written by Kim Ji-nam (1559–1631) notes, “A new house was built in Naju following the instructions of Minister Yu Cheon and was presented to Magistrate Woo Bok-ryong.” Jeongsuru, a two-story pavilion, features three bays in the front and two on the sides, with only the two sides of the first floor composed of walls. The gambrel roofs are overlapped with double eaves, and there is a large drum on the second floor of the pavilion.  Every time they passed through Jeongsuru, government officials would re-tie their hat strings and tidy up their outfit. This is because right in front of the pavilion is Geumseonggwan Hall, which symbolizes the king,. The neatly tied hat strings and attire symbolize, in a broad sense, upright and open politics whereas the drum represents benevolence towards the people.  Jeongsuru was not just any gate; it was a gate of government officials of integrity who, acting on behalf of the king, would in turn, help instill an ethical attitude into village governors.

stories.title: Naju-mok Cultural Center
stories.script: A look at the history of Cheonnyeon Moksa Goeul Naju-mok Cultural Center  Naju is a land fattened by the Yeongsangang River, which is originated in Yong-myeon, Damyang-gun, Jeollanam-do Province and passes through Gwangju, Naju and Yeongam before flowing out into the West Sea of Mokpo. Naju Plain, stretching endlessly in the midstream of the Yeongsangang River, is the greatest breadbasket of Jeollanam-do insomuch that people used to say, “If Naju has a year of good harvest, the entire Jeollanam-do enjoy a year of good harvest as well.”  In the Later Three Kingdoms period when Wang Geon occupied the Naju area and established Goryeo, he changed its name from Geumseong to Naju. The name, Jeolla Province, originates from combining Jeonju (jeon or jeol- as prefix) and Naju (na or -la as suffix). Wang Geon married to Ms. Oh he met in Naju, and she became Queen Janghwa. Queen Janghwa gave birth to Goryeo’s second king, Hyejong, which made Naju a region that produced a king.  From the days of King Seongjong of Goryeo to the installation of Naju Magistrate's Office in 1895, Naju is where Naju-mok was maintained for more than 1,000 years. Here, “mok” is an administrative unit during Goryeo and Joseon dynasties, similar to today's unit of city and county. Naju was the only area designated as a mok in Jeolla Province, and Naju-mok Cultural Center organized an exhibition of relics and materials so that people can understand its importance.  The elaborately constructed model of Naju Walled Town shows well the living conditions of Naju at the time, and the 2,000-year history from the era of Mahan confederacy is exhibited in a fun, interesting way, including the heated battles between Gyeon Hwon and Wang Geon, the attack of Sambyeolcho, the advance of the Mongolian army, the uprising of Donghak Peasant Army, formation of anti-Japan righteous armies, and the scenes of exploitation during the Japanese colonial era.  People from the Joseon dynasty called Naju as “Sogyeong,” which means “little Hanyang” (capital). Around Naju, Geumseongsan Mountain stands behind while the Yeongsangang River flows in front, and this topography resembles that of Seoul’s Samgaksan Mountain and the Hangang River. So Naju downtown was established with four gates, guest houses and government offices similar to Hanyangdoseong, the Seoul City Wall.  Until the end of the Joseon dynasty, Naju was the administrative, military, economic and cultural center of Jeolla Province. The city suffered a great damage by the invasion of Japanese after the opening of the port and became a mere satellite city as Gwangju became the administrative capital of the province. However, it is still a history museum filled with traces of Honam's greatest city.  The history that Naju holds in its arms is deep and wide. You can see as much as you know, right? It will be a much more meaningful trip to Naju if you first study the city at Naju-mok Cultural Center before slowly taking one step at a time.

stories.title: Geumhakheon the Magistrate's Living Quarters
stories.script: Feel the great fidelity of a scholar Geumhakheon the Magistrate's Living Quarters  The living quarters of the magistrate of Naju was referred to as moksanaea. The name of the building is Geumhakheon, which means “a house with the fidelity of a scholar who wishes to live detached like a crane while listening to the sound of Geomungo.” We can feel the spirit of the scholar who valued fidelity and integrity more than his own life.  As it was used as the official residence of the governor of Naju-gun from the Japanese colonial era to the 1980s, its original form was changed significantly. But it eventually recovered the original appearance of the Joseon government office architecture through dismantling and restoration work, which is why it is considered as an important material in the research of government office architecture.  “If you have an important business, stay for a night in the room of Magistrate Yu Seok-jeung or Kim Seong-il. Something good will definitely happen. If you cannot stay overnight, at least make a wish to the hackberry tree on the side of the yard.” This is something that Mr. Kim Jong-shin, a cultural commentator who guides through Naju, always tells his tourists. You may want to know why, right?  Magistrate Yu Seok-jeung served two terms as magistrate of Naju, and he ruled with such compassion that the people of Naju actually requested to further extend his term by offering rice to the country. Meanwhile, Magistrate Kim Seong-il commanded to install a drum in the magistrate's and government offices to collect cases and stories of unfair treatment suffered by the people, and he is also especially famous for his wise judgments in litigations.  It is said that good things often happened after sleeping here since these are rooms named after renowned magistrates whom the people of Naju admired. If you have a chance, how about spending a special day on which you can gather your thoughts and calm your emotions at the magistrate's living quarters where the spirit of dignified scholars dwells.

stories.title: Former Geumnam Financial Association
stories.script: Wealth accumulated by the blood and sweat of Joseon people Former Geumnam Financial Association  Traces of Japanese exploitation remain in different corners of Gosat-gil to force us to remember the painful history. One of such traces is a building that is used by “Koh Jo Hyun Surgery Clinic” today. It is the former Geumnam Financial Association. Geumnam Financial Association was located near the entrance of Jinggosat-gil, which was known as Bonjeong-tong as it was mostly inhabited by Japanese people at the time. Jinggosat-gil was home of a silk yarn factory run by a Japanese and Jukmul Corporation, which was a bamboo tree processing company, thus making it the busiest street of Naju during the Japanese colonial era.  Founded during the Korean Empire days, the association was a financial institution for commoners that lends farming funds to farmers but, during the Japanese occupation period, it mainly carried out the loan-sharking business, which is how many Japanese accumulated wealth.  Ironically, Geumnam Financial Association was also a place for anti-Japanese movements. Since it was located near the entrance the Naju 5-day Market, the number of people who traveled to and from this area was the greater than anywhere in Naju. On Nov. 27, 1929, the year in which the anti-Japanese movement was at its height, Naju student protesters shouted, “Students of Joseon, Hurrah!” in this place together with a crowd. Serious anger erupted before the scenes in which Japanese are exploiting the blood and sweat of the Joseon people.  Though it owns a conventional Japanese structure decorated in the European style, Geumnam Financial Association is typical Korean modern architecture that has an incredible architectural value. It is also a popular photo spot with red bricks and blue roofs shown in contrast. In a place where travelers today take commemorative photos, students from a century ago let out roars of their anger. Even though you are no longer able to capture the shouts from the day when students of Joseon waved the Taegeukgi in cold winter winds and cried out, “Students of Joseon Hurrah!” I hope that it will still remain in the travelers’ memories.

stories.title: Nampa Historic House (House of Park Gyeong-jung)
stories.audioTitle: Nampa Historic House (House of Park Gyeong-jung)
stories.script: Noblesse oblige of anti-Japanese movement and modern education Nampa Historic House (House of Park Gyeong-jung)  At 5:35 PM on Oct. 30, 1929, a school commuter train from Gwangju arrived at Naju Station. Soon after, an incident occurred in which Japanese male students harassed two female students from Gwangju Girls’ High School named Park Gi-ok and Lee Gwang-chun by grabbing their hair. Upon seeing this, a Gwangju High School student named Park Jun-chae protested and ultimately led to a group fight. This resulted in a massive student protest in Gwangju on Nov. 3, 1929, and did not take long to spread to anti-Japanese movements nationwide in which over 54,000 students participated. This historic event is referred to as the Gwangju Students' Anti-Japan Independence Movement. Park Gi-ok and Park Jun-chae were descendants of the famous Miryang Park clan as well as the main characters of the “Naju Station Incident,” which became the trigger for the aforementioned student movement.  The Park clan is a famous anti-Japanese movement family of Naju that produced three righteous army generals and three independence fighters, including Park Jeong-eop who carried out righteous army activities and made Taegeukgi during the Japanese occupation period; brothers of Park Jun-sam and Park Jun-chae who served time in prison due to their involvement in the March 1st Movement and Gwangju Students' Anti-Japan Independence Movement. The Taegeuki made by Park Jeong-eop was also used during the March 1st Movement. These great individuals were born and raised in the same house, which is Nampa Historic House, the pride of Naju.  Nampa Historic House was built in 1884 by Nampa Park Jae-gyu and has been inhabited for generations over 200 years of time, and is the largest private house in the entire Jeollanam-do. It imitates the look of a government office building and clearly shows the structure of the house of an upper class family in the Namdo region. Consisted of seven buildings including Anchae, Chodang and Outer Sarangchae, Nampa Historic House was designated as National Folklore Cultural Heritage No. 263 because of its architectural as well as folk values.  In particular, the kitchen has maintained the original appearance from a century ago and, even to this day, a bowl of water is offered to Jowangsin, a god in charge of the kitchen. The anchae, or the women's living quarters, preserves a variety of household items from a rice-bin capable of storing ten bags of rice to a small dining table from a hundred years ago and and lunch boxes. In addition, it is full of materials that you can typically find in a museum such as a faded Taegeukgi once used during the March 1st Movement, textbooks from the Japanese occupation period, and baseball rule book of the YMCA Baseball Team, all of which make you feel as if you are in a contemporary museum.  Nampa Historic House also played a big role in the history of education in Naju. A higher-level public school was operated after the Liberation and Cheongun Night Middle School was also established from the 1960s to 1980s, providing opportunities for poor students to study without cost.  Nampa Historic House is the cradle where famous independence activists of Naju were born and raised and the birthplace of Naju social movements and modern education. Today, Park Gyeong-jung lives here and looks after the house dearly so many people also call it the House of Park Gyeong-jung.  Mr. Park always keeps the main gate of the house open and extends his invitation to visitors by saying, “It is a privately house house but I believe Nampa Historic House is the city of Naju’s. It is a place that cannot be overlooked in Naju’s modern history. You can visit here anytime.” The gate is always open but it is a house where a person actually lives, not an exhibition hall, so please look around politely and quietly.

stories.title: Naju Nabillera Cultural Center
stories.script: Memories of silk reborn as a cultural rest area Naju Nabillera Cultural Center  When people think of Naju, some of the things that first come to mind are pears, beef broth stew and skate fish. There are many others that are known to be unique to Naju, such as ancient tombs and natural dyes. But if there is one specialty product that you would not have expected to be associated with Naju, it is silk.  Korea has quite a long history of silk. Since the Samhan period, silk had been weaved into fabric, and the techniques of silk weaving were also exported to Japan. As you can see from the name of Naju, which means “silk village,” Naju had been well-known as the home of silk since the Samhan days.  That is why the Japanese who encouraged sericulture as a military industry set their eyes on this region. In 1910, a Japanese named Senga first established the company Naju Sericulture Co., Ltd. in Naju and supplied the entire production as raw materials to be used by the Japanese military industry. The sericulture performance of Naju was known to be some of the best in Jeollanam-do as of 1928, which is probably why so much exploitation took place in the region.  The sericulture factory operated by the Japanese was temporarily shut down during the Korean War. Then, in 1954, Naju Sericulture Co., Ltd. re-opened, but this time by a man named Kim Yong-du.  The business thrived. However, the production of cocoons plummeted due to the 1973 oil shock. The synthetic fibers that inundated the market also prompted a decline in the sericulture industry, ultimately forcing the factory to shut down in the 1990s.  Since then, Naju Sericulture, once treated as a wasted industrial facility, has been reborn into Naju Nabillera Cultural Center, a space for culture and arts education, as part of the project to regenerate waste industrial facilities that started in 2015. Various spaces for culture and arts including exhibition halls and small theaters have been created in the six pre-existing buildings, and currently, culture and arts projects are being carried out for local residents.

stories.title: House Site of Choe Bu and Yang the Wealthy Man
stories.audioTitle: House Site of Choe Bu and Yang the Wealthy Man
stories.script: Cradle of Pyohaerok, the Joseon version of the Story of the wreck of the Sperwer yacht 500 years ago House Site of Choe Bu and Yang the Wealthy Man  Are you familiar with Pyohaerok, one of the world’s top three travel literature of China along with The Travels of Marco Polo by Marco Polo and Ennin’s Diary by a Japanese Buddhist monk named Ennin? Pyohaerok is a travel essay written by a scholar of Naju named Choe Bu. It is essential historical records for not only those majoring in Korean history but also those who study the history of the Ming dynasty of China.  By the way, why and how did Choe Bu come to write a Chinese travel essay? If you look more into the story, you would not believe how ridiculous it is.  In the 18th year of King Seongjong’s reign, Choe Bu was appointed as the Commissioner of Registers to Jeju Island to catch escaped slaves but, in the following year, his father passed away. On his way back to his hometown of Naju, his ship drifted due to a violent storm. After 14 days of being adrift, Choe Bu arrived on the southeastern coast of the Ming dynasty. He barely saved his life but got into trouble again when he was falsely accused of being a Japanese. He was eventually able to prove that he was a Joseon official and even enjoyed the good fortune to travel from the Southern China region to Beijing as a guest of the Ming dynasty and observe the dazzling aspects of the country. Having returned to Joseon after five months of difficulties and hardships, Choe Bu meticulously recorded the events of the 150 days in obedience to a royal command, and this is Pyohaerok.  “The houses in Southern China were tile-roofed and spread with bricks, and the stairs and pillars were all made of stones, all of which were large and splendid. In contrast, in Northern China, those who live in small thatched houses accounted for nearly half of the population.”  Pyohaerok contains details records of specific places and names of related people, which include the issues of Japanese raiders in the Ming dynasty, coastal defense system, grand canal transportation routes, economic situation in Southern China, and mindset of the Chinese people. Thus, it is highly regarded both in Korea and worldwide.  Choe Bu was an outstanding talent insomuch to participate in the compilation of historical and geography books, such as Dongguk Tonggam and Dongguk Yeoji Seungram, and wrote Pyohaerok with remarkable insight. However, he was unfortunately impeached for writing a diary while he was mourning his parents’ loss.  Today, Ihwa Apartment stands on the site of the house of Choe Bu who lived such a tough life. There was once a wealthy man named Yang Dong-ho who lived on this site where Choe Bu had dwelled, which is why the house today is known as the House Site of Choe Bu and Yang the Wealthy Man. Although there are few traces of Choe Bu now, the great travel essay of Pyohaerok is published in various forms so read it and take a look into his scholarly spirit, leadership and wisdom with which he overcame crises with a confident attitude and cleverness without losing his pride and fidelity as a Joseon scholar.

stories.title: Naju Hyanggyo
stories.script: The best school district in Honam and the pride of Naju Naju Hyanggyo  Hyanggyo was a place where students learned academics and trained their minds, which is why a sense of piety exists in it. Naju Hyanggyo, which is said to have been the second largest after Seonggyungwan, is antique and dignified as told by its long history. The exact timing of its construction is unknown but it is presumed to have been founded in 1398 during King Taejo’s reign. It consists of Daeseongjeon Hall that enshrines a memorial tablet of Confucius, Myeongryundang Lecture Hall where students learn, and Dongjae and Seojae, which were a kind of dormitories.  A typical Hyanggyo follows Jeonhak Humyo, an arrangement in which the lecture hall or Myeongryundang is in front and the ritual hall or Daeseongjeon is in the back. The arrangement of Hyanggyo is usually divided into the aforementioned Jeonhak Humyo and Jeonmyo Huhak that places Daeseongjeon in front of Myeongryundang.  Naju Hyanggyo, which is known to have been designed and built after Seonggyungwan in Seoul, was established on a flat land to express the hierarchy of its buildings. The most important building, Daeseongjeon, was located in the very front and at the highest place on a slope. Established on a flat land, Naju Hyanggyo owns the arrangement of Jeonmyo Huhak in which Munmyo, the Confucian shrine, is located in front and Myeongryundang is in the back.  The reputation of Naju Hyanggyo was truly great. When constructing the Hyanggyo, a carpenter was invited from China and stories say that its walls were built with the soil brought from Qufu in Shandong Province, China, which is the hometown of Confucius. Also, in the 11th year of King Seongjong’s reign, nine students from the Hyanggyo passed the state examination in the same year, boasting the greatest educational power in the country. The spirit of Confucius must be flowing through here.  Moreover, after Seonggyungwan was burned to ashes during the Japanese invasion in 1592, it was rebuilt by copying the appearance of Naju Hyanggyo. In other words, Naju Hyanggyo is the model of today's Seonggyungwan. The filming location of the drama Sungkyunkwan Scandal (2010) was also Naju Hyanggyo.  Like any other Confucian school, a ginkgo tree has been standing in its place by Daeseongjeon in Naju Hyanggyo for over 600 years. Every Hyanggyo planted a ginkgo tree because of the story that Confucius taught his disciples under a ginkgo tree, and it symbolized a desire that all Confucian scholars would have upright spirits just like a ginkgo that is not infested with insects.  Naju Hyanggyo, which produced a countless number of scholars as the best school district in Honam, is the pride of the Naju gentry as well as the city.

stories.title: Seoseongmun Gate and Seoseongbyeok-gil
stories.script: The roars of the Donghak Peasant Army Seoseongmun Gate and Seoseongbyeok-gil  Jeolla Province is a granary with an abundance of local products so the country’s finances heavily relied on this area and, at the same time, it was subject to exploitation throughout the Joseon dynasty, leaving helpless farmers to suffer from the extortion of taxes by the corrupt officials. On Feb. 10, 1894, the anger of the extensive peasant class resisting the excessive extortion of the magistrate of Gobu, Jo Byeonggap, exploded, and, thus, the peasants and followers of the Donghak religion joined forces and raised an uprising led by Jeon Bongjun, another follower of Donghak. This is famously called the Donghak Peasant Revolution.  In the 7th lunar month of 1894, the Donghak Peasant Army and government troops engaged in two fierce battles at Seoseongmun Gate. Most other provincial government offices in Honam had already fallen into the hands of the Donghak Peasant Army but Naju, which was paying the largest volume of grains as tax to the country, firmly withstood.  The force of the Donghak Peasant Army was powerful but the resistance of Naju was even stronger. Magistrate, local officials and their entire families fought like their lives were at stake in order to protect their vested interests. In the end, the Donghak Peasant Army faced a huge defeat, leaving 3,000 casualties. Afterwards, Nokdu Janggun Jeon Bongjun went into Naju Walled Town for consultation with Min Jong-ryeol, magistrate of Naju at the time, and the gate he walked through was Seoseongmun Gate.  Constructed during the early Goryeo dynasty, Naju Walled Town is the oldest walled town built in Korea. As the population increased and military importance grew, the walled town expanded in the 3rd year of King Sejo’s reign and has reached its present state. It has a perimeter of about 3.7 km and an area of 972,600 m2, and there are four main gates—Dongjeommun, Seoseongmun, Namgomun and Bukmangmun Gates.  However, these gates and walls having been protected and guarded by our people fighting and bleeding against each other faced a brutal demolition by the Japanese imperialists. As part of its policy to obliterate the Korean spirits, Japan destroyed the four gates and walls between 1910 and 1920, and left only the foundation stone at the site of Bukmun Gate.  The city of Naju has since restored the four gates through in-depth research and a carefully designed town restoration plan. The restored Seoseongmun Gate has a signboard that reads Yeonggeummun. This was installed in accordance with the record in the preface of the Augmented Survey of the Geography of Naju-mok published in 1815 that reads, “There was a plaque on which it writes Yeonggeummun.”  You can also find traces of the old Naju Walled Town about 250 meters from Seoseongmun Gate where the houses were torn down and Seoseongbyeok-gil was restored. Today, this path of low walls will not give you the strong dignity they once possessed in the past but it is cozy and friendly like a low hill behind our own neighborhood.  The wavering flag on top of Seoseongmun Gate looks quite confident. Along with the wind, it feels as if we can hear the shouts of the proud, high-spirited Donghak peasants.

stories.title: Borimadang Street
stories.script: A community culture of living together Borimadang Street  Tapping in step with the sound of Ongheya The whole yard is full of barley grains in an instant The exchange of melodies is getting higher and higher There is only dust of barley on the roof what I can see  It is part of a poem called Bori Tajak by Dasan Jeong Yakyong who wrote it after watching farmers threshing barley while he was in exile. It realistically depicted the image of a lively threshing ground in which farmers who gain energy from barley rice and makgeolli threshing with a flail to the beat of the labor song Ongheya. It contains the sincere heart of Jeong Yakyong who admired the healthy lives of the farmers and reflected on his own life.  There is nothing more pleasant and healthy than genuine labor. If the proposition, “All together,” is added to it, this will lead to a much more rewarding and healthy life. Borimadang Street here is a symbolic space that presents such a life.  In the late spring when barley harvest finishes, stacks of dried barley plants carried by A-frame carriers and carts were piled up on Borimadang Street because it was the largest alleyway in the castle so it was suitable for threshing barley. Barley threshing was something that all residents of the neighborhood performed together. This is called Ullyeok. Ullyeok is a beautiful cooperation custom only found in Korea through which villagers help one another without expecting remuneration or labor cost in return whenever there is an urgent farming work to do that cannot afford to be missed out. Dure and Pumasi are perhaps more familiar to you but these are ways of exchanging labor with the expectation of reciprocity so they have quite a different meaning than Ullyeok.  You won’t be able to see any barley threshing these days but, instead, look at the stone wall. It is a royal palace-style wall built by an engineer who built the walls of Gyeongbokgung Palace towards the end of the Korean Empire days. Considering that the local officials lived here, the house is big and has magnificent walls while the road is wide.  Borimadang Street was created by our hearts that could find comfort only if we all gathered together and worked on everyone’s tasks without separating your business from mine. With the advent of threshing machines in the 1960s, the scenes of barley threshing has long been disappeared but this street still remains as a place of warm, affectionate memories for the walled town residents.

stories.title: Samaegi and Hyangcheong Site
stories.script: Traces of history encountered on Naju Gosat-gil Samaegi and Hyangcheong Site  It is a dry, barren land now but water used to flow here even until the Joseon dynasty. If you see the old map of Naju from 1872, it tells us that water flowing from Geumseongsan Mountain passed in front of Naju Hyanggyo and flowed to Indeokji in the back of Geumseonggwan Hall. People had to cross this bridge to get to the local school and square where Sachang was located. It must have been quite a big and strong bridge.  In 1011 when King Hyeonjong of Goryeo came to Naju on a royal visit to get away from the attack of the Khitans, he also crossed this bridge on a cart driven by four horses. It was a royal procession of the king himself so you can imagine what a great spectacle it must have been. The name Samagyo Bridge was also acquired at this time, according to history. And, as it was talked about and pronounced for a long period of time since then, the name transformed into Samaegi. The water ran dry over the years to become land, and Samagyo disappeared without a trace. The only trace remaining in the Samagyobi Monument in the yard of Geumseonggwan Hall.  Hyangcheong site remains in the open space behind Geumseonggwan Hall. Hyangcheong was a regional autonomous governing body that used to regulate local officials called Hyangri, and it consisted of native aristocrats who had the knowledge and economic power.
