More specifically, a Beomjong is used to redeem those in hell, a Beopgo is used to redeem those in the animal world, a Mokeo is used to redeem those in the water world, and Unpan is used to redeem winged creatures in the sky.

stories.title: Geungnakbojeon Hall
stories.script: Geungnakbojeon Hall  Geungnakbojeon Hall is dedicated to the Amitabha Buddha, who governs the Western Paradise of Sukhavati and leads humankind to nirvana. It is also referred to as the Muryangsujeon Hall or Mitajeon Hall.  The rear wall features a “Banyayongseon” (Dragon Boat of Prajna), a ship that travels across the rough seas to reach Paradise. As its name suggests, the bow and stern of the Banyayongseon are designed to resemble the head and tail of a dragon, respectively. At the front, the ship is led by the Guiding Bodhisattva and Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva, and in the middle, the ship has a number of people with their hands clasped together in prayer.

stories.title: Yeongsanjeon Hall
stories.script: Yeongsanjeon Hall  Yeongsanjeon Hall features several murals depicting various stories and items from the Buddhist religion, such as the Dabotap Pagoda, Willow Branch Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva, and Arhats. Given the rarity and artistry of the murals, Yeongsanjeon was designated as Treasure No. 1711. Also, Yeongsanjeon is known to house “Palsangtaeng” (The Eight Great Events, Treasure No. 1041), one of the greatest depictions of the eight great events that transpired during the life and times of Sakyamuni’s life still remaining in existence.

stories.title: Three-story Stone Pagoda
stories.script: Three-story Stone Pagoda  The Three-story Stone Pagoda at Tongdosa Temple (Treasure No. 1471), is presumed to have been built during the latter years of the Unified Silla.  The pagoda was moved approximately 1.5m to the northeast from its original position when it was disassembled for repairs in 1987. The new location was chosen to better align the pagoda with the Geungnakbojeon Hall and Yeongsanjeon Hall. When the pagoda was disassembled, white porcelain from the Joseon Dynasty was found inside the upper tier of the pagoda, and two small gold bronze statues and bronze spoons were found in the earthen section of the pagoda at its base. These artifacts are currently on display at the Tongdosa Seongbo Museum.

stories.title: Yaksajeon Hall
stories.script: Yaksajeon Hall  Yaksajeon Hall enshrines Bhaisajyaguru Buddha as its main Buddhist statue. In Buddhism, Bhaisajyaguru Buddha is the Buddha that heals diseases, prolongs life, eliminates disaster, and helps people attain great enlightenment. The Bhaisajyaguru Buddha Painting housed inside the hall has been designated as Gyeongsangnam-do Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 419.

stories.title: Manseru Pavilion (Buddhist Supplies Store)
stories.script: Manseru Pavilion (Buddhist Supplies Store)  Originally, Manseru was built as a pavilion to host Buddhist services or other major events. At one point in its history, Manseru was used as an exhibition hall as well. Today, Manseru serves as a store selling Buddhist supplies.

stories.title: Myeongwollyo Hall
stories.script: Myeongwollyo Hall  Myeongwollyo is currently used for small-scale exhibitions and meetings. Tongdosa Temple is famous for the beautiful scarlet plum blossoms in spring, and the scarlet plum blossom tree standing right next to Myeongwollyo is regarded as one of the most striking trees in the entire temple.

stories.title: Bulimun Gate
stories.script: Bulimun Gate  “Buli” in Buddhism means “equality” and “no discrimination.” According to legend, Bulimun Gate at Tongdosa Temple was built by a carpenter, who used nothing but a simple axe. Apparently, the carpenter did not even use any metallic components to build the gate from the ground up. The main girder is supported by a tiger and an elephant. The tiger represents the Manjusri Bodhisattva and wisdom, while the elephant represents the Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and practice. In other words, the gate encourages people to take the wisdom they learn at the temple and practice it in real life.

stories.title: Hwaeomjeon Hall (Prayer Session Application Office)
stories.script: Hwaeomjeon Hall (Prayer Session Application Office)  Currently, Hwaeomjeon Hall at Tongdosa Temple is used for administrative purposes (e.g. prayer session applications, membership registration, etc.).

stories.title: Yeonggak Shrine
stories.script: Yeonggak Shrine  Yeonggak is a shrine built to commemorate all of the Chief Monks who served at Tongdosa Temple throughout its history.  It houses more than 80 portraits, including the portrait of Jajang Yulsa. These Buddhist portraits depict not only the physical appearance of each monk, but also the character and philosophy of the particular monk.

stories.title: Hwanghwagak Hall
stories.script: Hwanghwagak Hall  Hwanghwagak, also known as Cheonjagak, serves as a dormitory for the sangha university, where Buddhist monks from Tongdosa Temple study Buddhist scriptures. It earned its name when Queen Seondeok of Silla stayed overnight at Tongdosa Temple.

stories.title: Daegwangmyeongjeon Hall
stories.script: Daegwangmyeongjeon Hall  Daegwangmyeongjeon Hall is considered as the second most historically significant building in Tongdosa Temple, behind only its Daeungjeon Hall.  Inside, Vairocana Buddha from Avatamsaka Sutra is enshrined as the main Buddha statue. In Buddhism, Vairocana Buddha is the Buddha that strikes a balance between truth and the Buddhist mantras, and is the Buddha symbolizing the body of the universe. The Buddha Triad Painting hanging behind the Buddha statue is considered one of the best among all Buddha Triad Paintings remaining in existence. Thanks to its artistry and historical significance, the Buddha Triad Painting inside Daegwangmyeongjeon Hall has been designated as Treasure No. 1042.

stories.title: Yonghwajeon Hall
stories.script: Yonghwajeon Hall  Yonghwajeon was named after the place where Maitreya Buddha was born - under a Yonghwasu Tree.  Inside, the hall features a magnificent Maitreya Buddha statue that stands roughly 2m tall. Maitreya Buddha is the Buddha of the future, or the Buddha to come after Sakyamuni.  The walls to the east and west have murals illustrating episodes from the Journey to the West. These murals are unique in Buddhism, and so far, they are the only examples of their kind in the world.

stories.title: Bongbaltap Pagoda
stories.script: Bongbaltap Pagoda  Bongbaltap Pagoda at Tongdosa Temple (Treasure No. 471) is considered to be a sculpture symbolizing Sakyamuni’s robes and his alms bowl (i.e. Buddha’s clothes and crockery), which Maitreya Bodhisattva (the main Buddha enshrined in Yonghwajeon Hall) is expected to inherit when he manifests in the world.  Bongbaltap Pagoda is unique and rare in terms of its shape, and unlike any other sculpture in Korea.

stories.title: Gwaneumjeon Hall
stories.script: Gwaneumjeon Hall  Gwaneumjeon Hall enshrines the Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva. On its inner walls, Gwaneumjeon has murals depicting Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva on the slopes of Mount Potalaka, murals of Sudhanakumara, and murals of the 32 different iterations of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva.  Since Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva is known as the great and merciful Bodhisattva who brings salvation to humankind, Gwaneumjeon Hall is a popular attraction for Buddhists visiting Tongdosa Temple.

stories.title: Wontongbang Hall
stories.script: Wontongbang Hall  Wontongbang at Tongdosa Temple, along with Gamnodang and Hwanghwagak, is a venue where apprentice monks at the sangha university meditate and study.  The name “Wontong” comes from the phrase “Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva Igeunwontong.” Here, “Igeunwontong” means to “focus on listening to attain enlightenment.”

stories.title: Gamnodang Hall
stories.script: Gamnodang Hall  Gamnodang, along with Wontongbang, is a venue where apprentice monks at the sangha university meditate and study.

stories.title: Haejangbogak Hall
stories.script: Haejangbogak Hall  Haejangbogak, which enshrines Jajang Yulsa who originally built Tongdosa Temple, was named so because the content of the Buddhist Sutras (“Jang”) was like numerous treasures (“Bo”) from the vast ocean (“Hae”).  Currently, Haejangbogak houses Buddhist sutras, and the Tripitaka Koreana. Parts of the Buddhist sutras are exhibited in the Tongdosa Seongbo Museum as well.

stories.title: Geumgang Gyedan Stairs (Ordination Platform)
stories.script: Geumgang Gyedan Stairs (Ordination Platform)  The Geumgang Gyedan Stairs are a symbol of Tongdosa Temple, and a representation of its spirit. Underneath, Geumgang Gyedan houses the Sarira of Sakyamuni, which Jajang Yulsa brought back from the Tang Dynasty to build Tongdosa Temple. The reason why Tongdosa Temple earned the status of a “Buddhist Treasure Temple” was because of the genuine Sarira of Sakyamuni and the Geumgang Gyedan Stairs. As such, people believe that attending a Buddhist sermon on the Geumgang Gyedan Stairs is akin to attending a sermon led by Sakyamuni himself.  During the final years of Goryeo, and on multiple occasions during the Joseon Dynasty, Japanese pirates attempted to plunder the temple and steal the Sarira. However, the monks at Tongdosa Temple sacrificed their lives to protect the Sarira and keep it away from the hands of the pirates. The Geumgang Gyedan Stairs, which is very important in terms of its value as a cultural heritage and its significance in Buddhist history, is designated as National Treasure No. 290 along with the Daeungjeon Hall at Tongdosa Temple.

stories.title: Daeungjeon Hall
stories.script: Daeungjeon Hall  Given that Tongdosa Temple houses the genuine Sarira of Sakyamuni in its Geumgang Gyedan Stairs, it does not feature a statue of Sakyamuni in its Daeungjeon Hall. There is an interesting legend involving Tongdosa Temple. Jajang Yulsa, who received Sakyamuni’s Sarira from the Tang Dynasty, was looking for a site to build a temple. One day, Manjusri Bodhisattva appeared in Jajang Yulsa’s dreams and told him to build a temple and enshrine the Sarira in Silla. When he woke, Jajang Yulsa sent a wooden duck to the east, and to his surprise, the duck soon returned with an Arrowroot flower in its mouth. Jajang Yulsa took this as a sign. So, he immediately went out to search for an Arrowroot flower despite the cold of winter. A few days later, he found two Arrowroot flowers next to a pond near Yeongchuk Mountain. Finally, Jajang Yulsa had the perfect place to build his temple. He filled the pond, built the Geumgang Gyedan Staircase, and created Tongdosa Temple.

stories.title: Eungjinjeon Shrine
stories.script: Eungjinjeon Shrine  Eungjinjeon Shrine was built to enshrine the 16 Arhats, who pledged to defend the teachings of Buddha. Inside, Eungjinjeon Shrine at Tongdosa Temple features a Seated Sakyamuni Buddha statue, a Maitreya Bodhisattva statue, and a Dipamkara Bodhisattva statue along with the 16 Arhats. Together, these artifacts represent the past, present, and future forms of Sakyamuni, and his 16 disciples.

stories.title: Myeongbujeon Hall
stories.script: Myeongbujeon Hall  “Myeongbu” in Korean refers to the afterlife people travel to when they die. Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva is a merciful bodhisattva who refused to reach the enlightenment of nirvana and vowed to remain in the Myeongbu world until all of humanity suffering in hell was reformed and redeemed. Originally, Myeongbujeon Hall was named Jijangjeon Hall since it housed a statue of Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva. However, it was renamed Myeongbujeon during the Joseon Dynasty.

stories.title: Sallyeonggak Shrine
stories.script: Sallyeonggak Shrine  Sallyeonggak Shrine houses a hanging painting depicting pagan mountain gods. The reason why Tongdosa, a bona fide Buddhist temple, has a building that enshrines a pagan god is because Buddhism organically became intertwined with folk religions after it was first introduced in Korea.

stories.title: Samseonggak Shrine
stories.script: Samseonggak Shrine  Inside, Samseonggak Shrine features Hanging Painting of Samseong, Hanging Painting of Seven Stars, and Hanging Painting of Pratyeka Buddha. Here, “Samseong” refers to Buddhist monks Jigong, Naong, and Muhak, all of whom were revered high priests during the Goryeo Dynasty. Aside from housing these paintings, Samseonggak also serves as a venue to pray for the longevity, happiness, and enlightenment of humankind.

stories.title: Guryongji Pond
stories.script: Guryongji Pond  At first glance, Guryongji Pond seems like a nondescript pond (13~17m2) with a small bridge. But it plays an important role in the origin story of Tongdosa Temple.  When Jajang Yulsa, the founder of Tongdosa Temple, received the genuine Sarira of Sakyamuni from Manjusri Bodhisattva in the Tang Dynasty, he wanted to come back and enshrine the Sarira in Silla. At the time, the site where Jajang Yulsa wanted to build his temple had a large pond. So, he tried to fill the pond and build what we call today as the Geumgang Gyedan Stairs. But unfortunately, the pond turned out to be the home of nine evil dragons. Jajang Yulsa tried extremely hard to teach these dragons the ways of Buddhism. In fact, he succeeded in reforming eight. The last dragon, however, was blind as a bat, and he asked Jajang Yulsa’s permission to become a guardian dragon for the temple. Jajang Yulsa granted the blind dragon’s request, which is why he left one small corner of the pond to make sure it had a place to live.

stories.title: Seolbeopjeon Hall
stories.script: Seolbeopjeon Hall  Built in 1993, Seolbeopjeon Hall currently serves as a Buddhist sanctuary. As the largest stand-alone wooden building in Korea (approximately 1,653m2), it can accommodate up to 3,000 people at any given time. Seolbeopjeon Hall is often used for morning and evening prayers, as well as other large services where monks preach the teachings of Buddha.

stories.title: Seounam Hermitage
stories.script: Seounam Hermitage  Seounam Hermitage was originally built by the great Chunghyeon Daesa in 1326 (2nd year of King Chungmok’s reign, Goryeo Dynasty), then renovated by Nambong Hwasang in 1859, and more recently by a Buddhist monk named Seongpa. It features  Samcheonbuljeon Hall, Sansingak Shrine, Seonwon, and Yosa. The Buddha statue created during the late Joseon Dynasty period, which was originally enshrined at Seounam Hermitage, is now on display at the Seongbo Museum.  Also, Seounam Hermitage is home to 160,000 porcelain Buddhist sutras created to deliver peace all over the world, and unification of North and South Korea. The porcelain sutras are replicas of the Tripitaka Koreana. Moreover, the wildflower colony (165,289m2) with tens of thousands of flowers and more than 100 wildflower species near the Hermitage is currently used as an “outdoor nature classroom” for students and visitors.

stories.title: Baengnyeonam Hermitage
stories.script: Baengnyeonam Hermitage  Baengnyeonam Hermitage was built by Buddhist monk Wolhwa Daesa in 1374 (23rd year of King Gongmin’s reign, Goryeo Dynasty), then was rebuilt by Hyeonam Daesa in 1634 (12th year of King Injo’s reign, Joseon Dynasty). Hanging Scroll of Sakyamuni, Painting of Divine Guardians, Painting of Ksitigarbha and ten kings, etc. at Baengnyeonam have all been designated as cultural heritage properties. At present, these scrolls are housed at the Seongbo Museum. During the Joseon Dynasty, Baengnyeonam was one of the most famous hermitages in the country. At the end of the Korean Empire, it became particularly famous as a hermitage in the southern provinces of the country and attracted numerous hermits. According to records, Buddhist monk Seongcheol studied and practiced Buddhism at Baengnyeonam for two years after receiving his dharma name of Seongcheol from Beomeosa Temple in Busan (1937).

stories.title: Jajangam Hermitage
stories.script: Jajangam Hermitage  Jajangam is best-known as the hermitage where Jajang Yulsa, the founder of Tongdosa Temple, used to practice Buddhism. Between its sanctuary and Jajangjeon Hall, Jajangam features a 4m-tall statue of Buddha, which was erected in 1896.  This hermitage is also known for its golden frog story. Jajangam has a natural spring behind its sanctuary where water spouts through a large rock. According to legend, this spring was created by Jajang Yulsa when he carved out a hole with nothing but his fingers to give a golden frog a place to live. Ever since, the mythical golden frog has been referred to as the “Geumwa” (golden frog) Bodhisattva. Dressed in green and golden clothes, it is said that Geumwa Bodhisattva can transform into a bee or butterfly, and never leaves the Sanmun Gate at the Hermitage. To this day, people flock to Jajangam Hermitage to see the legendary Geumwa Bodhisattva living inside the rock.

stories.title: Geungnakam Hermitage
stories.script: Geungnakam Hermitage  Geungnakam Hermitage was originally built in 1332 (2nd year of King Chunghye’s reign, Goryeo Dynasty), then renovated as a hermitage with nine buildings and 104 rooms by Buddhist monk Gyeongbong in 1968. Famous for being the home temple of Gyeongbong, who is widely regarded as one of the wisest monks of modern and contemporary times, Geungnakam Hermitage has been the destination of choice for numerous senior monks and is touted as the best patriotic hermitages south of the Hangang River.  Geungnakam Hermitage also features a small pond named Geungnakyeongji Pond, which often offers a reflection of the peaks at Yeongchuksan Mountain on its surface. Together with Honggyo Bridge, which stretches across the Pond, Geungnakyeongji blends in well with its surroundings and creates a magnificent view.

stories.title: Biroam Hermitage
stories.script: Biroam Hermitage  Biroam Hermitage was originally built by Buddhist monk Yeongsuk Daesa in 1345 (the first year of King Chungmok’s reign, Goryeo Dynasty). More recently, it was repaired by Buddhist monk Wonmyeong Hwasang. Biroam has two main halls - Birojeon Hall, which houses statues of the Vairocana Buddha and Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva, and Bukgeukjeon Hall, which houses artifacts revered in a folk religion known as “Chilseong” (Seven Stars religion).  Moreover, Biroam is home to a number of hanging Buddhist scrolls painted during the Joseon Dynasty. In particular, Hanging Scroll Behind the Budda, Painting of divine guardians, Painting of Pratyeka Buddha, Painting of Mountain God, and Painting of Seven Stars hold significant historical value on par with other national treasures. Among the variety of Hanging Scrolls at Biroam, the Painting of Seven Stars features not only the Buddha Triad, but also Taoist gods such as the Chilwonseonggun (the Seven Original Kings of Stars), which makes it a rarity among Buddhist paintings.

stories.title: Chongnimmun Gate
stories.script: Chongnimmun Gate  Chongnimmun Gate at Tongdosa Temple features a signboard that says, “Yeongchuk Chongnim.” The word “Chongnim (Vindhyavana)”, which means “a dense forest with trees and plants” in the literal sense, was often used in the past among Buddhist circles to describe a mass gathering of monks and people from all over the country convened to study the teachings of Buddha. Today, the term Chongnim is used to refer to major temples featuring a “Seonwon” (training facility for Buddhist monks specializing in zen meditation), a “Seungga Daehak” (university that teaches Buddhist scriptures), a “Yulhak Seungga Daewon” (an academic institution specializing in religious precepts), and “Yeombul Daehakwon” (an academy for experienced Buddhist monks). Chongnimmun Gate at Tongdosa Temple is a symbol that represents the status of the Temple as a Vindhyavana, and it serves as a portal to the inner sanctum of the Temple.

stories.title: Changuimun Gate
stories.script: Changuimun Gate, also known as Jahamun Gate, is one of the Four Small Gates built amid the Four Great Gates during the construction of the City Wall in 1396 (the 5th year of King Taejo's reign). Later, in 1416 (the 16th year of King Taejong's reign), the gate was temporarily closed, allowing entry only upon the king's command. This action was due to the pungsujiri (geomancy) interpretation suggesting that Changuimun Gate was exerting pressure on Gyeongbokgung Palace. Located in Baegaksan Mountain between the Seodaemun and Bukdaemun gates, Changuimun Gate is the only gate among the Four Small Gates to retain its original structure.  During the Injobanjeong or the Coup of 1623, Yi Gwal and Yi Gwi washed their swords at Segeomjeong and entered the palace through Changuimun Gate. Additionally, an image of a pair of phoenixes was carved atop the rainbow shape to ward off numerous centipedes that gathered in front of the gate, as they were believed to fear hens and roosters.  The gate tower, which stands to this day, was constructed in 1741 (the 17th year of King Yeongjo's reign). Notably, its stonework is identical to that of the Sungnyemun and Heunginjimun gates. The gate's roof, characterized by double eaves and a gentle slope, exudes an elegant appearance. Gyeomjae Jeong Seon, a renowned Korean landscape painter from the Joseon Dynasty, depicted the gate within the natural setting of Baegaksan Mountain, surrounded by pine groves, a valley, and Buchimbawi Rock.  Originally serving as a route leading to both Yangju and Bukhansanseong Fortress), Changuimun Gate had been closed for centuries due to pungsujiri analysis (geomantic principles) until its reopening in 1506 (the 1st year of King Jungjong's reign). Presently, the gate, which overlooks Seoul, is closed to traffic, as its original function has been supplanted by the western road.

stories.title: January 21, Pine Tree
stories.script: Whilst walking along Seoul City Wall towards Sukjeongmun Gate, you will encounter a pine tree adorned with strips of red paint, known as the January 21 Pine Tree, a living witness to the armed communist guerilla.  January 21 commemorates the date in 1968 when 31 North Korean officers from Unit 124 of the Korean People's Army attempted to raid Cheongwadae (The Blue House). They managed to infiltrate as far as present-day Cheongun-dong, engaging in gunfire with South Korean military and police officers. At that time, the unit members disguised themselves in South Korean Army uniforms to blend in with civilians.  While passing through the Jahamun Gate hill, their identities were exposed during a random police investigation, leading to a shootout. They then fled towards Inwangsan and Baegak mountains. The red paint marks on the pine tree are bullet traces from the shootout, resulting in 28 of the 31 commandos being shot dead, two fleeing, and Kim Sin-jo being captured alive. This incident led to the permanent closure of Baegaksan Mountain and the establishment of the National Reserve Army.

stories.title: Sukjeongmun Gate
stories.script: Sukjeongmun Gate serves as the north gate among the Four Great Gates of Seoul City Wall. While the name Sungnyemun Gate signifies 'to hold good manners in high esteem,' Sukjeongmun Gate's meaning is 'to govern solemnly.' Originally named Sukcheongmun, Sukjeongmun Gate was erected in September 1396 (the 5th year of King Taejo's reign) along with the other great gates and the Four Small Gates.  Geomantic expert Choi Yang-seon remarked, 'Changuimun and Sukcheongmun gates are the arms of Gyeongbokgung Palace, and road construction in these areas should be avoided as it would damage the veins.' Consequently, the two gates were closed, and pine trees were planted to restrict public access in 1413 (the 13th year of King Taejo's reign). However, during a severe drought, Sukjeongmun Gate was opened while Sungnyemun Gate remained closed, reflecting the principle of yin in the north and yang in the south. Sukjeongmun Gate remained closed because it was believed that when opened, the yin air flow would make women immoral and lewd.  The tale of Ssalbawi Rock, located outside Sukjeongmun Gate, stands as an iconic folktale of Seoul. According to the legend, around two kilograms of rice poured out from this rock every morning, afternoon, and evening. The first person to witness this was a woodcutter, who lived without concerns of food thanks to the rice obtained from the rock.  However, one day, consumed by greed, he stood next to the rock with a sack all day long, refusing to return home until the sack overflowed with rice. Sadly, after a month, the rock ceased producing rice, pouring out only water. Following this legend, the rock was named Miam or Ssalbawi, signifying 'rice rock.' The story's moral lesson cautions against succumbing to greed, as it leads to no lasting satisfaction.

stories.title: Waryong Park
stories.script: Waryong Park is a relaxation spot in Seongbuk-dong, where a ridge shaped like a dragon stretches close to the flatland, culminating at Hyehwamun Gate located at the end of the long ridge below. To the left of Hanyang City Wall lies Seongbuk-dong, previously situated outside the capital city, while to the right is Myeongnyun-dong, once positioned within the city. The park overlooks Seongbuk-dong, displaying a distinct contrast between affluent and poorer neighborhoods.  Lined with renowned restaurants, including those specializing in pork cutlets, such as Majeonteo and Yongmaru, Waryong Park also features an adjacent badminton court bustling with residents until late at night. The park's charm lies in the breathtaking nightscape of the city, offering views of the N Seoul Tower. At times, sitting on the stone stairway near the observatory allows one to gaze upon the brightly lit neighborhood amidst the mountainous terrain of Seongbuk-dong. This view evokes deep emotions?yearning, sadness, tranquility, and peace.  Waryong Park is a popular spot for couples seeking respite from the city's hustle and bustle at night. Additionally, it attracts individuals seeking solace and consolation in a serene environment. Every visit to the park leads to an appreciation for the magnificence of nature.

stories.title: Hyehwamun Gate
stories.script: Hyehwamun Gate is one of the Four Small Gates situated in the northeast area of the city wall. Despite its categorization as one of the Four Small Gates, it has historically encountered heavy traffic due to its connection with the Gyeongwon Highway, linking Seoul and Wonsan. Hyehwamun Gate assumed the role of Sukjeongmun Gate, which had been permanently closed.  The gate was constructed in 1397 (the 6th year of King Taejo's reign) during the Hanyang City Wall's construction, but the gate tower of Hyehwamun was dismantled in 1928, and the remaining stonework was removed in 1939 for the construction of Sinjak-ro. A phoenix was depicted on the gate tower's ceiling to protect the surrounding area, which had long served as an important bird habitat. Initially situated on the Dongsomun-ro hill below the present-day gate, it was referred to as the East Small Gate due to its location between the east and north gates. Hyehwamun Gate, initially named Honghwamun, was the last of the eight gates to be restored in 1994.  In 1924, while observing this gate, the renowned novelist Hyeon Jin-geon conceived a short story titled Unsujoeun Nal (A Lucky Day). Although not completely confirmed, Hyehwamun Gate seems to have served as its backdrop. The short story revolves around Kim Cheom-ji, a pedicab driver, who sets out to work in the rain and hunger. On a day when there were exceptionally more customers than usual, he could earn enough money to buy ox bone soup for his sick wife. Tragically, upon his return home, he discovers his wife has passed away. The narrative depicts the harsh reality faced by Koreans, particularly those in the lower socioeconomic class, during the Japanese occupation period, where luck and miracles were scarce.

stories.title: Jangsu Village
stories.script: The trail along Hanyang City Wall from Hyehwamun Gate to Naksan Park has a gentle slope amid the low mountainous terrains, which makes it a perfect place to enjoy a stroll. Naksan Mountain has the lowest elevation among the four main mountains, but it still has a towering peak. Left to the trail, there is Jangsu Village on Samseondong 1-ga, surrounding Hansung University, where a redevelopment project is being implemented with resident participation. The entryway to the village is found halfway along the trail, where there is a pavilion and a bench for visitors to rest and enjoy the natural scenery.  Jangsu Village is where people settled after the liberation from the Japanese and the Korean War. The majority of the residents in this area are seniors, and the earnest wish for the village to be preserved for a long time is reflected in its name, Jangsu, which literally means 'longevity.'  Most of the houses and buildings were built without authorization or development plans, but this is why the natural environment and topography seem to be harmonized. The narrow and winding roads and the low stone walls are characteristic of this modern-day village. It has potential for alternative development, maintaining the culture and traditions unique to the village, such as Daraengi Village in Namhae and Dubrovnik in Croatia.

stories.title: Gakjaseongseok Rampart at Dongdaemun Seonggwak Park
stories.audioTitle: Gakjaseongseok Rampart at Dongdaemun Seonggwak Park
stories.script: Dongdaemun Seonggwak Park (formerly the site of Dongdaemun Church) is connected to the end of the Naksan section of the Hanyang City Wall. Gakjaseongseok Rampart is also situated near the fortress's end, speculated to have been constructed in 1706, the 32nd year of King Sukjong's reign. It is a stone inscribed with the words 'Chaegeung' and 'Dogyeok,' referring to the planning and supervision work performed for the Ilpaedu project.  When discussing this rampart, one must be mentioned in the story of filial daughter Dorijang, who became the story of the town at the time of the City Wall construction. Her father, hailing from Jinwon, Jangseong in Jeolla-do Province, traveled to Hanyang to take part in the construction work but had to stay in a medical relief station called Pangyowon after being sick. Upon learning this, Dorijang disguised herself as a man and traveled hundreds of kilometers to reach Hanyang in winter. During her journey, whenever encountering someone afflicted by disease, she checked if it was her father. After enduring numerous hardships, she finally reached Pangyowon, but her father was on his deathbed. With great earnestness, she cared for him, nursing him back to health before returning together to their hometown. Her exemplary filial devotion earned praise from her neighbors, and upon hearing her story, King Taejo bestowed her with fine cloth.  If you take a lengthy walk along the Hanyang City Wall, Dongdaemun Seonggwak Park will serve as an excellent spot to rest and appreciate Gakjaseongseok Rampart.

stories.title: The Five Floodgates
stories.script: The Ogansumun Gate, the Five Floodgates, was created during the construction of Hanyang City Wall during the Joseon Dynasty, there exists no defensive record of its inception. Ogansumun, meaning “Five-bay Water Gate,” was built under the fortress wall at the south of Heunginjimun Gate, or Dongdaemun (Great East Gate), designed to help the Cheonggyecheon water flow freely through the wall into Hangang River. However, Ogansumun Floodgate and the surrounding City Wall were demolished in 1907 and 1908. The current Ogansumun Floodgate is a replica of the original structure, reconstructed in 2004.  Originally, in each bay of Ogansumun Gate featured gratings to obstruct passage while allowing water flow. Despite these bars, the floodgates served as covert passageways for individuals seeking entry or exit from the capital without official authorization. This is depicted in the tale of Im Kkeok-jeong, a butcher turned leader of a band of thieves, hailed as a hero among the commoners during the Joseon Dynasty for redistributing wealth from the affluent to the impoverished.  One fateful night, a sudden commotion shattered the tranquility. A raid ensued, torches ablaze, voices cried, 'It's Im Kkeok-jeong!' He assisted the escape of his family from prison and fled toward Cheonggyecheon Stream. Pursued by royal forces, he vanished near Heunginjimun Gate. His disappearance likely occurred due to Ogansumun Floodgate, situated at the confluence of Cheonggyecheon Stream, flowing from west to east, and intersecting with the Hanyang City Wall. Im Kkeok-jeong forcibly bent the floodgate's bars, evading capture and seeking refuge in Gatbachi Village. Hidden for several days before fleeing to Baeogae, his status as a folk hero shielded him, with Baeogae residents refraining from disclosing his whereabouts to authorities

stories.title: The Two Floodgates
stories.script: The Ogansugyo Bridge, located below Hanyang City Wall, leads to Dongdaemun History & Culture Park, where Igansumun Floodgate, the Two Floodgates, can be found. Igansumun literally means ‘two arches.’ Igansumun Gate was where water from Namsan Mountain passed through and featured wooden bars to restrict unauthorized travel to and from the city.  The excavation of Igansumun Gate is intertwined with the history of Dongdaemun Stadium. In 1925, the Japanese constructed a stadium, initially named Gyeongseong Stadium, to commemorate the crown prince of Japan's marriage. During this time, Igansumun Gate was buried along with segments of the Hanyang City Wall. After the Seoul Sports Complex's construction in 1984, the stadium was renamed Dongdaemun Stadium. Upon its demolition in 2008, Igansumun Gate, buried underground for over 80 years, was unearthed and subsequently restored.  Dongdaemun Stadium was the backdrop for significant historical events. It hosted the funeral of Sunjong, Korea's final emperor, in 1926, along with football matches between the teams of Gyeongseong and Pyongyang. Additionally, it served as the venue for the funerals of public leaders Baekbeom Kim Gu and Mongyang Yeo Un-hyeong. Notably, the stadium witnessed the first home run in Korean baseball history, welcomed the renowned soccer player Pele, and hosted a farewell match for soccer player Cha Bum-kun before his departure to Germany.  Following the stadium's demolition, the discovery of historical structures and relics transformed it into valuable cultural and historical resources. Presently, Dongdaemun History & Culture Park comprises the Dongdaemun History Museum, Dongdaemun Stadium Memorial, Relics Exhibition Hall. The remnants of architectural structures dating from the Joseon Dynasty, unearthed at the former Dongdaemun Stadium site, are displayed at the Relics Exhibition Hall.

stories.title: Heunginjimun Gate
stories.script: A story of Dongdaemun Streetcar  288 Jong-ro, Jongno-gu, Seoul... This is the place that you will step on to, immediately after leaving Exit #6 of the Dongdaemun Station on subway line no. 1 and 4. After having an early dinner, one can take a stroll to Heunginjimun Gate (Treasure No. 1), the Dongdaemun Gate of the city wall that has turned into a fashion district. This gate features the architectural style of the late Joseon Dynasty that is characterized by simplicity and delicateness. It was constructed along with the other gates in 1396 (5th year of King Taejo's reign). It was originally called Heunginmun before being renamed as Heunginjimun in 1869 (6th year of King Gojong's reign).   Heunginjimun means a gate which promotes benevolence, and because its name contains more letters than the names of other games, it had to be written in two vertical lines on the signboard. According to a legend, the letter, ji (之), was added to the name because the area containing Naksan and Heunginmun, exhibited low terrains. Ongseong, a secondary wall built in front of the fortress gate, as an enclosure so that the gate cannot be viewed from the outside, as the topographic features of Seoul characterized by high western and low eastern grounds made the city vulnerable to foreign invasions.   The view of the old gate standing tall amidst the hustle and bustle of the fashion district strikes people with reverence. While recalling the history of Seoul, one may remember the streetcars that traveled across the streets in the past. The streetcars, which traveled at a relatively slow speed, were costly to maintain and they've long become a faded memory here in Seoul.   In some parts of the world, where streetcars are still in operation, they are on the verge of extinction, yet ironically, they've become a popular attraction. Although there are no traces of streetcars that remain in Seoul, there was a time when they served as an important transportation method for the people.   Hanseong Electrical Company, established in Hanseong in 1898, claimed that there was a need for more vassals to accompany King Gojong whenever he made a trip to Hongneung to visit the tomb of Empress Myeongseong and pushed for the temporary establishment of the streetcar system. The following year, the Japanese demolished a part of the city wall to install the streetcar tracks. Because the system was built, relying on American technology, the Korean and American flags were raised at the opening ceremony of the streetcar system. Streetcars, which became a new mode of transportation within the Four Great Walls, were operated from Donguimun Gate to Cheongnyangni through Jongno and Heunginjimun Gate. However, there were a large number of people, who traveled on foot in Jongno, because they didn't want to spend money on the fare.   The streetcars accompanied the tumultuous and tragic modern history of Korea. For instance, reeds and weeds grew up to a grown man's height along the streetcar tracks in Seoul at the time of the Korean War, which added to the dreary and desolate appearance of the city in ruins after the war. The streetcars came to a halt at midnight on November 30, 1968, which marked the end of the era of streetcars.

stories.title: Gwanghuimun Gate
stories.script: Gwanghuimun, meaning ‘light illuminates far in all directions,’ was built in 1396 during the fifth year of King Taejo's reign in the Joseon Dynasty. Gwanghuimun Gate was destroyed during the Imjin War. Subsequently, it was reconstructed in 1711 during the 37th year of King Sukjong's reign. Gwanghuimun Gate was left in a damaged state after its pavilion was destroyed during the Korean War. However, in 1975, it was situated in the middle of the road. Restoration work commenced by relocating it 15 meters south of its original position, concluding in November 1975.  Historical records indicate that in the second year of King Injo's reign (1624), the king fled through Gwanghuimun Gate. Similarly, during the Byeongja Horan in 1636, the king also passed through the gate, relocating to Namhansanseong Fortress. In the Joseon Dynasty, Japanese envoys crossed the Hangang River at Dumofonaru, Oksu-dong, and proceeded through Gwanghuimun Gate to Dongpyeonggwan, a designated accommodation in Inhyeon-dong.  Moreover, there exist poignant stories associated with Gwanghuimun Gate during the Joseon Dynasty. At one point, stone dust from Sigumun Gate was believed to be a remedy for all ailments. Consequently, rural inhabitants advised travelers heading to Hanyang, 'Scrape off and bring back some stone dust from Sigumun Gate in Hanyang.' This belief stemmed from the notion that no disease in the world could surpass the suffering that Sigumun Gate endured.

stories.title: Namsan (Mokmyeoksan) Octagonal Pavilion
stories.script: The Namsan Octagonal Pavilion overlooks the city center of Seoul, boasting a stunning view, but its history is far from ordinary. This site once housed the Guksadang Shrine, constructed to honor the mountain god of Namsan Mountain when King Taejo of Joseon selected Hanyang as the capital city. At that time, Guksadang Shrine held the utmost significance in the country. However, during the Japanese occupation period, Guksadang Shrine was relocated to Inwangsan Mountain to make way for a Japanese shrine. In 1925, the Japanese displaced Guksadang Shrine from its original location, where it had stood for over 500 years, asserting that it was improper for a colony's shrine to occupy the same site as their Emperor's shrine, which they worshipped.  Since then, Namsan Mountain has transformed into a public park. Yet, almost a century ago, the mountain, representing the grandeur of Joseon and the royal family, suffered under Japanese rule. On the mountain's foothills lies Dongpyeonggwan, where Japanese envoys lodged between the early Joseon Dynasty period and prior to the Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1592. During the invasion, the Japanese established camps here, serving as residences for Japanese generals, with the camps extending to present-day Jeongdong.  In 1884, the Japanese consular office was constructed on Namsan Mountain's foothills, housing the legation, Residency-General, Government General offices, and others. The current Seoul Youth Hostel occupied the former legation office and the Residency-General's residence, while the Seoul Animation Center now occupies the former Residency-General Office and Government General's residence. Namsan Mountain was considered the core of the Japanese settlement until the Government General office and residence were relocated to Gyeongbokgung Palace.

stories.title: Mokmyeoksan Beacon Mound
stories.script: King Taejo of the Joseon Dynasty recognized the strategic significance of Namsan Mountain and built the Mokmyeoksan Beacon Mound in 1394.  A beacon is a communication tool installed to alert the central agency of emergencies and urgent situations in border areas and vice versa, allowing swift responses to prevent crises. There was a series of five beacons, emitting smoke signals for various situations: smoke was produced once regularly, twice upon sighting enemy forces, thrice when enemies approached the boundaries, four times upon infiltration, and five times at the start of a battle. Mokmyeoksan Beacon Mound is considered the last among the nationwide beacon series. A single stream of smoke from these beacons symbolized a time of peace and tranquility, enabling people to focus on their daily activities without concern for survival.  Isabella Bird Bishop, an English explorer, visited Korea during the late Joseon Dynasty period and mentioned in the book 'Korea and Her Neighbors' that 'Seoul, surrounded by mountains, offers its most picturesque view from the beautiful Namsan Mountain.' Due to its geographical location, Namsan Mountain was regarded as a holy and dignified mountain. Rituals were conducted there, and it held the noble title of Jinsan, signifying a guardian mountain protecting the national territory and the royal capital from the Joseon royal family. At Namsan Mountain's peak stands the Mokmyeoksinsa Shrine, where rituals occurred in spring and autumn until the mid-Joseon Dynasty. According to the Sejongsillokjiriji (Annals of King Sejong), 'Mokmyeoksan Shrine was situated at Namsan Mountain's summit, where minor rituals took place.' Initially, as the site where state-organized rituals were conducted, it was known as Guksadang Shrine. However, the shrine was dismantled for the construction of the Japanese shrine and subsequently rebuilt on Inwangsan Mountain.

stories.title: An Jung-geun Memorial Hall
stories.script: An encounter with the revered patriot, An Jung-geun   While taking a stroll in Namsan Mountain, you will soon come across the An Jung-geun Memorial Hall, which has remained relatively obscure. Most people, upon sighting the memorial hall, enter it without any great expectations, but they all leave with a strong impression.     The An Jung-geun Memorial Hall was built to honor the independent activist, who assassinated Hirobumi Ito at the Harbin train station in Manchuria in October 1909. The original memorial hall, built by An Jung-geun Memorial Association in 1970, was demolished and a new memorial hall was erected on October 26, 2010. Upon entering, visitors will be welcomed by the seated statue of An Jung-geun in the central hall along with Taegeukgi, the national flag of Korea. This particular flag holds a symbolic value, as An cut his little finger and used the blood drawn to write  Independent Korea on it. The An Jung-geun Memorial Hall is a must-visit place, even for those who have little or no interest in history, and parents are urged to visit this place with their children as it will instill good values.  While touring the memorial hall, you will discover information that you were previously unaware of. Until now, it was popularly believed that patriot An wrote the words in blood directly using his fingers, but actually, he used a brush. Also, the account of the assassination of Hirobumi Ito, considered as a public enemy by An, can be viewed inside Exhibition Hall 3.   On the third floor, inside the glass showcase on the left side, there is a model reenactment of the assassination at Harbin train station. When movement is detected as a visitor enters the area, the figures begin to move and the audio starts to play in the background. Walk a bit further, and you will see a model depicting An Jung-geun on trial for the assassination.

stories.title: Sungnyemun Gate
stories.script: Sungnyemun Gate is Korea’s National Treasure No. 1, the largest castle gate, and it is unofficially named Namdaemun Gate. Sungnyemun Gate’s tablet has its name written vertically, differing from other gates. Sungnyemun was destroyed by fire in 2008, but the gate was re-opened in 2013 after a 5-year reconstruction.  When King Taejo of the Joseon Dynasty named the four great gates, he reflected the principles of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom, which were befitting as Confucianism deeply influenced Korean culture. They are pronounced in Sino-Korean as In, Ui, Ye, and Ji, respectively, and were incorporated into the names of the great gates. Specifically, Sungnyemun Gate got its name from pungsujiri or geomancy. Gyeongbokgung Palace, the main palace of the Joseon Dynasty, faces Gwanaksan Mountain, and according to the pungsujiri principles, the fire energy of Gwanaksan Mountain was very intense. Therefore, Gyeongbokgung Palace was slightly turned away from the fiery mountain.  Haetae, a mythical creature, was placed on the sides of Gwanghwamun Gate, the main gate of Gyeongbokgung Palace, to suppress the fire energy emanating from Gwanaksan Mountain. Traditionally, Haetae was believed to bring and exude water energy. There was a need to create fire energy stronger than that of Gwanaksan Mountain, and this is why Namdaemun, the south great gate, was named Sungnyemun. The Chinese character for 'Sung' is reminiscent of fire, while the character for 'Ye' represents fire in the principles of yin-yang and the five elements. When these two characters are placed on top of each other, it appears as though an intense fire is burning. Therefore, Sungnyemun is a name given to prevent the fire energy of Gwanaksan Mountain from penetrating inside the city wall by overpowering it with a greater fire.

stories.title: Site of Souimun Gate
stories.script: In the Joseon Dynasty, there were numerous markets inside the Hanyang City Wall, each in its respective neighborhood. Chilpae Market, one of the three major markets in Seoul during that period, was situated along present-day Tongil-ro. To reach it from the office of the Korea Chamber of Commerce & Industry near Sungnyemun, one crossed the Yeomcheongyo Bridge, and a landmark stone now marks the location of the former market. The name 'Chilpae' derived from the division of the Hanseong region into 8 'pae' for patrol by Hunryeondogam, Geumwiyeong, and Eoyeongcheong in the late Joseon Dynasty. A 'pae' represented a small military unit comprising 40 to 50 officers, roughly equivalent to a present-day platoon or company.  Chilpae had easy access to seafood due to its proximity to Yongsan and Mapo. This is evident in the 'Hanyang Song,' a depiction of Hanyang's history and appearance in the mid-19th century, which includes the lyrics 'there is a variety of fish in Chilpae,' introducing diverse seafood such as freshwater fish, bream, slender shad, octopus, conch, shellfish, shrimp, and gizzard shad.  Chilpae was infamous for cornering and hoarding. An old book describes it as, 'Unauthorized selling booths were scattered throughout Chilpae, outside the south gate, set up by merchants arriving in the morning and departing by nightfall. It was a chaotic scene filled with people and horses, and everyone shamelessly engaged in rampant selling.' Merchants in this area procured seafood directly from rural areas or during transportation to Hanyang, engaging in wholesale trade. They manipulated prices as they saw fit, adversely affecting authorized sellers. Moreover, many counterfeit goods were sold; records indicate merchants 'sold nickel as silver, goat horns as tortoise shell, and dog leather as sable leather.

stories.title: Ewha Girls' High School
stories.script: Ewha Hakdang is a modern secondary educational institution established in 1886 and is one of the early women's educational institutions in Korea. The name Ewha originates from Ewha Hakdang and is the predecessor of Ewha Girls' High School and Ewha Girls' University, the first and most famous women’s university in Korea.  At that time, it was uncommon for women to receive higher education. Ha Ran-sa (her maiden name was Kim), the first Korean woman to acquire a degree in the U.S., aspired to devote herself to her studies. She applied to Ewha Girls' High School with great scholastic ambitions. However, her application was rejected three times because she was a married woman. Relentless in her pursuit, she sought other means to enter the school of her choice. She lit a lamp and went to Ewha Girls' High School to meet the principal, L.E. Frey. When the principal asked her why she came, she turned off the lamp and said, My life is just as dark as this. Please lift the darkness from my life with the light of education. Her statement left a strong impression on Frey, and she was accepted into the school.  Ha Ran-sa studied at Ohio Wesleyan University, becoming the first Korean woman to study abroad and earn a bachelor's degree. In 1910, when an undergraduate program was launched at Ewha, she became the only professor with Korean nationality.  At the museum, you can get a glimpse into what it was like to graduate from Ewha. At the time, there was no formal graduation ceremony; instead, school administrators introduced the graduates to affluent families for marriage purposes and issued marriage certificates that indicated the women were graduates of Ewha Girls' High School.

stories.title: Russian Legation Office
stories.script: After the Russo-Japanese War ended with Russia's defeat, the Japanese began to interfere in everything in Joseon, prompting the emperor's lament at that time. Left with no choice, Emperor Gojong and Empress Myeongseong sought assistance from Russia to prevent further Japanese encroachment on their territory. In response, the Japanese committed a brutal assassination of Empress Myeongseong, known as the Eulmi Incident. This led to Emperor Gojong abandoning Gyeongbokgung Palace and seeking refuge in Agwanpacheon, the Korean royal refuge within the Russian Embassy.  Tensions continued to escalate. Russia demanded the right to a gold mine in exchange for protecting the emperor, while the U.S. and France demanded rights to install the railway and electrical systems. During this turmoil, Gojong found comfort and solace in coffee, which he tasted for the first time while seeking refuge in the Russian legation. He soon became a coffee enthusiast, and the only enjoyment he felt was when he drank coffee with the crown prince.  The old Russian legation was built in the Renaissance architectural style. Located on the highest hill of Jeong-dong, it offers views of Gyeongbokgung and Gyeongungung palaces, as well as the legations of other countries. Unfortunately, only the watchtower remains today. The solitary white building stands, seemingly conveying the emotions felt by Emperor Gojong.

stories.title: Site of Donuimun Gate
stories.script: Donuimun Gate, the west great gate of the city wall, is commonly known as Seodaemun Gate. The gate was erected near Sajikdan Altar in 1396 (the 5th year of King Taejo's reign), but it was closed in 1413. Seojeonmun Gate was newly built during King Taejong's reign to serve as the city entrance. In 1422, during the repair of the city wall, the gate was relocated to the south and renamed Donuimun Gate. Because it was newly constructed, it was also referred to as Saemun or Sinmun, both meaning a new gate. Due to the noise from people and horses passing through, King Yeongjo, staying in Gyeonghuigung Palace, ordered the gate to be closed and opened only on special occasions. Unfortunately, Donuimun was torn down by the Japanese in 1915, and its remnants were sold off as firewood for a mere 205 Korean won, which could buy only 17 bags of rice at the time.  In the 1920s, the Donuimun Gate area was also renowned for its streetcars. Operating since 1899, these streetcars traveled between Donuimun Gate and Cheongnyangni. Crowds were plentiful around the gate's final stop, and incidents of people falling off the streetcars due to overcrowding were not uncommon.  During the late 1920s, a shop selling saekdongbingsu, or colorful ice treats, was established near Donuimun Gate. This is considered the precursor to today's patbingsu (shaved ice with red beans) and gwailbingsu (shaved ice with fruits). The ice treats were colorful, made from ice shavings mixed with yellow, blue, and red water, believed to be sugar water containing food dyes. The shaved ice shop had a bush clover fence and a wooden curtain for shade, where people could cool down. Even today, shaved ice with red beans or various flavors remains a popular summer treat for people of all ages.

stories.title: Dilkusha (Taylor's House)
stories.script: While walking along the Seoul City Wall toward Inwangsang Mountain, one will notice a two-story red brick building in Western architectural style called Dilkusha. The house was the origin of the news about the March First Independence Movement that traveled across the world. In 1923, the house was built by an American reporter named Albert Taylor. With a keen interest in Korea's independence movement, he served as a correspondent for United Press International in 1919 and was the first to inform the world of the March First Independence Movement. Consequently, he was imprisoned by Japanese authorities at Seodaemun Prison (present-day Dongnip Park) for six months. After his release, he stayed at Dilkusha until he was forcibly vacated and deported by the Japanese in 1942. Taylor, who came to Korea with his father, considered Joseon his second home.  The manner in which Taylor delivered the news of the independence movement is quite intriguing. On the day of his son Bruce’s birth, he visited Severance Hospital to see his wife and their newborn. During his visit, the nurses hid the Declaration of Independence, which was being printed, under Bruce's cradle when the Japanese police raided the hospital. Taylor discovered the document later. This event occurred just the day before the March First Independence Movement. He clandestinely brought the document from the hospital and published a news report.  While residing in Dilkusha, he hosted foreign missionaries and businessmen from Gyeongseong to discuss the state of affairs in Korea. After his deportation, he passed away in the US in 1948. Per his final wish, he was buried in Yanghwajin, Korea.  Across from the house stands the ginkgo tree planted by General Kwon Yul. Cultural heritage experts believe that the site originally contained the general's house.

stories.title: Overview of Hanyangdoseong, the Seoul City Wall
stories.audioTitle: Overview of Hanyangdoseong, the Seoul City Wall
stories.script: Hanyangdoseong, the Seoul City Wall, was built to protect Hanyang (currently Seoul) against invaders in the Joseon Dynasty as fortress walls. The series of walls is 18.6 kilometers long.   Originally the wall had four main gates, Heunginjimun Gate in the east, Donuimun Gate in the west, Sungnyemun Gate in the south, Sukjeongmun Gate in the north, and four auxiliary gates. During the early 20th century, the wall underwent severe disruption mainly due to urbanization and the Korean War. However, some parts were reconstructed, and you can see the original part of the fortress in Samcheong-dong and Jangchung-dong, and in some gatehouses such as Heunginjimun Gate.    You can walk along the six trails of Baegak, Naksan, Heunginjimun Gate, Namsan (Mongmyeoksan), Sungnyemun Gate, and Inwangsan Sections. Hanyang City Wall will provide you with a breathtaking experience to see the wall-building techniques and architectural features as a significant historical site and feel the spirit of the Joseon people’s patriotism.

stories.title: Nakji Alley
stories.script: There is a street known for Nakji or small octopus, one of the attractions of Muan-gun.    It is called “Nakji Street,” which is lined with small restaurants around the Muan-eup Bus Terminal.   After a television entertainment program about this street was aired, this place began attracting more tourists, and a three-story parking building is now available for tourists in the middle of the street.    There are about 20 small restaurants on Nakji Alley, serving various kinds of nakji cousins such as Gigeol Nakji (knocked out small octopus), Nakji Hoe Muchim (seasoned baby octopus salad), Nakji Bibimbab, Nakji Yeonpo Tang (soup with boiled stir-fried octopus), and Nakji Horong (small octopus skewer).

stories.title: Muanhyanggyo Local Confucian School
stories.script: Muanhyanggyo Local Confucian School was a Confucian school in Muan, first built in 1394 at Namsan Mountain (then Mt. Gongsusan). Since wild tigers often appeared during the New Year’s ritual events; however, it was moved to its current location in the first year of the reign of King Seongjong (1470), 77 years after its establishment.   Today, buildings including Daeseongjeon, Jegichanggo, Myeongryundang Sinmun Gate, Dongje, Seoje, Dongbyeoldang, and Oesammun Gate still remain in here, but Hongjeonmun Gate, Samaje Hall, and Muhakdang Hall are now gone.     All the remaining buildings have been practically reconstructed since the late Joseon Dynasty. Only the 600-year-old ginkgo tree in front of Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall holds the whole history of the school.

stories.title: Mulmajigol Forest Park
stories.script: Forest Park  The Mulmajigol Forest Park is a wooden place with three themes: the forest of encounter, the forest of contemplation, and the forest of view.   The place got its name Mulmajigol because people suffering from neuralgia, skin diseases, and arthritis feel better if they wet themselves with the water from the waterfall in Yeonjingsan Mountain. As the news spread, more people began visiting the waterfall from nearby areas.    Afterward, the waterfall started to be called Mulmaji Falls (wetting with water) instead of Seolang Falls, and the valley area is called Mulmajigol.

stories.title: Forest of Contemplation.
stories.script: As you walk for about 1.5 km on a slight slope enjoying fresh forest bathing from the Forest of Encounter, you will get to the Forest of Contemplation.    Once you get there, you will notice a very attractive small spring filled with Mulmajigol’s freshness.  This is a delightful place to enjoy forest bathing with many pine trees, nut pine trees, and cedar trees.   Gazebos, low wooden benches, and other resting facilities are available for visitors in the Forest Bathing Area.   The Forest of Contemplation

stories.title: Heron Sanctuary
stories.script: Do you know that there is a Yongwolri Village in Muan-gun where  white and grey herons, natural monument animals, come to breed collectively?   Every year in March and April, white and grey herons come to this Yongwolri area to breed collectively after spending winter in East Asia, and again migrate southward in October for overwintering.  Thanks to their migration, we can enjoy the beautiful scenery of many white and grey herons in Cheongyongsan Mountain. White herons have been well-protected as auspicious animals as their collective breeding is believed to bring prosperity and fortune.

stories.title: Yaksasa Temple
stories.script: Yaksasa Temple in Muan-eup, Muan-gun of South Jeolla was founded with the original name Namaksa in 918. The size of the Buddha stone statue suggests that there was a considerably large temple from Goryeo.   The current Yaksasa building was built in 1972. It is located behind Daerimjang Inn across Muan Bus Terminal. It takes five minutes on foot from the Bus Terminal to get to the site.

stories.title: Floating Glass Greenhouse
stories.script: There is a creatively built glass building surrounded by water lilies in the Hoesan White Lotus Pond.  Because of its unique shape, a lotus flower, the Floating Glass Greenhouse received the Excellence Prize in Architectural Building at the 2006 Korean Architecture Cultural Awards.   There is a water lily exhibition hall in the Floating Glass Greenhouse. On the second floor is an exhibition hall featuring subtropical and other aquatic plants.  You can see the sky inside through its all-glass Green house ceiling, which makes it warm in winter.

stories.title: Introduction of White Lotus Pond
stories.script: Muan Hoesan White Lotus Pond is located in Ilo-eup of Bogyong-ri, and it measures 313313.   This pond was built with the sweat of Korean people during the dark era of Japanese Imperialism, providing water for nearby farmlands.     Today, the pond is one of the largest white lotus habitats in the Eastern world. According to an old story, its lotuses began to flourish with the work of one villager. He planted twelve white lotuses on the banks of the pond and dreamed that night that twelve cranes landed from the sky as if white lotuses bloomed. After the dream, he continued to care for the lotuses more diligently, creating today's beautiful pond.

stories.title: Outdoor Water Playground
stories.script: Every summer, the Heosan White Lotus Pond opens a water playground. It has five pools including pools for toddlers, children, and adults and wave pool that makes artificial waves up to 1.2m high.     The water playground attracts more visitors every year because of its fun water play equipment such as water tunnel and convenient facilities such as snack bar, changing room, shower facilities, and canopy.

stories.title: Muan Seungwoo Oh Museum of Art
stories.audioTitle: Muan Seungwoo Oh Museum of Art
stories.script: The Muan Seungwoo Oh Museum of Art was established when first-generation western painter Oh Seungwoo donated his art pieces in 2003.   The museum was established to promote the value of Oh Seungwoo’s works and development of culture and art of Muan-gun. The two-story museum exhibits various artworks in its exhibition halls.

stories.title: Memorial Exhibition Hall
stories.script: Visitors can get more information through a documentary video of the life and thoughts of Zen Master Choui here in the Memorial Exhibition Hall. You can also see the tea sets and books on tea etiquette such as Dongsasong and Dasinjeon in the Hall.   Visitors can enjoy the poems and paintings made by Zen Master Choui after visiting Wolchulsan Mountain in Baekundong with Dasan Jeongyakyoung, such as Baekundo and Dasanchodangdo.

stories.title: Joseon Tea History Museum
stories.script: In the Joseon Tea History Museum, visitors can get a glimpse of the tea culture of the Joseon period.   The museum exhibits the tea sets of the early, middle, and late eras of the Joseon period and books on Chinese tea sets as well as the tea culture of the Joseon period.  Visitors can watch a video of Korea’s tea-producing areas and tea cultures by era as well as the tea-making method of Zen Master Choui and tea-drinking etiquette.

stories.title: Iljiam Chodang
stories.script: Iljiam Chodang is restored here as a replica of Iljiam in Daeheungsa Temple where Zen Master Choui practiced Buddhism his whole life and passed away.  This place has the Iljiam tea room and Jawoosanbang that was used for daily life with the statue of Buddha.     This was also the center of tea culture in the late Joseon Dynasty and the birthplace of Namjeonghwa, one of the Eastern painting styles, and a venue of sharing traditional poems.

stories.title: Choui Seon Institution
stories.script: The Choui Seon Institution is the place that shows the tea philosophy of Monk Choui -- “Tea helps control, behavior and Seon brings enlightenment.” It is a wooden building for Chamseon meditation and tea ceremony.   There are meditation rooms on the first floor and tea rooms on the second floor. Each represents the human world and the heavens.    Try to experience tea in the tea room on the second floor and imagine the life of Monk Choui in the building.

stories.title: Keumoh chodang House
stories.script: Keumoh chodang House is a tea house of famous Joseon Dynasty poet Maewoldang Kim Siseup, restored based on historical documents.  After wandering across the country, Kim Siseup retreated to a place around Mt. Keumoh, Namsan of Gyeongju, where he built a small house and named it Keumoh chodang. The Korean first novel in Chinese known as Keumoh Mythology is said to have been written here.    He served tea to Japanese monk Junjangro who stayed in Ulsan and made a poem for him. He dug a ground to make a ground furnace in Keumohdang to brew tea.  After the monk went back to Japan, he made a ground furnace to make tea. This was how the culture of ground furnace was created and spread widely in Japan.

stories.title: Bojeru Pavilion
stories.script: Bojeru Pavilion is a place to experience making Choui tea.  The word Boje from the two-story pavilion means saving people from their sufferings, originating from the pen name of Daegak deunggye boje jonja Chohui seonsa (大覺登階普濟尊者 艸衣大禪師) bestowed by King Heonjong.

stories.title: Military Theme Park
stories.script: The Military Theme Park was built with financial support from General Ok Manho, the former Air Force Chief of Staff whose hometown is Sachang-ri, Mongtan-myeon.   The large park displays eleven aircraft that include the military aircraft used in the Korean War and Vietnam War and even North Korean airships. Transport airplanes are open for visitors to get into for observation.    This park was renovated on May 1, 2018 by expanding the former Honam Aerospace Exhibition. It has exhibition experience facilities for visitors to share  exhibition education and experience Korean aviation history and culture.    There are many experiential learning facilities such as exhibition halls of weapons of the army, navy, and air force, indoor shooting range, Homeland Security Exhibition hall, flight simulation experience center, and outdoor training center.

stories.title: Hodam Aerospace Exhibition
stories.script: The Hodam Aerospace Exhibition was established through the donation of trainer and fighter aircraft by former Air Force Chief of Staff Ok Manho to promote the dreams and hopes of children and realize his love of hometown.    The exhibition halls consist of four kinds of theme halls.   Visitors can enjoy special exhibitions about Aerospace history. The first exhibition hall is themed Humans Dream, Flight, the second hall, Realization of Dream, Airplane, the third hall, Human’s New Challenge, Space Travel, and the fourth hall, Footsteps of the Korean Air Force.

stories.title: Survival Shooting Range
stories.script: Survival Shooting Range is a popular place for all people to play a shooting game.  Visitors can choose either combat shooting or clay shooting by paying 2,000 won for one person or 3,000 won for two people.   Come and have fun playing a point-earning shooting game with friends.

stories.title: Military Training Experience Place
stories.script: Behind Nike Missile is the Military Training Experience Place with various kinds of facilities.  Visitors can use twelve facilities safely for military training experience such as climbing the ladder, walking across swinging panels, passing through suspended tires, and trench experience.     Kids below 12 years have to be accompanied by their guardian or parents when using the facilities.

stories.title: Observation Aircraft D-1G Bird Dog
stories.script: After you walk across the simulation experience center, you can see the impressive fighter, tank, armored vehicle, and missile on a bed of wide blade grass. Let me introduce the two relatively little aircraft  among them. First, Bird Dog is an observation aircraft introduced in 1972 from the United States. The two-seater aircraft was used in primary flight training mission for training pilots.   Second, MIG-15 Fagot was the first jet fighter for which the Soviet Union adopted sweptwing. The single-seater aircraft was supplied to many pro-Soviet countries including North Korea and China and operated until the 1980s.

stories.title: Fighter F-5 Freedom Fighter
stories.script: Would you like to take a look at one of the fastest and sleekest fighters on the outdoor education field in the Military Theme Park?  The first fighter is Freedom Fighter F-5A. It is a one-seater fighter introduced in 1965 from the United States, opening the era of supersonic aircraft in the Republic of Korea.   The second fighter is F-4D Phantom. The Phantom fighter is a fighter bomber reinforced with electronic equipment. It carried out covering, rear interdiction, and reconnaissance in the Vietnam War in 1964 and destroyed about 140 MIG fighters from Soviet.   The third aircraft is F-86F Saber whose nickname is Ssaegssaegi. In the Korean War, it was operated by the United Nations’ Air Force, destroying 792 enemy fighters after the first shutdown of the enemy’s new fighter MiG-15 on December 17, 1950; thus showing its superiority in the air raid. After the Korean War ended, five F-86F were introduced for the first time, opening the jet era for the Korean Air Force. A total of 201 F-86F were deployed by 1968.   The fourth aircraft is the Independence-day airplane T-6 trainer. This was introduced in May 1950 as one of the ten trainers purchased using the donations of the people to improve the military power of the Korean Air Force, which was separated from the Army in 1949.

stories.title: Tank M48
stories.script: Across from the jet fighter exhibition on the outdoor education field, tanks and self-propelled artillery are displayed elegantly.    First is the M48 A2C tank. It is a modified version of the M48 tank, playing a key role in the Korean army from the 1960s. Most of the M48 AC2 tanks are now retired.   Second is the 8-inch self-propelled artillery. It is similar to the field gun tank but has a thinner armor than a tank, without a 360-degree rotatable turret. It has superior maneuverability compared to a field gun. Most of them are retired.   Third is the M47 tank. The effective firing range of the anti-tank is 2000m. It is the first mass-produced tank equipped with a rangefinder.

stories.title: Air Boat
stories.script: Next to the tanks in the outdoor education field are the Marine Corps armored vehicles with the mark of a shark.   The first air boat was designed for river and swamp operation. It was operated by the 2nd marine division of the Korean Marine Corps during the Vietnam War and used by the Korean Marine Corps from 1970 to 1975.   Second is the Marine Corps armored vehicle LVT-P7. Introduced by the Korean Marine Corps in 1974, the vehicle had been used as key landing equipment until 2002. Its body was made of special aluminum.   Third is the Marine Corps armored vehicle LVT-C7A1. It is a command-controlled armored vehicle with the commander of the amphibious assault unit onboard. It is capable of rotating 360 degrees in place on land and at sea.   Fourth is the Light Armored Vehicle. It was adopted to defend against counter-guerrilla warfare in case of an attack by the special forces of the enemy. Its body is made of 8mm steel plate to be protected from small arms or fragments.

stories.title: Nike Missile
stories.script: If you pass the jet fighters and tank displayed on the outdoor education field, you can see two sleek and big missiles on the hill. They are Nike missiles.   They are surface-to-ground, surface-to-air guided missiles capable of attacking a target on the ground and in the air.   They were often operated by Korean air defense artillery but were retired on May 30, 2014.

stories.title: Beopcheonsa Temple
stories.script: Beopcheonsa Temple located in Seundalsan Mountain is a small temple of Daeheungsa Temple, the headquarters of the 22nd Diocese of the Korean Buddhism Jogye Order. It is Traditional Temple No. 69 designated by the Ministry of Culture, Sports, and Tourism. Monk Jeong Myeong from the Forbidden Western Regions is said to have founded the temple in 725 of Unified Silla. The temple was burned in 1030, remaining in ruins for 100 years until it was rebuilt by Monk Won Myeong in the late Goryeo.    It went through several destructions and reconstructions. During the last reconstruction in 1913, Jeong Beongwoo built a small temple there; in 1962, the temple was expanded by Monk Hwalyeon into a Buddhist sanctuary that remains today.

stories.title: Buncheong Ware Master Exhibition
stories.script: Buncheong Ware Master Exhibition Hall was opened on August 5, 2016. The two-story building was designed in the image of tea bowl. It displays the stoneware made by Kim Oksoo, Korean Master no. 459, and the artifacts excavated around the region.    There is also a space where visitors can enjoy a pottery-making experience and a place for purchasing one of the masterpieces.

stories.title: Jogeum Naru Beach
stories.script: Jogeum Naru Beach showcases breathtaking nature with a sandy shore more than 4km long and a lush pine forest.   In addition, the beach is well-equipped with convenient facilities such as shower and toilet. Thus, it is the best place to camp overnight and enjoy the beach atmosphere.  In particular, visitors can see the splendid sunset at the West Sea. They can also enjoy various tasty sashimi and gijeol nakji (knocked-out octopus), the region’s specialty, in seafood restaurants.

stories.title: Tando Island
stories.script: Tando Island is about 2.5 km west of the Jogeum Naru beach in Songhyeon-ri, Mangun-myeon.  During high tide, the home of about five hundred people is a remote island. During low tide, however, the black silk mud flats appear, practically spreading to the Jogeum Naru beach with river-like water 30m to 50m wide between them. The boat is available twice a day, going to the island from the beach and vice versa.    Octopus and kajime seaweed from Tando Island are well-known to have been used as offerings for kings as regional specialties, and they are still loved by many. Let’s go visit the island for the special food, octopus and kajime seaweed.

stories.title: Topmeori Beach
stories.script: Topmeori Beach is located around Muan International Airport. The white sandy beach has shallow and clean water and slight slope,  making it a popular attraction in the summer season.   A 200-year-old black pine forest behind the white sandy beach provides a beautiful resting area for visitors.   Visitors can enjoy a beautiful sunset against the plane-shaped lighthouse at Topmeori port.   The seashore around the Topmeori beach is a breeding place for fish such as small octopus and silver bream. The Topmeori embankment raised against Changpo Bay is a popular spot for fishing silver breams and grey mullet, attracting more people to fishing during the fishing season. Try to enjoy fishing leisurely to catch silver breams!

stories.title: Muan Ecological Tidal Flat Land
stories.script: The Muan Ecological Tidal Flat Land is Ramsar Wetland No. 1732 and is also a theme park to promote the value of Muan wetland called Black Silk, designated as a provincial park of South Jeolla.   This place plays the role of promotion, education, and exhibition of the tidal flat. Youths and children can learn marine ecology here through ecological experiences in a large ecological park, a wetland learning area, and an ecological experience spot.

stories.title: Camping spot
stories.script: Muan Ecological Tidal Flat Land opened the Auto Caravan Camping Site in 2012. For camping lovers, it is equipped with various facilities such as caravans, auto camping site, experience site, and convenience facilities including washroom.   This place has attracted more camping lovers across the country since it was featured in the reality show Happy Sunday 1 Night and 2 Days broadcast by the KBS2 network. How about going camping here to enjoy Muan’s fun wetland?

stories.title: Ecological Mudflat Science Museum
stories.script: The Ecological Mudflat Science Museum is built in the Muan tideland where visitors can explore various animals and plants.   It provides various learning experiences with over 250 species of benthic animals including endangered species such as milky fiddler crab and Ellobium chinense or small snail as well as migratory birds that come to the Muan wetland every season.  With Muan’s wide wetland, this museum serves as a real experience field for youths and children.

stories.title: Pot Planting Exhibition Hall
stories.script: The Pot Planting Theme Museum is an exhibition hall to commemorate pot planting master Dr. Moon Hyungyeol and promote pot planting.  It offers all kinds of information on pot planting such as the meaning, aesthetics, growth environment, cultivation and gardening of pot planting, and uses of gardening tools.    In the Pot Planting Exhibition Hall right next to the Pot Planting Theme Museum, visitors can enjoy outstanding plants in pots that have been managed carefully like Japanese yew, fraxinus, evergreen spindles, Chinese quince, crow persimmon tree, Japanese apricot flower, and camellia.

stories.title: Bird Observatory
stories.script: At the Bird Observatory next to the Ecological Mudflat Science Museum, visitors can observe rare migratory birds coming to Muan Tideland with a telescope.  On a lucky day, visitors can see migratory birds designated as natural monuments such as whooper swan, cormorant, Asian dowitcher, Chinese egret, Eastern curlew, and common buzzard.

stories.title: Sunrise Observation Deck
stories.script: If you walk in the middle of the mudflat leading toward the water, you can get to the Sunrise Observation Deck with a monument of the Ocean Charter.     At the deck, you can closely observe the migratory birds inhabiting the mudflat in the direction of Doripo port with a telescope. You can also enjoy a stunning sunrise with the harmonious view of the wide sea and wetland.

stories.title: Milky Fiddler Group Habitat
stories.script: Around the area leading to the Sunrise Observation Deck in the Muan Ecological Tidal Flat Land is a preservation area for the milky fiddler group habitat.  Visitors can occasionally find milky fiddler crabs.    As members of the family Ocypode, milky fiddler crabs are class Ⅱ endangered wildlife. They are small, about 1.5cm, including the leg of about 1cm. They inhabit burrows in the upper mudflat with lots of sand.

stories.title: Seungdalsan Mountain
stories.script: Seungdalsan Mountain is not high at 333m above sea level, but it has a breathtaking view of the sea at the peak because it is near the west sea. Even in winter, it is not cold in the mountain.
