The land plots reserved for pine trees from Hamgyong and Pyongan provinces remain vacant even to this day with hopes that one day pine trees from all across the Korean peninsula may stand side by side in front of Yeongbingwan.  The main attraction of Yeongbingwan is found outside the building. The landscape seen from facing Yeongbingwan, with Ingwansan Mountain to the building’s left, is just like a landscape painting by Gyeomjae Jeongseon, a famous painter in the late Joseon dynasty.

stories.title: Official Residence of the President
stories.script: President and Family’s Living Quarters  The presidential residence that served as the living quarters of the president and his family, is nestled in the deepest and highest point within the Cheong Wa Dae compound. The residence was built in 1990 to separate the president’s personal life from their public affairs. The building was designed in a traditional Korean house style, featuring an architectural design similar to the main building, complete with a hipped-and-gabled roof.  The residence is comprised of a living room with a fireplace, a piano, a bedroom, a dressing room, and a bathroom with sauna facilities. The living room has a hidden staircase that connects to a secret underground passageway, built as an emergency escape route for the president, leading to Cheong Wa Dae Square. Additionally, there is an annex building housing a powder room used for guest reception and banquet events.  At one side of the yard stands a sarangchae (guest room) named Cheongandang, where the president can take a break from his executive duties. While the presidential residence tour is typically limited to the general public, visitors can catch a glimpse of the interior through the windows.

stories.title: Sugungteo
stories.script: Fifty-four years of Service as the Executive Office  Sugungteo, or the site of Sugung, is a historical location within the Cheong Wa Dae complex, situated on the path between the main office building and the presidential residence. It is also called the site of Gyeongmudae or the old main office building. During the Joseon Dynasty, this site was inhabited by the guards of Gyeongbokgung Palace.   Later on, the site served various roles, including as the governor-general's office during the Japanese colonial administration and as the residence of General Hodge of the U.S. Military Government. After the establishment of the Korean government in 1948 following liberation, President Rhee Syngman moved his office and residence to this site, naming it Gyeongmudae. Over time, the site was eventually renamed to Cheong Wa Dae and served as the presidential office and official residence until President Roh Tae-woo’s term in office.  In 1991, following the construction of the main office building, the site was completely demolished and restored to its original state as Sugungteo by November 1993. During the restoration process, a rock engraved with the inscription the most blessed land in the world was discovered at the foot of Bugaksan Mountain, proving the site's historical significance and auspicious nature.  Currently, Sugungteo retains only a few relics from its past. Notable among them is the rooftop ornament that once adorned the entrance of the governor-general's office, as well as a 700-year-old evergreen tree. This ancient tree has witnessed centuries of Korean history, dating back to the Goryeo dynasty, and is a testament to the nation's historical vicissitudes. The rooftop ornament, shaped like a bottle gourd, was often used as a central decoration on roof ridges. These two remnants, the old tree and the bottle gourd ornament, are aligned in a straight line at the site and are notable features to seek out during your visit.

stories.title: Sangchunjae
stories.script: The Only Traditional Hanok in Cheong Wa Dae Sangchunjae  Bearing the meaning “a place of eternal spring,” Sangchunjae was designed to demonstrate the beauty of Korea’s traditional house, hanok. It was used to hold informal meetings, meals, and events. This was also where the former presidents Lee Myeong-bak and Barack Obama, and Moon Jae-in and Donald Trump shared meals, respectively.  This space was originally occupied by Maehwa Hall, an annex building of the Japanese General Government Building. However, President Rhee Syngman renamed the building to Sangchun Hall during his term in office. In 1978, the building was remodeled into a western-style design with a natural slate roof and renamed again to Sangchunjae. In 1983, Sanchunjae was remodeled once again, designed to be the hanok building seen today.  The first thing to take note of at Sangchunjae is the pine wood used as columns and beams. Crafted from 200-year old pine trees from Chunyang-myeon in Bonghwa-gun, Gyeongsangbuk-do, these natural woods are considered the finest and the best materials for building hanok. Another key point to keep in mind is the stairway from Nokjiwon Garden to Sangchunjae. As you go up the stairs, the first thing that comes into view is the hanok roof with its graceful curve against the sky, followed by red pine beams, and finally, the full façade of Sangchunjae.  The beauty of hanok stands out even more when it is in harmony with the surrounding nature. Enjoy the charms of hanok during your visit to Cheong Wa Dae. Sangchunjae is a surprise that’ll make your time in Cheong Wa Dae more pleasurable.

stories.title: Nokjiwon Garden
stories.script: The Most Beautiful Garden in Cheong Wa Dae  In spring, Nokjiwon Garden holds annual events in recognition of occasions such as Children’s Day, Parents’ Day, and Disability Day. This enchanting garden is one of the most picturesque spaces within the Cheong Wa Dae complex and serves as the one location where the general public can meet the President.  During the Joseon Dynasty, Nokjiwon Garden was the backyard outside the Sinmumun Gate of Gyeongbokgung Palace. It was initially served as the venue for civil service examinations and was later changed into an outdoor garden used for banquets and stock yard.  Nokjiwon Garden consists of approximately 120 different tree species, which are thoughtfully arranged around a 170-year-old Korean pine tree standing at an impressive height of 16 meters. In addition, you can find anniversary trees that were personally planted by former presidents. Korean pine trees are renowned for their elegant and umbrella-like growth shape. During the 2018 Inter-Korean Summit, a Korean pine tree that had been nurtured since 1953 was planted at the Peace House in Panmunjeom to commemorate this historic event.

stories.title: Chunchugwan
stories.script: Chunchugwan  Chunchugwan was built in 1990 and named after the organizations that were responsible for keeping historical records during the Goryeo and Joseon dynasties. The name bears the meaning “a place where history is recorded in a fair and critical manner.”  With the opening of Chunchugwan, a photo zone was installed where visitors can pose as a spokesperson of Cheong Wa Dae. In the front lawn is a tent where visitors can stop by for a break and take in the view of the Bugaksan and Inwangsan mountains.

stories.title: Chilgung Palace
stories.script: Tablet Hall for the Seven Consorts  Chilgung Palace is a tablet hall that enshrines the ancestral tablets of seven royal concubines who gave birth to the kings of the Joseon dynasty but were not crowned queens. Chilgung Palace consist of Yuksanggung Palace, housing the tablet of Consort Choi Suk-bin of King Sukjong; Jeogyeonggung Palace, housing the tablet of Consort Kim In-bin of King Seonjo; Daebingung Palace, housing the tablet of Consort Jang Hui-bin of King Sukjong; Yeonhogung Palace, housing the tablet of Consort Yi Jeong-bin of King Yeongjo; Seonhuigung Palace, housing the tablet of Consort Yi Yeong-bin of King Yeongjo; Gyeongugung Palace, housing the tablet of Consort Bak Su-bin of King Jeongjo; and Deogangung Palace, housing the tablet of Consort Eom of Emperor Gojong.  The ancestral tablets of the kings and queens of the Joseon dynasty are all enshrined in Jongmyo, but the kings who were born from consorts made a separate shrine to pay respect to their birth mother. Originally, only Yuksanggung Palace was located here, and the other six palaces that were scattered throughout Seoul were also moved to this location in 1908. Hence, the name Chilgung means “the seven palaces.”  Chilgung Palace was closed to the public since 1968. In 2001, it began allowing entry to special visitors of Cheong Wa Dae. Eventually, it was opened to the public completely in 2018. The palaces are not as large and fancy as the other palace buildings, but they create a peaceful and cozy atmosphere.

stories.title: Chimnyugak
stories.script: Enjoying Leisure at Cheong Wa Dae Chimnyugak   Chimnyugak Pavilion is designated as a Seoul Tangible Cultural Heritage. The name Chimnyu means “rest on flowing water as if it were a pillow.” The exact date of when Chimnyugak was built remains unknown. Based on the hanok style of the 1920s and the fact that Chimnyugak is missing on the map of Gyeongbokgung Palace after palace renovations in 1867, it is speculated to have been built sometime in the early 1900s.  At the center is a room and spacious maru, a raised wooden floor, with another raised maru in the front. The overall design demonstrates the beauty and practicality of a hanok.   Originally located on the western side of the premises, Chimnyugak Pavilion was moved to the current location with the construction of the official residence. On the right side of Chimnyugak is a traditional thatched house with a small garden, where the president and family personally grew a variety of garden vegetables.

stories.title: Ounjeong Pavilion
stories.script: Colorful Clouds Leading to the Heavens  If you proceed up the forest trail behind the official residence, you will soon arrive at Ounjeong Pavilion, meaning “the heavenly five-colored clouds.” The name is believed to have originated from Oungak Pavilion, which was originally constructed in the back garden of Gyeongbokgung Palace in 1868. Ounjeong Pavilion was originally located at the site of the official residence but was relocated to its current site due to the construction of the residence.  Oujeong Pavilion was assumed to be built during the presidency of former President Rhee Syngman. The signboard bears the personal calligraphy of President Rhee, known for his proficiency in brush calligraphy.  The pavilion is square shaped with a hipped and gabled roof, with all four corners converging at the central peak. Each side of the building features doors that allow visitors to open them and enjoy panoramic views of the city from the pavilion. The green forest scenery stretch out below the pavilion, providing a stunning backdrop. From this vantage point, you can take in views of Gwanghwamun Gate and Jongno, making it a highly recommended spot to appreciate both the natural beauty and the urban landscape.

stories.title: Minambul
stories.script: Smile that Withstood the Test of Time Minambul  A little further from Ounjeong Pavilion toward the main building is The Stone Buddha Seated on a Square Pedestal. This statue is also referred to as Minambul, meaning “handsome Buddha,” due to its gorgeous appearance. Inspired by the main statue of Seokguram Grotto, Minambul was carved in the 9th century. The statue is characterized by a compassionate smile, confident and balanced posture, and good physique, demonstrating styles that were prominent in Unified Silla during their prime.  Minambul was originally based in Namsan, Gyeongju, but was moved to the Namsan area in Seoul during the Japanese administration. It was brought to the current location after the construction of the official residence.   The square pedestal which the Buddha statue sits on has an exquisite lotus pattern that is rarely seen on works crafted during the Unified Silla period. In addition, the statue was relatively well preserved and was designated as a Seoul Tangible Cultural Heritage in 1974. In 2018, it was promoted to a state-designated heritage as a National Treasure.  Cheong Wa Dae is facing a dawn of a new era with the relocation of the presidential office to Yongsan. Minambul continues to oversee the change with his compassionate smile as he had for the past thousand years.

stories.title: Inwang Hall and Chungmu Hall on the 1st Floor (Main Office Building)
stories.audioTitle: Inwang Hall and Chungmu Hall on the 1st Floor (Main Office Building)
stories.script: Inwang Hall, the conference room holding press conferences with foreign leaders; Chungmu Hall, a room for holding appointment ceremonies  The Inwang Hall was used for holding joint press conferences with foreign leaders and as a banquet room to honor the guests. Many social gatherings, lunch meetings and dinner parties were held in the hall. Different from other halls located in the main office building, Inwang Hall has a sophisticated western style interior design. Amidst the predominantly white-themed room, a mural depicting the Tongyeonghang Port, created by artist Jeon Hyeok-nim from Tongyeong in 2006, draws attention. The blue mural on the wall creates a sense of gentle waves, in contrast to the room's white ambiance.  Conversely, Chungmu Hall is located in the right-wing annex of the main office building. It's a spacious hall capable of accommodating a large number of people, making it suitable for hosting appointment ceremonies, award commendations, and large-scale meetings. The hall also features folding screen paintings and banquet paintings from the Joseon Dynasty. Please be aware that the placement of artworks in Cheong Wa Dae may vary depending on events and other circumstances.

stories.title: 2nd Floor (Main Office Building)
stories.script: The working office of the president and various artworks of the main office building  As you ascend the red-carpeted staircase, you will arrive on the second floor of the main office building. The painting installed on the wall in the middle of the staircases, titled “Painting of Splendid Rivers and Mountains,” is an art piece of Korean contemporary artist Kim Shik. If you view from a distance, it provides an overview of the entire Korean Peninsula. However, when you go upstairs and look at the painting up close, you can appreciate all the intricate details of the peninsula. It is believed that successive presidents must have had various contemplations as a leader of the country when passing by this painting on their way to their offices.  Looking up the ceiling, you can find an astronomical chart that looks as if the stars are about to fall. Created during the reign of Yi Sung-gye, the founder of the Joseon Dynasty, it's known as the Cheonsang Yeolcha Bunyajido. This chart is said to depict 1,467 stars that were observed and engraved. This astronomical image is also drawn on the back of the 10,000 won bill, representing a cultural heritage that illustrates the creative and scientific mindset of the Joseon Dynasty. In addition, a resplendent chandelier graces the space, radiating light like falling stars.  As you proceed to the second floor, you'll encounter an oval-shaped office to your right. The desk used by former presidents still occupies the room, where numerous historic decisions were made. A blue phoenix flag symbolizing the president is prominently displayed. On the wall behind it, you can observe a golden Rose of Sharon, the national flower of South Korea, flanked by two golden phoenixes.

stories.title: Mugunghwa Hall and Sejong Hall on the 1st Floor (Main Office Building)
stories.audioTitle: Mugunghwa Hall and Sejong Hall on the 1st Floor (Main Office Building)
stories.script: Mugunghwa Hall, the working space of the First Lady; Sejong Hall, the former State Council Room  Upon entering the main building, you can see a lengthy staircase adorned with a red carpet, representing the presidency. Before going upstairs, let’s take a look of the first floor. The first floor houses various important rooms, including the First Lady's office, a banquet room for hosting foreign dignitaries, a conference room for political discussions, and a reception room for welcoming distinguished citizens.  Mugunghwa Hall, situated on the left side of the central staircase, used to serve as the First Lady's office and reception area. Its white-themed interior design has symbolized the elegance of successive First Ladies, with portraits of the First Ladies hanging on the white wall.   The hall next to Mugunghwa Hall is Sejong Hall. It was previously functioned as a meeting room and reception room for the president. It features a carpet woven with Korean vowels and consonants characters. Portraits of former Korean presidents are displayed on the walls. The spacious room, which once hosted State Council meetings, exhibits various items related to past presidents.  ‘Ilwolobongdo,’ displayed on the wall near the entrance, is a landscape painting by Song Gyu-tae, a master of Korean folk painting. This folding screen painting depicts the Korean landscape with mountain peaks, the sun, and the moon, similar to those found behind the king's seat during the Joseon Dynasty. The reason for hanging this painting, which was traditionally placed behind the king’s seat, in the president’s office is its significance as a traditional and symbolic artwork from the Joseon Dynasty.  Adjacent to ‘Ilwolobongdo,’ ‘Hunminjeongeum’ is a work by Baek Geum-nam. This artwork depicts the Korean alphabet created by King Sejong, the fourth king of the Joseon Dynasty. King Sejong developed the Korean characters to simplify writing and reading by replacing the complex Chinese characters which were challenging for many people. ‘Hunminjeongeum’ in the State Council room prompts contemplation on the necessity of state governance for the people.

stories.title: Yeongdo Tourism Information Center
stories.script: The observatory at the Yeongdo Tourism Information Center, where Yeongdo gets closer to you  What do you look for when you're traveling? Some look for famous restaurants and good food, and some scenic routes for a nice walk. Like this, the theme of the travel is decided based on the goal or the means of the trip. This is a great place to plan and start your journey in Yeongdo. It is Yeongdo Tourism Information Center, inspired by the Yeongdo Bridge's appearance.   The Center that boasts a striking look consists of the ground floor to the third floor and an outdoor observatory. On the ground floor, you are greeted by intuitive touchscreens that introduce various legends and stories about Yeongdo, as well as renowned tourist attractions and the Eight Scenic Places of Yeongdo. The second floor is the Yeongdo modern history exhibition room. It invites you to learn about Yeongdo's modern history through comparative timelines between now and 1920. The third-floor houses Bongrae Lighters Wharf gallery, which exhibits unique artists active in Yeongdo.   The observatory on the top floor is the highlight of the Information Center! You can watch the famous bascule bridge of Yeongdo opening and closing. You can look down upon the busy pier of Busan with moored fishing boats through the framed photo zone. It is also a great spot to take memorable photographs.    Yeongdo Tourism Information Center is open all year round except for January 1st, the Lunar New Year's day, and the day of Chuseok to provide information to the tourists, so please make sure to stop by if you have planned for a Yeongdo trip!

stories.title: Sky Observatory
stories.script: Sky Observatory  What is your impression of Busan’s seascape? Usually, people think of a blue ocean, waves crashing under the sparkling sun and the blue sky. Yeongdo’s Sky Observatory, just like its name, invites you to enjoy the picturesque view of the open sky and sea. Here you can truly appreciate Busan’s marine landscapes.    The Sky Observatory features a semi-transparent floor from which everyone, even children, can observe the breathtaking view from above. A corner for couples allows them to attach padlocks as a romantic gesture. From the observatory, you can see many different islands. You can even see Daema Island using telescopes installed in the observatory on a clear day.    The Sky Observatory is located on the Jeoryeong Coastal Walk between Huinnyeoul Culture Village and Taejongdae. It’s also connected to the 75 Plaza. Enjoy the feeling of walking on clouds at the Sky Observatory, from which you can immerse yourself in the view of the open sea to the front and rich, green forests to the back, all enveloped in a cool marine breeze. Here you can start your day refreshed and clear your head at the end of the day.

stories.title: Taejongdae Observatory
stories.script: Taejongdae Observatory, where you can appreciate the gift of nature  The name 'Taejongdae' originates from King Taejong Muyeol of the Silla Dynasty. While touring the country, the king was captivated by the breathtaking coastal scenery and enjoyed practicing archery in the park area. Spanning about 440 acres, the Taejongdae Recreation Area centers around its highest peak, standing 250 meters above sea level, and boasts an array of approximately 120 tree species, including the sea pine. Along the coast, one can marvel at cliffs, uniquely shaped rocks, and views of the Korea Strait. On clear days, Japan's Tsushima Island, about 56 km away, is visible.  The Taejongdae Observatory was designated as a tourist attraction representing Busan in 1969, designated as National Cultural Heritage Site No. 17 in November 2005, and declared a National Geopark on November 27, 2013. It stands as the only destination in Busan to be selected five times consecutively as one of the '100 Best Korean Tourist Destinations' by the Ministry of Culture, Sports, and Tourism and the Korea Tourism Organization. The observatory offers convenient indoor tourist facilities, including picnic-themed cafes, Korean restaurants, and convenience stores. Visitors are greeted with panoramic views of the azure sea upon arrival.  However, before becoming a prominent tourist spot, Taejongdae Observatory witnessed tragic incidents. In the 1970s, despairing individuals jumped from the cliffs to commit suicide where the observatory now stands. It was once infamously known as 'Suicide Rock.' To address this social concern, Gumyeongsa Temple was built in 1976, serving as a poignant reminder of the value of life for visitors. Additionally, a statue portraying a mother embracing two children was installed at the entrance of Taejongdae Observatory, symbolizing profound maternal love and offering solace and hope to those contemplating suicide.  Immerse yourself in the beauty of nature at Taejongdae Observatory?leave behind life's daily hardships and adversities and relish the gift of serene moments bestowed by nature.

stories.title: Cheonghak Reservoir Observatory
stories.script: Cheonghak Reservoir Observatory, where the lights of the city and the port dance together  The port city of Busan has many attractions near piers. What comes to mind first when you think of Busan's night view? Recently, places with a panoramic view of Busan's harbor have emerged as new night view spots. They are called 'harbor view' spots.  The Yeongdo Cheonghak Reservoir Observatory is one of the most popular harbor view spots. It overlooks Yeongdo and its surrounding seas as well as the Busanhangdaegyo Bridge, which shines with different lights every minute. Lights from the city and docks harmonize together here, creating an admirable view. The scenery created by the high mountains, waterways, and the urban landscape of Busan is spectacular.  The way to the observatory features public exercise facilities in an ample open space. The facilities include exercise equipment and acupressure pebbles. The surrounding area of the observatory is also well-known as a filming location for famous TV shows and movies.  There are sculptures of Jeolyeong horses and a farmer carrying sweet potatoes at the observatory, all of which symbolize Yeongdo.  Jeolyeongdo, which was the original name of Yeongdo, was known for the farm that raised national horses.    Its production of many famous horses is recorded in historical documents, including Samguk Sagi, Goryeosa, and Dongguk Yeoji Seungram, and is now celebrated by statues that represent Jeolyeong horses. Yeongdo's sweet potatoes are also famous. Yeongdo was the first planting site for sweet potatoes, which were introduced by Chosun's diplomat Jo Eom. Raw sweet potatoes used to relieve hunger in the past. The gentle smile of the farmer carrying the sweet potato comes through.   Below the deck is a map that introduces Yeongdo's attractions. Check out the Busanhangdaegyo Bridge as well as downtown Yeongdo. The harmony of Busan's iconic pier and the splendid city center will forever stay in your memories.

stories.title: Sunrise Observatory
stories.script: Sunrise Observatory, where the sun rises with hope  The Sunrise Observatory is the first place to see the rising sun in Busan. Sunrise Village, which houses the Observatory, is located at the highest point in Yeongdo. The lush, crimson sunrise emerges from the eastern slopes of Bongrae mountain. It is said that the village’s name reflects the residents’ wish to prosper together with the rising sun.  Sunrise Village was originally a cemetery. During the Korean War, North Korean refugees wandered in search of a place to live. They built houses with stones and soil and established a village. Later, refugees living near Busan Station joined, expanding the town. The village stood upon the sorrows of life, buried along with the lives of refugees.  Sunrise Village stands where the top road of the village, a long walk down the steep alleyway between the narrow houses, and the Bongraesan trail meet. Its connection to the path makes the village part of a popular hiking course. During the day, you can enjoy the beautiful view of Bongrae Mountain, a pride of Yeongdo. The fantastic night view of Busan from the Sunrise Observatory is also worth checking out.   The Sunrise Observatory was built in 2016. Its terrace features a photo zone, a cafe where you can enjoy a cup of coffee and a view of the village, and an observation deck overlooking the village. The colorful houses of the village at sunrise add to the fun of looking at the scenery.  It is a place where the scenery is as incredible as the height of the tall town. How about greeting Busan’s morning at the Sunrise Observatory?

stories.title: Seobok Observatory
stories.script: Seobok Observatory, a wish for immortality in nature  Have you ever heard of a person named Seobok? Qinshihuang, the first emperor to unify mainland China, and his subject, Seobok, were inseparable. The story of their relationship continues to this day.  In Yeongdo, there is a park that thematizes Seobok’s story as a tourist attraction. At the ‘Bulocho Park,’ which is based on Qin Shi Huang’s long-lasted dream of immortality, you can see an observatory after passing the Bulomun, the door of eternal youth. The name of this observatory is ‘Seobok Observatory.’ The name comes from a legend that one of the places where Qinshihuang sent Seobok to find the elixir plant was Bongrae Mountain.  The legend goes, Bongrae Mountain that Seobok visited is located in the middle of the eastern sea and houses gods, elixir plants, and elixirs of eternal life. The Bulocho Park, completed in 2014 on Busan’s Bongrae Mountain, fosters various medicinal herbs and numerous ecological resources. Yeongdo residents, as well as visitors from all over the country, come to this place.  The Seobok Observatory stands on the other side of the Bulomun Gate of Bulocho Park. Bullomun is a gate that symbolizes longevity and contains the wish of Qinshihuang, who wanted to find elixir plants that promised eternal youth and immortality.   The scenery from the observatory here is just as spectacular as the folk tales handed down over the years. From here, you can see Busan Port and Busanhangdaegyo from sunrise to nightfall. Please enjoy the superb view that nature offers from the Seobok Observatory.

stories.title: Jungni Sunset Observatory
stories.script: Jungni Sunset Observatory, where you can enjoy a golden sunset  What do you think when you see a sunset that burns red and then sets? Busan has a lot of famous spots known for sunrise and sunset, and Dadaepo Beach is one of the best-known spots. But did you know that Yeongdo also has excellent places to watch the sunset?   You can safely and comfortably enjoy the sunset in the scenery that harmonizes a red lighthouse and blue waves at the Jungni Sunset Observatory on Jungni Beach, the starting and ending point of the Jeolyeong Coastal Trail in Yeongdo.  Yeongdo Jungni Beach, a gravel beach with a sunset observatory and Haenyeo Village, is also known as ‘Jungri Haenyeo Village.’ This is where the Jungni Sunset Observatory is. Unlike other beaches, the waves here are calm, and the coastal road is beautiful, making it one of the most scenic driving routes.  The Jungni Sunset Observatory features a square frame-shaped photo zone and a unique viewing facility with one end fixed and the other unsupported. It is also connected to Yeongdo Galmaetgil, which provides an opportunity to enjoy the fresh air, take a walk during the daytime, and wrap up a long day by watching a sunset in Jungni.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 1. Yeongdodaegyo
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 1. Yeongdodaegyo
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Kangkangee Culture Village: 1. Yeongdodaegyo  Welcome to Yeongdodaegyo, the country's first-ever bridge connecting the mainland to an island as well as the only bascule bridge in Korea to this date! Although it has been remodeled into a more contemporary look, the birth of the bridge dates back to the Japanese occupation period. On November 23, 1934, the news of a bridge that would break in half and rise high into the sky brought onlookers from not only Busan but also Miryang and Yangsan. The number of people who gathered at the completion ceremony was a whopping 50,000, which is a significant figure considering that Busan's population at the time was only 150,000. Following the completion ceremony, “Chodosik” during which the first steps taken on the bridge were held as well. A Japanese sacred rituals official led the way with a sacred piece of wood with the spirit of heaven in his hands and then 124 children selected from primary schools around Busan walked over the bridge. It was a slightly different scene from the traditional Chodosik of Korea in which households with 3 generations living in harmony were chosen and the eldest men from those households walked over the bridge first. In the following year, railroad tracks were installed so trains departing from Dongnae also passed over this bridge, which meant that it truly became a bridge for the Yeongdo residents.  The birth of this bridge, however, was not easy. According to the original plan, Yeongdodaegyo was going to be built as a common bridge. But, as soon as the plan was announced, a strong opposition followed. If the bridge was installed as it had been planned, it was convenient for people and cargo to move on land but large vessels that go in and out of Busan Port had to make a detour all the way around Yeongdo even with a shortcut laying right in front of them. Owners of ships complained because of the increase in cost, which led to an abrupt change of design. In the early days of its operation, the bridge was repeatedly lifted and lowered seven times a day to fulfill its duties but due to the considerably large maintenance cost, this number began to gradually decrease as time went by. From 1966 to 2013, the bridge was not lifted once over four decades, and this was an unavoidable choice for the growth of Yeongdo.  Until the 60s, people could not access tap water in Yeongdo because no waterworks system was installed that could bring water from the mainland. But, as industries and the population grew in Yeongdo, people could no longer bear the inconvenience so a big decision was made to install water pipes along Yeongdodaegyo. Having lost its character since then, the bridge was treated as the less preferred brother to the juxtaposed “Busandaegyo ” before eventually facing the risk of being demolished. However, the people of Busan would not let a bridge that had been with them through the ages of turbulence be torn down so easily. For nearly 3 years, they put a great amount of efforts into building a sturdy, durable bridge while trying to reproduce the old appearance as much as possible. Looking at the stone steps and walls at the entrance of the bridge, you will see old, stained stones meshed with new, smooth stones. This seems to show the age of Yeongdo Bridge that embraces the turbulence of yesterday while protecting the daily lives of today with great vigor.

stories.title: Busan Bridge
stories.script: Busan Bridge, a symbolic bridge of Busan  There are a total of 7 coastal bridges in Busan that connect land and sea. Busan Bridge, built as a symbol of the development of Busan Port, broke its ground in 1976 and was completed in 1980. Before the bridge's opening, the current Yeongdo Bridge was called Busan Bridge. It has been connecting Jung-gu and Yeongdo-gu in Busan ever since its completion.  Busan Bridge has replaced the current Yeongdo Bridge, which was built under Japanese rule, as a representative structure of Busan. Its name comes from the fact that it represents Busan as the longest arch bridge in Korea. This gorgeous bridge celebrated the 100th anniversary of the opening of Busan Port and symbolizes Korea's industrial development.   Busan Bridge functions as an industrial road and a port road that easily handles the traffic volume of the Yeongdo district, a shipbuilding industrial complex, and a new port. Large trucks weighing 54 tons that cannot pass through the Yeongdo Bridge can pass Busan Bridge. The bridge also connects to Busan's urban expressway and thus directly links Busan Port and Gyeongbu Expressway.  Busan Bridge was designed and constructed by Korean engineers and is considered a turning point in developing domestic architectural engineering and construction technologies. Its size and complex structure make it meaningful that Korean engineers completed it with Korean materials.  The size is truly impressive. It is 260m long and 20m wide and has four-lane roadways and sidewalks 2m wide on each side.   Steel arches made of the tide arch method, a design method that connects the bridges at both ends of the arch with horizontal tension members, rise to a height of 31m, becoming a symbol of Busan. The original color of the bridge was orange, but it is now gray and white, reflecting modern beauty. Its new hues harmonize with the surrounding area, stabilizing the vibrant harbor nearby and downtown atmosphere.  Please take a closer look at the Busan Bridge, which shows the true nature of the port city of Busan and its value as a magnificent bridge.

stories.title: South Port Bridge
stories.script: South Port Bridge, connecting the South Port and Yeongdo with beautiful lights  Busan has many bridges that let you walk on the sea road. South Port Bridge is particularly famous for its landscape lighting in Yeongdo-gu, where four bridges are connected. Although it does not have remarkable sculptures or statues, the installed lighting gracefully harmonizes with the structural beauty of the bridge. South Port Bridge is a maritime bridge that connects Amnam-dong, Seo-gu, Busan and Yeongseon-dong, Yeongdo-gu. Its name comes from it linking the South Port to Yeongdo.   South Port Bridge has 3m wide sidewalks, allowing pedestrians to stroll and enjoy the scenery of the South Port area freely. Visitors can also enjoy views of Yongdusan Park, Jagalchi Market, Huinnyeoul Village, Jeolyeong Coastal Walk, and Songdo Beach.  South Port Bridge has unexpected charms. Its day and night are 180 degrees different. It provides a reliable walking trail during the day and presents a beautiful night view of the South Port adorned by a state-of-the-art LED lighting system. The visual feast of ships sleeping at the anchorage amidst the dazzling lights from sunset to midnight is also a sight to behold.  The 360m-long main route, where ships pass, decorates the night view with a dynamic colorful lighting spectacle every hour on Saturdays and public holidays. Enjoy the splendid display of lights on South Port Bridge.

stories.title: Busan Port Bridge
stories.script: Busan Port Bridge, the landmark of Busan  Busan Port Bridge, whose name comes from its function of connecting across Busan Port, was built on the North Port, the largest port in Busan. It is Korea's first steel-composite cable-stayed bridge and is rated as the world's fifth-largest steel-composite cable-stayed bridge. The bridge has received many external awards and honors, including the Grand Prize for Civil Structures by the Korean Society of Civil Engineers in 2015, the Grand Prize in Civil Engineering and Construction Technology in 2014, and the Best Artwork Award by the Concrete Society in 2014.  Busan Port Bridge connects Gamman-dong and Cheonghak-dong. This 3,331m-long bridge crosses the North Port and consists of a 1,114m-long cable-stayed section and a 2,217m-long connecting bridge. It forms the central axis of the coastal ring road connecting Gwangan Bridge, Yeongdo Highway Overpass, and South Port Bridge. The bridge has a reputation as a luxury bridge for providing a safe structure for transportation and beautiful scenery. Its diamond-shaped pylon offers an unforgettable spectacle and, at the same time, functions to resist wind more effectively.   Busan Port Bridge has a unique space—a camping ground in the city center. Yeongdo Marino Auto Camping Ground, a place where you can see the whole of Busan Port, represents the sea and the O-shaped circular path coming together in harmony. This eco-friendly campground has 52 sites (40 for cars, 12 for regular tents) where you can set up your tent and enjoy camping. There are also 7 fixed caravans where you can stay overnight, 107 parking lots, a walking trail, and an event plaza.  Please enjoy the leisure provided by Busan Port Bridge, the representative coastal bridge of Busan, and take memorable photographs, too.

stories.title: Introduction: Overview of Hantan River Columnar Joint Road
stories.audioTitle: Introduction: Overview of Hantan River Columnar Joint Road
stories.script: Welcoming comments & Introduction of the audio guide application Hello, welcome to the Hantan River Columnar Joint Road in Cheorwon, Korea. We are Haeshik Shin, Jeong-eun Park, and Sunhee Kim, and we are geopark Interpreters of Cheorwon County. It is an honor to introduce you to the attractions of our county while walking along the road today.   We'd like to not only show you the scenery but also share with you many interesting hidden stories as we walk along the road. Therefore, the Cheorwon County Office and the Korea Tourism Organization have developed an audio guide application called Odii. With this application on, you will be able to feel as if you were on a personal guided tour along this Hantan River Columnar Joint Road. Please listen to the first three audio clips and start your own guided tour with this app on.  The tour will begin in front of the tourist map of the Hantan River Columnar Joint Road near the ticket booth. Please make sure to purchase an admission ticket and you may use the public restroom before meeting back up in front of the map.

stories.title: Introduction: Overview of Hantan River Columnar Joint Road
stories.audioTitle: Introduction: Overview of Hantan River Columnar Joint Road
stories.script: Introduction of the Hantan River Columnar Joint Road Are you ready to get started with your tour? This area here is called the Hantan River Columnar Joint Road in Cheorwon, Korea. This trail consists of gallery roads on the riverside cliffs along the river. Many of you may know them as gallery roads, a type of cliff-hanging access road. Some of you might have experienced walking on the gallery roads while sightseeing or trekking in mainland China. The gallery road is a kind of a cliff road or a plank road, which you're going to walk on for the next hour or so.  Overview of the UNESCO Global Geoparks You are now inside the Hantangang UNESCO Global Geopark, which is the very first geopark focused on a river in Korea. The river begins at Jangamsan Mountain in Pyeonggang County, North Korea and meets together with the Imjin River downstream. The whole Hantan River and some of the Imjin River were formed with volcanic eruptions between 540,000 and 120,000 years ago. The lava ran through old channels, later developing various interesting volcanic shapes such as basaltic gorges, columnar joints, and waterfalls. Located in the central part of the Korean Peninsula, this particular geopark was added to the list by UNESCO back in July, 2020 for its valuable geological, ecological, historical, and cultural heritage. You can probably recognize the blue UNESCO logo on the map. Hantangang UNESCO Global Geopark is the fourth designated in Korea after Jeju Island, Cheongsong, and Mudeungsan Mountain. Not only are the citizens of Cheorwon proud of this but all Koreans throughout the country are proud of our Geoparks.

stories.title: Introduction: Overview of the Hantan River Columnar Joint Road
stories.audioTitle: Introduction: Overview of the Hantan River Columnar Joint Road
stories.script: Overview of the different sections of the Trail Would you please look closely at the big tourist map of the Hantan River Columnar Joint Road? The trail was opened to the general public on November 19th, 2021 after three years of construction from 2018. The trail is 3.6 km long, 1.5 meters wide and it takes about one and half hours for a one-way trip tour. There are 26 points including 13 bridges, 10 rest areas, and 3 observatories. You can start your own tour either from the Sundam Entrance or from the Deureuni Entrance. Either way will be fine. The bridges and rest areas in the photos on the map are named from the geological features or scenery along the routes, so understanding the meanings of each point will help you appreciate the river and its associated scenery better. The audio guide commentaries are available when you touch the play button at each point. Each audio clip lasts about 1 to 2 minutes; you'll get to know this trail in the same you would if you were on a guided tour led by a well-informed tour guide.  Safety Precautions Before we get started, I'd like to remind you of a few things. First, please be sure to stop by the public restroom before you start walking along the gallery road. Also, please note that drinking any alcoholic beverage is strictly forbidden before or during the tour as a safety precaution. We'd like to recommend to some local foods and drinks to enjoy at a nearby restaurant AFTER enjoying your scenic experience along the routes.  Secondly, the whole trail has many uphill and downhill slopes consisting of about one thousand steps. We recommend you prepare some water and energy snacks for the journey just in case. Another thing is, as there are no trash bins available along the cliff-hanging routes, please remember to take back whatever you have brought along with you for the breath-taking scenic excursion along the river.  Last but not the least, the surfaces of the trail can be very slippery when rainy or cold, so be cautious when taking each step. Now that you are ready, shall we start our exciting and scenic journey?

stories.title: Sundam Valley Rest Area
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at the Sundam Valley Observation Rest Area The deck you are now standing on is a great spot to view the panoramic scenery of the Hantan River. You're in the Sundam Valley, one of the most scenic locations here in Cheorwon looking down to the streams of the river.  Origins of the Name Sundam literally means watershield growing pond. The scientific name of the plant watershield is Brasenia schreberi, which is a medicinal herb well-known for its detoxifying effects such as cooling down a fever and soothing swelling. It was used in the royal palaces during the Joseon Dynasty in Korea. A high-ranking official named Kim, Kwanju about 200 years ago stayed around here for ten years while growing watershields in a pond nearby and drinking the extract of the sprouts to help him heal from a physical disease. The white building to the far right on the ridge is where the Sundam pond used to be located.  Scenery of the Sundam Valley 5 kilometers downstream from here in Sundam Valley is one of the most popular locations to whitewater rafting companions especially in Summer, as the valley has a great environment including odd-looking rocks, vertical cliffs, abundant water flowing, and naturally formed white sandy fields along the shore, which is not common to find on a riverside. You can also find a pine trees and an oak tree fused together on the left-hand side of the gallery road near the top of the access steps to the rest area. Viewing fused trees, especially between different species is not something you get to see every day, so make sure to not miss this romantic sight. It would be a good idea to preserve this memory with your heart as well as with your camera. They say traveling is not just about making time but following your heart. We hope you will enjoy your time with all your heart. Those of you starting from the Sundam Entrance, please enjoy the rest of the scenery along the columnar joint road till the Deureuni entrance. Those of you starting from the Deureuni entrance are about to leave the gallery road soon, so we hope that you will cherish the pleasant memories from here along the Hantan River. Thank you very much for visiting our town.

stories.title: Sundam Valley Sky Observation Deck
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Sundam Valley Sky Observation Deck You have walked on the gallery road with lots of holes in it so far. Was it scary? If you feel afraid, please don't look at the surface of the road, but try to look far to the scenery around. You have arrived at Sundam Valley Sky Observation Deck.  Overview of Sundam Valley Sky Observation Deck While walking along on the Sundam Valley Sky Observation Deck, please enjoy the natural mysteries harmonized with the Hantan River and rocky cliffs alongside while.   Structure of the Sky Observation Deck. You can have an even better look at the surrounding scenery if you walk to the middle of the observation deck. The observation deck itself weighs nine tons and it can hold up to 180 tons including the visitors on it. Each of the nine steel cables holds 20 tons respectively. It is obviously amazing to see the natural beauty, but the human technology that allows us to appreciate it more closely is also absolutely mind-blowing. Safety guards as well as the geopark commentators are stationed at every important stop for your safety and pleasant travel, so that you will always be able to enjoy the scenic views along the Hantan River in Cheorwon to your heart’s content.

stories.title: Dancheung Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Dancheung Bridge You have now arrived at Dancheung Bridge. Dancheung literally means a geological fault in English, or a large crack in the rocks that form the Earth’s surface. This bridge is named so because it's a good location to view such a geological phenomenon.  Overview of Dancheung, or Geological Fault. Earth's crust is known not to stay in one permanent location, but to move slightly from location to location. In such a process of rock-mass movements, some part of the crust is pulled or pushed sideways and when this happens, the earth’s crust can also bend or some geological formations could also be cut off the  A fault plane represents the fracture surface of a fault. A fault trace or fault line is a place where the fault can be seen on the surface. In other words, you're now at a location where such geological displacement can be best viewed.   Location of the Geological Fault If you look at the rock cliff from around the center of the bridge, you can find a crack in the middle of the cliff. The crack is Dancheung, or a geological fault. As the bridge is narrow and there are a lot of passers-by, please be careful when viewing the geological fault on the cliff.

stories.title: Seondol Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Seondol Bridge Now, you are at Seondol Bridge. Seondol in Korean literally means an upright rock. Those of you coming from the Sundam Entrance will find the upright rock standing on the closer shore of the river just before crossing the bridge while those of you from the Deureuni Entrance will enjoy the view of the vertical rock slightly slanting toward the upstream of the river right after passing the bridge. The bridge is named Seondol because of this extraordinary rock formation.  Overview of Seondol When you look down to the river, you can find various rock formations reduced or destroyed gradually by fast-flowing water in an especially steep decline. Such a gradual reduction process is called erosion, and the upright rock, or Seondol in Korean, is formed by the erosion process. Isn't it amazing that hard rock such as granite has been changed into an upright formation over a long period of time? Looking at these rock formations sometimes reminds me how our rigid mindset can be smoothed down to rather a than dull, more understanding state over time. As we gradually age, don't we have a certain personality that stands out just like this upright rock?

stories.title: Guriso Rest Area
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Guriso Observation Rest Area Those of you a little tired of walking so far can take a break at this rest area. We'd like to recommend that you take a rest on the bench while listening to the water flowing below here as it is the main reason why people are drawn here and want to take a break at this rest area.  Overview of Guriso Rest Area How does the name Guriso sound to you? Isn't it cute? There are two theories about the origin of this name; first, some people thought the water flowing in the rapids of the Hantan River sounded like water boiling in an iron pot as the Korean word guri is a sound symbolism of boiling water. Second, some people also thought they could hear nine different sounds from the water flowing here as gu in Guriso refers to the number nine in the Korean language. Well, why don't you try to find nine different sounds while listening to the flowing water below?  Pop Quizzes for Rock Formations Can you find the protruding rock to the right near the river below from around the center of the rest area? What do you think it looks like? It is called Lion Rock because some say it looks like the front part of a lion. The rock itself has no specific name. You can name it whatever image comes into your mind first. Why don't you find and name your own rock here in the Hantan River? For your information, I personally call the rock on the far left of the river side ET Rock as it looks like the E.T. in the famous Hollywood movie.  Zoning Out While Looking into Water Some people say they love camping because they can enjoy zoning out while sitting around a bonfire. Letting your mind wander while staring at a fire is one of the best ways to  shift your attention away from hectic daily routines. One of the most popular activities here in Cheorwon is zoning out while looking into flowing water. Guriso Rest Area is one such place where you can enjoy letting your mind wander. Why don't you take some time to pace while looking into the flowing water of the rapids and take a rest away from your busy modern life? Now, shall we take off our earphones and listen to the water below here in Guriso Rest Area to let your mind wander for a while?

stories.title: Dolgaegumeong Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Dolgaegumeong Bridge You're now crossing a bridge called Dolgaegumeong Bridge. Dolgaegumeong literally means potholes in a river bed in Korean. We'd like to suggest that you look for as many potholes hidden around here as you can. Are you ready?  Overview of Dolgaegumeong Bridge A pot hole is a smooth, bowl-shaped hole in the ground. You can see many such round holes on rocks along this river side. Have a go at finding as many potholes as you can. How many did you manage to find? No matter how many, you did a good job as the number of the potholes is different depending on the amount of the flowing water. Dolgaegumeong, or a pothole, is created by the erosive forces of pebbles moving around quickly in a circular movement in dented surfaces of the river bed. In other words, smaller rocks make holes bigger in larger rocks. Such phenomena are commonly found in a river bed, especially riverbeds made of hard rocks such as granite. The English name pot hole is named so because of its physical similarity to a metal cooking container. When rapids are slowed down with the amount of water decreasing, you can see some pebbles in these potholes. These pebbles look small but quite heavy, and so you may find them quite adorable. Now, shall we walk on while finding more potholes?

stories.title: Hanyeoul Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Hanyeoul Bridge Many landmarks are named in native Korean expressions here in the Hantan River. The name of this bridge is one such example.  Overview of Hanyeoul Bridge When you look down into the river, some of the river beds are quite steep and have faster flowing water. So, these rapid water flowing sections are called yeoul in Korean. Hanyeoul in Korean literally means large rapids in a river. These rapids are also called lungs of a river. When water flows faster, these rapids generate oxygen and so purify water. Do you see small bubbles in the calm sections past the rapids in the river? People say that these yeoul, or rapids, naturally purify the water in the Hantan River. Another thing is these rapids are in good harmony with the surrounding setting and make elegant layouts together.   Overview of a Mysterious Rock Those of you coming from the Sundam Entrance will find a moss-covered rock to the left-hand side past Hanyeoul Bridge while those from the Deureuni Entrance can see it on the right-hand side just before the bridge. A slight crack is also visible on the right-hand side of the rock; the marks on the rock surface seems to be soaked in water. Something seems to be coming out of the crack. Yes, warm air and heat are coming from the crack and so the narrow open space on the rock is lined with silver frost. It is one of the most mysterious phenomena found in nature.

stories.title: Hwagangam Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Hwagangam Bridge We’re approaching Hwagangam Bridge, one of the most attractive bridges along this cliff-hanging road. Why don't you stop and look around while crossing the bridge here? You'll see a lot of light gray smooth stones scattered everywhere around here. The name of the bridge, Hwagangam, literally means granite stones. The bridge is named so because there are a lot of granite stones found around here.  Overview of granite Can you see all the Granite? Granite is one of the most common rocks here in Korea. The Hantan River was formed by lava flowing from the lava eruption. The Granite already existed before the Cheorwon Plains were covered with lava; it had already been formed deep in the ground about 110 million years ago.  When a candle is lit, melted wax flows down; when the candle light is off, the soft flowing wax is slowly cooled down and hardens again. Rocks formed from volcanic activities are basically the same as hardened candle wax. Deep in the ground below the surface of the Earth is hot molten rock, or magma, heated from the extremely high temperature inside the Earth. Granite refers to the rock slowly cooled down and hardened deep underground. As granite is usually light-colored and has large grains hard enough to withstand heat and physical change, it is frequently used in building. As you are probably aware, many stone pagodas in Korean Buddhist temples are made of granite for that reason.  Overview of the Granite Rock Bed Across Would you take a look at the valley across the river? The stones on the shore are actually granite. Do you see different rocks on top of the granite? They are basalt columnar joints. Here in the Hantan River, the two different types of rocks you can see are found here because the granite existed long before the basalt lava flowed through.  Overview of Mysterious Rocks Those who started from the Sundam entrance, try to find the gorilla shaped rock upstream from where the gallery road curves past the bridge. Two smooth rocks on the shore across the river downstream also look like two dolphins cuddling with each other.

stories.title: Supyeongjeolri Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Supyeongjeolri Bridge You have now arrived at Supyeongjeolri Bridge. This is one of the shortest bridges along the Columnar Joint Road. The stone layers on top of each other across from here are called Supyeongjeolri in Korean, or horizontal columnar joints in English. The columnar joints here are best viewed from the right-hand side of the Saemso Rest Area.  Overview of Joints We will first introduce geological joints. A geological joint is a break found in a rock. It usually starts as a small crack, but it becomes apparently bigger through weathering and erosion over time. Do you see the big empty narrow space in the middle over there? Joints vary according to the type of rock and its circumstances and appear in various shapes when the unknown covering layers are removed. You can view  many columnar joints and horizontal joints here near the Hantan River. There are especially a lot of horizontal joints found along the Hantan River in Cheorwon. You can also view staircase-like rock formations all the way down the granite on the left center section. It's very interesting to see different patterns and shapes mixed in one rock. There is a rock formation that resembles a gorilla upstream from the point where the gallery road is curves past the bridge from the Deureuni direction. Two smooth rocks on the shore across the river downstream also look like two dolphins cuddling with each other.

stories.title: Saemso Observation Rest Area
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Saemso Observation Rest Area You have reached the Saemso Rest Area now. Those of you feeling a little bit tired can take a rest while listening to what we have to tell you.  Overview of Saemso Saemso is a mysterious spot where a natural spring water comes out from the cracks on the rock bed surrounded by odd-looking rocks in the river. The best spot to view the underwater spring is the center of the boardwalk, where you can see bubbling water in the middle of the river with your back toward the public restroom. The bubbling water has the appearance of a school of small fish rising upward in the water. Please note that you may not be able to see the natural phenomena depending on the weather.  Overview of Stony Slopes You can see more and more basalt from the Saemso Observation Rest Area. Do you see the small basalt stones falling on the opposite slope across from here? These stony slopes are pretty common in Korea. They were formed with natural causes.  Public Restrooms The Saemso Rest Area is the only location with public restrooms throughout the whole 3.6km length of the Columnar Joint Road. It is 2.7 kilometers to the Deureuni Entrance and 0.9 km to the Sundam Entrance from here. So don't forget to stop by the restroom before you start the rest of your experience here along the Hantan River.

stories.title: Bawigeuneul Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Bawigeuneul Bridge You're now at Bawigeuneul Bridge. Bawigeuneul in Korean literally means shades from rocks. So, the tourist attraction here is not the bridge but the shades from the rocks nearby. Are you wondering how to get to the shades here? Here's how. Those of you coming from the Sundam Entrance will find the shades on the left in the middle of the boardwalk past Bawigeuneul Bridge while those from Deureuni Entrance will find a big dent in the rock on the right half way down the wooden staircase. The dent looks just like a shade from the rock.  Overview of Bawigeuneul Bridge Water from rainfalls or nearby rivers enters and flows through rock cracks deep underground to create very thick layers of weathered rock soil. Weathering refers to changes in color, condition, etc., because of the effects of the sun, wind, rain, etc., over a long period of time. In other words, rocks become aged just like humans getting wrinkled with age. Granite is weathered into various physical forms. Onion skin weathering, or exfoliation, on the inside the granite rock is best viewed around here. You may think people could live here if the shade were a little bit bigger. Actually, people used to live in these types of rock shades in the prehistoric times. Hard materials such as granite can be weathered and changed into something smaller over time. We shouldn't take granite for granted.

stories.title: Jjokbitso Rest Area
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Jjokbitso Observation Rest Area You have come to Jjokbitso Observation Rest Area. Let me tell you about this area while you're taking a rest.  Overview of Jjokbitso Have you heard the name Jjokbitso before? The name Jjokbitso literally means indigo waterway. It is named so because the water in this river has the color from the plant indigo. Indigo is a natural dye extracted from the leaves of the plant. Jjokbit, or indigo color, is commonly used to describe an attractive natural bluish color. This area is named after the natural dye because the water in this river resembles the dye of the plant.  Overview of Waterfalls Would you come to the center of the rest area? Many of you may be wondering what that place over there is or what that area is for on the opposite side of the river. The opposite side does not belong to Cheorwon County, but to Gwanin-myeon in Pocheon City where people grow rice at the top of the cliffs. Do you see water fall down the cliffs? The water overflows from the rice paddies during the rice growing season usually from May till early November every year.    Overview of Buildings Do you see the two buildings that stand out below the cliffs? There is a mysterious natural spring coming from the rock bed there. The white building on the left is a water-intake facility, which is used for as much as 1,900 tons of the tap water in Gwanin-myeon in Pocheon City. The yellow building on the right is a pumping station that supplies the rice paddies with agricultural water. People often say that travel is not a conquest, but rather should be enjoyment to the fullest. Rather than finish the journey here as soon as possible, we'd like to recommend that you take your time to enjoy the indigo-colored scenery.

stories.title: The 2nd Hole Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at the 2nd Hole Bridge The bridge you are crossing now is named the 2nd Hold Hole Bridge. Aren't you curious why a golf term is used in a geopark?  Overview of the 2nd Hold Bridge This area is famous for the fact that golf balls flow from the 2nd hold of the Valley Course in the Hantan River Country Club nearby. However, don't worry about the golf balls flying from there. As you can see, the whole bridge is covered with guard nets to protect the tourists. The guard nets are installed in a flowing curve so that you may still get a great photo shot angle from the middle of the bridge.  You will find a lot of white or fluorescent-colored golf balls below the bridge while walking across it. You can even play a game about who is going to find more golf balls with your friends in your group till you get to the next stop.

stories.title: Cheorwon Hantan River Sky Observation Deck
stories.audioTitle: Cheorwon Hantan River Sky Observation Deck
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Cheorwon Hantan River Sky Observation Deck Didn’t you feel dizzy already when you saw this viewing point from far away? This is the second sky observation deck on this road, which is named Cheorwon Hantan River Sky Observation Deck.  Overview of the Sky Observation Deck (Glass-bottomed) Cheorwon Hantan River Sky Observation Deck is located halfway on the Columnar Joint Road, with the same structure as Sundam Valley Sky Observation Deck. It has a glass bottom in the middle of the deck where you can look at the river bed under the deck. You can also take a closer look at the basalt columnar joints on the cliffs across from here.  Overview of the Sky Observation Deck (Columnar Joints on the river bed) Do you see the dark stones on the river bed? This is where you can see deep holes in the basalt columnar joints caused by the downcutting of the river water and sometimes, you can see the spring water coming upward. If you look around, you will find that this valley is U-shaped, and unlike other locations along the river, the river bed here is made of basalt columnar joints. It is assumed that the river bed was probably even deeper before the lava eruption occurred.  Overview of the Next Stop. Those of you coming from the Sundam Entrance will walk for the next three to four minutes till Dongjuhwangbyeok Rest Area along the Columnar Joint Road. It would be a good idea to walk while paying attention to the columnar joints, plants blooming on the cliffs, and the water flowing downstream. Why don't you feel the atmosphere with your earphones off?

stories.title: Dongjuhwangbyeok Rest Area
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Dongjuhwangbyeok Observation Rest Area How are feeling walking along this part of the red clay-colored Columnar Joint Road reflected with the sparkling sun shine? You have now reached Dongjuhwangbyeok Rest Area.  Overview of Dongjuhwangbyeok Rest Area You can enjoy viewing the yellow-clay-colored wall across from here. Dongju was an old name of Cheorwon while hwangbyeok refers to a yellow-clay-colored wall. So, the name Dongjuhwangbyeok means the yellow-clay-colored wall here in Cheorwon. Usually, walls of columnar joints are dark-colored, almost black, but the drain water from the rice paddies on top of the columnar joints over there has permeated into the cliffs enough to make them look distinctly like yellow clay. These yellow-clay-colored cliffs become an even more attractive golden color when touched by sunlight. While walking along this part of the road I sometimes imagine what I’ll look like when I grow old. Those of you coming from the Deureuni Entrance will walk along the Columnar Joint Road for the next three to four minutes until you get to Cheorwon Hantan River Sky Observation Deck from Dongjuhwangbyeok Rest Area. We'd like to recommend that you take a walk while paying attention to the nearby columnar joints, plants blooming on the cliffs, and the water flowing downstream. Why don't you enjoy the natural settings with your earphones off?

stories.title: Hyeonmuam Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Hyeonmuam Bridge Hyeonmuam Bridge is one of the shortest bridges on the Columnar Joint Road, and this is where you can observe various Hyeonmuam, or basalts along the way. You don't have to stop walking; rather, please walk slowly looking around as you can see many different basalt formations everywhere from here.  Overview of Basalt Most of the stones you're now viewing are basalt. As you can see here, the common types of basalt found around here are not as porous as some of you may expect. There are two typical volcanic rocks; granite and basalt. Granite is formed from lava slowly cooling and solidifying deep in the ground while basalt is formed from the rapid cooling of low-viscosity lava when exposed to the air. Basalt is known to have fine grains and a rather coarse surface. It is amazing to see how different rocks show off their distinct characteristics. It's just like the human world full of different people with various personalities. We hope you'll be able to enjoy observing the basalt columnar joints around here.

stories.title: Hyeonhwa Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Hyeonhwa Bridge This is Hyeonhwa Bridge. Its name is made up of the first syllables of two distinctive rocks; hyeonmuam and hwagangam in Korean, or basalt and granite. As its name implies, this the bridge is where you can observe these two types of rocks together near here.  Overview of Hyeonhwa Bridge You have understood so far that the Hantan River is related with volcanic activities from a long time ago. Would you like to know where the volcano started? There is a small mountain named Orisan Mountain with an elevation of 452 meters above sea level, which is located 25 kilometers north from here. It belongs to North Korea, but it is located in the very center of the Korean Peninsula. So, the mountain has the nickname of the belly button of the Korean Peninsula. Lava from the crack between this mountain and the neighboring 680m-high plateau flowed covering the whole Cheorwon to make it a lava plateau. When we think about a volcanic explosion, we always imagine lava erupting from a mountain, but an explosion did not occur here in Cheorwon, rather a gradual flowing eruption took place. As Lava as thin as honey water flowed here, it presented a wide plain with rivers instead of gigantic, volcanic mountains such as Baekdusan Mountain or Hallasan Mountain. At the moment, you're looking at the basalt columnar joints which were formed by lava covering the area about 540,000 years ago after granite was created about 100 million years prior. Do you feel the weight of the time over the years? While currently taking a moment off your hectic daily routines, would you like to compare the weight of your time with that of these geological changes? The coexistence of granite and basalt can be witnessed here at Hyeonhwa Bridge.

stories.title: Doldanpung Rest Observation Area
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Doldanpung Rest Area You're now at Doldanpung Observation Rest Area. Let's suppose the Columnar Joints Road was only about the geological formation. Although, it would still be interesting, wouldn't it lack the attractive qualities that make people happy? Many people find the road so attractive because this road is also where you can find various plants living together on it.  Overview of Doldanpung One of the signature plants that make this Columnar Joints Road even more inviting is the Maple-leaf mukdenia, or Doldanpung in Korean. Its scientific name is Mukdenia rossii. The literal translation of its Korean name Doldanpung is stone maple, which implies its natural habitat and physical resemblance to maple leaves. Maple-leaf mukdenias usually grow in the narrow openings of the vertical walls of columnar joints or granite cliffs which are being weathered. Tiny white or light reddish star-shaped flowers are produced in late spring, when people start to feel amazed by the changes in nature once again.  Overview of the scenery You will see lots of Maple-leaf mukdenia, the signature plant of the Hantan River, here at Doldanpung Observation Rest Area. Please try to locate and enjoy viewing the maple-leaf-shaped plants hidden in the columnar joints and rocks. Their green leaves are in good harmony with clay-yellow cliffs in spring and summer, and they turn burgundy or reddish orange in autumn, presenting us with an opportunity to appreciate the seasonal changes and natural beauty.

stories.title: Doldanpung Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Doldanpung Bridge Here at Doldanpung Bridge, you can take a closer look at the maple-leaf mukdenia growing close by.  Overview of Doldanpung Bridge Let me give you a few more details about the maple-leaf mukdenia. This particular plant lives for several years and has a short thick stem that creeps underground. It usually grows up to 30 centimeters high. Its leaves come out from the root and usually have 5 to 7 points like maple leaves. Its human-hand-like leaves are saw-toothed on the edges. It's amazing and pitiful to see these tiny plants rooted between hard rocks; sometimes we feel the urge to root for the plant as much as we feel awe towards its tough survival instincts. It would be worth remembering how these tiny plants survive their challenging environment when you feel overwhelmed under the weight of occasionally challenging moments in life.  Those of you coming from the Sundam Entrance are going to walk about five minutes till the next stop, Ssangjarabawi Bridge. I'd like to recommend that you walk slowly enjoying the company of the maple-leaf mukdenias along the path with your earphones off. Don't forget to check out the rock shades here and there on the way there. I'll get back to you at the next stop.

stories.title: Ssangjarabawi Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Ssangjarabawi Bridge The name of this bridge means a terrapin couple in English. As the name implies, this bridge is located near a rock formation which resembles two terrapins, or small turtles. You will find the terrapin couple turning their heads up on the granite rocks across from you either before crossing the bridge from Sundam direction or past the bridge from Deureuni direction. This particular rock formation is usually called a terrapin couple. What does it look like to you? (pause) Whatever it may be, there's no correct answer as it should probably have the appearance of whatever your heart desires.   Overview of Geological Dikes You can also view other interesting rock formations from Ssangjarabawi Bridge. There are darker basalt columnar joints standing on the light-colored granite rocks. Do you see remarkable stem-shaped stones in the granite on the opposite side? These are called dikes in geology. A geological dike is a flat body of rock that cuts through another type of rock. Here across from Ssangjarabawi Bridge, geological dikes were created when magma was squeezed into narrow openings in the granite. These types of geological dikes are among the clear pieces of evidence that show the existence of volcanic activities in the past. Irregular geological dikes in the granite seem to highlight that we are living with various characteristics but in good harmony with each other in the world. Those of you coming from the Deureuni Entrance are going to walk about five minutes till the next stop, Doldanpung Bridge. It is highly recommended that you walk slowly looking for maple-leaf mukdenias along the path with your earphones off. Don't forget to check out the rock shades spotted along the way, too. I'll be with you again at the next stop.

stories.title: Jusangjeolri Bridge
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Columnar Joints Bridge Upon arriving at this bridge, please try to locate a rock formation with the appearance of a fish. It can be located either before crossing this bridge from the Sundam direction or past the bridge from the Deureuni direction. The rock formation looks like a mudskipper with a big head and bulging eyes. This will definitely make you smile at this cartoon-character-like and yet mysterious appearance of rock in nature.  Overview of Columnar Joints Bridge Now, would you turn your eyes to look at the columnar joints on the other side? The columnar joints at this point are not only vertically grained, but also horizontally layered because the lava erupted several times with time lags. One of the most apparent differences between the Hantan River and other rivers is that almost the entire section is in the form of a valley dug about 30 to 40 meters below the flat ground around it and the valley is made up of extraordinary cliffs, or columnar joints. Geological joints appear in various forms depending on the type of rock and the surrounding environment; columnar joints usually appear in the form of a hexagonal or polygonal column. It is the three-dimensional effect that attracts people to the columnar joints with their regular and irregular distributions of the convex and concave sides. You'll notice that the columnar joints at the top of the cliffs look like tens of meters of egg cartons attached on top of each other. When you see various water birds such as mallard ducks, egrets, and grey herons flying over around here, you may even feel like you're in the middle of a nature documentary film or a land of your dreams.

stories.title: Deureuni Sky Observation Deck
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Deureuni Sky Observation Deck Have you heard by any chance that a Korean historic figure by the name of Gung Ye established a state named Taebong on the Korean Peninsula in the year 901 during the Later Three Kingdoms Period? Deureuni Sky Observation Deck means to drop by in Korean. Gung Ye dropped by this area when he was chased off after Wang Geon's rebellion in the early 10th century.  Overview of the Hantan River Let me tell you a little bit about the Hantan River. It is 140km in length. It begins from Jangamsan Mountain in Pyeonggang County, North Korea, flows through Cheorwon and Pocheon, and joins with the Imjin River at Dogampo in Yeoncheon County, South Korea. It is also known as a volcanic river where basalt rocks can be observed on the riverside rather than near the seaside. The pronunciation of the name of the Hantan River is spelled and sounds the same as the Korean noun extreme grief, so there are a couple of folk tales associated with this homonym about the origin of the river name; Gung Ye is said to have given way to big grief, saying Ah, my fate is doomed. at the sight of dark basalt stones with many pores in them on the river bank after fleeing from the war against Later Baekje in the early 10th century. Some people even say that a lot of Koreans sighed and sighed at this river running through the demilitarized zone, the symbol of national division after the Korean War. In fact, the meaning of Hantan is big rapids as the river is well-known for its deep valleys alongside rapid streams flowing through them. Whatever origin of the name you choose to believe, the Hantan River is popular with its attractive and variable scenery as it flows through the basalt lava field with lots of vertical cliffs and narrow valleys.  Overview of Deureuni Sky Observation Deck Deureuni Sky Observation Deck is located in the middle of the Columnar Joints Bridge, where you can view extraordinary columnar joints together with combinations of granite and basalt. I hope you will enjoy the Hantan River with various hints of its 100-million-year history.

stories.title: Neoreunbawi Observation Rest Area
stories.script: Arrival Announcement at Neoreunbawi Observation Rest Area You have arrived at Neoreunbawi Observation Rest Area  Overview of Neoreunbawi Neoreunbawi can be translated word for word into spacious rock in English. Look to your left down the river, and you'll find two large flat granite plates leaning against each other. You can see a lot of spacious rocks like this around this area. These spacious rocks are found a lot around the Hantan River, and they are called various names with meanings such as a yard rock or an attic rock locally. A legend named Wang Jeong Lang has it that Gung Ye of the ancient kingdom Taebong showed his shins with his pants rolled up when he was chased off by his opponent named Wang Geon while crossing the river.
