However, there is something that still has not been restored until present. It is Woldae. Woldae is a broad platform visible from Geunjeongjeon, the main hall Gyeongbokgung Palace, the main hall of Jongmyo Shrine, and the pavilion of the Royal Tombs of Joseon, where the king and the public met to interact during important national events. The Cultural Heritage Administration is currently undertaking the restoration of Woldae, which is scheduled for completion by 2023.  Gwanghwamun underwent countless destruction and restoration throughout history, but its front road has always been the central heart of Korea. It served as the symbol and venue of democracy throughout modern and contemporary history. This main thoroughfare has finally regained life as a public square in August 2022. It passes on the historical significance of the road, while connecting ordinary events, such as rest and strolls, with non-ordinary events, such as festivals, to serve as a major public space for citizens.  The newly renovated square is twice as large than before, with over five thousand trees planted that make a green landscape. New spaces, such as rest areas, water fountains, and open plazas, enable the public to enjoy history, culture, entertainment, and rest.  Gwanghwamun Square, a cultural space for everyone that connects the past and present. This is where the people of Korea can come for peace of mind.

stories.title: Buried Cultural Heritage
stories.script: Gwanghwamun Square has a longer history than Gyeongbokgung Palace. It was where government offices were located, established before the construction of Gyeongbokgung Palace. Uijeongbu, along with six government agencies, or Yukjo (i.e. Ijo, Hojo, Yejo, Byeongjo, Hyeongjo, and Gongjo), were located on either sides of the street in front of Gwanghwamun. The street was also called Yukjo Geori (Street of Six Ministries) for this reason. In other words, Gwanghwamun Square was where countless government officials passed by to commute. Yukjo Geori was the heart of Joseon politics and administration, and the most developed area in Hanyang (now Seoul).  This street also underwent a lot of changes with Gwanghwamun. Yukjo Geori that was restored after the Imjin War became a road by the Japanese governor-general, leaving important relics buried underground. However, the in-depth excavation and inspection that began in 2020 discovered buildings, ponds, and roads that form historic sites at the west side of Yukjo Geori, revealing the location and foundation of the six ministry buildings.   The site assumed to be that of Samgunbu and Yejo showed traces of external rooms of Samgunbu, drainage, and the Yejo building of the early Joseon times.  Saheonbu and Byeongjo areas had a well, main gate, walls, drainage, and rooms. A drainage was also discovered in the Hyeongjo section, as well as in the Gongjo area, together with stone foundations that formed a barrier.  The excavated heritage are exhibited in the Gwanghwamun Square. leaving the traces of wells, drainage, and other relics in the site of the gate of Saheonbu. That place is the Time Garden. Old structures of Samgunbu, Byeongjo, and Hyeongjo are covered in soil again for preservation, and replicas are placed over them to exhibit the traces of Yukjo.  Gwanghwamun Square also features Yukjo Yard that represents Yukjo Geori. It is right in front of Gwanghwamun. It is covered in grass to add beauty to the magnificent scenery of Gwanghwamun. Also, this is where the History Waterway of 630 years begins. The starting point of the waterway was made referring to “Yeolsangjinwonsaem” of Gyeongbokgung Palace and “Yeolcheon” of Changgyeonggung Palace. History Waterway flows around the whole Gwanghwamun Square and to Hangeul Fountain. It flows over 630 stone plates with historic events engraved on them.  The first section of the waterway is from 1392 to 1910, with inscriptions of events such as the establishment of Joseon in 1392, the creation of Hunminjeongeum in 1443, and the victory of the Battle of Myeongnyang in 1597. This section was created along the drainage that was installed then. The second section of the waterway is from 1910 to 1946, the time of the Japanese occupation. The March 1st Movement in 1919, victories of the Bongodong and Cheongsanri battles in 1920, and national liberation on August 15, 1945, are engraved in this section. The last section is from the Korean independence to present, covering the Seoul Olympics in 1988, Korea–Japan World Cup in 2002, and the promotion of Korea’s status as a developed nation by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development in 2021.  This waterway also serves to cool off citizens in hot summers. A lot of citizens sit around the waterway with their feet in the water and enjoying their time in Gwanghwamun. The cultural heritage that was buried underground has been found. The history of 600 years flows along the waterway, and the story of the Gwanghwamun Square continues on.

stories.title: Media Art @ Haechi Lounge
stories.script: Gwanghwamun Square is recognized as a night attraction for its fancy media art that shines after sunset. Media artwork are screened on the facades of Haechi Lounge, KT building, and the National Museum of Korean Contemporary History. The media wall of a large LED panel with a length of 53 meters and maximum height of 3.25 meters installed at the entry of Haechi Lounge displays 4K media art.  The artwork that is screened with the opening of Gwanghwamun Square is Gwanghwa Hwacheop, created with a theme of Cheonjiin, the root of Hangeul. Artworks created by Hong Yu-ri and Lee Ye-seung, who are actively engaged in media art, feature New Painting of Gwanghwa and Dream in Dream in “Heaven Opens,” Forest in Seoul and Gwanghwa Meta-Landscape in “Earth Enjoys,” and Gwanghwa Aquarium and Moment of Gwanghwa in “Humanity Awakens.” Dandelion, Dung Beetle, and Soap Bubbles are other entertaining artworks displayed to connect each chapter.   The main characteristic of the media art of Gwanghwamun Square is that it is a two-way media art that allows all citizens who visit Gwanghwamun Square to participate to complete the work. Citizens can post their own drawing or photo they took on the media wall by scanning a QR code with smartphones. The glaring images and lights of media art is lighting Gwanghwamun Square every night.

stories.title: Statues of King Sejong & Admiral Yi Sun-sin
stories.audioTitle: Statues of King Sejong & Admiral Yi Sun-sin
stories.script: Do you know who is the most admired king by Koreans? Most people will agree it is King Sejong. King Sejong made remarkable achievements in the areas of science, national defense, agriculture, culture, and arts. He is probably the king that best fits the meaning of Gwanghwamun—a king that shines the nation with his great virtue.  The bronze seated statue of King Sejong is 10.4 meters high and 4.3 meters wide. This statue that was built in 2009 erects in the middle of Gwanghwamun Square. The king has one hand holding a copy of Hunminjeongeum and the other raised, giving a benevolent impression. In front of the statue, there is the sundial, rain gauge, and a celestial globe, which represent the technologies of Joseon. On the rear side, there are six pillars with the achievements of the great king engraved, such as the installation of Jiphyeonjeon (royal research institute), modification of the printing technology, the conquest of the Jurchens and Waegu, modification of Aak (court ritual music), and observation.  King Sejong’s greatest achievement that shows his love for his people is Hunminjeongeum. Hunminjeongeum, which literally means “the proper sound system for teaching the people”, is an easy and practical script to learn, composed of 28 characters that can represent all sounds of the Korean language. The 28 characters of Hangeul are hidden throughout the ground and tables of Gwanghwamun Square. Try to look for the hidden letters while walking around the square. You will experience an unexpected excitement.   Along with the statue of King Sejong, the statue of Admiral Yi Sun-sin is also guarding Gwanghwamun Square for over five decades. This 17-meter bronze statue that was built in 1968, depicting a standing figure of the admiral, who is holding a sword after winning a battle. A miniature turtle ship is placed on the base, and two war drums are placed in front. An advancing battleship is engraved on the side. Newly installed in front of the statue is what's called Myeongnyang Fountain. This fountain features 133 spouts that represent the 133 battleships of the Japanese that the Admiral destroyed during the Battle of Myeongnyang.  The achievements of King Sejong and Admiral Yi Sun-sin can be seen and experienced at Gwanghwamun Square. There are two exhibitions titled “The Story of King Sejong and The Story of Admiral Yi Sun-sin” in the basement that connects Gwanghwamun Square and the Sejong Center for the Performing Arts. King Sejong's love for his people and his overall achievements can be seen at The Story of King Sejong exhibition, comprised of sections that showcase King Sejong as a human being, his people-oriented thoughts, invention of Hangeul, science and arts, and military policies.  The Story of Admiral Yi Sun-shin conveys Yi Sun-sin as a human being through sections of the life of Yi Sun-shin, vessels of Joseon, naval battle of seven years, and his war diary Nanjung Ilgi, as well as his life story through another section that features his leadership and a theater.  Furthermore, the Media Glass installed in a form of a cube at the entrance to the underground exhibition at the rear side of the statue of King Sejong also features the achievements of King Sejong and Admiral Yi Sun-shin, Hangeul content, as well as creative media arts of young artists. Gwanghwamun Square is more complete with the statue of King Sejong, who led the golden era of the nation, and the statue of Admiral Yi Sun-sin, who saved the nation from crisis.

stories.title: Rest Area & Culture
stories.script: Gwanghwamun Square is a like a park. It has 5,000 native trees planted for the public to enjoy the ordinary beauty and relaxation in nature.   The pine garden at the entrance is planted with a long, evergreen pine species native to Gangneung, Gangwon-do Province. The landscape of Gwanghwamun and Bugaksan Mountain along the trail is also a magnificent view. This is the photo zone of Gwanghwamun Square. The Four Season Garden connected along the stone garden features Japanese cornus, Sargent's cherries, Korean dogwoods, Crepe-myrtles, three-flowered maples, and maples that change in color every season.  The rest area by the entrance of the Sejong Center for the Performing Arts is an oak forest. Two small and nice water tanks with flowing freshwater is placed in the middle of the forest, making visitors feel as if they are in a relaxing forest. Celtis sinensis, Japanese elms, and Japanese horse-chestnuts are planted in the gathering area by the statue of Yi Sun-sin, and the ground paved with eight kinds of stones brought from different parts of the nation.  Exit 7 of Gwanghwamun Station is connected with the Forest Square filled with tall trees, such as zelkovas and Japanese elms, as well as shorter ones, including Hydrangea serrata, Cercis chinensis, and Weigela subsessilis. Celtis sinensis that appeared in the popular Korean drama series Extraordinary Attorney Woo can also be found.  Gwanghwamun Square also features several water facilities that are especially loved by children. The ground well with sprinkling water inspired by the well discovered at the entrance of the site of Saheonbu, a tunnel fountain that creates a water arch with 77 water spouts that represent the 77th anniversary of Korea's national liberation, Hangeul fountain that symbolizes the Hangeul characters, inspired by Cheonjiin, the principle of the invention of Hangeul, Myeongnyang Fountain that symbolizes the sea battle of Admiral Yi Sun-sin, and the Wall Fountain that visualizes the time flow are some examples.   Enjoy the ordinary life and culture at this park-like square where one can relax feeling the nature. Gwanghwamun Square is an oasis of culture and leisure open to the public all year round.

stories.title: Story of Hangyeryeong Pass A Rugged Mountain Pass Connecting Between Yangyang and Inje
stories.audioTitle: Story of Hangyeryeong Pass A Rugged Mountain Pass Connecting Between Yangyang and Inje
stories.script: Hangyeryeong Pass is a hill located on the boundary line between Yangyang and Inje. Ryeong means hills. This word is often used in the names of rugged hills. As such, Hangyeryeong Pass is a rugged hill. Hangye, a word meaning limits, was added to the name. Some joke about this name, exclaiming, “I’ve reached my limits,” when crossing over this rugged hill.   In the past, the part of the mountain in Yangyang-gun was called Seoraksan Mountain and that in Inje-gun was called Hangyesan Mountain. The name, “Hangyeryeong,” came from the name of the mountain, “Hangyesan Mountain.” Hangyeryeong Pass has been serving as a transportation hub connecting the East Coast and the inland area. This hill was used for the transportation of people and supplies. Measuring 1,004m in height, Hangyeryeong Pass is a part of the main ridge of Seoraksan Mountain and belongs to Seoraksan National Park.   Up to the Joseon period, which lasted from the 14th century to the early 20th century, there were many thieves in the area. In response, geumpyo, a sign warning people not to pass over the hill after sunset, was engraved on a rock at the entrance to the hill. The rock still remains. Geumpyogyo Bridge can be crossed over on the way leading up to Hangyeryeong Pass.  Despite the beautiful valleys and magnificent features, Naeseorak did not attract many tourists other than trekkers because of the inconvenient transportation. The opening of National Road No. 44 in 1971, however, improved accessibility to Naeseorak.

stories.title: Yangnim Visitor Center
stories.script: Hello, welcome to Yangnim Visitor Center. The Yangnim Visitor Center highlights tourist attractions and offerings, while promotes its history and story on important historical figures. For visitors, onsite public parking and recharging of mobile devices are available. To enjoy the free docent-guided tour, please book a reservation. Shall we get started to learn what Yangnim Village is all about?

stories.title: Penguin Village
stories.script: In Yangnim-dong, the old downtown area of Nam-gu, Gwangju, there started to be empty houses one after another as the residents who have been living there for a long time became old, and a fire broke out in those empty houses in 2013. Since then, garbage was left unattended and became an eyesore of the town.  Then, one day, Donggyun Kim, the current village head of the Penguin Village, started to take out garbage, decorated the area with clock waste materials, created a garden, and called it the Penguin Garden, which became the beginning of the Penguin Village. Afterward, with the help of the residents, he was able to collect unique and interesting garbage and turned the vacant lot of the village into a level of junk art, making it into its current unique and interesting look.  At the entrance of the village, there is a Statue of Peace that reminds us of the historical pain that should not be forgotten. On the opposite side of the Statue of Peace, there is Yangnim Penguin Studio. As ‘Hope Song at Noon’ of Music FM and ‘Amazing 3 O’clock’ of Standard FM are broadcasted live from Monday to Friday, you can watch the live broadcast or participate and enjoy various events.  As you enter the Penguin Village and walk down the alleys, you will be able to find not only the junk art pieces made by the village residents themselves but also unique murals and eye-catching messages on the walls, so please feel free to enjoy the atmosphere of the Penguin Village. There is also a mural commemorating the birthday of J-Hope from BTS, so why not leave a commemorative photo for yourself?

stories.title: Yangnim-dong Penguin Village Craft Street
stories.script: Yangnim-dong Penguin Village Craft Street is a street that has been remodeled from about 20 surrounding houses in the Penguin Village into workshops, experience centers, and exhibition shops.  As Hanok are remodeled as-is, it gives children the feeling of nature that cannot be felt in urban areas and gives adults the memories and nostalgia of their childhood hometown. In addition, you can purchase works devotedly made by craftsmen in various fields such as ceramics, metal crafts, and wood crafts from 14 workshops created to promote the craft industry of Gwangju. There are also one-day classes available where you can try making your own work. In the center of Craft Street, there is Welcome Center, which is an information desk where you can get various leaflets and information. If you go to the back of the Welcome Center while walking around the alleys in between, there are stairs leading to the observatory where you can see the Craft Street at a glance. As you walk up the stairs, there is not only the observatory but also a photo zone for you to take pictures. After enjoying the scenery of Craft Street and looking around the workshops, you will be able to come to an old well pump called Jakdusam where you can experience the old well and pump. Regardless of age and gender, anyone can feel the memories and newness at the same time by pumping water together.  Please enjoy various crafts and immerse yourself in the charm of the Craft Village.

stories.title: Owen Memorial Hall
stories.script: Hello! This is the Owen Memorial Hall. Owen Memorial Hall is a Western-style building built to commemorate Owen and his grandfather, William L. Owen, who worked in Gwangju as the first missionary in Jeollanam-do together with Pastor Yuji Bae. It is also designated as Tangible Cultural Property No. 26 of Gwangju Metropolitan City.  Then, who is Owen? Owen came to Korea in November 1898 and started missionary work in Mokpo with Missionary Eugene Bell, and with Pastor Yuji Bae in Gwangju in December 1904 until he died of acute pneumonia due to overwork on April 3rd, 1909. After his death, his relatives from the United States sent donations to build a memorial hall for him and his grandfather to commemorate his missionary achievements and that is the Owen Memorial Hall.  For this reason, the marble sign reads “IN MEMORY OF WILLIAM L. AND CLEMENT C. OWEN” and it is not only written in English but also in Chinese as a memorial hall.   Owen Memorial Hall, which served as a dissemination center for Western culture and art, was the cradle of cultivating national consciousness during the Japanese colonial era and is considered a representative meeting house and culture and art center in Honam. The first civic movement organization in Gwangju also started here and had a profound impact on the entire Jeollanam-do region. Not only that, it was a place where all modern cultural and artistic events such as Western theater, opera, and modern dance, which are different from Korea’s ‘Changgeuk’, were presented, and the first concert in Gwangju, the ‘Pilrye Kim Concert’ was also held here in 1920 as well.  Owen Memorial Hall not only served as a medium to spread Western culture and art in Gwangju but also served as a space where the traditional and the modern met and combined. At that time, it is said that seats for men and women were separated in the center of the Owen Memorial Hall. At a performance by the Vladivostok Korean Music Troupe held in 1921, they performed a social dance or tap dance in which men and women dance in pairs, which surprised many people. It is a representative example of the open modern Western culture meeting with the closed feudal Confucian culture, interacting with each other and causing conflict.  This place, built with donations, is a building built by Missionary Swinehart who hired Chinese engineers. Chinese engineers were chosen as Japanese engineers had high labor costs and Korean engineers lacked experience at that time. With a beautifully decorated semicircular arch, pillars made of tin that were not seen in traditional Korean architecture, and a two-story structure with a sloping roof, the unusual and unique appearance caught people's attention.    Owen Memorial Hall, a Renaissance-style building, is composed of Dutch-style walls with granite wall footings at the bottom and gray bricks on top. The exterior was symmetrically balanced, and a porch was placed in the center of it. Two pairs of circular columns made of cast iron were placed on it with a semicircular arch to enhance the decorative beauty and openness by placing windows symmetrically on the left and right. The upper part of the window is a vacancy arch and the lower part is a horizontal bar, and there are solid square wooden pillars on the inside to support the seats on the second floor and the wooden truss. The flat shape is square, but the internal structure is symmetrical from side to side with the pulpit located at the corner, and the floor is slightly inclined toward the pulpit, so it is thoroughly designed to be suitable for a place of worship or assembly. Of course, the second-floor balcony is inclined toward the pulpit. The entrance opening has a north door called Sungilmun and a west door called Supiamun. There are small side entrances on the east and south corners. If you enter through this entrance, you will see the stairs leading to the second-floor balcony.  The overall finish was made of bricks, but on the elevation, horizontal bands dividing the layers and pilasters, which are vertical supporting walls, are formed, and this is also a masonry structure. It is presumed that the arched windows are for a decorative effect in the structure of the building, and an opening under the floor is also visible in the lower part of the east side for ventilation. Also, the corners are faceted with straight lines. The form of the window is a tall high window and has a rectangular shape in the longitudinal direction. The truss still forms a large space with a sturdy wooden truss and the shape of the roof is covered with copper plates at a right-angled angle.  Please enjoy Owen Memorial Hall, which is also famous as a filming location for Bridal Mask, and its unique Western-style architecture that drew a lot of attention at that time, attracting spectators not only from Gwangju but also from nearby towns.

stories.title: Eugene Bell Memorial Hall
stories.script: This is the Eugene Bell Memorial Hall to commemorate Paster Eugene Bell, who is known as “the father of missions in Gwangju and Jeollanam-do” and his co-workers.   Eugene Bell’s Korean name is Yuji Bae and he was born on April 1st, 1868 in Kentucky, USA. After graduating from Central University in Kentucky, he graduated from Kentucky Theological Seminary and Louisville Theological Seminary in succession, and came to Korea in 1895 with his wife, Lottie Witherspoon Bell, as a second-generation Southern Presbyterian missionary.  He learned Korean customs and language from Changyeon Byun, from ‘Dixie House’ in Jeong-dong, Seoul. Afterwards, he went to Naju with Changyeon Byun for missionary work and explored from November 3rd to 6th, 1896 but was unable to find a place to stay due to strong opposition from Confucian students. He went to Mokpo that year and began his missionary work in earnest. After the first worship service with 8 people gathered at the thatched house, he bought land, dug a well, built a church, and started holding the worship service in earnest. Thanks to Owen, who was soon appointed as a medical missionary, Eugene Bell's missionary work became more active.  Eugene Bell’s wife, Lottie Witherspoon Bell, was born in the United States, graduated from Augustus Women's Seminary, and came to Korea with her husband, Eugene Bell. She gave birth to their son Henry on May 27th, 1896 in Seoul and their daughter Charlotte on January 6th, 1899 in Mokpo. Unfortunately, Bell died of an endemic disease of the name not known.   After sweat and tears in Mokpo Mission from March 1898 to April 12th, 1901, Lottie Witherspoon Bell left behind her beloved husband and son and daughter who were still little.  After the funeral, Eugene Bell took his children who lost their mother to the United States and left them with his sister to come back to Korea in 1902. While he was away, he gathered the few remaining believers and had them build a church that could accommodate 200 people and there were 101 members who were preparing for baptism. Not only that, but he also founded Jeongmyeong School and Yeongheung School  In 1904, he got remarried to Margaret Bull, opened a mission in Gwangju, purchased land near the southern wall of Gwangju, and built a church. The first worship service in Gwangju was held on a snowy Christmas Day in 1904 at Eugene Bell’s temporary home and Eugene Bell, the Owen family, language teacher Changyeon Byun, and the villagers attended the worship service. Together with Missionary Owen, he opened a modern hospital, Jejungwon, in Yangnim-dong. It is said that within 6 years of the founding of the church, the church grew to five hundred members, and the church was extended three times. In 1910, there were 1,500 baptized members. Eugene Bell was loved by many church members as a capable missionary who captured people's hearts with a relaxed personality.  In 1907, he started teaching 2 boys in Eugene Bell’s guest room and 3 girls in a hall bedroom in the same year, which developed into Gwangju Sungil School and Supia Girls’ School.   On March 26th, 1919, Margaret, who remarried Eugene Bell, died in an accident at a railroad crossing on her way back from a missionary meeting in Seoul. Afterwards, Eugene Bell became a professor at the Pyongyang Presbyterian Seminary, but his health deteriorated due to overwork, died at the age of 57, and was buried in the Gwangju Missionary Cemetery.   On the 100th anniversary of missionary work in Korea, the 4th generation descendants of Missionary Eugene Bell established the Eugene Bell Memorial Foundation in the United States, and in 2002, a foundation with the same name was established in Korea.  Eugene Bell Memorial Foundation started a food aid and tuberculosis treatment medical system support project in North Korea, and over the past 10 years, it has provided medicines to 13 tuberculosis prevention centers and 63 tuberculosis sanatoriums in North Korea and treated 200,000 North Korean tuberculosis patients.   When you visit the Eugene Bell Memorial Hall, you can see the missionary activities of Pastor Eugene Bell, the history of the Gwangju Mission that began when he planted the seeds of the gospel in Yangnim-dong in 1904, and the Southern Presbyterian missionaries. You can also see the tombstone of Eugene Bell’s wife, Missionary Lottie Bell, and the original copy of the quarantine commemorative fan.

stories.title: Sajik Park Observation Tower
stories.script: Sajik Park Observation Tower, a landmark of Sajik Park, is an observation tower located on the site of the old octagonal pavilion in Sajik Park and is a representative space leading the night view culture of Yangnim-dong. It was completed in November 2014 and opened to the public in March 2015.   Starting with the 1st floor, the main entrance, there are a deck shelter on the 2nd floor, an exhibition room on the 3rd floor, and an observatory on the 4th floor. In the exhibition room, there are various experience spaces such as a book cafe, a media façade, an observation telescope, and an interactive zone where you can experience the planets of the solar system. Originally, there was an observatory, but it disappeared through 3 extensions and renovations and after the octagonal pavilion was built, Gwangju citizens climbed the octagonal pavilion to look down on the city of Gwangju including the four seasons of Mudeungsan Mountain at a glance. Then, the old octagonal pavilion was demolished, and the observation tower was built afterwards.   Another specialty, the observation tower, which opened in March 2015, is a three-story tower with a height of 13.7m. The representation of the shape of Sajikdan and the exterior of the image of light that symbolizes Gwangju is literally a masterpiece. The view of Mudeungsan Mountain from the Sajik Park Observation Tower is also amazing as Gwangju embodying Mudeungsan Mountain is amazingly beautiful.  If you come down from the observation tower after enjoying the beautiful Gwangju, you can see building materials that you didn't see when going up. This is the remnant of the now lost octagonal pavilion. The old octagonal pavilion was demolished and some of its appearance at the time were left with photos, which seems to be a good example of allowing citizens to know what it looked like before.   To get to the observatory on the 4th floor, you have to use the elevator or go up the circular stairs installed on the tower pillars. Only if you go up the circular stairs, you can have the opportunity to see the East, West, South, North, and North Gwangju in various ways.   Currently, there are many new facilities around Sajik Park. One of them is KBS Gwangju Broadcasting Station, the first radio station in Gwangju and Jeollanam-do, which opened in 1941. It has now been moved to Sangmu New City Center, and since 2003, it has been used as the Gwangju Visual Arts Center and Gwangju English Broadcasting Station. At the western foot of the top, Gwandeokjeong Pavilion was installed to create a palace site for flying bowstrings, and Sajik Library and Yangnim Art Museum are located at the foot of the mountain. In addition, a Live Guitar Street is formed at the entrance of Yangnim Police Station, making it a special place where you can reflect on the memories of the 1970s and 1980s.   Time does not stop but continues to flow, creating a new history. Although the history is less than 100 years old, Sajik Park holds a lot of time and memories. In it, there are remnants of the Japanese colonial rule and the pride of the nation. Even though the appearance of Sajik Park has changed, the meaning of Sajikdan will never be forgotten.    Why not go up to the observatory with your loved ones and take a look at the beautiful Gwangju through the telescope installed while reflecting on the meaning of Sajikdan together?

stories.title: Dwing-gul Dong-gul
stories.script: Contrary to its funny name, Dwing-gul Dong-gul, this underground cave is a remnant of the Japanese colonial rule. It is an air defense shelter that began construction in the 1940s to evacuate the Japanese living in downtown Gwangju during the Japanese colonial era from American air raids. The construction of the air defense shelter started because it was close to the Japanese residential area and the ground of Yangnimsan Mountain was hard to allow for a stable evacuation, but due to the solid granite ground, the original plan to create four entrances and a central square was not completed, and the war ended.    After liberation, the site where construction was neglected was restored, and now the four entrances remain as separate caves. How about walking through Dwing-gul Dong-gul, which used to be a resting area for the elderly of the village in the summer, to learn the truth about history and take time to reflect on the justice of history?

stories.title: House of Choi Seung-hyo
stories.script: Do you know Sanghyeon Choi, an independence activist? The House of Choi Seung-hyo is Sanghyeon Choi’s house and is designated as Gwangju Metropolitan City Folklore Material No. 2.   Sanghyeon Choi, the original owner of the house, was a wealthy man who accumulated enormous assets through trade with China and he used that wealth to finance the independence movement to relieve the poor. His father, Myeonggu Choi, built Heunghakgwan, a two-story wooden building, near the old city hall, and donated it so that it could be used as a national spirit training center. Since then, various educational and cultural activities have been held in Heunghakgwan in addition to civil society group activities, and in 1929, the Gwangju Student Independence Movement was also plotted there.  In addition, enlightenment campaigns, including night school, to inspire anti-Japanese spirit was developed and it was also used as a sports facility to supply tennis and boxing.  Although Heunghakgwan was demolished after 1966, it has been used by various organizations such as Shinganhoe and has played an important role in the history of the Gwangju Student Independence Movement.  The current owner is the late Seunghyo Choi, who played a leading role in the founding of Gwangju Cultural Broadcasting and was a journalist who rose to the position of president and a cultural figure who collected many works of art.   House of Choi Seung-hyo, built in the east on a large site of nearly 800 pyeong (around 2,645m2), is a very large-scale traditional Hanok with 6 rooms in the front and 2 rooms on the side with smaller rooms in the front, back, left, and right.  The layout of the building uses the sloped site as it is in its natural state and forms a semi-basement floor on the left, giving the whole building a sense of rhythm. The pond was decorated with clean water flowing down from small hills and rock walls, which further enhances the building's elegance.  Jaidang, the main building, is a flat, gambrel-roofed building commonly seen in this area. Inside, from the left, there are a room, 2 rooms for the main floored room, 2 rooms, and 1 and a half room for the pavilion site. Although the flat style is in the form of a house with several wings, there is no wall dividing the top and bottom, so the rooms form a large space overall.  The semi-basement floor was constructed using the small room space in the part where the front small room and the small room on the right meet, and a storeroom was placed on the side where the small room on the left and the small room in the back meet. The rest of the small rooms were decorated as open spaces to form an asymmetrical floor plan and elevation so that it is not monotonous. On the west-facing back, a 60cm-wide floor is laid and a sliding window is made to block out light from the west. The wisdom of our ancestors who placed a transom window on the top of the wall to solve the darkening of the master bedroom due to sliding windows stands out. With the exception of the main floored room, which has a lantern ceiling, there were large attics, and a beautiful story is told that independence activists were sheltered here.  Except for the semi-basement part in front of the right end, a pillar and a plinth with two stone columns were placed on the stylobate, which was built with rectangular stones at a height of about 1m. The width of the stairs leading up to the stylobate is exceptionally wide compared to other houses, reaching about half the length of the stylobate. Unlike other traditional tiles, you can see a lot of colorful aspects with the tiles with an orange tint. It is said that the building material of the house was made of wood near Baekdusan Mountain and the Yalu River, so it is not only thick and straight but also very well trimmed and weaved, which makes it look like a high-class building. In particular, the ends of the rafters were covered with copper plates to prevent them from easily rotting.   Unfortunately, the House of Choi Seung-hyo now only has the main building with no other buildings such as the guesthouse. However, it still is a very well-built Hanok in the time of enlightenment, with a thick wood frame, wide door dividers, and excellent trimming.   In particular, since it is a space that contains the process of changing from the traditional houses of the Late Period of Joseon to the modern Korean wooden architecture, please visit in person and have a special opportunity to know more about the House of Choi Seung-hyo, which has a lot of value as an architectural-historical material. Also, please feel free to enjoy the healing time of Yangnimsan Mountain, Gwangju River, and Mudeungsan Mountain.

stories.title: Monument to the Filial Piety of Mr. Jung Eom and the Sculpture to His Loyal Dog
stories.audioTitle: Monument to the Filial Piety of Mr. Jung Eom and the Sculpture to His Loyal Dog
stories.script: You can see the monument to the filial piety of Yangchon Jungeom and the sculpture to his loyal dog that used to run his errands for him on the right on the five-way street in Yangnim-dong along the Gwangju River in Nam-gu, Gwangju Metropolitan City, which has been known as the clan village of Gwangju Jung clan.   Jungeom was a civil official of the mid-Joseon Dynasty era with a nickname of Yangchon from the Gwangju clan. He was also the son of Jogye Manjong who served as the governor. He was born in Yangnim-dong, Nam-gu, and studied under Monk Pou, thanks to his father’s close relationship with Monk Pou. In 1552, he passed in first place among 200 in Saengwonsi (a type of civil service exam in the Joseon Dynasty) and passed in third place in Jinsasi (a type of civil service exam in the Joseon Dynasty), spending his youth in Yangnim-dong.  In 1558, he passed the civil service exam, got appointed as Seungmunwon Jeongja (a type of government post in the Joseon Dynasty), and entered Hodang to study further with other scholars. After that, he held various government posts such as Yejojeongrang, Byeongjojwarang, and Saganwon Jeongeon.   In 1574, Jeolla Governor Minheon Park spoke of Mokmingwan Jungeom, saying, “Namwon deputy governor Jeongeom warmly takes care of the people and administers with kindness, but when dealing with documents, he personally monitors and executes all documents and does not block civil complaints, which people appreciated a lot.” He left his mark as a hardworking, sincere, impoverished, and energetic Mokmingwan and was selected as an internal position and appointed to the Seungjeongwon Dongbuseungji, but when he heard the news that his mother was ill in his hometown, he immediately ran to see her. In order to provide for his mother, he volunteered to serve as Najumoksa and showed an exemplary administration, taking care of his mother day and night, suffering more than his own pain. He prayed for his mother while taking medicine, even tasting the stool, and caring for her with sincerity, but eventually, his mother passed away. Unable to overcome the sadness, he went to burial, sang morning and evening, and decided to live next to the grave for 3 years, however, got sick the following year and died. At the time, in order to make this noble filial piety a model for all, in 1611, filial piety was ordered at the entrance to the site of his birthplace, the position was increased to the Saheonbu Daesaheon, and Jeongryeogak was built with an appeal by Yejopanseo Jeonggu Lee. As this Jeongryeo was old, it was rebuilt primarily in 1705, but over the years, it collapsed. In 1975, descendants took the lead and repaired it again, giving it its present form.   Then, what is the Sculpture to His Loyal Dog that is with the Monument to the Filial Piety of Mr. Jung Eom?  Yangchon Jungeom had a native Korean dog, and she was so smart that she was able to protect her owner and do his errands well. At this time, communication and transportation were inconvenient, so people hung a note on the ankle of a pigeon to send a letter, and was dependent on a post horse. However, as this dog helped to greatly save time and money by doing simple correspondence errands, Yangchon used to use his dog for urgent communication.  It is said that he sent letters through this dog while staying in Yangnim-dong to take care of his mother's illness. It is also said that the letters he frequently sent to his father and various appeals and documents of the court were also sent through the dog he had raised. It is said that Yangchon put a bag with coins on the dog along with the paper bag with the letter, and when the dog is hungry, she would stop at the inn to get food and the owner of the inn would take money from the bag. An interesting anecdote is that when the dog ate her food and the owner of the inn takes too much money for the food, she would growl without leaving, so all the innkeepers treated this dog like a human being.   This dog, who became Jungeom's hands and feet, went on an errand to Hanyang and came home from a mission one day, giving birth to 9 pups under a bridge by the river in Jeonju, and died from exhaustion on the road in front of the house.  Yangchon lamented that he killed the dog by sending her on an errand without knowing whether the dog was having babies, ordered a mason to carve a sculpture of the loyal dog, and left it in the yard to commemorate the dog. It is said that filial piety was ordered down for this sculpture to the loyal dog in 1611 after Jeongeom's death, and his descendants built Yangchongong Jeongryeogak, and then erected the sculpture next to Jeongnyeogak to commemorate Yangchongong and his dog.    Yangchon Jungeom's filial piety and dog's loyalty to her master still touch our hearts.

stories.title: Lee Jang-woo's House
stories.script: Try finding a large house in Yangnim-dong, where the wealthy people of Gwangju used to live. That’s the Lee Jang-woo's House, which is also famous as a filming location for Clash of the Families and is designated as Gwangju Metropolitan City Folklore Material No. 1.   When you enter the Sangryangmun Gate of the main building, you can see that it was built in 1899 as it is written “February of the 3rd year of Gwangmu.” The owner at the time of construction is Byeongho Jeong, and it was bought by Jangwoo Lee in 1965, so it is called Lee Jang-woo's house now.  Jangwoo Lee, who contributed to the development of education in Honam, is the founder of Donggang Academy and Dongshin University in Naju, and the house is still managed by Dongshin University's school corporation.  Lee Jang-woo's house, distributed along Yangnimsan Mountain and placed along the Gwangju River, is a tiled house in the style of upper-class house that is arranged in a long line from east to west, and with the gatehouse, barn, building for servants, guesthouse, and main building arranged slightly off the axis.  As for the overall composition of the house, after passing the three-room gatehouse with a soaring gate, there are a large yard for the guesthouse, and the building for servants with a central gate, the guesthouse with one-room and three-room main floored room, and the main building are arranged side by side in front and back. Also, next to the main building, there is a recently restored building with a kitchen of 5 rooms. The main building has 6 rooms in the front and 4 rooms on the side, with small rooms on the front, back, left, and right. Unlike the straight guesthouse, the main building has an L-shaped floor plan. The floor plan of the main building, which is a large house of about 36 pyeong (around 119m2), from the left, is composed of a veranda floor, 1 small room, the main floored room of 2 rooms, a big room of 2 rooms, a kitchen of 1 room and 1 small room, and a small room of 2 rooms bent in the L shape. However, the L-shaped part of the main building has a small room in the front, a basement is placed under the two-room room, and a kitchen is placed at where it is bent in the L shape, which is out of the legend of the general L-shaped house configuration. This kind of transformation from the stereotype is a phenomenon commonly found in modern Hanok, and it seems to be an effort to make the activities of the women easier and secure a space for the family.  Round pillars were placed on the pedestal of Sebeoldae, columns and square pillars were built, and crossbeam supporters and camber beams are connected to girders. The structure is 2 Goju 5 Ryang of a tiled house with an octagonal roof. It is made with thick wooden rafters and has double-eaves and a skylight window in the central part of the gable. The door of the main floored room is a quartered partition door, a turtle ornament is placed in the middle and a sparrow-shaped ornament is placed on a strip of wood supporting a beam to fix the door.    Lee Jang-woo's House is a traditional house with a well-preserved architectural prototype. Since the trimming and the structure are outstanding and pedestal and stairs, round cornerstones and Shinbang stones are well finished, it is appraised as a masterpiece.   Let’s go and see Lee Jang-woo's House in Yangnim-dong, where the history of traditional culture is intact.

stories.title: Samirundong-gil Road
stories.script: On March 10th, 1919, many students and residents, who participated in the independence movement started at Supia Girls’ School in Yangnim-dong, passed Owen Memorial Hall and headed to Yangnim Upper Church, waving the Taegeukgi (the national flag of Korea) and singing Arirang on a small hill road here. Since then, this place became Arirang Hill. The March 1st Independence Movement in Gwangju was secretly planned at Pastor Gunghyuk Nam’s house, and about 100 people were arrested and the church (currently Gwangju Yangnim Church) got confiscated. After that, in 2009, a stone monument to 33 national representatives of the independence movement was installed in the hillside park on this road, and in 2014, it was named Samirundong-gil (March 1st Independence Movement Road) according to the implementation of the new address system.   Please imagine and feel the shouts of the time by walking along the Samirundong-gil Road, where patriots shouted for national independence.

stories.title: Cho Ara Memorial Hall
stories.script: . Cho Ara Memorial Hall is a special place where you can get a glimpse of the spirit of Ara Cho, who devoted her life to the women's movement, philanthropy, and the democratic human rights movement.   Ara Cho, who is called the mother of Gwangju, was born on March 28th, 1912, during the Japanese colonial era, in Daedan-ri, Bannam-myeon, Naju-gun, Jeollanam-do, as the second daughter out of 3 sons and 3 daughters to her father Hyungryul Cho and mother Seongeun Kim. She was influenced by her father Hyungryul Cho, a Christian elder, and grew up to be a devout Christian from an early age. In April 1927, she came to Gwangju and met the teacher Pilrye Kim at Supia Girls’ School in Yangnim-dong, and her relationship with Pilrye Kim became an opportunity for Ara Cho to dedicate her life to Gwangju YWCA. Pilrye Kim was a teacher at Gwangju Supia Girls’ School, a teacher at Jangheung Night School, and a person who laid the foundation for local women’s education, including the establishment of the Gwangju YWCA.  In January 1933, Ara Cho graduated from Supia Girls’ School and was a teacher at the Eeil School run by Missionary Seopyeong Seo. However, she was implicated in the ‘White Youth Crops Incident’ that participated in the Gwangju Student Movement, served a year in prison, and unfortunately, was also forcibly dismissed from her teaching position.  However, Ara Cho did not give in and constantly tried to regain our spirit, which had been cut off by the Japanese colonial rule, through the reconstruction of the Gwangju YWCA and the reconstruction of the Supia Girls’ School.   Ara Cho, who started as a managing director of Gwangju YWCA and then rose to the honorary chairman of Gwangju YWCA, established Gwangju YWCA as the stronghold of the women's movement and the democracy, human rights, and social justice movement. Thanks to this, Gwangju YWCA became the center of the women's movement and human rights movement in Gwangju together with women's activist Ara Cho. In July 1959, when the Gwangju YWCA Hall was built in Daeui-dong, Dong-gu, Gwangju, she made a great contribution as the chairperson of the establishment.  In the 1980s, when the Korean women's movement began in earnest, the Gwangju YWCA raised the status of women's organizations in the history of the Korean women's movement and contributed to society. Ara Cho's drive, perseverance, and dedicated leadership have made Gwangju YWCA solid.   In November 1984, she moved to a new building while serving as the construction chairperson of the Gwangju YWCA Yudong Hall. Gwangju YWCA Hall, located in Daeui-dong, Dong-gu, Gwangju, was a precious historical space where bullets and bloodstains of citizens remained during the Gwangju Uprising, so not being able to protect the site of the Gwangju Uprising is a great regret.   In addition, Ms. Ara Cho showed a steady interest in social welfare. She took the lead in social welfare work to become a true friend to the society's absurdity and marginalized neighbors by establishing Seongbinyeosa for war orphans, Honamyeosuk, which is a three-year night middle school, ‘Starlight Academy’, which is a night school for youth, in 1961, and ‘Gyemyeongyeosa’ for marginalized women.   During the Gwangju Uprising in 1980, Ara Cho worked as a member of the probation countermeasures committee and was taken to the martial law army and sentenced to 6 months in prison, but after being released from prison, she still took care of the families of the dead from Gwangju Uprising and Gwangju Uprising related detainees and their families even under the turbulent Fifth Republic. She also participated as a representative of the Korean women's community at the first inter-Korean women's debate after division.  Ara Cho was like the light of the Gwangju human rights movement and social movement, working as an advisor to the May 18th Democratization Movement Commemorative Project Promotion Committee, the Gwangju Jeonnam Headquarters for the National Movement, and the 21st Century Women’s Development Committee.  In recognition of her achievements, she received the Gwangju Citizens' Grand Prize, Jeong Ilhyeong Free Democracy Award, Mudeung Women's Grand Prize, and the Korea YWCA National Competition Grand Prize, and after her death, the National Order of Merit, Mugunghwa, was conferred.  In a lecture to commemorate Ara Cho’s 2nd anniversary, Mrs. Heeho Lee said “Elder Cho never gave up on finding and caring for the needy and starving neighbors and the lonely and sick neighbors and always prayed for them. Truly, Elder Ara Cho was a brave woman who carried the cross of the Lord and followed the Lord ceaselessly, and was an extraordinary person who created something out of nothing.”  Father Jovio Monsignor recalled Ara Cho in a lecture to commemorate the 6th anniversary of Ara Cho by saying “She deeply understood that the greatest suffering of the poor is not because of poverty, but the hardship of being despised and discriminated against because of poverty. She devoted her caring maternal love to opening and supporting Seongbinyeosa, Honamyeosuk, Starlight Academy, and Gyemyeongyeosa in an atmosphere of equal home and family without discrimination. With a motherly love that was enough to be set as an example for others, she sacrificed herself and devoted herself with the affection of a family.”

stories.title: Obang Choi Heung-jong Memorial Hall
stories.script: This is a memorial hall to commemorate Obang Heungjong Choi, who has dedicated his life to eradicating Hansen's disease, relieving the poor, independence movement, missionary activities, and educational activities.  . Obang Heungjong Choi's real name is Youngjong Choi, and he was born in 1880 in Bulo-dong, Gwangju, as the second son of 7 children to his father, Hakshin Choi and his mother, Mrs. Guk  Heungjong Choi was influenced by missionaries Eugene Bell and Owen, who were conducting missionary activities in Yangnim-dong, Gwangju as Southern Presbyterian missionaries in the United States in 1904, and became Christian while attending the first Christmas service in Gwangju held at the home of Missionary Eugene Bell in December 1904.  In 1905, with the help of Yunsu Kim, Heungjong Choi got a job as a patrolman at the Jeollanam-do Police Department of the Korean Empire, and the anecdote of him freeing the righteous army who were caught fighting the Japanese at the time is quite famous. He secretly released 12 subordinates of Gyuhong Ahn, the general of the righteous army from Boseong while transporting them from Hwasun. He also helped 6 soldiers of the righteous army who were about to be shot to escape from prison. The Japanese police adviser, who was suspicious of Heungjong Choi due to the two escapes of the soldiers, gave an order to Heungjong Choi to arrest the leaders of the Gwangju-area national debt repayment movement. At this time, Heungjong Choi boldly submitted a resignation letter and left the police force, where he had worked for three years.  Afterwards, he worked as an evangelist at the Yeomsan-ri Church of Glory, which was established in 1908 while preaching the gospel by Eugene Bell, and took on the turning point of his life.  In 1909, Missionary Forsythe, who was active in Mokpo, came to Gwangju to treat Missionary Owen, who was dying of acute pneumonia. Heungjong Choi meets Yunsu Kim, who had taught him Christianity, to pick up Missionary Forsythe at the request of Eugene Bell. On his way back to Gwangju, he meets a Hansen's disease patient who is shivering in the cold wearing rags stained with blood and pus. However, at this time, Missionary Forsythe takes the Hansen's disease patient on his horse all the way to Gwangju as if nothing is wrong and even gives his coat to the patient. This incident was a shock to young Heungjong Choi, and it became a compass for the rest of his life.  As a result, rumors spread that “a missionary in Yangnim-dong took a leper and treated him”, and lepers from all over the country flock to Jejungwon in Yangnim-dong. Unable to handle the influx of patients, Heungjong Choi donated 1,000 pyeong (around 3,306m2) of his land in Bongseon-dong to open ‘Gwangju Leper House’, the first hospital specializing in Hansen's disease in Korea. Heungjong Choi, who became a passionate member of the church through a fateful meeting with Forsythe, founded Bongseon-ri Church in 1912 and entered Pyongyang Theological Seminary in 1917 to become a paster by being appointed as an evangelist at the church outside the north gate. However, he was more enthusiastic about the work at Gwangju Leper House.  As the number of patients in Gwangju Leper House has since increased, rumors have spread that “Leprosy is attached to vegetables grown in the vegetable garden in Bongseon-ri”, which led to strong protests from the citizens. Accordingly, Heungjong Choi, along with Missionary Ilsun Woo from Jejungwon, received donations from the community leaders, purchased land of 150,000 pyeong (around 495,870m2) by the seaside in Sinpung-ri, Yulchon-myeon, Yeosu-si, built a community for lepers, and moved 60 lepers in September 1926 to provide a new home. This is ‘Aeyangwon’ of today.  In 1932, Heungjong Choi consulted with Seopyeong Seo, who was active in Yangnim-dong as a nursing missionary, decided to ask the Government General to build a facility for receiving and treating lepers, and went to Chiho Yun, Byeongok Cho, Seongsu Kim, Jaehong Ahn, Jinwoo Song, and Byeongro Kim from Seoul to explain their purpose. When everyone agreed to the proposal of Heungjong Choi, they organized the first National Leprosy Association in Korea with Chiho Yun as the resident and Heungjong Choi as the general secretary. After sending the proposal written by Jaehong Ahn to the Government General, they depart for the Government General from Gwangju with about 150 people at first, which became about 400 people by the time they arrived in Seoul. Pastor Heungjong Choi, who invaded the Government General with lepers, received a promise to greatly expand Jahyewon, a facility for receiving lepers, into a rehabilitation center, and to support those who received treatment to walk the path of rehabilitation. This is the famous Gura March, the leper march.   Heungjong Choi chose his nickname as 'Obang', which means 'letting go of the five things', which is to get rid of the obsession. The five things he let go of were family affairs, social prestige, economic interests, political activity, and sectarian activity. He declared, “I will depart from earthly affairs and live freely in God” and went into the Jeungsimsa Valley of Mudeungsan Mountain to live in retirement at Obangjeong, but his interest was still on beggars and patients. It was him who created ‘Samaewon’, a self-supporting village for the poor in Jeungsimsa Valley, and ‘Hohyewon’, a self-supporting village for inactive leprosy patients in Sanpo, Naju. He sets up a hut sanatorium in the valley of Mudeungsan Mountain for tuberculosis patients who have given up even at the hospital. Heungjong Choi himself built a mud house called ‘Bokeumdang’ in ‘Mudeungwon’ and works with tuberculosis patients. This is why beggars near Gwangju, tuberculosis patients from Mudeungsan Mountain, and lepers from Yeosu and Naju called “Father, Father” and cried at the funeral of Pastor Heungjong Choi, who was called the Mudeungsan Saint.   When the March 1st Movement broke out, Heungjong Choi was sent to prison for hurray at the Pagoda Park and was appointed as the senior pastor of the church outside the north gate, which was separated from the church inside the north gate. Afterwards, he led the founding of the Gwangju Christian Youth Group and vigorously developed labor, peasant movements, and national movements.  When Gyeongyangbangjuk was doomed to be landfilled by Japanese colonial rule, he formed the Gyeongyangbangjuk Anti-Landfill Struggle Committee and served as the chairman. The argument of the sixth out of 6 reasons for opposition, “In preparation for the development of Gwangju into a metropolis, the scenic area with beautiful scenery should be beautifully preserved” is an excellent idea that looked for the future value of Gwangju even when thought about it now. In 1939, Japan changed its original plan and landfilled only two-thirds of it due to strong opposition by Heungjong Choi and others, but in 1967, the rest disappeared into history along with Taebongsan Mountain.  On August 15th, 1945, Obang hears the long-awaited news of liberation from Mudeungsan Mountain. As Mongyang Woonhyeong Yeo and others formed the National Foundation Preparation Committee in Seoul, the National Foundation Preparation Committee was also formed in Jeollanam-do. In the election of officers of the Jeonnam National Foundation Preparation Committee held at the Gwangju Theater, Obang Heungjong Choi was unanimously elected as the Jeonnam Chairman of the National Foundation Preparation Committee. Then, on August 25th, at the ‘Gwangju Citizens Liberation Celebration Contest’ held at Gwangjuseojung with tens of thousands of crowds, Heungjong Choi emphasized, “Let’s all unite and build an independent nation.” Afterwards, Obang Heungjong Choi also served as an advisor to the U.S. Military Government, showing that he was the most trusted person in the area at the time.   In 1990, the government conferred the Order of Merit for National Founding to Obang Heungjong Choi, and the Gwangju YMCA established the Obang Scholarship Society in 1978 to commemorate the high will of Obang, taking care of inactive leprosy patients and their children.  Recently, Obang Heungjong Choi was drawn as a cartoon, and in 2009, the road from Bangnim 1-dong Community Center in Nam-gu to the entrance of Mudeung Park Apartment complex in Bongseon 2-dong was designated as 'Obang-ro' to honor the first pastor, independence activist, and social activist in Gwangju.

stories.title: House of Missionary Wilson
stories.script: The House of Missionary Wilson is the oldest surviving Western-style residential building in Gwangju. It was also designated as Gwangju City Designated Monument No. 15.   It is said that this building was built in the 1920s by an American missionary named Wilson, whose Korean name is Ilsun Woo. He is the person who took the lead in curing Hansen's disease, starting with the first orphanage in Gwangju for children with disabilities and orphans.   The House of Missionary Wilson later served as an important space when Soonee Park established Choonghyun Orphanage for war orphans. Soonee Park had experience living in the house of Missionary Ilsun Woo with his children as a child. While working as a piano player, Soonee Park dedicated her life to helping orphans when her husband Saengok Kim died in the Yeosu Suncheon Incident.   This place, overlooking the city of Gwangju, is located on a 10° slope of Yangnim-dong hill. It has a floor plan of a nearly square and consists of a basement, 1st floor, and 2nd floor with a porch, which is a protruding entrance to the front. The building does not particularly prefer south-facing, and it seems that the building is placed in the southwest direction to fit the topography. The exact date of construction is unknown because there are no records left, but it is presumed that it was built around 1911 to 1927, given that the same color gray bricks were used in the Supia Hall and the Curtis Memorial Hall built at the same time. On the other hand, some say that it was built in 1910 and that it was extended in 1921.   The planar shape is square, partially symmetrical and various rooms for various functions are properly arranged. At the front, the high and large porch is protruded to emphasize the frontality and symmetry. Of course, there was also a single door leading to the backyard on the backside, and the first floor was raised slightly from the site to make a basement floor with storage and boiler room, which went down from the side to the stairs. Glass windows were placed in the front to provide ventilation and light. A building with one basement floor and two above-ground floors can be found in Western-style residential architecture. At the bottom of the wall, two tiers of pedestals were placed as wall footings, and on top of that, a Dutch-style stacking of 55mm thick gray bricks was done. The first floor and the second floor were divided with a wall truss stacked with four protruding bricks, and the windows were made of glass windows that go up and down. Openness was secured by installing multiple windows not only on the front but also on the sides and back.  When you enter from the porch, the living room is right there, and the family room is right on the right. After passing the living room, there are stairs to the second floor on the right, and on the other side, there is a utility room, bathroom, and kitchen with a separate path to the family room. The second floor enters the interior stairs and through the hallway, bedrooms and bathrooms, which are private living spaces, are located. There is also a sunroom on the upper porch on the second floor. In the attic, it is written as “GUN ROOM”. Since Missionary Ilsun Woo enjoyed hunting on horseback, it is assumed that this was a place where the guns were stored at the time.    This building drew attention as a Westerner embodying the architectural style of their own country in another country. The trees planted around are also brought from overseas, so they are even more special. In particular, you can get a glimpse of the Western-style house through the chair-style living, fireplace, the brick building with basement and two floors, the rare gray brick, the porch, and the sunroom.   The appearance of these Western-style buildings and the way of life of missionaries must have been a subject of curiosity to Koreans and a spectacle of many citizens. Thanks to the exotic scenery, the House of Missionary Wilson, which appeared as the house where the main character Taehee Kim lived in the Tv show 'Forbidden Love', is said to have been used as a social gathering place for the upper class of Gwangju society.

stories.title: Yangnim-dong Horned Holly Hill
stories.script: The horned holly in Yangnim-dong, planted in the Joseon Dynasty, is 410 years old. It is a tree designated as Gwangju City Designated  Monument No. 17.  This tree is located in the backyard of the Christian Presbyterian Church Mission at the southern foot of Yangnimsan Mountain where Sajik Park is located. The place where the tree is located is the base of two American Southern Presbyterian missionaries, Yuji Bae and Clement Owen, who moved from Mokpo to Gwangju and started evangelism in 1899. They established ‘Supia Girls’ School’ and ‘Sungil School’ in 1907 and then established ‘Jejung Hospital’ in 1911 to further expand their missionary activities. This tree has grown wild in this area since the Joseon Dynasty and has been continuously protected as an ornamental by the Presbyterian Church. Some say that the horned holly, which has been designated as cultural property and is relatively well protected, must have been planted by early Western missionaries who settled in Yangnim-dong. This evergreen tree with pointy leaves has bright red berries that bear in autumn, looks quite familiar to us as the holly berries and leaves are often used as Christmas decorations. Considering that it is closely related to Christian culture and is still used as a decoration for Christmas cards, the story that missionaries planting it is not an outrageous story.   Horned holly is an evergreen broad-leaved small arboreous tree that grows mainly on the southern coast of Jeollanam-do and the west coast of Jeju. The Byeonsan Peninsula is the northern limit line, and it is also distributed in China, but it can be said that it is a tree in Jeollanam-do in particular. The leaves are thick leathery and glossy, and there are five thorn-shaped serrates on the edge of the leaf. The flowers are white in summer and bloom in the leaf axils, and the fruits ripen red in the fall, and in the winter, they are red in the snow, making them suitable as ornamental trees. This tree is about 6m high and has a circumference of 1.15m at the root of the tree, making it a large tree that is rarely seen in this species. The width of the branch and leaf part of the tree is 7m from north to south and 5m from east to west, and it is split in two at chest height. The lower part of the tree has a lot of cuts because the road is next to it, but the upper part is in the shape of a ball and is healthy.   The area around Yangnim-dong, where the residences of missionaries who came to Gwangju were built, was a habitat of horned holly. This tree, given its unusual name due to its five-pointy serrate on its leaves that resemble tiger claws and the myth that it was used as a back scratcher for an itchy tiger, is actually familiar to Westerners as well.  On the so-called Horned Holly Road that leads from Honam Theological University and Seminary to Supia Girls' High School, guesthouses and art studios that have been converted from missionaries' residences are opened, offering special inspiration and healing unique to Yangnim-dong.   A few years ago, a village company called ‘Holly Story’ was created, which made and sold food according to the recipes of missionaries and practiced sharing. Artists younger than Hyunseung Kim, who is a Christian poet, came together and published a literary coterie magazine titled ‘Horned Holly, On the Edge’ as well. In the gallery of artist Heewon Han from Yangnim Church, you can find stories and other works related to the horned holly.   On the Horned Holly Road, where small light bulbs illuminate the warm light, the dark path is lit up again, and the red fruits wrapped in green leaves are lit up.  If you climb up behind Horned Holly Hill, you can overlook Yangnim-dong and the beautiful surrounding scenery at a glance. The exact administrative address where the tree stands is 20, Jejung-ro 47beon-gil, Nam-gu, Gwangju for your reference.

stories.title: House of Missionary Cheolseon Heo
stories.script: Charles Betts Huntley is a missionary from the United States who came to Korea in 1965 and his Korean name is Cheolseon Heo. Missionary Cheolseon Heo started working as a hospital chaplain at Gwangju Christian Hospital and devoted himself to establishing a welfare system. In addition, he was a journalist and the last missionary in Gwangju who played a role in telling the world the terrible truth of Gwangju on May 18th, 1980.    Let’s look at the most meaningful space in the House of Missionary Cheolseon Heo. It is the darkroom. It is said that photos of the May 18th disaster were printed here. He also evacuated the May 18th protesters and foreign correspondents, including Jurgen Hinzpeter, in his house. He received the May Mother Award for his devoted efforts. Currently, the darkroom displays photos of people who did missionary work in Gwangju.   It is said that the deceased Missionary Cheolseon Heo loved Gwangju enough to leave a will before his death saying, “I want to go to Gwangju, I want to be buried in Gwangju.” So, the bereaved families came to Korea with some of the remains and buried them in the Missionary Cemetery located in Yangnim-dong.   We must not forget the sacrifice of Pastor Cheolseon Heo, who never gave up for the people of a distant country in the midst of a city where gunshots and death were rampant.

stories.title: Missionary Cemetery
stories.script: This is the group cemetery of Southern Presbyterian missionaries who took the lead in curing Hansen's disease, tuberculosis, and helping the poor by practicing sacrifice, sharing, and love in a distant foreign land. It is said that it is rare in the world to have a cemetery for missionaries of a specific denomination in one place.  The area around Yangnim-dong, where the missionaries settled in 1904, was called the Baekyeosigol, and it was a place where people who died of a terrible disease were wrapped up in blankets and thrown away. The missionaries built houses on 50,000 pyeong (around 165,290m2) of such a place and carried out missionary activities.  Missionary Cemetery is the place where 27 people were buried and 25 tombstones built as a monument to those who spread Christianity for the first time in Gwangju and Jeollanam-do, and their families during the Japanese colonial era. It is a noble place also with tombstones that were moved to this place after being buried in another area on one side of the cemetery.  On Yangnimsan Mountain, which climbs the missionary cemetery, there is a trail named after the missionaries, and there is a stone staircase with the missionaries' names engraved on them one by one.  From Owen, who tried to practice the love of Christ through healing and empathy, to Seopyeong Seo, who founded the Korea Nursing Association, established the Eeil Bible School to provide educational opportunities to women, and donated her own body for education while dying of malnutrition. How about giving thanks to the blue-eyed angels who died on this land while climbing up this stone staircase?

stories.title: Choonghyunwon
stories.script: Choonghyunwon was built by Soonee Park, who was influenced by her mother, Aeshin Park, an interpreter in the mission with Missionary Ilsun Woo, a member of the Southern Presbyterian Church in the United States to provide a home for war orphans that occurred before and after the Korean War under the Christian spirit of “Honor your father and mother, and, you shall love your neighbor as yourself”.   Thanks to her mother, Aeshin Park, who made a living by sewing for Missionary Ilsun Woo’s family in Yangnim-dong, Soonee Park, the daughter, was able to naturally grow up with them. Soonee Park grew up as a modern female pianist and became a hot topic as he married Saengok Kim, a singer and a student studying abroad in Tokyo, in 1994, but faced a turning point in her life due to his husband’s death after 4 years. After her husband’s death, Soonee Park was offered to move to the United States by foreign missionaries but she refused. Instead, he requested to rent a vacant building of Yangnim-dong Mission and established ‘Choonghyun Orphanage’ in 1949 and started taking care of infant orphans, which is the beginning of Choonghyunwon.   After that, for the increasing number of orphans, Choonghyunwon, which received the help of 13 missionaries from the Southern Presbyterian Church in the United States, moved to 210 Yangnim-dong in 1952.  In addition to caring for orphans, with the development of industrial society, from social problem treatment project to social problem treatment prevention project, it was operated for the purpose of financial support for boys and girls in charge of their households, a children’s hospital for orphans, dental treatment for orphans, and the return of runaway teenagers as    Gwangju’s first child counseling center, daycare center, domestic and foreign adoption agency, and housing protection project.  In 1976, with the support of the Dutch Children's Foundation, Gwangju's first children's communal playground was prepared and donated to Gwangju City. Also, a donation for the construction of a hospital dedicated to orphans arrived from the Netherlands, and it was planned to be built, but the Choonghyunwon site was tied to an urban park plan from 1976, so the funds were sent to 887-5 Ssangchon-dong to build the first Honam Welfare Center in the region, which continues to this day. Meanwhile, although the Yangnim-dong site has been mostly neglected, its historical value was recognized by Korean War veterans in 2005.   In particular, there is a statue of Lieutenant Colonel Blaisdell in the backyard. Lieutenant Colonel Blaisdell, who took care of the orphans during the Korean War, tried to evacuate the orphans from Incheon to Jeju with a landing ship, but the situation was unsatisfactory, as the ships could not arrive. At the same time, Colonel Rogers, the head of the Operations Department of the 5th Air Force Command, heard about the situation and promised to support the transport aircraft. However, for Lieutenant Colonel Blaisdell, there was no way to transport more than 1,000 children to Gimpo.  At that time, Lieutenant Colonel Blaisdell, who discovered the trucks of the US Marine Corps, ordered that the children be moved by truck, saying that it was an order from the superior. The Marines immediately traveled to Gimpo several times with 14 trucks, transporting 960 children and Korean workers. In this way, 16 C-54 transport aircraft safely transported them to Jeju, and this is the Operation Kiddy Car.  Although he is not directly related to Choonghyunwon as he did not transport the orphans of Choonghyunwon, a statue was still built to commemorate Lieutenant Colonel Blaisdell as he tried to save the lives of children even by breaking the orders.   Currently, Choonghyunwon is a child care facility of 37.8 pyeong (around 125m2), with all red brick exterior walls and a gable-shaped building. It has a structure that considers the health of the orphanage children by having windows all over the south side as children with jaundice or tuberculosis in particular need a lot of sunlight. The 1st floor used to have 4 rooms with hardwood floors, but now it is being used as an exhibition space. The 2nd floor, going up the steep stairs, is an attic and this was the room for newborns. To the south of the front, there is a wide window where you can see the Missionary Cemetery at a glance. At that time, there were doors on both sides leading to the outside veranda, and the chimneys were to the east and west. It is a building built in the same format as the Caddington Christian Hospital Director's house, built with red bricks. Now, the site is divided with Honam Theological University and Seminary by a road, but it used to be possible to climb up and down a gentle slope as it was a single area.   Here, photos of Korean War veterans who took care of orphans in the Korean War and rare materials related to the Korean War owned by Choonghyunwon are available in the experience hall, which restored the orphanage buildings from the time when Choonghyunwon was opened, in 2009.  There is also an experience of Korean etiquette culture for overseas adoptee families, so why not go to Choonghyunwon together and try it out?

stories.title: Leeleenam Studio
stories.script: Located on the site of Missionary Peterson's residence, Leeleenam Studio is a complex cultural space composed of media art artist Leenam Lee's creative studio, media art museum, and media cafeteria.  The artist continues to work on reinterpreting old paintings in a modern way based on media. The ‘Reborn Light’, a Pieta statue displayed in the courtyard of the studio, is a famous work that leads the magnificent atmosphere of the studio. At the studio that is composed of a space to share the values of culture and art with the public by reinterpreting the dedication of Missionary Peterson, who was devoted to the Christian spirit, you can meet the artist’s new works and various projects in the 220 pyeong (around 727m2) main exhibition room. In the moving space inside, you can enjoy not only monitor works but also media works through projection mapping. You can also experience media art outdoors with an LED media wall installed on the exterior wall. After viewing the exhibition, if you go to the rooftop, the open scenery of Yangnim-dong will give you a time of healing.  Why not enjoy a time that satisfies your senses at Leeleenam Studio, a space where you can relax and enjoy culture and art together?

stories.title: Yangpajeong
stories.script: Try going up the wooden stairs behind the Yangnim-dong Public Security Center. You will see a pavilion there. It is Yangpajeong, which was built by Nakgyo Jeong, a wealthy man in Gwangju.   Nakgyo Jeong, who built Yangpajeong, was a wealthy man born in Yangnim-dong, Gwangju, who owned huge farmland in the Gwangju area. At that time, he ran an onion farm to manage a lot of lands, and the corporate address was 157 Yangnim-dong. Considering that the corporate address and home address are often the same, 157 Yangnim-dong seems likely to be his home address.  In the year the Japan-Korea Treaty of 1905 was signed, he was appointed to the Gyeonggijeon Chambong, which is a type of government post, but he quit immediately and built Yangpajeong at the foot of Sajiksan Mountain overlooking the Gwangju River in 1914 and donated it to Gwangju. Because Nakgyo Jeong was well versed in poetry and had accumulated many merits for tenant farmers, tenant farmers near Gwangju built a memorial to Nakgyo Jeong. Nakgyo Jeong had two sons. The eldest son, Byeongho was adopted by his uncle, which led his second son, Sangho to become the eldest son in the family register. The best Hanok in Yangnim-dong known today as ‘Lee Jang-woo’s House’ at 128 Yangnim-dong was originally owned by Jeong Byeongho Jeong, who was adopted by his uncle. Sangho, who became the eldest son, studied in Germany thanks to the wealthy financial condition of the family. He is also known as a person who brought baseball equipment to Gwangju and introduced baseball to Gwangju in earnest. He also published ‘Yangpajeongshigo’ by collecting his father's poems and ran for the mayor of Gwangju in 1958, but after losing the election, the family’s financial condition started to be on decline. It was around this time that the Hanok owned by Byeongho Jeong, his brother, was handed over to Jangwoo Lee.   Behind Yangpajeong Pavilion, Chunghontap Tower was built in 1981 to commemorate 3,196 people who gave their lives for the country and people during the October 10th Yeosu Suncheon Incident and the Korean War. The Gwangju Video Center is located behind the Police Chunghontap Tower, and it is a great place to see Mudeungsan Mountain, downtown, and Jotanbo of Gwangju River at a glance. When Yangpajeong was built, there was Jotanbo at the site of the old Red Cross Hospital. Then, what would this Jotanbo with the unfamiliar name be?
