There was ‘Jotanbo’, also known as ‘Jochambo’, which was about 10m deep by blocking the Gwangju River under Yangpajeong to bring water to Gyeongyangbangjuk. It is quite large as the water was filled from Yangnim Police Station under Yangpajeong to the front of the old Red Cross Hospital where Jotanbo was located. Yunsang Choi, who serialized ‘60 Years of Gwangju’ in the monthly magazine ‘New Jeonnam’ published by Jeonnam Gongronsa in the 1970s, introduced that “Jotanbo not only served as a source of water for Gyeongyangbangjuk but was also used as a swimming pool for nearby children.”   When you climb the recently built Sajik Park Observation Tower, you can see Gwangju at a glance and Sajiksan Mountain is in the form of extending in the north-south direction alongside Gwangju River. Sajiksan Mountain, extending from north to south, met and bumped into a rocky mountain with its head protruding toward the Gwangju River, creating a deep puddle of water beneath it, and people called this place ‘Kotbasim’. Since Yangpajeong is built on top of that rocky mountain, the scenery must be outstanding. Kot of Kotbasim refers to a terrain where a part of the land protrudes into a river or sea due to a change in the cape.   Yangpajeong has a structure with 3 rooms on the front and 2 rooms on the side with a corrugated tile roof and an octagonal roof and the floor is made of cement, making it look a bit barren. Originally there was a floor, but it seems to have been made of cement during the repair process that came later. The pavilion usually has a signboard stating the history of building the pavilion or the atmosphere of the surrounding area. Yangpajeong also has many such signboards, some of which were written by Unram Bonghyeon Jeong from Gokseong. Few people remember this person's name today, but he was a famous scholar at the time. Perhaps it's because of the decline of Chinese studies, even his name feels unfamiliar now. If we go back to his name and look for a relationship, there is playwright Woojin Kim, who committed suicide in Hyeonhaetan along with Shimdeok Yun, who was the best soprano singer of the time and sang 'Praise of Death' in the 1930s. Woojin Kim's father-in-law is Bonghyeon Jeong.  The name of the pavilion, Yangpajeong, is derived from the nickname of Nakgyo Jeong, ‘Yangpa (meaning onion)’, who built the building.   Yangpajeong is built on a rock protruding from the top of Kotbasim. However, there was another pavilion built on an artificial island in Gwangju River where there was Kotbasim under Yangpajeong long before Yangpajeong was built. It is Seokseojeong, which was built by Gwangju Pastor Sang Kim during the Goryeo Dynasty. Even in the Joseon Dynasty, when there were many pavilions, Seokseojeong was famous enough to be counted as one of Gwangju's most scenic spots. It is not clear when the famous Seokseojeong disappeared, though. Judging from the record that “it is now in ruins” in ‘Gwangjueupji’, compiled around 1800, it is only estimated that it disappeared before the reign of King Jeongjo.  According to an article written by Nakgyo Jeong, the place of Yangpajeong was originally the place of Seokseojeong. It is the record that says, “I rebuilt the ruined site where the old Seokseojeong used to be and built this pavilion today.”  However, this seems a little different from the description of the topography in ‘Seokseojeonggi’ written by Saek Lee. Perhaps there was a mistake by Nakgyo Jeong.   Now, as the Gwangju Stream is straightened, the famous Kotbasim is filled, and Jotanbo, an amusement park where they used to ride boats, is disappeared and gone. Even though the old scenery is no longer available, Yangpajeong, which embraced the scenery in its heart, is still standing there today, embracing the history of Gwangju. Why not take the time to go up to Yangpajeong and look back at the countless history of Gwangju?

stories.title: Gallery S
stories.script: Gallery S is a commercial art gallery located at the center of Gwangju and Jeonnam art since its opening in 2012. It moved to this unique place with an orange half-moon-shaped exterior at the entrance of the beautiful Yangnim History and Culture Village overlooking the Gwangju River in the fall of 2021.  How about enjoying contemporary art at the gallery café CAVE, which contains a 25-meter-long cave that was used as an air defense shelter during the Japanese colonial era, and the unique exhibition hall where the granite bedrock of Yangnimsan Mountain is exposed? You can fully enjoy the scenery of the Gwangju River from the rooftop.

stories.title: HANHEEWON Museum of Art
stories.script: In July 2015, Heewon Han opened the ‘HANHEEWON Museum of Art’ at 27-6 Yangchon-gil, Yangnim-dong, where he first started his art. It is a cultural space converted from a small Hanok.   Western painter Heewon Han was born in 1955 in Songjeong-dong, Gwangju. His father, Yijik Han, was born in Pyongyang and started as a poet at the recommendation of Chunwon Kwangsoo Lee. Pastor Kyungjik is his uncle. His father, Yijik Han, came to Gwangju before the Korean War and worked as a teacher. After moving to places such as Damyang, Hampyeong, Gwangyang, and Naju, they settled in Yangnim-dong and started to live there. Following his father Yijik Han, Heewon Han started living in Yangnim-dong when he was in the 3rd grade of elementary school. He grew up in a house under Yangnim Church in Gijang, which was the pastoral space of Pastor Changguk Kim, the father of poet Hyunseung Kim, and spent his childhood reading literature in his father's library. It is a famous fact that he lived in a neighborhood with novelist Suntae Moon and broadcast writer Sohye Cho. He graduated from Hakgang Elementary School, Sungil Middle School, and Sungil High School. After graduating from high school, he visited Seungyoon Oh's studio and first encountered painting. So, for a year, he fell in love with art and drew, and then went on to the fine arts education department of Chosun University. In his senior year, in 1978, he drew a large-scale painting depicting the poor people in the basement of Yanglim Church. It is one of the works of Minjung Art. After graduating from the Department of Fine Arts Education at Chosun University, he also became a member of the Gwangju Artists Community founded in 1988 and was appointed as a teacher at Suncheonyeosang in 1981, where he worked for 10 years. . From then on, Heewon Han held the ‘Market Exhibition’ for 3 years, in which he carried paintings on a truck and toured the marketplaces in Gwangyang, Hwagae Market, and Guryejang to exhibit. It was called the first ‘moving museum’.  Heewon Han, who moved to Gwangjusanggo in 1991, immersed himself in oil painting in earnest while living away from his family. The reason was to look back on his inner world. At night, he used to draw the night scenery of Sinchang-dong, which was dark blue. In 1993, he went to Seoul with 150 works and held his first solo exhibition. His works captured and expressed fundamental human emotions such as death, despair, pain, and joy through the most common materials such as wind, ginkgo trees, stars, villages, and roads.  In addition, he went to the site where old houses in Yangnim-dong were being demolished due to redevelopment and drew the scenery of Yangnim-dong on the relics and window frames of the village. Thanks to this, Yangnim-dong, known only as a Western missionary village, was able to transform into an artist's village.  Although Heewon Han's works are paintings, they give us the feeling of looking at a poem drawn in color. The poetic paintings tell the inner story, and they received a lot of love from artists and audiences with ‘Poetry-like Paintings’ and ‘Picture-like Poems’. He crossed the boundaries of ‘poetry’ and ‘painting’ and showed a rich imagination and depth of life. His works breathed life and added warmth to things that were forgotten, alienated, and abandoned in everyday life. The warm gaze on life shown in his works comforted the modern people who were weary of the bleak world.   In the meantime, Heewon Han has participated in exhibitions such as 'Working People Exhibition', 'The Field of Life', 'Minjung Art 15 Years Ago', 'Gwangju Unification Art Festival', 'Korean Spirit of Namdo', 'In Search of the Origin of Namdo Culture', 'Northeast Asia and the Third World Art Exhibition', 'Meeting of the Tradition of Namdo Lyrics Literature and Contemporary Art', 'Collective Creation Village Project', 'Portrait of Young Artists', 'Korean Contemporary Art Projection Exhibition', 'New York Art Expo', 'Gwangju Istanbul Exchange Exhibition' ', and also served as the chairman of the 'Good Morning Yangnim Festival Organizing Committee'.   HANHEEWON Museum of Art aims to instill awareness of Yangnim-dong as an art village by exhibiting works of artists from Yangnim-dong and to show the spirit of art alive in Yangnim-dong through planning related to Yangnim-dong. In addition, anyone who visits the art museum can drink tea freely, so it serves as a space for artworks and a resting place. Above all, it is planned to be operated as a space that mainly exhibits exhibitions related to the history and culture of Yangnim-dong, so why not go before it's too late?

stories.title: Jeong Yulseong Street Exhibition
stories.script: At the entrance of Yangnim-dong, there is Jeongyulseong-ro. The distance from the bust of Yulseong Jeong next to the Blue Road Park to the birthplace of Yulseong Jeong is called Jeongyulseong-ro. In 2009, the Jeong Yulseong Street Exhibition was created by collecting various photos and video materials related to Yulseong Jeong.   Yulseong Jeong is a musician representing modern Gwangju, and he is revered as an anti-Japanese activist and the best popular musician in China. He is one of China's three great revolutionary musicians who composed the Chinese People's Army Song. He was born in Gwangju, but not many people know about it.   In 2009, among the 100 Founding Heroes of New China selected by the Chinese, Yulseong Jeong was proudly named. The sheet music for the Eighth Route Army March, which he composed, is cast and displayed on the walls of the Museum of the War of Chinese People's Resistance Against Japanese Aggression near Beijing. However, there is not much information about him compared to his fame. Even his place of birth is unclear. Recently, the ‘Yulseong Jeong Birthplace Verification Committee’ concluded the controversy by stating that Bulo-dong is the place where he was born and Yangnim-dong is the place he grew up after birth among 79 Yangnim-dong and 163 Bulo-dong, Gwangju, where the birthplace of Yulseong Jeong was controversial, and that both places are considered as his birthplace.  Born as the fifth of 5 sons and 3 daughters to his father, Haeeop Jeong, who was a teacher at Supia Girls' School, Yulseong Jeong moved to Neungju, Hwasun at the age of 3, and entered Neungju Public School in 1922. After moving to Gwangju again in 1924, he transferred to Gwangju Sungil School and entered Jeonju Shinheung Middle School in 1929 at the age of 15.  In 1933, the year he turned 19, he went to Nanjing, China with his fourth older brother, Euieun Jeong, who infiltrated Korea as a recruitment agent for the Korean Revolutionary Military and Political Officer School, and entered the Korean Revolutionary Military and Political Officer School. Since this school was a training center for the anti-Japanese struggle officers of Uiyeoldan led by Yaksan Wonbong Kim, he started walking the path of the anti-Japanese movement in earnest. Afterwards, he received spy training at a special school in Nanjing, and after spying against Japanese forces in Nanjing and Shanghai, he joined the Korean National Liberation League.  After graduating from the Korean Revolutionary Military and Political Officer School, his life, while performing a secret mission as a member of the Korean Revolutionary Party, hits a turning point when meeting Prof. Krinowa, a graduate of the Leningrad College of Music, in Shanghai, where he learned vocal music and composition. Krinowa highly valued Yulseong Jeong's musical quality, saying, If you go to Italy to study, you will become the Caruso of the East. After entrusting Yulseong Jeong as a tenor singer of the ‘World Masterpiece Concert’ held in Shanghai, Krinowa advised him to study in Italy, but he was not destined to leave China or to deviate from the path of the anti-Japanese struggle. It was around this time that the name of Bueun Jeong as a child was changed to ‘Yulseong’ in the sense of ‘succeeding through melodies’.  In 1934, after graduating from the Political, Military, and Revolutionary Caucus School, he got a job at the National Telephone Bureau in Nanjing and started espionage to dig up information about the Japanese consulate making phone calls to his home country. Then he moved to Shanghai and was active in 'May Literary History', etc. In 1937, as a special envoy of the Korean National Liberation League centered on his brother-in-law Geonwoong Park, he passed through the Eighth Route Army office in Xi’an and entered Yan'an. While attending the Island North Engineering and Lu Xun Art School in Yan'an, he created immortal songs such as ‘Yan'an Song’, ‘Eighth Route Army March’, ‘Yeonsuyo’, showing off his musical talents to the fullest. It is said that even Mao Zedong, who was leading the Communist Party of China in Yan'an at the time, liked Yulseong Jeong's songs and hummed his songs often.  In the 1940s, he participated in the Joseon Independence League organized in Yan'an, and joined the Korean Volunteer Army, a military organization, to participate in the Battle of Taihang Shan. He was an international anti-Japanese fighter who fought fiercely with the military. After returning to Yan'an, he became the training officer of the Joseon Revolutionary Military Government School and was in charge of the education and training of the Joseon Volunteers. The Jeong Yulseong Memorial Hall, which contains his anti-Japanese deeds, is located at the foot of Taihang Shan along with the Memorial of the Joseon Volunteers.  Immediately after liberation, he entered Pyongyang under the orders of the Chinese Communist Party to compose the Korean People's Army March, which became a military song for the North Korean People's Army. This Korean People's Army March song was played at an official event venue during the historic June 15th inter-Korean summit between President Daejung Kim and Supreme Leader Kim Jong-il in 2000.  His eventful later years were a series of misfortunes. Even Yulseong Jeong, who composed the military songs for the People's Army of China and North Korea, was deprived of opportunities to perform and restricted from his artistic activities in the wake of the Cultural Revolution that took place for 10 years from 1966. In December 1976, at the end of the Cultural Revolution, he collapsed from a brain hemorrhage while taking his granddaughter Eunju for a walk along a river near Beijing. He was only 62 years old. Today, he is buried at the Babaoshan Revolutionary Cemetery in downtown Beijing, China's national cemetery.   Yulseong Jeong's inscription reads, the Chinese people sang his song to drive out the Japanese invaders, overthrew the old China, and built a new China, which shows his status in China. Respected as a people's hero who founded the People's Republic of China only after his death, his brilliant achievements were also the fruit of Joseon's aspiration for freedom and independence.   In 1993, after Yulseong Jeong's death, the Jeong Yulseong Music Festival was held at the Sejong Center for the Performing Arts, hosted by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, to commemorate the first anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic ties between Korea and China. In 2005, the Jeong Yulseong International Music Festival was hosted by Nam-gu Office in Gwangju. Starting from 2007, a music festival to commemorate him has been held in Gwangju and Beijing back and forth.  Not only Yulseong Jeong, who was a fierce anti-Japanese fighter before an anti-Japanese musician, but also his father and 5 siblings all participated in the anti-Japanese independence movement. Yulseong Jeong's family from his mother’s side also had a great influence on the anti-Japanese independence movement of the Jeong family.  Heungjong Choi, his older uncle, was the first pastor in Gwangju who led the Gwangju March 1st Movement, and it was Heungjong Choi who provided the opportunity for Yulseong Jeong to grow into the godfather of Chinese revolutionary music. By listening to Heungjong Choi's phonograph, Yulseong Jeong met a new world of music and was encouraged by his uncle saying I want you to become a musician which made him dream. If the older uncle Heungjong Choi led Yulseong Jeong on the path of the independence movement, the younger uncle Youngwook Choi provided a strong background for them.   There are not many traces of Yulseong Jeong in Gwangju. In the yard in front of the Hiddink Hotel at 163 Bulo-dong, there is a monument engraved with the words ‘Birthplace of Musician Yulseong Jeong,’ and at 79 Yangnim-dong, there is a monument engraved with the words ‘Musician Yulseong Jeong’s Birthplace’. At the entrance to Jeongyulseong-ro from Daenam-ro towards Yangnim-dong, there is a statue of Yulseong Jeong donated by the Youth Association of Haizhu District, Guangzhou, China in 2008 for friendly exchange between Korea and China. It reproduced his life by showing one hand writing songs and the other hand conducting. In Jeongyulseong-ro, there is the Jeong Yulseong Street Exhibition, where street records expressing the scale of ‘Yan'an Song’ and kiosks where you can enjoy the world of Yulseong Jeong’s music are installed. The name ‘Yulseong’ is engraved under the signboard of Jeong Yulseong Street Exhibition, which is written by Seolsong Jeong, wife of Yulseong Jeong.  Although the length of 233m is short, I have a feeling that Jeongyulseong-ro will become a highway connecting the future of Korea and China!

stories.title: LEEKANGHA Art Museum
stories.script: The LEEKANGHA Art Museum is a place where you can see the works of Kangaha Lee expressing the identity of the nation and the life of the Namdo people based on our traditions.   Kangaha Lee learned how to use pigments and paint Dancheong from his father, who makes Dancheong paintings and decorative items for biers. The skill and spirit he learned from his father became the background for later making works based on our national tradition.  The life-changing meeting for Kangaha Lee was when he was in elementary school and met Yeongyun Kang, a sophomore in the art department of Chosun University, and Yeonseop Choi, a freshman, thinking that he would go on to become an artist. At the same time, in high school, he learned the art from the Western painter Jongsoo Kim and learned about the Namdo Western Painting Group. He even won a national art practice contest while studying in the art department. At the recommendation of his parents, he entered the Department of Electrical Engineering at Chosun University, but continued his studies during the day and continued to draw in Yeongyun Kang’s Rodin studio at night, walking the path of an artist. In 1980, at the age of 30, he entered the Department of Fine Arts Education at Chosun University's College of Education and formed Nammaekhoe in that year.   Gwangju Uprising had a great influence on Kangaha Lee's art world. After witnessing a paratrooper beating a girl on the school campus during the Gwangju Uprising in May 1980, Kangaha Lee participated as a member of the militia and started making promotional banners for the militia. However, in the historical reality where the mass media and media cover up the truth and turn those who cried for democratization into a group of evil, he was imprisoned for one month, sentenced to prison life, was chased as a wanted person, and led a difficult life in seclusion for 2 years.  After Gwangju Uprising, he stayed in a relative's house during his seclusion for about 2 years, and became acquainted with Yangnim-dong, Nam-gu, Gwangju, and lived there for the next 30 years.  After that, Kangaha Lee won the Silver Award for 2 years in a row at the Le Salon exhibition in France with a work called ‘Maeg (meaning pulse)’ as Yangnim-dong became a place to find peace for his mind during difficult times physically and mentally, allowing him to immerse himself in his work.  In 1985, he held his first solo exhibition at the Namdo Arts Center and exhibited about 100 works produced from the late 1970s to the early 1980s, including ‘Road to the Port’, ‘Hyang (meaning scent)’, and the ‘Maeg’ series. There was a time when ‘Road to Spring’ became an issue in the art world by exhibiting at the ‘Realism of Korea’ exhibition held at the Lotte Jamsil Museum of Art. At that time, the Gwangju Ilbo said, “An exhibition that gathers the works of Korea’s leading realism artists has been held and has become a hot topic in Korean art circles. In this exhibition, Kangaha Lee shows his uniqueness in his perception of reality, and in particular, he shows a section of realist painting that linearly depicts the real landscape of a fishing village.”    In commemoration of the 50th anniversary of the liberation of Korea, the 5th solo exhibition ‘For the Future through True Change’, which exhibited masterpieces from the 1990s, was an important exhibition. It was held from mid-August to the end of November as an exhibition touring 7 cities across the country, including Seoul. From 1988 to 2005, Kangaha Lee traveled to Japan, China, Central and South America, Russia, the Mediterranean Sea, Europe, India, and other overseas countries to create artworks and also contributed travel journals along with his works to the Mudeung Daily, Gwangju Ilbo, and Jeonnam Ilbo. In 2003, he was diagnosed with rectal cancer and spent 5 years fighting the disease. During his battle with illness, he burned his artistic soul, leaving behind a number of unfinished works. Over the past 30 years as an artist, he has published 5 collections of paintings and held more than 100 group exhibitions and 8 solo exhibitions, including ‘Today’s Local Artists Exhibition’, ‘DMZ Work Exhibition’, and ‘Korea-China Exchange Exhibition’.   The Maeg series by Kangaha Lee is based on the Dancheong technique and contains Korean traditional ideas and colors such as Buddhism and folklore. It is a work that seeks to find a new state of art and beauty in search of the pulse flowing in the history of the nation and it was drawn by studying the pulse of our culture. In the Maeg series, the boundary between life and death, and the real and the ideal world, is implicitly expressed through the ‘Bal’, which is made by weaving a long and thin cord with a string or hanging several strings side by side. In other words, the world in front of the ‘Bal’ is the real world, and the world inside the ‘Bal’ is the invisible world, the ideal world, and the world of the mind.   Based on the mountains and rivers of Namdo, Kangaha Lee drew works that researched and interpreted the lives of the Namdo people and our traditional culture. The spirit of Koreans was expressed through Dancheong and traditional patterns, and the spirit that is ingrained in the lives of our people was put into the work. These works represent the human-centered spiritual world flowing at the base of our nation with the grassroots that lead the life in the sky and Namdo, which symbolize heaven and earth.  In other words, Kangaha Lee wanted to say through his work that the string that connects heaven and earth is unity based on the history of our nation, and that love for humans is love.   If you are interested in knowing more about Kangaha Lee’s works, please visit LEEKANGHA Art Museum and take a look at his art world.

stories.title: Copper Plate Street
stories.script: When the residences or writing sites of famous writers and artists were demolished when Yangnim Humansia Apartments were built, Copper Plate Street was made with copper plates with contents related to them in honor of the artists. When these copper plates were installed on the sidewalk, Copper Plate Street was created naturally.  Enjoy the works of artists of Yangnim-dong, including Spring Rain by Poet Soobok Lee, the residence of Broadcast Writer Sohye Cho, Yan’an Song by Musician Yulseong Jeong, works by Artist Dongshin Bae, Autumn Prayer by Poet Hyunseung Kim, while walking along Copper Plate Street between Yangnim Humansia Apartment Complex 1 and 2.

stories.title: Neul Workshop
stories.script: The Craft Gallery Neul Workshop is the workplace and exhibition space of artist Seokhyeon Choi, a master of lacquerware, a traditional Korean craft.   This is an exhibition space specializing in crafts, and the lacquer works of Najeon lacquer by craftsman Seokhyeon Choi, who has been creative for decades in Yangnim-dong, are on permanent display. Artist Seokhyeon Choi is specializing in the exhibition and R&D of Najeon lacquerware, including barrel lacquerware, which are lacquer relics excavated from the Sinchang-dong site in Gwangju. As a space to increase contact points with the public and promote the excellence and beauty of lacquerware, you can find many works with traditional beauty and works with modern beauty, so please feel free to enjoy various crafts.

stories.title: Horned Holly Art Polygon
stories.script: Horned Holly Art Polygon, a complex cultural space, has been newly opened behind the horned holly.  As the name ‘Art Polygon’ suggests, it is a ‘complex cultural space that allows all cultural activities that are approached with multilateral and multifaceted thinking’. This was originally a space of about 10 pyeong (around 33m2) that was used as a garage for Missionary Yohan Won’s house, but ARTZOO, a culture and art agency, expanded it while preserving the original structure and transformed it into the current space. It is a place where the rich historical stories of Yangnim-dong meet current artists and planners and are reborn into various works and programs.  How about visiting this place as various events are held here in addition to exhibitions and performances?

stories.title: Monument for Dahyeong Kim Hyeon-seung
stories.script: On the Monument for Dahyeong Kim Hyeon-seung in Honam Theological University and Seminary, his representative work, Autumn Prayer, is written. What was Hyeonseung Kim's life would have been like, who used to like to contemplate while looking at Mudeungsan Mountain?  Hyeonseung Kim was born to a Christian family, father Changguk Kim, and mother Eungdo Yang, as the second son of 6 children right after the forced annexation of Korea and Japan.  He was born in Pyeongyang, Pyeongannam-do, and was from the Gimhae clan with the nickname of Dahyeong and Nampung, but he did not consider Pyeongyang his hometown. He mentioned several times in his poems “Gwangju is my hometown”, where he shared the major phases of his childhood, youth, and middle age. After his father was ordained as a pastor, he was sent to Jeju and lived in Jeju-eup until the age of 6, and at this time, his father, Pastor Changguk Kim, actively participated in the March 1st Movement.  In 1919, when the March 1st Movement spread across the country, Pastor Kim was sentenced to prison for raising 10,000 won for the independence movement and secretly remitting it to the Shanghai Provisional Government. The father's anti-Japanese movement in Jeju is also connected with Jeju Uprising in the future. Hyeonseung Kim watched all of his father's anti-Japanese independence movement, prosecution, trial, and mother taking care of his father's imprisonment through the eyes of a six-year-old. This process was a shock to him, who had a delicate and sensitive disposition.  Then, the following year, in 1920, his father moved the trading point to Gwangju, Jeolla-do, and served in this area for 30 years. Accordingly, Hyeonseung Kim also started living at 78 Yangnim-dong, Gwangju at the age of 7. Afterwards, he was sent to Pyongyang, where his older brother was studying first, and entered Sungil Middle School, and during vacations, he went back and forth to his hometown of Gwangju. He lived in the school dormitory and became engrossed in literature. At this time, he read the British poet Robert Browning’s ‘Pippa's Song’ and was impressed, began to study poetry, and started showing his literary talent from an early age by posting and publishing his own poem ‘Volcano’ in the school magazine ‘Sungsil’. Around this time, he also developed the gastrointestinal disease, which later became a chronic disease.  He entered the liberal arts department at Sungsil Vocational School in 1932 and listened to lectures from Yangjudong Hyoseok Lee, who was a professor, and immersed himself in his studies with a strong creative desire. As a result, the gastrointestinal disease got worse, and in 1933, the following year, he inevitably stopped school and returned to Gwangju, where his parents were, to recuperate. He returned to school in a hurry after recovering his health, and even after winter break, he stayed alone in the dormitory and wrote poems late into the night. The poems he wrote at that time were ‘When the Lonely Winter Evening Comes, You’ and ‘Young Dawn Comes to Us’. He submitted these to the school magazine, which caught the attention of Prof. Yangjudong, and had ‘When the Lonely Winter Evening Comes, You’ published in the literary section of the Dong-A Ilbo. Through this, Hyeonseung Kim entered the literary circles regardless of the annual spring literary contest or magazine recommendations, which is the customary practice of appearing, and he was 21 years old at this time.  After his debut, Critic Hyomin Hong praised him as “a poet who appeared like a comet”, and his senior writers also praised him. As such, he became a noted poet from the beginning of his career.  Unfortunately, the gastrointestinal disease recurred, and he had to go to Gwangju for recuperation again. On the other hand, he gets a job as a teacher at his alma mater, Sungil School, and hardship comes to him one day. In March 1937, when a refusal to worship a shrine occurred at the church in attendance, Hyeonseung Kim was arrested as the leader and thought-provoking criminal and subjected to severe torture and abuse for more than 15 days. In this incident, Pastor Changguk Kim and his younger sister were also imprisoned and tortured, and his lovely sister died in that incident. This made him stop writing poetry and end his writing career less than 3 years after his debut. While continuing with ending his writing career, he married Eunsoon Jang, the daughter of a Christian elder in February 1938, but lost his mother in April of that year, extending ending his writing career. He resumed writing poetry when Korea was liberated on August 15th, 1945 at the age of 32 in Gwangju.    Hyeonseung Kim wrote poems after losing his respected father during the Korean War in 1950 and wrote the poem ‘Tears’ as he watched his four-year-old son get ill and die without being able to get medicine properly due to poverty. He also wrote poems for Midang Jeongju Seo, who was suffering from schizophrenia due to the shock of the Korean War, after becoming a professor of Korean literature at Chosun University by co-founding the literary coterie magazine ‘Poetry Literature’ with other writers from Gwangju. He wrote poems while watching his tortured older brother die from aftereffects and wrote poems while experiencing dictatorship. Hyeonseung Kim wrote poems for many reasons.  So, starting with ‘Hyeonseung Kim’s First Poems’, he published 5 collections of poems, including ‘Advocate’s Song’, ‘Sturdy Solitude’, ‘Absolute Solitude’, and ‘Hyeonseung Kim Poem Collection’, leaving a total of 275 poems on the ground. In addition, he wrote ‘Explanation of Korean Contemporary Poetry’, ‘Study on the History of World Literature’, posthumous collection ‘In the Last Earth’, essay collection ‘Solitude and Poetry’, and ‘Let Me Pray in Autumn’.  Along with poetry writing and writing work, he also taught students as an educator.  After that, even after moving to Soongjeon University as a professor in the cold north, he did not let go of his attachment to his hometown Gwangju, leaving behind the words, “My hometown is Gwangju in the south of Jeolla-do, which is warm.”  Dahyeong Hyeonseung Kim collapsed while praying in the chapel class of Soongjeon University, where he was serving as a professor, on April 10, 1975, and it was due to the returned high blood pressure. He could not return to his hometown of Gwangju until the last and died at the age of 62.   Poet of Coffee and Solitude, Tears and Prayer. A poet who showed the metaphysical depth of human existence through poetry, which is rare in Korean contemporary history. A great poet who embodied the poetics of salvation through his patriotic presence. People refer to him as a representative poet who wrote poetry from a Christian worldview in this country by often abbreviating to these phrases.   If you are interested in finding traces of Poet Dahyeong Hyeonseung Kim, who is called ‘Poet of Solitude’ or ‘Poet of Tears’, try looking for the Monument for Dahyeong Kim Hyeon-seung in Honam Theological University and Seminary.

stories.title: Yangnim Art Center
stories.script: Yangnim Art Center is an art exhibition space located in Yangnim-dong, modern history and culture village. It opened in December 2012 and is loved by many art lovers. It is operated to provide a wide range of opportunities to enjoy culture and arts to Yangnim-dong visitors and local residents and to support free space for local artists to work. In addition, the exhibition space is rented free of charge to local artists, and you can enjoy free exhibitions of artists in various fields, such as Korean painting, Western painting, sculpture, and photography, held 20 times a year. Around 20 works of art are exhibited on 2 floors so people of all ages and genders can comfortably enjoy the art. Please note that the operating hours are from 10 am to 6 pm, closed on Mondays and public holidays.

stories.title: May Mother House
stories.script: In May 2000, the 20th anniversary of the Gwangju Democratization Movement, in order to inherit the spirit of Gwangju Uprising, former Chairman Seongrye Ahn, who led the ‘May 18th Restrainer Family Association’, Myungja Lee, Haengsoon Park, Jeonghee Na, Hyeonae Jeong, and Youngsuk Roh founded the ‘May Women’s Association’ with former Gwangju YWCA President Ara Cho as an advisor.   When the ‘May Women’s Association’ was established, the ‘Gwangju Community Association’ members, which had been inherited from the ‘May 18th Restrainer Family Association’ in the past, were naturally absorbed into the ‘May Women’s Association’. The members of the ‘May 18th Restrainer Family Association’ gathered again to create a new role for the women’s human rights NGO in transition, and they came together to give each other strength and to properly inform the descendants of the greatness of Gwangju Uprising that they experienced.  The ‘May Women’s Association’ held monthly meetings to strengthen the camaraderie of its members and began to heal tired minds and bodies. The families of the ‘May Women’s Association’ published a book based on their experiences and stories to inform neighbors of the truth of Gwangju Uprising, and moved forward step by step towards their goal of spreading the Spirit of May, which was completed at the cost of countless sacrifices.   At first, there was no space to gather together, so they had a meeting at a tea house, etc., but in May 2006, young people from the Gwangju movement, including the late Daejong Kim, Youngkwan Kim, Cheongbae Jeon, Kangryeol Kim, and Jeonghoon Kim, rented out and donated a small Hanok at 15-17 Jang-dong, Dong-gu, Gwangju for them. This space was the great beginning of ‘May Mother House’. Chairman Seongrye Ahn was appointed as the first director of ‘May Mother House’, and in November 2006, ‘May Women’s Association’ was renamed ‘May Mother Association’, and full-fledged activities began by registering as an incorporated association in Gwangju Metropolitan City. The members of May Mother House, who now have prepared a resident space, begin to build a variety of activity programs on their own. They started in earnest the education project for the succession of the spirit of May, May Mother Award presentation project, exchange project with domestic and foreign movement groups for national reconciliation, and Mother's Class program to heal the mind and body of members suffering from deep wounds and trauma.   Thanks to these May Mother House programs, the lives of May Mothers have undergone major changes. Although many mothers felt the loss of their family to be too great, they were unable to express it and had to live a lonely life with the people around them, making it even more difficult to live lonely, especially in old age. However, after gathering at May Mother House, they were able to comfort each other, gain strength, regain vitality, and gradually developed an attachment to life. As a result, although May Mother House started as a human rights NGO at first, it has now been reborn as a multi-purpose human rights center with multiple functions as an education and rehabilitation center.   ‘May Mother House’, a shelter for mothers who have dedicated themselves to democracy in Korea, is currently operating at 18, Cheonbyeonjwa-ro 418beon-gil, Nam-gu, Gwangju.

stories.title: Entrance to the Changnyeong Museum
stories.script: Hello everyone! It’s great to have you here at the Changnyeong Museum. This museum is open to everybody and informs visitors about the cultural heritage of Changnyeong. So now, let us start our journey into the priceless cultural treasures of this area.

stories.title: Shell Mound in Bibong-ri, Changnyeong
stories.script: Let me introduce you to the first shell mound of the Neolithic period discovered in Bibong-ri, Changnyeong. A shell mound is a heap consisting chiefly of the shells of edible mollusks discarded by prehistoric people settled in the area. Around this mound, archaeologists discovered an ancient wooden boat, which provides clues about the life of Neolithic people.

stories.title: Changnyeong-style Earthenware
stories.script: There are ancient tombs of Gyo-dong and Songhyeon-dong around Changnyeong Museum. Have you spotted some of the tombs from here? Archaeologists found at the tombs, which date back to the Three Kingdoms Period earthenware now called “Changnyeong-style earthenware”. This unique earthenware was made by combining the newly arrived techniques of Silla earthenware with the technique of Gaya earthenware native to the area.

stories.title: Songhyeoni, a Gaya Girl (Human Sacrifice of the Songhyeon-dong Tomb No. 15 in Changnyeong)
stories.audioTitle: Songhyeoni, a Gaya Girl (Human Sacrifice of the Songhyeon-dong Tomb No. 15 in Changnyeong)
stories.script: This girl named Songhyeoni is a reproduction of the human remains and relics excavated at the Tomb 15 of the Songhyeon Zone I. You many wonder how they made this reproduction of a girl sacrificed for religious purposes. A group of specialists in different academic fields participated in the excavation, dating, DNA analysis of the relics and, finally, assembling the bones through 3-D scanning. The reproduction of Songhyeoni is currently on public display at the Changnyeong Museum.

stories.title: Monument in Changnyeong Commemorating the Border Expansion by King Jinheung of Silla.
stories.audioTitle: Monument in Changnyeong Commemorating the Border Expansion by King Jinheung of Silla.
stories.script: This monument was set up to mark the boundary of the Silla territory expanded to the Changnyeong area of today when the kingdom was under the reign of King Jinheung. The monument was discovered in 1914 at the village of Malheul-ri and moved to its current location at Manokjeong Park in Changnyeong. You can see the actual monument if you got the Manokjeong Park.

stories.title: Relics of Bobusang (Relics of the Sangmujwasa Office in Changnyeong)
stories.audioTitle: Relics of Bobusang (Relics of the Sangmujwasa Office in Changnyeong)
stories.script: This collection of objects at the Changnyeong Museum is the relics of the Sangmujwasa Office in Changnyeong, an organization of travelling merchants called Bobusang. It consists of a total of 35 items including the documents such as the regulations of the Department of Commerce in the Donga Advancement Education Society, as well as seals and name plaques. These items are inscribed in the list of the National Folk Cultural Heritage. It is an admirable act to donate or entrust precious heritage items to a museum, allowing open public access to them.

stories.title: Entrance to the Ancient Tombs in Gyo-dong
stories.audioTitle: Entrance to the Ancient Tombs in Gyo-dong
stories.script: The ancient tombs in Changnyeong, Gyeongsangnam-do consists of two sections called the Gyo-dong Zone and Songhyeon-dong Zone, each of which is further subdivided into two, which are Gyo-dong Zones I & II, and Songhyeon-dong Zones I & II. The old tombs in Gyo-dong and Songhyeon-dong are known to have been connected to Bihwa Gaya located on the border between the Gaya confederation and Silla and a strategic point forming the hub of transportation through the Nakdonggang River. The geopolitical condition of the site explains why it produced a variety of archaeological relics showing its cultural exchange with neighboring Baekje, Silla and Japan. According to the structure of and archaeological findings, most of the old tombs in the area were built between the 5th and 6th century. The tombs are regarded as important monuments providing clues about the origin and development of Bihwa Gaya, the process of transition from Gaya to Silla, and the relationship between political powers within and beyond the Korean Peninsula of this period. Gyo-dong Zone I contains large tombs on the hilltop west of the tomb complex, mid-size tombs surrounding them, and smaller ones situated along the ridge running southwest. Gyo-dong Zone II includes the mountain slopes extending toward the west from Hwawangsan Mountain and a hill west of Changmil-ro running along the front of the Changnyeong Museum.

stories.title: Gyo-dong Zone I - Tomb No. 7
stories.script: The largest of the tombs in Gyo-dong Zone I, Tomb 7, is located at the highest point of the zone. The tomb was built between the late 5th century and early 6th century. It is characterized by a round mound containing a stone-lined pit tomb. Archaeologists found at the tomb a large number of diverse artifacts including a gilt-bronze crown, bronze horn cup, saddle, and personal ornaments.

stories.title: Gyo-dong Zone I - Tomb No. 12
stories.script: Tomb 12 of Gyo-dong Zone I is, unlike other tombs of the zone, is a wooden chamber tomb with stone mound, commonly known for Silla-style tombs. The tomb is characterized by a subterranean wood-lined chamber used to contain the body of the tomb occupant alongside grave goods. The chamber is covered with a large heap of cobblestones and finally encrusted with a layer of earth. It is the only example of the Silla tomb type discovered in the Changnyeong area and artifacts from this tomb are similar objects to those discovered at the small and medium-size Silla tombs in and around Gyeongju area.

stories.title: Gyo-dong Zone II - Tomb No. 3
stories.script: Tomb 3 of Gyo-dong Zone II is a stone chamber tomb with horizontal entrance dating back to the late 5th century. It is the oldest among all the ancient tombs clustered in the Gyo-dong and Songhyeon-dong area. The stone burial chamber had been looted when the tomb was found, but the large size of the chamber and mound, in which it is contained, along with the relics of human sacrifice found at the horizontal passage suggests the occupant of the tomb had been the supreme ruler of the area.

stories.title: Gyo-dong Zone II - Tomb No. 10
stories.script: Tomb 10 of the Gyo-dong Zone II is one of the largest among the ancient tombs clustered in Gyo-dong and Songhyeon-dong. It was surrounded by a group of small and medium-sized tombs. It is a stone chamber tomb with horizontal entrance dating back to the late 5th century and built with rectangular stone slabs.

stories.title: Entrance to the Ancient Tombs in Songhyeon-dong
stories.audioTitle: Entrance to the Ancient Tombs in Songhyeon-dong
stories.script: The ancient tombs in Changnyeong-gun, Gyeongsangnam-do are divided into the Gyo-dong Zone and Songhyeon-dong Zone, and each is further subdivided into Gyo-dong Zones I & II and Songhyeon-dong Zones I & II. The Songhyeon-dong Zone covers the area around the South Gate site of Mongmasanseong Fortress, the ridge east of the valley southwest of the gate site, and the middle slope of Hwawangsan Mountain. Songhyeon-dong Zone I contains the tombs arranged in a row along a mountain ridge with a gourd-shaped burial mound on the top of the ridge surrounded by several tombs and smaller tombs scattered further away. Songhyeon-dong Zone II covers the area 340 to 435 meters above sea level linking Jahagok with the summit of Hwawangsan Mountain, containing 31 tombs, 6 with mounds, and 25 without them.

stories.title: Songhyeon-dong Zone I - Tombs No. 6 and 7
stories.audioTitle: Songhyeon-dong Zone I - Tombs No. 6 and 7
stories.script: Tombs 6 and 7 of Songhyeon-dong Zone I are dubbed a “gourd-shaped burial mound” due to the shape formed by the two mounds connected to each other. Both are the stone chamber tomb with horizontal entrance linking the chamber to the outside. Tomb 6 was built prior to Tomb 7 but both between the late 5th to early 6th century.

stories.title: Songhyeon-dong Zone I - Tomb No. 15
stories.script: Tomb 15 of Songhyeon-dong Zone I was made after Tomb 16. The mounds of both tombs are called a gourd-shaped burial mound because of the shape made by the two mounds attached to each other. Tomb 15, featuring the style of the stone chamber tomb with horizontal entrance, was built in the early 16th century. Archaeologists discovered at the burial chamber leading to the entrance relics of four human sacrificial victims.

stories.title: What is pottery?
stories.script: The ceramic vessels known as jilgeureut are made by shaping easily obtainable clay into the desired form and firing it at a temperature of about 1100℃. This is lower than the temperature required for another type of vessel, called sagigeureut in Korean, which is fired at a higher temperature and therefore has a harder body than jilgeureut. Celadon, white porcelain, Buncheong and black-glazed wares, all of which are sagigeureut, are made from more refined clay. The preferred clay for these high-quality vessels is kaolin, a fine, white clay containing hard aluminous minerals such as feldspar, which is hard to find as deposits usually exist in the form of veins. The production of higher-quality wares requires more advanced techniques as they are fired at temperatures of over 1200℃. Western pottery of the modern period is largely divided into three major types, namely, earthenware, stoneware, and porcelain, of which the last two are largely glazed wares. Glazing creates a hard, translucent layer over the surface of a ceramic ware, effectively protecting it from moisture and pollutants, although it can crack easily. Earthenware and porcelain differ from each other mainly in terms of their function and use. The clay used to produce stoneware is typically easy to obtain, and is used in the production of large storage vessels and even architectural structures, in addition to ordinary tableware, whereas kaolin, which is much harder to obtain and requires more complex techniques to deal with, is used in the production of smaller items of tableware, stationery items, and ritual vessels.

stories.title: The Global Development of Ceramics
stories.script: It was about 10,000 years ago that humans first began to make vessels by shaping clay and firing it at a high temperature. The development of pottery in the Neolithic period resulted in the formation of pottery cultures through Asia and Europe. During this period, pottery decorated with incised comb patterns spread from Scandinavia to the Korean Peninsula via Siberia. Meanwhile, pottery with painted designs was developed in the four major ancient civilizations that emerged in Mesopotamia, the Nile delta in Egypt, the Indus valley in India, and the Yellow River in China. The early potters of the ancient world continued to develop the materials and techniques of their art, using higher temperatures to fire the shaped clay and glazing the surface of the vessels. The early pottery makers in East Asia were able to use fine-quality clay and abundant resources of fuel to produce high-quality vessels fired at high temperatures, whereas the potters of West Asia and Europe continued to produce ceramics fired at lower temperatures for quite a long period of time due to a lack of fuel and fine clay such as kaolin. In the medieval period, potters in China and Korea were able to produce fine-quality celadon with a body as hard as stone and a shiny jade-like surface, unlike its predecessor, which was marked by ash glazing, thanks to the technique they had developed of firing pottery at a high temperature. It was in the fourth or fifth century that the techniques of celadon ware production began to be introduced from China to Korea, whose own distinctive celadon ware began to emerge in the ninth century. Chinese celadon was carried to Southeast Asia, India, West Asia, Turkey and Egypt via the Silk Road and maritime routes, ultimately introducing the outstanding functionality and beauty of Chinese porcelain to the Western world. The West Asian potters of that period developed pottery decorated with painted motifs under the influence of the luxurious decoration of Islamic art. The expansion of Islam and the Crusades resulted in the spread of West Asian pottery culture to southern Europe, including Italy and Spain, exerting a strong influence on the development of ceramics across Europe.  In the fourteenth century, Chinese potters achieved techniques for producing white porcelain comparable to those of modern porcelain art. The art was introduced to Korea, where it reached its zenith in the fifteenth century, and to Japan in the seventeenth century, thus bringing all three East Asian countries into the porcelain culture. It was also during this period that Europeans began importing Chinese porcelain wares, starting with Italy and spreading northward to the Netherlands, Germany and even to England. The arrival of porcelain in Europe led governments and royal households across Europe to compete fiercely with each other to develop their own porcelain techniques, resulting in the development of Medici porcelain in Italy in the sixteenth century and Delftware in the Netherlands in the following century. Then, in 1710, the German alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger manufactured Europe's first porcelain ware, heralding a new dawn for that continent's own porcelain arts.

stories.title: Pottery in Korea (Prehistoric Times - Three Kingdoms - Unified Silla - Goryeo)
stories.audioTitle: Pottery in Korea (Prehistoric Times - Three Kingdoms - Unified Silla - Goryeo)
stories.script: It was around 8,000 years ago, during the Neolithic period, that earthenware began to appear in the Korean Peninsula. The early Neolithic potters produced pottery using the natural clay they obtained from their surroundings, creating the ceramic culture represented by shell-shaped comb-pattern pottery. In the following Bronze Age, comb-pattern pottery was replaced by a type of plain, undecorated pottery called Mumun earthenware. It was also in this period that the early Korean potters produced ceramic works for special purposes, including the red- or black-burnished wares, pottery with a painted design, and earthenware jar coffins.  The ancient Korean kingdoms that flourished on the Korean Peninsula between the third and mid- seventh century produced a wide range of ceramic vessels that featured characteristic elements of their respective cultures. Potters in Goguryeo, for example, produced a variety of soft- and hard-paste earthenware vessels under the influence of China's pottery culture, while Baekje potters developed a pottery culture that was more vibrant than that of its two rival kingdoms, creating more diverse items such as tiger-shaped chamber pots, ink stones, funerary urns and other items also influenced by Chinese ceramic works. Meanwhile, in Silla and Gaya, potters made elaborate grave goods, figurines and vessels that departed from the established forms. In the following Unified Silla period, the ruling class in Gyeongju, the capital of the kingdom, used ceramic vessels imported from China together with metal items, while the native potters favored vessels decorated with impressed floral motifs. In the ninth century, Korean potters were introduced to the production techniques of celadon ware developed by Chinese potters in Yuezhou in Zhejiang, resulting in the historic transition from stoneware to porcelain in the history of Korean ceramics. The potters of Goryeo began to manufacture their own celadon vessels in the eleventh century, making great advances in techniques and aesthetic beauty between the late eleventh and twelfth century. The celadon vessels made in Goryeo during this period were widely praised even in China for their attractive jade blue surface, which surpassed that of contemporary Chinese celadon ware. The growing political influence of Yuan over Goryeo in the late thirteenth century and the luxurious lifestyle of Goryeo's royalty and aristocracy disrupted the environment surrounding the ceramic art of Goryeo, leading to a drastic collapse in the technical and aesthetic merits of Goryeo celadon.

stories.title: Pottery in Korea (Buncheong Ware - Joseon White Porcelain - Public and Private Kilns)
stories.audioTitle: Pottery in Korea (Buncheong Ware - Joseon White Porcelain - Public and Private Kilns)
stories.script: The ceramic art of Joseon is largely represented by Buncheong ware and a type of white porcelain called Baekja. The term Buncheong is a shortened form of the term Bunjang Hoecheong, which referred to Joseon ceramic works whose surface was thickly coated with white slip. The birth of Buncheong ware is related with the Goryeo potters who consistently produced fine-quality celadon at their kilns in present-day Gangjin in Jeolla-do until they were forced to leave their original workplaces due to raids by Japanese pirates and the political turmoil of the Goryeo dynasty in its later phase. After dispersing all around the country, these potters focused on producing low-quality celadon ware simply to make ends meet, which eventually led to the creation of Buncheong ware. That is why the Buncheong wares of Joseon came to have similar features as those of the Goryeo celadon wares in terms of their shape and their decorative motifs. At the same time, Joseon's Buncheong is highly regarded today for its unique aestheticism and characteristic freedom from the established forms and decorative features. It was during the first half of the fifteenth century that the royal households of Joseon were supplied with Buncheong wares as tributes from the kilns in different parts of the country. The rulers of Joseon, King Taejong and King Sejong in particular, tried to secure the systematic management of Buncheong and improve its quality by introducing a policy by which Buncheong products were required to bear the names of both the potters who made them and the government agencies to which the vessels were supplied. Thus it may be said that the white porcelain ware of Joseon developed on the basis of the achievements of the celadon ware of Goryeo and the influence of the ceramic art of the Yuan and Ming dynasties of China. The art of white porcelain in Joseon underwent a significant development after the dynasty began to operate a public kiln in Gwangju, Gyeonggi-do, under the supervision of the Saongwon, the Joseon government agency responsible for management of the royal kitchen. However, Joseon's ceramic art industry suffered greatly between the late sixteenth and early seventeenth century as a result of a devastating series of invasions of the Korean Peninsula by the Japanese in 1592 and 1597 and the Manchu in 1627 and 1636. The price of imported cobalt blue pigment soared in the 1630s, which led many Korean potters to turn to the much cheaper, domestically produced iron oxide pigment. The economic depression that afflicted Joseon after these wars also resulted in a severe shortage in the supply of ceramic vessels, pushing the government-run kilns to turn to the mass production techniques traditionally used by private kilns across regional areas. For Japan, its invasion of the Korean Peninsula in 1592 presented a great opportunity to acquire the advanced production techniques of porcelain ware from the Joseon potters who were abducted to Japan by Japanese troops during the war. The knowledge and skills of these Joseon artisans played a crucial role in the creation of Arita ware in Kyushu during the early seventeenth century and the remarkable development of Japanese ceramic art in the following period. The economic recovery and revival of interregional trade in the eighteenth century led to cultural and industrial prosperity, and to the mass production of white porcelain ware represented by vessels decorated with cobalt blue designs

stories.title: Pottery Kilns of the Saongwon Operated by the Joseon Dynasty
stories.audioTitle: Pottery Kilns of the Saongwon Operated by the Joseon Dynasty
stories.script: The government of the Joseon dynasty established and operated a special kiln complex called the Bunwon, which - as the literal meaning of its name, affiliated agency, suggests - was run by the Saongwon, the government agency responsible for the culinary affairs of Joseon's royal family. Located in Gwangju, Gyeonggi-do, this state-run kiln complex produced a wide range of porcelain wares to meet the demands of government agencies and the royal household of Joseon. While the kiln complex was known by several different names, including Bunsaongwon and Bunjuwon, both of which reveal its association with the government and the royal family of Joseon, it was better known as the kiln of white porcelain ware affiliated with the Saongwon. Notably, in its early days, the Joseon royal court used the white porcelain and Buncheong vessels delivered to it as special tributary goods. However, the demand for white porcelain continued to increase due to the expansion of its use at various state and royal events, and as special royal gifts for meritorious subjects and foreign envoys. Eventually, the Joseon dynasty realized that the growing demand for high-quality porcelain could not be met by the traditional tributary system alone, and decided that it needed to operate its own production center. Accordingly, it chose Gwangju as the best location for the state-run porcelain kilns as it was easily accessible from the capital via the Han River, and was surrounded by dense forests that could supply enough firewood for the kilns.    The porcelain production complex run by Joseon's government was required to move its kilns about once every ten years as the resources of fuel around them were usually depleted in that period of time. That explains why as many as 340 kiln sites can still be found scattered around Gwangju, all of which were used to produce white porcelain for the Joseon dynasty. However, the frequent relocation of the kilns placed a significant financial burden on the dynasty; but this problem was resolved when the government of Joseon decided to operate a permanent kiln complex at one site, supporting it with fuel brought in from the upstream area of the Han River in Gangwon-do and Chungcheong-do, and funding its operation with the taxes imposed on commercial vessels that used the waterway.  According to the Gyeonggukdaejeon, or The Great Code of the National Government, published in 1485, a total of 380 potters were listed on the register of artisans employed by the Saongwon. They were selected from among the 1,140 artisans registered as ceramic artists across the entire country under a system which required each artisan to work for the government-run kiln once every three years. The system underwent continuous modifications to improve its efficiency such that, by the late Joseon period, successive generations of potters from the same family were hired to work for the state-run kiln complex. And that is how the potters and their families, amounting to several hundred in total, formed a large village around the government kiln complex.

stories.title: White Porcelain of the Bunwon
stories.script: The white porcelain produced at the Bunwon, the porcelain kiln complex operated by the Joseon dynasty, was characterized by a delightfully simple and austere form and limited decorative elements. These wares had a snowy white body and sometimes bore a decorative motif rendered with cobalt pigment to express the artist's inner world, and symbolism. The aesthetic austerity exemplified by the form and surface decoration of the porcelain produced by the artisans of the Bunwon is often compared with the sumptuous decorations of porcelain wares made for export in China, Japan, and Europe. The development of commerce in the late Joseon period lent vitality to the market in which some of the leading players dared to sell the products of the Bunwon kilns even to people of humble origin. In the nineteenth century, the imperial powers increased their pressure on Korea politically and economically, resulting in, among other things, the influx of cheap, mass produced foreign ceramic vessels into the Korean market. Amid the changed environment, the royal family of Joseon transferred the right to operate the government kilns to private traders in 1883. The transfer of ownership of the Saongwon kiln complex was followed by a period of turmoil that lasted for about thirty years until the early twentieth century.  In downtown Gwangju there are about 340 Saongwon kiln sites, some of which have been grouped together and collectively designated as National Historic Site No. 314. Some of the other kiln sites - such as Site No, 1 in Doma-ri, Site Nos. 2, 9 and 17 in Usan-ri, Site Nos. 5 and 9 in Beoncheon-ri, Site Nos. 2 and 3 in Seondong-ri, Site Nos. 5 and 6 of Songjeong-ri, and Site No. 1 in Bunwon-ri - have been excavated and researched by the Gyeonggi Ceramic Museum. The district of Bunwon-ri, whose name originates from Bunwon, the name given to the kiln complex operated by the government of Joseon, in Namjong-myeon, Gwangju-si, contains kiln sites that produced porcelain from 1752 until the early twentieth century, even after they were privatized in 1884. Excavations of these sites still uncover sherds of a variety of white porcelain vessels, kiln accessories, and pottery tools.

stories.title: White Porcelain Making (1) Clay Harvesting to Shaping
stories.audioTitle: White Porcelain Making (1) Clay Harvesting to Shaping
stories.script: The work of making a white porcelain vessel starts by harvesting clay of adequate viscosity, refractoriness, and color. Potters in Korea were able to find the white clay they needed for their art in their immediate vicinity relatively easily, but those who worked at the Bunwon kilns run by the Joseon dynasty preferred the clay harvested at the renowned mining sites in Hamgyeong-do, Pyeongan-do, Gangwon-do, Chungcheong-do, and Gyeongsang-do.  In the following process, harvested clay is mixed with water to form slurry and then sifted through a screen to remove impurities such as sand and iron particles. After levigation, the clay is spread on the floor and kneaded thoroughly by stomping it barefoot. It can then be cut to the right size and kneaded until it becomes fully plastic, whereupon it can be thrown on the wheel and shaped into the desired form.  Put a lump of porcelain clay on the wheel and shape it into the form of a vessel you want, bowl, dish, jar or bottle, while kicking the flywheel with your left foot. The process of shaping requires the clay to be placed on the center of the wheel and water to be sprinkled on it while it is rotated on the wheel in order to form it easily. You may choose to use clay slabs, cutting them into the shapes you need to make a vessel with a special form such as a polygonal bottle or a calligraphy water-dropper.   After shaping, the vessel is left half dry before putting it back on the wheel and trimming the entire surface of its body including the foot and, if necessary, carving a decorative design on it. It is then left in a shaded place until it has completely dried. There are four main techniques of decorative carving, including incising, whereby a design is engraved by cutting or scraping into the clay surface; and relief carving, whereby a design is applied by cutting out the background  in such a way that the desired image appears to rise up from the surface. The other two techniques are openwork carving, whereby decoration is produced by creating holes, piercings, or gaps right through the surface of the vessel; and inlaying, by which the desired decorative motif is incised on the surface of the vessel, and clay of contrasting colors is inserted into the incised depressions.

stories.title: White Porcelain Making (2) Bisque Firing and Gloss Firing
stories.audioTitle: White Porcelain Making (2) Bisque Firing and Gloss Firing
stories.script: Once a vessel has completely dried after decorative carving, it is placed in a kiln for bisque firing at a temperature of about 800°C. This initial firing transforms green ware into a durable, semi-vitrified porous form that can be handled safely during the glazing and decorating process. The bisque-fired vessel is then decorated with various images rendered with mineral pigments such as oxidized cobalt, iron or copper, resulting in a product called either Cheonghwa, a white-and-blue porcelain ware, or Cheolhwa, an iron-painted porcelain ware. Of the two types, the surface of the first is decorated with an image rendered with CoO2 (cobalt oxide) before glazing and firing it at a temperature of over 1200°C. The contrast between the cobalt blue design and the white background of the finished object is widely appreciated among connoisseurs.  During the Joseon period, such white-and-blue wares were extremely expensive because the cobalt pigment used in its decoration was of Persian origin and had to be imported from China. Historical records show that, during the reign of King Sejo of the Joseon dynasty, potters made great efforts to develop their own blue pigment to replace the expensive foreign product. Another pigment favored by the porcelain makers of Joseon was iron oxide, or FeO. Used to apply a decorative design on the white surface of a porcelain work, this pigment creates an attractive dark brown image after the decorated vessel has been coated with transparent glaze and fired at a high temperature. In Korea, this easily available iron oxide pigment was widely used by the potters of Joseon to decorate celadon, Buncheong and white porcelain wares. Even the court artisans of the state-run kiln complex (Bunwon) preferred iron oxide to the expensive cobalt blue pigment in the second half of the seventeenth century after the Imjin Wars. In the process of glazing that follows that of decorating the surface of a bisque ware, a bisque porcelain vessel is dipped into glaze prepared by mixing clay containing compositions of glass with a flux that aids the fusing of the compositions and color stabilizer. The glaze for white porcelain ware is made by mixing a number of materials obtained from nature, such as silica, feldspar, china clay, limestone and ash. Glazing helps strengthen porcelain ware, improves hygiene, and enhances the decorative effect.  The last stage of white porcelain making is that of gloss firing, which is generally regarded as the most important part of the entire process. In this stage, glazed clay objects are fired in a kiln at a high temperature of over 1200°C. The final result can vary according to the conditions surrounding the firing process, such as the kiln structure, fuel, firing method and duration, and even the weather on the day of firing, so potters need to take great care with every detail of the process. In the past, glazed objects were stacked high in large quantities for mass production; whereas, for the production of high-quality vessels such as those used by the royal households, each porcelain object was placed in a special container called a saggar to protect it from impurities or direct contact with fire.

stories.title: Production of Celadon and Goryeo Celadon and White Porcelains  (1 item)
stories.audioTitle: Production of Celadon and Goryeo Celadon and White Porcelains  (1 item)
stories.script: Celadon ceramics is an important cultural heritage of Korea from the Goryeo period. Celadon was first produced in the Korean peninsula around the 9th century, between late Unified Silla and the Later Three Kingdoms period, when the art of celadon making arrived from Yue kiln in China. In Goryeo, the world’s second country after China to produce celadon, celadon making was brought to its full potential thanks to the unparalleled craftsmanship and aesthetic acumen of its artisans. Celadon wares were mainly produced in Gangjin and other coastal areas in southwestern Korea to cater to powerful family clans and military warlords based in the region. Initially, Goryeo celadon wares were similar in style and appearance to Chinese ones. But their shapes and decorative styles and the color of glaze gradually changed over time to reflect Goryeo’s native culture and the taste of its people. By the 10th to11th centuries, Goryeo celadon acquired most of the characteristics that make them uniquely recognizable.    Along with Goryeo celadon, also on display here are white porcelain wares, a much less well-known type of Goryeo ceramics. This white porcelain cup with lotus petals in embossed carving is believed to be a tea cup. Lotus petals were carved on its outer surface using a burin and incised details were added along the edge.    In Goryeo, white porcelain wares were produced since early on, together with celadon. However, their production decreased over time due to the low melting point of the glaze, making it difficult to fire them at high temperatures, and the scarcity of materials. Because of this, white porcelain was frequently imported from China, from places such as Ding kiln or Jingdezhen kiln. Most surviving white porcelain items from this period are soft-paste porcelain wares, which are typically coated in glaze with a characteristic pale ivory hue. In terms of shape and decorative style, they are quite similar to celadon.

stories.title: Mystic Green-blue Hue of Celadon (1 item)
stories.audioTitle: Mystic Green-blue Hue of Celadon (1 item)
stories.script: By the 11th century, celadon ware were used in nearly all segments of Goryeo society, including royals, aristocrats, and ordinary people. The decorations they flaunted also became increasingly varied in reflection of the growing diversity of population they catered to. The types of celadon that was popular around this time was plain green celadon with designs in incised, press-embossed, or open work carvings. Some were figurative celadon, representing people, animals, or plants. Plain celadon came into its golden days during the first half of the 12th century when Goryeo’s celadon glaze acquired its beautiful signature green-blue hue referred to as “kingfisher blue.” Functional as well as aesthetically pleasing, Goryeo celadon came in a variety of shape, decorated with equally varied designs. These vessels, mirroring the lifestyle, hopes and dreams of Goryeo people, contain in them the images of the bountiful nature that supported their lives in this land.     The item you see here is a celadon bowl with an incised design of a parrot. A natural question that comes to mind is how an exotic bird, not found in the Korean peninsula, got to grace this bowl. The earliest mention of a parrot in a Korean historical record is in Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms and is in relation to a legend involving King Heungdeok. The legend reads as follows: “During the reign of King Heungdeok, the 42nd ruler of Silla, a government envoy to Tang China brought back with him a pair of parrots. Before long, the hen died. The bereaved cock was inconsolable. Seeing the parrot cry sadly every day, the king took pity on it and gave it a mirror. The parrot at first thought that the image in the mirror was its partner. But the bird soon realized, when it pecked at the mirror, that this image was its own reflection. The grief-stricken bird cried sadly and died eventually of the heartbreak.”   As suggested in this story, parrots are believed to form strong bonds with their partners. In Korea, parrots are a traditional symbol of marital bonds and conjugal bliss, most often represented in pairs rather than alone when they are used as decorative motif. Meanwhile, in the History of Goryeo, in its article about Song-dynasty merchants entering Goryeo, exotic birds like parrots and peacocks are listed among the items imported by Northern Song merchants as tributary gifts to the king. However, the fact that Song merchants brought parrots to Goryeo alone does not explain the high frequency with which parrots appear as design motifs in artifacts from this period. In no other period of Korean history did parrots enjoy such popularity. This is because Goryeo was a more cosmopolitan society open to the outside world than other Korean dynasties and its aristocrats, fond of landscaping, considered parrots as a rare and precious animal that is a flattering addition to their gardens.

stories.title: Intricacy of Inlaid Celadon and Decline of Celadon Making (1 item)
stories.audioTitle: Intricacy of Inlaid Celadon and Decline of Celadon Making (1 item)
stories.script: Inlay is an intricate process which involves incising designs on the surface of a ceramic object and, then, filling the carved spaces with slip, requiring both a thorough understanding of materials and a skilled hand. Inlaid celadon emerged as an important variety of celadon in the mid-Goryeo period. These wares were decorated with new design motifs that were never previously seen. The bluish surface of celadon became the sky or a body of water, providing a backdrop to white clouds or ducks. The range of underglaze motifs, both figurative and stylized, grew wider and greater emphasis fell on decorativeness. This led to the use of an increasingly transparent glaze, which resulted in a new style of celadon that was no longer as deeply hued as in previous eras. Inlaid celadon quickly became the synonym of high-end celadon wares produced in Gangjin and Buan and developed into a booming industry especially after the coming into power of the Choi clan and the establishment of the military rule.   The item we have here is a celadon flask with an inlaid scene of a lotus pond. A lotus pond is depicted both on the front and back of this flat bottle, inside an oblong medallion enclosed by two lines. Lotus flowers are fluttering in the breeze and ducks are swimming leisurely. The top and bottom edges of the flask are decorated with lotus petals and the area surrounding the medallion is densely filled with small clouds. This flask is an exquisite example of late Goryeo celadon, well known for the harmonious blending of realistic images with stylized designs.    However, the heydays of celadon were short lived. Toward the end of the 13th century, Goryeo was brought under the overlordship of the Mongol-led Yuan Dynasty, which exacted wealth and tributes from it. As the depletion of Goryeo’s national resources made it increasingly difficult to produce high-end celadon, potters started to inlay them with their dates of production in an attempt to control the quantity and quality of items supplied to the government. Conditions for celadon production further worsened in the 14th century due to the disintegration of Goryeo’s tax system and the opulent lifestyle of its ruling class. In 1350-1380, chronic attacks by the Wako, the Japanese marauders, in Goryeo’s southern coastal waters caused an almost complete suspension of the maritime transport of goods between Gangjin and Gaeseong. This led to the collapse of celadon industry in Gangjin and other cities with major kilns.

stories.title: Joseon-style Inlaid Celadon, Inlaid Buncheong (1 item)
stories.audioTitle: Joseon-style Inlaid Celadon, Inlaid Buncheong (1 item)
stories.script: Although Buncheong wares were produced during a relative short period of time between the 14th and 15th centuries, they are widely noted for their distinctive aesthetic and style, making them unlike any other types of ceramics produced in East Asia. After the collapse of Gangjin’s celadon industry amid social and political disruptions in late Goryeo, potters were dispersed across the country. Buncheong ceramics were originally low-quality celadon wares produced by Gangjin potters, tailored to local demand in new places where they settled. In other words, Buncheong was a transition type of ceramics that emerged after the decline of Goryeo celadon and before the rise of Joseon white porcelain.  A variety of decorative techniques were used in Buncheong wares, including inlay, stamping, underglaze iron-oxide painting, incision, deombeong (dipping vessels in white slip), and bakji (or sgraffito). Buncheong with inlaid designs, sprung from the marriage between the art of Goryeo celadon making and the lifestyle and taste of ordinary people, was the most popular variety. During the early 15th century, inlaid Buncheong wares were supplied to the royal family and government agencies. Inlaid designs were stylized designs, filled with white slip, which most often covered the entire surface of the vessel. The designs were frequently stamped instead of incised. After the early 15th century, Buncheong ceramics gradually became everyday tableware used by ordinary people as their use in the royal family or during official events by government agencies was gradually discontinued in favor of silver and white porcelain vessels. The item you see here is a Buncheong prunus vase with an inlaid floral design. Buncheong prunus vases, a Joseon version of Goryeo prunus vases, enjoyed popularity in early Joseon. Joseon prunus vases, used for storing wine, liquor, or honey, have a trumpet-shaped mouth with a narrow neck and round and broad shoulders that taper down toward a narrow base ending in a flared foot. Its gleaming surface is coated in a transparent glaze. The intricate design of this vase is enlivened by its dramatic curves.

stories.title: Tribute Tax System and Buncheong with Inscriptions of Government Agency Names (4 items)
stories.audioTitle: Tribute Tax System and Buncheong with Inscriptions of Government Agency Names (4 items)
stories.script: In the early 15th century, during the reign of King Taejong when Buncheong ceramics were still supplied to the government as tribute goods, they were sometimes engraved with the names of the receiving government agencies in order to prevent that they are stolen during transport. During the reign of Sejong, kilns were ordered to also inscribe the names of potters as a way of improving the quality of ceramics supplied to the government.
