The names of government agencies that are found inscribed in surviving Buncheong wares include Jangheunggo, Saseonseo, Yebinsi, Naejasi, Naeseomsi, Gonganbu, Gyeongseungbu, and Insubu.   This item we have here is inscribed with the word “Naeseom,” indicating that it was a vessel destined for Naeseomsi. Naeseomsi was a Joseon agency responsible for procuring wine, liquors, and refreshments for government officials of 2nd rank and above and food and textiles gifted to the Japanese and Jurchen. “Insubu,” the name inscribed on this plate, is an agency, established in February 1400, to manage the Crown Prince’s palace. The bowl next to it bears the inscription “Saseon,” meaning “Saseonseo.” Saseonseo, deriving from the late Goryeo agency Sangsikguk, prepared food for the royal family. The next item bears the inscription “Jangheunggo.” Vessels with the inscription “Jangheunggo,” an agency procuring rush mats and paper goods for the royal family, were most often produced in Gyeongsang-do and Chungcheong-do. Buncheong wares inscribed with names of government agencies were generally attractive, high-quality ceramics decorated with a harmonious combination of letters and stamped designs.

stories.title: Incised Buncheong, Sgraffito Buncheong (1 item )
stories.script: Incised and sgraffito Buncheong wares are made by covering the vessel with a generous amount of white slip and, then, incising patterns or scratching off some of the slip to allow the body color to show through. These techniques blends elements of sculpture with elements of painting. Compared to stamped Buncheong with a classic, elegant appearance, incised or sgraffito Buncheong displays a more naïve and rawer aesthetic. Two of the most striking decorative techniques for Buncheong ceramics, they were most often used in Jeolla-do-area kilns.   Here, we have an unusual animal-shaped Buncheong liquor carafe. This elephant-shaped carafe is a ritual ware. In China, vessels representing an elephant were frequently used during rituals since ancient times, along with vessels in the image of other animals such as sheep, pigs, tigers, phoenixes, hares, oxen, wild geese, and geese. In Joseon, animal-shaped ritual vessels were used during ancestral worship services by the royal family or national rites held at Hyanggyo, the Confucian shrine. According to the Annals of King Sejong, the positions of ritual vessels on an altar changed according to the season. In spring and summer, two liquor carafes, one in the shape of an ox and the other in the shape of an elephant were used since the elephant is an animal inhabiting warmer regions in southern China and northern Vietnam.   In this item, made of bluish gray clay, the elephant’s tail and legs were made separately and added later to the rest of the body. After the tail and legs were joined to the body, the vessel was then thickly covered with white slip. There is a round hole with a raised lip on the back of the elephant to pour in liquid, which looks like a jar. Notice the two incised lines that are meant to be the straps fastening the jar to the back of the elephant. Coarse yet polished, the vessel successfully conveys dynamic tension. The body and hind legs are massive but have well-defined silhouettes. The vessel, however, looks rather unfinished. This is likely due to the lack of experience with animal-shaped vessels on the part of the potter, who also probably had to look up the unfamiliar exotic animal in a picture book.

stories.title: Buncheong with Underglaze Iron-oxide Design and Deombeong Buncheong (3 items)
stories.audioTitle: Buncheong with Underglaze Iron-oxide Design and Deombeong Buncheong (3 items)
stories.script: Buncheong with underglaze iron-oxide design enhances the signature coarse beauty of this gritty variety of ceramics by combining it with abstract patterns and dynamic expressive techniques. Kilns in Hakbong-ri in Gongju, near Gyeryongsan Mountain, were famously known for this type of Buncheong; hence, the nickname “Gyeryongsan Buncheong.” In 1990, an ancient kiln site in Hakbong-ri was designated as Historic Site No. 333. There are several other kiln sites in this area stretching from Yuseong in Daejeon to the foot of Gyeryongsan, along the road leading to Donghaksa Temple, that are believed to have been in operation between the 15th and 16th centuries.  Buncheong wares with underglaze iron-oxide decorations were mainly produced between the late 15th century and the early 16th century, corresponding to the declining period of Buncheong ceramics. They were made of coarse dark brown clay containing significant amounts of grits and impurities and were covered with a thick layer of white slip as if to make them appear like white porcelain. Designs in black iron-oxide pigments on this thick white slip layer create a dramatic contrast between black and white. The result is most often an exquisite abstract painting, executed with bold and liberal brushstrokes that echo the unique aesthetic sense of Korean people. This highly original style of decoration, which appeared during the decline of Buncheong ceramics, flaunted simple motifs such as fish, peony blossoms and arabesque scrolls, or lotus flowers and arabesque scrolls, drawn in quick, free strokes.    Further right from this item are two other Buncheong wares, known as “deombeong Buncheong.” Deombeong Buncheong was made by dipping the vessel in white slip. The name “deombeong” comes from the onomatopoeia of the sound made by a vessel plunged into liquefied clay. Deombeong Buncheong, considered the last generation of Buncheong ceramics, were mostly produced during the 16th century in kilns located in the Jeolla-do region.

stories.title: Production of White Porcelain Before the Establishment of the Government Kiln (2 items)
stories.audioTitle: Production of White Porcelain Before the Establishment of the Government Kiln (2 items)
stories.script: Although ceramics used in Joseon’s royal household were mostly Buncheong wares up until the early 15th century, white porcelain was already produced around this time in some parts of the country, including Gwangju in Gyeonggi-do, Goryeong in Gyeongsangnam-do, and Namwon in Jeollanam-do, and were supplied to government agencies. Before 1467, the year when Bunwon, the state-run white porcelain kilns, was first established, hard-paste porcelain, although popular in Ming-dynasty China, was rarely produced in Joseon. The white porcelain produced in Joseon was instead soft-paste porcelain and inlaid white porcelain influenced by Buncheong ceramics. To understand how white ceramics changed over time in terms of quality and color, let us compare the items in these two display cases, one dating from before the establishment of the government kiln and the other dating from after its establishment.   This small plate with a yellowish hue is a white porcelain plate with the inlaid inscription “cheon.” The plate with a raised edge was fired by placing its foot on four stilts. Inside the plate, there is a round concave area inside which the character “cheon (天)” is inlaid using black slip. This plate is a typical example of soft-paste white porcelain-period ceramics with a relatively low density and unevenly-applied glaze, exhibiting a characteristic yellow hue.  To the right of this item is a white porcelain vessel with inlaid design. Inlay was a technique widely used in Goryeo for decorating celadon. The use of inlay continued into Joseon for decorating Buncheong and white porcelain ceramics. In early Joseon, white porcelain wares with black inlaid designs, inspired by inlaid Goryeo celadon, gained popularity and were produced in places such as Gwangju in Gyeonggi-do and Sancheong and Hapcheon in Gyeongsangnam-do.   This inlaid white porcelain bottle is a liquor bottle-type vessel with a trumpet-shaped mouth and a narrow neck. It has a round body that conveys a sense of stability. The surface is divided into three sections by two pairs of horizontal lines, with a row of lotus petals running along the top. At the center of the vessel, a lotus blossom is inlaid using black slip. The bottle is coated in a light blue glaze across its entire surface except for the tall straight foot.

stories.title: White Porcelain (1 item)
stories.script: The 15th century, which marked Europe’s transition into the renaissance period, was also a time of renewal and revitalization in the Korean peninsula. In this century which saw the birth of Joseon, the policy to promote arts and humanities by the new dynasty led to the rise of Korea as an advanced cultural nation. A similarly big stride was made in ceramics around this time. Joseon potters embraced hard-paste porcelain making technology, which was first developed in Jingdezhen kiln in China, to create a whole new type of porcelain that embodied Korea’s own native aesthetic. Joseon white porcelain wares were not regal or sumptuous like Chinese white porcelain, but instead had a sober and majestic beauty that the people of Joseon appreciated.  This display case contains several types of Joseon vases and jars with various different designs. Joseon was literally a kingdom of vases. An impressive variety of vases were produced in Joseon and equally various names existed for vases, depending on their use, such as “ho,” “hang,” “jun,” or “roe.” Some were used to hold wine, liquors, or flowers during big and small ceremonies and banquets. Others were everyday wares used by households to store water, grain, marinated fish or spices.   The piece in the middle of this display case is a white porcelain jar with cloud and dragon design, which is one of the most representative items in the collection of the Gyeonggi Ceramic Museum. It is a ritual vessel that used to be an indispensable item during national events and important royal family events for holding wine or flower arrangements. This jar, decorated with cintamani beads at the shoulders and the base, features a dragon amid clouds, depicted in a lively pose as if about to grab and swallow the beads. The dragon is considered a sacred creature connecting the sky with the earth and creating harmony in all things in the universe. The dragon was a popular symbol of the monarch and his authority as it stood for supreme power and was seen as the protector of the state. In Joseon, the face of a king was referred to as “dragon face,” his clothes “dragon robe,” his wisdom “dragon wisdom,” and his royal status “dragon status.” As dragon vases produced in the government kiln were also considered an important insignia of the king, court painters were dispatched to the Gwangju government kiln for the task of painting the dragon design. In this piece, while the dragon is painted in light blue, a more saturated blue is used for details such as the eyes and the scale for a subtle gradation of shade. The smooth surface is evenly covered in a bluish glaze. This beautifully crafted dragon vase of remarkable craftsmanship was deemed to be of great significance by Gyeonggi-do and was designated as Provincial Tangible Cultural Heritage No. 355.

stories.title: Establishment of the Government Kiln_”Cheonjihyeonhwang” (4 items)
stories.audioTitle: Establishment of the Government Kiln_”Cheonjihyeonhwang” (4 items)
stories.script: In early Joseon, ceramics used in the royal palace or government agencies were supplied by producers located in various parts of the country. This method of procurement proved to be inconvenient and prone to the inconsistency of quality. To resolve this problem, the government set up its own kiln under Saongwon, the royal court agency responsible for food-related matters, known as “Bunwon.” Located in Gwangju where it was relocated to several different sites over time, Bunwon produced white porcelain of the highest quality until it was ultimately privatized in 1883.    This display case and the one next to it contain an array of white porcelain bearing characters such as “cheon,” “ji,” “hyeon,” or “hwang.” The white porcelain wares supplied to the king were the best items produced in the government kiln, chosen among the ones that were pure white. Before they were delivered to Saongwon, one of these four characters was written on the underside of the foot. They were storage labels to help make it easier for Saongwon to sort through new shipments of inventory. Dishes used by the king and the royal family were kept in a storage called “Naetanggo.” Naetanggo was situated in front of Sajeongjeon, the king’s office quarters, for easy access. “Cheon,” “ji,” “hyeon,” and “hwang” were the first characters of the four sections of Naetango, named “Cheonjago,” “Jijago,” “Hyeonjago,” and “Hwangjago.”       Aside from these storage labels, there was no other information such as the names of responsible officers. This was because responsible officers were liable to change frequently. The dishes supplied to Saongwon were managed by four low-ranking officers, known as “jejo.” By using only the four labels, they could avoid unnecessary confusion and easily determine the inventory from the production stage on.    Dishes bearing these characters were reserved for the king’s use, but the king sometimes offered them to his courtiers as a fine gift. When court officials resigned or retired from their government positions and returned to their hometowns, they often took these cherished gifts from the king with them. This is the reason why dishes of this kind are sometimes unearthed during archaeological excavations outside the capital area. Vessels bearing these characters have also been discovered in major Buddhist temples located outside the capital area, dating from early Joseon. The white porcelain vessels excavated at the former site of Bowonsa Temple in Seosan Chungcheongnam-do were also marked with these characters, along with the names of monks, suggesting that the same characters were used in this temple for labelling ceramics.

stories.title: Placenta Jar (1 item)
stories.script: This white porcelain jar with four ears displayed here is believed to be a taehang, a jar used for storing the placenta of royal offspring.      In Joseon, the placenta was considered a sacred source of life. When a child was born in the royal family, they had the custom of burying the placenta at an auspicious site, which they believed will ensure the health and happiness of the child and help the country prosper. Such a cult of the placenta goes back to the Silla period and continued into Goryeo before it grew into a concrete custom with well-defined procedures in Joseon. After the birth of a royal, they built a taesil (or placenta chamber) in a place that was deemed auspicious. They, then, buried a white porcelain jar containing the placenta and a stone tablet recording the date of burial. Finally, to mark the burial site, a stone stele was erected. In early Joseon, a taesil was only built for a king, but in subsequent eras, one was also constructed for other royals. The status of a taesil was upgraded when its owner later became the king. When a taesil is promoted to “taebong,” its surrounding area was decorated with stone structures known as “gabong.”   The oldest surviving placenta jar is the one belonging to King Sejong, presumed to have been buried in 1397. In early Joseon, placenta jars were produced in kilns located outside the capital area, in various types of pottery, including earthenware and Buncheong. It was during the reign of Seongjong (1469-1474) that the classic type of placenta jar, consisting of an inner and outer urn, with four loops and a lotus bud-shaped knob on the lid, appeared for the first time. The lid was fastened to the jar by putting a cord through the four loops and, then, the hole in the knob for a secure seal.        During the Japanese rule of Korea, between the late 1920’s and 1934, all taesil nationwide were relocated to Seosamneung, the tomb cluster in Goyang, under the pretext that they were poorly maintained and neglected. This resulted in a serious undermining of the integrity and original intent of taesil and the taehang they housed. Taehang made in celadon or Buncheong were displayed as historical artifacts in places like the Yi Royal Family Museum for the viewing pleasure of the Japanese public, many of whom were aficionados of antiques at that time. People also brought dishes from their home and secretly buried them near a taesil in the hopes that some of the auspicious energy would rub off on them.

stories.title: Rising from the Ashes of War (1 item)
stories.audioTitle: Rising from the Ashes of War (1 item)
stories.script: The two successive wars between the late 16th century and the early 17th century, the Japanese and Qing invasions, took a toll on Joseon’s white porcelain making, which had flourished into a thriving industry following the establishment of the government kiln. Joseon’s economy was on the brink of collapse, and large numbers of potters were either killed or taken to Japan. White porcelain produced in the wake of these wars was a pale reflection of what it once was. Notwithstanding, as the country tried to rebuild from the ashes of war, the demand for white porcelain only grew larger. The government kiln looked for ways to increase its production, which led to the decline in quality. White porcelain produced during the 17th century had a dark gray hue. Despite the drop in quality, a significant stride was made in production techniques and productivity.     The item in the middle of this display case is a white porcelain bowl with an incised design of fish. This bowl was excavated from a mid-Joseon kiln site in Sindae-ri, Gwangju, Gyeonggi-do. The bowl is presumed to be a ritual hand wash bowl, known as “se.” Before the start of a rite, its officiants and participants washed their hands as a gesture of deference. This practice also had the symbolical meaning of cleansing the body and mind of impurities ahead of an important rite. Joseon ritual vessels were influenced by ritual bronzes of the Shang and Zhou dynasties of China in terms of their composition and classification. After the founding of Joseon, its rulers established national-level protocols for rites and ritual vessels as part of an effort to strengthen the legitimacy of the new dynasty.     Ritual vessels were normally made of metals, but ceramic wares replicating the appearance of metal wares were also sometimes made. During the period between late Goryeo and early Joseon, Korea was forced to send large quantities of gold, silver, and ginseng to the Yuan dynasty as tribute goods. Metals also became scarce due to the production of weaponry and the minting and casting of coins and metal type during Taejong’s reign to Sejong’s reign. The government called in brass, iron, and copper throughout the land and placed restrictions on the production of metal wares. The production of ceramics and wooden wares were encouraged instead. The demand for ceramics for use during royal family rituals increased progressively, leading to the establishment of the government kiln in Gwangju, Gyeonggi-do, in 1467. One major drawback of ceramic vessels was that they could easily break. The use of chipped or cracked vessels during rites was strictly prohibited. When ritual vessels were found to have chips or cracks, they were sometimes buried in the ground.

stories.title: White Porcelain with Iron-oxide Paintings (0 item)
stories.audioTitle: White Porcelain with Iron-oxide Paintings (0 item)
stories.script: Another major change brought about by the two successive wars in Joseon’s white porcelain making concerned pigments. Previously, blue pigments were most often to apply designs on high-end white porcelain produced in the government kiln. Iron-oxide pigments were used sparingly, only on special occasions. After the Japanese and Qing invasions, war-induced economic hardships were compounded by the cutting off of transportation routes from China. This made it extremely difficult to procure blue pigments, which were mostly imported from China. Hence, in the early 17th century, even the royal family used white porcelain with designs painted using iron-oxide pigments, rather than expensive blue pigments imported from Persia. Iron oxide-decorated white porcelain, therefore, appeared as a result of the willingness to compromise on prestige and luxury on the part of Joseon society amid a collective effort to weather the crisis facing the country.   Designs on some of the iron oxide-decorated white porcelain are quite elegant and sophisticated, as though the work of a court painter. The pottery fragments discovered at a 17th-century kiln site in Songjeong-dong, Seondong-ri, Gwangju, are fine examples of it. These fragments bearing the images of plum flowers, bamboos, and grapes reveal an interesting connection between mid-Joseon painting and pottery decoration.

stories.title: Nationwide Diffusion of White Porcelain with Underglaze Iron-oxide Designs (1 item)
stories.audioTitle: Nationwide Diffusion of White Porcelain with Underglaze Iron-oxide Designs (1 item)
stories.script: The perception of white porcelain with underglaze iron-oxide designs gradually changed over time. This pottery was produced amid social and economic upheavals as a substitute for blue and white porcelain until the mid-17th century. With the active use of white porcelain with underglaze iron-oxide designs by the royal house, they were no longer perceived as low-quality products. Starting in the late 17th century, iron oxide-decorated white porcelain wares inspired by those produced in the government kiln were widely produced across the country.     This white porcelain jar with a bluish gray hue features a humorously depicted dragon flying amid clouds. The design was realized using iron-oxide pigments. In Joseon, the use of a dragon’s image was restricted as this imaginary beast symbolized the king. This type of jars was considered special as they were used during important royal family events as wine jugs or flower vases. They were therefore crafted with care. Court painters drew the underglaze designs using blue pigments, according to set rules. Around this time, Joseon’s traditional social hierarchy started to show signs of weakening under the impact of its nascent market economy. By the late 17th century, white porcelain jars with whimsical images of dragon, created using cheaper iron-oxide pigments, were widely produced for use by members of its scholar-official class and affluent middle-class people. Government kiln sites where such dragon jars intended for private use were discovered include the Yusa-ri and Sindae-ri sites. Among private kilns located outside the capital area, only one such piece was discovered in 2008, at the Hapan-ri kiln site.  Although iron oxide-decorated white porcelain wares produced in local kilns were not the kind of classically elegant ceramics that could have appealed to the taste of royals or scholar-officials, they had an informal and humorous kind of beauty, reminiscent of Buncheong wares, of which this bluish-gray jar with a dragon drawn in a few quick strokes is a great example.

stories.title: Joseon Renaissance, White Porcelain Moon Jar (1 item)
stories.audioTitle: Joseon Renaissance, White Porcelain Moon Jar (1 item)
stories.script: In the 18th century, during the reigns of Yeongjo and Jeongjo, Joseon saw the flourishing of Silhak or “Practical Learning” and the booming of its ceramics industry. High-quality white porcelain wares produced during this period were characterized by their immaculate white color. The ceramics, produced near Geumsa-ri, Gwangju, were masterpieces of an understated elegance without flamboyant colors or complicated designs. One of the best-known examples is “moon jar,” a finely proportioned vase famous for its warm beauty and pure white color.    Large ceramics like moon jars are presumed to have been used on ceremonial occasions, for holding wine or flowers during royal family rites or banquets. Moon jars were produced mainly between the late 17th century and the 18th century. Government kilns that produced moon jars included the Sindae-ri and Geumdae-ri kilns.     As moon jars were not only large, but were also nearly spherical in shape, it was probably difficult to form them on a pottery wheel in one piece. They are likely to have been made by joining two hemispheres that were separately formed on a pottery wheel. The examination of the inside of large white porcelain vessels with a height of 40cm or more often reveals a visible joint along the circumference. Another reason that made it difficult to form a large white porcelain vessel on a pottery wheel was kaolin, its main ingredient, which is highly viscous clay.    Due to their unique shape, moon jars are often considered the variety of Joseon white porcelain that best embodies Korean aesthetic. Simple and unassuming, these generously-proportioned jars nevertheless arrest the eyes and rivet the attention. These jars of subtle and mysterious beauty have been a source of artistic inspiration for many modern Korean painters, installation artists, and photographers, of the likes of Kim Whanki Kim, Doh Sang-bong, Kuh Bon-chang, and Kang Ik-jung.    The circumstances of how these jars got to be called “moon jars” are not precisely known. However, according to some sources, this name was first used by Kim Whanki during the 1950’s and, then, by art historian Choi Sun-woo, who was a close acquaintance of his, in an op-ed Choi wrote for Donga Ilbo in 1963.

stories.title: Active Production of Blue and White Porcelain (1 item)
stories.audioTitle: Active Production of Blue and White Porcelain (1 item)
stories.script: In late Joseon, the flourishing of Silhak helped increase agricultural productivity, which, in turn, led to economic growth. As Joseon also traded more actively with its neighbors and became exposed to Western civilization through Qing China, this triggered shifts in perception and brought changes in all areas of industry. During the reigns of Yeongjo and Jeongjo, a period of extended economic stability, the government ended the practice of relocating the state-run kiln every ten years. The government kiln was permanently set up in Bunwon-ri, Gwangju for more stable supply of manpower and raw materials.  Moreover, progressive changes in Joseon’s class system, coupled with the enactment of Gyunyeokbeop, the equal taxation law, helped reduce inequalities and imbalances in its society and led to the emergence of a thriving merchant class and market economy. As the literati culture of the scholar-official class spread to wealthy middle-class people, government kiln-produced white porcelain became widely popular across broad segments of Joseon’s society. The demand for high-end porcelain grew in all segments of population. As a result, the government kiln, which previously only supplied to the royal family and government agencies, started to supply products to markets across the country. The active production of sought-after blue and white pottery, in particular, ushered in the heydays of Joseon white porcelain. Blue and white porcelain wares were now used by people of all social classes.   Here we have a tall blue and white porcelain jar decorated with longevity symbols. Jars like this one that have a tall straight neck, decorated with folk painting-style longevity symbols, were popularly produced during the 19th century. This piece features cranes flying low under the crown of a pine tree and two deer frolicking between bamboos with all four legs in mid-air. The jar, coated in a light blue glaze, has a smooth grayish blue surface with no crackling.

stories.title: Everyday White Porcelain Wares of the 19th Century (2 items)
stories.audioTitle: Everyday White Porcelain Wares of the 19th Century (2 items)
stories.script: After Bunwon, the government kiln, found its permanent home in Bunwon-ri, Gwangju, in 1752, it eventually began producing large quantities of white porcelain wares that combined practicality with decorativeness. This was because amid the continuous industrial growth in the 19th century, white porcelain was used by increasingly diverse segments of population. Everyday wares produced in Bunwon, such as bottles, plates, and bowls, were sturdy wares with thick walls, most often decorated with auspicious designs symbolizing happiness, good fortunes, and longevity.  Joseon’s trade with Qing-dynasty China between the late 18th and 19th century also had a profound impact on the style of ceramics produced in the government kiln. Government envoys and merchants traveled more frequently to China and brought back Qing-dynasty ceramics that were decorated with auspicious designs. As a result, design themes related to worldly happiness also became widely popular in Joseon. Peony blossoms, the ten symbols of longevity, fish, grapes, pomegranates, carps, cicadas, and butterflies were originally motifs used in Chinese painting, standing for prosperity, healthy and long life, and success. These Chinese motifs became dominant motifs in folk painting in 18th-19th century Joseon and also started to grace blue and white porcelain ceramics from this period after some modification to reflect the local taste.     The small plate at the far left end of this display case is a white porcelain dinnerware plate. The plate is inscribed with the character “bok” on the inside bottom. On the underside of the plate, there is a Hangeul inscription near its foot, stating that this plate was delivered in 1858 to the court kitchen of Changdeokgung, which was the residence of Hyojeong, the queen consort to Hyeonjong.    The exotic-looking bowl to the right of this item is a government kiln-made blue and white porcelain bowl dating from sometime in 19th century. Its design was influenced by Kraak, export ceramics mass-produced in kilns in Jingdezhen in the late Ming Dynasty. The rim is surrounded by a floral belt of stylized petals. The area below the rim is divided into four sections. Each section is enclosed by brackets and has a diamond-shaped medallion containing the image of flower stems. On the inside, there is a circle at the bottom of the bowl with three flower stems forming a radial design.

stories.title: Literati Stationery and Desk Accessories (2 items)
stories.audioTitle: Literati Stationery and Desk Accessories (2 items)
stories.script: Late Joseon was a period of economic stability and cultural revival. During this period, there was an infatuation among members of Joseon’s intelligentsia and learned class for refined blue and white porcelain wares embodying literati aesthetic. Stationery articles and everyday items used by scholar-officials, such as writing brush holders, water droppers, brush racks, ink jars, incense burners, vases, and wine carafes, were decorated with motifs related to literati lifestyle and ideals. Carps, dragons, peony blossoms, and the ten symbols of longevity were among the most popular motifs, as they expressed the hopes and dreams of scholar-officials; namely, success, peace in the household, wealth and prosperity, and healthy long life. Other popular themes such as landscapes and “Four Gentlemen” conveyed literati ideals.    This square-shaped blue and white porcelain piece is a water dropper used to dispense water for making ink. Made by joining six thin squares, the water dropper is almost a perfect cube. Each side of the cube has blue borders. The top side features a landscape and the four lateral sides plum blossoms executed in soft strokes. This landscape, inspired by the famous Chinese painting Eight Views of Xiaoxiang Rivers, depicts a delightful scene where two people standing on a tall cliff overlooking a river with a boat converse while looking at distant mountains.      However, in the mid- to late 18th century, Yeongjo prohibited the utilization of dragon vases and blue and white pottery. Evoking how cheaper iron-oxide pigments were used in the past, instead of blue pigments, the king is recorded to have expressed his concerns about the extravagant lifestyle of his subjects and people. During the reign of Jeongjo, his successor and grandson, an alternative to blue and white pottery. This new type of pure white porcelain had embossed designs, dispensing with the need for blue pigments. Embossed designs were made by incising patterns and then digging out clay from the surrounding areas of the patterns or pressing on them to create depression. At the far end of this display case, we have a white porcelain bottle with two blossomed chrysanthemum stems in embossed carving.

stories.title: White Porcelain Bottles, the Symbol of Joseon’s Upper-class Culture (2 items)
stories.audioTitle: White Porcelain Bottles, the Symbol of Joseon’s Upper-class Culture (2 items)
stories.script: Unlike in Goryeo where bottles and carafes were frequently made in celadon, in Joseon, these vessels were mainly made in white porcelain. This is because due to the low viscosity of white clay, white porcelain was best suited for making simple vessels without complicated details.     Most Joseon white porcelain wares for storing and dispensing wine, water, or tea had a round belly and a long neck to easily hold with a full hand. The mouth was slightly flared for the ease of pouring out liquids. In late Joseon, white porcelain bottles became a symbol of the lifestyle among its learned upper class members, characterized by the love of nature, tranquility, and poetry. They were a decorative object frequently found in a scholar-official’s room, which were also actually used as wine bottles. Some of them had dramatic curves and others had a more exotic square or hexagonally-shaped body.  This white porcelain bottle with plum, bird, and bamboo design in underglaze cobalt blue  we have here is decorated with the images of a bird perched on a flowered plum tree and bamboos. Varying shades of blue are used creating the impression of depth. Plum blossoms symbolize the honor and integrity of a scholar-official living in retreat from the world, and bamboos his rectitude. As a piece combining two favorite symbols of Joseon’s literati culture, this bottle is a great testament to a lifestyle that famously idealized nature and poetry.   This white porcelain bottle with a chrysanthemum and butterfly design in underglaze cobalt blue has a flat round body. The bottle resting on a generously-sized foot appears stable and conveys a sense of volume. Its overall appearance is sophisticated. The bottle is ringed by chrysanthemum flowers near its base and has a large butterfly flapping its wings on its belly. The contrast between the finely detailed design motifs and the white background gives the bottle a neat appearance. In Joseon, the butterfly was often compared to a scholar-official because of the metamorphosis it undergoes in its life cycle, from the egg to the caterpillar, from the caterpillar to the pupa, and finally from the pupa to the adult butterfly. The metamorphosis of a butterfly was considered analogous to the successive stages in the life of a scholar-official from an aspiring young scholar studying for the difficult civil service examination to a government official and, then, to a prominent statesman and scholar.

stories.title: Sarangbang (1 item)
stories.script: Sarangbang was men’s quarters in a Joseon upper-class home. It was a study or office for a scholar-official, doubling as a parlor to receive guests. Lively discussions with other scholar-officials about philosophy and arts took place in the sarangbang. As a prime site of intellectual exchange, a sarangbang had a thoughtful selection of furniture. In selecting furniture for a sarangbang, the emphasis fell on practicality. A simple, well-arranged interior, inspiring peace and calm was preferred. Furnishing was sober, most often made of pine or paulownia wood rather than other pricier and fancier woods. The basic furniture of a sarangbang included a bookcase, an open-sided cabinet, a stationery chest, a writing table, and a stationery table. Among the main accessories of a sarangbang were candlesticks, ink stones, water droppers, writing brush racks, ink jars, and seal stamps. Open-sided cabinets were most often used in pairs of two and were matched with a stationery chest, to store books, small objects, and place potted plants. Writing desks were made small to keep them portable. But they were never smaller than the size of an open book. A stationery table was placed next to the writing desk to provide extra space to stow away desk items.     Here, on top of this stationery chest, we have a white porcelain plate decorated with a carp. The carp leaping out of water depicted in this plate is a carp from a famous Chinese legend. The legend of the Dragon Gate, a waterfall in the upper reaches of the Yellow River, reads as follows:  “Hundreds of carps swam up the Yellow River toward the Dragon Gate to spawn. But few were able to leap over the Dragon Gate as this waterfall formed a narrow gorge barely 30m in width and the current was strong. The bravest and most adventurous of them swam through the current. Just when it succeeded in leaping over the Dragon Gate, a lightning struck from the sky and burnt away its tail. 36 scales suddenly appeared on its body and the carp was reborn as a dragon and ascended to heaven.”  In Korea, the legend of the Dragon Gate gave rise to the expression “deungyongmun,” which means a narrow gateway to success, admitting only very few capable of rising above the competition. The legend of the Dragon Gate was a popular design theme for ceramics and was also frequently made the subject of paintings. This theme was particularly well-loved by young scholars aspiring to succeed in the civil service examination and lead a prominent government career. It was therefore often used as a decorative motif for furnishings and accessories of a sarangbang. People also gave carp-themed objects to those who will be taking an exam in the near future to wish them success.          In ceramics, the carp is usually depicted on the surface of a water dropper, either while vigorously jumping above waves or leaping out of water with its head held vertically toward the sky. The popularity of carp design in late Joseon could be also explained by shifts that occurred in its rigid social class system during this period and the development of Silhak. More people perhaps felt that passing the civil service exam and climbing the ladders of Joseon’s bureaucratic society was a dream within reach.

stories.title: Pantry and Hall (0 item)
stories.script: Traditional Korean homes had a pantry, known as “chanbang,” located next to the kitchen. The pantry was used to prepare simple dishes or serve food on the tray tables before they were carried to the anbang, the main room, or to the sarangbang, the men’s quarters. Dishes were stored on “chantak,” furniture with open shelves. Chantak were made with hard and dense woods such as pine or oak, capable of withstanding the weight of heavy brass and ceramic dishes and resistant to warping and water damage from dishes left to dry.    The daecheong is a large wooden floor hall located between the anbang or sarangbang and other rooms, where many family activities take place. This space was most often furnished with a grain chest, an armoire, and an open-sided cabinet, and various household items hung from the wall. The grain chest was sturdily built using pine posts and oak panels as they had to hold the weight of grains and seeds, such as rice, barley, soybeans, and sesame seeds. This was also the place where food was prepared when there were large family gatherings and events. During memorial ceremonies, an altar was set up and spirit tablets were placed on it. As the daecheong is a well-aerated space, jars containing honey, medicinal ingredients, or crop seeds were often stored there, on top of the armoire or the grain chest.

stories.title: Dinnerware and Table Setting (item 1)
stories.script: “Bansanggi” refers to dinnerware used for traditional Korean meals. Composed of rice and soup bowls, various types of plates and small dishes for condiments, Korean dinnerware sets are a great testament to the rich diversity of Korean culinary culture. The number of dishes served, excluding condiments, was referred to as “gi.” As for “cheop,” the word used today to refer to the number of side dishes, it first appeared in the late 19th century.  An informative record about meals eaten in the royal family is Wonhaeng Eulmyo jeongni uigwe. This document describes in detail King Jeongjo’s trip to Suwon in 1795 (19th year of his reign) in the company of his mother Lady Hong and the banquet he held there for his late father Prince Sado’s 60th birthday. The document provides a comprehensive insight into the culinary culture of Joseon’s royal court as it lists the banquet menu, dishes served to the guests, the details of meals Lady Hong had during her eight day stay in Suwon as well as meals for royal court personnel. The meals for the king and royals consisted of seven gi, the meals for officials of third rank and above four gi or two gi, and the meals for low-ranking officials and people of upper middle class two gi. Regardless of the number of gi, all meals were served with rice and a soup.      Surasang, the king’s meal, was composed of a soup, a stew, gimchi, condiments, a steamed meat or fish dish or steamed vegetables stuffed with meat, and a hot pot. Rice served to the king was purplish-red rice, cooked in red water by leaching adzuki beans. Dishes were served on two or three small tables placed next to one another. Routine meals for the king were known as “wonsang.” Meals prepared for the king by an official’s household or special repasts were referred to as “gyeotsang.” Before the king began his meal, the food was inspected and tasted by two court ladies. To detect poisoning, the king’s eating utensils were made of silver, a metal that reacts to arsenic.     Brass, silver, or porcelain wares were used depending on the season to serve food in the royal court. Silver dishes were used from Chuseok, the mid-autumn harvest festival when the temperature starts to drop, to Dano in the following spring. Porcelain dishes were used during warmer months from Dano to Chuseok. Stews were, however, served in an earthenware dish throughout the year. Exceptions were therefore allowed for certain types of food.

stories.title: Grave Goods – Memorial Ceremony (1 item)
stories.script: With the flourishing of studies of rites in China during the 16th century, culminating in works such as Zhuzi jiali (Zhu Xi’s Family Rites), Confucian funeral and burial practices also became popular among members of Joseon’s scholar-official class. They felt that it was the duty of the living toward their dead to maintain the graveyard in a proper condition and bury suitable grave goods. It was a Confucian belief that dead ancestors should be buried at a sunny site and have access to personal items they used while living. However, dead ancestors being spirits and not living persons, they buried carefully-crafted ceramic miniatures of household items, known as “myeonggi.”       Myeonggi were dishes the dead would be using in the other world. The custom of placing myeonggi with the deceased, usually in a separate chamber on the south side of the tomb, was to express filial respect toward ancestors. Much like dinnerware, the allowable number of myeonggi was restricted by the rank of the deceased. According to Gukjooreui, a 15th-century book on five major types of rites, this number was up to 30 for deceased scholar-officials of 4th rank and above, up to 20 for officials of 5th rank and below, and up to 15 for those who had not held a government office. These limits were increased during the 17th century to 30 for 5th and 6th-rank officials and 20 for 7th and 8th-rank officials. The custom was discontinued during the 18th century when the size of tombs for the scholar-official class was reduced and had no longer room for myeonggi. One exception was the royal family which continued to inter myeonggi with dead royals.  In addition to myeonggi, a deceased scholar-official was also buried with a ceramic jiseok, a burial tablet containing family history and a short biography detailing his life and work. Along with personal information about the deceased and the genealogy of his family, the precise location of the tomb was indicated. This was to prevent the dead from becoming forgotten should the tombstone become defaced, lost, or destroyed one day. Jiseok were usually placed inside the tomb toward the end of the burial during its final stage. In Joseon, ceramic jiseok were preferred over stone jiseok, as clay is more malleable than stone and is easier to engrave. Initially, ceramic tablets were used mostly by scholar-official households, but were later adopted also by the royal family. As blue and white porcelain was the most prized variety of ceramics, blue and white porcelain tablets were reserved for royals and high-ranking government officials. In late Joseon, ordinary household ceramics with ink-written inscriptions were sometimes used as jiseok, instead of standard rectangular tablets.    Memorial rites were another way of remembering their dead for people of Joseon. Known as “jerye” or “gillye,” memorial ceremonies were one of the five basic types of rites held in Joseon. Jerye included ancestral worship ceremonies by the royal household or private households, national ceremonies worshipping the gods of the earth and harvest, as well as memorial ceremonies at the town or village level. Metal vessels were the norm for memorial ceremonies. But when the dead were of modest social status or in situations where metal vessels were not readily available, they were sometimes replaced by ceramics. According to Jegidoseol (or Illustrated Guide to the Production of Ritual Vessels), a wide variety of ceramic ritual vessels were produced, including “bo” or “gwe” for holding grains, incense burner, “jun” for holding wine offered at the altar, “jak,” the wine cup, “se,” the hand wash bowl for the officiant, and “yi,” the water dispensing basin.

stories.title: West Coast Period of Goryeo Celadon + Goryeo White Porcelain (1 item)
stories.audioTitle: West Coast Period of Goryeo Celadon + Goryeo White Porcelain (1 item)
stories.script: In Korea, celadon and white porcelain were first produced during the 10th century, under the influence of the Yue kilns of Northern Zhejiang in China. Their production began in the central western Korean peninsula, in places such as Siheung, Yongin, Goyang, Yangju, Yeoju, Baecheon, and Seosan. In towns along the west coast, such as Wonheung-dong in Goyang, Bangsan-dong in Siheung, Bugok-ri in Yangju, which were the first to be exposed to the advanced celadon technology of the Yue kilns, large Chinese-style brick kilns were built. As it was a time when tea drinking gained popularity in Goryeo, a variety of teawares, including bowls with a halo-shaped foot, were produced in these kilns, in addition to everyday wares and ritual vessels.    Next, we have a variety of Goryeo white porcelain wares that were produced in Gyeonggi-do. The production of white porcelain began around the same time as celadon. In Goryeo, white porcelain wares were mostly produced as a substitute for Chinese white porcelain ceramics that were in high demand among Gaegyeong-based aristocrats and influential family clans based outside the capital area. These ceramics were first produced in Seo-ri in Yongin, Bangsan-dong in Siheung, and Jungam-ri in Yeoju. As Goryeo white porcelain wares were produced using celadon making techniques, they had a low level of density and were affected by problems such as peeling glaze. Similar in quality to soft-paste white porcelain, these ceramics were not as popular as celadon. However, their production continued in places including Bisan-dong, Anyang and Sillim-dong, Seoul until the end of the Goryeo period to later serve as the foundation for Joseon white porcelain.  In the middle of this display case, we have a white porcelain bowl with a halo-shaped foot. This bowl, excavated from a kiln site in Seo-ri, Yongin, is known as a “halo bowl” or “jade disc bowl” as the underside of its foot is in the shape of a halo or a jade disc. Although this type of bowls are mostly of Chinese origin and were  popularly made only after tea drinking became widespread in China, some were discovered at archaeological sites of Unified Silla, such as Anapji in Gyeongju and Mireuksa Temple site in Iksan. This is because as the practice of tea drinking eventually spread to the Korean peninsula, teawares were imported from China during the Unified Silla period and were used by the royal family and at Buddhist temples. Domestically-produced teawares only became available when the production of ceramics began in the Korean peninsula during the Goryeo period. This bowl with a halo-shaped foot, produced in Seo-ri, Yongin, dates back to the early days of Korean ceramics making.

stories.title: Inlaid Celadon Kilns + Open Storage (0 item)
stories.audioTitle: Inlaid Celadon Kilns + Open Storage (0 item)
stories.script: In the mid-14th century, Goryeo was plagued by the Wako, the Japanese pirates, raiding its southwestern coastal region. As this led to the shutdown of the sea transportation routes, it dealt a severe blow to the ceramics industry based in this region. Celadon potters of kilns producing high-end celadon in places like Gangjin and Buan, Jeollanam-do left the region and became dispersed across the country. In Gyeonggi-do, they settled near Bukhansan and Dobongsan Mountains and produced inlaid celadon for the local community. The variety of vessels shrank as the potters now produced everyday wares primarily. Changes also occurred in the method of creating inlaid designs. Most of inlaid designs were now repetitive stamped patterns. After the founding of Joseon, inlaid celadon was continuously supplied to its royal family, but gradually underwent transformation to give rise to Joseon-style Buncheong ceramics.  At the opposite end of this room, there is an open storage with glass storage cases. These storage cases contain pottery fragments discovered during the survey and excavation of former kiln sites. Due to their vast quantity, not all of them are brought to the museum for sorting and classification. Although all pottery fragments are documented by specifying their types and sizes, only those that are deemed to be of significance are added to the collection of the museum. The rest are reburied in the ground at their original sites of discovery after thoroughly recording details of the excavations that were completed and what was done to artifacts that were discovered to avoid causing confusion during future excavations. Those that were brought to the museum are analyzed, measured, and photographed and, then, are registered into the national cultural heritage database.   Compared to metals, wood, textiles, and paper, ceramics are much less sensitive to their preservation environment or conditions. Notwithstanding, given that these pieces, even if only fragments, are valuable cultural heritage that should be passed down to future generations, they need to be carefully preserved and managed. They have to be stored in a temperature and moisture-controlled environment. The lighting in this storage has a minimal impact on the stored artifacts. The positions of LED lights on the shelves are periodically changed so that light is not continuously shone on certain specific items.

stories.title: Large Display Case + White Porcelain Kilns (items from Hapan-ri, Gapyeong and Hwagok-ri, Anseong)
stories.audioTitle: Large Display Case + White Porcelain Kilns (items from Hapan-ri, Gapyeong and Hwagok-ri, Anseong)
stories.script: This large display case contains ceramics excavated from kiln sites in Hapyeong-ri, Gapyeong and Hwagok-ri, Anseong. The items in this display case are shown in a rather unusual position. Vessels are stacked up on top of one another, which is the way they were arranged inside the kiln for firing.   - Ceramics are sometimes fired stacked up on each other especially when they are of similar types. To separate the vessels more easily after firing, sand or refractory soil was inserted between them. The outer surfaces of vessels that were fired this way sometimes show impurities and traces left by ashes. This firing method is used most often for low price ceramics intended for mass markets.      - Here, in the middle of this display case, we have several round lumps of clay. They are a kind of kiln furniture known as “stilts.” In Korean, they are known as “dochim” or “dojimi.” Stilts are placed either at the bottom of the kiln or the saggar to prevent vessels from sticking to the kiln or the saggar and to raise their positions for increased thermal efficiency.    -The photos you see here on this wall are excavation scenes at a former kiln site. They show the plan of the kiln and the layers of waste. The kiln is a multi-chamber stair-type kilns, consisting of three firing chambers built on a gentle slope with an inclination of about 15 degrees. The firing chambers are wider at the top than the bottom, which is a typical characteristic of kilns dating from the 17th century and later. Between the firing chambers, there are fire tunnels through which the fire travels from the front compartment to the one above. The second compartment has its own fuel entrance on one side for an additional source of fire.

stories.title: Bunwon Kiln (1 item)
stories.script: This display case shows a collection of fragments of government kiln-made white porcelain wares dating from the 15th to 19th centuries, along with a saggar.  The white porcelain pieces with inscriptions in Chinese characters are fragments of myojiseok, a tablet buried with a deceased person, containing his name and the dates of birth and death and biographical information. Unlike in Goryeo where burial tablets were most often large rectangular stone blocks with carved inscriptions, in Joseon, they were made in Buncheong ceramic or white porcelain with inlaid, blue or iron-oxide inscriptions.  The artifact on the right side is the saggar used in the government kiln. A saggar is a protective case used in a kiln, made of refractory soil. It shields vessels from impurities such as flying ashes and dirt falling from the ceiling of the firing chamber. The one shown here is cylindrical in shape. Saggars are made of clay with high silica content, which can withstand high firing temperatures. Using a saggar, potters could produce high-quality ceramics, fired at high temperatures, in an immaculate condition. In Joseon, government kiln-made white porcelain wares fired using a saggar were referred to as “gapbeon” and were considered the finest ceramics.

stories.title: Local Kiln-made White Porcelain Emulating Government Kiln White Porcelain (1 item)
stories.audioTitle: Local Kiln-made White Porcelain Emulating Government Kiln White Porcelain (1 item)
stories.script: Even during the period when Bunwon, the government kiln, was in operation, private kilns located in various parts of Gyeonggi-do also sometimes supplied ceramics to the government. Pottery villages were formed near white clay quarries and in valleys and thickly vegetated corners of the countryside, in places like Gapyeong, Yongin, Yeoju, and Paju. The government kiln’s white porcelain making techniques were eventually transmitted to the kilns in this area, often through the movement of potters who were scouted to work for the government. A great example of this was white porcelain with underglaze iron-oxide designs. After its first appearance during the 17th century in the aftermath of war, iron oxide-decorated white porcelain gave rise to local variants.   This striking looking piece is a dragon vase excavated from the white porcelain kiln site in Hapan-ri, Gapyeong. Gapyeong had a high concentration of private kilns in its environs and was also a supplier of high-quality kaolin for the government kiln. It was therefore both a major producer of ceramics and an important supplier of ceramic materials during the late Joseon period. Prior to the discovery of this piece, dragon vases with iron-oxide designs have only been found at government kiln sites. The dragon vase from the Hapan-ri kiln site is currently the only known example of dragon vase produced by a private kiln. This vase was made by joining two hemispheres. The dragon with interesting details like hair swept in the wind above its face is depicted in its entirety including all four limbs and the tail and is featured together with potted flowers.

stories.title: Gyeonggi-do Ceramics at Marketplaces (1 item)
stories.script: In the 18th century, Joseon’s stable social environment led to a boom in the production of ceramics in the government kiln as well as private kilns across the country, resulting also in the broadening of distribution channels. In addition, ceramics produced in different parts of the country began showing distinctive local styles and flavors around this time. Blue and white porcelain, until then only produced in the government kiln, were now made in kilns in Sanbon-dong, Gunpo and other private local kilns.    - The lack-glazed ceramic in this display case was excavated from the former site of a kiln presumed to have been in operation sometime during the late 19th century, located in Seolma-ri, Paju. Black ceramics covered in ebony-colored glaze were continuously produced from the Goryeo period through to the Joseon period. Although reduction-fired, these vessels had an opaque black hue due to the high iron content in the glaze. Black-glazed ceramics are often unevenly glazed and tend to be plain without any underglaze decorative design. In late Joseon, there were specialized private kilns producing only black-glazed wares.

stories.title: The fading glory of the national branch kiln (Artifact 1)
stories.audioTitle: The fading glory of the national branch kiln (Artifact 1)
stories.script: With the opening of Korea’s ports to foreign trade in 1876, cheaper porcelain wares imported from Europe and Japan dominated the domestic market, while operation of the national branch kiln became increasingly difficult as the financial condition of the royal family, the biggest client of the branch kilns, deteriorated. Eventually, the branch kiln proved unable to overcome these difficulties and its management rights were transferred to the private sector in 1883, thus ending the proud, 420-year-long history of the kiln, which had produced royal white porcelain of the very highest quality during the Joseon Dynasty. The Branch Porcelain Manufacturer run by a private operator in 1883 made some profits by supplying porcelain to the royal palaces and domestic markets, but it was unable to pay off its rising debts. Thus, during the Gabo Reforms (1894-1896), the main privileges of the branch kiln, notably state support and the delivery of porcelain wares to royal palaces and government offices, all came to an end. Then in 1897, the branch kiln established the Branch Ceramic Company under a joint investment and operation method, followed by the establishment of Branch Ceramic Co., Ltd. in 1911 with the capital (KRW 40,000) of the kiln’s employees, transforming it into a modern-funded company. However, the small capital sum and inferior ceramic techniques inevitably failed to revive the branch kiln, which disappeared into the mists of history in the 1930s.   The White Porcelain Jar in Underglaze Cobalt Blue Inscribed with the Chinese Character “Bun” and the Buddha’s Hand Plant Design is the representative artifact of the dying efforts of the branch kiln. In particular, rather than “Bun” (分) for the branch kiln, the Chinese character “Bun” (汾) meaning “large” was inscribed inside the foot of the jar. This same character (汾) is also found in the Chinese name of the Branch Ceramic Company (Bunweon jagi jusikhoesa), whose establishment was registered in 1911. This fact proves that this white porcelain object was made after the privatization of the branch kiln. It is characterized by the Buddha’s hand plant design painted using cobalt blue chrome pigment.

stories.title: Regional porcelains maintain their slender existence. (Artifact 1)
stories.audioTitle: Regional porcelains maintain their slender existence. (Artifact 1)
stories.script: Despite the difficult business environment of the Joseon porcelain industry due to the decline of the branch kiln and the influx of industrial and imported porcelains, kilns in different regions continued to produce pottery characterized by rich local colors for everyday use. Although the market was dominated by Japanese products, ordinary people still favored low-quality, relatively cheap porcelain (sangsagi). However, in 1912, the Japanese Government-General of Korea established the Central Laboratory to generate technical benefits by dispatching technicians to excellent production areas around the country under the pretext of investigating the production methods and raw materials of the porcelain industry; however, it was also used as a policy measure to facilitate Japan’s colonial rule over Korea. Among the areas which produced excellent porcelain areas were Yeoju, Bongsan, Haeju, Yanggu, and Gochang.  In North Korea, Haeju White Porcelain from Hwanghae-do and Hoeryeong Porcelain from Hamgyeongbuk-do were produced during the modern period. Although kiln sites in other regions were losing their traditional characteristics due to the influx of modern production techniques, Haeju White Porcelain and Hoeryeong Porcelain maintained their originality by maintaining their traditional methods.  The White Porcelain Jar in Underglaze Cobalt Blue Inscribed with “Geomdanje” and Peony Design, which is displayed in an independent showcase in the center of the exhibition hall, is the representative Haeju White Porcelain Jar of the Gyeonggi Ceramic Museum. It is characterized by a design created by freehand brush strokes. Its shoulder is adorned with a chrysanthemum stamp  design, while its body features a large chrysanthemum design created with loose strokes. The inscription “Geomdanje” indicates that the production area was the town of Geomdan in Haeju County, Hwanghae-do.

stories.title: Japanese industrial porcelains dominate Joseon’s markets. (Artifact 0)
stories.audioTitle: Japanese industrial porcelains dominate Joseon’s markets. (Artifact 0)
stories.script: Japanese industrial porcelains, called waesagi, flooded into Korea following the opening of Korea’s ports to foreign trade and the advent of the Japanese colonial era. Korean dining tables were filled with cheap Japanese bowls characterized by a thick, smooth texture, and even royal palaces favored imported dishes from England and France, rather than dishes made by the country’s branch kiln. With the advent of full-blown Japanese colonial rule after the signing of the Japan-Korea Treaty of 1910, the Japanese took over Korean kiln sites and focused on producing industrial porcelain objects such as insulators and, consequently, kilns run by Koreans increasingly lost ground.   As European export routes were blocked because of the war, the Japanese ceramic industry enjoyed a boom. Thus, they established Joseon Hard Porcelain Co., Ltd. in Yeongdo, Busan as a subsidiary of Japanese Hard Porcelain Co., Ltd. in 1914. This company was run by Joseon Hard Porcelain Co., Ltd. from 1920 to 1945, and was renamed as Daehan Hard Porcelain Co., Ltd. from the time of National Independence to 1950, when it became a Korean company under the name of Daehan Porcelain Co., Ltd. Japanese Hard Porcelain Co., Ltd. was a giant Japanese company established with Japanese capital and techniques, but after Korea regained its independence, it became a leading company of Busan’s economy.    This showcase displays imported Japanese white porcelain dishes inscribed with a pattern of Chinese characters, including 壽 (longevity) and 福 (fortune), which were very popular among the people of Joseon; bowls made by Japanese Hard Porcelain Co., Ltd., whose name was changed according to the era; oil lamps, which attest to the country’s importation of oil in modern times; and porcelain insulators, which were used in the supply of electricity.

stories.title: Korean porcelain emerges as an industry.
stories.audioTitle: Korean porcelain emerges as an industry.
stories.script: A number of industrial porcelain companies, which were established with Korean finances during the difficult period of Japanese colonial rule, laid the foundations for the emergence of Korea’s major porcelain companies in the future. Miryang Jedo Company (today’s Miryang Ceramic) was established in 1939, while Haengnamsa Company (today’s Haengnam Ceramic) and Chungbuk Jedo Company (today’s Hankook Chinaware) were both established in 1942. These companies are the original producers of Korea’s industrial porcelain wares. Compared to Japanese porcelain imported to Korea from the end of nineteenth century to the early twentieth century, the quality and degree of completion of the products of domestic porcelain was slightly inferior, but there was a remarkable change as Korean producers were able to manufacture large quantities of industrial porcelain wares.  Although the branch kiln failed to make a successful transition to the modern era at the end of the nineteenth century, some fifty years Korean porcelain companies set out to develop traditional porcelain into a major industry.

stories.title: The determination to preserve tradition and the love of celadon
stories.audioTitle: The determination to preserve tradition and the love of celadon
stories.script: As the branch kiln was unable –after its privatization–to produce the best quality white porcelain in Joseon, the royal family established the Hanseong Art Work Factory in a bid to restore the excellence of Korean traditional crafts in 1908. But with the loss of national sovereignty in 1911, the Department of the Royal Household (Kungnaebu), which was in charge of royal household affairs, was renamed as the Office of the Yi Dynasty (Yiwangjik), while the Hanseong Art Work Factory was renamed as the Yiwangjik Art Work Factory.  The Yiwangjik Art Work Factory was run with the royal family’s financial aid in the early days, but its actual operators were Japanese stockholders. The design of a plum flower, which was originally the emblem of the Korean royal family’s authority (and also symbolized an artwork made by the Yiwangjik Art Work Factory), was exploited by the Japanese to raise the value of their products.   At that time, a huge number of relics were illegally excavated from ancient Goryeo tombs by Japanese individuals or during investigations of historic sites overseen by the Japanese Government-General of Korea, and sent to Japan. There was a craze for collecting celadon among Japanese people, who were charmed by the mysterious color of Goryeo celadon. In order to generate profits from this passion for collecting celadon, some Japanese entrepreneurs moved to Joseon to run a business reproducing celadon. Among them, Tomita Kisaku, one of the major figures, established the Samhwa Goryeo Factory in Jinnampo, Pyeongannam-do in 1908, took over the Yiwangjik Art Work Factory and changed its name to Joseon Artwork Factory Co., Ltd. in 1922, and ran it until the late 1930s. It is said that Biwonso porcelain, which received favorable reviews from the public at the time, was baked at the Secret Garden of Changgyeonggung Palace by the Yiwangjik Art Work Factory, although the true location of the kiln remains unknown.    This showcase displays reproductions of celadon wares complete with their wrapping box, which were made by the Yiwangjik Art Work Factory, Joseon Artwork Factory Co., Ltd., and Samhwa Goryeo Factory.

stories.title: Pioneering inheritors of tradition Ⅰ& Ⅱ
stories.audioTitle: Pioneering inheritors of tradition Ⅰ& Ⅱ
stories.script: Hanyang Goryeo Factory was originally established in Mukjeong-dong, Seoul in 1911 by Umii Benzo (海正瓣藏, the owner of Haesi Sanghoe Co.). However, when business became difficult due to the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923, the factory was taken over by Tomita Kisaku in 1924. In the early days, it was mainly Japanese technicians who led production, but around seven to eight years after its establishment, they transferred their skills to Korean apprentices such as Hwang In-chun (1894-1950) and Yu Geun-hyeong (pen-name: Haegang, 1894-1993), who later established the Goryeo Celadon Research Institute in Gaeseong, North Korea. They devoted themselves to the study of both traditional Korean porcelain techniques and the celadon reproduction techniques of the factory, and led the production of creative porcelain in Korea after national independence.   However, the porcelain factories remaining after national independence were finally destroyed during the Korean War. Despite the difficult circumstances, the Korea Formative Culture Research Institute (known as the Seongbuk-dong Kiln) was established in Seoul in 1955 and the Korea Artworks Research Institute (known as the Daebang-dong Kiln) was established in 1956, and many artisans including Yu Gang-yeol, Kim Wan-bae, Jeong Gyu, Ji Sun-tak, and Yoo Geun-hyeong worked together to revive Korean ceramics. Despite their efforts, the institutes soon ran into financial difficulties and closed. The artisans scattered, and some of them settled in Icheon, Gyeonggi province, where they were able to work with difficulty.  From the late 1960s on, Korea’s rapid economic growth and cultural revival provided an opportunity for Korean ceramics to blossom once again. In 1965, when diplomatic relations between South Korea and Japan were normalized, many Japanese people showed great interest in the Korean ceramics market, and amid such a positive environment the kilns in Gwangju, Icheon, and Yeoju, Gyeonggi-do boomed again.  Meanwhile, in the decade after the Korean War, North Korea established the collective creative system in the 1960s and used art as a tool to propagate the Party’s revolution, rather than to create artworks. The Mansudae Art Studio, which is still active, is the cradle of this collective art, and its main ceramists are Wu Chi-seon and Lim Sa-jun. Some of their family members are also currently active members of the ceramic creative group of the Mansudae Art Studio. North Korea’s ceramics industry is focused on reproducing traditional ceramics using only limited techniques.

stories.title: Dream of Being a Tree - Artist Moon Byeong-Doo
stories.audioTitle: Dream of Being a Tree - Artist Moon Byeong-Doo
stories.script: This sculptural work titled “Dream of Being a Tree” was created by the artist Moon Byeong-Doo in 2010. It takes the form of a deer made of stainless-steel wire. Made of steel mesh, the work allows sunlight, wind, rain and snow to pass through it while fitting in harmony with its surroundings by blending into the background. Inside, there is a snail-shaped form symbolizing life. This snail grows in a form and shape resembling deer antlers, which grow like tree branches towards the sky, while the deer gradually assimilates with nature. The artist aimed to deliver a message of hope “Happiness, Love, Prosperity and Success” and to represent a small universe where man and nature coexist. The artist’s idea included themes of the cycle and symbiosis of nature.

stories.title: Reincarnation - Artist Lee Jeom-Won
stories.script: Here, this artwork is called “Reincarnation” created in 1993 by the artist Lee Jeom-Won. Inspired by life, the artist aimed to symbolically depict the phenomena of life where birth and death repeat in a cycle. In search of the origin of life that formed the foundation of his world of sculpturing, the artist researched forms embodying life. He wanted to explain that the form which he believed to be the origin of life would be round in shape with something protruding in one corner, not unlike a seed about to sprout. So, this work displays that form of life conceived by the artist. Look! Doesn’t it look like a seed about to sprout, or an egg about to hatch? It appears to figuratively capture the very moment when the energy of life bursts open.

stories.title: Ant - Artist Moon Shin
stories.script: This stainless-steel work titled “Ant” was created by Moon Shin in 1991, who was a well-known abstract sculptor in Korea. This artwork includes one of the most characteristic features found in the late sculptor’s world of art with its expression by using a symmetrical structure in the geometrical form. Since the feel of volume, streamlined yet full, was symmetrically designed, the work naturally displays a sense of vitality, while being restrained yet refined. Of note, the artist made sure to manifest a consistent principle of sculpturing in the purely abstract form by connecting straight and curved lines based on harmony and balance. We cannot know either the beginning or end from this round shape called “Ant,” but it represents the progress of birth and development of a life form, in tandem with the principle of the cycle of life, as it comes and goes back to life.

stories.title: Salvation 03-6 - Artist Kang Kwan-Wook
stories.script: Here is an old man standing, engaged in deep thought. This artwork of marble was made in 2011 by the artist Kang Kwan-Wook, who has incorporated the earthy image of the Korean people. It is called “Salvation 03-6.” This sculpture is part of the artist’s “Salvation” series that realistically captured destitution and pain through the image of a maternal figure who led and supported the Korean people. In the crude image of a mother, a wretched life of unending fatigue and cold reality is portrayed. From deep-set wrinkles, parched breasts and coarse hands, we can imagine how hard this mother had toiled away. A strong sense of authenticity towards life, which is derived from the completely unadorned, natural look. is like a consolation for our soul fatigued by the rough life. The sight of her can touch even the most hardened person’s soul that has grown numb to the burdens of life.

stories.title: Gravity Nongravity -Artist Kim Young-Won
stories.script: Here we see two human bodies. This work, cast stainless steel, is called “Gravity Nongravity” by the artist Kim Young-Won, and was completed in 1981. These anatomically correct human bodies are horizontally attached. One body has haphazardly set his foot on the ground, while the other is floating upside down in mid-air, and thus, we’re not sure whether the person on the ground is holding the other or whether the person on top is holding the other below. Even so, they are supporting each other. Through these realistically depicted bodies, the artist aimed to tell a narrative of man’s situations in reality, which he believed could transcend an existence that follows the natural law of gravity. The work embraces the artist’s view of the world where there might be an existence that obeys life and death and another one that wants to go beyond this constraint.

stories.title: Relatum - Artist Lee Ufan
stories.script: Composed of steel plates and natural stone, this work is part of the “Relatum” series by the artist Lee Ufan and was made in 2018. With the purpose to “make the most of a relationship with the world but through the least interventions,” the artist has incorporated points, lines, stones and steel plates in his artworks. Steel plates, placed either upright or laid down, and a stone or two on the plate form a relationship of contrast. What appears to be simple can make multiple relationships depending on the viewpoint, complicating them as well. Viewers can observe dialogues possible between materials formed by these relationships. To carry on in coexistence faced with differences in materials, according to the artist, is not to integrate relationships. The idea invites meditation on open relationships or time for our consciousness to recognize existences that are different from ours – an important premise in life as ever.

stories.title: For Reconciliation - Artist Chun Kook-Kwang
stories.script: This sculptural work titled “For Reconciliation” was created by the artist Chun Kook-Kwang in 1988. It represents the style of the artist who intensively explored the notion of mass unique to sculpturing. Made by carving Pocheon granite, the sculpture comprises three masses, each of which takes the form of layered boulders facing one another. The late artist found his inspiration from nature and aimed to express the abstract experience he found in nature. With this, the smooth curve created by the stone strata resembles sloshing waves in the sea, or curvy ridges between rice paddies or sand dunes being formed. The soft and melodic rhythm found in the simple stonework allows us to feel a sense of weight that is quite different from the stone’s weight. This inspiration also allows us to perceive a sense of volume that this work exudes while getting closer to the artist’s world of sculpturing.

stories.title: Works 0.10-21-01 - Artist Choi Man-Lin
stories.script: Characteristic by a smooth sense of volume, this work of bronze is titled “Works 0.10-21-01“ by the late artist Choi Man-Lin, and was completed in 2010. Evocative of human’s placenta, the artwork captures its theme “life,” while the sculpture’s swelling, contracting, and twisting features mimic a movement. Going with the flow of the work, viewers can feel the lively energy of the form, being so lively that they might even forget about the property of bronze, which is hard and static. That feel of kinetic energy created by expansion and contraction can evoke the cycle of life, where birth and death repeat. Perhaps, our ability to directly feel the force of life from an abstract work of art perhaps is due to the artist’s creative intention to create a particular meaning.

stories.title: Community - Artist Lee Ung-Bai
stories.script: This artwork looks like someone drew a 3D line using a thick color pen. It is by the artist Lee Ung-Bai, who called it “Community” in 2010. The 3D “scribble” is made of round metal duct pipes, which were welded together. With this organic form that is comprised multiple units, the artist found and captured the concept of “community” and “communication.” Due to its bright colors, freely formed curves and a soft sense of volume, this work can stimulate viewers’ senses in appealing ways to make them think it is a toy. Naturally, the sculpture cannot be simply visually enjoyed but rather actively experienced. As the artist intended, you can touch it, tap it, or sit down on it. As a result, viewers who directly experience the sculpture in person and communicate with the artwork can think about “community.”

stories.title: Dwelling - Artist Yi Gee-Chil
stories.script: Doesn’t this sculpture remind us of an architectural work? This artwork, titled “Dwelling,” made by welding steel plates, was created by the artist Yi Gee-Chil in 2013. It compressively represents basic components of a building, such as floors, ceilings, walls, windows and doors. The outer surface of the steel plate was left to naturally rust in the open and be altered as viewers were allowed to touch. The windows and doors on the four sides indicate outward directions, through which viewers can look out onto the outside world, so that viewers being on the inside can be connected to the outside. The artist wished our attitude and ways of life could be determined by the sculpture, an artwork that is fused with life. In other words, “Dwelling” can be the artist’s studio and dwelling.
