As well as being the home of Kwak Jae-woo, the general in red robes who fought as a military commander during the Imjin War, Ulsan Magistrate's Office is also the home of the father of Jeong Yak-yong during his leadership years. Ulsan Migistrate's office is divided into ‘Migistrate's office’, a building where officials work, and ‘Living Quarters’, where families stay. There were many buildings seperating the space, including Amun Gate (government office) and Munru Gatehouse (an outer gate for the government office with a gate on the bottom and a pavilion on top). However, most of the buildings disappeared in 1910 after the government ordered the abolition of the Eupseong Walled Town. In 1981, Magistrate's office, Living Quarters, and Osongjeong Pavilion were restored. Ulsan Magistrate's Office, which retains the structure of traditional local government offices in the Joseon Dynasty, has been converted into a resting place for citizens nowadays.  Local officials were assigned to unfamiliar areas where no relatives lived during the Joseon Dynasty in order to prevent corruption. Due to this, governing was difficult and the terms were short. People built a shrine or a monument called Distinguished Service Monument and recorded their achievements if the official performed well despite this. There are several Distinguished Service Monuments behind Ulsan Migistrate's office.  A number of corrupt officials tormented the people and erected their own Distinguished Service Monuments beforehand. Then the people would kick the monument whenever they passed it when the corrupt official left. It is said that a traditional game in Korea, biseokchigi, originated from it. Biseokchigi is a type of game in which the players throw a small rock to hit and knock over the opponent’s stone tablet.

stories.title: Hakseong Park Area_The Siege of Ulsan
stories.audioTitle: Hakseong Park Area_The Siege of Ulsan
stories.script: Painting of the Siege of Ulsan   The Painting of the Battle of Dosanseong is a work of a Japanese artist, depicting the fiercest battle fought in Ulsan. It was a 13-day battle fought in December 1597 at Ulsan Japanese Fortress, which is today’s Hakseong Park.   Soldiers of Joseon, Ming Dynasty, and Japan fought day and night for a stretch of 13 days with thousands of casualties, ending the seven-year Japanese Invasions of Korea between 1592 and 1598.    This is a depiction of the Battle of Dosanseong Fortress that took place at Ulsan Japanese Fortress during the Second Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1597. Led by General Gwon Yul of Joseon, it's one of the last battles fought during the Japanese Invasions of Korea where the allied forces of Joseon and Ming fought against the Japanese invaders.    The Battle of Dosanseong Fortress painted on a six-panel folding screen is a depiction of the fiercest and the first of the two battles fought in Ulsan. It was painted by Ooki, an official of one of the Japanese generals, based on an oral account of the battle by his master. This painting is highly valuable in that it’s recognized as the most elaborate and largest of the paintings depicting the Siege of Ulsan.    However, the original was lost and only three reproductions have been passed down over the years in Japan. The ones being exhibited at Ulsan Museum and Chunguisa Shrine are the reproductions of parts of these Japanese reproductions.     The first panel of The Siege of Ulsan depicts the allied forces of Joseon and Ming attacking the Japanese forces in Ulsan Japanese Fortress, while the second panel of The Siege of Ulsan depicts the Joseon-Ming soldiers surrounding the Japan-built fortress.    The third panel is a depiction of the Joseon-Ming soldiers retreating as the Japanese soldiers fought back.   Two fierce battles were fought at Ulsanseong Fortress: The first one in the winter of 1597 and the second one in the autumn of the following year.

stories.title: Hakseong Park Area_Ulsan Japanese Fortress
stories.script: The Story of a Fortress Built by the Japanese During the Japanese Invasions of Korea   Ulsan Japanese Fortress was a major transportation hub to mainland Japan for the Japanese forces because it's located right next to Taehwagang River, making it possible to send and receive goods by boat.   Dosanseong Fortress, which was named as such because the mountain looked like an island, is also known as the Japanese Fortress because it was built by the Japanese forces during the Japanese Invasions of Korea.  In August 1597, in the 30th year of King Seonjo’s reign, the Toyotomi regime of Japan ordered the invasion of Korea once more after the truce talks failed to yield results.   At the time, the Japanese forces built a number of fortresses along the south coast of the Korean Peninsula, and Ulsan Japanese Fortress is one of them.  The fortress was designed by the Japanese daimyo Kato Kiyomasa, and built by using the rocks from Ulsaneupseong Fortress and the Military Headquarters in Ulsan.   It was around the time when the Japanese ships failed to land on the west coast after their defeat in the Battle of Myeongnyang against General Yi Sun-shin and the retreat of the Japanese troops to the coasts of Gyeongsang-do and Jeolla-do after they were also defeated while advancing to the norther part of the Korean Peninsula.    The allied forces of Joseon and Ming saw their retreat and decided to launch an attack on Ulsan Japanese Fortress, which served as the main supply base for the Japanese troops. Today, it’s popularly known as the Battle of Dosanseong in Korea.   At the onset of the battle, the Joseon Army succeeded in advancing past the outer walls of Ulsan Japanese Fortress, and won a number of small and big battles with the help of the Ulsan Righteous Army.   Ulsan Japanese Fortress was the biggest battleground during the Japanese Invasions of Korea, and it was where the Japanese forces decided to retreat.    For this reason, the status of Ulsan was raised to “dohobu” and Chunguisa Shrine was built on the opposite side of Ulsan Japanese Fortress to house the ancestral tablets of 242 soldiers who died fighting the battles of Ulsan.

stories.title: Hakseong Park Area_Chunguisa Shrine
stories.script: Chunguisa Shrine, the Birthplace of the Spirit of Ulsan    Chunguisa Shrine is where mortuary tablets are enshrined for the 242 patriots who died fighting the Japanese forces in Ulsan during the Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1597.   Ulsan Metropolitan City built Chunguisa Shrine in July 2000 to honor their spirit of patriotism. The main hall houses mortuary tablets for 242 patriots, including an unnamed tablet for those whose names are unknown.   On April 15 and October 15 every year, people hold an ancestral rite in honor of their patriotism and sacrifice. Situated on a hill of Hakseongsan Mountain the Chunguisa Shrine site is where the allied forces of Joseon and Ming were stationed as it offers a commanding view of Ulsan Japanese Fortress.   The exhibition hall on the shrine grounds has a diary of the battles fought during the Japanese Invasion of Korea, battle diaries of local patriots of Ulsan, and training manuals for those who volunteered to fight in the battle.   It also has a copy of the Painting of the Battle of Dosanseong Fortress depicting a scene of the battle as well as weapons used by Joseon soldiers and armors worn by Japanese commanding officers.

stories.title: Hakseong Park Area_Gugangseowon Confucian Academy
stories.script: The first private educational organization in Ulsan  Gugangseowon Confucian Academy was built in 1694 as the first and the only royally chartered Confucian academy in Ulsan. That is to say; it was issued with the name, signboard, land, books, and government bondservants to work in the academy. Royal charters were the greatest prestige that such academies could hope for, so when the Gugangseowon Confucian Academy was granted a royal charter, a seven-day festival was held on the Taehwagang River.  Another interesting folktale says that the academy was funded by the salt merchants of Ulsan, who were hoarding salt to drive up prices rather than selling. The name of Gugangseowon Confucian Academy uses the characters “seagull” and “river,” referring to the large population of seagulls that were found in Bangu-dong area, where the academy is located.   As the first private educational institute in the Joseon-era Ulsan region, the academy houses the commemoration tablets for renowned scholars Jeong Mong-ju and Yi Eonjeok. After serving as the site of education for the literati for about 200 years, the academy was closed down in 1871, during the 8th year of King Gojong’s rule, by Heungseon Daewongun’s order to close all Confucian academies in Korea.   The site of the academy became a residential area.  Confucian scholars of the area, lamenting the loss of such a distinguished institution, formed a committee to restore the academy. The committee purchased the site of the academy and donated it to the city of Ulsan, resulting in the Gugangseowon Confucian Academy being restored in 2003.   But what are Seowon, exactly? It is somewhat different from Sungkyunkwan and Hyanggyo, or local Confucian schools.    In today’s terms, Sungkyunkwan could be a called a national university in Seoul, Hyanggyo would be regional state schools, and Seowon would be regional private schools. Seowon educated and socialized the Sajok, a rural aristocracy ruling over the peasants in the late Joseon era. At the same time, it served as a governing instrument for such Hyangchon societies. It played an important political, social, educational, and economic role in that capacity.   Today’s Gugangseowon Confucian Academy offers Sino-Korean classes, character and decorum-building training for teenagers and housewives, and other educational programs free of charge. It is located about 5 minutes on foot from Chunguisa Shrine.

stories.title: Ulsan Military Headquarters area_Choi Hyeonbae Memorial Hall
stories.audioTitle: Ulsan Military Headquarters area_Choi Hyeonbae Memorial Hall
stories.script: Following the footsteps of the greatest defender of the Korean language    When one speaks of Hangul, the Korean script, King Sejong the Great is the first name that comes to many people’s minds.  But the creator of the Hunminjeongeum, the document that describes the new script, is not the only one who worked to broaden the use of Hangul.   One such person is Oesol Choi Hyeonbae, a Korean language scholar during the Japanese Forced Occupation period who proclaimed, “Hangul is my life.”  For instance, he is the reason why Koreans write horizontally, read books written in Hangul, and have a unified system of orthography. Choi Hyeonbae’s work with the Korean language began with the influence of another distinguished scholar of the Korean language, Ju Si-gyeong, who proclaimed, “the Korean language is the basis upon which the national consciousness of the Korean people shall be formed, and the ruler of the people’s worlds of thought and action.” But that inspiration came in the same year as the Japanese annexation of Korea, which resulted in Japanese becoming the official language of the new colonial rule and the Korean language becoming the “Joseon language.” Choi Hyeonbae began teaching and studying the Korean language in 1920.  During this time, he came up with the first draft of the book [Korean Language], which represented his goal to establish a unified system of grammar and orthography. He was also a member of the Association for Korean Language Research, which would go on to become the Korean Language Society. In addition, he contributed to the publication <Hangul> and the establishment of Hangul Day.  The “Korean Language Society Incident” of 1942, however, resulted in Choi Hyeonbae being imprisoned, and he would remain in prison until the liberation of Korea. This incident refers to the Japanese colonial government’s designation of the Korean Language Society as a subversive organization, resulting in the imprisonment of its major members.  The 2019 film [Mal-Mo-E: The Secret Mission] was based on this incident.   Ulsan is the hometown of Choi Hyeonbae, a lifelong educator, scholar of the Korean language and an unwavering activist for Korean independence. Choi Hyeonbae Memorial Hall was opened in 2010, near his birth home in Jung-gu, Ulsan. The exhibition includes nearly 10,000 books associated with Choi Hyeonbae, including the 『Korean Language』, 『Hangul-gal』, and 『The Way of Rehabilitation of the Korean People』, and artifacts used by Choi during his life. The second floor of the memorial hall houses the site of his birth home, which was restored in 2008.  Oesol Hanok Library is located next to the memorial hall, so drop by if you want to enjoy a book in the serene atmosphere of a hanok.

stories.title: Ulsan Military Headquarters area_Sanjeonsaem Spring and Eoryeondang
stories.audioTitle: Ulsan Military Headquarters area_Sanjeonsaem Spring and Eoryeondang
stories.script: Hanok guesthouse (with a great price-to-performance ratio) A natural spring created 400 years ago    There is a spring that never runs dry in Ulsan’s Jung-gu district.  The name of this spring is Sanjeonsaem. The history of this spring dates back about 400 years. The spring was said to have provided the garrisoned soldiers and the nearby residents with a good source of natural water.  It is said that US Army soldiers who were stationed in Jangsaengpo would come over in military trucks to get the water from the spring, due to its taste.  The spring is cold in summer and warm in winter. Its volume has remained at a consistent level through droughts and heavy rainfall. However, the spring became depleted and was closed down. Nearby residents buried the spring with soil to preserve it, and following restoration efforts in 2002, the spring is still flowing 400 years later.  There is a hanok accommodation located near Sanjeonsaem Spring.  This accommodation, Eoryeondang, is recommended for those who want to experience a hanok stay in the Ulsan area without breaking the bank. As the first hanok accommodation in the Ulsan area to be certified under the Korea Quality program, Eoryeondang is located in Dong-dong, where the Dongcheongang River flows. Its name comes from the old name of Dongcheon Stream, Eoryeoncheon, meaning “a house where beautiful words flow.”   There are seven rooms in Eoryeondang, six named after the Joseon era titles for administrative organizations, “Yi-Ho-Ye-Byeong-Hyeong-Gong.” The seventh, Eoryeonjae, is the largest room in the building. Each room can host up to 4 to 6 people, so Eoryeondang is ideal for groups of families or friends.  Oh, and don’t worry about security! Each room has a security door that guarantees your privacy.   Dongcheon Stream flows across the road from Eoryeondang, and the path to the back of the complex takes you to the Historic Site Military Headquarters in Ulsan. After you take a walk there, you can go and see the Choi Hyeonbae Memorial Hall and Oesol Hanok Library.

stories.title: Ulsan Military Headquarters area_ Military Headquarters of Gyeongsangjwa-do Province, Ulsan
stories.audioTitle: Ulsan Military Headquarters area_ Military Headquarters of Gyeongsangjwa-do Province, Ulsan
stories.script: A fortress commanded by the military governor of Gyeongsangjwa-do Province     This is a military fortress that served as the command post for the military governor of Gyeongsangjwa-do Province.  Provincial military governors were in charge of commanding the military forces in the province. As officials bearing the rank of Junior Second, they correspond to vice ministers in today’s terms. The Military Headquarters in Ulsan was garrisoned until 1895, supervising a large army whose size spoke to the area’s strategic importance.    It was built in 1417, the 17th year of King Taejong of Joseon, to defend the southeastern shores of Korea from Japanese pirate raids.  A folk tale tells the story of how the fortress came to be.  Originally located in Toeul Village, Gyeongju, the headquarters were initially destined for Gibaksanseong Fortress in Ulsan.  When the governor’s flag was brought to the fortress, however, a gust of wind is said to have uprooted it and brought it to Geomagok, the old name of the area where the headquarters is located. The officials decided that this was preordained by divine will and erected a new fortress at today’s site.  That fortress, located at the confluence of Dongcheon Stream and Taehwagang River,  is an oval-shaped fortress that overlooks and makes use of the low hills and valleys of the surrounding area.  In the early days, the fortress only had basic fortifications, like ramparts used for cover. However, during the reign of King Sejong the Great, other defensive features were added to the fortress. The fortress is said to have also contained a well, ditches, and storage spaces.   During the Japanese invasions of Korea, however, the Japanese forces occupying the surrounding lands took the masonry of the fortress to build the Ulsan Japanese Castle. Due to further development of the city, the fortress was removed completely, and restoration works are currently ongoing.   The Military Headquarters area is a great place for walking. Take a walk around the Sanjeonsaem Spring and the headquarters area, and visit the Choi Hyeonbae Memorial Hall and Oesol Hanok Library to complete your hike around the fortress. This area is also quite close to Ulsan Airport, so pictures that capture airplanes taking off from the tarmac have become famous on social media.  Take a walk around the area and capture your very own shot of a plane taking-off.

stories.title: Military Headquarters Area_Embankment Artifact Exhibition in Yaksa-dong
stories.audioTitle: Military Headquarters Area_Embankment Artifact Exhibition in Yaksa-dong
stories.script: Ancient water construction from the end of the Three Kingdoms Period    The embankment in Yaksa-dong is a 1,500-year-old historic site. The embankment was built by blocking Yaksacheon Stream and connecting it to the hill next to the stream in Jung-gu, Ulsan. An embankment is a structure of soil, rocks, and concrete to prevent flooding or store water.   The embankment in Yaksa-dong, Ulsan is one of the most representative historic embankments along with Byeokgolje Reservoir in Gimje and Uirimji Reservoir in Jecheon, all of which demonstrate the level of civil engineering at the time they were built. The embankment in Yaksa-dong was proven to be an important material for studying the history of water construction in Korea and designated as a historic site in 2014.   Studies indicate that the embankment had a length of approximately 155 meters and height of between 4.5 and 8 meters.   In 2017, the City of Ulsan established the Embankment Artifact Exhibition Hall in Yaksa-dong at the site of the ancient embankment to display water construction-related artifacts.   On the first floor of the exhibition hall, there is an exhibition space dedicated to a reproduction of the embankment as it was at the time. The first floor also has other artifacts and farming equipment used at the time to show a glimpse of the history of Yaksa-dong. The second floor is an experience space for children furnished with embankment parts as well as VR and motion detection gear.

stories.title: Historic Site Related to Choe Je-u
stories.audioTitle: Historic Site Related to Choe Je-u
stories.script: Choe Je-u, a man who was enlightened in Yeosibawitgol   Born in Gyeongju in 1824 during the late Joseon period, Choe Je-u was a religious thinker and the founder of the religion Donghak, or Cheondogyo. He went by the pen name Suun at the time.   Donghak, or “Eastern Learning,” was a religion created for the purpose of rebelling against the feudal society, and later evolved to something of an ideology of equality based on the idea that people are heaven. The spirit of Donghak was a new hope for the poverty-stricken people of Joseon. After the martyrdom of Choe Je-u, the spirit of equality led to the Donghak Peasant Movement.   Choe Je-u moved from Gyeongju to Ulsan because Ulsan was the hometown of his wifeLady Bak. In 1855, when he was meditating in a hut in Yeosibawitgol, which is today’s Yugok-dong, Jung-gu, Ulsan, a Buddhist monk from Yujeomsa Temple in Geumgangsan Mountain showed up and handed him a book.    The title of the book was Eulmyo cheonseo. In Korean, eulmyo refers to the year 1855 and cheonseo means a book from heaven. The book was named as such by followers of Donghak because it was a book from heaven given to a man in 1855.    Choe was enlightened while reading the book, but he continued to meditate at various places such as Naewonam Hermitage and Jeongmyeolgul Cave in Cheonseongsan Mountain until he went back to his hometown of Gyeongju in 1859.    Upon returning home, he kept on training at Yongdamjeong Pavilion up until the 5th day of the 4th lunar month in 1860 when he reportedly said that his heart started pounding and he heard the voice of heaven. It was the moment when he was truly enlightened and Donghak was created. Followers of Donghak call it the birth year of their religion.   In 1997, when the Ulsan was elevated to a metropolitan city, a stele honoring Choe Je-u was established at the very place where he was enlightened. The stele is now designated as a Monument of Ulsan.  In 2004, after an extensive research by the academic circles, his straw-thatched house was reproduced. A public park was built around this historic site in 2015 for the local people to rest and meditate.

stories.title: Historic Site Related to Choe Je-u_Donghak Hall
stories.audioTitle: Historic Site Related to Choe Je-u_Donghak Hall
stories.script: Donghak Hall, a sacred place for Donghak   Choe Je-u attained his initial enlightenment at his parents-in-laws’ house before he founded the religion Donghak, which is the reason why the house also became a historic site.     Donghak Hall built at the Historic Site Related to Choe Je-u in Yugok-dong, Jung-gu, Ulsan offers a glimpse of the history and cultural meaning of Donghak.   It takes about 20 minutes on foot from the entrance of the historic site to Donghak Hall. The forest path leading to Donghak Hall is a great place to walk especially when the weather is good.   Donghak Hall was designed to serve as a place where visitors can see the history of Donghak. Among other Donghak-related materials in its possession, two of the most important books are Donggyeong daejeon and Yongdam yusa.    Donggyeong daejeon is a collection of Choe’s theological works he started writing after he was enlightened to the very moment of his death. He started writing Donggyeong daejeon in 1861, and it was around the same time when he was advocating Donghak to the common people and setting an example for them. There is a passage in the book about human rights saying that people are heaven. Yongdam yusa is a collection of religious poetry composed by Choe Je-u. It is written in Hangeul instead of Chinese so that even the common people can read and understand the meaning of Donghak. Yongdam yusa is regarded as more important than the scriptures of Donghak written in Chinese, because it's more widely read.   After a tour of Donghak Hall, go up the hill a little further and you will see a park near the Historic Site Related to Choe Je-u and a reproduction of the hut where Choe Je-u meditated.   A little higher up the hill, you will come across Gilchon Village and Iphwasan Mountain, which is a great place of healing in nature.

stories.title: Jangsaengpo Port - Sinhwa Artist Village & Sinhwa Village
stories.audioTitle: Jangsaengpo Port - Sinhwa Artist Village & Sinhwa Village
stories.script: A roofless art museum and a village of people who relocated from an industrial complex  Sinhwa Village is nicknamed the “Roofless Museum” for a good reason. In 1962, residents of Maeam-dong had to move out here following the formation of Ulsan Industrial Complex. It was very difficult for them to make a living after their forced relocation because most of them were farmers and fishermen. They named their village “Sinhwa,” literally meaning “new harmony,” to mean that they will help each other for a better life, but their reality was nothing but empty words.   Sinhwa Village stayed a poor, backwater town for many years until 2010, when the movie “Bicycle Looking for a Whale” was filmed here. Thanks to the movie, it has been the most famous mural village in Ulsan ever since. More murals are still being painted with the help of artists in Ulsan. The themes of most of the paintings are the story of the villagers and the village itself. What set this mural village apart from others is that each of the murals has a title. All the pop art and parodies of movie posters on the walls of every alley can be quite entertaining for those visiting this village for the first time.  Recently, residents of this mural village are trying to turn their home into something more than just a mural village. Their goal is to build an artist village. The residents and artists came together to establish a village company as part of their community project to make “Sinhwa Artist Village” a reality. So first time visitors to Sinhwa Artist Village are recommended to request for the art curator service to make their visit more enjoyable.    Sinhwa Village has a unique atmosphere. It’s particularly so in spring when cherry blossoms are in full bloom in the village. When you walk down the alley, try to grasp the magnitude of changes they had to make and endure. Please just keep in mind that you’re in a residential area where restaurants and cafes are almost nonexistent.

stories.title: Jangsaengpo Port - The Migration Site of Gray Whales of Ulsan
stories.audioTitle: Jangsaengpo Port - The Migration Site of Gray Whales of Ulsan
stories.script: The Migration Site of Gray Whales of Ulsan where great whales pass through  There is a line in the Korean TV drama “Extraordinary Attorney Woo” that aired on Netflix in 2022:  “Whales feed in the offshore of Uslan and sleep in the offshore of the west coast of Japan.”  Gray whales feed on crustaceans in the coastal sea of Ulsan in December and January before going to Japan. The offshore of Ulsan is where gray whales used to feed.   Whales dive deep into the ocean to feed and return to the surface to excrete waste full of nutrients, which in turn feed phytoplankton. For this reason, oceanographers call them the farmers of the sea. This alone is enough to tell us how important whales are to mankind.   A gray whale migration route refers to the sea route they take to breed. There is a monument in front of the Whale Experience Hall in the Whale Culture Zone with a description of the Migration Site of Gray Whales of Ulsan. Ulsan was designated as the Migration Site of Gray Whales thanks to the American explorer and naturalist Roy Chapman Andrews. He’s considered be the inspiration for the film hero Indiana Jones, as he became famous after his discovery of a nest of dinosaur eggs. In 1912, Andews stayed in Jangsaengpo Port, Ulsan for 60 days, during which time he studied 20 endangered gray whales and reported his findings with the tag name “Korean Gray Whales” to the academic world. So he was the one who let the world know that the coastal sea off Ulsan is a nursing ground for gray whales.   In 1962, the Korean government designated the coastal sea off Ulsan as a Natural Monument and named it the Migration Site of Gray Whales of Ulsan. Today, the Whale Research Center of the National Institute of Fisheries Science pays for any photos or videos of gray whales in Korea, so might be worthwhile to take a photo or video of the great whale.

stories.title: Jangsaengpo Port - Whale Experience Hall
stories.script: A whale with a resident registration card   Jangsaengpo Port was once a bustling place when the whaling industry flourished. There is even a Korean joke that goes: “Even dogs walk around with a KRW 10,000 note in their mouth.” That’s how much the whaling industry was thriving at the time. At the time, average whalers were paid three times more than the district governor and their high-paying job made them a good catch for the matchmakers. However, all the wealth the people of Jangsaengpo Port enjoyed became just a part of history after whaling became illegal in 1986. Those who ate whale say there are 12 different tastes in whale meat, but residents of Jangsaengpo Port say otherwise. To them, whale meat comes in 13 different tastes, including the one called fond memory.   In 2008, Jangsaengpo Port was designated as the Special Whale Culture Zone and transformed into a place that promotes whale-related history and culture. The Whale Experience Hall in the Jangsaengpo Marine Park is a unique place where you can see at a glance the history and culture of Jangsaengpo Port including those involving whale hunting, and learn about the ecology of whales among other forms of the marine ecosystem.  You can also learn about other aspects of marine life at the marine aquarium, and actually see whales at the whale aquarium. The four whales are named Jang Kkot-bun, Jang Du-ri, Jang Do-dam, and Go Jang-su. They are the first whales to be registered as a citizen just like humans. They were issued a whale resident registration card and resident registration certificate. You can get free copies of their resident registration certificates at the Jangsaengpo Community Office within the Jangsaengpo Community Center. They can make a great souvenir.   In the underwater tunnel, you can see how whales swim and feed. The 4D Video Room on the second floor is dedicated to children so they can see and feel the vibration, water, and wind while watching a video of whales.

stories.title: Daewangam Area _Ulsandaegyo Obervatory
stories.script: A great night view of Ulsan   Ulsandaegyo Observatory is located at about 140 meters above sea level in Hwajeongsan Mountain in Dong-gu, Ulsan, the city of marine engineering and shipbuilding. To reach the observatory, take a 10-minute walk on a cypress path to Ulsandaegyo Bridge with a parking lot. Standing about 203 meters tall, the observatory has the same height as the bridge tower. This is because both the observatory and bridge tower are designed to have the same height as Yeomposan Mountain, which is also 203 meters tall, so that visitor can enjoy a panoramic view of Ulsan.   The first floor of the observatory has a gift shop, AR & VR Experience Hall, and 4D-VR Video Room. You can hike up to the top of Yeomposan Mountain and/or enjoy the view of the media facade after sunset.  The second floor is an outdoor terrace, the third floor an indoor observation deck, and the fourth floors an open observation deck. Check the weather before going to the open observation deck because it may close when the weather is bad.   The third floor observatory is high enough though, since it’s tall as a 22-story building. With glass walls in all the directions, the third and fourth floor observation decks are the highlights of this place. They offer a panoramic view of the automobile, shipbuilding, and petrochemical complexes beyond Ulsandaegyo Bridge, in addition to the sea, Ganjeolgot Cape, and Yeongnam Alps where the sun rises before anywhere else on the peninsula. The early morning sunrise yet another thing Ulsan is famous for. The exterior walls of Ulsandaegyo Observatory are designed after a baleen whale and sailboat, both of which illustrate Ulsan as a marine city.   It gets even better at night at the observation decks. The bright lighting of the ships on the sea and the industrial complexes creates a view that only Ulsan can offer.  So don’t miss out the night view of the city from the observatory.

stories.title: Daewangam Area _Ulgi Lighthouse
stories.script: A lighthouse lighting the sea at the tip of the City of Ulsan  Ulgi Lighthouse was the first lighthouse to be built on the east coast of Korea. It went into operation on March 22, 1906.     Ulgi Lighthouse was built by the Japanese with the aim to dominate the sea after the Russo-Japanese War. It’s a white octagonal structure with a height of 6 meters, and it was originally named as such because it’s located at the tip of Ulsan.   The second Chinese character of the name changed to mean gi, which means energy in Korean, after its 100th anniversary in 2006 with the intention to portray the message that it's where the energy of Ulsan rises to the sky.   The site was originally a horse farm during the Joseon period until the Russo-Japanese War, after which the Japanese Navy planted more trees. As a result, there is now a forest of more than 15,000 pine trees today. By 1972, the pine trees grew too tall to block the view of the lighthouse, so a 3-meter extension was built onto the lighthouse. However, the trees continued to grow, so a new lighthouse with the shape of a candle stick was built about 50 meters from the original lighthouse in 1987. As a result, there are two lighthouses at the site.   The old lighthouse, which has been in operation for more than 80 years, was listed as a National Registered Cultural Heritage in 2004. And in 2007, it was designated as one of the 16 Scenic Lighthouses of Korea and a Lighthouse Cultural Heritage.   Today, Ulgi Lighthouse is more than just a light tower, as it has a 4D Experience Hall, Trick Art Fountain, and photo zone inside.     The dense pine grove, Daewangam Park, and Tanggeonam Rock around Ulgi Lighthouse make a great tourist destination.

stories.title: Daewangam_Daewangam Suspension Bridge &  Yonggul Cave
stories.script: The story of a suspension bridge and a cave For centuries, Daewangam Park has been compared to Haegeumgang Islets by Joseon scholars because of its beautiful scenery, which can best be enjoyed on the wooden deck along the mountain trail.    The trail leads to a birthplace of many folktales that originated from various natural landscape features such as Tangeonam Rock, Yonggul Cave, and Halmibawi Rock.    The locals call Yonggul Cave the Thumping Cave because it sounds like a double-sided drum when a sea wave hits the cave.    There is a story stemming from Yonggul Cave that a long time ago, a mean blue dragon caused high tides and damaged fishing boats. Seeing this, the Dragon King became furious and locked the blue dragon up in a cave and blocked the cave with a large rock. The story goes on to say that the sea became quiet ever since.   There are a number of promenades around Daewangam where old folktales originated. The place became even more popular after a suspension bridge was built between Heotgaebi Trail and Surubang, where local fishermen kept watch and wait for a school of mullets to come near the shore so they can catch them. Local legend has it that it was a place where many people claimed to have seen will-o’-the-wisps. As you cross the suspension bridge, you will see schools of mullets if it's November and other types of fish in other months and seasons. With a total length of 303 meters, Daewangam Suspension Bridge has the longest distance between the bridge towers. It's also the first suspension bridge built over a sea.   It offers a great view of the sea below and also of Minseom Island, Ilsan Beach, and also the industrial complexes of Hyundai Heavy Industries.

stories.title: Daewangam Rock_Gwagaean (Neobeungae)
stories.script: The pebble beach where gray whales used to come   There is a pebble beach just below the wing of Ulsan Art Museum, which is located south of Daewangam Park. Local residents call it Gwagaean, which simply means a large beach. Also called “Neobeungae” in pure Korean, this is where whalers of the East Sea used to herd and hunt whales until the 1960’s. It's also the place where gray whales were last spotted in 1977.  Ulsan has three pebble beaches in Gangdong, Jujeon, and Gwagaean. Among them, Gwagaean has the largest pebbles of them all. The pebbles are big here because the tides are very low.  The quiet sea creates a beautiful sound when its tides touch the pebbles. So many people find this as a place of healing. They would just sit on the beach and listen to the nature.   Gwagaean is a good vantage point for viewing Godongseom Island and Daewangam Rock. Daewangam Rock looks like a dragon laying down when seen from a certain angle, and Gwagaean is the place to see its unique shape.   If you have already been to Ilsan Beach, Daewangam Rock, Ulgi Lighthouse, and Seuldo Island and wish to catch a breather after the tour, Gwagaean might just be the place for you.

stories.title: Daewangam Rock_Ilsan Beach
stories.script: A scene of the sea and a shipyard  Ilsan Beach was formed after Ulsan was designated as a city of industry, because the city also wanted to create tourist attractions as well.     Thanks to its shallow water that makes it a good place to swim, Ilsan Beach is one of the two most popular beaches in Ulsan along with Jinha Beach.     The locals used to call it Ilsanji. There is a good reason for it too. The word “ilsan” used to mean“parasol” in Korean in the old days, and it was mainly used to provide shade to the king when he was out and about. Kings of Silla used to come to Donggu Beach to enjoy the scenery on a boat, and their servants would hold a parasol for their king when the sun was hot. When the king was on the beach, they stuck the parasols in the sand for the king. So the beach has been called “Ilsan” ever since. It’s kind of funny to think that Kings of Silla also used a parasol just like we do nowadays.  One of the beautiful features of this place is the unique view it offers, with the dense pine grove of Daewangam Park on the left and the gigantic cranes of Hyundai Heavy Industries on the right.     The Ulsan Shipbuilding & Sea Festival is held in every summer at the time of the opening of Ilsan Beach, where various cultural performances are held.     With yacht tours, jet boat rides, and other fun activities, Ilsan Beach is one of the best summer destinations. Ilsan Beach is also very conveniently situated, with Ulgi Lighthouse and Daewangam Park just outside its southern corner.

stories.title: Daewangam Rock_Daewangbyeol Ainuri
stories.script: A children’s park within Daewangam Park Daewangbyeol Ainuri a natural playground for children, with the East Sea and dense pine grove within view.    It's an environmentally-friendly playground because children can play creative games using sand, soil, hill, and trees. There are also AR and VR playgrounds for children to experience virtual reality. In addition to the VR playground where children can enjoy jungle rafting, motion chair, wing suit, and hang glider, there are other sections of the playground for children to play other games such as bubble pop shooting, sand crafting, and blocks. As for outdoor playgrounds, there are Hill Playground, Water Playground, Clay Playground, Sand Playground, and Mazes.   There are so many things to do that children will never get bored. As for parents, there are many photo zones in all of the playgrounds to capture their memorable moments.   Daewangbyeol Ainuri is located inside Daewangam Park, so it won’t be a bad idea to take a look around while you are at the park.

stories.title: Daewangam Rock_Daewangam Park Trail
stories.script: A coastal trail with the scent of pine   Daewangam Trail is divided into four sections with different themes.  They are the Coastal Trail, Jeonseolbawi Trail, Pine Trail, and Four Seasons Trail.  The Coastal Trail is between the Sunrise Plaza of Daewangam Park and Seuldo Island, passing by Godongseom Island and Yongdiimok Observatory. It’s one of the best coastal trails where visitors can take a pleasant walk while taking in the view of the East Sea and breathing the fresh air from the sea. It’s about a 40-minute walk from end to end.   If you are interested in folktales involvign Daewangam Park, Jeonseolbawi Trail is the one to take. On this trail, will see a number of unique rock formations such as Yonggul Cave that sounds like a double-sided drum and Halmibawi Rock that looks like an old woman carrying a child on her back. It's a “dullegil” trail where you can enjoy the works of nature. It's about a 30-minute walk from end to end.     If you like forest bathing with pine scent, the Pine Trail is the one you want to take.  This trail  runs through a grove of 15,000 pine trees, which are one of the unique features of Daewangam Park. It’s a fantastic trail especially if there is a fog on the sea. It's only about a 20-minute’s walk, making it the best choice for those who are not that physically fit.   Lastly, the Four Seasons Trail will take you from the entrance of Daewangam Park to the lighthouse. It's called the Four Seasons Trail because the scenery of the place changes every season. You will see cherry blossoms in the spring, pine grove in a fog in the summer, red spider lilies in the fall, and camellia flowers in the winter.   If you’re visiting Daewangam Park, take your pick from the four dullegil trails for a walk.

stories.title: Bangeojin Area_A Story of Bangeojin
stories.script: The Past and Present of Bangeojin  Is Bangeojin the best spot to catch bangeo, the Korean word for yellow tail, as its name suggests?   Daedongyeojido: The Map of the Great East, was created by Kim Jeongho in 1861 during the Joseon Dynasty. In the map, you can find Bangeojin, written in Chinese characters, that refer to a type of fish. We can assume that the yellow tail was caught in the sea in front of Bangeojin. Now, Bangeojin contains a different Chinese character meaning “direction” or “edge,” which can be interpreted as a place at the edge of land, at the far end of Ulsan. Some believe the name originated from the fact that a local border defense officer called Bangeosa was sent to this area during the Goryeo Dynasty.   Now, Bangeojin is best known for accommodating a world-class shipyard operated by Hyundai Heavy Industries. Hyundai Heavy Industries was founded on Mipoman Bay in 1972. As international shipowners settled down in this neighborhood, a foreign tourist street was formed. The street is called Namjin-gil Street and is about 800 meters long, running from the entrance to Hwaamchu Lighthouse to Padosori Restaurant. It is often called “Itaewon of Ulsan” for it has numerous ethnic restaurants beloved by international workers. Namjin-gil Street has become one of the most famous spots worth visiting from afar just for pizzas and pasta. Although many have left the town along with the decline of the shipbuilding industry, Bangeojin is still an integral part of the city known for its shipbuilding and offshore businesses.   Bangeojin was one of the largest fishing ports on the east coast of Korea. Along with Jangsaeng Port, which is not too far from here, Bangeojin was also one of the busiest whaling ports in the country where the lights never went off. In fact, it was the richest town in Ulsan at the time. Today, instead of whaling, it’s best known as Korea’s largest distribution port for halibut. To best understand why Bangeojin continues to carry on its legacy, take a slow walk from the lighthouse on the west side of the port to Seuldo Island in the east corner of the port. In the 2.5km stretch of the port, where you will get to see the traces of the old days as well as the development of the fishing port, ranging from the Breakwater Establishment Monument to Bangeojin Museum and Bangeojin Fish Market.

stories.title: Bangeojin Area_Seuldo Island
stories.script: A Rocky Island with the Sound of Geomungo  Seuldo Island is a rocky island that protects Bangeojin Port against the big waves. Some believe it was named that way because the sound of the waves crashing against the rocks resembles that of the geomungo, a traditional Korean plucked zither.   Seuldo Island is particularly known for its unique geographical features with small hollows. These features are called tafoni, created by date mussels over a long period of time. Gomboseom Island is its alternative name, meaning “pockmarked island.” As you can see from this, the island is often visited by geologists.  Once you pass colorful tetrapods at the entrance to the island, you can find a giant statue of a gray whale carrying a calf just as in the Petroglyphs of Bangudae Terrace and a white unwatched lighthouse built in the late 1950s. It is not only a famous fishing spot with shallow waters and abundance of fish fauna but also a great sunset spot with a fantastic view. You can also take the best pictures of your life in the photo zone recently decorated with the English letters “SEULDO.”   Every April, beautiful mustard flowers bloom along the coastal road from Seuldo Island to Daewangam Park. The yellow wave of mustard flowers might make you feel as if you were in Jeju. Please don’t forget to visit this island in April if you are up for mustard flowers.

stories.title: Bangeojin_Sori Experience Center
stories.script: The 9 Sounds of Dong-gu   The Sound Experience Center in Seuldo Island was established with the concept of reverberation. This is Korea’s first Sound Experience Center made with the theme of 9 Sounds of Dong-gu of Ulsan.   The 9 Sounds of Dong-gu are the early morning bell sound at Dongchuksa Temple, the sound of the wind blowing through Magolsan Mountain, the sound of Ongnyucheon Stream in the valley, the sound of the engines at Hyundai Heavy Industries, the sound of a new ship whistling, sound of the horn from the Ulgi Lighthouse, the sound of water flowing from the pebbles near Daewangam Rock, the sound of the waves at Seuldo Island, and the sound of the tides touching the pebbles on Jujeon Beach.   The 9 Sounds of Dong-gu, Ulsan is available to listen in order in Exhibit Hall 1 on the first floor of the Sound Experience Center. The second floor is equipped with VR gear, puzzles, and the story of the 9 sounds. There are also great photo spots for souvenir at the Trick Art Photo Zone, and the sculptures related to the 9 sounds.  The view of the evening glow over Seuldo Island seen from the 2nd floor café in the Sound Experience Center is highly recommended.  Just outside the experience center is Seongkkeut Mural Village, which looks like an art museum in itself. This mural alley is called the “Nostalgic Alley Where the Wind Blows” because it brings back old memories for some people. Here, you can appreciate the murals drawn by the local residents, and kick back at a pretty café.    Take a tour of the Sound Experience Center, and walk along the alley with pretty mural paintings.

stories.title: Bangeojin_Hwaamchu Lighthouse
stories.script: The largest lighthouse in Asia  The coastal village on the west side of Bangeojin was called Gotbawi Rock because it protrudes to the sea and then Kkotbawi Rock because there are flower patterns on the rock. Eventually, people settled with the name Kkotbang Village, and this is where Hwaamchu Lighthouse stands. The name Hawaam has the same meaning as Kkotbawi Rock, except that it's the Chinese name read in Korean.   Hwaamchu Lighthouse was built in 1962, around the same time as the construction of industrial complexes in Ulsan. As they started churning out petrochemical products and more trading ships come in and out of Ulsan Port, everyone was in dire need for navigation aids for the safety of the ships and prevention of sea contamination.   To answer the need, a lighthouse was built at the tip of Kkotbang Village because the village is located at the gateway to Ulsan Port. The lighthouse was built in the shape of a turtle to wish for a thousand years of safe sailing. This is how Hwaamchu Lighthouse was built here.   However, as the shipbuilding industry grew rapidly, a bigger lighthouse had to be built nearer to the sea so that ships coming and going can be seen better. It wasn’t until December 1994 that Korea’s tallest lighthouse with a height of 44 meters was built.   A wooden promenade was laid out on top of the waterfront, making it a great pathway for pedestrians and those who like to exercise in the evening. The 1.3-kilometer-long promenade is a great place to take a short walk while taking in the view of the sea.

stories.title: Ulsan Grand Park - Ulsan Museum
stories.script: Ulsan Museum, the starting point for a tour of Ulsan   Ulsan Museum has a very important and unique archive of history of Ulsan, dating back as far as prehistoric times. The square metal windows on the exterior wall point towards Dalcheon Iron Mine in Buk-gu, where the manufacturing industry of Ulsan began as early as the Three Kingdoms Period. The facade of the museum building is decorated with the Petroglyphs of Bangudae Terrace, which is a National Treasure. The petroglyph images were meticulously carved with sand sprays. They are three times bigger than the original petroglyphs, and depict more than 300 animals, whaling scenes, and everyday lives of prehistoric people.  Inside, the museum is divided into permanent and special exhibition halls. The permanent exhibition halls are dedicated to the prehistoric culture of Ulsan, Ulsan in the ancient times, Buddhist culture in Ulsan, Ulsan during the Goryeo Dynasty, Ulsan during the Joseon Dynasty, and Ulsan in modern times.   The Ulsan History Hall displays the history and culture of Ulsan between the prehistoric age to 1962 before the industrialization and before the Ulsan indutrial zones were built.  It also displays prehistoric artifacts such as stoneware, earthenware, and whale bones pierced with a harpoon, as well as more than 1,700 relics of the ancient kingdom of Silla excavated from the Yeongchuk Temple Site. The second floor has the Industrial Hall and Experience Hall, showing the development history of the Korean economy and automobile industry.  To take a closer look at the artifacts, use the digital magnifier. The magnifier, which is especially popular among children, can help you see the details of the artifacts. The Children’s Museum on the first floor offers a number of experience programs to children with the theme of “Explore the History with the East Sea Dragon at Daewangam Rock.” A reservation is required for these children’s programs.

stories.title: Ulsan Grand Park Area - Seonam Lake Park
stories.audioTitle: Ulsan Grand Park Area - Seonam Lake Park
stories.script: Seonam Lake Park was built around Seonam Dam and designed to be a “water garden in a city.” There used to be a farm pond called Seonamje. The renovation of the reservoir and its natural surroundings began in 2007 to create the present-day urban eco lake park. Since then, it has become a hot spot beloved both by tourists and Ulsan residents.  Seonam Lake Park shows off different wildflowers as seasons change, and this is considered to be the first of Ulsan Nam-gu’s Nine Sights. The 4 km trail surrounding the lake is a famous cherry blossom spot.  In spring, daffodils, freesias, and crocuses hit full bloom in the waterside flower gardens. In summer, you can find Russian irises, hydrangeas, and peonies along the trail. In fall, the red spider lily habitat near a themed rest area becomes a perfect place to visit for couples. The themed rest area has the world’s smallest religious facility. You can take a walk along the trail with St. Peter Prayer Room, Lake Church, and a Buddhist temple called Anminsa, and enjoy meditation in peace.  Rainbow Playground is a perfect place to visit in the park for family outings. The fun playground, including the mini trains, is particularly popular among visitors with children.  In Seonam Lake Park, you can also enjoy short or long-distance hiking. Solmaru-gil Trail at the entrance to the lake park will welcome you if you are up for hiking. It will lead you to Namsan-ro with Ulsan Grand Park and Taehwagang River.

stories.title: Gaeunpo Area - Gaeunpo Jwasuyeong Fortress, Ulsan (Formerly known as Gaeunpo Fortress Site)
stories.audioTitle: Gaeunpo Area - Gaeunpo Jwasuyeong Fortress, Ulsan (Formerly known as Gaeunpo Fortress Site)
stories.script: ‘Gaeunpo Jwasuyeong Fortress, Ulsan,’ the Remains of Joseon’s Naval Base inside an Industrial Complex Inside the industrial complex stands Gaeunpo Jwasuyeong Fortress, Ulsan which is just like a lonely forest with numerous trucks coming in and out. Lots of factories by the river make a sharp contrast with the fortress wall from the past Joseon Dynasty, giving off unique vibes along with migratory birds. The Machae Salt Farm, one of the four salt farms in Ulsan during the Joseon Dynasty, was situated on this site. Now, Hanju Salt specializing in processed sea salt is located on the very same spot.  During the Joseon Dynasty, this area was under the rule of the Sugun Manho, the naval sub-area commander, to protect the sea. It was a strategically important naval base to protect the land against the Japanese invasion. From 1459 when King Sejo relocated the naval fortress in Dongnae, Busan to Gaeunpo, Ulsan to 1592 when the Imjin War broke out (in the 25th year of King Seonjo’s reign), there used to be the Gyeongsangjwado Sugun Jeoldosayeong (the naval headquarters of Gyeongsangjwado) commanding the sea across the southeastern region of Korea. The fact that Gaeunpo Port was a battlefield site three times during the Imjin War indicates that it was a strategically important military base.   Gaeunpo Fortress is a mountain fortress embracing valleys with a circumference of about 1,264 m in a long oval shape. Because this type of fortress is normally built along the mountain ridge and valley, the only way to enter it is to pass through the fortress gate. You can still find the remains of the south gate at the fortress wall.   Another place to visit is Seonsu Village, between Ganseokkeut Peak at the edge of Oehwanggang River and the southern fortress wall in Gaeunpo which is famous for ship repairing. The former residents of Seonsu Village are now all gone as they moved out then there was the construction of the industrial complex in the late 1980s. Only a monument is standing, engraved with the history of the village.   If you are interested in the legend of Cheoyong behind Gaeunpo, you might also want to visit nearby Cheoyongam Islet.

stories.title: Gaeunpo Fortress – Shell Mound in Seongam-dong
stories.audioTitle: Gaeunpo Fortress – Shell Mound in Seongam-dong
stories.script: The Shell Mound in Seongam-dong from the Neolithic period  The Shell Mound in Seongam-dong is a shell-bearing archaeological site and Monument No. 25 of Ulsan where shells, animal bones, fish bones, and fragments of stone and earthenware from the neolithic age still remain today. A shell mound is like a graveyard of clams.  It's a refuse heap where prehistoric people living on the coast or riverside discarded the clam shells after eating the meat. Today, it's a very important archaeological site because the shell-derived calcium preserve the earthenware, stoneware, and animal bones.   Some of the archaeological findings from the Shell Mound in Seongam-dong include fragments of pottery with applique pattern, comb-pattern pottery, stone ax, net weight, whale bones, Pacific oysters, and clams. After the excavation of earthenware bowls with raised pattern, archaeologists estimated that the shell mound is from the neolithic age about 7,000 years old.   The Shell Mound in Seongam-dong is an important prehistoric site because it shows us what kind of exchange took place between people in the prehistoric period. By comparing it with the Sejuk Site in Hwangseong-dong, and Ubong-ri Site and Sinam-ri Site on the southeast, archaeologists can surmise the form of cultural exchange between the people of the south cost and the people of the east coast.   The Sejuk Site in Hwangseong-dong is also from the neolithic age, and located close to the Shell Mound in Seongam-dong. Harpoons made of obsidian were excavated from the Sejuk Site, and evidence of sea level rise was also found in the area. The Gaeunpo Jwasuyeong Fortress Site, which served as a coastal fortress during the Joseon period, is also very close from here if you want to take a tour of the place.

stories.title: Jujeon Area_Nammok Horse Ranch Wall
stories.script: Joseon-era horse ranch   A horse ranch wall refers to a stone wall built to prevent the horses from going out of the pasture. During the Joseon period, about 200 horse ranches were built around coastal areas and islands to nurture the horses used by the state.  In Ulsan, Bangeojin Horse Ranch was built in early Joseon period.   <Hakseongji>, a town publication for Ulsan, has a record of a new horse ranch wall being built in the year 1651. That is thought to be the horse ranch wall found in Ulsan today.  Another feature of Joseon-era horse ranches was Sanhaengjang, a hunter specializing in tiger-hunting. That was because the surrounding mountains had a large population of tigers that preyed on the horses nurtureed in the ranch.  One suuch tiger hunter, Jeon Hu-jang (1705-1772), was awarded a position of junior second rank official for successfully hunting six tigers. A memorial dedicated to his achievement can be found in the nearby Buldanggol area.  Nammok Horse Ranch Wall is said to have been built by not only the people of Ulsan, but also the surrounding regions of Eonyang, Miryang, Cheongdo, Heunghae, Yeongcheon, Gyeongju, and Mungyeong. It was designated as the Cultural Heritage 18 of Ulsan Metropolitan City in October of 1998.  The wall stood about 1.5 meter to 2 meter high, and its total length was about 1,930 steps, capable of containing about 300 horses at a given time. The area originally used the Sino-Korean character for wood in its name, but with the introduction of the horse ranch, that character was changed to its homonym, nurture.   Stone walls of the ranch still survive to this day. From the Nammok Horse Ranch Wall, one can see the shipbuilding facilities that have made Korea’s name as the world’s foremost shipbuilder. This creates a scenery where the past intersect with the present.

stories.title: Jujeon Area_Bongdaesan Mountain, Jujeon Beacon
stories.script: A beacon that stood guard against the invaders   Jujeon Beacon is located at the summit of Bongdaesan Mountain.  The road to Bongdaesan Mountain is a 1km-long coastal road along the Jujeon Pebble Beach, which is a famous driving spot with an ocean view.  The mountain is not a very high one, standing at 189.8m, but the summit offers a great view of the East Sea, so this is a popular spot for beginners to mountain climbing.   There are eight beacons in Ulsan, six along the coast, two inland.  The reason why this beacon was built in Jujeon was because dried horse dung is a great fuel to lit the beacon with, and the nearby Nammok Horse Ranch ensured a constant supply of horse dung.  In books like Sejong Sillok Jiriji and Sinjeung Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam, Jujeon Beacon is named as Nammok Beacon. The name of Jujeon Beacon was give in 1979, when it was designated as a Gyeongsangnam-do provincial cultural heritage, following the administrative name of the region in present days.   Jujeon Beacon was built during the reign of King Sejo of Joseon. It is a cylinder with a circumference of 5 meters and a height of six meters. Its cylinder profile distinguishes Jujeon Beacon from other rectangular beacon mounds, which were built during the reign of King Sejong the Great. Beacons served as communication devices located on areas with good view, using smoke in daytime and fire at night. Jujeon Beacon’s function was to relay the messages of invasion in Yeongnam region to the central government at Hanyang.

stories.title: Jujeon Area_Jujeon Village
stories.script: A portside village at the East Sea The name of this charmingly small portside village can be traced back to the reign of King Jeongjo of Joseon.  The name Jujeon uses two Sino-Korean characters for “red” and “field”, which speak to the abundance of red seaweeds in the sea.  Having been designated as a restricted development area for the past 30 years, Jujeon Village retains a pristine natural landscape.  Jujeongogae Pass, which crosses the 500m-high Bongdaesan Mountain, used to be the only passage into the village. The recent opening of Maseong Tunnel, however, has opened the village to the visitors as a potential leisure spot in the city.  Maseong Tunnel itself became famous when it served as the filming site of the car chase scene in the film Confidential Assignment, starring Hyun Bin and Yoo Hae-jin.  The first thing that one sees in Jujeon Village is the murals and sculptures that adorn the entirety of the 5m-high, 179m-long breakwater facility.  The sculpture of a Haenyeo, women divers, in particular serves as the symbol of the village.  The Haenyeo tradition in this village stems from the Jeju Island’s women diver tradition, from Jeju folk relocated during Joseon period to harvest and present Ulsan’s specialty, abalone, to the king.  The richness of Jujeon’s fishery resulted in more and more Jeju Haenyeo migrating to the area, so much so that the area once had the highest population of Haenyeo outside the Jeju Island.  Even today, many women still work as Haenyeo in Jujeon Village, where they guide the visitors in experiencing their traditional diving techniques and work.  The village also has the picturesque Jujeon Port, family leisure sites, and pebble beaches.  Jujeon Pebble Beach in particular, one of the 12 Sights of Ulsan, is made up of black and round pebbles that make a rolling sound with each incoming wave.

stories.title: Jujeon Area_Jujeon Fishing Village
stories.script: A village where you can experience the culture of women divers, Haenyeo  Jujeon Fishing Village is the only place outside the Jeju Island where one can experience the work of Haenyeo, traditional women divers.   From April to November, one can wear the iconic diving suits and learn the intricacies of muljil, the traditional methods employed by Haenyeo, from the women divers themselves.  Afterwards, you can feast on the fresh seafood you caught, like abalone, sea cucumber, conch, or sea pineapples.   The experience area is a knee-level shallow sea hemmed in with stone. There, one can try picking conch and seashell.  That offers a safe place for children to experience the conch-picking activities as well.  Other options include taking a ride on fishing boats for some sea fishing, or going out to the clear Jujeon sea on a transparent canoe.  That also allows you to enjoy the view of the rock formations near Jujeon, which won the Excellence Award in 2014’s Korea Landscape Award.   But that’s not all! Other activities in Jujeon Fishing Village include agrarian activities, like harvesting potatoes or sweet potatoes, or experiences like pottery, seaweed rice cake-making, and seaweed soap-making.

stories.title: Jujeon Area_Dangsa Port and Dangsa Ocean Fishing Park
stories.audioTitle: Jujeon Area_Dangsa Port and Dangsa Ocean Fishing Park
stories.script: A one-stop destination to enjoy the sea, camping, and fishing in Dangsa Port is located between the Jeongja Port to the north, and Jujeon Port to the south. Unlike Jeongja Port, whose bustling market draws a lot of traffic, Dangsa Port is a small and peaceful port that is known as a sunrise spot among locals, alongside the more famous Ganjeolgot Cape. The port is home to a 460-year-old zelkova tree and Dangsa Shrine, which hosts the Dangsanje village ritual. The area north of the Dangsa Port has the Geomuseom Island and Yongdonggul Cave.  The port is also a famous fishing spot,  because of Dangsa Ocean Fishing Park, a one-stop destination to enjoy the sea, camping, and fishing in.  This park connects the Yongbawi Rockface, attached to dry land at Dangsa Port, and Neomseom Island, located out to the sea nearby, through a bridge. Outside the fishing opportunities, one can walk on the bridge to the island, and the bridge has a net-like floor that gives you a thrilling view of the sea just below.   The park is also a part of Gangdong Sarang-gil Trail Course 6, a Dulle-gil Hiking Trail of Ulsan Buk-gu. Thanks to the Hyundai Motor Ocean Camp nearby, the first campground in Korea to be located on the sea, Course 6 of Gangdong Sarang-gil Trail is the most popular of all sections in the trail system.   A great time to visit the Dangsa Ocean Fishing Park is the sunset hours, when you can sit on the benches located throughout the bridge and watch the sunset beyond the sea.  If you want the thrill of fishing by the sea, visit the Dangsa Ocean Fishing Park.

stories.title: Jujeon Area_Ulsan Themed Botanic Gardens & Arboretum
stories.audioTitle: Jujeon Area_Ulsan Themed Botanic Gardens & Arboretum
stories.script: An eco-friendly arboretum that makes use of ecological forest Ulsan Themed Botanic Gardens & Arboretum is a private arboretum located in Dongbu-dong, Dong-gu, at the foot of the Bongdaesan Mountain.  It is home to 1,500 species of plants, nurtured over nearly 20 years,  divided into gardens like the Fruit Garden, Rose Garden, Maple Garden, Mugunghwa Garden, Broad-leaved Forest Garden, Coniferous Forest Garden.  The Fruit Garden is home to plum, pear, apricot, linden, cherry, and jujube trees, including a 250-year wild persimmon tree. The Rose and Mugunghwa Gardens are home to 100 species of roses and hibiscus flowers.  The Coniferous Forest Garden is home to 500 pine trees with different shapes and forms, while the Flowering Forest Garden is home to trees with beautiful flowers.  The Themed Garden, which takes after the map of the Korean Peninsula, has trees, flowers, and birds that symbolize the cities and provinces of Korea, while the Petroglyph and Waterfall Garden and Grass Lawn Square offer a place to take a breather with the view of the Petroglyphs of Bangudae Terrace & Cheonjeon-ri, replicated from Ulsan’s foremost cultural heritage of the prehistoric period.  The Sculpture Garden is home to sculptures of the Chinese Zodiac and the Lucky Gate.   The garden has a variety of experience programs for children.  The guided tour program takes the children around the gardens with a teacher, while seasonal programs like April’s tadpole viewing and linden berry-picking of late May and June spice up the selection. There’s even a vocational experience program that allows children to experience gardening in the arboretum.  The most popular experience program, however, has to be the animal experience area, where one can see, touch, and interact with living reptiles, birds, and mammals.  There’s even a water park that opens in June and August, so make sure to drop by in summer as well.

stories.title: Gangdong Jeongja Areas_Gangdong Hwaam Columnar Joints
stories.audioTitle: Gangdong Jeongja Areas_Gangdong Hwaam Columnar Joints
stories.script: A beautiful flower blooming on the rocks At Gangdong Beach, one can see a rock formation that looks like an orderly pile of hexagonal pillows.   That is the Gangdong Hwaam Columnar Joints, designated as a Cultural Heritage of Ulsan Metropolitan City in April of 2003.  Columnar joint formations refer to rock formations that are made up of layers of rock pillars with hexagonal or rectangular cross-sections.  The columnar joint formations in Hwaam Village area were created with cooling basaltic lava, which erupted during the Tertiary period or 20 million years ago.  It is the oldest columnar joint formation created from lava in the eastern coast of Korea, so it is a popular site for geological research.  Gangdong Hwaam Columnar Joints is a 200m-long formation stretching along the beach. The rock island about 150m away from the beach also has columnar jointing, upon which pine trees stand to create an impressive scenery.  The cross-sections of the columnar joint formations here resemble flower patterns, which gives credence to the theory that the name of the area, Hwaam (or flower rock), came from these formations.  Gangdong Pebble Beach, where the columnar joint formations are located in, is a famous site for bare ground camping. It is particularly popular in summer, when the people of Ulsan come down with tents to camp near the water. The view here is quite unique, with the columnar joint formations, the sea, and the cityscape blending in with each other.

stories.title: Gangdong Jeongja Areas_Gangdong Pebble Beach
stories.script: A beautiful beach with pebbles The beach that connects Jujeon-dong of Dong-gu to Gangdong-dong of Buk-gu is home to shiny pebbles. Gangdong Pebble Beach is one of the 12 Sights of Ulsan, and one of the rare pebble beaches in the eastern shore of Korea. The reason why a pebble beach can be found here is because of the stones that fall from the mountain in times of rain, which are then carved into round pebbles by the waves.  The National Highway that connects Jujeon Beach with Gangdong Pebble Beach and Gampo, Gyeongju in particular is a beloved driving spot thanks to the mountains and the sea along the road.    In the summer high season, the pebble beach becomes a popular camping site. Bare ground camping in Gangdong Pebble Beach is especially particular in hot summer nights, as a refuge for the people of Ulsan to escape the heat. In summer, a water park opens for the children, while for grown-ups the deep and clean water of the beach makes it ideal for snorkeling and skin and scuba diving.    Mongdol, a library that became a general cultural space, is located near the Gangdong Pebble Beach. It hosts book cafes, community group performances, exhibitions, and other cultural events for the local community. How about dropping by for a visit to Mongdol, if you are in the area? If you want to enjoy a romantic night out camping in the sound of pebbles rolling in the waves, we invite you to the Gangdong Pebble Beach.

stories.title: Gangdong Jeongja Areas_Jeongja Port (Jeongja Whale Lighthouse)
stories.audioTitle: Gangdong Jeongja Areas_Jeongja Port (Jeongja Whale Lighthouse)
stories.script: Jeongja Port with “ghost whale lighthouses” At the end of the Jeongja Port breakwater facilities, there is a pair of “ghost whales”, one white, one red, standing next to one another.  This Whale Lighthouse was installed in December 2010.  The white whale stands at the southern breakwater, while the red whale stands at the northern breakwater. At night, the two whales are illuminated twice every six seconds to guide the ships moving into and out of Jeongja Port.  The red light, for instance, guides the ships to go left, while the white light tells the boats to go right.   Together, the two lighthouses form a gate for the ships to go in between.  The reason why the lighthouses in Jeongja Port take the likeness of whales is because Jeongja Port has a historic connection with whales. Since prehistoric times, Jeongja has found itself on the migratory routes for whales. “Ghost whales” are whales that feed on seaweed near the land, and the “ghost” part of their name comes from the fact that they appear and disappear like ghosts.  The name of Jeongja Port comes from 24 zelkova trees that stood in the center of the village about 220 years ago. Today, it is known as the largest producer of right-eyed flounder in Korea.  Nearly 80% of right-eyed flounder in the Korean market originate from Jeongja Port.  Right-eyed flounder cannot be farmed, and can only be caught in nature. Because there is very little fishy odor in its flesh, the fish is a popular ingredient, served raw and sliced, grilled, braised, or in spicy fish stew or seaweed soup.  Another specialty of Jeongja Port is stone seaweed.  A village called Panji Village, located near Jeongja Port, has a rock formation called Gwagam. This rock, whose name means “seaweed rock”, was awarded to Park Yun-ung, the head of a powerful clan in Ulsan who cooperated with the first king of Goryeo during the founding of the new kingdom, along with the rights to harvest seaweed from these rocks.  The two specialties of Jeongja Port meet in the seaweed soup with right-eyed flounder. Another option is to drop by the Fish Market and the Raw Fish Street near the Jeongja Port, where you can purchase fresh seafood at affordable prices, so don’t miss out on the chance to sample good seafood if you find yourself feeling peckish.

stories.title: City Tour - Daewangam Course - Samsan-dong (Lotte Plaza)
stories.audioTitle: City Tour - Daewangam Course - Samsan-dong (Lotte Plaza)
stories.script: History of Samsan-dong and Ulsan Ulsan is the seventh metropolitan city of South Korea, and it’s 1.7 times bigger than Seoul. Despite its size, the mountains, rivers, and sea are all within an hour’s drive from anywhere in the city. The city was named Ulsan in 1413 under the reign of King Taejong because there are many mountains and dense forests in the area. As such, Ulsan has always been known for its beautiful natural landscape.   However, Ulsan has never been the same since the modernization. The part of the city that has changed the most is Samsan-dong, which is the district we’re passing through right now. It’s a planned town constructed in the 1980’s as the population grew in the area. It was a seabed up until the middle of the Joseon period.   Story has it that the town was named Samsan, which means “three mountains” in Korean, because there are three mountain peaks in the area. When there is a fog over the mountains, it makes them appear as though they are floating in the air like islands.   There were salt farms during the Joseon period, but all of them had to give way to airstrips since it was where the first private international airport was built. Today, it’s the busiest part of the city.

stories.title: City Tour - Daewangam Course - Jangsaeng Port Tourist Information
stories.audioTitle: City Tour - Daewangam Course - Jangsaeng Port Tourist Information
stories.script: “Whales feed in the offshore of Uslan and sleep in the offshore of Japan.”  This is a line from the popular Korean TV drama “Extraordinary Attorney Woo” that aired on Netflix.  Jangsaeng Port is the birthplace of whaling in Korea. The 52 whales engraved on the Petroglyphs of Bangudae Terrace in Daegok-ri, Ulju-gun show that the people of Ulsan have been whaling since the prehistoric age. The whaling industry of Jangsaeng Port is a part of Korean history dating back to prehistoric times. Jangsaeng Port has always been the forerunner of the whaling industry until Korea joined the International Whaling Commission in 1986.   The Special Whale Culture Zone in Jangsaeng Port is the only special zone dedicated to whales in Korea, and it’s where you can get a glimpse of the history of whaling in the Korean Peninsula from the prehistoric age to the point when whaling became illegal in 1986. There is a monorail train to the Special Whale Culture Zone in Jangsaeng Port offering many things to see and enjoy.   There are Whale Culture Village and Whale Park, which is a reproduction of a whaling village, Whale Museum with a gray whale model, and the Whale Experience Hall where you can learn about whales.   You can also take the Whale Excursion Ship to see the whales or get on Korea’s first frigate made with Korean technology.  The old cold storage was rebuilt as the Culture Storage where you can enjoy a great view of the sunrise over the East Sea. Also, don’t miss out the Ulsan Whale Festival held every year in the Special Whale Culture Zone.

stories.title: City Tour - A 1 Dollar Crane past the Ulsandaegyo Bridge
stories.audioTitle: City Tour - A 1 Dollar Crane past the Ulsandaegyo Bridge
stories.script: On the way to Daewangam, we pass the Hyundai Heavy Industries shipyard.  Hyundai Heavy Industries is a very important company in the history of Korean shipbuilding industry,  and here, we have something that stands as a testament to that symbolism, the Kockums Goliath Crane that was purchased from Sweden at the low price of 1 dollar.  There was a very famous shipyard in the Swedish city of Malmö, called Kockums.  The goliath crane owned by the company had to be sold off because of bankruptcy. Nobody wanted to purchase the crane, so it found itself in a bind, until Hyundai Heavy Industries, a rising star in the shipbuilding industry at the time, offered to purchase it in 2002. Their price was 1 dollar. That single dollar was a formality to complete the purchase agreement. After all, even if the crane was purchased at 1 dollar, it took a further twenty two billion Korean won to disassemble, transport, install, modify, and test the crane in its new home. That astronomical cost was the reason why nobody wanted to purchase the crane.  Malmö was a city with a long and proud tradition of shipbuilding. When the goliath crane, which symbolized the city’s status and wealth as a shipbuilding giant, was purchased by Hyundai Heavy Industries, it is said that the people of Malmö came out to the harbor and wept. That is why some have dubbed the crane “Tears of Malmö”.   This goliath crane thus symbolizes that transition in the global shipbuilding industry, when the leadership of the industry passed from Sweden to Korea. Hyundai Heavy Industries, which purchased the crane, became the foremost and the largest shipbuilder in the world. The goliath crane, purchased with a single dollar, now stands at the shipbuilding facilities in Hyundai Heavy Industries shipyard.

stories.title: City Tour - Daewangam Course - Ulsan Port and Shipbuilding (Ulsandaegyo Bridge)
stories.audioTitle: City Tour - Daewangam Course - Ulsan Port and Shipbuilding (Ulsandaegyo Bridge)
stories.script: Samyang was the first company in Korea to have a modernized factory, which can be seen on the left side of Ulsandaegyo Bridge. The bridge also commands a view of Ulsan Port. Ulsan Port ranks first in Korea and fourth in the world in terms of handling liquid bulk cargo. The deep water and low range of tides make Ulsan Port one of the most ideal ports in the country along with Jangsaeng Port. Cross Ulsandaegyo Bridge, and you will be able to see all the heavy, chemical, and auto industry complexes at a glance.  Ulsandaegyo Bridge opened in June 2015. The distance between its two bridge towers is the third longest in the world. Korea built this bridge with its own technology. The same bridge engineering was employed to construct the world’s longest 1915 Canakkale Bridge in Turkiye.   Ulsandaegyo Bridge was also where a chase scene was filmed for the highlight of the 2017 Korean movie “Confidential Assignment” starring Hyun Bin and Yoo Haejin.   Both Ulsandaegyo Bridge and Ulsandaegyo Observatory command a view of Korea’s largest chemical complex where the lights never go out. Some Koreans say that turning off the lights here is like stopping the heart of the country.  The night view with the sunset over the city and lighting from the industrial complexes was listed in the KTO’s Top 100 Night Views of Korea and the 12 Scenic Views of Ulsan.  While Pudong Port in Shanghai and Victoria Harbour in Hong Kong are famous for their night view, the industrial complexes of Ulsan create a night view with a unique atmosphere and beauty like no other.

stories.title: City Tour  –  Daewangam Course –  Daewangam Park Information
stories.audioTitle: City Tour  –  Daewangam Course –  Daewangam Park Information
stories.script: Daewangam Park, adorned by centuries-old pine forest There are two places in Korea that are known under the name Daewangam, meaning “the great king rock”.  The first is the Daewangam in Bonggil-ri, Yangbuk-myeon, Gyeongju, the resting place of King Munmu of Silla. The second is the Ulsan Daewangam, which is said to be the resting place of the queen. Just as King Munmu wanted to protect the country after his death as a dragon, the queen is also said to have chosen Ulsan’s Daewangam as her resting place to protect the country in death.
