In the early 1900s, a Frenchman named Laporte was appointed as head of customs in Gunsan. He came to Korea with his pet French bulldog. People who saw his pet dog first time called it Mugbangi, which means a “dog with good appetite,” because its nose resembled that of a pig.  Gunsan made the characters of five animals that lived in the old days of Gunsan including Mugbangi into its mascot. Mugbangi and Friends are actively starring in tourist content and marketing of Gunsan’s specialties, such as music videos, animations, and YouTube videos.  At café Jeongdam, Mugbang Bread baked with the faces of Mugbangi and Friends on it is highly popular. Kneaded with white glutinous rice barley, the bread is chewy and sweet with red bean paste made with local ingredients. Another recommended menu in this place is King Gojong Coffee, which commemorates the independent opening of the port in Gunsan.  As opened by the will of citizens, Humanities Warehouse Café, Jeongdam is used as a new culture and arts platform. It holds humanities lectures on various daily topics of culture, music, travel, and arts. If you have taken pictures in front of the Old Customs House and looked inside around, why not come by Jeongdam to have a cup of King Gojong Coffee and Mugbang Bread with a book in your hand?

stories.title: Leesungdang
stories.script: In Gunsan, a city of gourmets and good restaurants, there is Leesungdang, a nationwide-popular bakery. Opened around 1910, Leesungdang is a bakery that represents Gunsan and the oldest bakery in Korea. Its name was originally “Izmoya.” Hirose Yastaro, a Japanese man, opened the bakery at the time and named it after his hometown.  Izmoya was famous for cracker called “arare,” which was made of glutinous rice pounded in the mortar and added with shrimp. Besides, it sold Japanese traditional refreshments, such as mochi and wagashi. Laker, the two sons of Hirose started to make bread with new machines and techniques after they had learned baking in Tokyo, which made their bakery prosper.  Expanded, Izmoya Bakery had a residential quarter, factory, and dormitory for workers. On one side of the bakery on the first floor, there were also a restaurant and coffee shop. The number of workers was almost 20, all people of Joseon.  When Korea regained independence in 1945, the family of Hirose went back to Japan. The bakery was taken over by Lee Seok-woo, who named it Leesungdang to mean a “bakery where the Lee’s family make bread.” Afterward, Lee’s descendants have been operating the bakery for almost 80 years.  Its representative items are sweet red-bean bun and vegetable bread. The sweet red-bean bun is filled with sweet and savory red bean paste. The vegetable bread is baked with vegetable stuff mainly made with cabbage, tasting clean because it is not fried like croquettes. On the weekend, Leesungdang is crowded with tourists and about 10,000 sweet red-bean buns are sold. People come to this place to enjoy the taste that survived the history of 100 years.

stories.title: Gunsan Museum of History of the Japanese Colonial Period
stories.audioTitle: Gunsan Museum of History of the Japanese Colonial Period
stories.script: Gunsan has a great number of painful traces of the Japanese colonial period. After it forcedly opened the Gunsan Port in 1899, the Japanese Empire took Gunsan as its foothold for plundering rice from Honam region. About one-fourth of rice that was taken from Korea was shipped from Gunsan to Japan. The Gunsan Museum of History of the Japanese Colonial Period is where you can take a glimpse into the history of exploitation and people’s lives in Gunsan of the time.  The exhibition hall on the third floor holds different exhibitions, providing diverse materials that illustrates the aspects of life of old days. Gunsan, the Memory of Exploitation shows the materials related to the Japanese plunder of rice during the Japanese colonial period, such as the delivery order and the booklet of estimating rice production in Gunsan, as well as more than 300 rare materials that depict how Gunsan looked like in those old days, including the panoramic map of Gunsan Port until the 1930s and the history of Gunsan Port opening.   1930 Gunsan Store shows the materials that demonstrate the industry and life in Gunsan during the Japanese colonial period, such as the postcard of Minakai Department Store Gunsan Branch and the Map of Gunsan with Lot Numbers with place names and 67 stores in Gunsanbu in 1935. Resistance and Treachery in Writings and Pictures is the first exhibition to display more than 50 paintings and calligraphies, including the autographs of the late Maecheon Hwang Hyeon, who took his own life in rage of losing the country to Japan–Korea Treaty of 1910, the calligraph of Oh Se-chang, one of 33 Korean leaders who declared independence, the letter and eight-panel folding screen painted with the painting Ilsaengdo by Choi Ik-hyeon, a patriotic martyr who was killed after being sent to Daemado Island, and an eight-panel folding screen of Lee Bang-ja.  Visit the Gunsan Museum of History of the Japanese Colonial Period, a storage of memories, to learn the history of Gunsan that has been hidden to us and create the future of the Republic of Korea based on what you learned from the exploitive history during the Japanese colonial period.

stories.title: Jangmi Theater and Jangmi Gallery
stories.script: There are as many as more than 170 modern buildings that remain in Gunsan, including those on Gunsan Modern Culture Street. The modern buildings that have been preserved without being demolished after liberation are now great resources for tourism. Among them, there are Jangmi Gallery and Jangmi Theater together with Miz Coffee located in Jangmi-dong, where Japanese trade companies, banks, and commercial facilities were clustered.  “Jangmi” of Jangmi-dong refers to rose in Korean, but it does not so in this case. It is how “藏米,” the Chinese characters that compose the name of the village, is pronounced in Korean, meaning a “barn of plundered rice.” During the Japanese colonial period, Gunsan Port was expanded by the Japanese Government-General of Korea and became a channel through which Korean agricultural products were transported to Japan. The Japanese Empire built a large warehouse in front of the port, stored grains from Honam and Chungcheong there, and loaded ships with the grains. It named the area Jangmi-dong.  Jangmi Gallery was first built in the Japanese colonial period and used as for recreational purposes after liberation in 1945. In 2013, it was refurbished into a gallery. On the first floor, foreign tourists and visitors with their family can enjoy various experience programs, such as making a coaster, candle, wooden necklace, and original handkerchief.  Jangmi Theater, next to Jangmi Gallery, is a performance hall with 77 seats. It was renovated from a warehouse where the Joseon Granary Corporation stored plundered rice in the 1930s. Miz Coffee, a café located across Jangmi Gallery, was once a trade company in the 1930s. It was moved from in front of Gunsan Modern History Museum for remodeling and renovation. Between the two buildings, there is a beautiful garden with garden rocks and a stone lamp, famous as a good spot for tourists to take pictures.

stories.title: Mallaengi Village
stories.script: Mallaengi Village is a new rising tourist destination in Gunsan. It is a poor hillside village that was formed by refugees who lived on the hillside of Haemang-dong and Sinheung-dong during the Korean War. The word “Mallaengi” means a hillside in dialect of Jeolla-do Province. It was once an impoverished village where small houses built closely side by side stood along the narrow uphill path, but as many people moved out, a number of houses became empty.  Gunsan-si Office decided to purchase the empty houses and land to create a new space for recollection. It built nine residences for artists and eight exhibition halls, making the place reborn into a village resided by both artists and residents.  Every nook and cranny of Mallaengi Village diffuses warmth of life, allowing visitors to look into loving lives of ordinary people. Affectionate are the wall paintings that remind us of families of the 1980s, the clock sculpture that is suggestive of time travel, and the small spring that was once used by villagers.  The Memorial Hall displays the photos featuring the Japanese colonial period, the open port, colonized land, refugees, Japanese landowners, and people who had weary days working at Gunsan Port. The exhibits of old stores, alleys and old dresses may have visitors feel as if they travel into the past in a time machine.  Climbing up a little to Wolmyeong Park from Mallaengi Village, you can see a friendly face. It is Kim Soo-mi, an actress who was born in Gunsan. Following the Kim Soo-mi Trail, you can see the house she lived in her childhood and her village. In the site of the house, a painting of Kim with makeup on as Madame Iryong, a character she played in Country Diaries. At the end of Kim Soo-mi Trail, you can see a pavilion where you can look down a wide view of Wolmyeong Park and coastal waters of Gunsan.  Jayu Theater, located at height in the village, is where you can enjoy the story about the village. The nostalgic entrance resembles that of an old theater. The theater also has a front yard where you can play squid game. The studio in the village displays various souvenirs made by village residents and runs experience programs.  Mallaengi Village is a living space of modern history and culture. It is filled with villagers’ past memories and with artists’ new stories at the same time.

stories.title: The Site of Simdo Textile
stories.script: As the center of the Korean peninsula for a long time, Ganghwado Island can be called a microcosm of Korea history, preserving a long and massive history. In prehistoric times, there lived a people of the Bronze Age who formed a strong ruling class, and Dangun, a legendary founding father of Gojoseon, worshiped god at the Chamseongdan Altar on Manisan Mountain to follow the Providence. In the Goryeo period, the capital was moved to Ganghwado Island from Gaegyong against the invasion of Mongolia and the palace was newly built in the island. The palace has not remained as it was demolished under the conditions to make peace with Mongolia. In the Joseon period, kings took refuge in the island during wars, and powerful nations often coveted the island in the modern age. Representative examples are the French Disturbance of 1866, or Byeongin Yangyo; the American Disturbance of 1871, or Sinmi Yangyo; and an armed conflict between Japan and Korea in 1875, known as Unyo Incident.  Until the 1970s, Ganghwado Island was one of three major textile cities together with Daegu and Suwon in the Republic of Korea. There were more than 30 textile factories, including Joyang Textile, Pyeonghwa Textile, Simdo Textile and Ihwa Textile, with more than 4,000 workers in total.   However, they declined going through two times of oil crisis and the government’s policy to move the center of textile industry to Daegu, where they produced synthetic fabrics. Currently, there are a few small factories that produce sochang, or natural fabric made of cotton.  If you visit Yongheunggung Park in Ganghwa-eup, you can see the traces of once glorious textile industry: the site of Simdo Textile. Founded in 1947, Simdo Textile was a massive textile company hiring up to 1,200 workers until the 1970s. It faded into the mists of history as any other companies did.  Ganghwa-gun Office cut the upper part of the chimney of Simdo Textile to commemorate the history of textile industry and erected it beside the park. As cotton tree is planted near the site, you can see the cotton flowers in August. Charming white cotton flowers blossom beautifully as if they want to tell us that this place once led the textile industry of Ganghwado Island contributing to the development of the national economy.

stories.title: Ihwa Textile Street
stories.script: Ganghwado Island is well known for its ginseng, scaled sardine, and turnip, but some time ago, hwamunseok, or a flower-patterned rush mat, was the best of all among its specialties. A rush mat was a must-have item during summer. It blocked heat and soaked sweat. The rush produced in Ganghwado Island was white, glossy, and strong. People in this island produced handmade white rush mats with no patterns since the mid-Goryeo period. In the Joseon period, the royal family ordered them to make rush mats with flowery patterns, which led to the development of hwamunseok. Hwamunseok was a masterpiece created from the elaboration using warp weights by women of Ganghwado Island who are famous for their dexterity.  In the modern age, Ganghwado Island became the mecca of textile industry. The dexterity of women who once made hwamunseok started to be used in making textile. From the Japanese occupation period, almost all households in Ganghwado Island had “jokdapgi,” or a hand-operated loom. It was used for women to make rayon. It is said that white fabrics that were hanging to dry over the field looked like a giant wave across the island. The women of Ganghwado Island crossed the sea to peddle nationwide, selling rayon. Their relentlessness is often called bold-faced, from which we could assume their life of twists and turns.  The foundation of Joyang Textile in 1933 by brothers Hong Jae-mook and Hong Jae-yong, the businessmen of Ganghwado Island, marked the beginning of the modern textile industry sfrom the hand-operated form. With other companies, such as Simdo Textile, Namhwa Textile, Ihwa Textile, and Pyeonghwa Textile, coming in the industry, the textile industry continued its heyday until the 1970s.  Established by Namgung Hyeong, Ihwa Textile was quite a large company with more than 300 employees. Most buildings were demolished already, but the wall has well been preserved as a remembrance of the pain and memories of people who lived in Ganghwado Island in those days. Ihwa Textile Street displays the stories and photos about the history of textile industry in Ganghwado Island, the incident of the labor union of Simdo Textile, introductions to Ihwa Textile, Simdo Textile, Joyeong Textile, Namhwa Textile, and Pyeonghwa Textile, and the view of the street where Simdo Textile was standing in the 1970s. The structures of a loom and a view of the factory are manufactured in the form of relief, showing how they looked.  Due to the textile factories, people of Ganghwado Island could use electricity and telephone earlier than those living in most onshore cities. Even people from the land came to see the electric lights. In those days, Ganghwado Island was a famous wealthy region in the country with a population more than double of the current population. Read storyboard to look into the old days when the island was prosperous following the Ihwa Textile Street.

stories.title: Sign Stone of Labor Ministry
stories.script: Until the 1970s, the streets of Ganghwa-eup were filled with young female workers who commuted to factories twice a day to their shift timetable. Female workers from poor family couldn’t receive school education and had to become the breadwinners of their family working at textile factories until they got married. Not being rich, most people in Ganghwa-eup could work at textile factories to make a living.  Among all factories, Simdo Textile was of great scale, and more than 1,200 workers worked there for 12 hours a day with two shifts. “Wembley Necktie,” the product of Simdo Textile, was its representative product for exportation to different from advanced countries including the United States, praised as a mainstay of the nation’s exports.  However, such achievement was only possible due to sweats of laborers. The company forced laborers to work too much citing shortage of manpower. Already swamped with 12 hours of work, the laborers had to work for almost 24 hours before holidays. Young female workers often had nosebleed suffering overtime work at night, coughing constantly due to dust in the factory.  In order to improve such poor environment, a labor union was organized in May 1967 with participation of 300 workers, prompted by the Korean Young Christian Workers (JOC) with pastor Michael Jeon as a leader. As the labor union started to fight against the textile company for the rights of laborers, the company tried to disorganize the labor union and suppressed the laborers, creating conflicts. In February 9, 1968, when the episcopate issued a joint statement entitled “We advocate social justice and the laborers’ rights” to support laborers, Ganghwa Textile Association in which Simdo Textile belonged to withdrew the suppression on the labor union and its members and promised their reinstatement.  The accident of the Simdo Textile labor union is being commemorated on the Sign Stone of Labor Ministry at the Ganghwa Catholic Church. It is the first accident in which the Korean catholic church was actively engaged in labor issues to address them, having significance in the Catholic labor history. To celebrate the accident, the Catholic Diocese of Incheon established the Sigh Stone of Labor Ministry at the Ganghwa Catholic Church.  The textile industry, which needed long-time labor and cheap labor force, and the women of Ganghwa, who boasted strong vitality, were a necessary and sufficient condition for each other. Tough and poor life of Ganghwa women who naturally worked as laborers of the textile industry and built the economy of the region nourished the history of democratic and labor movement in the 1970-80s.

stories.title: Memorial Stone for Kim Sang-yong
stories.script: One of the most painful past memories of Ganghwado Island would be the Qing Invasion of Joseon in 1636. Ganghwado Island was a fortress blessed with natural barriers that even Mongolia couldn't collapse. However, the Qing Invasion of Joseon in 1636 was the time when a great number of people had to be killed or captured by a force of 3,000 men of Qing.  Founded by Manchu people, who was called barbarians by the people of Joseon, Qing won victory after victory replacing Ming, the dynasty founded by Han, to occupy the ruling position. As Joseon strongly believed that the Chinese legitimacy is possessed by Ming, it kept regarding Qing only as barbarians, which led them to the Qing invasion.  On December 9, 1636, the military force of Qing swept away everything in their way crossing Amnokgang River. It took less than a week for them to capture Hanyang. King Injo, who first planned to take refuge to Ganghwado Island, had to leave refuge to Namhansanseong Fortress with Crown Prince Sohyeon and some of his retainers as the road was blocked by the Qing’s forces. The royal concubines of King Injo and other princes departed earlier and could arrive Ganghwado Island. It was Kim Sang-yong who accompanied them for escort.  He was a senior minister who served as the first royal secretary, inspector-general, minister of Justice, and third state councilor. He had excellent diplomatic finesse and dealt with tricky issues related to Ming. During his stay in Ganghwado Island, he collected news from Namhansanseong Fortress and tried to raise an army to provide a military support for the king. However, when the military forces of Qing surrounded the fortress of Ganghwa, he decided to take his own life, went up on the southern gate tower of the fortress, and lit the explosives on which he was standing. This made him the symbol of fidelity of the late Joseon period together with his younger brother, Kim Sang-heon, who is known as a minister who opposed peace negotiations.  If you go to Yongheunggung Park, you can see the Memorial Stone for Kim Sang-yong to commemorate his loyalty. There are two memorial stones in the monument house. One was erected in 1700 with the epitaph composed by Kim Chang-hyup and written by Kim Chang-jip, both great-grandchildren of Kim Sang-yong. The other was established again in 1817 as the original epitaph was worn away. Ganghwado Island preserves the spirit of resistance and elevation from the Goryeo period to modern times. Its fierce history is still shining in the beautiful landscape.

stories.title: Ganghwa Literary House
stories.script: Do you know what is common among Lee Gyu-bo, a great writer in the Goryeo period, Jeong Cheol, the master of lyrics in the Joseon period, and Jeong In-bo, an independence movement activist and educator? They are all literary men and scholars closely related to Ganghwado Island. Lee Gyu-bo wrote many writings as he stayed in Ganghwado Island and Songgnag Jeong Cheol left many poems in Korean called “Gasa” before he died in Songjeong Village in Ganghwado Island. The literature and thoughts of literary persons of Ganghwa School enriched the traditional literature of Ganghwa, starting with Jeong Je-du of the mid Joseon period, followed by Lee Gwang-sa, Lee Chung-ik, and Lee Si-won, along with Lee Geon-chang of the modern times, and Jeong In-bo of the contemporary times.  Established by bequest of the late Jo Gyeong-hui, an essayist who was born in Ganghwa, Ganghwa Literary House inherits such great spirit of national literature, showing the pride and integrity of literature of Ganghwa. The world of Ganghwa literature is unfolded in various exhibits, proving its production of many writers and works in its long history. The exhibition hall on the first floor invites you to the introduction to literary men related to Ganghwado Island who left their names in the Korean literature, such as Lee Gyu-bo, Jeong Cheol, and Jeong Je-du.  The exhibition hall on the second floor shows the literature world and life of Woldang Jo Gyeong-hui with more than 9,000 items of her donated relics, illuminating her lofty spirit. Jo Gyeong-hui was born in Onsu-ri, Gilsang-myeon, Ganghwa-gun in 1914, serving as a representative writer of the island as she worked as the president of the Korea Essayists Association, the president of the Federation of Artistic & Cultural Organization of Korea, and the second state Minister for Political Affairs.  Before finishing the visit, visitors can also experience the woodblock printing at the woodblock printing experience section. Ganghwa Literary House displays the historic culture and the tradition of national literature of Ganghwa. It cultivates dream and hope of the next generation in literature, serving as a rest area for those who love literature.

stories.title: Yeongnam Alps Complex Welcome Center
stories.script: There is a place where you can get the feeling of the Alps without having to visit Europe — it is the Yeongnam Alps. This place was named after the Alps since the mountains that are connected with nine high peaks rising 1,000 m above sea level are comparable to the European Alps.  The Yeongnam Alps Complex Welcome Center is located underneath the high peaks of the Yeongnam Alps. As an open space that combines nature and culture, this center was constructed as a complex cultural space and the foothold of mountain tourism. This multi-purpose center allows hikers, tourists, and nearby residents to understand the Yeongnam Alps, enjoy various cultural activities, and hold domestic and international events.  The center has the Mountain Culture Center, International Climbing Center, Lightning Man Experience Center, and a Theater. The Artificial Falls, Talking Tree, and Square are available in the outdoor space. The Mountain Culture Center includes: the Mountain Theme Exhibition Hall, which reproduces the nature and culture of the Yeongnam Alps; the Interactive Art Wall of Hongnyupokpo Falls, which presents the four seasons of Hongnyupokpo Falls of Sinbulsan Mountain with a touchscreen video; and the Alps Cinema. This is a place to appreciate the nature, ecology, history, and culture of the Yeongnam Alps.  The Lightning Man Experience Center, the favorite of children, is a hands-on theme park where children can see, listen to, and experience Lightning Man. Play facilities, trains, and spaceships inside the experience center are available to all children regardless of age.  The International Climbing Center is Korea’s largest artificial rock climbing center, designed for 20 standard courses for domestic and international competitions. Anyone can try out rock climbing with the help of experts.  The Yeongnam Alps Complex Welcome Center has many gorgeous mountains on its back, including Sinbulsan, Gajisan, Ganwolsan, and Odusan Mountains. Come and feel the grandeur of the mountains and enjoy various cultural and leisure sports activities.

stories.title: Eonyangeupseong Walled Town, Ulju
stories.script: Walled town, or eupseong in Korean, refers to a fortress that protects residents of a county or district and plays military and administrative roles. Inside are various government offices, guesthouses, and Hyanggyo, or local Confucian schools, as well as facilities like wells and ponds. They had administrative functions during ordinary times and military functions in case of emergencies. Eonyang also had this walled town, implying that this place used to have administrative and military importance in the past. In fact, the old town of Eonyang was a transportation hub connecting Gyeongju, Ulsan, Miryang, and Yangsan.  The Eonyangeupseong Walled Town was built as an earthen fortress during the Three Kingdoms period. Later, it was expanded and rebuilt into a stone fortress by Governor Lee Dam-ryong in 1500 the 6th year of King Yeonsangun's reign. Fortresses are normally built by neatly piling square stones or mountain stones, but the Eonyangeupseong Walled Town was built by rolling gigantic rocks, polishing the rock surface, placing large stones on top of the rocks, and inserting numerous small stones to fill the gap. The fortress built this way becomes extremely sturdy and can endure a considerable impact. That is why a substantial portion of this walled town remains to this date.   The circumference of the Eonyangeupseong Walled Town is 1,500 m, and there are four gates each on the north, south, east, and west. Pavilions like Yeonghwaru (south gate) and Mangwollu (east gate) were constructed on top. Pavilions were built around the corners of the fortress for guards to keep watch, and a crescent-shaped defensive wall was built nearby the gate. The outer semi-circular wall was intended to defend the gates against enemies effectively. Protrusions can be found on the fortress walls, corresponding to the bastions of the fortress. It is presumed that these protrusions were designed by someone who had considerable experience in defense and military knowledge.  Yeonghwaru Pavilion in the south gate has been restored. If you stand atop Yeonghwaru Pavilion, you can clearly see the entire walled town area. There used to be government offices to the east, guesthouses to the west, a road headed in all four directions, and a waterway crossing from the east gate to the west gate. It is said that there even existed four wells inside the fortress. Of course, we cannot find their traces nowadays.  As we slowly walk through the restored walled town area, a gentle breeze blows above the fortress walls, piled up in several layers of time. This breeze must have blown in the Three Kingdoms period and also in the Joseon period. The breeze connecting the past and present delivers the history of Eonyang.

stories.title: Eonyang Alps Market
stories.script: There are mills with the savory smell of sesame oil and perilla oil, forges that have been making farming equipment and tools for over 50 years, grocery stores selling tasty side dishes such as water kimchi made of bean leaves and pickled bean leaves, bakers that make donuts and twisted bread sticks, and street vendors selling wild greens and vegetables picked up on the mountain or green farms. Eonyang Alps Market is a countryside market that has a variety of products, from industrial products to daily necessities.  The name of the Eonyang Alps Market has a contemporary feel, but this market boasts a long history of over 100 years. In the Joseon period, Eonyang was a place with much traffic as roads were connected to Gyeongju, Miryang, and Yangsan. It was a trading center where products came from seven regions, including Cheongdo, Miryang, Dongnae, Yangsan, Gyeongju, Yeongcheon, and Ulsan. That is why such a huge market was formed. This market was called the Eonyang Market or Seven-Town Market.  The Eonyang Market became what it is today in the late 1960s. The marketplace used to be a riverbed and a water parsley garden. Eonyang had many fields of water parsley with a taste and fragrance so great that it was even offered to kings. The Eonyang Market, opened by reclaiming water parsley fields, became widely known until the early 1980s. The market was crowded with merchants and customers on the 2nd and 7th days of every month.  The market shrank with the appearance of large-sized supermarkets but began to revive with the development of Gyeongbu High-Speed Railway station area near the KTX Ulsan Station. Ulju-gun reorganized the surrounding environment by conducting a commercial vitalization project, and the market was renamed the Eonyang Alps Market to reflect the regional characteristics. With such efforts, more people are visiting the market on market days nowadays.  Thanks to the vast pastureland, Eonyang raised many cattle, resulting in the advancement of beef food products with a cattle market and slaughterhouses. Eonyang Bulgogi is the representative food product. However, Eonyang Bulgogi was too expensive for commoners. Commoners bought inexpensive cuts of beef at the cattle market and cooked beef rice soup using wild greens growing everywhere. That is why Eonyang Alps Market has several restaurants selling beef bone soup from the old days.  The simmering rice soup inside the iron pot in front of the restaurant makes passersby stop walking. The soup, made by boiling beef leg bone all day long and adding sirloin and brisket, has a plain yet refreshing taste. Seasoned chives add flavor to the soup.  Even if you do not intend to buy something in particular, looking around this traditional market is fun. It is full of warm hearts and energy. Even if you are not familiar with bargaining, you can still benefit from the generosity of the merchants. Come and experience the taste and warmth of the Eonyang Alps Market. It is full of things to see and eat.

stories.title: Namchang Onggi-Jonggi Market
stories.script: The origin of the Namchang Onggi-Jonggi Market goes back about 400 years. Located in Namchang-ri, Onyang-eup, Ulju-gun, this place was named “Namchang” because the warehouse that used to store grains in the Joseon period was located to the south of Ulsan-bu. The Namchang Market was naturally formed as products and people gathered. The Donghae Nambu Line, currently known as the Donghae Line connecting Ulsan with Pohang and Busan, was opened in the Japanese colonial period, and the Namchang Station was created. This station attracted more products to the Namchang Market, and the market prospered even more.  Due to its proximity to the sea, this market is rich in seafood. It is also rich in farm products, such as “Seosang Pear,” a specialty of Ulsan. When the market opens on the 3rd and 8th days of each month, old ladies come from nearby farming villages to sell wild greens and vegetables, and the market is full of boisterous bargaining and laughter.  The pottery shop is the most famous in this market. Potteries, or onggi in Korean, of this shop are made in the Oegosan Onggi Village nearby. Oegosan Onggi Village is the village that produces most of the domestic potteries circulated in Korea. You can check out the traditional pottery-making process in the village, and reproduction of Silla pottery. This village was the reason why the Namchang Market was renamed as Namchang Onggijonggi Market.  We cannot miss out on the delicious food when it comes to traditional markets. Popular foods in this market are gukbap, known as rice soup, and makgeolli, or unrefined rice wine. About 10 rice soup restaurants are lined up on one side of the market. Rice soup and noodles made of ox blood, or seonji, are famous.  Namchang makgeolli paired with rice soup is a traditional liquor with a clean taste, made by maturing groundwater from the Daeunsan Mountain in a 60-year-old pottery. Imagine tasting the hot seonji and rice soup with a cup of makgeolli. It will relieve your fatigue from the trip.

stories.title: Former Namchang Station
stories.script: If you step out of the Namchang Onggijonggi Market, the Namchang Station, a train station on the Donghae Nambu Line, comes out across the road. During the Japanese colonial period, Japan linked Ulsan, Busan, and Pohang through the Donghae Nambu Line to transport wood, mineral, coal, and seafood products. The Namchang Station was opened as an ordinary station in December 1935. Later, after the Donghae Nambu Line was transformed into the Donghae Line, this station continued to operate due to the prosperity of the Ulsan Industrial Complex in the 1970s. The station was abolished after a new station was built with the installation of a double-track railway between Busan and Ulsan in 2016.  The former Namchang Station is a wooden building with unusually overlapping roof ends with an upside-down V-shape. This roof is the typical style shown by stations that were built in the Japanese colonial period. At the time of construction, the windows were double-hung windows. We can no longer find these double-hung windows because most of the window frames have been replaced and downsized. The Namchang Station was slightly changed on the interior and exterior, but it has kept the structure and spatial composition of stations from the Japanese colonial period. This station was designated as the Registered Cultural Heritage No.105 in 2004.  This time-traveling site cherishes its old form, full of the friendly rural landscape. Countless people would have boarded and stepped down from the trains at this station. And all those people probably had their own stories. The old station yielded its position to the new station, but it functioned as a gateway to the world for nearly 100 years. This small and plain station seems to be piled up with memories and longings.

stories.title: National Center for Forest Therapy, Daeunsan
stories.audioTitle: National Center for Forest Therapy, Daeunsan
stories.script: Ulju, a place known as the Yeongnam Alps with beautiful mountains often compared to the Alps in Europe, has natural pathways that offer forest therapy experience. In particular, the Daeunsan Mountain, the last place where Great Monk Wonhyo practiced asceticism, has sceneries that comfort people’s bodies and minds.  The National Center for Forest Therapy, Daeunsan, is nestled in a dense primeval forest with the Naewonam Hermitage depicted as the best propitious site in Yeongnam, a 500-year-old hackberry, and the Dotonggol Guryongpokpo Falls where it is said that Great Monk Wonhyo became enlightened. The dense forest of oriental cork oak trees and cypress trees is an optimal place for forest bathing.  Forest therapy refers to an activity that boosts the immunity of the human body and stabilizes the mind by utilizing various therapeutic elements in forests, such as phytoncide, anions, oxygen, and scenic views. The first human beings lived in nature, such as dugout huts and caves. Contemporary people still love nature and feel secure in nature because the memory of living in nature remains in human DNA. Perhaps this is why our body and mind feel comfortable and refreshed when we visit forests.  Forests provide a resting experience to people who are tired of everyday life.  The National Center for Forest Therapy, Daeunsan, has various therapy paths on a wide site of 250,000 ㎡, such as the Grass Scent Path, Wind Garden Healing Path, and Premium Forest Path. There are various experience facilities like the Sharing Healing Center with health checkup and thermotherapy rooms, Water Healing Bath, and Red Clay Garden. The center operates many healing programs based on exercises, yoga, breathing, meditation, and tea ceremony. The programs are available for children, teenagers, adults, seniors, and persons with disabilities. It is also inexpensive as it is operated by the national government. Since taking a walk around the forest path is enough, you can take a short time to visit this center during your trip.  Forests provide a resting experience to people who are tired of everyday life. There is a saying that goes, “Walking makes you healthy.” Come to the National Center for Forest Therapy, Daeunsan, a place that offers green rest and healthy breath to tired people. Walk on the forest paths to turn on the healing switch in your body.

stories.title: Jeonju Handicraft Exhibition Hall
stories.script: Jeonju Hanok Village is full of things to see, enjoy, and buy; in this Hanok Villgae, there is one place where you can do everything at once. It is the Jeonju Handicraft Exhibition Hall, which offers diverse crafting cultures with gorgeous craft works and many experiential programs.  Jeonju Handicraft Exhibition Hall, located in Jeonju Hanok Village, consists of the Experience Hall, where you can gain experience in crafting cultures; the Exhibition Hall, which introduces traditional and contemporary craft works; the Sales Hall, which gathers and sells excellent craft works from around the nation; and the Premium Hall, which exhibits intangible cultural properties.  About 800 craft works are exhibited in the Exhibition Hall, carefully selected among outstanding craft works from around the nation. In the Sales Hall, there is the fun of seeing various craft works sold. In the Premium Hall, you can find intangible cultural properties of Jeollabuk-do Province and “own brand” products made in collaboration with designers. You can also try making a handicraft of your own. Show off your crafting skills by making pretty wish boats, spinning tops, folding fans with folk paintings, bracelets, mask straps, mother-of-pearl chignon ornaments, and knot bags.  The Jeonju Handicraft Exhibition Hall is a place where the traditional styles of Jeonju and Korea breathe alive. Come and enjoy the joy of seeing, buying, and experiencing.

stories.title: Jeonjuhyanggyo Local Confucian School
stories.script: Hyanggyo, or local Confucian schools, are secondary educational institutions founded by the national government in the Goryeo and Joseon periods to educate Confucianism. In the beginning, the Goryeo Dynasty sent experts and professors to different regions to educate talented individuals in an attempt to strengthen the centralization of power. In the Joseon period, the functions of the local Confucian schools have been reinforced, and they were installed in all counties and towns around the nation. The purpose was to foster talented individuals into government officials and educate and spread Confucianism as the central ideology of Joseon instead of Buddhism, which was the mainstream culture of Goryeo.  The Jeonjuhyanggyo Local Confucian School was founded in 1354, the 3rd year of King Gongmin's reign from Goryeo. After the foundation of Joseon, this school was relocated to Hwasan-dong by constructing the Gyeonggijeon Hall, a hall to seal the memorial portrait of King Taejo, in 1410 or the 10th year of King Taejong's reign. It is because people believed that the sound of students reading books out loud made the deceased soul of King Taejo restless. After 139 years, the Jeonjuhyanggyo Local Confucian School was relocated again to the current location because it was far away from the city, had inconvenience in crossing the Jeonjucheon Stream, and violated the rule of placing the Confucian shrine on the left and Sajikdan Altar on the right side of the guesthouse.  The Jeonjuhyanggyo Local Confucian School was a large-sized Confucian school with buildings comprising 99 kans (a unit of measurement referring to the distance between two columns), including the Daeseongjeon Hall, Manhwaru Pavilion, Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall, Dongjae, Seojae, and Gyeseongsa Shrine. This school was also known as the Capital Confucian School because it resembled the look of the Seonggyungwan Academy in Seoul. Similar to the Najuhyanggyo Local Confucian School, this school has the front-shrine, rear-school arrangement with the Manhwaru Pavilion, Irwolmun Gate, Daeseongjeon Hall, and Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall forming the central axis. The Gyeseongsa Shrine is placed behind them to the northwest. As you enter the Manhwaru Pavilion at the entrance of the school, you pass by a tall gate called the Irwolmun Gate to reach the space for sacrificial rites.  The front yards of the Daeseongjeon Hall and Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall have two large ginkgo trees that are over 400 years old. Peculiarly, the ginkgo tree on the right side of the Daeseongjeon Hall is a hermaphrodite tree that turned from a male into a female to produce ginkgo nuts. These ginkgo nuts are gathered to perform rites. A legend says that people who pick a ginkgo nut from the 250-year-old ginkgo tree in front of the Irwolmun Gate and pray can pass the state examination. To this date, people who are about to take an examination keep a ginkgo nut like a charm. With longevity and strong resistance to harmful insects, ginkgo trees represent the spirit of classical scholars who are adamant to temptations. For this reason, all Confucian schools planted ginkgo trees in their yard.  The Jeonjuhyanggyo Local Confucian School used to play the role of an educational institution in the Goryeo and Joseon periods, but it lost its educational function with the implementation of theology after the Gabo Reform. The school once again became a cradle of education through the national liberation in 1948. There was no university in Jeonju until the liberation. Accordingly, the Jeonjuhyanggyo Local Confucian School led the efforts to form a foundation and establish Myeongnyun College in 1950. People had a great passion for learning, even during the Korean War. The facilities of the college were inferior, and students had to study with desks placed on muddy grounds, but the poor conditions could not suppress the desire of students to study. With the support of the Confucian school, Confucian scholars, and local leaders of Jeollabuk-do Province, the college was promoted into Jeonbuk National University in 1953. Jeonbuk National University relocated to the Deokjin Campus, which stood the test of time until today. The Jeonjuhyanggyo Local Confucian School was the forerunner of Jeonbuk National University.  In 1983, the Jeonjuhyanggyo Local Confucian School opened Korea’s only Sunday school in Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall to teach ethics, morals, Chinese characters, calligraphy, and courtesy. The school also runs the Children’s Courtesy School for children to learn courtesy at young ages.  This Confucian School opened its doors to the public to become a place for culture and art education. As the school operates various programs, take a moment to visit and experience the culture of classical scholars. The school will make your trip to Jeonju more worthwhile.

stories.title: Omokgyo Bridge
stories.script: You can find the Omokgyo Bridge in front of the red gate after coming out of the Jeonjuhyanggyo Local Confucian School through its front entrance. It is a bridge that connects Jeonju Hanok Village with the National Intangible Heritage Center. Standing on this bridge, you can appreciate the clear wind and water sound of the Jeonjucheon Stream. Cross the stepping stones underneath the Omokgyo Bridge if you want to hear the sound of clear water flowing in the Jeonjucheon Stream. The stepping stones were used as a bridge before the construction of the Omokgyo Bridge and are considered a photo zone that presents the beauty of the Jeonjucheon Stream.  The Omokgyo Bridge hoists five-colored flags that cannot be found on any other bridge. These flags are the flags of Joseon kings installed to spread the image of Jeonju as a city of traditional culture and remind people of the historical significance of Jeonju Hanok Village, the hometown of the royal family of Joseon. The Hongmundaegi flag has a blue dragon on the red background, and there are five-colored flags showing the dignity and dynamics of kings known as the Yellow Dragon Flag, White Tiger Flag, Vermilion Bird Flag, Black Tortoise Flag, and Blue Dragon Flag.  As you walk along the bridge flapping with king's flags, you can feel as if you have become a king guarded by many civil and military officials, dignified with elegant footsteps.

stories.title: Jeonjucheon Stream
stories.script: The Jeonjucheon Stream is a stream that originates from the Seulchi Pass, Sanggwan-myeon, Wanju-gun that passes by the old downtown of Jeonju, and flows to Mangyeong. This stream is the heart of Jeonju that keeps joys and sorrows from the memories and stories of Jeonju people. This stream was so clean that children could catch fish and swim until 1970. However, as domestic sewage and garbage flowed into the Jeonjucheon Stream with the urbanization trend, it turned into a dead stream where neither people nor fish could live. As fish died, birds no longer visited the stream. People stopped visiting the stream too.  In 1998, the Jeonjucheon Stream began to revive slowly with the natural stream development project. As water became clear, fish returned, and so did birds. The development project, continued until 2002, was acknowledged as an exemplary model for successful restoration of the ecosystem at the “River Day” contest held in Japan in 2002.  The Jeonjucheon Stream recovered its old shape through the hometown river project carried out from 2013 to 2017. As concrete is removed from the underwater beams and reservoirs, reeds and Amur silver grasses grow thick to present a magnificent sight in the fall. The stream has been reborn as an ecological space in the city, where people mingle with animals and plants.  The stream has many bridges as it cuts across Jeonju, and each bridge is full of stories to share. The Wansangyo Bridge was previously known as the “Salt Field Bridge” because salt stores were lined up underneath the bridge in the past. It used to be a “women-only zone” where women gathered and bathed on summer nights in the 1960s. The Seochongyo Bridge appears if you come down from the Wansangyo Bridge toward the Nambu Market, and there is a place below this bridge that used to be a public wash place. Flat-shaped laundry stones and drying stones stand in a row. The bridge that links the Seocheongyo Bridge to the Maegokgyo Bridge was named the Yeonjukgyo Bridge or Seoldaejeondari Bridge after the merchants who opened stores selling tobacco underneath the bridge. The Ssajeondari Bridge connecting Wansan-dong and the Nambu Market was the birthplace of the March First Independence Movement in Jeonju.  The Jeonju Stream, currently classified as a 1st class stream, is a habitat for various plants and 11 species of fish, including slender shinner, dark chubs, striped shinner, goby minnow, Korean spine loach, carp, minnow, and Chinese minnow. Natural monuments like otters, mandarin ducks, and kestrels live in the upstream, and reeds and Amur silver grasses fully bloom in the downstream to decorate the streamside.  The nightscape from the Namcheongyo Bridge under the Jeonjuhyanggyo Local Confucian School to the Jeonju Eco Museum is also beautiful, so you may look up into the stars and moon while strolling.

stories.title: Hanbyeokdang Pavilion
stories.script: The Hanbyeokdang Pavilion, located in the Jeonjucheon Stream near Jeonju Hanok Village, was a pavilion built in 1404 or the 4th year of King Taejong's reign as a villa by Choi Dam (pen name: Woldang), a founding contributor of Joseon and a Jikjehak of the Jiphyeonjeon Hall. This pavilion was constructed on a rock next to the Ongnyudong Pass and was originally named the “Woldangnu Pavilion” after Choi Dam’s pen name. Later, the pavilion was renovated several times and renamed the Hanbyeokdang Pavilion. This name means that the cold and clear water of the Jeonjucheon Stream flows down and splashes like white jade after crashing into the rock.  Poets and artists visited the Hanbyeokdang Pavilion to recite poems and enjoy the arts. This place has many poems left behind by passersby. A poem titled the Hanbyeokdang Pavilion is included in Misanjip, a poetry book written by a literary man of the late Joseon period named Han Jang-seok. The poem goes as follows.  The Hanbyoekdang Pavilion is colored in sunset,  thinking long about farewell with a willow standing next to the pavilion. A wanderer who spent the spring on a horse is  busy looking for places to travel in the south of the river. A green curve in the stream has two peaks rising between the creek,  and a higher one rises in a place blooming red flowers. As I worry about my hometown in the north that cannot be seen from here,  I turn the head towards the north of the Hangang River.  There is also a story of folding fans told by Lee Sam-man (pen name: Changam), one of the three master calligraphers of the late Joseon period. On a midsummer day, a folding fan seller visited the Hanbyeokdang Pavilion to avoid the summer heat. The seller complained about slow-selling folding fans before falling asleep. When he woke up from a sweet sleep, there was a classical scholar writing letters on his folding fans. When the seller got angry and said, “Why are you writing letters on my folding fans? If you ruin them, I can no longer sell them.” The scholar replied, “You will be able to sell them all before the sun sets, so go ahead and sell them.” The seller checked the location of the scholar’s house, thinking about demanding compensation if the folding fans were not sold, and went back to Jeonju to sell the products. And what happened next was that the seller sold all the fans within a short period of time. With his money pouch full of money, the seller visited the scholar's house to thank him and asked for the scholar’s name. The scholar was Changam Lee Sam-man.  The Hanbyeokdang Pavilion is three kans in width and two kans in depth with a hipped and gable roof. It is only about 16.5 square meters wide, but the view is fine with traditional Korean-style rafters, floor, and eaves surrounded by handrails. The current building was renovated in 1828, and the Yowoldae Pavilion was recently restored on the side.  The Hanbyeokdang Pavilion was designated as a tangible cultural property of Jeollabuk-do Province, having an exquisite landscape chosen as one of the Eight Scenic Views of Jeonju known as “Hanbyeokcheonyeon,” indicating the fog on the rock. Together with the 	Gwanghallu Pavilion in Namwon and the Hanpungnu Pavilion in Muju, the Hanbyeokdang Pavilion is called the Three Pavilions in Honam. The pavilion does not look exactly the way it did in the past, but people of Jeonju love this place for its graceful appearance harmonized with the scenery of the Jeonjucheon Stream.

stories.title: Baramssoeneun-gil
stories.script: Baramssoeneun-gil is a forest path that extends about 3.4 km from the Hanbyeokgul Tunnel below the Hanbyeokdang Pavilion to Wonsaek Myeonghwa Village in Saekjang-dong. It is recommended for those who want to walk silently in nature. This path became well known after it was walked by the two main characters of a drama series called Twenty-Five, Twenty-One.  Baramssoeneun-gil was originally a railroad for the Jeolla Line, but the rail track was removed to turn the path into a walkway and a bicycle road. The Jeonjucheon Stream flows gently on the right side, and the Seungamsan Mountain stands firmly on the left side. While walking along this path, you can find many tourist attractions like the Hanbyeokgul Tunnel, Jeonju Eco Museum, Seungamsa Temple, Entrance to Chimyeongjasan Sanctuary, Jeonju World Peace Hall, and Gaksibawi Rock.  The green forest path appears on both sides after you pass the Entrance to the Chimyeongjasan Sanctuary. Full of cherry trees, ginkgo trees, maple trees, and zelkova trees, this beautiful path boasts beautiful flowers in the spring, cool shades in the summer, and gorgeous fall foliage in the fall.  Baramssoeneun-gil has the halfway point after the Chamsarang Mental Recuperation Center. You can come back from the halfway point by following the streamside of the Jeonjucheon Stream. You can appreciate the ripples shining under the sunlight, watch fish swimming, and touch silver grasses along the way. Baramssoeneun-gil is a refreshing place accompanied by the forest breeze and stream breeze.

stories.title: Gaksibawi Rock
stories.script: The Jeonjucheon Stream has many stories that flow along the waterway. One such story is a legendary story of ardent love and parting. The Gaksibawi Rock on the bank of the Jeonjucheon Stream in the middle of Baramssoeneun-gil is the very place.  In the early Joseon period, Yeonhwa, the daughter of the district magistrate, and Jeong Yong, the grandson of Minister Jeong, had a fateful encounter and got married. One day, Jeong Yong went hunting and died from an attack by an ox-sized tiger. His dead body was carried by the Jeonjucheon Stream. Yeonhwa saw the corpse of her husband and threw herself into the water. The place where Yeonhwa threw her body into the stream was called the Gaksibawi Rock.  The story of the Gaksibawi Rock appears in a literary work. It is an incomplete full-length novel by Choi Myung-hee titled Jemangmaega. Born in Jeonju, Choi became a leading author of contemporary literature and wrote epic novels like Honbul, Collapsing Light, and Manjong.  Jemangmaega is a novel that illustrates the Jeonjucheon Stream and the lives of people who rely upon the Jeonjucheon Stream. This novel tells a sad story of a beautiful bride who became the legend of the Gaksibawi Rock.  People who looked into the Jeonjucheon Stream felt heartbroken. The water reaching the skirt right underneath this Gaksibawi Rock collided with the steep cliff, scattering as vivid indigo color. Once the water reached the rock, it became so quiet as if it stopped flowing. Under the sunlight, the wave of water resembling the silver scales of fish shattered like a mirror, making the eyes dazzle. The flower palanquin arrived at this place just in time, precariously passing by the narrow path that barely existed on the side of the risky cliff. If one were to lose one’s footing, one would fall off the cliff and have one’s body smashed by the rock. Suddenly, the palanquin bearer turned his head. For some reason, the blue and quiet rapids of the stream underneath the cliff came into his eyes. Oh, the water is truly marvelous. And it happened in a moment. The moment the palanquin bearer looked away, the palanquin slipped and plunged into the rock, swirling right into the rapids. The bride did not float to the surface of the water. Only the shafts of the palanquin that bumped into the rock when falling from above the cliff left their traces on the dented rock. The lonely soul of the drowned is nowhere to be found. <Excerpt from Jemangmaega>  The mournful love story of Yeonhwa is still carried by the blue water flowing in the Jeonjucheon Stream.

stories.title: Jeonju Eco Museum
stories.script: Jeonju Eco Museum, located between Jeonju’s representative mountain Seungamsan in the back and Jeonjucheon Stream in the front, is a place for learning the history and ecosystem of the Jeonjucheon Stream. Children particularly love this place because they can see fireflies.  The first floor has Pain, Healing, and Memories of Jeonjucheon Stream, River and Its Ecosystem, Slender Shinner and Friends of Jeonjucheon Stream, Digital Pond, and Garden of Life (Doctor Fish, Aquarium) under the theme of “The Story of Lives in Jeonjucheon Stream.”  The Pain, Healing, and Memories of Jeonjucheon Stream introduces the stories of Jeonjucheon Stream until the end of the 1990s when water pollution was severe due to the Deokjinbo Reservoir and the Stream that became clean again through the natural river restoration project, In the Slender Shinner and Friends of Jeonjucheon Stream, there is an experience zone where you can closely observe the features and growth of slender shinners representing clean grade 1 water.  The second floor covers various life forms, from endangered otters to birds, mammals, insects, amphibians, and reptiles of Jeonjucheon Stream. The highlight is the Garden of Fireflies which introduces the types, ecology, and habitats of fireflies. You can see and experience live fireflies in the tank.  The unique exterior of Jeonju Eco Museum is also attracting attention. The front entrance is the mouth and the back entrance is the tail of the slender shinner. The flowing line of traditional eaves shows a harmony of tradition and modernity. Don’t forget to enjoy the architectural beauty of the building from outside.

stories.title: Hanbyeokgul Tunnel
stories.script: Hanbyeokgul is a tunnel built in 1931 by opening the Jeolla line between Jeonju and Namwon. The Jeollaseon line trains passed this tunnel for 50 years until the track relocated to the eastern part of Jeonju in 1981. At the time, the Jeollaseon railroad track started from the Iri Station and headed toward Namwon, passing Samnye, Deokjin, Jeonju Station where the current Jeonju City Hall used to be located, Omokdae, Imokdae, Hanbyeokgul, and Saekjang-dong along the lower west of Jungbawi Rock. In May 1981, the section between Dongsan and Shilli was relocated to the east of Jeonju and excluded from the main Jeollaseon line, closing down the old track from North Jeonju to Shilli.  Jeonju city government removed the track from the closed line and recreated it into a bicycle road currently known as Baramssoeneun-gil. It is designated as the Jeollabuk-do Tangible Cultural Heritage and has a high value as a modern cultural tradition.  Hanbyeokgul, beloved by Jeonju citizens, is filled with memories of citizens who visited here and took photos. Now thousands of tourists come here to take photos. Don't forget to capture the different atmospheres of the entrance and exit of the tunnel.

stories.title: Jaman Mural Village and Imokdae
stories.script: There are many mural villages in Korea. These villages are born as part of urban regeneration by beautifully decorating the deteriorated villages and adding stories to boost the pride of villagers. They have become a great touristic spots, and Jaman Mural Village is one of them.  Jaman Mural Village is located on the Seungamsan Hill between Jeonju Hanok Village and a road. Refugees settled down in this hillside town one after another during the Korean War and it became famous when murals were painted on houses as part of the 2012 Green Trail Project.  More meaningful about this village than murals is that it is the root of Joseon. Mokjo Yi An-sa, the forefather of Taejo Yi Seong-gye who found Joseon, lived here. The name of the village means that “descendants will flourish.” King Gojong granted the “Jaman Donggeumpyo,” a gold label for controlling entrance to protect Jaman-dong, and converted this home of forebears into a sacred place. You can still find the landmark stone in the village.  Next to the landmark stone, there is a mural of Prince Yi wu. Yi wu is the prince of misfortune who was taken to Japan and became the Japanese colonel under the Rule of the Joseon Royal Family during the Japanese colonial period. His body was returned to his home after ending his life from the Hiroshima atomic bomb, but the ancestral tablet remains at the Yasukuni Shrine. The mural of Prince Yi wu holds painful history we should never forget.  At the entrance of the village, you will find Imokdae. There is a monument on which King Gojong himself wrote the inscription, Mokjodaewanggugeoyuji, meaning that Mokjo Yi An-sa lived here. The monument was originally on the high ground east of Omokdae, but it was moved next to Omokdae in 1986 because of road construction. Now only Imokdae remains. Jaman Donggeumpyo and Imokdae are heritages instilled with King Gojong's effort to strengthen the faltering discipline and the spirit of the Joseon Dynasty.  Trails of narrow alleys are filled with murals of various themes. You can find the portraits of famous stars from Michael Jackson to Anne of Green Gables, Marilyn Monroe, and Mexican artist Frida Kahlo. There are paintings of fairy tales such as the Altair and the Vega missing each other as well as Pinocchio and Geppetto. Murals of ordinary people, like a grandma with a big smile who has a red basin over her head and a woman by the well will also catch the eyes of visitors.  The alleys are steep but murals painted in various styles with memories and innocence of childhood are a delight that will charm away the difficulty of an uphill. As you look around colorful artworks, you will reach the top of the village overlooking Hanok Village.  Jaman Mural Village is like a giant museum with excellent and well-kept murals. Make sure to take enough time to look around. And keep the message from the villagers in mind.  “Welcome to Jaman Village once left and forgotten. We hope the winding and steep walkways will be a place for making happy memories by helping and guiding each other. We hope each step you make is a chance to communicate with the loved one next to you.”

stories.title: Omokdae
stories.script: Jeonju, which became the cornerstone for the establishment of Joseon, has many historic sites. Omokdae is one of them. Designated as the Jeollauk-go monument, Omokdae is a pavilion you can encounter when you cross the pedestrian overpass from Jaman Mural Village to Hanok Village. The hill from Jeonju Hanok Village is slightly steep, but it is popular because you can enjoy the view of Hanok Village.  Omokdae is a place where Yi Seong-gye stopped to celebrate his victory on his way home from a war with Japanese invaders at Hwangsan Mountain in Unbong in 1380 at the end of the Goryeo Era. It is also a place where Mokjo, one of Yi’s forefathers, had once lived. Yi Seong-gye recited Daepungga sung by Yoo Bang who founded the Han Dynasty. In other words, he hinted at his ambition to build a new country. Jeong Mong-ju who noticed this went to the Mangyeongdae Overlook in Namgosanseong Fortress, and recited a poem about his concern for Goryeo.  After declaring the Korean Empire in 1897, King Gojong built a monument written with Taejogohwangjejupiryuji in his handwriting in 1900 while he was converting the roots of the imperial family into sanctuaries. This monument and pavilion are located next to Omokdae.  If you go up the hill to the top of Omokdae, you can see the magnificent view of the whole Jeonju Hanok Village. The hipped and gable roofs aligned against eaves create a friendly atmosphere, while straight alleys look neat and clean. From the new observatory on the hill headed toward Jeonjuhyanggyo Local Confucian School, you can see Moaksan Mountain from afar.  Omokdae also boasts a beautiful nightscape. Omokdae illuminating with lights and the night view of Hanok Village from Omokdae are noted for the scenic beauty.

stories.title: Hanok Village Dangsan Tree (Omokdae Dangsan Tree)
stories.audioTitle: Hanok Village Dangsan Tree (Omokdae Dangsan Tree)
stories.script: On the way from Hanok Village to Omokdae, you will find a zelkova tree that has been protecting the village for over 5,000 years. There is a sad story behind this Dangsan Tree.  One day, the parents that got the epidemic left their children and went deep into the mountain, worrying that they will spread the disease to their children. The brother went on a journey to find their parents and froze to death from the blizzard, and the sister also died waiting for her brother to come back. It is said that the tree grown from the spot where the sister died is the Omokdae Dangsan Tree. The village holds an ancestral rite on the first full-moon day to comfort the spirit of the sister and pray for the peace of the town.  If you write down your wish in a lucky bag and hang it under the Dangsan Tree, your wish will come true. The spirit of the zelkova tree may grant your prayer with the 500 years of energy.

stories.title: Deokjin Park
stories.script: Deokjin Park with the lake formed during the Goryeo Dynasty is a place that embraces the grace of Jeonju and holds the memories and daily lives of Jeonju citizens. It also hosts the Dano festival on May 5 of the lunar calendar.  The lake is covered with lotus in the early Summer and it offers a variety of attractions including a pavilion, bridge, artificial waterfall, Iris Garden, Wild Flower Hill, amusement park, waterside stage, and music waterfall. The landmarks of Deokjin Park are the Yeonhwagyo Bridge and Yeonhwajeong Pavilion. The Yeonhwagyo Bridge crossing the lake was originally a suspension bridge but was reborn as a stone bridge, blending curves and straight lines beautifully. The railing is decorated like a fence to add the beauty of Korea. As you walk along the Yeonhwagyo Bridge, you can see the Yeonhwajeong Pavilion, a Hanok library newly built on the artificial island in the middle. Seating down and reading a book in an elegant and refined library will make you feel like a person of taste.  Deokjin Park is beautiful all year round but in the early Summer, large green lotus leaves and colorful lotus petals that cover half of the lake create spectacular scenery. You also can’t miss the nightscape. When the darkness falls, Yeonhwagyo Bridge is filled with warm and romantic lights. Yellow lights over the bridge give the impression as if you are walking on water under the moonlight. You can enjoy the fascinating night view of Yeonhwagyo Bridge and Yeonhwajoeng Pavilion over gentle water every night and all year round.

stories.title: Jeonju Arboretum
stories.script: Jeonju Arboretum is more beautiful and lush than any other arboreta. You can walk around the arboretum all day long to enjoy the plants and flowers.  Operated by the Korea Expressway Corporation, Jeonju Arboretum is Korea’s only arboretum run by a public company. It was built in the 1970s to restore the nature damaged during the road construction. 20 themed gardens including the aquatic botanical garden, rose garden, Mugunghwa garden, bamboo garden, the garden of southern plants, herbal garden, and rock garden span over an area of 290,000㎡. The most popular place is the rose garden. Tens of thousands of roses are in full bloom against elegant and antique sculptures that remind of Hanok Village to create unique beauty.  Jeonju Arboretum has eight sceneries you cannot miss for each season. Scenery 1 is the fringe tree path covered with white flower blossoms in Spring, and Scenery 2 is the Western garden with a variety of flowers by season. Scenery 3 is the hanging garden made of a stylish glass house. Scenery 4 is the bamboo garden where you can walk along the bamboo and forget about the worries of daily life. Scenery 5 is the scenic aquatic botanical garden with various aquatic plants. Scenery 6 is the grass garden where zinnia flowers are in full bloom in Summer, and Scenery 7 is the landmark square that catches your eyes with purple alliums. And lastly, Scenery 8 is the mountain stream garden with beautiful fall leaves that should not be missed in Fall.  Jeonju Arboretum also hosts the Garden Expo every September. Various programs such as busking, bubble show, magic show, mime show, gardening experience, and flea market add excitement to the event.  Jeonju Arboretum operates the “Jeonju Arboretum in My Hands” content for visitors to enjoy the beautiful sceneries and stories of plants through 360-degree VR videos. Visitors can watch VR videos using QR codes found across the arboretum.  Enjoy and experience various plants at Jeonju Arboretum, a healing place in the city. Tranquil and refreshing plants will comfort your tired body and mind.

stories.title: Jeonju National Museum
stories.script: Museums nowadays are transforming from solemn and formal spaces for viewing exhibitions and studying history into open spaces of history and culture where anyone can have a relaxing and pleasant time; and so is Jeonju National Museum.  Opened in 1990 to study, preserve, and exhibit cultural heritages of the Jeollabuk-do area, Jeonju National Museum has been leading its role as a national museum by possessing and exhibiting about 40,000 artifacts, including the cultural heritages of the prehistoric era and Mahan and Baekje period excavated in the Jeollabuk-do area, Buddhist arts, potteries, metal objects, and historical folk materials. But due to its narrow and complicated structure, the place was far from a general museum. In 2021, the permanent exhibition hall was completely renovated with visual images to experience the history in more fun and interesting way.  The “History Hall” of the permanent exhibition hall on the first floor exhibits the history of Jeollabuk-do from the Old Stone Age to the Joseon Dynasty period, and the “Jeonju and Royal Families of the Joseon Dynasty” exhibits the culture of the royal families of Joseon rooted in Jeonju.  You can see the works of famous calligraphers of Korea and China in the “Scholar’s Calligraphy Hall” and enjoy premium cultural heritages related to Buddhist arts, potteries, and crafts of Korea and Jeollabuk-do. On the second floor, you can watch videos that show the beauty of Jeollabuk-do and Jeonju. The Children’s Museum is popular among children as it offers a place for experiencing the civil service exam of the past, Sarangbang education and more.  In the newly renovated lobby on the first floor, you can enjoy the view of the garden while drinking warm tea. A nation that forgets its past has no future. Learn the history and culture of Jeollabuk-do and Jeonju at Jeonju National Museum, a great place to study history and take a rest.

stories.title: Jeonju Museum of History
stories.script: In any city, visiting a museum is the start and end of a history trip. Jeonju Museum of History, which shows how Jeonju has progressed in its long history, is the right place to start a historical journey in Jeonju.  Jeonju Museum of History opened in May 2002 is a museum that collects, manages, and exhibits over 10,000 historic and cultural artifacts of Jeonju. It discovers the regional content and operates various educational programs for citizens to establish local pride and identity.  The exhibition space is classified into the Jeonju History Hall which exhibits artifacts from the prehistoric era to the modern age; Jeonju Culture and Art Hall which looks into the culture of Jeonju through hanji, publication culture, food, sound, and paintings and calligraphic works of Jeonju; and Donghak Peasant Revolution Hall that shows the spirit and ideology of the Donghak peasant movement.  Meet the glorious history of Jeonju at the Jeonju Museum of History keeping on the tradition and pride of Jeonju.

stories.title: Korea Traditional Culture Center
stories.script: A tall, refined modern building in the heart of downtown Jeonju catches your eyes. It's the Korea Traditional Culture Center. The Korea Traditional Culture Center is a facility for connecting the dynamically-changing traditional culture of Korea to the modern and next generations and recreating future values instead of limiting the culture to the time, people, and region.  The center consists of the Hanji Project Support Center, Traditional Culture Creation Center, Creative Korean Food Center, Craft Exhibition Hall, Playground Marudal, and Jeonju Cheonnyeon Hanji Hall. You can enjoy various experiences, exhibitions, and programs from making hanji to cooking traditional Jeonju food.  Tradition is a valuable asset to preserve and inherit in terms of learning the old and finding the new. Even if you haven't had a chance to visit the Jeonju National Museum or Jeonju Museum of History, make sure to visit the Korea Traditional Culture Center to feel the traditional beauty, taste, and excitement of Jeonju.

stories.title: National Intangible Heritage Center
stories.script: The spirit of artists and the brilliant skills of masters shine brightly at the National Intangible Heritage Center. Intangible heritage is a cultural heritage spanning oral tradition and expression, performance art, ceremony, festival, and traditional craft. Korea’s intangible heritages registered in UNESCO include the royal ancestral ritual in the Jongmyo shrine and its music, pansori epic chant, Gangneung Danoje festival, Ganggangsullae, Taekkyeon, Arirang, Kimjang, Nongak, and more.  The National Intangible Heritage Center located by the riverside of Jeonjucheon Stream is a place for organizing, preserving, and passing down these intangible assets. You can see how people never lost the relaxed attitude toward life against natural environments and adversities and elevated in the form of art in the Permanent Exhibition Hall 1 consisting of traditional performances, arts, rituals, ceremonies, traditional plays, martial arts, and traditional knowledge. 3D projection mapping that projects videos made of light related to music, dance, and festivals on the target surface makes the experience more realistic.  In the pavilion, visitors can enjoy the arts in nature on a large screen along with instruments and musical notes. The five Pansori chants are shared through the interactive sensor and multi-digital mapping for a more live experience. Visitors also can enjoy Cheoyongmu of the past and today.  The Permanent Exhibition Hall 2 for displaying the works of those with craft and artistic accomplishment is even more interesting. It reminds us that there are so many brilliant and interesting intangible heritages, such as court embroidered Hwarot which was used as a ceremonial costume for the princesses of the Joseon Dynasty, the Jinju Geommu costumes worn by the Jinju Geommu Society, and the Cheoyong mask worn by master Kim Jung-seop.  The National Intangible Heritage Center uses immersive content for visitors to get more familiar with and enjoy national intangible cultural heritages. Intangible cultural heritages are something that cannot be touched, but you can feel, touch, and experience them here. The National Intangible Heritage Center opened its door in 2014 and therefore is not well-known, but considering its grand size and content, it is a place not to be missed. Epitomizing the intangible heritages of Korea, this center could be the highlight of your Jeonju trip

stories.title: JIFF Film Street
stories.script: Every spring, quiet Jeonju becomes boisterous. It's because the Jeonju International Film Festival (JIFF) that invites the movie people from all around the world is held. Started in 2000, the JIFF is a festival for introducing alternative films, digital films, and independent films of Asia that break the common notions and ideas on films instead of mainstream films.  When the JIFF begins, red lights symbolizing the festival fill the JIFF Film Street and “Jeonju Dome” specially installed during the festival period plays unique and high-quality independent films. Visitors can also enjoy shopping at booths that sell the JIFF goods.  At other times, it is a popular place with famous stores, restaurants, and cafes beloved by young people like Hongdae and Gyeongnidan Street in Seoul. On weekends, artists in Jeonju participate in the festival to show musical, dance, and busking performances, and young entrepreneurs gather and open a flea market for selling handmade souvenirs.  As its name suggests, there are many cinemas including CGV. Originally, it was a famous cinema street, having 15 theaters from the mid-1980s to the mid-1990s. After the Korea Cinema and Samnam Cinema opened in 1963, small and large cinemas were built and became the hub of local culture for showing various performances, including plays, classic and popular music, and traditional Korean music in addition to the screening of films. They are all gone now when a multiplex cinema entered in the early 2000s, but their vestiges remain and lead the JIFF.  There is a “Guide Map of Old Jeonju Cinemas” at the entrance of the street. It guide the pictures and map of old cinemas, bringing good memories for Jeonju citizens and creating a retro mood for tourists.

stories.title: Ajunghosu Lake
stories.script: Only a few years ago, Ajunghosu Lake located in Inhu-dong was called Ajung Reservoir or Ingyo Reservoir. This large reservoir was recreated into a resting place for citizens and its name was changed to Ajunghosu Lake when the supply of agricultural water decreased with urbanization.  The waterside trail around the lake is a great place to stroll. When you walk along the trail, all kinds of thoughts whirling around in your mind become calm like the placid waters of the lake.  The beauty of Ajunghosu Lake can be found in the morning. A wet fog over the lake creates a mystical landscape. The lights are lit along the trail at night and create a special mood. A soft glow of lights is reflected on the water, making the lake look even more romantic. Ajunghosu Lake which shows different sceneries from morning to night is one of the spots of Jeonju that attract both local residents and tourists.

stories.title: Donggosa Temple
stories.script: Donggosa Temple is a Buddhist temple of Taego Order nested in Seungamsan Mountain. It is named Donggosa because it is located in the east of Jeonju. It is one of the temples that Doseon Guksa established in north, south, east, and west of Jeonju in 876. It is said that the second prince of Gyeongsun of Silla trained himself spiritually to soothe the sorrow of losing the country after Gyeongsun of Silla surrendered to King Taejo of Goryeo. The prince carved the figures of five people including his parents and Prince Maui on the trees and enshrined them in Donggosa Temple.  Donggosa Temple was burnt down during the Imjin War against Japan, but Monk Heoju rebuilt it in 1844. In 1946, Monk Yeongdam newly built the Main Hall to have the integrity of now.  The temple houses are lined up around the Main Hall as if birds are spreading their wings. The halls were built one by one along the mountain bend to preserve nature. The prayer room, Simwudang Hall, Samseonggak Hall, and bell are built around the Main Hall, arranged in a form of a lotus flower in bloom.  Although Donggosa Temple is not a large temple, it is worth a visit because you can find portraits of high priests and the wooden panel with Buddhist images in relief. You can also enjoy the picturesque view of downtown Jeonju from here.

stories.title: Chimyeongjasan Sanctuary
stories.script: Nested in the slope of Seungamsan Mountain, this Catholic pilgrimage place is called the Chimyeongjasan Sanctuary. Chimyoengjasan means the mountain of the “people who sacrificed their life.” Yoo Jung-cheol (Joannes), the son of Yoo Hang-geom who propagated the Catholicism in the Honam area in 1784 and was executed as a political offender, and his wife Lee Sun-yi (Lutgarda) were martyred during the Catholic Persecution and buried under the top of the mountain. The couple are famous for dying after keeping virginity for four years for a devout religious life. The mountain is also called as Lutgarda named after Lee Sun-yi’s baptismal name.  Under the graves of the martyrs, there is a memorial church that stands on the rock. This church built with granite is praised as the best Catholic church in Korea with mosaic fresco design. “The Way to Golgotha Cross” from the entrance of the sanctuary to this church is filled with flowers and it is considered as the best pilgrimage route and trail.  Above the graves, there are strange rock called Jesus and Mary rock and the cross.
