The serpent, finding her lover whom she had not forgotten even in her dreams, wrapped her body around the young man as if she were complaining. However, the young man was so engrossed in the practice that he did not even realize that the serpent was wrapped around him. After a while, the young man who felt something wrong with his body opened his eyes and tried to move around but couldn't.  The serpent around his body said,   “I was your lover. I died waiting for you and couldn't go to the afterlife, so I came here as a serpent. I still want to be with you even after death. I won't leave this world without you. Let's become serpents together and go to the otherworld with me. Let's live together there.”  In spite of the serpent's earnest plea, the young man continued to recite Buddhist scriptures. He couldn't give up his practice for the love of a woman. The serpent, who believed that she could not break the will of her beloved lover, slowly unwound her body. After falling off the young man's body, the serpent disappeared away.  Soon the sun rose and the day was bright. Climbing up a large rock, the young man stared down the sea as if he had washed away his agony from the night before. After looking at it for a while, he looked around and found a serpent lying dead under a rocky cliff.  It was only then that the young man realized that the woman he had left in his hometown had died, and that she had come to visit him last night and asked him to be together even if they were to die together. The young man held a rite for his lover who had passed away while longing for him. He named this rock the Sangsaam Rock and appeased the woman's spirit.

stories.title: Stone Pagoda of Buseoksa Temple
stories.audioTitle: Bonghwangsan Mountain in Andong, Gyeongsangbuk-do / Stone Pagoda of Buseoksa Temple
stories.script: A stone pagoda built with stolen offering  There is Hakgasan Mountain, which rises behind the village of Cheonji in Jeapum-ri, Seohu-myeon, Andong-si, Gyeongsangbuk-do, is the highest peak in Andong with a height of 882 m. It is situated on the boundary of three different counties, Andong, Yecheon, and Youngju. In Hakgasan Mountain, there is Neungingul Cave, where Neungindosa trained for 10 years in the Shilla Dynasty. Clear stone water sprung from this Neungingul Cave, which was a mysterious cave that did not decrease in volume no matter how severe the droughts were.  There is Buseoksa Temple in Bonghwangsan Mountain in Yeongju, 78 km away from Neungingul Cave. Buseoksa Temple is famous for its numerous cultural assets and treasures. It was a huge temple where 3,000 monks practiced asceticism. One day, a quarrel broke out between Neungindosa and the monks of Buseoksa Temple, and as a result, a huge stone pagoda was built in the valley north of Hakgasan Mountain.  What had happened between Neungindosa and the monks of Buseoksa Temple? As there were as many as 3,000 monks living in Buseoksa Temple, making food offerings was a big deal. Each monk had to be served rice, side dishes, and spoons. Thus, the bodhisattvas were always on alert to prepare all the meals.  In the offering time in one morning, upon discovering that a bowl of rice was empty, a monk requested more. Bodhisattva who prepared the offering said that it was provided correctly. That evening, however, the bowl of rice that had been missing that morning was missing again. Likewise, the bowl of rice continued to be missing the next day and the day after that.  Suspicion began to spread among the monks, and disputes arose. In the end, they turned to the high monk, told him the story and asked for a solution.   “There is nothing wrong about it. When a bowl of offering is missing, it means that somebody has eaten it. But the thief is not in the temple. The one who has been eating the offering at Buseoksa Temple is Neungindosa of Hakgasan Mountain, 78 km to the south from here.”   Hearing this, the monks went to see Neungindosa. They were each holding a stone in their hands.  Neungindosa, who had anticipated this, appeared in front of the monks as he performed a magic trick when they reached the mountain's northern ridge.  He laughed and said,   “Thieves are said to have one sin, while losers are said to have ten. Have the losers come to punish me?” When the angry monks tried to hit him with stones, Neungindosa widened his eyes and scolded them in a more stern voice. “As monks, we forbid killing and seek mercy. What kind of insolence is this? Instead of being upset for the stolen offering, you should rather provide offerings to the others. Do you want to kill like the people of the world because your food is taken away?”  The monks of Buseoksa Temple had an epiphany from the harsh rebuke of Neungindosa and built a pagoda from all the stones they brought together. This pagoda stands across the valley north of Hakgasan Mountain, and it remains as a huge natural stone pagoda with 16 meters in length and 15 meters in height.

stories.title: Guryong Village
stories.script: The village where nine dragons ascended to the sky  Maenam-ri, Yongseong-myeon, Gyeongsan-si, Gyeongsangbuk-do is a mountain village located in the mid-slope of Guryongsan Mountain. It is composed of natural villages such as Maeam, Jangjae, Gamangol, and Guryong. “Maeam,” also known as Maenam, is named because there is Maebawi Rock. “Jangjae” is a name created by a scholar named Park, who wished a longevity and talent when a person is born. Jang means longevity and Jae means talent. “Gamangol” is located in a deep mountain valley. The name was given for the reason that it could hardly be seen due to its long distance. It was the last village that was formed in this area. “Guryong” was named because it is located at the bottom of Guryongsan Mountain. The following story is told about its name.  Once upon a time, the Dragon King of the East Sea had three daughters. The queen, the mother of three daughters, suddenly died one day due to an illness. The sad Dragon King married to a new queen shortly after. However, the new queen mistreated the daughters of the ex-wife every time she had a chance. The Dragon King felt sorry and sent his youngest daughter to live on land.  “It hurts to let you go, but watching you here is just as painful. Find a good place on the land and control the rain and clouds there.” The youngest daughter comforted her father while shedding tears. “Don't worry, father. I will do my duty as a great dragon.”  Upon coming up to the mainland, the youngest daughter searched for a good place to live, but couldn't find anywhere suitable. She liked Geumgangsan Mountain, but the Dragon King's brother already lived there. Turning her eyes, she traveled south along the Taebaeksan Mountain range. She finally found a mountain with thick trees and grass, a wide and flat top, full of good energy. The youngest daughter, who thought this was the perfect place, started living on the mountain.  She governed clouds and rain, and got married and gave birth to nine dragons. The nine dragons occasionally gave birth to clouds and sprinkled rain as they grew bigger. But there was a troublemaker among the nine dragons. It was the youngest one.  All the other siblings were filial and listened to their mother, but the youngest son was particularly mischievous. She coaxed him and scolded him, but he did not fix his behavior. Finding him unbearable, she asked her father, the Dragon King of the East Sea, to punish him.  Hearing this, the Dragon King summoned his youngest daughter, who had suffered a lot in the human world, to the dragon palace. He sent the nine dragons to the wider world of heaven to be in charge of rain and clouds there. After leaving his home and living in a new place, the youngest dragon missed his mother and hometown, shedding tears as he reflected on his actions.  However, he didn’t do his job properly and only longed for his hometown. Eventually, he made the Dragon Kim upset, got ill and died. Later, people called the mountain where the nine dragons lived “Guryongsan Mountain,”meaning the Nine Dragon Mountain, and named the village at the foot of the Mountain “Guryong.” At the top of Guryongsan Mountain, “Mujiteo,” a spring where dragons lived, is still said to exist.

stories.title: Hwanggeumsan Mountain
stories.script: The coastal waters of Hwanggeunsan Mountain where the yellow croakers disappeared  There is a mountain called Hwanggeumsan in Dokgot-ri, Daesan-eup, Seosan-si, Chungcheongnam-do. Originally, it was called “Hanggeumsan Mountain,” but as gold was discovered in the mountain, it was called “Hwanggeumsan Mountain.” Hwanggeumsan Mountain was initially an island, but it became connected to the mainland.  As there were many yellow croakers in the offshore of Hwanggeumsan Mountain, most of the villagers made a living by catching them. At the top of Hwanggeumsan Mountain, there was even a shrine where rites were conducted to pray for the safe return of boats fully loaded with fish. Until the mid-1900s, boats were full of yellow croakers, but for some reason, they began to disappear, and the rites were not held and forgotten ever since. Since 1996, the shrine was restored as “Hwanggeumsansa Temple,” and rites have been held every spring. But why did all the yellow croakers disappear? The story of yellow croakers disappearing off the coast of Hwanggeumsan Mountain has been passed down for generations in Seosan and nearby areas.  As the number of fishes in the coastal waters gradually decreased, more and more people began to leave the village.  The remaining villagers lived in worries. Then one day, a blue dragon appeared in Park Hwal-ryang’s dream and said, “I am the Blue Dragon of the sea in front of Hwanggeumsan Mountain. The number of fishes decreased because the Yellow Dragon of Hwanghae-do drove away all the yellow croakers to Yeonpyeongdo Island.  I will fight the Yellow Dragon in the field in front of the village and have them back.”   Park Hwal-ryang told the story of his dream to the villagers. The people wished that the Blue Dragon would win in the fight so that they can catch the fish again.  Days later, the Blue Dragon appeared again in Park's dream and said, “In a few days, I will fight the Yellow Dragon in the field in front of the village. But I can't defeat the Yellow Dragon on my own.  You must come and help me. When I fight with the Yellow Dragon, aim at me and shoot your bow.”  Park Hwal-ryang was the best archer in the village.  After repeatedly asking him to aim at himself, the Blue Dragon disappeared. Park was puzzled by the Blue Dragon's request to aim at him, but he decided to give it a try and went out to the field on the day the Blue Dragon were to fight the Yellow Dragon. Soon after, the two dragons appeared and began to fight. Park Hwal-ryang prepared to shoot with his bow and arrows. But at that moment, he thought to himself.  ‘I have never missed an arrow. If I shoot an arrow at the Blue Dragon as he told me, he will die right away. If that happens, this village will be unable to catch the fish forever. I can't let it happen. Let's just shoot the Yellow Dragon.” He made up his mind, aimed at the Yellow Dragon and made his shot.  At that moment, the Yellow Dragon twisted his body, making the arrow to hit the Blue Dragon straight on. After the Blue Dragon was struck by an arrow and died on the spot, Park finally understood what the Blue Dragon had meant. Although he regretted it, there was no way of undoing his mistake. Since then, it is said that no yellow croakers have been caught in the coastal waters of Hwanggeumsan Mountain.  It is said that the Blue Dragon appeared again later in Park's dream and said, “If the Hwanggeumsan Mountain turns green three times, you will find yellow croakers again.” According to the villagers, it has been green twice so far. When will the mountain turn green for the last time? Will yellow croakers really come back like the Blue Dragon said?

stories.title: Daejeon Flower Village
stories.audioTitle: Daejeon Flower Village, where the daughter-in-law baked flower skewers and offered them to her father-in-law
stories.script: Kkotjeokgol is a valley between Cheongeun Village in Munhwa-dong, Jung-gu, Daejeon and 88 Park, and it has the following legend. Once upon a time, there was an old man living with his daughter-in-law in Kkotjeokgol. The old man was in poor health, so her daughter-in-law worked hard every day to get food for him. “Father, are you hungry? Just wait a minute. I’ll make you a delicious salad today.” “Father, I finished work early today. My boss gave me a piece of fish thanking me for the hard work. I will bake it right away.” “Father, today I went to the neighboring village where there was a party celebrating the 70th birthday of one of your friends.” When the daughter-in-law came back from work, she would always tell her father-in-law who was lying in the room all day what she had seen. “You are suffering so much because of me. It would be better off for me to die soon so you can live in comfort. Why is it so hard to die!” “Father, don’t talk like that. I can live because of you. I'm so sorry that I couldn't even throw a 70th birthday party for you like your friend did.” “My daughter, don’t say such things. I'm having my party every day. It's a feast to be able to eat like this every day thanks to you.” “I'm very sorry and feel ashamed.” The old man and his daughter-in-law exchanged these words and tried to live every day with satisfaction, although they barely made ends meet.  One year, the drought was so severe that it was impossible to find a work. The daughter-in-law did not tell her father-in-law that she couldn't get a job, fearing that her father-in-law would be worried. After leaving her house quietly, she climbed a mountain to pick some flower petals. She picked out flowers that her father-in-law would like. “Father, today I went to the mountain to pick some flowers and make you some skewers. Please wait a little.” “The smell of making skewers is good. With flowers on top, it must be even more delicious!” “Yes, please wait a moment.” “Here, try it. How does it taste?” “You are a good cook. It's savory and has a floral scent. It's very delicious.” “What a relief that you enjoyed it.” The old man and his daughter-in-law happily ate the food.  A few months passed and the father-in-law passed away. Before his departure from life, he called his daughter-in-law and said, “I have buried a gold tray under that mountain rock. In the distant future, if a female Buddhist monk comes looking for that tray, please tell her where it is. And it would be nice to receive her teachings. My child, thank you for all the things you have done for me. Even if I go to the other world, I will never forget what you did.” She cried and responded that she would do as he told her. Three years after the father-in-law's death and funeral, a female Buddhist monk visited the house. “I came here to find out where the golden tray is buried,” the monk said while bowing her head. The daughter-in-law, bowing her head as well, said “You must be the one my father-in-law talked about.” She guided the monk to where the gold tray is buried. The Buddhist monk dug a little under the rock and took out a golden tray. The gold plate was in its original form. While rolling her rosary, she said, “You are truly a high Buddha!” Then suddenly, the golden plate floated high into the sky, giving off an incredibly bright and beautiful light. The light dazzled the daughter-in-law so much that she could not see open her eyes. The Buddhist monk and the gold tray disappeared, and the daughter-in-law turned into a stone Buddha on the spot. Afterwards, the villagers called the stone Maitreya, and the village “Kkotjeokgol or “Kkotjeok Village” because it was the place where the daughter-in-law used flowers to make skewers for her father-in-law.

stories.title: Giringogae Pass
stories.script: The hill where Maeng Sa-seong met a black giraffe  In Jung-ri, Baebang-eup, Asan-si, Chungcheongnam-do, there was a place called Giringogae, meaning the Giraffe Pass. It was called the Giringogae Pass because it was the place where the black giraffe, which Maeng Sa-seong rode, appeared. Maeng Sa-seong, along with Hwang Hui and Park Soo-ryang, is widely known as the three great uncorrupted government officials of Joseon. Maeng Sa-seong lived in where Jung-ri is now after quitting his work.  Currently in this village, there is Asan Maengssi Haengdan House. “Haengdan” comes from the anecdote of Confucius who taught his disciples under a ginkgo tree, which generally refers to a place where one devotes himself to learning. Maeng also planted a ginkgo tree in his house and taught his disciples, so it was called the Asan Maengssi Haengdan House.  When Maeng traveled to Hanyang, he rode a black cow. Usually, a state councilor of Joseon Dynasty rode on a palanquin carried by four people. Maeng Sa-seong, however, despite his high official title as state councilor, always maintained a frugal lifestyle, saying, “Everyone lives a hard life. I cannot live comfortably.”  When Maeng returned home from the courthouse one day after completing his work, he was reading a book. When he went out for a walk, he saw a black mountain beast heading towards Seolhwasan Mountain, the mountain in front of the village. A group of young men climbing the mountain to collect firewood also discovered this beast. The beast had never been seen before, so they tried to catch it. When the beast became angry, it rushed towards the young men, who brandished sticks to stop it.  Maeng Sa-seong saw this and ran towards it, thinking something terrible might happen. When Maeng Sa-seong appeared, the startled young men bowed, and the mountain beast stopped attacking and circled around him like a puppy meeting its owner. “You shouldn't mistreat even the wild animal. Now, go away and collect firewood,” said Maeng to the young men. He petted the wild beast and headed home.   Then, the animal begin to follow Maeng Sa-seong. As Maeng Sa-seong saw the mountain beast following him, he decided to keep it at home. Maeng told the servants, “Never mistreat it, and you should take good care of it.”  The mountain beast that lived in Maeng Sa-seong's house grew into a tall black giraffe. The black giraffe was docile and behaved well, especially with Maeng Sa-seong. Since then, Maeng always rode the black giraffe when he traveled to Hanyang. Later, people called the pass where Maeng Sa-seong and the black giraffe first met the Giringogae Pass.   It is known that Maeng Sa-seong actually rode a black cow. Maybe it was a cow that looked like a giraffe. After Maeng Sa-seong passed away, the black cow is said to have cried sadly for several days at the tomb of Maeng Sa-seong and died. People gave a funeral for the black cow who was loyal to the owner and died together. They made a tomb near the grave of Maeng Sa-seong, which is called “Heukgichong.” It is located about 10 m to the left from the entrance of the Tomb of Maeng Sa-seong in Gwangju, Gyeonggi-do. If you visit the tomb, take a look around the tomb to find Heukgichong.

stories.title: Uirimji Reservoir
stories.script: Reservoir created by the collapse of a wealthy family  There is a wide and deep reservoir called Uirimji in Mosan-dong, Jecheon-si, Chungcheongbuk-do. Uirimji Reservoir is one of the three major irrigation facilities built during the Three Hans period. It is a cultural heritage that shows the development of agricultural technology. The rice fields around Jecheon still use water from Uirimji Reservoir. In addition, the landscape created by pavilion and grove is so beautiful that it has been designated as the scenic site No. 20. Uirimji Reservior holds a sad legend.  There lived a very rich man in Mosan-dong, Jecheon. One day, a monk came to the the rich man's house and asked for alms. The greedy rich man ignored him. But the monk persistently asked for alms. The rich man was angry and poured manure into the monk's alms bag. The monk who had been given manure turned away without saying anything. “Father, how could you give manure to him?” Said the rich man's daughter-in-law, and she came out with a scoop of rice.  “Sir, leave the manure and take this rice. I ask for your forgiveness on behalf of my father-in-law.” “Thank you very much. Please get out of the house and follow me. No matter what you hear, never look back!” Keeping those words in mind, the daughter-in-law silently followed the monk. As the monk and daughter-in-law climbed the hill, a loud bang came from the village. The daughter-in-law was very curious. However, because of the monk's words to never look back, she wasn't sure whether it was okay to look back. It seemed that the loud noise was coming from close to the house, so she couldn't hold it anymore. She turned around.  It was then that the house she lived in collapsed, filling with water and becoming a blue lake. And the daughter-in-law who turned around became a stone. It is said that on the mountain the daughter-in-law climbed, there is a rock in the shape of the daughter-in-law. It is also said that if you look closely at the water at Uirimji Reservoir, you could see pieces of earthen pots.

stories.title: Beomgol Village
stories.script: A village where a hunter raised a tiger cub On the hill road from Ho-dong, Jung-gu to Daemyeong-dong, Daejon, there is a village called Beomgol. Once upon a time, there lived a strong and clever hunter in Beomgol. He liked hunting but he was not interested in farming at all, so he didn't even cultivate a small vegetable garden. And he never ate the meat of wild animals he hunted.  One day he visited an ill friend with a rabbit he had hunted. The hunter gave the rabbit to the friend. “That's the only thing I caught today. It's not big, but eat this and get well soon.” “Thank you for coming, and thank you for bringing me a precious rabbit.”  The friend who received the rabbit hesitated for a long time before saying: “I have a request for you.” “What is it? I'll do what I can.” “The doctors told me that my illness would be cured only by eating a tiger's foreleg.”  For a moment, the hunter stopped breathing when he heard the word tiger. Then he asked, “Did you just say a tiger?” “Yes, a tiger's foreleg.” “But why the tiger?” “I know it’s difficult for you.”  The hunter thought for a while. Then he said, “I’m worried because it’s been a while since I caught a tiger. But if you must eat a tiger’s foreleg to be healed, then you should. I get it. I will go and bring a tiger. Take a good care of yourself.” Then he left his friend’s house.  From the day, the hunter had looked for a tiger to cure his friend’s disease. One day, wandering in the mountain, he found a tiger. The tiger knew that the hunter was looking for him, so he went deep in the mountain and hid himself. The hunter reached a big cave, following the footprints of the tiger. He knew intuitively that the tiger was in this cave. He heard the roaring sound of several tigers in the cave. They were the mother tiger and the tiger cubs.  The hunter hid himself and waited for a tiger to come out. After several days passed, a big tiger came out, looked left and right, and ran somewhere. Seeing the opportunity, the hunter went inside the cave and brought out a tiger cub. When he was going back to the village, the mother tiger jumped onto him to save her cub. The hunter defeated the tiger with all his might and brought the tiger to his friend. The friend who ate the tiger's foreleg was miraculously cured.  When the hunter returned home, tiger cubs were hovering around the hunter's house. The hunter, who was feeling sorry for killing their mother, fed and raised them. He thought of the mother tiger that he killed and poured his heart into raising the cubs.  Watching this, village people told the hunter to leave the village. They said that if there are tiger cubs in the village, a big tiger would come and hurt the people. The hunter’s friend visited village people around and explained that it would never happen, but they did not listen to him. Seeing this, the hunter said, “There is nothing good about having tigers in the village. I have to take responsibility for what I did. I am going to the mountain with the tiger cubs and live there. I will visit you sometimes,” and went into the mountain.   The hunter, who went into the mountain with the tiger cubs, lived in the cave. It is said that from then on, he didn’t hunt, and farmed by planting the mountain. As time passed, villagers called the place “Beomgol,” meaning the tiger valley.

stories.title: Gullebawi Rock
stories.script: Cursed Gullebawi Rock of the propitious site There is a village in Ssangdeok-ri, Gundong-myeon, 4 km southeast of Gangjin-eup. This village is on the way to Maryang-myeon, and it was called Ssangdeok-ri because there were two villages in the place, Pyeongdeok Village and Gwandeok Village. There is Gullebawi Rock in Pyeongdeok Village which has a sad legend. Gullebawi Rock was also referred to as “Guyubawi” or “Gusibawi.” In other places, it is also dubbed the Janggobawi because it looks like Janggu.  Gullebawi Rock stands tall in the middle of the rice fields in front of the village. It is made up of two large rocks. The distance between the two rocks is 1 meter. The height of the bigger rock is 2 meters, and that of the small rock is about 1.8 meters. These rocks used to be one rock in the old days.  According to geomancy, the rock represents a trough for cows’ food. It is said that the mountain of the Bae clan is located about 100 m behind this rock, which resembles a cow's head, and the streams nearby resemble cow reins. Three hundred years ago, this village had many people from the Bae clan, but now, there is only one household left. The rest of the villagers are from the Kim and Wi clans. Where did all the people of Bae clan go? And why did Gullebawi Rock split in two?  According to legend, this is what happened.  Once upon a time, there lived a boy named Kim In-seon in this village. Everyone envied the boy's good looks and his excellent academic performance. He crossed the river to go to school in town which was about 4 km away. On the way home one spring day, he met a pretty girl for the first time. This girl secretly flirted with the boy. She began to seduce the boy more and more every day. The girl begin to boldly seduce him, such as hugging him and rubbing her cheeks against him.  It embarrassed him at first, but he didn't hated it, so he let her do what she liked. She even kissed him without hesitation. The boy, however, begin to become thinner and thinner every day. Even in school, he often dozed off. Finding this strange, the school's headmaster called the boy to ask why. Despite not telling anyone in the meantime, the boy revealed everything when the headmaster asked him kindly.  The headmaster surprised after hearing his story. He was certain that a 100-year-old fox was trying to steal the spirit of the boy in disguise as a girl. In order to prevent him from being shocked, the headmaster explained clearly and told the boy what he had to do.   “In-seon! That girl is stealing your spirit. You will die eventually if you don't get off her. You will notice a bead on the tip of her tongue when she kisses you. Immediately after the bead enters your mouth, push her away, take off your shoe, and hit her on the back of the head.”  He met the girl on his way home that day. When she kissed him, he did what the headmaster told him to do. Then the girl fell down on the ground and turned into a white fox. It was so shocking to the boy that he lost consciousness. And he swallowed the bead without even knowing it.  On the next day, the headmaster came to him and asked to show him the bead, but it had already been swallowed. In a very sorry tone, the headmaster said:  “The bead you swallowed is a treasure. With the bead, you will understand all the principles of the universe. Since you swallowed it and fell to the ground, you will one day become a famous governor.”  Perhaps because of the bead he swallowed, the boy grew up to become a famous governor. When his father passed away, he looked around himself to find a place for grave. After walking around the mountain for a while, he found a place that he thought was a propitious site.  Kim In-seon dug a grave pit on the spot so that no one else could use it. After the father’s funeral, Kim In-seon went to the place to bury him. But the pit was filled with water inside.  There wasn't any rain. It seemed very weird, but since he couldn’t bury his father in water, he found another spot.  Meanwhile, Kim In-seon had a younger sister who married into the Bae clan. After the funeral of his father, his younger sister said that she had a favor for her brother. “As you know, we are in a difficult situation where we cannot find a burial site, let alone a good one. I would like to bury my father-in-law at the grave site that you dug to bury our father. Could you give it to me since it's the site of the grave that's already been dug?”  Kim In-seon agreed because it was his younger sister's request. But as it turned out, his younger sister was trying to take over the spot.  Knowing that the place was a propitious site, the younger sister, wishing to bury her father-in-law and be blessed, poured water into the pit. The Bae clan, who buried the father-in-law in the propitious site, became very wealthy.  One day, a mendicant monk came and stood at the door of the sister’s house, who became wealthy, asking for alms. There way no way that the mean younger sister would be willing to give alms.  Instead of offering alms, she drove the monk away by saying all sorts of harsh words. After receiving such poor treatment, the monk left the gate and muttered to himself.   “I don’t know whose grave it is but it’s a shame that if you break that big rock in front of the grave and get rid of it, you'll be even richer.”  The younger sister, who had been driving the monk out, heard this and immediately took a worker and broke the rock. When they cracked the rock open, a pair of blue birds flew out of the rock. The bluebirds circled the village and fell into the lotus embankment 700 m below the rock and died. After that, the younger sister's family slowly began to fall apart. The rock that the younger sister broke was the Gullebawi Rock that symbolized cow’s trough. As punishment for the younger sister's excessive greed, the monk split the Gullebawi Rock in half, symbolizing the abundance.

stories.title: Hwajinpo Lake
stories.script: The site of the house of the rich miser Lee Hwa-jin that turned into a lake  Hwajinpo Lake, located next to Hwajinpo Beach in Gangwon-do, is a lagoon where seawater and freshwater intersect. The lake circumference is 16 km, the largest one in Gangwon-do with beautiful scenery. Located in the sea off Hwajinpo Lake is Geumgudo Island, a small island where legend says the tomb of King Gwanggaeto the Great is located. There are rugosa rose flowers all around the lake. Eight Scenic Views of Hwajin selected by Kim Sat-gat in the late Joseon Dynasty include the waves of Geumgudo Island and rugosa rose flowers. It is a beautiful lake that attracts swans in winter, a natural monument.  There is an interesting legend about Hwajinpo Lake, designated as Gangwon-do Monument No. 10, about a miserly old man named Lee Hwa-jin and his kind daughter-in-law. Hwajinpo Lake is named after Lee Hwa-jin.  Long ago, there lived a father-in-law named Lee Hwa-jin and a kind daughter-in-law in Hwajinpo. One day, an old monk came to request for alms. Lee Hwa-jin, who was a miser, donated only a small amount of millet despite his barn being full of grain. After saying thank you, the monk went back to his monastery. Three years later, the monk came again. Lee Hwa-jin gave him a spoonful of millet this time. The monk again said thank you and prayed for the prosperity of his family. Three years later, the monk came again. Lee Hwa-jin hated the monk who kept visiting him, so he shoveled cow dung in the barn and donated it.  “I have nothing to give, so take this.” “Thank you. Save us, merciful Buddha, Bodhisattva of compassion.” The monk opened his long sleeves to receive the cow dung, blessed the miser, and went back.  The kind daughter-in-law, who was watching this scene while working in the kitchen, hurriedly went into the storehouse, wrapped several bags of rice in a dishcloth skirt, and ran after the monk. The monk didn't look back even though the daughter-in-law called him, “Sir! Sir!” “Please forgive my father-in-law for his sins and take this alms instead,” shouted the daughter-in-law. However, the monk went up to the mountain without responding. He went up the mountain for a while. Stopping at a place called Gochongseonang, the monk looked back at the daughter-in-law and asked, “Why do you keep following me?”  “Please forgive my father-in-law for his sins and take this alms instead,” said the daughter-in-law and handed him the rice. Then the monk said, “Turn your head and look at the house where you lived.” The daughter-in-law was stunned when she looked at her house. The house where she lived and the vegetable garden were all gone, and the place was filled with blue water. The daughter-in-law, in shock, looked for the monk, but the monk disappeared without a trace.  The daughter-in-law was so devastated by what had happened that she untied her belt and hanged herself. For some reason, there were great floods throughout the country after that. People in this region died because of the bad harvest every year and due to epidemics.  There was a rumor that this was caused by the rice fields and houses of Lee Hwa-jin flooding. A woodcutter from the village found the daughter-in-law who had killed herself while collecting firewood. As the story of the kind daughter-in-law who committed suicide spread, the villagers built a grave without a name and a shrine to honor her spirit. Since then, there was a good harvest and epidemics have disappeared. And people named this lake Hwajinpo after Lee Hwa-jin.

stories.title: Yonggungsa Temple
stories.script: Stone Buddha statue rescued from the sea  There is a temple called Yonggungsa at the eastern foot of Baegunsan Mountain in Unnam-dong, Jung-gu, Incheon. Yonggungsa Temple was founded by Great Monk Wonhyo in 670 during the Shilla Dynasty. At the time it was called Baegunsa Temple. In 1854, it was renovated by Heungseon Daewongun and became Yonggungsa Temple. A stone Buddha statue was enshrined in Yonggungsa Temple until it was plundered by the Japanese during the Japanese colonial era. It is said that there is a legend behind this stone Buddha statue.  Once upon a time, there lived a poor fisherman named Son on Yeongjongdo Island. Although Son was poor, he was kind and sincere and was well-received by the villagers. Using a small fishing boat, he caught fish like the other fishermen in the village.  Fishermen from Yeongjongdo Island went to Yeonpyeongdo Island to catch yellow croakers one year when it was April. Son also joined the villagers and went to Yeonpyeongdo Island. Son, who had arrived near Yeonpyeongdo Island, threw the net and waited for the fish to appear.  After a while, when he pulled the net up, it felt heavier than usual. It was with expectations that he pulled the net, but instead of yellow croakers, he found a stone Buddha caught in the net.   It was sunk in the sea for a long time, so the stone Buddha was covered with moss. It seemed useless, so he threw it back into the sea. The other fishermen who went to Yeonpyeongdo Island with Son caught enough yellow croakers to fill their boats, but Son returned empty-handed. He threw the net again to try to catch some fish. He pulled up the net thinking that he had caught enough fish, but this time again, there was only a stone Buddha statue in the net. Son, who got angry, grumbled and threw the stone Buddha statue into the sea and returned home with an empty boat.  That night, a gray-haired Taoist appeared in Son's dream and rebuked him severely. “The stone Buddha statue you rescued from the sea today should have been at Yonggungsa Temple in Baegunsan Mountain. Tomorrow, when you go out fishing, you will retrieve the stone Buddha statue again. Put it on top of Taepyeongam Rock in Yeongjongdo Island.” Son got up and wondered what had happened and went to Yeonpyeongdo Island the next morning before dawn to cast the net. Indeed, the stone Buddha statue that he retrieved yesterday was inside the net. Son thought the words of the Taoist who appeared in his dream are true, and took the stone Buddha statue to Yeongjongdo Island and put it on top of the Taepyeongam Rock. After that, fish were caught every day and Son became rich. His descendants also prospered from generation to generation.  Meanwhile, near Taepyeongam Rock, where the stone Buddha statue is enshrined, there were loafers who spent their time shooting arrows without doing anything. A loafer shot an arrow for fun when he saw a stone Buddha statue standing on top Taepyeongam Rock. However, the arrow hit the right arm of a stone Buddha statue and the arm fell off. After a while, however, the fallen arm was put back on its place, and a bottle of medicine was held in the hand. The loafer who shot an arrow at the stone Buddha statue died instantly on the spot.  The stone Buddha statue on top of Taepyeongam Rock was brought to Yonggungsa Temple by a monk after a long time. The medicine held in the stone Buddha's hand is said to have cured many people with diseases.

stories.title: Dorau
stories.script: A wandering old man who completed his house with the flat stones that were given by the god of mountain  Dorau is a village located in Seorigol, Sangdong-ri, Sang-myeon, Gapyeong-gun, Gyeonggi-do. It is a village located under Seorisan Mountain and is the hometown of the Eonyang Kim clan. There is a legend about flat stones in this village.  Once upon a time there was an old man. The old man, who wandered around many villages when he was young, settled down in Sangdong-ri when he got older. He thought he could spend the rest of his life comfortably in this place. The old man cut down a tree in the mountain to build a house to live in. It took several days to build the columns and rafters and erect the skeleton of the house. He kneaded the soil, attached the walls, and plastered them. Then, the house was in shape. All that remained was to put flat stones to warm his back. The house only needed flat stones to be completed, but even after walking around the mountain for several days, there was no stone that was thin and wide enough to be used for it. No matter how much he went around, he couldn't find a flat stone, so the old man was worried about whether he should abandon the house he had built and move to another place. The old man finally decided to leave and begin to pack up his belongings. Unlike everyone else at his age, he couldn't even build a single house, while everyone else at his age spent their lives enjoying with their family. It was all the more lamentable that he was separated from his family due to wanderlust and was unable to return to his hometown.  The old man, who did not want to live any longer, climbed a high cliff to throw himself. At that moment, the mountain god appeared before the old man and said,  “I am not unaware of how difficult your life journey has been. Death here would mean you had wandered for your entire life and had eventually died. Even after death, your soul will not settle down and will wander the human world forever. In consideration of your situation, I give you a flat stone to finish your house.”  The mountain god gave the flat stone to the old man and disappeared. He carried the flat stone and laid it on the floor that had already been built, finally completing the house. Until his death, he plowed the fields and gathered wild vegetables and lived comfortably.  When the old man started living there, other people came in and formed the village. The name Dorau means a place where people can settle down and live. Furthermore, it has a lesson that if you set your mind on something and do it, you can achieve it with someone's assistance.  Another legend has it that when a scholar was on the verge to death due to being bitten by a beast, a woman wearing mourning clothes appeared and called to him, “Sir, Dorau,” meaning to come back.

stories.title: Ihwa-ri
stories.script: Whose brazier is this?  Ihwa-ri, Gapyeong-eup, Gapyeong-gun, Gyeonggi-do is a village under Jangseunggogae Pass. The story of a fox who returned a favor is passed down in this village.  A long time a go, a man named Hwang lived in Gapyeong-eup. The tombs where Hwang's ancestors were buried were located near Yeomchang Village. Hwang had to cross Jangseunggogae Pass to get there. One day, Hwang went to the mountain where the tombs were to cut grass to feed the cattle he was raising. When he went to check on the tombs of his ancestors after cutting down grass, he saw someone carrying his belongings and climbing Jangseunggogae Pass. Hwang hurried up the pass following him. As he climbed the pass, he saw that the man was resting for a while. Interestingly, the person carrying the grass was a woman wearing a white dress.  Hwang asked the woman, “Thank you for carrying my belongings. May I ask your name? I live right down there. Would you like to come and have dinner?” But the woman replied unexpectedly. “I am a fox and I live here. I will turn one hundred years old tomorrow.” Hwang’s legs trembled as he heard that she was a fox. Then he asked in a very small voice.  “Why did you have to carry someone else's belongings?” “I have a favor to ask you.” “What is it?” “Under this hill, a woman's body is buried. But the body is not buried properly so the feet are sticking out. Could you bury the body well?” As Hwang awoke in shock, it had all been a dream. He had fallen asleep in front of Seonangdang Shrine on the top of the hill after cutting down the grass.  Hwang went to the place the woman told him in his dream just in case. There, the woman's body was covered with dirt, and both of her feet were sticking out of the dirt. Hwang buried the body with care and even held a ancestral rite.  Many days had passed since what happened that day. Hwang was catching a breath on Jangseunggogae Pass as he walked to the tombs of his ancestors. He saw something sparkling beside the road. As he looked closely into it, it was a brazier made of gold. Hwang took the gold brazier and went to the tombs to make the area clean and went to the village to find the owner of the brazier. “Does this brazier belong to anyone? Whose brazier is this? He shouted and walked around the village but no one showed up. In the end, the brazier became Hwang's, and he became rich by selling the gold brazier. This is the man who is known as the rich man Hwang in Gapyeong. The fox repaid the favor.  Later, the village where Hwang lived was named after him and called Hwangcheongol, and Yeomchang Village under his ancestors' tombs was called Ihwa-ri. As Hwang used to shout, “I hwaro nugu geosiyo?” (Whose brazier is this?) the area became “Ihwa-ri.”

stories.title: Pagoda Trees in Gyeran Village
stories.audioTitle: Siheung, Gyeonggi-do / Pagoda Trees in Gyeran Village
stories.script: The pagoda trees around the tomb of Hayeon  In Sincheon-dong, Siheung-si, Gyeonggi-do, there is the tomb of Hayeon, who served as the chief state councilor. Hayeon was praised as the best chief state councilor for his 20 years of working for the government in the early Joseon Dynasty.  Hayeon spent the rest of his life in a village called Gyeran in Sincheon-dong, Siheung-si after retiring from a government post for many years. He died in 1453, and before he passed away, he set up a site for his own tomb and planted pagoda trees around the site. The pagoda trees formed a big forest after hundreds of years. All the villagers coveted the trees around Hayeon's tomb. But at some point, Hayeon's descendants begin to sell the trees around the tomb.  One year, something strange happened to the government office. As soon as the new governors came to the village, they died unexpectedly without knowing the cause. When this happened several times, everyone was reluctant to go the village to work as a governor. In response, the court selected people with strong and courageous spirits and sent them to the village. The newly appointed governor called all the subordinates and gave the order, “I will stay up all night, so light up the lights everywhere in the government office.”  Time passed and it was midnight. The new governor suddenly heard a call out for high-ranking person somewhere, and a person wearing the chief state councilor's official uniform appeared The bewildered new governor soon came to his senses and went down to yard to greet the chief state councilor. Then, after asking to go up to the government office, he bowed his head and said, “Greetings from the new governor.”  The chief state councilor said, “Thank you. I am Hayeon, the chief state councilor. I have a wish to make so I have visited new governors but they all died in shock. I am grateful that you are welcoming me. And I am very happy so that I can tell you my wish.” “Please let me know. I will do what I can do for you.” “There were a lot of pagoda trees around my tomb on Soraesan Mountain. I sometimes played there at night, but my stupid descendants sold the trees, so most of them are gone. Please do not let them cut down the trees anymore.” “I will certainly do what you told me.”  The governor, who had made a promise with Hayeon, went to visit Hayeon's descendants the next day and told them not to cut down the trees. And he asked them to replant the pagoda trees on the spots that they cut down. Hayeon’s spirit was happy that the governor did his favor, so he occasionally appeared and stayed with the new governor. But no matter how great Hayeon is, he was a long-gone person. Meeting Hayeon's soul was a burden for the governor. As Hayeon was the chief state councilor in the past, dealing with him was not only inconvenient, but it also seemed that bad things might happen if people met spirits frequently.  So one day when Hayeon’s spirit came, the governor asked, “What is the thing a dead person hates the most in this world?” “Ghosts and spirits hate peaches the most.” After hearing this, when Hayeon’s spirit revisited, the governor peeled off a peach and served it to him. Then, the spirit of Hayeon, who was sitting silently, said to the governor, “It seems that you don’t like me coming. If you don't want me here, I will not come again.” It is said that he has not appeared again since then.

stories.title: Hyoyangsan Mountain
stories.script: Golden calf from Hyoyangsan Mountain guarded by the mountain god  Hyoyangsan Mountain is located between Sanchon-ri and Maam-ri, Bubal-eup, Icheon-si, Gyeonggi-do. Also referred to as Suyangsan Mountain, Hyoyangsan Mountain has the meaning of “the mountain that raised a filial son.” Hyoyangsan Mountain was named after a filial son who lived in it in the old days. 187-meter-high Hyoyangsan Mountain is located at the end of a wide field, and has the shape of a sitting tiger. And at the top of the Mountain there is the Golden Calf Statue, and the reason is as follows.  Once upon a time, a golden calf was on Hyoyangsan Mountain. The rumor even reached the ears of the Chinese emperor. The Chinese emperor ordered a trusted servant to find the golden calf in Hyoyangsan Mountain and bring it to him. After receiving an order from the emperor, the servant walked for months to reach Icheon, Gyeonggi-do. It was around the time when the sun was setting and the sky was getting dark. He couldn’t see clearly because it was dark but he kept on walking towards a place that somehow looked like Hyoyangsan Mountain.  He passed a village in what is now Jakchon-ri, Majang-myeon, Icheon-si. He met an old man in the village who was holding an iron cane, and the old man said that he had just been to Hyoyangsan Mountain. His happiness of meeting the old man made him treat the old man well and ask the way to Hyoyangsan Mountain. He also explained in detail why he was going. The old man then explained in detail how to reach Hyoyangsan Mountain.  “If you follow this road all the way, you will come across Ocheon. Pass through Icheon-eup, Eogeokdari Bridge, and Guman-ri yard, and you will find Hyoyangsan Mountain on the other side of the road.”  The servant who heard the old man's words was very disconcerted. The journey from China took several months, but he was stunned when he heard that he had to go to Ocheon-ri again and go to Guman-ri from there. Besides, the old man said, “Originally, this iron staff was longer than 90 cm, but it has become so short.”  The servant had no more courage to head to Hyoyangsan Mountain. Thinking that it would be better to give up and go back now, he re-checked the location of Hyoyangsan Mountain with the old man and returned to China. However, it turned out that the old man was the mountain god who was guarding Hyoyangsan Mountain. To protect the golden calf, he made the servant give up by deliberately saying that the mountain was very far. The village where the servant and the old man from China met was called “Jakbyeori Village” because it was the place where the two parted. In fact, Hyoyoangsan Mountain is located very close to Jakbyeori Village.  In addition to this story, there is another story about the golden calf. There were twin caves in Hyoyangsan Mountain, and a golden calf was enshrined in the middle. This golden calf was made using gold mined at Hyoyangsan Mountain during the Shilla Dynasty, and the king of Silla devoted himself in holding ancestral rites there. He believed that the golden calf contributed to Silla's expansion to the north. The king tried to expand the territory further by moving the site of the ancestral rite to the north. Then the mountain god appeared and told him to bury the golden calf on Hyoyangsan Mountain.  Meanwhile, a golden calf was reflected in the washing basin of the emperor of the Tang Dynasty. It was a golden calf of Hyoyangsan Mountain. Rumors spread that if the golden calf was left where it was, Silla's fortune would spread to China. Despite the emperor's effort to take the golden calf to China, it stayed where it was thanks to the mountain god's tact, and Silla became even more prosperous.

stories.title: Seonanggogae Pass
stories.script: A filial son who loved a fox There are several passes with the name Seonanggogae across the nation. Among them is the story of a filial son who loved a fox in Seonanggogae Pass in Bongseong 2-ri, Haseong-myeon, Gimpo-si, Gyeonggi-do.  Long time ago, Deokchil, an extremely filial bachelor, lived with his old single mother in a remote place away from the village. Deokchil, who supported his mother by cutting down firewood and selling it at the market every day, was very kind-hearted. So the villagers often made fun of him by treating him as a fool.  One cold winter day, young village men offered to help him get married. “Deokchil! We will help you get married. Let’s go to Seonanggogae Pass.” “A marriage? Sure. Ha-ha” What they meant was marrying a woman passing Seonanggogae Pass. The young village men who arrived at Seonanggogae Pass said, “I will marry the first woman passing by,” “And me the second woman,” and “Me the third one.” Deokchil said that he will marry the last woman passing by.  The young village men and Deokchil hid near Seonanggogae Pass and watched the women passing by. The first woman to cross Seonanggogae Pass was an old woman, the second was a young girl, and the third was a middle-aged wife. And at the end, a young and beautiful woman rode on a donkey and crossed Seonanggogae Pass. The village bachelors laughed and joked with each other whenever girls appeared. After playing for a while, Deokchil and the village bachelors returned home.  When Deokchil got home that night, he couldn't sleep, wandering around the yard thinking about the woman he saw at Seonanggogae Pass. And suddenly, there came a woman he saw on the hill coming into his house. The woman approached and bowed to Deokchil, saying, “Sir, I have nowhere to go.” She asked, “Please let me stay at your house.”  Duckchil liked it very much and readily accepted the woman. From that day on, she lived in Duckchil's house. Like magic, the woman managed to transform the hut where Deokchil lived with his old mother into a tile-roofed house overnight, and filled the warehouses with grains, making them rich. Deokchil married her and lived a happy life, supporting his mother with utmost sincerity.  The villagers who saw this became jealous, saying that it was the work of a hundred-year-old fox. “Get your senses straight. The despicable fox will eat you.” “Foxes like rotten meat, so if you want to know if it’s a fox or not, put rotten meat by your wife’s bedside.” After a while, the wife who really turned into a fox ate the rotten meat. Shocked by the sight, Deokchil opened the door. Then the fox rushed at Duckchil and said,  “I am a fox who trained to become a human for a hundred years in a deserted mountain. I have to eat your liver until the dawn of today's full moon to become a human. I will die if I don't eat your liver within the time.” Hearing this, Deokchil closed his eyes and said,  “I am willing to give you my liver to repay your kindness. But, please do not harm my mother. She knows nothing about this.”  The fox looked at Deokchil after hearing his words and went outside. Another fox outside said, “Go ahead and eat his liver. If you don't eat his liver before dawn today, you will die without becoming a human.” The fox pushed her. Then the hundred-year-old fox said, “I can't. Even though it hasn’t been long, he is my lover. So, I can’t.”  While the foxes were fighting, the day dawned and the other fox disappeared somewhere and the fox who had been his wife left the house and died on a snowy hill. Deokchil, who had been searching for his wife all night, found a dead fox on the snowy hill, and buried her in a sunny place. Then he left his house with his mother.  Seonanggogae, the pass where the sad love story of Deokchil and the fox is told, is named after the Seonangdang Shrine. The shrine is gone now, leaving only its name behind.

stories.title: Simboksa Temple
stories.script: Stone Buddha statue rescued from the sea  Simboksa Temple, where there is the legend of a Buddha statue rescued from the sea, is located in Deongmok-ri, Hyeondeok-myeon, Pyeongtaek-si, Gyeonggi-do. Simboksa Temple is said to have been constructed during the Goryeo Dynasty, but the exact year of its foundation is unknown. There are only records that it has been reconstructed several times during the Joseon Dynasty. Deongmok-ri, where Simboksa Temple is located, is adjacent to Pyeongtaek Lake, and it was famous as a blessed fishing ground until the Asan Embankment was built. During that time, most residents worked in the fishing industry, and yet even today this area still has a unique culture associated with fishermen. The story of Simboksa Buddha is also closely related to the lives of fishermen whose lives are dependent on the sea.  In the 5th year of King Myeongjong's reign of the Joseon Dynasty, a fisherman named Cheon Eul-mun lived in Munsanpo, Paju. Cheon lived fishing in the sea off Munsanpo with fellow fishermen living in the same village. Then one day, while catching fish, a large stone was caught in the net. Cheon threw the stone into the sea and moved to another place to cast the net again. After a while, the net was pulled up, and there was the stone in the net again. The second time Cheon got the same stone, he looked at it carefully, thinking it was very strange.  Surprisingly, the big stone was a stone statue of Buddha. His great devotion to Buddha led him to bow deeply to the Buddha and tell his fellow fishermen, “To have rescued Buddha twice from the sea is not a coincidence. Let us take good care of him,” and with his colleagues, he took the stone and headed for Gwangdeoksan Mountain  Cheon carried the Buddha statue on his back. Although it was made of stone, it was very light. After walking for a while, he came to the site where the temple stands now, and took a break. He tried to carry the Buddha statue again, but this time it was so heavy that he couldn't move at all. His intuition told him that the place had been chosen by the Buddha. Cheon set up a temporary shelter and enshrined the Buddha there. They had to build a temple to enshrine the Buddha, but they couldn't build a temple on their own. Cheon and the fishermen worried all night and finally went to bed late at night.  That night, the Buddha appeared in Cheon's dream and said, “Don't worry about it and go to the sea tomorrow morning. There will be a black cow and a broken boat. Use the black cow and the broken boat to build a temple and a shrine.”  Cheon woke up and went to the beach with his colleagues. He found a broken boat and a black cow just like Buddha’s words. Cheon loaded the timbers of the wrecked ship onto the cow, brought them to the spot, built a temple, and enshrined the Buddha. This temple is “Simboksa Temple.” After building Simboksa Temple, Cheon and his colleagues always caught a big amount fish and became very rich. Their descendants also prospered.

stories.title: Pyeongchang intro
stories.script: Thank you for using the Pyeongchang Tourist Taxi. Pyeongchang is situated in a mountainous region, with nearly 60% of the total area being more than 700m above sea level. That’s the reason why the area has plenty of resorts, farms, and healing forests. It also has a long winter with plenty of snow, so it is deeply connected to winter sports as well. After all, it served as the venue of the 2018 Winter Olympics.  Other famous things include buckwheat, found in abundance in Bongpyeong; Korean beef, raised in the highlands of Daegwallyeong; and pollack, dried in the cold winds of winter. Don’t miss the view of nature from the Balwangsan Cable Car and healing under the stars at Sanneomi Farm and Yukbaekmajigi.

stories.title: Woljeongsa Temple, Odaesan Mountain
stories.script: Woljeongsa Temple is a famous temple created nearly 1,300 years ago, in 643 CE. The most notable features of this temple are the Octagonal Nine-story Stone Pagoda and the Stone Seated Bodhisattva, located at the center of the temple complex. These valuable cultural heritage sites retain their appearance from a millennium ago. The Octagonal Nine-story Stone Pagoda was built during the early Goryeo Period. It is known as Korea’s largest and most beautiful octagonal stone pagoda. Next to it sits a stone Buddha in a half-kneeling position, the Stone Seated Bodhisattva of Woljeongsa Temple. It is home to a story of a Buddhist saint who willfully turned into stone to protect the Sarira pagoda.  When one passes through the first gate of the Woljeongsa Temple, one finds oneself on a 1km-long fir forest trail. The popular 2016 show “The Guardian” made this forest even more famous. With nearly 1,700 old fir trees making up the forest, it is also known as a millennial forest. There are two forest trails, one earthen, the other decked in wood.  It connects to the Seonjae-gil Trail, which connects Woljeongsa Temple with Sangwonsa Temple along a valley. Buddhist monks used to walk this trail for meditation, so you could join them and attain some inner peace on this road.   A storage facility located above the Woljeongsa Temple housed the records of the  Joseon Dynasty. One can find the origin of the Hangang River further above.

stories.title: Sangwonsa Temple, Odaesan Mountain
stories.script: Sangwonsa Temple is a historic temple constructed in 705 CE. Though it is small in size, it has two National Treasures of Korea, which testify to its long history.   This temple has an interesting story associated with King Sejo, the 7th king of Joseon. When Sejo was heading to Sangwonsa Temple to treat his chronic skin condition, he bathed in clear water from the valley. That was when the Buddha Manjusri appeared to him in the form of a boy and wiped his hands across the back, which removed the boils that no drug nor doctor could cure. The valley has a marker stone that the king had reportedly hung his clothes on. To commemorate this event, Sejo is said to have built a statue of the Buddha Manjusri and donated it to the temple, which is the Wooden Seated Child Manjusri of Sangwonsa Temple, a National Treasure.   The other National Treasure in the complex is the Bronze Bell of Sangwonsa Temple, which was donated by the king as the bell with the clearest and the most beautiful sound in the country. It is said that when this bell was relocated from Andong, it suddenly stuck to a pass and refused to budge. It was only able to be moved after a piece was broken off from the bell and sent to where it was. If you look closely at the bell, you will indeed see that one of the thirty-six lotus flowers carved onto the surface of the bell is missing.  A short climb toward Birobong Peak brings one to the Shrine of Sakyamuni Buddha's Sarira. This shrine, located on a tomb-like hill, has a subdued and elegant appearance. The reason why Odaesan Mountain was considered a holy place is probably because of the sarira enshrined in this shrine.

stories.title: Hyo-seok Moonlight Hill
stories.script: Lee Hyo-seok’s “When Buckwheat Flowers Bloom” is thought to be one of the greatest short stories in Korean literature. The story is set in Bongpyeong-myeon, in Pyeongchang-gun, Gangwon-do. Opened in 2018, Hyo-seok Moonlight Hill takes one along the footsteps of the short story’s protagonist, with plenty of things to see and enjoy on the way.  It is particularly spectacular in September, when buckwheat flowers fill the area from the Hyo-seok Moonlight Hill to the fields of Bongpyeong. When the full moon rises, and moonlight falls over the buckwheat flowers, the view is indescribably romantic. It is just like the story, where “flowers are beginning to bloom like large grains of salt, scattered across the moonlight. The view took my breath away.”  Hyo-seok Moonlight Hill is also home to places with their own stories, like the house that Lee Hyo-seok had lived in Bongpyeong; the Blue House, which recreates Lee Hyo-seok’s house in Pyeongyang; the Dreaming Moon Cafe, a place where one can enjoy a cup of coffee and read; the Dream Garden, where one can feel the nature and the four seasons; and a place to feed a donkey, just like the protagonist of the short story. You can also climb the Donkey Observatory to get a birds’-eye view of the area.  At the top of the Hyo-seok Moonlight Hill lies the Lee Hyoseok Memorial Hall. Climb the flat hill to find a statue of Lee Hyo-seok at his desk at the entrance to the garden. The exhibition traces Lee Hyo-seok’s life and legacy through artifacts and magazines that published his works.

stories.title: Filming Location of “Welcome to Dongmakgol”
stories.script: “Welcome to Dongmakgol” was a film that drew nearly 8 million people to the box office in 2005. It begins with an American pilot crashing in Dongmakgol, a small village located deep within the Hambaeksan Mountain, at the height of the Korean War in November of 1950. The people of Dongmakgol live in peace, thanks to the mountain hiding the war raging outside. Soldiers from the Allied forces and North Korea end up in the village for different reasons, creating a humorous and touching tale of humanity in war. Rather than emphasizing the meaning or the ideologies behind the war, the film sought to capture human warmth, anti-war messages, and humanism. As a result, it is still remembered fondly as a light-hearted, yet touching masterpiece.  This place, which served as the filming location for the movie, was originally a bustling village centered around the mining industry. When the mines closed at the end of the 70s, the village disappeared as well. However, it was revived as a filming location for the film and a number of subsequent TV shows and advertisements, which established it as a popular tourist site in Pyeongchang.  Fans of the film will recognize places like the tunnel, which doubled as the entrance to the old mine; a 500-year-old village, where soldiers from the two sides came together; and the American plane that kicked off the plot.  Even those who didn’t watch the film are sure to have fun here, and some might even go on to look up the film afterwards.

stories.title: Pyeongchang Olympic Market
stories.script: Pyeongchang Olympic Market is a traditional market with a 70-year history that traces its roots to 1955. Its proximity to the bus terminal means that it serves as a place of livelihood for the people of Pyeongchang and the surrounding areas. What makes it so charming is the fact that you can enjoy both the ambience of a traditional market and regional foods in the market. Pyeongchang Olympic Market was originally named Pyeongchang Traditional Market. To commemorate the hosting of the 2018 Winter Olympics, its name was changed to its present name in 2012.  Pyeongchang Olympic Market includes both the permanent market, which opens for business every day, and the fifth-day market, which opens on days ending with 5 or 0. The fifth-day market includes a large selection of temporary stalls that add to the bustling atmosphere of the traditional market.  Like other markets across Korea, Pyeongchang Olympic Market offers fresh foodstuff and a large selection of household items. Its greatest appeal, however, is the selection of dishes using buckwheat, the local specialty of Pyeongchang. After all, this is the origin of buckwheat pancakes, the most well-known specialty of Gangwon. As a result, many stalls continue to serve the same delectable buckwheat pancakes in the alleys within the market.  At the end of the market, one can find bakeries, cafes, and other shops catering to the younger crowd. Bakeries that use buckwheat, the signature foodstuff of Pyeongchang, are particularly popular. So why not sample the bread when you’re in the area?

stories.title: Daegwallyeong Sky Ranch
stories.script: Daegwallyeong Sky Ranch was built in 1974. Visitors were prohibited from entering the farm until 2014, however. The Sky Ranch has a land area of 10 million meters squared, equivalent to 1,400 soccer stadiums. About 400 dairy cows, 100 sheep, and 40 horses graze freely on this field.  The defining attraction at Daegwallyeong Sky Ranch is the tractor carriage. One can explore the four corners of the Sky Ranch on the carriage, so it is quite popular. When one gets on the 32-seater carriage, the carriage takes one from the entrance of the Sky Ranch to the Haneulmaru Overlook, located 1,000m above sea level. The view of the open field and the surrounding areas is nothing short of spectacular. When you see the view, you will understand why this is often said to be the “Alps in Korea” or one of the “top 3 ranches in Korea”.  You can also follow the trails taken by the shepherds in Daegwallyeong Sky Ranch. There are four walking trails on the grounds, from the “Wide Scenery Trail” that connects the ranch to Seonjaryeong Pass, the highest point of Daegwallyeong, to the “Forest Waves Trail”, which brings one to the virgin forest and the wildflowers of the area. Other activities onsite include the sheep and goat feeding experience, where one can even pet the farm animals, and the horseback riding experience accompanied by an expert coach.

stories.title: Bangadari Mineral Spring
stories.script: The quality of Bangadari Mineral Spring is said to have been recognized during the reign of King Sukjong of Joseon. Local legends say that an old man, who was wasting away from an unknown disease, met the spirit of a mountain deity in a dream, who instructed him to dig a hole in the ground. A clear mineral spring sprouted forth from the hole, and the old man was healed after drinking the water from the spring. Afterward, he set up an altar and began offering ceremonies to the deity.  Indeed, water from the Bangadari Mineral Spring has nearly 30 types of minerals, including carbonates and iron, which help to mitigate stomach disorders, anemia, and neuralgia.   Bangadari Mineral Spring and the surrounding areas were left in ruins after the Korean War. Mr. Kim Ik-ro, an educator dedicated to reforestation, spent nearly 50 years from 1964 onward restoring the area to its former beauty.  Nearly 70 species of trees are planted around the area, including Korean pine, spruce, and almost 100 fir trees. In addition, fir trees line the 1km-long stretch of the trail connecting the entrance with the mineral spring, so you can enjoy a leisurely walk there.

stories.title: Tourist attractions and popular food in Dong-gu, Daejeon
stories.audioTitle: Tourist attractions and popular food in Dong-gu, Daejeon
stories.script: Thank you for using the Tourist Taxi. Daejeon’s Dong-gu is a beautiful district flanked by Daecheongho Lake to the right. It also serves as a commercial hub thanks to its commercial center. Furthermore, mountains representing Daejeon, such as Maninsan Mountain, Sikjangsan Mountain, and Gyejoksan Mountain, are all located in Dong-gu, in addition to prehistoric sites, Uam Historic Park, retro-style Soje-dong Cafe Street, and Daedong Sky Park’s famous sunset and night view.  The Meditation Garden by the Daecheongho Lake and Sannae-dong’s Plane Tree Street are popular destinations as well, where one can enjoy the traditions and romantic views in the city center. Don’t forget to explore the shopping arcades and market food at Jungang Market, the largest traditional market in the Daejeon area.

stories.title: Meditation Garden (Daecheongho Lake)
stories.script: Daecheongho Lake is known for its beautiful scenery. The Meditation Garden, located by the Lakeside Romance Trail, the 4th section of the Daecheongho Obaengni Road, is said to be the high point of any visit to Daecheongho Lake. The Meditation Garden is known for its seasonal scenery, from the verdant green of spring to snow-covered winter. In particular, a mystical scene unfolds in the morning hours, when mist rises from the lake over the reflection of trees and the shadow of the mountains beyond. The Meditation Garden also served as the filming location of the 2005 MBC show Sad Love Story. Since then, different TV shows and movies have been filmed in the garden, establishing it as a popular tourist site.  The garden was built on a plot of land submerged under water when Daecheongho Lake was completed in 1980. The area's stone fences, earthenware pots, and other sculptures pay homage to the lost village. Barrier-free decked roads allow children, visitors with disabilities, and others to access the area as well. When the water level falls, you can also walk along a road that connects the Meditation Garden with the island.

stories.title: Sannae-dong Sycamore Street
stories.script: The former National Highway 17 in Sannae-dong, Dong-gu, is home to a specialized street designated by the city of Daejeon. It is the Sannae-dong Sycamore Tree Street, which won the Excellence Award in the Beautiful Street category of the national Beautiful Forest Contest, hosted for the first time in the year 2000.  The street is a product of labor that began with the planting of a few trees back in the 60s. Today, it has 2,000 sycamore trees creating a tunnel over a 10km-long stretch of road between Nangwol-dong and Haso-dong toward Maninsan Recreational Forest. This tunnel came to be because the branches were trimmed to be bent inward toward the road. Why? So that the branches wouldn’t obstruct the sunlight too much for the rice paddies next to the road. No matter the reason, that decision created a new model of landscaping that resulted in this beloved street.  Since 2022, Sannae-dong Sycamore Tree Street has also been hosting a festival. Villagers from 10 villages connected by the 10km-long road come together to tell 10 stories from their villages. If you are interested, visit the area in September, when the festival is held.

stories.title: Jecheon intro
stories.script: Thank you for using the Jecheon Tourist Taxi. Jecheon, where clear winds blow under a bright moon, is home to handsome sights: Oksunbong Peak, crowned by mysterious rocks, and Cheongpungho Lake’s greenery and flowers across the seasons are but two examples. Cheongpungho Lake’s cable car, Jeongbangsa Temple, and the historic Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex are the must-visit sites. Don’t miss the Uirimji Reservoir, a reservoir with nearly 1,500 years of history, and Jecheon Jungang Market’s new Food Alley, made up of four areas specializing in spicy fishcakes, galbi, and noodles. But whatever you do, be sure to leave plenty of time and space to enjoy the living history of Jecheon and its flavors.

stories.title: Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex
stories.script: Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex was established as a cultural heritage site that recreates the appearance of an old town that was submerged underwater. This area, Cheongpung-myeon, was known as a commercial center in the old days, thanks to the river traffic following the Namhangang River. A government office was installed here to govern the surrounding areas about 400 years ago, which led to the proliferation of cultural heritage in the area. Unfortunately, the construction of the Chungju Dam jeopardized the existence of these heritage sites. Still, the  government of the Chungcheongbuk-do Province established this site at the foot of the Mangwolsanseong Fortress in 1983. Over the next 3 years, the village was relocated to create this complex. The area is home to two Treasures, Hanbyeongnu Pavilion and the Stone Standing Buddha in Multae-ri, as well as Paryeongnu Pavilion, which served as the gateway to Cheongpung, and Geumnamnu Pavilion, a gateway built in 1825 that leads to the administrative center of the region. It is also home to 43 cultural properties, including hyanggyo, or local Confucian school; government buildings; private homes; monuments; and nearly 1,600 everyday objects. The highest point of the complex can be found at Mangwolsanseong Fortress. Climb to the top to get a bird’s-eye view of the complex and Cheongpungho Lake.    You can also find traditional performances at weekends. From Taekgyeon, a traditional martial art, to traditional music and promotional performances displaying Jecheon as a city of naturopathy, there are plenty of things to see and do in the complex.

stories.title: Jecheon Jungang Market Cheongchunmatgil Food Street
stories.audioTitle: Jecheon Jungang Market Cheongchunmatgil Food Street
stories.script: Jecheon has several traditional markets that are connected with each other by a food street, which you can stay on until you have finished a complete tour of the city’s oldest traditional market called Jecheon Jungang Market as well as Naeto Market and Dongmun Traditional Market. These markets were formed next to each other because, in the past, some stayed open every day of the year while some opened occasionally like a flea market. Jungang Market mostly deals with textiles, clothes, and dishware while Naeto Market sells food and snacks. Dongmun Market is mainly comprised of fruit and vegetable shops, but there also unique and delicious traditional snacks you don’t want to miss such as red fishcake, half-moon rice and acorn cake, and sweet rice cake with red bean filling. The streets in these traditional markets also lead to the main cultural street of Jecheon that can make your trip more enjoyable.  There is another market called Yeokjeon Hanmaeum Market right in front of Jecheon Station. You will find an array of restaurants near the entrance to the market, and stores selling locally-produced vegetables and medicinal herbs inside the market.  Some traditional markets in Jecheon are called fifth-day markets because they open once every five days, on the 3rd, 8th, 13th, 18th, 23rd, and 28th of every month. On these market opening days, you will see that the place is even more packed with street vendors. Conveniently situated next to Jecheon Sation and Bus Terminal, these markets are where  you might want to start and end your trip to Jecheon.

stories.title: Oksunbong Suspension Bridge
stories.script: Oksunbong Peak was named so because the green and white rock formation at its tip resembles a bundle of bamboo sprouts. It is said to be the most beautiful in the Cheongpunghoban area which encompasses Jecheon and Danyang. The Oksunbong Suspension Bridge is a famous scenic spot where you can enjoy the beauty of Oksunbong Peak up close.  The Oksunbong Suspension Bridge was opened in October 2021. This 222-meter long and 1.5-meter wide suspension bridge is visited by many people, especially during the autumn foliage season. Once you cross the suspension bridge, you will reach a wooden eco trail partly covered with palm mats.  Next to the Oksunbong Suspension Bridge is the vivid red Oksundaegyo Bridge and the Oksunbong Shelter. It is the starting point for Goegokseongbyeok-gil, the 6th course of the Cheongpungho Jadrak Trail and also a parking lot. After crossing the road from the parking lot, visitors can reach the Oksunbong Observatory where they can enjoy a spectacular view of the Oksunbong Peak after a five minute climb up wooden stairs.

stories.title: Andong intro
stories.script: Thank you for using the Andong Tour Taxi. Andong has the largest land area among all cities in Korea. It was also home to the largest number of independence activists during the Japanese colonial rule. In addition, it is known as the capital of Korean spiritual culture, because of its long Confucian tradition and the number of head families descending from the yangban class, or traditional aristocracy. Indeed, Andong is home to several UNESCO World Heritage sites, such as Hahoe Folk Village, Dosanseowon Confucian Academy, and Bongjeongsa Temple. In addition, other sites like Woryeonggyo Bridge, Andong Dam, Manhyujeong Pavilion, filming locations for K-dramas and movies, and Andong hemp and traditional paper-making experiences ensure that you can feel the unique culture of Korea.  Andong also boasts specialty dishes that have captivated the tastebuds of its visitors. From Andong-style Salted Mackerel’s nostalgic appeal to Bibimbap with Soy Sauce, made with food used for ancestral rituals, and Andong Braised Chicken, which brings together chicken with vegetables and sauce, the city can offer a rich culinary experience as well. Feel the traditional culture and taste of Korea in Andong.

stories.title: Yekki Village
stories.script: Yekki Village was built in 1976, when people displaced by the construction of the Andong Dam moved to the top of the hill where they could overlook their former homes. Before it was submerged underwater, the village at Yean-myeon was actually pretty big. That’s also why Yekki Village has multiple names hearkening back to Yean, such as Yean Church, Yean Barber Shop, and Nonghyup Yean.  Today’s Yekki Village is full of colorful murals, drawn throughout the alleyways and walls. The old Myeon Office building now houses a gallery, and traditional houses are refurbished into cafes. The whole village is one big outdoor art museum and photo area. Many other shops like breweries, mills, and hardware shops still retain their old appearance.  There are plenty of things to do in Yekki Village as well. Seonseonghyun Cultural Heritage Complex, named after the area’s old title, offers experiences like traditional costumes, weddings, and traditional Korean liquor tasting.
