Despite being considered a beautiful ecological site, the DMZ is viewed as a symbol of division associated with the dark history of war or a place we cannot visit. People think of it as a terrifying and dangerous place before anything else. Although we might think of it as a “place where we cannot visit” or “a place where no one can visit,” the DMZ would be a magical and meaningful place for us if we thought of it as a “place that will become our lives’ foundation.”  The DMZ holds value as a carefully preserved pristine environment supporting diverse flora and fauna. It also carries a symbolic meaning that reminds us of the division between the South and the North. Although it is currently not freely accessible to the public, I hope you can experience the DMZ more closely and vividly through various virtual experiences and realistic media experiences at the DMZ Live Immersive Media Center.

stories.title: Introduction of DMZ Live
stories.script: Hello. DMZ Live is located at the Korean Peninsula Ecological Peace Tourism Information Center in Imjingak, Paju. Here, you can get a closer and more vivid experience of the DMZ. It is designed to provide visitors with enjoyable and meaningful experiences with the theme “various values, such as historical, symbolic, and ecological significance” through realistic media content.   In the experience space, visitors can engage in physical activities and digital experiences designed to deliver DMZ-related content and other information, as well as video experiences integrated with simulators and virtual reality (VR) devices, digital interactive experiences, and more.   The first floor consists of six experiential zones: “Drone Rider” and “Shuttle Rider” for an indirect immersive experience of the DMZ and main tourist attractions by using cutting-edge information and communication technology (ICT), and “DMZ 248km,” “DMZ Four Seasons,” DMZ Coloring Zoo,” and “DMZ Secret Forest,” which are focused on the DMZ’s ecological environment. On the second floor is DMZ Live Media Hall, where various media art centered around the large, 24-m L-shaped media wall are found.

stories.title: Shuttle Rider
stories.script: “Shuttle Rider” is designed to provide information and guidance about the DMZ by traveling around major tourist attractions while riding on a futuristic shuttle. While enjoying videos on a moving futuristic shuttle, visitors can watch a tour of the peaceful DMZ. This also conveys the wishes for the Korean Peninsula’s reunification to the audience.  “Shuttle Rider” offers different content per day, providing visitors with various delightful experiences.   ① The video of a transcontinental train journey from the Gwanghwamun Gate to Paris on a futuristic train is scheduled every Tuesday and Wednesday.  ② The virtual video showcasing the Korean Peninsula and the opening of the Trans-Korean Railway, seen from the universe, is scheduled every Thursday and Friday.  ③ Videos exploring historical relics related to the DMZ’s history are scheduled on Saturdays.  ④ Videos introducing tourist attractions in adjacent areas of the DMZ and providing a preview of the places are scheduled on Sundays or public holidays.  Children below 110 cm are not allowed to ride for safety reasons. Safety is our top priority, and we kindly ask for your understanding.

stories.title: Drone Rider
stories.script: “Drone Rider” allows viewers to experience as if they are flying across the entire Korean Peninsula by integrating a high-definition, live-action video with simulators and VR devices. Once the viewer wears the VR device inside the ride, the simulator synchronizes with the video in up-down and right-left motions, adding a sense of immersion. Each content is approximately 5 minutes and 10 seconds long, and viewers may choose to watch one of the four themed videos.   ① World Cultural Heritage: A video showcasing Korea’s tourist attractions designated as World Heritage sites, such as the Hwaseong Fortress in Suwon or Hahoe Folk Village, Namhansanseong Fortress,  Beopjusa Temple, Magoksa Temple, Sosuseowon Confucian Academy,  Dosanseowon Confucian Academy.  ② Baekdudaegan Mountain Range: An introduction video of the Baekdudaegan Mountain Range, including the Jirisan or Seoraksan Mountains.  ③ Baengnyeongdo Island: An introduction video of the major tourist attractions of Baengnyeongdo Island, a UNESCO World Heritage.  ④ DMZ off-road: Videos featuring virtual traveling in the DMZ border area in a vehicle, showcasing the ecological environment and more.  Children below 110 cm are not allowed to ride for safety reasons. Safety is our top priority, and we kindly ask for your understanding.

stories.title: DMZ Secret Forest and DMZ Four Seasons
stories.audioTitle: DMZ Secret Forest and DMZ Four Seasons
stories.script: “DMZ Secret Forest” is a photo zone of the secret and tranquil night landscape of the DMZ seen inside a rusted iron helmet. When you touch the handprints of the iron helmet in the middle, a beautiful and mysterious scenery unfolds, showcasing war ruins now home to various animals and plants. You can have an immersive experience of walking into a place inside the cozy and peaceful DMZ.   The central space is named “DMZ Four Seasons,” where you can feel as if you are sitting on top of a beautiful pond with its colorful and open space. When you sit on the pebble-shaped chair in the center, sensors will be activated, and you will be greeted by marvelous and refreshing nature with flowers, butterflies, grass, frogs, and more. Through the screen on the opposite side, you can see DMZ’s four beautiful seasons, including flowers, autumn leaves, snow, and more, while experiencing the interactive effects of butterflies fluttering around your reflection on the screen.

stories.title: DMZ Coloring Zoo and DMZ 248km
stories.script: “DMZ Coloring Zoo” is a “live sketch” space with content where you can choose and uniquely color the drawings of nine endangered animals in the DMZ. After scanning the animals you have colored, they come to life on the screen, interacting with each other and playing in the forest. They also respond when you touch the screen.  “DMZ 248km” is an ecological experience in the 248-km–long DMZ, which crosses east to west of the Korean Peninsula. It is a play-type interactive content where you choose from the DMZ regions and quickly touch the screen to find animals that inhabit each region. Once you clear the game by finding all the animals hidden in the video, such as spotted seals, black-faced spoonbills, white-naped cranes, Asiatic black bears, long-tailed gorals, and more, you may take commemorative photos with these adorable animals.

stories.title: Second-floor DMZ Live Media Hall
stories.script: The media hall on the second floor shows media art on a large, 24-m L-shaped screen with various themes, such as the history of the DMZ, natural ecology, tourism resources, and more.   ① The Forest of Hope: Interactive content where an audience’s touch triggers a response. It shows light from the sky to the DMZ and illuminates the path. The images of South and North Korea coexisting on the Korean Peninsula are projected onto the sun and moon, and the scattered beams on the ground represent the DMZ’s lookout posts and barbed wire fences, symbolizing the history of interaction between South and North Korea. The light beams created by the sun and moon flow under the Peace Tree, a symbol of peace and prosperity, and reach people’s feet as they represent “connectedness as one.” ② THE WALL: It is a viewing content–show, a fusion of cinema and writing. The sun and the moon, whose coexistence is difficult to witness, meet and open up a fantastic world that expresses the emotions of war and healing through color, abstract graphics, and writing. The content is designed to heighten the audience’s immersive experience with a direction that shows grandeur, beauty, and tension at the same time. ③ Dream of the Train: This media art captures the tense and tragic moment of the train destruction on December 31, 1950, while the Korean army was retreating, by freezing the scene and using stopped camera movements. The audience can experience a condensed story encompassing war, armistice, recovery, and healing. The content naturally guides the audience to learn about the Cheolma (train) and the Peace Tree, landmarks in Imjingak Pyeonghwa Nuri Park, representing the story’s outcome. ④ DMZ and East Sea: The Hwajinpohaebyeon Beach, located at the northernmost tip of Korea’s eastern coast, is shown through the video, and the seascape is captured in stunning detail by a 12K panoramic camera and an 8K drone, bringing a vibrant scenery of the sea to the screen. ⑤ DMZ Fantasia: You can witness the breathtaking harmony of animals and plants inhabiting the DMZ, a land that dreams of hope and peace. The DMZ’s natural beauty that we could only dream of comes to life in a splendor that changes and harmonizes with the flow of four seasons, as it conveys the value of connection, coexistence, peace, and harmony.  ⑥ DMZ Odysseia: You can witness the DMZ, a place filled with the pain of the Korean War that we should never forget, through the Korean calligraphy artworks of Kim So-Young.   We invite you to experience media art’s vivid and dazzling beauty at DMZ Live.

stories.title: ﻿Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP)
stories.script: ﻿There is a massive structure that looks like a UFO in Dongdaemun, Seoul. This bizarre building is Dongdaemun Design Plaza, or DDP, a multifunctional cultural space where visitors can enjoy exhibitions, events, and relaxation. Its name, DDP, also stands for Dream, Design, and Play.  The DDP is famous for its striking architectural design. It was designed by Zaha Hadid, the first female architect to win Pritzker Prize. DDP is the world’s largest three-dimensional, asymmetrical building. According to Zaha Hadid, DDP reflects the dynamism of Dongdaemun, a district that changes constantly, from dawn to dusk. She created a space that seamlessly connects natural and artificial forms, using her unique architectural style of curves, slopes, and lines. Such design added a new layer to Dongdaemun’s significance in Korea, making the DDP a landmark of the area.   Dongdaemun Design Plaza consists of the Art Hall, Museum, Design Lab, DDP Market, Oullim Square, and Dongdaemun History and Culture Park. The Art Hall, Museum, and Design Lab host various exhibitions, conferences, and forums while visitors can enjoy cultural content and events, as well as purchase unique items at the DDP Market. Oullim Square, which is open for 24 hours, is designed for visitor convenience and to revitalize local commerce. The Dongdaemun History and Culture Park is a place where visitors can learn about the history of the area.

stories.title: Mudeungsan National Park
stories.script: Mudeungsan National Park  Mudeungsan National Park was designated a provincial park in 1972 and became Korea’s 21st national park in 2013. Located on the slopes of Mudeungsan Mountain, the highest and largest mountain near Gwangju Metropolitan City, it stands at 1,187 meters above sea level. The name Mudeungsan means incomparably high mountain or a mountain beyond grading. Its name might make it sound like a tall and difficult mountain to climb, but Mudeungsan Mountain is actually known for its gentle slopes and rounded shape.  Mudeungsan Mountain offers numerous sights to explore. The summit, known as the Three Peaks, includes Cheonwangbong Peak, Jiwangbong Peak, and Inwangbong Peaks, surrounded by famous rock formations like Gyubong Peak, Ipseokdae, and Seoseokdae. Gyubong Peak is particularly renowned for its stunning scenery, inspiring the saying, Don’t say you’ve seen Mudeungsan Mountain without seeing Gyubong Peak, as its views resemble a traditional Korean painting. Ipseokdae, with its crescent-shaped stone pillars, presents a unique landscape rarely seen on other mountains. Additionally, temples such as Jeungsimsa Temple, Wonhyosa Temple, Cheonmunsa Temple, and Miyeoksa Temple add more dazzling sights to see.  Mudeungsan Mountain boasts beautiful views in every season. In spring, wildflowers bloom in vibrant colors, and in summer, lush green leaves create a cooling effect across the landscape. Autumn brings stunning views of foliage at Gyubongam Rock, along with fields of silver grass at Jangbuljae and Baekma Ridge. In winter, frost and ice flowers create breathtaking scenes. Walking through Mudeungsan Mountain and breathing in the fresh mountain air with each changing season allows you to appreciate the wonder and value of nature.

stories.title: Mudeungsan Columnar Joint Cliffs
stories.script: Mudangs Columnar Joint Cliffs  Formed from volcanic activity, Mudeungsan Mountain is well-known for its well-developed columnar joint cliffs. Columnar joints are created when lava cools and contracts after eruption, forming polygonal cracks that result in columns with pentagonal or hexagonal cross-sections.  The columnar joints of Mudeungsan, formed about 70 million years ago, are prominently displayed at Seoseokdae, Ipseokdae, and Gyubong Peak. The columns at Ipseokdae and Gyubong Peak, shaped into upright stone pillars through extensive weathering, stand in stark contrast to Seoseokdae, which is less weathered and resembles a folding screen. The stone pillars at Ipseokdae and Seoseokdae are among the largest reported in South Korea, attracting particular attention. Moreover, Seoseokdae, stretching from east to west, becomes especially stunning at sunset, when the pillars are bathed in the warm glow of dusk, this breathtaking scene rarely found on other mountains.  With its grand columnar joints, Mudeungsan Mountain has been designated a UNESCO World Geopark, recognized for its significant scientific and scenic value. It’d be a shame not to visit! So, why not hike up and experience the beautiful columnar joints and lush greenery that Mudeungsan Mountain has to offer?

stories.title: Temples of Mudeungsan Mountain
stories.script: Temples of Mudeungsan Mountain  Mudeungsan Mountain is home to several temples, including Jeungsimsa Temple, Wonhyosa Temple, Cheonmunsa Temple, Miyeoksa Temple, Dongguksa Temple, Bodeoksa Temple, Baegunam Hermitage, Yaksaam Hermitage. These temples add unique charm and interest along the way up the mountain. Among them, Jeungsimsa Temple and Wonhyosa Temple are considered the most prominent.  Located on the western slopes of Mudeungsan Mountain, Jeungsimsa Temple was founded during the Unified Silla Period. It sadly burned down during the Japanese Invasion of Korea in 1592. While it was rebuilt, much of it was again destroyed during the Korean War. The temple’s buildings, including the Daeungjeon Hall, were restored in 1970. Jeungsimsa Temple is designated as a cultural heritage site in Gwangju and houses many heritage treasures such as Obaekjeon Hall, the Iron Seated Vairocana Buddha, and the Three-story Stone Pagoda of Jeungsimsa Temple from the late Silla Dynasty. Obaekjeon Hall, is quite significant, dating back to the early Joseon Dynasty and featuring a multi-bracketed roof design.  Wonhyosa Temple is renowned as a traditional temple with the most beautiful pavilion in Korea. As the name suggests, it is closely associated with Buddhist Monk Wonhyo, who was inspired by the mountain’s beauty to establish the temple here. The temple was lost alongside Jeungsimsa Temple in the Korean War and was only later restored. During its reconstruction, several bronze relics, including a Bronze Standing Buddha Statue and a bronze mirror, were discovered. These relics spanning periods from late Unified Silla to the Joseon Dynasty, attesting to the temple’s long history. These artifacts are now preserved at the Gwangju National Museum. Wonhyosa Temple is also well-known as a prime spot for viewing the majestic Seoseokdae rock formations. The view of Seoseokdae from Wonhyoru Pavilion alone is reason enough to visit Wonhyosa Temple.

stories.title: Dokdo
stories.script: Dokdo, located at the far eastern tip of our country, is an island formed by volcanic eruptions. It consists of two large islands, Dongdo (East Island) and Seodo (West Island), along with 89 smaller islets scattered around them. The island is home to many uniquely shaped rocks, like Chotdae Rock, which looks like a candle, Buchae Rock, which resembles a fan, and Neopdeok Rock, which has a flat shape. These rocks, blending harmoniously with the surrounding sea, create a breathtakingly beautiful view.  Dokdo has been Korean territory since the Silla period. In 512, General Isabu of Silla conquered Usan-guk, the kingdom that included both Ulleungdo and Dokdo, as recorded in historical texts. Later, references to the island as Usando, the old name for Dokdo, can be found in books like Goryeosa (History of Goryeo) and Sejong Sillok (The Annals of King Sejong), confirming that Dokdo has always been recognized as part of our territory. This led the Korean Empire to issue Imperial Decree No. 41 on October 25, 1900, to formally declare Dokdo as Korean territory. Unfortunately, with Japan's annexation of Korea, Dokdo was taken from us.  Even after Korea's liberation, Japan continues to falsely claim that Dokdo belongs to them, despite it clearly being part of Korean territory. Why does Japan persist with such claims? This is because Dokdo, though small and made up of rocks, holds immense strategic, natural, economic, and military importance.  A country's territory is not just its land, but also the surrounding sea and airspace. Losing Dokdo would mean losing control over the vast surrounding waters and skies. Dokdo is home to a variety of wildlife, and its waters are rich in marine resources and natural gas. Moreover, it is crucial for monitoring the naval and air movements of neighboring countries like Russia, Japan, and North Korea, making it a highly strategic location. For all these reasons, Dokdo has been designated as a natural monument.  Moreover, Dokdo is not just a small island but a symbol of the history and independence of the Republic of Korea. It is important to understand the history of Dokdo and continuously pay attention to protecting it.

stories.title: Entrance of Daereungwon Ancient Tombs
stories.script: Daereungwon Ancient Tombs, the Tomb Complex, is a site where numerous ancient tombs from the Silla period are concentrated.  These ancient tombs are akin to museums in their own right. In ancient period, the dead were buried along with their personal belongings, grave goods, and sometimes even their servants. Consequently, ancient tombs serve as repositories of historical records and offer valuable insights into the culture of those times.  Daereungwon, in particular, boasts a remarkable collection of numerous old tombs, including the resting places of renowned kings and aristocrats. Here, 37 tombs are clustered together, and among them is the Hwangnamdaechong Tomb, the largest tomb in Gyeongju, a city famous for the discovery of a remarkable golden crown.  To begin your exploration, let's start with the tomb nearest to the entrance, which is the tomb of King Michu. As you enter, follow the path to your left, and then take the right fork. You will soon come across the protective walls that encircle the tomb.

stories.title: Tomb of King Michu
stories.script: The large tomb enclosed and protected by the walls is the tomb of King Michu. King Michu was a significant figure in Silla history, serving as the first King of Silla from the Kim family. During his reign, he exhibited a strong commitment to the development of the kingdom, defended it against foreign invasions, and promoted agricultural advancement. These efforts earned him profound respect from the people, a respect that continued even after his passing.  King Michu's tomb is also known by the nickname the bamboo tomb. This name has an interesting story behind it. During the reign of the 14th king of Silla, the kingdom faced an invasion from a neighboring nation. Silla was struggling in the battles, and the situation looked dire. Then, seemingly out of nowhere, an army of resolute soldiers appeared. Each of them wore helmets adorned with bamboo leaves and fought valiantly on behalf of Silla, eventually leading the kingdom to victory.  After the battle, these mysterious soldiers vanished without a trace, leaving only bamboo leaves behind. People came to believe that these bamboo leaf soldiers originated from the bamboo forest surrounding King Michu's tomb, and thus, they began to refer to it as the bamboo tomb. The legend persisted, with people thinking that King Michu was still watching over and assisting Silla, the kingdom he loved, even after his passing.

stories.title: Entrance of Cheonmachong Tomb
stories.script: If you take the left path from the Tomb of King Michu and continue until you pass a small lake, you'll come across the information office of Cheonmachong Tomb, located to the west of the lake.  The name Cheonmachong Tomb refers to the “tomb of a heavenly horse.” What makes it particularly noteworthy is that typically a tomb is named after its owner, the person who is buried under it. However, in the case of Cheonmachong Tomb, the identity of the owner has never been uncovered. As a result, it is named after the most famous treasure discovered within it, which is the painting of a heavenly horse.  Cheonmachong Tomb stands at a height of 12.7 meters and has a diameter of 47 meters. Researchers estimate that its construction would have required the efforts of approximately 200 workers laboring full-time every day for over six months. These grand and opulent royal tombs underscore the ruler's desire to display their authority and the strength of the regime.  Venturing inside the tomb provides a glimpse into Silla culture. The internal structure and interior of the tomb are adorned with replicas of artifacts that were excavated from it. The original artifacts are on display at the Gyeongju National Museum.

stories.title: Cheonmachong Tomb
stories.script: Inside Cheonmachong Tomb, you can see the coffin of the owner of the tomb. It is an exact replica of what was discovered during the excavation.  The tomb is constructed in the typical Silla style. To build this tomb, first you lay the coffin and put up a wooden chamber around it. Then, you pile a mound of stones on the chamber and put a layer of mud on it.  Take a look into the glass case. When the site was excavated, a golden crown was found near the head of the body. It was covering the face like a mask. Also, a sword and a golden belt were hung around its waist, and the axe and a pair of gilt-bronze boots were found at the feet.  Much of the artifacts that were once kept in ancient tombs of Korea were lost due to robbery and foreign invasion. However, here in Cheonmachong Tomb, it seems most of them were kept safe. It owes to the unique structure of tombs of Silla.  If you look at the replica of the tomb, you’ll see the mound of stones on the wooden chamber. If grave robbers attempted to get into the tomb, the stones would crash and block the entrance. There was no way any robber could reach the artifacts inside.

stories.title: Cheonmado(Mudguard with a Painted Flying Horse)
stories.audioTitle: Cheonma Painting, The treasure of Cheonma Tomb
stories.script: Cheonma Painting, The treasure of Cheonma Tomb  This painting of a heavenly horse is an invaluable piece of Silla art.  It is designated as a national treasure and the original painting is kept in the National Museum of Korea.   This one is painted on a saddle flap, depicting a mythical horse similar to the unicorn.   The horse seems like flying in the sky, with its tongue sticking out and its tail curled upward.  This depicts a heavenly horse carrying the soul of a dead man to heaven.   But a more recent interpretation is that the animal is not a horse, but another mythical animal with a horn on its forehead.   This interpretation was offered after an infrared image of the painting revealed a horn-like shape on the forehead of the horse.   Whatever the animal in the painting is, its value as a precious cultural heritage from Silla does not change.    Now, let's take a look at the golden artifacts on the opposite side.

stories.title: Golden artifacts
stories.audioTitle: Golden artifacts, The pride of the Silla court
stories.script: Golden artifacts, The pride of the Silla court  A wide range of golden ornaments, including golden crowns, have been excavated from historical sites of Silla.  Let's learn about the fascinating art of Silla from the golden crown and ornaments here.   Let's take a closer look at the crown. On the front top part, there are three tree branch-shaped prongs.  These prongs are decorated with the shapes of sprouting plants and jade ornamentations that look like fetuses, which are believed to symbolize vitality.    Such a variety of ornamentations on the golden crown are associated to Silla people's belief of reincarnation.   Now, let's look at the golden belt.  The golden belt is heavily decorated with ornaments in the shape of fish, comma-shaped jade, whetstones and tongs.  These ornamentation must be important symbols of the Silla period. But the meaning attached to them has not been fully figured out yet.   But certainly these golden artifacts are the world-class cultural heritage that show the fabulous art and sophisticated craftsmanship of Silla.    Well, shall we now move to Hwangnam Tomb which is the largest tomb in the Tomb Complex? It is the two-humped tomb you see across the pond.

stories.title: Daereungwon Tomb Complex - Gold Crown of Silla in Daereungwon Tomb Complex
stories.audioTitle: Daereungwon Tomb Complex - Gold Crown of Silla in Daereungwon Tomb Complex
stories.script: Daereungwon Tomb Complex - Gold Crown of Silla in Daereungwon Tomb Complex  Secret of Silla gold crowns  [Teacher] Silla’s gold crowns have beautiful and splendid looks unprecedented in history of the entire world. But, as we can imagine, some people question whether or not the Silla people actually lived with these gold crowns on their heads.  [Student] Huh? Then, where did they use the crowns?  [Teacher] They say the gold crowns were used as death masks, a type of funeral product.  [Student] If you say death mask, does it mean gold crowns served to hide the faces?  [Teacher] Yes. It is said that the gold crowns discovered in Geumryeongchong Tomb near Daereungwon have standing ornaments in the shape of cones with a converging end. Also, the crowns were not worn on the heads but rather were dropped down to the shoulders of the corpses. The gold crowns of Cheonmachong and Hwangnamdaechong Tombs displayed similar looks. So, considering their excavated appearances, we presume that these gold crowns cover entire faces instead of wearing on heads. Also, the standing ornaments are too weak and bend easily even when the crown is moved by just a millimeter, which makes it unsuitable to be worn on the head.  [Student] So that's why people say that gold crowns were funeral items that were not actually used in real life.  [Teacher] That’s right. But it's still quite difficult to give a definitive answer on the usage of these gold crowns. Which can be said for the origin of these Silla gold crowns as well.  [Student] Huh? Are you saying the Silla gold crowns are not from Silla?  [Teacher] Regarding the origin of Silla gold crowns, there are two theories - one is the northern race theory and the other is the independent development theory.  [Student] The northern race theory sounds like Silla's gold crowns may be related to a northern race, no?  [Teacher] Yes. According to the northern race theory, the Silla gold crowns stemmed from shamanism from regions like Siberia. On the crowns worn by Siberian shamans, there are decorations in the shape of antlers, which are believed to have led to Silla’s gold crowns. Also, various tribes in Siberia and other northern regions worshiped a tree that connects the heavens and the earth, and the theory claims that the symbolic meaning of this tree traveled to Silla and evolved into the shape of twigs.  [Student] Ah, that’s why Silla gold crowns have standing ornaments.  [Teacher] Yes. But the other theory saying that the gold crowns were internally developed within Silla interpret the standing ornaments in a different way.  [Student] How?  [Teacher] They claim that the standing ornaments and decorations in the shapes of sprouts and an embryo on the Silla gold crowns are closely related to Gim Al-ji’s legendary birth story.  [Student] Gim Al-ji is the progenitor of the Gim royal family of the Silla Dynasty who was born in a golden box, right?  [Teacher] Right. Gim Al-ji was born from a golden box in the forest of Gyerim, and the twig ornaments on the Silla gold crowns symbolize these trees of Gyerim, according to some scholars. And tree leaves and magatama, which symbolize birth, were hung on this sacred tree.  [Student] Then, Gyerim would be the origin of Silla’s gold crowns.  [Teacher] Yes, they say that what the Silla gold crowns symbolizes is none other than Gyerim itself. What do you think? Silla’s gold crowns are as glamorous as they are secretive. But, if all of you continue to study and research our history and cultures, I believe those secrets will be solved naturally over time.  Now, let’s go out of Cheonmachong Tomb and walk over to Hwangnamdaechong Tomb, which is the largest tomb in Daereungwon, shall we?  Hwangnamdaechong is a twin-grave tomb located on the other side of the pond next to Cheonmachong.

stories.title: Hwangnam tomb
stories.script: Hwangnam tomb  This is Great Hwangam Tomb, which is the largest tomb in Korea.   If you take a closer look at it, you'll see that it is not a single tomb but is actually two linked mounds.   A tomb consisting of two linked grave mounds just like this one is considered the tomb of a married couple.  Supporting this explanation, male bones were found in the southern part of this tomb and a woman's belt in the northern part.     Numerous artifacts were excavated from this tomb. A golden crown, necklaces, bracelets and comma-shaped jade were found in the northern part, and a gilt bronze crown and weapons were discovered in the southern part.  So it is believed that the northern tomb belongs to a queen and the southern tomb to a king.    What's notable is that bone fragments of a girl of about 15 years of age were found along with the bones of a man in the southern part. This indicates that the girl was buried along with the dead man. According to historical records, burying the slaves alive along with of the dead was prohibited in Silla. But this tomb suggests that the practice was actually alive.    Well, this is the end of the tour of the Tomb Complex.  When you exit, try the back route of Hwangnam Tomb. You'll see many other tombs on your way out.

stories.title: Daereungwon Ancient Tombs
stories.script: The massive ancient tombs at Daereungwon Tomb Complex are an important remembrance of Silla. However, it’s not known yet to whom the 23 tombs belong. Researchers are assuming that the tombs were made for kings and other members of the royal family, but we have no historical record to prove this.  Excavated between 1973 and 1975, Hwangnamdaechong is the largest among all the tombs. It is a set of twin tombs that belong to a couple. More than 58,000 pieces of golden artifacts were discovered along with the bone fragments of a man in his 60s and a woman around the age of 16. It’s presumed that they were married.  In the Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms written by Il-yeon Daesa, there is an interesting story regarding the tomb. It dates all the way back to the reign of King Soji, the 21st monarch of Silla. Being the smallest of the three kingdoms on the Korean Peninsula back then, Silla used to suffer from a never-ending stream of wars and battles before the unification. The old king often had to patrol along the border areas himself.   One night, the King was about to stay in Yeongju, which is now a city in Gyeongsangbuk-do. A local nobleman asked the King to take his daughter as his wife. She was a beautiful woman named “Byeokhwa.” Embarrassed by the age gap, the King declined the offer at first. However, Byeokhwa’s beauty wouldn’t leave his thoughts. Spending a few nights tossing and turning in his bed, the King decided to begin dating Byeokhwa in disguise. Even though he hid himself hard, rumors about the King’s relationship quickly spread across the kingdom. King Soji left Byeokhwa and tried to forget her, but the love was so intense that he couldn’t bring himself to get over her. At last, he ended up smuggling Byeokhwa into his palace where he spent the rest of his days deep in love. Since a couple was discovered in it, it’s been assumed that Hwangnam-daechong is the remains of the iconic love of the King and the young woman.   A magnolia tree stands between the two mounds of the tomb, and each year, it blossoms with white magnolias, seemingly celebrating the enduring love between the two lovers.

stories.title: Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond: Entrance
stories.audioTitle: Anap , The pond of the moon
stories.script: Anap , The pond of the moon  [Teacher]  This pond which shows a romantic moonlight reflection is called Anap. But its original name was Wolji, meaning the moon pond.  [Student]  Oh, the moon pond sounds like a place for fairies. This place must have been very beautiful.  [Teacher]  Yes. This pond was created in the 7th century when Silla was at its height.  It was like a royal vacation home and also used as the palace of the crown prince. At that time, the pond was surrounded by beautiful flowers and trees, and the king and aristocrats loved this place.  But as time went by, the moon pond lost its light and its name was changed to the current name, Anap.     [Student] What happened to this pond?  [Teacher]  The word Anap refers to ducks and geese. After Silla collapsed, the pond lost its glamour.  Poets who visited the pond long afterward gave the name, from the sight of ducks and geese swimming in the deserted pond.   [Student]  It's a sad story.  [Teacher]  Yes. But the pond has been beautifully restored. And many relics showing the everyday lives of Silla people were excavated and are now exhibited in Gyeongju National Museum.  [Student]  Then let's go see the moon pond now!  [Teacher]  OK. Let's go inside to the first building in front of the pond.

stories.title: Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond: In front of the first building
stories.script: What is Anap Pond like  Let's have a look at the pond.  About 13 centuries ago, 26 buildings were here. But today, only a large pond and three buildings are restored.   The stones lining up on the grass show where the buildings used to be.  The three restored buildings are known to be the largest of the 26 buildings.   In these buildings, Silla nobles held banquets; foreign envoys were received; and important ceremonies were held.    Now, let's move to the second building where you'll see a miniature of the pond, which will help you imagine how big and magnificent it was back in the 7th century.

stories.title: In the second building (Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond)
stories.audioTitle: In the second building (Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond)
stories.script: Did you notice that many of the artifacts on display are wooden objects. Isn’t it a wonder how they lasted without rotting for over 1300 years?  The secret lies at the bottom of the pond. During the excavation, numerous items were found on the bed of the pond, buried in a thick layer of mud. The mud kept the objects from air, preventing any form of erosion.  Among the items in this building are a 14-faced wooden dice and a scissors-like tool. The scissors were used for cutting candle wicks, and the dice was used for games that involved drinking. The wooden dice was found at the bottom of the pond during the excavation in 1975. Made from an oak tree, the dice was as big as a child’s fist and had fourteen sides instead of six. On each side, an interesting penalty was inscribed.   Types of penalties included things like drinking three glasses of alcohol, hitting one’s own nose, dancing without music, and laughing hard after drinking.

stories.title: Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond: Strolling around the pond
stories.script: Gardening secrets  This is a man-made pond which is representative of the relics of the Silla kingdom.  By the name pond, most people would expect a small body of water. But this one seems a little too big to be called a pond.    In fact, it is the gardening technique that does the magic.  First, have a look at the western part of the pond and then the eastern part.  Have you noticed the difference? While the western boundary is straight, the eastern side shows many curves and irregular bends.   What makes this pond look larger than its actual size is the contrast between a linear open space and a curvy closed space.  Another secret is the uneven height, which many of you would have already noticed. The western bank of the pond is twice taller than its eastern counterpart. Anyone who stood on the western bank overlooking the east side would have the impression that he is looking down on a vast sea.     Indeed, that was precisely the key to the pond's design, making a limited space of a pond look like an open sea. As a result, you cannot have a complete view of the pond from any single point of location.   So it feels like there is some unknown world on the other side of the pond.  It makes you wonder how big this pond is and what lies over there.    Why don't you take another look at it? You'll see the artistic sensibility of Silla people in every corner.   Now, let's move to the next stop, the waterway that draws water to this pond.  Walking along the pond, you will find a stone waterway at the western end.  It is the device that pipes water into the pond.

stories.title: In front of the Anap waterway (Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond)
stories.audioTitle: In front of the Anap waterway (Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond)
stories.script: Let's explore the surroundings of the pond. Anapji, a manmade pond, means ‘a pond with geese and ducks.’ Abandoned for an extended period, historical records about the pond and palace gradually surfaced starting from 1980, documented within the History of the Three Kingdoms. Since 2011, it has been officially referred to as Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond, reinstating its original names. Approximately thirteen centuries ago, this area was occupied by twenty-six structures. Presently, only the pond and the three largest buildings have been restored, marked by stones arranged on the grass to indicate the locations of the former buildings.  These buildings served as venues for Silla nobles' banquets, receiving foreign envoys, and hosting significant ceremonies.

stories.title: Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond
stories.script: Taking a leisurely walk in the evening is one of the more romantic things you can do when you travel to a new place. Glittering lights excite adults and children alike. If you are looking for a place along the eastern seaboard that offers a spectacular nightscape, Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond in Gyeongju (along with Daewangam Park in Ulsan and the steel mills in Pohang) are the places to be.  Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond were built by King Munmu the Great (the 30th monarch of Shilla) to celebrate the unification of the three kingdoms. Here, Donggung refers to the residential palace for the Crown Prince, and Wolji means a moonlit pond. One historical record states, “King Gyeongsun hosted a banquet at Imhaejeon to welcome Wang Geon.” Another record says, “[Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond] were home to rare flowers and animals.” Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond gave people a place to rest, just as parks do in modern times.   King Munmu the Great brought peace after centuries of war. He would have wanted to build the greatest garden in the world in hopes of securing eternal glory for unified Shilla. Nevertheless, Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond were not an ostentatious display of victory. They were built upon the spirit of harmony. The King invited artisans from Baekje and Goguryeo to construct them. That is why Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond featured sweeping curves that were distinct in Baekje structures, and powerful straight lines that were typical of Goguryeo architecture. It seems, King Munmu the Great was indeed a great visionary!  Today, we can still enjoy leisurely breaks at Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond. In that sense, we are the same as our ancestors who lived during the Shilla Dynasty. Naturally, large quantities of historical artifacts from the Shilla period were discovered at the bottom of Wolji Pond. In fact, there were so many artifacts the Gyeongju National Museum had to create a dedicated hall (Wolji Hall) to exhibit them. Particularly noteworthy is the ‘Canoe’ which is an important resource that shows how the Shilla people built boats.  Surprisingly, a drawing of a boat similar to the canoe discovered in Wolji Pond has been found in the “Petroglyphs of Bangudae Terrace” in Ulsan, which is believed to have been created during the prehistoric age. Where do you think people would have traveled to on their small canoes? To the sea, the pond, or somewhere else? If you watch the shimmering moonlight and shadows reflected on the surface of Wolji Pond, you might find yourself transported back in time to the Shilla Kingdom.

stories.title: Cheomseongdae: On a way to observatory
stories.script: Cheomseong Observatory, A star-gazing tower  [Teacher]  This structure is called Cheomgseong Observatory, the star-gazing tower.            [Student]  Well, for me, it’s more like a tower. But as a tower, it's neither gorgeous nor tall.  So... I first guessed it might be a storage or chimney. To be honest, I don't understand why it is a famous cultural heritage.             [Teacher]  Judging from its appearance, you may think so. Well, you might be surprised if I tell you this is the oldest astronomical observatory in the East built in the 7th century.          [Student] An astronomical observatory? Did they really observe stars there? An observatory is supposed to be in the mountain.            [Teacher]  Today, observatories are built in the mountains to stay away from the bright lights of cities. But in Silla, they didn't have to climb up high to watch stars because there was no air pollution or bright lights at that time.    [Student]  I see. Then why were Silla people so interested in astronomy?   [Teacher]  Yes. In ancient agricultural societies, astronomical observation was extremely important.  By observing stars, people were able to predict floods and draughts and astronomical events like solar and lunar eclipses. And they believed a sudden appearance of a new star or death of a large star were the signs that something important might happen to their kingdom.          [Student]  Oh, so they were keen on studying the movement of stars to foretell the future of their kingdom.           [Teacher]  Exactly. Then why don't we go to see how Silla people observed stars up there?

stories.title: At the Cheomseong Observatory (Cheomseongdae)
stories.script: The astronomical observatory of Cheomseongdae has both rectangular edges and round parts with graceful carves. The round part and the rectangular part each represents the sky and the earth.  According to the records, the square window opening in the middle was the hole through which people went in and out of the observatory. Supporting this explanation are the small holes that were found inside. It’s believed that they were made by people leaning a ladder against the inner wall. This indicates that people went into the observatory through the window opening using a ladder, and then climbed up another ladder from the inside to the top, to observe stars. Below the window opening is filled with dirt and gravel, which makes a strong platform for people to stand on.  A total of 362 blocks were used to build the observatory. The number of blocks represents the number of days in a year in a lunar calendar. The 12 layers of stone blocks represent 12 months that make up a year. This suggests that the observatory might have served as a calendar for people of Silla.  This observatory was near the royal palace of Silla. An astronomical observatory needed to be close to the palace, so that any changes observed in the sky could be promptly reported to the king.  Since Cheomseongdae Observatory was built, records of observations of solar and lunar eclipses, appearance of comets and extreme weather events were made more frequently. The observations are also known to be very accurate. Cheomseongdae Observatory carries both a significant scientific value and beautiful appearance, making it a perfect example of Silla’s advanced knowledge of science and refined artistry.

stories.title: Look Around Cheomseongdae Observatory (Cheomgseongdae Observatory)
stories.script: The fact that ancient people observed stars doesn't solely indicate their curiosity but also reflects their grasp of 'astronomy,' the study of celestial changes. Astronomy held significant importance in agricultural societies due to its direct correlation with weather patterns, crucial for farming.  It was intricately intertwined with politics. Believing that royal authority was divinely bestowed, people regarded celestial changes as indicative of human world transformations. For instance, meteors or comets were perceived as ominous omens signalling the imminent demise of someone important.  Hence, interpreting celestial phenomena served as a means to validate political legitimacy for both nobility and the populace. Astronomy remained a closely guarded secret, accessible only to a select few. National calendars were also confidential due to their inclusion of pivotal astronomical occurrences like solar and lunar eclipses. This notion stemmed from the belief in governing the country in alignment with the will and supremacy of heaven.  The prevailing view of Cheomseongdae Observatory suggests it was an astronomical observatory, but its actual function remains controversial. Let's explore the divergent perspectives.  Some researchers argue that during the Silla period, Cheomseongdae was used solely to measure sun-induced shadow lengths and not for astronomical investigations. They contend that its structure, including the square window and the installation of observation instruments like Honcheonui, seems unsuitable. Climbing in and out of the tower daily would have been inconvenient for astronomers. Instead, they posit that people utilized it to understand various solar terms like Chunbun, Chubun Haji, and Dongji, applying this knowledge to agriculture, serving as a sundial hub.  Others perceive Cheomseongdae Observatory as an object or altar for religious purposes. Queen Seondeok, the tower's builder, expressed in her will a desire to be buried in Doricheon after her death. Doricheon symbolizes the sky at the summit of Sumisan Mountain, a sacred place in Buddhism. Advocates of this view assert that Cheomseongdae Observatory 's design mirrors Sumisan, suggesting a religious connotation.  Lastly, some scholars view Cheomseongdae Observatory as a 'space well,' a passage connecting the celestial realm (inhabited by gods) and the earthly world (inhabited by people). The Silla people perceived wells constructed of piled stones on the ground, akin to Cheomseongdae Observatory, as such passages. Given Queen Seondeok's various political challenges during her reign, she might have sought to fortify her authority by establishing a connection to the heavens through Cheomseongdae Observatory.  Having acquainted yourself with these theories, take a moment to observe Cheomseongdae. Envision the Silla people coming and going. Which story resonates the most with you?

stories.title: Cheomseong Observatory
stories.script: Cheomseongdae Observatory was built under the reign of Queen Seondeok, the 27th monarch of Silla. She was the first queen ever recorded in the written history of Korea. Undoubtedly, she faced considerable pressure from those who questioned her leadership.  During that era, people held a deep fear of celestial signs. The prevailing belief was that only those chosen by the heavens were fit to rule the land. Cheomseongdae Observatory was intended as a celestial gateway for the royal family, allowing them to observe the stars to predict human destiny.  In the waning years of Queen Seondeok's rule, a rebellion led by Bidam emerged against the Crown. As the uprising gained momentum, a significant shooting star streaked across the sky. Witnessing this celestial event, Bidam's followers interpreted it as a sign of the Queen's impending downfall, emboldening their rebellion.  General Kim Yu-sin devised a shrewd strategy to restore order to the kingdom. He affixed a large fireball to a kite, releasing it into the sky near the Cheomseongdae Observatory. The intention was to create an illusion that the fallen star had returned to the heavens. When the rebels saw the bright fireball ascend once more, they believed it to be the Queen's star and were seized by terror, resulting in their swift dispersal.  Historical records indicate that Queen Seondeok passed away before the rebellion was completely quelled. Nonetheless, her government's resolve and dedication to safeguarding the country endure, resonating through the legacy of the Cheomseongdae Observatory.

stories.title: Gungnamji Pond
stories.script: The Royal Pond of Baekje  Welcome to Gungnamji Pond! The Pond was the first artificial pond to be built on the Korean Peninsula in 634 A.D. Surrounded by serene willow trees, it embodies the gentle beauty characteristic of the Orient. Historical records reveal that the pond was linked to a 7.8-kilometer-long waterway, drawing water from a distant source. At its center stood an artificial island symbolizing the Bangjangseonsan Mountain, evidenced by the discovery of its original stone foundation at the pond's bottom. The advanced technology demonstrated in the pond's construction reflects the progressive capabilities of the people of Baekje. The island and the pavilion were restored in the 1960s in accordance with historical records.  Crossing the bridge to the island, visitors can consider visiting Gungnamji Pond during the summer to experience the annual lotus festival. The air becomes infused with the delightful scent of fully bloomed lotus flowers, presenting a magnificent spectacle. Over 1,400 years ago, the king of Baekje would enjoy the pond's scenery from the pavilion, amidst the sweet fragrance of lotuses. Why not take a moment to relax in the pavilion and appreciate the stunning views?  While resting in the pavilion, would you like to hear a love story associated with the pond? King Mu, who commissioned the construction of Gungnamji Pond, was raised outside the palace, unaware of his lineage due to political circumstances. As he grew older, he fell in love with the beautiful Princess Seonhwa from the Silla kingdom. However, their love faced obstacles not only due to his lower social status but also because Silla was an adversary of Baekje at that time. To communicate his feelings, he taught Silla's children a song implying that the princess was secretly enamored with a man from Baekje. When the Silla king heard this song, he was infuriated and banished the princess from the palace. Subsequently, she met King Mu outside the palace and reciprocated his feelings. Eventually, King Mu brought her back to Baekje and married her. Upon ascending the Baekje throne, he ordered the creation of the pond, presenting it as a gift to the princess.  What do you think of this story? It is akin to the Baekje version of Romeo and Juliet. Keep an eye out for statues of the couple scattered throughout Buyeo as you explore!

stories.title: Poseokjeong Pavilion: At the entrance of Poseokjeong Pavilion
stories.audioTitle: At the entrance of Poseokjeong Pavilion
stories.script: At the entrance of Poseokjeong Pavilion  [Teacher]  Now, we are at Poseokjeong Pavilion. This was a place for entertainment. Here, the king and the nobility held banquets and spent their leisure time, setting drinking glasses afloat on the winding waterway and composing poems while waiting for the glasses to come in front of them.                   [Student]  Wow, they maintained their dignity even when enjoying entertainment.    [Teacher]  Yes. But it is also a place related to the tragic end of the Silla Kingdom.          [Student]  The end of Silla?  [Teacher]  Yes, records say that during the late Silla period, a neighboring kingdom attacked Silla when the king of Silla was holding a banquet here.  Later, the king was forced to kill himself, and that led to the collapse of Silla.    [Student]  I see. But how can the king have a banquet when the enemy was attacking his kingdom?   [Teacher]  Well, that's what the records say. But there are different views as well. History is written by the victors, so the saying goes.  Maybe the kingdom which overthrew Silla wrote the story in their favor.       And as some records say that kings performed rituals here when the kingdom was in a crisis, it seems that this pavilion was not just a place for entertainment.             [Student]  I see. Anyhow, I'm sorry that the 1,000-year history of Silla ended just like that.   [Teacher]  Indeed. Now, shall we talk about that more, while looking around this pavilion which witnessed both glamorous life of the Silla nobility and the demise of the kingdom?

stories.title: Poseokjeong Pavilion: In front of the waterway
stories.script: The waterway  Currently in Poseokjeong Pavilion, only the waterway remains which was used to set drinking glasses afloat.  Now there's no water flowing in this waterway, but Silla people would set drinking glasses afloat in it to pass them to others.   Let's take a closer look at it. You'll see that the stones are carved to create a gently bending waterway.  It was built in a curve to slow down the stream which carries the drinking glasses.  They enjoyed the waiting time until the stream brought the glass to them, composing and reciting poems.  But if this pavilion had not been a place of entertainment where people would drink and write poems, what would have been the purpose of this waterway?   Some say that this place was a shrine. And this waterway is believed to have been a place where sacred rituals were performed for gods or ancestors.      Water has long been considered purifying and clearing people both spiritually and physically.  So maybe Silla people performed rituals at this waterway to ward off misfortunes and pray for peace and well-being of the kingdom.   If that is true, the Silla king, who was known to have a banquet here when his kingdom was invaded, might have actually been praying for the kingdom.   As there are no accurate records about this place, it is still unclear when this pavilion was constructed and why the waterway was built.   Still, the tragic story of Silla's collapse still lingers in many corners of this pavilion.

stories.title: Najeong Well: At the entrance of Najeong Well
stories.script: Najeong Well,The beginning of Silla  [Teacher]  This is Najeong Well where the founder of Silla, Park Hyeok-geo-se, was born.  [Student]  Park Hyeok-geo-se?   [Teacher]  Yes, before Silla, six tribes were competing with one another in the city of Gyeongju.  In the 1st century BC, Park Hyeok-geo-se emerged to unify these tribes and built the Silla Kingdom.  So, you can say that the 1,000-year history of Silla began with him.   [Student]  Wow, that's cool! Is there any legend about him? Every great person in history has one.                [Teacher]  Yes. The legend says that he was born here at Najeong well, from an auspicious red egg.   [Student]  Born from an egg? Well, it seems that even his birth was unusual because he was destined to build a kingdom.  Then did his descendents succeed the throne?  [Teacher]  Not exactly. In Silla, three families-Park, Seok, and Kim-took the throne in turn.  That was because in early days of the Silla Kingdom, the power of the king was relatively weak and politics and society was not very stable. So the three families took turns to succeed the throne, sometimes competing with external forces who brought new cultures to the society. But although the throne was shared, Silla remained a coherent kingdom.           [Student]  I see. I want to learn more about Park Hyeokgoese, the founder king!   [Teacher]  OK, let's go to Najeong Well and learn some more about him.

stories.title: Najeong Well: At Najeong Well
stories.audioTitle: At the excavation site of Najeong well
stories.script: At the excavation site of Najeong well  This is Najeong Well where Silla's founder king was born.   The excavation has been completed, but the restoration is not done yet. So what we're seeing is the site of the well.    During the excavation, the site, surrounding fences and waterways of the well were found.  Look at the circular space in the center.  Here, a set of pottery used for rituals and an octagonal building site were found during the excavation.     Historical records say that a shrine for the founder king was built on the site.    Bronze Age house sites were also discovered around Najeong well, which indicates that this place was inhabited even before the foundation of Silla.    The founder king derived his power from this place to unite the six tribes competing in the city of Gyeongju and ultimately built the Silla Kingdom which lasted a thousand years.   So Silla people considered this place sacred.   Now, shall we hear the legend of the king's birth? It is about a birth from an egg.    Park Hyeokgeose - Born from an egg  [Narration]  Before Silla was founded, the city of Gyeongju was divided by six tribes.  One day, the tribe leaders gathered to choose a new king. During their meeting, a mystical energy came down from the far southern sky.   [Tribe Leader 1]  What an auspicious sign! The energy seems to be coming from Najeong Well,   Let’s go find out what it is.   [Narration]  As the tribe leaders arrived at Najeong Well, they discovered a large, red-colored egg.   They also found a white horse kneeling in front of the egg, with its head bowed, but the horse flew away into the sky as soon as the men stepped closer to the egg.   The tribe leaders were astonished. They decided to crack open the egg. Incredibly, they discovered a beautiful baby boy inside.   The tribe leaders took the baby to a nearby spring and bathed him. All cleaned up, the baby shone with sacred light. The ground began to shake, the skies began to thunder, and the birds and beasts started dancing with joy.   [Tribe Leader 1]  Do you see what is happening? This baby boy must be a gift from heaven!   It is an omen, he is to become our king!  [Tribe Leader 2]  You are absolutely right! He will become a king worthy of our praise and rule with dignity to make a better world. Just look at the signs? the birds and beasts are dancing joyfully before him and the sun and moon are glowing!  [Tribe Leader 1]  Let's name him ‘Park Hyeok-geo-se'.  We wish you rule the kingdom with a pure heart to make the world a better place in the future.    [Narration]   In 57 BC, Park Hyeok-geo-se was crowned the king of Silla with the blessing of the six tribes. And true to his name,   he wisely ruled the kingdom and made his people's lives better.

stories.title: In front of Gyerim Forest
stories.script: Gyeryeom, the site celebrating the birth legend of Kim Alji, the founding ancestor of the Silla Kim dynasty, holds significant importance. Originally known as ‘Sirim,’ signifying a sacred forest, it later acquired the name ‘Gyerim’ due to its association with Kim Alji's birth legend, involving a chicken. ‘Gyerim’ translates to a forest where chickens cry.  However, why did the legend feature a chicken? Chickens, which we commonly encounter today, held a unique place in the beliefs of the Silla people during those times. Birds, in general, were perceived as creatures bridging the heavens and the earth. Chickens, in particular, were revered as sacred animals capable of dispelling darkness and heralding the morning. This reverence for chickens as bird totems is a significant part of the Gyerim Forest legend.  Within the western pine forest connected to Gyerim Forest, a shrine is dedicated to the 17th King Nae Mool of Silla. King Nae Mool, as the second member of the Kim family to ascend the throne, played a pivotal role in securing the ongoing reign of the Kim family.  While Kim Alji is often regarded as the founding ancestor, it's important to note that he never became a king. The first Kim to ascend the throne did so during the reign of King Michu, the 13th king. Silla's rulership alternated among the Park, Seok, and Kim families. Following King Nae Mool, the Kim family predominantly retained the throne, producing a total of 38 Kim kings out of the 56 in Silla's history.  Despite not ascending to the throne, Kim Alji is indeed a figure deserving of admiration, as his legacy laid the groundwork for the Kim family to hold the throne across numerous generations.

stories.title: Walking around Gyerim Forest
stories.script: On a March night, a radiant light emanated from the forest to the west of the Geumseong Palace. A rooster crowed, though it wasn’t yet time. King Talhae, the fourth king of Silla, found this occurrence strange and opted to wait until daylight before dispatching his servant to investigate.  Upon reaching Gyerim Forest, the servant saw a small golden chest hanging from a tree branch, with a white rooster crowing beneath it. Surprised, the servant hurried back and reported the discovery to the king. King Talhae then went to Gyerim Fortress and opened the golden chest, revealing a cunning-looking baby boy inside. Deeming the child as a celestial blessing, the king bestowed upon him the title of prince.  The birth legend of Kim Alji emphasizes the sacredness of the character through various symbolic elements. First, the rooster crowed when Kim Alji was born from the golden box. In that era, the people of Silla regarded birds and gold in reverence. Birds were viewed as creatures bridging heaven and earth, while gold served as a jewel symbolizing the authority of royalty and nobility.  The tree from which the golden chest hung symbolized the link between heaven and earth, signifying the mythological aspect of Kim Alji’s descent from heaven.  Thus, with his mysterious birth highlighting his sanctity, Kim Alji was recognized as a prince by King Talhae. However, he later relinquished the throne in favor of his cousin. It was his seventh-generation descendant, King Michu, who eventually ascended to the throne.  Gyerim Forest, where the legend of Kim Alji's birth is enshrined, remains a sacred site to this day. Relics from the Kim Alji birth legend, erected during the reign of King Sunjo in the Joseon period, still exist. It is highly recommended to visit and explore these remnants.

stories.title: In front of Wolseong Fortress (Wolseong Fortress)
stories.audioTitle: In front of Wolseong Fortress (Wolseong Fortress)
stories.script: Wolsong Fortress, an ancient historical royal palace is located in Gyeongju, a city renowned for its profound history and cultural heritage. It is also known as the ‘Moon Castle,’ owing to its distinctive half-moon-like shape.  In the 22nd year of King Pasa's reign, a fortress, named Wolseong or Jaeseong was built to the southeast of Geumseong. Wolseong Fortress subsequently served as the royal palace until the decline of Silla.  Originally, the hill-shaped terrain resembling a crescent moon is believed to have accommodated several palaces. However, the actual appearance of Wolseong has faded over time, leaving only traces documented in historical records.  Only the site of the palace remains, with a few surviving structures yet to be restored. Most of the palace buildings no longer exist. Nevertheless, the site encompasses remnants of various structures, holding significant archaeological site in unraveling the history and architectural aspects of the Silla Dynasty.

stories.title: In front of Seokbinggo (Wolseong Fortress)
stories.script: According to historical records, the people inhabiting the Korean peninsula built their first ice storage facilities around the first century, overseen by government officials.  Seokbinggo, the ice storage, was built in 1783. It was utilized for storing naturally formed ice to be utilized during hotter periods.  How did they prevent the ice from melting before summer? The interior is made of slanting granite, aiding in the drainage of melting ice while maintaining a cool environment. Additionally, the design effectively insulated the storage from warm external air. Externally, the rounded roof featured a stone vent that released warm air, allowing people to enjoy ice even in hot summers.  Historical records indicate that ice storage structures were first built in Korea around the 1st century, with government officials even having their own storage units. Korea boasts a lengthy history of ice storage. However, for an extended period, ice was primarily reserved for those in prominent positions and used for preserving bodies and cooling patients.

stories.title: Oreung(Five Royal Tombs in Gyeongju): At the entrance of Oreung
stories.audioTitle: Descendents of Park Hyekgeose and Queen Alyeon
stories.script: Descendents of Park Hyekgeose and Queen Alyeon  [Teacher]  This is Oreung which refers to five tombs. These tombs belong to five members of the Park family, Park Hyeok-geo-se, the founder king; his queen Alyeong; and three kings from the family.    [Student]  So these are royal tombs. Then why do people call these “five tombs and not specify which tomb belongs to whom?    [Teacher]  That's because it is unclear to whom each of the tombs belong. And also there is another reason for the name.  [Student]  Oh, what is it?   [Teacher]  According to historical records, Park Hyeokgeose went up to heaven after he died.  And seven days later, his body fell from the sky in five pieces.   [Student]  A corpse cut in five pieces? Ooh, that's creepy!   [Teacher]  So, people tried to put his body back together for burial.  But suddenly a giant snake sprang from the ground and blocked them.  So they ended up burying each of the five pieces separately.             For this reason, these tombs are called Oreung meaning “five tombs or sometimes Sareung, meaning “snake tombs.  [Student]  It's kind of scary but also interesting.    [Teacher]  Yes, it is. Now, why don't we go to Oreung Tombs and Alyeong Well where Queen Alyeong was born?  [Student] Okay.

stories.title: Oleung - Look Around Oleung
stories.script: Oleung - Look Around Oleung  Looking at Oleung  Have you arrived in front of Oleung? Although the interior structure of Oleung is unknown, its exterior appearance is similar to other typical Silla tombs; with earth that is piled up in the shape of a semispherical mound. This type of grave appeared after the 4th century in Silla and was not the kind used during the time of Bak Hyeokgeose.  According to the records of Samguk Sagi, however, the five tombs of Oleung are regarded as those of Bak Hyeokgeose Geoseogan; his wife, Queen Aryeong; the second king, Namhae Chachaung; the third king, Yuri Isageum; and the fifth king, Pasa Isageum. You may have realized the variety of names that were used to call the Silla kings. Shall we briefly talk about the changes of the titles of Silla kings? In the early stages of Silla, the governing ruler was not designated as the king; instead, he was called Geoseogan, Chachaung, Isageum and Maripgan, and it was only during the reign of Jijeung, the 22nd king of Silla, when the designation, king, started to be used.  First of all, Geoseogan was used during the reign of Bak Hyeokgeose, the progenitor of Silla, and the name, which meant a precious person, referred to the leader of a small nation.  The second ruler following Bak Hyeokgeose was known as Chachaung, which meant a shaman. As the name suggests, Chachaung was a leader who communicated with gods and oversaw both rituals and politics.  Isageum, which literally means a person with many teeth, is the term that refers to an elder. Silla at the time was a league of several states, and the leaders of the states took turns to inherit the throne. Then, Yuri and Talhae, the son and the son-in-law of Namhae Chachaung, respectively, wanted the other person to become the next ruler and, as they continued to yield to each other, stories say that they both bit into a rice cake and the one with more teeth marks, which was Yuri, ended up taking the throne first.  After Isageum, the term, Maripgan, was used. Maripgan means the chief who sits on a high peak and refers to a great leader. As the Kim Clan monopolized the hereditary right to the throne, they began using the title, Maripgan, to manifest their desire to strengthen the royal authority.  Since then, the father-son inheritance system was solidified and the political structure (6-bu) was reformed to achieve centralization of power. In the process, the title of king started to be used.  As you can see, the terms to call the king of Silla continued to evolve together with the changes in the scope of royal authority.  Now, shall we move to Aryeongjeong where Bak Hyeokgeose's wife, Queen Aryeong, was supposed to be born from? Aryeongjeong is located to the east of Oleung.

stories.title: Oreung(Five Royal Tombs in Gyeongju): At Alyeongjeong well
stories.audioTitle: Queen Alyeong, who was born of a dragon
stories.script: Queen Alyeong, who was born of a dragon  [Narration]  This place is Alyeong Well where Queen Alyeong was born. This is the only place in Korea linked to the birth legend of a queen.   Now, shall we find out how Alyeong, the first Queen of Silla and Park Hyeok-geo-se's wife, was born?    On the day Park Hyeok-geo-se was born from an egg, another strange thing happened at the well named Alyeong.  An old woman who came to the well to draw water found a dragon inside.   And a baby girl was born from the dragon's left side.  Then the dragon flew into the sky.    The baby girl had fair skin and beautiful eyes. But her lips were shaped like the beak of a chicken.   [Old Woman]  How odd.. Such a pretty baby girl has the beak of a chicken.   [Narration]  The old woman took the baby to a nearby stream to bathe her, then suddenly the beak fell off.  Later the old woman named the baby Alyeong, after the name of the well where she was found, and raised her with love. Alyeong grew up to become a bright and beautiful woman, and became the Park Hyeok-geo-se’s queen.

stories.title: Hwangnyongsa Temple: The site of Hwangyongsa Temple
stories.script: Hwangnyongsa Temple that protected Silla  [Teacher]  Here we are at the site of Hwangnyongsa Temple. Although it no longer exists, the temple is known as the largest Buddhist temple from Silla.     [Student]  Really? I'm sorry that such a grand temple is gone. By the way, what does the name Hwangnyong mean?    [Teacher]  Hwangnyong refers to a yellow dragon. Originally, a royal palace was supposed to be built here.   But when the construction work was about to begin, a yellow dragon suddenly appeared to the site.             So the king thought it was a message form Buddha and decided to build a Buddhist temple instead of a royal palace.            [Student]  A temple of a yellow dragon... well, it sounds cool. But what happened to the temple? Why doesn't it exist now?  [Teacher]  The temple had been here even after the Silla Kingdom collapsed.  But it was destroyed by fire during a foreign invasion in the 13th century.  The famous 9-story pagoda in the temple was also burned down at that time.    [Student]  I see... and why did Silla build such a huge Buddhist temple?   [Teacher]  Well, you know that kings in the West often built large churches or cathedrals for certain purposes or to show off their power.  It was the same in the East. As Silla was a Buddhist kingdom, the king wished to strengthen his kingdom and unite the people with the help of Buddha.                     [Student]  Oh, yes. In Silla, building a large temple was not just to promote a religion. Rather, it was a national project that served various political purposes, right?  [Teacher]  Exactly. Well, now shall we look at the site where the main building of the temple was located?  The site is where a number of foundation stones lie.

stories.title: Hwangnyongsa Temple: The site of the main building
stories.audioTitle: The Giant Buddha Statue and the well of Hwangyong Temple
stories.script: The Giant Buddha Statue and the well of Hwangyong Temple  Walk down the path and you'll see two sites where a number of foundation stones lie.  The smaller one is where a pagoda stood and the larger one is where the main temple building was.   At the center of the building site there are three large stones. They mark the place where a 5-meter-high statue of Buddha stood.  The statue was one of the three most famous treasures of the Silla kingdom.  The giant Buddha statue is believed to have protected Silla from foreign invasion.   And there is a mysterious story about the statue. The story goes that a King of India had tried to build a Buddha statue but repeatedly failed.  So he gave up and put a huge amount of gold, bronze, iron along with models of a statue in a boat and shipped them away.  The boat arrived in Silla, and the king of Silla ordered carftsmen to build a statue with the materials.  Surprisingly, the statue was successfully built on the first try. That statue was kept in this temple.     And there was also a famous painting of a pine tree. A famous artist of Silla painted an old pine tree on a wall of this building.  The painting was so lifelike that birds saw it as a real tree and flew into it.   Also, this temple was home to another of the three treasures of Silla, the 9-story wooden pagoda.    Now, shall we go to the site of the pagoda? It is to the south of this site.

stories.title: Hwangnyongsa Temple: At the site of the 9-story wooden pagoda
stories.audioTitle: The 9-story wooden pagoda- One of Silla’s top three treasures
stories.script: The 9-story wooden pagoda- One of Silla's top three treasures  The famous pagoda which stood here was a 80-meter-high wooden pagoda, as high as a 30-story apartment building. On the first floor of the pagoda was a space for a Budda statue and a staircase that led up to the 9th floor. The roof of each floor was covered with roof tiles, and small wind chimes were hung on the edge.       But the pagoda was burned down during foreign invasion and today only the site remains.   Currently a large stone lies where the pagoda stood. It is a foundation stone which supported the main pilar of the pagoda. To build a pagoda, you first set the main pillar on this stone and then other pillars around it.   Then why did Silla people construct such a high pagoda? Well, they built this pagoda with the hopes that 9 kingdoms surrounding Silla at that time would one day surrender.   Although the pagoda no longer exists, we can still imagine Silla people's wish to protect their kingdom with the power of Buddha.    And there's an interesting story about the construction of the pagoda. Let's listen to the story while looking around the temple.   Master architect and the 9-story wooden pagoda  In the Silla Kingdom, there was a famous monk. In his journey to the China, an old man told him that a wooden pagoda needed to be built as high as nine stories at Hwangnyongsa Temple in order to bring peace to the kingdom. He immediately returned home and summoned a master architect of wooden pagodas from a neighboring kingdom to begin the construction right away.  But one day, the master architect had an ominous dream about his kingdom coming to ruin. The next morning, he could not get over how real the dream felt.  [Master architect] I can’t do this. If the construction of this pagoda is completed, it might lead to the collapse of my country. I cannot be part of this. I must go back to my country!  Suddenly the sky became dark and a whirlwind began to blow, shaking the earth. Then a monk appeared from nowhere with a group of strong men, put up the pillars for the pagoda. And in the next instant they were gone.  [Mater Architect] I can’t believe it! Is it really the will of heaven?  After that night, the master architect redoubled his efforts to complete the construction of the pagoda.  In this magical episode, we can guess how eagerly Silla people wished to bring peace to their kingdom.

stories.title: Jeongnimsa Temple Site: Five-story Stone Pagoda of Jeongnimsa Temple Site
stories.audioTitle: Five-story Stone Pagoda of Jeongnimsa Temple Site
stories.script: Five-story Stone Pagoda of Jeongnimsa Temple Site  Do you see the stone pagoda reaching high into the sky? The spectacle presented by the solid pagoda, standing in the middle of the open Jeongnimsa Temple Site, is overwhelming. Jeongnimsa Temple was located in the middle of the capital of Baekje. The Five-story Stone Pagoda represents the desire of Baekje to strengthen public solidarity and build a stronger kingdom by honoring Buddhist principles. There were many stone pagodas in the Buddhist kingdom of Baekje, and as such it was known as the ‘kingdom of the stone pagoda’. Unfortunately, only two of them have survived to the present day.  This stone pagoda was constructed during a period of transition, when artisans switched the material used to construct pagodas from wood to stone. Wood was easier to work with, so why do you think they chose to begin making the pagodas out of stone?  Although wood was traditionally a popular material, it was susceptible to fire and decay over time. To signify eternal desires, stone was a more suitable material. Another reason was that granite was readily available and abundant in Baekje. Please take the time to appreciate the beauty of the stone pagoda.  Each story of the pagoda becomes progressively smaller and narrower as the tower ascends. The harmonious proportions of the structure give those who view it an impression of stability. Another feature worth noting is that this stone pagoda appears simultaneously weighty and delicate with its beautiful, soft curves, a balance that would have been almost impossible to achieve had the pagoda been constructed out of wood.  If you look at the four pillars supporting the first story, you will see that each one has convex curves in the middle. This Korean traditional technique was applied to enhance the visual stability of the construction, and surprisingly, similar technique was also used for the pillars in the Temple of the Parthenon, ancient Greece's most legendary building. The thin, broad roofing stones are gently lifted at the four edges. This feature is influenced by the style of earlier wooden pagodas, and accentuates the elegance and delicacy of the pagoda.   This pagoda is gently charismatic and dignified. It typifies Buddhist art in Baekje. However, the tragic sentiment of Baekje is also evident here. Upon the fall of Baekje, a Chinese commander defaced the pagoda by carving on it the phrase ‘Monument commemorating the suppression of Baekje’. The traces of the inscription can still be seen on the broad wall of the first story of the pagoda.   The pagoda, which has been standing here for 1,400 years, is a symbol of Buddhism in Baekje and a sad reminder of the kingdom’s tragic history.
