There is an ancient Korean ritual for making a wish called tapdori. Why don’t you relax now, walk slowly around the pagoda, and make a wish?

stories.title: Jeongnimsa Temple Site: Entrance
stories.script: What is Jeongnimsa Temple Site?   This site is located is at the center of Buyeo, surrounded by Geumseongsan Mountain in the east and Busosan Mountain in the north.  Situated at the core of Baekje’s Sabi capital, this site contains an imposing stone pagoda, whose surface is inscribed with writing that commemorates the collapse of Baekje brought about by the Tang Dynasty of China. This suggests that Jeongnimsa Temple served as a symbolic space directly related to the fate of the Baekje Kingdom.  Jeongnimsa Temple was built in the typical “one pagoda, one prayer hall” style of Baekje. The temple also had a lecture hall. This practice of building lecture halls within temples continued until the Goryeo Period.  The only relic from Baekje that still remains at the site is the Five-story Stone Pagoda, and it deserves our attention. This pagoda is an example of the unique Baekje artwork featuring structural characteristics of wooden pagodas. Stone pagoda construction technology used for this and other pagodas in Baekje was later transferred to Silla, contributing to the abundance of stone pagodas in ancient Korea.

stories.title: Jeongnimsa Temple Site: Tiled platform
stories.script: Tiled Platform    Tiled platforms became popular among Buddhist temples of the Ungjin and Sabi Periods. Tiled platforms, which are created by piling roof tiles, have not been found in the former Goguryeo territory. However, in the former Silla territory, at Cheongwansa Temple Site and the former Inyongsa Temple Site, and numerous other temple sites, platforms likely derived from the tiled platforms of Baekje were discovered. Moreover, in Japan, such tiled platforms were found not only in Buddhist temples but also in traditional government office buildings. It is highly likely that these platforms were created by Baekje engineers, and their widespread use indicates their popularity. As such, Baekje’s unique tiled platforms spread to neighboring Silla and Japan, and came to be established as a technology shared across international borders.

stories.title: Jeongnimsa Temple Site: Lecture Hall Site
stories.script: Lecture Hall Site   Today, a protective pavilion for the Stone Seated Buddha at Jeongnimsa Temple Site stands at this site, which is located 57.5m to the north of the pagoda. The building was 39.1m long and 16.3m wide in the shape of a rectangle. In comparison, the lecture hall built during the Goryeo Period was confirmed to have been smaller than this one.

stories.title: Sikjangsan Mountain
stories.script: Located in the southeastern part of Daejeon, Sikjangsan Mountain stands at a height of 598 meters, forming a border between Gunseo-myeon and Gunbuk-myeon in Okcheon-gun, Chungcheongbuk-do. The mountain's name is said to originate from historical records, which note that during the Baekje era, soldiers built a fortress here and stored large quantities of provisions to defend the Daejeon area from Silla's invasions. A Different legend suggests that the name Sikjangsan (or Sikgisan) comes from the belief that numerous bowls, symbolizing abundant food, were buried at its summit.  At the foot of Sikjangsan Mountain lie several historic temples, including Gosansa, Gujeolsa, and Gaesimsa. Gosansa was founded during the Silla dynasty by Monk Doseon Guksa and later reconstructed by Monk Sudeng Guksa during the reign of King Injo in the Joseon dynasty. The temples are surrounded by striking rock formations, ancient pine trees, and crystal-clear streams, offering a refreshing retreat for visitors.  Sikjangsan Mountain, recognized as one of Dong-gu, Daejeon’s top attractions, offers a safe and peaceful travel option in Korea. The mountain's observatory is especially renowned for its breathtaking nighttime views, making it a favorite destination for couples and families. Its stunning scenery has also gained popularity as a picturesque spot for taking and sharing photos online.  Why not plan your next outing to Sikjangsan Observatory for a memorable date or family trip?

stories.title: Daecheongho Lake
stories.script: Daecheongho Lake, an artificial reservoir created by Dam blocking the Geumgang River with the Daecheong Dam, is the third-largest lake in South Korea. Its crystal-clear waters and the harmony of islands scattered across the lake resemble the scenic beauty of Hallyeohaesang National Park. Behind the lake lies Cheongnamdae, formerly a presidential holiday villa. Known for its pristine natural environment and stunning landscapes, many migratory birds nest here.  Beloved by many visitors, various trekking courses around Daecheongho Lake offer personalized healing experiences, providing comfort for both mind and body. Among these, the 500-ri (Korean traditional unit for measuring length) Trail , section 5, famous for being the longest cherry blossom road in the world, begins at the Shinsanggyo Bridge. Walking along the well-maintained path under the bridge, visitors can enjoy views of Daecheongho on the left and Heungjin Village on the right. The trail leads through the serene reed fields of the Heungjin Village peninsula and connects to the Odong Cherry Blossom Path.  The Daecheongho Haengboknuri Trail is another popular route, stretching about 4 km from Bakgatagam to the Shinchon Ae-hyang Tower, with an easy-to-walk decked path. Additionally, the cherry blossom road along Local Road 517, extending from Shinsang-dong in Dong-gu, Daejeon, to Hoenam-myeon in Boeun-gun, Chungcheongbuk-do, features approximately 26.6 km of Yoshino cherry trees planted in the 1960s. This road has been recognized as one of the 20 Most Beautiful Cherry Blossom Roads by the Korea National Arboretum.  Every spring, Daecheongho Lake welcomes visitors with its breathtaking cherry blossoms. Why not take a moment to admire the lake's beauty, reflect on life, and take a break?

stories.title: Maninsan Mountain
stories.script: Maninsan Mountain, whose name means “a mountain as high or deep as ten thousand gil (a traditional Korean unit of measurement),” stands at height of 538 meters and boasts a stunning landscape. The mountain is home to picturesque valleys, including Bongsuremi Valley, the source of Daejeoncheon Stream. While Maninsan Mountain is beautiful year-round, it is especially captivating in spring, when its vibrant azaleas and cherry blossoms are in full bloom, showcasing the peak of its natural beauty.  According to a legend, Muhak, a revered monk, proclaimed this mountain a geomantic treasure. This led to King Taejo Yi Seong-gye, the founder of the Joseon Dynasty, relocating his royal placenta chamber from Hamgyeong Province to Maninsan Mountain. Reflecting this story, Maninsan Recreational Forest offers a serene retreat amidst dense deciduous forests and crystal-clear streams that flow through the valleys. It has become a beloved, easily accessible haven for city dwellers seeking relaxation in a pristine natural setting.  Located conveniently near Daejeon, the Maninsan Recreational Forest is an ideal destination for day trips. Visitors can enjoy the local specialty Bong-i Hotteok (sweet Korean pancakes) or enhance their experience by trying skewered fish cakes, grilled rice cakes and jochung (a traditional sweet syrup). The forest's ever-changing scenery promises a memorable visit, making it a perfect spot for a refreshing day trip.

stories.title: Daedong Sky Park
stories.script: Recognized by the Korea Tourism Organization as a Small-Yet-Strong Potential Tourism Destination and one of the Top 100 Night Tourism Spots, Daedong Sky Park is located in the city center making it easily accessible by foot from Daejeon Station. Situated on a hill in the Daedong area, the park attracts not only Daejeon residents but also travelers seeking a light urban getaway.  Historically, the hills of Daedong area were used for cultivating pears and cotton. However, after the Korean War, refugees settled at the foot of the hill, transforming it into Daejeon’s first shantytown. Even today, visitors can spot unique sights uncommon in urban settings, such as wooden utility poles, narrow winding alleys, and stray cats going about their day.  The alleyways leading up to Sky Park are adorned with vibrant murals. At the park itself, a panoramic view of the historic city center awaits, offering a serene and heartwarming experience. The romantic sunset coloring the old town is breathtaking. The glow of lights gradually illuminating the village as the sun sets creates a cozy and inviting atmosphere. Create unforgettable memories in Daedong, a tranquil getaway in the heart of the city!

stories.title: Uam Historical Park
stories.script: Uam Historical Park is a site where Uam Song Si-yeol, a prominent scholar of the late Joseon Dynasty pursued his studies. The park was renovated into its current form from 1991 to 1997. Total of 16 buildings including Jangpangak, an exhibition hall, and a Confucian academy, spanning over 16,000 pyeong (approximately 52,800 square meters) were restored.   Uam Historical Park holds great historical significance, as it includes Namganjeongsa, where Song spent his later years teaching and studying, and Gigeukjeong, a structure known for its exceptional architectural beauty. Additionally, the park preserves valuable cultural assets such as the wooden blocks of Songja Daejeon, a collection of Song Si-yeol’s writings.  Beyond its historical value, Uam Historical Park serves as a well-maintained urban oasis, offering a serene retreat for city residents. Namganjeongsa, in particular, is a favorite spot for photographers, especially in spring when magnolias and other blooms create a picturesque scene.

stories.title: Soje-dong Café Street
stories.script: With wild grass and trees sprouting between low fences, rusty window grilles, and an old-town atmosphere, Soje-dong is a neighborhood steeped in nostalgia. Preserving its 100-year history, Soje-dong feels as though time has stood still. However, it has recently undergone significant changes as part of the Soje-dong regeneration project. Once an overlooked area, it has now gained fame as a café street in what was formerly the Railway Workers’ Residential Area. To truly understand Soje-dong Café Street, we must first delve into the history of Soje Lake and the railway residences that shaped its story.  Behind Daejeon Station, there once lay a lake known as Soje Lake. This charming body of water, present since the Joseon Dynasty, was said to rival the beauty of a lake in Suzhou, China, earning it the name, Soje Lake. With blooming lotus flowers, the lake was a picturesque spot for leisure and poetry. The advent of the railway in 1905 brought increased attention to the Soje-dong area behind the station. Streams flowing from Daejeon’s major mountains converged here, but frequent flooding during the rainy season became a recurring issue. During the Japanese colonial period, a water drainage project was undertaken to reclaim the lake area, leading to the lake’s disappearance.  The reclaimed site was developed into a planned residential area with over ten railway workers’ houses. Today, traces of Soje Lake remain in the area. For example, the road name Saeduk-gil reflects the dike road that once surrounded the lake, and the present-day Cheolgabgyo Bridge once crossed the lake’s center. Even aerial photographs of Soje-dong reveal remnants of the lake’s outline.  The railway workers’ residences built on the reclaimed land had a distinctive multi-family design, with two homes under a single elongated roof divided by an internal wall and yard fences. The interior featured tatami-style rooms, and some homes even had indoor restrooms, which were rare for the time. These houses, constructed between the late 1920s and the late 1930s, were concentrated in Soje-dong and nearby Samseong-dong. Although many were modified into smaller, single-room dwellings as the population grew in the 1960s, some original structures remain, preserving the unique layout of the railway houses.  In the past, these residences were home to affluent families, and the yards were often adorned with fruit trees such as persimmon, pomegranate, and trifoliate orange. Even today, a walk through the railway residential area in autumn reveals vibrant orange persimmons ripening on the trees. Why not embark on a journey to the past through Soje-dong and experience its rich history and nostalgic charm?

stories.title: Sangso-dong Forest Park
stories.script: Sangso-dong Forest Park, officially selected as a Small-Yet-Strong Potential Tourism Destination for 2023 by the Korea Tourism Organization, is one of the must-visit hotspots in Dong-gu, Daejeon. Nestled between the slopes of Maninsan Mountain and Sikjangsan Mountain, the Park is adorned with a picturesque sycamore tree tunnel along its entrance road. The Park offers a variety of facilities for nature exploration and relaxation.  A particularly notable feature is the 17 Stone Pagodas, often referred to as the ‘Angkor Wat of Korea.’ These were built by Lee Deok-sang, a resident born in Buyeo in 1931. With a heartfelt wish for everyone’s health, he carried carefully selected stones up the mountain on his back from 2003 to 2007, starting at the age of 74. His dedication has left behind an inspiring legacy. This unique and exotic site has become a popular spot among young visitors looking for the perfect photo spot.  The Park also offers spaces where visitors can build their own stone towers, making it a meaningful experience for couples, families, and friends who want to express their wishes. From spring to fall, visitors can enjoy vibrant wildflowers, while amenities such as a children’s forest playground, forest experience zones, and water play areas make it an ideal destination for family trips. In winter, the Park transforms into a magical wonderland with ice hills and frozen waterfalls, creating an enchanting atmosphere.  Sangso-dong Forest Park is part of Sangso Cultural Park, which is also home to the famous Sangso-dong Auto Camping Site—Daejeon’s top camping destination, beloved by camping enthusiasts nationwide. With attractions like the stone pagoda plaza and the Metasequoia Road, the park has long been cherished as a city-center retreat. Why not create joyful memories with loved ones at Sangso-dong Forest Park?

stories.title: Archeological Site in Gwanbuk-ri: Entrance
stories.script: Archeological Site in Gwanbuk-ri    Excavations at the Archeological Site in Gwanbuk-ri discovered numerous remains of facilities and artifacts, such as a large building site, roads, royal workshops, storage facilities, a pond, water supply and drainage facilities, and a stamped roof tile whose inscription reads subu (首部), or capital city. All of these provide glimpses into the royal palace of Baekje during the Sabi Period.

stories.title: Archeological Site in Gwanbuk-ri: Large Building Site
stories.script: Large Building Site   The site is 35m wide in the east-west direction and 18.5m long in the north-south direction. Considering the structure of the building, composed of a tiled roof supported by pillars erected on cornerstones, it was presumably the main hall of the palace. A building site of almost identical size and structure was found at the Archeological Site in Wanggung-ri, Iksan. The building’s platform had two layers, but only 50cm of it remains.

stories.title: Buyeo Royal Tombs
stories.script: The Buyeo Royal Tombs are a cluster of burial sites from the Sabi period of the Baekje Kingdom, located just outside the Sabi Capital City Wall. The tombs are primarily grouped into three sections, with seven main tombs at the center and additional tombs spread across the eastern and western areas. Based on their size and location, the central tombs are believed to be the royal tombs of Baekje's kings from the Sabi period.  All the tombs in the Buyeo Royal Tombs are stone-chamber tombs. This type of tomb consists of a burial chamber (neolbang) to house the coffin and a passageway (neolgil) connecting the chamber to the outside. The burial chamber and passageway are constructed with stones and covered with soil to form a mound.  Stone-chamber tombs are categorized by the shape of their ceilings. The ceilings can either be tunnel-shaped or flat. The flat ceilings are further divided into hexagonal or rectangular structures, depending on their cross-sectional design. These architectural styles later influenced Japan's tomb designs.  Among the tombs, Tomb No. 2 is considered the oldest, leading to speculation that it might belong to King Seong, who moved the Baekje capital to Sabi. However, further evidence is needed to confirm this theory. Tomb No. 1 features murals depicting the Four Guardian Deities (Sasindo), showing that Baekje inherited mural traditions commonly seen in Goguryeo tombs. Additionally, the lotus and cloud patterns painted on the ceiling are invaluable resources for studying Baekje art.  Designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Buyeo Royal Tombs offer visitors a glimpse into the excellence of Baekje culture.

stories.title: On the way to Seokguram Grotto
stories.audioTitle: On the way to Seokguram Grotto
stories.script: Seokguram Grotto is a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage Site and represents the pinnacle of Silla’s sophisticated architectural skills.  A grotto refers to a temple built within a cave, offering Buddhist monks a cool space for meditation during summer. This 1200-year-old grotto was constructed uniquely, blending the concept of caves from India with the dome-style roof from the West, showcasing Silla’s distinctive architectural techniques.  This grotto is an artificial stone cave assembled by stacking granite blocks, akin to an igloo. The process involved carving granite blocks, stacking them in a mound shape, and covering them with dirt. Constructing such a sophisticated architectural marvel necessitated extensive knowledge of mathematics, geometry, and advanced architectural skills.  Kim Dae-Seong, an aristocrat of Silla, constructed the grotto. Legend has it that he built Seokguram Grotto for his parents in a previous life and Bulguksa Temple for his parents in the present life.  Visitors must climb some stairs to reach Seokguram Grotto. In Buddhism, stairs symbolize life's hardships. However, let's not dwell on it too much ? instead, notice how the ascent helps to pacify your mind as you ascend.

stories.title: Seokguram Grotto - Inside of Seokguram Grotto
stories.audioTitle: Seokguram Grotto - Inside of Seokguram Grotto
stories.script: Seokguram Grotto - Inside of Seokguram Grotto  Seokguram Grotto locked in glass walls  It is our precious and proud Seokguram but, unfortunately, it is difficult to look inside closely because it is blocked by glass walls. The reason for the installation of the glass was because Seokguram was damaged while dismantling and repairing the grotto in the Japanese colonial period.  Originally, cold underground water flowed under Seokguram, which kept the temperature of the stone chamber at a constant level. Therefore, it prevented the formation of dews that can be caused by the temperature difference between the outside and the inside.  And, to enable the interior of the stone chamber to breathe, the walls and the ceiling were fitted uniformly with granite and then covered by roof tiles and soil, which naturally helped remove moisture.  During the Japanese occupation era, however, repairs were carried out without sufficient understanding of the scientific structure of Seokguram. That is why underground water was cut off to prevent permeation of water, and the roof tiles and soil on Seokguram's circumference were removed before completing the repair work with cement, which was a relatively new material at the time.  Because of this, moss grew inside the grotto due to moisture, and the stone structures that constitute Seokguram were in danger of corrosion.  So, inevitably, glass walls and thermostats were installed during the rework performed in the 1960s in order to control the temperature and humidity in an artificial manner.  If we understood and paid more attention to our ancestors’ wisdom and scientific technology during the repair construction process, our precious cultural heritage probably wouldn't have faced such a sad reality?

stories.title: At the entrance of Seokguram Grotto
stories.audioTitle: At the entrance of Seokguram Grotto
stories.script: Before we explore Seokguram Grotto, let’s observe its exterior. You'll notice that the grotto is encompassed by wooden structures designed to shield it from the erosive effects of rain and wind.  Seokguram faces the East Sea. Prior to the construction of these wooden structures, the rays from the rising sun reached the Buddha statue, illuminating it.  The strategic placement of Seokguram at a high altitude overlooking the sea is no coincidence. This location choice reflects the Silla people's aspiration for it to radiate over the country like the morning sun.  Upon entering, you'll find the layout arranged in a circular fashion. The main Buddha statue resides in a rounded chamber, encircled by stone statues along the rotunda's wall. In Buddhism, a circle symbolizes a world in complete harmony, signifying this grotto as an embodiment of the yearning for a harmonious world.  Notice the ceiling arched in a dome shape and believed to weigh as much as 20 tons. The stones protruding from the ceiling support this substantial weight, maintaining balance and distributing the load.  Recreating this remarkable architectural achievement even with today’s technology remains challenging. Considering it was built 1,300 years ago, it's truly astounding not to marvel at the remarkable skills of the Silla people.

stories.title: Inside the Seokguram Grotto 1
stories.script: The inside of the grotto is enclosed with glass to preserve it. As you continue the tour, you’ll hear more of these aspects. For now, let’s focus on what we can see.  First, observe the main Buddha in the center. Notice its serene appearance, it is perfectly in tune with the surrounding silence.  In fact, the statue is not placed at the precise center of the rotunda. Instead, it slightly set back. The head of the statue appears relatively larger than its body. Both the position and size were deliberately calculated to provide viewers with viewer a sightline exuding grandeur. Similarly, the lotus petals on the back wall create the illusion of a halo when you gaze into the statue’s eyes.  Nevertheless, the statue itself exhibits ideal body proportions, adhering to the “golden ratio,” accentuating its beauty and a sense of harmony.  Take note of the hand gesture depicted by the statue. In the Buddhist tradition, each gesture of Buddha carries a different meaning. The gesture on this Buddha symbolizes warding off demons.  Curious about how this sizable statue was placed inside the cave? Interestingly, the statue was carved first, and afterward, the grotto was constructed around it.  Behind the glass walls, various statues and intimidating figures stand like guards. At the center of the rotunda stands the Buddha's statue, surrounded by diverse wall images. These statues and drawings represent highly esteemed pieces of Buddhist art.

stories.title: Inside the Seokguram Grotto 2
stories.script: Seokguram Grotto is designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site, evoking significant pride among the Korean people.  However, the grotto's interior remains inaccessible due to its enclosure with glass walls. This protective measure was implemented because the grotto suffered damage during the Japanese colonial era when its structure underwent dismantling and reassembly.  Beneath this grotto flows naturally cold underground water, maintaining a stable temperature within the stone chamber. This flow prevents dew condensation resulting from temperature disparities between the grotto's interior and exterior.  The walls and ceiling of the stone chamber were constructed using granite blocks, subsequently covered with tiles and earth. They serve the purpose of dehumidifying the space and ensuring the grotto can breathe.  The grotto’s structure was delicately designed. However, the repair work conducted by the Japanese imperialists was carried out without a proper understanding of the structure. They impeded the flow of underground water, removed the tiles and earth covering the grotto, and concluded the repair work by encasing the grotto in cement, a novel material at that time.  This led to increased humidity and moss growth, exposing the stone structures to the risk of erosion. As a result, further repair work was undertaken in the 1960s, involving the installation of glass walls and a temperature controller to artificially regulate temperature and humidity.

stories.title: Seokguram
stories.audioTitle: Everything there is to know about Buddha in one place
stories.script: Did you know that Seokguram, a masterpiece of Buddhist art created by the Shilla people, was originally named “Seokbulsa” Temple? Seokguram was originally built as a temple by a prime minister named Kim Dae-seong who served during the reign of King Gyeongdeok (the 35th monarch of Shilla). The domed ceiling of Seokguram shows the influence India and the Tang Dynasty had on Gyeongju, as an international city at the time. One thing to note is that Seokguram was built using an entirely different technique compared to other temples that preceded it. Instead of digging a cave, the architect used tomb-building techniques available in Shilla to erect the stone walls. UNESCO designated Seokguram as a World Heritage Site in 1995, and lauded the temple as a culmination of architecture, mathematics, and geometry brought together under the umbrella of religion and art.   Art historian Yu Hong-jun has also singled out Seokguram as the most valuable heritage site in Korea on multiple occasions. More specifically, Seokguram features the main Buddha statue (widely regarded as the best artifact from our Buddhist art history), statues of Buddha’s 10 disciples, bodhisattvas, heavenly gods, and other artifacts that can teach people about Buddha. Direction-wise, Seokguram faces the East Sea. Interestingly, you can connect Seokguram and the underwater royal tomb of King Munmu in a straight line. That is why some people believe that Buddha and King Munmu the Great protected the Shilla Kingdom.   Seokguram also offers a great view of the sunrise, which is why Gyeongju is part of a “Sunrise Alliance” with Ulsan and Pohang. It might be a good idea to spend a night and see the sunrise standing on the very spot where Buddha has been looking over Gyeongju for more than a millennium. If you do get a chance, welcome the sun rise over the ocean at the top of Tohamsan Mountain with the main Buddha statue at Seokguram beneath your feet.

stories.title: Gongju Tomb of King Muryeong and Royal Tombs
stories.audioTitle: Gongju Tomb of King Muryeong and Royal Tombs
stories.script: The Tomb of King Muryeong and the Royal Tombs, located in Geumsong-dong, Gongju, are the burial grounds of the kings from the Woongjin period of Baekje. This site features a total of seven tombs, including the Tomb of King Muryeong, whose owner has been identified. The seven tombs are divided by a valley: the Tomb of King Muryeong and Tombs No. 5 and No. 6 lie to the west, while Tombs No. 1 to No. 4 are placed to the northeast. Tombs No. 1 to No. 6 were studied during the Japanese colonial period, which revealed their structure and form, whereas the Tomb of King Muryeong was discovered by chance in the summer of 1971 during drainage work near Tomb No. 6. This discovery surprised the world, as the tomb was found in an almost perfectly preserved state, maintaining its form for over 1,500 years. In terms of construction style, Tombs No. 1 to No. 5 are traditional Baekje stone-chamber tombs, while Tomb No. 6 and the Tomb of King Muryeong are brick tombs influenced by Chinese design. This highlights the international and open nature of Baekje society. The structures and artifacts from these tombs are displayed at the exhibition hall of the Tomb of King Muryeong and Royal Tombs. The hall features replicas of the tomb interiors, offering visitors a vivid understanding of their original state. After visiting the exhibition hall near the entrance, the serene cluster of seven tombs comes into view. Take a stroll along the paths surrounded by lush pine trees to explore these Baekje-era burial sites. The scenic trail also leads to the National Museum of Gongju.

stories.title: The Six Tombs
stories.script: The tombs, including the Tomb of King Muryeong and others within the Royal Tombs of Songsan-ri, are located on the southern slopes of Songsan. These tombs can be categorized into two types based on their construction style: stone-chamber tombs and brick tombs.  First, stone-chamber tombs are built by creating a room using stones to house the coffin, with an entrance leading to the outside, which is then covered with soil. Think of it as a tomb with a room and a door, like a house. This traditional Baekje style can be observed in Tombs No. 1 throughout No. 5. While all these tombs share the same basic form, their structures and sizes vary slightly. For instance, Tombs No. 1 to No. 4 have pebble-lined floors to support the coffins, whereas Tomb No. 5 incorporates bricks into its construction.  On the other hand, brick tombs are constructed using bricks, following a style influenced by China. Tomb No. 6 is an example of this type, showing a design clearly inspired by the Southern Dynasties of China. This tomb features a tunnel-shaped double passageway and a rectangular burial chamber, constructed with bricks engraved with the Wuzhu coin design. One unique aspect of Tomb No. 6 is the presence of murals depicting the Four Guardian Deities (Sasindo) on its walls, intended to protect the tomb’s occupant.  Similar to Tomb No. 6, the Tomb of King Muryeong, located nearby, is also a brick tomb. Let’s move on to the Tomb of King Muryeong to explore the treasures unearthed there.

stories.title: Tomb of King Muryeong
stories.script: The Tomb of King Muryeong is located in a low hill area behind Tomb No. 6. Unlike other tombs referred to simply as Tomb No. 1 or Tomb No. 2, this burial site was named specifically after King Muryeong. Why is that?  During the excavation of the tomb, an epitaph stone (myojiseok) was discovered inside, identifying the owner as King Muryeong, the 25th ruler of Baekje. As royal tombs in Korea are traditionally called neung, the tomb was named after the king, hence the name, Tomb of King Muryeong.  Initially, the tomb was mistaken for an artificial mound constructed to surround Tomb No. 6, and it went unnoticed for years. In 1971, the tomb was discovered out of pure chance; while building a drainage system to prevent water infiltration into Tomb No. 6, the entrance to the Tomb of King Muryeong was accidentally uncovered, prompting an investigation.  Because the Tomb of King Muryeong had not been previously recognized as a royal tomb, it was spared from looting. Allowing its contents to be preserved in their original condition. The excavation revealed numerous artifacts believed to belong to the king and queen, including gold ornaments and accessories, bronze mirrors, bronze dishes and utensils, a bronze iron, and white porcelain lamps. In total, approximately 4,600 artifacts were unearthed, with 12 categories and 17 items designated as National Treasures.  The Tomb of King Muryeong is a valuable asset for research on Baekje history and Korean art history in that it is the only royal tomb from the Three Kingdoms period whose owner has been definitively identified. Moreover, the dated artifacts provide invaluable insights for researchers. Many of the artifacts excavated from the Tomb are now on display at the National Museum of Gongju. A visit to the museum is highly recommended.

stories.title: Royal Tombs in Neungsan-ri
stories.audioTitle: What are the Ancient Tombs in Neungsan-ri?
stories.script: What are the Ancient Tombs in Neungsan-ri?   The Ancient Tombs in Neungsan-ri are royal tombs from Baekje’s Sabi Period. They are located right outside Baekje’s Sabi capital, on the southwest foot of Neungsan Mountain, which is 121m in altitude and connected to neighboring mountains in the east-west direction. The tombs are surrounded by mild hills to the left and right, and the Wangpocheon Stream flows in front.  There are seven tombs in total: a set of three tombs are placed front and back in two rows, and there is one other tomb approximately 50m behind them to the north.  All of the Ancient Tombs in Neungsan-ri are stone chamber tombs with a corridor. However, by this stage of tomb development, the chamber had become smaller and the structure more refined. Such a style was transferred to neighboring Silla and Japan, a testament to the vibrant exchanges of tomb construction technology between Baekje and other regions.

stories.title: Outstanding Universal Value of the Ancient Tombs in Neungsan-ri
stories.audioTitle: Outstanding Universal Value of the Ancient Tombs in Neungsan-ri
stories.script: Outstanding Universal Value of the Ancient Tombs in Neungsan-ri   The Ancient Tombs in Neungsan-ri are stone chamber tombs with a corridor. Based on the design of the ceiling, these tombs from Baekje are categorized into a vault-ceiling type and a flat-ceiling type. The flat-ceiling type is classified again into hexagonal and rectangular ceilings. The Ancient Tombs in Neungsan-ri consist of all three types of tombs. The excavations also found that the ceilings evolved from the vault type to hexagonal flat type to rectangular flat type.

stories.title: ﻿Sindang-dong, Seoul
stories.script: Have you heard of Hipdang-dong? It is a trendy nickname for Sindang-dong on social media and online, literally meaning hip Sindang-dong. Sindang-dong used to be popular for tteokbokki but it now emerging as the next cool spot, following Euljiro, Seongsu, and Hannam-dong. There are many trendy restaurants, cafes, and small shops. Growing number of people are flocking to the area.   Sindang-dong has a harmonious blend of old and new, especially Seoul Jungang Market, where traditional market meets art. The Market was formed after the Korean War and is a place for fresh food ingredients and daily necessities. Markets always bring to mind delicious street food, right? Seoul Jungang Market is famous for glutinous rice hotteok, and cooked barley rice sold at the entrance. Visitors can find Sindang Creative Arcade in the basement floor of the Market. Here, visitors can watch young artists and creators in action, buy their works, or even join in on art-related experiences. It’s a unique combination of traditional market and art, isn’t it?   Taking left from the Market is the street frequently featured on social media, the Ssajeon Street. Ssajeon means rice and grain shops. True to its name, the Street is lined up with sacks of rice. Hidden along Ssajeo Street are trendy shops. There are shops with industrial-style interiors that still retain the old factory framework, cafes renovated from rice storage warehouses, and small boutiques selling adorable trinkets, all side by side with traditional rice shops. Combined, the old and new shops on Ssajeon Street create the unique vibe of Hipdang-dong.  Take time to explore every nook and cranny of Sindang-dong, where old and new coexist. Who knows, you may discover a yet unknown hidden jems. Throw on your most stylish outfit, enjoy tteokbokki, and snap a few photos for social media. It’ll be a day to remember!

stories.title: ﻿Haenggung-dong, Suwon
stories.script: Haenggung-dong in Suwon is an area that encompasses 12 administrative districts around Hwaseong Fortress, including Jangan-dong, Sinpung-dong, and Buksu-dong. From 220 years ago, when the Fortress was built, to a few decades ago, Haenggung-dong was the most populated part of Suwon. But as Hwaseong Fortress was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage in 1997, strict development regulations were imposed on the area, leaving its landscape nearly unchanged. Haenggung-dong was revitalized when its residents, working with artists, began decorating the town with murals. Along with the Fortress, the area is now filled with unique spots like the mural village, craft shops, and Jidong Market, scattered along the alleys of Haenggung-dong.   The Suwon Hwaseong Haenggung is the starting point for the tour around Haenggung-dong. Haenggung refers to a temporary palace for kings to stay during their royal visits. Hwaseong Haenggung is the largest of its kind in Korea, boasting both beauty and grandeur. King Jeongjo from the Joseon Dynasty stayed here whenever he visited his father Prince Sado’s tomb, Hyeollyungwon. He also held many events at Bongsudang, the main building of Hwaseong Haenggung, including the 60th birthday celebration of his mother, Lady Hyegyeong. Although it has lost many of its original features during the Japanese colonial period, restoration efforts have brought back its stately elegance. The majestic, tiled roofs of Hwaseong Haenggung and the cars passing by on the road in front creates an ironically harmonious view.   ﻿After exploring Hwaseong, Haengung, it is time to look around the nearby streets. Jidong Market, located near Paldalmun, the southern gate of Hwaseong Fortress, creates a scenic view alongside Suwoncheon Stream. This area is also popular for street foods. There is Sundae town, known for stir-fried blood sausage, and Suwon Chicken Alley, perfect for fried chicken lovers. Take a walk around Hwaseong Haenggung and indulge in mouthwatering street foods.

stories.title: Daejeon Station
stories.script: Did you know that Daejeon Station is emerging as an exciting spot to visit in Daejeon? While it may seem like an ordinary train station, its name has given it a unique charm. If you remove ‘dae’ from the name, you get ‘jeonyeok’ which, in Korean, refers to a soldier's transition to reserve status after completing mandatory military service.  This is why some soldiers choose to celebrate their discharge by taking photos in front of Daejeon Station. They stand in front of the station in their uniforms, covering the first syllable ‘대’ (dae) of the station’s name with their face, leaving only ‘전역’ (jeonyeok) visible. This quirky tradition has grown in popularity, and now the station even features a dedicated photo spot where visitors can easily capture the perfect shot. From newly discharged soldiers to influencers and tourists, many people stop by this spot to take photos in a saluting pose.  Just outside Daejeon Station, you'll find Daejeon Jungang Market, the largest traditional market in the central region of Korea. Stretching from the station to Daejeoncheon Stream, the market is vast, with different sections such as dried fish street, tools street, fish alley, herbal medicine street, hanbok street, and food alley. A visit to the market isn’t complete without trying some of the region’s distinctive and delicious foods. If you’re in Daejeon, don’t miss out on trying kal-guksu. The market boasts several kal-guksu restaurants, many of which have been serving locals for decades. You’re sure to enjoy a hearty, flavorful bowl wherever you go. And, of course, no trip to Daejeon would be complete without a stop at the iconic bakery Sungsimdang. Established in 1956 as a small, steamed bun shop near Daejeon Station, Sungsimdang has grown to become a source of pride for Daejeon residents and a symbol of excellence in Korea’s baking industry. Known for its use of fresh and local ingredients, the bakery now offers over 400 types of bread. With locations throughout the city, including a branch inside Daejeon Station, it’s a must-visit spot for anyone exploring Daejeon.

stories.title: Busan Yeongdo Mulyangjang Street
stories.script: In Yeongdo, Busan, you'll find the charming Mulyangjang Street, where ships are neatly docked along the expansive sea. The term Mulyangjang refers to a wharf structure designed for ships to dock and handle cargo or passengers, with a vertical wall facing the sea. True to its character, aren’t those little boats adding to the charm of Mulyangjang Street? Along this street, you can see various boats, each with its own unique shape, creating a beautiful and lively seascape.  Mulyangjang Street has become a popular coffee destination in Busan. The city has transformed a 600meter stretch of Bongnae Naru in the area into a coffee-specialty district. This area, once filled with factories and warehouses, is now home to several trendy cafes that have popped up in repurposed industrial spaces. Notable spots like Cotton Diary, a cultural space in a former factory. At Momos Coffee, you can watch the entire coffee-making process from bean storage to roasting and packaging, which adds a special charm to this part of town. As a result, Mulyangjang Street is now a perfect spot to stroll, coffee in hand, and enjoy a delightful walk.  When evening falls, the waterfront is lined with food stalls, offering a great way to enjoy local delicacies while taking in the night view of Busan. On Yeongdo's Pocha Street, you can savor dishes like live octopus, grilled mackerel, and grilled eel. The sight of the food stalls along the beach might tempt you to sit down and enjoy some fresh seafood. And if you're in Yeongdo, don't miss visiting the original Samjin Fish Cake shop, which has been making fish cakes since 1953. It's the oldest fish cake brand in Korea, offering a variety of fish cakes with a space where you can taste them freshly made.  It’s not often you come across a scene where the unique atmosphere of the area blends with a trendy vibe. How about taking a stroll down the Mulyangjang Street, enjoying the refreshing charm of the place, with a cool drink in hand?

stories.title: Gyeongju Woljeonggyo Bridge
stories.script: Woljeonggyo Bridge in Gyeongju is a beautiful structure originally built during the Unified Silla period. The name “Woljeonggyo” appears in the Samguk Sagi (History of the Three Kingdoms), which records that in the 19th year of King Gyeongdeok’s reign, two bridges, Woljeonggyo and Chunyanggyo, were constructed over the Namcheon stream, south of the palace. Although the bridge was lost during the Joseon Dynasty, it was carefully restored over more than a decade, with the reconstruction completed in April 2018. Isn’t its long, straight form simply stunning?  Woljeonggyo Bridge is also full of fascinating stories. If you take a moment to look down at the Namcheon stream below, you’ll find yourself in a place tied to the famous tale of Wonhyo, a monk known for the “skull water” legend. When a royal envoy came with a decree from the king, Wonhyo deliberately fell into Namcheon stream, which caused the envoy to take him to Yoseokgung Palace to dry his clothes. It was there that Wonhyo spent a night with Princess Yoseok, resulting in the birth of Seolchong, a celebrated scholar. Nearby, you’ll also find Jaemaejeong, known as the site of General Kim Yushin’s home. Historical accounts tell us that he often crossed Woljeonggyo Bridge on his way to Cheongwansa Temple. Even Arab merchants who brought glass to Silla and troops departing for war are said to have crossed this historic bridge.  You can reach Woljeonggyo Bridge easily from either the parking area or the Gyodong side. As you approach, the wide entryway and the rows of thick pillars create a striking first impression. From the bridge, you can take in the picturesque views of Namcheon stream, with Seondosan and Byeokdosan mountains to the west and Wolseong to the east. Don’t forget to explore the second floor of the pavilion, where you’ll find an exhibition hall showcasing artifacts and the story of Woljeonggyo Bridge’s restoration.  For a truly unforgettable experience, step onto the stepping stones in front of the bridge and take in the full view of Woljeonggyo as it gracefully stretches over the stream. During the day, you’ll be able to admire the bridge’s elegant structure in the sunlight, while at night, the soft glow of the lights transforms it into a magical sight, revealing a whole new side to its charm.

stories.title: Sacheon Samcheonpohang
stories.script: Samcheonpo refers to the southern urban area of Sacheon, Gyeongsangnam-do. In the past, it was a separate administrative district called Samcheonpo City, but in 1995, it was merged with Sacheon County during an administrative reorganization and became part of ‘Sacheon City’. Samcheonpo is known for its mild climate, beautiful coastal scenery, and abundance of food, making it a very livable place.  Having developed as a fishing port, Samcheonpo attracts many visitors with its charming fishing village landscape. The beautiful port, filled with small fishing boats, has captured the hearts of many, making people return for a second or third visit.  The waters off Samcheonpo Port are rich with marine life, with fishing boats constantly moving between the islands. The area around the port is a clean, fast-flowing current zone, which results in high-quality shellfish and fish.  Near Samcheonpo Port, there is the Samcheonpo Yonggung Fish Market, where freshly caught seafood is sold. This fish market, with over 50 years of history, is centered around Samcheonpo Port. It sells fresh seafood caught straight from the sea. The market is themed around Yonggung(palace of sea kings), with sculptures of rabbits and turtles evoking the traditional Korean tale of The Rabbit and the Turtle. The market also hosts various cultural performances and events that bring joy to both locals and visitors.  Around the fish market, you can find street vendors lining the coastline, known as Yonggung Pocha Village. This charming spot is where you can savor fresh, seasonal seafood. But it’s not just about the food, Yonggung Pocha Village offers stunning scenery. Especially at sunset, the view of the sun setting over the horizon is breathtaking, with the vibrant red hues of the sunset contrasting beautifully against the deep blue sea when you can enjoy the beautiful view of the setting sun.   Once you’ve taken in the fresh sea air amid the charming scenery of Samcheonpo and enjoyed its charm by tasting seasonal seafood, might you find yourself wanting to visit again?

stories.title: Suncheon Naganeupseong Walled Town
stories.script: Travel back to a Joseon Dynasty village  During the Joseon Dynasty, Naganeupseong Walled Town was the vibrant center of the Nagan area. Initially a mud fortress, it was transformed into a stone fortress in the mid-Joseon period by General Im Gyeong-eop, who was appointed as the governor. Inside its 1.4 km stone walls, you'll find a charming village with thatched-roof houses that continues to thrive today.  This village is a rare and living example of a historical site. While some residents relocated outside the walls during renovations, many chose to stay and still run guesthouses, craft shops, and restaurants. This allows the village to remain a lively, authentic fortress, rather than a simple folk village.  No matter which of the four gates you enter, starting your visit by strolling along the fortress walls is highly recommended. Be cautious as there are no railings, but as you stroll, you can take in the view of the village filled with thatched roofs and the green fields and mountains surrounding the fortress. For the best scenery, head to the hill located between Seomun (West Gate) and Nammun (South Gate).  The homes where villagers live are mostly located near Nammun (South Gate) and Dongmun (East Gate). In contrast, the areas around Seomun (West Gate) and Bukmun (North Gate) feature historic sites such as the Gyeoksa (guesthouse), Dongheon (administrative office), and the filming location for the Korean drama Dae Jang Geum.  Among these, the Stele Pavilion dedicated to General Im Gyeong-eop, situated in front of the Gyeoksa (guesthouse), is honored as a protector of the village. Throughout the fortress, you’ll also find ancient trees that offer a window into its rich history and cultural heritage.  Naganeupseong Walled Town is historically significant, having been visited by Admiral Yi Sun-sin during the Japanese invasion. Behind the Gyeoksa (guesthouse) there is a tree believed to have been planted by the Admiral. During that time, 'Paljinmi,' a dish made with eight locally grown ingredients, was served. You can still enjoy this traditional dish at local restaurants inside the fortress. Taste history with every bite and feel as if you've stepped into a village from the Joseon Dynasty!  Just a five-minute walk from Nammun (South Gate) is the Deep Rooted Tree Museum, dedicated to Han Chang-gi, the founder of a magazine that promoted the preservation of Korean traditions. The museum displays his collection of artifacts, reflecting his efforts to preserve and revitalize aspects of Korean culture that had been overlooked and undervalued due to urbanization.  After visiting the modern museum, you can explore the traditional hanok of the respected Kim Mu-gyu, also known as Baek Gyeong, which was moved here in 2006. Built in 1922, this home gives you a glimpse into a typical southern-style Korean house. Baek Gyeong was a holder of the Important Intangible Cultural Heritage, specifically the Gurye Hyangje Julpungnyu, a traditional performing art. The house features a clear distinction between the sarangchae (men’s quarters) and anchae (women’s quarters). Don’t forget to remove your shoes before stepping inside, so you can fully enjoy the authentic atmosphere of this beautiful hanok.

stories.title: Mujinjang Bus Terminal
stories.script: Have you ever heard of Mujinjang? This term refers to the combined area of Muju, Jinan, and Jangsu in Jeollabuk-do. The name comes from the first characters of each of these regions. Located in the rugged Jinan Highlands, Mujinjang was not home to many people in the past, due to the difficult terrain. Even today, it remains one of the least populated areas in Jeollabuk-do, but that's part of its charm.  As a result of its shrinking population, Mujinjang region has implemented a regional bus system to improve transportation between rural villages and key town centers. The Mujinjang buses have such charming looks. These buses, often in cheerful orange or red, with the words Happy Mujinjang written on the front, make them stand out. There's something about riding a Mujinjang bus that makes you feel as though happiness is right around the corner. As you ride, the peaceful rural scenery adds to the calm, and these buses transport happiness throughout Muju, Jinan, and Jangsu.  The buses in the Mujinjang area are mainly used by elderly residents heading to local markets or by hikers visiting nearby mountains like Deogyusan, Maisan, and Gubongsan. As the bus service doesn't run frequently, it's important to check the schedule before traveling. Also, note that the buses usually stop operating by 7 p.m.  Once you've confirmed the bus schedule, take the Mujinjang bus to visit the iconic mountains of Muju, Jinan, and Jangsu. In Muju, you can enjoy Deogyusan, known for its gondola. In Jinan, you'll find Maisan, with peaks that resemble horse ears. Jangsu’s Gubongsan, famous for its nine sharp peaks, also awaits your visit. The autumn season, with its vibrant foliage, offers the perfect opportunity to experience the stunning landscapes of the Mujinjang region.

stories.title: Gwangju Yangnim History & Culture Village
stories.script: Gwangju Yangnim History & Culture Village is a space where Western-style modern buildings and traditional Korean hanok come together, creating a harmonious blend of history and culture. Located in the heart of a bustling city, this charming village is a place where the past and present coexist.   Yangnim-dong was once called the “Jerusalem of Gwangju” or the “Western Village.” This nickname dates back to 1904, when the Southern Presbyterian Mission settled here after passing through Mokpo. Even after all these years, traces of those times are still alive in every corner. A great example is the Missionary Wilson’s House, perched on Horanggasinamu Hill. Missionary Wilson, who once lived here, dedicated his life to caring for those in need, including Hansen’s disease patients. This house is the oldest Western style building in Gwangju and retains its historical charm. Its picturesque setting makes it feel like stepping into a movie scene, making it an ideal spot for photos.  Yangnim-dong isn’t just about Western-style buildings. As you wander through the Yangnim Cultural and Historical Village, you’ll come across the Lee Jang-woo’s House, a traditional Korean home. Its size alone tells you it once belonged to a wealthy family. Built in 1899 during the Korean Empire era, the house still stands strong, as if time stopped around it. How about taking a stroll through the garden, sarangchae (men’s quarters), and anchae (women’s quarters) of this timeless house built during the Korean Empire in 1899? It’ll feel as if you’ve stepped back in time to experience the life of a noble family member.  One of the most delightful spots in Yangnim-dong is Penguin Village. This quirky little area is filled with junk art made from recycled materials, creating a unique and playful vibe. Isn’t it charming? While you’re in the area, don’t miss the chance to visit Migwang Clothing Store, located on the first floor of the Budulsup Youth Creative Center. Here, you can rent everything from missionary outfits to retro clothes from the ’70s and ’80s. The mix of nostalgic and trendy styles fits perfectly with Yangnim-dong’s retro atmosphere.  There’s so much more to see in Yangnim History & Culture Village such as art galleries, museums, and cozy streets lined with delightful cafes and restaurants. Take your time to soak in the warm and welcoming vibe of this unique neighborhood.

stories.title: Ansan Reed Marsh Park
stories.script: Ansan Reed Marsh Park is a large-scale artificial marsh designed to improve the water quality of Sihwa Lake and create a new ecological environment. There are about 380 plant species in the park, and they serve as “Natural Purifiers” to provide a pristine space for relaxation and nature learning for citizens of all ages. People aren’t the only ones who come to the park to relax.  Since its opening in May 2002, around 170 species and 200,000 migratory birds visit the park every year. The park has birdwatching towers where you can observe migratory birds as well as herons hunting fish in the water. The communities of aquatic plants, reeds, and other plants supporting the breeding birds are also one of the important ecological environments at the park. Before visiting, bring your telescope, cameras, and pens to make your own bird guides.  This will help you feel the park’s charms even more deeply. Now, let’s move on to a trail with an ecological pond.  As you walk along the trail, you will see golden wave tickseed, rugosa roses, and daisy fleabane. Standing on the wooden bridge crossing the marsh gives visitors a sense of being embraced by the wetland’s lush flora and fauna.     The park presents visitors with seasonal charms and natural beauty that guarantee pleasant memories that are sure to last a lifetime.

stories.title: Ansaneupseong Walled Town
stories.script: Hongi: Hello, everyone. Today, we will take a trip to “Ansaneupseong Walled Town and Local Government Building Site.” Meogi, do you know what a walled town is?  Meogi: Well, isn’t it a place where prince and princess live?  Hongi: Hmm, it’s a place where people lived, but not only prince and princess. Inside a walled town, there were ordinary people’s homes and administrative buildings. Have you ever heard the phrase, “go inside the walled town?” Meogi: You are right! When I think of a town, it feels like a place closely connected to ordinary people’s lives!  Hongi: Exactly! You made a good point. The walled town united the people of counties and the province within the communal hub and defended them against external invaders.   Meogi: But why did our ancestors build such a walled town at Suam-dong of Ansan?  Hongi: Our ancestors built the walls to defend against the Japanese invaders from the West Sea during the late Goryeo and early Joseon Dynasty periods. Take a look behind the wall site. Do you see that huge rocky mountain? Since it had Suambong Peak behind the wall, it was a perfect strategic point to defend against enemy invasions from the coast.  Meogi: But isn’t it better to build a wall over that high cliff to see the enemies better? This wall isn’t that high.  Hongi: You have really sharp eyes. That’s another characteristic of Ansaneupseong Walled Town. There are mainly three types of fortresses. First is a mountain fortress in high places and the second one is a flat land fortress. The last one is a hybrid type.     Meogi: (Interrupts) So, it’s a mixture of two types!  Hongi: Yes. It combines hilly areas and flat lands together to serve military and administrative roles at the same time. Meogi : That’s really cool.  Hongi: The perimeter of the wall is about 772 meters. Considering the lost parts, it is assumed that the wall was once longer. Unfortunately, most of walled towns on the Korean Peninsula disappeared due to wars and demolition policy during the Japanese colonial era. It’s sad that we couldn’t preserve these walled towns.  Meogi: I feel the same way. I hope we can preserve the remaining walled towns better.

stories.title: Ansan Gaeksa Inn
stories.script: Hongi: In Ansaneupseong Walled Town, you can find a building that looks like an eagle spreading its wings. The place is called Gaeksa, and it was used as a local inn where foreign envoys and central government officials stayed. Ansan Gaeksa Inn was restored in 2010, and it consists of a central room with royal plaques, and a left-side room, and right-side room. The central room has a gabled roof with openings on both sides, and two rooms in each side have half-hipped roofs. Ansan Gaeksa Inn is also called Ansan Royal Palace because King Jeongjo spent a night at this place when he visited Prince Sado’s tomb in 1797.

stories.title: Ansan Industrial History Museum
stories.script: Do you want to find out the miraculous growth of Korean industries and their history?  Visit Ansan that has been leading the industrialization of South Korea based on establishment of large-scale industrial complexes.  Ansan Industrial History Museum opened in 2002 and it introduces the industrial history by exhibiting over 100,000 industrial artifacts and offering many engaging experience programs.    Let’s take a look around the corners of the three-storied building  The first floor has a 4D theater where you can watch realistic materials.      On the other side of the first floor is a special exhibition hall.  Since the special exhibition hall has different themes, I recommend checking to see what’s being exhibited before visiting the museum.  Now, let’s go up to the second floor.  On the second floor, you’ll see the permanent exhibitions, which are the main exhibitions.  The three permanent exhibition sections have different themes.  The first theme is “Industry and City.”  This section portrays 40 years of Ansan that grew alongside the industrial complexes.   You can also use the touch screens to see the changing history of towns in panoramic photos.   The second section’s theme is “Industry and Technology,” and it exhibits the history of root industries that have been sustaining South Korea.  This section also exhibits life-sized retro cars and machines.  The last theme is “Industry and Daily Life.”  In this theme, you can take a closer look at how industrialization changed people’s lives.  The section exhibits the machinery and finished goods for textile processing, paper, and printing industries.   Is that all for the second floor?  Nope! The second floor also has a special place.  It’s the VR experience hall. In this section, you can enjoy various realistic console games.  Lastly, the third floor has places for diverse educational programs.   At the rooftop space, you can enjoy the whole view of Hwarang Park as well as concerts and performances for citizens of all ages.  Visit Ansan Industrial History Museum. It’s a relaxing site full of history and culture.

stories.title: Nojeokbong Park
stories.script: Nojeokbong Park of Ansan has Korean’s largest artificial waterfall. The name, Nojeokbong, comes from its geographical features. The mountain behind the waterfall was named “Nojeokbong” because it looks like piles of harvested rice.  The true charms of Nojeokbong are its ever-changing scenery in tune with the seasons and even times of the day.   At the summit of Nojeokbong, experience a memorable sunset as the sun slowly sinks in the west.    At night, the park is illuminated by a rose garden with LED lights.  You can also enjoy cherry blossoms in the spring and the hills covered with beautiful flowers in autumn.   There is more than just scenery.  The park has a 2.6-kilometer-long trail surrounding the park, which is perfect for a short stroll or a long, leisurely walk.  Photos of you among the vast garden of roses and azaleas will capture a special moment of your life.

stories.title: Kim Hong Do Theme Trail
stories.script: Kim Hong Do was a gifted and celebrated painter, and his paintings extend from King Yeongjo and King Jeongjo’s cultural renaissance to the early years of King Sunjo. He was born in Ansan, studied under one of the greatest painters and calligraphers Kang Se Hwang, and became a painter of Dohwaseo at an early age.   Kim talents were evident in landscape painting, Taoist and Buddhist figure painting, flower and bird painting, and genre painting. He is held in very high regard for his landscape and genre paintings. In 1990, Ansan was designated as the “City of Danwon” by the Ministry of Culture, Sports, and Tourism for the birth and growth of Danwon Kim Hong Do. Since then, Ansan has been inheriting and developing his artistic spirit and working on projects to become a traditional city of history, culture, and tourism.    As a part of such projects, Ansan opened Kim Hong Do Theme Trail by imagining the street that Kim used to pass as he started learning painting in childhood. The trail starts from Nojeokbong Trail of Seongpo-dong, which is believed to be the birthplace of Kim.        The trail connects KIMHONGDO ART MUSEUM with Nojeokbong Park, Cheongmundang, and Seongho Park, and it has three themes—Kim Hong Do Modern Trail, Kim Hong Do Old Trail, and Cheongmundang Old Trail. The first course is Kim Hong Do Modern Trail, which features a pedestrian overpass connecting Nojeokbong Park and Seongho Park, and offers a photo zone with the Painting of Cat and Butterfly, Hongdorang designed by upcycling a relief mural with Kim’s folk painting at Danwon Sculpture Park, and a ceramic mosaic sculpture inspired by colors from the piece titled Painting of Cat and Butterfly.  Walk along Kim Hong Do Theme Trail in the City of Danwon and become immersed in the artworks, artistic spirit, and touches of Kim Hong Do.  The second week of October heralds the Kim Hong Do Festival where you can see and sample the art and cuisine while learning about the customs, humor, and artistic spirit in Kim’s paintings.

stories.title: Wongok-dong Multicultural Food Street
stories.script: Imagine a street with steamed Yanbian-style rice cake, spiky durian with thorns, and Russian shashlik.   Can you guess where it is?   It’s actually in Korea. Ansan’s Multicultural Food Street offers tasty delicacies from around the world.   Take Exit 1 from Ansan Station where Subway Line 4 and Suin-Bundang Line pass. Then, cross the main road and the aroma of exotic food will lure you to the right spot.  The signage is written in multiple languages and foreigners fill the streets.  Suddenly longing for local Vietnamese rice noodles? Visit Multicultural Food Street for the best this side of Hanoi.   The restaurants are run by locals from China, Indonesia, Vietnam, Mongolia, and Uzbekistan to create authentic tastes.   Street food choices abound, so let your curiosity help you decide which snack will satisfy your appetite.  Cars are banned from 11 am to 8 pm so the street is pedestrian-friendly.

stories.title: Sihwa Lake Tidal Power Station
stories.script: Drive freely along the wide-open coastal road without complicated signals or tall buildings blocking your sight.   Come to Sihwa Lake Tidal Power Station  The road from Oido Island to Daegudo Island offers a great view of the 11.2 kilometer-long Sihwa embankment.  When you pass about two-thirds of the length of the embankment, you will see Sihwa Lake Tidal Power Station and Sihwa Narae Rest Area.  Sihwa Lake Tidal Power Station is the world’s biggest tidal power station and generates 552,700MWh of electricity annually, which can be used by 500,000 people for one year.  The power plant is operated by using the differences between the rise and fall of tides at the embarkment The demand for green energy is increasing due to serious climate change caused by environmental pollution.  Sihwa Lake Tidal Power Station is a distinguished eco-friendly energy producer by replacing over 860,000 barrels of annual oil import and preventing the emission of 310,000 tons of carbon dioxide.

stories.title: Sea Fragrance Theme Park
stories.script: Sea Fragrance Theme Park is designed by filling a vast and open land with waterways and beautiful decorations.   In spring, a colorful array of flowers welcome you to the Sea Fragrance Theme Park.  The waterside park is created with 1.2-kilometer-long natural waterways along Bangameori Beach, which has now become an ecological museum.   Be amazed at the diversity of life in and around the ponds and marsh observational deck, and get a great photo with the operating windmill.  When a pleasant wind blows, the fields of wheat and reeds play a beautiful symphony. How about taking a walk along metasequoia tree road like young couples from romantic movies? The park is 4 kilometers long and home to over 1,000 metasequoia trees.    Come alone or stroll with your loved one for a beautiful memory.

stories.title: Daebu Mine Sedimentary Rock Layer
stories.script: Daebu Mine Sedimentary Rock Layer lets you look back 70 million years!  This place was originally a quarry.  One day in 1997, an important event happened here and completely changed the historical significance of the space.  In 1997, footprints of Mesozoic herbivorous dinosaurs were found here.  Then, 23 dinosaur footprints were found, immediately attracting the attention of the press and public. Later, a plant fossil called cladophlebis was uncovered and Daebu Mine Sedimentary Rock Layer became an important place for studying vegetation and the environment of dinosaur habitats in the midwestern section of the Korean Peninsula.   What do you think? Do those rocks around the lake feel more special now?  Sedimentary rock is mainly composed of tuffs, sandstones, and mudstones from the Cretaceous period.   Some layers are sedimented by volcanic activities, so volcanic rocks and geological layers are available for viewing at the same time.  The sedimentary layer has been subjected to potassium-argon dating and found to be 70 million years old.   In 2003, the sedimentary rock was designated as a monument of Gyeonggi-do for its preservation value.  You can look down to the pond from two observatories on the cliff, or look up to the sedimentary rock layer from the grass park at the bottom.   Enjoy a relaxing time with the beautiful lake and examine the dinosaur footprints to imagine life on the peninsula millions of years ago.  Daebu Mine Sedimentary Rock Layer is a wonderful place for learning and resting.

stories.title: Daesong Wetland
stories.script: Daebudo Island is often called the “Treasure Island of the West Sea” for its beautiful coastline stretching 100 kilometers, vast mudflats, Daebu Hasol-gil, and Daesong Wetland.   Daesong Wetland is an ecological tourist spot located at southern Siheung Lake, and it’s also a friendly habitat that attracts many migratory birds every year.  This ecological tourist spot offers viewings of the rarely seen whooper swans and spoonbills in the winter.   Daesong Wetland is also one of the main feeding areas for winter migratory birds together with Sihwaho Lake and Hwaseong Hyeongdo Island.  In 2014, Daesong Wetland was designated as the first metropolitan ecological tourist spot by the Ministry of Environment for its crucial ecological resources.  Daesong Wetland is a great place to escape from congested cities and restore your natural affinity for nature with the majestic views of the vast mudflats and reed fields.

stories.title: Daebu Haesol-gil
stories.script: Daebu Haesol-gil is a welcoming trail offering stunning views of the west coast highlighted by the scents of the sea and pine trees.  The trail takes you around the island along the coastline. Several courses are available covering a total of 91 kilometers.  Each course has unique features, but the Daebu Hasol-gil course is the highlight.  When you pass Sihwa embankment, you will soon see the starting point at the Daebudo Tourist Information Center.  You may not be able to resist the temptations of the restaurants but walk along the fine sand beach of “Bangameori Beach” to reach the Bukmangsan-gil Trail.   Climb to the top of the mountain and enjoy the view of the coastal trails you have passed. A paraglider site is available for those seeking an adrenaline rush.  After taking a short break, walk by one of the favorite campsites for car campers.  By the time you cool down along smooth trails, you will reach the Gubongdo Forest Course. Its name reveals the nine peaks of the course.  Quench your thirst at the “Gubong Mineral Spring.”  After crossing an arch bridge connecting islands and enjoying a beautiful unobstructed view of the coastal deck road, you will arrive at the famous “Gubongdo Sunset Observation Deck.”  It’s a must-take photo when the sunset paints the sky with brilliant colors.  Sunset is the recommended time for visiting this popular site.   You can also walk a little farther to see “Grandma Rock” and “Grandpa Rock” which are also famous for sunset photos.  As you walk along the paved road toward Jonghyun Farming and Fishing Experience Village for a mudflat experience, an abundance of restaurants and cafes beckon hungry hikers. Take a break with a delightful coffee and then continue to reach the end point with Donji Island Observatory.

stories.title: Nueseom Island Lighthouse Observatory
stories.script: Nueseom Island Lighthouse Observatory opened in 2004 to create a safer environment for coastal fishing boats along the west coast and provide nature study programs and a fishing village tour program.  Let’s take a close look.  You can enter Nueseom Island by Tando Sea Parting Trail but it is only open twice a day at low tide.    Nueseom Island got its name because it resembles a silkworm when you see it from afar.  When you arrive at the island, the lighthouse observatory looks like a spaceship crash landed on the top of the island.    The building’s first of four floors introduces Nueseom Island and exhibits photographs of Daebudo Island’s tourist spots.  On the second floor, you will see stories of different islands around the world.  Stroll among the exhibits and read stories of islands, such as Easter Island’ moai statues and the island that Robinson Crusoe was based on.   The third floor has an observatory offering great views of Daebudo Island, Jaebudo Island, Seongamdo Island, Tando Island, and Buldo Island.  The fourth floor functions as an actual lighthouse.  When the sun sets, the lighthouse lights up the dark sea with its yellow light.

stories.title: Sea Fragrance Arboretum
stories.script: Daebudo Island has a beautiful arboretum located near the sea.  It’s called appropriately the “Sea Fragrance Arboretum.” The name comes from a story describing a hermit who left his mundane world and came down to take a bath in the clear water.   In 2017, Gyeonggi-do planned to open an arboretum in the provincial forest to preserve plant genetic resources and provide forest recreation space along the west coast. Since opening in May 2019, the arboretum has been a popular stop for countless visitors.,   The arboretum covers about 100 hectares and is home to 1,000 species of coastal, central, and inland plants.    As you enter the arboretum, you will see a large splashing fountain and a diverse array of flowers and trees.  Follow the beautiful trails for great views from the sea observatory, uniquely themed gardens with sea swell, rocks, roses, and comfortable resting areas including Lily Rest area and a quaint concert hall.    Taking a walk around the arboretum refreshes your body and comforts your mind.

stories.title: The Origin of Life
stories.script: "The motif here is based on the nut-bearing torreya tree, and the light and mirrors make it feel like you are in a forest of nut-bearing torreya trees. Take a moment to pause and gaze upon the forest reflected in the mirrors. If you listen closely, you can hear the sounds of life. I hope you experience it as if taking a stroll through the woods. "

stories.title: Tactile Box
stories.script: "Explore the many natural resources of Naejangsan National Park at your fingertips. Place your hand inside the box and feel with your fingertips to guess what they are from right to left. In the first section, you can feel a smooth and round shape. In the fall, you can hear them crackling in Galcham oak (Oriental white oak) forests. These are acorns, a winter food source for chipmunks, squirrels, and other wildlife. In the second section, you’ll feel something rough, slightly convex, and with ring-shaped patterns. It is the shell of a Unio douglasiae, about the size of a palm. They live in symbiosis with Korean rose bitterlings in the pond in front of Ilgwangjeong Pavilion. In the third section, you can feel something cold, sharp, and uneven. What could it be? It is volcanic rock from Baekhakbong Peak in Naejangsan National Park. The last section, marked with a question mark, holds one of the natural resources of Naejangsan National Park for each month. What will you encounter this month? Feel it with your fingertips. "

stories.title: Flagship Species and Representative Plants in Naejangsan Mountain
stories.audioTitle: Flagship Species and Representative Plants in Naejangsan Mountain
stories.script: "Use your senses of touch, sight, and smell to immerse yourself in the allure of nut-bearing torreya trees.  First, look at the bark. You will notice that there are tightly packed cracks. Then, focus on your fingertips to feel the texture of the hard bark. When you observe nut-bearing torreya (called “bija namu” in Korea) leaves with a magnifying glass, you will see pointed leaves arranged neatly on both sides like the strokes of a brush, resembling the Chinese character “非.” 非 is pronounced as “bi” in Korea. This is why Koreans call this tree “bija namu” (namu means tree in Korea), named after the character “非.” Walking into a nut-bearing torreya forest, you will smell a bitter aroma, a phytoncide with head-clearing, stress-reducing, immunity-boosting, and antibacterial properties. Walk along the trail through the nut-bearing torreya forest between May and September, when the aroma grows stronger. "

stories.title: Poetry, Calligraphy, and Painting in Baegamsan Mountain
stories.audioTitle: Poetry, Calligraphy, and Painting in Baegamsan Mountain
stories.script: "Ssanggyeru Pavilion is renowned for being a place where scholars and poets of the Goryeo and Joseon dynasties sang about its outstanding scenery. It stands at the point where waters from two branching valleys meet; hence, the name “Ssanggyeru” is derived from the characters “ssang” (pair), “gye” (valley), and “ru” (pavilion).  The poem and calligraphy in this scroll came from the original writing by Jeong Mong-ju (1337–1392, pen name: Poeun), the first work composed after the pavilion’s name changed to “Ssanggyeru Pavilion.” The titles of the next 200 or so poems are all Ssanggyeru Pavilion, borrowing the characters 僧 (monk), 能 (ability), 增 (increase), 澄 (clear), and 登 (ascend) from Jeong’s original poems. I hope you experience the picturesque beauty of Ssanggyeru Pavilion, a captivating sight even after hundreds of years. "

stories.title: Plants and Trees in Naejangsan National Park
stories.audioTitle: Plants and Trees in Naejangsan National Park
stories.script: "This space showcases plants and trees you could find along the trail. With an enlarged model of a yellow surprise lily, about three times its actual size, in the center, plants are at the right section, and trees are at the left. In the right section, you will find plants such as the spring-blooming common corydalis, Byeonsan winter aconite, the summer-blooming dwarf woodland Korean iris, white-flower bittercress, the fall-blooming orange-flower surprise lily, field touch-me-not, the winter-blooming Amur adonis and red spurge. In the left section, you will find trees such as plum blossoms and early-blooming ivory honeysuckles in spring, trilobed-leaf alangium and East Asian orixa in summer, palmate maple and mono maple in autumn, and Oriental cork oak and macropodous daphniphyllum in winter. Stroll along the path through the Oriental white oak tree forest, which transforms into a fairyland, as if splattered with watercolors in the fall. "

stories.title: Animals in Naejangsan National Park
stories.script: "In Naejangsan National Park, you can encounter various mammals and birds. You will find roe deer, weasels, raccoon dogs, moles, chipmunks, squirrels, and birds like bluebirds, kingfishers, white-backed woodpeckers, and Korean black-naped green woodpeckers. Male roe deer have antlers on their heads, while females do not and are covered in yellow fur with white fur on their rumps. Weasels are intelligent creatures with a cute appearance that prefer solitude. They emit a pungent odor and flee when they sense danger. Raccoon dogs are timid and uniquely hibernate among Canidae animals. They have no stripes on their tails and pointed snouts.  Moles spend most of their time underground, using their large, sharp claws to dig tunnels. They detect vibrations and sound waves caused by moving insects with sensory hairs along their muzzles and bodies. Chipmunks and squirrels differ in appearance and ecological habits. Chipmunks hibernate, have five dark stripes on the top of their bodies, and spend most of their time on the ground. On the other hand, squirrels do not hibernate, are gray all over, and live in trees. Bluebirds are common summer migratory birds, about the size of pigeons, and easily identifiable by their distinctive loud calls. Kingfishers have large heads and beaks, making them adept at catching fish. White-backed woodpeckers have short black lines on their bellies, while Korean black-naped green woodpeckers have dull green feathers all over. "

stories.title: Autumn at Cheongnamdae
stories.script: Cheongju, Cheongnamdae in Autumn Warm Southern Cheongwadae Nestled within a forest vibrant with autumn foliage, the striking blue roof of Cheongnamdae immediately captures the eye. Located in Cheongju, Cheongnamdae served as a presidential villa where former presidents spent their vacations from 1983 for approximately 20 years. Since opening to the public in 2003, it has become a popular tourist destination.
