Spanning an impressive 1.825 million square meters, Cheongnamdae boasts over 100 species of ornamental trees and wildflowers that showcase their beauty with each passing season. The area is also home to a rich natural ecosystem, where animals like otters and flying squirrels roam freely.  Be sure to stroll along the trails former presidents once enjoyed. These paths, ranging from one to three kilometers, wind through the forest and along Daecheongho Lake. One of the most popular spots is the 645-steps-long Stairway of Happiness, and an observatory. From there, visitors are treated to a breathtaking view of Daecheongho, reminiscent of the scenic Dadohae archipelago.

stories.title: Spring at Cheongnamdae
stories.script: Cheongju, Cheongnamdae in Spring Vacation Retreat for Former Korean Presidents  Cheongnamdae, meaning ‘Cheongwadae in the South,’ served as the vacation retreat for six presidents over a span of about 20 years. During this period, it was visited 89 times for a total of 472 days. Known for its stunning natural scenery, the site is a popular destination for leisurely walks, but it also offers intriguing spaces that reflect the lives of past presidents.  The building in the photograph is the main hall of Cheongnamdae, notable for its neatly maintained lawn and striking blue roof. The first floor of the main hall includes meeting rooms, reception rooms, a dining hall, and VIP rooms, while the second floor served as a private space for the president. It housed the president’s bedroom, study, and living room. Since June 2011, an annex building has been expanded to include exhibition halls where visitors can explore the diverse lives of former presidents.  The Presidential Memorial Hall, a scaled-down replica of the main building of Cheongwadae, offers experiences such as reenactment of national addresses, military honor guard inspections, and summit meetings. Additionally, the Korean Provisional Government Memorial Hall provides a glimpse into the lives of Korea’s leaders during the Provisional Government era. Take a tour around Cheongnamdae. Retrace the footsteps of past presidents and delve into the history of the Republic of Korea.

stories.title: Entrance to Gamcheon Culture Village (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.audioTitle: Entrance to Gamcheon Culture Village (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.script: The Beginning of Gamcheon Culture Village  The stream flowing at the foot of Cheonmasan Mountain used to be called “Gamnae,” which literally means sweetness in Korean, referring to its sweet taste. During the period of Japanese occupation and the Korean War, approximately 4,000 Taegeukdo religion believers gathered in this area. Subsequently, more people, including merchants and refugees, moved to the area, forming a village. Initially named Cheondeok-dong, the area eventually split due to increased population, forming a new area named “Gamcheon-dong,” which further separated into “Gamcheon 1-dong” and “Gamcheon 2-dong.”  Gamcheon-dong was initially constructed with around 1,000 shacks on slopes when the Taegeukdo followers relocated to this site. In the aftermath of the war, severe shortages of supplies and living spaces afflicted the residents. Originally, the village was built as a communal residence village, all inhabitants shared wells and bathrooms, leading to increased inconvenience as the population grew. Moreover, shacks were susceptible to fire hazards. Therefore, three 6-meter-wide vertical stairs were installed as a safety measure, which still exist in the village today.  From its initial planning stages, Gamcheon Village was designed to ensure houses at the back would not obstruct the view and to maintain a pedestrian lane in front of the houses. These planning considerations contribute to the colorful and well-organized village seen today. Unfortunately, the village started to decline as its facilities deteriorated, prompting residents to seek better living conditions elsewhere. To revitalize the village's atmosphere, the government initiated the “Gamcheon Village Art Project.” This project involves installing artwork in the village annually, aiming to enhance residents' quality of life. The renovated village eventually became a popular tourist spot for visits and photography.  An information center is situated at the village entrance, where visitors can purchase a map of the village. Additionally, visitors can converse with village guides who provide course guidance and explanations. It's essential to note that touring the village is permitted only between 9 AM and 6 PM, and visitors should refrain from peeping into residents' houses or taking photos without their consent.

stories.title: Haeundae Beach
stories.script: Haeundae Beach  Haeundae Beach is the first name that probably pops up in your head when talking about the beaches of Busan. The beach became even more popular thanks to the film “Haeundae” and is one of the beaches in Busan that attracts the most visitors.  The name, “Haeundae”, comes from Choe Chiwon, one of the geniuses from the Silla Dynasty, who built a stone platform here and engraved “海雲臺 (Haeundae)” in Chinese characters. One of the pen names used by Choe Chiwon was “Haeun (海運)” but the character “Un” is different when it comes to the name and place. But, because they are both pronounced as “Haeun”, people theorize that one of those two names was created here. The letters known to have been engraved by Choe Chiwon are located on the southern rock face.  Haeundae Beach spans broadly between Dongbaekseom Island and the Dalmaji-gil cliffs, and thanks to the cool sea breeze that continues to blow, no matter how hot the day is, it has the advantage to letting you enjoy yourself in the water. Parks and trails are nicely set up around the beach making it great to go for a walk to warm up.  Haeundae is most known for its view at night; fancy hotels and high-rise apartments near the beach allows for an urban night view, which can be enjoyed from a variety of chic cafes nearby. It is visited by a grand number of people during the summer but there are many tourists wanting to take photos of their trip to Busan who come to Haeundae even during the winter, so it is a beach that is always filled with people all year long.

stories.title: Gwangalli Beach
stories.script: Gwangalli Beach  A place to visit at least once, every time you're in Busan, to see the view of the night sea, Gwangalli Beach is where Gwangandaegyo is located. It is where the Busan International Fireworks Festival is held, which splendidly decorates the black sky and sea every fall.  Gwangalli Beach is named after its location in Gwangan-dong, which was created during division of administrative districts during the Japanese occupation period. Gwangan-dong means, in Chinese characters, “wide coast.” It is the region that was guarded by the naval forces of Gyeongsangjwa-do Province during the Joseon Dynasty. A long time ago, the sand at Gwangalli Beach used to break and disappear easily, so it was deemed unfit to swim in. So, instead, it was used as a shore where small fishing boats were tied up or a place people could go for a walk at.  When Gwangandaegyo was constructed by the sea in front of Gwangan-ri in 2003, the landscape of Gwangan-ri began to change. At the time of the construction, it was the longest bridge in Korea and people from all over the country gathered to see the beautiful sight of Gwangandaegyo reflecting the night sea with various colored lights that changed hourly. Fully living up to its wonderful nickname the “Diamond Bridge”, Gwangandaegyo and its bright lights that shined on soon became a landmark of Gwangan-ri.  Subsequently, a beach was formed there and the Fireworks Festival came around, making the area a tourist attraction with various facilities. Especially during the Fireworks Festival in the fall, the beach is full of people from the shore all the way to the roads so some people even camp out starting midday in order to secure the best spots.  If you are interested in seeing Gwangalli Beach from a different angle, you could try driving over Gwangandaegyo by car. Gwangandaegyo is a bridge made of two levels, each of which is one-way only. If you take your car, there is a toll fee so make sure to prepare it in advance.

stories.title: Dadaepo Beach
stories.script: Dadaepo Beach  “Dadaepo,” one of the oldest names in Busan, is located where Nakdonggang and the South Sea meet. In 『Samguk Sagi (historical record of the Three Kingdoms of Korea: Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla)』, there appears a place named “Dapdal”, and this is presumed to refer to “Dadae” of Dadaepo. During a similar period, a book named 『Nihongi』 revealed the names of places such as “Dadara” or “Dadarajin” and it is assumed that these words eventually evolved into “Dadae”.  Japanese invaders frequently appeared in this area so, during the Joseon Period, a military camp was installed here to make it one of the 7 military zones that protected the Gyeongsangjwa-do Province. This is also the ground for the historic “Battle of Dadaepo”, which was one of the earliest battles that took place during the Japanese invasion of 1592 along with the Battle of Busanjin. Today, it has become a peaceful and relaxing coast thanks to its beach and Sunset Fountain of Dreams.  You can get to the beach and park by getting off at Dadaepo Beach Station (Morundae Station), the final stop of Busan Subway Line 1. Known as the “Fantastic Music Foundation”, the Dadaepo Sunset Fountain of Dreams is located inside the beach park.  Operating from April to October of every year, the Sunset Fountain of Dreams first opened in 2010. The first music fountain installed in Busan, it is a beautiful fountain that shoots streams of water upward in sync to the music and lighting. Thanks to its enormous size and height, it was listed as the “world's largest ground fountain” by the Guinness World Records in 2010.  As the name suggests, the Sunset Fountain holds music performances in the evening for about 20 minutes, and, since the hours of operation and frequencies vary depending on the season and date, we recommend you to check the times in advance. Music performances are popular even on weekdays and the seats are on a first-come, first-served basis in an open space so you need to be there early in order to get good seats.  If you post a story and song request in advance onto the Saha-gu District Office website, you may be able to see the music fountain dancing to the song you want. It's a great opportunity to do something special for your loved one or for families to make long-lasting memories.

stories.title: 3. Gukje Market (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.audioTitle: 3. Gukje Market (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.script: Would you believe that the vast Gukje Market emerged as a result of chance, stemming from a series of overlapping historic events? Since the mid-Joseon Dynasty, numerous Japanese immigrants resided in the Choryang-Waegwan area. Consequently, the region was densely populated with buildings during the Japanese occupation. As all these structures were made of wood, any fire outbreak quickly escalated into a large inferno. Before liberation, while the Allied Forces’ continuous attacks that inflicted significant damage, the Japanese imperialists left Lighting Street, currently named as such, vacant as a refuge area. This strategic measure aimed to contain any fire outbreak within this street and prevent it from spreading.  Following liberation, many Japanese gathered at the port to depart from Korea. Due to restrictions on the number of carry-on luggage, numerous sold their bags at scrap value, containing items collected over decades. Some bags contained not just expensive household goods but also valuable artworks and rare antique books. Setting up goods for sale in the vacant refuge area marked the inception of Guje Market. Locals often refer to Gukje Market as Doddegi Market, derived from the Japanese term “Dori,” meaning grab and take, illustrating the fierce competition among Joseon merchants striving to acquire Japanese items.  With the outbreak of the Korean War in 1950, a multitude of refugees fled to Busan, and the U.S. Army brought in an overflow of war supplies and munitions, significantly expanding Gukje Market. However, its success was short-lived as a massive fire in January 1953 reduced the entire market to ashes. A small bar fire engulfed over 4,000 stalls within 7 hours, resulting in a catastrophic event that caused 1.4 billion won in damages and nearly 10,000 victims. Amid Busan's mourning, General Whitcomb, commander of the U.S. Logistics Supply Base, brought hope and support. He erected tent villages for those who lost homes overnight, rebuilt schools and churches, and remained committed to safeguarding Busan's citizens throughout his life. Recovering from this tragedy, Gukje Market once again thrived until the 1990s, trading aid goods and contraband from America. It served as an all-in-one marketplace that met various life needs. Though the market's peak has passed, it retains its status as Busan's foremost traditional market.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 5. Bosu-dong Book Street
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 5. Bosu-dong Book Street
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 5. Bosu-dong Book Street  “The very first to start here was Mr. Son Jeong-rin who fled from the North and built a shack over there on the hillside slums. He had to feed himself so he put everything he had brought from his hometown up for sale. The first things to sell were books. Why? It was because there were many schools in Daesin-dong on this street and a lot of students at the time did not have enough money so they walked instead of taking the tram. And this was on their way to school and many of them would be around the area in the mornings and evenings so books were the first to sell. That's when he realized that he should become a bookseller. I asked him about 2 or 3 years later. I was studying under adversity and I wanted to make a living out of something so I asked, Can I do this, too? and he said yes. So, I put a box out here and bought books from him to sell them myself.”  This is the story of Mr. Kim Yeo-man, a first generation Bosu-dong resident who still runs his bookstore to this day since it first opened in 1953. During the days when everyone was facing tough times, there were not a lot of books being published so students had a hard time finding books even though they wanted to study. Students were grateful if they could even get a hold of used books. A few refugees who had realized the circumstances opened up street stalls for used books, and Bosu-dong thrived as the number of stalls grew from 6 to 7 in the beginning to over a few dozen in just a couple years. One of the more popular items here were English magazines and other foreign books, which had mostly been left behind by U.S. troops who frequently traveled to and from the Busan Port. They were collected by the booksellers and resold to refugee intellectuals. There were also those who made great profit by selling antique books that they had purchased inexpensively without much thought from the Japanese after Liberation. Merchants who secured seed money from their stall operations opened stores and officially launched the used books business, which has become the Book Street that we see today. When a frequent customer orders a book he or she needs, the bookseller finds and secures it from another used book street in Cheonggyecheon, Seoul or near Daegu City Hall, and makes a trip around the country once a month to transport the books before delivering it to the customer. At the time, books in specialized fields such as law or engineering had a waiting period of about 1 to 2 months. Refugees or students facing hard times would sell relatively high-priced books among the ones they owned and then buy the other used books that they needed. In the 60s and 70s when there were over 70 bookstores, Bosu-dong street was always crowded especially before the start of new semesters with people carrying around bags of books, looking to buy and sell textbooks and reference materials.  “A bookstore is innocent. 90% of those who come to buy a book are good people. When you talk to them, there is a lot of things you can learn. There are no better teachers. Everyone who comes to buy a book is a teacher. I have lived my whole life in gratitude.” In an era where online bookstores dominate the publishing world, these words of an old bookstore owner who still protects a corner of the alley seem to symbolize the unchanging value of the Bosu-dong Book Street.

stories.title: Busan Modern History Museum
stories.script: Built in 1929 during the Japanese colonial period, it is the history museum where you can see the modern history of Busan. In the beginning, it was used as the Busan Branch of Oriental Colonization Company, an agency responsible for exploiting colonies, but after the Liberation, it started to serve as Busan Cultural Center for the United States Information Service in 1949. However, due to ceaseless demands from Busan citizens for its return, the American cultural center left the building in the end. It was returned to the Korean government in 1999 before the city of Busan took it over in June of the same year. As it was a symbol of invasion and exploitation, the building became the Busan Modern History Museum to be able to utilize it for education to teach the citizens on our painful history. The museum opened on July 3, 2003. The exhibition hall has a map that shows the opening and reclamation of Busan Port with modern stories of the city through various videos. Busan Modern History Museum tells us a lot of interesting stories about the city's modern history.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 8. Gwangbok-ro Fashion Street
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 8. Gwangbok-ro Fashion Street
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 8. Gwangbok-ro Fashion Street  What attracts people to this street, which would thrive even when put up against the likes of Myeongdong in Seoul, is perhaps the stores that tightly populate the street. This particular area on Gwangbok-ro was known as the Fashion Street because these stores led the trends of not just Busan but the entire country during the 80s.  But it was actually long before that when this area first began to be crowd with people looking to buy and sell goods. The history of commerce on Gwangbok-ro started along with the installation of Waegwan in the late Joseon Dynasty. Joseon people were not allowed to enter Waegwan, which was a Japanese-only residence, and even the Japanese could not travel beyond certain limits. That is why the markets, near the three gates into Waegwan, that sold fresh vegetables, fruits and fish to the Japanese prospered. As the Japanese population grew even more after opening the port, development of the commercial district of Gwangbok-ro took off. By the Japanese occupation era, many restaurants, movie theaters and department stores were established so the area began to be known as “Jangsutong”, which means “Prospering”. Two-story store buildings began to populate either side of the street and an increasing amount of energy came about every day to the point where it was nicknamed Byeoncheonjeong, which stood for “the look of the sky has changed”. In 1902, street lamps were lit on this street for the first time in Busan to be able to set up a night market, enabling the street to gain extreme popularity as one of the leading commercial districts within the city.  The Gwangbok-ro shopping district continued to maintain its fervor even after Liberation, and Mihwadang Department Store, established in 1949, was at the center of it all. It was the first-ever department store in Busan and the second in the country, behind Seoul's Hwasin Department Store, built by our own national capital. The concrete annex building constructed in 1956 was not only the tallest building in Busan at the time but also an advanced structure with elevators and escalators. In particular, the pedestrian overpass leading from the roof of the annex to Yongdusan Park made a name for itself as a romantic date hot spot for young lovers. Thanks to its reputation, Mihwadang was considered as a place of gathering amongst Busan people. Everyone from Busan probably has fond memories of briskly walking along Gwangbok-ro towards the main entrance of the department store, filled with excited anticipation of seeing a friendly face.  Where the people gathered, so gathered tea houses on the streets. Gwangbok-ro especially featured many music cafes. It was a natural outcome of cultural artists, who had fled to Busan due to the war, gathering in cafes at Gwangbok-ro. Here, the artists transcended the pain of our history into literary, artistic, and musical works to motivate themselves to carry on. A novel by Kim Dong-ri written in the setting of “Mildawon”, a cafe on Gwangbok-ro, depicts a writer who refuses a comfortable bed and instead takes naps in a corner spot of the cafe. Through a confession stating, “I can't stand not being in the midst of our crowd of refugees,” we are given a glimpse of an artist's conscience in desiring to be with history and destiny. As a result, the Nampo-dong area became the mecca of Busan culture teemed with musical halls and movie theaters until the 70s. Today, many of the traces from those times have disappeared but the dignity of the original city center, built by a long history, can be felt anywhere.

stories.title: What is the UN Memorial Cemetery? (UN Memorial Cemetery)
stories.audioTitle: What is the UN Memorial Cemetery? (UN Memorial Cemetery)
stories.script: The United Nations Memorial Cemetery is the only UN-certified cemetery. It is a place where fallen UN soldiers, who sacrificed their lives for world peace and freedom, rest in peace. There are several main sites and memorials including the Memorial Service Hall, Memorabilia Hall, two Turkish Monuments, Greek Monument, Australian Monument, British Commonwealth Monument, and two ponds.  As soon as the Korean War broke out on June 25, 1950, the UN immediately dispatched Allied Forces to fight. This was the only incident in history where UN forces were sent to a troubled region worldwide. A total of 22 nations participated in the war, with 16 providing combat forces and weapons, and 5 contributing hospital ships, medical staff, and supplies. Throughout the war, which lasted about 3 years (from June 25, 1950, to July 27, 1953), 40,896 UN soldiers from the 17 participating nations lost their lives, including those who provided medical assistance like Norway.  From 1951 to 1954, around 11,000 fallen UN heroes were buried at the UN Memorial Cemetery. However, the remains of soldiers from 7 countries including Belgium, Colombia, Ethiopia, Greece, Luxembourg, the Philippines, and Thailand, along with some from other nations, have since been repatriated to their home countries. Currently, 2,309 fallen soldiers from 11 countries, including 36 Korean soldiers who died in battle alongside the UN troops, are buried in this cemetery.  Every year on November 11, the Turn Toward Busan International Memorial Ceremony in honor of the Fallen of the Korean War is held at the cemetery. Under the slogan of “Moment to Be One, Turn Toward Busan,” the entire world observes a minute of silence towards Busan at 11 AM on November 11. Let us all remember this day and pay a silent one-minute tribute to the deceased heroes.

stories.title: South Port Bridge
stories.script: South Port Bridge, connecting the South Port and Yeongdo with beautiful lights  Busan has many bridges that let you walk on the sea road. South Port Bridge is particularly famous for its landscape lighting in Yeongdo-gu, where four bridges are connected. Although it does not have remarkable sculptures or statues, the installed lighting gracefully harmonizes with the structural beauty of the bridge. South Port Bridge is a maritime bridge that connects Amnam-dong, Seo-gu, Busan and Yeongseon-dong, Yeongdo-gu. Its name comes from it linking the South Port to Yeongdo.   South Port Bridge has 3m wide sidewalks, allowing pedestrians to stroll and enjoy the scenery of the South Port area freely. Visitors can also enjoy views of Yongdusan Park, Jagalchi Market, Huinnyeoul Village, Jeolyeong Coastal Walk, and Songdo Beach.  South Port Bridge has unexpected charms. Its day and night are 180 degrees different. It provides a reliable walking trail during the day and presents a beautiful night view of the South Port adorned by a state-of-the-art LED lighting system. The visual feast of ships sleeping at the anchorage amidst the dazzling lights from sunset to midnight is also a sight to behold.  The 360m-long main route, where ships pass, decorates the night view with a dynamic colorful lighting spectacle every hour on Saturdays and public holidays. Enjoy the splendid display of lights on South Port Bridge.

stories.title: Busan Port Bridge
stories.script: Busan Port Bridge, the landmark of Busan  Busan Port Bridge, whose name comes from its function of connecting across Busan Port, was built on the North Port, the largest port in Busan. It is Korea's first steel-composite cable-stayed bridge and is rated as the world's fifth-largest steel-composite cable-stayed bridge. The bridge has received many external awards and honors, including the Grand Prize for Civil Structures by the Korean Society of Civil Engineers in 2015, the Grand Prize in Civil Engineering and Construction Technology in 2014, and the Best Artwork Award by the Concrete Society in 2014.  Busan Port Bridge connects Gamman-dong and Cheonghak-dong. This 3,331m-long bridge crosses the North Port and consists of a 1,114m-long cable-stayed section and a 2,217m-long connecting bridge. It forms the central axis of the coastal ring road connecting Gwangan Bridge, Yeongdo Highway Overpass, and South Port Bridge. The bridge has a reputation as a luxury bridge for providing a safe structure for transportation and beautiful scenery. Its diamond-shaped pylon offers an unforgettable spectacle and, at the same time, functions to resist wind more effectively.   Busan Port Bridge has a unique space—a camping ground in the city center. Yeongdo Marino Auto Camping Ground, a place where you can see the whole of Busan Port, represents the sea and the O-shaped circular path coming together in harmony. This eco-friendly campground has 52 sites (40 for cars, 12 for regular tents) where you can set up your tent and enjoy camping. There are also 7 fixed caravans where you can stay overnight, 107 parking lots, a walking trail, and an event plaza.  Please enjoy the leisure provided by Busan Port Bridge, the representative coastal bridge of Busan, and take memorable photographs, too.

stories.title: Songdo Beach
stories.script: Songdo Beach  Korea's first public beach  Teacher: 	 Welcome to the Songdo Beach Trip!   Student:	 Wow, it’s the ocean! Why is this place called Songdo?   Teacher:	 This place was named Songdo because it has had many pine forests since old times, and it was the first public beach in Korea that opened in 1913. It was the No. 1 tourist spot in Busan and was called the Naples of the East. It was a great beach that was selected as the best tourist destination in the country from the 1960s to the 1970s because of its clean white sandy beach and clear water.  Student:	 I heard this from my grandma. She said she came to Songdo Beach for her honeymoon, hehe.  Teacher: 	 At that time, there were many things to enjoy, including the cable car, and the surrounding scenery of nature was also very good, so many tourists came to visit. It is a place that holds the memories and romance of lovers and newlyweds of that time.  Student:	 There are not that many people here now compared to Haeundae or Gwangalli Beach.   Teacher:	 As development accelerated in the 1980s, a lot of sand was lost, and the cable car and surrounding facilities were damaged by Tropical Storm Selma in 1987 and Typhoon Maemi in 2003, so the number of visitors to the beach significantly decreased.  However, with the restoration of old Songdo landmarks such as the Busan Air Cruise, marine diving platform, and Yonggung Suspension Bridge, tourists are coming back again. Now, shall we go together to see the famous Busan superstar Songdo Beach?

stories.title: Introduction of Pyeongtaek
stories.script: Welcome to the citizen-centered city of Pyeongtaek, the name of which means “flat land.”  Pyeongtaek is situated in southwestern Gyeonggi-do Province, Korea, Today, it can be roughly divided into three regions: Pyeongtaek in the south, Songtan in the north, and Anjung in the west. Topographically speaking, it largely consists of flat land and low hills of a few tens of meters in elevation, with no large mountains. The highest mountain is Mubongsan, which is 208 m above sea level. Adjacent to the Anseongcheon and Jinwicheon streams, flowing into Asanman Bay are vast plains, which have been further expanded due to reclamation around Asanman Bay.   Pyeongtaek is flat terrains and it served as a portal between Seoul and the southern part of the country. The current population is 580,000, as of July 2023. It is home to Camp Humphreys, the largest overseas U.S. military base in the world, and the Osan Air Base, Samsung Electronics Pyeongtaek Campus, Poseung National Industrial Complex, and Pyeongtaek Port International Terminal are areas with a lot of foreign traffic.  Due to such regional characteristics, it has come to be known for its distinctive cityspace, with the Songtan Special Tourist Zone and Anjung Rodeo Street among others attracting tourists wishing to enjoy a different atmosphere.   Pyeongtaek Station, the gateway to the city, PyeongtaekJije station and the eight scenic sites of Pyeongtaek are also major tourist attractions. Seohaedaegyo Bridge, Pyeongtaek Port, Sopung Garden, Baedari Ecological Park, Pyeongtaekho, Oseong Riverside, Jinwicheon Recreation Area, and Wonpyeong Dock are places where visitors can feel the distinct charm of the natural environment unique to Pyeongtaek.   Pyeongtaek not only offers an abundance of fascinating spectacles of nature but also tourist sites providing a glimpse into local history and culture. There are a number of Buddhist temples such as Sudosa, Honghaksa, Mangisa, and Simboksa, as well as places where you can understand the history and culture of Pyeongtaek such as Pyeongtaekhyanggyo Confucian School, Jinwihyanggyo Confucian School, Paengseong Guesthouse, and Nongseong Fortress in Paengseong, and places where you can trace the footsteps of great figures from Pyeongtaek such as the Shrine of Jeong Do Jeon, Shrine of Won Gyun, and Shrine of Shin Suk-ju. In addition, there are the Korean Modern and Contemporary Music Center, Korea Soriter Arts Center, Jiyeonghui Music Pavilion, and Pyeongtaekho Art  Museum that present the traditional sounds and arts of Pyeongtaek.  Pyeongtaek is a city with a beautiful future ahead! Come for a healing experience with the breathtaking sea and land as a backdrop and enjoy various sights and local food.

stories.title: Port of Pyeongtaek/Seohaedaegyo Bridge (1st Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.audioTitle: Port of Pyeongtaek/Seohaedaegyo Bridge (1st Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.script: Welcome to the citizen-centered city of Pyeongtaek, starting with the Port of Pyeongtaek, the first of the eight scenic sites of the city.  The Port of Pyeongtaek is the gateway to the Seoul Metropolitan Area and central region of Korea, an outpost for trade with China and Southeast Asia, and a logistics hub of Northeast Asia. It is located in Asanman Bay, which historically has played key roles in economic, cultural, and military aspects, as it is a massive water system situated deep inland and thus protected from the open sea.   Now the port is being developed as a multifunctional harbor of the West Sea for production, distribution, commerce, and human resource exchanges.  At the PR center showcasing the port’s inception, development, and future vision at a glance.  From the observation deck of the Pyeongtaek Port Marine Center, you can see the Seohaedaegyo Bridge, a landmark symbolizing Korea’s national power that astonished people at home and abroad as the largest bridge in Korea and the 9th longest in the world at the time of its opening.   It took 7 years, 2.2 million people, and 450,000 pieces of equipment to build the bridge, the total length of which is 7,310 m, with the height of the main pylon being 182 m, similar to the 63 Building. It has become a popular tourist spot on the west coast with tourists visiting just to see the bridge.   Take a stroll around the Port of Pyeongtaek, where the red sunset glow presents picturesque scenery and gaze out at the West Sea in the distance!

stories.title: Sopung Garden (2nd Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.audioTitle: Sopung Garden (2nd Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.script: Sopung Garden is located in Gung-ri, Godeok-myeon, Pyeongtaek, it is the eight scenic sites of Pyeongtaek. It’s a beautiful waterfront park. Sopung Garden means a garden where smiles and winds stay. So, why do people come here for a picnic in search of smiles and winds?  Sopung Garden is a waterfront park built in 2013 on riversides that were like islands with ponds that formed after the waterway of the Jinwicheon Stream became cut off,  and in 2018, a theme garden was built on each of the four islands.   Let’s first visit the Ihwa Garden, where “ihwa” means “pear blossoms.” Pyeongtaek, a city becomes dotted with pear blossoms in the springtime not a pink cherryblossoms. Pear trees greet visitors along the traditional wall surrounding Sopungjeong, an octagonal pavilion.  Our next stop is the Mujigae Garden. Symbolizing the astounding potential of diversity and multiculturalism, the garden presents rainbow sculptures and nests that represent the people of Pyeongtaek. There are smaller gardens inside the Mujigae Garden including the Mujigae Forest, Miso Garden, Oreum Garden, and Dungji Garden, so be sure to take your time and enjoy each one.  Our third stop is the Garden of Light, which is inspired by the M?bius strip, and it symbolizes Pyeongtaek’s prosperity and development. The Garden of Light looks especially stunning when its light balls sparkle during sunset, and is a unique nighttime place with its sparkling light balls.  The fourth thematic garden is the Jijibebe Garden. Jijibebe, representing the sound of larks, is the sound of communication and harmony pursued by Pyeongtaek. As a symbolic space for communication between society and its citizens and nature and humans. In the center of the garden, bamboo grove and a sound-sharing pipe and a birdhouse. here can communicate with Mother Nature.  In addition to the four thematic parks, Sopung Garden has many other fascinating places. How about spending a day with your family, significant other, or friends searching for smiles and winds at Sopung Garden.

stories.title: Baedari Ecological Park (3rd Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.audioTitle: Baedari Ecological Park (3rd Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.script: Baedari Ecological Park is situated in Jukbaek-dong, Pyeongtaek. The request from the public for an ecological corridor connecting the wetland and pine forest and a library was answered, and the area was transformed into an ecological park.  The promenade along the perimeter of the Baedari Reservoir is a popular place for a pleasant stroll in the morning and evening. The waters of the reservoir will help soothe the mind and soul after a hard day’s work, while the fountain shooting water into the sky alongside exquisite lighting seems and a cup of tea on cafe streets to give people the much needed strength and energy.   People are not the only ones who find solace in Baedari Ecological Park. It is a sanctuary for a number of endangered species, including wintering bean geese, whooper swans, and Eurasian spoonbills and home to gold spotted frogs, Suwon treefrogs, and boreal digging frogs, which have been migrating here since 2014. Ducks leisurely drying their feathers, gold spotted frogs skimming the surface of the water, grey herons soaring into the sky, and a school of carp leaping out of the water are sights to behold, and the park truly feels like a gift of nature, especially to those who are exhausted from the hustle and bustle of city life.   Once planned to be developed as a recreation area, Baedari Ecological Park was able to maintain a part of the forest and ecological resources thanks to the efforts of socially responsible civil society and the Pyeongtaek City Council.   How about enjoy a pleasant respite at Baedari Ecological Park, where a balanced coexistence between urban and natural environments can be found?

stories.title: Pyeongtaekho Tourist Complex (4th Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.audioTitle: Pyeongtaekho Tourist Complex (4th Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.script: Pyeongtaekho Tourist Complex, where you can take in magnificent views of the sea and a lake, is the fourth scenic site of Pyeongtaek.   The complex overlooks Pyeongtaekho, an enormous artificial lake that formed when a seawall was built around Asanman Bay along the 2km seaway connecting Pyeongtaek and Asan.   To get the first impression of Pyeongtaekho, we recommend visiting the Pyeongtaekho Tourist Information Center. From the observation deck on the second floor of the tourist information center, you can see the glistening surface of the lake and check out the marine natural history exhibition. You can also enjoy marine leisure such as duck boats and water boats on the first floor.  The 1.5km-long wooden walkway connecting the Pyeongtaekho Tourist Complex and Pyeongtaekho Art Park has been designated as Seohaerang-gil Course 85. And every April, it attracts visitors with exquisite cherry blossoms. so it is definitely worth a visit.  There are photo spots and benches producing the sounds of various musical instruments throughout the promenade, but the highlight is arguably the Baenmeori Observatory. The observation deck, which has been hosting Pungeoje, a ritual for bountiful catch, every year since 2007.  Pyeongtaekho Art Park contains a variety of cultural facilities, including Pyeongtaek Farming Village, Ji Young-hee Hall, and Pyeongtaekho Arts Center. Pyeongtaek Agro-Ecological Park has a large grass field, a children's playground, a garden, and a picnic area, which is why it’s especially popular with families for weekend outings.  And there are various exhibitions and performances, hanbok experience, haegeum experience, and a space where you can take a dip while looking at Pyeongtaekho.  The Pyeongtaekho Tourism Complex, which is expected to power the local tourism industry, is poised to take a giant leap forward.

stories.title: Pyeongtaek Agro-Ecological Park & Agricultural Museum (5th Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.audioTitle: Pyeongtaek Agro-Ecological Park & Agricultural Museum (5th Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.script: Did you know that Pyeongtaek is the city with the second largest farming population in Gyeonggi-do Province? As an urban-rural area, Pyeongtaek seeks ways for urban and rural areas to coexist in harmony, and the Agro-Ecological Park is an agriculture-themed park built to promote urban-rural exchanges. Under the slogan, “Leading the development of the agricultural industry together with citizens,” the park highlights the forgotten value of agriculture and rural areas and operates an agricultural museum and rural cultural experience and agricultural education programs under the theme of “healthy relaxation through agriculture.”   The Agro-Ecological Park contains the Agricultural Museum, which sheds light on the history of agricultural development from prehistoric times to the present day, along with seasonal farming tools, farming artifacts, processed products under Pyeongtaek City’s agricultural brand, “Super Oning,” and crops on display. Here, you can witness how Pyeongtaek is cultivating the value of its locality and local specialties.  Throughout the year, the Agro-Ecological Park holds flower-themed festivals.   In mid- to late-April, a flower festival is held, and the tulip complex in the garden is a must-visit. Meanwhile, the Autumn Harvest Festival is held every October when chrysanthemums burst into full bloom.   If you’re interested in learning more about how Pyeongtaek maintains a balance between urban and rural areas, or if you’d like to enjoy seasonal flowers, we recommend visiting the Agro-Ecological Park!

stories.title: Oseong Riverside (6th Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.audioTitle: Oseong Riverside (6th Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.script: Pyeongtaek may not have any mountains, but it is a city of water with more water resources than any other city in the country. From Pyeongtaekho, which resembles the sea, to Tongbokcheon, Seojeongnicheon, Jinwicheon, and Anseongcheon streams, you can enjoy a variety of waterscape. Let’s take a look at the Oseong Riverside, which is said to be the finest of the eight scenic sites in Pyeongtaek.   Along the Oseong River, there is a scenic agricultural complex where seasonal crops are grown, and it presents a breathtaking view throughout the year, regardless of the season. With rape flowers and cosmos in full bloom in spring and fall, respectively, making the Oseong Riverside provide a healing moment for anyone to put their worries aside.  There’s one experience you shouldn’t miss out on while you're here, and it’s cycling. It’s a favorite spot among cyclists from all over the country, and riding alongside the striking landscape is an experience you can’t get anywhere else. If you don’t have a bicycle, you can rent one for free at the bicycle rental shop, Happiness on Two Wheels. So we hope you enjoy the Oseong Riverfront with your bike.  Changnae Wetland, extending from the Oseong Riverside, is a treasure trove of nature, being home to a wide variety of creatures that are rarely seen on inland wetlands. Six rare protected species can be found here, including the Suwon treefrog, which is classified as a Class 1 endangered species, and adorable otters.   Enjoy a cup of tea at one of the many teahouses along the Oseong River while gazing at the calm waters of the Pyeongtaek River and chatting with friends and family.   The sight of the sun setting over the Paengseongdaegyo Bridge and Danggeori Railroad Bridge against the unique backdrop of the U.S. military base on the other side of the Oseong River can only be savored on the Oseong Riverside, so why not stop by and spend a relaxing evening here?

stories.title: Jinwicheon Amusement Park (7th Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.audioTitle: Jinwicheon Amusement Park (7th Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.script: Jinwicheon Amusement Park, the seventh scenic site of Pyeongtaek, is widely popular with local residents. The Jinwicheon Stream flowing through the northern part of Pyeongtaek, a city of water, has been designated as a water source protection area, which is indicative of its excellent water quality. Jinwicheon Amusement Park built on an area of about 2 km along the streamside opened in 1999. Admission is free, making it a perfect picnic spot that can be enjoyed all day long, as long as you pay for parking.  When you enter Jinwicheon Amusement Park, you will be greeted with a panoramic view of the 13ha site, with spacious areas for caravanning, rail bikes, and foot volleyball, allowing visitors to enjoy leisure and recreational activities in the bosom of nature.  There is also an auto campground, consisting of around 130 campsites in total, with excellent amenities such as restrooms and showers, and it is quite an affordable way to enjoy a vacation.   The most popular spot across all seasons is the large shaded shelter where visitors can cook food for free. Bring a mat and meat to grill or other food to cook under the shade.   Across the Yeoul Stepping Stones, there is railbike that takes you across a 1.2km-long flower garden, and it is popular with young and old alike.   Also, located in the vicinity of the recreation area is the U.S. military base, which is a sight that excites the kids.  The sunset in Pyeongtaek has been famous since ancient times, and the sunset at the Jinwicheon Stream is simply awe-inspiring. If you visit Jinwicheon  Amusement Park, be sure to stay to watch the sunset. Consider Jinwicheon Amusement Park for your next trip.

stories.title: Wonpyeong Dock (8th Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.audioTitle: Wonpyeong Dock (8th Scenic Site of Pyeongtaek)
stories.script: Wonpyeong Dock is one of the eight scenic spots in Pyeongtaek. You might be wondering why the riverside has been selected as one of the eight scenic sites. It is because of the stunning sight that can be witnessed when the sun sets over the reeds and silver grass along the riverside of Wonpyeong Dock.   Have you ever heard this song?  “From the field where the wind lingered, the evening smoke rises. On the autumn hills that have changed into colorful clothing burns the red sunset glow.”  The words to the long-loved children’s song, “Sunset,” which won the top prize at the Creative Children’s Song Festival in 1984, were written while watching the sunset from Wonpyeong Dock.   It is said that before the Pyeongtaekho breakwater was built, it was a maritime transportation hub with seawater reaching all the way here, and Hwangpo sailboats transported seafood such as shrimp to Hwachon, Sindae-ri, and Sapgyo via this area. Gunmungyo, which can be found at Wonpyeong Dock, was formerly Gunmunpo, one of the top 10 ports in Joseon, and there was also Sindeokpogu. Over the years, as the breakwater changed the course of the water and boat traffic declined, the area no longer received sea water or merchants and visitors.  On the 50ha wetlands of the Gunmungyo Bridge area of the Anseongcheon Stream, you can see endless stretches of the silver grass and reeds, and in autumn, you can enjoy a spectacular view of cosmos flowers. Not only that, but you can also see wildflowers as well as insects  Every October, against this backdrop of outstanding natural scenery, the Wonpyeongnaru Mung Bean Festival, which has been held annually since 2012, is held. How about visiting Wonpyeong Dock, which is a great spot for cycling or walking while watching the beautiful sunset and not far from Pyeongtaek Station, for a pleasant retreat away from the city?

stories.title: Pyeongtaek Station
stories.script: Pyeongtaek Station serving as the gateway to southern Gyeonggi-do Province was built as a regular train station in 1905 with the opening of the Gyeongbu Line. It has gradually emerged as a center of administration, commerce, finance, and transportation, as roads and squares got built nearby.  Pyeongtaek Station has borne witness to Korea’s 100-year modern history.  The original Pyeongtaek Station was located in Wonpyeong-dong, further west than the current station. Because of its proximity to the Anseongcheon Stream and Gun-mun-po. Water transportation was highly accessible, and it was easy to transport grains from the Anseongcheon Stream area and seafood from the Asanman Bay, which was why the location was chosen by the Japanese, who had the right to build a railway. At the time, the downtown area around Pyeongtaek Station was divided into a Japanese neighborhood called Honmachi, and a Korean market called Pyeongtaekjang, situated south of Honmachi.  The first Pyeongtaek Station was destroyed due to a flood in 1946 and bombing during the Korean War in 1950. The second station, built in 1953, was demolished in 1988, and the third station, built in 1988, was demolished in 2006.   Built at the time of the opening of the extended line of the Seoul Metropolitan Subway Line 1 with private investment, the construction of the fourth station began in 2006 and was completed in April 2009.  Just like Pyeongtaek Station, Pyeongtaek Station Square has been a site of many historical events.  During the March 1 Movement in 1919, as well as for rallies of youth and social organizations in the 1920s and 30s. Due to its high foot traffic, street performances and various festivals are held at Pyeongtaek Station Square.

stories.title: Tongbok Market / Tongbok Market Youth Forest
stories.audioTitle: Tongbok Market / Tongbok Market Youth Forest
stories.script: Tongbok Market is the largest and oldest traditional market in Pyeongtaek that opened in 1953. It initially started as a cattle market and was relocated to the old Pyeongtaek Market, but when the old Pyeongtaek Market was destroyed by UN bombing during the Korean War, it was moved to its current location.  Today, it is home to about 700 shops, including those selling a variety of merchandise and historic restaurants.  Since 2008, the market has been modernized with convenient amenities such as toilets, parking lots, and cultural facilities, and it is a prominent traditional market that has been keeping pace with the latest trends while addressing complaints and inconveniences. There is a permanent market that is always bustling with people and an oiljang(five-day-market) that opens on days that end in 5 or 0.   Walk through the alleyways of Tongbok Market and you will find the Youth Forest Mall, which emanates a different atmosphere from the traditional market. Youth Forest is a youth mall complex created in 2017 by remodeling some of the empty stores and idle spaces in the alleyways that were originally part of Judan Alley from the 1960s and 70s. The shops with distinctive concepts lining both sides of the alley with tables and parasols in the middle create a different atmosphere from other alleys in Tokbok Market.   Pyeongtaek Market, which is only about 10 to 20 minutes on foot from Pyeongtaek Station, is a fascinating place to explore! Enjoy the unique experiences and merchandise offered by the traditional market and grab some grub at Youth Mall!

stories.title: Baramgil Forest
stories.script: Have you heard of “Baramgil Forest”? The Baramgil Forest of the Tongbokcheon Stream in Pyeongtaek is an urban forest area. In 2018, the area was selected for a project jointly supervised by the Ministry of Economy and Finance and the Korea Forest Service, and for a total of three years from 2019 to 2021, urban forests were created in four sections: 14 km of the Tongbokcheon Stream, 21 km of National Road 1, 7 km of National Road 38, and 0.5 km of Anseongcheon Stream. The Baramgil Forest project is aimed at mitigating air quality and urban heat island issues by directing clean and cool air generated by forests on the outskirts of the city into the city center. The project in Pyeongtaek was initiated to improve the environmental problems of the city center, whose forest and tree ratio stood at 16.9% compared to the national forest ratio of 62.6%.  The Baramgil Forest section of National Road 1, which sees significant car traffic, not only helps reduce carbon emissions but also improves the roadscape with the application of a “forest tunnel” concept in consideration of the location characteristics around the road.   The Baramgil Forest of the Tongbokcheon Stream, which traverses the city center of Pyeongtaek, is a forest path that runs from the beginning of the Anseongcheon Stream to the Dongsak District above Yangseonggyo Bridge. And those with special themes such as the history, culture, and famous figures of Pyeongtaek. In total, there are six history-themed spaces and ten Baramgil forests.   In 2022, the Baramgil Forest won the Minister of Agriculture, Food, and Rural Affairs Award at the 12th Landscape Award, co-hosted by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, and Transport and the Korean Institute of Landscape Architecture, and the National Top Prize at the Green City Best Practice Awards, hosted by the Korea Forest Service, and was selected as Korea’s first exemplary urban forest. Thanks to this, people from all over the country are visiting Pyeongtaek to see the Baramgil Forest.

stories.title: Naeri Tourist Site (Naeri Culture Park)
stories.script: Naeri Culture Park is found along the Pyeongtaekgang River, formed by the convergence of the Jinyucheon and Anseongcheon streams. With a grass plaza, children’s playground, forest, trails, and campground, it is a perfect place to enjoy a healing experience while looking at the Pyeongtaekgang River.   Many people visit to take once-in-a-lifetime photographs of hydrangeas in summer and pink muhly in autumn. Of particular note, Pyeongtaek has become a garden of hydrangeas with over 20,000 plants of 29 varieties planted over the course of three years from 2021. Every June, we hold a hydrangea festival.   In fall, pink muhly bloom in the muhly garden, which is a great spot to take photos. Albeit small, the pink muhly grass field along the S-shaped trail against the backdrop of Anseongcheon Stream stop people in their tracks with its striking beauty.  At night, the Stroll of Light, which is based on a tale of a goblin site in Pyeongseong-eup, is screened at the grass plaza. The 3D film effects tells the story of Dari, living on the Pyeongtaekgang River, who goes on an adventure to explore the goblin world hidden in the Naeri Culture Park together with Kkaebi, and it is popular among children.  Naeri Culture Park, which is part of Gyeonggidulle-gil Pyeongtaek Course 44, and Naeri Campground is stated on one side of culture park. You can enjoy the everything in Naeri Cuilturl Park.

stories.title: Buraksan Culture Park / Ichung Leports Park
stories.audioTitle: Buraksan Culture Park / Ichung Leports Park
stories.script: Buraksan Cultural Park is a place that both adults and children can enjoy with towering trees and dirt trails, as well as forest experience programs, forest shelters, sports facilities, the Forest Experience Center, and the Sky Forest Trail.   Buraksan Cultural Park is a place that both adults and children can enjoy with towering trees and dirt trails, as well as forest experience programs, forest shelters, sports facilities, the Forest Experience Center, and the Sky Forest Trail.   Buraksan Mountain standing 148 m high is one of the few famous mountains in Pyeongtaek, where the terrain is mostly flat. It is said to have been the main mountain of Songjangbugok in the past, and during the Joseon Dynasty, it was called Joraksan, Buraksan, and Yoyaksan among others.  There is also a dulle-gil trail that starts and ends at the Chorok Library and consists of four sections: the city trail, the forest trail, the cherry blossom trail, and the historical exploration trail.   At the entrance of Buraksan Cultural Park, there is Pyeongtaek Artificial Waterfall, and there are also a thematic playground, a forest experience center for toddlers, and a forest experience center for people of all ages, making it popular with families with kids.  The forest experience center, in particular, is a nature-friendly leisure facility with wooden structures and ropes that allows visitors to enjoy nature and develop a sense of adventure. It is a famous place in Pyeongtaek where you can enjoy leisure sports in the nature of Buraksan Mountain. There is an adventure course consisting of 10 programs, including flying straw.  Next to Buraksan Cultural Park is Ichung Leports Park, which was established in 2001. It is a sports park that hosts various sports competitions and events such as those of the K3 League, the third highest division of the Korean football league, and local volleyball tournaments, and it is frequently used by local sports clubs and organizations.

stories.title: Utari Cultural Village
stories.script: Utari Cultural Village is a former elementary school site that has been repurposed as a space for creative culture and arts. Utari Cultural Village, an experiential arts and culture space situated in Geumgak-ri, Seotan-myeon, opened in August 2006 after Pyeongtaek City and the Pyeongtaek Cultural Center renovated Geumgak Branch School in 2005 under a free lease agreement with  from Pyeongtaek Office of Education.   Utari is a type of nongak, or farmer’s music, and the name refers to the nongak of the Gyeonggi and Chungcheong regions.   In 1985, Pyeongtaek Nongak was designated as Important Intangible Cultural Heritage in recognition of its status as a representative form of Utari Nongak.  Utari Cultural Village will be remodeled in August 2021 to make another change to an exhibition-based complex cultural space. In the 10 exhibition halls, you can see various genres of works by famous artists as well as local artists in Pyeongtaek.  In addition, exhibition-linked experience programs are operated at all times so that visitors can enjoy the exhibition easily and interestingly, and artists and visitors are building cultural and artistic bonds together.  I hope you can experience various experiences at Utari Culture Village, an open complex cultural space where everyone can hang out together.

stories.title: Korean Modern and Contemporary Music Center / Jiyeonghui Music Pavilion
stories.audioTitle: Korean Modern and Contemporary Music Center / Jiyeonghui Music Pavilion
stories.script: The Korean Modern and Contemporary Music Center and Jiyeonghui Music Pavilion located at the Korea Soriter Arts Center in the Pyeongtaekho Tourist Complex, were established to preserve and promote the tradition of Korean modern and contemporary music and to pass on the legacy of Jiyeonghui, the father of modern gugak from Pyeongtaek.   The Korean Modern and Contemporary Music Center houses the first and largest collection of 70,000 Korean modern and contemporary music materials in Korea, and is a place where traditional Korean music, western music, and modern and contemporary music coexist.   It is a multifunctional cultural space with the functions of a museum, library, and archive that allows visitors to view and understand history in a new light through the cultural perspective of music.   Among the materials held by the Korea Museum of Modern and Contemporary Music, Geunhwa Changa, which was designated as Gyeonggi-do Provincial Registered Cultural Property No. 14 in April 2022, is also a representative cultural heritage of the Korea Museum of Modern and Contemporary Music.  The Jiyeonghui Music Pavilion introduces visitors to Jiyeonghui, the father of modern gugak, and showcases his achievements in popularizing, modernizing, and globalizing gugak.   Born in Naegiri, Poseung-eup, Pyeongtaek-si, he was the holder of Important Intangible Cultural Property No. 52 Sinawi, a folk music that paved the way for piri sanjo through haegeum sanjo and flute sinawi. He also preserved folk songs by collecting oral folk songs and transcribing them into music notation for the first time, and as a teacher at the Gugak Arts School, he worked to preserve and modernize traditional music. In particular, he wrote the first modern gugak textbook and created the Gugakwan String Orchestra to modernize traditional music.  The Jaehaegeum housed in the Jiyounghui Gugak Museum is a prefabricated haegeum that can be detached for portability, and is the only one of its kind left in Korea.

stories.title: Korea Soriter Arts Center / Pyeongtaekho Arts Center
stories.audioTitle: Korea Soriter Arts Center / Pyeongtaekho Arts Center
stories.script: The Korea Soriter Arts Center and Pyeongtaekho Arts Center are cultural facilities within the Pyeongtaekho Tourism Complex.   Pyeongtaek is the birthplace of Korean music, having produced prominent artists who played major roles in the history of modern and contemporary Korean music including Pansori Junggoje master, Lee Dong-baek; the founder of Gyeonggi Sinawi Dongnyeongje, Bang Yong-hyun; the fathers of modern gugak, Ji Young-hui and Seong Geum-yeon; Pyeongtaek Nongak master, Choi Eun-chang, who developed Dure Nongak into a form of art; Pyeongtaek folk song master, Lee Jong-gu, who depicted the lives of the people of Pyeongtaek; and Korean rhapsodist Jeong Tae-chun. The artists of Pyeongtaek have been at the center of Korea’s nearly 200-year history of modern and contemporary music, and their legacy has permeated throughout Korean music into traditional Korean arts such as pansori, sinawi, sanjo, nongak, and folk songs as well as and popular music.   Korea Soriter Arts Center, a hub of traditional culture and a base for local culture and arts, is a cultural facility established in the Pyeongtaekho Tourist Complex through the Pyeongtaek Special Support Project for the Relocation of the US Military Base to preserve and pass on Pyeongtaek Nongak and local traditional arts.   Since 2012, around 100 permanent and special performances, including the Pyeongtaek Nongak and Pyeongtaek folk music performances, have been held annually, and it has become an important platform for traditional culture and general performances.   The Pyeongtaekho Arts Center, which opened in 2001, is an exhibition hall and multipurpose hall that showcases artworks by local artists and hosts small-scale performances and events. The building is designed as a pyramid with the first floor in a rectangular shape and the second and third floors finished with glass. The exhibition hall on the first floor features exhibitions of Eastern and Western paintings, sculpture, photography, calligraphy, and visual design, and there is also a pottery experience room. The second floor contains a multipurpose hall, while the third floor serves as a meditation space.

stories.title: Anjeong-ri Rodeo Street / Anjeong-ri Art Square
stories.audioTitle: Anjeong-ri Rodeo Street / Anjeong-ri Art Square
stories.script: Anjeong-ri Rodeo Street is famous for its distinct features.  Anjeong-ri in Pyeongtaek, where the US Army Garrison Humphreys is located, became home to the largest US army garrison in Korea around 2020 when the Eighth United States Army and the Yongsan garrison, the headquarters for U.S. military forces stationed in South Korea, were relocated to Camp Humphreys. Anjeong-ri Rodeo Street is a commercial district that developed nearby.   Anjeong-ri Rodeo Street is reminiscent of an American town, similar to what can be seen inside the military base, with unique restaurants, clothing stores, and souvenir shops for American soldiers and foreign tourists. The last Saturday of every month, the Mato Festival is held for cultural exchanges between US military officers and their families and Korean citizens, offering a variety of delightful things to see and experience.   There are a total of 10 buildings, including a fine arts center, an everyday arts center, a performing arts center, and a creative workshop, where various exhibitions, performances, residency programs, and art education are held. Diverse events and festivals take place in the open-air plaza, which is designed to allow audiences to get a clear view of the stage with a slope of 3.75%.    'Gilmatrak', which represents Dongjangni Artists' Square, is a combination of 'Gilma', an old Korean word for Anjeong-ri, the administrative district where the square is located, and 'tteurak', a Korean word for garden. You can learn more about Stability and the various events taking place at Anjeong-ri on the Gilmatrak app.  With a rise in the number of U.S. troops stationed with their families, the area is fast-transforming from a military base to a family-friendly, safe, and dynamic urban area. There are also tourist guide services available, so please visit and enjoy this one-of-a-kind place where there is culture and history.

stories.title: Wonhyo Realization Experience Center / Sudosa Temple
stories.audioTitle: Wonhyo Realization Experience Center / Sudosa Temple
stories.script: Sudosa Temple, renowned as a sacred site where Wonhyo attained enlightenment, shares the famous story of the skull and water and provides Korean Buddhist temple food experience.  The temple is said to have been founded in 852 during the Silla Dynasty by Monk Yeomgeo, further north than where it is today. However, but as the power of the state weakened in the late Silla period and early Goryeo period, the Namyangman Bay became overrun by pirates, forcing the monks to abandon the temple and it closed down in the 15th century. The current temple was built in 1960 by Monk Yeongseok.   Sudosa Temple also offers temple stay, with programs that include a wide range of Buddhist practices and lifestyle that can only be experienced at a temple, such as alms bowl meal, tea ceremony, worship, and Seon meditation.  The temple also offers seasonal programs for making traditional temple food, which is an integral part of Buddhist culture, and for cultivating and collecting wild plants that are the main ingredients for temple food.   There is also an overnight program that includes a tour of the temple, walking meditation, Seon meditation, recitation of Buddha’s name, 108 prostrations, tea ceremony, and a demonstration of temple food, as well as hands-on experience programs such as trying ink rubbing, making wood block printings of the Tripitaka, prayer beads, and lotus flowers, and more.   Visit Sudosa Temple in Pyeongtaek with your entire family to learn about the story of Wonhyo and the water from the skull and enjoy a variety of experiences.

stories.title: Spatial Aesthetics
stories.script: Pyeongtaek has a renewed space called Spatial Aesthetics, a modern interpretation of the city’s traditional agricultural history, which developed along with rice cultivation.   In 1992, a mushroom cultivation company was established in Sin-ri, Oseong-myeon, Pyeongtaek as a rural living environment settlement project to operate a special crop complex. However, it closed down in 2001 and the building was virtually neglected for two decades. Then, in 2020 and 2021, it was selected for the Idle Space Cultural Regeneration Project of Gyeonggi-do Province, and the building was remodeled in March 2023 to be given a second life under the name of Spatial Aesthetics. The warehouse, which once housed agricultural products and machinery, has been transformed into a repository of memories and a place that cultivates culture and the arts.  The theme of the newly created gallery and cafe is “rice.” Spatial Aesthetics is divided into an exhibition building and a cafe building, where you can view artworks in a gallery and buy the rice bread of Sin-ri from Babi Bread.   If you visit Spatial Aesthetics, be sure to pay special attention to the architecture.  At first glance, the building’s exterior seems to retain the appearance of the former mushroom cultivation company. At the same time, the roof representing rice embodies the desire for the multicultural space to move toward the future with agriculture.  It is a spatial aesthetic that coexisted with the locals and created a new culture and locality.

stories.title: Mubongsan Youth Training Center
stories.script: Mubongsan Youth Training Center, a public youth facility established by Pyeongtaek City in 1999 and operated by the Pyeongtaek Youth Foundation, is a place where youth, the leaders of tomorrow, can learn through experiences in nature, training of the mind and body, activities for personal and emotional development, intellectual inquiries, sports and culture, and volunteer activities.   Most of the twelve youth facilities in the city are located in the living spheres, but Mubongsan Youth Training Center is situated in the natural environment.  Mubongsan Youth Training Center is equipped with accommodations for more than 500 people. Located at the foot of Mubongsan Mountain, it is used as a nature-friendly training facility that offers differentiated educational and training programs not only for youth but also for various other groups such as public institutions, corporations, social organizations, and religious organizations.   It operates the Youth Training Activity Certification System, which is a national certification system, and a variety of programs for different group sizes and age groups. The themes of these programs include competence, conflict resolution, problem-solving skills, motivation for achievement, interpersonal skills, leadership skills, and physical health.  The Youth Training Center is also home to the Mubongsan Observatory, a dome observatory where you can observe all kinds of astronomical phenomena that was completely renovated in 2020. Why not pay a visit to go stargazing late at night?

stories.title: Pyeongtaekhyanggyo Confucian School
stories.script: Pyeongtaekhyanggyo Confucian School was first built in 1413 (the 13th year of Taejong’s reign) in the early Joseon Dynasty, but it was burned down during Byeongjahoran, the second Manchu invasion of Korea.   It was repaired several times afterwards to take on the present-day appearance. It was built on gentle slopes, with Myeongnyundang, the lecture hall, in front, and Daeseongjeon, a ritual space, at the top. That is, the school is at the front and the shrine is at the back.  Past the Hongsilmun Gate of the entrance, you’ll see the Myeongnyundang Hall in the center of the fence as well as Dongjae and Seojae. Myeongnyundang is a single-story building with hip-and-gable roof in the Mindori architectural style meausing five rooms in the front and two rooms on the sides, while Dongjae and Seojae are buildings with gable roofs measuring three rooms in the front and two rooms on the sides.  Behind the Myeongnyundang Hall is Soseul-sammun Gates, inside of which there is the Daeseongjeon Hall, an enshrinement hall that is a single-story gable-roofed building measuring five rooms in the front and three rooms on the sides where rubble cornerstones were placed on the base and columns were erected to create complex brackets in the shape of bird wings in Ikgong architectural style. The Daeseongjeon Hall inside the Naesammun enshrines the tablets of Confucius, Mencius, and other sages, and the Chunchu Rite is held every spring and fall.   In the early Joseon Dynasty, hyanggyo were run smoothly and played a major role in local development, but their primary purpose gradually transitioned from education to ritualistic functions, a center for the villages code, and a local cultural center, which has continued to this day. Based on the village code called hyangyak, hyanggyo helped local residents help one another and live harmoniously together. So, how about visiting Pyeongtaekhyanggyo Confucian School to learn more?

stories.title: Jinwihyanggyo Confucian School
stories.script: It is said that Jinwihyanggyo Confucian School was founded in the early Joseon Dynasty in 1398 during the 7th year of King Taejo’s rule, but this is not certain as no accurate records remain. When it was completely destroyed by fire during Byeongjahoran, the second Manchu invasion of Korea, the tablets of the sages were taken by Gyohasa Choi Eung-su to be kept safe in his home, and he later built a thatched house to enshrine them.  There are records that it was renovated several times since then, starting with the renovation of Hyanggyo Jungsu in 1644 by Jinwi Hyenryeong Namduguk in 1646, 1660, 1665, 1839, 1889, and later. Today, Jinwihyanggyo Confucian School is composed of the Daeseongjeon Hall, Myeongnyeondang Hall, the Naesammun, the Oisammun, and Dongjae and Seojae, which feature a layout that reflects the 18th-century architectural style. Myeongnyundang, Dongjae, and Seojae are located at the bottom of the sloping site, while Daeseongjeon is located above. There is a staircase to Naesammun  at the back of Myeongnyundang and a ritual space centered around Daeseongjeon near the rear gate.  Daeseongjeon displays the architectural style unique to the late Joseon Dynasty, as a single-story building measuring three rooms in the front and three rooms on the sides with a gabled roof consisting of Korean-style barrel tiles, double-layer eaves, and windbreak panels on both sides. Myeongnyundang, on the other hand, is a single-story building with hip-and-gable roof measuring four rooms in the front and two rooms on the sides, while Dongjae and Seojae feature hip-and-gable roofs and measure two rooms in the front and one rooms on the side. The Oisammun which originally had a gable roof, underwent an extension work in 1990.  Located at the foot of Mubongsan Mountain overlooking Jinwicheon Stream, Jinwihyanggyo Confucian School offers a striking view of the surrounding landscape. We recommend that you pay a visit to enjoy the breathtaking scenery of Jinwihyanggyo Confucian School, where local Confucian scholars would gather to study and share their thoughts and wisdom.

stories.title: Paengseong Guesthouse
stories.script: Paengseong Guesthouse for Pyeongtaek County during the Joseon Dynasty was built in 1488 (19th year of King Seongjong’s reign). Documents show that it was built in 1279 (5th year of King Chungryeolhwang’s reign over Goryeo), but it is believed that envoys started staying here in the early Goryeo period. During the Joseon Dynasty, a tablet symbolizing the king was enshrined here, and a rite was performed toward the royal palace on the first and fifteenth days of each month. It was also used as an accommodation for foreign envoys and government officials from the capital.   The center of Pyeongtaek County during the Joseon Dynasty was Gaeksa-ri, Pyeongtaek-eup, but since Pyeongtaek County was the smallest of the 330 counties in the country, the original guesthouse was quite small and humble. However, it was significantly expanded during the reign of King Hyeonjong in the late Joseon Dynasty, rebuilt during the reigns of Yeongjo in 1760 and Sunjo in 1801, and maintained as such until the Japanese occupation. During the Japanese colonial period, the guesthouse was repurposed and structurally changed in accordance with the colonial policy to eliminate Joseon government offices. While many government office facilities were destroyed, the Paengseong-eup guesthouse was sold to an ordinary citizen who turned it into a brewery.   As the brewing industry declined in the 1970s and 80s, civilians moved in, and the building gradually fell into disrepair until 1993, when Pyeongtaek City initiated a repair and extension project to transform it into its current state.   The Paengseong Guesthouse may not be large in size, but it retains the appearance of a typical guesthouse from the late Joseon Dynasty. Of the nine rooms of the main building, three rooms belongs to Jungdaecheon, with Dongheon and Seoheon to its left and right. Enshrined in Jungdaecheong was a tablet symbolizing the king, and the head of the village prostrated toward the royal palace twice a month here. In addition, single-wing brackets are connected to cylindrical columns and the roof is a gable roof that is one level higher than that of Dongheon and Seoheon, which makes the building look especially majestic. There are dragon heads sculptures at the two ends of the top of the roofs of Jungdaecheong and the main gate to signify the authority of the government office. The space between Jungdaecheon, Dongheon, and Seoheon is left open, and there are hearths of Dongheon and Seoheon ondol, or heated floor rooms, in this space.   We invite you to visit Paengseong Guesthouse of Joseon that has been well-preserved to capture the changes of time and witness the majestic beauty of this timeless building.

stories.title: Nongseong Fortress of Paengseong
stories.script: Nongseong Fortress of Paengseong spanning 300m in circumference is an oval-shaped earthen fortress found northern Anjeong-ri, Paengseong-eup, Pyeongtaek-si that has been designated as Gyeonggi-do Monument No. 74.   Encircling the summit of a low hill reaching 24m above sea level, Nongseong Fortress is located in the center of a fertile plain where the Anseongcheon Stream flows into the Asanman Bay. Surrounding the fortress are low hills of 20 to 30 meters in altitude, with the Anseongcheon Stream to the north and vast plains to the west and south.   The inside of the fortress is shaped like a convex lens, with the north side being about 2 m higher and the east, west, and central sections at high levels, and there are gate sites on the east and west sides.   Nongseong Fortress was a town fortress built around the local government office and private residences. It was built by piling up the inner and outer surfaces with earth using the slope of the hill, and the plan is rectangular with the long axis in the north-south direction.   The walls of Nongseong Fortress of Paengseong envelop a total area of 14,900 ㎡, and the wall is around 6 to 8 m in height, on average, with a circumference of about 300 m, a length of 101.9 m from north to south, and a length of 73.2 m from east to west. There is a dense pine forest to the north of the fortress, and it is said that there was once a well and Seonghwangsa a government office building of Pyeongtaek County inside the fortress.   The cultural value of Nongseong Fortress had been unrecognized until July 1980 due to an initiative to build an officer's and historian's house on the fortress site that prompted the Ministry of Culture and Public Information to conduct a survey, which revealed its cultural value. As a result, it was designated as Gyeonggi-do Cultural Heritage on July 16, 1981.

stories.title: Monument House of Honghaksa Temple
stories.script: The Monument House of Honghaksa Shrine was built to protect the stele of Hwapo Hong Ik-han, one of the three scholars of Cheokhwapa who were taken to the Qing Dynasty of China and killed during the Byeongjahoran. Hong Ik-han, whose family clan was based in Namyang, is known as one of the three scholars of the Cheokhwapa faction. His family is also known as the Ohyungmunjip.  Honghaksa is a building that protects the monument, which is currently located in Anjeong-ri, Pangseong-eup. Hong Ik-han lost his two sons and son-in-law during the Byeongjahoran and was taken to the Qing Dynasty with the rest of his family.  He refused to become a vassal of the Qing and was tortured into martyrdom to maintain his integrity. The country praised his loyalty and exploits, and he was enshrined in the court of Yongzheng.  According to folklore, Hong Hak-sa's family is called the Ohyungmunjip House because his wife, son, daughter, and daughter-in-law all went into hiding when news of his death in Shenyang reached them.  We invite you to visit Honghaksa Temple to honor Hong Ikhan's loyalty and jizo, and to feel the historical significance.

stories.title: Simboksa Temple
stories.script: Simboksa is a temple of the Jogye Order of Korean Buddhism located at the foot of Godeungsan Mountain, which used to be called Gwangdeoksan Mountain when it was the main mountain of Gwangdeok County during the Goryeo Dynasty. Its name means to be “blessed by the grace of the Buddha,” and its main attraction is the Stone Seated Vairocana Buddha.   Although there are no exact records of the founding of the temple, it is believed to have been built in 1375 during the Goryeo Dynasty based on a legend concerning the Buddha statue.  According to the legend, in the late Goryeo Dynasty, an old fisherman who lived in Mongsanpo, Paju cast his net off the coast of Deongmok-ri and caught a large stone, so he threw it back into the sea, moved to another spot, and cast his net again only to retrieve the stone again.
