Using his personal connections, Yeo Unhyeong arranged a meeting with Charles Crane and asked him, ‘In service of its , independence, Joseon wishes to dispatch an envoy to speak about the situation in Joseon to the international community. Will there be any issue?’ Charles Crane answered that there were no issues with that.  Only 8 years ago, no state in the world listened to Korea as its sovereignty was stripped away by Japanese imperialism. But now, the U.S.  demonstrated a different attitude.  Encouraged by this, Yeo Unhyeong sought to dispatch a Korean delegation to the Paris Peace Conference. He came up with a group, ‘Shinhan Youth Party’, as a new representative of the Korean people, and dispatched Kim Gyusik as the head of the delegation. There was a problem, though. There was no proof of the Korean people’s will for independence, save for the documents that Kim Gyusik was bringing to the conference.  So, a number of people were immediately sent to various places where Koreans lived to spread the news of  the Paris Peace Conference and urge them to prepare for the independence movement. Jang Deoksu was sent to Joseon, while Yeo Unhyeong himself headed to Manchuria and the Primorye region.   Therefore, the March First Independence Movement was not just an expression of resistance against the Japanese but also a proclamation of the Korean people’s will for independence. I myself heard the news in Tokyo and started preparing for the independence movement, which in turn led me to come to Korea with that news.  When it comes to the March First Independence Movement, Yeo Unhyeong’s name is often left out, but it is clear that he is a figure of great importance if one looks into the details. The next figure we will be meeting is of equal importance. In fact, he can be said to be the one who symbolizes the : March First Independence Movement: Son Byeonghui.  The site of Son Byeonghui‘s House is located near here. Let’s move on and continue our discussion there.

stories.title: Son Byeonghui’s House
stories.script: This is the site of Son Byeonghui’s House. One can find a single stone post that details the history today, but the significance of this place cannot be understated.  After all, it is a memorial dedicated to Son Byeonghui, who was one of the central figures of the March First Independence Movement. As I said, the news I brought to Korea eventually reached Son Byeonghui. He made the final decision to start the independence movement, and Christian and  Buddhist organizations decided to join. I imagine the weight of being the head of Cheondogyo weighed heavily in his mind. Although Park Inho was the Head of Cheondogyo at the time, everyone thought that Son Byeonghui was the center of Cheondogyo.  I cannot imagine the weight of that decision. Donghak, the predecessor of Cheondogyo, staged its second uprising in September 1894, with Son Byeonghui as one of its leaders. Fight back against the West and Japan! Despite its righteous fervor, the Donghak Peasant Revolution ended in massive sacrifices. After that, Donghak members sought to fight against pro-Japanese Koreans, and eventually changed its name to Cheondogyo to expand its presence in Korea. In the end, it became much bigger than the entirety of Chritianity in Korea, but the odds of facing the might of Japan were not favorable. As the activists prepared for the March First Independence Movement, Cheondogyo handled the funding for the movement and the printing of the Korean Declaration of Independence. Those deeply involved with Cheondogyo became the national leaders, while Son Byeonghui‘s name became the first to grace the Korean Declaration of Independence.  Of course, their decision not to go to Tapgol Park, the starting point of the movement, is thought to be an unfortunate one. But I personally think that it is unproductive to focus only on one’s failings in pursuit of great projects.  Nationalist activists were the ones who carried the torch for the March First Independence Movement, but another important factor drove the spread of the movement. In retrospect, one can think of three groups involved in the March First Independence Movement: The ones who prepared, the ones who acted, and the ones who spread the movement. Added to that, some of us still remember the March First Independence Movement even though more than a century has passed.  Ah, there’s actually something that many, including myself, are curious about: The method of protest involved in the independence movement. The chant was ‘Long Live Joseon Independence’ or ‘Long Live Korean Independence’. The words Joseon, Korea, and independence are easy to understand, in that they invoke the names of states that preceded the Japanese colonial rule.  But in Korean, ‘manse’ or ‘long live’ is an expression normally used to celebrate something. It is not known who came up with this in the first place, but the March First Independence Movement was also known as the Manse Movement, and most protests took similar forms. If I had to hazard a guess, I would imagine that it was something like ‘Hurray if Joseon or  Korea becomes independent!’  Let’s move on to our next stop. It is the Central Temple of Cheondogyo, at the center of March First Independence Movement Road in Gyeongun-dong. It is a rather unique building that one can easily identify even from afar, particularly its red brick construction.

stories.title: The Central Temple of Cheondogyo
stories.script: The Central Temple of Cheondogyo is a very famous building, a must-see sight in Seoul. But do you ever wonder why Cheondogyo, a folk religion of Korea, decided to build a Western-style place of worship?   The Japanese, since the  installation of the Resident-General of Korea, sought to oppress the religions in the country. In 1906, the Resident-General of Korea established that religions other than Shinto, Buddhism, and Christianity are to be restricted, as they are not considered to be religions. Because of that, folk religions like Cheondogyo or Daejonggyo, which were quite strong at that time, had to struggle to maintain their identities.  One of the measures taken then was to build a new place of worship. The decision came about with the fact that Catholicism and Protestantism were drawing considerable interest with their new places of worship at the time. Despite Cheondogyo being a Korean religion, it sought to establish itself as a religion equal to others with the construction of new buildings.   Under this strategy, Cheondogyo decided to build its central temple in today’s Gyeongun-dong area and began preparing for its construction. The issue was finding an architect. Catholic or Protestant churches had priests who doubled as architects or had buildings for reference in other countries, but Cheondogyo had no such connection.   What’s more, Korean modern architecture was only in its infancy, so architects who could handle massive constructions like that of the Central Temple of Cheondogyo were quite rare.   In the end, the Japanese architect Nakamura Yoshihei, who designed the main branch of Chosun Bank, today’s Bank of  Korea Money Museum, was chosen as the architect.   With the planning out of the way, Cheondogyo began fundraising for the new building in 1918. The cost of construction varies a bit depending on the source, but it seems to be around 220,000 to 270,000 won. Given that the church's membership reached 2 to 3 million at the time, the total amount raised was likely much higher. It is estimated that a significant portion of that went to fund the March First Independence Movement. So because of that, despite the central temple building not yet existing in 1919, it is nevertheless a space that is deeply related to the March First Independence Movement.  Construction began in December 1918, and after being interrupted by the March First Independence Movement, it was completed on February 28, 1921. The building is two stories tall, and the Central Tower is four stories tall in height. The first floor has a land area of 700 meters squared, and the total floor area is 925 meters squared. Initial designs called for a total floor area of 1322 meters squared, but the Government-General of Korea refused to issue the permit, claiming that the hall was too extravagant and that the lack of a central pillar made the building dangerous.   This was also the place where Son Byeonghui‘s funeral was held. Although he led the construction of this place, he would only get to enter the building after his death, as his involvement in the March First Independence Movement resulted in his imprisonment and rapidly deteriorating health.   There is a signboard in front of the Central Temple of Cheondogyo that shows the place where the Korean Declaration of Independence was distributed to the people. It is also the site of Lee Jongil’s House, who was the president of Boseongsa, the company that printed the Korean Declaration of Independence for the , March First Independence Movement, and one of the  national leaders.  The original title of the Korean Declaration of Independence was simply the ‘Declaration’. I personally think that the title is significant. While many agreed on the need to fight the Japanese through the independence movement, it was often the case that people had different opinions on how.   Some argued for petition, some argued for declaration, and others for struggle. Some even fought among themselves, rather than facing off againstJapan together. But since the document that was spread at the time of the March First Independence Movement was titled the ‘Declaration’, our independence movement can be called a ‘ declaration of independence’. At least, that was a commonality for everyone.  There were some typos in the Korean Declaration of Independence because it was printed in a hurry. If you look at the first line, you will find that ‘Joseon’ is written as ‘Seonjo’. But despite the typo, my comrades and I read it as ‘Joseon’, so that wasn’t a big issue.   Next, we will move on to the site of Taehwagwan, where the national leaders had gathered.

stories.title: Taehwagwan Site
stories.script: As we’ve seen before, Taehwagwan was where the national leaders were to meet on February 28. The decision not to join the students at Tapgol Park was to avoid the possibility that the Japanese would use that as a pretext to initiate a wide-scale crackdown.   Indeed, when police arrested the national leaders, it sought to charge them with sedition, which could carry the death penalty. But there is a rather unfortunate story related to this.  Were the national leaders truly representative of the movement? Is it true that most of the  national leaders changed sides in the end? Let’s look at the context to find the answers to these questions.  On that faithful March 1, all the national leaders were to come to Taehwagwan. In practice, four were not able to come to the place. Gil Seonju, Jeong Chunsu, and Yu Yeodae arrived late and went straight to the police on their own, while Kim Byeongjo fled the authorities and thus became the only one among the national leaders to not be arrested.   The 29 national leaders who gathered at Taehwagwan read the Korean Declaration of Independence, had a toast, and were led off to the police station by Japanese police. They were led off in a car in groups of three. Son Byeonghui was the first, while Choi Lin and Han Yongun were the last. The reason why they were moved directly to police station rather than Jongno Police Station shows just how serious this matter was to the Japanese. The Chief of Police, the core of  Government-General Police, also served as the Commander of Military Police.   This part is widely known. What is not widely known is the subsequent trial. The 32 national leaders were subject to terrible torture. They were questioned first by the police and then by a pretrial judge. However, the trial is known as the Trial of 48 because 15 people were tried in addition to national leaders. Yang Hanmuk passed away in prison, so in the end, 47 were on trial.   The laws that they were charged under were the Security Act,Publication Act and others. To avoid the controversies that could arise from sedition charges, such as the legitimacy of the forced occupation of Korea, sedition was deliberately excluded from the trial. The logic was that the protesters were there of their own volition, so the national leaders were not responsible for the conspiracy. The Security Act, Publication Act carried maximum sentences of 2 or 3 years in prison, so all national leaders received the maximum sentence.   Furthermore, most of the ones arrested during the March First Independence Movement, including the national leaders, suffered greatly at the hands of authorities during their questioning. Yang Hanmuk passed away in custody, while Son Byeonghui, Park Junseung, and others passed away due to the aftereffects of their interrogations and imprisonment. So I hope that the national leaders are given their due respect. However, it is understandable if the trio of Jeong Chunsu, Park Huido, and Choi Lin, who had changed sides to serve Japanese imperialism, come under criticism. I find it truly unfortunate that my teacher, Choi Lin, is one of the three.  Now, it seems that we can feel the passionate fever of the March First Independence Movement a bit closer. We now head to Seungdong Church, located right next to Taehwagwan. It is a red-bricked building, so you can find it quite easily.

stories.title: SeungDong Church
stories.script: This place is something that I really want to focus on. After all, this is the place where the students and youths prepared  for the March First Independence Movement. Kim Wonbyeok, who was a member of the parish here, was the one who played the leading role in preparing the March First Independence Movement. Kim Wonbyeok was a student of Yeonhui College. Along with the likes of Kang Gideok and Han Wigeon, he had planned the Namdaemun Protests on March 5.  To be honest, we young ones find it a bit difficult to work with seniors in the movement: We often have to worry about their opinions, and we sometimes find their cautious approach to be too slow.  I’ve been told that Kim Wonbyeok had to struggle against these things as well. For one, national leaders’ decision to eschew Tapgol Park in place of Taehwagwan was something that threw off his expectations. He sought to bring the national leaders to Tapgol Park to no avail. I think they did their best in the context they had. The space below this church is where the students came together to build the fire of independence.  Now, let’s move onto Tapgol Park, where you can truly feel the heat of the March First Independence Movement.

stories.title: Tapgol Park
stories.script: Why this place, out of all places, for .the March First Independence Movement? There’s a story. Let’s explore why.   Tapgol Park was built in 1899. Like its name, Tapgol, or “place with a pagoda”, was home to a Buddhist temple, specifically, Wongaksa Temple, which was erected during the rule of  King Sejo of Joseon. There was a stone pagoda at the site of Wongaksa Temple, whose marble white color has lent it the name ‘White Pagoda’.  Wongaksa Temple began to lose its form during the rule of Prince Yeonsan. The temple was first replaced by Jangagwon, an institute specializing in music, then a space where the gisaeng, female entertainers during the Joseon period, stayed. It was such a spiteful decision. When Prince Yeonsan was expelled, government offices moved into the area. What remained of the temple was destroyed when it was torn down for repair materials.   However, the ten-story white tower made out of marble served as a landmark of Seoul for its beautiful and rare form. When famous poets in the late Joseon period came together to this place, they were even called ‘Baektapsipa’.   So, this historic site ended up becoming a park during the Korean Empire period. It is said that a British man working in customs named  Brown came up with this idea, but it is not certain. Others say it is Korea's first park, but this is false. The first park was in  the foreign concession in Incheon. It was named ‘Gakuk Park’, which was renamed as Jayu Park later.   So it’s not the first in Korea, but it is the first park to be in Hanseong, the capital of the Korean Empire. A special building was erected here around 1900, namely the octagonal pavilion. Octagonal pavilions appear to have a circular roof, which symbolizes the authority of the king or the emperor. For instance, the octagonal Hwanggungu of Wongudan, which was built in 1899, also symbolizes the authority of the emperor.   So this octagonal pavilion is said to be a gift of King Gojong to the people. Franz Eckert, the leader of the Korean Empire’s marching band, composed a song for the emperor, which was performed at the octagonal pavilion.   If one thinks about it, a park is also a space where people can come together freely. While the park was created by the emperor and the state in the beginning, people came together and created a different space.  On March 1, 1919, the Korean Declaration of Independence was read aloud at the octagonal pavilion. It was read by Jeong Jaeyong from Hwanghae-do. What a wonderful event. Above all, you can feel its significance as the proclamation of an ‘independent nation’ and ‘liberated people’. This meant that the emperor was there when our country was taken away from us, but we did not need the power of emperors to take it back.   I imagine that people came to the idea that they were the ones who were at the helm of the country as time went by. This concept seemed to become clearer as the March First Independence Movement went on. After all, the imperial house did not fulfill its role in any capacity during the movement.  In the end, the independence movement arose in Seoul and spread to the rest of Korea. Following the example of the national leaders, students, and leaders began to move, and soon, the entire nation rose up. This brings us back to the idea of the people, or citizens, as the holders of sovereignty. It brings us back to the idea that, in the end, it is our thoughts, our minds, and our strength that will take back our country.  These thoughts led people to think about the idea of ‘nationalism’, a political system that none had imagined for Korea. It was the dream of a republic in Korea, excluding the crown that had been on the ruler’s head since the founding of the Korean nation. This wish, led to  the temporary Korean government in Shanghai adopting the declaration ‘Korea shall be a democratic republic state’ in its provisional charter in its founding on April 11, 1919. The ruled became the citizen, and the kingdom became the republic.   The first goal in the movement was to drive away the Japanese, but its ultimate goal now became the establishment of a democratic republic state. So those working toward the goal of the independence movement between 1919 and the liberation of Korea were working toward two goals.   So the fact that the March First Independence Movement began at Tapgol Park signifies that the time of the emperor was over, and the time of citizens was beginning. Keep this in mind as you look around Tapgol Park to see it in a different light.   Today’s  Tapgol Park still has traces of the Crown Prince of Joseon’s piety when it was Wongaksa Temple, the emperor’s prestige in the octagonal pavilion, and the March First Independence Movement, which transformed this space to that of the citizens, standing with the statue of Son Byeonghui. This space captures different periods of time, as symbols of the independence movement transforming the future of Korea and the history of the Korean Empire becoming the Republic of Korea. It lights a fire in my heart.

stories.title: Information for the Starting Point of Course 7
stories.audioTitle: Information for the Starting Point of Course 7
stories.script: So, this is the last stop with me, Song Gyebaek, on this March First Independence Movement Road. In the end, I passed away to the next world after imprisonment and torture in a prison in Japan. But I do not regret the road that I had walked.  Now, you move on to the next road. The starting point of Course 7 is Tapgol Park. The next guide is waiting for you to share a perspective that is different from mine. As we say goodbye, I hope you enjoy your walk in Modern Jongno, the trail that connects Jongno’s modern and contemporary history.

stories.title: Introducing the Presenter 5
stories.script: "Hello, nice to meet you all! I'm Hong Yeongsik, your guide for the Jongno Modern Street Course 5. Have you ever heard my name? Haha. I heard that the theme for this Course 5 is 'The Path to Enlightenment.' The period leading to modernization in the late Joseon era is referred to as the Enlightenment Period, and it's during this time that a historical event unfolds, where I come into the picture. It's none other than the coup d'état, the Gapsin Coup, that took place in 1884.  Enlightenment. It feels refreshing. I didn't anticipate that I would have the opportunity to share my story about enlightenment with all of you again. It's a word to which I dedicated my brief life.  Oh, let me briefly explain the Gapsin Coup. After the  Japan-Korea Treaty of 1876 opened a port to the world, the Joseon Dynasty faced a crucial decision. It had to choose between rapid and comprehensive modernization, like Japan, or a more selective approach focusing on military and industrial aspects, similar to the Qing Dynasty. My comrades and I closely observed the changes in the West and Japan. With a great mentor and supportive friends by my side, I believed that we could achieve something significant.  So, on the day the modern postal system, the Wujung Chongguk (Central Post Office), was opened, we saw it as an opportunity to seize power through a banquet. I'll explain more later, but the coup initiated by our Enlightenment Party failed just three days later.  Comrades who joined me in the Gapsin Coup, and those who opposed my stance, we all must have wrestled with many thoughts. It was a time of novelty and confusion, as it had been less than ten years since the country had opened its doors to the world.  Now, let's delve into the history after 1884. During that time, our dreams and perhaps aspects we hadn't considered coexisted. Some things progressed as quickly as we had envisioned, while in other aspects, progress was not as swift as we had hoped.  However, it's fortunate that the path towards enlightenment has consistently continued. Despite the hardships and the challenges to our country's sovereignty, the efforts to construct a new society never ceased. Although progress may have been slow and sometimes we had to make a long way around, it's heartening to have this moment to comfortably share these stories with all of you.  Wow, the thought of sharing these stories makes my heart flutter. With an excited heart, let's embark on the Jongno Modern Street Course 5, 'The Path to Enlightenment. "

stories.title: Constitutional Court of Korea (Lacebark Pine Tree)
stories.audioTitle: Constitutional Court of Korea (Lacebark Pine Tree)
stories.script: The first place to introduce is the Constitutional Court of Korea, where the Lacebark Pine Tree is located. Stepping into this special space brings a bittersweet sense of nostalgia. While you can now see the spacious Constitutional Court of Korea, it might take me a bit of time to recall its appearance from when I lived there.  Hmm. To the north of the parking lot, there was a house where I used to live. And over there, where the white-lined Lacebark Pine Tree stands, was Daegam Park Gyusoo's residence. Additionally, in the location of the Constitutional Court of Korea building, there used to be the government office responsible for diplomatic affairs, the Tongni Gyoseop Tongsang Samu Amun.  Standing here brings back fresh memories. I have a long story to share, so please have a seat on one of the chairs near the Lacebark Pine Tree. The majestic presence of the natural monument, the Lacebark Pine Tree, and the atmosphere created by the President Yun Posun Residence in the background - all of it adds a charming touch, doesn't it?  Alright, let me delve into the history of this place. Joseon underwent a significant shift in its diplomatic direction starting from 1873. Until then, Heungseon Daewongun, who had been in power, pursued a firm policy in foreign relations. The Byeonginyangyo against France and the Shinmiyangyo against the United States, are events that clearly illustrate his approach. However, during the Shinmiyangyo, Oh Gyeongseok advocated for opening up and modernization. He argued that Joseon needed to evolve rapidly by engaging with the world.  Mr. Oh Gyeongseok, though not a Yangban, was a middle-class interpreter and my mentor. Oh Gyeongseok was a disciple of the interpreter Lee Sangjeok, who, in turn, learned from the Silhak scholar Kim Jeonghui - the protagonist of the painting 'Sehando' by Kim Jeonghui. Lee Sangjeok sent valuable books obtained in Peking to Kim Jeonghui when he was exiled to Jeju Island. In return, Kim Jeonghui painted the famous 'Sehando' for Lee Sangjeok. So, you could say that Oh Gyeongseok, as Lee Sangjeok's disciple, continued the academic lineage of Kim Jeonghui. Oh Sechang, the son of Oh Gyeongseok, also played a significant role as the representative of the people in the March First Independent Movement.  In 1873, when Heungseon Daewongun stepped back from politics and King Gojong took a direct role, the diplomatic course shifted to an open-door policy. During this time, Japan demanded trade and caused the Unyo Incident - an event where the Japanese warship Unyo illegally invaded various places, including Yeongjongdo Island, and launched attacks. This incident led to the signing of the 1876 Treaty of Friendship, also known as the Japan-Korea Treaty of 1876, between the ambassadors of Joseon and Japan.  People often misunderstand the Japan-Korea Treaty of 1876 as 'yielding to Japan's pressure and establishing diplomatic relations.' Although the Unyo Incident led to Joseon trading with Japan, Joseon was not a country to yield easily to a foreign warship. During the Byeonginyangyo, Joseon repelled the French forces, and in the Shinmiyangyo, stood against the American forces.  While this treaty had unfavorable terms, Joseon analyzed diplomatic documents signed between the Qing Dynasty and Western countries as precedents. The person who advised and provided counsel during the treaty negotiations was none other than Park Gyusu, who lived right here beside Lacebark Pine Tree.  In 1866, after the American merchant ship General Sherman illegally sailed up the Daedonggang River, kidnapping Joseon officials and attacking civilians inPyeongyang while demanding trade, Park Gyusu, who was the governor of Pyeongan at the time, set fire to the General Sherman. In 1869, he became the mayor of Hanseongbu and lived here. Park Gyusu advocated for the modernization of Joseon's future. Alongside individuals like Yoo Hongki and Oh Gyeongseok, who were knowledgeable about international affairs, young people with dreams of modernization gathered at Park Gyusu's house.  I, Hong Yeongsik, lived right next door, and other young men lived nearby as well. Individuals like Kim Okgyun, Seo Kwangbum, and Seo Jaepil gathered together during that time. Even Min Yeongik, an outer relative of the Joseon Dynasty with a keen interest in modernization, joined the group.  After that, I became busy establishing diplomatic relations with Japan and the United States. I went to Japan to examine their military system and reported to King Gojong. I also traveled to the United States as one of the ambassadors to meet U.S. President Chester A. Arthur. At that time, Min Yeongik served as the head of the embassy, and I, Hong Yeongsik, served as the deputy ambassador. During my time in the United States, I was amazed by the exhibitions, factories, military, hospitals, railways, and electric companies.   At that time, I took charge of diplomatic affairs. Recognizing the importance of postal services in international exchanges, I prepared for the establishment of the Wujung Chongguk (Central Post Office). Not to brag, but during that process, the first postage stamps of Korea were created. There were a total of five types, ranging from 5 mun to 100 mun. Initially, when the Ujeong Chongguk was established, we issued and used two types of stamps for a brief period.  As you may well know, there were many challenges on the path to modernization. After the Soldiers’ Riot of 1882, interference from the Qing Dynasty posed significant difficulties for Joseon. They even sent thousands of troops, exerting pressure on our government. Additionally, the atmosphere within my own household was another hardship. My father opposed modernization, always telling me that supporting it would ruin our family. (Depressed) In the end, my father's words proved to be true.   Taking advantage of the opening of the Wujung Chongguk, my comrades and I staged a coup, known in Korea as the Gapsin Coup. After removing the opposing party in the Ujeong Chongguk, we went to Changdeokgung Palace, informed King Gojong of the coup, and directed him to move to Gyeongugung Shrine. Since the military support from the Japanese Legation was limited, we chose a location with a narrow space for protection and privacy.  However, a problem arose when, at the request of the queen, we moved to Changdeokgung Palace. As Qing troops stationed in the provinces entered, the Japanese forces retreated without much resistance, and ultimately, the coup ended in failure. At that time, my comrades suggested that we should seek asylum in Japan or another country.  But I chose to stay behind to legitimately clarify the reasons for staging the coup. In truth, King Gojong had expressed his support for modernization to me on several occasions. However, unlike my will, the Qing troops arrived unexpectedly, and...  Afterward, I was killed by the Qing troops. Upon hearing the news of my death, my father took his own life, and my wife and son also departed from life. The government confiscated our home, and we were labeled as traitors. (Sighs deeply) Even now, it's horrifying to think about. Trusting Japan was my biggest mistake, but I should have also focused on building skills and preparing to gain more support from the people.  Yet, the world is truly ironic. Min Yeongik, who once led the modernization efforts, turned against the coup, and was stabbed during the Ujeong Chongguk event but narrowly escaped death. Subsequently, upon seeing Dr. Allen, who treated Min Yeongik, the government developed an interest in Western medicine and decided to establish Western-style hospitals.  As a result, Korea's first modern hospital, Gwanghyewon, which later became Jejungwon Clinic Center, was established. Jejungwon Clinic Center first opened in the house where I used to live. From my perspective, as someone who dreamt of modernization, it was a positive development to see Jejungwon Clinic Center come to life. However, the fact that it all started because of Dr. Allen, who treated Min Yeongik, shows how unpredictable the world can be.  Well, I've talked a lot, but I'll tell you one more thing. In this space symbolizing modernization, the first public women's school in Korea was established. Hansung Girls' High School was founded in 1908 in Doryeom-dong and later moved to this location in 1910.  This school later became Gyeonggi Girls' Regular High School, which is now Gyeonggi Girls' High School, then moved to another location. Subsequently, Changdeok Girls' High School, originally in Sindang-dong, relocated here. After the school moved to Bangi-dong, the current Constitutional Court of Korea was established in this location.  Now, let's move on to the next destination on Jongno Modern Street Course 5. After leaving the Constitutional Court of Korea, if you walk along the main road towards Bukchon, you will come across the Gahoe-dong Community Service Center. Take the alley right in front of the community center, and you'll find the next destination, Baek In-je House. There are also signs installed for guidance, so please refer to them.

stories.title: Baek In-je House
stories.script: Now, here we are - Baek In-je House. I've looked into this person separately, and he was truly remarkable. At some point, his vision aligned well with the direction I had in mind for modernization. It is also interesting that such an individual owned this house.  First, let's take a tour of the house, and then I'll explain the individuals associated with this place.  Baek In-je House is incredibly spacious. The land area alone is almost 2,500 square meters, containing a sarangchae, anchae, byeoldang, byeolchae, daemunchae, and jungmunchae. What's most astonishing is the innovative architectural design. For instance, originally, the sarangchae and anchae were divided into a space for men and a space for women, but in this house, they are joined together.  As the times and lifestyle changed, the architecture followed suit. This kind of construction was probably possible because it was the early 1910s. The use of Japanese housing-style corridors and the incorporation of bricks and glass windows reflects the architectural characteristics of this period. Moreover, making one side of the anchae a second floor can be considered a modernized hanok.  Now, recalling my explanation, let's go through the daemunchae, Jungmunchae, and carefully examine the sarangchae, anchae, and byeoldang area. The architecture is sophisticated, and the decorations are refined, don’t you agree? This house often appears in movies, typically portrayed as the residence of an affluent pro-Japanese traitor. It even made an appearance in the movie <Assassination.>  However, the actions of the Baek In-je House's owner and the actual use of the house differed from its atmosphere or the portrayal in movies. Now, please make yourself comfortable and listen to the story. Or, while listening to my story, feel free to explore different areas of the house and discover parts you haven't seen yet.  Baek In-je House was built in 1913 by Han Sangryong, who was the executive director of Hanseong Bank at the time. Soon after, ownership transferred to Hanseong Bank, and it became a gathering place for followers of Cheondogyo, a Korean indigenous religion. Cheondogyo believers, who were key figures in the March First Independent Movement, gathered here to discuss the direction of the country's independence. In 1935, Choi Sunik, a young magnate in Gaeseong, acquired the house. Choi Sunik was also interested in the press and took over the Chosun Joongang Daily, appointing Yeo Woonhyung as its president. Chosun Joongang Daily was the newspaper that closed due to the Erasure of the Japanese National Flag by Sohn Kee-chung.  Later, the name we use today, Baek In-je, acquired this house. Baek In-je, too, is a historical figure worth remembering. Despite being a top student at Osan School and Kyungsung Medical School, he faced expulsion due to his participation in the March First Independence Movement. After overcoming many challenges, Baek In-je returned to the medical field, graduating as the top student from Kyungsung Medical School. However, once again, his involvement in the March First Independence Movement became an issue, and he was ultimately denied a medical license.  He managed to obtain a medical license after two years of working as a second assistant, a position lower than an assistant, in the Japanese Colonial Government Hospital. Later, while employed at the Japanese Colonial Government Hospital, he earned a doctoral degree in medicine from the University of Tokyo. Following studies in Europe, he established Baek Hospital. After the liberation, he served as a chief professor and hospital director at Seoul National University College of Medicine. Unfortunately, during the Korean War, he was captured by North Korea, and his whereabouts remain unknown. Thanks to the preservation of Baek Hospital and this house, we can still remember Dr. Baek In-je.   He paved a path similar to the modernization I had envisioned. I hoped we could produce excellent doctors and establish good hospitals with our own efforts. Although opportunities dwindled and were delayed due to the Japanese colonial period, it's fortunate to see someone succeed in this way.  Alright, let's move on to the next location. The next place to explore is the Seoul Museum of Education, located next to the entrance of the Jeongdok Library.

stories.title: Seoul Museum of Education
stories.script: "Here we arrived at the Seoul Museum of Education. The museum seems to embody history even from its exterior. Let's first take a look around the outside and then explore the exhibits inside, shall we?  This charming red brick building here is, as you might have guessed, an old school building. It was constructed in 1925 during the time of Kyungsung Jeil Regular High School. The inner Jeongdok Library was built in 1938, so the Seoul Museum of Education building is even older.  Enlightenment and education are deeply intertwined. Enlightenment implies embracing change with an open mind. In that sense, the coup that I and my comrades initiated might have been seen as rushed. Although we were impatient, the efforts of those who consistently showed interest in education paved the way for the present-day Republic of Korea. At the Seoul Museum of Education exhibition hall, you can catch a glimpse of the history of our education. Explore vivid scenes from traditional education to the education during the Enlightenment period, the resistance period, liberation, and the Korean War.  I find the education during the Enlightenment period particularly interesting. Among the exhibits, <Saminpilji> catches my eye. Saminpilji is the first Korean Hangul textbook written by Dr. Hulbert. Thanks to Hangul, our education was able to grow rapidly. This textbook, in particular, covers world geography, allowing many students to learn about and develop an interest in international affairs.  If you explore the exhibition hall, you can see the scenes from each era, and interesting things as well. If you graduated from a school in Seoul, you might be able to find the badge of your alma mater. Take a moment to look around. Shall we move on to the next location?  The next destination is the Jeongdok Library, right behind the Seoul Museum of Education. There are several benches in the library courtyard, so let me explain further there. "

stories.title: Jeongdok Library
stories.script: "Now, are you ready to hear the story about the Jeongdok Library? Jeongdok Library is a municipal library in Seoul—a place where many people come to read books and study. As widely known, this library was originally the building of Gyeonggi High School.  However, for me, it's a place that stirs complex emotions. Originally, this was where my two comrades, Kim Okgyun and Seo Jaepil, lived. After the coup, both of them went into exile. Kim Okgyun was assassinated by Hong Jongwoo in Shanghai, China, in 1894, and his body was sent back to Korea, only to be quartered again—an indescribably horrific event. Seo Jaepil went to the United States from Japan, eventually obtaining U.S. citizenship.  The house, once a prestigious residence in Seoul, became a house of rebels after the Gapsin Coup, so no one paid it any attention. Or rather, it would be more accurate to say people avoided it. In the meantime, the house fell into ruin.  However, an interesting transformation took place here as well. Just as my former residence became the Western-style hospital Jejungwon Clinic Center, this place evolved into a public middle school. In other words, it became the birthplace of modern secondary education in Korea, dating back to the year 1900. While the first public elementary school, Gyodong Elementary School, was established in 1894, public secondary education was created about six years later.  Modern secondary education, representing the enlightenment, takes place where two individuals, who once led the charge for modernization but met tragic ends, once lived. The flow of history is truly intriguing, isn't it? If it were not the homes of Kim Okgyun and Seo Jaepil, would a school have been established here?  Inside the Jeongdok Library, there's another intriguing feature. If you head east from the main library building, you'll come across a well. It's uncommon to find a well inside a school, but this particular well signifies the location of someone's former residence. Yes, it happens to be the site where Park Jesoon, one of the Five Eulsa Traitors and a former Minister of External Affairs, once lived. Interestingly, Park Jesoon's career aligns well with his role as a Minister of External Affairs.  Park Jesoon was not only one of the first diplomats sent to China but also assumed control of a Legation Office from the Qing Dynasty. Highly knowledgeable about international affairs, he was regarded as an elite figure during the late Joseon and the Daehan Empire. However, sometimes knowledge can lead people down the wrong path. From his international perspective, the Daehan Empire might have appeared extremely precarious.  Nevertheless, as an intellectual and a bureaucrat tasked with leading the nation, he should have navigated the challenging path to discern the right direction and protect the country, rather than conforming to prevailing currents.  Alright, let's move on to the next location. As we leave the Jeongdok Library, we'll head towards Duksung Girls' High School. There might not be any prominent buildings in sight, but our next destination is the place where the Central Temple of Cheondogyo was once located, as indicated by the guidepost. "

stories.title: Former Central Temple of Cheondogyo
stories.script: "Wasn't it hard to get here? The streets might be bustling with both passersby and foreign tourists. Witnessing them enjoy Seoul, Korea makes me emotional. In the past, under the name 'Enlightenment,' I earnestly sought to engage with various countries, welcoming knowledge and culture.  Haha, I find myself tearing up. I'll calm myself and continue the guide of Jongno Modern Street, the 'Path to Enlightenment.' The place you're currently standing in is a bit lively, isn't it? You can hear the chatter from the streets and the laughter or cheers of students coming from the schoolyard across the guidepost. Welcome to the front of Duksung Girls' Middle School.  If you look at the guidepost, it mentions that the Central Temple of Cheondogyo was located here. Cheondogyo - a name that sounds unfamiliar to me, but I'm not entirely ignorant of it. During my time, it was referred to as Donghak, and it changed its name to Cheondogyo in 1905.  Looking back, I regret not showing more interest in Donghak. We believed that the path to modernization was outside the country. In some short period, we even thought that Japan's path was exemplary. However, one of the things that showed the way to modernization within Korea was Donghak. Donghak’s teaching of 'considering people as high as the sky and advocating equality for all' was profoundly significant. While we also claimed the abolition of lineage during the Gapsin Coup, we fell far short compared to Donghak's principles.  Many people were deeply moved by Donghak's teachings, and as Donghak spread widely, the government viewed it as a threat. As Donghak began gaining popularity, the government falsely accused its founder, Choe Je-u, of misleading the innocent people and executed him. Despite this, Donghak continued to thrive under Choe Sihyeong, leading to the Donghak Peasant Revolution. However, as Donghak's power and influence grew, internal issues arose, such as the infiltration of pro-Japanese sentiments. In response, the leader at the time, Son Byeong-hui, expelled the pro-Japanese faction and changed the name to Cheondogyo.  After changing its name, Cheondogyo, despite its image as an indigenous religion, embraced new elements without hesitation. This ranged from small changes like removing Goreum and adding buttons to the attire of believers, to more significant ones such as constructing Western-style buildings for their places of worship. Before building the Western-style Central Temple, the Central Temple of Cheondogyo was right here.  In 1919, Cheondogyo played a crucial role in planning a significant historical event. It collaborated with Christianity and Buddhism to initiate a movement for independence. In other words, it laid the foundation for the March First Independence Movement as a national movement in which everyone could participate. The movement started right here. Then, in 1921, Cheondogyo, having built a new church, relocated to Gyeongun-dong.  Alright, now let's move on to the next stop on Jongno Modern Street. As we head to the Jeongdok Library, if you take a left into a small alley, you'll come across the Seoul Hall of the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art. In front of it, there's the Office of the Royal Genealogy, where we’re going to explore. "

stories.title: Gyeonggeundang and Okcheopdang Halls of the Office of the Royal Genealogy
stories.audioTitle: Gyeonggeundang and Okcheopdang Halls of the Office of the Royal Genealogy
stories.script: "Here we have the Gyeonggeundang and Okcheopdang Halls of the Office of the Royal Genealogy. If you see two buildings that look different from the current atmosphere of Seoul, you're in the right place. The larger building is Gyeonggeundang Hall, and the smaller one is Okcheopdang Hall. These two structures were constructed during a time when the concept of modernization was under consideration, although they may not perfectly align with the modernization movement.  , Gyeonggeundang and Okcheopdang Halls together are called the Office of the Royal Genealogy. The Office of the Royal Genealogy is a government office responsible for tasks related to the descendants of the royal family. In 1866, Heungseon Daewongun significantly expanded the Office of the Royal Genealogy. At that time, the Office of the Royal Genealogy was an extravagant office with over 300 Kan. It's hard for me to understand why they built such a grand office for the royal descendants. Even if it was to enhance the authority of the royal family, was it necessary to invest such enormous resources and effort? However, this building also underwent unintended changes. In 1981, it was decided to build a tennis court for the Security Command here, so the Office of the Royal Genealogy that remained was moved to the Jeongdok Library. Yes, that's the place we just explored. Therefore, the buildings stood in the garden of Jeongdok Library for a while, not quite fitting in with the surroundings.  And in 2013, they were moved back to their original location, taking on the appearance you see now. Looking at the two buildings, you can tell that Gyeonggeundang Hall is a bit more important. It's larger, the Woldae in front of the building is more extensive, and the building is positioned more prominently. Oh, it's a small thing, but there's a corridor connecting the two buildings, giving us a glimpse of what the administrative offices looked like back then. When I worked in administration, the office buildings were somewhat similar.  Even within the same building, we can discuss modernization or maintaining the old appearance.  Now, let's move on to the next location. We'll need to take a bit of a walk this time. Follow the path east of Gyeongbokgung Palace towards Samcheong-dong. Once you find the Korea Banking Institute, look for the Chinese-style building inside. Our destination is the  Foundry of Joseon-Dynasty Arsenal. "

stories.title: Foundry of Joseon-Dynasty Arsenal
stories.script: "The  Foundry of Joseon-Dynasty Arsenal inside the Korea Banking Institute exudes a strong sense of modernization. The brick walls and double roof create a uniquely distinctive atmosphere.  Let me explain about the Joseon-Dynasty Arsenal. It started from the Tongni-Kimu-Amun in 1880, which was a special office set up to deal with domestic and international matters after the country opened up. Tongni-Kimu-Amun had 12 departments, and one of them, focused on weapons, handled machinery and military equipment tasks. Modernization aimed to boost national prosperity and defense, so these weapon-related tasks held significant importance.  To accomplish this aim, a substantial mission known as the Yeongseonsa was sent to the Qing Dynasty in 1881. Yet, due to the lack of cooperation from the Qing Dynasty and the disparity in knowledge, substantial achievements were not attained.  Two years later, in 1883, the Joseon-Dynasty Arsenal, tasked with weapon manufacturing, was established in the former Office of Gunpowder Weaons. Within the Joseon-Dynasty Arsenal, the Foundry was constructed - a factory specifically for casting weapons. While Chinese technicians contributed to its construction, the structure also bears elements of Korean architecture, indicating the involvement of Korean carpenters.  The Foundry was set up with the aim of creating a new rifle to replace the matchlock. However, hindered by the Qing Dynasty's lack of cooperation and financial difficulties in Joseon, the focus shifted toward repairing firearms. Despite this shift, the Foundry stood as a symbol of Joseon's modernization during that period. Looking back, I've come to realize that modernization wasn't simply about emulating foreign nations. It encompassed the need for a robust military, which demanded the capability to manufacture and handle weapons. This called for societal shifts in governance, nurturing skilled weapon craftsmen, and, crucially, unwavering leadership from administrative or political figures. Unfortunately, during my era, despite abundant ideas, we lacked the necessary political continuity to implement them effectively.  Given the time and social latitude to learn from our mistakes and forge ahead, we might have accomplished more. It's regrettable, yet comforting, to see the legacy showing our efforts for modernization.  I learned later that the Foundry was initially perceived as nothing more than a storage facility. It's intriguing, considering how distinct warehouses and factories are.  Now, onto our last stop on 'The Path to Enlightenment': Bukchon Hanok Village. "

stories.title: " Information for the Starting Point of Course 6"
stories.audioTitle: Information for the Starting Point of Course 6
stories.script: "It's time to say goodbye. The guidance through Jongno Modern Street Course 5 by Hong Yeongsik has come to an end. Course 6 begins at Choongang High School. From your current location, make your way down towards Bukchon road and then ascend the eastern hill. There, I hope you'll discover another charming aspect of Jongno Modern Street.  Thank you and goodbye.  "

stories.title: Introducing the Presenter 4
stories.script: Hello, I'm Yeom In-yeong, a literary critic. I'll be taking you to Course 4 of Jongno Modern Trail. I hear that this course is titled the ', Modernists, the Trail of Literature.' It seems that I was recommended because there will be a number of stories related to literature.   Literature has always been a popular genre. Novels are especially loved by many people. It's human nature to be interested in exciting stories. And it seems that poetry is still an effective way to express our emotions and feelings. When we're overwhelmed by emotions, singing is often more empowering than simply talking. It seems to be related to the effects of poetry, too.  By the way, there's something that we need to think about when we look at literature, which is its relationship with history. A well-written novel or poetry is valuable material with which to look into a certain period of the past!  We can live through the characters in books and experience an age or someone else's life that we've never thought of before to gain a fresh view of ourselves and our society. Some novels serve as textbooks, showing us more vivid visions of history. In short poems, we can read about poets’ passion for idealistic and beautiful worlds that they dreamt of, as well as their life and agonies.  Today's theme is 'Modernists, the Trail of Literature'. Modernism is an artistic trend that emerged in the early 20th century. Modernism states that art begins from criticism of the prior system and styles. Modernism was a trend in Korea in the 1920s to 1950s. It seems that the nation was experiencing rapid changes back then.  In this sense, the Trail of Literature may help you understand literature and our modern and contemporary history.  Now, let's visit our modernist writers.

stories.title: Birthplace of Bang Jeonghwan
stories.script: The first man of literature we'll come across on this trail is Sopa Bang Jeonghwan.  Oh, it is hard to find the trails of Bang Jeonghwan in this concrete forest. But if you look carefully, a stone post is in a small garden in front of Royal Building, marking the birthplace of Bang Jeonghwan.  Thanks to this little stone post, we can talk about Bang Jeonghwan. Bang Jeonghwan is also known as the 'friend of children.' He’s the one who designated the Children's Day and established '' 'Saekdonghoe Club' to lead Children's Movement. He also asked Yoon Seokjung, a Korean children's literature writer and Jeong Suncheol, an educator who dedicated himself to training younger students and a children's rights activist, to compose a song.  Some of you may think that Bang Jeonghwan is not a great fit for the theme of this course. But, mind you, Bang Jeonghwan translated foreign fairy tales and published them in a fairy tale book called < Gift of Love>. Published by Gaebyeoksa, < Gift of Love> may be a translated work, but it showed the need for children's literature. Literature for children... During the Joseon Dynasty, people thought of children as someone who needed discipline, and there were no books for children.   Hmm, it does seem that Bang Jeonghwan was ahead of his time. Inside <Gift of Love>, there are 10 classical children's stories picked from <Andersen's Fairy Tales> and <Grimm's Household Tales>.  The reason he published this children's book is very touching. Let me read it for you. 'I published this book as the first loving and sympathetic gift for our children that grow in abuse, devastation, and cold and dark.' Even if you leave out 'children' in this sentence, it presents a perfect need for literature.  Of course, Bang Jeonghwan also wrote children's stories and published essays himself. On this note, Bang is a true writer in children's literature.  If you ask me about Bang Jeonghwan's greatest accomplishment, it would be creating the unique word ' children' in Korean. Children in Korean is a formal way of calling minors like we call ' seniors' or ' the youth.' It is often pointed out that one of the backgrounds that motivated Bang Jeonghwan to have such an idea was being the son-in-law of Son Byeonghui, a Korean Cheondoism leader.  In Cheondoism, it is said that 'striking children is like striking Hanul-nim,' indicating that children are full persons. To practice this belief, the religion instructs its devotees that they must speak formally when addressing children. In fact, in Korean, it sounds most natural when you finish a sentence with the word 'children' in a formal manner. In English, for example, it might sound like 'dear young children.'  By the way, it is very difficult for newly created words like ' children' to survive. One of the reasons that this word survives is thanks to the presence of the magazine < Eorini>. This magazine was issued in March 1923 by ' Gaebyeoksa' and was hugely popular. ' Eorini', which means ‘children’ in Korean, was the name of the magazine, and people became familiar with the word. Oh, but it makes me sad because I can barely see popular children's or young adult magazines. This is my opinion, but I believe that rather than saying 'kids' book' or 'kids literature', it is better to say ' children's book' or 'children's literature'.   Bang Jeonghwan left many other footprints as well. For example, at the Central Temple of Cheondogyo, there is Monument of the Birthplace of World Children's Movement' that commemorates Bang Jeonghwan for first beginning the children's Movement and Korea for designating a Children's Day for the first time in the world. But did you know this? Bang Jeonghwan's grave is located in ' Mangu History and Culture Park'. His tombstone says, 'The hearts of children are like those of celestial beings.'  It seems to imply the emergence of literature for children and changes to a new world.  Let's go to our next destination. We will be heading to the front yard of Kyobo Books, a massive bookstore located at Gwanghawmun Intersection. Walk past Sejong Center for the Performing Arts and Gwanghawmun Square, and you're there. Continue on with the view of General Yi Sun-shin, and Gwanghawmun Gate and Bugaksan Mountain and Bukansan Mountain as the backdrop of King Sejong the Great makes you realize that you are walking in the very center of Seoul. I think it's a good idea to enjoy a slow pace when you walk here.  Cross the road and head for the statue that is sitting at the entrance to the bookstore, facing Jongno.

stories.title: Yeom Sangseop's Statue
stories.script: Did you find a gentleman sitting on the bench in front of the bookstore? Good. He is Yeom Sangseop, a writer that I'll be introducing to you. He was such a prolific writer, so I couldn't read all his works. But I read a few novels and critiques of him so that I can talk about him with you.  There's some space on the bench. You can sit on it or go to the other side for some extra space to be comfortable listening to my story. I think you'll be able to see many people going into the bookstore to buy books while we talk. I never consider someone buying many books as spending too much of their money. Well, that someone's family might think otherwise, though.  Now, let's begin the story of writer Yeom Sang-seop. Yeom Sangseop has a pen name, and it's Hoengbo. It means walking sideways, which also means 'staggering'. Like when you had too much drink. I never walked sideways myself, but it does have a writer's vibe , doesn't it?  But the literary world of Yeom Sangseop is reviewed as straightforward and upright, unlike his pen name Hoengbo. He based his novels on the age that he lived in. In that sense, his novels feature studying abroad in Japan, the declaration of independence, moving to Manchuria, and returning to his homeland after the nation's liberation.   He is regarded as a writer that represents the modern or contemporary times, because Yeom Sangseop has never written a historical novel based on ancient history. But, in a sense, he was a writer who represents Korean history, or rather, the contemporary history of Korea, the best. Reading his novels helps us to understand Korean society between the 1930s and 1950s.   Yeom Sangseop's iconic work is < The Tree Frog in the Specimen Gallery>. His work < Mansejeon> is based on The March First Independence Movement and <Sampalseon> describes the complicated situation after the liberation. The protagonist of Mansejeon is a student returning from Japan, and Sampalseon a family that returns home from Manchuria. Perhaps you can say that they are based on the author's experiences as a student who studied in Japan and worked as a businessman in Manchuria.  Reading this novel helps you to better understand The March First Independence Movement and the complicated situations of the division of North and South Korea. For example, the protagonist, who was relatively free during his days studying in Japan, feels the oppression of the Japanese Empire as he comes home to Korea after leaving Japan. From the story of the protagonist feeling a surge of hostility toward the words and behaviors of Japanese people, you can learn why so many participated in The March First Independence Movement.  But you come to realize that you can't easily judge the time or anyone who is torn between going pro-Japan and continuing independence activities after The March First Independence Movement. Or people with different behaviors to their thoughts.  <Sampalseon: The 38th Parallel>, however, shows the complicated social situation after liberation. The story tells of a Korean family's return to South Korea from Manchuria after the country's liberation. They crossed the Amnokgang River easily, but the protagonist's mind is torn between crossing the 38th parallel, a border drawn by the Soviet Union and the United States.   I wondered about the significance of the 38th parallel to the people of the time; whether it's like a border or something less important. Through this novel, I could learn more about it. You'd think that people would be overjoyed about the country's liberation. It's sad that they couldn't really feel so. It's also difficult to imagine how Japanese people, whose lives turned upside down overnight, quite literally, would've felt.  Like this, Yeom Sangseop, or Hoengbo's novels, help us to understand the time. However, some critics say that his works are patriarchal and center around men.   You may think that people know the time that they live in the best, but perhaps it's not necessarily like that. Perhaps, with more materials, it'll be easier for us to judge our history. Yeom Sangseop's works remind us that to write literature, one must have sharp insights.   What would he think there, sitting on the bench and watching people passing by? Perhaps he'd be observing today's Korea and looking into its traits? If so, I wonder how he would perceive the day-to-day life of the 2020s.  Now, to the next stop. A recently restored stream flows next to a bench. It's Junghakcheon Stream. We will follow the trail next to it and head north toward Gyeongbokgung Palace. At the end of the Kyobo Building stands a post that marks the Site of Park Inhwan's House. Let's continue our conversation there.

stories.title: "Site of Park Inhwan's House "
stories.script: It's a small post in the concrete jungle. It tells us the site of Park Inhwan's House.   Park Inhwan is known for, like the post says, his work <Wooden Horse and a Lady>. People may not know Park Inhwan, the poet, but many know a phrase in his poetry that goes, 'We drink as we speak of Virginia Woolf, and  a skirt fluttering away on a wooden horse.' And the improvised poem <When Time Passes>, which is also a song, is his work. I think we have a genius poet right here.  Park Inhwan is also known as the post-war poet. He debuted in 1946 and passed away from a heart attack on March 20, 1956. World War II and the Korean War that he lived through were major materials for his works.  Perhaps that's why his works have a touch of nihilism. Critics regard him as a modernist writer, saying that such a characteristic stems from his anxiety from living in wartime.   One of the reasons why he could compose such a new style of work is that he debuted in 1946. Because he was not active during the Japanese Occupation of Korea, there was no need for him to overcome the Japanese Empire like many other writers of the time. He was consumed by the idea but able to write works that the time demanded. Also, Park Inhwan's used bookstore 'Mariseosa' was a place where many writers exchanged their thoughts and ideas.   Let's have a look at one of his works.  There is a poem called 'A Poem to the People of Indonesia'. Wow, Indonesia. Haha. This work sends support to Indonesia which was trying to break free of the Dutch rule. Also, Park Inhwan wrote ' South Wind' that supports the fight for the freedom of people of Southeast Asia, 'Incheon Port' that describes Koreans returning home from overseas after the liberation of the nation, showing his acute observation of the time.   Myeongdong was one of many things that made Park Inhwan famous. At Myeongdong, a neighborhood that kept the vibe of the city even in the desolation of the Korea War, Park Inhwan was called the 'Count of Myeongdong' thanks to his good looks. This prominent neighborhood figure, Park Inhwan, passed away in March 1956 from a heart attack which was caused by excessive drinking to celebrate I Sang.   Although critics evaluated his poems to display the nihilism of death rather than as magnificent, he was surely a poet loved by people.   Now, we'll be heading to the Site of Kim Suyeong's House. But make sure to pay attention on the way there because we'll be passing Pimatgol Alley. It's a small alley behind the main streets of Jongno. It's slowly disappearing these days, but we still have an alley-like setup at the foot of new high-rise buildings. Let's talk more when we get there.

stories.title: Pimatgol Alley / Gongpyeong Historic Sites Museum
stories.audioTitle: Pimatgol Alley / Gongpyeong Historic Sites Museum
stories.script: This small space under a towering building used to be an alleyway. It was called Pimatgol Alley. It was a very lively place with the smell of mung bean pancakes, hangover soup, and octopus dishes. People studying literature and art, poor office workers, and students with unkempt hair trying to have some fun came here. People who lived in the 80s and 90s of Seoul and Jongno might have a memory or two about Pimatgol Alley.  Oh, I think some of you might be misunderstanding the origin of Pimatgol Alleys. Let's talk about this before we go. The word Pima means avoiding horses. You might know Pimatgol Alley as alleyways that common folks used to avoid horse-riding high civil officials during the Joseon Dynasty. But the word Pima actually means 'the place where a lower-ranked civil official would turn his horse away to avoid a higher-ranking official on horseback.' Lower-ranked officials had to get down from their horses to pay respect to their senior officers, but that would delay their time and make them late for their official duties. So, the law allowed junior officers to go around to avoid running into their seniors.  This means that Pimatgol Alley was the path that junior civil officers used. But later, merchants and common folks also came to use it, creating a commercial area.  In some 18th-century maps, you can already see Pimatgol Alley. The Pimatgol Alley north of Jongno, the main street of Hanyang, continues from near Gwanghwamun Gate to Dongdaemun Gate. But, the Pimatgol Alley south of Jongno cuts once near Jonggak and continues again. This means that the north Pimatgol Alley of Jongno better preserves its old looks.   During the Japanese Occupation of Korea, parts of Pimatgol Alley were called Pima-dong. Because the neighborhood was a residential area for Koreans, they didn't develop or expand the Jongno area, leaving Pimatgol Alley intact. After the liberation, when Jongno was undergoing expansion, south Pimatgol Alleys all but disappeared because north Jongno was the focal point. Time passed, and large buildings sprouted up in the north part. It made Pimatgol Alley today to keep its name and some of its history only.  Let me briefly introduce the gathering place for writers that used to be in Pimatgol Alley. It was <Siin Tongsin>, which used to be at 300, Cheongjin-dong. Many artists and writers frequented this cafe that doubles as a pub. But, sadly, it closed permanently in 2008 after moving around several times.  Pimatgol Alley, the side alley in Jongno that pedestrians take for quicker travels, is a place that adds rich vibes to Jongno. It's a good idea to catch your breath at a place that lets you take in the vibes of Pimatgol Alley. Have a delicious meal, or allow yourself a tea break. But, better yet, you can visit a place that allows you to take a glimpse into what was happening at Pimatgol Alley with your own eyes: Gongpyeong Historic Sites Museum. It has quite a long name. Gongpyeong is the name of the neighborhood. And it's a museum that exhibits the urban ruins. Simple. This museum is located in a basement of a modern-looking building. That's because it kept the historic site that they found during the construction process. Gongpyeong Historic Sites Museum shows four distinctive strata. 0.6M to 1.5m below the soil is the Japanese Occupation of Korea and the 19th century, 1.5m to 2.4m is the 18th to 19th century, and so on. To put it simply, as we dig 1 m down the ground of Seoul, we find 100-year-old history. At Gongpyeong Historic Site Museum, you can see the outcome of the excavation of the 16th and 17th-century stratum that is the most well-preserved. The path running between the remains was also an alleyway 400 years ago. Let's walk the alley and imagine the old appearance of Pimatgol Alley.   Now! Next, we're headed to the birth home of poet Kim Suyeong. You can find the site of the Birth Home of Kim Suyeong can on the other side of Tapgol Park, at the cluster of foreign language academies. Let's continue our conversation when we get there.

stories.title: Site of the Birth Home of Kim Su-yeong
stories.audioTitle: Site of the Birth Home of Kim Su-yeong
stories.script: Let's resume our journey on the Trail of Literature. The owner of this post, poet Kim Suyeong, is also a known modernist. Like his reputation as a modernist poet, he is known for poems that criticize modern civilization.   But Modernism originated from the West. How could it criticize modern civilization? But, Kim Suyeong has many fans as he describes Korea's current situation as well as modern society in detail.  Often, the age in which a poet lives influences his works. But did you know that Kim Suyeong had an unexpected side to his character?   First, let's trace his life briefly. Born in November 1921 at he was the third son of Kim Taewook and An Hyeongsun. We are standing at that very address. He went to Joyang Kindergarten at the age of four and then to Gyemyeongseodang Village School to learn Chinese characters. When he turned 8, he entered Eoui-dong Public Primary School. The school is still here, but under the name of Hyoje Elementary School.   When he was in the 6th grade, he ate a banana, a rare imported fruit then, and got indigestion. His indigestion got worse, and Kim Suyeong, who was born with a sickly health condition, could not even attend his graduation.  Later, it is said that he continued to suffer from his weak body constitution. As the family business declined, he went to Seonlin Commercial School. He was aiming to get employed. But Kim Suyeong, who longed to get into a university, left for Japan to further his studies.   But, he comes home, failing to enter a university in Japan. The cost of studying abroad was one issue. But, the main reason was to flee the conscription of Korean international students by the Japanese Empire.   He later transferred to Yonhee College but dropped out. During the Korean War, he was conscripted to the Communist Army as he failed to flee home at the right time. Because of that, he ended up in Geojeodo POW Camp, where the UN force detained the Communist Army prisoners after the war. Later, he also served briefly as an interpreter at the US Army and worked at a news agency for a short while. But, in 1968, he passed away from a traffic accident.  As we look back, he lived through the decisive moments in Korean history, such as the Korean War and the April Revolution. But fans of his work are most impressed by the description of April Revolution, a democratic movement against the corruption of Rhee Syngman's government.  Let's read a poem by Kim Su-yeong about the April Revolution.  Titled < For the Blue Sky>  A poet's words of envy On a skylark That conquers the blue sky Must be corrected.  Those that soared up  For freedom Will surely know What a skylark sees And sings Why freedom has The scent of blood  Why revolution  is a solitary thing  Why revolution Must be a solitary thing  How is that? Perhaps now you can see the atmosphere of the April Revolution, felt by the poet. In this poem, poet Kim Suyeong refers to the soaring for freedom as' revolution.' That naturally makes the poet view the soaring bird differently. As he knows that flying is a hard ordeal, he sings that advancing forward to gain freedom is a hard, arduous, and solitary struggle.   He emphasizes that revolution is a lonely path to tread and the imperativeness of it being a solitary deed; he argues that the path of revolution requires willpower.  It is essential to recognize the history of April Revolution that begins at the Bloody Tuesday of April 19, 1960, and the Victory Tuesday in April 26 when president Rhee Syngman finally announces his resignation. But, of course, we encounter the revolution's different aspects through Kim Suyeong's poetry.   Most of all, his works emphasize the power of citizens, showing his passion for freedom.  Civil rights, and fights for freedom. Here history meets literature yet again.  Now, let's visit the space of a poet who fought for freedom in a bit of a different way. We'll be going to a cafe called 'Guicheon (歸天), which means going back to Heaven, and it's inside Insa-dong.    Insa-dong is a popular tourist destination as well. In the past, many came here to find old texts, vintage items, paintings, and old stationary items. Thanks to their visits, restaurants and tea houses sprung up.   In turn, the area became a popular tourist destination. Recently, we're seeing more trendy shops here as well.  Nowadays, the area is nothing but an old neighborhood, but you can still enjoy the unique vibes of Insa-dong on its main street. Keep walking and enjoy your surroundings, and you'll arrive at the alley where Guicheon is.

stories.title: Poet Cheon Sangbyeong’s Working Space, <Guicheon>
stories.script: A small cafe inside an alleyway, Guicheon is a place that commemorates poet Cheon Sangbyeong. The cafe used to be run by his wife, Mun Sunok. Guicheon, while poet Cheon Sangbyeong was alive, was the place where his friends would come to talk to him.  Poet Cheon Sangbyeong is known for his innocent nature. Once, he met up with poet Jung Gwang, who is also known as the Ragged Monk, a name given after his representative work 'I am a Rag', and novelist Lee Oisu and argued who has the most innocent nature. What do you think?  But what made Cheon Sangbyeong famous was the brutality of the state. He suffered twice. The first incident was being swept into the ' East Berlin Incident' and taken to the Korean Central Intelligence Agency for torture.   Another incident was his being forcibly imprisoned in an asylum for being mistaken as a mentally ill homeless person while he was wandering the streets, suffering from the aftermath of the East Berlin Incident.   There is a funny story about this. As the whereabouts of Cheon Sangbyeong fell into a mystery, his fellow poets thought he was dead and published a collection of his poems in memory of him. Thankfully, he returned after its publication, but now we have a very rare case of having a collection of poems dedicated to a late but very much alive poet in the Korean literature scene.   Cheon Sangbyeong's two keywords, 'innocence' and 'poetry collection in memory of the late poet' come from the East Berlin Incident in 1968. The poet himself said that the incident 'killed' his life.  So, what has happened? As many know, the East Berlin Incident was a fabricated spy incident created by the Central Intelligence Agency. At that time, the Central Intelligence Agency announced that about 200 European and Korean intellectuals went back and forth between East Berlin, the North Korean Embassy, and Pyeongyang to be trained as spies for espionage activities against South Korea. Around then, 70 people were arrested and imprisoned for allegedly violating the National Security Act and Anti-Communist Act.  The persons at the center of this incident were Lee Eungno and Yun Isang, students who studied abroad in Pyeongyang. Cheon Sangbyeong was arrested for allegations of 'not reporting crimes despite knowing they had been committed' regarding a fellow student, Kang Bingu, at Seoul National University School of Commerce, and threatening him and extorting a total of KRW 50,000 on dozens of occasions.   This meant that the point of the allegation was whether or not Cheon Sangbyeong knew Kang Bingu was a spy.   But as the investigation authorities released the suspect's personal details to the public early on, he was taken as a criminal even before the trials. But none of the persecuted received any sentence for the crime of espionage in the final stage of the trial. Those who were persecuted and were serving terms under other charges were all freed, so you can easily see the truth of this incident.   Cheon Sangbyeong underwent electrical torture three times while being forced by the Central Intelligence Agency to a confession. Later, he was sentenced to 1 year of imprisonment and 3 years of probation and served 6 months of prison time. He saved his friends from the talons of the authorities but suffered physically and mentally. He lost his teeth and reproductive ability, which also took his power to compose poetry.   Cheon Sangbyeong had such natural innocence, but before the East Berlin Incident, he was a totally different man. Cheon Sangbyeong was born in Japan and came to Korea after the nation's liberation. He served as an interpreter for the US during the Korean War and served as the press secretary of the Mayor Kim Hyeonok of Busan for 2 years.  Not long after that, the commemorative poet collection came out, and he married Mok Sunok. Thanks to the dedication of Moon Sunok, who loved and respected Cheon Sangbyeong, her husband, he managed to slowly resume his literary works and be his old self. Which meant he could buy a bowl of makgeolli with a KRW 1,000 note and be a happy man.   In this period, we begin to see Cheon Sangbyeong with his much-celebrated innocence.  He passed in 1993, after having resumed his literary work thanks to his loving wife. Perhaps his work, <Back to Heaven> is Cheon Sangbyeong's most iconic work.   Let me read it for you.  Titled, <Back to Heaven>  I shall return home to Heaven Hand in hand with morning dew Fading at the touch of dawn.  I shall return home to Heaven Together with the color of the sunset. When the clouds beckon at me on the slope,  I will return home to Heaven When my journey in this beautiful world I will go home and tell them it was beautiful.   How is that? It's a beautiful yet sad poem. After you know more about Cheon Sangbyeong's life, it will make you choked up. Perhaps his life can be summed up with this very word, Guicheon, and his poetry.  Now, let's go to the last destination in the Trail of Literature, the Trail of Modernism. We must cross Yulgok-ro, the path heading north of Insa-dong, and head to Bukchon. Walk pass Seoul Museum of Craft Art and Deokseong Girls High School. The next stop is near Former President Yoon Bo-seong's House, and it's a stone post that marks the site of the Korean Language Society.

stories.title: Site of the Korean Language Society
stories.audioTitle: Site of the Korean Language Society
stories.script: Now, this is where the office of the Korean Language Society used to be. The exact location is inside this narrow alley in front of this post. It was a two-story building. The second floor was the society's office, while the first floor was the living quarters of Lee Geukro, a Korean linguist from North Korea and a politician.   Korean Language Society is not a literature club, but it's deeply related to literature. We cannot have literature without our own language, letters, and grammar.
