The Korean Language Society was where the < Complete Korean Dictionary> was published, and the Korean spelling and loanword orthography were organized.    The Korean Language Society also went through a huge ordeal, namely, the ' Korean Language Society Incident' in 1942. The Japanese Empire arrested Hangeul researchers for a small fault that they found in a diary of a student girl in Hamheung, and tortured them to get confessions for treason.   In the process, the linguist Lee Yun-jae and Hangeul researcher Han Jing passed away tragically. The Japanese Empire sentenced 5 researchers to 6 years in prison for violating the Public Order Act. This implies that protecting the Korean language was equal to the independence movement.  Without Hangeul in the modern and contemporary literature scene, writers would have had much narrower areas of activity. And readers wouldn't have been able to read Korean literature. Let's remind ourselves of the value of Korean language and Hangeul through literature.  By the way, this building was built and donated by Jeong Segwon, the first real estate developer in Korea who built Hanok Village in Ikseon-dong and Bukchon Hanok Village, the hottest tourist destinations these days.   * Information for the Starting Point of Course 5 – The Constitutional Court (Lacebark Pine Tree) We've walked Jongno Modern Trail: Modernists, the Trail of Literature. Did you enjoy it?   Today, I learned that literature gives significance to the space as well as the time that the writer lived as we walked around Jongno that tells the stories of writers.   Actually, Jongno has many more traces of people in literature, but we've run out of time now. But if you are interested in literature, you will find more writers at Jongno.   You will find special stories and the history of Jongno in course 5. It will begin at the Lacebark Pine standing inside the Constitutional Court, which is in the House of Yun Posun, a former president of Korea. Please continue on the trails of modern history, Modern Jongno.   I will say goodbye to you here. Thank you.

stories.title: Introducing the Presenter 3
stories.script: Hello, nice to meet you. I am Mary Lynley Tailor, and I will guide you to the Ginkgo Trail of Strangers, course 3 of Jongno Modern Street. Perhaps you recognize me by my voice. I was one of the British residents living in the house named Dilkusha. I’ve heard that Dilkusha is quite famous in Jongno.   'Ginkgo Trail of Strangers' is a tour route that passes through the sites where foreigners like me lived more than 100 years ago. They have experienced the Joseon society like no other foreigner during their time in this country. Some of them have made great achievements, so it would be more fitting for them to guide you to this street. But I am honored to serve in their stead.   Oh, I forgot to introduce myself. I was born and raised in Great Britain. While pursuing a career as an actress, despite my family's opposition, I met Albert, an American entrepreneur, while we were in Japan, and married him. And in 1917, I came to Joseon, the land of the morning calm. We lived in Joseon from 1917 to 1942, but we were deported from the country after the outbreak of the Pacific War.   My husband and I loved Joseon very much. In particular, Albert had been pursuing his career in mining and trade businesses in Joseon since 1896, after he came to the country with his father. For him, Joseon was a special place because it’s where he lived most of his life. That is why the forced deportation by Imperial Japan was such a tragedy to us, and it was much more than just losing our home.    Albert was even imprisoned for 6 months at Seodaemun Prison for refusing to leave the country. I was under house arrest for the same period. It was a terrible ordeal for us. In the end, Albert had to sell his mine at a giveaway price and go back to the United States. Hmm, in some ways, America felt more foreign than Joseon to both Albert and I.  When Albert died after a heart attack in 1948 in the States, I brought Albert's remains to the foreigners' cemetery in Yanghwajin. I buried him next to his father because he asked me to before he passed away. It saddens my heart to recall our leaving Joseon and bringing my husband's remains back to Korea.   We were so happy for the 26 years we were in Joseon. We befriended many people from diverse countries that lived around the legation street. People of Joseon may have considered us foreigners, but Joseon was our home.  Let us go to the places where we had the happiest moments.

stories.title: Dilkusha
stories.script: First, take a look at the ginkgo tree there. That ginkgo tree in such a narrow space between buildings has been there for centuries. I’ve heard that it was the residence of General Gwon Yul, the provincial military marshal who controlled the army in wartime during Japanese invasions of Korea between 1592 and 1598. The name of the town, Haengchon-dong, has a ginkgo tree in it. '' The district came to be when Eunhaeng-dong and Sinchon-dong merged together, and Eunhaeng-dong was named as such because of this ginkgo tree.  I still cannot forget the day when I first saw this tree. One day, my husband and I took a walk around Hanyang fortress trail. When we encountered this tree, we were climbing down by the fortress wall of Inwangsan Mountain.   With a height of 30 meters, the tree was so huge that you would need two people to embrace the trunk. I just loved it. Since then, I called it 'our tree.' I was determined to build a house of our own here someday. I used to come here frequently and look down at the city of Seoul with this ginkgo tree next to me.  And in 1923, my dream came true. It’s the red brick house behind you, called '' Dilkusha.     Dilkusha is a Persian word meaning ‘the palace of heart’s delight.' When we went to India, we saw the ruin of an old palace and decided to name our house '' Dilkusha in the future. But I hadn’t the slightest idea that it would be here in Joseon.   Because of the Joseon Shrine that was built by the Japanese on the skirt of Namsan Mountain, we couldn't build our house on higher ground than the shrine. Nevertheless, Dilkusha was a big house situated in the second-highest place in Seoul, after Joseon Shrine.   To understand how I felt at the time, you must erase all those tall buildings you see in front of you from your mind, one after another. Do that, and you will only see the old fortress walls and hills, and Namsan Mountain and Inwangsan Mountain on the other side. Oh, this ginkgo tree would also be standing tall right in front of it.   Can you see how it was when Dilkusha was first built? It was quite a sight to see. Haha.  Thanks to the recent efforts of many people, Dilkusha's interiors were restored to the state when I was living in it. Some of the decorations include my paintings of some honest and good Joseon people whom I have met in person. And don't forget to look for the amber necklace that connected Albert and I with Joseon.    Albert proposed to me with a large amber necklace, saying that people of Joseon, too, cherish amber. The past glories of Dilkusha were restored thanks to the cornerstone that has the name Dilkusha on it. It also made it possible for my son Bruce, who must be in his old age by now, to visit the house of his childhood.  In fact, Bruce has a special relationship with Korea. It was 1919. At that time, I was hospitalized in Severance Hospital near Seoul Station to give birth to him. Albert, a correspondent of A.P. News of the U.S., was preparing to cover the royal funeral of Emperor Gojong, the day before the March First Independence Movement.   My son Bruce was born on February 28th while I was wondering why there were so many Japanese soldiers inside and outside of the hospital. In a flurry of activity, the nurse stuck a bunch of paper under my bed and disappeared. I only realized the presence of those papers when Albert entered the room.   It was the Korean Declaration of Independence. I can still recall Albert's expression when he saw it. He seemed to be more in awe than when he held our son Bruce for the first time. To be honest, I was kind of sad to see that.  That night, my brother-in-law Bill hid the Korean Declaration of Independence and Albert's article in the heels of his shoes and left for Tokyo. It was to send them to A.P. News via telegraph. That was how they could send an article on the March First Independence Movement that declared the independence of Korea overseas.   After that, Albert spread the news of the March First Independence Movement as well as the royal funeral of King Gojong to the world as a correspondent of A.P. News. In April, he also covered the incident of the massacre of 29 Joseon people at a church at Jeam-ri in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi-do, and the burning of the village by the Japanese Military Police.  It was truly amazing to see Korean people hurraying for their independence with bare hands before the Japanese soldiers armed with knives and rifles. They established the Provisional Government of Korea at Shanghai, China.   Seeing such a resolution, I believed that the Japanese colonial rule would not last long.  Now, I believe I've said enough about Dilkusha. Shall we take a look inside Dilkusha for a moment? As you can see, it has been restored to resemble the house we lived in. It looks like a small museum. Please see how our family lived back in the day. We will go to the next destination after that.   A short walk along the alley between and the ginkgo tree will take you to a small red brick house. We'll be heading there next.

stories.title: Hong Nanpa's House
stories.script: This is another beautiful house. It is known as a house built by a German missionary in the 1930s. See the special window structure that opens up and down.  This place, too, used to be home to another foreigner. But now, it's known as the house of Hong Nanpa, a Korean musician who is known for composing 'Garden Balsam' and 'Spring of the Hometown.' It's said that Hong Nanpa lived the last 6 years of his life here.   Hong Nanpa is a man who left a significant footprint in modern Korea's Western music. He first took an interest in Western music when he was going to Saemunan Church.   He was a musician who learned to sing and play the violin at Joseon Musical Academy, the first educational institute to teach Western music in Korea, and he went on to Japan and America to study Western classical music. After returning to Korea, he earned the love of many Koreans by hosting recitals and leading an orchestra.  However, after his imprisonment for the Suyang Club incident in 1937, Hong Nanpa turned pro-Japan due to the pressure from Japan, and some say that his music changed after that. How unfortunate.  This place also has an interior design like that of a small museum such as Dilkusha. Perhaps it would be a good idea to take a look around here for a while. And then we'll go to the next place. Let us climb up the stairs in what appears to be the garden of Hong Nanpa’s house and go uphill. A small stone post there is our destination.

stories.title: Site of Bethell's House
stories.script: Can you see the stone post? Yes, This is the site of the house of Ernest Bethell, a fellow Brit like myself. Unfortunately, I never had the pleasure of meeting Bethell. It’s because he passed away long before I came here. But many Koreans remember Bethell as a good Brit. Some of them even remember the newspaper that Bethell established, <> <Korea Daily News>.   Bethell was a British journalist. In Korea, he issued <> <Korea Daily News>, which was in Korean, as well as <Korea Daily Mail>, which was in English.  It's said that there is a reason why Koreans have special feelings for this newspaper. It's related to a couple of incidents; namely, Eulsa Unwilling Treaty or Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905. The treaty allowed the Japanese to rob Korea of its diplomatic sovereignty. Jang Ji-yeon, enraged by this incident, issued an article called '' 'Si Il ya Bangseong Daegok' which means 'I Wail Bitterly Today' in <> <Hwangseong Sinmun>, but the Japanese stopped his article from being issued. However, <> <Korea Daily News> took the article and published it.   Also, the handwritten letter of King Gojong to the international society that claims the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1905 as null and void was published in <> <Korea Daily News>. At that time, Japan lied that King Gojong endorsed this treaty, but the newspaper called them right out.   Also, <> <Korea Daily News> led the National Debt Repayment Movement that began in Daegu in 1907. This movement began with the idea of earning independence with the full payment of loans granted by Japan, and it quickly spread across the nation. Newspaper articles and names of people who made donations to the newspaper significantly helped the movement. Although the movement failed because of Japan's sabotage, this movement that involved tens of thousands of people ignited the passion for independence.  As such, <> <Korea Daily News> was a nuisance to Japan, but they couldn't do anything because Bethell was a British, a citizen of an allied nation. In the difficult time, <> <Korea Daily News> was a medium that helped Koreans to breathe. In the end, Japan amended the Newspaper Act to control foreigner-issued newspapers and pressured the British Consulate General of Korea to press charges against Bethell, giving him a hard time with trials. Not long after that, Bethell passed away.  Oh, it's also said that Bethell lived in a hanok. Quite a few foreigners fall in love with the charms of hanok.  We would have been great friends if we ever met in Korea. What a shame. But I'm glad that we can find Bethell's footprints from this stone post. Now, let's travel down along the fortress walls from Bethell's House.

stories.title: Hanyangdoseong Fortress Wall
stories.script: "When I lived there, the north part of the fortress wall was almost in ruins due to Japan.   But I heard there's something special about this fortress. It is like the symbol of Seoul, as the founding king of Joseon, King Taejo, moved the capital from Gaesung to Hanyang and built the fortress walls. Since then, many of the Joseon dynasty's kings refurbished it. I loved walking along this fortress wall. It felt like I was walking through centuries of history. Also, Korea's fortress wall blends in with nature, giving a cozy feel.   Now, the next destination is the National Meteorological Museum of Korea. Follow the trail and exit on the left. It's quite a lengthy walk from the entrance to the museum, so keep a leisurely pace. "

stories.title: National Meteorological Museum of Korea
stories.script: Well done for climbing all the way up here. It'll be well worth your hard work. You'll see the weight of time draped on an old building, a wide garden, and a few meteorological instruments. A sight that you can rarely see.  As I said previously, it's the National Meteorological Museum of Korea. Now, it's hidden behind skyscrapers, but a century ago, you could see the entire Seoul from here. It was in 1932. Joseon built a new building for meteorological observation here at a high ground. That is the building that we see in front of us.  From January 1st, 1933, this place became the standard point of Seoul's weather. The museum's garden is still the standard point of Seoul's weather. They say the garden's maple tree is about 120 years old. It must've been here when I came here for the first time. Of course, it was only a small tree back then.  Oh, the building of the National Meteorological Museum of Korea is in a style that was trending in the 1930s. It's made with a focus on practicality as much as possible.  It's a museum, so there are several exhibition halls where you can have hands-on experiences. The museum also exhibits an artifact that Korea prides itself on. That is Cheugugi, the first rain gauge in the world. People say that the West has advanced science in general. But, Cheugugi was invented 200 years before a similar one in the West. How marvelous is that? That is why Korea celebrates May 19th as 'Invention Day,' in celebration of Cheugugi's invention in the 23rd year of King Sejong's reign, which is May 19th, 1441.  By the way, among many Cheugugis that were made during the Joseon Dynasty, this Cheugugis in this museum is the only one left. This Cheugugi is Cheugugi of Gongju in Chungcheong Gamyeong, called Geumyeong Cheugugi, made in 1837. It's a rare and famous piece that was featured in <Nature> in 1911.   But, after the liberation of Korea, you could no longer find Cheugugi in Korea. Because (和田雄治) Wada Yuji, a Japanese meteorologist, took it to Japan without any permission. Thankfully, it was returned after going through much trouble in 1971 with the negotiation for returning cultural assets.  Other than this, Cheugudae, a part of Cheugugi, which is a supporting stone on which Cheugugi was placed for easier measurement of rainfall, is another rare artifact. Let us look around the museum for a while and go to the next place. When you leave the museum and walk down the hill, you will see Kangbuk Samsung Hospital. Walk along the road inside the hospital grounds, and you'll find Gyeonggyojang House, a building in the 1930s style. This is our next destination.

stories.title: Gyeonggyojang House
stories.script: Gyeonggyojang House is where Kim Gu, also known as Baekbom, stayed once he returned to Korea after the nation's liberation. He was the premier of the Provisional Government of Korea in Shanghai, which led the nation's independence movements. The ground floor was the office of the Provisional Government, and the first floor was Kim Gu's office and residential quarters.   This building was originally a personal residence built by Choi Changhak, a gold mine millionaire. I remember it by the name of Jukcheomjang House' as it's a building in Jukcheomjeong. When the staff of the Provisional Government returned home from Shanghai in November 1945, he gifted this building to Kim Gu. It was then that the name changed to Gyeonggyojang House.   Actually, Choi Changhak wasn't a very patriotic man. He only provided this building to in an attempt to cover up his pro-Japanese activities during the Japanese Occupation of Korea.   After the liberation, Korea was in turmoil. The United States and Soviet Union installed their military governments in the south and north of Korea in September 1945, respectively. Albert once briefly stayed in Korea as a consultant to the U.S. military government.   At that time, Korea was in turmoil, as its people argued over remaining as a trustee territory ruled by the U.N.'s designation or establishing a new government. Gyeonggyojang House was the stronghold of the group that rejected the trusteeship and attempted to establish a unified government of South and North Korea.   In 1948, the Government of Korea was established. And Kim Gu began the unification movements. However, in June 1949, Kim Gu was shot by Ahn Duhui, an army second lieutenant at Gyeonggyojang House, and passed away. The death of Kim Gu, the iconic figure of Korea's independence movement, shocked many.  Today, Gyeonggyojang House, too, is restored to when Kim Gu was staying here. Provisional government staff stayed on the ground floor, and on the first floor is Kim Gu’s personal quarters. The basement is a small exhibition area where you can learn about the provisional government of Korea, Kim Gu, and Gyeonggyojang House. Take your time to look around, and we'll go to the next place.  We are headed to Schofield Memorial Hall located inside <Donuimun Museum Village>. Donuimun Gate was also called Seodaemun Gate. It's a complex area, so see the map to find your way around it. It's a cozy little place.

stories.title: Schofield Memorial Hall
stories.script: There you are. This small two-story house here is Schofield Memorial Hall. 33 representatives of the people of Joseon signed the Korean Declaration of Independence announced in the March 1st Movement, and the man who lived here, Dr. Frank Schofield, is often called the 34th representative of the people of Joseon, despite being a British Canadian. Unlike me, Dr. Schofield is a figure that occupies an intimate place in Korean history. That’s why we can call him an independence activist for Korea.  I knew Dr. Schofield through my husband. You remember that Albert became a correspondent of A.P. News before March 1st Movement, yes? My husband covered the massive demonstration by students at Namdaemun Gate on March 5th with Schofield as an A.P. News correspondent. At first, I thought Schofield was a correspondent like my husband. It turned out that Schofield was a professor who teaches microbiology and sanitary science at Severance College of Medicine.    Schofield gave himself a Korean name, '' Seok Hopil, and worked as a doctor and missionary. Schofield taught students at Severance College more than his medical knowledge. He encouraged responsibility as intellectuals and social participation. Schofield himself practiced these principles in his movements and gained strong faith from those around him. I heard that is why the Korean independent activities who planned the March First Independence Movement considered Schofield as the person to promote their movement to the outside world.  In fact, we foreigners didn't know of the plan of the March First Independence Movement in advance, except for one person, Schofield. Lee Yongseol, a student of Severance College, came to his house the day before and handed Schofield the Korean Declaration of Independence that he hid in his coat, and asked him to send it to the White House. Lee Gapseong, a member listed in the Korean Declaration of Independence as a staff member of Severance College, asked him in the morning of March 1st to take photographs of the movement to spread the news internationally.   Schofield put the camera on his bicycle and headed to Tapgol Park. And so was Schofield able to capture the day of the March First Independence Movement in photographs.    Schofield didn't stop here. Many Koreans were arrested by the Japanese military and suffered injuries from their brutal crackdown at the scene of the movement. Schofield went to the scene, captured the facts, and reported the brutality of Japan through newspapers. He was also in Seodaemun Prison, in which he met many students, including Yu Gwansun, and the scenes of the massacre at Jeam-ri and Goju-ri in Suwon.  Despite the threats made by the Japanese Empire, Schofield never stopped his movement against Japan. They couldn't do anything because Schofield was a British journalist. But, as Japan's pressure on Severance College mounted and his life was under threat, Schofield was forced to leave Korea in 1920.   Schofield was a true intellectual who stood up for people in a foreign land who faced injustice, risking his own life, and a doctor and missionary who loved Korea and its people. He was decorated with an Independence Medal in the Order of Merit for National Foundation, and his remains rest in the Independence Activists' section of the Seoul National Cemetery, which is a rare honour for a foreigner.  You can also find these descriptions inside the memorial hall. The 1st floor also has a small terrace where you can rest. After finishing our tour here, we will be heading to a place honouring yet another stranger who loved Korea.   Let's go to Ju Sigyeong Garden behind Sejong Center for the Performing Arts.

stories.title: Ju Sigyeong Garden (Hulbert's statue)
stories.script: This is Ju Sigyeong Garden. Named after Ju Sigyeong, a Hangeul scholar and a pride of Korea.  But now, aren't you curious why Ju Sigyeong and Hulbert's busts stand side by side?  In 1907, Emperor Gojong of the Korean Empire sent special envoys to the Hague, where the Hague Convention was being held, to regain Korea's diplomatic sovereignty that Japan had forcibly taken. As many of you would know, volunteered for the mission and attempted to help the Korean Empire by negotiating with the United States. If you don't see the name and just focus on his achievements, you'll picture a Korean independent activist.  One of the many reasons why he loved Korea was Hangeul. Hulbert researched Hangeul and promoted the value of the alphabet system.   Hulbert first visited Korea in 1886. He was appointed as an English teacher at Yukyeong Academy, an institute that Joseon established to teach English. But he was more fascinated by Hangeul and researched and taught it with passion. He learned the Korean language and the alphabet to teach his students and discovered the excellence of Hangeul.  Hulbert was certain that he couldn't find an alphabetic system that could rival Hangeul anywhere in the world. In 1889, Hulbert published an article in a New York newspaper that introduced the value and excellence of Hangeul, and in 1892, he even analyzed the outstanding characteristics of Hangeul in a journal article. And he also authored 'Saminpilgi', also known as Geographical Gazetteer of Korea, the first Korean textbook that has the meaning of things that all nobility and common folks must know.   Ju Sigyeong is the person who learned linguistics from Hulbert at Pai Chai Academy, a modern secondary academy established by missionary Appenzeller in 1885. Ju Sigyeong and Hulbert participated in the production of Tongnip Sinmun, a newspaper issued by the Independence Club, and continued their studies in Hangeul. Now, we take spacing in Korean for granted, but guess what? Hulbert was the person who adopted spacing in Tongnip Shinmun! Wow, I'm surprised as well.   Hulbert believed that a people with such an outstanding letter system, Hangeul, could not be colonized. Hangeul made him fall in love with Korea and the motivation to carry out independent movements for Korea. Homer Hulbert was yet another stranger who loved Korea more than some Koreans. Now you know why Ju Sigyeong and Hulbert's statues stand side by side!

stories.title: Information for the Starting Point of Course 4 – Birthplace of Bang Jeonghwan
stories.audioTitle: Information for the Starting Point of Course 4 – Birthplace of Bang Jeonghwan
stories.script: Did you enjoy the trail? I was delighted to tell you about Dilkusha that I loved and the beautiful scenery around it and the people who lived during the same age as me.   Course 4 will begin at the Birthplace of Bang Jeonghwan, a child rights activist. I am certain that course 4 will have more special stories about Jongno for you. Continue walking the trails of modern history, Modern Jongno.

stories.title: Introducing the Presenter 2
stories.script: "Hello? My name is Kim Gyeonghwa, and I'm here to be your guide on 'The Path of Independence and Quislingism.' 아, I understand my name might not ring a bell for most of you. I attended Paiwha Girls' School more than a century ago, and I'm proud of the meaningful role I played during that era. Now, since my old school, Paiwha Girls' School, is part of this course, I've been given the honor of being your guide.  I hold a deep affection for this neighborhood. It warms my heart to revisit the paths I once walked to school and the places where I used to spend time with my friends. But most of all, I'm overjoyed that my alma mater, nestled on the foot of Inwangsan Mountain, still stands warmly and proudly.  But it does bring about some mixed feelings when it comes to introducing the events that took place here and the people who lived in this neighborhood. Now, let's embark on the 'The Path of Independence and Quislingism.' The route I'll be guiding you through traces the footsteps of modern historical figures on the eastern side of Inwangsan Mountain.  First, let's introduce the neighborhood. The backdrop of this area is Inwangsan Mountain which surrounds the northwestern part of Hanyang, the capital of the Joseon Dynasty, which is present-day Seoul. Located to the west of Gyeongbokgung, the grandest royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, Inwangsan Mountain is a majestic rocky mountain, adorned with lush forests and clear streams. So, in the early days of the Joseon Dynasty, it was a place where royal family members, enjoying high social status but somewhat distant from political power, chose to reside and embraced the beauty of nature.  The atmosphere underwent a significant change from the late Joseon period to modern times. Those in power began to visit Inwangsan Mountain to appreciate its landscapes, and during the period when our sovereignty was threatened, pro-Japanese collaborators even built elaborate homes here. Furthermore, Its proximity to Hanyang, Gyeongseong, and later Seoul, which now lies at the center of the city, made it a place where modern scholars and artists contemplated and created their works while trying to capture the spirit of their times. Speaking of literature, it is still a bit challenging for me  Now, would you like to take a walk with me through the beauty of nature and the rich history along the slopes of Inwangsan Mountain? Our first stop is the Yun Dongju Literary Museum. "

stories.title: Yun Dongju Literary Museum and  Yun Dongju Hill
stories.audioTitle: Yun Dongju Literary Museum and  Yun Dongju Hill
stories.script: This place is quite famous. The Literary Museum here has a unique appearance. Yun Dongju Literary Museum was established by renovating the Cheongun Waterworks Booster Station and its water tank. It's truly remarkable to think that a massive water tank has been repurposed into an exhibition space. While literature might still be a bit challenging for me, I have a sense that this space, which once carried water through the waterworks, now conveys an abundance of literary spirit to people. The concept of using the waterworks booster station as a literary museum was inspired by the image of a well depicted in Yun Dongju's poem 'Self-Portrait. Though the space isn't very large, it houses Yun Dongju's works, letters, and personal belongings, offering a vivid recollection of the young poet who cherished our language and our literature.  The presence of the Yun Dongju Literary Museum in this spot has a strong connection to Yun Dongju Hill situated just above it. It's told that Yun Dongju, during his years of study in Seoul, used to stroll and contemplate in this area with friends, where he contemplated and composed some of his most renowned poems, including 'Seo-si' and ‘The Night of Counting Stars.’   Yun Dongju Hill is home to a memorial stone commemorating the exquisite poem ‘Seo-si.' Reading this poem has a soothing effect on me, and at the same time, it also evokes a warm feeling. I might have gone on a bit of a tangent there. Here's an interesting story. When they put in this memorial stone, they apparently brought soil from the poet's grave in Bukgan-do Yongjeong to this location. So, you could say it's yet another space where the poet's footsteps are preserved.  Now, shall we take a moment to learn more about the poet Yun Dongju? It took a bit of research, but it was truly rewarding.  Poet Yun Dongju was born in 1917 in Myeongdong-chon, Bukgan-do. He's actually much younger than me, isn't he? Haha. By the way, Myeongdongchon was a Korean settlement established by immigrants from Hamgyeong-do in 1899, and it was a place where new learning and Protestantism were embraced from an early age. The poet attended Myeongdong School in this area.   Yun Dongju began composing poetry and reading numerous books from a young age, but it was when he entered Yeonhui College in 1938 that he truly blossomed. There, he attended lectures by Korean linguist Choi Hyeonbae on the Korean language, historian Son Jintae on history, and English scholar Lee Yangha on literature. These experiences helped nurture his sensitivity towards our nation's language, writing, and spirit.  In fact, I hold the teachings of my alma mater, Paiwha Girls' School, in high regard as well. Especially, I miss figures like Mr. Namgung Eok, a journalist and modern Enlightenment thinker, and Mrs. Cha Mirisa. Mrs. Cha Mirisa guided us on how to think and act as Koreans and intellectuals, regardless of being a woman.  Now, Let's continue with the story of Yun Dongju, the poet. Yun Dongju grappled with the harsh reality of his homeland being a colony and his own identity as someone born in Bukgan-do, which was beyond the ambiguous border of the nation. He expressed these thoughts through his poetry.   Yun Dongju, who often viewed life and the world through his poetry, went through a period of not writing any poems for a whole year. It was when the war began engulfing everything. The poet couldn't write poetry for a while due to his inner struggles, but later, he presented verses that candidly expressed his wanderings and dilemmas. His famous work, ‘Seo-si' was created during this period.  After graduating from Yeonhui College, Yun Dongju left for Japan in 1942 to pursue his studies. However, while in Japan, he and his cousin Song Mongkyu were arrested by Japanese police on charges related to the 'Joseon independence movement.' As it is widely known, he tragically became a subject of human experimentation and lost his life in Fukuoka Prison.  While his pure and innocent soul was extinguished, Yun Dongju possessed another dimension to his character.   In 2010, the trial records of Yun Dongju were made public. During his trial in Japan, he courageously voiced his beliefs, saying, 'We must nurture the skills and national identity of Joseon peoples to establish the groundwork for the independence movement,' and he emphatically declared, 'For the liberation of Joseon, Japan must be defeated in the Greater East Asian War.’  Yun Dongju had intended to publish his poems before going to study in Japan, but under Japanese colonial rule, his poems couldn't be published. It was only after liberation that his poetry collection, titled 'Heaven, Wind, Stars, and Poetry,' could finally see the light of day.  Let's now take our steps to another location where his legacy is preserved. Yun Dongju may have once walked the path you're on right now. How does that make you feel? Doesn't it evoke something special within you? It's indeed a blessing that we can now freely read and appreciate Yun Dongju's poems.  Now, from here, I'll lead you along the Inwangsan Forest Trail towards Suseong-dong Valley. This is the path that follows the Inwangsan Beltway, a creation that emerged as a result of the 1.21 Incident' we talked about earlier. It's a trail consisting of wooden walkways and hiking paths along the foothills of Inwangsan Mountain. It might be a bit of a journey, but shall we walk together while listening to his poems?  (Recites several poems)  <Seosi (Prelude)> Until the day I die, I wish I will have no shame when I look up at the sky. It pains me to see even the wind rustling the leaves. I will love every dying thing like singing the stars. And I will walk the only path that is laid out before me.  Tonight again, the wind is rustling the stars.  <Jahwasang (Self-portrait)> I walked around the spur of the mountain  to a remote well by the rice field and I looked into it, in silent solitude.  In the well, the moon was bright, the clouds were passing, the sky was big, the blue wind was blowing, and the autumn was there.  And there was a man. I didn't like the man I saw for some reason, so I turned around and left.  On second thought on my way back though, I felt sorry for the man. So I go back there, and see the man still in the well.  I didn't like the man I saw again, so I turned around and left. On second thought on my way back though, I missed the man.  In the well, the moon was bright, the clouds were passing, the sky was big,  the blue wind was blowing, the autumn was here, and there was a man like an old memory.  <Gil (Street)> I lost something. I didn’t know what and where I lost it, so I rummage through my pockets with both of my hands and I go out to the street.  There are stones, stones, and stones and the street winds through the endless stone wall.  The wall with a locked iron gate casts a shadow over the street  and the street runs from the morning to the evening. It runs from the evening to the morning.  I touch the stone wall and shed some tears. But when I look at the sky, it’s so blue that it makes feel ashamed.  The reason I walk this street that is so barren without any plants, is because there is another me from the past on the other side of the wall.  I just keep on living only because I’m still looking for something I lost.  Strolling with his poems feels like strolling beside the poet. The view is breathtaking as you reflect on his verses. It's truly remarkable, isn't it?  When I was in school, more than a hundred years ago, Seoul was called Gyeongseong. The atmosphere of the Joseon era and the essence of the Korean Empire, established in 1897, were still very much alive. Giwajip, where Joseon people congregated, adorned the city and the hillsides.  However, there were new, massive buildings that had emerged, unlike anything seen before. The most notable among these was the immense Japanese Government-General of Korea that stood across from Geunjeongjeon Hall of Gyeongbokgung Palace. Additionally, the Joseon Shrine on Namsan, was constructed as if to dominate the land of Joseon.  But now, it has become the Seoul we are familiar with today. Seoul—what an inspiring name it holds. As I look at Seoul, it feels as though tears could well up. When you think about it, 'we' are truly remarkable and extraordinary individuals. Let's move forward with our journey to the next destination.

stories.title: Guard Post Book Café
stories.script: This place offers a stunning view of Seoul while enjoying a cup of tea and reading a book. It's said that this place wasn't always this romantic. It was originally built as a military facility to protect Cheong Wa Dae after the 1.21 Incident and served as a guard post on Inwangsan for over 50 years.  However, in 2020, its purpose changed. It became a book cafe where you can enjoy tea. Over time, things often change in their use. If the direction is towards a more peaceful one, that's all the better. From a stark guard post to a book cafe – isn't it truly wonderful? Since we've been walking for quite a while, how about taking a short break?  If you intend to continue your journey past the Guard Post Book Cafe, the next destination is a bit further along the Inwangsan slope path. You'll encounter a sign guiding you to Suseongdong Valley. Simply follow the left path, which indicates the direction of Suseongdong Valley, and make your way downhill.  I'll meet you again at Suseongdong Valley.

stories.title: Suseongdong Valley
stories.script: Thank you for coming all the way. We're currently at Suseongdong Valley, one of the valleys within Inwangsan Mountain. This place, where water flows between the steep and rugged cliffs on the eastern side of Inwangsan Mountain, was renowned for its resonant and pure water sounds. That's why it's called Suseongdong, which means a neighborhood where the sound of water is loud. There have been significant changes in this area, and I'll provide more details shortly.  Not far from here, you can find Yun Dongju's boarding house. Yun Dongju used to leave his residence in the morning, walk up the middle peak of Inwangsan, and wash his face with water from Suseongdong Valley before heading to Yeonhui College.  Now, let's dive into the history of this neighborhood. In fact, there was a notable figure who had already appreciated the beauty of Suseongdong Valley. This person was Prince Anpyeong, the third son of King Sejong, the creator of Hangul. Prince Anpyeong built a villa known as ‘Bihaedang’ in this beautiful and scenic area near Gyeongbokgung Palace. Prince Anpyeong, who had an appreciation for arts and culture, had to maintain a certain distance from the political power of his era.  However, it appears that his interactions and associations with various individuals became problematic. Unfortunately, he was compelled to undergo a purge due to the actions of his own brother, Prince Suyang, who later ascended to the throne as King Sejo after dethroning his nephew King Danjong. Nevertheless, the memory of Prince Anpyeong's residence in Suseongdong Valley was esteemed throughout the Joseon era, and many visitors came to explore his footsteps.  You can still witness the evidence of its grandeur here, the ‘Giringyo Bridge’, situated in the heart of the stream, crafted from the rocks at the center of the water. A great artist like Gyeomjae Jeong Seon, reknowned for his Jin-gyeong sansuhwa during the late Joseon Dynasty, depicted this very bridge in his famous work, ‘Jang-dong palgyeong cheop.' I'm genuinely grateful that this bridge was depicted in the artwork by the artist from two centuries ago and remained in the same spot during my time, a century ago.  Back when I was attending school, the waterways of Suseongdong were so refreshing. The stream that originated from Inwangsan Mountain's Ongnyudong converged with the waters of Suseongdong Valley, forming the Ongnyudongcheon Stream. It then flowed downstream, joining with Baegundongcheon Stream and Nugakdongcheon Stream, ultimately forming what we know as Cheonggyecheon Stream today. Ah, here, the term 'Dongcheon,' in contrast to the name Baekseokdongcheon on the first route, actually means 'the village's waterway.’  But sadly, the waterway that used to flow along the foothills of Inwangsan Mountain is no longer visible in the village. Over time, they covered the waterway with concrete to create roads, which is why it has disappeared from view.  Apartments also encroached upon Suseongdong Valley. If you follow the road on the right side leading up towards the valley, you can see the remnants of apartments that seem out of place here. These are the remains of the Ogin-dong Experimental Apartments, a vast complex with a total of nine buildings, constructed in 1971. In 2008, they demolished the apartments, and the valley was restored to its current state. It's interesting how both removing nature and restoring its original form are considered progress. The assessment of values in this world indeed carries a profound and intriguing essence, doesn't it?  Now, it's time to leave Suseongdong Valley. Our next destination is down the road beneath the valley. If you walk a bit, you'll find a sign on the right side of the road that says ‘Yun Dongju’s Boarding House Site.' We'll continue our story from there.

stories.title: Yun Dongju’s Boarding House Site
stories.script: ‘Nusang-dong No. 9th.' This is the residence of the novelist Kim Song, where Yun Dongju used to board during his time at Yeonhui College. Unfortunately, the Hanok from that time is no longer standing, but you can still get a glimpse of what it was like through the sign on the building's wall that says 'Yun Dongju's Boarding House Site' and the photos displayed here.  In truth, during that era, there were many hanoks like this one here. So, the neighborhood had quite a charming atmosphere back then.  But Yun Dongju's stay here wasn't all that long. During his stay, he engaged in discussions about life, the era, and literature with his landlord Kim Song, roommate Jeong Byeonguk, and other literary figures who often visited. Perhaps those five months spent here were a contented time for him. It's said that he wrote several poems while living here.  Before departing for Japan to pursue his studies, he gathered 19 of his poems written here into three copies of poetry. One of these copies was presented to his mentor, Professor Lee Yangha, another was given to his junior, Jeong Byeonguk, and he kept one for himself.  However, the copies of poetry that Professor Lee Yangha and Yun Dongju possessed were lost during difficult times. Only one copy, the one that was held by his junior, Jeong Byeonguk, remains.  Jeong Byeonguk entrusted the manuscript to his hometown's mother, considering it 'as precious as life,' even as he was drafted into military service.  So, Yun Dongju's poetry, which had been concealed in the crockpot beneath Jeong Byeonguk's hometown house porch, could finally be published as a poetry collection named 'Sky, Wind, Stars, and Poetry,' along with other poems Yun Dongju had written during his lifetime, thanks to the efforts of his friends, poets Kang Cheojung and Jeong Jiyong.   Thanks to the friendship of Jeong Byeonguk, who treasured his friend's poems, and the mother's love that protected her son's heart, Yun Dongju's poems, which were as invaluable as the poet's life, could be preserved for future generations.   Alright, let's move on to the next location. As we walk a bit, I'll quietly recite one of my favorite poems by Yun Dongju. On the left, you'll see the Bak Nosu Art Museum.  아, here, you'll encounter traces of someone who led a life quite distinct from the poet Yun Dongju.

stories.title: Bak Nosu Art Museum (House area of Yun Deokyeong)
stories.audioTitle: Bak Nosu Art Museum (House area of Yun Deokyeong)
stories.script: The quaint two-story brick house in front of you is the Bak Nosu Art Museum, opened in 2013. The house belonged to the painter Bak Nosu, who resided here for over 40 years after purchasing it in 1973. Eventually, he donated both the house and his artworks to Jongno-gu, and now it serves as the  Jongno Park No-soo Museum. While it's a heartwarming story, the history of this house has a somewhat different atmosphere.  This house was built in 1937. Yun Deokyeong, a figure who constructed several houses in this neighborhood, built this Western-style house for his daughter and son-in-law.   The name Yun Deokyeong sends shivers down my spine, just hearing it.  When we talk about traitors or pro-Japanese collaborators who signed the Eulsa Treaty (Eulsa Neugyak) in 1905, relinquishing diplomatic rights to Japan -commonly known as the Five Eulsa Traitors- one of the initial names that comes to mind is Lee Wanyong. However, Yun Deokyeong is no less significant among them. In 1910, he played a part in the signing ofJapan’s annexation of Korea, betraying the country as one of the ‘Gyeongsul Traitors.' It's infuriating to think that his house was situated next to my alma mater, Paiwha Girls' School.  What's even more astonishing is that Yun Deokyeong was a member of the imperial family, being the uncle of Empress Sunjeong, the last empress of the Korean Empire. When his niece, the daughter of his younger brother Yun Taekyeong, ascended to the position of empress in 1906, Yun Deokyeong was on his way up. However, all his influence and power were purely self-serving.   Though Yun Deokyeoung was a royal relative, he took on a prominent role in supporting Japan and even received commendations from the Japanese government. Additionally, he became a member of the Daedong Hakhoe sponsored by Ito Hirobumi. After Ito's death, he proposed a 'Memorial Ceremony for Ito' and recited a eulogy for Ito Hirobumi.  In 1910, he took a leading role in surrendering the country's sovereignty. In recognition of such actions, Japan rewarded him with the title of Marquess and a staggering 460,000 won, equivalent to 2.3 billion in today's currency.  Yun Deokyeong used the money gained from betraying the country to purchase land above the Ongnyudongcheon Stream, in the area of Ogin-dong. On more than half of the land in Ogin-dong, he built an extravagant Western-style mansion called 'Byeoksusanjang,' often referred to as the palace of Hanyang. This mansion, resembling European castles, was a two-story brick house with a basement and attic, using only materials imported from abroad. The living room ceiling even had an aquarium for raising goldfish, earning it the nickname 'Goldfish House.' Yun Dukyoung's collaboration with the Japanese was so notorious that everyone looked at the mansion with disdain.  In the midst of such collaborators, I found myself questioning the significance of a powerless student like me participating in the independence movement. However, despite my limited strength, I wholeheartedly shouted 'For the independence of Korea' because the independence movement is a righteous cause. I learned that the collective will of many people has the potential to change the world. Even now, recalling the rallying cry of 'For the independence of Korea' from March 1919 warms my heart.  Perhaps in response to the criticism, Yun Deokyeong repurposed Byeoksusanjang into a facility for the religious group 'Hongmanjahoe.' Subsequently, he constructed a traditional Korean house within its premises, where he resided. Additionally, he built several other houses nearby, and the house constructed for his concubine still stands today.  And just below Byeoksusanjang, near Ongnyudongcheon Stream, is where his daughter's house was constructed, now transformed into the Bak Nosu Art Museum.   Observing these traces, it becomes evident that the footprints of collaboration hold a significance as profound as those of the independence movement.   Indeed, the location where Yun Deokyeong built his house has been a favored location for influential families such as the Andong Kim clan and the Uiryeong Nam clan since the Joseon era. They have long established their residences, and appreciated the clear water flowing beneath Inwangsan and the splendid forest. Roughly 200 years ago, middle-class technicians formed a poetry gathering called 'Sisa' in this very area.   Among them, the renowned ‘Songseogwon Sisa' was portrayed in paintings by artists like Kim Hongdo and Lee Insang. Moreover, Chusa Kim Jeonghui was commissioned to carve the Sisa name 'Songsukwon' on a cliff. The cliff bearing the inscription ‘Songseogwon’ is situated near the art museum.  Byeoksusanjang, renowned as the palace of Hanyang, functioned as the headquarters for the United Nations Commission for the Unification and Rehabilitation of Korea (UNCURK), established by the UN in 1950 after liberation. Following a fire in 1966, it was left abandoned and eventually completely demolished in 1972. Even though the structure is no longer standing, the history of collaboration, selling out the country, and betraying the nation will never be erased.  Let's continue our journey. As we walk down the path, we'll encounter Tongin Market.

stories.title: Tongin Market
stories.script: Tongin Market might seem like any other market, but there's something interesting hidden within. Haha, there's a dosirak cafe right inside the market.  The sight of delicious food brings back memories of my school days, chatting with friends while munching on snacks. Here, you can purchase traditional Korean coins, called 'yeopjeon,' and use them to acquire rice and side dishes to assemble your own lunchbox.  It's a Joseon-era-style activity I've never experienced. If you're hungry, how about trying a lunchbox from there? Just describing it is making my mouth water. If you continue down the path of Tongin Market, you'll reach the main road, 'Jahamun-ro.' When you head right, you'll come across a sign indicating the birthplace of King Sejong. King Sejong, was the third son of King Taejong, born here in 1397 at the Junsubang.  So, that's why they named this area Sejong Village. Just a year after King Sejong was born, King Taejong moved to Gaeseong, following King Jeongjong. If King Sejong had been born just a little later, his hometown might have been Gaeseong.  Now, the place we're heading to is a small Giwajip called ‘I Sang's House.'

stories.title: I Sang's House
stories.script: "This small building, covered with glass windows, concrete walls, and Giwa, is ‘I Sang's House.' It stands as a remnant of the birthplace where the poet and novelist I Sang, who was active in the 1930s, spent about 20 years of his life from the age of 3.  I Sang's real name was Kim Haegyeong. He was adopted by a childless uncle and began living here. During that era, this place featured a quite spacious Hanok, surpassing 300 square meters. However, it's challenging to find such a grand sight in today's landscape.  During his youth, I Sang showed talent in both art and writing. However, under pressure from his father to revive the declining family, he graduated from the architecture department at Kyungsung Institute of Engineering. He later became an architectural technician under the Japanese Colonial Government of Korea. Even while working in this field, he continued to publish poems and stories under the pen name ‘I Sang.'  Growing up in a colonized land stripped of sovereignty and an indifferent family, I Sang expressed his anxiety, fear, self-division, and self-awareness in the harsh reality in a uniquely unconventional manner.  His innovative and radical writing was embraced as a new experiment in the literary world, labeled as 'Modern.' However, I Sang's attempts also faced significant criticism. His poem 'Ogamdo,' serialized in the Chosun Joongang Daily, received strong protests from readers and was even discontinued. I've also read the poem that starts with ’13ChildrenRunDownTheRoad.’, and the only thing that stuck with me was the 'Child' who fled in panic—it was quite a perplexing poem. I Sang often used mathematical symbols or disrupted grammar, making his works challenging for readers to grasp.  Though I Sang lived a short 27 years, he left behind a wealth of works. His poems, novels, and essays showcased a unique language, exceptional psychological portrayal, and a combination of grammar disruption and creation. After his departure, I Sang was acclaimed for paving a new path in modern literature.  ‘Do you know the genius turned into a specimen?’ This is the beginning of his famous novel 'Wings.' Some view it as a comforting word he offered to himself, unrecognized in his lifetime.  I Sang's House is a place where his writings and materials are exhibited. In one of the inner rooms, you can watch a short video lecture to understand I Sang's literary world. "

stories.title: House of Hong Geonik
stories.script: As you follow Pirundae-ro 1-gil, you'll come across a refined modern Hanok on the right side within a small alley. It's the House of Hong Geonik, built in 1936.  The building is a large-scale modern Hanok comprising Daemunchae, Haengnangchae, Sarangchae, Anchae, and a Byeolchae, which even features Binggo, a traditional ice storage facility and a courtyard. It's a spacious Hanok that you don't come across every day.  This place is designated as a Seoul Folk Cultural Heritage, and anyone can take a break and relax here. If you've been walking for a while and feeling tired, how about stretching your legs and taking a moment to enjoy the ambiance of the Hanok?  The next destination is my alma mater, Paiwha Girls' School. Once you leave I Sang's House and head towards Inwangsan, you'll reach an intersection. From there, walk to the left and follow Pirundae-ro on your left side. You'll find ‘Pirundae-ro 1-gil’ leading to the main gate of Paiwha Girls' High School and Baewha Women's University.  Now, the next place that we will visit is the university tthe place we're heading to is a small Giwajip called ‘I Sang's House.'  Our next stop is Paihwa Girls' School where I attended.

stories.title: Baewha Women's University (Women’s Monument for Anti-Japanese Resistance Movement, Pirundae)
stories.audioTitle: Baewha Women's University (Women’s Monument for Anti-Japanese Resistance Movement, Pirundae)
stories.script: Finally, we've arrived at Baewha Women's University, my alma mater. But it looks quite different from when I attended. Back then, it was a small building known as Paiwhahakdang Academy or Paiwha Girls' School. Now, it has evolved into Paiwha Girls' Middle School, Paiwha Girls' High School, and Baewha Women's University. However, you can still spot the building where I used to study on one side of the campus. It's truly prideful that, after over a century, it still stands as a school for Korean girls. Oh, by the way, outsiders are not allowed inside on weekdays, so you can only visit the campus on Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays when the school is not in session. Be sure to check the days before you plan your visit!  The person who founded our school was Missionary Josephine Campbell. She arrived in Korea in 1897 and dedicated 23 years to the education of Korean women. Mrs. Campbell believed that through learning, we could become better Koreans. At school, we had the opportunity to study a variety of subjects, including the Bible, English, Korean, Chinese classics, history, and geography.  Oh, Mr. Namgung Eok, who taught history, was a remarkable man. He was a famous figure who founded the Independence Association, served as the president of the Hwangseong sinmun, and played a leading role in the patriotic enlightenment movement. Mr. Namgung Eok came to our school and taught us English grammar and Korean history from 1910. With his personally written history book, 'Stories of Joseon,' he instilled in us a sense of national pride and the awareness that we must reclaim our country.  We also attempted the Independent Movement in 1919, but it failed due to pre-censorship. However, we couldn't stay silent. On March 1, 1920, exactly one year after the 3.1 Independence Movement, around 40 students and I climbed to the top of Pirundae behind the school.  And from the top of there, where you can see the entire Seoul city, we fervently shouted ‘For the independence of Korea.' We carried out the March First Independence Movement that had failed even after receiving the Korean Declaration of Independence the previous year due to detection. It was the day when female students from Paiwha Girls’ School resolutely shouted, ‘For the independence of Korea.'  ‘For the independence of Joseon,' ‘For the independence of Korea.' Saying these words still stirs something passionate in my heart, even when I think about it now.   My alma mater and our country remember and commemorate our efforts. Next to the Paiwha Memorial Hall, there's a special sculpture depicting a woman from over a hundred years ago, adorned in elegant Hanbok. She is illuminating a present-day female student in the current Paiwha Girls' High School uniform, printing the Tae Guk Gi. It's a touching scene of our past selves lighting the way for future generations. Oh, and I spot my name written on the back of the sculpture: ‘Kim Kyunghwa.'  Though my time in Seodaemun Prison was tough, I have no regrets. It was the right path, and now, with many people in Korea remembering and honoring not just me but 'us.'  Now, shall we go find Pirundae where we once shouted, ‘For the independence of Korea?’ You can easily locate it by heading back behind Paiwha Girls' High School. The red letters carved into the rock, spelling Pirundae,' are quite impressive, aren't they? This spot, nestled in the middle of Inwangsan, offers a breathtaking view of the entire Hanyang, present-day Seoul. It was once the residence of Yi Hangbok, who served as the Daejehak (First Academician) and Young Euijung (Premier) during the Joseon Dynasty in the time of King Seonjo. And ‘Pirun’ is his pen name. On the right side of the Pirundae inscription, his descendant Yi Yuwon shared his reflections after visiting this place in 1889.  When I was in school, climbing up Pirundae provided a panoramic view of Seoul. So we shouted ‘For the independence of Korea’ from here, making our voices echo across all directions of Seoul. It's a bit disappointing now that the view of Seoul is obstructed by the school.  Now, let's take our steps to the final destination, Hwanghakjeong Archery Range. Pass through the main gate of the school, head down towards the Sajikdan where ceremonies for the gods of land and grain were held during the Joseon Dynasty. Follow the path to the right around the Sajikdan wall, and you'll reach Hwanghakjeong Archery Range.

stories.title: Hwanghakjeong Archery Range
stories.script: Hwanghakjeong Archery Range was originally a pavilion constructed in 1898 during the Daehan Empire era under the reign of Emperor Gojong, where it stood not here, but in Gyeonghuigung. In an effort to promote traditional Korean archery, Emperor Gojong relocated Hwanghakjeong Archery Range near the northern wall of Hoisangjeon in Gyeonghuigung Palace and opened it to the public. During that period, Gyeonghuigung Palace had most of its buildings either demolished or relocated to reconstruct Gyeongbokgung Palace. The remaining land was distributed as farmland for other palaces, rendering it incapable of serving as a palace any longer.  In 1910, Japan established Kyungsung Middle School in Gyeonghuigung Palace, utilizing the remaining structures as school buildings. Upon signing Eulsa Neugyak (Japan-Korea Treaty of 1905), Japan ensured that no place related to the Korean royal family remained intact, including Gyeongbokgung Palace, the primary palace of Joseon. Then, in 1922, citing the construction of the Official Residence for Monopoly Department on the Gyeonghuigung site, Japan relocated the remaining Hwanghakjeong Archery Range.  They relocated it to the vicinity of Sajikdan, where ceremonies were conducted during the Joseon Dynasty to pray for a prosperous harvest from the gods of land and grain. Japan's intention was to destroy both Gyeonghuigung Palace and Sajikdan Altar.  It's a place marked by the pain of history, but still, Hwanghakjeong Archery Range is referred to as ‘The First Place of Traditional Korean Archery.' Despite the change in location, it's fortunate that it still serves its original role as a pavilion for archery. Near Hwanghakjeong Archery Range, there's an archery exhibition hall where you can explore more about traditional Korean archery. If you're interested, it's definitely worth a visit.  Oh, among the women I know, many enjoy shooting arrows. Archery doesn't discriminate between genders. The thrill of releasing the arrow from the bow and watching it pierce the target after leaving the string is truly exhilarating.

stories.title: Information for the Starting Point of Course 3 - Dilkusha
stories.audioTitle: Information for the Starting Point of Course 3 - Dilkusha
stories.script: We've walked many paths together, read heart-wrenching poetry, and shared deep anger. We've sought out the sites where the spirit of independence was awakened, shouting ‘For the independence of Korea.'  Contemplating how to live is a task given to everyone, regardless of the era. I, too, always learned and dreamed of a better life, a better world at school. As a result, I concluded that independence was imperative. Despite the Japanese claim of equality between Korea and Japan on the surface, there was always discrimination. Some argued that collaborating with the Japanese was for the good of the country, but in the end, it was just an excuse for a traitor to prosper while others suffered.  Which path should we walk? I believe we should choose the path of righteousness and consideration for all people, rather than the path of mere success and certainty.  Now, it's time for us to part. The next guide awaits at Dilkusha, a little uphill from Inwangsan Mountain towards Jongno Culture and Sports Center. Someone with a different perspective from mine will be waiting at the door to guide you on a new path.  Thank you, and until we meet again someday.

stories.title: Segeomjeong
stories.script: "Hello? Testing, testing. Hello? Can you hear me? Haha. This is my first time as a guide, so it feels a bit awkward.  Welcome to Jongno Modern Street, everyone. It is my pleasure to be your guide for the first tour course. I’m originally from Gangwon-do, and I studied in Busan, so my way of speaking might have a bit of a rustic flavor, but I hope you can bear with it.  I'm Choi Gyusik, Chief of Police at Jongno Police Station. Did you know that in January 1968, a North Korean special force attempted to attack Cheong Wa Dae? It is known as the Kim Sinjo Incident in South Korea. You might have heard it from the news. At the time, I was responsible for containing them at Jongno Police Station during that incident.   This tour course is titled <-gil,> because it has a lot to do with the January 21st Incident that took place on January 21, 1968. It was an incident where 31 armed communist guerrillas sent from North Korea attempted to cross the military demarcation line (MDL) and attack Cheong Wa Dae. Fortunately, it ended in failure, but nevertheless, it shocked the nation at the time and triggered some significant changes in South Korea.  One of them was a change of the law that required any Korean over 17 to carry an ID card called the Resident Registration Card. And the reserve forces system, which requires individuals to undergo military training again after completing their mandatory military service, was also introduced after this incident. Most importantly, it brought back memories of the tragedy of the Korean War, which began on June 25th. During the war, many Koreans had to flee across the Han River to escape North Korean attacks. As industrialization progressed, and the population in the northern part of Seoul, Gangbuk, increased rapidly, the government made efforts to develop Gangnam starting in 1963, but progress was slow. Leaving a familiar place is not easy, after all. However, the incident served as a catalyst for substantial development in Gangnam, accelerating its growth. The increased awareness of North Korean aggression led to a shift in people's attitudes, and plans were implemented.   Well, I guess it's hard to view the January 21st Incident as just an event involving a few dozen armed communist guerrillas infiltrating. I'll provide more details related to this as we continue. Now, let's begin our journey.   Before you stands a neat yet elegant pavilion, Segeomjeong. While this place isn't a 'modern,' contemporary space, there are several reasons why I chose Segeomjeong as the starting point for the first leg of our journey.   The first reason is the beautiful scenery of Segeomjeong. It's still beautiful today, but during the Joseon period, it was a place frequented by many scholars called ‘seonbi’, including the renowned Confucian scholar Jeong Yagyong. In the past, the layout was a bit different, with a courtyard on the side where the road is now, so Segeomjeong must have had an even more delightful ambiance. The second reason is that the name of this pavilion, Segeomjeong, is related to today's journey. The name, 'Sword-Washed Pavilion,' originates from the fact that key figures of the Injo Restoration, which dethroned Prince Gwanghae and established King Injo, made their oath here before entering the capital city. As such, Segeomjeong has its origins in a coup event, symbolizing the gateway to Hanyang. During the 1.21 Incident, armed communist guerrillas were also found in this area at that time.  My introduction and explanation did get a bit lengthy, didn't they? Well then, let's proceed to the next location. Shall we take a short walk along the road next to us, ''Segeomjeong-ro'? "

stories.title: Tangchundae Historical Marker
stories.script: "This historical marker indicates that this area was once known as Tangchundae. Tangchundae was located around the current Segeomjeong Elementary School area, and was named for its spacious and flat terrain. Since the Silla period, there was a Buddhist temple called Jangeuisa here, and during the early Joseon period, scholars were granted a form of sabbatical to study in this area. It is also known as a playground used by Prince Yeonsan, infamous for his tyrannical behavior. Prince Yeonsan engaged in immoral activities with palace ladies here and ultimately faced his downfall. Perhaps due to this history, King Yeongjo relocated Chongyungcheong, which had been responsible for military affairs in this area, and changed the name from Tangchundae to Yeonyungdae, symbolizing its military significance.   By the way, following the Japanese Invasions of Korea between 1592 and 1598 and the Second Manchu Invasion of Korea in 1636 during the Qing Dynasty, King Sukjong developed a strong interest in the defense of the city wall, Hanyangdoseong, or the Seoul City Wall. Above all, having experienced two wars, King Sukjong came to believe that it was not desirable for a king to flee but thought that he should fight alongside the people of Hanyang. So, he decided to reconstruct the fortress on Bukhansan Mountain, which had previously been an earthen fortification, and fortify it with stone walls. During this period, the soldiers of Bukhansanseong Fortress built a storage facility for military provisions in the south of the fortress, which was named ' Pyeongchang’, that's right. The name ‘Pyeongchang-dong' has its origins in this place.  However, with Bukhansanseong Fortress to the north and Hanyangdoseong to the south, it left ‘Pyeongchang’ vulnerable to external threats. So, there was a need for an additional fortress to protect the valuable food storage. To address this issue and establish a connection between Hanyangdoseong and Bukhansanseong Fortress, a new fortress was built, which is the fortress known as Tangchundaeseong Fortress, named after this place, Tangchundae.  After the January 21st Incident, significant changes occurred in this area.  Also, the northern part of Jongno, which is the current Baegak area, experienced transportation problems, making it difficult to receive external support. That's why plans were made to construct roads in the Baegak and Inwangsan Mountain area to ease the movement of many people. It marked a significant change in mindset. We came to realize that attempting to enforce strict control to protect Cheong Wa Dae was actually leading to more problems.  Here we have the path known as the 'Bugak Skyway,' originally named Bugaksan Road. 아, The original name of Bugak was Baegak. Bugak Skyway is a path that starts at Changuimun Gate and passes through Baegak, connecting to Jeongneung and Miari. During its construction, Inwang Skyway was established, linking Jahamun Gate to Sajikdan Altar, which is now known as Inwangsan Road. It's a road that allows you to enjoy the scenic beauty of Seoul. Midway along the Bugak Skyway, they even built octagonal pavilions, creating an unexpected tourist attraction for the people of Seoul. They also significantly widened the once narrow and winding Segeomjeong-ro and developed the Pyeongchang-dong area.  At that time, this area was quite remote and desolate after sunset, which is hard to imagine now.  Now, our next destination is just a short walk away. You'll find a small park with a marker, and this is where Jojiseo used to be. There's a small milestone here. "

stories.title: Jojiseo Site
stories.script: "Within the tidy sports park, you'll find a signboard. This is the location where Jojiseo, originally an office for paper production, used to stand. When it was first established during King Taejong’s reign, it was called Jojiso, but during the reign of King Sejo, it was renamed Jojiseo.  According to historical records, around 90 skilled artisans worked here to produce high-quality paper, which was used for diplomatic documents. In Korea, paper was primarily made from the mulberry tree, ensuring its excellent quality. After the scholars compiled the Joseonwangjosillok, or Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, which is recognized as a UNESCO Memory of the World, they would wash the draft in the Segeomjeong Stream here to remove the ink. Then, they would provide the cleaned parchment to Jojiseo for recycling and the production of new paper.  The Korean word ‘hanji’ was coined to distinguish it from Western paper and Japanese paper called ‘washi’. During the Joseon period, it was simply called 'johi,' which means 'paper.'  The reason they established the office for paper production here was due to the presence of a clear stream in this area. Now, we'll cross the stream and head into a somewhat special space. While there are many side trails, the main path is not too intricate. Our destination is ‘Baeksasil.'  First, cross the bridge from this point, then follow the path beside the convenience store, heading towards Hyuntongsa Temple. As you continue along the path leading to Hyuntongsa Temple, and you reach a peaceful forest with a narrow trail, you're on the right path. Walk a little on that trail, and you'll come across the remnants of an old building to your left.  I'll provide further guidance from that spot "

stories.title: Baeksasilgyegok Valley and Byeolseo
stories.script: "Hello, I’m Choi Gyusik. I hope you haven’t forgotten my name in the meantime.  Throughout your walk, I hope you’ve been filled with amazement. Many people entering this path often express their astonishment, saying, ‘How can such a place exist in the heart of Seoul?’ Yes, indeed. What a tranquil and inviting forest path! They even say there are salamanders in the gently flowing brook.  Now, to listen to my story, you might want to take a seat on one of the building’s foundations or benches.  The preservation of the Baeksasilgyegok Valley that you’ve seen today is also connected to the January 21st Incident. This incident not only led to the establishment of new pathways but also increased security measures around Baegak near Cheong Wa Dae. As a result, access and development in the Baeksasil area have been restricted. These measures have allowedBaeksasil to retain its current appearance. When we delve into history, we sometimes discover that unexpected outcomes arise from particular events.  Now, let’s talk about the story of the building that used to be here, even though it’s now an empty space. During the Joseon period, scholars who had a deep appreciation for the arts and culture couldn’t resist the charm of this beautiful scenery. If you look to the left at the end of this valley, you’ll find a large rock with the inscription ‘Baekseokdongcheon.’ This inscription signifies that Baekseok is a place where even a divine hermit would choose to stay.  Here, Baekseok refers to the area behind Baegak. The name Baegak means ‘the foremost mountain,’ and also means ‘a mountain with gleaming white rocks.’ So, this area, nestled at the foothills of Baegak, was named ‘Baekseok,’ and from there, it seems the name ‘Baeksasil’ was given, representing the neighborhood within Baekseok.  For a while, the focus was on the word ‘Baeksa’ in ‘Baeksasil,’ and it was thought to be related to ‘Baeksa Yi Hangbok.’ The buildings in this area were also presumed to be associated with Yi Hangbok, a historical figure from the Joseon period. However, doubts arose regarding whether ‘Baeksasil’ truly carried that meaning. Researchers conducted searches for related documents and found records that in the 19th century, a person named Hong Woogil owned a place called ‘Baekseoksil’ in the vicinity of Baekseokdongcheon. Before that, this area had connections with notable calligraphers of the late Joseon period, like Kim Jeonghui and Cho Myeonho.  Discovering historical roots can be quite a challenging task, can’t it? The building that used to be here was called ‘Byeolseo,’ much like the villas of today. Therefore, they highly appreciated the scenic beauty. Above, you can find buildings like Sarangchae and Anchae, while below, there’s a pond and the remnants of a hexagonal pavilion platform.  To be honest, I haven’t seen this building in person either. Like you, I’ll have to imagine it. After taking your time to explore, let’s move on to the rock with Baekseokdongcheon carved into it. "

stories.title: Buam-dong Baekseokdongcheon
stories.script: "How was it? The path we’ve been through is truly wonderful. Despite a slight incline, it’s not too steep, and it provides an atmosphere where you can peacefully enjoy nature.  Right here, we have the rock with the inscription Baekseokdongcheon. The term ‘Dongcheon,’ signifying a place where a divine hermit resides or a path leading to the heavens, can be found not only here but in other place names as well. In Jongno alone, you can find Cheonggyedongcheon and Samgye dongcheon. Also, in Buyong-dong Garden on Bogildo Island, you can find Dongcheon Stone Chamber, created by the prominent mid-Joseon poet Gosan Yun Seondo. We’re standing in a place just like that.  Now, if you walk just a bit further from here, the forest path of Baeksasil will come to an end. 아, But there’s no need to be disappointed because the following path is also exceptionally beautiful.  As you leave the valley, you’ll transition from a natural setting to man-made spaces. It feels like you’ve traveled through time from the Joseon period to the present day. The path from here to our next destination, Changuimun Gate, is also beautiful.  After leaving the forest path, make sure to turn left and follow the road. Don’t forget to enjoy the scenery on both sides of the road. As the road winds and inclines slightly, you’ll be rewarded with splendid views of Bukhansan and Inwangsan Mountains in the distance. There are cafes along the way, so feel free to take a break.  A bit further up, there's a downhill section on the road. On the left side of our path, you’ll see the road we previously explored – the Bugaksan Road, which is the former Bugak Skyway. To the left of the point where the road and the path meet, you’ll find our next destination, Changuimun Gate. It’s one of the gates in the Hanyangdoseong, also known as Jahamun.   Now, let’s head to Jahamun and continue our story. "

stories.title: Changuimun Gate
stories.script: "Thank you for making the effort to reach Changuimun Gate. Changuimun Gate is one of the gates in Hanyangdoseong. Located between the northern gate Sukjeongmun Gate and the western gate Donuimun Gate, it served as the northwest entry point to Hanyang. The area below Changuimun Gate is presently Cheongun-dong, but was formerly calledJaha-gol, which is why the gate is often more commonly known as Jahamun Gate.  During the Joseon period, it functioned as a space separating the inside and outside of Hanyangdoseong. Today, it serves as an entrance to the heart of Seoul's city center in Jongno. During the Injo Restoration, the event in which Prince Gwanghae abdicated and King Injo ascended the throne, the rebels were compelled to open the sealed gate and enter the city. Even today, the names of those involved in the Injo Restoration are inscribed on the memorial stone.  After the Japanese Invasions of Korea between 1592 and 1598, Bukhansanseong Fortress was constructed, and subsequently, Tangchundaeseong Fortress was also constructed. With the opening of Changuimun Gate, it began to function as an entrance gate like other city gates. Despite its small size, it played a vital role in connecting Hanyangdoseong with the northwest.  Even during the January 21st Incident, 31 armed communist guerrillas tried to enter Cheong Wa Dae by passing through here. It was a tense situation, and I'll continue the story as we pass through Changuimun Gate and go a little further down.   You'll be able to spot me there too. "

stories.title: In front of the Statue of Police Chief Choi Gyusik and the Bust Sculpture of Sergeant Jung Jongsoo
stories.audioTitle: In front of the Statue of Police Chief Choi Gyusik and the Bust Sculpture of Sergeant Jung Jongsoo
stories.script: "Now, can you see me? Yes, that's right. The person depicted in the bust sculpture is Sergeant Jung Jongsoo, and the full-body statue standing beside him is me, Choi Gyusik. I served as the Chief of Jongno Police Station in 1968.  On the night of January 21, 1968, I received a call from the Jahamun Checkpoint, which was under the jurisdiction of Jongno Police Station, reporting that there were some suspicious individuals.
