They identified themselves as members of a special forces unit and disregarded police intervention, proceeding towards the city center. We received a report stating that something seemed suspicious.  I also found it suspicious, so without any delay, I rushed to the Changuimun Gate area with the Quick Reaction Force(QRF). There, we encountered the armed communist guerrillas. At that moment, a city bus happened to pass by, and the guerrillas, mistaking it for our reinforcements, began throwing grenades and firing their weapons. This led to a life-and-death firefight.  As the communist guerrillas realized that advancing further on the main road was difficult, they attempted to scatter. I also moved forward at that moment.  But heavens, I was shot. However, with my last ounce of strength, I managed to regain consciousness and gave the order to 'protect Cheong Wa Dae.' As you may be aware, a joint effort by the police and the military resulted in a fierce battle, leading to the deaths of the majority of 31 armed communist guerrillas. The only one we managed to capture alive was Kim Sinjo.  In fact, we suffered significant casualties on our side as well. A total of 75 people, including myself and Sergeant Jung Jongsoo, were injured or lost their lives. There were also 7 civilian casualties, which is truly tragic.  Such tragedies should never happen again. Nevertheless, if a similar incident were to occur, I believe that our younger police officers would do their best, just as I did.  After January 21, 1968, I was no longer able to carry out my duties. However, while standing here, I've witnessed South Korea undergo significant changes and development. I’ve seen this place, which resembled a battlefield at the time, transform into a welcoming destination for both locals and foreigners to enjoy. Though there is still some lingering attachment, I can now smile, knowing that I fulfilled my duty. Also, I'm delighted to share with all of you the things I've witnessed and heard in this place.  My guidance isn't over yet. If you cross the street and walk on the right side, in the opposite direction of the city, you'll find Buam-dong Community Center. Follow the alley next to the community center, and you'll arrive at Mugyewon, which was established in 2014. That's where I'll conclude today's mission.   I understand it's been quite a walk to reach this point, but just a little more effort as we make our way to the final stop of Route 1. "

stories.title: Mugyewon
stories.script: "Here, we've reached Mugyewon. How about taking a seat on the porch and listening to the story? First, let me share a bit about this space. This hanok was initially a high-class restaurant called Ojinam, and it was relocated here from near Ikseon-dong in Jongno.  The reason this place is named Mugyewon is because it was situated near Mugyejeongsa Temple, the villa of Prince Anpyeong, who was a member of the royal family and a patron of the arts during the early Joseon period. Many people used to visit this place, along with his other villa, Bihaedang. Among those close to Prince Anpyeong, there was an outstanding artist of the early Joseon period named An Gyeon, renowned for his painting Mongyudowondo. The landscape depicted in the painting resembles the scenery we've passed by, including Segeomjeong, Baeksasil, and the distant slopes of Bugaksan Mountain.  Suddenly, I briefly felt that this place might not fit with the last part of the January 21st Road, but in fact, it is closely related to a very important event. Ojinam is where Lee Hurak, the Director of the Korean Central Intelligence Agency, met with Park Seongcheol, the Vice Premier of North Korea. What was discussed here led to the ‘North-South Joint Statement' announced on July 4, 1972.  The 1.21 Incident led to other incidents, such as the capture of the US spy ship Pueblo by North Korea, as well as the appearance of armed communist guerrilla units in Uljin and Samcheok regions. Tensions escalated to the point where it felt like a prelude to war.  However, both South and North Korea believed that maintaining a state of tension was not desirable. We believed that we should independently address our issues without relying on other countries. As a result, we issued the Joint Statement, emphasizing the importance of resolving inter-Korean issues based on the principles of self-reliance, peace, and national unity.   Looking back, inter-Korean relations have shifted between confrontation and peace at different times. Please remember that, after experiencing extreme tension, we were able to achieve the North-South Joint Statement of July 4th, 1972.  Doesn't Mugyewon look a bit special when you think this way? Doesn't it feel like you've spent a truly special and meaningful day walking this remarkable path together so far? At Mugyewon, various history and culture programs organized by Jongno-gu take place, so please pay them a lot of attention. "

stories.title: Information for the Starting Point of Course 2 – Yun Dongju Literary Museum
stories.audioTitle: Information for the Starting Point of Course 2 – Yun Dongju Literary Museum
stories.script: "Now that the <Jongno Modern Street> 1st Course journey has come to an end, the 2nd Course begins at the Yun Dongju Literary Museum. You'll find the Yun Dongju Literary Museum right across from where I'm standing. If you've completed the 1st Course, you should have no trouble finding it.  It seems like my mission is complete now. I've heard that a special guide will accompany you on the next course. I hope you enjoy your journey on the <Jongno Modern Street> 2nd Course as well.  Thanks to all of you, I've been happy. Goodbye, and take care! "

stories.title: Saengildo Island (Birthday Island), Wando
stories.script: Saengildo Island (Birthday Island), Wando  When talking about birthdays, it is always filled with familiarity and excitement, right?   Saengildo Island (Birthday Island), located in the Saengil-myeon area of Wando-gun, Jeollanam-do, maybe a perfect example. Its name derives from the Chinese characters of birth (生) and day (日), symbolizing the innocence akin to that of newborns.  As special as its name suggests, Saengildo Island offers different attractions related to birthdays. At Seoseong Harbor, a street on Saengildo Island, stands a 6-meter-tall cake model and a more than 200-year-old Haesong (Cedar Tree). With the cedar tree now renamed Saengil Song (Birthday Song), this place has transformed into a photo zone.  Saengildo Island is not just about its name because the entire island serves as a tourist destination. From Baekunsan Mountain, where clouds linger on top; Yongryangdo Island said to have been ascended by a dragon; Mongdol Field in Yongchul, which seems like sown go stones; to Hakseoam, where the auspicious cranes stay.  Notably, Geumgok Beach is famous for the beauty of the cedar and camellia forests surrounding the golden sand field. As a well-known sunset spot, the sky and sea are dyed in the sunset, which has a truly spectacular view.  Saengildo Island is an island that gives you excitement like a birthday and presents a new look every day. How about celebrating your big day with a large cake and the Birthday Song on Saengildo Island?

stories.title: Jodo Island, Hodo Island, Namhae
stories.script: Jodo Island, Hodo Island, Namhae  Jodo Island in Mijo-myeon, Namhae-gun, is an island located in front of Mijo Fishing Port. It is referred to as Saeseom (Bird Island) because its shape resembles a flying bird. When viewed from a distance, it appears to be two islands; the larger one with a village is called Keunseom“ (Big Island), while the smaller one is called Jodo Island. It was originally two separate islands, but they were connected to one by an embankment.  Mijo Fishing Port, a cozy harbor surrounded by mountains, is the gateway to Jodo Island and Hodo Island derives its name from the legend the village helped by Mireuk. Visitors can enjoy the picturesque coastline and the blue sea while immersing themselves in a quiet and leisurely rest. The representative historical site in Mijo Fishing Port is Muminsa Shrine and it was built to honor General Choi Yeong from the Goryeo Dynasty, who embodied the spirit of patriotism. It sits on an auspicious site that overlooks Mijo Fishing Port.  Jodo Island and Hodo Island provide a special experience through the Namhaebarae-gil, a trail that was created on the island, allowing visitors to walk around these two beautiful islands in Namhae in just a day. On the first island trail of Namhaebarae-gil, Jodo Island, and Hodo Barae-gil, visitors can view the scenic views composed of various unique rock formations.   This autumn, why not take a walk on Jodo Island, Hodo Island in Namhae, a rising trekking destination, with your family and friends?

stories.title: Daebudo Island, Ansan
stories.script: Daebudo Island, Ansan  Daebudo Island, located in Danwon-gu, Ansan-si, Gyeonggi-do, is often referred to as the Hawaii of Ansan. It's the largest island of the West Coast and is named after the significant size of the slope. Daebudo Island has also attracted many visitors who are looking for a suburban getaway.   Daebudo Island's representative tourist attractions include the Glass Island, which combines the sea, light, and glass and is with various attractions, including the Glass Island Art Museum, the Mac Art Museum, a fairytale-like children's art museum, and an outdoor sculpture park where the sea and reed forests are well harmonized, and a glass craft experience space.  Besides, Daebudo Island is also known as a healing destination near the metropolitan area that allows you to experience the diverse charms of a trip to the beach. By taking the ferry across the Sihwaho Lake, when you arrive at the Daebudo Old Bangameori Dock, you can enjoy the beautiful natural scenery of Daebudo Island, including nearby Bangameori Beach, Haesol-gil, and Daebu Badahyanggi Theme Park. The nearby Mudflat Experience Center, operated by the fishing community, is equipped with convenient facilities such as a water supply station, so it is one of the attractions that tourists of all ages can visit and join a field trip that is beneficial and enjoyable.  Why not spend a day enjoying the colorful marine tour on Daebudo Island, an island with a beautiful sunset?

stories.title: Gyodongdo Island, Ganghwa
stories.script: Gyodongdo Island, Ganghwa   Gyodongdo Island, located in Ganghwa-gun, Incheon Metropolitan City, is only 2.6 km away from North Korea. During the Korean War, it was an island where displaced people fled to establish their livelihoods. Although it was alienated for a long time, with the opening of Gyodongdaegyo Bridge in 2014, it has become a little more convenient to go.  Recently, Gyodongdo Island has gained popularity as a retro travel destination, thanks to its unique charm, as time seems to have stopped at some point around the 20th century. Daeryong Market, a place filled with such a retro vibe, was remodeled as the Yeonbaekjang in Hwanghae Province after the displaced people who fled from North Korea and were unable to return after the ceasefire. From vintage signs to murals by young artists, Daeryong Market has created a subtle charm.  When talking about Gyodongdo Island, it's impossible to overlook Hwagae Garden. Designed under the concept of a garden containing the history and nature of Gyodongdo Island that accumulated over a long time, Hwagae Garden boasts 180,000 types of trees, shrubs, and perennial plants. The garden is composed of five nature-friendly themed sections, featuring an unmanned monorail that leads visitors to the Hwagaesan Mountain Observatory. From the observatory, visitors can enjoy the breathtaking scenery of the Yeonbaekpyeongya and the beautiful landscape of the West Sea along the Yeseonggang River.  In addition, there are many other things to see on Gyodongdo Island, such as Gyodong Eupseong Fortress, a pleasant place to take a walk that is located south of Hwagaesan Mountain. Gyodonghyanggyo Local Confucian School, which is the first Confucian school in Korea, with a history spanning 900 years.

stories.title: Seokmodo Island, Ganghwa
stories.script: Seokmodo Island, Ganghwa  Seokmodo Island, located in Samsan-myeon, Ganghwa-gun, Incheon Metropolitan City, is a special island where you can view the beautiful scenery of the West Sea and enjoy watching the sunset over the horizon. Seokmodo Island has various attractions and activities, and it is loved as a nearby travel destination because it is close to the metropolitan area.  Seokmodo Mineral Hot Springs is the representative tourist attraction on Seokmodo Island. You can enjoy a bath in the hot spring while appreciating the sunset over the West Sea from the open-air bath located adjacent to the beach. If you soak in the mineral hot spring water that elutes from 460 m of underground granite, the accumulated fatigue and stress will surely be relieved, right?  Seokmodo Natural Forest, being the only recreational forest in the Seoul and northwest Gyeonggi regions, offers a variety of walking and hiking trail courses of different difficulty levels, allowing visitors of all ages to walk around leisurely. Especially, the sunset that you encounter while walking along the trails gives you a breathtaking experience.  Besides, you can also feel the beauty and the scent of nature on Seokmodo Island, including Bomunsa Temple, one of Korea's three largest Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva sites, where you can see beautiful sunsets; Minmeoru Beach, where you can experience both white sand and mudflats; and the Suaeda japonica Makino site, which interprets each season in different colors.

stories.title: Dochodo Island, Sinan
stories.script: Dochodo Island, Sinan  Dochodo Island, located in Docho-myeon, Sinan-gun, Jeollanam-do, is the largest island among the surrounding islands. It is often referred to as Dochido Island because the shape of the island resembles that of a hedgehog.  Dochodo Island is particularly popular during the summer because of its iconic flower, the hydrangea. Dochodo Island Hydrangea Park boasts over 100 types of hydrangeas, with more than two million blooms creating a breathtaking view.  The Fantasy Garden, a combination of hydrangeas and hackberries, is a representative attraction on Dochodo Island. More than 700 hackberry trees form a tunnel, and hydrangeas, rainbow pink flowers, and red-hot pokers bloom underneath to add to the beauty. The Fantasy Garden extends about 3.5 km from Hwapo Wharf, known as the 'Hackberry 10 ri-gil.' The hackberry trees were donated and transplanted from various regions, and each one has a name tag indicating its place of origin.  Other attractions include the dazzling beaches of Simok Beach, which is part of Dadohaehaesang National Park; a walking trail between Black Pine Grove and the heart beach of Bigeumdo Island, which is connected by Dochodo Island and a bridge. Come enjoy and experience the diverse charms of Dochodo Island, where the sea, flowers, and trees all come together in harmony.

stories.title: Aphaedo Island, Sinan
stories.script: Aphaedo Island, Sinan   Aphaedo Island, located in Aphae-eup, Sinan-gun, Jeollanam-do, is an island of an administrative center with the vision of becoming a new maritime city. It is also the home of the Sinan-gun Office. The name Aphaedo derives from its shape, which resembles an octopus's legs stretching out in three directions, pressing against the sea and mudflats. This name fits well for an island floating in the middle of the mudflats along the west coast.  There is a Cheonsaseom Bonsai Park on Aphaedo Island, where you can appreciate bonsai art with the backdrop of the Dadohae. It is like a natural art gallery exhibiting various bonsai trees such as pine, yew, Korean Hornbeam, and golden pine, as well as various Shona sculptures.  Songgongsan Mountain on Aphaedo Island is famous for its mountains, seas, and leisurely hiking trails. No matter which course you choose, the presence of the sea and islands will be accompanying the hikers, their families, and their friends.  Aphaedo Island is particularly popular in winter because baby camellias bloom red alone in the snowy winter. The baby camellia flower, which is the highlight of Sinan-gun's representative festival, Island Winter Flower Festival, blossoms with around 40 million flowers from over 20,000 baby camellia trees planted at the foot of Songgongsan Mountain in Aphaedo Island on a scale of 50,000 pyeong.   Why not visit Aphaedo Island and create an unforgettable memory with the red baby camellias blooming in the white snow?

stories.title: Heuksando Island, Sinan
stories.script: Heuksando Island, Sinan  Heuksando Island, located in Heuksan-myeon, Sinan-gun, Jeollanam-do, is located in the southwesternmost part of Korea, which is part of the Dadohaehaesang National Park. As the central island of the Heuksangundo, it is named “Heuksando Island” because it seems to be covered in black when viewed from a distance due to the thick pine forest. The island is also known as the birthplace of the Hongeo(fermented skate) and is also famous for its marine cultural heritage.  As Heuksando Island is far from the land, it has been the place where many people were exiled to. Jeong Yak-jeon, the second elder brother of Dasan Jeong Yak-yong and a civil servant of the late Joseon Dynasty, wrote the Jasan-eobo, which documented 155 species of fish and other marine products he collected during his exile here on Heuksando Island. The book recorded the details of the species' names, forms, distributions, and characteristics. The Sachon Seodang in Sari Village, where he nurtured younger students during his exile, has now been transformed into a Exile Culture Park. The park features the Heuksando Island Exiles Chart, which provides information about the people who had their exile on Heuksando Island.   Other attractions on Heuksando Island include Heuksando Port Angel Lighthouse, Heuksando Island Lady, the beautiful landscape of Sangrabong Peak, and the Migratory Bird Museum.  Among all the attractions, the 24 km-long coastal road of the island is the perfect drive course to see the beautiful nature and cultural relics round the island. Come and feel the scent of nature and history on an island that retains ancient mysteries, Heuksando Island in Sinan.

stories.title: Gageodo Island, Sinan
stories.script: Gageodo Island, Sinan   Gageodo Island, located in Heuksan-myeon, Sinan-gun, Jeollanam-do, is named after the quote “an island that people can live” by Admiral Jangbogo in the Silla dynasty. Besides this remark, Gageodo Island also takes pride in its magnificent view created by the steep mountain shape and towering cliffs.  Getting to Gageodo Island is not easy without certain determination because it takes four and a half hours even if you ride a high-speed boat from Mokpo Port without stopping. However, as difficult as it is to get there, the island preserves its natural scenery and remains untouched by human hands. It is an island that matches the nickname of an unexplored island with such intoxicating beauty just by looking around.  The entire island is made up of unique rock formations that are centered around Doksilsan Mountain. The sea cliffs and sea caves developed around the coastline boast stunning scenery. Some of the major attractions of Eight Scenic Views of Gageodo Island include Doksilsan Mountain Peak, Janggunbawi Rock, the cliffs of Seomdeungbando Peninsula, the panoramic view of Kukheuldo Island, and Kalbawi Rock.  Designated as a scenic point on September 2, 2020, Gageodo Island holds symbolic significance as the southwesternmost island of Korea, recognized for its diverse vegetation and terrain. Apart from its breathtaking landscapes, Gageodo Island also plays an important role in geography and diplomacy because it safeguards the southwestern part of Korea.

stories.title: Uido Island, Sinan
stories.script: Uido Island, Sinan   Uido Island, located in Docho-myeon, Sinan-gun, Jeollanam-do, is the main island of Ui-gun, which consists of 27 islands. The name Uido Island is derived from the two peninsulas protruding on both sides of the island, resembling the ears of a cow.  On this island, there is a rare and endangered species named white daphne and it is famous for its pure white flower and far-reaching fragrance. The white daphne is sometimes referred to as Cheonrihyang because its scent is said to travel for miles. Therefore, when white daphne blooms, Uido Island is known as an island that is filled with the fragrance of these heavenly flowers.  Uido Island is also named Island of Mystery because it has many different attractions. The name Dalteunmollang-gil came from the beauty of the moon that hangs from the high peak when looking at Sangsanbong Peak from the village. Mollang is the Jeolla-do dialect for mountain peaks, so Dalteunmollang-gil means moon-floating mountain peak, referring to its scenic beauty, and it is an old road that extends from Jinri Village to Donmok Village through Yeri Village.  Another attraction is the Pungseong Sand Dune, which is a massive dune about 50 m in height, known as the Desert in the Island. It was created purely by wind and time without any artificial structures; this unique attraction draws many tourists to visit Uido Island.  The marks of Uido Island being a strategically important site during the Joseon Dynasty can be found throughout the island. Uido Wharf will be a suitable example, as it was built in 1745 during the reign of King Yeongjo and is the oldest and most well-preserved wharf in South Korea. Hence, Uido Wharf is also designated as Monument No. 243 of Jeollanamdo Province.  Uido Island, with its exceptional natural beauty and well-preserved historical and cultural heritage, is a perfect island to walk on while enjoying leisure time.

stories.title: Maldo, Myeongdo, Bangchukdo Island, Gunsan
stories.script: Maldo, Myeongdo, Bangchukdo Island, Gunsan  Maldo Island, Myeongdo Island, and Bangchukdo Island, located in Gunsan-si, Jeollabuk-do, are popular tourist destinations best known for their stunning natural landscapes. As an archipelago, these islands have different and unique features that are waiting to be explored at once.  Maldo Island, located at the end of the Gogunsan Islands, is also known as the Kkeutseom. It is famous for the “Thousand-Year Pine Tree” rooted on a large rock and the last manned lighthouse in Korea, the Maldo Lighthouse. Visitors can also observe the natural monument of the Precambrian wave rock formations, dating back to nearly 590 million years ago.  Myeongdo Island is also called Yaksan Mountain because dozens of medicinal herbs have grown withstanding the sea breeze, and the name Myeongdo Island was given because the water is clear and clean as if the moon and the sun are combined.  As for Bangchukdo Island, it has a lot of rocks and strong waves, but many people visit this island because it is famous as a sea fishing spot. Besides fishing, there are other attractions with unique forms of rocks, such as Dongnimmunbawi Rock and Sirutteokbawi Rock. You can also enjoy island trekking while walking on the bridge connecting Bangchukdo Island and Gwangdaedo Island and immersing yourself in the variety of charms that the island brings.  Maldo Island, Myeongdo Island, and Bangchukdo Island in Gunsan are known as the must-visit K-Tourism Islands.” Let’s join us and experience the outstanding natural landscape!

stories.title: Sapsido Island, Boryeong
stories.script: Sapsido Island, Boryeong  Sapsido Island, located in Boryeong-si, Chungcheongnam-do, is the third-largest island in Chungcheongnam-do, named after its shape resembling an arrowhead.  On Sapsido Island, the three treasures that the local community cherishes and takes pride in are the Golden Black Pine Tree, Myeonsapji, and Mulmangteo.  The Golden Black Pine Tree, which is the first treasure, is a globally rare plant with golden-hued pine needles. Since it is just a young tree that is about 50 years old, the pillars are not thick, but it is mysterious to see the color of the leaves sparkle golden.  The second treasure, Myeonsapji, means land that separates from Sapsido Island during high tide but reconnects during low tide. When the tide is high, it becomes an isolated land that is not able to reach, but when the tide recedes, it rejoins the main island.  The third and final treasure, Mulmangteo, is a mysterious natural wonder unique to Sapsido Island. When cool, fresh water rises from the cracks in the rocks, it will reappear after being submerged in seawater.  In addition to these three treasures, there are attractions such as Geomeolneomeo Beach, with fine white sand and dense pine forests, and Jinneomeo Beach, renowned for its uncontaminated sea areas with clean water. Enjoy the beautiful scenery and dense pine forests while walking along Sapsido dulle trail, which is built in the shape of the island's arrowhead.

stories.title: Hansando Island, Tongyeong
stories.script: Hansando Island, Tongyeong  Hansando lsland, located in Hansan-myeon, Tongyeong-si, Gyeongsangnam-do, is the main island of Hansan-myeon and the largest among the 29 islands comprising the Hansan-myeon. Hansando Island is famous as a travel destination that has a wide variety of attractions connected by Yeondogyo Bridge, including Chubongdo Island and historical sites such as Jeseungdang Hall, along with fresh sashimi, fishing, swimming, and various sea experiences. It is also known for being the site of the historical Chubong Prisoner-of-War Camp, providing a combination of leisure and historical exploration.   As the beginning of Hallyeo Haesang National Marine Park and the site of the renowned Hansan Battle, Hansando Island attracts tourists throughout the year. Many visitors come to see historical sites such as Jeseungdang Hall, built when Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin moved the navy headquarters of the three provinces to Hansando Island.  Visiting Hansando Island in April allows you to see the beautiful cherry blossoms blooming along the Hansanilju-ro. It is said that the cherry blossom trees were planted by the residents to commemorate the opening of the Hansanilju-ro, creating a beautiful landscape that harmonizes with the sea.  Besides Hansando Island, Tongyeong also takes pride in owning other islands with various charms, such as Somaemuldo Island, known for its stunning coastal cliffs; Chubongdo Island, renowned for its beautiful nights; and Yokjido Island, famous for its suspension bridge. Why not take the chance to explore these islands along with Hansando Island to fully experience the charms of Tongyeong?

stories.title: Jangsado Island, Tongyeong
stories.script: Jangsado Island, Tongyeong  Jangsado Island, located in Hansan-myeon, Tongyeong-si, Gyeongsangnam-do, is named for its shape, which resembles a snake slithering out. It was once called Jamsado Island or Nueseom Island due to its long shape, which resembles a silkworm (Nue, 누에).  Jangsado Island is a beautiful island known for its scenic beauty created by over 100,000 camellia trees, Machilus thunbergii, and Castanopsis sieboldii, along with a camellia habitat that reaches its peak bloom in February and March. Not only camellias but also over 200 species of native flowers and over 1,000 species of diverse plants bloom and wither throughout the four seasons, allowing visitors to fully experience the beauty of nature.  Besides, there are various themed gardens such as the Dongbaek tunnel-gil, Miro Garden, and Herb Garden, located all over the island, provide many nice photo zones. Taking photos along the Dongbaek tunnel-gil, where fairy lights combine nicely with the camellia trees, is considered the highlight of a trip to Jangsado Island.  Apart from that, there are numerous large and small observatories where you can enjoy the natural environment of Hansando Island and the atmosphere of Hallyeo Haesang National Marine Park at a glance. There are some other attractions, such as an outdoor performance venue and an outdoor gallery.  Enjoy the superb view of Hallyeosudo and the harmony of camellia on the beautiful Jangsado Island, which was reborn as a cultural maritime park in December 2011.

stories.title: Gwanmaedo Island, Jindo
stories.script: Gwanmaedo Island, Jindo  Gwanmaedo Island, located in Jindo-gun, Jeollanam-do is the representative island among the six islands designated as part of the Dadohaehaesang National Park. It is highly valued as an ecological tourist destination with beautiful views and stunning landscapes.  In the calm sea surrounding Gwanmaedo Island, there are various attractions created by nature itself, including the beautiful landscapes known as the Eight Scenic Views of Gwanmae, a bright rapeseed field that signals the arrival of spring, and an 800-year-old natural monument, the Machilus thunbergii.  In particular, transforming the farmland of 30,000 pyeong into a rapeseed field has turned it into a beautiful sightseeing spot that attracts a large number of tourists. From April to late May, the blooming rapeseed flowers give both the mind and body a rest.  If the rapeseed flowers represent spring on Gwanmaedo Island, then the 2 km-long white sand beach with stunning sunsets and the pine forest enveloping the sky-blue sea and coastline represent one of the most beautiful pine forests in Korea, where visitors can enjoy camping under the beautiful stars.  There is an interesting legend in Gwanmae-do Island, and it has been said that since early times on rainy days, Halmi-dokkaebi(goblin) appeared in Halmi Jungdeuraengigul Cave, one of the eight scenic views of Gwanmae. Rumors have it that even if you walk into the cave with a torch, the light will switch off and you will hear a mysterious sound. It is said that even the people who are known as the bravest cannot make it to the end. Hence, even now, the length of the cave remains unknown. Fascinating, right?  Come and feel the charm of the colorful island at Gwanmaedo Island, Jindo.

stories.title: Hahwado Island, Yeosu
stories.script: Hahwado Island, Yeosu  Hahwado Island, located in Hwajeong-myeon, Yeosu-si, Jeollanam-do, is named Flower Island because, during the Japanese invasions of Korea, Jang from Indong was the first to set foot on the island, and camellias, sedges, and azaleas were in full bloom at that time. Sanghwado Island, located in the north, is given the nickname Utkkotseom, while Hahwado Island, located in the south, is given the nickname Araekkotseom.  On Hahwado Island, you can enjoy the natural landscapes such as breathtaking sea cliff and a dulle trail where you can enjoy the beautiful flowers. Also, at the suspension bridge named “Kkotseom Bridge”, you can glance the stunning scenery, which is why this island is a representative attraction in Yeosu-si that attracts many visitors.  Besides the suspension bridge, there is a flower-adorned dulle trail, named “Kkotseom-gil,” and is considered the treasure of Hahwado Island. This trail also has a 5.7 km trekking course along the coastline. If you choose to walk around by following the trail from the pier, it takes approximately 3 hours. While you are on your way, remember not to miss the flowers on Hahwado Island! Also, if you look closer to the surroundings, you will notice some murals along the way, even if the murals are not created by famous artists, they are still some of the simple yet carefully crafted works. Since there are no dangerous areas around the island, it will be the best place for someone looking for an easy and leisurely around-the-island trip.  If you need some healing time in nature, why not enjoy the moment on Hahwado Island that filled with wildflowers?

stories.title: Sonjukdo Island, Yeosu
stories.script: Sonjukdo Island, Yeosu  Sonjukdo Island, located in Samsan-myeon, Yeosu-si, Jeollanam-do, is one of the islands comprising the Sonjugyeoldo, along with Sogeomundo Island, Pyeongdo Island, and Gwangdo Island. It is situated on the route to Geomundo Island. The origin of its name comes from the time during the Japanese invasions of Korea when General Lee Dae-won of Nokdo Manho sacrificed himself on this island. It was initially called Sondaedo Island, meaning suffered great loss from losing a great figure, but was then renamed Sonjukdo Island in 1914. Upon arriving at Sonjukdo Port, you will see the statue of General Lee Dae-won. Every year on March 3rd of the lunar calendar, a ceremony called Sungmojae is held to honor General Lee Dae-won.  The coastline stretching along the clear sea and soft sand beach is perfect for many tourists to enjoy camping and swimming, where they can also experience the vitality provided by nature.  In addition, the trail is connected by three mountains where General Lee Dae-won raised a beacon in Bonghwasan Mountain, Gittaebong Peak, which is the highest peak of Sonjukdo Island, and a large rocky mountain named Samgaksan Mountain. The trail guides tourists along the rugged coastline that is harmonized with the coastal scenery created by rough waves, attracting visitors to explore the island.  Sonjukdo Island is referred to as a paradise for fishermen because it has a variety of fish species, such as octopus, mackerel, yellowtail, and sea bream. In addition to abundant fishing opportunities, Sonjukdo Island also has a variety of delicious food and various attractions. Let's experience the richness of nature and the warmth of a quiet life on Yeosu’s Sonjukdo Island.

stories.title: Jangbongdo Island, Ongjin
stories.script: Jangbongdo Island, Ongjin  Jangbongdo Island, located in Ongjin-gun, Incheon Metropolitan City, is an exquisite island with protruding rocks and sea cliffs around the coastal area. It is a 40-minute boat ride from Sammok Quay, Yeongjongdo Island. The name Jangbongdo Island comes from its elongated shape and numerous mountain peaks. There are various trekking courses with different difficulty levels along the mountain peaks, making it a popular place for trekking.  During spring, especially in the cherry blossom and azalea blooming seasons, Jangbongdo Island will be dyed pink. Visitors can enjoy a beautiful spring filled with the fragrance of flowers while walking along the blooming trekking trails and promenades.  Besides Malmungogae, which is famous for its cherry blossom, and the Ongam Cloud Bridge, where you can enjoy the scenery of the sea of Jangbongdo Island, there are various attractions such as Gamakmeori Observatory, Handeul Beach, and Jinchon Beach with the beautiful glow of sunset.  Ongam Beach in particular, which is the representative beach of Jangbongdo Island, takes pride in its 1 km-long fine white sand beach. Behind the beach is a forest full of pine trees, making it a popular place for campers. Ongam Beach has also been known as a Golden Fishing Ground since the Joseon Dynasty, and legends related to the abundant marine resources are also passed down. It is said that a fisherman named Choi, who used to cast nets every day, once discovered a mermaid caught in his net. He was delighted at first, but her eyes looked so sad that he released her back into the sea, and since then, every time he cast his net, it was filled with fishes. In fact, upon arriving at the wharf on Jangbongdo Island, you are welcomed by the mermaid sculpture erected in memory of the mermaid's blessing.

stories.title: Jawoldo Island, Ongjin
stories.script: Jawoldo Island, Ongjin  Jawoldo Island, located in Ongjin-gun, Incheon Metropolitan City, is named so because the full moon is exceptionally red and beautiful. After arriving at Jawoldo Island by taking a ferry from the Incheon Coastal Passenger Terminal, you will be greeted by a red crescent-shaped arch.  Incheon, home to Jawoldo Island, is the region in Korea with the latest cherry blossom blooming season. The 4 km-long cherry blossom path around Jawoldo Island's Guksabong Peak boasts a dazzling view where you can enjoy the essence of spring. Climbing to the top of Guksabong Peak, which is only 166 m above sea level, allows you to overlook Daeijakdo Island, Soijakdo Island, and Seungbongdo Island at a glance. On a bright and clear day, you can also enjoy the panoramic view of nearby islands such as Incheon Harbor and Daebudo Island. This is an island where you can enjoy both trekking and going on a trip to the sea all at once.  Jawoldo Island has a variety of attractions. The Jawaldo Dulle trail is surrounded by many broadleaf trees, making it a forest path where ecological exploration and observational learning are possible. It is also a popular healing tourist destination that people of all ages come to visit as it can soothe their minds and bodies.  At Janggol Beach, the representative beach of Jawaldo Island, you will find fine sand and groves of acacia trees and black pine. Another beach, called Keunmal Beach has a small but cozy atmosphere that is best suited for quiet relaxation. You can also enjoy the experience of clamming, gathering shells, and catching crabs in the mudflats.

stories.title: Daeijakdo Island, Soijakdo Island, Ongjin
stories.script: Daeijakdo Island, Soijakdo Island, Ongjin  Daeijakdo Island and Soijakdo Island, located in Ongjin County, Incheon Metropolitan City, belong to Deokjeokgundo. In the past, they were known as havens for pirates, so they were called Daeijakdo Island and Soijakdo Island, meaning large pirate island and small pirate island, respectively.   Daeijakdo Island is known as a clean and pleasant island that has been designated as a marine eco-conservation area. It is an exotic island where you can observe the mysterious Puldeung that submerges at high tide and is exposed at low tide twice a day. Puldeung refers to a sand island, which is called a sand pool due to the abundance of sand. It is called Puldeung because the sandbar resembles the back. Puldeung, which is fully exposed at low tide, is said to boast a large scale of about 300,000 pyeong (0.99 km2) from Daeijakdo Island to Soijakdo Island nearby.  Besides Puldeung, other attractions on Daeijakdo Island include the Red Cloud Bridge before reaching the top of Buasan Mountain. There is also Jageunpuran Beach, where the golden sands sparkle and the oldest rock formations in the Korean Peninsula are estimated to be around 2.51 billion years old.  While Soijakdo Island is smaller in scale, there is Yakjinneomeo Beach, which has very fine sand and a pine tree forest; Beolan Beach with rocks on the seashore; and Soijakdo Gaetti-gil, a trekking course that passes both mountains and seas.  All beaches on Daeijakdo Island and Soijakdo Island have gentle slopes and fine sand, so children can enjoy playing in the water comfortably. Why not spend your next summer vacation in Daeijakdo Island, Soijakdo Island, Ongjin?

stories.title: Daehangno
stories.script: Daehangno  Daehangno is a cultural street in Seoul's Jongno District, stretching from Jongno 5-ga to Hyehwa-dong Rotary. It is renowned as the heart of performing arts in South Korea. Centered around Marronnier Park, Daehangno is home to numerous artistic organizations, theater companies, and cultural facilities, making it a beloved landmark in Seoul that attracts many visitors.  In Daehangno, you can enjoy different kinds of street performances as well as plays and musicals in small to medium-sized theaters. Actors such as Song Kang-ho, from the Academy Award-winning film “Parasite,” and Choi Min-sik, who starred in “Oldboy”, a thriller film that ranked third among the classics of modern South Korean film by The Guardian in 2020, nurtured their acting dreams here. It can truly be called the cradle of K-culture, loved worldwide.  Every day, Daehangno hosts a variety of festivals, both large and small. Among these, the “Welcome Daehakro Festival,” held annually every autumn since 2017, is a representative performance tourism festival. The festival features a lot of K-performance showcases, along with delightful eateries, cafes, and guided tours of the storied alleyways of Daehangno. The highlight of the festival is the opening ceremony, which features a grand performance.  If you are interested in the performance arts atmosphere and looking for a relaxing day in downtown Seoul, come and spend a day in Daehangno with someone special!

stories.title: Introduction of Seong An Olle Route 2 Audio Guide
stories.audioTitle: Introduction of Seong An Olle Route 2 Audio Guide
stories.script: (Guide) Mr. Bong-su Go (Cast) Mr. Bong-su Go  Hello. My name is Bong-su Go. I was born in the original city center of Jeju, where my family has lived for five generation, and I am a representative of the Citizen Council for Revitalizing the Original City Center of Jeju.  I run an architecture firm in Hanjitgol near Gwandeokjeong Pavilion, and work as an adjunct professor of Architectural Design at Cheju Halla University.  As Jeju’s original city center has various stories, it offers a variety of themed tours such as dark tour related to Jeju April 3rd Incident, Jeju’s modern and contemporary architecture tour, or Jeju historical tour, allowing visitors to explore based on their interests. Today, as a local of original city center, I would like to share some of the stories of Seong An’s residents I have searched for, heard, seen, and experienced.  Now, let’s set off together, taking small steps to uncover the hidden tales along Seong An Olle Route 2.

stories.title: Jeju Chinese Immigrants’ Story
stories.script: Around Sanjicheon Stream, which crosses Sanjimul Plaza, there were once eight natural spring water sources, also known as Yongcheonsu (Jijangkkakmul, Geumsanmul, Norinmul, Sanjimul, Geupgocheon, Gamaekcheon, Panseojeong, Garakutmul). The residents of Seong An used these spring waters for cooking, washing vegetables, and doing laundry. However, due to the jumbling problem of shantytown, Sanjicheon Stream was covered in 1966 through a process called “bokgae” (covering a river with structure such as concrete and so forth). Later in 2002, Sanjicheon Stream was restored as an ecologic stream, making it the first of such restoration projects in Korea after a stream had been covered. It also served as a model for the restoration of Cheonggyecheon Stream.  Today, I would like to talk about the story of Jeju’s first-generation Chinese immigrants that is related to Sanjicheon Plaza. In 1948, as a civil war erupted in China, fifty-four people from a landowner’s family from Changhai County in Liaoning Province boarded the “Haesangho Ferry” to flee to Taiwan. However, the boat encountered difficulties and ended up in Incheon. During the Korean War, as they attempted to head toward Taiwan again, they suffered a mistaken airstrike by the U.S. Army near Wando-gun, which partially damaged the boat. With assistance from the Korean navy, the Haesang-ho Ferry was towed to Sanjicheon Stream in Jeju. By the time they reached Jeju-do, only twenty-two people remained.  For seven years, these individuals lived on the boat, surviving by making and selling twisted donuts from flour. In 1957, when the boat was dismantled, they moved onto land and opened a Chinese restaurant in Jeju City. Making them the first generation of Chinese immigrants in Jeju, and today, restaurants like Bukgyeong Banjeom and Yuil Banjeom in Jeju City are run by their descendants.   On the second and third floors of my house building, Chinese immigrants also rented space to operate Chinese restaurants. Every Chuseok (Korean Thanksgiving), I remember receiving mooncakes, a traditional Chinese holiday pastry, as gifts from them, which I enjoyed greatly. At the time, the Chinese immigrants held onto the belief that they might return to the mainland one day and that Chinese should receive Chinese education. For primary education, children attended Chinese Elementary School in Jeju; for middle and high school, they studied on the mainland; and for college, they went to Taiwan.   In some ways, Chinese Elementary School in Jeju could be considered the first international school in Jeju-do. Around 1995, when my children were entering kindergarten, there was a trend among the parents in Jeju-si to send their children to Chinese kindergarten to learn Chinese.   After the Chinese Elementary School in Jeju was officially recognized by the Taiwanese government in 1965, six classes were operated until 2006. Afterward, it ran after-school Chinese language classes, though it has since closed, the building remains, so I encourage those interested to visit and take a look.

stories.title: Memory of the Meokdol Beach
stories.script: Today’s Tapdong Plaza was created through two rounds of land reclamation. Before the reclamation, there was a 2 km long Meokdol Beach here, which the residents of Seong An called the Apbadang (front sea).  In the mid-summer, Tapdong Apbadang was a swimming pool, a marine ecological experience center, and a playground for local kids. After playing in the water, we’d lay our wet clothes on the hot black stones, and they’d dry in no time. When water filled our ears, we’d press our ears to a warm stone and stomp our feet to let it drain out. During low tide, we’d head out to the Apbadang with a kettle filled with lots of Gingi (crab) and Brown Turban Shell back home and boil them to eat. Family members would sit together, competing to see who could pull the longest brown turban shell meat out using a pin. Back then, these were treats we never imagined paying for, but now they've become the most popular local foods: Gingijuk (crab porridge) and Bomal kalguksu (Brown Turban Shell noodle soup).  During the first phase of reclamation, the breakwater was not as high as it is now, so we could still see the Meokdol below. At low tide, we could even climb down to them. On hot summer evenings as the sun was setting, we’d each buy a bottle of wheat makgeolli in a beer bottle and gather in small groups on top of the breakwater. It was a treasured spot for young people of modest means, a place to relax, sing shoulder-to-shoulder, and share stories. It served as a beloved retreat and dating spot for many during those times.   With the second phase of reclamation, the landscape completely changed. Originally, there were two purposes of the first reclamation. One was to make a road for coastal tourism, and the other was to enhance safety as the area was considered a disaster-prone zone. However, even after the reclamation, this area remains classified as a disaster-prone zone.   Today, traces of the black stone can still be seen in a few spots along Tapdong, like the Jipdam (stone wall) of some traditional thatched houses. The best-preserved example is (Old) Mandeokgwan Memorial Hall at the Sarabong Mochungsa Shrine. Before the first reclamation project, students were mobilized to move Meokdol to help build the Sarabong Mochungsa Shrine. It’s hard to imagine such a thing happening now, but that’s how it was back then.  After the first reclamation in Tapdong, Jeju Seoul Hotel (now Cheonma Tower) and Jeju Palace Hotel were built, and Meokdol Beach was completely damaged. If Meokdol Beach had been preserved, it could have served as a valuable asset as a marine ecology experience center in the city, allowing people to experience the value of Jeju. We would now be able to walk along the shoreline, listening to the gentle sound of waves mingling with the crunch of Meokdol underfoot.  ⓒ 기억재생프로젝트-리마인드 원도심(2017). All rights reserved.

stories.title: A Grandma Maitreya protecting Jeju Doseong
stories.audioTitle: A Grandma Maitreya protecting Jeju Doseong
stories.script: There are two Maitreya statues near the Jeju Doseong Fortress. The one to the east is called Dongjabok, and the one to the west is called Seojabok. Dongjabok stands at 286 cm, while the Seojabok is slightly smaller at 273 cm. Sometimes people regard Donjabok as “Hareubang (grandfather)” and Seojabok as “Halmang (grandmother).”.  Seojabok is located within a small temple named Yonghwasa Temple. Next to Seojabok, there is Namgeunseok, which was made later, symbolizing the folk belief of Gija, the desire to bear a son. Seojabok represents a combination of Buddhism and folk beliefs.  When holding an ancestral rite in Jeju, a separate ritual table is set up for Munjeonsin (guardian deity of the gate) to perform a ritual in their honor. This practice is observed not only for weddings, funerals, and ancestral rites but also for significant events within the household. It’s a unique Jeju custom combining Confucianism and folk beliefs. I have also experienced Munjeonje rituals at dawn for important occasions, such as my university entrance exam and wedding.   Gautama Siddhartha is depicted as a “Seated Buddha,” while the Maitreya is depicted as a “Standing Buddha”. The faith in Maitreya centers around the belief that after Buddha’s Nirvana, he will return to save all beings, hence his standing posture, symbolizing readiness to foresee and alleviate people’s worries and concerns. Seojabok, as well as Donjabok, is to serve as a guardian of Jeju Doseong Fortress.   Herefrom, I think it would be good to use the term “Jeju Doseong Fortress” as recorded on ancient map, rather than the term Jeju Eupseong Fortress, whose origin is unclear.  In the Tamna Sunryeokdo, the middle of the painting titled Jeju Jojom (a valuable source for the restoration of the Jeju Fortress and Jeju-mok Government Office buildings due to its detailed depiction) clearly labels it as Jejumok Doseong Fortress. Additionally, the map titled Jejumok Doseong Jido also uses the term Jejumok Fortress. This suggests a lingering awareness of Tamna's stature as an ancient state, even though it had been incorporated into the Joseon Dynasty. So why not start calling it Jeju Doseong Fortress instead of Jeju Eupseong Fortress from now on?

stories.title: Memory of Yongyeondari Bridge
stories.script: In the past, Yongyeondari Bridge was a suspension bridge with its downward middle part, and it also shook more than now.  When I was in fourth grade, Yongyeondari Bridge was temporarily turned into a toll bridge. Residents of Yongdam-dong could cross for free, while everyone else had to pay a small amount, which I found quite frustrating. I often crossed the bridge with a friend who lived in Yongdam-dong. Back then, living in Yongdam-dong meant you couldn’t attend Jeju Buk Elementary School, but people would sometimes change their addresses as a workaround to enroll. Jeju Buk Elementary School was considered a prestigious school at the time, much like the elite schools of the Gangnam School District 8 today, and many parents went to great lengths to secure a spot for their children due to their strong educational aspirations.  Neighborhood friends would swim at Meokdol Beach, known as the Apbadang, and dive from the high rocks at Yongyeon. The difficulty varied depending on the height of the rocks, from level 1 to level 10. The ultimate goal was to dive from the Yongyeondari Bridge itself. Tourists passing by seemed to find our diving exciting and entertaining. Sometimes they would even give us pocket money or snacks, asking us to dive again, and we would jump every time.   With Yongyeondari Bridge in between, there are two rock formations, Donghandugi and Seohandugi, about 20-30 meters apart. My friends said only being able to swim across that distance while holding your clothes in one hand to keep them dry was considered a real man.  People from Jeju often learned to swim by instinct, battling waves for survival rather than receiving formal training, so our poses were very clumsy. My cousin, who majored in Physical Education, said that during his first swimming class, the professor immediately recognized the posture and said, “You’re from Jeju-do, aren’t you?”  We learned to live with the waves, often swallowing seawater in the process.

stories.title: Mugeunseong Where the Past and the Present Coexist
stories.audioTitle: Mugeunseong Where the Past and the Present Coexist
stories.script: When I was young, Mugeunseong was known as the neighborhood where the noblemen and officials lived, and the residents here took great pride in that identity. Back then, I considered the entire area, including Tapbarae before it was reclaimed, to be part of Mugeunseong. However, as I did more research, I discovered that Mugeunseong and Tapbarae aren’t actually the same area. Even though my wife, who is also an elementary school classmate of mine, grew up in what is technically Tapbarae and not Mugeunseong, she insists to this day on identifying herself as being from Mugeunseong.  Mugeunseong means Old Fortress, indicating an ancient fortress. Records show that a fortress was built here during the Kingdom of Tamna, even before the Jeju-mok Government Office was established.  During elementary school, I had many friends who lived in Mugeunseong, so I often visited this area. If you come to Inja Pharmacy at the entrance to Mugeunseong, the fierce sea breeze would hit, making me think, “Ah, I’m in Mugeunseong now.” Some of the familiar shops are still around. Where Inja Pharmacy once stood, there’s now “Munhwa Laundry Service,” and the phone number on its sign is 58-5309, a telltale sign of its age. The “Dongnae Supermarket” with a green roof on the left side of the laundromat has been open since my elementary school days and continues to operate even now.  In Mugeunseong, there were three rich families, and they are the Go, Moon, and Kang families. Among them, members of the Go and Kang families held the title of Manho, a rank equivalent to today’s regiment commander, and were thus referred to as “Go Manho” and “Kang Manho.” During the Korean War, when 150,000 refugees flocked to Jeju, a descendant of Kang Manho donated his farmland so that refugees could build temporary shelters and have a place to stay.  The Mugeunseong-gil you’re walking along now passes near the former home of the Go Manho family. It is said that, in his house, there was ‘Malbanga’ which means a horse mill, a testament to their wealth.

stories.title: Jeju Buk Elementary School and Soo Library
stories.audioTitle: Jeju Buk Elementary School and Soo Library
stories.script: No discussion of Mugeunseong would be complete without mentioning Jeju Buk Elementary School. Originally established in 1907 as Jeju Government Elementary School, it was Jeju’s first public elementary school. However, according to the historical newsletter of Ildo 1-dong, the school may have opened in 1897 as Jejumok Public Elementary School. If this is accurate, it would mean that modern education in Jeju began a decade earlier and that the school was founded not during the Japanese colonial era but in the Joseon Dynasty.   Three generations of my family are all alumni of Jeju Buk Elementary School. My grandfather graduated from the school when it was Jeju National Primary School, my father when it was Jeju Public Primary School, and I graduated when it was Jeju Buk Elementary School. The number of students during my time was two thousand seven hundred, but now, the entire school body is fewer than three hundred.  From what I've heard from my elementary school classmates, many of their families moved to Mugeunseong around the time they started school. This was likely to enroll them in Jeju Buk Elementary School, the first modern educational institution in Jeju, known for its history and tradition. It seems that parents' dedication to their children’s education hasn't changed much, even after fifty years.   Jeju Buk Elementary School features Kim Young-soo Library, built in 1968. It was donated to the school by alumnus Kim Young-soo, who graduated in 1930, as a birthday gift for his mother. In 2018, it was remodeled and reopened as part of an educational and urban regeneration project by the Office of Education. This building then won the Grand Prize at the 2020 Korea Public Architecture Awards.  The “Kim Young-soo Library” sign on the exterior wall is also impressive. It is a handwriting completed by collecting each consonant and vowel written by all the children attending the kindergarten attached to the Jeju Buk Elementary School at the time. On the ceiling, a newly installed commemorative plaque features writings from current students. It was designed by an architect who was one of the parents of a student there at the time, and I think he worked with greater affection, knowing their own children would be using the library.   After the library was completed, I visited it with some elementary school classmates, and a friend said, My life might have been different if I had a library like this when I was in school. I thought, “Yeah, maybe.  It is open as the village children's library on weekday evenings and weekends. If you have a chance, I highly recommend you visit the reading room on the second floor, where you can enjoy a night view of the Jeju-mok Government Office.

stories.title: Story Behind Gwandeokjeong Pavillion and Dolhareubang
stories.audioTitle: Story Behind Gwandeokjeong Pavillion and Dolhareubang
stories.script: Gwandeokjeong Pavillion is the oldest existing architecture in Jeju and a symbolic space that is inseparable from Jeju's history and the lives of its people. During the Joseon Dynasty, it served as a venue for the civil service exams, a military training ground, and the final inspection site for tribute items to be sent to the royal court. In 1901, it was the site of the Yi Jae-Soo's Rebellion, where many Catholics were killed, and in 1947, it was the location of the police shooting incident that sparked the Jeju April 3rd Incident. When I was in elementary school in the 1970s, the area around Gwandeokjeong Pavilion was the only plaza in Jeju to be the main stage of several events, including the Halla Culture Festival (now the Tamna Culture Festival).   Inside Gwandeokjeong Pavilion, murals are painted on the walls, depicting various scenes and stories, including Sipjangsaengdo, Daesuryeopdo, and Jeokbyeokdaecheopdo. Many people assume that entry is prohibited due to its cultural heritage status, but you’re welcome to take off your shoes, go inside, and appreciate the murals and inscriptions up close.  The Dolhareubang in front of Gwandeokjeong Pavilion has an uncertain date of origin. Given their placement in front of the fortress gate, it is believed they served either as boundary markers or as spiritual guardians, ensuring safety within the fortress. Recently, one researcher argued that, in comparison with Jeju’s King Cheonji myth, the Dolhareubang should be interpreted as deities overseeing life and death. In such a sense, the Dolhareubang with its right hand on top represents Daebyulwang, the God of the afterlife; while the one with the left hand on top represents Sobyul-wang, the God of the living world. Unlike the Jangseung totem, which was set up at village entrances by the local people, the Dolhareubang were placed in pairs at the fortress entrance by the government office.  Before the liberalization of the overseas trip in 1989, Jeju was the best destination for honeymoons. At that time, one popular belief was that one can conceive a son after touching the nose of Dolhareubang or grinding it into powder to drink with water, making newlyweds, whether in earnest or just for fun, touch the Dolhareubang’s nose in hopes of having a boy.   If you sit in Gwandeokjeong Pavilion and look forward, you can find that the plaza in front is lower than the road. It was the original surface height of the government office at that time in the Joseon period. Over the years, the road level has gradually risen, creating a noticeable difference from the ground level of the Joseon Dynasty.  Although it no longer exists, there was a fountain in front of Gwandeokjeong Pavilion until the 1990s. It was installed in 1961 as a donation from a group of Korean Japanese. The fountain was a popular photo spot, even having an exclusive photographer on site. Nearly everyone who lived in the original city center has at least one photo taken in front of the fountain. Above all, the fountain played a role as a meeting place. Unfortunately, during the Jejumok Restoration Project, this fountain was demolished in July 1999 to align with the surface ground level of the Joseon Dynasty.   ⓒ 기억재생프로젝트-리마인드 원도심(2017). All rights reserved.

stories.title: Ohyeondan, a Shrine of Jeju’s Education
stories.audioTitle: Ohyeondan, a Shrine of Jeju’s Education
stories.script: Ohyeondan is an altar dedicated to five people who were either exiled to Jeju or appointed as officials there during the mid-Joseon period and contributed to the development of the region, and they are Kim Jeong, Song Insu, Kim Sangheon, Jeong On, and Song Siyeol.  This site, with traces of institutions like Jangsudang (1660), Gyulrimseowon (from 1682 to 1871), Gyungshinje (1875), Uisin School (1907), Jeju Public Agriculture School (1909 to 1940), and Ohyeon Academy (1909 to 1940), can be regarded as a truly sacred place for Jeju education.  The three-story red brick building, north of the Korean Federation of Community Credit Cooperatives, and the W Stage Building below Jeigak were once classrooms used by Ohyeon Academy. It is still there, it remains standing to this day, providing an interesting glimpse into 1960s school architecture.  During the Korean War, Major Gilbert, who came to Jeju, became the first to introduce wind music to the island. He taught wind instruments at Ohyeon Academy, and there was a music room named ‘Gilbert Hall’. Thanks to his influence, an orchestra was founded in Ohyeon High School in 1952 and went on to participate in the Gaecheon Arts Festival and National Brasswind Competitions from 1953 to 1969, winning the top prize fifteen times.  In a way, the international recognition of the Jeju International Wind Ensemble Festival, held today with global interest, can be traced back to this very place, Ohyeondan.

stories.title: Story about Jeigak and Garakutmul
stories.script: According to the “Jeungbo Tamnaji,” Jeigak Fortress was built by Minister Seong Yunmun to defend against foreign invasions in 1599. It is thought to have been built under the influence of Eulmyo Waebyeon in 1555 and Imjin Waeran in 1592.  “Eulmyo Waebyeon” was a battle that took place in 1555, when the Japanese army, after plundering the Jeolla region with around seventy ships, retreated but arrived in Jeju with forty remaining ships and about one thousand soldiers. Facing a significant shortage of troops, Jeju Magistrate Kim Su-mun formed the Hyoyonggun, a special task force of seventy brave and agile soldiers to launch a preemptive strike. He also deployed a cavalry unit called the Chima Storming Party to suppress the Japanese forces. In Namsarok, written by Kim Sang-heon around fifty years later, it’s noted that “within the Jeju fortress, there were five hundred male soldiers and eight hundred female soldiers.” It indicates that the forces were even smaller during the Eulmyo Waebyeon fifty years ago, yet they achieved great combat results. King Myeongjong commemorated the battle by naming it the Great Victory of Jeju in the Eulmyo Waebyeon.”  Jeju Doseong Fortress began construction during the Tamna period and remained standing through the Joseon Dynasty. Sadly, during the Japanese colonial era (1925–1928), much of the fortress wall was dismantled to develop Jeju Port, using the stones to reclaim the sea.  Below the northern side of Jeigak was a natural spring called “Garakutmul.” There were eight sites of spring water near around Sanjicheon Stream, and Garakkutmul was the one I frequented most as a child.   Garakutmul was the best place to swim in summer. While the sea was great on hot summer days, sometimes we preferred to dip our feet in the cool spring water, setting leaves afloat as boats to see whose “boat” would go the fastest or competing to see who could last the longest in the icy spring water. I remember so vividly that, even though our lips became blue, we enjoyed that time.  The spring water at Garakkutmul, which remained until the mid-1970s, dried up due to nearby development. In 1974, when Jeju KAL Hotel was built to the south of Jeigak and began using groundwater, the spring, Garakutmul, which had been a cherished gathering place for local residents, dried up. Looking back now, especially with the hotel now closed, I feel a great sense of loss.   At Ohyeondan, the Jeongnyeo Yuheobi, a memorial stone dedicated to Chungam Kim Jeong, stands in two pieces, with only the top half remaining. I once heard that someone found the missing half being used as a washboard at Garakkutmul and relocated it to its current position. It seems it must have served quite well as a washboard.

stories.title: The Centre of Jeju, Chilseong-ro
stories.script: The name “Chilseong” is said to come from the Chilseongdae with the form of the Big Dipper. Another origin is thought to be the “Sashinchilseong” which means the seven snake deities from “Chilseongbonpuri (Shamanism in Jeju).” As a maritime culture, the people of Jeju seem to have a close connection with the stars, and this might be why, after the Unified Silla period, the rulers of Tamna were referred to as Seongju, or Star Lord.  During the Japanese colonial era, Chilseonggol was known as Bonjeong-tong because many Japanese lived there. After liberation, it became known as Chilseong-tong or Chilseong-ro. Chilseong-ro was like a combination of Myeongdong and Chungmu-ro in Seoul.   Chilseong-ro was home to many of Jeju’s firsts, including Jeju-Chilseong Dabang, Gyeongseongsil, Dongyeongsil (bakery), Seoksong Yeogwan, Jeju Sinbo (press), and Ilchultang (sauna). It was the commercial center, housing three of the six movie theaters in Jeju City: “Jungang Theater,” “Jeil Theater,” and “Daehan Theater.” The area was also a hub of fashion and shopping because it was packed with shoe shops, boutiques, department stores, jewelry shops, light western restaurants, bakeries, and music cafés.  During the Korean War, 150,000 people sought refuge in Jeju, and Chilseong-ro was the main area for them. It is described as “walking shoulder-to-shoulder.” As Chilseong-ro was so crowded that it was impossible to walk without bumping into each other, Chilseong-ro became a pedestrian-priority street, with neither cars nor even bicycles able to pass through.   Park Jongsil, a representative businessman in Jeju, opened “Park Jongsil Store” on Chilseong-ro. “Park Jongsil Store” was a general store selling groceries, cotton clothes, hardware, and textiles. Later, it moved to the current location of Hana Bank on Jungang-no, and he founded Jeju Sangseon (1922), Jejusangsa (1935), Jeju Sangwun Inc. (1939), and more. During the 1950s and 1960s, when the national finance situation was difficult, he contributed to the community by building the Jeju Provincial Library and Cheongamjeong Pavilion, a senior citizens’ center. When I was in middle and high school, the Provincial Library near the Citizen Hall Bus Stop was a popular spot where mothers would line up on weekends to get reading passes for their children, showing the strong commitment to education both then and now. Park Jongsil served as the first branch president of the Korean Red Cross in 1948. When he passed away in 1966, his funeral was held at Gwandeokjeong Pavilion, marking Jeju’s first public funeral.  The busy appearance of Seong An has declined a lot since the 1990s due to the urban expansion, but signs of change have emerged recently. Thanks to the urban regeneration projects and the involvement of young planners, unique spaces have started to open, attracting diverse groups of independent travelers. I think Chilseong-ro is particularly well-suited for travelers on foot, thanks to its convenient public transportation and well-developed infrastructure. It’s expected to reborn as a shopping district where visitors can meet the expectations on the first day of the Jeju trip and forget your regrets on the last day.

stories.title: Story of Jeju Water
stories.script: In the past, water was rare in Jeju-do. People living beside the sea relied on natural springs, while those in the mid-mountain areas used harvested rainwater Bongcheonsu (Jishinmul, Billemot) and river water.   There’s a Jeju proverb that says, “When you use lots of water to wash your face, in your afterlife, you have to drink water that you have used during your lifetime.”  In the past, people in Mugeunseong primarily drank water from two natural springs near the sea, “Seonbanmul” at low tide and “Nonkkakmul” at high tide. My father was a pharmacist, and he told me that in the early 1960s, the two best-selling medicines were headache pills, mostly taken by haenyeo to relieve pressure-related headaches, and liver medicine, commonly taken by locals. With the salty and likely polluted water near the coast, people’s liver health suffered from drinking it regularly, which led to a high demand for liver medicine.   My grandparents ran a shop that was extremely successful, and their secret was simple. Every morning, my grandfather would fetch jars full of water from Sanjitmul and offer it to their customers. It was the best service at the time. Of course, it was my grandfather's job to haul Sanjitmul.  Nowadays, with Samdasoo and a well-developed water supply infrastructure, we don’t experience water shortages. However, recently, there have been reports of water cuts in the western regions. It seems like a time for reflection on our lifestyles considering climate change and environmental shifts.

stories.title: Introduction of Seong An Olle Route 1 Audio Guide
stories.audioTitle: Introduction of Seong An Olle Route 1 Audio Guide
stories.script: (Guide) Prof. Tae-Il Kim (Cast) Prof. Tae-Il Kim  Hello. My name is Tae-Il Kim, a professor of Architecture major in Jeju National University. Although I wasn’t born in Jeju, I have lived here for about 30 years, teaching students at Jeju National University. With the affection for Jeju, I share stories about Jeju’s cities and architecture with the public through books and lectures.  Cities and architecture reflect the history and cultural essence of life that have naturally accumulated over time. In this way, they also become important elements that shape our lives. The original city center of Jeju holds numerous stories and historical traces, accumulated over the years. This is why understanding the original city center of Jeju is a meaningful process in rediscovering Jeju’s unique identity.  Today, we’ll be exploring Seong-an Olle Course 1 together, an Olle path that leads you through every corner of Jeju's original city center. I’ll be your guide, introducing the charming urban and architectural values of this historic area.  The 6-km Seong-an Olle Route takes about two hours to walk at a leisurely pace. Along the way, you’ll find many cafes operated by unique local brands, making it perfect for a relaxed and casual stroll.  So, shall we begin our time travel together to the heart of Jeju’s original city center?

stories.title: Seong An Olle Rest Area ‘Kkodak kkodak’ (Jeju bookstore)
stories.audioTitle: Seong An Olle Rest Area ‘Kkodak kkodak’ (Jeju bookstore)
stories.script: The area around Sanjicheon Stream is home to many architecturally significant buildings. Here, you’ll find traces of Jeju's ancient fortress from thousands of years ago, structures from the Japanese colonial period, and buildings constructed from the 1950s to the 1970s. It’s like a living history museum once you get to know it.  To revitalize the original city center, many buildings were demolished during the Sanjicheon Restoration and Tamna Culture Plaza projects. Fortunately, the area around Jeju Bookstore, Kewhat, and Sanjicheon Gallery has been well-preserved. This location maintains buildings constructed between 1949 and 1999, including houses, a grocery store, and two inns, all in one space. It’s a great example of urban regeneration, showcasing diverse architectural uses within a single area.  Jeju Bookstore, which also serves as a rest area for Seong-an Olle, is sometimes called Gossi's House, named after the surname of a previous resident. According to the building register, it was built in August 1949, and its preserved condition allows visitors to appreciate the residential style from around the time of liberation, showing an eclectic blend of Japanese and Jeju architecture.  The inner and outer structure is centered around a courtyard, resembling traditional Jeju architecture, with walls made from Jeju stone. Due to Jeju’s strong winds, traditional thatched roofs are typically low, but this building features an unusually large roof with a striking 1:1 ratio to the main structure. The roof tiles are in a Japanese style, without the paired concave and convex tiles of traditional Korean roofing, and the slope is very steep. The glass doors and storage spaces in front of the veranda serve to block heavy rainstorms. While the exterior resembles Jeju’s traditional thatched houses, the interior layout and roof design reflect Japanese style. Kewhat, a building located in front of Jeju Sarangbang, was originally a building of Youngjinfood (built in 1999). After Jeju Island purchased it along with Jeju Sarangbang, it was transformed into a cultural space for residents. The nearby Sanjicheon Gallery serves as an exhibition space, created by merging two former inns, Noksujang (built in 1989) and Geumseongjang (built in 1976), into a single structure. Originally, each inn had its own chimney and bathhouse, but today, only one chimney remains as a symbolic feature.  In addition, many buildings from the 1970s remain around the Sanjicheon Stream area. Architects can often determine the construction period based on the design and materials used. Many buildings from the 1970s feature tile finishes on their exterior walls, and the consistent tile designs throughout the city center suggest they were likely sourced from just a few suppliers. Around the Seong-an Olle area, you can still find Japanese-style houses like Jeju Bookstore and other buildings from the 1970s, so be sure to keep an eye out for them.

stories.title: The Trace of Jeju Eupseong Fortress
stories.audioTitle: The Trace of Jeju Eupseong Fortress
stories.script: Seong An means inside the fortress (城) and is an ancient name referring to the original city center of Jeju. This name stems from a time when the Jeju-si area was surrounded by a solid fortress. But why did the Jeju Eupseong Fortress that once encircled the city center disappear?  During the Joseon Dynasty, Jeju Island's administrative structure consisted of Jeju-mok, Jeonguihyeon, and Daejeonghyeon. In Kim Jeong-ho's “Daedongyeojido”, map of Jeju, the administrative regions of Jeju-mok, Jeonguihyeon, and Daejeonghyeon, along with the defense network of 3-seong 9-jin 25-bongsu 38-yeondae, are depicted. Jeju-mok was the primary hub for administration, defense, and daily life, with its core centered around Jeju Eupseong Fortress. However, when Korea became a Japanese colony, one of Japan’s initial actions was to dismantle defense sites and government buildings. It was during this period that the Jeju Eupseong Fortress disappeared.  Currently, eight remnants of Jeju Eupseong Fortress remain, with the best-preserved being Jeju Seongji (濟州城址) near Ohyeondan, designated as a monument. The other seven locations have largely vanished, leaving only scattered fragments. After discussions began about restoring Jeju Eupseong Fortress, a staircase leading up to W360 was newly discovered through excavation.  This site, a defensive point on higher ground within the otherwise flat Jeju Eupseong Fortress, was highly visible to residents. However, the Japanese made it symbolic. In photos from the colonial era, the area housed a shrine, a meteorological balloon (now part of the KMA), and Gongsinjeong Pavilion. Simply put, they demolished parts of the fortress to build these stairs, which led up to the shrine, and the site was also used for meteorological observations to exploit Jeju’s resources.  So, where did the stones from the demolished Jeju Eupseong Fortress go? They were used to reclaim land for Jeju Port near Seobudu breakwater. In other words, the Japanese dismantled the defensive structures, reclaimed Seobudu breakwater with the stones, expanded Sanji Port, and built Jeju Port, marking the beginning of full-scale exploitation. And what was necessary to ensure the safe transport of these plundered goods? A lighthouse, of course. That’s why Sanji Lighthouse was constructed during the Japanese colonial era.

stories.title: Lighthouse of Hope, Deungmyeongdae
stories.script: Deungmyeongdae is a lighthouse built by residents, and it can only be seen in Jeju.  During the Joseon Dynasty, many Jeju residents faced hardship and attempted to migrate to the mainland, disrupting military service and tribute collections. To control this, a travel ban was imposed from the reign of King Injo to King Sunjo, lasting about 200 years, prohibiting Jeju residents from leaving the island and effectively isolating them from the mainland. To prevent escape, residents were banned from building sturdy fishing boats, and even their fishing activities were restricted. As a result, they relied on “Teu,”, simple boats carved from a single Korean fir or cedar tree, limiting them to nearby waters and causing a decline in shipbuilding skills.  During the period of Joseon Modernization and the Japanese colonial era, Jeju fishermen began to venture further out to sea. In this context, Deungmyeongdae became a Lighthouse of Hope for many Jeju fishermen.  Since Deungmyeongdae were built voluntarily by residents, their shapes vary. For instance, the Deungmyeongdae at Yongdam Port resembles a radiation tower. The Gosan Deungmyeongdae you see is a reconstructed version, styled similarly to a Japanese lighthouse, due to the presence of a naval base nearby in Gosan-ri, Hangyeong-myeon, Jeju-si during the Japanese colonial era.  Although the structure resembles Japanese style due to the assistance of stonemasons who came to work at the naval base, it was still constructed by the local people of Jeju. Therefore, it can be considered part of Korean cultural heritage.

stories.title: Dongjabok, Seojabok, and Dolhareubang protects Jeju Eupseong Fortress
stories.audioTitle: Dongjabok, Seojabok, and Dolhareubang protects Jeju Eupseong Fortress
stories.script: Inside Jeju Eupseong Fortress, there were seven orchards dedicated to cultivating mandarins as a tribute to the king. The fortress layout was organized around Chilseongdae Peak, symbolizing the seven stars of the Big Dipper constellation. Outside the fortress stood Dongjabok and Seojabok, which were considered guardians of Jeju Eupseong Fortress.  While eight Dolhareubang statues guard the fortress at the East, West, and South gates, Dongjabok and Seojabok protect it from the outside. If the Dolhareubang statues served as government-initiated guardians at the main entrances, then the Maitreya statue can be seen as guardians with spiritual significance created by the local people.  Dongjabok was originally a Maitreya statue located in Mansusa Temple, estimated to have been crafted during the Goryeo Dynasty, though the temple no longer exists. It resembles the Dolhareubang statue due to its hat, which is believed to have been added later. Dongjabok and Seojabok remain significant spiritual sites for the people of Jeju, who still visit to make wishes.  Dongjabok and Seojabok can be seen as a Maitreya statue that bestows blessings, blending Jeju’s indigenous shamanistic beliefs with Buddhist faith. However, their orientation is particularly intriguing. If they were intended to guard against Japanese invaders, they would be facing the sea.
