The sight of Saebyeol Oreum completely engulfed in red flames is spectacular, so visiting during the festival to experience Jeju’s unique traditional culture would be a great idea.   In October, white silver grass blooms all over Saebyeol Oreum, creating a stunning backdrop for a hike up the oreum. Hiking amidst the beautiful silver grass is the perfect way to enjoy Jeju Island’s autumn. How about experiencing the special landscapes created by the spring Fire Festival and the autumn silver grass waves at Saebyeol Oreum, shining like the evening star?

stories.title: Geomunoreum Lava Tube
stories.script: Geomunoreum Lava Tube, at an elevation of 456 meters, is a very special oreum among the 360 oreums more in Jeju Island. It is the only oreum to be designated as a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site in 2007 due to its high geological value.   The name Geomunoreum Lava Tube  is believed to have two origins. One is that, unlike other bare mountains, Geomunoreum Lava Tube has a dense forest, which, when covered in greenery, appeared dark and was called Black Oreum, eventually evolving into Geomunoreum Lava Tube . The other theory is that the name comes from the old word Geomun, meaning sacred or spiritual, thus giving the meaning Sacred Oreum.   In the past, lava from Geomunoreum Lava Tube flowed northeast to the coast, creating over 20 lava caves, such as Manjanggul Lava Tube and Gimnyeonggul Lava Tube. These lava caves are large in scale, have existed for a long time, and are well-preserved, with excellent scenic views. Some even show features of limestone caves, which are not typically found in other lava caves, giving them unique global value. This is one of the reasons why Geomunoreum Lava Tube  and its lava caves were designated as a World Natural Heritage site.   Unlike other oreums, Geomunoreum Lava Tube requires a reservation to hike. Same-day reservations are not possible, but from the 1st of each month, reservations are accepted on a first-come, first-served basis through the internet or by phone. It is recommended to check in advance before your visit. Reserved participants depart with a guide every 30 minutes, providing an opportunity to experience the beautiful natural heritage with expert commentary.   At the summit of Geomunoreum Lava Tube , you can see the volcanic crater at a glance, and within the crater are small, low hills. Surrounding the area, you can encounter various volcanic terrains, including lava caves, dense forests, rare plants, and cool breezes emerging from wind holes. How about experiencing the unique geological history and natural wonders of Jeju Island at the globally recognized Geomunoreum Lava Tube?

stories.title: Daejeon Municipal Museum
stories.script: The Daejeon Municipal Museum is located in Daejeon Doan New Town, where visitors can explore the rich history and culture of the city in a single visit. The museum, which opened in 2012, preserves traces of the past that have shaped Daejeon, a region once known as 'Hanbat' and blessed with a beautiful natural landscape.   The museum consists of several sections: the Permanent Exhibition Hall, the Donated Artifacts Hall, the Special Exhibitions Hall, and the City Promotion Hall. Let's start by exploring the Permanent Exhibition Hall. Here, you can learn about Daejeon’s history as a desirable living space throughout the ages, from the Paleolithic Era to the Modern Era. The exhibition tracks the footsteps of the people who lived in the Daejeon region, showcasing their daily life and culture. A particularly striking exhibit is a diorama of a Baekje-era village restored in Yuseong Yonggye-dong, which vividly depicts life in that period.   In addition to historical artifacts, the museum showcases cultural heritage that embodies Daejeon’s identity as a region historically known for its flat fields, rolling hills, and rivers—an ideal living environment. Daejeon has served different roles throughout history: a battlefield during the Three Kingdoms period, a space of change during the Goryeo Dynasty, a refined space during the Joseon Dynasty, and a time of upheaval in the modern era. All of these transformations can be seen and appreciated in the museum's exhibits, offering a comprehensive look at the city's evolution.   The Donated Artifacts Hall displays a variety of items donated by the citizens of Daejeon, offering a personal connection to the city's history. Meanwhile, the Special Exhibitions Hall hosts one or two special exhibitions each year, providing diverse and unique cultural experiences. The museum also offers a range of interactive programs, lectures, and performances, making it a space where visitors can not only learn about Daejeon but also engage with and enjoy its rich culture.   Why not visit the Daejeon Municipal Museum to explore the vibrant history and culture of Daejeon, and experience the city’s past in a lively and engaging way?

stories.title: Sunrise Observatory
stories.script: Sunrise Observatory, located in Dong-gu, Daejeon, is one of the city's most iconic viewpoints. It is especially famous for its annual New Year’s Day celebration, which offers breathtaking panoramic views of the entire city of Daejeon.   Sikjangsan, the highest peak in Daejeon at 623.6 meters, stretches across Dong-gu, Okcheon-gun Gunbuk-myeon, and Gunsu-myeon. It is home to a 4.82 million square meter natural ecological preservation forest. The mountain is a biodiversity hotspot, with over 200 plant species, 45 mammal species—including deer, squirrels, wildcats, and raccoons—and more than 100 species of birds. The surrounding mountains, including Seodaesan and Daeseongsan, further enhance the scenic beauty of the southeastern part of Dong-gu.   From Secheon Park to the Sunrise Observatory, Sikjangsan Cultural Park, developed between 2016 and 2018, is a vibrant ecological park. A traditional pavilion built within the park adds to the landscape’s charm, and the Sunrise Observatory is located here as well. Once considered the best spot in Daejeon for enjoying night views, this place has become a popular tourist destination for people of all ages with the addition of the cultural park.   When you reach the Sunrise Observatory, you’ll be greeted by spectacular views in every direction. You can see Daejeon’s surrounding mountains, such as Daedunsan along the border with Honam, Seodaesan in Okcheon, Gyeryongsan in Gongju, and Gyejoksan and Bomunsan in Daejeon. Additionally, the sparkling blue waters of Daecheong Lake create a stunning vista. Whether it’s the majestic mountain landscapes during the day or the mesmerizing city lights at night, Sikjangsan Sunrise Observatory is a must-visit attraction in Daejeon.   How about welcoming the New Year at the Sikjangsan Sunrise Observatory, where you can enjoy a breathtaking view adorned with beautiful nature?

stories.title: Dongsan Valley
stories.script: Dongsan Valley, located in Gunwi County, Daegu, is a pristine stream nestled within the lush forests of Palgongsan. Palgongsan, one of Korea’s most famous mountains, is renowned for its majestic peaks and dense forests. Dongsan Valley, which stretches over 4 kilometers through the heart of Palgongsan, has historically been called Myeokbau due to its abundant water.   Dongsan Valley is not only a place of stunning beauty but also a popular retreat. As you follow the valley, you’ll encounter over 20 large and small waterfalls. The refreshing sound and sight of the waterfalls enhance the tranquil atmosphere of the valley. In summer, the valley is especially popular with visitors looking to cool off and enjoy water activities, all set against the backdrop of Palgong Mountain’s breathtaking scenery.   While Dongsan Valley itself is a captivating destination, its appeal is amplified when combined with nearby attractions. The valley is located within Palgongsan that is surrounded by scenic beauty year-round. In spring, you can enjoy the view of blooming cherry blossoms, and in autumn, the vibrant colors of fall foliage make it an attractive destination throughout the seasons. There are also several other places worth visiting nearby, such as the Gunwi Buddha Triad Grotto and Palgongsan Provincial Park, making it an ideal area to explore. Lastly, the drive along Local Road 79, which leads from Daegu through the Palgongsan Hanti Pass to Gunwi, offers a scenic journey, making the trip to Dongsan Valley itself a memorable experience.   Why not embark on a trip to enjoy the pristine forests and crystal-clear waters of Dongsan Valley, surrounded by the stunning landscapes of Palgongsan?

stories.title: Baekdamgyegok Valley
stories.script: Baekdamgyegok Valley, is located in Inje-gun, Gangwon-do, is a stunning destination where you can fully immerse yourself in the beauty of Inner Seorak. Its name, Baekdam, translates to a hundred pools, referring to the numerous natural ponds of various sizes scattered along the valley.   Stretching 8 kilometers from Yongdaeri to Baekdamsa Temple, Baekdamgyegok Valley is the main waterway of Inner Seorak, collecting streams from across the western region of Seoraksan Mountain. The crystal-clear waters, pristine rocky beds, and majestic mountain scenery combine to create a breathtaking landscape. The valley's unpolluted waters are so pure that they are home to rare fish species like eurymen gill and lenok. Another must-visit is the upper stream of Baekdamgyegok Valley, called Suremdong Valley, which is equally renowned for its serene beauty.   At the heart of Baekdamgyegok Valley lies Baekdamsa Temple, a historic Buddhist monastery famous for being a site of meditation for the independence activist and poet Han Yong-un. Once a remote and hard-to-reach location, Baekdamsa Temple is now easily accessible via shuttle buses, making it a popular destination for visitors.   There are many ways to enjoy Baekdamgyegok Valley. You can take a leisurely hike along the 8-kilometer stretch, soaking in the natural scenery, or cool off by dipping your feet in the refreshing waters of the valley. A convenient option is to take the shuttle bus to Baekdamsa Temple and then stroll down the valley while taking in the majestic views.   Why not plan a peaceful retreat to Baekdamgyegok Valley, where the awe-inspiring landscapes of Inner Seorak promise a refreshing escape into nature?

stories.title: Achimgari Valley
stories.script: Achimgari Valley, is nestled in Inje-gun, Gangwon-do, is a pristine natural haven known for its lush, untouched forest and breathtaking scenery. It’s the perfect retreat for those looking to escape the hustle and bustle of daily life and immerse themselves in tranquil wilderness.   Achimgari Valley is located deep within Bangtaesan Mountain, in an area known as Samdun Sagari, a term referring to remote, untouched regions. Samdun signifies three hidden villages, and Sagari represents four deep valleys. Among these, Achimgari Valley is especially notable. Its name, which translates to Morning Plow Valley, comes from its unique geography—sunlight briefly graces the valley in the morning, allowing farmers just enough light to plow their fields before the dense forest casts it into shade once again.   This secluded location is entirely cut off from modern communication; no cell signals penetrate its dense forest canopy. There are no paved paths or clearly marked trails, making the area a natural escape. Visitors often embark on the Achimgari Valley Trail, which begins at Bangdong Mineral Spring and leads up to the valley before descending along its watercourse. With no set trails, hikers must follow the stream’s flow, offering a truly immersive experience in nature.   For those seeking an extended stay, nearby accommodations include rustic clay houses and camping spots at Bangtaesan Natural Recreation Forest. The campsite is ideal for enjoying the preserved beauty of the forest and the serenity of the valley.   If you’re yearning to disconnect from the world and explore a clear, untouched valley surrounded by dense, primeval forests, Achimgari Valley is an unparalleled destination to recharge and reconnect with nature.

stories.title: Maebawi Artificial Waterfall
stories.script: Maebawi Artificial Waterfall, is located in Inje-gun, Gangwon-do, is a stunning spectacle where water cascades down an impressive 80-meter rock face. As a man-made feature, it boasts a striking height and a refreshing torrent of water, offering a cooling retreat and drawing numerous visitors during the warmer months.   However, the waterfall’s charm doesn’t end with the seasons. Did you know that in winter, Maebawi Artificial Waterfall transforms into a breathtaking ice wall? While it’s a popular destination for its soothing water sounds from spring to fall, the colder months reveal a frozen masterpiece, turning the area into a hotspot for ice climbing enthusiasts. The nearly 100-meter frozen cascade becomes a playground for climbers who seek the thrill and exhilaration of scaling its icy surface.   The ice climbing course in Achimgari Valley is renowned among climbers nationwide. Every winter, the valley becomes a bustling hub as climbers gather for the Maebong Ice Wall Climbing Competition. This event attracts numerous challengers, drawn by the opportunity to test their skills on the stunning frozen walls of the valley. For those who prefer to stay on the ground, the frozen waterfall offers an extraordinary sight, resembling a massive pillar of ice, making it a beloved photography spot.   Whether you visit to cool off with the roaring waters in summer or to witness the awe-inspiring frozen formation and adventurous climbers in winter, Maebawi Artificial Waterfall is a destination that captivates in every season. Why not plan a visit to experience its year-round charm?

stories.title: Hwanseongul Cave
stories.script: Hwanseongul Cave, located in the Daei-ri Cave Area of Samcheok-si, Gangwon-do, is the largest limestone cave in Korea. Estimated to have formed 530 million years ago, its grandeur is so remarkable that it was documented in Cheokjuji, written by Heo Mok in 1662. Along with Daegeumgul Cave and Gwaneumgul Cave, Hwanseongul Cave serves as the centerpiece of the Daei-ri Cave Area, designated as Natural Monument No. 178.   The cave stretches over 6.5 kilometers, making it the largest and most visited cave in Korea. Inside, you'll find well-developed cave formations such as stalactites, stalagmites, and columns. There are also formations resembling figures like the Beauty Statue, Maria Statue, a turtle, and a jar, offering visitors the fun of seeing how closely they resemble their namesakes. Additionally, the cave features various unique rock formations, waterfalls, and underground plazas that are worth exploring.   Hwanseongul Cave also holds immense scientific value. Researchers have identified 47 animal species within the cave, including the Hwanseon Blind Beetle and three other species that are either endemic to or first discovered in the cave. The uniqueness of these creatures underscores the ecological importance of this subterranean habitat.   Since 2010, a monorail system has made the journey to the cave more accessible, and visitors can explore its wonders within about an hour. Hwanseongul Cave offers a fascinating glimpse into Korea's geological and biological history, wrapped in an awe-inspiring natural setting.   Why not venture into Hwanseongul Cave to experience its ancient beauty, learn about its unique wildlife, and marvel at the natural artistry of this incredible underground world? It promises a journey unlike any other.

stories.title: Geumjinhaebyeon Beach
stories.script: Geumjinhaebyeon Beach, is located in Gangneung of Gangwon-do, offers a peaceful and quiet retreat compared to the bustling tourist spots around the city. If you're looking to escape the crowds and enjoy a more tranquil coastline, Geumjinhaebyeon Beach is the perfect choice. Though it is small in size, the beach boasts beautiful scenery where the soft white sands meet the clear blue waters.   With a length of about 150 meters, Geumjinhaebyeon Beach may be modest, but its unique location right next to the road makes it easily accessible. As you drive along the road from Jeongdongjin to Heonwa-ro Road, the mesmerizing view of the blue sea stretches out before you. The beach has a gentle slope and shallow waters, making it ideal for families with children or beginners trying surfing for the first time. In fact, the beach has become a popular spot for surfing enthusiasts, which gives it a unique and laid-back vibe.   Despite its small size, Geumjinhaebyeon Beach is known for its serene and cozy atmosphere, and visitors often return for its peaceful environment. However, it lacks some of the facilities found in larger, more crowded beaches, so it's a good idea to plan ahead before visiting.   On a small hill near the beach sits Geumjin Hot Spring, a perfect spot to relax after a day of water activities or surfing. The spring water is rich in healing minerals such as calcium, magnesium, and selenium, offering therapeutic benefits.   If you're looking to enjoy stunning coastal views on a scenic drive and escape the crowds to experience a private beach, why not visit Geumjinhaebyeon Beach?

stories.title: Cheongyang Market
stories.script: Cheongyang Market, located in Cheongyang-gun, Chungcheongnam-do, is a traditional marketplace that represents the region. It was originally situated along the river in Eupnae-ri, and was relocated to its current site in 1971. In 2003, it underwent modernization as part of a traditional market revitalization project, resulting in the current structure. Today, Cheongyang Market hosts both a permanent market and a five-day interval market, known as the Fifth-Day Market, held on dates ending in 2 or 7.   The market, situated west of Chilgapsan Mountain, offers easy access to specialty products unique to the mountain area. These include various medicinal herbs like licorice and cinnamon, as well as the renowned reishi mushrooms sourced from the deep mountain forests of Chilgapsan.   One must-try specialty at the market is wolfberry. Cheongyang produces over 70% of the country’s wolfberries, making it a significant hub for this valuable plant. Every part of the wolfberry —fruit, stem, and flower—has beneficial uses. The fruit is said to purify the blood and treat acne and boils. The stems can be used as cough medicine, and the flowers serve as a tonic. On market days in the past, collectors would flock to buy wolfberries, making the market bustling with activity.   Other regional specialties, such as Cheongyang’s chili peppers and medicinal herbs, are also easily available at Cheongyang Market. Visitors can enjoy a variety of experiences, including the Cheongyang Constellation Night Market and the Saturday Market, which feature diverse foods and cultural performances.   Since the addition of a public parking lot in 2018, it’s become even easier to visit. Why not take a trip to Cheongyang Market to enjoy the fresh produce and unique local specialties grown in the pristine environment of Cheongyang?

stories.title: Yeongildae Beach
stories.script: Yeongildae Beach, the representative beach of Pohang, Gyeongsangbuk-do, is famous for its vast sandy shore and the beautiful Yeongildae Pavilion. Stretching 1,750 meters in length and 40 to 70 meters in width, the beach covers an area of 380,000 square meters, making it the largest beach on the East Coast of South Korea. Along with nearby Songdo Beach, Yeongildae Beach is considered one of the key attractions in Pohang.   Conveniently located near Pohang's city center, the beach is easily accessible by public transportation, and the surrounding area offers various amenities and attractions. In the summer, the beach becomes a lively gathering spot for families, friends, and couples, all enjoying the water and the sun. The beach is well-equipped with facilities such as showers and changing rooms, making it ideal for a comfortable beach experience.   A major highlight of Yeongildae Beach is the Yeongildae Pavilion, the first of its kind on the water in South Korea. Originally called Pohang North Beach, it was renamed after the pavilion opened in 2013. Visitors can walk along the 80-meter-long Yeongil Bridge to reach the Yeongildae Observatory, which won the 2013 Korea Space Culture Award. The pavilion is designed with traditional Korean architectural style, featuring a beautiful tiled roof, offering panoramic views of the sea. At night, the bridge and pavilion are illuminated, creating a spectacular nightscape with views of POSCO and Yeongil Bay.   Additionally, Yeongildae Beach hosts exciting events such as the Pohang International Fireworks Festival and the Yeongildae Sand Festival every year, providing even more reasons to visit. With plenty of attractions and activities, why not dive into the charm of Pohang's beautiful sea at Yeongildae Beach?

stories.title: Biyangdo Island
stories.script: Biyangdo Island is a small island situated in the western part of the Jeju Island, near Udo. Despite sharing the same name as another island in Udo, it is a distinct and separate island. Covering an area of about 0.52㎢, Biyangdo Island is small enough to be explored in just two to three hours.   To reach Biyangdo Island, you can take a ferry from Hallim Port. The ferry operates four times a day, and the journey takes around 15 minutes. From nearby Hyeopjae Beach, you can even catch a glimpse of Biyangdo Island, as it's close to the mainland.   Biyangdo Island offers two main walking routes for visitors. One is a complete loop around the island, while the other is the Biyang Oreum Trail, which leads to the highest point, Biyangbong Peak, where a white lighthouse offers stunning panoramic views of the island. The island's coastline is dotted with unique rock formations, such as the Baby-Carrying Rock and the Elephant Rock, both popular landmarks.   Another intriguing feature of Biyangdo Island is its salt marsh, a rare sight that is difficult to find on the mainland. Formed through volcanic activity in 1002 and 1007, Biyangdo Island is considered Jeju Island's youngest island. It is historically significant, with the in the third volume of “Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam”, a historical document, describing it as a mountain rising from the sea, highlighting its geological importance. For a peaceful and scenic experience, visiting the unique landscape and natural beauty of Biyangdo Island would be a perfect way to explore Jeju Island's remarkable geography.

stories.title: Seodeokchul Park
stories.script: Seodeokchul Park  Seo Deok–chul, born and raised in Ulsan wrote Snowflake symbolized by white flowers with which hope blossomed during the Japanese occupation in Korea.    It was just a moment. With a thud! sound, a boy child's loud cry broke out a quiet house. The startled mother frantically ran to her child. There, six-year-old boy, Deokchul, fell over from the main floor. Having slipped over, he injured one leg. His parents put their best efforts into healing his leg, but his leg worsened and the inflammation in the leg spread out to his spine.   After all, Seo Deok-chul ends up living the life of a physically disabled person, with his back bent and his lower body paralyzed owing to the accident. Seo Deok-chul, who could not move his body properly on his own, had difficulty completing formal education courses. So he learned Hangul from his mother. He opened his eyes through literary magazines and books his father brought for him, understanding the world. However!! The more he learned about the world, the more the darker sadness seeped into Deok-chul's heart.    (as if resigned) Why only to me…. (Suddenly got mad). Why does this misfortune happen only to me?! Seo Deok-chul suffered a great ordeal due to physical disability at a young age. He sometimes became angry and felt too sad. Besides, the era in which Seo deok-chul lived was those times when the Japanese occupied in Korean Peninsula. It was a time when all Koreans had to live a hard and sad life as they lost their country. Seo Deok-chul was not only physically disabled but was also thrown into the dark sad times.   He faced a reality where one could collapse countless times and despair endlessly.  Seo Deok-chul, however, never gave up hope. Instead of despair, he picked up a pen and started to write poetry. Spring Letter(봄편지) Seo Deok-chul wrote, offered the Koreans great hope. His poem comforted the people oppressed by the military Japanese. Through his achievement from his writings for children's literature, Seo Deok-chul overcame his physical disability and the pain. Above all, Seo Deok-chul published many of his works, giving hope to the nation with optimistic and bright emotions.  Snow Snow like a white flower / White flowers form the sky …   This is the song, Snowflake, one of the songs Seo Deok-chul wrote. The song expresses the snow falling from the sky as beautiful flowers. In this song, Seo Deok-chul's innocence and childlike mind are well presented.   Currently, Seodeokchul Park along with the exhibition hall is being built in Boksan-dong, Jung-gu, Ulsan. At the Park, you can see the statue of Seo Deok-chul. At the Exhibition Hall, you can find his chronicles and works. In addition, Ulsan holds various cultural events every year such as the Seodeokchul Literary Award, Seodeokchul Creative Children's Song Festival and Seodeokchul Spring Letter Song Monument to commemorate Seo Deok-chul's achievements in bringing hope up in dark times.   With his pure, innocent, and kind heart, Seo Deok - chul sang about a beautiful world. His lovely mind reached and touched the sky. So, his songs make us feel beautiful now.   In the trees, in the field, and even outskirts / snowing softly and beautifully.”

stories.title: Children's Education Center for History and Science
stories.audioTitle: Children's Education Center for History and Science
stories.script: Children's Education Center for History and Science   Hi folks, let's study with fun. Children's Education Center for History and Science in Jung-gu, Ulsan!  Rattle, Clatter. Children's little hands become busy. The soft scuttle of children around the center. Children's little feet also become busy. With wide smiles and twinkling eyes like stars, children truly enjoy studying with fun here in the Children's Education Center for History and Science. This is the world of children where children learn while playing, thinking, and laughing. Children's Education Center for History and Science is a complex cultural experience space exclusively for children.   The first floor of the center is for History education. You can take a look at the achievements of Oesol Choi Hyeon-bae and Shinwol Seo Deok-chul as both are from Jung-gu, Ulsan. Also, you can explore the history of Jung-gu including Jung-gu Fortress that protected Ulsan area, the ruins of Bangu-dong which was called the Sea Gate of Silla, and the dinosaur footprints in Yugok-dong.   Going up to the second floor, you will find a cultural hall where you can learn about the history of Jung-gu. You can explore the proud cultural heritages such as the Gyeongsangjwa-do Military Fortress. Finally, the third floor is designed as a science hall, stimulating and inspiring children's scientific curiosity to foster imagination and creativity. This Science hall enhances to connect the historical, cultural resources of Jung-gu, Ulsan.  Children's Education Center for History and Science in Jung-gu, Ulsan helps children learn about the excellence and originality of Ulsan Jung-gu history and culture through the eyes and the hands along with the hands-on experiences. This Education center is the place where children learn while playing, thinking, and laughing. Anyone is always welcome here.

stories.title: Dinosaur Footprint Park
stories.script: Dinosaur Footprint Park  You can see the vivid traces of dinosaurs in Ulsan Dinosaur Footprint Park. The dinosaur theme park is in Yugok-dong, Jung-gu, Ulsan. Here, three footprints of the carnivorous dinosaur Maniraptora and 77 footprints of the herbivorous dinosaur Coreanosaulopus from the Early Cretaceous period, about 100 million years ago, were discovered. Those footprints were preserved in good condition, becoming a valuable resource for research on the natural history of the Korean Peninsula. As such, it was designated as Ulsan Metropolitan City Cultural Heritage Material No. 12 on November 9th, 2000. The entire area was created as a Dinosaur Footprint Park.    Looking at the dinosaur footprints in Yugok-dong, Ulsan, some of the footprints have the appearance of dinosaurs running at high speed. Those footprints appear to be traces made by one carnivore dinosaur chasing several herbivorous dinosaurs. Based on the Yugok-dong dinosaur footprints, the international geological community estimates that the area was a lakeside developed on a plain during the Early Cretaceous Period. Like the savanna area which is considered an important ecological space for African animals, Yugok-dong in Ulsan was also an important ecological space for dinosaurs. Herbivorous dinosaurs gathered here on the lakeside and were hunted by carnivorous dinosaurs, and their traces appear to have been left in what is now Yugok-dong, Ulsan.   At Ulsan Dinosaur Footprints Park where traces of dinosaurs are vividly left, life-like dinosaur models such as Tyrannosaurus, Stegosaurus, Brachiosaurus, and Spinosaurus are on display. In addition to operating the interpretation program about dinosaurs, a fossil excavation playground is lodged so children can dig up dinosaur fossils. Also, children can enjoy a dinosaur egg photo zone, a dinosaur sculpture telling the story of dinosaur footprints fossils, and a door and bench shaped like a dinosaur's head.  	 A long way off, dinosaurs lived and breathed just like us on this land where we humans live now. Although we cannot see their actual appearance now, their existence can be identified through such dinosaur footprints in Yugok-dong, Jung-gu, Ulsan.

stories.title: Sangil Sanghwe (Sangil Store)
stories.script: Sangil Sanghwe (Sangil Store)  The Sangsaeng Hall, our town where imagination becomes our daily life!  The places where entire cities have been turning into village gardens are here. This is Jung-gu, Ulsan Metropolitan City. Ulsan is well known for the Taehwa River National Gardern. Jung-gu, Ulsan is going one step further up, making efforts to turn the entire city into a village garden by connecting the veins of the Taehwa River National Garden to the original city center. With this effort, a beautiful glass greenhouse was created in the original downtown of Jung-gu, Ulsan on September 28, 2021.   The name of this glass greenhouse is Sangil Sanghwe. Sangil Sanghwe stands for a center where  local residents coexist whereby our imagination becomes a daily life. So, the store keeps its unique function as it is. In this beautiful glass greenhouse garden café, you can enjoy fragrant flower tea as well as coffee.    Jung-gu, Ulsan has supported residents' participation and professional education to revitalize alley gardens. It has also raised Ulsan Keunaegi Village Gardens. The Keunaegi Village gardeners trained under the specialized programs have been transforming the cityscape into a beautiful village garden.   Sangil Sanghwe is an important activity base for gardeners in Keunaegi Village. The greenhouse, yard, and rooftop of the store are all well-maintained by Keunaegi Village gardeners. Thanks to the systematic operations by professional gardeners, the landscape of the Sangil Sanghwe is full of vitality and beautiful colors. Here, a cup of tea you enjoy will quench your thirst and soothe your tiredness.   Currently, Sangil Sanghwe holds exhibitions and hands-on events by emerging artists. Also, it is planning to organize a fun cultural experience in which all tourists can participate.  Prettily looking, Sangil Sanghwe would appear even more beautiful when you know the meaning behind it. Today, Sangil Sanghwe creates a new culture with vital spirits as a complex cultural space. The store is awaiting your visit someday.

stories.title: Hamwollu
stories.script: There was a mountain that embraced the moon. On that mountain, even the passing wind seemed to carry the scent of the moon.  People named this mountain Hamwolsan which means a mountain that embraces the moon.  At a site with a view of Hamwolsan, a pavilion resembling the mountain was built.  The pavilion faced Hamwolsan when the sun rose, and when the moon rose,  it gazed down at the world, embracing the moon like the mountain.   Therefore people gave this pavilion the name Hamwollu.  Hamwollu offers serene views of the city of Ulsan along the Taehwa River. It faces the moon-hugging Hamwol mountain and the millennium-old Baekyangsa Temple.  Many people visit to enjoy the stellar night scenery.  When you go up to Hamwollu and gaze down at a world that sparkles even in the dark, it will appear that the moonlight is scattered in the sky and the earth is sprinkled with starlight.  A place where you can feel the stirring promise of the night surrounded by beautiful hues.   This is Hamwollu in Jung-gu, Ulsan, where you can embrace the moon.

stories.title: The Birth and History of Ganjanggejang
stories.audioTitle: The Birth and History of Ganjanggejang
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Let’s dive into the story of Ganjanggejang—Korea’s beloved Rice Thief with its salty, savory charm.  Ganjanggejang is a well-known Korean dish made with blue crab, loved for generations at family tables. As blue crabs get plumper, meat turns sweeter and richer in flavor. Ganjanggejang was first made as a way to keep that fresh taste a little longer.  A written recipe of Ganjanggejang appears in Sallim Gyeongje, a 17th-century book by scholar Hong Man-seon. By the 1800s, another book called Gyuhap Chongseo even described different types of soy sauce used in the dish. That shows just how long Ganjanggejang has been part of Korean food culture.  Incheon’s Ganjanggejang is known for its deep umami flavor, thanks to the use of super fresh blue crab. That’s no surprise—Incheon has long been a center for seafood. The West Coast, with its wide mudflats and rich marine life, has supported fishing communities for generations. Incheon’s seafood industry really took off after Jemulpo Port opened in 1883. Today, the city is one of the top places in Korea to enjoy blue crab.  Each spring and fall—between April and June, and again from October to November—fishing boats head out to Korea’s biggest blue crab grounds near Incheon and Yeonpyeongdo. They bring back fresh crabs that you can enjoy right away at the Incheon Complex Fish Market.  Spoon some soy sauce–marinated crab over warm rice, and you’ll understand why Koreans call it the ultimate rice thief. How about trying fresh Ganjanggejang in Incheon, where the salty sea breeze fills the air?

stories.title: The Birth and History of Jjajangmyeon
stories.audioTitle: The Birth and History of Jjajangmyeon
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Let’s talk about Jjajangmyeon—a glossy, black-sauced noodle dish that holds a special place in every Korean’s heart.  You can trace Jjajangmyeon back to the early 1900s in Incheon, where it first started to appear. When Incheon Port opened in 1883, workers from China’s Shandong region came to Korea. They brought with them a noodle dish called zhajiangmian(炸醬麵), which slowly changed to fit Korean tastes—eventually becoming Jjajangmyeon.  In 1905, a restaurant called Gonghwachun opened in Incheon’s Chinatown—and it’s known as the very birthplace of Jjajangmyeon. They came up with a new sauce by adding caramel to a Chinese paste called mienjang. Later on, they started stir-frying the sauce with pork and onions—and that gave us the Jjajangmyeon we know today.  Today, the old Gonghwachun building is home to the Jjajangmyeon Museum, where you can see the full history of the dish in one place. The museum recreates the restaurant’s interior from the 1930s and shows scenes from the 1970s and ’80s—when Jjajangmyeon became a go-to favorite. Together with the museum, Incheon’s Chinatown gives visitors a real sense of the dish’s history and culture.  Jjajangmyeon is now one of Korea’s most iconic dishes. Now that you know the story behind this bowl of noodles, why not try it for yourself—and taste it in a whole new way?

stories.title: The Birth and History of Wanggalbi (Grilled Jumbo Galbi)
stories.audioTitle: The Birth and History of Wanggalbi (Grilled Jumbo Galbi)
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! This time, we’re digging into Suwon Wanggalbi—a local favorite from Suwon, Gyeonggi-do.  One thing that makes Suwon Wanggalbi stand out is its size—these ribs are much bigger and meatier than regular galbi. They used to be about 17 centimeters long, and even now, they’re still over 10. They’re seasoned with just salt and sugar—not soy sauce—so you really taste the meat itself.  Suwon Wanggalbi traces its roots back to the Suwon cattle market, which began in the late Joseon Dynasty. When King Jeongjo built Hwaseong Fortress, livestock farming in the area started to grow. At the time, butchering was banned in Seoul, so Suwon naturally became the center for Korean beef distribution. In 1905, the opening of the Gyeongbu Line railway gave the local cattle market a big boost. During the Japanese colonial era, it grew into one of the three largest cattle markets in Korea.  In 1945, a haejangguk place called Hwachunok opened in Suwon’s Yeongdong Market. Haejangguk is a traditional Korean soup known as a hangover cure, often made with beef, vegetables, and spicy broth to help you feel better after drinking. Hwachunok added beef ribs to their soup—and it was such a hit that by 1956, they started serving Suwon Wanggalbi as a separate dish. What made Hwachunok special was its use of large, fresh ribs and simple seasoning—just salt and sugar, no soy sauce. It quickly became popular, and by the 1960s and ’70s, it was famous all over Korea—even attracting well-known politicians.  When Hwachunok closed in the 1980s, chefs who had trained there opened their own galbi restaurants in East Suwon. That’s how Suwon Galbi Street came to be. Today, there are over 30 Wanggalbi restaurants in Suwon. And the traditional way of preparing these hearty ribs is still loved by both locals and visitors.  Craving Wanggalbi—the kind you can enjoy any time of year? Then head to Suwon and treat yourself to a meal that’s rich, hearty, and deeply satisfying.

stories.title: The History Behind the Warmth of Budaejjigae
stories.audioTitle: The History Behind the Warmth of Budaejjigae
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Let’s explore the story of Budaejjigae—a spicy, comforting stew born out of hardship and resilience.  Budaejjigae is Korea’s first fusion dish—made by mixing Western ingredients like ham, sausage, and baked beans with Korean favorites like kimchi, tofu, and gochujang. It has a spicy, savory broth that people of all ages enjoy. And part of the fun is adding extra toppings to match your taste.  So where does the name Budaejjigae come from? It goes back to right after the Korean War in the early 1950s. After the war, large U.S. army bases were set up all across Korea. Food was scarce, so many locals made do with ingredients from the bases. Ham and sausage—called Budae gogi, or army meat—were often used in Korean-style dishes. One of those was Budaebokkeum, where the meat was stir-fried with butter and vegetables. That stir-fry became the starting point for what we now call Budaejjigae.  In the 1960s, a vendor in Uijeongbu who sold fish cakes turned Budaebokkeum into the stew-style Budaejjigae we know today. As more restaurants opened nearby, the area slowly grew into what we now call Uijeongbu Budaejjigae Street.  Today, Budaejjigae is seen as true Korean soul food—a dish that reflects the country’s strength and resilience after the war. So why not visit Uijeongbu, where it all began, and enjoy a hot bowl of Budaejjigae with rice?

stories.title: How Dakgalbi Turned a Crisis into an Opportunity
stories.audioTitle: How Dakgalbi Turned a Crisis into an Opportunity
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Get ready for Dakgalbi—spicy chicken that sizzles on a hot grill and fills the air with mouthwatering aroma.  Chuncheon Dakgalbi is made with bite-sized pieces of chicken marinated in a spicy sauce, then stir-fried on a hot iron plate with vegetables and rice cakes. It’s often wrapped in fresh greens or eaten with garlic and chili for an extra kick.  Did you know Chuncheon Dakgalbi was originally called Dakbulgogi? In the late 1960s, when beef was hard to get and pork was in high demand, a small tavern in Chuncheon switched to chicken, marinated it, and sold it as Dakbulgogi. That was the start of today’s Chuncheon Dakgalbi.  Thanks to the many poultry farms in Chuncheon, fresh chicken was easy to get at a good price. It soon earned nicknames like College Student Galbi and People’s Galbi, and gained popularity fast. Soon, other eateries joined in—and that’s how Dakgalbi Street was born, making the dish a true symbol of Chuncheon.  Just thinking about spicy Dakgalbi sizzling on the grill is enough to make your mouth water, isn’t it? Take in the rich aroma rising from the hot grill—and soak up the warm, local charm of Chuncheon.

stories.title: The Hanu That Even Our Ancestors Fell in Love With
stories.audioTitle: The Hanu That Even Our Ancestors Fell in Love With
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Up next on our K-local food trip is Hanu—Korean beef so tender and flavorful, it practically melts on your tongue.  Hanu is premium Korean beef, known for its fresh quality, soft texture, and juicy, rich flavor. It’s graded based on several factors—like marbling, texture, maturity, meat color, and fat color. You can choose from the highest grade, 1++, which has lots of marbling, or grade 3, which is leaner and more affordable. Each one has its own appeal.  Hoengseong Hanu is especially known for its fine marbling and nutty flavor. It earns some of the highest quality ratings in Korea. That’s because Hoengseong’s mountains and rice farms provide great feed, like rice straw. With clean water and fresh air, too, you get the deep, signature taste that makes this beef so special.  To really enjoy Hanu, head to the Hoengseong Traditional Market. Many butcher shops there also run restaurants, so you can pick your cut and have it grilled on the spot. The meat is fresh, the prices are fair, and both locals and visitors love the experience.  This way of grilling meat at the table shows just how much Koreans have loved barbecue for a long time. In the past, people held winter gatherings called Nallohoe, or stove meetings. They’d sit around a charcoal fire and grill marinated meat on a flat pan called a beoncheol—it looked like an upside-down pot lid. Of all the meats, Hanu—with its soft texture and deep flavor—was always the favorite. Even today, it’s still a big part of Korean food culture.  So why not try Hanu grilled over warm charcoal in Hoengseong—the hometown of Korean beef?

stories.title: Chodang Sundubu—A Creation of Nature and Tradition
stories.audioTitle: Chodang Sundubu—A Creation of Nature and Tradition
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Next on our K-local food trip is Chodang Sundubu—Gangneung’s soft tofu, light and airy like clouds in the sky.  Sundubu is tofu in its softest form—it’s made before the soy milk sets in a mold. It has a smooth texture and a mild, nutty soybean flavor, making it both healthy and comforting. And when it comes to Sundubu, you can’t leave out Chodang Sundubu from Gangneung.  Chodang Sundubu is made in Chodang Dubu Village. It uses Haekong soybeans grown in Gangwon’s clean mountain areas and deep ocean water that’s full of minerals. That’s what gives it its rich flavor and soft, silky texture.  The name Chodang comes from the pen name of Heo Yeop, the father of Heo Nanseolheon—one of the most famous poets of the Joseon Dynasty. He made soy milk using water from his own well, and used seawater from the East Sea to turn it into tofu. The tofu was so good that people in the village started selling it. Over time, the area became known as Chodang Dubu Village, famous for its tofu.  Come visit Chodang Dubu Village, where the story of Sundubu meets the ocean breeze. Have a warm bowl of soft, nutty tofu and enjoy the true taste of local Korean flavor.

stories.title: The Unique Charm of Daejeon Kalguksu
stories.audioTitle: The Unique Charm of Daejeon Kalguksu
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Next on our K-local food trip is Kalguksu—steaming handmade noodle soup that’s perfect on a rainy day or a snowy one.  There’s a saying in Korea: When it comes to kalguksu, it has to be Daejeon. That’s how seriously this city takes its noodle soup. Daejeon’s Kalguksu has its own local twists you won’t find anywhere else, which keeps food lovers and travelers coming back. Daeheung-dong was once called Kalguksu Street, with noodle shops filling every alley. The street is smaller now, but a few long-time restaurants still serve rich, flavorful broth made with care.  Kalguksu broth usually comes in two main types—one made with beef bones, and another made with seafood like anchovies or clams. But in Daejeon, you’ll find something different. Here, there are unique versions like Stir-fried Kalguksu, Dongjuk Kalguksu made with clams, and Stew-style Kalguksu.  One unique version is tofu duruchigi kalguksu—a bold, stir-fried dish made with spicy meat, tofu, and noodles cooked all together. Another favorite is dongjuk kalguksu, made with dongjuk clams. These small clams are full of umami and give the broth a deeper, more distinctive flavor. Some restaurants even serve squid stew with kalguksu noodles tossed in like toppings. It’s just one more way Daejeon keeps putting a new spin on this classic dish.  In Daejeon, kalguksu is more than just a bowl of noodles. Come and feel the warmth of a food culture that’s full of local flavor and heart.

stories.title: Dwaejigukbap—A Hearty Meal That Combines Taste and Warmth
stories.audioTitle: Dwaejigukbap—A Hearty Meal That Combines Taste and Warmth
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Let’s dive into Dwaejigukbap—a rich, comforting pork and rice soup that reflects the bold energy of Busan.  Dwaejigukbap is a well-loved local dish from Busan, made with a milky pork broth served alongside rice and side dishes. You can mix the rice into the soup or eat it on the side—whatever you prefer. The broth is pre-cooked, so when you order, it’s reheated quickly over high heat, making it a fast and filling meal.  For centuries, Gukbap—rice served in hot broth—has been known as the go-to meal for travelers. Merchants and scholars on long journeys would stop at roadside taverns to get something warm and filling. A simple bowl of Gukbap was just what they needed to rest and recharge.  After Korea’s industrialization in the 1970s, more pig farms made it easier and cheaper to get quality domestic pork. In Busan, a major port city, the rise of meat-processing plants meant fresh pork and by-products could be used to make rich, flavorful broth. That’s how dwaejigukbap grew into a local favorite—something like Korean-style fast food, but also warm and comforting like soul food. Over time, this led to the creation of Busan’s famous Dwaejigukbap Street.  How about a hot, hearty bowl of Dwaejigukbap to feel the flavor and history of this harbor city? It’s a meal that captures the warmth of Busan—one you won’t forget.

stories.title: The Crispy Sound That Cools Off the Hot Summer Heat—Daegu Chicken
stories.audioTitle: The Crispy Sound That Cools Off the Hot Summer Heat—Daegu Chicken
stories.script: Welcome to the K-local food trip! Let’s talk about a true Korean favorite—fried chicken, crispy outside and tender inside.  No matter the season, chicken always brings something different to the table depending on how it’s cooked. From lean, oven-roasted chicken to golden, crispy fried chicken, there’s a style for every craving. It’s a go-to choice for watching sports or grabbing a late-night bite—chicken makes any moment more fun.  This beloved national snack got its start in the 1960s in Myeong-dong, Daegu. A restaurant called Original Nutrition Center opened there and became popular for serving whole roasted chicken. In the 1970s, people began frying chicken in vegetable oil. By 1977, it was cut into bite-sized pieces to make it easier to eat—what we now know as fried chicken. Then in 1981, a new type of chicken coated in a sweet and spicy sauce, known as Yangnyeom Chicken, was introduced. This helped Daegu establish its position as Korea’s veritable chicken capital.  Another local favorite in Daegu is dakttongjip—deep-fried chicken gizzards. They’re thoroughly cleaned and fried until golden, giving them a chewy texture and lots of flavor. Because of their unique bite, they’ve become a popular snack to enjoy with beer.  What could be better than freshly fried chicken and an ice-cold beer? Every summer, Daegu hosts the Chimaek Festival—where chicken (chi) meets beer (maekju). Come and make tasty memories in Korea’s fried chicken paradise!

stories.title: Andong Jjimdak—Perfect in Both Flavor and Quantity
stories.audioTitle: Andong Jjimdak—Perfect in Both Flavor and Quantity
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Let’s check out Andong Jjimdak—flavorful braised chicken that goes perfectly with a warm bowl of rice.  Andong Jjimdak is one of Korea’s most beloved dishes, enjoyed by people of all ages. It’s made with tender chicken, vegetables, and chewy glass noodles, all simmered in a rich soy-based sauce that’s both sweet and savory.  The story of Andong Jjimdak goes back to the 1980s. At the time, vendors at Andong’s traditional market would prepare chicken based on customer requests and sell it on the spot. One restaurant did something different—it braised the chicken in soy sauce instead of frying it, and people loved it. Before long, other shops started doing the same, and that’s how Andong’s famous Jjimdak Street got its start.  Andong is also known for a similar dish called Jjolimdak. It’s simmered longer than Jjimdak, which gives it a deeper, more concentrated flavor. This dish blends traditional cooking with a modern twist, creating a taste that’s uniquely Andong.  Now it’s your turn to experience the charm of Andong Jjimdak for yourself. Visit Jjimdak Street in Andong and enjoy a hearty meal full of local flavor and warm hospitality.

stories.title: Jeonju Bibimbap—Crafted with Tradition and Care
stories.audioTitle: Jeonju Bibimbap—Crafted with Tradition and Care
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip. Up next is Jeonju Bibimbap—a colorful bowl that looks as good as it tastes.  Bibimbap is warm rice topped with spinach, bracken, bean sprouts, beef, and egg—then mixed with Gochujang (Red Chili Paste) and sesame oil. This traditional Korean dish, with its sweet and spicy kick, has long been loved by everyone—from kings to everyday folks.  Among all regions, Jeonju is known as the true home of Bibimbap. As you wander through the narrow alleys of Jeonju’s Hanok Village, you’ll come across quiet old homes serving Bibimbap made with a traditional touch.  There’s one special ingredient you’ll only find in Jeonju Bibimbap. It’s called Hwangpomuk—a yellow mung bean jelly known as a gourmet delicacy. This yellow jelly is made by adding natural coloring from gardenia to white mung bean jelly. It gives Bibimbap a brighter and more beautiful color.  The rice is cooked in beef bone broth, which gives it a rich and deep flavor. Each grain stays separate, so when you mix it with the toppings, it doesn’t stick or break apart.  The real charm of Jeonju Bibimbap comes from its name. Bibim means mixing everything together with a spoon, right at the table. Don’t you wonder how it will taste when all those colors and flavors come together? Come to Jeonju and try the deep, rich flavor of Bibimbap—only found here.

stories.title: The Taste of Time and Effort—Damyang Tteokgalbi
stories.audioTitle: The Taste of Time and Effort—Damyang Tteokgalbi
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip. Up next on our K-local food trip is Tteokgalbi—a melt-in-your-mouth favorite that even royalty couldn’t resist.  Damyang-style Tteokgalbi is made by carefully removing the bones from beef short ribs, chopping the meat very finely, and grilling it over charcoal. The result is a soft, tender patty with sweet and juicy flavor in every bite.  Making Tteokgalbi takes time and care. First, fresh beef is chopped until sticky, then shaped into round, even patties. The patties are aged for a short time and then grilled slowly over low charcoal heat. While they cook, they’re brushed again and again with oil and sauce to keep them soft and full of flavor.  Long ago in the Joseon Dynasty, Tteokgalbi was a luxury dish served at royal banquets for the king. Because it took so much time and care to make, it was only served to important guests or on very special occasions. Today, you can enjoy Tteokgalbi at elegant Korean restaurants called Hanjeongsik. One of the best things to do in Damyang is to try Tteokgalbi near Juknokwon, the beautiful bamboo forest. Try it with Juktongbap, rice steamed in bamboo that has a gentle forest aroma. You might feel like you’re part of nature.  Do you enjoy food fit for a king? Then come to Damyang, where bamboo forests stretch out in every direction. Try Tteokgalbi here, and enjoy its deep flavor and soft, tender texture.

stories.title: The Irresistible Allure of Gwangju Yukjeon
stories.audioTitle: The Irresistible Allure of Gwangju Yukjeon
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip. Let’s talk about Gwangju Yukjeon—thinly sliced beef, pan-fried to bring out a warm, nutty flavor in every bite.  Yukjeon is made by dipping thin slices of beef in flour and egg, then pan-frying them until lightly browned and tender. In the past, it was a special dish served only during holidays or ancestral ceremonies. Even today, it’s often served when welcoming important guests.  What makes Gwangju Yukjeon special is its high-quality Korean beef and a unique way of cooking. It uses a tender cut of Hanu beef called Arongsatae, often from Hampyeong. One special feature is that it’s cooked to order and served hot, straight from the pan. Because it’s made fresh and served right away, you can really enjoy its soft texture and warmth.  Take a walk through Chungjang-ro in Gwangju, and you’ll find everything from traditional restaurants to stylish modern spots. Each place has its own way of making Yukjeon. Here, Yukjeon is usually dipped in salt mixed with ground perilla seeds, or eaten with spicy scallion salad. Some places even serve Tohajeot, a salty sauce made with fermented freshwater shrimp. It adds a strong, savory flavor that makes Yukjeon taste completely different.  Yukjeon is one of Gwangju’s famous 7 Flavors, and a true local favorite. Come to Gwangju and taste the real Yukjeon, handmade with care by local chefs who keep the tradition alive.

stories.title: Jeju Black Pork—The Island’s Precious Treasure
stories.audioTitle: Jeju Black Pork—The Island’s Precious Treasure
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip. Let’s head to Jeju for our next K-local food trip highlight—Heukdwaeji, the island’s prized black pork often called its black gem.  Because Jeju is an island, it was hard for people to travel to and from the mainland in the past. During the Joseon Dynasty, a 200-year travel ban made the island even more isolated, and that led to the development of a culture unique to Jeju.  Since they couldn’t build large boats, people in Jeju turned to farming and raising livestock instead of fishing. Among livestock, pigs were especially hard to raise because their diet was similar to what humans ate. But black pigs were strong and could grow well even on weeds, so they became more popular than white pigs. Because they were raised in hard and isolated conditions, black pigs were special to Jeju island people. People only ate black pork on holidays or special occasions. Today, black pork is one of Jeju’s most famous foods. There are even streets full of restaurants that serve only black pork.  Compared to regular pork, Jeju’s black pork is known for its chewy texture and rich, juicy flavor. Popular dishes include grilled black pork and dombe gogi, which is boiled and sliced pork served on wooden plates. There’s also pork noodle soup made with rich black pork broth. Another special dish is Jeopjjakppyeoguk, a thick soup made with black pork bones and buckwheat flour which is something you can only find in Jeju.  Imagine listening to the sound of Jeju’s waves while enjoying black pork in so many delicious ways.

stories.title: The Vibrancy of Spring Captured in Pyeongchang’s Sanchae
stories.audioTitle: The Vibrancy of Spring Captured in Pyeongchang’s Sanchae
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Next on our K-local food trip is Sanchae—wild mountain greens from Pyeongchang, packed with the pure scents and flavors of nature.  When the snow melts and new sprouts push through the soil, Koreans know spring has arrived—not just outside, but right on their plates. They welcome the season with Sanchae, a variety of wild greens that grow naturally in the mountains. These include pickled garlic leaves, thistles, bitter herbs, dandelions, valerian root, wild parsley, plantain leaves, Chamnamul, and more. Each one has its own flavor and texture, making every Sanchae meal a celebration of spring.  When spring comes to Pyeongchang, its traditional markets and local restaurants are filled with dishes made from freshly picked mountain greens. Every corner is bursting with the colors, scents, and flavors of the season—it's the kind of place where you can truly feel that spring has arrived. One of the best spots to enjoy these greens is Odaesan Sanchae Baekban Street. Here, you can try Sanchae dishes made with wild greens harvested from the slopes of Mt. Odaesan. While you're here, you can also visit the peaceful Woljeongsa Temple or take a slow, refreshing walk along the Seonjae-gil Trail that runs through the forest. Together, the food and scenery make Pyeongchang a perfect place to enjoy the full experience of spring—with your eyes, your taste buds, and your soul.  Butterbur is usually mixed with soybean paste, giving it a deep, earthy flavor. Durup, or angelica tree shoots, can be blanched or grilled with pork belly—their slightly bitter taste balances out the richness of the meat.  If you want to try many kinds of mountain greens in one meal, go for Sanchae Bibimbap or Sanchae jeongsik, a full-course meal with a table full of wild greens.

stories.title: The Taste of Nature—Yangyang Pine Mushrooms
stories.audioTitle: The Taste of Nature—Yangyang Pine Mushrooms
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Now let’s take a closer look at the pine mushroom from Yangyang—a delicacy known for its amazing aroma and satisfying texture.  Pine mushrooms grow in harmony with living pine trees, usually near ones that are more than 20 years old. They have a gentle aroma, an earthy flavor, and a pleasantly chewy texture. You can enjoy them in several ways—lightly cooked in a clear-broth shabu-shabu, steamed over rice in a hot stone pot, or grilled with beef. Each way brings out a different side of their unique flavor and texture.  Often called Nature’s Gift, pine mushrooms are nearly impossible to farm, so they can only be gathered from the wild. They grow in just a few mountainous areas, and Yangyang in Gangwon-do is one of the most famous. With clean air and thick pine forests, Yangyang offers the perfect environment for them to grow. Mushrooms from this area are 100% wild-harvested. They’re usually 1 to 2 centimeters larger than those from other regions, and because they hold less moisture, they have a firmer texture and a stronger aroma.  Want to taste the deep flavor and rich aroma of pine mushrooms, only found in autumn? Come to Yangyang, where the sea meets the pine forests, and enjoy this seasonal treat surrounded by nature.

stories.title: The Harmony of Aroma and Taste—Geumsan Ginseng
stories.audioTitle: The Harmony of Aroma and Taste—Geumsan Ginseng
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Let’s turn our attention to Geumsan ginseng—Korea’s signature health food, known for its deep flavor and nourishing power.  For centuries, ginseng has been used in Korea not just as medicine, but also as a way to nourish the body. Geumsan, in Chungcheongnam-do, is known as the birthplace of Korean ginseng. Today, it’s still the center of ginseng production and trade. In Geumsan, ginseng isn’t just a health food—it’s turned into tasty dishes that are full of flavor.  If you walk through Geumsan’s traditional markets or along Ginseng Street, you’ll find all kinds of dishes made with ginseng. The most popular one is samgyetang, a ginseng chicken soup—sam actually means ginseng in Korean. This healthy dish features a whole chicken simmered in a rich broth with ginseng, making it both flavorful and good for your body. In Geumsan, the soup is especially fragrant and smooth, thanks to the generous use of mild, high-quality ginseng.  If you’re feeling a little adventurous, try fried ginseng. It might sound strange to fry an herb, but once it’s cooked, it turns into a crispy snack with a hint of sweetness and a surprisingly nice flavor. You can also enjoy ginseng in other ways—like red ginseng candies, lattes, or snacks made with concentrated ginseng extract.  In Geumsan, ginseng isn’t just healthy—it’s also delicious. Come and taste all the different ways this traditional root is enjoyed, right where it’s grown.

stories.title: Hongseong Egg Cockles, a Gift from the Blue Winter Sea
stories.audioTitle: Hongseong Egg Cockles, a Gift from the Blue Winter Sea
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! The star of this culinary journey is Hongseong’s Egg Cockles, celebrated for their wonderfully chewy texture and savory, umami-rich flavor.  The Korean name for Egg Cockles, Saejogae, literally means Bird Clam. It refers to the clam's soft flesh, nestled inside a hard shell, closely resembling the shape of a bird. In the late Joseon Dynasty, scholar Jeong Yakjeon vividly described the striking appearance of these cockles in his book Jasan-eobo: The shell is thick and smooth, with a color resembling a sparrow. Its patterns are so similar to sparrow feathers that one might even suspect it was transformed from a bird. With their appealing appearance and delightful taste, Egg Cockles have been enriching Korean cuisine for generations.  Cheonsu Bay in Hongseong—especially Namdang Port—is well-known nationwide as one of Korea’s leading producers of Egg Cockles. In the past, the mudflats near Cheonsu Bay were sandy. However, after seawater was blocked by the construction of the Seosan District seawall nearby, these mudflats became muddier—creating a perfect habitat for Egg Cockles. Every winter, Namdang Port hosts an egg cockle festival, attracting food enthusiasts from all over Korea who come to enjoy the fresh and plump Hongseong Egg Cockles at their seasonal best.  The best way to savor Egg Cockles is definitely through shabu-shabu. When briefly blanched in a broth made from vegetables, anchovies, and kelp, their tender texture and the clean, savory taste of the ocean will fill your mouth. With the leftover broth, making fried rice or adding kalguksu, traditional Korean knife-cut noodles, creates another delicious experience.  Visit Hongseong and experience the true essence of fine dining with a bite of Egg Cockle, set against the beautiful sunset views and peaceful atmosphere of the West Sea.

stories.title: Puffer Fish: Busan's High-End Gourmet Dining
stories.audioTitle: Puffer Fish: Busan's High-End Gourmet Dining
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! The highlight of this culinary journey is Busan’s Puffer Fish, an exquisite winter delicacy that's not to be missed.  Known for its unique appearance and strong toxins, Puffer Fish is often considered dangerous. Despite this, its pleasantly chewy texture and mild flavor have long made it a beloved delicacy among gourmet food lovers. Because only licensed professionals can handle Puffer Fish, it’s not readily available everywhere.  If you want to truly experience Puffer Fish cuisine at its best, Busan is the perfect destination. Busan’s Puffer Fish cuisine began in the 1920s, when chefs from Japan—the birthplace of Puffer Fish dishes—moved to Busan. They brought their culinary traditions with them, introducing the city to authentic Japanese-style Puffer Fish cooking. Busan soon became a major hub for fresh Puffer Fish caught off Korea's southern coast. Easy access to fresh catches helped the local Puffer Fish culinary culture flourish naturally.  During the cold winter months, Puffer Fish comes into peak season—its flesh growing plumper, richer, and even more flavorful. There are many delicious ways to enjoy Puffer Fish—from hot Bokguk (Puffer Fish soup) and spicy Bok-bulgogi, to marinated chewy Puffer Fish skin. But the most beloved dish of all is definitely Bokguk, or Puffer Fish soup. Bokguk features a clear, mild broth filled with tender Puffer Fish meat, crunchy bean sprouts, and aromatic water dropwort. Gentle and soothing for your stomach, it's the perfect remedy for a hangover or as a nourishing meal in the cold winter months. When Koreans describe a hot soup as Siwonhada, meaning Refreshing, they're not referring to its temperature. Instead, they're expressing the soothing sense of relief and comfort it brings.  Enjoy a bowl of warm, comforting Puffer Fish soup that refreshes both your body and mind. Experience the true depth of fine dining in Busan, a romantic coastal city known for its stunning ocean views.

stories.title: Snow Crab: Long, Meaty Legs from the East Coast
stories.audioTitle: Snow Crab: Long, Meaty Legs from the East Coast
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! The highlight of this culinary journey is Uljin Snow Crab, a prized delicacy freshly harvested from the deep blue waters of Korea’s East Sea.  Did you know that the Dae in Daegae (Snow Crab) doesn't mean big? It actually refers to Bamboo. According to a story from the Goryeo Dynasty, an official inspecting the Chuksan area in Yeongdeok caught a crab near a village facing Jukdosan Mountain. He noticed its long, straight legs resembled bamboo, so he named it Daegae, meaning Bamboo Crab.  Snow crabs thrive in deep waters over 200 meters, especially on ocean floors where mud and sand mix. Growing in cold ocean currents, they develop firm, succulent meat known for its rich umami flavor. Snow crabs are commonly found in the northern Pacific, the Sea of Okhotsk, and the waters off Alaska. In Korea, they're especially famous in Uljin and its northern coastal areas in Gyeongsangbuk-do.  Uljin Snow Crabs are especially prized for their exceptionally long legs packed with tender meat, and their uniquely delicate and savory flavor. The best time to enjoy Uljin Snow Crab is in January and February, when their flavor is richest. Steamed whole in a deep steamer, you can fully appreciate their delicious taste.  Around Hupo Port in Uljin, you'll find numerous restaurants steaming freshly caught Snow Crabs right on the spot. The crab’s savory aroma and tender, flaky meat fill your mouth with the fresh, briny taste of the ocean. Another local favorite is Crab Shell Rice, where steamed rice is mixed with flavorful crab innards and served right in the shell.  Why not take a culinary trip to Uljin this winter to savor the delicate texture and rich, savory flavor of Snow Crabs raised in the cold, pristine waters of the East Sea?

stories.title: The Ocean's Flavorful Treasure of the Winter
stories.audioTitle: The Ocean's Flavorful Treasure of the Winter
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! The highlight of this culinary journey is Tongyeong Oysters, a jewel of the winter sea known for their exquisite flavor.  Oysters are seasonal seafood, at their best from November through March, when the cold winter waters give them an especially deep, rich flavor. During this period, Tongyeong oysters are full of nutrients, offering a plump, juicy texture and a rich, savory umami flavor.  South Korea accounts for about 5% of the world's oyster production, most of which comes from the southern coast between Tongyeong and Geoje. This area's winding coastline, where mountains and valleys meet the sea, creates an ideal habitat rich in plankton. The intersection of warm and cold ocean currents further provides the perfect environment for oysters to thrive. These unique geographic features and climate conditions are exactly what make Tongyeong oysters so special.  Tongyeong Port serves as the central hub for fresh oysters harvested from nearby farms, with numerous restaurants specializing in oysters located throughout the area. Most restaurants in Tongyeong offer oyster dishes only during winter, using delicate cooking methods to highlight their natural flavors. Whether you choose oyster bossam with crisp kimchi, oysters grilled in their shells over an open flame, or comforting oyster rice soup, each dish brings out the freshness of seasonal oysters and the authentic taste of Tongyeong’s ocean.  If you miss out on the deep, rich flavor of Tongyeong oysters this winter, you might find yourself craving them all year long. Come experience the culinary delights of winter in Tongyeong, the true home of Korea's finest oyster cuisine!

stories.title: A Treasure of the Bountiful Ecosystem of Seomjingang River
stories.audioTitle: A Treasure of the Bountiful Ecosystem of Seomjingang River
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! The highlight of this culinary journey is Hadong Freshwater Marsh Clams, a delightful spring delicacy that will awaken your taste buds.  Hadong marsh clams, small yet packed with savory flavor, thrive in the lower reaches of the Seomjingang River. The lower reaches of the Seomjingang River, where fresh and saltwater meet, provide an ideal habitat for marsh clams to thrive. From March, when flowers begin to bloom, to June, just before the rainy season, the Seomjingang River area bustles with people gathering marsh clams.  Freshwater marsh clams are gaining attention as a healthy food due to their high content of nutrients like glycogen, methionine, and vitamin E, known to relieve fatigue and help ease hangovers. The most delicious way to enjoy these nutritious clams is undoubtedly Jaecheopguk, a traditional Korean clam soup. The clear broth from boiling these clams has a clean, refreshing taste.  Hadong Freshwater Marsh Clam Village is home to specialty restaurants serving various clam dishes, including Jaecheopguk, tangy clam salads mixed with spicy red pepper paste, and savory golden-brown clam pancakes cooked with fresh chives. When warm spring arrives, food lovers from all over Korea come here to savor the distinct aroma and flavor of Hadong's freshwater marsh clams.  Visit Hadong, where refreshing breezes blow along the Seomjingang River, and enjoy a bowl of soothing clam soup that fills your senses with the taste of spring.

stories.title: The Story Behind Sunchang's Renowned Flavors
stories.audioTitle: The Story Behind Sunchang's Renowned Flavors
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! The highlight of this culinary journey is Sunchang Gochujang—a special ingredient known for enhancing the flavor of any dish.  The deep, rich taste of Sunchang Gochujang comes from the precise fermentation of Meju—traditional blocks of fermented soybeans. During fermentation, beneficial molds called Nuruk develop in the soybeans. These molds break down proteins to create rich umami flavor and convert starches into natural sweetness, giving Gochujang its uniquely addictive taste. By carefully controlling temperature, humidity, and mold maturation, this meticulous process ensures that Gochujang develops an even deeper and richer flavor as it matures.  Sunchang has long been renowned throughout Korea for the exceptional taste of its traditional sauces, known collectively as Jang. As early as 1809, the household encyclopedia Gyuhap Chongseo praised Sunchang Gochujang as a specialty famous throughout Korea, affirming its outstanding quality and historic reputation. Thanks to abundant sunshine and mild daily temperature changes, farmers in Sunchang harvest fresh chili peppers earlier than those in other regions—typically in August and September—which is perfect timing for making Gochujang. Unlike regular Gochujang fermented with common white mold, Sunchang Gochujang uses a special yellow mold known for its excellent protein-breaking properties. This unique fermentation enhances the Gochujang’s signature sweet and spicy flavors, creating a richer and deeper taste.  At the Sunchang Traditional Gochujang Folk Village, you can try making Gochujang yourself and sample a variety of delicious dishes that highlight its unique flavor, including spicy Tteokbokki and savory Gochujang Chicken. Why not visit Sunchang, the hometown of authentic Gochujang, and enjoy an unforgettable culinary adventure, where traditional craftsmanship and scientific precision create a magical harmony of flavors?

stories.title: Freshwater Eel: Crispy on the Outside, Rich and Oily on the Inside
stories.audioTitle: Freshwater Eel: Crispy on the Outside, Rich and Oily on the Inside
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! The highlight of this culinary journey is Gochang’s renowned Pungcheon Eel—crispy on the outside, with a wonderfully rich, oily flavor inside.  Did you know freshwater eels, much like salmon, migrate between rivers and the ocean? Located in the Pungcheon area, where rivers flow into the sea, Gochang provides an optimal habitat for these migratory eels.  Freshwater eels are typically raised in farms, starting from young eels collected at sea. The region around Juchincheon Stream in Gochang is particularly famous for combining advanced farming techniques with an ideal natural environment, producing superior-quality eels. Thanks to these ideal conditions, Gochang has established itself as one of Korea’s leading freshwater eel producers, accounting for more than 30% of national production.  Interestingly, freshwater eel became a widely enjoyed delicacy relatively recently. Its popularity began in the 1970s when locals in Gochang first started grilling and selling Pungcheon Eel. By the 1990s, eel had gained fame as an energizing and stamina-boosting food, turning the Seonunsa area into a nationwide hotspot for eel cuisine.  There are many delightful ways to savor Pungcheon Eel. Grilled over charcoal and lightly seasoned with just a pinch of salt, it offers a wonderfully rich and smoky flavor. Or, for a completely different taste, wrap the eel in fresh greens such as lettuce or perilla leaves, and pair it with aromatic ginger and garlic to enjoy an exciting combination of textures and flavors.  In August and September, when the warmth of summer gently fades into autumn, Gochang brims with the rich flavors of Pungcheon Eel. Come enjoy the deep, savory taste of this local delicacy amid Gochang's beautiful seasonal scenery.

stories.title: A Nourishing Specialty of Wando
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! The highlight of this culinary journey is Wando Abalone—a nourishing delicacy cherished by Koreans for generations.  Abalone has long been considered a luxury seafood ingredient. Across many East Asian cultures, including Korea, abalone—with its sturdy shell and powerful suction cups—is traditionally seen as a symbol of health and longevity. And indeed, abalone is packed with beneficial nutrients known to help relieve fatigue and improve metabolism, making it a wonderfully nourishing food.  Today, most of the abalone enjoyed in Korea is farmed in Wando. In fact, Wando accounts for about 74% of the country's total abalone production, largely thanks to another local specialty—kelp. Since kelp is a primary food source for abalone, farmers in Wando strategically place their abalone farms alongside kelp farms, providing an ideal environment for abalone to feed and thrive.  Abalone can be enjoyed in many delicious ways. Abalone Porridge, made by gently simmering finely chopped abalone with rice, is the perfect comfort food for when you're feeling exhausted, stressed, or simply lacking an appetite. Another delicacy is thinly sliced raw abalone, served with soy sauce or spicy Cho-gochujang (a sweet and tangy red pepper sauce), offering a refreshing taste of the sea. Steamed or grilled abalone dishes are always popular, and buttery sautéed abalone with fresh vegetables is another local favorite.  Freshly harvested abalone in Wando has a distinctively stronger ocean aroma compared to those you might taste inland, offering an authentic, briny flavor of the sea. This fall, visit Wando to savor fresh, nutritious abalone dishes—delighting your palate while boosting your health!

stories.title: The Pioneering K-Food Captivating the World
stories.audioTitle: The Pioneering K-Food Captivating the World
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! The star of this culinary journey is Wando Laver, a beloved, nutrient-rich side dish enjoyed throughout Korea.  Laver is a type of seaweed from the genera Porphyra or Pyropia. Traditionally, it's dried into thin sheets, then cut into rectangular shapes. Koreans commonly enjoy laver by wrapping it around rice, creating small, bite-sized parcels, or simply as a crispy side dish lightly dipped in soy sauce. Thanks to its crispy texture and savory taste, laver is loved by people of all ages, and it's also a must-buy souvenir among tourists visiting Korea.  In the past, laver was known as Haetae, literally meaning Grass from the Sea. According to tradition, when a man named Kim Yeo-ik successfully cultivated haetae in the 17th century, it was renamed kim, after his family name, to commemorate his achievement.  Today, Wando accounts for about half of Korea's total laver production, thanks to its pristine coastal waters, abundant sunlight, and mudflats ideal for cultivating laver. Gogeum Island, one of Wando’s islands, is especially renowned for its high-quality Dolgim, a type of laver. Here, locals maintain the traditional cultivation method, in which laver nets are attached to wooden stakes set into the mudflats. Thanks to this traditional cultivation method, Wando laver receives the perfect amount of natural sunlight, resulting in its uniquely rich aroma and deep, savory flavor.  Imagine savoring a crispy sheet of laver infused with the fresh, clean energy of Wando's blue seas. To experience this distinctive texture and delightful aroma, why not visit Wando today?

stories.title: A Chewy, Nourishing, and Delicious Dish
stories.audioTitle: A Chewy, Nourishing, and Delicious Dish
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! The highlight of this culinary journey is Muan Octopus—famous for its chewy texture and outstanding nutritional benefits.  Have you ever heard the Korean saying, Feed live octopus to an exhausted ox, and it'll regain its strength? Indeed, octopus is well-known for being rich in taurine, a nutrient known to help relieve fatigue and boost energy. It's especially popular in autumn, when it's in season and considered particularly nourishing.
