Cafes, bakeries, and boutiques moved in, keeping the original concrete walls and steel structures to create a unique atmosphere. Thanks to this, young people and foreign tourists visit constantly. Every weekend, various brands open pop-up stores here, making it a center of trends.  Seongsu-dong Cafe Street is full of stylish and creative cafes. One special place is Grandfather's Factory, a cafe with an old exterior but a very modern interior that creates a unique vintage charm. This cafe also appeared as a location in the drama Vincenzo. There's a funny scene where Hong Cha-young suggests a cool iced americano to Vincenzo, an Italian mafia lawyer who orders espresso double shots. This scene made many viewers laugh.  Vincenzo: In Italy, americano is no different from dirty water. Hong Cha-young: (Looking at the part-time worker) I'll have one iced dirty water, please.  Vincenzo reveals the truth about her father's death and tells her to stay away from Babel Group. Hong Cha-young becomes angry at this truth and insists she will fight until the end. This scene takes place on a terrace surrounded by plants. Unlike their heavy conversation, the atmosphere feels warm and relaxed. Viewers watching these two people in conflict hope that someday they will become strong partners fighting against evil together.  Now Seongsu-dong Cafe Street has become more than just a trendy place. It has become a cultural space where new feelings and stories bloom every day. Take a cup of coffee and walk slowly through this street. An ordinary day here can become a special memory.

stories.title: A House that Holds the Spirit of Korea's Modern Era, Baek In-je House
stories.audioTitle: A House that Holds the Spirit of Korea's Modern Era, Baek In-je House
stories.script: "Welcome to K-Culture Travel! This cultural journey features a famous landmark in Bukchon where traditional Korean hanok and modern architecture blend together beautifully. This is the story of Baek In-je House.  Baek In-je House is a traditional house located in Bukchon Hanok Village in Gahoe-dong, Jongno-gu, Seoul. It was built in 1913 by Han Sang-ryong, who was an executive director of Hanseong Bank. The house is named after its last owner, Dr. Baek In-je, a surgeon. he house has the main reception hall (sarangchae) in the center, with the family living quarters (anchae) and a large garden around it. At the highest point, there is a small separate pavilion. Although it was built during the Japanese colonial period, it is well-preserved and maintains the beauty of traditional hanok while accepting modern changes like red bricks and glass windows. Because of this value, it was designated as Seoul Folk Cultural Property in 1977. Today, it is open to the public as a special place where people can experience the atmosphere and history of Bukchon.   Baek In-je House, where you can feel the layers of history, is also the filming location for a dramatic scene in the drama ""Reborn Rich."" In this scene, Jin Do-jun reveals to Chairman Jin Yang-cheol that he is the major shareholder of Miracle Investment. Jin Do-jun discovers that Soonyang Group was behind his mother's death. He then begins his fight to take control of Soonyang Group through Miracle Investment, the company he established.  Jin Do-jun: ""I plan to buy Soonyang. With my own money.""  Chairman Jin Yang-cheol is furious and feels betrayed to discover that the major shareholder of Miracle Investment, which threatens Soonyang Group, is his own youngest grandson. Meanwhile, Jin Do-jun boldly declares he will buy Soonyang Group, breaking the tradition of eldest son inheritance. At that moment, the darkness filling the sarangchae of Baek In-je House contrasts sharply with the light coming through the windows, creating maximum tension between the two characters. This scene was a key turning point in the drama, the symbolic moment when Jin Do-jun fully revealed his revenge and ambition toward Soonyang Group.  After the tense scene fades away, Baek In-je House returns to its peaceful quiet. The clean lines and open spaces of Baek In-je House still stand quietly in their place today, holding traces of many years of history. Take a slow walk through the courtyard and feel the peaceful atmosphere around you."

stories.title: Where the Reform Spirit of Joseon's King Still Echoes, Gyeonghuigung Palace
stories.audioTitle: Where the Reform Spirit of Joseon's King Still Echoes, Gyeonghuigung Palace
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel! This cultural journey features a palace in the heart of Seoul that truly lives up to its bright and beautiful name. This is the story of Gyeonghuigung Palace.  Gyeonghuigung Palace was completed in 1623 during the reign of King Gwanghaegun, the 15th king of Joseon. The name means bright and fortunate palace. The palace has several important buildings that show the finest examples of Joseon palace architecture. These include Sungjeong Hall as the main hall, along with Hoesang Hall, Heungjeong Hall, Jonhyeon Pavilion, and others. Jonhyeon Pavilion is especially significant as it served as the royal library where crown princes studied.   Among Seoul's ancient palaces, Gyeonghuigung Palace is relatively quiet and peaceful, keeping its calm and serene atmosphere. This makes it a perfect quiet retreat in the busy city and a place where visitors can feel like they are traveling back in time. The elegant and dignified beauty of Gyeonghuigung Palace, along with its peaceful atmosphere, has attracted many movie and drama producers. In particular, the movie The Fatal Encounter perfectly captured the charm of Gyeonghuigung Palace on screen.   The movie The Fatal Encounter is set one year after King Jeongjo, the 22nd king of Joseon, came to the throne. It tells the story of Jeongjo constantly pushing for reforms. In the movie, Jonhyeon Pavilion at Gyeonghuigung Palace serves as the main stage for King Jeongjo's activities. There is a tense scene on a rainy night where the top assassin Salso breaks into Jonhyeon Pavilion to kill King Jeongjo. This thrilling moment, combined with the quiet and mysterious nighttime atmosphere of Gyeonghuigung Palace, created heart-pounding suspense for the audience.   The story of King Jeongjo set at Gyeonghuigung Palace wasn't limited to just thrilling moments. In scenes set at Sungjeong Hall of Gyeonghuigung Palace, King Jeongjo's voice rang out with absolute confidence as he revealed his strong beliefs.  King Jeongjo: Only those who give their absolute best with sincere dedication can work with me to change the world.  The grand columns and elegant rooflines of Sungjeong Hall perfectly matched King Jeongjo's strong will, adding weight and depth to his words. The powerful cinematography, meaningful dialogue, and the beautiful atmosphere of Gyeonghuigung Palace came together to create a deeply moving experience that touches hearts across time.  How about taking a walk through Gyeonghuigung Palace and thinking about King Jeongjo's struggles and determination from the movie The Fatal Encounter? In this peaceful palace setting, feel the breath of history around you. Take a moment to pause and reflect deeply on your own will and determination.

stories.title: Where Parallel Worlds Cross in Central Seoul, Gwanghwamun Square
stories.audioTitle: Where Parallel Worlds Cross in Central Seoul, Gwanghwamun Square
stories.script: "Welcome to K-Culture Travel! This cultural journey features a place where centuries of history and modern city life come together beautifully. This is the story of Gwanghwamun Square.   Gwanghwamun Square has been a symbolic space at the center of Korean history from the Joseon Dynasty until today. This square is located in front of Gwanghwamun Gate, the main entrance to Gyeongbokgung Palace. Since ancient times, many historic moments and national events have taken place here, giving it deep symbolic meaning. On the north side of the square stands a statue of King Sejong, and on the south side is a statue of Admiral Yi Sun-sin. These represent Korea's spirit and pride, attracting many visitors to this special place.   Gwanghwamun Square is located on Seoul's central axis, connecting Gyeongbokgung Palace to the north, Cheonggyecheon Stream to the east, and Sejong-ro intersection to the south. The wide walking paths, green spaces, and refreshing fountains provide a peaceful break in the busy city. Important government and cultural buildings like the Government Complex and Sejong Center for the Performing Arts surround the area. At night, the beautifully lit Gwanghwamun Gate and Gyeongbokgung Palace blend with the modern city lights, creating a unique beauty where Seoul's past and present come together in one view.  This unique contrast between old and new often appears in movies and dramas, showing Seoul's special visual charm. In particular, in the drama ""The King: Eternal Monarch,"" this becomes the symbolic place where the main characters from two different worlds first meet each other. One world is the Korean Empire and the other is the Republic of Korea.  Lee Gon: ""Finally, I get to see you. Detective Jung Tae-eul.""  In the drama, Emperor Lee Gon from the Korean Empire crosses into a parallel world and arrives in the Republic of Korea. The scene where he first meets detective Jung Tae-eul made viewers' hearts race with excitement.  The footsteps of modern people walking through Gwanghwamun Square and the lights of cars on the roads come together to create a special scene. Against this backdrop, a story that crosses time and space begins, making the fantasy setting of the drama even more magical.  Gwanghwamun Square has been the stage for countless stories throughout centuries. A day spent here might bring you dramatic moments too. Why not start your own special story today with the beautiful views, city lights, and gentle breeze of Gwanghwamun Square as your backdrop?"

stories.title: A Peaceful Place Among the City Buildings, Bukchon Hanok Village
stories.audioTitle: A Peaceful Place Among the City Buildings, Bukchon Hanok Village
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel! This cultural journey features a place that holds 600 years of Seoul's history. Located between Gyeongbokgung Palace and Changdeokgung Palace, this is the story of Bukchon Hanok Village.  Bukchon was a historic village where aristocratic families and royalty lived during the Joseon period. It is a special place where tradition and modern life exist together beautifully in the heart of the city. The view of traditional hanok houses from Gahoe-dong 31st street hill is one of Bukchon's 8 Scenic Views and shows the finest example of Seoul's traditional architecture.  The hanok houses along narrow alleys have stood close together for many years. The tile roofs connect like waves, and the peaceful atmosphere beyond the stone walls brings comfort and peace to visitors' hearts. This quiet and beautiful mood of Bukchon Hanok Village has made it the perfect setting for many stories that want to show deep emotions.  Maybe that's why the drama Personal Taste, which shows the love and friendship of two very different people living together, chose Bukchon Hanok Village as the setting for their story. This place was more than just a beautiful location. The emotions and feelings in the drama matched perfectly with the peaceful mood of Bukchon.   Park Gae-in: Sanggojae is the name my mother gave to this place. She wanted it to be a place where people love each other... Let's live here together happily for a long, long time.   In the drama, the place that appears as Sanggojae is actually a peaceful hanok called Yeorangjae. It is the first house on the right side of the alley going from Bukchon's 5th scenic view to the 6th scenic view. The name Yeorangjae means beautiful and virtuous, which fits perfectly with the meaning of Sanggojae in the drama.   There are old gates and walls covered with ivy, and alleys that seem to hold old memories. In this place, the two characters slowly open up to each other and learn to understand one another. Even though they are awkward at first, they gradually build a deep and genuine relationship. The scenery and atmosphere of Bukchon became the source of authenticity and emotion that flows throughout the entire drama.  Take a walk through Bukchon Hanok Village today and enjoy the sunlight shining between the traditional roofs and the gentle breeze over the tile roofs. In that moment, you might find yourself looking at someone's heart in a new way. How about finding your own special place for love here in Bukchon Hanok Village?

stories.title: Where Love and Longing Stay, Deoksugung Stone Wall Path
stories.audioTitle: Where Love and Longing Stay, Deoksugung Stone Wall Path
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel! This cultural journey features a place where you can fully experience the peaceful charm of a stone wall path. This is the story of Deoksugung Stone Wall Path.  Deoksugung Stone Wall Path is located in the heart of Seoul. This beautiful walking path features a 1,100-meter stone wall built in traditional Korean style and many green trees. The trees change with each season, so you can enjoy different beautiful views all year round. Here, you can see both the traditional Joseon palace and modern Seoul together, creating a stunning scene.  Deoksugung Stone Wall Path has an old superstition that says couples who walk together here will break up. In the past, Seoul Family Court was located along this stone wall path. Couples who came to the court for divorce were often seen walking together on this path. This is how the story naturally began.  Maybe that's why the main characters in Discovery of Love, Han Yeo-reum and Kang Tae-ha, carefully avoided this path when they were dating. But after they broke up and met again, they could now walk side by side along the stone wall path without any worry.  Han Yeo-reum's thoughts: I guess Kang Tae-ha and I really can't just be friends. I want to hold his hand so badly. Kang Tae-ha's thoughts: Should I pretend to be drunk and hold her back? Should I pretend to be drunk and... kiss her?  In this quiet night scene, they walk along the stone wall path having calm conversations. You can feel their deep emotions for each other and the weight of all the time that has passed. The path they once avoided because of the superstition, they now walk together naturally. This reality makes their hearts even more complicated. The peaceful atmosphere of Deoksugung Stone Wall Path makes the longing and lingering feelings between these former lovers even deeper.   Why don't you take a walk along Deoksugung Stone Wall Path and think about your own precious memories? As you walk and remember the past, you might naturally create wonderful new memories!

stories.title: Where Our Beloved Summer Story Stayed, Jaha Super
stories.audioTitle: Where Our Beloved Summer Story Stayed, Jaha Super
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel! This cultural journey features a place that may not be fancy, but has a special way of touching your heart. This is the story of “Jaha Super”, an emotional spot that moves people's hearts.  This small supermarket sits quietly at the end of an old alley in Jongno, Seoul. With just an old sign, a low roof, and a wooden deck in front, it brings back the feelings and atmosphere of the past. As you walk slowly along Hongjecheon stream, you will naturally come across this place. It keeps the simple and warm scenes that are hard to find in the city. Here, you can feel like time has stopped.  This place has appeared in many Korean dramas because of its special emotional atmosphere. The most memorable scene was from the drama Our Beloved Summer, which tells a sweet story of young love.  Here, university students Yeon-su and Woong learn to accept their differences and become stronger as individuals. The scene at Jaha Super, with spring wind blowing and yellow lights twinkling, was the perfect setting that beautifully showed the sweet moments between the two characters.  Yeon-su: We saw the cherry blossoms together.  This short line carries much deeper feelings than words can express. Cherry blossoms were falling in the spring wind. These two people, who had missed each other in their busy daily lives, sat facing each other on the wooden platform in front of Jaha Super. In the spring breeze, they shared their hearts again. The falling cherry blossoms, together with this simple dialogue, blended beautifully with the quiet mood of Jaha Super. This scene perfectly showed the growing understanding between the two characters.   For some people, Jaha Super is a place to stop by for a quick break with an ice cream. For others, it becomes a place where they shared unforgettable conversations. Why not take a break from the busy city life and create your own special day here, just like in Our Beloved Summer?

stories.title: Home of the Lonely and Great Goblin, Unhyeongung Yanggwan
stories.audioTitle: Home of the Lonely and Great Goblin, Unhyeongung Yanggwan
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel! This cultural journey features the story of Unhyeongung Yanggwan, a place that has quietly kept its original beauty among Seoul's beautiful royal palaces.   Unhyeongung Yanggwan is a Western-style building located within Unhyeongung Palace, where the spirit of Korea's late Joseon royal family still remains. Unhyeongung Palace features beautiful traditional Korean design with detailed wooden structures and elegant classic beauty. Within this traditional setting, Unhyeongung Yanggwan stands out with its curved roof, stone columns, and Western decorative elements. Though it contrasts sharply with the traditional Korean buildings around it, the two styles blend together beautifully to create a unique and special scene.   These two places show how different architectural styles can exist together beautifully. Among them, Unhyeongung Yanggwan became famous again after appearing in the drama Goblin as the home where the immortal Goblin Kim Shin and the Grim Reaper live together. These are beings who live forever but never truly belong anywhere in the world. The Goblin and Grim Reaper are neither gods nor humans. This place where they stayed creates a mysterious feeling that naturally moves between reality and fantasy.  Kim Shin: My life of meeting you was a gift. I love you. I‘ve already done even that.  This short confession contains the deep feelings of someone who lived alone for hundreds of years and the end of a life that seemed eternal. To show the love and waiting of the Goblin, a being beyond this world, for his bride, Unhyeongung Yanggwan became the perfect stage.   Here at Unhyeongung Yanggwan, foreign beauty meets traditional Korean style. This is a place where countless stories and moments in time have passed through. And now, with your visit, this place welcomes the start of a new story. How about creating your own special moment here today?

stories.title: Gyeongju Daereungwon Ancient Tomb Complex: An Iconic Legacy of Silla’s Tomb Culture
stories.audioTitle: Gyeongju Daereungwon Ancient Tomb Complex: An Iconic Legacy of Silla’s Tomb Culture
stories.script: Welcome to the K-Culture Tour! Today’s journey takes us to “Gyeongju Daereungwon Ancient Tomb Complex,” a unique place where a thousand years of Silla history flow together with the rhythms of everyday life.  Located in Hwangnam-dong, Gyeongju, Daereungwon is a vast cluster of tombs built for the royal family and nobility of the Silla Dynasty. The tombs are classified into three main categories: royal tombs, mound tombs, and common tombs. When a tomb is confirmed to belong to a king, it is called a “royal tomb.” If the artifacts suggest it might be a king’s or queen’s tomb but are not verified, it is called a “mound tomb.” Tombs  of nobility below the royal family are simply called “tombs.” The name “Daereungwon” comes from the Samguk Sagi (The History of the Three Kingdoms), which records that King Michu was buried in Daereung. Indeed, one of the tombs here is believed to be the resting place of King Michu himself.  This area is home to several renowned ancient tombs, including Cheonmachong, Hwangnamdaechong, and Geumgwanchong Tombs. These tombs were built by digging a pit into the ground, placing a wooden outer coffin containing the body and burial goods inside, and then covering it with layers of large stones and earth to form a mound. Their sturdy construction helped protect the tombs from looters and preserved them remarkably well. Thanks to this, archaeologists have uncovered precious artifacts such as gold crowns and intricate gold ornaments, which reveal the artistic skill and rich funerary traditions of the Silla period.  In 1973, Daereungwon was developed into an ancient tomb park and has since become a beloved walking spot for both locals and visitors. The site also blends seamlessly with the several scenes from the film Gyeongju, in which the main character, Choi Hyeon, rides his bicycle through the city and is even scolded by a security guard for lying down on a tomb. One particularly memorable scene shows Choi Hyeon arriving at Yoon-hee’s house, pulling back the curtains to reveal the massive tombs of Daereungwon stretching out before him.  Gong Yoon-hee: “Isn't it strange to have the royal tomb right in front of the house?” Choi Hyeon: “I think it's nice.” Gong Yoon-hee: “It's hard to live in Gyeongju without seeing the royal tomb.”  As Yoon-hee points out, the “royal tombs” are not just historical landmarks to the people of Gyeongju; they are part of the everyday landscape, quietly woven into the fabric of daily life. Like the tombs scattered across the city that have silently watched over the passing of time, the moments you encounter here seep gently into your heart. Take a moment now to observe the gentle flow of time along the ridges of these ancient mounds. You may find yourself breathing a little slower, immersed in the calm atmosphere and deep history that surround you.

stories.title: Introduction of Seong An Olle Route 3 Audio Guide
stories.audioTitle: Introduction of Seong An Olle Route 3 Audio Guide
stories.script: (Guide) Guide Amy Kim (Cast) Guide Amy Kim   Hello, my name is Amy Kim, and I am working as a guide in the Seong An Olle program with narration. I have been working in the tourism industry for 35 years as a licensed tour interpreter. Having long been interested in village tours, I was delighted to find the wonderful opportunity of Seong An Olle and am enjoying my work with great enthusiasm.   The word Seong An in Seong An Olle refers to the inner part of Jeju Eupseong, which has now almost disappeared. It was also called Seong Nae or Mokgwan, meaning inside Jejumok. In comparison to Seoul, it would be the area inside the four gates, or in today’s terms, the downtown. Visiting Seong An , where government offices and major commercial facilities were concentrated, was considered a grand outing for Jeju people in the past. Adults used to say that whenever they went to Seong An , they left home dressed up in their finest.   The total length of Course 3 is 5.3 km, which is perfect for walking. Now, let’s begin our journey to hear stories of Seongan that even many Jeju locals may not know.

stories.title: Gallery Remicon
stories.script: Why is it called Remicon? The reason is that the person who purchased this old building and transformed it into a beautiful gallery was none other than the president of a ready-mix concrete company (Remicon). Thanks to that, the gallery’s name alone has drawn great attention, making it a landmark in the old downtown. Although demolishing the old structure and building anew would have been cheaper and easier, the owner couldn’t forget the memories of going to kindergarten via the stairs next to this building as a child. So, he decided to preserve as much of the original form as possible when renovating. As a result, Gallery Remicon has become an open cultural space for everyone today. Originally, this place was Myeongseung Hotel, which opened in 1962 as Jeju’s first modern-style accommodation. The building was painted entirely pink, earning it the nickname “Pink Hotel” at the time. Now, when we say “modern accommodation,” what is the criterion? It is the installation of flush toilets. In the early 1960s, even in Jeju City, the typical toilet culture was what locals called dottongsi — an ecological toilet system connecting human latrines with pigsties. At such a time, Myeongseung Hotel introduced flush toilets. The first floor of the hotel was used as the Jeju branch of the Government Central Public Information Office, where newsreels were shown. The second and third floors housed the front desk and guest rooms. Interestingly, in the 1960s, there were more Western-style rooms than Korean-style rooms. The fourth floor was designed as a banquet hall. When you stepped outside, a terrace opened up, serving as a social gathering place for local leaders and celebrities. During dance parties and banquets, the hotel chef presented special dishes — extraordinary for the time — such as pork cutlets, Hamburg steak, and macaroni. If you look at the building’s façade, you can see it decorated with tiles. Tile construction methods were actually popular in the 1970s, but Myeongseung Hotel introduced them in the early 1960s, making the building itself the talk of the town.

stories.title: Marine Soul Tower and the Jeju April 3 Incident
stories.audioTitle: Marine Soul Tower and the Jeju April 3 Incident
stories.script: The Marine Soul Tower stands tall at Dongmun Rotary, near Dongmun Market, yet many Jeju residents who pass by daily know little about it. The tower was built in 1960 by the 3rd and 4th class units of the Marine Corps, composed mainly of Jeju natives who survived the Korean War, to honor their comrades who never returned.  Shall we take a closer look at the inscription? In the phrase Marine Soul written in Chinese characters, you may notice something unusual about the character “魂” (soul). The calligrapher, Mr. Kim Gwang-chu, deliberately left out one stroke from the radical “鬼” (ghost) at the top. This omission symbolized that it was not the soul of the dead, but the immortal soul. Thus, the Marine Soul Tower was built with heartfelt devotion.  The Republic of Korea Marine Corps was established on April 15, 1949, with 380 men. By the outbreak of the Korean War, there were barely a thousand. After the war began, the Navy Headquarters relocated to Jeju, and to reinforce the insufficient forces, Marine Corps recruitment began. On August 5, 1,500 men were recruited for the 3rd class, and on August 30, another 1,500 for the 4th class. These 3,000 Jeju men, with little training, departed Jeju Port on September 1. To this day, September 1 is remembered as “Jeju Marine Corps Day.”  But why did so many Jeju youths volunteer for a war where death was almost certain? I believe the main reason was the Jeju April 3 Incident. The conflict was still ongoing in 1950 when the Korean War began, and it wasn’t until September 21, 1954, when the martial ban on Hallasan was lifted, that it officially ended. Under Syngman Rhee’s regime, bereaved families, teachers, and village leaders were arrested and massacred under the pretext that they might “collaborate with the North.” Witnessing this, islanders lived in constant fear. For the young, volunteering to fight in the war carried a faint hope: “If I fight against the North Korean army, perhaps my family will no longer be branded as communists, and we can live safely.” Tragically, many of them never came home.

stories.title: Dongmun Market and the Story of Omegi Tteok
stories.audioTitle: Dongmun Market and the Story of Omegi Tteok
stories.script: Dongmun Market is known nationwide as one of the most vibrant permanent traditional markets. Since it was included in Olle Course 18, it has become a destination for many travelers, gaining popularity and nationwide recognition.  The market attracts all kinds of visitors. Once mainly frequented by Jeju locals for cheap and diverse goods, it has now become a hotspot for travelers from all over the world. Dongmun Market is also a paradise for food lovers. At Gate 1, you’ll find what many call the tastiest hotteok in Korea, and in the alleys near Hyundai Pharmacy, you can try local specialties hard to find elsewhere, like pheasant buckwheat noodles or bingtteok. From fresh sashimi at family-run restaurants to hearty pork rice soup, the food choices are endless. With the influx of visitors, shops specializing in Jeju traditional liquor and even wine stores have appeared, and stalls run by young people selling food with performances have become attractions in themselves.  So, what is the most popular item in Dongmun Market? I’d say it’s omegi tteok. Anyone who has visited Jeju has likely tried it. Interestingly, omegi tteok was not originally meant to be eaten as rice cake. It was a type of sul-tteok (fermented cake) brewed to make a traditional Jeju liquor called omegi-sul.  Because Jeju’s volcanic soil made rice farming difficult, people relied mainly on millet and barley. Naturally, these grains were also used for brewing. Barley was used to make yeast, while millet was used for fermentation. Since millet rice did not ferment well, they made cakes out of it to brew alcohol. Mostly green-colored foxtail millet was used, giving omegi tteok its distinctive greenish hue. Though it should be made from 100% millet, today’s omegi tteok in Dongmun Market is usually made with glutinous rice and mugwort, since millet is expensive and hard to work with.  But what does the name “omegi tteok” actually mean? Curious myself, I visited the master craftsman of omegi-sul, recognized as Jeju Intangible Cultural Asset No. 3, in Seongeup Folk Village. He explained: “When you make rice cakes with millet, they often don’t cook properly, leaving the center raw. So people would press the center with their finger to shape it. The standard word is omok (concave), but in our village we pronounced it omek. Over time, people said omek tteok or omegi tteok. That’s how the name was passed down.” And so, the name of omegi tteok, now little known even to Jeju locals, was born.

stories.title: Jeigak(制夷閣)
stories.script: Jeigak is one of Jeju’s hidden gems, little known even to locals. In 2013, during investigations for the restoration of Jeju Eupseong, the site of Jeigak was discovered. As its name Jei (制夷: “to subdue the barbarians”) suggests, it was originally a military watchtower. After the Imjin War ended in 1599, King Seonjo ordered the reinforcement of national defense facilities, and records show that Magistrate Seong Yun-mun of Jeju established Jeigak at that time.  Jeigak stands atop a protruding bastion of Jeju Eupseong. Bastions were special structures designed to repel enemies climbing the fortress walls with arrows, and Jeju Eupseong had as many as 19 of them.  But what does bastion (chisung) mean? You know pheasants, right? When a pheasant encounters people on the road, sometimes it flutters away, but more often it just runs and, upon finding a gap, shoves its head into it to hide. A pheasant thinks, “If I can’t see the enemy, then the enemy can’t see me either.” Bastions resemble pheasants hiding their heads while their bodies stick out, which is why the character for pheasant (鴩) was used to form the word chisung. However, the Map of Jeju Mok Fortress from the late Joseon Dynasty shows that Jeigak, once a military watchtower, had been renamed Cheongpungdae and repurposed as a scenic spot for enjoying panoramic views.

stories.title: Finding Life Quotes in the Alley of Four-Character Idioms
stories.audioTitle: Finding Life Quotes in the Alley of Four-Character Idioms
stories.script: As you walk along the Sanjicheon stream toward Samseonghyeol, take a moment to glance aside. A narrow, old alley comes into view. Rows of Western-style houses, likely built around the 1980s, stand there. On the timeworn walls, heartwarming murals appear alongside four-character idioms written in Chinese characters. The old alley and the ancient sayings seem to harmonize beautifully.  Shall we take a look at a few of the murals? First, Tian Chang Di Jiu (天長地久), meaning “Heaven and Earth endure forever.” I remember this phrase as the title of a film starring Anita Mui and Andy Lau that I once watched at the cinema. The poignant love story they portrayed still lingers in my memory. The movie was likely titled this way to suggest that their love, like heaven and earth, would never change.  The one that struck me most was Xiaomen Wanfulai (笑門萬福來), meaning “A smiling gate brings ten thousand blessings.” It reminded me of a TV show from my childhood, Smile and Fortune Comes, which my whole family enjoyed watching together. Such fond memories.  But perhaps the phrase most beloved by many is Huayang Nianhua (花樣年華), which means “the most beautiful and happiest moment in life.” Isn’t the very moment we are walking down this alley one of the most beautiful and happiest in our lives?

stories.title: Gwangyangdang Site
stories.script: Gwangyangdang was the largest shamanic shrine in Jeju, dedicated to the guardian spirit of Hallasan Mountain. According to the Sinjeung Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam (1530), “Gwangyangdang, along with Chagwidang, was one of Jeju’s representative shrines. Each spring and autumn, men and women would gather to offer wine and meat in rituals.” Before Confucian rites became the norm during the Joseon dynasty, it was regarded as the national shrine (gukdang) of the Tamna Kingdom, and it is presumed that state rituals were conducted here.  This assumption is supported by records in the Sejong Sillok Jiriji and Dongguk Yeoji Seungnam. They note that during the Goryeo period, a Taoist practitioner named Hojongdan tried to sever Jeju’s spiritual energy before leaving the island. Enraged, the deity of Gwangyangdang transformed into a hawk and sank the ship he was sailing on. As recognition of this, the state conferred the title of “King Gwangyang” upon the guardian spirit of Hallasan and decreed annual rites in his honor. This shows the shrine had official recognition at the national level.  What is unusual here is that “Hojongdan,” who appears in the myth, was in fact a real historical figure. He was a man from the Song dynasty who naturalized in Korea during King Yejong’s reign (1105–1122) and even served as an official. What happened between him and Jeju remains a mystery.  In 1105, King Yejong downgraded the Kingdom of Tamna to Tamna-gun, an administrative district of Goryeo, reducing its semi-independent status. In 1153, King Sukjong further downgraded it to Tamna-hyeon and dispatched local officials. Scholars view this as the point when Tamna was fully annexed into Goryeo. Considering this historical background, the myth may have been a way for the people to express their resentment and resistance against annexation through symbolic narrative.  According to oral shamanic traditions, the deity of Gwangyangdang was said to be the eldest brother of the Seonangdang deity of Jeongui-hyeon and the Gwangjeongdang deity of Daejeong-hyeon. The three brothers shot arrows to decide their respective territories, with the eldest, Gwangyangdang, claiming Jejumok. This story sounds familiar, doesn’t it? Let’s go seek out other tales with similar motifs.

stories.title: Samseonghyeol (Three Clans Cave) and the Samseong Myth
stories.audioTitle: Samseonghyeol (Three Clans Cave) and the Samseong Myth
stories.script: Samseonghyeol is known as the place where the ancestors of the three clans—Yang Eulna, Go Eulna, and Bu Eulna—emerged from three holes to found the Tamna Kingdom. However, the name Samseonghyeol itself is relatively recent; until the mid-Joseon period, it was called Mohunghyeol (毛興穴). According to texts such as Tamna Ji Chobon, “The three holes were arranged in the shape of the character 品, and from them arose the Three Eulna (三乙那). When the three ‘Eul’ (乙) are combined, they form the character 毛, hence the name.”  In the myth, the three divine beings (sinin) who emerged were all men. They lived by hunting animals and gathering fruits until they discovered a wooden chest drifting from the eastern sea. Inside were three women from Byeokrang-guk (碧浪國). They married the men, formed families, and thus began the Tamna Kingdom. The women also brought seeds of five grains and livestock such as cattle and horses. However, the Goryeosa Jiriji identifies the origin as Japan instead of Byeokrang-guk, leading to some debate. In any case, the Samseong myth reflects how the island’s indigenous people, once hunters and gatherers, accepted outsiders with agricultural knowledge, leading to the formation of a more advanced state system—through peaceful union represented by marriage.  In 1526, Magistrate Yi Su-dong built a memorial stone (Hyeolbi) and a red gate (Hongmun) north of Samseonghyeol and instituted Confucian-style rites. From this, the site began to be sanctified, and ritual ceremonies continue to this day.  Meanwhile, in 1786, Magistrate Yi Myeong-jun reported to the king: “In the past, no shrine was built here and no ancestral rites were performed. It was only Gwangyangdang, where shamans prayed and held rituals. But in the 21st year of King Jungjong, Magistrate Yi Su-dong piled an altar next to Mohunghyeol and had the descendants of the Sam Eulna perform annual rites in the second lunar month.” This suggests Samseonghyeol and Gwangyangdang were originally the same place. It also makes sense that the Gwangyangdang myth of three brothers deciding their territories with arrows overlaps with the Samseong myth. What do you think?

stories.title: Finding Hidden Eateries at Boseong Market
stories.audioTitle: Finding Hidden Eateries at Boseong Market
stories.script: Boseong Market, established in 1972, is home to a bustling “sundae alley,” where about 30 shops compete fiercely. Some have even won prizes at national sundae contests, while others are beloved local favorites recommended by residents. One shop was even featured in Heo Young-man’s famous comic Sikgaek. Above all, the sundae here is affordable and generously portioned, making it popular among loyal regulars for decades—and I’m one of them.  Jeju-style sundae differs slightly from that of the mainland. While mainland sundae typically uses pig small intestines, Jeju sundae is made with large intestines or the rectum, giving it a chewier texture. Pairing a bowl of Boseong Market sundae soup with a glass of Jeju makgeolli is pure happiness—you really must try it.  The market is also famous for its fried chicken. For big gatherings, ordering branded chicken can be expensive, so Jeju locals often choose the market chicken known for its large portions. Many of the market chicken shops are in Boseong Market, with some operated by families for generations, preserving this tradition.  Beyond the main building, a small outdoor market has also formed nearby. Here you’ll find fish shops drying seafood in the open air, friendly butchers, a grandmother’s rice cake shop famous for keeping 1990s flavors and prices, and an aromatic oil shop you shouldn’t miss. The only downside is that the outdoor market tends to close early. Adding to the charm, trendy pubs run by young people have sprung up nearby, creating a vibrant mix of old and new.

stories.title: A Stroll in Sinsan Park
stories.script: Sinsan Park is a beloved resting place for citizens in Jeju City. Along Sanjicheon Stream next to the park, native Jeju king cherry trees grow in clusters, creating a breathtaking scene of blossoms every spring. During this season, many foreign couples come to take wedding photos, and at night people gather to enjoy the spectacular cherry blossom night views.  At the center of Sinsan Park stands a large monument commemorating the arrival of the Olympic flame for the 1988 Seoul Olympics in Jeju. The flame first landed here, circled the island once, and then traveled to the mainland. Just by looking at the monument, one can sense the excitement and passion of that Olympic era.  To the south, a tall tower and stone markers can be seen—the Korean War Memorial. During the war, 10,000 Jeju residents served in the Army and 3,000 in the Marine Corps. The stone markers bear the names of all the soldiers, including those who died in service. Seeing them made me think, “This is how Jeju people express their gratitude to those who fought in the war.”  On one side of Sinsan Park lies a gotjawal forest path, a rare sight within the city. I was amazed when I first discovered it. Beyond the king cherry trees, there are also flowering trees such as chinaberry and crape myrtle, making it both mysterious and pleasant to walk through. For tired legs after walking the Seongan Olle, this path feels like the perfect gift.

stories.title: Jeju Dining Table at the Jeju Folklore & Natural History Museum
stories.audioTitle: Jeju Dining Table at the Jeju Folklore & Natural History Museum
stories.script: The Jeju Folklore & Natural History Museum, which opened in 1984, was designated as one of Jeju’s Outstanding Architectural Assets in 2024. The museum presents Jeju’s traditional culture, the ecology of local flora and fauna, and the everyday life of Jeju people in an accessible way.  The museum has seven exhibition spaces, including the lobby. There is the Natural History Hall, which explains in detail the formation of volcanic Jeju; the Folklore Hall, displaying diverse artifacts such as leather socks and Jeju earthenware; the Modern and Contemporary Life Hall, which recreates the bustling streets of old Jeju City; and the Marine Hall, which children especially enjoy. In the Marine Hall, you can see the skeleton of a Bryde’s whale and rare marine species like the oarfish, making it a must-visit for families with children. There is also a Special Exhibition Hall for rotating exhibits and an Outdoor Exhibition Area with guardian statues and large volcanic rocks.  Among these, my favorite is the Folklore Hall, because it features Jeju’s dining table. A Jeju-style table is distinct from one on the mainland. On the mainland, a stew dish is placed at the center and rice bowls are served individually. The stew, with little broth and more solid ingredients, is shared.  On Jeju’s table, however, a large communal bowl of rice sits in the middle, while each person has an individual soup bowl. Soup is separate, but rice is shared—the opposite of the mainland. Why did this custom emerge? It likely relates to Jeju’s volcanic soil.  Because wet-field rice farming was difficult on Jeju’s volcanic terrain, people primarily ate millet and barley. These grains were coarse and not easy to eat. Eating them with soup made them easier to swallow and created a greater sense of fullness than eating rice alone. For Jeju’s ancestors, who often faced food shortages, sharing soup was a way to feel satisfied. Even today, many Jeju people over 60 prefer soup to stew, and in many households a meal is incomplete without soup.

stories.title: Gyeongju National Healing Park: A Magical Place That Inspires Love
stories.audioTitle: Gyeongju National Healing Park: A Magical Place That Inspires Love
stories.script: Welcome to the K-Culture Tour! Today’s journey takes us to “Gyeongju National Healing Park,” a place where you can enjoy a variety of activities throughout the year.  Nestled in the mountains of Sannae-myeon, Gyeongju, National Healing Park offers a unique natural healing experience, surrounded by a peaceful atmosphere that feels far away from the busy world. It is especially famous for its breathtaking winter scene: a calm lake flowing between towering walls of ice. Canoeing here feels like stepping into the magical world of Frozen. But the park’s charm doesn’t end with winter. In spring, the rose garden bursts into bloom; in summer, the water park offers a cool escape from the heat; and in autumn, you can enjoy a gentle canoe ride surrounded by brilliant fall colors. Truly, it is a place for healing all year round.  The unique charm of Gyeongju National Healing Park is vividly captured in the drama A Good Day to Be a Dog. In an episode where students from Garan High School go on a field trip, the park serves as the backdrop for both romance and tension on its peaceful lake, as the love triangle between the main characters—Hae-na, Seo-won, and Bo-gyeom—grows more intense.  Cheon Song-yi (school’s music teacher): “Oh, I think things will work out for them this time, don’t you think?”  Just as the music teacher, Song-yi says while canoeing with Seo-won and watching Hae-na and Bo-gyeom, Gyeongju National Healing Park is a magical place that makes couples’ romantic moments feel even more special. Even without any grand gestures from Hae-na and Bo-gyeom, the autumn leaves and warm sunlight naturally surround the two in a romantic atmosphere.  Seo-won’s jealous gaze as he watches the scene reveals the park’s unique power. Simply seeing his beloved Hae-na here with someone else sparks a feeling of urgency. The beauty of this place can turn even a simple moment together into a special date.  Just like the scene from A Good Day to Be a Dog, this park has the power to captivate the heart without any elaborate staging. Gyeongju National Healing Park will capture your heart, becoming the perfect setting for a romantic story in any season. Why not create your own romantic and dra  matic tale here?

stories.title: Oksan Seowon, Gyeongju: Where Contemplation and Dignity Abide
stories.audioTitle: Oksan Seowon, Gyeongju: Where Contemplation and Dignity Abide
stories.script: Welcome to the K-Culture Tour! Today’s journey takes us to “Gyeongju’s Oksan Seowon,” a place rich with Joseon Dynasty tradition and the spirit of scholarship.  Located in Angang-eup, Gyeongju, Oksan Seowon is a prominent Confucian academy from the Joseon Dynasty. Founded in 1572 to honor the virtues and teachings of Neo-Confucian scholar Yi Eon-jeok, it received official royal recognition just a year later, becoming a “Royally Chartered Confucian Academy” supported by the king.  As you pass through the main gate, Yeokrakmun, the first building you encounter is Mubyeonru, meaning endless pavilion. This pavilion served as a resting place for Confucian scholars. Its signboard is famous for the calligraphy of the renowned master Han Seok-bong, also known as Seokbong Han Ho. Opposite Mubyeonru is Guindang, the hall where lectures and discussions were held, which also displays a plaque bearing Han Ho’s calligraphy.  Next to Guindang are Dongjae(Mingujae) and Seojae(Amsujae), dormitories for the scholars. Behind Guindang, beyond the Chein Gate, stands the Cheinmyo Shrine, which houses the spirit tablet of Yi Eon-jeok. The term “Chein” means “putting virtuous and kind hearts into action,” symbolizing Yi Eon-jeok’s philosophy of practice. The buildings to the right of Dongjae(Mingujae) are administrative buildings, and behind them stands Munjippangak, which preserved the woodblocks created by the seowon.  Oksan Seowon is one of the 47 seowon that survived the abolition decree of such academies during the late Joseon period under Heungseon Daewongun. Its value was reaffirmed in 2019 when it was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site as part of the “Korean Seowon.” This sacred and dignified site also served as the setting for the drama Under the Queen’s Umbrella, which depicts the queen’s fierce struggle within the palace over royal education.  Im Hwa-ryeong (Queen): “Next time, you will have to go through every single formality.” Hwang Won-hyeong (Prime Minister): “If I go through said formality, are you willing to be questioned yourself, Your Majesty?” Im Hwa-ryeong (Queen): “Certainly. If I am responsible for something, then I shall accept the request. However, if anyone tries to frame me, I don’t care who it is, I will gnaw on them and slowly finish their last breath.”  This scene, set here, shows the Queen standing resolutely against the Prime Minister’s attempt to accuse Lady Sin of causing the Crown Prince’s death. Her cold and unwavering demeanor perfectly embodies the dignity of a Joseon queen.   As the wind drifts gently over the tiled roofs and time passes quietly beneath the trees, the reflections of the Josun era still linger throughout Oksan Suhwon. Take a leisurely stroll today, and let the enduring wisdom and serene dignity of this place touch your heart.  As the wind flows gently between the tiled roofs and time quietly passes under the shade of the trees, the contemplations of the Joseon era still quietly resonate throughout Oksan Seowon. Take a leisurely stroll today, and let the enduring wisdom and serene dignity of this place softly touch your heart.

stories.title: Gyeongju Gampo Haeguk-gil: A Place Where the Love of Family Blooms
stories.audioTitle: Gyeongju Gampo Haeguk-gil: A Place Where the Love of Family Blooms
stories.script: Welcome to the K-Culture Tour! Today’s journey takes us to “Gyeongju Gampo Haeguk-gil,” where the deep blue sea meets the soft, pale purple of sea chrysanthemums, creating a view that warms the heart.  When people think of Gyeongju Gampo Haeguk-gil, they often picture clusters of pale purple sea chrysanthemums blooming along the coastline, set against the deep blue of the East Sea. In fact, this place has preserved its natural beauty while also offering a charming mural street, a modest village landscape, and sweeping ocean views from the famous “Haeguk Stairs.” It is filled with healing spots where you can relax, take in the scenery, and feel at peace.  The charm of the sea, blended with the warmth of everyday life, has even drawn the attention of television. Gampo Haeguk-gil was featured in the drama Family by Choice, a heartfelt story that explores the true meaning of family. Here, the ordinary setting becomes something special, more than just a backdrop. It’s where bonds beyond blood ties turn into cherished memories.  As you walk along the stairs painted with a “sea chrysanthemum” scene, depicting the childhood of San-ha, Joo-won, and Hae-joon, you step right into the drama’s memories. A little further on, you’ll find a small café that served as the kalguksu restaurant run by “Jeong-jae,” the father figure to the three main characters. Each spot still holds traces of the show’s warm, makeshift family.  Yoon Joo-won: “What’s so important about family on paper? If we consider ourselves family, we’re family. Why should that be proved with a piece of paper?”  Even without blood ties, sincere love and care flow gently here in Gampo Haeguk-gil.  Today, Gampo Haeguk-gil is more than a scenic coastal path. It’s a living story, a place that holds the essence of family, affection, and treasured memories. Why not follow the emotional journey of the drama and create lasting memories with the people who matter most to you?

stories.title: Golden Ginkgo Tree Roads, Gyeongju Dori Village
stories.audioTitle: Golden Ginkgo Tree Roads, Gyeongju Dori Village
stories.script: Welcome to the K-Culture Tour! Today’s journey takes us to “Gyeongju Dori Village,” a charming place filled with warm natural beauty and the cozy friendliness of village life.  Located in Seomyeon, Gyeongju, Dori Village is a peaceful farming community surrounded by deep valleys and gentle mountain slopes. It is said that people have lived here for more than 2,000 years, long before the Silla Dynasty was founded. Since ancient times, the villagers have held local gatherings called “Hyanghoe,” where they discuss community matters and live by principles of justice and moral conduct. Thanks to this tradition, the village was once called “Doui” or “Dojil,” but following an administrative reorganization in 1914, it was renamed “Dori.”  What Dori Village is best known for is its beautiful ginkgo forest. Every autumn, the ginkgo trees planted throughout the village turn a brilliant golden color, creating a breathtaking sea of yellow leaves. This stunning sight attracts visitors from all over Korea. During peak foliage season, food stalls and specialty markets run by the villagers open, offering delicious local treats and unique products that make the experience even more enjoyable.  This picturesque village was also featured in the drama The Good Bad Mother. One memorable scene shows Kang-ho searching the entire village for the rubber balls belonging to Ye-jin, Seo-jin’s twin sister, perfectly capturing the warmth and calm of Dori Village. Kang-ho races along paths lined with bright yellow cosmos flowers in his wheelchair, while his mother, Young-soon, desperately searches for him. Late at night, just after sunset, Kang-ho finally finds the rubber ball in the middle of the ginkgo forest and shouts with joy:  Choi Kang-ho: “I found it! I found it!!! Ye-jin, Seo-jin, I found it! I found it!”  Like a scene from a drama, Dori Village gently helps you heal, even if just a little, restoring pieces of your heart that you may have lost. If your daily life feels hectic, come here and take a slow, peaceful walk. As you stroll beneath the fluttering golden ginkgo leaves, your busy thoughts will calm, and precious memories long forgotten may quietly return.

stories.title: Gyeongju Samreung Forest: A Dreamlike Forest With Green Hues
stories.audioTitle: Gyeongju Samreung Forest: A Dreamlike Forest With Green Hues
stories.script: Welcome to the K-Culture Tour! Today’s journey takes us to “Gyeongju Samreung Forest,” a magical pine forest that beautifully blends Korean history with a sense of calm and healing.  Located west of Namsan Mountain in Gyeongju, Samreung Forest is home to the tombs of three Silla kings: King Adalla, King Sindeok, and King Gyeongmyeong. The forest is filled with dense Angang-type pine trees, known for their low, twisting branches, creating a lively atmosphere where you can feel the freshness and energy of every season.  Pine forests like Samreung have long been cherished as symbols of the Korean spirit. Their deep green needles stand strong through harsh winds and storms, reminding us of patience, perseverance, and an unbreakable will. For this reason, pine forests in Korean dramas often reflect fateful meetings and changes inside the characters. They stand for values that should be kept, even when times change.  Young Eugene Choi: “I watch because I feel a single black bird could spoil the whole sky.” Go Sa-hong: “Live with your eyes on the ground. The sky is far away. When a servant looks far away, their life tends to be short”  In Mr. Sunshine, young Eugene Choi, once a slave, speaks with Ae-shin’s grandfather, Go Sa-hong, while carrying a wooden carrier. This scene takes place in Samreung Forest, which reflects Eugene Choi’s struggle to overcome his social limits while staying true to his beliefs, deepening viewers’ emotional connection to the story.  Why not take a peaceful walk among these vibrant pine trees and listen to your inner voice? Like sunlight shining through the branches, this forest may bring a gentle comfort to your busy life.

stories.title: Andong Hahoe Village — A Village Rich in Deep Tradition and Aspiration
stories.audioTitle: Andong Hahoe Village — A Village Rich in Deep Tradition and Aspiration
stories.script: Welcome to the K-Culture Tour! Today’s journey takes us to “Andong Hahoe Village,” a place rich with historic homes and deep-rooted traditions.  Located in Pungcheon-myeon, Andong City, Hahoe Village is a typical clan village where the Pungsan Ryu family has lived for over 600 years. The name Hahoe, meaning encircling stream, comes from the unique S-shaped bend of the Nakdong River that flows around the village. The village is filled with beautiful traditional Korean houses, known as hanok.  At the heart of the village are the tile-roofed homes of the Ryu clan, including Yangjindang and Chunghyodang, surrounded by well-preserved thatched-roof houses. These buildings showcase the lifestyle and architectural beauty of the Joseon Dynasty aristocracy. Today, descendants of the original families still live there, continuing their heritage.  The traditional culture of Hahoe Village is still very much alive today. One of its most treasured customs is the “Hahoe Byeolsingut Talnori,” also known as the Mask Dance Drama of Hahoe. This mask dance is performed as part of the village’s communal ritual called Byeolsingut, and it is the oldest surviving mask dance in Korea. The performance is held to pray for the village’s well-being and a bountiful harvest.  Besides the mask dance performed mainly by commoners, there is a traditional performance enjoyed mostly by scholars called the “Seonyu Fire Play.” This fireworks display takes place against the breathtaking scenery of Buyongdae Cliff and the Nakdong River. During the Joseon Dynasty, noblemen would enjoy this show while floating on boats and reciting poetry. The Seonyu Fire Play was also memorably featured in the final episode of the drama Revenant.  Yeom Hae-sang: “This is the Seonyu Fire Play. It carries the meaning of driving away disease and misfortune and inviting good luck. It also symbolizes sending lost and wandering spirits to a better place. This grand purification ritual is filled with countless white papers, fireworks, and the heartfelt wishes of many people. Can you see the ghosts?”  Hae-sang mentions he comes here whenever he struggles with seeing ghosts. San-yeong says the ghosts here all look happy. Hae-sang wishes happiness not just for San-yeong, but for everyone. Meanwhile, San-yeong, determined to live fully by her own will rather than for anyone else, smiles brightly even in the face of her impending blindness.  Just as San-yeong regained her will to live, Andong Hahoe Village still deeply resonates with us today. Take a walk through the village and experience the spirit of tradition and the beauty of nature. As you watch the calm flow of the river and the dazzling fireworks lighting up the night, you may find the strength to rise again.

stories.title: Art Blossomed in the Alleyways: Busan Hocheon Village
stories.audioTitle: Art Blossomed in the Alleyways: Busan Hocheon Village
stories.script: Welcome to the K-Culture Tour! Today’s journey takes us to “Busan Hocheon Village,” where the layered rooftops hold stories of life and warmth.  Located in Beomcheon-dong, Busanjin-gu, Hocheon Village gets its name—meaning “Tiger Stream”—from the frequent tiger sightings along the nearby stream. As striking as its name, it is one of the villages along Busan’s famous Sanbok Road, alongside Gamcheon Culture Village. Sanbok Road is a path carved into the mountainside, where houses densely built along steep slopes form a maze-like and distinctive landscape.  The alleyways, worn by time, and the vibrant colors of the houses create a unique atmosphere found only in Hocheon Village. As you wander the narrow, winding streets, you’ll naturally feel the nostalgic spirit of old Busan and the simple, warm charm of village life. Murals and artworks scattered throughout, created by residents and artists alike, add life and stories to the village.  Hocheon Village gained attention as a filming location for the drama Fight for My Way. Next to the Hocheon Cultural Platform, a faithful recreation of “Namil Bar,” the hangout spot for the main characters, attracts many fans. “Namil Bar,” where the characters shared their dreams during their youth, overlooks a tightly packed neighborhood that lights up like a starry night sky.  Go Dong-man: “Do you really need a plan for life? Sometimes it’s better to just take things as they come. What’s the point of planning? If things don’t go your way, just go for it.” Choi Ae-ra: “Isn’t this where I stand—the major league?”  Just like the encouraging words spoken to youth, Hocheon Village sends a small but powerful message of courage to all of us living today. As you follow the colors and stories left in each alley, you’ll feel a gentle warmth settle in your heart.

stories.title: Seomyeon Busan Youth Street: A Street Pulsing with Busan’s Vibrant Energy
stories.audioTitle: Seomyeon Busan Youth Street: A Street Pulsing with Busan’s Vibrant Energy
stories.script: Welcome to the K-Culture Tour! Today’s journey takes us to “Seomyeon Busan Youth Street,” a vibrant place alive with sparkling neon lights and buzzing with dynamic energy.  Seomyeon Busan Youth Street is Busan’s largest and busiest shopping district, filled with bright neon lights, bustling shops, and a nightlife that comes alive after dark. But it’s more than just a place for shopping and entertainment—it’s where Busan’s warm and welcoming spirit shines through, and real-life stories are shared. From cozy cafes and restaurants to cultural spaces and lively streets, this vibrant area offers a rich mix of experiences, creating a special stage where dreams and reality come together.  Seomyeon Youth Street, full of urban energy and Busan’s unique local spirit, was a key filming location for the movie Man of Men, a heartfelt story about true friendship and the meaning of life. In the film, Seomyeon Youth Street isn’t just a backdrop; it almost becomes a character itself, a vibrant space where two very different men form a deep bond.  The story follows “Young-gi,” a flashy gangster who lives to show off, and “Jang-soo,” a terminally ill man with money but little time. Together, they check off items on their bucket lists, building a true friendship that’s reflected throughout the streets of Seomyeon Youth Street. In one touching scene, Jang-soo, who usually insists on wearing suits, dresses like Young-gi and walks beside him—vividly showing how their hearts have come together.  Jang-soo: “Do you accept this as Jinppae?”  The friendship between these two men, marked by matching “Jinppae” tattoos on their collarbones, a Busan dialect word meaning “real” or “genuine,” blends seamlessly with the street’s vibrant energy. The strong local spirit of Busan and the unique charm of this street, where “past and future coexist,” highlight the touching story of two imperfect people who become true partners by complementing each other.  On Seomyeon Busan Youth Street, why not create your own perfect day inspired by the film’s lasting impression of two men completing their bucket lists together and learning to accept each other? Here, amidst Busan’s vibrant energy, you might discover warm friendships where imperfect people complement and support one another.

stories.title: Daegu Modern History Streets: Home to Retro Charm and Fiery Youth
stories.audioTitle: Daegu Modern History Streets: Home to Retro Charm and Fiery Youth
stories.script: Welcome to the K-Culture Tour! Today’s journey takes us to “Daegu Modern History Streets,” a place brimming with timeless retro charm.  Daegu Modern History Streets hold a timeless, nostalgic beauty. With red brick walls and old buildings lining the alleys, this special area stretches from the March 1st Independence Movement Road to Gyesan Cathedral and Cheongna Hill. Here, the footsteps of Korea’s modern history remain alive. Past and present blend naturally, offering a mysterious experience that feels like traveling through different eras with every step.  It’s no surprise that the drama Love Rain, which captures the pure spirit of youth in the 1970s, was filmed throughout Daegu Modern History Streets. This area offered the perfect setting to portray the excitement and innocence of first love, transcending generations and time. Drama fans will especially appreciate the music café “c’est la vie,” which served as the main characters’ hideout. Located on Gukchaebosang-ro 102-gil, it is a set that perfectly recreates the 1970s atmosphere and appears as a “nostalgic place” where the characters’ friendships, loves, and struggles naturally unfold.  Seo In-ha: “One, two, three—I fell in love in just three seconds.”  Though brief, the intensity of that first love leaves a deep impression, harmonizing with the quiet and nostalgic atmosphere of Daegu Modern History Streets. The scenery created by the old alleys and retro buildings perfectly holds the powerful moment of first love. The pure innocence spanning the 1970s and 2010s still feels as if it remains somewhere along these streets today.  Why not follow the tender, pure feelings of Love Rain as you stroll through this timeless place? Like that love that came in three seconds, create a dramatic and unforgettable day here in Daegu Modern History Streets.

stories.title: Ulsan Nasa Breakwater Lighthouse: Where Emotion and Romance Surge
stories.audioTitle: Ulsan Nasa Breakwater Lighthouse: Where Emotion and Romance Surge
stories.script: Welcome to the K-Culture Tour! Today’s journey takes us to the “Nasa Breakwater Lighthouse,” a steadfast guardian that lights up Ulsan’s sea and hearts.   Situated at the tip of Nasari Beach’s breakwater in Ulsan, the Nasa Breakwater Lighthouse is a small, white, rounded tower featuring a blue roof and door. Since 2006, it has faithfully guided ships navigating the open waters.   The waves crashing against the breakwater and the deep blue sea create a breathtaking view at any time of day. At night, the lighthouse’s glow brightens the surroundings, adding a romantic touch. Nearby, the fishing village alongside the lighthouse gives off an exotic yet peaceful vibe.   Thanks to its unique atmosphere, this place was the backdrop for a touching scene in the drama See You in My 19th Life, where the protagonist Moon Seo-ha opens up to Ban Ji-eum, who feels somehow familiar.   Moon Seo-ha: “Ban Ji-eum, do you realize how strange this is? I told you it was my first love, didn’t I? My first love never came true. I’m sure it’s the same for you, Ban Ji-eum.”   Moon Seo-ha, unable to forget his first love, finds it hard to accept Ban Ji-eum’s feelings. At the same time, Ban Ji-eum cannot reveal that the first love she yearns for is her own past self before reincarnation. Their emotions, intertwined with the lighthouse’s glow shining through the rain, convey their deep sorrow and heartfelt longing even more poignantly.  Spend some time at Nasa Breakwater Lighthouse and think of someone dear to you. The refreshing sound of the waves and the tranquil, exotic scenery will bring warm comfort to your heart.

stories.title: Local destinations, relaxing drive
stories.script: “A drive in Seoul? Most people think of Bukak Skyway or Gangbyeonbuk-ro. But the perfect place to slow down lies in the east, in Gangdong District. I’ve been driving for years, and whenever I need a break, this is where I go. It’s still in the city, but peaceful — and the view outside always clears my mind.”  Let’s start at Amsa Ecological Park. It’s close to Amsa Station, but once you step inside, it feels as if you’ve left Seoul behind. A narrow trail winds through tall reeds, and the river flows quietly beside you. In winter, mist rises from the water. In summer, soft sunlight shimmers on the surface. Park your car, roll down the window, and the scent of nature you’ve forgotten in the city drifts into your taxi.  Next, follow the Gangdong Greenway, a calm road that runs along the river. Few cars pass here, and biking and walking paths stretch alongside it. Drive slowly, and you’ll feel as if the breeze itself is leading the way. In spring, cherry blossoms blanket the road. In autumn, golden ginkgo leaves pile up until the path looks like a scene from a movie. My passengers often say, “I never knew Seoul had roads like this.”  The last stop is the Iljasan Trail, one of the greenest drives in the city. Much of the road is open to cars, with small rest areas and outdoor gyms where you can stop for a short walk. In late autumn, sunlight filters through crimson leaves, and at night, the sound of insects and rustling trees fills the air — sounds you’ll rarely hear anywhere else in Seoul.  Take a moment to discover that Seoul still has quiet drives like this. On days when you just want to slow down, remember this drive.

stories.title: Coastal drive, relaxing drive, local destination
stories.audioTitle: Coastal drive, relaxing drive, local destination
stories.script: “I’ve been to Haeundae, and Gwangalli is always crowded. But isn’t there a drive that really captures Busan?”  When people ask me that, I never hesitate to recommend this drive. It starts at Oryukdo Skywalk, follows the Igidae Coastal Trail, and ends at the Jangja Village Observatory on Busan’s southeast coast.  At Oryukdo Skywalk, you can walk across a glass bridge that makes you feel like you’re floating above the sea. There are plenty of photo spots, and on clear days you can even see Tsushima Island across the water. It’s the perfect place to start your drive, breathing in the fresh sea air.  The next stretch, the Igidae Coastal Trail, is perfect for both driving and walking. Here, waves crash against rocky cliffs, and the coastline unfolds beside you. It’s quiet and peaceful, and you can feel nature even while you’re behind the wheel. If you park and take a short stroll, it helps you relax and clear your head.  The final stop is the Jangja Village Observatory. Perched above a seaside village, this lookout offers a sweeping view of Busan’s coast. At sunset, the sky turns gold and boats move slowly across the water, like a scene from a movie. Be sure to pull over and take a few minutes just to sit and breathe.  They’re not as famous as Gwangalli, but locals and regular visitors to Busan often come here. These are quiet spots that capture the real Busan. When you want to cruise along the coast and forget the city noise for a while, this is the drive for you.  Today, let’s go for a seaside drive in Busan, one recommended by Uber Taxi drivers.

stories.title: Cherry blossom spots, relaxing drive, year-round scenery
stories.audioTitle: Cherry blossom spots, relaxing drive, year-round scenery
stories.script: “When people think of Changwon or Jinhae, they picture the cherry blossom festival. But there’s a quiet drive just as beautiful, but without the crowds.”  Among Uber Taxi drivers, the most recommended drive is the Jinhae Dream Road. It starts at Jehwangsan Mountain, crosses Anmin Hill, and leads to Jangboksan Park — a drive that captures the hidden charms of Changwon.  At Jehwangsan, the monorail and observatory are well known to visitors, but few people know the quiet road below. In spring, cherry blossoms line both sides of the street. In summer, cool green shade covers the way. Each season gives the drive a different mood.  Anmin Hill connects Changwon and Jinhae and offers a wide view of Jinhae Bay. Locals often come here for a walk, and by car, you can take it slowly and enjoy the scenery at your own pace.  At Jangboksan Park, park your car and walk up to the observatory. The city of Jinhae spreads out below, where the sea and the naval port meet in the distance, like a scene from a film.  This drive changes with the seasons — blossoms in spring, deep greens in summer, and red and gold leaves in autumn. It’s a drive worth taking all year round. If you want to avoid the festival crowds and feel a quieter side of Jinhae, drive this road.  Today, let’s drive the Jinhae Dream Road, a drive recommended by Uber Taxi drivers.

stories.title: Local destinations, urban nature, relaxing drive
stories.audioTitle: Local destinations, urban nature, relaxing drive
stories.script: “When a passenger tells me they’re looking for a quiet place for a walk, I always recommend the forest drive that winds along Mucheoksan Mountain in Jangyu, Gimhae.”  Just a ten-minute drive from downtown, it feels like a completely different world. Mucheoksan Foothill Drive is a quiet stretch known mostly to locals. Early in the morning, when a light mist settles over the road, you can feel the city noise fade away.  Near the Mucheoksan Sports Park parking lot, it’s nice to pull over and take a short walk. The forest trail here is well maintained, so anyone can enjoy an easy stroll. Surrounded by green trees and fresh air, you can feel yourself slowly unwind.  Get back in the car and follow the foothill drive again. In spring, you’ll see how breathtaking it is when cherry blossoms are in full bloom. There are plenty of curves, but the road stays wide and smooth — easy even for new drivers.  “Among Uber Taxi drivers, this is one of the drives we recommend most. It’s quiet, peaceful, and lets you feel the real Gimhae.”  If you arrive at Gimhae Airport in the morning, why not take this relaxing drive and start your day with a moment of calm? Let an Uber Taxi driver show you the real Gimhae — a drive we know by heart. Shall we go?

stories.title: Forest drive, family-friendly drive, relaxing drive
stories.audioTitle: Forest drive, family-friendly drive, relaxing drive
stories.script: “Just driving along the coast won’t show you the true Jeju. If you really want to experience Jeju’s quieter side, I recommend a peaceful forest drive. This drive starts in Seonheul-ri, passes through Gyorae Recreation Forest, and ends along the serene Jeju Arboretum Road.”  Seonheul-ri is a quiet inland village in eastern Jeju, more of a place where locals live than a tourist spot. But as you drive through its calm roads, you’ll see volcanic landscapes blending with patches of Gotjawal forest, spreading gently around you. In the morning, a light fog hangs low over the trees, and the scent of the forest drifts in through your open window along with the sound of birds.  Turn toward Gyorae, and soon you’ll arrive at Gyorae Recreation Forest. From a small information center by the parking lot, a gentle trail of wooden steps leads into the woods. It’s an easy walk for both kids and older visitors, making it a favorite spot for families. Sunlight filters through the cedar trees, and when the wind stirs the leaves, it feels as if time in Jeju slows down.  When you leave the forest and drive along Jeju Arboretum Road, you’ll find a quiet place where locals come for a stroll or to relax. It’s a spot that captures Jeju’s calm, unhurried spirit. Each season paints the road with different colors — bright greens in spring and crimson leaves in autumn.  “Many who go on this drive tell me it’s the first time they’ve really felt just how peaceful Jeju can be. For us Uber Taxi drivers, it’s one of the drives we’re most proud to recommend. So how about a quiet drive through the forest, feeling the gentle breeze of Jeju around you? I’ll be happy to guide you along the way.”

stories.title: UNESCO World Heritage, nature retreat, scenic suburban drive
stories.audioTitle: UNESCO World Heritage, nature retreat, scenic suburban drive
stories.script: “If you’re looking for a quiet place in Daegu, there’s a drive Uber Taxi drivers love to recommend. It’s a short but fulfilling drive from the foothills of Biseulsan Mountain to Dodong Seowon.”  Leaving behind the busy city, this drive takes you through nature and history — perfect for starting or ending your day.  The Biseulsan Foothill Drive winds gently along the base of the mountain, surrounded by green scenery rare within Daegu. Each season brings a different breeze, and spring and autumn are the best times to roll down your window and drive slowly. As you pass through the shade of the forest, you’ll feel your mind clearing with every turn.  About halfway through the drive, stop at Bonni Village, home to the Nampyeong Mun Clan — a hidden gem few people know about. Old traditional houses line the narrow alleys, and the quiet air fills you with calm. Here, the sound of the wind is louder than the sound of people. It feels like a rare gift of silence.  The destination is Dodong Seowon, a Confucian academy nestled in a pine forest. It’s one of Daegu’s treasures and a UNESCO World Heritage site, preserving the grace of traditional hanok architecture. Sitting under the golden ginkgo trees in autumn, even a cup of coffee here offers a rare sense of peace.  On a calm afternoon, take this road that winds quietly outside the city. More than any destination, it’s the slow journey itself that becomes the reward. With Uber Taxi, your peaceful escape begins the moment you set off.

stories.title: Harmony of nature and tradition, autumn foliage, suburban drive
stories.audioTitle: Harmony of nature and tradition, autumn foliage, suburban drive
stories.script: “In Gyeongju, every road leads to history. But if you want to feel the city’s quieter side, I highly recommend this drive. It’s especially popular among older travelers and families.”  Most people think of Bulguksa Temple, Seokguram Grotto, or Daereungwon Tomb Complex when they hear “Gyeongju.” Yet beyond these famous sites, there are peaceful places that reveal a deeper charm of the ancient city. Local Uber Taxi drivers often suggest a route that begins at Seoak Seowon, passes through Dori Village, and continues along the Namsan Foothill Road.  The first stop, Seoak Seowon, sits beside royal tombs from the Silla period. It’s a serene place where quiet traditional beauty lingers in the air. Broad lawns and neatly preserved hanok buildings unfold outside your car window, offering a glimpse into Gyeongju’s heritage. With few visitors, it’s a perfect starting point for those seeking calm away from the city.  Next comes Dori Village, a modest countryside village that carries traces of long-standing tradition. Old tile-roofed houses and wooden cottages line the roadside, and in autumn, when golden rice bows in the fields, the scenery turns deeply Korean. Keep your windows open as you drive—sunlight and wind mingle in the air, filling your car with the gentle scent of the season.  The final highlight is Namsan Foothill Road, a winding drive that follows the lower slopes of Mount Namsan. When autumn leaves reach their peak, the entire route becomes a golden tunnel of trees. On weekdays, traffic is light, allowing you to enjoy the stillness of Gyeongju’s nature. Some sections even have small spots where you can park, take a walk, or capture photos.  If you want to experience Gyeongju beyond its crowded landmarks—where nature and tradition meet in quiet harmony—follow this tranquil and heartfelt route. Guided by an Uber Taxi driver, you might just discover a new side of Gyeongju, one that feels entirely your own.

stories.title: Gyeongpo Lake, Gangneung
stories.script: "Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Gyeongpo Lake in Gangneung. Here, the soft moonlight and the calm water create a peaceful and beautiful scene.  Located in Jeo-dong, Gangneung, Gyeongpo Lake is a natural lake that connects to the East Sea. Its water is so clear and still, it's also called Gyeongho, which means ""mirror lake."" The lake shines with a special beauty in every season. In spring, soft pink cherry blossoms surround the water. In summer, deep green trees cast a cool, shady canopy. Autumn brings a gentle golden field of reeds. And in winter, a magical mix of fog and snow creates a truly dreamlike atmosphere.  Thanks to its stunning scenery, Gyeongpo Lake is a must-visit spot for both locals and travelers. As you walk along the peaceful trail, you can feel the pure breath of nature and just be amazed by the views. The lake is also a special nature reserve. It's home to various fish like carp and mullet, and in winter, it becomes a resting place for migratory birds, including mallards and mandarin ducks. It's a true sanctuary for wildlife. When the sun goes down, people say five moons appear over Gyeongpo Lake. There's one in the sky, one on the lake's surface, one reflected in the sea, one in a cup of wine, and one shining in the eyes of your loved one. Searching for these five moons with someone you care about is a truly romantic moment.  And the best place to experience all those moons is Gyeongpodae Pavilion.
