This famous spot sits on a hill north of the lake and is considered one of the Eight Scenic Views of the Gwandong region. Long ago, scholars called the most beautiful places along the eastern coast the Eight Scenic Views. They would admire the breathtaking scenery stretching from Chongseokjeong in what is now North Korea all the way down to Wolsongjeong in Pyeonghae. Gyeongpodae was always the first on the list. When you stand here at night, the view of the lake and the moonlight feels so peaceful, it's like time has stopped.  The night at Gyeongpo Lake is like a quiet poem that gently touches your heart. Just looking at the view brings a sense of comfort without saying a word. Tonight, we hope you'll take a quiet step into the moonlit nightscape of Gyeongpo Lake and let its beauty embrace you."

stories.title: Namdaecheon Stream, Gangneung
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Namdaecheon Stream in Gangneung, a place where festivals and city life flow together.  Flowing through Gangneung and out to the East Sea, Namdaecheon Stream is a local river that provides water for daily life and farming. It also has wide riverbanks that offer a peaceful place for locals to relax. After a major cleanup project in 1992, the riverbanks were transformed into an even more beautiful space. The area is also home to great spots for families to visit, including Dano Park, the Gangneung Dano Culture Center, and the Imyeonggwansammun Gate, among many other historical and cultural sites.  Each year on the 5th day of the 5th lunar month, the Gangneung Danoje Festival turns the Namdaecheon riverside into a grand stage of traditional culture. Here, you can experience everything from shamanic rituals where gods and people come together, to the nation's largest open-air market, lively folk games, and performances recognized as national cultural heritage. It's a place overflowing with special memories and experiences for everyone. When night falls, Wolhwa Bridge, a landmark of Namdaecheon Stream, transforms into a dazzling musical fountain. The entire 160-meter-long bridge comes alive with water, lights, and music, creating a truly spectacular show. As you watch the dancing streams of water, you might just feel your daily worries and fatigue melt away.  Right next to Wolhwa Bridge, Wolhwa Street comes alive with a night market and themed festivals. The sparkling lights and delicious food create a lively atmosphere where visitors and locals can share in the fun and make lasting memories together.  No matter the season or time of day, Namdaecheon Stream is always full of charm. Why not come with someone special and immerse yourself in the beautiful night views and lively festivals along this river?

stories.title: Anbandegi, Gangneung
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Anbandegi in Gangneung, a place where the quiet comfort of nature meets a dazzling world of stars.  Located 1,100 meters above sea level, Anbandegi is a plateau so close to the sky that it's called the first village beneath the sky or the land above the clouds. Its name comes from anban, a wide wooden board used for making rice cakes, which looks like the village's unique flat and hollowed-out landscape.  Beneath this unique landscape, you'll find a small village and terraced fields stretching out in layers along the steep mountainside. These fields were created by slash-and-burn farmers who, starting in 1965, used only pickaxes and shovels to carve out a living. Today, the cool breeze and warm sunlight blend together to create a view as picturesque as a painting.  As the sun sets and darkness falls, Anbandegi seems to be under a spell, revealing a sky full of glittering stars and the Milky Way. Thanks to its clean air and pristine landscape with no light pollution, the night sky here shines with a brilliance you could never imagine in the city.  From the Meonge Observatory and Sunrise Observatory, you'll have a truly magical experience. In the quiet darkness, it feels like thousands of stars are raining down on you. Between April and August, the Milky Way shines its brightest on nights with little moonlight. This is a dreamy sight that fills the entire night sky.  Wrapped in a blanket against the cold mountain wind, the quiet moment of gazing at the night sky brings a feeling of pure wonder, just like being a child again. As you look at the endless stars sparkling in the darkness, why not hold a special wish close to your heart? We believe the starlight of Anbandegi will send you its warmest encouragement.

stories.title: Gangmun Beach, Gangneung
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Gangmun Beach in Gangneung, where the sea washes away the noise of everyday life, offering a moment of quiet comfort and peace.  Gangmun Beach, which means the mouth where the river flows, is a beautiful place where soft white sand meets the blue East Sea. It's much quieter and more peaceful than nearby Gyeongpo Beach. Here, you can enjoy a calm walk and deep thoughts, with the sound of the crashing waves and the cool sea breeze by your side.  When the sun starts to set, Gangmun Beach shows a different, more beautiful side. The walking path along the coast lights up, and the beach glows with a warm light. The Sotdae Bridge, which connects Gangmun Beach to nearby Gyeongpo Beach, lights up with a spectacular rainbow of LED arches. This creates a magical scene that blends perfectly with the charm of the night sea.  Sotdae Bridge is a modern cultural space that was inspired by the traditional sotdae, a totem pole once used to pray for a village's peace and good fortune. Below the bridge, you'll find the Jjinttaebaegi Wish Sculpture where you can make your own wish and experience a part of Korean folk culture. When you stand on the bridge, you'll get a beautiful, panoramic night view that connects the two beaches. From a distance, the bridge looks like a giant rainbow of light floating over the sea.  As night gets deeper, Gangmun Beach turns into a stunning stage of light. The glowing LED lights of Sotdae Bridge blend beautifully with the ocean waves. Whether you're looking at the bridge or walking on it, you can feel the stress of daily life disappear, replaced by a gentle sense of peace.  Step away from your noisy daily life and find true rest and comfort at Gangmun Beach. Here, the quiet night and the bridge of light come together to offer a moment of peaceful calm.

stories.title: Namsan Park, Gangneung
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Namsan Park in Gangneung, an emotional space where the romance of a spring night seems to linger all year long.  Namsan Park, located in the heart of downtown Gangneung, is a peaceful retreat during the day. But when the sun goes down, it shows a completely different charm. As hundreds of lights in the park begin to turn on, the once ordinary walking paths transform into a magical trail of light.  Beautiful in every season, Namsan Park is at its most stunning in the spring when the cherry blossoms are in full bloom. Under the lights, the blossoms shine like white popcorn, creating a truly romantic atmosphere. But the park's charm doesn't fade when the blossoms do. In summer, lights filter through the green leaves to create cool, shady spots. In autumn, warm lights mix with the colorful leaves. And in winter, the snow and lights combine to create a quiet, beautiful scene.  The most beloved spot in Namsan Park is Oseongjeong Pavilion. This pavilion is a perfect photo spot. With its elegant tiled roof and graceful columns, it creates a tranquil atmosphere that looks beautiful with both cherry blossoms in spring and autumn leaves. When deep darkness falls, the white cherry blossoms stand out in stunning contrast, creating an even more breathtaking scene.  Walk along the path from Oseongjeong Pavilion, and you'll find an observatory. From here, the city lights of Gangneung spread out beneath you, and in the distance, you can even see the flow of Namdaecheon Stream. No matter the season, the night view from this spot is a dreamy and romantic sight.  The greatest charm of Namsan Park is how comfortable and safe it feels. With well-lit and wide paths, you can walk here with ease, even late at night. Because of this, it's a popular spot for couples on a date or families enjoying a night walk all year long. Sitting on a bench, you can spend time gazing at the city lights and the unique beauty of each season. As you do, you might just feel the stress of daily life melt away as if by magic.  From the cherry blossoms of spring to the snowy scenes of winter, Namsan Park always welcomes people with its seasonal beauty and warm lights. Come and enjoy a walk here and let the night fill you with quiet emotion.

stories.title: Expo Bridge, Daejeon
stories.script: "Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Expo Bridge in Daejeon, a landmark that carries the legacy of the Daejeon Expo and has been reborn as a bridge of love.  Spanning the Gapcheon River and connecting Expo Science Park with Hanbat Arboretum, Expo Bridge was built to celebrate the 1993 Daejeon Expo. Now, more than 30 years later, it still stands as one of the city’s most beloved landmarks.  The two giant arches at the center of the bridge are a modern take on the traditional Korean taegeuk symbol, representing harmony and balance. These arches cross over each other gracefully, creating a beautiful sight. They look like a rainbow that has come down from the sky and settled elegantly over the Gapcheon River.  Expo Bridge also has a romantic nickname, the ""Gyeonu and Jingnyeo Bridge."" This name was chosen by the public, and it comes with a touching belief. The story goes that if you confess your love on this bridge, your love will come true. It's said that the bridge is like the Milky Way over the Gapcheon River.  By day, Expo Bridge looks grand, blending beautifully with the blue waters of the Gapcheon River. But by night, it shows off a spectacular view as it lights up with dazzling colors. Starting at sunset and lasting until 11 p.m., the lights cover the bridge in brilliant colors. They reflect off the calm water of the Gapcheon River, creating a magical scene that looks like another bridge is floating beneath the water.  The night view from the bridge shows a stunning contrast between the city and nature. You'll see the glowing high-rises of Dunsan New Town and the beautiful media façade on the majestic Hanbit Tower. These sights add a touch of brilliance to the city. In contrast, the dark green of Hanbat Arboretum and the gentle flow of the Gapcheon River create a sense of calm and peace.  A gentle breeze along the Gapcheon River, starlight shimmering on the water, and the legend of Gyeonu and Jingnyeo that lives on in this bridge. At Daejeon Expo Bridge, why not write your own special love story?"

stories.title: Daejeon Couple Bridge
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Daejeon’s Couple Bridge, a place that lights up even the darkest night with the glow of love.  Couple Bridge spans the Daejeoncheon Stream, connecting Jung-gu and Dong-gu. It was designed to be a place of connection, communication, and meeting for people. With its unique S-shaped curve, the bridge looks futuristic, almost like a spaceship that has landed on the Daejeoncheon Stream.  As the sun sets, Couple Bridge begins to show a completely different kind of beauty. Colorful LED lights cover the entire bridge, making its spaceship-like shape glow softly. This creates a spectacular night view. With the shining lights as a backdrop, you can take amazing photos. The large moon sculpture and Mokcheok Bridge in the distance create a perfect frame for your pictures, giving you unforgettable memories.  True to its name, Couple Bridge has a special yeonriji tree nearby, which is a symbol of everlasting love. The legend says that just as two trees intertwine to become one, couples who promise their love here will see their bond last a lifetime.  With its two levels, Couple Bridge offers different views of the Daejeoncheon Stream and the old downtown area. Thanks to its unique S-shaped design, you get a new view with every step you take. The bridge also has a round stage and an event space, which are used for various cultural events.  The dazzling lights on the bridge blend with the calm flow of the Daejeoncheon Stream to create a dreamlike scene. The reflection of the lights twinkling on the water gives couples a moment they’ll want to cherish for a lifetime, and it offers families a chance to create warm memories.  How about making your own promise of forever here on Couple Bridge? Beneath the moonlight, as you walk side by side, the night in Daejeon is gently colored with love.

stories.title: Media Art Park, Daejeon
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Media Art Park in Daejeon, where the city’s futuristic spirit meets the timeless beauty of tradition.  Located in the front yard of Studio Cube, Daejeon Media Art Park is an open-air exhibition space that's open 24/7. It's a place where Daejeon's scientific identity and artistic imagination come together. This park changes its look depending on the time of day. But after sunset, when the lights and media shows begin, it transforms into one of Daejeon's most popular night attractions.  At the center of the park stands the grand “Eternal Life Cosmos.” This multimedia artwork is 25 meters tall and 29 meters wide, and its theme is the light of the universe, nature, and humanity. With its colorful LED lights and music, the piece fills the park with a light show. As the lights flow to the rhythm, they light up the park. When you follow their movement with your eyes, you'll feel like you're standing in the middle of the Milky Way, lost in a dreamlike sensation.  Lining the walking paths in the park are eight sculptures that tell a single story called “Eternal Light – The Four Seasons of Hanbat.” Inspired by the painting Dream Journey to the Peach Blossom Land by the Joseon-era painter An Gyeon, the artwork blends traditional Korean painting with modern images of Daejeon, like the Expo Science Park and Daecheong Dam. At night, the sculptures light up, bringing together the flowing lines of tradition with the brilliant light of modern technology. This creates a breathtaking scene that shows the past, present, and future all at once.  The greatest charm of this park is how tradition and modernity are naturally connected through light. Past and future coexist in a single space here, and the moment the lights turn on, the park transcends time itself, becoming one beautiful scene.  The night view of Daejeon Media Art Park, with its light, music, and technology, offers more than just a beautiful sight. It feels like a journey through time. Why not take a walk here beneath the starlit sky, where science and art come together?

stories.title: Daedong Sky Park, Daejeon
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Daedong Sky Park in Daejeon, a hilltop nightscape spot where a small shining windmill stands and the city unfolds in a single sweeping view.  Daedong Sky Park is a small, charming park located in Daedong, Daejeon. It was created in 2009 as part of the “Rainbow Project.” Selected as one of the Eight Scenic Views of Dong-gu, the park's symbol is a white windmill with bright red blades. The sight of the windmill turning slowly on the hilltop blends with the park’s peaceful feel, creating a special charm. Although it’s small, the park has a pavilion, benches, and a wooden swing. It’s the perfect place to get away from the city's noise and bustle for a moment of quiet rest.  The greatest charm of Daedong Sky Park is its sunsets and night views. The nightscape here isn't dazzling, but it has a gentle, emotional feel. It's like the warm comfort you get at the end of a busy day. Standing in front of the windmill, you can take in a sweeping panorama of Daejeon. From here, you'll see the ridges of Mount Gyejok in the northeast all the way to Mount Bomun in the southwest, surrounding the city in beautiful layers.  At sunset, the sky glows with a deep red. As the city lights start to come on one by one, the scene becomes as beautiful as a painting. As night gets deeper, colorful lights illuminate the windmill and the walking paths, and together with the sparkling night view of Daejeon, they create a scene straight out of a fairy tale.  Why not spend a relaxing moment at Daedong Sky Park, where the humble but warm charm of the place blends beautifully with the night view of Daejeon?

stories.title: Bomunsan Observatory, Daejeon
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Bomunsan Observatory in Daejeon, where you can enjoy a 360-degree panoramic view of the city along with the glowing nightscape of the baseball stadium.  Located at 197 meters above sea level on the mid-slope of Bomunsan, this spot was once called “Treasure Mountain” because of the treasures said to be buried here. For a long time, it's been a special observatory and a place for the people of Daejeon to relax and heal. Just a five-minute walk from the “Wood Culture Experience Center,” it offers a quick break from your busy life. By day, you can see the wide-open cityscape of Daejeon, and as the sun goes down, the city lights begin to twinkle like little stars.  The greatest charm of Bomunsan Observatory is its 360-degree panoramic night view. From the retro streets of the old downtown districts of Dong-gu and Jung-gu all the way to the modern high-rises of Dunsan New Town, the city lights that unfold before your eyes offer a nightscape that is special to Daejeon. This unique view lets you fully enjoy the city's many different sides all at once.  But the charm of Bomunsan Observatory doesn’t end there. From here, you can also look down on Hanwha Life Eagles Park. During baseball season, from April to October, you can vividly feel the stadium's atmosphere even from the observatory, with its bright lights and the roaring cheers of fans. This unique blend of the city’s nightscape and the passion of the ballpark is a special experience you’ll only find at Bomunsan Observatory.  Here, you can enjoy not only the city lights but also the sounds of nature. As evening falls and the birds become quiet, the gentle sounds of crickets and the soft mountain breeze create a natural melody. This beautiful sound makes the night view even richer.  Why not create your own special memories here, where the city lights, the bright glow of the baseball stadium, and the sounds of nature all come together in perfect harmony?

stories.title: Yongdusan Park, Busan
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Yongdusan Park in Busan, a place that embraces the beauty of both day and night  Located in Jung-gu, Busan, Yongdusan Park is an urban park named for the mountain's shape, which is said to resemble a dragon's head. The park is home to Busan's famous landmark, Busan Tower. It also has peaceful walking trails, various sculptures, and a large grassy plaza, making it a welcoming place where everyone can relax and have fun.  On sunny days, the bright blue sky and the park’s colorful flower clock make it the perfect place to create special memories with loved ones. From the proud Busan Tower observatory, you can take in the sweeping view of Busan Port, leaving you with a refreshing sense of openness that clears away any lingering worries.  As time passes and the sky glows with golden sunset, another charm of Yongdusan Park begins to awaken. Lights that had been resting quietly under the sun start to come on one by one, and the colorful illumination surrounding the white Busan Tower creates a magical atmosphere, as if the stars themselves had descended.  The softly glowing lights along the walking paths make it feel as if you’re strolling through the Milky Way itself. n particular, nighttime programs such as the Busan Tower fireworks mapping show create treasured memories for families and spark romantic emotions for couples, offering special moments you can experience only here.  A night filled with special memories, no matter who you’re with. At Yongdusan Park, where the romance of Busan shines brightly, take a moment to capture a night that is truly your own.

stories.title: Dadaepo Sunset Fountain of Dream, Busan
stories.audioTitle: Dadaepo Sunset Fountain of Dream, Busan
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to the Dadaepo Sunset Fountain of Dream in Busan, a magical stage of light and water where cool streams dance in harmony with the night.  Located at the entrance of Dadaepo Beach, the Sunset Fountain of Dream is Busan's first ground fountain and is one of the largest in the world. Just past the plaza, Dadaepo Beach is known as one of Busan's most beautiful sunset spots. The fiery red glow of the setting sun over the sea and the grand fountain come together to create a truly special atmosphere.  During the day, the beach and walking trails sparkle under the hot sun, and the nearby eco-paths are also filled with visitors. From May to September, the water play fountain is especially popular with families and children. Splashing through the cool streams offers a great way to beat the heat, filling the air with endless sounds of joyful laughter.  As the sun slowly sets in the west and paints the sky red, the dazzling night fountain show begins. From April to October, the evening fountain performance offers a spectacular display synchronized to more than 60 songs, ranging from pop to classical music. Streams of water soar up to 55 meters high, blending with vibrant LED lights to create a breathtaking sight.  The fountain show also features a special event. If you apply in advance, your personal message, whether it's a birthday greeting, a proposal, or something else you wish to share, will be displayed along with the music and fountain performance. It’s a one-of-a-kind experience that gives couples, families, and friends an unforgettable memory to treasure.  Welcome a special night by the sea in Busan, as the Sunset Fountain of Dream soars high into the sky. Here, you'll encounter magical moments where light, music, and water blend together in perfect harmony.

stories.title: Yeongdo Sky Observatory, Busan
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to the Yeongdo Sky Observatory in Busan, a breathtaking walkway where the sea and sky meet.  Located along the Jeoryeong Coastal Walk, the Yeongdo Sky Observatory is a spot where you can take in sweeping views of the blue sea and open sky, just like its name suggests. On clear days, the sight stretches all the way to Tsushima, Geoje Island, and Gadeokdo, making it the perfect place to pause and reflect while listening to the sound of the waves.  The main highlight here is the Skywalk, an experience space where visitors of all ages can enjoy a thrill. Standing on the transparent reinforced glass, you can look straight down at the sea and coastline beneath your feet, feeling the exhilarating sensation of walking on air.  On the deck benches beside the observatory, you can enjoy a simple picnic or leave a memory with loved ones by placing a lock on the fence. Surrounded by the calm of nature, quiet conversations with someone special soon turn an ordinary day into an unforgettable memory.  The true charm of the Yeongdo Sky Observatory shines as dusk settles and night deepens. Beyond the horizon, the golden sunset slowly spreads across the sky, offering a sense of tranquility you can only experience here. As night falls, the twinkling harbor lights and the city’s nightscape blend with the gentle sound of the waves, creating an atmosphere filled with romance.  Why not step away from the dazzling city lights for a while and embrace the quiet night offered by the Yeongdo Sky Observatory? The special nightscape where sea and sky come together will leave a gentle afterglow and warm comfort deep in your heart.

stories.title: Yongho Starlight Park, Busan
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Yongho Starlight Park in Busan, a place where starlight and serenity flow together.  Located in Nam-gu, Busan, Yongho Starlight Park is a community-friendly healing space where open coastal trails meet the city’s stunning night views. Once closed after a Russian vessel collided with the Gwangan Bridge, the area was temporarily opened to the public through cooperation between Nam-gu District and the Busan Port Authority, making it a special place to enjoy until the full redevelopment of the Yongho Pier begins.  Returning to the community after 30 years, Yongho Starlight Park has become a welcoming space where everyone can relax, combining beautiful scenery with engaging experiences. From its viewpoint, you can take in Busan’s iconic sights, including Haeundae and the Gwangan Bridge, all at once. Seasonal festivals and a variety of hands-on programs add to the excitement, giving every visitor something to look forward to.  As dusk settles in, Yongho Starlight Park, true to its name, comes alive. The glow of city lights blends with the gentle illumination along the walking paths, creating a beautiful nightscape. A once-abandoned management building has been remodeled into an exhibition and experience center. Here, visitors can enjoy a permanent exhibition hall, the media art program Starlight Sea Journey, and observation and rest areas, offering plenty of ways to explore and relax.  How about spending a romantic moment with someone special beneath the shining stars of Yongho Starlight Park? Here, where the night sky meets the night sea, unforgettable memories are waiting just for you.

stories.title: Hwangnyeongsan Mountain, Busan
stories.script: Nightscapes of Korea takes you to places where the night shines even brighter. Today, we journey to Hwangnyeongsan Mountain in Busan, where green peaks offer breathtaking scenery.  Stretching across four districts of Busan, Hwangnyeongsan Mountain embraces the bustling city with its dense forest trails. It’s a lively destination beloved not only by hikers who enjoy its walking paths, but also by visitors seeking the nighttime charm that reveals a completely different beauty from the day.  A hike of about two to three hours from the trail entrance will bring you to the summit, where a beacon mound stands. Once used during the Joseon Dynasty to signal enemy invasions with fire, this beacon mound is now a symbol of Hwangnyeongsan's peak and a unique photo spot beloved by visitors.  Climbing up to the Hwangnyeongsan Observatory at sunset, you’ll see the city lights turn on one by one between the mountain peaks, unfolding a panoramic view of Busan like a painting. Blended with the red glow of dusk, the scene offers a special harmony created by both city and nature.  As full darkness settles over downtown Busan, the lights from countless buildings blend with the night sea, completing the dazzling nightscape unique to Hwangnyeongsan. Standing before this view, anyone can feel a liberating sense of escape from the everyday.  When you need a pause from the busy rhythm of daily life, come to Hwangnyeongsan, where the sea and city of Busan meet in harmony. The wide-open panorama will clear your heart and leave you feeling refreshed the moment you see it.

stories.title: A place where words awaken the mind, the Forest of Wisdom
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel. This time, our journey takes us to the Forest of  Wisdom in Paju, a peaceful place where the spirit of knowledge quietly resides.  Located on the first floor of the Asia Publication Culture & Information Center in  Paju Book City, the Forest of Wisdom is an open library created to collect,  preserve, and share books of enduring value. Open to everyone, this space invites visitors to read, reflect, and share ideas, offering a place where the meaning and value of books can be felt in everyday life.  The Forest of Wisdom consists of three main sections. Hall 1 features collections donated by scholars, intellectuals, and research institutes. It is filled with rich resources across the humanities, from literature and history to art and the social sciences. Hall 2 is filled with books donated directly by publishing houses.   Here, visitors can catch a clear glimpse of Korea’s publishing culture and the distinct character of each publisher. Hall 3, known as Munbal Salon, serves as the lobby of Library Stay Jijihyang. It offers broader cultural inspiration through books donated not only by publishers, but also by distributors, museums, and art galleries.  This quiet yet deeply moving space also served as an important setting in the drama Yumi’s Cells 2. After their first kiss, Yumi and Babi came here for a date, the very place where Yumi came face to face with her true dream.  Kim Yumi: “A contest? I’ve tried preparing for contests before.” Yoo Babi: “I bet someone like you’ve already won a contest. Maybe not Kim  Yumi the assistant manager, but Kim Yumi the writer.” Kim Yumi: “Oh, come on… that’s not true.”  After her short chat with Babi, Yumi spots a poster for a web novel contest on a bookshelf and suddenly remembers the dream she had long kept buried in her heart. The next day, Yumi boldly turns in her resignation and takes her first step toward a new life as a writer. The Forest of Wisdom in Paju became a beautiful turning point in Yumi’s life at thirty-three. As you walk slowly between the shelves, you may suddenly find yourself meeting a voice in your heart you had long forgotten. May you, too, discover your own true story here today.

stories.title: A place where the grandeur of nature meets thrilling excitement, the  Hantan River Sky Bridge in Pocheon
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel. This time, our journey takes us to the Hantan River Sky Bridge in Pocheon, where excitement meets the beauty of nature high above the valley.  Nestled in Yeongbuk-myeon, Pocheon, Gyeonggi-do, the Hantan River Sky Bridge is a 200-meter-long suspension footbridge that opened in May 2018. Rising 50 meters above the ground, the bridge offers visitors a breathtaking view of the Hantan River Gorge, where the deep valley unfolds beneath your feet. Designed to support up to 1,500 adults at once, each weighing about 80 kilograms, the bridge perfectly balances excitement and safety.  The Hantan River Sky Bridge connects the Ecological Landscape Complex and the Theme Park, and is also known for its scenic walking trail. The 6-kilometer trail begins at the bridge, winds along the Meonguri Gorge, and loops back, offering breathtaking views of the columnar joints shaped by volcanic activity and erosion. The trail offers an easy and relaxing walk where visitors can take in the beauty of nature, making it a favorite spot for families with children.  Renowned for its breathtaking scenery, the bridge was also featured prominently in the drama Crash Landing on You. While standing on the Hantan River Sky Bridge, Ri Jeong-hyeok shares a story with Yoon Se-ri from his days studying abroad, when he asked a woman he met by chance on a bridge to take his photo. He admits that the image of the woman, who nervously took the camera with trembling hands, has stayed with him ever since.  Yoon Se-ri: “Where was that?” Ri Jeong-hyeok: “On the Sigriswil Bridge in Switzerland.” Ri Jeong-hyeok: “That woman stayed in my mind for a long time. / I sometimes  wondered if she was doing all right, if she ever felt down... / Because, well... she  was my type.”  At that moment, Yoon Se-ri realizes that she was the woman he had been talking about. She says nothing, just gazes at Ri Jeong-hyeok in silence. The scene, where emotions spoke louder than words, captured the destiny of the two reunited lovers and left a lasting impression on viewers.  As the cool breeze drifts across the Hantan River Sky Bridge, take a moment to pause and look around you. Perhaps that long-awaited feeling will find its way into your day.

stories.title: A place filled with laughter and memories, Donggwang Theater in  Dongducheon
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel. This time, our journey takes us to Donggwang Theater in Dongducheon, a place that has preserved the memories of an era.  Opened in 1959, Donggwang Theater is the longest-running single-screen theater in Korea that shows commercial films. Since its opening, it has long served as a cultural and social hub for the citizens of Dongducheon. Around the theater, dentists, clinics, photo studios, and cafés began to open, turning the area into a lively symbol of the town. Even through the 1990s and early 2000s, long lines of moviegoers filled the street on weekends and holidays.  Today, Donggwang Theater still operates while keeping much of its original appearance. The ticket booth outside is no longer used, but the old schedule board still greets everyone who walks in. Tickets are sold inside the theater, and guests can choose any seat they like. This system preserves the nostalgic, analog charm of Korea’s classic single-screen theaters.  With its vintage and distinctive atmosphere, the theater also appeared in the drama Reply 1988. In one scene, three friends from Ssangmun-dong, Dong-ryong, Jung-hwan and Sun-woo, put on reserve uniforms and sneak into the theater, hoping to watch an adult movie.  Dong-ryong: “Three soldiers here.”  His nervous eyes as he delivers the line to the ticket clerk made countless viewers laugh. That awkward yet sincere moment reflected the innocent and playful spirit of youth in the 1980s.  Even today, Donggwang Theater still quietly serves as a place of shared memories across generations. As you stand here today at Donggwang Theater, may you find yourself smiling at the simple warmth and quiet joy that time has left behind.

stories.title: A garden filled with exotic charm, Wolhwawon in Hyowon Park,  Suwon
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel. This time, our journey takes us to Wolhwawon in Hyowon Park, Suwon, a place of exotic beauty and gentle charm.  Located on the west side of Hyowon Park in Suwon, Gyeonggi-do, Wolhwawon faithfully recreates the traditional garden architecture of Guangdong Province, China. In 2003, Gyeonggi Province in Korea and Guangdong Province in China signed a friendship exchange agreement, pledging to build traditional gardens in each other’s cities. This resulted in a beautiful cultural exchange. Wolhwawon was built here in Suwon, and in return, Guangzhou received a reciprocal garden, Haedong Gyeonggiwon, which was modeled after Korea's famous Soswaewon in Damyang. The Chinese character 'Wol' (粤) in Wolhwawon is actually the old name for Guangdong Province.  In particular, Wolhwawon beautifully captures the essence of Guangdong-style gardens, where architecture and nature exist in perfect harmony. The buildings are perfectly situated to frame the garden views through their windows. The rear garden features an earthen mound, an artificial pond, a boat-shaped pavilion, and a waterfall, all working together to infuse the space with calm and grace.   This special and exotic place is also known as a filming location for the drama Moon Lovers: Scarlet Heart Ryeo. Hae Soo, the young Goryeo girl who arrived at the palace with the Eighth Prince Wang Wook and Lady Hae, unexpectedly meets the Fourth Prince Wang So in the Wolhwawon garden. He no longer has the rough appearance he had when they first met. Hae Soo is struck by Wang So’s more dignified and mature presence.  Wang So: “Why are you here? This isn't a place for someone like you.” Hae Soo: “You’ve completely changed. Now you really look like a prince!” Wang So: “I was born one.”  Wang So was locked in a brutal struggle for the throne and had been rejected even by his own family. Yet, whenever he was with Hae Soo, he slowly began to open the heart he had kept closed for so long. The sunlight and the shimmering water of Wolhwawon quietly mirrored their feelings, leaving behind a lovely, warm atmosphere.  Wolhwawon in Hyowon Park is where their story began. Just as the title Scarlet Heart suggests, take your time walking through this beautiful place and let your own heart-stirring story begin.

stories.title: A place filled with King Jeongjo’s filial devotion, Hwaseong  Haenggung in Suwon
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel! This time, our journey takes us to Hwaseong Haenggung in Suwon, a palace that beautifully captures the spirit of filial devotion and the legacy of the Joseon Dynasty.  Suwon Hwaseong Fortress was completed in 1796 by King Jeongjo, the 22nd king of the Joseon Dynasty. He built it after moving his father, Crown Prince Sado’s tomb, from Baebongsan in Yangju to Mount Hwasan in Suwon, and created a new city for the people who would live there. Located inside Suwon Hwaseong Fortress, Hwaseong Haenggung is the largest of all temporary palaces in Korea. It is considered so beautiful that people often call it the “secondary palace of Gyeongbokgung.”  The word Haenggung means a temporary palace where the king stayed when he traveled away from the main palace. While Hwaseong Haenggung usually functioned as a local government office, it became the king’s temporary residence and a venue for royal functions whenever the king visited Hwaseong. When you pass through the central gate of Hwaseong Haenggung, you’ll see Bongsudang Hall, famously known as the site of King Jeongjo's magnificent 60th birthday celebration for his mother, Lady Hyegyeong. The name literally means a wish for ten thousand years of longevity. It was chosen to honor Lady Hyegyeong’s long life and beautifully reflects King Jeongjo's deep filial devotion.  Bongsudang, a place steeped in this devotion, is memorably featured in the drama Love in the Moonlight. In the scene, Crown Prince Lee Yeong passes by the hall after hearing that Queen Kim is expecting a child. In that moment, he vividly recalls a warm childhood memory with his mother, Queen Yoon.  Queen Yoon: “How was the music, my son?” Lee Yeong: “When you moved your fingers like that, it sounded like young  leaves trembling in the spring breeze.” Queen Yoon: “Exactly. That technique is called nonghyeon. Shall I teach you how to play the geomungo?”  As he recalled that cherished, happy day, a deep sense of longing crossed Lee Yeong's eyes. In that moment, his true, tender feelings quietly came to light. His usual playful sternness gave way to deep emotion. The calm scenery of Hwaseong Haenggung perfectly enhanced the scene, giving their story even greater emotional depth.  Beneath these quiet tiled roofs, the old stories of devotion still breathe around us today. As you walk the paths of Hwaseong Haenggung, why not take a moment to feel King Jeongjo’s filial devotion and the lingering warmth in Lee Yeong's heart?

stories.title: A place filled with romance and love, Nami Island in Chuncheon
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel! This time, our journey takes us to Nami Island in Chuncheon, known as the island of pure love.  Nami Island, located in Namsan-myeon, Chuncheon, Gangwon Province, is a natural paradise where lush green forests meet the river. In spring, cherry blossoms fill the air. In summer, the trees offer a cool, pleasant shade. In autumn, the paths are lined with red and gold leaves. In winter, white snowflakes bloom like flowers. The island becomes a colorful fairy-tale world throughout the year. In 2006, the island was transformed into a unique theme park called Naminara Republic, a special place where culture, art, and nature seamlessly blend together.  One of the highlights of Nami Island is the Metasequoia Road and the majestic pine forest that lines the walking path. As you stroll along the forest path filled with the scent of pine and fresh greenery, you’ll feel as if you’ve been transported to another, exotic world. Thanks to this romantic atmosphere, Nami Island became the filming location for the most famous scenes in Winter Sonata, the drama that is considered the starting point for K-Wave pilgrimages.  Jun-sang: “Why is the snowman’s mouth like that?” Yu-jin: “He’s got something he wants to say to you.” Jun-sang: “What is it?” Yu-jin: “I’ll tell you later, later.”  The scenes of Jun-sang and Yu-jin are still cherished memories for many people. They deepened their bond while walking side by side along the forest path, or sitting on a wooden bench to make a snowman. The peaceful scenery of Nami Island allows you to completely immerse yourself in their love story. It feels calm and romantic, as if time itself has stopped.  Why not create your own special memories on Nami Island, the island of love?  The sparkling river and the gentle sound of the forest will stay in your heart as a warm and lasting memory.

stories.title: A place that brings destiny to life, Jumunjin Beach in Gangneung
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel. This time, our journey takes us to Jumunjin Beach in Gangneung, the place where a lonely and radiant god once stayed.  Located at the northern tip of Gangneung, along the blue East Sea, it's a beautiful beach where clear, shallow waters, white sand, and the sound of waves blend harmoniously with the charm of a small fishing village. Beyond the cool shade of pine trees and cozy camping spots, the nearby Hyangho Reservoir is a peaceful place for freshwater fishing and quiet conversations. By day, the sea shines blue, and by night, the gentle glow of the waves lights up the shore. It’s a place where the romance and youth of Gangneung flourish, and friends,  couples, and families can share unforgettable moments.  With its mysterious and magical atmosphere, Jumunjin Beach became the filming location for one of the most iconic scenes in the drama Goblin. The scene of the first meeting was filmed right here at Jumunjin Beach. Here, Kim Shin, the goblin living under an immortal curse, meets Ji Eun-tak, the human bride destined to free him, for the first time.  Kim Shin: “Is it you?” Ji Eun-tak: “What?” Kim Shin: “Were you the one who called me?”  Ji Eun-tak, who has grown up in hardship, sits alone on the breakwater at Jumunjin Beach, spending her lonely birthday. As she makes a lonely wish and blows out the candle on her cake, Kim Shin, the goblin, appears right behind her. When Kim Shin hands Ji Eun-tak the buckwheat flower, the cloudy sky suddenly turns clear. The buckwheat flower, which means “lover,” perfectly symbolizes this moment as the beginning of their shared fate. Their hearts slowly grow closer.  Now, amidst the silver waves of Jumunjin Beach, why not create a magical moment with someone you love? Here, where time seems to stop, your memories will drift on the gentle waves and shine brightly.

stories.title: A place where memories and emotions flow like waves,  Nongoldam-gil in Donghae
stories.script: Welcome to K-Culture Travel. This time, our journey takes us to Nongoldam-gil in Donghae, a seaside village where white waves and tender feelings drift together.  Nongoldam-gil is a charming mural village in Mukho-dong, Gangwon Province. It stands near Mukho Port, which opened as an international trading port in 1941. Countless stories of everyday life still linger in the air. The name Nongoldam-gil comes from two things: a small rice field that once existed on the hillside, and the lives of the old fishermen who walked its muddy alleys. As you walk through these alleys, now filled with colorful murals, you can feel the hardships and bittersweet stories of this old seaside village.  Thanks to its cozy atmosphere and the simple, warm stories of its residents, the village became the main character’s place of refuge in the drama The Heirs.  Cha Eun-sang: “Why are you here? If you show up like this again, what should I do?” Kim Tan: “I’m sorry.” Cha Eun-sang: “If you’re sorry, then go. I ran away to escape you, so why did you find me again?”  Cha Eun-sang is in love with Kim Tan, the son of a wealthy family. Trapped by the harsh reality of poverty, she hides her feelings and lives with her mother in a small orange-roofed house along Nongoldam-gil. Cha Eun-sang gazes at the T-shirt hanging in the yard, which holds precious memories of Kim Tan. She is lost in deep longing. This scene blends with the view of Nongoldam-gil's mural alleys, where the sea breeze gently blows through, stirring even deeper emotion.  Kim Tan finally finds her after a long search. But he stops in front of the wall between their worlds that even love cannot overcome. He is afraid of hurting her again. His sadness lingers, like the deep, wide sea surrounding Nongoldam-gil. It leaves behind a quiet ache.  As you walk along this peaceful path, why not think back to the memories of someone special? The many stories in the colorful murals and the gentle sound of the East Sea waves might leave a gentle echo in your heart.

stories.title: Introduction to the Mongolian Folk Museum
stories.audioTitle: Introduction to the Mongolian Folk Museum
stories.script: The Mongolian Folk Museum is a symbolic exhibition space located within the Mongolian Cultural Village, established through the sister city relationship between Namyangju City and Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia. The Mongolian Cultural Village opened in April 2000, and the Mongolian Folk museum, modeled after a traditional ger, opened in 2009 and remains in operation to this day. This unique space—the only one in Korea dedicated to the comprehensive exhibition of Mongolian culture—showcases hundreds of significant Mongolian artifacts.  In addition to the general information of Mongolia, you can see the grasslands, life, faith, and art-related artifacts that give you a glimpse of Mongolian life, as well as Mongolian livestock, wildlife, natural and cultural relics.  These artifacts vividly portray the lives of Mongolians who lived in vast nature and unique environments. Traditional clothing, household items, and crafts go beyond mere everyday objects to embody the Mongolian spirit.  We hope you will discover a new charm of Mongolia by indirectly experiencing the Mongolian way of life at the Mongolian Folk Museum.

stories.title: Mongolia Overview
stories.script: Mongolia's land area is approximately seven times that of the Korean Peninsula. Considering its size, its population is relatively small, with approximately half of its population living in the capital, Ulaanbaatar. Ulaanbaatar, meaning Red Hero, has become a center of politics, economy, and culture, with a history spanning more than 360 years. The main ethnic group in Mongolia is the Khalkh Mongols, making up approximately 80% of the population. Kazakhs, Chinese, and other ethnic minorities also live alongside them. The official language is Khalkh Mongol, particularly widely spoken in the eastern region which is the center of the country.  The national flag is also a key to understanding Mongolia. The Mongolian flag, known as the Turiin Dalbaa consists of two colors: blue and red. Blue symbolizes the eternal sky, and red represents the development of the nation. The Soyombo pattern, located on the left side of the national flag, is a comprehensive symbol that embodies the spirit of the Mongolian people. The flame symbolizes the past, present, and future; the sun and moon represent the life and glory of the Mongolian people; the fortress and walls symbolize sincerity and unity; the two fish symbolize masculinity and femininity; and the spear and arrow signify courage. A single, small pattern embodies the identity of the entire nation.  Mongolia has a unique natural environment. With the average altitude is about 1,580m, decreasing from west to east, and it is a place where various natural landscapes, from grasslands and deserts to forests and lakes, exist in harmony. This environment has profoundly influenced the Mongolian lifestyle and culture. Traditional pastoralism and agriculture, and more recently, mining, are Mongolia's primary industries. With 75% of the country being pastoral land, pastoralism and livestock herding are crucial to the livelihood of Mongolians. At the same time, the country's abundance of mineral resources, such as copper, molybdenum, and oil, has fueled the rapid development of modern industries.

stories.title: Blessing of the Grasslands
stories.script: Blessing of the Grasslands features artifacts related to the nomadic lifestyle of Mongolians, who seasonally herded their livestock across the vast grasslands of Mongolia. The leather pouches, called Bogts and Khos Bogts, displayed in the center, were used to store items on the saddles of horses or camels during nomadic migrations, providing a glimpse into their nomadic lifestyle on the grasslands.  Mongols migrated four times seasonally. On the eve of each migration, Mongolians cleaned their houses, horses, and saddles. They performed a ritual in which they poured milk into the sky using the Tsatsal displayed in the upper right corner, expressing gratitude to the heavens and the earth. These artifacts also reveal the Mongolian tradition of living in harmony with nature.

stories.title: A Day in the Grasslands
stories.script: A Day in the Grasslands presents a diorama of Mongolian life on the grasslands. Mongols built gers on the vast grasslands and raised horses, cattle, sheep, goats, and camels—the five types of livestock they called the Five Livestock. They also hunted for living. The ger was constructed with a wooden frame and felt for easy transport. It can be disassembled and reassembled, and when unfolded, it becomes a single room structure, like an umbrella erected with walls surrounding it. Furthermore, the Five Livestock were not merely a means of livelihood, but lifelong companions. Horses were essential for transportation, grazing, and long-distance travel, while cattle contributed to all aspects of life, including transportation, dairy products, and leather. Camels were used for transportation across deserts, and sheep and goats were used for living as meat and dairy products, fur and leather.

stories.title: Scent of Nature
stories.script: Scent of Nature offers a glimpse into the lives of Mongolian hunters on horseback. They utilized various tools and methods for hunting. Tools such as the bow and arrowheads  (Num and Bultsuut sum), the hunting gun (Tsahiur buu), the stirrup  (Doroo) for riding a horse, the Khot tseneg (a container for gunpowder or bullets), the whip (Tashuur), the cowhide strap (Chodor), and the Khusuur (a device used to remove horse sweat) reveal how hunting was practiced on the grasslands. Hunting took place in autumn and early winter, excluding spring and summer, when animals give birth and raise their young. Rituals were performed at home before hunting, and rules were observed in harmony with nature, such as not harming other animals in the hunting grounds.

stories.title: Mongol Etiquette
stories.script: Mongols considered it polite to serve tea and milk when welcoming guests. Various types of tableware have been developed for nomadic life including bowls used for serving guests. Guts, small copper jugs, were used to hold Mongolian butter, a staple in Buddhist meals. Mongon ayaga, made of silver, was used to serve milk, tea, and alcohol to guests. Copper and brass containers such as Saakhuu, Guulin sav, and Savkhanwere also used to store tea, milk, and water.

stories.title: Mongolian Life
stories.script: “Mongolian Life” exhibits various tools used by Mongolians in their daily lives. In particular, tools like irons, mortars, and scales are similar to those used by our Korean ancestors. For example, the Tsognii induu is an ancient iron made of cast iron, with a wooden handle and a lit charcoal inside. Mortars such as the Shirmen uur, Uur, and nuduur, Were used to grind medicine or tea leaves into powder, and the Jing, a scale used to measure weight, were similar to those used by Koreans. You can also see tools for nomadic life, such as the Myadu, a wooden and threaded tool used to mark clothing lines and for various other purposes; the Erguuleg, Uut, and Olom, used to tie camels and calves; and the Mongol tsooi, a lock engraved with traditional patterns. It is said that a brazier was usually placed in the center of the ger, with an altar and valuable items placed on top, and on the left was the man's place with horse and weapons, and on the right was the woman's cooking utensils and dairy products making tools.

stories.title: Taste of Mongolia
stories.script: Taste of Mongolia features artifacts that offer insight into the traditional Mongolian diet. Because the nights and winters on the grasslands were extremely cold, a brazier was essential. It was placed in the center of the ger to provide both heat and a means for cooking. Furthermore, most kitchen utensils were designed for easy portability to accommodate the nomadic lifestyle.  Mongolians consumed a lot of high-calorie foods to endure the harsh winters and depended on livestock milk, which provided a complete source of nutrition. The wooden plate Modon tavag was used to hold dairy products, while the Bagvar was a vessel for tea, food, and dairy products. Mongols typically enjoyed light meals such as Suutei tea and fried lamb, like Khuushuur, for breakfast and lunch. Dinner usually consisted of boiled meat, noodles, and a thin soup with grains. Whole steamed meats were served when entertaining guests or during holidays.  Containers such as Togoo, Sav, and Uisen Sav were used to store and prepare food on the move. Ul boovnii khev was used to make Lunar New Year cookies. Tsar was used to store meat and cookies.  Additionally, tools like the Khaluun toggo, Shanaga, Tulga, and Galiin khaich were used to start fires and cook food.

stories.title: Mongolian Currency
stories.script: In this section, we can observe the changes in the Mongolian economy and lifestyle through the history of Mongolian currency. From the far left, the Ikh Sangiin Tes, used from 1860 to 1918, was a certificate issued in exchange for green tea or currency. This indicates that green tea was rare in Mongolia at the time, so it functioned as a form of currency. Next to it are round, flat, and square-hole Russian and Chinese coins, primarily used before 1912.  Next to it is the Bagaburzud, issued in 1921. Its high denomination prevented it from being widely used. Next to it is another currency, issued by the then Minister of Finance, which was also discontinued for various reasons. Eventually, in 1925, a new currency unit called the Tugrik, was established, and silver coins and banknotes were issued. Following this, currency featuring the portrait of Sükhbaatar was issued in 1939, and beginning in 1941, currency with modern Mongolian script was introduced. Since 1993, eleven banknotes of various colors and sizes have finally been in circulation.

stories.title: Colors of Mongolia
stories.script: Colors of Mongolia showcases Mongolian clothing and accessories. With the development of nomadic culture in Mongolia, traditional clothing was adapted to suit the nomadic lifestyle, emphasizing convenience and practicality. Mongols endured harsh winters by making clothing from fur and leather obtained through livestock rearing and hunting; hats were also essential. The Malgai, shown above, is a traditional women's hat made of colorful silk. The Arisan malgal, worn by the mannequin on the right, is a winter hat made from sheepskin turned inside out, offering exceptional warmth.  The Mongolian Gutal shoes feature an upward-curved toe, symbolizing the Mongolian philosophy of respecting the land and preserving nature. Inside, they wore Oims made of wool as overshoes, and there were also special shoes, such as the Ugalztai Mongol gutal, which featured decorative patterns.

stories.title: The Style of Mongolia
stories.script: Style of Mongolia section showcases traditional Mongolian clothing, reflecting the distinctive style of the Mongolian people. Traditional Mongolian clothing transcends everyday wear, embodying distinct tribal and regional characteristics. The men's and women's clothing you are viewing now most exemplifies the characteristics of the Khalkh people.  Men wore traditional garments called Khalkh nokhor deel and carried knives, cigarettes, and a het—a kindling tool—at their waists. Women wore elaborate garments called Khalkh ekhner deel, including a puffy-shouldered Tengger Mur made from camel hair. Since clothing, belts, and hats varied according to gender, age, and social status, they served a symbolic role in revealing an individual's status and identity.  Standing in front of the map on the glass case on the right, you can compare the names of various Mongolian tribes from each region with their traditional costumes, as depicted on the map inside the artifacts exhibition.

stories.title: Men's Accessories
stories.script: Here, you can see the accessories worn by Mongolian men. Nomadic men carried the tools they needed at all times and places on their belts. A prime example is the development of tobacco culture. Khoorog a traditional tobacco used for sniffing, was exchanged as a form of greeting. You can also see Gaans, a pipe, and Soyoo and Tsokhior, tools used for shaking off ash. Khavtag, a pouch for wrapping tobacco, was made of silk or leather, and its opening was ornately decorated.  Furthermore, the Khet, a fire starter, and the Khutga, a knife essential for hunting and daily life, were indispensable items for men. Knives were more than mere weapons; they served as essential tools for food preparation and survival, often adorned with intricate decorative designs.

stories.title: Women's Accessories
stories.script: Here, we see the accessories worn by Mongolian women. While it varied across tribes, the Khalkha accessories are particularly ornate and representative. Just like the men's accessories, the intricate and elaborate craftsmanship is also evident. Women wore their hair in pigtails, silver hairpins, and Khavchig and Öröövchiadorned with beads and jewels. They wore Süikh earrings made of pearls and silver, and around their waists, they carried Tavang Savagui containing a nail file, earpicks, toothpicks, and a perfume bottle. They wore necklaces made of jade or coral around their necks and sometimes wore Engeriin Mungugol—small amulets case containing Buddhist scriptures. Furthermore, rings and bracelets made of gold, silver, and copper were adorned with various gemstones, further enhancing the women's beauty.

stories.title: Faith in Life
stories.script: “Faith in Life” showcases artifacts from Mongolian Lamaism, a religion practiced by over 90% of the current Mongolian population. Buddhism was introduced to Mongolia from India via Tibet, becoming the religion of the empire during the Kublai Khan era and soon becoming the most important faith in Mongolia. From the left, there is Gush bumba, which sprays holy water using feathers; Khorol, shaped like a disk; Khurd, which contains several scriptures; and Erkh, which turns Buddhist prayer beads and symbolizes wishes for the health and happiness of humans and animals. All of these instruments were used in Lamaist rituals to fulfill people's wishes and to cleanse them of their sins.  They also carried Buddha images made from molds, such as the Suvraga and Khev, which are small stupas containing people's prayers. On the right are the Manal, a picture believed to cure illness; the Sudar, a Buddhist scripture; and the Bar, a woodblock used to create Buddhist scriptures. This clearly demonstrates the Buddhist characteristics of Mongolian Lamaism, which are similar to those of Korean Buddhism. Next to it, various tools are on display, including musical instruments used by monks such as Denshig, Tungiin Khalbaga, and Khonkh, as well as the Artsnii uutand Sanggiin boipor—powders used to burn incense—offering a glimpse into the unique characteristics of Lamaism.  Finally, on the rightmost mannequin, you can see the attire of the Lama monks.

stories.title: Worship of Heaven
stories.script: Worship of Heaven features shamans performing rituals and showcasing artifacts. This evokes the shamans performing rituals in Korea, demonstrating shamanism—the most representative religion of Mongolia before Lamaism and a belief deeply rooted in Mongolian consciousness. For the Mongols, faith was a profound aspect of their culture, inseparable from their nomadic way of life. Nature was not an object of conquest but of worship; their faith arose from gratitude and reverence for nature, their ancestors, and Heaven. At the center of this belief system was the Tengri faith, or Heaven, with the shaman serving as a link between Heaven and humanity. The shaman's hat, the Orgoi, and the Manjilack, a decorative element on his clothing, exemplify his majesty and authority. The Ongo, a shamanic drum hung on the back wall during rituals, was believed to be inhabited by the gods. The drumsticks of the shaman's drum, called the Khengereg, were considered tools that connected the shaman with Heaven. The Toli, mirrors used by shamans, were employed to ward off evil spirits and for fortune telling.

stories.title: Songs of the Grasslands
stories.script: Songs of the Grasslands displays artifacts used in Mongolian music that resonate across the grasslands. From the top left, you can see traditional stringed instruments such as the Bishguur, Tovshuur, and Khuuchir. The Khuuchir resembles the Korean Haegeum, but its bow is made from horsetail hair, and its body is covered with snakeskin, producing a unique tone. The Morin Khuur, positioned at the center, is a traditional Mongolian instrument and a UNESCO World Heritage. It features two strings attached to a carved wooden horse's head, enabling it to produce a variety of melodies. Next to it, the Yiheuhel resembles the Morin Khuur but features carved heads of sheep, camels, and cows, providing insight into Mongolia's animal culture. In addition, the religious instrument Tsan is used not only in Lamaist rituals but also in modern art. The Dun, also employed in Buddhist ceremonies, is believed to dispel evil spirits.

stories.title: Arts in the Grasslands
stories.script: Arts in the Grasslands showcases a diverse array of visual arts and handicrafts. These include masks used in Lamaist Buddhist rituals, such as the Bag or Yamandag Bag; the Bodisadvaa, a carved figure of the first animal to hear the Buddha’s words; and the Burkhani Hulul, the animal on which the gods ride. These are beautifully detailed and ornate. Next to these are paintings, arranged from top to bottom, depicting the Mongolian naadam festival (Danshig naadam); the Khuree tsam, a Lamaist mask dance; and the Mongoliin neg odor, which illustrates scenes from traditional Mongolian daily life. In particular, Mongoliin neg odor” was commissioned by the Bogd Khan, the last Mongol emperor, to depict the daily life of his people at a glance. Completed by the artist Sharav, it is considered a representative painting of Mongolia.Furthermore, the Tsaini uut and Ayagni uut which were made of wool, used to store household items such as teapots, bowls, tea leaves, and camel hair, they along with the Kazakh rug, the Tekelik, showcase handicraft that combine practicality with decorativeness.

stories.title: Mongolian Games
stories.script: Here, you can see traditional Mongolian games. Starting from the innermost area, we see Shagai, made from sheep peach bones. Each player chooses a piece to move, and it was enjoyed by both children and adults. The Shagain khasa and Shagain sum, located nearby, were used as auxiliary tools, often serving as targets or pedestals for the game. Next, you can explore various game tools, including Khorol, Onis, and Shatar, each accompanied by detailed explanations. Shatar, in particular, is Mongolian chess, introduced from Arabia in the 13th and 14th centuries. The final display features the Shataring Kholog, a piece used in the game of Shatar. The diverse and colorful appearances of the pieces provide a vivid glimpse into Mongolia's horses, people, traditional customs, and nomadic lifestyle.

stories.title: Animals of Mongolia
stories.script: You can see small models of the diverse animals that have coexisted with Mongolia's vast lands. Mongolian animals are not merely livestock; they are invaluable companions who have supported and coexisted with the lives of Mongolians. In particular, camels, cattle, goats, horses, and sheep—collectively known as the Five Livestock were an essential part of the nomadic lifestyle. The first animal to be introduced is the camel. In Mongolia, camels have long been an important means of transporting cargo, and their broad soles allow them to walk steadily in the desert. The long hair around their noses, eyes, and ears is a characteristic that has adapted them to life in the desert. Camels are resistant to both cold and hot weather of the desert, can survive long periods without water, and have a highly developed sense of smell that prevents them from getting lost even in the vast desert. These characteristics made them the most reliable means of transportation across the Mongolian desert.  You can see cattle on the right. Cattle were indispensable not only for transportation but also for sustaining life on the grasslands. Their milk was used to produce dairy products and Milk liquor; their dung served as firewood; their meat was used for soup and dumplings; and their leather and fur were crafted into clothing, shoes, and everyday necessities.  Next up are goats. Goats herded sheep, protected them from wolves, and guarded the pastures. Their soft, warm, and lightweight fur made them the ultimate fabric. Their exceptionally fine fur, in particular, was processed into cashmere, making it a globally recognized Mongolian resource. Next is the Mongolian horse. Although small in stature, it was strong and durable, making it an essential companion for long-distance travel. It was also used for horseback riding, horse racing, and hunting. Its milk, which is easily digestible and rich in vitamin C, was fermented and enjoyed as horse milk liquor. Horses were not merely livestock; they were loyal companions and an integral part of life. They were the symbols of good luck and were even featured in ger patterns.  The final livestock is sheep. Sheep, prized for their delicious meat, became a staple food for Mongolians. Even their internal organs were utilized, ensuring that no part went to waste. Their rich, nutritious milk was processed into dairy products and beverages, while their hides were used to cover gers. Now, let's turn our attention to wild animals. Antelopes thrive in the deserts of Mongolia. Antelopes can survive for six months without water, run at speeds exceeding 90 kilometers per hour, and migrate northward by the thousands each year to breed.  Next to them are eagles. Because they hunt rodents with eyesight three times better than that of humans, the Mongolians trained the eagles for about five years, used them for hunting for approximately three years, and then released them back into the wild.  In the alpine forests, owls hunt small birds, mice, and rabbits, while in the grasslands, ground squirrels dig burrows and live in groups.  Next to them, we see wolves and foxes, native to Mongolia's forests and grasslands. Wolves sometimes live in hiding places in grasslands, sometimes in deserts and forests. A month after birth, the mother feeds her pups chewed food, gradually acclimating them to hunting. This behavior demonstrates the wolf's social nature and intelligence. Foxes also live in burrows within grasslands and deserts, where they hunt small animals, playing an important role in maintaining the balance of the ecosystem.

stories.title: Mongolia's Representative Natural Heritage Sites
stories.script: This section showcases Mongolia's representative natural heritage sites. In the upper left corner, you can see the Gobi Desert, the first thing that comes to mind when thinking about Mongolia. The Gobi means rough land where grass does not grow well. Mostly rocky deserts dominate the landscape, with some sandy deserts interspersed. Within these areas, grasslands also exist, creating a vast and diverse environment. Northeast of Ulaanbaatar lies Terelj National Park. The massive granite boulders and sheer cliffs are spectacular, and climbing Turtle Rock offers a panoramic view of the surrounding landscape. In the middle of the second row, Altai Tavan Bogd National Park is part of the Altai Mountains, one of Mongolia's three major mountain ranges. Its highest peak rises above 4,300 meters and is perpetually covered with snow and glaciers. Next to it, Bayanzag is called the Grand Canyon of Mongolia. In the 1920s, numerous dinosaur fossils and dinosaur eggs were discovered here, and Paleolithic artifacts continue to be unearthed to this day.  To the right of the lower row, you can see Khan Khentii National Park, where Genghis Khan was born. It has been designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its outstanding natural beauty as well as its significant historical and cultural heritage. Lake Khuvsgul, visible at the center, is Mongolia's largest lake and is known as the Blue Pearl of Mongolia. It is one of the world's cleanest lakes, with clear waters that support a diverse ecosystem of fish, wildlife, and birds.

stories.title: Mongolia's Representative Cultural Heritage
stories.script: This section presents Mongolian cultural heritage sites through photographs. Starting from the left of the top row, Gandan Monastery is a Lamaist Buddhist temple built in the 17th century. It still stands today, serving as a religious center where lamas reside. Next to it is Erdene Zuu Monastery, Mongolia's first Buddhist temple and another significant historical site. Built within a city founded by Genghis Khan's son, Ögedei, it features 108 stone pagodas symbolizing the 108 afflictions in Buddhism. The Bogd Khan Palace, located on the right side of the top row, was the winter residence of Bogd Khan, Mongolia's last emperor, who was also known as the Living Buddha. It now serves as a museum showcasing artifacts and historical materials from his era. Sukhbaatar Square, visible in the lower left, symbolizes Mongolia's independence. Located in the center of Ulaanbaatar, this site is where independence was declared in 1921 and where the first popular assembly was held in 1989. You can also see various cultural heritage sites that showcase Mongolian history and traditions, such as the Folk Museum, which exhibits Mongolian folklore; the Natural History Museum, renowned for its dinosaur fossils; the Zaisan Memorial, commemorating Mongolia's victory in World War II; and the Choijin Lama Temple, a prime example of Mongolian architecture from the early 20th century. So far, you have explored Mongolian life, culture, and art, as well as the natural landscapes and cultural relics that inspire them. Through your experience with various artifacts, I hope you will remember the stories of the Mongolian grasslands and skies, as well as the Mongolian people who have lived there.

stories.title: Greetings!
stories.script: Hello! Welcome to Beopjusa Temple in Boeun! Located on Songnisan Mountain, Beopjusa Temple was founded by the Spiritual Patriarch Uisin in 553, the 14th year of the reign of King Jinheung of the Silla dynasty. Beopjusa Temple, whose name literally means “a temple where the Dharma of the Buddha resides,” was named thus because Patriarch Uisin, who had traveled to India to seek the Dharma, returned to Korea with the Buddhist scriptures. In 776, the 12th year of the reign of King Hyegong of Silla, when Beopjusa Temple was rebuilt by Master Jinpyo and his disciple Yeongsim, the temple became the center of Maitreya worship. Those who worship the Maitreya Buddha follow the doctrine that Maitreya will appear and save the world from chaos in the future.  During the Goryeo Dynasty, Beopjusa Temple was rebuilt several times under the patronage of the royal family, and its prestige was raised further when King Gongmin relocated the Buddha’s sarira from Tongdosa to Beopjusa. Even during the Joseon dynasty, when Buddhism was oppressed by the Confucian regime, both King Taejo and King Sejo visited the temple to pray and hold a Buddhist service there. During the late Joseon period, a votive shrine, or Seonhuigung, was built there for Crown Prince Sado’s mother, Royal Noble Consort Yeongbin Yi, and the Placenta Chamber of King Sunjo was established at Songnisan Mountain. Thanks to this deep relationship with Joseon’s royal family, Beopjusa remained the country’s central Buddhist temple. Today, Beopjusa is home to some fifty national treasures, treasures , and other cultural heritages that embody its long history and profound Buddhist belief, including the Stone Lotus Basin and the Twin Lion Stone Lantern, which date from the Unified Silla period, and the Palsangjeon Wooden Pagoda, which was built in the Joseon period. In 2018, Beopjusa Temple was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage in recognition of its value as a mountain temple that exists in perfect harmony with nature, and as a repository of Buddhist traditions and the Maitreya belief for over a thousand years. Now, let’s take a look around Beopjusa Temple, which preserves the brilliant culture and history of Korean Buddhism!  Stone Lotus Basin The Stone Lotus Basin made of granite is believed to have been made in the eighth century during the Unified Silla period. It consists of an octagonal base placed on top of a rectangular foundation stone, a three-tiered stone platform carved with an upturned lotus flower design, and a short stone pillar decorated with a cloud design in which a lotus flower appears to be floating above the clouds. Additionally, the main body is shaped like a partially bloomed lotus flower, and is hollowed out to form a large bowl capable of holding a large volume of water. The basin’s outer surface is engraved with small and large lotus petals, each of which features a sophisticated floral medallion motif of lotus flower and ivy. The basin is surrounded by stone railings supported by posts, which are carved in the shape of a child. Although no exact record about the purpose of this basin remains, in Buddhism a lotus pond symbolizes “the pond in the Buddhist Land of Bliss”, so it is presumed that the basin was filled with water in which lotus flowers were left to float as an offering to Buddha. This Stone Lotus Basin, which is regarded as a sophisticated cultural heritage symbolizing the Buddhist belief of the Unified Silla period, has been designated as a National Treasure in recognition of its artistic and historical value.  Flagpole  Next to the Stone Lotus Basin, You  can see an iron flagpole standing between two stone pillars. A flag, called a “dang” in Korean, is hung at temples whenever important Buddhist events or ceremonies are held. In addition, the pole from which a flag is flown is called a “dangan”, while the pair of stone pillars used to support the flagpole is called a “dangan jiju.”  At Beopjusa, the flagpole, which is made of copper and measures about 16 meters in height, was initially erected in 1006 during the reign of King Mokjong of the Goryeo dynasty. However, in 1865, when Heungseon Daewongun, the regent of Joseon, confiscated metal artifacts from temples all around the country and issued the Dangbaekjeon coins in order to raise funds for the reconstruction of Gyeongbokgung Palace, the copper flagpole of Beopjusa was also removed. Then, in 1907, during the reign of King Sunjong, a 22-meter-high iron flagpole was re-erected there. The current flagpole was completed in 1972 after several repair works.

stories.title: Rock-carved Seated Buddha
stories.script: This Rock-carved Seated Buddha of Beopjusa Temple was carved out of a giant, six-meter-high rock using a sophisticated carving technique. It is presumed to have been made in Goryeo in the eleventh century. In particular, the Buddha’s hair is densely engraved to express the curly “nabal” style, which is rarely seen in rock-carved Buddhas. The Buddha is characterized by a round face, a big, long nose, arched eyebrows, and thick lips that form a smile. The Buddha also has broad shoulders and a slim waist, and wears a flowing robe that covers his left shoulder, chest, and legs in beautiful curves. The Buddha’s earlobes, which are so long that they nearly touch his shoulders, represent the sacredness of the Buddha; while the three wrinkles on his neck are a characteristic feature of early Goryeo rock-carved Buddha images. The Buddha holds his right hand in front of his chest, with the palm facing outwards and the middle finger and thumb put together, and his left hand horizontally, with the palm facing upwards. This hand gesture is called the Dharmacakra Mudra, which symbolizes the spread of the Buddha’s teachings to redeem mankind. The Buddha is seated on a lotus pedestal with both feet placed on large lotus petals. This posture is rarely found among rock-carved Buddhas in Korea. As such, the image clearly displays the profound Buddhist belief and unique artistry of the Goryeo dynasty, and accordingly was designated as a Treasure in recognition of its great value in 1963. In addition, on the right of the rock we can see a person leading a loaded horse, and a cow kneeling in front of the horse. This image is believed to be associated with a legend that this person is Uisin, the founder of Beopjusa Temple, bringing the Buddhist scriptures there, while the cow is begging to be taught about Buddhism. Meanwhile, on the left of the rock we can see a rock-carved Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva which is also presumed to have been made during the early Goryeo period. Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva is known for his vow to save all beings in heaven and hell - from the death of Sakyamuni Buddha until the future appearance of Maitreya Buddha. In particular, it is believed that Ksitigarbha saves the souls of the dead and leads them to Nirvana; so many Buddhists dedicate to him prayers  for the dead to be reborn in paradise.

stories.title: Iron Pot
stories.script: The Korean word “cheolhwak” refers to an iron pot, while the word “hwak” means a large pot used for cooking a large amount of food. The giant iron pot at Beopjusa Temple stands 1.2 meters tall and has a diameter of 2.7 meters, and weighs an astounding 20 tons. As there is no record or pattern left on the body, its exact date of production and purpose are unknown. Although there is a legend that it was made during the reign of King Seongdeok of Silla, it is more likely that it was made during the Goryeo or Joseon period. It is said that this iron pot was used to present large-scale offerings to Buddha or for holding ceremonies, and that it was used to cook food for some 3,000 monks during the Japanese Invasions of Korea (1592-1598).  Although it has a simple structure, the fact that it is a huge object cast in iron, which has a much higher melting point than bronze, attests to the high standard of the casting techniques used at that time.
