In recognition of its status as both a symbol of Korea’s Buddhist culture and a cultural heritage made with outstanding techniques, the iron pot of Beopjusa Temple was designated as a Treasure in 2004.

stories.title: Palsangjeon Wooden Pagoda
stories.script: This is the Palsangjeon Wooden Pagoda of Beopjusa Temple. It is the only five-story wooden pagoda in Korea to be designated as a National Treasure. It is known to have been built by Great Master Uisin during the reign of King Jinheung of Silla. During the Japanese invasion of Korea in 1597, however, the pagoda was burned down by the Japanese, but it was restored in 1626 under the supervision of Great Master Samyeong (Dharma name: Yujeong). The current pagoda is well preserved, having undergone various repair works. The pagoda has a very unique structure in which its surface area decreases with each additional story, creating a pleasing sense of balance and stability. The first to fourth stories feature a complex column-top bracket system in which the brackets are only placed above the column, not in between them. So, when looking at them from the inside, these stories are not divided, but rather are connected as one through an open middle, thereby forming a single-story structure. However, the fifth story features a complex multiple-bracket system in which the brackets are fixed both on top of each column and in between them in order to support the roof more effectively, while further emphasizing the grandeur of the structure.  The pagoda is covered with a pyramidal style of roof with a finial, which features a series of wheel-shaped decorations stacked in layers on top. This type of finial is usually erected on top of a stupa or a stone pagoda, and represents hopes that the Buddha’s teachings will spread throughout the world.  In addition, the pagoda boasts very impressive exterior decorations. The fearsome demon face carved on the edge of the eaves is a symbolic decoration that emphasizes the sacredness of the building and prevents evil spirits from entering it. While the statue of Rakshasa supporting the hip rafters is an external guardian deity that protects the Buddhist scriptures, and carries the meaning of “guarding a sacred place”, the dragon carved at the end of the eaves and rafters has been considered a sacred animal that rules over water since ancient times, and has the symbolic meaning of protecting the building from fire.  As for the interior of the pagoda, it is largely divided into three areas: the first area enshrines the relics of eminent monks; the second houses Buddha statues and paintings depicting the eight major phases of Shakyamuni’s life; and the third area is used for prayer meetings. The hanging paintings depicting the eight important phases in the life of Shakyamuni Buddha are arranged into four spaces, two panels per space.

stories.title: Twin Lion Stone Lantern
stories.script: The Twin Lion Stone Lantern of Beopjusa Temple is believed to have been made in 720 during the reign of King Seongdeok of Unified Silla. Known to be Korea’s oldest existing stonework carved in the shape of a lion, it was designated as a National Treasure in 1962 in recognition of its value as a major Buddhist work of art and a magnificent piece of stonework from the Unified Silla period.  Notably, the lantern is supported by two stone lions rather than lantern posts. At that time, lantern posts were mostly octagonal or cylindrical in form, but this one has a unique shape consisting of two lions facing each other, supporting the upper stone with their front legs and snouts. As such, it was very rare and exceptional for its time. In addition, the lions’ manes, muscles, and even facial expressions are depicted very realistically.  In Buddhism, the lion is regarded as a creature that protects and guards the Buddha’s teachings, and symbolizes strength, courage, and wisdom. In particular, the roar of the lion represents the spread of the Buddha’s teachings throughout the world.  The supporting stone, upper stone, and light chamber are all octagonal in structure, and each side is engraved with a lotus design symbolizing enlightenment and purity. In particular, the light chamber is designed with four windows to allow light to radiate outwards in all directions. This octagonal structure symbolizes the “Noble Eightfold Path” consisting of the eight Buddhist practices that lead to enlightenment: namely, (the) right view, right resolve, right speech, right conduct, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right Samadhi, which refers to meditative absorption. Another unique feature of this stone lantern is that it was intricately hewn from a single large stone. In general, stone lanterns are made by assembling several stones, but this one was completed by carving the supporting stone, two lion posts, and upper stone from one large stone.  The lion carvings and the overall structure of the stone lantern form an excellent harmony as well as fulfilling a simple function, clearly exhibiting the high level of artistry and the sculptural skills of the Unified Silla period. This unique style had a great influence on sculptors of later periods, and similar stone lanterns were made in many places throughout the country.

stories.title: Daeungbojeon Hall
stories.script: The word “Daeung” of the hall’s name “Daeungbojeon” refers to “the Buddha”, while “Bojeon” means a “precious Buddhist hall of worship”. Daeungbojeon Hall of Beopjusa Temple was founded by Great Master Byeogam in 1624, the 2nd year of the reign of King Injo of Joseon. The current building was completed after several repair works.  Daeungbojeon Hall is a two-story building that measures seven kan (a unit of measurement referring to the distance between two columns) at the front and four kan at the sides. It exhibits the characteristic features of structures of the mid-Joseon period. The roof is supported by a complex type of bracket system which is fitted on top of each column and in between them, evenly distributing the weight of the building and increasing its stability, while also adding to the splendid decorative features. In particular, its hip-and-gable roof, whose eaves extend in all directions, makes the interior space look wider and higher, giving the viewer a sense of piety and sacredness.   The blue roof tiles were granted by King Injo to Great Master Byeogam and some monk-soldiers for their contribution to the construction of Namhansanseong Fortress.  Daeungbojeon Hall of Beopjusa Temple, a major structure of the mid-Joseon period, is regarded as one of the three biggest Buddhist worship halls in Korea, along with Geungnakjeon Hall of Muryangsa Temple, which dates from the Goryeo period, and Gakhwangjeon Hall of Hwaeomsa Temple, which was built in the late Joseon period. Therefore, in 1987, it was designated as a “Treasure” in recognition of its architectural perfection and profound historical significance.

stories.title: Stone Standing Bodhisattva
stories.script: This Stone Standing Bodhisattva of Beopjusa Temple is a unique statue of a Bodhisattva that was made during the Unified Silla period. In general, such statues depict the Bodhisattva holding a lotus flower or a pagoda in his hands, but this statue depicts the Bodhisattva carrying a large incense burner on his head, suggesting that he is offering incense to the Buddha.  As the statue’s face is severely damaged, it is difficult to determine the appearance of its original features. The statue is characterized by the vivid expression of the two arms holding the incense burner and the realistic expression of the chest. In particular, the exquisite rendering of the hem of the robe attests to the excellent carving techniques of the time.  Although this statue is known as the “Bodhisattva (that is) Gladly Seen by All Living Beings”, its origin remains unknown. In Buddhism teachings, it is said that this Bodhisattva burned his body as an offering to the Buddha. When his body was consumed, he was reborn as the Bodhisattva Medicine King, who has the power to cure illness and alleviate the suffering of living beings. At present, this statue stands next to Wontongbojeon Hall at Beopjusa Temple, but it was originally located to the left of the temple’s Palsangjeon Wooden Pagoda, along with the Stone Lotus Basin and the Stone Lantern of the Four Guardian Kings. While the basin symbolizes “purified water”, and the stone lantern signifies “the lantern that illuminates the teachings of Buddha”, this Stone Standing Bodhisattva represents “the incense used to burn fragrant oil.” As such, these three artifacts seem to represent the making of three offerings within a Buddhist sanctum. This arrangement has led us to conjecture about the faith and significance of Beopjusa Temple during the Unified Silla period.  This Stone Standing Bodhisattva of Beopjusa Temple, which is distinguished by its elaborate carving techniques and the unique appearance of the Bodhisattva offering the incense, was designated as a Treasure in 2004 in recognition of its value as an important cultural heritage that sheds light on the Buddhist belief and the artistic sensibility of the Unified Silla period.

stories.title: Stone Basin
stories.script: The Stone Basin of Beopjusa Temple, which was made during the Unified Silla period, is the largest extant stone basin in Korea. It is 1.3 meters high, 4.45 meters long, and 2.42 meters wide, and is large enough to fill 80 sacks of rice, which is equivalent to about 6,400kg.   This simple stone basin was hewn from one giant stone, and has no decorative features on its outer or inner surfaces, although its upper edges look smoothly trimmed. The basin varies in thickness by about 10 cm different on its long and short sides, which helps to distribute weight and pressure evenly, showing that it was meticulously designed in consideration of balance and stability. This basin appears to have been used to store water. It has a hole at the bottom with a diameter of 11 centimeters, which served to drain rainwater; and it seems highly likely that many people lived in the temple at that time and kept and used the water it contained. In fact, the existence of such a large stone basin indicates that Beopjusa was a large and extensive temple.  Although parts of the basin are damaged, overall it has been well preserved in its original form, and it displays the outstanding stone masonry skills of the Unified Silla period. In recognition of its value, the Stone Basin of Beopjusa Temple was designated as a “Chungcheongbuk-do Tangible Cultural Heritage” in 1980.

stories.title: Neunginjeon Hall
stories.script: Neunginjeon Hall of Beopjusa Temple was rebuilt by Great Master Byeogam in 1624, the second year of the reign of King Injo of Joseon, during the reconstruction of Beopjusa Temple, which had been burned down about three decades earlier during the Japanese Invasions of Korea (1592-1598). It measures three kan (a unit of measurement referring to the distance between two columns) at the front and two kan at the sides. The hall’s name, “Neungin,” refers to one of the Chinese renderings of the name of Sakyamuni Buddha, and means “the one who can teach and benefit all living beings.”  It is known that Neunginjeon Hall was originally used as the Jeokmyeolbogung, which refers to a hall in which the stupa enshrining the Buddha’s sarira was venerated. Given that Neunginjeon Hall is marked as “Sarigak”, meaning “a pavilion enshrining the Buddha’s sarira”, on the painting titled A Panoramic View of Beopjusa Temple produced by Ho Yeong in the late Joseon period, it seems that the Sakyamuni stupa was initially a closed space in which Buddhists worshipped the Buddha’s sarira. Although Jeokmyeolbogung Hall did not house any Buddhist statues in the past, it now enshrines a statue of the Sakyamuni Buddha and the Sixteen Arhats, whose date of production is unclear. The Arhats are disciples of Sakyamuni Buddha who have achieved Nirvana, and who guide sentient beings and protect the Buddhist scriptures.   Just behind Neunginjeon Hall there is a Sakyamuni Stupa consisting of an octagonal foundation stone engraved with an elaborate lotus design, and a body stone with a round roof stone, on top of which there is a bead-shaped finial, which signifies the Buddha’s sarira: These three elements are characteristic features of stupas of the Goryeo dynasty. Generally, stupas are sacred towers that enshrine the sarira of the Buddha or those of high Buddhist priests. According to historical records, in the year 1362, when King Gongmin of Goryeo was taking refuge during the Red Turban Rebellion, he brought a piece of the Buddha’s sarira from Tongdosa Temple in Yangsan and enshrined it here in Beopjusa Temple. And it is this Sakyamuni Stupa that was eventually built to house the sarira. As a sacred stupa that houses Sakyamuni Buddha’s sarira, the Sakyamuni Stupa is a symbol of Buddhists’ deep faith and reverence.

stories.title: Four Guardian Kings Gate
stories.script: To enter Beopjusa Temple, one must pass through three gates: the first is the Iljumun or “One Pillar Gate,” which marks the boundary between the temple and the secular world; the second is the Geumgangmun Gate, where wrathful guardians protect the temple; and the third is the Four Guardian Kings Gate. The current Four Guardian Kings Gate was rebuilt by Great Master Byeogam in 1624, during the second year of the reign of King Injo of Joseon. Measuring five kan (a unit of measurement referring to the distance between two columns) at the front and two kan at the sides, the gate has a gable roof which resembles the shape of the Chinese character “In” (人) when viewed from the side. The central space of the gate is the entrance, which is flanked by the statues of the four guardian kings, two on each side.  As the protectors of the temple, the Four Guardian Kings are the deities of the four cardinal points. As such, they play the role of protecting the Buddhist laws and repulsing evil spirits. Dhrtarastra, the King of the East, is depicted holding a Korean lute (bipa); and he is said to praise and propagate the teachings of the Buddha. Meanwhile, Virudhakais , the King of the South, is depicted holding a long sword, with which he is said to cut down mental afflictions and defeat evil. As for Virupaksa, the King of the West, he is depicted holding both a dragon and a wish-fulfilling jewel that symbolizes the fulfillment of wishes and the Buddhist faith. Finally, Vaisravana, the King of the North, is depicted holding a pagoda and a spear, and he is said to protect and spread widely all the Buddha’s teachings.  Unusually, the red-spiked gate at the Four Guardian Kings Gate of Beopjusa Temple is not a common feature of Buddhist temples, and is more often seen in Confucian buildings. However, as a votive shrine, or Seonhuigung, was built here for Crown Prince Sado’s mother, Royal Noble Consort Yeongbin Yi, it seems likely that a red-spike gate was built here due to the prevailing influence of Confucianism, the state religion of Joseon.  Both the Four Guardian Kings Gate and the Clay Statues of the Four Heavenly Kings of Beopjusa Temple are the largest of their kind in Korea. They were designated as Treasures in recognition of their religious significance and architectural value.

stories.title: Great Gilt-bronze Maitreya Buddha
stories.script: This enormous Gilt-bronze Maitreya Buddha of Beopjusa Temple, which measures 33 meters in height, is the largest Maitreya statue in the East.  The history of this statue began in 776, during the twelfth year of the reign of King Hyegong of the Silla dynasty, when a 5-meter-tall Buddha statue was created under the leadership of Master Jinpyo, and has continued for about 1,000 years. However, in 1865, when Heungseon Daewongun, the regent of Joseon, confiscated the metal artifacts from all the temples in the country and issued the Dangbaekjeon coins in order to raise funds for the reconstruction of Gyeongbokgung Palace, this Buddha statue was also removed. In 1939, during the Japanese occupation of Korea, Kim Bok-jin, Korea’s leading sculptor, began producing a great Maitreya Buddha statue, using cement, based on the Principal Buddha of Seokguram Grotto. He aimed to match the head of the Buddha with the overall proportions of the statue, but he was unable to complete the work during his lifetime. Afterwards, several attempts were made to create a great Maitreya Buddha statue using cement, but the process was interrupted repeatedly, and it was not completed until 1964. From 1987 to 1990, an attempt to remake the Maitreya Buddha statue using bronze was carried out, and during this period about 116 tons of bronze were used. However, as the bronze corroded over time, in 2000 the builders began to use gilding to coat the surface of the statue. The current gilt-bronze Maitreya Buddha was completed at this time, taking about seventeen months and requiring some eighty kilograms of pure gold.

stories.title: Stone Lantern with Reliefs of the Four Guardian Kings
stories.audioTitle: Stone Lantern with Reliefs of the Four Guardian Kings
stories.script: This Stone Lantern with Reliefs of the Four Guardian Kings has been dated to the mid-eighth century.  The stone lantern is octagonal in shape overall, and has a three-tiered pedestal. Each face is engraved with an “ansang”, in other words an arched pattern enclosing the design of an elephant’s eye or a water droplet, which symbolizes protection and stability, and is often seen in Buddhist art.  The lantern’s light chamber has four rectangular open windows and features images of the Four Guardian Kings carved in relief on all four sides, while its supporting stone is intricately carved with a lotus pattern symbolizing enlightenment and purity. As the Four Guardian Kings are deities who watch over the four cardinal points and protect the Buddha and his teachings, this stone lantern clearly plays a symbolic role in protecting Beopjusa Temple as well as the Buddha’s teachings. The roof stone at the top of the lantern has eight corners that are slightly raised, enlivening the structure. As we have seen, this Stone Lantern with Reliefs of the Four Guardian Kings of Beopjusa Temple is a valuable cultural heritage that represents the typical style of stone lanterns of the Unified Silla period. It was designated as a Treasure in 1963 in recognition of its cultural and historic value.

stories.title: Clay Seated Vairocana Buddha Triad
stories.script: Located in Daeungbojeon Hall of Beopjusa Temple, this Clay Seated Vairocana Buddha Triad expresses a fundamental Buddhist doctrine called the Trikaya, which refers to “the distinct bodies or aspects of the Buddha.” The triad consists of the Vairocana Buddha, flanked by the Rocana Buddha on his left and the Sakyamuni Buddha on his right.  The Vairocana Buddha symbolizes the essence of the universe and the eternal truth, and is also known as the Dharmakaya (law-body), who represents the truth that is the basis of all the different Buddhas. The Vairocana Buddha forms the “Bodhyangi mudrā” with his right hand clasping his left hand, which signifies that the Buddha and all sentient beings are essentially one. The Rocana Buddha represents the Buddha’s asceticism and virtue. The Enjoyment-body of the Buddha manifests his great compassion and wisdom. The Rocana Buddha is shown forming the “Vitarka mudrā” with his left hand held in front of his chest, and his right hand placed on his knee, which represents the Buddha teaching living beings. The Sakyamuni Buddha represents the human-like body that the Buddha manifested on Earth to save mankind. He forms the “Bhumisparsa mudrā” in which he places his left hand on the stomach, while his right hand rests on top of the knee, with the fingers spread downwards in a gesture representing the expulsion of evil just before the Sakyamuni attained enlightenment.  This Clay Seated Vairocana Buddha Triad of Beopjusa Temple was made in 1626, when the temple was rebuilt after the Japanese invasions of Korea (1592-1598) and the Qing invasion of Korea (1636-1637) . It was created using a method of molding and sculpting clay in the desired shape, and then adding colors to complete it. This imposing 5.5-meter-high Buddha Triad is known to be the largest clay statue of its kind in Korea, and is regarded as a representative work of Buddhist art from the late Joseon period . In 2003, it was designated as a Treasure in recognition of its historical significance and artistic value.

stories.title: Wontongbojeon Hall
stories.script: Wontongbojeon Hall is a place of worship that enshrines a statue of Avalokitesvara, the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion. Its name, Wontongbojeon, means Hall of the Permeation of All Things, which signifies Avalokitesvara's compassion and his ability to provide salvation from suffering for all living beings, wherever they may be.  The temple was burned down during the Japanese invasions of Korea (1592-1598), and was rebuilt in 1624, during the second year of the reign of King Injo, and it has since undergone several repairs. It is a typical wooden structure with a tiled roof, and measures three kan (a unit of measurement referring to the distance between two columns) at the front and three kan at the sides. The hall is covered with a pyramidal roof with four symmetrical sides, enhancing the formal, elegant beauty of the structure.  The roof of the hall features a bracket system that combines the column-top complex bracket style, in which brackets are used only above the columns, and not in between them, which lends an impression of simplicity and stable impression  to the ceiling’s structure, and the multiple complex bracket style, in which brackets are fixed both on top of each column and in between them, creating a splendid ceiling with many decorative elements. This combination of two styles of bracket enhances the stable structure and refined beauty of Wontongbojeon Hall. Situated inside the hall is a Wooden Seated Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva which stands 2.35 meters tall. As the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, Avalokitesvara is clearly a symbol of compassion, a Buddhist savior who listens to all mankind’s afflictions and saves humanity. This statue looks upon all living beings with a compassionate expression, and wears a crown on its head, symbolizing divinity. In addition, the statue is placed on an octagonal wooden pedestal in the shape of a lotus flower, adding to its grandeur.  Standing next to the Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva are the Dragon King and the Sudhana . While the Dragon King, the ruler of water and sea, symbolizes the compassion and protective power of Avalokitesvara, Sudhana, a practitioner of Buddhist doctrines, seeks enlightenment and wisdom through the teachings of the Bodhisattva. In general, only the statue of Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva is enshrined in a temple’s Gwaneumjeon Hall, but as Wontongbojeon Hall is a higher level of worship hall, it houses these two statues together.

stories.title: Goteo·Sebit Special Tourist Zone
stories.script: Welcome to the Goteo·Sebit Special Tourist Zone, the only tourist district that embraces the Han River.  If you want to enjoy shopping, art, leisure, and night views all at once in the heart of Seoul, the Goteo·Sebit Special Tourist Zone is your best choice. The vibrant energy of the Express Bus Terminal area naturally flows into the relaxed atmosphere of Banpo Hangang Park, allowing you to create a fulfilling day even with a short itinerary.  First, head to Goto Mall's underground shopping center. This is where you can feel the pulse of K-fashion up close, making it a great place to start your journey regardless of the weather. After browsing through stylish accessories, fashion items, and lifestyle goods to gently set the rhythm for your trip, slow down for a moment at Picasso Mural Street, Seoul's 24-hour mural street that connects to Goto Mall's G2 exit.  Picasso Mural Street is an artistic corridor connecting Goto Mall's underground shopping center with Banpo Hangang Park, where the pathway itself feels like a gallery. Why not capture a photo on this street, which beautifully bridges the transition from shopping excitement to the tranquility of the Han River, then sit in the lounge for a moment to catch your breath and prepare for the next scenery?  We especially recommend visiting during May and October, when K-fashion and beauty coaching events are held every Sunday on Picasso Mural Street in connection with the Jamsugyo Bridge Festival.  The journey is completed at Banpo Hangang Park. Centered around the Moonlight Rainbow Fountain, the waterfront scenery comes alive with lights and ripples, and Seoul's night approaches in the most Seoul-like way. After fully enjoying the harmonious blend of the fountain, night view, and river breeze, satisfy your hunger with Hangang ramyeon. Let the warm soup gently wash away the day's fatigue with each sip. It will make for a trip that stays even more vividly in your memory.  Oh, and here's a tip to make your experience at Banpo Hangang Park even more special. Take the Golden Blue Marina yacht or Han River Tubester to feel the river breeze brushing against your face and the sparkling waves. Even familiar scenery will feel refreshingly new when viewed from close to the water's surface.  A place where the excitement of shopping, street art, and Han River night views all come together in one course. Experience today's Seoul in its most brilliant way at the Goteo·Sebit Special Tourist Zone.

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 29
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 29 marks the beginning of the Gangwon-do section, connecting Wondeok-eup and Geundeok-myeon in Samcheok. The route passes through villages, streams, coastlines, and forests, tracing what was once the main road linking Gyeongsang-do and Gangwon-do, a passage that long connected the lives of people in both regions.  The starting point, Hosanhang Port, is a small but charming harbor. Today, large power-generation industrial complexes stand on either side, but the area was once known for its beautiful stretches of black pebble beaches and rocky outcrops. It offers a glimpse into the changing face of Korea's east coast, where traditional fishing villages and modern industrial facilities now exist side by side.  The trail follows the Hosancheon Stream along a relatively gentle path, passing villages, farmland, and the newer communities that have grown alongside the industrial complex. This region carries a story tied to Hwang Hui, the renowned prime minister of the Joseon Dynasty. During the reign of King Sejong the Great, a severe famine struck the Gwandong region, and the people here were able to escape disaster thanks to the relief measures led by Hwang Hui, who was serving as the provincial governor at the time. In gratitude, the residents built the Sogongdae Stand to honor his achievements. The name ""Sogong"" refers to a celebrated prime minister of China's Zhou Dynasty, and giving Hwang Hui this title was the highest form of praise. When the original pavilion eventually fell into ruin, the Sogongdaebi Monument was erected in its place to preserve his memory.  Just past the Sogongdaebi Monument signpost, a short climb over a small hill opens up views of the Nogokhang Port and Bihwahang Port area. This stretch of coast retains the classic character of an East Coast fishing village and is famous for its wild rock laver. Growing directly on the rocks, this laver thrives in rough waters, which is said to give it an exceptional aroma and texture.  Next comes Imwon Port, the largest fishing port in Samcheok. Interestingly, the same snow crabs prized in Yeongdeok are also caught here in great numbers. On the hill across the harbor, beyond the observation deck, lies Lady Suro Heonhwa Park. The park's centerpiece is a statue of Lady Suro standing 10.6 meters tall, 15 meters wide, 13 meters deep, and weighing 500 tons, said to be the largest natural stone sculpture in Asia. Unfortunately, the Haeparang Trail does not pass through the park itself.  After Imwon Port, the trail turns inland toward the mountains. Once you pass Imwon Station, the coastal scenery quickly gives way to mountain village landscapes. In a small village just across from Imwon Station stands a pine tree known as the ""Millennium Pine."" Though its exact age is uncertain, it is believed to be well over 500 years old. Every year on Chilseok, the seventh day of the seventh lunar month, villagers hold a ritual beneath its branches, a tradition said to have been carried on for a thousand years.  From here the trail moves into the Geombongsan Mountain area. Near the entrance to Geombongsan Mountain Recreational Forest, the path turns toward Achilmokjae Pass, climbing gently along a valley and over a low ridge. In earlier times, this pass was considered dangerous. The name ""Achilmokjae"" comes from the word ""ajjil-ajjil,"" meaning a feeling of nervousness or unease, reflecting travelers' fear of running into bandits on the mountain. According to a village elder, until as recently as the 1970s, cattle merchants used this very road to drive dozens of cattle at a time between Uljin and Bukpyeong. Beyond the pass, the trail descends back toward the coast and arrives at Yonghwa Village. The area around Yonghwa Beach and Yonghwa Rail Bike Station is now developed as a hub for marine activities and tourism.  Haeparang Trail Course 29 weaves together fishing villages, streams, and forested mountains in succession, offering walkers a chance to experience the local way of life, natural terrain, and historical heritage all in one route. Please note that some sections run close to vehicle roads, so be especially mindful of traffic while walking."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 30
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 30 runs from the Yonghwa Rail Bike Station to Gungchon-ri, tracing on foot the route of Samcheok's celebrated Ocean Rail Bike.  The starting point, Yonghwa Beach, flows seamlessly into Janghohang Port, an area prized for its stunning coastal scenery and wide range of marine activities. Jangho Fishing Village has grown into one of the region's most popular ocean experience sites, taking full advantage of these natural conditions. Visitors especially love riding clear-bottomed canoes that reveal the seabed below and snorkeling above calm, transparent waters where the underwater landscape is on full display. A marine cable car also operates here, offering sweeping aerial views of the coastline. Thanks to this combination of scenery and experiences, Janghohang Port has earned the nickname ""Naples of Korea.“  The first stretch of the trail runs alongside the Samcheok Ocean Railbike, which parallels Course 30 from Yonghwa to Gungchon and keeps you remarkably close to the sea. Among the rail bike routes along Korea's east coast, this one is on the longer side, and it stands out for its tunnels, coastal cliffs, and tracks that seem to skim right over the water.  At the end of Yonghwa Beach, the path climbs up to Malgupjae. In the old days, this was the only road wide enough for travel on horseback. Wealthy people who could afford horses would ride along this route, but at this particular pass, they were required to dismount and walk over on foot. The reason was a village shrine, or Seonghwangdang, that stood at the top of the hill. The shrine was believed to hold such powerful spiritual force that any rider foolish enough to cross without dismounting would find his horse's hooves bent out of shape. That belief gave the pass its name, Malgupjae, meaning ""Horse Hoof Pass."" Whatever you make of the legend, the view of Yongho and Jangho beaches from the observation deck here is simply breathtaking.  At the far end of the pass stands Hwang Young-jo Memorial Park, perched on a hill overlooking Chogok Port, the hometown of the famed marathoner. Known as the ""Hero of Montjuïc,"" Hwang Young-jo is honored here with a photograph of him mid-stride displayed at the entrance to the tunnel, along with a monument capturing the moment of his Olympic victory. Inscribed at the base of the monument is a line from a poem by Do Jong-hwan: ""He ran like the waves.“  Descending from the pass brings you down to Chogok Port, the gateway to the Chogok Yonggul Chotdaebawi Rock Trail. Here, a striking array of rock formations awaits, including Chotdaebawi Rock, which resembles a candlestick, Geobukbawi Rock, shaped like a turtle, and Yonggul, a sea cave wrapped in dragon legend.  From Munam Beach onward, the trail rejoins the rail bike tracks and stays beside them for the rest of the way. A footpath winds alongside the rails through a grove of pines, making for an especially pleasant walk. Unlike other stretches, this section even features a rest stop at the rail bike's midway point, designed like a small seaside park where you can pause for coffee and a snack. Beyond the pine grove, the trail follows Wonpyeong Beach until it reaches Gungchon Port. This is the place where King Gongyang, the last king of the Goryeo Dynasty, is said to have settled after handing over the throne to Yi Seong-gye. The name ""Gungchon"" itself means ""the village where a king once lived,"" and indeed, just above the port lies the Royal Tomb of King Gongyang.  Course 30 ends in front of the rail bike station that overlooks the harbor. All in all, Haeparang Trail Course 30 lets you take in the full beauty of the east coast as you walk alongside the rails."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 31
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 31 stretches from Gungchon to Maengbang Beach. The path begins with the final chapter of a fallen dynasty and unfolds into stories of local life, of choices made by a community, and of scenery that opens out toward the sea.  Just across from the start of the course lies the Royal Tomb of King Gongyang. Within the burial grounds stand four mounds, traditionally said to be the graves of King Gongyang and his two sons. The identity of the fourth mound remains a matter of folklore, with some saying it belongs to a lady-in-waiting and others insisting it is the grave of the king's loyal horse. Yi Seong-gye, the founder of the Joseon Dynasty, deposed King Gongyang during his rise to the throne and ultimately ended his life. Yet it is said that Yi Seong-gye later ordered memorial rites to be held at Samhwasa Temple by the East Sea, to pray for the late king's repose. That ritual, known as the Suryukjae, is still performed every October to this day. This trail begins right at that crossing point, where the close of one dynasty meets the dawn of another.  The path moves on through villages and open fields toward the Bunam-ri area, a typical rural community where farmland and homes sit side by side, showing how everyday life here has long bridged the coast and the interior. The Bunam-ri and Maeupcheon Stream area also holds significance in more recent local history. Plans were once put forward to build a nuclear power plant in the Samcheok area, but a determined campaign by local residents led to the project being withdrawn. A monument stands here to commemorate that effort, a quiet reminder of a community that chose the course of its own future.  The trail then follows the Maeupcheon Stream. Walking beside the water, you can sense the rhythms of everyday life in this region and the slow passage of time. The path eventually turns back toward the sea and arrives at Maengbang Beach. Rising just ahead is Deokbongsan Mountain, with Deoksan Beach spreading out below. According to legend, three brother mountains once drifted south from Yangyang. The eldest came to rest here as Deokbongsan, the second became Haemangsan Mountain in Wondeok-eup, Samcheok, and the youngest settled in Uljin as Biraebong Peak.  Deokbongsan is significant enough to appear on the Daedongyeojido, the famed 19th-century map of Korea, where it is recorded as ""Deoksan."" It was originally an island standing apart from the shore, but as sand gradually accumulated, it became a tombolo, an island linked to the mainland by a natural sand bridge. Locals once called it ""Deomeongsan,"" after a ""muldeomeong,"" a gourd dipper half-sunken in water, which the mountain's silhouette was said to resemble. Over time, the name shifted into its Sino-Korean form, becoming ""Deokbongsan."" At the summit, you can still find the remains of a pavilion known as Hoeseondae and an old well. The site was once used for rituals praying for rain during droughts, and legend has it that a jar filled with wild ginseng water lies buried somewhere on the mountain.  Today, a coastal walking trail winds around Deokbongsan, offering sweeping views of the East Sea in every direction. It is the most striking finale this course could offer. "

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 32
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 32, running from Maengbang to Chuam Beach, is a journey through history that traces the footsteps of Isabu, the legendary general of the Silla Kingdom.  The course begins at Maengbang Beach, one of the most iconic stretches of sand on Korea's east coast, distinguished by its wide, gently sloping shoreline. Rather than crashing in heavy breakers, the waves here roll in long and easy and slip quietly back out to sea. Just behind the beach lies a broad open plain that, in spring, bursts into a sea of bright yellow canola flowers. Following the line where ocean meets field, the trail climbs over Hanjae Pass.   Today, Hanjae is a quiet country pass, but in centuries past, it was the only way for travelers from the south to reach Samcheok or Gangneung. Isabu himself crossed this very pass on his way from Gyeongju to take up his post in Samcheok, and King Gongyang, the last monarch of Goryeo, almost certainly traveled the same path on his journey into exile at Gungchon.  Beyond the pass, the trail follows the Osipcheon Stream. Its name, meaning ""Fifty Streams,"" comes from the stream's many bends, said to require some fifty crossings to travel from its mouth to its source. For the people of Samcheok, these waters have long been the source of daily life. The International Cave Expo was once held along its banks, and on a cliff above the stream stands Jukseoru Pavilion, one of the celebrated Eight Scenic Wonders of the Gwandong region.  Jukseoru is perched on what is widely considered the most beautiful clifftop along the Osipcheon Stream. The name comes from its original location, just west of a temple called Jukjangsa. Built directly atop the natural rock face, with the cliff itself serving as its foundation, the pavilion is regarded as one of the finest examples of Joseon Dynasty architecture. Rather than leveling the ground, the builders adjusted the length of each pillar to match the uneven contours of the rock beneath, a traditional technique known as “graengi”, which allows the structure to settle into its surroundings as though it had grown there naturally. Inside, the rafters are crowded with wooden tablets bearing poems and calligraphy by some of the great literary figures of their day, among them a poem composed by King Jeongjo himself, alongside works by the scholars Yi Yul-gok and Yi Seung-hyu.  This site was once home to the Samcheok Dohobu, the local government office of the old administrative district. Jinjugwan, the guesthouse that once received visiting officials, has been restored, and excavation and reconstruction of the rest of the complex are still underway.  Continuing downstream along the Osipcheon, just before Samcheokhang Port, you'll find the Cheokjudonghaebi Monument standing atop Yukhyangsan Hill. In earlier times, the seas off this coast were so violent that waves swept inland into the villages, and floods caused devastating damage to local residents. Moved by their suffering, the scholar Heo Mok composed an inscription said to hold mystical power and carved it onto stone in his own distinctive calligraphic style. According to local lore, once the monument was raised, the seas grew calm and the floods never returned. Believed to ward off misfortune through the strength of its words, the stele also came to be known as Toejobi, ""the Stele That Turns Back the Tides.“  Right next door is the Isabu Dokdo Memorial Center, a modern reinterpretation of General Isabu's conquest of Usan-guk and what it meant for early Korean awareness of the East Sea. Isabu was the figure who brought Usan-guk under Silla rule in the 6th century, during the reign of King Jijeung. The exhibition relies less on text and explanation than on immersive video and media art. Large-scale projections and interactive displays let visitors feel as though they are crossing the sea themselves and stepping straight into the historical moment. The exhibition space is also designed so that the interior flows out toward the ocean, letting the view of the sea become part of the exhibits themselves.  Past Samcheokhang Port, the path climbs up to Naritgol Gamseong Village. This neighborhood was once home to dock workers and their families, and the steep alleys, stairways, and sea-facing houses still carry traces of the hard but honest lives once lived here. In autumn, the hilltop blushes pink with fields of pink muhly grass, drawing visitors from far and wide.  Continuing past Hujin Port and Samcheok Beach, the trail keeps following Isabu's path. Beyond Sol Beach Resort, you'll come to Haega Song Site and Imhaejeong Pavilion, where the legend of Lady Suro, wife of Lord Sunjeong, has been passed down from the reign of King Seongdeok of Silla. Lady Suro, renowned for her unrivaled beauty, was traveling with her husband, who had been appointed governor of Gangneung, when they stopped at Imhaejeong Pavilion. Suddenly, a dragon rose from the sea and carried her down into the depths. The villagers gathered and sang a song to call her back, and she was returned safely to shore. That song, ""Haega,"" survives today as one of the rare lyrical pieces from the Silla Kingdom.  At the end of the trail lies Isabu Lion Park, a tribute to General Isabu's conquest of Usan-guk. According to the Samguk Sagi, the Chronicles of the Three Kingdoms, Isabu loaded wooden lions onto his ships and sailed across the sea toward Usan-guk. There he threatened the islanders, declaring, ""If you do not surrender, I will set these lions loose upon you."" Terrified by the sight, the islanders gave in without a fight. The episode is read today not as mere legend but as a real chapter in Silla's gradual unification of the East Sea islands. Isabu Lion Park brings this story to life through a modern lens, blending lion sculptures with sweeping ocean viewpoints.  Just beyond the park lies Chuam, with its iconic Chotdaebawi Rock rising sharply from the sea at sunrise. This is the very scene that appears in the music video of Korea's national anthem. With the sun climbing out of the East Sea behind it, the rock creates one of the most dramatic views along the entire coast, a fitting and symbolic finale to the trail."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 33
stories.script: "This trail begins at Chuam and follows the scenery of the East Sea, but woven into its landscape are the writings of Joseon era scholars, the changes of the modern era, and old folktales passed down through generations.  The first sight that catches your eye at Chuam Beach is Neungpadae, the cluster of rock formations spreading out beneath Chotdaebawi Rock. During the reign of King Jeongjo, the celebrated painter Kim Hong-do was sent by royal command to capture the scenic wonders of Geumgangsan Mountain and the East Sea coast, and his depictions of Chuam and Neungpadae are among the works that have survived. The name ""Neungpadae"" is said to have been given by Han Myeong-hoe, a powerful court official of the early Joseon period. When he came to Gangwon to serve as a regional inspector and laid eyes on this place, he is said to have remarked that the rocks looked like ""the graceful steps of a beautiful woman drifting lightly across the water,"" and so he named it Neungpadae, meaning ""Pavilion of Stepping Over the Waves.“  Just in front of Neungpadae stands Haeamjeong Pavilion. The pavilion is said to have been founded by Sim Dongro, regarded as the progenitor of the Samcheok Sim clan. The wooden signboard that hangs there today is believed to bear the calligraphy of Song Si-yeol, a renowned scholar of the late Joseon Dynasty. From here the trail continues toward Hohaejeong Pavilion and Mangyeongdae. This stretch, where cliffs meet the open sea, has long been treasured as a place to take in the splendor of the East Sea. True to its name, which means ""Platform of Ten Thousand Views,"" Mangyeongdae is celebrated for the sweeping panorama of the ocean it offers.  Walking along with Donghae Port in view, you will come upon Bukpyeong Fifth-Day Market. One of the largest five-day markets in Gangwon-do, it has long served as a traditional hub linking the east coast with the inland regions. In earlier days, this was also the site of the largest cattle market in the southern part of Gangwon-do, where buying and selling of cattle was a thriving daily affair.  The city of Donghae was created by merging Bukpyeong in Samcheok with Mukho in Gangneung. Bukpyeong Port and Mukho Port served as the centers of these two communities, and what was once Bukpyeong Port is today's Donghae Port. This harbor was once the departure point for cruise ships bound for Geumgangsan Mountain, a symbolic gateway for inter-Korean exchange.  When you reach Gamchusa Temple, a tale from the Silla Kingdom unfolds. According to legend, after Princess Seonhwa married King Mu of Baekje, she fell ill with a mysterious disease called baekpung-byeong. None of the remedies tried could cure her, until a monk staying at Sajasa Temple on Mount Mireuksan in Iksan, in present-day Jeollabuk-do, advised her to travel to Gamchu on the east coast. The princess made the journey here, and for three years she enshrined a Buddha statue in a natural cave and bathed and prayed each day at Naksan Yongso Pond. In time, her illness was healed. To honor the Buddha's grace in restoring her health, the princess is said to have built Gamchusa Temple. The temple sits tucked between cliffs and the sea, and a natural spring of medicinal water flows from its entrance, drawing a steady stream of visitors to this day.  The trail then follows Hanseom Beach and Hapyeong Beach. This is a relatively quiet stretch of coast, with the path running alongside the seaside railway, revealing a calmer, more secluded side of the East Sea, set apart from the busier towns.  At last, you arrive at Mukho Station. Long a key hub on the east coast railway, this was once the center of an industry built on coal and seafood passing through its tracks. On the hillside across from the station once stood the company housing where railway workers and their families lived. Today, that hillside has been reborn as the Pencil Museum and Book Village.  A place where harbor, railway, and town grew up together, Mukho is perhaps the clearest window into the rise of modern industry along Korea's east coast."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 34
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 34 starts in front of Mukho Station and runs all the way to Okgye Beach in Gangneung. The route follows mostly level coastline, making it a relatively easy stretch to walk.  As soon as you set out, the East Sea Central Market and Mukho Port appear right ahead. This area has long been the heart of daily life for the people of Donghae and a familiar base camp for travelers. Even today, you can see the lively scene of fresh seafood being bought and sold straight from the morning boats. The writer Sim Sang-dae, in his work Do You Know Mukho?, once described it as ""a sea like a shot of soju.“  Unlike other ports along the east coast, Mukho was a distinctively modern industrial harbor, where coal, seafood, and freight all moved through together. Around it grew up railways, warehouses, and tight-knit neighborhoods. There was a time, locals say, when the port was so prosperous that ""even the neighborhood dogs ran around with ten-thousand-won bills in their mouths."" From behind Mukho Port, the trail leads up to Nongoldam Village, a community where dock workers and fishing families built their homes on the steep hillside above the harbor. The lanes and stairways of Nongoldam-gil Street are filled with murals and small handmade touches, each one carrying a deep, nostalgic echo of the hard but heartfelt lives of the seafaring people who lived here.  Continuing up through the village brings you to Mukho Lighthouse. Standing watch over the port since it opened in 1941, the lighthouse holds within it both the history of Mukho Port and the memories of the people who built their lives around it. The view down over the harbor and the town below makes it instantly clear why the city took root in this particular spot. In front of the lighthouse is Dojjaebigol Sky Valley, and below it, the trail descends past Kkamakbawi Rock at Eodal Beach. From here, the path winds through a small alley known for gomchiguk, the local moray eel soup that fishermen have long favored as a morning pick-me-up after a hard night at sea, and arrives at Eodal Port. From this point on, you'll pass through a string of small but charming seaside villages where the atmosphere of a traditional fishing community still lingers.  Beyond Daejin Beach, known as a great spot for beginner surfers thanks to its shallow water and steady, gentle waves, the trail reaches Mangsang Beach, the midway resting point of Course 34. As one of the earliest stretches of the east coast to be developed with both beach facilities and campgrounds, Mangsang played an important role in transforming the region from a quick stopover into a true overnight destination. A camping resort and a traditional hanok village stay area now stand here like local landmarks, though the Haeparang Trail itself runs slightly inland and does not pass directly through these facilities.  After passing beneath the Donghae Rest Area on the Donghae Expressway, the sight of the Halla Cement plant signals that Okgye is just ahead. This is also the point where the administrative boundary shifts from Donghae City to Gangneung City. The final leg of the course leads into the pine forest along Okgye Beach. The dense pines bring this long and varied 34th course to a quiet close, gently helping you catch your breath as the trail comes to an end."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 35
stories.script: "The starting point of Haeparang Trail Course 35 is right in front of the Korean Women's Center. Follow the gentle scent of pine drifting through the air, and a short walk will bring you to Okgye Beach. Beyond the surfers riding the waves, you can already see Geumjin Port in the distance. From here on, the trail hugs the coast itself. This is one of the stretches along the entire Haeparang Trail where you walk closest to the sea.  In a small rest area in front of Geumjin Port stands a stone marker commemorating the Legend of Lady Suro. The story goes like this: ""Long ago in the Silla Kingdom, as a newly appointed governor of Gangneung was traveling to take up his post, his wife, Lady Suro, asked someone to pluck for her an azalea blooming on the edge of a coastal cliff. The terrain was so dangerous that no one dared try, until an old man passing by, leading his ox, climbed up and brought down the flower, presenting it to her with a song.“  This tale gave the road its name, ""Heonhwa-ro,"" meaning ""the road of the offered flower,"" and the spirit of the legend lingers all along this coastal route. Past Geumjin Port, the seaside Heonhwa-ro Road unfolds before you, a road that has earned a place on Korea's list of the 100 Most Beautiful Roads. As you wind your way along the curving coastline, Simgok Port suddenly appears, looking like a scene from a film, its atmosphere entirely different from anything you've just passed. You may find yourself wondering how a harbor could exist tucked into such a hidden cove. In the old days, the village was so cut off from the outside world that, according to local lore, residents didn't even hear about the outbreak of the Korean War until long after it had begun.  To the right of Simgok Port, the Badabuchae-gil Trail continues on toward Jeongdongjin. The Haeparang Trail, however, takes the mountain path to the left and climbs over the ridge toward Jeongdongjin. This was once the everyday route used by Simgok villagers to come and go. The shrine and stone walls at the edge of the village, and the narrow footpath that leads on from there, still bear the quiet marks of generations who walked this way.  When you reach the top of the ridge, a striking view opens up before you, a railway running right alongside the sea. This is Jeongdongjin. As you enter the village, you'll first pass through Hourglass Park, home to a giant hourglass built to mark the new millennium in the year 2000, designed to complete one full turn over the course of a year. A sundial and a clock museum nearby are also well worth a visit. The trail then continues past Jeongdongjin Station, the iconic filming location of the 1995 hit drama Sandglass. On the platform, the pine tree fondly nicknamed the ""Go Hyun-jung Pine,"" after the drama's leading actress, still stands facing the sea, just as it did in the show.  Jeongdongjin Station also holds a Guinness World Record as the train station closest to the sea anywhere in the world. The rails meeting the horizon, and the rhythm of the East Sea waves seen from that very platform, make for the perfect closing scene to this leg of the journey.  A word of caution: Heonhwa-ro, the most beautiful stretch of this course, calls for as much care as it does admiration. Avoid climbing onto the rocks or descending to the shoreline for photographs. On days when the surf is high, even when there are no formal restrictions, stay on the inland side of the road. In winter, many sections of the path can be slippery, and the trail often runs close to vehicle traffic, so caution is needed throughout. That said, you'll find plenty of places along the way to stop for a meal or a rest, in Okgye, Simgok, Geumjin, and Jeongdongjin, which makes this a relatively comfortable walk overall. Enjoy the beautiful scenery, and have a safe walk."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 36
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 36 begins at Jeongdongjin and follows the ridgeline of Gwaebangsan Mountain all the way to Anin Beach. Although it's a mountain route, it offers stunning views of the East Sea unfolding far below your feet. The name ""Jeongdongjin"" means ""the ferry landing due east of Gyeongbokgung Palace."" This name appears even in the travel writings of Heo Mok, a scholar of the Joseon Dynasty, attesting to its long history.  The trail begins with a steep climb that connects to the hiking path up Gwaebangsan Mountain. In days gone by, passing the civil service exam was a cause for celebration not just for one family but for the entire village. When word of someone's success arrived, the news was hung high on the mountain so that the whole region might share in it. Here in Gangneung, the names of those who passed the exam were posted on this very mountain, which is how it came to be called Gwaebangsan, meaning ""the mountain where the notice was hung."" It is also said that many scholars studying for the exam stayed at Nakgasa Temple at the foot of the mountain, climbing up each dawn to gaze out over the East Sea and pray for success.  As you walk along the ridge, you'll come upon a small village shrine. These shrines were dedicated to the local guardian spirits, and from ancient times, the fishing communities here have offered prayers at this spot for safe seas and bountiful catches. To this day, villagers still gather here to perform the rites, keeping that tradition alive. From near the shrine, several notable places come into view below. The first is Haslla Art World. ""Haslla"" is the old name for Gangneung, a beautifully native Korean phrase meaning ""bright land by the sea."" That name was later rendered into Sino-Korean characters as ""Myeongju,"" before eventually becoming ""Gangneung.“  Imhae Natural Recreation Forest and the Unification Security Exhibition Hall also come into view, showing how this area carries both natural beauty and a layered military history. The 1996 Gangneung Submarine Infiltration Incident, in particular, is one of the defining stories of this region. When North Korean operatives came ashore at Anin Beach, they fled inland along this very ridge of Gwaebangsan Mountain, triggering a massive 49-day search operation across the area. For this reason, the trail is also known as the ""Unification and National Security Hiking Trail.“  Midway along the ridge, you'll also come upon an ancient fortress site. This is a coastal defense fortress built during the Goryeo Dynasty, raised by the local people working together to repel raids by the Japanese and the Jurchen. Of the original wall, which once stretched roughly 451 meters, some sections still remain, and you'll walk briefly along the surviving stones. Past the old Goryeo fortress site lies an open paragliding launch point, with views that open out in every direction. It is the finest vantage point along the entire ridge. As the ridge descends, the trail turns back toward the sea and eventually arrives at Anin Beach.  Beginning at the old ferry landing of Jeongdongjin and following the spine of Gwaebangsan Mountain back down to the coast, Course 36 holds within it the hopes of scholars who once dreamed of passing the royal exam, the resolve of villagers who built fortresses to protect their land, and the more recent memories of modern Korean history all woven into a single path."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 37
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 37 runs from Anin Beach to the Gulsansa Temple Site. As the path leaves the sea behind and winds through rivers, fields, and mountains, you'll discover another, quieter face of Gangneung.  The course begins along Anin Port. In the name ""Anin,"" the character ""in"", meaning ""benevolence,"" is traditionally used to refer to the east. Just as Seoul's Dongdaemun gate is formally called ""Heunginjimun,"" meaning ""Gate of Rising Benevolence,"" ""Anin"" carries the meaning of the eastern ferry landing of the old town of Gangneung.  On Bonghwasan Mountain, just behind the harbor, stands a village guardian shrine called Haeryeongdang, the ""Shrine of the Sea Spirit."" Legend has it that long ago, a county magistrate of Gangneung took his court entertainers on an outing to Bonghwasan, where one of the young women fell into the sea while playing on a swing. Her body was never recovered. In the years that followed, fishing dwindled and the catch grew poor, so the villagers, saying that ""even spirits need a partner,"" carved a wooden phallus and offered it in ritual. Mysteriously, the fish returned in abundance. Similar legends are found at fishing villages all along the East Sea, but unlike elsewhere, the people here did not continue to offer wooden phalluses. Instead, they enshrined a male deity alongside her as her bridegroom, and the two are worshipped together to this day.  Rounding the harbor, you'll come within sight of Korea's last coal-fired power plant. Past the plant, you'll arrive at Gunseongang Stream, whose name means ""the stream where immortals gathered to play."" Living up to its name, the stream is home to otters, designated a Natural Monument of Korea. Otters have a curious habit of arranging their catch neatly along the water's edge, which led people of old to say that ""the otter is performing a rite."" If you happen to glimpse one darting through the water as you pass, consider it a special gift from Gunseongang Stream.  Beyond Dongmak Reservoir lies Eodan Village. The story goes that when the Goryeo Dynasty fell, scholars who refused to serve the new regime returned to their hometowns, and those who settled here built an ""Eodan,"" a memorial altar to enshrine the spirit tablet of the Goryeo king, keeping their loyalty alive in quiet defiance. At the entrance to this small village stand a stone-stacked village guardian shrine and two great pine trees, known as the ""Husband and Wife Pines."" They were planted, the story says, to honor the souls of a couple who lost their lives praying at the shrine to ward off a calamity that had befallen the village.  Cross the stream and pass the flagship branch of Terarosa coffee, and when you see two tall stone pillars rising in the middle of the open fields, you've arrived at the Gulsansa Temple Site. Those two pillars are the Flagpole Supports at the Gulsansa Temple Site, the largest of their kind in all of Korea.  Gulsansa Temple was founded in the year 847 by the National Preceptor Beomil. It was one of the Nine Mountain Schools of Korean Seon Buddhism in the Silla Kingdom, and the largest temple in the Yeongdong region of Gangwon-do. The mountain rising behind the temple site is Haksan, the ""Crane Mountain,"" named for a crane-shaped rock found on its slopes. That name is also tied to the birth legend of the monk Beomil.  According to the tale, a young woman drawing water from a well on this site noticed an unusually bright sun floating on the water's surface. She took a single sip, and soon found herself with child. To hide the birth, her family abandoned the baby in a crevice on the mountain, but cranes flew down and watched over him. Moved by what they saw, the villagers retrieved the child and raised him as their own, and that child grew up to become the great National Preceptor Beomil. The legendary well still remains within the Gulsansa Temple Site, alongside the stupa enshrining Beomil's relics.  During the Gangneung Danoje Festival, the spirit of the National Preceptor is invited down from Daegwallyeong Pass to take part in the celebrations, and that National Preceptor is none other than Beomil himself. For this reason, the festival cannot begin until rites are first performed at this very village shrine before the procession sets off for Daegwallyeong.  In front of the Gulsansa Temple Site is the Odokttegi Training Center. Odokttegi is a long, drawn-out farmers' song in which a single phrase can take nearly a full minute to sing. One theory traces its origins to the songs of the Hwarang warriors of Silla, while another suggests the name comes from the technique of breaking and bending the high notes five times in succession. Records show that even King Sejo of Joseon, hearing the song in person, was deeply moved, and the tradition has carried on for centuries since. In each long, lingering note, you can still hear the labor, the joy, and the quiet sorrows of generations who lived close to the farmland."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 38
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 38 carries you through the very heart of Gangneung. Beginning at the Odokttegi Training Center, the trail passes the Danoje Festival Training Center, Myeongju-dong neighborhood, the Gangneung-daedohobu Government Office, and Jungang Market, before reaching Namhangjin.  The first stop along the way is Haksan Village. So deeply rooted is this village in tradition and history that locals have an old saying: ""If you must live somewhere, live in Haksan."" It is the birthplace of National Preceptor Beomil, the principal deity of the Danoje Festival, as well as Cho Soon, the former Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs who laid the foundations of modern Korean economics, along with countless other scholars, statesmen, and entrepreneurs.  Past the Gujeong-myeon Office, the trail brings you to Janghyeon Reservoir and Mosanbong Peak. Though only 105 meters tall, this gentle peak goes by several names. It is called Mosanbong, ""Mother Mountain Peak,"" after its resemblance to a mother carrying a child on her back. It is also called Babbong, ""Rice Bowl Peak,"" because of its shape like an overturned bowl, and Munpilbong, ""Brush Peak,"" because so many gifted minds have come from this area. During the reign of King Jungjong of the Joseon Dynasty, a county magistrate of Gangneung, said to have been jealous of how many talented people the town was producing, ordered the top of the peak shaved down. In 2005, local civic groups restored the summit, and it is said the old spirit of the mountain has returned with it.  Coming down from Mosanbong, the trail leads to the Danoje Festival Training Center and the festival grounds along Namdaecheon Stream. The Gangneung Danoje Festival is one of the world's great cultural treasures, inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The celebration begins on the fifth day of the fourth lunar month with the brewing of sinju, the sacred liquor offered to the gods, and unfolds over the course of about a month, closing in early May with a farewell rite for the deities. Three principal gods are honored at the festival. There is General Kim Yu-sin, the unifier of the Three Kingdoms, enshrined as the mountain spirit of Daegwallyeong; the National Preceptor's Guardian Deity, the spirit of Beomil, founder of Gulsansa Temple; and the Female Guardian Deity, the spirit of a woman from the Jeong clan who is said to have been taken by a tiger. In this gathering of three deities, Confucianism, shamanism, Buddhism, and Daoism all flow together, reflecting the deep, communal soul that has long bound the people of Gangneung.  Cross Namdaecheon Stream and you arrive in Myeongju-dong, the heart of Gangneung's millennium of history. The seat of local government has stood here since the Goryeo Dynasty, and even after the Japanese colonial era, the courthouse, prosecutor's office, city hall, and other major civic buildings remained clustered in this neighborhood. As the years passed and Myeongju-dong slowly fell into decline, young artists and one-of-a-kind cafes began to move in, one by one. Today, it has been reborn as Gangneung's most beloved neighborhood for atmosphere and creative spirit.  Just across the road sit the Gangneung-daedohobu Government Office and Chilsadang Shrine. Of all the structures that have survived, the oldest is the Imyeonggwan Sammun, the gate of the old official guesthouse. As a building, it is the only National Treasure in all of Gangwon-do, and the wooden plaque above it, said to have been written in the hand of King Gongmin of Goryeo, still hangs in its original place. Chilsadang Shrine was the office where magistrates of the Joseon Dynasty oversaw the seven duties of local governance, including farming, household registers, education, and military conscription. Most of the complex was dismantled during the Japanese colonial period, but ongoing restoration is gradually bringing back the appearance of the thousand-year-old government office. Stepping out from the government office, you enter the duty-free shopping street known as the Myeongdong of Gangneung, and at its far end lies Jungang Market.  The road in front of Jungang Market was once a railway line. Today, the trains run underground, and above them stretches Wolhwa Street, a walking promenade created around one of Gangneung's most enduring legends. The story dates back to the Silla Kingdom. During the reign of King Jinpyeong, an official named Muwollang was sent from Gyeongju to take a post in Myeongju, where he met and fell in love with Yeonhwa, the daughter of a powerful local family. But when Muwollang was recalled to the capital by royal order, he gradually let her memory slip away. Faced with an arranged marriage to another man, Yeonhwa entrusted a letter to a carp in the pond where she often visited and sent it out toward the sea. The carp swam all the way to Gyeongju, delivered the letter, and brought Muwollang back to her. The two were married and had a son, who grew up to become the King of Myeongju, the founding ancestor of the Gangneung Kim clan. The street takes its name from this tale, said to be the inspiration for the famous love story Chunhyangjeon, by combining ""wol“, meaning ""moon,"" from Muwollang's name with ""hwa"", meaning ""flower,"" from Yeonhwa's. Alongside Wolhwa Street, an old railway bridge over Namdaecheon Stream has been converted into a pedestrian crossing called Wolhwagyo Bridge. Cross it, and you'll find Wolhwajeong Pavilion, said to mark the very spot of Muwollang and Yeonhwa's legend.  Course 38 ends at Namhangjin. The name ""Namhangjin"" comes from its origin as the ferry landing on the southern route from Songjeong to Hansongsa Temple, ""namhang"" meaning ""the southern way."" In every step, Haeparang Trail Course 38 lets you feel, more deeply than perhaps anywhere else, the layered depth of time that the city of Gangneung has quietly held within it."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 39
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 39 is where Gangneung's most glamorous face, its deepest history, and its quietest natural rhythms all come together in a single stretch of road.  The trail begins at Namhangjin, crossing the Solbaram Bridge to lead you straight into Anmok Port. The story of how this small harbor became a pilgrimage site for coffee lovers across the country is a humble one. Back in the 1980s, a handful of vending machines were installed at the beach entrance for fishermen and merchants starting their workday before dawn. At the height of the trend, more than 300 machines stood lined up along the shore. Each one offered a slightly different blend of beans, strength, and ratio of sugar and cream, and over time, locals developed their own favorites, with regulars and enthusiasts forming around individual machines. On top of that culture, a new generation of masters dedicated to traditional hand-drip coffee began to set up shop here, one by one. Today, Gangneung is celebrated as Korea's ""City of Coffee,"" and Anmok is recognized as the birthplace of Korea's artisan coffee culture.  From Anmok Port, a black pine forest stretches all the way through Songjeong to Gangmun. This is a protective coastal forest that has shielded the town of Gangneung from wind and tides since the Joseon Dynasty.  Gangmun, as its name suggests, means ""the gate of the river,"" the very point where the waters of Gyeongpoho Lake flow out into the sea. At this boundary stands a sotdae, a tall wooden pole topped with a carved bird, known here as “Jinttobaegi.” It is a folk symbol of Gangneung used in prayers for the safety of the village, raised together with community rites each year at Jeongwol-Daeboreum, the first full moon day, and at the Danoje festival in early summer. It stands today as one of the most enduring symbols of Gangneung's folk traditions.  Crossing the Gangmun Sotdae Bridge, Gyeongpoho Lake opens up before you. Long ago, this was an open inlet of the sea, gradually closed off as sand built up along the shore. It is said the lake was once three times its present size. The Legend of Jangja Pond lives on in these waters. As the story goes, ""Long ago a miserly rich man, when a monk came to his door seeking alms, gave him cow dung instead of rice. In that very moment, his home collapsed and sank, becoming this lake, and all the grain piled high in his storehouses turned into clams."" Strangely enough, in the years when the harvest is poor, clams are said to be plentiful here, and in good years, scarce. Sweet and fragrant in flavor, they came to be called ""Jeokgok clams,"" meaning ""clams of stored grain.“  In Chodang Village, just south of the lake, the poet Heo Nanseolheon was born in 1544 1563. At only eight years old she stunned those around her with her verse, and she was married at the age of fifteen, only to die at twenty-seven. Before her death, she asked that all her poems be burned. But her younger brother, Heo Gyun, gathered the verses he remembered and passed them to a Ming Chinese envoy. Her collection was published in China and Japan before her own country, and her name soon spread across East Asia. The painful irony, that a brilliant poetic voice unheard at home for being a woman shines first in distant lands, still moves the heart today.  On a low hill on the north side of Gyeongpoho Lake stands Gyeongpodae Pavilion, considered the finest of the Eight Scenic Spots of the Gwandong region. The four characters inscribed on the plaque hanging inside, “Jeil- Gangsan”, ""the most beautiful land and rivers on earth,"" speak to the standing of this place. Hanging alongside it is the Gyeongpodaebu, a rhapsodic verse composed by the great scholar Yi Yulgok when he climbed Gyeongpodae at just ten years old.  Right next to the pavilion sit the Chamsori Gramophone & Edison Science Museum and the Son Sung-mok Film Museum, side by side. The world's only theatrical film projector of its kind, and the bamboo carbon filament incandescent bulb with which Edison first brought light to the world, are among the many exhibits here, each carrying labels marked ""world's only"" or ""world's first.“  Continuing toward the coast, the trail leads you past the Gangneung Submarine Park Observatory and Sunpo Wetland. The name ""Sunpo"" comes from sunchae, an aquatic plant that once grew wild here. Today, sunchae is designated as an Endangered Wild Species Class 2 by Korea's Ministry of Environment, and this wetland remains one of its rare habitats.  A little further along, through more black pine forest, you reach the “mulhoe village” of Sacheonjin Port. Mulhoe, a chilled raw fish soup made by slicing the day's catch thin and mixing it with red pepper paste, vinegar, and cold water on the spot, began as the simple, hearty meal of working fishermen. Today, that same dish is the signature dish of this harbor.  In all of this, Haeparang Trail Course 39 holds Gangneung's most luminous moments within a single course. With a cup of coffee in hand and the romance of the ""Five Moons"" of Gyeongpo in your heart, take your time, and let yourself walk slowly."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 40
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 40 runs from Sacheonjin all the way to Jumunjin Beach. Along the way, sea, people, and stories flow into one another, making this perhaps the most complete and immersive stretch of Korea's east coast you can experience on foot.  The starting point, Sacheonjin Beach, was once a military installation. The stretch of coast that was for so long closed off behind barbed wire has now opened up as a path anyone can walk. Ironically, having been spared from human traffic for decades, this section has held onto its clean, untouched natural beauty.  Past the beach, the trail continues along Yeongok Beach. Known for the unusually clear water where stream meets sea, the beach is also home to Solhyanggi Campground, set among decades-old black pines, and considered one of the most popular campgrounds in all of Korea.  Beyond Yeongok Beach, the trail goes slightly inland, and here you'll come across “Bohemian Coffee.” This is the home of the master who first introduced specialty coffee culture to Korea. Park I-choo, a Korean-Japanese who returned to Korea, opened the very first ""Bohemian"" in Seoul's Hyehwa-dong in 1988. At a time when instant coffee was the norm, this small shop, where every bean was roasted in-house and every cup carefully hand-poured, became the cradle of Korea's artisan coffee culture. When he moved his base to Gangneung in the 2000s, coffee enthusiasts followed him here, and Gangneung's reputation as a coffee city took root.  Once you reach Yeongjin Beach, cafes appear lining both sides of the road. At the northern end of the beach, a long breakwater stretching out toward the sea is the famous filming location of the K-drama Goblin. It is the very spot where Kim Shin, the goblin himself, first appears before Ji Eun-tak with a bouquet of buckwheat flowers in his hand. As soon as the show aired, fans from across the country flooded in to recreate the scene, red scarves around their necks and buckwheat flowers in hand. Today, still affectionately known as ""Goblin Breakwater,"" it has become one of the must-visit stops on any trip to Gangneung.  Beyond Yeongjin Beach lies Jumunjin Port. It was developed in 1927 as a key stopover on the East Sea shipping route between Busan and Wonsan. Its breakwater alone stretches 920 meters, and the harbor can shelter more than 500 fishing boats at a time. Three markets stand side by side around the port. The oldest, Jumunjin Fish Market, is filled with stalls that also operate as raw fish restaurants, so you can buy your seafood and have it sliced on the spot. Jumunjin Boardwalk Traditional Market is where you can pick out the day's seasonal catch by the fish, with the variety changing throughout the year. And the newest, Jumunjin Fishermen's Seafood Market, is reserved for local fishermen. Only their own catch is sold here, displayed in simple baskets with prices written by hand, a touch that gives the market its warm, local charm.  On the hill above the markets is the Lighthouse Village. The atmosphere recalls Mukho's Nongoldam Village. The lighthouse here, built in 1918, was the first ever erected in Gangwon-do, and to this day its beam still reaches some 37 kilometers out to sea.  Just below the lighthouse stands the Jumunjin Haesindang, a village shrine to the sea god whose rites trace back to the Joseon Dynasty. The Legend of Jin-i is told here. A woman named Jin-i, who once lived along this coast, took her own life rather than yield to the demands of the magistrate of Yeongok, who tried to force her into his service. When poor catches and sickness plagued the village in the years that followed, the prefect of Gangneung had Jin-i enshrined in the village shrine and ordered rites in her memory, and from that time on, the fish are said to have returned. To this day, spring and autumn rites called “Seonangje” are held here, and every three years, in the ninth lunar month, a grand ritual for an abundant catch called “Pungeoje” takes place. The Donghaean Byeolsingut, the elaborate East Coast religious ritual performed on such occasions, is designated as a National Intangible Cultural Heritage of Korea.  Descending from the lighthouse hill, you arrive at Sodol Port, named for its resemblance to the shape of a resting cow. Beside the harbor stands a cluster of strange and striking rock formations that took shape on the seafloor some 150 million years ago. An old story is told here of an elderly couple who, longing for a child, prayed before these rocks for one hundred days. In time they were blessed with a son, and ever since, the place has drawn visitors who come hoping for the same blessing.  Past Sodol Port, the trail finally arrives at Jumunjin Beach. With a shoreline 700 meters long, the beach has shallow, crystal-clear waters where you can see right down to the shells beneath your feet."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 41
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 41 begins at Jumunjin Beach and runs all the way to the edge of Jukdo Beach in Yangyang. Rather than monumental ruins, the impressions here come from the small, quiet expressions of the sea, the beach as a stage for youth, the rock wrapped in legend, the working harbor at the heart of daily life. This is a stretch of coast that shows how the East Sea is remembered, believed in, and lived alongside by the people.  The trail begins at Jumunjin Beach, also known as ""Cheong-Si-Haeng Beach,"" from the Korean phrase meaning ""Youth Begins with a Journey."" With the rise of surfing and a new generation of young travelers, the once-quiet beach has gotten a livelier vibe.
