At the northern end of Jumunjin Beach, where its 700-meter stretch of white sand comes to a close, you'll find Hyangho Beach. Its name, Hyangho, means ""Fragrant Lake,"" after the small lagoon that sits right next to the beach, a stretch of still water created when the sea was sealed off from the shore. At the edge of this beach stands a modest, weathered bus stop. It was here, in 2017, that BTS shot the cover of their second studio album, You Never Walk Alone. The original set, put up briefly and then taken down, has been faithfully recreated and now stands on the same spot. Fans from around the world have made pilgrimages to find the sea and bus stop from the album, and Hyangho Beach has quietly become a small shrine born of K-pop. Just as the album's title suggests, someone, somewhere, will always remember the wind of this sea.  Cross over Hyangho Beach and you arrive at Jigyeong Beach. From here on, you are in Yangyang. The very name, Jigyeong, meaning ""the border of the land,"" makes that clear. At the nearby Hwasangjeong Pavilion, a local legend lives on. The story tells of an old monk who, deeply moved by the Buddhist devotion of a young boy releasing creatures back to the sea, brought his hands together in prayer. In that moment, the boy vanished, and a rock in the likeness of a monk rose up in his place. In summer, the pavilion is surrounded by the deep red blossoms of rugosa roses, making it seem to sit on a bed of flowers.  A little further on, you arrive at Hyuhyuam Hermitage. The name means ""Rest, and Rest Again."" Founded in the late 1990s as a small Buddha hall, the hermitage rose to fame once a great rock along the shore, shaped like a reclining figure of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, was recognized. From a wide ledge of stone called Yeonhwadae, ""the Lotus Platform,"" visitors can spot the Avalokiteshvara Rock, the Turtle Rock, the Toe Rock, and the Fist Rock scattered along the coast. Another remarkable sight unique to this place is the school of yellow chub, a migratory fish, that linger close to the shore here rather than heading out to deeper waters.  Beyond Hyuhyuam, Namae Port comes into view. Together with Simgok Port in Gangneung and Chogok Port in Samcheok, it is counted among the three most beautiful ports in Gangwon-do. A red lighthouse and a white lighthouse stand facing one another across the harbor, with small rocky islets and breakwaters wrapping around the port, a scene so striking that Namae has earned the nickname ""the Venice of Gangwon-do."" Beloved as a sunrise spot, it is also where director Bae Chang-ho filmed the final scene of his 1984 film Whale Hunting. The maritime observation deck at the entrance of the breakwater stands on what was once a small island called “Yangyado” during the Joseon Dynasty, a site that held a beacon. Where signal fires once rose into the sky, a glass-floored deck now lets visitors look straight down into the East Sea beneath their feet.  The final stop on this course is Ingu Port and Jukdo Island. Jukdo, true to its name, was once an island covered in bamboo. Over long centuries, however, sand carried by waves and coastal currents built up until the island became joined to the mainland. A landform like this is called a tombolo, an island connected to the shore by a natural sand bridge. The bamboo of Jukdo was famed for its unusual strength, and records from the Joseon Dynasty show that it was offered as a royal tribute. The trail makes a full loop around the small island. Along the way you'll come upon Buchaebawi Rock, ""Fan Rock,"" spread open like a folding fan, Sinseonbawi Rock, ""Immortal's Rock,"" where a Taoist sage is said to have rested, and Seonnyeotang, ""the Heavenly Maidens' Pool,"" where heavenly maidens are said to have come down to bathe.  In all of this, Course 41 is a stretch where the texture of an old fishing community and the quiet breath of the natural world remain wholly alive, side by side."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 42
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 42 runs from Jukdo Beach to Hajodae Beach. Along the way, it crosses one of the most consequential lines ever drawn into the history of the Korean people.  Just two decades ago, Jukdo Beach was a quiet, unremarkable fishing village. As the surfing boom swept across Korea, surf schools began to set up shop here, and the character of the village began to shift. Today, around half of all surfers in Korea make their way to Yangyang, and roughly 70 percent of the country's surf-related businesses are clustered along this coastline.  There are good geographic reasons that Jukdo Beach became Korea's surfing mecca. Jukdo Island acts as a natural breakwater, blocking the wind and creating shallow, steady waves that break close to shore. Those conditions are said to be ideal for surfing.  Right next to Jukdo Beach lies Dongsan Port. There's a warmth here that you only find in small fishing harbors, where young surfers and fishermen heading out before dawn share the same patch of sea. A fishing village and a surf town living side by side: it's a sight unique to this stretch of coast.  Past Jangyori Beach you arrive at the 38th Parallel Rest Stop. This modest little roadside rest stop sits directly on the 38th parallel itself. The line was drawn in August 1945, just days after the fall of the Japanese Empire. Not a mountain range, not a river, but a single parallel of latitude on a map, severing the Korean Peninsula in two. Stretching 312 kilometers in total, the line ran from the Yellow Sea in the west, through Yeoncheon in Gyeonggi-do, and Hwacheon, Yanggu, and Inje in Gangwon-do, before reaching this very point on the east coast.  That line was broken on the early morning of October 1, 1950. The success of the Incheon Landing had turned the tide of the war, and as North Korean forces began to retreat, the 3rd Battalion of the 23rd Regiment of the 3rd ROK Infantry Division, pursuing them up along the East Sea coast, reached the 38th parallel near Yangyang at five o'clock that morning. With two companies in the lead, they became the first to cross the line in the history of the war. The official orders from the United Nations Command had not yet been issued, and no UN resolution authorizing the crossing had been passed. With wartime operational control already transferred to the U.S. military, this was an action taken on the independent judgment of the Korean Army. To commemorate that day, the South Korean government later designated October 1 as Armed Forces Day in 1956. The origin of the Armed Forces Day that Korea observes each year traces back to this very beach, this very line.  Next to the rest stop is a small 38th Parallel Mini Exhibition Hall, where visitors can find materials on the division of Korea and the Korean War.  Behind the rest stop, Gisamun Port comes into view. The narrow lanes of the harbor are painted in blue murals, and the bright, colorful walls give the village a feel almost like a small Mediterranean town.  Gisamun Beach is often called the birthplace of surfing in Gangwon-do. Before Jukdo Beach rose to fame, it was here at Gisamun that the very first surf school was established, planting the seed that would eventually turn all of Yangyang into Korea's surf capital. Even today, Gisamun holds a special place for intermediate and advanced surfers. In winter, the waves here curl into the cylindrical hollow known as a barrel, an exceptionally rare phenomenon in Korean waters, and surfers from across the country come to Gisamun just for the chance to ride one.  Past Gisamun Port, the trail brings you to Hajodae. This is where Ha Ryun and Jo Jun, two of the founding contributors to the Joseon Dynasty, are said to have lived in seclusion. In the late Goryeo period, as the dynasty fell into decline, the two men are said to have retreated to this place and laid the plans for a new kingdom together. Ha Ryun, who had opposed General Choe Yeong's expedition against the Liaodong region and was exiled to Yangju, later joined Yi Seong-gye in founding the Joseon Dynasty following the famous return of his army from Wihwado Island, and became one of King Taejong, Yi Bang-won's longest-trusted confidants. Jo Jun, who had lived in seclusion for four years at the end of the Goryeo period, was sought out by Yi Seong-gye to take part in establishing the new dynasty. He went on to compile Gyeongje Yukjeon, the first written legal code of Joseon, laying the legal framework of the new kingdom and earning him a reputation as one of the true architects of Joseon.  Just in front of the pavilion, an old pine tree more than 400 years old stands gracefully atop the craggy cliffs. Having weathered every kind of storm, the pine appeared in the sequence of Aegukga, the South Korean national anthem, broadcast at the start and end of each day on national television, and from then on came to be known affectionately as the ""Patriotic Pine.“  In every step of the way, Course 42 carries you alongside both the waves of history and the waves of the sea."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 43
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 43 runs from Hajodae Beach to Susan Port.  The starting point, Hajodae Beach, first opened to the public in 1976. The white sands stretch 1.5 kilometers in length and 100 meters in width. Fresh water flowing in from the Gwangjeongcheon and Sanguncheon streams gently raises the temperature of the seawater, making the water here noticeably warmer than at other beaches along the coast. For that reason, Hajodae has long been a favorite of families with children.  Heading north, you arrive at Surfyy Beach. Did you know that this beach, now packed with parasols, sun loungers, and people carrying surfboards, was a military zone fenced off behind barbed wire only a little over a decade ago?  Off-limits to civilians for more than forty years, the beach had, ironically, preserved a stretch of pristine sand and ocean precisely because no one was allowed to set foot on it. In 2014, a man who had worked as a snowboard instructor, as the head of an advertising agency in Seoul, and as an employee at BC Card came to this place, saying he wanted ""to learn the sea."" In July of 2015, he set up two shipping containers and hung up a sign reading ""Korea's First Surf-Only Beach."" At the time, there wasn't a single sunshade on the entire stretch of sand, the barbed-wire fence still ran the length of the shore, and visitors could only enter when a soldier on duty opened the gate for them. After the Seoul-Yangyang Expressway opened and the first Sunset Festival was held here in 2017, word spread quickly, and Surfyy Beach became a magnet for Koreans in their twenties and thirties.  Past Surfyy Beach lies Dongho Beach. Tucked right beside Yangyang International Airport, it is not large, but it is well known for the fineness of its sand.  Right next to Dongho Beach is Yangyang International Airport. The project began as a campaign promise of former President Roh Tae-woo in 1987 and was pushed forward in earnest under the Kim Young-sam administration. Originally scheduled to open in 2000, the airport's launch was delayed by the fallout from the Asian Financial Crisis and finally opened its doors in April 2002. But just months before its opening, the expansion of the Daegwallyeong section of the Yeongdong Expressway had already dramatically improved access to the east coast. Passenger numbers fell sharply, and when Korean Air withdrew its services in 2008, the airport effectively ceased operating. Even after being designated the official airport of the 2018 PyeongChang Winter Olympics, increases in passenger traffic remained modest, and by May 2023, regular scheduled flights had stopped once again.  Past the airport, the trail continues along the coast and brings you to the final stop of this course, Susan Port.  The waters of Susan Port are so clean that eelgrass grows here naturally. Eelgrass is a marine plant that cannot survive in polluted waters, and the very presence of an eelgrass colony inside the inner harbor itself is proof of how pure these waters remain.  Step further into the harbor and a striking scene unfolds before you, rows of yachts with white sails moored side by side. This is the largest yacht marina on Korea's east coast. National competitions including the President's Cup Yacht Race and the Korea Coast Guard Commissioner's Cup Yacht Race are held here, and the Yangyang County-run yacht academy sees some 300 graduates a year hoist their first sail over the waves of the East Sea. A fishermen's port and a yachtsmen's port sharing the same waters, this is Susan Port today.  In every step, Course 43 brings together a sea that was once closed off and is now opened wide, an airport that still dreams of taking flight, and yachts setting their sails to the wind: the dreams, the setbacks, and the new beginnings that this coast has long held, all unfolding along a single path. "

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 44
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 44 leads from Susan Port through Naksan Beach to Seorak Sunrise Park. It passes the 8,000-year-old traces of Neolithic life and the devotion of a thousand-year-old temple, until at last it touches the mountain shadows of Seoraksan.  Right at the starting point, just in front of Susan Port, rises Susanbong Peak. Only 63 meters above sea level, this is a low hill, but from its summit, the full ridgeline of Seoraksan Mountain spreads out before you. Along the shore at the foot of Susanbong Peak stands a row of strange and striking rock formations. Among them is one shaped like a toad, and according to a village tale, wishes made before this rock are sure to come true.  A short walk along the road from Susan Port brings you to the oldest known settlement on the entire east coast, a prehistoric site dating back to the Neolithic era. The area was originally a lake called “Ssangho”, meaning ""Twin Lakes."" During the work of filling it in to create farmland, large quantities of pottery shards and stone tools were unearthed, revealing a Neolithic site some 8,000 years old.  Archaeologists uncovered stone mounds used for crafting tools, along with raised pattern earthenware, fishhooks, and net sinkers. These finds offer a vivid picture of a people who lived here by fishing the sea and hunting the land. Most remarkably, a clay sculpture in the form of a human face, Toje-Inmyeonsang, and small clay figurines of animals, To-Wu, were recovered, revealing that even these Neolithic people had a religious and spiritual life of their own. A scientific analysis of obsidian tools unearthed at the site traced the raw stone back to Mount Baekdusan in the far north, a discovery that stunned researchers at the time. To this day, the Osan-ri site remains a key to understanding the origins of Korea's Neolithic culture and the connections that linked early cultures across Northeast Asia.  Past the Osan-ri site, the trail crosses Namdaecheon Stream. Rising in the foothills of Mount Odaesan and flowing into the East Sea, it is the longest and cleanest river in the Yeongdong region. More than 70 percent of all salmon returning to Korean waters come home to this very stream. Salmon born in Namdaecheon swim out into the East Sea, range across the North Pacific from Alaska to the Bering Sea for three to five years, and then return to the exact stream of their birth to spawn and end their lives. Every spring, millions of young salmon are released into the river here, and every autumn, the return of the adults is celebrated with eco-experience events. At the Salmon Ecological Park built at the river's mouth, you can witness the salmon's entire life cycle up close.  Crossing Namdaecheon Stream brings you to Naksan Beach. At 1.8 kilometers long, it is one of the most expansive beaches on the east coast. On one side of the beach stands Donghae Sinmyo, the Shrine of the East Sea God. This was the official site where the state once performed rites to the Dragon King of the East Sea, and together with the shrines of the West and South Seas, it was one of the three royal sea shrines maintained by the central government. Dating back to the Goryeo Dynasty, the shrine's stele was broken and its buildings demolished under the Japanese colonial regime's policies of cultural erasure. It was restored in 1993. Every year, when the beach opens for the summer season, the Dragon King Rite is still held here, carrying on the old tradition of prayer for safe seas and an abundant catch.  Overlooking Naksan Beach is Naksansa Temple, a thousand-year-old temple founded in the year 671 by the great monk Uisang during the reign of King Munmu of Silla. Having returned from Tang China where he had studied the Hwaeom doctrine, Uisang heard that the true form of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara had come to dwell in a sea cave along this coast, and so he made his way here. He prayed before the cave for seven days, and the guardian spirits of the heavens and the seas guided him within, where he received a crystal rosary and a wish-fulfilling pearl. After praying for another seven days, he at last beheld the true presence of Avalokiteshvara. The site where this took place is Hongnyeonam Hermitage, and the pavilion built later by his followers on the coastal cliff where Uisang had sat in meditation is Uisangdae Pavilion. According to Samguk Yusa, after Uisang founded Naksansa Temple, the great monk Wonhyo also came seeking to behold Avalokiteshvara. Yet on the way, he met the Bodhisattva's incarnation without recognizing them, and in the end was unable to enter the Avalokiteshvara cave of Hongnyeonam Hermitage.  In April 2005, this thousand-year-old temple was lost in just one hour to a forest fire. The great bronze bell, designated Treasure No. 479, cast during the reign of King Yejong of Joseon in honor of King Sejo, melted in the flames. Today, the molten remains of that bell are displayed at the Uisang Memorial Hall, a silent testament to the devastation of that day. And yet, in the very midst of that vast inferno, Uisangdae Pavilion and Hongnyeonam Hermitage, perched on the seaside cliffs, alone were spared from the fire.  Turning past Naksansa, the trail continues along Seorak Beach and Hujin Port. Past Jeongam Beach lies Mulchi Port, alive every winter with the energy of the sailfin sandfish festival.  The final stop on this course is Seorak Sunrise Park. On the rocks behind the park, a pair of mermaid figures sit side by side on the shore. At first glance, the sculpture brings to mind the Little Mermaid of Copenhagen, but the story behind this one is its own, and it is a sorrowful one. According to local lore, a young couple who had promised to marry were torn apart when the man was lost at sea in a storm. The woman waited for him on these very rocks until her own life slipped away. To console their broken love, the villagers raised the figures here in their memory. It is a mournful story, but a saying has grown up around the spot that those who take a photograph here will see their love come true. So each year, countless couples come to make their own promises. The scenery of the two mermaids sitting side by side on rocks washed endlessly by the waves, gazing out at the East Sea, brings this stretch of the trail to a quiet and unforgettable close."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 45
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 45 begins at Seorak Sunrise Park, passes through the downtown of Sokcho, and ends at Jangsa Fishing Village.  Setting out from the Jamboree Memorial Tower at Seorak Sunrise Park, you arrive almost immediately at Daepo Port. On old maps of this region, the name ""Sokcho"" was sometimes left out entirely, but Daepo Port always made the cut. The name ""Sokcho"" itself dates back to the Joseon Dynasty, but in those days, it was only a small village, while Daepo functioned as the true port of the area. It wasn't until 1937, when the township office moved from Daepo-ri to Sokcho-ri and Sokcho Port began to be developed, that Sokcho took its place as the administrative and maritime center.  Right next to Daepo Port lies Oeongchi, a name said to come from the area's resemblance to an earthenware jar. Though it has long been counted among the Eight Scenic Views of Sokcho, the coast here was closed off to civilians after the 1953 armistice. The barbed-wire coastal fence put up after an armed infiltration incident in 1970 sealed off the area entirely. It wasn't until April 2018, with the opening of the ""Bada Hyanggi-ro,"" meaning ""the Road of Sea Fragrance,"" that this stretch of coast was finally returned to the public after 65 years.  Looping around Oeongchi, the trail flows into Sokcho Beach. Just off the shore lies the small island of Jodo, ""Bird Island,"" named for the seagulls that flock there. It is the only island in all of Sokcho. According to local geological lore, Jodo is in fact a continuation of one of Seoraksan Mountain's ridges that travels beneath the sea and resurfaces here, meaning that Seoraksan and Jodo are, geologically speaking, one and the same. For fishermen returning from the open sea, the sight of Jodo also meant that home was near.  When you reach Cheongchoho Lake, the cityscape shifts. So renowned was its beauty that Lee Jung-hwan, author of the Joseon-era geographical treatise Taengniji, argued that this lake should have been counted among the Eight Scenic Views of the Gwandong region in place of Naksansa Temple. During the Joseon Dynasty, a naval garrison was stationed here, and warships were anchored on these waters, making the lake a key military stronghold. Today, along the lakeshore stand Sokcho Expo Symbol Tower, rising 73.4 meters and built in 1999 to commemorate the Gangwon International Tourism Expo, and a lakeside park.  Crossing Seorak Bridge brings you to Abai Village. This village began as a temporary refuge during the Korean War. Believing they would only need to wait briefly before returning home, refugees built shacks on the sand here in what is now Cheongho-dong, Sokcho. In the end, they were never able to go back, and the village they founded by accident became permanent. On this barren stretch of sand, where even drinking water was hard to come by, they made their living through fishing and odd labor, all the while holding on to the foods of their lost homeland in Hamgyeong-do. Sikhae made from pollack and flounder, abai sundae blood sausage, and Hamheung-style cold noodles topped with raw flounder are the flavors that grew from their hands.  From Abai Village, visitors cross over to the fish market by “gaetbae”, a hand-pulled cable ferry. Passengers themselves take hold of a steel hook and haul the boat across by hand. It may be the shortest ferry route in the world, but for many years that short stretch of water was the only road connecting Abai Village to the rest of Sokcho. After the gaetbae appeared in scenes of the K-drama A Fairy Tale of Autumn and was broadcast across the country, it became a tourist attraction in its own right. Even so, the longing for the homelands left behind still lingers in the murals painted along the village's narrow alleys.  Following the shoreline, you arrive at Dongmyeong Port. True to its name, which means ""the port where the eastern sun rises bright,"" it is famed as a sunrise spot. At the harbor's end stands Yeonggeumjeong Pavilion. The site was once home to a great rock, and the sound of waves crashing against it was said to ring out like the music of a sacred geomungo, the six-stringed Korean zither, which is how the place came to be called Yeonggeumjeong, ""the Pavilion of the Divine Geomungo."" During the Japanese colonial period, however, the rock was broken up to build a breakwater for the new port, leaving behind only the broad, flat stone shelf that remains today.  The path continues past the lighthouse next to Dongmyeong Port. What makes this lighthouse special is the lamp housed inside it. Burning every night since 1957, the apparatus uses a one-meter-diameter lens rotated by the weight of a 230-kilogram counterweight. It is said to be the only one of its kind still in operation in all of Korea. With each full winding, the lens turns for seven hours, and the beam reaches some 35 kilometers out to sea.  Past the lighthouse beach, the trail loops around Yeongnangho Lake before heading on to Jangsa. With a circumference of 8 kilometers, this lagoon owes its name to Yeongnang, a young hwarang warrior of Silla. On his way back from training in Mount Geumgangsan, Yeongnang is said to have been so taken by the beauty of the lake that he forgot the very martial arts competition he was traveling to, and lingered here instead. The Sokcho poet Lee Seong-seon once wrote that ""Sokcho can be Sokcho because it shines with two clear eyes, Cheongcho and Yeongnang."" The finest view at Yeongnangho is Beombawi, ""Tiger Rock,"" named for its shape resembling a tiger crouched and ready to spring. Sinjeung Dongguk Yeoji Seungram, a 16th-century Korean geographical encyclopedia, records that ""this was the place where Yeongnang and his fellow immortals came to wander and admire the view,"" confirming the rock as one of the spots once climbed by the hwarang of Silla.  Completing the loop around Yeongnangho Lake brings you to the end of the course, the Jangsa Fishing Village. Course 45 carries you past the wounds and quiet endurance of the displaced families of Abai Village, and brings you to a close at the edge of the very lake that once enchanted a hwarang of Silla."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 46
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 46 runs from the Jangsa Fishing Village to Sampo Beach.  The starting area around Jangsa Port and Yeongnangho Lake was originally open sea. Over long centuries, sand accumulated along the shore until Yeongnangho was sealed off as a lake, and a village took root on the new sandbar. The place was once called ""Moraegi,"" meaning ""sandy ground,"" and was later written in Sino-Korean as ""Sayaji"", eventually becoming ""Sajin-ri."" In 1973, when the area was incorporated into Sokcho City, it was combined with Jangcheon-ri to form Jangsa-dong. The harbor, originally known as Sajin Port, was renamed Jangsa Port in 2008.  Heading north from Jangsa Port brings you to Bongpo Port. Just beyond its breakwater lies a small cluster of rocks, including one stone that has been gradually rolled and rounded by the waves over time, ground between the surrounding rocks like a millstone. Locals call it “Maetdolbawi,” ""Millstone Rock,"" and on stormy days, they say you can sometimes hear a low grinding sound, as though the millstone is still slowly turning.  Past Cheonjin Port, Cheongganjeong Pavilion comes into view. Long regarded as the finest of the Eight Scenic Views of the Gwandong region, this pavilion has drawn poets and painters in unbroken succession for centuries. The pavilion once held a collection of writings by some of Korea's greatest figures, including calligraphy by the renowned Yang Sa-eon, prose by Jeong Cheol, and a royal poem composed by King Sukjong of Joseon. All of these were lost in 1884 when fire spread to the pavilion during the upheaval of the Gabshin Coup. For more than forty years afterward, the site lay empty, until the pavilion was finally rebuilt in 1928. The wooden plaque reading ""Cheongganjeong"" that now hangs beneath its eaves bears the personal calligraphy of former president Rhee Syngman. The great Joseon-era landscape painter Gyeomjae Jeong Seon also left behind a painting of this pavilion, ""Cheongganjeong-do."" Yet the pavilion in his painting differs in both location and form from the one that stands today. In the old painting, the pavilion is shown high atop a rocky outcrop rising sharply from the sea, suggesting that both the site and the surrounding landscape have shifted with the passage of time.  Above Cheongganjeong lies Ayajin Port. The name “Ayajin” was once written as “Daeyajin.” During the Japanese colonial period, however, when the use of the character “Dae,” ""great,"" was restricted by the colonial government, the name was changed to Ayajin.  A short climb over a hill from Ayajin brings you to Gyoam Port, known throughout Gangwon-do for its abundant catches of herring. Just at the entrance to the village stands Cheonhakjeong Pavilion. If Cheongganjeong's fame comes from its long history, Cheonhakjeong's comes from the sheer beauty of its setting. Built in 1931 through the joint efforts of local notables, the small pavilion stands alone at the tip of a sheer coastal cliff, encircled by pine trees more than a century old, facing out to sea. From the pavilion, you can look south and just make out Cheongganjeong and Baekdo Island in the distance, while to the north, the rugged rock coastline around Neungpadae unfolds before you.  Across from Cheonhakjeong, beyond Munam Port, lies Neungpadae. The characters ""Neungpadae,"" carved into the rock here, are believed to be the personal calligraphy of Yang Sa-eon, also known by his pen name Bongnae, one of the greatest masters of calligraphy in the Joseon Dynasty. The honeycomb-like surface, pocked with countless small hollows, is a geological formation known as tafoni, said to have formed over an astonishing 180 million years. The site was designated as part of the Gangwon Peace National Geopark in 2014. In 2020, when BTS filmed scenes for their photoshoot video ""2021 Winter Package"" here, Neungpadae was introduced to fans around the world.  Munamcheon Stream, flowing alongside Neungpadae, carries within it the long memory of this coast. On the low hills near the stream, Neolithic remains dating from roughly 5,000 to 3,000 BCE have been excavated, including some of the earliest traces of farming ever found along Korea's east coast.  Past Baekdo Port, the trail at last reaches Sampo Beach, the end of this course. Opened in 1977 and designated a National Tourist Site in 1980, the beach is famous for its ""singing sand,"" which gives off a soft, musical sound when stepped on. Just offshore lie the small islets of Heukdo, Baekdo, and Homiseom, scattered across the water, while behind the beach stretches a dense pine forest. "

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 47
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 47 runs from Sampo Beach to Gajin Port. It is a rich tapestry of a route, weaving together strangely beautiful rocks, a serene coastal lake, and a centuries-old traditional village.  Leaving Sampo Beach, you quickly arrive at Bongsudae Beach. Long ago, a smoke-signal beacon, or bongsudae, is said to have stood on the hill behind the beach, and traces of that beacon, along with its name ""Bongsudan,"" remain to this day. This beach was developed to provide new homes for residents who lost everything in the 1997 Goseong forest fires, making it the most recently established beach in all of Gangwon-do.  At the northern end of Bongsudae Beach lies Oho Port, the birthplace of Korea's deep-sea water industry. Goseong County was a pioneer in this field, entering the business of deep-sea water development in the early 2000s, and the waters off Oho Port are the very source from which it is drawn. Pulled up from depths of more than 200 meters, deep-sea water is prized for its purity and rich mineral content. It is now used to produce beverages, cosmetics, and bio-products that are exported to Japan and other countries around the world.  Right beside Oho Port stands Seonangbawi Rock. The name, ""Village Shrine Rock,"" comes from the fact that the shrine of Oho-ri village sits just beside it. The rock is geologically remarkable: its head is made of granite, while its slender waist is composed of rhyolite. The formation has earned several nicknames, ""Buchaebawi,"" or ""Fan Rock,"" for its fan-like silhouette, and ""Snoopy Rock,"" for its resemblance to the famous cartoon dog.  Beyond Seonangbawi, you arrive at Songjiho Beach, where a wide, fine-grained stretch of white sand runs four kilometers along the shore. A new pedestrian bridge now connects the beach to the small island of Jukdo just offshore, adding a striking element to the seascape.  The trail then turns inland and passes Songjiho Lake. With a circumference of 6 kilometers, this lagoon rarely freezes over even in winter thanks to the salt in its waters. Its clear water and even depth allow saltwater fish like sea bream and gizzard shad to coexist alongside freshwater species such as carp and mullet.  The secret to this remarkable mingling of fresh and salt water lies in the very nature of a lagoon. A few times each year, channels open between the lake and the open sea, and migratory fish such as mullet, yellow chub, gizzard shad, and pond smelt swim in to spawn and feed. When the channels close again, these fish remain, sharing the waters together. In winter, the lake transforms once more into a stage for migratory birds, with whooper swans, designated Natural Monument No. 201, alongside mallards and wild geese arriving in great flocks.  Following the path west of Songjiho Lake brings you to Wanggok Village. Nestled in a basin enclosed by five peaks, this village holds within it the quiet weight of more than 600 years of history. The village traces its origins to the late 14th century, when Ham Bu-yeol, a scholar of the Hongmun Academy and one of the famed ""72 Loyalists of Dumun-dong,"" refused to serve the new Joseon Dynasty founded by Yi Seong-gye, and retreated here to live in seclusion. He was later joined by the Choi clan of Gangneung and the Kim clan of Yonggung, and together they formed the close-knit clan community that endures here today. As a designated Traditional Architecture Preservation District, the village does not allow renovations of its houses, and so the northern-style traditional homes, built around the late 1800s to early 1900s, have been preserved entirely in their original form.  Interestingly, there is not a single well in all of Wanggok Village. According to local geomantic belief, the village is shaped like a boat, and digging a well would sink it. For that reason, no resident has ever drilled one, generation after generation. Even more remarkably, the five peaks surrounding the village are said to have shielded it so completely that not a single artillery shell fell within the village throughout the Korean War, a fact that locals regard as nothing short of a miracle.  Leaving Wanggok Village and returning to the coast, you arrive at Gonghyeonjin Port. In front of the harbor stand three rocks rising side by side from the sea, known as Sumutgae Rocks. Old records refer to them as “Samsokdo,” ""Three Bundled Islands,"" for the way they appeared to be lashed together. Over time, the pronunciation drifted through forms like ""Syeomutdwi"" and ""Seumutdae"" before settling as ""Sumutgae."" Rising at three different heights toward the sea, the rocks are one of the most popular sunrise photography spots on the east coast.  The final stop on this course is Gajin Port. Long ago, the village was known as ""Deokpo,"" meaning ""the harbor of bounty,"" named for the abundance of seafood that brought prosperity to its people. When another small ferry landing was later added, the area came to be called Gapojin, and in 1914 it was officially renamed Gajin-ri. Today, Gajin Port is known as one of the finest places in Korea for wild-caught mulhoe, a refreshing cold raw fish soup. Freshly caught flatfish, rockfish, and flounder are sliced paper-thin, mixed with red pepper paste and crisp vegetables, and topped with chilled broth. That single bowl, served cold, is the signature dish of this port.  In all of this, Course 47 carries you past beautiful beaches, a vast and serene lagoon, and a traditional village that has held its ground for centuries."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 48
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 48 begins at Gajin Port and continues northward to Geojin Port. Winding through a string of small, quiet harbors along the northern stretch of Korea's east coast, this is a path where the traces of national division and a deep coastal stillness walk side by side.  Leaving Gajin Port and heading north, you arrive at Dongho-ri. As the name suggests, this is a tranquil village, written with the characters meaning ""a village like a lake to the east."" In its earliest days, reeds grew so thickly across the land that it was simply called “Galbeol,” or ""Reed Field."" Later, it was renamed Seonyu-ri, and from the 1940s onward, the name changed once more to Dongho-ri.  Past the shore at Dongho-ri, the trail reaches the mouth of the Bukcheon Stream, where you come upon a rusted railway bridge. Only the piers still stand, yet within these weathered columns lies the entire arc of modern Korean history. This bridge was once part of the old Donghae Bukbu Line, the Eastern Sea Northern Railway. Built in the 1930s, it carried sightseers bound for the Geumgangsan Mountains and goods traveling north toward Wonsan. Damaged during the Korean War, it has since been reborn as a bicycle and pedestrian path.  Across the bridge lies the Salmon Welcome Square. Together with the Namdaecheon Stream in Yangyang, the Bukcheon Stream is one of the east coast's signature salmon-spawning rivers. Each autumn, salmon that have roamed the North Pacific return to this very stream. Remembering the scent of the river where they were born, they swim thousands of kilometers home, guided by a homing instinct that scientists have yet to fully explain.  Beyond Banam Beach, the trail reaches its final destination: Geojin Port. About five hundred years ago, the story goes, a scholar passing through on his way to the civil service examinations in Hanyang paused here, surveyed the surrounding ridges, and declared that the land took the shape of the Chinese character “Geo”, meaning ""great,"" and would surely give rise to many wealthy households. From that observation came the name Geojin-ri. This port was once the largest producer of pollock in all of Korea. Only a few decades ago, villagers would carry pollock inland and trade it for rice or meat.  Pollock is a cold-current species that thrives in waters between one and ten degrees Celsius. Each autumn it migrates south from the Sea of Okhotsk to spawn along Korea's coasts, returning north again in spring. Of all the fish in these waters, none has shared a longer or deeper history with the people of the Korean Peninsula. The pollock drying racks stretching along Geojin Port, set against the sea as the evening sun washes over the water, remain to this day the enduring emblem of this harbor.  Course 48 is a path where many stories travel together: the dream of a train halted on rusted piers, the instinct of salmon returning home, and the memory of pollock that once filled these seas. Take your time walking along the coast, and read with your feet the long, quiet hours that these small harbors have held. "

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 49
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 49 stretches from Geojin Port to Unification Security Park. Traversing mountains, lakes, and sea in a single stretch, this is a course where the history of national division and the splendor of nature meet at every step.  Leaving Geojin Port, the trail follows the walking path of Geojin Lighthouse Sunrise Park up to Eungbong Peak. From the summit of Eungbong, Hwajinpo Lake and the Geumgangsan Mountains open up in a single sweeping view. To the south lies Geojin Port and the East Sea you have just walked along; to the north, the heart-shaped Hwajinpo Lake and beyond it the ridgelines of the Geumgangsan Mountains. It is for this panorama, where mountain, lake, and sea overlap in one frame, that many travelers count Course 49 as the most beautiful stretch of the entire Haeparang Trail.  Hwajinpo is the largest natural lagoon on the east coast, with a circumference of about 16 kilometers. The name Hwajinpo means ""the ferry landing where flowers bloom,"" and the lake lives up to its name. All around its shores, the rugosa rose, the official flower of Goseong County, blossoms in abundance.  Descending from Eungbong, you arrive at the Hwajinpo History and Security Exhibition Hall. Three villas stand on these grounds. The first, set among pines and facing Hwajinpo Lake, is known as the Castle of Hwajinpo, or more commonly, Kim Il-sung's Villa. Originally built in 1938 by a German missionary as a chapel, the building served from 1948 to 1950 as a summer retreat for Kim Il-sung, together with his wife Kim Jong-suk, his son Kim Jong-il, and his daughter Kim Kyong-hui. At the entrance hangs a photograph of a six-year-old Kim Jong-il posing alongside the son of Major General Lebedev, the Soviet political commander of the time. Inside this two-story cylindrical stone building, shaped like a medieval European castle, you will find exhibits on the Korean War and on North Korea.  Just below it stands the villa once used by Lee Ki-poong. Built by foreign missionaries during the Japanese colonial period, it is the oldest of the villas in the area. After liberation, it was used as a retreat for North Korean Communist Party officials, and after the Korean War it became the private summer house of Lee Ki-poong's wife, Park Maria. Park Maria founded Daejin Church and is said to have visited often. A short distance off the trail, you will also find the villa of Rhee Syngman, the first president of the Republic of Korea. The three villas, standing side by side along the same lakeshore, seem to bear silent witness to the twists and turns of modern Korean history.  Walking a little further along the lake, you reach the Hwajinpo Marine Museum. The museum displays a wide range of specimens gathered from the East Sea and from oceans around the world, including rare shells, crustaceans, corals, and fossils. It is a place where you can encounter the deep time of the sea from indoors.  Beyond Hwajinpo lies Chodo Port. Famous for its abundant sea urchin harvests, it is also known as the ""Sea Urchin Village,"" and a sea urchin festival is held here each year from May through June. At the edge of the harbor stands a monument inscribed with the lyrics of the popular song ""A Love Pledged at Hwajinpo,"" adding a touch of romance to this quiet port.  A few hundred meters offshore floats a turtle-shaped rocky islet known as Geumgudo, ""the Golden Turtle Island."" Traces of granite fortress walls remain on this small island, leading some historians to suggest that it may be the underwater tomb of King Gwanggaeto the Great of Goguryeo. The waves breaking against Geumgudo, known as “Geumgu-nongpa,” are also counted among the Eight Scenic Views of Hwajinpo.  Following Chodo Beach, the trail leads to Daejin Port, the northernmost national fishing port that South Korean vessels are permitted to reach. Here you will find Starlight Galaxy Marine Park, a park built out over the sea itself. Designed around the octopus, the local specialty of Daejin Port, the park welcomes visitors with an octopus-shaped sculpture at its entrance, followed by rainbow-colored tetrapods and a Y-shaped deck stretching out over the water.  Above Daejin Port lies Machajin. On one side of the beach stands a marker stone inscribed with the words ""Starting Point of the Territorial Waters of the Republic of Korea."" It is from this point that Korea's maritime territory begins. At the center of the beach floats Musongdae, a small island crowned with a dense grove of pines, picturesque as a painting. It is said that during the Joseon dynasty, Yun Ja-un, the Prince of Musong, retreated to this island to enjoy its scenery and the arts, though today the island lies within a military protection zone and cannot be entered.  From Machajin, the trail passes in front of the Geumgangsan Condominium and reaches its terminus at Unification Security Park. Visitors wishing to continue on to the Unification Observatory must register here and complete a brief orientation.  Course 49 carries you across the panorama of Eungbong Peak, past the villas of three powerful figures and a lake alive with migratory birds, on through the northernmost fishing port, and finally to this place, where the Geumgangsan Mountains stand just within reach."

stories.title: Haeparang Trail Course 50
stories.script: "Haeparang Trail Course 50 begins at Unification Security Park and continues to the Unification Observatory. It is the final stretch of the entire Haeparang Trail, though this section is traveled by car rather than on foot.  The journey begins with a registration stop at Unification Security Park. Visitors must present identification, state the purpose of their visit, and complete a brief security orientation before being permitted to enter the Civilian Control Line. At the checkpoint just ahead, soldiers will verify identification once more and inspect the vehicle.  Immediately beyond the checkpoint lies Myeongpa Beach. Those who wish to walk may reach this point from Unification Security Park along a mountain path. The northernmost beach in South Korea, Myeongpa, meaning ""clear waves,"" lives up to its name with luminous waves and fine white sand. The mouth of the Myeongpacheon Stream meets the shore here, offering the lovely scenery of freshwater and sea coming together, and the beach is equipped with both a campground and a hotel.  Continuing past the checkpoint, you soon arrive at Jejin Station, the northernmost railway station in the Republic of Korea. From here, it is only 28 kilometers to the Geumgangsan Mountains. The station first opened in 1935 along with the Donghae Bukbu Line, the Eastern Sea Northern Railway, carrying tourists and goods bound for the Geumgangsan Mountains. After the Korean War, however, the tracks were destroyed and the station lost all function. Fifty-three years later, in 2006, in the warming spirit of inter-Korean reconciliation, Jejin Station was reopened. As part of the project to reconnect the Donghae Line across the inter-Korean border, tracks were laid all the way to Gamho Station in North Korea, and on May 17, 2007, a test run of inter-Korean trains was carried out. The rails that came briefly back to life that day, however, did not remain connected for long. As inter-Korean relations cooled, the trains came to a halt, and in 2024 North Korea demolished its portion of the line, severing the tracks once again. Today, the rails at Jejin Station extend only northward; to the south, no tracks remain. Construction of the Donghae Bukbu Line linking Gangneung to Jejin Station is currently underway, with completion scheduled for 2027. Inside the station, the Gangwon State Office of Education has set up a Peace Train experience hall.  Right beside Jejin Station stands the DMZ Museum. Opened in 2009, the museum uses the Demilitarized Zone, the symbol of the world's last remaining divided nation, to retrace the events surrounding the outbreak of the Korean War, to convey the historical meaning of the Armistice Line, and to introduce the ecology of the DMZ itself. Inside, the pain of division and the longing for peace meet, and the story of this land can be encountered in the closest way.  A little further on lies the destination of this course and the final terminus of the entire Haeparang Trail: the Unification Observatory. Since opening in 1983, the observatory has welcomed roughly 20 million visitors and remains the northernmost point in South Korea that civilians may approach for tourism. From its viewing platform, the last peak of the Geumgangsan Mountains, Guseonbong, feels almost within arm's reach, and on clear days the ridgelines of Birobong, Ongnyeobong, and Chaehabong unfold before you. Below your feet runs the line of barbed-wire fence, and the Donghae Line road and railway stretch onward across the Military Demarcation Line. Out toward the sea lies Haegeumgang, the ""Sea Geumgang,"" so named because the ridges of the Geumgangsan Mountains extend into the East Sea, scattering strange rocks and sheer cliffs across the water. Manmulsang, Sagongam, Hyeonjongam, and Bucheobawi rise above the waves, and at sunrise, when Haegeumgang glows red with the dawn, the view has long been counted among the finest in all of the Geumgangsan Mountains. That this sea lies so close at hand and yet cannot be reached speaks of the reality of division more clearly than any words.  Haeparang Trail Course 50 ends here, beyond the identification checks and the barbed-wire fences, past a station of halted trains and seventy years of silence, before the Geumgangsan Mountains that seem almost close enough to touch. Read with your feet the stories of this sea, these mountains, and these people that have carried you all the way to this place, and pause for a while in the hope that one day the journey may continue beyond that distant fence. "

stories.title: Gumi Saemaul Jungang Market
stories.audioTitle: Filled with happiness in Saemaul, the New Village
stories.script: As you get off at Gumi Station, look up, and you can see Saemaul or New Village Jungang Market right across the street. Since it is right downtown in Gumi City, it has always been a popular market for city dwellers. Then, one day, a green symbol of happiness began to fill this bustling place.  Starting from the entrance of the market, store signs decorated with three-leaf clovers come into view. The three-leaf clovers became popular decorations after the merchants decided to use these symbols to promote the market. Through the meaning of the three-leaf clover, “happiness,” merchants hope that all market visitors will be happy.  Saemaul Jungang Market is an all-inclusive Korean traditional market, with Soondae, or Blood Sausage Street; Jokbal, or Pigs’ Feet Street; Hanbok, or Korean Traditional Clothing Street, and Food Alley. Store signs are displayed clearly by each door, as well as street names, so they can be seen easily. Also, stores with many patrons also hang signs bearing a caricature of the store’s owner, to emphasize the trust customers have in that vendor.  Furthermore, visitors can join a tour program, and be guided around the market. They can even take part in a number of Korean cultural activities: rice cake making, trying on Hanbok, or traditional clothes, and picking fruits or vegetables. These will be a chance for hands-on experience, so visitors can add more memories to their rich lives.

stories.title: The Crispy Sound That Cools Off the Hot Summer Heat—Daegu Chicken
stories.audioTitle: The Crispy Sound That Cools Off the Hot Summer Heat—Daegu Chicken
stories.script: Welcome to the K-local food trip! Let’s talk about a true Korean favorite—fried chicken, crispy outside and tender inside.  No matter the season, chicken always brings something different to the table depending on how it’s cooked. From lean, oven-roasted chicken to golden, crispy fried chicken, there’s a style for every craving. It’s a go-to choice for watching sports or grabbing a late-night bite—chicken makes any moment more fun.  This beloved national snack got its start in the 1960s in Myeong-dong, Daegu. A restaurant called Original Nutrition Center opened there and became popular for serving whole roasted chicken. In the 1970s, people began frying chicken in vegetable oil. By 1977, it was cut into bite-sized pieces to make it easier to eat—what we now know as fried chicken. Then in 1981, a new type of chicken coated in a sweet and spicy sauce, known as Yangnyeom Chicken, was introduced. This helped Daegu establish its position as Korea’s veritable chicken capital.  Another local favorite in Daegu is dakttongjip—deep-fried chicken gizzards. They’re thoroughly cleaned and fried until golden, giving them a chewy texture and lots of flavor. Because of their unique bite, they’ve become a popular snack to enjoy with beer.  What could be better than freshly fried chicken and an ice-cold beer? Every summer, Daegu hosts the Chimaek Festival—where chicken (chi) meets beer (maekju). Come and make tasty memories in Korea’s fried chicken paradise!

stories.title: Andong Jjimdak—Perfect in Both Flavor and Quantity
stories.audioTitle: Andong Jjimdak—Perfect in Both Flavor and Quantity
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Let’s check out Andong Jjimdak—flavorful braised chicken that goes perfectly with a warm bowl of rice.  Andong Jjimdak is one of Korea’s most beloved dishes, enjoyed by people of all ages. It’s made with tender chicken, vegetables, and chewy glass noodles, all simmered in a rich soy-based sauce that’s both sweet and savory.  The story of Andong Jjimdak goes back to the 1980s. At the time, vendors at Andong’s traditional market would prepare chicken based on customer requests and sell it on the spot. One restaurant did something different—it braised the chicken in soy sauce instead of frying it, and people loved it. Before long, other shops started doing the same, and that’s how Andong’s famous Jjimdak Street got its start.  Andong is also known for a similar dish called Jjolimdak. It’s simmered longer than Jjimdak, which gives it a deeper, more concentrated flavor. This dish blends traditional cooking with a modern twist, creating a taste that’s uniquely Andong.  Now it’s your turn to experience the charm of Andong Jjimdak for yourself. Visit Jjimdak Street in Andong and enjoy a hearty meal full of local flavor and warm hospitality.

stories.title: Andong Soju, Korea's Premier Traditional Liquor
stories.audioTitle: Andong Soju, Korea's Premier Traditional Liquor
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! The highlight of this culinary journey is Andong Soju, a traditional Korean spirit treasured for its rich history and deep, distinctive flavor.  Andong Soju is a traditional distilled liquor produced in the Andong region of Gyeongsangbuk-do, widely recognized as one of Korea’s signature spirits. Historically abundant in clean water and high-quality rice, Andong naturally became home to many noble families, who established clan villages where brewing alcohol for ancestral rituals became an integral cultural tradition. Today, the Andong Soju Museum operates alongside production facilities to promote the historical value and traditional crafting methods of Andong Soju, preserving this important cultural heritage for future generations.  Dating back to the Goryeo Dynasty, Andong Soju carries a deep-rooted tradition and was highly prized during the Joseon Dynasty, frequently served at royal banquets and state rituals. Crafted from pure, locally sourced ingredients, Andong Soju is known for its crisp bite derived from its high alcohol content, harmonious balance of nutty richness and depth, and a smooth finish that leaves a pleasant, lingering aftertaste.  With its harmonious and balanced flavor, Andong Soju has been cherished by countless people throughout generations. In Andong, Soju has also been traditionally valued as a medicinal remedy—applied topically to wounds or used as a folk treatment for stomachaches and indigestion.  Indeed, Andong Soju is much more than just an alcoholic beverage; it is a precious cultural heritage that embodies the very essence of Korea’s traditional liquor craftsmanship. Each bottle carries within it the skills, dedication, and artisanal spirit passed down through generations. Even today, Andong Soju stands as one of Korea’s most prestigious traditional liquors, widely recognized for its cultural and historical significance both at home and abroad.  Why not savor the rich history and flavor in every sip of Andong Soju, while immersing yourself in the unique culture and charm of Andong?

stories.title: Seokguram Grotto - Inside of Seokguram Grotto
stories.audioTitle: Seokguram Grotto - Inside of Seokguram Grotto
stories.script: Seokguram Grotto - Inside of Seokguram Grotto  Seokguram Grotto locked in glass walls  It is our precious and proud Seokguram but, unfortunately, it is difficult to look inside closely because it is blocked by glass walls. The reason for the installation of the glass was because Seokguram was damaged while dismantling and repairing the grotto in the Japanese colonial period.  Originally, cold underground water flowed under Seokguram, which kept the temperature of the stone chamber at a constant level. Therefore, it prevented the formation of dews that can be caused by the temperature difference between the outside and the inside.  And, to enable the interior of the stone chamber to breathe, the walls and the ceiling were fitted uniformly with granite and then covered by roof tiles and soil, which naturally helped remove moisture.  During the Japanese occupation era, however, repairs were carried out without sufficient understanding of the scientific structure of Seokguram. That is why underground water was cut off to prevent permeation of water, and the roof tiles and soil on Seokguram's circumference were removed before completing the repair work with cement, which was a relatively new material at the time.  Because of this, moss grew inside the grotto due to moisture, and the stone structures that constitute Seokguram were in danger of corrosion.  So, inevitably, glass walls and thermostats were installed during the rework performed in the 1960s in order to control the temperature and humidity in an artificial manner.  If we understood and paid more attention to our ancestors’ wisdom and scientific technology during the repair construction process, our precious cultural heritage probably wouldn't have faced such a sad reality?

stories.title: Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School
stories.audioTitle: (22) Modern Streets of Daegu: Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School
stories.script: There is a stone sign that reads “Hamabi” by the stairway to the Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School. “Hama” means to get off the horse and walk. This sign was put in front of palaces, royal tombs, temples of Confucius, and royal ancestral shrines during the Joseon Dynasty, where it was necessary to pay respect to a subject. Those who ignored the sign were severely punished. The reason why this sign was placed here was because this place was a school where the scholars of the Joseon Dynasty studied Confucianism and admired ancient sages, including Confucius.  Hyanggyo was a national secondary education institution of the Joseon Dynasty. Scholars of over 16 years of age who completed seodang, or a private village school, were eligible to enroll. The students practiced proprieties and studied and learned Confucianism. The history of hyanggyo begins from the Goryeo Dynasty, but it was most appreciated after the establishment of the Joseon Dynasty in 1392. As hyanggyo were established in large and small villages throughout the country, Joseon was able to strengthen its position as a Confucian nation. 600 years since then, there are about 200 hyanggyo left on the Korean Peninsula today.  Past an outer three-door gate with a message that wishes you good luck and health, you will be greeted with a marvelous and peaceful landscape as if you have entered a different world. Inside the school you can find: Daeseongjeon Shrine where the tablets of Confucius and other ancient sages are enshrined; Myeongnyundang Lecture Hall that was used as the classroom of scholars; Dongjae East Dormitory and Seojae West Dormitory; and a white statue of Confucius who founded Confucianism. Imagine the young scholars of the period passing through Daeseongjeon Shrine, studying hard without break, and going in and out of the dormitories.  Built in 1398, the Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School saw a lot of events take place throughout history. It suffered a series of fires and repairs, reconstruction and relocation, until it finally settled down in 1932 at the current location. Despite the fact that all villages that had or have a hyanggyo are called “Gyo-dong”or “Myeongnyun-dong,” the Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School is currently located in Namsan-dong. It was the Japanese colonialists that forced the relocation of the school to the outskirts of Daegu, so that it could not be used as the base of independence movement by scholars.  Confucianism is often misinterpreted as an old-fashioned idea that does not fit in with the contemporary world. The belief in the relationship of people and the true meaning of being human as promoted by Confucianism, nevertheless, still has a place in contemporary life. Especially so in this hyper-competitive world where courtesy, respect, social order, and stability often take a back seat. Take a moment to get a deeper insight into Confucianism values from the Daeguhyanggyo Local Confucian School.

stories.title: Manhyujeong Pavilion
stories.script: The 82nd Scenic Site of Korea is Manhyujeong Pavilion, a pavilion with a view of a valley and a forest. There’s a log bridge that goes across the waterfall and the valley in front of it. Wide rocks and clear pools add to the beautiful scenery of this place. Manhyujeong Pavilion was made famous by the TV show Mr. Sunshine, where it served as the backdrop for Eugene’s declaration of his love for Ae-shin. The famous line, “What is love? Would you like to do it with me?” still captures the hearts of K-drama fans worldwide. The log bridge that the two lead characters stood upon is the only bridge leading to Manhyujeong Pavilion. For those who want to recreate the iconic scene from the show, you can take the side path down to the valley.   When you cross the bridge to get to the pavilion, you can take off your shoes and sit down as well. The rock near the log bridge bears the inscription “bobaekdang”, which translates to “even though I have no treasure in my house, I value as treasures my upright integrity.” It is also the courtesy name of Kim Gye-haeng, the owner of this house.  Kim Gye-haeng was an early Joseon period scholar who hailed from Andong. He held a government post called “Daesagan”, an equivalent of today’s Censor General. During his service, he sought to criticize the improper conduct of the king’s relatives in the government. He, however, lost hope of things changing, and is said to have come down to his hometown, built the Manhyujeong Pavilion, and focused on teaching the next generation.

stories.title: UNESCO World Heritage, nature retreat, scenic suburban drive
stories.audioTitle: UNESCO World Heritage, nature retreat, scenic suburban drive
stories.script: “If you’re looking for a quiet place in Daegu, there’s a drive Uber Taxi drivers love to recommend. It’s a short but fulfilling drive from the foothills of Biseulsan Mountain to Dodong Seowon.”  Leaving behind the busy city, this drive takes you through nature and history — perfect for starting or ending your day.  The Biseulsan Foothill Drive winds gently along the base of the mountain, surrounded by green scenery rare within Daegu. Each season brings a different breeze, and spring and autumn are the best times to roll down your window and drive slowly. As you pass through the shade of the forest, you’ll feel your mind clearing with every turn.  About halfway through the drive, stop at Bonni Village, home to the Nampyeong Mun Clan — a hidden gem few people know about. Old traditional houses line the narrow alleys, and the quiet air fills you with calm. Here, the sound of the wind is louder than the sound of people. It feels like a rare gift of silence.  The destination is Dodong Seowon, a Confucian academy nestled in a pine forest. It’s one of Daegu’s treasures and a UNESCO World Heritage site, preserving the grace of traditional hanok architecture. Sitting under the golden ginkgo trees in autumn, even a cup of coffee here offers a rare sense of peace.  On a calm afternoon, take this road that winds quietly outside the city. More than any destination, it’s the slow journey itself that becomes the reward. With Uber Taxi, your peaceful escape begins the moment you set off.

stories.title: Kim Kwang Suk Road & Bangcheon Market
stories.audioTitle: 13. Kim Kwang Suk Road & Bangcheon Market
stories.script: Kim Kwang Suk Road & Bangcheon Market The neighborhood of an one-in-a-generation singer   Daegu has a street that commemorates Kim Kwang Suk, a poetic, one-in-a-generation singer who still moves and touches the hearts of many today even after decades of his passing. Kim was born and raised here in Daebong-dong until he was five. In 2009, 11 teams of artists came together to establish Kim Kwang Suk Road. The walls of the street feature the lyrics of his songs and images and artworks that suit the lyrics. The street is filled with his songs all year round, so you will become imbued with the atmosphere.  Bangcheon Market is a traditional market located next to the Suseonggyo Bridge in Daegu. The market's history began when people who had fled from Japan and Manchuria after the Liberation in 1945 set up sales stands. It is said that merchants at the time used straw ropes to divide the chaotic market in the shape of the number sign (#). In the old days, the market actively sold grains brought from Namdo. Today, there is a makgeolli (rice wine) shop where the market adjoins the Kim Kwang Suk Road. Take your time to appreciate the vibe while listening to the singer's music.

stories.title: Bongsan Culture Street
stories.script: Bongsan Culture Street The Insa-dong of Daegu   Bongsan Culture Street is an area crowded with art galleries, antique shops, ateliers, and mounters, showing similar traits as Insa-dong, Jongno-gu in Seoul. Daegu is a city of arts that gave birth to outstanding artists like Lee In-seong and Lee Kwae-dae. The city is the province of many artists to date. Bongsan Culture Street is famous nationwide as you can see from the fact that over 80% of those who purchase artworks at galleries here are from outside Daegu. In addition to the galleries, various exhibits and performances are held in Bongsan Cultural Center, which expands the spectrum of cultured life for the citizens.  All kinds of stores you need for cultural and artistic activities are available on Bongsan Culture Street, from private galleries, calligraphy stores, and handicraft shops to ateliers, old bookstores, publishers, and printing shops. For those who are not sure where Bongsan Culture Street starts and ends, look at the sewers on the ground and you will know it right away!

stories.title: The ARC
stories.script: Waves attracting attention day and night   The ARC Culture Center is located at the point where Nakdonggang and Geumhogang Rivers meet. Opened in September 2012, The ARC Culture Center is an architectural work of art that contains everything about rivers and water. The ARC, which is an acronym of “Architecture of River Culture” and “Artistry of River Culture,” refers to not only an elegant, geometric approach to the sky, earth and culture but also architecture and art that holds and values everything about the river culture.  This building was designed by world-famous architect Hani Rashid who was inspired by stone skipping that cuts across the river surface and fish jumping out of the water. Inside the ARC Culture Center, various exhibitions are being held under the theme of “Sympathy of River and People.” In particular, the blue “Greeting Men,” which fills the entire wall of the first floor lobby, are welcoming its guest.  If you go up to the observatory through stairs or the elevator, you can see Geumhogang and Nakdonggang Rivers at a glance. At night, beautiful lights shine brightly on the exterior walls of the building, adding to the night’s beauty.   <This guide was recorded by Baek Ji-yoon of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Daegaya Museum
stories.script: The Daegaya Museum comprises the Daegaya Wangneung Royal Tomb Exhibition Hall and the Daegaya History Hall. The Daegaya History Hall consists of the Permanent Exhibition Hall, which displays relics and provides explanations on the history of Daegaya and the Goryeong region from the Paleolithic to the present, and the Special Exhibition Hall, which holds special themed exhibitions. There is also the Outdoor Exhibition Space, which displays reproductions of an ancient dwelling hut and an iron kiln site of the Daegaya Period, and various stone cultural properties. The Daegaya Museum boasts more than 9,000 exhibits, and uses a variety of exhibition techniques, including video, diorama, model and signage, to present the exhibits in the best possible conditions. Please come and enjoy the rich and interesting culture of the Daegaya!

stories.title: Daegu National Museum
stories.script: The Daegu National Museum first opened its doors in 1994. It is established to preserve, research, and exhibit the cultural heritage of Daegu and Gyeongsangbuk-do. In 2006, the museum expanded with the addition of a storage facility to the south and the construction of Haesol Hall and a special exhibition hall to the north. Additionally, in 2010, the museum was revamped with new exhibits, including the Ancient Culture Hall, the Medieval Culture Hall, and the Textiles and Clothing Hall, making it a continuously evolving museum.   Now, let’s take a closer look at the museum’s highlights. First, in the Ancient Culture and Medieval Culture halls, you can explore the cultural heritage of different eras. The museum showcases artifacts from the Paleolithic period to the Joseon Dynasty. You can learn about the earliest human cultures in the Paleolithic era, the cultures of Silla and Gaya during the Three Kingdoms period, and the culture of the Joseon Dynasty, which was based on Confucian ideals. The exhibits offer a fascinating journey through the diverse cultures that shaped Korea’s history.   Next, let’s explore the newly opened Textiles and Clothing Hall, which replaces the former Folk Hall. This exhibition offers a unique focus on Daegu’s history, highlighting how the city's rise as a modern industrial center was largely driven by its textile and clothing industry. In this hall, you can learn about the evolution of clothing, a fundamental part of our daily lives. It is regularly updated, incorporating both domestic and international materials to create a richer and more diverse display.   The outdoor exhibition area is also filled with fascinating sights. As you walk around the grounds, you’ll encounter Bronze Age dolmens and house sites, pottery kilns from the Three Kingdoms period, and stone pagodas from Unified Silla, among other historical artifacts. In addition, the museum hosts a variety of special and themed exhibitions in its planned exhibition halls, and educational programs are offered at Haesol Hall, making it an enriching experience for all visitors.   Visit the National Daegu Museum and immerse yourself in the vibrant culture and history of Daegu and Gyeongsangbuk-do!

stories.title: Suam Valley: Kim Tak-goo Exhibition Hall
stories.script: Kim Tak-goo Exhibition Hall  [Traveler] Can you see the oven-shaped exhibition building? That is the exhibition hall for King of Baking, Kim Tak-goo, which was a famous Korean drama watched by one out of every three Korean people. Aired in 2010 against a background of the rapid growth of the Korean economy in the 1980s, this drama told the story of a man who overcame many hardships to succeed as a baker.  This place used to be a cigarette factory. Although old and a bit torn, this historic building was ideal as a set for a drama based in the 1980s.  The exhibition hall was built by remodeling the interior of the factory. The grey warehouse was colorfully painted, and the actual sets and props used in the drama were brought in. Usually, drama sets are disassembled as soon as a drama ends, but because of the fame of Kim Tak-goo, this set has still been kept. The structure and even the circulation system of the exhibition hall were all designed to recall the touching scenes of the drama. So, if you have seen the drama, imagine yourself as being in the kitchen with Kim Tak-goo and Gu Ma-jun.

stories.title: Jayu and Muhak Markets
stories.script: Jayu and Muhak Markets   A visit to markets where the liveliness of local people can be directly felt cannot be left out of the schedule. In particular, the fun of eating and people watching as well as touring traditional attractions can all be enjoyed in Chungju’s traditional markets. Five markets gathered along Chungjucheon Stream are located where the north gate of the old Chungjueupseong Walled Town was. Each market has its own characteristics, making it fun to visit each one. Among the markets, Jayu Market is easily accessible due to its location near a big road and has many stores that handle dry goods, clothes and jewelry. Muhak Market, where various kinds of food such as vegetables, fish and side dishes are sold, is also worth visiting.  In particular, Sundae-Mandu Alley stretching from Jayu Market to Muhak Market is a course you should take: Blood sausage and rice soup with dried radish leaves and chewy-textured potato dumplings are popular. After filling your stomach, why not check out Jayu Café run by the Jayu Market Merchants’ Society. A variety of beverages can be enjoyed at a low price, and the joy of requesting the music you want to listen to from a DJ can be experienced.     Also at Nuri Market near Jayu and Muhak Markets there is the Samhwa Blacksmith’s Shop run by Kim Myeong-il, a blacksmith designated as Chungcheongbuk-do’s intangible cultural heritage. Watching the master craftsman, who has handled iron for about 60 years, work the bellows and hammer and temper the iron to make a variety of tools is phenomenal. Nearby there is Banseonjae House, the house where UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon lived in during his school days.

stories.title: Liquorium
stories.script: Liquorium   There is a unique museum in Chungju, a place of glorious beauty, full of flavor. It is Liquorium, a museum with exhibits on global liquor cultures next to the Pungnyu Culture Center. Liquorium is a compound of “Liquor” and “-rium,” which is a Latin word for space. It introduces various kinds of liquor and culture from around the world.    At the entrance to the museum are two stills that were actually used to distill whiskey for over 100 years, acting as a main gate. Also, the oak casks from around the world stacked at the entrance of the exhibition hall will delight your eyes even more. The first exhibition hall is the History of Wine, Wine Culture Hall. It is full of exciting exhibits, from the history of wine to the variety of grapes, how to read the labels on bottles of world-famous wines and trademarks, and how to choose wine. The next exhibition hall, the Cooperage Hall, displays oak casks that were used for storing, aging and transporting wine, brandy and whiskey. The exhibition corner called “The Angel’s Share” is eye-catching. It explains that “Alcohol and fragrances evaporate when alcohol is matured in oak barrels, and the amount that evaporates is called ‘the angel’s share.’”  In addition, you can learn about the history and culture of liquor while touring around the Beer Hall, Aqua Vitiate Hall, Tradition Hall, Korea Liquor Hall, and Fermentation Education and Science Hall. If looking around the exhibition halls is not enough for you, you might want to try some wine or make a cocktail yourself.

stories.title: Yukgeori Traditional Market
stories.script: This is Cheongju's most famous traditional market formed in the 1950s, considered one of the top five traditional markets in Korea. With fresh agricultural and marine products, fashion items, and a sumptuous spread of food, the market is full of life all year round. The sellers are usually happy to throw in extras for a sweet-talking customer. The street is covered by a shelter that stretches over one kilometer, protecting visitors from rain and snow. Yukgeori market is full of things to see, eat and buy, a place for shopping with the human touch.

stories.title: Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral: Entrance
stories.audioTitle: Front of Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral
stories.script: Front of Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral   [Traveler] Hello!  The word ‘Maegoe’ from the name of Gamgok Maegoe Catholic Cathedral is composed of the Chinese characters for ‘rosario,’ which means rosary in English. It’s used in Catholicism and symbolizes the rose bouquet dedicated to the Virgin Mary. As its name indicates, this church, which has more than one hundred years of history, is dedicated to the Virgin Mary. The church was founded by Father Camille Bouillion from Lourdes, France, a town famous for an apparition of the Virgin. You can see a statue of the bearded priest holding his hat in front of the priest’s office built with red bricks. Inscribed below the statue are the words he always used to say.   [Bouillion] “I loved you long before I ever met you.”  [Traveler] After entering the clergy in 1893, Father Bouillion entered Korea to carry out missionary work. While searching for a location to build a church, he found just the spot he was looking for, but there was already an extravagant house there. The Father asked the townspeople who the owner of the house was. People told him that the house belonged to a family of the empress. So the Father had no choice but to give up on the location.   Soon after October 1895, there was a national tragedy in Korea. Japan assassinated the empress in order to gain control of Korea, and the big house that belonged to the family of the empress was also burned down. After hearing the news a little later, Father Bouillion acquired the land from the owner and built a small church there for temporary use.   As the small church attracted more and more believers, it was expanded through a number of reconstructions until it gained the appearance it has today.   Father Bouillion was French, but he loved Korea as much as any Korean. Maybe because of the Father’s endless love, an astounding miracle occurred in this church. I’ll tell you a couple of stories from the Korean War in the next file.

stories.title: The Birthplace of General Kim Yu-sin
stories.audioTitle: The Birthplace of General Kim Yu-sin
stories.script: The Birthplace of General Kim Yu-sin 1  [Traveler] Born in this place, General Kim Yu-sin is one of the most famous military leaders in Korean history. He played a key role in the unification of three ancient Korean kingdoms.   He was born in 595 and thereafter devoted his life to winning the battles which led to the unification of the three ancient Korean kingdoms, namely, Silla, Baekje and Goguryeo. The three kingdoms fought against each other for over 700 years until their unification.  Few expected that Silla, the weakest of the three for much of that long period, would be the ultimate winner in the conflict for unification. General Kim Yu-sin was one of the few leaders who nurtured Silla’s strength to enable it to overpower its two rivals. History says that he was a brave fighter and outstanding strategist who left no record of defeat during his forty years as a battlefield commander.  His decisive role in Silla’s success in the unification of the early Korean kingdoms has been widely admired among the Korean people, and both his birthplace and his grave have been transformed into a major place of pilgrimage. The village you are currently visiting is where he was born and grew up. Before you stands a stone monument erected in his honor, and on your left is his birthplace, which was restored in 1983. The mountain behind his home contains a well used by his family during the period when his father served as a government official. And, on the peak of the mountain is a mound in which his placenta is buried.  Another interesting point is that his home was in Jincheon, a town situated about 200 km from Silla’s capital, although he was one of Silla’s most powerful political figures in the unification period.
