This is particularly interesting, given that Silla’s aristocrats at that time clung to the capital as it was the source of their power and wealth. The situation surrounding Kim Yu-sin at the time is closely related with the history of the three preceding generations of his family.  While Kim Yu-sin was a great warrior who obtained fame and power through his successive victories on the battlefield, he was always careful about his family background. The fact that he overcame his inferior social status using his own outstanding personal capabilities makes his life comparable to that of Julius Caesar.  History tells that he was born in a country which was later defeated and incorporated into Silla. His grandfather, the last king of the fallen country, surrendered to Silla and became a Silla aristocrat. However, he was ostracized by the Silla aristocracy because he had not been born in Silla. The fallen king felt that he needed to achieve distinguished exploits in battle to prove his loyalty to Silla and open up a new future for himself. He succeeded, and was eventually promoted to the highest position in government.  His remarkable success, however, did not prevent further discrimination. His son, that is, Kim Yu-sin’s father, came up with a new plan, and seduced a Silla princess. His behavior infuriated the Silla royals, who sent him into exile here, which was at the time a remote border area. Meanwhile, the Silla princess had fallen in love with the seducer and fled the palace to the border town, where she married him and gave birth to a boy who would later become General Kim Yu-sin.    Grown into a man of noble character and looks, Kim Yu-sin was admitted to his maternal grandmother as a royal offspring, but he could never remove the tag that he was a descendant of a foreign, ruined country. He had to repeat what his grandfather had done to be accepted by the Silla aristocracy; that is, fighting and winning victories for Silla. He continued to rush to the battlefield and brought numerous victories to Silla until he was 70. His spirit of self-sacrifice and devotion to the dynasty moved the Silla ruler to honor the general with a title and a position of the highest rank. These remarkable achievements made through three generations finally brought Kim Yu-sin what he and his ancestors had longed for.

stories.title: Sanmagi Trail: Roh Su-sin’s House of Exile
stories.script: Roh Su-sin’s House of Exile  [Traveler] Roh Su-sin was a scholar who lived in the 16th century. He made his debut in politics at the age of twenty-nine, and was praised for his competence during his period of service, but was ousted by the powers that controlled the Joseon Dynasty. He was exiled to an isolated town where he lived for twenty-three long years.   The Joseon Dynasty lasted for six centuries, until the beginning of the 20th century. In those times a common form of punishment was exile. The sentence was usually passed to eliminate officials who failed to adjust to the harsh power struggles between the various factions. The king, being reluctant to kill nobles, sent them far away from the capital. They had to live in isolated villages where they would wait, sometimes for many years, for the king to summon them once more. But unlike what most people might think, life in isolation was not always bad. For many scholars who had lived busy and hectic lives, it was a chance to read in peace and silence. Poems and writings by exiled nobles constitute a major genre in Joseon literature. Roh Su-sin was sent from village to village where he continued his studies. After twenty years of roaming, he was finally reinstated. Later, he made his way to the highest government post in Joseon. All this was possible because he continued to study despite the seemingly hopeless conditions.   This house is the last place he stayed in during his time of exile. Shall we go in?.  The house is a bit rugged , but can you see the wooden board inscribed with Chinese characters hanging under the roof? From right to left, each character represents water, moon, and pavilion. It means that the only things you can see from here are the moon and water. There is a wood-floored space separating two rooms: one was for Roh Su-sin, while the other was for his servant.

stories.title: Sangdang Fortress: On the Way to the Gate
stories.audioTitle: On the Way to the Gate
stories.script: On the Way to the Gate   [Traveler] Welcome to Sangdang Fortress, a symbolic site of North Chungcheong Province. This mountain fortress serves as a place of relaxation for many Chungju citizens and is a hotspot where various historical dramas have been filmed. Today, the 4.2-km-long fortress trail is open to citizens who want to take a walk, but the original purpose of this fortress was to prevent enemies during war.  European countries or Japan usually built their fortresses on plains with moats and waterways around them as a defensive measure. However, Korea has a lot of mountains that served as refuges for the king and his citizens. They fought off enemies from the mountaintop. This kind of history led to the country being described as “a nation of fortresses.”  Sangdang Fortress, which you are about to enter, has gates on the east, west and south. The northern gate was omitted because the steep slope of the mountain acted as a natural defense mechanism. This fortress was situated at an important crossroads in the central plain, and was successively ruled by Baekje, Goguryo and Silla. The large number of relics discovered in the area indicates the importance and value of this location.  Then, let’s go to the first gate, Gongnam Gate, and find out what treasures are hidden there.

stories.title: Beopju Temple: Seated Rock-carved Buddha
stories.script: Seated Rock-carved Buddha  [Traveler] Let's move to a rock cliff carved with a Buddha image, which attracts Buddhist followers from all over the country. The Buddha is carved in low relief on a rock cliff, but it has been preserved for about a millennium. While other images carved on the front of the large rock have been worn away, this particular image has survived to reveal the original condition.  This Buddhist image is regarded as a rare piece of art largely because of the position it takes. The Buddhist figure is seated on a fully-bloomed lotus flower.  Please look at the figure's characteristic curly hair style. The conch-shaped hair is one of many characteristic physical features of the Buddha. But what is truly remarkable is the skill that the carver used to create such a fine piece of art work. Just imagine how hard and intricate was the working process required to carve these clear-cut images in such a high place.

stories.title: Okcheon Confucian School
stories.script: Okcheon Confucian School  [Traveler] On the way up to this Confucian school, the first thing you will see are the red doors. Red doors were built in dignified buildings such as palaces, lecture halls, and Confucian schools. To the right, there is a headstone inscribed with the words: “Get down from your horse and walk from here.” As the saying suggests, this place is very solemn and important.   Confucian schools were built by government offices to educate local residents and hold commemorative rites for great scholars during the Joseon Dynasty. In 1398, the king who founded the Joseon Dynasty built Okcheon Confucian school. It consists of an educational facility for students at its front and a shrine for commemorative rites at the back.   Now, are you at the entrance to the Confucian school? The big building you saw on the way up here was the lecture hall, where students used to learn. The building to the right, which stands opposite the lecture hall on the left of the entrance, is a shrine to Confucius of China and Korean scholars.   As a place of education and ritual, even the building’s location and position follow strict rules. Let’s look at the lecture hall first. The splendid roof with the ears pointing upwards is a traditional style of Joseon architecture designed to avoid rain with wide eaves. The wide floor was used to hold lectures, and the teachers dwelled in the two rooms. For heating, the traditional under floor heating system called ondol was used.  Now let’s look at the shrine across the lecture room. There’s a reason why the entrance consists of three doors. The middle door was built for deities, so ordinary people didn’t use it. It was customary to enter through the door on the right and exit through the one on the left.  The roof looks different from the one we saw before. It looks like a half-closed book hanging on the top. This type of Korean roof architecture has its own meaning. For buildings that emphasized tradition, such as shrines, a simple and humble roof was used, while for residential buildings such as schools and temples, more extravagant roofs were used.   During the Joseon Dynasty, Confucius’ teachings were selected by the elite as the national ideology, and the general way of life including customs, manners and traditions were formed within a Confucian framework. That’s why the ancestral tablets of Confucius, the founder of Confucianism, and those of four additional scholars are housed inside this shrine. It also houses the tablets of 18 people who contributed to the development of Korean Confucianism.   Finally, the humble building between the hall and the shrine is a dormitory for students. Originally, there were an east building and a west building, but only the latter remains now. The next course will take us to where Korea’s first lady used to live. We will see a traditional Korean house there. Shall we move on?

stories.title: Eight Beautiful Sites of Danyang: Dodam Peaks
stories.script: Dodam Peaks  [Traveler] Welcome to the most mysterious and peaceful valley in the Korean Peninsula. The word “danyang” means “a sunlight-filled hidden paradise of gods.” Which is why Danyang is one of the most beautiful cities not only in Chungcheongbuk-do, but also in all of Korea.   This heavenly city is well known for eight very beautiful landscapes. All these famous places can be seen along the wide and deep meandering river in front of you. Oh no! Not enough time to see all eight? Don’t worry! There is a ferry that will take you up and down the river. Although you can’t see every corner of the eight beautiful sites, it’s a convenient way to take in the landscapes, and the whole trip only takes an hour. Okay, are you ready for the trip?   The first place you’ll see is Dodam Peaks, or the Three Peaks of Dodam. The word “dodam” means “isle and water” while “sambong” simply means “three peaks” in Korean. It became even more famous after one of the most revered scholars named ‘Jeong Do-jeon’ nicknamed himself ‘Sambong’ because he liked the view so much. Jeong Do-jeon is one of the founders of ‘Joseon’, the dynasty that ruled over Korea from the 14th century to 20th century. He’s one of the most prominent figures in history for being the one who laid the foundation for the new kingdom, and brought about some important economic changes by giving land to poor peasants. He often visited Danyang because it was his birthplace, and he was very fond of his hometown. There is an interesting story about him. Would you like to hear it?   These three rock peaks were originally located at the mouth of the river, but after a flood, they were moved here. So the folks living in the upper side of the river demanded the townspeople here to pay taxes since the peaks were originally theirs. This didn’t make any sense, not even to the 7-year-old Jeong Do-jeon. So Jeong Do-jeon stepped forward and said to the grownups, “Take them back then! Because we don’t need them!” Humiliated by a little boy, the folks from the upper town gave on collecting taxes. Whether the story is true or not, no one knows, but if it were, wasn’t he such a clever boy?  Each of the Dodam Peaks has a name, and they were named for a special reason. The peak in the middle is the tallest one, and it’s named the “Husband” peak. The one nearest to it is called the “Concubine” peak, and the one farthest from them is the “Wife” peak. They say it’s because the three peaks look like a married couple with a concubine, with the wife turning her back to them because she didn’t want to look at her husband, who had brought in a concubine to bear a son for him.  For some reason, the “Concubine” peak looks conniving and flirtatious next to the “Husband” peak.

stories.title: Uirim Reservoir: Yongchu Falls
stories.script: Yongchu Falls  [Traveler] Looking down from the bridge above the waterfall, is a dazzling cliff about 30 meters in height, and a cool waterfall. Interestingly, on one side of this bridge there is a gentle flow of water and on the other there’s a dynamic waterfall.  A long time ago, people thought this waterfall resembled a dragon penetrating the valley before flying up into the sky. That’s why the word ‘Yong,’ which means ‘dragon’ in English, forms part of its name - Yongchu Falls. The high copper content in the water makes the waterfall look red, so the area is also called, the Red Dragon Valley. Look where the dragon left his mark, and listen to a folk tale. The story of <Five strong men and a python> has been passed down for generations here at Uirim Reservoir.  Once upon a time, there were five very strong brothers. Not only were they strong, but they also had scales on their bodies like dragons. One day, while the five brothers were playing around in Uirim Reservoir, a gigantic python came up behind the eldest brother. A python is an imaginary beast that frequently appears in Korean legends. It’s basically a baby dragon that has yet to acquire its mysterious powers. While the eldest brother fought with the creature under the water, his four brothers watched in shock, hoping for their brother to come back safe.   The brothers picked up wooden sticks from the waterside and started attacking the python. With help from his younger brothers, the eldest finally struggled back on land, while the angry beast whipped its tail at the five brothers.  The five brothers quickly dodged the attack, and the creature’s tail got stuck in a giant pine tree. The brothers beat down the evil beast with their bare hands and feet.   The beast’s scales broke off and were scattered all around, and its blood turned the waterfall red. The python was so big that when they hung it from the top of a giant tree, its tail reached all the way down to the ground. Thanks to the five brothers who defeated the python, the townspeople were able to go to Uirim Reservoir without fear.

stories.title: Hwayang Valley: Entrance
stories.script: "Towards the Valley  [Visitor] This valley, where an abundance of cold, clear water flows, is called Hwayang Valley. It is also a popular summer resort. Besides the clear water of the valley, there are other nine tourist attractions that are worth seeing. This place was selected by Song Si-yeol, who has had a huge impact on Confucianism and politics in Korea since the 17th century.  Song Si-yeol, the top politician of his day, wrote a large number of books and achieved excellent academic results. Also, a lot of his disciples entered government services, so he was very influential in the political sphere. In particular, his name appears over three thousand times in The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, which has recorded the 500-year history of the Joseon Dynasty, and historically speaking it’s hard to find a comparison. Therefore, he is sometimes likened to the Confucius of Korea. He was a teacher of King Hyojong, the 17th King of the Joseon Dynasty, as well as a supporter and a faithful servant of the King. In a history book, it was recorded that a close relationship between the King and the servant was recognized.    However, he was famous for his stubborn character, and when he thought he was right, he never compromised. Thus, when he was in government service, there was often friction between him and the King, which resulted in him being exiled several times. Eventually, he died insisting on the principle regarding the succession to the 18th throne of Joseon.  He studied and taught his disciples while staying here, and visited this place 23 times. Then, in his late 60s, he settled down here while filled with anguish about a crisis following the death of the King.   It takes about one and a half hours to look around the nine attractions and their beautiful landscapes. The first attraction, Gyeongcheon Cliff, is located slightly to the rear of the parking lot. After getting off the bus, walk back a bit to the road you came along. You will see the fantastic site of the cliffs supporting the sky.  "

stories.title: "Jeongbukdong Toseong Fortress "
stories.script: "The earthen fortifications of Jeongbuk-dong have been built in a square shape in the middle of the plain where Mihogang River and Musimcheon Stream merge. The fortress is the oldest of its kind in Korea along with Pungnap Toseong Fortress in Seoul and the only one maintained almost in its original form. Thus it is considered a valuable resource for the study of earthen fortifications in early Korean history. It was designated a Monument of Chungcheongbuk-do on December 14, 1990, then promoted to Korean Historic Site No. 415 in 1999 when its importance was recognized. The Jeongbukdong Toseong Fortress becomes the best sunset watching spot in the evening. People flock to photograph the brilliant sunset and the trees atop the earthen fortifications each day. "

stories.title: Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex: Entrance
stories.audioTitle: Entrance to the Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex
stories.script: "Entrance to the Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex  [Traveler] Welcome to Cheongpung. Blessed by beautiful scenery and waterways extending in all directions, Cheongpung was the center of regional commerce. As indicated in its name, it is a complex of cultural relics of the area. When the relics were at risk of being immersed underwater due to plans to build a dam, local residents and civil workers joined hands to transfer the precious relics here, to the Cheongpung Cultural Heritage Complex, and ultimately formed a small folk village.   At the entrance of the complex, Paryeong Pavilion welcomes visitors. It was originally the entrance to the village. Let’s walk through the gate and go up to where we can see the entire place.   Please look up as you pass through the gate. Can you see the big tiger? It was drawn there so that it will protect the village from negative energies and floods.  Have you come up? Can you see the writing on the ceiling? It says ""paryeongsi,"" which means “paryeong poem.” This pavilion was named after this poem, which was written an official of the Joseon Dynasty about the 8 scenic views of this town. The original name of the gate was Namdeok Gate, and there is an inscription with the name on the inside. Okay, now let’s go and take a closer look at a traditional house of the Joseon era house. "

stories.title: Jeungpyeong Folk Museum
stories.script: In front of the Museum  [Traveler] Welcome to our museum! This museum features exhibits and experience corners where you can learn about and experience Korea’s traditional rural cultures. In Hall No. 1, located in front of the parking lot, you can learn about agricultural folksongs and try playing some traditional Korean instruments. Every second week of June, the villagers hold a festival in the vicinity of the museum and invite visitors to attend. The festival features planting rice in the local paddies, and ploughing fields with oxen. Of course, tourists are welcome to join in these events. You can also catch mud snails and dig up potatoes. Since experienced farmers are ready to help, this is your chance to try your hands at farming.    Hall No. 2 features a collection of folk dolls from all around the world. Some 700 dolls from about 100 countries are displayed here. Each doll is pretty and unique. Korean blacksmith’s tools and a variety of ancient weapons are also exhibited in Hall No. 2.   Hall No. 3 exhibits native materials. Over 90 percent of them were donated by local residents. Another corner showcases the four-season farming, and ancient market places and other agriculture-related items.  After taking a tour of the museum, you can take a look at the Buddha images that are believed to guard Jeungpyeong Village. This tangible cultural heritage was discovered at a temple site. The Buddha images were thought to serve as guardians of the village. First, you will see the Namha-ri Stone Maitreya Bodhisattva next to the museum. The other Buddha images are a 10-minutes drive away from here. These Buddhas are not elaborate or fancy, rather they are a bit old but give off a friendly aura. Shall we go to meet the Namha-ri Stone Maitreya Bodhisattva?

stories.title: Chungju Museum
stories.script: "Chungju Museum   Due to its geographical location, Chungju was a fierce battlefield for fights over territory among the three ancient states of Goguryeo, Silla and Baekje(A.D. 57-668) as well as a major traffic hub. Therefore, lots of cultural properties and historic sites are scattered throughout the area. Among others, Chungju Museum in Jungangtap Park houses representative relics from the Three Kingdoms period.      The museum comprises two exhibition halls and an outdoor exhibition area. Hall 1 consists of the History Hall with Buddhist art pieces including Buddha statues, Buddhist paintings and shaman paintings on display, and the Folk Hall, where visitors can take a look at the lives of our ancestors in the Chungju area. Hall 2 is composed of four connected exhibition halls: The Prehistoric-Three Kingdoms Hall, Goryeo-Joseon Hall, Noted Men of Chungju Hall, and Chungju’s Struggle Hall. The Prehistoric-Three Kingdoms Hall exhibits replicas of the Goguryeo Monument, Chungju and the Jeokseongbi Monument of Silla, Danyang, representative relics of the Three Kingdoms period. The Goryeo-Joseon Hall displays celadon and white porcelain from the Goryeo and Joseon periods, while Chungju’s Struggle Hall houses reproductions of battles in Chungju including the Chungjuseong Fortress Battle, Tangeumdae Battle during Imjinwaeran(Japanese Invasion of Joseon in 1592), etc. The outdoor exhibition area exhibits stone relics.   For more about the exhibits, a commentary service on the exhibits is available upon request. You can apply for the service at the Information Center from 10 am to 4 pm on all days except Mondays when the museum is closed. Currently, commentary in English is available. You can contact the Tourism Promotion Team in the Tourism Division of Chungju City Hall.  "

stories.title: Pungnyu Culture Center
stories.script: Pungnyu Culture Center   The Pungnyu Culture Center, inside a stylish hanok(traditional Korean house), is located in front of the quiet scenery of the Namhangang River. It is a place of relaxation and learning to recall the beauty and wisdom of the arts left by our ancestors in beautiful nature. Pungnyu refers to the enjoyment of tasteful activities that combine the elements of nature, life, and art.   Anyone visiting here can get a taste of pungnyu while looking at the gentle flow of the river and the low hills. It is also great to have some relaxing moments over a cup of healthy tea made with apple blossoms, the symbol of Chungju, or chrysanthemum, the flower of the city. You can also experience a tea ceremony where you can learn about the origins of tea, and the etiquette of making and drinking tea with an application in advance.  Various experience programs are also available. In the Writing a Family Motto corner, you can write a phrase that you want to let your descendants know or a lesson passed down from ancestors(called gahun, or family motto) or you can ask a calligrapher to write it for you. You can also try making traditional Korean cookies, tea confectionery, or playing traditional folk games such as tuho(throwing arrows), biseokchigi(hitting stone slabs), etc. However, since the programs available may vary depending on the season, it is recommended to check before visiting the Pungnyu Culture Center. Sitting with a brush and writing on traditional Korean paper will make you feel calm and relaxed both physically and mentally.

stories.title: "Chungbuk Cultural Center "
stories.script: "In 1937, when the Chungbuk Provincial Office was relocated from Jungang Park to its current location, the governor's official residence was established near the provincial office in 1939. The building was built in Western style in the front and Japanese style in the back, differentiating its public and private spaces. It was used as the governor's official residence for a long time, and then opened to Chungbuk residents in September 2012 as a new cultural space.  Now, the House of Culture, a book cafe, the Forest Gallery, and an outdoor concert hall are operated under the Chungbuk Cultural Center. The floral landscaping alongside the unique building creates a welcoming atmosphere. The site has been designated as National Registered Cultural Heritage No. 353. "

stories.title: Gyeonghwa Market (Fifth-Day Market)
stories.script: Do you smell something delicious?   Gyeonghwa Market is held every five days in front of the Gyeonghwa station. Although it is held throughout the Gunhangje Festival, it is a normal road where cars pass by on regular days. The market takes place on days ending in a 3 or an 8. There are so many people and stores gathered that you may forget this is a regular car road. As the market is held regularly, there are a variety of good eats ranging from puffed rice cakes that pop with a loud sound to freshly extracted perilla oil with a nice nutty smell, hotteock, which is the griddlecake with sugar filling, hot rice soup, and even crispy fried chicken! The market is full of delicious smell that it makes you crave more food. In addition to delicious gourmets, you can also buy horticultural plants, agricultural equipment, pottery, handicraft accessories, and every other daily necessity at a relatively low price. Another thing to see is mid-aged women shopping with a basket and their bargaining skills. Why don’t you look around the Gyeonghwa Market with food in one hand?

stories.title: 1. Jagalchi Market (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.audioTitle: 1. Jagalchi Market (Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market)
stories.script: What do you think Jagalchi means in Jagalchi Market? One might assume it's the name of a famous fish in Busan, like hairtail or sauries, but Jagalchi actually refers to the beach here, named for the large number of pebbles (jagal in Korean). The name is a blend of Jagal and Chi, the Chinese character for hill. Originally, this fishing village, where pebbles chattered along with the waves, was known as Nambin, meaning southern waterside. Interestingly, the land you're standing on was once the rippling sea, not the top of a pebble hill. Traces of the embankment, built to prevent seawater from flooding, can be found from BIFF Square, indicating extensive land reclamation.  In 1928, Japanese invaders reclaimed Nambin and established Namhang Port, named after Nampo-dong. The port facilitated frequent incoming and outgoing fishing boats, leading to the establishment of a fish market called Nambin Market. It primarily traded seafood, agricultural produce, and vegetables. Later, some merchants began selling small amounts of fish caught by small boats, marking the inception of the Jagalchi Ajimae. Following the Liberation and subsequent war, Busan's population nearly doubled. Facing financial constraints, many opted to start small seafood stands. The Busan Metropolitan City cracked down on these stands post-war. Despite this, the resilient Jagalchi Ajimae fiercely resisted. In one incident, an elderly woman, desperate about the situation, hugged a police officer, dragging both into the sea. Subsequently, Busan City abandoned restrictions on the Ajimaes, instead constructing a three-story building to house all the stands.  Officially, Jagalchi Market refers only to the glass building adorned with a structure resembling a flying seagull. However, locals consider all the old markets and stores, between the stock fish market near Yeongdodaegyo Bridge and the fish market in Chungmu-dong, as part of Jagalchi Market. This is because Jagalchi Market was a community-created space. It boasts over 300 fish types, including hairtail, mackerel, minke whales, great white sharks, and sunfish. You can glimpse into the lives of Busan's people here. Undoubtedly, Jagalchi Market reflects the map of Busan citizens’ lives.

stories.title: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 4. Bupyeong Kkangtong Market
stories.audioTitle: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 4. Bupyeong Kkangtong Market
stories.script: Original City Center of Busan - Gukje Market, Jagalchi Market: 4. Bupyeong Kkangtong Market  Just across the street from Gukje Market, there exists another enormous market. It is rare to see two such large-sized markets right next to each other even when looking throughout the whole country. While Gukje Market was a market that came about by chance during a period of historic upheaval through Liberation and war, the Bupyeong Market had been a major marketplace in the area since the Joseon Dynasty.  After the port was opened to foreign trades, the Japanese came into this market that had been here since the days of Joseon and began to call it “Ilhan Market”. “Ilhan Market” opened everyday except for the first day of every month, and since during the time, a market that would open five-days a week was the norm, many Joseon people stood in lines to check out the first permanent market they had ever seen in their lives. Thanks to this Bupyeong Market was able to stably and also endured the troubled times of Liberation and the war in a relatively peaceful manner. It was definitely a different vibe from Gukje Market, which was also known as Doddegi Market with its many shabby stands. As the Joseon people took over the stores that had been abandoned by the Japanese, Bupyeong Market was reborn as a market of Joseon. This was also around about the time when “Busan Fish Cakes”, one of the most famous foods of Busan, was created. In 1910s, many stores that cook and sell fish cakes were set up here to respond to the needs of the increasing Japanese population. In one of the official records of the Japanese Government-General of Korea, it even describes how “rice, fish cakes, vegetables and fruits were primarily sold at Ilhan Market”. The fish cake alley in Bupyeong Market was also a natural outcome of merchants who had taken over stores from the Japanese after Liberation, while competitively developing their own recipes.  Bupyeong Market began to enjoy great prosperity when American soldiers replaced the fleeing Japanese. The name, Kkangtong Market, was coined around this time because the main goods sold and purchased then were canned foods that trickled out from the U.S. Army bases in the aftermath of the Korean War. Then, as those who had taken part in the Vietnam War brought and sold C-ration, a type of combat food of the U.S. Army, the name stuck for good. Another name for Bupyeong Market is Dokkaebi Market. Even after the Vietnam War, peddlers obtained foreign goods and sold them to the Bupyeong Kkangtong Market, however, the trading of items that had not gone through customs was not legal at all. So merchants would briefly unpack their bags of goods, and once the police showed up, quickly pack up everything and disappear. The nickname, Dokkaebi, stems from how they repeatedly appeared and disappeared.  During the days when supplies were nowhere near abundant, Bupyeong Kkangtong Market was a new world for the Busan people. There were no “foreign imports” that one could not buy at the market, from the latest electronic devices to liquor and cigarettes, and even cosmetics. The reputation of Bupyeong Kkangtong Market has slightly faded in an era where it is not so difficult to find foreign products or travel overseas, but for tourists, the market still offers a variety of things to see.

stories.title: Dwaejigukbap—A Hearty Meal That Combines Taste and Warmth
stories.audioTitle: Dwaejigukbap—A Hearty Meal That Combines Taste and Warmth
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! Let’s dive into Dwaejigukbap—a rich, comforting pork and rice soup that reflects the bold energy of Busan.  Dwaejigukbap is a well-loved local dish from Busan, made with a milky pork broth served alongside rice and side dishes. You can mix the rice into the soup or eat it on the side—whatever you prefer. The broth is pre-cooked, so when you order, it’s reheated quickly over high heat, making it a fast and filling meal.  For centuries, Gukbap—rice served in hot broth—has been known as the go-to meal for travelers. Merchants and scholars on long journeys would stop at roadside taverns to get something warm and filling. A simple bowl of Gukbap was just what they needed to rest and recharge.  After Korea’s industrialization in the 1970s, more pig farms made it easier and cheaper to get quality domestic pork. In Busan, a major port city, the rise of meat-processing plants meant fresh pork and by-products could be used to make rich, flavorful broth. That’s how dwaejigukbap grew into a local favorite—something like Korean-style fast food, but also warm and comforting like soul food. Over time, this led to the creation of Busan’s famous Dwaejigukbap Street.  How about a hot, hearty bowl of Dwaejigukbap to feel the flavor and history of this harbor city? It’s a meal that captures the warmth of Busan—one you won’t forget.

stories.title: Puffer Fish: Busan's High-End Gourmet Dining
stories.audioTitle: Puffer Fish: Busan's High-End Gourmet Dining
stories.script: Welcome to your K-local food trip! The highlight of this culinary journey is Busan’s Puffer Fish, an exquisite winter delicacy that's not to be missed.  Known for its unique appearance and strong toxins, Puffer Fish is often considered dangerous. Despite this, its pleasantly chewy texture and mild flavor have long made it a beloved delicacy among gourmet food lovers. Because only licensed professionals can handle Puffer Fish, it’s not readily available everywhere.  If you want to truly experience Puffer Fish cuisine at its best, Busan is the perfect destination. Busan’s Puffer Fish cuisine began in the 1920s, when chefs from Japan—the birthplace of Puffer Fish dishes—moved to Busan. They brought their culinary traditions with them, introducing the city to authentic Japanese-style Puffer Fish cooking. Busan soon became a major hub for fresh Puffer Fish caught off Korea's southern coast. Easy access to fresh catches helped the local Puffer Fish culinary culture flourish naturally.  During the cold winter months, Puffer Fish comes into peak season—its flesh growing plumper, richer, and even more flavorful. There are many delicious ways to enjoy Puffer Fish—from hot Bokguk (Puffer Fish soup) and spicy Bok-bulgogi, to marinated chewy Puffer Fish skin. But the most beloved dish of all is definitely Bokguk, or Puffer Fish soup. Bokguk features a clear, mild broth filled with tender Puffer Fish meat, crunchy bean sprouts, and aromatic water dropwort. Gentle and soothing for your stomach, it's the perfect remedy for a hangover or as a nourishing meal in the cold winter months. When Koreans describe a hot soup as Siwonhada, meaning Refreshing, they're not referring to its temperature. Instead, they're expressing the soothing sense of relief and comfort it brings.  Enjoy a bowl of warm, comforting Puffer Fish soup that refreshes both your body and mind. Experience the true depth of fine dining in Busan, a romantic coastal city known for its stunning ocean views.

stories.title: Royal Tomb of Queen Suro
stories.audioTitle: Princess from Ayodha became Queen Suro - Legend of Marriage
stories.script: Princess from Ayodha became Queen Suro - Legend of Marriage  This is the Royal Tomb of Queen Suro. There is a legend about the marriage of King Suro and his Queen.   According to this legend, Queen Suro was originally an Indian princess. One day, her parents received a divine revelation that she was destined to marry King Suro, and so the princess travelled to Gaya and married the king in accordance with her parents' instructions.   The power of destiny was strong enough to lure the princess to Gaya from faraway India. Although it is impossible to verify and is only a story that has been passed down through the generations, there is a clue that may support the legend at the entrance to the Royal Tomb of King Suro. At the entrance gate, there’s a drawing featuring a motif of two fish facing each other. These fish are representative symbols of Ayodhya in India, believed to be the hometown of the princess, and appear on public buildings, on police insignia, and even on taxi number plates in the area.   Similarities in the motifs of the two fish at the entrance to the tomb and in Ayodhya are cited as proof of ancient links between Gaya and India. It may be coincidental that King Suro’s tomb features the motif representative of Ayodhya, but it is surprising, nonetheless.  On the other hand, some historians insist that Queen Suro was not from India. According to the legend of her marriage, she brought with her many goods from China. This suggests that she may have migrated from China or have been a merchant visiting China.   There’s no way to conclusively determine the heritage of the Queen. We only know that she was a mysterious and courageous woman who travelled to Gaya to marry King Suro.

stories.title: Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace
stories.audioTitle: A whale’s dream, embarking on a journey back in time
stories.script: [Man]	  Whales seem to spend an eternity swimming across the deep blue ocean. Where could they be right now?  [Woman] Whales swim across the ocean, but so do fishermen.They sail across the open sea, hoping to catch a glimpse of whales breaking the surface.   [Man] Whalers were the envy of all fishermen! Today, our destination is Jangsaengpo in Ulsan, a port that used to be a forward base for whalers. It’s a place with fascinating tales from the waters off the coast of Ulsan!  [Together] A whale’s dream. Let’s embark on a journey back in time.     Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace    [Man] Daegokcheon is a tributary of the Taehwagang River in Ulsan. The sound of water rushing through the tranquil valley is the only thing that breaks the silence here. There is a special boulder here.A special boulder in Ulsan.. Hey Suji, can you guess which boulder I’m talking about?  [Woman] Of course, I can. You’re talking about the “Petroglyph Rock,” right? Petroglyphs are found almost all over the world across different points in time, and they are known as the oldest form of art created by humans.  [Man] You’re absolutely right. features more than 300 pieces of illustrations scattered  across an 8m x 5m patch of rock face on a cliff. Most of the illustrations depict marine animals such as sharks and seals, or land animals such as deer and tigers. But, if you take a closer look, you might find something strange.  [Woman] Let me see... you said most of the drawings are about animals...But here, the Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace seem to have a lot of whales!   [Man] You’re right. In total, there are 58 whales. Whales live in the deep ocean. Why do you think people drew whales on a rock in the middle of the mountain?  [Interview with Park Ki-nam, a Cultural and Tourism Commentator working in the Ulsan area.] Given the high concentration illustrations created using a side relief technique, we can estimate that the drawings were created 7,000 years ago during the prehistoric era. The Neolithic Era to be precise. The reason why there are so many whales is because our ancestors who settled in Ulsan 7,000 years ago hunted whales. Nearby, we have found artifacts such as a harpoon embedded in whale bone. That is why we think there are so many illustrations related to whaling in Bangudae.  [Woman] Now I get it. The illustrations are so detailed, I can’t believe they’re from the Neolithic Era. Some pictures even show the detailed features of whales and depict how they like seaweed. They are so intricate, I almost think people may have actually gone into the water to observe the whales with their own eyes.  [Man] We can enjoy these amazing pieces of art thanks to the artists astonishing powers of observation. You can spend several hours looking at different illustrations, but there is one particular picture that attracts my attention. It’s the picture of people dragging a whale that appears bigger than their boat.  [Woman] How on earth did they manage to catch a whale that appears to be as large as a house?  [Male] The key to answering that question lies in the Petroglyphs. Do you see that long, sharp thing jutting out of the whale’s back?  [Woman] Is that a ‘harpoon’? You mean, those prehistoric people fought whales with harpoon?  [Man] That’s correct. They caught giant whales with tiny harpoons that appear ridiculous compared to the size of the whales. This is a remarkable series of events that happened 7,000 years ago in the sea.  [Woman] But, there are several other parts at the Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace, apart from whale hunting, that do not make much sense. How did people manage to preserve these Petroglyphs for thousands of years?  [Man] That involves some sophisticated calculations. Did you know that archaeologists discovered the foundations of old houses from the prehistoric period near the banks of Taehwagang River?  [Woman] They found it on the banks of Taehwagang River... isn’t that almost 30km away from Bangudae?  [Man] That’s right. But there is a reason why prehistoric humans traveled all the way from their houses to Bangudae. The answer lies on the top area of the rock. Bangudae has a rock that juts out between 2m to 4m out at the top like a roof. In other words, the Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace was the only place in the area where people could find protection against wind, rain, or snow.  [Woman] Wow!.. I guess all the leg work looking for clues linked to the Petroglyphs paid off.  [Interview with Park Ki-nam, a Cultural and Tourism Commentator working in the Ulsan area. ] The Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace are widely acknowledged as the first record of humans hunting whales. It contains information about the distinct maritime culture in the North Pacific during the prehistoric period, which is why it has been included in the tentative list of World Heritage Sites. Also, the illustrations of whales seems to indicate that whales were an important food source for Neolithic humans. They caught whales together as a group, and shared the meat as well  [Man] Whalers who fought the rough seas with high hopes of a good catch tried to pass on the wisdom of whaling to their children with petroglyphs because they did not yet have a written language system. That’s why prehistoric humans drew the illustrations on the Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace    Ulsan Petroglyph Museum    [Man] If you travel a little further from Bangudae, you’ll arrive at the Ulsan Petroglyph Museum.Also nearby is the Cheonjeon-ri valley. Cheonjeon-ri valley used to be a popular road for Hwarang cadets during the Shilla Dynasty. They even created a visitor’s log on the rocks. That’s just another thing that makes the Ulsan Petroglyph Museum so special. First of all, it’s the only petroglyph museum in Korea.  If you want to visit a petroglyph museum, Ulsan is the only place you can go to. Also, from the sky, the museum looks like a whale. The museum was built thanks to the sheer fact that Bangudae Terrace had such historically important petroglyphs.  [Woman] If you want to learn more about petroglyphs, it might be a great idea to visit the museum and take your time touring its exhibits.  [Man] Bangudae Terrace has beautiful petroglyphs, but it is also famous for its gorgeous scenery. “Gyeomjae” Jeong Seon, a famous painter who lived during the late Joseon Dynasty used to come to paint the landscape near Bangudae...enough said, right? Meanwhile, “Poeun” Jeong Mong-ju, a noble official who lived during the late Goryeo Dynasty, was so enamored with the strange rock formations of Bangudae when he was exiled, called it “Poeundae.”  [Woman] Historical figures loved this place, too. All those whales in Ulsan and the Petroglyphs...I feel like really want to go on a trip now.  [Man] If you’re heading to Ulsan, there’s another place I want to recommend.    Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village    [Man] I’m talking about Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village.  [Woman] I’ve heard of Jangsaengpo in Ulsan. Apparently, you can see whales in the area from time to time.  [Man] In fact, there is an interesting story about Jangsaengpo Village. In the not-so-distant past, whaling made the entire village so rich that, people used to say, “even the village dogs carry rolls of cash.”   [Woman] Haha! Imagine dogs around the village carrying rolls of 	cash... I know there’s a 		statue of a dog holding money in its mouth. How did people catch so many whales near Jangsaengpo?  [Man] Well, that requires a little history lesson. In 1899, a whaling company in Russia decided to butcher whales in Jangsaengpo because they needed a whaling base to process large whales caught in the East Sea. After that, when Japan defeated Russia in the Russo-Japanese War, Japan monopolized the whaling base in Jangsaengpo. During the Japanese colonial rule of Korea, the waters near Jangsaengpo remained extremely profitable. Each year, whalers caught more than 100 whales, including gray whales and white whales. Here, Korean people mostly served as petty crewmen. But after our country won independence, Korean fishermen opened a company named the Joseon Whaling Corporation.  [Woman] Wow. That just seems so much fairer.  [Man] During the 1970s, whalers began using 100-ton iron ships, the whaling industry became much more substantial in size. But soon, the success story of Jangsaengpo came to an abrupt halt.    [Interview with Park Chang Hye-gyeong, a Cultural and Tourism Commentator working in the Ulsan area. ] Jangsaengpo in Ulsan is a port city that has a rather unfortunate history. It suffered from numerous raids and attacs from Japanese pirates, and it had to endure wars such as the naval battle of Ulsan and the Korean War. Today, it has become a place where countless people visit to get a taste of how things were during the days when whaling was a prominent industry.  [Man] Despite countless raids and attacks from Japanese pirates, Jangsaengpo survived. But, after some reckless whaling practices around the world drove a few whale species into extinction, the International Whaling Commission decided to ban all commercial whaling as of 1986.  [Woman] That means the fishermen at Jangsaengpo lost their livelihood literally overnight.  [Man] That’s right.. Whaling ships were moored in port, never to sail again. Soon, they disappeared into the history books.  [Woman] Whaling used to represent a glowing dream for the fishermen in Jangsaengpo. It took up their entire lives. Does Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village tell the same story you just told me?  [Man] Yes it does. Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village was created to show people how things looked and felt during the heyday of whaling.   [Woman] If you take the monorail from Whale Cultural Square, you will pass by the blue skies and arrive at Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village! Jangsaengpo Whale Cultural Village offers plenty of features to see and enjoy, including the “Goraemadang (Whale Plaza)” that shows you the history of whales since prehistoric times, and the Whale Sculpture Park with a life-size representation of a whale.  [Man] In particular, “Jangsaengpo Old Town” which features a diorama-like reproduction of people carrying out everyday activities is the most popular attraction among tourists.  [Woman] From the butchery where people would butcher freshly caught whales, then onto the whale restaurant that used to sell boiled whale meat! Walking through every single street makes me feel like I’ve been transported back in time to the bustling village of Jangsaengpo.  [Man] At one point, ‘being the county mayor or being the harpoon gunner’ was a legitimate debate.That’s how popular whaling was Another popular feature at the village is the harpoon gunners home. Wouldn’t it be fun to actually see a real harpoon gun?  [Woman] Was harpooning like the next up-and-coming job? I bet people were rewarded quite handsomely because the success rate was so high.  [Man] Back then, people could tell which ship had caught a whale just by listening to the horn. Watching butchers butchering a whale was like a game for the village people.   [Woman] As the butchering comes to an end, the sun begins to set. I think I can almost hear someone’s mom yelling, “Come on in for dinner.” Jangsaengpo is an old town that brings up the nostalgia of home and feels warm and generous.  [Man] When the time comes, whales travel the East Sea for thousands of kilometers, and return to the waters of Jangsaengpo. The reason why whales return to Jangsaengpo in Ulsan is because it is their home.   [Woman] Jangsaengpo, on the shores of the East Sea, used to be the home of gray whales. Today, the gray whale is an endangered species. Why did gray whales call Jangsaengpo their home?  [Interview with Park Chang Hye-gyeong, a Cultural and Tourism Commentator working in the Ulsan area. ] The tidal changes in Ulsan are not as severe as some other regions. The water is relatively shallow, and has a higher degree of salinity. These conditions make Jangsaengpo the perfect place to give birth to new calves. People also believe whales would have eaten the seaweed in Ulsan, which grows in vast quantities, to recover after giving birth to their babies.  [Woman] Apart from Jangsaengpo, you can also see whales migrating back to Korea at ‘Cape Ganjeolgot which is the very first place in Korea where you can see the sunrise. Cape Ganjeolgot is such a popular destination, right?  [Man] Tourists from all over country head over there on New Year’s Day. Along with Jangsaengpo, Bangeojinhang Port in Ulsan and Guryongpo Port in Pohang are famous for whale-watching. Bangeojinhang is also known for its modern history street. So, taking a tour of Bangeojinhang after Ganjeolgot and Jangsaeongpo might just be the final touch that finalizes your travel plans. Watch the sunrise at Cape Ganjeolgot, watch some whales at Jangsaengpo, and learn about local history in Bangeojinhang.   [Woman] If you walk along the seawall at Bangeojinhang, you’ll get to see sculptures inspired by whales.Apparently, they were created on the theme of “Wish towards the sea.” If you look closer, though, you might realize that they are reproductions of illustrations from the Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace.   [Man] Thousands of years ago, prehistoric people used to hunt whales and draw their achievements on the Petroglyphs at the Bangudae Terrace.  [Woman] Fishermen from Jangsaengpo also set sail into the open ocean with dreams of catching whales.For the locals, whales were a symbol of hope and dreams.  [Man] The East Sea, where all the wales used to be, has a warmth that makes it feel like home. Like the whales returning home to the East Sea, we hope you can travel to Ulsan, with hopes and dreams of a better tomorrow.

stories.title: Hakseong Park Area_Ulsan Japanese Fortress
stories.script: The Story of a Fortress Built by the Japanese During the Japanese Invasions of Korea   Ulsan Japanese Fortress was a major transportation hub to mainland Japan for the Japanese forces because it's located right next to Taehwagang River, making it possible to send and receive goods by boat.   Dosanseong Fortress, which was named as such because the mountain looked like an island, is also known as the Japanese Fortress because it was built by the Japanese forces during the Japanese Invasions of Korea.  In August 1597, in the 30th year of King Seonjo’s reign, the Toyotomi regime of Japan ordered the invasion of Korea once more after the truce talks failed to yield results.   At the time, the Japanese forces built a number of fortresses along the south coast of the Korean Peninsula, and Ulsan Japanese Fortress is one of them.  The fortress was designed by the Japanese daimyo Kato Kiyomasa, and built by using the rocks from Ulsaneupseong Fortress and the Military Headquarters in Ulsan.   It was around the time when the Japanese ships failed to land on the west coast after their defeat in the Battle of Myeongnyang against General Yi Sun-shin and the retreat of the Japanese troops to the coasts of Gyeongsang-do and Jeolla-do after they were also defeated while advancing to the norther part of the Korean Peninsula.    The allied forces of Joseon and Ming saw their retreat and decided to launch an attack on Ulsan Japanese Fortress, which served as the main supply base for the Japanese troops. Today, it’s popularly known as the Battle of Dosanseong in Korea.   At the onset of the battle, the Joseon Army succeeded in advancing past the outer walls of Ulsan Japanese Fortress, and won a number of small and big battles with the help of the Ulsan Righteous Army.   Ulsan Japanese Fortress was the biggest battleground during the Japanese Invasions of Korea, and it was where the Japanese forces decided to retreat.    For this reason, the status of Ulsan was raised to “dohobu” and Chunguisa Shrine was built on the opposite side of Ulsan Japanese Fortress to house the ancestral tablets of 242 soldiers who died fighting the battles of Ulsan.

stories.title: Dongbaekseom
stories.script: Dongbaekseom  Named Dongbaekseom due to its abundance of Dongbaek Trees, it was transformed into a place for the 2005 APEC Summit Meeting in Busan and has since become a famous attraction where many world leaders have visited.  Dongbaekseom used to be a small island just off the coast of Haeundae however due to sedimentation, over a long period of time, became connected to the mainland. The island was also called “Darimiseom” for its resemblance to an iron. In “Come Back to Busan Port”, a song by Cho Yong-pil, there is a line that goes, “Spring came to Dongbaekseom, where flowers are”, and the Dongbaekseom in the lyrics is in fact this island itself. Every spring, it becomes a red island on top a blue sea due to its complete covereage in red flowers.  Dongbaekseom is where the “Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit Meeting” was held in November 2005. APEC is an international organization and summit of countries on the Pacific Rim that discuss a variety of topics such as economics and politics while solidifying their partnerships. When the summit was held in Busan, the status and details of the meeting were reported in real time around the world showcasing the amount of attention that the event had gotten globally.  No cars are allowed on Dongbaekseom. Instead, one can only walk throughout the island because while the yacht club side has flat paths, the Haeundae side is made of cliffs. Where the flat road meets the cliffs sits the “Nurimaru House,” the place where the APEC Summit Meeting was held. The inside of the meeting house still remains as it was so visitors can see with their own eyes the desks and chairs that were used by the leaders of the countries in attendance.  On the side where the Dongbaekseom lighthouse is, there is a stone on which the story of Choe Chiwon, who is known to have created the name “Haeundae,” and the name in Chinese characters are engraved. As you walk along the cliff path from the lighthouse you will see a short suspension bridge and a mermaid statue depicting the legend of Princess Hwangok who came for marriage from the kingdom of mermaids. The cliff section is narrow and has steep steps so make sure to pass safely and let other people pass by first, if needed.

stories.title: Hwawangsan Mountain in Changnyeong
stories.script: Hwawangsan Mountain in Changnyeong Fortress surrounded by azalea and silver grass  Hwawangsan Mountain is a famous mountain of Changnyeong-gun. Its old name is “Bulmoe,” meaning a mountain blowing out the fire. The current name Hwawang originated from the meaning of the old name. There are many tourist spots in Hwawang Mountain, including Hwawangsanseong Fortress and Eoksae Plain which can be reached only when you climb up the mountain as it is located at the top of the mountain.  You need to choose the most suitable course to get to the peak. The most common course is from Jahagok Ticket Booth close to the downtown of Changnyeong and the Okcheon Ticket Booth nearby the Okcheon Reservoir. Since each course has a different level of difficulty, it is recommended you start climbing with hiking equipment. However, if you just want a casual hike with sneakers on, taking the Jahagok Course 3 that passes the Doseongam Hermitage to the West Gate of the Hwawangsangseong Fortress would be a good choice.  If you go up to the top along the hiking trail, you can see the view of winding mountain ranges and Changnyeong. Inside the fortress, you can see the beautiful silver grass waves at the Eoksae Plain. The fortress was built for the purpose of defense by using the cliffs and ridges at the top, but it is unknown when it was built. Still, the story of the General Gwak Jae-u, dubbed the Red Robe General, defeating the Japanese army led by Kato Giyomasa here at Hwawangsanseong Fortress is well-known.  Landscape around Hwawangsanseong Fortress changes every season. In spring, the place is filled with pink-colored azalea along the trail. During fall, a vast silver grass field creates a splendid view of golden silver grass waving in the wind. Due to these beautiful sceneries, many Korean TV series including Dae Jang Geum (Jewel in the Palace), Sangdo, Wangcho, and Mr. Sunshine were filmed here. Nearby the East Gate, you can visit an actual filming site of the legendary series Hur Jun.  When enjoying the view, watch your step at all times as there are many cliffs at the top. Since no safety fence is installed here, walking the inner road of the fortress is highly recommended.  <This guide was recorded by Kim Ha-rim of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Changnyeong Uponeup Marsh (1988)
stories.script: In Changnyeong, which has been long referred to as the “Fire Village” from the Gaya Era, there is a large marsh. Uponeup Marsh, located about 10 minutes by bus from downtown Changnyeong, is the second marsh designated as the Ramsar Wetland in Korea. It is the largest of the wetlands in the country.  Uponeup Marsh is so large that, depending on where you depart from, you can see and experience whole different things. In general, visitors start at the Ecological Center. This route is suitable for a walking trip or bicycle trip, which is recommended to those who want to take a slow stroll. If you want to see migratory birds, start at the parking lot of Somok Village.  Uponeup Marsh includes Upo, Sajipo and Mokpo sections, as well as Jjokjibeol and sanbakbeol wetlands.These are the names made during the Japanese colonial period, and their original Korean names are Sobeol, Namubeol, and Moraeboel. People who lived here for a long time prefer to call them by their old Korean name. The marsh was created by Topyeongcheon Stream and Nakdonggang River nearby. It is assumed that the bank was piled up following the flow of the river and stagnated water, thereby creating the Uponeup Marsh today. It used to play the role of the reservoir in the past. It was also a fishing spot to catch freshwater fish by riding a boat or throwing a net. Now is the home to migratory birds, freshwater fish, and wild plants. Ecological Wetland School and Ecological Experience Center provide both educational and scientific opportunities to see and learn about the ecosystem of the wetland and experience dugout canoe riding, loach fishing, and aquatic insect hunting. Come and see the famous Uponeup Marsh.   <This guide was recorded by Kwon So-hyun of Korea Tourism Organization through talent donation.>

stories.title: Cape Ganjeolgot
stories.audioTitle: New hope rises in the East Sea
stories.script: Ganjeolgot Cape is a popular natural tourist attraction thanks to the fact that it is the very first place on mainland Korea where you can see the sunrise.     The name “Ganjeolgot” comes from the Cape’s distinct shape - it resembles a long pole if you look at it from the sea.      The Cape Ganjeolgot lighthouse has guided seafarers for close to a century now. Built under the Japanese colonial rule of Korea, the lighthouse has witnessed all the joys and sorrows of the Korean people as they endured war and earned their peace. You can climb up the lighthouse, look out into the vast East Sea, and imagine a pack of whales swimming by the Cape.      The Wishing Postbox is another popular feature at Cape Ganjeolgot. Don’t you want to sit down next to the 5m-tall, giant postbox and write a little postcard as a keepsake?    Meanwhile, Pohang is home to Cape Homigot, one of the best places to enjoy the sunrise in Korea along with Cape Ganjeolgot. Pohang is also known for its “Sunrise Alliance” with Ulsan and Gyeongju.     Every year, Cape Ganjeolgot hosts a Sunrise Festival on the 1st of January, and it invites everyone to witness the hope of a new year rise above the horizon.

stories.title: Taehwagang Grand Park
stories.audioTitle: King Seongjong’s favorite pavilion Taehwaru and Simnidaesup (Simni Bamboo Grove) at the Taehwagang Grand Park
stories.script: The Simnidaesup (Simni Bamboo Grove) at the Taehwagang Grand Park sits along Taehwagang River, a major river that flows through the heart of Ulsan.      In summer, the Park is home to more than 8,000 White Herons, and in winter, it offers shelter for 100,000 or so Rooks and Jackdaws. Moreover, Taehwagang Grand Park is well-known for having the largest bamboo forest trail in the country  Taehwaru Pavilion offers panoramic views of Taehwagang River. But it has more than just beautiful views. It also has plenty of secrets to tell.  King Seongjong was the sixth monarch of the Goryeo Dynasty. One year, on his way to Seorabeol (capital city of the Shilla Dynasty), the King made his way to Ulsan. There, he hosted a banquet at the Taehwaru Pavilion which was hailed as one of the eight must-see attractions in the Ulju region at the time.   Taehwaru Pavilion was originally built as a bell tower for Taehwasa Temple by Buddhist monk Jajang during the reign of Queen Seondeok of Shilla.   Thanks to its outstanding views, Taehwaru Pavilion has been quoted in more than 100 poems written by top poets in Korean history such as Kim Si-seup, Kwon Geun, and Seo Geo-jeong.    According to the History of Goryeo, King Seongjong hosted a banquet and ate a large fish caught from the sea.  Historians have hypothesized that Taehwaru Pavilion was near the East Sea, rather than the Taehwagang River.  Based on this theory, some have argued that the large fish the King ate may have been a whale which used to inhabit the waters off the coast of Ulsan since prehistoric times.            Meanwhile, the dense bamboo forest of Simnidaesup (Simni Bamboo Grove) has become a popular place for healing and recuperation along with Bomun Tourist Complex in Gyeongju and Sabang Memorial Park in Pohang.

stories.title: Entrance to Gamcheon Culture Village (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.audioTitle: Entrance to Gamcheon Culture Village (Gamcheon Culture Village)
stories.script: The Beginning of Gamcheon Culture Village  The stream flowing at the foot of Cheonmasan Mountain used to be called “Gamnae,” which literally means sweetness in Korean, referring to its sweet taste. During the period of Japanese occupation and the Korean War, approximately 4,000 Taegeukdo religion believers gathered in this area. Subsequently, more people, including merchants and refugees, moved to the area, forming a village. Initially named Cheondeok-dong, the area eventually split due to increased population, forming a new area named “Gamcheon-dong,” which further separated into “Gamcheon 1-dong” and “Gamcheon 2-dong.”  Gamcheon-dong was initially constructed with around 1,000 shacks on slopes when the Taegeukdo followers relocated to this site. In the aftermath of the war, severe shortages of supplies and living spaces afflicted the residents. Originally, the village was built as a communal residence village, all inhabitants shared wells and bathrooms, leading to increased inconvenience as the population grew. Moreover, shacks were susceptible to fire hazards. Therefore, three 6-meter-wide vertical stairs were installed as a safety measure, which still exist in the village today.  From its initial planning stages, Gamcheon Village was designed to ensure houses at the back would not obstruct the view and to maintain a pedestrian lane in front of the houses. These planning considerations contribute to the colorful and well-organized village seen today. Unfortunately, the village started to decline as its facilities deteriorated, prompting residents to seek better living conditions elsewhere. To revitalize the village's atmosphere, the government initiated the “Gamcheon Village Art Project.” This project involves installing artwork in the village annually, aiming to enhance residents' quality of life. The renovated village eventually became a popular tourist spot for visits and photography.  An information center is situated at the village entrance, where visitors can purchase a map of the village. Additionally, visitors can converse with village guides who provide course guidance and explanations. It's essential to note that touring the village is permitted only between 9 AM and 6 PM, and visitors should refrain from peeping into residents' houses or taking photos without their consent.

stories.title: Kim Daljin Literary Museum and Birth Home of Kim Daljin
stories.audioTitle: Kim Daljin Literary Museum and Birth Home of Kim Daljin
stories.script: Kim Daljin Literary Museum was constructed by his disciple to pass down the passion for Buddhism and literature of Kim Daljin who lived as a scholar of the Chinese classics, teacher, monk, and poet by restoring his private house in Jinhae. This hall is highly appreciated as the “Best Literature Hall in 2016” by the Korean Literature House Association. The museum consists of an underground and a ground floor. The birth home of Kim is located nearby. The appearance of the museum gives off a benevolent feeling like an old country school. Before entering the museum, visitors can appreciate the creative artwork of children. The actual size of his photo greets the visitors at the entrance. Visitors can see actual items used by Kim as well as his research documents to look back on his life and literature work. Art Street near the museum reenacts scenes from daily life in the 1930s. The birth home of Kim Daljin has a wide yard as well as a vegetable and flower garden, giving off a homely atmosphere that well demonstrates his warm and soft personality. If you want to learn about Korea's past and literature of Kim, how about visiting Kim Daljin Literary Museum in Changwon?

stories.title: Eulsukdo Island — Nakdong River Culture Pavilion
stories.audioTitle: Eulsukdo Island — Nakdong River Culture Pavilion
stories.script: " Nakdong River Culture Pavilion was first opened to tell the diverse stories of Nakdonggang River, which flows up to 317 miles and holds beauty and lives in its arms. Nakdonggang Estuary is a brackish water zone where river water and sea water meet. It features reed fields and an abundance of foods, which makes it a perfect seasonal home for over 170 kinds of migratory birds.  Inside the culture center, you may not only check out the culture surrounding the river but also enjoy world-renowned artworks with the theme of river. It is also a great experiential learning space that teaches why living organisms in water cannot live in a polluted river or what we have to do to protect our environment in a very detailed and transparent manner even for children to easily understand.  When you look at Nakdonggang Estuary from the rooftop garden of the building, you may witness once in a while fish that jumps out and back into the river as if it were dancing. You can also find birds who are waiting for those fish. The culture center offers a live view of the river, which you have only learned through pictures and texts.  Now, shall we move onto Nakdonggang Estuary Eco Center?  "

stories.title: Bangeojin_Sori Experience Center
stories.script: The 9 Sounds of Dong-gu   The Sound Experience Center in Seuldo Island was established with the concept of reverberation. This is Korea’s first Sound Experience Center made with the theme of 9 Sounds of Dong-gu of Ulsan.   The 9 Sounds of Dong-gu are the early morning bell sound at Dongchuksa Temple, the sound of the wind blowing through Magolsan Mountain, the sound of Ongnyucheon Stream in the valley, the sound of the engines at Hyundai Heavy Industries, the sound of a new ship whistling, sound of the horn from the Ulgi Lighthouse, the sound of water flowing from the pebbles near Daewangam Rock, the sound of the waves at Seuldo Island, and the sound of the tides touching the pebbles on Jujeon Beach.   The 9 Sounds of Dong-gu, Ulsan is available to listen in order in Exhibit Hall 1 on the first floor of the Sound Experience Center. The second floor is equipped with VR gear, puzzles, and the story of the 9 sounds. There are also great photo spots for souvenir at the Trick Art Photo Zone, and the sculptures related to the 9 sounds.  The view of the evening glow over Seuldo Island seen from the 2nd floor café in the Sound Experience Center is highly recommended.  Just outside the experience center is Seongkkeut Mural Village, which looks like an art museum in itself. This mural alley is called the “Nostalgic Alley Where the Wind Blows” because it brings back old memories for some people. Here, you can appreciate the murals drawn by the local residents, and kick back at a pretty café.    Take a tour of the Sound Experience Center, and walk along the alley with pretty mural paintings.

stories.title: Ocheon Seowon
stories.script: There has been a saying in Daegu since ancient times, “Il-Pa-I-Mu.” It refers to what are considered the best places to live in Daegu. First is Pa-dong, Suseong-gu, where Ocheon Academy of Classical Learning is located, followed by second, Mutae in Buk-gu. In fact, Pa-dong has been a good place for people to live for a long time, to the extent that Neolithic and Bronze Age remains can be found nearby. It can also be said that this place is clean enough to introduce it as Ocheon Academy of Classical Learning in a valley of paradise. As you can see, Ocheon Academy of Classical Learning located in Seodanggol to the southwest of Mount Beobisan in Pa-dong is cozy and quiet, making it a good place for scholars to study or immerse themselves in character development.  Built in 1786 in the 10th year of King Jeongjo, Ocheon Academy of Classical Learning was designed to commemorate Daebong Yang Hee-ji. Daebong Yang Hee-ji passed the government exam in 1474 and met King Seongjong, who gifted him with the new name Yang Hee-ji. The pronunciation of Hee-ji is the same, but the meaning of the Chinese characters is different.   “In a willow tree, few branches are precious. So how about Hee as scarce and Ji for branch?”  “That would be a great honor for me.”  In addition, when Yang Hee-ji asked to resign to take care of his old mother:  Yang Hee-ji has a talent for both literature and defense. So should I dissuade him from resigning?“  Yang Hee-ji is talented in both literature and defense and is a useful person. I would be very happy if you were to dissuade him.“  In this way, Yang Hee-ji, who was recognized by the king and his subjects, later returned to the original name, Hee-ji, received from his parents, and concentrated on learning and nurturing future students. His book, Daebongjip, is enshrined here at Ocheon Academy of Classical Learning.

stories.title: Bongsan Seowon
stories.script: There are many academies of classical learning in Gyeongsang-do, the hometown of nobility, but there are more than 20 in Daegu, the large city. Nestled among residential areas, Bongsan Academy of Classical Learning is situated more like the house of the head of a village rather than an imported structure.  Bongsan Academy of Classical Learning commemorates Muntan Son Rin, a Joseon scholar from Daegu. It all begins with Bongsanjae, which was built in Sang-do, Suseong-gu, when Son Rin was alive. It was later changed to Bongamsa Temple and Bongsan Academy of Classical Learning, but unfortunately was demolished by ordinance during the Daewongun period. However, in 1996, the Bongsan Academy of Classical Learning was rebuilt by the descendants of the Iljik Son clan.  Son Rin held a variety of posts after passing three exams for high office. Should I tell you a story about Son Rin? At the time of the Japanese invasions of Korea in 1592, Son Rin was reading a book in a chestnut forest after enshrining his parents' ancestral tablet in a safe place. But then six or seven Japanese soldiers appeared in front of Son Rin with swords drawn. But Son Rin continued to read his book without any emotion on his face.  What's the matter with this man? He doesn't even look at us, but continues reading. Isn't he even afraid of us?“  After staring at Son Rin for a long time, the Japanese soldiers simply withdrew. Later, Son Rin wrote a poem about this:  White swords looked around, but saw only someone reading. How deplorable not to learn Sono's strategy and wipe away the filth for the sake of the country.

stories.title: Cheongho Seowon
stories.script: This is Cheongho Academy of Classical Learning, neighboring the Deoksan Academy of Classical Learning. Cheongho Academy of Classical Learning is the cradle of education in Daegu. In today's terms, it can be regarded as the most prestigious private university in the eastern part of the city. Just as Suseong-gu is now the center of education in Daegu, it was the same during the Joseon Dynasty.  Cheongho Academy of Classical Learning was built by the Iljik Son family to commemorate Modang Son Cheonul, a Confucian scholar representing Daegu in the mid-Joseon Dynasty and active from the late 16th to the early 17th centuries. In order to follow the principle, If the country is in turmoil, you must sacrifice, Modang Son Cheonul marched out at the head of resistance forces when the Japanese invaded. But Son Cheonul, who lost his parents during the invasion and was unable to bury them properly, was said to have been a devoted son to the point where he built Yeongmodang once the war ended, as if to say, I will never forget you and will adore you forever.“  Son Cheonul is a representative scholar of Daegu, but it is said that he did not pass the exam for high office. It is said that he expressed his disappointment in this way:  From the beginning, gaining and losing is beyond the power of the man. How can we be happy when we have gained, or how can we be sad when we lose? Since ancient times, even those like Yu Bun have been rejected. So now I understand that time and life are always connected.“  Life is timing. You can feel Son Cheonul's belief that the time will come when the world recognizes you. Although he did not pass the exam, the people acknowledged Son Cheonul's studies and told him not to dwell on the results of the exam. Time and life are always connected. It is a quote on which to anchor your thoughts.

stories.title: Deoksan Seowon
stories.script: Finally, after 400 years, a family's hidden secret is revealed. Deoksan Academy of Classical Learning was built to commemorate Nameun Seo Seop, who was a civil servant during the early Joseon Dynasty and remained loyal during hard times. Seo-seop was founder of the Dalseong Seo clan, Panseo Gongpa, and after passing a major exam under King Sejong the Great, served as Ijo-panseo during the reign of King Danjong. But strangely, nothing has been known about Seo Seop. Who erased the records?  In 1920, while Seo Ui-gon, the descendant of Seo Seop, was repairing his house, a box fell on his head. In fact, it was strictly forbidden among the members of the Panseogong family to open the box. However, Pandora's box was suddenly opened, and being curious, So Ui-gon looked inside. Immediately he realized why they said to never open it, and why was there no information on Seo Seop.  Here's what was inside the box. Seo Seop, who saw how the young King Danjong became a scarecrow king under his uncle, Grand Prince Suyang, so the latter could wield power, published Cheokganso, telling Danjong to get rid of his subordinates that were not loyal to him. However, when Grand Prince Suyang learned of this, he flew into a rage and forced Seo Seop into exile. Seo Seop remained loyal to Danjong, but the family, worried that his family and relatives would be angry, sealed Seo Seop's information inside the box. Seo Seop's son, Seo Gam-won, also died in prison after speaking directly to Seongjong. The son was like his father.  400 years later, Seo Seop's descendants and scholars discovered Seo Seop's loyalty and built Cheommoje, the birthplace of Deoksan Academy of Classical Learning in Hwanggeum-dong, where his grave is located. In 1995, it was extensively renovated and expanded to become the Deoksan Academy of Classical Learning you see today.  Lastly, shall we recite a poem that Seo Seop left behind?  I heard there was a person who was exiled to Changsa in the past. Today, I too have been framed by others. Heaven has bestowed upon man the same disposition. Who is the man of evil, and who is the man of good?

stories.title: Gosan School, Ganghak Memorial
stories.script: Gosan, located at the eastern end of Suseong-gu, is called “Lonely Mountain” because it rises out of the fields alone. At the northern foot of this mountain is a historic school, said to have been taught directly by Toegye Ihwang, who was known as the best Confucian scholar in Korea during the Joseon Dynasty.  Gosan School was designated as Cultural Property Material Number 15 of Daegu Metropolitan City in 1984. As a school commemorating the scholars Ihwang, representative of the middle Joseon period, and Ubok Jeong Kyung-se, a student of Ryu Seong-ryong, it began from Gosan Library, built in 1560, later called Gosan Academy of Classical Studies. The school was demolished in 1868, fifth year of King Gojong, due to the abolition of academies by Heungseon Daewongun. It was rebuilt by local scholars in 1879. Only the auditorium on the old site was remodeled and a signboard hung. Since 1964, it has been preserved in its renovated state. In 1879, only the auditorium was restored and named Gosan Seodang. The shrine was restored in 2020. Unfortunately, a fire broke out in 2021 and destroyed the entire auditorium, so only the shrine remains.  It is said that Gosan, used as the name of the school, and Gudo, used as the name of the gate, were designated by Ihwang himself. The two characters, Gudo, written by Ihwang, were put on a signboard which was hung on the door to the Academy of Classical Studies. However, the sign was destroyed during the Japanese invasion. Likewise, at its peak, Gosan Academy had an auditorium, a shrine, a building, a study, and a gatehouse. But now only the shrine, Sunghyeonsa, remains.
