In 2020, Donggo Seo Sa-seon was also listed to commemorate Ihwang and Jeong Kyung-se in the shrine, Sunghyeonsa. Now, Gosan Academy, School of Confucian Scholars Association, is in the process of being promoted to an academy itself.  On the site of the old shrine behind Gosan school, there is a memorial stone for Toegye Ihwang and Ubok Jeong Kyung-se. In 1872, Lee Heon-so, then governor of Gyeongsan, had the stone set up. The inscription records three reasons for setting up the memorial stone. The first is to record the fact that Ihwang and Jeong Kyung-se lectured here. The second is to mark the site of the Academy of Classical Studies that was abolished. The third is a record to prevent feng shui experts from determining it to be an auspicious location and claiming it for feng shui purposes after it was demolished during the reign of Heungseon Daewongun. The memorial stone remained on this site of the vacant shrine for 148 years until being moved to the side of the shrine after restoration of Sunghyeonsa Temple in 2020.  Toegye Ihwang, who can be said to have been the spiritual teacher of Yeongnam School, lectured the younger students at Gosan School right here.   “Studying is a lifelong business, so even if you reach the top, you cannot say that your studies are complete. How much truer would this be for the person below you?”   If you look at Jaseongnok, written by Ihwang, who lived as an honest official all his life, you can guess the mindset he had while teaching the younger students here.  Gosan is the name of the mountain where Gosan School is located. The area between Daegu and Gyeongsan has been called Gosan for a long time. It belonged to Gyeongsan throughout the Goryeo, Joseon, and modern periods, and was incorporated into Suseong-gu, Daegu in 1981. The reason Gosan continues to exist even after 500 years is because of the Gosan Academy of Classical Studies, where the footsteps of Toegye Ihwang remain. Lee Man-seung, a descendant of Ihwang and mayor of Gyeongsan at the time, left this as a record:   Gyeongsan was just a small town in Yeongnam, but became known to the world when my ancestor Toegye came to it..   This is an important passage that reminds us of why Gosan, a small lonely mountain, became widely known and the meaning behind Gosan School.  Next to the wall that surrounds the building stands a dignified Ihwang and Jeong Kyung-se Zelkova tree, which has been protected for about 300 years. It was called Ihwang and Jeong Kyung-se Zelkova tree to commemorate Toegye Ihwang, who devoted his whole life to teaching rather than taking a post, and Jeong Kyung-se, who worked to prevent popular unrest while serving as governor of Daegu. In the past, the village near Gosan School was called the Academy of Classical Studies Village, and it was here that the residents prayed for peace and serenity each year to commemorate the deep will of the two scholars they respected.  Let's hope that the school, which was destroyed by fire, will be restored as soon as possible so that the once unique Gosan Academy of Classical Studies can stand proud once again.

stories.title: Mudongjae
stories.script: Mudongjae is an altar belonging to the Oksan Jeon clan in honor of Jeon Kyeong-chang, a Confucian scholar representing Daegu during the middle Joseon period.  Mudongjae has its roots in Gye-dong Jeongsa, where Jeon Kyung-chang studied. It was a thatched house constructed on the site of Gye-dong Jeongsa in 1900 and rebuilt in 1978. Because it is located in Pa-dong, Suseong-gu, it is also called “Pasanjae” or “Pajae.” Mudongjae, which stands out by the soaring gate, has an octagonal roof in the form of six kans in the front and 1.5 kans on the side, which is a considerable size. The memorial to Gye-dong and the memorial to Imran Gongsin's guard are to the east.  As a student of Toegye Ihwang, Jeon Kyung-chang first spread Toegye studies in Daegu. He and Lee Sook-ryang were the main persons responsible for establishing Yeongyeong Academy of Classical Studies, the first academy of classical studies in Daegu. Yeongyeong Academy of Classical Studies fostered many Confucian scholars, and the lectures were so well attended that it could be said that the renaissance of studying in Daegu had begun.  When we talk about Jeon Kyung-chang, we can't leave out “Susin-Jega.” Jeong felt family rules were particularly important, thus creating Gaheon and ten sets of family rules which he taught to his descendants.   “The goal of a scholar is not to pass exams. If you put in your best effort, success depends on the gods, so it is much more valuable to put effort into training yourself.”   He went to the cemetery every morning and evening for three years to greet his deceased parents, setting an example for his descendants.  Jeon Kyung-chang served in a variety of government posts in the central and provincial areas and was buried in Pa-dong. He is highly regarded, as people say studying in Daegu began with Jeon Kyung-chang. After his death and in recognition of his achievements, a mortuary tablet was enshrined in Hyanghyeon Temple at Yeongyeong Academy of Classical Studies, the first academy of classical studies in Daegu.  When talking about Mudongjae, one must also talk about Ocheon Academy of Classical Studies. Ocheon Academy of Classical Studies belongs to the Junghwa Yang clan, and the Mudongjae shrine to the Oksan Jeon clan. These two clans have maintained relations through inter-family marriage for over 500 years.

stories.title: Haksanjae, Yeongmojae
stories.script: Haksanjae is the Junghwa Yang clan's shrine for Yang Dal-hwa, a scholar during the late Joseon period. It was originally called Haksan School, and it was here that Yang Dal-hwa taught. In 1890, Haksan School was enlarged and reconstructed, and Haksanjae was completed as it is now. The building consists of a beautiful exterior with a standing gate and a single eve, an octagonal roof with five kans in the front and three kans on the side. Signboards of famous people active during late Joseon line the building's interior and exterior. Hyojagak is five minutes away.  Yeongmojae is located near Hwanggeum intersection, about two kilometers from Haksanjae, and was built in 1913 to protect and manage the tomb of Yang Dal-hwa.  There is a famous legend among those associated with the Junghwa Yang clan, who settled in Jisan-dong. It is the legend of “Daedeogsanha Hwalman-in”, which means “10,000 people live in the Mount Daedeog.” Around 360 years ago, Yang Si-jin and his son Yang Dal-hwa, a 14th generation descendant of the Junghwa Yang clan, initially set up their home in Beommul-dong next to Jisan-dong for the prosperity of their descendants. But one day, Monk Il-yi, who had only one ear, came down from Mount Geumgang and saw the site of his house and said this:  This place is not good for the children.“  Monk, then where should we go that will make our descendants virtuous?“  There are people who live in the mountains of Daedeog. For your descendants to see virtue and become wealthy, Jisan-dong is much better than here.“  The family listened to the monk and moved back to present-day Jisan-dong.  The story that the monk looked for Yang Dal-hwa's grave is also interesting. The tomb of Yang Dal-hwa, which is enshrined behind Yeongmojae, was originally the seat of another surname, but it is said that it was abandoned because the site was not good.  If a tomb is used on the site without changing the direction, a 12th generation empress will arise from the Yang clan in Jisan-dong.“  After listening to this, the descendants prepared the tomb of Yang Dal-hwa accordingly. It would be interesting to see whether an empress with the Yang surname will come out of this place, as the monk predicted.

stories.title: Chunghyojae, Moundang
stories.script: The Chunghyojae and Moundang shrines belong to the Cheongju Jeong clan, built to commemorate the father, Jeong Dong-beom, and the son, Jeong Ji-eon. In 1803, the Moryeonjeong pavilion was expanded and renamed Moundang. In 1996, when Chunghyojae was built next to Moundang, Jeongchunggak and Jeonghyogak were moved slightly to where they are now.  Jeong Dong-beom was famous for quelling a rebellion when Yi In-jwa tried to take power during the late Joseon period. Pastor Lee Bo-hyeok, a local official at the time, wanted to honor his contribution and recommend him for a government post. But Jeong Dong-beom politely rejected the honor and returned home to Nobyeon-dong.  As virtuous scholarly gentlemen should meet a bright world, illuminate humanity, and be known for learning, it is not right to make a name for yourself as a military officer.“  As a scholar, Jeong Dong-beom refused the honors and said that it was not right for him to receive an official military post. It is surprising as he was only 19 at the time. Returning to his hometown, he spent the rest of his life as a lecturer while caring for his parents. In fact, it is said that he was known for his filial piety and loyalty from an early age.  Father, mother, have some of this.“  My son, isn't this chestnut and jujube?“  Yes, I got it at a party and brought it home for you and father.“  He is growing big.“  Legend says that he was so faithful that he began bringing food home for his parents when he was only four or five years old. When he was 15, he heard the news of the king's passing and mourned for three years while looking towards the north, saving up carp during the cold winter for his sick parents. In the end, legend says that no grass grew in the place where Jeong Dong-beom's tears fell as he wept so bitterly after the death of his parents.  There is a saying that filial piety comes from a filial family. Jeong Dong-beom's son, Jeong Ji-eon, was even more faithful than his father. From an early age, he made innerwear for his parents and used to make them laugh by dancing to please his elderly parents and grandparents. Also, when his grandparents died, he spent six years beside their grave with his father Jeong Dong-beom. Where is the end of their filial piety?  Among the famous records of Jeong Ji-eon's filial piety, there is a story that almost seems myth, which happened when Jeong Ji-eon's father, Jeong Dong-beom, fell seriously ill.  Dear God, stars of the sky, I beg of you. Please help me heal my father.“  He begged and prayed day and night, and then fell asleep. His grandfather appeared in a dream.  Grandfather, please help my father. No matter how good the medicine is, he's not improving.“  There is only one way for your father to get better.“  What is that?“  Dog oil is an immediate medicine for your father's illness. So if he puts it on and eats it, he will soon get well.“  After waking up from the dream, Jeong Ji-eon looked outside and was terribly surprised. A big tiger was standing outside with a six-legged dog in its mouth. When the tiger saw Jeong Ji-eon, it threw the dog into the yard and disappeared into the forest. Recalling his grandfather's words in the dream, he immediately pressed out some oil from the dog and gave it to his father, who was healed that day.  Why don't you say hello to your parents today while looking around Jeongchunggak and Jeonghyogak, which records the loyalty and filial piety of one family?

stories.title: Deoksanjae
stories.script: Deoksanjae is a shrine belonging to the Asan Jang clan, who have lived in Siji-dong for 600 years. The shrine is a hall that commemorates Jang Ja-won, a scholar who passed the official exam in the early Joseon period, and served as a Cham-gun in Hanseong-bu, which is today known as Seoul.  Deoksanjae was first built in Daeheung-dong, where the Daegu Stadium is today. It has maintained its legacy throughout a few relocations and new names. First built in 1740, it was called “Gokgye-jeongsa”, then renamed “Irojae”, and moved to Siji-dong. When it was moved to Daeheung-dong, it took on the name Deoksanjae, before finally settling in Siji-dong, where it remains today.  Why did Deoksanjae move and have its name changed a few times? Deoksanjae moved from Siji-dong to Daeheung-dong in 1870, and an interesting record states that the reason for this was a tiger. At that time, Siji-dong and Daeheung-dong were adjacent to Beommul-dong at the foot of Daedeog Mountain. It is said that it was impossible to go outside at night as tigers would appear. Legend has it that there was always roaring in Beommul-dong 150 years ago, and that tigers often came to Siji-dong. Sounds scary, doesn't it?  In 1498, Jang Ja-won resigned from government office before Muosahwa occurred and returned to his hometown in Siji-dong to spend the rest of his life as a scholar. At Deoksanjae, there is a poetry board that was exchanged between Jang Ja-won and Gim Jong-jik, another scholar who represented the Sarim school of the early Joseon period and an outstanding literary writer.

stories.title: Soriljae
stories.script: Soriljae is a shrine belonging to the Miryang Park clan, Daesaheon Gongpa, built to commemorate Park Hae, who served as Daesaheon in the early Joseon period. Although the exact date of its initial construction is not known, it was demolished in 1995 for urban planning and rebuilt in 1998 in its current form. In 2019, the Martyr Monument was established outside Soriljae's gate for Park Eung-seong and his three sons, and in the spring of 2022, a monument for Park Hae was added.  The name of the shrine, Soriljae, comes from the Book of Changes and refers to the phrase meaning When a king has a shrine, it is deeply honorable. This can be seen by looking at the meaning of the shrine in the first place. Our ancestors considered the shrine to be a gathering place for the spirits of our ancestors, ourselves, and our descendants. Therefore, many people visited the shrines of great families and thought that it was the best place for minds from all over the world to gather.   “Just as the king built a shrine and gathered the good hearts of the people of the world, we also built a chapel here in Siji and called it Soriljae in honor of the great spirits of our ancestors.”  In this way, Park Hae was honored by his descendants. He entered politics after being selected by Yi Seong-gye, the founder of Joseon. Park He served as Saheonbu, equivalent to today's prosecutor general. Then, even though he was in a position where his family could enjoy wealth and power from generation to generation, he married a native of Daegu who was part of the Oksan Jeon clan and settled here in Siji-dong.  I know what I want and I know the way to go.“  As the title “Gwirim” suggests, Park He followed the principle of moderation. He had no interest in power or wealth, which serves as a great example to remind young people of how important it is to know the right way to go.

stories.title: Momyeongjae
stories.script: Momyeongjae is one of the representative cultural heritages of Suseong-gu and is located in the city center. It is a shrine for General Du Sa-chung, who served in the Ming army during the first Japanese invasion and the second, after which he became a naturalized Korean with his two sons. The name of the shrine, Momyeong, engraved on the signboard, refers to a longing for Ming China.  So, who was General Du Sa-chung? He was a descendant of Du Fu, a famous Chinese poet from Tang China, and worked as an operational assistant for Ming during its battles with the Japanese. He then became part of the operational staff who looked at the battlefield's topography and decided on tactics or camp locations. When the war ended, he chose to stay in Joseon instead of returning to Ming China.  Why did Du Sa-chung settle in Daegu and not in Hanyang? Du Sa-chung, who was a famous strategist who selected camp and barracks locations in war using feng shui, referred to the site of today's Gyeongsang-gamyeong Park in Pojeong-dong, Jung-gu, Daegu.   “This site is where a thousand coins are produced in a day and a truly famed place among famed places.”   Du Sa-chung lived in Pojeong-dong and Gyesan-dong and chose to be buried under Hyeongje-bong Peak, which is behind Momyeongjae.  Mandongmun, the entrance gate to Momyeongjae, is derived from “Manjeol-Pildong”, which is an old saying that means even if the river bends ten thousand times and flows through, it will always flow eastward. It is an old saying that talks about the unwavering dedication of a loyal person. Momyeongjae is divided into two rooms: Gyeongmodang, which honors Du Sa-chung, and Sungjeong-Yuru, which pays tribute to Sung Jeong Je, the last Ming emperor. The tomb of Du Sa-chung is preserved in the back. In the front yard is Du Sa Loyalty Memorial.  In Momyeongjae, the special relationship between Admiral Yi Sun-sin and General Du Sa-chung cannot be left out. It is said that their descendants continued to exchange and carry on the will of their ancestors. This inscription on the memorial was written by Admiral Yi In-su, the 7th generation descendant of Admiral Yi Sun-sin. Admiral Yi In-su served as a naval officer in three provinces, including Jeollanam-do, Gyeongsang-do, and Chungcheong-do, and was known as a great commander whose achievements rivaled Admiral Yi Sun-sin's.  When did the relationship between Yi Sun-sin and Du Sa-chung first begin? As mentioned earlier, Du Sa-chung was a famous feng shui strategist and a master of amphibious landings. Do you remember the thrilling moment in the movie Myeongryang, when Yi Sun-sin, commanding three fleets, routed 330 Japanese warships with only 12 turtle ships? Just as Admiral Yi Sun-sin used the surrounding landforms to lead his forces to victory, Du Sa-chung was also a key strategist, using Feng Shui and terrain. Yi Sun-sin and Du Sa-chung had a lot in common.  Momyeongjae Altar has a poem expressing the friendship between the two. Can you see the poems hanging on all five pillars? This is called “Bongjeong Dubogya” and is a poem for Yi Sun-sin to Du Sa-chung.  Bongjeong Dubogya. Going north, we shared our troubles. When we came to the east, we lived and died together. Under the moonlight night on the south side of the castle, today we share our friendship with a glass of alcohol.“  In this poem, Yi Sun-sin's thoughts toward Du Sa-chung are fully revealed. It is said that Du Sa-chung also looked for the grave site where Yi Sun-sin would be buried later. So we can see their deep admiration for each other. Yi Sun-sin and Du Sa-chung lived life and death together on a battlefield in ruins. That relationship has been passed down through the generations to this day.

stories.title: Dongmujae, Donmokjae
stories.script: Dongmujae and Donmokjae are shrines belonging to the Dalseong Ha clan, who have a legacy of over 350 years in Manchon-dong.  Dongmujae was erected for Ha Si-chan, who studied Confucianism in the late Joseon period. Ha Si-chan was a Neo-Confucian scholar who learned under Lee Ui-jo and Song Hwan-gi, but did not go into the civil service. He built a small house called “Dongmu-Amseo” by himself and while studying, devoted himself to teaching younger students while interacting with the scholars of his time. He left such books as Palrye Jeonryo and Yeolam Collection.  Of the stories related to Ha Si-chan, there is one that reveals his tenacity and integrity. One day, a Gyeongsang-do inspector who had heard of his fame came to visit. The inspector said he wanted to recommend Ha Si-chan to the government on one condition.  I would like to recommend you to the government. There's only one condition.“  What is that?“  I'm uncomfortable about you having the same name as my father. Haven't there been taboos against that in Joseon since ancient times? If you change your name, I will recommend you.“  In response, Ha Si-chan refused, saying this:  Official positions have no meaning to me. But even if they did, how can I change the name my parents gave me? I don't want to pay that price for a post.“  As such, Ha Si-chan is admired for keeping to his beliefs and principles. Later, future generations and scholars built Dongmujae to commemorate him, about 500 meters from its current location. In 1968, it was moved to its present spot with the opening of the road.  In fact, Dongmujae has a rather unusual structure for a shrine. It is composed of Dongmujae, a space to study in the form of an academy of classical studies; Gyeongdeoksa, a space where ancestral tablets are kept for memorial ceremonies; and Jangpangak, where books and woodblocks are stored.  Donmokjae is another shrine belonging to the Dalseong Ha clan and erected near Dongmujae.

stories.title: Junghwa Yang Clan, Hyoja Jeongryeogak
stories.script: Hyoja Jeongryeogak, a memorial building to commemorate the strong bond between Yang Hae-il and Heon-bang, was built in 1891 during the reign of Joseon's King Gojong. The entrance to Jeongryeogak is low and narrow, so that you bow your head and remain reverent. You can see the records and stories of the dutiful son and the animals in the story painted as murals inside Jeongryeogak.  The fact that the filial piety of the two was great enough to be recognized by the king makes us want to learn more about the story. Yang Hae-il, who had always loved his parents, is famous for a story wherein he gave blood from an injured finger to revive his dying father. However, the filial piety shown by the other son, Yang Heon-bang, was even greater. When his father, Hae-il, was too sick to rise, Heon-bang broke the ice on a frozen pond in the winter and caught some carp.  Sir, something terrible is going to happen from this!“  ”My father is suffering, and the cold does not bother me. I will do whatever I have to do to save my father's life.“  Yang Heon-bong stopped eating and drinking when his father did not recover, even after eating the carp.  God of heaven and earth, I offer my life. Please save my father instead of me.“  We have heard many stories of parents sacrificing for their children. But stories of children risking their lives for their parents are rare. In today's reality, where the relationships between parents and children are growing further apart, the story of filial piety among the Yang clan as they offered their lives to save their parents inspires us.

stories.title: Yeongyeongchukseongbi, Daegu-bu Suseongbi
stories.script: Yeongyeongchukseongbi, Daegu Tangible Cultural Heritage Number 4, and Daegu-bu Suseongbi, Daegu Tangible Cultural Heritage Number 5, can be found in Yeongnam jeilgwan overlooking the Geumho River.  Yeongyeongchukseongbi is a monument that records the history of the Daegu Eupseong Fortress, which was destroyed during the Japanese Imjin invasion of Korea. The record of repairs to the Daegu Eupseong Fortress is engraved on the Daegu-bu Suseongbi located next to it.  So let's take a look at the record engraved on Yeongyeongchukseongbi. Daegu Eupseong Fortress had a circumference of about 2.5 kilometers and its walls were about 8 meters high. It took about five months and a lot of people to complete the castle. The workers mobilized to build the fortress were from local armies, known as Sok-oh-gun, Yeong-gun, Seung-gun, and Mo-gun. Sok-oh-gun were local soldiers during late Joseon, and Yeong-gun were draftees. These two were mobilized only in winter, not in the farming season. There are records of Seung-gun, made up of monks, working on the castle during the farming season, and Mo-gun, who worked for a fixed wage.  Daegu-bu Suseongbi is a precious treasure that records in detail why the fortress was built, why the repair work was necessary, how long it took and the scale, and how the manpower was mobilized and construction materials became available. It's like a database. The two monuments originally located in front of Yeongnam jeilgwan Gate were moved to the old Dalseong-gun office and Daegu Hyanggyo when Daegu Eupseong was destroyed in 1906. Finally, it was moved to its current location in 1980 when Yeongnam jeilgwan was restored to its present location.  Yeongnam jeilgwan is one of the most representative gates in Daegu. It was one of the four gates of Daegu Eupseong built during the Joseon Dynasty. The original structure was destroyed during the Japanese invasions and was rebuilt during the reign of King Yeongjo. It was remodeled in 1980 and is now the only gate that has been restored from the original fortress. The name Yeongnam jeilgwan means it is the best gateway in Yeongnam. If you climb the watchtower, you can see Geumho River immediately. Such scenery is refreshing.  Defend the castle! Don't give up an inch!“  It seems that the earnest cry of our ancestors who sweat, shed blood, and sacrificed themselves is still alive today.

stories.title: Du Han-pil Myeongjeonggak
stories.script: Myeongjeonggak is a memorial to commemorate the filial deeds of Du Han-pil, the seventh generation descendant of General Du Sa-chung. The entrance to Myeongjeonggak is low and narrow, so you must bow your head before entering. It is designed to keep visitors reverent and respectful. The signboard of Myeongjeonggak is full of records of the filial acts of Du Han-pil.  So what exactly did he do to deserve such honor? Han-pil's mother was ill for a long time. One day she became so ill that she couldn't eat anything. She suddenly called for Hanpil and said that she wanted to eat matsutake mushrooms.  He was a very devoted son, but mushrooms in the dead snowy cold of winter?   “Huh, what should I do? Mushrooms only grow in midsummer. Where does one go to get matsutake mushrooms in winter? What should I do about this?”  However, Du Han-pil put away his fear and began looking for matsutake mushrooms.  God of heaven and earth, it has already been several days since my mother stopped eating. Please let me find just one mushroom.“  Du Han-pil who climbed a snowy winter mountain every day in search of mushrooms. Did heaven hear his earnest prayer?  Oh! There's one! And there! There are actually some mushrooms! Thank you God, thank you!“  Finally, he found some mushrooms after hiking up and wandering through the snowy mountains. After his mother ate the matsutake mushrooms, she recovered fully. In this way, the filial deeds of Du Han-pil were so great that they reached heaven. The king was moved by this and praised the achievement. Plaques and monuments celebrating these actions have been preserved at Myeongjeonggak.

stories.title: Lee Deuk-sim Monument
stories.script: This monument was established to commemorate the gainful spirit of Lee Deuk-sim, who after serving the royal court during the reign of King Gojong in the final years of the Joseon Dynasty, returned to her hometown and voluntarily spent her fortune on the poor.  Born in Jung-dong, Daegu around 1850, Lee Deuk-sim began life as a court lady at a young age and rose to the highest royal position as an official, Jeong 5th rank, the highest. After resigning from her post, Lee Deuk-sim settled into her hometown of Daegu and shed tears of sorrow as she saw the people struggling in poverty.  The law is too harsh. With what money do people pay taxes when they barely survive long famines and poverty? And what kind of hope can they live on?“  Lee Deuk-sim was the daughter of Lee Je-yeon, who served as the Hyeonpung governor in late Joseon. Unfortunately, there are no exact records of her, but she is known for her good deeds, such as paying taxes for the residents and opening up her barns to provide food.  The grace that the lady has given is like the ocean. Let's work together to build even a small monument.“  Residents who did not want the good heart and sacrifices of Lee Deuk-sim to be forgotten built the monument. The place where it was first erected in 1923 was a place where prayers for village prosperity and abundance were offered. In this prayer area, there was a Dangsan tree, holy tree, and Toad Rock.  Later, the monument was moved from Jung-dong Market to the Jung-dong Senior Citizens Hall and to the Jung-dong Administration and Welfare Center. As the inscriptions wore away over the years, a new monument was erected next to the old one in 1980 to commemorate its meaning. Currently, it is protected as a non-designated cultural property in Suseong-gu.

stories.title: Lee Seo Monument
stories.script: This monument was erected to commemorate Lee Seo, a Daegu magistrate during the reign of King Jeongjo, and was designated as Daegu Tangible Cultural Property number 23 in 1988. The monument is protected by a structure at Lee Seo Park by Sincheon stream.  Walking along the stream beside the sound of water is refreshing, but in the 18th century, the area suffered great damage every time there was a flood. In Daegu, people were divided until recently as to whether Lee Seo, a Daegu magistrate, turned the course of Sincheon stream or built an embankment to prevent flooding.  In our area, there is a big flood every year, and the damage suffered by residents is great. In the section that is regularly flooded, build a strong embankment to minimize damage for the residents.“  In 1778, Lee Seo, a Daegu magistrate, built a new embankment with his own money. Residents who were able to avoid great damage thereafter were so moved that they decided to call the embankment “Lee Gong Je.” In August of that year, a monument was erected in honor of Lee Seo. However, the first stone monument disappeared and another one was erected again in 1797. In 1805, another monument was set up next to it to commemorate the meaning.  Gunsu Ihubeomseon Yeongsebulmangbi is a monument built to commemorate Lee Bum-sun, who served as the governor of Daegu. In 1898, there was a major flood and the downstream part of the embankment was in danger of collapsing. Lee Bum-sun, then governor of Daegu, had it repaired within a short time to prevent its loss. The following year, the people built and protected a monument, and it is now together in the Lee Seo Monument House in Lee Seo Park, Sincheon-byeon.  Recently, something new has been discovered about the monument, which was built in 1808. It is that a boy named Lee Hak-cheol wrote the words “Lee Gong Je” on its front. Isn't it surprising that the boy was only 12 years old at the time? The monument almost never appeared in public view, and until 1987, there were separate monuments in the memorial house for Lee Seo and Lee Bum-sun. However, during construction of Sincheon-daero in 1987, another monument was unearthed on the west side of the now famous Kim Kwang-seok Street. This was the memorial monument with Lee Hak-cheol's handwriting on it. On the back of the monument is a record that states the large front letters were written by 12-year-old Lee Hak-cheol. Unfortunately, it is still unknown who Lee Hak-cheol is.  There is an annual ancestral ritual held on the day of the first full moon in the first month of the year in front of the monuments to Magistrate Lee Seo and Lee Bum-sun. Since 2000, the ritual has been held for all three monuments. Since 2010, the ritual has been renamed Lee Seo Gong Hyangsa and is hosted by Daegu Suseong Cultural Center.

stories.title: Beobisan Beacon Site
stories.script: “Light the fire!”  This is where the Beobisan beacon stood, one of the five beacons in Daegu. The beacon was used to alert the capital city of Hanyang that war was coming. Light from the fire would be used during the night to communicate the alert, while during the day, smoke would serve the same purpose. The message would be received and delivered onward from another beacon. In some senses, it was like a present-day mobile phone during the Joseon Dynasty, and was the means of warning the Joseon Kingdom at a time when foreign invasions were frequent.  In normal times, one fire was lit, two when an enemy appeared, three when the enemy approached the border, four when the enemy crossed the border, and five when a battle broke out.  Unfortunately, the original beacon tower has disappeared and only the site remains. Still, the site of the Beobisan beacon tower was the first in Daegu to be designated a cultural property in recognition of its high academic value in understanding the military communication techniques used during the Joseon Dynasty.  Light one fire today. Everything is calm.

stories.title: Beomeo Station Site
stories.script: Beomeo intersection, where Dalgubeol-daero and Dongdaegu-ro meet. What kind of old story is here, where the largest roads in Korea cross, where people and cars come and go?  “Beom” in Beomeo stands for tiger, while “eo” means fish. Its name comes from the fact that the old terrain was shaped like a fish. It is said that Beomeo Station has existed since the Joseon Dynasty. Of course, not as a subway station.  During the Joseon Dynasty, Beomeo Station was a transportation facility where horses were available for traveling personnel on official journeys. In those days, the station was like a highway rest area, indispensable for those traveling long distances on horseback. This was the place where they prepared for their next trip while resting, eating, and giving water and feed to the horses. Government officials were assigned horses here, sometimes replacing tired ones with fresh mounts before continuing their journey.  Unfortunately, there are currently no remains of Beomeo Station in the Beomeo intersection. In 1895, the station system was abolished. And in 1970, the only relic related to Beomeo Station, Ipmasi Jeong-jeon-bang-geum Jeolmokbi, is currently on display at Kyungpook National University Open Air Museum.

stories.title: Sijiwon Site
stories.script: Do you know the origin of the name Siji-dong in Suseong-gu, Daegu? The etymology of the place name “Siji” is derived from the word Sijiwon.  So, what is the won in Sijiwon? During the Goryeo and Joseon dynasties, public inns were called won. These inns acted as lodging facilities for those traveling to the provinces on official business. The won that we have heard a lot in such names as Itaewon, Janghowon, and Jochiwon, were where lodging facilities known as won were located in the past. These places also had stations where horses were available.  It is said that during the Goryeo dynasty, when Korea was largely Buddhist, temples served as won. That is why temples are popularly known as sawon. In the Joseon dynasty's Sinjeung Dongguk Yeoji Seungram, it is mentioned that there were 1,310 won across the country. However, by late Joseon, won had been replaced by inns, and the station system was abolished in 1895. Unfortunately, Sijiwon remains only as a name.  Dongguk Yeoji Seungram states that Sijiwon is located 11 Chinese miles west of Gyeongsan-hyeon. It is said to be almost identical to Siji-dong, where today's Gosan Elementary School is located. Won in other locations like Itaewon, Janghowon, Jochiwon, and Sariwon no longer exist, but we often hear them spoken. In this way, Sijiwon should remain in our memory.

stories.title: Sungsan Beacon Site
stories.script: Sungsan Beacon was one of the five in Daegu, along with Beobisan Beacon. The signals received from Beobisan Beacon go to Sungsan Beacon, which passes it on to Sisan Beacon in Gyeongsan, Gyeongsangbuk-do.  According to the result of an urgent excavation in 2020, the Sungsan Beacon site is shaped like an elongated ship when viewed from above. The circumference of the protective wall that once surrounded the beacon is similar to that of Beobisan Beacon, which is more than three times larger than the average circumference of the interior beacons scattered across the country.  However, the site of Sungsan Beacon tower has been severely damaged due to unauthorized cultivation. Besides the piles of stones scattered around, it is difficult to recognize the old appearance. Once a site is destroyed, it is difficult to restore it to its original state. Hopefully, Sungsan Beacon Tower will be repaired as soon as possible.

stories.title: Pa-dong Shade Rock Ruins
stories.script: Sincheon is a rock that has remained in place during Daegu's lifetime. (There is a rock that has remained in place in Sincheon during Daegu’s lifetime.) It is a ruin of a rock that has silently watched the winds and waves of the world over the ages. The word shade of the rock was given because it gives way on one side, allowing people to shelter from the rain and wind. The age of this rock is said to be unknowable, but it has been around since the Paleolithic Age.  During an academic excavation, remains from the Joseon Dynasty were found from the bottom of the rock to the top, with earthenware and porcelain sculptures from the Goryeo, Unified Silla, and Three Kingdoms eras confirmed layer by layer. Further down, artifacts from the Bronze and Neolithic ages, such as pieces of plain earthenware, relics, grooves, and stone blades were discovered. And on the bottom level, a large number of remains that appear to have been made by human hands about 10,000 years ago have been recovered.  It almost feels strange that the history has gradually piled up under the surface of the ground. In fact, it is said that people come here to make wishes because of the magical energy of the place.  Don't damage the rock. It is an old stone that is precious to all of us.

stories.title: Sang-dong Bronze Age Village
stories.script: How did people live in prehistory? The prehistoric period refers to time during which there were no written records of humans. It can be broken up into the Paleolithic, Neolithic, Bronze, and Iron Ages. At Sang-dong Bronze Age Village, catch a glimpse of the Bronze Age in prehistoric times.  Korea has the largest number of dolmens in the world and is known as the country of dolmens. Daegu in particular had more dolmens than anywhere else in the world. But now, most of them have been lost due to urbanization and industrialization, which brings greater meaning to Sang-dong Bronze Age Village.  Sang-dong Bronze Age Village is a rare expedition site where dolmens and the site of a Bronze Age house can be seen at the same time. “Goindol” are representative remains of the Bronze Age. The word is pure Korean for cutting stones. On this site, Suseong-gu office directed the installation of a model of the Bronze Age house and tomb inside that once stood here so visitors can see it with their own eyes behind glass.  There is a theory that dolmens are tombs, but others say they are also altars for ancestral rites or territory markers dividing the four districts. We hope that no more of the proud Bronze Age dolmens will disappear, but stay with us forever.

stories.title: Remains of Chiso, Silla of Suchang-gun
stories.audioTitle: Remains of Chiso, Silla of Suchang-gun
stories.script: “Huh? What's in the apartment complex?”  The name “Suseong” in Suseong-gu has been used since the Goryeo Dynasty. Before that, during the Unified Silla period, Suseong-gu was known as Suchang-gun. It is said that during that time, Suchang-gun was the representative area of Daegu.  Evidence of this includes several ruins buried beneath this apartment complex. During construction of this complex here, an excavator was used, uncovering a variety of relics and remains from the Bronze Age to the Joseon Dynasty, including evidence of housing sites, tombs, and wells. The excavation of precious tiles, such as Sumaksae, Amaksae, Gwimyeonhwa, Chimipyeon, which have the characteristics of the Unified Silla period, suggests that the site is an important place.  Local scholars explain that it used to be the site of a Chiso, one of the local administrative organizations mentioned in Samguk Sagi, in the section on the Shinmun Dynasty. So, Suchang-gun, now Suseong-gu, was the regional administrative base. In short, it is the core area of Daegu chosen by our ancestors, Chiso of Silla's Suchang-gun.

stories.title: Toad Rock of Jung-dong
stories.script: Why are you crying, Kongji?“  My mother told me to put water in that pot, but there's a hole in the bottom.“  Don't worry, I'll block it with my body.“  Oh my! Thank you so much, Mr. Toad.“  Like the toad in the story Kongji Patji, in Korean legends and myths, the toad was a valuable animal that drove away bad things and brought good fortune. There's a toad next to you right now. Can you see it? In fact, the rock in front of you is the Toad Rock, the guardian deity of Suseong-gu. Where is this toad? It's just a rock.  It is said that this Toad Rock has been under the Dangsan tree at the three-way intersection of Jung-dong Market for a long time. It was also used as an altar for ancestral rites in the village, which involved praying for the well-being and prosperity of the village. Since Jung-dong, where the rock was placed, was on the banks of the Sincheon River, flood damage was the biggest concern before the embankment was built. That's why the people prayed at the Dangsan tree and at the Toad Rock. Now, it is protecting the future of Suseong-gu in front of Suseong-gu Office.  I pray that we all may be at peace.

stories.title: Uksucheon Dinosaur Footprints
stories.script: It's extraordinary that the road we're walking on is the way the dinosaurs used to walk. Although the times are different, we share the same space. It feels like going back to prehistoric times, 100 million years ago.  So, there's a lot of delicious grass in Daegu!“  It's perfect for herbivores like us!“  The footprints on the floor are said to have been left by a plant-eating dinosaur that walked on all four legs. Dinosaur fans are familiar with it, and it is believed to have been a sauropod with a long neck and round body. Like the big elephant that eats only grass, the sauropod was a herbivore, but it was huge. Was it a Cetiosaurus? A Brachiosaurus? Close your eyes and imagine two dinosaurs lumbering along Uksucheon stream.

stories.title: Take in the Magnificent Columnar Joints at a Glance Along the Mulwitgil Water Trail
stories.audioTitle: Take in the Magnificent Columnar Joints at a Glance Along the Mulwitgil Water Trail
stories.script: "The Mulwitgil, or ""Trail Over the Water,"" is a path of floating pontoon bridges laid across the Hantangang River, running from Sundamgyegok Valley past Goseokjeong Pavilion to the Songdaeso columnar joints and on to Taebong Bridge, for a total length of 8.5 kilometers. The trail operates only from October, when the water level of the Hantangang River drops, until March of the following year, when the water begins to rise again.  Goseokjeong, one of Cheorwon's notable geological sites and the first of the region's Nine Scenic Views, is said to take its name from a pavilion built during the reign of King Jinpyeong of the Silla Dynasty. Today the entire area is known as Goseokjeong. Rising 15 meters beneath the pavilion is Goseokam, a granite rock. This granite had already formed underground long before the land of Cheorwon was covered by lava. Around 500,000 years ago, volcanic activity buried it beneath basalt, and over time erosion revealed it once more above the river. Standing like a scene from an ink-wash painting, Goseokbawi Rock and the vast Madangbawi flat rock that you meet here offer views that simply cannot be seen from the Jusangjeolli Skywalk or the cliffside boardwalk.  As you begin the trek in earnest, heading north along the Hantangang River from Goseokjeong, you soon come upon Seungilgyo Bridge. Construction of the bridge began under North Korea in August 1948 and was completed by South Korea on December 3, 1958. Because the two sides used different construction methods and the work was carried out by different builders, the differences are visible even from the outside, such as in the differing sizes of the arches and the shapes of the piers. A place of singular significance born of national division and the Korean War, it now serves as a pedestrian-only bridge. In recognition of the symbolism it carries through its unique construction history, it was designated Registered Cultural Heritage No. 26 on May 31, 2002. An artificial waterfall has been installed at the bridge, its cool cascade tempering the summer heat, while in winter the frozen falls form a spectacular wall of ice.  Continuing past Seungilgyo Bridge toward the Songdaeso columnar joints, you reach Songdaeso, where the river deepens into a pool. Also one of Cheorwon's Nine Scenic Views, it is renowned for its richly colored and varied basalt columnar joints, and perhaps because the trail brings you so much closer here than the cliffside boardwalk does, the scenery feels truly magnificent. Songdaeso is where basaltic lava, flowing across the Cheorwon Plain, passed through a narrow channel formed of metamorphic rock. The basalt that once filled this channel has since eroded away, with only portions remaining along its inner walls, leaving behind steep cliffs and columnar joints of striking beauty. The layered basalt cliffs reveal seven or eight distinct strata, each reaching 30 to 40 centimeters in height. The columnar joints here formed as lava erupting onto the surface cooled rapidly into vertical columns, and you can also observe fan-shaped joints tilted to the side. Depending on the layer, the basalt columns take on a range of colors such as red, gray, and black, and the hues of these strata at sunset glow with a beauty almost beyond words, inviting travelers to pause for a moment.  The Milky Way Bridge is an asymmetrical suspension bridge, 180 meters long and 3 meters wide, connecting Jangheung-ri in Dongsong-eup, part of Course 1 of the Hantangang River Jusangjeolli Trail, with Sangsa-ri in Galmal-eup, part of Course 2. Before crossing the Milky Way Bridge and continuing up the pontoon trail toward Taebong Bridge, you can climb the Torchlight Observatory for a sweeping view of the Songdaeso columnar joints together with the endless expanse of the Cheorwon Plain. Standing about 45 meters tall, the observatory is shaped like a flaming torch, expressing a wish for peaceful reunification.  Taebong Bridge, where the Mulwitgil water trail comes to an end, takes its name from the Taebong Kingdom of Gungye. It is striking that both Deureuni Rest Area, the first stop along the skywalk, and Taebong Bridge, the final stretch of the water trail, are connected to Gungye.  Here you will find Jiktang Falls, the third of Cheorwon's Nine Scenic Views, located just about 700 meters further up from Taebong Bridge. Sitting on the main course of the Hantangang River, Jiktang Falls formed atop flat basalt, and unlike other waterfalls in Korea, it spreads broadly across the width of the river. As water flowed for ages over the basalt, formed from lava that had cooled and hardened layer upon layer, weathering and erosion gradually broke the rock away along its columnar joints, creating a stair-stepped waterfall. Though only about 3 meters high, it stretches 80 meters wide. "

stories.title: Where Traces of History and Modern Culture Coexist
stories.audioTitle: Where Traces of History and Modern Culture Coexist
stories.script: "Standing across from Cheorwon History and Culture Park, the Cheorwon Korean Workers' Party Headquarters is a sight that commands attention. From a distance, only the building's frame remains, giving it an almost eerie, haunting appearance. It was built in 1945 by North Korea's Workers' Party to administer Cheorwon-gun and the surrounding area. Constructed of unreinforced concrete, it rises three stories above ground over a floor area of 1,850 square meters. The labor and funds of local residents were forcibly mobilized to build it, and the building served as a place to control the population and suppress ideological dissent. A vivid reminder of the painful chapters of modern Korean history, today only the ruins remain. Visitors were once able to tour the interior, but it is now fenced off and can only be viewed from the outside. Walking around the building, you can see bullet and shell marks still embedded in the walls. Though this was a place where those engaged in anti-communist activities were brought to be brutally tortured and killed, the red glow of sunset that seeps through the gaps in its skeletal frame seems only serene. Having endured intact even as nearly every other building was destroyed during the Korean War, it was designated and is now managed as Registered Cultural Heritage No. 22 on May 31, 2002.  Cheorwon History and Culture Park, which opened in July 2022, recreates the downtown of Cheorwon-eup as it was in the 1930s. At that time, Cheorwon-gun was home to more than 80,000 people, making it one of the three largest cities in Gangwon-do. Its streets were lined with modern facilities such as the county office, a police station, a theater, Cheorwon Station, and banks. Before exploring the park and its attractions, it is wise to buy your ticket for the Soisan Monorail first, as it sells out quickly, so that you can ride at the time you want.  The first stop is the Cheorwon Theater, a hall of new culture that brought the arts of Gangwon-do into full bloom. As the opening of the Gyeongwon Line and the Geumgangsan Electric Railway made the Cheorwon area the heart of northern Gangwon, the urban population surged and demand for performing arts grew. In 1934, the Cheorwon Theater opened its doors as the region's first modern theater. It was a stage where some of Korea's most celebrated artists performed, including Choi Seung-hee, the foremost dancer of her time, and Lee Eun-gwan, the master singer of Baebaengi-gut, who made his debut here. Beyond live performances, the theater also screened silent films, and after its 1939 renovation it was reborn as a cultural venue with the full character of a professional performance hall, a rarity among provincial theaters. Silent films are still screened here accompanied by a byeonsa, a live narrator, so that visitors today can fully appreciate the spirit of that era.  In front of the Cheorwon Theater stands a red iron tower, a device known as the “ojeongpo,” which announced the time. In the late Joseon period and during the Japanese colonial era, when clocks were not yet widespread, a cannon was fired at noon, twelve o'clock, to mark the hour. This was called ojeongpo or simply opo, the ""noon gun."" Just as the bell of Bosingak Pavilion was rung to tell the time in Seoul during the Joseon Dynasty, here a cannon was used, and over time a siren came to replace it. Beyond marking the hour, it was also used to signal dangers such as fires and air raids. The ojeongpo typically stood next to a fire station garage, which is why it was managed by the fire department, and the manner in which the sound was produced was varied to convey different messages.  Cheorwon Station was the driving force behind the region's economic growth. Located in the heart of the Cheorwon Plain, the station opened in 1912 with the inauguration of the Yeoncheon-Cheorwon stretch of the Gyeongwon Line connecting Seoul and Wonsan. With the opening of the Geumgangsan Electric Railway in 1931, it came to play a vital role in driving Cheorwon's development. The Gyeongwon Line put Cheorwon Station two hours from Yongsan in Seoul and four and a half hours from Inner Geumgang, and Cheorwon rapidly grew into the center of transportation, logistics, and industry in northern Gangwon. According to the Cheorwon County Gazetteer published in 1937, around 280,000 passengers boarded and alighted here, about 63,000 tons of freight passed through the station, and some 80 staff worked on site.  The monorail is a miniature train carrying eight passengers per car, traveling the 1.8 kilometers from the modern culture street to the summit of Soisan. As the monorail begins to glide slowly along what appears to be a level track, you may feel at ease, but the moment it heads down a steep slope, even at its gentle pace, you will feel a touch of thrill. Taking in the views of Soisan, the Workers' Party Headquarters, and the modern culture street through the open windows on either side, you reach the final stop after a climb of about ten minutes. Climbing roughly 700 meters more to the summit of Soisan, you can look down from the observatory pavilion onto the Cheorwon lava plateau. This plateau was formed in the late Quaternary period of the Cenozoic era, when basaltic lava erupting from Hill 680 and Orisan in the Pyeonggang area of North Korea flowed across the valleys and lowlands of the Cheorwon region, burying the underlying bedrock of granite. The bedrock, made up of granite and other rock formed about 100 million years ago, was not entirely covered by the lava in some granite highlands, which remain as low hills with gentle slopes. These are known as ""steptoes."" Representative steptoes such as Baengmagoji Hill and Ice Cream Hill enjoy many strategic advantages and are therefore militarily significant.  Soisan is a small mountain, 362 meters high, rising sharply above the plain. Since the Goryeo Dynasty it has been the site of the First Route beacon station, which warned of approaching enemies. For decades the mountain lay untouched, sealed off within minefields and a civilian-restricted zone beyond military control, but through consultations between the military and developers, a trail is now open that links the Landmine Flower Path (1.3 kilometers), the Ecological Forest Path (2.7 kilometers), and the Beacon Station Ascent Path (0.8 kilometers)."

stories.title: Savor Spring and Autumn Along the Goseokjeong Flower Field
stories.audioTitle: Savor Spring and Autumn Along the Goseokjeong Flower Field
stories.script: Now one of Cheorwon's most popular hotspots, the Goseokjeong Flower Field is a place that has been completely transformed from a military training ground that once echoed with the roar of tanks on maneuvers. Since its official opening in September 2022, the Goseokjeong Flower Field has welcomed more than 600,000 visitors each year, all drawn to admire its beautiful blooms in every color.  Of the field's total area of 24 hectares, 15 hectares burst into a spectacular display of one million flowers across 18 varieties, including candle celosia, gaura, and verbena. At night, landscape lighting installed among the flowers creates a strikingly different scene from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m., a rare and special touch. The Goseokjeong Flower Field came to life through the hands of Cheorwon's residents, who planted the flowers and carved wood to craft each sculpture, sharing in every step until the colorful blooms came into full flower. Korea is home to many celebrated flower festivals, but the Cheorwon Goseokjeong Flower Festival truly stands out, offering a scale and an overwhelming beauty worthy of being called the very best. As waves of purple verbena ripple in a grand display, the zinnia field dazzles the eye with an almost dizzying splendor, while the kochia, looking like cartoon characters with playful expressions and adorable little eyes, forms rounded, rolling hills. The candle celosia, unmistakable even from afar with its vivid hues, sends its fragrance drifting on the wind across the vast plain, giving everyone who visits an exotic, unforgettable moment that feels like an unexpected gift.

stories.title: Experiencing an Unknown World Firsthand at the DMZ Ecology and Peace Park
stories.audioTitle: Experiencing an Unknown World Firsthand at the DMZ Ecology and Peace Park
stories.script: "The sharp line of division at the 38th parallel, the winding curve of the meandering Hwagang River, and the arcs traced along the river's course are all drawn upon the map. Through the long winter, migratory birds fly into the plains and reservoirs of Cheorwon in triangular formations. Their order, moving between horizon and waterline, is the law of nature and a route that no human may cross. There are also strictly controlled front lines. The line that divides the Korean Peninsula into north and south is a forbidden boundary that cannot be crossed without agreement. The DMZ Ecology and Peace Park, where Cheorwon's spring, the last to arrive at the tail end of the long and bitter winter, finally begins, was created through a joint agreement among the Ministry of Environment, the Army's 3rd Infantry Division, and Cheorwon-gun. As a space carrying the symbolic message of a DMZ where war, peace, and nature coexist, it lets visitors explore the pristine ecosystem that has remained untouched by civilian development for the 60 years since the armistice.  There are two trails to explore: the Yongyangbo Trail, which takes in Chungnyeolsa Shrine, Amjeonggyo Bridge, Yongyangbo, and the Yongyangbo gateway, and the Sipjatap Trail, which runs from the rear command post past the Cross Tower Observatory and back to the starting point.  The Yongyangbo Trail is a path full of anticipation, where you can walk inside the Civilian Control Line on your own two feet rather than by car, starting from the Yongyangbo parking lot. Yongyangbo is a reservoir created during the Japanese colonial era, using the piers of the Geumgangsan electric railway as its embankment. Built on the upper reaches of the Hwagang River to supply water to the farmland of the Saengchang-ri area, it became a ""land of life"" after the war, where, untouched by people for some 60 years, a colony of Korean willows grew into a pristine wetland. This was once a place that civilians could not dare to approach, and the trail in particular runs right up to the fence of the Southern Limit Line, bringing the South's General Outposts and Guard Posts close enough to seem within reach. The tension grows all the greater, and so does one's curiosity. The most striking sight at the reservoir is the suspension bridge once crossed by soldiers on DMZ border duty after the war. With its footboards all gone and only the steel pylons and cables left standing bare, it conveys the weight of bygone years. The crumbling, ruin-like structure set against the vitality of the Korean willow colony, just turning a soft green with the spring waters, creates a curious contrast. The embankment of Yongyangbo was once a railway pier where the Geumgangsan Electric Railway used to run.  The Geumgangsan Electric Railway, designated Registered Cultural Heritage No. 112 on September 4, 2004, was a 116.6-kilometer railway line that opened in 1924 during the Japanese colonial period and was completed in 1931. With the construction of the Geumgangsan Railway connecting Cheorwon to Inner Geumgang, along with the Geumgangsan Electric Railway Bridge, the journey to Geumgangsan took four and a half hours at the time. The line was laid to carry off the region's abundant mineral resources to Japan, and it was also used for tourism, though with a fare reportedly equal to the price of a sack of rice, it was hardly within reach of ordinary people. When Korea was divided into north and south in the 1950s, the railway fell out of use, but the electric railway bridge still remains. Built in 1926 during the construction of the Geumgangsan Railway, the bridge confronts you with severed tracks above a river that continues to flow beneath, making the reality of the world's only divided nation vividly tangible.  The Sipjatap Trail spans 13.1 kilometers and takes about five hours round trip. Set atop Seongjae Mountain, this was the site of a Christmas tree lighting ceremony, and here you can see the fences and fortified positions of both North and South Korea with your own eyes. It is a trail where you can feel, firsthand, the natural environment within the DMZ and the Cold War reality of the Korean Peninsula. The Sipjatap Trail makes use of the Cross Tower erected along the ridge of Seongjae Mountain by the Army's 3rd Infantry Division as an observatory, to send a message of peace and love to North Korea. Adjacent to this course is the site of the Battle of Sniper Ridge, also known as the Battle of Triangle Hill, the most ferocious of the hill battles fought on the central front during the Korean War. It is a place of palpable tension, where you can even see with the naked eye the North Korean guard posts on Oseong Mountain, now part of North Korean territory. The vast plain that stretches out below the Cross Tower may look like a lawn, but it is in fact a field of reeds standing over two meters tall. Because the Sipjatap Trail lies right alongside the DMZ in an area off-limits to civilians for the past 60 years, its natural ecosystem remains in a pristine state. This mountain trail, winding along forest paths through areas of uncleared landmines, is a rare and precious place unlike anywhere else."

stories.title: Festivities That Run from the Heart of Winter to the Height of Summer
stories.audioTitle: Festivities That Run from the Heart of Winter to the Height of Summer
stories.script: "True to a people who would break into a shoulder dance at a single cry of ""Strike up the music!"", Cheorwon hosts a variety of spirited festivals throughout the region every year. In the face of such revelry, neither the cold of midwinter nor the heat of midsummer holds anyone back. Here we explore the distinctive festivals of Cheorwon, set against its blessed natural scenery and sure to make you forget the summer heat entirely.  Playing freely in a pristine river: the Cheorwon Hwagang Freshwater Snail Festival The Cheorwon Hwagang Freshwater Snail Festival began as a village event and grew steadily in scale as it took fuller shape. First held as a village festival in 2007 under the lead of a local community development association, it became established as a regional festival in 2009 with the formation of the Cheorwon Hwagang Freshwater Snail Festival Organizing Committee. It has since grown into one of the region's flagship cultural tourism festivals, drawing as many as 300,000 visitors a year. Each summer, the Hwagang Swiri Park and the Gimhwa Sports Park area in Gimhwa-eup, Cheorwon-gun, Gangwon State, bustle with people enjoying the festival in the heat of midsummer. In the clean, natural surroundings of the Hwagang, a first-grade river, visitors can not only enjoy the water to their heart's content but also gather freshwater snails by hand, offering plenty of fun for families. There is also a large swimming pool, a children's pool, and a water slide, all summer essentials. On top of the festival itself, early August brings a true gathering of harmony, where visitors can encounter military culture through the 3rd Infantry Division's recruit graduation ceremony and displays of military equipment.  Capturing both fun and historical value: Taebongje Festival Now well past forty in human years, the Taebongje Festival carries within it the story of Gungye, a figure inseparable from Cheorwon itself. The festival has long been held to commemorate how Gungye, founder of Later Goguryeo, established the Taebong Kingdom in Cheorwon-gun, Gangwon-do, and to wish for the inheritance and growth of local culture and for bountiful harvests. In 1982, October 21, the day Cheorwon-gun was recaptured during the Korean War, was designated ""Cheorwon County Citizens' Day,"" and the first Citizens' Day celebration held that year has continued to this day. From 1991, the festival was renamed ""Taebongje,"" taking its name from the Taebong Kingdom founded by Gungye. Living up to its name, the festival embraces not only simple entertainment but also the historical and local significance tied to the Taebong Kingdom and King Gungye, the historical roots of Cheorwon-gun, through events such as a ritual for peaceful reunification combining waters from across the country, a royal procession of King Gungye, the Taebong writing contest, the Taebong sketching contest, and the Taebong calligraphy contest. With its efforts to honor historical value alongside the enthusiastic participation and support of local residents, the Taebongje Festival is regarded as the largest festival in Cheorwon-gun.  Strolling over the Hantangang River in the depths of winter: the Hantangang River Ice Trekking Festival There is a festival where the wind may be cold against your face, yet the scenery is so breathtaking that you forget the cold entirely. It is the Cheorwon Hantangang River Ice Trekking Festival, held every year in mid-January. Ice trekking at the peak of winter may sound surprising, but this festival is the only time you can walk across the Hantangang River while taking in its magnificent natural scenery. Already a quiet favorite among mountaineering enthusiasts, the festival debuted in 2013 with a 5.5-kilometer experience course running from Taebong Bridge on the Hantangang River to Seungilgyo Bridge, in answer to that enthusiasm. Today the course has been extended to a total of 8.5 kilometers, starting at Taebong Bridge and passing Songdaeso, Madangbawi Rock, and Seungilgyo Bridge before continuing to Goseokjeong and Sundamgyegok Valley. As a winter trekking event launched under the theme of ""Like spotting a flower in the depths of winter,"" it lets you fill your eyes with the splendid crags, cliffs, and columnar joints of the Hantangang River canyon, while also offering a range of attractions and activities such as sledding and large ice sculptures. Overcome the cold and take just one step, and you can set off into a winter world beyond anything you imagined."

stories.title: The DMZ That Embraces Cheorwon, Where Nothing Is Ordinary
stories.audioTitle: The DMZ That Embraces Cheorwon, Where Nothing Is Ordinary
stories.script: """A place where restriction and control have become a way of life, the DMZ embraces people and culture."" Though it carries the wounds of history, this too is a place where people have lived and continue to live. Here we explore the festivals of coexistence in the Cheorwon DMZ, where untouched nature and people become one.  Running in pursuit of peace: the Cheorwon DMZ International Peace Marathon Is there any better way to savor autumn than to run beneath a sky so blue it stings the eyes, gazing out over the golden hue that washes across the vast plain? The Cheorwon DMZ International Peace Marathon lets runners take in the autumn scenery of Cheorwon with their whole bodies, carrying the added meaning of running together in a shared wish for peace on the Korean Peninsula. Runners gather at the lawn plaza of Goseokjeong in Jangheung-ri, Dongsong-eup, Cheorwon-gun, set off at 9 a.m., and run into the afternoon. The event features five categories in all: the DMZ full course of 42.195 kilometers, the DMZ half course, the 21-kilometer course, the 5-kilometer course, and the Milky Way Trail Walk. The Milky Way Trail Walk is an outing well suited to taking in the magnificent scenery of the Hantangang River and the golden Cheorwon Plain while feeling the autumn breeze. As the first DMZ course in Korea to be officially certified by the Korea Association of Athletics Federations, it stands comparison with any race in the world. Beyond the joy of running, the DMZ Marathon has earned great popularity by offering hands-on activities for families, such as rides on the tin can train, silkworm experiences, making blueberry ice cream, baking apple cookies, dyeing, making cosmos flower photo cups, and tractor wagon rides.  Breaking down the boundaries between us to coexist: the DMZ Peace Train Music Festival The DMZ Peace Train Music Festival is a music festival held for just three days a year in Cheorwon, Gangwon-do. It began in 2018 with the aim of transcending politics, economics, and ideology through music, and experiencing freedom and peace. Now in its seventh edition this year, Peace Train honors the music that has shaped its times and brings together artists with distinct voices and individuality. Placing the diversity of music above all else, with no headliners, it offers audiences a wide range of musical experiences. Cheorwon, where the festival takes place, bears the scars of division, with parts of it assigned to South Korea and parts to North Korea after the Korean War, and it embraces the Demilitarized Zone, a ""zone of peace where no hostile act may occur."" The astonishingly peaceful and beautiful natural environment here, together with the stories of its residents, merges with the musical values of Peace Train to form a unique festival identity found nowhere else.  Peace Train carries on its own distinctive sense of festival, breaking down the boundaries between people and coexisting by singing together music that transcends rankings, genres, nationalities, and generations, and by simply ""dancing together before any lines are drawn,"" with no hostility. It seeks to continually rediscover, through culture, the universal values of life that we can grow indifferent or numb to in our daily routines, in the hope that the spirit of freedom and peace, inclusion and tolerance, will endure unchanged into the future.  Peace Train has no headliners. It guards against drawing distinctions between musicians who sell tickets well and those who do not, and it breaks the usual formula of putting only young, famous musicians who appeal to the key audience of those in their twenties and thirties on the festival stage. Instead, Peace Train actively introduces legendary musicians of genuine significance in music history alongside musicians who, outside the reach of digital algorithms, deliver outstanding live performances with their own individuality. Rather than lining acts up by fame, it weaves together music of different genres, nationalities, and generations through its curation, creating a narrative that only Peace Train can tell.  At Peace Train 2018, the legendary Glen Matlock, founder of British punk rock with the Sex Pistols, performed and presented a collaborative stage with Crying Nut and ChaCha. In 2019, John Cale of The Velvet Underground, regarded as one of the most important avant-garde and experimental rock bands of the 1960s, performed and sang together with So!YoON!. In 2023, the festival welcomed 26 acts from 10 countries, including Michael Rother of the legendary band NEU!, founders of krautrock, Germany's signature genre of popular music which greatly influenced post-punk and post-rock, along with Korean legends Choi Baek-ho, Lee Sang-eun, Silica Gel, and ADOY."

stories.title: DMZ Peace Tourism: A Zone of Peace Where No Hostile Act May Occur
stories.audioTitle: DMZ Peace Tourism: A Zone of Peace Where No Hostile Act May Occur
stories.script: "Now, as life stirs in the once-frozen earth, you may wonder how Cheorwon's flower buds have stretched awake, and whether peace has arrived along with spring. Frozen solid one moment and quietly melting the next, Cheorwon's winter and spring bear a striking resemblance to our own lives. This is a place that carries a quiet melancholy, conveying the beauty of spring while having to soothe wounds not yet healed, tracing the crossing curves of joy and sorrow. Into the Civilian Control Line of Cheorwon, where people live dreaming of coexistence, spring comes rushing in with open arms.  The DMZ Crane Peace Town on Yangji 2-gil in Dongsong-eup, Cheorwon-gun, is one of the starting points for DMZ peace tourism in the Cheorwon area. From here, a course takes in the Cheorwon Peace Observatory, Woljeong-ri Station, and the Second Tunnel, all located within the Civilian Control Line. After buying tickets, visitors travel in their own vehicles under the guidance of a tour leader, and the warning lights mounted on the cars lend a tension unlike any other kind of tour.  Passing through the Civilian Control Line checkpoint and drawing one step closer to that forbidden boundary, you arrive at the Cheorwon Peace Observatory, which looks out over the Demilitarized Zone, the Pyeonggang Plateau, and a propaganda village. A monorail carries you conveniently up to the observatory as you take in the surrounding scenery. The observatory consists of an exhibition hall on the first floor and a viewing room on the second, and the usual route is to gaze out at distant North Korean land from the second floor and then tour the exhibits.  From the observatory, the vast Pyeonggang Plateau rises in the distance like a folding screen wrapped around the surroundings, standing up like an embankment. Below it spreads the Pungcheonwon Plain, encompassing Cheorwon and Pyeonggang. It is both a migratory bird habitat of Cheorwon and the site of the Taebong Kingdom's fortress capital, founded by Gungye, who established Later Goguryeo. Gungye's dream of unifying the Later Three Kingdoms was never realized, but traces of the fortress capital remain on the Pungcheonwon Plain. Using the high-precision telescopes in the viewing room, you can fill your eyes with historic battle sites such as Camel Hill, Bloody Ridge, and Kim Il-sung Highland, along with the untouched nature of the Demilitarized Zone, a sight that draws spontaneous admiration. The first-floor exhibition hall features displays on the Battle of Baengmagoji Hill, the fiercest of the Korean War, a Second Tunnel experience, the history of the Cheorwon battles, and a virtual journey through North Korea. This is a place where you can come to understand both war and peace.  Cheorwon was where the fighting was most ferocious among all the Civilian Control Line areas of Korea bordering the DMZ fence. Baengmagoji Hill in particular was the scene of a fierce ten-day battle beginning on October 6, 1952, during which the hill, only 395 meters above sea level, changed hands no fewer than 24 times. Originally a small, nameless hill on one slope of Hyoseong Mountain, it came to be called Baengmagoji Hill, or White Horse Hill, because the relentless shelling of the time toppled every tree along its ridge, leaving it stripped bare and white, so that from the sky it looked like a white horse lying down. The battle left around 3,500 South Korean and some 10,000 Chinese casualties, and with roughly 280,000 shells reportedly falling here, the scale is hard to imagine. When South Korean forces brought this brutal battle to a victorious close, the Cheorwon Plain became the land of the Republic of Korea. Baengmagoji Hill is off-limits today, but a memorial battlefield site honoring the battle has been established in the southern area within view of the hill. It includes a memorial monument honoring the souls of those who fell in the Battle of Baengmagoji Hill, a memorial hall displaying records and artifacts from the time of the battle, a commemorative monument, and a memorial tower.  Now closed, Woljeong-ri Station is the railway station nearest to the Southern Limit Line of the Demilitarized Zone. It was the northernmost station on the Gyeongwon Line running from Seoul to Wonsan. Beside a sign reading ""The iron horse longs to run"" stand the wreckage of a North Korean freight train destroyed by bombing during the Korean War, along with the No. 4001 locomotive used at the time to tow the derailed train, conveying the tragedy of the war. The Gyeongwon Line was an industrial railway connecting Seoul and Wonsan over 221.4 kilometers, serving as a trunk line that carried agricultural products from Cheorwon and seafood from Wonsan, among other goods. Originally located north of the Civilian Control Line, the station building was relocated to its present site and restored in 1988 for the purpose of security tourism. Nearby, the King Gungye Taebong Kingdom History Park has been established.  The Second Tunnel, discovered in the Demilitarized Zone along the Military Demarcation Line, was a tunnel dug by North Korea for a surprise invasion of the South. A South Korean sentry on guard duty heard the sound of explosions underground, and modern equipment was used to drill and confirm the tunnel's location. After dozens of days of excavation, it was discovered on March 19, 1975, the second such tunnel found within the South Korean area. Lying in a solid granite layer at a depth of 50 to 160 meters underground, the tunnel runs a total of 3.5 kilometers, of which 1.1 kilometers was dug south of the Military Demarcation Line. An arched tunnel two meters high, it was specially designed to allow large-scale infiltration of about 30,000 heavily armed troops along with field artillery and other equipment in a single hour, making it a striking site of North Korean provocation.  The Seungni Observatory stands at the very front line, on the hill in front of Mahyeon 2-ri village in Geunnam-myeon, Cheorwon-gun. Located 108 kilometers from Seoul and 74 kilometers from Chuncheon, it sits at the exact center of the 155-mile Armistice Line. From here, Daeseong Mountain, Jeokgeun Mountain, and Samcheon Mountain come into full view, while across to North Korea you can take in sights such as Oseong Mountain, a fierce battlefield during the Korean War, and the Geumseong area of North Korea. In particular, you can clearly see the Geumgangsan electric railway tracks, now buried under weeds. Opened by Cheorwon-gun on February 18, 2002, the Seungni Observatory is staffed by tour guides who manage it."

stories.title: Sejong National Arboretum
stories.script: In Korea, there are 73 arboretums registered with the Korea Forest Service. Of these, only a handful are managed directly by the state, and the Sejong National Arboretum in Sejong Special Self-Governing City is one of them. As a national arboretum, it has many features that set it apart.  To begin with, while most arboretums sit at the foot of a mountain or deep in the hills, the Sejong National Arboretum is located within the city. It was created by leveling flat land that had once been rice paddies during the construction of the Multifunctional Administrative City. Opened in 2020, it is Korea's first urban arboretum. True to that identity, it runs a wide range of programs for the public, including various cultural events and educational activities.  The arboretum is home to the largest four seasons exhibition greenhouse in the country, a place where you can encounter a diverse array of plants rarely seen elsewhere in Korea. The greenhouse itself is shaped after the petals of an iris flower. In the Mediterranean Greenhouse, modeled after the Alhambra Palace in Spain, plants native to the Mediterranean region grow in abundance, including the baobab tree that appears in the novel The Little Prince and the bottle tree, whose trunk resembles a jar. The Tropical Greenhouse, meanwhile, recreates the jungle of a tropical rainforest in vivid detail. Here, plants of unusual color and form catch the eye, such as Darwin's orchid, named for the clues it offered to Darwin's research on the theory of evolution, and the pink-hued Musa velutina banana.  Beyond these, the arboretum features a Korean Traditional Garden, created to carry forward the garden culture of our ancestors; Cheongnyujiwon, a place of learning where waterways drawn from the Geumgang River allow visitors to observe wetland ecosystems; and a Bonsai Garden displaying bonsai regarded as works of art. Each space has its own distinct charm, so wherever your steps lead you, you are sure to enjoy it.  Whether you come to learn about plants, to take a leisurely stroll, or to capture lovely memories in photos, the Sejong National Arboretum is the perfect place. Why not spend some time unwinding among its many plants?

stories.title: The Four Seasons Greenhouse
stories.script: "The Four Seasons Exhibition Greenhouse, the largest greenhouse in Korea, is made up of three areas: the Mediterranean Greenhouse, the Tropical Greenhouse, and the Special Exhibition Greenhouse.  The Mediterranean Greenhouse recreates the Alhambra Palace in Spain, a space where you can appreciate the balanced beauty of proportion and symmetry. Along with a 20-meter-high observation deck, it is home to a rich variety of plants from Europe, Asia, and Africa, including the baobab tree that carries the very scent of the Mediterranean, the olive tree, the Wollemi pine known as the ""dinosaur tree,"" the Ceiba speciosa with its bottle-shaped trunk, and the vividly colored bougainvillea.  As you enter the Tropical Greenhouse, you are met at once by a majestic waterfall.
