The space evokes the tropical climate that is home to half of all the world's living species, and with its theme of exploring mysterious rainforests and secret woodlands, it makes you feel as though you have stepped into a world of tropical forest. Here you can encounter a wide range of tropical fruits such as Alstonia and papaya, carnivorous plants of many curious shapes, the Victoria water lily with its large spined leaves, and mangroves that take root and live in the water.  The Special Exhibition Greenhouse hosts displays that change by season and by theme. At the center of the greenhouse is a courtyard flower bed, and each time the exhibition changes, you can take in a fresh atmosphere and lose yourself in a space where plants and culture come together."

stories.title: The Korean Traditional Garden
stories.script: "The Korean Traditional Garden is an exhibition space designed to express the ways our ancestors related to plants and the culture surrounding them. It is made up of a palace garden, a scholar's villa garden, and a folk village garden.  The palace garden recreates the Juhamnu and Buyongjeong Pavilion of Changdeokgung Palace at their actual size, though the names of the buildings and their features have been rendered in pure native Korean. The point to look for here when observing the plants is the hwagye, which means ""flower steps."" A hwagye is a terraced flower bed where flowers are arranged in tiers so they can all be taken in at a glance, while naturally assigning the flowers a kind of rank, or hierarchy. The closer the planting is to the building, the more it features plants that the king loved and cherished, such as peonies and Korean cherry trees.  The villa garden was a space for scholars of old, not a place of everyday residence but one where they read books and discussed learning with fellow scholars and younger students. The villa garden at the Sejong National Arboretum takes its inspiration from Soswaewon Garden in Damyang. Here, a waterway flows in a natural course, expressing the wish to draw nature into one's own embrace. It is a space where you can feel the graceful, refined lives of our ancestors and their unhurried desire to live in harmony with nature. The folk village garden is laid out to feel familiar and comfortable, incorporating garden elements once seen in old villages, such as a village shade tree and a stone wall.  This is the Korean Traditional Garden, where you can experience firsthand the freedom shared between nature and people, and the worldview of our ancestors."

stories.title: The Bonsai Garden
stories.script: The Bonsai Garden is an exhibition space for displaying and appreciating bonsai, often called nature in miniature held within a pot. It consists of an outdoor exhibition hall, a permanent exhibition area where bonsai can be viewed throughout the four seasons, a special exhibition area where bonsai education programs are held, and a seokgasan, a rockery that recreates the form of a mountain in miniature.  The Bonsai Garden displays bonsai of many different species, such as black pine, Chinese juniper, and Japanese apricot, and even within the same species, each bonsai reveals an entirely different mood and character.  To appreciate a bonsai properly, it is important to stand where the whole tree comes into view and take your time observing the finer details, such as the flow of the branches, the texture of the bark, and the shape of the roots. As you take in the form of the tree, you can even read the heart of the person who cultivated it.  The greatest charm of the Bonsai Garden is that each bonsai feels like a single landscape of nature, compressed within a small pot.

stories.title: The Rare and Endemic Plants Exhibition Greenhouse
stories.audioTitle: The Rare and Endemic Plants Exhibition Greenhouse
stories.script: The Rare and Endemic Plants Exhibition Greenhouse, set against the backdrop of Cheongnyujiwon where waterside plants grow in lush profusion, is designed in the shape of a leaf floating on a bowl of water. It is made up of two greenhouses: one displaying plants native to the southern regions, and one displaying rare orchids.  As its name suggests, the Rare and Endemic Plants Exhibition Greenhouse displays endemic plants that grow only in Korea, along with rare plants that are disappearing from their natural habitats. It is also the themed exhibition space that best fulfills one of an arboretum's core roles, the conservation of plant species. Here you can see plants such as the gulgeori tree and the Japanese holly fern, while the orchid greenhouse is planted with a wide range of orchids, including terrestrial orchids that root in the ground, epiphytic orchids that root on trees, the noble orchid, and the wind orchid.  The Rare and Endemic Plants Garden located in front of the greenhouse presents its collection across five zones, organized according to the growth characteristics of the plants. Korea is home to some 350 endemic plant species and around 570 rare plant species. The Sejong National Arboretum focuses on displaying endemic and rare plants found in the central temperate region and the southern regions, raising awareness of the importance of habitat conservation.

stories.title: The Folk Plants Garden
stories.script: The Folk Plants Garden is the place that best reveals the value of plant resources, an exhibition space planted with over 100 species of folk plants that our ancestors used in daily life across the various regions of Korea.  The garden is arranged into nine areas according to the plants' representative uses. Made up of sections for rice-planting experiences, medicinal plants, natural insecticides, edible plants, spices, dyes, fibers, sap, and timber, it offers the pleasure of both gaining knowledge about plants and observing them up close.  Rather than simply planting the plants that have become part of our lives, the garden is laid out so that you can also take in the atmosphere of a traditional living environment. Along with a garden shaped like the Korean Peninsula, it is designed with curving lines to emphasize a natural garden form, and the plants are arranged along Cheongnyujiwon, making it an exhibition space that is pleasant to visit throughout all four seasons.

stories.title: The Sensory Garden
stories.script: The Sensory Garden is an exhibition space themed around the five human senses. Plants that stimulate sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch make up its four exhibition areas.  In the Fragrance Garden, you can smell for yourself the scents of what we call herbs, such as apple mint, peppermint, and lemon balm, along with native plants like Korean thyme. The Color Garden is home to plants that bloom in bright, varied colors, such as Korean winter hazel, nandina, and the silk tree. In the Touch Garden, you can feel the texture of plants by touching them yourself, including silver mound artemisia, blue fescue, and Japanese forest grasses. In the Wind Sound Garden, you can enjoy the sound of the wind brushing past the plants through silver grass, Japanese spindle, and giant bamboo.  For us humans, who long ago lived amid nature and made the forest our home, it lets us feel the color green. Why not take a moment to rest while gazing at the green leaves and the flower petals of many colors that fill the Sensory Garden?

stories.title: Walk Gimhae, Course 1 Opening
stories.script: "Today's walk takes you along a route rich with the story of the ancient Gaya Kingdom. We will visit the Tomb of Queen Heo, the final resting place of Queen Heo Hwang-ok, wife of King Kim Suro, the founder of the Garak Kingdom. We will also see Gujibong Peak, home to the legend of the ""Guji-ga,"" one of the oldest songs in Korea, along with the Gimhae National Museum, which holds the history of Gaya, and the Street of Gaya, one of Korea's 100 most beautiful roads.  One quick note before we begin. The Gimhae National Museum on today's route is closed every Monday, on January 1st each year, and on major national holidays, so please keep that in mind when planning your visit.  Now then, shall we set off together?"

stories.title: Tomb of Queen Heo
stories.script: The site before you is the tomb of Queen Heo, wife of King Suro, the founder of the Garak Kingdom.  According to the Record of the Garak Kingdom in the “Samguk Yusa,” the queen's surname was Heo and her given name was Hwang-ok. It is said that Heo Hwang-ok, a princess of the Ayuta Kingdom in India, crossed the sea at the age of sixteen to marry King Suro. Of their many sons, two were given the queen's surname, Heo, and their descendants continue to this day.  The tomb is a round earthen mound about five meters high. A low square stone wall surrounds and protects it, and a retaining wall built of long stones stands at the front. Within the grounds you will find Sungbojae, along with attached structures such as the outer and inner triple gates.  Unlike typical tombs built on flat ground, the Tomb of Queen Heo stands atop a hill, a distinctive feature. In front of the tomb is the Pasa Stone Pagoda, whose stones are said to have been brought from India.  In 1446, the 28th year of King Sejong's reign, the protected area was expanded along with the Tomb of King Suro. The tombstone and stone altar that remain today are believed to have been installed during renovations in 1647, the 25th year of King Injo's reign.  Take a moment to pause here, and as you take in the Tomb of Queen Heo, imagine the story of a queen who, two thousand years ago, crossed a distant sea to help shape the history of Gaya.

stories.title: Gujibong Peak
stories.script: "You are now standing at Gujibong Peak. This is the sacred birthplace of the Gaya Kingdom, the very spot where King Kim Suro, founder of Geumgwan Gaya, is said to have descended from heaven.  Gujibong Peak in Gimhae is also known as Gusubong or Gubong, because the shape of the hill resembles a turtle, and it is closely tied to the founding legend of Gaya. According to the Record of the Garak Kingdom in the Samguk Yusa, in the year 42, King Kim Suro descended here by the will of heaven. Chosen by the nine chiefs, including Adogan and Yucheongan, and by the people, he became the king of the Garak Kingdom. The Guji-ga, the song the nine chiefs and the people are said to have sung and danced to as they welcomed King Suro, is also known as the Yeongsin-ga, or ""Song of Welcoming the Deity."" As one of the oldest epic songs in Korea, it is an important source for the study of ancient literary history.  At the summit of Gujibong Peak stands a southern-style dolmen believed to have been built around the 4th century BC. Carved on the capstone of the dolmen are the characters reading ""Gujibongseok,"" said to have been written by Han Seok-bong, a renowned calligrapher of the Joseon Dynasty.  Here at Gujibong Peak, the founding legend of Gaya, the Korea's earliest epic song Guji-ga, and a prehistoric dolmen all remain together in one place. As you look around at the surrounding scenery, imagine the cheers and songs of the people who gathered here some two thousand years ago, and the sense of anticipation as they awaited the birth of a new nation.  Gujibong Peak is the starting point of Gaya's history and an important cultural heritage site that reveals the origins of Gaya culture and the process by which Korea's ancient states were formed."

stories.title: Gimhae National Museum
stories.script: "If you are curious about the story of Gaya, which flourished along the Nakdonggang River two thousand years ago, you can discover it at the Gimhae National Museum.  Through relics excavated from the heartlands of Byeonhan and Gaya, such as the Daho-ri site in Changwon and the Yangdong-ri and Daeseong-dong tomb complexes in Gimhae, you can vividly encounter the lives of the Gaya people, who connected to the wider world through trade and cultivated an outstanding ironware culture.  The exhibition halls present Gaya's history in an easy and engaging way. On the first floor, ""The Road to Gaya"" follows the journey from prehistoric times through the rise and eventual disappearance of Gaya. On the second floor, ""Gaya and Its People"" lets you look closely at the daily life and culture of the Gaya people through splendid ornaments, pottery, and weapons. Be sure not to miss the Children's Museum and Gayanuri, where special exhibitions are held. After your visit, you can stroll along the Gaya Garden and Gujibong Peak walking path behind the museum and take in the scenery of Gimhae, where the myth of King Suro lives on.  At the Gimhae National Museum, a place where the Gaya you once knew only as a name in textbooks comes to life before your eyes, enjoy a truly special journey through time."

stories.title: The Street of Gaya
stories.script: "The path we will now walk is the Street of Gaya, a road of about two kilometers stretching from the Gimhae National Museum to the Bonghwang-dong Archaeological Site. Its scenery is so remarkable that it was named one of Korea's 100 Most Beautiful Roads by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport.  Beginning near Yeonjigyo Bridge close to the Gimhae National Museum, the Street of Gaya is a pathway that links the sites of Gaya's brilliant history. Across from the museum, you will see the Nine Chiefs Monument Stones and an outdoor performance stage. If you look closely at the wall of the stage, you will find carvings depicting the founding myth of Gaya and the story of the bridal journey of Queen Heo.  A little farther along, you will come upon life-sized sculptures of a horse, a mounted warrior, and foot soldiers. Cast in bronze, these figures were modeled on the Cup with a Warrior on Horseback, designated National Treasure No. 275, and on relics excavated from Gaya tombs. They express the advanced ironware culture and formidable military strength of the Gaya people, vividly capturing their brave and majestic spirit to inspire pride in Gimhae.  Walking a little more, you will find a sculpture in the shape of a horn cup. This is a reinterpretation of the “gakbae,” a drinking vessel shaped like a horn, rendered with modern artistry as a large fountain five meters high, expressing the bold and powerful spirit of the Gaya people.  Across from the Daeseong-dong Tombs Museum stands a work by the artist Lee Ufan titled ""Hill of Infinity."" Combining rusted iron plates with stone and wood, this piece draws the eye with its distinctive form, capturing both the iron of Gaya and the passage of natural time.  As you continue on, admiring the sculptures that stand at every turn, you will reach the ""Bell of the Gimhae Citizens."" Look closely at its design and you will find not only the original patterns of Gaya pottery, but also the spirit of the six Gaya states, symbolizing the unity of the Gaya Confederacy.  We hope the Street of Gaya has become for you a storehouse of memories, carrying with it the brilliant breath of Gaya."

stories.title: Walk Gimhae, Course 1 Closing
stories.script: And with that, today's walking guide, Walk Gimhae, comes to a close.  The traces of Gaya remain not only within its historic sites, but live and breathe here as well, in the paths we walk, in the wind, and in the scenery around us.   We hope your time in Gimhae today has become a journey that stays with you for a long time. Thank you for walking with us. We look forward to meeting you again with more wonderful stories on your next journey.

stories.title: Walk Gimhae, Course 2 Opening
stories.script: Hello, and welcome to Walk Gimhae, a walking guide series that invites you to stroll slowly along the history and scenery of Gimhae.  Today we will walk Course 2, the Aeguji Course. On this route, you will experience the Royal Tomb of King Suro, one of Gimhae's most iconic cultural treasures, along with the Daeseong-dong Ancient Tombs, which were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in September 2023. The course also takes you to the nearby Daeseong-dong Tombs Museum and Sureungwon Garden.  Beyond the walls that hold the history of the Royal Tomb of King Suro, a grove of pine trees and Chinese trumpet vines draped over the stone walls create a serene atmosphere, while the hackberry tree standing high on the hill of the Daeseong-dong Ancient Tombs, close to the sky, is a favorite photo spot.  One quick note. The Daeseong-dong Tombs Museum on today's route is closed every Monday, on January 1st, and on the days of Seollal (Lunar New Year) and Chuseok (Korean Thanksgiving), so please keep this in mind when planning your visit.  Now then, shall we make our way to our first stop, the Daeseong-dong Tombs Museum?

stories.title: Daeseong-dong Tombs Museum
stories.script: The Daeseong-dong Tombs Museum is a public museum dedicated to exhibiting, preserving, researching, teaching, and making use of the artifacts excavated from the Daeseong-dong Ancient Tombs. Since opening in 2003, it has held special exhibitions each year, introducing the history and culture of Gimhae, the heartland of Gaya culture.  The museum consists of a permanent exhibition hall and a special exhibition hall. The permanent hall presents excavated relics and vividly recreates the structures of the tombs, while the special exhibition hall offers displays on a variety of themes drawn from Gaya's history and archaeological research.  Here you will find artifacts that clearly reveal the remarkable cultural sophistication and international character of Geumgwan Gaya. Among the highlights are two treasures: the necklace excavated from Tomb No. 76 and the gilt-bronze belt excavated from Tomb No. 88, both of which showcase outstanding craftsmanship and the prestige of Gaya.  In this way, the Daeseong-dong Tombs Museum displays a wide array of artifacts that capture the very essence of Gaya culture. As you explore the museum, we hope you will come to appreciate the brilliance of the Geumgwan Gaya civilization.

stories.title: Ancient Tombs in Daeseong-dong, Gimhae
stories.script: The Daeseong-dong Ancient Tombs are one of the most representative tomb complexes of Gaya, set on a gently sloping ridge between the Gimhae National Museum and the Royal Tomb of King Suro.  Here lie the tombs of the ruling class of Geumgwan Gaya, the leading power of the Gaya Confederacy from around the 1st to the 5th century. Through the various types of burials found here, including pit tombs, wooden-chamber tombs, and stone-lined tombs, you can trace the changing styles of tomb construction over time and the active cultural exchange of the era.  To date, more than ten rounds of excavation have investigated 149 tombs and unearthed countless artifacts, providing vital evidence for understanding the history and culture of Geumgwan Gaya. In recognition of this value, the Daeseong-dong Ancient Tombs were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2023 as part of the serial property known as the Gaya Tumuli. We invite you to meet, right here, the lives and history of the Gaya people from sixteen hundred years ago.

stories.title: Sureungwon Garden
stories.script: Sureungwon is an ecological park created in honor of King Kim Suro, the founder of Gaya. Covering about 39,600 square meters, Sureungwon was designed around the theme of the meeting between King Suro and Queen Heo. Throughout the park, various spaces have been arranged so that visitors can experience the story of these two figures alongside nature.  The eastern walking path is a space dedicated to King Suro, the founder of the Garak Kingdom. Here you will find trees that grow tall and strong, such as the Japanese chinquapin, oak, and sawtooth oak. The western walking path, by contrast, honors Queen Heo. It is planted with fruit-bearing trees such as wild persimmon, wild pear, apricot, and wild peach.  At the heart of Sureungwon lies a pond. Around its edges, plants such as prickly water lily and yellow floatingheart have been cultivated to recreate the wetland environment of the Gaya period. As they stroll, visitors can naturally encounter the history of Gaya and the stories of its people.  Another charm of Sureungwon is its connection to the surrounding historical and cultural resources. The Royal Tomb of King Suro and the Daeseong-dong Ancient Tombs are nearby, and right next door stand the Gimhae Folk Museum and the Gimhae Hanok Experience Center. In one place, then, you can explore Gaya's history and culture together with traditional ways of life.  Sureungwon is a place where nature, history, and the story of Gaya come together in harmony. As you walk slowly through it, we hope you will feel the breath of Gaya from two thousand years ago and the story of King Suro and Queen Heo.

stories.title: Royal Tomb of King Suro, Gimhae
stories.audioTitle: Royal Tomb of King Suro, Gimhae
stories.script: The Royal Tomb of King Suro is the burial place of King Suro, the founding monarch of Geumgwan Gaya, and one of Gimhae's most representative historic sites.  King Suro is known as the founder of the Garak Kingdom and the progenitor of the Gimhae Kim clan, and his tomb is also called “Namneung.” The tomb is a round earthen mound about five meters high, and the surrounding grounds of roughly 18,000 pyeong (about 59,500 square meters) have been developed into a royal tomb park.  Within the grounds stand Sungseonjeon, the shrine enshrining the spirit tablet of King Suro, along with buildings such as Anhyanggak, Jeonsacheong, Jegigo, Namneung Gate, and Sungjae. Various stone monuments also remain, including a memorial stele, civil and military stone figures, stone horses and sheep, and monuments of achievement.  The Annals of King Sejong record measures taken to protect the tombs of King Suro and his queen. At first, boundary stones were set within a range of thirty paces in each direction around the tomb. In 1446, the 28th year of King Sejong's reign, the protected area was expanded to one hundred paces in each direction.  Through renovation projects in 1580, the 13th year of King Seonjo's reign, in 1647, the 25th year of King Injo's reign, and in 1878, the 15th year of King Gojong's reign, the tomb came to take on the form we see today.

stories.title: Walk Gimhae, Course 2 Closing
stories.script: Today's walk, Course 2 of Walk Gimhae, the Aeguji Course, has followed the beginning and the heart of Gimhae's Gaya culture.  Along the way, we have encountered the dreams of the Gaya people from two thousand years ago and the traces of their international exchange. The story of Gaya, which began in legend, is not a history that has ended. It continues still, woven into the lives and culture of the people of Gimhae today. Pause for a moment and look around you. Between the quiet royal tomb and the wooded paths, two thousand years of time still live and breathe.  Thank you for walking with us.

stories.title: Walk Gimhae, Course 3 Opening
stories.script: Hello, and today we will walk Course 3 of Walk Gimhae, the Bonghwangdae Course.  Starting from the Gimhae Hangeul Museum, we will explore the Archaeological Site in Bonghwang-dong, the Shell Mound Exhibition Hall, and the charming, atmosphere-filled Bonghwangdae-gil. At each stop, we will slowly encounter the traces of a royal palace, the footsteps of Gaya as an international maritime kingdom, and the stories of people still living and breathing within these old alleyways.  Today, rather than simply looking at the sights, try walking while imagining what life was like for the people who once lived here. It will make your time all the more special.  Please note that the Gimhae Hangeul Museum is closed every Monday and on the days of major holidays, so do keep this in mind when planning your visit.  Now then, shall we set off together?

stories.title: Gimhae Hangeul Museum
stories.script: The Gimhae Hangeul Museum opened in November 2021 as Korea's first public museum devoted to Hangeul, created to share widely the history and value of Hangeul, one of our people's most precious cultural treasures. In particular, the museum honors the scholarly achievements and research spirit of two leading Hangeul scholars from Gimhae, Yi Yun-jae and Heo Ung, and offers a look at the culture and history of Hangeul that has unfolded since the script was first created. Yi Yun-jae devoted himself to the systematic study and dissemination of Hangeul, laying the foundation for the study of the Korean language, while Heo Ung established Korean linguistics on a scientific footing and played a major role in the development of modern Korean language studies.  On display are precious documentary treasures written in Hangeul, including the Royal Edict of King Seonjo Written in Hangeul, a treasure composed entirely in Hangeul during the Japanese invasions of the 1590s so that ordinary people could read and understand it easily, and the Kim Seung-tae Independence Movement Song, which records the unfolding of the Jangyu March First Independence Movement of 1919 and the scenes of that time.  These materials show that Hangeul is far more than a mere writing system. It is a precious heritage that has recorded our history, our culture, and the very lives of our people.

stories.title: Archaeological Site in Bonghwang-dong, Gimhae
stories.script: "The Archaeological Site in Bonghwang-dong, Gimhae encompasses the Hoehyeon-ri Shell Mound and Bonghwangdae. It is a complex site containing cultural layers from many periods, ranging from the Bronze Age all the way to the Gaya period. Here, remains such as dolmens, shell mounds, a docking site, and an earthen fortress have been identified, allowing us to examine the traces of human life sustained over a long span of time.  The Hoehyeon-ri Shell Mound is well known as the very first site in Korea to undergo archaeological excavation. A variety of artifacts have been unearthed here, including iron implements, bone and antler tools, pottery, and carbonized rice, revealing the daily lives of the people of the Gaya period. The discovery of the huoquan, a Chinese coin, is regarded as important evidence that Gaya carried on active international trade at the time.  The name Bonghwangdae originated with Jeong Hyeon-seok, a magistrate of Gimhae during the Joseon Dynasty, who thought the shape of the hill resembled a phoenix spreading its wings. He built a terrace here and named it Bonghwangdae, meaning ""Phoenix Terrace."" At its summit stand Yeouigak and Hwangse Rock, connected to the legend of General Hwangse and the Maiden Yeoui. To the west, a Gaya-period earthen fortress and the sites of large warehouse-style buildings have been identified, showing that this was an important living space at the time.  As you explore this site, we hope you will feel the everyday culture of Geumgwan Gaya."

stories.title: Bonghwang-dong Shell Mound Exhibition Hall
stories.script: "The Shell Mound Exhibition Hall before you opened in 2006 to preserve and present the Hoehyeon-ri Shell Mound, regarded as the starting point of archaeological excavation in Korea. The roof of the building was designed in the shape of a seashell, and inside, an actual layer of shells from the excavation site is preserved and displayed.  A shell mound is a site formed when the shells that people long ago gathered and ate from the sea and rivers were thrown away and piled up, layer upon layer. In Korean it is called “jogaedeomi” or “jogaemuji.” A shell mound holds not only the shells the people of that time ate and the bones of animals and fish, but also discarded everyday tools such as pottery, stone implements, and bone tools. Traces of graves, house sites, and hearths can also be found. For this reason, a shell mound can be thought of as a treasure trove that shows us today how people lived in the distant past.  The Hoehyeon-ri Shell Mound is a heap of shells that ancient people gathered, ate, and discarded over more than 400 years, from before the Common Era to the 4th century. It forms a hill about 7 meters high, 30 meters wide, and roughly 130 meters long, running east to west.  This was also the first site in Korea to undergo archaeological excavation. In particular, the carbonized rice unearthed here provided important evidence about rice cultivation, and the discovery of oracle bones, the bones used to foretell the future in ancient society, offers a vivid picture of how people lived at the time. Beyond the Hoehyeon-ri Shell Mound, many other shell mounds have been found in Gimhae, telling us that the areas around them were all once sea. This, one might say, is why the place name Gimhae contains the character hae, meaning ""sea.“ It would be no exaggeration to say that the standing of Gaya as a maritime kingdom began right here, at the Hoehyeon-ri Shell Mound.  As you explore the Bonghwang-dong Shell Mound Exhibition Hall, we hope you will feel the lives of the Gaya people and the long history of Gimhae."

stories.title: Bonghwangdae-gil
stories.script: "The place we will now walk together is Bonghwangdae-gil, Gimhae's iconic old-downtown street full of character, often affectionately called “Bongni-dan-gil.”  This street is a place where old alleyways and youthful sensibility coexist, the very spot to feel what people today call a ""newtro"" atmosphere, a blend of the new and the retro. Houses and buildings decades old have been remodeled into cafés, workshops, and restaurants, so that the charm of the past and a modern sensibility mingle naturally. As you walk the alleys, you may feel as though you are traveling through time. In fact, this area was once so full of fortune-tellers' shops that it was known as the ""Street of the Gods,"" and traces of that can still be seen throughout the alleys today.  Bonghwangdae-gil as it is now is also a successful example of urban regeneration, created by residents and young artists together. Once worn and quiet, the alleys regained their vitality through the efforts of cooperatives and cultural communities, transforming into the Bonghwangdae-gil we see today. Tucked within the alleys are beloved eateries, distinctive gift shops, and craft workshops, so there is great joy in wandering and stumbling upon them by chance. At the far end of the alleys, you will find the Dwitgogi Street, home to one of Gimhae's signature dishes, so you can enjoy a delicious journey as well. “Dwitgogi” refers to lesser-known cuts of pork grilled over the flame, a local favorite.  As you walk along Bonghwangdae-gil, you come to realize that even a single weathered wall or an old signboard holds the time of this neighborhood. So do pause for a while, take some photos, and step into a café you like to rest a moment. After all, travel is remembered not by how long we stayed, but by how slowly we took it all in."

stories.title: Walk Gimhae, Course 3 Closing
stories.script: The Course 3 Bonghwangdae Course we have walked today has been a special path where the ancient time of Gaya and the sensibility of the present connect so naturally.  From the story of those who protected Hangeul, to the lives of the Geumgwan Gaya people two thousand years ago, and on to the Gimhae of today, blooming once more between the alleyways. Perhaps travel is less about seeing many famous places than about how closely we come to feel the breath of a single city.  Thank you for walking with us. We hope to meet you again on another path, with yet more of Gimhae's charm and stories to share.

stories.title: Gimhae Gaya Theme Park
stories.script: "Gimhae Gaya Theme Park was created as part of the restoration of Gaya's history and culture, transforming what was once the set of the popular 2010 MBC drama ""Kim Su-ro, The Iron King"" into a space where visitors can see, feel, and experience the history of Gaya. Spanning an area of 165,078 square meters, it was built with an investment of 63.5 billion won over a construction period of six years, and was completed in May 2015.  Centered around a space that recreates the royal palace of Gaya, the park offers a variety of exhibitions along with hands-on programs such as pottery making, warrior experiences, and creative activities, helping visitors understand the daily life and culture of the Gaya period in an easy and engaging way.  The park also offers a wide variety of content, including festivals and “Painters Gaya Kingdom”, a nonverbal performance that turns the very process of a painting coming to life into an enjoyable story. It welcomes around 300,000 visitors a year. In spring and autumn, it draws children on picnics and outings and young people coming to experience Gaya culture, while in summer and winter its water play area and sledding hill attract many guests. At night in particular, dazzling landscape lighting lends the park a charm quite different from the daytime, establishing it as one of Gimhae's leading tourist attractions."

stories.title: Gimhae Astronomical Observatory
stories.script: Gimhae Astronomical Observatory, the very first citizens' observatory in Gyeongsangnam-do, sits right at the top of Bunseongsan Mountain! The building has a unique shape, almost as if it were cradling an egg, and that design was inspired by the birth legend of King Suro of the Garak Kingdom, according to which the king was born from an egg.  The observatory is packed with programs that are both rewarding and genuinely fun. First, in the Virtual Constellation Program, a state-of-the-art planetarium projector gives you a preview of the seasonal constellations and the celestial objects you can spot that night. During the day, the Solar Observation Program lets you see sunspots and solar prominences with your own eyes. And at night, the Nighttime Stargazing session brings the Moon, planets, star clusters, and nebulae to life through six telescopes of various sizes. On top of that, there are quarterly special programs and hands-on events, plus fun special events timed to occasions like solar and lunar eclipses.  And here's a bonus: you get to enjoy Gimhae's glittering night view as well! Come and take in the stunning night scenery and the wonder of the cosmos with all your senses.

stories.title: Gupo Obstacle-free Trail
stories.script: "<A Path of Consideration and Companionship, the Gupo Obstacle-free Trail>  To some, a mountain summit is a steep challenge to be conquered, but here it becomes a peaceful place of rest that anyone can enjoy. Set on the slopes of Beombangsan Mountain in Gupo-dong, Buk-gu, Busan, the Gupo Obstacle-free Trail is, just as its name suggests, a path open to all, free of obstacles.  A gently sloping wooden deck trail zigzags all the way to the summit, so that someone in a wheelchair, a parent pushing a stroller, and those with weak knees alike can make their way deep into the embrace of the forest without ever running out of breath. As you walk this path, which does not have a single step, you come to feel in your heart the true meaning of ""walking together.“  As you climb along the trail, the fresh scent of pine that brushes past your nose and the songs of unnamed mountain birds become your companions. Making your way along in easy conversation, before you know it you arrive at the wide-open Sky Wind Observatory. The view here, taking in the Nakdonggang River stretching coolly below, the Gupodaegyo Bridge, and even the distant Gimhae Plain all at once, brings a rush of exhilaration that seems to open up your whole chest.  At dusk in particular, the golden sunset over the Nakdonggang River seen from here is counted among Busan's hidden scenic wonders. As you gaze at the river blazing red as if to swallow up every color in the world, the warm conversations you shared on the way up deepen into even richer memories.  Take the hand of family, a friend, or someone you love, and walk slowly. Step away for a moment from a world that competes over speed, and here at the Gupo Obstacle-free Trail, we hope you will rediscover the joy of walking at the pace of the slowest person among you."

stories.title: Hackberry of Gupo-dong
stories.script: <A Green Breath That Connects Time, the Hackberry of Gupo-dong>  Gupo-dong, Buk-gu, Busan. In a spot where the bustling noise of the city gradually fades away, there is a mysterious grove preserved as if by a miracle. It is a space where past and present coexist, a place that has held the well-being of the village for hundreds of years. This is the Hackberry of Gupo-dong.  For a very long time, this grove was home to a great hackberry tree, the village's guardian deity, designated a Natural Monument. For some 500 years it stretched its branches high toward the sky, watching over the joys and sorrows of the village. Sadly, however, it could not withstand the weight of the years and died in 2017. It then fell during the monsoon rains of 2021, and today only its weighty stump remains in place.  Though the once-lush leaves are gone, the life of the grove did not stop here. Beside the fallen old tree, seven fresh young successor trees are stretching out their tender branches, preparing for a new 500 years and destined to make the grove lush again centuries from now. The remaining stump and the growing young trees show us firsthand the tenacious vitality of nature and the value of its cycles.  The spirit that wraps around the grove is still as green as ever. Two hundred-year-old pine trees, keeping the hackberry tree's empty place from feeling lonely, carry themselves with the dignity of scholars, while the bright crape myrtle blossoms that bloom each season breathe vivid life into the colorless cityscape.  Is this a moment when you need a brief pause within the city? If so, come and visit the Hackberry of Gupo-dong. The great tree may have departed, but the whisper of life told by the young trees beginning anew upon its roots will warmly embrace your weary heart.

stories.title: Geumbit Noeul Bridge (Golden Sunset Bridge)
stories.script: "<Where the Sunset Lingers, the Geumbit Noeul Bridge>  Gupo-dong, Buk-gu, Busan. Here stands one very special landmark that connects the city with nature. It is the Geumbit Noeul Bridge, or Golden Sunset Bridge, which at a total length of 382 meters is the longest pedestrian bridge in Busan.  The Geumbit Noeul Bridge holds a value greater than that of a mere bridge. It is a space like a ""comma,"" a place to catch your breath for a moment amid the busy day. Bringing together spaces that once felt far apart, cut off by railways and roads, it lets the energy of the lively Gupo Market and the youthful streets of Deokcheon-dong flow across the bridge and down to the Nakdonggang River.  As you step onto the bridge and move forward one step at a time, the noisy sounds of the city drift far away, and the crisp river breeze fills the space they leave behind. The far end of the bridge, where your steps lead, connects to the green embrace of Hwamyeong Eco Park. It is the comfort of green nature, met in just a few minutes from a forest of gray buildings. At the end of this path, which unfolds like a secret passage, the ever-changing scenery of the ecological park, dressing in new colors with each season, will warmly welcome you.  The true beauty of the Geumbit Noeul Bridge reveals itself only when the sun hides itself beyond the horizon. As the sky begins to be dyed in deep orange and mysterious purple, the calm river starts to shimmer in gold. When the blazing red sunset reflects off the water and gently wraps the entire bridge, you will find yourself standing within the most beautiful moment of sunset in all of Busan. It is the very moment you finally understand why this place had to be named ""Golden,"" and nothing else. For this dazzling moment, at least, we hope you will set your smartphone down for a while and capture this enchanting scene with your own two eyes before your camera lens."

stories.title: Gamdong Narutgil River Walk
stories.script: "<Walking Over the River, from the Edge of the City to the Start of Nature, the Gamdong Narutgil River Walk>  Gupo-dong, Buk-gu, Busan. Here is a very special waterway where you can walk over the river, moving between city and nature. It is the Gamdong Narutgil River Walk, a 320-meter waterside pedestrian bridge stretching from Gupo Station on Subway Line 3 all the way to Hwamyeong Eco Park.  Does the name ""Gamdong"" sound a little unfamiliar? This was a historic place, home to Gamdongchang, a granary that stored tax rice during the Joseon Dynasty, and to Gamdong Ferry, one of the three great ferry crossings of the Nakdonggang River in the Joseon era. This path calls back to life the name ""Gamdong,"" which had been fading into forgetfulness. Once a place where boats bustled to and fro, it has now been reborn as a path of connection where people meet one another.  The Gamdong Narutgil River Walk reinterprets this historical spirit with a modern sensibility. Its graceful design, drawing on the motifs of a ferry boat and rippling water, stands out beautifully. As you walk along the bridge stretching out over the riverside, you feel as though you are walking over the water itself, and the colors of the riverbank that change with each season, together with the migratory birds dancing in flocks across the sky, awaken once more the vitality you had forgotten within the city.  Pause for a moment on the observation deck set at the middle of the bridge, catch your breath, and give yourself over to the river breeze. The cool wind blowing in from the heart of the river washes away the clamor of everyday life. After the sun has set, the soft lighting that flows along with your steps glows as beautifully as afterimages of light spreading across the water's surface. Stop your busy steps for a while and set your pace to the leisurely flow of the river. We hope you will linger in the quiet ease the Nakdonggang River offers, filling your heart with precious memories."

stories.title: Byeongpungam Seokbulsa Temple
stories.script: "<A Heartfelt Prayer Carved in Rock, Byeongpungam Seokbulsa Temple>  Mandeok-dong, Buk-gu, Busan. On the southern slopes of Sanggyebong Peak of Geumjeongsan Mountain, there is a mysterious temple nestled snugly among enormous rocks, as though wrapped in a folding screen. This is Byeongpungam Seokbulsa Temple. Though it is not far from the city, the moment you pass through the Iljumun, the temple's one-pillar gate, a serene atmosphere envelops your whole body, as if you have stepped into another world.  The temple was founded in the 1930s, during the Japanese colonial period, amid the pain of an oppressed era. Its greatest attraction is, without question, the group of Buddhist images carved directly into the enormous rock face. The eleven-faced Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva and the Four Heavenly Kings, intricately sculpted onto the sheer rock surface, are more than worthy of being called the essence of modern Korean Buddhist art. The moment you come face to face with them, they present a spectacle so overwhelming it can take your breath away.  Climbing the narrow stairs between the rocks, you look out over the whole of downtown Busan, and the view moves you as though the Buddha's compassionate gaze were quietly watching over the world. If you visit in the morning hours in particular, when sunlight softly plays across the rock, the three-dimensional depth of the carvings comes alive, and you can meet an even more exquisite scene.  Called ""Busan's hidden gem,"" Seokbulsa Temple is full of beautiful scenery and quiet charm, so much so that the world-renowned travel magazine Lonely Planet selected it as one of Asia's hidden wonders. It is a wonderful place to visit along the walking paths that lead from Mandeok Pass or Geumjeongsanseong Fortress, and for those in need of quiet reflection, it is the perfect place to mark a pause in the heart.  A great flower of rock, completed by tens of thousands of strikes of the chisel, Byeongpungam Seokbulsa Temple. Here, why not set down the clamor of daily life for a while and feel a deep resonance? The weighty comfort offered by the great rock face will make your steps want to linger."

stories.title: Flagpole Supports of Mandeoksa Temple Site
stories.audioTitle: Flagpole Supports of Mandeoksa Temple Site
stories.script: <A Quiet Moment Met at the Threshold of an Old Temple, the Flagpole Supports of Mandeoksa Temple Site>  Mandeok-dong, Buk-gu, Busan. As you walk along to the sound of the Sagicheon Stream, two neat stone pillars come into view that quietly bring your steps to a halt. These are the Flagpole Supports of Mandeoksa Temple Site, which once guarded the entrance to Mandeoksa, a great temple that long ago stood here.  Flagpole supports are the bases that hold, from either side, the tall pole known as a “danggan,” from which a banner called a “dang” was hung high whenever the temple held a great ceremony. To the people of old, they were like a signpost marking that the sacred temple grounds began from here.  Yet behind the complete form we now see lies a long span of waiting. In truth, for a very long time only one of the pillars stood here alone. Because a banner can only be raised when two pillars face one another, the other pillar, missing for many long years, was carefully restored in 2014, giving the monument the form it has today.  An old pillar in which the grain of time can be felt just as it is, and beside it a restored pillar that has newly filled the empty space. Like past and present walking side by side, the sight of these two stone pillars, each holding a different time, standing face to face offers the comfort of scattered fragments of history fitted back together at last.  Pause for a moment and listen to the sound of the wind passing between the two stone pillars that now face one another once more. Their lines, rising straight toward the sky without any elaborate ornament, become a comma that lets you quietly gather your thoughts amid the busy city scenery.

stories.title: Mandeoksa Temple Site
stories.script: <Traces of a Vanished Great Temple, the Mandeok Temple Site>  Mandeok-dong, Buk-gu, Busan. Cross the road from the Flagpole Supports of Mandeoksa Temple Site, and you come to the place where Mandeoksa once stood, a temple that represented Busan during the Goryeo Dynasty. Only its grounds remain today.  For a long time, the Mandeoksa Temple Site lay quietly asleep beneath the village. Then, through excavations that began in the 1990s, it finally revealed itself to the world once more. The main hall site, some four times the size of the main hall of Beomeosa Temple, the raised stone terrace built up from enormous stones fitted together with precision, and the “chimi,” a large decorative roof tile rivaling those of the Hwangnyongsa Temple Site, which is said to have been the largest temple in the East, all bore silent witness to just how grand this temple's scale once was.  Today it may look like nothing more than an ordinary park. But stand on the main hall site, once the heart of the temple, look around you, and for a moment close your eyes and imagine. Picture the majestic scene of countless monks in their robes, filling this valley as they devoted themselves to their spiritual practice. The splendid painted decoration and the gentle smile of the Buddha statues can no longer be seen, yet it is precisely because the space is empty that we can imagine the scenery of those days all the more freely.  A sorrowful record also tells us that Mandeoksa was the place of exile for a prince named Seokgi, an illegitimate son of King Chunghye, the 28th king of Goryeo. Having left the splendid palaces of Gaegyeong for this far-off place at the southern end of the land, what must the prince have felt in his heart? Perhaps that is why the stillness of the Mandeoksa Temple Site is not merely quiet, but resembles the deep peace that comes after laying everything down.  All things change and vanish in the flow of time, but the land's memory, which has kept this place, never disappears. Leaving behind its splendid past, the Mandeoksa Temple Site has now returned to the embrace of nature. Here, we hope you will slow your steps for a while and feel with your whole being the depth of time that lies beyond what the eyes can see.

stories.title: Gupo Japanese Fortress
stories.script: "<A Quiet Rampart Path Where Time Lingers, the Gupo Japanese Fortress>  Climb to the summit of Uiseongsan Mountain in Deokcheon-dong, Buk-gu, Busan, and you come face to face with a quiet rampart that has silently endured hundreds of years. This is the Gupo Japanese Fortress, standing and gazing out over the distant Nakdonggang River.  The Gupo Japanese Fortress is a fortification built by Japanese forces in 1593, during the Imjin War, to secure their supply route along the Nakdonggang River. Take a close look at the walls. Wide at the base and growing narrower toward the top, leaning at a slant, they are built in the distinctive style of Japanese fortifications, quite unlike our traditional fortresses, and they vividly reveal the fortress-building techniques and history of that time. Hundreds of years have passed, and though moss now clings to every crevice in the walls and grass has sprung up between the stones, the stone blocks stacked layer upon layer still seem to remember the time of this land carried down from the distant past.  An interesting fact is that the Gupo Japanese Fortress is also called ""Uiseong,"" meaning ""the righteous fortress."" This is because of a legend passed down that long ago, General Hwangnyong of Silla, together with five hundred soldiers, defended the fortress to the very end against an invasion by Japanese raiders and met a heroic death here. Though the structure may have been built by unfamiliar hands, the steadfast will of our ancestors to protect this land lives and breathes within the name ""Uiseong.“  Hundreds of years ago, the Gupo Japanese Fortress was a fiercely contested strategic stronghold charged with tension. Now it has become a place of rest, full of the light footsteps of passersby and the songs of grass insects. Why not lend an ear to the old stories this wall softly tells, having kept its place in silence over the long years, and move for a while at a slow and easy pace?"

stories.title: Hwamyeong Rose Garden
stories.script: "<A Neighborhood Garden Full of the Scent of Roses, the Hwamyeong Rose Garden>  Hwamyeong-dong, Buk-gu, Busan. Here is a ""palace of flowers"" where, each May, tens of thousands of roses create a magnificent spectacle. More than 50 varieties of roses show off their own colors and fragrances. From the ""passion"" whispered by red roses to the ""friendship"" conveyed by yellow roses, this is a place where, with every step, you can feel the colorful language of flowers unfolding before your eyes. This is the Hwamyeong Rose Garden.  Throughout the garden you will find lovely rose tunnels and charming sculptures. The spot beneath the tunnel where climbing roses bloom in profusion is the perfect place to capture today's treasured photo of a lifetime. Pause for a moment and press the shutter. The brightest record of this moment today will be captured within your frame.  Inside the Hwamyeong Rose Garden, a cool fountain and a small pond add a sense of refreshment throughout your walk. Thanks to the flat pathways, strollers and wheelchairs can move about with ease, and since the garden connects to the nearby Hwamyeong Library, it is just right for enjoying the leisure of a good book as well.  When the sun sets, the Hwamyeong Rose Garden changes into another set of clothes. When night comes, with moonlight and soft lighting crossing one another, the roses light up the darkness and become stars that bloom in the night. Though not showy, this deep nighttime mood grows richer along the silhouettes of the roses cast by the light, and as you stroll slowly through the garden settled in darkness, even a troubled heart will gently melt, before you know it, into the deep rose fragrance carried on the night air. At the end of your unhurried steps, gentle rose-tinted memories will gather quietly within your heart. On this path, happy enough even without any special destination, why not bring today to its most fragrant close?"

stories.title: Hwamyeong Eco Park
stories.script: "<A Blue Canvas in the City Where the Breath of the Nakdonggang River Lingers, the Hwamyeong Eco Park>  There is a vast green field spreading wide, held in the embrace of the Nakdonggang River. Stand with your back to the forest of gray buildings, and before you lies a boundless expanse of land. This is the Hwamyeong Eco Park. It is a space like a great watercolor painting, one that nature itself paints, changing its own colors with each season.  In spring, waves of yellow daffodils ripple across the field, and in summer, the graceful forms of the lotus colony greet visitors. When autumn arrives, silvery silver grass, colorful kochia, and cosmos dance along with the autumn wind, and in winter, the park becomes a peaceful resting place for migratory birds that have journeyed from afar. Wherever you walk, there is not a single wall to block your view. Only the crisp river breeze and the blue sky will fill your journey completely.  Within the park, well-laid bicycle paths and walking trails stretch out, more than enough to fill you with the lively energy of everyday life. Sit quietly for a while on a bench beneath the trees lining the riverside. Time spent gazing blankly at the gently flowing waters of the Nakdonggang River, a moment of ""water-gazing,"" offers a magical rest that briefly stops the winding spring of your busy daily routine.  As the sun slowly sinks, the Hwamyeong Eco Park meets its most dramatic moment. The hour of sunset, when the sky and the river are dyed entirely in red, is the most enchanting scene you can encounter here. When the city lights across the river flicker on one by one in the place the glorious sunset has left behind, the park at last takes its rest in deep stillness.  On this vast meadow that stretches beyond sight, set down your heavy burdens for a while and match your steps to the pace of nature. Here, where nature, people, and the river breathe together. At the Hwamyeong Eco Park, we hope you will fill your weary heart with the color blue."

stories.title: Daecheoncheon Stream and Daecheoncheon Nurigil Trail
stories.audioTitle: Daecheoncheon Stream and Daecheoncheon Nurigil Trail
stories.script: <A Green Pause Flowing Through the City, the Daecheoncheon Stream and the Daecheoncheon Nurigil Trail>  A clear stream that begins on Geumjeongsan Mountain winds its way down, and before it merges into the Nakdonggang River, it opens up a great breathing space in the heart of downtown Hwamyeong-dong. A place where people, nature, and daily life come together in delightful harmony. This is the Daecheoncheon Stream.  As you walk along the Daecheoncheon Stream, you can easily meet a family of ducks swimming leisurely on the water and a gray heron searching for food. The wildflowers and silver grass that bloom with each season offer an ecosystem so rich that it is hard to believe you are in the middle of the city. Thanks to this, it becomes a lively place of learning for children, and for adults, a resting place that awakens dulled senses and helps them read the first sentence of the season.  There is a way to savor the embrace of this living, breathing Daecheoncheon Stream even more deeply and more comfortably. It is to walk along the Daecheoncheon Nurigil Trail, which seamlessly links the green nature of Buk-gu, from the Hwamyeong Ecol Park to the Hwamyeong Arboretum and on to Geumjeongsan Mountain. Walk with the cool breeze of Geumjeongsan Mountain and the sound of clear water as your companions. As you follow the well-maintained deck trail, a lush canopy of trees overhead and cool valley water flowing beneath your feet carry the noise of the city ever farther away.  On a summer day, the star of the Daecheoncheon Nurigil Trail is, without question, the hydrangea. Wherever your steps lead, bouquets of hydrangeas blooming in soft, round clusters of blue and purple are set like jewels throughout the trail. Slow your busy steps for a moment and sit on a bench. The colonies of hydrangeas swaying in the wind offer a photo of a lifetime wherever you shoot. The scenery, fresh enough to make you forget the sweltering heat, pleasantly lowers the temperature of a weary heart. Why not rest a while at the Daecheoncheon Stream and the Daecheoncheon Nurigil Trail, a green pause that washes away the city's heat?

stories.title: Archaelogical Site of Rock Shelter in Yul-ri
stories.audioTitle: Archaelogical Site of Rock Shelter in Yul-ri
stories.script: "<A Journey Through Time to Thousands of Years Ago, the Archaelogical Site of Rock Shelter in Yul-ri>  Geumgok-dong, Buk-gu, Busan. Just a few steps from the modern apartment complexes and the subway station, a special door opens that takes you back through time. It is the oldest site in Buk-gu where traces of human presence can be found. This is the Archaelogical Site of Rock Shelter in Yul-ri, once the home of people of the Neolithic period.  The name ""rock shelter"" sounds a little unfamiliar, doesn't it? It refers, quite literally, to a place where an enormous rock juts out like a roof, naturally creating a space beneath it that offers protection from the wind and rain. Thousands of years ago, our ancestors made this their natural apartment, a gift of nature, and built their lives here while looking out over the Nakdonggang River.  Here, comb-pattern pottery was found, along with a shell mound formed from layer upon layer of the shells that the people of that time ate and discarded. Standing quietly beneath the great rock, you can almost picture before your eyes the lively scene of the Neolithic people, who caught fish in the Nakdonggang River and gathered here to sit and share their stories. The charm of the Archaelogical Site of Rock Shelter in Yul-ri lies in the fact that this is not a structure built by human hands, but a nook granted by great nature, upon which human history has layered itself over a long span of time. The weighty heft of the massive boulder and the river breeze blowing through it offer a curious peace, hard to find within the city.  The Archaelogical Site of Rock Shelter in Yul-ri is very close to Yulli Station on Subway Line 2, making it perfect as a light stroll. Before walking the nearby Hwamyeong Arboretum or the Garam Sunset Trail, why not stop here for a moment and feel the warmth of the rock, which has held thousands of years of time just as they were? Beneath the rock shelter, not showy but silently keeping its place, we hope you will set down for a while the busily turning routine of modern life and experience the leisure of the distant past."

stories.title: Park Entrance: Introduction to the Park
stories.audioTitle: Park Entrance: Introduction to the Park
stories.script: "“Meeting General Gim Jong-seo: The Immortal Tiger Who Defended Joseon” Welcome to Gim Jong-seo History Theme Park, a place dedicated to commemorating the life and achievements of General Jeoljae Gim Jong-seo, a renowned commander who played a pivotal role in the development of Joseon's northern frontier and the stabilization of its borders. When you hear the name Gim Jong-seo, what comes to mind? Many people may picture the white-haired veteran general portrayed in films and television dramas, who met a tragic end while resisting Grand Prince Suyang. Yet General Gim was much more than a brilliant military commander. He was also a distinguished scholar-official who passed the highest state civil service examination. Earning the deep trust of King Sejong the Great, he was entrusted with the important task of managing Joseon's northern frontier and made significant contributions to the nation's defense and territorial expansion. In particular, he played a leading role in the establishment of the Four Garrisons and Six Posts (Sagun-Yukjin), strengthening Joseon's northern border against incursions by the Jurchen tribes. He is also remembered as a loyal statesman who remained faithful to the young King Danjong and ultimately gave his life during the Gyeyu Jeongnan (the royal coup of 1453). Centered around the general's burial site, this History Theme Park offers visitors an opportunity to reflect on his remarkable life, his military accomplishments, and his unwavering loyalty to his country. As you explore the park, you will encounter the courage of the commander who endured the rugged terrain and harsh climate of the northern frontier, as well as the steadfast conviction that led him to remain true to his king and his principles until the very end. Now, let us journey back more than six centuries and follow in the footsteps of General Gim Jong-seo, the ""Great Tiger of Joseon"" who devoted his life to defending Joseon's northern frontier."

stories.title: "Hongsalmun (Red Spike Gate): The Border of Sacred Ground "
stories.audioTitle: "Hongsalmun (Red Spike Gate): The Border of Sacred Ground "
stories.script: “The Red Gate to a Sacred Place” Standing before you is the Hongsalmun or Red Spike Gate. If you look closely at the top of the gate, you will notice a row of pointed wooden spikes resembling arrows or spearheads. Traditionally, the Hongsalmun was erected at the entrance to places of great significance, such as royal tombs, Confucian academies, shrines, and the burial sites of loyal officials. It serves as a symbolic boundary separating the everyday world from a sacred space, reminding all who pass through to enter with respect, humility, and a reverent frame of mind. The Hongsalmun standing before General Gim Jong-seo's burial site carries the same meaning. It honors the general's lifelong dedication and loyalty to his country, while marking this as a place deserving of respect and remembrance. By the command of King Sejong the Great, General Gim Jong-seo led the development of Joseon's northern frontier and played a vital role in defending the kingdom's borders against the Jurchen tribes. His strong leadership and outstanding military ability helped strengthen Joseon's northern defenses and he continues to be remembered today as a symbol of loyalty, responsibility and unwavering devotion to his nation. As you pass through the Hongsalmun, you will enter the grounds surrounding the general's burial site and the historical spaces dedicated to his life and legacy. We invite you to leave behind the distractions of everyday life for a moment and quietly follow the footsteps of a man who devoted his life to the service of his country.

stories.title: Chunguimun Gate and Chungiksa Shrine: Everlasting Loyalty
stories.audioTitle: Chunguimun Gate and Chungiksa Shrine: Everlasting Loyalty
stories.script: “A Promise Stronger Than Death” As you pass through Chunguimun Gate, the outer gate before you, you will arrive at Chungiksa Shrine, a shrine dedicated to the memory of General Gim Jong-seo. Now, let us journey back more than six centuries. Following the deaths of King Sejong the Great and his successor, King Munjong, the responsibility of supporting the young King Danjong fell upon the senior officials of the royal court. Before his death, King Munjong entrusted General Gim Jong-seo and other high-ranking ministers with the important duty of protecting and guiding the young king. Having earned the deep trust of both kings, General Gim became one of the leading statesmen of the court. In 1453, Grand Prince Suyang launched the Gyeyu Jeongnan (the royal coup of 1453) and seized political power. During the coup, General Gim Jong-seo was attacked and killed while serving as one of the principal officials supporting King Danjong. His death marked a major turning point in the political history of the early Joseon Dynasty. The shrine before you is named Chungiksa. The name was bestowed by King Jeongjo as a mark of royal recognition, honoring General Gim's loyal service, distinguished achievements, and unwavering integrity. General Gim Jong-seo is remembered not only as an accomplished scholar-official and military commander, but also as a visionary strategist who helped secure Joseon's northern frontier and remained faithful to his duty until the very end. As you explore Chungiksa Shrine, we invite you to reflect on the enduring values of loyalty, responsibility, and devotion embodied in the life of General Gim Jong-seo.

stories.title: Chunghyo Jeongnyeo: A Legacy of Loyalty and Filial Devotion
stories.audioTitle: Chunghyo Jeongnyeo: A Legacy of Loyalty and Filial Devotion
stories.script: "“Before He Was a Loyal Minister, He Was a Devoted Son” Before you stands the Chunghyo Jeongnyeo, a commemorative gate erected by the state to honor General Gim Jong-seo's loyalty to his country and his devotion to his parents. In the Joseon Dynasty, such gates were among the highest honors bestowed upon individuals whose lives exemplified virtues such as loyalty, filial piety, and moral integrity. Despite bearing the immense responsibility of defending Joseon's northern frontier, General Gim never forgot his duty to his family. Historical records tell us that when he learned of his parents' illness, he even requested leave from public office so that he could care for them personally. After the death of his parents, he observed the traditional mourning rites, including a period of simyo (living beside their graves in accordance with Confucian custom) to fulfill his duties as a son. For General Gim, loyalty to his country and filial devotion to his parents were not separate ideals, but two guiding principles that shaped his life. Entrusted by Kings Sejong and Munjong, he helped secure Joseon's northern frontier and remained loyal to King Danjong until he lost his life during the Gyeyu Jeongnan (the royal coup of 1453). This Chunghyo Jeongnyeo commemorates both his loyalty and his filial devotion. It also invites us to remember the sacrifices endured by his family during the political turmoil of the coup, reflecting the enduring spirit of honor and integrity that they upheld together. Today, the values of loyalty and filial piety may seem distant from our everyday lives. Yet General Gim Jong-seo's unwavering commitment to his principles and to those he cherished continues to inspire people across generations. As you pause here, take a moment to reflect on the values that you, too, would choose to uphold throughout your own life. "

stories.title: Sindobi (Sacred Path Stele): A Legend Carved in Stone
stories.audioTitle: Sindobi (Sacred Path Stele): A Legend Carved in Stone
stories.script: """A Record of Great Victory, Carried Upon the Back of a Toad"" Before you stands the Stele of General Gim Jong-seo, resting upon a magnificent stone toad pedestal. A stele is a monument erected to preserve and commemorate the life and achievements of a distinguished individual, serving as a lasting historical record for future generations. Take a moment to look at the stone toad beneath the stele. In Korean tradition, the toad symbolizes longevity, endurance, and the passage of history through the ages. The inscription above records General Gim's achievements in developing Joseon's northern frontier, including his contributions to the administration of the Four Garrisons and Six Posts (Sagun-Yukjin), which helped strengthen and stabilize the kingdom's northern borders. It also honors him as an upright and incorruptible public official. Yet General Gim's life was not remembered only for its triumphs. Following the Gyeyu Jeongnan (the royal coup of 1453), he was declared a traitor, stripped of his official titles, and for many years his accomplishments were not fully recognized. As time passed, however, his legacy was gradually reexamined. During the reigns of Kings Sukjong, Yeongjo, and Jeongjo, his loyalty and distinguished service were reassessed, and his honor was progressively restored. Today, General Gim Jong-seo is remembered as one of Joseon's foremost strategists, a pioneer of the northern frontier, and one of the dynasty's most respected loyal officials. This stele is more than a stone monument. It is a lasting testament to a remarkable life and an enduring record of history. As you take a closer look at the inscription, we invite you to reflect on the legacy of General Gim Jong-seo, whose contributions continue to resonate more than six centuries later. "

stories.title: The Gim Jong-seo Family Burial Grounds: A Place of Eternal Rest
stories.audioTitle: The Gim Jong-seo Family Burial Grounds: A Place of Eternal Rest
stories.script: “The Final Resting Place of General Gim Jong-seo” You have now arrived at the final stop of our journey the Gim Jong-seo Family Burial Grounds. Situated at the highest point of the park, this peaceful site is the final resting place of General Gim Jong-seo and members of his family. The burial mound at the top belongs to General Gim Jong-seo. Nearby are the graves of his father, Gim Chu, and his grandfather, Gim Tae-yeong, allowing visitors to trace the history of three generations of the Gim family in one place. After the Gyeyu Jeongnan (the royal coup of 1453), General Gim was declared a traitor and his family suffered greatly. It is believed that his funeral could not be conducted in the customary manner. According to a local tradition, a portion of his remains was recovered and quietly buried here in his family's ancestral burial grounds. Although this story has been passed down through generations, it is regarded as a local oral tradition rather than a confirmed historical fact. As the centuries passed, General Gim Jong-seo's loyalty and achievements came to be recognized once again. Today, these burial grounds serve as a place to honor his life, his accomplishments, and the enduring spirit he left behind. As you walk through this quiet resting place, take a moment to remember not only General Gim Jong-seo, who devoted his life to defending Joseon's northern frontier, but also the family who shared both his triumphs and hardships. More than a burial site, this is a place where the history of Joseon and the enduring values of loyalty continue to live on.

stories.title: Fermented Sauce Cave The King's Sauce Storehouse: The Fermented Sauce Cave
stories.audioTitle: Fermented Sauce Cave The King's Sauce Storehouse: The Fermented Sauce Cave
stories.script: Welcome, from the bottom of our hearts, to the Fermented Sauce Cave, a place filled with the fragrant aroma of fermentation.  Have you ever heard of the “eojanggo,” the storehouse where, in the palaces of old, the fermented pastes eaten by the king were kept as great treasures? This Fermented Sauce Cave where you now stand is a very special space, a modern reinterpretation of that royal storehouse.  This site was originally a set of terraced rice paddies. A building was raised upon them and covered with earth to create an artificial cave. Thanks to this, a cool and pleasant temperature of 15 to 20 degrees Celsius is maintained all year round. Can you feel the cool air?  Now, shall we step inside the cave together? The moment you enter, more than 200 kinds of colorful sauces from some 50 countries around the world will be here to greet you.  Did you know that ketchup, which we so often enjoy, actually began not in the United States but in China? Remarkably, a salted fish sauce from China made its way to Europe, and there, meeting inexpensive onions and mushrooms, it transformed into the delicious ketchup we know today. The history of food is truly fascinating, isn't it?  Of course, we cannot leave out the deep charm of Sunchang's pride: gochujang (red chili paste), doenjang (soybean paste), ganjang (soy sauce), and vinegar. Sunchang's fermented sauces have steadfastly preserved their deep, rich flavor by adding modern science to fermentation secrets passed down over hundreds of years. This is the pride of our fermentation, capturing both taste and health at once. Now then, shall we walk together into the fun stories of the world's savory and sweet sauces?

stories.title: Hongme Hall: Food Science Museum The History of Food and War: The Food Science Museum
stories.audioTitle: Hongme Hall: Food Science Museum The History of Food and War: The Food Science Museum
stories.script: Do you see the distinctive building shaped to represent the world's five oceans and six continents? This is the pride of the Fermentation Theme Park, the Food Science Museum. Step inside, and you will find yourself full of the joy of discovering, one by one, the fascinating science and history hidden within the food we meet every day.  Did you know that humanity's food preservation technology advanced dramatically alongside war? On the battlefield, combat rations were more important than anything else, food that could save precious mealtime while quickly replenishing energy. The dried pollack and grain powder carried by the Silla army during the Three Kingdoms period became the forerunner of misugaru, the roasted grain powder we enjoy today, and the idea of preserving military provisions in glass jars, devised in the age of Napoleon, led to today's canning technology.  Now, shall we take a deeper look inside the building? One thing that catches the eye is the retort pouch, used as food for the Apollo 11 astronauts in 1969. A retort pouch is easy to picture if you think of the instant curry or black bean sauce packets we often eat at campsites. It is a magic pouch that completely blocks out light and air and is sterilized at high temperature, allowing food to be kept fresh for a very long time without any preservatives.  Thanks to this technology, a hearty meal became possible even in space, and today the retort pouch has become the star of the most convenient ready-to-eat meals on our tables. From the ordinary food on our dining table all the way out into space, the boundless world of food science now awaits your own hands-on discovery. Enjoy your journey of exploration!

stories.title: Pangi Hall: Microorganism Museum The World Unseen by the Eye: The Microorganism Museum (Pangi Hall)
stories.audioTitle: Pangi Hall: Microorganism Museum The World Unseen by the Eye: The Microorganism Museum (Pangi Hall)
stories.script: Here at Pangi Hall, you can meet the hidden heroes who bring fermentation to completion. From now on, we go to meet the true stars behind fermentation. So small they cannot be seen with the eye, yet present since the very beginning of all life, these microorganisms invite you into their astonishing world.  Isn't it truly amazing that the one who first breathed oxygen into the Earth, allowing living things to breathe, was not a plant but a microorganism called cyanobacteria? These mysterious microorganisms live abundantly inside our bodies as well. Depending on which microorganisms live in greater numbers in our gut, even our body shape can change. This is exactly where the familiar talk of fat bacteria and slim bacteria begins.  Now, shall I share a special secret about our animal friends? The koala lives on nothing but the leaves of the eucalyptus, an extremely toxic plant. In fact, these leaves are dangerous, and other animals get a stomachache if they eat them. So how is it that the koala does not fall ill? It is because the mother koala passes on to her baby, in advance, the special microorganisms that can digest this toxic plant. It is just like a mother handing down a magical gift of health to her child.  People, too, are connected to one another through microorganisms. Did you know that when we kiss someone we love, as many as 80 million microorganisms are passed between each other? Perhaps the way old friends or family members come to resemble one another is because sharing microorganisms has brought them even closer.  How did you find the mysterious and delightful world of microorganisms?

stories.title: Kongi Hall (1F Champions Sports Park / 2F Onggijonggi Play Library and Science Hall) A Playground Overflowing with Lively Energy: Kongi Hall
stories.audioTitle: Kongi Hall (1F Champions Sports Park / 2F Onggijonggi Play Library and Science Hall) A Playground Overflowing with Lively Energy: Kongi Hall
stories.script: Hello! This place, where cheerful laughter never stops, is Kongi Hall. The first and second floors of Kongi Hall are filled with entirely different charms throughout all four seasons, no matter the time of year.  First, the Champions Sports Park on the first floor is a dynamic indoor activity space where not only children but adults too can work up a sweat and have fun. From thrilling indoor climbing to screen clay shooting and quick jump! Brimming with energy whenever you visit, and blessed with a comfortable indoor environment, this is the perfect place for children to run and play to their hearts' content in every season.  Head up to the second floor and the Onggijonggi Play Library and Science Hall opens up for our children. Here they can read all kinds of books to their hearts' content and nurture their imagination, while learning the principles of science naturally through play. Once they start romping in the large ball pit and on the mini slide, they will lose all track of time. Here at Kongi Hall, where body and mind grow ever taller with the rich energy of fermentation, make joyful memories all year round!

stories.title: Yeast Hall The Wizard of Bread and Liquor: The Yeast Hall
stories.audioTitle: Yeast Hall The Wizard of Bread and Liquor: The Yeast Hall
stories.script: Have you ever heard of yeast, the magical star hidden within the bread and liquor we eat and drink every day? The Yeast Hall of the Fermentation Theme Park is a space for fascinating exploration into the history of yeast and nuruk (fermentation starter), which enrich our tables.  This hall is divided largely into a first floor and a second floor. The first floor is an exhibition hall where you can take an in-depth look at the history of yeast and nuruk, made up of three exhibition rooms in all.  In the first exhibition room, you can encounter the long history of yeast, which has evolved alongside humanity, and the birth of the traditional nuruk that our ancestors used with such wisdom. Step into the second exhibition room, and through videos and displays you can take in, at a glance, the colorful fermented foods, liquors, and the history of bread from countries around the world. And in the final third exhibition room, you can learn the deeper story of just how the special nuruk and traditional fermented sauces made in Sunchang, the home of fermentation, come to completion.  Go up to the second floor, and a hands-on space awaits where you experience it all for yourself. Here you will find not only fermentation science programs but also a range of activities such as fermentation cooking classes where you make delicious food with your own hands, all hugely popular with children.  But that is not all! A special treat you simply must enjoy at the Yeast Hall is waiting for you: the Yeast Car Play Zone. As you have fun zipping around in bumper cars, the scientific principles of fermentation will slip right into your mind before you know it. Experience the magic of yeast that enriches our lives, right now, for yourself at the Yeast Hall!

stories.title: Gogo Hall A Place for Body and Mind to Rest: Gogo Hall
stories.audioTitle: Gogo Hall A Place for Body and Mind to Rest: Gogo Hall
stories.script: If you have played to your heart's content at the Fermentation Theme Park, now it is time to catch your breath and take a rest. Known as the Fermentation Therapy Center, this Gogo Hall is a cozy resting space that soothes a weary body and mind. Up on the second floor, you will find a foot bath area where you can soak your feet in warm water and ease your fatigue, along with a nap room where you can quietly close your eyes.
