There is also a café where you can enjoy fragrant coffee and tasty snacks, making it just right for the whole family, from children to adults, to recharge together. Lively play is wonderful, but every now and then, why not add a leisurely pause like this? At Gogo Hall, take some time for healing that leaves your body and mind refreshed.

stories.title: Maekom Hall
stories.script: Spicy and sweet! A place where joy bursts and sparkles all through your mouth! This is Maekom Hall, the food court that adds to the joy of your journey with delicious snacks!  Step inside and you will see a special resting spot called “Sikchibang.” Sikchibang means a space for healing the body and mind through food. As you share tasty snacks that add to the joy of travel, and laugh and chat heartily with your loved ones, the fatigue that has built up will melt away like snow.  If you would like to add some delicious energy to today's journey, come on over to Maekom Hall without a moment's hesitation! Tasty delights are waiting for you.

stories.title: The Classroom of Memories
stories.script: Shall we hop aboard a time machine for a moment and travel back to those days in the black-and-white photographs? With its creaky wooden desks, an old stove, and the teacher's handwriting pressed firmly onto the blackboard in chalk, this place is the Classroom of Memories.  This is no simple exhibition space. For parents, it brings back the flutter and nostalgia of school days long forgotten, and for children, it becomes a place of generational connection, where they can see and touch their parents' childhood with their own eyes. As you put on old school uniforms and take photos in the style of that era, before long conversation blossoms between parent and child. Gather round together with friends, or with the whole family, and once again feel the laughter of those days.  In a fast-changing world, this is a place where you can pause for a moment and meet the warmest version of yourselves. This is the Classroom of Memories.

stories.title: Sunchang Souvenir Shop
stories.script: Would you like to keep your happy memories from the Fermentation Theme Park in an even more special way? Let us introduce you to the Souvenir Shop, where Sunchang's fermentation microorganisms have been brought to life as characters!  Adorable character souvenirs developed by our very own Sunchang Fermentation Tourism Foundation are waiting for you. From stationery for children to everyday household goods you can use in daily life, come and discover special items well worth collecting.  Oh, and one more thing! This is not only a place to find souvenirs but also serves as a tourist information center full of travel tips. If you are curious about your next stop on the journey, or if there is anything more you would like to know about Sunchang, please feel free to ask our friendly staff anytime. Here, at the place that accompanies both the beginning and the end of your journey, complete your precious trip to Sunchang in all its rich color!

stories.title: Perennial Plant Garden
stories.script: Slow your steps for a moment and step into the Perennial Plant Garden, brimming with fresh green. This is a place where a variety of plants breathe, grown by Sunchang's clean air and healthy soil. In particular, you can meet up close the plants of our land that form the very foundation of fermentation, and feel the comfort that nature offers. As you stroll slowly through this garden, green all year round, you may feel as though even the inside of your body is being cleansed. In the midst of a busy daily life, we hope you will fully feel here the pace of nature you had briefly forgotten.

stories.title: Sunshine Lounge
stories.script: After happily roaming all around the Fermentation Theme Park, you will surely need a place to rest for a while. When that time comes, please find your way to the Sunshine Lounge.  Where warm sunlight settles softly through the windows, this is a comfortable haven and a cozy charging station for you, our visitors. Lean back in a chair for a while and chat quietly about the stories of fermentation and science you have seen today. Simply gazing at the scenery spread out beyond the window will become the sweetest rest of your journey today.  So that your steps may feel all the lighter, the Sunshine Lounge will always welcome you warmly.

stories.title: Seoul Station, Where the City Meets the Airport
stories.audioTitle: Seoul Station, Where the City Meets the Airport
stories.script: Seoul Station brings together mainline rail, the subway, and the Airport Railroad (AREX) in one place, making it one of the city's key transport hubs. Trains to major cities nationwide, downtown transit, and the line running out to the airport all connect here, serving visitors arriving in Seoul as readily as travelers heading on to other parts of the country. The route through the station stays relatively simple even on an itinerary that has you hopping from place to place, so Seoul Station serves as a dependable anchor at the start and the finish of a visit to Seoul.  Seoul Station opened in 1900 and has stood as the city's flagship railway station ever since. Its layout today is built so that passengers can move easily between the trains, the subway, and AREX. The ground level handles KTX, ITX-Saemaeul, and other services running to and from major cities nationwide, while the levels below connect to Subway Lines 1 and 4 and to AREX.  Signage and amenities inside the station are clear enough that first-time visitors find their way without much trouble. Shops and a row of restaurants also occupy the third floor, which makes it easy to eat or rest for a while before or after a journey. It's a convenient spot to take a short breather while waiting for a train or before moving on to the next thing on the itinerary.  Seoul Station is especially useful for travelers combining rail and air, since the AREX Express Train and the City Airport Terminal both operate here. The Express Train runs quickly from Seoul Station to Incheon International Airport. International passengers on selected airlines can also complete check-in and departure immigration in advance at the Seoul Station City Airport Terminal. Anyone who completes those formalities at Seoul Station on the day of departure can then use the dedicated departure lane at Incheon International Airport and enter the duty-free area more smoothly. Send your luggage on ahead, whatever time your flight departs, and spend the time you have left enjoying downtown Seoul with nothing weighing on you.  Begin and end your time in Seoul at Seoul Station, where easy connections and efficient transfers make each moment that much more comfortable.

stories.title: Seoul Station, Where Culture and Pathways Meet
stories.audioTitle: Seoul Station, Where Culture and Pathways Meet
stories.script: Seoul Station is more than a transport hub: it's a place where Seoul's past and present sit side by side. A building that still carries traces of the old station stands alongside a newly built pedestrian walkway, and together they give the Seoul Station area a look unlike anywhere else in the city. Slow your steps for a moment and another side of Seoul surfaces in the middle of the busy downtown.  Culture Station Seoul 284 catches the eye first. The building is a cultural complex created by restoring the former Seoul Station, and it hosts a range of arts programs including exhibitions, performances, and workshops. Its red brick exterior, in particular, preserves the Renaissance architectural style of Gyeongseong Station as it stood in 1925, allowing you to look closely at what the old Seoul Station once was.  A short walk on brings you to Seoullo 7017. The walkway occupies the old Seoul Station overpass, which was once slated for demolition but was instead rebuilt as a pedestrian path. Walk it slowly, and the city opens up from a little above street level, in a view of Seoul unlike the everyday one. After sunset, the lamps along the path come on one by one, and the night view of the station district and the downtown beyond arrives all at once. Take in the city's energy by day, and after dark, the glittering lights that give Seoul another kind of appeal.  Culture Station Seoul 284 and Seoullo 7017 each connect Seoul's timelines in their own way. One offers the beauty of modern architecture; the other shows an aging overpass reborn as a walking route for the people who live here. Walk both, and the way Seoul's past runs into its present becomes something you can feel up close.  Take your time and look around the Seoul Station area on foot. Traces of the old station and the shape of a city that has changed around it come together into something only Seoul offers.

stories.title: Walking the Seoul of K-Dramas from Gongdeok Station
stories.audioTitle: Walking the Seoul of K-Dramas from Gongdeok Station
stories.script: Anyone who watches K-dramas knows the scene: office workers closing out a busy day at a restaurant tucked into an alley. Brightly lit restaurants, people moving up and down the lane, warm laughter and the smell of good food — that combination is Seoul's evening at its most vivid. Gongdeok is where the familiar mood of those scenes exists off-screen.  Start with Gongdeok Jokbal Alley, the strip that defines the neighborhood. It stands today as Gongdeok's signature food alley, but it began as a small restaurant off a market lane. The alley's history began about 30 years ago, with sundaetguk (Korean blood sausage soup) simmered for market traders and jokbal (braised pig's trotters) served alongside their drinks. More shops opened nearby one after another until the jokbal alley took the shape it has now. Today, people finishing their day gather here in the warm light and the smell of cooking, and they make a warm evening scene that belongs to Gongdeok alone. You half expect to find the authentic local eateries a drama's characters would head to after work tucked somewhere along it.  Mapo Jeon Alley sits directly beside it, and it's much loved for the nutty aroma of batter browning in the pan and for its warm, familiar atmosphere. Jeon are Korean savory pancakes: vegetables, seafood, meat, and other fillings are coated in batter and pan-fried until golden brown, and the appeal lies in the crisp texture and clean, mild flavor. Conversation never stops in this alley, carried over plates of jeon fresh from the pan, and it gives Gongdeok's evenings more depth.  Gongdeok's appeal has less to do with spectacle than with showing an ordinary Seoul evening at its warmest. Footsteps on the way home from work, the layers of time settled into old alleys, and the plain warmth that good food gives off all come together into the deep, unmistakable mood of the neighborhood. Head for Gongdeok Station if you want to walk through the familiar Seoul evenings of K-dramas yourself. Follow Gongdeok Jokbal Alley and Mapo Jeon Alley, and the city's nights and the character of its back lanes come to you of their own accord.

stories.title: Hongik University Station, Alive by Day and by Night
stories.audioTitle: Hongik University Station, Alive by Day and by Night
stories.script: Head for Hongdae if you want to feel the young, free-spirited mood of Seoul. Trend and sensibility feed off each other in this neighborhood: by day, it opens onto streets full of character and unhurried places to walk, and by night, music, lights, and the energy of the crowd bring out everything youthful in it.  Start with Hongdae by daylight. Hongdae Street gathers distinctive shops, cafes, performance venues, and cultural spaces of all kinds, which makes it a good place to soak up the free-and-easy air you only get here. Red Road in particular, where musicians busk every day, puts a young sensibility and a lively street culture right in front of you. KT&G Sangsangmadang brings the arts-and-culture feeling that defines Hongdae into sharp focus.  Make for Gyeongui Line Forest Park, better known as Yeontral Park, if you want a slower hour in Hongdae. The path follows a route trains once ran along, and it has become a much-loved place to rest in the middle of the city. Green trees and grass line the way, with charming little cafes and shops strung along it, and walking it slowly buys you an easier stretch of time in a busy downtown. It offers a different kind of ease from the energy of Hongdae Street, which is why so many people stop here for a while.  Hongdae shifts again once the sun goes down. Lights flick on one after another along Hongdae Street and Red Road, and music and laughter fill the air. Street performances run near the venues and at points throughout the area, while distinctive shops and cafes stay busy well into the night. Streets that by day are for wandering after whatever catches your eye now fill with the heat of youth and an energy that runs free.  Hongdae sits at the center of youth culture, where trend and an unbound sensibility come together. Spend the daytime taking it slow along its distinctive streets and through Yeontral Park, then come back at night for the mix of music and light that gives the neighborhood its charge. Day and night each hold their own appeal here, so come and take in the young, lively spirit of Seoul.

stories.title: A K-Content Journey Starting at Digital Media City Station
stories.audioTitle: A K-Content Journey Starting at Digital Media City Station
stories.script: Step off at Digital Media City Station, and the first thing you notice is the atmosphere of a place that sits at the center of Korea's broadcasting and media industry. MBC and SBS, two of the country's leading broadcasters, are based here, which puts you close to the energy of a city where dramas of every kind, variety shows, and music programs are made. Walk slowly through the streets around the studios and the particular mood of the place where K-content is born comes through on its own.  The area around the station holds more than broadcasting and media; it also has places to enjoy nature without leaving the city. Haneul Park, an ecological park within World Cup Park, is chief among them: a former landfill site that nature has since reclaimed and that has been reborn as a beautiful green expanse. Follow the walking trails and a wide-open view unfolds, with broad fields of silver grass, a rock garden, and wind turbines set against one another. The park shows a different face in every season, which makes it a good place to slow down for a while in the middle of the city. It's best known in fall, when silver grass and pink muhly grass come together and draw visitors in numbers.  Oil Tank Culture Park also stands a short distance from Haneul Park. The site is a cultural complex built from the huge cylindrical tanks that once stored petroleum, now converted into exhibition halls, performance venues, and other cultural spaces. Walk slowly between the tanks and a distinctive scene emerges: the red of the industrial structures set against green trees. Traces of the old industrial facility and the new cultural spaces hold together in balance, and the effect is hard to find anywhere else. A range of exhibitions and performances runs here, so the park is also a place to encounter Seoul's newer culture.  Broadcasting and media meet nature and culture around Digital Media City Station, in a part of the city that shows off another side of Seoul. The energy of K-content, the ease of nature in the middle of the city, the character of a cultural venue given a second life: Digital Media City Station offers a view of Seoul all its own.

stories.title: Magongnaru Station: Walking Through Nature, Meeting Culture
stories.audioTitle: Magongnaru Station: Walking Through Nature, Meeting Culture
stories.script: Magongnaru Station offers an unhurried rest when you want to catch your breath in the middle of a forest of high-rises. The Airport Railroad (AREX) and Subway Line 9 meet here, in a new restorative corner of Seoul where green nature and the arts come together, and stepping off the train sets the pace of the city aside for a while.  Seoul Botanic Park comes first. It was built in Magok, once the last remaining development site in Seoul, and is the country's first botanic park, combining a botanical garden and a public park in one. The conservatory's distinctive shape, like a shallow bowl, is what the park is best known for. Walk the paths where the scent of flowers meets green trees, and the ease that nature offers arrives slowly, even with the busy city close by.  Carry the garden's afterglow with you, then head to LG Arts Center Seoul. The venue moved to Magok in 2022 and is also well known for its building, designed by the world-renowned architect Tadao Ando. Between architecture that keeps company with its natural surroundings and a full slate of performances, the arts take on another dimension here. Take your time with the building itself, and let the beauty of the space register alongside everything else.  The unhurried walk continues at Gangseo Hangang Park. It runs from Gayangdaegyo Bridge to the boundary between Seoul and Gimpo, combining a wetland ecological park with a sports park under a single theme. Walk slowly along the Hangang River, and a cool breeze comes off the water while another view of Seoul opens up. It's a good place to slow right down with nature close at hand, and toward sunset the color spreading across the river deepens the calm.  Being out among the greenery of a botanical garden, enjoying the arts, walking slowly along the Hangang River: that is a day here. Magongnaru Station gives you room to breathe in the middle of a busy Seoul and find another side of the city. Nature, culture, and views of the Hangang River all come together at Magongnaru Station, so come and give a few unhurried hours of Seoul to this corner of the city.

stories.title: A Small Trip of Your Own at Gimpo Airport
stories.audioTitle: A Small Trip of Your Own at Gimpo Airport
stories.script: Take a pause at Gimpo Airport if you have time before your flight. You can shop and eat here, and watch the planes moving along the runway — a view you'll find at an airport and nowhere else.  The National Aviation Museum of Korea, near the station, is the country's first national museum devoted to aviation and houses a valuable collection documenting Korea's aviation history. Aircraft on display carry a presence that looks ready to lift off at any moment, and that is the pleasure of the place.  Lotte Mall Gimpo Airport, Korea's largest lifestyle shopping complex, connects underground to Gimpo International Airport Station. Shopping is only part of it: a range of restaurants, cafes, and rest areas make it a comfortable place to settle before heading to the terminal. Wander the wide, airy levels at your own pace and the hours before departure pass more easily. The airport itself also carries K-beauty brands of all kinds, so there's time to browse and shop for beauty products before you fly.  Lotte Mall Gimpo Airport is also a good place for one last Korean meal. The restaurants on the second basement level serve gukbap (rice in hot soup), ssambap (rice and fillings in leaf wraps), sujebi (hand-torn dough soup), jjukkumi (webfoot octopus), and more, so a taste of Korea is easy to come by. Sit down to an unhurried meal and take the time to look back over your trip through Korea.  Head for the observation deck on the sixth floor of Lotte Mall once the meal is done. The deck puts you close enough to watch planes taking off and landing, and the whole restless business of an airport comes into a single frame. By day the aircraft keep up a constant motion that gives the view its life; toward evening the runway takes on the color of the sunset and offers something else again. Stop for a while and look at the sky and the runway together, and the particular feeling of an airport settles on you.  Shopping, good food, and the planes moving along the runway. Gimpo Airport turns the wait before departure into part of the trip itself. Rest here until it's time to board, and enjoy the last moments of your journey through Seoul at your own pace.

stories.title: Gyeyang Station, Better the Slower You Take It
stories.audioTitle: Gyeyang Station, Better the Slower You Take It
stories.script: "Gyeyang Station is where eco-friendly slow travel comes into its own: staying a while, letting the landscape come to you. The Gyeongin Ara Waterway runs through the area around the station, so a trip here can mean moving slowly along the water and taking in the views from the bank as you go.  If slow travel from Gyeyang Station appeals to you, go by bicycle. The cycle paths here have no serious gradients and run more or less flat, which makes them easy going for anyone. Bike rental points along the Ara Waterway make it simple to pick one up, so you can set off without any special preparation. Riding along the water is enough on its own to give you the easy pace of the area around Gyeyang Station.  Move slowly along the channel and the view over the Gyeongin Ara Waterway draws closer. Cruise boats pass over the broad open water, and sculptures set along the path add something else to look at. Riding into the wind through that wide-open scenery brings an ease that faster travel never does. Pausing at one of the rest areas along the way to look out over the water is another large part of the route's appeal.  Gyulhyeonnaru is a good place to break the ride. It sits on both banks of the wide waterway, with Gyeyangdaegyo Bridge joining the two halves in the middle. Wooden boardwalks and cycle paths around it are well maintained, so it's easy to get off the bike for a walk or take in the view over the water.  Carry on riding and the route can take you as far as Aradaegyo Bridge in Gimpo. Pedal steadily along the path and the bridge is upon you before you know it, with a cool wind off the canal to make the end of the ride that much fresher. Slow travel is about enjoying the journey itself rather than reaching the destination quickly, letting the scenery change at its own pace. Why not start yours at Gyeyang Station?  "

stories.title: Geomam Station, Where Passion and Calm Sit Side by Side
stories.audioTitle: Geomam Station, Where Passion and Calm Sit Side by Side
stories.script: "Geomam Station lets you take in the heat of K-pop and the ease of open nature all in one day, at a destination where the city and the natural world sit in balance. It is also a key hub on the Airport Railroad (AREX) between Seoul and Incheon International Airport, where all kinds of journeys and daily routines converge. Start your trip with a full day at Geomam Station.  Geomam Station is a place to catch K-pop at its most charged. Incheon Asiad Main Stadium, close to the station, hosts K-pop concerts and events of every kind. On concert or fan-meeting days, you'll see crowds of fans filling the hours before the doors open, buzzing with anticipation. If K-pop is your thing, check the schedule and feel that heat for yourself.  Once you've had your fill of the crowd, head for the Ara Waterway and slow down. The Gyeongin Ara Waterway is a man-made canal linking the Hangang River to the West Sea, with broad water and walking paths laid out along it, made for taking your time. Walk with the water beside you and a calm settles in, quite unlike the energy of the stadium. Ease your pace, and let the cool air and the still canal do the rest. After sunset, the sky and the water change color together, and once the surrounding lights come on, the mood settles further.  The anticipation the Airport Railroad carries with it, the heat of a K-pop concert, and the ease of the Ara Waterway all come together at Geomam Station. Make a day of it that belongs to you. "

stories.title: Cheongna International City Station, Where the Light Turns from Sunset to Night
stories.audioTitle: Cheongna International City Station, Where the Light Turns from Sunset to Night
stories.script: "The area around Cheongna International City Station holds both the moment the sun goes down and the city lights that sharpen as night deepens. Red spreads across the sky toward the West Sea; turn your eyes to the waterfront downtown and a night view of glittering lamps takes over. Watch the mood of the day shift slowly in one place, and the particular appeal of Cheongna International City comes to you on its own.  Jeongseojin is the place to start. The name means the westernmost ferry landing, taking Gwanghwamun in Seoul as the starting point, and it is known as one of the best spots to watch the sun set over the West Sea. Jeongseojin Square features the Sunset Bell, the site's signature sculpture, along with a marker stone; both are worth a look. Walking paths, a sunset observatory, and nearby rest areas make it easy to take in the West Sea slowly and let an hour pass.  Cheongna Central Lake Park shows a different face after dark. As the evening deepens, the park's unhurried scenery extends to Canal Way, and the surroundings take on a more urban character. Canal Way follows the water with walking paths, cafes, and shops strung along it. Watch the red of the West Sea sunset from Jeongseojin, then spend the night hours on the waterfront at the lake park and Canal Way. The contrast that opens up as day turns to night is another kind of appeal unique to Cheongna International City.  "

stories.title: Yeongjong Station, Riding Closest to the West Sea
stories.audioTitle: Yeongjong Station, Riding Closest to the West Sea
stories.script: "Yeongjong Station puts you close to the West Sea, with wide-open coastal paths to walk and water-based leisure activities that make for a different kind of day.  Seaside Park is the signature destination around Yeongjong Station. It is a large coastal park running from the Sea Breeze Garden and the Salt Field Theme Garden through the Waterfront and Sky Cloud Square to Yeongjongjin, and each zone offers its own scenery and activities.  The walking paths along the shore come with a cool sea breeze and the wide-open West Sea. Observation decks, sculptures, sports facilities, and playgrounds are set throughout the park, so families can look around at their own pace.  The one thing to do at Seaside Park is the Seaside Rail Bike. It's a bike that runs on rails, and you pedal it yourself along the West Sea coastline. The open sea fills the view ahead, and the sea breeze adds to the pleasure of the ride. Rolling slowly with the water ahead brings you alongside coastal scenery that's hard to reach any other way. Bring family, friends, or someone you love, and pedal the West Sea together.  Yeongjongjin makes a good final stop. It's a historic site that once guarded the waters off Yeongjongdo Island, and today it offers the story of the area alongside the sea view. Take in the lively coastline of Seaside Park and the quiet of Yeongjongjin together, and you come away with a deeper sense of Yeongjongdo's nature and its history.  Riding the rail bike with the West Sea in view, walking without hurry along a broad coastal park. Nature, leisure and the story of Yeongjongdo all come together at Yeongjong Station. Come and make a day of the sea here.  "

stories.title: Unseo Station, the Start of a Quieter Kind of Trip
stories.audioTitle: Unseo Station, the Start of a Quieter Kind of Trip
stories.script: "Unseo Station sits close to Incheon International Airport, yet the mood here is quiet and unhurried, nothing like the bustle of the terminals. Eungol Cafe Street stands out as the best place to explore the area around Unseo Station at a slow pace. Cafes and restaurants of all kinds line the roughly 800-meter lane, with murals appearing here and there, which makes it a pleasant walk. You don't need a destination in mind; part of the pleasure is coming across somewhere you like along the way.  The appeal of Eungol Cafe Street is how easy it feels. Each cafe has a character of its own, so it's simple to walk the lane, step into whichever one draws you, and settle in over a coffee. Why not give the street the cafe tour it's made for, and let an hour or two go by?  Go a little farther from Unseo Station and the Sinsimodo Islands come within reach. Sinsimodo is the collective name for three islands: Sindo, Sido and Modo. Bridges link all three, so you can take them in one after another by car or bicycle, with no ferry transfers. Sindo is known for its mountain and coastal scenery, Sido for views where mountains and sea play against each other. Modo carries the quiet, easy air of an island village.  The three sit close together, but each holds its own look and its own mood. If time allows, take a bicycle along the roads that link them and go slowly. Blue water, small villages and beautiful stretches of coast open up one after another as you ride. Stop wherever you like for a photo, or look out at the sea and let the pace drop.  A cafe crawl within sight of the airport, and a run across three islands with the sea alongside. Unseo lets you take in both landscapes in a single day. Come and make a memory that stays.  "

stories.title: Airport Cargo Terminal Station, Where the Thrill of Flight Lingers
stories.audioTitle: Airport Cargo Terminal Station, Where the Thrill of Flight Lingers
stories.script: "Airport Cargo Terminal Station puts both planes and cars within arm's reach. It sits near Incheon International Airport, so aircraft taking off and landing are in plain view, and there is somewhere to get behind the wheel yourself, which adds up to a few hours you won't spend anywhere else.  If cars interest you, visit the BMW Driving Center. You can drive a BMW yourself on a professional track. It suits travelers who love cars, and just as much anyone looking for something they haven't tried before.  There are hands-on programs for families too. Junior Campus uses a range of activities to show how a car works and make the science behind it easy and fun to grasp. The whole thing is built around seeing, touching, and doing, so children take to it without much prompting.  Once the driving is done, it's time to look up. Sky Garden at Incheon International Airport is the place to see aircraft up close. Flowers bloom across the wide grounds in every season, making it a good place for a walk with the airport landscape around you. The main draw at Sky Garden is the traffic in and out of the airport. Aircraft gather speed down the runway and lift away, or drop slowly toward the ground on approach, and you see all of it from close range. When one seems to pass directly overhead, you stop merely knowing how near the airport is and start feeling it.  It's worth taking a photo with a plane above the flower beds. The seasonal colors and a large aircraft land in a single frame, producing a picture you won't find in many other places. Simply pausing mid-walk to watch the planes move is a pleasure in itself. Watch aircraft take off and land from close by, get behind the wheel yourself, and let Airport Cargo Terminal Station show you the appeal of the machines that move between sky and ground. "

stories.title: Incheon International Airport, Where the Journey Begins and Ends
stories.audioTitle: Incheon International Airport, Where the Journey Begins and Ends
stories.script: "Incheon International Airport opened in 2001 and became more convenient and varied when Terminal 2 came into service in 2018. It holds both the anticipation of a journey beginning and the good feeling of one ending well.  To take in the sweep of Incheon Airport at a glance, stop by the Incheon Airport Observatory. Close to Terminal 1, it overlooks the entire airport and the aircraft moving in and out.  The indoor viewing area on the first floor gives an easy view of the runways and airport facilities, along with a bird's-eye plan of the site and aviation information. Go up to the open-air deck on the second floor, and the runways, Terminals 1 and 2, and the Concourse all come into view at once.  Paradise City is a good choice if you want rest and a slower pace. It sits on Yeongjongdo Island in Incheon, an integrated resort that brings art, relaxation, and plenty to do under one roof. Paintings, sculptures, and media art are installed throughout, so looking around the place means looking at art whether you planned to or not.  If what you need is proper rest, try CIMER inside Paradise City. CIMER combines a European-style spa with Korea's jjimjil tradition. A jjimjilbang is one of Korea's signature ways of resting: you warm your body through in the heated rooms, then take your time in the lounge areas.  CIMER lays out rest areas on a range of themes and runs programs that change with the season. It's a good place to work the fatigue out in the warmth and let time pass at its own pace.  Paradise City offers art as a form of restoration and a high-end spa in one place, minutes from the airport. Why not look at the art, then let the spa do the rest?  Incheon Airport brings together culture and art, good food, and proper rest. If you want the beginning and the end of your trip to count for more, take that time slowly at Incheon Airport. "

stories.title: Dailycation: A New Way to Travel Like a Local
stories.audioTitle: Dailycation: A New Way to Travel Like a Local
stories.script: "An ordinary Saturday for someone who lives in Seoul can be a special day on someone else’s travel itinerary.  You sit by the river and order fried chicken, then buy tteokbokki at the neighborhood market. At a convenience store, you pick out a snack that has just come out, and you step into a Life Four Cuts photo booth with a friend.  This kind of trip is called “Dailycation,” a blend of daily and vacation. It means traveling by living the way locals live day to day. All you need to know is where to go and what to order.  Hangang Park in Seoul has designated delivery zones. Settle in by the water, order chicken on your phone, and it will be brought to the appointed spot. Try chimaek by the Hangang River, chicken and beer together. It is one of those everyday thrills that visitors from abroad make a point of trying once.  Hangang Park stretches across Seoul, and each stretch has its own character. At Banpo Hangang Park you can watch the Moonlight Rainbow Fountain play from the bridge after dark. People heading for Mangwon Hangang Park tend to pick up food at the nearby market first and carry it down to the water.  That market is Mangwon Market. It has more than 40 years of history behind it and now counts as a favorite with Seoul’s younger generation too — spicy tteokbokki worth queuing for, oversized fried stuffed peppers, thick tteokgalbi, handmade cream makgeolli. Walking the market and tasting your way through it is the whole pleasure.  If getting out to the Hangang isn’t practical, head to a convenience store instead. Korean convenience stores are the fastest place to find whatever snack has just started trending on social media. Random products that give no hint of what’s inside, desserts made with famous bakeries, giant instant noodles built for a mukbang challenge. Plenty of them sell out the moment they launch.  For something a little more particular, try a personal color analysis. A consultant holds up fabrics in different colors to your face to determine which ones suit you. Come without makeup for an accurate reading; each session runs 40 minutes to an hour.  There are also cafes that open for a single day only. These are idol birthday cafes, where fans rent out a whole cafe to celebrate an idol’s birthday. The interior is dressed with photos and props, and there are special menu items and merchandise. Most happen around Hongdae, Seongsu, and Gangnam, and you can find dates and venues on social media.  Four-cut photo booths are where you leave Korea with a memory in hand. They work more like small self-service studios: hats, sunglasses, scarves, and other props are free to use, and you can shoot with special frames made in collaboration with idols and actors.  Copy what people in Seoul actually do with their weekends. You don’t need a special destination; an ordinary day holds a trip that could only be Seoul. "

stories.title: The Neighborhoods Where Seoul’s Trends Gather
stories.audioTitle: The Neighborhoods Where Seoul’s Trends Gather
stories.script: "Which neighborhood you head for in Seoul depends on what you want to buy. In Seongsu, you try things out; in Hongdae, you find new brands; and in Myeongdong, you fill a bag with what you like.  Seongsu-dong is less a place where brands sell things than a place where you try them first. From the 1970s to the early 2000s, it was an industrial district full of leather factories, auto repair shops, and warehouses. The factories closed after the Asian financial crisis and the neighborhood sat empty for a while, but cheap rents drew young creators in one by one. Now every made-over warehouse holds a brand showroom or a pop-up store.  At AMORE SEONGSU, you can freely try more than 2,000 cosmetic products. Even a washbasin is set up inside the store, so you can test cleansers on the spot. There are showrooms too, from brands like OIMU, which redesigns familiar objects such as matches, erasers, and incense.  Hongdae draws young creators and new brands, so every alley has its own character. Korean street fashion labels often open their first store here. The first thisisneverthat flagship and the first offline store for MUSINSA’s own label are both in Hongdae. KAKAO FRIENDS and LINE FRIENDS have stores on the same street.  Myeongdong brings together street-level shops, department stores, duty-free stores, and an underground arcade on a single street. Cosmetics stores are especially dense here, and at Olive Young Myeongdong Town you can compare, test, and buy across many brands in one place. The nearby Daiso Myeongdong Main Store occupies all 12 floors of its building. Stationery, kitchenware, socks, accessories, and much more can all be scored for a few thousand won without a second thought.  For a souvenir with more to it, try the gift shops at the palaces and museums. Hand mirrors finished in mother-of-pearl inlay, keyrings cut from the same shell, silk bokjumeoni fortune pouches, travel mugs carrying traditional patterns, Hangeul name stamps: things you will not easily find elsewhere. If you want the same sorts of things at a friendlier price, Namdaemun Market, with more than 600 years of history, is a good option.  Look for clothes in Seongsu and Hongdae, cosmetics and household goods in Myeongdong, and traditional souvenirs at the palace gift shops. The three areas are within 30 minutes of one another by subway, so a single day covers all of them. "

stories.title: From the Herb Market to the Spa: Korea’s Lifestyle Trends
stories.audioTitle: From the Herb Market to the Spa: Korea’s Lifestyle Trends
stories.script: "In Korea, food, cosmetics, and bathing culture are not far apart from one another. All of them originally began from the same way of caring for the body.  Samgyetang, the summer restorative dish, is a whole chicken simmered slowly with a range of other ingredients. The ginseng, jujube, and garlic that go into it are both medicinal herbs and foodstuffs. Most ingredients used in Korean medicine work that way. They are eaten as food, simmered down and drunk like tea, and applied to the body.  There are markets that deal in medicinal herbs and nothing else. More than half of all the herbs distributed in Korea pass through Seoul Yangnyeongsi in Dongdaemun. At the Seoul K-Medi Center inside the market, a reservation gets you a foot bath and a consultation with a Korean medicine doctor, and you can join a cooking class using medicinal herbs.  Traditional Korean medicine held that the same illness calls for different treatments and different remedies depending on a person’s constitution. That idea still runs through a range of fields today. Forest Resom in Chungcheong-do runs a spa tailored to your constitution, and Tea Therapy in central Seoul pairs a foot bath program with a medicinal tea matched to the same reading.  Cosmetics can be understood as part of the same continuum. Sulwhasoo builds on formulations drawn from traditional medicine, and its flagship store offers spa programs based on these formulations. Where Joseon medicine sorted people by constitution, cosmetics stores today recommend products by skin type. BEAUTY PLAY, with branches in Myeongdong and Hongdae, is an experience space run by the Korea Cosmetic Industry Institute, where you can have a skin diagnostic and a personal color consultation free of charge.  The most popular spa culture of all is the jjimjilbang. You move between ocher rooms, charcoal kilns, and salt rooms, sweating it out and bathing as you go. Many stay open around the clock, and the snack counter will have baked eggs and cold sikhye. Eating eggs in a sauna may look a little strange at first, but in Korea it could not be more natural.  What people eat shifts a little from region to region too. Jeolla-do has a mild climate and rich soil, so ingredients are abundant, and it is called Korea’s capital of flavor. In mountainous Gangwon-do, you will often find a table laid with wild mountain greens, and on Jeju there is a standing tradition of eating hairtail raw.  There is food to be had at the temples as well. Temple food is built around beans, tofu, and vegetables and is described as food that nourishes the body and mind. Korean cooking uses vegetables in so many ways to begin with that bibimbap and gimbap are easy enough to enjoy if you simply ask for them without the meat.  What you eat, what you apply, and even the culture of warming the body. In Korea, all of it is connected within a single current. "

stories.title: A Travel Course for K-Pop Fans
stories.audioTitle: A Travel Course for K-Pop Fans
stories.script: "A park bench in Seoul carries the names of the BTS members and lyrics from their songs. The park is Seoul Forest, in the city’s Seongdong-gu. K-pop agency headquarters are clustered around this area, and since most of the addresses are public, plenty of fans go and see them for themselves. Step into the lobby of the SM Entertainment building in particular, and a large LED media wall is the first thing you see. The merchandise store KWANGYA@SEOUL is inside. You can browse albums and all kinds of goods, and take in exhibitions on the label’s artists while you are there.  The second place to go is Gangnam. At COEX by Samseong Station, there is Ktown4u, a dedicated merchandise store. It is run by a company that ships to 240 countries, and it stocks everything from the newest albums to older ones, light sticks, photocards, and keyrings. The screens inside the mall sometimes run videos celebrating an idol’s birthday or comeback.  Four music programs are broadcast live from Seoul. The main venues are the SBS Open Hall in Gangseo-gu, KBS Hall in Yeouido, and MBC and the CJ ENM Center in Sangam. How to get into the audience differs from program to program, so check the official site before you go.  The spots the stars frequent are open to fans as well. Leesle, in Mapo, is a hanbok brand that has made stage costumes for idols. The traditional hanbok worn at the palaces and the outfits worn on stage come from the same workshop. HAN Collection on Sejong-ro in Jongno carries around 200 Korean designer labels, including the designer behind a Grammy Awards outfit. At BEAUTY PLAY in Myeongdong, you can try makeup and hair styling yourself.  Around Apgujeong and Seolleung are the salons that do idols’ nails and actors’ makeup. Most require a booking, but if you book in advance, you can receive the same service in the same room as the idols.  Everywhere named here is another kind of destination for experiencing K-pop. Not concert halls or exhibition spaces, but office lobbies, park benches, and the salons the stars keep going back to. Less a trip to see a star on stage than a walk through the places their ordinary days brush past. "

stories.title: From Palaces to Templestay: Korean Tradition, Experienced Firsthand
stories.audioTitle: From Palaces to Templestay: Korean Tradition, Experienced Firsthand
stories.script: "In the middle of Gangnam in Seoul, there is a king’s tomb. It belongs to a Joseon king who ruled 500 years ago. Come lunchtime, it is easy enough to spot office workers walking laps around it. The five Joseon palaces also remain in the city center, and people here treat them as familiar ground.  Gyeongbokgung Palace is the largest of the five. It was built in 1395 as the primary royal palace of Joseon and still stands looking down Seoul’s central avenue. The Changing of the Royal Guard takes place at the main gate three times a day. It runs about 20 minutes at 10 a.m., 1 p.m., and 3 p.m., and anyone can watch without entering the palace grounds.  Many people come to Changdeokgung Palace for the rear garden. Huwon, as the garden is called, was laid out to keep the natural setting as intact as possible. Rather than felling trees or rerouting streams, the builders left the terrain as it was and set pavilions into it.  Changgyeonggung Palace was originally where the queens lived. During the Japanese colonial period, a zoo and a botanical garden were installed, and the palace was turned into something closer to a park. A restoration project in 1983 brought it back to its current form.  Deoksugung Palace is the only one of the five open until 9 p.m., so you can see the halls lit up. It is also the only one with Western-style buildings mixed in, and the stone-wall path around it is a walking route in its own right.  A short walk from the palaces brings you to Jongmyo Shrine. Jongmyo is where the ancestral rites for the kings were performed, and on the first Sunday of every May, their descendants gather to perform the ceremony exactly as it was done more than 500 years ago. It counts as one of the longest continuously observed rituals in the world.  Leave Seoul, and you can reach even further back. Two hours by train brings you to Andong. Hahoe Folk Village still has its Joseon-era hanok exactly as they were. This is not a place built for tourism; it is a village where people actually live. You can stay in a hanok and take part in a tea ceremony, pottery making, and traditional games. Yangdong Folk Village in Gyeongju has some 160 old houses and thatched-roof homes more than 500 years old. It too is a village where people still live. Bulguksa Temple, in the same city, was founded in the eighth century during the Silla period. The wooden buildings have been rebuilt several times, but the stone bridges, steps, and pagodas have retained their original form to this day.  Just as people live in the villages, monks live in the temples, and travelers can stay a night as well. This is called a Templestay: you sleep at the temple and take part in 108 prostrations, meditation, a tea ceremony, and lotus lantern making. There are Templestay temples within Seoul, and you can also do it at Haeinsa Temple in Hapcheon or Beomeosa Temple in Busan.  None of these places is merely a relic of the past. The rites are still performed at Jongmyo, people still live in the villages, and travelers can still spend a night at the temples. "

stories.title: A Must for Shopping in Korea: The Tax Refund Guide
stories.audioTitle: A Must for Shopping in Korea: The Tax Refund Guide
stories.script: "Goods sold in Korea have value-added tax included in the price. If you are a foreign traveler, you can get that tax back. It comes to about 10 percent of the price, though the amount you actually receive is slightly less after the agency handling fee is deducted. The procedure is easier than you might expect, and there are only three things to remember. Duty-free stores sell at prices that exclude the tax to begin with, so there is nothing to refund. Everything explained below applies to goods bought at ordinary stores.  First, check whether the tax was deducted when you paid at the store. If you already paid a price with the tax taken off, that is the end of it. This is called an immediate refund. Show your passport and the tax is deducted at the register, with no refund procedure to go through at the airport. Immediate refunds apply to purchases under KRW 1,000,000 at a time, up to KRW 5,000,000 across your entire stay. Above those limits, the immediate refund does not apply, and you will need to take a refund slip and claim it later.  Second, check whether you paid the full tax and received a refund slip. In that case, the refund comes later. You can collect it at a downtown refund counter or at the airport. Take care not to lose the slip; without it, no refund is possible.  Third, decide where you want to receive the refund. Customs confirmation must be completed when you leave the country, regardless of where you collect the refund. The only thing that changes is when you get the money.  To be refunded downtown first, you need your passport, your refund slips, and a credit card. Even if you have already received the money, you must still show the goods you bought to customs when you depart.  If you are being refunded at the airport, get customs confirmation first and then go to the refund counter. Reverse the order, and you will not be refunded because the counter pays out based on that customs confirmation.  In short: customs first, refund second.  Customs officers personally verify that the goods are actually leaving. So do not open the packaging on what you bought. Items already opened or used do not qualify, nor do items that leave nothing behind, such as prepared food or a massage.  As an exception, hotel accommodation is refundable for up to 30 nights for independent travelers only; group packages are excluded.  There are three eligibility requirements: a stay of less than six months, a single purchase of KRW 15,000 or more, and export within three months of the purchase date. Anyone earning income in Korea or staying longer than six months does not qualify.  At Incheon Airport Terminal 1, customs is on the third floor near counters E and J, and the refund counter is near Gate 28. The staffed counter is open until 10 p.m., and the self-service kiosks run 24 hours.  Remember: bring your passport, leave the packaging sealed, and go to customs first. "

stories.title: The Many Faces of Seoul’s Landmark Shopping Malls
stories.audioTitle: The Many Faces of Seoul’s Landmark Shopping Malls
stories.script: "In the middle of the COEX mall in Seoul stands a 13-meter-tall bookcase. More than 70,000 books are shelved on it, and people sit beneath them and read. Everything here is free to read without having to buy it.  Every large shopping mall in Seoul has a place like this. The point is not to be a place for shopping and nothing else, but to become a destination people set out for on purpose.  The Hyundai Seoul in Yeouido built a forest indoors. Its garden is called Sounds Forest. Natural light streams through the glass ceiling, and off to one side, a 12-meter waterfall cascades from the third floor to the first.  Starfield COEX Mall in Samseong-dong has a library. It is where that bookcase stands. Starfield Library sits among more than 100 cafes and restaurants, and people read there or simply take a break. The building was originally a convention center, with the ground floor and the first basement level connected to the mall. It also connects to the City Airport Terminal, from which a bus to Incheon Airport takes about an hour.  Lotte World Tower in Jamsil is where you go to experience the sky. At 123 floors and 555 meters, it is the tallest building in Korea. The SEOUL SKY observatory sits at 500 meters. Its Sky Deck, where you can look down through a glass floor, holds the Guinness World Record for the highest glass-floored observatory. At 541 meters, there is the further option of stepping outside the building and walking the Sky Bridge.  Inside Dongdaemun Design Plaza, there are exhibitions of all kinds on architecture, fashion, comics, and more, and Seoul Fashion Week is held here each spring and fall. After dark, the whole building lights up, becoming one of Seoul’s signature night views. It was designed by Zaha Hadid, the first woman architect to win the Pritzker Prize, and because it is asymmetrical, with almost no straight lines, many people say it looks like a UFO.  Dongdaemun Fashion Town runs directly beside it. Some 30 shopping malls and more than 30,000 shops are gathered there, and some stay open until dawn. One street separates a cultural venue by a world-renowned architect from a busy wholesale market, and that pairing is a sight you will find nowhere else.  A forest, a library, the sky, and a building that looks like a UFO. These are places that hand you an experience before they hand you anything to buy. That is exactly why a shopping mall counts as a destination in Seoul. "

stories.title: A 570-Meter Man-Made Alley: Triple Street in Songdo
stories.audioTitle: A 570-Meter Man-Made Alley: Triple Street in Songdo
stories.script: "A city of the future usually calls to mind somewhere you drive. Songdo in Incheon is the opposite. Here you have to walk to see where a future city’s appeal lies.  Songdo began as land with nothing on it to walk to. The city was built on reclaimed tidal flats, leaving nothing on the ground and, naturally, no streets either. So somewhere to walk had to be designed and built.  Triple Street is a street 570 meters long. Except that it is not really a street; it is a single building. It is a shopping mall made up of four blocks, A through D. It opened in 2017 and was designed by Minsuk Cho, an architect who won the Golden Lion at the Venice Architecture Biennale. He called the building an artificial topography laid over the blank page of a city.  The Triple in the name refers to its three streets. They do not run side by side but stack one above another. Below ground is Under Street, a dining floor gathering Korean and international restaurants and franchises. At ground level is Ground Street, lined with brand stores, pop-ups, cafes, and a cinema. And the rooftop is Park Street, with lawns, a sports field, and an observation point. Hyundai Premium Outlet adjoins it, so you can keep walking in that direction. Technopark Station on Incheon Line 1 connects underground.  Songdo has water too, a 1.8-kilometer canal cutting through Songdo Central Park. It is not a natural stream but a man-made channel. You can take out a canoe or a duck boat, and there is a water taxi that runs along the surface. The crescent-shaped Moon Boat lights up at night.  Beside the canal is a building that looks like three bowls joined together. This is Tri-Bowl. The three stand for sky, sea, and land, and performances and exhibitions are held inside. A hanok hotel stands in the same park. Tiled roofs ringed by glass high-rises make it a good spot for a photograph.  For the whole city at a glance, there are two places worth going. The observation point on the Triple Street rooftop, and the G-Tower observatory. Why not go up and take in Songdo’s beautiful sunset and the night view that follows? "

stories.title: The Hip Alley Made by an Old Fortress Wall: Haengridan-gil
stories.audioTitle: The Hip Alley Made by an Old Fortress Wall: Haengridan-gil
stories.script: There is an alley in Suwon that young people have been flocking to lately.  Walk the alley, and unusual buildings start to catch your eye. A galbi restaurant has its sign mounted on top of a chimney. The building used to be a bathhouse; the chimney was still standing, and the owner used it as signage instead of tearing it down. A cafe next door was once a fortune-teller’s, and the teahouse beyond it opens onto a hanok. Rather than demolishing the buildings, people layered a contemporary sensibility over them, creating an alley humming with young life.  Hwaseong Fortress, which encircles Haengridan-gil, was completed in 1796 and designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997. Development around a World Heritage Site is subject to restrictions, so the height and shape of buildings cannot be changed at will. Because of that, time in this neighborhood has run slowly for a long while.  Things began to change in 2013. An international festival was held to bring life back to a district that had stalled, and in the process, the alleys were tidied up, and old signs were restored. Then, in 2017, Hwaseong Fortress opened at night as well; its nighttime view spread widely on social media, and from that point, Haengridan-gil began to fill with visitors.  Cafes opened in every alley, and the ones that opened their rooftops are the most popular of all. Go up and the entire fortress wall comes into view. The wall was built to watch what was outside. A wall raised to look out for an enemy is now being looked at by people holding coffee.  After sunset, the lights come on between Hwaseomun Gate and Janganmun Gate. People who have been walking the ramparts and people coming out of the alleys mix under the same light. A fortress wall well over 200 years old, and beneath it the smell of coffee. Perhaps what makes this neighborhood hip is not that it sits beside a wall, but that the wall slowed its time down.

stories.title: Gangneung Gyoridan-gil
stories.script: Cross a single road from Gangneung Station and you are in Gyo-dong. The neighborhood takes its name from the hyanggyo, a Confucian school that has stood on the hill since the Goryeo period. It was Gangneung's center for a long time, though it lost its energy for a while. What drew people back to these alleys was, unexpectedly, that very oldness. Young people began arriving one by one, repairing the old houses instead of tearing them down. Cafes converted from homes people had lived in, workshops that kept their narrow courtyards intact, and small goods shops in the spaces of former stores filled the alleys. The mood of the old neighborhood and a young sensibility came together beautifully. That is how it came to be called Gyoridan-gil, by analogy with Gyeongnidan-gil in Seoul. True to a city known for coffee, many cafes roast and brew their own. Between the cafes, small workshops and goods shops are tucked away. They sell handmade bowls, hand-drawn postcards, and vintage objects, and usually the owner is the maker.  One of the dishes Gangneung is known for is Gyodong jjamppong, and this alley is where it was born. Gyodong jjamppong differs a little from ordinary jjamppong. The broth is clear and clean rather than red and thick, and the clams and mussels are served out of the shell, which makes them easy to eat. One long-established restaurant, said to be the first to sell Gyodong jjamppong, has held the same spot since 1979. Head a little south from the crossroads and you pass Seobu Market, a modest market where local residents shop for daily life, and arrive at Myeongju-dong.  Finally, at the top of the alley on the lower slopes of Hwabusan Mountain, there is also the Gangneung Museum of Art. Set on the hill, it offers a view of the city at a glance and showcases work by local artists based in Gangneung.

stories.title: Gwangju Dongmyeong-dong
stories.script: If Yangnim-dong lies west of Geumnam-ro, the street that represents Gwangju's history and culture, then Dongmyeong-dong lies east. Where Yangnim-dong shows the city's modern-era culture, Dongmyeong-dong is an alley where contemporary culture is alive.  A trip to Dongmyeong-dong starts at the Asia Culture Center (ACC). Walk a few steps into the alleys and a quiet neighborhood appears, lined with low walls and old detached houses. This alley of cafes and restaurants is where Gwangju's wealthy once lived. High walls and large gates, gardens set deep inside, traces of hanok here and there: all of it is left over from those days. Major government offices stood nearby, including the old South Jeolla Provincial Office, city hall, the courthouse, and the prosecutors' office, so people with power and means naturally settled here in numbers. When the city and provincial offices moved away in the 2000s, the residents left one by one too, and only the old houses remained.  What woke this sleeping neighborhood was, unexpectedly, private academies. Well-known academies moved into Dongmyeong-dong, close to downtown yet cheap, and parents gathered to drop off their children and wait for classes to end. Places for those parents to pass an hour sprang up alongside. That is how Dongmyeong-dong Cafe Street began.  Then the Asia Culture Center opened right beside it, drawing artists and cultural producers as well, and the alleys grew steadily more varied. The living quarters of wealthy households became cafes, and old hanok became bookshops. Each place began infusing its own character into its interior, menu, and atmosphere, and young people started coming to enjoy them.  Traces of a railway remain in Dongmyeong-dong as well. Trains on the Gyeongjeon Line once ran through this area. Residents themselves brought the abandoned track back as a wooded walking path, the Gwangju Greenway. Nongjang Bridge sits on this path. Inmates of Gwangju Prison, which was in this area until the 1960s, crossed it going to and from farm labor. A cultural space called the Greenway Culture Spring has opened on the bridge, so the space beneath it is now an exhibition hall and the steps are seating where people gather. In Dongmyeong-dong, then, the old houses, the abandoned railway, and the bridge the inmates crossed have all found new uses.

stories.title: Daejeon Euneungjeongi Cultural Street
stories.script: Stand with your back to Daejeon Station, the gateway to a trip through the city, and a small stream called the Daejeoncheon flows ahead of you, with the Eunhaeng-dong area spreading out beyond it.  As the subway station name Jungang-ro, meaning Central Road, suggests, this was long the heart of Daejeon's commerce, enough to be called the city's Myeongdong. A large ginkgo tree and a pavilion are said to have stood here in the past. People called the place Euneungjeongi, meaning the village with the ginkgo pavilion. Euneung is an old word for ginkgo. When the village was organized into an administrative district, the neighborhood took the name Eunhaeng-dong from eunhaeng, the modern word for the same tree, and the old place name Euneungjeongi survived as the street name.  Step onto the street and the first thing you see is Sky Road, an enormous screen covering the whole street like a roof. It is an LED video arcade 214 meters long and 20 meters high, modeled on Fremont Street in Las Vegas. In the evening, brilliant footage runs across the vast ceiling, and on the last night of the year, the countdown event held here packs the street shoulder to shoulder.  Alongside this tunnel of light, the street's greatest attraction is without question Sungsimdang. Sungsimdang started in 1956 as a small steamed-bun shop and won a national reputation with breads found nowhere else, such as fried soboro and chive bread. It is also known as the bakery that made the bread for Pope Francis's meals during his 2014 visit to Korea. What is most remarkable is that Sungsimdang opens no branches in other cities, despite all its popularity. To taste its bread, you have to come to Daejeon. That stubborn principle has become the force drawing people from across the country into this old downtown.  Walk on a little past Sungsimdang and you reach Urideul Park, the former site of the Jung-gu district office. A government building has turned into a cultural yard where outdoor performances, busking among them, are at their liveliest. Mokcheokgyo Bridge crosses the Daejeoncheon right beside it. Built during the Japanese colonial period to move military supplies, it was originally a wooden bridge. During the Korean War, it was a meeting place where refugees parted and found one another again. Cross Mokcheokgyo and the way continues to the old Jungang Market.

stories.title: Busan Jeonpo Cafe Street
stories.script: Cross a single road from Seomyeon, Busan's signature downtown, and you step into an alley where the feel of the place shifts entirely. This is Jeonpo Cafe Street.  The first thing that catches your eye in the alley is not a cafe at all. It is the old shops with signs reading Tools and Hardware. An automobile plant and a US military base stood nearby, so shops selling car parts and machine parts naturally gathered here, and at the peak in the 1960s and 70s, the alley is said to have held close to 500 tool shops.  Change began in this alley around 2010, when young people who wanted to open their own places cheaply moved into the spaces the tool shops had left. They opened up shop while keeping the old tool stores and worn warehouses as they were. In places a trendy cafe stands directly beside a tool shop still in business.  That makes for a curiously mixed experience. From one side come the dull sound of machines working metal and the smell of iron; from right next door, the sound of beans grinding and the rich aroma of coffee. It is a scene you will rarely come across anywhere else. Another pleasure of this alley is that walking it feels like a treasure hunt. A cafe you could see clearly from the main road turns out to need a maze-like loop upward once you approach, and it sits quietly on the second or third floor of a worn building with no sign at all. You climb a narrow staircase, open a door, and a handsome space you never expected opens up. Not hiding what is old but making it the attraction instead: that is the sensibility particular to Jeonpo.  What is interesting is that this alley is still unfinished. Small shops appear and disappear so quickly that the alley wears a slightly different face each time you visit. Another alley, Jeonpo Saitgil, has grown up across the main road, so the district is still expanding.

stories.title: Busan: Haeridan-gil and Yeongdo's Bongnae Market
stories.audioTitle: Busan: Haeridan-gil and Yeongdo's Bongnae Market
stories.script: A trip to Busan usually brings to mind Haeundae, Jagalchi Market, or Gwangan Bridge. Yet the real interest and appeal of Busan hide, unexpectedly, just behind those famous sights. Haeridan-gil at Haeundae on the eastern edge and Bongnae Market on Yeongdo, an island in the sea to the southwest, are two such places.  Both sit directly behind the glamorous tourist sites, yet neither is dressed up for tourism. They are the real Busan, where the people of Busan actually live.  Mention Haeundae and everyone pictures the wide, glittering beach. Turn your back on the sea there, though, and you meet an entirely different face. This is Haeridan-gil. The alley starts at the former Haeundae Station. Behind that closed station, where trains on the Donghae Nambu Line stopped running, a new alley has flowered on the ground the tracks left. What defines this alley most is how foreign it feels. Walk the narrow lanes and Thai rice-noodle shops, Hong Kong-style dim sum houses, Italian home cooking, and Japanese ramen and dessert shops stand packed together, so that you feel like you are traveling through several countries in a single alley. Each shop has its own strong character. Charming murals on the walls, goods shops, the occasional flea market: your eyes never go idle the whole way.  Bongnae Market, by contrast, is on Yeongdo. Yeongdo means something particular to the people of Busan. It is the ground where refugees who poured in from across the country during the Korean War mostly settled, and a port town that has made its living from shipbuilding, building and repairing vessels. Bongnae Market sits in the middle of it. It was once considerably larger, but part of it was absorbed into the road when Busan Bridge was laid in 1980, and it is a little more compact now.   Even so, more than a hundred stalls still lay out vegetables, fruit, and freshly caught fish to meet their customers. Seeking out the long-established places in the shabby lanes deeper inside is a pleasure in itself. A plate of raw fish or a bowl of gukbap eaten among the people of Busan is the taste of the real Busan, something no ordinary tourist site can offer. The market's most remarkable story is eomuk, or fish cake. Bongnae Market is quite special in the history of the Busan fish cake we commonly eat today. Samjin Fishcake, famous across the country, opened in a small shack in this market in 1953. Busan's oldest fish cake company was born right here. The Samjin Fishcake main store still stands beside the market, where you can taste fish cakes hot from the fryer, then go upstairs to see how they are made and learn their history.  A real face of Busan left behind the glittering front of the tourist sites, the traces of old industry that the railway and the sea left behind, and an appeal that opens only when you wander the alleys wherever your feet take you. Walk these two alleys and the city of Busan will look a little different to you.

stories.title: Andong Jungang Culture Street
stories.script: Andong's Jungang Culture Street is a walking route through the city's old downtown, running from the front of the former Andong Station to Jjimdak Alley in Andong Old Market. It offers plenty to look at and is a street of youth, thronged these days with young people. The path is shaped after the courtyards and alleys of traditional houses, and a small stream runs along it, its bed patterned with the movements of the Hahoe mask dance and the floors of Byeongsan Seowon. You can dip your feet at the water's edge or sit on a bench and talk. There is also the Perfect Match Date Trail, with sculptures and photo zones for couples, which makes it great for walking and taking pictures.  What makes this street special is that it is pleasant to walk in its own right while also serving as the hub that brings together the scattered attractions of the old downtown. One point along the way anchors your route: Mammoth Bakery. This bakery, more than forty years old, is an Andong landmark, and the line for its cream cheese bread is always long.  The street runs naturally on to the entrance of Andong Old Market, and Tteokbokki Alley sits at that junction. A dozen snack stalls that have held their spots for more than thirty years stand in a row, numbered from one, and the sight is a warm one. A little farther in is Jjimdak Alley, which made Andong known nationwide. This alley originally sold whole roast chicken, and when fried chicken and seasoned chicken came into fashion in the late 1980s, it created a new dish: Andong jjimdak. Proud of being the original, the alley changed its name from Tongdak Alley to Jjimdak Alley. More than thirty jjimdak restaurants gather here today, and beside them, Boribap Alley, more than fifty years old, continues as well.  Step out of the food alleys and you meet Andong's history instead, at Ungbu Park. This is the site of the government office when Andong was raised to a Daedohobu, a grand protectorate, under King Gongmin of Goryeo, and it held the Andong county office until recent years. In the park stand Yeonggaheon, a restoration of the old government hall, and the gate tower Daedongnu, and the Citizens' Bell hangs there, a reproduction of the Sangwonsa Bronze Bell, a national treasure said to have been taken from Andong. Right next door is the Andong Traditional Culture Content Museum, a museum without artifacts. It turns Andong's traditional culture into digital content and presents it through 4D video and virtual reality. You can try notdaribalpgi, a traditional group game, as though it were a video game, and learn the Hahoe mask dance.  Say Andong and images of tradition come first: Hahoe Folk Village, Dosan Seowon, head families and ancestral rites. Walk the Culture Street, though, and you will get a feel for how that city of tradition has lived and changed over the past hundred years.

stories.title: Jeonju Gaengnidan-gil
stories.script: The area around Jeolla Gamyeong and the gaeksa, the old government guesthouse, was Jeonju's center in earlier times. During the Joseon period, the spaces that stood for Jeonju's administration, its commerce, and the royal house were all gathered here. The road that runs from the gaeksa past Jeolla Gamyeong to Gyeonggijeon Shrine and the Hanok Village holds Jeonju's yesterday and today intact. This area was Jeonju's foremost downtown as late as the 1980s, but people drained away in the 1990s and, tied up in redevelopment plans, it filled with nothing but empty shops. Then, about a decade ago, young entrepreneurs began gathering one by one to open cafes, restaurants, and small shops inside old buildings left as they were. Young people came back for the appeal of that reversal, an exterior unchanged from the old days and a stylish space appearing when you open the door. And by analogy with Gyeongnidan-gil in Seoul, the area came to be called Gaengnidan-gil.  Jeonju's gaeksa stands at the center of this street. Its formal name is Pungpaejigwan. Pungpae is a figure of speech for the ancestral home of the founder of a dynasty. Jeonju was the ancestral home of King Taejo Yi Seong-gye, so it was called Pungpaejihyang, and the Jeonju gaeksa took the name Pungpaejigwan to carry that meaning.  Jeolla Gamyeong stands not far from the gaeksa. It was the provincial office that covered what are now North Jeolla, South Jeolla, and Jeju. Unlike other provincial offices, which moved from time to time, this one never left Jeonju throughout the Joseon dynasty. It is said to have been second in size only to the Pyongyang provincial office, so large was its scale and so considerable its authority.  If the Hanok Village is the traditional Jeonju, Gaengnidan-gil is called the new Jeonju. Murals cover the old walls, small spaces host exhibitions by local artists, and on weekends you may come across flea markets of handmade goods and busking performances. Nobody ordered any of it; the culture grew naturally from the hands of the young creators gathered on this street. Coffee brewed from beans roasted on the premises, Jeonju-style desserts, and craft beer from small breweries are tucked away in the alleys as well.  These character-filled spaces lead to Film Street. Several cinemas and screening halls line the street, and the Jeonju International Film Festival is held every spring. Because the festival puts independent and art films ahead of commercial ones, Jeonju is known as the city of film.  On Gaengnidan-gil, then, even the old buildings each have a color of their own, open-air tables are set out in the narrow lanes, and music drifting from the shops adds warmth. The vintage alleys of daytime turn into a snug, romantic street after dark. So peer in wherever you feel drawn, and take this alley slowly.

stories.title: Jeju: Songdang-ri and Sehwa-ri
stories.script: Jeju is often called the Land of Oreum. More than 360 of these volcanic cones are scattered across the island, and the area of Gujwa-eup in the east, where they cluster most densely, is known as the Kingdom of Oreum. The village at its center is Songdang-ri. It is a quiet countryside village in the mid-mountain zone, but the people of Jeju have long regarded it as the home of the gods. The village holds Songdang Bonhyangdang, Jeju's oldest shrine, and the children born to Geumbaekjo, the goddess of Jeju myth enshrined there, are said to have become the guardian deities of villages across the island.  Leave Songdang and oreum with soft ridgelines follow one after another, Abu Oreum and Andol Oreum among them, while nearby Pyeongdae-ri holds Bijarim Forest, where thousands of old nutmeg yews form a wood. Past that forest, Darangswi Oreum, the Queen of the Oreum, rises. It takes its name from its round hollow crater, said to look like a full moon, and at a depth of some hundred meters it matches Baengnokdam on Hallasan in scale. This oreum is a source of pride for Jeju and at the same time the symbol of the village for the people of Sehwa, who look up at it to the south.  Cross the oreum and come down to the sea, and fields of red volcanic soil spread out between black stone walls. These are the carrot fields that stand for Jeju. Gujwa-eup accounts for roughly half of the country's carrot production, making it Korea's largest growing area, and Gujwa carrots, raised in well-draining volcanic soil, are known for being unusually sweet and firm.  Follow the field paths and you arrive at Sehwa-ri, a seaside village on Jeju's eastern edge. Above all, this is a village of haenyeo, the women divers. The culture of the Jeju haenyeo, a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, is preserved here better than anywhere, and the Haenyeo Museum holds their lives and their history. Alongside the divers' household goods and their working tools, such as the tewak float and the mangsari net, the museum lays out a haenyeo's whole life, from her first dive to the day she leaves the sea, through the true story of one woman. The village is also known as a place where the haenyeo, acting on their own initiative, carried out anti-colonial and human rights campaigns during the Japanese colonial period. A memorial park commemorating those days stands beside the museum.  Sehwa's appeal does not lie in old things alone. Young, polished shops line the village throughout. Cafes where the sea fills a wall of glass, charming goods shops selling hand-drawn postcards, independent bookstores made for turning pages quietly: a new sensibility has soaked into every alley of the old diving village. Because the old sea and the young shops come together this way, Sehwa was named one of the world's Best Tourism Villages by the UN World Tourism Organization in 2023.

stories.title: Jeju Handam Coastal Trail
stories.script: Handam Beach, on the western side of Jeju, is counted among the finest places to watch a sunset and a hot spot where distinctive cafes, select shops, and good restaurants line the shore. Word spread about a cafe opened by a well-known entertainer, and visitors began flocking to this quiet fishing village.  A traditional Jeju house also sits midway along the cafe street. It is the birthplace of Jang Han-cheol, a scholar of the Joseon period. At twenty-nine, on his way to sit the state examination, his boat drifted off course and carried him as far as an uninhabited island near present-day Okinawa; rescued by a Vietnamese merchant ship, he passed through several countries and did not return for half a year. Remarkably, he left a meticulous record of the entire journey. That record is no simple castaway's diary. It captures the sea routes and currents of eighteenth-century East Asia, the customs of unfamiliar islands, and even the waverings of a human mind at the threshold of death, and it is recognized as a valuable source in both maritime history and literature.  So the walking route along Handam Beach was named the Jang Han-cheol Coastal Trail. It runs about 1.2 kilometers to Gwakji Beach, forms part of Jeju Olle Route 15, and is one of the 31 Hidden Scenic Spots recommended by Jeju City. The path was originally the route the haenyeo used to and from their dives. These women divers descend ten meters into the sea with no equipment. The sound of the breath they release as they surface is called sumbisori, and it is sometimes described as the boundary between life and death. In this way, the path holds the hard, resilient lives of the Jeju women who have made their living treating the sea as a field.  Walk on and black rocks and stones run endlessly along the sea. They are the traces of the volcanic island's birth. This is basalt, formed when lava that flowed from erupting volcanoes tens of thousands of years ago cooled in seawater and hardened. Holes riddle it where gas escaped from the lava, and it is black and rough, no two pieces alike. Waves breaking against this basalt ring unusually loud and long.
