It is a sound you will hardly hear on another shore, a sound that belongs to Jeju.

stories.title: Jeju: Hallasan, the Olle Trail, and Seongsan Ilchulbong
stories.audioTitle: Jeju: Hallasan, the Olle Trail, and Seongsan Ilchulbong
stories.script: Jeju is an exceptional island, because the whole of it was made by volcanic activity. Eruptions over hundreds of thousands of years shaped the island and every landform on it. The world has recognized that worth. Jeju holds all three of UNESCO's natural designations: Biosphere Reserve, World Natural Heritage Site, and Global Geopark.  The first key to understanding Jeju is its mountain. Hallasan rises at the exact center of the island. At 1,947 meters, it is Korea's highest mountain, and Baengnokdam sits at its summit. The name means the pond where the white deer drinks, and the lake formed as water gathered in the volcanic crater. Around Hallasan, more than 360 small volcanic hills called oreum are scattered. Having hundreds of oreum gathered on one small island is extremely rare anywhere in the world. The people of Jeju have long made their villages between one oreum and the next, in the places where the mountain slopes gently down to the sea. A high mountain at the center, hundreds of oreum ringing it, and a life settled in between: this is Jeju as it truly is.  On the eastern shore stands Seongsan Ilchulbong, a volcanic body that formed separately from Hallasan. Magma surged up from beneath shallow water about five thousand years ago and made it. Its shape is therefore nothing like an ordinary volcano on land. It looks like an enormous fortress risen from the sea, with a hollow crater at the top and jagged rock peaks ringing the rim like a crown. This distinctive volcanic landform was recognized for its scientific value and inscribed as a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site. At the same time, Seongsan Ilchulbong draws more visitors than anywhere else on a trip to Jeju. The walk to the summit takes thirty or forty minutes, and the sunrise over the sea seen from there is especially famous.  Beautiful as it is, Jeju also has a walking route that circles the island: the Jeju Olle Trail. Olle is a Jeju word for the narrow lane that runs from the main road to the front of a house. The trail began in 2007, inspired by the Camino de Santiago in Spain, and was made by joining existing coastal paths, forest tracks, and village lanes; it now has 27 courses and runs about 437 kilometers. A single course is usually around 15 kilometers and takes five or six hours to walk. Meeting volcanic coastline and oreum, black basalt walls and mountain villages along the way is the heart of the Olle. Remarkably, the Jeju Olle has become a global model. The Jeju Olle advised directly on course development and provided its brand, and Kyushu Olle was created in Japan in 2012, with an olle of the same kind established in Mongolia as well. A walking journey born on Jeju now reaches across borders into the wider world.  Walk even one section of the Olle Trail for yourself. You will feel this world-recognized volcanic island whole, starting from the ground beneath your feet.

stories.title: Section 1 Battle of Okpo
stories.script: "[The First Victory: Turning Fear into Hope]  Welcome to the Battle of Okpo section, the starting point of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail and the site of the Joseon navy's first victory in the Imjin War. This trail follows the waters that first brought hope to a nation gripped by fear after a string of defeats—the hope that Joseon, too, could fight and win.  On the fourth day of the fifth lunar month in 1592, Admiral Yi Sun-sin set out for battle for the first time, leading a fleet of 91 vessels, including 28 panokseon warships. After receiving word that the enemy was stationed there, the fleet was heading toward Gadeokdo Island when, around noon on the seventh day of the fifth lunar month, a singijeon signal rocket was fired into the sky to announce that the Japanese forces had been sighted in the waters off Okpo. It was the moment the Joseon navy first came face to face with the Japanese forces.  On land, Busan and Dongnae had already fallen, and the Japanese army was advancing rapidly northward. The men of the Joseon navy, too, must have felt fear as they faced real combat for the first time. Admiral Yi gave his commanders a short but weighty order.   ""Mullyeong mangdong, jeongjung yeosan."" In other words, do not act rashly, and remain as calm and steady as a great mountain.  Some 30 Japanese ships lay anchored in the waters off Okpo. The Japanese soldiers had moored their vessels close to shore and gone ashore to plunder the village. When the Joseon navy appeared, they rushed back to their ships to fight or fled inland.   At Okpo, the Joseon navy did not choose to board the enemy vessels and fight hand to hand. Using the panokseon's high hull and sturdy construction, the Joseon navy kept their distance and attacked the enemy ships with cannon and fire arrows. The Japanese were strong in close combat with matchlock muskets and swords, but they struggled to respond to the Joseon navy's sustained bombardment from a distance. Admiral Yi directed the fleet so that its formation never broke, and his commanders, working in concert, attacked the enemy ships one after another. As a result, 26 Japanese ships were burned, and three Joseon captives held by the Japanese were rescued.  The Joseon navy won its first battle with little damage to itself. At a time when defeat followed defeat on land, this first news of victory from Okpo brought hope to Joseon. The victory also proved that the warships, cannon, military training, and command system Admiral Yi had prepared before the war were effective in actual combat.  Along the trail, you will pass Okpo Sculpture Park, the Okpo Great Victory Stairs, a Turtle Ship (geobukseon) replica, and Okpo Port Waterfront Park. Beyond Okpo Port, a coastal boardwalk and observation deck offer views of the now-peaceful waters off Okpo. Today, fishing boats share the view with a large shipyard, but more than 400 years ago, these waters were the scene of the first naval battle that would determine the fate of the nation. Past the simple fishing-village scenery of Pallangpo Village, you will reach Okpo Great Victory Commemorative Park.  Here you can look once more at how the Battle of Okpo unfolded and what the victory meant.  The Battle of Okpo section is about 4.6 kilometers long and takes about one hour, making it a relatively short and gentle course. As you look out to sea along the way, keep one thing in mind. Admiral Yi's first victory was no accident. It was won through preparations begun long before the war, accurate judgment of conditions at sea and the enemy, and the teamwork of a Joseon navy that held its formation to the very end.  This first victory, which began in the waters off Okpo, led directly to the Battle of Happo later the same day and to the Battle of Jeokjinpo the following day. It also became the starting point of the many victories that followed at Sacheon, Dangpo, Hansando Island, and Noryang.   As you look out over the calm sea before you, imagine the moment when the Joseon navy first overcame its fear and gained confidence. Thank you for joining us on the Battle of Okpo section, the first step along the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail. We hope to see you again on the next section of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail. "

stories.title: Section 2 Battle of Happo (Jinhae)
stories.script: [As the Sun Set, the Joseon Navy Took Up the Oars Again]  Welcome to the Jinhae section of the Battle of Happo on the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail. This trail follows the historic waters where the Joseon navy, having won its first victory at Okpo, went on to win another battle.   The Battle of Happo took place on the seventh day of the fifth lunar month in 1592, the same day as the Battle of Okpo. After defeating the Japanese at Okpo, the Joseon navy did not become complacent. Instead, it maintained formation and continued to scout the surrounding waters carefully.  As the sun was setting, Admiral Yi spotted five enemy ships fleeing toward Happo and immediately ordered a pursuit. As the Joseon navy pursued them relentlessly, the Japanese abandoned their ships and fled ashore, and the Joseon navy burned all five vessels. The engagement was smaller than the Battle of Okpo, but its significance was no smaller. With two consecutive victories in a single day, the Joseon navy began to seize the initiative at sea from its very first campaign.  In particular, the battle showed the Japanese forces that the sea routes along the southern coast were no longer safe. It also seriously disrupted their plans to move troops and supplies by sea. The Battle of Happo demonstrated Admiral Yi's prudence. He pursued boldly when the enemy was sighted, but did not push the chase once they fled ashore.  He had calculated that his men could be caught in an ambush on unfamiliar terrain. Instead, he made sure the enemy's ships were destroyed so they could never be used again. It showed his sound judgment about when to fight and when to stop. At the time, there was no wireless communication.  On the darkening sea, the only ways to exchange signals were flags, drums, and horns. Even so, the ships kept their spacing and moved as one, thanks to the training they had practiced repeatedly and the deep trust among the commanders. It shows that the Joseon navy was not simply strong in weapons, but exceptionally well organized.   Today, opinions differ about the exact location of the Battle of Happo, but this trail follows the area around Jinhaeman Bay and Hapgye, recalling that day.  At the starting point, around the Republic of Korea Naval Academy, you can sense the spirit of today's Republic of Korea Navy, which carries on the legacy of Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin. Next, at Sokcheon Port and Jinhaeru Pavilion, look out over the broad expanse of Jinhaeman Bay and imagine the Joseon navy advancing while exchanging signals. Past Jangcheon Port, Haengam Village offers a distinctive landscape where the sea meets the railway. And finally, at Hapgye Village, the Battle of Happo Victory Monument and an observation deck await you.  Walking on from here while recalling the long voyage of that day, from Okpo all the way to Happo, you will arrive at quiet Suchi Village. Today's long journey comes to an end there.  The Jinhae section of the Battle of Happo is relatively long, at about 15.2 kilometers. With a moderate difficulty level, it takes about five hours at a leisurely pace, so allow enough time and make sure you have the stamina for the walk. Some stretches run close to roads with vehicle traffic, so please stay alert.   The Battle of Happo was less a large-scale naval engagement than a fierce pursuit that turned one victory into the next. As you walk beside the blue waters of Jinhaeman Bay, feel the intensity of that day, when the Joseon navy took up the oars once more to chase the enemy before news of the victory at Okpo had even spread. Thank you for joining us on the Jinhae section of the Battle of Happo, which traces that day's second victory, achieved as the Joseon navy took up the oars once more. We hope to see you again on the next section of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail.

stories.title: Section 3 Battle of Happo (Masan)
stories.script: "[Under the Moonlight, Following the Records and the Sea]  Welcome to the Masan section of the Battle of Happo on the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail. This trail follows the blue waters of Masanman Bay and invites you to reflect on the historical significance of the Battle of Happo, fought immediately after the Battle of Okpo.   Fought on the seventh day of the fifth lunar month in 1592, the Battle of Happo was the second engagement of the Joseon navy's first campaign under Admiral Yi Sun-sin. That morning, the Joseon fleet had dealt a major blow to Japanese ships in the waters off Okpo in Geoje. Even after the victory, however, it did not stop to rest.  The fleet kept moving and scouting the surrounding waters until it spotted five Japanese ships fleeing toward Happo. Admiral Yi immediately ordered a pursuit. As the Joseon navy pursued them at high speed, the panicked Japanese forces abandoned their ships and fled ashore. The Joseon navy burned all five vessels so the enemy could never use them again.  The chase was brief, but its significance was great. While the Battle of Okpo was the stage where the Joseon navy first showed its strength, the Battle of Happo proved that the victory was no accident. By winning twice in a row in a single day, the Joseon navy took the initiative at sea. What deserves our attention at Happo is speed and restraint.  Admiral Yi swiftly pursued the fleeing enemy, but he did not push the chase once they had escaped ashore. This was because the navy's strength lay at sea, and on unfamiliar land there was the risk of an ambush using the terrain. Rather than pursuing a small victory within reach, he made a cool-headed judgment with the safety of the fleet and the war ahead in mind. He eliminated the enemy's means of movement while keeping his own losses to a minimum. It was, in every sense, a wise victory.  In fact, old records contain no modern road names or coordinates. The sites of battles are therefore estimated by matching place names, terrain, winds, and tides. Because ""Happo"" was the name for the Masan area in older times, Masanman Bay here is also regarded by some as the site of the Battle of Happo.  This section is about 9.9 kilometers long, rated moderate in difficulty, and takes about three hours at a leisurely pace. Some stretches run close to port facilities and roads, so please watch for traffic and walk safely. This section begins around Gapo Waterfront Culture Park and continues through Gapo Coastal Park, 3.15 Marine Nuri Park, Masan Port Central Pier Park, and Masan Port Pier 2 before reaching Happo Waterfront Park, letting you take in the history of the Battle of Happo together with the urban waterfront scenery of Masanman Bay. A calm coastal path, broad waterfront parks, sea views toward Dotseom Island, and the lively atmosphere of Masan Port and Masan Fish Market follow one after another, revealing the many faces of Masanman Bay.  The Masan section of the Battle of Happo is not about confirming a single settled version of history. Instead, it invites travelers to follow the questions that remain between the historical record and the places before them. As you look out over the moonlit sea and consider the old place names, try comparing records from more than 400 years ago with the map of today. Thank you for joining us on the Masan section of the Battle of Happo, a journey in search of answers. We hope to see you again on the next section of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail."

stories.title: Section 4 Battle of Jeokjinpo
stories.script: "[Closing the First Campaign]  Welcome to the Battle of Jeokjinpo section on the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail. This trail leads through a meaningful site of victory, where the combined fleet of Admiral Yi Sun-sin and Won Gyun won battle after battle and gave the Joseon navy the confidence that they could not be defeated—the belief that ""we will surely win.""   Early on the morning of the eighth day of the fifth lunar month in 1592, Admiral Yi did not let down his guard even after the two victories at Okpo and Happo the day before, and immediately scouted the surrounding waters again. Just then a report came in that Japanese ships were lying at Goriryang in Jinhae. Admiral Yi ordered the fleet out without delay, and the Joseon navy searched thoroughly among the islands before reaching Jeokjinpo in Goseong.  Thirteen Japanese ships stood in a row at the mouth of the inlet. The Japanese forces had left their vessels empty and entered the village, setting fires and seizing food. When the Joseon navy appeared, the Japanese forces were so taken aback by the sight of them that they fled into the mountains without putting up a proper fight. At this point Admiral Yi did not follow them onto land.  This was because pushing recklessly into unfamiliar mountains could have meant an ambush and would have meant leaving the sea, the Joseon navy's greatest strength. Instead, the Joseon navy fired its powerful chongtong cannons from the water, concentrating its attack on the enemy ships and burning them. The Joseon navy ended the engagement by destroying no fewer than 11 of the 13 ships. It was a cool-headed judgment. Rather than getting carried away trying to catch the enemy in front of them, they concentrated on decisively eliminating the ships that served as the Japanese forces' means of supply and movement.  With this, the Joseon navy set a great record on its first campaign: three consecutive victories in two days, at Okpo, Happo, and Jeokjinpo. At a bleak time when only news of defeat came from land, this news of victory from the sea became a powerful signal of hope that Joseon could hold the southern coast. Scholars hold a range of views on the exact location of the Battle of Jeokjinpo, with the Georyu-myeon and Donghae-myeon areas of Goseong among the candidates. The Battle of Jeokjinpo section was therefore designed not to focus on a single site, but to let you explore the waters and terrain of several possible locations.  The Battle of Jeokjinpo section is about 21.8 kilometers long and takes about six hours. It is a demanding route that crosses Gujeolsan Mountain, combining mountain trails, roads, and coastal stretches, so be sure to allow plenty of time and prepare yourself physically.  The trail begins at Goseong Sunrise Park and continues through Jeondo Village, the administrative center of Donghae-myeon, the summit of Gujeolsan Mountain, Pokpoam Hermitage, Jeongnam Village, and Dangdongman Bay before reaching Hwadang Village. From Gujeolsan Mountain, you can take in a broad view of Goseong's intricate coastline, including Danghangpo and Dangdongman Bay. Looking at how the mountains, islands, and inlets are arranged, you can understand why the Joseon navy divided its ships to search among the islands. At the time, it was vital to watch the sea from high ground and check the inlets where enemy ships could hide, one by one.  After descending Gujeolsan Mountain, you will pass the calm harbor and fishing-village scenery of Dangdong Port and Hwadang Village. The sea is peaceful today, but for the Japanese forces at the time, ships were essential for transporting troops and food. Burning enemy vessels meant more than destroying ships; it severely restricted the Japanese forces' ability to move troops and supplies. The key to the Jeokjinpo victory, worth remembering as you walk this trail, was thorough vigilance that never slackened, even after a string of victories.  Admiral Yi's wisdom lives on in these waters. He never got carried away by a single success, instead choosing the most advantageous way to fight whenever he encountered the enemy. Remembering the great victory won that day through thorough reconnaissance, swift maneuvering, and cool-headed judgment, we invite you to continue along the trail with the blue sea of Goseong beside you. Thank you for joining us on the Battle of Jeokjinpo section, the final part of today's journey of unbeaten victories. We hope to see you again on the next section of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail."

stories.title: Section 5 Battle of Sacheon
stories.script: "[As the Tide Returned, the Turtle Ship Appeared]  Welcome to the Battle of Sacheon section, where the Turtle Ship made its first appearance in battle.  This trail lets you learn, as you walk, not only about the first deployment of the Turtle Ship, a new kind of warship, but also about the patience and judgment of Admiral Yi Sun-sin, who read the timing of the ebb and flood tides and turned an unfavorable sea into a sea of victory.   On the twenty-ninth day of the fifth lunar month in 1592, Admiral Yi began his second campaign. Setting out with 23 panokseon warships, he was joined at Noryang by three warships under Won Gyun, for a total of 26. On the way to Sacheon, a Japanese ship was sighted leaving Gonyang and heading toward Sacheon.  When the fleet gave chase, the Japanese abandoned the ship and fled ashore. The Joseon navy broke up and burned the ship they had left behind. Then, looking toward the Sacheon wharf, the fleet saw 12 Japanese ships anchored in a row. Admiral Yi did not go straight in.  This was because it was ebb tide, and the water was going out. If the heavy panokseon warships entered the shallows, they could run aground and become unable to move. The moment a ship stopped, it would be exposed to the guns of the Japanese on shore. So Admiral Yi waited for the tide to turn.  Then he told his commanders: ""If we feign a retreat, the enemy will surely board their ships and come out to fight. The best plan is to draw them out into the open sea and destroy them there."" Instead of forcing his way in, Admiral Yi carried out a clever decoy operation that used the flow of the sea. As the panokseon slowly turned away, the Japanese forces, mistaking this for a Joseon retreat, rushed out from the shore and prepared to fight. At that very moment, the tide began to come in.  As the water deepened, the panokseon could move in close to the wharf. Admiral Yi turned the fleet around and ordered an immediate attack. At the very front of the Joseon navy was a ship unlike any other. It was the Turtle Ship.  The Turtle Ship was built on the basis of the panokseon. A dragon's head was fitted at the bow so that cannon could be fired from the dragon's mouth, and iron spikes and awls were set into its back so that the enemy could not climb aboard. Its crew could see out, but the enemy could not see in, making it an assault ship that could charge without hesitation into the midst of even hundreds of enemy vessels and fire its cannon. The Turtle Ship charged into the heart of the enemy position, firing cannon in every direction and shattering the Japanese formation in an instant. The panokseon following behind fired their cannon all at once, and after fierce fighting, all 13 Japanese ships were destroyed, including the one destroyed earlier. It was a spectacular debut for the Turtle Ship and a great victory, but the Joseon navy did not come through unharmed.  During the battle, Admiral Yi was shot in the left shoulder. Na Dae-yong, who had taken part in building the Turtle Ship, was among the commanders and soldiers who were also wounded. The Battle of Sacheon was not won by the Turtle Ship alone. The key decisions came first: not to enter at low tide, to lure the enemy out, and to commit the Turtle Ship when the flood tide returned. The new weapon showed its power only under a commander who could read the flow of the sea and within a well-trained fleet.  The Battle of Sacheon section is about 20.6 kilometers long and rated moderate in difficulty. It takes around five hours, so allow enough time and make sure you have the stamina for the walk.  The trail begins at Seonjin Waterfront Park and continues through Jongpo Village, Geobukseon Rural Village, Daepo Port, Mojarangpo, Mochung Park, Sanbullyeong Port, and Samcheonpodaegyo Park before reaching Daebangjin Port. It is said that Turtle Ships were hidden at Daebangjin Port during the Imjin War. Another story that survives is that Daebangjin Port was filled with fresh water to keep oysters and seaweed from clinging to the bottoms of the warships. These are stories passed down locally, however, and should be understood as distinct from the historical record.  Starting from the symbol of the Turtle Ship, the route takes you in turn past villages and tidal flats, harbors and sunsets, the broad waters around Samcheonpodaegyo Bridge, and the old naval-harbor atmosphere of Daebangjin Port. Because the route is fairly long, please watch for vehicle traffic and other walkers, and stay safe. The victory at Sacheon did not come simply from the power of the new weapon, the Turtle Ship. It was the fruit of Admiral Yi's cool-headed strategy—reading the tides precisely and drawing the enemy out to where the Joseon navy had the advantage.  As you look out over the blue waters of Sacheon, feel deep in your heart the courage and wisdom of the Joseon navy, which turned the tide even in a moment of crisis and never doubted its victory. Thank you for joining us on the Battle of Sacheon section, the first voyage of the Turtle Ship. We hope to see you again on the next section of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail."

stories.title: Section 6 Battle of Dangpo
stories.script: "[The Turtle Ship That Brought Down the Red-Draped Flagship]  Welcome to the Battle of Dangpo section on the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail. This trail follows the historic sites of the Battle of Dangpo, where the Joseon navy won a complete victory by first bringing down the enemy's command ship and its commander.   On the morning of the second day of the sixth lunar month in 1592, just four days after the Turtle Ship's first victory at Sacheon, a report came in: ""Japanese ships are anchored at the Dangpo wharf."" When the Joseon navy under Admiral Yi reached Dangpo, some 300 Japanese soldiers were busy plundering inside the fortress and in the village. Twenty-one Japanese ships were lined up at the wharf, and among them one large ship stood out.  It was the Japanese command ship, with a tall tower draped with red silk curtains and marked with a single large character reading ""hwang."" Rather than taking on all the enemy ships at once, Admiral Yi ordered his forces to concentrate first on this command ship. At the order, the Turtle Ship was the first to charge into the enemy formation. It charged beneath the towering command ship and fired its cannon from the dragon's head and hull.  The panokseon warships following behind kept up the momentum, firing cannon and arrows one after another. Then Gwon Jun, center commander of the squadron, charged forward and shot the enemy commander with an arrow, and Kim Wan, garrison commander of Sado, and the military officer Jin Mu-seong cut off the enemy commander's head. Having lost their commander, the Japanese forces instantly fell into utter confusion. The soldiers scrambled to abandon their ships and flee, and the Joseon navy destroyed and burned all 21 Japanese ships without leaving a single one.  The key to the Battle of Dangpo was a strategy that struck precisely at the enemy's vital point and concentrated force there. It was a battle in which perfect teamwork shone. The Turtle Ship tore through the enemy formation and struck the command ship directly, while the panokseon warships provided cover with powerful cannon fire from behind.  This section starts at Changnyangmyo Shrine, built by the people of Tongyeong to honor Admiral Yi Sun-sin. From the shrine, the route leads to the Tongyeong Undersea Tunnel, which connects downtown Tongyeong with Mireukdo Island and offers the unusual experience of walking beneath the sea. From there, it continues through Tongyeong Marine Tourism Park, Sepo Rural Village, Sanyang-eup, Dangpo Port, and the Dangposeong Fortress Site before reaching Dara Park.  At the end of a long journey, this is a place to reflect on both the history of the Battle of Dangpo and the beauty of the Tongyeong sea.  From Dara Park, islands and waterways unfold in layer upon layer. Today it is a place to enjoy beautiful sunsets, but during the war, these waters were where the navy had to determine which islands the enemy ships were hiding behind and decide the direction of the next sortie.  The Battle of Dangpo section is about 14.9 kilometers long and takes about four hours at a leisurely pace. The course is rated moderate, but the repeated climbs and descents in the latter half call for careful pacing. Some stretches also combine village lanes, coastal roads, and mountain paths, so please watch for vehicles and other pedestrians and walk safely. The Battle of Dangpo was a battle of wisdom. It showed how important it is to find the most important target and concentrate force on it, rather than simply using force blindly.  Picture the proud Turtle Ship and panokseon warships charging toward the heart of the enemy across the calm waters of Tongyeong, and hold in your heart the memory of that day's stirring victory. Thank you for joining us on the Battle of Dangpo section and recalling that day's masterstroke, which brought down the red-draped command ship. We hope to see you again on the next section of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail."

stories.title: Section 7 Battle of Yulpo
stories.script: [The Unsung Soldiers Who Rowed Through the Headwind]  Welcome to the Battle of Yulpo section on the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail. This trail honors the spirit of the nameless soldiers who rowed without rest, overcoming the headwind to pursue the fleeing enemy to the very end.   Around noon on the seventh day of the sixth lunar month in 1592, the combined Joseon fleet, fresh from consecutive victories at Sacheon, Dangpo, and Danghangpo, was moving toward the waters off Geoje. When it reached the waters off Yeongdeungpo, seven Japanese ships appeared far off in the direction of Yulpo. On sighting the Joseon navy, the Japanese forces chose not to fight and began fleeing toward Busan, their stronghold.  Admiral Yi immediately ordered a pursuit, but as ill luck would have it, the wind was a headwind blowing from the opposite direction. It was a desperate situation. They could never catch the Japanese ships by sail alone. But Joseon's panokseon was a warship that could use both sail and oars. To drive such a large, heavy ship into the wind, dozens of men had to row in unison, pulling together with every stroke.  To the beat of the drum, the oars dipped into the sea. Once, and then again. No single ship could race ahead on its own. The entire fleet had to hold its positions and move forward together in the same direction.  As the heavy panokseon warships closed in at a remarkable speed without breaking formation, the panicked Japanese fled, throwing even their cargo into the sea to lighten their ships. But the Joseon navy pushed through the headwind and pursued them until they were within range, and poured in chongtong cannon fire and arrows, destroying and burning all seven enemy ships. The Battle of Yulpo may have been small in scale, but it showed the fierce tenacity of the Joseon navy. Once it found the enemy, it pursued them to the end and cut off their escape. Above all, it was a precious victory won by the cooperation and discipline of the countless gyeokgun, or oarsmen, whose sweat and hard work lay behind the record of victory.  The Battle of Yulpo section starts at Guyeong Beach, once a major lookout post for the navy. From there, it continues through the entrance to the Daebongsan forest trail, Nongso Mongdol Beach, Bause Observatory, Gwanpo Port, and Dumo Port before reaching the Guyulpojinseong Fortress Site. The full route is about 14.7 kilometers long and takes about four hours at a leisurely pace. Rated difficult, it is a long-distance course combining coastal paths, forest trails, and scenic viewpoints.  Because the route rises and falls repeatedly, allow enough time and make sure you have the stamina for the walk. Some stretches also connect coastal roads, village lanes, and mountain paths, so please watch for vehicles and other pedestrians and walk safely. The great victory at Yulpo was no mere stroke of luck. It was the inevitable result of the resolve of Admiral Yi, who never let unfavorable conditions deter him and never gave up, and the sweat of the oarsmen.  As you look out over the blue sea, feel deep in your heart the fierce perseverance and the very breath of the Joseon navy as it drove powerfully through the waves against the rough wind. Thank you for joining us on the Battle of Yulpo section and remembering the perseverance shown at the oars that day, rowing against the headwind. We hope to see you again on the next section of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail.

stories.title: Section 8 Battle of Danghangpo
stories.script: [A Sheltered Bay Becomes a Giant Trap]  Welcome to the Battle of Danghangpo section on the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail. This trail follows the historic sites of the Battle of Danghangpo, where the Joseon navy won two separate victories.   Two naval engagements were fought at Danghangpo during the Imjin War. The First Battle of Danghangpo took place on the fifth day of the sixth lunar month in 1592, while the Second Battle of Danghangpo was fought from the fourth to the fifth day of the third lunar month in 1594. Although they took place in the same waters, the two battles differed in timing, fleet size, and the course of operations.  The First Battle of Danghangpo took place as the Joseon navy, fresh from its victories at Sacheon and Dangpo, continued its second sortie. Yi Eok-gi's Right Jeolla Naval Force joined Admiral Yi Sun-sin's Left Jeolla Naval Force in the waters off Dangpo, and Won Gyun's Right Gyeongsang Naval Force also took part. It was a combined operation of the three provincial naval forces: the Left Jeolla, Right Jeolla, and Right Gyeongsang naval forces. At that point, residents of Geoje reported that the Japanese ships that had been defeated at Dangpo and fled had entered Danghangpo in Goseong.  The combined fleet under Yi Sun-sin, Yi Eok-gi, and Won Gyun headed for Danghangpo. Rather than sending every ship into the narrow bay at once, Admiral Yi first dispatched three warships to check the depth and terrain. If the Japanese followed them, they were to feign a retreat and lure the enemy into open water. Danghangpo has a narrow entrance and a broad inner bay. It offered the Japanese a sheltered place to hide their ships, but once the Joseon navy controlled the entrance, escape would be difficult.  The Joseon navy concealed part of its force outside the bay and waited for the scout ships to draw the Japanese forces out. When the Japanese vessels began to move, the Joseon navy tightened the encirclement. The Turtle Ship led the way, disrupting the enemy formation, while the panokseon warships followed with concentrated cannon fire. With their escape route blocked, the Japanese either fled ashore or resisted from their ships.  The Joseon navy destroyed or burned all 26 Japanese vessels. The key to the battle was not charging blindly into the narrow bay, but carrying out reconnaissance, deception, ambush, and encirclement in sequence. Admiral Yi first studied the terrain, then drew the Japanese out, and finally cut off their retreat. He turned the geography of Danghangpo from a refuge for the enemy into a place where the Joseon navy could encircle them.  About two years later, in 1594, the Japanese forces again gathered ships at Danghangpo. The Joseon navy fought the Second Battle of Danghangpo over the fourth and fifth days of the third lunar month, destroying 31 Japanese ships. Taking the first and second battles together, a total of 57 Japanese ships were destroyed here.  There is also an intriguing story behind this victory that has been handed down to the present day. At Danghangpo, the story of a figure named Wol-i is passed down. According to local legend, Wol-i altered the sea routes on a map the Japanese carried so that they would sail deep into Danghangpo. Trusting the map, the Japanese thought they had entered by a safe route, but it was a dead-end sea with only one way out. The story of Wol-i, however, is not a fact confirmed in the official battle records of the time, but it is a legend passed down in the region over many years. It is important to distinguish between the historical battle and the local legend, but the story of Wol-i shows how special this victory has remained in the memory of the people of Danghangpo.  The trail begins at the Chungmugong Victory Memorial Tower in the Danghangpo Tourist Area and continues through the Gate of the Sea, Danghangpo Port, and the Danghangpo Marine Footbridge to Donggoseong Sports Park. The Danghangpo Tourist Area brings together places that commemorate the Battle of Danghangpo and Yi Sun-sin, including the Chungmugong Victory Memorial Tower, Sungchungsa Shrine, and a Turtle Ship exhibition facility. It is a good idea to first learn about when the two battles took place and how they unfolded before setting out on the trail. Along the Danghangman Trail, you can see up close the shape of the long, narrow bay surrounded by low hills.  Looking over the calm water, you can understand why the Japanese thought of this as a safe anchorage and, conversely, why it was so hard to escape once the Joseon navy had taken control of the entrance.  The Battle of Danghangpo section is about 4.3 kilometers long. Short and gentle, it takes about an hour and a half at a leisurely pace. Rated very easy, it can be walked comfortably by families and by those taking their first steps in exploring history. The Battle of Danghangpo was a battle in which the Joseon navy first read the terrain, then lured the enemy out, and finally cut off its retreat. As you look over the calm waters of Danghangman Bay, picture the moment when the scout ships and the ambush ships, the Turtle Ship and the panokseon warships, each played their part.  Thank you for joining us on the Battle of Danghangpo section, where the terrain was turned into a trap and two victories were won. We hope to see you again on the next section of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail.

stories.title: Section 9 Battle of Hansando (Inland – Mireukdo Island – Hansando Island)
stories.audioTitle: Section 9 Battle of Hansando (Inland – Mireukdo Island – Hansando Island)
stories.script: [The Crane Wing Formation Born from a Cowherd's Report]  Welcome to the Battle of Hansando section, the dramatic climax of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail. This trail follows the events of the Battle of Hansando, which completely changed the course of the Imjin War, as well as the stories of the people of Tongyeong and Hansando Island who supported that victory.  On the seventh day of the seventh lunar month in 1592, a cowherd came running into the Joseon naval camp, gasping for breath. His name was Kim Cheon-son. While tending cattle on Mireukdo Island, he had seen Japanese ships massed in Gyeonnaeryang Strait, the narrow channel between Geoje and Tongyeong, and had come to report it.  Admiral Yi did not dismiss the report that a large Japanese fleet was lying at Gyeonnaeryang. At dawn the next day, the eighth day of the seventh lunar month, the Joseon navy headed for Gyeonnaeryang. The Japanese fleet numbered 73 vessels in all: 36 large ships, 24 medium ships, and 13 small ships. The Japanese commander, Wakisaka Yasuharu, had already put to sea in search of the Joseon navy.  Admiral Yi, however, did not fight inside Gyeonnaeryang. Gyeonnaeryang is a narrow channel with many reefs and complex currents. The large, heavy panokseon warships would have had difficulty spreading into formation, and there was a high risk of the ships colliding with one another. And if the battle went against them, the Japanese forces could flee to the nearby shore.  Admiral Yi decided to fight not where the enemy had chosen, but where the Joseon navy could fight at its best. Five or six panokseon warships entered Gyeonnaeryang first. They approached the Japanese, then suddenly turned their ships around and appeared to flee. Wakisaka thought the Joseon navy was retreating in fear.  The 73-ship Japanese fleet gave chase all at once and began streaming out of Gyeonnaeryang. The decoy ships drew the Japanese into the open waters off Hansando Island. The moment enough enemy ships had come out, the fleeing Joseon ships turned around.   Across the sea, a vast pair of crane wings seemed to unfold. It was the hagikjin, or Crane Wing Formation. Admiral Yi took a formation used on land and executed it flawlessly with his fleet at sea. The scattered panokseon warships formed up in an instant. While the center of the fleet blocked the Japanese from the front, the panokseon warships on both wings spread wide and enveloped the enemy on the left and right. As if a crane were slowly folding its wings, the encirclement tightened from three directions. Cannon fire and arrows poured down on the Japanese ships from all sides.  The Japanese tried to get close to the panokseon warships and board them, but they came under concentrated fire before they could get near. In the battle, 47 Japanese ships were burned and 12 were captured by the Joseon navy. Fifty-nine ships in all were destroyed or captured, yet the Joseon navy did not lose a single warship. Wakisaka barely escaped in a small boat.  It is said that he hid on Hansando Island and survived by eating seaweed, and a story is also told that the Wakisaka family thereafter ate only seaweed every year on the eighth day of the seventh lunar month. This, however, is a tradition separate from the official battle records. It can be understood as a story symbolizing the shock the defeat at Hansando Island caused among the Japanese. With the victory at the Battle of Hansando, Japanese plans to advance into the West Sea suffered a heavy blow.  Plans to send troops and supplies to the Japanese army by sea also became difficult. Admiral Yi later established the Joseon navy's command headquarters on Hansando Island. Hansando Island preserves not only the memory of the battle's heroes, but also a number of village names said to be linked to the navy's supply activities. At Daegopo and Sogopo, salt was made for the navy, and at Mangsan Mountain, beacon fires signaled the enemy's movements.  Jindu is said to have had a naval guard post, and Yaso a forge where weapons and equipment were made. Uiam is said to have been a place where military uniforms were made and mended. The victory at the Battle of Hansando was not made on the water alone. It was a victory made together by the information Kim Cheon-son brought, the soldiers' cannon fire, the oarsmen's rowing, and the salt, clothing, and weapons prepared by the people of the island villages.  The trail is made up of three parts with a total length of 32.1 kilometers: inland Tongyeong, Mireukdo Island, and Hansando Island. The inland part runs from Yi Sun-sin Park through Nammangsan Sculpture Park and Gangguan Harbor to Changnyangmyo Shrine. The Mireukdo part continues from Changnyangmyo Shrine over Mireuksan Mountain and through Sinbong Village, Yeongun Port, and Tongyeong Suryuk Beach to the Donam Tourist Area.  The Hansando part runs from Jeseungdang Pier through Jeseungdang Shrine, Uihang Port in Dueok-ri, and Muneopo Village to the Monument for the Battle of Hansando. From the top of Mireuksan Mountain, Gyeonnaeryang and the waters off Hansando Island spread out before you, offering the view the cowherd Kim Cheon-son would have seen. At Suru Pavilion in Jeseungdang Shrine, you can look out over the sea that Admiral Yi would have gazed upon as he commanded his navy. As you walk this trail, keep one scene in mind.  A cowherd comes running, gasping for breath, to report that the enemy has appeared. The admiral does not overlook even this small report and draws the enemy out into open water. And across the sea, vast crane wings unfold. The Battle of Hansando was not a victory won by a brilliant admiral and a strong fleet alone.  It was a victory created by countless people, each doing their part, whose efforts came together as one. Thank you for joining us on the Battle of Hansando section, a victory made possible by the admiral, the soldiers, and the people. We hope to see you again on the next section of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail.

stories.title: Section 11 Battle of Ungpo
stories.script: [A Month of Battle and a Handful of Seeds]  Welcome to the Battle of Ungpo section on the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail. The Battle of Ungpo was the longest battle Admiral Yi Sun-sin ever fought, and one in which he carried out a combined land and sea attack. This trail honors the Joseon navy, which spent about a month persistently pressuring an enemy that would not come out to sea, as well as Admiral Yi Sun-sin, whose sense of responsibility led him to withdraw so that the people could plant their spring crops.  From the tenth day of the second lunar month to the sixth day of the third lunar month in 1593, seven battles took place one after another in the waters off Ungpo. Wakisaka Yasuharu, the Japanese naval commander who had suffered heavy losses at Hansando Island, no longer came out readily into open water.  To protect their main bases in Busan, the Japanese forces made use of the narrow inlets and land strongholds around Ungcheon and Ungpo. They hid their ships close to shore, while their troops took position on high ground and in defensive works and resisted with matchlock fire. The combined fleet under the three commanders Yi Sun-sin, Yi Eok-gi, and Won Gyun tried to draw the Japanese forces out to sea. This was because on the open sea, the maneuverability of the panokseon warships and the firepower of the Joseon navy's cannon could be used to full effect.  The Joseon navy's decoy ships approached close to the inlet. Small Japanese boats showed themselves, but the moment the Joseon navy gave chase, they fled straight back toward land. Having experienced the Joseon navy's decoy tactics at Hansando Island, the Japanese forces would not carelessly follow them out. Admiral Yi did not give up.  He used some ships to lure the enemy while keeping others in ambush outside. The fleet fired its cannon close to the inlet, withdrew, regrouped, and came back again. For nearly a month, attacks and decoy maneuvers, reconnaissance and blockade were repeated. Admiral Yi also conceived a plan for the army and navy to attack together.  He twice asked Kim Seong-il, the Provincial Inspector of Right Gyeongsang Province, for army support, but the reply came back that there was no capacity to spare because of the work of receiving the Ming troops, and that too few soldiers remained. Admiral Yi did not simply wait for the army to arrive. On the twenty-second day of the second lunar month, he called together Yi Eok-gi and his other commanders to discuss a new way of attacking. The Japanese forces, cowed, would not come out to sea, and with no land forces attacking from behind, there was no way to wipe them out completely. Repeated fighting, however, had badly broken Japanese morale, and Admiral Yi judged that the inlet had enough room for seven or eight panokseon warships. So he selected five light ships in good condition from each of the Joseon navy's three provincial fleets. These 15 panokseon warships charged in turn toward where the Japanese ships lay lined up. When the lead ship entered the inlet, fired its cannon, and withdrew, the next ship went in and continued the bombardment.  As the cannon struck the Japanese ships and positions one after another, about half of the enemy ships were smashed, and many Japanese soldiers were killed or wounded. At the same time, another operation began. Monk soldiers and archers selected from the three provincial naval forces were divided among some ten ships and sent to set up positions at Angolpo and Jepo. The Japanese forces were thrown into great confusion by the prospect of being attacked from both sea and land.  They had to run back and forth between the inlet and their positions to respond to the attacks. With victory in sight, the Joseon commanders vied with one another to charge the enemy. But as confidence in victory grew too great, an accident occurred. As they attacked the Japanese and pulled out of the inlet, two Joseon ships collided.  The collision tore away the shields, and the soldiers crowded to one side of the ship to avoid the Japanese musket balls. In the end, one of the ships capsized, and soldiers were killed or injured. Admiral Yi did not see this accident as mere bad luck. He recorded that repeated victories had made the soldiers overconfident, and that the accident happened because they rushed into the enemy position, each vying not to be left behind.  The Battle of Ungpo showed not only the courage of the Joseon navy, but also the importance of order and restraint even at the moment of victory. As the fighting dragged on, the spring farming season was approaching. If soldiers and civilians kept being mobilized for battle, they could miss the time to sow their seeds. If they could not sow in spring, there would be no grain to harvest in autumn, and both the people and the navy would face a food shortage.  Records tell us that Admiral Yi, mindful of this, brought the operation to a close so that the people could return home and farm, even though he regretted not having driven the Japanese forces out completely.  The trail begins at the Battle of Ungpo Victory Monument in Huindolme Park and continues through Ungcheon Japanese Fortress, Jedeok Pier, and Myeongdong Pier before reaching Jinhae Marine Park.  The Battle of Ungpo section is about 8.6 kilometers long and takes about two hours. The route is rated moderate, but it includes a stretch that climbs up to the Japanese fortress, so please take it slowly there and continue your journey safely. From the top of Ungcheon Japanese Fortress, you can look down on a narrow sea channel. Today it has been reclaimed and looks like land, but in the past, this was part of the sea.  Looking out from here, you can understand why the Japanese relied on narrow inlets and high land strongholds, and why the Joseon navy could not end the fighting by naval bombardment alone. Take a moment to imagine the scene as it was. Fifteen panokseon warships charge into the inlet one after another. Cannon fire echoes across the sea.  At the same time, ships carrying monk soldiers and sailors approach the shores of Angolpo and Jepo. As the troops land and set up positions on land, the Japanese forces are thrown into great confusion, caught between sea and land. The Battle of Ungpo was not a battle in which the Joseon navy simply waited for army support. It was a battle in which the navy reorganized the troops and ships available to it and landed sailors and monk soldiers directly to open a new way forward.  It was also a battle in which Admiral Yi reflected on an accident among his own forces amid the momentum of victory and, at the end, knew when to stop for the sake of a handful of seeds the people would sow in their fields. What Admiral Yi showed in the waters off Ungpo was not only unwavering persistence. It was the judgment to change tactics as the situation demanded, the restraint to reflect on himself even in victory, and a sense of responsibility that looked beyond the war to the lives of the people.  Thank you for joining us on the Battle of Ungpo section, the longest fight and a day that called for the greatest caution. We hope to see you again on the next section of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail.

stories.title: Section 10 Battle of Angolpo
stories.script: [Why Some Enemy Ships Were Left Behind]  Welcome to the Battle of Angolpo section on the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail. This trail follows the wisdom and compassion of Admiral Yi Sun-sin, who overcame the disadvantage of narrow, shallow waters by attacking in turns and, even at the moment of victory, placed the lives of civilians first.   The Angolpo before you is a snug inlet surrounded by mountains. The sea is calm, and the waters farther inside are so shallow that in places the seabed is exposed at low tide. In the seventh lunar month of 1592, the Japanese navy made use of exactly this terrain to anchor its ships deep inside Angolpo.  The Joseon navy, however, did not force its way into the narrow, shallow waters where the enemy was hiding. The Battle of Angolpo was a battle in which the Joseon navy watched the changing tides and depths and sent its ships in by turns, attacking the Japanese navy relentlessly. The Battle of Angolpo took place on the tenth day of the seventh lunar month in 1592, two days after the great victory at the Battle of Hansando. It was the final naval battle of Admiral Yi's third campaign of the Imjin War.  On the ninth day of the seventh lunar month, Admiral Yi received a report that some 40 Japanese ships were lying at Angolpo. But it was already dusk, and a strong wind was blowing in a direction unfavorable to a Joseon advance. For that reason he did not rush into battle. The fleet spent the night at Oncheondo Island in Geoje, regrouping, and at dawn the next day, after informing Yi Eok-gi's Right Jeolla Naval Force and Won Gyun's Right Gyeongsang Naval Force of the plan of operations, headed for Angolpo.  At the Angolpo wharf lay 42 Japanese vessels in all: 21 large ships, 15 medium ships, and 6 small ships. It was the fleet led by the Japanese naval commanders Kuki Yoshitaka and Kato Yoshiaki. Angolpo had a narrow entrance and shallow inner waters, and the space in which the large panokseon warships could move changed with the ebb and flow of the tide.  Relying on this terrain, the Japanese kept their ships moored close to shore and refused to leave the inlet. Admiral Yi first tried to draw them into open water. Joseon vessels repeatedly approached and withdrew, attempting to lure the enemy out, but the Japanese forces held their position.  This was because they knew that only two days earlier, in the waters off Hansando Island, the Japanese forces had suffered heavy losses after being drawn into a Joseon decoy operation. The Japanese kept their ships anchored in shallow water and held out, firing matchlock muskets from land and from the decks of their ships. Admiral Yi did not fight in the way the enemy expected. This was because if the large panokseon warships entered the narrow inlet all at once, they could collide with one another, or be left stranded on the exposed seabed as the tide went out.  So Admiral Yi sent his ships into the inlet one after another. When the lead panokseon warship entered the inlet, fired its cannon, and withdrew, the next ship waiting behind went in and attacked in its turn. As one ship pulled back, the next came in, and as that ship came out, yet another kept up the bombardment. While watching the changing tides and depths, the Joseon navy rotated its fleet so that the attack could continue without interruption.  Instead of letting the narrow inlet become a weakness, the Joseon navy turned it into a place where the Japanese found it hard to escape. When Yi Eok-gi's Right Jeolla Naval Force joined in as well, the Joseon attack grew even stronger. After a bombardment that lasted all day, most of the Japanese ships had been destroyed or badly damaged, and the Japanese forces aboard them fled ashore. The Joseon navy could have burned every remaining Japanese ship as well.  But Admiral Yi ordered the fleet to pull back about 400 meters from the inlet and spend the night there. The reason was the Joseon civilians hiding in the mountains. If every Japanese ship were burned and their escape route cut off, the cornered Japanese forces could go ashore, hunt down the people hiding from the war, and kill them. So Admiral Yi left a few ships so that the Japanese could flee by sea.  This was not a matter of giving up the chance to wipe out the enemy before him. He left the enemy an escape route open in order to prevent the loss of the people's lives. The Battle of Angolpo shows both Yi Sun-sin's resourcefulness and his love for the people. When the enemy would not take the bait, he changed tactics to a rotating bombardment, and at the moment victory was within reach, he put the people's lives before military gains. Badly shaken by the heavy blows suffered in quick succession at the Battle of Hansando and the Battle of Angolpo, the Japanese navy withdrew to the Busan area.  The Japanese forces lost control of the southern seas and began to struggle to supply troops and provisions to their army by sea. The Battle of Angolpo was an important victory in which the Joseon navy blocked the sea approaches to Busan, the Japanese forces' main forward base.  This trail begins at Angol Japanese Fortress and continues through Angolpo Gulgang to the Battle of Angolpo Victory Monument in Ancheong Park. Climbing up to Angol Japanese Fortress and looking over the inlet, you can understand why the Japanese moored their ships so far inside the inlet, and why the Joseon navy attacked in rotation rather than sending in every ship at once. As you descend along the narrow lanes of Angol Village, you can still sense the atmosphere of an old harbor village. Angolpo Gulgang was a Joseon-era facility where ships were moored and repaired and protected from rough waves.  The remaining stone structures suggest that Angolpo had long been an important base for the navy and its ships. At the final point, Ancheong Park, stands the Battle of Angolpo Victory Monument.  The Battle of Angolpo section is about 2.1 kilometers long, a short and relatively easy walk, but take care on the approach to Angol Japanese Fortress and along some stretches of road. As you look over the calm waters of Angolpo, picture the panokseon warships entering the inlet one after another to keep up the bombardment, and recall Admiral Yi's decision to pull the fleet back for the sake of the people in the mountains. What Admiral Yi blocked at the Battle of Angolpo was the Japanese route toward Busan. And what he protected to the very end were the lives of the people trying to survive behind that sea.  Thank you for joining us on the Battle of Angolpo section, where Admiral Yi put the lives of the people before victory. We hope to see you again on the next section of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail.

stories.title: Section 12 Battle of Noryang
stories.script: "[A Great Star Falls at Gwaneumpo: Walking in Memory of Yi Sun-sin]  Welcome to the Battle of Noryang section, the final section of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail and the battle that brought the seven-year war to its close. This trail honors the final moments of Chungmugong Yi Sun-sin, who gave everything he had to save his country, as well as the countless heroes who fought beside him to the end.   On the night of the eighteenth day of the eleventh lunar month in 1598, torches and fire arrows burned brighter than moonlight over the waters of Noryang. The seven-year Imjin War was drawing to a close. Japanese forces were preparing to withdraw from Joseon, and a large fleet headed for Noryang Strait to rescue Japanese troops isolated in Suncheon.  The Joseon navy under Admiral Yi Sun-sin and the Ming navy under Chen Lin blocked the Japanese retreat. Noryang Strait is a narrow stretch of sea between Namhaedo Island and Hadong. Its currents are strong, and there are many islands and reefs, so that once ships become entangled there, they cannot easily get out. As the night deepened, the allied Joseon and Ming navies launched their attack.  Drums and cannon fire echoed across the dark sea as fire arrows streaked through the night sky. Caught by surprise, the Japanese fought back desperately because their last route home had been blocked. Japanese ships closed in on the Joseon and Ming vessels, firing matchlock muskets and trying to board them.  Hundreds of ships became entangled in the narrow waters of Noryang. Smoke from the cannon and from burning ships covered the sea, and the battle became a melee in which friend and foe were hard to tell apart. At the center of the battle, Admiral Yi beat the drum as he directed his men. The drumbeat told the men where their commander was, serving both as an order and a source of courage.  The battle went on all night. As dawn approached, the Japanese formation began to collapse. The allied Joseon and Ming navies pursued the fleeing Japanese forces to the last. Just then, a bullet fired by the Japanese struck Admiral Yi.  Admiral Yi was mortally wounded. But if his death became known, the soldiers might waver, and the course of a battle that was nearly over could change. His last words are passed down as follows: ""The battle is at its height. I beg you, do not speak of my death."" Admiral Yi's death was made known only to a few people close by, including his son Yi Hoe and his nephew Yi Wan.  Accounts differ as to who concealed the admiral's death and carried on commanding, but the drumbeat from the flagship and the commands given from there continued until the battle was over. The Joseon navy fought on through the final battle without knowing that the admiral had passed away. The drum did not stop, and the Japanese fleet withdrew after suffering heavy losses. Only after the battle ended was Admiral Yi's death made known.  Over the sea where victory had been won, wailing spread rather than cheers. The Battle of Noryang was the last victory of the Imjin War. The withdrawing Japanese fleet suffered heavy losses, and the war that had lasted seven years came to an end. But this sea is not simply a site of victory. It is the sea where Admiral Yi Sun-sin fought his final battle, holding his post until the very moment the war ended.  Now, let us follow the path along the sea where cheers of victory and deep sorrow met that day. The trail runs from the Gohyeon-myeon area, home to the Tripitaka Koreana Woodblock Culture Center, along the Gwaneumpo embankment and past Gwaneumpo Cheommangdae Observatory, Yi Sun-sin Sea Park, Iraksan Mountain, Gupomisan Mountain, Wolgok Village, Gamam Village, and the Namhaedaegyo Cruise dock to Chungnyeolsa Shrine. Passing Gwaneumpo, where the admiral's remains are said to have first been brought ashore, we follow the footsteps of that sorrowful funeral procession to Yi Sun-sin Sea Park. From Yi Sun-sin Sea Park, you can pass Iraksa Shrine to reach the memorial stele and Cheommangdae Observatory, from which you can look out over the sea where Admiral Yi gave his life for his country.   Seen from here, Gwaneumpo is quiet today. But on that night in 1598, cannon fire, drumbeats, and the light of burning ships filled the sea. Standing before the water, imagine the sound of the drum. The admiral has already fallen, but the drum does not stop. The soldiers press forward, not knowing that their commander has died.  That last drumbeat drove back the Japanese forces and marked the end of the seven-year war. When, with the cool sea breeze on your face, you reach the final destination, Chungnyeolsa Shrine in Namhae, today's meaningful journey comes to a close. Chungnyeolsa Shrine is where the admiral's remains were kept for a time before being taken to his hometown of Asan, a fitting place to quietly bow your head and honor his noble sacrifice.  The Battle of Noryang section is about 11 kilometers long and follows the coast on relatively gentle terrain. Rated moderate, it takes about three hours. Rather than walking quickly, we hope you will pause for a moment at each key point, look out over the wide sea, and reflect together on the meaning of Admiral Yi's death for his country. Admiral Yi's great voyage, which began at Okpo, ended here at Noryang.  Though the great star fell into the sea, his loyalty and devotion to duty until the very last moment, along with the courage of countless soldiers, still flow through these blue waters more than 400 years later. Thank you for walking with us all the way to the Battle of Noryang section, the final sea of the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail. We hope to see you again on your next walk along the Yi Sun-sin Victory Trail.  "

stories.title: Galmaemot Martyrs Sacred Place: A Place of Reflection and Healing by the Sea
stories.audioTitle: Galmaemot Martyrs Sacred Place: A Place of Reflection and Healing by the Sea
stories.script: "Galmaemot lies near the scenic Ocheon Port in Boryeong, Chungcheongnam-do, looking straight out over the West Sea. Its name, in native Korean, means “the pond where a thirsty horse drinks.” Just as horses that have galloped a long way pause to quench their thirst, this meaningful place today offers true rest and peace to pilgrims and travelers from Korea and abroad who arrive carrying the weariness of everyday life. Behind the scenery of blue sea and the quiet sound of the waves lives the fervent story of those who gave everything to defend the noble values they held. In 1866, some 160 years ago, the Byeongin Persecution broke out in Joseon, a brutal campaign of repression against Catholics. Heungseon Daewongun, the regent, wanted no blood shed in the walled capital of Hanyang (present-day Seoul), and on his orders the condemned were marched several hundred ri, a traditional Korean unit of distance, to the sandy shore at Galmaemot near the Chungcheong Naval Command. Even on that cruel road to death, Bishop Antoine Daveluy, who had come from France, held a single sentence close to his heart. “Whoever has Jesus has everything.” For 21 years he had shared the joys and hardships of the people of Joseon. Fearing that innocent people would face greater danger if he stayed in hiding, he chose to give himself up. Fr. Pierre Aumaître and Fr. Martin-Luc Huin of France, together with the Korean lay leaders St. Luke Hwang Sok-tu and St. Joseph Chang Chu-gi, joined him in his resolve and willingly drank the cup of death. Though they differed in nationality, language, and social status, they were wholly united in steadfast faith, and they shed their sacred blood on the shore at Galmaemot.  In the eyes of the world, these five men may have looked like failures, stripped even of their freedom and their lives. Yet, true to Bishop Daveluy's motto, they proved through their deaths the unchanging worth of a noble life. That is why Galmaemot is at once a horrific execution ground and a sacred place where true peace, born of suffering overcome, has blossomed. Solemnly proclaimed saints by Pope John Paul II in 1984, these five left behind a story that, even after so many years, still shines as an eternal light to the sound of the waves of the West Sea.  Galmaemot reaches beyond any one religion. It is a place of reflection that offers warm comfort to every traveler drawn here by its natural beauty and history. Whatever their religious or cultural background, visitors from any country will find in its message of sacrifice and love something that moves them deeply. Feel the cool sea breeze and gaze quietly out over the open sea. The devotion of missionaries who crossed rough seas to reach a distant land, and the steadfast hearts of Korea's forebears in the faith, who did not waver even before the executioner's blade, reach across the ages to put a question to you who walk here today. “What do you value most in your life?” At Galmaemot Martyrs Sacred Place, let the wind of peace blowing in from beyond the sea wash over you. May it quench the thirst of a heart wearied by daily life, and may you leave filled with true rest and the firm courage to walk back out into the world. "

stories.title: About Gongseri Catholic Church
stories.script: "# Gongseri Catholic Church, Asan: From a Tax-Grain Storehouse to a Shrine of Martyrdom In Inju-myeon, Asan-si, Chungcheongnam-do, a red-brick Gothic church stands on a hill overlooking Asanman Bay. This is Gongseri Catholic Church, a historic church that is the oldest parish in the Diocese of Daejeon and the ninth parish established in the Catholic Church in Korea as a whole.  ## From a Tax-Grain Storehouse to a Place of Prayer The name Gongseri comes from Gongsegotchang, a state tax-grain granary that stood on this hill during the Joseon dynasty. It was one of the transport granaries where tax grain from the Chungcheong, Jeolla, and Gyeongsang regions was collected and shipped by boat to the capital, Hanyang. In the late Joseon period, however, the state tax-grain transport system was effectively abolished during the reign of King Yeongjo, and the granary was abandoned. The hill where tax grain had once been gathered turned into a forsaken land of fear, and only much later was it reborn as a hill where prayers gather.  ## Fr. Devise and the Construction of the Church Gongseri Catholic Church traces its origins to Ganyanggol Church in Yesan, founded in 1890. In 1894, the aftermath of the Donghak Peasant Revolution made it impossible to continue pastoral work in Yesan, and the church at Gongseri began when the succeeding pastor, Fr. Émile Devise, known in Korea as Seong Il-lon, was assigned here. Before his first winter, he built a hanok-style church. A second hanok church and a rectory followed, and in 1920 he finally set about building the Western-style Gothic church that stands today. The site chosen for the church, however, was the very ground where the old children's graves and a structure known as the Chimhaedang had stood. While workers were moving a zelkova tree on the hill to prepare the site, the tree fell and crushed two of them to death. Fr. Devise then sought the intercession of St. Benedict, long renowned for his power against evil spirits: he buried three St. Benedict medals beneath the altar and prayed for three days, and the construction was completed without further incident. From that time on, St. Benedict has been the patron saint of Gongseri Catholic Church.   ## Those Who Gave Their Lives for the Faith Gongseri is also a land of martyrdom. Through the Sinyu Persecution of 1801 and the Byeongin Persecution of 1866, 32 martyrs from this area alone died bearing witness to their faith. Best known among them are three brothers from nearby Geolmae Village: Sabbas Bak Ui-seo, Mark Bak Won-seo, and Bak Ik-seo. Won-seo, the second brother, had been lax in his faith, but at the moment of his arrest he repented, saying, “Today God has called me.” Ui-seo, the eldest, then led his brothers with the words, “Let all three of us be martyred for the Lord,” and in 1867 the three walked the path of martyrdom side by side.  ## The Korean War and the Martyrdom of Three Priests Gongseri's history of martyrdom continues into modern times. Fr. Joseph Bulteau, a French priest known in Korea as O Pil-do, became pastor of Gongseri Parish in 1950. When war broke out and the faithful urged him to flee, he stayed to guard the church, saying, “A shepherd cannot leave his sheep.” Accused of being a spy and arrested by North Korean forces, he died in North Korea in January 1951 at the end of the so-called Death March. Fr. Joseph Cadars, known in Korea as Gang Dal-sun, who was assigned to Gongseri that same year but was martyred before he could take up his post, and Fr. Gang Man-su, a native of Gongseri who was the first Korean priest of the Diocese of Daejeon and was then pastor of Hongseong Parish, were likewise captured by North Korean forces during the war and martyred at Mok-dong in Daejeon. All three priests are now included in the cause for the beatification and canonization of the 81 Korean War martyrs.  ## Gongseri Catholic Church Today The former rectory, designated Chungcheongnam-do Monument No. 144, has been reborn as the church museum. Its exhibits present the history of the Diocese of Daejeon and the work of Fr. Devise, who ministered here, while the second floor documents the lives of the 32 martyrs from Gongseri. The tradition of the Eucharistic procession, which began in the Diocese of Daejeon, continues every year. The zelkova and hackberry trees standing guard beside the church, more than 400 years old, show a different face with each season, and the tranquil scenery has made Gongseri a favorite filming location for television dramas and films. "

stories.title: About Darakgol Shrine
stories.script: "Darakgol Shrine in Cheongyang is a historic Catholic village, where Fr. Thomas Choe Yang-eop, the “Martyr of Sweat,” and his father, St. Francis Choe Kyeong-hwan, were born, and where the graves of unnamed martyrs lie in rows. On the hill behind the village, the graves and headstones of unnamed martyrs stand in several rows, but no one knows whose graves they are. According to oral tradition, the bodies of Catholics martyred during the Byeongin Persecution of 1866 at the provincial offices in Hongju and Gongju were spirited away at night, past heavy surveillance, and buried here on the Choe clan's burial ground.  The Catholic faith came to Fr. Thomas Choe Yang-eop's family through his great-grandfather Choe Han-il, who, together with his younger brother Choe Han-gi, learned Catholic doctrine in Seoul from Ludovico Gonzaga Yi Jon-chang, the Apostle of Naepo, and joined the Church. Fr. Choe's grandfather, Choe In-ju, lost his father at the age of 12 and lived in Seoul caring for his widowed mother, a woman of the Gyeongju Yi clan, until he moved here, to Saeteo, to escape the Sinhae Persecution of 1791 and settled. Choe In-ju grew up, married, and had six children, the youngest of whom was St. Francis Choe Kyeong-hwan, the father of Fr. Thomas Choe Yang-eop. Here, St. Francis Choe Kyeong-hwan met and married Blessed Mary Yi Seong-rye (1801–1840), and together they raised a devout Catholic family with their eldest son, Fr. Thomas Choe Yang-eop (1821–1861), and his five younger brothers. Fr. Thomas Choe Yang-eop was born here on March 1, 1821. Almost no records survive of his childhood, but in his letters Fr. Choe wrote that the Catholic faith had taken root in his family through the influence of his grandfather. It was here that his grandfather, Choe In-ju, instilled in the whole household the commandment of “love of neighbor,” the first step for any person of faith, teaching them how to live together through hard times. That spirit passed intact to St. Francis Choe and Fr. Choe Yang-eop.  The Choe family must have been well known in the village. Believers and nonbelievers alike would have respected them, and most people would have treated them with goodwill. Within the Catholic village, too, they would have been a model of religious life and the family at the center of the community. The trouble is that those who receive people's respect and affection often lose sight of what is essential. St. Francis Choe Kyeong-hwan realized this. So he resolved to leave, in order to live the word of the Lord more fully. After overcoming their initial hardships, the family came to enjoy a life of comfort and plenty here. What is more, with frequent contact with non-Catholic relatives and a growing laxity in the family's religious practice, St. Francis urged his parents and brothers again and again to leave their wealth and relatives behind and abandon their hometown for the sake of a better life of faith. When his words had no effect, he made up his mind to leave home alone. He wrote a long letter, gave it to a child of the household, and told the child to open it six days after his departure. Then he set out in search of a place with the right conditions for living his faith fervently. When St. Francis was found missing from home, the whole household was thrown into an uproar. Even after his brothers received and read the letter, the entire family wept aloud and did not know what to do. So all the brothers went out to find him and returned home with him. Afterward, the whole family, 25 people in all, agreed unanimously to give up their hometown, relatives, and property and leave Darakgol. They gave up everything for Christ. Francis's family moved from one mountain valley to another, clearing thickets of brambles and stony fields with their own hands to survive. Though they had once been wealthy, they willingly accepted such poverty and hardship for Christ. They lived contentedly, holding as their one hope the knowledge that in doing so they were following the example of Jesus Christ and the saints more completely. (Fr. Choe Yang-eop's eighth letter, written at Jeolgol, October 15, 1851) Fr. Choe Yang-eop's family moved first to Nakdong in Seoul (near present-day Hoehyeon-dong, Jung-gu), then to Gimseong in Gangwon-do (present-day Gimhwa-eup, Gimhwa-gun, Gangwon-do, also called Geumseong) and to Jeoppeuri in Bupyeong, Gyeonggi-do, before settling in the Catholic village on Surisan Mountain in Anyang (present-day Dwitteumi in Anyang 9-dong, Anyang, Gyeonggi-do, also known as Dambaechon), where they lived until they were martyred in the Gihae Persecution of 1839.   Even after Fr. Choe Yang-eop's family left, Darakgol remained a Catholic village. During the Gihae Persecution of 1839, Fr. Pierre-Philibert Maubant and Fr. Jacques-Honoré Chastan hid here. After receiving a letter from Bishop Laurent Imbert (known in Korea as Beom Se-hyeong), the second Vicar Apostolic of Korea, urging them to give themselves up, they surrendered to constables near Hongju and were martyred at Saenamteo. The Darakgol Catholic Village survived into the early days of the Byeongin Persecution of 1866. But after Ernst Oppert's attempted robbery of Prince Namyeon's tomb in 1868, many Catholic villages across the country vanished without a trace, and Darakgol did not escape the persecution either. Gradually forgotten, the site has come down to the present day through the efforts of many people. "

stories.title: Seonggeosan Shrine, Cheonan
stories.script: "After the Sinyu Persecution of 1801, Catholics fleeing persecution took refuge on the slopes of Seonggeosan Mountain and formed several gyowuchon, or hidden Catholic villages, among them the Sohakgol Catholic Village. Firing onggi earthenware and clearing hillside plots for slash-and-burn farming, the faithful relied on one another through bitter poverty and kept the thread of their faith alive. The Seodeulgol Catholic Village, close to the Sohakgol Catholic Village, has an especially deep connection with Fr. Thomas Choe Yang-eop, the second priest of the Catholic Church in Korea. His father's older brother, Choe Yeong-ryeol, settled there, and after Fr. Choe's parents, St. Francis Choe Kyeong-hwan and Blessed Mary Yi Seong-rye, were martyred, the second of his younger brothers, Andrew Choe Seon-jeong, was entrusted to that household and grew up there.  The Sohakgol Catholic Village on Seonggeosan Mountain was a pastoral base for Fr. Choe Yang-eop, the “Martyr of Sweat,” and for the French missionaries. Located at a strategic point linking Gyeonggi, Chungcheong, and Gyeongsang provinces, it served as a key center of pastoral work during the persecutions. Fr. Choe, who traveled the length and breadth of Korea on foot to administer the sacraments to the faithful, often visited Seodeulgol, Sohakgol, and the other Catholic villages on the slopes of Seonggeosan Mountain to care for their communities. Seonggeosan Mountain was also a hiding place and a place of rest for the French missionaries of the Paris Foreign Missions Society (MEP) who had slipped secretly into Joseon. Bishop Antoine Daveluy, the Vicar Apostolic of Korea, along with Fr. Joseph-Ambroise Maistre, Fr. Stanislas Féron, and Fr. Michel Petitnicolas, rested here and wrote letters to send back home. Fr. Adolphe Calais in particular made Sohakgol his pastoral center from 1864 until just before the Byeongin Persecution, and in one letter he described Sohakgol as “a very good place to take refuge, perched high up like an eagle's nest.” In 1866, the wave of the Byeongin Persecution swept mercilessly over the Catholic villages on Seonggeosan Mountain as well. Constables stormed in and arrested a great many of the faithful, who were sent to the provincial office in Gongju, the Podocheong, the capital police bureau in Seoul, and elsewhere, where they gave their lives. The remains of those martyred at this time, among them Peter Bae Mun-ho, Peter Choe Cheon-yeo, Lazarus Choe Jong-yeo, Joseph Go, and a woman from the Chae family, were buried here on Seonggeosan Mountain together with those of countless unnamed martyrs. Because the burial mounds lie in rows, the two burial grounds are known as julmudeom, or row graves.
