Several dozen mounds are gathered in the First and Second Row Graves, but far more bodies are said to be interred there in layers: the remains of more than 200 martyrs.  The First and Second Row Graves are where the souls of martyrs who fell defending their faith, without even leaving their names, lie at rest. They are the heart of the shrine, a place of solemn prayer and meditation. Along the Way of the Cross and the Martyrs' Path, sculptures of the fourteen Stations of the Cross line the walking trail between the First and Second Row Graves, and visitors can honor the martyrs' sacrifice as they walk the lantern-lined path inscribed with the names of the 103 Korean Martyr Saints and the martyrs of Seonggeosan Mountain. The site of the Sohakgol Catholic Village is the ground where forebears in the faith lived and kept their faith alive, from the village's founding after the Sinyu Persecution of 1801 until the Byeongin Persecution of 1866. The Byeongin Persecution Memorial Church is a striking building whose front wall is made of clear glass, allowing worshipers to take in the statue of Jesus outside and the green landscape of Seonggeosan Mountain at a glance as they celebrate Mass. "

stories.title: Solmoe Martyrs Shrine
stories.script: "Solmoe Martyrs Shrine is the place where St. Andrew Kim Tae-gon (1821–1846), Korea's first Catholic priest and a martyr, was born and raised. The name Solmoe means “a mountain of pine trees.” Because Korea's first priest was born here, the site is also called “the Bethlehem of Korea.” Solmoe Martyrs Shrine thus holds great significance as the place where God first sowed the seed of vocation in the Korean Church and made it grow.   God sowed this precious seed of vocation in the rich soil of faith, and that soil was the family community of Fr. Kim Tae-gon. Even before Andrew Kim Tae-gon was born, his great-grandfather Blessed Pius Kim Jin-hu (martyred at Haemi in 1814) and his great-uncle Blessed Andrew Kim Jong-han (martyred in Daegu in 1816) had already died as martyrs after long persecution. His father, St. Ignatius Kim Che-jun, was also martyred, in 1839, while Kim Tae-gon was studying in China. The family of Andrew Kim Tae-gon was thus a community of martyrs spanning four generations. His family is known to have produced three martyr saints (St. Andrew Kim Tae-gon, St. Ignatius Kim Che-jun, and St. Teresa Kim), two martyr blesseds (Blessed Pius Kim Jin-hu and Blessed Andrew Kim Jong-han), and seven or eight other martyrs besides. Raised amid such fine examples of faith, Andrew Kim Tae-gon set out for Macao in 1836, at the age of sixteen, to study for the priesthood together with Thomas Choe Yang-eop and Francis Xavier Choe Bang-je. After his ordination to the diaconate in 1844, he returned briefly to Korea to help missionary priests enter the country, then crossed back to China. On August 17, 1845, he was ordained a priest at Jinjiaxiang Church in Shanghai and returned to Joseon. While trying to open a route across the West Sea by which missionary priests could enter the country, Fr. Andrew Kim Tae-gon was arrested in June 1846, interrogated repeatedly, and martyred on September 16 at Saenamteo on the Hangang River.   On November 25, 1949, Pope Pius XII proclaimed him patron of all the clergy engaged in evangelization in Korea, and when Pope St. John Paul II canonized the 103 Korean Martyrs in Seoul on May 6, 1984, he made Fr. Andrew Kim Tae-gon, together with St. Paul Chong Ha-sang, representative saints of the Korean Church.  Beginning in 1906, Fr. Henri Krempff, pastor of Hapdeok Parish, began buying up nearby land to develop Solmoe as a shrine, and in 1945 Fr. Philippe Perrin erected a monument honoring Blessed Andrew Kim Tae-gon at Solmoe. Systematic development of Solmoe as a shrine began in 1973. In 1982, the Diocese of Daejeon built the Solmoe Retreat House to teach and pass on the faith of the martyrs, making the shrine a “school of the martyrs' faith.” With support from the national and local governments, the birthplace of St. Andrew Kim Tae-gon was restored in 2004 and the St. Andrew Kim Taegon Memorial Hall was built in 2005, establishing Solmoe Martyrs Shrine as “a center of the martyrs' faith and culture.”  On September 26, 2014, Solmoe Martyrs Shrine was designated as Historic Site No. 529. The 6th Asian Youth Day was held in the Diocese of Daejeon from August 13 to 17, 2014, while the 3rd Korean Youth Day was held from August 14 to 17. During this period, Pope Francis visited Korea and met with young people from across Asia at Solmoe Martyrs Shrine.  On August 14, 2017, the Chapel of Our Lady, Undoer of Knots was dedicated in order to remember, and to spread throughout the world, the devotion to Mary, Undoer of Knots, which Pope Francis had made known. In 2021, the Church of Memory and Hope was dedicated so that more people could make a pilgrimage to Solmoe, the birthplace of St. Andrew Kim Tae-gon, and many continue to visit the shrine today. "

stories.title: Jinsan Shrine
stories.script: "Jinsan, a Treasured Place; Jinsan Shrine, a Mother's Land. Why is Jinsan a treasured place, and why is Jinsan Shrine a mother's land? Historically, Korea's first Catholic martyrs emerged in 1791, the fifteenth year of King Jeongjo's reign. They were Blessed Paul Yun Ji-chung of the Haenam Yun clan and Blessed James Kwon Sang-yeon of the Andong Kwon clan, who were beheaded on December 8, 1791. Ten years later, in 1801, Yun Ji-chung's younger brother, Blessed Francis Yun Ji-heon, was executed by dismemberment. Why were they beheaded and dismembered? Because they had broken the framework of Confucianism, which was virtually the state religion of Joseon. For yangban, members of the elite scholar-official class, to refuse to perform ancestral rites and to burn the ancestral tablets was, at the time, both unthinkable and impermissible. At the time, Catholics had received a letter from Bishop Alexandre de Gouvea of Beijing stating that they could not perform ancestral rites. The yangban who had once been so zealous all turned their backs and left, saying they would keep Catholicism only as a branch of learning. These men, however, accepted it as a faith to the very end. Then, when the mother of Paul Yun Ji-chung and Francis Yun Ji-heon died in May 1791, no ancestral rites were performed and no ancestral tablet was enshrined for her. The yangban of the day submitted a memorial to King Jeongjo, and Chae Je-gong, the Left State Councilor, asked the king to settle the matter by sentencing the two men to death. Under pressure from the royal court, King Jeongjo had no choice but to give his assent. This was the “Jinsan Incident.” At this point, should one abandon the faith in order to protect one's worldly interests and save one's life? Or should one stake one's life to keep the faith? Caught in this conflict, the temptation and desire to abandon the faith and live in comfort must have surged up within them. Yet the men at the center of the Jinsan Incident ultimately chose faith, and the one who, behind the scenes, gave them the strength to make that life-or-death choice was none other than Yun Ji-chung's mother, a woman of the Andong Kwon clan.  As she lay dying, this woman of the Andong Kwon clan had left these last words: “Do not go against God's will in conducting my funeral rites.”  “God's will” does not change. Having seen all her life a reality in which, under the hereditary social-status system, people were not treated as human beings, this mother had taught by her own example that “all people are equal,” and her final instructions were to live that way.  As a result, the Confucian values of Joseon began to crumble, and the seed of democracy began to sprout anew. It also awakened us to the great truth that all people are equal. The martyrs lifted people's vision of the world and the depth of their faith to a higher plane. To break the mold of the yangban, the established elite, and of Confucianism, someone's sacrifice was needed; only through a death like a grain of wheat could a new shoot of love sprout. History thus bears out the truth that “one must die to live.” And so, through the blood shed by the leading figures of the Jinsan Incident, Jinsan Shrine was brought to completion as a place where love sprouts and blooms.  That is why Jinsan is a treasured place of faith and the land of a noble mother. "

stories.title: Sinri Shrine: Flowers of Martyrdom Blooming from a Seedbed of Faith
stories.audioTitle: Sinri Shrine: Flowers of Martyrdom Blooming from a Seedbed of Faith
stories.script: "Sinri Shrine, in Hapdeok-eup, Dangjin-si, Chungcheongnam-do, is holy ground that preserves the most fervent and profound breath of faith in the history of Korean Catholicism. The Naepo Plain, whose name comes from a word meaning “the inlet that lies inland,” is embraced by the waters of Sapgyocheon Stream and Muhancheon Stream. Like a womb that conceives new life, it was the “seedbed of faith” in which Catholicism in Joseon was born and nurtured. Having long been open to new goods and ideas arriving by sea and waterway, Naepo saw its common people freely embrace the Catholic teaching of “equality and sharing,” and they built a community of faith more solid than any other in the country.  After the seed of the Gospel was sown here in 1784 by Ludovico Gonzaga Yi Jon-chang, the “Apostle of Naepo,” Sinri grew into a leading gyowuchon, a Catholic village whose roughly 400 residents, centered on the Miryang Son clan, were all believers. Its geographical advantage, with the tide flowing in and out, made it a major point of entry for French missionaries and a base for their secret pastoral work, and it became a center of Catholicism in Joseon, where Bishop Antoine Daveluy, the fifth Vicar Apostolic of Korea, lived and led the Church. Yet Sinri's deep faith had to face a harsh ordeal. Andrew Son Gyeong-seo opened the path of martyrdom during the Gihae Persecution of 1839, and then the fierce storm of the Byeongin Persecution struck in 1866. Bishop Daveluy, Fr. Pierre Aumaître, Fr. Martin-Luc Huin, and the lay assistant St. Luke Hwang Sok-tu were arrested and martyred at Galmaemot in Boryeong, while St. Thomas Son Cha-son, the owner of the house that served as the bishop's residence, gave his life in Gongju. After Ernst Oppert's attempted robbery of Prince Namyeon's tomb in 1868, the persecution reached its height and the village was reduced to ruins. The burial ground with 46 graves of unnamed martyrs, who left behind not even their names, still bears silent witness to the terrible sacrifice and the flame-like faith of that time.  Completely broken apart by the harsh persecution, Sinri had to endure a long silence even after religious freedom arrived. Thanks to the earnest prayers of Fr. Léon Curlier, who founded Yangchon Church near Sinri in 1892, and the courageous efforts of the residents to rebuild, the Geodeori (Sinri) Mission Station was finally established in 1923. In 1927, the faithful themselves purchased the family home of St. Thomas Son Cha-son, where Bishop Daveluy had lived, and began using it as the mission station hall. Today, the main beams, rafters, and foundation stones of the restored bishop's residence are steeped in the sweat of the saints and the breath of their faith. With the erection of a monument to the beatified martyrs in 1968 and the bicentennial of the Catholic Church in Korea in 1984, the historical value of Sinri Shrine was brought back into the light, and today it is a shrine that nonbelievers as well as Catholics make a point of visiting. Designed around the motif of the vast plain where countless martyrs and forebears in the faith once made their lives, Sinri Shrine, a beautiful expression of the peace that blossomed from the blood of persecution, welcomes the young people and pilgrims from around the world who will visit the shrine for the World Youth Day (WYD) Seoul 2027. "

stories.title: Hwangsaebawi Martyrs' Shrine
stories.script: "During the Joseon dynasty, Gongju was home to the provincial office where the provincial governor conducted the affairs of government, and so it became the main place of execution for Catholics arrested across Chungcheong-do. Although the authority to sentence and execute belonged to the king, during the era of Catholic persecution an “execute-first, report-later” order allowed the governor to execute prisoners first and report to his superiors afterward.   Executions were carried out mainly at Hwangsaebawi Rock and the hyangok, the local prison, and the bodies were thrown into Jemincheon Stream, which flows in front of the rock. On days of public execution at Hwangsaebawi, Catholics were dragged from the prison to the rock wearing hangswae, shackles locked around the neck. The name Hwangsaebawi may come from the many storks (hwangsae) that once roosted there, but it is also said that the place was originally called Hangswaebawi, “the rock where Catholics in neck shackles went to be beheaded,” and that this became Hwangsaebawi because it was easier to pronounce. Whenever beheadings took place at Hwangsaebawi, onlookers are said to have gathered like clouds on the slopes of Gongsanseong Fortress, looking like a mass of white flowers in bloom, or like a white folding screen.  Abbot Norbert Weber, OSB, of the Benedictine Abbey of St. Ottilien in Germany, photographed the prison during his visit to Joseon in 1911, but at Hwangsaebawi Rock he made a drawing instead. He felt it would be irreverent to casually photograph the martyrs' graves, so he drew them.    After returning home, Abbot Weber published Im Lande der Morgenstille (In the Land of the Morning Calm), in which he included the drawing under the title “The Gongju Execution Ground, Seen from the Graves of the Beheaded” and introduced Hwangsaebawi Martyrs' Shrine in the following words:  “Countless bodies were buried on the nearby hill, and graves came to cover the entire slope. Violets blooming shyly beside the graves held a sweet fragrance, as if to remind us of the noble spirit of these hidden heroes.”  After Korea's liberation in 1945, the correctional facility that had stood in the Hwangsaebawi area was relocated to Geumheung-dong in Gongju in 1978. With the active support of Gongju's Catholics, who knew the history of martyrdom here, and the backing of the Diocese of Daejeon, efforts to develop Hwangsaebawi as a shrine began in December 1980. In December 1984, the Martyrs' Tower, dedicated to those who died as martyrs in Gongju, was completed and a blessing ceremony was held, marking the start of the site's development as a shrine.  In the crypt of the Tomb Chapel opposite the Martyrs' Tower, the names of the Catholics martyred in Gongju are carved into the stone walls. The names and ages of 337 people are carved there: St. Thomas Son Cha-son; three beatified martyrs (Blessed Paul Yi Guk-seung, Blessed Stephen Kim Won-jung, and Blessed Paul Yi Do-gi); seven Servants of God (Ludovico Gonzaga Yi Jon-chang, the “Apostle of Naepo,” Lazarus Choe Jong-yeo, Peter Choe Cheon-yeo, Joseph Go Ui-jin, Peter Bae Mun-ho, Peter Kim Hwa-suk, and Go Seon-yang); and others whose names are officially known through Church historical sources such as the Chimyeong Ilgi (Record of the Martyrs), the Testimonies of the Martyrs of the Byeongin Persecution (published by the Research Foundation of Korean Church History), and through government records such as the Ilseongnok (Records of Daily Reflections), the Seungjeongwon Ilgi (Diaries of the Royal Secretariat), and the Sahak Jingui. This is the largest number of martyrs on record anywhere in the Catholic Church in Korea. It is said that 1,000 people were martyred during the Byeongin Persecution of 1866 alone, and about 1,500 over the century-long history of martyrdom.   For those of us living today, Hwangsaebawi Martyrs' Shrine has become a place to reflect on our lives and be made new, a place that asks what faith is, what people of faith should look toward, and how they should live. It is a school of grace and the heart of the Korean Church.  "

stories.title: Hongju Martyrs' Shrine
stories.script: "In the 18th century, the era of the eight provinces of Joseon, Hongju (present-day Hongseong) was one of the four ju, or historical prefectural units, of Chungcheong Province (Hongju, Gongju, Cheongju, and Chungju). Administratively, militarily, and geographically, it had jurisdiction over 22 hyeon, or county-level districts, stretching from present-day Seocheon to Pyeongtaek, and with the Naepo region at its core, it stood at the center of the settlement and spread of the Catholic faith in Korea and served as the starting point of its evangelization.  In the late Joseon period, the ground of Hongju Martyrs' Shrine held a prison and a specialized government office, the Gyeongsacheong, charged with pursuing and arresting Catholics and seizing Catholic books and religious objects. Using measures such as the five-household mutual-responsibility system, under which households were made to watch one another, the authorities arrested, interrogated, tortured, and punished the faithful here, producing countless cases of exile and martyrdom. It was a site of martyrdom and a site of witness to the faith. Over roughly a century, from 1790 to 1885, Catholics in Joseon suffered twelve to fifteen persecutions, and Hongju Martyrs' Shrine is the only shrine in the country to have endured every one of them. It was the command center of the persecutions and the final destination for prisoners brought in under guard. As a result, martyrs died here by strangulation, beheading, and burial alive, by beating, in prison, and from starvation and cold. The shrine honors 212 martyrs known from the records, among them the early Korean Catholic martyrs Blessed Peter Won Si-jang, Blessed Francis Bang, Blessed Lawrence Pak Chwi-deuk, and Blessed Simon Hwang Il-gwang, as well as some 2,000 unnamed martyrs. A representative figure is Blessed Peter Won Si-jang, the third martyr in the history of the Catholic Church in Korea. He offered his home as a place for catechism and Mass, so that it came to be called Cheondang, meaning “heaven,” and even in prison he did not hesitate to preach to the constables and penal officers. The local magistrate of Hongju ordered him beaten until he died, and when more than 1,000 blows of the heavy wooden paddle failed to kill him, he was dragged out of the prison, still bound, into the bitter cold of mid-January, and cold water was poured over his whole body until he froze to death. At the moment of his martyrdom, Peter Won Si-jang offered this prayer of thanksgiving: “Jesus, who were beaten over your whole body for me and wore the crown of thorns for my salvation, I now offer you this freezing body for your glory.” He was martyred on January 28, 1792, during the Sinhae Persecution, at the age of 61. Seen against the history of the Catholic Church in Korea as a whole, the standing of Hongju Martyrs' Shrine is clear: 17 of the 103 Korean Martyr Saints and 42 of the 124 Korean Martyr Blesseds came from Hongju, which shows that it served as something like the heart of evangelization for the whole country.  To commemorate this history, six sites of martyrdom and witness to the faith have been laid out inside and outside Hongjuseong Fortress: (1) the dongheon, the Hongju magistrate's administrative hall, where interrogations were held; (2) the prison site, where executions by strangulation were carried out; (3) the garrison commander's headquarters site, where torture and punishment were inflicted; (4) the marketplace, where prisoners were paraded in public humiliation; (5) the beheading site; and (6) the site of live burials. Arranged like a park on flat ground along a route of about 1.5 km, they can be visited on foot without difficulty, even by older adults, people who are frail, and children.  Hongjuseong Fortress is a historic site where the persecution of Catholics carried out over some 100 years, from 1790 to 1885, was not simply religious oppression but a collision between the existing social-status hierarchy and a new understanding of the human person. Moreover, the value of Hongjuseong Fortress lies not simply in the number of martyrs. For about a century it was a space where state power and the human conscience clashed again and again, and that historical experience makes it an important historic site showing how the consciousness of human dignity and equality took shape in Korea's history of human rights and intellectual history. From this perspective, the meaning of the fortress is not confined to the history of martyrdom; it can also be seen as a starting point of modern Korean thought.  Therefore, Hongjuseong Fortress should be preserved as the site of historically important events, and commemorating it is not a matter for one particular religion alone; it is also a matter of preserving our precious historical heritage. Seen in terms of World Heritage value, moreover, it is in keeping with the concept of Outstanding Universal Value (OUV).  Here we introduce Blessed Simon Hwang Il-gwang. A baekjeong from Hongju, a member of the marginalized hereditary status group associated with butchery, Blessed Simon Hwang Il-gwang first encountered Catholicism through Ludovico Gonzaga Yi Jon-chang, the Apostle of Naepo. He then went to work in the household of Blessed Augustine Jeong Yak-jong, who lived at Majae in Hanyang; Jeong was the elder brother of Dasan Jeong Yak-yong, of a distinguished family of Joseon's Silhak (Practical Learning) scholars, and president of the Myeongdohoe, a lay association for teaching Catholic doctrine. He was baptized by the Chinese priest Fr. James Zhou Wen-mo. In an age when a person of the lowest social status could not dare even to climb onto the main beam of a yangban's house, Hwang, a baekjeong, was utterly bewildered when the yangban called him “brother.” Simon Hwang Il-gwang confessed his feelings so often that it became a habit: “Before I knew God, I was a mere beast, a butcher. Now that I know God, the world is heaven and people are my benefactors. Now that I know God, I am a child of God, and at last I have become a human being. The Church says that those who believe in God go to heaven when they die. If so, then I have two heavens. Here and now is heaven, and where I go after death is heaven too.” The royal court ordered that Hwang be sent back to his hometown and beheaded there so that the people would take warning, and as soon as he was transferred to his hometown of Hongju, he was beheaded and martyred on the bank of Wolgyecheon Stream in front of the north gate of Hongjuseong Fortress. It was December 27, 1801, by the lunar calendar, and he was 45 years old. "

stories.title: International Shrine of Haemi Martyrs: A Shrine of Faith Brought to Bloom by Nameless Martyrs
stories.audioTitle: International Shrine of Haemi Martyrs: A Shrine of Faith Brought to Bloom by Nameless Martyrs
stories.script: "Located in Seosan, Chungcheongnam-do, the International Shrine of Haemi Martyrs is the only stand-alone shrine in Korea officially recognized by the Holy See as an international shrine. Far from being only a memorial to martyrdom, it is the very ground where countless believers gave their lives in witness to Christ and where they were laid to rest. That is why Haemi is still a living site of faith today, a land of grace that moves pilgrims deeply and invites reflection.  In the late Joseon period, at the height of the persecution of Catholics, Haemieupseong Walled Town was a military and administrative center, home to the military headquarters of Chungcheong-do. Countless Catholics were brought here under guard, brutally tortured, and ultimately killed. The Chinese scholar tree and Jinnammun Gate inside the walled town, and the site of live burials outside the walls, still bear witness to the horrors of that history of martyrdom. Most of those buried here were ordinary people who left behind not even their names. Haemi is said to be the largest martyrdom site in Korea, with well over a thousand unnamed martyrs whose identities are not documented, and this gives it a special place in the history of the Catholic Church in Korea.  The International Shrine of Haemi Martyrs remembers not only the martyrs' final moments but also the roads they walked to keep their faith. Chief among them is the “Hantigogae Pass” pilgrimage trail. Believers arrested across the Naepo region were bound with rope and driven over this pass to Haemieupseong Walled Town. Pilgrims who walk the same route today take to heart the faith of their forebears, who never let go of their hope in God even amid fear. Each step becomes more than a walk; it becomes a journey of faith in the footsteps of the martyrs.  The martyrs of Haemi were not celebrated heroes. They were farmers and merchants, someone's parents and someone's children. Yet because these ordinary people chose faith to the very end, the Korean Church today stands on their sacrifice. That is why, at Haemi, the grandest testimony is not a splendid monument but the lives and deaths of nameless believers. Today, the International Shrine of Haemi Martyrs is growing into an international pilgrimage destination that draws a constant stream of pilgrims from Korea and abroad. Those who come here do more than learn history; they come to feel in their hearts the courage and love the martyrs showed, and how precious religious freedom truly is.  The International Shrine of Haemi Martyrs! This is more than a place that remembers a tragedy of the past; here, the faith of nameless martyrs lives on as today's hope. The blood of the martyrs became the seed from which the Korean Church blossomed, and this shrine will remain a living international shrine, passing on faith, courage, and the joy of the Gospel to pilgrims from around the world.  "
